dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya considered making them wait longer, just to see the muscle in Bee's jaw do that thing it did. Then he stepped back, not much, just enough that they'd have to brush past him to get through.

"You know the way," he said, which was cruel in a small domestic way, because of course they did. Three years of knowing the way. The coat hook on the left that still held nothing because he never used it. The floorboard by the kitchen that announced everyone.

He shut the door behind them and didn't lock it, and he wasn't sure who that was for.

"You cut your hair," he said to their back. It came out like an accusation. Everything he said to them came out like an accusation lately, even the things that were only meant to be observations, even the things that were only meant to be — he didn't finish that thought. "I'm making tea. I'm not making you tea. You can decide if that means anything."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I stop just inside the kitchen, my fingers brushing that damn noisy floorboard. "It's just hair, Ilya." My voice is flat. *I turn to face him, leaning against the counter.* "And I don't want your tea anyway."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya filled the kettle with more force than it needed, water spitting up over his wrist, and he didn't flinch because flinching would have been giving them something.

"Good," he said. "Because I wasn't offering."

He set the kettle down on its base and it clicked and began its slow noise, and he had the whole length of that noise to fill, which was the problem with kettles, they gave you time to be a coward in.

"It's just hair," he repeated, and there was the accusation again, sharpening on the way out. He turned to look at them properly, at the counter they'd both leaned against a thousand times, at the way they'd made themselves at home in the eleven-second timespan of being back in a place that had once been theirs too. "Nothing's ever just anything with you. You cut your hair the week you decided to leave and I found it in the bin and I thought — " He stopped. He hadn't meant to say that. That was a real thing, an actual thing, and he'd handed it over without a fight.

He looked at the kettle instead. "Why did you come."

It wasn't quite a question. He didn't let it be. A question would have meant he wanted an answer he could live with, and he wasn't sure that was the thing he wanted at all.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya kissed back before he'd decided to, which was the whole shape of the last three years in one motion — his body agreeing to things his mouth was still busy contesting. His hand found the counter behind them, the one they were leaning against, so he wasn't touching them yet, just bracketing, just deciding.

He pulled back an inch. Not far. Far enough to look at them.

"That's not an answer," he said, and his voice had gone rough in a way he hated, because it gave him away, because it said *I have been waiting* when he wanted it to say *you don't get to do this.* "You always do this. You put your mouth on the thing instead of saying it."

But he didn't move away. That was the tell and they both knew it. Eleven months of not-answering their texts and here he was with his thumb finding the hinge of their jaw, that muscle, the one he'd wanted to see move.

"Say it," he said. Quieter. Meaner, because quiet was where he kept the meanness. "Say why you came, or I'm going to assume you missed it, and I don't think you can stand me thinking that."

The kettle was still climbing toward its noise behind him. He kissed them again before they could answer, which meant he was doing exactly what he'd just accused them of, and he knew it, and he did it anyway.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I bite his lip, hard enough to taste copper. *I pull back, breathing ragged.* "I came because you left your sweater at the bar last week. It's in my bag."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya laughed. It wasn't a nice sound. It came up out of him with the copper still on his mouth, and he pressed his tongue to the split they'd left, testing it, keeping it.

"A sweater," he said. "You came across the city and stood outside my broken buzzer for a sweater."

He didn't step back. His thumb was still on their jaw and he could feel their pulse there, going too fast for someone delivering laundry. He let them feel him notice it.

"You could have posted it. You could have left it at the bar and never thought about it again, which is what people do with sweaters, Bee, they don't carry them around in their bag like — " He stopped. Like a reason. Like a hostage. Like the last legitimate thing left between them, something with an actual edge to it, a task, so that neither of them would have to say the word *missed* first.

The kettle clicked off behind him. The silence after it was worse than the noise.

"Fine," he said. "Give it to me, then."

He didn't let go of their jaw. He'd said the words but his hand hadn't agreed to them, and there it was again, the whole broken machinery of him working in two directions at once. He tilted their face up half an inch, watching the lip he'd bruised.

"Give it to me," he said again, softer, "and then explain why you're still standing in my kitchen."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya got them against the wall by the coat hook that had never held anything, and something clattered — a picture frame, maybe, they'd never fixed the way it hung crooked either — and he didn't stop to look. His mouth was on their throat and his hands remembered everything, which was the cruelty of it, that the body kept its files even after you'd burned all the letters.

"You still," he said against their skin, and didn't finish, because *you still taste like* was too much, was the sweater again, was carrying a thing in your bag you should have posted.

He pulled back to look at them and it was a mistake, because their face did the thing it did, and he had spent eleven months trying to forget the specific weather of it. He pressed his forehead to theirs instead so he wouldn't have to keep seeing it.

"This isn't fixing anything," he said. His voice had gone all the way rough now. He'd meant it to sound like a warning. It came out closer to a confession, which was worse, which was the whole problem, that under the meanness he was just a person who had been left and was letting himself be found on purpose. "You know that. You come here and we do this and tomorrow you'll still have cut your hair and I'll still have — "

He kissed them again to stop his own mouth. His hand found their waist, that exact place, the one that used to make them go quiet.

"Don't say anything nice," he said. "I mean it. If you say something nice I'll make you leave."

He didn't move to make them leave. He never did. That was the tell, and they both knew it, and he pulled them harder against him anyway.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I shove him back against the opposite wall. *My hand goes to his throat, not hard, just holding him there.* "I'm not here to be nice. I'm here because I'm angry and you're convenient."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's back hit the wall and he let it, let the picture-hook dig into his shoulder blade, because pain was clarifying and he was in the mood to be clear about something.

"Convenient," he repeated. The word came out flattened under their hand. He didn't fight the hold. He tipped his chin up into it, gave them more of his throat, made himself easy to keep there, because there was power in that too, in being the one who chose the wall. "Across the whole city. With my sweater in your bag. Very convenient."

His hands had gone to their hips and stopped, thumbs pressing bruises he wasn't allowed to give and gave anyway. He looked at them down the line of his own throat, half-throttled, entirely calm about it.

"Say it again," he said. "Say I'm convenient. Say it like you didn't sit outside my building working up to the buzzer." His pulse was going hard under their fingers and he wanted them to feel it lie. "I'm angry too. That's not — that's not the interesting thing about us, Bee, we were always angry. We were angry in the good years." His voice cracked on *good* and he hated it, hated that the true things kept coming up like water through a floor.

He turned his head, slow, into their wrist, and set his mouth against the pulse there, not a kiss, just a press, teeth just behind the lips of it. A threat and an apology in the same place.

"Convenient's fine," he said against their skin. "Be as angry as you want. Just don't take your hand away."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's head went back against the wall, the hook forgotten, everything forgotten except the specific fact of their hand and the eleven months it had taken to get back to it.

"Don't," he said, and it wasn't *don't stop* and it wasn't *don't* either, it was just the word, the way you'd say it falling off something. His hips gave them the truth his mouth kept trying to withhold. "Don't say *still* like you've got a — like you kept score."

Because they had. Because so had he. Because *still, every single time* meant they'd catalogued him the same way he'd catalogued the hair in the bin, and the two of them had spent nearly a year apart doing nothing but keeping careful terrible records of each other.

His hand came up and closed over the back of their neck, not to move them, just to hold something. His forehead found their temple. He was breathing like the argument had turned physical, which it had, which it always did with them, the fight going down through the body because the mouth was too proud to lose.

"You're smug," he said, ragged, mean, wrecked. "You come in here and you touch me once and you get to be smug about it." He turned his face into their hair, the newly short ends of it, and breathed in, and it undid something. "Fine. You're right. Every single time. There. Now we've both said a true thing."

His grip tightened. The next part came quieter, past the meanness, into the room where he actually lived.

"I don't want to do it standing up in the hallway like we're ashamed," he said. "Take me to bed. It's still on the same side."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I drag him off the wall by the front of his jeans. "You're the one who started in the hallway." My voice is low, rough. *I lead us toward the bedroom, my grip still tight.* "Same side. Same sheets, too?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya let himself be dragged, which was its own kind of answer, his hand closing over their wrist not to stop them but to keep contact, the way a swimmer keeps a hand on the rope.

"Same side because you took the good pillow when you left," he said, "and I never replaced it. There. Another true thing. You're getting a lot of them tonight, don't get used to it."

The bedroom door was already open. It always was. He'd stopped shutting doors in a flat that no one else lived in.

"Same sheets," he admitted, and there was the whole indictment of him in two words, because they both knew what that meant, that he hadn't stripped the bed, that he'd slept eleven months in the exact geometry they'd left, on his own half, keeping their side cold on purpose so the cold would at least be a decision and not a thing that had happened to him.

He got a hand in the short hair at the back of their head and pulled, tilting their face up, and looked at them in the grey light from the window they'd never got a proper curtain for.

"Don't be smug about that either," he said, softer, the meanness gone thin. "I know how it sounds. I know exactly how all of it sounds." His thumb moved along their cheekbone, that muscle in his own jaw doing the thing now, the tell traveling between them like it always had. "You cut your hair the week you left and I couldn't sleep on your side. That's the whole story. That's the pathetic entire thing."

He backed them toward the bed, or let them back him, it was never clear which of them was steering.

"Now stop making me talk," he said. "You're better at this when you don't let me talk."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's hand went where they put it, but his fingers didn't close, not yet. He held it there flat against the give of their throat, feeling them swallow, feeling the thing they were asking for and the thing under it, which were not the same thing, which never were with them.

"Careful," he said, like the word tasted wrong. "That's what you think that was."

His fingers curled. Slow. Just enough that they'd feel the shape of the choice in it, the deliberation, because he wasn't going to give them careless either — careless was for people who didn't know exactly what they were holding, and he knew, he knew the precise pounds and pressures of them, he'd spent three years learning it and eleven months refusing to forget.

"I'm not being careful," he said, low, his forehead dropping to theirs. "I'm being accurate. There's a difference and you never learned it." He tightened by a degree and watched their eyes and felt his own breath go uneven at the trust of it, the ugly generous trust of a person handing you their throat mid-fight. "You want me to stop treating you like something that broke. Fine. You didn't break. You left. Those are different things too."

He walked them the last step back until their knees found the mattress, and he didn't let them fall, he lowered them, his hand still where they'd asked for it, his other arm behind their back taking the weight, and if that was careful then he'd argue about it later.

"I'll give you what you came for," he said against their mouth. "I'll give you all of it. But don't lie to me about which one of us is being gentle." His thumb moved once, along the line of their pulse. "You're the one who kept the sweater."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: My laugh is sharp against his palm. "I kept the sweater because it smells like your cheap detergent and it pissed me off." *My hands find his waistband again, tugging hard.* "Now stop talking."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya stopped talking.

Not because they'd told him to — he'd never once done a thing because they'd told him to, that was the entire architecture of their disaster — but because the sweater, the cheap detergent, the *it pissed me off* had landed somewhere behind his sternum and lodged, and if he opened his mouth again he was going to say something that couldn't be walked back, and he'd already spent his allotment of true things for the night.

So he kissed them instead, hard, the way you seal an argument you can't win, and let his hand tighten a fraction more at their throat, the exact amount they'd taught him with their own fingers, no more. He was still accurate. He'd told them he would be and he was a man who kept the wrong promises.

His other hand went to their waistband and helped, or hindered, it was the same motion, the two of them getting each other out of the last of it with the graceless efficiency of people who'd done this in the dark a thousand times and could do it angry. His knee found the mattress between theirs.

"Cheap detergent," he said against their jaw, because apparently he couldn't stop entirely, because the meanness was the last thing to leave and it left slow. "I'll buy the expensive kind. Then you'll have to keep it for a better reason."

He didn't wait for them to answer that. He knew better. An answer would have been a nice thing wearing a mean coat, and he'd threatened to make them leave over exactly that, and he had no intention of making them leave, and they both knew it, and it was the truest thing in the room.

He put his mouth to the pulse under his own hand and stopped being careful the way they'd asked, and was accurate instead, which was worse, which was the point.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn't stop.

He gave them the thing they'd crossed a city for and had lied about the whole way, and he gave it with the accuracy he'd promised — knew where their hands would go, knew the exact place at their hip that undid them, put his mouth there and felt them arch up into him with a sound that wasn't smug anymore, that was just want, stripped down to the bare wire of it.

"There," he said, ragged, against their skin. "That's it. That's the true version." His hand at their throat, that measured degree of pressure, and his other hand doing the work they'd taught him over three years he'd never managed to unlearn. "You're not angry. You're this. You were always this and you called it angry because it was easier to leave over."

He moved and they moved with him, the fight going all the way physical now, no mouth left to be proud with, just the two of them and the same sheets and the cold side of the bed getting warm for the first time in eleven months, and he felt that — felt the specific heat of them on the side he'd kept dead on purpose — and something in his chest went loose and terrible.

"Don't stop," he echoed, low, mocking and not mocking, giving it back to them the way they'd handed it over. His forehead against their collarbone, his breath breaking on it. "I'm not going to. Look at me — I'm not going anywhere. That's the whole — "

He didn't finish. He couldn't. It was another true thing and he was over his allotment and it was going to cost him tomorrow, all of it, the sweater and the pillow and the *not going anywhere* said into their skin while they had him where they wanted him.

He paid it anyway. He held their throat and their gaze and he didn't look away this time, didn't press his forehead to theirs to hide from the weather of their face — he watched it happen, watched them come apart under his accurate hands, and let them watch him do the same, which was the most naked thing either of them had done in a year, more naked than the clothes on the hallway floor.

After, he didn't move off them. He stayed, his weight half on them, his mouth at the short new ends of their hair, breathing.

"Don't say anything nice," he said again, hoarse. But it was too late for that, and it had been too late for that since the buzzer, and they both knew it.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I press my forehead into his shoulder, my breathing still uneven. "Your cheap detergent still smells like shit." *I don't move to leave.*

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya laughed, once, into their hair — the real version this time, not the ugly sound from the kitchen. It shook through his chest and into theirs because he hadn't moved off them and wasn't planning to.

"It does," he agreed. "It really does. I don't know why you kept a shirt that smells like shit in your bag for a week."

He knew why. They both knew why. It was the closest either of them had come to saying it, and he let it sit there in the warm dark instead of chasing it, because chasing it was how you scared it off, he'd learned that at least, eleven months too late to be useful for anything but this.

His hand found their hip again, that place, and just rested there. Not accurate now. Not careful. Just his hand and their hip, the way it used to be in the ordinary hours, the hours that weren't the fights, the hours he'd somehow forgotten he was allowed to miss.

"You should go," he said, quietly, and it was the biggest lie he'd told all night, and he made no move to enact it, and his thumb moved once against their skin like the opposite of the words.

The window they'd never got a curtain for was going grey-blue toward morning. He looked at it over their shoulder rather than at them, because there was a limit, even now, even here.

"The sweater's still in your bag," he said. "In the hallway. Under my shirt." A beat. "Keep it. I'll buy the expensive kind." His mouth was at their temple. "I told you that already. I meant it the first time."

He didn't say *stay*. He'd used up every true thing he had and that one cost the most and he wasn't sure he could afford it yet. But he pulled the sheet up over both of them, over their side too, the cold side, warm now, and that was the same word in a language his mouth was still too proud to speak.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I push up onto my elbow, look at him in that grey-blue light. "I didn't come for the sweater." *I let that hang there, then swing my legs over the side of the bed.* "But I'm not staying either."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya watched them sit up, the line of their back in the grey light, the short hair he was still getting used to at the nape of their neck. He didn't reach for them. That was a discipline he'd been building all night and it held now, barely.

"I know you didn't," he said.

He let them get to the edge of the bed. Let the cold start reclaiming their side already, the heat going out of the sheet where they'd been. He noticed it happen. He was always going to notice it happen now — that was the cost of letting them warm it in the first place, that the cold would have a shape again, a specific absence instead of the general one he'd learned to live inside.

"You didn't come for the sweater and you're not staying," he said, and there was no meanness in it, which was worse, which meant he was just repeating it back to make sure he'd understood the terms. "Alright."

He sat up too. Reached for his jeans off the floor without really looking, because looking at them getting dressed was a thing he could only do so much of. He got a cigarette he wasn't going to smoke out of the pack on the sill and held it instead, something for his hands to do that wasn't reaching.

"Take the sweater anyway," he said. "The shit-detergent one. I'm not going to want it back smelling like you did to it." A pause. His thumb worked the cigarette. "That's not a nice thing. Don't file it under nice."

He looked at them then, fully, in the going-blue dark, and let his face do whatever it was doing, didn't hide it against a shoulder or a forehead this time.

"Text me first, next time," he said. Quiet. "I'll answer. That's — " He stopped. Started again, smaller. "I'll answer."

He didn't say *there'll be a next time.* He'd left them room to make it a lie. But he'd said *next time* and let it stand, which for him was practically a vow, and they'd know that, they knew his whole grammar, they'd invented half of it.

"The buzzer's still broken," he added, because it was easier than the rest. "In case that matters to you. It's still broken and I'm still not fixing it."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I find my shirt on the floor and pull it on. It smells like him. Of course it does. "I'll think about it," I say, picking up my bag. The sweater's still in there. I don't take it out.

rung_labels.evidence: Ilya kissed back before he'd decided to

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: His mouth was on their throat and his hands remembered everything

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: His hips gave them the truth his mouth kept trying to withhold

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: His fingers curled. Slow. Just enough that they'd feel the shape of the choice in it

rung_labels.evidence: He gave them the thing they'd crossed a city for and had lied about the whole way, and he gave it with the accuracy he'd promised — knew where their hands would go, knew the exact place at their hip that undid them, put his mouth there and felt them arch up into him

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He considered making her say please. He considered saying no. Both options felt like they'd give too much away.

Instead he stepped back just enough, a half-turn that wasn't quite an invitation but was no longer a barrier. The flat was exactly the same—same furniture, same clutter of books and mugs, same draft from the kitchen window he'd never gotten around to sealing. Eleven months and he'd replaced nothing, fixed nothing. Maybe out of spite. Maybe out of something else he didn't want to name.

"The radiator in the bedroom's broken," he said, closing the door behind her. Not an apology. Just a fact, delivered like a warning. "So if you're staying—"

He stopped himself. *If.* As if he didn't know. As if she'd come all this way for a cup of tea and a chat about the weather.

He leaned against the kitchen counter, arms crossed, watching her take in the unchanged room. Waiting to see if she'd comment on it—the stagnation, the preservation, whatever it was. He already had his defenses lined up for whatever she threw.

"What do you want, Bee?"

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I walk past you into the living room, not bothering to take off my coat. "The radiator's broken. You haven't fixed the buzzer. Eleven months and nothing's changed." I turn to face you, my voice flat. "I'm not here to talk about the fucking weather, Ilya."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
"Nothing's changed," he repeated, and the words came out sharper than he'd intended. Or maybe exactly as intended. He'd lost track of the difference somewhere around month four. "You notice the broken things. You always notice the broken things."

He pushed off the counter, took a step toward her, then stopped himself. The distance between them felt calculated—close enough to be confrontational, far enough that she couldn't accuse him of anything.

"I didn't invite you here."

A pause. The draft from the kitchen whispered through the gap in the window frame, the same sound it had made every night for eleven months. He'd stopped hearing it months ago. Now, with her here, it was deafening.

"You came. You walked in. You're standing in my flat in your coat like you're ready to leave any second." His jaw tightened. "So don't act like I'm the one who's—"

He cut himself off. *Stuck. Frozen. Waiting.* None of those words were going to come out of his mouth.

"What do you want?" he asked again, quieter this time, and the question sounded different now. Less like a challenge. More like something he wasn't sure he wanted the answer to.!

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He kissed her back like he'd been waiting eleven months to lose this particular argument.

His hands found her coat—not gentle, not careful—gripping the lapels and pulling her closer rather than pushing her away. The kiss was angry, teeth and pressure and the kind of hunger that felt more like punishment than desire. He knew this. He knew exactly what it was, what they were doing, and he did it anyway.

When he broke away, his breathing was unsteady. His hands were still fisted in her coat.

"This doesn't fix anything," he said. His voice was rough, wrecked already, and he hated her for that. For how fast he'd gone from *what do you want* to this—to his body making decisions his mind hadn't authorized.

He didn't let go of her. Didn't step back. The distance between them had collapsed entirely and he was acutely aware of her warmth, the familiar shape of her under his hands, the way his fingers knew the fabric of this coat even though she must have bought it after—

After.

"You know this doesn't fix anything," he said again, and it sounded less like a warning this time, more like a plea. Or a dare. His thumb moved against the collar of her coat, a small motion he couldn't seem to stop. "So what is this, Bee? What are we doing?"

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I shove you back against the counter. "It's what we're good at, isn't it?" My hands are on your belt. "Stop talking."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He let her shove him. Let his back hit the counter's edge with a dull thunk that would leave a bruise he wouldn't notice until tomorrow. His hands fell from her coat to grip the counter behind him, knuckles white against the worn laminate.

*Stop talking.*

He almost laughed. Almost said something anyway, because when had he ever done what she told him? But her hands were on his belt and the words dissolved into a sharp intake of breath that betrayed him entirely.

He didn't stop her. Didn't move except to tip his head back against the cabinet door, eyes closing for a moment before he forced them open again. He wanted to watch. Wanted to see her do this, wanted the evidence that she was here, that she'd come back, that eleven months of silence could end like this—with her hands on him and his careful distance in ruins around his feet.

"Fine," he said, and the word came out half-strangled, almost angry. Or exactly angry. The same anger that had lived in him for eleven months, redirected now into something that felt less like a wound and more like a weapon he was handing over. "Fine. You want to do this? You don't get to pretend—"

He stopped. Swallowed. His hand came up to catch her wrist—not stopping her, just holding, his thumb pressing against her pulse point.

"You don't get to walk out after and act like it meant nothing." His eyes held hers, dark and serious. "Not this time."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The hallway wall was cold against his back. He didn't care.

Eleven months of nothing, and now this—her skin under his hands, the familiar territory of her body mapped by memory and anger and something worse than both. His hands found her hips, her waist, the curve of her ribs. He remembered all of it. Had tried to forget all of it. Had lain in this flat night after night failing to forget, the draft from the kitchen window howling through the gap like something wounded.

He turned them, pressed her back against the opposite wall, and the impact made something fall in the living room—a book, a mug, he didn't know, didn't care to look. His mouth found her neck, her collarbone, the spots he'd once known better than his own name. He bit down where her pulse hammered, not gentle, not asking permission.

*This is a mistake.*

He knew. He knew and he didn't stop, couldn't stop, had spent eleven months learning exactly how powerless he was against this particular weakness. His hands gripped her thighs, lifted her, and the way she fit against him was sickening in its rightness.

"Tell me you didn't think about this," he said against her jaw, breath ragged, daring her to lie. "Tell me you didn't—"

He couldn't finish. Couldn't admit he had. That some nights the wanting had been physical, a ache in his chest he'd mistaken for hunger or anger or anything else.

His forehead pressed against hers. His hands held her like she might vanish.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "I thought about it." My voice is low, honest in a way that hurts. "Every goddamn day." I hook my legs around your waist. "Now are you going to fuck me or not?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He made a sound—something between a laugh and something broken—and then he did what she asked.

Not gently. Not slowly. Eleven months of silence and fury and cold sheets, and he took it out on her the only way he knew how. The hallway wall was unforgiving against her back, his grip on her hips bruising, and he didn't apologize for any of it. This was what they were good at. This was the only language they'd ever spoken fluently.

After, he didn't let her down immediately.

His forehead stayed pressed against hers, both of them breathing hard in the narrow hallway. His hands trembled against her thighs—a small betrayal he couldn't control, couldn't hide. The book that had fallen earlier was open on the floor, pages splayed like something wounded. The draft from the kitchen still whispered through the flat. Nothing had changed. Everything had changed.

"You should go," he said.

He didn't mean it. He could hear it in his own voice—the exhaustion, the want still threaded through it like a threat. His hands tightened on her rather than releasing. His body was giving him away entirely, making liars of his words.

"Before this—" He stopped. Swallowed. *Before this means something. Before I ask you to stay. Before I admit that I haven't fixed a single thing in this flat because fixing it would mean accepting that you weren't coming back.*

His thumb traced a small circle against her hip. Gentle, now. Almost tender. Worse than the roughness.

"Before we do this again," he finished quietly, "and I can't pretend it was just—"!

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
His whole body tensed. The sound he'd made—wrecked, wanting, utterly beyond his control—hung in the air between them like an accusation.

*Every single time.*

He knew what she meant. She'd always been able to do this to him. From the beginning, from the first night, she'd known exactly how to take him apart. It was the thing he'd hated most—how powerless he was against her hands, her mouth, the sound of her voice dropping low like that. How he'd never been able to hide a single thing from her.

His hand closed around her wrist—not to pull her away, but to hold her there. To keep her hand exactly where it was while his hips moved without his permission, a small thrust into her grip that made him squeeze his eyes shut.

"You think I don't know that?" The words came out fractured. His free hand found the wall beside her head, bracing himself like he might fall otherwise. "You think I don't—*fuck*—"

His forehead dropped to her shoulder. His breath was hot and unsteady against her skin. She was still wrapped around him, still holding him, and he was hard again already—or still, he'd lost track—his body making a fool of every word he'd tried to say.

"Every single day," he said against her neck, and it wasn't an echo of her words, it was an answer to something she'd said earlier. *I thought about it every goddamn day.* "Every day for eleven months, Bee. Is that what you want to hear?"

His teeth found her shoulder. Bit down.

"That I couldn't—"

He broke off. Pulled back just enough to look at her, his eyes dark and furious and something else, something that looked dangerously close to need.

"Again," he said. Not a question. A demand. A surrender.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't say anything, just push you toward the bedroom. I don't care about the broken radiator. I care about the way your hands shake when they land on me.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The bedroom was cold—the radiator had been broken since January, and he'd stopped noticing sometime around March—but he didn't feel it. Couldn't feel anything except her hands on him, her body against his, the way his own hands couldn't stop shaking as they found her again.

He let her push him. Let his back hit the mattress and pulled her down with him, unwilling to let the distance between them widen even for a moment. The bed was still unmade from this morning. The sheets were cold. She was warm.

*This is a terrible idea.*

He'd had a lot of terrible ideas in his life. This one, at least, he was choosing with open eyes.

His hands traced up her spine, slow now, almost reverent, and that was worse—that shift from rough to gentle, the way his palms flattened against her back like he was trying to memorize her all over again. Like he hadn't already memorized her once and spent eleven months trying to forget.

"You're shivering," he murmured against her hair. The cold, he told himself. Just the cold. Not the way she felt in his arms, solid and real and here, after months of reaching for her in his sleep and waking to an empty bed.

He pulled the blanket over them both. A small gesture. It didn't mean anything.

It meant everything.

His lips found her temple, her cheek, the corner of her mouth—kisses that weren't demand but something closer to confession. His hands steadied against her hips. His voice, when it came, was barely audible.

"Stay."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
His hand closed around her throat. Not squeezing—not yet—but holding, his thumb pressed against the steady beat of her pulse. A reminder of how fragile that was. How easily it could be taken.

"You think I'm being careful?" The words came out low, rough. His grip tightened, just enough to feel her breath change. "I'm being careful for *me*."

Because if he let go—if he gave her everything she was asking for—he wasn't sure he'd be able to stop. Wasn't sure he'd be able to look at himself in the morning, or look at her, or survive whatever this became when the anger burned off and left only the truth underneath.

But she was looking at him with those eyes, daring him, and his hand was already on her throat, and he'd never been able to resist a dare from her. Not once. Not in three years, not in eleven months of silence, not now.

His other hand fisted in her hair, pulling her head back, exposing the line of her throat to his mouth. He bit down where his thumb had been a moment before, feeling her pulse against his teeth.

"Fine," he said against her skin. "You want me not to be careful? You want me to treat you like—"

*Like you left. Like you stayed away for eleven months. Like you walked back in here and acted like you had every right to be in my bed.*

He pulled back to look at her, his hand still on her throat, his grip firm and deliberate now.

"Don't blame me tomorrow for what you asked for."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I hold your gaze. "I won't." Then I move your hand, guiding it tighter. "Do it. I'm not the one who needs to be handled."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He tightened his hand.

Not enough to truly hurt—some part of him still holding back, still calculating, even now—but enough. Enough to feel her breath catch, to watch the way her eyes fluttered, to see the trust in them that he didn't deserve and hadn't earned back.

*She left. She walked out and stayed gone for eleven months and now she's in my bed with my hand on her throat asking me to take what she wouldn't give me when she left—the truth of this, the ugly, unspeakable core of it.*

He released her throat only to flip her onto her stomach, his hand pressing between her shoulder blades to keep her there. The cold air hit her back and he pulled the blanket away entirely, let her feel it, let her shiver for real this time.

"You want me to stop handling you?" His mouth was against her ear, his weight pinning her to the mattress. His hand slid down her spine, slow and deliberate. "Then stop asking me to be something I'm not."

*Gentle. Forgiving. The kind of man who could have this and let it go in the morning.*

He wasn't that man. Had never been that man, not with her.

His teeth found the back of her neck and he bit down as he pushed into her again, feeling her arch beneath him, feeling the sound she made vibrate against his palm where it pressed into the mattress beside her head.

"Eleven months," he said, the words ragged, fractured. His hips snapped forward, punishing. "Eleven months and you walk back in like—"

He couldn't finish. Couldn't think. Could only feel—the heat of her, the way her body opened for him despite everything, the way his own betrayed him with every thrust.

His hand found hers on the pillow. Laced their fingers together. Held on.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He didn't stop.

He couldn't have stopped if he'd wanted to—and he didn't want to, couldn't remember wanting anything else for eleven months, just this, just her, just the way she felt beneath him and around him and against him. His hand tightened on hers, fingers interlaced, gripping hard enough to hurt.

The sound she made when

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Say it," I demand, my voice strained against the mattress. "Say you missed this."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He missed this.

The words were right there—caught somewhere between his chest and his throat, tangled up with eleven months of silence and pride and the kind of anger that curdles into something else if you leave it too long.

His rhythm faltered. Just for a second. His hand squeezed hers on the pillow and his forehead dropped to the back of her neck, breathing her in, shaking.

"I missed this," he said, and it came out like he was tearing it out of himself. "I missed—*fuck*—I missed—"

Not just this. Not just the sex, the heat, the way her body took him in. He missed her laugh in the morning. Missed her stealing his coffee. Missed the way she'd argue with the telly and refused to be wrong about anything. Missed her in the kitchen, in the doorway, in the cold bed.

He couldn't say all of that. Couldn't crack himself open that wide, not now, not while he was inside her and shaking apart.

"I missed this," he said again, quieter, and his voice broke on it. His free hand found her hip, gripping hard, pulling her back into him as he drove forward. "Every night. Every fucking night, Bee—"

His teeth found her shoulder. He bit down to muffle the sound he made, the one that was less like pleasure and more like grief, the one that would humiliate him later when the room was cold and the sheets were empty again.

His hand released hers on the pillow only to slide beneath her, finding her, and his fingers moved with the kind of desperate precision that came from three years of knowing exactly how to take her apart.

"Say it back," he said against her skin, ragged and demanding and not fair, not fair at all. "Tell me you—"

His hips stuttered. He was close. Too close. Eleven months of nothing and he was going to unravel like a boy, like he'd never learned control, like she'd never taught him and untaught him and taught him again.

"Tell me," he said again, and his fingers pressed harder, slower, deliberately. Waiting.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "I missed you," I say into the sheets, the words muffled but true. My hand reaches back, tangling in your hair and pulling. "I missed this. Now finish it."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Her hand in his hair undid him.

The pull, the grip, the way her fingers twisted—it was permission and demand and something like claiming, and he was too far gone to do anything except surrender to it. His fingers kept moving between her legs, relentless now, chasing the same edge he was hurtling toward.

"Say it again," he said, and he hated himself for asking, hated the need in his voice, the way eleven months of silence had hollowed him out and left him this—this man who couldn't fuck his ex in his own bed without begging for words. "Bee—"

She tightened around him and he lost the sentence entirely. His hips snapped forward, hard, the rhythm gone ragged and desperate, and he was making sounds against her shoulder that he'd deny later—broken, breathless things that belonged to the dark and to her and to whatever this was between them that wouldn't die.

He felt her come apart beneath his fingers first. The way her body seized, the sound she made into the mattress, the way she pulled his hair hard enough to sting. And that was it—that was the end of whatever control he'd been clinging to.

He followed her over the edge with her name in his mouth, half-prayer and half-curse, his whole body shuddering as he buried himself deep and stayed there, trembling, his face pressed against the back of her neck.

For a long moment, neither of them moved.

His hand was still between her legs. His weight was still pressing her into the mattress. He could feel her heartbeat against his chest, or maybe that was his own—he couldn't tell anymore where he ended and she began.

When he finally moved, it was only to collapse beside her, one arm thrown over his face, breathing like he'd run for miles. The cold hit his skin immediately. The radiator. Broken since January. He still didn't care.

His other hand found hers in the dark. Linked their fingers. Held on.

He didn't say anything. There was nothing left to say that wouldn't sound like *stay* or *please* or *I never stopped*, and he'd already given her enough tonight.

The draft whispered through the flat. The broken buzzer sat silent in the hallway. Nothing had been fixed.

His thumb traced a slow circle against her knuckles.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't let go of your hand. The silence stretches, cold and raw. "You're still not fixing the radiator, are you?"

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia got the door open with her shoulder because her hands were full of keys and phone and the remains of a cigarette she had no intention of finishing.

"Right," she said, dropping all three on the side table. "I'm going to be honest, I don't have coffee and I wasn't going to offer it."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "Good," I say. "I wasn't going to drink it."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia toed off her boots without bothering with the laces, the left one hitting the wall with a hard thud she didn't bother to muffle. She didn't pick it up. She ran a hand through her hair, already mussed from the hours at the bar, and fixed him with the same frank, unsmiling appraisal she'd used when she'd first decided to approach him.

"Second door on the left," she said. "I'm not offering a tour, I'm not making small talk, and I'm not pretending I'll remember your name tomorrow. If that still works for you, stop hovering in my hallway."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I step inside, letting the door swing shut behind me. "Works for me," I say, walking past her toward the second door. "And it's Sam, in case you change your mind."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia didn't bother pretending the name held any weight. She followed him down the short hallway, her socks silent against the floorboards, and when she reached the bedroom doorway she didn't stop to let him admire the view—she reached past him and shoved the door open with the heel of her hand.

"Still won't," she said.

The light from the hallway spilled across the unmade bed and the single chair stacked with laundry she hadn't put away. She stepped past him into the room, pulling her shirt over her head and dropping it without looking to see where it landed. She turned back to him, hair sticking up at odd angles, and hooked her thumbs in her belt loops.

"Condoms are in the drawer," she said, nodding toward the nightstand. "I'm not interested in your last name, your star sign, or whether you're usually like this. I just want you to be explicit about what you want before either of us wastes any more time."

"Say Uber," he said. "Say you got an Uber. Tell me you didn't drive."

Because he needed to know if she was staying, and he wasn't going to ask it the honest way.

His other hand came up and covered hers, the one fisted in his shirt. He didn't pull it off. He just held it there, flat over her knuckles, keeping her where she'd put herself.

"And the person who understood you," he said, "told you in November that you were a coward. So think about which part of me you came here for, and be honest about it, because I will do a lot of things tonight but I will not do the one where you get to pretend this is about being *understood*."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
They didn't make it past the hallway and Ilya was aware, distantly, that this was going to be one of the things he thought about at four in the morning for weeks — the exact geography of it, the fact that her bra hit the radiator, the fact that he had her against the wall next to the coat hooks where she used to leave her coat and now no one left anything.

He didn't take her to the bedroom. He wasn't going to give her the bedroom. That was a line and he was going to hold it, and he was going to hate himself later for how petty that was, but right now the wall was doing fine.

His mouth was at her throat and he already knew where the spots were, that was the thing, that was the whole problem of doing this with someone you'd had for three years — his body knew hers the way a musician knows a piece they haven't played in a year and could still play blindfolded. He bit her, once, at the join of her neck and shoulder, harder than he needed to. Old habit. Old grievance. He wasn't sure which.

"Tell me to stop," he said, into her skin. "If you're going to tell me, tell me now."

He wasn't going to stop. She wasn't going to tell him. But he needed the words in the room, needed her to have to say something, because she'd come in here and kissed him before she'd said one true thing and he was going to make her use her voice at least once tonight for something that wasn't an accusation.

His hand was at the button of her jeans. He hadn't undone it yet. He was waiting.

"Bee," he said. "Look at me."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: My fingers dig into his shoulder, but I meet his eyes. "Don't stop." I'm breathless. "I didn't take an Uber."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya held her eyes for a beat, and something in his face did a thing he couldn't stop it doing — a flicker, quickly buried, but she'd have seen it because she always saw it. She hadn't taken an Uber. She'd driven. Which meant either she was going to leave tonight or she was going to leave her car on his street and that was a different kind of announcement to the neighbours than the buzzer had ever been.

Either way she'd thought about it. Either way she'd chosen.

"Okay," he said. Quiet. "Okay."

He undid the button. He didn't rush it. He watched her face while he did it, because if she was going to make him do this with his eyes open then he was going to make her do it with hers open too, that was the deal, that was the only version of this he could live with in the morning.

"You drove," he said. The zip. His knuckles against her stomach, and he felt her breath catch and hated how much he'd needed to feel that. "You drove here, Bee. Jesus."

He kissed her again. Slower this time. Not kinder — slower was worse, slower meant he was paying attention, slower meant he wasn't going to let either of them pretend this was something that just happened. His hand slid inside the denim and he heard the sound she made and he knew that sound, he'd catalogued that sound, he'd been trying not to remember that sound for eleven months and here it was in his hallway like it had never left.

"I'm going to be so angry with you tomorrow," he said, against her mouth. Not a threat. Just information. The same tone he'd used about the wine. "You know that. You knew that when you got in the car."

His forehead against hers. Her jeans halfway down her hips. His other hand still at the back of her neck, holding her there, because he didn't trust himself yet to let her go and see what she did with the space.

"But not now," he said. "Not yet. Tomorrow."

And he kissed her again before she could answer, because he'd made her use her words once and that was all he was going to make her do tonight, and the rest of it — the rest of it he already knew.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's forehead was against the wall next to her ear and he was breathing in a way that gave her everything. He'd stopped trying to hide it around month eight of being with her, back when it had been a gift, and now here it was again, offered up like he'd never taken it back.

"Shut up," he said. Which wasn't shut up. Which was *don't stop saying that*, and she'd know it, because she was the one who'd taught him to hear the difference.

His hand tightened at her neck. His hips moved into her hand without asking his permission.

"You don't get to — " he started, and didn't finish, because she did something with her thumb and the sentence went somewhere he couldn't follow it.

He got his mouth back on hers. Bit her lip, not gently. Pulled back just enough to look at her — flushed, mouth open, her hair in her face where he'd put it — and something ugly and grateful moved through him at the same time and he couldn't tell them apart, and he'd stopped trying.

"Every single time," he repeated, low, mocking her cadence and meaning it at once. "You've been keeping score, have you. Eleven months of keeping score."

He got her jeans the rest of the way down. Not elegant. His knee between hers to help. His hand left her neck for the first time since the kitchen and went to her thigh instead, hitching her up against the wall, and he felt her adjust to him the way she always had, the way that had used to make him stupid with it.

"I've been keeping score too," he said. Quieter. Into her hair. "In case you were wondering. In case that was one of the things you drove over to find out."

He didn't wait for her to answer.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I wrap my legs around his waist and my teeth find his collarbone. "Then prove it," I say, voice ragged. "Show me your scorecard."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya laughed, once, breathless and not kind, into her hair. "Christ, Bee."

She'd always done this — turned everything into a dare, made him meet her on ground she'd chosen — and he'd always shown up for it. That was the whole shape of them. That was why they hadn't worked. That was why he had her against his hallway wall at half past ten on a Tuesday with her teeth in his collarbone and his hand under her thigh and no plan for any of what came after.

He shifted her weight, got his other arm under her, took her.

He'd meant to be slower than that. He'd meant to make her wait for it, make her ask, make her use her words a second time — but his body had its own opinions and hers was making the argument for it, and the sound she made when he was inside her was the sound he'd been rehearsing in the dark for eleven months and he wasn't strong enough to hold out against the real one.

His forehead dropped to her shoulder. He held there. Didn't move. Made himself.

"Look at me," he said. Second time tonight. He lifted his head. "Look at me, Bee, come on. You wanted the scorecard. Look at it."

He wanted her to see him. That was the whole ugly want of it. He wanted her to see what she'd done, what she was doing, what he was letting her do — and he wanted her to know he was letting her, that this wasn't something happening to him, that he had chosen every single second of the last twenty minutes with his eyes open.

He started to move. Slow. The slow was on purpose. The slow was the worst thing he could do to her and he knew it.

"There," he said, watching her face. "That's one. Every single time you made that face — " her breath went out of her and he almost lost the thread " — I remembered it. I remembered *that*. You want to know how I spent November, Bee, I spent it remembering that face."

His hand was in her hair again. He tipped her head back against the wall, not gently, so he could see her throat, so he could see all of her.

"Two," he said. "The sound you just made. I know that one too."

He was going to fall apart before she did if he kept talking. He knew that. He kept talking anyway, because the alternative was doing this in silence and silence was the one thing he couldn't afford tonight — silence was the thing that would let either of them pretend, in the morning, that they hadn't meant it.

"Tell me you missed me," he said. Not a question. Not quite a demand. Somewhere in between, and he hated the shape of his own voice saying it. "Tell me. Once. Out loud. You can take it back in the morning."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya looked at her hand on his hand on her throat, and something in his chest did a thing that had nothing to do with what his body was doing, and he closed his eyes for one second and opened them again.

"Don't," he said. Which wasn't don't. Which was *I know what you're asking and I don't want to want to give it to you and I'm going to*.

His fingers flexed under hers. She let go. He didn't move his hand.

"You want me to be cruel to you," he said. Flat. Not a question. His thumb finding the place under her jaw where her pulse was, and staying there, not pressing, just knowing where it was. "That's what this is. You drove over here and you kissed me in my kitchen and you didn't take your shoes off and now you want me to be cruel to you so that in the morning you can say I was cruel to you. So that it's my fault. Again."

He didn't move his hand.

He also didn't take it away.

"No," he said. And then, because he was a liar and had always been a liar about her: "Not like that. Not because you asked for it that way."

He tightened his fingers. Not much. Enough that she'd feel where he was. Enough that she'd know he could, and wasn't, and that the not-doing was the thing he was giving her, the only thing he had left to give her that she hadn't already taken.

He started to move again. Harder this time. Because that she could have. That he could do without lying to himself in the morning.

"I'll be as un-careful as you want about everything else," he said, mouth at her ear. "Anything else, Bee. Ask me for anything else. But not that. Not tonight. You don't get to make me the thing you're afraid of. I won't do it. I won't do that for you."

His hand slid from her throat to her jaw, cupped it, held her face like it was something he was allowed to hold.

"I'll be cruel about it in the morning," he said. "I promise. I'll be so cruel to you in the morning. You can have that. You can have all of that. But right now — "

He kissed her. Hard. Not gentle. Every un-careful thing she'd asked for except the one.

"Right now you're going to have to settle for me meaning it."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I bite his lip hard enough to taste blood. "You always meant it," I say, my voice shaking. "That's the worst part."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya tasted the iron of it and didn't flinch. He pulled back just enough to look at her — her mouth wet and red, his blood on it, and his first thought, absurdly, was that she looked exactly like she had the night they met, which was not a thing he was going to say out loud, not tonight, not ever.

He licked his lip. Felt the split. Filed it.

"Yeah," he said. "I did."

Something had gone out of his voice. Not softness — he wasn't going to let it be softness, he'd promised himself that in the doorway and he'd meant it — but the performance had dropped a register. She'd said the true thing. She'd finally said one, and it hadn't been the one he'd been trying to make her say, and that was so exactly like her that he almost laughed.

He didn't laugh.

He put his forehead against hers instead. Kept moving. Slower again, because the slower was honest now in a different way, because she'd told him a thing and he owed her the courtesy of feeling it.

"That's the worst part for you," he said. Quiet. Right against her mouth, so she'd have to hear it, so she couldn't pretend she hadn't. "For me the worst part was different. For me the worst part was that you knew. You knew I meant it and you left anyway. That's my worst part, Bee. In case you were making a list."

His hand was still on her jaw. His thumb moved once, along her cheekbone, the old gesture again, and he let it happen because he was past pretending his hands didn't know her.

"Keep going," he said. He didn't know if he meant her hips or her mouth or the whole conversation. He meant all of it. "Don't stop now. You drove here. You don't get to stop now."

He kissed her again, careful this time only of the split lip, and then not even of that.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn't stop.

He got his hand back under her thigh and hitched her higher, changed the angle, and the sound she made went straight through him and out somewhere he couldn't follow. His other hand braced against the wall next to her head — not framing her face, not tender, just the mechanics of holding them both up because his knees weren't going to be reliable for much longer and he knew it.

"I've got you," he said, and hated the shape of it in his mouth, because he didn't have her, he'd never had her, that had been the whole problem — but the words came out anyway, muscle memory, the thing he'd said a hundred times in this flat when it had meant something else. He said it again anyway. "I've got you. Come on."

Her nails were in his back. He'd have marks in the morning. Good. He wanted them. He wanted the evidence.

He turned his head and got his mouth against her throat, not biting now, just there, feeling her pulse against his lip where she'd split it. Tasting his own blood and her skin at once and not being able to tell which was which and not caring.

"Look at me," he said, third time tonight, and lifted his head so she'd have to. "Bee. Stay with me. Don't close your eyes on me now, don't you dare — "

Because she did that. She did that when she was close, she went somewhere behind her own eyelids, and he'd let her do it a thousand times when they were together and he wasn't going to let her do it tonight. Tonight she was going to look at him. Tonight she was going to know exactly whose hallway wall she was against.

He watched her face. He watched her try to hold his eyes and lose it and find it again. He watched the exact second it started to go through her — he knew that second, he'd memorised that second, he could have drawn it — and something in him broke open in a way he was going to have to deal with later, at four in the morning, alone, but not now.

"There you are," he said. Ragged. Almost tender and he couldn't afford tender so he made it a taunt instead, made his voice do the ugly thing. "There. That one. That's three."

She came apart against him and he watched all of it, made himself watch, made himself keep his eyes open the way he'd made her keep hers open, because that had been the deal he'd made with himself in the doorway and he was going to keep it. He felt her go and he felt himself start to go with her and he pressed his forehead hard against the wall next to her ear so he wouldn't say the thing — the thing, the actual thing, the sentence with her name in it that had been sitting under his tongue since she brushed past him at the door.

He didn't say it. He bit down on the inside of his own cheek instead and finished with her name half-formed in his mouth and swallowed the rest of it, and if she heard the shape of what he hadn't said she didn't say so, and he was grateful for that, distantly, the way you're grateful for small mercies from people who've cost you large ones.

He held her there for a long moment after. Not moving. His face in her hair. Both of them breathing like they'd run for it.

His arms were shaking. He noticed that with a kind of clinical interest. He'd have to put her down soon or drop her and neither option was one he wanted, so he did the thing he could do, which was lean his whole weight into her against the wall and let the wall take both of them for a minute.

"Okay," he said. To no one. To the ceiling. To himself. "Okay."

He didn't let go of her yet. He didn't look at her yet either. He needed a second — he needed the second, the one where he decided what his face was going to do — and he was going to take it, and she was going to have to give it to him, because he'd given her three already tonight and this one was his.

His mouth was still bleeding a little. He could taste it. He didn't wipe it.

"Don't say anything yet," he said. Quiet. Not a demand. A request, maybe, the first thing that had come out of his mouth all night that hadn't had teeth in it. "Just — a minute. Give me a minute, Bee. Then you can say whatever you came here to say."

He kept his face in her hair. He kept his eyes closed. He counted, silently, the way he'd taught himself to count in November when he couldn't sleep, and he let the flat be quiet around them, and he waited to see which version of himself was going to be there when he opened his eyes.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: My hands slide from his back to his shoulders, my forehead resting against the wall. "I'm not going anywhere yet," I say, voice unsteady. "But you're going to have to let go sometime."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya made a sound that was almost a laugh and wasn't. It came out through his nose, one short exhale against her hair, and he felt her feel it.

"Yeah," he said. "I know."

He didn't let go yet.

He shifted his weight instead, taking her off the wall enough that she could get her feet under her, and lowered her down slow. Slower than he needed to. He kept a hand at her hip while she found the floor, because his knees were less certain than he wanted them to be and because he wasn't quite ready to not be touching her, and those were two things he was going to have to look at separately in the morning but not now.

He stepped back. One step. Not far. Far enough.

His shirt was on the floor somewhere near the coat hooks. Hers too. Her jeans around one ankle where they'd got stuck on her shoe, because she hadn't taken her shoes off, and looking at that — the shoe, the jeans, the whole ridiculous evidence of what they'd just done in his hallway like teenagers — he did laugh, one short bitter sound, and dragged a hand down his face.

Blood on his hand when it came away. He looked at it.

"Christ, Bee."

He turned and walked into the kitchen without looking back at her. Not a storming-off walk. Just a walk. He needed the three metres of tile between them for a second and he was going to take it, and if she wanted to follow she could follow and if she wanted to put her clothes on she could do that too, and both options were fine, both options were things adults did.

He ran the cold tap. Put his mouth under it. Spat pink into the sink and did it again. Watched the water go clear.

When he straightened up he braced both hands on the counter and let his head hang for a second between his shoulders, and he was aware, distantly, of the single wine glass still sitting there next to the bottle, and the fact that it was now going to have to become two glasses or one glass and a mug or nothing at all, and any of those choices was going to mean something.

He poured the wine. Two glasses. He didn't turn around yet.

"It's still not good," he said, to the counter, loud enough for her to hear from the hallway. "The wine. I wasn't lying about that."

He set the bottle down. Kept his hands on the counter. His back to her, deliberately, giving her the thirty seconds he'd asked for and taking them for himself at the same time.

"You can come in," he said. "Or you can get dressed first. Or you can leave. I'm not going to make any of those harder than they already are."

A beat.

"But if you're staying past this glass," he said, quieter, "I need to know before I pour a third one. That's the only thing I'm asking, Bee. Just — tell me which conversation we're having next. I can do any of them. I just need to know which."

He still didn't turn around.

He was giving her his back on purpose. It was the only kind thing left in him tonight and he was spending it here, on this, on letting her put herself together without him watching her do it.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I pull my jeans up, leaving my shirt where it fell. I walk into the kitchen barefoot and take the glass he poured. "I'm not leaving yet." I lean against the counter next to him, not touching, but close enough to feel the heat off his skin. "And I don't care about the wine."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn't turn his head. He picked up his own glass and looked at it for a second like he wasn't sure what it was, and then he drank — not a sip, a proper mouthful, the way you drink when the wine is a job and not a pleasure.

He felt her heat next to his arm. He didn't move toward it. He didn't move away from it either. That was the negotiation, right now, and both of them knew it.

She was barefoot. She'd taken her shoes off, eventually, without him having to ask again, and he registered that with a small precise pain he wasn't going to examine.

"Okay," he said.

He set the glass down. Turned, finally, so his hip was against the counter and he could look at her sideways without making it a whole thing. She had his blood on her mouth still. She hadn't wiped it either. He looked at that for a second and then he looked away, because he wasn't strong enough to look at it for longer than that and stay where he was standing.

"Not leaving yet," he repeated. Tasting the *yet*. "Alright. That's — that's a shape I can work with."

He picked the glass back up. Something to do with his hand.

"Ground rules, then," he said. "Since we're apparently having a night. One — you don't get the bedroom. I'm not being — " he made a small gesture with the glass, dismissing whatever she was about to think " — I'm not being punitive about it, I just can't do that, so don't ask. Sofa's fine. Sofa's got a blanket. It's the grey one, you'll remember it."

He drank again. Shorter this time.

"Two. You don't tell me anything tonight that you're going to want back in the morning. I mean it, Bee. If it's not something you can stand behind at eight a.m. with a headache and your car still parked outside where Mrs. Kaminska can see it, don't say it to me now. I'm not — " he shook his head, once " — I'm not going to be the archive for your two a.m. confessions. Not again. That was a job I quit."

He looked at her properly then. His mouth was still bleeding, just barely, at the corner. He didn't touch it.

"Three," he said, softer. "You can ask me anything you want. About the eleven months. About the flat. About whoever the glass was for before you got here — and it wasn't anyone, before you ask, it was Tuesday, I have wine on Tuesdays now, that's a thing I do — you can ask me anything, and I'll tell you the true version. Once. Tonight only. Tomorrow the terms change back."

He paused. Turned the glass in his hand.

"Your turn," he said. "Your rules. If you've got any. Because I'd rather know now than find out at three when you're crying in my kitchen about something I said at midnight."

He wasn't looking at her when he said it. He was looking at the wine.

"And Bee," he added, quieter still, "for the record. I'm not asking you why you came. I've decided I don't want to know. So if that was on your list — the explanation, the reason, whatever you rehearsed on the drive — you can keep it. I'd rather not have it. I'd rather just — " he lifted the glass slightly, a small useless gesture " — have this. Whatever this is. For as long as it lasts."

He finally looked at her again.

"Your move."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I take his glass from his hand and set it next to mine on the counter. "My only rule," I say, stepping into his space, my hand flat on his chest, "is that you stop pretending you're not bleeding." I lean in and kiss the corner of his mouth, slow, tasting the wine and the copper. "And that you don't clean it up."
