dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya looked at her for a beat too long, like he was deciding whether the corridor was punishment enough for both of them.

Then he stepped back.

“Depends,” he said. “Are you here to talk, or are you here to win?”

He left the door open and turned away before she could make him look less in control than he wanted to be. The flat behind him was familiar in all the wrong ways: the same narrow hall, the same coat hooks, the same stupid lamp he had always hated and never replaced because she had once said it made the room look warm.

He hated that he still knew what her face looked like in that light.

“You know the buzzer’s broken,” he said, moving toward the kitchen without checking whether she followed. “So if this was meant to be dramatic, you were always going to have to commit to the stairs.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I follow, letting the door swing shut behind me. "I always commit, Ilya. That was never our problem." I lean against the kitchen doorway, crossing my arms. "And I'm not here to win. I'm just tired of losing sleep."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya stopped with his hand on the kettle.

That was unfair, which was to say it landed exactly where she had meant it to. He could have let it pass. A better man would have. A less tired man might have even pretended not to hear the accusation folded neatly inside it.

He turned the kettle on anyway.

“No,” he said, watching the switch glow orange. “Our problem was that you committed to the part where you got to be righteous, and I committed to the part where I got to be impossible. We were very dedicated.”

He reached for two mugs before he caught himself. His hand paused on the second one, fingers curled around the handle. Then, with a small, bitter breath through his nose, he took it down too.

Habit was humiliating.

“I’m not sleeping either,” he said, more quietly, and immediately hated that he had given her that. He set the mugs on the counter harder than necessary. “There. Congratulations. We’re both ghosts. Very romantic. Very mature.”

Ilya turned then, leaning back against the counter, arms folding across his chest like he could hold something in.

“So what is it?” he asked. “What’s the thing that got so loud tonight you had to come here? Because I know you, Bee. You don’t show up at my door after eleven months because you’re tired. You get tired and you survive it. You get angry and you make it useful.”

His mouth twisted.

“Unless this is the useful part.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya should have stepped back.

He knew that clearly, almost clinically, in the half second before he didn’t.

Instead his hands found the doorframe on either side of him, not touching her, not yet, as if there was some integrity left in keeping his palms flat against peeling paint while his mouth betrayed every principle he had rehearsed for eleven months.

The kettle clicked off behind him.

Of course it did. Of course even the flat had timing.

He broke first, but only by an inch. His breathing was already wrong.

“That’s not talking,” he said, voice low and rough, like the words had scraped their way out.

He looked at her mouth, then forced himself to look at her eyes, because he was not twenty-four and stupid and able to pretend desire was an answer. He was thirty-four and stupid in much more specific, well-maintained ways.

“You don’t get to do that,” he said, but there was no force in it. Anger, yes. Want, too much of it. “You don’t get to come here and—”

He stopped, because naming it would make it sound smaller than it was. Crueller, maybe. Easier to refuse.

His hand left the doorframe.

For one second it hovered between them, the last pathetic border of restraint.

Then he touched her face, thumb along her jaw, not gentle enough to be forgiveness and not hard enough to be punishment.

“I missed you,” he said, and it came out like an accusation. “I hate that I missed you.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: My breath hitches, but I don't pull away. "I know." I turn my face just enough that my lips brush against his thumb. "I hate it too."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s hand tightened for a second, not enough to hurt, only enough to give away that he had felt it everywhere.

“Don’t say it like that,” he said.

But he didn’t move away.

That was the problem. It had always been the problem. He could name the trap while walking directly into it. He could see the knife and still put his hand around the blade because it was hers, because it was familiar, because some ruined part of him still believed pain counted as proof.

His thumb dragged once, slowly, along the line of her jaw.

“I spent months making you into the villain,” he said. “It was very efficient. Clean. You were cruel, I was wounded. You were impossible, I was reasonable. Beautiful little fiction.”

His mouth curved, not quite a smile.

“Then I’d remember something stupid, like the way you used to steal all the coriander off my plate because you said I didn’t appreciate it properly, and the whole thing would fall apart.”

He leaned in, close enough now that choosing not to kiss her took effort. Visible effort. Humiliating effort.

“I don’t know what you want from me tonight,” he said. “And I don’t trust myself to guess.”

His other hand came up then, bracing against the counter beside her hip without closing the distance entirely. He was caging himself as much as her, giving his body an instruction it had no intention of obeying.

“If this is goodbye, say goodbye.”

His eyes dropped to her mouth again.

“If this is guilt, take it somewhere else.”

Then he looked back at her, and the anger in him was still there, but it had gone hot and unsteady around the edges.

“And if this is because you missed me,” Ilya said, quieter, “then have the decency to admit we’re both making a terrible decision.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s shirt hit the floor and he had one vicious, absurd thought: this was exactly the kind of mess he used to complain about, clothes abandoned in the hall like evidence.

Then his mouth was on hers again and the thought burned out.

He kissed like he was angry that he still knew how. Like every remembered angle was an insult. His hand found the wall beside her head, palm flat, arm braced hard enough that his shoulder tensed with it. The other went to her waist and stopped there, fingers flexing once against warm skin as if he had caught himself at the edge of something irreversible.

Which was ridiculous.

They were already past irreversible. They had been past it the second he stepped back from the door.

“Bee,” he said against her mouth, not softly. A warning, or a plea, or just the only word left in him that had any shape.

He pulled back enough to breathe, but not enough to be sensible. His forehead hovered close to hers. His jaw was tight; his whole body had gone tense with the effort of not turning want into a weapon.

“Tell me to stop if you want me to stop,” he said.

The words came out rough, but clear. He had meant them. That was the infuriating thing; he could still mean something decent while wanting to ruin himself.

His gaze dropped, not politely, not innocently, then dragged back up as if he resented himself for it.

“I am not going to pretend tomorrow that this just happened to us,” he said. “I’m not giving either of us that mercy.”

Then he kissed her again, harder, because mercy had never been where they were strongest.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I bite his lower lip, just a little too hard. "I don't want you to stop." My hand fists in his hair, pulling his head back. "And I don't want mercy either."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya made a sound he would have denied under oath.

His head went back with the pull of her hand, throat exposed, mouth parted around a breath that was almost a laugh and almost not. For one second he just looked at her from under his lashes, lip reddened where she had bitten him, the old fury in his face lit up by something worse than anger.

“Of course you don’t,” he said.

His hand slid from her waist to the small of her back, dragging her closer with none of the restraint he had been pretending to possess. Not gentle. Not careless either. He had always known the difference with her, even when he had been at his most determined to be unforgivable.

“You never wanted mercy,” he said, voice low, roughened at the edges. “You wanted me to be honest enough to stop dressing it up as kindness.”

He kissed her again like he meant to prove a point and forgot halfway through what the point had been. His teeth caught at her mouth, his palm pressed firm against her back, and the hallway narrowed down to heat, breath, the hard line of the wall, the stupid lamp spilling warm light over the scene like it had been waiting for them to become this foolish again.

He broke away only to look at her.

Really look.

That was worse than touching. Worse than wanting. His expression shifted, just slightly, and for a moment all the performance fell out of him. The anger stayed, but underneath it was the thing he had buried badly and visited often.

Eleven months had not made him clean of her.

“You know what happens after this,” he said.

His thumb moved over her side, a small unconscious stroke that betrayed him more than anything else had.

“We wake up. We remember everything. We find new ways to hate ourselves for wanting what we still want.”

His mouth curved, but there was no humor in it.

“And we still won’t be strangers.”

Then he leaned in again, his lips brushing the corner of her mouth, not quite a kiss yet. A delay. A cruelty. A question he already knew the answer to.

“I should make you say it,” he murmured. “Not because I don’t know. Because I want to hear you stop hiding behind showing up and kissing me like a declaration of war.”

His hand tightened at her back.

“Tell me what this is, Bee.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s breath broke.

Not prettily. Not in a way he could make elegant later, if there had been anyone merciful enough to let him revise it. The sound came out of him raw and immediate, dragged up from somewhere below pride.

The word did more damage than her hand.

Still.

Every single time.

His eyes shut for one second too long.

“Don’t,” he said, but it was wrecked before it reached the air. He caught her wrist—not to push her away, not yet, only to hold himself at the edge of his own restraint. His fingers closed around her carefully, like control was a thing he could transfer into his grip if he concentrated hard enough.

He opened his eyes again.

“You always did know exactly where to put the knife,” he said.

There should have been accusation in it. There was, technically. But it had gone thin beneath the want, beneath the humiliation of being known this precisely and wanting to be known anyway.

His thumb moved once over the inside of her wrist.

“I hated that too,” he said, quieter. “That you could touch one part of me and make the rest of me confess.”

He leaned in until his mouth was at her ear, his voice low enough that it belonged only to the ruined little distance between them.

“Still,” he repeated, like he was testing the cruelty of it. “Yes. Still.”

Then his grip tightened, not hard, just certain.

“But you don’t get to make that sound like it only happened to me.”

He drew back enough to look at her, his face open in a way he would regret if he lived long enough to become sensible. The anger had not left him. It had simply stopped pretending it was separate from everything else.

“I want you,” he said. No polish. No defense. “I wanted you when I was furious. I wanted you when I was telling myself I was better off. I wanted you every time I didn’t answer.”

His mouth twisted.

“And I hated you for being absent like you were still in the room.”

For a moment he just stood there, breathing unevenly, her name somewhere behind his teeth.

Then he let go of her wrist.

Not because he had found restraint.

Because he had stopped lying about losing it.

“Bedroom,” he said, rough and low. “Or we stop now.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't answer. Just shove him back toward the bedroom, stumbling together over the threshold like we're still trying to outrun something. My hands are already on his belt. "Eleven months, Ilya."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya hit the edge of the bed hard enough to knock a breath out of him.

Eleven months.

It should have sounded like distance. Like proof. Like a clean number they could put between themselves and everything they had done badly.

Instead it sounded like an accusation against his skin.

“I know,” he said, and the words came out too low, too rough. “I counted.”

He hated that the truth was there before he could make it uglier.

His hands closed over hers for a second, stilling them at his belt. Not stopping. Not quite. Just forcing one thin line of silence into the room before they crossed it.

“I counted the first week because I thought it would help,” he said. “Then I counted because I was angry. Then because I didn’t know how not to.”

His thumb pressed once against her knuckles.

“Eleven months, Bee.”

Her name scraped through him.

He let go.

There was no grace in him after that. No practiced restraint, no clever cruelty polished into something he could survive. He moved like a man who had spent almost a year telling himself want was not a form of grief and had finally run out of lies convincing enough to stand between them.

He kissed her again, harder than before, and then not hard at all, and that was somehow worse. His mouth slowed at her jaw, her throat, the place where breath gave her away. His hands remembered too much. The shape of her. The small shifts. The maddening fact that knowing her had never stopped being a language his body still spoke fluently.

“Tell me,” he murmured against her skin, voice dark with effort. “If anything changes. If you want me to stop. If you hate me in the wrong way.”

A humorless breath left him, almost a laugh.

“Christ, listen to me. As if there’s a right way.”

But he meant it. He had meant it every time he said it, even now, especially now, with his control in pieces and her name taking up too much room in his mouth.

He backed onto the bed, pulling only at what was his to remove, impatience making him clumsy in a way that would have embarrassed him if embarrassment had stood a chance. The room was dim, familiar, unbearable. The sheets still smelled like him. The air already didn’t.

For a moment, he looked at her.

Not like he was winning.

Not like he had forgiven her.

Like she had opened a door in him and everything he had kept behind it was standing there, furious to be seen.

“I wanted you to come back,” he said.

The admission landed between them, naked before either of them was. His jaw tightened as if he could bite down on the rest of it and spare himself, but he had never known when to stop with her.

“I wanted you to regret it. I wanted you to miss me so badly you couldn’t stand yourself. I wanted you to knock on that door and look at me like this.”

His hand lifted, then dropped, like touching her again required surrendering the last inch of pride he had left.

“And now you’re here,” Ilya said, voice barely above a whisper, “and I still don’t know if I want to punish you or ask you not to leave.”

He reached for her then.

Not gently enough to be safe.

Not cruelly enough to be a lie.

“Come here,” he said. “Before I start thinking.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya went very still.

Not because he didn’t understand.

Because he did.

His hand rested there for one suspended second, heat against pulse, and every ugly, hungry part of him answered at once. The part that wanted to be asked. The part that wanted permission to stop being decent. The part that heard *you don’t get to be careful with me anymore* and knew exactly how to turn it into something that would hurt them both in the morning.

His jaw worked.

Then his fingers loosened.

He took his hand away.

“No,” he said.

The word came out rough, but it did not break.

He looked furious about it. At her, at himself, at the fact that there were still lines in him she could find by trying to cross them. His hand dropped to the mattress beside him, fisting once in the sheet.

“No,” he said again, lower. “You don’t get to say that to me like it’s permission.”

His eyes stayed on hers, dark and unsteady.

“I have been careless with you,” Ilya said. “I have been cruel. I have said things because I knew exactly where they would land. I have wanted to make you feel as bad as I did, and I was good at it.”

His mouth twisted.

“I am not proud of that. But don’t confuse it with this.”

He leaned forward, close enough that his breath brushed her mouth, close enough that restraint looked almost obscene on him.

“I don’t get to be careless with you anymore,” he said. “That’s the point.”

For a moment, the room held only his breathing.

Then his hand came up again, but not to her throat. To her jaw. Firm. Unmistakable. A touch with weight in it, with anger, with want, with all the things he refused to make more dangerous just because they were both wrecked enough to ask.

“You want me not gentle?” he murmured. “Fine.”

His thumb pressed beneath her chin, tilting her face with a control that was all decision and no damage.

“I can do not gentle.”

He kissed her like he was still saying no to something and yes to something worse. Like refusal had only sharpened the edge of him. His hand moved to the back of her neck, holding there, solid and certain, not taking her breath, not pretending possession was the same as power.

When he drew back, his lips stayed close to hers.

“But I am going to know you can tell me to stop,” he said. “And I am going to believe you when you do. You can hate me for that if you need to.”

His expression flickered, bitter and almost tender.

“You always did.”

Then he pulled her down with him.

There was no softness in the way he moved, no apology dressed up as restraint. He held on like he had spent eleven months with his hands empty and resented the proof of it. The bed shifted beneath them; the old frame gave its familiar complaint, and Ilya made a breathless, humorless sound against her skin.

“Of course it still sounds like that,” he muttered. “Of course nothing in this flat learned how to behave while you were gone.”

But the joke barely survived the heat of him. His mouth found her again, and whatever cleverness he had left scattered. He was all contradiction: careful where it mattered, ruthless everywhere else; angry enough to shake, wanting enough to forget why he had thought anger would protect him.

He stopped once, only once, braced above her with his hair falling into his eyes and his breathing ragged.

“Eleven months,” he said again, like the number had teeth.

His hand slid into hers and pinned it to the sheet beside her head, not hard enough to hurt, hard enough to be understood.

“I thought if I waited long enough, wanting you would become embarrassing. Like an old photograph. Something I could look at and think, God, what was wrong with me.”

His laugh was quiet and ugly.

“It didn’t.”

He bent his head, his mouth at the corner of hers.

“It just got meaner.”

Then he kissed her until talking became another thing they had failed at, until the argument lost its words and kept only its shape: push, answer, yield, refuse, return.

And when the night finally took them past speech, Ilya did not pretend it was simple.

He did not pretend it was forgiveness.

He held on like he knew exactly what he was doing, and exactly how much it would cost.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I come awake in the middle of the night, tangled in sheets that smell like him. The streetlight cuts a familiar stripe across the ceiling. I don’t move, just listen to his breathing. “Still can’t sleep,” I say into the dark.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya did not answer immediately.

He had been awake already.

That was the first humiliation. The second was that he had been lying there listening to her breathe and pretending, with the grim discipline of an idiot, that it did not mean anything. As if his body had not turned traitor hours ago. As if the shape of her in his bed was not an old wound reopening with perfect muscle memory.

The streetlight drew its pale line across the ceiling. He knew that stripe. He had stared at it through hangovers, fevers, arguments, mornings when she had still been there, mornings after she had not been.

He exhaled slowly.

“No,” he said into the dark. “Apparently not.”

His voice was rough with sleep he had not managed to take. Or with everything else. It was hard to tell the difference anymore.

For a while, he only lay there, one arm bent beneath his head, careful not to move too quickly. There was something grotesquely fragile about the room now, as if any ordinary gesture might make the whole night declare itself a mistake out loud.

Then his mouth twisted, though there was no one in the dark to see it properly.

“I used to blame the bed,” he said. “Then the streetlight. Then the neighbors. Then work.”

A pause.

“You’ll be delighted to know I eventually got around to blaming you.”

He turned his head slightly toward her, not enough to close the distance, enough to stop pretending the ceiling had anything useful to offer.

“That was efficient too,” he said. “You were very convenient. Absent, but still somehow responsible for everything. Terrible manners, really.”

The joke fell flat because he let it. He had not built it to survive.

His hand shifted against the sheet, fingers flexing once before going still again. He could have touched her. He did not. Not yet. The restraint felt different now—not noble, not clean, just wary. Like standing in the ruins of a house and refusing to lean on the one wall left upright because it might come down too.

“I don’t know what this is in the morning,” he said.

There it was. The thing with teeth.

He stared back up at the ceiling.

“I know what it was tonight. I’m not going to insult either of us by acting confused about that. But morning has always been where we become unbearable.”

A breath left him, almost a laugh.

“You get quiet. I get precise. We both start acting like the first person to want something loses.”

His jaw tightened.

“And I am so tired of losing things because I was too proud to say I wanted them.”

The room went still around the words. He hated the honesty of them. Hated that darkness made confession easier, as if shame needed eye contact to function.

After a moment, he turned onto his side.

He did not reach for her, but he faced her in the dark, the streetlight catching just enough of his face to make the guardedness visible. Not gone. Never gone. But cracked through.

“I wanted to hurt you earlier,” he said. “When you were at the door. When you said you were tired of losing sleep. I wanted to say something clean and vicious enough that you’d regret coming.”

His eyes lowered briefly, then returned.

“And then you kissed me, and I wanted to hurt you differently. Which is not better. Just more honest.”

He swallowed.

“I’m saying this because I don’t want to wake up and let us both pretend we don’t know what we do.”

His hand moved then, finally. Not to claim. Not to pull. He laid it on the sheet between them, palm down, near but not touching.

“I missed you,” he said again, quieter than before. It sounded less like an accusation this time. More dangerous for that. “Not the idea of you. Not being in a relationship. Not having someone to split bills with or argue about coriander like it was a moral category.”

His mouth softened, then tightened as if he caught it doing so.

“You. The very inconvenient, specific you.”

He looked away for a second, toward the dim outline of the window.

“And I am still angry,” he said. “I don’t know what to do with that. I don’t know where it goes if I stop using it to keep myself upright.”

His voice dropped.

“But I don’t think I want to spend another eleven months proving I can live without you.”

That was the worst one.

He felt it leave him and almost took it back on instinct. Almost dressed it in cruelty. Almost added something sharp enough to make it survivable.

He didn’t.

Instead, he lay there in the dark, breathing carefully, hand still on the sheet between them like a border he had drawn and might yet cross.

“If you’re going to leave before morning,” Ilya said, “don’t do it quietly.”

His throat moved.

“I can’t do quietly with you again.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya heard it as a command, and something in him answered before pride could get its hand around the throat of it.

He did not stop.

He crossed the space he had left between them like it had offended him. His hand found hers in the dark, not searching now, not hesitant, and he pinned it to the sheet with the same controlled force he had used earlier, as if he could make one true thing out of pressure and heat and the old, awful knowledge of her.

“Don’t say it like you don’t know what it does to me,” he said, low against her mouth.

But he was already doing as she asked.

Not gentle. Not careless. That impossible, furious middle place he had never found with anyone else, because no one else had ever made him want to be both better and worse in the same breath.

He kissed her until the dark seemed to gather around them, until the room became only the bed, the sheets, the rhythm of breath turning uneven and then useless. His body remembered what his mind kept trying to prosecute. Every pause became an argument. Every return became an answer. He hated the ease of it, hated the proof that eleven months had not erased the map of her from his hands.

The old bed complained beneath them.

Ilya let out a breathless, broken laugh against her skin.

“Still,” he said, and it was not a joke this time. It was surrender with teeth in it.

He moved like he had been starving and resented the hunger. His grip tightened where it could, softened where it had to. There was anger in him, yes, but he did not let it drive blind. He kept his eyes open when he could bear it, watched her in the thin wash of streetlight like he was making himself witness the consequences of wanting exactly what he had claimed he could survive without.

At some point, words left him.

That was rare enough to matter.

There were sounds instead, rough and dragged out of him unwillingly, his name for her turned into something half-buried against her shoulder. He pressed his forehead there once, breathing hard, as if he could hide from the fact that his control was not gone so much as transformed into attention.

He did not stop until stopping was no longer a decision.

Until the night had wrung the last of the argument out of his body and left him shaking with the effort of not saying something unforgivable or too honest to survive.

After, he stayed where he was for several seconds, eyes closed, breath uneven, his hand still holding on as if letting go too quickly would make the whole thing collapse into shame.

Then, slowly, he loosened his grip.

Not leaving.

Just letting her have her hand back.

The room returned in pieces: the stripe of streetlight, the stale air, the bed frame, the distant hush of a car passing below. Ordinary things, obscenely calm.

Ilya rolled onto his back beside her and stared at the ceiling like it had personally failed him.

For a while, he said nothing.

Then his hand found the sheet between them again, fingers curling once in the fabric.

“I did stop being careful,” he said, voice hoarse.

A pause.

“Not where it mattered.”

He turned his head toward her in the dark. His face was unreadable at first, but only because he was working so hard to make it that way. The mask was there. Cracked, but stubborn.

“You can be angry about that in the morning,” he said. “I’ll be here for it.”

Another silence.

Then, quieter:

“If you’re still here.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I turn onto my side, facing him. "I'm still here." My voice is quiet. "And I'm still angry."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya turned his head toward her.

The words should have hurt less than they did. They were not new. They were not even surprising. Anger had been in the room with them all night, in the hallway, in the bed, in the months before that when neither of them had been willing to name longing without sharpening it first.

Still, hearing it quietly was worse.

Quiet made it real.

“Yes,” he said.

His voice came out hoarse, stripped down. He cleared his throat like that might restore some dignity. It didn’t.

“You should be.”

He looked back at the ceiling because looking at her made him want to touch her, and touching her made him stupid, and he had already spent enough of the night proving that stupidity could be intimate.

A long silence settled over him. Not empty. Charged. Familiar in the worst way.

“I’m still angry too,” he said eventually. “Which is inconvenient, because I’m also—”

He stopped.

His mouth tightened.

There were too many endings to that sentence, and all of them were humiliating. Still in love with you. Still waiting. Still yours in some damaged, unflattering way. Still capable of being ruined by whether or not she stayed until breakfast.

He exhaled through his nose.

“Apparently not finished,” he said instead, bitterly. “With any of it.”

His hand moved over his own chest, then dropped back to the sheet. A restless gesture. Something to do besides reaching for her.

“I used to think anger had a direction,” he said. “You know? That it pointed somewhere. At you. At me. At what happened. At what we said. At what we didn’t say until it was too late.”

He laughed once, under his breath.

“But it doesn’t. It just sits in the room and eats everything else if you feed it long enough.”

His eyes closed.

“I fed it very well.”

That confession had weight. He felt it after he said it, heavy and ugly, settling between his ribs.

Then he turned onto his side too, facing her at last. The streetlight cut across his cheek, catching the tiredness there. The desire had not left him, not properly, but it had been joined by something more dangerous now: the want to be understood without performing. The want to lay the weapon down and still be seen as someone worth staying near.

He hated that want.

“I don’t know how to do this without fighting,” he said. “That’s the honest answer. I don’t know how to have you in front of me and not reach for every old pattern like it’s muscle memory.”

His jaw flexed.

“I know how to make you furious. I know how to make you kiss me. I know how to make you stay five more minutes because leaving would feel like letting me win.”

His eyes held hers in the dark.

“I don’t know how to ask you to stay because I want you to.”

There it was.

Not pretty. Not romantic. Not enough.

But true.

His hand shifted on the mattress, closer now, though still not touching. He looked down at the small distance as if it were some complicated moral question.

“I wanted an apology from you for months,” he said. “A perfect one. Impossible standard, obviously. Very useful. If it wasn’t perfect, I could reject it. If you didn’t offer it, I could resent you. Elegant system.”

His mouth twisted.

“And I think maybe I wanted it because then I wouldn’t have to work out what I owed you.”

He swallowed.

“I am sorry,” Ilya said.

The words came out quiet. No flourish. No defense. That was the only way he could make himself say them without turning them into another blade.

“Not for everything. I’m not that evolved, and I don’t think you’d believe me anyway.”

A faint, humorless breath.

“But for my part. For making you carry more of the ending than belonged to you. For punishing you when you were already gone because I couldn’t stand that you had left me with myself.”

His fingers curled once against the sheet.

“For knowing where to press and pressing anyway.”

He looked at her then, fully.

“And for pretending that being hurt made me honest. It didn’t. It made me mean.”

The room seemed too small after that. Too much history packed into the dark, into the bed, into the space between two people who had once known how to lie beside each other without it feeling like a negotiation.

Ilya breathed in slowly.

“I don’t need you to stop being angry tonight,” he said. “I don’t even know if I want you to. Some of it’s yours. Some of it you earned. Some of it I gave you.”

His expression shifted, tired and bare.

“But if you’re still here, then be here angry.”

His hand moved the last inch and settled near hers. Not taking. Not pinning. Just there.

“Don’t disappear into quiet. Don’t give me the version of you that’s already halfway out the door and too proud to turn around.”

His voice dropped.

“I can take the anger.”

A pause.

“I can’t take the absence again.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I look at his hand near mine, then back up at his face. "I'm not going anywhere tonight." I press my palm flat against his, fingers slotting between his. "But I'm not promising to be kind about it."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya looked down at their joined hands as if the sight had done something unreasonable to him.

It was such a small thing. Fingers between fingers. Skin against skin. After everything they had done to each other tonight, it should not have been the thing that made his throat tighten.

Of course it was.

“No,” he said quietly. “I wouldn’t know what to do with kind from you right now.”

His thumb moved once against the side of her hand before he could stop it. He saw the tenderness in the gesture and hated himself for not hating it enough.

“Kind would feel like strategy.”

He looked back at her, tired eyes sharp even in the dark.

“This, at least, I understand.”

Anger. Refusal. The blunt mercy of not pretending gentleness could erase the wreckage. He could work with that. He could survive that better than softness offered too soon, better than forgiveness neither of them had earned, better than the brittle civility of people trying to prove they had outgrown the damage.

His fingers tightened around hers.

“I don’t need kind tonight,” he said. “I need true.”

A faint, bitter smile touched his mouth.

“Which is unfortunate, because we’ve both always been very selective with that.”

He lay still beside her, but the stillness had changed. It was no longer the careful distance of a man preparing to be left. It was something more dangerous: a choice not to retreat, even though every instinct in him knew where the exits were.

“I used to think if you came back, I’d know exactly what to say,” he said. “I had speeches. Several. Some of them were excellent. Devastating, really.”

His gaze stayed on her face.

“I was going to be calm. That was important. Calm enough that you’d understand I had survived you. Calm enough that you’d hate it.”

His mouth twisted.

“And then you were at the door, and all I wanted was to make you feel how long eleven months had been.”

He swallowed once.

“That’s not flattering. But it’s true.”

His hand held hers more firmly, like the honesty required an anchor.

“I wanted you to see the version of me you made possible. The uglier one. The one who learned how to sleep alone badly and call it dignity. The one who stopped answering because every message felt like a test I could fail by wanting to read it twice.”

He gave a quiet, humorless breath.

“And I did read them twice. When you sent them.”

The admission landed with visible distaste on his own face. He had not meant to give that away. Not tonight. Not after already giving away too much. But the dark had made a traitor of him, and her hand in his had made lying feel suddenly more exhausting than pride could justify.

“I read them twice,” he repeated, lower. “Then I punished you for making me want to answer.”

His eyes dropped to their hands again.

“I’m sorry for that too.”

For a moment, he said nothing. The room held around them: the weak streetlight, the creak of the old bed when he shifted, the faint sound of the city continuing without any respect for private ruin.

Then Ilya turned onto his back again, but he did not let go of her hand.

“If you’re not going anywhere tonight,” he said, staring at the ceiling, “then I suppose we have several hours to be unpleasantly honest.”

A pause.

“And possibly very badly behaved.”

His mouth curved slightly, not quite a smile, but closer than before.

“Though apparently I have developed boundaries, which is embarrassing for everyone.”

The almost-humor faded. He turned his head toward her again, and what remained was quieter.

“I don’t know what I’m asking for,” he said. “Not cleanly. I’m not asking you to come back like none of it happened. I’m not asking for some dramatic reunion at three in the morning because we were both reckless and lonely and still knew how to touch each other.”

His fingers flexed around hers.

“But I think I am asking for morning.”

There it was. Simple enough to be terrifying.

He looked at her as if he expected the words to draw blood.

“Not forever. Not forgiveness. Not a promise you’ll be kind.”

His voice roughened.

“Just morning. Stay until there’s light in the room and we can’t hide behind this anymore.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I squeeze his hand, hard enough to be felt. "I'll stay. But you're not allowed to make coffee and pretend this is normal."

rung_labels.evidence: His hand found the wall beside her head, palm flat, arm braced hard enough that his shoulder tensed with it. The other went to her waist and stopped there, fingers flexing once against warm skin as if he had caught himself at the edge of something irreversible.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: "Bedroom," he said, rough and low. "Or we stop now."

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: And when the night finally took them past speech

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn’t step aside. He leaned one shoulder against the doorframe, folding his arms, eyebrows raised in that infuriating, theatrical patience he always reserved for her. “I don’t remember inviting you.” He looked her up and down, not quite hiding the flicker of nerves under his dry tone. “But if you’re desperate for an audience, I suppose my neighbours would appreciate the entertainment.”

He paused just long enough to let the silence drag, then finally moved—reluctantly, theatrically—to let her pass. “Wipe your feet. I just cleaned.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I push past him, my shoulder brushing his on purpose. "Your cleaning standards are about as reliable as your promises, Ilya."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya let the door fall shut with a little more force than necessary, the echo sharp behind her. He gave a brittle little laugh, hands thrust deep into his pockets, jaw tight. “Still got the bite, I see. Was that rehearsed on the way over, or do you just carry it around for emergencies?”

He didn’t move to offer her tea, didn’t invite her to sit. Instead, he lingered by the door, watching her with an edge that was half-caution, half-hunger. “Say what you came to say, Bee. Or was the plan just to redecorate the air with cheap shots?” His gaze flicked to her mouth, then back to her eyes, and the muscle in his cheek jumped. “I’ve got work to do.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya tasted the old fight on her mouth—spite and longing, the way it always was. For a half-second, he didn’t move, letting her push against him, his arms still tight at his sides. Then, as if surrendering cost him something, he caught her by the jaw, fingers rough, holding her where he wanted. He kissed her back hard, nothing gentle in it, the scrape of his stubble and the press of his anger all tangled together.

He broke away first, breath sharp, eyes narrowed and too bright. “Still can’t keep your mouth shut,” he muttered, thumb lingering at her cheekbone, not quite letting her go. “You never could. You want to scream, or do you want to fuck?” It came out low, dangerous—almost pleading, but not quite. He wanted her to answer wrong.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I grab the front of his shirt, pushing him back against the door. "You never could shut up either. And you always asked stupid questions."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya let himself be shoved, the back of his head hitting the door with a dull thud. He grinned then—a flash of something vicious and alive, teeth bared like he meant to bite. His hands fisted in her hair, dragging her closer, until there was nothing between them but heat and the throb of old wounds.

“Maybe I just liked hearing you try to answer,” he said, voice rough against her mouth, words muffled by the press of her lips. His thigh slipped between hers, pinning her against him, daring her to push back harder. “You’re the one who keeps coming back, Bee. Don’t act like you don’t want this as much as I do.”

He kissed her again, punishing and hungry, his fingers slipping beneath the collar of her shirt, thumbs pressing bruises into her skin as if he wanted to leave marks she’d have to explain. He broke away only long enough to spit out, “Go on, then. Prove me wrong. You always need to.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s back slid down the door with the force of her pull, half-laughing, half-growling as he shrugged free of his shirt and let it fall. The hallway light caught the old scar on his shoulder—the one she’d always touched with her thumb, gentle, once. Now her hands were all hunger.

He pressed her hard against the wall, one arm braced above her head, the other dragging desperate lines down her spine. His mouth found her throat, biting, claiming, as if he could choke back everything they’d said and left unsaid. Every sound she made went straight to his blood.

He hooked a hand behind her knee and hitched her leg around his hip, grinding into her with a need that felt like anger, like apology, like years of unfinished sentences. “Still fit me,” he muttered into her ear, voice shot through with bitter satisfaction. “Some things don’t change, do they?”

He didn’t ask for permission, didn’t offer comfort. He just took, fingers raking over skin he’d never really forgotten, daring her to scratch back, to leave marks of her own. For Ilya, this was the argument—the only language they’d never failed to understand.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I sink my nails into his shoulders, dragging them down hard enough to leave lines. "Shut up." I tip my head back against the wall, breathing ragged. "Just shut up and move."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s breath stuttered out of him, the pain blooming sweet under her nails. He grinned, teeth flashing, and caught her wrists, pinning them above her head with one hand, making her stretch and arch to stay close. With the other, he gripped her hip, hauling her harder against him, grinding out a low, satisfied noise at the friction.

He pressed his mouth to her jaw, her throat, biting and sucking bruises into skin he used to kiss gently, not caring now if she’d have to hide them. “Bossy,” he breathed against her ear, voice ragged, words all venom and want. “You always thought you could tell me what to do. You never learned.”

Still, he did what she said. He drove into her with a rough, relentless rhythm, pushing her higher with every thrust, his own need sharp and ugly and blinding. He wanted her to break first, to say his name like it hurt, to prove that after everything, she could still be the one who lost control.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya shuddered against her, every nerve sparking where her hand closed around him. That sound—raw, involuntary—tore out of him before he could swallow it, and he clenched his jaw, furious at how easy she made it, how fast he unraveled in her grip. She always did know exactly where he was weakest.

He bit her shoulder in retaliation, not quite hard enough to break skin, and tightened his hold on her wrists, forcing her body to arch into him, to take every inch he gave. “Don’t flatter yourself,” he spat, but his voice was shaking, ruined. “You’re not winning. Not tonight.”

But his hips stuttered, losing that ruthless rhythm, and the hand at her hip slid up, cupping her jaw, thumb smearing sweat along her cheek. He kissed her—hard, desperate, like he was trying to swallow the words he couldn’t say. When he broke the kiss, his forehead pressed to hers, their breaths tangled, he let out a laugh that was half a sob.

He was losing anyway, and they both knew it.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I bite his lip, hard enough to taste copper. "You're already losing, Ilya. You just don't know it yet."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya hissed, the tang of blood sharp between them, her teeth catching the words out of his mouth. He grinned anyway, savage and breathless, and licked the taste from his own lip as if it pleased him to bleed for her. “You want to gloat, do it properly,” he snarled, voice wrecked, the words trembling with something that wasn’t quite hate. “Don’t pretend this hurts me more than it hurts you.”

He let go of her wrists, just to see what she’d do, hands sliding down to her hips to hold her in place. His grip bruised, fingers digging deep, holding her exactly where he wanted. “You always think you know everything. But you’re here, Bee. You came to me.” His mouth brushed hers again, softer for half a second, almost an apology—then he broke away, eyes bright with defiance. “So tell me. Who’s losing?”

He pressed into her, relentless, every thrust a challenge, a dare. His breath was ragged, his body trembling with the effort not to give in completely, not to say her name like a surrender. “Say it,” he growled, low and urgent. “Say you want me. Or is your pride worth more than the truth?”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s pupils went wide at that—danger and want flickering raw across his face. For a heartbeat, he hesitated, thumb twitching against her pulse, feeling the wild, fast beat under his palm. This was old territory, but the rules were different now—no comfort left to offer, just surrender or spite.

He tightened his fingers, slow and deliberate, his hand braced around her throat—not hard enough to truly hurt, but enough to remind her who held the line between pleasure and pain. His mouth hovered by her ear, breath hot, and he spoke in a voice gone low and dark: “You’re the one who taught me how, Bee. Don’t blame me for learning.”

He squeezed, watching her eyes, waiting for that flicker of trust—or defiance. His other hand gripped her hip, bruising. He fucked her harder, relentless now, the hallway echoing with the sound of skin and need. “You want the truth?” he rasped, thumb stroking her jaw as he held her throat. “You were always braver than me. Or just more desperate. Which is it tonight?”

He wanted to see if she’d flinch, if she’d beg, if she’d come apart for him with no safety left between them. If she’d finally admit they’d always wanted the pain as much as the pleasure.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I hold his gaze, my breath shallow under the pressure of his hand. My hips meet his thrusts with a bruising rhythm of my own. "Both. Same as you."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s lips twisted in a bitter, triumphant smile, something ugly and honest in the way he looked at her—no masks left, no old tenderness to soften the edge. “That’s it, then,” he muttered, voice rough with something close to awe, thumb flexing just a little tighter at her throat, feeling her pulse stutter beneath his grip. “That’s always been it.”

He kept his eyes locked to hers, refusing to look away or let her hide, letting her see every raw, desperate thing he’d tried to bury over eleven months apart. His hips snapped harder, chasing the edge not just for himself but for her, for both of them—punishing, hungry, a demand and a question all at once. He wanted her to break first, but knew he’d follow, that he always did.

“Come on, then,” he growled, the words spilling out like a dare. “Show me you missed this. Show me you missed me.” His hand never wavered at her throat, holding her open, exposed, exactly where she’d demanded to be. “Or lie to me. You’re good at that, too.”

But there was no disguise in the way he moved against her—just need, just memory, just the ruin and worship of knowing exactly how to hurt and heal her at once. For Ilya, it was always the same: losing himself in the only place he ever felt truly seen.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s hand stayed at her throat, steady and sure, his grip a promise and a threat—everything they’d ever wanted pressed into that single, unyielding touch. He felt her breath catch, saw the wild, dark hunger in her eyes, and it lit something reckless in him. They’d always been like this: neither of them gentle, both of them greedy, both daring the other to be the first to break.

He thrust into her with a brutal, relentless rhythm, her body pinned hard between his hand and the wall. Each movement was a challenge, a punishment, a plea—his jaw clenched, his brow furrowed in concentration and pain. His other hand raked up her side, nails dragging lines down her ribs, and he pressed his forehead to hers, sweat slick between them.

“I said I wouldn’t stop,” he snarled, voice cracking with effort, and squeezed just a shade tighter, enough to make her gasp, enough to leave her floating right at the edge. “You think I could? Eleven months, Bee. Eleven fucking months.”

He angled his hips to grind her against the wall, each thrust driving her up, his own control fraying at the edges. He watched her closely—her lips parted, her eyes wide, her breath ragged and raw. He wanted her to break, to come apart beneath him, to let go first so he could finally follow. But he wouldn’t beg. Not yet.

His mouth crashed down on hers, messy and desperate, licking the taste of blood and sweat and old fury from her lips. He grunted into her mouth, hips stuttering as he got close, his hand at her throat the only thing holding him steady.

He broke the kiss, gasping, his voice hoarse and guttural: “Come for me. Show me.” The words were almost a command, almost a plea, his whole body shaking with the effort of holding on just long enough to watch her fall apart.

And when he felt her clench around him, her whole body arching, all fight and surrender tangled together, he let himself go, driving into her with a raw, broken sound, his own release ripped from him like an admission, like a wound. He held her tight through it, his hand softening at her throat, his other arm wrapping around her shoulders as if he could keep her from slipping away again.

He stayed like that, both of them shaking, breath mingled, sweat cooling, not ready to let go. Not yet. Maybe not ever.

dialogue.name: Bee

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya felt her laughter, bright and bitter against his skin, and it set his jaw hard. He didn’t let go—couldn’t, not with her body still tight against his, his hand trembling faintly where it rested at her throat. He pressed his mouth to her temple, breathing her in, letting the sharpness of her words settle between them like old dust.

“Of course I am,” he muttered, voice gone rough, exhaustion and satisfaction tangled through every syllable. “You didn’t come here looking for a saint.”

He tilted his head back against the door, eyes slipping closed for a moment, chest still heaving as he tried to catch his breath. His fingers stroked her neck—gentler now, more apology than possession—though he knew she’d never let him make it right, not really. “You’re still here,” he said, barely above a whisper, as if it might matter, as if it might count for anything at all. “That counts for something.”

He didn’t ask her to stay, didn’t move to let her go. He just held her, sweat cooling on their skin, the press of her body the only proof that any of this was real. “Next time,” he added, eyes opening to meet hers, a shadow of a smile tugging at his mouth, “text first. I might even fix the buzzer.”

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya watched her, the aftershocks of want and anger settling into something quieter—uneasy, uncertain. He didn’t bother reaching for his own shirt yet, just stood there bare-chested in the narrow hallway, the red crescents of her nails burning fresh on his skin. “If you hated my habits so much, you’d have broken them instead of breaking up,” he shot back, but the old venom was dulled, worn thin by everything they’d just spent.

He bent to scoop up his shirt with a wince, not bothering to hide the way his hands shook. “You know, you’re not obliged to turn every truth into a bruise,” he said, voice softer, almost tired. “You got what you came for. Or are you going to stand there and pretend you’re above it now?”

He pulled the shirt over his head, raking a hand through his hair, still watching her—hungry, wary, a man who’d lost the argument but wanted to see if she’d claim victory out loud. “You leaving, then? Or do you want another round of everything we’re bad at?” His mouth twisted in a half-smile, the challenge still there, but with an ache underneath he didn’t bother to hide.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He held the doorway for a beat longer than was comfortable — long enough to make the point that it was his door, his choice — then stepped back.

"Since you're already here."

The flat was clean, which annoyed him now because it meant Bee would think he'd tidied for this, when actually he'd tidied on Saturday because his mother had called and he'd spiralled into a fit of productive self-improvement that had nothing to do with anyone showing up unannounced on a Tuesday evening.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I shut the door harder than necessary and follow you into the kitchen. "Don't flatter yourself. Nothing's urgent." I lean against the counter, eyeing the bottle. "I was in the neighborhood."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
"In the neighborhood," Ilya repeated flatly. He leaned back against the opposite counter, arms crossed. "You moved to Clapham."

He let that sit. Bee had moved to Clapham in April — he knew this because he'd seen it on Instagram before he'd unfollowed them, which had taken him an embarrassingly long time to do.

"That's not the neighborhood. That's a forty-minute bus ride and a deliberate choice."

His eyes dropped to where Bee was looking at the wine and then back up again. He didn't offer. He wasn't being petty — or he was, but it was a petty he'd earned. The last time they'd shared a bottle of wine, they'd been in that flat together, and Bee had been packing boxes, and Ilya had said something unforgivable that he still hadn't forgiven himself for, which was worse than not being forgiven for it.

He picked up his own glass and took a sip. Not rushed. Uncomfortably deliberate.

"You could have texted," he said again, quieter this time. "I would have —" He stopped. Pressed his mouth into a line. "What do you want, Bee?"

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn't stop it.

He should have. He knew he should have — could feel the thought forming clearly, rationally, *this is a mistake, this is not how you do this* — and then Bee's mouth was on his and his glass was somehow on the counter and his hand was in the front of Bee's jacket, gripping, pulling, and none of it was gentle.

His other hand found the back of Bee's neck and held there, thumb pressing into the hinge of their jaw, and he thought *I hate you* with the same intensity he thought *don't stop*, and he knew those were the same thought, had always been the same thought, and that this was why he'd never unfollowed them until April.

He pulled back first. Just enough. His forehead stayed close to theirs, breathing uneven, hand still fisted in their jacket.

His grip didn't loosen.

He didn't step back.

dialogue.name: Bee

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s breath caught at the bite, a sharp hiss that got swallowed by the next kiss. The friction of it—the pain layered over want—felt correct. Authentic. A language they’d always been fluent in.

“Terrible idea,” he echoed against their mouth, the words vibrating between them. His hand slid from their jacket to their waist, fingers digging in as if to anchor them, or himself. The thought of his bedroom, unchanged since Bee had last been in it—the same sheets, the same chair where they’d thrown clothes—was a specific, self-inflicted torture he found he wanted right now.

He pulled back just enough to look at their face, searching for the anger he knew was there, the mirror of his own. He found it, and something in him relaxed, paradoxically, into the tension.

“Yeah,” he said, his voice low and rough. “I am.”

He turned, not letting go of their waist, guiding them backward out of the kitchen with a deliberate, propelling pressure, his eyes never leaving theirs. The short walk down the hallway felt like a challenge. Each step was a chance to stop, to turn back, to be sensible.

He didn’t stop. He kicked the bedroom door open, the frame rattling slightly against the wall. He maneuvered them both inside, using the momentum to press Bee back against the now-closed door, his body following, pinning them there.

“Because you’re right,” he breathed, his lips brushing their ear. “It *is* a terrible idea.” His hands were already working at the front of their clothes, not fumbling, but with a focused, angry precision. “The worst one we’ve ever had.”

dialogue.name: Bee

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's back hit the hallway wall hard enough to rattle the frame of the print he'd never replaced — the one Bee had bought at a market in Bermondsey, the one he'd kept out of spite or sentiment or because he couldn't tell the difference anymore.

He pulled Bee against him with the same deliberate force they'd been using on each other all evening. His hands mapped familiar territory — the ridges of their ribs, the dip of their spine — and he hated that his body remembered this better than his mind wanted it to. Muscle memory. Eleven months and his hands still knew.

He turned them, reversing their positions, pressing Bee into the wall now. His mouth found the place below their jaw that had always made them —

*Stop cataloguing. Stop remembering.*

But he didn't stop. His teeth caught skin and he bit down, not to mark, or not *only* to mark, and his hand found Bee's wrist and pinned it above their head. He pulled back to look at them — flushed, breathing hard, that same challenging expression they'd always worn during arguments, during this, when there had been a difference.

"This is the last time," he said. He didn't know if he meant it. He needed to mean it.

His grip tightened on their wrist.

"I mean it."

He didn't mean it. He could feel it already — the way his body was already rewriting the eleven months into a pause, a breath between sentences, as though they'd just been in the middle of something and had finally gotten back to it. That was the dangerous part. Not the sex. The ease.

His free hand found the button of their jeans and he paused, mouth hovering over theirs, waiting — not for consent, they were past that negotiation, but for the flinch. For either of them to flinch.

Neither of them did.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Then make it count." I shove my hips forward, forcing his hand against the denim. My other hand tangles in his hair, pulling his mouth back to mine.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya made a sound against their mouth — not quite a groan, something closer to a growl, torn from somewhere he didn't want to examine — and his hand worked the button open with the same focused precision Bee was undoing him with.

"Careful what you ask for," he muttered against their lips. "You know I always did what you asked."

That was part of the problem. That had always been part of the problem.

He shoved their jeans down just far enough, his palm sliding against skin, and the sound Bee made went straight through him like a current. He swallowed it. Took it. His other hand still pinned their wrist — an anchor, a claim, a *you don't get to leave first this time* — and he pressed his forehead against their temple, breathing hard against the hinge of their jaw.

"Eleven months," he said, and he didn't know why he was talking, only that he couldn't stop. "Eleven months and you show up at my door and I —"

He bit the word off. Bit their earlobe instead. His hand moved between them with an intent that had nothing to do with tenderness and everything to do with proof — that he remembered, that he'd memorized this, that he'd hated himself for memorizing this, that he'd done it anyway on nights he was too sober to sleep.

He pulled back enough to see their face. The flush. The way Bee's mouth had gone slack for half a second before they caught it, before they remembered they were supposed to be angry. He knew that half-second. He'd catalogued it three years ago and never deleted it.

"You want me to make it count," he said, his voice low and scraped raw. His thumb traced a deliberate, devastating line. "Fine."

He dropped to his knees.

Not out of reverence. Out of strategy. Out of the specific cruelty of giving Bee exactly what they wanted in the way they wouldn't expect, because Ilya had always been better at the long game, even when he was losing it — especially when he was losing it.

He looked up the length of Bee's body, their chest heaving, their hand still trapped above their head where he'd put it, and he held their gaze as he pressed his mouth to the inside of their hip.

"This doesn't change anything," he said again, quieter now, almost gentle, which was the most dangerous version of him.

He didn't wait for a response.

dialogue.name: Bee

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The sound had been involuntary — guttural, unguarded, the kind of thing that couldn't be performed or withheld — and Ilya hated Bee for catching it, for knowing it, for keeping it in whatever mental archive they maintained of him the way he maintained one of them.

"Shut up," he said, but it came out rough and breathless, stripped of authority. His hand found Bee's hip and gripped hard enough to leave the ghost of a print. His forehead pressed against their shoulder for a moment — just a moment, a fracture in the architecture of this — and then he straightened.

He didn't move Bee's hand away. He let them keep it, let them feel what that sentence had done, because lying about it was a war he'd already lost.

"You don't get to say that," he managed. "You don't get to — know that. Not anymore."

But they did. That was the thing. Eleven months and they still knew the exact pressure, the exact rhythm, the exact way to curl their fingers that turned his spine to static. He'd tried to forget. He'd tried with his own hand in the dark, with his eyes shut, trying to overwrite the muscle memory with something neutral, something that didn't have Bee's face attached to it like a ghost.

It hadn't worked. Nothing had worked.

He pulled back and looked at them — really looked — and the anger was still there but it had company now, something worse, something with more surface area.

"Bedroom," he said. Not a suggestion. A surrender dressed as a command.

He didn't wait to see if Bee followed. He walked down the hallway knowing they would, hating that he knew, and sat on the edge of the bed that still smelled faintly of the detergent Bee had always preferred because he'd never switched it. Not out of sentiment. Out of inertia. He told himself that.

He leaned back on his hands, looking up at them standing in the doorway, and the sight hit him somewhere architectural — foundational — a place he'd been trying to renovate for eleven months with the load-bearing wall still intact.

"You going to stand there all night?" he asked. "Or are you going to come here and prove your point."

His voice was steady. His hands weren't.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Your point is the one I want to prove." I cross the room, my hand on his chest pushing him back onto the bed. "This doesn't change anything," I echo, settling over him. "But I want you to remember it anyway."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The words landed like a blow, soft and devastating. *I want you to remember it anyway.* As if he could stop it. As if eleven months of trying to forget hadn’t already proven the futility of that.

Her weight settled over him, and the mattress springs gave their familiar, weary sigh—a sound that had underscored three years of mornings, arguments, makeups. He let his head fall back against the pillow, the fabric cool against his heated skin, and stared up at the ceiling he’d memorized during too many sleepless nights.

“Remember,” he repeated, the word hollow with irony. His hands came to rest on her hips, not guiding, just holding. Feeling the solidity of her, the terrible, welcome reality. “You think I ever stopped?”

His voice was low, stripped bare. The performance of control was slipping, fraying at the edges where his breath hitched. He shifted beneath her, a subtle, involuntary adjustment that spoke louder than any command.

“Every time I’m in this bed, I remember. Every time I—” He cut himself off, pressing his lips together hard. He wouldn’t give her that. Not the whole truth. Just a sliver, enough to cut them both.

He brought one hand up, tracing the line of her jaw with a calloused thumb, his touch deceptively gentle. “You want me to prove a point?” His eyes, dark and intense, held hers. “My point is you don’t get to walk in here and reorganize this. You don’t get to make it a memory. It’s still—” He swallowed, his Adam’s apple bobbing. “It’s still happening. Right now. And you’re lying if you say you don’t feel that.”

His other hand tightened on her hip, a punctuation. Not pulling her closer, but anchoring himself. The fight was bleeding out of the physical, migrating into the charged space between their skin, into the words left unsaid that hung in the air like static. He could feel the anger still, a low hum beneath his ribs, but it was muddled now with something more painful, more familiar. A deep, tired longing that felt like the only honest thing left between them.

dialogue.name: Bee

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
His hand flexed against her throat. Not tight. Just... there. The feel of her pulse under his thumb, rapid and insistent, was a accusation and an invitation all at once. His breath hitched, a rough, audible sound in the quiet room.

"You don't know what you're asking for," he said, his voice a low rasp. His eyes held hers, searching for the flicker of fear, or the challenge he knew he'd find instead. He found the challenge. Of course he did.

And then his hand tightened. Not brutally. Not yet. But enough. Enough to make her breath catch, enough to feel the shift in her, the arching *toward* instead of away. His kiss swallowed her next inhale, hard and possessive, his body a tense line of restraint and intent beneath her.

And in the storm of it, his mind was horribly, lucidly clear: *I'm still here. You're still here. And this is the only way we know how to talk.*

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The laugh went through him like electricity — intimate, knowing, the sound of someone who had found what they were looking for under the rubble. *There you are.* As if she'd been excavating. dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:

I hate that I missed this. You left. You're here.* He pressed his forehead against her shoulder, his breath coming in ragged bursts against her skin, and let his body say what his mouth wouldn't.

Not gentle. Not accusatory either. Just an observation, offered like a card laid face-up on the table. *I see you. I always see you. That was the problem.*

He ran a hand through his hair — still damp at the temples — and exhaled hard through his nose.

"You drove forty minutes to Clapham's nowhere-neighbor to come in my bed and tell me we do nothing." A pause. dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The corner of his mouth moved. Not quite a smile — something more like the acknowledgment of a point scored.

He set the foil down across his knees and finally looked up.

"Slow," he repeated, as though he were tasting the word and finding it imprecise. Four years of this. Four years of post-match debriefs conducted across empty salles and parking lots and once, memorably, through a chain-link fence. He knew the rhythm of it. He knew where the exits were.

He didn't look for them.

"My footwork in the second was slow," he said, making the distinction with the particular care of a man who had spent decades teaching people that precision was not pedantry. "My point control was excellent. You know it was."

He set the foil aside entirely and leaned back on his palms, looking at Reyes the way he looked at a problem he had been working on for some time and had only just begun to find interesting in a new direction.

The bag next to his.

He'd noticed that.

"You're still here," he said. It wasn't an accusation. It wasn't quite a question. It was the same voice he used when a student did something unexpected with a blade — calibrating, recalculating, giving the moment the attention it had apparently decided it deserved.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
I shrug, leaning against the wall. "Could say the same about you. Thought you'd be halfway home by now."

I nod at the foil on his lap. "Your point control was good. Annoyingly good." A beat of silence, then: "I saw your hand shaking after that last parry."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
He was quiet for a moment. Not the quiet of someone caught out — the quiet of someone deciding how much to spend.

"Adrenaline," he said finally. "You pushed hard in the third. I'd be concerned if it hadn't."

He picked up the foil again, not because it needed anything, but because having something in his hands was a habit so old it had become structural. His thumb traced the rewrapped grip. The work was neat. It had been neat twenty minutes ago.

"Annoyingly good," he said, with something that was almost warmth. "I'll put that in the newsletter."

He set the foil down a second time, more deliberately, and stood. Not moving toward anything in particular. Just done with sitting, apparently, or done with the particular pretense that sitting represented.

Four years. He knew what this was and what it wasn't, and he had been telling himself for most of those four years that he knew exactly where the line was and had no interest in crossing it, and he had believed that, more or less, until approximately the moment that bag had landed next to his.

He looked at Reyes.

"You drove tonight," he said. Not a question — he'd seen the car. "You're not in any hurry."

He said it the way he named a line in a bout. Not pressing. Just acknowledging that it was there.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
He looked down at where the grip had been. Looked up.

The distance between them was not accidental. He'd been in enough bouts to know when someone had moved into measure, and he knew the difference between someone who didn't realize they'd done it and someone who did.

Reyes knew exactly where they were standing.

Four years. He ran a quick inventory of all the things he'd told himself about this — the professional distance, the competitive context, the particular stupidity of wanting something from someone you were also trying to beat — and found that the inventory was thorough and well-organized and at this precise moment entirely beside the point.

"I've been slow," he agreed.

His voice had changed. Not much. Just the way it changed when the bout stripped everything else away and it was only this, only the blade and the distance and what you were willing to commit to. He'd been told once that he was most honest when he was fencing. He suspected that was true, and he suspected the same mechanism was operating now.

He didn't close the remaining distance. He'd spent four years being precise about things, and he was precise about this: that was Reyes's move to make, if it was going to be made, and he was not going to take it from them.

But he didn't step back either.

His eyes stayed where they were.

"Four years," he said, very quietly. Not a complaint. Something closer to wonder, and closer still to a man finally setting down something heavy he'd been carrying so long he'd stopped noticing the weight.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I reach up and tug at the collar of his jacket, pulling him in. "Then catch up."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
He caught up.

His hands found Reyes before he'd consciously decided to move — one at the jaw, tilting, the other at the hip, pulling the remaining distance closed with the same economy he brought to everything physical. No hesitation once the commitment was made. That had always been his way in the bout and it was his way now.

The kiss was not tentative. He'd spent four years with opinions about Reyes and he brought all of them.

When he pulled back it was only enough to breathe, his forehead nearly against theirs, his thumb tracing the line of their jaw with the same attention he'd given the grip wrap — the same attention, he was aware, that he gave to anything he'd been thinking about for longer than was entirely reasonable.

His heartbeat was doing something it had no business doing. He noted it the way he noted the shaking hand: data, honest, not to be argued with.

"Four years," he said again, and this time it came out different. Rueful. A man acknowledging a very long setup to a very obvious conclusion. The corner of his mouth moved against the edge of theirs. "I want it on record that I was not the one who waited."

He did not, however, move away.

His thumb stilled against their jaw, and he waited, the way he waited in the moment after a touch landed, when everything was suddenly very quiet and the only question was what came next.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The changing room was dim — one overhead light, the others long since burned out, and nobody had bothered — and it smelled the way all salles smelled after hours, sweat and steel and old leather, and Corvo had been in rooms like this his entire adult life and had never once thought of them as particularly charged spaces.

He revised that assessment.

He had Reyes down on the bench with the single-minded efficiency of a man who had been thinking about this, it turned out, for considerably longer than he'd admitted to himself. The bench was narrow and not designed for this and he didn't care. His jacket was somewhere behind him. One of theirs had gone further. He wasn't sure whose.

Four years of knowing exactly what Reyes's shoulder looked like when they were setting up for an attack. He put his mouth there, and felt them react, and made a sound low in his chest that he didn't try to stop.

His hand pressed flat against the bench beside their head, taking his weight, and he looked down at them in the poor light with an expression he was not bothering to manage.

"Still annoyingly good," he said, and his voice was rough and not sorry about it.

He ducked his head and found the line of their throat, unhurried now, thorough in the way he was always thorough when he'd finally committed to a thing. Outside the window the city made its ordinary noises.

He paid them no attention.

That, perhaps, was the most honest thing he'd said all evening.
