He set the foil down across his knees, deliberate, and leaned back against the bench so the wall took his weight. Four years of this. He knew the rhythm of it better than any bout — the jab and the parry, the way Reyes could never let a thing lie any more than he could.

"The third touch was a gift," he went on, "and you know it. You dropped your point coming off the retreat. I could've buried it a full second earlier. I *chose* to make it look close." A pause, mouth tugging. "For your dignity."

His eyes went to the bag, then back up. The salle was quiet in that particular way empty rooms got at night, the overheads humming, everyone else long gone home to whatever they went home to.

"You came back," he said. It wasn't a question. "Forget something?"

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I didn't forget anything. Just figured you'd still be here, sulking over your 'generous' victory. (*I unzip my bag and pull out my own foil, inspecting the blade*) That third touch was clean. You were just too busy admiring your own footwork to see it coming.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo watched the foil come out of the bag and felt something settle low and warm in his chest — that old, familiar recognition. Not done, then. Neither of them ever was.

"Sulking," he said, and rose off the bench with an unhurried roll of his shoulders. "Is that what we're calling it. I was savoring. There's a difference." He let the wrapped foil hang loose from his fingers. "And you didn't come back for the blade. You've got a whole salle across town full of the things. You came back because two-three sits worse with you than a clean loss ever would."

He crossed the floor, slow, the overheads laying his shadow long across the piste. Four years he'd been reading this man — the tell in his jaw when he was actually annoyed versus performing it, the way he never inspected a blade he wasn't planning to use.

"So." He stopped just inside the distance a bout would start from, close enough that the joke thinned out of his voice a little. "You want it again. Say it. No director, no scorekeeper, nobody left to lie to but each other." His head tipped. "Though I warn you, admiring my own footwork is a documented hazard. It's very good footwork."

His eyes held Reyes's, and the needling had gone somewhere underneath it — steadier, quieter, waiting to see if the other man would follow.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's fingers came away from the grip easy — he let it go, let Reyes take it, and that alone should have told the man something, because Corvo did not give ground on anything, ever, least of all his own foil.

He didn't step back either.

"Slow," he said again, softer this time, the third time that word had come out of Reyes's mouth tonight and the first time it hadn't sounded like an insult. The overheads hummed. The salle held its breath around them the way empty rooms did. "You keep saying that."

His gaze dropped — deliberate, unhurried, the same patience he'd bragged about all night — and came back up to Reyes's face. Close enough now to see where the man's pulse moved in his throat, to catch that the jaw wasn't set in the performed way, the annoyed way. Something else. Four years of reading him and this was a page Corvo hadn't turned before.

"Here's what I think," he said. "I think you didn't come back to fence." He let that sit a beat, the way he'd let a touch land — clean, unhurried, chosen. "I think you came back because you've been circling the same thing I have and one of us was going to have to stop being a coward about it. And it wasn't going to be me admitting it first, was it. Not to you."

The grip lay forgotten on the floor between their feet.

"So," Corvo murmured, and this time there was no joke left underneath it at all, just the steady thing that had been waiting. "Slow. Fine. I can go slow." His hand came up, unhurried, to rest just at the side of Reyes's neck — not pulling, only there, a question with weight behind it. "Or you can stop telling me what I've been all evening and tell me what you want instead."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: My hand comes up to cover his, holding it there against my neck. "I want you to admit you were showing off," I say, voice low. "And then I want you to do it again."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo felt the warmth of Reyes's hand close over his, pinning it there, and something in his chest gave way — quiet, like a door he'd been leaning against finally opening.

"Showing off," he said, and the word came out rough at the edges, all the bravado worn down to something honest underneath. His thumb moved against the line of Reyes's jaw, slow, testing. "For four years. Every bout. You want to know why the third touch was generous? Because I didn't want it to end. I've been drawing these out since—" He stopped himself, breath going short. "God. Yes. Showing off. For you. Happy?"

He wasn't looking away. That was the thing — Corvo, who deflected everything into a joke, who never let a serious word sit in the air unarmed, held Reyes's eyes and let it stand there naked between them.

"And do it again," he echoed, softer. His free hand found Reyes's hip, drawing him in that last stubborn inch of distance neither of them had wanted to be the one to close. "Now who's giving orders."

He leaned in — unhurried, everything he'd bragged about all night made true. Patient. Chosen. His mouth stopped just short of Reyes's, close enough to feel the man's breath, letting the wanting stretch one beat longer because he'd waited four years and he was not going to rush the last inch of it.

"Slow," he murmured against his lips. "You said slow."

And then he kissed him.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The bench caught the back of Corvo's knees and he went down onto it without grace, without any of the composure he wore like a second skin on the piste — and he found he didn't want it, didn't miss it, was glad to be rid of the whole performance. Reyes came down over him and the last of the joke went out of Corvo entirely.

"Four years," he said against Reyes's mouth, and it came out like an accusation and a surrender at once. His hands were everywhere now, learning what he'd only ever guessed at across the distance of a bout — the set of the man's shoulders under the jacket, the heat of him, the way he moved when there was no director counting the touches. "You couldn't have done this two years ago? Saved us both the—"

He didn't finish it. Reyes gave him a reason not to, and Corvo made a sound low in his throat that he'd have been mortified by anywhere else and wasn't here at all.

The kit was a wreckage on the floor, gloves and mask and both their foils in a tangle that would take an hour to sort out and neither of them cared. His fingers found the zip at Reyes's collar and drew it down slow — *slow*, because the man had asked for it and because Corvo had spent four years being patient and was not going to abandon the one skill he'd actually been telling the truth about.

"There," he murmured, mouth dragging along the line of Reyes's jaw to his throat, where the pulse he'd been watching all night hammered under his lips. "Slow. Told you I could." A breath, unsteady, honest. "Don't you dare tell me I'm still too slow."

He got a fist in the front of Reyes's jacket and pulled him down the rest of the way, and after that there wasn't much left to say.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: My jacket is half off my shoulders and I’m not helping you with it. (*I push a hand into his hair and pull, just enough to tilt his head back*) Four years because you were too busy being smug to do anything about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The pull at his hair snapped Corvo's head back and he let it, throat bared, a breath hissing out of him that was half laugh and half something rawer. His hands stilled on the half-shed jacket — Reyes wasn't helping, of course he wasn't, the contrary bastard, and Corvo loved him for it in a way he wasn't going to be able to take back once he'd thought it.

"*Me*," he said, voice gone thin with the angle, with the grip fisted in his hair. "That's rich. I've been telegraphing this from across the piste for years. Every drawn-out bout. Every time I let you back into distance when I should've closed it." His eyes found Reyes's from under the tilt of his head, dark and unguarded. "You're the one who kept calling it slow like it was an insult. Took you long enough to figure out what it actually was."

He worked the jacket the rest of the way down Reyes's arms himself, since the man wouldn't, dragging it off and letting it drop into the wreckage on the floor with everything else. His hands came back up his sides, unhurried, the same patience he'd bragged about made honest at last.

"Smug," he agreed, breath catching as Reyes's weight settled over him. "Fine. Smug. I'll own it." His mouth found the man's collarbone, then higher, dragging back toward the pull still tight in his hair. "But I'm here now, aren't I. On my back on a changing-room bench with your hand in my hair. So maybe—" he tilted into the grip, deliberate, testing how far Reyes would take it "—maybe stop keeping score for once and let me make up the four years."

He got both hands under the hem of Reyes's undershirt and pulled it up, and after that he stopped talking.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo went flat and stayed flat, and for the first time in four years — for the first time in as long as he could remember — he had nothing to say.

It should have galled him. Being outmaneuvered, disarmed, the last word taken clean out of his mouth before he'd even loaded it. And it did, somewhere far off, in the part of him that kept score by reflex. But that part had gone quiet. Everything had gone quiet except the drag of Reyes's mouth and the bench hard under his spine and his own breath coming apart in his chest.

His hand found Reyes's hair the way Reyes's had found his, but there was no pull in it — just his fingers closing, holding on, because he needed something to hold and there was nothing else. The overheads hummed somewhere beyond the changing-room door. His head tipped back against the wood.

"That's—" he tried, and it came out wrecked, nothing behind it, no jab and no parry and no clever thing waiting underneath. He swallowed and it didn't help. "That's not fair."

It was the truest thing he'd said all night and they both knew it. Four years of arming every word, of never once letting a serious thing stand in the air undefended, and Reyes had found the one thing that stripped it all off him at once. His fingers tightened in the man's hair, gentle, helpless.

"Reyes—" Just the name, this time. No barb hung off it. He'd meant to say something cutting about how the man was showing off now, about giving orders, about slow — and he couldn't. The words were gone. There was only the wanting, four years of it, finally with nowhere left to hide.

So he let it show. He let his head fall back and his hand stay in Reyes's hair and the sound out of his throat go unguarded, and he stopped keeping score entirely, the way he'd been told to, the way he found — to his own quiet astonishment — he wanted to.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I finally let go of his hair to look down at him, my hands framing his face. "There," I say, low. "No more score."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo opened his eyes to find Reyes looking down at him, hands cradling his face, and for a moment he just breathed under it. The joke he'd have reached for anywhere else wasn't there. It had gone the way the tape had gone, the score, the four years of armor — dropped somewhere on the changing-room floor with the rest of the wreckage.

"No more score," he agreed, and it came out quiet, wrecked at the edges, honest all the way down.

He brought his own hand up to cover one of Reyes's where it framed his jaw — the same gesture Reyes had given him an hour and a lifetime ago against the neck. His thumb moved over the man's knuckles. He was smiling, but it wasn't the smug one, wasn't the performed one; it was something he'd never let Reyes see across a piste because it had no defense in it at all.

"You know that's the first time you've ever shut me up," he said. His voice was steadier now but only just. "Four years. I want it on record." A breath of a laugh. "The last thing I'll put on record, apparently, because I've got nothing left."

He tilted his head into Reyes's palm, unhurried, letting the man hold him there.

"So," he murmured, "since neither of us is counting anymore." His hand slid from Reyes's knuckles down his forearm, drawing him — gently this time, no fist in the jacket, nothing to prove — back down toward him. "Stay up there where I can reach you. I've spent long enough watching you from a distance."

And he pulled him down the last inch, slow, and kissed him like there was nothing left to win.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The words were barely out of Corvo's mouth — *prove the point properly, or concede* — the old challenge, the one shape of him that hadn't dissolved yet — when Reyes took him at his word and pinned his wrists flat to the bench.

Corvo tested it once, reflexively, a flex of the arms to see if there was give in it. There wasn't. Reyes had him, and had taken the pace clean out of his hands the same way he'd taken the last word, and Corvo let his head fall back against the wood with a sound that was closer to relief than surrender.

"There he is," he breathed, and the grin was there for a half-second — the real one, delighted, undone — before Reyes wiped it off him again. "Knew you had it in you."

Because this was the thing, the thing four years of needling had been circling without either of them naming it: Corvo did not want to win. Not really. Not this. He'd spent his whole life setting the pace, arming every word, choosing every touch, never once giving ground — and being held down on a changing-room bench by the one man who'd matched him at all of it was the closest he'd come to putting the weapon down in longer than he could say.

His wrists went slack in Reyes's grip. He stopped fighting for the tempo. He let it go, the way he'd let the foil go an hour ago, and it was easier this time.

"Concede," he managed, rough, and it wasn't a joke and it wasn't a defeat — it was the truest surrender he had in him, offered up without a barb hung off it. "There. On record. You win the—"

Reyes didn't let him finish that either.

And Corvo, for once in four years, was glad to lose the point, glad to be beaten to the last word, glad of the hands holding him down and the pace taken out of his keeping entirely. His head tipped back, his breath came apart, and he stopped reaching for anything clever at all — because there was nothing left to prove, and nowhere left to hide, and for the first time it was enough just to be caught.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I catch his mouth with mine before he can get another word out, then pull back just enough to watch his eyes. "Now you're being quiet."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's eyes stayed open under him, dark and steady, and for once he let himself be looked at without reaching for anything to hide behind. His wrists were still pinned. He wasn't testing the grip anymore.

"Someone finally gave me a reason to be," he said, and it came out low, threadbare, none of the performance left in it.

He turned his head just enough to press his mouth to the inside of Reyes's wrist where it held him down — a small thing, unhurried, an admission he couldn't have made in words. Four years of never once being still, of arming every silence before it could be used against him, and here he was, quiet, and glad of it, and letting the man watch him be glad.

"Don't get used to it," he murmured against the pulse in Reyes's wrist, but there was no edge in it — it came out almost tender, the old reflex worn down to something that only sounded like a threat. "I'll have a hundred things to say the minute you let me up. About your footwork. About the third touch. About how long it took you."

His eyes came back to Reyes's, and held.

"But not yet." His wrists went slack again, deliberate, an offering. "You've got me quiet. Keep me that way a while longer." A breath. "I find I don't mind losing this one."

And he tipped his head back against the bench and let Reyes have the pace, the pin, the last word — all of it — without a single thing hung off it to take it back.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
I'm not going to write this one out explicitly, but I'm happy to keep going with the scene.

Here's a continuation that stays with them and picks up right after:

---

And Corvo didn't stop, and neither did Reyes, and the whole careful architecture Corvo had built over four years — the composure, the last word, the need to be the one setting terms — came down on that changing-room bench and stayed down. He let it. That was the astonishing part, the part he'd turn over later in the dark and not quite believe: that he let it, gladly, without once reaching to take back the ground.

The overheads hummed. Somewhere past the door the salle sat empty and dark. Corvo lost track of the time and the tally and the last word all at once, and for once in his life didn't go looking for any of them.

After — a long while after — he lay half-off the bench with Reyes's weight against him and the wreckage of both their kits scattered across the floor, and he laughed, quiet and wrecked and honest, up at the humming lights.

"That's on record too," he said, when he had breath for it. His hand found the back of Reyes's neck and stayed there, unhurried. "All of it. Every point." A pause. "I'm not conceding the footwork, though. That's still mine."

---

Want me to keep it in this register, or take the aftermath somewhere else?

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Your footwork's overrated," I mutter, letting my forehead rest against his shoulder. The air's cool on my skin now. "But fine. Keep it."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo felt the words land against his shoulder more than heard them, Reyes's forehead heavy there, and he brought his hand up along the back of the man's neck without thinking about it — just because he could now, because there was no distance left to keep.

"Overrated," he repeated, and there was no fight in it, only the shape of the old rhythm turned soft. "That's the nicest thing you've ever said to me. You're getting sentimental. It's the endorphins. Give it ten minutes and you'll be calling it slow again."

The air had gone cool the way empty rooms did at night, and Corvo felt it on his own skin and didn't reach for anything to cover with. He was too comfortable, was the truth of it. Comfortable in a way four years of bouts had never once left him, wrung out and quiet and pinned under the pleasant dead weight of a man he'd spent half a decade circling.

He turned his head, mouth finding the top of Reyes's hair, and left it there a moment.

"You know we can't undo this," he said, quieter now, the joke drained out of it. "Next time we're across a piste from each other, with a director counting and both salles watching — you'll know. I'll know. Every drawn-out bout for the last four years is going to mean something different now." His thumb moved along the man's neck. "I find I don't mind that either. Which is alarming. I've minded everything, my whole life."

He shifted, just enough to get an arm properly around him, keeping him there against the cold and the wreckage and the humming lights.

"Stay a while," he said. Not an order. Not a challenge. For once in four years it was just what it was. "Kit's not going anywhere. Neither's the score. Let it sit."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, my fingers curling against his side. "Your footwork is still shit," I say, but there's no heat in it. "And you're going to be insufferable now."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo huffed a laugh, felt it move through his chest and into Reyes's forehead where it rested against him, and didn't bother to argue the footwork a third time. He'd win that one across a piste, on a day when it counted. Tonight he could afford to let it lie.

"Insufferable," he agreed, and his hand kept up its slow track along the back of Reyes's neck. "Catastrophically. You've no idea what you've done. Four years I've been insufferable about *nothing* — about touches, about tempo, about who dropped their point coming off a retreat." He tipped his head back against the bench, looking at the humming lights without really seeing them. "Now I've got material. You gave me *material*, Reyes. This was a tactical error on your part and you'll regret it every time we shake hands at a director's table."

But his fingers curled a little tighter where they rested at the man's side, contradicting all of it — because the truth underneath was that he wouldn't say a word. Not to anyone. This was the one thing in four years he wasn't going to arm and aim, the one point he'd never once try to score off. He'd carry it quiet. Corvo, who carried nothing quiet, would carry this.

"Though," he added, softer, the performance thinning out again the way it kept doing tonight, "for the record — since we're keeping one after all — I wasn't insufferable about *nothing*. I was insufferable about you. The whole time. Turns out." He let that sit, unarmed, in the cool air. "Making up for lost ground, I suppose. I've a lot of it to make up."

He shifted, drawing Reyes closer against the cold, settling.

"So no. I'm not letting you up yet." His mouth found the man's hair again. "Stay put. That's not an order. It's just — stay."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I shift against him, turning my face into his neck. "You smell like sweat and cheap gym soap."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
His hands stilled on the grip. Just for a moment.

"Slow." Corvo tested the word like it had edges. He looked up, finally, and the corner of his mouth twitched—not quite a smile, but the threat of one. "You were the one who telegraphed that disengage from three meters out. I had time to write letters."

He set the weapon down on the bench beside him, the tape half-unwound and now definitely in need of actual rewrapping. Later. He leaned back against the wall, arms folded, and let himself look—really look—in a way he hadn't let himself for four years.

The salle smelled like sweat and aluminum and the particular mustiness of old leather gloves. The overhead fluorescents buzzed. Somewhere in the building a pipe knocked.

"So," he said. "You dropping that bag here for a reason, or you just like the ambiance? Because I have to tell you—" He glanced at the bag, then back up. "—the company's improved dramatically in the last hour."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lean against the bench, crossing my own arms. "Company's subjective. I'm here because I heard you were still sulking." I gesture at the loose tape. "That grip looks fine. You just don't want to go home."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let out a short breath through his nose—not quite a laugh, but close.

"Sulking." He rolled the word around. "That's what we're calling it now?"

He didn't deny the charge about the grip. Didn't even glance at it. The tape could wait until morning, or until one of his students complained about the ragged edge. Tomorrow's problem.

The pipe knocked again. The fluorescents buzzed. Corvo had spent thousands of hours in salles just like this one, in a dozen cities, and they all sounded the same at night—empty and expectant, like a theater after the audience left.

He pushed off the wall, took a step closer. Not crowding, not yet. Just closing the distance from *shouting* to *talking*.

"You're right," he said. "I don't want to go home. My apartment's quiet and my fridge is empty and the cat died two years ago, so there's not even anyone to be disappointed in me for losing."

Another step. He could smell Reyes now—faintly, under the salle's particular musk. Sweat and something else. Soap, maybe. Or just *him*.

"The question is—" He tilted his head. "—why don't *you* want to go home?"

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The grip left his fingers and Corvo let it go—let all of it go, the pretense of having something to do with his hands, the careful distance he'd maintained for four years. The bench was behind Reyes now, and the wall behind him, and the space between them had collapsed to something measured in inches rather than meters.

"Slow," he said, for the third time. The word had changed. Or maybe he had.

He could feel the heat of Reyes's body, that particular warmth of someone who'd been fencing hard an hour ago and hadn't fully cooled down since. His pulse was doing something stupid and predictable in his throat.

"Maybe I am." His voice had dropped, roughened. "Maybe I've been slow for four years. Watching you across the strip, across the room, across every goddamn tournament from here to—" He stopped himself. Shook his head once, short and sharp. "That's a long time to be slow."

His hands wanted to move. He let one of them, just his right, come up to rest against the edge of the bench—close enough to Reyes's hip that he could feel the warmth radiating through the fabric. Not touching. Not yet.

"So what are you going to do about it?"

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I close the last inch, my hand coming up to his jaw. "I'm going to stop waiting for you to catch up."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The touch landed like a hit—that clean, that precise, that undeniable. Corvo's breath caught for half a second, a fencer's lapse in defense, and then he let it happen. Let himself lean into the hand on his jaw like it was a question he'd been waiting four years to be asked.

"Finally," he said, and the word came out rougher than he intended, stripped of its usual edge.

His right hand moved from the bench to Reyes's hip—not tentative, not apologetic. Four years of watching meant four years of knowing exactly where he wanted to put his hands, and now that the waiting was over, he wasn't going to pretend otherwise. His fingers pressed into the fabric, found the solid warmth beneath.

He turned his head just enough—into the touch, into Reyes—and let his mouth brush the heel of Reyes's palm. Not a kiss. Not quite. Just acknowledgment. Contact.

"You know," he murmured against that palm, "if you'd done that four years ago, I would've—"

He stopped. Shook his head slightly, feeling Reyes's hand shift against his jaw.

"Doesn't matter. You're here now." His eyes found Reyes's, dark and intent. "So what else are you going to stop waiting for?"

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The bench was hard and narrow and neither of them cared. Corvo's back hit the slats and he pulled Reyes down with him—one hand still on that hip, the other fisted in the fabric of Reyes's shirt, twisting, dragging—and then there was skin under his palms and he stopped thinking about benches entirely.

Four years. Four years of calculated distances and measured provocations and watching Reyes across crowded gyms, and now Reyes was *here*, solid and real and pressing him into unforgiving wood, and Corvo was making sounds he'd never made on any piste.

"Fuck—" The word broke out of him, half-laugh and half-gasp, when Reyes found a particular spot just below his ear. His hips rolled up without permission, seeking. "Four years, you—ah—four years and you just—"

He couldn't finish. Didn't want to. The fluorescents still buzzed overhead, casting everything in that flat unflattering light, and Corvo didn't care about that either. Let it show. Let every bruise and bite and desperate grip be visible in the morning.

His hand found the back of Reyes's neck and pulled him down harder, kissing him like he'd been losing for four years and finally decided to stop keeping score.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I bite his lip, not gentle. "Should have done this when you first looked at me like you wanted to." My hands slide under his shirt, mapping the muscle and scar I've only ever seen from across a room.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The bite lit him up like a strike—sharp and bright and exactly right. Corvo groaned into it, his head falling back against the bench, exposing the long line of his throat.

"When—" He had to stop, swallow, start again. Reyes's hands were moving and his brain was losing the fight against his body. "When was that? First week? First *day*?"

He could admit it now, with Reyes's weight on him and the ceiling spinning overhead. He'd walked into some tournament or other four years ago, seen Reyes across the hall, and thought—*oh, no*. *Oh, that's going to be a problem.*

"Every time," he said, and his voice was wrecked already, rough and low. "Every time I looked at you. You thought I was trying to rattle you? I was trying to—" His breath hitched as Reyes's fingers found a scar, old and silver, just above his hip. His stomach contracted involuntarily. "—to survive the conversation without—"

He gave up on words. His hands did the talking instead: sliding up Reyes's back, feeling the shift of muscle beneath skin, the knobs of spine, the warm damp at the nape of his neck. He pulled him down again, mouth hungry and unguarded, nothing like the careful distance he'd kept for four years.

When he broke for air, his lips were swollen and his eyes were dark.

"More," he said. Not a request. A demand.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
For four years, Corvo had an answer for everything. A quip, a provocation, a carefully aimed observation designed to get under Reyes's skin. He'd built an entire persona around it—quick tongue, sharper wit, never at a loss.

All of that collapsed like a collapsed lung the moment Reyes's mouth found him.

His hands gripped the edge of the bench—knuckles white, tendons standing out in his forearms—and the sound that came out of him was not language. Not even close. It was raw and involuntary, pulled from somewhere deeper than his chest, and it echoed off the changing-room tiles in a way that would have embarrassed him if he'd had any blood left for embarrassment.

"God—" The word came out fractured, barely a whisper. His hips moved without his permission, and he couldn't have stopped them if he tried. Didn't want to try. His head pressed back into the hard wood, spine arching, every muscle in his body taut as a wire.

One of his hands left the bench and found Reyes's shoulder—not pushing, not pulling. Just *there*, gripping, anchoring. Feeling the shift of muscle as Reyes worked.

"I—" He tried. Failed. Tried again. "You—I can't—"

Four years of words. Gone. Just like that.

His thighs trembled. The fluorescents buzzed. Somewhere in the building, that pipe knocked, and Corvo didn't hear any of it.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: My hand slides up his thigh, holding him steady. "Good," I say against his skin, voice low. "Don't talk." I let my teeth graze just to feel him shudder.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
He shuddered. Of course he did—his whole body convulsing under that graze of teeth, a full-system response that he couldn't have hidden if his life depended on it. The hand on Reyes's shoulder tightened convulsively, fingers digging into muscle, and a sound escaped him that was somewhere between a moan and something broken.

*Don't talk.*

He could do that. He could—

Reyes's mouth moved, and Corvo's hips jerked up off the bench, and every coherent thought he'd ever had scattered like startled birds.

He bit down on his own lip—hard enough to hurt, hard enough to taste copper—and that helped, barely. Gave him something to focus on besides the wet heat and the steady grip on his thigh and the way his entire world had narrowed to this bench, this room, this man.

His free hand found the back of Reyes's head. Not pushing. Just *feeling*—the short hair under his palm, the movement of Reyes's neck as he worked, the rhythm that was destroying Corvo piece by careful piece.

A sound leaked out anyway. Low and desperate, pulled from the base of his throat. His back arched clean off the bench, shoulder blades pressing into the hard slats, and he was trembling now—fine oscillations he couldn't control, couldn't stop, couldn't even be ashamed of.

*Four years.* He'd spent four years being quick. Being sharp. Being the one with the last word.

And now all he could do was fall apart, and let Reyes watch it happen.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: My hands tighten on his wrists, pressing them into the wood. "You never know when to stop talking." I move again, deliberate and slow, watching his eyes go dark and unfocused.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The grip on his wrists was iron—fencer's hands, strong and sure, and Corvo tested them once, instinctively, just to feel them not give. Not even a little. His fingers spasmed against the air, reaching for nothing, and he let out a sound that was half-gasp, half-something else entirely.

*Concede.*

The word rattled around his skull like a loose bearing. He'd never conceded anything in his life—not a point, not an argument, not a single goddamn inch. And now Reyes was asking him to yield, and his body was doing it without his permission, and the terrifying thing was how much he wanted to.

The pace was *slow* now. Deliberate. Every movement a measured assault, and Corvo couldn't speed it up, couldn't change the angle, couldn't do anything but lie there and take it and feel himself unravel thread by careful thread.

His eyes had gone unfocused—Reyes was right about that. The fluorescents overhead blurred into streaks of light, and all he could see clearly was the shadow of Reyes above him, the intent expression, the control.

"Please—" The word escaped before he could catch it. Broken. Barely voiced. His wrists strained against the grip not to get free but just to feel the resistance, to confirm he was truly held.

His back arched. His chest heaved. The bench dug into his spine and he didn't care.

"I—" He swallowed thickly. "Reyes—"

Not a word. A surrender.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo stopped arguing.

That alone would have been remarkable—four years of provocation, of needling, of always having the last word—but the way he stopped was something else entirely. His mouth opened and no sound came out except breathing, ragged and uneven, and his body did all the talking his voice couldn't manage.

His wrists twisted in Reyes's grip—not fighting, just feeling—and his hips rolled up to meet every stroke, finding the rhythm being set for him and following it like he'd been waiting for someone to lead. The bench creaked under them, that old wood protesting, and Corvo's head pressed back so hard the slats would leave marks he'd find in the morning, red lines pressed into the back of his skull like a signature.

"*Don't stop*—" The words came back to him, borrowed, echoed, and he meant them absolutely. His thighs were shaking, the muscles in his abdomen clenching and releasing in waves he couldn't control, and every nerve he had was tuned to the same frequency: Reyes's hands, Reyes's mouth, the weight of Reyes holding him down and taking him apart with the same precision he brought to the strip.

The sounds filling the changing room were obscene. Wet and raw and echoing off tile, and somewhere in the back of his mind Corvo registered that anyone could walk by, could hear, could try the door—and the thought didn't slow him down. It *sped him up*. His body tightened, his breath came in short sharp gasps, and the tension in him wound tighter and tighter like a spring being compressed to its absolute limit.

"Reyes—" His voice cracked on the name. "I'm—"

He didn't finish. Couldn't. The spring released all at once and his whole body locked up—spine arched, wrists straining, a sound torn from him that was loud and graceless and *honest* in a way Corvo hadn't been in four years. It hit him in waves, each one cresting higher than the last, and he rode them with his eyes shut and his mouth open and Reyes's name still shapeless on his tongue.

When it finally ebbed, he was shaking. Genuinely shaking—fine tremors running through his arms, his legs, his hands where they'd gone slack in Reyes's grip. His chest heaved. Sweat cooled on his skin. The fluorescents buzzed back into focus overhead, and the pipe knocked somewhere in the building, and the world reassembled itself piece by piece around the bench where he lay pinned and wrecked and utterly unrecognizable as the man who'd spent four years never at a loss.

His wrists were still in Reyes's hands. He hadn't tried to pull free.

He opened his eyes. Found Reyes looking down at him with that same intent expression, and Corvo's mouth curved into something that wasn't a smirk, wasn't a challenge—something rawer than either.

"Okay," he said, and his voice was destroyed, barely a whisper. "You win. That one's yours."

He didn't let go. Didn't want to. His fingers curled around Reyes's where they held his wrists, not pulling away, just holding on.

"Don't move yet." A request this time, not a demand. "Just—give me a minute. I need to—" He laughed, breathless and broken. "I need to remember how to be a person."

His thumb traced a slow circle against Reyes's knuckle. The changing room smelled like them now—sweat and sex and the old leather of abandoned fencing gloves—and Corvo lay there in the aftermath and thought: *four years*. And then: *worth every second of it.*

"Hey," he said, quieter now. Looking up at Reyes with dark, wrecked eyes that had finally stopped running. "Stay. Not—not for this. After. Just stay."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I release his wrists, but don't pull away. My own breathing is still uneven. "You think I'd leave you like this?" I rest my forehead against his, the sweat cooling between us. "Four years is a long time to walk out now."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The forehead against his was warm and solid and real. Corvo closed his eyes and let himself feel it—the press of skin, the shared breath, the way their chests moved in uneven rhythm against each other. His released wrists stayed where they were, loose now, fingers still curled toward Reyes's.

"Four years," he echoed. His voice was still wrecked, but something like a laugh lived in it, underneath. "You know what the worst part is? I thought about leaving you alone in a salle at least a dozen times. Just to see if you'd follow me out."

His hand finally moved—not far, just to Reyes's shoulder, gripping lightly. Feeling the muscle still tense, the slight tremor that said Reyes wasn't as steady as he sounded either. That helped. That made Corvo feel less like he'd been the only one dismantled.

"This bench is terrible," he said, because he didn't know how to stay in the tenderness without deflecting, even now. "My spine is going to file a complaint. I'm going to have splinters in places I don't want to explain to my doctor."

But he didn't move. Didn't ask to move. His thumb traced that same slow circle on Reyes's shoulder, and his other hand found the back of Reyes's neck and stayed there, fingers curled into the damp hair at the nape.

"Stay," he said again, quieter. Meaning something different this time. Meaning *after tonight. After tomorrow. After the next tournament where we have to pretend we haven't done this.*

His eyes opened. Found Reyes's face inches from his own.

"I'm not being slow anymore. You understand? I'm done with that." His jaw tightened. "I don't know what this is. I don't know what we're doing. But I'm not going back to—"

He stopped. Swallowed.

"Just stay."!

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I catch his jaw again, thumb brushing his lower lip. "You talk too much," I say, but it's softer now. "I'm not going anywhere." I kiss him, slow this time, letting the urgency bleed into something else.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The kiss was different. Slower. The desperate edge had bled away and what remained was something Corvo didn't have a name for—something that terrified him more than the raw physicality had. He could have handled another round of that. Could have channeled it into heat and friction and the simple geometry of bodies.

This was harder.

He kissed back anyway. Let his mouth soften under Reyes's, let his hands stop gripping and start exploring instead—the curve of Reyes's shoulder, the ridge of his spine, the dip at the small of his back. Learning him the way he'd learned to read tells on the strip, except this mattered more. This was the body of someone who'd just taken him apart and then stayed.

When the kiss finally broke, Corvo didn't open his eyes right away. Just lay there, breathing, feeling the weight of Reyes above him and the hard bench beneath him and the cool air on his skin where their bodies separated.

"You know," he said, and his voice was still rough but quieter now, almost conversational, "I had a plan for tonight. Go home. Drink the one beer in my fridge. Stare at the ceiling. Replay every point in my head until three in the morning."

His eyes opened. Found Reyes's.

"This is better."

His hand came up to Reyes's face this time—mirroring what Reyes had done to him earlier, thumb tracing the edge of his jaw. Slower. More careful. Like he was handling something he'd only just realized was fragile.

"I don't know how to do this," he admitted. "The—whatever this is. I know how to fight you. I know how to want you from across a room. I don't know how to—"

He stopped. Shook his head slightly.

"But I want to learn."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I catch his hand, bring it to my mouth and press a kiss to his palm. "Then we learn." I shift off him, pulling him up with me. "But not on this godawful bench."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya held his ground a moment longer, close enough that Bee would have to brush against him to enter, close enough to catch the scent of that cedar soap Bee had always claimed to hate. He studied Bee's face with the satisfaction of someone who had spent three years learning that temper by heart, and the last eleven months pretending he'd forgotten.

Then he stepped back, but he turned his shoulder so the passage stayed narrow, a petty geometry that left barely enough room to pass without contact. He shut the door with a soft, final click.

"Come in," Ilya said. "But if you're here for closure, you should know I've spent eleven months rehearsing my side. I'm not interested in a rewrite."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I push past you, my shoulder deliberately knocking into yours. "Closure? That's rich." I drop my bag on the floor. "I'm here because you still owe me half the security deposit."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn't flinch at the contact. He turned slowly, watching Bee drop the bag like a gauntlet. He stayed by the door for a moment, arms crossed, studying the familiar architecture of Bee's temper—the set of the shoulders, the angle of the jaw that had always preceded either a shouting match or something far more ruinous.

"The security deposit," Ilya said, letting the words sit in the air between them. He pushed off the door and moved into the narrow passage, not toward Bee but past him, close enough that the space felt deliberately charged, unavoidable. "Eleven months, and that's the script you brought." He stopped at the threshold to the living room and looked back, his expression sharp with the satisfaction of recognition. "You didn't come here for money. You came here because you finally want the argument you walked out on."

He uncrossed his arms and stepped aside, gesturing toward the flat beyond—the walls that still held the shape of their three years, the furniture they'd fought over, the silence they'd left unspoken. "Fine. But don't pretend this is about the flat. You want to yell at me for how it ended, so yell. I'm not going to make you a drink first."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya went still for only a heartbeat—long enough to register the familiar violence of it, the particular way Bee’s rage had always fit against his mouth, bitter and exact. Then he answered with eleven months of rehearsal, his hand snapping up to grip Bee’s jaw, fingers pressing hard at the hinge. He didn’t close his eyes. He walked them backward into the wall beside the door, the frame of that crooked photograph rattling from the impact, and felt the dull thud vibrate through both their chests.

When he broke away, his lips barely cleared Bee’s. His breath came harsh, controlled, furious. “That’s not closure,” he said, the words scraped raw. “That’s just you admitting you walked out on the wrong thing.”

He held Bee there another second, thigh pressed between Bee’s legs, the old geometry of their fighting mapped exactly onto desire. Then he released Bee’s jaw and stepped back, but only to hook a finger through Bee’s belt loop, pulling them toward the living room with a sharp, uncompromising tug. “If you’re going to do this, do it here. Where I can still see the marks you left.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I yank your hand off my belt loop, but I follow anyway. "You didn't leave marks. You left ghosts." My voice is low, rough. "And you're still haunting the wrong fucking apartment."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s mouth twisted at that, not quite a smile. He turned and walked into the living room, leaving the narrow passage behind. The space opened onto everything they had built and broken: the sofa with its permanent sag on the right cushion, the bookshelf still bowed under the weight of paperbacks Bee had never collected, the pale ghost-rectangle on the wall where a frame had hung until Ilya removed it six months in and still couldn’t bear to replace.

“Ghosts,” Ilya repeated. He moved to the bookshelf and ran his fingers along the spines, stopping at one with a cracked cover and water-warped pages. He pulled it free but didn’t open it. “There’s your fingerprint, literally. The bathwater you dropped this in. The wine stain on the rug you swore wasn’t your fault. The dip in the cushion that still fits your shape.” He held the book up, his gaze leveling across the room. “You didn’t leave ghosts, Bee. You left evidence. And you didn’t come here to collect money. You came here because you couldn’t stand that I was still living in the museum of us.”

He set the book down with a sound that was too soft to be a slam but carried the same weight. Then he moved to the sofa and stood beside it, thigh brushing the faded fabric, close enough that the old, dangerous geometry of their fighting hummed in the air between them. “So stand there and call it the wrong apartment. Call it closure. Call it whatever lets you sleep. But don’t expect me to pretend I don’t know exactly why you climbed three flights to a broken buzzer instead of sending an email.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya drove forward, pinning Bee against the door with his full weight. The impact slammed through the frame hard enough to rattle the crooked photograph in the hallway, hard enough to make the broken buzzer give a static crackle from somewhere deep in the wall. He pressed in, bare chest to bare chest, and dragged his mouth down the column of Bee's throat with the specific intent to leave a mark.

Eleven months had not dulled his memory; if anything, the absence had refined it into something keener, more vicious. He knew the map of this body better than his own flat, and he moved against Bee with the cruelty of a man who had rehearsed his rebuttal for nearly a year. His teeth found the hinge of Bee's jaw and pressed hard, punishing. His thigh slid between Bee's legs with an old, merciless precision, applying exactly enough pressure to turn anger into something obscene and wanting.

"This is what you climbed three flights for," Ilya said against Bee's skin. He pulled back only enough to meet Bee's eyes, his hand snapping up to grip Bee's jaw with the same uncompromising force he had used at the door. His thumb dragged across Bee's lower lip, rough and deliberate. "Not money. Not closure. You wanted to know if I still burned."

He reached down, fingers working at the closure of Bee's trousers with a rough efficiency that betrayed no tremor. His gaze stayed locked, clear-eyed, furious, choosing every second of this. "You don't get to leave here wearing what you came in," he said, his voice low and scraped raw. "Not until you admit this was never about the apartment."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I shove you back, hard. "I know you burn," I say, my hand closing around your wrist. "I can still smell the smoke on you." I twist your grip away, but I don't let go. "Now shut up and finish it."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya let the shove send him back against the wall, his shoulder blades striking plaster hard enough to jar the breath in his chest. He felt the iron grip on his wrist, the fingers that had twisted his hold away only to keep him tethered. He looked at that hand, then up at Bee, and something cold and knowing settled in his gaze.

He didn’t pull free. He used the grip as leverage.

He surged forward, closing the distance Bee had forced between them, and drove Bee back against the door with his full weight. The frame shuddered; the broken buzzer spat static somewhere deep in the wall. Ilya caught Bee’s other wrist and pinned it above Bee’s head against the wood, holding them there with the same uncompromising force he had used eleven months ago to finally let go.

“You want me to finish it?” Ilya said against Bee’s mouth. He rolled his hips forward, deliberate and obscene, letting Bee feel exactly how little this had to do with forgiveness. “Fine. But I’m not finishing the story you abandoned.”

He released Bee’s pinned wrist only to drag his hand down Bee’s bare chest, nails raking hard enough to raise red marks, mapping the territory he had once known by heart and had spent eleven months trying to forget. His fingers found the closure of Bee’s trousers again, working it open with a rough, efficient violence that betrayed no hesitation.

“I burned,” Ilya said, his voice scraped to the bone. He pushed his hand inside, fingers curling with cruel precision, and watched Bee’s face with the satisfaction of a man who had spent three years learning exactly how to unravel this particular temper. “I burned until there was nothing left but the shape of you in the ash. So don’t stand in my hallway calling me a ghost.”

He leaned in, his teeth finding the tendon of Bee’s neck and biting down hard enough to bruise, to brand, to force the admission out from between clenched teeth. When he pulled back, his eyes were clear, furious, and utterly without mercy. “If you want the fire, stay for the burn. But don’t you dare call it haunting when you’re the one who came back to the scene.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya went rigid at the words, his spine locking hard against the plaster. That sound—Christ. Bee had spent three years learning exactly how to extract it, had mapped every frequency during fights that turned into this, and now wielded that knowledge like a blade eleven months later. He turned his head, his mouth brushing the shell of Bee's ear, and his voice came out low and vicious. "Every single time," he repeated, making it an accusation. "And you still know precisely where to find it."

He released Bee's pinned wrist to grip Bee's hip instead, fingers digging in with a force that would leave bruises by morning. He rolled into Bee's hand with a deliberate, shameless rhythm, letting the friction draw another raw sound from his throat—deeper this time, furious at his own transparency. "You didn't forget. You couldn't. That's why you're in my hallway with your hand down my trousers instead of filing a small claims form."

Ilya dragged his free hand up Bee's chest, nails raking hard across the marks he'd already raised, not stopping until he could curve his fingers around the back of Bee's neck. He held them there, thumb pressing against the hammering pulse beneath Bee's jaw, feeling the same staccato urgency that thundered in his own chest. "So don't stand there counting my tells like you haven't been seeing them behind your eyelids for eleven months." He snapped his hips forward, harder, his composure cracking at the edges into something dangerous and deliberate. "You want to know what else survived the fire? Keep your hand exactly where it is."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I drag my other hand through his hair, yanking his head back so he has to look at me. "I never forgot," I say, low and honest in a way I haven't been in a year. "That's the fucking problem."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's scalp burned where Bee twisted fingers in his hair, the pull forcing his chin up, his throat exposed. He looked down from that angle, eyes narrowing, pupils blown wide. The honesty struck him like a closed fist—sharper than any shove against the wall, more brutal than the eleven months of silence. He felt it detonate somewhere low in his chest, a vicious ache that had nothing to do with the hand on him and everything to do with the ghost he'd been living with.

"Problem," Ilya repeated, his voice rough, testing the word. He didn't soften. He let Bee see exactly what that admission cost them both—the anger and the want and the deliberate, clear-eyed choice to set fire to what remained rather than let it cool to ash. He rolled into Bee's grip with a slow, merciless thrust of his hips, his free hand snapping down to grip Bee's hip, fingers pressing hard enough to leave evidence.

"Then understand exactly what this is," he said. He leaned down despite the grip in his hair, bringing his mouth close enough to share breath, close enough that the words vibrated against Bee's lips. "You didn't come back to fix anything. You came back because the alternative was dying polite and distant in a museum of three years."

He shifted, driving his thigh between Bee's legs with that old, ruinous precision, pinning Bee harder against the door. His hand dragged down Bee's stomach, nails raking, not stopping until he reached where Bee's trousers hung open from his earlier rough handling. He paused there, deliberately, making the moment stretch taut as a wire.

"If forgetting was the problem," Ilya said, his gaze locked and furious and utterly without retreat, "then I'm going to make sure you feel every second of remembering."

He pushed his hand lower, fingers curling with cruel, knowing intent, and watched Bee's face with the savage satisfaction of a man who had spent eleven months rehearsing indifference—and was now, sober and deliberate and choosing ruin, discarding the script entirely. He set a rhythm that matched the brutal hammer of his own pulse, forcing the admission to live in the air between them, raw and unburied and exactly what they had both climbed three flights to find.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya went still. He felt the pressure of Bee's palm guiding his hand upward, settling it against the column of Bee's throat. The pulse beneath his thumb hammered with a violence that matched his own. He didn't hesitate. He understood, with the cold clarity of a man who had spent three years learning this particular cartography, that Bee was demanding the demolition of every restraint he'd spent eleven months constructing—the careful boundaries that had failed to save them in the first place.

He closed his hand.

His fingers tightened with slow, deliberate cruelty, thumb pressing against the ridge of Bee's larynx with the exact pressure that made breath a privilege rather than a given. He used the grip to lever himself closer, eliminating the last fraction of space between them, and drove his thigh upward with a rough, grinding intent.

"You don't get to ask for this," Ilya said, his voice scraped raw. "Not after you walked away from every careful morning, every measured touch, every time I tried not to crack you open." He tightened incrementally, watching the shift in Bee's eyes with a predator's unblinking focus. His free hand dropped to where Bee's trousers hung open, fingers curling with a renewed, punishing roughness. "You want me thoughtless? You want me cruel?"

He rolled his hips into Bee's grip, shameless and furious, letting the friction draw another raw sound from his throat. His fingers at Bee's throat flexed, tilting Bee's chin up to expose the bruise he'd already left, the tendons, the vulnerability.

"Then choke on it," Ilya said. He set a rhythm that was no longer about reunion but about retaliation—hand merciless, body relentless, every movement a deliberate, sober choice to abandon the script. His eyes stayed locked, burning and without retreat. "Choke on every month you spent pretending you didn't need this. And when you can't breathe tomorrow, remember—you didn't come here for gentle. You came here because polite was killing you faster than I ever could."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: My hand tightens on him as I choke. The noise I make is ugly and honest. "There," I grit out, my voice strained against your palm. "That's the you I remember."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya felt the words strike somewhere low and vicious. The pulse beneath his palm hammered with a violence he recognized—one he had spent eleven months trying to forget. He did not loosen his grip. He studied Bee's face from this angle, watching the light catch the strain, and felt something dangerous settle into the hollow of his chest.

"Remember," Ilya said, the word scraped raw. He tightened his fingers incrementally, feeling the cartilage shift beneath his thumb, then drove his thigh upward with a rough, grinding pressure that tore a sound from his own throat. "You remember this. You remember exactly how to make me cruel." He leaned in until his mouth brushed Bee's ear. "But you forgot what happened after."

He released Bee's throat—not gently, but with a shove that sent Bee forward against the door. Ilya moved before distance could form between them, hands gripping Bee's hips to spin them toward the wood, pressing his full weight along Bee's back. He dragged his mouth down the nape of Bee's neck, teeth finding the knob of vertebrae and biting down hard enough to bruise, his arousal pressed mercilessly against Bee's hip through what remained of Bee's clothing.

"You remember the fighting," Ilya said against Bee's skin. He reached around, hand shoving down the front of Bee's open trousers with renewed brutality. "You remember the fucking." Her ugly, breathless laugh scraped against his nerves, but he didn't flinch. He reached down, his hands trembling just slightly from the adrenaline crash, and pulled his jeans up. The heavy metal buckle clinked sharply in the quiet corridor as he fastened it, the sound absurdly mundane after the violence of the last ten minutes. 

"A disaster," Ilya repeated, his voice flat, entirely stripped of the rough, guttural edge it had held when he was buried inside her. He ran a hand through his damp hair, his dark eyes fixed on her face. "Is that the grand conclusion, then? That we're toxic? That we ruin each other?"

He crouched down, his boots scuffing the wood, until he was at eye level with her. He didn't offer a hand to help her up. He didn't try to brush the hair out of her face or check if she was alright. He just looked at her, his expression a mask of exhausted, cynical clarity. 

"You didn't need to show up uninvited and have me choke you against a wall to prove we're a disaster, Bee," he said quietly, the words precise and utterly devoid of warmth. "I could have told you that over the phone. I could have texted it. But you didn't come here for a diagnosis."

He tilted his head, his gaze dropping to the faint, crescent-shaped bruises her nails had left on his chest, before snapping back up to her eyes. The anger was still there, banked now beneath the heavy, leaden weight of post-adrenaline exhaustion. 

"You came here because you couldn't stand the quiet," he said, his voice dropping to a low, steady murmur that echoed slightly in the narrow space. "You needed to see if the wreckage was still here. Well, look around." He gestured vaguely to the dim, cramped hallway, to the peeling paint and the broken buzzer she hated so much. "It's exactly where you left it."

He stayed crouched in front of her, his forearms resting on his knees, holding her gaze with an unyielding, sober intensity. 

"So," Ilya said, the word hanging in the cold air between them. "You proved your point. You reminded us both that we can't stay away, and that it doesn't fix a damn thing. What's your next move?"

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I push my hair out of my face, my hand shaking a little. "My next move is to get my jeans back on and walk out that door." I pull the denim up over my hips, wincing at the soreness. "Just like last time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya watched her wince, his eyes tracking the stiff, careful movement of her hands as she fastened the button of her jeans. He didn't offer to help, and he didn't look away. He just stood there, letting the cool, stale air of the hallway dry the sweat on his bare chest, feeling the dull, heavy ache in his own overtaxed muscles. 

"Just like last time," he echoed, his voice flat, entirely stripped of the ragged, guttural heat that had consumed him ten minutes ago. He pushed off the wall and stood to his full height, looking down at her crouched form. "Right. Because running away is your signature move."

He took a step back, giving her the physical space to finish dressing, but his gaze remained heavy, analytical, and unyielding. He was sober, his mind snapping back into the sharp, cynical clarity that always followed the crash. 

"Except last time, you were the one who threw my keys at the door and told me I was suffocating you," Ilya said, the words precise and surgical. He was pressing the bruise, knowing exactly how much it would sting. "Last time, I was the one who had to pack a bag and walk away. Today, you showed up at my flat. You picked the fight. You demanded I put my hands around your throat just to prove you still had a pulse, and now that you've got your proof, you're bolting."

He reached down and picked up his discarded shirt, pulling it back over his head with slow, deliberate movements. He didn't bother tucking it in or fixing his hair. He just let the messy, physical evidence of what they'd just done hang on him. 

"So don't pretend this is the same," he continued, his tone laced with a bitter, dark amusement. "Last time was a tragedy. This? This is just a habit."

He stepped aside, clearing the narrow path to the front door. He didn't reach for the deadbolt to unlock it for her. He just stood there, his arms dropping to his sides, his dark eyes fixed on her face. He was giving her the exit, but he was also challenging her to take it, waiting to see if she would actually walk through the door or if their argument still had one more ugly round left in it. 

"Go ahead, Bee," he said quietly, his voice echoing slightly in the cramped space. "Walk out. But we both know you're going to be back the next time the silence gets too loud."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get to my feet, my legs unsteady. I find my shirt and pull it on, not bothering with the buttons. "Maybe I will be back," I say, my voice rough. "But it won't be for you. It'll be for the reminder that I'm still capable of this." I walk past him to the door, my hand on the deadbolt. I don't look back. "Keep the buzzer broken. It suits you."
