rung_labels.evidence: He kissed her back with the exact same bruising, combative force, his mouth moving against hers in a rhythm that was far more fight than affection

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: His hands dropped to the waistband of her jeans, fingers working the button and zipper

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: He drove into her, a single, deep thrust that was entirely devoid of gentleness, burying himself to the hilt

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: His long fingers wrapped around the column of her throat, his thumb resting against the frantic, fluttering beat of her pulse. He didn't squeeze, not yet. He just let the weight of his hand settle there, a heavy, undeniable threat.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: His hips snapped forward in a relentless, punishing cadence, the heavy, wet slap of their bodies colliding echoing off the narrow walls. He drove into her with a brutal, single-minded focus, burying himself as deep as he could go

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's mouth twitched. He set the grip down and finally looked up, the overhead lights catching the silver threading through his dark hair.

"Slow," he repeated, tasting the word. "You say that like it's an insult and not just a description of someone who lets you come to him."

He rose from the bench in a single fluid motion, rolling his shoulder the way he always did after a bout, and crossed to where his own bag sat by the strip.

"For the record, the third was a corps-à-corps you initiated. I had right of way."

His back was to Reyes now, and his voice had dropped half a register without him seeming to notice.

"You're welcome for not bringing it up with the referee."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lean against the wall, arms crossed. "Right of way, maybe. But you were the one who hesitated." I watch his back. "And you didn't bring it up because you knew it was messy."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo turned around, slow, the way he turned around on the strip when he was measuring distance.

"Messy," he agreed. His gaze traveled from Reyes's crossed arms to his face, unhurried. "I don't like messy. You know that."

He took a step closer. Just one.

"But you were also the one who stayed to argue about it instead of heading to the locker room with your students."

Another step. The overhead lights were doing something inconvenient to the line of Reyes's jaw, and Corvo was not going to be the kind of man who pretended not to notice that.

"So either you wanted the last word," he said, voice low enough now that it was clearly not for a salle that had emptied an hour ago, "or you wanted to see what I'd do if you pushed."

He stopped just inside Reyes's space. Not touching. Not yet.

"Which was it?"

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's fingers stayed where the grip had been for a beat too long. Then he let them close on nothing.

"Slow," he said, and the word came out different this time — less like an accusation, more like he was turning it over in his mouth to see what was underneath it.

He didn't step back either. If anything, the removal of the grip had narrowed the distance between them to something that couldn't be blamed on the strip or the bout or the hour. His gaze flicked down to Reyes's hands, then back up.

"That's interesting," he murmured. "Because earlier you were telling me to be faster. And now you're telling me I've been slow. Make up your mind."

His hand came up — not to Reyes, not yet, but to the wall beside his head, palm flat, forearm close enough that Reyes would have been able to feel the warmth off his skin if he'd shifted an inch.

"Or," Corvo said, quieter, "don't. I like watching you try to box me in with the wrong words."

He tilted his head. The silver at his temples caught the light again.

"You still haven't answered my question."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I push off the wall, closing the last inch between us. "Maybe I wanted both." My hand finds the front of his jacket, grip tight. "You going to do something about it?"

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo looked down at the fist on his jacket, then back up. His expression didn't change — or rather, it changed in a way that only someone who'd spent four years across a strip from him would recognize: the slight settling of his jaw, the way his eyes went very still right before he committed to an attack.

"Both," he repeated, as if confirming a call. "Greedy."

He didn't move Reyes's hand. Instead he leaned into it, just slightly, the way he'd lean into a bind — testing whether the pressure would hold or give.

"You want to know what I'm going to do about it." His voice was low, almost conversational, which was worse than if he'd raised it. "I'm going to do exactly what I did on the strip. Wait for your shoulder to drop. Wait for you to overcommit."

His free hand came up — slowly, deliberately, the pace of a man who wanted there to be no misunderstanding — and settled over Reyes's knuckles where they gripped his jacket. Not pulling them away. Holding them in place.

"And then I'm going to take what you offered me," he said, "and make sure you remember that you did."

The overhead lights buzzed. The strip was ten feet away, abandoned, still scuffed from the bout.

Corvo's thumb shifted against Reyes's knuckles, just barely.

"Your move, instructor."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's laugh was short, bitten off against Reyes's mouth — the kind of sound he'd never have let out on the strip.

"Four years," he said, pulling back just far enough to breathe. His hair was wrecked and he hadn't noticed. "Four years of you calling my footwork a joke and it took you losing a bout to get you in here."

He had Reyes half-back onto the bench, one hand braced on the wood beside his hip, the other still working at the collar of the jacket Reyes had been wearing for some reason after their own — stubborn, proprietary, unwilling to be the first one stripped.

"Let me — " Corvo muttered, fingers finding the fastener. "You always wear too many layers to train. It's a weakness. I've been telling you that for seasons."

His mouth found Reyes's throat, the hinge of his jaw, the corner where he'd nicked him earlier with the button and hadn't apologized for.

"And for the record," he added, low, between marks he was leaving with intent, "this is not slow."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I shove his shoulder, tipping us both off-balance until we're a tangle on the floor between the benches. "Shut up about the bout," I mutter, my hands already at his belt. "And it was still three-two."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's back hit the floor and he exhaled — half laugh, half something that wasn't, his head tipping back against the tile. His hand found the bench leg above him and held on, knuckles going white for a second before he remembered himself and made his grip relax.

"Three-two," he said, to the ceiling, "is a score you only got because your lateral was cleaner in the second period. I out-touched you. You know I out-touched you."

His hips shifted under Reyes's hands, not helping and not hindering, the way he shifted when he was trying to keep his distance on the strip and not quite managing it. His eyes had gone dark, the overhead lights catching the damp at his temples.

"And if you think I'm going to shut up about the bout," he added, voice gone rough-edged, "you haven't been paying attention for four years."

He let go of the bench leg. His hand came up to Reyes's jaw — not guiding, not pushing, just there, the way a guard sits in a bind, waiting for the exchange to begin.

"You can have the score," he said, quieter, his thumb brushing the corner of Reyes's mouth. "I'm about to take something that counts for more."

His knee drew up beside Reyes's hip, opening the tangle the least possible amount, and he watched his rival's face with the same focus he'd given the strip an hour ago.

"Come on, then. Show me what you do when you actually win."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's hand found Reyes's hair and held on.

Not pulling. Not guiding. Just gripping, the way a man grips when he's lost the line and is trying to find it again by feel. His breath left him in a sound he would have denied making under oath, and his head tipped back against the bench, throat exposed, the tendons standing out in the harsh overhead light.

"Christ," he said, to no one.

The silver at his temples had gone damp. His hips shifted once — a betrayal his body made without consulting him — and then he made himself still, because if there was one thing four years across a strip from a man like Reyes had taught him, it was that overcommitting cost you the exchange.

He lasted about ten seconds before his fingers tightened in Reyes's hair and his other hand came down hard on the bench seat.

"Four years," he said again, and his voice had gone somewhere he didn't recognize it. "Four years you've been trying to get under my guard. And this is — this is how you —"

The sentence didn't finish. His back arched off the bench, the movement economical and entirely involuntary, the kind of commitment to an action he would have called premature on the strip.

He made himself breathe. In through the nose, out through the mouth — the cadence he used between touches when he was down a point and needed to reset.

"Still three-two in my head," he managed, and it was a lie, and his voice cracked halfway through it, and he didn't seem to care.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I laugh against his skin, the sound low and rough. "Liar." My fingers dig into his hip, holding him still. "You haven't thought about the score since we hit the floor."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's fingers tightened in Reyes's hair, a sharp involuntary pull that he couldn't quite catch and file away as deliberate.

"I'm — thinking about it," he managed, and his voice had gone ragged in a way he didn't bother trying to smooth over. "I'm thinking about it between — between every time you —"

He broke off, his jaw clenching, the tendons in his neck standing out. His hand came up from the bench seat and found Reyes's wrist where it held his hip, and for a second it looked like he might try to pry it loose — four years of muscle memory, four years of refusing to let a competitor pin him without a fight.

He didn't.

His grip on Reyes's wrist stayed where it was, but his thumb pressed against the pulse point, which was a different kind of acknowledgment entirely. His breath came out shaking.

"Fine," he said, to the ceiling, to the empty salle, to whatever gods watched fencers make idiots of themselves in their own changing rooms. "Fine. The score is gone. Are you happy."

His hips shifted under Reyes's hand — not breaking the hold, not testing it, just *moving*, in a way that was going to make the lie of his composure very obvious very quickly.

"You've been trying to get me to admit that for four years," he added, and his laugh was short and breathless and aimed mostly at himself. "Should've just — should've just done this from the start, would have saved us both the post-bout arguments about right of way."

His head tipped forward off the back of the bench, and he looked down at Reyes, hair fallen across his forehead, expression caught somewhere between a sneer and something much more honest than a sneer.

"Don't let go," he said, quieter, and his thumb was still pressed against Reyes's pulse, counting the beats. "Don't you dare let go."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo went still when his wrists hit the wood.

Not the calculated stillness of a fencer setting up for a parry — the other kind. The kind that happened when every planned response in a man's body was suddenly unavailable and he had to find a new one from scratch. His fingers curled against the bench, testing the hold, and then uncurled, because there was nothing to find.

"There he is," Corvo said, and his voice had gone rough at the edges, softer than he'd let it get all evening. "There's the fencer I've been trying to get on the strip for four years."

His chest rose and fell under Reyes, the rhythm uneven in a way his breathing had never been during the bout. His wrists stayed where they'd been put, which was the closest thing to surrender Corvo had ever made in his life and probably ever would. The tendons in his forearms stood out, the only thing in his body still trying to fight.

He watched Reyes from under the mess of his own hair. The overhead lights were unforgiving and he didn't look away from them. His pupils had blown wide, the dark of his iris almost gone, and his mouth was parted slightly — not a sneer, not the set line he wore on the strip, just his face, unguarded, in the way it probably hadn't been since he was twenty.

"Don't," he said, and the word came out broken in the middle, "don't you dare go gentle on me now. I'll know. I'll know you went easy and I'll never let you hear the end of it."

His head tipped back against the bench. His throat worked.

"You've got me," he said, to the ceiling, to the empty salle, to no one in particular, and the words cost him something he couldn't quite name. His hand twitched in Reyes's grip — not a pull, not a fight, just his body registering what his mouth had already admitted.

"Four years," he murmured, and his ankle hooked behind Reyes's calf, the only anchor he'd let himself have. "Four years and the only person who's ever pinned me is the one person I never wanted to lose to."

A breath. Two. His thumb pressed against Reyes's palm where it had him pinned, the only part of him still moving.

"So make it count," he said, quieter. "You waited long enough for it."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lean down, my mouth nearly at his ear. "Who said I was waiting?" Then I take him apart, piece by piece, exactly the way he asked for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
vo's laugh came out broken, somewhere between a gasp and something he'd deny making if anyone were still here to hear it.

"Waiting," he repeated, the word dragged out of him like a parry that had come a fraction of a second too late. "You — you absolute — "

His sentence didn't finish. Reyes had always been good at finding the line, and he'd just crossed it, and Corvo's back arched off the bench in a way that had nothing to do with footwork.

His wrists twisted in the grip — not to break it, not anymore, just to feel it, the way he'd test a blade's flex before a bout. Reyes held. Corvo's breath left him in a sound that was almost a laugh and almost not.

"Piece by piece," he managed, through his teeth. "That's what you said. Piece by piece." His head tipped back against the bench, throat working. "You're enjoying this. You've been enjoying this. I can tell because you — Christ — because you keep — "

His hand found Reyes's wrist in the grip, thumb pressing against the tendon there, not pulling, not fighting. Counting something. The overhead lights buzzed and the strip sat empty ten feet away and neither of them was thinking about the bout anymore.

"You're not — " Corvo said, and then stopped, because whatever he'd been about to say got lost somewhere between Reyes's mouth and his hip and the hand still pinning him to the bench. "You're not even being subtle about it. Four years and you've — you've been patient. Patient for this. That's — that's — "

His voice cracked on the word, and he didn't bother trying to cover it. His ankle tightened behind Reyes's calf. The silver at his temples was damp, his hair a ruin across the bench, and his face had gone open in a way he would have hated if he'd had any presence of mind left to hate it.

"I should've known," he said, quieter now, the words coming out of him like a man conceding a touch he couldn't argue. "I should've known it was going to be you. In the — the changing room after — after you — "

He gave up on sentences. His chest was heaving under Reyes, his fingers curled tight against the bench, and the only sound he was making was the in-out of his breath, ragged, nothing like the cadence he used between touches.

He didn't beg. He'd never beg. But his thumb on Reyes's wrist pressed harder, and his hips shifted once under the hand holding him, and the look he gave Reyes from under his ruined hair said what his mouth couldn't: *more*, and *don't stop*, and *I will never say either of those words out loud, so don't make me.*

"Four years," he murmured again, and his voice had gone somewhere small and honest. "Four years and you — and this is — "

The sentence ended in a sound he would absolutely deny making, his back off the bench, his grip on Reyes's wrist gone white-knuckled. The overhead lights buzzed. The strip sat empty. Somewhere in the building a door clicked shut.

Neither of them noticed.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's hand found Reyes's hair again and pulled, hard, and the sound that came out of him was not a word in any language.

He'd stopped trying to hold the line. He'd stopped trying to keep the cadence of his breath, stopped trying to keep his hips still under Reyes's hand, stopped trying to do anything except the one thing he'd been refusing to do for four years: let someone inside his guard without a parry ready. His wrists stayed where Reyes had pinned them because he had nothing left in him to fight with, and the only movement left in his body was the involuntary kind, the kind that didn't consult him first.

"Don't stop," he repeated, and his voice had gone somewhere he didn't recognize. Smaller. Younger. The voice of a man who'd never lost a touch he couldn't explain, never let anyone see him on the floor of a changing room with his wrists held and his hair in ruins. "Don't — Reyes. Reyes. *Don't stop.*"

The second time he said the name it came out broken in the middle, and he didn't try to repair it.

His back arched off the bench and his fingers went white on the wood and his ankle tightened behind Reyes's calf hard enough to leave a mark, and the sound he made when it broke over him was something he'd be furious about later — something ragged and bitten-off and too honest, the kind of sound a man made when he'd finally stopped fighting a bout he was going to lose anyway. He held on to Reyes's wrist and Reyes's hair and the bench leg above him and let it take him, and for three full seconds Corvo was not a fencer and not a rival and not an instructor, he was just a man on a bench in an empty salle, undone.

Then it passed.

His grip loosened on Reyes's wrist. His ankle unwound from behind Reyes's calf. His chest heaved once, twice, three times, the cadence coming back to him by degrees — in through the nose, out through the mouth, the reset between touches, except there was no bout to reset for and no touch coming and no one to fence except the man still on top of him.

He opened his eyes.

The overhead lights were still unforgiving. His hair was still a ruin across the bench. Reyes was still close enough that Corvo could feel the warmth off his skin, and his wrists were still pinned, and his face was doing something it never did on the strip: nothing. No sneer. No set jaw. No competitive edge. Just his face, post-exchange, the way it looked when a bout had actually gotten to him and he hadn't had time to rebuild it.

"Off," he said, finally, and his voice had come back rough-edged but mostly his. He tugged at Reyes's grip on his wrists, not seriously — the kind of tug that was really asking for a hand to help him sit up. "I'm not — I'm not going to lie on this bench all night. There are hygiene considerations."

He sat up slowly when Reyes let him, one hand braced on the wood, the other going to the back of his own neck as if he could feel the muscle memory of being held down still written there. He didn't look at Reyes for a long moment. He looked at the strip, abandoned, ten feet away, still scuffed from the bout. He looked at the grips on the floor. He looked at his own hands, which were shaking slightly, which he put in his lap to hide.

"That," he said, and stopped, and started again. "The second touch. In the second period. You had me. I was off-line and you had me and I knew it and you knew I knew it and that's why we ended up here instead of in the locker room. So. You can have that one. For free."

He glanced at Reyes sideways. The silver at his temples had gone damp and was drying in uneven patches. His mouth twitched.

"Three-two still stands," he added, and his voice had found its footing again, mostly, the old edge creeping back in. "But I'm granting you the moral. Off the record. Unrepeatable. If you tell anyone I conceded a touch in this changing room I'll deny it and I'll be more convincing than you."

He reached down and picked up the grip he'd been rewrapping when this whole thing had started. Turned it over in his hands. Set it down again without doing anything with it.

"Same time next Tuesday," he said, to the grip, to the bench, to anywhere except Reyes's face. "I'll be faster. You won't have to stay behind to argue."

A pause. His thumb ran over the leather of the grip, the same gesture he'd made on Reyes's knuckles twenty minutes and a lifetime ago.

"Bring a better lateral," he added, quieter, and the corner of his mouth did something that on anyone else would have been called a smile. "I want a closer match next time. Closer than three-two. Closer than tonight."

He stood, finally, and pulled on the jacket he'd let fall on the floor, and did up the fastenings with hands that were almost steady. He didn't look at Reyes again. He looked at the strip.

"You coming," he said, "or are you going to lie on my bench all night. There are hygiene considerations."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I push off the floor and grab my bag, my jacket still in a heap somewhere. "Three-two stands," I say, shouldering past him toward the door. "But you're buying the post-bout drinks. Hygiene considerations."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo watched him go, and the smirk that crossed his face was the real one — the one he'd never have let Reyes see across the strip.

"Post-bout drinks," he said, to the empty changing room, and then laughed once, short, at the ceiling. "Post-bout drinks. As if we needed a tradition to justify —"

He stopped. Picked up his own bag. Checked the floor for anything that needed picking up — grip, glove, the jacket Reyes had left in a heap by the second bench.

He picked the jacket up. Held it for a second. Then folded it, properly, the way he'd fold his own before a competition, and set it on top of Reyes's bag where he'd find it.

He locked the door behind him. The hallway was colder than the changing room and the lights were worse, and he could hear Reyes's footsteps two turns ahead, moving at the pace of a man who thought he was going to walk out of this building alone.

Corvo lengthened his stride to catch up. He didn't run. He'd never run.

"Loser buys," he said, falling into step beside Reyes, close enough that their shoulders brushed once in the narrow corridor. "By tradition. So you understand I'm conceding the score, not the argument. The argument you were wrong about. You're still wrong about right of way. You'll be wrong about it next Tuesday too."

He held the exterior door open with one hand, the night air coming in cold and smelling of the metro and someone's cigarette two streets over. He didn't gesture Reyes through. He just stood there, holding it, until Reyes had to pass close enough that Corvo could see the marks he'd left at the hinge of his jaw and the collar of his shirt and not pretend he hadn't.

"The place on Rue Lacuée," he said, once they were out on the pavement. "The one with the narrow bar. You know it." He shouldered his bag and set off in the direction he always set off, which happened to be the same direction Reyes's car was parked in. "They have a decent Malbec and they don't ask questions when two fencers walk in at eleven looking like they've been in a strip, which I am told we do."

He glanced sideways. Just once. The streetlight caught the silver at his temples again and Reyes's jacket was still in his bag, folded properly, and the bench was still warm behind them, and Corvo's thumb was still pressing against his own palm where he'd been pressing against Reyes's pulse.

"If you tell anyone I conceded a touch," he said, "I will end you. On the strip. In the second period. With a flèche you won't see coming."

He turned the corner. Kept walking.

"Coming," he added, without looking back, because Reyes had not yet moved, and because Corvo was not the kind of man who asked twice.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I fall into step beside him, my shoulder bumping his in the dark. "You already tried a flèche in the second period. It was slow." I nod toward the bar's dim sign up ahead. "But I'll let you buy me that Malbec anyway."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's shoulder stayed where it had bumped, a fraction of a second longer than physics required.

"Slow," he said, for the third time that evening, and the word had gone through so many meanings tonight that it had almost come back around to its original one. "You know, most people when they've just — when they've —"

He stopped. Started again.

"Most people don't review the second period on the walk to the bar. Most people let things settle. You —" He shook his head, the silver at his temples catching the light from the bar's sign as they got closer. "You've always been like this. I used to think it was a weakness. Now I think it's just — you. Whatever *you* is."

He held the bar door open. The place was exactly as dim and narrow as he'd described, half-full of people who weren't going to look twice at two men with marks on their throats and the particular posture of people who'd recently been horizontal. The barman nodded at Corvo, who nodded back, and they ended up at the far end of the bar in two stools that had clearly been meant for one.

"Two Malbecs," Corvo said, without looking at the wine list, because there was no wine list, and because he already knew. He set his bag down between his feet and his jacket on the back of the stool and only then did he let himself settle, his elbow on the bar, his posture going slightly loose in a way it never did in the salle.

He didn't look at Reyes for a long moment. He looked at the bar top, at the small circle of wet his elbow had made, at the barman pouring.

"That was messy," he said, finally, and the word didn't sound the way it had sounded an hour ago in the empty salle. Quieter. Almost fond. "What you said earlier. That it was messy. You were right."

He picked up his glass when it came. Didn't drink yet. Held it by the bowl, the way his old instructor had taught him, and turned it once so the wine caught the low light.

"I'm not —" He stopped. Started again. "I don't do that. I don't stay after. I don't go to the floor. I don't say *don't stop.*" The words came out flat, factual, the cadence of a man making a confession he hadn't planned to make. "I don't let anyone pin me. I don't let anyone in the changing room at all. The door was locked and you were — you were already in there because of course you were, you'd been trying to get in there all season, and I —"

He drank. Set the glass down. Looked at Reyes sideways, finally, the streetlight and the bar's dim fixtures doing something unfortunate and entirely to his advantage.

"I don't regret it," he said, and his voice had gone firm again, the competitive edge creeping back in like a man reclaiming his own territory. "For the record. The third touch was generous and the bout was three-two and you were wrong about right of way and you are still buying me the second bottle when we get to it. But I don't regret — the rest of it."

His thumb ran around the rim of his glass. Once. Twice.

"Same time next Tuesday," he said, and the corner of his mouth did the thing again — the almost-smile, the one that on the strip would have looked like a sneer but here, in the dim bar, with his hair still a ruin and his collar still undone and the marks Reyes had left visible above his collar, looked like something else entirely. "Bring the lateral. Bring the patience. Bring —"

He stopped. Drank again. Set the glass down.

"Bring yourself," he said, quieter, and didn't take it back, and didn't look at Reyes, and his thumb kept moving on the rim of the glass as if he could keep the word turning over in the air between them forever.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take a long pull from my glass, watching him over the rim. "You talk too much after a bout," I say, but my boot nudges his under the bar. "Tuesday, then."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: His hand came up — not to Reyes, not yet, but to the wall beside his head, palm flat, forearm close enough that Reyes would have been able to feel the warmth off his skin if he'd shifted an inch.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: His mouth found Reyes's throat, the hinge of his jaw

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: The silver at his temples had gone damp. His hips shifted once

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: Don't you dare go gentle on me now

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: His back arched off the bench and his fingers went white on the wood and his ankle tightened behind Reyes's calf hard enough to leave a mark, and the sound he made when it broke over him was something he'd be furious about later — something ragged and bitten-off and too honest

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Slow. Corvo's hands stilled on the grip.

"Generous," he repeated, and finally looked up. "The blade was past your guard before you started moving. I counted."

He set the foil down. The salle felt smaller with Reyes standing that close, with the smell of exertion and the faint tang of metal still hanging between them.

"You know what your problem is?" Corvo said, but there was no venom in it tonight. Just that familiar, crooked almost-smile. "You fight like you're angry at the sport."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I snort, leaning against the wall. "And you fight like you're trying to seduce it. All that flourish." I nod toward the foil. "Generous my ass."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo stood, the chair scraping softly against the worn floorboards.

"Seduction requires a willing partner," he said, and there it was—something different in his voice, something that had no business being there after four years of sharp words and sharper blades. "I wasn't sure you qualified."

He stepped closer. Not into Reyes's space, not quite. Close enough to see the dried sweat at his temple, the slight rise and fall of his chest still settling from the match.

"Three-two," Corvo said again, quieter now. "With two points in it, you'd usually be halfway through explaining how the ref missed something. Tonight you're still here." He tilted his head, studying Reyes with the same focused intensity he'd brought to every bout. "Why are you still here, Reyes?"

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's breath caught. Barely, but Reyes was close enough to notice—he was sure of it.

"That's not—" he started, then stopped. His jaw tightened, that familiar stubbornness warring with something softer underneath. "I've been *patient*. There's a difference."

He didn't move away. Didn't close the remaining distance either. Four years of circling each other on the piste, four years of comments that cut and compliments that stung, and Corvo had always been the one to pull back first. Safer that way. Kept the competition clean.

But Reyes was still here. Reyes had taken the grip from his hands and put it down like it was nothing, like it was everything.

"You're not usually this slow either," Corvo murmured. His fingers, still slightly numb from the rewrap, twitched at his side. "Should I be worried you're concussed?"

He watched Reyes's mouth. Just for a moment. Then made himself look up again, steady, the way he did before a match, when everything narrowed down to a single point of focus.

"Your move," he said.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
I huff a quiet laugh, my eyes still on his. "Maybe I'm just tired of being patient."

I reach out and push a damp strand of hair back from his forehead. "Is that concussed enough for you?"

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo closed his eyes for half a second. Just half. Reyes's fingers were rougher than he'd imagined—callused from years of gripping foils, hilts, the world like it owed them both something.

"Considerably concussed," he heard himself say, and his voice had gone rough at the edges. "Dangerous, even."

He let his hand come up. Not to push Reyes away, but to rest against his jaw, thumb settling at the hinge where tension lived. Corvo knew tension. Had mapped every point of it across four years of matches, watching Reyes tighten up before an attack, loosen when he thought he'd won a exchange. He knew this tension now—the kind that came from wanting something for too long.

"I've been patient," Corvo said again, but the word sounded different in his own ears this time. "I want to be clear about that."

He opened his eyes. Reyes was still there, still close, still waiting like Corvo had been waiting, like they'd both been circling this for longer than either would admit.

"Three-two," Corvo said softly. "Final score. And I'm not going to be generous this time."

His thumb traced Reyes's cheekbone once, deliberate, the same way he'd trace a target before a strike. Then he leaned in and stopped, breath mingling, close enough that the choice was Reyes's to make.

Corvo had been patient long enough. Now he could wait a little longer.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo had imagined this exactly once, in the kind of quiet moment he'd told himself not to examine too closely. The reality was better. Messier. Reyes's hands were in his hair now, pulling, and Corvo made a sound he would have denied later if anyone had asked.

The bench creaked under them. Theirs was the only kit on the floor—Reyes's bag still by the wall where he'd dropped it hours ago, Corvo's chair abandoned by the stripped-down grip. The overhead lights buzzed faintly, the only witness to four years of careful distance collapsing into this.

"You're still wearing half your gear," Reyes muttered against his collarbone.

Corvo laughed—a real one, not the sharp bark from the piste or the careful deflection at awards. "Your fault. You distracted me."

He worked his fingers under the hem of Reyes's jacket, felt the heat of skin, the shift of muscle. Reyes was solid everywhere Corvo touched—years of footwork had carved him into something that could take a hit and stay standing. Corvo appreciated that. Had always appreciated that, in the way he'd trained himself not to think about.

"Here," he said, and pulled back just enough to work the knotted laces at Reyes's collar. "Let me."

Reyes watched him with dark eyes. "You're slow when it matters."

"I've been told I'm thorough."

The jacket came open. Corvo traced the line of a recent bruise, yellowing at the edge of Reyes's ribs—sweep from last week's bout, the one Reyes had won four-one. He remembered the moment. Remembered the twist in his chest when Reyes had dropped him with a flick Corvo still hadn't figured out.

"Here," Corvo said again, softer, and pressed his mouth to the bruise.

Reyes's breath stuttered. His fingers tightened in Corvo's hair.

"*God*—" The word came out rough, broken. Reyes's hips rolled forward, and Corvo forgot, for a moment, that this was supposed to be something he'd have to explain later. There was no later in this room. There was only the bench beneath them and Reyes shuddering against him and the low sound Corvo made in answer, something he didn't try to swallow.

The salle was empty. The mats were rolled in the corner. The foils waited in their rack, gleaming under the dim lights like they'd know exactly what happened here.

Corvo lifted his head, just enough to meet Reyes's eyes. His mouth was wet. His hands were shaking—just slightly, just enough.

"I want a rematch," he said. The words came out hoarse, wrecked.

Reyes grinned. It was the same grin from the piste, from every match, except now it was pressed against Corvo's jaw.

"Best of five," Reyes said.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I push him back against the bench, straddling his waist. My hands brace on his chest. "Three-two," I repeat, my voice low. "And the next one's mine."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let himself be pushed back. That was the thing about Reyes—give him an opening and he'd take it, every time, relentless in a way that made Corvo's chest tight in ways that had nothing to do with exertion.

"Three-two," he said, but his hands found Reyes's hips anyway, pulling him closer. "Bold of you to assume you won't need a full five."

The bench was harder under his back than he'd expected. He'd need to oil the joints of it tomorrow—assuming he could remember how to stand tomorrow, with Reyes looking at him like that, with Reyes *on* him like that.

Corvo ran his thumb along the ridge of Reyes's hip bone, feeling the muscle shift. Watched Reyes's eyes go heavy-lidded. Four years of studying that face across the piste, reading the micro-expressions before an attack, and Corvo had never seen this particular look before. It made him want to lose on purpose.

He didn't, of course. That wasn't who he was.

But Reyes was warm and solid and still wearing half his gear, and Corvo's careful composure was unraveling thread by thread every time Reyes moved.

"Your point," Corvo admitted, rough and quiet. His fingers curled into the fabric at the small of Reyes's back. "Take it."

He arched up to meet him, and the salle's fluorescent lights buzzed overhead like a crowd that had gone silent, waiting for the next exchange.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo stopped talking. That was the thing—not silence, but the complete absence of anything resembling words. His hands found the edge of the bench and gripped until the wood creaked. His spine arched off the bench without his permission. A sound escaped him that he'd never made on the piste, that he'd never made anywhere, something raw and involuntary that Reyes swallowed like he'd been waiting four years for it.

He probably had. They both had.

"Re—" Corvo started, and then lost the thread entirely when Reyes did something with his tongue that should have been illegal. "*Reyes*."

Reyes didn't stop. Didn't even slow down. Just looked up with that same sharp grin, except softer now, except ruined, and Corvo understood with sudden clarity that Reyes had been thinking about this too. That the sharp comments and the harder-than-necessary parries and the way Reyes always lingered after matches had meant something all along.

Corvo's hand found Reyes's hair—still damp, still tangled from the bout—and held on. Not guiding. Not controlling. Just anchoring himself to something solid while the rest of him came apart.

"You—" Corvo managed. Then, quieter, almost awed: "You absolute *menace*."

Reyes hummed in response, and Corvo forgot what he was going to say next entirely.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I pull back just enough to watch his face go slack, my thumb brushing his lower lip. "Menace wins points," I say, and my voice is wrecked too.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's breath came uneven, his chest still rising and falling too fast. Reyes's thumb on his mouth was an anchor and a taunt both, and Corvo did the only thing he could—he turned his head and pressed his lips to Reyes's palm, tasting salt and exertion and something that might have been triumph.

"Point taken," he said against Reyes's skin. His voice came out wrecked, which was infuriating, which Reyes clearly knew, given the way his mouth curved. "Menace does win points."

He reached up and pulled Reyes down to him. No more talking. No more counting. Just the weight of Reyes settling over him, the friction of fabric against bare skin, the fluorescent lights humming their indifferent witness overhead.

The bench creaked. Their kit lay scattered on the floor where it had fallen. Somewhere in the rack, foils caught the light like they were applauding a bout well-fought.

Corvo stopped counting points. Stopped keeping score. Let Reyes have this one, and the next, and the one after that.

There'd be time to reclaim the lead tomorrow. Or the day after. Or never. Corvo found he didn't mind the uncertainty nearly as much as he'd expected to.

Reyes's mouth found his throat, and Corvo's thoughts scattered like a scattered guard.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo had spent four years setting the pace. Every exchange, every encounter, every barbed comment across the piste—always him pulling back first, always him deciding when to press and when to retreat. It was control he'd never even acknowledged having until Reyes took it from him in a single move.

His wrists hit the bench. The wood was cool against his skin. Reyes's fingers pressed firm, not bruising but immovable, and Corvo felt something crack open in his chest that he hadn't known was sealed.

"*Reyes*," he said, and it came out like a challenge. Like a surrender. Like both at once.

Reyes didn't answer. Just held him there, gaze steady, waiting for Corvo to fight or concede or do something other than lie there with his pulse hammering visibly at his throat.

Corvo did the only thing that made sense. He stopped trying to win.

His body went lax against the bench. Not submission—Corvo didn't do submission—but acknowledgment. Recognition that Reyes had found an opening and deserved to exploit it. The tension bled out of his shoulders, his arms, even his jaw, until he was just *there*, chest heaving, wrists pinned, entirely at Reyes's mercy.

"Fine," Corvo breathed. His eyes found Reyes's and didn't look away. "Fine. *Your* pace."

The words tasted foreign. So did the smile that pulled at his mouth after—something unguarded, something he'd never worn on the piste where anyone could see. Reyes had asked for proof. This was the only proof Corvo had left to give.

He tilted his chin up, baring his throat, and let Reyes decide what happened next.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I kiss the line of his throat, slow and deliberate. "Better," I murmur against his skin, letting go of one wrist to trace the line of his collarbone. "Now keep still."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo kept still. That was the hardest part—not the vulnerability of his throat exposed, not the loss of his wrists, but the stillness itself. Four years of calculated movement, of measuring every step and breath against an opponent, and now he was lying on a changing-room bench being told to do nothing while Reyes mapped his skin like it was new territory.

Reyes's freed hand traced his collarbone with the same focus he'd bring to a feint. Slow. Deliberate. Cataloging every shiver, every twitch of muscle. Corvo could feel himself being studied, and worse—he could feel himself *responding* to it. The heat building low in his belly, the way his breath kept catching on nothing.

"You're staring," Corvo said. His voice was hoarse, barely above a whisper.

Reyes's mouth curved against his skin. "Learning."

The word sent a tremor through Corvo that had nothing to do with the touch. Learning. Like Corvo was a technique to be mastered, a sequence to be practiced until it was perfect. And the infuriating thing—the *wonderful* thing—was that Corvo wanted him to. Wanted Reyes to take him apart and study the pieces and figure out exactly how to undo him.

His free hand found the back of Reyes's neck, fingers curling into damp hair. Not to pull him away. Just to hold on.

"Get on with it, then," Corvo managed. "I haven't got all night."

A lie. He would have given Reyes all night, all morning, every point in every match he'd ever won or lost, if this was what waited on the other side.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo stopped pretending he had any dignity left. There was none to be found on this bench, under Reyes's hands and mouth, with the fluorescent lights buzzing overhead and the scent of them both filling the small room. Reyes worked him over with the same relentless focus he brought to everything—the same precision that made him dangerous on the piste, now turned to entirely different ends.

Corvo's fingers found the edge of the bench again, gripping hard enough to ache. His other hand stayed tangled in Reyes's hair, guiding without directing, surrendering without giving up entirely. There was a difference. He clung to that difference like it mattered.

"*There*," Corvo heard himself say, and his voice was someone else's, wrecked and wanting. "Reyes, *there*—"

Reyes knew exactly where there was. Reyes always had.

The salle went blurry at the edges. Corvo's spine arched, his head pressing back into the bench, and for a moment he forgot everything—the points, the matches, the four years of circling each other like wolves. There was only Reyes, and the sound Corvo made when he came, and the way Reyes didn't stop, just gentled through it until Corvo was shaking and oversensitive and making sounds he'd never admit to.

When he opened his eyes again, Reyes was watching him. Of course he was. Cataloging the aftermath like it was another point scored.

Corvo laughed. It came out breathless, unsteady. "Satisfied?"

Reyes's grin was sharp enough to cut. "Not even close."

He wasn't done. Corvo could feel it—the heat still coiled in his own limbs, the way Reyes was still hard against his hip. The match wasn't over. Corvo had been stupid to think it was.

"Best of five," Corvo rasped, and pulled Reyes back down to him.

The next one was his.

---

Later—minutes or hours, Corvo couldn't tell—the bench creaked as they shifted. Reyes had gone lax against him, one arm draped across Corvo's chest, both of them breathing hard. The changing room smelled like sweat and something else, something that would be embarrassing in the morning light.

Corvo should move. Should start gathering their scattered kit, should offer to lock up, should do any of the things practical people did after. Instead he stayed exactly where he was, staring at the water-stained ceiling tiles, Reyes's weight warm and unfamiliar and entirely welcome.

"Three-two," Corvo said quietly. "Going on four."

Reyes snorted against his shoulder. "You didn't score four."

"I'm scoring now. In the standings. Mentally." Corvo's hand found Reyes's hair, stroked absently through the damp mess of it. "Personal satisfaction counts double."

"Since when?"

"Since tonight." Corvo turned his head, pressed his lips to Reyes's temple. The gesture felt strange in his own mouth. Soft. Unearned. "I'm rewriting the rules."

Reyes was quiet for a moment. Then, quieter than Corvo had ever heard him: "What rules?"

Corvo considered the question. The salle around them, empty and dim. The bench that would need oiling tomorrow. The way Reyes fit against him like a geometry problem finally solved.

"All of them," he said finally. "Whatever we need."

Reyes shifted, propped himself up on one elbow to look down at Corvo. His hair was a disaster. There was a bruise forming on his collarbone that Corvo didn't remember giving him. He looked wrecked and satisfied and something else, something Corvo wanted to keep looking at.

"Rematch tomorrow?" Reyes asked.

Corvo smiled. It felt different from his usual smile—less sharp, more honest. "Every tomorrow," he said. "Best of five. Best of ten. Best of whatever you want."

Reyes shook his head, but he was smiling too. "You're slow tonight."

"I've been patient." Corvo reached up, traced the line of Reyes's jaw. "Now I've got all the time I need."

The lights hummed. The foils gleamed in their rack. Somewhere outside, the city went on without them, and neither of them cared.

Corvo pulled Reyes back down, and they stayed.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
I push up on my elbow, looking down at him. "I'll still beat you on the piste tomorrow."

My fingers trace the new mark on his collarbone. "But this stays off the record."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo caught Reyes's fingers against his collarbone, held them there. The mark would bruise, dark and visible, and Corvo found he liked that. Evidence. Proof that tonight had happened outside the fever-dream of it.

"Off the record," he agreed. His thumb traced circles on Reyes's wrist. "But I'm keeping the scoreboard in my head."

"And when you lose tomorrow?"

"Then I'll know the debt's owed." Corvo smiled—that new one, the softer version he was still getting used to. "Payable in kind."

The salle sat quiet around them. Somewhere a radiator clicked. Their kit lay in a scattered pile that would require sorting in the morning, whites tangled with whites, foils leaning against the wall where they'd been discarded mid-motion. Evidence enough for anyone paying attention.

But no one would be paying attention. This was theirs.

"I should go," Reyes said, without moving.

Corvo didn't let go of his wrist. "Should you?"

Reyes looked at him for a long moment. The sharp edges of him had softened, or maybe Corvo was finally seeing what had always been underneath—something that matched the ache in his own chest, the one he'd spent four years fencing around.

"Tomorrow," Reyes said finally. "Piste. Five o'clock."

Corvo nodded. "I'll be slow."

"You're always slow."

"I prefer *patient*." Corvo released Reyes's wrist, let his hand fall to the bench between them. "But yes. Five o'clock."

Reyes pushed himself up, off the bench, off Corvo, and the loss of warmth was immediate and unwelcome. Corvo watched him gather their kit from the floor—his whites, then Corvo's, folded with surprising care and draped over the bench beside him.

"You're doing my laundry now?" Corvo asked.

"I'm making sure you don't walk out half-dressed." Reyes tossed Corvo's jacket at his chest. "Some of us have standards."

Corvo caught the jacket, held it against him. "You have standards?"

"One or two." Reyes was pulling on his own trousers, movements efficient despite the ache Corvo could see in his shoulders, the way he moved like something was tender. "Left over from when I had a reputation to maintain."

Corvo sat up slowly. His body protested—the bench had not been designed for this, and he would feel it tomorrow in ways that had nothing to do with fencing. He pulled on his own whites, wincing as fabric dragged across sensitive skin.

"Your reputation," Corvo said. "As a menace."

"Among other things." Reyes found his shoes, sat on the bench to tie them. The posture was ordinary, domestic almost, and Corvo was struck again by how strange this was—not the sex, but the after. The ordinary. Reyes in his salle jacket, lacing up his shoes, while Corvo sat half-dressed and ruined beside him.

Reyes looked up. "What?"

Corvo shook his head. "Nothing. Just—" He stopped, started again. "I thought you'd leave faster."

"Sorry to disappoint." Reyes finished the laces, straightened. Looked at Corvo with something unreadable in his expression. "I'll see you tomorrow. Five o'clock. Try to show up on time for once."

"I always show up."

"Late. You always show up late." Reyes stood, grabbed his bag from where it had fallen hours ago, and paused at the door. The light from the corridor caught his profile—sharp jaw, tired eyes, a softness at the corner of his mouth that Corvo had put there.

Corvo committed the image to memory. Another entry for the scoreboard in his head.

"Three-two," Corvo said quietly.

Reyes's smile flickered. "Not anymore."

Then he was gone, the door swinging shut behind him, and Corvo was alone in the salle with the smell of Reyes still on his skin and the ghost of his warmth still pressed into the bench.

He sat there longer than he should have. Thinking about tomorrow. About the piste, and the foils, and the way Reyes would meet his eyes across the en garde line like nothing had changed.

Everything had changed.

Corvo smiled to himself, reached for the grip he'd already rewrapped twice tonight, and started to plan his next move.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
I pause outside the salle door, one hand still on the frame. I can see the strip of light under the door, hear him moving around inside. I should leave. I told him I would.

Instead I push the door back open, lean against it. "Forgot something," I say, my voice rough.

He's still sitting on the bench, jacket in his hands. He looks up, and I see the question in his eyes before he can hide it. "Your dignity?" he says, but it's quiet.

I walk back over, stop in front of him. "Yours." I lean down and kiss him once, hard and fast. "Keep it safe for me."

Then I'm gone for real, the night air cold on my face. My steps are slower than usual.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo sat there with Reyes's mouth still burning on his and the door swinging shut for the second time. His hands had gone still on the jacket in his lap. He'd been about to put it on. About to gather the last of his things, lock up, walk home through the cold to an empty apartment that would feel different now. Quieter. Like something was missing that he'd only just found.

Reyes had come back. Reyes had come back and called Corvo's dignity *his* and kissed him like a promise and then left.

Corvo touched his own mouth. Pressed his fingers to his lips where the ghost of it lingered.

"Menace," he said to the empty room.

The salle didn't answer. The foils caught the light, still gleaming. The bench held the shape of them both, and Corvo thought about oiling it tomorrow and decided he'd rather leave that particular evidence intact.

He stood. His body ached in new and interesting ways. The mark on his collarbone throbbed faintly, and Corvo pressed his jacket closed over it, hiding nothing, wanting to feel it.

Outside, Reyes's footsteps had faded into the night. Corvo listened anyway, as if he could track them by sound alone.

Five o'clock. Tomorrow.

He turned off the lights. Locked the door. Walked home through streets that felt familiar and strange all at once, carrying the taste of Reyes on his tongue and a warmth in his chest that had nothing to do with the cold.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I'm halfway home before I realize I left my keys in my bag. Back at the salle, the lights are off. I lean my forehead against the cool wood of the door and laugh, the sound swallowed by the empty street.
