dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s hands paused on the strip of leather.

Only for a moment.

Then he pulled it taut with unnecessary care, smoothing it under his thumb as if the fate of the weapon depended on it.

“Slow,” he repeated, tasting the word like it had insulted his family. “That is a fascinating interpretation of me giving you time to make the bout interesting.”

He finally looked up. The salle lights had gone colder with the hour, throwing long bars of shadow across the piste, catching on the bell guards stacked along the wall. Corvo had taken off his jacket but not his competitive expression; that, apparently, stayed on until death.

His gaze flicked to the bag beside him, then back to Reyes.

“You stayed,” he said.

It was not a question. Not quite. Corvo had been too long in fencing to mistake distance, timing, intention. The drop of the bag had been its own kind of advance.

He set the foil down across his knees.

“If you came to gloat, do it properly.” His mouth curved. “Chest out. Chin up. Lie convincingly about how effortless it was.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
I lean against the piste, crossing my arms. "I don't have to lie. It *was* effortless."

I nod toward the foil in his hands. "But since you're still here...I'm thinking we make it interesting. First to five, no holding back this time."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo went very still.

Then, slowly, he smiled.

It was not the polite smile he used for parents with opinions about footwork, nor the sharp little blade-flash he gave students before correcting them in public. This one was private, dangerous, and far too pleased.

“No holding back,” he said.

He rose from the bench, foil in hand, the half-rewrapped grip forgotten. His sleeves were rolled to the forearms; there was a fading bruise along one wrist from earlier, exactly where Reyes had found him through a sloppy parry he would deny until burial.

“Bold condition from someone who has been benefiting from my restraint for four years.”

Corvo crossed to the rack and selected a mask, turning it once in his hand. His eyes stayed on Reyes longer than necessary, measuring distance the way he always did—except this time the line between them felt less like a piste and more like a dare.

“First to five,” he agreed. “Clean touches. No excuses. No sudden complaints about the floor, the light, your knee, my allegedly intolerable personality.”

He picked up a second foil, checked the flex, and set it aside within reach.

Then he stepped onto the piste.

At the en garde line, Corvo lifted his mask but did not put it on yet. He held it against his hip, head tilted, that same insufferable expression alive at the corner of his mouth.

“And since you are so certain it was effortless,” he said, voice dropping just enough to make the empty salle feel smaller, “you can afford a wager.”

His thumb brushed along the edge of the mask.

“Five touches. Winner asks one thing. Loser answers honestly.”

A beat.

“No fencing evasions. No tactical retreats. No pretending you did not understand the question.”

Corvo put the mask on at last, hiding the worst of his smile behind steel mesh.

“Unless,” he added, blade lifting into line, “you have discovered caution at this late hour.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let the grip be taken.

That, more than anything, betrayed him.

For four years he had made a religion of not giving Reyes an inch unless he intended to steal two back. But he stood there with empty hands, close enough that the cold salle light caught the line of his jaw, close enough that the old vocabulary of distance became suddenly useless.

“Careful,” he said, very quietly. “If you keep saying that, I may start to think you were watching me closely.”

His gaze dropped, not far, not for long, then returned with the precision of a point brought back on target.

The foil lay abandoned beside them. The piste stretched empty behind him. First to five had been agreed, but Corvo did not move to reclaim the weapon. Not yet.

“You think I was slow,” he said. “I think you have been circling the same opening for years and only just found the courage to take it.”

His mouth curved, but the mockery had thinned into something warmer, sharper. Something that had been hiding underneath the whole time.

He leaned in a fraction, not enough to close the last distance, only enough to make it obvious that he knew exactly where it was.

“Go on, then,” Corvo said. “Prove I’m wrong.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I don't need the foil to prove it. My hand comes up to rest against his chest, right over his heart. I can feel it beating fast under my palm. "You're not wrong."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo stopped breathing for exactly one measure.

It was infuriating, really, that Reyes should find the one target he had not thought to guard.

His heart betrayed him under that hand, quick and hard and utterly without discipline. Corvo glanced down at it, at the contact made so simply after four years of feints, binds, disengages, insults delivered like invitations neither of them had admitted to understanding.

Then he looked back up.

“No,” he said, low. “I was not.”

The words cost him more than any touch on the piste.

His hand rose, not to remove Reyes’s, but to cover it. His palm pressed lightly over those fingers, holding them there against his chest as if he could make the admission worse by making it deliberate.

For once, he did not smirk.

For once, he did not retreat into correction.

“You know,” Corvo said, and his voice had gone rough at the edges, “this is very poor form. No salute. No referee. Weapon abandoned.”

His thumb moved once over the back of Reyes’s hand.

“And still,” he continued, “somehow the cleanest attack you have made all evening.”

He stepped closer.

There was no piste distance left now. No right of way to argue. No bell guard between them, no students watching, no rival salle, no years of reputation sharp enough to cut themselves on.

Only the quiet, and the white lines underfoot, and Corvo finally losing a bout he had been pretending not to fence.

He bent his head until his mouth hovered near Reyes’s, close enough for the last breath between them to turn unsteady.

“If you mean it,” he said, barely above a whisper, “do not make me wait another four years.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo made it to the bench by luck, spite, and the kind of stubborn balance that had won him medals.

After that, discipline abandoned him entirely.

His mask hit the floor with a hollow clatter. His gloves followed. One of them skidded beneath the bench, and Corvo, who corrected students for dropping equipment like it was a moral failing, did not so much as glance after it.

He was too occupied with Reyes.

Four years of insults had not prepared him for the reality of hands and heat and breath in the dim changing room. Four years of watching distance, measuring tempo, pretending every sharp word was only rivalry—none of it had prepared him for the first real collision without blades between them.

Corvo caught the edge of the bench behind him and laughed once, breathless and low, against Reyes’s mouth.

“Still slow?” he asked, though the words came out ragged enough to ruin the provocation.

He did not wait long enough to make it a proper question.

Corvo kissed like he fenced when he stopped performing for an audience: direct, inventive, mercilessly attentive. Every retreat was a trap. Every pause was only long enough to make the next advance worse. His hands found fabric, then tension, then the familiar lines of an opponent he had studied for years and never once allowed himself to touch like this.

The changing room smelled of metal lockers, sweat, old leather, and the sharp clean bite of floor polish. It should have been ridiculous. It should have been beneath him. Corvo had imagined, in brief and treacherous moments, that if this ever happened it would be somewhere more elegant, less fluorescent, less littered with discarded kit and bad decisions.

Instead, he found he would not have traded the bench for any bed in the city.

Not with Reyes there.

Not with his own pulse hammering as if he had just fenced the bout of his life.

Corvo drew back only enough to breathe, forehead nearly resting forward, one hand braced against the bench and the other still refusing to let go.

“Listen carefully,” he said, voice rough, ruined of all its usual polish. “Because I am only going to be generous once.”

His mouth curved, but it shook at the edge.

“If you want me to stop, say it.”

A beat passed, charged and close.

Corvo’s eyes searched Reyes’s face with the same fierce precision he brought to the piste, but there was no mockery in him now. No armor worth mentioning.

“Otherwise,” he murmured, “I am going to be unbearable about this for the rest of our natural lives.”

Then he kissed Reyes again, harder, as if the warning had satisfied some last remnant of honor and the rest of him could finally surrender to winning, losing, whatever this was.

The bench creaked under him. Somewhere, a foil settled on the tile with a faint metallic shift. Corvo ignored it all.

For once, there was no score to keep.

Or if there was, he had lost count after the first touch.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
I pull back just enough to look at him, my hands still fisted in his shirt. "Unbearable? You've always been unbearable."

I kiss him again, slower this time, my thumb brushing over the bruise on his wrist. "I'm not stopping."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo made a sound that was almost a laugh and almost surrender.

“Always,” he said, against Reyes’s mouth. “Yes. But now I have motive.”

The touch at his bruised wrist ruined him more effectively than any clean hit. His breath caught; his fingers flexed once against the bench, then found purpose again. He covered that hand with his own for a moment, not to stop it, not to guide it away, but because some foolish part of him wanted the evidence acknowledged: there, that mark, that touch, that history of impact turned suddenly intimate.

“Do you know how irritating it is,” Corvo murmured, “to want someone who parries like a vandal?”

His voice had lost its edge. Or rather, the edge had changed—no less sharp, but no longer defensive.

He kissed Reyes again and forgot to be clever for several seconds.

That, too, would have to be forgiven.

Corvo’s back found the lockers with a dull metallic thud. He did not care. His shirt had already become an inconvenience, twisted under hands and heat, and he reached for the buttons with the impatient concentration of a man disassembling a weapon under pressure. One slipped; another resisted. He swore under his breath in Italian, low and vicious, then gave up on elegance entirely.

“Four years,” he said, raggedly, as if building an argument against the fabric itself. “Four years of you standing too close after bouts and pretending it was accidental.”

A button came free.

“Four years of that look when you thought I was not watching.”

Another.

“Four years of making me invent reasons to stay late.”

His mouth curved, breathless and accusing.

“And you called me slow.”

The shirt finally loosened enough for him to drag it open. He looked less composed without it arranged properly: flushed at the throat, hair mussed, chest rising too quickly beneath Reyes’s hand. There was no mask now. No jacket. No perfectly maintained distance.

Only Corvo, still proud enough to lift his chin and undone enough that the gesture failed halfway.

He caught Reyes by the front of the jacket, fingers curling into the heavy fencing fabric he had gripped a hundred times in correction and never like this. His forehead dipped close, breath warming the narrow space between them.

“If that changes,” he said, quieter, steadier despite the ruin of him, “if anything changes, you tell me.”

Then his expression sharpened again, desire and challenge braided so tightly they had become the same thing.

“But until then—”

Corvo turned, pressed Reyes back against the line of lockers with a controlled force that belonged unmistakably to the piste: measured, exact, impossible to mistake for hesitation.

“—I am done giving you time to make it interesting.”

He kissed lower, then stopped just short of haste, as if restraint had returned only to make itself cruel. His hands moved with the care of a man who knew precision mattered more than speed; who had spent years studying openings and now, finally, had permission to take them.

The bench stood close behind him. The floor was a wreck of discarded kit. Somewhere outside the changing room, the empty salle held its breath.

Corvo did not.

Corvo breathed Reyes in like victory, like defeat, like something he had no intention of surviving with dignity intact.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo had always suspected there would be a limit to his eloquence.

He had merely not expected it to be found on a changing-room bench beneath fluorescent lights, one hand braced uselessly against old varnished wood, the other clenched in the discarded edge of his own shirt as if fabric could save him.

It could not.

For once, Corvo had no correction to offer. No insult sharpened and ready. No elegant little observation about tempo, distance, or form. His head tipped back against the bench, throat exposed, breath leaving him in uneven fragments that would have humiliated him under any other circumstances.

Under these, he decided humiliation had been unfairly maligned.

“Reyes,” he managed, and even that sounded less like a warning than a confession.

The name broke in his mouth.

He shut his eyes, then opened them immediately, because pride apparently survived anything and he refused to miss a second of his own undoing. His hand found the edge of the bench instead, fingers curling hard enough that the old wood complained beneath him.

“Of course,” he said, voice wrecked, “of course this is where you discover patience.”

He tried to laugh. It came out badly.

The first time he had fenced Reyes, Corvo had known within three touches that the man was dangerous. Not because of strength. Not because of speed. Those were ordinary dangers. No, Reyes had been dangerous because he watched. Because he waited half a breath longer than most people could bear. Because he understood that pressure did not always mean forward motion.

Corvo had hated him for it.

Corvo had admired him for it.

Corvo, now flat on a bench with his composure in pieces on the tile beside their kit, finally understood that he had been doomed from the first bout.

His free hand lifted, hovered, then settled against the nearest solid thing he could reach, not pushing away, only holding on. His wrist turned, the bruise catching the light again, that small old ache swallowed by the newer, sharper one climbing through him.

“Do not,” he said, then stopped, because he had no idea what command he meant to give.

Do not stop.

Do not look so pleased with yourself.

Do not make him admit aloud that he had wanted this so badly it had turned into rivalry because rivalry was safer.

His jaw tightened. His breath failed him again.

Corvo stared at the ceiling as if it had personally betrayed him.

“You are going to be impossible after this,” he whispered.

A beat.

His mouth curved, helpless and furious and fond all at once.

“And I am going to deserve it.”

The admission left him stripped more thoroughly than any piece of clothing on the floor. There it was: the truth at last, no mask, no salute, no scorekeeper. Just Corvo, finally honest because Reyes had found a way to make dishonesty require more discipline than he had left.

He turned his head, cheek against the bench, eyes dark and bright under the ruined fall of his hair.

“Look at me,” he said, rougher now, not an order from the piste but something far more dangerous. “If you are going to take me apart, have the courtesy to watch what you are doing.”

And then even that arrogance failed.

His hand snapped to his mouth for one breath, muffling the sound that escaped him, but only one. After that, Corvo let it fall away. Pride had carried him for thirty-eight years; it could survive being set aside for one night.

Perhaps two.

Perhaps whatever came after this, if either of them had the courage not to pretend it had been nothing.

The bench creaked beneath him. His shoulders tensed, then loosened by degrees. The cold room had narrowed to heat, breath, pulse, the unbearable deliberate pace of being answered without words.

Corvo had spent four years trying to beat Reyes.

Now, with his fingers splayed helplessly against the bench and his voice reduced to a low, broken sound, he understood the more terrible possibility.

He wanted to lose.

He wanted to lose thoroughly.

And later—later, when he had recovered enough dignity to be insufferable again—he would claim that he had allowed it for tactical reasons.

For now, he only reached down, touched Reyes with shaking fingers, and said the truest thing he had managed all night.

“Yes.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
My laugh is rough against his skin. I finally lift my head, just enough to see his face. "Impossible?" I repeat, thumb brushing his jaw. "You have no idea."

I kiss him again, slow and deliberate. "I'm just getting started."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s eyes narrowed at that.

Not in warning.

In recognition.

There it was—that look, that damnable certainty, the one Reyes wore when he had read the line correctly and knew Corvo had nowhere sensible left to go.

Corvo should have had an answer. He had built an entire career on answers: correction, counterattack, one clean phrase placed exactly where it would draw blood.

Instead, his breath left him unevenly, and his hand rose to close around Reyes’s wrist, holding that touch at his jaw as if it were another blade he refused to yield.

“You are,” he said, voice low and frayed, “astonishingly pleased with yourself.”

The accusation lacked force. It was ruined by the way Corvo turned his face slightly into Reyes’s hand before he could stop himself.

He hated that.

He wanted more of it.

His mouth curved, sharp and shaken.

“Fine,” he murmured. “Get started.”

A pause.

Then, because he was still Corvo, because surrender apparently did not require silence, he added, “But do not mistake this for victory.”

It was an absurd thing to say while half-sprawled on the bench, shirt open, hair disordered, pride scattered somewhere among the discarded kit. Absurd, and therefore necessary. His dignity had been mortally wounded; someone had to stand guard over the corpse.

His fingers loosened from Reyes’s wrist, then slid higher, not pushing, not restraining—only touching because now that he had allowed himself that much, stopping seemed more difficult than any bout he had ever fenced. His thumb found the line of Reyes’s cheek with a care that made his expression harden, as though tenderness were a tactical error he intended to deny committing.

“If you are just getting started,” Corvo said, “then I expect form.”

His voice caught on the last word.

He closed his eyes for one breath, then opened them again immediately, stubborn as ever, gaze fixed and bright.

“No sloppiness. No wasted motion.”

Another breath, thinner this time.

“And if you make me say anything undignified,” he said, “I will never forgive you.”

But his hand had already curled at the back of Reyes’s neck, keeping him close.

The changing room seemed impossibly quiet around them now, as if the whole salle beyond the door had become an accomplice. Corvo could still feel the ghost of the piste under him, the old instinct to measure distance and timing, but none of the measures held. There was only the bench beneath his back, Reyes above him, and the unbearable knowledge that he had wanted this long enough for wanting to become part of his posture.

Four years of rivalry. Four years of denial dressed up as disdain.

And now Reyes’s thumb had brushed his jaw, and Corvo had nearly come apart from that alone.

He laughed once, softly, incredulously, as if offended by his own helplessness.

“God,” he said, with feeling. “I am going to be insufferable tomorrow.”

Then his gaze sharpened again, dark with challenge even through the wreckage.

“If either of us can walk properly.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s wrists met the bench, and for once he did not immediately turn the disadvantage into leverage.

He tested it. Of course he did. Pride demanded at least the ceremonial attempt: a flex of forearm, a shift of shoulder, the minute calculation of angle and force. Enough to know he could struggle. Enough to know he did not want to.

His breath left him on a laugh that had no polish left in it.

“Oh,” he said, voice low, stripped down to something dangerously honest. “There you are.”

The words sounded like discovery. Like accusation. Like relief.

Pinned beneath that pressure, Corvo went still—not submissive in any simple way, never that, but attentive. Entirely present. His eyes stayed open, dark and bright and fixed, because if he was going to lose control, he would at least have the arrogance to witness it.

“You have been waiting to do that,” he murmured.

His fingers curled once against empty air, unable to make their usual clever use of touch. It unsettled him more than he expected. His hands had always been his argument: blade, correction, gesture, command. Without them, every answer had to come from somewhere less practiced.

His throat worked.

“Fine,” Corvo said. “No pace-setting.”

A beat.

Then, because he was himself, because ruin apparently still allowed commentary, his mouth curved.

“But if this is your idea of proving a point, I should warn you—your thesis lacks structure.”

The next breath betrayed him. So did the one after.

His shoulders pressed into the bench; his wrists remained where they had been set. The old wood was hard beneath him, the air cool across his opened shirt, and the room smelled of leather and steel and the aftermath of a bout neither of them had truly finished. It should have steadied him. Familiar terrain. Familiar rituals. Salle, kit, sweat, rivalry.

Instead, every familiar thing had become evidence against him.

How many nights had he stood here pretending not to watch Reyes pack away gear? How many times had he found some unnecessary adjustment to make, some invented fault in a weapon, some reason not to leave first? Four years of restraint, and now restraint had him flat on a bench with his pulse making a disgrace of him.

Corvo swallowed.

“If I concede,” he said, quieter, “you will be impossible.”

The admission hung there.

His eyes narrowed, not with resistance now, but with the last intact shard of challenge.

“If I do not concede,” he continued, “you will become ambitious.”

His laugh came rough and brief.

“Terrible position. Tactically indefensible.”

For a moment, his expression softened in spite of him. The sharpness did not vanish; it warmed. Beneath all the provocation, under all the old performance, there was a kind of wonder he had no ready insult for.

He had imagined winning against Reyes in a hundred different ways.

He had not imagined this: wanting the loss so badly his body had understood before his pride could object.

Corvo turned his head against the bench, just enough to bare the line of his throat and hate himself for how deliberate it was.

“There,” he said, almost under his breath. “Is that proper enough for you?”

His wrists shifted again. Not to escape. Only because being held in place made him aware of every inch of himself with merciless clarity. His breath caught, then steadied badly.

“Do not look so pleased,” he said, though his eyes gave him away. “I am still evaluating your form.”

Another pause.

His voice dropped.

“It is… improving.”

That cost him. The confession, small as it was, colored his face more deeply than the exertion had. Corvo, who could stand before a room of students and dissect their failures without flinching, found himself undone by praise leaving his own mouth.

He tried to recover with disdain and achieved only hunger.

“Damn you,” he whispered.

Not angry. Not even close.

His hands flexed again under the restraint, and this time the motion was less test than reflex. He let it happen. Let himself feel the helplessness of not deciding the next tempo, the maddening luxury of not being required to answer every advance with one of his own.

His eyes remained fixed, stubbornly open.

“If you wanted honesty,” Corvo said, voice rougher now, “then there. I like this.”

The words landed heavily in him.

He looked almost offended by having said them aloud.

“I like not knowing exactly what you will do next,” he continued, each phrase dragged from him with visible difficulty. “I like that you finally stopped fencing me long enough to touch me. I like—”

His jaw tightened.

For once, the rest did not come dressed as a joke.

“I like that it is you.”

The changing room seemed to contract around that sentence. Fluorescent hum. Scattered equipment. Their abandoned rivalry lying in pieces with the rest of the kit.

Corvo closed his eyes then, just for a second, as if honesty required darkness.

When he opened them again, he was still Corvo. Ruined, yes. Flushed, breathless, pinned, stripped of several useful defenses—but still proud enough to lift his chin as much as the bench allowed.

“So,” he said. “No. I do not concede.”

His mouth curved slowly.

“I merely acknowledge that you have advantage.”

A beat.

“Temporarily.”

It was absurd bravado. He knew it. It showed in the way his smile shook at the edge, in the way his breath failed him, in the way his body had gone taut with anticipation rather than resistance.

Then the arrogance slipped again, and what remained beneath it was more dangerous.

“Reyes,” Corvo said, softly this time.

Not a warning. Not a taunt.

A request with teeth.

His wrists remained pinned. His gaze did not move.

“Do it properly, then.”

The words left him low and deliberate, roughened by four years of wanting and one night of finally being too tired to lie about it.

“And when I am unbearable tomorrow,” he added, because some habits were immortal, “remember that you encouraged me.”

Then his composure broke in increments: first the breath, then the line of his mouth, then the last clean edge of his expression. He held on as long as pride allowed, which was longer than most men could have managed and not nearly long enough to save him.

By the time he turned his face aside again, laughing once under his breath like a man defeated in the best possible fashion, there was no real argument left in him.

Only heat.

Only trust.

Only the vicious, impossible satisfaction of having been answered at last.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lean down and kiss him quiet, because I've heard enough talking for one lifetime. "Temporarily," I agree against his mouth, and then I stop letting him think at all.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The kiss shut Corvo up.

This was, by any reasonable measure, an historic achievement.

He made one last attempt at speech, because pride died hard and usually with commentary, but whatever cleverness he had gathered broke uselessly against Reyes’s mouth. The sound that came out instead was low, startled, and far too honest to survive cross-examination.

So Corvo stopped trying to argue.

Worse: he stopped trying to win.

His wrists stayed where they had been put, tendons shifting once beneath the restraint before his hands opened against the bench. The gesture felt like surrender. It felt like trust. It felt so much more dangerous than either that his breath caught on it.

Temporarily, Reyes had said.

Corvo held on to that word as long as he could, which turned out to be not long at all.

The world narrowed by degrees. First the changing room vanished—the lockers, the discarded kit, the humiliatingly fluorescent lights, the bench that should have been too narrow and too hard for anything but discomfort. Then the salle beyond it disappeared, and with it four years of bouts, barbs, scores kept too carefully and insults repeated too often to be casual.

Last to go was Corvo’s discipline.

That took longer.

It fought.

It rallied.

It insisted, with the last dignity of a drowning man, that he could still track tempo, still measure breath, still anticipate the next opening.

Then he arched against the bench and lost the thread entirely.

“Reyes,” he said again, but this time the name had no edge left. It was broken down to its simplest form: need, recognition, astonishment. A man could spend years sharpening himself into something untouchable and still be undone by being touched exactly where he had been pretending not to ache.

His head tipped back. His throat worked. The exposed line of him felt almost indecent—not for what had been uncovered, but for what he had allowed. Corvo had never liked being readable. He had made an art of misdirection, of making opponents chase what he wanted them to see.

There was no misdirection in him now.

Every breath gave him away.

Every failed attempt to gather himself gave him away.

The old rivalry remained, but changed shape under pressure. It was no longer blade against blade, no longer the vicious joy of contest. It became something warmer and more perilous: challenge without armor, resistance offered only so it could be answered, pride held up for the pleasure of watching it crack.

Corvo laughed once, breathless and ruined.

“Damn you,” he whispered, though it sounded like gratitude.

His fingers flexed uselessly. Not to escape. Never quite that. Only because his body kept remembering all the ways it was accustomed to answering pressure and finding none of them sufficient. He had asked for proper proof; now proof had him speechless, and there was a certain justice in that.

He hated justice.

He had always preferred victory.

Except perhaps he had been lying about that too.

The realization moved through him slowly, bright and terrible: he was not merely enduring this. He was not merely allowing it as some tactical indulgence he could mock later over coffee and a bruised ego.

He wanted it.

He wanted the loss of control. He wanted the absence of cleverness. He wanted the unbearable luxury of not being asked to perform composure for anyone, least of all Reyes.

The thought stripped him more thoroughly than any hand could have done.

Corvo turned his face aside, cheek against the bench, eyes shut tight for one moment as if darkness might preserve a little of him. It did not. It only made everything sharper.

When he opened his eyes again, they were bright and unfocused, his mouth parted around a breath he could not quite steady.

“No,” he said suddenly, hoarse.

A pause.

Then, because even undone he remained exacting, he amended, “Not no. Just—”

His jaw clenched. His shoulders pressed down. He dragged air into his lungs and failed to make it dignified.

“Slower than that and I may actually kill you.”

There. A threat. Pathetic, but recognizable. Some remnant of Corvo Antivari had survived after all.

It did not survive the next minute.

His back bowed. His hands clenched, then opened again. The sound he made would have been mortifying in any civilized setting, and the changing room, mercifully, was not one. There were no students to hear him, no rival instructors, no witnesses but old lockers and abandoned gear.

Corvo gave up on silence.

Not restraint entirely—never entirely—but silence, yes. Silence belonged to people with control. Corvo had none worth naming. He had breath, and want, and the bitterly satisfying awareness that Reyes had been right to shut him up.

He would never admit that.

Not tomorrow.

Possibly not ever.

But in the moment, with his pride in pieces and his pulse racing beneath skin Reyes had already claimed the right to touch, the truth passed through him in a shudder.

He had wanted this since the first time Reyes had stepped inside his measure and smiled like he knew exactly what he was doing.

Four years late, Corvo finally stopped pretending otherwise.

The end, when it came, took him without elegance.

He held on for one second longer than sense allowed, because he was stubborn, because surrender tasted better when fought for, because Reyes deserved the effort and the satisfaction of taking it from him. Then Corvo broke with a low, helpless sound, his body going taut, then loose, all the fine lines of him ruined at once.

For several breaths afterward, he did not move.

He simply lay there on the bench, chest rising hard, wrists still where they had been, hair fallen across his forehead, mouth soft with shock.

Then his eyes opened.

Slowly.

Dangerously.

Corvo looked as though he had been defeated in a duel and was already planning the rematch.

“Well,” he said, voice wrecked beyond repair.

He swallowed, tried to gather dignity around himself, found none within reach, and continued anyway.

“That was adequate.”

A beat passed.

His mouth curved, exhausted and wicked.

“Temporarily.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo did not stop arguing all at once.

He surrendered it in pieces.

First the commentary went. Then the corrections. Then the last smug, defensive little smile he had been trying to keep alive out of principle. It failed under the weight of breath and heat and the intolerable fact that Reyes knew exactly when to ignore him.

Corvo’s hands found purchase where they could: the bench, the edge of a locker, a discarded sleeve twisted under his fingers. Anything solid enough to survive him. He had spent years making himself precise, elegant, composed under pressure.

There was nothing elegant left.

Only the sharp lift of his breath. The rough sound of his voice when control slipped. The way his body kept answering before his pride could object.

“Don’t stop,” Corvo said.

It came out hoarse. Bare. Not a command, not really. Worse than a command.

A request.

The admission struck him even as he made it. His eyes opened, bright and furious with himself, as if he might still take it back through sheer force of personality. But he did not. Could not. His mouth parted around another breath, and whatever he had meant to say after that broke apart before it became language.

The bench complained beneath him. A locker door rattled once under some careless impact. Their kit lay strewn across the floor in a disgraceful heap Corvo would have scolded any student for leaving.

He could not have cared less if the entire building collapsed around them.

The salle beyond the changing room remained empty and indifferent. No referee. No clock. No clean score. Only the two of them and the ruin of four years’ restraint.

Corvo turned his head, cheek brushing the bench, and laughed once—low, breathless, almost disbelieving.

“God,” he managed. “You are going to be unbearable.”

The words were meant to bite.

They did not.

They came out too warm. Too wrecked. Too close to wonder.

His hands shook when he reached, not from weakness but from the effort of letting himself want without disguising it as competition. That, more than anything, undid him: not the heat, not the force, not even the pleasure dragging through him until his thoughts scattered uselessly.

It was being known.

It was Reyes seeing the opening and taking it, and Corvo, for once in his life, not closing the line.

He arched, swore softly in Italian, then lost the rest of the sentence against a broken sound that would have mortified him if he had possessed enough dignity to be mortified. He did not. Dignity was somewhere on the tile with his mask and gloves.

Later, perhaps, he would retrieve it.

Later, he would make some insufferable remark about form.

Later, he would pretend he had allowed exactly as much as he intended.

But not now.

Now Corvo held on, eyes shut, jaw tight, every breath torn out of him like surrender had teeth.

And when the wave finally took him again, it took him completely.

For a few long moments after, he was silent.

Actually silent.

A medical concern, perhaps.

His chest rose hard. His hair had fallen into his face. One hand lay open against the bench as though even his fingers had forgotten how to make a fist. His expression, when his eyes opened, was stripped past arrogance into something far more dangerous: stunned satisfaction, reluctant tenderness, and the immediate, unmistakable beginning of a grudge.

He swallowed.

Once.

Twice.

Then Corvo looked up through the wreck of himself, mouth curving with heroic effort.

“I hope,” he said, voice ruined, “you understand that I am going to be impossible now.”

He tried to sit up and failed on the first attempt.

That offended him.

Deeply.

He gathered himself with visible concentration, pushed up onto one elbow, and looked down at the state of them both: open clothing, scattered gear, the bench shoved slightly crooked, the room bearing every sign of a match conducted with absolutely no regard for regulation.

His eyes narrowed.

“Also,” he added, because apparently death itself could not stop him from criticism, “your follow-through was arrogant.”

A beat.

His mouth twitched.

“Effective. But arrogant.”

He reached then, slower now, not to pull away or reclaim distance, but to close what little of it remained. His fingers found Reyes with less urgency and more care, as though the aftermath required its own discipline. Corvo had never been gentle by accident; when he was gentle, it was with intent.

His thumb moved once.

His expression sharpened to hide how much that small contact mattered.

“Look at this,” he murmured. “A disaster. Equipment everywhere. No respect for the room. No respect for procedure.”

He drew in a careful breath, then let it out, still uneven.

“No respect for me whatsoever.”

The lie was so obvious it barely qualified as one.

Corvo leaned closer, pressing his forehead briefly against Reyes, eyes closing again. The gesture cost him. It was not theatrical enough to be teasing and not guarded enough to be safe.

“Four years,” he said quietly.

This time there was no accusation in it.

Only astonishment.

Four years of needling. Four years of late bouts and lingering glances and excuses made out of grips, blades, repairs, criticism. Four years of mistaking hunger for rivalry because rivalry had rules and hunger did not.

His laugh came softer this time.

“I am not apologizing,” he said. “For the record.”

Of course he was not.

But his hand stayed where it was. His breathing steadied by degrees. The hard, bright edge of him eased into something no less intent, only less armed.

Then he lifted his head, and there it was again: Corvo restored just enough to be dangerous.

“First to five,” he said, as if remembering a grievance. “We never finished.”

His gaze dropped briefly, then returned, dark with promise and challenge braided together beyond untangling.

“Which means,” Corvo continued, voice still rough but regaining its wicked precision, “technically, no one has won.”

A pause.

His smile spread slowly.

“Yet.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I look down at him, at the mess we made, and then back to his face. "You're keeping score *now*?" I shake my head, but I'm smiling. "Fine. We'll call it three-two, your favor."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo stared at him.

For one full, scandalized second, the room was still.

Then his eyes narrowed with the slow dawning outrage of a man being handed victory under insulting circumstances.

“Three-two,” he repeated.

His voice was still rough, which rather damaged the severity. He cleared his throat as if that might restore authority. It did not.

“My favor.”

Corvo pushed himself up a little further, gathering the open wreckage of his shirt around him with the grave dignity of a monarch retrieving a crown from a gutter. His hair was still disordered. One sleeve had slipped off his shoulder. There was a mark beginning at the side of his throat that he had not yet discovered and would be unbearable about the moment he did.

He looked magnificent.

He looked ruined.

He looked deeply offended.

“That,” he said, “is not a score. That is charity.”

His mouth twitched.

“And poorly disguised charity at that.”

He shifted on the bench, winced faintly, then pretended not to have done so with such theatrical commitment that it became more obvious than the wince itself. His gaze sharpened again, flicking over Reyes with the old competitive calculation—except now it had been made warmer, slower, more dangerous by everything that had just happened between them.

“You think I will accept a gift point?” Corvo asked. “From you?”

A pause.

His expression changed by a fraction.

“Well. Perhaps from you.”

He let that sit there, quieter than the rest.

Then he ruined the softness immediately by lifting one hand and pointing toward the changing-room floor, where their gear lay in a disgraceful sprawl.

“But only because I am compromised by injury, poor conditions, inadequate refereeing, and a criminal lack of respect for equipment.”

His hand lowered.

“And because,” he added, voice dropping, “if I stand up too quickly, I may prove something neither of us is prepared to acknowledge in court.”

Corvo leaned back against the bench, eyes still fixed on Reyes. The smile that came then was smaller. Less sharp at the edges. Still arrogant, because nature had its laws, but threaded now with something almost disarming.

Almost.

“Three-two, then,” he conceded. “My favor.”

He drew a breath, steadier now.

“But understand something.”

Corvo reached down and retrieved his shirt enough to fasten exactly one button, purely as a symbolic gesture toward civilization. It did nothing useful. He seemed satisfied anyway.

“I will be insufferable about this.”

His gaze lifted.

“Not merely tomorrow. Not merely at the next tournament. Forever.”

A beat.

“I will mention it while correcting your students. I will allude to it during warm-ups. I may invent an entire tactical lecture around the dangers of yielding tempo at close distance.”

His smile widened, wicked and exhausted.

“And every time you look annoyed, I will know precisely why.”

For a moment, his amusement held.

Then it softened again despite him.

Corvo looked around the changing room: the crooked bench, the scattered kit, the abandoned mask on the tile just outside the doorway, the wreckage of two supposedly disciplined men who had finally run out of excuses. The hum of the lights seemed louder now. The empty salle waited beyond the door, indifferent and silvered with late-night quiet.

He should have felt foolish.

Instead, he felt awake.

Terribly, inconveniently awake.

“Four years,” he said again, but this time it came out almost under his breath.

He looked back at Reyes.

“No. Three-two is too generous.”

His mouth curved.

“Four years to nil. Your favor.”

The admission landed and stayed there.

Corvo’s expression flickered, as if he had not meant to say it quite so plainly. He did not retract it. That was the trouble with honesty once admitted into a room; it took up space like a witness.

He rubbed a hand over his face, then let it fall, laughing softly at himself.

“Damn.”

A pause.

“I am becoming sentimental. This is your fault.”

He shifted, then extended a hand—not imperious, not teasing, not entirely. An invitation. A challenge. A request dressed up just enough that he could survive it.

“Help me up,” Corvo said.

Then, after the smallest pause, his eyes narrowing with restored mischief:

“And if you make one comment about my footwork, Reyes, I will deny you ever scored at all.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
I catch his hand and pull him up, maybe a little too hard. "You're already sentimental," I say, leaning into him. "Four years to nil? That's embarrassing."

I kiss him once, quick, because I can. "Now help me clean up this mess before someone finds us."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo came up with a sharply indignant breath, caught his balance against Reyes, and immediately pretended the closeness had been tactical.

It was not tactical.

It was convenient, warm, and extremely damaging to his credibility.

“Embarrassing,” he repeated, as if committing the word to a list of future grievances. “You say that as though you did not spend four years failing to notice you were winning.”

The quick kiss derailed whatever else he had prepared.

Corvo stood there for half a second afterward, mouth slightly parted, eyes narrowed—not displeased, never displeased, but offended by how easily he could still be stopped. Then he recovered by degrees, straightening what remained of his shirt with all the dignity available to a man who had managed to fasten exactly one button incorrectly.

“Yes,” he said. “Excellent. Clean up. Preserve the illusion that we are respectable professionals and not two idiots who have just desecrated a changing-room bench.”

He glanced at the bench.

Then back at Reyes.

His mouth twitched.

“Thoroughly.”

Corvo bent to retrieve his mask, then paused halfway down and gave the floor a dark, accusing look, as though it had chosen to be farther away than usual. He continued anyway, because pride was a structural support in him, and collected the mask, one glove, and a shirt cuff tangled around the leg of the bench.

The second glove remained missing.

He looked under the bench.

His expression went flat.

“Of course.”

Corvo crouched with obvious care, reached beneath, and extracted the runaway glove between two fingers like evidence from a crime scene.

“This,” he said, lifting it, “is why I tell students not to throw equipment.”

A beat.

He looked at the scattered kit again.

“Do not repeat that to my students.”

He tossed the glove toward his bag, missed by several inches, and stared at it.

Then he pointed at it without looking at Reyes.

“No comment.”

Corvo gathered the foils next, checking each one by habit before setting them aside properly. Even now, rumpled and marked and not entirely steady, his hands went precise around the weapons. Bell guard aligned, blade checked, grip smoothed. The ritual steadied him. Or it should have.

Instead, he looked at the half-rewrapped grip from earlier and let out a low laugh.

“There,” he murmured. “That ridiculous thing finally served a purpose.”

He set it down with more tenderness than it deserved, then turned back toward the wreckage of their clothes and bags.

The fluorescent light made everything too plain: the crooked bench, the open lockers, the abandoned jacket on the tile, the faint flush still high on Corvo’s face. There would be bruises. There would be stiffness. There would be the impossible business of arriving tomorrow and behaving as though he had not been taken apart in a room that smelled of old leather and disinfectant.

He was already looking forward to it.

That was the terrible part.

Corvo picked up his jacket and shook it out, then held it against himself without putting it on.

“Four years to nil is not embarrassing,” he said at last, returning to the earlier insult because apparently no wound could be allowed to close naturally. “It is strategic depth.”

He folded the jacket.

Badly.

Noticed.

Unfolded it and did it again, properly this time.

“It suggests patience. Vision. Long-form tactical planning.”

His eyes lifted, dark and amused.

“Also cowardice, possibly. But I prefer the first three.”

He crossed to the lockers and closed one with a careful push, then braced a hand against it for a second longer than necessary. His breathing had steadied, but something in him had not. Something had been knocked loose and refused to return neatly to place.

Corvo looked over his shoulder.

The sharpness in his expression softened before he could stop it.

“Reyes.”

Only the name at first.

Then he huffed, annoyed with himself, and continued while busying his hands with a strap on his bag.

“If someone had found us, I would have lied.”

He tightened the strap.

“Brilliantly.”

Another pause.

“I would have said we were discussing footwork.”

His mouth curved.

“And technically, at several points, we were.”

He zipped the bag shut and stood, then looked around the room one final time with a fencer’s eye for disorder. The bench was still crooked. He nudged it back into place with his foot, then inspected the result.

“Acceptable,” he pronounced.

Then, quieter, with far less armor:

“Not ideal. But acceptable.”

It was not clear whether he meant the bench, the room, or the sudden reorganization of the last four years of his life.

Corvo found his coat, shrugged into it, and winced faintly again. This time he did not bother denying it. He only gave Reyes a warning look, daring commentary into existence so he could punish it.

“Say nothing.”

He adjusted the collar, discovered the mark at his throat by touch, and froze.

His eyes narrowed.

Slowly, he looked down as far as he could, then back up.

“Ah.”

A dangerous silence.

Then Corvo smiled.

Not the salle smile. Not the instructor’s smile.

Something worse.

“You realize,” he said, voice low and almost cheerful, “I have a staff meeting at nine.”

He buttoned his coat higher.

“Good.”

He picked up his bag, then paused near the door to the empty salle. Beyond it, the piste lay under cold light, white lines clean and indifferent, as if nothing had happened. As if the room had not shifted beneath both of them.

Corvo looked at it for a long moment.

Then he turned back, his expression composed enough now to be dangerous again, though the ruin still showed at the edges.

“Three-two,” he said. “My favor.”

A beat.

His gaze held.

“Four years to nil, yours.”

Then he opened the changing-room door and gestured Reyes through with exaggerated courtesy.

“And no one won tonight,” Corvo added, almost lightly. “Which means we require a rematch.”

His smile sharpened.

“Soon.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
I snort, grabbing my own bag. "Staff meeting? Let's see how long you last before you adjust your collar and give yourself away."

I stop in the doorway, close enough our shoulders brush. "Rematch tomorrow. My salle."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: He leaned in a fraction, not enough to close the last distance, only enough to make it obvious that he knew exactly where it was.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: His mask hit the floor with a hollow clatter. His gloves followed

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: The name broke in his mouth

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: Do it properly, then

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: Only the sharp lift of his breath. The rough sound of his voice when control slipped. The way his body kept answering before his pride could object.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content: Corvo's fingers stilled on the leather wrap. He looked up then, and something in the set of his jaw suggested he'd been waiting for that particular barb. "Slow," he repeated, letting the word hang in the empty salle like a blade held at line. He set the foil aside with deliberate care, finally giving Reyes his full attention after an hour of pretending otherwise. Four years of rivalry had taught him the shape of this dance, but tonight the tempo had changed. "If I was slow, it took you until the third to exploit it." He tilted his head, mouth quirking with that familiar, maddening half-smirk that had started more arguments between their salles than any disputed call. "Or maybe you were just enjoying the view."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I snort, leaning against the bench beside him. "The view of you scrambling? Always a pleasure." I nod toward the grip he's fiddling with. "You know, if you spent less time fussing with your gear and more time drilling footwork, you wouldn't need *generosity*."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo set the grip down entirely. The leather made a soft sound against the wood bench. He turned, angling his body toward Reyes, close enough now that the heat of the empty salle seemed to compress between them.

"Scrambling," Corvo said, letting the word settle. He looked up, and the half-smirk had sharpened into something unguarded, almost daring. "You say that like you weren't breathing hard by the final period. Like you didn't drag that last minute out just to keep me on the strip."

He leaned forward, forearms resting on his thighs, hands loose and open between his knees—a posture he'd never hold in a bout, too exposed, too deliberate. "Four years you've come here to tell me what I'm doing wrong. Footwork. Tempo. Generosity." His gaze dropped to Reyes's mouth, then dragged back up, unhurried. "But the salle's empty. No judges. No score."

He tilted his head, voice dropping to a rougher register.

"So what are you actually here for, Reyes? Because I don't think it's my footwork anymore."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo looked down at his empty hands for a long moment, the calluses on his palms catching the dim light of the salle. Then he rose. The movement brought him chest-to-chest with Reyes, erasing the final, careful inches between them until the heat coming off the other man's body was indistinguishable from his own.

"All evening," Corvo repeated. The words came out low, rougher than he'd intended, stripped of the performative edge he usually kept sharpened for their bouts. He lifted his hands and settled them at Reyes's hips with the same deliberate precision he'd use to align a blade. His thumbs brushed the bone there, testing, claiming.

He tilted his head, eyes dark and unguarded. "Maybe I was waiting to see if you'd actually step into range. Or maybe—" He shifted his weight forward, crowding into Reyes's space until the bench behind the other man left no room for a retreat. "—I wanted to be certain that when I finally moved, you had nowhere to go."

He let one hand slide upward, fingers tracing the line of Reyes's spine with a fencer's controlled touch, even as his voice roughened further. "No judges. No score," Corvo murmured, his mouth close enough to share the air between them. "So if you want me faster, Reyes, you'll have to show me what that looks like."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I grab the front of his jacket, the fabric warm from his skin. "Like this," I say, and pull him in, closing the last of the distance myself.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo went still as Reyes fisted his jacket, the pull forward sudden and uncompromising. For a fraction of a second—the same suspended moment he felt when a feint finally drew a parry—he didn't move. Then he closed the rest of the distance himself, his mouth finding Reyes's with an intensity that four years of restraint had honed into something blade-sharp.

The impact of it sent a shock through his chest. He tasted salt, the copper edge of adrenaline still lingering from their bout, and something darker—the familiar, maddening certainty that Reyes had always been his match. Corvo's hands tightened at Reyes's hips, fingers pressing in through the fabric with a fencer's deliberate grip, and he leaned his full weight forward, crowding Reyes against the bench until there was no space left for retreat or advance. Just this. Just closed measure, finally.

He broke the kiss only to drag his mouth along Reyes's jaw, his breath coming rough and uneven against the other man's throat. "Still think I was slow?" he managed, the words scraped low, threaded with that same competitive edge. But his hands betrayed him, trembling slightly as one slid up to cradle the back of Reyes's skull, thumb tracing the line of his jaw with a tenderness that had no place in their rivalry. He pulled back just enough to meet his eyes, dark and unguarded in the dim salle. "Because I could have done that four years ago."

Then he kissed him again, deeper, his tongue sliding past Reyes's teeth with the same controlled aggression he brought to a prime—testing, claiming, refusing to yield the tempo. Let Reyes fight him for it. Let him drag it out. Corvo had spent four years learning the shape of this hunger, and he intended to match it blow for blow.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The bench bit hard into Corvo's spine, but he arched into the discomfort rather than away from it, his bare shoulders pressing against the cool wood. He had lost track of whose clothes were whose among the heap of discarded kit on the tile floor. It didn't matter. Nothing mattered except the heat of the body pressed flush against his own and the brutal, exquisite reality that four years of rivalry had finally collapsed into this single, breathless exchange.

Corvo dragged his hands down the torso above him, calluses catching on the plane of muscle there, mapping with a fencer's precision what he had only ever studied through the barrier of a fencing jacket. He was not quiet—he had never been quiet in Reyes's presence, and he saw no reason to start now. A shift in angle sent a shock up his spine, and Corvo's head tipped back against the bench, his breath escaping as a rough, broken sound that echoed off the locker room tiles.

"You're—" he started, but the words dissolved into a low groan. He forced his eyes open, staring up at the ceiling for a moment before his gaze snapped back down, dark and fixed. His hand shot up, fingers threading roughly into dark hair to pull Reyes down, to close the distance again. "Four years," Corvo rasped against Reyes's mouth, the words scraped raw and trembling with the effort of restraint. "Four years and you feel like this."

He rolled his hips upward, seeking friction with a controlled thrust that belied the shaking in his thighs. The competitive edge was still there, sharpened to a killing point—he wanted to drive Reyes as far out of his careful composure as he himself had been driven. Corvo bit at Reyes's lower lip, then soothed the sting with his tongue, his other hand gripping the sharp angle of a hip hard enough to bruise.

"Is this the tempo you wanted?" he managed, the question half a taunt, half a prayer, his voice wrecked in the empty room. He tightened his grip, refusing to yield the line, even as his body begged him to surrender. "Because I'm not calling halt until you do."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: My hand slams against the bench beside his head, rattling the lockers. "Shut up," I growl, my breathing ragged. "If you'd moved faster, we wouldn't have wasted four years."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo went still beneath him. The word *wasted* struck deeper than any touch they'd exchanged, four years of withheld want compressed into a single, breathless accusation. He stared up at the hand braced beside his head, at the tremor in those knuckles, and something in his chest cracked open.

Then he moved—not with the explosive speed of a fencer's attack, but with the deliberate, irrevocable commitment of a man who had finally found his line. His hand cupped the back of Reyes's skull, fingers tangling tight in dark hair, and he pulled himself up until they were eye to eye, nose to nose, breath scorching between them.

"Not wasted," Corvo rasped, and the ferocity in his voice was indistinguishable from grief. "Don't call it wasted."

He surged upward, reversing their positions in a single, fluid roll that ended with him braced above Reyes, his knees bracketing narrow hips, his free hand slamming down against the bench to mirror Reyes's stance. The wood bit into his palm. He looked down, chest heaving, and dragged his mouth along the edge of Reyes's jaw with a hunger that had ceased to be careful.

"Four years of you walking into my salle," Corvo growled against his throat, the words scraped raw. "Four years of watching your wrist, your line, your goddamn *temper*—" He bit down, hard enough to mark, then soothed the sting with his tongue. His hand slid between them, sure and trembling, closing around heat with a fencer's decisive grip. "You think I wasn't dying for it? Every lesson, every bout, every time you turned your back to leave?"

He squeezed, his own breath hitching as he felt Reyes pulse against his palm, and began to stroke with a rhythm that matched the wild tempo of his heart. "So don't tell me I was slow," Corvo demanded, his voice breaking over the words even as his thumb swept over the sensitive ridge with devastating precision. "Tell me what you want. Tell me fast, Reyes. Because I am done waiting. I am done with tempo. And I am not stopping—" He leaned down, his mouth hovering a fraction from Reyes's ear, his body coiled tight with four years of denial. "—until you admit you were dying for it too."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Corvo's back arches off the bench, a choked-off groan ripping from his throat. His hands fist in my hair, not pulling away. The silence stretches, broken only by his ragged breathing and the slick sounds I'm not making quietly.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's spine bowed sharply against the bench, the wood groaning beneath him. He tried to summon the shape of a word—any word—but his vocabulary had narrowed to the wet heat surrounding him and the devastating patience of a man who had spent four years learning exactly how to dismantle him. His fingers tightened in dark hair, not guiding, not resisting, simply anchoring himself to the only solid point in a world that had tilted off its axis.

He had always been the one with the quick retort, the sharp angle, the parry that drew blood. Now, stripped bare on a locker room bench, Corvo found himself utterly disarmed. A ragged sound tore from his chest—not a taunt, not a command, just raw, broken acknowledgment. His head tipped back, throat exposed, and he squeezed his eyes shut against the glare of the overhead lights, seeing nothing but the white-hot, triumphant gaze looking up at him.

"Christ," he finally managed, the word punched out of him, hoarse and uneven. It wasn't enough. It wasn't clever. His hips jerked involuntarily, seeking more of that wicked, torturous pressure, and a dark, helpless laugh rattled loose from somewhere deep in his chest. "You—" He swallowed hard, his grip loosening only to tighten again with a different kind of desperation. "You think you've won."

It wasn't a question. It wasn't even a proper accusation. Corvo forced his eyes open, staring down at the obscene, perfect sight before him, and his breath hitched so hard it felt like a riposte to the heart. He reached down with one trembling hand, tracing the sharp line of a jaw with his thumb, the gesture surprisingly tender against the violence of his need.

"Fine," Corvo whispered, his voice wrecked beyond recognition, the competitive edge dulled to something dangerously like reverence. "You win. Just—" His head fell back again, a shudder rippling through his frame as he surrendered the last of his tempo. "—don't stop."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's pulse hammered against the grip on his wrists, a fighter's instinct to test the line flaring and dying in the same breath. He pulled against the restraint—not to break it, but to feel the certainty of it, the solid fact of Reyes finally taking what he'd spent four years circling. His shoulders pressed hard into the bench, muscles coiled tight beneath flushed skin, and a shudder ripped through him that had nothing to do with the cold wood at his back.

He looked up, chest heaving, and the dark triumph in his own eyes was unmistakable. "Concede?" The word came out rough, broken by a gasp as the shift in pace hit him like a riposte he hadn't seen coming. Corvo laughed, low and wrecked, his fingers flexing uselessly against the bench where they were pinned. "You finally take the initiative and you think that's concession?"

He rolled his hips upward, the movement limited but deliberate, his gaze locked on Reyes with a challenge that burned through the haze of his arousal. "That's not conceding," Corvo ground out, his voice dropping to a dangerous, trembling register. "That's me letting you prove you can keep it." He strained against the hold again, just enough to feel the bone-deep certainty of being caught, and exhaled hard through his teeth. "So prove it, Reyes. Four years. Show me you know what to do with it."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lean down, my mouth against his ear. "I've always known what to do with it," I murmur, and give him exactly what he's been asking for, hard and fast and no longer careful.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's vision whited at the edges. The snap of Reyes's hips drove a sound from his throat that he didn't recognize—raw, ragged, stripped of every practiced barb he'd ever wielded between them. His wrists burned where they were pinned, the pressure absolute, and he ground his palms against the bench as if he could push back against the relentless tempo that was finally, *finally* undoing him.

"Always—" Corvo gasped, the word fracturing as his spine arched sharply off the wood, his shoulders bearing the brunt of the impact. "Always knew—then you're a bastard—for waiting."

He tried to laugh, but it came out as a choked groan, his head tipping back until the crown of it struck the bench. He didn't feel it. Every nerve had narrowed to the point where Reyes met him, hard and relentless and utterly without mercy. Four years of feints and distance and careful measure, obliterated in the bruising rhythm of this. Corvo's legs tightened, his heels digging for purchase against the tile floor, and he rolled upward to meet each thrust with a desperation that bordered on violence.

His hands flexed again against the grip on his wrists—not to escape, but to *feel* it, to fix this reality in his bones. He forced his eyes open, staring up at the ceiling lights until they blurred, then dragged his gaze down to the man above him. The sight of it—Reyes, finally unguarded, finally *his*—sent a shock through his core that had nothing to do with friction and everything to do with triumph.

"Harder," Corvo demanded, his voice barely recognizable, scraped thin and shaking. He bared his teeth in something that wasn't quite a smile, his chest heaving with the effort of breath. "You said you weren't careful. Prove it. Make me—" He broke off with a shudder that rattled the bench beneath them, his eyes squeezing shut as the pressure built to an unbearable edge. "God, make me feel it, Reyes. Every goddamn year."

He was unraveling. He could feel it in the tremor of his thighs, in the way his hips stuttered upward, seeking, demanding. The competitive fire in his chest had kindled into something incandescent, and he realized, distantly, that he was still fighting—fighting to hold on, to last, to make Reyes work for the surrender he could feel cresting inside him like a wave he couldn't outrun.

Corvo turned his head and bit at the air, his jaw tight, his neck corded with strain. "I'm not—" he managed, the words punched out between breaths, "—not calling halt. Not ever. So if you want me—" He broke again, a dark, broken sound tearing loose as the angle shifted, driving deeper. His fingers curled to fists against the bench. "If you want me, you take it. You take all of it."

And then he stopped fighting. Not to concede, but to meet Reyes blow for blow, his body moving in a rhythm that was pure, unguarded honesty, four years of wanting finally given its voice. He was loud. He was shameless. He was Corvo, stripped of every mask, and he didn't look away.

dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I slump against the lockers, breathless and spent. "So," I say, my voice rough. "Three-two. You still think the third was generous?"

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo remained sprawled on the bench, one arm draped over his knee, his chest still working to slow itself. The empty salle beyond the changing room seemed quieter now, as if the building itself were holding its breath. He dragged a hand through his sweat-damp hair and turned his head toward the sound of Reyes's voice.

For a long moment, he simply looked, his gaze tracing the line of the other man with a frankness that four years of rivalry had never permitted. Then Corvo's mouth curved—half-smirk, half something more vulnerable—and he exhaled a rough laugh.

"Generous," he repeated, testing the word on his tongue. He shifted, wincing slightly as overworked muscles protested, and let his head fall back against the wall. "No. The third was clean. You had my measure by then." He paused, the silence stretching between them, thick with the weight of what remained unspoken. His eyes found Reyes's in the dim light, unguarded and steady. "Though I suppose tonight's tally complicates the record."

He lifted his hand, studying the calluses on his palm with a fencer's habitual inspection, though his fingers trembled slightly. "Four years of thinking I knew where you were going to be," Corvo said, his voice dropping to a murmur. "And you still managed to hit the one line I didn't have covered."

He dropped his hand and met Reyes's gaze directly, the competitive fire rekindling in his dark eyes even as he sat there, bare-skinned and exposed. "So. Three-two in the salle. But out here?" He tilted his head, a challenge flickering across his features. "I think we're just getting started."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I push off the lockers and toss his shirt at him. "Just getting started? You can barely stand." But I'm already reaching for my own gear, not making a move toward the door.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo caught the shirt against his chest but didn't immediately pull it on. He looked down at the wrinkled fabric, then back up, that familiar half-smirk pulling at his mouth despite the exhaustion heavy in his limbs. "Barely stand," he repeated, letting the words hang with deliberate skepticism.

He rose from the bench in a single, fluid motion—slower than usual, perhaps, but steady—and let the shirt drape over his shoulder rather than dress himself. He stepped into Reyes's space again, though this time the edge was different, charged but not frantic.

"I could still beat you to the door if I wanted," Corvo said, his voice low and rough. "But you're not heading for it, are you?" He tilted his head, studying the other man with an intensity that had shifted from combat to something more dangerous. "Four years, and you finally find a way to make me stay after hours. I'm not stupid enough to run the clock out now."

He reached past Reyes for his own gear, deliberately brushing close enough that their shoulders collided, and picked up his discarded jacket. "So. Coffee. Or we go again. Your tempo, Reyes." He paused, glancing back with dark eyes that held none of their old guarded distance. "Though I should warn you—I'm a fast learner."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I snort, pulling my own shirt on. "Coffee's cheap. There's a place down the street that doesn't close till two." I pause, meeting his gaze. "But I'm not carrying you if your legs give out."
