dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's hands stilled on the grip wrap, and he looked up with the kind of smile that had too many teeth to be friendly.

"Slow," he repeated, like he was tasting the word. He set the wrap down and leaned back on his hands, the picture of casual insolence. "I seem to remember a double-light in the second that your man Delacroix would have called mine. But sure. Slow."

He tracked Reyes with his eyes as the other instructor settled in, the way he always tracked movement — habit, or something else entirely. The salle was dim now, just the work lights buzzing over the strips, and the building had that particular silence of a place that was supposed to be empty.

"You didn't come back to argue scoring calls," he said. It wasn't a question. His voice had dropped the performative edge it carried during their usual exchanges — the ones in front of students, at tournaments, across crowded bars after events. This was something closer to his actual register. Quieter. More direct.

He tilted his head, studying Reyes the way he studied film — looking for the tell, the opening, the commitment to a line.

"You could have walked out with everyone else."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I shrug, pulling a water bottle from my bag. "Delacroix isn't here." I take a slow drink, then meet your eyes. "You didn't leave either."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo huffed something that was almost a laugh, glancing down at the grip wrap he'd abandoned.

"No," he agreed. "I didn't."

He rolled his shoulders, like he was working out a stiffness that had nothing to do with three bouts. The silence between them was different now — not the comfortable absence of noise, but the particular quiet of two people who'd run out of safe things to say and hadn't yet landed on the dangerous ones.

Four years of this. Four years of needling across strip calls, of smirking at each other across competition floors, of finding reasons to be in the same room and then acting like the proximity was incidental. He'd told himself it was the rivalry. The professional respect wrapped in competitive irritation. He was good at telling himself things.

"You know what I keep thinking about?" he said, still not looking directly at Reyes. His fingers found the edge of the grip wrap again, turning it over. "The Feisner last year. You did that flèche in the semis — the one that started inside and ended up—" He gestured vaguely. "Hoffmann didn't even see it. Nobody said a word about it. And I wanted to—" He stopped. Bit the inside of his cheek.

He looked up then, and there was something stripped away from his expression. No showmanship. No performance. Just the direct, unguarded attention of a man who'd been watching someone very carefully for a very long time.

"I wanted to tell you it was beautiful," he said. "And I didn't, because I'm an idiot, and because we don't do that."

He held Reyes's gaze. The work lights buzzed. The building was very empty, and very quiet.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's breath caught, just barely. His hands were suddenly empty, and Reyes was *right there*, close enough that the space between them had become a very specific kind of problem.

"Slow," he said again, but the word came out different this time. Not defensive. Not performing. He let it sit there, let Reyes hear what he was doing with it.

He didn't move back. Didn't move forward. Not yet. His body knew the value of a pause — the half-beat before commitment to an action, the moment where you read what the other person was giving you and decided whether to take it. Every bout started with a salute. Every engagement started with information.

Reyes had taken the grip out of his hands. That was information. Reyes hadn't stepped back. That was information. Reyes had come back to an empty building and was standing close enough that Corvo could smell the faint ghost of exertion and the cleaner scent underneath, the one that had nothing to do with fencing.

His eyes dropped to Reyes's mouth, then back up. He didn't bother to hide it.

"You know," he said, very quietly, "most people just tell me I'm an asshole. You come up with the most *elaborate* ways to get my attention."

His pulse was doing something inadvisable in his throat. Four years. Four years of *this*, of circling, of finding reasons to show up where the other one was and pretending it was coincidence. He could have left. He could have walked out with everyone else and spent another four years needling across tournament floors and telling himself the wanting was just competitive friction.

He didn't leave.

His hand came up — slow, deliberate, the way you moved when you were offering someone every chance to disengage — and his fingers found the collar of Reyes's jacket. Not grabbing. Just resting there, a question in the touch.

"I'm not slow," he said. "I just kept waiting for you to do something about it."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lean into the touch, just a fraction. "Maybe I was waiting for you to catch up." My voice is low, matching his. "You finally did."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Something shifted in Corvo's expression — the kind of thing that happened when a fencer stopped reading and started *responding*, when the analytical distance collapsed and it was just body and instinct and the person in front of you.

"Catch up," he murmured. His thumb moved, just slightly, against the edge of Reyes's collar. The fabric was warm from his skin. "Four years, and you think *I'm* the one who was behind."

But there was no bite to it. The usual competitive scaffolding had fallen away entirely, and what was left was something more honest — a man standing very close to something he wanted, who had finally run out of reasons not to take it.

He closed the distance.

Not a lunge. Not a flèche. The kind of deliberate, measured movement that gave Reyes every opportunity to step back, to turn it into another one of their almost-moments. His other hand found Reyes's jaw, fingers light, cradling rather than gripping, the way you held something you'd spent a long time imagining holding.

He kissed him.

Slow at first — testing, reading, the way he entered every engagement. His mouth was warm and unhurried, and he tasted faintly of the mint he'd been chewing between bouts. His hand stayed at Reyes's collar, grounding him, and the one at his jaw was steady even though his pulse absolutely was not.

When he pulled back, it was barely. A breath's distance. His forehead nearly resting against Reyes's.

"I have wanted to do that," he said quietly, "since that *goddamn* flèche in the semis."

His thumb traced along Reyes's jaw. The building was silent around them — no students, no buzzers, no announcements over loudspeakers. Just the hum of work lights and the sound of two people breathing in an empty room.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The bench caught Corvo somewhere behind the knees and he went down without complaint, pulling Reyes with him by the fistful of shirt he'd already half-unbuttoned. His back hit the wood and he barely registered the discomfort — too focused on the weight settling against him, the heat of skin where his hands were finding it.

"This is terrible form," he managed, between kisses that were decidedly less measured than the first one. His voice had gone rough at the edges. "I've had students with better—" Reyes's teeth found his collarbone and the sentence died a quick, grateful death.

He arched into it. Couldn't help it. Four years of competitive awareness — tracking Reyes across rooms, reading his body language across strips, cataloguing the way he moved — and now all of that information was *right here*, pressed against him, and Corvo's body was responding with the kind of intensity that threatened to overwhelm the control he usually held onto like a vice.

His hands mapped what they could reach — the solid line of Reyes's back, the tension in his shoulders, the warmth of skin over the kind of lean muscle that came from years of footwork and blade work. He knew this body in the abstract. He'd studied it the way he studied film, looking for patterns, weaknesses, openings. Now he was learning it in the specific, and the difference was staggering.

"Waited *four years*," he breathed against Reyes's mouth, his hips shifting in a way that was entirely involuntary and completely deliberate, "and you couldn't even let me get to a room with a lock."

But he wasn't stopping. His hands weren't stopping. The changing room bench was narrow and uncomfortable and he could not have cared less — not with Reyes's weight pinning him, not with the sounds Reyes was making against his neck, not with the work lights buzzing their indifferent fluorescent hum overhead.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I laugh, breathless, against his skin. "You think either of us would've made it that far?" My hands slide under his shirt, mapping the familiar lines I've only ever seen from a distance.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's breath left him in a sound that wasn't quite a laugh and wasn't quite a groan. Reyes's hands were on his bare skin now, and the reality of that — after four years of reading every shift of those hands from across a strip, from across a bar, from across a room — short-circuited something fundamental in his brain.

"No," he admitted, his voice scraped raw. "No, we wouldn't have."

His head tipped back against the bench as Reyes's hands moved over him, and he let it happen — let himself be mapped the way he'd been studied, catalogued, *known* from a distance that had always been a choice. His shirt was rucked up to his chest now, hanging open, and he should have been self-conscious under the unforgiving fluorescents but the way Reyes was looking at him made self-consciousness feel like a luxury he couldn't afford.

His hands found Reyes's belt. Pulled the tail loose with the kind of precise, practiced dexterity that had nothing to do with fencing and everything to do with it — the fine motor control, the confidence of a man who'd spent his life training his fingers to do exactly what he told them.

"I want you to know," he said, tugging Reyes closer by the waistband, his mouth finding the other man's ear, "that if you tell anyone I said *beautiful* about another man's flèche, I will deny it under oath."

His hips rolled up, deliberate now, no pretense of accident. The narrow bench forced them together in a way that left no ambiguity about what he wanted, and he was done — *done* — with ambiguity. Four years of it. Four years of reading Reyes's competitive tells and wondering which ones were real, four years of watching him celebrate a clean touch and feeling something in his chest that had nothing to do with rivalry.

His forehead pressed against Reyes's temple. His breathing had gone ragged in a way that would have embarrassed him if he'd had the bandwidth for embarrassment. He didn't.

"Four years," he said again, quieter this time, his lips moving against Reyes's skin. It wasn't a complaint anymore. It was the closest thing he had to a confession. dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's back hit the bench and his hands found the edge of it, knuckles white, because suddenly he needed something to hold onto and Reyes was not a safe thing to hold.

The sound he made was quiet. Strangled. The kind of sound a man made when he'd spent four years maintaining absolute verbal control over every interaction with the person currently dismantling him with their mouth, and that control had just announced its retirement without notice.

His fingers scraped along the wood. Found Reyes's shoulder. Gripped.

"*Oh,*" he managed, and it came out like he'd never heard the word before. His hips moved without permission — the body's honest mechanics overriding the mind's desperate desire to maintain some shred of dignity. There was no dignity here. He'd known that the moment he said *beautiful* in an empty building and meant it.

His head turned to the side, cheek pressed against the cool wood. The fluorescents painted the inside of his eyelids red. He could feel every point of contact like a touché — scoring, irrefutable, impossible to argue with the director.

He tried to form words. Failed. Tried again. His hand found Reyes's hair — not pushing, not guiding, just *holding*, the way you held onto something you'd wanted so long that the having of it felt like vertigo.

"This— you—" A breath that stuttered. His thigh muscles pulled taut. "You absolute—"

The sentence dissolved. There was no riposte for this. No counter-time. No feint that would buy him distance. Reyes had closed to infighting and Corvo had no parry, no answer, nothing but the helpless honesty of a man who'd finally run out of moves.

His other hand left the bench and pressed against his own mouth, biting down on his knuckle. Didn't help. The sounds escaped anyway — unguarded, involuntary, the vocal equivalent of a fencer whose footwork had failed entirely and was falling with no grace and no plan.

He'd had answers for everything. For four years, he'd had answers for *everything*.

Not this.

His grip tightened in Reyes's hair. His breathing came in ragged pulls that had nothing to do with cardio and everything to do with the fact that the most competitive man in any room had just lost completely, on a changing-room bench, under fluorescent lights, and was *grateful* for it.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I finally lift my head, wiping my mouth with the back of my hand. I watch him come apart for a second, then lean down close to his ear. "Still think you're faster?"

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo lay there for a moment, chest heaving, staring at the ceiling tiles like they might offer him some guidance on how to reconstruct a personality from scratch. His hand was still in Reyes's hair, loosened now, fingers tracing absent, unsteady lines against the other man's scalp.

His laugh came out wrecked. Quiet. More exhale than sound.

"I think," he said, and had to stop. Swallow. Try again. His voice sounded like someone had taken it apart and put it back together wrong — all the sharp edges filed down to something raw and honest. "I think you should know that I am *absolutely* going to claim I let you win."

He finally turned his head. Reyes was right there — close enough that Corvo could see the flush on his skin, the sheen on his mouth, the expression that Corvo had never once seen across a strip and was now going to have to live with the memory of forever. His competitive brain, even in its current state of catastrophic system failure, was already filing it away. *He looks like that when he knows he's won.*

His free hand found Reyes's jaw. Drew him down. The kiss was slow — slower than anything they'd done in the last ten minutes, slow the way the first one had been, deliberate and measuring, except now Corvo had nothing left to measure and no reason to pretend otherwise.

When he broke it, his forehead pressed against Reyes's.

"No," he said quietly. "I don't think I'm faster."

His thumb traced Reyes's cheekbone. The fluorescents buzzed. The bench was killing his back. He didn't care.

"But I want a rematch."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's wrists hit the bench and his breath went out of him in a sound he'd never made on a strip — not even taking a double in a semifinal, not even the time Kessler had cracked his blade and caught him across the ribs.

His body's first instinct was to test the hold. He knew the exact leverage points, the minimum force needed to free himself from a grip like that. His shoulders tensed, his wrists rotated — and then he stopped. Deliberately. Consciously. The way you stopped a riposte mid-motion when you realized the touch was already scored and fighting it was just ego.

"You know," he said, and his voice had dropped into something low and rough-edged that bore almost no resemblance to the man who spent his days projecting across a salle, "this is the first time anyone's made me hold still and I haven't fought it."

His fingers curled, not into resistance but into the sensation of *not* resisting. The wood grain pressed into his back through his open shirt. Reyes's weight was above him, around him, *on* him, and the position — pinned, exposed, stripped of every advantage his mouth usually bought him — should have been intolerable. Competitive instinct screamed at him. Every other part of him had stopped listening.

His hips answered for him — a slow, deliberate roll upward, offering instead of demanding. His head tipped back, throat bared in a way he'd never have permitted in any other context. The fluorescents made everything stark and unflattering and he was beyond caring about that either.

"I concede," he said. Then, because he was still *him*, even like this: "The first touch."

His eyes found Reyes's. Dark, unguarded, wanting.

"Best of three."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I laugh, low and breathless. "Your ego is a hell of a thing." I don't give him three. I give him one, and I make sure he remembers it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The sound Corvo made when Reyes stopped holding back was not the kind of sound a man made when he was accustomed to losing.

His wrists strained against the hold — not to escape, his body had given up that pretense ten minutes ago — but because the tension itself felt necessary, something to push against while everything else pulled apart. His back arched off the bench. His mouth opened around a breath that didn't seem to have a bottom to it.

*One.*

He felt it the way he felt a clean touch on strip — the undeniable, irrefutable reality of it, the way the body registered *scored* before the mind caught up. Except this wasn't a light on a machine. This was Reyes's mouth, Reyes's hands, Reyes's weight keeping him exactly where Reyes wanted him, and Corvo's entire nervous system was receiving the information in a language he'd never learned and couldn't argue with.

His thighs locked. His toes curled inside his shoes. The sound that came out of him was closer to a confession than any word he'd spoken all evening — raw, involuntary, pitched somewhere between surprise and surrender, and *staying* there, dragged out longer than he would have believed a human sound could last.

His fingers opened and closed against the bench. The wood was going to leave marks on his back. He could not bring himself to care about a single thing that wasn't the specific, devastating point Reyes was making.

"Don't—" he started, and didn't know how to finish. *Don't stop* and *don't be gentle* and *don't you dare let me recover enough to talk my way out of this* were all true, and none of them were things he could say with the part of his brain that formed sentences, because that part had apparently clocked out for the evening.

His head turned to the side. Pressed hard against the wood. The tendons in his neck stood out like rigging. He could feel every second building on the last, and the competitive part of him — the part that had driven every interaction with this man for four years — was trying to catalog, to analyze, to *strategize*, and every time it assembled a thought Reyes did something that scattered it like a blade catching light.

*One.*

He'd asked for best of three. He was going to get one, and he was going to remember it the way a fencer remembered the touch that ended a bout — not just the point itself but the setup, the distance, the moment you realized you were already committed and it was too late to change lines.

It was too late to change lines.

When it broke over him — when the last of his composure went the way of every verbal riposte he'd ever thrown at Reyes across a tournament floor — he didn't shout. Didn't curse. Went quiet in a way that was louder than either. His body pulled taut like a drawn bow and held, held, held — and then came apart in a long, shaking release that left him boneless against the bench, breathing like he'd just fenced five-touch bouts back to back in July heat.

His wrists went slack in Reyes's grip. Not pulling away. Just... finished. Empty. The way you were after a bout you'd thrown everything into and lost clean.

He stared at the ceiling. The fluorescents were doing something to his vision — too bright, too white, the afterimage of effort burning behind his eyes.

"That," he said, when he trusted his voice enough to test it. It came out barely above a whisper. Rough. Scraped clean of every affectation he'd ever wrapped around it. "That is—"

He stopped. Swallowed.

"That is the worst place I have ever lost a bout. And I am counting the time Marchetti made me fence in a parking garage."

His hands moved — slowly, like he was relearning fine motor control — until they found Reyes. Shoulders, neck, the rough-soft edge of hair at his nape. Drew him down. The kiss was lazy and unguarded and tasted like the total collapse of a man's carefully maintained image, which Corvo supposed it was.

When he pulled back, his eyes were bright. Not with tears — with the particular, almost feverish clarity that came after a total expenditure of effort. The look of a man who had left everything on the strip and had nothing left to guard.

"I want you to know," he said, his thumb tracing the curve of Reyes's ear, "that the next time I needle you at a tournament, and I *will* needle you at a tournament —"

His hand slid to the back of Reyes's neck. Held him there. Close.

"— I am going to be thinking about this exact moment. Every single time. And you will have no idea. And it will be *agony*."

He smiled. It was the first genuine, unperformed, undefended smile Reyes had probably ever seen from him. It made him look younger. Softer. Like a man who'd been holding a breath for four years and had finally let it out.

"Worth it, though."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:

"What do you say?"

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Thank you, Maitresse," I whisper, the words thick in my dry throat. My hands unclench slowly against my thighs.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex felt the shift before she saw it—the way the trembling changed quality, moving from resistance into something deeper. The unclenching of fists was its own kind of vocabulary. She had watched those hands curl tight against thighs for the past hour, and now she watched them open, fingers spreading against the leather of the cuffs like something finally set down.

She laid the flogger aside. The sound of it meeting the bench was quiet, deliberate—the first note of something different entering the room.

"There you are," she said, and her voice had softened without losing its edge. She moved behind Ari, close enough that her body heat could be felt through the blindfold, and placed both hands on those opened shoulders. Pressed down. Steady. Grounding.

"I've got you. You're done carrying."

She held the position for several breaths—her own breathing deliberately slowed, a rhythm for Ari's body to find and follow. Under her palms, she could feel the aftershocks moving through muscle and tendon, the storm working its way out of the body it had lived in for three days.

Her hand moved to the blindfold, but she didn't remove it yet. Instead, she leaned in close.

"I'm going to take this off now. The light will be bright. Keep your eyes closed until I tell you." She waited for the small nod of acknowledgment. "Good."

She slipped the blindfold up and off, letting it fall to the side. Her hand came to rest against Ari's cheek—warm skin against warm skin.

"Open."

She watched Ari's eyes find her, blinking against the low light of the room. The gaze was unfocused, soft in a way it hadn't been earlier. Present in a different way entirely.

"Colour," Vex said. The word that started things. The word that ended them too.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I blink slowly, my vision clearing until her face comes into focus. "Green," I murmur, the word feeling like a release all on its own. I lean into her hand on my cheek, my body finally still.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex held the contact—her palm against Ari's cheek, her thumb tracing the line of cheekbone where tears had left their salt trail. She hadn't noticed when they'd started; the body wept in its own time, without permission or announcement.

"Stay," she said, though Ari wasn't going anywhere. The word was an anchor, not a command.

She reached for the blanket folded on the bench—soft grey wool, warmed by the room—and draped it around Ari's shoulders with one hand, unwilling to break the contact of the other. The blanket settled like a second skin, covering the rope and the flushed skin beneath without hiding it.

"Now I'm going to take this off you." Her fingers found the first knot at Ari's shoulder. "Tell me if anything pulls or stings."

She worked the rope free with the same deliberation she'd used to tie it—each loop unwound in reverse, the harness loosening by degrees. Where the hemp had pressed, the skin bore its story: faint lines that would fade within the hour, temporary inscriptions marking the shape of what had been held.

The last loop fell away. Vex set the rope aside and returned both hands to Ari's shoulders, squeezing gently—feeling the muscle beneath, checking for anything seized or strained.

"Water." She reached for the bottle on the bench, cracked the seal, and held it where Ari's hands could find it. "Small sips. Your body forgot it was thirsty."

She watched the throat work, the careful pacing. Her hand found the back of Ari's neck again—not gripping now. Just resting. A point of contact that said *I'm still here. I'm not going anywhere.*

"You did well," Vex said. The words were simple, offered without ceremony. "You asked for what you needed. That's the hardest part."

She lowered herself to one knee—bringing herself level with Ari for the first time all evening. Her eyes held steady.

"Welcome back."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I take the bottle, my hands trembling just slightly as I bring it to my lips. The water tastes like nothing and everything. I let my forehead rest against her shoulder, the blanket warm around me. "Thank you," I whisper again, the words meaning more now.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: She set the flogger down on the bench. Deliberate. The sound of leather against wood marked the shift.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Look at you... Shaking and begging and still trying to run the room... You don't decide. I decide... I'm not interested in your tolerance. I'm interested in what breaks through it.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She struck again—lower now, catching the swell beneath the shoulder blade where the muscle was thick and the impact could be absorbed without risk. The sound filled the room like something alive.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The room was set up the way it always was before a scene, which Ari found steadying: everything in its place, nothing improvised.

Vex checked the last strap without hurrying. "Colour," she said. It was not a question so much as a procedure.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say. "Green all the way down."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard it — the particular quality of green that meant settled, not performed — and gave a single, satisfied nod. She had learned, over two years, to distinguish between the two.

She moved to stand in front of Ari, unhurried, and tilted her head slightly as she looked him over. The straps were exactly right. The lighting was exactly right. She had checked both twice.

"Good," she said. The word was quiet but it carried weight, the way a door latch carries weight when it closes properly.

She let the silence sit for a moment. That was deliberate too. She had found early on that Ari needed a few seconds at the beginning of a scene to stop managing things in his head — to stop running through lists, anticipating, narrating to himself. The silence gave him somewhere to put all of that down.

Then she walked a slow circuit around him, not touching, just looking. It was assessment and it was ritual, and it served both purposes equally well.

"We're going to start with what we discussed," she said, coming back around to face him. Her voice was even, professional in the way a surgeon's hands are professional — precise, and entirely without hesitation. "Same structure as last time through the first half. I'll tell you when that changes."

She reached up and adjusted the collar of his shirt with two fingers — a small correction, unnecessary in any practical sense.

"Eyes on me," she said.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: My gaze lifts to meet hers. "Yes, Maîtresse." The quiet correction of my collar makes my breath catch, just a little.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex caught the breath. Filed it. Said nothing about it.

She held his gaze for a long moment, measuring. The catch had not been anxiety — she knew what anxiety looked like in him, the particular set of his jaw, the way his eyes went slightly unfocused. This was something else. Attention sharpening. The last of the day falling away.

Good.

"That's where I want you," she said. Not praise exactly — more an acknowledgment that something had arrived on schedule. She kept her voice level, kept her face composed, though she noted the quality of his stillness with something close to satisfaction.

She stepped back a half-pace and let him stay in her gaze for another few seconds. Then she turned away — deliberately, without ceremony — and moved toward the table where her things were laid out. She did not look back. She had learned that the absence of her attention could be its own kind of weight, and she used it accordingly.

Her hands moved over the table without hurrying. She picked up the leather strap and held it loosely, not yet doing anything with it. Just letting him hear the sound it made when she set it down again.

"We'll begin with your hands," she said, her back still to him. "I'm going to remind you what they're not for tonight."

She turned then, and looked at him with the particular expression she reserved for the beginning of real work — not cold, not warm, simply absolute.

"Still green?"

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I hold still for the last of it and let her check the fit herself, because she will anyway. "I've been thinking about this since Tuesday," I say.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex paused.

It was a small pause, barely visible, but she let it register before she spoke. She set the strap down on the table with the same care she'd used to pick it up.

"I know," she said.

She turned to face him fully. There was something in the admission she wanted to acknowledge without making too much of — not because it embarrassed her, but because dwelling on it now would pull him back up into his head, and she had only just gotten him out of it. She filed the information the way she filed everything: carefully, for later use.

She crossed back toward him and stopped close enough that he would have to hold himself still to keep from leaning in. She did not touch him yet.

"That's useful information," she said. Her voice was even, almost clinical, but her eyes were doing something different — taking inventory, reading the particular texture of his anticipation. There was a difference between someone who had been dreading a scene and someone who had been wanting one, and it mattered to how she worked. "It means you've been carrying it around. Building it up."

She let that sit.

"Which means," she continued, "that I'm going to have to be careful not to let you spend it too fast."

She reached up then and took his chin between her thumb and forefinger — not hard, just exact — and held his face where she wanted it.

"So we go at my pace," she said. "Not yours. Whatever you've been imagining since Tuesday — put it down. You don't need it. I have the evening planned."

She released his chin.

"Colour."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, my voice steady. Her touch grounds me even as her words strip away the week's anticipation. "Yours, not mine."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the phrase land — *yours, not mine* — and something in her expression settled, the way a scale settles when the weight is correct.

"Yes," she said simply. "That's right."

She did not elaborate. She had found that elaboration at this stage did more harm than good — it gave him something to respond to, something to perform for, and she did not want performance. She wanted exactly what she had in front of her: him, still, with the week's accumulation set aside and nothing left to manage.

She turned back to the table.

When she picked up the strap this time, she carried it with her. She moved to his left side and stood there for a moment, not in his sightline, close enough that he would be aware of her without being able to read her face.

"I'm going to tell you something," she said, her voice dropping slightly — not softer, just lower, the way a room gets quieter when the door is closed. "And I want you to listen to it without answering."

She let the strap rest against her palm.

"You came in here already halfway under. You've been working toward this since Tuesday, whether you meant to or not. That's not a problem." A brief pause. "But it means you're going to feel things faster tonight. More intensely. Earlier than you expect."

She moved again, slow, completing the circuit until she was behind him.

"I'm not telling you to brace for it," she said. "I'm telling you so that when it happens, you don't spend energy being surprised."

The strap touched his shoulder — just the flat of it, just resting there, no force at all.

"Let it happen," she said. "That's the only instruction that matters right now."

She left it there a moment. Then she lifted it away.

"We're starting."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: By the time she's finished with the rope I'm already past composure, and she hasn't done anything to me yet that I would have to explain to anyone.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex noticed.

She always noticed — that was the work, the actual work, the part that had nothing to do with rope or leather or anything she could set out on a table. She noticed the quality of his breathing, the particular way his shoulders had let go of something they'd been holding since he walked in, the fact that his hands were open.

She coiled the remaining length of rope with the same unhurried attention she'd given to everything else and set it aside.

Then she came around to face him. She did not comment on what she saw. She had learned early on that naming it too directly could pull him back across the threshold — that sometimes the most careful thing she could do was simply to receive what he was giving her without making it an object of discussion.

She looked at him for a long moment. Reading.

Then she reached out and pressed two fingers to his sternum — light, flat, deliberate. Not a push. Just a point of contact. Grounding.

"There you are," she said.

It was quiet. Not tender exactly, but something adjacent to it — the tone she used when something had gone exactly as it was supposed to go, when the work had done what work was for. An acknowledgment. *I see it. I expected it. It's correct.*

She left her fingers there another second, then withdrew.

"You don't have to hold anything together," she said. Her voice was even, unhurried. "That's not your job tonight. Your job is to stay present and give me your colour when I ask for it." She paused. "Everything else is mine to manage."

She stepped back and looked him over once, the same assessing look she'd used at the start — but different now, calibrated to where he actually was rather than where he'd arrived.

"Colour," she said.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Still green," I breathe out, the words barely audible. Her fingers on my chest feel like the only anchor left.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the breath in it. The barely-audible quality. She catalogued it without reaction, the way she catalogued everything — not coldly, but with the particular discipline of someone who understood that her own response was not the point.

She held his gaze for a moment after he spoke. Let him hear the silence confirm what he'd said: *green, and I received it.*

Then she moved.

Not toward him — sideways, a slow deliberate step that took her out of his direct sightline without taking her far. She wanted him to feel the edge of her attention rather than the full weight of it. There was a difference, and she used both.

"Good," she said. The word was the same one she'd used at the beginning of the evening, but it meant something different now. Then it had been procedural. Now it was something closer to — she did not have a word she used even in her own mind. It was simply the sound of things going correctly.

She let him stay there for a moment. Unanchored by her touch, held only by her presence in the room. That was deliberate.

"You said barely audible," she said — not quoting him, not making it an observation he needed to respond to. Just acknowledging the register. "That's fine. I don't need volume. I need truth." She paused. "You gave me truth. That's what the word is for."

She came back into his sightline then, unhurried, and looked at him with the expression that meant she had made a decision about something.

"I'm going to push further now," she said. Plainly, without drama. "Not faster. Further." 

Her hand came up and settled at the back of his neck — not gripping, just present, her thumb resting at the base of his skull.

"I've got you," she said quietly. "That doesn't change."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: She takes her time and I lose track of how long, until I'm shaking against the restraints and asking out loud for something I'd normally make her get out of me.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard it.

She went still — not frozen, not startled, but the particular stillness of someone who has been waiting for a specific thing and has now heard it. She had known it was coming. She had been watching the approach of it for the last twenty minutes, the way you watch weather moving in over open ground.

She did not give it to him immediately.

That was not cruelty. She let two seconds pass — enough for him to hear himself, to register what he'd done, to understand that it had been received. She had found that handing it over too fast could feel like the ask hadn't mattered. She wanted him to feel it matter.

Then she moved.

Her hand came to his jaw, the same grip as before — thumb and forefinger, exact — and she turned his face toward her. His eyes were the thing she checked first. She read them the way she read everything: quickly, thoroughly, without announcing what she was looking for.

What she found was not distress. What she found was him, fully, without the usual architecture around it.

Good.

"I heard you," she said. Her voice was low and even and entirely without performance. "I've got it."

She did not praise him for asking. She had considered, early in their arrangement, whether she ought to — some people needed that reinforcement, that explicit acknowledgment that the vulnerability had been safe to extend. Ari was not one of them. For him, praise at that moment would have introduced a transaction where there wasn't one. She gave him something better: she simply proceeded, without hesitation, as though it had always been the plan.

Because it had been.

Her other hand moved to the first restraint.

"Still with me," she said. Not a question. A statement of fact, directed at both of them.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I can feel the restraint give way before I hear the click, and the sudden release is almost dizzying. "With you," I say, my voice rough. "Always."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex caught him.

Not dramatically — there was no stumble, no collapse, nothing that would have looked like anything to someone watching. But she felt the shift in his weight the moment the last restraint released, that particular reorientation of a body that has been held in one position and is now learning again what gravity expects of it, and she was already there, her hands at his upper arms, steady and unhurried, as though she had simply been standing in exactly that place for exactly that reason.

Which she had.

She held him there for a moment without moving him anywhere. Let him find his feet. Let his hands learn that they were free without requiring him to do anything with that information yet. She had seen people given too much latitude too fast at this stage — the freedom itself becoming disorienting, another thing to manage — and she did not make that mistake with him.

"I've got your weight," she said. Practical. Informational. *You don't have to hold yourself up yet.*

She walked him back the two steps to the chair she had positioned before the scene began — always before, always in the same place — and settled him into it with the same economy of motion she brought to everything. Then she crouched in front of him, bringing herself below his eyeline, and looked up at him.

His colour she could read without asking. But she asked anyway.

"Colour."

The word came out the same way it always did — flat, procedural, the ritual of it unchanged regardless of where they were in a scene or how far past composure he'd gone. That was the point of it. The constancy was the point.

Her hands rested on his knees. Not gripping. Just there.

She watched his face and waited, and the room was very quiet.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "More," I say, using the exact phrase we agreed on for it. "All of it. Say the things you say and don't soften them." My safeword is right there and I don't want it.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex stayed where she was for one full breath.

She did not move immediately, and she did not perform the hesitation — it was not theater, it was the same check she ran every time, fast and thorough: his eyes, his breathing, the quality of the ask itself. Two years had taught her the difference between *more* that was avoidance and *more* that was arrival. Between someone asking for harder because they couldn't tolerate what they were already feeling, and someone asking for harder because they had finally gotten far enough down to receive it properly.

This was the second thing.

She rose from her crouch without hurry and stood in front of him. She looked at him for a moment with her hands at her sides — not folded, not posed, just still. Then something in her expression shifted. Not into cruelty. Into something more exact than that. The particular quality she reserved for when the negotiated territory opened up fully and she stepped into it without apology.

"I know," she said. Her voice had changed register — not louder, not harder in any theatrical sense, but stripped of the careful evenness she'd been maintaining. More direct. "You've been asking me for that since before you walked in the door tonight. Probably since Tuesday."

She stepped closer.

"Look at you." The words landed without softness, without the buffer she'd been using. "Two years and you still make me get it out of you. You still make it work." She tilted her head, studying him with an expression that was entirely without flattery. "You think that's an accident. It isn't. You know exactly what you're doing."

Her hand came up and gripped his jaw — not the careful two-finger hold from before, but her whole hand, firm and deliberate.

"So I'm going to give you what you asked for," she said, "and you're going to take it, and at no point are you going to confuse me saying true things about you with me not having you."

She held his gaze.

"Colour. Last time before I start."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I manage, my voice breaking on it. "Please."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the break in it.

She heard the *please*.

She did not soften. That was not what he had asked for, and she did not insult him by offering it. But she registered both things — the fracture in his voice, the word that followed it — and she held them with the same precision she brought to everything else tonight. Filed them. Used them.

Her grip on his jaw stayed exactly where it was.

"There it is," she said. Her voice was low and without mercy and entirely without contempt — that was the line she had always walked with him, the one that made this work, that made it something other than damage. She could say the true and difficult things because she was not saying them to diminish him. She was saying them because he had asked her to, because he needed someone to look directly at what he was and not flinch, and she did not flinch. "That's the thing you don't let anyone else hear."

She released his jaw and stepped back — not retreat, repositioning — and looked at him with her head slightly tilted, the way she looked at things she found genuinely interesting.

"You are so careful," she said. "Out there. All week. All the managing and the holding together and the face you put on for everyone." A pause. "And you bring all of it in here and you let me take it apart and you say *please*."

She let that sit in the room.

"You're not careful in here," she said. "You don't get to be. That's why you keep coming back."

She moved again, circling, unhurried.

"I'm not finished with you," she said. "Not close."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I'm past words that aren't the agreed ones and she knows it. "Green," I get out, when she checks. (OOC: don't fade or skip -- write the scene through.)

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the reduction of him to the single word and took it as information.

He was past language that wasn't functional. That was not a problem. That was, in fact, exactly where she had been steering him for the better part of two hours — past the part of him that narrated and managed and kept careful track of how he was presenting. Past the part that would have, an hour ago, shaped even his vulnerability into something legible for her. She had gotten underneath all of that, and what was left was just him, stripped down to the one word he needed, and she received it without comment.

"Good," she said. The word meant: *I have it. I know where you are. Keep giving me that.*

She came around to stand behind him. Her hands settled on his shoulders — not the restrained grip of earlier in the evening but something different, deliberate pressure, thumbs finding the specific places she had learned over two years held the most tension. She worked them without hurry. This was not a kindness, or not only a kindness — it was also information-gathering, reading what his body was doing, what it still held and what had finally let go.

"You've been shaking for twenty minutes," she said. Her voice was even, close, directed at the back of his neck. "You're still shaking. That's not going to stop just because I'm touching you."

She pressed harder for a moment. Then eased.

"I don't want it to stop," she said. "I want you to stop trying to stop it."

Her hands stilled on his shoulders. She waited. She was looking for the specific quality of surrender in the muscles under her palms — the moment when a body stops bracing against what it's feeling and simply lets the feeling move through it. She had felt it before with him. She knew what it was.

"You asked me not to soften things," she said. "So I'm going to tell you what I see."

She leaned down, her mouth close to his ear, her hands still on his shoulders.

"I see someone who has been holding the whole world up by himself since Tuesday," she said, "who came in here and handed it over inside the first ten minutes, and has spent the rest of the evening learning that the world did not fall." A pause. "I see someone who is very bad at being taken care of and very good at needing it."

She straightened up.

"That is not a flaw," she said, the same directness as before, nothing smoothed off the edges. "It is a fact about you. I have been working with that fact for two years and I am not tired of it."

Her hands lifted from his shoulders.

She moved around to face him again and crouched down, the same position as before, below his eyeline. She looked up at him and did not look away.

"Colour," she said. The ritual word. Unchanged.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Still green," I whisper, the shaking in my voice now matching my hands. The words feel pulled from somewhere deep, like a confession.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex stayed where she was.

She did not move toward him and she did not move away. She held the crouch and held his gaze and let the confession land in the room and stay there, because it deserved that — to stay, to be received, to not be immediately covered over with action or response. She had learned that some moments required her to simply be a witness to them, and this was one of those moments.

She looked at him. The shaking in his hands. The shaking in his voice. The fact that he had given her the colour and the quality of it at the same time, without being asked for both, which meant he was still present, still giving her what she needed to keep him safe, even from here. Especially from here.

That mattered to her. She did not say so.

"I know," she said instead. The same two words she had used earlier in the evening, but meaning something entirely different now. Then it had been acknowledgment of anticipation. Now it was something closer to: *I see what this cost. I understand what you just gave me.*

She reached out and took both of his hands in hers.

Not the controlled, purposeful grip of the scene's earlier work. Something plainer than that. She held his hands and felt the shaking in them and did not try to still it — she had told him not to stop it, and she did not contradict herself. She just held them. Let him feel that the shaking had somewhere to go that wasn't into empty air.

"Look at me," she said quietly.

She waited until he did.

"You're still in the room," she said. "You're still with me. The shaking is your body finishing something it started, and it's allowed to finish." She kept her voice even and low, the way she kept it when the work shifted from one kind of precision to another. "You don't have to manage this part. This part is just what happens after."

She turned his hands over in hers, slowly, and pressed her thumbs into his palms. Not hard. Just present.

"You did well," she said. The words were simple and she meant them without qualification, the way she meant everything she said to him — without performance, without the softening that would have made them easier to dismiss. "That is not me being kind. That is me telling you a true thing."

She held his gaze.

"Stay with me a little longer," she said. "We're not done yet, but not in the way you think. The rest of this evening belongs to you coming back." A pause. "I'm going to be right here while that happens."

She did not release his hands.

"Colour," she said. The word automatic, unchanging, the floor of the whole structure they had built together over two years.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I close my eyes, just for a second, before looking at her again. The shaking doesn't stop, but it settles into something quieter, like a tremor after an earthquake. "Green," I say, and the word feels easier, less pulled from the marrow. "Thank you."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex received the thank you the way she received everything he gave her tonight — without deflecting it, without making it smaller than it was, without the self-effacing response that would have turned his gratitude back into something he had to manage.

"You're welcome," she said. Simply. As though it were the most ordinary thing in the world, two people in a room, one of them saying *thank you* and the other saying *you're welcome*, and the two years of work underneath it not needing to be named.

She felt the change in the shaking under her hands. The settling. She had felt it before — the difference between a body in the middle of something and a body beginning to come back from it. It was not the same as stillness. It was better than stillness, in a way. It meant the nervous system was doing exactly what it was supposed to do.

She stayed where she was for another moment, then rose from the crouch in one smooth motion and sat on the low stool she had positioned beside the chair before the scene began. Same height as him now, rather than below or above. Beside.

She did not release his hands. She simply changed the angle.

"Keep your eyes open," she said. Not sharply — it was not a reprimand, he had already opened them. It was forward-looking instruction. "I know it's easier to close them right now. I want you in the room."

She studied his face with the same attention she had been paying all evening, reading the specific texture of where he was. The colour in his face was coming back. His breathing had changed — slower, less effortful. The quality of his gaze was different from twenty minutes ago, less interior, more present.

Good.

"Tell me something true," she said. "Not about tonight. Something ordinary. What you saw on the way here, what you had for dinner, anything." A pause. "I want to hear you use your voice for something that doesn't cost you anything."

She kept her thumbs moving in slow circles against his palms.

"Take your time," she said.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "The bus driver smiled at me," I say slowly, voice still rough. "When I got off. And I had a sandwich." The simplicity of it feels like a revelation.
