He waited until Wren moved, then followed the lead of it — if they sat, he'd crouch to work their shoes off; if they lay down, he'd start with getting them out of anything that had a waistband. Practical hands, unhurried. Nothing that asked to be reciprocated.

Horizontal, and talk or don't."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas had been kneeling by the end of the bed for about four minutes, which Wren knew because he had started counting somewhere around the point it became obvious he intended to wait as long as it took.

"You could have said something," Wren said.

"I could have," Tomas agreed, not moving.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I put my hand in his hair and tip his head back so he has to look up at me. "Say it now, then."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
A small sound caught in his throat at the grip in his hair—more reflex than anything else—but his eyes stayed steady on Wren's face.

"I wanted you to notice," he said. "That I was waiting. That I—" He stopped, jaw working for a moment. "I wanted you to tell me what to do with myself. I've been restless all day and I can't settle my head down and I thought if I just knelt here eventually you'd—" He cut himself off with a short exhale. "I wanted to give it over. The deciding. I didn't want to ask for it because then it felt like I'd still be the one choosing."

His hands rested on his thighs, palms down, fingers curled slightly inward. He hadn't moved from the position he'd found on his own. Four years and he still sometimes circled around the direct ask—not from shame, but from the stubborn lingering want to be *seen* and met without having to explain first.

"I know that's not fair," he added, quieter. "You're not in my head. I just wanted it anyway."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: My thumb strokes over his temple, a soft counterpoint to the hold in his hair. "It's not about fair. It's about you." I let go, my hand dropping to his shoulder. "Stand up. Then tell me one thing you need, clearly."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas rose to his feet in one clean movement, steadier than he'd felt kneeling. The directive helped. Directives generally helped.

He stood facing Wren, close enough that the space between them felt deliberate rather than distant. His jaw worked once—old habit, the one that surfaced when he was trying to line words up in the right order—before he exhaled and just said it.

"I need you to take the reins tonight. Fully. Not—" He paused, recalibrating. "Not checking in every few minutes to see if I'm still with you. I'll tell you if I'm not. I need to not be the one steering for a while. I need it to not feel like I'm co-piloting my own surrender."

His eyes held Wren's, steady and clear. Four years had taught him how to ask for what actually lived under the roundabout impulses. The wanting to be seen without explaining had been real, but so was this: the relief of putting it into words once the moment demanded it.

"That's one thing," he said. "It might require several of yours to make it work."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I've had a week," he says. "I'd like not to make any decisions for a few hours, if that's on offer."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas held still after the words left his mouth, feeling the shape of them in the air between himself and Wren. There it was—the whole thing, laid out clean. No hedging, no indirect routes. Just the ask.

His shoulders had dropped somewhere in the last sentence, tension bleeding out of them without his permission. That was the thing about finally saying it plainly: his body seemed to recognize it as done, as handed over, even before Wren had responded.

He didn't look away. Didn't fidget. Four years had also taught him that the space after an ask was Wren's to fill, and filling it himself—with justification, with backpedaling, with nervous chatter—would only undercut what he'd just built.

His fingers uncurled slightly at his sides. The restless buzz under his skin was still there, but it had shifted from aimless static into something with a direction. Anticipation, maybe. The particular kind of quiet that came from having set something down.

*Your move*, his posture said, clearly and without apology. He'd made his ask. Now he'd wait to see what Wren did with it.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I nod once, a firm, final gesture. "Consider it taken." I step closer and take his chin between my thumb and forefinger, holding his gaze. "Go shower. Use the cold water at the end. Then put on the grey sweats and nothing else and wait for me in the living room. Don't touch yourself while you wait. Understood?"

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas's breath caught—just barely, just enough that Wren would feel it through the grip on his chin. The specificity hit him like relief. Not vague permission, not an open-ended suggestion, but *instructions*. Concrete and exacting. The cold water. The grey sweats. The living room. The restriction. Each detail a handhold on the way down.

"Understood," he said. His voice came out quieter than he expected, already settling into something smoother. The restless hum under his skin had sharpened into focus.

He didn't move yet. Wren still had his chin. The protocol was old and automatic: you didn't step away from a grip until it was released. Four years of small negotiations had carved that one deep.

His eyes stayed on Wren's face, and something in his expression had shifted—less tension in his jaw, less calculation behind his eyes. The part of him that had been spinning gears all day, trying to figure out what to do with himself, had gone quiet. Or not quiet—*directed*. The energy was still there, but it wasn't his to manage anymore.

When Wren released him, he would go. Shower. Cold water. Grey sweats, bare chest. Living room. Hands off. The sequence was clean and simple, and his mind could wrap around each step instead of spiraling around the shapeless *want* that had been driving him up the wall all day.

He waited.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I take him at his word and stop asking after that, and he stops needing to be asked, and neither of us has any clothes on within about a minute of the decision.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The shower had been quick—efficient, the way everything felt when it had a structure attached. The cold water at the end had been a shock that locked his breath in his chest for a long second, skin prickling into tight goosebumps, the last of the aimless static in his skull crystallizing into something sharp and singular. By the time he'd toweled off and pulled on the grey sweats, his hands were steady.

The waiting had been harder. Not difficult—Wren had said *don't touch yourself*, and that was clear enough to obey—but the stretch of minutes in the living room, standing because he hadn't been told to sit, had let the anticipation build into something thick and heavy in his gut. He'd heard Wren moving in the bedroom. Hadn't called out. Hadn't asked how long. Just waited.

And then Wren had come into the living room, and Tomas had seen the decision on his face before any words, and something in his chest had unlocked.

Now—clothes discarded somewhere between the living room and the bed, Wren's hands on him, Wren's mouth—Tomas stopped tracking the sequence. That was the gift of it. He didn't have to anticipate the next move or plan three steps ahead or wonder if he was doing this right. He just had to be here, responsive, present.

His hands found the sheets, gripping, and a sound escaped him—unrehearsed, unguarded. His back arched off the mattress without his permission, body answering before his mind could catch up.

*This*. This was what he'd been chasing all day. The place where his head went quiet because it didn't have to run anything.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I smile against his skin, feeling the arch of his body beneath me. "Good," I murmur, my voice low. "Just like that. Let go of everything else." My hand slides up his side, mapping the tremor that runs through him.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The word *good* landed somewhere beneath his ribs, and Tomas felt himself unlock further at the sound of it. Praise did that—always had, from the start—but tonight it hit differently. Less like encouragement and more like confirmation. Evidence that he'd done the right thing by asking, by waiting, by handing it over instead of spinning his wheels for another hour trying to will himself calm.

The tremor under Wren's hand wasn't something he could have stopped if he'd tried. His skin was still cool from the water, sensitive in a way that made every point of contact feel magnified—Wren's mouth, Wren's hand, the brush of chest against chest. He was hyperaware and somehow not overthinking it, which was the paradox of this particular headspace. Everything felt more vivid, but none of it required analysis.

His grip on the sheets tightened, knuckles going white, and he let out a breath that shook on the way out. Not distress—something closer to the release of pressure from a valve that had been sealed too long.

"Yeah," he managed, the word rough and half-swallowed. Not a response that required answering, just a sound he couldn't keep in. Affirmation without articulation. His head tipped back against the pillow, throat exposed, another small surrender he didn't think about offering.

The part of his brain that had been running calculations all week—work deadlines, social obligations, the low-grade anxiety that hummed under everything when he went too long without this—had gone mercifully, temporarily offline. There was only this room, this bed, Wren's hands deciding where to put him and how.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's shaking by the time I've finished with my mouth and he still hasn't been told he's allowed to move, which is most of why he's shaking.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The shaking wasn't dramatic—nothing that would show on camera, nothing that looked like distress from the outside. It was fine-grained and constant, a vibration running through muscle and bone that he couldn't have stopped any more than he could have stopped his own heartbeat. His thighs trembled where they'd been positioned. His stomach clenched and released in uneven rhythm. His fingers ached from how hard he was gripping the sheets, but he hadn't been told to let go, so he didn't.

His cock was hard and flushed against his stomach, untouched, unattended, and that was almost worse—or better, depending on how you measured it. The wet heat of Wren's mouth had been there and then withdrawn, and the absence was its own kind of intensity. He didn't know if it was coming back. That was the point. He didn't get to know.

His breathing had gone ragged somewhere in the last few minutes. He could hear it in the quiet of the room—harsh, unsteady pulls of air that he couldn't quite smooth out. His chest heaved with the effort of staying still when every nerve ending was screaming for movement, for friction, for *something*.

"Please—" The word slipped out before he could catch it, and he almost bit down on it after, uncertain whether he was allowed to ask, whether asking counted as trying to steer. But Wren had said he'd speak up if he needed to stop, and this wasn't that. This was just—overflow. The pressure finding a crack in his control.

He didn't finish the sentence. Didn't specify what he was asking for. That wasn't his to decide anymore, and some part of him—the part that had been spinning all week—found an almost savage relief in the not-deciding.

His eyes were closed. He didn't remember closing them. When had he closed them?

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I lean in, my breath warm against his ear. "Please, what?" I keep my voice soft, deliberate. "Use your words, Tomas. Tell me what you want right now."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The question landed like a hand pressing on a bruise—not cruel, just exact. Tomas's breath stuttered in his chest, and for a moment he almost laughed, because there it was: the thing he'd said he didn't want. Being asked to steer. Being asked to choose.

But this wasn't the same as checking in. This was something else. Wren wasn't asking *if* he was okay or *whether* he wanted to continue. Wren was asking him to say it. To claim it. And maybe that was the point—maybe the surrender wasn't complete until he could name what he was surrendering to.

His eyes opened, unfocused, finding Wren's face close to his. The words caught somewhere behind his teeth.

"I want—" He stopped. Swallowed. His throat worked around the admission that felt like pulling a hook out of his own chest. "I want you to decide whether I get to come tonight. I want it to not be mine. I want—"

His voice cracked, and he hated that, the way it exposed how far down he'd already gone.

"I want to stop talking now. I want you to just—" His hands released the sheets and found Wren's shoulders instead, gripping hard, anchoring. "Whatever you're going to do, just do it. Don't ask me again. Please."

The *please* came out raw, stripped of pride. He'd said his piece. He'd used his words. Now he wanted to stop having them.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Please," he says, and then the phrase we use when he wants it harder than that. "Rough. You know how. I'm not going to break and I'd tell you."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The word hung in the air between them—*rough*—and Tomas felt it land in his own chest like a dropped weight. There it was. The thing he'd been circling around all night without naming, even when he thought he'd been naming it. Not just surrender. Not just the handing over. The other part. The part that wanted to be overwhelmed past the point of thinking, wanted the sharp edge that would cut through everything else still spinning in his head.

His grip on Wren's shoulders tightened. He could feel his own pulse in his fingertips.

"I know you'd tell me," he added, quieter now, steadying himself on the certainty of that. Four years. The safeword they'd never had to use but had always been there. The checks that had become unnecessary because they'd learned each other's edges so well. "That's why I can ask for this."

He let out a slow breath, forcing his hands to loosen their death-grip on Wren's shoulders. Not letting go—just shifting from desperation to something more deliberate. An invitation instead of a clutch.

His body was still trembling, still wound tight, but something in his expression had cleared. The last piece of hesitation had burned off in the asking. He'd said the thing. He'd made himself known. Now there was nothing left to negotiate, nothing left to explain, nothing left to decide.

*Do it*, his posture said, the line of his throat, the way his back arched slightly off the mattress in anticipation. *Take me apart.*

He didn't close his eyes this time. He wanted to see it coming.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: My hand slides to the back of his neck, firm and grounding. "Then stop asking." My voice drops, a low command. "I've got you." I shift my weight, pressing him deeper into the mattress, and lean down to bite his shoulder—not a tease, a claim.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The sound that came out of him when Wren's teeth sank in was not something he would have chosen. Raw and startled, punched from somewhere beneath his diaphragm. His body jerked under the weight pressing him down—a reflexive attempt to move that had nowhere to go, which was exactly the point.

The pain was clean. Bright and specific, unlike the muddy static that had been cluttering his skull all week. It carved a line through everything else, left no room for thought beyond *yes* and *more* and *there*.

His hands flew up—not to push away, but to hold on. His fingers found Wren's back, nails digging in, and he didn't moderate the pressure. He'd been told rough. He'd asked for it. That permission unlocked something in his own responses, let him stop calculating whether he was being too much, too loud, too hungry.

The bite hurt, and the hurt was a relief, and the relief made him gasp something that might have been Wren's name or might have been nothing coherent at all.

He could feel the indent of teeth, the slow release as Wren's mouth lifted, the throb that settled in after. His shoulder would mark. He wanted it to mark. Wanted the evidence tomorrow, something to press his fingers against and remember this: the weight, the claim, the permission to stop holding himself together.

His hips shifted under Wren's weight, seeking friction without permission, and he didn't try to stop them.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's stopped forming sentences and I'm not much better. "Don't stop," he manages. (OOC: no fade, no time-skip -- write it through, including the end.)

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The words landed somewhere outside the part of his brain still capable of parsing language. *Don't stop.* Like he could. Like there was any version of this where his body would let him do anything but exactly this—hands clawing down Wren's back, hips bucking up into whatever friction he could find, sounds spilling out of him that he'd stopped trying to shape into words.

There was no more sequence. No more steps. Just Wren's weight driving him into the mattress, Wren's hands repositioning him whenever they wanted him somewhere else, Wren's mouth and teeth finding new places to mark—his collarbone, the curve of his neck, the soft skin below his ear. Each one a fresh shock that wiped whatever had come before, left him gasping and arching and reaching for more.

He was making noise. He couldn't stop making noise. Broken-off syllables that might have been attempts at Wren's name, groans that he felt originate somewhere in his spine, whimpers when the pressure let up for even a second. His throat was going to be raw tomorrow. He didn't care.

When Wren's hand wrapped around him—finally, *finally*—Tomas's whole body seized. The sound that tore out of him was embarrassingly close to a sob, relief and desperation tangled together so tight he couldn't separate them. He'd been so hard for so long, had been held on the edge without knowing when or if he'd be allowed over, and now—

"Don't—" He couldn't finish. Didn't know what he was warning against. Don't stop. Don't make me wait anymore. Don't let me think.

His hands found the sheets again, twisting, his back bowing off the bed as Wren's grip tightened and moved. He was close—he could feel it building at the base of his spine, coiling tight, threatening to snap with every stroke. But he hadn't been told—

"Can I—" The words fractured. He tried again, forcing them through a throat that didn't want to cooperate. "Please, I need—I'm going to—"

He was begging. He'd asked not to steer and here he was, asking anyway, because his body was past the point of obedience without direction. The tension had wound too tight. If Wren said no, if Wren made him wait—

His eyes found Wren's face, desperate and pleading and stripped of every pretense he'd ever had. This was what he'd wanted. To be this far gone. To not recognize the sounds coming out of his own mouth. To need permission because he couldn't give it to himself anymore.

"Please," he said one more time, barely a whisper, and then his body decided for him—the orgasm hitting hard and sudden, his vision whiting at the edges, a sound ripping from his throat that he'd never made before. His hips jerked erratically, riding it out, and he couldn't have stopped if he'd wanted to, couldn't have done anything but let it shudder through him in waves that felt like they'd never end.

When they finally did end—or when they subsided enough that he could feel his own limbs again—he was trembling for a different reason. Empty. Undone. His hands had released the sheets at some point and now lay slack at his sides, and he couldn't seem to make them move.

His breath came in ragged pulls. His chest heaved. The bite on his shoulder throbbed in time with his heartbeat, and the marks on his neck and collarbone pulsed with the same rhythm, and he could feel where his nails had dug into Wren's back without knowing he'd done it.

He didn't say anything. Couldn't, for a long moment. Just lay there with his eyes closed, his body loose and pliant in a way it hadn't been in weeks, the restless static in his skull finally, *finally* gone quiet.

When he opened his eyes, they were wet. Not crying—not quite—but close. The kind of raw that came from being cracked open and not having the energy to close back up yet.

His hand found Wren's wrist. Held on. His grip was weak, fingers barely curling, but it was an anchor. A thread connecting him back to the world outside his own skin.

"Stay," he managed. Just that. One word. Everything else was still too far away.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I stay, of course. I don't pull away. My hand slides from his hip to rest over his heart, feeling the frantic beat slow under my palm. I shift my weight off him, but only enough to settle beside him, keeping the contact he's seeking. I press my lips to his damp temple, a soft, grounding kiss. "Right here," I murmur. "I'm not going anywhere."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The hand on his chest was an anchor. Tomas focused on it—the weight of Wren's palm, the steady pressure against his sternum, the way his heartbeat thudded against that contact like it was trying to reach something solid. His own breathing was still ragged, still catching on the exhale, but it was slowing. The trembling had shifted from intensity to something more like aftershock, small involuntary shivers that rolled through him in decreasing waves.

He turned his head toward the kiss on his temple, a small movement that felt enormous. His hand was still wrapped around Wren's wrist, and he didn't let go. Couldn't, yet. The contact was the only thing keeping him tethered to the room, to the bed, to his own body. Without it, he suspected he might float somewhere up near the ceiling and not know how to get back down.

The quiet in his head was almost startling. He'd spent the whole week with noise in his skull—deadlines, anxieties, the low hum of *something's wrong that you can't name*—and now there was nothing. Just the echo of his own breathing and the warmth of Wren's body beside him and the throbbing reminders scattered across his skin.

He shifted closer, pressing himself against Wren's side with a clumsiness that would have embarrassed him an hour ago. Now he couldn't bring himself to care about how desperate it looked. His face found the curve of Wren's neck, nose pressed against warm skin, and he breathed in deep. Sweat and sex and something underneath that was just *Wren*, familiar and grounding in a way nothing else ever had been.

"I didn't—" His voice came out wrecked, barely more than a whisper against Wren's throat. He stopped, swallowed, tried again. "I didn't know I needed it that much."

The admission felt important. Not an apology—he wouldn't apologize for this, not after four years—but an acknowledgment. He'd been restless all week and hadn't understood why. Now, emptied out and held together only by Wren's hands, the answer seemed obvious.

His fingers loosened their grip on Wren's wrist, but only so he could shift his hand up, find Wren's hand, guide it back to his chest. *Keep it there. Keep feeling this.* He didn't have the words for what he was asking, but he hoped Wren understood anyway.

The marks on his shoulder and neck pulsed with his heartbeat, and he let himself focus on that sensation instead of trying to form sentences. Pain settling into ache. Ache settling into something that felt almost like gratitude.

He was drifting. Not asleep—too present for that, too aware of every point of contact between their bodies—but suspended somewhere softer than full consciousness. The room felt hazy at the edges. Time had gone strange.

"Thank you," he said eventually, the words muffled against Wren's skin. "For—for not making me ask twice. For just—" A small exhale. "For taking it."

His free hand moved tentatively, finding the marks he'd left on Wren's back, fingertips tracing the raised lines with a gentleness that felt incongruous with how he'd made them. He didn't apologize for those either. They were part of the same exchange. Given and received.

He closed his eyes again, letting himself sink deeper into the mattress, deeper into Wren's warmth, deeper into the quiet. The hand over his heart anchored him. The marks on his skin reminded him where he'd been. The body beside him promised he wasn't alone in coming back.

"I'm okay," he added, quieter still. Not because he needed to reassure, but because he wanted Wren to know. "Really okay. Just—give me a minute. Or ten."

His mouth curved against Wren's neck. A small thing, barely a smile, but real. The first expression that had felt like his own all week.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I press my forehead against his, my breath evening out with his. "You never have to ask twice," I say quietly. "Not for this." My thumb strokes over his chest, slow and steady. "Take all the minutes you need."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The words settled into him like warm water, easing out the last knots he hadn't realized he was still holding. *You never have to ask twice.* Four years, and somehow that still landed like something new. Like something he had to relearn each time his brain tried to convince him he was asking for too much.

His hand stilled on Wren's back, palm flat against the raised lines his nails had left. He could feel the slight heat of them, the evidence of how far he'd gone, and something in his chest loosened further at the realization that he didn't have to feel guilty about it. Wren had given him this. Wren had wanted to give him this.

"Mm." The sound was nonverbal, more vibration than word, hummed against Wren's skin. Agreement, acknowledgment, something too formless to be either.

His breathing had evened out now, each inhale and exhale matching the steady rhythm of Wren's thumb against his chest. The trembling had stopped. His body felt heavy in the best way—sunk into the mattress, held down by Wren's warmth beside him, no longer buzzing with the restless need to move or think or figure anything out.

He let his hand slide down from Wren's back to rest against his hip instead, a loose curl of possession that asked nothing and received nothing except proximity. His legs shifted until one of his knees was hooked over Wren's thigh, tangling them together with a laziness that would have been impossible an hour ago.

The marks on his shoulder and neck had settled into a dull ache now, the kind that would be tender tomorrow in a way he'd press into on purpose. A reminder. Evidence that someone had wanted him enough to mark him, that he'd trusted someone enough to let them.

He should probably say something about water. About cleanup. The practical voice in the back of his head—the one that was slowly coming back online—pointed out that there was come cooling on his stomach and the sheets were a disaster and they'd both need to hydrate eventually.

He ignored it.

"Later," he mumbled, apparently aloud since Wren was right there. "Everything else later. Just—"

He pressed closer, tucking himself more firmly against Wren's side. His hand on Wren's hip squeezed once, a gentle pulse of pressure.

"This."

The word came out sure despite the exhaustion behind it. This was what he'd needed. Not just the roughness, not just the surrender, but this—the aftermath where he could be soft and held and not responsible for anything except staying present in his own skin.

His eyes were still closed. His breathing had gone slow and deep. The hand over his heart had stopped its stroking and now just rested there, warm and steady, and Tomas focused on that weight like it was the only thing keeping him from floating away entirely.

"Thank you," he said again, because it felt important. Because after four years, he'd learned that gratitude didn't diminish with repetition—it deepened. "For seeing me. For—not making me explain the whole thing before you understood it."

His voice was drowsy now, soft around the edges. The kind of voice that preceded sleep, if sleep was willing to take him.

He turned his head just enough to press his lips against Wren's jaw—a kiss that was barely a kiss, just contact, just closeness, just the physical expression of something he didn't have words for anymore.

The quiet in his head held. The restless static stayed gone. And for the first time all week, Tomas let himself stop running.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, my own exhaustion catching up now that his has settled. My hand moves from his chest to stroke through his hair, a gentle, repetitive motion. "You're easy to see," I murmur. "Always have been." I don't say anything else for a long moment, just let the quiet sit between us. "Sleep if you want. I'll be here when you wake up."

dialogue.content:
Tomas had been kneeling by the end of the bed for about four minutes, which Wren knew because he had started counting somewhere around the point it became obvious he intended to wait as long as it took.

"You could have said something," Wren said.

"I could have," Tomas agreed, not moving.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I put my hand in his hair and tip his head back so he has to look up at me. "Say it now, then."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas's breath caught once at the pull in his scalp, and then settled. He didn't fight the angle — let his throat stretch, kept his eyes on Wren's face. He liked this part, the moment where the waiting turned into permission. It made everything after it feel earned.

"I want you to hit me," he said. Plain. No preamble. "Not a lot. I want to count them."

He shifted his weight on his knees, the only fidget he'd allow himself, and added, "And then I want you to let me stay here. After. Even if I fall asleep on the floor."

A pause, then, quieter: "I missed you this week."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: My thumb brushes his temple. "You could have told me you needed this sooner." I let go of his hair, stepping back to give him space to rise. "But if you're counting, get up and bend over the bed."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas rose in a single motion, unhurried but without hesitation — the way he always did when Wren gave him something concrete to move toward. The stretch in his thighs felt good after the kneeling, a small dullness he catalogued and set aside. He'd feel it more later, probably. That was fine.

He crossed the short distance to the bed and bent at the waist, bracing his forearms against the mattress. He didn't fuss with his position — knew how Wren wanted him by now. Hips square, head down, feet steady on the floor. He let his weight settle into his shoulders and exhaled slowly through his nose.

"Like this?" he asked, because he always asked, and because sometimes Wren adjusted him, and Tomas liked that too — being moved into the exact shape someone else wanted.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I've had a week," he says. "I'd like not to make any decisions for a few hours, if that's on offer."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas felt something shift in his chest — not the usual loosening of giving up control, but something a little different. A gear he didn't usually reach for. He looked at Wren for a long moment, taking in the tired set of his shoulders, the way the week seemed to be sitting visibly on him, and made a quiet decision.

"Yeah," he said. "I can do that. If you want me to."

It wasn't a no. It wasn't resistance. It was just — honest. He hadn't done this before, not like this, and they both knew it. But the way Wren had asked mattered more to him than his own uncertainties.

He held out his hand. "Come here, then. First — what do you need from me right now? Not what you think you *should* need. What actually feels good in your body right now, if I'm not doing anything to you, just being near you?"

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't realize I was holding. "Just... quiet. And not having to think." I take his hand, letting my fingers lace with his. "Your weight against me would help."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas's expression softened — not pity, not concern, just a quiet kind of recognition. He understood the difference. He didn't comment on it, didn't try to make it more than it was. He just gave Wren's hand a small squeeze and let himself be pulled.

"Come on," he murmured, guiding them both toward the bed. He didn't rush. Wren was the one who'd said he didn't want to make decisions, and Tomas wasn't about to hand him another one by hurrying.

He sat first, then tugged gently until Wren was settled between his knees, back to chest. Tomas arranged himself slowly, letting Wren control how much weight he took — and then more, when Wren sagged back against him with a sound that wasn't quite a sigh and wasn't quite a groan, just the audible loosening of someone letting go of something heavy.

Tomas curled around him. One arm settled low across Wren's stomach, the other coming up to rest along his collarbone, palm flat against his chest. Not holding. Just there. A steady, warm presence that asked for nothing.

He pressed his mouth to the back of Wren's shoulder — a brush, not a kiss, barely anything — and let the quiet do the work.

They stayed like that. Tomas didn't speak, didn't shift, didn't try to make it into something. He just breathed with Wren, slow and even, and let the room go still around them. After a while, he felt Wren's weight change — going heavier, more surrendered — and Tomas eased them both down onto their sides, rearranging carefully so he could stay curved around Wren's back.

He tucked his face against the nape of Wren's neck and closed his eyes.

*I've got you*, he thought, and didn't say. Wren didn't need words right now. He just needed someone to stay.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I take him at his word and stop asking after that, and he stops needing to be asked, and neither of us has any clothes on within about a minute of the decision.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas took his time.

Not because he was uncertain, but because he'd heard what Wren had asked for, and this was how it looked — not rushing, not building toward something urgent, just a slow and thorough attention that let Wren's body be the only thing that mattered in the room.

He moved with his hands first. A long pass down Wren's side, learning the shape of him in the dim light — the ridge of a rib, the dip of a waist, the way his breath stuttered when Tomas's palm skimmed the sensitive place just below his hip. Tomas catalogued it without commentary. No *that feel good?* No *tell me what you want.* He wanted to keep Wren out of his head entirely.

When he finally pressed in — slow, careful, watched Wren's face the whole way — he kept still for a long moment. Just weight. Just presence. Let Wren feel the fullness of not being alone in his body without having to do anything about it.

Then he began to move, barely at all. A slow roll of his hips that barely changed the angle, more a rhythm than a thrust. He kept his forehead against the back of Wren's neck, breathing warm against his skin, one hand curled loosely around Wren's where it was fisted in the pillow, the other resting low on his belly — not reaching, not pushing, just grounding him. Reminding him where he was.

*Here. With me. Nowhere else to be.*

He could feel the tension in Wren's shoulders, the way the week was still living in his body even now. Tomas smoothed his thumb in slow circles against Wren's stomach and shifted the angle — a fraction deeper, a fraction slower — until he found the one that made Wren's breath catch and then release in a way that sounded almost like relief.

He stayed there. Held the pace. Didn't escalate.

When Wren's hand tightened around his, Tomas squeezed back — *I know, I'm here, stay with me* — and kept moving with him in that same unhurried current, the kind of pace that wouldn't let Wren's mind rebuild anything. There was only the next breath, the next slow shift, the next point of contact.

Tomas watched the back of his neck, the way his shoulders had finally, finally dropped. Felt the moment Wren stopped waiting for it to end and started letting it be what it was.

That was when Tomas let himself move a little deeper. Not faster — just *more*. A slow filling that asked nothing back.

He brought Wren's hand up to his mouth and pressed a kiss to his knuckles — one, then another, soft and unremarkable — and kept going until the only sounds in the room were their breathing and the small, almost surprised sound Wren made when he realized this was actually it. This was the whole thing. There was nowhere to go but deeper into it.

Tomas held him there.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath, my fingers curling tight in his hair. "God— Tomas." The week's tension finally shatters in my chest, and I press my forehead into the mattress, letting him carry all my weight.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas felt the exact moment Wren stopped holding himself up — felt the weight transfer into his body, felt the last of that rigid, carried-alone thing in his frame finally give. Something in Tomas's chest went very quiet and very sure at the same time.

He didn't change his pace. Didn't pull back to check. Just adjusted the angle of his hips a fraction and let Wren press into the mattress, let him be heavy, let him have that.

"I know," Tomas murmured against the nape of his neck. Low, almost not a word. "I've got you. Stay down."

His hand stayed fisted loosely in Wren's hair — not pulling, just there, a reminder that someone else was in charge of where his head went for a while. He shifted his weight onto his forearm so he could curl more fully over Wren's back, chest to shoulders, and the new depth made Wren's breath stutter in a way Tomas catalogued without comment.

He kept moving. Slow. That same steady current. He was nowhere close to coming — had decided somewhere around the third minute that this wasn't about him at all, and his body had quietly agreed. There was something in him that liked this more, in a way he didn't usually let himself look at directly: being the structure someone else rested on. Being the thing that held.

He pressed his mouth to the curve of Wren's shoulder. Then the knob of his spine. Then back up to the place behind his ear where the skin was damp.

"You're doing so well," he said, barely above a breath. "Letting go like this. I've got you. I won't stop until you tell me to."

A promise and a permission, both at once.

He tightened his fingers in Wren's hair — gently, a little, just enough to feel — and kept moving with him, slow as tide, until the only thought left in the room was *more of this, more of this, more of this.*

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's shaking by the time I've finished with my mouth and he still hasn't been told he's allowed to move, which is most of why he's shaking.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas's fingers had gone white-knuckled in the sheets. He didn't know when that had happened — only that his hands were shaking too hard to keep flat anymore, and gripping the fabric was the only thing keeping them from doing something he hadn't been given leave to do.

He wasn't making sound. Hadn't for the last minute or so — just breathing, ragged and too fast, through his nose, his jaw locked so tight it ached. Every pass of Wren's mouth sent a jolt up his spine that made his hips twitch forward a fraction before he caught himself and stilled them again, teeth gritted.

"Please," he got out, and it came out broken in a way he hadn't meant it to. He cleared his throat. Tried again. "Wren. I need — I need you to tell me. If I can."

That was the rule. They both knew it. He wasn't going to hump the air until he got permission, wasn't going to take what he hadn't been offered, even shaking apart like this. His body didn't belong to him right now. He knew whose it was, and he wasn't going to forget it just because the rest of him was forgetting how to breathe.

A sound escaped him that was nearly a whine. He bit it off, hard, the inside of his cheek catching between his teeth. A copper tang bloomed.

He kept his forehead pressed to the mattress. Kept his hips still. Kept his hands in the sheets and not reaching for Wren, not pulling him closer, not trying to set the pace he so desperately wanted. His thighs were trembling with the effort of it — holding himself back from a thing his whole body was screaming for.

He waited. The only movement in him was the shaking, and the rise and fall of his ribs, and the way his fingers kept flexing tighter in the fabric.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I take my time, letting my thumb brush the inside of his thigh before I finally sit back on my heels. "Alright. Go on." My voice is low, granting the permission he's been holding himself so still for.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas made a sound he'd deny making later — something low and broken in the back of his throat — and then he moved.

Not frantically. Even now, even shaking apart, he didn't lose the shape of what they were doing. His hips stuttered forward once, twice, finding the rhythm Wren had set, and then he was pressing into it, and the relief of finally — *finally* — being allowed to take what he needed hit him so hard he nearly sobbed with it.

"Thank you," he gasped, and he didn't know if he was saying it to Wren or to the air or to the permission itself. "Thank you, thank you—"

His hands released the sheets — he'd have small red weals across his palms, he registered distantly, later — and found Wren instead. One hand splayed across his back, the other bracing against the headboard, and then he was moving with intent, not the careful measured pace from before but something real, something that matched the ragged edge in his breathing.

He kept his forehead against the mattress. Kept most of his weight braced on his arms so he wasn't crushing Wren. Kept the shape of *taking without taking over*, because even desperate, even shaking, he knew this was Wren's to give and he was only allowed what Wren had offered.

"Tell me—" he managed, voice wrecked, "tell me if this is — if you want—"

He couldn't finish the sentence. His hips were moving on their own now, the rhythm he'd been holding back for what felt like hours finally loose in his body, and the only thing keeping him from driving hard and fast was the iron will of four years of practice. He was still checking. Still making sure.

But he was close. So close it was making his vision blur at the edges, his whole body wound tight as a wire, every muscle trembling with the effort of not just *taking*.

He turned his head against the mattress, cheek pressed to damp fabric, and found Wren's hand with his. Laced their fingers together. Held on.

"I'm — I need —"

A breath, ragged.

"Please tell me I can come. I need to — Wren, *please*—"

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Please," he says, and then the phrase we use when he wants it harder than that. "Rough. You know how. I'm not going to break and I'd tell you."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas heard the words land somewhere deep in his chest — felt them rearrange the architecture of the next thirty seconds — and then he was moving.

The careful restraint he'd been holding himself in for what felt like hours cracked open at once. Not a slow loosening, a fracture. His hips drove forward with a force that punched a sound out of Wren that made Tomas's whole body go electric, and he didn't check, didn't pull back to ask if it had been too much, because Wren had said he wouldn't break, Wren had said he'd tell him, and Tomas trusted that the way he trusted gravity.

"Yes," he breathed, half a word, half a sound. "Okay. Okay—"

His hand tightened in Wren's and he braced the other against the headboard and *took*. The measured pace from before was gone, replaced by something urgent and real, hips snapping forward in a rhythm he couldn't have slowed if he'd wanted to. The bed was hitting the wall — he'd worry about the neighbors later, if he remembered to — and the sound of it, the sound of them, filled the room in a way that was almost indecent.

He could feel the difference in Wren's body immediately. The way he took it, absorbed it, gave back. The small sounds he was making that weren't protests. Tomas's hand found the back of Wren's neck and pressed — not hard, not a restraint, just weight, just *I'm here, take it* — and Wren's shoulders dropped another fraction, and something in Tomas's chest went so tight it nearly hurt.

"There," he managed, voice wrecked. "Like that. You're so — *fuck*—"

He wasn't going to last. He knew it the way he knew his own name — the wire he'd been wound into had nothing left to give, and every thrust was bringing him closer to the edge at a speed that made his vision swim. His hand was shaking where it held Wren's. His breath was coming in short, torn sounds against the damp skin of Wren's shoulder.

He curled himself more fully over Wren's back, chest to shoulders, mouth finding the shell of his ear. "Tell me you're close," he said, and it came out barely a whisper. "I need to feel you — I want to feel you finish, I want to—"

He didn't finish the sentence. Couldn't. His hips were driving harder now, the rhythm going ragged at the edges, and the only thing left in his body was the climb and the desperate, aching need to feel Wren come undone underneath him before he did.

His hand found Wren's and held on, knuckles white, and he pressed his forehead to the back of Wren's neck and let himself fall the rest of the way.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I press back against him, my own breath coming in ragged gasps. "Yeah— close. Don't stop." I push up onto my elbows, arching my back to meet his pace. "Come with me."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas felt Wren push back against him and the sound that came out of him was nothing he'd planned — a low, broken thing that sounded almost like a sob, almost like a name.

"Yeah," he managed, the word barely formed. "Yeah — I'm—"

He couldn't finish. His hips were already driving harder, meeting Wren's arching back, the new angle sending a shock up his spine that made his whole body clench. His hand was crushing Wren's where their fingers were laced together, and he couldn't make himself let go, couldn't make himself do anything but hold on and *take* and give at the same time.

He felt it building in Wren before it happened — the way his rhythm faltered, the way his breath caught on a sound that wasn't quite a word, the way his whole body went suddenly taut beneath Tomas's chest. Tomas pressed his mouth to the back of Wren's neck, tasting salt, tasting the week finally leaving his skin, and he held himself there — deep, still, shaking with the effort of not yet, not yet, *waiting for it* — and then Wren was coming apart under him, and the sound of it, the feel of it, the way his body clenched and released and clenched again was the only thing in the room.

Tomas let himself go. Just — let go.

The first spasm hit him like a wave, then another, and he drove into Wren one last time, hard enough that his vision whited out at the edges, and he made a sound he didn't recognize as his own voice, something low and wrecked and honest in a way he usually wasn't. His hand was still crushing Wren's. His forehead was still pressed to the nape of his neck. His whole body was trembling with it, aftershocks rolling through him in slow, devastating waves that left him slack and gasping against Wren's back.

For a long moment he couldn't move. Could barely breathe. His weight had sagged down onto Wren and he didn't have the strength to push himself back up, didn't want to, his body heavy and boneless in the aftermath in a way that made the bed feel like the only solid thing in the world.

He turned his head just enough to press his mouth to Wren's shoulder. Not a kiss. Just contact. Just — *I'm here, I'm still here, did I do okay, are you still with me.*

"Hey," he got out, and his voice was ruined. Wrecked. Barely a whisper against damp skin. "You still with me?"

He eased his weight off slowly — carefully, because Wren had given him everything and the least he could do was be gentle now — and then his hand found Wren's face, thumb brushing his cheekbone, tilting his head just slightly so he could see him.

His own face was a mess. He knew it. Eyes wet, mouth slack, hair plastered to his forehead. He didn't try to fix any of it. Just looked at Wren like he was the only thing in the room worth seeing.

"That was—" He stopped. Swallowed. Tried again. "Thank you. For letting me. I know you didn't — I know this week was—"

He gave up on words. Pressed his forehead to Wren's instead, breathing him in, still shaking faintly in the aftermath, and curled his body around him as best he could on the ruined sheets.

He was going to need to get a washcloth. He was going to need to get them water. He was going to need to do all the aftercare things they'd both come to rely on. But that could wait thirty seconds. Right now, the only thing he needed to do was stay exactly where he was.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's stopped forming sentences and I'm not much better. "Don't stop," he manages. (OOC: no fade, no time-skip -- write it through, including the end.)

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas heard it. He felt it land — felt the shape of it, the way Wren wasn't asking for anything active, wasn't asking for more of what they'd just done, was just asking for *this*. The contact. The proximity. The not-being-left-alone-yet.

"Okay," Tomas said. The word came out barely a whisper against Wren's cheek, his hand still cradling his jaw, his thumb still tracing that slow absent path along his cheekbone. "I'm not going anywhere."

He shifted closer instead of pulling away. The angle was awkward — he was half-propped on his elbow, still braced above Wren, and his body was shaking faintly in the aftershocks and his thigh muscles were starting to cramp — but he didn't move to fix any of it. He just let his weight settle back down, chest to Wren's back, hips to hips, the whole long line of him curved around Wren like he was trying to be a wall between him and the rest of the week.

The mess between them was cooling. He'd deal with that in a minute. He'd get the washcloth. He'd get them water. He'd do all of it — but not yet. Wren had said *don't stop* and what that meant was obvious to anyone who'd been doing this for four years.

Tomas pressed his mouth to the back of Wren's neck. Not a kiss. Just warmth. Just the reminder of a body against his body, someone who was still here, who hadn't dissolved out from under him while he was shaking apart.

He stayed.

His breathing was evening out slowly, the ragged gasps softening into something longer, deeper. Every few breaths he'd feel a small aftershock roll through him — a flicker of tension in his abdomen, his thigh, the small of his back — and each time he just let it move through him, didn't fight it, the way he'd learned to over the years. The shaking was the body's way of finishing. You just let it finish.

His hand found Wren's again — the one he'd been crushing, he realized belatedly, and loosened his grip with a small guilty sound against the nape of Wren's neck. He massaged the tension out of Wren's fingers gently, one by one, working out the ache he'd put there. *"Sorry,"* he murmured, barely a sound. *"I didn't — sorry."*

Wren's breathing was slowing under him. Tomas could feel it — the way his ribs expanded and contracted with more space between each one, the way his shoulders had dropped so far they were nearly touching the mattress, the way the tension had finally drained out of his body in a way that hadn't been there at the start of the evening. Heavier. Quieter. Given over.

Tomas had seen him like this before, but it never stopped meaning something to him — the trust implicit in it, the way Wren let go so completely here in a way he didn't anywhere else. It wasn't something Tomas took for granted. He never had. He didn't think he ever would.

He rearranged them slowly, carefully, easing Wren onto his side so they could curl around each other properly. It took a minute — Wren was heavy with exhaustion, uncooperative in the boneless way of someone half-asleep, and Tomas had to do most of the work, shifting his weight, guiding Wren's arm, tucking a pillow under Wren's head where he wanted it. He didn't ask which way Wren wanted to face. Just settled him on his side facing the room, and then slid in behind him, chest to shoulder blades, knees tucked up against the backs of Wren's thighs.

He pulled the blanket up over them — the one at the foot of the bed, the one that didn't smell like sex or sweat, because that's the one they always used for aftercare. A small rule they'd never formalized but had always followed.

"There," Tomas murmured, his mouth against Wren's shoulder blade. "There you go."

He tucked his face against the nape of Wren's neck and breathed him in. Sweat and sex and the faint clean smell underneath that was just *Wren* — the smell he knew better than his own.

His hand came up to rest flat against Wren's chest. Not over his heart — lower, against his sternum, where he could feel the rise and fall of his breathing. Just monitoring. Just present. A pulse check of a different sort.

The room was quiet. The only sound was their breathing, slowly synchronizing without either of them trying, the way it always did after. Outside, a car passed on the street below. Inside, the house was still.

Tomas thought about the washcloth. About the water on the nightstand, the one he should have filled before they'd started. About the fact that Wren had had a hard week and he hadn't asked what it had been about, and he wondered if he should, if Wren would want to talk about it now or later or at all. He decided he wouldn't bring it up. Wren would, when he was ready. Or he wouldn't, and that would be okay too.

For now — just this.

His thumb brushed Wren's sternum in slow circles. Idle. Reassuring. *I'm here, I'm here, I'm here.*

After a long moment, he pressed his mouth to the knob of Wren's spine and let out a long slow breath against his skin. His eyes were heavy. His body was heavy. The shaking had stopped entirely, leaving him with the pleasant exhausted looseness that always came after — the feeling of having been wrung out and hung up to dry.

"Don't go to sleep yet," he murmured against Wren's back. Quieter: "I want to get you water first. And clean you up a little. Is that okay? Can you stay awake for two more minutes?"

He shifted his weight, just barely, enough to see Wren's face over his shoulder. His own face was still a wreck — eyes swollen, mouth slack, a faint smear on his cheek he'd have to wipe off — but he was smiling, just barely, the soft private smile he didn't show anyone but Wren.

"You're still here," he said, like he'd just confirmed it. "I was worried you were going to fall asleep on me before I could get back."

A beat. His smile softened.

"I love you," he added, quieter, because the moment felt like it wanted it. "I'm glad you came home."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, turning my head just enough to press a kiss against his arm. "I'm here. I'm not going anywhere." I push myself up onto my elbows, wincing at the protest in my muscles. "Get the water. I'll wait."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas made a small sound against Wren's shoulder — something almost like a laugh, except softer, the exhale of someone who'd been holding a breath he hadn't realized he was holding.

"Half a minute," he said, and then he was moving.

The getting up was unglamorous. His thighs protested immediately — that dull ache he'd catalogued earlier coming back with interest, joined now by a deeper one in his lower back, the kind that meant he'd been tensing muscles he didn't usually tense. He sat on the edge of the bed for a moment, hand braced on his knee, just breathing. The room was cool against the sweat drying on his skin. He could feel the mess on his stomach, tacky and cooling, and decided he'd deal with that after Wren.

He stood, and his knees popped audibly — loudly enough that he winced and glanced back at Wren with a self-conscious grimace. "Twenty-seven," he muttered, half to himself, half an apology, and padded barefoot toward the bathroom.

The washcloth came from the stack on the counter — the clean ones, the top of the pile, because there was a small dignity in the choice. He ran it under warm water, wrung it out thoroughly, and then stood there for a moment with both hands braced on the edge of the sink, head bowed, just breathing.

*Okay.*

He looked at himself in the mirror. The face looking back was exactly the wreck he'd expected — eyes puffy, mouth bitten, hair sticking up at angles that defied physics. There was a faint red mark on his cheekbone he didn't remember getting. He looked, he thought distantly, like someone who'd been thoroughly used in the best possible way.

He touched the mark on his cheekbone with his fingertips, gently, and felt something warm shift in his chest.

He wet a second washcloth. Filled a glass with water. Paused, then filled a second one, because Wren always drank more than he admitted to after, especially after a hard week. Took both glasses in one hand, the washcloths folded over his shoulder, and went back.

"Hey," he said softly, settling on the edge of the bed near Wren's hip. "C'mere. Let me."

He didn't wait for an answer — just leaned in and pressed the warm washcloth to Wren's stomach first, gentle, methodical, the way he'd done a hundred times. He cleaned him carefully, watching the cloth pick up the mess of it, the evidence of what they'd just done, and felt a quiet satisfaction in the act. The domesticity of it. The small way his hands knew the rhythm of this, knew when to press and when to lift, knew where Wren was tender.

He took his time. Moved the cloth to Wren's thighs, then lower, the inside of one knee, the crease of his hip. Gentle. Not clinical — present. The way you touched someone you knew.

When he was done he set the cloth aside on the towel he'd spread on the nightstand for exactly this purpose, and held out one of the glasses.

"Drink," he said. Not a suggestion. The same tone he used when he was reminding Wren to eat, or to sleep, or to do the small maintenance things Wren was bad at remembering about himself. "All of it. I know you."

He watched Wren drink, and something in his face went soft in a way he didn't bother hiding. Not worship. Not awe. Just — the ordinary, unremarkable fact of looking at someone you knew that well, and being glad.

Once the glass was empty he took it from Wren and set it aside, then did the same with his own — drank half in one long pull, the other half slower, feeling the water settle cool in his stomach. He wiped his mouth with the back of his hand, then picked up the second cloth and cleaned himself off, quick and efficient, the same unhurried attention but turned on his own body. Tossed the cloth toward the bathroom door without looking. It landed close enough.

Then he came back to bed.

He didn't ask which side. Just slid in behind Wren, chest to back, and pulled the blanket up over them both, tucking it around Wren's shoulders with a care that bordered on fussy. His arm came around Wren's waist, hand splaying flat against his stomach, thumb finding the same idle path it had traced before. His forehead pressed to the back of Wren's neck.

"For the record," he said, and his voice was rough still, the wrecked texture of it not quite smoothed over yet, "tonight was — "

He paused. Not because he didn't have the words, but because the ones he had felt too small for the shape of what he meant.

"You took care of me," he said, quieter. "I know that's not — I know you were tired, and I know you came home needing to not be in charge of anything, and you were anyway. For me. I noticed."

A beat. His thumb stilled against Wren's stomach, then resumed its slow path.

"I'm not going to make a thing of it," he added, even quieter. "But I noticed. And I — thank you. For wanting to. For asking me to let you."

He pressed his mouth to the nape of Wren's neck, lingering there, breathing him in.

"How's your body," he asked after a moment, shifting into the practical. "Honest. Anywhere sore I should know about? You took a lot of impact earlier, I wasn't exactly — " A pause. "I wasn't exactly gentle at the end. I would've remembered being told to stop, but I want to check in anyway."

His hand moved from Wren's stomach up to his chest, palm flat over his sternum again. The pulse-check position. The grounding position.

"And your week," he added, even more quietly, because Wren might want to talk about it now, and Tomas wanted to leave the door open without pushing it. "Whenever. Or not. I'm here either way."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, sinking back against him. "Nothing that won't feel better tomorrow." I cover his hand with mine, pressing it more firmly against my chest. "The week was just... long. Missed this."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas felt the press of Wren's hand over his, felt the way he pulled it more firmly against his chest like he wanted to feel Tomas's palm there even more than Tomas did, and something in his chest went very quiet.

"Yeah," he said, his voice still rough at the edges, still a little too honest to hide behind. "Me too."

He didn't elaborate. Didn't need to. The week had been long for both of them, in different ways, and the *this* of it — the particular shape of what they did, the particular shape of what they were — was something neither of them could get anywhere else.

His thumb resumed its slow idle path against Wren's sternum. He was quiet for a long moment, just breathing with him, feeling the rise and fall under his palm.

"Let me check," he said, softer, a request rather than a question. "Just — quickly. Then I'll let you sleep."

He didn't wait for an answer. His free hand came up and found the back of Wren's neck first, fingertips gentle against the muscle there, feeling for any knots, any tension that hadn't let go yet. He worked a small one loose with his thumb — felt Wren's breath catch and then release on a small sound that wasn't quite a sigh — and moved on. Down the slope of his shoulder. Across the meat of his trapezius, where the week had clearly been living. Across the ridge of one shoulder blade, then the other.

His hand drifted down Wren's back, slow and methodical, not clinical but not entirely not either. The kind of touch that was half-tenderness, half-assessment. He paused at the base of his spine where the impact had landed, pressed gently with his palm, felt Wren shift into it rather than away.

"Here?" he murmured.

When Wren didn't tense or pull away, he moved on. Down over the curve of one hip, the swell of one glute — not lingering, just touching, just making sure. The back of one thigh. The other. He checked the backs of his knees, the places where strain sometimes hid. Found nothing that made him stop. Found nothing that felt wrong.

He came back up and pressed a kiss to the knob of Wren's spine.

"You feel okay," he said, an observation more than a question. "Bruised in a few places, probably. Nothing that needs anything but time."

His hand came back to rest on Wren's chest, finding its place again over his sternum like it belonged there. Because it did.

"Drink more water when you wake up," he said, quieter now, the edges of the practical starting to blur into something sleepier. "And if anything's sore in the morning, tell me. Don't just — power through it because you think I want you to. I don't. I want you to tell me."

A beat. His mouth curved against the nape of Wren's neck, hidden where Wren couldn't see it.

"I want you to tell me a lot of things," he added. "You've gotten out of practice this week. I noticed that too."

Not an accusation. Just — observation. The kind of thing a partner said when they wanted the other to know they'd been paying attention, and that the paying attention wasn't going to stop just because the crisis was over.

He shifted his weight, settling them both more comfortably, pulling the blanket up a fraction higher around Wren's shoulders. His arm tightened briefly around Wren's chest — a small squeeze, a reminder of presence, of *still here* — and then relaxed again into the same loose hold.

The room was very quiet. Outside, a car door slammed somewhere down the street, and then nothing. The house settled around them, the old familiar sounds of cooling pipes and the tick of the baseboard heater they both pretended not to hear.

Tomas's eyes were getting heavy. The wrecked feeling in his body had settled into something pleasant, a kind of heaviness that felt earned, that felt like a job done right. He was aware, in the dim way of someone half-falling-asleep, that his breathing had slowed to match Wren's. That his thumb had stopped moving against Wren's sternum and was just resting there now, warm and still.

"Hey," he murmured, even quieter than before. "Wren."

A pause.

"I'm glad you told me what you needed. The — the way you did. Earlier. At the start."

He didn't elaborate on what he meant. He thought Wren probably knew. The way Wren had said *I'd like not to make any decisions for a few hours* — not asking, exactly, but not pretending either. Just saying it. Just trusting Tomas to know what to do with it.

"I like taking care of you," he said, almost inaudible now, his mouth against the curve of Wren's shoulder. "I know that's not — I know I usually want you to take care of me. But I liked it. I liked being the thing you rested on. I'd do it again. Whenever you needed."

He pressed his face into the nape of Wren's neck and breathed him in one more time — sweat and sex and *Wren*, the smell that meant home — and let his eyes close.

"Stay," he said, even though Wren had already said he would. Just — a small, sleep-drunk insistence. A last check. A last reminder that the door was still open. "Stay, and sleep, and I'll be here when you wake up."

His hand found Wren's under the blanket, their fingers loosely lacing together in the dark. His breathing was slowing. Evening out. The kind of slow that meant he was already half-gone, slipping into the warm exhausted place where nothing hurt and nothing was asked of him and the only thing left in the world was the steady rise and fall of Wren's chest under his palm.

"Love you," he murmured, half-asleep, half-awake, the words barely formed against Wren's skin. "Love you. G'night."

And then, softer, almost not there at all:

"...glad you came home."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I turn my head just enough to press my lips against his knuckles. "I'm glad I came home too." My voice is thick with sleep already. I shift, just a little, to feel him more fully against my back. "Love you. Sleep."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The room was set up the way it always was before a scene, which Ari found steadying: everything in its place, nothing improvised.

Vex checked the last strap without hurrying. "Colour," she said. It was not a question so much as a procedure.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say. "Green all the way down."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content: Vex noted the colour in the small leather-bound log—*"Green, 21:14"*—and set the pen down with a precise click. "Acknowledged," she said. She surveyed the row of implements on the linen-draped side table, each cleaned and placed according to their written agreement. After a moment, she selected the weighted leather paddle, testing its heft in her palm before moving to stand at Ari's left side. "Impact to start," she stated. "Thirty strikes. Count them. Do not thank me until I instruct you." She let the paddle rest against her own thigh, watching with unhurried attention.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I take a deep breath, letting my muscles relax into the restraints. "Yes, Maitresse," I say, my voice steady. I can feel my heart already beginning to race.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content: Vex adjusted her grip a fraction, finding the weighted paddle's balance point with the familiarity of long practice. She let a measured silence settle—three seconds, four—before pivoting at the hip and delivering the first strike with controlled, unhurried force. The leather connected with a sharp, resonant crack that seemed to absorb the room's quiet. She held her follow-through, wrist steady, and studied the result with unblinking attention, her breathing unchanged, her focus absolute.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I hold still for the last of it and let her check the fit herself, because she will anyway. "I've been thinking about this since Tuesday," I say.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex let the paddle rest against her thigh, her eyes tracking the minute rise and fall of Ari’s breath. She noted the stillness, the unspoken mention of Tuesday, but it was the missing number that held her focus. She allowed three seconds of silence to elapse before she spoke.

"You did not count," she said. There was no reprimand in her voice, only the flat exactitude of a record that refused to close. "That strike is void. We begin again at one. Keep the count, Ari. Keep it exact."

She adjusted her stance by a fraction, revisited the angle with unhurried precision, and delivered the blow to the same plane with controlled, unwavering force. The crack of leather filled the room. She held her wrist steady, breathing unchanged, and watched with absolute attention.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I suck in a breath, the sting blooming sharp. "One," I say, voice a little tighter. I feel my face flush—not from the pain, but from the slip.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content: Vex held the paddle’s balance for a measured four seconds, allowing the sting to settle and Ari’s breath to find its rhythm. She did not speak; the correction had already been delivered, and further words would have been imprecise. Without altering her stance, she pivoted at the hip and brought the leather down in a clean, unhurried arc—same plane, same controlled force, same absolute precision. The crack resonated in the stillness. She held the follow-through, wrist steady, her gaze fixed on the rising flush and the minute tension across Ari’s shoulders, cataloguing every signal with unblinking attention.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: By the time she's finished with the rope I'm already past composure, and she hasn't done anything to me yet that I would have to explain to anyone.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex finished threading the rope, secured the last knot with a precise tug, and set the remaining coil on the linen-draped table beside the paddle. She did not rush. She stepped back, her gaze moving methodically over the network of lines across Ari’s skin before lifting to study the face: the flush high on the cheeks, the parted lips, the unfocused quality of the eyes that told her composure had already unraveled. She counted four of Ari’s breaths—each one shallow, uneven—before she spoke.

“You have not been asked to explain anything,” Vex said. Her voice was low and flat, clinical, stripped of both comfort and cruelty. “You have been asked to count, and to report your colour. Those are your only obligations.” She let a measured silence elapse, watching the faint tremor in Ari’s shoulders. “If you are past composure, you are not past protocol. State your colour, Ari. Then we will see if you can still keep your numbers straight.”

She adjusted her grip on the weighted paddle, letting it rest once more against her thigh, and waited with unblinking attention.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I swallow, focusing on the feel of the rope against my skin. "Green, Maitresse," I say, my voice a bit rough. "Still green."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex received the confirmation with a slight inclination of her head, though she did not reach for the log. The record remained open; the protocol had been satisfied. She lifted the paddle from her thigh, adjusting her stance to account for the ropes now framing Ari’s body, and found her distance with unhurried exactness.

She allowed three seconds of measured silence—sufficient for anticipation, insufficient for recovery—then pivoted at the hip and brought the weighted leather down in a clean, controlled arc. The strike landed with the same sharp, resonant crack, precisely placed against the plane she had established earlier. She held the follow-through, wrist steady, breathing unchanged, and watched the immediate bloom of colour beneath the skin, the minute recoil against the ropes, the flutter beneath Ari’s eyelids. Her attention was absolute, cataloguing every signal.

She did not speak. The count was Ari’s obligation, and she waited for it with unblinking patience, the paddle resting once more against her thigh.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: She takes her time and I lose track of how long, until I'm shaking against the restraints and asking out loud for something I'd normally make her get out of me.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex held her position without moving, the weighted paddle resting motionless against her thigh. She watched Ari shake against the ropes with the same unblinking attention she had given every strike, cataloguing the tremor in the shoulders, the shallowness of the breath, the unguarded openness of a composure that had fully unraveled. She counted five of Ari’s ragged exhalations, letting the silence stretch until the room seemed to settle around the sound of Ari’s heartbeat.

“You have spoken without leave,” Vex said. Her voice was flat and clinical, devoid of reprimand or warmth. “That is a protocol breach. Your obligations are the count and the colour. Nothing more.”

She paused, adjusting her grip on the paddle with unhurried precision, and studied the flush high on Ari’s cheeks, the desperate angle of the frame.

“However,” she continued, “you have just offered me something freely. Something you would normally require me to extract.” She let the observation hang in the still air, her breathing unchanged. “That interests me. Name it precisely, Ari. What are you asking for? Do not make me interpret your noise.”

She held her stance, wrist steady, and waited with absolute patience.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Permission to come," I say, the words shaky and raw. I can feel my face burning even hotter. "Please, Maitresse."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex held the paddle motionless against her thigh, her gaze tracking the tremor in Ari’s shoulders with unblinking scrutiny. She let eight seconds of silence elapse—sufficient for the request to settle, insufficient for hope to form—before she spoke, her voice flat and clinical.

“Permission to orgasm is not granted from a breached protocol,” she said. “You spoke without leave. You lost your count. The last confirmed entry in my record is one. That is unacceptable disorder.”

She lifted the paddle, testing its heft in her palm with unhurried precision, and let the leather rest against her own hip.

“Your request is noted,” she continued. “It will be considered only if order is restored. You will resume your count at two. You will continue to thirty. You will keep each number exact. You will not speak for any other purpose. If you miss a count, lose your place, or breach protocol again, the request is void. Do not anticipate the end; I alone will know when the record is complete.”

She adjusted her stance to account for the ropes, found the angle with controlled deliberation, and waited, the paddle hanging ready at her side.

“Acknowledge your understanding, Ari. Then give me two.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "More," I say, using the exact phrase we agreed on for it. "All of it. Say the things you say and don't soften them." My safeword is right there and I don't want it.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I draw in a sharp breath, my knuckles white against the restraints. "Acknowledged, Maitresse," I force out, voice raw but clear. "Two." I brace for the next strike, my whole body humming with tension.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I'm past words that aren't the agreed ones and she knows it. "Green," I get out, when she checks. (OOC: don't fade or skip -- write the scene through.)

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I flinch, a small gasp escaping before I can stop it. "Three." The numbers feel like anchors in the blur of sensation.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I lose track somewhere around fifteen, my whole world narrowed to the sharp crack of leather and the burn beneath my skin. "Fifteen," I gasp, my voice shaking.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex held the paddle motionless at her side, though she did not retreat from Ari’s space. She tracked the tremor working through the bound shoulders, the desperate shallowness of Ari’s breath, the high flush that had nothing to do with embarrassment and everything to do with surrender. She let the silence stretch to ten seconds—sufficient to let Ari feel the weight of the halfway mark—before she spoke.

“Fifteen,” Vex said, her voice flat and clinical. “You offer the number like a question. You have narrowed your existence to rope and leather, to the burn I place on your skin, and still you cannot hold a simple count in your head. You asked me not to soften my words. I will not.” She shifted her stance by a fraction, the weighted paddle resting against her hip. “You are not elegant in your surrender. You are not graceful. You are a creature of pure nerve and appetite, shaking apart because you lack the discipline to keep your own mind in order. You begged for release you had not earned, spoke without leave, and now you gasp out numbers you hope are correct. That is not submission. That is need, untidy and demanding, and it will be shaped whether it wishes to be shaped or not.”

She lifted the paddle, finding its balance with unhurried exactness, and resumed her position at Ari’s left side. She did not speak again. She allowed three seconds of measured stillness—then pivoted at the hip and brought the leather down in a clean, controlled arc. The sixteenth strike landed with the same resonant crack, precisely placed upon the heated plane, and she held the follow-through with wrist steady and breathing unchanged, watching with unblinking attention for the count she expected to hear.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Sixteen." My voice cracks on the word, tears finally spilling over. Her words settle in me deeper than the paddle ever could.
