dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun had planned to say something when the door opened. He had in fact planned several things, over roughly nineteen weeks, and had rehearsed at least two of them.

Halle got the door open and he forgot all of them.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I don't say any of the things I planned either. I drop the bag and close the distance.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The bag hit the floor somewhere behind him. Jun didn't register it going — only the collision of Halle against his chest, the familiar weight of her, the smell of her that five months of recycled air and strangers' coffee and his own unwashed skin had not managed to overwrite.

He made a sound he would be embarrassed about later. Something low and broken in the back of his throat. His hands came up and found her face, her hair, the curve of her skull, her shoulders, like he was checking she was assembled correctly. Like if he stopped touching her she might disassemble.

"You're here," he said, or tried to. It came out rough and too quiet.

He kissed her before he finished the sentence.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I kiss him back, hard and desperate, my fingers curling into the fabric of his shirt. When we finally break apart, I'm breathless. "*Finally.* I thought that rotation would never end."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun laughed against her mouth, or tried to — it came out wet and unsteady, more breath than sound. His forehead dropped to hers and he just stayed there for a moment, breathing her in, his thumbs tracing slow arcs against her jaw like he was memorizing the shape of her again.

"*Finally,*" he repeated, the word ragged. "You — I had this whole thing. I had a whole *speech*, Halle. I was going to be — I don't know. Charming, or something." His voice cracked on the last word and he didn't try to hide it. His hands slid down to her waist and pulled her in flush against him, like the half-inch of space between them was an insult he'd been waiting five months to correct. "I was going to say something about missing you. Something *good*. And then you opened the door and I just —"

He kissed her again, harder this time, one hand fisted in the back of her shirt, the other pressed flat against the small of her back. When he broke off he was trembling slightly, which he hated, which he couldn't seem to stop.

"Nineteen weeks," he said, his mouth against her temple. His voice had gone low and rough, stripped of any pretense. "Nineteen weeks of — I couldn't even *look* at anyone, Halle. I just counted days. I counted them on the back of my hand and then I ran out of hand."

He pulled back just enough to look at her, and whatever was in his face was completely unguarded — no composure, no deflection, just five months of wanting written plainly across his features.

"Tell me you didn't change the sheets," he said, and the corner of his mouth tugged up despite everything, despite the way his eyes were bright and wet. "Tell me you haven't washed them since I left."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I kiss her and keep kissing her and we don't manage to get further into the flat than the hallway for a while.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun made a sound against her mouth — half laugh, half something else entirely — when she didn't answer him about the sheets. He didn't ask again. He was too busy kissing her, too busy pressing her back against the wall of the hallway with his whole body like he could somehow make up for five months of absence through sheer contact.

His hands were shaking. He noticed it distantly, the way you notice a thing about someone else, and was annoyed by it, and then forgot to be annoyed because Halle's fingers were in his hair and he was making that sound again, the embarrassing one, and he couldn't seem to stop.

He broke off just long enough to breathe. Just long enough to press his forehead to hers and say, rough and wrecked, "We are not — I am not making it to the bedroom. Halle. I can't. I need you right *here*, I need —"

He kissed the corner of her mouth. Her cheek. The hinge of her jaw. The place below her ear that he remembered, that he'd been remembering for nineteen weeks in a bunk that smelled like nothing he wanted.

"You have to tell me to stop," he said against her skin, and his voice had gone somewhere low and serious that he didn't entirely recognize. "Because I am not going to be the one to — Halle. I have been thinking about this for so long. I don't — I don't trust myself to be patient right now."

His hand found the hem of her shirt. He didn't pull. He just rested there, fingertips against warm skin, and waited, breathing unevenly against her neck.

"Tell me," he said again, quieter.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath, my own hands sliding under his shirt and mapping the familiar planes of his back. "*Don't* stop," I murmur against his lips, my voice just as wrecked as his. "I haven't washed the sheets."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun made a sound at that — at *both* things, her hands on his back and the admission about the sheets — and it was not a dignified sound. It was the kind of sound that would have made him die of embarrassment in any other context, a raw, relieved noise pulled from somewhere behind his ribs that he hadn't known existed until this moment.

"You kept them," he said, and his voice broke on it completely. He pressed his face into the curve of her neck and breathed, just breathed, his shoulders shaking with something he wasn't going to call crying because he was a grown man and he'd held himself together for nineteen weeks in a place where falling apart was not an option. "You *kept* them, Halle, you —"

He couldn't finish. Her hands were moving on his back and he was coming apart under them, every pass of her fingers undoing some knot he'd carried across an ocean and three time zones. His own hands finally moved — pulled her shirt up and over her head in one motion, dropped it somewhere he didn't look, and then his palms were flat against her stomach, her ribs, learning her again like a language he'd been afraid he'd forgotten.

"I have you," he said, and it wasn't a question. It was a confirmation, spoken into her skin like a vow. His mouth followed his hands — her collarbone, the dip of her sternum, the soft underside of her breast — and every point of contact felt like a small homecoming. "I have you, I have you."

He lifted her. It wasn't graceful — his knees were unsteady and his arms were trembling and he almost overbalanced — but he got her up against him, her legs around his waist, her back against the wall, and the sound she made when he did it went straight through him like a current.

"*Halle.*" Her name in his mouth like a prayer he'd forgotten the words to and just remembered. He was looking at her, close enough to count her eyelashes, and whatever was in his face was completely naked — five months of loneliness and longing and the particular ache of wanting someone you can't reach. "I'm going to — we don't have to — I just need to be *inside you*, Halle, I need to — please, can I —"

He was asking. Even now, even wrecked and shaking and desperate, he was asking, because he'd spent five months being afraid of exactly this: the moment where wanting tipped over into taking, and he needed to know she was with him. Needed to hear it.

He pressed his forehead to hers and waited, breathing ragged, his whole body taut with restraint he was rapidly running out of.

"Tell me," he said one more time, the words barely a whisper. "*Please.*"

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: The bag stays where it fell. So do most of our clothes, in a line down the hall that we are both going to find funny tomorrow.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun heard her — heard the *don't stop*, heard the thing about the sheets, heard both of them like they were the same sentence — and something in him came unspooled.

He kissed her. He kissed her like he was trying to apologize for every missed call and every late night and every morning he'd woken up in a bunk that didn't smell like her. His mouth moved from hers to her jaw to her throat, and he felt her pulse jump under his lips, and the small animal sound he made against her skin was not something he was going to be able to explain away later.

"Halle —" Her name again, because it was the only word left in his mouth, the only word that mattered. He said it into the hollow of her throat, against her collarbone, against the rise of her breast. "*Halle.*"

He was moving. He didn't remember deciding to move — only that they were suddenly in motion, her legs around his waist, his hands steadying her against him, and they were bumping into the wall and the hall table and each other in a graceless, shaking, half-blind progress down the corridor. He registered the edge of the doorframe against his shoulder and thought *ow* and did not slow down. Her laugh — or his, he couldn't tell anymore whose it was — broke against his mouth, and he swallowed it.

They made it to the bedroom. Barely. He got them through the door and then the backs of his knees hit the edge of the mattress and they went down together in a graceless collapse that knocked the breath out of him. He lay there for a second, looking up at her, and something about the angle of her — hair falling forward, light from the hallway behind her, the particular expression on her face — made his chest constrict so hard he had to close his eyes.

"Don't move," he said, and his voice was wrecked. "Just — give me a second. I need to —"

He didn't need a second. He needed to look at her. He needed to memorize this, the way the pillow hadn't been plumped since she'd last slept alone, the way the sheets still held the faint impression of *her* and not of him, the way she was sitting astride him in the half-dark looking down at him like he was something she'd been waiting for.

He reached up. His fingers found the clasp at the back of her — he'd done this a thousand times before, his hands knew the way, but they were shaking badly enough that he fumbled it, and the sound he made was half laugh, half groan.

"I can't — my hands won't —" He laughed again, helpless and embarrassed and entirely undone. "Five months and I can't even — Halle, I'm sorry, I'm —"

She helped him, or he helped her, or they figured it out together in the dark, and then her hands were on his chest and he stopped talking entirely because there wasn't a word in any language for what it felt like to have her skin against his skin after nineteen weeks of nothing.

He arched up into her. His hands found her hips, her waist, the curve of her ribs, and he held on like she was the only solid thing in a world that had just liquefied. He pressed his face into the curve of her neck and breathed, just breathed, his whole body trembling with the effort of going slowly when every nerve in him was screaming to *go*.

"Look at me," he said, and it came out rough and pleading. "Halle. *Look at me.* I need to see you. I need —"

He waited until she did. Until her eyes found his in the dark. Until he could see, in the faint light from the hallway, the way she was looking at him — not with pity, not with patience, but with the same raw, unguarded want that was tearing him apart from the inside out.

"*Now,*" he said, and it was half question, half plea. "*Please.*"

And when she answered — when her hands tightened on his shoulders and her hips shifted and she said whatever she said, whatever sound she made — he stopped holding back.

Later — much later, in a different kind of quiet, the kind that comes after — Jun lay with his face pressed into the pillow that still smelled like her shampoo and not like his own absence, and his arm was heavy across her waist, and he was tracing absent patterns on her hip with his fingertips because if he stopped touching her he thought he might actually die.

His breathing had finally steadied. His hands had finally stopped shaking. He was boneless and wrung out and absurdly, stupidly happy, and he was not going to think about the fact that his eyes were wet again because he'd already cried once tonight — *once*, against her stomach, at some point he was going to have to live down — and that was his limit.

"Hey," he said, into the dark. His voice was hoarse. It was barely a voice at all.

He pressed his mouth to her shoulder. Just rested it there, breathing her in.

"I had a whole speech," he murmured, and the laugh that came out of him was small and exhausted and real. "I really did. It had — I think it had *rhymes*, Halle. I wrote it on a napkin in a C-17 and I've lost the napkin and I cannot remember a single line of it."

He lifted his head just enough to look at her. His hair was a disaster. His eyes were red-rimmed. He looked like a man who had been taken apart and put back together by someone who knew exactly where all the seams were.

"You're not going to let me live this down, are you," he said, and it wasn't a question. He was already smiling — slow and helpless and completely gone for her. "The shaking. The crying. The *rhyme*. You're going to hold all of it over me for the rest of our marriage."

He kissed the corner of her mouth. Then the other corner. Then her nose, which she hated, which was why he did it.

"I'm home," he said, quieter. The smile had faded into something steadier, something that looked more like the man he'd been before deployment and less like the man he'd been in the hallway. He rested his forehead against hers and closed his eyes. "I'm *home*, Halle. I'm — I'm here."

His hand found hers under the sheets — the unwashed sheets, the ones that had waited for him — and laced their fingers together, and held on.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I let out a soft laugh, my fingers tightening around his. "Your terrible poetry is safe with me. But the shaking... that I'm keeping." I shift to press closer, my head fitting into the hollow of his shoulder. "I missed the way you feel."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun felt the laugh move through her before he heard it — the small tremor of it against his ribs, where her head was tucked into the hollow of his shoulder like it had been designed to fit there. Which, he thought distantly, it probably had been. Six years of sleeping beside someone. The body learns the shape of the other person the way water learns the shape of a glass.

"The shaking," he repeated, and the sound he made was something between a groan and a laugh. "Of course you're keeping the shaking. Of *course* you are."

He didn't move. He didn't want to move. His arm was heavy across her waist and his body had taken on that particular weight that comes after — not sleep, not yet, but the heavy, liquid stillness just before it, when every muscle has finally remembered it's allowed to unclench. He was aware, distantly, that he was still trembling. Faintly. In the way that aftershocks work — the big one already past, the smaller ones still rolling through.

He pressed his mouth to her hair. Breathed in. The shampoo. The sweat. The particular smell of *her*, which was not one smell but a composite, layered, the way a chord is layered — something floral underneath, something warmer on top, something underneath *that* that was just skin and sleep and the specific chemistry of the person he had chosen.

"I missed the way you feel too," he said, and his voice was so quiet it barely disturbed the air. "I missed it in a way I didn't — I didn't have a word for. I'd be lying in that bunk and I'd try to remember what your — the weight of you, specifically. Like, not *a* person. *You*. And I couldn't get it right. It kept coming out wrong. Too light, or too warm, or the breathing was off."

He shifted just enough to pull her closer, his hand sliding up her back, palm flat between her shoulder blades. Holding her there. Feeling her breathe.

"It was the breathing I kept getting wrong," he murmured. "Because you breathe in this — I don't know how to describe it. Three short and then a long one. Like you've got your own personal rhythm and nobody taught you it but you figured it out anyway."

He was quiet for a moment. His thumb traced a slow line up her spine, vertebra to vertebra, the way he used to when they were falling asleep. The way he'd done a thousand times before deployment. The way he was going to do a thousand times again, if he had anything to say about it.

"I tried to write it down once," he said. "What it felt like. Being here. Being with you. I thought if I got it on paper I could — I don't know. Read it back to myself. Like a letter from a better version of me. And I wrote the whole thing and then I read it back and it was just — it was just a list of your *parts*, Halle. Your hands, your mouth, the back of your neck. Like I was inventorying you. Like if I catalogued enough of it I could keep it."

A sound escaped him — small, self-conscious, the laugh of a man who has just admitted something embarrassing and is trying to walk it back even though he knows he can't.

"I crossed it out," he said. "And then I crossed out the crossing-out. And then I folded the paper into a C-17 and flew it home and now it's somewhere in that bag in the hallway and I genuinely do not know if I want to look at it again or burn it."

He tilted his head just enough to look down at her — at the curve of her cheek against his shoulder, the fall of her hair, the way her hand was still laced in his under the sheets.

"You're keeping the shaking," he said again, softer now. Almost wondering. Like he was turning the fact of it over in his hands. "Of all the things from tonight. The shaking and the — did I actually — Halle, did I actually *cry*? I feel like I remember crying. I feel like I have a memory of that happening. I'm choosing to believe that was a hallucination brought on by jet lag and physical exertion and we will never speak of it again."

He was smiling. He could feel it — the slow, helpless pull of it at the corner of his mouth, the way it kept arriving uninvited, the way it kept being *real* in a way his face hadn't felt in five months. He pressed his smile into her hair because he didn't know what else to do with it.

"I love you," he said, and the words came out simple and plain and completely unadorned, which was not how he'd planned to say them either. He'd planned a speech. He'd planned rhymes. What came out instead was just the fact of it, offered up into the dark like something he'd been carrying in his pockets for nineteen weeks and had finally set down on the kitchen table.

"I love you," he said again, quieter, "and I'm home, and your sheets smell like you, and I'm going to fall asleep on you in approximately four minutes and I am *sorry* in advance for the elbow you're about to take to the ribs."

His eyes were closing. He could feel it happening — the slow, irresistible pull of it, the way his body had finally, *finally* decided it was allowed to rest. His hand was still in hers. His arm was still around her. He was still here.

"Hey," he murmured, half-asleep already, the word slurring at the edges. "Halle."

A pause. His breathing was already changing — slowing, deepening, the three-short-and-a-long rhythm of hers beginning to sync with his own.

"Don't wash the sheets tomorrow, either," he said. "Just — leave them. One more day. I want to remember what this smelled like when I wake up."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I get her onto the bed and take her apart slowly with my hands and mouth, five months of intending to do exactly this and no reason left to wait.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun made a sound when Halle's mouth found the place below his ribs — a low, involuntary thing, more breath than voice, the kind of sound that had lived in his chest for nineteen weeks and only now had somewhere to go.

His hands found her hair. Her shoulders. The knobs of her spine, one by one, like he was reading her in braille. He couldn't keep still — his hips kept shifting, his breath kept catching, and every time she did something with her hands he arched off the bed like she'd touched a nerve that had been sleeping for five months and was now, very rudely, awake.

"*Halle* —" Her name, again, the only word he had left. He said it into the dark, into her hair, into the pillow that smelled like her shampoo and not like his absence. He said it like he was trying to get her attention even though she was *right there*, like he needed to confirm she was real every thirty seconds or he'd float away.

She was going slow. He could feel it — the deliberate, unhurried pace of her, the way she was taking him apart in pieces instead of all at once, and some distant part of him that still had access to language wanted to laugh, because *this* was the woman who'd dropped her bag in the hallway and closed the distance before he'd finished his first sentence. This was the woman who'd said *don't stop* before he'd even asked. And now she was here, unhurried, methodical, like she had all the time in the world.

Like she knew exactly what she was doing to him.

"You're —" He tried to form a sentence. Gave up. Tried again. "*You're doing this on purpose.*"

His hand found the back of her neck. Held on. His breath was coming in short, ragged pulls now, and the trembling had come back — not the desperate shaking from the hallway, something slower, something that moved through him in waves, something that crested every time her mouth found a new place and broke against him.

He was not going to last. He could feel it building — five months of wanting, compressed into a single point, and she was taking her time about it, she was *enjoying* it, and he was going to die here, he was going to die in this bed that still smelled like her shampoo and it was going to be her fault and he was not even going to be sorry about it.

"Look at me," he said, and his voice was wrecked — lower than he'd known he could go, rougher than he wanted it to be. "*Halle. Look at me.* I want to — I need to see you while you —"

He waited until she did. Until her eyes found his in the dark. Until he could see, in the faint light from the hallway they'd never bothered to turn off, the expression on her face — focused, intent, completely in control of a situation that had him coming apart at the seams.

"You're beautiful," he said, and it came out broken and honest and nothing like a compliment, more like a fact he was reporting from the field. "You are so — Halle, I can't — *I can't* —"

She did something with her hands. He lost the sentence. Lost the next one too. Lost, briefly, the ability to form words in any language at all.

When it broke over him it was quiet — no sound, really, just a long, shuddering exhale and his whole body going taut and then boneless, his hand tightening in her hair, his face pressed into the curve of her shoulder, his breath coming in ragged, broken pulls against her skin.

He didn't move for a long time. He couldn't. His body had become a thing that was mostly liquid and a small, stubborn part of his brain that was still trying to remember how to operate his limbs.

"Halle," he said, eventually, into her shoulder. His voice was barely there. "I am going to need approximately a week to recover from that and also I am going to need you to do it again in about eleven minutes."

A pause. His thumb traced a slow, absent circle against her hip.

"Okay," he said, quieter, "maybe eight minutes."

He turned his head just enough to look at her. His hair was worse than before. His eyes were worse than before. He looked like a man who had been thoroughly, comprehensively, *expertly* disassembled, and who was not remotely upset about it.

"I take back every word I said about you keeping the shaking," he murmured, and the smile that came over his face was slow and helpless and entirely without defense. "You can keep *everything* from tonight. Every embarrassing sound. Every — did I say your name that many times? I feel like I said your name that many times. You can keep all of it. It's *yours*."

He pulled her up against him, tucking her into the hollow of his shoulder, his arms wrapping around her like he was trying to keep her from escaping back to the hallway.

"I'm home," he said, again, like he was still getting used to the shape of it. Like it was a word he'd practiced in his head for nineteen weeks and was now, finally, allowed to say out loud.

His eyes were closing. His breathing was slowing. The three-short-and-a-long was starting to sync with hers, the way it always did, the way it had done for six years and would do, he was promising himself now, for a very long time after.

"Don't wash the sheets," he murmured, half-asleep. "Don't wash them tomorrow. Don't wash them the day after. I want to remember this. All of it. Every — "

He was gone. Mid-sentence. Mid-breath. Asleep against her hair with his arms still wrapped around her and his hand still tangled in hers and the smallest, most exhausted smile still on his face.

The bag stayed in the hallway. The clothes stayed where they'd fallen. The sheets stayed unwashed.

In the morning, he would wake up with his elbow in her ribs, exactly as promised, and he would not be sorry about that either.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I smile against his skin, my own body heavy and sated. "Eight minutes, huh? I'll set a timer." I shift just enough to pull the blanket up over us both, my fingers still laced with his. "Sleep. I'll be here."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun made a sound against her hair — half laugh, half something too tired to have a name — and his arms tightened around her, a reflex more than a decision, the way a hand tightens around something it's afraid of dropping in its sleep.

"Set a timer," he mumbled, into her hair, into the dark, into the place where his voice was already dissolving at the edges. "Set a — yeah. Do that. I'll be ready. I'll be —"

He didn't finish. His breathing changed — the three-short-and-a-long giving way to something slower, deeper, the particular rhythm of a man who had not slept properly in five months and whose body had finally, irrevocably, decided it was done waiting for permission. His hand stayed laced in hers. His face stayed pressed into her hair. The smallest, most exhausted smile stayed on his mouth, even after the rest of him had gone.

He slept like the dead. He slept like the living, too — heavily, completely, with the particular abandon of a person who has finally been given back the one thing they were missing and is now refusing, on a cellular level, to let go of it. His body curled around hers in sleep the way it always did — knee hooked over her hip, arm heavy across her waist, face tucked into the curve of her neck — and he didn't stir, not once, not through the small hours when the flat went quiet and the city outside dimmed to its lowest murmur and the only sounds were their breathing, slowly syncing, slowly becoming one rhythm.

He dreamed. He wouldn't remember it in the morning — something formless, something warm, something that had Halle's shape and Halle's voice and none of the specific anxieties that had lived in his chest for nineteen weeks. Just her. Just the fact of her, repeated, like a word he was finally allowed to keep saying.

---

He woke up slowly. The way a person wakes when their body has decided, for once, that there is nowhere it needs to be. Light was coming through the curtains — early, gray, the particular quality of a London morning that hasn't quite committed to being morning yet. The flat was quiet. The bag was still in the hallway. The clothes were still on the floor.

He registered these things in no particular order, the way you register things when you're surfacing from a very deep sleep and your brain is still booting up. Then he registered Halle. Warm. Present. Real. Tucked into the hollow of his shoulder like she'd been designed to fit there, which, he thought muzzily, she probably had been.

His elbow was in her ribs.

He became aware of this approximately three seconds before she did. He considered, briefly, the possibility of moving it. He considered the probability of waking her up by moving it. He considered, with the strategic mind of a man who had been married for six years, the possibility of pretending he hadn't noticed and dealing with the consequences later.

He moved it.

Halle made a sound. He pressed his face into her hair to hide the smile.

"I'm sorry," he said, and his voice was rough with sleep and completely unconvincing. "I warned you. I specifically — I believe I *apologized* in advance. I believe I said the words *elbow* and *ribs* in the same sentence. You were *informed*, Halle. This is on you."

His hand found her hip under the blanket. Rested there. He could feel her breathing — the three-short-and-a-long, exactly as remembered, exactly as missed.

He was quiet for a moment. Just breathing. Just being in a bed that smelled like her, in a flat that was his, in a city that had carried on without him for five months and was now, very patiently, allowing him to catch up.

"Hey," he said, softer. His mouth was against her hair. His eyes were still closed. "I'm still here."

A pause. The smallest smile.

"I didn't dream about the sheets," he murmured. "I dreamed about you. Just so you know. In case you were wondering what I — what the nineteen weeks were *for*, in the end. They were for this. This, specifically. Waking up with my elbow in your ribs and the flat smelling like us and you being *here*."

He opened his eyes. The morning was gray and quiet and entirely without ceremony. The bag was still in the hallway. The sheets were still unwashed. Halle was still warm against him.

"I'm going to make you coffee," he said, into her hair, into the morning, into the first day of the rest of it. "And you're going to tell me everything that happened while I was gone. And I'm going to pretend to remember most of it."

He kissed the top of her head.

"And *then*," he said, and the smile was audible now, "I'm setting the timer myself. Eight minutes. I stand by it."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "Stop being gentle," she says. "Nineteen weeks. I don't want gentle, I want to feel it tomorrow." She pulls me down by the back of the neck to make the point.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun made a sound against her mouth — something low and startled and entirely undone — when her hand closed around the back of his neck and *pulled*.

The sleepy softness of five minutes ago evaporated. Just — gone. Replaced by something that had been waiting underneath it the whole time, coiled and patient, something that had been listening to her breathe for nineteen weeks and was now, very clearly, *done* listening.

He shifted over her. Not gently. The word wasn't in his vocabulary right now — had been evicted from it somewhere between *nineteen weeks* and *feel it tomorrow*. His hand found her wrist — the one still wrapped around the back of his neck — and pinned it to the pillow beside her head, his fingers lacing through hers, holding it there.

"*Halle.*" Her name, low and rough, scraped out of him like something he'd been keeping in a locked room. "You can't — you can't just *say* things like that when I've been awake for thirty seconds. I have a *heart*. It's been through *things*."

But he wasn't pulling back. He was pressing closer, his weight settling over her, his free hand sliding up her side, her ribs, the curve of her breast — not careful, not reverent, just *present*, just *there*, like he was trying to take up more space against her body than physics should allow.

His mouth found the place below her ear. The place he'd remembered. He pressed his smile into it — he couldn't help it, the smile kept arriving, kept catching him off guard — and then bit down, gently, not gently, somewhere in between, and the sound she made went through him like a current.

"*Nineteen weeks,*" he repeated against her skin, his voice dropping into that low, serious register he'd found in the hallway and apparently couldn't get out of. "You think I've been *gentle*? Halle. I have been — I have been *so careful* with you. I have been *so* careful. I have been holding myself back since the *door*, do you understand that? Since you opened the door and I forgot every word I'd planned, I have been —"

He kissed her. Hard. The kind of kiss that wasn't a question.

When he broke off he was breathing ragged, his forehead pressed to hers, his hand still pinning hers to the pillow.

"I want to feel it tomorrow too," he said, and his voice was wrecked. "I want to feel it *next week*. I want to walk around this flat and know exactly where you touched me and have to — Halle, I'm going to have to sit at my own kitchen table and *remember* this, and you're going to be right across from me drinking coffee, and I'm going to be *ruined*, do you understand that? I'm going to be *ruined*."

He kissed her again. Slower this time, but not softer — slower the way a wave is slower when it's about to break. His hand released hers, slid down her arm, her side, her hip, and pulled her closer, flush against him, no space left between them, no space *allowed*.

"*Tell me again,*" he said against her mouth, his thumb tracing the line of her jaw. "*Tell me what you want. I want to hear you say it. I spent nineteen weeks not hearing you say anything and I need — Halle, I need to hear you say it.*"

His eyes were open. Looking at her. The gray morning light was doing something to her face that he wasn't going to survive, and he wasn't going to look away.

"I'm here," he said, quieter. "I'm *here*. And I'm not being gentle. I'm not being *anything* you don't ask me to be. So *ask*."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: My other hand fists in his hair, pulling his mouth back to mine. "*You,*" I bite out between kisses, hips arching against his. "Just you. Hard. Now."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun heard her — heard the *you*, heard the *hard*, heard the *now* — and something in him that had been holding very still for nineteen weeks finally, *finally* let go.

"*Halle* —"

Her name came out of him like a sound he'd been keeping in a locked room for five months, and the lock had just been broken from the inside. Her hand in his hair, her hips against his, the way she said *now* like a command and a plea in the same breath — it went through him like a current, like a thing with weight and heat and direction, and he followed it.

He kissed her. Not the careful, reverent thing from last night — not the slow, memorizing, trying-to-be-charming thing. He kissed her like a man who had been given permission to stop being careful and was discovering, in real time, how much of himself had been held back. His mouth moved from hers to her jaw to her throat and he didn't slow down, didn't pull back to check, didn't ask. She said *hard*. She said *now*. He was giving her both.

His hand found her hip. Gripped. Pulled her against him in a way that wasn't a suggestion, and the sound she made when he did it — the small, sharp intake of breath, the way her back arched off the bed — went straight through him and settled somewhere behind his ribs like a coal.

"*Like that,*" he said against her throat, his voice wrecked, scraped raw. "Tell me if it's — *Halle*. Tell me if it's too much. I need to — I need to know I'm not —"

She pulled his hair again. He lost the sentence.

He shifted over her. Settled his weight. His hand found hers — the one fisted in his hair — and pulled it free, pinned it to the pillow beside her head, his fingers lacing through hers and holding on. His other hand was already moving, already learning her again, but not carefully this time, not the slow mapping of last night — this was something else, something that had a rhythm to it, something that matched the way she was breathing now, faster, shallower, the three-short-and-a-long gone entirely, replaced by something ragged and wanting.

"Look at me," he said, and it wasn't a request. It was a demand. He wanted to see her. He wanted to watch her face while he — *while*. He wanted to see exactly what he did to her, exactly how she took it, exactly what she looked like when she stopped being careful and started being *honest*.

He waited until her eyes found his. The gray morning light was doing something to her face that he wasn't going to survive. Her hair was a mess. Her mouth was swollen. She looked like a woman who had been waiting nineteen weeks and was done being patient about it.

"*Now*,*" he said back to her, and the word was a mirror of hers, an echo, a confirmation. "*Now. Yes. Okay.*"

He didn't ask again.

---

Later — *later* — the flat was quiet in a different way. Not the heavy, liquid stillness of last night. Something sharper. Something that still had an edge to it. Jun was on his back, one arm flung over his eyes, his chest heaving, his whole body humming with the particular frequency of a person who has been thoroughly, comprehensively, *expertly* taken apart and is now lying in the wreckage trying to remember how to be a single coherent human being.

His other arm was around Halle. He was aware of this distantly — the weight of her against his side, her head on his chest, her hand somewhere over his heart. He was aware that his heart was doing something unreasonable under her hand and he was choosing not to think about it.

"Halle," he said, to the ceiling, to the morning, to the god of long deployments and complicated homecomings. His voice was gone. Completely gone. He had used it all up.

A pause. His chest moved under her head as he breathed.

"I am going to need you to know," he said, carefully, like he was picking his way through a sentence that had been blown to pieces, "that I have been awake for approximately ninety seconds. I have been awake for ninety seconds and you have already — Halle. I am a *pilot*. I fly multimillion-dollar aircraft. I have been in *combat*. I have *training*."

Another pause. His hand found her hair. Twisted a strand around his finger. Released it.

"And you," he said, with the slow, wondering air of a man delivering a field report, "have just ended me. Completely. In ninety seconds. I want that on the record."

He lifted his arm off his eyes. Turned his head to look at her. His hair was worse than before, which he hadn't known was possible. His eyes were — well. He was choosing not to think about his eyes.

"You said *feel it tomorrow*," he said, and the corner of his mouth tugged up despite everything, despite the fact that he was a man who had just been disassembled by his wife at seven in the morning on a Saturday. "I am going to feel it *next week*. I am going to be sitting across from you at that kitchen table and I am going to remember this *specific* morning and I am going to have to *excuse myself*, Halle. That is what's going to happen. You have created a *problem*."

He was smiling. He could feel it — slow, helpless, completely without defense. The same smile he'd fallen asleep with. The same smile that kept arriving uninvited, that kept being *real* in a way his face hadn't felt in five months.

He rolled onto his side, pulling her with him, tucking her into the hollow of his shoulder like she belonged there. Which she did. Which she always had.

"Coffee," he murmured into her hair. "I promised you coffee. I am a man of my word. Give me a minute. Give me — Halle, give me *several* minutes. I have to remember how my legs work."

His hand found her hip under the sheets. Rested there. The sheets that still smelled like last night. The sheets that were going to smell like *this* now too.

"Don't wash them," he said, quieter. Almost to himself. "Don't wash them for a *while*."

He pressed his mouth to her hair and closed his eyes and breathed, just breathed, the three-short-and-a-long syncing with hers, the way it always did, the way it had done for six years and was going to do, he was promising himself now, for a very long time after.

"I'm home," he said, one more time. Not because he needed to say it. Because he liked the way it sounded. Because it was true.

"I'm *home*."

Her name came out of him like something torn loose. He could feel it — the heat of her, the particular urgency of her body, the way she was pulling at him like she was trying to eliminate the last inch of distance between them. He pressed his forehead to hers and breathed, ragged, his eyes closed, his hand shaking again — the aftershocks, the five-month kind, the kind that didn't care that it was seven in the morning and the neighbours could *hear* —

"I can't — *Halle* —"

He said her name into the hollow of her throat. Pressed his mouth there. Felt her pulse jump under his lips, fast and unsteady, and the sound he made against her skin was low and wrecked and not at all quiet.

His hand found her. He learned her again — not carefully this time, not the slow reverent mapping of last night, this was something with *intent* to it, something that moved with the rhythm she'd set, something that matched the way she was breathing now, fast and shallow and broken. He watched her face. He couldn't look away. He wanted to see exactly what he did to her, exactly how she took it, exactly what she looked like when the careful, patient version of her finally stopped being careful and started being *honest* —

"*Like that*,*" he said against her mouth, his voice scraped raw. "Tell me — *Halle*. Tell me if it's —"

His hand found hers — the one fisted in his hair — and pulled it free, pinned it to the pillow beside her head, his fingers lacing through hers and holding on like he was afraid she'd disappear if he let go. He didn't ask again.

---

He moved into her like a man stepping into water after a long time in the desert — not slowly, not carefully, just *completely*, the whole length of him in one motion that knocked the breath out of both of them. The sound she made went through him like a current. The sound *he* made went through the wall, probably. The neighbours were going to have *thoughts*. He was not going to think about the neighbours.

"*Halle* — *Halle* —"

Her name, again, the only word he had left, repeated like a thing he was trying to get right. His forehead was pressed to hers. His hand was pinned with hers to the pillow. His whole body was trembling — not the shaking from last night, something else, something that moved through him in waves, something that crested every time she shifted her hips against his and broke against him.

He was not being gentle. She told him not to be. She told him to make her feel it *tomorrow*, and he was trying, he was *trying*, but the problem was that every time he moved she made a sound and every time she made a sound something behind his ribs came undone and he had to stop and just *breathe* for a second, just *exist* in the fact of her, just remind himself that this was real and not another one of the nineteen weeks of wanting.

"*Tell me*,*" he said against her mouth, his voice gone, completely gone, scraped down to nothing. "*Tell me what you want. I want to — Halle, I want to —"

She moved against him. He lost the sentence. He lost the next one. He lost, briefly, the ability to form words in any language at all, and what came out instead was a sound — low, broken, nothing like the composed man who'd walked through the door ninety minutes ago, nothing like the pilot who flew multimillion-dollar aircraft, just a man in a bed with his wife making sounds he was not going to be able to explain to anyone, ever, including himself.

He moved. Harder. The way she'd asked for. The way he'd been holding himself back from since the hallway, since the door, since the first moment he'd seen her face and forgotten every word he'd planned. His hand released hers, slid under her, pressed flat against the small of her back, and pulled her up against him, flush, no space, no distance, just *contact*, just *presence*, just the fact of two bodies learning each other again after nineteen weeks of forgetting.

"*I have you*,*" he said into her hair, into her throat, into the hollow of her shoulder where her pulse was jumping under his lips. "*I have you, I have you, I'm — Halle, I'm —*"

She said something. He didn't hear it. He felt it — the vibration of it against his mouth, the way her whole body tightened around him, the way her hands fisted in his hair and *pulled* —

He came apart.

It wasn't quiet. It wasn't the quiet, shuddering exhale of last night. It was a sound pulled out of him from somewhere behind his ribs, raw and wrecked and *loud*, and he didn't try to muffle it, didn't try to bury his face in the pillow, just let it happen, let it go through him like a wave, let it break against her and pull him under.

His whole body went taut. Then boneless. He collapsed against her, his face pressed into the curve of her neck, his breath coming in ragged, broken pulls against her skin. His hand was still pressed flat against her back. His other hand had found hers somewhere in the wreckage and was holding on, fingers laced, knuckles white.

"Halle," he said, eventually, into her shoulder. His voice was gone. Completely gone. He had used it all up. "Halle. I —"

He couldn't finish. He didn't need to. He pressed his mouth to her shoulder, to her throat, to the corner of her jaw, and just stayed there, breathing, trembling, *home*.
