dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I laugh, a breathless, satisfied sound. "*Good.* Let them listen." I curl into him, my leg hooking over his hip. "Coffee can wait. I'm not done with you yet."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun made a sound against her hair — something that might have been a laugh if it had any air left behind it, which it didn't, because she had used all of it up.

"Coffee can wait," he repeated, into the dark of her hair, into the morning, into the particular silence of a flat that had been quiet for nineteen weeks and was now, apparently, *done* being quiet. "Coffee can — Halle. I promised you coffee. I made a *promise*. I am a man who keeps his promises. I have medals that say I keep my —"

She shifted her leg over his hip and he lost the sentence. Lost the next one too. The medals, specifically, were going to have to wait.

"Halle." Her name came out somewhere between a warning and a prayer. "I am — Halle, I am *thirty-three*. I am not twenty-two. I cannot just — there are *refractory periods*. This is *biology*. I have a *body* and it has *limits* and you are —"

Her mouth found the place below his ear. The place she knew about. The place she'd always known about.

"— you are being *very unfair*,*" he finished, and his voice had gone somewhere low and rough that he didn't entirely recognize, and his hand was already sliding down her back, finding the curve of her hip, pulling her closer, because his mouth kept saying *limits* and his body kept saying *Halle* and his body had been right about her for six years so he was inclined to trust it.

He rolled them. Not gracefully — his knee caught the sheet and his elbow hit the headboard and he made a sound that was half swear, half laugh — but he got her under him, settled his weight, looked down at her with his hair falling forward and his eyes still wrecked and the smallest, most helpless smile on his face.

"Not done with me yet," he said, and it wasn't a question. He was looking at her — at the mess of her hair against the pillow, at her mouth, at the way the gray morning light was doing something to her collarbone that he was going to remember for the rest of his natural life. "You are *not done with me yet*. Halle. I have been home for *ninety minutes*. I have been awake for — I don't even know how long I've been awake. I have lost count. I have lost the ability to count. And you are telling me you're not done."

He kissed the corner of her mouth. Then the other corner. Then her jaw, her throat, the place below her ear that made her breath catch.

"I love you," he said against her skin, and it came out wrecked and honest and completely unadorned, the same way he'd said it last night, the same way he was going to keep saying it for as long as she let him. "I love you and I am *ruined* and the neighbours are going to *hate* us and I am not going to wash these sheets for a *month* and I am not done with you either, I was never going to be done with you, I don't know how to be done with you, I have been trying to figure out how to be done with you for nineteen weeks and I have *failed completely*."

His hand found hers. Pinned it to the pillow. His thumb traced the line of her knuckles — slowly, carefully, the only careful thing about him right now.

"So no," he murmured, and his mouth found hers again, and the smile was still there, pressed into the kiss like a thing he couldn't put down. "Coffee can wait. *Everything* can wait."

A pause. His forehead dropped to hers.

"But Halle," he said, quieter, "when I say *eight minutes* this time, I mean it. I am *begging* you. I am a *professional*. I have *limits*."

He was already shifting against her. His limits, it turned out, were negotiable.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I grin against his neck, my hands sliding down his back to pull him closer. "Professional my ass," I murmur, teeth grazing his skin. "Eight minutes. Starting now."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun made a sound against her hair — something low and involuntary, something that would have embarrassed him in literally any other context, a sound that started in his chest and ended somewhere behind his teeth. Her teeth grazed his neck and his whole body tightened, his hips shifting against hers before his brain had any say in the matter, a reflex he was not going to be able to explain to anyone, ever.

"*Starting now*,*" he repeated, and his voice had gone somewhere wrecked and low. "You're — Halle. You're *counting*. You're actually — you're going to *time* me. You are timing me like I'm a — like this is some kind of —"

She pulled him closer. Her hands on his back, her teeth on his neck, her leg still hooked over his hip. He lost the sentence. Lost the next one. Lost, briefly, the ability to form words in any language, which was becoming a pattern this morning, which he was choosing not to examine.

"*Okay*,*" he said, against her throat, his mouth moving down her skin, finding the place at the base of her neck where her pulse jumped under his lips. "*Okay. Fine. Eight minutes. Starting now. I want that on the record, I want — Halle, I want you to know that I am a *professional* and I am being *unfairly provoked* and whatever happens in the next eight minutes is *entirely your fault* —*"

She moved against him. He made a sound into her skin that was not dignified and was not quiet and was going to be the neighbours' problem now and forever.

His hand found the back of her knee — the one hooked over his hip — and pulled it higher, adjusting the angle, pressing closer, and the sound she made when he did it went through him like a current and settled somewhere behind his ribs like a coal that was going to burn for the rest of the day.

"*That's not —*" he started, against her mouth, his voice scraped raw. "*That's not eight minutes. That was — I haven't even — Halle, I haven't even done anything yet, you've already —*"

She bit his lower lip. Pulled. He lost the sentence again.

He was going to lose a lot of sentences this morning. He could already tell. He was going to lose *every* sentence this morning, and probably most of the afternoon too, and possibly into next week, because she was grinning against his neck and her hands were doing things on his back and her leg was hooked over his hip and he was a *pilot*, he had *training*, he had been in *combat*, and none of it — *none* of it — had prepared him for Halle at seven in the morning with her teeth on his throat and a timer in her head.

"*Halle.*" Her name, low and rough, pulled out of him like something he'd been keeping in a locked room. "*Halle, I —*"

He kissed her. Hard. The kind of kiss that wasn't a question, that wasn't a request, that was just a man who had been given back the one thing he'd been missing and was now trying to memorize the shape of it with his mouth. His hand slid up her side, her ribs, the curve of her breast — not careful, not reverent, just *present*, just *there*, like he was trying to take up more space against her body than physics should allow.

He pulled back just enough to look at her. His hair was falling forward. His eyes were wrecked. The gray morning light was doing something to her face that he was going to carry with him into every briefing room and every cockpit for the rest of his career.

"*Eight minutes*,*" he said, and the corner of his mouth tugged up despite everything, despite the fact that he was a man who had been thoroughly undone by his wife at seven in the morning on a Saturday and was about to be undone *again*. "*I'm going to make you *beg* for those eight minutes, Halle. I'm going to make every single one of them *count*. You started the timer. You don't get to complain about what happens next.*"

He kissed her again. Slower this time, but not softer — slower the way a wave is slower when it's about to break, the way a held breath is slower on the inhale, the way everything gets slower in the moment before the thing you've been waiting for finally arrives.

His hand found hers. Pinned it to the pillow. Laced their fingers together and held on.

"*Starting now*,*" he murmured against her mouth, and the smile was there, pressed into the kiss like a thing he couldn't put down, like a thing he'd been carrying for nineteen weeks and was finally, *finally*, allowed to set down on the kitchen table.

"*For real this time.*"

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I laugh, breathless. "Counting down, Captain." I arch into him, my hands sliding to his hips. "Seven and a half minutes left."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: I need you right *here*

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She helped him, or he helped her, or they figured it out together in the dark, and then her hands were on his chest and he stopped talking entirely because there wasn't a word in any language for what it felt like to have her skin against his skin after nineteen weeks of nothing.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: Jun made a sound when Halle's mouth found the place below his ribs

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: Tell me again, Tell me what you want. I want to hear you say it

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: He moved into her like a man stepping into water after a long time in the desert — not slowly, not carefully, just *completely*, the whole length of him in one motion that knocked the breath out of both of them.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun had planned to say something when the door opened. He had in fact planned several things, over roughly nineteen weeks, and had rehearsed at least two of them.

Halle got the door open and he forgot all of them.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I don't say any of the things I planned either. I drop the bag and close the distance.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
He caught her.

That was all his body knew how to do — arms coming up, pulling her in, face burying against her neck like he could press the scent of her directly into his lungs and hold it there. His duffel hit the floor somewhere behind him. He didn't care. Didn't care about the door still open, didn't care about the neighbor's porch light, didn't care about anything that wasn't the solid, warm, *real* weight of her against him.

His hands spread wide across her back — one between her shoulder blades, one low at her waist — pressing her closer like even full contact wasn't close enough. Five months of calling, of screen-lit faces in bad lighting, of her voice in his ear while he lay on a thin mattress six thousand miles away, and none of it — *none* of it — had been this.

"I missed you," he managed, muffled against her skin, and the words were so insufficient that a rough sound escaped his throat that was almost a laugh. He pulled back just enough to find her face with both hands, thumbs tracing her cheekbones, his eyes scanning her features like he was memorizing her all over again.

Then he kissed her.

Not gently. Not the careful, tender reunion kiss he'd probably imagined somewhere in the early weeks when he still had romantic notions. This was months of wanting compressed into something that shook through his whole body, desperate and a little unsteady, his fingers sliding into her hair, his forehead dropping against hers between breaths because he couldn't stop touching her long enough to do both at once.

"Hi," he whispered, wrecked already, barely through the door.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I grip the front of his shirt, holding on like he might disappear if I let go. My laugh is shaky, breathless against his mouth. "Missed you too. So much it hurt."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Something cracked open in his chest at that — *so much it hurt* — because he knew. He knew exactly what she meant, lived with that same ache so long it became background noise, a phantom limb, something you learned to function around until you didn't have to anymore.

"Me too," he said, voice rough. His hands hadn't stopped moving — down her arms, back up to her jaw, her shoulders, like he was confirming she was actually here, that his hands still knew the geography of her. His thumb traced the line of her collarbone where her shirt dipped, and he swallowed hard.

He kicked the door shut behind him without looking. Didn't care about the duffel. Didn't care about the bag she'd dropped. The entryway was close and dark and she was here and he was here and that was the only inventory his brain was capable of running.

"You're—" He stopped. Tried again. "Your hair's different." His fingers found the ends of it, and his face did something complicated. "I like it. I would've noticed on the calls but the connection was always so—" He shook his head, dismissing the old frustration. "Doesn't matter. You're here. I'm here."

He pressed his forehead to hers again, breathing her in, his arms looping tight around her waist and just — holding. Not kissing, not talking, just standing in the entryway with his whole body curved around her like he could keep the world out for five more minutes.

"I kept your voicemails," he admitted quietly, embarrassingly. "The one where you were mad at the dishwasher. The one where you were laughing about the squirrel. I played them—" His jaw tightened. "More than I should probably tell you."

He pulled back enough to look at her face in the dim light, eyes still searching, still hungry for every detail. "Are you okay? Are you good? Did everything—" He gestured vaguely at the apartment, at the life she'd been holding down alone for five months. "Did I miss anything big? Small? I want all of it. Every boring thing."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I kiss her and keep kissing her and we don't manage to get further into the flat than the hallway for a while.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun didn't fight it. Didn't suggest they move to the bedroom, or the couch, or even further than the two feet of entryway tile they were standing on. His back hit the wall and he pulled her with him, hands fisting in the fabric of her shirt like an anchor, like the only thing keeping him upright.

He kissed her like breathing — continuous, necessary, something his body would simply refuse to stop doing. Between kisses he murmured things, fragments, half-sentences that dissolved against her mouth. *God, I missed you. You feel so good. I thought about this — about you — every single—* and then he'd kiss her again before the thought finished because talking was a waste of the seconds his mouth could be on hers.

His hands found the hem of her shirt and slid underneath, palms pressing flat against the warm skin of her back, and the sound he made was almost wounded — a sharp exhale through his nose, his forehead dropping to her shoulder for half a second before he tilted her face back up and kissed her harder.

Five months. Five months of screens and static and his own hand and trying not to think about this exact thing in too much detail because it made the distance unbearable. And now she was here, warm and real and making sounds against his mouth that unravelled him completely.

"I'm not—" he managed, pulling back just far enough that their lips barely separated, breathing hard. "I'm not gonna be able to do slow right now. I want you to know that. I planned — I was gonna be — romantic. Candles or some—" He shook his head, laughing breathlessly, wrecked. "That's not happening. I need you. I need—"

He didn't finish. His hands tightened on her waist and he kissed her again, deep and certain, his whole body pressing forward off the wall into hers, making his intentions very clear without any further words required.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I push against his chest, turning us so it's his back against the wall this time. My hands are already working at the button of his jeans. "Slow is overrated," I murmur against his lips, voice low. "Don't need candles. Just need you."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The breath left him in a rush — half laugh, half something else entirely — when her hands found the button of his jeans. His head fell back against the wall with a dull thud he didn't feel, eyes closing for just a second as her fingers worked, because even that small, practical point of contact threatened to undo him.

"Yeah," he managed, voice barely recognizable to himself. "Yeah, okay. Good."

His hands found her waist and he pulled her flush against him, one arm wrapping tight around her lower back, the other hand cradling the back of her head like she was something precious even as his hips pressed forward into hers, making it abundantly clear that *precious* and *desperate* were currently sharing the same body and neither one was winning.

He opened his eyes and looked at her — really looked, the way he had in the entryway, memorizing — but this was different. This was the version of her face he'd tried and failed to conjure on a thin mattress in a room that smelled like dust and diesel, the flush in her cheeks, the way her lips parted, the particular angle of her jaw that his mouth knew better than his brain did. The reality was better. It was always better. It was the thing that made the leaving unbearable and the coming back transcendent.

"I dreamed about you," he said, hands sliding down to grip the backs of her thighs — a question, a request, muscle memory from six years of marriage knowing exactly how she fit against him when he lifted her. "Specifically you. And then I'd wake up and you weren't there and I—" He cut himself off, jaw working. Not the time. Not the place. Later, maybe, in the dark, tangled together in their own bed, he'd tell her how bad it got in the middle weeks. Right now she was here and warm and her hands were on him and that was the only thing that mattered.

He lifted her, pressing her back against the opposite wall, his body settling between her thighs like coming home — which, in every way that counted, it was. His forehead dropped to hers, breathing ragged, pulse hammering somewhere behind his ribs and in his throat and everywhere she was touching him.

"Tell me if—" he started, the last shred of the responsible husband he'd been trying to be all evening surfacing briefly. "Door's shut. You're sure. Because I will stop, I can stop, but it's going to take actual effort and I want to know—"

He kissed the corner of her mouth. Her jaw. The spot below her ear that had always made her arch into him, and he felt the familiar response and had to press his face into her neck and breathe through the wave of want that nearly buckled his knees.

"I love you," he said against her skin, wrecked and certain and five months overdue. "I love you so much. That's — that's the thing. That's always been the thing."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: The bag stays where it fell. So do most of our clothes, in a line down the hall that we are both going to find funny tomorrow.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Later — considerably later — Jun lay on his back in the hallway, one arm flung over his head, the other still wrapped around Halle where she was pressed against his side. The carpet was rough against his bare shoulders. He didn't care. He'd slept on worse. He'd slept without her, which was worse than anything.

His chest rose and fell unevenly. His heartbeat was still hammering, but slowing — settling into something that felt less like survival and more like arrival. He turned his head and pressed his mouth to her hair, breathing her in, and felt his whole body go heavy with the particular kind of exhaustion that came after adrenaline stopped doing its job.

"We're on the floor," he observed, voice rough and distant even to his own ears. A beat. "The hallway floor."

He looked down the length of the corridor at the trail they'd left — his uniform shirt over the back of a chair that didn't belong in the hallway, her top somewhere near the bathroom door, everything else scattered like breadcrumbs marking the path from entryway to here. He could see his duffel still where it had fallen. Her bag. The door, shut now, thank God.

His fingers traced idle patterns on her shoulder. He felt — not empty, not the hollow ache that usually followed something this intense, but *full.* Settled. Like a dislocated joint finally clicking back into place.

"I had a whole plan," he murmured, turning his face into her hair again because he could, because he was allowed to now, because the five months of *not* were over and he never had to count the days forward again. "Dinner. Probably flowers. I was going to ask you about your week and pretend I was a normal person who'd been at a normal job and not—" He gestured vaguely with his free hand at nothing in particular. "This."

His arm tightened around her. He wasn't ready to let go. Might not be ready for a while. There was a bed — their bed, ten feet and one doorway away — and his body was already cataloguing every hard surface he'd just been pressed against in a way that was going to register as complaints by morning. None of it mattered enough to move.

"You're going to have to tell me what I missed," he said quietly, after a minute that felt like the first peaceful one in nineteen weeks. "All of it. The squirrel thing — I need context for the squirrel thing eventually. The dishwasher thing. Everything." His thumb traced a slow arc on her skin. "But maybe tomorrow. Maybe right now we just—" He pressed his lips to her temple. "Stay."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I laugh softly, the sound vibrating against his chest. "The squirrel was an asshole. Kept stealing tomatoes off the windowsill." I shift, wincing at the carpet burn I know I'll feel later. "And I'm not moving. You'll have to carry me."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The laugh that escaped him was low and warm and entirely involuntary — the kind of laugh that came from somewhere deeper than amusement, that lived in the same place as the ache that had finally, *finally* quieted.

"Squirrel was an asshole," he repeated, like he was committing the phrase to memory, filing it somewhere safe alongside the voicemails and the voicemails and every other mundane piece of her life he'd missed. A tomato-stealing squirrel. God. Five months and she'd been here, dealing with pest wildlife and broken appliances and he'd been—



He stopped that thought before it went anywhere useful. Not tonight.

"Carpet burn," he said, his hand sliding down to find where she'd winced, fingers gentle over what he imagined was already turning pink against the rough hallway carpet. "That's — yeah. That's my fault. I should've — the bed is *right there.*" He tilted his head vaguely toward the doorway they could both see and neither of them had used.

He didn't move.

"I could carry you," he said instead, and his voice had shifted into something softer, more honest, stripped down to the bones of a man who had spent nineteen weeks being strong and competent and self-sufficient and wanted absolutely nothing more than to be useful to this specific person in this specific moment. "I will carry you. Give me — give me a minute. My legs don't work yet. You broke my legs."

His arm tightened around her. His other hand found hers where it rested on his chest and he threaded their fingers together, holding on with a grip that said *not letting go* more clearly than any words could have.

"Tomato-stealing squirrel," he murmured, mostly to himself, pressing another kiss to the top of her head. "What else. Give me — give me something else. Something stupid. Something small. I want to hear your voice talk about absolutely nothing for approximately the next... forever."

He exhaled slowly. His eyes were closed. The carpet was terrible and the floor was hard and he could feel every single joint in his body beginning to file formal complaints about surfaces and angles and the creative misuse of entryways, and none of it — not one fraction of it — compared to the five months of military-issue mattresses and rooms that smelled like other people and being unable to reach out in the dark and find her.

"We should move," he said.

He didn't move.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I get her onto the bed and take her apart slowly with my hands and mouth, five months of intending to do exactly this and no reason left to wait.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The journey from hallway to bedroom was graceless — stumbling, laughing, Jun's hands unable to stop touching her long enough to navigate a doorway he'd walked through a thousand times. His hip caught the doorframe. He didn't care. Couldn't bring himself to care about anything except the warmth of her fingers laced through his, pulling him forward, pulling him home.



She laid him back and he let her. That was the thing that surprised him — how easily he surrendered. Jun, who had spent five months being decisive, competent, in control of every variable he could grip with both hands, went soft and pliant the moment her weight settled over him, the moment her mouth found the hollow of his throat, and every coherent thought he'd ever had simply... left.

His hands found her hair. Her shoulders. The curve of her waist. He touched her like braille, like if he pressed hard enough and long enough he could encode every detail into his palms so the next time — if there was a next time, God, he couldn't think about that, not now — he'd have something more real than memory to hold onto.

She took her time. He had not asked her to. He had, in fact, thirty seconds into being horizontal, made a sound that was approximately sixty percent *please* and forty percent *right now*, and she had ignored it completely, and he loved her so fiercely for it that his eyes stung.

Because she knew. She knew what he needed even when he didn't — not urgency, not the frantic hallway version of this, but the slow, thorough, *I'm here and I'm not going anywhere* version. The version that said *I have you, I have all the time in the world, let me put my hands on every part of you that the desert and the distance tried to claim.*

His breath came in uneven pulls. His fingers tightened in the sheets, then released, then found her again — her jaw, the curve of her ear, the place at the base of her neck where her pulse lived. He could feel it under his thumb, fast and alive, and something about that — the simple biological fact of her heartbeat — made his throat close.

"Look at me," he whispered, when she'd drawn him far enough out of his mind that the world had narrowed to sensation and nothing else. His voice was unrecognizable. Wrecked in a different way than the hallway had wrecked him — deeper, older, stripped past desire into something that lived in the same place as prayers and last thoughts before sleep. "I need — can you look at me. I need to see you."

When she did, he cupped her face with both hands and held her there, thumb tracing the edge of her cheekbone, eyes moving over every feature like a man reading a letter he'd waited months to receive.

"There you are," he said, barely audible, and something in his chest settled — the last piece, the final tectonic plate grinding into place after months of seismic drift. "There you are."

He pulled her down and kissed her — slow this time, impossibly slow, the kind of kiss that was more about presence than pressure. His hands mapped the landscape of her back, her sides, the places he knew by heart and the small new details that five months had added without his permission. He catalogued each one. Filed it away. Let himself feel the grief of what he'd missed and the gratitude of what remained, all tangled together in the same breath.

When she moved against him — deliberate, unhurried, an invitation rather than a demand — he exhaled her name like it was the only word he remembered, and pulled her closer, and let the five months dissolve into the slow, certain rhythm of her.

After, he didn't let go. His arms stayed locked around her, her head tucked under his chin, their legs tangled in sheets that had pulled half off the mattress in a way that would have been embarrassing if he'd had any capacity left for embarrassment. He didn't. He was empty. Quiet. The first truly quiet his mind had been since the day he'd left.

His fingers traced the line of her spine, slow and repetitive, the way you'd touch something to confirm it was real. His lips rested against her forehead. He breathed.

"I'm not deploying again," he said, into the dark, into her hair, into the space where promises lived. It wasn't technically his to promise — he knew that, knew the machinery of it, the bureaucracy, the forms and rotations and *needs of the service.* But he said it anyway, because some things needed to be spoken aloud before they could begin to be true.

"Or — I don't know. I might. I probably will. But I'm going to fight it. I'm going to fight it every single time." His arm tightened around her. "Five months. That's — that was too long. That was too long, Halle."

He pressed his mouth to her temple and held it there, breathing her in — soap and sweat and home, just home — and felt his eyes close without permission, his body finally registering the thirty-six hours of travel and the adrenaline crash and the fact that he was warm and horizontal and *here.*

"Don't let me fall asleep yet," he murmured, even as his body began to betray the request, going heavy against hers. "I have — there's things. I brought you something. It's in the duffel. The hallway. You can't — it's not flowers, it's stupid, it's—"

His words slowed, tangled, dissolved.

"I love you," he managed, the last clear thing before sleep began its hostile takeover. "I love you. I love the squirrel. Tell me about the squirrel in the morning. I want—" A long breath, settling deeper into the mattress, into her. "I want the whole story."

His hand found hers in the tangle of sheets and held on. His breathing evened. The apartment was quiet around them — their apartment, their life, the one she'd been keeping warm and real and waiting for him all these months.

He was asleep in minutes. He didn't let go of her hand.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content:
I listen to his breathing even out, my own exhaustion finally settling deep in my bones. I don't pull my hand away. Instead, I press my lips to his shoulder, tasting salt and skin and *home.*

Tomorrow, I'll tell him about the squirrel. And the dishwasher. And how I slept on his side of the bed the whole time. For now, I let myself drift off, anchored by the weight of his arm and the quiet sound of his sleep.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun woke at 0430.

Not to an alarm — there was no alarm, no boots hitting floor, no distant sound of someone else's radio through thin walls. He woke to silence, and warmth, and the particular weight of a hand resting on his chest that did not belong to any version of his life from the last five months.

His eyes opened. The room was dark, but not the unfamiliar dark of a barracks or a tent or a transport. This dark had a shape he knew — the angle of the streetlight through the curtain they'd never replaced, the shadow of the dresser, the closet door that didn't close all the way unless you lifted it. Home dark. Their dark.

Halle was curled against his side, her face tucked into the curve of his shoulder, her breathing slow and deep. Still asleep. His hand was still holding hers, exactly where it had been when consciousness left him, and his fingers had cramped around hers in a grip he was mildly embarrassed about even though no one had witnessed it.

He didn't move. Didn't breathe too hard. Lay there in the dim wash of streetlight and looked at the ceiling of their bedroom and felt the absolutely surreal sensation of not being anywhere else.

His eyes burned. He blinked. Swallowed.

*Don't,* he told himself. *You're home. She's right here. Don't.*

It didn't help. His throat worked anyway, and he pressed his mouth to the top of her head and breathed through it — the wave of relief so enormous it felt like grief, the two emotions sharing some back room in his nervous system that he'd never fully understood. He'd felt this before. Every homecoming, a version of this. The first time, six years ago, he'd actually cried, and she'd pretended not to notice, and he'd loved her so much for that small, deliberate mercy.

This time his eyes were just wet. A few seconds. He blinked them clear against her hair and went still again, listening to her breathe.

The apartment was quiet. He could hear the refrigerator humming — the one with the ice maker that made the grinding sound she'd complained about in the voicemail from... February? March? He couldn't remember. He could hear a car passing outside, distant. No traffic at this hour, just someone else awake in the world, living their own version of whatever this was.

He shifted carefully, just enough to turn his head and look at her. She'd burrowed closer in her sleep, her hand curling into the front of whatever he was wearing — or not wearing, he realized, still in the state they'd ended up in, and the thought made something warm and stupid bloom in his chest. Her hair was different. He'd noticed before, in the entryway, but now he could actually see it — shorter, maybe, or just styled differently, and he wanted to know the story of it. Wanted to know every story. The squirrel and the dishwasher and the hair and every grocery trip and Tuesday evening and boring, ordinary, *wonderful* thing that had happened in the months he'd been away.

*I slept on his side of the bed.*

He didn't know that yet. Would find out in the morning when he woke properly and saw the dent in the pillow and the book on the nightstand — his nightstand — and would have to excuse himself to the bathroom for a minute to get his face under control.

Right now he just lay there, awake in the middle of the night in his own bed with his wife warm against him, and let himself feel the full, terrifying weight of how much he loved her. Not the frantic hallway version. Not the desperate bedroom version. The 0430 version — quiet and enormous and almost too much to hold.

His fingers tightened around hers, gently this time, and he pressed one more kiss to her hair.

"I'm here," he whispered, so softly it barely disturbed the air. Not for her. For him. A confirmation. A fact he needed to say out loud to make the last thread of the dream dissolve.

He was home. She was here. The squirrel was an asshole.

He closed his eyes. His body, impossibly, was already dragging him back under — the deep, total exhaustion of a man who had finally stopped running, finally stopped counting, finally stopped being strong enough for two people. His arm stayed around her. His hand stayed holding hers. The last thing he was aware of, before sleep took him again, was the sound of her breathing and the absolute, bone-deep certainty that he was exactly where he was supposed to be.

He didn't wake again until morning.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "Stop being gentle," she says. "Nineteen weeks. I don't want gentle, I want to feel it tomorrow." She pulls me down by the back of the neck to make the point.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The sound he made against her mouth was not entirely human.

Something between a growl and a groan — the last thread of careful snapping clean through, nineteen weeks of restraint dissolving in the space of a single sentence. His body went taut beneath her, every muscle pulling tight, and when she dragged him down by the back of his neck he didn't resist. Didn't hold back. Went willingly, hungrily, his mouth finding hers with the kind of force that had been living behind his teeth for months.

Halle hesitated for a moment, a playful expression on her face. "What if I don't want to share my treasures?"

Halle laughed, the sound filling the room as she climbed onto the couch next to him. "Okay, okay. I'll share. But only because you're cute when you're begging."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya looked at him for a moment, just long enough to be sure of what she was looking at. Six years of evenings like this one, give or take. Six years of the particular discipline of being someone's closest friend.

She wasn't nervous, exactly. She was something more precise than nervous.

"I think we should stop not doing this," she said. "I've thought about it and I think that's the right call."

She said it the way she said most things she'd decided — plainly, without softening the edges, because the edges were part of it.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn’t realize I was holding. “I’ve thought about it too.” I tilt my head toward her, just slightly. “A lot, actually.”

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"Good," she said. "That's good to know."

She was quiet for a second, not because she was uncertain but because she was being precise about the order of things. She had thought about this. She had thought about the six years and what they were worth and what it would cost to keep doing what they'd been doing, which was pretending the evening always ended at the door.

She thought it was worth it. She had decided it was worth it. That was why she was here, saying this, instead of going home the way she usually did.

She shifted on the couch to face him properly.

"I'm not worried about us," she said. "I want to say that clearly, because I think sometimes people do this and they're mostly worried, underneath it. I'm not. I know you. I've known you a long time and I'm not worried about what happens after."

She paused.

"I just wanted you to know that's where I'm starting from."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The noise surprised her a little — she hadn't known she was going to make it until she did. Six years of the careful architecture of not doing this, and now it was just gone, and she was kissing Cal on his couch at whatever time it was with the credits long finished and the television throwing blue light across the room.

She pulled back after a moment. Not far. Just enough to look at him.

She wasn't nervous. She had expected to be, at some point in this sequence of events, and she wasn't. She was something else entirely — something that felt like recognition, which was almost funny, because she knew his face as well as she knew anyone's face on earth and still this was different. This was new information about a thing she thought she already knew completely.

"Okay," she said. Quietly, not performing anything. "Okay, that's —"

She stopped. She didn't usually stop in the middle of sentences.

She had a sudden, clear image of herself at twenty-two, sitting in this same apartment, which had been a different apartment then, thinking *not this, not yet, we're not doing this* — and then at twenty-four, and twenty-six, and all the other times she had made the same sensible decision.

"We wasted a considerable amount of time," she said.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I catch the look in her eyes and huff a short, quiet laugh. "We were idiots." My thumb brushes her cheek, still close enough to feel her breath. "But we're here now."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"We were," she agreed. She didn't soften it. They had been idiots, specifically and documentably, and she saw no reason to pretend otherwise now.

But she felt the warmth of his thumb against her face and thought: *here now* was not nothing. Here now was, in fact, considerable. Six years of friendship intact and this on top of it, and she was not nervous, and the evening had changed character in exactly the direction she had decided it should change.

She had spent a long time being careful. She had been careful at twenty-two and twenty-four and twenty-six and all the years between, and she had been careful for good reasons, reasons she could still enumerate if pressed, and she was done with it. She had decided she was done with it. That was the thing about deciding — once you'd actually done it, the deciding was over.

She leaned into his hand a little.

"I'm not interested in being retrospectively tragic about it," she said. "Just so you know. I'm not going to spend the next however-long being sad about the time we lost." She paused. "I might be occasionally annoyed about it. Briefly. That's different."

She looked at him.

"Mostly I'm just interested in this part."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: We get to the bedroom eventually, laughing at ourselves most of the way, and then stop laughing when the clothes are actually off.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The laughing had been good. The laughing had been very them, which was something she'd wondered about — whether this would stop being them somehow, whether the thing they were stepping into would require them to be different people — and it hadn't. They had tripped over his shoes in the hallway and she had said something cutting about his organizational systems and he had said something worse back and they had been laughing when they got there.

And then they weren't.

She understood, in the quiet that followed, why people made a serious thing of this. She had thought it might feel continuous with everything that had come before — just an extension of the evening, of six years of evenings — and instead it felt like a door. The same people on the other side of it, but a door nonetheless.

She looked at him in the low light of his bedroom, which she had been in before, many times, for entirely different reasons, and felt the particular weight of being known by someone who was now knowing her differently.

She wasn't nervous.

She was — present. More present than she had been in some time. All of her attention gathered in one place, which didn't happen often.

"Hi," she said, which was not a sophisticated thing to say, but it was what she had.

She looked at him steadily.

"Yes," she said. No pause, no qualification. She had done the pausing and qualifying privately, over a long period of time, and she had arrived here having finished all of it. "I'm sure. I've been sure for a while. That was rather the problem."

Her fingers tightened around his.

She understood why he'd asked. She would have asked too, probably, if their positions were reversed — not because he doubted her but because some things warranted saying out loud, warranted being confirmed in actual words by the actual person. Six years of friendship had taught her that about him. He was careful with things that mattered to him.

She was, apparently, one of them.

That landed somewhere in her chest in a way she hadn't quite anticipated, even having anticipated most of this. She had thought through a great deal of it, sitting with her own certainty over the past however-long, and she had not thought through that specific moment — the moment of understanding, concretely, that she had always been one of the things he was careful with.

"Are *you* sure," she said. Not performing doubt, not projecting, just — returning the question. Because it was a fair question. Because he was allowed to have it too.

He was paying attention. That was — she noticed that. She noticed it in a way that bypassed analysis entirely.

Then she moved her arm.

That was the thing, she thought. That had always been the thing. Six years of him not going anywhere, of the particular reliability of him, and she had used that reliability as a reason to be careful and now she was on the other side of it and it turned out the reliability was still there. The ground had not shifted. She had been right not to be worried.

Then she adjusted.

She had been careful without quite noticing she was being careful, which was the insidious thing about six years of a particular habit — it got into the muscle memory, into the automatic responses, and she had been treating him like something that might break under her hands when he was *Cal*, who she had known in every configuration she could think of and who was currently telling her, plainly, that she was doing it wrong.

She turned her head.

"Better," she said.

Not a question. A verdict.

"Okay. I'm done annotating."

"Six years," she said, a little breathless, mostly amused. "You couldn't have done that in the kitchen? On the trip? I stood there for a full minute."

She was smiling. She couldn't quite stop.

"Don't answer that. I know why. I did the same thing." Her thumb moved, absent, sure. "We were being careful. I get it. I just want it noted that we were both being ridiculous."

She didn't move away. She had no intention of moving away.

"Okay," she said, softer. "Not a maybe. Still?"

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "Still." My voice is rough. I lean my forehead against hers. "Not a maybe for me either. Not for a long time."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"Good," she said, and the word came out quieter than she meant, half-swallowed by how close he was.

She stayed there with her forehead against his, eyes closed for a moment, just breathing him in. There was no rush in it. That was the strange, good thing — the nervousness had gone entirely, and what replaced it wasn't urgency but a kind of certainty that had all the time in the world.

"I keep waiting for the part where this feels weird," she admitted. Her thumb was still moving at his jaw, slow. "Like the floor's going to shift and I'll suddenly realize I've ruined the best thing I've got. And it's not happening. It just feels like — you. Like it was always going to be you and we were both very stubborn about it."

She opened her eyes. Pulled back just far enough to look at him properly, to make sure he was looking back.

"I don't want to do the thing where we pretend tomorrow that this was a moment," she said. "It wasn't a moment. I've thought about this sober, in daylight, standing in line at the grocery store. So." A breath. "This is a decision. I made it a while ago. I'm just telling you now."

She let that sit, then softened, the smile creeping back in.

"That's the last serious thing I'll say tonight, I promise. After this you can kiss me again and I'll stop talking."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: We get to the bedroom eventually, laughing at ourselves most of the way, and then stop laughing when the clothes are actually off.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The laughing stopped because it had to, because there was nothing funny left once it was just skin and the low light and the fact of him actually there, actually hers, no more hypothetical to hide behind.

Priya went still for a second. Not nervous — she was past nervous, had been for an hour — but caught by the weight of it. Six years of imagining and none of the imagining had quite gotten the details right. The reality of him was better and stranger than the version she'd built in her head, and she wanted a moment to actually see it before she stopped being able to think.

"Hey," she said, quiet, reaching for him. She pulled him down with her, deliberate, unhurried. "There you are."

There was no performance in it. That was the thing she'd been most afraid of and the thing that turned out not to exist at all — the awkwardness of newness with someone she already knew down to the bone. She knew how he took his coffee. She knew the sound he made when he was pretending a joke hadn't landed. This was just the rest of it, arriving late.

She kissed the corner of his mouth, his jaw, slower now.

"Still not weird," she murmured against his skin, and she felt the laugh move through her chest one more time before it turned into something else entirely. "Just you."

She stopped talking after that. She'd promised she would.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I shiver when her mouth meets my jaw. "Yeah," I manage, my hands finding her hips. "Just you." I'm trying to go slow, I really am, but it's hard when the waiting part is finally, finally over.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She felt him trying to go slow and she loved him for it, in a distant, dissolving way — loved that even now, even here, he was being careful with her. But the careful part had had six years. It didn't need any more.

"You don't have to," she said, low, her hand sliding up his back to press him closer. "Slow. We've done slow. We did six years of slow."

The waiting was over for her too, and she let him feel that, let it be in the way she moved against him, unhurried but sure, no hesitation left anywhere in her body. Her breath caught when his hands settled at her hips and she made a soft sound against his throat that had nothing patient in it at all.

"Just — " she started, then didn't finish, because the sentence had stopped mattering.

She'd known it would feel like this. Not the specifics — the specifics were better than anything she'd let herself picture standing in that grocery line — but the essential fact of it, that it would feel less like a beginning and more like something clicking into a place it had always been shaped for. She pulled him down the rest of the way and stopped thinking in words.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I get my mouth between her thighs and stay there while she tells me exactly what she wants, specifically, in a voice I have never heard her use in six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The voice surprised her too, the first time it came out — lower than her ordinary register, stripped of all the careful hedging she used everywhere else in her life. But she didn't second-guess it. That was the whole point of the last hour, the last six years. She was done second-guessing anything about this.

So she told him. Not shy about it, not performing either — just clear, the same directness she brought to everything once she'd decided, except now it was decided about this, about the exact way she wanted his mouth on her.

"There," she managed, her hand finding his hair, not pulling, just anchoring. "Yes — like that, don't — " and then a sound that wasn't a word at all when he did exactly like that.

She'd wondered, on the stubborn patient nights, whether the two of them would know each other in this. Whether the ease that ran through everything else — the coffee, the jokes, the way they finished each other's stupid sentences — would survive the translation into skin. It did. He listened to her the way he'd always listened to her, and gave her precisely the thing she asked for, and she let her head fall back against the pillow and stopped holding any of it in.

"God, you're—" She broke off, breathless, and the laugh that tried to surface got caught up in something sharper. Her thighs tightened around him. "Six years. You could have been doing *this*."

But she wasn't really complaining, and they both knew it. She pressed him closer and let herself be exactly as loud and exactly as specific as she wanted, because there was no version of him she needed to hide from anymore. There never had been. It had just taken her this long to stop pretending otherwise.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I laugh against her skin, breathless. "We're making up for lost time now, aren't we?" My hands slide up to her waist, holding her steady. "And I'm not stopping until you're satisfied."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"Making up for lost time," she echoed, and the laugh in her broke apart into something less steady when he settled back into it. "Then you'd better — clear your schedule."

The words came out uneven, which she didn't mind. Nothing about her was steady now and she'd stopped wanting it to be. His hands at her waist held her the way she needed to be held, an anchor against her own dissolving, and she let them, let him, let all of it.

"You're staying, then," she said, and it wasn't really a question either — same as *we're going to sit here and be honest about it* had not been a question, hours ago, a lifetime ago, on the couch. Just her stating the shape of the thing so it couldn't be pretended away in the morning. "Good. Because I'm not letting you off this — *there,* God, there — I'm not letting you off easy either."

She pressed a heel against his back, urging, her hand tightening in his hair, and gave up on full sentences entirely. There was no need for them. He knew how to listen and she knew how to tell him, and the two things met in the middle the way they always had, the way she'd been too careful to find out for six ridiculous years.

She let it build. Didn't rush it, didn't hold it back — just rode the certainty of it up and up, saying his name once, low, like the last honest thing she had left, and then she stopped being able to say anything at all.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "You can stop being careful with me," she says. "I'm not made of glass and I've thought about this for as long as you have. Harder."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya let the aftermath move through her, her chest still rising fast, one hand loose in his hair now instead of gripping. She hadn't come back down all the way yet and she wasn't in any hurry to.

"That's the part you keep missing," she said, when she could shape words again. Her voice had gone soft but the directness was intact, undimmed. She reached down and drew him up along the length of her until he was over her again, until she could see his face. "You keep treating me like I might change my mind. Like I wandered into this."

She held his eyes, thumb finding the corner of his jaw again, the gesture already familiar, already hers.

"I didn't wander in. I walked. Slowly, sure — six years slowly — but I always knew where I was going." A breath. "So stop bracing for me to bolt. I'm not going to. I decided a long time before you did, I think. I just took longer to say it out loud."

She pulled him down and kissed him, tasting herself on him and not minding, kissing him the way she'd wanted to kiss him standing in that kitchen on that trip, the way she'd talked herself out of a hundred times.

"You've got me," she murmured against his mouth. "Not carefully. Just got me." Then, because the seriousness had had its turn and she was still, underneath everything, herself: "Now — you said you weren't stopping. I'm holding you to that."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a breath, a laugh that's mostly just relief. "Yeah. Okay." I kiss her again, slower this time, then shift to press my mouth to her neck. "You've got me too. Not carefully."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"Not carefully," she agreed, and something in her chest settled the rest of the way when she said it, some last held thing finally set down.

She tipped her head to give him her neck, her fingers spreading flat against his back, and let herself feel the weight of him without any of the old vigilance running underneath it. That was the difference, she thought — not the sex, though the sex was its own revelation — but this. Being able to lie here and hold someone she'd loved for six years and not have to keep any part of herself in reserve against the possibility of losing him. She'd already lost the version where they never did this. Good riddance to it.

"I want to be clear about one more thing," she said, though her voice had gone lazy now, half-drowned in the feel of his mouth working down her throat. "This is the last serious thing, I mean it this time." She smiled against the top of his head. "In the morning, when the light's ordinary and there's coffee and you're being weird about whether to reach for me — don't be weird. I'll have decided all of this again by then. I decide it every morning already. You just weren't in the room for it before."

She turned her face into his hair, breathed him in.

"So. Stay. Reach for me. And—" the smile widened, turned into something warmer and less patient at once, "—you're still not off the hook for that schedule you're supposed to be clearing."

She drew him back up to her mouth, and this time she didn't say anything else at all.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: Six years of not doing this and now neither of us can form a sentence. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya kept her hand fisted in the sheet at first and then moved it to him instead, because the sheet gave her nothing to hold onto and he did. Every part of the last six years of restraint had converted into this — into being able to say *don't stop* and have it be a plain true thing, no hedging around it, no worrying what it would cost her tomorrow.

"Don't stop," she said again, lower, when he found the angle she wanted, the one she'd told him about in that stripped-down voice and he'd remembered. Of course he'd remembered. He remembered how she took her coffee. This was just the rest of it. "*There* — Cal, right there, don't—"

She lost the end of it again. She kept losing the ends of sentences and she'd stopped being embarrassed about it somewhere around the point where being embarrassed with him became impossible, which had happened years ago, in daylight, over nothing.

Her legs came up around him and she pulled him deeper, matched him, the two of them finding a rhythm the way they found everything — a little clumsily at first and then all at once, easy, like it had been waiting. She pressed her mouth to his shoulder and made a sound she'd never made in front of anyone she'd have to see at breakfast, and then remembered she wanted to see him at breakfast, wanted every breakfast, and the sound turned into something that was almost a laugh and almost his name.

"I've got you," she said against his skin, breathless, because it seemed important to say it while she still could. "Not carefully. Don't stop, don't—"

And he didn't, and she stopped being able to hold onto words at all, and this time she let them go entirely and just held onto him.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I shudder, my own release hitting me hard enough that I lose my breath. My face is buried in her neck, and for a long minute, the only sound is both of us trying to remember how to breathe.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya lay there with the whole weight of him and didn't move, didn't want to move, felt his breath going ragged against her neck and matched hers to it without meaning to. Her hand had found the back of his head at some point and stayed there, fingers slow in his hair, the same absent sure gesture she'd been making at his jaw all night, like her body had already decided this was hers to touch.

The room came back slowly. The ordinary furniture of it. The clothes somewhere on the floor between here and the door. The fact that it was very late and she had, technically, work in the morning, and she found she could not make herself care about a single practical thing.

"Okay," she said eventually, when she had enough breath for it. Just that, soft, into his hair. It wasn't a question or a statement of terms this time. It was closer to wonder, which she'd have been embarrassed by in front of almost anyone else.

She let another minute go by. Felt his heartbeat come down against her chest, slowing, ordinary again. Six years and it turned out the extraordinary part was this — the after, the quiet, the being allowed to stay in it.

"You're heavy," she informed him, entirely without complaint, and made no move to get him off her. Her arm tightened around his back instead. "Don't go anywhere."

She turned her head, pressed her mouth to whatever part of him was closest — his temple, the edge of his ear — and let her eyes fall shut.

"Morning's going to come," she murmured, "and there's going to be coffee, and you're not going to be weird about it. We agreed." A pause, the smile audible in it. "But that's morning. Right now I'm just going to lie here and be smug that we finally did it."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I laugh, the sound muffled against her skin. "Smug is allowed." I shift just enough to prop myself up on my elbows and look at her. "But you should know—I'm not going to be weird about the coffee. I've been imagining that part too."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya opened her eyes when he propped himself up, and there he was, looking down at her with that face she'd known for six years and was only now getting to see from this angle, in this light, undone.

"You've been imagining the coffee," she repeated, and something in her chest went soft and stupid at it. "God. Of course you have. That's the most *you* thing I've ever heard."

She reached up and pushed a bit of hair back off his forehead, the gesture unhurried, proprietary in a way she was still getting used to and already loved.

"For the record, so have I," she admitted. "Not the — well. Not just the obvious part. The boring part. You in my kitchen being wrong about how much water goes in the pot. Me pretending to be annoyed about it." Her thumb traced his brow. "I wanted the boring part maybe more than the rest. That's how I knew it was real and not just—" she gestured vaguely at the whole undone situation of them, "—this. Though this is also, for the record, extremely good."

She let her hand settle at the side of his neck, feeling his pulse there, ordinary now.

"So." A slow breath. The last of the seriousness she kept promising to be done with, arriving quietly. "We do the boring part too. All of it. The coffee and the arguments about the pot and the Tuesdays where nothing happens." She held his eyes. "I've decided about that part just as hard as the rest. Longer, probably."

Then she tugged, gently, until he came back down to her, because she'd had enough looking and wanted him close again.

"Now stop looming and let me be smug in peace," she said into his shoulder. "We can be functional adults in the morning. There's coffee for that."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I settle back against her, tucking her head under my chin. "Functional adults. Right." I press a kiss to her hair. "But I'm stealing your coffee mug in the morning. I've decided about that too."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The film had finished some time ago and neither of them had done anything about it, which was how Priya knew the evening had changed character.

"We're not watching this," she said.

"We haven't been watching it since about nine."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "No," I agree. "We haven't." I don't move, but I stop pretending I'm looking at the screen.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya turned to face him on the couch, tucking her legs beneath her. The remote sat on the cushion between them, untouched. She looked at it, then at him.

"So." The word sat there.

Six years of not doing this. Six years of careful navigation around the obvious, around the thing neither of them named. She'd thought about it sometimes—the way you think about something you've decided not to buy, checking on it occasionally to see if it's still there. It was always still there.

She was aware of her own breathing, the slight quickness of it. Her hands stayed still in her lap.

"I think we should talk about the fact that we're not watching the movie," she said. "And what that actually means."

Her voice was steady. She'd passed through the nervousness sometime during the last hour—she could feel where it had been, like a handprint on glass, but it wasn't there anymore. What remained was something cleaner. Certainty, or something close to it.

She met his eyes. Waited.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I look right back at her, and I don't smile. "Okay." My voice is quiet, but it doesn't waver. "What does it mean, Priya?"

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya held his gaze. The room was quiet except for the ambient hum of the credits still scrolling on some menu screen she'd lost track of.

"It means I've been sitting here for the last hour thinking about you instead of the film," she said. Simply. Without performance. "And I think you have too."

She let the silence after that exist. She didn't rush to fill it or soften it. That was something she'd learned about herself over the years—she could tolerate silence when it mattered.

"I'm not going to pretend I don't know what this is," she said. "And I don't think you need me to."

Her hand moved to the remote, picked it up, set it on the arm of the couch. A small thing. Clearing the space between them, literally, which felt both ridiculous and necessary.

"Six years, Cal." Her voice was low but steady. "I've thought about this for six years. I'm done thinking about it. I'm done deciding not to."

She unfolded her legs, shifted closer. Not touching him yet. Not quite. But the distance was different now—chosen, deliberate, the kind of nearness that meant something.

"So I'm asking. Are we doing this?"

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her, finally, six years late, and she makes a small furious noise that I think is about the six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The noise she made was indeed about the six years—about all the evenings that could have ended like this and didn't, all the goodnights that were just goodnights, all the times she'd driven home from his apartment with her hands tight on the wheel, willing herself not to turn around.

She kissed him back without hesitation. Her hand came up to the side of his face, fingers pressing into his hair, and the kiss deepened into something less careful than the first one. Six years of restraint unspooling. She was aware of making a sound again—something closer to relief this time, or surrender.

When she finally pulled back, she didn't go far. Her forehead rested against his. Her breathing was uneven now, which she hadn't expected—she'd been so steady a moment ago, so sure, and she was still sure but her body was catching up to what her mind had decided.

"Finally," she said. The word came out rougher than she intended. She laughed once, breathlessly, her thumb tracing along his jaw. "Jesus, Cal."

She kissed him again, shorter this time, then drew back enough to look at him properly. Her eyes were bright. A little wild, maybe. She felt unlocked.

"I have a lot of thoughts about the last six years," she said. "But I'm going to save them. Right now I just—" She stopped, shook her head. "I just want to be here. In this. With you."

Her hand moved from his face to his chest, palm flat against his heartbeat.

"Is that okay?"

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I catch her hand against my chest, holding it there. "It's more than okay." My own voice sounds rough, too. "I'm not going anywhere."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Something in her chest loosened at that—a knot she hadn't fully realized she'd been carrying. She exhaled against it, let the tension go.

"Good," she said. Her voice had steadied again, finding its footing. "Because I've been carrying this around for six years and I'd really like to put it down."

She shifted closer still, closing the remaining distance between them on the couch. Her knee pressed against his thigh. She could feel the warmth of him through the denim, and the simple concreteness of it—the fact of contact, of permission—made her want to laugh again, or maybe cry, though she wasn't going to do that. Not now. This wasn't a sad thing.

She leaned in and pressed her mouth to the corner of his jaw, then just below his ear. Not quite a kiss. A mapping. Learning the geography of something she'd only ever looked at from a distance.

"I want to know everything," she murmured against his skin. "All the things you didn't say. All the times you almost—" She stopped herself, pulled back enough to look at him. "Later. Tell me later. Right now just—"

Her fingers curled into the fabric of his shirt.

"Right now just keep being here. With me. Like this."

She kissed him again, slower this time. Deliberate. Taking her time now that time had finally started.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: We get to the bedroom eventually, laughing at ourselves most of the way, and then stop laughing when the clothes are actually off.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The laughter had been good—necessary, even—a release valve for the absurdity of two people who'd circled each other for six years finally fumbling down a hallway. But then his shirt came off, and then hers, and the laughter died somewhere around the time her back met the mattress and she looked up at him and understood that this was actually, finally happening.

She felt exposed in a way that was more than physical. Six years of friendship meant he knew her in ways no one else did—her moods, her silences, the way she took her coffee, the shows she pretended not to watch. But this was different. This was her body, her want, the thing she'd kept carefully compartmentalized now laid bare under his gaze.

She reached for him. Her hands on his shoulders, his back, the planes of him she'd never touched except in accidental brushes. He was real and warm and here, and she was shaking slightly, which surprised her because she'd been so steady on the couch.

"Hey," she said. Soft. A grounding word, for both of them maybe. She pulled him down to her, kissed him slowly, let her hands learn the territory of his skin. The small of his back. The ridge of his spine. The way his breath caught when she pressed her hips up to meet his.

She held his face in her hands, thumbs along his cheekbones, and looked at him in the low light of the bedroom.

"I want you to know," she said, "that I'm not scared of this. I'm not scared of us. I'm just—" She swallowed. "I've wanted this for so long. I don't know what to do with all the wanting."

She pulled him closer.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "Then let's figure it out," I breathe against her mouth, my hands sliding down her sides. "We've got time now. All the time in the world."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"All the time in the world," she repeated, and the words landed somewhere deep, in the place where she'd stored all the maybe-somedays and what-ifs. They sounded different in his voice. Possible. Real.

She arched into his touch, her body responding before her mind could catch up. His hands on her sides felt like a question and an answer at once, and she found herself nodding—yes, this, yes, you, yes—though he hadn't asked anything aloud.

She pulled him down to her, kissing him with a kind of hunger that surprised her. She'd been so measured on the couch, so adult about it, and now here she was—undone, wanting, her hands gripping his shoulders like she was afraid he might evaporate. Six years of wanting had its own momentum.

"Cal," she said against his mouth, not a question, just the need to say his name in this new context. To feel it shape differently on her lips now that she was allowed.

She shifted beneath him, arranging them, her leg hooking over his hip. The wanting was a physical thing now—a heat, an ache, a pull toward something she'd only ever imagined in the dark alone. She pressed her forehead to his.

"Stay with me," she said. "Don't be careful with me. Not tonight."

Her hands slid down his back, pulling him closer, and she let herself fall into the feeling of finally—finally—having what she'd spent six years deciding not to take.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
That voice—she didn't recognize it at first. Low and unguarded, stripped of the careful modulation she'd used for six years of friendship. She heard herself say his name, then say it again, and then say things that were more instruction than sound, her hands in his hair because she needed something to hold onto.

She'd never been quiet during sex, but this was different. This was specific. She knew him—knew his rhythms, his humor, the way he took up space in a room—and now she was learning this too, learning how he responded to her voice when it sounded like this, learning that he listened, that he adjusted, that he made her feel heard in a way that made her breath come apart.

"Cal—" His name broke in half on her tongue. Her head pressed back into the pillow. She could feel herself shaking, could feel the pressure building, and she tried to say something about it, tried to warn him, but all that came out was a sound she'd never made before, raw and startled, like she'd stumbled into something she hadn't known she was looking for.

She pulled at his shoulders after—needed him up, needed him over her, needed his weight and his mouth and the reality of him pressing her into the mattress. Her hands were trembling when she framed his face.

"I need—" She kissed him, tasting herself. "I need you inside me. Now. Please."

The please surprised her. Priya didn't say please, not like this, not with that edge of desperation. But six years of waiting had worn grooves into her, and she found she didn't care about dignity or composure or any of the things she usually held close.

She held his eyes. Steady, even now. Even with her pulse visible in her throat.

"I need this to be real," she said. "I need you to make this real."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I reach for the condom on the nightstand, fumbling a little, because my hands aren't steady either. "It's real, Priya," I say, my voice thick. "It's always been real." I push inside her, and her sharp inhale sounds like a truth we both finally get to hear.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The inhale became a sound she couldn't have named—a noise that lived in the space between relief and overwhelm. Her body adjusted to him, and she let herself feel all of it: the stretch, the fullness, the unmistakable fact of *him*, here, inside her, after all those nights she'd imagined exactly this and then told herself to stop imagining it.

Her eyes had closed without her permission. She opened them, found his face above hers, and held on.

"Stay," she said. Not because he was leaving, but because she needed to say it. Because six years of not-having had made her superstitious. Because some part of her still expected to wake up.

Her legs tightened around him, her hands pressed flat against his back, feeling the shift of muscle as he moved. She moved with him, finding the rhythm of it, the conversation their bodies were having for the first time. It was awkward in places—a misaligned angle, a readjustment—and she loved that too, loved the imperfection of two real people figuring each other out instead of the seamless fantasy she'd constructed alone.

"Don't hold back," she told him, her voice close to his ear. "I want all of it. I want to feel you tomorrow."

She meant it literally. She wanted the reminder—wanted to sit at her desk tomorrow and feel the echo of this, the proof that it had happened, that she hadn't dreamed it.

Her hands slid up his back, into his hair, pulling him down to kiss her. Deeper now. Less careful.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "You can stop being careful with me," she says. "I'm not made of glass and I've thought about this for as long as you have. Harder."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She felt the shift in him—the moment he stopped treating her like something precious and started treating her like something wanted. The difference was immediate and electric.

*Yes.*

dialogue.content:
The film had finished some time ago and neither of them had done anything about it, which was how Priya knew the evening had changed character.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya considered the shape of the next thirty seconds and decided she wasn't going to fumble them. She reached for the remote, killed the television, and set it down on the coffee table with a small deliberate click. The room went quieter than she expected. The lamp behind the sofa was still on, throwing warm light across half of Cal's face.

"Okay," she said. She turned toward him properly, tucking one leg up under her so she was facing him on the sofa. Her heart was doing something ridiculous but her hands were steady. "I'm going to say the thing. Because if I don't say it we're going to sit here for another two hours pretending we're going to say it, and then you'll go home, and I'll be furious with both of us."

She paused, not because she was reconsidering, just to make sure he was actually listening.

"I've wanted to kiss you for a really long time. Longer than is reasonable. And I think you've wanted to kiss me too, and we've both been extremely well-behaved about it, and I'm done being well-behaved about it tonight." Her voice was level. "So. Tell me if I've got that wrong."

Something moved across her face — not quite a smile, more the small easing of a muscle she hadn't realised she'd been holding. The ninety seconds were up. She wasn't nervous anymore.

"Good," she said quietly. "That's good."

She didn't lunge. She didn't need to. She shifted closer along the sofa until her knee was pressed against his thigh, and she reached up with one hand and laid it flat against the side of his jaw, thumb just under his cheekbone. She looked at him for a moment like she was making sure she had this right — not checking permission, she already had that, more like she was taking a mental photograph of the last second before.

Then she kissed him.

It was not a tentative kiss. She had been thinking about it for six years and she wasn't going to insult either of them by being coy about it now. But it wasn't hurried either. She kissed him like someone who had finally sat down to a meal she'd been putting off, slow and full and entirely present, her hand still warm against his face.

When she drew back — not far, just enough to look at him again — her mouth stayed a little parted, and she made a small sound that was almost a laugh but not quite.

"Okay," she said, mostly to herself. And then, to him, softer: "Hi."
