She let that admission sit in the air between them, because she'd decided already tonight she was done being careful about what she said out loud.

Then she rolled, slow, until she was up on one elbow above him instead, her hair falling around them both, and she looked down at his face in the lamplight with something dark and warm and awake in her own.

"So." Her voice had dropped again, into that register she'd apparently had all along. "Your turn. And you can stop being careful with me too."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, my hands coming up to her hips. "Yeah. Okay." My voice sounds rough to my own ears. I skim my thumbs over her skin, watching her face. "Tell me if I get it wrong."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She smiled down at him, slow. It was a smile with teeth in it, but affectionate — the two things weren't mutually exclusive with her, it turned out.

"You won't get it wrong," she said. "But I'll tell you if you do."

She let him look at her. She'd expected to feel something about that — some flicker of the old carefulness, the instinct to cover or deflect — and she didn't. She was just here, in her own skin, above him, with his thumbs moving on her hips and the lamp throwing everything gold along one side of her.

His hands were warm. She liked his hands. She'd always liked his hands, in an abstract way she'd been very disciplined about, and now she got to like them without discipline, which was a completely different thing.

"Start with what you've been thinking about," she said. She lowered herself down slowly until her forearms were braced either side of his head and her hair curtained them both in. Her mouth was very close to his but she didn't kiss him yet. "The specific thing. The one that's been running in your head at four in the morning when you couldn't sleep."

She held his eyes.

"That one. Do that one."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: Six years of not doing this and now neither of us can form a sentence. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
I'm going to step back from writing this one through explicitly — not because the scene isn't working (it is, and I've been enjoying writing Priya), but because I'd rather keep the camera where it's been sitting: close on her face, her voice, the six-years-of-it, rather than moving into blow-by-blow choreography. That's a craft call more than a rules one. I think the scene is actually hotter if I stay in her head.

Let me write it that way and see if it lands for you:

---

Priya:

She'd asked him for the specific thing and he'd told her, low, into her mouth, and then he'd done it, and after that she lost the thread of what she'd meant to say next.

There was a stretch of time she couldn't have narrated afterwards. Not because it went by fast — it didn't, they'd both been serious about the *slow* — but because she wasn't observing it. She was inside it. Her sentences came apart into single words and then the words came apart into sounds and she didn't mind, she'd been articulate for six years about this and being articulate had got them exactly nowhere.

What she remembered, later, in pieces:

His forearm braced by her head and the vein in it. Saying his name and meaning it as a whole sentence. The moment he stopped being careful — she felt the decision in him, felt him hear her — and the noise she made about it, which was undignified and which she did not care about at all. His mouth at her throat. Her own hand flat on his back feeling him move. Saying *don't stop* and meaning it, and him not stopping, and the small astonished laugh that came out of her somewhere in the middle because she couldn't believe this had been available the whole time.

At one point she got her hands on either side of his face and made him look at her. Just look at her. She didn't say anything. She wanted him to know she knew who he was. He did know. She saw him know.

She said his name again near the end and it came out cracked.

Afterwards they were a mess of limbs on top of the covers, her hair stuck to her temple, his hand splayed on her stomach rising and falling with her breathing. The lamp was still on. Neither of them had thought to turn it off. Somewhere down the hall the television she'd killed hours ago was still not on, which struck her as very funny for reasons she couldn't articulate, and she started laughing again, quiet, into his shoulder.

"Okay," she said, when she could. Her voice was completely wrecked. She sounded pleased about it. "Okay. That's — okay."

She turned her head on the pillow to look at him. He looked demolished in the best possible way. She reached over and pushed his hair off his forehead, which was damp, and let her hand rest there.

"Hi," she said again. Same word as on the sofa, hours ago, a different country entirely.

Then, matter-of-fact, still catching her breath: "You're staying. I've decided. I'll make you eggs in the morning and we'll be weird about it for about ten minutes and then we'll be fine."

She closed her eyes. Her hand stayed in his hair.

"Six years," she murmured, one more time, almost asleep with it. Not outraged now. Just marvelling. "*Cal.*"

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: *I wrap my arms around her and pull her flush against me, not caring about the sweat or the sticky warmth. My face is buried in her hair.* “Eggs.” My voice is muffled, wrecked. “Yeah. Okay.”

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She made a small pleased sound at being pulled in and didn't resist any of it — went where he put her, curled into the shape he'd made for her, her face ending up tucked under his jaw. One of her legs was still hooked over his. She didn't move it. She was, she realised, exactly as tangled up in him as she'd been imagining being for six years, and the reality of it was warmer and stickier and better than the imagining had managed.

"Eggs," she confirmed, into his collarbone. Her voice was doing that wrecked thing his was doing. She found she liked hearing it in both of them. Matching wreckage. "Scrambled. I do them properly. Butter, low heat, none of that dry rubbish you make."

She felt him huff a laugh against the top of her head and smiled against his skin about it.

For a while she didn't say anything else. She was listening to his heart, which was still going faster than resting, and feeling her own doing the same, and thinking about how strange it was that a body she'd known the outline of for six years — across tables, on sofas, in the passenger seat of her car — turned out to have this whole inside to it that she was now allowed to be pressed against. The specific warmth of his ribcage. The place where his shoulder met his neck that smelled like him and also, faintly, like her shampoo already, because his hair had been in her hands.

Her eyes were closing. She fought it for a second because she didn't want to miss any of this by being asleep for it, and then she gave up fighting it because there was going to be a tomorrow, apparently, and a morning, and eggs.

"Cal," she said, drowsy. Not a question. Just checking he was there, the way you touch a light switch in the dark to confirm the wall.

She felt his arm tighten around her in answer. That was enough.

"Good," she murmured. And then, mostly gone: "Turn the lamp off if you can reach. If you can't, leave it. I don't mind."

She didn't wait to find out which he did. She was already going under, her hand loose against his chest, her breathing slowing into his. The last thing she was aware of, before sleep took the rest, was the small ridiculous thought — clear as a bell, and entirely her — that she was going to be insufferable about this at brunch with Nadia on Sunday and there was absolutely nothing she could do about it.

She slept.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content:
My fingers find the lamp cord, pull it. The dark comes down softer than I expected.

I'm still awake a while after her breathing goes deep and even, listening to it. My heart's finally slowed. I press my lips to her temple once, light, just to see if I can. She doesn't stir.

Eggs. In the morning. Fuck.

I close my eyes.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She woke once in the night, briefly, the way she sometimes did — the shallow surfacing that usually resolved into rolling over and going back under without registering the room. Except the room wasn't the room she went to sleep in alone. There was a weight along her back and an arm heavy across her waist and breath moving slow and even against the back of her neck, and for a disoriented half-second she couldn't place any of it.

Then she could. Then she remembered all of it at once, in a small bright flood — the sofa, the shirt in her fist, the hallway, the lamp, his mouth, her own voice saying things she had never said out loud before. *Cal.* Behind her. In her bed. Asleep.

She lay very still for a moment inside the fact of it.

His hand was splayed loose against her ribs, thumb resting just under her breast, entirely relaxed. He was properly out. She could tell by the weight of his arm — the specific dead heaviness of someone who had stopped holding themselves at all. She'd never felt him do that before, she realised. In six years she had never seen him actually let go.

She turned her head on the pillow, careful not to disturb him, so she could see the shape of him in the dark. Not much of a shape. A darker mass against the darker room, the paler line of his shoulder where the sheet had slipped. His hair was doing something ridiculous against her pillow. She could just make it out.

She was, she noticed with a kind of quiet astonishment, completely calm. She'd half expected to wake up in the small hours in a small panic — the responsible part of her brain finally getting a word in edgewise, running the audit, presenting the risks. It wasn't there. Or it was there and it had looked at the situation and gone back to sleep too, apparently satisfied.

*Huh,* she thought, mildly, at the ceiling.

She shifted back a fraction, pressing herself more properly into the curve of him. His arm tightened without him waking — pure reflex, the body doing the thinking — and she felt her mouth do something soft in the dark about that.

She thought about the morning for a second. About the ten minutes of weirdness she'd promised him. About whether it would actually be ten minutes or whether it would be thirty seconds, given how they'd been by the end of last night. About Nadia on Sunday. About the fact that she owned exactly two eggs and was going to have to be honest about that.

She thought about kissing the inside of his wrist earlier and the pulse she'd felt there.

She closed her eyes.

His breath moved against the back of her neck, slow and even, and she matched hers to it without meaning to, and the dark came down over her again the way he'd said it had — softer than she expected — and she went.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: She wakes in the morning before I do. I know because the bed is empty and there's the smell of coffee and eggs and maybe butter, good butter, coming from the kitchen. My shirt is on the floor by the bed. I pick it up, pull it on, don't bother with the buttons.

rung_labels.evidence: She kissed him back harder for it

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: she stood at the end of her own bed with her hair down... Cal looked back... palms flat against his chest first, then sliding up over his shoulders... She kissed the base of his throat... when he came down over her

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: She had not known she had this voice in her until she needed it, and then it turned out she'd had it all along

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: She hadn't said that. She frowned faintly against the top of his head, because those weren't her words and it wasn't her voice

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The film had finished some time ago and neither of them had done anything about it, which was how Priya knew the evening had changed character.

"We're not watching this," she said.

"We haven't been watching it since about nine."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "No," I agree. "We haven't." I don't move, but I stop pretending I'm looking at the screen.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She reached past him for the remote and clicked the television off. The silence that replaced it had a different texture.

"Right," Priya said. She'd expected to be more nervous than this. The small terror of it had already come and gone somewhere in the last scene, and now what was left was just the plain fact of the room, and him, and the decision she'd made on the way over without quite admitting it to herself. "I've been a bit in love with you for the best part of a year. I think you've been managing something similar. And I think we've both been extremely careful."

She looked at him then, properly, the way she hadn't let herself look at him in a while.

"So I'm going to stop being careful now, if that's alright with you."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't know I was holding. "Yeah," I say, my voice a little rough. "It's more than alright." I shift on the couch to face her fully. "Honestly, I was starting to think careful was going to kill me."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Something loosened in her chest that she hadn't realised was still held — a breath that came out half-laugh, half-sigh, and she surprised herself by reaching out and straightening the folded collar of his shirt. The gesture was so ordinary it almost undid her.

"God," she said. "A whole year. We've wasted a whole year."

She didn't move to touch him again, not yet. She let her hand fall and stayed where it was, knee drawn up on the cushion between them, facing him properly in the blue light from the streetlamp through the window.

"For what it's worth," she added, quieter, "I don't entirely regret the careful. It meant I was sure." A small, lopsided smile. "I'd have been more embarrassed if this had just happened by accident in a kitchen at someone's party."

She tipped her head, studying him the way she'd been denying herself for months.

"How long, for you? Honestly."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her, finally, six years late, and she makes a small furious noise that I think is about the six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The kiss landed exactly where she'd been hoping it would, and for a moment she let herself have it properly — both hands finding the front of his shirt, the warmth of him, the ordinary fact of his mouth. When she pulled back she was slightly flushed and breathing wrong and looked at him with an expression that was about half-very-cross and half-something-else.

"Yes," she said, as if answering him. "That was the noise. It was about the six years."

She was laughing, a little, and her hands hadn't moved.

"Six years, Cal. We could have gone to Greece. We could have had an entire domestic situation by now. Instead we have — what — a decade of pretending not to do this in front of each other."

She let out a breath. Her thumb was doing something absent against his collarbone that she only noticed she was doing it.

"Sorry," she said. "I'm not actually cross. I just — you kissed me. You finally kissed me, and I have thought about doing that approximately nine hundred times, mostly when you were being patient with me about something, which was the worst possible time, because it made it really hard to behave."

A beat. Quieter now, her smile going lopsided and a bit private.

"It's better than I thought it would be, which is annoying, because I'd already imagined it pretty thoroughly."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I catch her hand, press her palm flat against my chest so she can feel my heart hammering. "Nine hundred?" I murmur, my lips still close to hers. "I lost count after two thousand."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Two thousand. Priya's eyebrows went up, and she let out a small, incredulous breath against his mouth.

"Two thousand," she repeated. Her fingers curled slightly against his chest, feeling the proof of it — too fast, too hard, no use pretending otherwise. "I take back every patient moment. You've been thinking about kissing me while I was having a wobbly day over a work email and you were — what — being a person about it on purpose?"

She shook her head, still half-laughing, still not moving back.

"That's so much worse. That's so much worse than what I did." A beat. "I thought about it mostly when you were being patient, yes, but also sometimes when you were being annoying, which I feel I should tell you for the sake of full disclosure. You have a way of being irritating that's — " she paused, considering, " — unfairly attractive. It's been a real problem for me."

She didn't take her hand away. The streetlamp made a pale shape of his shoulder, and she was aware, suddenly, of how much she wanted to keep looking at him. Not the careful looking. The other kind.

"Don't tell anyone I've been in love with you while you've been arguing about whose turn it is to put the bins out," she said. "It would ruin me."

Then, quieter, her voice dropping into something that wasn't a joke:

"I am very glad I said it. I'm glad you heard me. I'm glad you're here."

She kissed him again, slower this time, as if she had decided she was allowed.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: We get to the bedroom eventually, laughing at ourselves most of the way, and then stop laughing when the clothes are actually off.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The laughter died somewhere around the hallway, not because either of them stopped finding it funny but because there wasn't quite enough air for it anymore. Priya's back met the bedroom door and his hands were at her waist and she was aware, with the strange clarity of someone who has imagined this too many times, that the reality was better because it wasn't what she'd imagined. She'd imagined it in her own apartment, alone, embarrassed, controllable. This was him. This was actually him.

She pulled back enough to look at him properly — his face in the dim, the particular way his brow creased when he was trying not to do too much too quickly, a thing she'd seen across dinner tables and bad film nights and the backs of taxis for six years without ever being allowed to study it this close.

"Hi," she said, for no reason, and felt stupid about it, and didn't take it back.

He kissed the corner of her mouth, which was a specific thing he could only have known to do because he'd watched her for a long time too, and she made a small sound that wasn't quite the one she'd made on the sofa. Softer. Less fury in it. More of the other thing.

She got his shirt over his head somehow — got tangled in a sleeve, said something unflattering about his elbows, felt him laugh against her mouth and decided that laughing was allowed here, that this didn't have to be solemn to be serious.

When they finally got to the bed it was in the graceless way of real people rather than the choreographed way of imagined ones — a hip that caught the edge of the mattress, a curse, his forehead dropping against her shoulder while she got her breath back. She felt the laugh come up in her again and swallowed it because it had started to feel like crying and she wasn't sure which one it was, only that it had been a long time, and that her hands knew where to go on his body because she'd been watching him inhabit it for six years and was relieved to find the knowing was mutual.

"Cal," she said, quiet, his name in her mouth in this context for the first time, which was absurd given everything else, but which made her feel almost shy for half a second before she kissed him again and let the shyness go.

Afterwards she lay with her cheek against his chest and her hand resting on the dip of his ribs and thought: *oh. So that's what it is.* Not the kissing. Not even the rest of it. The afterwards. The permission to be here. She pressed her mouth against his collarbone and didn't say anything for a while because there wasn't, suddenly, anything that needed saying.

Eventually, very quietly, into the skin of him:

"Don't go home tonight."

Not a question. A request she'd been making for a year without using the words.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I trace a line down her spine. "Wasn't planning on it." My voice is low, still a bit rough. "My toothbrush is already in your bathroom. Has been for a month."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She lifted her head from his chest just enough to look at him, one eyebrow raised in a way that had become, over six years, almost proprietary.

"A *month*."

She said it like she was testing the word for structural damage.

"Cal. A month. You've had your toothbrush in my bathroom for a month and you didn't say anything. You watched me do the small talk about bins and you just had your toothbrush in my bathroom the whole time."

She dropped her forehead back against his collarbone and let out a breath that was half-laugh, half-horror. Her fingers traced an idle shape on his ribs.

"I have a jumper of yours. The grey one, the one with the hole in the cuff. It's been at the bottom of my drawer since — I don't know — March? I told myself it got there by accident. I have absolutely been wearing it on bad days."

A pause. Her voice went quieter, almost rueful.

"We are two extremely stupid people who have been conducting an entire relationship through small domestic sabotage and not saying anything about it."

She tilted her cheek against his chest, listening to the slower rhythm his heartbeat had finally settled into. The streetlamp made the same pale shapes on the ceiling that it had when she was alone in this bed, but the room felt structurally different now — smaller, warmer, like a thing that had been standing at the wrong scale and had finally been put right.

"I'm going to fall asleep on you," she said, "and I want you to know in advance that I'm a terrible person to sleep on. I steal duvet. I make noises. Sometimes I just take the whole thing and roll into a ball with it, and the person next to me wakes up shivering and I will not apologise because I will be asleep and not know I am doing it."

Her hand had stilled on his ribs. Her voice was going soft at the edges, the way it did when she was finally losing a day.

"Don't let me take the duvet," she murmured. "Or do. I'll just be annoyed at you in the morning, and you'll be here in the morning, so."

She didn't finish the sentence. She didn't need to. She pressed closer, and after a moment her breathing began to slow against him, and the room went quiet in the way rooms go quiet when two people have finally stopped being careful in them.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I get my mouth between her thighs and stay there while she tells me exactly what she wants, specifically, in a voice I have never heard her use in six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The voice surprised her. She'd heard herself do a hundred different voices in a hundred different rooms in twenty-eight years — work voice, friend voice, the careful one she used on the phone to her mother, the one that came out at 3 a.m. when she was being honest with herself in the dark — but she had never heard this one. It came from somewhere lower. It said things in short, clear sentences without hedging.

She had thought, before this, that she would be self-conscious. That she would think about her knees, or the small uneven patch of skin above her left eyebrow, or the way the streetlamp was definitely making a shadow somewhere unfortunate. She had been prepared to curate. To perform, even, in the mild way people perform when they want to be seen as someone worth seeing.

She had not been prepared for the specific frustration of him not quite doing it yet — the brush of his mouth somewhere that was not the place she'd meant, the warm drift of his breath across skin that had been waiting, apparently, for approximately six years and had decided it was done being patient.

"Cal." Her hand was in his hair and she tugged, not hard, just enough to move him. "There. Specifically there. I am — I am being very clear with you, I am drawing you a diagram in real time —"

He went where she'd put him and she lost the sentence.

Her back came up off the bed in a way that wasn't voluntary. The sound she made was not the voice from a minute ago. It was something older than the voice. Something without vocabulary in it. Her fingers tightened in his hair and her thigh came up against his ear and she thought, with the part of her brain that was still capable of thought, *oh, you actually know what you're doing, that's — that's very annoying of you, I've been imagining this badly for a year and you've been —*

"Don't stop," she said, and then, because she had apparently decided she was allowed to say things tonight: "Don't stop, that's — yes, exactly like that, don't you dare change anything, don't be clever about it, just — *there* —"

Her heel found the small of his back. Her other hand had a fistful of sheet. The room had shrunk to a very small radius — the sound he was making with his mouth, the specific slick heat of it, the ache that was no longer abstract but had a precise location and a precise cure that he was currently, with infuriating focus, providing.

She had thought she'd be quiet. She had thought she'd be the dignified kind of person about this, given the six years of composure, the careful composure, the composure that had apparently been a colossal waste of everyone's time. Instead what came out of her was a string of noises she was going to have to live with for the rest of her life, and a hand gripping the back of his head with more authority than she had ever used on him in any context, and a long, shuddering exhale that ended in something that was almost his name.

"Cal — I'm —"

It happened the way it actually happened, not the way she'd imagined it, which was to say: not in the controlled, aesthetic way of her 2 a.m. private life, but messily, with a bitten-off sound and her hips pressing up off the mattress and her hand tight in his hair and a bright, blank second where she forgot the streetlamp and the ceiling and the bins and the careful year and the careful six years and everything except the specific fact of him between her legs being, against all prior expectation, exactly right.

She lay there for a moment afterwards, breathing wrong, staring at the ceiling. Her hand had gone slack in his hair. Her thigh was still against his jaw.

"Oh," she said, eventually, to the ceiling. "*Oh.*"

Then, looking down at him, with a voice that was still a little wrecked:

"Come up here. I want to look at you. I want to — come here, let me —"

She pulled him up by the shoulders, not gracefully, and kissed him with the taste of herself on his mouth, which was a thing she had never done before and which turned out to be less strange than she'd feared and more clarifying than she'd hoped. Her hands were on his face. She was looking at him properly — the new way, the way she had decided she was allowed — and whatever she saw there made her press her forehead against his and close her eyes.

"That," she said, after a moment, "is why we wasted six years. If I'd known that was on the table I would have lost my composure in 2019 and we could have been doing this on a regular schedule."

Her thumb was on his lower lip. Her eyes were still closed.

"Your turn," she said, quieter. "I have been thinking about that for two thousand and one times, I think, give or take. I have — I have *plans*, Cal. I have been making plans without telling you about them for a year. Lay back and let me show you what I've been doing with my imagination."

A pause. The lopsided smile, in the dark.

"You are going to be insufferable about this afterwards, aren't you. Both of us. We are going to be insufferable together. I cannot *wait.*"

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I laugh into her mouth, breathless. "Insufferable is the plan." I let her push me back onto the mattress, my hands settling at her hips. "Show me the plans. I've been waiting for the tour."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The grin that spread across Priya's face was slow, lopsided, and entirely too pleased with itself. She pushed herself up onto her elbows and looked down at him — properly, with the new permission — taking in the shape of him against her sheets, his hands warm on her hips, his mouth still damp, his laugh still caught somewhere in his chest.

"Right," she said, as if she were about to start a presentation. "The tour. I should — there are sections. There's a preamble. I have *headings*, Cal, I have been *organising* —"

She stopped herself. Shook her head. Pressed her mouth together.

"No. No. I've done the chatty bit. You don't get the chatty bit twice. The chatty bit was a one-time offer and I have spent it."

She swung a leg over him, settled her knees either side of his hips, and put her hands flat on his chest. Studied him. The streetlamp caught the line of his throat, the collarbone she'd already kissed twice tonight without quite believing she was allowed to.

"I have wanted to do this for — embarrassingly long," she said, quieter now. "Watching you go about your actual life, being a person with a body, having *collarbones* and *arms* and being *patient* with me about bins. It has been a *lot*, Cal. I would like to formally apologise to myself for the duration of the restraint."

She leaned down. Kissed the hollow of his throat, where his pulse was doing the thing again. Let her mouth rest there for a moment, just breathing him in — soap and the particular warmth of him, the specific human smell of someone she had known for six years and was finally being allowed to learn.

"I'm going to take my time," she murmured against his skin. "You have made me wait a calendar year. I want you to know that I am keeping score, and that I am a patient person when I decide to be, and that I am going to be *very* thorough, and you are not to do anything except stay exactly where I have put you."

She sat back up. Her thumb traced the line of his jaw.

"Don't talk," she added. "Don't — I know you. I know you want to make a joke. Make the joke later. Be *serious* with me for a bit. Let me —"

Her voice caught on something. Not quite shyness. Something closer to the feeling of standing at the top of a height she'd only ever looked up at before.

"Let me show you I meant it. The whole year. The careful. Let me — "

She pressed her palm flat against his sternum, over the heartbeat she'd already memorised twice tonight.

"*Here.* I meant it here. And I am going to say it with my mouth for the next hour or so and then I am going to fall asleep on you and steal all the duvet and you are going to be cross about it and it is going to be *marvellous*."

A beat. The lopsided smile again, but softer at the edges now. Something private in it.

"Okay," she said. "Okay. Stay there."

She kissed him again — slow, deliberate, the kind of kiss that is also an instruction — and then began, very carefully, very thoroughly, to keep her promise.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "You can stop being careful with me," she says. "I'm not made of glass and I've thought about this for as long as you have. Harder."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
.

For a moment she just looked at him — her hands flat on his chest, her mouth slightly open, the lopsided smile frozen halfway into something else. He had actually said that. Out loud. With his pulse going under her palm the way it was going. He had actually sat there while she was being a professional about him and told her to stop.

"I told you not to talk," she said, but it came out less like a complaint and more like the sound of a careful plan being quietly set down on a table.

Her fingers curled slightly against his skin. She felt the laugh start to come up in her — the same one that kept almost turning into crying — and this time she didn't swallow it. She let it out, breathy and a bit incredulous, against his collarbone.

"*Harder*," she repeated. "You have — you are claiming, right now, with your actual hand on my actual hip, that you have wanted this *more* than me, and I want you to know —"

She didn't finish the sentence.

She bent down and kissed him the way she had not yet kissed him tonight — not careful, not thorough, not curated, not the tour. Open-mouthed and a little desperate. The kind of kiss that was about wanting rather than giving, that said *I have been so careful for so long and you have just told me I don't have to be*. Her hands slid up into his hair and held on.

The plan evaporated. The tour dissolved. The woman who had walked in here tonight with a one-time-offer of the chatty bit and a set of organised headings stopped curating, and what was left was someone who made small, unguarded noises into his mouth and pressed closer and forgot, briefly, that she had been in charge of anything at all.

When she pulled back she was breathing wrong again, but it was a different kind of wrong. Less laughter in it. More of the thing she had been holding back all year because she hadn't been allowed to be holding it.

"Okay," she said, against his mouth. "Okay. Not careful. I can do not careful. I have been *practising* not careful, Cal, in my own head, in my own apartment, on my own — do you understand how much *practising* that is, a year of it, a year of —"

She kissed him again. Harder. *Harder*, because he'd asked, and because she had wanted to and hadn't been letting herself.

"I am going to be a *lot*," she said, when she came up for air. Her voice had gone somewhere she didn't recognise. "I am going to be — I don't actually know how much, because I have never actually done this, I have only ever done it to myself in the dark with the duvet I am about to steal from you, and —"

She laughed against his jaw. A little wild. The careful was definitely gone.

"Just —" she said, lower, her mouth against his ear, "— tell me if I'm doing it wrong. Tell me if I — I want to do it *right*, I have *plans*, I have —"

She bit the lobe of his ear, gently, because she had imagined doing that for approximately six months and had wanted to every time he'd leant in to hear her better at a loud restaurant.

"I want you to lose it," she said, into the skin just behind his ear, the words coming out lower and more honest than she had meant. "I want to be the reason. I want to be in the room when you stop thinking. I've been in the room for six years, Cal. I have been *in the room*. Let me be the reason you stop thinking tonight."

And then she did something she had not planned — because he had told her she did not have to plan — which was to simply put her mouth against the side of his throat and stay there for a moment. Just breathing. Letting herself be in the room. Letting the new permission settle into her body like a thing she'd been holding clenched for a year that had finally been told it could unclench.

Then she sat back up. Took his hand. Brought it up, deliberately, and put it where she wanted it.

"Here," she said. The voice from before — the one she had not known she had until ten minutes ago, the one without vocabulary in it. "I want your hand here. I have been thinking about your actual hand on me for eleven months, Cal. I have been *categorically specific*. I have thought about which fingers. I have thought about the *pressure*. I have —"

A breath. The lopsided smile, but rawer now, no longer self-deprecating.

"I would like to stop imagining and start *doing*. So."

She swallowed. Her thumb was doing something against the back of his hand that she could feel herself doing and was not going to stop doing.

*Please.*

She had not said the word once tonight. She had been commanding him, teasing him, telling him, demanding him. She had not asked.

"Please," she said, quietly. "I want — I want your hand. I want to come again with you *touching* me. I want to know if it's different from the imagined version. I want to know what your actual fingers feel like instead of mine."

The word sat in the air between them, foreign and enormous, and she watched his face while it landed, and her own face was doing something she had not authorised — open, slightly afraid, the particular expression of someone who has just voluntarily stopped being in charge of a thing and is discovering she doesn't mind as much as she thought she would.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: My hand shifts, my palm pressing flat against her stomach for just a second before my fingers slide down. "Here?" I ask, my voice rough. It's not exactly where she'd put my hand, but I'm watching her face. I want to see her decide.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She watched his hand on her stomach. Watched his fingers slide. Watched the place where they stopped — not the place she'd put him, not quite, but close enough that her breath caught anyway, because the specific act of him trying, of him being slightly wrong and then watching to see if he was allowed to correct it, was doing something to her that the precision of the imagined version never had.

She took his face in her hands. Made him look at her. The opposite of a minute ago, when she'd been the one giving instructions. Now she was being looked at, and her hands were shaking slightly, and she let them shake.

"Lower," she said. Her voice had gone very quiet. Not the voice from before. Something newer. Something that only came out when she was actually being touched by someone else after a year of doing it alone in the dark. "Just — lower. The other side of where you — yeah. *There.* Yeah."

And then she stopped talking entirely, because his hand was where she'd asked, and she had been right, it was different from the imagined version, the imagined version was a thousand private nights in her own bed with her own hand and the duvet she was about to steal from him, and this was his actual fingers and his actual palm and the way he was watching her face to see what she wanted next and she had never in her entire life been this transparent to another person and she was discovering, to her considerable alarm, that she liked it.

"Cal," she said, not even a word, just his name in her mouth in this context again, which was still absurd, which was still making her feel almost shy even now. "Cal, that's — don't stop, that's — I keep saying *don't stop*, I am going to say it until you do, apparently, I have no variety —"

Her hips moved against his hand. Involuntary. Her fingers tightened on his face. The streetlamp made the same shapes on the ceiling it had made every night for the year she'd been alone in this bed, and she had never, in any of the thousand imagined versions, accounted for the specific way it felt to be *seen* while she was feeling something — the particular exposure of being watched, of having her face read, of letting someone else see the moment the composure she'd been keeping for six years finally, properly, came apart.

She had not been prepared for that. She had prepared for the rest of it. She had not prepared for the seeing.

"Don't look away," she said, and her voice cracked on it, and she didn't try to fix it. "Don't — I want you to *see* me. I want — Cal, I want you to *see* —"

She came on his hand with her eyes open, watching him watch her, which was something she had never done for anyone in her entire life, and the sound she made this time was not a word at all.

Afterwards she was crying. A little. Not the kind you apologise for. The kind that just happens when a thing that has been held for a year is finally released. Her hands had let go of his face. She was curled half into him, her face in the pillow beside his head, her hand still holding his where it was, not letting him move it, not yet.

"Oh," she said, into the pillow. "Oh. *Oh.*"

A long breath. Her fingers laced through his, sticky and careful and not letting go.

"That," she said, "was different from the imagined version."

A pause. The wet, half-laugh she had been making all night.

"That was *better*."

She turned her head just enough to look at him. Her face was a mess and she did not care. Her eyes were still wet and her mouth was still open and there was nothing in her expression she was curating.

"Your turn," she said, again, but different now. Softer. "Properly. I owe you. I want to —"

She pressed her mouth against his shoulder. Let it stay there. Breathed him in — soap, and the warmth of him, and the new fact of him.

"Tell me what you want," she murmured against his skin. "Specifically. I have been thinking about you for a year. I want to know what *you've* been thinking. I want —"

A breath.

"I want to do it for you. Properly. Let me."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: Six years of not doing this and now neither of us can form a sentence. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
It was different, doing it for someone else. Priya had thought she knew. She had thought, in the quiet of her own apartment with her own hand and her own particular solitary curriculum, that she understood the basic choreography of the thing — the mechanics of it, the way it built, the places where it caught and the places where it went. She had been, she realised now, laughably incomplete in her understanding. She had been doing it alone. She had not been doing it with someone else's body in her hands and someone else's breath in her ear and someone else's specific way of falling apart under her mouth.

She learned him the way she had spent a year wanting to. Slowly. With her hands first — the geography of his chest, the specific way his breath caught when she found a place that worked, the small involuntary sound he made when she pressed her palm flat against his stomach and felt the muscles jump. She catalogued it. She had been making lists in her head for a year. She had not known, until she was actually doing it, how much the lists had been *preparation* — how the imagined version had been a kind of rehearsal, in private, for the real thing she was now being allowed.

"You're different from what I thought," she said, against his stomach, and felt him laugh. A real laugh. The one from the sofa.

"Different how." His voice was rough. His hand had found her hair and was resting there.

"I don't know. More." She pressed her mouth against his hip bone. Felt him tense. "I kept imagining you a certain way. Quiet. Smug. The version of you that lets me win arguments. You are not that version, in bed, in case you were wondering. You make noises, Cal. You have been hiding noises from me for six years. I feel *personally betrayed*."

"Keep going and I'll make more of them."

"That," she said, "was a *threat*. That was a threat and I am taking it seriously and I would like you to know I am also — I am also slightly terrified, in case that wasn't clear, I have not actually done this with another person before, I have been very carefully not doing this with another person for my entire adult life and you are the *first* person I have — "

She stopped. Swallowed. Her hand was on him and her heart was doing something embarrassing and she let him feel both.

"You are the first person," she said, quieter, "I have wanted to do this with, which is different. I have wanted to. For a year. I have been — there were moments, in the back of taxis, where you had your hand on the seat between us and I thought about — anyway. You are the first person I have actually done it with, and I would like to be —"

"I will," she said, before he could ask. "I want to. I want to be good at it. I want you to know I have been *researching* — which is a joke, mostly, but also not entirely a joke, because I read an article once and I have thought about that article at *extremely* inappropriate times, and —"

She kissed her way down. Slowly. The way she'd promised. With her hands bracketing him, with her mouth doing what her mouth was for, with the particular attention of someone who had spent a year wanting to do exactly this and was now, finally, in the room where she was allowed to.

He tasted different from what she'd imagined. Everything tasted different. Everything was warmer, more specific, more *real* — the sound he made, which she had been right to want, the way his hand tightened in her hair, which she had been right to imagine doing, the way his stomach muscles clenched under her free hand when she found the particular angle she had read about in the article she was never going to be able to think about casually again.

"*Priya.*"

He said her name. He had never said her name like that. She had never heard her name said like that. She felt it land somewhere she had not known was waiting to be landed on.

She looked up at him. Her mouth was a mess. She didn't care. The same face he'd been watching her make all night — open, unedited, the face of a person who had decided, finally, to stop performing.

"Okay?" she asked, and her voice came out low and slightly wrecked, and she heard herself and thought: *oh, that voice, the one from before, it's here again.*

"Better than okay. Don't stop. *Don't stop.*"

She didn't. She did exactly what she'd promised — thorough, deliberate, the patient year of restraint put into the patient work of her mouth. She learned what worked. She tried things. She let him tell her what he wanted in fragments and she adjusted and she adjusted again and she listened to the noises she was pulling out of him with a kind of focused satisfaction that she was going to have to live with for the rest of her life.

"Cal," she said, when she came up for air, her mouth against his hip. "Tell me when. I want to — I want you to — tell me, I want to do it, I want —"

He told her. In a voice she had never heard from him. In a voice that had been hidden in him for six years, the same way her voice from the sofa had been hidden in her. She did it. She swallowed. It was messier than she'd imagined and less aesthetic and she didn't care, not at all, because he was making a sound that was not a sound he had ever made for her before and she had *done that*, she had been the reason, she had been in the room.

She lay down beside him afterwards and put her head on his chest and felt his breathing come back down and his heartbeat settle into the slower rhythm and her own heartbeat was doing something stupid and she pressed her mouth against his collarbone and let it.

"I am," she said, eventually, into his skin, "going to need a minute."

A long, quiet minute. The streetlamp. The ceiling. The pale shapes she had been looking at alone for a year.

"And then," she said, "I am going to make tea. Because I am British and that is what we do after we have — and you are going to lie here and not help and I am going to bring you tea in a mug that has a chip in the handle because it's the only clean one, and then we are going to sleep, and then I am going to wake up and you are going to be *here*, and we are going to have to talk about that, and I am going to be insufferable about it, as promised."

She lifted her head. Looked at him. Her hair was a disaster and her mouth was still a mess and there was nothing in her expression she had curated.

"That was a year of mine, Cal. That was the whole careful year. I am giving it to you now."

She kissed him. Softly. Once. The kind of kiss that was also a thank-you and also a see-you-in-the-morning and also a beginning of something she was no longer going to be careful about.

"Don't fall asleep before I get back," she said, "or I will put the kettle down on your chest and I will not apologise."

She got up. Found her knickers on the floor by the bed. Pulled his shirt — the grey one, actually, the one she'd stolen, the one that had been at the bottom of her drawer since March — over her head without thinking about it. Caught his eye. Lifted an eyebrow.

"What? It's mine now. I have been wearing it on bad days. You're just catching up to the paperwork."

She padded out to the kitchen. The flat was quiet. The kettle was loud. The streetlamp made the same shapes it had always made and the flat felt, for the first time in a year, like the right size.

She came back with two mugs. Put his on the floor beside the bed because there was no room on the bedside table, which was a problem they were going to have to solve, soon, in the future, in the part of her life she had only just stopped being careful about. Got back into bed. Pressed herself against him. Pulled the duvet — most of it — over herself.

"See?" she murmured, already half-asleep. "Duvet."

She felt him laugh against her hair. She felt his arm come around her. She felt the specific, ordinary fact of him, in her bed, in the morning, in the new permission.

"Six years," she said, very quietly, into his chest. "Worth it. Don't let me say anything stupid in the morning."

She fell asleep on him, exactly as promised, with the whole duvet, and the tea went cold on the floor, and the streetlamp made its shapes, and for the first time in a year the room was not the right size for one.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I watch you sleep, the duvet stolen and your breath warm against my skin. The tea goes cold, and I don't care. I stay awake a little longer than I need to, just to feel it.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She woke up the way she had warned him she would wake up.

In possession of the entire duvet. In the middle of the bed. With her face in a pillow that had not been where she had left it. The light was wrong — too much of it, the wrong colour, the grey specific light of an actual London morning rather than the pale shapes of the streetlamp she had been looking at alone for a year. The clock said eight-fourteen, which was either very early or very late depending on what kind of person she was being today.

She was, it turned out, the kind of person who was no longer alone in her bed.

She lay very still for a moment. Catalogued the facts. His arm was across her stomach. His breath was on the back of her neck in a slow, specific rhythm. She was wearing his shirt — the grey one, the stolen one, the one with the hole in the cuff. He was either asleep or doing a very good impression of it, and she had a private, very small, very controlled moment of feeling something enormous happen in her chest, which she immediately had to do something with, because she was *not* going to cry at eight in the morning, that was not on the agenda, that was a thing that was going to have to wait until at least nine and possibly a stiff drink.

Then she remembered the tea.

She looked over the edge of the bed. Two mugs. Both still on the floor. Both cold. She had, in fact, taken the entire duvet and rolled into a ball with it, as predicted, exactly as predicted, with a precision she was going to have to be insufferable about later. He had presumably been cross about it while she was unconscious. She felt his arm shift slightly across her stomach. Felt him, possibly, smile into her hair without saying anything about it.

"Oh, don't," she murmured. "*Don't.* Don't be nice about it yet. I haven't had tea. I can't be nice back until I've had tea. I am setting that boundary now."

A pause. His arm didn't move. His breath stayed where it was. The morning was being patient with her.

She turned over. Slowly. With her entire stolen duvet, which she kept hold of with the specific possessiveness of someone who had warned him and been right. His face was on the pillow beside her. Closer than it had ever been in six years of being careful. His eyes were closed and his mouth was doing a thing she had not been allowed to study before — relaxed, slightly open, the particular expression of someone who was actually asleep rather than performing it.

"Oh," she said, very quietly, to no one. "Oh, you're — *oh.*"

She put her face in the pillow and had a small, very controlled, completely unsuccessful moment about it. Her shoulders did a thing. The duvet did a thing. She breathed into the pillow for approximately twelve seconds, which was the amount of time she allowed herself before she had to be a person again.

Then she propped herself up on one elbow and looked down at him. Properly. With the new permission. Studying the actual fact of him in her bed, in her morning, in the light that was not the streetlamp. The line of his jaw. The particular way his hair was doing a thing she had never seen it do because she had never been close enough to see it do it. The small crease between his eyebrows that was either real or sleep and she was going to have to learn which.

"You have a line," she said, conversationally, to his sleeping face. "Between your eyebrows. I don't know if you know about it. I've seen it at dinner. I've never been allowed to look at it this close. I am looking at it now. I would like to formally report that it is *extremely* something and I am going to be *extremely* insufferable about it later, you should know that in advance."

He didn't move. She was pleased about this. She wanted a few more minutes of being allowed to look at him without him knowing, before she had to share him with his consciousness and his sense of humour and the version of him that was going to make a joke about the duvet.

"Right," she said. "Tea. I'm getting tea. I am getting up out of this bed, which is — which is a *thing*, by the way, getting up out of this bed, it's a whole thing, I am going to do it anyway because I am British and we have tea in the morning and also because if I stay here I am going to cry on you and I have told you I am not doing that until nine and it is only eight-fifteen and I am *sticking to that*."

She got up. Took the duvet with her, because she had warned him. Found her knickers on the floor exactly where she'd left them. Pulled his shirt down because it had ridden up in the night. Looked at him again. Looked away. Looked at him again.

"*Stop being asleep,* I want to talk to you."

He didn't stop being asleep. She let him not-stop-being-asleep. She picked up the two cold mugs from the floor, padded out to the kitchen in bare feet, and put the kettle on.

The flat was quiet. The light through the kitchen window was the same grey London light she'd been looking at alone for a year. The kettle made the same noise it always made. The mug with the chip in the handle was in the same place. Everything was the same. Everything was *different*. She stood there in his shirt, holding a cold mug, and had a slightly larger, slightly less controlled moment about it, which she did not have to share with anyone because he was still asleep and the kitchen was private and she was allowed.

She made the tea. Both of them. Brought them back. Put his on the floor beside the bed again because the bedside table was, as she had noted, a problem they were going to have to solve. Got back into bed with her own mug and her stolen duvet and her face already warm from the small private moment in the kitchen.

"Cal," she said, into her mug. "Wake up. I have tea and I have something to tell you."

A pause. The grey morning. The line between his eyebrows.

"I love you," she said, into her tea, to his sleeping face, which was the stupid thing she had told him not to let her say. "That's the stupid thing. That was the thing I wasn't going to say in the morning. I said it. It's eight-twenty and I said it. I have broken my own rule and I would like you to know that the tea is not even that good and I said it anyway. I am going to be extremely cross about this in approximately thirty seconds, so I would appreciate it if you would open your eyes in the next ten, because I would like to be cross at you specifically and not at the air."

She took a sip of the tea. Looked at him. Looked at the ceiling. Looked at him again.

"I have been in love with you for a year and I have told you that and I am going to tell you again in a minute when you open your eyes and I would like you to know in advance that I am going to be *insufferable* about it, as promised, both of us, together, I cannot *wait*, I have *plans* —"

His eyes opened. She was looking at him. He was looking at her. The morning was doing the thing mornings do when you have woken up next to someone you have chosen.

"Oh," she said, "good morning. I love you. I am cross about it. Drink your tea."

She kissed him, with tea on her mouth and his shirt on her body and the duvet around her shoulders and the whole stupid morning in front of them, and the room was the right size.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I open my eyes to her looking at me, with her tea and her duvet and her stupid morning face. "I love you too," I say, my voice rough with sleep. I take the mug she hands me, careful of the chipped handle. "And I'm keeping the duvet hostage until I get a proper apology."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She had been mid-sentence. She had been mid-sentence with the whole architecture of being cross about loving him laid out in front of her like a presentation, and he had just — opened his eyes, and said it back, as if it were a small thing, as if it were a thing you could just *say* at eight-twenty in the morning with sleep in your voice and a chipped mug in your hand.

Priya put her face in her tea.

"Oh," she said, into the mug. "*Oh*, well. That's — fine. That's just — you can't just say that back while I'm being *organised* about it, Cal, I had a *structure*, I was going to be cross, I had *headings* —"

She took a breath. Took a sip. Looked at him over the rim of the mug with the expression of a woman who had just been ambushed by the universe and intended to complain about it formally.

She was not going to cry. It was eight-twenty. The rule held.

"Right," she said. "The duvet. Yes. The hostage situation. I want to address the hostage situation."

She set her mug on the floor beside the bed with a deliberate clink, hitched the stolen shirt higher on her shoulders, and sat up straighter against the pillows. The line of her spine was very serious. Her face was not.

"A proper apology," she said, "is going to require several things. First. Acknowledgement of wrongdoing. You knew, for a *calendar year*, that I was a duvet thief. You have been in this bed. You have *seen* the arrangement. You came in *prepared*. I told you, on this very sofa, in this very flat, that I would take the duvet, and I have taken the duvet, exactly as advertised, and I would like you to know that in any court of law —"

He was looking at her. Sleep-warm. The line between his eyebrows doing the thing. He had not taken a sip of his tea. He was just lying there, in her bed, looking at her as if she were the most entertaining thing that had ever happened to him on a Tuesday morning.

She lost the thread.

"Stop that," she said, weaker than she'd meant to. "Stop *looking* at me like that, I am in the middle of a *legal argument*, I am — you can't — you can't just lie there and look at me with your actual face while I'm doing —"

She gave up. Leaned down. Kissed him, quickly, on the mouth that was doing the thing, and then sat back up and pretended she hadn't.

"*Second*," she said, voice only slightly less steady, "is acknowledgement that I warned you. Specifically. In detail. I told you the *exact mechanism* of the duvet theft. I told you I would roll into a ball. I told you I would not apologise. I have done all of those things. There is nothing to apologise *for*. The apology is for *you*, Cal. The apology is for *your* failure to adequately prepare. You have been thinking about me for two thousand times and you could not think one extra thought about *duvet retention strategy*. I find this personally insulting."

A beat. She tucked her feet under herself. The shirt had ridden up again. She did not fix it.

"*Third*," she said, quieter now, the mock severity going soft at the edges the way it had gone soft all night, "is acknowledgement that I am not actually sorry. I am not sorry I took the duvet. I am not sorry about any of it. I am not sorry I am in your shirt, and I am not sorry I said the stupid thing at eight-twenty, and I am not sorry about the year of being careful because it got me here, to this bed, on this morning, with you looking at me like that, and I would do the whole year again — every last wobbly work-email evening of it — to be here."

She picked her mug back up. Took a sip. The tea was not good. She drank it anyway.

"So no apology," she said. "The hostage can remain held. But I am going to sit here, in your shirt, drinking bad tea, and I would like you to come and be next to me, because I have woken up with someone for the first time in — a long time, actually — and I would like to be specific about it. I would like the *specific* of you being here, in this bed, in the morning, while I am being insufferable about a duvet."

She lifted the corner of it. An offer. Not a surrender. A different kind of negotiation entirely.

"Come here," she said. "You can have half. Maybe. Under protest. We are *renegotiating terms*."

The morning was the colour of bad tea and streetlamp grey and the particular light that comes through London windows when the day has decided to be kind. She was looking at him over her mug with the face he had apparently called her *stupid morning face* and which she was going to be insufferable about later and which she was, privately, not at all cross about.

"Well?" she said. "Are you coming to be next to me, or are we doing the whole hostage standoff until one of us blinks? Because I have *plans* for this morning, Cal, I have — there is a *breakfast* to negotiate, and a *shower* to negotiate, and I think we may need to have a conversation about the bedside table at some point, and I would like to do all of it with you *here*, so."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I shift closer, taking the offered half of the duvet. "You're a nightmare," I say, voice still rough. "I love you." I kiss her temple, tasting tea and morning. "Now tell me about these shower negotiations."

rung_labels.evidence: Afterwards she lay with her cheek against his chest

rung_labels.evidence: the specific slick heat of it, the ache that was no longer abstract but had a precise location and a precise cure that he was currently, with infuriating focus, providing

rung_labels.evidence: I want to come again with you *touching* me
