dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The film had finished some time ago and neither of them had done anything about it, which was how Priya knew the evening had changed character.

"We're not watching this," she said.

"We haven't been watching it since about nine."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "No," I agree. "We haven't." I don't move, but I stop pretending I'm looking at the screen.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya turned her head on the armrest. In the blue glow of the menu screen, she could see Cal's profile—the slight tension in the jaw, the deliberate way they weren't looking at her. Six years of this. Six years of not doing this.

"Okay," she said. Just that. Then she sat up, moved across the couch, and kissed them.

It was not the way she'd imagined it would be, which was a relief. She'd imagined a lot of ways, over the years. But she hadn't imagined the small, surprised sound Cal made against her mouth, or the way their hand came up to rest against the side of her neck, tentative and then not tentative at all. She hadn't imagined how simple it would feel, finally.

When they broke apart, Cal was looking at her like they were trying to recalculate something fundamental. Priya was breathing harder than she wanted to admit.

"So," she said.

"So," Cal repeated.

"We should probably talk about this."

"We probably should."

Neither of them moved.

"Or," Priya said, "we could not talk about it for a while and see what happens."

Cal laughed—that was the Cal she knew, the one who'd been her best friend through everything. "I vote for that."

"Good," Priya said, and pulled them back in.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I lean into the kiss this time, my hand sliding into her hair as I smile against her lips. "God, I've wanted to do that for years," I murmur, before pulling back just enough to see her face.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya felt the truth of it land somewhere beneath her ribs. Years. She pressed her forehead against Cal's and let herself laugh, too.

"六年," she said quietly. "Give or take."

Cal's eyes searched hers, and Priya watched them flicker over her face—the close scrutiny, the wonder. She knew what Cal was looking for: doubt, regret, some sign that this had been a mistake. Priya let her find none of those things.

"I'm sure," Priya said, answering the question Cal hadn't asked. "I've been sure for a while. I just didn't know if you—"

"I've been sure since the night you told me about your mother's diagnosis and fell asleep on my shoulder," Cal said. "That was the moment I knew I was in real trouble."

Priya kissed them again for that. Softer this time. A thank-you and a promise, wrapped into one. When she pulled back, she was smiling.

"Your shoulder is very comfortable," she said. "For the record."

"Wow. Romance."

"You love it."

Cal's answer was another kiss, and Priya decided that was sufficient commentary.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her, finally, six years late, and she makes a small furious noise that I think is about the six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya pulled back just enough to look at them, her hand still tangled in the hair at the nape of their neck.

"Six years," she said again, shaking her head. "Do you know how many dinners I've cooked for you where I was just—this—" She made a gesture that probably meant something. "And you sat there talking about some date that went nowhere, and I just—"

"You never said anything."

"I didn't think I could," Priya said. "I thought if I said it and you didn't—" She stopped. "No. That's not true. I knew you'd never make it weird. I was just scared. I was scared of losing the one person who—" She broke off.

Cal was watching her with that look again, the one that made her feel like she was the most interesting thing in the room.

"The one person who what?" Cal asked softly.

Priya kissed the corner of their mouth. "Ruins me," she said. "You ruin me. And I didn't want to be without you, so I just—" She shrugged. "I let it take up space in my chest for six years. Worked around it."

"That's the most unhinged thing you've ever said to me."

"I know." Priya smiled. "I meant it, though."

Cal pulled her closer, and she went, settling against them like she'd been waiting to do exactly this for six years—which, of course, she had been.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "Good." I breathe out, resting my cheek against her hair. "Because I'm not going anywhere. And I'm done working around it."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya let the words settle over her like a blanket. The TV menu had timed out by now, and the room had gone dark except for the faint streetlight filtering through the curtains. She could feel Cal's heartbeat against her shoulder, steady and real.

"Okay," she said softly. She pressed closer, fitting herself against the familiar shape of them in a way that felt new and ancient all at once. "Okay."

There was more to talk about. There always would be—they both knew that. The logistics of whatever this was becoming. The conversation they hadn't had. The adjustments that would need to be made, the questions neither of them had asked.

But not tonight, Priya thought. Tonight was for this: the dark, and the quiet, and the extraordinary relief of finally letting her guard down with the one person who'd always been safe.

She closed her eyes and let herself breathe.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: We get to the bedroom eventually, laughing at ourselves most of the way, and then stop laughing when the clothes are actually off.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya watched Cal watching her, and felt suddenly, strangely shy—which was absurd, given that Cal had seen her at her worst, at three in the morning, sick and crying and not caring. But this was different. This was choosing to be seen.

"You too," she said.

Cal undressed with the same careful deliberation they brought to everything, and Priya let herself look. She'd imagined this, too, late at night when she allowed herself to. But imagination was a pale thing compared to the reality of Cal's skin against her palms, the sharp intake of breath when she touched them.

"Priya," Cal said, and her name in that voice, in that context, undid something in her chest.

She kissed the hollow of Cal's throat, feeling the pulse jump beneath her lips. "I've got you," she murmured. "I've got you."

They found their way to the bed, and Priya thought: this is real. This is actually happening. She mapped the territory of Cal's body like she was memorizing it, because maybe she was, because she wanted to know this the way she knew everything else about them—thoroughly, completely, without uncertainty.

When they finally came together, Priya made a sound she didn't recognize as her own. Cal whispered her name again, and she answered with her mouth against their shoulder, with her hands, with everything she'd been holding back for six years finally given permission to surface.

Afterward, they lay tangled in sheets that smelled like both of them now, and Priya traced idle patterns on Cal's chest and thought: I get to have this. I actually get to have this.

"Say something," Cal said quietly. "You're too quiet."

Priya smiled against their skin. "I'm just thinking about all the time we wasted."

"We didn't waste it."

"No?" She propped herself up on one elbow to look at them. "What would you call it, then?"

Cal caught her hand, pressed a kiss to her palm. "Building something," they said. "Brick by brick."

Priya felt her eyes sting. "That's unbearably cheesy."

"I know. But it's true."

She lay back down, fitting herself against Cal's side, and let the silence hold them both. The room was dark and close, and she could hear Cal's heartbeat slowing toward sleep.

"I'm going to want to do that again," Priya said eventually. "In about an hour."

Cal laughed softly, the vibration traveling through them both. "I'm going to want to do that again in about five minutes."

"We'll figure it out," Priya said, and meant it as more than about sex.

Cal's arm tightened around her. "Yeah," they said. "We will."

Priya closed her eyes and let the exhaustion of six years finally, finally pull her under.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content:
I watch her sleep for a while, just letting myself feel the weight of her against me. Eventually, I slip out of bed to find my phone in the living room, still tangled in the blankets we'd abandoned. The screen lights up with a dozen missed texts from friends asking how movie night went.

I type back one-handed: *It went.*

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya woke to cool sheets and the absence of warmth beside her. She lay still for a moment, blinking in the dark, and then Cal's absence registered as wrong—not because it was unfamiliar, but because tonight everything had changed.

She pulled on Cal's discarded t-shirt from the floor and padded barefoot to the living room, where she found them sitting on the couch, phone in hand, bathed in the same blue glow from earlier.

"You're not in bed," Priya said, her voice rough with sleep.

Cal looked up, and something in their face made her cross the room before she consciously decided to move. She settled onto the couch beside them, leaning into their side.

"Who were you texting?"

"My friends," Cal said. "They were asking about movie night."

Priya raised an eyebrow. "And what did you tell them?"

Cal turned the phone screen toward her. *It went.* Two words, sent to a dozen people who'd been invested in this for nearly as long as they had.

Priya laughed, surprised and a little overwhelmed. "We have people who care about us that much?"

"We have people who have been waiting for us to figure it out for years."

"Hm." Priya took the phone, scrolled through the responses—exclamations, demands for details, at least one marriage proposal from an unknown third party. She handed it back and tucked herself against Cal's side. "They can wait until morning."

"You should go back to sleep."

"You should come with me."

Cal's arm came around her, pulling her closer. "Give me a second."

Priya waited, watching the streetlight play across the ceiling, feeling the rise and fall of Cal's breathing. After a moment, Cal set the phone aside and stood, pulling her up with them.

"Okay," Cal said. "Now."

Priya led them back to bed, and this time when they settled into each other, it felt like something that would happen again. And again. And again.

She fell asleep smiling.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I get my mouth between her thighs and stay there while she tells me exactly what she wants, specifically, in a voice I have never heard her use in six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya stopped mid-sentence, her train of thought dissolving entirely. She gripped the sheets, then found Cal's hair instead, her fingers curling against their scalp as they worked.

"Oh," she managed. "That's—you can't just—" But Cal could, apparently, and did, with a focus and determination that suggested they'd been thinking about this for a while. Maybe years. Priya had certainly been thinking about it, in the dark, alone, not allowing herself to want it too much.

She was allowing herself now.

"Cal." Her voice came out strange, thin at the edges. "I need you to—"

Whatever she needed, Cal either already knew or was determined to find out. Priya gave up on language and let her head fall back against the pillow, eyes squeezed shut, every nerve in her body narrowing down to the singular point where Cal's mouth met her skin.

She came like that, quietly at first, and then less quietly, her hand pressed against her own mouth because she didn't trust herself not to say something she couldn't explain later. Cal stayed with her through the aftershocks, patient and thorough, until Priya pulled them up by the shoulders and kissed the taste of herself from their lips.

"Hi," Cal said, grinning against her mouth.

Priya laughed, breathless and undone. "Where did you learn that."

"I had six years to research."

"That's—" She kissed them again. "That's a very long time."

"I told you," Cal said. "I've been sure."

Priya pulled them back down, and this time she did the research herself.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky laugh as her hands slide down my sides. "Okay, but fair warning—I've had a lot more time to think about this than actually *do* it."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya paused, her hand resting against the curve of Cal's hip. She looked up at them—at the vulnerability in their face, the slight tension in their shoulders, the way they were bracing for something.

"Hey," she said softly. She shifted upward, pressing a kiss to the corner of their jaw. "We have time. I'm not going anywhere."

"I know you're not."

"Do you?"

Cal's eyes searched hers, and Priya watched something shift in them—the last residual fear giving way to something steadier. She understood. She'd felt it too, the first time, the terrifying moment when the thing you'd wanted for years finally became real and you had to decide whether to step forward or run.

"Show me what you've been thinking about," Priya said. "For six years. Show me what you imagined."

She kissed them slowly, thoroughly, while her hands mapped the territory she'd been denied for so long. Cal made a sound against her mouth that suggested they'd imagined this too, probably in the same dark hours, in the same careful restraint.

"I want to know all of it," Priya murmured between kisses. "Every version. Every time you thought about it and then didn't."

She touched them the way she wanted to be touched—patient, attentive, with the kind of focus that came from years of knowing someone's boundaries and wanting to understand where the new ones were drawn.

"Tell me if I get it right," she said.

Cal pulled her down and answered by showing her exactly where to go.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "You can stop being careful with me," she says. "I'm not made of glass and I've thought about this for as long as you have. Harder."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya heard the challenge in those words and felt something shift in her chest—permission, finally, to stop holding back. She'd been so careful with Cal for so long. Careful not to look too long. Careful not to touch in ways that might mean too much. Careful not to want more than she was allowed.

She wasn't careful now.

"Harder," she repeated, and the word came out low, rough. She pressed Cal back into the mattress, held them there, and kissed them until neither of them could think. "You want harder? You want to know what I think about when I can't sleep?"

Cal's breath caught. "Yes."

Priya ran her thumb along the line of Cal's jaw, watched their eyes go dark. "I think about this," she said. "I think about you asking me for something and me giving it to you. I think about the sounds you make when you don't have to be quiet. I think about what it would be like to just—" She kissed the hollow of Cal's throat. "—take what I wanted."

She could feel Cal's heartbeat racing beneath her palm, could feel the slight tremor in their breathing that meant she was affecting them the way they were affecting her. Six years of wanting this. Six years of imagining it in detail she'd never admit to out loud.

And now Cal was beneath her, asking her to be less careful, and Priya discovered she was done being careful. She was done pretending this wasn't what she'd wanted, what she'd needed, what she'd dreamed about in the small hours when she told herself it was just friendship, just closeness, just the way best friends were supposed to feel.

It wasn't.

She showed Cal exactly what it was.

Later, tangled in sheets again, Priya traced the marks she'd left on Cal's shoulder and felt a flash of something fierce and possessive that she didn't try to hide.

"Yours," she said quietly. Not a question. A statement of something she was only now allowing herself to claim.

Cal pulled her closer, pressed a kiss to her hair. "Yours," they agreed.

Priya closed her eyes and let herself believe it.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, my fingers tracing the line of her spine. "We're going to have to tell people eventually. My friends are already texting me in all caps."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya made a soft noise of acknowledgment, her fingers still moving absently along Cal's skin. The streetlight had shifted, casting new shadows across the ceiling, and she watched them move as she considered the question.

"Let them wait," she said eventually. "A little longer."

She could feel Cal's laugh more than hear it, the slight vibration against her cheek where she'd resting it.

"It's been one night," Priya continued. "I want more than one night before we have to package this into something we can explain to people who aren't us."

"Even though everyone's already guessing?"

"Especially then." Priya propped herself up on one elbow, studying Cal's face in the dim light. "I don't want to have to defend this. I don't want to have to justify it or make it make sense to anyone. I just want it to be ours for a while."

Cal's expression softened in a way that made something tighten in her chest.

"That's fair," Cal said.

Priya leaned down and kissed them, slow and thorough, the way she'd been wanting to kiss them for six years.

"Your friends can have their all-caps moment," she murmured against their lips. "They'll get their details. Just not yet."

Cal's hand came up to cup the side of her face, thumb brushing her cheekbone. "You really don't want to share this."

"I really don't." She turned her head, pressed a kiss to Cal's palm. "I've been sharing you for six years. This part is mine."

"Mine too," Cal said.

Priya settled back against them, fitting herself into the space that had always been waiting for her, and decided the outside world could wait a little longer.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: Six years of not doing this and now neither of us can form a sentence. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya didn't stop.

She moved with the kind of intention that came from years of wanting, years of imagining, years of stopping herself three seconds before she would have done exactly this. Cal's hands found her hips, her waist, the small of her back, touching her like she was something precious and also something that belonged to them now—both true, neither contradictory.

"You're thinking," Cal said, breathless.

"I'm always thinking." Priya pressed her forehead against Cal's shoulder, breathed them in. "I'm thinking about how many times I almost said something. How many times I almost kissed you at the wrong moment, in front of the wrong people, and every time I talked myself out of it because I was scared it would ruin—"

"It didn't ruin anything."

"I know." She lifted her head, met Cal's eyes in the half-dark. "I know that now."

She kissed the corner of Cal's mouth, the line of their jaw, the pulse point beneath their ear where she could feel their heartbeat racing. Cal made a sound that went straight through her, and she smiled against their skin—fierce, possessive, finally allowed.

"Tell me what you want," she said. "I want to give you everything."

Cal's breath hitched. "I want—you. Just you. Everything you've been keeping back."

Priya felt the words land somewhere deep in her chest. She pulled back just enough to look at them properly, to memorize the way they looked right now—undone, wanting, finally asking for what they'd both been denying themselves.

"Okay," she said softly. "Okay."

She gave them everything.

And Cal gave it back, in ways Priya hadn't let herself imagine, in sounds and touches and whispered names that made her feel like the most wanted thing in the world. They found a rhythm together that felt less like choreography and more like conversation—asking, answering, responding in kind. Priya lost track of time, of words, of everything except the heat between them and the extraordinary relief of finally being allowed to want this.

When she came, it was with Cal's name in her mouth and Cal's hands holding her steady, and for a moment there was nothing in the world but sensation and belonging and the strange, overwhelming intimacy of being truly seen.

She collapsed against Cal's chest, breathing hard, and felt their fingers tracing lazy patterns along her spine.

"Hi," Cal said again, the same word as before but different now, weighted with something new.

Priya laughed, too exhausted and too happy to lift her head. "Hi yourself."

They lay like that for a long moment, heartbeats gradually slowing, bodies slowly relaxing into each other. The room smelled like them both—sweat and sex and something warmer underneath, something that felt like home.

"I should probably go clean up," Priya murmured eventually, making no move to actually do so.

"You should probably stay," Cal said.

Priya tilted her head up, pressed a kiss to the underside of Cal's jaw. "I should probably do both."

But she didn't. She stayed exactly where she was, fitting herself against the familiar-unfamiliar shape of Cal's body, and let herself drift in the aftermath of something that had been six years in the making and somehow still managed to surprise her.

"I love you," she said quietly, into the hollow of Cal's throat. She hadn't planned to say it yet. She hadn't planned anything about this night, really, except that she'd known for a long time that it was true. "I've loved you for a long time. I probably loved you before I knew what to call it."

Cal's arms tightened around her.

"I love you too," they said. "I should have said it years ago. I should have done a lot of things years ago."

"We both should have." Priya propped herself up, met their eyes. "But we're saying it now. That's what matters."

Cal reached up, brushed a strand of hair from her face. "That's what matters," they agreed.

Priya kissed them then—soft, unhurried, the kind of kiss that didn't lead anywhere except back to the same place they'd been heading all along. When she pulled back, she was smiling.

"Okay," she said. "Now I should probably clean up."

"Probably."

"But I'm going to stay here for another minute first."

Cal's laugh vibrated through them both. "I can live with that."

Priya closed her eyes and stayed exactly where she was, and thought: I get to have this. I get to have this tomorrow, and the day after, and every day after that. I get to stop working around it.

The thought was terrifying.

The thought was the best thing she'd ever felt.

She fell asleep with Cal's heartbeat steady beneath her ear, and didn't dream at all, and woke up exactly where she belonged.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I wake up first, which never happens. She's still asleep, hair everywhere, one hand fisted in the shirt I'm still wearing. I just...look. For a long time. Then I carefully untangle myself to make coffee.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya woke to sunlight and the absence of warmth.

She stretched, reaching for Cal before her eyes were fully open, and found only empty sheets. Her hand dropped back to the mattress, and she lay there for a moment, blinking at the ceiling, trying to remember where she'd put her feet, where Cal had gone, whether last night had actually happened or if she'd finally cracked from years of repression.

The sheets smelled like both of them. That was answer enough.

She sat up slowly, Cal's shirt hanging off one shoulder, and listened. From the kitchen came the soft sounds of someone navigating a space that wasn't quite theirs—cabinet doors, the hiss of the coffee maker, a quiet hum that might have been Cal trying not to wake her and failing.

Priya padded to the kitchen doorway, bare feet silent on the hardwood, and stopped.

Cal stood at the counter in one of her old college t-shirts, hair sleep-mussed, hands wrapped around a mug. Morning light caught the edge of their profile, the curve of their shoulder, the way they stood like someone who'd done this a hundred times before in their own kitchen but were still learning the geography of hers.

Except they hadn't done this before. They'd never stayed the night. They'd never been here in the morning, in this light, in this context.

Priya leaned against the doorframe and watched them for a long moment before speaking.

"You made coffee."

Cal turned, smiled, and the expression on their face was something Priya had never seen directed at her before—softer than friendship, more certain than desire. Just warmth, open and uncomplicated.

"I made coffee," Cal agreed. "There's toast, if you want it. I found the butter."

Priya crossed the kitchen, took the mug Cal offered, and let herself lean into their side. The contact was simple. The contact was everything.

"I don't remember where I keep the butter," she said.

"You don't keep it in the refrigerator."

Priya laughed, surprised. "How do you know that?"

"Because it would be congealed and gross." Cal pressed a kiss to her temple, casual and deliberate at once. "I pay attention."

Six years, and Cal had been paying attention. Priya had known that, of course—she'd known Cal noticed things about her that no one else did, remembered details she'd forgotten mentioning—but this was different. This was Cal in her kitchen, knowing her butter habits, making her coffee, looking at her like the morning after was something they'd been planning all along.

"Your toast is burning," she said.

Cal swore, lunged for the oven, and Priya watched them rescue two slices of slightly-too-dark bread and thought: this is my life now. This is actually my life.

She could get used to it.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I hand her a plate with the toast, still a little charred at the edges. "We can scrape it," I offer, leaning back against the counter to watch her take the first bite. My heart is doing something stupid in my chest, just from this.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya took the plate, scraped the charred edges, and took a bite. The bread was slightly burnt, slightly dry, and absolutely perfect.

"It's fine," she said. "It's toast."

"You don't have to be polite."

"I'm not being polite. I'm being honest." She took another bite, chewing deliberately. "I've eaten much worse. Remember the camping trip?"

Cal groaned. "The foil dinners."

"The foil dinners that you made wrong because you didn't pack enough aluminum foil and we had to eat half of them out of a cooler."

"We don't talk about the cooler."

Priya smiled around another bite of toast, something warm spreading through her chest that had nothing to do with the coffee. This was the thing she'd been afraid of losing, she realized. Not Cal themselves, but this—the easy teasing, the shared history, the way they could mock each other without any edge to it. She'd been terrified that adding sex to the equation would break something, make it strange, turn the comfortable into the complicated.

It hadn't. It was just more of what they'd always had, with new territory to explore.

"We should probably talk about logistics," she said, setting the plate down. "Eventually."

"Logistics."

"Where we're going to do this. Whose apartment. How often. Whether we tell people or just let them figure it out from context clues."

Cal raised an eyebrow. "That's very clinical."

"I'm a planner. You know this about me."

"I do." Cal took a sip of their own coffee, watching her over the rim. "But maybe not first thing in the morning. Maybe we just have toast first."

Priya considered this. "That's reasonable."

"And then maybe we sit on that couch and I kiss you while the neighbors complain about the noise."

"The neighbors already complain about the noise. You once made soup at an unreasonable hour and Mrs. Patterson from 4B threatened to call the HOA."

"That was one time."

"It was a very loud one time."

Cal laughed, and the sound made something settle in Priya's chest. She set down her mug and stepped closer, fitting herself against Cal's side the way she'd done in the kitchen of her imagination a hundred times and never had the nerve to actually do.

"Okay," she said. "Toast first. Then logistics. Then whatever comes after."

"Sounds like a plan."

"It does, doesn't it?" She tilted her head up, pressed a kiss to the corner of Cal's mouth. "I'm stealing your shirt back, by the way. It's mine."

"You can have it. I have others."

"I know. But I want this one." She tugged at the hem, which had belonged to her for years and would now belong to both of them. "It smells like you now."

Cal's expression shifted into something softer, more wondering. "Is that okay?"

"It's more than okay." Priya finished her coffee, set the mug in the sink, and decided that logistics could wait another few hours. They had time. They finally had time. "Now. Couch?"

"Couch," Cal agreed.

Priya took their hand and led the way.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let her pull me to the couch, my thumb stroking the back of her hand. "We're really doing this," I say, more to myself than to her, as I settle beside her and pull her into my lap.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The film had finished some time ago and neither of them had done anything about it, which was how Priya knew the evening had changed character.

"We're not watching this," she said.

"We haven't been watching it since about nine."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "No," I agree. "We haven't." I don't move, but I stop pretending I'm looking at the screen.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya turned her head on the cushion, looking at him properly now. The blue light from the paused screen made his face strange and familiar at the same time.

"I'm going to kiss you," she said. It wasn't a question. She reached for the remote and turned the television off entirely, and the room went dark and quiet except for the streetlight through the window.

Then she did, deliberately, like it was something she'd thought about and decided on.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't realize I'd been holding. My hand came up to cradle the back of her head, fingers tangling in her hair. "Finally," I murmured against her mouth.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya pulled back just far enough to see his face in the dim light, her hand still resting against his jaw. Her thumb moved once, a small stroke along his cheekbone.

"How long have you been waiting to say that?" she asked, and her voice was warm, a little amused, but mostly something quieter.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her, finally, six years late, and she makes a small furious noise that I think is about the six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya didn't pull away. She pressed closer instead, her hand sliding from his jaw to the back of his neck, fingers curling into the short hair there. The kiss had been brief but not tentative—nothing about it had been tentative. It had been the kind of kiss that acknowledged how long they'd both been not doing this.

When she spoke, her mouth was still close to his, her breath warm.

"Six years," she said. "Give or take." She let her forehead rest against his for a moment, her eyes closed. "I kept thinking about all the times I was in your bed. Just sitting there. Watching something. And I was thinking about you."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let my forehead rest against hers, my eyes closing. "You were thinking about me, huh?" My voice is rough. "I thought I was going to go insane."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya laughed, a soft exhale against his cheek, and when she opened her eyes the streetlight caught the edge of her smile.

"I know," she gasped out, her eyes flying open, dark and wet with tears of sheer sensation. She looked up at him, her face flushed, her breath coming in ragged, desperate hitches. "I know. Don't hold back, Cal. Come with me."

She tilted her pelvis, her inner muscles still pulsing around him, urging him on. She wanted him to break, wanted to feel him unravel completely inside her after all these years of waiting. She lifted her hips, matching his desperate, heavy thrusts with a fierce, unyielding rhythm of her own, her gaze locked onto his, demanding everything he had left.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "Fuck," I choke out, and I'm gone. I bury myself deep and stay there, shaking, while her name cracks in my throat again.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya absorbed the full, shuddering weight of him as he broke, her arms locking around his back to hold him flush against her. She felt the hot, pulsing rush of his release deep inside her, the fading tremors of her own body clenching around him one last time before finally, slowly, beginning to relax. 

She didn't try to shift or ease the heavy pressure of his chest against hers. Instead, she buried her face in the crook of his neck, breathing in the sharp, clean scent of his skin and the heat of his sweat. Her chest rose and fell in rapid, shallow hitches, matching the ragged rhythm of his breath as they both tried to find their air. 

As the violent shaking in his shoulders slowly subsided into a heavy, exhausted stillness, Priya began to stroke his back. Her movements were slow and deliberate, her palms tracing the damp line of his spine, smoothing over the tense muscles of his shoulders to ease him down. There was no rush to separate, no sudden return of the careful boundaries they had lived by for six years. That world was gone.

She turned her head slightly, her lips pressing a soft, lingering kiss to the warm skin of his shoulder, right over the faint, stinging mark her teeth had left. 

"I've got you," she murmured against his skin, her voice low, raspy, and completely steady in the quiet room. "Don't move." 

She tightened her legs around his waist, anchoring him to her, content to simply lie there in the dark and feel the slow, calming beat of his heart against her own.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I stay exactly where I am, my breathing slowly evening out against her skin. One hand comes up to push her hair back from her face, my fingers tangling in the damp strands. I don't think I could move if I tried.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She pulled him closer, closing the last remaining distance between them with a deep, deliberate hunger

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She stepped forward, closing the last of the distance between them. Her bare feet made no sound on the floor. When she reached him, she didn't hesitate; she placed her hands flat against his bare waist, her palms soaking in his heat, her fingers anchoring themselves against his hips.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Right there. Don't stop. Just like that.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: the sudden, uncompromising shift in his rhythm sent a jolt of pure electrical heat straight to her core. Priya let out a sharp, undone cry

rung_labels.evidence: When he drove into her, the sensation was so intense, so thick and deep, that the breath was knocked completely out of her lungs

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The film had finished some time ago and neither of them had done anything about it, which was how Priya knew the evening had changed character.

"We're not watching this," she said.

"We haven't been watching it since about nine."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "No," I agree. "We haven't." I don't move, but I stop pretending I'm looking at the screen.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya looked at the black mirror of the television for a moment longer, at their two dim shapes reflected in it, close enough on the sofa that the pretense had become ridiculous.

Then she reached for the remote and turned the screen off properly.

The room went quieter.

She set the remote down on the coffee table with unnecessary care, because her hands needed one last practical thing to do. After that, there was nothing left to tidy, nothing left to blame on the film, nothing left except the fact that she had been aware of Cal beside her for the last hour in a way that was no longer even trying to be friendly.

Priya drew in a breath, then let it out through her nose. The nervousness came up sharp and bright, exactly as expected.

She looked at Cal.

“I’m going to say something,” she said, steady enough. “And if I’ve misread this, we can pretend I didn’t. I’ll be mortified for about a week, and then I’ll recover.”

A small, almost disbelieving smile touched her mouth, but it didn’t last. She was past the point of making it a joke.

“But I don’t think I’ve misread it.”

Priya shifted, turning more fully toward Cal, one knee drawn slightly onto the sofa between them. She didn’t reach out. Not yet.

“I think we’ve been very, very disciplined for six years,” she said. “And I think tonight we stopped being disciplined.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn’t realize I was holding. My voice comes out rough. “You haven’t misread it.” My hand finds hers, tentative but certain.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya looked down at their hands.

For a second, all the six years were there at once: every almost, every careful joke, every time she had chosen the safer seat, the safer word, the safer version of herself. It made her chest ache, but not with regret. More like relief arriving too fast.

“Good,” she said softly.

Her fingers closed around his.

The nervousness lasted, as predicted, perhaps another thirty seconds. Then it went. It simply left her body, as if it had done its part by getting her to the edge and was no longer needed.

Priya shifted closer, not hurried, not coy. Her shoulder brushed his. Her gaze moved over his face with an openness she had not allowed herself before.

“I don’t want to be careful anymore,” she said. “Not like that.”

She paused, because the next thing mattered, and because she wanted it said plainly.

“I do want to be careful with us,” she added. “With you. But I don’t want to keep pretending this is nothing.”

Her thumb moved once over his knuckles.

“And I don’t want to do the noble thing where we talk ourselves out of it because friendship is important.” Her mouth curved faintly. “It is important. That’s rather the point.”

Priya leaned in slightly, close enough now that the decision had a shape.

“I want to kiss you,” she said. “Unless you tell me not to.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her, finally, six years late, and she makes a small furious noise that I think is about the six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya made that noise again, lower this time, and caught the front of his shirt in her fist as if she had discovered an injustice and meant to take it up with someone immediately.

Six years, she thought, with real indignation. Six years of sitting beside him, laughing too hard at things that were not that funny, pretending not to notice the exact shape of wanting because noticing would have required doing something.

Apparently doing something was excellent.

She broke the kiss only far enough to breathe, her forehead nearly touching his, her hand still closed in his shirt.

“That,” she said, voice unsteady but not uncertain, “was stupidly overdue.”

Her eyes opened. She looked at him from far too close, and now there was no careful version of herself left to perform. No friend-mask, no plausible deniability, no little escape hatch of irony.

Just Cal. Just her. Just this.

Priya swallowed once, then let out a quiet laugh, almost disbelieving.

“I’m a little angry with us,” she admitted. “Not enough to stop.”

Her hand loosened from his shirt and flattened there instead, over his chest. The contact felt both new and absurdly familiar, as if her body had known the route before she had permitted herself the map.

She kissed him again, slower this time, less like an argument with the past and more like an answer to it.

When she drew back, she stayed close.

“Just so we’re clear,” she said, her voice soft but direct, “this isn’t going back in the box tomorrow.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: My other hand comes up to cradle the side of her face, thumb brushing her cheekbone. "It better not," I say, my voice still rough. "I don't think I'd survive the re-packing."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya’s expression changed at that—something in her went visibly softer, and then steadier.

“No,” she said. “We’re not doing that.”

Her hand rose to cover his at her face, holding it there for a moment as if she needed the proof of it. She turned her head just enough to press a brief kiss into his palm, then looked back at him.

“I mean it,” she said. “I don’t want a dramatic overnight personality transplant. I don’t want us suddenly making everything fragile by staring at it too hard. But I am not going to sit next to you tomorrow and pretend I don’t know what this feels like.”

Her thumb moved over the back of his hand.

“And I’m not going to let you do that either.”

There was a little smile then, warm and dangerous in its confidence.

Priya leaned forward and kissed the corner of his mouth, once. Then his jaw. Then, because she could and because the permission of it still felt astonishing, she kissed him properly again.

When she pulled back, it was only by an inch.

“We can be sensible in the morning,” she murmured. “We can have the conversation. Labels, pace, consequences, the whole mature little agenda.”

Her nose brushed his lightly.

“But tonight I would like to be extremely unsensible for a while.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: We get to the bedroom eventually, laughing at ourselves most of the way, and then stop laughing when the clothes are actually off.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya had expected another joke to save them, one last bit of familiar scaffolding to lean on.

It did not come.

Without the clothes, without the sofa, without the television’s dead reflection giving them somewhere else to look, the whole thing became very simple. Not easy, exactly. But simple.

Her breath caught.

Not from doubt.

From the sudden, almost unbearable fact of him.

“Oh,” she said, very softly.

Then she gave a short, helpless laugh and covered her face with one hand for half a second.

“Sorry. Not sorry. Just—” She dropped her hand again and looked at him properly. Her cheeks were warm, but her gaze did not run away. “That has rather clarified things.”

Priya stepped closer.

The nervousness had not returned. That surprised her a little. She had thought this moment would make her self-conscious, that she would become awkward in her own skin under the weight of six years turning into one night. Instead she felt startlingly present. Awake. As if the room had sharpened around her.

She reached for him, slower now, not because she was uncertain but because she wanted to remember the difference between imagining and knowing.

Her hand settled against him, careful at first, then less careful when the world did not end. Her mouth parted on a quiet breath.

“I want to do this properly,” she said.

A beat passed, and then her eyebrows drew together.

“That sounded much more formal than I meant it to.”

Her smile flickered, affectionate and a little dazed. Then it faded into something more serious.

“I mean I want us to pay attention. I want you here with me. I don’t want either of us performing bravery because we’ve waited so long that stopping to ask feels embarrassing.”

She lifted her chin, direct again.

“So if anything feels wrong, or too fast, or strange in a bad way, you tell me. I’ll do the same.”

Priya’s hand moved up, finding the side of his neck, her thumb resting lightly at the edge of his jaw.

“And if it only feels strange because it’s us,” she added, voice lower, “then I think we can survive that.”

For a moment she simply stood there, close enough to kiss and not doing it yet, letting the wanting breathe between them instead of rushing to cover it. That was new too: not the desire, but the permission to let it exist openly.

Then Priya leaned in and kissed him.

Not hurried this time. Not angry at the lost years. Just certain.

She kissed him like she had finally stopped trying to be good at restraint. Like friendship had not been discarded but brought with them, transformed by heat and trust and the astonishing relief of not having to step back.

When she drew away, her forehead lowered briefly, her eyes closed.

“Still here,” she murmured, almost to herself.

Then she opened her eyes again, and the softness in her face turned intent.

“Good.”

Priya kissed him once more, then let her mouth trace, slowly and deliberately, the path she had clearly been refusing to think about for years. Her hand steadied at his shoulder. Her other hand found his waist. Every place she touched him seemed to make the fact of this less impossible and more inevitable.

A quiet sound escaped her, not furious now.

Wondering.

She paused close to him, breathing unevenly, and gave another small laugh under her breath.

“I keep thinking I should be shocked,” she said. “I’m really not.”

Her mouth brushed his skin as she spoke.

“I’m just annoyed by how much sense it makes.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her shoulder, then the hollow of her throat, because I need to see if her pulse is racing as fast as mine is. (It is.) "Tell me about it," I murmur, my breath warm against her skin.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya’s eyes closed.

For a moment she lost the sentence she had meant to say, because the touch at her throat had made language briefly seem like an overcomplicated system nobody really needed.

Then she laughed, breathless and quiet.

“Right,” she said. “That is not helping me sound clever.”

Her hand found the back of Cal’s neck, not to pull, exactly. To anchor herself. To confirm that this was happening in the same world where they had once argued for forty minutes about the best way to load a dishwasher.

Her pulse was racing. She knew he could feel it. There was no dignity in pretending otherwise.

“It makes sense,” she said, words coming slower now, “because I trust you. Because I know you. Because apparently my body has been waiting for my brain to stop being such a bureaucrat about the whole thing.”

That startled another small laugh out of her, but it dissolved almost immediately when she looked at him again.

“And because it’s you.”

The simplicity of that landed harder than she expected. Her expression softened, then steadied.

“I don’t want someone easier,” she said. “I don’t want some tidy version of this where nothing is at risk. I want you, and I want us, and I am done pretending those are separate things.”

Priya brushed her thumb once along the side of his neck. Her gaze moved over him with open want now, unhidden and unashamed, but still threaded through with care.

Then she stepped back just enough to breathe properly.

“I’m also done standing in the middle of the room giving speeches,” she said, though her voice had gone low enough to ruin the joke.

Her mouth curved.

“Mostly.”

Priya reached for him again, slower this time, giving the invitation rather than taking the answer for granted. Her palm settled against his chest, warm and steady. She let herself feel the rise and fall of breath beneath her hand, and the intimacy of that almost undid her more than anything else had.

For six years, she had known how to be near him.

This was different.

This was nearness without translation.

She drew in a careful breath.

“I’m here,” she said. “I’m not panicking. I’m not regretting it. I’m very much not regretting it.”

Her smile flickered again, smaller now.

“But I do need to say, just once, that I’m going to be absurdly fond of you during this, and that may be inconveniently obvious.”

Priya’s cheeks warmed, but she did not look away.

“Possibly ruinous for my mystique.”

Then the humor left her face, not because it had been false, but because there was something better than humor waiting underneath it.

She leaned in and kissed him again, deeply enough that the last of the evening’s carefulness seemed to leave her with a sigh. Her hand slid up to his shoulder, then down again, learning what she had only guessed at before. Not hurried. Not tentative. Attentive.

When she broke away, she stayed close, her breath uneven.

“Touch me,” she said softly.

The words hung there for a second, plain and irreversible.

Then Priya added, because she was still Priya, because trust did not mean abandoning precision, “And keep telling me you’re with me.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I get my mouth between her thighs and stay there while she tells me exactly what she wants, specifically, in a voice I have never heard her use in six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya had not known she could sound like that.

Not with him.

Not with anyone, if she was honest.

The first time the words came out of her, precise and low and unmistakably commanding, she almost laughed from the shock of it. Then the feeling took the laugh apart before it reached her mouth.

“Yes,” she said, her hand tightening in the sheets. “There. Exactly there.”

Her head tipped back. Her eyes shut, then opened again at once, because she did not want to disappear into it completely. Not yet. She wanted to know this was Cal. She wanted the room, the night, the impossible ordinariness of the lamp beside the bed and his clothes on the floor and her own voice becoming something she did not recognize.

“Slower,” she said, breath catching. “No—don’t stop. Just slower.”

Her face burned, but not with embarrassment. With the force of being listened to. With the terrible, gorgeous intimacy of asking clearly and being present for what happened after.

Priya drew one knee up a little, then let it fall open again, a movement less graceful than honest. She made another sound, sharper this time, and pressed the back of her hand briefly over her mouth before pulling it away.

“No,” she told herself, almost fiercely. Then louder, to him, “I want you to hear me.”

That seemed to undo some last private restraint in her. Not caution. Not care. Just the old habit of making herself smaller when she wanted too much.

She was done with that.

Her hand found his hair, not forcing, just there. Holding on. Grounding herself in the impossible fact of him.

“More pressure,” she said, and the words came easier now. “Yes. God, yes, like that.”

Her voice broke on the last word. She laughed once, breathless and wrecked, because it was absurd, because it was Cal, because it made such devastating sense that she wanted to scold the universe for not arranging this sooner.

Then her laughter vanished.

The pleasure had stopped being something she could comment on from a distance. It gathered low and bright, spreading until her thoughts narrowed around it. Priya’s hand twisted in the sheet. Her hips shifted of their own accord, and she let them. She let herself want openly. She let herself be inelegant. She let herself be known.

“Don’t make me be patient,” she said, voice rough now, almost pleading and almost a command. “Not tonight.”

Her breath hitched.

“Please.”

The word startled her more than the others had. It had no performance in it. No cleverness, no control. Just want.

Her eyes opened, unfocused, and she looked down toward him with an expression stripped bare of every careful compromise they had ever made.

“I’m here,” she whispered. “I’m here, I’m—”

The sentence broke.

Priya came apart with a sound she could not have planned or softened if she tried. Her back arched; her hand tightened; the whole room seemed to contract to a single white point and then shudder open again. For several seconds there was no language at all, only breath and heat and the helpless tremor of her body riding through it.

When she finally came back to herself, it was slowly.

Very slowly.

She lay there breathing hard, one arm flung over her eyes, her skin damp and alive and oversensitive. Then she lowered her arm and stared at the ceiling with the stunned expression of a woman revising several long-held opinions at once.

After a moment, she gave a small, ruined laugh.

“Well,” she said.

Another breath.

“That was inconveniently persuasive.”

Her hand moved, searching for him without looking away from the ceiling at first. When she found him, her fingers curled gently, tenderly, as if the enormity of what had just happened required careful handling afterward.

Then she turned her head.

Her face was open in a way she would not have permitted an hour ago. Soft, dazed, deeply fond, and still unmistakably hungry.

“Come here,” Priya said, voice quiet but certain. “I need to kiss you before I say something embarrassingly sincere.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I move up to meet her mouth, still tasting her on my lips. My laugh is shaky against hers. "Think we can manage both?" I kiss her again, slow, before pulling back just enough to see her face. "Because I'm about to say something embarrassingly sincere too."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya went very still.

Not cold. Not afraid.

Just caught.

The shaky laugh against her mouth had undone her almost as much as everything before it, because it was so unmistakably him. Not some abstract lover conjured out of six years of denial. Cal, laughing like he could not quite believe the ground still existed beneath them.

Her hand came up to his face. Her thumb moved over his cheek, slow and tender.

“Oh, excellent,” she said, voice quiet and a little wrecked. “Mutual emotional endangerment. Very on brand.”

She tried to smile, managed it for half a second, and then lost it.

The room seemed to hold its breath with her.

Priya looked at him properly. Not at the idea of him. Not at the risk. At him.

“I love you,” she said.

The words came out plainly. No tremor. No ornament.

Then her eyes widened slightly, as if even she had not expected herself to begin there.

“Well,” she added, after a beat. “Apparently we’re doing that sentence first.”

Her hand stayed against his face. She did not take it back.

“I love you,” she said again, softer now, because the first time had been the truth breaking the surface and the second was her choosing it. “And I don’t mean only the safe version. I don’t mean the version we could explain to other people without alarming them. I mean this. I mean you. I mean I have loved you in a way I kept filing under friendship because it was convenient and because I was a coward and because losing you would have been intolerable.”

Her breath caught, but she kept going.

“And I am not saying it because you just made me temporarily insane.” A faint, helpless smile touched her mouth. “Though, for the record, you did make a compelling argument.”

The smile faded.

“I’m saying it because it’s true. Because I think it has been true for a long time, and I am suddenly very tired of pretending precision will save me from consequence.”

Priya swallowed once. Her fingers slid lightly into his hair, then back to his cheek, as if she could not quite decide where she needed to hold him.

“You don’t have to answer it neatly,” she said. “You don’t have to make it symmetrical just because we are naked and everything feels enormous. I am not setting a trap. I am not asking for a performance.”

She paused, and her expression softened into something almost unbearably fond.

“But I am asking you to stay here with me. In it. Honestly.”

Her gaze moved over his face, open and intent.

“And if your embarrassingly sincere thing is even half as dangerous as mine, then I would like to hear it before I lose my nerve and start making jokes about hydration.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "You can stop being careful with me," she says. "I'm not made of glass and I've thought about this for as long as you have. Harder."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya heard herself say it and felt the sentence settle between them, blunt and necessary.

There. That was the line she had been circling.

Not reckless. Not careless.

Honest.

Her fingers tightened, then opened again, deliberately, because she did not want to clutch at him like fear. She wanted this chosen. She wanted every part of it awake.

“I mean it,” she said, voice low, roughened past elegance. “I know you’re trying to be good to me.”

Her eyes opened, dark and intent.

“You are being good to me.”

A breath shuddered out of her.

“But you don’t have to treat wanting me like it might break something.”

That made her throat tighten unexpectedly. Not with sadness. With the sheer intimacy of saying it aloud after all the years of carefulness. She had spent so long making herself manageable around him, so long believing restraint was the kindest thing either of them could offer.

Now kindness looked entirely different.

Priya’s hand slid to the back of his neck. Her mouth found his again, not gentle enough to be mistaken for uncertainty. When she broke away, she was breathing hard, but her gaze stayed fixed on him.

“I want you here,” she said. “All the way here.”

The words came out quieter than she expected, and more vulnerable.

For a second, that vulnerability opened under her like a drop. Then she did not fall. She stayed.

Because it was Cal.

Because he knew her.

Because she had trusted him with grief and bad decisions and terrible takeaway and the version of herself that snapped when exhausted and the version that cried at adverts and the version that pretended not to want this.

So she could trust him with this too.

Priya let her head fall back against the pillow, then looked at him again with something like wonder moving through her face.

“Yes,” she whispered, before anything else had even needed saying. “I’m still with you.”

Her laugh came out broken and breathless.

“I’m very much with you.”

Then the laughter vanished, replaced by a sound she did not soften. Her eyes shut. Her body arched into the moment, no longer trying to be composed, no longer translating desire into something polite enough to survive breakfast.

There was nothing polite about this.

There was care in it. Trust. Astonishing tenderness.

But not politeness.

“Don’t disappear on me,” she managed, her voice fraying. “Stay with me. Let me see you.”

Her hand moved blindly, found skin, held on.

The old friendship was still there, impossibly, underneath everything—six years of knowing how he took his coffee, how he went quiet when hurt, how he pretended not to be sentimental and failed constantly. It should have made this stranger.

Instead it made it devastating.

Priya’s eyes opened again, shining and unguarded.

“Oh,” she breathed, almost a laugh, almost a plea. “There you are.”

For a while after that, words became difficult and then unnecessary, except for the ones that mattered: yes, here, more, don’t stop, I’ve got you, I’m here.

And when she finally lost the thread of language altogether, she did not feel lost.

She felt found.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "I love you," I say against her mouth, my voice rough. "Six years. Should've said it six years ago." My hand slides into her hair, holding her there while I catch my breath. "But I'm not taking it back now."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya stopped breathing.

For one impossible second, everything in her went quiet. Not empty. Full. Too full to move.

Then her face crumpled.

Not dramatically, not beautifully. Just honestly. Her eyes stung, her mouth trembled, and she made a small sound that was half laugh, half protest, because apparently joy could be rude enough to arrive at the worst possible moment.

“You absolute idiot,” she whispered.

Her hand came up to his wrist, holding him where his hand was in her hair, as if she could keep the words there too. As if they might vanish if she did not physically anchor the moment.

Then she kissed him hard.

Not careful. Not composed. Not with any of the restraint she had once mistaken for wisdom. She kissed him like the sentence had gone into her bloodstream. Like six years had folded in on themselves and left only this: his mouth, his breath, his ridiculous timing, his love said too late and exactly when she needed it.

When she pulled back, her eyes were wet.

“Don’t you dare take it back,” she said, voice shaking now, but not from uncertainty. “I will be unbearable about it. I’ll make charts. I’ll bring witnesses.”

A laugh broke through her, fragile and bright, and she pressed her forehead to his.

“Six years,” she said again, softer. “God. We are so stupid.”

But there was no real anger in it now. Only awe. Only the grief of lost time dissolving under the weight of what had finally been said.

Her thumb moved over his cheek.

“I love you,” she said once more, because now that she had begun, she seemed unable to stop choosing it. “I love you. I love you. I love you.”

Each one came out different. One relieved. One fierce. One nearly broken.

Then Priya drew him closer, her breath catching as the moment shifted again, tenderness becoming heat without losing tenderness at all.

“Now stay,” she whispered. “Stay right here. With me.”

She did not mean the room.

She meant the truth of it.

She meant no retreating behind gentleness so careful it became distance. No disappearing into performance. No making love into something abstract when both of them were there, bare and breathing and finally, finally done lying.

Priya’s hands moved over him with a new certainty, not rushed but unhidden. She let herself want him without apology. Let herself be wanted without flinching away from the scale of it. Every touch seemed to answer something old in her, something she had trained herself not to ask.

Her eyes stayed open as long as they could.

She wanted to see him.

She wanted him to see what his words had done.

“You should have said it six years ago,” she murmured, breathless, mouth brushing his skin. “I should have said it six years ago.”

Her voice caught, then steadied.

“But we’re saying it now.”

That mattered. It mattered more than the waste. More than the fear. More than every careful evening they had survived by pretending not to know.

Priya pulled him down to her again, and after that the world narrowed to warmth, breath, the press of him, the astonishing intimacy of not having to translate anything. She was not graceful. She was not guarded. She was sometimes laughing, sometimes almost crying, sometimes whispering his name like it had become the only sensible word left.

And through it all, she stayed.

Present. Open. Devastatingly awake.

When pleasure rose again, it did not feel like being taken apart so much as being gathered. All the scattered versions of herself—the friend, the coward, the woman who had known and not known, the woman who had finally reached across the sofa—seemed to converge in one place.

Here.

With him.

Loved.

Loving.

Priya held on, her voice breaking around the words she had once been too careful to say.

“I’ve got you,” she whispered. “I’ve got you. I’m here.”

And when the moment finally overtook her, she did not try to make it quiet. She let it move through her, let him know, let the night have the whole truth of her.

Afterward, she lay still for a long time, breathing unevenly, one hand resting over her own eyes.

Then, very slowly, she lowered it.

Her face was flushed, tear-streaked, dazed. Entirely without mystique.

She turned her head toward him.

“Well,” Priya said faintly.

A pause.

Then her mouth curved, soft and helpless.

“I think the friendship may have escalated.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: Six years of not doing this and now neither of us can form a sentence. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya had said it before she could make it elegant.

“Don’t stop.”

The words left her raw and honest, and there was no taking them back. She did not want to take them back. She wanted them heard. She wanted this night to know that she had meant every reckless, careful, loving thing she had said.

Her hand slid into the sheets, then out again, searching for something steadier than fabric. Finding skin, warmth, him. She held on.

For a while, she could not manage language. Not properly. Only fragments.

“Yes.”

“Here.”

“Stay.”

Each word came from somewhere deeper than thought. Each one seemed to pull her further out of the old habit of restraint and into the astonishing present tense of being wanted by the person she trusted most.

Priya kept her eyes open until she couldn’t. Then opened them again because she wanted to see. Because hiding, even in pleasure, felt like a smaller version of the lie they had both been telling for too long.

Her breath broke. Her mouth parted around his name.

It was too much and exactly enough.

The tenderness was what undid her. Not just the heat of it, not just the years turning themselves inside out, but the care threaded through every second. The fact that she could be this unguarded and still feel safe. The fact that love had not made the want gentler so much as truer.

Her body trembled with the effort of staying present.

“I’m here,” she managed, voice barely holding together. “I’m here. I love you.”

That last part came out like a confession and a vow and a reminder all at once.

Then there was no cleverness left in her. No mystique. No version of Priya who could make a joke quickly enough to shield herself from how much this mattered.

She simply let herself feel it.

Let herself be known.

Let herself fall apart without making it smaller.

When the wave finally took her, she held on and did not quiet herself. She let the sound of it exist. Let the tears come when they came. Let the laughter break through afterward, startled and breathless and almost disbelieving.

For a few seconds, she could not move.

Then Priya turned her face into the pillow and laughed again, softer this time.

“Oh my God,” she said faintly.

A pause.

Then, with what little dignity she had left, “I may need to revise my entire personality.”

Her hand found him again, gentler now. Not grasping. Just touching because she could. Because the aftermath felt as important as everything before it.

She blinked slowly, eyes wet, face warm, utterly undone.

Then she looked at him with devastating fondness.

“Also,” Priya said, voice hoarse and sincere, “I am absolutely never letting either of us pretend this didn’t happen.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "Good," I breathe, still tangled in her. I kiss her forehead, her cheek, my own voice wrecked. "Because I'm not going to be able to stop."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya closed her eyes at the words.

Not because they frightened her.

Because they landed somewhere tender and permanent, somewhere that had already been altered beyond repair.

“Good,” she whispered.

The word came out almost soundless, but it was full of certainty.

For a while, she did not try to be articulate. She had spent years being articulate around him. Careful, funny, useful, composed. She had translated too much into friendship and timing and practicality, had turned longing into manageable little shapes and congratulated herself on being sensible.

Now sense had failed beautifully.

Priya’s hand moved to his shoulder, then to the back of his neck, holding there. Her touch had changed. It was not exploratory anymore, not astonished by permission. It was possessive in the quietest possible way. Not claiming him from anyone else. Claiming the truth from all the years they had hidden it.

“You don’t have to stop,” she said, voice rough. “Not loving me. Not wanting me. Not telling me.”

Her eyes opened.

She looked at him with the kind of steadiness that came after fear had burned itself out.

“Especially not telling me.”

A small smile tugged at her mouth, tired and radiant and entirely without defense.

“I may require a frankly embarrassing amount of telling.”

That should have been a joke. It was mostly not.

Priya breathed in, slow and uneven, then let it go. Her body still felt distant from itself in places, oversensitive in others, as if the night had rearranged her and then left her to discover the new floor plan. But emotionally, strangely, she felt clear. Wrecked, yes. Exposed. Tender to the point of absurdity.

But clear.

She loved him.

He loved her.

The fact existed now. Not imagined. Not implied. Not buried under a hundred reasonable excuses.

Said.

Her face shifted again, the humor softening into something more vulnerable.

“I’m going to wake up tomorrow and remember this in stages,” she said. “First I’ll remember the sofa. Then the kissing. Then the extremely unsensible portion of the evening.”

Her cheeks warmed, but she did not look away.

“Then I’ll remember you said you loved me, and I am going to be absolutely insufferable.”

A breath of laughter escaped her, and it trembled at the edges.

“Possibly smug. Definitely emotional. There may be tea involved. Possibly a spreadsheet, if I panic.”

Priya swallowed, and for a second her eyes shone again.

“But I don’t think I will,” she said more quietly. “Panic.”

That surprised her enough that she had to sit with it.

She had expected the fear to return after. Had expected some cold rush of consequence, some sober little voice asking what they had done and how they intended to survive it. But the voice did not come. Or if it did, it sounded embarrassingly reasonable.

What they had done was stop lying.

What they had to survive was being honest.

Priya’s thumb moved slowly against his skin.

“I thought this would make everything feel precarious,” she admitted. “Like one wrong move and we’d ruin the best thing in my life.”

Her mouth twisted faintly.

“And I’m not saying we get to be careless. We don’t. We’re still us. We still have to be kind, and honest, and not idiots in fresh and exciting ways.”

A pause.

“But it doesn’t feel like ruining it.”

Her voice softened.

“It feels like finding the rest of it.”

That was the part that almost broke her again. Not the desire, though God knew that had been enough to ruin her dignity several times over. Not even the love, though the love was vast enough to frighten her if she looked at it too sideways.

It was the continuity of it.

That friendship had not vanished under her hands. That it had come with them. That everything she had known about Cal had not made this smaller or stranger, but deeper. More intimate. More real.

Priya gave a slow, disbelieving shake of her head.

“We are going to be unbearable,” she murmured.

Then she leaned in, pressing her smile briefly against his skin.

“I am almost looking forward to it.”

Her hand stilled.

For a moment, she simply rested there, breathing, letting the silence settle around them without rushing to fill it. The quiet no longer felt like an unanswered question. It felt like the room after music had stopped, still holding the shape of it.

Then, softly, because the words still felt new enough to need practice, Priya said, “I love you.”

She closed her eyes as she said it.

“I love you, Cal.”

His name changed the sentence. Made it less abstract. Less like a declaration made in the high drama of the night and more like something she could say in a kitchen, in a doorway, over bad coffee, at the end of an ordinary day.

She opened her eyes again.

“And I want this,” she said. “Not just tonight. Not just because we finally lost our minds in a very coordinated fashion.”

Her smile flickered.

“I want the awkward morning. I want figuring out what we are. I want you texting me something stupid tomorrow and both of us knowing it means more now. I want to be your friend and whatever comes next. I don’t want to trade one for the other.”

Priya’s throat tightened.

“I want both.”

There it was.

The greedy, impossible, obvious truth.

She had wanted both for years.

She let out a breath that nearly became a laugh.

“And if that sounds like too much, I’m not apologizing. I have spent six years being restrained and I would like credit for time served.”

Her expression warmed, then sobered.

“But I’ll go slowly where it matters,” she added. “I will. I’m not going to drag us forward just because I’m relieved. We can be careful with the real things.”

A beat.

“Just not careful in the old way.”

Priya shifted closer, seeking warmth without shame now. Her head lowered for a moment, and she let herself be quiet against him.

The night had changed them. Not into strangers. Into something they had already been becoming, secretly, stubbornly, for years.

After a while, she gave a small sigh.

“I’m very tired,” she said, with great seriousness. “And very happy. Which is an alarming combination. I may say something appalling.”

Her mouth curved.

“Like that I feel safe.”

The smile faded almost immediately, because the sentence deserved better than deflection.

Priya lifted her head enough to look at him.

“I do,” she said. “With you. Even now. Especially now.”

Then, because she could not bear all that sincerity without at least one small act of self-preservation, she added, “But if you tell anyone I was this earnest, I’ll deny everything.”

Her eyes softened.

“Except loving you,” she said.

That, at least, she was done denying.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a breath that's half-laugh, half something else entirely. My hand's still in her hair, not pulling, just...holding. "We're going to be insufferable," I murmur, and it's not a complaint.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya’s smile started small and then spread, helplessly, across her whole face.

“Yes,” she said. “Catastrophically.”

She shifted just enough to look at him properly, still warm and tangled and not yet ready to return to any version of the world where people wore clothes and checked the time. Her hair was a disaster. Her voice had gone rough. Her body felt loose and oversensitive and deeply, absurdly content.

She had never felt less impressive in her life.

It was wonderful.

“We’re going to be the sort of people other people complain about after dinner,” she said. “You realize that. Someone will say, ‘Were they always like this?’ and someone else will say, ‘No, they used to be normal,’ and then everyone will look sad for our lost dignity.”

A pause.

Priya’s expression softened.

“Though, to be fair, I’m not sure we were ever normal.”

Her hand moved idly against him, not with urgency now, just contact. Reassurance. The strange new luxury of touching him without needing an excuse. She seemed unable to stop checking that he was there, that the night had not become imaginary the second she let herself relax.

There had been so many years of almost.

Now there was this.

Priya breathed in, and the breath caught a little.

“Oh,” she said quietly, and closed her eyes for a moment.

The emotion rose without warning. Not as a dramatic wave this time, but as something gentler and more dangerous: gratitude, huge and simple, pressing up under her ribs. She had expected desire to be destabilizing. She had expected confession to be frightening. She had not expected the after to feel like coming home to a room she had been standing outside for years.

When she opened her eyes again, they were bright.

“I keep thinking I’m done reacting,” she said. “And then I remember again.”

Her mouth curved, but the smile trembled.

“You love me.”

She said it softly, as if testing the words in the air. Not asking. Not doubting. Just learning the shape of a fact that had finally been allowed to exist.

Then she laughed under her breath and pressed the heel of her hand briefly to one eye.

“God. I’m going to be impossible.”

Priya lowered her hand and looked at him with open fondness.

“You’ll say something completely ordinary tomorrow, like ‘Do you want toast?’ and I’ll have to go and stand very still in another room because apparently toast will now have emotional implications.”

She considered this with genuine concern.

“This is going to be inconvenient in several practical ways.”

But the humor could only hold for so long. It thinned, leaving her face bare again.

Priya reached up and touched his hand where it rested in her hair, her fingers curling lightly around his wrist.

“I’m glad,” she said.

The words were too small. She knew that as soon as they left her. Glad was for cancelled meetings and trains arriving on time. Glad was ridiculous for this.

Still, it was what she had.

“I’m glad it was you,” she said, more carefully. “I’m glad it’s this. I’m glad we didn’t wreck it by wanting too much. I’m glad wanting you didn’t take you away from me.”

Her throat worked.

“That was the thing I was afraid of, I think. Under all the sensible reasons. That if we touched this, I’d lose the version of you I already had.”

Priya gave a small shake of her head, almost disbelieving.

“But you’re still here.”

She smiled again, softer now.

“And I’m still me. Slightly less mysterious, perhaps. Considerably less composed. But still me.”

Her thumb brushed once over his wrist.

“And you are still my favourite person.”

There. That one felt almost more intimate than I love you, somehow. Older. Worn smooth by six years of proof.

Priya let it sit between them.

Then, because she was tired and happy and entirely too exposed, she turned her face briefly toward the pillow and muttered, “This is awful. I’m going to have to be emotionally available now.”

A beat.

She glanced back, eyes warm.

“I shall expect compensation.”

Her smile lingered, then faded into quiet seriousness.

“But not tonight,” she said. “Tonight I don’t want to solve anything. I don’t want to get ahead of it. I don’t want to start building rules because we’re frightened by how much it matters.”

She shifted closer, the movement slow and drowsy, and rested there with a sigh that seemed to leave her whole body.

“I just want to stay here,” she said. “With you. Knowing.”

For a while, Priya said nothing else.

She let the silence settle. Let the room become ordinary again around the impossible thing they had done. The lamp. The sheets. The faint noises beyond the walls. The world continuing, unaware that six years had just been rearranged in the dark.

Her eyes grew heavy, then opened again stubbornly.

“One more thing,” she murmured.

There was, apparently, always one more thing.

“If either of us becomes noble tomorrow, I want us to remember this exact moment and be embarrassed.”

Her voice was sleepy now, but still direct.

“No speeches about protecting the friendship. No pretending we’re confused if we’re not. No running away just because the stakes finally admitted they were stakes.”

Priya’s hand tightened gently.

“We can be scared if we need to be. But we have to be honest.”

She was quiet for a second.

Then she added, softer, “I can do scared with you.”

The sentence surprised her. Not because it was untrue, but because it was so true she had not needed to polish it.

Priya looked at him, her expression open and tired and wholly sure.

“I love you,” she said again, with no drama left in it now. Only warmth. Only practice. Only the beginning of habit.

Then her mouth curved faintly.

“And yes. We are going to be insufferable.”

She closed her eyes, still smiling.

“But I think, on balance, people have survived worse.”
