dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit had made it as far as the kitchen doorway before Bear moved, which was further than usual and had clearly been allowed.

"You let me get that far," Kit said, backing up one step.

"I did," Bear agreed. "I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't be," I say, and go.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear let the words land, held still a beat too long — long enough to let Kit's pulse kick up into something sharper — and then launched after them.

The house was only so big. Bear knew every squeaking floorboard, every corner that killed momentum. He heard Kit's footsteps stutter past the dining table, and he took the long route, bare feet silent on the runner rug in the hall, cutting off the hallway toward the bedroom.

He didn't run so much as *hunt*. Palms grazing the wall for balance, slow when he needed to be silent, crashing loud when he wanted Kit to hear him closing in.

The bedroom door was half open. Bear hit it with a flat palm, sent it swinging wide, and stepped into the doorway, chest heaving, eyes pinning Kit wherever they'd tried to hide.

"Generous is off the table," Bear said, voice a rough rumble, still catching his breath. "You told me not to be. So I'm not."

He dragged two fingers across the old bite mark on his own shoulder — Kit's work, from last time — and grinned, all teeth.

"You owe me. And I'm counting."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I let out a sharp, delighted laugh and darted for the other side of the bed. "You don't hunt what you already own, Bear."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn't bother going around. One hand planted on the mattress, and he vaulted over the foot of the bed with a grunt, landing heavy on the other side, cutting off Kit's retreat.

"Who said anything about owning?"

He crowded in close, not touching yet, just letting his size do the work. His chest still rose and fell hard, and the smell of him — clean sweat, cedar soap, something sharper underneath — filled the space between them.

"Ownership's paperwork. This is *keeping*."

He reached up, slow this time, telegraphing it, and hooked two fingers into the collar of Kit's shirt, not pulling, just holding.

"And you, sharp little thing, know damn well I don't stop hunting just because I caught you once."

His voice dropped lower, almost a purr. "Now. You gonna make me work for it? Or you gonna let me even the score?"

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear caught Kit's wrist first, then the other, pressing them back against the wall with just enough weight to make the point. His breath was hot against Kit's temple, and he held there, savoring the surrender.

"There you are," he murmured, low and satisfied. "Knew you'd come to your senses."

He shifted his grip, gathering both of Kit's wrists in one hand, pinned above their head. His free hand slid down Kit's side, possessive, mapping the familiar territory of ribs and hip.

"Eight years," Bear said, mouth brushing the shell of Kit's ear. "Eight years and you still make me chase. Still make me earn it."

He pulled back just enough to meet Kit's eyes, his own dark and warm with something that wasn't quite tenderness — too hungry for that, too sharp.

"I love it," he admitted, like a secret. "Love that you never just roll over. Even when you let me win."

His thumb pressed into the soft dip of Kit's hip, a promise of pressure to come.

"Score's uneven, sweetheart. You got me good last time." He tilted his head, baring the side of his throat, showing the fading bruise Kit had left three nights ago. "I intend to return the favor. Thoroughly."

He leaned in, teeth grazing the curve of Kit's neck, not biting yet. Just the threat of it.

"Bedroom. Now. Unless you want me to start right here."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Bedroom," I agree, tilting my head back against the wall, baring my throat further. "But you're carrying me."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear let out a low, pleased growl that rumbled through his chest and into Kit's.

"Demanding little thing," he said, but there was nothing but approval in it.

He released Kit's wrists and bent, one arm hooking under their knees, the other bracing solid across their back. He lifted with an easy grunt, Kit's weight familiar and welcome in his arms.

"Arms around my neck," Bear instructed, already walking. "You know the rules. If I'm doing the hauling, you're doing the holding."

He carried them through the hallway, past the kitchen doorway where the chase had started, and nudged the bedroom door open with his shoulder. The bed was still rumpled from this morning, sheets kicked half off, pillows askew.

Bear didn't set Kit down gently. He dropped them onto the mattress with a bounce, following immediately, one knee pressing between their thighs, hands planting on either side of their head.

"Now," he said, looking down at them with that sharp, hungry grin. "Where were we?"

He dipped his head, mouth finding the curve of Kit's shoulder, and bit down — not hard enough to break skin, but hard enough to leave a mark. Hard enough to make his point.

"That's one," he murmured against the reddening skin. "I'm thinking three. Maybe four. You've been mouthy all week."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn't argue. The floor met his knees with a dull thud, and he followed Kit down, all heat and weight and urgency.

"Fine," he growled against Kit's mouth. "Floor's fine. *You're* fine. Clothes—"

He yanked at Kit's shirt, buttons scattering across the hardwood with tiny clicks, and shoved the fabric aside with a roughness that was half desperation, half devotion. His own shirt went next, dragged over his head and thrown blind, landing somewhere in the dark behind him.

"Problem solved," he breathed, already lowering himself, skin to skin, chest to chest. The contact punched a groan out of him.

His mouth found Kit's throat again, then lower, mapping collarbone and sternum with teeth and tongue. One hand braced beside Kit's head, the other working between them, dealing with belts and zippers with practiced, impatient fingers.

"Two," he counted, biting down on the meat of Kit's shoulder, harder this time. He soothed the sting with a slow drag of his tongue, then pulled back just enough to meet Kit's eyes in the dim light.

"Three's gonna be somewhere you can't hide. Gonna see it every time you look in the mirror."

He shifted his hips, grinding down with deliberate pressure, and his voice cracked just slightly — still rough, still in control, but fraying at the edges.

"Tell me you want this. Tell me now."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't make me say it," I breathe, arching into him, my hands finding his hair. "You already know I do."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear's breath caught, something fierce and tender twisting behind his ribs at the way Kit said it — *you already know I do* — like surrender and challenge all at once.

"Still like hearing it," he admitted, rough and quiet. "Still like knowing you'll give me that much."

He didn't make Kit say more. They'd given enough.

Instead, he lowered his head and bit down a third time, right at the junction of neck and shoulder, where the skin was soft and the mark would bloom dark by morning. Kit's hands in his hair tightened, and Bear groaned against their skin, hips pressing down in answer.

"Three," he rasped, pulling back to admire his work. The imprint of his teeth was already rising, red and claiming. "That one's my favorite."

He shifted lower, mouth trailing down Kit's chest, pausing to press a softer kiss over their heart — a brief, tender counterpoint to the sharpness — before continuing his descent.

"Still owe you one more," he murmured against the plane of Kit's stomach, breath hot and deliberate. His hands found Kit's hips, thumbs pressing into the hollows there, holding them steady. "But I'm gonna take my time with four. Make you earn it."

He looked up the length of Kit's body, eyes dark and warm, lips curved in that sharp, hungry grin.

"You good? You need a minute?"

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear pulled back just enough to look at the mark he'd left, thumb brushing the edge of it with something close to reverence.

"You want it harder?" His voice was gravel and smoke, barely above a whisper. "You sure?"

He didn't wait for an answer — didn't need to. Kit's hands were still fisted in his hair, body arched up against him, every line of them saying *yes, more, don't stop*.

"Alright," Bear breathed. "Alright, sweetheart. You asked for it."

He shifted his weight, one arm bracing solid beside Kit's head, the other hand sliding up to cradle the back of their neck. His mouth found the same spot, the already-tender skin, and this time he didn't hold back.

His teeth sank in deep, deliberate, the bite blooming hot and sharp. He felt Kit's whole body go taut beneath him, heard the breath they sucked in, and held — held until the edge of too-much, until the line blurred and sharpened all at once.

Then he let go, slow, pressing his mouth to the mark in a kiss that was almost apologetic. Almost.

"That's four," he murmured, voice wrecked. "And now we're even."

He pulled back to look at Kit, at the flush spreading down their chest, at the dark bruise already forming on their shoulder. His thumb traced the edge of it, feather-light.

"Gonna feel that tomorrow," he said, and his grin was all satisfaction. "Gonna feel it every time you move. Every time you turn your head. And you're gonna think of me."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I laugh, breathless and raw. "I think of you anyway." My hands slide down to his back, fingers pressing into the muscle there. "Now stop talking and finish what you started."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear huffed a laugh against Kit's skin, hot and rough and full of want.

"Bossy," he muttered, but it came out like praise.

He stopped talking.

His mouth found Kit's again, less biting now, more desperate — the kind of kiss that said *I've got you* and *I need you* all at once. His hands roamed, mapping familiar territory with the same hunger as the first time, because it never got old. Kit never got old.

The floor was hard beneath them, unforgiving, but neither of them cared. Bear's body covered Kit's like a shield, like a claim, moving with a rhythm they'd perfected over eight years of wanting each other.

When Kit's nails dug into his back — sharp, demanding — Bear groaned into the kiss and gave them what they asked for. What they both needed.

Later, much later, when they were tangled together on the floor, breathless and sweat-slicked and marked up on both sides, Bear let out a long, satisfied exhale.

"Score's settled," he murmured against Kit's hair, arm heavy across their waist. "For now."

He pressed a kiss to Kit's temple, softer than anything that had come before.

"You're gonna be sore tomorrow. Both of us are. Worth it."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went still.

Not the tense stillness of the chase, but something deeper — a quiet, focused attention that settled over him like a held breath. He lifted his head to look at Kit, really look, reading their face in the low light.

"Thursday," he repeated, voice careful. "You want them to last till Thursday."

It wasn't a question, but it was a check. A pause. The kind they'd learned to give each other over eight years, even when the want was sharp enough to cut.

He took Kit's wrists, one in each hand, and held them gently — a stark contrast to the grip he'd used earlier. His thumbs brushed over the delicate skin on the inside, tracing the veins there, the places where a bite would linger.

"Here?" he asked, low and serious. "You want my teeth here? Where you'll see them every time you reach for something? Every time you button a cuff?"

He lifted Kit's left wrist to his mouth, lips brushing the pulse point, feeling the quick flutter of their heartbeat against his kiss.

"I'll do it," he murmured against the skin. "But you tell me if it's too much. You tell me, and I stop. Same rules as always."

He waited, breath warm, teeth grazing but not yet biting, giving Kit the space to pull back or push forward.

"Thursday's a long time, sweetheart. Gonna hurt. Gonna ache every time you move your hand." His voice dropped, rough and reverent. "That what you want?"

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I hold my wrists steady. "That's what I want." I watch his face, letting the silence stretch for a beat. "Same rules. I'll tell you."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear held Kit's gaze for a long moment, something raw and grateful flickering behind the hunger. Then he nodded, once, a solemn promise.

"Okay," he said. "Okay, sweetheart."

He lifted Kit's left wrist first, pressing a kiss to the tender skin just below the palm — a benediction, a warning, a thank-you all at once. Then he opened his mouth and bit down, slow and deliberate, letting the pressure build until Kit's breath caught, until the edge of pain sharpened into something else entirely.

He held for a count of three, then released, soothing the mark with his tongue. The imprint of his teeth was vivid, already darkening, and he traced it with a feather-light thumb.

"One," he murmured, and moved to the right wrist.

This time he bit down faster, harder, drawing a sharper gasp. He held until Kit's fingers curled reflexively against his palm, then let go, pressing a kiss to the center of the bruise.

"Two."

He lowered Kit's wrists back to their chest, arranging them gently, almost ceremonially. The marks stood out against their skin — twin claims, impossible to hide.

"You're gonna see those every time you type," Bear said, voice hushed with something close to awe. "Every time you reach for a coffee cup. Every time you touch yourself and think of me."

He leaned down, forehead pressing to Kit's, breath mingling.

"Thursday," he repeated. "And every day till then, you're gonna feel me. Know I put them there. Know you asked for them."

His hand came up to cradle Kit's jaw, thumb brushing their cheekbone.

"Thank you," he said, so quiet it was almost lost. "For trusting me. For asking. For still wanting this after all this time."

He kissed them then, soft and deep, the sharp edges smoothed into something tender.

"Now let's get off this floor before my back gives out. I'm forty, not twenty."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear made a sound low in his throat — not quite a growl, not quite a groan, something caught between hunger and reverence. His forehead stayed pressed to Kit's, breath coming rough and uneven.

"No more score," he agreed, voice wrecked. "Just this. Just you."

He didn't stop.

His mouth found Kit's again, slower this time, deeper — the kind of kiss that wasn't leading anywhere because it was already the destination. His hands slid down Kit's sides, over ribs and hips, mapping the familiar landscape with the same desperate wonder he'd had the first time he'd been allowed to touch.

"I'm not twenty anymore either," Kit had said once, years ago, and Bear had laughed and said *good, neither am I, we'll be old and sore together* — and here they were, on the hard floor, forty and thirty-something and still unable to keep their hands off each other.

Bear shifted his weight, one arm sliding under Kit's lower back, lifting them just enough to press closer. The angle was awkward, the floor unforgiving, and he didn't care. He'd take bruises on his knees tomorrow. He'd take a stiff back and aching shoulders. Worth it. Kit was worth it.

"Don't stop," Kit had said, and Bear wouldn't. Couldn't.

He pulled back just long enough to drag in a breath, looking down at Kit sprawled beneath him — marked up, flushed, eyes dark and bright all at once. The bite on their shoulder was already purpling. The ones on their wrists stood out stark against their skin. Bear felt something fierce and tender lodge itself behind his sternum.

"Beautiful," he said, the word escaping before he could catch it. "You're so goddamn beautiful like this."

Then he stopped talking, because Kit had told him to, and because words weren't what they needed now.

He shifted lower, mouth trailing down Kit's chest, pausing to press a kiss to the hollow of their throat, to the center of their sternum, to the soft skin just below their ribs. His hands followed, broad and warm, gripping their hips with just enough pressure to anchor them both.

When he reached the waistband of their pants — already undone from earlier, shoved down but not off — he paused, looking up the length of their body.

"Still good?" he asked, because he always asked, because eight years hadn't dulled the need to check in. "You still want—"

He didn't finish the question. Kit's hand found his hair again, fingers tightening, pulling, and that was answer enough.

Bear huffed a laugh against their stomach, hot and wanting. "Alright. Alright, I hear you."

He dealt with the rest of their clothes with the same practiced impatience as before, dragging fabric down and off, tossing it somewhere into the dark. His own followed, and then there was nothing between them but heat and want and the cool air of the bedroom they hadn't quite made it to.

Bear crawled back up Kit's body, settling between their thighs, skin to skin everywhere it mattered. He braced himself on his forearms, framing Kit's face with his hands, and just looked at them for a long moment.

"Eight years," he said, quiet and rough. "Eight years and I still can't get enough of you. Still can't believe I get to have this. Have you."

He kissed them before they could answer — or maybe so they wouldn't have to, because Bear knew Kit wasn't always good with words, and that was fine. They'd said enough. They'd said everything that mattered.

He reached down between them, positioning himself, and paused with his forehead pressed to Kit's.

"Ready?"

A breath. A nod. A whispered *yes*.

Bear pushed inside, slow and steady, the way he knew Kit liked it — at least at first. The sound Kit made went straight through him, and he had to stop for a second, jaw clenched, holding himself still.

"God," he breathed. "Every time. Every single time, you feel like—"

He didn't finish. Couldn't. Instead he started to move, finding a rhythm that was part muscle memory and part desperate need, built on years of learning exactly what Kit liked, exactly how to make them fall apart.

The floor was hard beneath his knees. His back was going to hate him tomorrow. Kit's nails were digging into his shoulders, leaving marks of their own, and Bear welcomed the sting.

"Look at me," he said, voice cracking. "Want to see you. Want to watch you—"

Kit's eyes met his, dark and hazy with want, and Bear felt something in his chest crack open.

"There you are," he murmured, the same words from earlier, but softer now. "There you are, sweetheart. Stay with me. Stay right here."

He shifted his angle, one hand sliding down to grip Kit's thigh, hitching their leg higher around his hip. The new position drew a sharp gasp from Kit, and Bear grinned, all teeth, even as his own breath stuttered.

"Yeah? That good? Right there?"

He didn't need an answer. He could read Kit's body like a language he'd spent eight years learning, every gasp and arch and shudder a word he knew by heart.

"Come on," he urged, voice dropping to something dark and encouraging. "Come on, sweetheart. I've got you. Let go. I've got you."

His rhythm stuttered, his own control fraying at the edges, but he held on — held on for Kit, because Kit came first, always, that was the rule they'd never needed to say out loud.

When Kit finally broke apart beneath him, Bear watched every second of it, cataloguing the way their back arched, the way their mouth fell open, the way their hands clutched at him like he was the only solid thing in the world.

"That's it," he breathed, praise and prayer all at once. "That's it, sweetheart. Beautiful. So goddamn beautiful."

He let himself follow then, let the tension that had been coiling at the base of his spine finally snap. He buried his face in Kit's neck and groaned, long and low, as his own release crashed through him.

For a long moment, neither of them moved. Bear's weight pressed Kit into the floor, and he knew he was heavy, knew he should shift, but his arms weren't cooperating and Kit wasn't complaining.

Finally, with a Herculean effort, he rolled to the side, pulling Kit with him so they were sprawled together on the hard floor, tangled and sweat-slicked and still breathing hard.

"Floor," Bear said after a long silence, his voice a wrecked rasp. "We're still on the floor."

He turned his head to look at Kit, and a slow, satisfied grin spread across his face.

"Worth it."

He reached over, clumsy and uncoordinated, and brushed a strand of hair from Kit's face. His thumb lingered on their cheekbone, tracing the flush there.

"You okay? Need water? A blanket? My back is going to be furious in about twenty minutes, but right now I don't care."

He pressed a kiss to Kit's forehead, soft and lingering.

"Thursday," he murmured against their skin. "You're gonna feel me till Thursday. And I'm gonna see those marks on your wrists every time you reach for me, and I'm gonna remember this. Remember you, spread out on the floor, asking me for more."

His arm tightened around their waist, pulling them closer.

"I love you," he said, quiet and sure. "Don't have to say it back. Just wanted you to know."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I turn my head to kiss his palm, my throat too tight to speak. After a moment I find the words, rough but clear. "I love you too. Now help me up before we both need a chiropractor."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt those three words settle into his chest, warm and solid as a heartbeat. He didn't need them—hadn't needed them for years—but hearing them still hit different. Still mattered.

"Chiropractor," he repeated, huffing a tired laugh against Kit's hair. "Speak for yourself. I'm in excellent shape."

He wasn't. His back was already lodging formal complaints, and his knees were going to file a grievance any minute now. But he'd die before admitting it.

With a grunt that betrayed every one of his forty years, Bear pushed himself upright, then reached down to haul Kit up after him. He didn't let go once they were standing—kept one arm wrapped around their waist, steadying them both.

"Alright," he said, pressing a kiss to the top of Kit's head. "Shower. Water. Bed. In that order."

He steered them toward the bathroom, grabbing a discarded shirt off the floor on the way and draping it around Kit's shoulders without comment. The marks on their wrists caught the low light from the hallway, and Bear's thumb brushed over one of them, gentle.

"Thursday," he murmured, half to himself. Then, louder: "Come on. I'll wash your back. You can yell at me about the floor tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I lean into him, letting him take most of my weight. "You're washing my hair, too. And you owe me new buttons."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear snorted, steering them both toward the bathroom with one arm still firm around Kit's waist.

"Your hair. New buttons." He shook his head, but there was nothing but fondness in it. "You're expensive, you know that? High maintenance."

He flicked on the bathroom light, squinting against the sudden brightness, and guided Kit to sit on the closed toilet lid while he leaned over to start the shower. The water pipes groaned in protest — old house, old plumbing — and then the spray kicked on, steam already starting to curl in the cool air.

"Buttons I can do," he said, turning back to Kit. He crouched in front of them, hands resting on their knees, looking up at their face with an expression that was half exhaustion, half devotion. "Got a whole sewing kit somewhere. You can pick the thread color. Make it a whole thing."

He reached up, fingers gentle as they brushed the edge of the bite mark on Kit's shoulder — the deep one, the one that would last.

"Hair, too. I'll wash it. Condition it. Whatever you want." His voice dropped, losing the teasing edge. "You let me mark you up. You let me chase you through the house and bite you hard enough to bruise and pin you to the floor. Least I can do is wash your damn hair."

He stood, joints popping, and held out his hand to help Kit up.

"Come on. Water's hot. I'll be careful around the bites. Promise."

A beat, and then his grin crept back, tired but sharp.

"Still can't believe you made me chase you in my own house. Eight years. You're a menace."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I take his hand, letting him pull me up. "Your house? Pretty sure my name's on the deed too." I step under the hot water, letting it wash over the new marks with a hiss. "And I'm your menace."

dialogue.content:
Bear did not.

He gave it half a heartbeat—just enough mercy to make it sporting—and then he hit the doorway hard, one hand catching the frame as he pivoted through after the sound of movement.

“Generous is over,” Bear said, low and pleased.

He moved like he meant it: heavy, fast, unfairly quiet for his size. He did not grab wildly. Bear hunted properly. Cut the angle. Took the shortest line. Let the house do half the work for him.

His shoulder brushed the wall as he rounded the corner, mouth already curved in that sharp, delighted grin he got when Kit made him chase. Eight years had not dulled it. If anything, it had made him worse—more patient, more certain, more willing to enjoy the exact second before he closed the distance.

“There you are,” he said, though his voice made it clear he had known all along.

Bear surged forward, one hand shooting out—not to be gentle, not quite, but controlled with the ease of long practice. His fingers caught fabric, tugged, released, then caught again better. He used his weight next, a solid press and turn meant to pin without crushing, to crowd without harming.

His breath came warm and amused near Kit’s ear.

“Should’ve taken the generosity while it was offered.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I laugh, breathless, and twist against his grip. "Where's the fun in that?" I manage, arching my back to try and slip free.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear laughed too, deep in his chest, pleased enough that it sounded almost like a growl.

“That,” he said, tightening his hold just enough to answer the attempted escape, “is exactly the problem with you.”

He shifted with the twist instead of fighting it straight on, using momentum the way he always did when the game turned close and scrappy. One forearm braced across the doorway, boxing the space in. His other hand slid from fabric to hip with practiced certainty, not yanking, not careless—just there, heavy and claiming, making it clear he had no intention of giving back the inches he’d won.

Bear lowered his head, nose dragging slow along the line of shoulder and neck, breathing in like he was committing the moment to memory.

“Always wanting the fun.”

His teeth closed briefly, firmly, at the edge of muscle—not enough to break skin, enough to promise a mark if he decided one was earned. Then he let go only to press his mouth there after, warm and smug, like the bite had been punctuation.

“You run,” Bear murmured, voice rough with amusement, “then act surprised when I catch you.”

He crowded closer, using his size the way he knew was unfair and therefore excellent. His knee nudged into the space available, his weight pinning through hips and chest without crushing, every bit of him controlled, deliberate, familiar.

Then he paused.

Not releasing. Not softening.

Just holding that charged stillness, breath close, grin against skin.

“Score’s mine,” Bear said. “Unless you think you can steal it back.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear knew that kind of fight.

He knew the difference between escape and invitation, between a real bid for distance and the kind of resistance that existed mostly to make his hands tighten.

So he did.

“Lazy,” Bear accused, pleased and rough-edged, though there was nothing disappointed in him at all.

He shifted his grip higher, one broad hand spreading between shoulder blades, the other anchoring at the waist. Not trapping for necessity now. Trapping because he liked the shape of it. Because he liked winning when the win was warm and laughing and already half-given.

Bear pressed in until the hallway had no room left for mercy.

“Thought you told me not to be generous.”

His mouth found the side of the neck again, slower this time. Less warning. More decision. He took his time choosing the spot, teeth grazing once, twice, before he bit down with controlled pressure—enough to leave memory. Enough to count.

There.

Bear exhaled through his nose, satisfied, and soothed the mark with his mouth after, not gentle exactly, but affectionate in the way he had always been affectionate: possessive, physical, certain.

“One,” he said against skin.

His hand flexed at the waist, thumb pressing in like he was marking another point without teeth.

“Doorway was charity. Hallway was mine.”

Bear drew back only far enough to look, eyes dark and bright with the old game. The grin was still there, but it had gone quieter. More dangerous. More fond.

Then he leaned in again, voice low.

“You want another chance, you’d better make it good.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I push back against him, just enough to feel the resistance. "You're keeping score now?" I ask, turning my head to try and catch his eye. "That's new."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s grin widened, slow and wicked.

“New?” he said, like the accusation offended him deeply. “Kit, he’d been keeping score since the first time you thought a locked bathroom door counted as a strategy.”

He held firm against the push, letting the resistance travel through him without giving much ground. Just enough movement to prove he had felt it. Not enough to make it useful.

“Bites. Escapes. Ambushes. Cheap shots.” His hand tightened at the waist for emphasis. “That time with the ice cube, which still counted as cheating.”

Bear dipped his head, mouth close but not touching yet, letting the warmth of his breath do some of the work.

“He remembered all of it.”

Then he shifted, pinning with his body rather than his hands for one heavy, deliberate second while one palm slid up to brace beside the wall. The other stayed planted, broad and possessive, keeping the score exactly where he had decided it belonged.

“But if you want the official tally,” Bear murmured, “right now it’s one mark to me, zero clean getaways to you, and one very bad attempt at pretending you weren’t waiting to be caught.”

His teeth grazed just below the first mark, not biting yet. Teasing. Threatening.

“Could make it two.” 

Bear paused there, all patient pressure and amusement, eyes lifted enough to catch what he could of the look being aimed back at him.

“Or,” he said, voice dropping rougher, “you could try to earn one of yours.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear hit the floor with the same controlled violence he did everything else—hard enough to make it count, careful enough that nothing that mattered took the impact wrong.

One hand went behind Kit’s head before the last inch, palm broad and sure. The other braced, caught, shoved fabric out of his way with impatient efficiency.

“Floor’s fine,” Bear said, rough and amused, like that had been his decision all along.

It was not graceful. Bear had never cared much for graceful when fast was better and hungry was honest. Cloth bunched. A seam complained. His breath dragged in sharp through his nose, and then his mouth was back where he had already claimed one point, teeth finding the edge of the mark like he was checking his work.

“Two,” he murmured, and bit lower.

Not reckless. Never that.

But not gentle, either.

Bear had learned Kit’s edges by heart over eight years: where pressure turned into challenge, where challenge turned into heat, where to hold, where to leave room, where to stop everything dead and ask.

So he did, voice low against skin.

“Color.”

He held there, locked and waiting, all that weight and hunger banked behind restraint. His fingers flexed once against the floor. His jaw worked like patience was costing him something.

Then, only when he had what he needed, Bear moved again.

The scorekeeping went to hell after that.

Or maybe it just changed language.

No more neat tally of doorways and hallways. No clean points. Just Bear’s mouth, his hands, the press of him, the scrape of teeth followed by heat and breath and that pleased, possessive sound in his chest every time he found another place worth remembering.

“Still think it’s new?” he asked, voice wrecked with laughter and wanting.

He caught fabric between his fingers and dealt with it badly, exactly as promised. Too fast. Too impatient. Like the clothes had personally offended him by existing between him and what he wanted.

Bear lowered himself close again, pinning with care and intent, his grin gone darker now, quieter at the edges.

“Because he was absolutely keeping score.”

His mouth hovered near Kit’s ear.

“And he was winning.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I grin up at him, breathless. "Winning's a strong word," I say, getting a hand free to shove at his shoulder. "I recall a few victories of my own."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear let the shove move him exactly one inch.

Maybe two, out of respect for history.

Then he came right back down with a grin that was all teeth.

“A few,” he allowed, as if granting a legal technicality. “Some disputed. Some under review. One or two legitimate.”

He caught that freed hand and pinned it—not hard, not cruel, just with that infuriating certainty of his, thumb settling over the pulse like he was checking the tempo of the fight. His eyes stayed bright, hungry and fond.

“But tonight?”

Bear lowered his head, dragging his mouth along the line of jaw, not quite a kiss, not quite a bite. A threat with warmth in it.

“Tonight you got caught in the hall.”

His weight shifted again, controlled and deliberate, making the floor feel like part of the trap. The house had gone quiet around them, all the noise narrowed down to breath, fabric, the low sound Bear made when he was very pleased with himself.

“And then,” he continued, voice rougher, “you chose the floor.”

He paused there, mouth hovering, letting the words land before his teeth did.

“That’s not a victory.”

Bear bit—not where he had already marked, but close enough to make a constellation of the evidence. Firm. Careful. Mean in the way they both liked. Then he soothed it with his mouth, a low laugh pressed into skin.

“That’s surrender with attitude.”

His hand slid from the pinned wrist to lace fingers there instead, changing the hold without giving up the claim. His other hand braced beside him, arm corded, keeping most of his weight exactly where he wanted it and none of it where it would be too much.

He drew back enough to look down, breathing harder now, hair fallen forward, grin gone sharp and warm all at once.

“But if you want to argue the scoreboard,” Bear said, “he was listening.”

Then he leaned close again, voice dropping into that dangerous, pleased register.

“Make your case.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear did.

No hesitation that time. No teasing pass of teeth first, no pretending he had to think about it. He set his mouth to the same shoulder, shifted half an inch to keep from breaking the first mark open, and bit down again with slow, deliberate pressure.

Harder.

Not careless. Not out of control.

Hard enough to make it count.

A rough sound tore out of him, low and pleased, and his hand spread wide over Kit’s ribs like he could hold the whole moment still under his palm. He kept the bite until it had weight, until it had shape, until he knew it would be there later under bathroom light and wandering fingers.

Then he released by degrees.

Teeth first. Then mouth. Then breath.

“Three,” Bear said, wrecked and smug against damp skin.

He pressed a kiss there after, if it could be called a kiss with that much teeth still in the memory of it. His jaw dragged along the shoulder, beard scraping, mouth finding the edge of the new mark like he was admiring the work.

“That one’s mine.”

His hand flexed once, possessive and warm. The floor was unforgiving beneath them, clothes twisted wrong, the hallway too narrow and too familiar and absolutely perfect. Bear looked down at what he had made and smiled like an animal with blood on its teeth, even though there was none.

Just heat.

Just evidence.

Just eight years of knowing exactly how far was far enough.

He shifted his weight, pinning again with a care that did not look like care unless someone knew him very well. His forearm braced near Kit’s head. His mouth hovered over the shoulder, over the first mark, the second, the fresh dark promise of the third.

“Still want to argue victories?” he asked, voice gone rough and low.

Bear’s grin brushed skin.

“Because he could keep doing this all night.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I arch up against him, fingers digging into his back. "All night's a long time," I say, breath catching. "You sure you can keep count that long?"

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear laughed, rough and breathless, and the sound came out more dangerous than amused.

“Kit,” Bear said, dragging the name low against marked skin, “he had been counting you for eight years.”

He shifted under the dig of fingers into his back like it fed him, like every sharp little proof of being wanted only made him heavier, warmer, worse. His mouth traced the shoulder again, not biting yet. Just letting the threat of it sit there.

“Marks,” he murmured. “Sounds. Times you almost got away.”

His hand slid up to brace firm at the side of the neck, thumb careful along the pulse, not pressing—just feeling. Keeping measure.

“Times you started trouble and then looked surprised when trouble answered.”

Bear lifted his head enough to look down, grin dark and fond and entirely too sure of himself.

“He could count that long.”

Then he lowered again, slower this time, patience returning like a weapon. His teeth grazed the edge of the newest mark, and he paused there, making the choice obvious before he made it real.

“But if numbers got difficult,” Bear said, voice gone deep and wrecked at the edges, “he could always switch to landmarks.”

He bit again.

Not in the same place. Just beside it. Another deliberate claim in the map he was making by memory and mouth, held long enough to matter, released slow enough to be cruel.

Bear exhaled hard after, forehead dropping briefly against skin.

“There,” he said. “Four.”

His hand flexed, then softened. Controlled. Listening.

“Still with him?”

The question came quieter than the rest, buried under the heat but solid as bone. Bear did not move past it. Did not take the next inch just because he wanted it.

He waited, breathing hard, mouth hovering over the mark he had just made, every bit of him held on a leash he had chosen himself.

Then his grin returned, close and sharp.

“Because if you were,” Bear murmured, “he was nowhere near done counting.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went very still.

Not uncertain.

Listening.

Then his expression changed, the grin sharpening into something older and darker and utterly fond.

“Thursday,” Bear repeated, low.

He looked at the offered wrists like they were a dare, a gift, and a terrible idea he fully intended to honor.

Then he took them.

One broad hand closed around both, firm and practiced, thumb laid where he could feel pulse and heat and any shift that mattered. He drew them up and pinned them to the floor above Kit’s head, not crushing, not careless. Just certain. The kind of hold that said he had accepted the terms.

His other hand braced beside them, caging the space in.

“You wanted marks,” Bear said. “He heard you.”

He lowered slowly, because speed had its uses and so did making the next thing unavoidable. His mouth found the shoulder again, but not the places already darkening under his work. Bear chose fresh skin, safe skin, the kind that would bruise beautifully without turning into damage.

His teeth settled.

Paused.

Then bit.

Deep, controlled pressure. No breaking skin. No losing himself to it. Just a hard, deliberate claim held long enough to promise tomorrow, and the next day, and maybe Thursday if Kit kept pressing at it in the mirror like Bear knew would happen.

He released with a rough exhale.

“Five.”

His mouth soothed the bite after, but only barely. Affectionate. Possessive. Mean enough to make the kindness worse.

Bear shifted his grip on the wrists, tightening for one second when he moved lower, making sure the hold stayed clean. His knee braced. His weight settled. The hallway floor gave nothing back, and Bear used that too.

“You’re going to look,” he murmured against skin. “Turn this way and that. Pretend you’re checking damage.”

His teeth grazed another place.

“But you’ll be counting.”

Another bite. Slower. Harder at the end.

Bear’s eyes half-closed with the satisfaction of it, jaw working, breath hot as he held the pressure and then let go by degrees.

“Six.”

He pressed his forehead briefly to the marked shoulder, breathing rough through his nose. His hand at the wrists softened for a beat, thumb stroking once over the pulse before locking down again.

“Color stayed yours,” he said, voice quiet beneath the growl. “Always.”

Then his mouth moved to the upper arm, where the mark would be harder to hide from a mirror and easier to find by accident. His grin brushed skin.

“But the rest?”

Bear bit again.

Firm. Deliberate. Unapologetic.

He held this one longer, because Thursday had been asked for and Bear was a generous bastard only when it served him. When he released, he looked down at the shape of it like a craftsman admiring a clean cut.

“Seven.”

His voice had gone rough enough to scrape.

“There,” Bear said. “That one’ll complain when you move.”

He shifted higher again, still pinning the wrists, still keeping most of his weight where it belonged. His mouth hovered over the constellation he had made, choosing, refusing to rush now. The chase was over. The floor was won. The score had become something that would bloom later in purples and reds and tender heat.

Bear smiled against Kit’s skin.

“And when Thursday comes,” he murmured, “he wanted you remembering exactly who put them there.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I laugh, breathless. "You act like I'd forget." I twist under him, testing his grip. "You think I'm letting anyone else do this?"

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s grip tightened the instant the twist came, not enough to punish—enough to answer.

His eyes went dark and pleased.

“No,” he said, voice low, almost too calm. “He didn’t.”

He shifted his weight with the movement, followed it, stole the leverage out of it the way he always had. One knee braced. One hand pinned both wrists higher. His other palm spread over the marked shoulder, thumb skimming the edge of one fresh bite with deliberate cruelty.

“He knew exactly whose teeth you wanted.”

Bear lowered his head, slow enough to make it a choice and close enough to make it feel inevitable.

“And he knew exactly who you’d come back to when they still hurt.”

His mouth found the newest mark and pressed there, warm and possessive. Not a kiss. Not quite. More like a seal set over his own work.

Then his teeth grazed just beneath it.

“You said Thursday,” Bear murmured. “That means he had standards to meet.”

He bit again.

Not rushed. Not sloppy. A hard, steady pressure that built with intent, held until his shoulders went tense and his breath left him in a rough exhale through his nose. His hand stayed locked around the wrists, thumb still at the pulse, listening through the whole of it.

Then he released slowly.

“Eight.”

Bear drew back just enough to look at the collection of marks, satisfaction cutting sharp across his face. His grin came back mean and fond.

“That one was for suggesting he might have competition.”

His hand slid from shoulder to jaw, turning nothing, forcing nothing—just settling there, heavy and warm, knuckles brushing skin.

“He did not.”

The words came flat. Certain. No performance in them now.

Bear had played at jealousy before. Played at possession. Played at all the old teeth-bared things they both liked to drag into the light and wrestle with.

This was not quite play.

This was eight years of knowing the shape of what was his because it had been offered again and again, chosen again and again, never assumed and never taken for granted.

His voice dropped.

“No one else gets this unless you want them to. And if you don’t?”

His thumb stroked once, slow.

“Then no one else even gets close.”

Bear bent again, mouth brushing the line between throat and shoulder, right over the places that would bloom later.

“And he liked that,” he admitted, rough. “Too much.”

His grip on the wrists softened for half a breath, just enough to ask without words, then firmed again when he continued. He pinned them cleanly, carefully, like the hold itself mattered as much as the bites.

“Still with him?” Bear asked, quieter.

The hunger did not leave him. It just waited properly.

His mouth hovered over unmarked skin.

“Because he had at least one more in him before he let you up.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear did not stop.

He only went still long enough for the words to land in him properly.

Then his mouth curved against skin.

“No,” Bear said, voice rough and certain. “He wasn’t stopping.”

His hand stayed locked around the wrists above Kit’s head, grip clean and steady, thumb resting over the pulse like it was the only clock in the house. His other hand braced beside the shoulder he had already marked, fingers spread wide, holding the floor and the moment both.

“Color if it changes,” he said, low. “Otherwise he was going to give you Thursday.”

Then he lowered his mouth again.

Not to the same place. Bear had discipline even when he looked like he had none. He chose new ground: the upper arm first, where the skin would take the bite deep and remember it when sleeves shifted. His teeth set carefully, pressure building slow, deliberate, mean enough to count. He held it until his own breath roughened, until his jaw ached faintly with restraint, until he knew the mark would bloom.

Then he released.

His mouth stayed there after, warm over the bite, beard scraping as he dragged along the edge of it.

“That one,” Bear murmured, “was because you asked so nicely.”

He moved higher again, over the shoulder, past the constellation already forming there. His hand left the floor just long enough to cup the back of Kit’s neck, steadying, possessive, checking. He could feel heat, pulse, breath. He listened with his whole body.

Satisfied, Bear bit again.

Shorter this time. Sharper. A clean, bright mark near the shoulder’s slope, placed where a mirror would catch it immediately.

He exhaled hard when he let go.

“And that one was because you told him not to stop.”

Bear shifted his weight with care, keeping the pin exactly where he wanted it. Heavy enough to hold. Light enough to trust. His grip on the wrists loosened for one heartbeat, thumb stroking once across the inside, then closed again.

He was breathing harder now. Hair fallen forward. Mouth reddened from use. Eyes dark with the kind of hunger that had learned manners and kept them only because Kit mattered more than appetite.

Bear lowered himself until his chest nearly touched, until his voice was a rough scrape near the ear.

“You were going to feel these when you reached for something,” he said. “When you turned over in bed. When the shower hit them.”

His teeth grazed the side of the neck, not biting yet.

“When you forgot for half a second.”

Then he bit.

Careful there. Controlled. Enough to leave tenderness, not enough to be stupid. Bear knew the difference, knew the map, knew what was safe to mark and what was only for threat. His hand tightened on the pinned wrists as the bite held, not from losing control but from keeping it.

When he released, he pressed his mouth over the spot and stayed there, breathing.

“There,” he said, quieter. “That one was for Thursday morning.”

Bear lifted his head then, looking over what he had done.

The hallway light caught skin in uneven patches. Some marks were already rising red. Some would darken later. Some would be found by accident and cursed fondly under breath. Bear looked at them with open satisfaction, but not carelessness.

Never carelessness.

His hand left the wrists at last, but only to slide down slowly, checking, grounding, palm warm over the outside of the arm, the shoulder, the ribs. He did not move away. He did not give back the space all at once.

“Stay,” Bear murmured, though the word was more vow than command.

He bent again and put one last bite at the top of the shoulder.

Not the hardest.

The slowest.

Bear set his teeth and held, steady and deep, making it last until his own eyes shut and a rough sound broke low in his chest. He released by fractions, then soothed it with his mouth, again and again, like he was sealing the ache in.

When he finally lifted his head, his voice had gone quiet.

“That one was his.”

Bear stayed over Kit for another few breaths, still caging the space, still warm and solid and close. Then he eased the pressure from the pinned wrists completely, his hand sliding down to hold rather than restrain.

He looked at the marks again, then back down, expression softened around the edges even if his mouth still looked wicked.

“He was done biting for now,” Bear said, low. “Not because he ran out.”

His thumb brushed carefully near one fresh mark.

“Because Thursday needed a fighting chance.”

Then Bear lowered his forehead to Kit’s shoulder, between the bites, and breathed there. The hunting had gone out of his body by degrees, leaving only heat, weight, and the old familiar care beneath all the teeth.

After a moment, he turned his head and pressed his mouth to unmarked skin.

“Still with him,” Bear said—not quite a question this time, but still listening for the answer in every way that mattered.

His hand found the wrist again, gentle now, thumb over the pulse.

“Good.”

Bear stayed there on the hallway floor, clothes twisted, breath uneven, one hand holding and the other tracing careful paths around the damage he had made. Not over the worst of it yet. Around. Respectful of the ache.

Then his mouth curved, small and smug against skin.

“You were going to be insufferable tomorrow,” he murmured. “Standing in front of the mirror like you didn’t ask for every single one.”

He pressed one more warm kiss beside the darkest bite.

“And he was going to be worse.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, the ache settling in deep. "I'll be insufferable," I agree, shifting carefully under him. "And you'll be smug as hell about it." I turn my head to catch his eye. "Help me up. Floor's starting to complain."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear huffed a laugh, low and satisfied.

“Floor had a good run,” he said. “Better than yours.”

But his hands had already changed.

No more pinning. No more taking. Bear shifted back first, slow and careful, peeling his weight away in stages so nothing pulled sharp where it had been bitten. One palm slid under a shoulder blade, the other braced at the hip, steadying before lifting. He moved like a man handling something precious and pretending he was not.

Smug, yes.

Gentle, absolutely.

“Up you come,” Bear murmured.

He got a knee under himself, then brought Kit with him by degrees, supporting more than necessary because he liked having the excuse. The hallway was narrow, clothes were still a wreck, and Bear looked profoundly pleased with every bad decision that had led them there.

Once upright enough, he kept one arm wrapped firm around Kit’s back and the other hand cupped carefully behind the neck, avoiding the worst of the marks. His thumb moved once, slow, grounding.

“There,” he said, softer. “Easy.”

Bear looked over the shoulder, the upper arm, the place near the neck where the marks were already starting to show their opinions. His mouth curved despite himself.

“Smug as hell might be underselling it.”

He leaned in and pressed a careful kiss to unmarked skin, deliberately away from the bites. Then another, lower. Affectionate now, openly so, though there was still teeth in the shape of his smile.

“Bathroom,” Bear decided. “Water. Mirror, if you’re already committed to being a menace. Then bed before the floor files a complaint with management.”

He shifted again, taking more of the weight without making a production of it, one broad hand spread warm at Kit’s lower back.

“And tomorrow,” Bear said, voice going rough with amusement, “when you turn sideways in the mirror and try to act normal about it, he was going to stand behind you looking exactly as pleased as he deserved.”

His thumb brushed a slow path along the spine.

“Thursday too, if he did his job right.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I lean into him, letting him take the weight. "Bathroom," I agree, and then I grin, tired and satisfied. "But you're coming with. I want a running commentary on your handiwork."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s smile went slow and helplessly pleased.

“Obviously,” he said. “He wasn’t about to let art go uncritiqued.”

He kept an arm around Kit and started them toward the bathroom at an easy pace, one careful step at a time. The smugness stayed all over his face, but his body had gone attentive in that quiet, practical way—watching balance, watching breath, watching the little catches that said where the floor had been too hard and where his teeth had done exactly what they had been asked to do.

“Careful,” Bear murmured at the threshold, hand firm at the waist. “Doorways were dangerous tonight.”

He guided without rushing, broad palm warm at the lower back, the other hand reaching ahead to flick on the bathroom light. The sudden brightness made him blink once, then look immediately—shamelessly—at the marks coming up along shoulder, upper arm, neck.

Bear went still for half a second.

Then his grin returned, quieter and much worse.

“Oh,” he said, low. “Those are going to be beautiful.”

He eased closer behind Kit, not crowding now, just present. Solid. One hand settled at the hip; the other hovered near the worst of the bites before deliberately touching only clean skin around them.

“That one,” Bear said, nodding toward the shoulder with open satisfaction, “was when you told him to do it again. Excellent decision. Ten out of ten. No notes.”

His thumb traced a careful arc beside another mark.

“That one was for Thursday. Might make Wednesday jealous.”

Bear leaned down and pressed his mouth to the back of Kit’s head, a brief, warm pause between commentary.

“And that one,” he added, voice dropping into a pleased rumble, “was for implying he needed help remembering whose teeth you wanted. Personally, he thought the response was restrained.”

He reached for a washcloth next, running water until it warmed, then wringing it out with one hand while keeping the other lightly anchored at Kit’s side. The cloth touched first to unmarked skin, then around the edges of the bites, careful and slow.

“Color stayed good,” Bear said, softer now. “Breath came back good. No broken skin.”

His eyes lifted to the mirror again, meeting what he could through the reflection.

“He was proud of the work,” Bear said. “But he was prouder of the asking.”

Then, because he could not help himself, because smug as hell had indeed been underselling it, Bear tilted his head and surveyed the blooming evidence like a man appraising a trophy wall.

“Composition’s strong. Placement’s excellent. Variety could be called inspired.” His mouth twitched. “The artist was clearly motivated.”

He set the cloth aside and reached for water next, filling a glass before offering it over without fuss.

“Drink,” he said, low and fond. “Then he would continue the tour.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I take the water, my eyes not leaving the mirror. "Tour, huh?" I take a sip, wincing slightly as I turn. "Gonna charge admission?"
