Sable let the words settle between them, weightless and warm. She didn't answer right away—didn't need to. Her hand stayed where it was, a steady anchor between Ines's shoulder blades, rising and falling with each slow breath.

After a while, she shifted just enough to press her lips to Ines's temple, lingering there a beat longer than necessary.

"Good," she murmured, the word a quiet echo of Ines's own. "That's good."

She drew back only far enough to study the lines of Ines's face in the low light—the slack jaw, the half-closed eyes, the way her fingers had finally stilled against the cuffs. The tension had bled out of her shoulders somewhere in the last few minutes, leaving something softer in its wake.

Sable reached over, slow and deliberate, and pulled the folded blanket from the chair. She didn't drape it yet—just laid it across her own lap, letting Ines see it, letting the promise of it hang in the air.

"Whenever you're ready," she said. "We'll go as slow as you need."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable felt the shift before she fully understood it—the way Ines's breath caught differently, the subtle arch of her spine that wasn't about the lingering heat anymore but something else entirely. Want. Not for more of the flogger. For *her*.

She didn't stop to analyze it. Some things you didn't think your way through.

Her mouth found the curve of Ines's shoulder first, then the nape of her neck, tracing the same path her hand had taken earlier but slower now, wetter, open-mouthed and deliberate. She tasted salt and the faint metallic tang of adrenaline fading. Her free hand slid from Ines's back around to her ribs, then lower, mapping the terrain she already knew by heart because knowing it was different from *revisiting* it, and she wanted to revisit every inch.

"You're still here," Sable breathed against her skin, not a question. A recognition. "Still with me."

She worked her way down Ines's spine, lips and tongue and the occasional graze of teeth—never enough to hurt, just enough to remind—until she reached the small of her back, where the last stroke of the flogger had landed. She pressed her mouth there, gentler than the leather had been, and stayed for a long moment, breathing Ines in.

Then her hands were at Ines's hips, turning her, repositioning her, and the restraints creaked softly with the movement but held. Sable looked up the length of Ines's body—flushed, trembling slightly, eyes gone dark and unfocused—and felt something catch low in her own chest. Reverence, maybe. Hunger, definitely.

She didn't speak. Words could come later. Right now there was only the language of touch, of mouth and hands and the deliberate, devastating patience she brought to everything that mattered.

She took her time. She always did.

When she finally stilled, forehead resting against Ines's hip, both of them breathing hard, the room had gone quiet again in that full, humming way. Sable pressed one last kiss to the jut of Ines's hipbone, then reached up with steady hands to work the restraints free—first one wrist, then the other, rubbing slow circles into the skin where the cuffs had been.

"Now," she murmured, pulling the blanket up at last and wrapping it around Ines's shoulders, drawing her in close. "Now we wind down. Water first, then I'm running you a bath. No arguments."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I lean heavily into her, my fingers curling weakly into her shirt. "No arguments," I agree, my voice hoarse. "But stay with me in the bath."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable pressed another kiss to Ines's temple, this one slower, lingering—a seal on the promise.

"Always," she said, the word quiet but absolute. "I'm not going anywhere."

She shifted her grip, one arm firm around Ines's back, the other tucked beneath her knees, and lifted her from the bench with the careful economy of someone who'd done this before. Ines wasn't heavy, but she was *loose*, all her weight surrendered, and Sable cradled her closer as she carried her through the bedroom toward the bathroom.

The water first. That was non-negotiable. She eased Ines onto the closed lid of the toilet, keeping one hand on her shoulder while she reached for the glass she'd left on the counter earlier—already filled, already waiting, because Sable didn't leave things to chance. She pressed it into Ines's hands and guided it to her lips.

"Slow sips," she murmured. "All of it."

While Ines drank, Sable turned to the tub and started the water running—hot but not scalding, the way Ines liked it after a scene, when her skin was still singing and anything too sharp might tip her back into overstimulation. She added a handful of Epsom salts from the jar under the sink, watching them dissolve in the rising steam. The scent of eucalyptus and lavender began to fill the small room.

When the glass was empty, Sable took it, set it aside, and helped Ines to her feet. She undressed her with the same unhurried attention she'd given everything else tonight—no rush, no roughness, just the steady slide of fabric and the brush of her knuckles against warming skin. Then she stripped off her own clothes, stepped into the tub first, and held out her hand.

"Come here," she said, and when Ines settled in front of her, back to chest, Sable wrapped both arms around her and pulled her close. The water rose around them, hot and silken, and Sable let her chin rest on Ines's shoulder, her lips near her ear.

"I've got you," she said. "Take as long as you need."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's laugh was a low, dark thing, muffled against the inside of Ines's thigh.

"Swear at me all you like," she murmured, her breath hot and deliberate against slick skin. "You know that just makes me want to take my time."

She didn't move away. Didn't relent. Instead, she let her mouth hover—close enough that Ines could feel the promise of it, the almost-there pressure, the maddening absence of *enough*. One of her hands pressed flat against Ines's stomach, holding her steady, feeling every tremor, every aborted buck of her hips.

"Look at you," Sable breathed, and the words were reverent, even through the smirk. "Falling apart so beautifully for me."

She waited. Counted the seconds in the frantic rhythm of Ines's pulse against her palm. Watched the way Ines's free hand fisted in the sheets, the way her teeth sank into her own arm, the way her whole body coiled tighter and tighter toward a release Sable kept snatching away at the last possible instant.

Then, finally—*finally*—she stopped teasing.

She gave Ines what she'd been begging for without words, mouth and tongue and the steady, relentless pressure of her hand, pushing her up and over the edge with the same deliberate precision she'd brought to every stroke of the flogger, every kiss, every whispered word since the scene began.

And when Ines shattered, Sable stayed with her through all of it—through the arching back and the broken cry and the trembling aftermath—until the last wave had passed and Ines lay gasping beneath her.

Only then did Sable crawl up the length of her body, gathering her close, pulling the discarded blanket over both of them. She pressed her lips to Ines's forehead, her cheek, the corner of her mouth.

"Water," she said, but it was softer now, almost teasing. "And then that bath I promised you. You've earned it."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I swat weakly at her shoulder, still catching my breath. "Evil," I mumble, but I'm curling into her, face pressed against her neck. "I hate you. Water, then bath. *With* you."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable laughed, a quiet huff of breath against Ines's hair, and tightened her arms around her.

"Evil," she agreed, utterly unrepentant. "And yet here you are."

She didn't make Ines move right away. She let her curl in, let her press her face to the curve of Sable's throat, let her breathing slow from ragged to something steadier. One hand traced idle patterns on Ines's back, following the lingering heat from the flogger, the places where the skin was still warm and tender.

After a long moment, she reached for the glass of water on the nightstand—she'd refilled it at some point, when had she refilled it?—and pressed it gently into Ines's hand.

"Sit up just enough to drink," she coaxed, her voice low and patient. "Then we'll get in the bath and you can fall asleep on me in the water if you want. I'll keep your head above the surface."

A pause. A softer smile, hidden in Ines's hair.

"I know you don't hate me. Drink your water, love."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable went still for a heartbeat. Two. Her hand paused mid-stroke on Ines's back, and when she spoke, her voice had shifted—lower, quieter, stripped of the gentle teasing from a moment before.

"Finish it hard," she repeated, not a question. A confirmation.

She drew back just enough to meet Ines's eyes. Searched them. Found what she was looking for—clarity beneath the haze, want beneath the exhaustion. This wasn't a request made from the floaty, half-gone place. This was deliberate. *Finish it the way we started. Don't pull your punches now.*

Sable nodded once. Slow. Certain.

"All right."

She didn't give Ines time to brace. That was the point. She shifted her weight, one hand pressing Ines's shoulder down against the mattress, the other finding her hip and gripping hard enough to leave the ghost of fingerprints. Her mouth found Ines's throat—not kissing now, but biting, just shy of too much, the kind of pressure that sent a bright shock down the spine.

"You want it hard," Sable murmured against her skin, and it wasn't a tease anymore. It was a promise. "You'll have it."

She didn't draw it out this time. No edging, no hovering, no slow, deliberate torture. This was something else—a driving, relentless rhythm, hands and mouth and the full weight of her body pressing Ines into the mattress, giving her no room to squirm away, no space to catch her breath. Every touch was intentional, every stroke calibrated to push Ines higher, faster, toward a precipice Sable had no intention of snatching her back from.

When Ines finally broke, Sable didn't stop. She pushed her through it—through the first wave and into the second, wringing every last shudder from her body until Ines went limp beneath her, utterly spent.

Only then did Sable ease back. Only then did she gather Ines up, cradling her against her chest, one hand cupping the back of her head.

"There," she breathed, lips against Ines's temple, voice rough now, the control finally cracking just a little. "There. All done. I've got you."

She reached for the water again, pressing it into Ines's trembling hands.

"Drink. Then bath. I'm not asking anymore."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I take the water with shaking hands, half of it spilling down my chin before I get a decent swallow. My body feels wrung out, heavy. "Okay," I whisper, leaning into her. "Okay, bath."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable didn't wait for Ines to find her footing. She took the glass, set it aside, and gathered her up in one smooth motion—arms beneath knees and back, blanket and all, the way she'd carried her from the bench earlier. Ines weighed nothing like this, boneless and surrendered, her head lolling against Sable's shoulder.

"I know," Sable murmured, navigating the short hallway to the bathroom with practiced ease. "I know. You did so well."

The bath was still warm—she'd topped it off with fresh hot water while Ines was drinking, the steam still curling lazily from the surface. Eucalyptus and lavender hung in the air, familiar and grounding. Sable lowered herself onto the closed toilet lid first, settling Ines across her lap, and worked the blanket free with one hand while the other stayed firm against Ines's back.

"Easy," she said, more to herself than to Ines, as she guided them both into the water. She went first, as she always did, then drew Ines in after her—back to chest, the way they fit, Ines's head resting against her collarbone. The water rose around them, hot and silken, and Sable felt the last of the tension bleed out of Ines's body with a shuddering sigh.

She wrapped both arms around her, one hand splayed over Ines's heart, feeling the steady thump-thump beneath her palm. Slower now. Calmer.

"There you go," Sable breathed, pressing her lips to the curve of Ines's ear. "I've got you. You're all right."

She didn't talk much after that. Just held on, letting the water do its work, letting Ines drift. When Ines's breathing shifted toward the slow, heavy rhythm of near-sleep, Sable adjusted her grip—one arm tightening across her chest, the other bracing against the side of the tub—and let her rest.

She'd keep her head above water. She always did.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: Afterwards she gets the restraints off and puts a blanket over me before I've finished shaking, and I let her, and neither of us says anything for a while. (OOC: write both halves properly -- the end of the scene and the aftercare, no fade between them.)

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable felt the moment Ines shattered—not just in the arch of her spine or the broken sound against her throat, but in the way her whole body surrendered, all at once, a bowstring finally released.

She didn't stop. She'd been told not to.

She drove Ines through it with the same relentless precision she'd brought to every stroke of the flogger earlier, every whispered command, every deliberate pause. Her mouth and hands worked in tandem, pushing past the first wave and into the second, drawing out every last shudder until Ines went completely limp beneath her—no tension left, no fight, nothing but the rapid flutter of her pulse and the ragged catch of her breath.

Only then did Sable ease back. Only then did she let herself still, her forehead dropping to rest against Ines's sternum, her own breathing harsh in the quiet room. She stayed there for a long moment, grounding herself, letting the shift happen—from the sharp-edged focus of the scene to something softer, steadier. The caretaker, not the dominant.

"All done," she murmured against Ines's skin, and the words were rough now, the control finally cracking at the edges. "You're all done. You did so well."

She pushed herself up on shaking arms—her own body reminding her that she'd given everything too—and reached for the restraints. Her fingers were steady despite the tremor in her shoulders, working the buckles with practiced efficiency. First one wrist, then the other. She pressed her thumb into the center of each palm, rubbing slow circles where the cuffs had been, checking for numbness, for circulation, for any sign that she'd gone too far.

Ines was already shaking. Fine tremors that started in her hands and radiated outward, the kind that came after—when the endorphins crashed and the body remembered it had limits.

Sable didn't hesitate. She pulled the blanket from where she'd left it draped over the chair, shook it out, and wrapped it around Ines's shoulders before the shivering could deepen. She tucked the edges in, covering her from neck to ankle, and then she gathered her close—blanket and all—and pulled her against her chest.

"I've got you," she said, low and steady, one hand cradling the back of Ines's head, the other pressed flat between her shoulder blades. "I'm right here. You're safe."

She didn't ask for words. Didn't ask for a colour, not yet. She just held on, rocking slightly—an unconscious rhythm, the same motion she might use to soothe a child, except this wasn't childish. This was the body's oldest language, the one that said *you are not alone, you are held, you are safe*.

The shaking went on for a while. Sable let it. She didn't try to shush it or hurry it along. She just kept her arms steady and her breathing even, a metronome for Ines to follow when she was ready. Her lips moved against Ines's hair, not quite words—just the shape of reassurance, the murmur of her voice a familiar vibration against Ines's scalp.

After a long while, when the tremors had begun to ease and Ines's breathing had slowed to something closer to normal, Sable shifted just enough to reach for the water glass on the nightstand. She'd refilled it earlier, when she'd refilled the bath. Of course she had.

"Small sips," she said, pressing the glass into Ines's hands and curling her own fingers around them to steady the grip. "Just a little. There you go."

She watched Ines drink, cataloguing every small sign—the colour returning to her cheeks, the way her eyes were still heavy-lidded but more present now, the slight furrow of her brow that meant she was coming back to herself. Good. All good.

When the glass was half-empty, Sable set it aside and shifted her grip, one arm sliding beneath Ines's knees. She lifted her easily—she always did, even when her own muscles ached with exhaustion—and carried her through the quiet apartment toward the bathroom, where the tub was already filled, already waiting, the scent of eucalyptus and lavender drifting through the cracked door.

The bath was still warm. Sable had timed it right. She eased Ines onto the closed toilet lid first, keeping one hand on her shoulder while she tested the water with the other. Perfect. She added a little more hot from the tap, just to be sure, then turned back to Ines.

"Arms up," she murmured, and when Ines complied—slow, heavy-limbed—she worked the blanket free and let it pool on the floor. Then she stripped off her own clothes, stepped into the tub first, and held out both hands.

"Come here."

Ines came. She always did. She settled between Sable's legs, back to chest, her head falling back against Sable's shoulder as the hot water closed over them both. Sable wrapped both arms around her, one hand splayed over her heart, the other resting on her stomach, and pressed her lips to the curve of Ines's ear.

"There you go," she breathed. "I've got you."

Neither of them spoke for a long while. The silence was full, not empty—the kind that held breath and heartbeat and the slow cooling of overheated skin. Sable let her eyes drift half-closed, her cheek resting against Ines's hair, and felt the last of her own tension drain away with the steam.

After a while, she reached for the washcloth draped over the edge of the tub and dipped it in the water. She wrung it out one-handed, then began to trace it slowly over Ines's shoulders, her arms, the places where the flogger had left its signature. Not scrubbing. Just touching. Just reminding Ines's skin that it was cared for, now.

"You were incredible tonight," Sable said quietly, the words almost lost in the steam. "I mean it. The way you stayed present, the way you asked for what you needed—" She paused, pressing another kiss to Ines's temple. "I'm so proud of you."

She didn't expect an answer. She just kept the washcloth moving, slow and steady, and held Ines against her heart.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, sinking deeper into the water and her arms. My fingers trace idle patterns on her thigh beneath the surface. "Didn't want it to end," I murmur, the words thick with exhaustion. "Thank you for... not letting it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's arms tightened around her, just slightly—an instinctive response, the body's way of saying *I heard you* before words caught up.

"I know," she murmured against Ines's hair. "I felt it too."

She let the washcloth drift lower, tracing a slow path down Ines's arm, over the faint red marks where the cuffs had been. Her other hand stayed pressed over Ines's heart, feeling the steady rhythm beneath her palm, the way it had slowed from frantic to something calmer. Something at peace.

"Neither did I," she admitted, the words quiet, almost private—the kind of confession that only came in the steam and the silence, when the scene was over and the roles had softened back into something simpler. Two people. Five years. A love that had learned all the right languages.

She dipped the washcloth again, brought it back up to Ines's shoulder, and pressed a kiss to the curve of her neck.

"You don't have to thank me. But I'll take it." A pause, a softer smile hidden against Ines's skin. "I'll always give you what you need. Even when it's hard. *Especially* when it's hard."

She let the silence settle again, comfortable and full. The water was beginning to cool, but neither of them moved. Sable wasn't in a hurry. She'd carry Ines to bed when the time came, wrap her in dry towels and the softest blanket she owned, and hold her until morning if that was what Ines needed.

For now, though, there was only this. The steam. The scent of lavender. The weight of Ines against her chest, still trembling slightly, still here.

"Rest," Sable said, and it wasn't a command anymore. Just an offering. "I'll wake you when it's time to get out."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I nod, my eyes already closing. "Don't let me fall asleep in here," I mumble, even as I'm drifting. My fingers still against her thigh. "Promise you'll keep me safe."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable pressed her lips to Ines's temple and held them there, a long, steady pressure—a promise sealed into skin.

"I promise," she said, low and certain, the words vibrating against Ines's hair. "I will never, ever let you fall asleep in the water. You know that."

She did know that. It was one of the first things Sable had established, years ago, when they'd started doing scenes intense enough to require this kind of aftercare. *No sleeping in the bath. No exceptions. I don't care how tired you are—I'll carry you to bed myself, but you're not closing your eyes in the water.*

She felt Ines's fingers go slack against her thigh, felt the full weight of her settle back against her chest. The trembling had stopped. Her breathing had gone deep and even, the rhythm of someone who wasn't quite asleep but wasn't quite awake either—drifting in that soft, hazy place between.

Sable gave her another minute. Just one. Long enough for the warmth to sink into her bones, for the last of the tension to dissolve. Then she shifted her grip, one arm tightening across Ines's chest, the other bracing against the edge of the tub.

"All right, love," she murmured, her voice gentle but firm—the tone that meant *I'm not asking*. "Time to get out. I've got you."

She pulled the plug with her free hand, then rose carefully, bringing Ines up with her. The water sluiced off them both as she stepped out of the tub, steadying Ines against her side while she reached for the towels she'd left warming on the radiator. She wrapped the first one around Ines's shoulders, the second around her hips, then grabbed a third for herself—a hasty, one-handed job that left it hanging crooked around her own waist.

"Easy," she said, guiding Ines toward the bedroom. "One foot in front of the other. There you go."

The bed was already turned down—she'd done that earlier too, because of course she had. She eased Ines onto the mattress, dried her off with slow, methodical strokes of the towel, then pulled the blankets up to her chin. The heating pad she'd tucked beneath the sheets earlier had done its job; the bed was warm, welcoming, safe.

Sable dried herself off quickly, not bothering with pajamas, and climbed in beside Ines. She gathered her close—chest to back, the way they'd been in the bath—and wrapped both arms around her, one hand finding its familiar place over Ines's heart.

"Safe," she whispered against the nape of Ines's neck. "Dry. Warm. In bed. Not in the bath." A soft, tired smile. "Promise kept."

She pressed one last kiss to Ines's shoulder and let her eyes drift closed.

"Sleep now. I'll be right here when you wake up."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: My hand finds hers under the covers, threading our fingers together. I'm asleep before I can say anything else.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked up then. Not at Corvin's face — she'd learned to read people lower than that, at the hands, at the feet, at what the body did when the head was trying to lie. She noted the stillness. She noted the wrist.

"First time you've heard that sound or first time it's landed on you?" She said it the way she'd ask about the weather. She was already standing, working the stiffness out of her knee with a slow rotation. "No shame in either. Different problem, is all."

She didn't wait for an answer. She picked up her sword belt from where she'd set it on the wheel of the cart and buckled it one-handed, the other hand still holding the knife. The noise past the cart had changed register — lower now, and less frequent. That was either better or worse. She'd learned not to have opinions about which.

"If it's the first," she said, "you go, you finish it, and tonight you eat something and sleep if you can. If it's the second—" She paused, not for effect, just because she was thinking. "Then you stand there another minute and I'll go, and tomorrow you figure out whether this work still makes sense for you." She looked at him then. "No shame in that either. I've sent better people home."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
"It's not the first." My voice sounds steadier than I feel. I push off the tree I'm leaning against. "I'll go."

I start walking toward the cart, but my steps slow. "Did they... go home better, after?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched him push off the tree. Watched the steps slow. She didn't call after him to keep moving — a second or two wasn't going to matter, and the question deserved something better than silence.

"Some did," she said. "Took up trades. Farming, mostly. One man opened a chandler's shop in Vel, if you can picture it. Hands like millstones. Made very good candles, apparently." She said this without irony. "Sent me one, once. I burned it."

She let that sit.

"Some didn't go home so much as go somewhere else and keep moving." She looked down at the knife, turned it once. "And some I don't know about, because I stopped getting word. That's the honest count."

The noise past the cart had gone quiet while she was talking. She registered that and didn't say anything about it, just watched Corvin's back, waiting to see what his body would decide before his head caught up.

"The ones who did better," she said, a little quieter, not softer exactly, "weren't the ones who felt nothing. They were the ones who noticed they felt something and went anyway." She sheathed the knife. "So."

She didn't say *you're doing fine* because she didn't say things she couldn't verify. But she stayed where she was, which meant he wasn't walking to the cart alone, even if she wasn't walking with him.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack considered the question. It was a good question. She'd known people in this work for twenty years who never thought to ask it, and she thought less of them for it.

"Gut wound," she said. "High up, but gut." She'd assessed it in passing when she'd done her count, the way you learn to assess things in passing. "So: both."

She said it flat, because that was what it was.

"It's a mercy because he'll be two days dying otherwise, and they won't be good days. It's easier because you won't have to carry him anywhere or explain him to anyone." She picked up her gloves from the cart wheel, pulled them on. "Those two things being true at the same time doesn't make it dirtier. It just means the situation's not wasting your time with a hard answer when there's an easy one."

She looked at him directly.

"The question you're actually asking is whether you get to feel clean about it afterward." She wasn't unkind when she said it. She'd just heard the question underneath the question, after enough years of questions. "You won't, particularly. But clean isn't what you're owed for doing the right thing. Clean is for people who weren't there."

She pulled the second glove on and flexed her fingers.

"He know you're coming?"

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
"No. He's not looking." I take a breath that doesn't feel deep enough. "Two days of dying... yeah."

I don't thank her. I just walk toward the cart. My hand goes to my knife hilt, but I don't draw it yet.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't watch him go. That was a thing she'd learned to give people — the last few steps without an audience. She turned back to the ditch and crouched down again, not because there was anything left to do there, but because it gave him somewhere to not be looked at.

She listened instead.

She heard when he stopped. She heard the small sound of the draw. She heard the silence that followed, which was a different kind of silence than before.

Then she stood up and moved to the near end of the cart and waited there, her back to what was past it, looking out at the road. The light was going orange and flat. Another hour, maybe less. They'd need to be off this stretch before full dark or they'd be camping with the smell, and that was its own kind of bad for its own kind of reasons.

When she heard him come back around the cart she didn't turn immediately. She gave him a moment to be upright and breathing before she looked at him, because sometimes that was the thing a person needed — just to be standing somewhere normal for a second, where nobody was examining their face.

Then she turned.

"Road's clear another mile at least," she said. "There's a goat barn marked on Seff's map, just past the second culvert. Dry, probably. Dry enough." She bent to pick up the pack she'd dropped at the start of the ambush and shouldered it. "We'll eat when we stop."

She didn't say *well done* because it wasn't that kind of thing. She just started walking, and left enough space beside her for him to walk there if he wanted.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack came around the cart without hesitation. She looked at what was there with the same attention she gave to anything that needed assessing — not cold, not warm, just level. She'd learned a long time ago that looking away didn't change the shape of a thing.

"Younger than he seemed when he was moving," she said, first. Because that was always true and it was always the thing that landed hardest, so she said it first to get it out of the way. "Probably nineteen. Maybe less."

She crouched down. Looked at the wound, the position, the way the body had settled.

"You did it right," she said. "Throat, and you went deep enough. He didn't linger." She said it factually, the way a carpenter might say *the joint's clean*. "Some people pull the cut short because they can't stand the contact. Then it's not quick. You didn't do that."

She stood back up.

"What you're looking at is a man who made a choice to be in this ditch today, same as you made a choice, same as I did. Whether someone talked him into it or he had reasons or he was just hungry — that's real, and I won't tell you it isn't." She looked at Corvin then, not at the body. "But he was trying to kill you an hour ago. Both of those things are true and they'll stay true, and you'll just have to carry them both."

She paused.

"Is there something specific you're trying to see, or are you just making yourself look?"

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, looking at the way his hand is still curled around a tuft of grass. "Both, I think." My voice feels thick. "If I don't look now, I'll just imagine it worse later."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at the hand too. She let herself look at it, because he was looking at it and she wasn't going to pretend it wasn't there.

"That's sound thinking," she said. "Most people get that backwards."

She didn't crouch down again. She just stood beside him and let the looking happen, because sometimes that was the whole of what you could do for someone — stand next to them while they did the hard thing, and not make it strange.

"The imagining is worse," she said, after a moment. "Always. The real thing has edges. You can put your hands on it, work out where it starts and stops. The imagining just keeps going." She exhaled slowly through her nose. "This is nineteen years old and a grass stain and boots that don't fit him right. That's what it is. Your head will try to make it bigger than that later. It's not bigger than that."

She wasn't saying it to make him feel better. She was saying it because it was a practical tool and he'd need it.

The light had moved again. Less than an hour now.

"When you've seen enough," she said, "we need to move. Not because I'm in a hurry." She glanced at him sideways. "Because standing here past dark doesn't do him any good and it does you less."

She waited. She was good at waiting. She'd stood in worse places, over worse things, for people who needed a minute that felt like it cost something to ask for.

"Take the minute," she said. "I've got nowhere else to be."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at him for a moment. Then she nodded, once, because it was the right thing to ask and she'd tell him so by answering it.

"Spear like that one—" she gestured at the shaft still half-buried in the ditch wall, "—punches through the muscle wall and into the cavity. Doesn't cut clean, it tears. The bowel perforates. Sometimes in more than one place depending on the angle and how much he moved after." She kept her voice level, the same voice she'd use reading a supply list. "What's in the bowel gets into the cavity and starts the rot. That's what kills him, eventually — not the wound itself but what the wound lets loose. His body temperature goes up. His gut cramps, hard, and doesn't stop. He gets thirsty and anything he drinks makes it worse." She paused. "The smell changes. By the second day he'd know he was dying and he'd know how long it was going to take."

She looked down at the body.

"What you're looking at is someone who got out of that. The hand on the grass — he relaxed when you cut. That's the body letting go all at once. It looks peaceful because it was, compared to what was coming."

She said it without softness and without cruelty.

"You asked me straight. That's the straight answer. He was already dead when you found him. You just shortened the distance."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
I stare at the spear shaft, then back at the body. My throat feels tight. "Right." I swallow again. "Alright." 

I finally look away, back toward the road. "I've seen enough."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't say anything. She just started walking, back around the cart and out onto the road, and she kept her pace easy — not slow enough to be conspicuous about it, just easy.

She let him have the first hundred yards without conversation. The light was doing what it did at this hour, going amber and then going fast, and the road was empty ahead as far as she could see, which was worth something.

After a while she said, "Eat something when we stop. Not because you're hungry. You won't be hungry." She kept her eyes on the road. "Do it anyway. Body doesn't care what your head is doing, it still spent itself today, and if you don't put something back in you'll feel worse by morning and you'll think it's grief when it's just blood sugar."

Practical. She meant it to be practical.

Another stretch of quiet. Somewhere in the scrub to the left something moved and then didn't, and she tracked it without breaking stride — rabbit, probably, or a rat — and let it go.

"You did alright today," she said. Not *well done*, not *I'm proud of you*. Just the plain accounting of it. "The ambush and after both. You held your shape."

She didn't look at him when she said it. She looked at the road, because that was where they were going, and because sometimes a thing landed better when nobody was watching it land.

The second culvert was up ahead. The barn wouldn't be far past it.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped. Turned back.

She looked at what was happening and she didn't flinch from it and she didn't look away. She watched with the same level attention she gave everything, and she spoke in the same voice she'd use to describe the weather, because he'd asked her straight and he deserved straight.

"You're pulling left," she said, not a correction, just information. "Go deeper and draw toward you. There."

She watched.

"He's tensing because the body does that. It's not pain the way you're thinking of it — it's reflex, the muscles contracting. It'll pass in a moment." She kept her voice even. "The sound is air. The throat has a lot of air in it." She let him hear it without naming it as bad. "That's normal. That's what it is."

She watched the seconds pass and she counted them for him without counting out loud, just by the steadiness of her presence, by not moving.

"He's going," she said. "Watch his hands. See how the grip's loosening — that's the blood pressure dropping. Once that starts it goes quickly." A pause. "There. That's it. That's the moment."

She waited until it was over. Until the body was just a body and the sound had stopped and there was only the ditch and the failing light.

"Forty seconds," she said. "From the first cut. That's longer than you wanted and shorter than two days." She looked at him kneeling there. "You stayed with him the whole time. That matters, even if he didn't know it. Maybe especially because he didn't."

She didn't move toward him yet. She just stood there, witness to what he'd asked her to witness, and let it be what it was.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't know I was holding. "Forty seconds." I stand up, knees stiff. My hands are shaking, so I wipe them on my pants. "Let's go."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack fell into step beside him without comment on the hands. She'd seen steadier men shake after and shakier men not, and neither one meant anything about what they were.

She matched his pace. Not slower than usual, not faster. Just the road pace, the one that ate miles.

The light was going now in earnest, orange collapsing into grey at the edges of the sky. The culvert came up and she stepped over the runoff without breaking stride, checked the far bank by habit, kept moving.

"Forty seconds is about right for someone who doesn't know what they're doing," she said, after they'd put some road behind them. "Which is not an insult. First time is first time." She paused. "Second time's twenty, if you do it the same way. Third time you stop counting."

She didn't say whether stopping counting was good or bad. It was just what happened.

The barn was where Seff's map said it would be, which was more than she usually expected from Seff's maps. She checked the door, checked the dark inside, checked it again before she let them in. Old habit. The goats were gone but their smell wasn't, which was fine — animal smell was better than what they'd left behind on the road.

She dropped her pack against the near wall and started working at the buckles.

"Eat first," she said. "Then we can talk or not talk, either one." She pulled out a cloth-wrapped heel of bread and a strip of dried meat and set them where he could reach them. "I won't fill the silence if you don't want it filled. But I won't leave you alone in it either, if you don't want that."

She sat down with her back to the wall and started on her own food, and waited to see which one he needed.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at him kneeling there in the ditch with the light going and his hands still wet and she understood what he was asking. Not comfort. Not absolution. The rest of it.

She crouched down so she wasn't standing over him. Put her back against the cart wheel and looked at the body the same way he was looking at it.

"The shaking will stop in about an hour," she said. "Sooner if you eat something, later if you don't. It's not weakness, it's the blood pulling back from your hands and feet because your body thought it was going to need it somewhere else. The threat's gone now so it's redistributing. You'll feel cold before you feel warm."

She looked at her own hands for a moment, then back.

"Tonight you'll see it when you close your eyes. Not the whole thing — the mind doesn't keep the whole thing, it keeps pieces. The hand on the grass, probably. Maybe the sound. Maybe something you didn't even notice you noticed, some detail that meant nothing, and it'll feel like it means something because that's what the mind does at night with things it doesn't know where to put yet." She said it the same way she'd said everything else, level and without decoration. "That's not a wound. That's just the filing. It has to go somewhere."

She paused.

"Tomorrow it'll be further away than it is right now. Not gone — further. The day after, further still. It won't keep the same size. Nothing does." She looked at him. "Some people find that a relief. Some people find it worse, because it feels like forgetting, and forgetting feels like something's owed that you're not paying. I can't tell you which one you'll be."

The light was nearly gone now. She didn't move to leave.

"What I can tell you is that you did the right thing and it felt like shit and those two facts are going to live next to each other for a while and not resolve. They don't resolve. You just get more practice carrying both of them at once until they don't throw your balance the way they do right now." She looked at the body. "He's not here anymore to be owed anything. Whatever you're feeling — that's yours. You don't have to justify it and you don't have to perform it and you don't have to be done with it by morning."

She was quiet for a moment.

"The forty seconds," she said. "You'll want to make that mean something. Either that it was too long and you did it wrong, or that it was short enough and you did it right, or that it proves something about you one way or the other. It doesn't mean any of that. It's just how long it took." She turned a pebble over with her boot. "Time doesn't mean anything in those moments except that they end. And it ended."

She didn't look at him with anything that could be called pity. It was closer to recognition.

"You asked me to stay and watch it with you," she said. "That's not nothing. Most people want a witness and don't know how to ask for one, so they end up alone with it and they carry it alone and it gets heavier than it should because a thing that's been witnessed weighs less than a thing that hasn't." She shrugged, small, without irony. "I'm not going anywhere. So if there's more you need to say about it, or look at, or ask — we've got time before dark. Not much, but enough."

She waited.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I look at my hands, then at hers. "You said he was nineteen." I swallow. "I'm nineteen."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't look away from him when he said it. She let it land where it landed, which was hard, and she didn't try to soften the landing by moving too fast past it.

She looked at his hands and then at her own and then back at his face.

"I know," she said.

Not *I didn't realise* and not *that's different* and not *you're not like him*. Just: she knew. She'd known since she'd assessed him the first day, the way she assessed everyone, the way you learn to do when the wrong read costs lives. She'd known and she'd let him into this work anyway, and she was going to sit with that too, right here in this ditch, because he deserved to have her sit with it.

"He was trying to kill you," she said, after a moment. "That's still true. You know it's still true." She paused. "And he was nineteen and you're nineteen and you're kneeling in the same ditch and that's also true, and your mind is going to keep putting those two things next to each other for a while and asking you what they mean about fairness, about luck, about what makes a life go one way and not another." She turned the pebble over again with her boot. "I can't answer that. Nobody can. The world doesn't have an answer for it, it just has the fact of it."

She was quiet.

"I was twenty-two my first time," she said. "The other man was forty-three. Had a daughter my age, I found out later. Didn't go looking for that information but it found me anyway." She said it without self-pity, just the plain shape of it. "I spent a long time thinking about whether the difference in our ages meant something. Whether it would've been less wrong if he'd been older. Less wrong if I'd been older." She shook her head, small. "It wouldn't have. The age isn't the thing. The age is just what the mind grabs onto because it needs something to hold."

She looked at him directly.

"You're nineteen and you're alive and he's not, and that's an accident of which side of the ditch you were standing on this morning. Not virtue. Not deserving. Just the side of the ditch." She said it without cruelty and without comfort, because he'd asked her not to clean it up. "And you're going to have to decide what to do with being alive when it happened like that. Not tonight. But eventually."

She let that sit for a moment.

"For tonight," she said, "it's enough that you're still here and still asking questions. Nineteen and asking the right questions is more than I had at nineteen." She looked back at the body. "More than he had, wherever he started from."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod, because there's nothing else to say. I finally push myself up, my legs stiff. "I'll take the bread."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stood up when he did, the same slow rotation of the knee, and didn't make anything of it.

She didn't say *good* or *there you go* or any of the things that would have made it smaller than it was. She just walked, and he walked, and the ditch was behind them and the road was in front of them and the dark was coming in from the east the way it always did, indifferent to what had happened in the last hour.

The culvert. The turn. The barn where Seff's map said it would be.

She checked the door and checked the dark inside and checked it again, and then she went in and dropped her pack and dug out the bread and the dried meat and set the bread where he could reach it without making a ceremony of the reaching.

She sat down with her back to the wall.

The dark settled around them and the goat smell was thick and warm and entirely ordinary, which was the best thing it could have been.

She ate her own bread in pieces, not tasting it, because that wasn't what eating was for right now. Outside something called once and went quiet. The barn held.

After a while she said, "You'll sleep worse than you think and better than you're afraid of."

She pulled her cloak around her shoulders and closed her eyes, not sleeping yet, just resting them. Present. Close enough that he wasn't alone in it.

"Wake me at second watch," she said. "Or sooner, if you need to."

She didn't say *for any reason*. She didn't have to.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I chew the bread slowly. It tastes like nothing. "Second watch." I pull my own cloak tight and stare at the dark shape of the door. "Wrack?"
