dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack glanced up at that, just briefly, reading something in the way Corvin stood there. She'd seen that paralysis before—in new recruits, in people who'd thought they were ready for this until they weren't. The blood on his face wasn't his, and the stillness in his legs wasn't hesitation. It was something else.

She wiped the blade again, though it was clean enough. Gave her hands something to do while she waited.

"He'll keep making noise," she said. Not unkind. Just a fact, like the count. "Or he'll stop, and then you won't know if he's gone quiet or gone dead, and then you'll have to check anyway, except now it's dark and you're jumping at shadows." She stood, joints protesting as they always did, and sheathed the knife.

"I'm not doing it for you. That's not how this works." She squinted toward the cart, where the sound was—a wet, rhythmic breathing, the kind that meant chest wounds. "But I'll walk over there with you, if walking's the hard part."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: *I swallow, my throat dry.* "Right." I finally force my legs to move, falling into step beside you. "It's just...the quiet after."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack walked alongside him, her pace set to his—not rushing, not slowing to make a point. The ground was uneven, clotted with cart ruts and old mud. She kept her eyes forward.

"The quiet after," she repeated, like she was tasting the words. "Yeah. That part's the work. The killing's just—movement. Muscle and metal and luck. Any fool can do it."

The breathing from past the cart got louder as they approached. Wet, labored. Someone with a punctured lung, maybe, or a rib gone wrong into something soft.

Wrack stopped a few paces short. She could see him now—a young man, younger than she'd expected, pressed against the cart's broken wheel like it might shelter him. His hands were pressed to his side, and the dark spread beneath them wasn't shadow.

"First time I killed a man," she said, quietly enough that only Corvin could hear, "I sat in a ditch for an hour after, shaking. Couldn't stop. Thought something was wrong with me." She looked at the dying man, then back at Corvin. "Nothing was wrong with me. Nothing's wrong with you. It's just the body understanding something the mind hasn't caught up to yet."

She gestured toward the man with her chin. "He's got maybe a few minutes of making that noise. After that, he drowns in his own blood, which is a bad way to go and one I wouldn't wish on anyone, even someone who just tried to kill me." Her voice stayed even. "Or you end it, and it's quiet, and you sit with that quiet until you learn how to carry it. Most people do, eventually."

She stepped back, giving him the space. "Your call. I'll wait here."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at the man against the wheel. Really looked, the way she'd learned to look over ten years of making calls like this one. The breathing told her most of it. The color of his skin told her the rest—waxen, already going grey at the edges, the blood not pulsing from the wound but seeping steady and dark.

"Bad enough," she said. She didn't look away from him. "Gut and lung, from the sound. Maybe liver, if he's lucky." A pause. "He's not lucky."

She crossed her arms, not out of impatience but because standing with them at her sides felt wrong, somehow. Too casual.

"Mercy and easier aren't different things, not here. You're not choosing between them." She scratched at a dried smear of blood on her forearm, someone else's, from earlier. "He's dying. That's just fact. The only choice you've got is whether he does it in the next minute or the next hour, and whether he does it choking or not."

The man's breathing hitched, a wet rattle. His eyes were open but seeing something else now—some private place where the pain couldn't follow, maybe. Or maybe nothing at all.

"I've seen men survive worse," Wrack added, because it was true. "Surgeons, priests, clean beds, a month of fever and luck. None of those are coming down this road." She looked at Corvin directly. "So. It's not easier. It's just the only thing left."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take a slow breath, my hand finding the hilt of my knife. "Alright." I step past her, my boots crunching on the gravel. The man's eyes flicker toward me, glazed but aware.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't look away.

She watched Corvin approach the man, watched the way his shoulders had set themselves, the slight tremor in his knife hand that he probably thought nobody could see. The dying man's eyes found Corvin's face—there was something there, recognition maybe, or just the desperate hope that someone had come to help.

He didn't speak. Couldn't, probably, with what was filling his lungs.

Wrack had seen this part more times than she could count. The moment stretched out, longer than it actually was—time always went strange around death. She kept her breathing even, her weight settled back on her heels. Present but not hovering. A witness, if he needed one. Alone, if he needed that instead.

The road was empty both ways. No sound but the wet rattle and the creak of the broken cart shifting in a wind that hadn't been there before.

She thought about saying something—*quick and clean, don't hesitate*—but that was the kind of advice that only mattered before you were already standing there. Now it would just be noise.

So she waited, her arms still crossed, her eyes on Corvin's back. Whatever happened next, he'd carry it. She couldn't carry it for him.

But she could make sure he didn't walk away alone after. That much, she could do.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack moved up alongside him, close enough to speak low but not crowding. She looked down at the man the way she'd look at a broken axle—assessing, cataloguing, nothing more.

"His hands are where the pain is," she said. "See how he's pressing? That's gut. Something's torn open in there, spilling into places it shouldn't. The smell will tell you that in a minute, if it doesn't already." She pointed with her chin, not her hand. "The breathing's the other problem. Wet, rhythmic—means his lung's collapsed or filling. Every breath he takes is pushing blood where air should be. That's why he's grey. That's why his lips are going blue."

The man's eyes moved between them, slow and unfocused. A sound came from his throat, not words—just air escaping around something that shouldn't be there.

"He can probably hear us," Wrack added, quieter. "Might even understand. People hold on longer than you'd think. But he can't speak, and he won't get up, and nothing we pour down his throat or press against that wound is going to fix what's broken inside." She paused. "You're looking at a man who's already dying. This is just the part where his body hasn't accepted it yet."

She stepped back again, giving Corvin room.

"Throat or heart," she said. "Throat is faster but messier. Heart—you'll need to get through the ribs, find the right space. Push hard, don't stop until it's done." A beat. "Whatever you choose, commit to it. Half-measures are worse than none."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod, my grip tightening on the knife. "Throat, then." I kneel down beside him, my free hand coming up to steady his head. His skin is cold and clammy. "Close your eyes," I whisper, though I don't know if he hears me.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't look away.

She watched Corvin's hand steady the man's head, watched the way his fingers found the angle without fumbling. The dying man's eyes didn't close—maybe he couldn't hear, maybe he didn't want to, maybe his body just couldn't obey anymore. His lips moved, shaping something that might have been a word or might have been nothing at all.

"Press firm," Wrack said, quiet. "Don't let him roll. And when you start, don't stop halfway through."

The wind shifted. Somewhere back along the road, a crow called out and got no answer.

Then Corvin's knife moved, and the sound that came was brief—shorter than the breathing had been, shorter than anything should be that ends a life. The man's body tensed once, a single spasm that ran from his shoulders to his heels, and then went still. The quiet came down like a held breath finally released.

Wrack stood there a moment longer, watching the dark pool spread beneath the man's neck into the already-dark earth. Then she let her arms drop to her sides.

"Sit down," she said, not unkindly. "Not in that—over there." She nodded toward a stretch of ground away from the blood, away from the cart. "Sit down before your legs decide for you."

She didn't reach for him. Didn't touch his shoulder or offer any of the comforts that people reached for when they didn't know what else to do. She just stood nearby, solid and unhurried, waiting to see if he'd sway or if he'd hold.

The quiet after. He'd mentioned it before. Now he was in it.

"You did it clean," she said after a moment. "That matters. Might not feel like it right now, but it does."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack regarded him for a moment, something shifting behind her eyes—not surprise, exactly, but a recognition. She'd seen men refuse to look and men who couldn't stop staring. Fewer who asked to understand what they were seeing.

"Alright," she said. She crouched down beside the body, not touching it but close enough to point. "You want it straight, here's straight."

She gestured toward the man's midsection, where his hands had been pressing. "Spear went in here. Maybe four inches of blade, maybe six—doesn't take much with gut wounds. The belly wall's not armor. It goes through muscle, through fat, and then it's inside the cavity where your organs sit loose and wet. No bones to stop it, not there."

She pointed lower, toward the dark stain. "Intestines, first. They're folded up like rope in there, and when you pierce them, what's inside them—bile, waste, bacteria—spills into the cavity. That's what kills you slow, if nothing else does. The body can't handle its own filth in places filth shouldn't be. Sepsis. Fever. Days of it, if you're unlucky."

She straightened slightly, her voice still even. "But he also got the lung. See how the entry angles up? Something caught him on the way through or he twisted on it. Either way, it nicked the bottom of his lung. That's why he was drowning—blood filling the sac around it, pressing until no air could get in. You heard that rattle. That was him trying to breathe around his own blood."

She looked at Corvin directly. "He'd have been dead by morning regardless. Probably conscious for most of it, in pain most of us can't imagine, and unable to call for help because his throat was filling up too. That's what a spear does. That's what you ended."

She stood, her knees popping. "It's not clean. It's not quick, most times. What you gave him was faster than what was coming."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I look down at the blood on my hands. "Faster." I repeat the word like it's a prayer. "I'll sit for a minute." My legs feel hollow as I walk to the clean patch of dirt.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack let him go. Didn't follow, didn't hover. She turned back to the bodies instead—working through them the way she always did after a fight, checking pouches for intelligence, checking hands for signets or marks that might tell her who'd hired them. Grunt work. The kind of thing that kept the hands busy while the mind did what it needed to do.

She worked her way through three of them before she spoke, her back to Corvin, not turning around.

"Minute's fine. Two minutes is fine. Ten's fine." She rolled a dead man's sleeve up to check for tattoos. Nothing. "Just don't make it an hour. An hour is where it starts living in you. Gets comfortable. Harder to dig out after that."

She found a purse on the fourth body, cut it free, weighed it in her palm. Heavier than it should be for a road ambush. She tucked it into her belt without comment.

The wind had picked up, carrying the smell of blood and something sharper underneath it—the gut smell she'd described, which was worse than the blood, always worse. She was used to it. Corvin probably wasn't.

She moved to the fifth body, crouching. Glanced back over her shoulder once, quick, just to confirm he was still sitting and not lying down. Lying down was bad. Sitting was fine.

"Water's in my kit, if you need it. Left side." She turned back to the body. "Tastes like leather. It's not poisoned, it just tastes that way."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped mid-turn. Looked at him. Really looked, the way she'd assessed the dying man—except this was different. This was Corvin asking her to witness something he needed to witness himself.

She came back. Stood off his shoulder, close enough to see, far enough not to crowd.

"Alright," she said. "I'll tell you."

She watched him kneel. Watched the knife come up again—still bloodied, he hadn't wiped it. Maybe that was deliberate. Maybe he'd forgotten. Either way, it didn't matter.

"Your hand's steadier than you think it is," she said. "That's good. That'll matter later, even if it doesn't feel like it now."

The man beneath him wasn't the same one. This was another—older, grey-bearded, a wound in his chest that had soaked his shirt black. Still breathing. Still aware. His eyes found Corvin's face and stayed there.

"When you go in," Wrack said, her voice low and steady, "you'll feel resistance. Skin gives first—like pushing through wet canvas. Then muscle, which grips the blade. That's the part that surprises people. It holds on. You have to push through it."

She paused. The man's lips were moving. A prayer, maybe. Or just sound.

"The sound—" She considered her words. "It's not what you'd expect. Not a scream, most times. Something between a gasp and a sigh. The body knows. Sometimes it fights. Sometimes it just... lets go."

She fell silent as Corvin's knife found its mark. Watched the blade disappear. Watched the man's body arch once, then settle. The sound came—

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: *My eyes are fixed on the place where the knife went in.* "I felt it," I say, my voice rough. "The muscle. Like you said." I pull the blade free.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched him pull the blade free. The sound it made coming out was different than going in—a wet, sucking thing, the body reluctant to release what it had taken hold of.

"Yeah," she said. "That's the part no one tells you about. The holding on." She glanced at his face, checking. Not for tears—those didn't matter—but for the kind of blankness that meant a man had gone somewhere else in his head, somewhere he might not come back from easily.

He was still here. Still present. That was something.

"The blood's going to flow faster now," she said, nodding toward the wound. "Heart's still beating for a minute, maybe two. Pushes it out in pulses. You'll feel it on your hand if you're close." She paused. "That's normal. Doesn't mean you did it wrong. Just means the body's still trying to do what bodies do, even when it's over."

The man's eyes had gone glassy, seeing something far away or nothing at all. His chest rose once more, barely, then settled.

Wrack crouched down nearby, not beside him but adjacent. Close enough to talk. Far enough to give him room.

"There's two more still breathing, from what I counted," she said. Not a prompt. Just information. "Could be three—I missed one in the grass earlier, might still be there. You don't have to do anything about them. I will, if you're done."

She looked at the blood on his hands, on the knife.

"But you asked me to tell you what you're doing. So I'm telling you." Her voice stayed even. "You're learning something most people never have to. Whether you use it again or not—that's tomorrow's problem. Right now, you just did it, and you didn't look away." A beat. "That's all you can ask of yourself today."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't move. Didn't shift her weight or look away or find something else to do with her hands. She just stayed where she was, crouched in the dirt beside a dead man, and let the silence stretch until it became its own kind of permission.

Then she spoke.

"The rest is this," she said. "What you're feeling right now—that hollow place in your chest, the way your hands don't seem like yours, the sound of his breathing still in your ears even though it's stopped—that doesn't go away. Not tonight. Not tomorrow. Maybe not ever, not entirely."

She looked down at the blood soaking into the ground between them. Dark earth, dark blood. Hard to tell where one ended and the other began.

"You'll sleep tonight and you'll dream about it, or you won't sleep at all and you'll lie there seeing it anyway. Both of those are normal. Neither one means you're broken." She paused. "You'll eat tomorrow and the food will taste wrong for a while. Like it's not reaching you. That passes too, mostly."

The wind moved the grass along the roadside. Somewhere distant, that crow called again.

"The weight of it changes," she continued, her voice still even, still just facts. "Right now it's sitting on you like a stone. Heavy enough to press the air out of your lungs. That's the shock. The body doesn't know what to do with what the mind just told it. So it does the only thing it can—it goes still. Waits. Watches. Makes sure you're not next."

She shifted her weight, one knee settling into the dirt.

"After a while—days, maybe weeks—the stone gets smaller. Not lighter. Smaller. You learn where to carry it so it doesn't press on the parts that need to keep working. You learn how to walk with it, how to eat with it, how to sleep with it lying there next to you. It doesn't leave. You just get used to the shape of it."

She looked at him directly. Held his gaze.

"Some people carry it in their shoulders. They get tight, rigid, like they're bracing for something. Some carry it in their gut—they can't eat, or they eat too much, or they drink until the weight feels further away. Some carry it in their sleep. Nightmares, or worse, the nights when you don't dream at all and you wake up feeling like something's missing and you can't name it."

A beat. She let him absorb that before continuing.

"I carry mine here." She touched her sternum, briefly, then let her hand drop. "Like something's sitting right behind my ribs, pressing in. It's been there ten years. I notice it less now, but it's still there. I notice it most when I'm alone and it's quiet, which is why I don't like being alone when it's quiet."

She stood slowly, her joints complaining the way they always did. Stayed where she was, though. Didn't step closer or further.

"You'll find your place. The spot where it sits easiest, where you can reach around it when you need to. And most days, it won't stop you from doing what needs doing. Eating, walking, fighting, fucking—all the things living people do. You'll do them. It just won't feel the same as it did before today."

The light was going. The shadows stretching long across the road, swallowing the bodies by degrees.

"That's the part people don't tell you about," Wrack said. "It doesn't make you less. It just makes you different. The man you were this morning is gone. The man you are now has blood on his hands and weight on his chest and a quiet that'll follow him into every room he enters for the rest of his life. That's not a wound. That's a change. And changes don't heal. They just become who you are."

She looked back toward the road, where two more breathing shapes still waited in the gathering dark.

"You asked for the rest. That's the rest. No redemption in it. No honor that makes the weight lighter. No secret that makes it stop mattering." Her voice softened, just slightly—not pity, something closer to respect. "You did a hard thing because it needed doing, and you didn't look away when you did it. That's not nothing. But it's not enough to keep the weight off, either. Nothing is."

She let that sit between them.

"Two more out there," she said again, after a while. "I'll see to them if you're done. You don't have to. Nobody's counting. Nobody's keeping score of who did what tonight. You did enough."

She waited to see what he'd say.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit there, watching the blood dry dark on my fingers. "I'll do the last one." My voice sounds strange to me. "But I need you to tell me if I do it wrong. Not kind, not gentle — just if my form's bad."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack nodded once. No argument, no pause to check if he was sure. He'd asked for something specific, and she understood what it was—not permission, not comfort, just the work.

"This way," she said.

She led him to the far side of the cart, where the grass grew thicker and the shadows had already claimed the ground. The man was there, same as she'd guessed—young, barely more than a boy, curled on his side with his hands pressed to his belly. Same kind of wound as the first one. Same dark spread beneath him.

He was quieter than the others had been. Past making noise, maybe. Just breathing in shallow, rapid pulls, his eyes half-closed.

Wrack stopped a few paces back and looked at Corvin.

"Kneel beside him, not over him," she said. "Over him puts your weight forward—off-balance if he moves, and you'll be reaching down instead of in. Wasted motion, less force."

She watched him settle into position.

"Your grip's too tight. I can see it from here." She gestured at his hand. "White knuckles means you're fighting the blade instead of using it. Hold it firm enough that it won't slip, no more. You want your wrist loose enough to adjust if he shifts."

The boy on the ground made a sound—small, barely there. His eyes opened, found Corvin, and something crossed his face that Wrack had seen a hundred times. Not fear, exactly. Recognition. The understanding that this was the person who would end it.

"Support hand on his shoulder or his head," she continued, her voice steady. "Steadies him, steadies you. When you go in, angle slightly up toward the throat—you want the blade to find the space between the collarbone and the windpipe. There's a gap there. Easier entry, faster path to what needs cutting."

She watched him position his free hand on the boy's shoulder. Watched his grip adjust on the knife.

"Better," she said. "Don't look at his eyes. Look at where your blade's going. Eyes'll make you hesitate. The target won't."

A pause. The boy's breathing had sped up—aware now, maybe, of what was happening. His fingers twitched against his wound.

"When you commit, commit all the way. No half-push. You go in like you mean to come out the other side. Speed matters more than force—a fast blade cuts cleaner than a strong one." She shifted her weight, settling in to watch. "And when you pull out, pull straight. Same angle you went in. Twisting makes a mess and doesn't kill faster. Just hurts more."

The wind moved the grass. The light was almost gone now, everything reduced to shapes and shadows.

"Go when you're ready," she said. "I'll tell you after."

She fell silent. Waited.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I adjust my grip, the leather of the hilt creaking. My other hand presses down on his shoulder, feeling the bone beneath the wool. I look at the hollow of his throat, not his eyes. Then I move.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The blade went in clean.

Wrack watched it happen—the way his arm drove forward, wrist staying loose the way she'd told him, the angle finding the space she'd described. The boy's body jerked once beneath his hand, a reflex more than resistance, and the sound that came was what she'd said it would be. Not a scream. Something between a gasp and a sigh, air leaving a body that wouldn't draw more.

Corvin's support hand held steady on the shoulder. Good. That was good.

The boy's fingers spasmed against his wound, then went slack. His eyes stayed open, but the thing behind them was already gone—just flesh now, waiting to catch up. The blood came in pulses, slower than a heartbeat, fading. Wrack counted three before it stopped.

Corvin pulled the blade free. Straight out, same angle. The sound it made was wet, soft—the body releasing its grip the way bodies did when there was nothing left to hold on with.

Wrack stayed where she was for a moment, watching the stillness settle. Then she nodded.

"Form was good," she said. No warmth in it, no praise—just assessment, the way she'd promise. "Angle was right. Speed was right. You didn't twist on the way out." She paused, considering. "Your elbow came up too high on the follow-through. Wasted motion, puts your shoulder in a weaker position if you need to strike again. Keep it tight next time."

*Next time.* She said it like it was just a thing that might happen, which it was.

"Support hand held. That matters more than most people think. A man who's dying can still claw at you, grab the blade. You kept him pinned without pressing down hard enough to shift your weight. That's instinct doing the right thing. Trust it."

She looked at the body. At the blood on Corvin's hands, his knife, his knees where he'd knelt in the wet grass.

"Three," she said. "You did three tonight. That's more than most men do in a year of this." She straightened, her joints cracking. "You'll want to clean that blade before the blood sets. Harder to get off after, and a sticky blade catches when you need it smooth."

She turned toward the road, where the last of the light was fading.

"I'll check the grass for the one I missed. You sit. Drink the water that tastes like leather." A beat. "You earned both."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat too tight for words. I find the water skin and take a long pull. It does taste like leather. I sit there in the dark and I don't look at the bodies. I just listen to the quiet.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack finished with the knife and sheathed it, then sat back on her heels. The dead man's cloak she left where it was; she wasn't going to carry it home, but she wasn't sentimental enough to fold it for him either.

"Hmm," she said. That was about as much as she gave most silences.

She picked up a waterskin from the ground — hers, by the way it was tied — and took a mouthful, swilled, spat. Then she drank properly. When she spoke again, her voice had the flat, unhurried quality of someone stating the weather.

"Couple options. You go put him out clean, and we don't have to listen to him. You bring him in, and we got a prisoner to feed and mind, which is a pain in the arse, but sometimes worth a bit of silver. Or you leave him, and we walk away and maybe he lives and maybe he doesn't, and either way it's not our lookout by morning." She corked the skin. "But whichever it is, it'd be nice to know before the light goes. We've still got the road to make."

She glanced at Corvin then, briefly, the way a farrier glances at a horse that's shied at the same stone twice. Not unkind. Just measuring.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, the taste of blood still in my throat. "A prisoner," I say, forcing my voice steady. "They might know who paid for this." I start toward the cart, then hesitate. "You coming?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The question sat there a moment, and Wrack gave it the weight it deserved, which was not much.

"You don't need me to hold his hand," she said. She pushed herself up off her heels with a grunt that had nothing to do with effort and everything to do with her knees, and began the unhurried business of checking the dead for anything worth carrying. A purse, a good belt knife, a shortbow with a sound limb — those things paid for bread the same as prisoners did, and they didn't whimper.

She didn't say no. She didn't say yes. She just worked her way down the line of bodies with the focused disinterest of a woman picking blackberries.

"You go ahead," she said, over her shoulder. "I'll be along. If he tries anything clever, you put a knife in him and we'll discuss whether he was worth more breathing. If he doesn't, and you want him walking, you tie his hands proper — not that knot you tie, the one that looks like a knot. Use the rope on his own belt if you have to. He'll be slower, but he'll bleed less."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack paused in her work, a man's purse half-open in her hand. She didn't turn around. She let the question sit for a beat, as though she were weighing the coins inside it.

"Depends on who you ask," she said. "He'll live through the night if you bind the leg. Probably. Might not keep the leg, but he'll live through it, and that's a mercy to him and a problem for us, because a man with one leg is slow and heavy and he'll want us to carry him and then he'll want us to bury him proper, and somewhere in there he'll forget we cut him in the first place."

She tipped the purse into her palm, counted under her breath, and tucked it away. She moved to the next body.

"The other kind," she said, "that's the one where he won't see morning no matter what you do, and you're just choosing when. That's not a mercy. That's a favour to yourself so you don't have to listen."

She crouched, unbuckled a belt, considered the knife that hung from it, and took it too.

"So. Which is it for him?" She glanced over her shoulder then, and there was something in her face that wasn't quite impatience. "And while you're figuring that out, figure out which is it for you. Because the first one I can dress. The second one, you'd better sort out before we make camp."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I walk towards the cart slowly, my own knife out but held low. When I see him—a man with a deep gash in his thigh, pale and sweating—I stop. "He's the first kind," I call back, voice tight. "But I don't know if I've got the stomach to drag him."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't answer right away. She finished with the belt she was unbuckling, buckled it around her own waist over her sword-belt, and came trudging across the dead ground toward the cart. Not fast. Not slow. The pace of a woman who'd heard a thing and was coming to have a look for herself.

She came up beside Corvin and stood there a moment, looking down at the man the way you'd look at a horse with a thrown shoe. Clinical. Unromantic.

"Mm," she said. "Yes. First kind."

She crouched, not gracefully, and put two fingers to the man's throat without asking his permission. He flinched and made a sound. She ignored both.

"Pulse is up, which is bad, but it's there. He's bled a lot but not all of it. Thigh wound, you said — yes, there it is." She tilted her head, considering. "Femoral's missed, or he'd be gone already. That's the good news. Bad news is the muscle's in it, and once muscle's in it, you don't get a clean heal. He'll walk with a stick and a limp the rest of his life, assuming he keeps the leg."

She sat back on her heels and looked up at Corvin. Not judging. Just looking.

"Now. As to the dragging." She wiped her hands on her trousers, which were already past saving. "You don't have to like it. You just have to do it. And there's a trick to it, which is you don't think of him as a man. You think of him as a sack of meat that's worth silver, because right now that's all he is to you. You can go back to thinking of him as a man later, when there's a wall between you and him."

She jerked her chin toward the man's belt.

"Rope's there. Cut his belt off, use the belt to bind the leg above the wound — tight, tighter than you think, he'll forgive you when he's alive tomorrow. Then we truss him like a goose and take him by the wrists. You take the shoulders, I'll take the feet. He'll scream. That's all right. He's allowed one."

She paused, and something in her face shifted, just slightly.

"And Corvin." She said it flat, the way she said most things. "The stomach comes back. It just takes longer the first time."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack shifted her weight and leaned over the wound, pointing with the tip of her knife — not touching, just indicating.

"See how the skin's pulled back here, like a lip?" She traced the air above the gash. "That's because something went in deep and came out sideways. Whatever hit him — sword, most likely, given the width — it tore the muscle as it left. That's why it's bleeding like that and not in a clean pulse. If it were the artery, he'd be dead already and you'd be looking at a different problem."

She sat back and tapped her own thigh, high up near the hip.

"What you're worried about is up here. Feel under your fingers — no, don't actually put your fingers in the wound, just here, on your own leg." She waited. "That's where the big one's running. If that's cut, you bleed out in minutes. It's not cut. So he's ours to do what we like with, and that includes saving."

She gestured at the edges of the gash.

"See the dark bit? That's dead meat already. It'll have to come out later if he lives, or the wound'll go rotten and then he'll wish he hadn't. See the yellow? That's fat. Means the cut went deeper than the muscle. Means when it heals, if it heals, the skin's going to knit to the meat underneath and he'll always feel it pull when he bends the knee."

She looked up at Corvin then, and her expression was neither kind nor unkind. Just factual.

"That's what you're looking at. A leg that'll work, sort of, if we stop the bleeding and he doesn't get fever. Now you know."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel, my hands shaking slightly as I fumble with his belt. "Tighter than I think," I repeat under my breath, pulling until his knuckles turn white. He groans, his eyes fluttering open. "Sorry," I mutter, not sure if he hears me.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched Corvin work without offering to help. That wasn't cruelty; it was the same reason you don't take the knife from a man learning to gut his first deer.

"Good," she said, when the binding was on. "Now check the colour of his toes. If they're going blue, loosen it a finger's width. If they're pink, leave it."

The man's eyes had focused on her now, which meant he was coming round properly. That was either good or bad, depending.

"He'll want water in a minute," she said. "Don't give him any yet. Give it to him after we move him and he thinks he's earned it. Right now if you fill him up he'll just sick it back out on the road."

She stood, knees cracking again, and moved around to take his ankles.

"Right. On three. One, two—"

She didn't say three. She lifted on two, which was either an accident or a kindness, because it gave Corvin half a second less to think about what he was doing.

The man screamed. Wrack let him.

"There it is," she said, conversationally, already walking. "One's spent. Now we've got a quiet few miles before he finds his lungs again."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
They made it about twenty paces before the prisoner found his breath again and started in with the weeping — which was better than screaming, Wrack supposed, and worse in some other ways.

"Don't stop," she said, to Corvin, not to the man. "He'll quiet down when he sees you're not stopping."

She shifted her grip on the ankles. The man's boot slid off; she caught it by the toe and shoved it back on without breaking stride. Small mercies. She'd learned that the hard way, dragging a man barefoot over a stony road for a mile and having to listen to him beg for his boots the whole way.

"As to your question." She considered it as they walked, the way she might consider a piece of meat at a fire — turning it over, looking for the best place to bite in. "You said you wanted it straight, so. A spear's the worst of them, for the gut. Swords cut, and if you're lucky the cut's clean and the man bleeds out quick. An axe splits, and it's ugly but it's over. A spear — a spear's made for poking holes, and the holes it pokes are deep, and then somebody shoves it deeper, and then somebody twists it on the way out because that's what they teach you to do."

She paused, adjusting her grip on the ankles.

"And the gut — the gut's a long tube, and it folds back on itself, so when you put a hole in it, what comes out isn't just what's there at the time. It's everything that's behind it, working its way down. Which means a man gut-speared might bleed a little from the front hole, but what really kills him is the stuff that's leaking out into the space behind the muscle. That sits there. That goes bad. That eats him from the inside, and it takes days, and the whole time he's awake and he knows exactly what's happening because the gut hasn't got nerves that feel pain. The skin around it does. So he feels it at the edges, and he doesn't feel it where it matters, and he can't tell the doctor where it hurts, and the doctor opens him up and there's nothing to be done because it's already everywhere."

They walked a few more paces in silence.

"That's a spear," she said, flatly. "That's what it does. You wanted straight, that's straight."

She glanced back at Corvin, then ahead again.

"Now. You asked me not to clean it up. I'm not. But I'll say this, because somebody should've said it to me when I asked. Knowing what it does doesn't make it easier to do. It makes it harder, in some ways, because before you knew you could tell yourself it was quick, it was clean, he didn't suffer. Now you know different. So you'll do it anyway, because the work's there to do, but you won't have the lie to hold onto afterward. That's the cost of asking. I hope it was worth the price."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I don't say anything for a while, just keep walking with his shoulders in my hands. "Thanks," I finally get out, my voice rough. "For not lying."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't acknowledge it. She just walked, and the silence she left for him had a different texture than the ones she usually kept — a little more space in it, maybe, as though she'd made a gap in her usual armour for the word to fit into without being remarked on.

The prisoner had stopped weeping and started in with a low, continuous moan, which Wrack marked as an improvement. A man who could moan could be reasoned with. A man who only screamed couldn't.

They came to a bend in the road where the hedgerow broke and the last of the light slanted through. Wrack stopped, set the man's feet down carefully, and crouched to check the binding on his leg without being asked.

"Holding," she said, to no one in particular. "That's something, anyway."

She stood and looked back down the road the way they'd come, then forward, then at Corvin.

"We'll make the wood by dark if we keep on. There's a hollow I know off the track — out of the wind, a bit of cover. We'll water him there, see if he says anything useful before the fever takes him or it doesn't. If he talks, we get the name of who set this up. If he doesn't, we get a body to bury or leave, and we're out a hope but no worse than we were."

She nudged the man's boot with her toe, gently. Checking he was still in him.

"As to thanks." She said it to the road, not to Corvin. "You don't thank a woman for telling you what's true. You thank her for being the one who'd do it, and even that sounds strange in the mouth. But I heard it, and I'll keep it. Now let's walk."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped. She didn't turn around right away, and there was a beat — just a beat — where her shoulders rose and fell once in a way that might have been a sigh or might have been her resettling the weight of the body on her back.

"Alright," she said, and her voice was the same as it had been: flat, unhurried, factual. But there was something in it that hadn't been there before, a thin edge of something she wasn't naming. She set the man's feet down again, came back, and crouched opposite Corvin at the man's head.

"Hold him by the jaw," she said. "Both hands. You're going to want to let go, and you can't, because if you do he'll twist and you'll do worse than you mean to. Tilt his head back. Keep the airway open. That's your whole job now — keep that airway open and don't let him move."

She waited until Corvin had the man's face held steady. Then she reached across and put her hand flat on the man's chest, just to feel the rise and fall of it.

"He's still breathing. Good. That's where we start."

She looked at Corvin then, and her face was the farrier's face again, the one that measured without judging.

"You asked for all of it. So. The sound first. A man dying by the blade — by the throat — he doesn't scream. He makes a sound like he's trying to cough and swallow at the same time, because what he's doing is trying to breathe through a hole that's full of blood. It's a wet sound. You'll know it when you hear it. It's not like any other sound a body makes, because it isn't a sound the body means to make. It's just air and blood meeting wrong."

She paused.

"The length of it. It varies. Some go quick — a minute, maybe less, if you've done the cut right and the heart's still pushing. Some hang on. Five minutes. Ten. Longer. The ones that hang on are the ones you'll remember, because they look at you while they're doing it, and you can't do anything about that, you just have to take it. The eyes don't go blank right away. That's a lie. They go blank in stages."

She glanced down at the man's throat, then back up.

"The feel of it. Under your hands — and you'll feel this, you can't not — there's a pulse at first. Fast. It's the body trying to pump what's left. Then it gets slower. Then it gets strange. It skips. It doubles up. Then it goes thin, like a thread, and then it goes away, and your hands will know before your eyes do, because your hands are on the skin and the skin tells you. That's how you'll know it's over. Not the silence. Not the look. The pulse going out under your fingers like a tide."

She straightened up, slowly, and looked at Corvin's face. Whatever she saw there, she didn't look away from.

"That's what you're doing to him. Whatever else you are, whatever else you were before this morning, you're a man killing another man, and he's going to feel it, and you're going to feel it, and nobody in the world is going to tell you either of those things is honourable. It's just what it is. Work. Ugly work, and you asked for the description, so there's the description."

She reached out and put her hand over Corvin's on the man's jaw. Not to move it. Just to press it there, firmly, so he couldn't pull away.

"Now do it. I'll stay. I'll watch. And when it's done, you put your hands down, and you don't wash them yet, because the feel of it is part of the lesson, and the lesson's the only thing that'll keep you from hesitating next time when hesitation is what kills you."

She sat back on her heels, and waited.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take a breath, and my hands aren't shaking anymore. I look the man in the eye as I draw my knife. "Alright," I whisper. "Alright."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The road took them. Wrack didn't look back.

She walked with the man's ankles in her grip and her eyes on the track, and the silence she kept was the working kind — the kind that didn't need filling. By the time the last light had thinned to a seam between the trees, the prisoner had gone quiet in the way Wrack had said he'd go quiet, and the only sounds were their boots and the small noise Corvin was making with his breathing that he probably didn't know he was making.

She didn't remark on it.

When they reached the hollow — a scoop in the hillside where the roots of an old oak had pulled the earth into a kind of crooked room — Wrack set the man's feet down and stood a moment, listening. Nothing. Just the wind in the branches and the small settling sounds of a wood at dusk.

"We're here," she said, to no one in particular. She pulled the shortbow from her back, tested the string with her thumb, and leaned it against the trunk within reach. Then she crouched and began to clear a space in the leaf litter with her hands, scraping back to bare earth.

"Fire's out of the question. Smoke'll have every patrol in the hills down our throats by midnight. Cold camp tonight. We can manage a heat-stone if you've got one in your pack, and we've got cloaks." She glanced at Corvin. "Have we got cloaks?"

She didn't wait for the answer. She was already moving on to the next thing, the way she always did — one task after another, the way water finds its way downhill. She found a flat stone at the base of the roots and dragged it over, propped the man's bound leg up on it so the wound was higher than his heart, which she said was for the bleeding and which was also, Wrack suspected, so Corvin didn't have to look at it in the dark.

"Now," she said, sitting back on her heels. "We water him. We wait. We see if he's got anything to say before the fever finds him. If he does — good. We get a name, we get a direction, we get something to take to whoever's paying us, if anyone's still paying us, which is its own question."

She pulled the waterskin from her belt and held it out toward Corvin.

"You do it. He saw your face last. He's more likely to drink from your hand than mine, and besides — " she paused, and something in her mouth worked, as though she were tasting the next words before she let them out. "Besides, it does a man good to do a kindness with the same hands that did the harm. Don't ask me who told me that. I don't remember. Maybe nobody did. Maybe I just made it up to get through a night or two of my own."

She set the waterskin down in the space between them, and then she did something Wrack didn't usually do. She sat down properly, back against the root, and stretched her legs out, and let the quiet come back in.

"You did the work," she said, after a while, when the quiet had had its full say. "That's all there is to it. You did it, and it's done, and he's past hurting, and you aren't, which is the part that'll keep you up tonight. So if you've got something to say, say it now while I'm too tired to make a joke of it. Tomorrow I'll have my armour back on, and you'll have to do your grieving on the road like the rest of us."

She tipped her head back against the root and looked up at the last of the light through the branches, and waited.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack was quiet for a long time. Long enough that a bird settled in the branches above them and settled out again. When she spoke, her voice had a different grain to it — not softer, exactly, but worn, the way a stone is worn by water that's had years to work on it.

"Right," she said. "The rest."

She pulled her belt knife and began to clean her nails with the tip, not looking at Corvin. It was a thing she did when she was reaching back into herself, he would learn. A thing to do with her hands so the rest of her could go where it needed to go.

"I was nineteen. First real fight. There was a woman in the company — Halé, her name was, and she wasn't much older than me, and she was better than me at the work, which I hated her for in the way you only hate people you're trying not to love. We got caught in a skirmish outside a town I don't remember the name of. I don't even remember what the war was about by then. It had been about something, I'm sure. It always is, at the start."

The knife-tip found something under her nail. She worked at it.

"There was a man. I don't know who he was. I don't know what side he was on, in any way that mattered. He came at me with a pike — not a spear, a pike, the long kind, the kind that's meant to keep you away — and I was too slow getting my shield up, and he put it through my sword-arm. Clean through, the meat of it, missed the bone by a finger's width. I remember the sound it made going in. Not the wet sound, not yet. A kind of pop, like a ripe fruit. That's what flesh sounds like when it opens for something it wasn't expecting."

She set the knife down on her knee.

"I dropped my sword. He pulled the pike out to finish me, and that's when Halé came round behind him. She had a short blade, a little thing, not much longer than my hand. And she put it into the back of his neck, just at the base, just where the spine meets the skull, and she twisted it, and she left it in, and she stepped back, and she said to me — and this is the part I remember, this is the part I keep — she said, 'Stay with me now, Wrack. Stay with me, and I'll see to him after.'"

Wrack's hand had stopped moving.

"And the man was on the ground. And I was on the ground too, a few paces off, with my arm going wrong and my blood coming out faster than I wanted it to. And he was looking at me. Not at Halé. At me. Because I was the one he'd hurt, and I was the one who was nearest, and his eyes were doing the thing I told you about — going blank in stages — and he was trying to say something, and I couldn't hear it because of the blood in my own ear, but I could read his mouth. He was saying a name. I don't know whose. Maybe a wife's. Maybe a child's. Maybe his own, because he was afraid, and people say their own name sometimes when they're afraid, as though reminding themselves they're there."

She was quiet for a moment.

"Halé came to me first. She did my arm, because if she'd done his — and I'll say this careful, because I want you to hear it right — if she'd done his first, I might've bled out while she worked. She chose me. She chose to let him die slow so I wouldn't. I knew that while she was doing it. I knew what she was doing and why, and I didn't tell her not to, and I didn't tell her to stop, and I didn't even think about telling her, because I was nineteen and I was bleeding and I wanted to live."

She picked the knife up again and began to slide it back into its sheath, slowly, as though she were giving the words time to land.

"He died while she was tying off the stump of my arm. I don't know exactly when. I was looking at her hands. But when I looked up, he was quiet, and the thing he'd been trying to say was in his mouth unspoken, and that was the end of him. And Halé finished with me, and she sat back, and she didn't say a word, and I didn't say a word, and we stayed like that until the rest of the company came up."

She looked at Corvin then. Not the farrier's look. Something else.

"So. The rest. The rest is, you can do everything right and still carry the man you didn't help. You can choose the one you love over the one you don't know, and it can be the right choice, and you can know it was the right choice, and it can still come back to you on cold nights for the rest of your life. It doesn't go away. You just learn where to put it down so you can pick up your sword in the morning."

She drew her knees up and rested her arms across them.

"Halé died three winters later. Fever. Nothing to do with any of this. And I was the one who sat with her, and I was the one who closed her eyes, and I said her name, and not the other man's, because hers was the one I had left. That's the work. That's all of it. You do it, and it does you, and you keep going because the road's still there and the bread's still got to be earned."

The prisoner stirred. A small sound, a shifting. Wrack didn't look at him.

"Now you know what I know. And it's yours to do what you like with. I'd say don't tell anyone, but that's a lie — you'll tell someone, one day, when you've had enough years to make it sound like a story instead of a thing that happened to you. That's alright too. Stories are how we set the weight down." She tipped her head back against the root again. "Just don't tell it tonight. Tonight we rest, and we watch him, and we make the road in the morning, and we don't say another word about it unless you need to."

She closed her eyes. Not sleeping. Just done.

"There. That's the rest. Are you satisfied, or do you want the rest of the rest, because there's more, but it's older, and I'm tired, and I'd rather save it for the next time you ask, because there'll be a next time, there always is."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit there for a long time, listening to the trees. "I'm satisfied," I say, my voice quiet. I pick up the waterskin and go to him.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack kept her eyes closed. She listened to Corvin move to the man, to the small sounds of waterskin and throat working, and she let herself have the quiet the way you let yourself have a drink of clean water when you've been a long time in the dust.

She didn't open her eyes until Corvin had settled back.

"He drink?" she asked, without moving.

She listened to the answer, and to whatever else was in it.

"Mm. Good. That's something, then. Now we wait, and we watch, and we see what the night brings him."

She opened one eye, then the other, and looked at Corvin sidelong.

"Get some sleep if you can. I'll take first watch. You've done enough being awake for one day."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: He drinks a little. I sit back against a root, the damp of the ground seeping through my trousers. "I'll sleep," I say, but I don't think I will.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack let it lie. She knew the difference between a man saying he'll sleep and a man sleeping, and she knew better than to argue the point when the argument would only sharpen the thing he was trying to set down.

She drew her cloak off and tossed it across his knees without ceremony.

"You'll get the chill, sitting on the ground like that. Use that, don't thank me for it, and if you do sleep, sleep light. I've got the watch but I've only got the one pair of ears, and yours are closer to him than mine."

She settled back against her own root, the shortbow across her knees, and let the quiet come in.

The prisoner breathed. The wood settled. Somewhere out past the track a fox made a small, sharp noise and stopped.

Wrack didn't sleep. She watched the dark between the trees, and she listened, and she let Corvin have the time he thought he wasn't taking.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I pull the cloak over my legs, the smell of old sweat and leather familiar. After a while, I find myself watching the prisoner's chest rise and fall. "He's still breathing," I say, just to break the quiet.
