dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack finished with the knife and slid it home, then wiped her hands one against the other, which did nothing except move the mess around. She got up out of the crouch with the small, deliberate care of someone whose knees had opinions.

"You heard him," she repeated. Not a question. She looked at Corvin properly then, taking in the wet on his face and the fact that he hadn't wiped his hands the way she had, hadn't done anything with them at all. "Blood's not yours. In case you were wondering. It sits different when it's yours. Warmer for a second, then it isn't."

She let that sit, then jerked her chin toward the cart and whatever was making noise behind it. The sound had thinned. That was its own kind of answer, but not a fast one.

"Here's the shape of it," she said. "He's gut-shot or worse, from the way he's carrying on. That doesn't stop. It goes slow, and it gets worse, and then some hours from now it stops on its own and he's been screaming the whole time — or one of us walks over there and it stops now." She shrugged, not unkindly. "There's no clean version. I want to be honest with you about that, because people your first few times go looking for a clean version and there isn't one. There's only who does it."

She waited. She didn't reach for the knife again. Not yet.

"You don't have to. I'll do it. But if I do it, I want you to watch, because it's easier to send someone else to the cart the second time if you never had to see the first."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow, the taste of iron heavy in my mouth. My hands are sticky, and I still can't bring myself to look at them. "I'll do it," I say, voice low. I force my legs to move, taking a step toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack fell in beside him, half a step back, close enough to catch him if his legs quit but not close enough to make it look like she expected them to.

"Alright," she said. "Then listen, because I'm only going to say it walking and I'm not going to say it again once we're standing over him."

The noise past the cart had a wet edge to it now, a man breathing through something that shouldn't be there. Flies had started to find the others behind them. It was that hour.

"Don't do the throat. It's what people reach for and it's the worst of the lot — takes longer than you'd think, and he'll fight you, and you'll both remember it. You go here." She tapped two fingers below her own ear, along the hinge of the jaw, then drew them down the side of the neck. "Or under the ribs, up, if the throat's covered. Fast in, and you lean your weight into it, you don't saw. You commit or you don't go at all. Half a thing is worse than nothing."

They came around the cart's edge. The man was younger than the cloak had suggested. He was holding himself together with both hands and not managing it. His eyes came up and found Corvin's, and stayed there.

Wrack didn't look away from him either, but she spoke low, to Corvin. "He can see you. That's the part nobody warns you about. You do it anyway, and you do it kind, and kind means fast." She stepped back, giving him the room. "Knife's on your hip. Whenever you're ready. Not before."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack crouched — not to make a show of examining him, but because standing over a dying man to appraise him was a thing she didn't do — and looked at the way his hands sat, at the color coming up under his skin, at the shine of what he was holding in.

"Both," she said. "Because it's always both, and if you go looking for a version where it's only the clean one you'll be standing here past dark." She said it flat, but she wasn't dodging. "But you asked me straight, so. He's opened up low and it's the bad kind. That doesn't close. If we walked away right now and sent the best cutter in the company running, and he was already here with clean hands and light — he still dies. Slower. Screaming, most of the way. That's the mercy part, and it's real, and I'm not saying it to make it sit easier on you."

She glanced up at Corvin, brief.

"The easier part's real too. I'm tired, you're shaking, and I want to be off this road. Both of those are true at the same time as the mercy. That's what nobody tells you." She looked back at the man, whose eyes had drifted to her now, then swung back to Corvin like Corvin was the one who'd decide. "Doesn't make it a lie. Just means you don't get to do it feeling clean about it. You do it and you carry the both of them. That's the job."

She didn't move to take the knife herself. She stayed crouched, close, steady.

"He's listening to us talk about him," she added, quieter. "So whatever you're deciding, decide it soon."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath and pull my knife. "Alright," I say, more to myself than anyone. My eyes stay locked with his as I kneel down.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stayed where she was, just off his shoulder, and kept her voice down to nothing.

"Good. Don't look away now — you started it looking at him, you finish it looking at him. He's not asking you for anything except that you don't make a mess of it." She watched the knife in Corvin's hand, watched the grip, and reached over without fuss to turn his wrist a fraction — thumb here, edge angled up, the way you'd correct a child holding a spoon wrong. Practical. No weight to it.

"Under the ribs, then. His hands are in the way of the throat and I don't want you fighting them. Here." She set two fingers briefly against the man's side, low, under the arch of the bone, then took her hand back out of the way. "You go in soft-side and up, toward the middle of him. Lean. All your weight, straight through your arm into it. Then you hold it — you don't pull it right back out, you hold, count to yourself, slow. Let it do the work. Pulling out fast is for the man's benefit who's squeamish, not the man on the ground."

The soldier's breath hitched, a thin whistling thing. His eyes hadn't left Corvin's. There was less fight in them than there'd been a minute ago. That was the body starting to be sensible about it, whatever the man wanted.

"He's ready before you are," Wrack said. "They usually are." A beat. "Whenever your hand stops shaking, or in spite of it. Both work. Go."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack came up beside him, following his gaze down to the man on the ground, and gave the answer plainly, the way you'd read out a map.

"You're looking at a man about your own age who picked the same work you did and stood on the wrong side of a ditch this morning. That's the first thing, and you can set it down or carry it, but look at it once." She let that be there a second, then moved on, because dwelling wasn't a kindness to anyone here.

"Now the body." Her voice dropped into something even, almost gentle, the tone of someone naming parts. "See the color under his jaw — that grey coming up? That's him losing the fight quiet, from the inside. His hands are pressed low because that's where it hurts and where it's open. Don't watch his hands, they'll only make you sad. Watch here." Two fingers, a hair above the man's collarbone, at the pulse. "That's still going. Fast and thin. When it stops, he's gone, and you'll feel it stop under your hand if you're keeping one there, which you should. So you know. So you're not guessing."

The soldier's eyes had gone glassy but they still tracked Corvin, dull now, patient in the way of an animal that has stopped expecting anything.

"And him looking at you — that's not accusing you. People decide that's what it is because it's easier than the truth. The truth is he doesn't want to be alone in the last of it, and you're the face that's here. That's all it is. That's the whole of it." She looked at Corvin, steady. "So you're not looking at a thing you're doing to him. You're looking at the last company he gets. Now put your hand where mine was, feel the pulse, and put the knife where I showed you. And keep looking at him. You're doing right by him. Go on."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I reach out, my hand trembling as I press my fingers where hers were. His pulse flutters against my fingertips, weak and frantic. "Alright," I whisper, to him or to me, I'm not sure. I set the blade where she showed me, take one last breath, and lean in.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack said nothing while he did it. That was deliberate. There was a moment where a voice at your ear was the last thing you needed, and she knew where it was, and she held her tongue through it.

She watched the knife go in — clean, committed, his weight behind it the way she'd told him. Good. The man's breath caught and let go, one long shudder that ran the length of him and then didn't come back for more. His hands loosened. His eyes stayed on Corvin's, which was the part that would stay with him, and there was nothing to be done about that except let it happen.

"Hold it," she murmured. "Keep your hand on his pulse. Don't count out loud, just count." She watched Corvin's face more than the man's now, because the man was already most of the way gone and Corvin was the one still here. "You'll feel it go. Won't be dramatic. Just — thins out, and then there's nothing under your fingers. Wait for that. Don't pull the knife yet."

The soldier's chest gave one more small movement, and then it was still, and the flutter under Corvin's fingertips stumbled, skipped, and quit.

"There," she said quietly. "That's it. He's gone. You can feel it's gone." She reached over and, unhurried, put her hand over Corvin's on the knife's grip — not taking it, just steadying — and eased it out for him, slow, the way she'd said. She wiped the blade on the dead man's sleeve and folded it closed into Corvin's palm.

"You did it right," she said. "Fast, and looking at him. That's more than most manage their first time." She got up, knees complaining, and stood over him a moment — not judging, just present. "Now stand up. You'll want to sit down and you're going to stand up instead, because sitting down here is how it gets its hooks in you. Up you get."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at him a moment — a longer look than she'd given him all day — and something in her face shifted, not softer exactly, but like a door being held open where usually it stayed shut.

"Alright," she said. "Straight, then."

She crouched again, and this time she did put her hand near the wound, not touching, just indicating, the way you'd point out the parts of a thing you were teaching someone to butcher.

"Spear's a shove, not a cut. Goes in narrow and it doesn't care what's in the way. In the gut, that's rope — yards of it, coiled up soft. It'll nick the bowel, or open it, and that's the killing part, not the blood. Blood you can sometimes stop. What comes out of the bowel you can't put back, and it gets into the rest of him, into the meat of his belly, and it rots him from the inside while he's still awake to feel it. That's the smell — you'll have caught it. That's not death you're smelling. That's a living man going bad."

She let her hand rest on her own knee.

"Takes a day. Sometimes two, if he's strong, and strong's the cruelty of it — the strong ones last longest. Fever comes up. Belly swells hard as a drum. He'd have been thirsty and you couldn't have given him water, it'd have made it worse, so he'd have begged and you'd have said no, and that's its own kind of thing to carry. Toward the end he'd have stopped making sense, and then stopped making noise, and you'd have thought that was better. It isn't. It just means he's too far gone to tell you about it."

She stood, slow, and looked down at the dead man with the flat, level regard of someone who'd seen the long version more than once and preferred not to.

"That's what a spear does. That's what you spared him." She held Corvin's eye. "I'm not saying it to make you feel good about it. I'm saying it because you asked straight and you'll hear a hundred lies about this work before you're done. Wanted at least one true thing in you first." A beat. "Now up. I meant it about the sitting down."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I push myself up, legs feeling like they don't belong to me. My hand is still sticky with his blood. "Truth feels worse," I mutter, wiping my palm on my trousers. "But thanks."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched him get up on legs that clearly disagreed with the plan, and she gave a short nod, satisfied enough by it. Up was up.

"It feels worse because it is worse," she said. "That's the whole reason people don't tell it. Lies are lighter to carry. Trouble is they don't hold weight when you actually need them to, and then you're standing over the next cart with nothing true in your hands." She started walking, angling him back toward the ditch and the others and the horses beyond, away from the body, because standing there admiring your own work was another one of the small doors that let it in. "You'll get offered the light version plenty. Man'll clap you on the back tonight, tell you it was a clean kill, righteous, one less enemy. Some of that's kind and some of it's him needing to believe it about his own dead. Take what helps. Don't swallow it whole."

She glanced at his trousers, at the smear he'd made trying to be rid of it.

"That doesn't come off dry, by the way. You'll rub at it all evening and just work it in. Cold water and time, or leave it." A dry twitch at the corner of her mouth, the first of the day. "Most of us leave it. You stop seeing it after a while. That's either a mercy or the thing that's wrong with all of us, depending who you ask."

They reached the ditch. The flies were loud now. She stopped, and looked at him properly one more time.

"You did a hard thing right and you asked for the truth instead of the comfort. That's rarer than the killing, and it's worth more." She jerked her chin toward the horses. "Now come on. There's water in my saddlebag, and we're not spending the dark here."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped mid-turn. For a moment she just looked at him, at the boy who'd asked once already and was asking again, harder, and she understood what he was doing even if he didn't have a word for it yet. He was making himself see it so it couldn't sneak up on him later. It was either the healthiest thing a person could do with this work or the start of a long, quiet ruin, and she'd known men who'd gone both ways off the same instinct.

She came back. She crouched beside him, close, and did not tell him no.

"Alright," she said. "I'll tell it. You keep your hand where it belongs and I'll do the rest."

His grip was wrong for this one — the throat, because he'd chosen the throat this time, and she didn't correct him, because there was a lesson in the harder way and he'd asked for it. She kept her voice low and even, naming each thing as it came, the way you'd narrate a river you'd crossed a hundred times to someone learning the fords.

"He's fighting you. That's the first thing, and it's why I steered you off the throat before — the body doesn't agree to it even when the man does. His hands are coming up. Let them. You lean into it, you don't stop for them." A beat. "The sound now — that wet drag, that's the air trying to go the old way and finding the new one you made. It's loud and it's ugly and it means it's working. Don't ease off because of the sound. Easing off is the cruelty here, not the pressing."

The man's heels worked against the dirt, short and jerking, then slower.

"Feel that in his legs going soft? That's him leaving before he's dead. Takes longer this way — count of thirty, forty, maybe. His eyes'll stay open. They do that. Doesn't mean he's seeing you anymore." Her hand stayed near, not on. "Keep going. You committed. Halfway through is the one thing you're not allowed."

The drag thinned. The heels stopped. She watched it all the way down with him, and only when it was truly still did she speak again, quiet.

"There. That one was harder, and you did it, and now you know why I told you the jaw." She didn't get up. She stayed crouched beside him in the loud, fly-thick quiet, giving him the room to sit in it exactly as long as he needed — which was the one time she'd let a man stay down by the bodies, because he'd earned the sitting by asking for the truth twice.

"That's all of it," she said. "Nothing left out. Now you carry it, and I'll carry it next to you, and we'll go find that water."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at my hands, the blood thick under my nails. My voice comes out rough. "You ever get used to it?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't answer straight away. She looked at his hands with him, at the dark packed in under the nails where it always went, the last of it to come out, sometimes days.

"No," she said finally. "Not the way you mean. You don't get to a place where it doesn't touch you. Anyone tells you they're there, they're either lying or there's a piece of them already dead and they didn't feel it go." She shifted her weight off her knees, settling. "What happens is smaller than used-to. You get quicker at it. Your hands stop shaking sooner. You stop looking for the clean version because you finally believe me that there isn't one. And the nights it sits on you — those get further apart. Not gone. Further apart."

She was quiet a moment, and the flies filled it.

"I'll tell you the true thing, since you keep asking for those. The day it stops touching you at all — that's the day to worry. That's not strength coming, that's the rot I told you about, except in you instead of him. I've watched it happen to good men. They get smooth about it, easy, and everybody thinks that's them coping." She shook her head slowly. "It's not. It's them gone hollow. So if it keeps costing you something — keep letting it. The cost is the part that means you're still in there."

She reached over and, without ceremony, took one of his hands and turned it, looking at the blood under the nails like it was a thing to be assessed rather than shied from.

"You'll get this out with a knife-point and cold water tonight. Takes patience. Most don't bother." She let his hand go. "You will, though. I can tell that about you already." A beat, dry. "For better or worse."

She got up, and this time she offered him her hand to do the same.

"Come on. Water, and then we ride. The dark's not going to wait for you to make peace with your fingernails."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack lowered her hand when he didn't take it, and she didn't push. She looked at him sitting back on his heels in the churned dirt with two dead men's blood on him and the light going amber and low, and she understood that "the rest" wasn't a question with an end to it. It was him holding the door open now, the one she kept shut, and asking her to walk through it in front of him so he'd know the room was survivable.

So she sat. Not crouched — sat, all the way down, in the dirt beside him, the way you sat when you'd decided you weren't going anywhere for a bit. Her knees made their opinion known and she ignored it.

"The rest," she said. "Alright."

She was quiet a moment, gathering it, because the true things didn't come out in order.

"First one I did was on purpose, in a fight, and I don't remember it. That's the thing nobody warns you — the first one, the one you think is going to be the mountain, half the time you don't even keep it. It's just noise and then it's over and someone's telling you you did well. Mine's gone. I've tried to find it and it isn't there." She picked a stalk of grass, turned it in her fingers, didn't do anything with it. "The one I kept was three weeks later. A boy. Not younger than me — I was young too — but a boy the way this one was a boy. He was under a horse that had gone down on him and his leg was wrong and he couldn't get free and he wasn't going to. And there was no ambush about it, no heat, no one swinging at me. It was just quiet, and him looking at me, and me deciding. That's the one that stays. The quiet ones. The ones where you had time to be a person about it and did it anyway."

She let the grass fall.

"That one I did badly. I didn't know the jaw yet. Nobody sat with me the way I'm sitting with you — I got the back-clap and the clean-kill lie and I believed it for about a year and then I stopped believing it all at once, on a night that had nothing to do with anything, and I was sick behind a tent for it. That's how it comes for you if you swallow the lie whole. Not that day. Some other day, later, when you're not braced. It waits."

The flies were loud. She didn't hurry.

"There've been enough since that I couldn't give you a number and I won't pretend to. Some were mercy, like today. Some were the job — a man who'd have killed me if I'd been slower, and there's less to carry in those than people think, because he chose the ditch too. And some were neither. Some were orders I followed and shouldn't have, and men who weren't going to hurt anyone, and I did it because stopping would have cost me more than doing it, and I knew that at the time, and I did it anyway." She said it without dropping her eyes, without asking him to make it easier. "Those are the ones I don't get further apart from. Those come at the same rate they always did. You want the truth — that's the truth. Mercy fades. The job fades. The ones you knew were wrong, those keep their edges."

She was quiet again, and then she went on, lower.

"You lose the people you'd lose things for, too, and that's its own kind of it. I've got a few left. Fewer than I had. Every year the number goes down and it does not go back up — there's no season where you gather more of them, not in this. So you learn to be careful with the ones left, and stupidly loyal, because loyal's the only thing that's yours to give in a war that stopped meaning anything years back. I don't believe in the borders. I don't believe in either lord. I couldn't tell you what we're fighting over anymore and I don't think anyone up the chain could either. What's left, when you take all that away — and you should take it away, it's all lies — what's left is the person next to you. That's the whole of what I've got. That's it. That's the whole faith."

She looked at him then, direct.

"And here's the part I'd tell almost no one, so hear it once. There are mornings I don't know why I get up and do it again. No cause left, no coin worth this, most of what I loved already in the ground. And I get up anyway, and the reason I get up is small and stupid and it's usually just that someone I'm down to needs me to be there for the next bad thing. That's not glory. That's not even meaning. It's just the last rope holding, the one I told you about — narrow, and it doesn't care what's in the way, and it holds." Something dry moved at the corner of her mouth, tired. "You asked me to leave nothing out. That's the bottom of it. There's no clean version of the whole life either, same as there's no clean version of the cart. There's only who you stay for."

She let it sit. The light was nearly gone off the field.

"That's the rest," she said. "Or as much of it as fits in one sitting on cold ground, which is more than I've said out loud in years, so." She planted a hand and started the long argument with her knees toward standing. "Now I've bled for you, boy. Get up and come drink my water, so at least one of us got something out of it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I look at her, really look, for the first time all day. "You're staying for me, aren't you?" I ask, voice quiet. "Even though I'm just some new kid."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack got the rest of the way up, and she took her time about the answer — long enough that it wasn't a reflex, wasn't the easy thing said quick to close a wound. She looked down at him where he still sat, and she didn't soften her face into anything.

"Don't put words that big in my mouth yet," she said. "You're two dead men old. That's not nothing, but it's not a life spent, either." She held her hand out to him again, and this time she left it there. "I sat down for you. That's a thing I don't do. Read into that what you want, but read it careful."

He was still looking at her, so she gave him the rest of it, because she'd already opened the door and there was no closing it halfway.

"Here's what's true right now, this evening. You asked for the truth twice when you could've had the comfort, and you did a hard thing right, and then you did a harder thing worse and stayed in it anyway. That's not nothing in a person. Most bolt from the second one." Her hand stayed out, patient. "So no, I'm not staying for you. Not yet. You don't get that from me for one bad afternoon, and you shouldn't want it that cheap — the ones I stay for, I earned them and they earned me, over years, and half of them are dead for it. It's not a thing you'd wish on yourself if you understood the weight."

The corner of her mouth did the tired thing again.

"But I'll tell you what I am doing. I'm watching to see if you're worth staying for. That's different, and it's more honest, and it's the most anyone in this can promise a stranger without lying." A beat. "You keep asking for the true version instead of the kind one, you keep getting up when your legs vote against it — and you might get there. Might be one of my few, some year down the line, God help us both." 

She flexed her offered fingers, once, impatient now.

"That's the answer. Now take my hand, because it's getting dark and my knees have said their piece, and I'm not standing here holding it out like a fool while you decide whether I meant it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take her hand, my grip slick with blood. "Alright," I say, letting her pull me up. My legs hold. "And I'll take that water."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack hauled him up — she was stronger than the grey in her hair suggested, and she put her back into it without ceremony — and when he was on his feet and staying there, she let go and gave his shoulder one short grip, the kind of contact that meant *good* and didn't need saying.

"Legs held. Noted." She wiped her palm down her own thigh, transferring the slick of blood he'd left on it, and didn't remark on it beyond that. Just another thing that didn't come off dry.

She turned him with a hand between his shoulder blades, steering him toward the horses and away from the ditch, the flies, the two shapes going cold in the grass. She didn't look back at them and she made sure he didn't get the chance to either. Looking back was another door.

"Water's the skin on the left side, the one that isn't wine — don't mix them up, I'll want the wine later and I'll be short with you if it's gone." She walked half a step behind him again, that same easy distance, close enough to catch. "Drink slow. You'll want to pour it down all at once and your stomach's had a day. Small mouthfuls. Same rule as most things — commit, but don't rush the part that undoes you."

They reached the horses, which had stood through all of it the way horses did, patient and unbothered by the arithmetic of the men who rode them. Wrack loosed the water skin and put it in his hands herself, closing his fingers around it the way she'd closed them around the folded knife earlier.

"There." She swung up onto her own mount, settled, and looked down at him drinking in the last of the amber light with two men's blood drying on him and his legs still holding. Something in her face wasn't quite approval and wasn't quite grief. Close to both.

"We ride till full dark and then a bit past, till the smell's off us and this road's behind." She gathered her reins. "And you'll dig that muck out from under your nails tonight when we stop, like I said. Knife-point, cold water, patience." A dry beat. "I'll show you how. Seems I'm showing you everything else today."

She nudged the horse into a walk, and did not tell him to hurry, and left him room to finish the water first.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take a slow swallow, the water washing away the taste of iron. I cap the skin and tie it back in place, then haul myself into the saddle. My hands don't shake anymore. "Alright," I say, nudging my horse to follow hers. "Show me."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
They were most of the way through and both of them knew it, in the way you know a piece of music is nearly over before it ends.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's mouth curved into something that was not quite a smile, all sharp focus and pleased severity. Five years had etched the particular shade of Ines's stubbornness into her memory, but green was green, and she had never been in the habit of denying what was freely and clearly offered.

"Greedy," Sable said, letting the word settle between them like smoke. She resettled her grip on the flogger, leather creaking faintly against her palm, and stepped into the space she had carved out for herself. Her free hand moved to the nearest cuff—not to release it, but to verify the fit with a practiced twitch of her fingers, the reflex as automatic as breathing. "I was going to give you a moment. Now you'll wait longer for it."

The next stroke landed with a heavy, deliberate crack, placed precisely along the curve of Ines's shoulder where Sable had mapped her aim over half a decade of study. She held her stance, breathing steady, the impact shuddering up her own arm in a familiar jolt. She would not rush the end, not even for the water and the blanket she had already set aside in the next room; she would take Ines there only when the need was genuine and unmistakable, not merely because the hour suggested it.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stood, folded the knife, and slid it home. She looked at Corvin for a long moment -- not hard, not unkind, just assessing. Then she crossed the trampled ground toward the cart without comment.

The man was younger than she'd expected. He was trying to hold his insides in with both hands and doing a poor job of it. His eyes found hers. She crouched at the edge of his reach.

"Easy," she said. "I'm not here to hurt you." A pause. "I'm here to stop it."

He understood. You could see it in his face, the way the fight went out of him. She gave him a moment. Then she did the work.

When she came back, she wiped her hands on the nearest available cloth -- the dead man's trousers, by then there was no question of the cloth's prior cleanliness -- and looked at Corvin again.

"You don't have to watch," she said. "You don't have to do it either. But you do have to decide what you are. That man was holding his guts in with his hands and he was grateful when I made it stop." She let that settle. "The world's full of men who've made that choice one way or the other. You'll be one of them soon enough."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at the blood drying under my nails. "I know what I am." My voice is steadier than I feel. "Just didn't think it'd smell like this."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack snorted softly. Not quite a laugh.

"No," she said. "You don't think about it. You imagine steel and shouting and the glory of it, maybe. You don't imagine the smell." She flexed her fingers, looking down at them. The blood had dried in the creases of her knuckles, brown-black. "It gets easier. That's not a comfort, really. It's just what happens."

She started walking toward the horses, checking the straps on the saddlebags as she went.

"Smell lingers the longest. Then the sounds. Then the faces, but that takes longer still." She glanced back over her shoulder. "You remember their faces. Every one of them. That's how you know you're still a person."

The light was going thin and orange at the edges. Somewhere in the distance, dogs were starting up -- drawn to something, probably this. She'd want to be gone before they found their way to it.

"Take what you can carry," she said, already pulling herself into the saddle. "We'll make the river by midnight if we move. You can wash your hands then."

A pause. She looked down at Corvin, something unreadable in her expression.

"You did fine. Six's six, and you didn't freeze. That's more than some manage their first time." She nudged the horse forward. "Come on. We can fall apart somewhere that isn't here."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack paused, one hand on the reins. She looked back at the cart, then at Corvin, and her expression was flat in the way that meant she was thinking about it seriously rather than dodging the question.

"Both," she said. "It's both." She turned in the saddle, facing Corvin properly now. "The kind of man who'd set an ambush on a road like this one -- he's not going to die easy. Gut wounds don't. He'll have time to think about it, and he'll be in pain the whole way. By morning, maybe by noon tomorrow, he'll be dead no matter what. The difference is whether he spends that time screaming or not."

She let that hang.

"Easier for us is also better for him. That's not always the case. Most times there's no clean answer and you just pick the thing in front of you." She shrugged, one-shouldered. "This one was clean. Don't try to make it more than it was."

The horses shifted beneath them, restless. The dogs were louder now.

"He'll have people somewhere," Wrack said, matter-of-factly. "Wife, mother, someone. They'll wonder what happened to him. They won't know it was quick." She started riding, not waiting for a response. "That's the part that stays with you. Not the mercy. The knowing that somewhere there's someone who doesn't know."

She didn't look back again.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I mount up, keeping my eyes away from the cart. "Then maybe it's a mercy for them too." I tug the reins, turning my horse to follow hers.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack glanced back over her shoulder at that. She didn't slow the horse, but something in her posture shifted -- not softening, exactly. More like taking note.

"Maybe," she said. "I don't know that I'd lean on it too hard. Comfortable ideas have a way of curdling."

They rode in silence for a while, the horses finding their rhythm on the dirt road. The trees were thick enough here to cut the wind, which meant the smell would stay behind them. Good.

"Most people don't think about the people left behind," she said eventually. "You do. That's not a bad sign." She paused. "But don't let yourself believe you did it for them. You did it because it was the thing to do, and because he was suffering. Anything else is a story you tell yourself so you can sleep."

The road curved ahead, winding toward the river as she'd promised. The sky was bruising purple now, the first stars pricking through.

"You'll tell yourself stories," she added, quieter. "Everyone does. Just make sure you know they're stories. The ones who forget are the ones who stop being people."

She rode on, hands loose on the reins, watching the road ahead.

dialogue.name: Corvin

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack dismounted without a word. She crossed the trampled ground and crouched beside Corvin, close enough that their shoulders were nearly touching. She didn't tell him not to look away.

"See how he's curled," she said. "That's the body's last reflex. It tries to protect itself even when there's nothing left to protect. The arms come up, the legs draw in. Doesn't matter how he was positioned when it happened."

She pointed with one finger, not touching.

"Blood's darker than you expected, probably. Venous. Arterial's brighter, spurts. That's how you know where the wound is -- the blood's lighter near the source if it was a major vessel. This one's been pooling."

She paused, letting Corvin take it in at his own pace.

"His color. See it? Goes grey-blue after a while. That's the blood settling. Rigor comes later, then it passes. Then the smell changes." She said it matter-of-factly, not dwelling. "You'll learn to read it. How long they've been down, whether they suffered. Most of it tells you nothing useful except that it happened and it's over."

She stood, brushing her knees off.

"You wanted to know," she said. "Now you know. It's not knowledge that makes it easier. It's just knowledge." She looked down at the body, then back at Corvin. "Come on. He's past caring what you think of him."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
I swallow hard, my throat tight. "I thought he'd look more...angry." My eyes keep drifting back to the man's face, slack and empty now. "Or afraid."

(OOC: moving us along a bit) I turn away and start checking the saddlebags on their horses. "You said take what we can carry. Let's get this done."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack nodded once, approving. She moved to the nearest horse, already working the buckles on its saddlebags.

"Angry or afraid is when they're still in there," she said. "Once it's done, it's done. You saw him after. He was already gone before I ended it." She pulled a waterskin free, checked it, slung it over her shoulder. "The anger's for the living to carry. His people might imagine him fighting, defiant. Most do."

She handed Corvin a coil of rope, then a oilcloth bundle that turned out to be dried meat. Provisions.

"Anything small and valuable, you take it," she said. "Coin, jewelry, things that'll spend. Weapons if you use them. But mostly you're looking for letters, anything with a name. Might tell you who he was fighting for, whether there'll be more coming."

She found a small leather pouch, bit it open, tipped a few coins into her palm. Silver, not gold, but not nothing either.

"Six men and this is what they've got between them," she said, without much bitterness. "Company's not paying us enough either, but at least we get the certainty of a wage."

She passed the pouch to Corvin to carry. Then she paused, looking at him -- not the way she'd looked before, assessing whether he'd freeze. Something closer now. Just acknowledgment.

"You didn't vomit," she said. "Didn't faint. You asked questions and you did the work." She rolled her shoulders. "That's the job. Now you know."

The dogs were closer. Time enough.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack paused in the act of checking a saddle strap. She looked at Corvin for a moment, measuring something, then nodded once.

"Sit down," she said. "You don't want to hear this standing."

She settled onto a fallen log, gesturing for Corvin to do the same. When he was seated, she leaned forward, elbows on her knees.

"Spear's not like a sword," she said. "Sword cuts, tears. Spear punches through, drags everything with it when it pulls out. Gut's where it gets bad, because gut's not one thing. It's a coil. Peristalsis, you know -- the motion that moves food through. When you punch through that, you don't just make a hole. You contaminate the whole cavity. What's inside the gut gets into the rest of him."

She picked up a stick, traced a line in the dirt.

"Entry's small. Handled, mostly clean. It's what's behind it that kills. The blade tears the lining, hits the mesentery -- that's the thing that holds the gut to the wall. Rip that, and the gut loses its anchor. It starts to die. What doesn't die rots. And the body knows it, even when the man doesn't."

She broke the stick, let the pieces fall.

"Pain comes in waves at first. Then it doesn't. That's when you know it's bad, because the nerves are dying. But the body still fights. Fever sets in. The belly goes hard, not soft, because it's trying to wall itself off. It doesn't work. It can't."

She looked at Corvin steadily.

"Six hours, maybe twelve before the screaming starts if you don't finish it. Could be a day or more before the end, depending on where it hit. Some men hang on longer than they should. The body doesn't want to die even when it's already lost."

She leaned back.

"That's what a spear does. It's not quick like a blade through the throat. It's a process. It takes its time." She paused. "You asked. Now you know why I didn't let him suffer."

The dogs were very close now. Barking, excited. They'd be on the blood trail within minutes.

"Anything else you want to know, you ask now," she said. "After we ride, you carry it without knowing. That's how it works."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
I stare at the broken stick in the dirt. "Thanks." My voice sounds small. "Guess I'd rather know."

I stand up, brushing off my trousers. "What do we do if the dogs find us before we're gone?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack was already moving toward her horse.

"Depends on whose dogs they are," she said, swinging into the saddle. "If they're village dogs, just scavenging, they might scatter if you shout and wave. Wolves might, too, if you're lucky. But if they're trained pursuit dogs, the kind soldiers use—"

She reached down, offered Corvin a hand up.

"Then you don't let them catch you. You ride hard, you ride for thick cover where they lose the scent, or you find water. Running water washes the trail out." She pulled Corvin up behind her on the horse; they'd move faster this way than if he tried to catch his own mount while exhausted. "Dogs are fast on open ground. You're faster on horseback, but only if you don't hesitate."

She kicked the horse into motion, and Corvin had to grab her belt to keep from sliding off.

"Stay low," she said over her shoulder. "Keep your head behind mine. If they come at the horse, you kick, you shout, you don't stop moving."

The barking was ahead of them now, through the trees. Close. But the road curved toward the river, and there was thicker brush to the left.

"I'm going to cut left," Wrack said. "Hold on and don't fall. We hit the water, we don't stop."

She didn't wait for acknowledgment. The horse lunged forward, branches whipping past, and the last light of evening closed around them like a fist.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack turned back. She didn't say anything, just lowered herself to one knee a few feet away, close enough to guide but not close enough to crowd.

"Steady," she said. "Let your breath out slow. You're shaking."

She wasn't wrong. Corvin's hands were steady enough to get the blade in the right place, but there was a tremor underneath it, the kind that comes from holding yourself too rigid.

"First thing," she said, voice low. "You're looking for the throat. The carotid's the fastest. You cut sideways, not down. Sideways opens the vessels, doesn't crush them. Crush is slower."

The man on the ground was barely conscious, barely aware. The pain had hollowed him out, left him raw and simple. His eyes moved toward the blade, but there was no fear left in them. Just exhaustion.

"You're doing it," Wrack said. Not encouragement, just fact. "Now."

She watched Corvin's hand move. The blade bit. The sound was wet, deeper than you'd expect, and the man's body arched once and then went slack in a way that was different from before — final.

Wrack counted under her breath, not quite silently. "One. Two. Three."

The man stopped moving.

"Four seconds," she said. "You were fast. Good."

She stood, brushed off her knees.

"That's what clean looks like. Four seconds and he was gone. You didn't flinch, didn't hesitate." She looked at Corvin's face. "You're going to shake now. That's normal. Let it happen."

She wasn't wrong about that either.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I drop the knife and my hands won't stop shaking. "Four seconds," I repeat, staring at the blood on the blade. "That's all it takes."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack picked up the fallen knife, wiped the blade clean on her own sleeve, and handed it back to Corvin handle-first.

"Four seconds," she agreed. "Four seconds of work. The rest is what's in here." She tapped her own temple, then her chest. "That's the part that takes longer."

She stood, offering Corvin a hand up. When he was on his feet, she let go and didn't comment on the fact that his legs had gone unsteady.

"You did it clean," she said. "No excess. You found the right place and you ended it. That's the best you can do, and you did it." She paused, looking at him steadily. "Now you know what it costs. Not what it costs him. What it costs you. Keep that. The ones who forget what it costs are the ones who start to enjoy it."

She glanced toward the road. The sounds of pursuit were distant still, just at the edge of hearing. She didn't rush, but she didn't linger either.

"We make the river," she said, already walking. "You wash your hands, you drink water, you don't think about it for the rest of the night. Tomorrow we talk about what comes next." She looked back over her shoulder. "Tonight you fall apart if you need to. I'll keep watch. No one's dying except the people we mean to, and that's not tonight."

The horses were where they'd left them. She swung into the saddle and waited for Corvin to follow.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped. She didn't turn around, but she didn't move forward either. The horse shifted beneath her, restless, and she let it.

"Sit down," she said. "If you're going to hear it, sit down."

She dismounted again, came back, and settled onto the ground across from Corvin. The evening was going grey around them, the light draining out. She didn't seem to care about the time.

"The rest," she said. "You want the rest."

She picked up a handful of dirt, let it sift through her fingers.

"First few days, you won't sleep right. You'll close your eyes and see his face. Not the one on the ground just now -- the one he was wearing a minute before, when he still knew what was happening. That one's the worst. He'll look at you like he's asking why. You won't have an answer."

She brushed her hands clean.

"Weeks from now, you'll be eating, or talking to someone, or laughing at something stupid -- and you'll hear his voice. Not really. But you'll hear it. Asking why. Some nights you'll dream about the sound the blade makes, the way it moves through. You'll wake up and lie there in the dark and you'll hear it again. And again. And you won't be able to make it stop."

She looked at Corvin directly, not softening.

"Months from now, it gets quieter. Not better. Quieter. The sounds fade to something you can almost ignore. But the face doesn't. The face stays. And every now and then, usually when you're starting to feel alright about yourself, it'll come back. You'll be in the middle of something ordinary and you'll remember what your hands look like when they're covered in someone else's blood. And you'll have to decide what to do with that."

She paused, letting it settle.

"A year out, two years, you'll meet someone good. Someone you care about. And you'll think about telling them. And you'll know that once you do, they'll never look at you the same way. Not because you're a monster -- because you're something they can't understand. And you won't know if that makes you better or worse."

She leaned back against the log.

"That man on the ground had a name somewhere. He had people who'll never know what happened. That's the part that wakes me up at night, after all this time. Not the dying. The ones left behind who don't know. The ones who'll wonder forever."

She was quiet for a moment.

"You asked what it costs," she said. "It costs four seconds and everything after. Every morning you wake up still alive. Every night you don't. You carry it. That's the work. Killing's easy. Living with it is the thing that breaks most people."

She met his eyes.

"You wanted the rest. That's the rest. It's not done. It's never done. You just get stronger at carrying it, or you don't. Most do, if they last. The ones who don't stop being people."

The dogs had gone quiet in the distance. Moving away, maybe, following a different trail. Wrack didn't seem to notice or care.

"That's what you're signing up for," she said. "Every time you pick up that blade. Every time you make that choice. You're not just ending someone. You're starting something in yourself that doesn't have an ending."

She stood, slowly, and offered him her hand.

"Come on," she said. "River's waiting. You can fall apart on the way."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take her hand and let her pull me up. My knees don't buckle. "I don't want to fall apart," I say, and my voice sounds raw. "But I don't want to forget either."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at him for a long moment. Not assessing this time. Something else, something harder to name.

"Good," she said. "Don't forget. That's how you stay human."

She turned and walked to the horse, not waiting to see if he followed. But her pace was slower than before, measured, giving him time.

"You forget, you start to think it's nothing. Just what you do. Then you start to think you're entitled to it, or that it doesn't matter, or that the people on the other end aren't really people." She put her hand on the horse's flank, steadying it. "Once you start thinking that, you're already gone. Just a body walking around pretending to be a person."

She let him get settled behind her before she spoke again.

"Keeping it is the point. The weight, the faces, the why. You carry all of it, and it makes you careful. Makes you sure before you do it." She nudged the horse forward, and it moved into a steady walk. "Men who forget are dangerous. Men who remember are useful. There's a difference."

The road stretched ahead, dark now, the trees closing in on both sides. The river would be close. She could smell it already, the green wet scent of water moving over stone.

"You'll learn to live with it," she said. "Not because it gets easy. Because you decide it's the cost of being the kind of person who does the work and still sleeps at night. You pay it, and you keep going. That's all any of us can do."

She didn't look back again.

"Hold on," she said. "We're moving faster now."

And they rode toward the water, and the dark, and whatever came after.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
I hold onto her belt tighter, the horse's rhythm steady under me. "Thank you," I say, quiet. "For telling me straight."

The river sound's getting louder up ahead. My hands are still stained. I wonder if the water will really wash it off.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't turn around, but she reached back and adjusted the strap of her saddlebag, fingers brushing his hand where it rested on her belt. Not a gesture of comfort. Just acknowledgment.

"Water gets the blood off," she said. "It won't get it out of you. That's different."

The trees thinned ahead, and the river opened up between them — black and silver in the last light, moving fast over rocks. She slowed the horse at the bank.

"Doesn't have to," she added, quieter. "The ones who want it gone are usually the ones who shouldn't have done it in the first place. You did. You know why. That's what matters."

She dismounted, let the horse drink, and crouched by the water's edge. She cupped some in her palms and rinsed her own hands — not to clean them, just to feel the cold. The blood came away brown at first, then pink, then nothing.

"You'll know when it's clean," she said. "Doesn't mean you're done with it. Means you're ready to carry it instead of fighting it."

She sat back on her heels, watching the water move.

"There's a camp upstream. Half a mile, maybe. We can rest there. Fire if you want, or don't. Your call." She glanced up at him. "You did good today. Don't forget that either."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod and slide off the horse, my boots sinking into the soft mud at the river's edge. I kneel and plunge my hands into the water. It's cold enough to make my teeth ache. "I'll take the fire," I say, watching the last of the red swirl away. "I don't think I want the dark tonight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack glanced up at them then, brief and unreadable. The knife stilled in her hand.

"You want the knife, or you want to use your own? Either way, you're going to want to clean it after. Blood gets sticky if you let it sit."

She nodded toward the cart, where the sound was—a wet, hitching kind of noise, the kind you didn't need to be close to interpret.

"Take your time. But not too much. We're burning daylight and there's burying to do."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow, my throat dry. "I've got mine." My hand goes to the hilt of my short sword, but I still don't draw it. "You sure he's not just... bleeding out on his own?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack wiped the blade once more and slid it back into its sheath. The noise from past the cart went on, ragged and wet.

"He is. That’s the problem. Slow enough to feel it, loud enough to carry." She tilted her head toward the sound. "Fast is better—for him, and for us. If you can’t do it, say so. I’ll do it, but you owe me the next one."

She picked up her gloves and shook the dirt from them. "Don’t take too long. I’m not digging six holes by myself."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't answer right away. She pulled her gloves on, one finger at a time, listening to the sound from behind the cart—the hitch and gurgle, the wet pull of breath that wasn't finding what it needed.

"Took one in the gut," she said finally. "Low. Opened him up wrong. He'll go, but it'll be a while, and he'll feel most of it." She flexed her fingers, testing the fit of the leather. "So. Both."

She stood, joints cracking, and looked at Corvin without pity and without pressure. Just a woman who'd done this too many times and knew what it cost the first time.

"You want me to come with you, or you want to do it alone? Either way, you're the one holding the blade. I'm just there to make sure you don't hesitate wrong."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I shake my head. "No. I'll do it alone." I pull my sword free, the sound too loud in the quiet. "Better if I just... get it over with."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack gave a single nod, short and sharp. "Throat or heart. Throat's faster, if you can get the angle. Don't let him grab you—dying men hold on harder than you'd think."

She turned away, already reaching for the entrenching tool strapped to her pack. "I'll start on the holes. Shout if you need me."

She didn't look back. The sound of digging started up a moment later, steady and methodical, the scrape of metal in dry earth.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't stop digging, but her voice carried clear over the scrape of the shovel.

"Young. Maybe twenty. Took a blade low in the belly—see how his gambeson's torn? That's not a clean cut, that's a twist. Means whoever did it wanted him to feel it." She paused, tossing a shovelful of dirt to the side. "Gut wound like that, you're looking at bile and shit leaking into places it shouldn't. Infection'll kill him if the bleeding doesn't, but that takes days. He's not got days."

Another scrape of metal. "His eyes are open. He's trying to focus on you. That's shock—he's not really seeing anything. Don't let it stop you."

She straightened up for a moment, wiping sweat from her forehead with the back of her glove. "You see the way he's holding himself? Hands pressed to the wound, but not tight enough. He's already gone, he just doesn't know it yet. Make it quick. Throat. Angle the blade up, behind the jaw. He won't feel much after the first second."

She bent back to her work. "I've got three holes dug. You've got time, but not forever."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I move closer, my boots crunching on the dry dirt. His eyes find mine, glassy and wide. "Easy now," I say, though I'm not sure who I'm saying it to. I adjust my grip on the hilt, my knuckles white.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack kept her rhythm steady, the shovel biting into the earth with a sound like a heartbeat. She didn't look up.

"That's it. Don't look at his eyes. Look at the spot you're aiming for. Right under the jaw, where the skin's soft." Another shovelful of dirt. "You're going to feel resistance. Push through it. It's not like cutting meat on a board—there's gristle, and the spine'll stop you if you go too deep. Don't go too deep."

She paused, leaning on the shovel for just a moment, her voice dropping lower, almost gentle. "He's not a person anymore, Corvin. He's a job. That's all. Just a job that needs finishing."

Then the scraping started again, steady and unbroken.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack's shovel didn't pause, but her voice shifted—flatter now, clinical, the way a butcher might describe a cut of meat.

"Spear goes in low, under the ribs but above the hip. If the man holding it knows what he's doing, he twists on the way out. That tears the abdominal wall wide open. You're not looking at a puncture—you're looking at a rent. Peritoneum's shredded. Bowel's perforated in at least two places, maybe three, depending on the angle. That means whatever was in his guts is spilling into the cavity. Stomach acid. Bile. Shit. His body's poisoning itself right now, and he can feel it."

She straightened, resting her weight on the shovel, and looked at Corvin directly for the first time since they'd walked over.

"The blood you're seeing on his hands and his tunic—that's venous. Dark, steady. Means the spear nicked something important but didn't sever it clean. If it had, he'd already be gone. Instead he's leaking slow, and every breath pulls more of that filth through the tear. It burns. That's why he's making that noise. Not just pain. His diaphragm's trying to breathe around a belly full of blood and waste."

She let the silence hang for a beat, then two.

"You asked for straight. That's straight. Now finish it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I close my eyes for a second, then open them and step in. The blade goes in at the angle she said. There’s a horrible, wet sound, and then the noise stops. I pull back and my hands are shaking.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack was already walking toward him before the body finished its last twitch. She didn't rush—just crossed the distance with the same steady, unbothered stride she used for everything. When she reached him, she didn't touch him, didn't reach for the sword. Just stood there, solid and still, her shadow falling across the dead man's face.

"Good," she said. No praise in it, just fact. "Clean. He didn't suffer more than he had to."

She reached down and pulled the dead man's eyelids shut with two fingers, a gesture so practiced it looked like habit. Then she straightened and looked at Corvin's shaking hands, at the blood on the blade, at the tight set of their jaw.

"First one's the worst. Not because it's hard—because it's easy. You'll think about that later. Don't." She pulled a rag from her belt, the one she'd used on her own knife, and held it out. "Clean your steel. Then help me with the holes. Work's the only thing that makes it sit right."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't move. She crouched down beside Corvin, elbows resting on her knees, her expression unreadable but her attention absolute. When she spoke, her voice was low and steady, the same tone she might use to talk someone through field-dressing a deer.

"You're pulling the gambeson back now. See how the fabric's stiff? That's dried blood. It'll crack when you fold it. There—hear that? Like old leather. Underneath, the shirt's soaked through. Linen wicks fast. You're going to have to cut it away to see what you're working with."

She pointed, not touching, her finger hovering an inch above the wound.

"There's the entry. Ragged edges. That's from the twist I told you about. The skin's already starting to pucker—means the body knows it's dead, even if the nerves haven't caught up. You'll see the muscle underneath. Paler than you'd think. The blood's darker now, almost black. That's because his heart's stopped. No more pressure. What's left is just... settling."

She paused as Corvin's hands worked, watching without flinching.

"The sound you're hearing now—that wet, sucking noise—that's the wound pulling air. It'll stop in a minute. The body's still releasing. Don't let it throw you. He's not feeling it. He's not anything."

She shifted her weight, her voice dropping even lower.

"Now you're wiping the blade. Good. Get the blood off before it gums up the works. Use the cloth from inside his tunic if you need to—it's cleaner than the outside. There. See how it smears before it comes clean? That's the fat content. Human blood's greasier than animal blood. Sticks different."

She watched in silence for a long moment, then reached out and steadied Corvin's wrist—not grabbing, just a brief, grounding pressure.

"You're doing fine. Almost done. Last thing—close his mouth. Rigor hasn't set in yet, so it'll move easy. If you leave it open, the jaw locks that way. Looks worse than it is, but you'll remember it. Better to remember him quiet."

She let go, sat back on her heels, and waited.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I press my fingers to his chin and his mouth closes with a soft click. My hands aren't shaking anymore. They just feel cold. "Alright," I say. "Let's dig."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack rose to her feet without ceremony, brushing the dirt from her knees. She didn't offer a hand up—that wasn't her way, and Corvin didn't need it. Not anymore.

"Good," she said again, and this time there was something different in it. Not praise, exactly. Recognition. The tone you used when someone crossed a line and didn't break.

She walked back to the half-dug grave and picked up the shovel, then nodded toward the entrenching tool still lying in the dirt near the second hole.

"There's yours. We'll put him in the third one, over by the cart. Soft ground there—should go faster." She paused, glancing back at Corvin with something that might have been the ghost of a smile. "You did alright. Didn't freeze. That's more than most."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't move from where she stood, shovel still in hand, but she didn't start digging again either. She looked at Corvin—really looked, the way she'd looked at the wound, the way she'd looked at the body. Taking in the details. The way they sat. The way their hands rested on their knees. The way their voice had sounded when they'd asked.

She set the shovel down. Not with a sigh, not with reluctance. Just set it down, like she'd decided the digging could wait.

"You're going to remember the sound," she said. "Not the one he made before—the one your blade made going in. That wet, tearing noise. It'll come back to you at night, when you're trying to sleep. For a while, it'll be the first thing you think about when you close your eyes. That's normal. It fades."

She crouched again, not close enough to crowd, but close enough that she didn't have to raise her voice.

"You're going to remember how easy it was. You pushed, and he stopped. That's going to scare you more than the sound. You'll wonder what it says about you, that you could do that. You'll wonder if something in you is broken now." She shook her head, a small, firm motion. "It's not. It's just done. You did what needed doing. That's all."

She picked up a pebble from the dirt, turned it over in her fingers, then tossed it aside.

"You're going to feel cold for a while. Not just your hands. All of you. Like something drained out and hasn't come back yet. That's the shock. It'll pass. Eat something when we're done. Drink water. Don't let yourself sit empty—it makes it worse."

She met Corvin's eyes and held them.

"And you're going to hate me a little, for making it sound simple. For not flinching. For talking about it like it was butchering a hog. You're going to wonder if I'm even human anymore, or if I ever was." A pause. "I am. I just stopped letting it show. That's what ten years does. You don't have to stop. You can feel it. You can be sick if you need to—I won't watch. But don't let it stop you from getting up. Because there's still holes to dig, and the sun's going down, and if we don't finish, the coyotes will. And that's worse."

She stood, slowly this time, and offered her hand. Not to pull Corvin up—just there, an option, if they wanted it.

"That's the rest. You want more, ask. But that's the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take her hand and let her pull me up, my fingers still cold against her calloused palm. "I'm not going to be sick," I say, my voice steadier than I expect. "Let's just get the rest of them in the ground."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack's hand was rough and warm, and she held on for just a second longer than necessary—not soft, but steady. Then she let go, nodded once, and turned back to the shovel.

"Good," she said, and this time she used their name. "Corvin."

She picked up the entrenching tool and held it out to them, handle first.

"Second hole's over there. Ground's got more rock in it—watch your wrists. I'll take the third one by the cart." She paused, glancing up at the sky. "We've got maybe an hour of good light. Should be enough, if we don't stop."

She started toward the cart, then looked back over her shoulder.

"And Corvin? When we're done, I've got a flask in my pack. It's not good, but it's strong. You've earned a pull."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take the tool, the weight of it familiar and solid in my hands. "I'll hold you to that," I say, and start digging. The scrape of the metal is a better sound than the silence.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack moved to her own hole and set to work without another word. For a while there was only the sound of digging—two shovels biting into dry earth, the soft thump of dirt hitting the growing mound beside each grave. She worked fast, not rushing but not wasting motion either, her body falling into a rhythm that was older than the war, older than her name.

After a few minutes, she spoke again, not looking up from her work.

"The third one—the one with the grey in his beard—he had a letter in his boot. Folded up, sealed with wax. Didn't open it. Not my business." Another shovelful of dirt. "But I put it in his tunic, over his heart. Someone might come looking for him someday. Be easier to find if it's on the body."

She paused to wipe sweat from her forehead with the back of her glove, leaving a smear of dirt across her temple.

"I don't know if that matters. Probably not. But I do it anyway. Been doing it ten years." A short, humorless exhale that wasn't quite a laugh. "Habit, I guess. Or superstition. Hard to tell the difference, this far in."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stop digging for a moment, leaning on the tool. "What do you think it said?" My voice sounds hollow in my own ears. "The letter."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Took one in the gut. Low. Opened him up wrong. He'll go, but it'll be a while, and he'll feel most of it.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Took a blade low in the belly—see how his gambeson's torn? That's not a clean cut, that's a twist. Means whoever did it wanted him to feel it. Gut wound like that, you're looking at bile and shit leaking into places it shouldn't.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Spear goes in low, under the ribs but above the hip. If the man holding it knows what he's doing, he twists on the way out. That tears the abdominal wall wide open. You're not looking at a puncture—you're looking at a rent. Peritoneum's shredded. Bowel's perforated in at least two places, maybe three

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: That wet, sucking noise—that's the wound pulling air... See how it smears before it comes clean? That's the fat content. Human blood's greasier than animal blood

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: You're going to remember the sound... That wet, tearing noise... You're going to remember how easy it was. You pushed, and he stopped... You're going to feel cold for a while... And you're going to hate me a little

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack glanced up then, not at the cart, but at Corvin.

"Course you did."

She folded the cloak over once and dragged the knife through the wool again, slow and thorough. Blood came off in dark ropes. Not all of it. Never all of it.

"Noise has a way of climbing inside a skull when the rest goes quiet." She slid the blade back into its sheath and stood with a small grunt, one hand braced against her knee. "First time, it sounds like a person. Later, it sounds like trouble."

She looked toward the cart. A wheel had sunk halfway into the mud, and one of the dead men lay crooked under the axle like he'd tried to crawl beneath it and bargain with the ground. Past that, somewhere in the brush, the wounded one made a thin, wet sound. Breathing through blood. Maybe gut-cut. Maybe lung. Hard to tell at a distance.

Wrack spat into the ditch.

"Could leave him," she said. "He'll take a while. Might bring wolves. Might bring friends, if he's got enough voice left and the world's feeling mean." Her eyes returned to Corvin. "Could bind him, if you've a mind to ask questions. Though men in that state mostly answer the same thing: water, mother, gods, and lies."

She shifted her weight, calm as a butcher discussing weather.

"Or I can do it." A beat. "Doesn't have to be a lesson every time."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I look away from the cart, jaw tight. "It's not a lesson." I start toward the sound, my own knife still in hand. "Just... let me do it."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched him for a moment, then bent and picked up a fallen sword by the hilt. Not hers. Too much shine on the guard, too little sense in the balance. She tossed it aside into the mud where no one would trip over it.

"Then don't make it one," she said.

She followed at an angle, not close enough to crowd him, close enough to stop anything foolish that had teeth. Her boots sank and sucked in the ditch-muck. The evening had gone that ugly iron color it got after blood had been opened in wet ground.

"Keep your feet out of reach," she said. "Man dying still has hands. Sometimes that's all he has left, and he'll spend them on you."

The wounded raider lay half in the brush beyond the cart, one leg twisted under him, both hands pressed uselessly to his belly. The ambush had opened him low. Not neat. Nothing about it was neat. His breath bubbled in and out of him, each one smaller than the last, but his eyes still moved. That was the part that troubled green men. The body could be ruined beyond salvage and still the eyes went on working, accusing the sky, the mud, whoever stood nearest.

Wrack stopped a few paces off.

"Quickest from there is the throat, if you know where to put it," she said, voice level. "Under the jaw and across, hard. Don't saw at him like you're cutting rope. Or heart, if you can get between ribs, but folk miss that when their hand's shaking."

She rubbed at a dark smear on her knuckle with her thumb.

"And don't apologize. He won't hear it right, and you'll hear it forever."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack's mouth twitched, but it was not quite a smile.

"There's a question men ask when they've still got room in them for tidy shelves."

She looked down at the raider. He had gone grey around the lips. One hand had slipped from his belly, fingers digging into the mud as if there was a latch there he might find. The smell had changed. Blood, shit, opened gut. The body's old treacheries, all arriving on time.

"Bad enough he's dead already," she said. "His flesh just hasn't agreed to stop arguing."

Wrack crouched, out of reach, and studied the wound with the flat patience of long practice.

"Cut low. Filth in it. Belly open. Maybe a vein nicked, maybe not. If not, he'll last longer than you'd thank any god for. Fever if he sees morning. Rot after. Thirst first." She nodded toward his hands. "He knows. Look there. Not clutching a blade. Not crawling. Holding himself together because some part of him thinks that matters."

She rose again, slow.

"Mercy and easier aren't clean opposites. Folk like to pretend they are so they can feel noble when they pick one." Her eyes stayed on the dying man. "Leaving him is cruel and stupid. Binding him is cruel and maybe useful, if you've got a question worth the cost. Ending it is mercy for him and easier for us."

A breath passed, damp and cold.

"Both can be true. World won't split in two because you didn't choose a prettier word."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down, ignoring the mud soaking through my trousers. "Alright." My voice is lower than I mean it to be. I reach for his chin, turning his head to get a clean angle. He doesn't fight me.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stayed where she was, low enough to see, far enough not to make a crowd of it.

"Good," she said. "Don't chase the fear. It'll run faster than you."

The raider's eyes rolled toward her for a moment. Young, maybe. They were always young once the blood was out of them. His lips moved around something that might have been a word, or only air looking for a door.

Wrack's face did not change.

"Knife in close," she said. "Commit. Half a kindness is just another injury."
