She shifted her weight, watching the hands first, always the hands. One of his twitched in the mud, fingers curling and uncurling like a spider stepped on but not finished.

"If he grabs, don't pull back. Push through." Her voice stayed flat, almost bored. "And keep your mouth shut. Blood jumps when it wants to. Tastes like old pennies and bad decisions."

A thin wind moved through the brush, stirring the cart's torn canvas. Somewhere behind them, one of the dead men's boots knocked softly against a spoke as the wheel settled deeper into the muck.

Wrack added, quieter, "Eyes open or closed, doesn't matter. Yours, I mean. You'll see it either way."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at the man in the mud, then at the knife in Corvin’s hand, then back again.

“You’re looking at what a man is when the shouting’s done,” she said.

She crouched a little, forearms resting on her knees, businesslike as ever.

“See his color? Grey at the mouth, wax under the eyes. Blood’s leaving the places that make him a person and going where it’s no use to anyone. His breath’s wet because something inside him’s filling where air ought to be, or because blood’s coming up and he’s too weak to spit it clear.”

The raider made another sound. Small. Ugly. Not quite a word.

“That noise isn’t courage. Isn’t begging, most like. Body’s just trying every door it knows. Breath in, breath out, hold the guts in, don’t die. Same as a fish on a bank. Looks personal because it’s wearing a face.”

Wrack’s eyes stayed on the wounded man’s hands.

“His belly’s open low. That’s bad work if you mean to kill quick. Hurts like fire, stinks worse, takes its time. The gut’s full of filth. Once that spills where it shouldn’t, the body turns against itself. If blood loss doesn’t take him, fever will. If fever’s slow, thirst gets a turn. None of them are gentle.”

She tipped her chin toward him.

“You’re also looking at an enemy. Don’t polish that away. He came here meaning to put you in the mud instead. Maybe he had orders, maybe he had hunger, maybe he had a mother who kissed his forehead and told him he was good. Doesn’t change where his blade was pointed.”

A pause.

“And you’re looking at a person. Don’t polish that away either. That’s how men start laughing while they cut ears off.”

Wrack shifted, mud creaking under her boot.

“So. Hold both. Enemy and person. Dead already and not dead enough. Mercy and work. If you wait for one word that makes it clean, you’ll be waiting till he rots in front of you.”

Her voice dropped, not softer exactly, but lower.

“Look at his throat. Not his eyes. Eyes will ask you questions they’ve no right asking now. Throat’s just meat and breath. That’s the part you can answer.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat tight. "Throat," I repeat, and bring the blade up. My knuckles are white on the hilt. I breathe out and do it.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The cut went in hard enough.

Not clean. First times rarely were. The blade found skin, then the hot red under it, and the raider’s body gave one fierce, startled pull as if some rope had yanked him from inside. His hands clawed once at the mud. Breath came out of him in a wet rush, more spill than sound.

Wrack moved half a step closer, eyes on the work, not the dying.

“Hold,” she said. “Don’t snatch back.”

The worst of it passed quickly. Not quietly. Quick was not the same thing as quiet.

Blood sheeted dark over the raider’s neck and into the mud beneath him, turning the ground black. His mouth opened. Nothing useful came out. One heel scraped twice, then stopped. The hands took longer. Hands always had their own stupid little war to finish.

Wrack waited until the twitching had gone from purpose to leftover spark.

“Done,” she said.

She let the word sit there. Plain. No blessing, no praise, no sermon nailed to it.

After a moment, she crouched beside the body and looked without touching.

“Could’ve been cleaner,” she said. “Could’ve been worse. He didn’t last long.”

That was all the kindness she had to spend on it.

She pulled a ragged strip from the dead man’s own sleeve and held it out by one end.

“Wipe the blade before it dries. Blood gums in the join if you let it. Then your knife sticks when you need it not to, and some bastard gets to enjoy the joke.”

Her gaze flicked once to Corvin’s face, then away again. She had seen men break from less, and seen others grow too fond of how little they broke. Both were trouble.

“Don’t go looking for how you feel about it yet,” Wrack said. “Feelings are poor witnesses right after the fact. They shout, they lie, they change their story by morning.”

She straightened, joints complaining under her breath.

“Tonight, you clean your knife. Wash your hands if there’s water not full of horse piss. Eat something, even if it comes back up. Sleep if sleep’s fool enough to come near you.”

Wrack looked down at the dead raider one last time.

“Tomorrow you can decide what kind of scar it is.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack’s eyes narrowed a little, not in disapproval. Measuring, maybe.

“Straight, then.”

She looked back toward the body in the mud, then down at the churned mess of his belly.

“A spear isn’t a knife. Knife cuts what the hand tells it to cut. Spear’s got weight, reach, and a bastard’s amount of shove behind it. Goes in narrow enough, but it doesn’t stay polite. It parts skin, fat, muscle. If the point’s broad, it opens him like a split wineskin. If it’s narrow, it still drags dirt, cloth, rust, shit, whatever was on the head straight into the meat.”

Wrack hooked a thumb toward the wound without touching it.

“Gut’s not one thing. Folk say ‘belly’ like it’s a sack of porridge. It isn’t. There’s bowel coiled in there, stomach higher up, liver tucked under the ribs, bladder low if he’s unlucky, big blood vessels running deep where you don’t see them until they’re done emptying a man. Spear goes in, it can punch through one loop of bowel or three. Tear instead of cut. Rip little holes that leak what’s inside the gut into places it was never meant to be.”

Her voice stayed flat. Work-talk.

“That’s the stink. Not just blood. Bowel opens and you get shit, bile, sour stomach, half-digested food. Warm, too. Body-heat on it. First time you smell it, your own guts try to climb out in sympathy.”

She shifted her jaw, looking at the corpse with no tenderness and no relish.

“If the spear hits something rich with blood—the liver, the big vessels in back—then he bleeds inside fast. Belly swells. Skin goes pale, lips grey, hands cold. He gets thirsty. Always thirsty. Begs for water if he’s got words left. Give it to him if you like, but it won’t patch the hole. Mostly it just gives him something human to do while he dies.”

A faint, humorless snort.

“If it misses the big blood and only opens bowel, that’s worse in its own way. Slower. Pain like being burned from the inside. He curls around it because lying flat pulls on the torn parts. Fever comes after. Belly goes hard. Every breath hurts. He vomits. Sometimes what comes up smells like what should’ve gone down and out. That’s when even priests start standing upwind.”

Wrack wiped her thumb along the edge of her belt, though there was nothing on it.

“And pulling the spear out can kill quicker than putting it in. Shaft plugs what it broke, sometimes. Yank it free and the blood remembers the door. Leave it in and he suffers around the wood. No clean choice there, either. Just choices.”

She looked at Corvin then.

“So that’s what it does. It makes a man into damage that still knows its own name for a while. Opens him where he was never meant to be open. Spills private things into the weather. Turns all the fine talk—banner, pay, orders, honor—into meat trying not to leak.”

Wrack’s mouth twitched once.

“And it ruins your boots if you stand too close.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at the wound, the smell sharp in my nose. "I thought you said not to look for how I feel about it yet." I wipe my knife on the strip of cloth, slow and deliberate. "Guess I'm just looking."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack gave a dry little grunt.

“Looking’s allowed. Digging isn’t.”

She watched the cloth drag along the knife, red turning brown where air found it.

“There’s a difference. Looking says, there it is. That’s what happened. That’s what my hand did. Digging says, what does it mean, what am I now, where do I put the blame so it sits quiet.” She glanced toward the darkening trees. “That second lot can wait until you’re fed and less likely to decide you’ve discovered the truth of war because your stomach’s upset.”

The corpse lay between them and the brush, already losing the shape of urgency. That was another ugly trick of death. A moment before, a man could fill the whole world with his needing. Then he was a thing in the mud, cooling by inches, and the world had the nerve to go on creaking.

Wrack bent and picked up a fallen scabbard with the toe of her boot, checking beneath it for anything useful. Nothing but mud and a beetle making poor choices.

“First one I finished was older than me,” she said. “Had a beard full of frost and a hole under his ribs. Kept asking me if the mill had burned. No mill within ten miles. I told him no, because it cost nothing and he was past collecting debts.”

She straightened and looked over the cart, counting shapes in the gloom. Still six. Always count again anyway.

“Thought afterward there’d be some bell in me. Some mark. Like the gods would lean down and stamp murderer on my forehead so folk could tell at market.”

Her mouth pulled sideways.

“Nothing so tidy happened. I was cold. My hands stank. I wanted bread. Spent the next hour worrying I’d lost my flint. That offended me more than the killing, for a while. Felt like I’d failed to feel the proper grand thing.”

Wrack looked back at the body.

“Turns out most grand things are for songs and officers. Men die wet and frightened. Men kill hungry and tired. Then someone has to check the packs before dark.”

She nodded toward the dead raider’s belt.

“Speaking of. We need what they’ve got. Coin, dry tinder, food, orders if they’re literate enough to be dangerous. Don’t take trophies. Trophies are for boys who want nightmares with handles.”

A pause settled. The wind worried at the torn cart canvas again.

“And don’t stare too long at the opened parts,” she added. “Not because it’s forbidden. Because after a while you stop seeing the man and start seeing only the damage. That’s its own kind of lie.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped.

For a heartbeat she looked like she might tell him no. Not because of the blood. Not because of the sound. Because she knew the taste of what he was asking for, and it was not knowledge. Not all of it.

Then she came back and stood where he could hear her.

“I’m here,” she said.

Her eyes went to the man in the mud.

“That first sound is air finding the wrong door. Not a scream. He hasn’t got room for one. Throat’s full of blood, mouth’s trying to breathe around it, and the body’s too stupid to know the road’s gone.”

She watched without softening.

“That pull there, that’s fear and meat together. Body feels the cut and throws everything it has at not dying. Hands, heels, back, jaw. Doesn’t matter if the man inside understands. The flesh fights even when the fight’s lost.”

A wet rasp came from the ground. Wrack’s jaw worked once.

“That bubbling is blood in the breath. Sounds worse than it is, most times. Worse for us, I mean. For him it’s all one storm now. Pain, choking, cold coming in fast. He won’t sort it into pieces.”

She folded her arms, gaze fixed and hard.

“If the main vessels opened, he takes heartbeats. Maybe a dozen. Maybe fewer. Time stretches when you’re watching it, so don’t trust your head. Your head will tell you it’s been an hour because it wants out.”

The dying man twitched again.

“That there is leftover lightning. Nerves firing. Hands still looking for work. Don’t make a story of every movement or you’ll go mad granting meaning to every shiver. Sometimes a man reaches because he wants his mother. Sometimes because his hand forgot he’s dead.”

Wrack drew a slow breath through her nose, then regretted it.

“The smell changing now is warm blood hitting mud and old gut. Sharp first, then sweet underneath. Copper, shit, bile, fear-sweat. You’ll know it again even if you spend ten years pretending you don’t.”

She crouched, not touching, not helping, not hiding.

“He’s colder already at the edges. Fingers, ears, nose. Heart keeps what it can for the middle, like a miser counting coins in a burning house. Then it loses count.”

A pause.

“That rattle? That’s near the end. Not words. Not judgment. Just the last air dragging through wreckage.”

Wrack stayed until the body had nothing left but small motions, and then not even those.

When it was done, she did not say good. She did not say brave.

She said, “That long.”

Only then did her eyes move from the corpse.

“And now I’m leaving something out.”

Her voice went flatter.

“I’m leaving out the part where you use every detail like a hook and hang yourself from it tonight. I’m leaving out the lie that if you stare hard enough, suffer hard enough, count every sound, you’ll make it fair.”

She straightened, knees clicking.

“It won’t be fair. It’ll be dead.”

Wrack looked down at the mud-black blood.

“You wanted straight. There it is. A man was opened. He struggled. He emptied. He stopped. Took less time than boiling oats and longer than anyone decent would wish.”

Her mouth tightened.

“Now clean the knife again.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe the knife again, harder than it needs. The smell's in my mouth now, copper and something sour. "Alright," I say, but it comes out rough. I stand up, my legs stiff. "Let's check the packs."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack nodded once.

“That’s the spirit. Miserable, practical, and late.”

She turned from the body first, not quick enough to look like retreat and not slow enough to make a shrine of him. The mud sucked at her boots as she crossed back toward the cart, where the other dead lay in the dreary arrangement battle left behind when it stopped pretending to be motion.

“Start with belts and inner pockets,” she said. “Men keep coin near skin and lies near the heart. If there’s orders, they’ll be in oilcloth or tucked in a boot because some sergeant once told them that was clever.”

She crouched beside the nearest raider, a thick-necked man with a split lip and one eye gone cloudy already. Wrack rolled him with a hand on his shoulder and a knee braced in the mud, indifferent to the wet sound the body made.

“Don’t put your fingers where you can’t see them. Needles, little knives, broken buckles. Dead men still find ways to be irritating.”

She worked quickly. Knife from boot. Purse from belt. Two copper bits, a bent silver clipped thin enough to insult the mint, a twist of salt wrapped in waxed cloth. She held that up.

“Worth more than the silver if the cook’s feeling murderous.”

The salt went into her pouch.

She checked his mouth next with the tip of her knife, lifting the lip.

“Gold tooth,” she said. “Leave it.”

A glance toward Corvin, dry as dust.

“Unless you’ve found a sudden calling as a battlefield dentist. If so, congratulations. You can do it downwind.”

Wrack moved to the next corpse, the one tangled beneath the axle. Getting him out would have been effort, and effort had to earn its keep. She searched what she could reach: belt, sleeves, collar seam. Her fingers found a narrow packet under the jerkin, bound in greasy twine.

“There we are.”

She cut the twine and unfolded the oilcloth. Inside was a scrap of map, badly copied, showing the old ford, the ridge path, and three charcoal marks along the road.

Wrack studied it in the failing light.

“Not bandits, then. Or not only bandits.” Her mouth flattened. “Someone pointed them.”

She tucked the map away.

“We show this to Marek if he’s still breathing when we get back. If he isn’t, we show it to whoever’s clever enough not to wave it around the fire.”

A few paces off, the cart creaked again. The horse hitched to it had died in the traces, eyes wide, tongue dark between its teeth. Wrack gave it a look.

“Poor bastard. Only honest soul here, and it caught the worst bargain.”

She cut a saddlebag loose and opened it. Hard bread, damp at the edges. A heel of cheese wrapped in cloth. Flint. A little packet of lampblack. Three arrows with warped shafts. A child’s carved bird, worn smooth from handling.

Wrack paused with that last thing in her palm.

For a moment her face gave nothing away.

Then she set it back inside the dead man’s bag.

“Not useful,” she said.

She stood and rolled her shoulder, listening to the trees. No voices. No horns. No snap of brush under hurried feet. Just wet leaves, settling wood, and the small obscene sounds of cooling bodies.

“We take food, tinder, coin, blades worth carrying. Leave armor unless it’s better than ours and not full of holes. No helmets with skull in them. Learned that one in a summer heatwave and I’ll spare you the sermon.”

Wrack knelt by another man and tugged a ring from a cord around his neck. Not jewelry. A seal stamped in lead.

Her brows drew down.

“Company mark.”

She rubbed mud off with her thumb and angled it toward the light.

“Black rook. Eastern auxiliaries, unless some fool’s taken to copying their charms.”

She spat to the side.

“That means patrols, not hungry boys with rusty knives. Means we don’t sleep near the road tonight. Means if anyone asks, we saw nothing, killed no one, and were born blind besides.”

She put the seal in her pouch with the map.

Then she looked once toward the body beyond the cart, the one Corvin had finished.

“Leave him for last if you need to,” she said. “Or don’t. Dead don’t mind order. Living do.”

Wrack wiped her hands on the dead man’s cloak, then gave a short, humorless huff.

“Look at us. Six corpses, one ruined cart, no supper cooked, and now politics.”

She bent over the next pack.

“I hate politics. At least murder has the decency to bleed where you can see it.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack did not ask which rest.

She stayed bent over the pack for another breath, fingers still on the strap, then let it go. The buckle snapped softly against leather.

“Aye,” she said. “All right.”

She looked over the road, the ditch, the cart, the six dead men cooling in the mud. Her face had gone still in the way it did when she was taking stock of bad weather.

“The rest is this wasn’t chance.”

She hooked a thumb toward the map in her pouch.

“Road marked. Ford marked. Ridge path marked. That means someone knew a cart would come this way, or wanted whoever came this way stopped. These lads weren’t starving hedge-cutters hoping for a purse and a loaf. They had a point to stand on and a reason to bleed for it.”

Her eyes moved from body to body.

“And they bled badly. Which means either their officer was careless, or the job was worth spending them cheap.”

Wrack crouched beside the man with the black rook seal again. She took his wrist and lifted his hand. The nails were cracked, rimmed black. Calluses across the palm. Not noble. Not soft. She turned the hand once, then dropped it.

“Eastern auxiliaries draw pay from three purses depending who’s lying loudest that month. Crown says they’re irregulars. Border lords call them scouts. Villages call them bastards, which is the only honest rank any of us get. Black rook means they answer to Captain Veyr, unless he’s dead and another crow’s wearing his coat.”

She spat into the mud.

“Veyr doesn’t waste men on a cart unless there’s something in the cart, someone on the road, or a message being written with corpses.”

Wrack stood, slow. Her knees clicked again.

“So the rest is, we have to decide what kind of trouble we just stepped in.”

She pointed to the dead horse.

“Cart was coming west. Wheel dropped in the rut after the horse went down, not before. See the drag there? Shaft lurched when it fell. Horse took an arrow or spear from the side, panicked, died in the traces. Driver likely got pulled off or cut down first. There’s no driver here.”

Her mouth tightened.

“That matters.”

She walked to the front of the cart, boots sinking, and examined the churned earth. She did not touch the blood at first. She only looked.

“Two sets there. One heavy, one lighter. Heavy boots came in from the trees. Lighter ones staggered off roadward.” She tipped her head toward the ditch. “Blood drops. Not much. Could be wounded. Could be someone carrying something wet. Could be a man with a nosebleed and the gods playing jokes.”

She gave a dry, joyless snort.

“Gods love jokes. Never good ones.”

Wrack followed the marks with her eyes but did not go after them yet.

“The rest is someone may have run. If they ran, these six weren’t alone in the story. If they carried news, that news is moving. If they carried cargo, someone may come looking. If they were bait, we’re already standing in the mouth of the trap and admiring the teeth.”

She turned back to the bodies.

“And the other rest—since you asked—is that killing him doesn’t end with him.”

Her gaze went past the cart, toward the brush where the last man lay.

“It goes home if he had a home. Not in some grand bard’s way. No ghost over your bed with chains. Just a woman waiting two extra days before she admits he’s not late. A boy wearing boots too big because his father doesn’t need them. A mother hearing hoofbeats and knowing before anyone speaks because bad news has a sound to it.”

Wrack’s jaw shifted.

“Maybe he deserved it. Maybe he burned farms, cut throats, laughed while he did it. Maybe he was the sort who’d have opened you from crotch to sternum and called it supper-talk. Or maybe he was told to stand in the trees and stop a cart, and he was stupid enough to obey.”

She looked back at the dead.

“Dead doesn’t sort that for us. Dead’s lazy.”

She wiped her hand across her mouth, leaving a faint smear of dirt at the corner.

“The rest is you’ll remember the wrong pieces. Not the whole thing. No one remembers whole. You’ll remember his chin in your hand. Or the little jump when the knife bit. Or the sound. Or the way your own fingers felt too strong and too useless at once. You’ll forget what Wrack said, then remember it at a bad hour. You’ll tell yourself you should’ve done it cleaner. Then you’ll tell yourself wanting it cleaner means you cared. Then you’ll wonder if caring after is just another way to polish the blade.”

Her eyes narrowed against the dimming light.

“That’s all ordinary. Miserable, but ordinary.”

She crouched by another corpse and searched him while she spoke, because standing still too long around fresh dead gave the mind room to breed vermin.

“The dangerous part is if you start needing it to mean more than it does. Some men kill once and spend the rest of their lives trying to make that first body into an altar. Every drink, every brawl, every cruel thing they do after gets stacked on top of it. ‘This is what war made me,’ they say, like war held their prick when they pissed on someone weaker.”

Wrack found a purse and shook it. Two coins. She pocketed them.

“Other men go the other way. Decide if one death didn’t split the sky, none of them matter. They laugh too loud. Start counting kills like pay. Take teeth. Cut marks in bowstaves. Call mercy soft because mercy asks them to notice what they’re doing.”

She glanced toward Corvin then, not soft, not hard.

“Don’t become either kind. They’re both boring, and both get people killed who weren’t on the list.”

Wrack moved to the dead man half under the axle. She braced one boot against the wheel and pulled him just far enough to reach beneath his coat. The body came loose with a wet drag. She ignored it.

“The rest is the body has no dignity unless we lend it some. Not prayer. Not flowers. Dignity’s mostly not being an arsehole with what’s left. Don’t kick him because he frightened you. Don’t mock the noises he made. Don’t take what has no use just because your hand wants proof. Don’t pretend he wasn’t a man. Don’t pretend he was only a man, either, and forget his blade was meant for your ribs.”

Her fingers found a folded scrap tucked inside the lining. She eased it out.

“Ah.”

She unfolded it carefully. The paper was damp, ink feathered at the edges, but legible enough. Her eyes moved over it.

“Names,” she said.

She read in silence for a few moments, then folded it again.

“Three hamlets. Tollbridge. Wren’s Hollow. Eastmere. Marked beside them—grain, mules, sons fit for levy.” Her expression did not change, but something behind it shut like a door. “Recruiting list, or raiding list. Same handwriting either way. Someone’s hungry for bodies and bread.”

She tucked the paper away with the map.

“So the rest of that is simple. These six were not the war. They were a fingertip. Cut it off, and the hand still reaches.”

The wind shifted. The smell came with it again, thick and intimate. Wrack endured it without flinching.

“And the rest of him—the one beyond the cart—is already starting to leave himself. Warmth first. Then color. Jaw will stiffen. Hands curl harder before they loosen. Blood settles low. By morning he’ll look less like the thing you did and more like something the weather found.”

She picked up a serviceable short blade from the mud, tested the edge, and slid it through her belt.

“Flies will know before we do. They always get the news early. If sun comes out tomorrow, he’ll swell. If rain comes, he’ll soften. If wolves come, they’ll open him with less ceremony than you did and sleep well after.”

Wrack’s mouth twitched.

“Wolves are honest philosophers.”

She went still then, listening.

No hoofbeats. No voices. Only water in the ditch and the creak of ruined wood.

“The rest is we should bury them, if the world were kind and we had shovels, daylight, and no enemies. We have mud, two tired hands too few, and whatever comes after this wearing boots. So we won’t.”

She said it plainly. No apology.

“We’ll drag them off the road if we can spare the time. Not for them. For us. Bodies in a road ask questions. Questions bring riders. Riders bring ropes. A shallow ditch and some branches will have to serve as sermon.”

She looked toward the tree line.

“Maybe crows find them first. Maybe their own people do. Maybe some farm child comes looking for a lost goat and learns too much before breakfast. That’s another bit no one puts in songs. War scatters lessons where children can step on them.”

Wrack bent and took a waterskin from one of the dead men. She sniffed it, grimaced, and corked it again.

“Not horse piss. Close family.”

She tossed it aside.

“The rest, Corvin, is you are not ruined because your hand killed a dying enemy. Ruined is work. Ruined takes repetition and excuses. Ruined is waking each morning and choosing the easier cruelty until it fits like a glove.”

She paused.

“You are also not clean because you felt bad. Feeling bad is cheap. Any fool with a stomach can manage it. What matters is what you do when the next man is on his knees. What matters is whether you can still tell the difference between necessity and appetite.”

Wrack’s gaze rested on the corpse beyond the cart only briefly.

“Tonight it was necessity.”

Then she gave a humorless little breath.

“And appetite would’ve watched longer for pleasure, not punishment. Worth knowing the difference. Both like to stare.”

She knelt by the last pack near the wheel and opened it. Inside were hard biscuits, a coil of cord, a whetstone, and a pair of socks wrapped in oilcloth. Dry socks made her eyebrows rise.

“Well. There’s the first blessing all evening.”

She tucked them into her own pack without shame.

“The rest is your hands may shake later. Let them. They may not. Don’t go admiring that either. You may dream of him. Or you may dream of bread, wake ashamed, and think that proves something rotten in you. It doesn’t. The mind’s a drunk quartermaster. It puts supplies where it likes.”

She slung the pack aside and stood.

“If you vomit, vomit away from camp. If you cry, do it quiet or loud, but don’t expect it to wash anything off. If you sleep, take it as mercy and don’t insult it by standing guard over your own guilt all night.”

Wrack looked over the field again. Six bodies. One horse. One cart. The dark coming down.

“And if tomorrow you want to ask whether he had a name, I’ll tell you this: likely. If you want to know whether that changes what had to be done, I’ll tell you no. If you want to know whether no is a cruel answer, I’ll tell you yes.”

Her shoulders rose and fell once.

“There. That’s the rest.”

She reached down, caught one dead man under the arms, and started hauling him toward the ditch.

“Now grab boots or don’t. Philosophy’s lighter after the corpses are moved.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I grab the dead man's boots and haul, my own hands still tacky. "Names," I say, grunting with the weight. "Did you ever learn the first one's name?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack hauled until the corpse’s shoulders bumped over a root and dropped into the ditch with a wet, final sort of thud.

“No,” she said.

She stood a moment with her hands on her thighs, breathing through her nose and regretting it. The ditch water was black where the dead man had gone in, reeds bent under his weight.

“Not then.”

She wiped one palm down her trouser leg.

“Learned it later. Or thought I did. Hard to tell, after. Men get names wrong when they’re frightened, and officers get them wrong when they’re counting losses, which is most of the time.”

Wrack looked back toward the road and the remaining bodies.

“His name was Joric, maybe. Yorren, maybe. Something with a soft middle. He wore a bit of blue thread tied round his wrist. Had three teeth missing on the left. Kept asking about the mill.”

Her mouth went crooked.

“That’s what I remember. Not his name. The thread. The teeth. The mill that wasn’t there.”

She bent to catch the next corpse under the arms and paused, looking down at his face. This one had died with his eyes open and mud drying in the lashes. She closed them with two fingers, not gently, but not carelessly either.

“Names are funny things,” she said. “Folk think they make the dead heavier. Sometimes they do. Sometimes they make them easier to carry, because then they’re not every man at once.”

She got her grip and pulled. The body slid a handspan, then stuck on something beneath the coat. Wrack swore under her breath and shifted her hold.

“First years, I wanted names. Thought it was a debt. If I killed a man, I ought to know what his mother called him before I put him in the ground. Noble little idiot I was.”

The corpse came free with a sucking sound.

“Then I learned names don’t come alone. A name brings a village. A trade. A wife with bad knees. A brother who owes him money. A little girl who thinks he hung the moon because he once carved her a horse from kindling. Or else it brings worse. Burned barns. Split lips. Some boy he beat for dropping a spear.”

She dragged the dead man to the ditch and let him roll in beside the first.

“Knowing doesn’t cleanse it. Not knowing doesn’t spare you. It’s just another shape the weight takes.”

Wrack straightened and looked toward the brush, where the last dead raider lay out of sight beyond the cart.

“This lot may have names on that paper, if someone cared to write them. More likely numbers, marks, village tallies. Men fit for levy. Men fit for dying. Same ink.”

She gave a short, bitter huff.

“Captain Veyr used to say names made soldiers soft. Had them answer to file and rank when he could. Third spear. Left flank. Cart guard. Easier to spend a man if you’ve turned him into a place on a board.”

Her eyes narrowed toward the dim road.

“Veyr was always a tidy bastard. I distrust tidy bastards. They can stack corpses like firewood and call it order.”

She crouched by the next body and searched once more before moving it. Her fingers found nothing but a crust of bread gone soft with blood. She tossed it aside for the crows.

“Joric,” she said at last. “That’s the name I kept, anyway. Might be wrong. Doesn’t matter to him now. Matters to me some nights, which is rude of him.”

Wrack’s mouth twitched, dry and brief.

“Dead men have poor manners.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I don't want to know his name. I say it out loud, dragging the next body by its ankles. "I don't want it."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack dragged her end of the corpse until it tipped into the ditch with the others. Limbs settled wrong. They always did.

“Then don’t take it,” she said.

She wiped her hands on the dead man’s coat before letting go.

“Names aren’t holy. They’re not curses either. They’re just handles. Sometimes you need one. Sometimes grabbing hold only means the thing gets dragged after you longer than it should.”

She glanced toward the brush, then back to the road.

“If someone says it later, you can hear it or not. No law says you’ve got to build him a little room in your head and keep the fire lit.”

Wrack bent, picked up a broken spear shaft, and used it to push a slack arm farther down into the reeds.

“Only don’t make a virtue of not wanting it. That’s the trick. Men start saying, I don’t learn their names, as if that makes them hard. Then they stop seeing faces too. Then hands. Then throats. Soon enough it’s all sacks of meat making noise between one order and the next.”

She tossed the spear shaft aside.

“You’re allowed not to want more weight tonight. Sensible, even. Cart’s heavy enough.”

The sky had darkened another shade. The road was losing its edges, mud and blood and shadow all making one country together. Wrack did not like it. Dusk made honest distances lie.

She went to the next body and crouched, checking the belt, the sleeves, the boots. Her fingers moved quickly, practiced and ugly in their usefulness.

“Wanting matters less than folk think,” she said. “You didn’t want the smell either. Got it anyway. Didn’t want his blood on your hands. There it is. Didn’t want to know what a spear does to a gut. Asked, and now you know.”

She pulled a small knife from inside the corpse’s boot, looked at the edge, and tucked it away.

“Name’s one of the few bits you can refuse for now.”

Wrack stood, looked toward the ditch, then toward the cart.

“But if it comes to you later, don’t spend half the night pretending you didn’t hear. That’s all. Let things arrive when they arrive. Send off what you can. Keep what won’t leave without feeding it like a stray dog.”

A faint creak came from the cart as its broken axle shifted deeper into mud. Wrack turned her head sharply, then relaxed when nothing followed but settling wood.

“Shit cart’s got more life left than some men I’ve known.”

She moved to the last corpse by the road, the one with his cheek pressed into the rut. For a moment she only looked at him.

“This one had a scar behind the ear,” she said. “Old burn, maybe. That’s enough. Scar-behind-the-ear. Easier than a name. Less likely to bring a village with it.”

She rolled him over, searched him, and found a strip of dried meat wrapped in cloth. She sniffed it.

“Possibly food. Possibly punishment.”

It went into a separate pouch.

Wrack got her hands beneath his arms and began hauling him toward the ditch.

“War gives you too much and not enough. Too much blood, too much stink, too much knowing how men come apart. Not enough reasons. Not enough graves. Not enough time to be decent in a way that would satisfy anyone watching from a warm chair.”

She dragged the body another few feet.

“So you do the small decencies. Don’t gloat. Don’t steal foolish things. Don’t lie to yourself when truth’s cheaper. Don’t carry every name like a saint’s relic just to prove your back can bend.”

The corpse slid over the lip and dropped beside the others.

Wrack stood over the ditch a moment, breathing shallow.

“There,” she said. “Road’s less talkative now.”

She gathered dead brush with one hand, snapping off branches and tossing them over the bodies. Not a burial. Not close. But shadows and reeds would break the shape from a distance, and sometimes distance was all a man got between himself and a hanging.

“Help’s not coming for them,” she said, almost to the ditch. “Might come looking, though. Different thing.”

She paused with one branch in hand.

“And for what it’s worth, not wanting his name doesn’t make you cruel.”

Her eyes stayed on the bodies beneath the reeds.

“Wanting it wouldn’t make you kind.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I toss another branch over them, my hands still cold. "Right." I look away from the ditch, toward the cart. "We done with the road?"

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Cut low. Filth in it. Belly open. Maybe a vein nicked, maybe not. If not, he'll last longer than you'd thank any god for. Fever if he sees morning. Rot after. Thirst first.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: His belly's open low. That's bad work if you mean to kill quick. Hurts like fire, stinks worse, takes its time. The gut's full of filth. Once that spills where it shouldn't, the body turns against itself.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Spear goes in, it can punch through one loop of bowel or three. Tear instead of cut. Rip little holes that leak what's inside the gut into places it was never meant to be.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: That first sound is air finding the wrong door... Throat's full of blood, mouth's trying to breathe around it... That bubbling is blood in the breath... The smell changing now is warm blood hitting mud and old gut. Sharp first, then sweet underneath. Copper, shit, bile, fear-sweat

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: There. That's the rest.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stood up, her left knee making a dry, cracking sound that seemed loud in the sudden stillness of the road. She sheathed the knife, the iron guard clicking home against the boiled leather of her scabbard. 

She looked over at Corvin, her gaze lingering for a second on the smear of dark grease and blood across his cheek before she dismissed it. She didn't offer him a rag; she didn't have one that wasn't already stiff with old sweat or fresh gore. 

From past the overturned cart, the noise came again—a wet, rattling whistle, like someone trying to breathe through a mouthful of gravel. 

"Lung shot, by the sound of it," Wrack said, her voice flat and conversational. She leaned her weight onto her good hip, her hands resting easily near her belt. "He won't make it to midnight, but he'll make a lot of noise trying. If we're staying here to search the packs, we'll be listening to that the whole time. If we're moving, we leave a trail of noise behind us."

She tilted her head toward the cart, her expression entirely empty of malice or pity. It was just a logistical problem. "You want to go use the iron, or should I go do it? It's your turn to carry the water skin if I have to do the throat-cutting."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow, my throat tight. "I'll do it." My voice comes out steadier than I feel. I start toward the cart, then hesitate. "You check the packs. I don't want to... take too long."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched him for a beat, her eyes tracking the slight tremor in his shoulders. She didn't mock him for it; she'd seen stouter men than Corvin lose their breakfast over a simple throat-cutting. 

"Under the ear," she said, her voice dropping a register so it didn't carry. "Angle the blade down toward the center of his collarbone. One hard push. Don't go sawing at the windpipe, or he'll start thrashing and you'll get it all over your sleeves. Just put your weight behind it and step back."

She didn't wait to see if he took the advice. Turning her back on the cart, she walked over to the lead horse, which lay on its side in the mud, its ribcage still shuddering with the last of its heat. 

Wrack knelt by the beast’s flank, her boots squelching in the wet clay, and began unbuckling the saddlebags with practiced, efficient movements. She ignored the smell of spilled bowel and wet iron, her fingers working the stiff leather straps. The first bag held nothing but moldy barley and a spare pair of woolen hose, stiff with grease. She tossed the hose aside and reached deeper, looking for salt, dried meat, or anything else that didn't weigh more than it was worth.

Behind her, the whistling breath from the cart continued, a rhythmic, desperate rasp. Wrack kept searching, her ears tuned to the sound, waiting for it to stop.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn’t stop her fingers, though she did pause long enough to glance back over her shoulder at him. Her face was as neutral as a gray sky. 

"Both," she said, her voice dropping into that low, flat register she used when she was stating the obvious. "A lung shot in this weather, with no surgeon within three days' ride? He’s going to drown in his own chest. It’ll take him hours, and every breath will feel like he’s swallowing hot coals."

She pulled her hand out of the saddlebag, holding a small brass tin. She shook it—a dull, heavy rattle. Salt. She slipped it into her own pocket and reached back into the leather pouch. 

"So it’s a mercy because he’s finished anyway, and it's easier because I don't want his choking to bring every wolf and patrol within five miles down on us while we're trying to sleep." She looked at Corvin, her gray eyes steady. "Call it whichever one makes you feel better when you’re closing your eyes tonight. But do it now, before the light goes completely. The blood gets hard to see in the dark, and you don't want to slip."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take a slow breath, then move around the cart. The man is propped against a wheel, eyes wide and glassy. I kneel, pull my knife, and hesitate. "Hey," I say softly. He doesn't look at me.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped her fingers inside the second saddlebag. She closed her eyes for a brief second, a small, tired twitch tightening the corner of her mouth. 

"He's not checking your credentials, Corvin," she said, her voice carrying just loud enough to reach him over the horse's carcass. It was low, dry, and entirely devoid of anger. "And he isn't going to buy you a drink. Don't make it a conversation. It just makes the blade feel heavier."

She pulled her hand out of the bag, holding three copper bits and a half-eaten hard tack biscuit that was already fuzzy with green mold. She spat into the mud, tossed the biscuit, and pocketed the coppers. They were thin, cheap things, probably clipped at the edges, but they'd buy a cup of watered small beer at the next crossing if they lived that long. 

Standing up, Wrack let out another dry grunt as her bad knee protested the movement. She didn't look over the cart at Corvin and the dying man. Instead, she turned her face toward the tree line, squinting through the deepening gray of the dusk. The woods were quiet—too quiet, the birds having fled when the first arrows flew—but quiet was a relative term. The smell of blood was fresh, and the horse's bowels were letting go. It would draw things.

"If you're going to hesitate, step back and let me do it," she added, her hand resting casually on the pommel of her own sword. "But decide now. The light's dying, and I'd rather not be stumbling around in the dark trying to find where we dropped the spade."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack let out a short, sharp puff of air through her nose and walked around the tail of the cart. She didn't rush, but her stride was purposeful. She stopped a pace behind Corvin, looking down at the man propped against the wooden spokes. 

She didn't look at the man's face first; she looked at his chest. 

"See that pink froth bubbling around his lips?" she said, her voice dropping into the quiet, dry tone of a master mason explaining a cracked foundation. "That’s blood from the lung, whipped up with the air he’s trying to drag in. It looks like soap bubbles, but it tastes like iron. It means the lung is punctured and filling up fast."

She knelt beside Corvin, her bad knee giving its familiar protest, and pointed a dirty, blunt fingernail at the dying man's throat. 

"Look at his collarbones. See how they're jerking up toward his ears every time he tries to draw a breath? That's his body using every muscle it has to force air into a space that won't hold it anymore. It’s like trying to inflate a leather bladder inside a bucket of wet clay. The blood is pooling in his chest cavity, squeezing the lung flat."

She reached out, her hand entirely steady, and gripped the man's chin. She tilted his head up slightly. His skin was clammy, cold, and a strange, sickly shade of grey. His eyes rolled toward her, wide and unseeing, the pupils blown wide.

"Look at his lips," Wrack continued, her thumb brushing near his mouth without a hint of hesitation. "They're turning the color of a bruised plum. That’s the lack of air. In another ten minutes, his fingernails will go the same color, then his ears. He's drowning, Corvin. Just on dry land, in his own skin."

She let go of his chin and wiped her fingers on her trousers, leaving a dark smudge on the woolen cloth. 

"He isn't thinking about his home, and he isn't thinking about who won the skirmish," she said, looking up at Corvin. "His brain is just a animal in a corner, panicking because it can't get oxygen. It's a mechanical failure. Nothing more."

She reached down, took Corvin’s wrist—the one holding the knife—and guided it slightly, adjusting his grip so his thumb was pressed firm against the flat of the pommel. 

"Now," she said softly. "Do you want to leave him here to spend the next two hours trying to pump water out of a leaking boat, or are you going to stop the wheel?"

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I press the blade under his ear like she said, angle it down, and push. It goes in easier than I thought it would. I step back quick, wiping the knife on my thigh. "It's done."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stood up, her knees giving another small, dry pop. She looked down at the man's neck. The cut was deep enough; the rattling had died into a wet, heavy sigh, and then the road was entirely quiet. The silence that followed was thick and immediate, broken only by the wind in the pines.

She looked at Corvin's thigh where he had wiped his blade. A dark, wide smear was already sinking into the wool of his trousers. 

"That'll go stiff when it dries," she observed, her voice flat and conversational. "Hard to wash out once the cold sets in. Next time, use their clothes, not yours. They aren't using them anymore."

She didn't linger on it. She stepped over the dead man's legs, her boots clicking against the iron rim of the cartwheel, and reached down to grab the leather strap of the water skin she had set near the ditch. It was heavy, nearly full of stale, brackish well-water they’d drawn yesterday morning. She slung it over her shoulder, the wet leather cold against her collarbone.

"Since you did the throat-cutting, I've got the water," she said, nodding toward the lead horse. "Grab the small saddlebag I cleared out. The one with the salt. And look through the rest of the dead. If any of them have decent boots that fit you, take them. Yours are splitting at the welt, and we've got a long walk before we find a dry barn."

She turned her eyes back to the tree line. The shadows were stretching out, turning the gray trunks of the birch trees into long, dark bars. The air was getting sharper, the kind of autumn cold that smelled of rot and fallen leaves. 

"Ten minutes," she said, not looking at him as she started toward the rear of the cart to check the last body. "Then we get off the road. The smell of this horse is going to carry, and I don't fancy sharing our ditch with whatever comes to eat it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped her search of the dead man's belt. She didn't look up immediately, her rough fingers resting on a cheap pewter buckle. When she did raise her head, her eyes were narrow, assessing him in the gathering gloom. 

"You want it straight?" she said, her voice dry as dead leaves. "Fine."

She stood, her joints popping again, and walked three paces to where the third man lay. He was sprawled on his back in the ditch, his legs twisted beneath him, the front of his woolen tunic torn open and dark with a wide, wet stain that had already turned the color of old liver. 

Wrack stood over him and pointed down with the toe of her boot, nudging the edge of the tear in the cloth.

"A spear doesn't make a clean hole like a knife," she said, her voice dropping into that flat, instructional tone. "It's got weight behind it, and a wider head. When it goes into the belly, it doesn't just cut; it pushes. It drags the wool of his shirt and the grease on the iron right into the grease of his own fat."

She knelt beside the corpse, her face inches from the wound. She didn't flinch from the sour, heavy odor already rising from the split trousers. 

"The blade punctures the gut-pipes," she continued, her finger tracing a line an inch above the dead man's navel. "The bowel leaks. Everything he ate for his midday meal, and yesterday's supper, spills out into the hollow of his belly. That's the real poison. If the iron doesn't nick the big vein running down the front of the spine—which would let him bleed out in a couple of minutes, if he's lucky—then he gets to wait."

She reached down, took the dead man’s hand, and turned it over. The fingers were already stiffening, curled like dry twigs. 

"By morning, his belly will be hard as a shield. Swollen up with gas and rot. He’ll start to burn up with a fever that makes his spit dry up like salt. He’ll beg for water, but if you give him a drop, his stomach will just reject it. He’ll fetch it back up, green and black and smelling like an open privy. You can smell a gut-shot man from fifty paces by the second day. The flies find him before he’s even stopped breathing."

She dropped the dead hand back into the mud with a soft *slap*. 

"It takes three days," she said, looking up at Corvin, her gray eyes entirely empty of expression. "Sometimes four, if he’s got a strong heart. By the end, he’s out of his head, screaming at people who aren't there, his skin yellow as old lard. And then his kidneys give out, his blood goes black with his own waste, and he finally chokes on his own vomit."

She stood up, wiping her palms on her thighs. 

"That’s what a spear does to the middle of a man. It’s not quick, it’s not clean, and there isn't a surgeon from here to the coast who can fix it once the bowel is torn. If you see one of our lads take a point there, you don't waste your bandages. You give him his water skin, you tell him he did well, and you leave him your sharpest knife if he’s got the nerve to use it before the fever takes his senses."

She looked down at the dead man's boots. They were cheap leather, the soles held on with copper tacks, but they were whole. 

"These are better than yours," she said, her tone shifting back to business as if she’d just been discussing the price of hay. "Get his laces undone before the stiffness makes it hard to pull them off. And do it quick. The light's nearly gone."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at the man's boots for a second too long, my gut still tight from her description. "Right," I say, my voice a little rough. I kneel and start working at the stiff laces. "You ever have to do that? Leave someone the knife?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stood over him, her shadow long and thin in the dying orange light of the sunset. She watched him struggle with the wet, mud-caked leather laces. 

"Twice," she said. She didn't sound sad, just tired. "Once at the Red Ford, about six years back. A boy named Kess. He’d only been with the company three months. Took a billhook to the groin and the lower belly. We had to move; the Duke's horsemen were thirty minutes behind us and we had two miles of swamp to cross."

She reached down, took her own knife out again, and used the tip to pry at a stubborn knot on the dead man's other boot, saving Corvin the trouble. 

"I offered him mine," she continued, her voice level. "He took it. He was a sensible lad. We heard the pop about five minutes after we hit the reeds. He used his own small-sword, though. Said he wanted to go with his own iron."

She yanked the knot loose with a sharp tug. The dead man's foot flopped uselessly inside the leather. 

"The other was a fellow named Miller," Wrack said, pulling the boot off the foot with a wet, sucking sound. She tossed it near Corvin's knees. "A big bastard. Strong as an ox, but his head was soft. Took a spear in the gut during the retreat from the salt-pans. I tried to hand him my dagger. He threw it in the dirt. Started cursing me, screaming that I was a coward for not carrying him."

She reached for the second boot, her fingers working the leather with the same cold efficiency she used for skinning rabbits. 

"We couldn't carry him. He weighed sixteen stone and we had three miles of hill-country to climb before dark. We left him there with his canteen and his boots. The crows were circling before we even hit the ridge. He was still screaming when the wind shifted."

She stood up, holding the second boot by its collar. She tapped the heel against her own shin to knock the loose, dried mud off. 

"You do what you can," she said, handing the second boot to Corvin. "But you don't carry dead weight. If you're going to put those on, do it now. The damp is rising, and once your socks get wet, you'll be limping by midnight."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack did not turn away. She stood there in the purple twilight, her shadow swallowed by the larger darkness of the trees, and watched him struggle with the dead man's laces. Her face was a map of old scars and indifference, but her eyes stayed on his hands.

"He's already dead, Corvin," she said, her voice dropping into that low, even register. "But if you want the ledger, I'll give you the ledger."

She knelt back down, not next to the gut-shot man this time, but closer to Corvin, her knees clicking like dry twigs. She reached out and tapped the side of her own neck, just under the jawline, where the skin was thin and the pulse beat steady.

"When you put the point under his ear and pushed," she said, "you went through the skin first. That’s the hardest part—it’s tough, like old pig-skin, and it wants to slide. But you had the angle right. Once you were through, the blade cut the carotid. That's the thick pipe that carries the hot blood straight from the heart to the brain. You felt it give, didn't you? A little pop, like pushing a peg through wet canvas."

She watched his hands. He was holding the dead man's boot, but he wasn't pulling.

"The moment that pipe is split," Wrack continued, her tone as dry as if she were counting sacks of oats, "the pressure drops to nothing. The brain doesn't get its grease anymore. He didn't feel the cold or the dark coming; he just went dizzy. Like when you stand up too fast after a long sit by the fire, only it doesn't stop. Within five seconds, his eyes couldn't see you anymore, even if they were still open. Within ten, his mind was gone. The rest of it—the twitching in his fingers, the way his chest gave that one last, deep heave—that’s just the meat realizing the master’s left the house."

She reached down, took the heel of the boot Corvin was holding, and gave it a sharp, downward yank. The leather came off the dead foot with a soft, wet *shuck*. 

"The sound you heard—that wet sigh—that was just the air left in his windpipe escaping through the hole you made," she said. She took the empty boot from Corvin's hand and set it beside the first one. "It's the quietest way a man dies on a field. No screaming, no begging, no three days of smelling your own rot. You did him a favor, if you want to look at it that way. Or you just saved us a half-mile of noise. It’s the same difference to the road."

She stood up, her hand resting on her hip, looking down at him. 

"Now put them on," she said. "Your feet are smaller than his, so you'll want to stuff some dry grass or a bit of rag into the toes so they don't rub. If you get blisters tonight, you'll be trailing blood by tomorrow noon, and I'm not carrying you either."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stuff some dead grass into the toes and pull the boots on. They're loose, but better than my old ones. "I can walk," I say, standing up. "Let's get off this road."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack nodded once, a brief jerk of her chin that passed for approval. She didn't praise him; standing up and walking was the bare minimum required to stay alive, and she wasn't in the habit of handing out copper stars for basic survival. 

"Good," she said, hoisting her own pack onto her shoulder. The strap bit into her collarbone, right over an old scar from a crossbow bolt that always ached when the damp came up. "Stomp your heels down hard once or twice. Get the grass settled in the toes before we hit the slope, or it'll bunch up under your instep and give you a blister anyway."

She didn't look back at the dead men or the horse. The road was already fading into a uniform, dusty gray, the white birch trunks along the ditch-edge looking like pale ribs in the gloom. 

"Leave your old boots in the ditch," she added, turning her face toward the dark wall of the pines. "If some scout finds them, they'll think we're traveling light. If they find nothing, they'll look harder."

She stepped off the hard-packed dirt of the road, her boots sinking into the wet, rotting mast of the ditch. She climbed the far bank with a hand out to steady herself against a low pine branch, her bad knee making a dull *click* in the quiet. 

"Keep five paces behind me," she said, her voice dropping to a low murmur that barely carried over the sighing of the wind in the needles. "Watch where I put my feet. The ground's rocky here, and if you break an ankle, I'm not carrying you, and I'm not leaving you my knife either. You'll just have to sit in the wet and wait for the wolves to do the throat-cutting."

She didn't wait to see if he was following. She slipped into the deeper shadow of the trees, her gray cloak blending into the bark and the dusk until she was nothing but a shape moving slightly faster than the dark.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped. Her boots, halfway up the ditch-bank, slid slightly in the loose pine needles. She didn't turn back around immediately. She stood there with her back to him, her head tilted toward the dark canopy, listening to the wind rattle the dead leaves. 

Then, with a slow, heavy breath that hissed through her teeth, she turned. She walked back down into the ditch, her bad knee clicking, and stood three feet from where he sat on his heels. 

She didn't offer him a hand to get up. Instead, she leaned her shoulder against the splintered tailboard of the overturned cart, right near where the dead man’s head had been resting a minute ago. She looked down at Corvin, her face a pale, sharp wedge in the twilight.

"The rest," she said. Her voice was very quiet now, not because she was being gentle, but because the forest was getting dark and sound traveled further in the cold. "You think there's a part I'm keeping back to spare you. You think there's some secret to it that makes it make sense."

She reached into her pocket, pulled out a small piece of dry pine bark, and began scraping the dirt out from under her fingernails with the corner of it. 

"Here’s the rest," she said. "Tonight, once we’re five miles from here and we’ve crawled into some thicket where the wind can’t reach us, your fingers are going to start shaking. Not now—now you’ve still got the grease of the fight hot in your blood. But when we stop, when the dark gets heavy and we’re sitting there in the wet with nothing but cold water and raw fat to chew on, the cold will get into your bones. Your hands will start to twitch. You won't be able to hold the water skin steady. You'll think you're freezing, but you aren't. It's just the panic coming out of your skin like sweat."

She didn't look up from her fingernails, her voice remaining flat, rhythmic, and entirely devoid of pity.

"And the smell. You've got his blood on your trousers now. You'll smell it all night. It doesn't smell like iron when it gets old; it smells like sweet, rotten copper. It gets behind your teeth. You'll spit, and you'll think you taste it, even though your mouth is clean. You'll wash your hands in the first creek we find, you'll scrub them with sand until the skin is raw and bleeding, but when you put your fingers near your face to eat, you'll still smell him. You'll smell him for three days. Every time you sweat, you'll think it's his grease coming out of your own pores."

She tossed the piece of bark into the mud and finally looked at him, her gray eyes steady and hard as river stones.

"And then there's the sleep," she continued. "People who write the songs—the ones who stay in the taverns and never see a ditch—they think you dream of their eyes looking at you. They think you see ghosts. They're fools. You won't remember his face by next week. What you'll dream of is the weight of his chin in your hand. The way his skin felt like wet lard. You'll wake up in the dark because you think your own fingers are covered in that grease, and you'll reach for your knife because you think he's sitting on your chest, trying to put his fingers in your mouth to stop the whistling."

She pointed a blunt finger at the dead man propped against the wheel. 

"He had a name," she said, her voice dropping another notch. "He probably had some girl in a village three days north who's going to wait by the well until her hair goes grey, wondering why he didn't come back with the salt. He had a mother who cried when he went to the wars, and he had some dog he liked, and he had some stupid joke he told when he was drunk. And now he’s just a sack of meat we’re leaving for the crows. The world didn't tilt when you pushed the iron in. The sun didn't stop going down. The dirt just took his blood, and it'll take yours the same way, and it won't care about the difference between you."

She straightened up from the cart, her joint giving that familiar, dry pop. She adjusted the strap of her pack where it dug into her shoulder.

"That's the rest of it, Corvin," she said, looking down at him. "It doesn't get better. It doesn't get cleaner. You just get used to the taste of copper in your spit, or you die because you were too busy looking at your hands to see the next spear coming."

She turned toward the trees again, her gray cloak rustling against the dry weeds. 

"Now get up," she said, her tone returning to that flat, business-like rasp. "The wind is turning. If we aren't in the pines before the stars show, we'll be freezing in the open, and I've told you all the stories I have."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I get up. My legs feel heavy, like they don't belong to me. I follow her into the trees without looking back. "My turn with the water skin tomorrow," I say, my voice too loud in the quiet.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't stop, but she slowed her pace just enough that the gap between them didn't grow. She didn't look back, either, though she did reach up and catch a low pine branch, holding it aside with her shoulder so it wouldn't whip back and take his eye out in the dark.

"Keep your teeth together," she murmured, her voice so low it was barely more than the rustle of her wool cloak against the gorse. "The wind is dropping, and a voice carries like a bell in the cold. If you want to talk, you wait until we're deep enough in the brush that the needles muffle it."

They climbed a steep, slick bank of wet pine needles, Wrack using her boots to find the exposed roots for traction. Her bad knee twinged with every rise, a dull, throbbing heat that she ignored with the practiced ease of someone who had lived with a dozen such quiet miseries for a decade. 

"We'll see about the water skin tomorrow," she added, her breath pluming gray and faint before her. "If your shoulders are stiff from that cart-work, you'll just drop it and spill the only clean drink we've got. Let's see if we make the ridge first."

The forest closed in around them, swallowing what little remained of the twilight. The smell of the road—the wet horse, the spilled iron, the sour, sudden death—began to fade, replaced by the sharp, clean scent of crushed pine and damp earth. It was safer here, but only marginally. The dark was its own kind of trap if you didn't know how to walk in it.

"Five paces," she reminded him, her silhouette a slightly darker patch of blackness against the trees ahead. "And lift your feet. You're dragging your heels like a plowshare. If I can hear you, a scout with his ear to the ground can hear you from a mile off."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I lift my feet, trying to walk lighter. The new boots feel strange, the grass already shifting. "You talk like a scout," I whisper, the words barely there. "You ever do that?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn’t stop, her boots finding the firmest parts of the slope by touch alone. Her answer came back to him as a thin, dry thread of sound, barely louder than the pine needles brushing against her wool sleeves.

"Two years," she said. "Under the old Captain, before the company got split at the Red Hills. If you live long enough in this trade, you do a bit of everything. They put the light ones on the flank, and back then, I didn't have this knee."

She paused, her hand reaching back to touch a thick, mossy trunk, guiding herself around a drop-off he couldn't see in the dark. 

"Scouting isn't what they tell you in the songs," she whispered, her breath cold against the back of her neck. "It’s not creeping through the ferns with black grease on your face, waiting to slit a sentry’s throat. It’s sitting in a wet gorse bush for three days in the rain, staring at a crossroads to see if the Duke’s supply wagons have six mules or eight. It’s counting the shovels on the back of a pioneer cart to guess if they’re going to dig trenches or throw up a bridge."

She kept her pace slow, steady, her body leaning forward to balance the weight of the water skin and her pack. 

"And it’s dirty," she continued. "You don't light a fire. You don't chew dry meat because the cracking of your teeth sounds like a pistol shot when the air is still. You learn how to piss in your breeches because if you stand up to stretch your legs, some lad with a hunting bow on the ridge will put a goose-feather through your kidney. By the end of a week, you smell like a wet dog that's been rolled in a privy, and your toes are so rotted from the damp that the skin comes off with your socks."

She stopped for a fraction of a second, her silhouette head tilting as she listened to the deeper woods. Satisfied, she started forward again, her voice dropping even lower.

"But it teaches you to look at the ground. You stop looking at the trees and you look at what’s under them. You learn that a broken fern means someone was carrying something heavy, because a man with a light pack doesn't swing his hips wide enough to snap the stems. You learn that if the crows are sitting in the high pine branches instead of the birches, there’s someone walking under the birches."

She reached back and grabbed his sleeve, her grip tight and hard as iron, pulling him slightly to the left. 

"Watch your shin," she murmured. "There’s a fallen pine trunk under the needles here. It’s slick as grease. If you bark your bone on it, you’ll yell, and then we’ll both be dead."

She let go of his sleeve and pushed through a thick screen of young hemlock, the wet boughs brushing against her leather jerkin with a soft, sweeping sound. 

"If you want to live to see the spring, Corvin, you stop thinking like a man who’s walking down a road," she said. "You start thinking like a fox that’s got three different hounds behind it. You don't look for the easy path. You look for the one that doesn't leave a track."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I follow the way she pulls me, my shin just missing the hidden log. "A fox," I repeat, the word tasting strange. "What do the hounds smell like?"
