dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack finished with the knife and slid it home, then sat back on her heels and looked at him properly for the first time since it had started. Whatever she saw made her mouth do a small thing that wasn't quite a smile.

"Not yours," she said. "I checked while you were standing there. You've got a graze on your ear you haven't noticed yet, but the rest of it's somebody else's problem, and their problem's over."

She stood, joints complaining, and stretched her back until something in it clicked. The noise from beyond the cart hadn't stopped. It wasn't screaming — screamers usually stopped themselves one way or another inside a few minutes. This was the wet, tired sound of a man breathing wrong through a hole that shouldn't be there.

"Gut, probably," she said, matter-of-fact, cocking her head toward it. "Sometimes it's the lung. Gut takes longer. Could be a day, if he's stubborn about it, and out here that's a day of the crows working on him while he's still awake to notice." She rolled her shoulder, felt the pull of a bruise she hadn't accounted for yet. "So. Three ways it goes. You go over there and finish him. I go over there and finish him. Or we walk off and let the field have him."

She didn't say which she'd pick. She'd picked plenty of times, and she wasn't about to pretend it was a hard sum. But he was newer to this than she was, and there were things you had to work out with your own hands or they sat in you wrong later.

"Your call, Corvin," she said. "Not a test. Just a call."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod, not meeting her eyes. My sword feels too heavy in my hand. "I'll do it." The words come out quieter than I meant.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched him for a moment — the way the sword hung, the way his eyes stayed on the mud between them — and then she nodded once, like he'd told her the weather.

"Alright." She bent and picked up a fallen shortsword from the ditch, tested its weight, tossed it point-down into the earth so it stood between them. "Leave yours sheathed. That one's shorter and you won't have to think about the swing. Point-first, under the ribs, angled up. Left side of his chest, your right hand. You'll feel it go through the soft, and then you'll feel it stop. Push till it stops, then a bit more, then hold it there while you count to five. Don't saw. Sawing's for meat you mean to eat."

She said it the way a smith might explain a weld. There was no ceremony in it and she wasn't offering any.

"He might grab at you. Won't have much in him but it'll feel like more than you expect. Kneel on his arm if you have to. And don't look at his face until after — look at where you're putting the blade. After's different. After you can look at him all you want."

She picked her own knife back out, not because she meant to use it, but because her hands wanted something to hold while his did the work. Then she stepped aside, out of his line to the cart, and gave him the room.

"I'll be here," she said. "Won't watch if you'd rather. Won't leave, either."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack considered that. She could have given him the quick answer — the one that made it sit easier — but he'd asked the real question and he'd asked it straight, and she wasn't going to hand him a lie to carry around instead of the truth.

"Both," she said. "Mostly. Gut wound out here, no surgeon, no clean water, no roof — he's not walking out. That part's a mercy and it's a real one, not the kind people tell themselves after. He'd die tonight or tomorrow and it wouldn't be gentle."

She scratched at a fleck of drying blood on the back of her hand, worked it off with her thumbnail.

"But easier's in there too. Won't pretend it isn't. Easier for us — we don't sit here half the night listening to him. Easier for the horses, if they're still where we left them, because they don't like the smell of a man dying slow. Easier on the next people down the road, whoever they are, who don't have to walk past him."

She looked up, finally, and met his eyes properly.

"The two things live in the same house, Corvin. Anyone tells you they only ever did it for the one and never the other is lying, or hasn't done it enough times to know. Doesn't make it not a mercy. Just means you're honest about the rest of it."

She tipped her chin toward the cart.

"He's still making that noise. Whichever reason you go with, go soon."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take a slow breath, then pull the shortsword from the dirt. The grip feels foreign in my hand. "Alright," I say, more to myself than to her. I start walking toward the cart, my boots heavy in the mud.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stayed where she was. She didn't watch him go, exactly — she let her eyes rest somewhere in the middle distance, past the ditch, where a crow had already found something to think about on the far side of the road. But she tracked him with the rest of her. The sound of his boots. The pause when he'd have first seen the man properly, over the tail of the cart. The absence of a second voice, which meant the man on the ground was too far gone to beg or hadn't the breath for it.

She thumbed the flat of her knife against her knee, a small idle motion. Her own first one had been fifteen years back and she still remembered the weight of it, the specific give under the blade, the way the fellow had looked at her not with fear but with something more like recognition, as if she'd finally shown up. She hadn't thought about that face in years and it surprised her a little, arriving now, uninvited. That was how it worked. Someone else's turn brought your own back up out of the mud where you'd stamped it down.

The noise from beyond the cart changed. A shorter sound. Then quieter. Then the particular quiet that wasn't the same as the quiet before.

Wrack counted, in her head, to a slow ten. Gave him the time to do the holding-still part, and the standing-up-after part, without a voice at his back rushing him through it.

Then she called, low and even, not loud enough to carry past the cart to anywhere it shouldn't: "Corvin. Walk back when you're ready. No hurry on it."

She sheathed her knife and, because her hands still wanted work, began going through the nearest body's belt — not looting so much as checking, the old habit. A purse, thin. A folded bit of paper she didn't unfold. A knife better than the one he'd died with, which said something about him she didn't need to know.

She left it all where it lay for now, and waited.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack got up without hurry, wiped her palms on her thighs, and came over. She didn't stand too close to him — a pace off his shoulder, near enough to talk low, far enough that he didn't have to feel her breath on him while he was working out whatever he was working out.

She looked down at the man on the ground and let her eyes take stock the way they'd been trained to, one thing at a time.

"Alright," she said. "You did it right. Under the ribs, up. See where the hilt's sitting — that angle's what you wanted. Went through the soft and found the works. That's why it was quick at the end."

She crouched, not touching anything yet, just pointing with two fingers.

"Colour of his face — that grey under the dirt, round the mouth especially — that's blood not going where it should anymore. Lips'll go bluer in a bit. Eyes are already doing the thing they do; they don't track. You can wave a hand across and they won't follow. That's how you'll know, from now on, when you're not sure. Eyes stop working before the rest of him's finished, sometimes by a good few minutes. Don't let that fool you into thinking he's gone if the chest's still moving. But his isn't."

She let a beat pass, so he could see it for himself if he wanted to.

"Belly's the mess. That's the wound he was going to die of — see the dark on the front of his tunic, low down, and how much of it there is. That's a day of dying you spared him. What you did on top of that was maybe an hour, maybe less. So." She glanced up at him, sidelong. "Small mercy in real terms. Real one, still."

She stood again, joints doing their usual complaint, and rested a hand briefly on the tail of the cart. Not on him. On the wood.

"Now the part nobody tells you. In a bit — could be tonight, could be a week — you'll be doing something ordinary and you'll get his face back. Not because you did wrong. Because you did a thing, and the thing sits. Doesn't go away, exactly. Finds a shelf. You let it find one. Don't argue with it and don't build a shrine to it either."

She looked at the sword still in the man's chest, and then at Corvin's hand, which was probably shaking or probably wasn't; either was fine.

"Pull it out when you're ready. Foot on his hip for leverage, not his belly. Straight back, same angle you put it in. Wipe it on his cloak, not yours. Then we see to your ear."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod, swallowing hard. "Small mercy," I echo, my voice rough. Stepping forward, I brace my boot against the man's hip and pull. The blade comes free with a wet sound. I wipe it on his cloak, the motion mechanical. "Alright," I say, turning back to her. "Ear next."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack took the shortsword from him — not with any ceremony, just held her hand out for it like a farrier taking back a tool — and gave it a look, then bent and set it point-down in the mud a little way from the body. Someone would want it, or nobody would. Not their problem now.

"Sit," she said, and pointed at the cart's back edge. "Higher than a log, lower than standing. My back'll thank you."

She fished in the pouch at her hip while he settled, and came up with a small stoppered horn and a strip of linen that had started life whiter than it was now but was clean enough for the job. She uncorked the horn with her teeth, spat the stopper into her palm, and gave the contents a sniff more from habit than doubt.

"Spirits," she said. "The drinking kind, mostly. Going to hurt for about as long as it takes you to swear once. Don't swear at me, I didn't put the hole there."

She stepped in close, tilted his head with two fingers under his jaw — brisk, not gentle, the way you'd turn a horse's head to check a bit — and had a proper look at the ear in what light was left. The graze ran along the upper curve, shallow, a clean shave of skin gone. It had bled the way ear wounds bled, which was to say generously and out of all proportion to what had actually happened. Half his neck was tacky with it.

"Nothing," she pronounced. "You'll keep the ear. You'll keep the hearing. You'll have a nick in it come morning that you can tell girls about, or boys, whichever you're lying to."

She wet the linen with the spirits, put her other hand flat against the side of his head to hold him steady, and pressed the cloth to the graze without any warning worth the name. Warning made people flinch into it. Better to just do it.

"Breathe out," she said, after, keeping the pressure. "Not in. Out. Long one."

She held it there while she counted, and while she counted she watched his face — not for the pain, which was ordinary and would pass, but for the other thing. The after-thing. It usually showed up somewhere around now, when the doing was done and the hands weren't busy and somebody was touching you with something like care, even if the care was rough and smelled of cheap liquor.

She didn't say anything about it if it came. She just kept her hand where it was, and her count steady, and let him have the quiet.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't answer right away. She kept the pressure on his ear, finished her count, then peeled the linen back and had a look at the graze before she folded the cloth to a cleaner face and pressed it back.

"Alright," she said. "Hold that yourself. Firm. I'll talk while you press."

She stepped back half a pace, wiped her fingers on her thigh, and considered where to start. Not the way she'd have told it to another sellsword over a fire — that version had jokes in it, and shorthand, and the jokes were a kind of armour. He wanted it without the armour. Fair enough.

"Spear goes in easier than you'd think," she said. "Skin gives, then the wall of muscle, then you're in the belly proper, which is mostly bag and rope. Bag's the stomach and the guts. Rope's the guts uncoiled, which is what they are — one long tube, folded up clever. Spear doesn't care. Punches a hole in whatever's in front of the point. Might be stomach. Might be a loop of bowel. Might be liver, if it's angled high, and liver bleeds like a cut wineskin and doesn't stop."

She glanced at the body by the cart, then back at him. Kept her voice level.

"What kills him, out here, isn't the hole. It's what comes out of the hole and where. Stomach's got acid and half-eaten food in it. Bowel's got shit — I'm not being coarse, that's what it is, and it's the worst of the lot because it goes into the belly cavity and rots him from the inside while he's still using it. That's the fever you'd have watched come up on him by morning if you'd left him. Shakes first, then the sweat, then the talking to people who aren't there. Belly swells up hard as a drum. Skin round the wound goes the wrong colours in order — red, then a bad yellow, then black at the edge. Smell changes. You'd know the smell after once. You don't forget it."

She rolled her shoulder again, the bruise reminding her.

"Pain's the other part. Gut pain isn't like a cut on your arm. It's deep and it's everywhere and it doesn't let up between breaths. Men curl round it. They can't help it, the body just does. Some of them beg for water and you can't give it — water goes straight out the hole and hurries the rot. Some of them go quiet early and you think they're dying and they're not, they're just saving what breath they've got. Some of them ask for their mothers. Most of them, actually. That one stops being a surprise after a while and starts being — I don't know. A thing you notice, and then you don't."

She scratched under her jaw with the back of her thumb.

"His one, specifically — the one you just did — spear went in low left, out through his back a hand's breadth off his spine. I saw it when I walked round earlier. That's bowel and probably kidney on the way through. Kidney bleeds inside where you can't see it, fills the belly up slow. He'd have gone the fever way if we'd left him, and he'd have gone it thirsty, because the blood loss makes you thirsty in a way that doesn't quit. That's your day, day and a half. Crows would've started on his eyes before his heart stopped. They go for the wet parts first. They're not cruel, they're just birds."

She stopped there. Not because there wasn't more — there was always more — but because there was a point past which telling it became something other than what he'd asked for, and she'd been on the wrong end of that kind of telling herself, once or twice, from men who liked the sound of their own knowing.

"That straight enough," she said. It wasn't quite a question.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't know I was holding. "Straight enough." My hand holding the cloth to my ear is steady now, maybe from the pressure. "He asked for his mother?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't answer at first. She looked past him, toward the cart, and her mouth did that small thing again that wasn't a smile.

"Didn't say he did. Said most of them do." She met his eyes then, and there was nothing evasive in it, but nothing soft either. "This one — I don't know. I wasn't at his shoulder for it. He was making noise when we got close and he was making less of it when you got closer, and somewhere in there he might've said anything or nothing. You'd know better than me. You were the one who heard the end of it."

She let that sit a beat, in case he wanted to say. Didn't push.

"If he did, it wasn't for you. Wasn't really for her either. It's just what the mouth reaches for when the rest of you's run out of ideas. Comes up out of somewhere older than the man does." She shrugged, one-shouldered, careful of the bruise. "I've heard grown killers call for theirs. Men who hadn't spoken their mother's name in thirty years and probably hated her when they had. Doesn't mean anything about him. Doesn't mean anything about you for hearing it."

She reached over and lifted the edge of the linen at his ear with two fingers, checked the bleed, pressed it back.

"Slowing," she said. "Give it another count of fifty and we'll tie it off."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped mid-turn. She looked at him for a long moment — kneeling in the mud beside a man who wasn't yet dead — and then she came back, unhurried, and lowered herself onto her heels a pace off his shoulder. Close enough to see. Not close enough to crowd his hands.

She didn't ask him why. She had an idea why, and if she was wrong about it that was his business.

"Alright," she said, low. "You keep going. I'll talk."

The man on the ground was past most things but not all of them. His eyes were open and his eyes weren't seeing, not properly — they were fixed somewhere off past Corvin's shoulder, at nothing, and every few breaths they twitched like they were trying to focus on something that had already left. His mouth was slack. There was pink froth at the corner of it, thin, which said the spear had found lung along the way, or a nick of one, and the gut wound had had company all along.

"Lung too," she said. "See that pink at his mouth? Air getting into the blood in his chest. He'd have drowned in it before the belly finished him. So — smaller mercy than I said, or bigger, depending how you count."

Corvin's hands were doing what hands did when they hadn't done a thing before: too much force in the wrong places, not enough where it was needed. The shortsword's point was against the man's tunic, dimpling it, and the angle wasn't right yet.

"Higher with the point," she said. "Not the hilt, the point. Your wrist's dropped. There. Feel where the last rib runs — you'll feel the ridge of it under the cloth if you press with your off hand. Under that ridge, up toward his opposite shoulder. Not straight up. Angled. Like you're pointing at his far ear from underneath."

She watched his knuckles.

"Grip's too tight. You'll shake. Loose enough that it's the weight of you going through, not the squeeze of your hand. Lean on it. Don't stab. Lean."

The man's breath hitched — not from anything Corvin had done yet, just the ordinary hitching of a body running out. His fingers moved on the mud, a small crabbing motion, not reaching for anything, just the last of the nerves talking to themselves.

"That's not him," she said, quiet, before he could ask. "That's the meat. Body does that near the end whether the man's in it or not. Don't answer it."

She watched him lean.

"There. That's the give — feel that? Skin. Now the wall. That's the second give, thicker. Keep going. You'll feel it get easier, that's the belly proper. Don't stop there. Up. Up. — There."

The sound wasn't loud. It never was, when it was done right. A soft wet press, and then a smaller sound underneath it, which was the point finding what it had been sent to find. The man's chest jerked once, a shallow thing, and the pink at his mouth pulsed and then didn't.

"Hold it," she said. "Count. Slow. One. Two."

She kept her eyes on the man's face because Corvin's was busy.

"Three. Four. His eyes — watch them now. That flatness coming in. Like a film. That's what going looks like, from the outside. Five. Six. You can breathe, by the way. You're not. Seven."

A last small sound came out of the man that wasn't quite a word and wasn't quite a breath. Just the air in him leaving by the shortest road it could find.

"Eight. Nine. Ten. Alright."

She didn't tell him to pull it out yet. Some men wanted the blade out fast, like the thing wasn't over till the steel was clear. Some men needed a breath with their hand still on the hilt, feeling the weight of what they'd done sit properly in their arm before they let it go. She let him pick.

"He took about a count of ten from your lean to the last of him," she said, evenly. "That's fast. That's as fast as it gets, with a belly wound already working on him. You didn't drag it out. You didn't botch it. The noise you heard — that small one at the end — that's air, not him. He was gone before it. The body empties after. Like tipping a jug."

She didn't touch him. Didn't put a hand on his shoulder or his back. He hadn't asked for that and she wasn't going to give him something he hadn't asked for on top of everything else.

"When you're ready," she said. "Foot on his hip. Straight back, same angle in. Wipe it on his cloak."

A beat.

"And then you tell me if you want the walk back quiet or you want me talking. Either's fine. I've done both."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I pull the blade free, the sound thick and final. Wiping it on his cloak feels like cleaning a tool after a messy job. "Talk," I say, my voice rough. "Tell me about your first one."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack took the shortsword from him again, and this time she didn't set it in the mud. She held it flat across her palms for a moment, considering the weight of it, and then she slid it through her belt at the back where it wouldn't knock against her own knife. Someone's, now. Hers by default.

She stood, and offered him a hand up. If he took it, she'd pull; if he didn't, she'd let the hand fall without making anything of it. Then she started walking, slow, back toward where they'd left the horses tied off the road, and she waited till he was in step with her before she started.

"Fifteen years back," she said. "Give or take. I was younger than you are now, which is a thing to think about and I try not to. It wasn't a battle. That's the first thing to know. People think their first is a battle. Mine was a barn."

The light was going. The road ahead had that blue in it that came before proper dusk, when the shapes of things were still clear but the colours had started leaving.

"We'd taken a farm. Not we — the company I was with then, which was a different company, most of them dead now for reasons that had nothing to do with me. The fighting was done by the time I got put on the barn. My job was to walk through and check what was in it. Standard work. You look for stores, you look for anyone hiding, you look for anything that might come at your back later."

She scratched at her jaw.

"There was a man in the hayloft. Not a soldier. Farmer, or somebody's uncle, I don't know. He'd taken a cut across the thigh earlier in the day and climbed up there to wait it out, and the cut had opened an artery, the big one on the inside of the leg — you'll learn where that is, remind me — and he'd bled most of what he had into the hay before I found him. He was white as cheese. Couldn't sit up. Couldn't do anything but look at me."

She was quiet a few paces.

"He had a knife in his hand. Little thing. Eating knife. He wasn't holding it like he meant to use it, he was holding it like he'd forgotten he had it. And I stood there at the top of the ladder with my sword out and I did the sums the way you do — he's not walking out of here, he's not a threat, somebody's got to, and it's going to be me because I'm the one standing here."

The road bent. She adjusted her course without looking.

"Took me a long time. Longer than yours. I didn't know where to put it. I'd killed in the fight earlier — two, I think, maybe three, it goes blurry — but that had been arms and shoulders and the side of a neck, everything happening at once, and none of it had been a man lying still and looking at me while I decided. I ended up doing it wrong. Went for the throat because I thought it'd be quick and I nicked the side instead of the pipe and had to do it again. He didn't fight me. He made a noise I still hear sometimes. Not a scream. More like — disappointed. Like I'd let him down."

She glanced sidelong at Corvin, brief.

"That's the bit that stayed. Not the blood, not the mess, not the smell. The disappointment. Because he'd been waiting for someone to come up that ladder and finish it and when I finally did I made him wait longer than I should've. That's the thing I owe him, is that I was slow."

She let that walk with them a while.

"I tell you that not because yours was like mine. Yours wasn't. You did yours cleaner than I did mine, and you're carrying it better than I carried mine, which I carried by getting into a fight in a tavern three nights later and losing most of a tooth over it." She showed him, briefly, the gap on the left side of her smile — an old one, worn smooth. "Tooth was the bill. Everybody pays it somehow. Some pay it drinking, some pay it fighting, some pay it going quiet for a month and coming back thinner. You'll find yours. Don't pick the drinking one if you can help it. It's the most expensive in the long run and the company's worse."

The horses were where they'd left them, which was a mercy in itself. One of them lifted its head at the sound of her and went back to whatever it had been thinking about. She stopped a few paces short and turned to face him properly, in what was left of the light.

"That's the story," she said. "It's not a good one. First ones mostly aren't. But you asked, and it's yours to keep now if you want it, or to put down. I don't mind either way."

She waited a beat.

"Ear's stopped bleeding, by the way. You can take the cloth off when you remember it's there."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at him — really looked, in the way she mostly didn't, because looking at people that way was a thing that cost you and she was careful with her coin. He was still on his heels in the mud by the horses, not sitting properly, not standing, in that in-between crouch bodies went into when they hadn't decided yet whether the day was over.

She thought about telling him to get up. Decided against it. Instead she lowered herself onto the road across from him, slow, one hand on her knee for the descent, and settled cross-legged in the dirt like they had all night. Which, near enough, they did.

"Alright," she said. "The rest."

She didn't start straight away. She unstoppered the horn again, took a small pull of the spirits herself — small, because spirits on an empty stomach after a fight were how you woke up not remembering things — and passed it across to him without asking whether he wanted it. He could take it or not.

"The rest of the barn," she said, "was that I sat down. Right there in the hay. Didn't come down the ladder for — I don't know. Long enough that someone came looking. Long enough that the blood I was sitting in had started to go tacky under my thighs, which is a feeling you'll know now or you'll know soon. Wet blood and drying blood are different weights. Drying's heavier. Sticks."

She rolled her neck. Something in it popped.

"I sat there and I did a thing I'm not proud of, which was I talked to him. After. Kept talking to him for — I don't know how long. Told him I was sorry I'd been slow. Told him my name, which is a thing you do not do, to a dead man or a live one, when you're on somebody's farm you've just taken. Told him where I was from, which was a lie at the time and became true later in the way those things do. Told him I hadn't wanted to come up the ladder. Which was also a lie, because I had wanted to — that was the job and I'd wanted the job — but I'd wanted it to be empty up there, and it hadn't been, and I was making him carry the difference between what I'd wanted and what I'd got."

She scratched at the back of her hand.

"He didn't answer, obviously. But I remember being surprised he didn't. Not surprised he was dead — I knew that, I'd done it — surprised the talking didn't reach him. First time you understand, properly, that dead's a wall. Not a curtain, not a door, a wall. You can put your hand on it and it doesn't give. Everybody thinks they know that before it happens to them. They don't. You know it when you've talked at one for a while and heard your own voice come back at you off the hay."

The horse behind her shifted its weight, one hoof to the other. She didn't turn.

"Man who came looking for me was called Bel. Big fellow, older than me by twenty years, dead now — of the flux, three winters after, which is what most of us get in the end if the steel doesn't. He came up that ladder and he saw me sitting there and he saw the man I'd done, and he didn't say anything for a bit. Just leaned on the top of the ladder and looked. Then he said — I remember it exactly — he said, 'You want to come down, or you want me to come up.' Not a question the way I'm saying it. Flat. Like the weather."

She almost smiled. It didn't quite make it to her mouth.

"I said come up. So he came up. Sat down in the hay across from me the way I'm sat across from you now, more or less, and he didn't touch me and he didn't say anything kind. He asked me if I'd looked through the man's pockets yet. I said no. He said we should, because that was the work, and the work was what we were there for, and if I did the work now the rest of it would find its shelf faster. So we went through his pockets together. Bel did the actual going-through, because my hands weren't up to it, but he made me watch and he made me name what came out. Flint and steel. A bit of cord. Half a loaf wrapped in cloth. A wooden comb with two teeth missing. A folded paper that turned out to be a list of names, which we didn't read, because it wasn't ours to read and reading it wouldn't have told us anything we could use."

She held up a finger, one at a time, as if laying the items out on the road between them.

"Flint. Cord. Bread. Comb. Paper. Five things. He made me say them twice. Then he made me say them again the next morning, and again the morning after. By the fourth morning I couldn't remember them in the right order and he said good, that's the shelf, that's where he lives now, you don't have to dust him."

She let her hand fall.

"That was the trick he taught me and I'll give it to you for free because it was given to me for free. When one of them starts coming back up — the face, the sound, whatever's yours — you name what was on him. Five things. Doesn't have to be pockets. Can be the colour of his boots, the way his hair was cut, whether his teeth were straight, the shape of the wound, the weather. Five specific things. And you say them out loud if you can, or in your head if you can't. You're not making a shrine. You're making an inventory. Inventories go on shelves. Shrines don't."

She shifted, easing the bruise on her shoulder.

"Rest of what happened. I came down the ladder eventually. Bel came down first, which was decent of him, because it meant if my legs gave out on the rungs he'd catch me instead of me landing on top of him. They didn't give out. I got down. I went and washed my hands in the trough, which was a stupid thing to do because the trough was for the animals and now it wasn't good for anything, and Bel didn't stop me because he understood that some stupid things you have to do anyway. Then I sat against the barn wall in the sun for about an hour and didn't talk to anyone, and nobody made me, because that was a company that understood the hour after and gave it to you when they could."

She looked at him.

"Then I ate. That was the other thing Bel taught me, that first day. He brought me bread and cheese and made me eat it while I was still — you know. Still in it. I said I couldn't. He said that was exactly why I had to, because the body needed to learn that it got fed after, or it'd start associating the after with going hungry, and going hungry with the after, and I'd be a mess about food for years. I don't know if that's true. Might be one of those things old sellswords tell young ones to sound wise. But I ate the bread and the cheese and I've never had trouble eating after, so maybe he was right, or maybe I was going to be fine on that front anyway."

She took the horn back if he'd finished with it, or waited for it to come back to her, and stoppered it and put it away.

"The three nights later thing, with the tooth. That I'll tell you straight because I told you it already and I don't want you thinking I dressed it up. We were in a town — I won't name it, it doesn't matter, it's ash now anyway for other reasons — and I went into a tavern by myself, which was the first mistake, and I drank more than I could carry, which was the second, and I picked a fight with a man twice my size over nothing, which was the third. He wasn't even a bad man. He was just there. I hit him first and I hit him because I wanted him to hit me back, and he did, and he knocked a tooth loose and split my lip and Bel — Bel again, always Bel that year — Bel pulled me off him before it got worse and paid the man for the trouble and dragged me back to where we were sleeping and sat with me while I cried, which I did for about two hours straight and haven't done since about anything, that I remember. He didn't tell anyone. I didn't ask him not to. He just didn't. And in the morning he said, that's the bill paid, don't pay it twice. And I didn't. I've paid other bills for other ones since, but I didn't pay that one twice, and that's something."

She was quiet a while. The horses breathed. Somewhere off in the trees a bird that wasn't a crow made a small evening noise.

"The reason I'm telling you all of that," she said, and her voice had gone quieter, not softer — quieter, which was different — "is because you asked, and because you did a thing today that most people don't do the first time, which is you looked at it. You knelt down and you looked at it and you asked me to look at it with you and to say what it was. That's — that's not a small thing. Most first ones look away. Most first ones want the whole business gone from their head before the blade's out of the body. You wanted the details. And the details are how it doesn't rot in you. The details are the shelf. So you did, without knowing you were doing it, the thing that took me three nights and a tooth to figure out."

She looked at him levelly.

"Doesn't mean it won't come back up. It will. Face, sound, the give under the blade, the way his fingers moved on the mud that wasn't him moving them. One of those, or all of them, some night when you're doing something ordinary. And when it does, you name five things. Colour of his cloak. Shape of the wound. Sound of the cart wheel behind you. Whatever. Five. And you say them, and then you eat something, and then you sleep if you can. That's the whole of it. That's what I've got to give you, fifteen years in, and it's not much, but it's what worked."

She stopped there. Not because there wasn't more — there was more, there was always more — but because she'd said the thing she meant to say and the rest was talking for the sake of talking, and she'd never had much patience for that in others and less in herself.

"Ear," she said, after a beat. Nod at his hand, which had long since dropped the cloth into his lap. "Show me. Then we get on the horses and we go find somewhere to be that isn't here."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I hold the cloth out to her. The graze stings now, sharp and clean. "What were the five things for yours? Flint, cord, bread, comb, paper?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack took the cloth from him and gave it a look — bloody, but not soaked through, which was what she wanted to see — and then folded it into her pouch to be boiled later or thrown away depending on what water they found. She tilted his head with two fingers under the jaw again, brisk, checked the graze in the last of the light, and made a small satisfied sound at the back of her throat.

"Scabbing already. You'll live to disappoint your mother another day."

She let him go and sat back on her heels, and for a moment she didn't answer the question. Not because she was deciding whether to — she'd decided the moment he'd asked it, and the answer had been decided years before that — but because saying them out loud was a thing she hadn't done in a while, and she wanted to say them properly.

"Flint and steel," she said. "Bit of cord — hemp, frayed at one end, about a forearm long. Half a loaf of dark bread wrapped in a bit of linen that had a patch on it, blue thread on brown. Wooden comb, two teeth gone from the middle, the wood worn smooth on the back where his thumb had gone. Folded paper with names on it we didn't read."

She said them the way you'd count coin. No music in it. Just the count.

"That's five. That's him. That's where he lives."

She was quiet a moment, then she added, without looking at Corvin, in the same flat voice: "The comb's the one that comes up. If any of them comes up. The comb, because of the thumb-worn place on the back. Somebody used it every day for a lot of years. That's the one that walks around in my head, when one of them does. Not the man's face. The comb."

She got to her feet, joints doing their thing, and dusted the road off her palms.

"Yours'll pick itself. You won't get to choose which one. Might not be a thing at all — might be the sound the cloak made when you wiped the blade, might be the weight of the shortsword before you leaned. Whatever picks itself, that's the one. Let it. Arguing with it just makes it louder."

She turned toward the horses and untied the nearer one, ran a hand down its neck once, absent, more for herself than the animal.

"Up you get, Corvin. There's a stand of pines about two miles south we can be under before full dark, and I'd like to be eating something by the time I can't see my hands."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stand slowly, my legs stiff. "Alright." I take the reins from her, my hands steady now. "Lead the way."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack swung up into her saddle with the small grunt that had crept into the movement somewhere in her late thirties and hadn't left since. She settled, adjusted the sit of the shortsword at her back so it wasn't going to knock her kidney for two miles, and clicked her tongue at the horse, which flicked an ear at her in the way it did when it had opinions and was keeping them to itself.

She didn't set off at once. She waited until she heard him mount behind her — the creak of leather, the small shift of weight, the horse's answering breath — and then she nudged hers into a walk, southward, the road going grey ahead of them under a sky that had gone the colour of wet slate.

For a while she didn't say anything. The quiet after a fight had a shape to it, and she'd learned young not to fill it up with talk unless the talk was earning its keep. The horses' hooves made the small wet sound they made on this kind of road, and somewhere behind them a crow said something to another crow about the work they had ahead of them, and Wrack let all of it be what it was.

After the first mile she spoke, without turning her head.

"Pines have a spring at the north edge of them. Small one. Clean enough. We'll water the horses and fill the skins and I'll do your ear proper with the water instead of the spirits, which'll sting less and clean it better anyway — spirits were for the field, water's for when you've got the time. Then I'll see what I've got in the saddlebag that isn't hardtack, because you're going to eat something whether you want to or not, and I'd rather it wasn't hardtack for your first."

She let a beat go.

"Not a rule. Just a preference of mine. My first was hardtack because that's what Bel had, and I've held it against hardtack ever since, which isn't fair to the hardtack but there it is."

The road bent. She adjusted without looking.

"You can talk if you want, on the ride. Or not. I won't ask you anything. If something comes up you want to say out loud before we're at the pines, say it. Easier to say things moving than sitting still, sometimes. That's another one of Bel's, and that one I do think is true."

She rode on, easy in the saddle, her back to him and the last of the light going out of the west, and she didn't look round to see whether he was following. She could hear that he was.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I don't say anything for a while, just watch her back in the saddle ahead of me. Then: "He had a ring. On his left hand. Silver, simple."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Gut wound out here, no surgeon, no clean water, no roof — he's not walking out. That part's a mercy and it's a real one

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: that grey under the dirt, round the mouth especially — that's blood not going where it should anymore. Lips'll go bluer in a bit. Eyes are already doing the thing they do; they don't track

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Spear goes in easier than you'd think. Skin gives, then the wall of muscle, then you're in the belly proper... Punches a hole in whatever's in front of the point... stomach's got acid and half-eaten food in it. Bowel's got shit... goes into the belly cavity and rots him from the inside... Belly swells up hard as a drum. Skin round the wound goes the wrong colours in order — red, then a bad yellow, then black at the edge

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The sound wasn't loud. It never was, when it was done right. A soft wet press, and then a smaller sound underneath it, which was the point finding what it had been sent to find. The man's chest jerked once, a shallow thing, and the pink at his mouth pulsed and then didn't.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The rest of the barn, was that I sat down. Right there in the hay. Didn't come down the ladder for — I don't know. Long enough that someone came looking. Long enough that the blood I was sitting in had started to go tacky under my thighs

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched Corvin a moment, noting the set of his jaw and the way his boots stayed planted. She didn’t bother to stand; her knees were happier this way, and the cloak was thick enough to finish the job. 

"If you’re thinking he'll fix himself, he won't," she said, voice flat as a whetstone. "If you want me to do it, say so. But I won’t be pretty about it. Not my habit."

She flicked the knife clean, then sheathed it with a practiced motion. The groaning from behind the cart carried, thin and broken. Wrack glanced up at the sky, squinting at the lowering sun. "Flies’ll be on him soon. Worse things after dark." She shrugged, the gesture barely a lift of her shoulders. "Up to you, Corvin."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, forcing my eyes away from the blood on my wrist. "I'll do it." My voice comes out rougher than I meant. I start walking toward the cart, but stop halfway. "Just... tell me if I'm doing it wrong."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn’t nod or soften; she just pushed herself up with a grunt and followed, boots squelching in the rutted mud. She kept a careful distance, neither rushing nor lagging behind. 

"Don’t think there’s a right way," she said. Her tone was dry, matter-of-fact. "But there’s ways that are quick." She drew her knife again, holding it out hilt-first to Corvin. "You want steel, not mercy. Go behind him—don’t let him see your face. Blade goes under the ear, up. Or through the heart if you’ve got the angle. Fast hand, no talking."

The man’s breath rattled, wet and desperate, from behind the broken wheel. Wrack looked down at the torn tunic, the spreading stain. "Don’t wait too long. That’s the only wrong there is."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack knelt beside the cart, her eyes taking in the man’s wound with the same cool detachment she used for spoiled rations or broken gear. She angled her head so Corvin could see, not hiding any of it. The man’s guts were showing—wet and pale, threaded with mud—his breath hitching high in his chest, too ragged to last.

"Bit of both," Wrack said. "He’s got a half hour, maybe, if you want to see what drowning in your own spit looks like. Won’t be walking again, either way." She reached out, steadying the man’s shoulder as his head lolled. Her grip was impersonal; she’d steadied horses the same way before a cut.

"It’s not for him, Corvin. Not really. He’s already gone, just doesn’t know it yet. It’s for you and for us—so we don’t listen to this all night. So we don’t draw wolves or worse." She looked at Corvin, her eyes unreadable. "Do it for that, if you can’t do it for mercy. It all ends the same."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take the knife from her, the grip slippery in my palm. My throat feels too tight. "Okay." I step around the cart, trying not to look at his eyes.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack let Corvin go ahead, staying just far enough to be there if he needed steadying, but not close enough to crowd. She watched his hands, not his face—she’d seen enough faces at this part to know how much good it did. When the knife went in, Wrack didn’t flinch, didn’t speak. She just watched, counting heartbeats. The man gave a shudder, then sagged, the noise stopping all at once. That was always the worst part: how quick quiet came.

She waited a moment longer, to be sure it was done, then reached out and nudged the man’s jaw, checking for pulse or breath. Nothing. Wrack wiped her hands on her own trousers, less clean than before, and took the knife back from Corvin, her hand steady.

"That’s it," she said quietly. She didn’t offer comfort; she offered facts. "You did it right. He didn’t feel the end." She turned, already looking to the ditch and the fallen—calculating what needed burning, what needed burying, what could be left for the crows. "Sun’s going down. Help me with the bodies. Then we eat."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack came to stand beside Corvin, knife still bare in her hand. She didn’t soften her voice, didn’t shape the scene into anything easier; she just described what was there, plain as mud.

"Exit wound, low left," she said, pointing with the tip of her blade. "Blade nicked the lung. That’s why you hear the wheeze—blood filling it up, drowning him faster than the gut wound would. Guts are out, too. He’d have bled slow if you hadn’t done it. When the belly’s opened, you watch for color—see that pinkish stuff? That’s the fat. Gray is bowel. If it’s black, he’s already rotting inside." She squatted, boots braced against the churned earth, and nudged the corpse’s tunic aside for a better look.

"Hands are clenched. That’s the nerves firing off. Not pain, not anymore. Sometimes they piss themselves, sometimes not. If they’re still, you did it quick." She let the tunic drop. "This is what dying looks like up close. It’s ugly and fast, or ugly and slow. This was fast. Remember it." She straightened, rolling her shoulders, and turned to the others, sprawled in the ditch.

"Best thing you can do for the dead is get it over with. Worst thing you can do is watch too long. You done here?"

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod, stepping back from the body. "Yeah. I'm done." I start toward the ditch, then stop. "Thanks. For not... sugarcoating it."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack gave a grunt that might’ve passed for agreement, or just acknowledgment. She slid the knife home in its sheath, the motion practiced and unconscious, and set her boot in the mud beside Corvin’s.

“Sugar’s for tea,” she said, deadpan. “And we’re out of both.” She jerked her chin at the nearest corpse. “That one’s light enough to drag. Grab his boots—careful, the heel’s half-off. I’ll take the heavy bastard by the ditch.”

She moved toward the body she’d chosen, pausing only to roll a loose sleeve back from her wrist. The sun was low now, shadows stretching longer, and Wrack didn’t waste time with ceremony. She leaned into the weight, back braced, hauling the dead man by his armpits toward the pyre site they’d used before.

“Next time’ll be easier,” she said over her shoulder, not unkindly. “Not better. Just easier.” The sky above them was already streaked red. Wrack spat into the grass and kept moving. Work didn’t wait, not for sunset, not for grief.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn’t slow, boots digging furrows through the grass as she dragged the corpse. Corvin’s voice followed her, earnest and raw, and she gave it the same respect she gave a blade in her hand—treating it as something that could cut if misused.

“Straight, then,” she said, nodding once. “Spears are ugly. You catch the point in the gut, it slides between ribs easy, or slips off the bone and chews up the soft bits. Bowel’s worst—spill those and the stink’s like nothing else. Man starts dying right there, but slow. Gut wounds leak out shit, bile, half-digested food. Belly goes hard, skin slicks with sweat. Most scream, if they’ve got breath left. After a while, they don’t.”

She bent, getting a better grip on the armpits, hauling the weight up over the edge of the shallow pyre pit. “If the spear’s broad-headed, it rips coming out. Makes a bigger hole, more bleeding, faster death. If it’s narrow, it can punch straight through—neat wound, but worse inside. Bleeds into the belly, poisons from the gut. Takes hours, sometimes days, to kill if nobody helps.”

Wrack wiped her brow with a bloody wrist, not bothering with the mess. “Seen men try to crawl on their hands, spilling their insides. Some beg for water, some just for an end. It’s always the same: hurts like hell, and it’s slow unless you’re lucky.” She looked over her shoulder, meeting Corvin’s gaze. “That’s what a spear does. There’s no clean way. All you can do is finish it quick, when it’s on you.”

She turned back to the pyre, matter-of-fact. “Ask me about arrows if you want. Or swords. Best to know the work, if you’re going to do it.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Okay." I take a shaky breath, grabbing the dead man's boots. The heel comes off in my hand, just like she warned. "Tell me about swords next. I want to know how to... make it quick."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack glanced over, noting the broken heel, but didn’t bother with a smirk. She understood wanting answers—a clean edge on ugly work. She heaved the corpse the rest of the way and straightened, hands on her thighs, catching her breath.

“Swords are a better bet, if you know what you’re doing,” she said, voice low. “Long blade—go for the neck, just under the jaw or at the notch above the collarbone. Cuts the big veins, drops a man quick. Blood goes fast, brain goes quiet. If you miss and catch the windpipe, he’ll choke. That’s worse. Best to angle up—hard and fast.”

She gestured, tracing the strike in the air. “If you’ve only got time for a stab, aim under the ribs, up into the heart. That’s tricky—heart’s not where you think it is, sits more to the left. Stick too low, it’s just gut again. Too high, you catch lung, like the spear. If you’re behind, blade between the ribs and twist. Always twist. Stops the fighting fast.”

Wrack spat again, clearing her throat. “Don’t go for the belly, not unless you’re meaning to make him talk first. That’s slow. Thigh’ll bleed a man out, but it’s messier and takes longer. Wrist or ankle—hard to hit in a fight, but cuts the big arteries.”

She looked at Corvin, steady and sure. “You want it quick—neck or heart. Clean cut, hard thrust. Don’t hesitate. Think of it as work: get it done, get on to the next.”

The sun was almost gone now, the sky streaked dark. Wrack gave the corpse a nudge with her boot. “That’s all there is. You keep asking, I’ll keep telling. Someone should.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stayed where she was, folding her arms across her chest, boots planted firm in the bloody grass. She didn’t try to look away or soften her eyes—she watched, sharp and precise, as Corvin pressed the blade in. The first cut was off the mark: too shallow, catching more skin and fat than vein. The man spasmed, sound bubbling up from his throat—a wet, rattling gasp, like a bucket turned underwater.

“You missed the vein,” Wrack said, voice low but steady. “See how he’s grabbing at your wrist? That’s the nerves. He’s still got fight in him. Pull the blade higher—just under the jaw, angle toward the ear. That’s where the blood is.”

Corvin adjusted, the knife dragging through gristle and skin, and this time the blood came fast, dark and pumping. The body jerked once, legs drumming the dirt. There was a noise—half sigh, half gurgle—then a slackening, sudden and final.

“That’s it,” she narrated. “Sound you hear? That’s the airway going, blood in the throat. Twitching now—just the nerves firing off. He’s gone, even if the eyes stay open another minute. That smell? That’s piss letting go. Happens most times.”

Wrack squatted beside the body, pointing at the spreading pool beneath the chin. “See the color? Dark, almost black—means you hit the jugular. Fastest way out, short of a blade through the eye. Quieter, too, if you want it.”

She didn’t look away from Corvin. “Watch the hands. Fingers curl, then slack. If he’s still fighting, you missed something. If not—he’s done. That’s the measure.”

She let silence settle, heavy and honest. “You did it. Wasn’t clean, but it was quick enough. Next time, you’ll remember the angle. Next time, your hands won’t shake so much.”

Wrack stood, rolling her neck, then nodded once. “You wanted to know. Now you do. That’s the truth of it—no better, no worse.” She waited, giving Corvin a moment with it. Not for comfort—just for truth.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at my hands, still wrapped around the knife hilt. "Tell me how to clean it off. The blade, I mean."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack nodded, practical as ever. She crouched beside Corvin, eyeing the knife—slick with blood, fat clinging to the edge, bits of hair stuck along the spine.

“Best is hot water and a rag, but you take what you’ve got. For now—grass first. Wipe it down, both sides, away from the edge. Don’t use your sleeve unless you like the smell sticking.” She reached for a clump of rough grass and demonstrated, scraping the blade clean with short, sure strokes. Fat smeared green, flecks of red clinging to the stem.

“When you’re done with that, spit on the edge if you can’t find water. Wipe again. Gets most of the blood off so it doesn’t rust. If there’s black gunk in the handle, pick it out with a stick or your nail. Don’t cut toward yourself—seen too many fools nick a finger and rot it off by morning.”

She offered the grass to Corvin, her hands steady, voice unbothered. “When you get the chance—boil the blade, oil it if you’ve got any. Keeps it from pitting. If it still smells, drag it through fresh earth—dirt’ll pull out what the rag misses. Don’t leave it wet. Blood eats steel faster than rain.”

Wrack straightened, wiping her own hands on the grass, then on her trousers. “That’s all. Clean your tools, clean your work. Makes the next job easier. And it keeps you honest—can’t hide from the mess if you have to wipe it off yourself.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack knelt, boots sinking deep in the churned ground, and didn’t leave Corvin’s side. She didn’t rush; there was no hurry left, only this: the facts, hard-edged and unvarnished, same as she would’ve wanted for herself.

“First thing you notice is the noise goes quiet,” she said, voice flat but not unkind. “That’s true for every killing, no matter the tool. Man makes a hell of a racket when he’s alive—breathing, whimpering, trying to talk even if he can’t. Soon as you cut him deep enough, you get this silence. It’s not peace. It’s just empty.”

She reached out, turned the man’s face sideways so Corvin could see the slack jaw, the half-open eyes. “Eyes go wide, most times. You’ll see people say it’s fear, but it’s just nerves. Sometimes they roll up, sometimes they stay staring. Don’t mean much. If you see the pupils go big, that’s the body quitting. After that, you could cut his throat again and he wouldn’t care.”

Wrack ran a finger along the sticky handle of the knife, showing where blood pooled under the crossguard. “The hand shakes—yours, not his. That’s the truth. You’ll think it’s weakness, but it’s just your body catching up to what you did. You might want to puke. Might want to laugh. Both are normal. I’ve done both, years apart. Doesn’t change the work.”

She pointed at the blood, already browning at the edges where it touched the grass. “Blood starts bright, then turns dark. Smells sharp, like copper and shit. It’ll cling to your boots, get under your nails. You’ll keep finding it for days, even after you think you’ve cleaned it all.”

Her gaze flicked to the corpse’s hands, still curled tight. “If you look at his fingers, you’ll see them slowly loosen. That’s the tendons letting go. Sometimes they claw at you, sometimes at the ground. The last things a man’s body does are ugly—spit, piss, maybe shit himself. It’s not about him anymore, just the machine winding down.”

Wrack sat back, elbows on her knees, and let the wind shift the stink away for a moment. “You’ll remember the sound of it—the gurgle, the snap when you hit bone, the little sigh they make. You’ll remember it long after you forget his face. That’s normal too. Some folk try to drown it out with drink, or prayer. Some just stop feeling it. Don’t let it eat at you. You did what had to be done. If you hadn’t, he’d be here longer, hurting worse.”

She looked up at Corvin, steady as stone. “This is the truth of it. You kill a man, it doesn’t wash off. But you learn to carry it, piece by piece, until it’s just weight. Doesn’t make you evil. Doesn’t make you good, neither. Just means you’re here, and he’s not.”

Wrack let the silence stand a moment, letting Corvin breathe. When she spoke again, it was quieter. “If you need to spit, spit. If you need to swear, swear. Doesn’t matter to me. But don’t pretend it’s something it’s not. You did what needed doing. That’s all there is.”

She stayed there, close enough to share the silence, until Corvin moved. No hurry. No comfort. Just the truth, and the work.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I lean forward and vomit into the grass. It’s thin, mostly bile. My hands are still trembling. “It’s not like the songs,” I say, voice hoarse. “They never talk about the fucking smell.”

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched Corvin retch and didn’t flinch or turn away. She’d seen it before—she’d done it herself, first time, long years ago. She waited until the dry heaves faded and Corvin’s breathing evened out, then reached over and handed him a strip of rough cloth from her belt. Not clean, but clean enough to wipe his mouth.

“No songs for this part,” she said, tone flat as cold iron. “No one hums about piss and bile and the stink in your boots. Ballads are for the ones who never see it up close.” She let her gaze wander over the sprawled bodies, the purpling sky, the churned-up ground that stank of blood and fear.

She shifted her weight, knees popping quietly. “Smell’s the first thing you learn, and the last thing you forget. Gets in your hair, your tongue. You’ll taste it when you eat. You’ll dream it. After a while, you just stop noticing—except when you’re in a place where it isn’t, and that feels wrong too.”

Wrack glanced at the knife in Corvin’s hand, the blood drying in rusty patches. “You did it. That’s more than most. Some freeze, some run, some just stand and piss themselves. You didn’t run. Means you can be trusted to finish, when finishing’s what’s needed.”

She let out a long breath, steady and quiet. “First time’s always the worst. Doesn’t mean you’re weak. Just means you’re not a liar.” She stood and offered Corvin a hand up, her grip hard, her palm stained. “Come on. We burn them, we eat. You get used to the smell, or you find better company.” Her mouth twitched, not quite a smile. “Around here, that’s as close as it gets to a happy ending.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take her hand, my grip still unsteady, and let her pull me up. My legs feel like they're made of water. I wipe my mouth with the cloth she gave me, then tuck it into my belt. "What do we do with his gear? And his boots-- they're still good."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack steadied Corvin as he rose, not fussing over the tremble in his grip. She scanned the corpse with a practiced eye, already cataloguing what could be salvaged. “We strip them,” she said, matter-of-fact. “If it’s not torn or soaked through, we keep it. Blades, belts, boots—if the soles aren’t worn out, they’ll fetch something, or fit someone.”

She knelt beside the body, deft fingers unlacing the dead man’s boots. “Always check the insides,” she advised, turning one over and rapping the heel against her palm. “Folk hide things—coins, notes, little knives. Never found gold, but I’ve found worse.”

She pulled the boots free, setting them aside, then moved to the belt, testing the leather. “Belt’s decent. Pouch is empty, so he spent what he had, or someone else got to him first. Shirt’s too far gone.” She tossed it aside, unmoved by the sticky blood. “You want the boots, take them. If they fit, they’re yours. Otherwise, we trade them next time we see a friendly face.”

Wrack stood, hands slick but steady. “Gear’s worth more than words out here. Strip what you need, burn the rest. Don’t carry what’ll weigh you down, but don’t leave good leather for the scavengers.”

She fixed Corvin with a level look. “Taking from the dead isn’t stealing, not out here. It’s just the way of things. You leave them something—a coin, a word, whatever’s right for you—if it helps. The dead don’t mind. Only the living remember.”

She nodded toward the next body, already settling into the night chill. “Come on. The sooner we’re done, the sooner we eat. Let the songs talk about glory. We’ll take the boots.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I bend down and start unlacing the boots, my fingers fumbling with the knots. They're a little big, but I can stuff 'em with grass. "I'll take them," I say, my voice steadier than my hands. "Better they walk a few more miles."
