dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack finished cleaning the knife and slid it back into its sheath. She stood, her knees protesting the way they always did after a crouch, and looked at Corvin properly for the first time since the fighting stopped. The wet on his face. The way he was standing like a man waiting for something to happen to him rather than making things happen.

The sound from beyond the cart was irregular now. Wet. A man trying to breathe through what was probably a collapsed lung.

"Right," Wrack said. She didn't say it with any particular weight. She picked up one of the dead men's swords — decent steel, worth carrying — and walked past Corvin toward the cart without asking whether he wanted her to or not. She didn't look back to see if he followed.

She came around the cart and found him. Young, maybe twenty. Gut wound, which was the worst kind to leave someone with because it took so long. He was curled on his side with his hands pressed to his stomach and his eyes were open and very focused on nothing.

Wrack crouched again. She put two fingers to his neck, felt the pulse doing what pulses do when they're winding down, and then sat back on her heels.

She waited, listening to him breathe. After a moment she said, conversationally, to no one in particular, or maybe to Corvin if he was there: "He's not going to last the hour. Could be longer." She shrugged one shoulder. "Depends on what you can live with, I suppose."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, my throat dry. "We could... just leave him." The words taste sour, but I can't make myself walk over there.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack was quiet for a moment. She looked down at the dying man's face, then back at the way they'd come. The light was going. It'd be full dark within the hour.

"We could," she said. Nothing in her voice said yes or no about it. "He'll scream eventually. Maybe not loud, but loud enough if anyone's close enough to hear. And someone might be — his friends weren't out here for the scenery." She paused. "Then again, might not matter. Might be nobody within a league."

She stood up, brushing dirt off her knees. "I've left men before," she said, and there was no confession in it, no guilt, just a fact like any other. "Sometimes you don't have a choice. Sometimes you just don't want to do it and you walk away and that's the choice you made." She looked at Corvin, not unkindly. "But don't pretend it's kinder, is all. It's just easier to not be the one holding the knife."

She rolled her shoulders, settling the ache out of them. "Your call. I'll do it if you want. I won't think less of you either way." A beat. "Well. Not for that, specifically."

The man by the cart made a sound. Small. Like a hiccup, if a hiccup hurt that much.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack gave him a look that was almost patient. She crouched back down beside the wounded man and lifted his hands away from his stomach — gently, the way you'd move a child's hands to look at a scrape, though the man barely registered it. His eyes tracked her for a moment, then went back to staring at nothing.

The wound was below the navel. Dark, welling slowly. The smell was already there — bowel, unmistakable, the body starting to poison itself from the inside.

"Both," Wrack said. She let his hands go and they drifted back to his stomach on their own, muscle memory doing what the mind couldn't be bothered to direct anymore. "It's not a fast death, a gut wound. The body takes its time deciding to quit. He'll get feverish. Then the real pain starts — and I mean the kind that makes you wish you could stop being a person for a while. Sometimes they go quiet, sometimes they don't." She paused. "Most don't."

She wiped her hands on her thighs and stood again.

"I've seen men last two days on a wound like that. Two days is a long time when you're spending it dying in a ditch." She looked at Corvin steadily. "So it's a mercy because he won't have to go through that. And it's easier because *we* won't have to listen to it and know we could've done something. Both things can be true at the same time. Doesn't have to be one or the other."

The man on the ground made another sound. Quieter now.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: My hand goes to my own knife, but I don't draw it. "Would you have done it yet, if I wasn't here?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
"Yes," Wrack said. She said it without hesitation, without making a thing of it. "Would've been done before you walked over."

She looked down at the man again. His breathing had changed — shallower now, the spaces between longer. His eyes had closed. She didn't know if that meant he was losing consciousness or just tired of keeping them open.

"I'm not waiting because I think you need to watch," she said. "Or because I think it'll build your character or any of that horseshit." She rubbed the back of her neck where the muscle had knotted up. "But you're the one who has to sleep tonight and every night after this, and some men sleep fine knowing another man did the ugly work for them, and some men don't. I don't know which kind you are yet."

She shrugged. "So I figured I'd give you the option."

The silence stretched. A bird called somewhere off in the tree line — one of those grey things that sang at dusk regardless of what had happened nearby.

"If you want me to do it now, I will. No speeches. It'll take a second and it'll be done and we'll move on and find somewhere to camp before full dark." She shifted her weight, settling into practicality the way she always did when the moment of choosing had passed and only the doing remained. "Or you do it, and I'll watch the road. Either way, we need to decide soon. Light's going."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack moved to make room for him, shifting to one side of the dying man so Corvin could see. She didn't speak immediately. She was studying the man's face, his hands, the way his body had arranged itself around the wound — the body's instinct to protect what was already gone.

"His hands," she said first. "Notice how he's holding himself? Palms flat, fingers spread. He's not pressing anymore, he's just... there. The body does that after a while. Gives up trying to fix it and just holds on."

She pointed without touching him. "See the color of his lips? That grey. Means he's losing blood somewhere we can't see it — inside. The wound's not bleeding much now because it's all going into his belly. That's what kills you eventually. Not the blood you lose, but the blood that pools where it shouldn't be and starts poisoning everything around it."

She leaned forward slightly. "The smell. You're smelling his guts. Once that gets opened, it's only a matter of time. The body can't fight that kind of infection, not without a surgeon and a prayer and mostly just luck. We've got none of those."

She looked at his chest. Counted breaths for a moment.

"See how his belly's moving but his chest barely is? Means the pain's so bad his body's forgotten how to breathe right. It'll get worse. By morning he'll be making sounds you won't want to remember."

She sat back and let Corvin look.

"That's what you're looking at. A man whose body's already decided he's dead. It just hasn't finished the paperwork."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I draw my knife. My hand is steady, but I can hear my own heartbeat in my ears. "Will he know?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
"Probably not," Wrack said. She kept her voice low, matter-of-fact. "The body's shutting down. Pain does that—pulls you inward, away from everything. I've seen men with worse wounds who didn't recognize their own sergeants by the end."

She paused, watching Corvin's hand.

"But I can't promise you that. No one can. Might be he's still in there somewhere, just watching." She shrugged. "You do it quick, either way. That's the only part you control. Everything else is just luck and timing."

A beat.

"You know where to put it?"

Corvin:
"No," I say, my voice tight. "Show me."

Wrack:
Wrack moved behind Corvin, her presence solid and unobtrusive at his shoulder. She didn't reach for his hand or the knife. She just pointed.

"Base of the skull. Where it meets the neck. You'll feel a gap there, a soft place between the bones. That's the quickest way to reach the brain stem." Her voice was clinical, like she was explaining how to sharpen a blade or pack a wound. "Angle it upward, just a little. You're not trying to cut—more like driving a spike. The knife does the work if you get it in the right place."

She stepped back.

"It'll be fast. Probably faster than he'll feel it. Probably." She left the word hanging, not as an apology, but as a simple acknowledgment of uncertainty. "You ready?"

The man on the ground let out a slow, hitching breath, his eyes still closed.

Corvin:
I kneel. The ground is damp. I put my hand on his shoulder—still warm. "I'm sorry," I whisper, not sure if I'm saying it to him or to myself.

Wrack:
Wrack watched. She didn't look away. Her face was still, the kind of stillness that comes from having seen this particular motion hundreds of times—hands finding the place, the moment of hesitation, the resolve or the failure of it. She'd seen men weep doing this, and men go blank, and men vomit afterward. All of it was just weather.

She said nothing. This part wasn't for her.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack shifted her weight and looked at the wound again, the way you'd look at a piece of equipment you were trying to assess for repair. Except there was no repairing this one.

"Alright," she said. "Straight."

She pointed again without touching him. "Spear went in low, left of the navel. Angled upward — see the way the skin's torn on the top edge? That's the entry point pulling open as he moved. A clean thrust wouldn't have done that. Means he was moving when it went in, or the man who stuck him was pulling it out rough."

She squatted on her heels, arms resting on her knees.

"What it did inside — well. The spearhead's got a leaf blade, probably, maybe barbed. You've seen them. It punched through the abdominal wall, which is muscle and fat and membrane, and then it went into whatever was in the way. Small intestine, most likely, given the placement. Maybe nicked the large bowel on the way."

Her voice didn't change pitch. She spoke the way a carpenter might describe wood rot.

"The intestines are — imagine wet cloth. Soft. Full of everything you've eaten in the last two days, and the bacteria that come with it. When you put a blade through that, the contents spill out into the abdominal cavity. That's what you're smelling. His own body's rotting from the inside, started about ten minutes after he got stuck."

She scratched her jaw.

"The bleeding's mostly internal. The mesentery — that's the tissue that holds the guts in place, feeds them blood — it's torn somewhere we can't see. So he's slowly filling up with blood that has nowhere to go. The belly will swell. By now it's probably already started. You can check if you want."

She didn't wait for him to.

"That's what a spear does. It doesn't cut clean like a sword might. It tears, and it pushes things aside that shouldn't be pushed, and it leaves a wound that's wider inside than it is outside. Like driving a tent peg into mud — the hole closes up behind it, but everything underneath's been rearranged."

She met his eyes.

"That's straight. That's what happened to him. And there's no fixing it, and no medicine for it, and no prayer that makes the intestines unspill themselves. All that's left is how it ends."

The man between them breathed. Shallow. Slower than before.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod, my jaw clenched. My fingers find the base of his skull like she said. I take a breath, and then I push the blade up hard and quick. It's not as much resistance as I expected.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The body convulsed once — a full-body twitch, legs drawing up and then straightening — and then went still. The sound Corvin made with the knife was small. A wet click of metal on bone. The man didn't make any sound at all.

Wrack waited a beat. Then another.

"That's it," she said. "He's done."

She watched Corvin's hand for a moment — watched whether it stayed steady or started to shake, because that was the part that came after and it mattered which way it went. Some men locked up in the wrist, some in the shoulders. Some just dropped the knife like it had burned them.

"You'll want to pull it out slow," she added, quieter. "Quick going in, slow coming out. Otherwise—" She gestured vaguely. "You make a mess of the back of his skull and you'll be cleaning bone fragments off your blade for an hour."

She straightened up and looked at the sky. The last of the light was holding, but barely. Orange going grey along the treeline.

"We need to move," she said. "There's a farmstead about a mile south — burned out, but the walls are still standing. Good enough for the night." She paused, glancing down at the dead man, then at the others scattered across the ditch and the road. "We should drag him back to his friends. Won't help him none, but it's..." She trailed off, shrugged. "Something people do, I suppose. Don't ask me why."

She looked at Corvin's face in the fading light. Not studying him exactly — more like taking a reading, the way she'd check a horse's gait or a blade's balance.

"You did it right," she said. "First time's the worst. Not because it gets easier, exactly, but because you'll know what to expect next time. And there's—" She stopped herself. Shook her head. "Well. We should move."

She turned and walked back toward the bodies by the ditch, leaving him with the knife and the dead man and whatever came next.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped mid-turn. She looked back at him for a long moment — the kind of look that said she understood why he was asking, and also that she thought he might regret asking, but that wasn't her problem to solve.

"Alright," she said. She stayed.

She watched him grip the dead man under the arms. The body was heavier than it looked — they always were. The dead had a way of letting go of all the little adjustments the living made to carry themselves, and the result was dense, slack, uncooperative. Like moving a sack of wet grain with bones in it.

"You're going to feel the head lag," she said. "That's normal. The neck's got nothing holding it rigid now — you severed the connection, so it'll roll. Try not to let it drag on the ground or you'll take the skin off his face, and someone might want to bury him eventually. Probably not, but they might."

She walked alongside, not helping, just watching.

"See how the arms are sliding? You've got him under the armpits but the shoulders have gone soft. He'll start slipping. When he does, just set him down, get a better hold, and go again. No shame in stopping. He's not in a hurry."

She glanced ahead to where the other bodies lay in a loose cluster by the ditch where the ambush had funnelled them. Three of them had gone down in the first volley. One had made it another ten feet before Wrack caught him. The sixth was the one they'd just finished.

"You're doing fine," she said, without particular warmth. Just a fact. "The ground's soft here, so you're leaving tracks with the drag marks. Doesn't matter tonight, but it would in daylight. Something to remember."

She stepped over a root without looking down.

"About thirty more feet. You can put him down next to the one in the red cloak — they were probably together, the way they moved. Same unit, at least. That's something, if you believe in that sort of thing." Her tone suggested she did not, but that she wasn't going to judge those who did.

She was quiet for a moment, then: "The sounds you're hearing — that's the body, not him. Air pushing out of the lungs as you compress the chest. Sometimes it sounds like moaning. It's not. It's just physics. Remember that."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stop, breathing hard. The body slips from my grasp and lands with a soft thud. "I don't believe in that sort of thing," I say, my voice rough. "But I think I will tonight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at him for a moment. The light was almost gone now — just enough to make out shapes, the pale blur of faces, the darker smear of blood on cloth.

"Fair enough," she said.

She didn't say anything else about it. Didn't tell him it was foolish or tell him it was wise. Some men found religion the night they did something like this, and some men lost it, and most just sat somewhere in the middle feeling like the world had shifted two inches to the left and nothing quite lined up anymore.

She helped him set the body right. Pulled the dead man's cloak over his face — not for him, but because that was what you did, apparently, even if you didn't believe in that sort of thing. She straightened the arms, folded the hands over the gut wound she'd described in such clinical detail not twenty minutes ago. It looked almost peaceful if you didn't think about it too hard.

"There," she said. She wiped her hands on her thighs again. A habit. "We should go. Mile south, the farmstead I mentioned. There's a well that still had water last time I was through — two weeks back, maybe. Long enough ago that I wouldn't trust it without boiling, but it's water."

She picked up the sword she'd taken from the dead man earlier. She'd almost forgotten it.

Corvin was still kneeling. She didn't tell him to get up. She just stood there, holding the borrowed sword, looking at the tree line where the last of the light was bleeding out of the sky.

"You'll dream about this," she said after a while. Not a question. "Probably for a few nights. Maybe longer. The dreams aren't messages or omens or any of that — it's just your head trying to file something it hasn't got a folder for yet. It'll sort itself out."

She shifted the sword to her other hand.

"And if it doesn't — well. That's what drink's for." A pause. "I'm joking. Mostly."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't answer right away. She looked at the bodies, at the darkening sky, at Corvin kneeling in the dirt, and for a moment she looked older than her years in a way that had nothing to do with the lines on her face.

She sat down. Not gracefully — she lowered herself onto the bank of the ditch a few feet from him, sword across her knees, and stared at nothing in particular for a moment.

"Alright," she said. "The rest."

She scratched the back of her neck, a gesture he'd probably seen her do a dozen times now. A thinking gesture, or maybe just a way of buying a few seconds.

"The first one's the worst, like I said. Not because of what it does to them — that's done in a second, most of the time. It's what it does to you. The way your brain won't quite... settle afterward. You'll replay it. The angle of the blade, the resistance, the sound. You'll wonder if there was a better way, a faster way, if you missed something that would've meant you didn't have to do it at all. That's normal. It passes."

She pulled a piece of grass from the bank and turned it between her fingers.

"The second one's easier. That's the part nobody tells you, and it's the part that should worry you. It's easier because you've already done it once and the world didn't end, and your hands know what to do, and the shock isn't there anymore. You'll feel — not good about it. But competent. Like you've learned something useful. And that feeling is dangerous, Corvin. That's the one that changes people."

She let the grass fall.

"After a while — and I can't tell you how long because it's different for everyone — you stop counting. Not because you've decided to stop. Because the number just stops mattering. It becomes part of the job, like sharpening your blade or checking your boots for rot. You do it, you clean up, you move on. And one day you'll be sitting somewhere quiet and you'll realize you can't remember the face of the first man you killed. You'll try, and it'll be — just a shape. A blur. Maybe the color of his hair, maybe the sound he made, but the rest of it's gone. That's your head protecting you. Or maybe it's your head giving up on you. I've never been sure which."

She looked at him now, directly.

"You asked me to say the rest, so here it is. This won't make you hard. Not really. What it'll do is make you tired. You'll get tired of feeling things about it, and that tiredness will look like hardness if you don't know what you're looking at. You'll start making jokes. I do. You've heard me. They're not funny — they're just a way of putting distance between you and the thing. Everyone in the company does it. It's how we eat dinner after."

She rubbed her thumb along the edge of the borrowed sword, feeling the steel.

"You'll have nights where you drink too much, and nights where you can't sleep, and nights where you sleep fine and wake up feeling nothing about any of it, and that last one is the one that'll scare you the most, eventually. Because you'll wonder when you became the kind of man who sleeps well after killing someone. And the answer is — it just happened. Slowly, and then all at once. You just woke up one morning and the weight was less."

She paused. When she spoke again, her voice was quieter.

"The worst thing — the actual worst thing, not the dramatic worst thing people talk about — is that it becomes ordinary. This—" She gestured at the bodies, the ditch, the blood still wet on the grass. "This is extraordinary to you tonight. A year from now it'll be Tuesday. Two years from now you won't tell this story because it won't feel like a story worth telling. That's not toughness. That's erosion. Water on stone. And the stone doesn't get harder, it just gets smoother and thinner and more like all the other stones."

She was quiet for a moment. The bird in the tree line had stopped singing. The only sound was the wind in the grass and, somewhere far off, water moving over rocks.

"I've been doing this for ten years," she said. "Longer than some of the men in the company have been alive. And I can tell you honestly — I don't know if I'm a good person anymore. I don't mean that for pity. I mean I genuinely don't know. I do things that need doing, and I do them well, and I sleep at night, and I don't lie awake wondering about the men I've killed. But I don't know if that's because I've made peace with it or because I've lost whatever part of me would've kept score. And I don't think there's a way to tell the difference from the inside."

She looked at him, and her expression was — not hard, not soft. Something in between. Something earned.

"That's the rest. It doesn't get better. It doesn't get worse. It just gets... familiar. And familiar is the thing that should keep you up at night, if anything does."

She held his gaze for a moment longer, then looked away, toward the south where the farmstead was waiting.

"There's your truth. Do with it what you want." She stood, joints protesting again, and brushed the dirt off. "Now get up. We've got a mile to go and I'd like to make a fire before I'm too tired to care whether the smoke gives us away."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I get up. My knees are sore and the knife is still in my hand. "You don't have to tell me when it's Tuesday," I say, finally sheathing it. "I'll just watch for when you stop telling stories about it."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at him. For a moment, something shifted behind her eyes—not surprise, exactly, but recognition. The kind you get when someone else sees the shape of the thing you've been carrying.

"Clever," she said. It wasn't praise. It was an acknowledgment. She turned the borrowed sword over in her hand, then slid it through her belt beside her own. "Don't wait up for it. Stories dry up different ways. Sometimes they stop because they're not stories anymore. Sometimes they stop because you've told them so many times the words wear smooth and don't catch on anything anymore. Like a river stone."

She started walking, not waiting for him this time, but not leaving him behind either. Her boots found the path by habit. "This one's fresh. Might get a few tellings out of it yet. Might not." She shrugged. "Depends on the company."

The light was gone now, truly gone. The world had gone to shades of grey and black, and the only real things were the sound of their feet, the rustle of grass, the smell of blood and damp earth fading behind them.

"Fire'll be small," she said after a minute of walking. "Dug in. Smoke'll be thin if the wood's dry enough. There's an old hearth in the farmstead—chimney's half-collapsed but it'll draw enough. I'll show you how to bank it so it doesn't flare."

She paused at a fork in the path, listening. Then took the left one, stepping over a fallen branch without looking down.

"You did alright back there," she said, not looking at him. "The dragging. The cleaning. The—" She gestured vaguely with one hand. "The rest of it. It's ugly work. Most of it is."

She was quiet for another stretch. The sound of their footsteps filled the space.

"Your hands'll shake later," she said. "Probably when you're trying to light the fire or tie your bedroll. That's just the body letting go of what it held onto. Don't fight it. Let it shake. It passes quicker if you don't try to make it stop."

She glanced at him sideways in the dark. "And if you're sick, be sick. Don't try to swallow it down for my sake. I've seen men vomit after their first, and their tenth, and their fiftieth. There's no shame in it. The shame is in pretending you're made of stone when you're not. Nobody's made of stone. Not even me."

She said it simply, without irony. As if she were stating a fact about the weather, or the distance to the farmstead, or the number of bodies they'd left behind.

"We're almost there," she added. "I can smell the ash."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take a long breath and I can smell it too, sharp and cold. "Alright," I say, and my voice comes out steadier than I feel. "Show me how to bank the fire."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The farmstead was a black shape against a charcoal sky. The smell of old ash was stronger here, clinging to the stones. Wrack didn't head for the gap that had once been a gate; instead, she circled to the leeward side, where a section of wall had fallen inward, creating a low, defensible gap. "Through here," she said, crouching to duck under a sagging timber. "Mind your head."

Inside was a roofless courtyard, open to the stars. The remains of a long-house stood against the far wall, its roof timbers charred and broken. But the hearth she'd mentioned was there—a large, stone-built fireplace, half-collapsed on one side but with a recognizable chimney channel.

Wrack moved to it without hesitation, her boots crunching on gritty ash and broken tile. She knelt and began clearing debris from the hearthstone with her hands, scooping out handfuls of soot and fallen mortar. "The trick is the foundation," she said, her voice echoing slightly in the ruin. "You need a pit, down to bare earth if you can get it. Otherwise the heat just bakes the ground and you get a cold that seeps up through your bedroll."

She used the tip of the borrowed sword to dig at the packed dirt inside the hearth, loosening it. "Wood next. You want it dry, and you want it small. Finger-sized. We'll gather what's left in the morning, but for tonight—" She reached into her belt pouch and pulled out a twist of oilcloth. Inside were a few splinters of resinous pine, saved for this purpose. "Kindling. You place it in a cross in the pit, with space for air. The fire needs to breathe same as you do."

Her hands moved with surety, arranging the splinters. "The logs go on last, once the kindling's caught. Not too big. And you lay them so they're not touching—like a little cage. The flame gets in between, burns slower." She sat back on her heels, surveying her work. "Now. Flint and steel."

She passed him the fire-starting kit. "You do it. Let me see your hands."

It wasn't a command for performance. It was an instruction. She watched his fingers grip the flint and steel. They were steady enough. She didn't comment on it.

"When it catches, you feed it. Slowly. One small piece at a time. You're not building a bonfire, you're building a coal. The goal is a bed of embers that'll last the night. Once you've got that, you can bank it." She picked up a flat, wide stone she'd cleared from the debris. "This is your damper. You cover the pit, almost all the way. Leaves a gap, here—" She pointed to a space at the back. "That's your draft. The fire smolders instead of burning. It'll last till dawn if you've done it right."

She gestured for him to begin. The scrape of flint on steel was loud in the quiet ruin. Sparks fell, but the tinder didn't catch at first. She didn't offer to take over.

"Let me see the angle," she said. "You're striking down. Strike *across*. Let the steel kiss the flint, don't fight it."

A few more strikes. A spark caught in the dry pine splinters, glowed, and then a tiny, delicate flame licked up.

"There," Wrack said. "Now. Feed it."

He did. She watched his hands move, placing a twig, then another. The flame grew, steadied. The smell of burning pine cut through the ash.

"Good. Now the logs. Small ones first. See how I showed you? The cage."

The fire crackled, a honest, living sound. Wrack stood and went to the gap in the wall, peering out into the dark for a long moment, listening. Then she came back and sat down on a relatively whole stone a few feet from the hearth, laying the sword across her knees again.

"You'll need to watch it for the first hour," she said. "Add wood if it gets too low, but not too much. You're looking for that steady burn. When the logs have burned down to glowing coals—no flames, just red—you use the stone. Cover it. Leave the gap."

She fell silent, watching the fire he'd made. The light played on her face, deepening the lines. Her own hands were resting on the sword, still and relaxed.

"There's a bucket by the well," she said after a while. "Water's in it. Don't drink it yet. We'll boil it in the morning, or if we can find a pot in this rubble. The hunger'll pass by morning, too, usually. It's the thirst that matters."

She leaned her head back against the cold stone wall behind her, closing her eyes for a moment. Not sleeping. Just listening to the fire and the night.

"You're learning," she said, without opening her eyes. It wasn't high praise. It was an observation of fact, like noting the direction of the wind or the quality of the steel. "That's something. In this place, that's a lot."

The fire crackled. Somewhere out in the dark, an owl called, a low, questioning sound. Wrack let it hang in the air, a sound for a world that didn't care about men and their sharp, necessary work.

"Bank it when the coals are ready," she said, her voice quieter now, almost blending with the fire's whisper. "Then try to sleep. I'll take first watch."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I feed the fire slow, watching the flames settle into the coals like you said. My hands don't shake, not yet. "You take second watch," I say, my voice low. "I don't want to sleep first. Not tonight."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The wound was below the navel. Dark, welling slowly. The smell was already there — bowel, unmistakable, the body starting to poison itself from the inside.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: See the color of his lips? That grey. Means he's losing blood somewhere we can't see it — inside. The wound's not bleeding much now because it's all going into his belly.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: It punched through the abdominal wall, which is muscle and fat and membrane, and then it went into whatever was in the way. Small intestine, most likely, given the placement. Maybe nicked the large bowel on the way.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: You're going to feel the head lag

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The first one's the worst, like I said. Not because of what it does to them — that's done in a second, most of the time. It's what it does to you.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
She glanced up then, her face a roadmap of old scars and lines etched by sun and wind and things worse than either. Her eyes, the color of damp stone, fixed on the boy. He was shaking, not visibly, but she could see it in the way he held himself, tight as a drawn bowstring. Good, she thought. Fear was useful. It kept a man alive.

"Of course you heard him," she said, voice rough as gravel. "He's screaming loud enough to wake the dead. And he's got friends, somewhere." She cleaned a bit of grime from under her fingernail with the tip of her knife. "The question is, do we finish the job or do we leave him to bleed out? Personal opinion? Bleeding out is messy and it takes too damn long."

She stood up slowly, her joints popping like dry twigs. "Either way, we need to move. The sun's going down and I've got no interest in being here when whoever's with that screaming boy decides to come looking for their friends."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Finish it," I mutter, pushing myself up from the ground. My sword feels heavy in my hand. "I'll do it."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack nodded once, a sharp, decisive movement that was almost a twitch. "Good. That's the spirit." She slid her knife back into its sheath with a soft scrape of steel on leather. "Just remember to put the point in right. Messy throat work will only make him louder, and we don't have time for that."

She began to walk toward the cart, her movements unhurried but purposeful. She wasn't going to rush the boy. Let him get a good look at the people coming to finish the job. Fear was a teacher, and she'd learned her lessons well.

"Try for the kidney if you can," she called back over her shoulder, her voice carrying easily in the sudden stillness of the afternoon. "Messy, but it's quiet. Or the heart. If you can hit it right. Either way, be quick about it. I'll be watching the trees."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped walking and turned her head slightly, not fully facing the boy but giving him enough of her profile to see her expression. It was flat, unreadable, the kind of face that could deliver a terrible truth without a flicker of emotion.

"Mercy and easier are two different things," she said, her voice a low rumble like distant thunder. "That boy's got a spear in his gut, and I'm guessing not a clean one. He's not dying quickly, and he's certainly not dying quietly. So whether it's mercy or just getting the job done doesn't matter much right now. What matters is that he's a liability. He's bleeding, he's screaming, and he's going to bring whoever's with him straight to us."

She turned back to the cart, continuing her slow approach. "As for which it is... well, if you were lying in a ditch with your insides hanging out and two strangers walking toward you, and one of them is asking if it's mercy or just easier... you'd probably be praying for mercy to come from somewhere else entirely."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow, the taste of blood and dust thick in my mouth. "Right." I force my legs to move toward the cart, my boots crunching over broken gravel. I can hear the gurgling now, wet and desperate.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
She reached the cart first, positioning herself where she could see the boy and watch the tree line at the same time. The boy on the ground was younger than she'd first thought—barely more than a teenager, his face pale as parchment, sweat beading on his forehead. His eyes were wide, fixed on Corvin as he approached, the gurgles coming from his punctured lung.

"Say something to him," Wrack said, her voice just above a whisper. "Something final. Makes it cleaner that way."

She watched the trees again, her hand resting lightly on the hilt of her knife, her body coiled like a spring. The boy was still screaming, though the sound was growing weaker, ragged. Time was running short. The boy's friends would be coming. They always did.

"Don't think about it," she added, her eyes never leaving the forest edge. "Just do it. Fast and clean. That's the first lesson. The only one that matters out here."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Her eyes flicked to Corvin, then back to the trees. She wasn't looking at the boy anymore; he was just a fact of the landscape, like the cart or the ditch or the six bodies. "You're looking at a dead man with a few minutes of life left," she said, her voice flat. "That's a spear wound, went in just under the ribs, came out the back. Pierced the lung, maybe the liver. Blood's dark, so it's probably not arterial bleeding—that's a mercy. He's drowning in his own blood right now, breathing in it with every ragged gasp."

She took a half-step closer, her movements economical, practical. "The wound's dirty. By morning, even if you don't finish the job, he'll be feverish, delirious. If he lives through the night, and that's a big if, he'll be weak as a newborn kitten. He'll be a burden. Either to us, or to whoever finds him."

Her gaze finally settled on the boy's face, and for the first time, something flickered in her stony expression—something like pity, quickly buried under years of professional detachment. "He's already dead, boy. He's just fighting it. Your choice is whether to let him die slow and messy, or to make it quick and clean. Either way, he's not getting back up."

She straightened, turning her full attention back to the tree line. "So decide. The sun's getting lower, and we've got to move. Now."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: My grip tightens on my sword hilt. "Alright," I say, more to myself than anyone. I kneel next to him, and his eyes lock onto mine, wide with a terror I can almost taste.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
She watched, not watching, as the boy knelt. Her eyes scanned the trees, the fading light creating long shadows that could hide anything. She could hear the wounded boy's breathing now, that wet, desperate rasp that was growing weaker with each passing second. Good. Less time for hesitation.

"Don't look him in the eyes," she said softly, without taking her gaze from the forest. "Look at the wound. Look at what you're doing. Remember that detail. It helps."

She could hear Corvin's breathing, shallow and fast. The boy on the ground made a sound, something between a gasp and a whimper. Wrack's hand rested on her knife, her body ready to move in an instant. The shadows were lengthening, pooling between the trees. They were running out of time.

"Get it over with," she said, her voice barely above a whisper now. "One quick thrust. Right there. Do it."

And then she heard it—the snap of a twig, not from the wounded boy but from deeper in the woods. Her head snapped around, her hand going to her knife hilt. "Now," she hissed, her voice suddenly sharp as broken glass. "Do it now, boy. They're coming."

She took a half-step back, her body coiled, ready to move, ready to fight. But her eyes flicked back to Corvin, waiting, watching. The boy on the ground was still breathing, still watching, still alive. And the forest was no longer silent.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack's eyes narrowed, and for a split second, she actually looked at Corvin, really looked at him. Her expression was a fascinating study in conflict—annoyance at the delay, respect for wanting to understand, and a grim recognition that the boy was serious. She took a deep breath, the kind that sounds like air being let out of a punctured skin.

"Alright," she said, her voice dropping to a low growl that seemed to carry the weight of all the years she'd spent studying such wounds. "A spear in the gut... it's not like a clean cut. It's not like a knife. It's a tearing, a splitting. That boy's insides are probably hanging out, or at least they're being pushed against his skin. You'll see the purple bruising where the organs are swelling with blood. The spear head tore through muscle, through fat, through whatever was in its path. And now it's a channel. A channel for infection, for air to get into his belly where it doesn't belong, for blood to pool where it shouldn't be."

She gestured with her chin toward the wound, her eyes still scanning the trees, her hand never leaving her knife. "See that dark blood? That's from inside him. That's his liver, maybe his spleen. The bright red stuff would be from a cut artery, but thankfully, you're not seeing much of that. The wound is a mess. It's an open invitation to death, and it's coming for him slow and painful as anything."

Her voice dropped even lower, urgent now. "He can't eat, can't drink without it hurting like hell. He'll vomit blood. He'll get a fever. His body will turn against itself trying to fight an infection that's already won. He'll die screaming, if he's lucky. And if he's not, he'll just... fade. Weak and terrified."

She finally looked directly at him, her eyes hard as flint. "That's what a spear does to a man's gut. It undoes him, piece by piece. It turns him into a liability. It turns him into a problem. Now finish the job, boy. Before his friends come to turn us into problems too."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod once, sharp, then look away from her face and down at the wound. I see the mess she described—the purple bloom, the dark stain. My stomach clenches. I adjust my grip, angle the point of my sword. "Close your eyes," I tell him, and my voice sounds strange in my own ears.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched as Corvin adjusted his stance, her own muscles coiling tighter with every second that passed. The boy on the ground made a soft, wet sound, a final gurgle that seemed to hang in the air. His eyes, wide with terror and pain, flickered to Corvin's face, then closed, as if accepting the inevitable.

"Good," Wrack whispered, not taking her eyes off the tree line. The shadows were longer now, deeper, and the forest had fallen unnaturally silent. Even the wounded boy had stopped making noise. That wasn't a good sign. "Quick and clean. Remember that."

The sound came then—a rustle, not of a small animal, but of something larger moving through the undergrowth. Wrack's hand tightened around her knife hilt. She didn't look at Corvin, didn't dare take her eyes off the forest edge. But she could feel the tension radiating from him, the sudden stillness of his body as he held his breath.

"Now," she said, her voice barely audible. "Do it now."

There was a sudden movement in the trees—just a flicker, a moment of disruption in the gathering darkness. Wrack took a half-step forward, her body low and ready. "Corvin," she hissed, not looking away from the threat. "Finish it. Right now."

Her heart was pounding, but her breathing remained steady. This was it. The moment the quiet would be broken, one way or another. The moment the boy would either become a liability or a memory. The moment they would either fight or run. And in that moment, she was just a sellsword, doing her job. Waiting for the next move in a game that had no winners, only survivors.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped moving, her body a coiled spring of tension that suddenly froze. She didn't look at Corvin, but her head turned slightly, enough to take him in from the corner of her eye. The command in his voice, the steadiness that had replaced his earlier shaking—it was a surprise. A nasty, unwelcome surprise.

"The hell are you talking about?" she whispered, her voice like the scrape of a stone against another. Her eyes remained fixed on the tree line, where the shadows were now thick enough to hide an entire company of men. "We don't have time for this. We need to move. Now."

"The sound of it," Corvin insisted, his voice a low rasp. "How long he takes. Tell me everything."

Wrack finally pulled her eyes from the forest, turning to face him fully. Her expression was a storm cloud about to break. For a long moment, she just stared at him, this boy who had gone from trembling wreck to something... else. Something worse, in her eyes.

"You want a lesson?" she hissed, taking a step closer, her voice dropping to a venomous whisper. "You want a story? Fine. But we are not doing this here. We are not doing this now. The moment you put that blade in, the moment that boy takes his last breath, you become part of this. You become as much a killer as I am. And you'll see what it does to a man. You'll see what it does to you."

Her eyes flicked to the dying boy on the ground, then back to Corvin. "So don't ask for a story. Ask for a way to stay alive. Ask for a reason to move. Ask for anything but this. Because this... this is a thing you don't come back from. Not really."

She took another step, closing the distance between them, her presence suddenly overwhelming. "Now finish it. Finish it and we run. Finish it and we survive. Or don't finish it and we die. Those are the only options on the table. Choose."

Her hand hovered over her knife, her body vibrating with the need to move, to fight, to do anything but stand here and lecture a boy about the cost of killing. The shadows were closing in, and with them, the promise of more death. More work. More survival.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Then we die." I say it flatly, my eyes still on the boy's face. I let the point of my sword dip. "Because I'm not leaving until I know what I've done."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stared at him, the world seeming to slow down to the thud of her own pulse. A muscle twitched in her jaw, and for a moment, she looked like she might actually strike him. The boy had been holding himself together with frayed threads, and now he was talking about death like it was a choice to be made over a cup of ale. It was infuriating. It was... impressive.

"Fine," she spat, the word like a stone in her mouth. "You want to watch? You want to learn? Then watch this."

In one fluid motion, she stepped forward, her knife flashing. The wounded boy never saw it coming. It was a quick, efficient cut across his throat, a gush of dark blood, a final, wet gurgling sound that lasted no more than three heartbeats before it faded into the gathering silence.

Wrack wiped her blade on the dead man's cloak again, her movements practiced, unhurried. She didn't look at Corvin, didn't check to see if he was watching, didn't care. She was a professional, and she had a job to do.

"He's gone," she said, her voice devoid of emotion, of triumph, of anything. "That's the sound of it. That wet pop. That gurgle. That final sigh. It's fast. It's clean. It's over. And in about five minutes, we'll be the only ones who remember he made a sound at all."

She finally turned to look at him, her eyes cold and hard. "Now. Do you feel like you've learned something? Do you feel like you understand? Because I don't have time for your little philosophy lesson anymore. We have company coming, and if you want to see what comes after watching a man die, you'd better start running. Right. Now."

She started to walk away, her boots crunching softly on the gravel. "And if you decide you've had enough of this... if you decide you can't handle it... that's fine too. Just don't be surprised when they find you. Just don't be surprised when you join him. Choose, boy. Survive or die. It's the only choice that matters out here."

She didn't look back, but she could feel his presence behind her, the weight of his decision hanging in the air like a physical thing. She knew what he would choose. They all did, eventually. But the question was, would he make the choice before it was too late?

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped walking. She was about fifteen paces away when his voice reached her, and she froze, her back still turned to him. For a long moment, she just stood there, her shoulders rising and falling with each controlled breath. The forest around them was silent, that terrible silence that follows a sudden, violent death. She could hear the distant sound of a bird, a little squeak in the undergrowth, the creak of her own leather armor.

"Say the rest," he had said. And she knew exactly what he meant.

She didn't turn around. She couldn't look at him right now. Instead, she looked at the trees, at the growing darkness, at the shapes that might or might not be men hiding in the shadows. Her mind was racing, a hundred memories flashing through it—all the men she had killed, all the men she had watched die, all the moments that had shaped her into what she was now. A thing of leather and steel and old scars, a survivor in a world that didn't care who survived.

"Say the rest," he said again, his voice quieter now, not demanding, but pleading. Pleading for something she wasn't sure she could give.

Wrack closed her eyes. When she spoke, her voice was different. It was softer, older, coming from some place deep inside her that she rarely let out.

"After you watch a man die," she said, her words measured, each one a step into a memory she usually kept locked away, "you don't feel brave. You don't feel strong. You feel... small. Like a kid who found his father's hunting knife and thought he was a man until the first rabbit died in his hands. And you never look at a rabbit the same way again."

She took a step forward, her boots crunching on the gravel. "You'll see things, boy. You'll see the life leave a man's eyes, and you'll wonder what it is you're seeing. Is it his soul? Is it just the light? You'll wonder what he was thinking in his last moments. Was he thinking of his mother? His lover? Or was he just thinking about the pain? And you'll never know. Because he can't tell you. And you can't ask."

Another step. "The smell... you'll never forget the smell. Blood has a smell. And death has a smell. And when you mix them together, it's a thing that gets into your clothes, into your hair, into your nose. And no matter how much you wash, you can still smell it sometimes. On rainy days. When the wind blows a certain way. And you'll remember."

She was closer now, close enough to see his outline in the fading light. "And you'll start to see him everywhere. In the faces of other men. In strangers on the road. And you'll wonder... would I have killed him too? Would he have tried to kill me? And you'll never know. Because you took away his chance to answer."

She stopped walking, and finally, she turned to face him. Her expression was unreadable in the shadows, but her voice was steady, clear.

"After you watch a man die, you change. You become someone else. Someone who can do what needs to be done. Someone who can live with it. Or you don't. And you break."

She gestured to the dead boy on the ground. "So you're right. You should know what you've done. Because this... this is the thing that makes you a man. Or it breaks you. And there's no coming back from either one of them."

She looked at him, really looked at him, for the first time since the ambush began. "So now you know. You know the sound. You know the smell. You know the feeling. And now you have to choose. Do you have what it takes to be this person? Or do you run? The choice is yours, boy. It's always been yours."

And with that, she turned away, her hand resting on the hilt of her knife, ready for whatever came next from the forest. Ready for whatever he chose to do.

Corvin:
I push myself to my feet, my legs unsteady. "We go," I say, my voice hoarse. "We go now."

Wrack:
Wrack didn't turn around. She just nodded once, a sharp, decisive movement. "Good," she said, her voice back to its usual gravelly tone. "We go."

She started moving, her steps sure and purposeful now that a decision had been made. She didn't look back to see if he was following. She knew he would. They always did. Once you saw the darkness, you couldn't turn back to the light. Not really.

"The trail splits about a quarter-mile ahead," she said, her voice low as she led the way into the gathering shadows of the forest. "One path leads to the river, the other to the old watchtower. The river's faster, but it's open. The watchtower's slower, but it has a place to hole up if we need it."

She glanced at him, a quick, assessing look. "Choose. Now."

Corvin:
"Watchtower," I say. "We can see them coming from there."

Wrack:
"Good," Wrack said again, a note of approval in her voice. "Smart."

She veered off the main path, her movements silent despite the uneven terrain. "Keep close. And keep your eyes open. They'll be looking for two people. Two sets of footprints. We need to make them doubt what they're seeing. Break the pattern."

She led him into a thicket of thorn bushes, the branches scratching at his arms and face. "And if you see them before I do, you don't shout. You don't make a sound. You get behind something solid and you wait. You watch. You learn."

She glanced at him, a brief, hard look. "You're not a boy anymore, Corvin. Not out here. You're just another man with a sword, trying to stay alive. Act like it."

And with that, she melted into the shadows, a ghost in the forest, leaving him to follow or be left behind. The choice, as always, was his.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I keep my head down and follow, the thorns tearing at my sleeves. My sword feels heavier than before, but my hand is steady. "I'm watching," I mutter, more to the forest than to her.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't acknowledge his words. She was already scanning the tree line, her movements economical, her senses attuned to the forest around them. The thorns tugged at her own cloak, but she barely seemed to notice, as if pain was merely an inconvenience she had long learned to ignore.

"They'll be tracking us," she said, her voice barely above a whisper now that they were deeper in the woods. "They'll be looking for signs. Broken branches, disturbed undergrowth. The smart ones will be watching for trails we might try to fake."

She paused, holding up a hand for silence. In the distance, the faint sound of voices carried on the wind. They were still far off, but getting closer.

"When we get to the watchtower," she continued, her eyes never leaving the shadows between the trees, "you take the west side. I'll take the east. The ladder is on the north side. Don't go near it unless you hear me give the signal."

"What signal?" he asked, his voice sounding too loud in the sudden stillness.

Wrack finally looked at him, her expression unreadable in the fading light. "You'll know it when you hear it," she said simply. "Now move. And remember—quiet is your friend out here. Quiet and stillness."

She turned back to the forest, her body coiled like a spring, ready to move at a moment's notice. The voices grew a little louder, then faded, as if their pursuers were circling, trying to pick up the trail.

"And Corvin?" she added, her voice dropping even lower, barely a breath. "If they find us, don't hesitate. Don't think. Just act. Remember what we did back there. Remember what you have to do to survive. Remember everything."

And with that, she melted into the shadows, leaving him to follow in the gathering darkness, the weight of her words—and his new reality—pressing down on him like a physical thing.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I don't nod. I just follow, my boots finding the soft patches of moss between roots. The voices fade again. "They're circling," I whisper, my throat tight. "They don't know where we are yet."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack's lips thinned into a grim line, a small, almost imperceptible movement in the dim light. "Smart," she murmured, not to him but to herself, impressed despite herself. "They're learning."

She increased her pace slightly, her movements fluid and silent as she moved through the forest. The thorns that had been tearing at their clothes moments before seemed to part for her, as if the woods themselves recognized a predator and gave way.

"Keep your distance," she hissed over her shoulder, her voice barely audible. "Don't step where I step. Don't break what I break. We need to make them think one person went this way and the other went that. Confusion is our friend right now."

She gestured to a small, moss-covered rock to his right. "If we need to split up, that's your marker. Go west from there. Find a creek bed and follow it. It'll take you to the old stone bridge, and from there, you can either hide or keep running. But only if we get separated. Understood?"

Corvin nodded, and Wrack saw the movement out of the corner of her eye. She approved. He was learning. Fear could either paralyze a man or sharpen him, and so far, it seemed to be doing the latter for the boy.

"The watchtower is just ahead," she said, slowing her pace and becoming even more cautious. "It's been abandoned for years. The stairs are rotted, but the walls are still solid stone. We can see for miles from up there. And if they find us, they'll have to come up the ladder one at a time. It's defensible."

She stopped behind a large oak tree, her hand resting on the hilt of her knife. The voices were growing louder again, closer this time. They were coming from the north, cutting across their path.

"They're getting bolder," she whispered, her eyes scanning the tree line ahead. "They think they're closing in. They're right. But they don't know we're here. Not yet."

She took a deep breath, the sound like the rustle of dry leaves. "Ready?"

Corvin nodded again, his hand tightening on the hilt of his sword. "Ready."

"Good," Wrack said, and a faint, almost invisible smile touched her lips. "Remember what I said. Fast and clean. And if you can't be fast, be quiet. And if you can't be quiet..." Her smile faded, replaced by the hard, professional expression she wore when facing death. "...then be ready."

She stepped out from behind the tree, her body low and coiled, her eyes fixed on the approaching voices. The watchtower loomed ahead, a silent, crumbling sentinel in the gathering darkness. And in that moment, Wrack was no longer just a sellsword. She was a hunter, and the forest was her hunting ground. And she was ready to do whatever it took to survive.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I match her step, angling my body to break different branches. My breathing's too loud in my ears. "I can see the tower," I murmur, and my voice sounds strange. "How long do we hold it?"
