dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack flipped the cloak back over the dead man’s face and sheathed her knife. She did not look at Corvin as she straightened, though she noted the wet on his wrist and the way his boots had rooted to the mud. The sound past the cart was wet and rhythmic, like a bellows with a hole punched through it.

“You’re not obliged,” she said. She stretched her shoulders, rolled the stiffness from a decade of sword-work out of her neck. “But leaving him means listening to that until morning, and then digging the hole deeper so the dogs don’t pull him out by morning.” She started toward the cart, her boots squelching in the ditch-mud. “Or I can do it, and you can check the saddlebags for anything worth burning. Your choice. Either way, the work’s the work.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "I'll do it." My voice comes out a little rough. I push away from the ditch edge, sword still in hand. "Just... give me a minute."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped. She did not turn, but she lifted her chin toward the wet sound beyond the cart. "He's on his side. Come in from behind the jaw, or you'll catch the collarbone and have to lever it." She rolled her shoulders again, the leather of her harness creaking. "Take your minute. I'll start on the saddlebags."

She squelched past the cart without looking toward the wounded man, making a wide path through the mud so Corvin would have the room and the line of sight to approach clean if he chose. The horses were still shifting, rolling their eyes at the smell of opened bellies. Wrack caught the nearest by its bridle, murmuring something tuneless, and began unbuckling the first bag with methodical patience. From somewhere in the darkening trees, a crow called. Wrack ignored it, upending the saddlebag and sorting through the contents with the same care she might use field-dressing a deer: efficient, detached, looking for anything that would burn or barter.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack upended a tin of salt tablets into her palm, considered them, and pocketed them. She still didn't look toward the cart.

“He's got a punctured lung,” she said. “That wet bellows sound—air where it shouldn't be, blood filling the sack. He'll drown in it. Might take an hour, might take till dawn. Won't lose consciousness quick, though. He'll be scared, and he'll be loud.”

She tossed aside a pair of ruined gloves and pulled a leather purse from the bag, weighing it by heft.

“So it's not easier,” she continued. “Easier's walking away and letting him finish slow while we sleep upwind. If you want to call it mercy, go ahead. To me it's just the last job of the day, and better done before full dark when you've got to guess at the placement.”

She finally glanced back, not toward the dying man but at Corvin's boots planted in the mud.

“And don't hesitate once you're over him. A half-cut windpipe just makes more noise.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take a slow breath, then move toward the cart. The sound gets louder, more ragged. "I know." My knuckles are white around the sword hilt.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack pulled a half-empty flask from the second saddlebag, worked the cork free with her teeth, and smelled it. Sour apple brandy. She set it atop the cart’s splintered rail in the open, where a man might find it if he had need, and kept her eyes on the bags, on the horses, on anything but the mud beyond the cart.

The wet bellows sound stopped. The silence that followed settled like dust.

“Four silvers,” she said, “a decent whetstone, and a book of prayers. Good kindling.” She pocketed the coins and the stone and tossed the book onto the discard pile. She murmured something tuneless to the nearest horse, checking its hooves one by one with the same dispassion she’d shown the dead.

“If you’re done, come help me with the off-side horse. He’s picked up a stone,” she said. “If you’re not, take your time. But the light’s going, and I don’t fancy digging six holes in full dark.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack set the horse’s hoof down with a wet clop and straightened, her knees clicking. She looked across the mud at the shape by the cart, reading him with the same flat assessment she’d give a downed stag.

“You’re looking at a man drowning in his own blood, only he’s doing it sideways in the dirt,” she said. “Top side of his chest rises faster than the bottom—air pushing through the hole, collapsing the sack. Pink froth at the mouth. Means his heart’s still beating hard. Means he’s conscious. Means he’s looking at you while he fills up.”

She wiped her hands on her trousers and turned back to the saddlebag, though her voice carried over the mud without hurry. “Come in from behind the jaw, blade angled down toward the collar. Soft spot under the ear. Severs the cord and the big vessels both. Lights out. You go for the throat from the front and you’ll catch the windpipe, and he’ll just bubble at you while you work.”

She pulled a rag from the bag and began cleaning the stone from the off-side hoof. “You’re looking at meat taking too long to die. Same as that buck we dressed in the frost, only this one borrowed a face and knows how to beg. Finish the job. Standing over him like a priest just gives him time to ask, and I’ve no taste for hearing it.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down in the mud, my sword held steady. I find the spot she described. "Don't look at me," I tell him, but he does. My stomach turns. I close my eyes and do it anyway.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack set the horse’s hoof down with a wet clop and did not turn. There was a soft, wet sound behind her—a blade sinking home, a body going slack in the mud. Then silence, except for Corvin’s breathing. She counted three of his breaths, measured and ragged, before she spoke.

“Done is done,” she said. It was not praise. It was a statement of fact, same as noting a fire had caught or a horse was lame. She upended the last saddlebag, sorting through the spill with methodical fingers. “Flask on the rail. Sour apple. It’ll burn going down, and sometimes that’s the point.”

She pulled a half-empty tin of hardtack from the bag, pocketed it, and tossed the ruined leather onto the discard pile. The sky above the trees had gone the color of old iron. “Take your minute. But when you’re steady, start dragging them to the ditch line. I want the fire built before full dark, or we’ll be explaining ourselves to every patrol between here and the river.” She drew her knife and began cutting a length of rope from the dead man’s tack. “Work’s the work. It doesn’t wait.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack tied the rope off with a sharp tug and stood. She did not look at Corvin. Instead, she walked to the body nearest the cart’s wheel—the one who’d caught a spear low, just beneath the rusted edge of his breastplate. She nudged him onto his back with her boot.

“A spear to the gut doesn’t kill,” she said. “Not quick. Steel punches through the abdominal wall, perforates the bowel. Stomach, intestines, whatever’s in the pipe empties into the cavity. The body tries to wall it off, but it can’t. Blood poisoning, except it’s mostly shit—gut flora eating him from the inside. He bloats, he burns, he retches bile and can’t keep water down.”

She squatted, indicating the wound with a flick of her fingers, her voice level as a supply report. “Muscle clamps tight around the shaft. That slows bleeding, but it don’t stop the leak. If the spear stays in, it plugs the hole some. Pull it out, and the vacuum sucks more mess into the space. Either way, he dies screaming or he dies whimpering. Hours. Sometimes a day, if he’s young and fat.”

She stood, wiping her hands on her thighs, and finally looked at Corvin. Her eyes held no challenge, only the flat relaying of facts. “I had a man take a boar spear outside Hallow’s Ford. Two days before his heart quit. We ran out of anything worth drinking the first night, and he was still lucid enough to beg for his mother by dawn. That’s the straight of it. A gut wound’s not a wound—it’s a slow drowning in your own filth, and there’s nothing to be done but wait.”

The wind shifted, carrying the smell of iron and opened bellies. Wrack turned back toward the ditch.

“So you finish them clean if you can. Or you learn to sleep through the noise. Now take your minute, drink the flask if you need it, and help me drag these bodies. Fire won’t build itself, and the dark’s coming on.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at the body she just pointed out, my throat tight. "Alright." I push myself up, mud sucking at my boots. I don't reach for the flask. "Which one do you want me to start with?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack pulled the coil of rope over her shoulder and nodded toward the body by the cart wheel.

“That one,” she said. “He’s already on his back, and his boots point toward the ditch. Hook him under the arms, keep his hips low so he don’t snag on the ruts, and drag. Ground’s soft enough he ought to slide.”

She stepped to the man in the ditch—the one whose cloak she’d used earlier—and hooked her hands under his belt without ceremony. “Don’t lift unless you want to feel his insides shift against your knee. These lads ate barley and salt pork same as us. Dead weight’s dead weight.” She hauled the body toward the ditch line with a low grunt, her boots finding purchase in the sucking mud. “If your hands get slippery, wipe ’em on his shirt before you reach for your blade. Nothing worse than a loose grip when you’re elbow-deep in evening work.”

She paused just long enough to shove the hair out of her eyes with a muddy forearm, then bent to haul the second body. “And leave his cloak where it is. We don’t need him staring up while we work. The faces are for morning, if you need ’em. By then the light makes ’em look like anyone else.”

The first body hit the ditch line with a wet thump. Wrack straightened, rolling her shoulder against the pull of an old scar.

“Two more on this end,” she said. “Then we pile the tack for burning and dig the scrape shallow. Deep enough to keep the dogs busy, not deep enough to waste the dark. Move brisk, Corvin. I’d rather smell smoke than corpses by the time the dew falls.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I hook my hands under his arms and pull. There’s a wet, dragging sound as his body slides through the mud. “Tell me what I’m doing to him,” I repeat, my voice low and steady even though my stomach’s churning. “Don’t make it clean in my head.”

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack let the coil of rope fall from her shoulder into the mud. She planted her boots wide and watched Corvin haul the dead man, tracking the way the corpse’s heels dug twin ruts through the slop.

“You’re pulling too high,” she said. “Hips catch on the ditch rim and you’ll flip him facedown. Then you’re wrestling a hundredweight of slack meat to get him right-side up again.”

She watched the dead man’s head rock loose on the neck, his temple knocking against a rut with a dull, sodden thud. “His joints haven’t locked yet. Rigor’s two hours off, maybe three in this wet. Right now he’s just wet leather and loose pegs. Feel that hitch? That’s his shoulder separating a little more with every tug. Socket gives up once the blood stops feeding it, same as a chicken wing when you twist it off the carcass.”

She stepped closer, close enough to catch the smell. “You’ll get a stink soon. Stomach’s a sack, and moving him squeezes it. He’ll leak from both ends before you hit the ditch—bile, piss, whatever’s in the pipe. That’s not fear. That’s gravity. A gut-shot deer does the same, only deer don’t fill their trousers with last night’s salt pork.”

She nodded at the corpse’s arm, flopped outward so that his fingers traced furrows in the muck. “The sound you’re hearing—wet, sloppy—that’s his cloak tearing where it’s pinned under your boot, and his jaw knocking stones. If his eyes were open, they’d roll with each jerk. Lucky for you, he’s already staring at nothing. Count about forty seconds for the full drag at that pace. Long enough for your forearms to cramp and your knees to lock. Long enough to realize the mud doesn’t care, and neither does he.”

Wrack wiped her nose with the back of her hand, smearing mud across her cheek. “There’s no dignity in it. Not for him, not for you. You’re hauling meat to the midden, and the only difference between him and a slaughtered hog is that this one owed you coin or didn’t, and either way he won’t pay. The sound is flesh moving through dirt. The time is however long your back holds out. And what you’re doing to him? You’re rendering him into fuel for the fire instead of bait for the dogs. That’s the whole of it. Keep hauling.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack let the silence stretch until the crows called again in the darkening trees. She squatted on her heels beside him, close enough that her shoulder nearly brushed his, and reached out to straighten the dead man’s arm where it had twisted during the drag. She handled him with the same impersonal care she might use adjusting a saddle blanket.

“The rest,” she said, “is hours. It’s your hands going numb from the rope while you haul the other five to the same line. It’s checking every pocket for coin while your thumbs press into cooling belly-bloat, because dead men don’t need silver and we do. It’s the cold slick that coats your fingers when you pull a man’s rings—joints swell, or they shrink, either way you work them like greased nuts off a bolt until the skin gives.”

She wiped her fingers on her trouser leg. “The rest is building the pyre. You don’t just stack them. Green wood on the bottom, dry on top, because corpses are wet and they need help catching. You lay them on their backs with their arms crossed, not for respect, but because a limb left hanging contracts in the heat and points at you like a finger. Skin splits in the fire—across the thighs, the belly, the chest. Fat renders slow, and it smells like a hog roast, and that is the smell that finds you three nights later when you think you’re safe in your bunk and the wind shifts through the canvas.”

She paused, listening to the horses shift behind her. “The rest is the popping. Air in the lungs, air in the gut, fluid boiling in the skull. Sounds like wet kindling splitting. Teeth don’t burn; they grin up out of the ash. Finger joints curl into fists unless you break the small bones with a mattock before the fire catches high, and if you don’t break them, you sift them out later, scorched clean, and you think they’re twigs until you see the nail beds.”

She turned her head and looked at him. The failing light carved deep lines around her mouth and eyes, but her gaze held no challenge, only the flat relaying of facts. “The rest is your clothes stinking of smoke and rendered grease no matter how you beat them on the stones. It’s the taste in the back of your throat when the wind brings it round. It’s digging the scrape for what didn’t fit—the scraps, the half-burned bits that fell through, the buckle that survived the heat—and throwing lime over the mess so the foxes don’t dig. It’s sleeping upwind and still waking with the taste of pork fat on your tongue, knowing exactly what it is.”

She stood, her knees clicking, and looked down at the body between them. “The rest is doing this again. Maybe tomorrow, maybe next week. The rest is learning that the worst part was never the killing. It’s the weight. It’s the hours. It’s knowing the exact heft of a dead man when you lift him under the arms, and feeling that same heft in your own shoulders when you lay down to sleep. It’s your back hurting for ten years and never being sure if it’s your sword arm or all the bodies you dragged before the fires.”

She bent and retrieved a discarded belt from the mud, coiling it over her shoulder. “So sit there as long as you need. But the rest doesn’t wait. The pyre needs building, and the dark’s coming on, and those other four won’t walk themselves to the ditch line. Get up when you’re ready. Or don’t. But the work’s the work, and it keeps moving with or without you.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I get to my feet, my hands still slick with mud and whatever else. "Tell me how to build the pyre," I say, and my voice sounds steadier than I feel. "I want to know the right way to do it."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked toward the treeline, gauging the last grey of the sky. “Right way,” she said, picking up a dead branch and snapping it across her knee with a sound like wet kindling. “Right way means it burns hot enough to crack bone in three hours, not smolders all night and leaves us picking teeth out of half-cooked meat by morning.”

She pointed toward the stand of ash and birch at the ditch lip. “Gather anything dead and standing—dry as tinder. Stack it in the ditch first, a handspan thick across the bottom. Not a mound. A cradle. You need air underneath, or the fire suffocates on its own smoke and the wet ground steals your heat.”

She strode to the cart and yanked loose a splintered rail, testing its heft in both hands. “Green wood on the bottom if you’ve got it, but tonight we burn what we can lift. These rails, the wheels if we must. Lay them parallel, two spans apart, then weave cross-pieces like a ladder. Bodies go atop that grate. Keeps them out of the mud. Wet meat in wet dirt just steams and stinks and won’t catch.”

She tossed the rail down into the ditch, where it struck mud with a sodden clack. “Lay them head to foot, crossed at the ankles so they don’t roll. Break the fingers back if they won’t stay folded—use a rock, a knife pommel, whatever’s hard. Arms across the chest. Like I said, a hanging limb curls in the heat and points. You don’t want to look up from the flames and see a blackened finger tracking you across the fire.”

She pulled her knife and began stripping bark from a fallen branch, letting the pale curls fall. “Top layer’s brush, dead leaves, anything that flares quick. Their cloaks if the cloth isn’t too blood-wet. Blood doesn’t burn; it boils and crusts. You want dry, you want oil if any of them carried it, you want the saddle grease from the tack we’re burning anyway. Rendered fat catches where flesh won’t.”

She glanced at the sky, the iron-dark settling fast. “Light it from the downwind side, low and along the whole base. One torch in the middle makes a chimney—burns straight up and leaves the edges cold. You want a wall of flame racing in, eating the air, so everything catches at once. Then you stand back and let it roar. Don’t prod it. Don’t stir it. Every time you open the pile, you let heat out and you smell what’s inside.”

She straightened, rubbing her lower back with the heel of her hand. “If a body doesn’t burn through by midnight, you roll it with a pole—never your hands, not unless you want your palms blistered to the bone—and feed the gap underneath. The scrape comes after dawn, when the coals are grey. Break the brittle bits with a stone, shovel what you can into the hole, lime the rest.”

She looked at Corvin, mud-slicked and steady-voiced, and nodded once. “That’s the right way. Efficient. Thorough. No poetry to it. Now gather wood. I’ll break the cart down for the frame.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I start gathering wood, snapping branches with more force than needed. "Tell me if I'm doing it wrong," I say, my back to her. "And tell me which of these bastards had the oil."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack wedged the splintered cart rail beneath the axle and leaned into it, her weight grinding rust through dry wood until the wheel sagged with a shriek of nails. She paused, listening to the snapping behind her.

“You’re taking the green ones,” she called, not turning. “Hear that? Wet tear, not dry crack. That’s sap crying. Green wood smokes and spits and won’t give heat—you’d be better off burning the mud.”

She braced her boot against the bed of the cart and heaved the rail free, tossing it down into the ditch atop the others.

“Kick the trunk first. Bark comes off in dry plates, that’s your tree. You want standing dead, grey and hollow. Sounds like a dry bone when it goes. What you’re breaking now is sappy trash. It’ll steam the bodies, not burn them.”

She drew her knife and sawed at the leather traces still tethering the harness to the frame, slicing free strips of oiled leather that would catch fast.

“The oil’s on the tall bastard by the far rut,” she said, jerking her chin toward the tree line. “Bad shave, split lip, leather flask at his hip—not the brandy. Smells like cooking grease and old olives. Soldiers carry it for lamps. Pours thick, but it’ll take a spark if you splash it on dry brush first. Check his pack, too. Might be a second tin, or rags soaked in it.”

The last trace parted. She caught the harness before it fell into the mud and coiled it over her shoulder.

“Bring what you’ve got and lay it in the ditch. I’ll show you the weave once I’ve got this axle broke. And don’t wear yourself out snapping twigs like kindling. You need arm-length pieces, finger-thick, for the frame. The tinder’s on the ground—dead leaves, punkwood, the brittle stuff under the bracken. Let the forest do the work. Your back’s for hauling and lifting, not thrashing at wet branches like you’re sword-drilling a hay bale.”

She drove her knife into a warped spoke and twisted, the dry oak groaning.

“And when you find the flask,” she added, looking back long enough to meet his eyes in the failing grey light, “look at his face before you take it. Not for prayers. So you know exactly whose grease you’re pouring. Makes it simpler when the fire pops and sizzles. You’ll remember it was his lamp oil, not stolen meat, and you earned the use of it same as you earned the rest. Now move brisk. That sky’s fixing to drop on us, and wet pyres don’t light.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kick the trunk of a grey-barked ash and it shivers, dry plates of bark rattling down. "Better?" I ask, breaking off a branch that snaps clean. I walk over to the tall bastard with the split lip and kneel beside him. His flask is right where she said. I look at his face first — a boy, really, with a sparse mustache and mud in his eyelashes — before I pull it free. "Got it."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack gave the blade one final wipe and slid it into her sheath with a soft, practiced click. She stood up, her knees giving a faint pop that she ignored, and looked over at Corvin. She noted the blood smeared across his face but didn't comment on it. It was just weather, as far as she was concerned.

"Right," she said, her tone entirely conversational. "Then we have a choice. We walk over there and open his throat, which is quiet. We drag him back here and ask him who paid him, which is loud, messy, and takes time we don't have. Or we leave him to bleed out and hope his buddies don't come looking when he misses supper."

She spat into the ditch and adjusted her sword belt. "I vote we finish it. Interrogations give me a headache, and I'm too tired to run from reprisals in the dark." 

She didn't wait for his answer before she started walking toward the cart, her boots crunching steadily on the hardpack. The noise from the wounded man was clearer now—a wet, ragged wheezing, punctuated by the occasional scrape of armor against dirt. Wrack drew her knife again as she closed the distance. 

"You coming, or do I need to do the heavy lifting?" she called back over her shoulder.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I force my legs to move, my own steps less steady than hers. "You're always in such a damn hurry." My hand goes to my sword hilt, but I don't draw it yet.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
"Hurry is just a word for not lingering," Wrack said, not breaking her stride. "Sun's dropping, and fresh blood smells like dinner to every wolf and scavenger in a five-mile radius."

She rounded the rear of the cart. The seventh man was slumped against the splintered wood of the left wheel, clutching his chest. His hands were slick with dark blood, and his eyes were wide, rolling in panic as Wrack’s shadow fell over him. He tried to speak, to beg or curse, but it only produced a wet, bubbling cough. A punctured lung. He was dead already, just waiting for his body to catch up.

Wrack didn't offer any comforting words, nor did she hesitate. She stepped heavily on his forearm to pin his flailing hand to the dirt, knelt on one knee, and grabbed a fistful of his greasy hair to tilt his head back. The knife went in just below the ear, angled upward—a quick, brutal twist that severed the brain stem. 

The man went limp instantly, the awful wheezing cutting off mid-breath. 

Wrack withdrew the blade, wiped it clean on the dead man's tunic, and stood up. She looked down at the corpse for a second, then kicked his boot to ensure the reflexes were truly gone. 

"Seven," she said, turning her head to look back at Corvin. "He was a bleeder. Check the cart before we move on. If they were carrying coin, I want it. If they were carrying rations, I want that too." 

She sheathed her knife and rested her hand casually on her sword pommel, her eyes scanning the treeline as the light began to fail. "And try not to step in the puddle. It's getting cold, and I don't want to listen to you complain about wet socks all night."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack let out a short, dry breath that might have been a laugh if she had the energy for it. 

"Mercy's for priests and people who don't have to sleep in the dirt," she said, stepping over the dead man's legs to reach the back of the cart. "But if you need it to be mercy, he had a collapsed lung and was bleeding out inside his chest. He was going to drown in his own fluids in about ten minutes, gurgling like a backed-up drain the whole time. I saved us the noise."

She grabbed the heavy, oil-stained canvas tarp covering the cart's bed and yanked it back. The fading light spilled over the contents, revealing a thoroughly unglamorous haul. 

"Grab that corner and fold it back," she instructed, nodding at the other side of the tarp. "Sun's almost gone and I want to be three miles down the road before the wolves get bold."

Under the canvas, it was mostly survival gear and stolen staples: half-empty sacks of milled grain, a small barrel of salted pork, and a few bundles of rough-spun wool. Tucked near the front of the bed, however, was a heavy, iron-banded lockbox. 

Wrack tapped the lid of the box with the toe of her boot. It gave a dull, heavy thud. "Well. They weren't just out for a stroll. Check the bodies for a key. If you can't find it, I'll smash the lock with a rock, but it'll take time we're spending in the dark." 

She turned her back on the cart to keep her eyes on the treeline, the shadows between the pines growing long and thick. Her hand remained resting casually near her sword pommel. "And wipe that blood off your face before it dries," she added, her voice flat and practical. "It's going to itch, and I don't want to watch you scratch at it all night."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
"Mercy's for priests," I repeat under my breath, rubbing at the drying blood on my cheek with my sleeve. I move to fold back the tarp, my fingers clumsy. "You know, sometimes I think you actually enjoy this part."

I start pawing through the dead man's pockets, avoiding looking at his face.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack let out a slow, measured breath through her nose, her eyes never leaving the darkening pines. 

"I enjoy hot stew," she said, her voice carrying easily over the quiet rustle of his search. "I enjoy dry boots. I enjoy waking up without a new hole in my gut. This?" She gave a slight, dismissive tilt of her head toward the carnage. "This is just the commute."

She shifted her weight, the leather of her armor creaking faintly. The woods were getting louder as the light failed—the chirp of crickets, the distant, lonely call of a crow, the settling of the cooling earth. 

"Stop patting his thighs," she instructed, her tone entirely practical. "If he’s carrying a heavy iron key, it’s not stuffed in his breeches. Check his neck. Men who run for a living don't keep heavy keys on their belts unless they want them jingling like a fool. Look for a leather cord under his collar."

She finally glanced back at him, watching him deliberately avoid the dead man's face. "And look at him. He’s dead. He isn't going to judge you for picking his pockets, and he isn't going to bite you. Just do it."

She turned her attention back to the trees. The shadows were pooling thick and black between the trunks now, turning the forest into a wall of jagged silhouettes. "Seven men don't escort a lockbox just to guard half a barrel of salted pork," she mused, her voice dropping a fraction. "Whoever they were working for is missing a payroll, or a bribe. Which means someone is going to be very interested in where they ended up."

She drew her sword an inch from its scabbard, just to check the slide, then let it snap back into place with a sharp click. "Sun's touching the ridge. You've got one minute. If you don't find it, I'm taking a rock to the hinge and we're walking."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't sigh. Sighing was a waste of breath, and she needed all of hers for the dark. She kept her eyes fixed on the treeline, where the shadows were now bleeding together into a solid, impenetrable wall, but she pitched her voice to carry clearly over the cart.

"You're looking at a hundred and seventy pounds of cooling meat," she said, her tone as flat and instructional as a butcher explaining a cut to an apprentice. "The pump's stopped, which means the blood is settling in his back and his legs. That's why his face is going gray."

She risked a quick glance over her shoulder. He was still hovering, his hands uncertain. 

"Stop staring at his eyes," she instructed. "They're just glass now, and they aren't looking back. Look at his neck. See the line of road dirt caked right above his tunic? Slide your fingers under the linen. Feel for a leather thong. If he's got a key, it’ll feel like a cold, hard lump resting against his collarbone."

She shifted her weight, the leather of her armor creaking faintly in the quiet. A branch snapped somewhere deep in the woods. Probably a deer. Probably. She didn't take her hand off her sword. 

"And don't mind the wetness on his chest," she added, her eyes sweeping back to the pines. "That's just the bleed-out from where I stuck him, mixed with the fluid from his lung. It’s slippery, so grip tight. If you drop the key in the mud, I'm not digging for it. Just use his sleeve to wipe your hands if it bothers you, but don't wipe them on his cloak. I'm taking that for a bedroll."

The wind picked up, rustling the dry needles and carrying the sharp, coppery scent of the slaughter down the road. The temperature was dropping fast, the evening air turning brittle and cold. 

"Sun's dipped below the ridge," Wrack said, her voice dropping to a low, carrying murmur. "You've got twenty seconds before I take a rock to the ironwork. Work fast."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: My fingers fumble under the man's collar, and I find the leather cord. It’s slick and damp. I pull, and the iron key comes free, clattering onto his chest. I snatch it up, wiping my hands hastily on my own trousers. "Got it."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack turned away from the treeline, the rigid line of her shoulders easing just a fraction. She closed the distance to the cart in three long strides, holding out a blood-speckled hand. 

"Give it here," she said. 

She took the slick iron key from him, wiped it casually on the dead man's tunic to clear the worst of the gore, and fitted it into the heavy lock. It turned with a stiff, grinding protest, and the latch gave way with a sharp *clack* that seemed entirely too loud in the gathering dark. 

Wrack threw the heavy lid back. 

The fading light caught the dull gleam of stacked coins. They weren't gold, but thick, unclipped silver marks, stamped with the profile of a king who’d been dead for five years. Border pay. Beneath the neat rows of silver rested a heavy, wax-sealed leather tube. 

Wrack didn't smile, and she didn't gasp. She just stared at the haul, her eyes doing the rapid, practiced math of a veteran quartermaster. 

"Silver," she said, her voice flat. "Enough to buy us through the winter, if we don't get killed spending it. And a dispatch tube." She tapped the leather cylinder with a knuckle. "We don't open it. If it's troop movements, it's leverage. If it's a pardon, it's a retirement. Either way, it stays sealed until we're somewhere with walls."

She slammed the lid shut and threw the lock back into place, dropping the key into her own belt pouch. 

"Grab the salted pork and the bundles of wool," she ordered, stepping back and letting her eyes sweep the black wall of the pines once more. The wind was biting now, carrying the chill of the high ridges. "Leave the grain. It's too heavy, and we can't carry it and fight at the same time. Shove the lockbox into your pack, or carry it by the handle if it won't fit."

She adjusted her sword belt, the leather creaking in the quiet, and drew her cloak tighter around her shoulders. 

"We need to be off this road and under cover in five minutes," she said, her tone leaving no room for argument. "Whoever sent these seven is going to notice they're missing, and I'd rather not be standing over their payroll when the relief column rides up. Start loading."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't stop moving. She hauled the heavy bundle of rough-spun wool out of the cart and dropped it at Corvin's feet with a dull, heavy thud. 

"I don't clean it up to spare your feelings," she said, her voice a low, steady rasp in the dark. "I do it because staring at the mess gets you killed. But if you want the butcher's bill, here it is."

She grabbed the small barrel of salted pork, hoisting it under one arm with a grunt of effort. 

"A spear doesn't just cut. It pushes. If it goes into the gut and misses the big veins, it punches through the bowel. That spills shit, bile, and half-digested stew right into the belly cavity. He doesn't bleed to death. His gut swells up hard as a drum and he rots from the inside out. Takes about three days of sweating, shitting himself, and screaming before the fever finally cooks his brain."

She shoved the barrel toward his chest, forcing him to take it or let it drop into the dirt. 

"If it catches the liver or the spleen, it's like stabbing a wet sponge. The organ shreds. He bleeds out inside his own skin, turning pale and cold while his heart tries to pump sludge. Ten minutes, maybe fifteen, if he's tough."

Wrack turned back to the lockbox, grabbing its iron handle and dragging it to the edge of the cart bed with a scrape of metal on wood. 

"The guy by the wheel caught a thrust that slipped up under the ribs. Missed the gut, hit the lung. Air and blood fill the chest, the lung collapses, and he drowns in it. That's the wet wheezing you heard." 

She let go of the box and looked at him. Her face was a pale, hard mask in the starlight, entirely devoid of pity or malice. 

"It's not a tragedy, Corvin. It's just broken plumbing. Now put the pork in your pack, grab that box, and start walking. Because the only thing worse than looking at a gut wound is catching one."

She didn't wait to see if the anatomy lesson had settled his stomach. Wrack turned and began walking down the hardpack road, her boots keeping a steady, measured rhythm, her eyes already adjusting to the black of the treeline.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I heft the lockbox, the weight of it settling something cold in my stomach. "Broken plumbing," I mutter, falling into step behind her. "So we're just... fixing leaks."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
"Plumbers don't have to worry about the pipes fighting back," Wrack said, her voice dropping to a low, carrying murmur. "And they get to sleep in a bed. But if it helps you process it, sure. We're fixing leaks."

She shifted the heavy bundle of rough-spun wool on her shoulder, the coarse fibers scratching against her neck. The hardpack road was a pale ribbon in the starlight now, entirely too exposed. Anyone riding hard to catch up with their missing payroll would see them a hundred yards off, and Wrack had no intention of fighting a cavalry patrol in the dark.

"Step off the road," she ordered, veering sharply to the right and sliding down the steep embankment into the ditch. The dead grass crunched under her boots before she pushed through a thicket of scrub oak, letting the deeper shadows of the tree line swallow her. 

"Keep your head down and watch for low branches," she called back softly. She didn't wait to check if he was right behind her. She trusted him to follow; he always did, even when he was busy having a crisis of conscience. 

The forest closed in around them, thick and suffocating. The air under the canopy was colder, damp with the smell of rotting leaves and wet earth. Wrack kept her pace steady but quiet, placing her boots carefully to avoid dry twigs and loose stones. Her right hand hovered near her sword hilt, her thumb resting lightly against the cold iron of the crossguard. 

"We'll push two miles in, then find a hollow to bed down in," she said, her voice barely louder than the rustle of the wind through the pines. "No fire tonight. We eat the pork cold and sleep in shifts. You take first watch. If you hear anything that doesn't sound like a squirrel or a deer, you wake me."

She paused for a fraction of a second, glancing back just long enough to catch his silhouette in the gloom. 

"And Corvin?" she added, her tone flat and entirely serious. "If you do hear something, don't try to be a hero. Just wake me up. Heroes don't get to collect their pay."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped. She didn't sigh, and she didn't roll her eyes. She just let the heavy bundle of wool slide from her shoulder to the dirt with a soft thud, turned on her heel, and walked back. 

She found Corvin kneeling in the bloody grass beside one of the original six—a man who had taken a spear thrust to the belly during the initial clash and been left to linger. The man was pale, his breathing shallow and ragged, his hands weakly batting at Corvin’s wrists as Corvin tried to drive his knife into his chest. It was a messy, struggling tangle of limbs.

Wrack stepped up beside him, her shadow falling over them both. She kept her voice low, pitched only for him, her eyes flicking briefly to the dark treeline before settling back on the grisly work.

"You're fighting the ribs," she said, her tone as calm as if she were correcting his grip on a whetstone. "You're trying to push through the bone, and your blade is too narrow to pry it apart. You're just making him thrash."

She crouched down on one knee, close enough to smell the sour stench of the man's voided bowels and the sharp copper of his blood. 

"You want the details? Listen," she instructed. "That wet, tearing sound when you pull the blade back? That's the fascia peeling away from the muscle. You're sawing. Stop sawing. Put the point just below the sternum, angle it up toward the left shoulder, and push. Use your body weight, not your arm."

She watched his hands, ready to intervene if he completely botched it, but she kept her own hands resting on her knees. 

"When you pierce the diaphragm, you'll hear a hiss," she continued, her voice steady over the man's weak, gurgling gasps. "That's the vacuum in the chest cavity breaking. It sounds like a wet boot pulling out of deep mud. Once you hit the heart, the blood won't spray unless his heart is still beating hard. His pressure is too low. It'll just well up, thick and dark, like syrup."

The man's eyes rolled toward Wrack, wide and uncomprehending, his mouth opening in a silent plea. Wrack didn't blink. 

"He's trying to scream, but his lungs are filling with fluid and his vocal cords are paralyzed by shock," she told Corvin, her eyes tracking the clumsy plunge of Corvin's knife. "You've got the angle right now. Push deeper. You need to sever the aorta or pierce the ventricle, or he'll just bleed out internally over the next hour."

She leaned in slightly, watching the man's chest. 

"There," she said softly as a dull, wet *pop* vibrated through the hilt of Corvin's knife. "That's the pericardium. The sac around the heart. Now twist the blade a quarter-turn to keep the wound open. Don't pull it out yet."

The man's back arched off the ground in a final, violent spasm, his heels drumming a erratic rhythm against the dirt. A thick bubble of dark blood escaped his lips, popping with a faint, wet click. Then, the tension bled out of his muscles all at once, and he collapsed back into the grass, his eyes fixing on the starry sky.

"His brain is starved of oxygen now," Wrack said, watching the man's chest. "He's gone. But watch his legs."

For another ten seconds, the dead man's calves twitched and his fingers curled inward, the nervous system firing off its last meaningless signals. Then, stillness. 

"He takes about three minutes to lose consciousness from a heart strike, but the body keeps moving for a minute after," Wrack said, standing up and brushing the dirt from her knees. "The sound of it is mostly just air and fluid shifting. It's not dramatic. It's just a machine winding down."

She looked down at Corvin, her face unreadable in the gloom. 

"Pull the blade out. Wipe it on his cloak, not his tunic—the tunic is soaked and it'll just smear. Then get up. You've got your lesson, and we've got a schedule." She turned and walked back to where she'd dropped the wool, hoisting it back onto her shoulder. "And Corvin? Next time, don't hesitate on the thrust. Hesitation is what makes it ugly."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at the blood on my knife, then wipe it on the dead man's cloak like she said. My hands don't shake, but they feel like they belong to someone else. "You're a real good teacher," I say, my voice flat. "Ever think about taking up tutoring?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack let out a short, dry breath that sounded more like a cough than a laugh. 

"Tutors get summers off," she said, her tone entirely deadpan. "And their students don't usually try to gut them during the final exam. Stick to the sellsword trade. The dental plan is a joke, but the enrollment is steady."

She hoisted the bundle of wool higher on her shoulder, the coarse fibers scratching against her neck. The woods were fully dark now, the canopy above them blocking out the starlight and turning the forest into a maze of black trunks and deeper shadows. The air was growing sharper, the damp chill of the ditch seeping through the soles of her boots.

"Keep your voice down," she murmured, stepping over the dead man's legs and moving toward the tree line. "Sound carries in the cold. And if there's a second patrol on the road, they won't be as sloppy as the first."

She paused at the edge of the scrub oak, glancing back to make sure he was actually moving and not just staring at his hands in the dark. 

"You did fine," she added, offering the closest thing to a compliment she was likely to give. "You didn't puke, and you didn't drop your blade. That puts you ahead of half the conscripts they send us from the capital. Now shut your mouth and watch your step. We've got two miles of blind woods to cross before we can stop walking."

She turned and pushed into the thicket, the branches snapping back softly behind her. She kept her pace steady, her boots finding the solid ground beneath the leaf litter by memory and feel. Her right hand stayed near her sword, her thumb resting against the cold iron of the crossguard.

"If your conscience starts acting up," she called back softly over the rustle of the brush, "just remember that guy was going to die anyway. We just saved him three days of shitting himself in the dirt. You're welcome, by the way."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped. The heavy bundle of wool slid from her shoulder and hit the dirt with a muffled thud. She didn't sigh. She just turned around and walked back to where he was kneeling, her boots crunching softly on the dead leaves. 

She stopped a few feet away, looking down at him in the gloom. The starlight caught the hard, uncompromising lines of her face. She rested her hands on her sword belt, her thumbs hooked in the leather, and looked at the corpse, then back to Corvin.

"You want the rest," she said. It wasn't a question. Her voice was flat, stripped of any lingering dry humor. "Fine. Listen."

She gestured with her chin toward the dead man's midsection. "Right now, all the muscles are giving out. That means his sphincters are relaxed. His bladder and his bowels are emptying into his clothes. That sour, heavy smell you're trying not to breathe through your mouth? That's him. It's going to get worse before it gets better."

She took a slow step closer, her eyes tracking the stillness of the body. "In about an hour, his core temperature will drop to match the dirt. The skin will get clammy. Because his heart isn't pushing blood anymore, gravity takes over. The blood will sink to the lowest points—his back, his shoulders, the backs of his legs. It'll pool there and look like a massive, dark purple bruise. If you rolled him over, his back would be black and blue."

She shifted her weight, the leather of her armor creaking in the quiet woods. "By sunrise, the stiffness hits. It starts in the small muscles—the jaw, the eyelids, the fingers—and works its way down to the arms and legs. He'll lock up like a board. If you tried to bend his knee tomorrow morning, the ligaments would snap before the joint gave. He'll stay frozen in whatever shape he's in right now, right down to the curl of his fingers, until the rot breaks the tissues down."

Wrack didn't look away from the body. She was giving him the work, the details he had asked for, and she wasn't going to blink. 

"And the rot will come," she continued, her voice a steady, low rasp in the cold air. "The bacteria in his gut will start eating him from the inside out. They'll produce gas. His belly will swell up tight as a drum, and the skin will turn a mottled, sickly green. The pressure from the gas will force a pink, foul-smelling fluid up his throat and out of his mouth and nose. They call it purge fluid. It smells like spoiled meat and shit, and it'll stain the grass around his head."

She paused, letting the silence of the woods press in on them for a few seconds. A cold breeze rattled the dry branches above. 

"Then the environment takes over," she said. "The flies will find him by mid-morning. They lay their eggs in the wet spots—the corners of his eyes, his nostrils, his mouth, and the wound you just put in his chest. The maggots hatch in a day and start liquefying the soft tissue. They eat the eyes first, then the lips."

She looked down at Corvin, her gaze heavy and entirely unromantic. "If the scavengers don't get to him before the bugs do, he'll be a skeleton in a month. But the scavengers will come. The crows, the feral dogs, the wolves. They don't care about his soul or his sins. They'll tear his stomach open to get to the organs, and they'll drag his intestines through the brush. The dogs will crack his femurs for the marrow. That's the rest of it, Corvin. That's what you leave behind when you walk away. Every man you kill becomes a meal and a mess."

She stood there for a long moment, letting the grim reality of the biology settle over him in the dark. She didn't offer a comforting hand, and she didn't soften her expression. 

"That's why you don't hesitate," she said, her voice dropping to a quiet, absolute certainty. "Because the only part of this you can control is the moment the heart stops. The rest belongs to the dirt. So you make the kill clean, you wipe your blade, and you don't look back. Because looking back doesn't change the meat."

She reached down and grabbed the heavy bundle of wool, hauling it back up onto her shoulder with a grunt. She adjusted the strap, her eyes moving past him to the black wall of the pines. 

"You've got the whole picture now," Wrack said, turning her back to the corpse and facing the road ahead. "So get up. We're burning daylight, and the dead aren't going anywhere."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I get to my feet, my knees stiff. The sour smell is in my nose, in my clothes. "Alright," I say, my voice rough. I hoist the lockbox. "Let's go."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack gave a single, curt nod. It was the only validation he was going to get, and it was all he needed.

"Keep your breathing steady," she said, turning back to the treeline. "In through the nose, out through the mouth. The sour smell will fade once you stop thinking about it."

She pushed through the scrub oak, the dry branches scraping against her leather armor. She kept her pace deliberate, her boots finding the solid earth beneath the leaf litter by memory and feel. She didn't use a lantern; the dark was a tool, and she knew how to use it. 

They walked for the better part of an hour in silence. The woods grew denser, the canopy overhead knitting together so tightly that the starlight barely pierced the gloom. The air grew colder, biting at their exposed skin, and the damp chill of the earth seeped up through the soles of their boots. Wrack's shoulder ached where the coarse wool rubbed against her collarbone, but she ignored it. Pain was just another detail to file away.

Finally, she stopped. She had found what she was looking for: a shallow depression beneath the sprawling, moss-draped roots of a massive, ancient oak that had fallen decades ago. The hollow was sheltered from the wind and hidden from the main road by a thick screen of dead brambles.

"Drop it," she ordered, shrugging the bundle of wool off her shoulder and letting it hit the dirt. 

She unrolled the wool, revealing it to be a rough, lanolin-heavy blanket that smelled strongly of sheep and old woodsmoke. She spread it out in the deepest part of the hollow, beneath the overhang of the roots. 

"This is home for the night," she said, her voice a low murmur. She sat down heavily, her back against the solid wood of the root wall, and unbuckled her sword belt, though she kept the scabbard resting across her knees. "No fire. We eat cold, we sleep cold."

She pulled a small, waxed cloth bundle from her belt pouch and unwrapped it, revealing a chunk of hard, yellow cheese and a heel of dark bread. She broke the bread in half and tossed a piece toward where he was standing. 

"Eat," she instructed, taking a bite of the cheese and chewing methodically. "You need the salt. You lost a lot of it sweating over that corpse."

She wiped her hands on her trousers and looked at him, her eyes catching the faint, ambient light of the forest. 

"You take first watch," she said, her tone shifting into the crisp, authoritative cadence of a veteran giving orders. "Sit at the edge of the brambles. Don't stare into the dark until your eyes play tricks on you. Keep your gaze moving. Sweep left to right, right to left. Listen for the snap of a twig, the rustle of dry leaves, the smell of woodsmoke or unwashed bodies. If a wolf howls, ignore it. If the crickets stop chirping, wake me."

She pulled her cloak tighter around her shoulders and shifted to get comfortable against the hard wood, closing her eyes for a brief second to let them adjust to the absolute black of the hollow. 

"I'll wake you in four hours for the second watch," she added, her voice already dropping a fraction as she settled in. "Don't let your mind wander, Corvin. The dead are behind us. The living are what you need to worry about."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I catch the bread, my stomach turning at the thought of food. But I eat it anyway, the dry crust scraping my throat. I settle at the edge of the brambles, my sword across my lap. "You ever think about doing something else?" I ask quietly, not looking back at her.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack chewed the hard cheese, working it against her molars until it softened enough to swallow. She washed it down with a pull from her waterskin, the cold water shocking her throat and settling heavy in her stomach. She leaned her head back against the massive, mossy root, letting the solid wood support the ache in her neck.

"Something else," she repeated. Her voice was low, a dry rasp that barely carried over the rustle of the wind in the dead brambles. "Like what? I don't have the patience for farming. Turnips don't fight back, which means you have to care about the rain, and I hate the rain. I don't have the hands for a trade, and I certainly don't have the smile to pour ale for drunk mercenaries."

She capped the waterskin and tucked it back into her pouch, her movements slow and deliberate to conserve warmth. 

"I think about it the same way I think about the king's border policies," she said, her tone entirely conversational. "It doesn't affect what I'm having for supper, so it's a waste of breath. You start thinking about 'something else,' you start wondering if the guy you just gutted was on his way to 'something else.' You start wondering if he had a wife, or a dog, or a favorite pair of boots. And the second you start wondering about his life, you stop focusing on ending it."

She shifted her weight, wincing slightly as her left knee gave a faint, familiar pop in the cold. She rubbed the joint absently through her leather breeches. 

"Your thrust gets an inch too shallow, or your parry gets a fraction too slow," she continued, her eyes fixed on the black wall of the tree line. "And then you're the one lying in the dirt, waiting for the flies to find your eyes. So no. I don't think about something else. I think about the next meal, the next mile, and keeping my blade sharp. That's the whole world, Corvin. Don't make it bigger than it is."

She pulled her cloak tighter, tucking the edges beneath her boots to trap whatever body heat she had left. The hollow was freezing, the damp cold of the earth seeping up through the roots and into her bones, but it was a safe cold. It was the kind of cold that kept you awake.

"Now stop staring at the back of my head and watch the brush," she ordered, her voice dropping back into the flat, authoritative cadence of a veteran on watch. "Keep your eyes moving. If a patrol comes up that road, they won't be asking us about our career aspirations. They'll just be asking how heavy our coin purses are. Wake me if the wind changes direction." 

She closed her eyes, her breathing slowing as she forced her body to rest, though her right hand remained resting lightly on the pommel of her sword.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I watch the brush, my eyes straining in the dark. "You're a real poet, you know that?" I keep my voice low, the taste of bread and blood still on my tongue.
