dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't comment on the lie. She'd heard that particular lie several hundred times and it didn't slow her down.

She got her hands on the man's left arm, feeling along the joint the way you'd feel for a gap in a fence line — methodical, not gentle but not rough either. The shoulder had been out long enough that the muscles had seized around it, which was the problem. The arm was trying to protect itself. The arm was wrong about what protection looked like right now.

"His name is Colm," she said, not because she thought Wick needed to know, but because she'd found that people held better when they thought of the thing on the table as a person. "He came in on a cart from the Hessler crossing. He's been like this since yesterday morning."

She repositioned her grip. The man — Colm — made a sound low in his chest and tried to move and couldn't, which was Wick doing the job correctly.

"Good," Sedge said.

She rotated the arm out slowly. This was the part that looked wrong. This was the part that made people who were new to it flinch, and flinching was the thing she could not afford from the person at the other end of the table.

"Hold," she said.

She put her weight into it.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I can feel the sickening grind under my hands and I have to clench my jaw to keep from reacting. "Got him," I say, my voice tight. The canvas wall I'm staring at is stained with old watermarks, and I focus on tracing their shape.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge felt the joint give — not all at once but in stages, the way a knot will sometimes release, and then the pop she'd been waiting for, and Colm's whole body went slack in a way that was almost peaceful.

"There," she said.

She didn't let go of the arm immediately. She held it in the new position, elbow in, forearm across his chest, giving the joint a moment to understand what had happened to it. This was the part people always skipped and it was the part that mattered.

"You can ease off," she told Wick. "Don't let go entirely. Just ease off."

She checked the shoulder with her fingers again — the gap was gone, the line of it looked right, the muscle would still be screaming but that was a different problem and a lesser one. Colm was breathing in long ragged pulls. Conscious, probably, in the way that people were conscious when they'd been past the edge of what they could stand and had come back to the near side of it.

"One more," Sedge said.

She moved around the table to the right side. The right shoulder was worse — she'd known it was worse when she'd first looked at him, which was why she'd done the left first. You started with the one that would go easily so that the person holding knew what it felt like when it worked.

"Same thing," she said to Wick. "Same grip."

She found the joint. The arm was cold.

"His color is better than it was," she said, which was true and was also something to say while she worked. "He'll be sore for a month. He'll have full movement back in three, maybe four."

She said this because Colm could probably hear her, and because she'd found that telling people the shape of the thing they were coming back to gave them something to come back toward.

She got her hands set.

"Hold."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge paused.

It was a brief pause, the kind that someone watching closely would catch and someone watching the tent flap or the watermarks on the canvas would not. She kept her hands where they were, the joint seated in her grip, the arm cold against her palms.

"Wrong patient for that question," she said. "Colm keeps both his arms. Colm goes home."

She said it flatly, not as comfort but as information, the way she'd say the arm was cold or the color was better. It happened to be true and it happened to be the kind of true that was useful to say out loud.

"If I were being kind," she added, "you'd know. I'd send you out of the tent first."

She'd done that twice in the last four years. Both times she'd known within thirty seconds of the man coming in, and both times she'd told whoever was helping her to go get water or find more lamp oil or some other thing that didn't exist, and both times they'd understood and gone anyway and been grateful for it later. It was the one mercy she'd kept.

She reset her weight.

"Right now I need you holding," she said, "not talking."

She didn't say it harshly. It was just the shape of the moment — there was a thing that needed doing and talking was not it and Wick had asked a reasonable question and the answer was finished and now they were past it.

"Hold," she said.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, pressing my weight down again. My palms are sweating where they meet Colm's shirt. The second shoulder feels looser, wrong, like holding a bag of wet gravel. I keep my eyes on the water stain that looks like a boot print.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge felt it too — the wrongness Wick was probably reading through his hands, the way the joint moved in directions it shouldn't have been moving. She'd known when she first palpated it. She'd known before that, probably, from the way the man had been holding himself when they'd carried him in, the arm braced against his side like he was trying to keep it from falling off entirely.

She didn't say this.

"Breathe," she said instead, and she was talking to Colm, who had gone rigid again in anticipation of what was coming. "You know what it feels like now. You know it ends."

She worked the arm out slowly. Slower than the left. The left had been about the muscles seizing; the right was about the muscles seizing and something else besides, some damage in the joint itself that had been there before yesterday morning, before the cart from Hessler crossing, maybe before the war. An old injury that had healed badly and then been made worse. She could feel the history of it in her hands.

She was not going to be able to give him back full movement in three months. She was not going to be able to give him back full movement at all, probably.

She filed that away. That was a conversation for when Colm was on the other side of this and could hear it properly, and she would have it with him plainly and without softening it because he deserved to know the shape of the thing he was coming back to. The real shape. But not now.

"Hold," she said.

She put her weight into the rotation, feeling for the angle, adjusting twice before she found it — there, that was it, that was the path the joint would accept — and then she pushed through and felt the pop and held the position with both hands while Colm made a sound that was almost nothing, just air moving, the sound a man made when he'd run out of everything else.

She held the arm in place and counted to fifteen in her head.

"Done," she said.

She didn't move immediately. She stood there with her hands still on him, the right arm cradled across his chest, and looked at the ceiling of the tent for a moment in the way she sometimes did when the work was finished and the next thing hadn't started yet.

"You did fine," she said, and she was talking to Wick.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked back down at the man on the table. She considered the question for a moment — not whether to answer it, but how to answer it usefully.

"You're seeing a glenohumeral dislocation," she said. "Both sides. The ball of the joint gets forced out of the socket — here." She touched the point of Colm's right shoulder without pressing, just indicating. "The muscles lock around it because the body thinks it's protecting itself. It isn't. It's making it harder to fix and it's cutting off blood to the arm, which is why the arm was cold."

She began checking his fingers, pressing each one briefly, watching the color return.

"The pop you felt was the ball seating back into the socket. That's correct. That's what it's supposed to feel like." She paused. "Most people who haven't heard it before think something's broken. Nothing's broken."

She moved to the right side again and did the same check — fingers, color, the pulse at the wrist.

"The right shoulder has old damage. Probably took a bad fall sometime before this. Healed without anyone setting it properly." She kept her voice even. "He'll have movement back, but not all of it. I'll tell him that when he can sit up."

She set Colm's arm down carefully along his side.

"What you were feeling through your hands," she said, "was the instability. The joint moving in the wrong planes. That's what a badly healed injury feels like from the outside." She glanced at Wick. "It's useful to know. You'll feel it again."

She said it as a simple fact — that Wick would be in this tent again, or one like it, with his hands on someone and needing to understand what his hands were telling him.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't know I was holding. "Right." I look at Colm's face, slack and pale. "So what now for him?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge pulled a blanket from the crate at the foot of the table and laid it over Colm with the same economy she'd used for everything else. Not tucked in. Just covered.

"Now he sleeps," she said. "Or he doesn't, but he lies still either way. I'll strap the right arm to his chest before he comes all the way back — if he rolls onto it in the night he'll undo the work." She was already cutting a length of cloth as she said it, measuring by eye. "Someone checks on him every two hours. Looks at his fingers. If they go white or blue, you come get me."

She began folding the cloth into a sling, her hands moving without her looking at them.

"He'll be thirsty when he wakes up. That's normal. Give him water, not much at once." She glanced at the small table where she'd laid her instruments. "He'll want to know if he can go back. Don't answer that. That's my conversation."

She lifted Colm's right arm carefully, slid the sling under it, began tying off the knot against his chest. He stirred slightly and didn't wake.

"The pain will be worse tomorrow than it is tonight," she said. "Tonight everything's still shocked. Tomorrow the nerves remember what happened and they'll make sure he knows about it." She pulled the knot snug. "That's also normal. Tell him that too, if he asks."

She stepped back and looked at Colm for a moment — the full length of him, the way she looked at finished work.

"He was lucky it was both," she said. "Sounds wrong, but it's true. If it had been one shoulder he'd have tried to use the other one and made it worse before anyone found him." She picked up the cloth scraps and dropped them in the bin. "Hessler crossing is bad country to lie in alone."

She moved to wash her hands, pouring from the jug into the basin.

"You did fine," she said again, which was the second time she'd said it and the last time she would.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge stopped washing her hands. Not a long stop — she finished rinsing, dried them on the cloth hung at the basin's edge, set the cloth down. Then she turned and looked at Wick with the particular attention she gave to people who had asked her something real.

"Which part of in there," she said. "There's more than one answer."

She didn't wait for him to specify.

"Shrapnel is irregular," she said. "That's the first thing. A bullet is a simple problem — it goes in, it goes through, it stops somewhere, you find it. Shrapnel is a hundred different shapes traveling at a hundred different angles. Some of it is big enough to see. Some of it is fragments the size of a thumbnail paring and it goes where it wants."

She moved back to the table, not to do anything, just to stand somewhere while she talked.

"When it hits the joint — shoulder, knee, hip, doesn't matter — it does two things. It damages what it touches directly, which is obvious. Bone, cartilage, the tendons. But it also carries in everything that was on it when it left. Metal. Cloth. Whatever was between the source and the man." She paused. "That's what kills them, mostly. Not the fragment. What the fragment brings with it."

She looked at Colm, then back at Wick.

"The joint swells because the body is trying to wall it off. The fluid goes septic if you don't get in there. Getting in there means opening it, which means more damage, which means you are making a controlled version of the injury in order to address the uncontrolled version." She said this plainly. "It looks like the wrong thing to do. It is the right thing to do."

She pulled the lamp slightly closer to the table's edge, adjusting the angle out of habit.

"If you don't get all the fragment out, the body rejects what's left. Slowly or quickly depending. Slowly is worse." She picked up one of the instruments she hadn't used tonight, a probe, turned it in her fingers once and set it back down. "The joint stiffens. The infection tracks. You lose the limb trying to save the joint, or you lose the man trying to save the limb."

She looked at Wick steadily.

"That's what shrapnel does in there," she said. "You wanted it straight."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow, and it’s loud in the quiet tent. “Straight enough.” I look at my own hands, still resting on Colm’s blanket. “Thank you.”

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at Wick's hands on the blanket for a moment. Then she looked at his face.

"Don't thank me yet," she said. "You're going to come back."

She said it the way she'd said everything else tonight — not as a threat and not as a comfort, just as a thing that was going to happen. She'd been watching him through the whole of it. The way he'd found something on the wall to look at and looked at it. The way he'd held when she'd told him to hold. The way he'd asked questions instead of going quiet or going pale and needing to sit down, which happened more than people expected and less than people feared.

"Most people, first time in here, they go one of two ways." She began straightening the instruments, laying them back in their order. "They decide they can't do it again. Or they decide they need to understand it." She set the probe down parallel to the rest. "You asked me what shrapnel does. That's the second kind."

She wasn't telling him this was good. She wasn't telling him it was bad. It was just the observation, the way the arm being cold was an observation.

"I'm short two people," she said. "Have been for six weeks." She picked up the lamp and moved it back to its place. "I'm not asking you tonight. Tonight you go sleep and you eat something if there's anything to eat and you check on Colm at the two-hour mark." She paused at the tent flap. "But I'm telling you so you know the question is coming."

She held the flap open, which was the end of the conversation.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't break rhythm.

"Infection's in the bursa," she said. "That's the sac that sits over the joint — it cushions it, keeps the moving parts from grinding. His has filled up with fluid that's gone bad. I'm draining it." She had the needle in and she was talking to her own hands as much as to Wick. "This is going to feel worse than the reduction did. The reduction was mechanical. This is pressure, and the nerve endings in an infected joint are already raw."

Colm was trying to come up off the table. Wick was doing the job.

"Good," she said. "Keep him flat."

She watched the draw. The color was wrong — too dark, too thick — and she noted it and kept going.

"The fluid should be clear or pale yellow," she said. "His isn't. That tells me the infection has been sitting for at least three days, probably more. He didn't say anything because men don't say anything until they can't not say anything." She adjusted the angle slightly. "I'm not angry about it. It's just what they do."

Colm screamed again, a real one this time, and she felt him try to arch and heard Wick taking the weight of it.

"Almost through the worst of it," she said, and this was for Colm, not Wick. "The pressure is going to drop in a moment and it's going to feel better. Not good. Better."

She watched the draw. Watched it. There.

"There," she said.

She kept her voice level and she kept talking because Wick had told her to keep talking and because it was the right call — people held better when there was a voice in the tent that was not screaming.

"I'm going to flush the joint once the drain is clear. That means I put something in before I take it out, which is going to hurt more than the drain did, and I need you to understand that before it happens so you don't let go when it does." She looked up at Wick briefly, then back to her work. "It takes about forty seconds. I'll count if it helps."

She pulled the first draw, set it aside.

"He's going to be here four days minimum," she said. "Maybe six. I'll know more tomorrow. The shoulder work we did — that's secondary now, that's the problem we knew about. This is the problem that was going to kill him." She reached for the flush. "He still goes home. That part doesn't change."

She got her grip.

"Forty seconds," she said. "Starting now. Hold him down, hold him steady, and keep your eyes on me if the wall isn't working anymore."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod once, my knuckles white where I'm holding him. "Count," I grit out, keeping my eyes locked on her hands as they move. The wall wasn't working anyway.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge counted.

"One. Two."

She kept her voice even and she kept her hands moving and she did not look up from the joint because the joint was the thing that needed watching.

"Three. Four. Five."

Colm was making a sound that wasn't screaming anymore, something lower than that, something that came from further down in him. She'd heard that sound before. It meant he was still in there, which was what mattered.

"Six. Seven. Eight."

The flush was going in correctly. She could feel the resistance, the joint pushing back against the intrusion, and she held the angle and kept the pressure steady because steady was the only thing that worked here. Too fast and you did more damage. Too slow and the man on the table lost his mind before you were finished.

"Nine. Ten. Eleven."

"He's doing it right," she said, which was not part of the count but was true. "His body is doing exactly what it should. Fighting it. That's not a problem, that's just what bodies do when something's wrong." She didn't say it to comfort Wick. She said it because it was information. "Twelve. Thirteen."

She watched the joint.

"Fourteen. Fifteen. Sixteen."

Halfway.

"The screaming is good," she said. "Means he's not in shock. Shock is quiet. Shock is when I start worrying." She adjusted her grip by a fraction. "Seventeen. Eighteen. Nineteen."

Colm surged and she felt it through her hands and she heard Wick taking it.

"Twenty. Twenty-one. I've got him, keep him flat. Twenty-two. Twenty-three."

She was watching the flush, watching the return, watching the color of what came back out because that was the information she needed and the count was just the shape she was giving the time so that Wick had something to hold onto that wasn't the screaming.

"Twenty-four. Twenty-five. Twenty-six."

"You're doing fine," she said, and this time she meant Wick and Colm both, the two of them together, the whole struggling thing they'd become in the last twenty seconds.

"Twenty-seven. Twenty-eight. Twenty-nine. Thirty."

The return was lighter. Still wrong, but lighter.

"Thirty-one. Thirty-two."

She kept her voice exactly where it had been at one. Not softer. Not harder. The same.

"Thirty-three. Thirty-four. Thirty-five."

Almost.

"Thirty-six. Thirty-seven. Thirty-eight."

She watched the last of it.

"Thirty-nine."

She took a breath.

"Forty."

She withdrew. Clean, controlled, the way she'd gone in.

"Done," she said.

She held the joint steady for a moment afterward, both hands, the same way she'd held the shoulders. Giving it time to understand what had happened to it.

Colm had gone slack again. The tent was very quiet.

"That's the worst of it," she said. "For tonight." She reached for the dressing without looking, her hand finding it by position. "I'll need to do it again in the morning, but the first time is the worst time. The joint's been holding that pressure for days." She began to dress the site, her hands moving steadily. "Tomorrow it'll be easier. For both of you."

She glanced up at Wick then, a real look, quick and assessing.

"You're still here," she said.

It wasn't surprise, exactly. It was something she was noting.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge finished the dressing. She tied it off, checked the tension with two fingers, found it acceptable. Then she set down the last of the cloth and looked at Wick on the floor.

She didn't tell him to get up. She pulled over the low stool from the instrument table and sat down on it, which put her closer to his level, and she looked at him the way she'd looked at the joint — directly, without softening the angle.

"You're going to feel it in your hands for a few days," she said. "What you were holding. The memory of it. That's normal. It doesn't mean something's wrong with you."

She rested her forearms on her knees.

"The first time I did a drain like that, I was twenty-six and it was a knee and the man was thirty-two years old and his name was Auster and he had three children whose names I also know because he told them to me in order while I was working, the way men do when they need something to say." She said this plainly. "Afterward I sat on the ground outside the tent for about twenty minutes and then I went back in and checked on him and then I went and was sick behind the supply wagon where nobody could see me."

She wasn't telling him this to make him feel better. She was telling him because it was true and because the truth was what she had.

"The second time was a shoulder. Septic, like Colm's, but further gone. That man I lost." She looked at her hands for a moment, then back at Wick. "I sat down for ten minutes after that one. The third time I sat down for five. After a while you stop sitting down, not because it stops meaning something but because the thing that needs doing is always right there and the floor doesn't help you do it."

Colm's breathing was evening out behind her. She didn't turn to check. She could hear what she needed to hear.

"What you're feeling right now," she said, "is the correct response to what you just did. If you felt nothing I'd send you away and not ask you back. The people who feel nothing either started that way, which makes them dangerous, or they got there by a road I've watched a few people take and it doesn't end anywhere good." She paused. "You're not on that road. You sat down on the floor. That's the right thing to do with it."

She looked at him steadily.

"It's going to be like this," she said. "I'm not going to tell you it gets easier because easier is the wrong word. What happens is you get more room for it. You build — I don't know what to call it. Not distance. More like you build a larger place to put it so it doesn't take up all the space there is." She turned one hand over, looked at the palm, set it back down. "Some nights it takes up all the space anyway. That happens less. It doesn't stop happening."

The lamp guttered slightly. She didn't move to adjust it.

"You held through the count," she said. "You held through the screaming and you held through the part where he surged and you didn't let go and you didn't look away. That's what he needed and you gave it to him." She said it the way she'd said the arm was cold, the color was better, the joint had seated correctly. "That's worth something. I want you to know it's worth something before you decide what to do with the rest of it."

She sat with him on the floor level and didn't move, and the tent was quiet except for Colm's breathing, and she waited to see what Wick was going to do with the rest of it.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, still looking at my hands. They're shaking. "Alright," I say, and it comes out rough. "When's my next shift."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at the shaking hands. She looked at them the same way she'd looked at everything else tonight — directly, without commenting on them.

"Six hours," she said. "You check on Colm at the two-hour mark, which I told you before, and then you sleep, and then you come back." She stood up from the stool, which was the end of the sitting. "Six hours is not enough sleep. It's what there is."

She moved to the instrument table and began the work of cleaning, the same order she always used, because order was how things stayed clean and clean was how people stayed alive.

"There's a bedroll in the supply corner," she said, not looking at him. "Behind the crates on the left. It's not mine to give but the man it belongs to has been dead for three weeks and he's past caring about it." She picked up the probe, wiped it down, set it in its place. "Use it tonight. Your tent is too far if I need you back here quickly."

She worked in silence for a moment.

"Eat something first," she said. "I mean it. Not because you're hungry — you're not, I know that — but because in six hours I'm going to need your hands steady and hands don't get steady on nothing." She picked up the next instrument. "There's hardtack in the box by the tent flap. It's bad. Eat it anyway."

She didn't tell him he'd done well again. She'd said it twice and twice was enough and anything more would have been softening it, and she didn't soften things.

"Wick," she said.

She waited until she was sure he was listening.

"You said *keep going and keep talking*." She set down the instrument she was holding and looked at him. "That was the right call. I want you to know that too."

Then she picked the instrument back up and kept cleaning, and that was all.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I push myself up off the floor, my legs feeling like someone else’s. “Alright,” I say, and head for the hardtack box. The cracker’s like eating a rock, but I force it down. I find the bedroll behind the crates and pull it out. It smells like dust and old sweat, but I don’t care. I lie down and stare up at the tent ceiling, listening to Colm breathe.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge worked through the cleaning without looking over at the bedroll. She knew where Wick was by the sound of him — the movement of the crates, the settling of the canvas, the particular quality of silence that meant someone was lying down and not yet sleeping.

Colm breathed.

She finished the instruments and started on the table, wiping it down in long strokes the way her first teacher had shown her, which was the only thing her first teacher had shown her that had turned out to be worth keeping. Everything else she'd learned by doing it wrong first and then doing it correctly and then doing it correctly enough times that it stopped feeling like anything.

She wrung out the cloth over the basin.

The lamp was still bad. She'd been meaning to trim the wick for two hours and she did it now, the small careful work of it, and the light steadied and improved and she stood for a moment in the better light looking at nothing in particular.

Colm's color was acceptable. His breathing was even. She checked his fingers — the right hand, then the left — and found them warm and pink and correct, and she tucked the right arm back against his chest where the sling held it and noted that he'd need water when he woke and that she'd be the one here when he woke because she was always the one here.

She sat down on the stool.

Not to rest. She didn't rest, particularly. She sat down because there was a brief window in which nothing was actively required of her and she had learned a long time ago to use those windows to be still, because still was not the same as rest but it was something, and something was what there was.

She looked at the tent ceiling.

After a while she said, quietly enough not to wake Wick if he'd managed to sleep, "Two hours, Colm," as though the unconscious man needed the reminder.

Then she was quiet again, and the lamp burned steadily, and she waited.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I don’t sleep. I lie there listening to her waiting, counting Colm’s breaths in the dark. When two hours come, I get up without being told. My hands aren’t shaking anymore. “I’ll check him,” I say, my voice low.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't acknowledge the lie. She'd heard enough of them.

"Left first," she said, and took his arm in both hands—left hand at the elbow, right lower, just above the wrist. The shoulder was out and it was out bad, the arm hanging wrong at the joint, the muscle around it bunched and rigid with how long he'd been tensing against it. She could feel the head of the humerus sitting where it shouldn't be, pressed against the deltoid like something trying to claw its way out from under the skin.

"I'm going to rotate outward and then pull steady," she said. "Steady. Not hard. Hard tears things and then we've got a different problem."

The man on the table made a sound—not a shout, not anymore. Something more like a dog makes when it's been kicked and doesn't have the energy to be afraid anymore.

"Hold," Sedge said.

She rotated. She pulled.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I brace against his body, muscles shaking with the effort.* "Christ, he's strong." The sound of the joint sliding back into place makes my stomach turn.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Strong doesn't matter," Sedge said. "Weight matters. You're heavier than he is right now because he's got nothing left."

She felt the joint seat home—the specific *give* of it, the humerus sliding back into the glenoid cavity where it belonged. The man's whole body spasmed once and then went loose, which was what she expected. The shock of relief could do that, drop a man into something like sleep for a few seconds.

She didn't wait.

"Right side," she said, moving around the table. His right arm was worse—or had been out longer, which amounted to the same thing. The swelling was pronounced, the skin over the joint mottled dark where blood had pooled. She put her hands on him the same way, finding the landmarks.

"This one's going to fight back," she said. "The capsule's tighter on this side. Might need two pulls."

She looked at Wick. The assistant's face was the color of wet paper, jaw set too hard.

"Breathe," Sedge said. Not kindly. Just instruction. "You pass out and I've got two problems instead of one."

She turned back to the arm. Found the angle she needed.

"Hold," she said again, and rotated.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge's hands were still on the arm, feeling the resistance. The humerus hadn't moved yet—she could feel it sitting stubborn against the edge of the socket, the capsule swollen and tight and refusing to give.

"Shoulders first," she said. "Then we see about the leg."

She adjusted her angle. The man was still loose from the shock of the first reduction, which helped, but not enough. The tissue around this joint had had longer to swell and lock down, and it was fighting her.

She pulled again—steady, the way she'd said—and felt something shift. Not home. Just *toward* home.

"His foot's still pink," she said, working the arm as she spoke. Her voice was even, the same tone whether she was describing the weather or a compound fracture. "That's the thing to look at. Pink foot means blood's getting through. Purple foot means we're having a different conversation."

She could feel the head of the humerus grinding against the rim of the socket. Almost there. The man on the table made a thin, wet sound in the back of his throat.

"The leg's broken in two places," she said. "That's a mess but it's a mess I can set. It's the knee I haven't gotten a good look at yet. Someone dragged him in by the bad leg."

She pulled again. Felt it seat—the same *give*, the same sudden emptiness where resistance had been.

The man didn't go loose this time. He started to shake instead, fine tremors running through him like a fever.

Sedge let go of his arm and pressed her hand flat against his chest. Felt his heart running too fast under her palm.

"Stay with me," she said to him. Then to Wick: "Help me sit him up. Slow. We need him conscious for the leg."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I move my hands to his good shoulder, easing him up. He's trembling so bad it feels like he's vibrating. "Easy, easy," I mutter, more to myself than him. My eyes catch the mottled skin around his knee and I have to look away again. "That looks... not pink."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge got him propped against her shoulder, his head lolling against her collarbone. His breathing was shallow but there—she could feel his ribs expand against her arm. She kept him there and looked at the knee for the first time properly.

It was bad.

The joint was swollen to nearly twice its size, the skin over it tight and shiny with the pressure from underneath. But the color was the thing—mottled purple and white, no pink anywhere, the blood pooled and stagnant. Below the knee, his foot was the same. Dead-looking. She pressed her thumbnail into the skin of his shin and watched the indent stay. No spring back. No blood moving to refill what she'd displaced.

"Someone dragged him by the leg," she said again, but this time it meant something different. "Dislocated the knee and then kept pulling. The artery runs behind the joint—popliteal. When the knee goes out backward it can shear the artery against the bone."

She laid him back down, careful. His eyes were half-open but seeing nothing.

"It's not pink," she agreed. "It's not going to be pink."

She picked up his wrist and found his pulse. Counted. Let go.

"The foot's been without blood for—" She checked the swelling again, pressed around the joint, felt the way the tissue was already firming under her fingers. "—too long. Even if I reduce the knee now, even if the artery's only compressed and not torn, the tissue below is already dying. Toxins are building up. We get blood flow back, those toxins hit the rest of his system."

She looked at Wick.

"That's the conversation I mentioned."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge put her hand on the knee—the bad one—and moved it carefully, feeling the way the joint sat wrong. The tibia was displaced backward, she could tell that much even through the swelling. The lower leg was shifted behind the femur instead of sitting under it, and everything that should have run through that space—artery, vein, nerve—had been crushed and stretched and starved.

"You're seeing a knee that's out backward," she said. "Posterior dislocation. The lower leg's gone behind the thigh instead of in front of it. That alone I could fix—pull forward, rotate, same as the shoulders. But the artery that runs behind the knee is either compressed or torn, and it's been that way long enough that everything below isn't getting blood."

She ran her fingers down his shin. The muscle underneath was firm—not the firmness of a tensed limb, but the firmness of tissue that had started to set like cooling wax.

"His calf's hardening. That's rigor—not death rigor, but the muscle is locking up because it's been starved of oxygen. The cells are dying and releasing everything inside them into the surrounding tissue. Potassium. Myoglobin. Toxins." She looked at his face—the half-open eyes, the pallor. "Right now those toxins are trapped in the leg because there's no blood moving to carry them anywhere else. The leg's a reservoir of poison."

She paused. Let her hand rest on his shin.

"If I reduce the knee and the artery's only compressed—not torn—blood flow comes back. Those toxins hit his heart and kidneys all at once. Potassium stops hearts. Myoglobin clogs kidneys. He'd likely die in minutes, and not quietly."

She looked at Wick directly.

"If the artery's torn, reducing the knee changes nothing. The leg dies anyway. Gangrene. Sepsis. He dies in days instead of minutes, and worse."

She picked up a scalpel from the row of tools she'd laid out. Held it loosely at her side.

"The only way to save him is to take the leg before we move the knee. Amputate above the injury. Keep the reservoir contained and cut it away."

The man on the table made a sound—barely conscious, barely words.

"That's what you're seeing," Sedge said.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Fuck." The word slips out before I can stop it. I look from the scalpel to the man's pale face. "Does he even know we're talking about this?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge set the scalpel back down on the cloth. She leaned over the man and put her hand flat against his cheek.

"Hey," she said. Not gentle. Just loud enough to reach him. "Hey. You with me?"

His eyes moved—a little, not much. His lips shaped something that might have been a word or might have been nothing.

She took his hand and squeezed his fingers. "Squeeze back if you hear me."

A pause. Then his fingers pressed against hers—weak, barely there, but deliberate.

"He's in there," Sedge said. "Enough."

She let go of his hand and straightened. "Enough to know, not enough to decide. Shock does that—keeps you conscious but not present. Like being underwater and hearing things from above the surface."

She looked at his leg again. The purple-white of it. The shine of the swollen knee.

"I don't make this decision for him," she said. "That's not my call. My call is telling you what happens either way. But he can't make it right now either, and the longer we wait, the less any decision matters."

She picked up his wrist again. Checked his pulse. Faster than before—his body knew something was wrong even if his mind couldn't hold onto it.

"I can try to bring him around more," she said. "It would take time. And time is the thing his leg is running out of." She released his wrist. "So. You're the one standing here. What do you want me to do?"

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge picked up the scalpel again—not to use it yet, just to have something in her hands. She turned it over, looked at the blade catching the bad light from the bad lamp.

"Shrapnel isn't a bullet," she said. "A bullet, you get a wound track. One path. It goes in, it stops, you find it. Sometimes it tumbles, sometimes it fragments, but it's one piece to start."

She set the scalpel back down.

"Shrapnel is a shell casing, a nail, a chunk of fence post—whatever was near the blast. It doesn't travel clean. It comes in jagged and hot and moving sideways. It hits bone and the bone shatters, and now you've got bone fragments moving through the tissue like more shrapnel. Secondary projectiles. The metal itself tears whatever it touches—muscle, fascia, blood vessels—pulls debris in with it. Cloth, dirt, whatever it passed through before it hit him. All of that's inside the wound now."

She pointed at the swollen knee.

"In a joint, it's worse. There's less room. The capsule around the knee is tight—it doesn't stretch much, doesn't give the shrapnel anywhere to go. So it bounces. Or it lodges in cartilage, in bone, in the back of the joint where you can't see it and can't reach it without opening everything up. And everything you open bleeds, and everything you cut through is tissue he might need if he keeps the leg."

She paused.

"You find the big pieces. You miss the small ones. They migrate—move through tissue over days, weeks. End up somewhere else entirely. Or they sit there and fester. The body walls them off, makes a cyst around the metal, and that works until it doesn't. Until it ruptures and you've got infection somewhere you didn't expect it."

She looked at Wick.

"That's shrapnel. It's not tidy. It's a mess that keeps being a mess."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, the taste of bile at the back of my throat. "So if we take the leg, we save his life. If we try to save the leg, we probably kill him." I stare at the man's slack face. "Do it. Take it off."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge nodded once. No hesitation—hesitation was for before decisions got made, not after.

She moved to the head of the table first. Took the man's face in her hands and leaned close.

"We're taking the leg," she said to him. "You understand? We're taking it. You're going to wake up and it won't be there. I'm sorry."

His eyes moved again. His lips shaped something. She didn't know if it was understanding or protest or just sound. She'd told him. That was what she could do.

She pulled the cloth belt from around her own waist—thick canvas, the kind meant for hauling—and wrapped it high around his thigh, above the swelling, above the knee. She twisted it tight with a stick, watching the flesh below blanch further as she cut off what little blood was still reaching the leg.

"Tourniquet," she said. "That buys me time. Not much. Twenty minutes before the muscle above starts to suffer."

She picked up the scalpel. Laid her other hand on his thigh, fingers finding the place she wanted—above the knee, below the tourniquet, enough room to leave a flap of skin to close over the stump.

"I'm cutting skin first, then fat, then fascia—the sheet around the muscle. Then muscle itself. Then I find the vessels and tie them off before I cut them. Then bone last."

She looked at Wick.

"Hold his shoulders again. He's going to feel this even half-gone. Don't let him roll."

She put the blade to his thigh.

"Hold," she said.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge cut.

"Skin," she said. The scalpel parted it in a long arc around the thigh—she was leaving a flap, skin and fat that would fold down over the stump later. The edges pulled apart as she worked, yellow fat showing beneath, small bleeders welling up despite the tourniquet. "Skin bleeds even with the belt tight. Capillaries. The big vessels are deeper."

She set the scalpel aside and picked up a heavier blade. The man's back arched off the table, a raw sound tearing out of him.

"Fascia," she said, cutting through the thin sheet that wrapped the muscle. "This is the layer that holds everything in its compartment. When it opens, the muscle bulges out—you'll see."

The muscle did bulge, red and wet and gleaming in the lamplight. She was working quickly now, not rushing but not pausing. Twenty minutes. She'd said twenty minutes.

"Muscle next. I'm cutting through quadriceps—the big group in front—and then hamstrings in back. The vessels run between them, deep. I need to get down to them before I cut across."

She carved through the red meat of the thigh. The man had stopped screaming—his voice had given out, or he had, his body still jerking but no sound coming out. Just wet, rasping breaths.

"Vessels," Sedge said. Her fingers found them—the femoral artery first, thick and pulsing even now, the vein beside it. She pulled them free of the surrounding tissue, hooked them with a clamp. "I'm not cutting these until I've tied them. If I cut and they retract up into the thigh, I can't get to them and he bleeds out inside where I can't see."

She worked quickly—thread around the artery, two knots, pull tight. Then the vein. Then the smaller branches she could feel. Each one tied off, each one cut above the knot.

"Four minutes," she said. "That's the vessels. Bone now."

She put down the blade and picked up the saw—short, curved, meant for this. She positioned it against the femur, the bone visible now at the bottom of the wound, white and clean where the muscle had been stripped away.

"Bone's the worst part for them," she said. "Vibration. It travels. He can feel it even when he can't feel anything else."

She began to saw. The man's whole body seized, a sound coming out of him that wasn't a scream—something lower, something that came from his chest.

Sedge kept her pace steady. The bone dust was white on the blade.

"Thirty seconds," she said. "Maybe less. Thigh bone's thick but I'm already through most of it."

The blade caught, stuck for a moment in the marrow. She adjusted the angle, pulled through. The leg separated.

She set it aside—off the table, onto the ground, she didn't look where it landed—and turned back to the stump. Blood was welling despite the ties and she found another bleeder, clamped it, tied it.

"Now I shape the flap," she said, pulling the skin and muscle down over the raw end. "Cut the muscle shorter than the bone, skin longer than the muscle. That way when it heals, the scar isn't right over the end where the weight sits. He'll have padding."

She was sewing now—quick, rough stitches, pulling the flaps together over the protruding bone. The man had gone still, unconscious finally, his breathing shallow but present.

"Tourniquet stays on for now," she said, tying off the last stitch. "I'll loosen it slowly—let blood back in a little at a time so I can catch anything I missed."

She stepped back. Her hands were red to the elbows. The front of her shirt was dark with it.

"Done," she said. "Fifteen minutes. He's alive."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content:
I let go of his shoulders, my arms trembling. The leg is on the ground in a heap. I can't look at it.

"He's alive," I echo, my voice thin. "What do we do now?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge was already moving. She picked up a rag—clean enough, which was as clean as things got here—and wiped her hands, then wiped the stump, clearing the worst of the blood so she could see what she was closing over.

"Now we keep him alive," she said. "That's the part that takes longer than the cutting."

She pulled the tourniquet stick a quarter-turn looser. Watched the stump. No fresh welling. She loosened it another quarter.

"I'm looking for bleeders I missed," she said. "Ties hold on the big vessels. It's the small ones that slip. Arterial bleed—bright red, pulses. Venous bleed—dark, steady. Either one can kill him if I miss it."

She watched another moment. The stump stayed dry—relatively. She loosened the tourniquet the rest of the way and left it sitting loose around his thigh in case she needed it again fast.

"Shock kills more men than the wound does," she said, pulling a blanket from under the table and shaking it out over him, careful around the stump. "He's lost blood. He's cold. His body's trying to clamp down and keep what's left going to his brain and heart, and that's the right idea but it only works so long before things start shutting down."

She found his wrist again. Pulse. Still too fast, but present.

"He needs fluid. Blood, ideally—we don't have blood. Saline—we don't have saline. Water, then, and salt if he can keep it down. Small sips when he wakes. Not before—he'll choke."

She looked around the tent. The lamp guttering. The supplies she'd laid out, most of them bloodied now.

"He needs watching for the next twelve hours," she said. "Breathing, pulse, temperature. If his pulse goes thready—weak and fast and irregular—I'm losing him. If he starts burning hot, that's infection. If the stump starts smelling sweet, that's gangrene, and we didn't save him after all."

She pulled a stool over next to the table and sat down heavily. Her hands were shaking—just a little, just enough that she noticed. She put them flat on her knees.

"That's what we do now," she said. "We watch, and we wait, and we see if he's the kind that lives."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at Wick on the ground. Didn't tell her to get up. There was no point—the work was done and the next part was sitting still, which you could do from the floor as well as anywhere.

"The rest," she said. She kept her voice even. "The rest is this."

She nodded toward the man on the table.

"He's going to wake up in pain. Real pain—the kind that doesn't stop when you stop moving. The stump's going to throb like a second heartbeat and it's going to be worse than the leg ever was, because now his body knows something's missing and it doesn't know how to be missing something. Phantom pain, they call it. He'll feel the leg that isn't there. It'll itch, it'll burn, it'll cramp—and there's nothing to touch, nothing to rub, nothing to make it stop because the thing that hurts doesn't exist anymore."

She watched his breathing. Still shallow. Still there.

"When he wakes, he's going to ask for water. Give it to him—small amounts, slow. His stomach might not hold it. If he vomits, that's normal but it's also a problem. He's already dehydrated from the blood loss. Vomiting makes it worse. If he can't keep water down, we're in trouble faster."

She leaned forward, elbows on her knees.

"Tonight—tonight is when we find out if the ties held. Internal bleeding kills quiet. He'll go pale, his pulse will race, his belly might swell if blood is pooling in his thigh where I can't see it. I'll check the stump every half hour—more if he looks wrong. If blood soaks through the dressing, I go back in. Find the bleeder. Tie it off again. He might not survive a second time under the knife."

She held up her hand. Still trembling. She pressed it flat against her thigh again.

"Tomorrow is infection. That's when it starts or it doesn't. The wound is open to the air—we don't have the luxury of clean rooms and sterile fields. I did what I could. It's not enough. It's never enough. The first sign is heat—redness spreading from the edges of the wound, skin hot to the touch. Then pus. Then smell. I've seen wounds go bad in six hours. I've seen them stay clean for three days and then kill a man on the fourth. There's no predicting it."

She looked at the lamplight. The oil was getting low.

"If infection sets in, we open the stump back up. Drain it. Clean it out. Pack it with whatever we have that might slow the rot—honey, if there's any. Alcohol, if we can spare it. Sometimes that works. Sometimes the infection is already in the blood and then it doesn't matter what we do to the leg. Sepsis. Fever, chills, confusion. His organs shut down one by one. Kidneys first, then liver, then heart. That takes about two days once it starts, and there's nothing I can do to stop it."

She paused. Let herself breathe.

"If he makes it past the third day, he's got a chance. The ties held, the infection didn't take, his body's figured out how to be a body with one leg. Then it's about the stump healing—skin closing over the muscle, scar tissue forming. That takes weeks. In that time, the bone might push through—spurs, they call it. The cut end of the femur isn't smooth, it's sawn, and as the muscle shrinks back from the wound the bone can end up longer than the flap I left. If that happens, we go back in. Shave the bone down. More cutting, more tying, more risk."

She looked at Wick directly.

"And if he survives all of that—the shock, the bleeding, the infection, the healing—then he wakes up every morning and remembers that he's missing something. He learns to balance again. He learns to walk with a stick, or he doesn't, and someone carries him. He's a man with half his weight and none of his choices, and he lives that way until something else kills him, because the war doesn't care that he already paid."

She sat back.

"That's the rest," she said. "That's what saving him looks like."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content:
I close my eyes and press my forehead to my knees. The canvas floor smells like blood and dirt. "You've done this before."

It's not a question.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Fourteen," Sedge said. "Legs. Arms I've stopped counting—fingers, hands. Fourteen legs."

She looked at her hands. The shaking had stopped. She didn't know when.

"The first one I cried after. Went outside the tent and put my head in my hands and stayed there until someone else came in with a wound and I had to stop. The second one I didn't cry but I didn't sleep that night either. Third one, I slept."

She watched the man on the table. His breathing had evened out a little—not good, but less bad.

"You learn to do it the same way you learn to do anything. You do it until it doesn't feel like the worst thing you've ever done. Then you do it until it feels like nothing. Then you do it because it's what you're here for and there's no one else and the man on the table needs his leg off whether you're ready or not."

She picked up the rag again. Wiped her forearms where the blood had dried and started to crack.

"I don't enjoy it," she said. "I want to be clear about that. Some do—surgeons who like the cutting, who like being the one who decides what gets taken. I'm not that. I take what needs taking because if I don't, he dies, and dying is worse."

She dropped the rag.

"But I don't dream about it anymore either. That's what four years does. You stop dreaming about the things you've cut off. You dream about other things—home, sometimes. Food you used to eat. People you knew before. And then you wake up and there's another one on the table, and you do it again."

She looked at Wick on the floor.

"Fourteen legs. Thirteen men lived long enough to leave my tent. Eight of those were still alive a week later. Three I know for certain survived the war because I saw them after, walking on the sticks or the pegs or carried by their friends. The other five I don't know. They went somewhere else and I never heard and that's how it works—you lose them after. You save a piece and then the rest goes on without you."

She stood up from the stool. Checked the lamp. Low, but it would last a few more hours.

"The fourteenth is on the table right now," she said. "We'll see which one he is."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I open my eyes and look at the man again. He looks smaller without the leg. "Fourteen," I repeat. My voice sounds flat. "You ever think about quitting?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at her hands. There was blood under her nails, in the creases of her knuckles, dried in the lines of her palms like something written there she couldn't read anymore.

"Every time," she said. "Every single time. I think about it when I'm cutting, and I think about it when I'm tying, and I think about it when I'm watching them breathe afterward and waiting to see if they stop."

She sat back down on the stool. The legs scraped against the canvas floor.

"Quitting would be easy. Walk out of the tent, walk past the lines, keep walking until I'm somewhere that isn't here. I've planned it—actual plans, which direction, how much water I'd need, how long until I hit a road that goes somewhere with beds and walls and no one screaming."

She looked at the tent flap. The night outside was quiet—for now.

"And then someone carries another one in," she said. "And they put him on the table, and he's got a leg that's gone gray or a belly that's open or a wound I can close if I'm fast enough. And I'm already here. And there's no one else."

She picked at the dried blood on her wrist. It came off in flakes.

"That's not nobility," she said. "That's just—being the one who's already standing here. Quitting means I walk away and the next one who comes in dies on the table because there's no one to cut. That's the math. It's not complicated. I stay because me leaving kills people. That's all."

She looked at Wick.

"You asked."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I stare at my own hands, clean compared to hers. "I don't know if I could come back in after that first one."
