dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"I'm going to count," Sedge said. "On three. Not before. If you feel him start to go, you lean into it, you don't pull back. Understand?"

She picked up the bone saw. The blade was new that morning; it wasn't new now.

"One."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: My knuckles are white where I'm pressing down. "Understood." My voice is too tight. I keep my eyes fixed on a tear in the canvas.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Two."

She set the saw against the humerus, just below the head, where the bone was already fractured and the soft tissue was already a mess. She'd marked the line with a scratch from the buck knife earlier; the skin was too dark under the lamp to see the ink.

"Three."

She worked. Not fast, because fast meant ragged, and ragged meant a second cut. The sound was the part people always remembered afterward, and she never told them otherwise. It was a sound like nothing else and there was no preparation for it and no point pretending there was.

The man on the table made a sound that wasn't a word and his body went tight all the way down. She felt the shoulder under her left hand try to rise and felt Wick's weight answer it, and that was good. That was what holding meant.

"Stay on him," she said, not looking up. Her voice was flat, the way it got when the work was the only thing in the room. "Talk to him if you want. Doesn't matter what. Just keep him here."

She finished the cut. She set the saw down on the tray without looking and picked up the artery forceps. The bleeders were already starting. They always were.

"Wick." First time she'd used his name. "I need you to look at me now, not at that tear. Tell me what you see."

The stump was open and the lamp was bad and there was a lot of blood and she needed to know, before she went further, what kind of man she had holding the shoulders.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Both," Sedge said. She didn't look up. Her hands were busy with the forceps, finding the spurting ends of vessels that had no business being this large. "He's going to lose the arm, and this is the part where we're being kind. Those aren't different things."

The first bleeder rolled under the clamp and she tied it off with a length of catgut she pulled from her teeth. Her fingers were steady. They'd been steady for four years, which was longer than most people's.

"Stop asking what it means," she said. "Meaning is for after. Right now it's just work." She reached for the next clamp. "Talk to him. Tell him about your girl, tell him the weather, tell him a lie about a farm he doesn't own. I don't care. Just keep his eyes open and his mouth working."

The man on the table had gone quiet in the way men went quiet, which was worse than the shouting. She checked his pulse at the throat with the back of her wrist without breaking her rhythm. Still there. Still fighting, somewhere under the leather strap between his teeth.

"You're doing all right," she said, and it was the first thing she'd said that wasn't an instruction. She didn't look at Wick when she said it. She was watching the stump, watching for the next bleeder, watching the lamp throw shadows that made it hard to tell artery from vein until it opened.

"Next one," she said. "I need his shoulder down. Same as before."

She waited. She had learned, the hard way, not to count on people who weren't ready.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I shift my weight back onto his good shoulder, the canvas slick under my boots. I clear my throat. "Hey. You still with us? My girl writes me about her garden—says the tomatoes are coming in red as a sergeant's face." I don't have a girl. I glance at Sedge, my jaw tight. "Ready."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
She didn't look up from the tray. She was picking through the instruments with the quick, practiced fingers of a woman who had learned to do this in the dark and was now doing it in something worse than the dark.

"Tomatoes," she said. It was flat. "Fine. Keep going."

She didn't say *you don't have a girl*. She didn't need to. She'd been lied to by better men than Wick, and she'd been lied to by worse, and the lie itself didn't matter so long as the mouth kept moving and the eyes stayed on something that wasn't the stump. She'd heard confessions in this tent that would have got men hanged in a town. A garden that didn't exist was nothing.

She set the saw against the second humerus. The bone on this side was in worse shape — shattered higher up, closer to the joint, and the fracture had been grinding for two days in a sling that wasn't a sling. She'd smelled it when she cut the sleeve off. That smell meant the work was already half-done by something that wasn't her.

"Hold him," she said. "Same as before. He's going to know what the saw sounds like now and he's going to fight harder. You lean in."

She didn't count this time. She just worked.

The second cut was uglier than the first. The bone gave wrong halfway through and she adjusted without stopping, because stopping was worse, and the man on the table arched up off the canvas and Wick's weight came down hard and she felt the shoulder answer it under her hand. Good. Good enough.

She finished. She set the saw down.

"Both off," she said, and her voice had the same flatness it had carried through the whole of it. "Stumps next. I need you to talk the whole time. Don't stop. Don't ask him questions, he can't answer with the strap in. Just keep the sound of your voice in the room."

She reached for the catgut again. Her fingers were slick and she wiped them once on the man's ruined shirt and went back in.

"Wick." Still not looking up. "When this is done I'm going to need you to carry him to the corner and I'm going to need you not to think about it until tomorrow. Can you do that?"

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge's hands didn't stop. They couldn't. The next bleeder was already welling up under the flap of muscle she'd folded back and she got the forceps on it before it had a chance to teach her anything new.

"What you're seeing," she said, and her voice was the same flatness it had been all night, "is two open stumps just below the shoulder. The bone is cut clean on the left. Not clean on the right — that one shattered on me halfway through and I had to trim it. There's a little ridge of it you'll see if you look close, where the saw jumped. That's why the right one is going to bleed more. That's why I'm here first."

She tied off the vessel. The catgut pulled wet through her fingers and she snapped it with her thumbnail the way she always did, because her teeth were busy with the next length.

"What you're seeing," she said again, "is muscle. Red, wet, trying to close on itself because that's what muscle does when it's cut. It doesn't know it's supposed to stay open. It's going to keep trying to close all night and all tomorrow and that's fine, that's what we want, that's how a man keeps his blood on the inside."

She reached for another clamp. Her wrist found the man's throat on the way and she checked his pulse without breaking stride. Still there. Thready but there.

"What you're not seeing is the bone marrow, because the bone is back inside the muscle where it belongs. What you're not seeing is the nerves, because I cut them high and they're tucked back out of the way. What you're not seeing is the joint, because I took it off below the head and the head is in the bucket with the rest of him."

She didn't look up. She was watching the right stump, the ugly one, the one that had fought her.

"The blood," she said, "is mostly venous. That's the dark red. When you see a spurt, bright red, that's arterial and that's the one I'm after. You'll know the difference in about two minutes because I'm going to miss one and you're going to see what a real bleeder looks like."

She worked for a moment in silence. The only sounds were the small wet ones of the work and the man's breathing through the leather, and somewhere outside the tent the low murmur of a camp that didn't know what was happening in here.

"There," she said quietly. "Now you know what you're looking at."

She glanced up at him for the first time since she'd told him to hold. It was a quick look, the kind she gave instruments to make sure they were where she'd left them, but it stayed on him a beat longer than that.

"Good," she said. "Now keep talking. He's still in there and I can feel him listening."

She went back to the stump. Her fingers found the next vessel and the forceps followed.

"Tomatoes," she said, almost to herself. "That's a new one. I had a man once tell a dying corporal about his chickens for forty minutes. Detailed. Names, egg counts, the whole business. Corporal lived. The chickens, I don't know."

She tied off the bleeder. Snapped the gut.

"Talk," she said. "Tell him about the farm he doesn't have."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "My mother had a farm," I say, the words coming out low and rough. "Back home. She'd spend all morning pulling weeds, said it was the only quiet she got." I press my weight down as the man twitches. "She grew roses. Not tomatoes."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Roses," Sedge said. She didn't look up. Her hands were deep in the right stump, fishing for a bleeder that had tucked itself up under the clavicle and was being coy about it. "That's better. That's a real thing. He'll hear the difference even if he doesn't know he does."

She found it. The forceps went in past her knuckles and she felt the vessel roll under the curve of the blade and clamped down. The man on the table jerked once and Wick's weight answered it and that was still good, that was still what she needed.

"Keep going," she said. "The weeds. What kind."

She tied off the bleeder. Snapped the gut. Reached for the next clamp without thinking about it, because thinking about it was how you lost time you didn't have.

"Your mother," she said, and her voice was the same flatness it had been all night but there was something under it now, something that had decided to stay, "did she teach you to pull them or did you learn after."

The lamp flickered. She didn't look at it. The lamp always flickered. The lamp had been flickering since before this war started and it would flicker after, and the work didn't care.

She worked in silence for a moment. The next bleeder was a small one and she got it with a single motion, the kind of motion that took four years to make look like nothing. Then another. Then a third that wasn't really a bleeder at all, just a slow ooze from a muscle bed, and she packed it with a square of gauze and moved on.

"Left side's clean," she said. "Right side's got two more I can feel and one I can't, and the one I can't is the one that's going to try to kill him at three in the morning when nobody's watching. So I'm going to find it now."

She went back in. Her wrist found the throat again. Pulse still there, thready but there, the heartbeat of a man whose body was still arguing with his situation.

"Talk," she said. "The roses. What color."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"It does four things," Sedge said. Her hands were deep in the right stump again, working by feel because the lamp had decided to make the shadows worse. "I'll tell you what they are while I find this last bleeder, because I've got a hand free and you asked."

She didn't look up.

"One. It punches a hole in. That's the entry wound, and the entry wound is the lie, because the entry wound is small and clean and looks like something a man could be sewn up from. It's the size of a thumbprint on a good day. Sometimes smaller. You see the entry wound and you think *this isn't so bad*, and that's the last hopeful thought you have about it, because—"

She found something under the clavicle. Not the bleeder. A fragment of cloth, wadded tight, black with old blood. She pulled it out with the forceps and dropped it on the tray without looking.

"—two. It tumbles. Whatever came out of that shell, it wasn't moving straight by the time it got to him. It hit something on the way in — a buckle, a bone, the strap of his own pack — and it changed direction, and now it's traveling through him like a drunk through a doorway, and it's taking pieces of him with it. Muscle. Bone splinters. Bits of the uniform he was wearing. All of that is now distributed along a track through his shoulder that doesn't go in a straight line."

She wiped her fingers once on the ruined shirt. Went back in.

"Three. It leaves pieces behind. That's the part that's going to kill him if anything does, and it's not the part people think. People think it's the bleeding. The bleeding is what I can fix. The pieces are what I can't get to without killing him to do it. There's metal in there I can't see and won't come out without taking more of him than I'm willing to take. There's cloth. There's bone fragments from the original fracture that are too deep to fish and too small to leave where they are. They're sitting in there right now, under the muscle I'm packing, and his body is going to spend the next six weeks trying to decide whether to fight them or fold around them, and I won't know which way it goes until it goes."

She paused. Not to think. To feel. Her fingertips were reading the underside of the muscle bed the way a blind woman reads a page, looking for the vessel that was hiding.

"Four. It kills the thing it touches on the way through. Not cuts. Kills. A vessel that gets nicked but not severed seals itself off, mostly. A vessel that gets *killed* — that gets pulped, that gets the inside of it crushed sideways so the wall doesn't know what shape it's supposed to be — that vessel doesn't seal. It just leaks. Slowly. Into the space around it. And that's the one I can't see, because it's not bleeding out, it's bleeding *in*, and I won't know it's there until his pulse starts to climb and his skin starts to go the wrong color and I open him back up at three in the morning to find out I've been wrong about him all night."

She found it.

"Here," she said quietly. "There you are."

The forceps went in past the second knuckle. She felt the vessel — small, deep, tucked behind a shelf of muscle that had tried to close over it the way she'd told Wick muscle would. The wall was pulpy under the blade. She knew before she clamped it that it was going to hold, and it held.

She tied it off. Snapped the gut. Sat back on her heels for the first time in longer than she could remember, and looked at the stumps.

"That's what shrapnel does," she said. "It lies to you on the way in, it wanders, it leaves souvenirs, and it kills things quietly. Four things. Every time."

She reached for the saline.

"His shoulders," she said. "Both of them. Whatever came out of that shell hit him from the front and tumbled back through both joints at once, which is the kind of wound you only see when a man is standing in the wrong place at the wrong time and God is taking notes. The bones were broken before I touched them. The joints were full of fragments before I touched them. The muscle was torn before I touched him. I just finished what the war started."

She began to irrigate. The fluid ran pink, then clearer, then pink again as it stirred up what was left in the bed.

"Now you know," she said. "And it's still just work."

She glanced up at him. Quick, the way she had before. Then back to the stump.

"Tell me about the roses," she said. "I'm almost done and he's still in there and I can feel him listening."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Red," I say, my voice sticking. "She said red was the only color worth the trouble." The man's breathing's changed—shallow, but steady. I lean into it. "They'd get black spot every damn year. She'd curse and cut them back to nothing."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Black spot," Sedge said. "That's the one that gets them every time. You can cut and spray and pray and it comes back the next wet season like it owns the place."

She was irrigating the left stump now, the clean one, running saline through the muscle bed until it ran clear. The right one she went over twice more because twice was what the ugly ones got, and she'd learned not to trust them on the first pass.

"Your mother was right about the red, too," she said. "Reds are the ones that black spot takes first. The yellows and the whites can hold out a season longer, sometimes two. The reds just fold."

She set the saline bottle down. Reached for the gauze packing.

"Both stumps are clean as I'm going to get them," she said. "I'm not closing him. Not tonight. There's too much I can't see in there and his body needs a way to drain if it decides to make more of what I left behind. So I'm packing them loose and wrapping them and we're going to let the muscle do what muscle does, which is close on itself around whatever it's got, and in six weeks I'll know if I was right or if I was wrong."

She packed the left stump first. Long strips of gauze, worked into the bed with the tips of her fingers, packed firm but not tight. The right one she packed the same way, taking longer, because the muscle bed was ragged and she wanted the gauze to find every pocket where fluid could pool and sit and decide to rot.

"Talk," she said, not because he needed reminding but because the silence had started to creep in and she could feel the man on the table beginning to surface. "The black spot. Did she burn the cuttings or did she leave them."

She reached for the bandage roll. Her fingers found it without looking, the way they found everything in this tent now, by feel and by memory and by the four years of muscle that had learned this room in the dark.

His pulse was still there at the throat. Thready, but there. The strap between his teeth had gone slack and his jaw was working and she knew what that meant — he was coming back, and coming back was going to be worse than going under, because coming back meant he was going to feel what was missing and what was left.

"Wick." She didn't look up. She was wrapping the left stump, figure-eight passes around the chest to hold the packing in place. "When I tell you, you're going to take the strap out of his mouth. Slowly. He's going to want to bite down on whatever's nearest and if that's your finger you're going to lose the finger and I'm not sewing you back together tonight. Give him the rolled gauze instead. Four thicknesses. Let him have it."

She tied off the bandage on the left side. Moved to the right. Began the same passes.

"Keep talking," she said. "The roses. The black spot. Whatever she did with the cuttings. He's almost back and I need him to land somewhere soft."

The lamp flickered. She didn't look at it.

"Almost done," she said, and it was the first time she'd said it twice.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
She didn't break stride. The scream was a sound she could work around — louder than the silence, worse for the ears, but better for the patient, because a man who was screaming was a man whose lungs still had air in them and whose brain was still telling his body there was something worth complaining about.

"Right stump," she said. Her hands kept moving, the bandage rolling under her fingers in the same figure-eight passes she'd done on the left. "Same wrap as the other side. The bandage is clean. It came out of the crate this morning. It's not sterile — nothing out here is sterile — but it's clean and it's dry and that's the best I can give him."

She tucked the end of the roll under the last pass and tore it with her teeth, the way she always tore it, because her hands were busy and her teeth were the only tool she had left.

"The packing underneath is going to feel strange to him when he comes all the way back. It's going to feel like pressure. Like something sitting in the wound that doesn't belong there. That's because something is sitting in the wound that doesn't belong there. That's the gauze. It's supposed to be there. Don't let him claw at it. If he gets his hands free he'll go for the dressing first because the dressing is the thing he can feel, and he'll tear it off and then I'll have to do all of this again and he won't survive me doing it twice."

She reached across the table without looking and found the rolled gauze she'd told Wick to have ready. She held it out in his direction without looking at him.

"Four thicknesses," she said. "When I tell you to take the strap out, you roll this between his molars on the left side. He bites down on instinct. Let him. It's better than biting down on you."

The scream was tapering. Not because the pain was less — because the lungs were emptying. She'd seen it a hundred times. A man could scream for about forty seconds on a full breath and then the breath ran out and the body had to choose between breathing and making noise, and the body always chose breathing, because breathing was older.

"He's going to pass out again in about ten seconds," she said. "Or he's going to go quiet and start shaking. Either way, you keep your weight on him. Don't lift off because it seems like it's over. It's not over. The shaking is worse than the bucking because the shaking goes on longer and you'll start to think you're hurting him, and you are, and you have to anyway."

She tied off the right bandage. Sat back on her heels for the second time that night and looked at the man on the table. He was going grey under the bad lamp. His lips had that blue edge she didn't like. But his pulse was still under her wrist when she found it again, and his chest was still moving, and that was the only ledger she kept.

"Both wrapped," she said. "Packing's in. Bandages are holding. He'll need changing tomorrow and the day after and the day after that until the beds start to close or until I decide they won't, whichever comes first. He won't die tonight. I don't think he's going to die tomorrow either. After that I won't promise you anything because after that it's his body and the war and the pieces I left in him that I couldn't get out."

She wiped her hands on the ruined shirt one last time. The shirt was more blood than cloth by now. She reached for the clean water basin and washed the catgut off her fingers and the blood out from under her nails, and she did it slowly, because slow was the first thing she let herself do since she'd picked up the saw.

"Now," she said, and she looked at Wick, and this time the look stayed. "When I nod, you take the strap. You take it slow. You give him the gauze. You don't say anything yet. You let him find out what happened to him on his own, because there's nothing you can say that will make it smaller, and trying will just give him something to be angry at later when he needs to be angry at the right thing."

She rested her hands on her knees. They were still steady. They'd be steady all night if she needed them to be.

"The right thing to be angry at," she said, "is the war. Not you. Not me. Not the roses. The war."

She waited. The man on the table had gone quiet and his body had started the long slow shake she'd told Wick was coming, and the lamp threw their shadows around the tent in shapes that didn't look like anything.

She nodded.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my fingers under the strap, pulling it gently from between his teeth. My other hand is ready with the gauze roll, pressing it into the space as he gasps. His eyes are wide and wild, staring at the canvas ceiling. I keep my weight on him. "Easy," I mutter, though I know it's not.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't move. Her hands stayed on her knees, still wet, and she watched the man's face the way she watched everything in this tent — for what it was telling her, not what she wanted it to tell her.

The gasping went on for longer than she liked. It was the kind of breathing that came from a body that had forgotten how to do it on purpose and was trying to remember, each breath a small negotiation between the lungs and the throat and whatever was left of the man's will.

"He's in shock," she said. Not to Wick. To the room. To the part of her that kept the ledger. "Not deep yet. The shaking is the giveaway. When the shaking stops and he goes still, that's when I worry."

She watched his eyes. They were moving but they weren't tracking. They were sliding across the canvas ceiling like a man reading something written in a language he didn't have, and she knew that look, and she knew it didn't last.

"Don't let him see his shoulders," she said, quieter now. "If he tries to lift his head, you put your hand on his forehead and you push it back down. Gentle. You don't have to be rough about it. He's not going to fight you hard right now because he doesn't have the strength yet. He will in about two minutes and that's when you need to be ready."

She reached for the canteen on the tray without looking. Her fingers found it, uncapped it, set it beside her on the canvas where she could reach it.

"When he starts to come all the way back," she said, "he's going to ask you what happened. Or he's going to ask me. Or he's not going to ask anything and he's going to try to roll onto his side because that's what a man does when he doesn't understand where he is. You keep him on his back. You keep his head back. You don't answer the question if he asks it. You tell him his name is — "

She stopped. She looked at the man on the table. She looked at him for a long moment, the way she looked at stumps before she closed them, reading what was there.

"I don't know his name," she said. "Nobody told me his name. They brought him in and said *both shoulders* and I started working. Call him what you want. Call him Tom. Call him what your mother's roses were called. Give him something to land on."

The shaking was slowing. She watched it slow the way she watched a bleed — for the moment it crossed from one thing into another.

"There," she said softly. "There it is."

The man's body was going still under Wick's hands. His breathing was evening out into something that sounded almost like sleep but wasn't. His eyes had stopped sliding and had fixed on a point on the ceiling that didn't exist.

"He's going under," she said. "That's the body's second answer. The first was the shaking. The second is this. Don't let it fool you. He's not asleep. He's just somewhere the pain can't get to for a little while, and when he comes back from there he's going to be worse than he was before he went, because this time he'll know what he's coming back to."

She picked up the canteen. Wet a square of clean gauze with it. Reached across and laid it across the man's lips, not in them, just across, the way she always did, because a mouth that had been open behind a leather strap for an hour was a mouth that had cracked in three places and would crack in more if she let it.

"His name," she said again, to Wick, and this time her voice had something in it that might have been, on another woman, in another tent, in another war, a kind of apology. "Tell him his name is whatever you want him to be. Just make it real when you say it."

She sat back. Her hands found her knees again.

"You did all right," she said. "Now carry him to the corner. Set him on the cot with his head on the folded blanket. Don't put him on his side. Don't take the bandages off. Don't look at what's under them."

She paused.

"And don't look at the bucket," she said. "Not tonight."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't answer right away. She was doing what she always did after — putting the room back in order so the next man who came in wouldn't have to do it, and so she wouldn't have to think about anything but her hands.

She stripped the canvas off the table and folded it once and dropped it in the slop bucket with the saw and the clamps and the lengths of catgut that hadn't been used. She wiped the table down with the rag from the basin until the wood was clean enough to lay a clean canvas on for whoever came in next. She laid the canvas. She tucked the edges under. She did it the way she always did it, the same motions in the same order, and she didn't hurry because hurrying was how you forgot a step and a forgotten step was how a man died of infection three days later because somebody left a soiled dressing under the fresh one.

The man in the corner was breathing. She could hear him from the table. That was enough for now.

She picked up the bucket with the arms in it and carried it to the back of the tent and set it down by the flap she'd have to take it through later. She didn't look in it. She'd told Wick not to, and she didn't, and that was the rule she kept for herself too.

Then she sat down on the other side of the tent from him, across the table, with her back against the canvas pole and her legs out in front of her and her hands in her lap. They were still wet. She wiped them on her trousers, slow, the way she'd washed them in the basin — one finger at a time, the way you cleaned a rifle you were going to use again.

She looked at him. He was on the floor. He hadn't moved since he'd sat down.

"All right," she said. "The rest."

She didn't make it gentle. She wasn't built for gentle and he hadn't asked for it.

"There's a man in the corner of this tent who is going to wake up in the morning and find out he doesn't have arms. That's going to be the worst morning of his life. It will be the worst morning of his life for a long time, and then one day it won't be, and that day will come sooner if the people around him don't treat it like a special kind of tragedy every time they look at him."

She picked at a piece of catgut stuck under her thumbnail. It came away wet.

"He's going to want to die. That's normal. That's the body's first answer to a thing the mind can't hold, and it's an answer I've heard from every man I've sewn up who lost something he couldn't get back. Most of them don't mean it by the third day. Some of them mean it longer. A few of them mean it forever, and those ones I can't help, and neither can you, and you don't take it personal when you can't."

She set her hands back in her lap.

"He's going to need to be fed. You do it. Don't make a production of it. Put the spoon in his mouth the way you'd put it in a child's, and don't look at his face while you do it the first few times, because he'll be watching yours to see what you see when you look at him, and if you look like you pity him he'll hate you for it, and if you look like nothing happened he'll hate you for that too. So you look at the spoon. You get good at looking at the spoon."

The lamp flickered. She glanced at it, then away.

"He's going to want to know if he can learn to do things. The answer is yes. He'll feed himself inside of a month if he has the right kind of hooks. He'll write if someone teaches him to hold a pen between the stumps. He'll dress himself with buttons on loops if someone is patient enough to sew them on. He'll ride a horse if someone breaks the horse first. He'll do all of it or none of it depending on whether the people around him decide he can or they decide he can't, and that decision gets made in the first week, before he's had a chance to make it for himself, and it sticks."

She looked at the canvas wall above his head. Not at him. At the wall.

"He'll ask you about the war. Not what happened in it. What happens next. Whether the war is going well, whether it's almost over, whether somebody won. You don't know the answer to any of those questions and neither do I, so you tell him the truth, which is that you don't know, and you tell him you'll find out, and then you find out, and you come back and tell him. That becomes the thing you do. You become the man who comes back and tells him. It's a small thing. It's not nothing."

She was quiet for a moment. The man in the corner shifted on the cot. She listened to the sound of him settling and then to the sound of him not settling and then to the sound of him breathing again.

"You," she said, and her voice came back to him now, and it was the same flatness it had been all night but it had something under it that had been there a long time, "are going to sit on that floor for as long as you need to. That's fine. The floor is clean. I swept it this morning before anybody came in, and nothing has spilled on it tonight that I didn't wipe up, and you're not in anybody's way."

She paused.

"When you get up you're going to feel it in your forearms and your shoulders and the small of your back. That's from holding him. It's not an injury. It's just what holding costs, and it goes away in a day or two, and the next time you hold a man for me it'll cost you less because you'll know what you're holding for."

She looked down at her own hands in her lap. They were very still.

"The first one I held for somebody else was a sergeant from the Ninth. Both legs below the knee. Took them off at the knee because there wasn't enough left below to save. I held him for the second one because the man who was supposed to hold him for the first one had gone outside to be sick and hadn't come back. I was two months in. I didn't know what I was looking at. I held him anyway and I watched her work and I didn't say a word and I didn't move and I didn't leave and when it was done I sat on the floor of that tent the same way you're sitting on the floor of this one, and an orderly I didn't know brought me a cup of water and didn't say anything and went away."

She was quiet for a long time. The lamp flickered and steadied and flickered again.

"I don't know where that sergeant is. I don't know if he's alive. I don't know if he learned to use the legs they made him or if he decided he didn't want them. I don't know his name either, because nobody told me his name, and I called him Tom in my head for years after, because Tom was the name of a boy I'd known as a child and it was the only name I had that wasn't already taken by somebody who mattered to me."

She wiped her hands on her trousers one more time. They were dry now.

"So that's the rest," she said. "There's a man in the corner who is going to wake up in the morning without arms, and you're going to be the one who feeds him, and you're going to be the one who tells him what you know about the war, and you're going to be the one who looks at the spoon until you can look at him, and that's the work, and the work is the same work I do, only mine is the part with the saw and yours is the part after, and neither of them is more important than the other, and both of them are going to take something out of you that you don't get back."

She looked at him. Looked at him the way she'd looked at the man on the table, reading what was there.

"You'll do it again," she said. "Not because you want to. Because there's going to be another man on another table and you're going to be the one in the tent and there's not going to be anybody else to hold him, and you'll hold him, and it will cost you less than it cost you tonight, and the night after that it will cost you less than that, and one day you'll stop counting the cost because counting it is the part that breaks you, and the work is the part that doesn't."

She sat with that for a moment. Then she reached behind her for the canteen and held it out to him across the tent the way she'd held out the rolled gauze, without looking.

"Drink," she said. "Then go outside. The air is cold and it'll do you good. When you come back, check the man in the corner. Pulse at the throat. If you can't find it, come get me. If you can, write the time on the slate by the cot and go to sleep. I'll be here for the next one."

She set the canteen down between them when he took it, or when he didn't, and she leaned her head back against the pole and closed her eyes, and her hands stayed in her lap, and they were steady, and they would be steady for the next one, whenever the next one came.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I take the canteen. The water's warm and tastes like metal. "I'll call him Rose," I say, my voice too quiet. I don't get up yet. "The black spot kind."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge opened her eyes. She didn't lift her head from the pole.

"Rose," she said.

She said it the way she said the names of instruments when she picked them up — testing the weight of it, finding where it sat in her mouth. She said it once and then she didn't say it again, and the tent was quiet except for the man in the corner breathing and the lamp doing its small flickering work against the canvas.

"That's a good name," she said. "That's a name a man can carry."

She was quiet for a while. Her eyes stayed closed. Her hands stayed in her lap.

"I had a lieutenant once," she said, "who held a boy for me. Just a boy. Couldn't have been seventeen. Lost the leg above the knee, and the lieutenant held him, and when it was done the lieutenant sat on the floor the same way you're sitting, and I asked him what he was going to call the boy, and he said *Edward*, and I said *why Edward*, and he said *because that's my brother's name and my brother died last week and I want his name to still be somewhere*."

She opened her eyes. She was looking at the canvas wall above Wick's head, the way she'd looked at it earlier, the way she looked at things that weren't anything in particular.

"The boy lived," she said. "I don't know if the lieutenant ever found out. I don't know if the lieutenant is alive himself. But the name was in the tent that night, and it did what names do, which is give a man somewhere to land when he comes back from wherever the pain takes him."

She was quiet again. The lamp steadied for a long moment, then flickered, then steadied.

"Rose," she said, softer now, almost to herself. "The black spot kind. Reds that fold. Your mother's farm."

She let it sit. She didn't add anything to it. She let it be what it was — a name, and the story behind it, and the fact that a man on the floor of a tent in the dark had decided to give both of them to a stranger who'd lost both arms and would wake up in the morning to find out what kind of man had been holding him while it happened.

"Go outside when you're ready," she said. "The air's cold and the sky's doing that thing it does before dawn where it isn't dark anymore but it isn't light either. It's just grey. That's a good color for right now. Grey is a color that doesn't ask anything of you."

She closed her eyes again. Her head settled back against the pole. Her hands stayed in her lap, one over the other, and they were still.

"I'll be here," she said. "When you come back, check Rose. Pulse at the throat. Time on the slate. Then sleep if you can."

A pause. Long. The kind of pause that meant she was deciding whether to say the next thing or leave it unsaid.

"You did all right tonight, Wick," she said. "You'll do it again. And the next man you hold for me won't know your name either, and you'll give him one anyway, and that's the work, and the work is enough."

She didn't open her eyes. The lamp flickered. The man in the corner — Rose — breathed. Outside, somewhere past the canvas, the sky was doing the grey thing she'd described, and the camp was quiet in the way camps get quiet in the small hours, when the only people awake are the ones who have to be.

Sedge stayed where she was. Her hands were steady. They would be steady for the next one.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I stay on the floor a while longer. Then I get up, go outside, and don't throw up. When I come back in, I go to the corner and put my fingers on the man's throat. His pulse is there. I write the time on the slate. I look at his face. "Rose," I say, quiet. Then I go find a blanket and lie down where I can see him.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge heard him come back in. She didn't open her eyes. She heard the pause at the cot, the small sound of chalk on slate, the single word spoken quiet to a man who couldn't hear it, and the heavier sound of a body finding the ground with a blanket under it.

She kept her eyes closed. She kept her hands in her lap.

The lamp had stopped flickering. That happened sometimes, toward morning — the oil running low, the wick settling into whatever shape it was going to burn out in. It threw a steadier light than it had all night, and she could feel the difference on her eyelids even with her eyes shut.

Rose breathed. Wick breathed. Sedge breathed.

She listened to both of them the way she listened to everything in this tent — for what they were telling her, not what she wanted them to tell her. Wick's breathing was the kind that came after a thing like this, ragged at the edges and too deliberate, a man reminding his lungs how to work on purpose. It would even out. It always evened out.

She reached behind her, slow, without lifting her head, and found the canvas pole with her fingertips and used it to pull herself upright. Her back complained. Her forearms complained. The small of her back had a knot in it that had been there since the Ninth and would be there until the war ended or she did, whichever came first.

She got to her feet. Quiet. The way she moved in this tent now, the way she moved in every tent now, so as not to disturb the men who were trying to find the place the pain couldn't get to.

She crossed to the tray. She picked up the lamp and carried it to the corner where Rose lay, and set it on the crate beside the cot, where it would throw the least shadow across his face. She looked at him for a long moment. She didn't touch the bandages. She didn't need to. She could read the rise and fall of his chest from across the tent and what it was telling her was *still here, still fighting, still arguing with the situation*.

She went back to the table. She sat down on the floor on her side of it, back against the pole again, and pulled the second blanket off the shelf behind her and laid it across her knees. Not over her shoulders. Across her knees. Because over her shoulders was a thing you did when you were going to sleep, and she wasn't going to sleep, and pretending she was would be a kind of lie she didn't allow herself in this tent.

She sat with her hands in her lap and her eyes open now, looking at the grey light coming in under the canvas where the sun hadn't quite decided to commit to the morning yet.

"Rose," she said, very quiet, to no one in particular. Testing the name again. Finding where it sat.

She let it go.

The camp was quiet. The next one would come when the next one came. She would be here for it. Her hands would be steady for it.

She closed her eyes, and she didn't sleep, and she waited.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I watch her sit in the lamplight, her hands still and her eyes closed but not sleeping. "You ever sleep?" I ask, my voice rough from not using it.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content: Wrack continued to clean her knife, her movements economical and precise. She did not look up, but her voice was even and matter-of-fact. "He's not going to stop making noise on his own. You can leave him, or you can put him down. Your call." She paused to inspect the edge of her blade, then returned to cleaning it. "If you're going to do it, do it now. We don't want to be here after dark if we can help it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take a slow breath, the coppery smell of blood thick in the air. "Right." My boots feel heavy as I walk toward the cart, trying to ignore the low, wet gasping coming from behind it.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched Corvin walk away, her eyes following the line of his shoulders until he disappeared behind the cart. She did not look away, even when the sound of his footsteps stopped. The only noise was the distant, labored breathing of the wounded man, and the faint rustle of Wrack's knife moving across the cloth.

After a moment, Corvin reappeared, his face set in a grim expression. Wrack looked away, her gaze dropping back to her knife. She sheathed it at her belt, the leather creaking softly as it slid home.

"Seven," she said, without looking up. Her voice was flat, uninflected. "Let's get out of here before it gets any darker."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack's gaze flicked up to Corvin's face, her expression unyielding. "Bad enough," she said, her voice devoid of emotion. "He's not going anywhere, and he's not going to get any better. It's easier, and it's a mercy. Same difference either way." She stood, her movements fluid and practiced, and brushed off her knees.

She glanced around the ambush site, her eyes taking in the sprawled bodies and the scattered gear. "We should get moving," she said. "We don't know how long it'll take for someone to come looking, and I don't want to be here when they do." She nodded toward the cart. "We can scavenge what we can, but let's not linger."

Wrack started to walk toward the cart, her boots scuffling against the dirt. "We need to get as far away from here as we can, before nightfall. We can't risk being caught out in the open." She glanced at Corvin, her expression grim. "We'll have to keep moving, even in the dark. It's not safe to stop now."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow, the taste of blood still in the air. "Right." I follow her toward the cart, trying not to look at the shape in the grass as we pass. "Think they had anything worth taking?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack's eyes scanned the cart as she approached, her gaze taking in the scattered gear and supplies. "Doubt it," she said, her voice skeptical. "These guys were barely equipped to start with. Probably just scraps and leavings." She reached out to rummage through the cart, her hands moving quickly and efficiently as she searched for anything of value.

As she searched, Wrack's mind was already moving on to the next step. They needed to get as far away from the ambush site as possible, and fast. They couldn't risk being caught out in the open, not now that the sun was starting to set. She glanced up at the sky, her eyes narrowing as she judged the time.

"Let's move," she said, her voice crisp and decisive. "We need to put as much distance between us and this place as we can, before it gets any darker." She started to gather up what little they had found, her movements swift and practiced.

As they moved out, Wrack kept a sharp eye on their surroundings, her senses on high alert for any sign of danger. She knew that the aftermath of an ambush was always the most dangerous time - the enemy could be anywhere, and they would be looking for revenge. Wrack's hand rested on the hilt of her knife, her fingers curled around it like a talon.

"We need to keep moving," she said, her voice low and urgent. "We can't stop now, not even for a minute. We have to keep pushing forward, no matter what." She glanced at Corvin, her eyes locked on his face. "You with me?"

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack's gaze flickered to Corvin's face, her expression unyielding. She moved closer to the body, her eyes taking in the wounds. "He's got a hole in his gut, and probably a broken ribcage from the fall," she said, her voice flat. "He's bleeding out, and he's not going to make it."

She glanced at Corvin, her eyes searching his face. "You want to know what it looks like when someone dies?" she asked, her voice even. "It looks like this. It looks like a lot of blood, and a lot of pain, and a lot of fear." She paused, her gaze dropping back to the body.

"It's not pretty, and it's not noble," she said. "It's just death. And sometimes, it's a mercy." She straightened, her movements fluid, and turned away from the body. "Let's get out of here," she said, her voice crisp. "We've got what we need. Let's go."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at the man's face, his eyes wide and unseeing. "Alright." My voice comes out quieter than I meant it to. I turn away, following Wrack. "Let's get this over with."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack led the way, her boots crunching against the dry underbrush as she navigated through the dense forest. She moved swiftly, her senses on high alert for any sign of danger. The sun was setting, casting long shadows across the forest floor, and Wrack knew they needed to find shelter before nightfall.

As they walked, Wrack's mind turned back to the ambush site. She replayed the events in her head, analyzing what had gone right and what had gone wrong. They had been lucky, she knew. The enemy had been poorly trained and poorly equipped, and they had been caught off guard. But Wrack knew that luck wouldn't last forever. They needed to be prepared for the next time, and the time after that.

After a while, Wrack slowed, her eyes scanning the surrounding area. She spotted a small clearing up ahead, partially hidden by a screen of trees. "This way," she said, her voice low. "We can set up for the night."

She led Corvin into the clearing, her eyes taking in the lay of the land. It was a good spot, she decided. There was a small stream running through the center, providing a source of water, and the trees offered decent cover. Wrack nodded to herself, satisfied.

"Let's get a fire going," she said, her voice crisp. "We need to get warm, and we need to get some rest. We've got a long day ahead of us tomorrow." She started to gather firewood, her movements swift and efficient.

As the fire crackled to life, Wrack sat back on her haunches, her eyes scanning the surrounding area. She knew they weren't safe, not yet. They still had a long way to go before they could consider themselves secure. But for now, this would have to do.

"Get some rest," she said, her voice low. "We'll take turns keeping watch. I'll go first." She stood, her movements fluid, and drew her knife. "I'll be back in a few hours. Try to get some sleep."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack's eyes narrowed, her expression unyielding. "Fine," she said, her voice flat. "A spear to the gut is a slow way to die. It tears open the intestines, and the victim bleeds out internally. It's painful, and it's messy." She paused, her gaze locked on Corvin's face.

"The spear probably punctured his stomach, his intestines, and possibly his liver or spleen," she continued, her voice even. "He's probably bleeding out, and he's going to die from shock and blood loss. It's not a quick death, and it's not a clean one."

Wrack's gaze dropped back to the body, her eyes taking in the wounds. "You can see the entry wound, just below his ribcage," she said, her voice matter-of-fact. "The spear probably went in at an angle, tearing open his stomach and intestines. The blood is pooling in his abdomen, and it's going to keep bleeding out until he dies."

She glanced up at Corvin, her eyes searching his face. "That's what a spear to the gut looks like," she said. "It's not pretty, and it's not noble. It's just death. And sometimes, it's a mercy." She straightened, her movements fluid, and turned away from the body. "Let's get out of here," she said, her voice crisp. "We've got what we need. Let's go."

She led Corvin into the clearing, her eyes taking in the lay of the land. It was a good spot, she decided. There was a small stream running through the center, providing a source of water, and the trees offered decent cover. Wrack nodded to herself, satisfied.

"Let's get a fire going," she said, her voice crisp. "We need to get warm, and we need to get some rest. We've got a long day ahead of us tomorrow." She started to gather firewood, her movements swift and efficient.

As the fire crackled to life, Wrack sat back on her haunches, her eyes scanning the surrounding area. She knew they weren't safe, not yet. They still had a long way to go before they could consider themselves secure. But for now, this would have to do.

"Get some rest," she said, her voice low. "We'll take turns keeping watch. I'll go first." She stood, her movements fluid, and drew her knife. "I'll be back in a few hours. Try to get some sleep."

Wrack walked to the edge of the clearing, her eyes scanning the surrounding area. She knew that they couldn't stay here for long, not if they wanted to stay alive. They needed to keep moving, to put as much distance between themselves and the ambush site as possible.

As she stood watch, Wrack's mind turned back to Corvin. She had seen the way he had hesitated, the way he had struggled to bring himself to kill the wounded man. She had seen the way he had looked at her, the way he had asked her to stay and watch.

Wrack's expression didn't change, but a flicker of something like approval danced in her eyes. She had seen something in Corvin, something that gave her hope. She had seen a spark of steel, a spark of determination.

As the hours passed, Wrack returned to the fire, her movements silent. She glanced at Corvin, her eyes searching his face. He was asleep, his body tense and guarded even in rest.

Wrack nodded to herself, satisfied. She knew that they still had a long way to go, but for now, this would have to do. She sat down next to Corvin, her back against a tree, and closed her eyes. She would sleep lightly, her senses on high alert for any sign of danger.

But for now, she could rest. For now, she could let her guard down, just a little.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I jerk awake sometime later, the fire low and the forest quiet. My hand goes to my knife before I remember where I am. "Your turn," I rasp, rubbing the stiffness from my neck. "I'll watch."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack's eyes flickered open, her gaze locking onto Corvin's face. She nodded once, her movements economical, and stood up, her joints creaking softly. "I'll get some rest," she said, her voice low. "Keep watch. If you see anything, don't hesitate."

She walked over to a nearby tree, her boots scuffling against the dirt, and sat down at the base of the trunk. She leaned her back against the tree, her eyes scanning the surrounding area one last time before she closed them. Her breathing slowed, her body relaxing as she let herself drift off to sleep.

But even as she slept, Wrack's senses remained on high alert, her ears tuned to the slightest sound, her body tense and ready to spring into action at a moment's notice. She knew that they weren't safe, not yet, and she knew that she had to be ready for anything.

As she slept, Wrack's mind turned back to the ambush site, to the sound of gunfire and the smell of blood. She replayed the events in her head, analyzing what had gone right and what had gone wrong. They had been lucky, she knew. The enemy had been poorly trained and poorly equipped, and they had been caught off guard. But Wrack knew that luck wouldn't last forever. They needed to be prepared for the next time, and the time after that.

After a few hours, Wrack's eyes flickered open, her gaze locking onto Corvin's face. She nodded once, her movements economical, and stood up, her joints creaking softly. "My turn again," she said, her voice low. "Get some rest."

She walked over to Corvin, her boots scuffling against the dirt, and nodded at him. "I'll keep watch," she said. "You get some sleep." She glanced at the fire, her eyes narrowing. "We'll need to get moving soon," she said. "We can't stay here for too long."

Wrack sat down next to the fire, her back against a tree, and closed her eyes. She would sleep lightly, her senses on high alert for any sign of danger. But for now, she could rest. For now, she could let her guard down, just a little.

As she sat there, Wrack's mind turned back to Corvin. She had seen the way he had hesitated, the way he had struggled to bring himself to kill the wounded man. She had seen the way he had looked at her, the way he had asked her to stay and watch.

Wrack's expression didn't change, but a flicker of something like approval danced in her eyes. She had seen something in Corvin, something that gave her hope. She had seen a spark of steel, a spark of determination.

As the hours passed, Wrack's eyes never left the surrounding area. She was on high alert, her senses tuned to the slightest sound. She knew that they couldn't stay here for too long, not if they wanted to stay alive. They needed to keep moving, to put as much distance between themselves and the ambush site as possible.

But for now, they could rest. For now, they could let their guard down, just a little.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare into the dying fire, watching the embers pulse. "You ever get used to it?" I ask, my voice quiet. "The part after."
