dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not look up from the row of instruments. "You're not ready. That's fine. Nobody's ready. Just keep your arms locked and your feet planted."

She wet a cloth and cleaned around the wound with quick, unbothered strokes, the way a person wipes down a table. The man on the board flinched at the cold of it and she rode the flinch with one flat hand.

"There's a piece in there, up under the collarbone. Metal. I can feel the edge of it." She said it to the room, to herself, to Wick — it didn't much matter which. Saying it made it a thing with steps. "I'm going in with the forceps. He'll feel that. The shout you heard earlier, that was nothing. This is the part where he means it."

She picked up the forceps, checked the light such as it was, adjusted the man's arm a quarter turn.

"I don't like this part either, if that helps you. It doesn't help him. But you asked with your face, so." She set the tips against the ragged edge of the wound. "Hold."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I lock my arms and brace my feet in the dirt.* "Go on." *My voice is tight. I don't look at his face, just at the stained canvas where the lamp throws our shadows.*

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge went in.

The forceps found the wound and then the meat of it, and she pushed past the give of tissue with a patience that had nothing to do with mercy — mercy was for after, if there was an after. The man came off the board with everything he had. His whole body arched, heels drumming, a sound tearing out of him that wasn't shouting anymore, that was lower and worse, the noise a body makes when it has stopped negotiating.

"There it is," she said. Not to comfort. Just marking the place. "Hold him. Hold."

Wick's arms held. Good. She felt the man surge under them and kept her own hand steady against his chest, riding it, the forceps not moving because she would not let them move, because moving them wrong now meant fishing twice.

"Almost. Edge of it — there." Metal kissed metal, a small dry click she felt more than heard. "Got the corner. It doesn't want to come. They never do. Keep holding, he's going to fight harder in a second, this is the part that matters —"

She adjusted her grip, drew a breath through her nose, and began to work the piece loose in small careful degrees, the tendons in her forearm standing up with it.

"Talk to him if you want," she said, flat, eyes down. "Or don't. He can't hear you. But it gives your voice somewhere to go, and yours is climbing." A pause, a fraction more pressure. "Steady. Nearly."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't look up. The piece shifted a hair under the forceps and she chased it.

"Wrong end. It's his shoulder, not his leg." A flat correction, no heat in it — she'd stopped expecting anyone to keep track of anatomy at this hour. "Your eyes went somewhere. Bring them back."

The man bucked again, weaker now, the body running out of the money to pay for it.

"How bad." She weighed the metal against the resistance, feeling the way it was hung up on something that had a name she didn't have time to say. "Bad like if I get this out clean and it hasn't torn what I think it hasn't torn, he keeps the arm and hates it in cold weather for the rest of his life. Bad like if I'm wrong about the vessel behind it, we find out in about ninety seconds and there's nothing either of us does about that." She drew a slow degree of pressure. "So it's the first kind of question, not the second. We're not being kind yet. We're being careful. Kind is later or it's not at all."

The corner came free of whatever had held it. She felt the whole shape of the thing pivot toward her.

"There. Moving now. Don't ease off — this is when he's got the most left in him." A breath. "Keep holding. I'm bringing it out."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: My knuckles are white against his shoulder, my own muscles trembling with the strain. "Just get it done," I grit out, still staring at the same damn patch of canvas.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge brought it out.

The piece came the way they came — grudging, then all at once, dragging a thin dark rope of blood behind it before she got the cloth there. She dropped the metal into the tin without ceremony and it rang once, a small ugly sound, and then she had both hands on the wound with the pad pressed down hard.

"Out. It's out." She said it plainly, the way she said everything, but there was a fraction less iron in it now that the worst degree of it was behind her. "You can ease off him. Slow. Not all at once — he'll try to move and he can't afford to yet."

The man had gone loose under Wick's hands, the fight spent, his breath sawing but there. Sedge leaned her weight into the pad and watched the color of what soaked through it, counting something behind her eyes.

"Vessel held," she said after a moment, to the tin, to the canvas, to nobody. "I was wrong about it and I'll take being wrong about that every day they let me." She glanced up then, quick, the first time she'd looked at Wick's face since the start. "You held. That patch of canvas you've been in love with — you can let go of that too."

She didn't tell him he'd done well. She didn't do that. But she nodded once, short, and it meant the same thing to anyone who'd learned to read her.

"Sit down before you fall down. I've got him from here."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge kept her weight on the pad and let him look.

"All right. You want to know, you know." She tipped her chin at the man's shoulder without moving her hands. "Under here there's a hole about the size of your thumbnail where the metal went in. It's not neat. Metal doesn't go in neat — it tears more than it cuts, so the edges are ragged, and that's what all that dark is. Muscle bleeds a lot and it looks worse than it is. That's the first thing to learn. Red and a lot of it isn't the thing that kills people."

She eased the pad up a fraction, showed him the wound wet and open for a second, then pressed back down.

"The thing that kills people is the color and the speed. Bright and fast and pushing — that's a vessel, that's arterial, that's the ninety seconds I told you about. What you're seeing here is dark and slow and seeping. That's the good kind, if there's a good kind. That means I got the piece out without opening the thing behind it that I was afraid of."

She nodded at the tin where the metal sat in its own small mess.

"That's what was in him. Bent. See the corner? That's the part that hung up on the way out. That's what made him make that noise." She said it without apology. "Now — the color's staying dark and it's slowing under my hand, which is what I want. If it went bright while you were watching, I'd stop talking to you and you'd know why."

She looked at him again, steadier now.

"That's what you're seeing. It's a man who's going to keep his arm and be angry about the weather. Better than what you were imagining. It usually is."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn’t know I was holding. “Yeah. That’s better.” I scrub a hand over my face, finally looking away. “What now?”

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge worked as she talked, because there was always a next thing and the next thing was hers.

"Now the boring part, which is the part that keeps him. Bleeding's stopping on its own, so I stop leaning on it and I clean it out — really clean, not the wipe I gave it before. Anything I leave in there festers. Cloth, dirt, a chip of bone, a splinter of that metal I can't see. Wound like this, it's never just the one piece. It's the one piece and the mess it dragged in with it."

She reached for the water without looking, hand knowing where the row was.

"Then I flush it. Then I decide whether to close it or leave it open. Dirty wound, you leave it open, pack it, let it drain — close it too soon and you seal the rot in and lose the arm anyway three days from now when I'm not here to watch it. So it stays open. Looks worse. Is better." A flat glance up. "Everything worth doing tonight looks worse and is better. You'll get used to that or you won't."

She wet her hands, shook them off.

"You — you sit. Drink something if there's anything to drink. Your hands are going to start shaking now that they've got permission, and I don't need them for this part." She pulled the lamp a hair closer with two fingers. "You did the hard thing already. The hard thing was holding when everything in you wanted to let go. This next bit's just patience."

She bent back to the shoulder.

"Stay where I can talk at you. Next one, you're doing more than the shoulders."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't look up. She liked the question, in the flat way she liked anything that made a person less useless later.

"Straight. All right."

She flushed the wound as she talked, water carrying pink out over the board.

"Bullet's simple. It's shaped to go in and it goes in, punches a channel, and if you're unlucky it tumbles. Shrapnel isn't shaped for anything. It's whatever the shell felt like tearing itself into — jagged, hot, spinning. So it doesn't make a channel. It makes a mess. It goes in and it slows down and everything it slows down against, it dumps that speed into. Tears sideways. Shreds what's next to it, not just what's in front of it."

She probed the edge of the wound with a clean finger, reading it.

"And it's dirty. Hot metal picks up cloth on the way through — his coat, his shirt, whatever he was wearing — and drives it in ahead of itself. That's the part that kills slow. Not the wound. The cloth. It sits in there where the light doesn't reach and it rots and it takes the man with it, days later, when everybody's decided he's saved." She fished something free, examined it, dropped it in the tin. "There. Thread. Told you it's never just the one piece."

She kept going, methodical.

"And the heat's a lie. People think hot metal cauterizes, seals as it goes. It doesn't. Not clean. It cooks a rim of dead tissue around the track, and dead tissue is exactly what rot wants — no blood getting to it, so nothing of mine gets to it either. Antiseptic, the man's own body, none of it reaches dead meat. So I cut it out. That's the part I'm doing now that looks cruel. I'm trimming back to tissue that bleeds, because tissue that bleeds is tissue that lives."

She glanced up, brief.

"That straight enough? Shrapnel doesn't wound a man in one place. It wounds him everywhere it touches and leaves the worst of it where I have to go looking." Back down to the shoulder. "Which is why I go looking. Drink your water."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I pick up the tin cup, but my hand's shaking so bad I have to brace it against my leg. "What happens to the piece? You just throw it out?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge glanced at the tin, then back to her work.

"Some men want it. That surprises you." She said it as fact, not judgment. "They live, they get it out of me later, they carry it in a pocket. The thing that nearly killed them, and they want to hold it. I don't ask why. I've got theories and none of them are my business."

She trimmed a rim of dead tissue, dropped it, kept talking.

"So no. I don't throw it out yet. It goes in the tin, the tin sits by his cot, and if he wakes up and wants it, it's there. If he doesn't wake up, or wakes up and doesn't want it, then it goes out. Metal's metal. Nothing sacred about it once it's out of a man." She flushed the wound again. "The sacred part was that it was inside him. Now it's in a tin. That's just the arithmetic of it."

She noticed his hand braced against his leg and didn't remark on it. The shaking was allowed. The shaking meant the body was doing what it should now that the work didn't need it steady.

"You keep asking the right questions," she said, quieter, not looking up. "That's not nothing. Most people in that chair go somewhere behind their own eyes and stay there. You're staying in the room. Keep doing that." A beat. "Small sips. You'll bring it back up if you gulp, and I've got enough on this board without your supper on my boots."

She bent closer to the lamp, working the last of it.

"Piece stays. Man decides. That's the rule I keep."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge kept both hands where they were and let the scream break over both of them like weather.

"He's not waking up. That's the meat remembering, not the man. There's a difference and you'll learn to hear it — the man screams words, the meat just screams. That's meat. Hold him anyway, it moves the same."

She worked as she talked, the words and the hands the same motion.

"Right now I'm debriding. That's the word for cutting away the dead. I've got the scissors, curved, and I'm trimming the cooked rim I told you about — the gray-yellow edge, there, that doesn't bleed when I cut it. That's how I know to take it. Living tissue argues with the blade. Dead tissue just comes away quiet. I follow the quiet out until I hit the argument, and then I stop. That's the whole skill of it. Knowing where to stop."

Snip. She dropped a sliver in the tin. Flushed. Kept on.

"Now I'm going deeper than I like, because I can feel a hard spot my finger doesn't trust, up against the bone. Could be bone chip. Could be another sliver of the piece that broke off the corner on the way out. That's why he's making that noise — I'm in against the periosteum, the sheath on the bone, and there's no numbing that, there's only through it. I'm sorry for it and it changes nothing." Her finger found the edge. "There. Chip. Small. Coming out — now."

Clink in the tin. She let out a short breath.

"That's the last of what I can find. From here it's flush, pack, dress. No more cutting. The screaming stops when the cutting stops, give it a few breaths." She glanced up, fast, steady. "How much longer — you want the true number, not the kind one. Five minutes of packing, and then he's off this board and he's your problem for six hours while I do the next one. So five minutes. Then the hard part's mine and the long part's yours."

She wet the packing, began feeding it in, slow and even.

"You held. He's quieting. Feel it? — there. Told you. Meat runs out of money too."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I feel the fight drain out of him under my palms. My own hands are slick with sweat. "Six hours," I say, voice hoarse. "What am I watching for?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge fed the packing in a slow inch at a time, not looking up, giving him the list the way she gave everything — as steps, because steps were survivable.

"Fever's the big one. He'll run warm — that's normal, that's the body working. What you're watching for is warm turning to hot, the kind you feel off his skin before you touch him. That's the cloth I missed, or the chip I didn't find, waking up. If he goes hot and stays hot, you come get me, I don't care what I'm elbow-deep in."

She smoothed the dressing, reached for the cloth to bind it.

"The dressing. It'll seep — that's fine, that's expected, dark and slow like I showed you. What's not fine is if it soaks bright and fast, or if it soaks through faster than it should. You learn the pace of it in the first hour. Whatever it looks like at the end of the first hour, that's your baseline. It gets worse than that, you come get me. Same rule."

She began wrapping, firm, even turns.

"His color. Right now he's gray because he lost blood and hurt like hell. Over the six hours he should come back toward himself — lips, the beds of his nails, that's where you read it easiest. If he goes the other way — grayer, or the lips going blue, or the breathing turning shallow and quick like a dog in summer — that's the vessel I said held deciding it didn't after all. That one you don't come get me for. That one you shout, and you shout while you're already pressing on it."

She tied off the binding and finally straightened, hands going still for the first time in an hour.

"And him. If he wakes and he's here — knows his name, knows the year, curses you for the weather — that's good, that's the best thing you'll see all night. If he wakes and he's somewhere else, talking to people who aren't in the tent, that can be the fever or it can be the blood loss and either way you keep him from tearing the dressing off and you keep him warm and you wait it out."

She wiped her hands on the cloth at her belt, looked at him — really looked, the gray face and the slick hands and the eyes that had stayed in the room the whole time.

"That's it. Fever, blood, breath, and whether the man's still a man when he wakes. You watch those four and you come get me for three of them and you shout for the fourth." A short nod. "He'll likely just sleep. Most of them just sleep, and you sit there sick with waiting for nothing to happen, and nothing happening is the whole prize."

She glanced at the flap, at the next thing already waiting past it.

"Get him off my board. Sit where you can see all four of those things at once. And drink the rest of that water — you've earned the shakes, but you can't watch a man from the floor."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge crouched down to his level, which she almost never did — she was a stander, a leaner, a person who talked at people over her own busy hands. But she came down onto her heels in front of him, forearms on her knees, and let the next one wait a minute longer past the flap.

"The rest." She turned the phrase over. "You mean the part I didn't say because it isn't a step."

She looked at him a moment.

"All right. Here's the rest. You did a thing tonight that the doing of doesn't reward. Nobody's going to thank you. He won't — he was meat by the end, he doesn't know your face. I'm not going to, not the way you'd want. There's no line where somebody says *well done* and it settles in your chest and stays. That's not how this works. You held a man down while he screamed and the whole of your prize is that he's breathing and you feel like something scraped out of a boot. That's the trade. I'm telling you that straight because nobody told me, and I spent the first year thinking there was a feeling waiting at the end of it that never came."

She rubbed her thumb along a knuckle, absent, the way a person worries a thing they've worried before.

"The shaking's fine. I keep saying it because you keep not believing it. The body holds still because you make it, and then it sends the bill. Every time. Four years and my hands still shake after, in the dark where the next one can't see. You do it in front of me, that's allowed. You did the work. The shaking is the work leaving."

A beat. The lamp guttered and steadied.

"Here's the part I actually want you to keep, though. You asked. All night, you asked. *What am I seeing, what does it do, say it straight.* Most people don't. Most people take the not-knowing because not-knowing feels safer, and it isn't — it's just quieter, and the quiet fills up with the worst thing they can imagine, and then they carry that instead of the truth. The truth's ugly but it's the right size. What you imagine is always bigger. You kept making me hand you the right-sized thing. That's the only trick there is to lasting at this. You didn't learn it tonight, you already had it. That's rare. I don't say that to flatter you. I don't flatter. I say it because you're going to be the one holding the forceps sooner than you think, the way this war eats us, and you should know now that the thing you've got is the thing that matters more than a steady hand."

She stood, joints telling her about it, and looked down at him where he sat.

"Now the last of the rest, and then I've got a man past that flap who's been patient longer than he should've. It doesn't get easier. That's the true one. It gets *familiar*, which people confuse for easier, and it isn't. What happens is you get faster and cleaner and better at handing out right-sized things, and inside it costs exactly what it cost tonight, every time, and you just carry the cost better. That's not a comfort. I don't have a comfort. What I've got is: you're not broken because it hurt. It's supposed to hurt. The day it stops hurting is the day I don't want you near my table."

She wiped her hands one more time, unnecessarily, and jerked her chin at the man breathing on the board.

"Sit as long as you need. Watch your four things. I'll be twelve feet away with my arms in someone else. Shout for the fourth."

And she was already turning toward the flap.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I stay where I am, watching the rise and fall of his chest. "Sedge." My voice is raw. "The piece in the tin. If he doesn't want it, I'll take it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge stopped with her hand on the flap. She didn't turn around right away.

"Will you," she said. Not a question. Just weighing it, the way she weighed the color of blood, reading the shape of a thing before she decided what it was.

Then she did turn, and looked at him a long moment — the man on the floor, the tin by the cot, the metal sitting in it dark and bent and useless now that it was out of anyone.

"You know why they keep them," she said. "The men. I told you I had theories and none of them were my business." A pause. "It's not a souvenir. It's not that. It's that the thing was inside them and doing its work in the dark where they couldn't see it, and they lay there feeling it and not knowing its shape, and it got to be the size of the whole world. And then somebody dug it out and put it in a tin and it turned out to be a bent little scrap the size of a thumbnail. Small. You could close your hand around it. So they carry it to remind themselves it was small. That the worst thing that ever happened to them fit in a pocket."

She let that sit.

"That's not his reason yet. He's asleep. Maybe he won't want it — some don't, some can't stand the sight of the thing." She crossed back, two steps, and picked the tin up off the cot. The metal shifted with a small dry sound. She held it a moment, then held it out to him.

"But you're not asking for his reason. You've got your own." She wasn't smiling — she didn't — but something in the set of her mouth had eased. "You held a man down through the worst of it and you want to keep the shape of what you were holding him against. So it isn't the size of the whole world in your head either. That's a good reason. Better than most of theirs."

She set the tin down in reach of his hand rather than making him take it from hers.

"If he wakes and wants it, it's his, and you'll give it over and not argue. That's the rule and it doesn't bend. But if he doesn't —" she nodded, short, "— then yeah. You take it. Put it somewhere you'll find it on a bad night. Close your hand around it and remember it was small."

She straightened, and this time she did go, but she paused once more at the flap, without looking back.

"Watch your four things."

And she was through, into the next lamp, the next board, the next man who'd been patient longer than he should have.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content:
I reach for the tin and close my fingers around the piece. It’s warm from the lamp, rough at the edges. I look at the man sleeping on the cot, then I push myself up off the floor. My legs hold.

I take the stool by his side. I watch his chest rise and fall, the slow seep on the dressing, the color of his lips. I keep the metal in my pocket. It’s small.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge worked through the night twelve feet away, and she did not look over, because a person who looks over is a person who doesn't trust, and she'd decided somewhere in the last hour that she trusted him.

She could hear him, though. Not words — there weren't any — but the quality of the quiet on that side of the tent. The particular stillness of someone watching properly. Most men filled the waiting with fidgeting, with pacing, with getting up to be useful in ways that were really just fear looking for somewhere to put its hands. He didn't. He sat. He watched his four things. Now and again she heard the small scrape of the stool as he leaned in to check a color or a pace, and then the settle of it as he sat back, satisfied, and waited again.

Nothing happened. That was the prize, and he was earning it the hard slow way, sick with waiting for it.

Somewhere past the third hour the man on the cot stirred — a shift, a groan, the sound of meat becoming a man again — and Sedge caught the change in the quiet on that side, the sharpening of it. She didn't stop what her hands were doing. She just raised her voice enough to carry, flat and even, without turning.

"Talk to him. Name, year, curse the weather. You know what you're listening for." A beat, elbow-deep in the next one. "That's the good sound. That's the best thing you'll see all night."

And she left him to it, because it was his to have.

Toward dawn, when the board in front of her was finally empty and the light through the canvas had gone from black to the color of dirty water, she came back. Wiped her hands. Looked at the man sleeping — properly sleeping now, color come back toward himself, the dressing dark and slow and no worse than its baseline — and then looked at Wick on the stool, who'd been there the whole six hours and hadn't shouted once.

"He kept his arm," she said. "You kept him." She didn't say *well done.* She still didn't do that.

But she pulled up the other stool, and sat, and that was the thing she did instead.

"Now you sleep," she said. "Before the next lot come in and you're standing where I stood. Go on. I've got him."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I look up at her, then down at the sleeping man. I don't want to leave, but I know she's right. I nod once, stand, and feel the piece heavy in my pocket. "Yeah," I say, my voice rough from disuse. I don't thank her. I think she'd hate it.

rung_labels.evidence: The corner came free of whatever had held it. She felt the whole shape of the thing pivot toward her.

rung_labels.evidence: Under here there's a hole about the size of your thumbnail where the metal went in. It's not neat. Metal doesn't go in neat — it tears more than it cuts, so the edges are ragged

rung_labels.evidence: It goes in and it slows down and everything it slows down against, it dumps that speed into. Tears sideways. Shreds what's next to it

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Right now I'm debriding. That's the word for cutting away the dead. I've got the scissors, curved, and I'm trimming the cooked rim I told you about — the gray-yellow edge, there, that doesn't bleed when I cut it.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Here's the rest. You did a thing tonight that the doing of doesn't reward. Nobody's going to thank you.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge picked up the forceps. The lamp threw shadows that made the wounds look deeper than they were, or maybe not deeper enough.

"Brace," she said, and sank the first instrument into the entry wound below his left clavicle.

The man's body convulsed once, a full-body reflex that drove his head back against the table. Wick held. Sedge kept working, fishing for the shard she'd felt when she'd pressed her fingers to the wound an hour ago. Metal moved through tissue with a sound like someone turning a key in a lock.

"You're going to feel that," she said to no one in particular. The man had stopped screaming again. Either the pain had finally crested or he'd found somewhere else to go. Didn't matter. The body was just a machine. You fixed the broken parts or you didn't.

She pulled the shrapnel free and dropped it in the basin without looking. It rang against the other pieces already in there — a small collection, all from this one man. Someone had tried to put him back together with whatever ordnance the other side had lying around.

"Left side's clear. Right one's deeper. Thirty seconds."

She adjusted the lamp. The flame guttered, steadied. In the bad light, she could see the second entry wound was uglier — ragged, the metal having tumbled through muscle instead of cutting clean. She'd need to cut around it, debride the torn tissue before she could reach the piece.

She reached for the scalpel.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, trying to ignore the wet sound of the forceps. "Right," I manage, shifting my grip. The man's breathing is shallow and quick under my hands.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge made the first incision. Scalpels were honest in a way most things weren't — they did exactly what you told them to do, no more, no less. The body, now. The body was a liar. It screamed when it should have been quiet, went silent when you needed it to tell you things, bled when you were trying to work and clotted when you needed it not to.

She spread the wound with the retractor and looked.

"Clipped the subclavian," she said. "That'll be the bleeder they couldn't find. I can tie it off, but he'll need a transfusion after. Ask someone if they've got B-negative. He's B-negative. Check his tags."

Wick nodded. Sedge watched the man's chest rise and fall — too fast, but steady enough. The retractor pulled the skin taut and the lamp lit the interior of the wound in shades of red and yellow. Muscle. Fat. Blood she was trying not to let her gloves get too slick with.

"Hold him again," she said. "This one's going to be worse."

She found the second piece with her fingers — not where she'd expected it, displaced deeper by however many hours had passed since the injury. The body had tried to protect itself. It had swelled around the foreign object, walled it off. Good for him, bad for her. She'd have to cut through that wall before she could get to the metal.

Sedge took a breath. Not because she needed to steady herself — she'd done this enough times that it required no steadiness — but because the next part would require her to push through tissue that had already been damaged, and she wanted to remember that there was a man attached to this body, even if the man had left the tent an hour ago.

"Hold," she said, and began.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge's hands didn't stop moving. She worked the scalpel around the second shard, keeping her eyes on the wound and not on Wick's face.

"Not that bad," she said. "Not yet. Subclavian's tied off, the lung's intact, and his heart's still beating on its own. He gets out of here with both shoulders and both arms if I can get this piece clean. If I can't—" She cut through another layer of tissue. "Then we talk about what comes next. But that's my problem, not yours. Your problem is keeping him on the table."

She found the edge of the shrapnel and gripped it with the forceps. This one had been in longer. The tissue had grown around it, and pulling it free would take pieces of that tissue with it.

"His tags say B-negative. When you're done here, find someone with a kit. If there isn't one, there wasn't one for the last six men either and we'll manage. But check."

The forceps gripped and Sedge pulled. Slowly — you always went slowly on the second piece, on account of the swelling. The man convulsed again, and this time Wick could feel the muscles in his shoulders turning to iron under the skin, every muscle firing at once. Sedge kept pulling.

"He's still in there somewhere," she said, almost to herself. "Somewhere under all that."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I tighten my grip, feeling his muscles strain against me. "He's B-negative," I repeat, my voice tight. "I'll check right after." *God, I hope we have it.*

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The shrapnel came free with a wet, sucking sound. Sedge dropped it in the basin without ceremony and immediately pressed a gauze pad to the wound. Her fingers found the bleeder she'd created when she severed the tissue around it, clamped it off, held.

"Got it," she said. The words meant nothing and everything. She'd gotten it. The man would live long enough to lose more blood than he could afford, long enough to get infected if the field dressings failed, long enough to make it someone else's problem three days from now when he was supposed to be somewhere else, doing something else, being someone other than the body on this table.

None of that was her problem.

"Hold pressure there," she said, guiding Wick's hand to the gauze. "Don't lift it to check. I know you want to. You won't be able to see anything useful and you'll let more blood through. Twenty seconds, then I close."

She threaded the needle herself, not handing it off. Her stitches would be ugly — she wasn't built for cosmetic work and didn't pretend to be — but they'd hold. That was the only metric that mattered. Would it hold. Would he stay together.

The man on the table had gone somewhere else entirely. His eyes were open but empty, tracking nothing. Sedge had seen that look before. It wasn't death. It was the body protecting the mind from what the mind couldn't process. He'd come back eventually, or he wouldn't. Either way, she'd done what she could with the machine.

"Closing now," she said, for Wick's benefit as much as the patient's. "Shoulder first, then the subclavian repair. Another hour, maybe less if you actually hold pressure and don't lift that gauze."

She began to sew.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't look up from her work. The needle moved in and out, pulling the wound closed one stitch at a time.

"You're seeing the fascial layer," she said. "The white stuff under the skin. That's connective tissue, holds everything in place. I'm suturing that first because if I just close the skin on top, the inside heals wrong and he gets adhesions that limit his range of motion for months. Sometimes permanently."

She tied off a stitch, cut the thread, started another.

"Now I'm closing the subcutaneous layer. Fat under the skin, see how it varies in thickness? Depends on the man, depends on where the shrapnel traveled. This one's pretty standard. The yellow is just fat. Doesn't mean anything except that this part of his body stored energy for later use. Later didn't come."

She worked the needle down the length of the wound, pulling it closed like lacing up a boot.

"Top layer's skin. I'll do a running stitch, cleaner that way. Leaves less for the body to reject. The black thread is silk — holds well, doesn't break down, comes out in a week or two when the tissue underneath has had time to strengthen. By then he'll be somewhere with better equipment and someone with steadier hands than mine."

She finished the suture, tied it off, trimmed the excess.

"You're seeing a man who was whole this morning," she said, finally glancing up. "Shell fragment opened him in three places and tumbled through his chest cavity. I took two pieces of metal out of him that had no business being inside a human body. He's closed now. He'll scar. He'll have two ugly lines on his shoulders and he'll feel them when the weather changes for the rest of his life."

She stepped back, peeled her gloves off.

"That's what you're seeing. That's all of it. Now hold that pressure while I prep the dressings. And when you go looking for blood, tell them I said the right shoulder's the priority. Left one's already clotting."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, my eyes fixed on the neat black line she’s made out of what was a ragged hole. "Okay," I say, my voice low. "I'll hold." The gauze under my hands is warm and damp.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge moved to the supply table and began assembling the dressings. Her hands knew the work well enough that she didn't need to watch what she was doing — gauze, antiseptic, adhesive tape, the same combination she'd used a hundred times before. The man on the table breathed in shallow rhythms that told her he was still running, still fighting whatever war had put him on her table, even if his mind had gone somewhere quieter.

"He might seize when I move him," she said, not turning around. "Muscle reaction to the trauma. If he does, don't try to hold him down. Just keep his head from hitting the table and stay clear of his arms. Seizing looks worse than it is, provided you don't get thrown into something."

She soaked a gauze pad with antiseptic and set it aside for the second shoulder.

"When you come back, there'll be a woman with a stomach wound two cots down. I've stabilized her but she needs the table next. Don't tell her it's urgent. She's the worrying kind and worrying makes her bleed."

Sedge wrung out her gloves in the basin, watching the water turn pink with diluted blood. She'd need to change it before the next one. She always needed to change it before the next one.

"He's stable enough to move," she continued, carrying the dressings back to the table. "Barring complications, he'll make it to evacuation. That's not the same as making it home, but it's closer than he was an hour ago. Sometimes that's all the margin we get."

She lifted the gauze from Wick's hands — the bleeding had slowed to a seep, exactly what she'd wanted to see — and pressed the antiseptic pad to the wound. The man didn't react. His body had finally run out of ways to tell her it was listening.

"Dress it. I'll handle the second one."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge paused with the second gauze pad in her hand. Wick wasn't looking away this time.

"It tears," she said. "That's the simplest version. Tissue doesn't want to be cut — it has structure, it has integrity, and a piece of metal coming through at speed doesn't care about any of that. It tears muscle fibers, nicks vessels, sometimes crushes more than it cuts because the metal tumbles. You see the entry wound and think you know how big the damage is. You don't. The inside is worse."

She pressed the pad to the second shoulder, began taping it down.

"Metal carries dirt, fabric, whatever it picked up on the way in. Burns the tract as it travels — heat from friction, even if the shrapnel itself isn't hot. That burn introduces bacteria into places that shouldn't have bacteria. So now you've got a foreign object embedded in tissue, plus contamination, plus the body's own response to both."

She smoothed the tape, checked her work.

"The body tries to wall it off. Surrounds the invader with inflammation, traps it in scar tissue. That's what you felt when I was digging for the second piece — the swelling, the resistance. The body was doing its job. Problem is, the body doesn't know the difference between something that will kill it and something that won't. So it keeps swelling, keeps fighting, and eventually the pressure inside a closed space starts cutting off circulation to everything else."

She stepped back from the table, looked down at the man who was no longer screaming, no longer fighting, just breathing in small mechanical increments.

"If it's near a major vessel, it nicks it and you bleed out before you get to a table. If it's near a nerve cluster, it severs something that doesn't grow back. If it's in the chest cavity like this one was, it tumbles until it hits something solid — heart, lung, spine — or it slows down enough to let the body finish the job. Sometimes it bounces. Shrapnel doesn't follow rules. It's physics and bad luck."

She stripped her gloves off, dropped them in the basin with the others.

"That's what it does. Tears, burns, contaminates, and waits to see if the body can outlast the damage. Most of the time the body can't. That's why they're on the table instead of walking around."

She nodded at the man.

"This one got lucky. Both pieces missed the important parts. The important parts being anything that pumps blood or breathes air. Everything else is negotiable."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I take a shaky breath, my hands still pressed to the dressing. "So he got lucky," I repeat, my voice hollow. "And we're the ones who get to clean up the mess."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge began cleaning her instruments. The forceps, the retractor, the scalpel — each one went into the basin with the same methodical care, as if the tools themselves deserved respect for having done their work without failing.

"That's the job," she said. "Someone makes the mess, someone cleans it. We clean it. Other people make different messes elsewhere and someone else cleans those. Round and round it goes until there's no one left on either side who knows how to throw metal at each other, or until we're all out of tables to put them on."

She dried her hands on a towel that had seen better days.

"You want to know what I figured out in the first year? Thinking about it that way doesn't help. Clean up this mess, move to the next mess, clean that one. That's all it is. You start thinking about luck, about fairness, about whether any of it means something — you'll go somewhere you can't come back from. The body on the table doesn't care what you think about its circumstances. It just needs you to be here and doing the next thing."

She looked at Wick — still holding pressure, still steady, still present.

"You're doing fine. You didn't throw up, didn't look away, didn't let go when he bucked. That's more than some manage. Go find your B-negative. The woman's stomach wound won't wait forever, and she bleeds faster when she's anxious."

She turned back to the instrument table, already preparing for the next procedure.

"And Wick? Don't make it mean more than it is. He's a man with two holes I closed. Tomorrow he'll be a statistic or a miracle depending on who writes the report. Right now he's just breathing. That's enough. That's all we get to keep."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The man's voice hit a pitch that meant he was back in the room, back in the body, back to feeling everything she'd done to him in the last hour. Sedge didn't flinch. She'd learned that much.

"Second dressing going on now," she said, loud enough to carry over the screaming. "I'm taping the edges down because the first layer is soaked through and I need a dry layer on top to keep contaminants out. The screaming is good. Screaming means the nervous system's still connected. Quiet is what worries me."

She smoothed the tape along the edge of the second shoulder dressing, her movements unhurried despite the noise.

"Thirty seconds on the right side. I need to check the sutures under this pad before I commit to it. Hold him — I know, I know, just hold."

She lifted the edge of the gauze, peered at the line of black stitches she'd made, watched the slow seep of blood that wasn't arterial, wasn't dangerous, was just the body's way of saying it had been opened and wasn't happy about it.

"Sutures are holding. Good. Closing the dressing now. Two more pieces of tape and I'm done with the shoulders."

The man on the table was weeping — actual tears, mixing with sweat, running back into his hair. That was a good sign too. Tears meant the autonomic nervous system was working, meant the brain had reconnected to the body well enough to produce a physical response to distress. Sedge had seen men come off the table empty-eyed and catatonic, and she'd seen this, the raw animal grief of someone who had survived something they hadn't expected to survive.

"He's crying because it hurts," she said, not unkindly. "The body cries when it hurts. Doesn't mean anything except that he's alive enough to feel it. I'm not giving him more morphine because I need him coherent for evacuation and his blood pressure's already lower than I'd like. He can hurt for the next four hours until someone with better resources takes over."

She finished the second dressing, stepped back, and pressed her palm flat against the man's sternum. His heart was still beating — she could feel it through her glove, a rhythm that said the machine was still running even if the operator had temporarily left the cockpit.

"Heart rate's elevated but strong. Breathing's shallow but even. You let go now and he won't convulse — the seizure risk drops once the immediate trauma response passes. But don't let go yet. I've got one more thing."

She reached for a bottle of saline and began flushing the wounds — the entry points on the chest, smaller, less critical, but still open enough to let in whatever the shrapnel had carried with it.

"I'm irrigating the chest wounds now. Salt water, sterile, gets into places my instruments couldn't reach and washes out the worst of the contamination. He'll feel that. He already does. Hold him through it."

The saline ran pink across the man's chest, diluted the blood, pooled on the table beneath him. Standard. Expected. Nothing in her work that she hadn't seen before, done before, described before.

"Thirty seconds more," she said. "Then we're done and you can go find your blood type and I'll start on the woman with the stomach wound. He's going to quiet down soon — exhaustion will take him before the pain does, one way or another. His body's already deciding to shut down the parts it doesn't need right now. That's normal. That's him surviving."

She emptied the saline, set the bottle aside, stripped her gloves.

"Done," she said. "You can let go now. Gently — lower his shoulders back to the table and step away. He'll sleep for a few hours and when he wakes up he'll be someone else's problem. For now, he's just a man with two ugly shoulders who isn't dead."

She moved to the basin, began washing her arms to the elbow, the water running cold.

"That's everything. That's all of it. Now go."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let go slowly, my hands stiff from holding. The man’s crying softens into ragged breaths. I wipe my palms on my trousers. "B-negative," I mutter, and head for the tent flap. I don't look back.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge watched the tent flap fall closed behind Wick. The canvas shuddered once, settled, and then the only sound in the tent was the man's breathing and the wet drip of the saline draining off the table's edge.

She dried her arms and moved to the supply table without looking at him. There wasn't anything to look at now that she hadn't already seen. The man would sleep or he wouldn't. He'd make it to evacuation or he wouldn't. Either way, her part in his survival was finished and there were others waiting who still had a chance.

She checked the saline count, noted they'd need more by morning, added it to the list pinned to the tent pole. The woman with the stomach wound was awake — Sedge could hear her talking to someone in the adjacent tent, voice thin but steady. That was good. Steady meant she wasn't bleeding internally. Bleeding internally made you quiet. Quiet was the kind of problem you didn't solve with field surgery.

Sedge pulled a fresh pair of gloves from the box and snapped them on. The list was long tonight. Two shoulders, one stomach, something with an arm that someone had bandaged wrong, and a fever case that was probably just a fever but she'd need to check the evacuations log to see who'd come through recently and from where. Typhus moved through camps the way water moved through cracks — find the smallest opening, take the path of least resistance, arrive before anyone expected it.

She heard footsteps outside. Wick, probably, back with news about the blood supply. Or someone else entirely. Didn't matter. She had work waiting and the work didn't care about anything except being done in the right order.

She pulled the lamp closer, adjusted the flame, and began laying out instruments for the next procedure.

The man on the table behind her breathed in and out, shallow and mechanical, the machine still running without an operator. Sedge didn't turn around. She'd learned not to turn around.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't stop laying out instruments. Her hands kept moving — forceps, sutures, gauze, the same arrangement she used every time, muscle memory that didn't require her attention.

"The rest of what," she said. Not a question. She knew what he meant.

"Everything. What happens when we leave. What happens if he doesn't make it. What happens to us."

Sedge set down the forceps. Turned. Looked at Wick on the floor of the tent, back against the canvas, legs stretched out in front of him like a child who'd worn himself out playing.

"You want the rest of it," she said. "Alright."

She pulled a stool over and sat, not across from him but adjacent, close enough that she didn't have to raise her voice. The lamp threw her shadow across the table where the man lay breathing his shallow mechanical breath.

"When we leave, he'll wake up in pain and confusion and probably ask where he is. The answer changes depending on who answers — a field hospital, a aid station, a place where people go to not die. He'll get water if he can keep it down, broth if someone's made any, and a cot that will feel like concrete after what his body's been through. Someone will check his dressings in an hour. Someone else will check them in two. He won't remember our faces. He won't remember yours. That's normal. That's how it's supposed to work."

She interlaced her fingers, rested her hands on her knees.

"If he doesn't make it — if the subclavian clot breaks loose, or the infection takes hold, or his blood pressure drops and doesn't come back — someone will note the time. They'll write his name on a tag and tie it to his wrist. The tag goes with him to wherever they take the bodies. That's not morbid. That's administrative. Someone has to account for everyone, and the tags make sure no one gets lost."

She watched Wick's face in the lamplight. He wasn't crying. He was just sitting, breathing, being present in the way someone is present when they've used up everything they had and there's nothing left to spend.

"What happens to us is we move to the next one. The woman with the stomach wound is awake and asking questions she doesn't need answers to. I need to get her stable before she tears something open by worrying. The arm case is wrapped wrong and if I don't fix it in the next three hours he'll lose the hand. The fever case — could be nothing, could be the start of something that moves through the camp like fire through dry grass."

She leaned forward, elbows on her knees.

"That's what happens to us. We don't sleep enough and we eat when there's time and we stop thinking about the ones who came before because there's no room in your head for ghosts and live patients at the same time. You pick the live patients. Every time. You pick them until there aren't any left to pick."

She stood, walked back to the instrument table, resumed her work.

"You did something tonight you probably didn't think you could do. You held a man together while I cut him open and you didn't look away and you didn't let go. That's not nothing. That's not small. But it doesn't change anything except that this one man will wake up with two ugly shoulders instead of bleeding out on a table. The war keeps going. The bodies keep coming. We keep cleaning up the mess until we can't anymore."

She picked up the scalpel, tested its edge against her thumbnail, set it down.

"That's the rest of it, Wick. There's no meaning in it. There's no lesson. There's just the next thing that needs doing and us doing it. You can sit on that floor for five more minutes or you can get up and find me B-negative blood and help me keep three more people alive tonight. Either way, tomorrow comes and we start over."

She turned back to the table, began arranging the second set of instruments. The woman with the stomach wound had gone quiet — either sleeping or getting worse, and she wouldn't know which until she checked.

"The floor's cold," she said. "And I'm going to need you standing up when I start on the next one. Up to you how long you take to get there."

The lamp flickered. The man on the table breathed. Somewhere outside, someone was calling for a medic, voice thin and distant, one more voice in a war that had run out of voices to answer it.

Sedge waited. She was good at waiting.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I push myself up, my hands braced on my knees. "I'll find the blood," I say. "And I'll be back." My voice sounds rough. "I'm not staying on the floor."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't turn around.

"Good," she said. The word carried no particular warmth. It was an assessment, nothing more. Wick was standing and that meant he was functional and that meant she had one more pair of hands available for the next several hours. That was the only thing that mattered.

"The supply tent's north, third row past the latrines. Ask for Dara — she's the night shift and she'll give you what we have without asking questions. If there's no B-negative, A-positive is close enough in an emergency. Tell her I said priority two, not priority one. The man on the table's not critical anymore. The woman with the stomach wound is."

She finished arranging the instruments and moved to the basin, began washing her hands again. The water was still clean from the last round. It wouldn't stay that way.

"When you come back, I'll be in the middle of her. Don't interrupt unless she's coding. If she starts bleeding out, I'll tell you what to do. If she doesn't, stay out of my way and watch. That's how you learn the next part."

She dried her hands, snapped on fresh gloves, flexed her fingers to settle the latex against her skin.

"Go," she said. "Dara's efficient but she likes to talk. Don't let her tell you about her grandchildren. You'll be there all night."

She heard Wick move toward the tent flap, heard the canvas rustle as he pushed through into whatever was waiting outside — the dark, the cold, the other tents full of other people with other problems. He didn't look back. Good. Looking back was a habit that killed you slowly in work like this.

Sedge turned to the supply table and began the count for the next procedure. Sutures, gauze, saline, clamps. The list ran through her head like a prayer she didn't believe in, each item a small祈祷 against the thing that waited for all of them — not death, exactly, but the slow erosion of everything that made a person a person instead of a collection of parts that happened to be breathing.

She checked the lamp. Adjusted the flame. The light steadied, steadied, held.

The woman with the stomach wound was next. Sedge walked over to the cot where she lay awake, watching the ceiling with the fixed stare of someone who had already calculated her odds and wasn't satisfied with the arithmetic.

"Name?" Sedge asked, pulling on a fresh pair of gloves.

"Maren," the woman said. Her voice was steady. Sedge respected that.

"Maren. I'm going to ask you some questions and I need you to answer honestly. The only thing that matters right now is whether you can do exactly what I tell you when I tell you. Can you do that?"

Maren nodded. Sedge began her examination, hands moving with practiced efficiency across the woman's abdomen, feeling for the distension that meant internal bleeding, the rigidity that meant peritonitis, the small clues that told her whether this was a problem she could fix in the field or a problem that needed to be somewhere else entirely.

Behind her, the man on the table slept. His breathing had steadied into something closer to natural. The dressings held. The sutures held. The machine was still running, operator still absent, but running.

Sedge found the edge of the wound and pressed.

"Tell me about the pain," she said. "Where is it and what does it feel like?"

Maren told her. Sedge listened. She always listened. The body lied but the voice sometimes told the truth, and it was the only instrument she had that couldn't break.

The tent flap settled. Wick was gone, out in the dark, looking for blood. Sedge hoped he found it. She hoped there was enough. She hoped for a lot of things she knew better than to count on.

She focused on what was in front of her. The next thing. The only thing.

The woman was talking. Sedge heard her. She always heard.

Outside, somewhere, a vehicle was starting. Engines had their own language, and this one said evacuation, which meant the night was moving people and supplies toward wherever people and supplies went when the field hospitals filled past capacity. The man on the table would be loaded onto one of those vehicles eventually, if he lived long enough. He would be someone else's patient then. Someone else's chance to keep a man breathing.

Sedge pressed her fingers deeper and felt the edge of what she was looking for. Not good. Not good at all.

"You're going to need surgery," she said to Maren. "Real surgery, not what I can do here. But I can buy you time. I can stop the bleeding long enough to get you there. It's going to hurt."

Maren nodded. Her jaw was set. Sedge had seen that expression before — the particular grimace of someone who had decided to survive regardless of what survival required.

"Good," Sedge said. "That's what I need from you."

She raised her voice toward the tent flap.

"I need a light over here. Someone. Now."

Then back to Maren, voice lower, steady, a rhythm she knew how to maintain.

"When I tell you to hold your breath, you hold your breath. When I tell you to breathe, you breathe. Between those two things, you scream if you need to. No one's going to think less of you. No one's going to remember what your voice sounds like in the morning. But what you feel right now, what we do right now — that stays between us and this table."

She reached for the instruments. The lamp steadied. The night continued.

Somewhere in the dark, Wick was looking for blood.

Sedge got to work.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I step back into the tent, a small cooler in my hands. "Dara gave me two units. Said it's all she's got left for the night." My eyes go to the new woman on the table. "Where do you want it?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge glanced up from Maren's abdomen, her hands still pressed to the woman's side where she'd found the problem.

"Counter," she said, nodding toward the supply table. "Put it there, next to the saline. I'll need it in about twenty minutes once I get her open and see what we're actually dealing with. If it's what I think it is, she'll need both units before we even close her up."

She returned her attention to Maren, fingers probing the distension along the lower abdomen. The woman was holding still, breathing in shallow sips, every muscle locked against the pain.

"Your handiwork?" Sedge asked, tilting her head toward Maren's midsection. "Or did she come to us like this?"

"Fall," Maren managed. "Three days ago. Didn't think—I thought it was just bruised."

Sedge's jaw tightened. Three days. Three days of internal bleeding, slow and quiet, the body compensating until it couldn't anymore.

"Three days," she repeated, for Wick's benefit. "Internal bleed that's been building for three days. The fall ruptured something — spleen, liver, one of the mesenteric vessels, I won't know until I'm in there. What I know is she's out of compensatory reserve. Her blood pressure's bottoming out and her pulse's running rabbit-fast to make up for it. She's dry inside. That's why we need both units."

She stepped back, stripped her gloves, reached for a fresh pair.

"I need you at the head of the table," she told Wick. "You're her second set of hands again. Same as before — hold her shoulders, keep her still, don't let her flinch when I cut. The difference is she's going to feel more of this than the last one. I've got local anesthetic for the outer layers but I can't deaden the inside and keep her conscious. She needs to stay conscious so I know her brain's still getting oxygen."

She snapped her gloves into place, moved to the instrument table, began selecting tools with the same practiced efficiency as before. Scalpel, retractor, clamps — the list she'd run through her head like a prayer she didn't believe in.

"Maren," she said, not looking up. "I'm going to give you something for the pain now. It won't take it away, but it'll make the edge softer. You might feel dizzy. You might feel like you're floating. That's the drugs. Don't fight it. Let it happen."

She filled a syringe from the vial, moved to Maren's side, found the IV line someone had started earlier, injected the contents.

"Twenty seconds," she said. "Then we start."

She looked at Wick, standing ready at the head of the table, the cooler of blood waiting on the counter behind him.

"Two units," she said. "That's not enough if it's the liver. It's enough if it's a mesenteric tear. I'll know in five minutes which one we're fighting. Until then, you hold her like she matters. She does. Even if she doesn't feel like it right now."

She picked up the scalpel. The lamp steadied.

"Maren. You feel it yet?"

Maren nodded, her eyes half-closed.

"Good," Sedge said. "Now we find out what's been killing you."

She lowered the blade.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I brace my hands on Maren's shoulders. Her skin is clammy. "I've got her," I say, my voice low. "Do it."

rung_labels.evidence: She cut through another layer of tissue... The forceps gripped and Sedge pulled. Slowly — you always went slowly on the second piece, on account of the swelling.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Shell fragment opened him in three places and tumbled through his chest cavity. I took two pieces of metal out of him that had no business being inside a human body.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: It tears muscle fibers, nicks vessels, sometimes crushes more than it cuts because the metal tumbles... Metal carries dirt, fabric, whatever it picked up on the way in. Burns the tract as it travels

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She lifted the edge of the gauze, peered at the line of black stitches she'd made, watched the slow seep of blood
