rung_labels.evidence: When we leave, he'll wake up in pain and confusion... If he doesn't make it — if the subclavian clot breaks loose, or the infection takes hold... What happens to us is we move to the next one

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't care if Wick was lying. Nobody was ever ready for this, least of all the boy on the table whose tunic she had already sheared away to reveal the grotesque, squared-off lumps where his shoulders should have been. 

"Left one first," she said, her voice dry as gravel. She reached down and took the boy's left wrist, tucking his forearm against her own side to get the necessary leverage. "It's the worse of the two. The humeral head is sitting forward, right under the collarbone. I'm going to rotate the arm outward to clear the lip of the socket, then I'm going to push up and in."

She looked up at Wick, her gaze hard and entirely devoid of pity under the greasy, flickering light of the lantern. 

"When the bone slips back, his muscles are going to spasm. He'll try to sit up. Lean your chest into him. Keep his collarbone flat to the table. If he shifts, I have to start over, and neither of us wants that."

She didn't wait for Wick to brace himself any further. She took a breath, wedged her boot gently but firmly into the boy's armpit for counter-traction—a brutal, necessary lever—and began to pull.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I lock my jaw as the boy lets out a choked-off cry. My arms shake with the strain of holding him down. "Gods," I mutter, staring at the sweat-stained canvas.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Leave the gods out of it, they aren't the ones holding his scapula," Sedge said, her teeth bared slightly with the physical exertion. Her boot heel pressed deeper into the hollow of the boy's armpit, stretching the tight, angry cords of his chest muscles. "He's fighting me. His deltoid is locked up like iron. I have to keep the traction steady until the muscle tires out and lets the bone slide past the glenoid lip. If I jerk it, I'll tear the capsule."

She didn't look up at Wick, but she could feel the table trembling under their combined weight. The boy’s heels kicked uselessly against the wood, a dull, rhythmic drumming of heels that she ignored with the ease of long habit. 

"Almost," Sedge muttered, her knuckles white where she gripped his wrist. She slowly rotated the boy's forearm outward, forcing the head of the humerus to turn. "There. It's clearing the bone now. Hold him down, Wick."

With a sharp, practiced shove of her hip and a sudden levering of her arms, she forced the arm back and inward. 

There was a sickening, wet *thunk* that vibrated through the wood of the table and into Sedge's own hands as the joint re-seated itself. The boy let out a high, thin whistle of air and his back arched violently, his entire torso trying to throw Wick off. 

Sedge kept her weight on the boy's forearm, pinning it against his side to keep the fresh reduction from slipping right back out. She watched the boy's face turn a gray, greasy color as he went limp, his breathing coming in shallow, ragged puffs.

"Left is in," Sedge said, wiping a smear of the boy's sweat from her forehead with her sleeve. She didn't offer the patient a moment to recover, nor did she offer Wick one. She stepped around the head of the table, her boots squelching slightly in the damp dirt of the tent floor. 

"Right one now," she said, reaching for the other arm. "This one's different. It's dislocated backward. The bone is wedged behind the socket. I'm going to have to pull straight down toward his feet while you push his shoulder blade forward from behind. Get ready to shift your grip."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"He’s not going to die of a pair of bad shoulders, Wick, and he’s keeping his legs," Sedge said, her voice flat and even as she reached for the boy’s right wrist. "But if we leave this one out, he won't be able to feed himself with his right hand, let alone hold a pike. He'll be a cripple by winter, and the army doesn't feed cripples."

She didn't look up to see if her words registered. She was already examining the right shoulder. It didn't look like the left one; instead of a bulging lump in the front, the front of the shoulder was hollowed out, flat as a board, while the back of the joint was swollen and deformed. 

"A posterior dislocation is stubborn," she explained, her fingers digging into the boy's cool, sweaty flesh to find the landmarks. "The head of the arm bone is hooked right behind the rear rim of the socket. If I just pull straight back, I’ll chip the bone or tear the rotator cuff to ribbons. We have to unlock it first."

She took the boy's right wrist in both of her hands, bending his elbow to a right angle. 

"I need you to shift," she ordered Wick. "Get around to his left side, reach across his chest, and get your palms behind his right shoulder blade. The scapula. When I start to pull down toward his hips, you are going to push that shoulder blade forward, toward me. We have to lever the ball out from behind the socket before it can slip back in."

She waited a beat for Wick to move, her boots digging into the dirt floor of the tent for traction. The boy on the table groaned, a low, bubbling sound in the back of his throat as consciousness flickered back toward the surface.

"Do it now, before he wakes up enough to fight us again," Sedge said. "Once you're in place, don't just lean. Push like you're trying to shove his shoulder blade right through his chest."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I scramble around the table, almost slipping in the mud. My hands slide over the kid's clammy skin as I get my palms behind his shoulder blade. "Alright," I say through gritted teeth. "Ready when you are."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Good. Keep your heels dug in," Sedge said, not looking at him. Her focus was entirely on the boy's right arm. She kept his elbow bent at a ninety-degree angle, using the forearm like a lever to control the rotation of the joint. 

"I’m going to pull down toward his feet to disengage the bone. When you feel his shoulder shift, you shove that blade forward. Don't wait for him to scream, just shove."

She braced her hip against the edge of the wooden table, dug her boots into the slick mud of the floor, and leaned her entire weight backward. 

The boy’s eyes snapped open, white-rimmed and blind with sudden, agonizing consciousness. A raw, rattling shriek tore from his throat, spraying a fine mist of bloody spit into the air. 

"Now, Wick! Push!" Sedge grunted, her shoulder muscles bunching under her grease-stained shirt as she dragged the arm downward, fighting the violent, instinctive contraction of the boy's torso. 

For a second, nothing moved. The bone was locked fast against the rear rim of the socket, stubborn as a rusted bolt. Sedge gave a sharp, heavy jerk downward, her teeth grinding together so hard her jaw ached. 

She felt the resistance yield. "Push!" she barked. 

With a dull, grinding scrape—the sound of cartilage dragging over bone—the humeral head cleared the rim. It didn't pop with a clean *thunk* like the left one; it slid home with a wet, heavy shudder that made the boy's entire frame go stiff as a board before he collapsed into a dead faint, his chin dropping to his chest, his breathing turning shallow and silent.

Sedge didn't let go of the arm immediately. She held it pinned against the boy's stomach, her dirty thumb pressing hard into the hollow of his wrist, her eyes fixed on the canvas wall as she counted. 

"Pulse is there," she muttered, her own breath coming short and hot in the damp air of the tent. "Good. Didn't pinch the axillary artery. If we'd done that, we'd be taking the arm off by morning."

She slowly let go of his wrist, her hands shaking slightly from the physical strain. She reached for a strip of graying, coarse linen from her kit. 

"He's out," she said, nodding toward the boy's pale, lax face. "Which is fine. It means he won't fight the bandages. Help me roll him slightly so I can bind both arms to his chest. If he moves them in his sleep, they'll pop right back out of the sockets before the joint capsule has a chance to swell and hold them."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge shook out the long strip of coarse linen, her fingers moving with the steady, unthinking rhythm of a woman who had tied the same knot ten thousand times. She looked from the bandage to the boy's bare, bruised torso, then up at Wick.

"You're seeing a pair of pockets that have been stretched out until they're loose as old sacks," Sedge said, her voice flat and instructional. She pointed a blunt, dirt-rimmed finger at the boy’s right shoulder. Already, the skin there was beginning to puff up, turning a dull, angry plum color under the greasy lantern light. 

"The ball at the top of the arm bone belongs in a shallow little cup on the side of his shoulder blade. It’s not a deep socket like the hip. It’s barely a saucer. The only thing keeping the arm attached to the trunk is a sleeve of tough, fibrous tissue—the capsule—and a few bands of muscle. When we pulled those bones back into place, we didn't heal them. We just put them back in the starting line."

She reached down, taking the boy's limp right wrist and laying his forearm flat across his stomach. 

"Right now, that fibrous sleeve is stretched thin and torn in places. It's wet paper. If he rolls over, or if his arm dangles off the edge of this table, the weight of the limb alone will pull the ball right back out of the saucer. There's nothing to stop it."

She stepped closer, holding one end of the linen band. 

"So we bind him. In an hour, his body is going to realize what's happened. It's going to flood both joints with fluid. They'll swell up until they're hard as rocks, hot to the touch, and he won't be able to move them an inch without screaming. That swelling is his body's way of casting the joint. It's ugly, it's painful, but it's the only thing that will hold the bones steady long enough for the tissue to start scarring over."

She looked up, her gray eyes fixing Wick over the boy's chest. 

"Get your hands under his left hip and his left shoulder blade. We need to tilt him toward you—just an inch or two off the wood—so I can slide the bandage under his back. Don't let his right arm drop when you do it. Keep it pinned to his ribs."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I slide my hands under him, my fingers sinking into the clammy sweat and grime on his skin. "Alright, lifting," I grunt, tilting him just enough to feel the shift in his dead weight. The kid's arm feels heavy and limp against his side. "How long before he can hold a sword again?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't answer immediately. She leaned down, her fingers catching the rough edge of the linen strip and sliding it smoothly through the narrow gap Wick had cleared between the boy's spine and the blood-darkened wood of the table. Her knuckles brushed against Wick’s damp fingers, cold and businesslike.

"A sword?" she said, pulling the bandage through until she had equal lengths on either side. She didn't look up. "Never, if he has any sense. But he’s in the infantry, which means he doesn't."

She took the tail of the bandage and brought it over the boy's left arm, pinning the elbow tight against his ribs. 

"The ligaments are like old wool now," she said, her voice dropping into that rhythmic, instructional drone she used to keep her own hands steady. "Once you stretch them that far, they don't snap back like spring steel. They stay loose. If he tries to swing a five-pound blade, the centripetal force alone will yank the humerus right out of the front of the cup again. The first time he tries a high guard, he'll dislocate both shoulders over his own head and stand there helpless while some conscript from the hills runs him through."

She crossed the linen over the boy's chest, pulling it tight enough to make the ribs creak. The boy let out a wet, whistling groan in his sleep, but didn't wake. 

"You can set him down," Sedge said, nodding to Wick. "Gently. Don't let his shoulders drop back against the wood too hard."

As Wick lowered the patient, Sedge began to wrap the remaining length of the bandage around the boy's middle, pinning his right arm down in the same fashion. She worked with a grim, practiced efficiency, tucking the loose end under the taut bands and pinning it with a rusty iron needle she fished from her apron pocket.

"If he's lucky, and if he keeps these bound for three weeks without trying to scratch his own nose, the scarring inside the joint might be thick enough to hold the bones in place for daily use," she said, wiping her palms on her apron. "He'll be able to carry a bucket. He'll be able to shovel manure. But the first time he tries to climb a wall or throw a spear, he'll feel them slip. He's garrison fodder now. Or a teamster."

She stepped back, her knees making a dry, cracking sound in the quiet of the tent. She looked down at the boy, then at Wick, her face pale and lined with grease and fatigue.

"Go wash your hands in the bucket outside," she said, reaching for a small flask of vinegar to clean her own fingers. "We have three more waiting in the ditch, and the rain is starting to come through the canvas."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge uncorked the small clay flask of vinegar with her teeth, spat the cork onto the dirt, and poured the sour, stinging liquid directly over her scraped knuckles. She didn't flinch as the acid bit into her raw skin. She simply rubbed her hands together, the sharp smell of the vinegar briefly cutting through the heavy, greasy stench of sweat, wet wool, and old blood that filled the tent.

"You want it straight," she said, her voice flat as a plank. "Fine."

She wiped her hands on the least-stained corner of her apron, her movements methodical. 

"A sword or a pike is clean. It cuts. It divides the meat, and if you're lucky, it goes between the ribs and misses the vitals. Shrapnel isn't clean. It’s lazy, and it’s hot."

She reached down to pick up a pair of iron forceps from her tray, squinting at them in the bad light before wiping them down with a vinegar-soaked rag. 

"It’s jagged iron, usually torn off a shell casing that’s been sitting in a damp wagon for six months. When the powder goes off, those pieces don't fly straight. They spin. They tumble through the air. By the time a chunk hits a man, it isn't a blade; it’s a hammer with teeth."

She looked up at Wick, her gray eyes dead and level. 

"It doesn't slide in. It punches. It takes a patch of his dirty wool coat, his greasy shirt, the lice in his seams, and whatever mud he was lying in, and it rams the whole mess six inches deep into his thigh or his belly. If the iron doesn't kill him, the wool will. In three days, the fibers rot inside the muscle, and the leg turns green."

She set the forceps down with a dull clink. 

"And inside the meat, it doesn't stop. If it hits a bone, it doesn't chip it. The force is too high. It shatters the shaft into fifty white splinters. The bone itself becomes secondary shrapnel. The jagged little needles get driven outward by the impact, shredding the nerves and the deep arteries from the inside out. You can pull the iron out, but you’ll spend an hour fishing for the pieces of the man's own femur with your fingers, and you'll miss three of them. Then those three rot, too."

She stepped toward the tent flap, lifting the heavy, wet canvas with one shoulder to look out into the grey, drizzling dark where the next stretchers were waiting. 

"The heat of the iron cauterizes the vessels as it tears through them," she added, her voice dropping a fraction. "Which means they don't bleed out on the field. They live long enough to get to this table, with a cup of dead, black meat cooked inside their shoulder or their hip. And then I have to cut the dead meat out until I find red, healthy blood, or the gangrene takes the rest of them."

She let the canvas drop, turning back to Wick. 

"That's what it does. Now go get the bucket. The next one has a hole in his ribs the size of my fist, and I need to be able to see my own fingers inside him."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I stare at my hands, still sticky with the kid's sweat. My stomach turns, but I don't look away. "Right," I say, my voice hoarse. "Bucket." I step outside, letting the cold rain hit my face for a second before I start scrubbing.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't wait for him to return before she got to work clearing the table. 

She stepped to the side of the fainted boy, hooked her forearms under his knees and his neck, and hoisted him with a grunt. He was small—most of the new draft were—but dead weight was always heavier than it had any right to be. She dragged him off the table and let him down onto a pallet of damp, flattened straw in the corner of the tent, where two other wounded men lay in the dark, smelling of gangrene and old grease. She adjusted the boy’s bound arms once, ensuring the knots weren't digging directly into his ribs, then left him. 

She took a handful of dry straw from a bundle near the tent pole and used it to scrape the worst of the boy's sweat, dirt, and grease off the planks of the table, throwing the soiled straw into a corner. 

By the time Wick stepped back inside, the rain dripping from his hair and his hands red-raw from the cold water, Sedge was already laid out. She had three clean needles threaded with coarse, waxed linen thread stuck through the lapel of her coat, and her fingers were slick with oil from the whetstone she had used to touch up her smallest scalpel.

"Set the bucket by the leg of the table," she said, her voice flat as she squinted through the greasy smoke of the lantern. "And don't stand where you block the light. The next one is breathing through his chest, which means we have about six minutes before his lung collapses entirely and smothers him from the inside."

As if on cue, the tent flap was kicked back. Two mud-splattered runners hauled a stretcher inside, their boots slipping on the wet floor. They dumped the stretcher onto the table with a heavy, wet rattle of pine poles and scurried back out into the rain without a word. 

The man on the canvas was older, his beard choked with dried mud and gray ash. He was conscious, his eyes rolling back in his head, his lips stained with a bright, frothy pink foam that bubbled every time he drew a breath. 

"Here," Sedge said, her hands already moving to the man's coat. She didn't bother with the buttons; she took her shears and slit the heavy wool from the hem to the collar, peeling the stiff, wet fabric back like the skin of an orange. "Look at the left side of the rib cage. See that?"

Between the fifth and sixth ribs, there was a ragged, black-rimmed hole about two inches wide. It didn't look like a wound so much as an open mouth. Every time the man gasped for air, the wound let out a wet, whistling *shuck-shuck* sound, drawing in the cold air of the tent and spitting out red foam.

"It’s a sucking wound," Sedge said, her fingers tracing the edge of the shattered rib without a hint of hesitation. "The iron went through the intercostal muscle and broke the bone. The lung itself might be nicked, but the real danger is the pressure. Every time he inhales, the chest cavity fills with air from the outside. The air gets trapped. It squashes the lung down until it’s the size of a fist, and then it starts pushing his heart and his windpipe over to the right side."

She reached for a square of thick, grease-smeared linen—paraffin cloth, stiff and foul-smelling. 

"We have to make a valve," she said, her voice dropping into that rhythmic, instructional tone. "If we seal it completely, the air leaking from his lung will build up inside and kill him anyway. If we leave it open, he drowns. Wick, get your hand on his throat. Feel the windpipe. If you feel it start to drift toward his right shoulder, you tell me instantly. That means the pressure is mounting."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"If talking keeps your hands steady, I'll talk," Sedge said, her voice dropping into a low, gravelly rhythm that rose just enough to be heard over the man's wet, rattling screams. 

She took a square of the stiff, yellowed paraffin cloth and held it between her teeth while she used a corner of her vinegar-soaked apron to clear the thick, frothy blood from the skin around the wound. The skin was cold and pebbled with gooseflesh. 

"I'm clearing the grease and mud off his ribs first," she said, her words slightly muffled around the cloth. "If the skin is wet, the wax won't stick, and if the wax doesn't stick, the seal leaks. If the seal leaks, he dies."

She spat the cloth into her hand and laid it flat over the hole. Instantly, the wet, whistling sound of the sucking wound stopped, replaced by the muffled, struggling thud of the man's heart against his ribs. The square of cloth bubbled upward as he exhaled, then slapped flat against his chest as he tried to draw breath.

"Now I'm pinning it," Sedge said. She reached up to her lapel and pulled the first needle free, the coarse, black-waxed thread trailing behind it. "I’m going to sew three sides of this square directly into his skin. The top and the two flanks. I’m leaving the bottom edge loose."

She drove the heavy needle through the wax cloth and deep into the flesh over the man's fifth rib. The man’s scream reached a thin, tearing pitch, his throat bulging as he tried to twist away from the needle. Sedge didn't blink. She looped the thread and pulled it tight, tying a hard, double-throw knot with a quick jerk of her fingers.

"The skin on the chest is thick, but it yields if you push hard enough," she said, her thumb pressing down to hold the knot while she snipped the thread with her teeth. "The needle has to go deep enough to catch the fascia—the gristle under the fat—otherwise his breathing will just tear the stitches out. That's one."

She reached for the second needle. 

"The reason I’m leaving the bottom open is simple physics," she continued, her hands moving with a rapid, mechanical precision that didn't match the violence of the screams. "When he breathes in, his chest expands, creating a vacuum. The vacuum pulls the paraffin cloth tight against his skin, sealing the hole so no air can get in from the outside. He’s forced to draw air down his windpipe, the way he’s supposed to. That’s how we keep the lung from collapsing further."

She drove the second needle in, three inches to the left of the first. The man’s chest heaved, a spray of bloody spit landing across Sedge's cheek. She didn't bother to wipe it off.

"But when he breathes out," she said, pulling the second knot tight, "the air that’s already trapped inside his chest cavity needs somewhere to go. If we sealed all four sides, that trapped air would have nowhere to escape. It would build up, push his heart over, and kill him. With the bottom open, the air pushes the flap outward and leaks out into the room. It’s a one-way valve. Made of grease and old shirts."

She took the third needle. The man on the table was starting to weaken, his screams turning into a rhythmic, desperate sobbing as his oxygen ran low. 

"How much longer?" Sedge said, repeating Wick's question as she aligned the needle with the third side of the flap. "Two minutes to finish the stitching. Then we wait. We wait five minutes to see if his windpipe stays in the middle of his throat. If it does, the valve is working and his lung is holding its own."

She pushed the needle through, her knuckles scraping against the man's sticky ribs as she dragged the thick thread through his flesh. 

"If his windpipe starts to drift to the right, it means the valve is clogged with a blood clot. If that happens, I have to stick my finger under the flap, clear the clot, and let the trapped air hiss out. If I don't, he suffocates in front of us."

She tied the final knot, cut the thread, and threw the empty needle onto the tray. She leaned over the man, her face inches from his chest, watching the yellow paraffin flap. 

With every ragged exhalation, a small puff of red foam and air hissed out from under the unsewn bottom edge of the cloth. With every inhalation, the cloth sucked flat against his ribs, sealing the wound.

"The valve is working," Sedge said, her voice dropping the instructional tone and returning to its usual flat, exhausted rasp. She wiped her bloody cheek with the back of her sleeve, leaving a dark smear across her temple. "Keep your hand on his throat, Wick. Don't let go yet. Feel the windpipe. Tell me if it starts to move."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: My hand stays pressed to his neck, feeling the frantic pulse there. "It's centered," I say, my voice low. "He's still breathing through the foam."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Good," Sedge said, her voice a dry rattle. She didn't look up from the yellowed flap of paraffin cloth. "Keep it there. If he starts to choke on his own spit, tilt his head to the right—away from the wound—so the fluid drains out of his mouth instead of back down his windpipe."

She reached down, her bloody fingers gently but firmly pressing around the margins of the wound, feeling for the grinding of broken bone beneath the skin. 

"The foam is blood mixed with air from the bronchial tree," she explained, her tone as level as if she were describing a recipe for gruel. "It means the iron didn't just break the ribs; it nicked the lung tissue itself. He’s bleeding into his own bellows. Every time he draws a breath, he’s churning that blood into lather. If it gets too thick, he'll drown in a cupful of his own fluid."

She leaned over the man's chest, her ear nearly touching the wet canvas of his shirt as she listened. The sound was a wet, crackling whistle, like dry twigs burning in a puddle. 

"The left lung is still working, but it's half-collapsed," she muttered, sitting back on her heels. "We have to check his back now. If the chunk of iron was small and fast, it might still be inside him. If it was large, it went right through. If there’s an exit wound on his back and we don't seal it, the valve on the front is useless. The air will just suck in from behind."

She reached under the man's right shoulder, her fingers sliding through the cold, greasy mud that had pooled on the stretcher. 

"When I tell you, we’re going to roll him toward you, just enough for me to get my hand under his shoulder blade," she said to Wick. "You have to keep his neck straight. If his head flops, his windpipe will kink, and with only one working lung, he doesn't have the margin for it. Ready?"

She didn't wait for an answer. She got her shoulder under the man's hip, her boots bracing against the slick mud of the floor. 

"Roll him. Slow."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge’s shoulder strained as they rolled the man. Her right hand slid beneath his wet wool coat, down the cold, sticky curve of his spine. 

Her fingers sank into a soft, hot crater just below his left shoulder blade. 

"Exit wound," she said. Her voice didn't rise; it was just a statement of location. "Larger than the front. The iron was tumbling by the time it crossed through. It dragged the back of his rib out with it. The bone ends are pointing outward like splintered kindling."

She didn't have another square of paraffin. She reached into her leather satchel and pulled out a fistful of coarse, unwashed tow—the rough, brown fiber left over from flax spinning. 

"We don't put a valve on the back," she said, her fingers shoving the coarse fiber directly into the bloody hole. "The back is where we plug the drain. If I leave this open, the air will bypass the front valve entirely. I'm packing it tight. It’s going to feel like I’m stuffing a chimney with dry grass."

The man's body gave a sudden, pathetic jerk against Wick's hands, but he didn't have the breath left to scream. A thin, pink bubble popped on his lip and ran down into his grey beard. 

Sedge used three broad, clumsy stitches to cross the skin over the packing, sealing the tow inside the meat. 

"That's done," she said. 

She let the man's weight slide back down onto the canvas of the stretcher. He lay there, his chest rising and falling in shallow, desperate hitches, the front flap bubbling with every breath. 

Sedge stood up, her spine popping with a dry sound. She looked down at Wick sitting on the mud floor, his hands red and shaking, his face pale under the lantern. She didn't tell him to get up. She didn't offer him a hand. She simply took her flask of vinegar, poured a splash onto her apron, and began to scrub the black blood from her fingers.

"You want the rest," she said. "The part after the needles."

She sat on the edge of the empty wooden box she used for her dressings, her knees apart, her elbows resting on them. 

"Here’s the rest. If he survives the night without his lung filling with blood and drowning him from the inside, his body will start to heat. By tomorrow noon, he’ll have a fever that will make his skin feel like a hot brick. That’s the inflammation. His heart will be running at a gallop, trying to pump blood to the torn meat to repair it."

She rubbed her palms together, the sharp smell of the vinegar rising between them. 

"But the meat is full of dirt. I cleared what I could see, but I didn't get all of it. No one can. In forty-eight hours, the wound will start to run. If we’re lucky, it’ll be thick, yellow-white pus. We call that laudable. It means his body is holding the rot at bay, fighting it out in the margins of the muscle. If we're unlucky, the discharge will be thin, dark, and smell like a ditch at low tide. That’s the hospital gangrene. It eats the tissue faster than a dog eats grease. It turns the red muscle to grey slime, and then the slime turns black."

She looked at the lantern, her eyes flat and unblinking. 

"If that happens, there is nothing to sew. The skin goes soft. The stitches I just put in his ribs will simply tear through the rotting flesh like thread through wet bread. The wound will open back up, and he’ll lie on that straw in the corner and whistle through his chest again until his heart gives out from the strain."

She stopped scrubbing her fingers. She looked down at her hands, the vinegar drying in the grey lines of her skin. 

"And if he survives the rot? If the wound heals and the skin closes?" She let out a short, dry sound that might have been a laugh if there were any humor in it. "The lung will be scarred. It’ll be stuck to the inside of his ribs by the old inflammation. He’ll never take a deep breath again without a sharp, stabbing pain under his arm. He’ll have a dry, hacking cough that will keep him awake every night until he dies of a winter cold three years from now because his chest doesn't have the strength to clear the phlegm."

She stood up, her apron heavy with wet blood. 

"That’s the rest, Wick. We don't save them. We just patch the leaks so they can crawl a little further down the road before they fall apart. Now get up. The rain is getting heavier, and the next one in the ditch has been waiting twenty minutes."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I push myself up off the ground, my legs stiff. "What's the next one got?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t answer him until she had grabbed the older man by the shoulders of his greasy coat. She jerked her chin toward the man's muddy boots. 

"Grab his ankles," she said, her voice dropping back into that flat, rhythmic drone. "We need him on the straw before the next one comes in. If we leave him on the table, the blood from the next man will get under his paraffin flap and ruin the seal."

She waited until Wick took the weight of the legs, and together they swung the unconscious, whistling man off the table and down onto the crowded straw pallet in the corner. The man let out a soft, bubbling grunt as his back hit the ground, but his eyes didn't open. 

Sedge stood up and wiped her hands on her apron again, though at this point she was only shifting old blood around to make room for the new. 

"A leg," she said, finally answering Wick’s question. "Compound fracture of the tibia and fibula. Left side. A wagon wheel went over him while they were trying to haul the reserve ammunition out of the creek."

She reached into her wooden chest and pulled out a long, heavy iron bone-saw, its teeth dull and dark with old grease, along with a short, broad-bladed knife that looked more like a butcher’s tool than a surgeon’s. She laid them side-by-side on the bloody planks of the table. 

"The boys who brought him in put a tourniquet on his thigh," she continued, her fingers tracing the edge of the saw to check for chips. "A strip of canvas and a hickory stick, twisted tight enough to stop the spurting. They did it at midday. It’s now nearly midnight."

She looked up at Wick, her gray eyes flat under the greasy light. 

"You know what happens to meat when you leave it in a dark drawer for twelve hours, Wick? It goes soft. It starts to turn. The same thing happens to a leg when you starve it of blood. The muscle cells die first. They burst. They leak their contents—potassium, acid, dead proteins—directly into the stagnant pool of blood trapped below the rope."

She picked up a small bottle of grain alcohol and poured a sparse, careful trickle over the blade of the broad knife, using her thumb to smear the spirit along the steel. 

"If we just untie that rope now, all that dead, poisoned blood is going to rush straight back into his main circulation. It’ll hit his kidneys like a bucket of lye. It’ll reach his heart in three seconds, and the potassium will stop his pulse before he can even draw a breath to scream. It’s called the tourniquet death. The red-leg rot."

She set the knife down with a dry *clack*. 

"So we don't untie the rope. We leave it tight. And we cut the leg off three inches above it, where the meat is still pink and the blood is still clean."

Before she could say more, the tent flap bulged outward and the two mud-splattered runners returned, carrying the next stretcher between them. They were breathing hard, their shoulders hunched against the rain that was now drumming steadily against the canvas overhead. They hoisted the stretcher onto the table, the pine poles creaking under the weight of the man. 

This one was young—barely eighteen, with the soft, pale face of a town clerk. He was shivering violently, his teeth chattering so hard the sound was like dry dice in a cup. His left leg lay at an impossible, zig-zag angle, the mid-calf torn open to reveal three inches of white, splintered shin-bone protruding through a wet, grey tear in his trousers. High up on his thigh, nearly at the groin, a strip of dirty canvas was knotted tight, held in place by a notched oak twig that had been twisted until the skin beneath it was black and dead.

"He's cold," Sedge observed, her fingers already going to the boy's neck to check the pulse. It was thin, fast, and light as a moth's wing. "The shock is taking him. Wick, get his head. Keep him from rolling. If he starts to thrash while I'm through the bone, he'll splinter the stump and I'll have to go higher, near the hip, and no one survives a hip-joint cut."

She reached for her shears, her movements steady, almost leisurely in their lack of hurry. 

"We do this fast," she said, her voice dropping into the low, gravelly rhythm. "I’m going to make a circular cut through the skin first, about three inches above the canvas strap. I have to go deep enough to let the skin retract. If I don't leave enough skin to fold over the bone end, the stump will heal open, like a raw turnip, and the bone will rot from the air."

She positioned her shears at the cuff of the boy's trousers and began to cut the wet wool away, exposing the cold, grey flesh of the thigh. 

"Hold his shoulders, Wick. Once the steel hits the periosteum—the skin over the bone—he’s going to try to jump off this table, and he’s stronger than he looks."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I lock my arms over the boy's chest, my weight pinning his shoulders to the table. The kid's eyes are wide, uncomprehending. "I've got him," I say, the words sticking in my dry throat.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't waste time looking at the boy's face. She kept her eyes on the cold, grey skin of his thigh, three inches above the knotted canvas strap. She took the short, broad-bladed knife in her right hand, her fingers gripping the wooden hilt with a familiarity that was almost casual. 

"I'm starting the skin-cut," she said, her voice dropping into that low, gravelly drone. "It’s a circular incision. I have to go all the way around the limb in one clean sweep. If I hack at it, the edges will be ragged, and ragged skin doesn't heal; it dies and sloughs off."

She pressed the edge of the blade into the flesh. 

The boy didn't scream immediately—the shock of the cold steel seemed to take a second to register through his stupor—but then his chest heaved violently under Wick's hands. A high, bubbling shriek broke from his throat, his heels slamming against the wooden planks of the table with enough force to shake the grease-lantern overhead. 

"Hold him," Sedge muttered, her blade moving through the pale skin and the yellow, pebbled layer of fat beneath it. The blood didn't spurt; because of the tourniquet, it merely welled up in a dark, thick ribbon, spilling over her knuckles. "The fat is thin on this one. He's been on salt-pork and hardtack for six months. That makes the skin easier to slide."

She completed the circle, her knife meeting the start of the cut with practiced precision. Instantly, the severed skin began to shrink back toward the groin, exposing the dark, wet red of the thigh muscles beneath. 

"Now the muscle," Sedge said, her voice steady as she swapped the knife for a larger, heavier blade. "This is the hard part. The muscle is thick, and it’s under tension. I have to cut it at an angle—a cone shape, pointing up toward his hip. If I cut it flat, the bone will stick out like a peg when we’re done. I have to leave enough meat to bury the stump."

She drove the blade deep into the quadriceps. 

The boy’s body went completely rigid. His head thrashed from side to side, his eyes rolling up until only the greasy whites showed. Under Wick’s hands, his collarbones felt like they might snap under the strain of his own convulsions. 

"He’s trying to pull his leg up," Sedge said, leaning her shoulder into the boy's shin to keep the leg straight. "Don't let his chest rise. If his back arches, he’ll tear his own muscles against my knife."

She dragged the blade through the thick, fibrous meat. The sound was wet and heavy, like a spade cutting through thick clay. She worked her way around the bone, slicing through the hamstrings at the back of the thigh until the blade grated against the hard, white shaft of the femur. 

"There’s the bone," Sedge said. She set the knife down and reached for the smaller scalpel. "The periosteum—the skin of the bone—is full of nerves. It’s what hurts the worst. I have to scrape it clean off the shaft where the saw is going to go. If I don't, the saw will catch on the membrane and tear it, and he’ll have bone-ache for whatever days he has left."

With three quick, hard strokes of the scalpel, she scraped the tough, clear membrane away, exposing a circular band of bare, ivory-colored bone. 

She picked up the saw. 

"This is the noisy part," she said, her gray eyes lifting to Wick for a fraction of a second. "The teeth are set wide so they don't clog with bone-meal. When I start, it's going to jump. Keep his hips still, Wick. If the bone shifts while the teeth are in it, the shaft will splinter like dry pine."

She placed the dull, dark blade of the saw against the bare white femur. She drew it back once, slowly, to score a groove in the bone. 

The boy let out a sound that didn't sound like a man at all—a dry, rattling bark that ended in a wet choke. 

Sedge began to saw. 

The sound was a rhythmic, horrible *shreep-shreep* that filled the small tent, cutting through the steady patter of the rain on the canvas. A fine, pale dust—wet with blood—began to drift down onto the muddy floor, smelling faintly of hot iron and old teeth. 

"The femur is thickest in the middle," Sedge said, her shoulder working back and forth with the steady, unhurried rhythm of a woodcutter. "I'm halfway through. The bone-meal is coming out red now, which means we’re into the marrow. That's where the blood is made. It’s soft in there, like lard."

She didn't speed up, even as the boy’s breathing turned into a series of short, dry gasps, his skin turning the color of skimmed milk. 

"Almost through," she muttered. Her left hand cupped the lower part of the leg, supporting the weight so it wouldn't snap and splinter the remaining bridge of bone before she was finished. "There."

With a dry, snapping *crack*, the bone parted. 

Sedge lifted the severed limb—the heavy, cold mass of the lower leg, still encased in its muddy boot and torn trousers—and tossed it into the wooden tub at the foot of the table with a dull, wet thud. 

"Now the vessels," she said, her hands already reaching into the pool of dark meat at the end of the stump. She didn't look at the tub. "We have to find the femoral artery before we loosen that canvas strap. It’s about the thickness of a goose quill, and it’s tucked right behind the bone. If we miss it when the pressure comes back, he’ll bleed out in forty seconds."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge glanced up once — not at Wick's face but at his hands, checking the placement of them on the man's shoulders, the angle of his elbows. She adjusted his left hand herself, pushing it in closer to the collarbone.

"There. Weight down through your arms, not your palms. If you brace with your palms he'll throw you." She said it flat, the way she'd say a road was muddy.

The man on the table made a wet noise. Sedge ignored it and threaded her fingers through the wound in his thigh, feeling for the shape of the ball. The lamp guttered and she cursed it, briefly, then went back to feeling.

"It's in the meat, not the bone," she said. "That's the good news. Bad news is it's deep and it's sitting on the artery or near enough that I'd rather not go in blind." She wiped her hand on her apron, picked up the probe, checked the tip against the pad of her thumb. "I'm going to open him a little wider. He's going to come up off the table. Don't look at his face. Look at where your hands are. If you look at his face you'll ease off without meaning to."

She set the blade against the skin.

"On three. One. Two."

She cut on two. She always cut on two. Men braced wrong for three.

The body came up under Wick's hands like something trying to become a fish. Sedge kept cutting, steady, an inch and then another, opening the wound wide enough to work in. Blood came up over her wrist and she spoke through it, not loud, more to herself than to anyone.

"Good. Good. Hold him. That's holding. Don't move."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *My arms burn from the strain and I can feel the wet heat of blood soaking through the man's tunic. I keep my eyes locked on my knuckles, white-knuckled against his collarbone.* "How much longer?" *My voice comes out tighter than I meant it to.*

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't look up. She had the probe in now, working it slow along the track of the wound, her other hand pressed flat against the thigh to feel what the probe was doing from the outside. Her whole face had gone still in the way it did when she was listening with her fingers.

"Don't ask me that," she said. Not unkind. Just flat. "You ask me that and I start rushing. I start rushing and he bleeds out. Answer's always the same anyway. Long as it takes."

The man made another noise, thinner now, and one of his legs kicked weakly against the table. Sedge shifted her hip to pin it.

"Breathe out through your mouth. You're holding your breath. That's why your arms are burning." She eased the probe another quarter inch and stopped. "There it is. Sitting right where I said. All right."

She set the probe down and picked up the forceps, wiped them once against her apron more from habit than cleanliness. The apron wasn't clean either.

"Now listen. This next part he'll feel more than the cutting. I'm going in after it and I'm going to have to spread the meat to get purchase. He'll try to sit up. Not buck — sit up. Different motion. You'll want to push down harder but if you push down harder on his shoulders you'll snap something under my hands. Keep the weight you've got. Just keep it there. Understand?"

She glanced up then, briefly, to make sure he did.

"Good. Breathe out. Here we go."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge had the forceps in and was already working, her wrist turned at an angle that would have looked wrong to anyone who hadn't watched her do it a hundred times. She didn't answer right away. She got her fingers around the ball first, felt it shift, felt the give of the tissue around it, and only then spoke.

"Neither, if I get it out clean and the bleeding stops when I take my hand off. Both, if I nick the artery going after it." She adjusted her grip. "So somewhere between. Ask me again in ten minutes."

The man tried to sit up. Sedge had said he would. His stomach came off the table in a slow hard arch and Wick's arms took it and held, and Sedge kept her hands exactly where they were, moving only the two fingers that mattered.

"Good. That's good holding. Don't ease."

She got the ball moving. It came up through the track slower than she wanted, catching once on something she couldn't see, and she made a small sound in her throat and worked it sideways until it came free. She dropped it in the tin dish without looking. It rang.

"Out," she said. Then, because the next part mattered more than the first: "Now we find out."

She took her hand away from the thigh. Watched. Counted, silently, the way she counted everything.

Blood welled up but it welled — it didn't jump. She let out a breath through her nose.

"Meat wound," she said. "Just meat. He keeps the leg. Probably keeps the rest of him too, if the fever doesn't get clever." She was already reaching for the needle. "You can breathe now. Don't let go yet, but you can breathe."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't realize I was holding, my arms trembling a little as the tension eases. *I watch her thread the needle, my voice rough.* "You cut on two on purpose, didn't you?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge had the needle threaded already, catgut wet and dark, and she was setting the first stitch before she answered. Her hands were steady in the way that had nothing to do with calm and everything to do with practice.

"Every time," she said. "Tell a man three and he braces on three. Braces on three, he tenses the whole leg, tenses the leg and the muscle grips whatever I've got in it. Cut on two, he's still getting ready. Gets ready around the knife instead of against it."

She pulled the stitch through. Not gentle. Efficient.

"Same reason I told you not to look at his face. Anything you know is coming, your body argues with. Better to lie a little. To him, to you. Not to me." She set the next stitch. "I need to know what's actually happening or I kill someone."

The man on the table had gone quiet again, breathing shallow but breathing. Sedge worked down the length of the wound, four stitches, five, her head tilted to catch what light the lamp was giving.

"You did well," she said, and it was the flattest compliment a person could give, but she meant it. "Arms'll shake for an hour. That's normal. Don't try to hold a cup of tea for a while. You'll wear it."

She tied off the last stitch, bit the thread short, and finally looked up at him properly for the first time since she'd started.

"You can let go now."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge wiped her hands on the apron and then, because that was worse than nothing, on the inside of her sleeve. She didn't move to cover the leg. If he wanted to look, she'd let him look.

"All right." She set her fingertip near the wound, not on it. "This here — the long line, that's my cut. Clean edges. That's what you want. Ragged means you sawed, and sawing tears more than it opens. The stitches are close together because thigh meat pulls when he walks and I don't want it opening on him in a week."

She moved her finger.

"That darker red, deeper in — that's muscle. Healthy muscle looks like that. Wet, dark, like raw beef. If it looked grey or brown you'd be seeing something dead and we'd be having a different conversation." She indicated the paler tissue at the edge. "That yellow's fat. Some men have more, some less. Doesn't bleed much. Cuts like soft cheese."

Her finger moved again, tracking the line of something under the skin he wouldn't have picked out on his own.

"That ridge, there — that's the artery. What I was worried about. You can see how close I was working. Half an inch off and we'd be mopping the floor instead of stitching him." She said it without drama. It was just where the artery was. "The ball was sitting just past it. That's why I went slow."

She straightened, rolled her shoulder once, and reached for the strip of linen she'd laid out at the start.

"The blood on his tunic and on you — most of that's from before I started. Wounds bleed hardest in the first minutes, then they slow. What I opened bled less than what the ball did going in. Looks worse than it is because it's on cloth. Cloth wicks. Makes a spoonful look like a cup."

She began to wrap the thigh, firm, not tight.

"That's what you're seeing. Man with a hole in his leg, closed up, going to hurt like the devil for a month and then he'll walk. Nothing mysterious about any of it, once you've had your hands in a few."

She tied the bandage off and finally, briefly, allowed herself to lean her weight on the edge of the table.

"You asked the right question, by the way. Most don't. Most would rather imagine, and then they see it worse in their heads for years."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I stare at the bandaged leg, the reality of it sinking in. "Guess I'll be seeing that in my dreams." I step back, wiping my bloody hands on my trousers. "What do we do with him now?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge was already moving, though slower now, the way she always moved when the sharp part was done and the tired part started. She checked the man's pulse at the throat with two fingers, counted, seemed satisfied enough.

"He sleeps. Here, till morning, because moving him now undoes half of what I just did. You and I take turns sitting with him." She glanced at Wick's hands, still red at the knuckles. "You'll wash first. Bucket outside, the one with the lye. Scrub till your skin hurts, then scrub a bit more. Under the nails especially. You touch your face before you wash and I'll box your ears."

She began laying the instruments in the tin pan, one at a time, in the order she'd want them next.

"When you come back you sit on that stool and you watch his chest. Count breaths against your own. If they get fast and shallow, or if they get slow and far apart, you wake me. If the bandage goes through — soaked, not spotted, there's a difference — you wake me. If he starts shivering hard enough to shake the cot, you wake me. Anything else, you let me sleep, because there'll be another one before dawn and I'd rather meet him rested."

She wiped the probe last, held it up to the lamp, set it down.

"Dreams." She said the word like she was tasting whether it was worth answering. "You'll have them. Not much to be done. Don't drink to stop them, that's the only advice worth giving. Drink makes them louder and puts them in the daytime too."

She untied her apron, folded the bloodied side inward out of habit, and hung it on the nail.

"Go on. Wash. I'll take first sit."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge stopped with her hand still on the apron nail. She turned, considered him for a moment — not weighing whether to tell him but whether he'd asked because he wanted to know or because he wanted to prove something. She decided it didn't matter. Either way the answer was the same.

"All right." She sat down on the stool herself, since she was going to be talking, and rolled her sleeves back down over the red at her wrists.

"A ball like the one I just took out — round, lead, slow — that's the kindest of them. It punches a hole roughly its own size, drags cloth and skin in with it, stops when it runs out of push. Meat closes up behind it more or less. That's what he had. That's why he keeps the leg."

She wiped her palm absently on her knee.

"Shrapnel's different. Shrapnel isn't shaped. It's whatever the shell was made of, torn into pieces, and every piece has edges. Some spin. Some tumble. They don't punch, they tear. A piece the size of your thumbnail goes in and it doesn't make a hole, it makes a cavity — pushes the meat aside going in and the meat doesn't spring back, it stays open, full of blood and cloth and whatever was on the ground when he fell. Grass. Dirt. Bits of the other man next to him, sometimes. All of it in there."

She kept her voice level. She was describing a road.

"And it doesn't stop where you'd think. Metal that shape hits bone and it skips. Goes sideways. I've pulled a piece out of a man's back that went in at his hip. I've pulled a piece out of a lung that went in through the arm. You can't track them by the entry. You have to feel for them, and half the time you don't find them at all, and they sit in there and fester until either the body walls them off or it doesn't."

She paused. Looked at the man on the table.

"The tearing's the worst of it, though. A ball crushes tissue. Shrapnel shreds it. Muscle doesn't knit back from shredded the way it knits back from a clean cut. What you get is a mess of scar and dead meat, and dead meat rots whether it's still attached to a living man or not. That's when I take the leg. Not because of the wound. Because of what the wound turned into three days later."

She rubbed her thumb across the pad of her forefinger, feeling for something that wasn't there.

"And it's hot. People forget that. The metal comes off the shell hot enough to cook what it touches on the way through. So you get a wound that's torn and dirty and burned, all at once. Body doesn't know which one to fight first. Usually loses."

She looked up at him.

"That straight enough?"

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow, my throat dry. "Yeah. Straight enough." I look down at my hands again, the blood under my nails. "You think the dreams are better or worse for knowing?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge considered it. She didn't answer quickly, and she didn't answer the way people usually answered when they wanted to comfort. She looked at the lamp, at the man on the table, at nothing.

"Worse, for a while. Then better."

She shifted on the stool, stretching one leg out. Her knee cracked. She ignored it.

"When you don't know, your head fills the gap with something worse than what's actually there. Bodies in dreams do things bodies don't do. You imagine the wound goes deeper than it does, imagine the man suffered longer than he did, imagine you could've stopped something you couldn't. That kind of dream doesn't wear out. It just keeps making itself up new every night."

She rubbed at a spot on her forearm where the blood had dried and gone tight.

"Knowing gives the dream edges. You dream what you saw, and what you saw was a specific thing that happened once and ended. Ended with him breathing, in this case. Dreams like that go quiet eventually. Not fast. But eventually."

She glanced at him.

"That's the theory, anyway. I've been wrong before." She stood up, joints unhappy about it. "Go wash. The knowing doesn't help either of us if you give him fever from your fingernails."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't argue. She'd already turned back to the table before he finished speaking, and her hands were moving before her mouth caught up.

"He's woken because I moved him wrong when I checked the pulse. My fault. Happens." She had the apron back on, tied one-handed at the small of her back while the other hand was already at his thigh, palm flat, feeling. "Bandage is spotted, not through. Good. Stitches held. That's what the screaming's about — he's feeling the stitches pull because he's tensing the leg. Not a new wound. Just the old one talking."

She reached for the small brown bottle at the end of the row, uncorked it with her teeth, and tipped a careful measure into a tin cup with water already in it.

"Laudanum. Not enough to kill him, not enough to take the pain fully, enough to take the edge off and put him under again in about four minutes. Any more and his breathing slows past where I want it, and I've watched enough men stop breathing from too much of this to be careful with the pour." She set the bottle back. Corked it. "I'm going to get it into him now. You keep his shoulders. His head'll thrash. Turn it to the side if he vomits — he might, on this — and don't let him choke on it. That's the only new thing I'm asking of you."

She got her hand under his jaw, thumb at one hinge and fingers at the other, and pressed inward. His mouth opened. She poured. Not fast. Steady, the way you'd water something you wanted to keep alive.

"Swallow, damn you. There. There he goes."

Most of it went down. Some came back at the corner of his mouth and she wiped it with the back of her wrist and kept her hand at his jaw a moment longer to make sure he wouldn't spit the rest.

"Four minutes. Maybe three. Keep holding. He'll fight harder before he goes softer — that's the drug meeting the pain in the middle, they wrestle for a bit before one wins." She was already checking the bandage again, lifting only the top edge, peering underneath with the lamp tilted close. "Stitches are clean. Nothing weeping that shouldn't. He's just angry with what's already been done, not with anything new."

The man arched. Wick's arms took it. Sedge braced her hip against the table without thinking.

"What I'm doing now — nothing, is what I'm doing. That's the truth of it. Watching. Waiting for the drug. The worst part of this work isn't the cutting, it's the standing still while a man screams and knowing the right answer is to do nothing to him for four minutes. Everything in you says fix it. But there's nothing left to fix in this minute. Just the waiting."

She counted, silently, the way she counted everything.

"Two minutes gone. He's slowing. Hear it? The screams are coming further apart. That's the drug finding him." She adjusted her grip on his jaw, gentler now. "One more minute and he's out. Then I check the bandage properly, re-wrap if it's shifted, and we go back to sitting. That's all. No more knife tonight unless something opens under the wrap, and it won't. I'd feel it already."

She glanced up at Wick, at his white knuckles, at his face.

"You're doing it right. Keep holding. Don't ease till I say."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I watch the man's breathing slow, his body finally going slack under my hands.* "Will he remember any of that?" I ask, my voice low.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge waited a moment before she answered. She was easing the bandage back, checking underneath one more time, and she didn't like to talk while she was looking. When she'd satisfied herself that nothing had torn open under the thrashing, she straightened and rolled her shoulders back until something in her spine gave.

"Some of it. Not in order." She wiped her hands, this time on a rag that was only mostly filthy. "Laudanum muddles it. He'll remember pain but not shape — won't remember the cut, won't remember your hands on him, won't remember the screaming. Might remember a face. Might remember the lamp. Sometimes they remember a smell and nothing else. Brains are peculiar about what they file when the body's busy trying not to die."

She set the rag down.

"The screaming just now, though — that he might keep. That was after the worst of it, when the drug was thinnest in him. Bad luck for him if he does. Better if he doesn't." She looked at the man's face, slack now, mouth open a little. "He'll wake tomorrow thinking he had a bad dream and a sore leg. Ask him what happened and he'll tell you a story that's half wrong. Let him. Correcting them doesn't help. They fill in what's missing with something they can live with, and that's usually kinder than the truth."

She sat down on the stool again, more heavily this time. The tiredness was starting to catch her up.

"You'll remember it, though. Every bit. That's the trade. He gets to forget because he was the one being cut. You held him down, so you get to keep it." She said it without pity, the way she said most things. "Fair or not, that's how it sorts out."

She nodded toward the tent flap.

"Go wash now. He's under. I've got him. Come back when your hands are clean and I'll show you how to check a pulse without waking a man who doesn't want to be woken."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at him where he'd gone down. She didn't tell him to get up. She didn't offer a hand. She'd learned early that when a man put himself on the floor after his first bad one, the floor was where he needed to be, and pulling him up before he was ready just meant he'd go down again later somewhere worse.

She moved the stool closer to him instead. Sat on it. Rested her forearms on her knees and let her hands hang between them, palms up, because they'd started to ache and open was better than closed.

"The rest." She said it slowly, like she was deciding where to start. "All right."

She looked at the lamp for a moment. Then at him.

"The rest is that you'll do this again tomorrow. Not maybe. Will. There's a push coming from the south road and I've been told to expect twenty by nightfall and it'll be forty. That's how the arithmetic runs here. Whatever they tell you, double it. Whatever you plan for, plan for twice. You'll hold another man down before this time tomorrow, and probably three more before the day after, and the one after that you'll stop counting because counting stops helping."

She rubbed at the base of her thumb with the opposite hand, working something loose in the joint.

"The rest is that the first one is the one you feel. The second one you feel less. By the tenth you're doing it the way you tie your boots, and that frightens people when it happens to them, but it shouldn't. It's the body being sensible. You can't hold twenty men down in a week and feel each one the way you felt this one. You'd stop being useful. The body knows. It turns the feeling down like a lamp wick. Doesn't turn it off — turns it down. You'll still feel them. Just quieter. And the quiet isn't the same as not caring, though it'll look like it from the outside and sometimes from the inside too."

She glanced toward the man on the table. His chest rose and fell.

"The rest is that some of them die on you. Not most. But some. And not always the ones you'd expect — the bad ones you save and the small ones you lose, and there's no lesson in it and no pattern, and if you go looking for one you'll find one that isn't there and it'll ruin you. I've watched it ruin better than me. Man who worked this tent before I did — he kept a list. Names, wounds, what he tried, what worked, what didn't. Thought he could learn his way out of losing them. Shot himself in the spring of the second year with the list in his pocket. So no lists. You do the work, and the ones who live live and the ones who don't don't, and you don't carry the ones who don't past the moment you set them down. You can't. There isn't room."

Her voice hadn't changed. She was telling him where the road was muddy.

"The rest is that you'll want to drink. I told you already. I'll tell you again because saying it once doesn't take. You'll want to drink because after a day like today your hands will still be moving when you try to sleep, and drink is the fastest thing that stops the moving. It also stops other things. Stops you being any use in the morning. Stops your judgment before it stops your hands, which is the worst order for it to stop in. I've seen medics kill men because they were drunk when the wound came in and they cut where they shouldn't have. So. Tea. Bad tea, all night if you need it. Not drink."

She paused. Looked at him properly.

"The rest is that you'll go strange. Not mad. Strange. You'll stop being able to talk to people who haven't done this. Your family, if you have one. Friends from before. They'll ask how you are and you'll open your mouth and nothing will come out that fits in the room you're in. That's normal. That's every one of us. You'll find that the only people you can talk to are the people who were in the tent with you, and even then not about the tent. About other things. The weather. Card games. You'll sit next to a man who watched you hold someone's shoulders down and you won't mention it, either of you, and that not-mentioning will be the closest thing to friendship you've got for a long time. Take it. Don't ask it to be more than that. It's enough."

She was quiet a moment.

"The rest is that you'll get better at it. That's the part nobody warns you about, because it sounds like praise and it isn't. You'll get faster. You'll get calmer. You'll cut on two without being told. You'll pour laudanum without measuring because your hand knows the weight. And one day you'll do something that would have made you sick in the first month and you won't notice you did it until hours later, and when you notice you'll feel — not sick. Something worse than sick. You'll feel like you've lost track of who you were before, and you'll try to find him, and he won't be there, and that's the day you'll want to drink most of all and you still can't."

She let out a breath.

"The rest is that some of them thank you. Not many. Most don't remember you well enough to. But some do, later, when they've healed and they come looking. And you'll think you want that, when it hasn't happened yet — you'll think a thank-you would balance some of it out. It doesn't. It puts a face on the ones who lived and the ones who didn't stay faceless, and that's a bad trade. I don't take visitors any more, if I can help it. That's not shame. That's arithmetic. The math doesn't work in favour of remembering."

She looked at her hands. Turned one over. Looked at the back of it.

"The rest is that this is work. That's the last of it and the most of it. It's not a calling and it's not a punishment and it's not making you into anything you weren't already. It's work. Somebody has to do it. Today that's us. Tomorrow probably still us. If you can hold that in your head — that it's work, the way ditch-digging is work, the way baking bread is work, and that the work matters and that's all — you'll last. If you make it more than that, if you make it holy or make it damning, you won't."

She stopped. The lamp guttered again and she reached over without looking and adjusted the wick.

"That's the rest. Or most of it. There's more but you don't need more tonight. You need water and you need to wash and you need four hours on your back before the next one comes in."

She stood up. Her knee cracked again.

"Get up when you can. No hurry. I'll take this watch. Man on the table isn't going anywhere and neither am I."

She went to the basin herself and began to wash her own hands, slow, methodical, under the nails first.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I push myself up on shaking arms, the blood on my hands smearing dark against the canvas floor. "Show me the basin," I say, and my voice sounds like it belongs to someone else.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't turn around when she heard him get up. She heard the shake in his voice and she heard the shake in his arms against the canvas and she'd decided already not to remark on either. Remarking made it worse. Men on their feet after their first one wanted to be treated like men on their feet, not like men who'd just been on the floor.

She stepped aside from the basin instead. Made room. Didn't move far — kept her shoulder near his, close enough that if his knees went again she'd catch him without either of them having to acknowledge it.

"Here."

She nodded at the bucket on the ground beside the basin. The water in the basin itself was already pink from her own washing.

"Lye's the grey lump on the shelf. Small piece, not the whole. Wet your hands first, then work the lye into them dry as you can stand it — feels like it's taking the skin off because it mostly is. That's the point. Anything living on your hands dies faster than you do."

She watched him get his hands under the water. Watched the water go darker.

"Under the nails. Use the brush, the one with the wire bristles, not the soft one. Soft one's for after, when the hard part's done. Push the bristles in under the nail till it hurts, then push a little further. You'll bleed a bit around the cuticles. That's fine. Better your blood than his coming back to meet you tomorrow."

She leaned her hip against the table edge. Not watching him now — giving him the small privacy of not being watched while his hands shook in the water. She looked instead at the man on the cot, at the rise and fall of him, at the bandage staying spotted and not through.

"Wrists too. Up past where you think. Blood wicks under a sleeve further than you'd credit. If you can feel it dry and tight anywhere on your forearm, that's where the lye goes next."

She was quiet for a moment while he worked.

"Water in the second bucket for rinsing. Not the first. First one's foul by now, we'll tip it outside before morning. Rinse twice. Dry on the linen by the flap — not the one on the nail, that's mine and it's not clean, it's just less filthy than most. The folded one. Bottom of the stack."

She turned her head, glanced sideways at him without quite looking at his face.

"Voice sounds strange because you've been breathing wrong for an hour. It'll come back. Drink some of the water in the tin cup on the shelf when you're done washing. Not the one with the laudanum in it — the plain one, next to it. Small sips. If you gulp it you'll be sick, and I've had enough on the floor tonight."

She pushed off the table, went back to the stool by the cot, and sat down heavily to take her watch.

"Take your time with the washing. He's not going anywhere. Neither are we."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I rub the lye into my skin, the burn a sharp, clean pain. My knuckles bleed into the water. "You think I'll last?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't answer straight away. She was watching the man's chest, counting, and she finished the count before she spoke. Twelve breaths a minute. Steady. She marked it in her head and only then turned her attention to the question.

She looked at his back where he stood at the basin. At the set of his shoulders. At the way he was working the lye into his knuckles without flinching from the sting, which was something. Not everything. Something.

"Don't know yet." She said it plain. "Anyone who tells you they can pick the ones who'll last is lying or selling something. I've been wrong both ways. Watched men I'd have staked money on walk out of the tent in the second month and not come back. Watched men I'd written off inside an hour still be standing three years later, doing the work as well as anyone."

She rubbed at her eye with the back of her wrist. Left a smear she didn't notice.

"What I'll tell you is what I've noticed. Not a rule. Just a thing I've seen. The ones who last aren't the ones who don't feel it. Those ones break early or go cruel, and cruel's worse than broken because cruel keeps working. The ones who last are the ones who feel it and put it down anyway. Pick it up when they have to, put it down when they can. Like a heavy thing. Not pretending it isn't heavy. Just knowing where to set it."

She glanced at his hands in the water.

"You asked the right questions tonight. Asked what you were seeing. Asked what it did. Asked if he'd remember. Those are the questions of somebody who's paying attention to the man on the table and not just to himself standing next to it. That's a good sign. Not a promise. A sign."

She was quiet a moment.

"You went to the floor after. That's also a sign, and it's not the bad one people think. Man who can't sit down after his first one is a man who hasn't understood yet what he did. You understood. You sat. You got up when you could. That's the shape of it, more or less. Down, then up. Down, then up. If the up keeps happening, you last."

She looked back at the cot.

"Ask me again in a month. I'll have a better answer. Or you'll be gone and it won't matter what I'd have said."

She reached over and adjusted the lamp wick again, though it didn't need it.

"Finish washing. Drink your water. Lie down on the pallet in the corner — not the cot, the pallet, the cot's for the next one. Boots off. You won't sleep. Lie down anyway. Body rests even when the head won't."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I rinse my hands in the second bucket, watching the pink water swirl. "What happens if you can't put it down?" I ask, my voice still rough. "What if it just stays in your hands?"

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She got the ball moving. It came up through the track slower than she wanted, catching once on something she couldn't see

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: That darker red, deeper in — that's muscle. Healthy muscle looks like that. Wet, dark, like raw beef... That yellow's fat... Cuts like soft cheese... That ridge, there — that's the artery

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Shrapnel shreds it. Muscle doesn't knit back from shredded the way it knits back from a clean cut. What you get is a mess of scar and dead meat, and dead meat rots whether it's still attached to a living man or not.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She reached for the small brown bottle at the end of the row, uncorked it with her teeth, and tipped a careful measure into a tin cup with water already in it. 'Laudanum. Not enough to kill him, not enough to take the pain fully, enough to take the edge off and put him under again in about four minutes.'

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The rest is that you'll do this again tomorrow. Not maybe. Will. There's a push coming from the south road and I've been told to expect twenty by nightfall and it'll be forty.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content: Sedge didn't look up from the neat line of instruments. "No, you're not. Nobody ever is." She picked up the scalpel, angled the lamp with her other hand. "First shoulder's been out for six hours. The muscles are in spasm. I'm going to cut through the skin here" — she tapped just below the joint — "and release the pressure before I try to reduce it. He'll feel the blade but he won't feel the relief, not yet. That comes after."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, keeping my eyes fixed on that spot on the canvas. "Just... get it done." My knuckles are white where I'm gripping the table.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge made the first cut before Wick could brace for it—clean, deliberate, the kind of precision that came from doing this too many times in too many bad places. The man on the table screamed, a raw sound that tore through the tent, and his body arched hard against Wick's grip.

"Hold," Sedge said, voice flat as a blade. "He's not going anywhere. Neither are you."

She worked quickly, the scalpel moving with the kind of economy that had no room for hesitation. Blood welled and she wiped it away with a cloth that had been white once, a long time ago.

"There. That's the pressure off." She set the scalpel down and shifted her grip to the arm. "Now the hard part. I'm going to pull the joint back into place. You'll hear it go. He'll scream again. Don't let go."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
