“That will happen again,” she said. “Maybe ten times. Maybe more. Each time is the same. Orient him. Keep him still. Check the hands after. Panic can do injury if it gets arms involved.”

She looked toward the dark tent flap.

“And if the camp gets shelled, you put your body over his middle and keep his arms from being thrown. If fire comes through the canvas, then we move him because burning outranks shoulders. Otherwise he stays. Triage is just cruelty with arithmetic, and fire changes the sum.”

She took a breath, then another. Her face had gone grey with fatigue, but her hands stayed steady.

“The second hour is the same as the first unless it is worse. If it is better, do not trust it too much. If he sleeps, check him anyway. Sleep is not permission to stop. If he snores wet, wake me. If he cannot be roused, wake me. If his lips turn blue, wake me. If one pupil goes wide and stupid while the other behaves, wake me. I do not expect a head injury from what I saw, but expectation is not evidence.”

She touched the bruised cheekbone with the back of her fingers.

“He took some knock. Not the worst. Still, if he vomits without reason, grows confused after being clear, complains of a splitting head, or will not wake, that joins the list.”

The list had become long enough to stand in the tent like another person.

Sedge seemed to see it too and snorted once without humor.

“Yes,” she said. “It is a lot. Keeping people alive is mostly noticing all the ways they are trying not to be.”

She picked up the waterskin, weighed it, then set it down.

“Water in another few minutes if he rouses. Not before. If his tongue swells dry and he cannot drink, wet rag. If he keeps two mouthfuls down over time, good. If he vomits once, we slow. If he vomits twice, no more by mouth until I say. Vomit steals more water than it gives.”

She checked the first mark on the sling and glanced toward whatever sense of time she kept in her bones.

“Not quarter yet. Feels longer. It always does.”

The man lay shivering now, small tremors running through him.

Sedge laid another blanket over his legs and belly, carefully leaving the hands out.

“Shivering. Warm him. Do not cover the hands. Warning flags stay visible. If he complains his hands are cold while they feel warm, nerve insult. Note it. If they are cold to touch, worse. Fetch me.”

She pressed her knuckles into the small of her own back until something clicked.

“By morning, if he has no fever, hands still working, shoulders still shaped right, and breath dry, I will call him stubborn and continue. Then he gets binding for travel if travel cannot be avoided. He does not march. He does not carry. He does not get thrown in a wagon without padding. Every jolt will try to undo us.”

Her mouth twisted.

“Someone will say there are worse wounded. They will be right. That will not make his shoulders stronger.”

She went back to the crate and opened the bottle at last, only to smell it, judge it, and stopper it again.

“Still no draught. He is not quiet because he is well. He is quiet because he is spent. There is a difference. If he starts straining again, I use it. If he sleeps with decent breath, I don’t.”

The first true quarter hour arrived by Sedge’s reckoning. She took the charcoal and pointed.

“Now. First check after the first mark.”

She did it aloud.

“Right hand: visible. Pink enough. Not blue. Warm.” She pressed the nail. “Color returns slow but returns.” She pinched. The fingers twitched. “Moves to pain. Pulse present.”

She marked a second small line beside the R.

“Left hand: visible. Pink. Warmer. Nail returns faster. Moves to pain. Pulse present.”

She marked the L.

“That is how boring it should sound. If the words change, the night changes.”

She set the charcoal down again.

“There. That is the rest for now. The rest after that is doing it again. And again. And again. Until dawn or trouble.” 

Sedge looked at the man’s face, then at his hands, and her voice went a shade lower, though no softer.

“He may live. He may keep both arms. He may still lose strength, feeling, sleep, pride, and a clean memory of tonight. Those

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I take the charcoal from her and copy her marks on the slings, my own hand shaking a little. "What happens if he does live?" I ask, not looking up. "After all this."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge watched the charcoal marks go down crooked and did not correct them. Crooked marks still counted if a person could read them.

“If he lives,” she said, “then he learns how long a body takes to forgive force.”

She took the charcoal back only long enough to darken the R on the worse sling, then set it down again.

“First day, he hurts. Not brave hurt. Not song hurt. Real hurt. Shoulders, neck, chest, back, arms. Everything that fought the dislocation will ache like it lost a private war. He will think something is wrong because it hurts after being put right. That is ordinary. Right does not mean painless. It means placed.”

She checked the right hand again with her eyes only.

“He stays bound. Both arms supported. Elbows in. Wrists up. Hands visible. He does not use them just because fingers move. Fingers moving is not permission. It is evidence we have not lost them.”

The man’s breath shuddered out. Sedge waited through it. His shoulders did not shift.

“Good,” she said, to the room more than to him.

Then she went on.

“Second day, swelling may be worse. Bruises spread. He may look uglier and be less dying. That confuses people. They want wounds to look better when men are better. Bodies don’t care what people want.”

She touched the edge of the right sling.

“Right shoulder worries me. If it was only out and angry, then time and stillness may give him an arm he can use. If it tore deep, he may never lift it properly. If the socket rim chipped, it may slip again later. If the nerves were bruised, he may get burning, numb patches, weak grip, clumsy fingers. Some of that can come back. Some stays and charges rent.”

She looked to the left.

“Left has better odds. Not good. Better.”

The lamp steadied for a moment, as if it had decided to pretend competence.

“After the first few days, if fever does not come, we start caring about stiffness. Not by flapping his arms like laundry. Gentle fingers. Hands opening and closing. Wrists, maybe. Elbows when the shoulders allow. The joint must rest, but the rest of the limb must not turn into rope.”

Sedge rubbed two fingers over her brow, leaving a faint streak of grime there.

“If he is lucky, in a week he can sit with help. Maybe walk with someone steadying him at the back, not hauling on his arms. If he is stupid, he tries sooner and pays for it. If the camp is stupid, they make him move sooner and he pays for their arithmetic.”

Her mouth tightened.

“In two weeks, if the shoulders hold and the swelling settles, I may change how he’s bound. May. Not will. He might begin small movements with the arms close to the body. Nothing overhead. Nothing behind the back. No pushing himself up. No carrying a bucket. No musket. No pack. No wrestling with his own shirt because pride itches.”

She glanced toward the patient’s face.

“He will hate being helped. Most do. Let him hate it. Hate is cheaper than another reduction.”

The man swallowed dryly. Sedge wet the rag again and touched it to his mouth, careful and ungenerous.

“Wet,” she told him. “Not drinking yet.”

She set the rag aside.

“After that, weeks. Not days. Weeks of guarded use. Pain with motion. Weakness. Maybe clicking. Maybe the feeling that the shoulder wants to leave again when the arm goes certain ways. That feeling matters. He listens to it or he becomes a regular customer.”

Sedge’s eyes narrowed at the right shoulder as if it had character flaws.

“If he had been in a city hospital before the war ate the cities, someone might examine him properly later. Splints made by a person with time. Exercises done in order. Maybe a surgeon if bone was loose inside. Here, he gets me, cloth, orders, and whatever sense survives in his skull.”

She checked the pulse at the right wrist again. Present.

“If infection comes, all that changes. Then living becomes fever work. Open wounds. Drainage. Cutting dead tissue if there is dead tissue. Stink. Chills. Sweat. Maybe delirium. Maybe blood poisoning. Then his shoulders are no longer the main trouble; they are simply the door the trouble walked through.”

She let go of the wrist.

“If the hands fail, all that changes too. Cold hand, dead fingers, no pulse, no feeling, no movement. Then I loosen anything I can, check whether swelling is choking him, and do what can be done with poor tools. Sometimes the hand returns. Sometimes it does not. I won’t perfume that for you.”

Her gaze moved from the slings to the black marks.

“If he lives cleanly through the night and the next, he may still not return to what he was. That is the part soldiers hate hearing. They think alive means restored. Alive often means altered.”

The man made a small noise. Sedge listened to it and found no new warning in it.

“He may not sleep right. Pain does that. The memory of being held down while someone pulled his shoulders back into place may come for him when the tent is quiet. He may wake fighting. He may curse anyone who touches his arms. He may laugh about it too loudly because some men would rather make a joke than admit the body frightened them.”

Sedge’s face did not soften.

“That is living too.”

She took the charcoal and tapped the crate once with it.

“If he has sense, he will ask what he can do. The answer will be: little. Keep still. Move fingers. Tell the truth about numbness. Drink when allowed. Piss when helped. Eat if he can. Do not prove anything. Proving things is for officers and young fools.”

A pause.

“If he does not have sense, someone else must have it for him.”

Sedge looked back down at the patient, at the sweat drying in dirty tracks along his temples.

“And if he lives long enough to be sent away from my table, then I write what happened. Both shoulders dislocated. Reduced. Right worse. Watch nerves. Watch vessels. No load bearing. No overhead work. No marching kit. Needs rest.”

She gave a short, humorless breath.

“Then some clerk may lose the note, some sergeant may call him fit because he has feet, and some wagon may shake him until he begs. That is also what happens after all this. War does not stop being stupid because one man survived a tent.”

She leaned over and checked the left hand again. Warm. Pink. Responsive enough.

“But if luck keeps its boots on,” she said, “he gets pain, then stiffness, then weakness, then work. Slow work. He learns to lift a cup before he lifts a rifle. Learns to dress himself before anyone asks him to carry. Learns that a shoulder is not one thing but a crowd of small things, and every one of them has an opinion.”

She straightened.

“Best case? Months from now he uses both arms. Maybe not as strong. Maybe weather aches in the right one. Maybe he avoids throwing, climbing, sleeping on that side. But he works. He eats with his own hands. He buttons his own coat. He can hate the memory privately.”

Sedge’s eyes returned to the right sling.

“Worst case, short of dying? Recurrent dislocation. Dead patches of skin. Weak grip. Arm that hangs pretty and does little. Infection in the joint. Fever that takes him piece by piece. Or a hand that lives but does not obey.”

She let that sit in the tent without dressing it up.

“Most men land between. Bodies are vulgar negotiators. They give some things back and keep others.”

The next tremor ran through the man’s legs. Sedge tucked the blanket firmer around him, still leaving both hands out in the lamp’s poor yellow light.

“If he lives,” she said, “he will be bored before he is healed. That is dangerous. Bored wounded men start bargaining with themselves. One button. One step. One lift. One small thing. Then the shoulder goes and everyone acts surprised.”

She looked at the marks again.

“So we make the rules simple enough to survive boredom. Arms stay in. Hands checked. Pain reported. Fever reported. No work. No pride. No sudden heroics. If anyone asks what he can do, the answer is breathe and complain.”

Sedge reached for the cup, considered the man’s face, then set it back down.

“Not yet.”

She counted his breaths in silence for a few moments.

“Breathing still rough. Dry. Pulse fast. Hands warm. That is tonight’s victory, such as it is.”

Then she picked up the charcoal and made the next tiny mark when the time came close enough by her reckoning.

“Living after this is not a door he walks through,” she said. “It is a ditch he crawls out of by inches. Tonight we keep the mud from filling over his mouth. Tomorrow we see whether he still has the strength to crawl.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I watch the marks on the slings blur a little in the lamplight. "Will you be here when he wakes?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at the man first, not at Wick.

“If I can be,” she said.

She checked the right hand again because the question had come too close to wanting comfort, and comfort was a poor substitute for circulation.

“Right still warm. Color still coming back. Fingers still answer.” She moved to the left. “Left still better.”

Only then did she straighten.

“I won’t promise what the camp can break. If they bring in a belly wound, a sucking chest, a child with half a foot, I go where the hands are needed most. That is not affection. That is triage. Arithmetic with blood on it.”

She wiped charcoal dust from her fingers onto her apron.

“But if I am alive, standing, and not elbow-deep in someone else’s disaster, I will be here when he wakes properly.”

The man stirred under the blankets. His eyelids trembled, then settled. His mouth moved again with no sound worth naming.

Sedge leaned close enough to hear his breathing.

“Still dry,” she said. “Still rough. No wet in the chest.”

She sat back on the crate, not far from the table.

“If I’m not here, the note is here. The marks are here. The rules are here. You keep his hands visible. You keep him still. You do not let anyone haul him by the arms. You do not let anyone decide screaming means dying or quiet means well.”

Her gaze went to the slings.

“When he wakes, he’ll likely wake wrong. Pain first. Sense later. He may not know where he is. He may think he is back where he was hurt. He may try to fight what already happened. That is why whoever is here speaks before touching him.”

Sedge pointed with two fingers toward the man’s face.

“Name the place. Name the injury. Name the rule. Aid tent. Shoulders back in. Arms still. Same words every time. Don’t decorate them. A frightened mind does not need a sermon. It needs a post to tie itself to.”

The lamp flame bowed and lifted again. Sedge watched it until it steadied.

“If he asks whether he’ll keep the arms, the answer is: for now. If he asks whether he’ll use them, the answer is: we watch and find out. If he asks whether he’s dying, the answer is: not this minute. Those are true enough to stand on.”

She glanced at the stoppered bottle.

“If he wakes wild and tries to tear loose, I dose him. If I am not here, you call me before you touch that bottle. If I cannot come and he is going to ruin both shoulders, then whoever has authority and sense gives a small dose, not a generous one. Generosity with opiates is just murder wearing clean gloves.”

Her mouth tightened.

“And if some soft-hearted fool says he deserves sleep, ask whether they plan to sit with their fingers on his pulse until dawn. Sleep is not free. Not tonight.”

The man made a low, broken sound. Sedge rose at once, one hand hovering over his chest, waiting to see whether the sound became motion. It did not. She waited another breath before lowering her hand.

“Pain dream,” she said. “Maybe memory. Maybe only the body shouting down a well.”

She touched the back of his right hand with the backs of her fingers.

“Still warm.”

Then she marked the sling again.

“Another check. Right: pink enough, warm, moves to pain, pulse present. Left: pink, warm, moves to pain, pulse present.”

She set the charcoal down.

“That is what being here is. Not grand. Not tender. Here means counting the same ugly facts until one changes.”

Sedge looked toward the dark tent flap.

“I have slept in worse places than beside a man with both arms tied to his chest. If nothing else comes through that flap, I’ll stay close.”

She looked back at the patient.

“But understand this: when he wakes, my being here will not make it hurt less. It may make him believe less nonsense about it. That matters. Men in pain invent punishments. They think the bandages are traps, the sling is cruelty, the medic is holding back relief out of spite.”

Her expression stayed flat.

“I’m not. I take no pleasure in this. I took none when I pulled his shoulders in. I take none watching him shake now. Pain is not a lesson I’m teaching him. It is the bill his body presented, and I am making sure he lives long enough to argue about the price.”

She picked up a clean rag, folded it, and placed it within reach.

“When he wakes, if I’m here, I’ll tell him the truth. Both shoulders were out. Both are back. Right was worse. Hands still live. Cuts cleaned. No promise beyond the next check. That is enough truth for a man coming up from pain.”

Sedge sat again.

“If I’m not here, you tell him that. Then you call me when you can.”

She rested her forearms on her knees, hands hanging loose but ready.

“And if he wakes before dawn and hates every face he sees, let him. Hatred uses less muscle than panic.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, my eyes tracing the dark marks on the cloth. "Alright." I shift on the floor, my back against a crate. "I'll tell him."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The joint shifted under her fingers, not the neat little clunk the left had given, but a thick, reluctant slide... Then the shoulder went home with a deep, ugly thunk.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Both shoulders were pulled out. They're back in now. That does not mean fixed. It means the bones are where they're meant to be, and everything soft around them is angry.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Skin opens. Muscle splits. Fat bruises. Blood vessels get nicked, ripped, or pinched shut by swelling. Nerves get stretched, crushed, or sliced. Bone, if it meets bone, may chip, crack, or explode around it.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She poured water over the rag, wrung it once, and pressed it to the torn skin. The man's scream broke into a choked curse. 'Yes,' Sedge said. 'That is the part where water finds open flesh.'

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She took the charcoal back long enough to mark the first strokes herself... Here is the rest.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t look up. Her hands were already slick with blood, though most of it was old—nothing had pumped for a while now. She checked the line of her scalpel against the swollen mess that had once been a shoulder. The joint bulged where it shouldn’t, flesh mottled and purple, the skin stretched so thin it looked like an overripe fruit about to split.

“Hold,” she said, and didn’t wait for affirmation. Her left hand braced above the clavicle. With the right, she cut through the skin—one clean line, no hesitation. The man under Wick spasmed, making a noise like a saw catching. Sedge ignored it. She peeled back the skin, blunt fingers following the blade, talking as she worked: “Out of all the joints, this one’s the worst to put back. Ball and socket don’t want to play nice.”

She hooked a finger under the head of the humerus and levered. The man screamed again, sharp and short. Sedge’s jaw worked, grinding out words. “Don’t look away, Wick. I need you to watch the color. If he goes gray, you let me know. Otherwise—hold.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: My eyes snap back to his face, which is already pale and slick with sweat. "Still... still pink," I manage, my own knuckles white where I'm pressing him down. The smell of blood and sweat is thick in the tent.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge grunted acknowledgment, not wasting a syllable. With the skin open and the joint exposed, she pressed her palm flat against the man's chest for leverage. The ball of the humerus bulged, slick with blood and the yellow shine of fat. She worked her fingers deeper, feeling for the edge of bone, cursing the swelling that fought her every inch.

She bore down, sweat prickling along her own brow, and jerked the arm forward and down. There was a crunch—deliberate, not accidental—a pop as the ball slid back into place. The man's whole body bucked beneath Wick’s grip; Sedge kept her hold steady, like pinning a wild animal.

“That’s in,” she said, voice flat. She didn’t let go until the joint settled. “Now, we’re lucky or we aren’t. He’ll need it bound, and he’ll scream again. Get ready. If you feel him sag, you tell me right then.” She took the cleanest cloth in reach and pressed it firm to the wound, blood seeping through instantly. “I don’t take pleasure in this, you know. It’s just what’s left to do.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge paused, hands stilled on the cloth, her face shadowed in the lamplight. "Not the leg. Shoulder’s hell to heal, but it won’t kill him if infection doesn’t set in. He’ll lose the arm before he loses the leg—and I’m not giving up that easy." She kept her eyes on the wound, watching the sluggish ooze of blood.

She rolled her shoulders, careful not to shift her weight from the man’s body. “Pain’s going to stay with him. Might not ever lift that arm above his head again. But I’ve seen worse walk out—if he listens, if we keep the rot out, he’ll live.” She spoke with a mechanical certainty, like listing the steps of a task she’d done a hundred times. Sedge didn’t soften her words; she didn’t have softness to spare.

She reached for the splints and bandages, already stained from the last dozen casualties. “Hold him steady. I’m going to set him up. I’ll wrap it tight—you press here.” She guided Wick’s hand to the pulsing, angry edge of the wound. “Firm, but don’t crush. Blood means he’s got something left to fight with. That’s more than some tonight.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: My hand presses down where she showed me. I can feel the heat of his skin through the cloth. "He's still fighting," I say, more to myself than her. The guy's breathing is ragged but steady. "What do we do after this?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge’s fingers moved quick and sure, winding the bandage in a figure-eight around ruined muscle and collarbone. “After this,” she said, “we bind him tight, keep him warm, and pray the fever doesn’t come. He gets water if he can swallow, nothing by mouth if he can’t.” She tore the end of the bandage with her teeth and knotted it off. “I’ll check every hour—if the swelling gets worse or the skin goes black, we cut again. If not, he rests.”

She checked the man’s pulse at the wrist, counting under her breath. “Someone sits with him. Keeps him from picking at the wrap, keeps him turned so he doesn’t choke if he vomits. You know the drill.” Her eyes flicked to Wick’s, sharp and unsentimental. “Pain’ll keep him half-mad for a day. If he starts thrashing, you hold him. If he gets cold and quiet, you call me. That’s when we worry.”

Sedge wiped her hands on a rag, streaking it crimson. “You did well. Most people let go when it gets ugly. You didn’t.” She didn’t offer comfort—just the facts, as plain as she found them. “I’ll get morphine if there’s any left. If not, he screams. Either way, we’re done for now.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge nodded, a flicker of respect passing through her expression—practical, not sentimental. She tugged the lamp closer, letting its weak glow spill over the wound. “Right. You see the skin, stretched and angry red? That’s bruising from the joint tearing out. Cut edges—those are mine, straight as I could manage. You’ll notice muscle bunched up where I had to pull it aside; it’ll be sore for weeks if it heals at all.”

She lifted the edge of the cloth so Wick could see the pad of yellow fat and the shadowed socket beneath. “That shine there—that’s subcutaneous fat, means I cut deep but not too deep. The pinkish-gray? That’s the head of the humerus, back where it belongs. If it were sticking out, or if you saw white splinters, we’d be talking shattered bone. We’re not.”

She let the cloth fall back. “There’s blood, but not arterial. It’s sluggish. That’s good: he’s not bleeding out. If it pulses hard, that’s trouble; if it stops, that’s worse. The wrap’s to keep the joint immobile and the wound closed. If it starts to stink, or turns green, that’s infection. If the fingers go blue—” she tapped his hand, limp on the table, “—it means the blood supply’s choked off. That’s when we cut, and it gets uglier.”

She straightened, voice low but steady. “It’s not pretty, but it’s not a death sentence—not tonight. What you’re seeing is a joint forced home and a body trying to decide if it wants to heal. That’s all.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, forcing my eyes to trace the lines she pointed out. "Okay," I say, voice rough. "What do we do if the fever does come?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t flinch from the question. She began clearing her tools, dropping blood-slick instruments into the basin with practiced movements. “If the fever comes, we strip him down, keep him cool. Water on the cloth, not in his mouth unless he’s awake enough not to choke.” She reached for a battered tin cup, filling it from the canteen, her eyes still fixed on the injured man.

“We watch his breathing. Too fast, too shallow, or he starts rattling—means the infection’s won. Red lines running up the skin? That’s blood poisoning. If it gets that far, not much we can do but make him comfortable.” There was no judgment in her tone, just the flat truth. “I’ve boiled rags, packed wounds with honey or spirits, but mostly, it’s waiting.”

She pressed the cup to the patient’s lips, coaxing him to swallow. The man managed a sip, then slumped again. Sedge nodded, satisfied for now.

“If he burns, we keep him from tearing the stitches. If he goes cold and stops shivering, that’s the body giving up. We watch, we wait, we try not to hope for miracles. That’s what’s left.” She met Wick’s gaze, eyes tired but unwavering. “You sit with him tonight. If he worsens, you come get me. If he gets through the dark, he might just make the dawn.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t hesitate, didn’t soften the answer. She set the tray aside and moved to the foot of the table, voice flat and practical. “Shrapnel tears. It’s not clean, like a bullet. Metal goes in jagged, twists through flesh, rips muscle, nerves, blood vessels. Doesn’t pick a path—just shreds what’s in the way. Sometimes it splinters bone; sometimes it buries itself so deep I can’t reach it, not without a saw.”

She pulled at the edge of the blanket, exposing a jagged scar on another patient’s thigh—a demonstration, not a warning. “See that? Shrapnel opened him hip to knee. I had to dig metal out with forceps, piece by piece. Every bit I missed is a chance for rot. If it nicks an artery, he bleeds out before I can tie it off. If it lodges near bone, the bone might die. If it carries cloth in with it, infection sets in faster.”

She wiped her hands again, voice still low and steady. “It’s not the hole that kills. It’s what happens after—muscle dies, pus builds, fever burns out what’s left. I cut away what I must. Sometimes I take the limb to save the man, but even then, there are no promises. That’s shrapnel: ugly, random, and never fair. That’s as straight as it gets.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I look at the man on the table, then back at her. "So we just... wait to see if his body decides to die." My voice is low. "And you do this every night?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge met Wick’s eyes, the lines in her face deepening with fatigue that was older than the war. She didn’t try to soften the truth. “Every night,” she said. “Every day, too. Sometimes I know they’ll make it, sometimes I know they won’t. Most times, I can’t tell until their body makes up its mind.” Her hands hovered over the man’s chest, feeling for the rise and fall, the heat radiating from the wound.

“There’s no trick to it. I cut, I clean, I bind. I wait. Sometimes I watch a man fight all night and lose him at dawn. Sometimes I think one’s a lost cause, and he surprises me.” She started to wrap the soiled cloths, setting aside the ones that might survive another use. “It’s not courage. It’s what’s left to do—same as you, holding him when he bucked. There’s no meaning in it, not for me. Just work to be done, and bodies that need it.”

She glanced at the lamp, light flickering and uncertain. “If you want hope, you won’t get it from me. But if you want the work done, I’ll do it. That’s all this is.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t hesitate, already reaching for another strip of bandage, her voice steady and clinical over the man’s cries. “He’s thrashing because the pain’s burning through the last of the shock. I’m checking the wrap—making sure it’s tight enough to keep the joint stable, not so tight I cut the blood flow. I’m pressing above the wound, here—” she pressed two fingers, hard, to the pulsing skin just above the elbow, “—to be sure his artery is open. If it’s weak or gone, I’d have to loosen the wrap or we’d lose the arm.”

She worked one-handed, the other bracing the man’s forearm, keeping it locked against his chest. “I’m tucking his hand in under his armpit—keeps the joint from slipping. Now I’m tying a sling. Knot at the back of the neck, tight enough to hold but not enough to choke.” Her fingers moved in practiced loops, the rough cloth scraping over raw skin. “He screams because torn muscle knots up, and every heartbeat pounds against the bruise. That’s normal. If he stops screaming and goes limp, you shout for me—means his heart’s giving up.”

She leaned over the man, checking his face, his lips. “His color’s holding. That’s time buying us another hour. I’ll need another set of hands if he starts seizing—jaw clenched, eyes rolling. If that happens, I wedge cloth between his teeth, keep him from biting through his tongue. If he vomits, roll his head sideways—don’t let him choke.”

She tied the final knot, her grip unyielding. “Now I’m checking the fingers. Pink, warm, nail beds blanch and fill again when I press—means blood’s moving. If they go cold or blue, or if he starts to stink with sweat and can’t answer when you talk to him, that’s fever.”

She stepped back, eyes on the clock nailed to the tent pole. “Five more minutes. If he’s still fighting, I’ll give him water. If not, I’ll sponge him down, pack the wound again, and we wait. If you want every detail, that’s what I’m doing, every minute, until we know which way he’ll go.” She glanced at Wick, expression as plain as the blood on her hands. “Nothing left out. You hold him. I’ll do the rest.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: My arms are burning from the strain of holding him, but I don't let up. "The fingers are still pink," I report, voice tight. "What's the first sign that we're losing him?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge gave the faintest nod, not praise but acknowledgment. She reached to check the man’s forehead, her touch impersonal, measuring the heat. “First sign is the breathing,” she said, eyes on the rise and fall of the man’s chest. “If it gets shallow and fast, or rattles in the throat, that’s the body failing. Next is the skin—he’ll go gray or waxy, lips blue at the edges. Pink fingers mean blood’s moving; if they go dusky or cold, the heart’s losing ground.”

She shifted her hand to the man’s wrist, feeling for the pulse. “If the pulse stutters, gets weak, or speeds up too much, that’s shock setting in. He might go quiet, stop thrashing—don’t trust it, that’s not peace, that’s the body giving up.” She pressed down on the bandage again, firm and sure. “Eyes rolling back, jaw slack, sweat turns cold—those are last signs. By then, there’s not much I can do.”

Sedge met Wick’s eyes, unflinching. “You see any of those before I do, you shout. Until then, you keep pressure steady, keep talking if he can still hear you. That’s your job. Mine’s the rest.” She checked the wrap one more time. “We watch the signs. Nothing else to be done.”

dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t look away, didn’t offer comfort Wick hadn’t asked for. She crouched by the wounded man, methodical even as her own knees cracked. She wiped the sweat from the man’s face with a damp bit of rag, voice low, plain as fieldstone.

“The rest is this,” she said, keeping her eyes on the work. “If he lives through the hour, I go over every knot, make sure nothing’s soaked through. I check the fingers again—press the nails, watch the color come back. If it doesn’t, I loosen the wrap, but not so much the bone slips. If it slips, I cut again. I keep a knife close for that.”

She nudged the basin aside with her boot, not bothering to look away from the man on the table. “If he shivers, I cover him. If he sweats, I strip him down, wipe him with water—never cold, always warm, or the shock will kill him faster. I check his pulse, once every minute, until my mind goes slack or I lose count. If he moans, I listen. Sometimes they mumble nonsense, sometimes their eyes roll back and they piss themselves—means the body’s had enough, brain stops talking to muscle.”

She gathered the dirty cloths and dropped them in the bucket, her hands bloody to the wrists. “I boil what I can, scrape the rest for bandages. If there’s morphine, I give it. If not, I hold their jaw shut when the screaming gets bad, so they don’t bite off their tongue or swallow it. I keep water in reach, but never more than a sip—if his throat swells, the water goes to his lungs and he drowns choking, not bleeding.”

She checked the bandage again, fingertips pressing firm, eyes never leaving the wound. “If the wound leaks thick, yellow, or starts to stink, I cut the stitches, drain the pus, pack it with whatever’s clean—sometimes honey, sometimes spirits, sometimes just rags. I watch for the skin to go black, means the flesh is dying. I cut that away too—cut and cut until there’s nothing left to cut, or until I find live tissue and pray it stays that way.”

She finally straightened, wiping her hands on a rag that would never be clean again. Her eyes met Wick’s, steady, unsentimental. “If he makes it to dawn, I change the dressing. If not, I wrap him tight, bind his hands so he doesn’t claw at his own chest in the end. Sometimes I sit with them, sometimes I have to leave them for the next. When it’s over, I clean the table, throw out what I can’t salvage, and start again on the next body that comes through the flap.”

Her voice didn’t waver; there was no pride, no bitterness—just the plain recitation of what the work required. “That’s the rest, Wick. It’s ugly, and it’s never enough, but it’s all there is to do.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I stay on the floor, watching the man's chest rise and fall. "So we just... do it again." My voice is quiet. I push myself up, my knees protesting. "I'll sit with him. You go clean your hands."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge gave a short nod—no argument, no gratitude, just a silent hand-off from one body to another. She bent to check the man’s pulse one last time, fingertips pressed to the inside of his wrist, counting out ten steady beats. “Let me know if he stops making sense, or if the dressing seeps through. Don’t move him unless you have to. If he goes still, you come get me, fast.”

She straightened, stretching the ache from her own shoulders, and moved to the battered basin in the corner. She plunged her hands into the water without flinching, scrubbing hard enough to make her knuckles sting, watching the cloud of blood and grit swirl away. The soap was thin and the water already tinged red, but she worked until the lines of her palms showed through. She dried her hands on her trousers, already stiff with old stains.

She looked over at Wick—not softened, just steady. “If you need me, shout. I’ll be close.” She checked the supply crate—gauze, a strip of morphine if luck held, a battered tin of boiled water. “If he lasts the night, I’ll change the dressings. If not, I’ll help you lay him out.”

She paused, the lamp’s glow catching the sharp set of her jaw. “You don’t have to stay, but if you do, you’ll see it all. That’s what it takes.” She set the lamp where the light fell full on the man’s face and wound, then ducked out of the worst of the shadows, already rolling up her sleeves for whatever came through the flap next.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, pulling the stool over. The man's breathing is shallow but there. I keep my hand on his good shoulder, just to let him know someone's here. "I'm staying," I say, to her and to myself. "Just... tell me if there's morphine."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge glanced back, eyes flicking over Wick and the man on the table. She rummaged through the battered tin, shaking out packets, weighing them with her thumb and forefinger like a butcher at market. The smallest glass vial surfaced—one last ration of morphine, the label washed blank by sweat and time.

She held it up so Wick could see, her voice flat as ever. “One dose left. Not enough for everyone, but I’ll use it here.” She snapped open the vial with a practiced twist, drew the liquid into the syringe, tapping out air with the tip of her fingernail. The needle was clean—or clean enough—boiled in the last water hours ago.

She came to the bedside, rolling the man’s sleeve up from the uninjured arm. “Vein’s here—crease of the elbow. I go shallow, not deep. Too deep, I lose the vein and waste the dose.” She slid the needle in smooth and fast, thumb steady on the plunger. The man’s body twitched, then slackened, the ragged edge of his breathing softening just a hair.

Sedge watched for a beat, making sure the morphine took. “He’ll drift now—less screaming, more sleep, if we’re lucky. Don’t let him roll onto the bad side. If he starts to choke or spit up, turn his head. If you can’t rouse him, slap his cheek and call loud. Don’t be gentle. Gentle gets them dead.”

She recapped the spent syringe, tossed it in the basin, and met Wick’s gaze once more. “You’ve got what’s left, and so does he.” Her tone was neither cruel nor kind—just what the night required. “If he makes it through this, it’ll be because he fought, not because of anything we did. But we keep doing it anyway.” She nodded to Wick, turned, and set about scrubbing the next set of instruments, already listening for the next footsteps outside the tent.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept the lamp steady. The water threw its light back at them in slow, oily ripples — whatever had thrashed it up was settling now.

"Good," she said. "That's the right answer. Wrong shape is the first thing you learn to notice." She moved the lamp a fraction to the left, sharpening the shadow along the far wall. "Tell me *how* it's wrong. Proportions. Where the mass is sitting. Whether the limbs — if those are limbs — match each other."

She didn't look at Pike while she waited. She kept her eyes on the thing at the far end of the cellar, watching for the small movements that looked like stillness. In thirty years she had twice made the mistake of trusting a thing to be dead before she'd confirmed it, and she still had the scars from the second time to remind her that once was not sufficient lesson.

The water was very cold. She could feel it through her boots already, which meant Pike could certainly feel it, which meant they had perhaps ten minutes before the footing became unreliable.

"Take your time," she added, which from Halloway meant the opposite — it meant *you have until I decide you've had enough*, and if Pike had been paying attention these past weeks, they would know that. "But not too much of it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I squint, trying to ignore the cold seeping into my boots.* "The left side's... bulkier. Like it's swollen. And that's not a limb, it's too thick. Maybe a growth?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway finally moved — two steps forward, slow, displacing as little water as possible. The lamp went with her.

"Swollen or structural," she said. "That's the question." She angled the light downward along the thing's flank. Up close the smell was worse: rot, yes, but underneath it something chemical, something that didn't belong in a cellar. "Swelling means injury or disease. Structural means it was built that way. Matters because one of those tells you it was suffering, and suffering things make bad decisions. The other tells you it was doing exactly what it was designed to do."

She crouched, which put the water at her coat hem. She didn't look thrilled about it.

"Count the limbs," she said. "All of them. Don't assume symmetry — that's a mammal bias and it'll get you killed down here." She prodded the thing once with the end of her lamp-pole, a short sharp movement, and watched. Nothing. She prodded it again, harder. "You're looking for four, six, or eight, most likely, but I've found things in cellars that didn't fit any of those and I want to know which category we're in before I start cutting."

She stood back up, water dripping from her coat.

"And tell me if you can see a head," she said. "Or something that might have been one."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway was quiet for a moment. Not the quiet of someone who didn't know the answer — she'd seen enough to know the answer before Pike had finished asking the question — but the quiet of someone deciding how much of it to give.

"No," she said. "Not recently." She moved the lamp in a slow arc. "See the integument — the outer layer, there, where it's split. That's not skin anymore. Hasn't been for a while." She kept her voice level, the same tone she used for everything down here. "Whatever it started as, it had been in the water long enough to change. The water does that sometimes. Speeds it up."

She paused.

"You're asking because of the hands," she said. It wasn't a question. She'd seen Pike's eyes go to them. There were things at the end of what might have been arms that looked, in the wrong light, too familiar. "Don't look at the hands. Look at the ribcage — or where the ribcage should be. Count the cavities. A person has one. This has three. That's your answer."

She moved the lamp closer so Pike could see it properly.

"I need you to stay with the question I gave you," she said, not unkindly, but firmly. "Head or no head. Limb count. You can have your horror afterwards — everyone does, there's no shame in it — but you have to finish the work first." She glanced sideways. "The water's not getting warmer."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I force my eyes away from the hands. "No head. Or... it's merged with the torso. And I count... six limbs? But two of them look melted into the side."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway filed that away with the efficiency of someone updating a ledger.

"Six, two fused," she repeated. "All right." She moved around the thing's flank, keeping her steps careful, testing the floor through the water before she committed her weight. The cellar floor was uneven down here — she'd noted that from the doorway, the way the waterline wasn't level. "That rules out the obvious candidates. Six-limbed with fusion at the lateral aspect, three thoracic cavities, structural asymmetry on the left." She said it the way someone else might read a shopping list. "We've had something like it before. Not here — further north, wetter climate. Different water table."

She crouched again at the head-end, or the end where the head wasn't.

"Merged with the torso is right," she said. "That's not damage, that's development. It grew that way, or it grew into it." She pressed two fingers briefly against the place where the neck should have been and felt the resistance there, the density of it. "Means it couldn't turn to look at anything. Hunted by sensing movement in the water, most likely. Vibration." She stood. "Which tells us how the Aldren boy ended up the way he did, because he was probably standing very still and thought that was keeping him safe."

She looked at the thing for another moment.

"Good work," she said, which from Halloway was not a small thing, though she said it the same way she'd said everything else. "You stayed with it." She pulled a folded cloth from her coat and dried her fingers. "Now we find out if there's another one. Cellars like this don't usually run to single occupancy."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway accepted the lamp without comment and began working her way around the thing's underside, pulling back the split integument with two fingers to look at what was beneath.

"Something bigger," she said. "That's the plain version." She tilted her head, angling her view into the cavity she'd opened. "See this — here, along the ventral surface. Those aren't wounds from a struggle. Something fed on it after. Possibly while." She let the flap fall back. "There's a hierarchy in water this old. You don't always find the thing at the top of it."

She moved to the fused-limb side and studied the margin where the appendages had grown into the body wall.

"It came in through that drain grate," she said, nodding toward the far corner without looking. "Or it was always here and the flooding this spring gave it room to get larger. Either way it outgrew its usefulness to whatever else is sharing this water." She pressed her thumb against one of the fused limbs and measured the resistance. "The damage to the thoracic cavities is recent. Hours, not days. Something opened it from underneath."

She stood up and took the lamp back.

"That's what happened to it," she said. "It got eaten by a thing that operates below our current waterline, which is why I want us both moving toward the stairs in approximately ninety seconds." She looked at Pike steadily. "You wanted it plain. That's plain."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, my own boots feeling suddenly too heavy in the water. "Right. And you think that other thing is still down here with us?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway was already moving toward the stairs, slow and even, disturbing the water as little as possible.

"I think the water moved wrong when we came in," she said. "Not our movement. Something below us reacting to our movement." She kept her voice at the same flat register she used for everything. "There's a difference. You learn it."

She paused at the midpoint of the cellar and held the lamp low, close to the waterline. The surface was still now, or nearly still. She watched it the way she watched everything down here — not for what it was doing but for what it was about to do.

"The thing we found died in the last two hours," she said. "We've been in this cellar for four minutes. Whatever killed it knows we're here." She straightened and resumed her measured progress toward the stairs. "So yes. It's still down here. It was here before we were and it will be here after, ideally after we've left it to its business and gone back upstairs to have a conversation about what we do next."

She reached the foot of the stairs and put one boot on the first step, testing it.

"Walk in my wake," she said. "Exactly. Same footfalls, same pace. Don't make a different pattern in the water than the one I'm already making." She glanced back, lamp steady. "And don't run. Running is a decision made by your legs without consulting your brain, and your brain is the only part of you I have any use for."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stopped on the second step.

She was quiet for long enough that it might have looked like reluctance. It wasn't. She was deciding what order to put it in, because order mattered — give the worst part first and the rest didn't land properly, give it last and you'd lost them before you got there.

"All right," she said. "Come up to the third step. Not for the distance — for the angle. You need to be able to see the ventral surface from here."

She held the lamp out over the water and waited for Pike to move.

"It doesn't take organs," she said, when she had the angle she wanted. "That's the first thing. People assume predation means consumption and they look for what's missing. That's wrong. Look at the three thoracic cavities — you see how the margins are clean? No tearing. It opens things along the natural seams and it lays something in." She moved the lamp fractionally. "Eggs is the wrong word but it's the closest word. Call them eggs. The Aldren boy had eleven of them distributed through his abdominal cavity and one in the chest. The chest one was the problem, structurally speaking."

She said it the same way she said everything.

"It needs warmth and movement to incubate them," she said. "That's why it doesn't kill outright. A living body is better than a dead one for about six days. After six days it doesn't matter anymore." She paused. "The boy was found on day four. That's why the question of what we do next is a conversation and not a foregone conclusion."

She looked at Pike steadily over the lamp.

"The fused limbs are relevant to your question," she continued. "It can't see. It finds entry points by pressure — it reads the body from outside before it opens it. Which means it spent time on him first. Which means if you're in water with one, you'll feel it before it acts." She let that settle. "That's your warning. That's the only warning you get. You feel something reading the shape of you through the water, you move. Immediately. Straight up if you can. It doesn't do well with vertical movement — the anatomy doesn't allow for it."

She lowered the lamp.

"That's what it did to him," she said. "And that's what it will do to you if you're standing still in four feet of water when it decides you're more useful than we are inconvenient." She turned and continued up the stairs. "Now come out of the cellar."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I follow her steps exactly, my eyes locked on the water behind us as I climb. "So the plan is to come back down here and kill it before it finds someone else."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway waited until Pike was clear of the door before she pulled it shut. Not slammed — a slow, deliberate close, the latch seated without noise. She stood with her hand on it for a moment, listening, then apparently decided whatever she was listening for wasn't there and turned around.

"The plan," she said, "is to sit down somewhere dry and think before we do anything that commits us to a course of action we can't reverse." She moved toward the kitchen, pulling her wet coat off as she went. "Killing it is probably the right outcome. I want to know more about it before I decide how."

She draped the coat over a chair and looked at it with mild distaste.

"Here's what I don't know yet," she said, as though reading from a list she'd been composing since the cellar. "Whether it came in or was always here. Whether there's one or whether the thing we found is evidence that there's already a territorial dispute happening, in which case we have at minimum two. What it does when threatened in a confined space, because I have a theory and I would prefer not to test it by accident." She held up three fingers and folded them down one at a time. "Those are the questions that change the method. Method determines whether we walk out of this house or get carried."

She pulled out a chair and sat, not heavily, but with the deliberate quality of someone who understood the value of conserving herself.

"The boy," she said. "Day four. That's the other piece." She looked at Pike directly. "Before we talk about killing it, you and I need to agree on what we're doing about him. Because if we go back down there and we do this wrong and we flood the cellar or we collapse something, that conversation becomes much shorter and considerably worse." She set her hands flat on the table. "So. What did you see down there that I didn't tell you to look for."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't stop cutting.

"Integument layers first," she said. "Three of them, which is two more than it should have. The outermost is what you saw from the stairs — that's the original, the thing it came with. The two underneath grew in response to the water. Adaptive. It was here long enough to change." She peeled the second layer back with two fingers and held it so the lamp caught it properly. "Feel the texture if you want. You don't have to, but you should. It'll help you identify one in conditions where you can't see clearly."

She didn't look up to see whether Pike did it or not. That was Pike's decision.

"The smell changes as we go deeper," she said. "What you're getting now is the top layer — that's the rot, that's just decomposition, that's nothing. The chemical smell underneath is what matters. Sulfurous, but not quite. Closer to struck flint. You smell that in a space, you treat it as confirmation rather than suspicion." She worked the blade along the seam she'd opened. "File that away. Struck flint in standing water."

She opened the first thoracic cavity.

"Empty," she said. "Already hatched or never laid. The margins tell us — see how the tissue has relaxed here, how it's gone soft at the edge. Something was here and isn't anymore." She moved to the second cavity. "This one too." She was quiet for a moment, working. "That's relevant. That's more relevant than most of what we've found so far, actually, so keep the lamp exactly where it is."

She opened the third.

"One remaining," she said. "Unhatched. Developmental stage unclear." She studied it without touching it. "Roughly the size of a closed fist. Gray-white. The casing is still intact, which means either it was laid later than the others, or the host died before it was ready." She sat back on her heels and looked at it. "The smell is strongest here. You're getting the full version of it now. That's what you're looking for — that's the source concentration. In a living host it would be fainter. Masked by the body. But it would still be there."

She set down her blade and picked up the folded cloth.

"It got into the abdominal cavity through the left lateral aspect," she said, wiping her hands with the methodical thoroughness of someone who had done this ten thousand times. "Natural seam, as I told you. No tearing. The precision is — " she paused, which was unusual for her — "notable. It knew exactly where to go. Which means it has done this before, many times, and it has a preferred method." She folded the cloth and set it aside. "It got as far as it needed to get. No further. It's not wasteful and it's not cruel, which I mention not because cruelty matters taxonomically but because it tells you something about how it thinks. It doesn't damage what it's using."

She looked up at Pike then, directly, with the lamp between them.

"That's everything," she said. "That's what's underneath. That's how far it got." She let a beat pass. "Now you know what we're dealing with, and knowing is the only advantage we have down there, so I need you to hold onto all of it." She picked up her blade and cleaned it. "Ask me anything you didn't understand. Once. Then we talk about the boy."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I lean forward, my shadow falling over the cavity. "The egg that's left... can you tell how long it had?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked at it for another moment without touching it. The lamp threw the cavity into sharp relief — the pale casing, the way it sat nestled in the tissue with a kind of horrible snugness, like it had always belonged there.

"Not precisely," she said. "Not from the outside." She leaned in close, close enough that her breath would have moved across it if she'd breathed wrong, and she didn't. "The casing color is my best indicator. Gray-white is early to middle. By the end it goes translucent — you can see movement through it." She sat back. "This one is gray-white throughout. No translucency at the margins."

She picked up the lamp from Pike and held it at a different angle, studying the surface of the casing.

"No surface tension changes," she said. "When they're close, the casing gets tight. Drum-tight. This one is still soft." She handed the lamp back. "So. Not hours. Days, probably. Two to four, if the developmental rate matches what I've seen before." She paused. "It doesn't always match. This one has been in colder water than the northern case, and cold slows things. So possibly longer."

She stood up, her knees making a sound she ignored.

"That's the honest answer," she said. "Two days at the optimistic end. Longer if the cold bought us something." She looked at Pike with the flat steadiness she used when she was about to say something that mattered. "Which means the question of the Aldren boy is not academic. If there are hatched ones already in this water, that changes every part of what we do next."

She picked up her blade again.

"I need to know if you understand what I mean by that," she said. "Say it back to me."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked at Pike for a moment. Then she looked at the egg.

She crouched back down beside the opened cavity without any particular ceremony about it. She picked up the blade and turned it once in her hand, finding the grip she wanted.

"The casing first," she said. "You want to do it in one motion. If you hesitate in the middle you can get a partial rupture and that's worse than either outcome — the intact version or the opened one." She set the tip of the blade against the casing at its uppermost point. "You score it along the long axis and then you open it like a book. Then you look at what's inside before you do anything else."

She scored it.

The casing opened without resistance, the way something engineered for opening opens. Not like tissue. Not like anything with a natural defense. She held both halves back with her fingers and held the lamp close.

Inside was nothing that had finished becoming anything yet. Gray-white throughout, consistent with what she'd said on the stairs, and it had not moved when the casing opened. She watched it for ten seconds. It did not move.

"Not viable," she said. "The host died too early." She kept her voice the same. "Sometimes they are. You have to check. You don't assume."

She set the blade down, picked up the cloth, and removed what was inside with two careful movements. She wrapped it thoroughly and without looking away from what she was doing. The smell was at its worst now — struck flint, concentrated, filling the cellar air — and she breathed through it with the practiced neutrality of someone who had learned that nausea was a response she could defer.

"The wrapping goes in the bucket," she said, and put it there. "Not in the water. The water's already compromised and we're not adding to it." She sealed the bucket with its lid and stood up.

She looked at the opened cavity for a moment. Then she looked at the whole of it — the thing from the far end of the cellar, opened along its seams, its three cavities counted and accounted for, its integument layers catalogued, its limbs numbered.

"Right," she said.

She picked up her blade and cleaned it properly, every surface, the way she always did at the end of a job. She folded the cleaning cloth and put it in her coat pocket. She picked up the bucket.

"That's finished," she said, which was the only obituary she gave for anything down here, and she meant it the same way every time — not dismissively, but finally. A door closing. "Come up when you're ready."

She walked to the stairs and went up them, her boots leaving wet prints on each step, and she left Pike the lamp.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stay where I am for another minute, watching the water go still around the thing's body. Then I get up, my legs stiff with cold, and follow her prints up the stairs.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway was at the kitchen table when Pike came up, the bucket set by the door and her coat spread over the back of a chair. She had made tea, or something approximating tea — the kettle had been on the range when they arrived and she had used it without asking permission, which was the kind of decision she made in other people's houses without thinking about it.

She pushed a cup toward the empty chair across from her.

She didn't say anything for a moment. She looked at her own cup and turned it once on the table, a small rotation, and then left it alone.

"The cold gets into the joints," she said finally. "Knees especially. You'll feel it tomorrow more than now." She said it the way she said everything down there — plainly, without softening — but it was a different kind of plain. The kind that acknowledged something without naming it directly. "Drink that before it goes cold. It won't help with much but it'll help with that."

She had the folded notebook open in front of her, and she'd been writing in it — her entries were small and close, no wasted space on the page. She didn't close it when Pike came in. She added one more line and then set down the pencil.

"I'm going to need you to tell me about the Aldren house," she said. "The layout. Whether there's a second cellar or a crawl space beneath this one. Whether the flooding came from inside or outside." She wrapped both hands around her cup. "Not because I'm in a hurry. Because my mind works better when it has something to do and yours probably does too, right now."

She looked at Pike across the table. The lamp was between them, still lit, throwing its ordinary light across the ordinary kitchen.

"Take a minute if you need one," she said. "I'll still be here."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I take the chair and wrap my hands around the cup. The heat feels distant. "There's a storm drain that backs up from the river. That's how the water gets in."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway wrote it down.

"Storm drain from the river," she said. "So it's not contained to this property." She didn't say it with alarm — she said it the way she said everything, as a fact being filed in its correct place, but she was still for a moment after she wrote it. "That's the piece I was missing."

She turned back a page in the notebook, looked at something she'd written earlier, and turned forward again.

"The river connects to what," she said. It wasn't quite a question. She was already thinking through the answer and she wanted to know if Pike's answer matched hers. "Downstream, I mean. What's the next property with a cellar. What's the next place with standing water that backs up from the same source."

She picked up her cup and held it without drinking.

"The hatched ones," she said. "That's the problem with a connected system. The ones that were already gone when we opened it — they didn't stay in that cellar. They went where the water goes." She set the cup down. "Which means this isn't a cellar problem anymore. This is a watershed problem, and those are considerably less tidy to resolve."

She looked at the notebook, then at Pike.

"How long has the drain been backing up," she said. "Not this season. Altogether. Who in this town has had standing water in their cellar over the past two years and didn't think it was worth mentioning to anyone."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Old man Aldren complained about it every spring," I say, my voice steadier than I feel. "Said the town council never fixed it. His house, the mill further down... probably three or four others along that stretch."

rung_labels.evidence: three thoracic cavities — you see how the margins are clean? No tearing. It opens things along the natural seams and it lays something in
