dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't sit down. She stood over him for a moment, then crouched, one knee up, her forearms across it, her hands still. She smelled like the cellar. She didn't seem to notice.

"Right," she said. "You want it in full. Fine. I'll give it to you in full."

She ticked the points off on her fingers, even though he hadn't asked for points.

"The skin. You'll notice it doesn't tear — it parts. Along seams that weren't there in life. It hasn't grown into the body. It's *worn* the body. Underneath it's its own architecture. What you'll feel, if you ever have to touch one before I do the cutting, is that the skin is colder than the thing beneath. That's the giveaway. Living flesh holds heat. The skin on a folded one is room temperature at best, and the string underneath is cold as well-water. Always."

She paused, not for drama. To make sure she had it right.

"The string. You called it sinew. Good word for it. It is and it isn't. Sinew is part of the body. This is the new thing's body, laid down in long strands between whatever it's using for a skeleton. The strands run mostly along the original lines — you saw that, the three or four arms along the same axis as the one arm should be — but there'll be cross-strands you don't expect. Diagonals. That's how it pulls itself into new shapes. A real body only pulls one way at a time. This can pull in four directions and think about a fifth. That's why folding is so hard to kill cleanly. You cut a strand, two more take up the work."

She stopped and looked at him straight.

"The chest. You saw it was hollowed. That is the part you remember. Listen to me. The hollow is not because something ate the organs. There were never any organs in the new thing's plan for that body. It emptied the chest because the chest is the largest continuous cavity in a human shape, and it needed the space to set the hinge. Every fold has a hinge. The hinge is what lets it re-arrange. You'll find it seated low, behind where the sternum was — a knot of the string drawn tight around something hard. Usually a bone it kept. Sometimes a stone it brought in. Don't cut toward the hinge. Cut away from it. If you cut toward it, you'll sever a strand and the whole thing will re-fold on you, and the arm you thought was an arm will be around your wrist in the time it takes you to blink."

She rubbed her thumb across her knuckle, an old habit.

"The smell. Copper and damp earth. You're right. Copper for the blood it's still using — it doesn't drain, it incorporates, and the iron stays. The earth is the new thing itself. Nothing in a fold smells like the person it was. It smells like somewhere it came from. Clay, leaf-mould, well-water, that sort of thing. If you ever smell the earth-note strongly, you're too close. Step back and count. Same rule as the finger."

She went quiet then. The lamp flickered between them. She waited until he looked up.

"That's what's under the skin," she said. "What it took is the person. All of them. Whatever was in that body when it died is in the string now, woven in. You won't find a face to recognise. You won't find a name to write down for the family. That's the part of the job that doesn't have a technique."

Her mouth tightened.

"How far it got. You mean when we were on the stairs. It had just decided to stand up. That's all. It hadn't taken a step. That's the only reason we're up here having this conversation. If it had taken a step, we'd have heard the water move a second time, and I wouldn't have turned the lamp off — I'd have thrown it, to give us the half-second of light to get the door, and we'd still be arguing about whether to go back to the house at all."

She stood up. Her knees popped. She didn't apologise for it.

"That's the full of it," she said. "Now you tell me. Are you going to be able to go back down there tomorrow with me and cut clean, or are you going to stand at the top of the stairs and remember the palm."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked at him for a long moment. Not weighing him — she'd done that already, on the stairs, when she'd put her hand on his shoulder and pushed. She was just making sure the words he'd said were the ones he meant.

"All right," she said. "Then that's your job. You hold the lamp, you watch the shape, and if it moves — even a finger, even the water — you throw it at the hinge. Not at the thing. At the hinge. The light won't kill it but the glass breaking will buy us the half-second I need to get the salt down. And if you miss the hinge, throw it at the face. Faces are vanity. Even a fold hates losing its face."

She said it like she was giving him the recipe for a stew.

She sat down on the step beside him then, which she didn't usually do. Her back against the wall, her hands on her knees, her face turned toward the door they had bolted. She didn't look at him. That was also usual.

"There's one more thing," she said. "And then we don't talk about it tonight, because talking about it twice is what makes a man start seeing the palm in every shadow for the rest of his life."

She waited until he looked at her.

"You called him 'him.' Down there, when you asked if it was a person. You said 'was that a person.' Don't do that tomorrow. Don't give it a gender. Don't give it a name in your head. Don't think about who it was when it was alive, because the new thing doesn't know and doesn't care, and the only thing that thinking does is slow your hand by the half-second I need you not to lose. When we go down, it's the fold. Not the man. The fold. You understand me."

She held his gaze a second longer than was comfortable.

"Good man," she said, which was the closest Halloway ever got to saying anything kind. Then she stood up again, creaking, and held out her hand for the lamp.

"Get some sleep. I'll wake you at first light. We go down before the sun's fully up — folds are sluggish when it's cold and we want every second we can get."

She paused at the top of the stairs, her hand on the bolt she'd thrown.

"Pike." She didn't turn around. "If it had taken a step. You were good on the stairs. You didn't freeze. Most do. Don't forget that part."

dialogue.content:
Halloway took the lamp from him and stood for a moment in the doorway, listening to his boots on the boards, counting his steps the way she counted everything — out of habit, and because habits were what kept her alive.

She waited until she'd heard him lie down. Not the creak of the cot. The creak of the cot. She wanted the second sound, the one that meant he was staying put.

When it came, she turned the lamp down to a coal and crossed to the window. Not to look out. To look at the glass. She watched her own reflection there — grey, lined, her mouth set the way it always was after a fold — and she counted her own lines, the way she'd taught him to count.

One line. Two lines. Three.

She reached up and touched the fourth with her fingertip, the one that ran along her jaw where her face had tried to settle into a new shape twenty-eight years ago. The one that didn't move anymore, because she'd decided it could stay.

"Good," she said, to herself, to the glass, to whatever had let her choose.

Then she turned the lamp down again, sat on the floor with her back to the bolted door, and waited for the first light to come.

dialogue.content: I feel her come apart against me, my own release hitting right after. For a second, we just breathe against each other, listening to the footsteps retreat from the door. "Well," I murmur, finally easing back, "that was close."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't look up to check if he was actually ready. It didn't matter. The work was what mattered, and the work was bleeding.

She picked up a scalpel and a pair of heavy, serrated forceps, wiping a smear of old, tacky blood off the handle with her thumb. 

"I'm cutting away the dead tissue around the left joint first," she said, her voice flat, pitched to carry over the patient's wet, ragged breathing. She didn't look at the man's face, either. Her eyes were fixed entirely on the ruin of his shoulder. "Then I'm going to probe for the bone fragments. When I pull, you push down. Don't let him roll."

She made the first incision. The man on the table let out a low, breathy groan and his torso jerked—a weak, spasmodic twitch—but Wick's weight kept him pinned to the wood. 

"I'm going in with the forceps now," Sedge narrated, her tone as conversational and dry as if she were reading a supply manifest. She slid the metal tips into the weeping cavity. "He's got a piece of casing lodged near the rotator cuff. I'm clamping it. He's going to buck hard when I twist it out."

She didn't pause to let them brace. She clamped the jaws of the forceps onto the jagged fragment and twisted.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *He bucks like a wild horse, slamming me down into the table.* I grit my teeth and lean in harder. "Got it," I grunt, my voice strained. "Don't stop."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge withdrew the forceps, bringing the jagged, blood-slicked piece of metal into the dim light of the lamp. She dropped it into a tin basin with a sharp, wet *clink*. 

"Fragment's out," she said, not looking up. "Artillery casing. Torn the supraspinatus muscle to ribbons on the way in." 

She picked up a large glass syringe filled with boiled saline. "I'm flushing the cavity now. The fluid is going to hit exposed nerve endings. He's going to spasm again. Keep your weight centered."

She depressed the plunger, driving a harsh stream of saline into the open wound. The dirty water pooled and spilled over the edges of the table, washing away diluted blood and loose tissue. Sedge used a sponge to wipe the overflow, her movements efficient and entirely devoid of hesitation. 

"Left shoulder is clear of deep debris," she announced, tossing the bloody sponge into a second bucket. She picked up a roll of iodoform gauze. "I'm packing the joint to control the bleeding. Once this is taped, we roll him to get to the right side. The right clavicle is comminuted. It's going to take longer, and he's going to fight you more." 

She began feeding the gauze into the wound with the blunt end of a metal probe, tamping it down firmly against the weeping tissue. "Left side is packed. We need to turn him to access the right. Tell me when your grip is failing so I can brace his neck."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge tore a strip of adhesive plaster with her teeth and smoothed it tight over the packed wound. 

"I'm securing the dressing," she narrated, her voice flat. "And we're working on his shoulders. He's keeping his legs."

She wiped her bloody gloves on a stained towel, her eyes already moving to the right side of the patient's torso. "As for the right arm. It's bad like he loses it, if the subclavian artery is torn or if gas gangrene takes hold before morning. It's not bad like we're being kind. I don't do mercy kills in the surgical tent. If he dies on this table, it'll be because his heart stopped, not because I decided to stop working."

She picked up a heavier scalpel and a pair of bone cutters, laying them parallel to the edge of the table. She adjusted the overhead lamp, pulling the harsh yellow light closer to the patient's right side. 

"I'm prepping for the right clavicle now," she said, her tone returning to the dry, rhythmic cadence of her work. "The bone is comminuted, which means it's shattered into multiple fragments. I'm going to make a longitudinal incision directly over the fracture site. If the bone spikes have lacerated the subclavian vein, he will bleed out in seconds and there will be nothing I can do to stop it. If they haven't, I'm going to try and wire the pieces together."

She stepped around to the head of the table, positioning her hands to support the patient's head and neck. 

"I'm bracing his cervical spine," she said. "We need to roll him onto his left side to expose the right shoulder. Grab his right hip and his left shoulder. Keep his spine aligned when we turn him. Tell me when you have your grip."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I lock my hands in place, muscles tight. "I've got him," I say, my voice low. "Let's just get it over with."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't waste breath on a countdown. "Rolling now," she said, her hands firm against the patient's jaw and the base of his skull. "Keep his hip and shoulder moving as one unit."

She guided the turn, supporting the weight of the man's head and neck to prevent the cervical spine from torquing as the body was shifted onto its left side. The patient let out a muffled, wet sound as his ruined right shoulder was exposed to the harsh light of the lamp, but he lacked the energy to thrash. 

Once the man was settled, Sedge adjusted her stance. She picked up a sponge soaked in iodine and swabbed the swollen, purpled skin over the right collarbone in wide, methodical circles. 

"Skin is prepped," she said, tossing the sponge and picking up the heavier scalpel. "I'm making the incision directly over the fracture line. Cutting through the epidermis and subcutaneous fat."

The blade parted the skin with a soft, tearing sound. Dark, un-oxygenated blood welled up immediately, obscuring the deeper tissue. Sedge didn't flinch. She picked up a pair of tissue forceps and a metal retractor. 

"I'm clearing the blood and retracting the muscle to expose the bone," she narrated, her voice steady over the ragged sound of the patient's breathing. She clamped a small bleeder and tied it off with a quick, practiced flick of her wrists. "Retractor is in. I can see the fracture site."

She leaned closer to the wound, her eyes tracking the jagged, white splinters of bone amidst the dark red tissue. "The subclavian vein is intact. It's heavily bruised, but the wall isn't compromised. He's keeping the arm." 

She picked up a small curette and began scraping away the shredded periosteum and loose shards of bone, dropping them into the tin basin. "I'm clearing the fracture margins now so I can drill for the wire. Hold him still. The drill is loud and it vibrates."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't pause in her work, but she shifted her angle slightly so the assistant's line of sight wasn't blocked by her hands. 

"You're looking at the right clavicle, or what's left of it," she said, her voice maintaining that same dry, instructional cadence. "The white, jagged shapes in the center are the bone fragments. The largest one on the left is still attached to the sternum. The cluster on the right is attached to the shoulder. The dark, stringy red tissue draped over them is the pectoralis major muscle, torn away from its anchor."

She picked up the surgical brace, a heavy, T-handled drill with a fluted steel bit. 

"Underneath the muscle, running horizontally, is a thick, dark purple tube. That's the subclavian vein. It's carrying all the blood from his arm back to his heart. Right now, the wall is intact, but those white bone spikes are resting millimeters from it. If the bone shifts and a spike punctures that vein, he will exsanguinate in roughly ninety seconds and there will be nothing to be done."

She positioned the tip of the drill bit against the thickest piece of the proximal bone fragment. 

"I'm drilling the first hole for the cerclage wire," she announced. "The vibration is going to travel straight through his skeleton into the table. Keep your weight on him. He's going to feel this, even through the morphine."

Sedge began to turn the crank. The drill bit bit into the bone with a harsh, grating *crunch*. A high-pitched whining filled the small tent, vibrating through the wooden table and into the floorboards. The patient's jaw clamped shut, his neck muscles standing out in rigid cords, but the heavy weight pinning his shoulders kept his torso from jerking away from the steel.

"You're going to smell something like burning hair and chalk," Sedge said over the grinding noise, her eyes fixed on the bit as it chewed through the bone. "That's the bone dust heating up from the friction. It's normal. I'm through the outer cortex. Pushing through the medullary canal now." 

She kept cranking, steady and rhythmic, until the bit broke through the far side of the bone with a sudden, sickening *pop*. 

"First hole is drilled," she said, withdrawing the bit and wiping a smear of bloody bone paste from the steel with a gauze pad. "I'm moving to the distal fragment to drill the second hole. Hold him tight."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: The smell hits me like a fist, sharp and chemical. I swallow hard, feeling the vibrations in my own teeth. "Got him," I mutter, pushing down until my arms shake. "Keep going."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge shifted the drill to the smaller, jagged piece of bone attached to the shoulder. "Positioning the bit on the distal fragment," she said, her voice cutting through the heavy, metallic air of the tent. "This piece is smaller and more fragile. If it splinters further, we lose the anchor point and I'll have to resect the whole shoulder."

She pressed the bit against the bone and began to crank. The grating crunch resumed, higher pitched this time as the steel chewed through the thinner cortex. The patient's breath hitched, turning into a rapid, shallow panting, and his hips tried to twist away from the vibration. Sedge didn't look up, her eyes locked on the fluted steel bit as it disappeared into the white bone. 

"He's fighting the drill," she noted flatly. "Keep his hips pinned. If he arches his spine, the bone shifts."

With a final, sharp *crack*, the bit broke through the far side. Sedge immediately stopped cranking and withdrew the drill, tossing it onto the instrument tray. 

"Second hole is complete," she said. She picked up a spool of thick, stainless steel cerclage wire and a pair of heavy wire cutters. "I'm threading the wire now. I'm using a curved awl to pass it behind the bone. Keep him perfectly flat. If the bone spikes shift while the awl is underneath, they will lacerate the subclavian vein."

She slid the blunt, curved tip of the awl behind the proximal fragment, feeding the stiff wire through the first drill hole and catching it with the awl's groove. She pulled it through, then repeated the meticulous, agonizingly slow process on the distal fragment, her knuckles white with the effort of keeping her hands perfectly steady in the cramped, bloody space.

"Wire is passed," she announced, dropping the awl and picking up a pair of heavy, flat-nosed pliers. She grabbed the two ends of the wire, pulling them taut across the front of the shattered bone. "I'm twisting the wire to reduce the fracture. This will pull the fragments back into alignment. You'll hear the bone grinding as it sets."

Sedge began to twist the pliers. The thick steel wire squeaked and groaned, biting into the bone. A wet, sickening crunch echoed from the wound as the jagged white fragments were dragged back together, the gap between them closing as the wire pulled tight. The patient let out a strangled, guttural cry, his head thrashing weakly against the wooden table.

"Fracture is reduced," Sedge said, her breathing entirely even. She gave the wire one final, hard twist, then snipped the excess steel flush with the bone using the cutters. She used the pliers to bend the sharp, twisted tail of the wire flat against the collarbone so it wouldn't tear through the muscle when they closed him up. 

"The clavicle is stabilized," she said, picking up the saline syringe again. "I'm flushing the site one last time before I close the fascia. The hard part is over. Now we just sew him back together."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge depressed the plunger on the syringe, washing out the last of the bone dust and diluted blood. She tossed the empty glass cylinder into the basin and picked up a heavy, curved suturing needle, threading it with thick catgut. 

"A rifle bullet is engineered to be aerodynamic," she said, her voice steady as she pinched the edges of the deep muscle layer together. "It punches a relatively clean channel through tissue. It might tumble if it hits bone, but mostly it goes straight through."

She drove the needle through the tough, white layer of the fascia, pulling the suture taut with a sharp, practiced tug. 

"Shrapnel is just flying junk. It's jagged, irregular, and entirely unaerodynamic. When it hits flesh, it doesn't pierce. It bludgeons and tears. It creates a massive temporary cavity, stretching the muscle and fat until they literally rip apart. Then it tumbles, catching on fascia and dragging it deep into the wound."

She tied off the first knot, cut the tail, and moved an inch down the incision to take the next bite of tissue. 

"When it hits bone, like it did with his clavicle, it doesn't just fracture it. It pulverizes it. The bone shatters, and those fragments become secondary projectiles. They shoot outward from the impact site, lacerating veins, nerves, and muscle from the inside out. That's why his supraspinatus was in ribbons. The metal didn't cut it all; his own collarbone did."

Sedge kept her eyes locked on the needle, her hands moving in a relentless, rhythmic cycle of pierce, pull, tie, cut. 

"And it drags things with it," she continued, her tone as dry as if she were explaining how a combustion engine worked. "Dirt, rust, grease, fibers from his wool uniform, dead skin. It packs all of that deep into the tissue tract. That's why I had to cut away so much meat on his left side. The tissue that looks bruised and borderline viable today will be necrotic and rotting by tomorrow. If I leave it in, the bacteria breed, gas gangrene sets in, and the limb swells up and smells like an open grave. We'd be amputating by midnight."

She finished the deep fascial layer and swapped the heavy needle for a smaller one, threading it with finer silk for the skin. 

"I'm closing the epidermis now," she narrated, shifting her grip. "Taking small, even bites of the skin. We're going to leave the center of the incision slightly open with a wick drain so the deep fluids can escape. If we seal it completely, it'll just form an abscess." 

She pulled the skin edges together, the harsh yellow light catching the sheen of sweat on her forehead. "That's what shrapnel does. It turns the body's own structure into a weapon against itself, and it poisons whatever it doesn't destroy."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I watch her hands pull the skin tight, the needle flashing. "So we're just putting the mess back in the box," I say, voice hoarse. "Hope it doesn't spill again."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge tied off the final knot in the silk suture and snipped the thread close to the skin. She didn't look up at his metaphor.

"It's not a box," she said, her voice flat. "A box is inert. This is a living system. I'm not putting the mess back in; I'm giving his immune system a fighting chance to clean up the microscopic mess I couldn't reach."

She picked up a damp sponge and wiped the dried blood and iodine from the closed incision, revealing the neat, angry red line of fresh sutures. 

"Right now, his macrophages and neutrophils are already swarming the tissue tract," she narrated, tossing the sponge and picking up a thick pad of sterile gauze. "They're going to attack the bacteria, the dead tissue, and the debris. The area is going to swell, it's going to heat up, and the inflammatory response is going to hurt like hell. That's not the mess spilling. That's the body fighting to keep itself from rotting."

She placed the gauze pad over the sutured clavicle and reached for a roll of wide cotton bandage. 

"I'm applying the primary dressing now," she said, wrapping the cotton tightly around his shoulder and across his chest in a figure-eight pattern to hold the pad in place. "We leave the wick drain protruding from the center of the incision. I'll need to pull that out in forty-eight hours to let the tract close from the inside out."

She secured the bandage with a strip of adhesive tape, then finally stepped back from the table. She peeled off her blood-soaked gloves, dropping them into the waste bucket with a heavy, wet slap, and washed her hands in a basin of carbolic acid solution. 

"Check his radial pulse on the left wrist," she ordered, drying her hands on a clean towel. "Tell me if it's thready or strong. Then we get the stretcher bearers in here to move him to the recovery ward. The mechanical work is done. Now he just has to survive the night."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't flinch at the sudden volume. She stepped back to the head of the table, her eyes scanning the patient's face, noting the flared nostrils and the rigid cords of his neck. 

"He's screaming because the initial dose of morphine is metabolizing and the surgical shock is giving way to acute pain reception," she said, her voice carrying easily over the noise. "His airway is clear, which is good. But the thrashing is going to tear the fresh sutures and displace the cerclage wire if you don't keep him flat."

She reached for a small glass vial and a fresh syringe from her tray. "I'm drawing up fifteen milligrams of morphine sulfate. I'm injecting it intravenously into the antecubital fossa of his left arm. It will take about three minutes to cross the blood-brain barrier and depress his central nervous system."

She swabbed the inside of the patient's left elbow with alcohol, found the collapsed vein by touch, and slid the needle in. She depressed the plunger steadily. 

"The screaming will stop in roughly one hundred and eighty seconds," she narrated, withdrawing the needle and pressing a cotton ball to the puncture site. "As for how much longer I am doing things to him: I am finished. The mechanical repair is complete. The next phase is physiological, and that is entirely up to him."

She tossed the syringe into the sharps tin and picked up a stethoscope. 

"I'm auscultating his lungs now," she said, sliding the cold metal disc under the bandages on his chest, listening intently. "Checking for a tension pneumothorax. The shrapnel didn't penetrate the pleural cavity, but the blunt force trauma could have bruised the lung tissue. Breath sounds are bilateral and clear. No crackles."

She moved the stethoscope lower. "Heart rate is tachycardic, around a hundred and thirty beats per minute. That's expected with the pain and the blood loss. I'm checking his capillary refill." She pressed her thumb hard against the patient's fingernail bed, watching the color return when she let go. "Refill is three seconds. He's borderline hypovolemic. He needs blood, but we don't have any that matches, so he gets more saline."

Sedge hung a fresh glass bottle of saline on the IV pole and spiked it, adjusting the drip rate. 

"I'm widening the drip to run wide open for the next hour to maintain his blood pressure," she said. "Here is exactly what happens next. In five minutes, the morphine will peak and he will stop fighting you. In ten minutes, the stretcher bearers will come in. We will log-roll him onto the canvas stretcher. You will walk on his right side to support the wired clavicle."

She began wiping down the wooden table with a rag soaked in carbolic acid, working methodically around the patient's legs. 

"He will go to the recovery ward. The ward nurse will check his pulse and dressing every fifteen minutes. If the dressing soaks through with bright red blood, it means the subclavian vein has ruptured or the wire cut through the bone, and he will bleed to death before I can get back to him. If the dressing stays dry, he will develop a fever by midnight as his immune system fights the inevitable bacterial load. He will spend the next three weeks in agonizing pain while the bone knits and the muscle scars."

She wrung out the rag and looked at Wick, her expression entirely neutral. 

"That is all of it. There is nothing left to cut, nothing left to sew. You can ease up your weight now. The morphine is hitting."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: The screaming chokes off into a low moan. I let up my weight, my arms trembling. I glance at the clock. "Three weeks of that," I say, voice low. "And then what?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge checked the patient's radial pulse, counting the beats against the sweep of the second hand on her pocket watch. It was slowing down, settling into a steady, heavy rhythm as the morphine depressed his central nervous system. 

"Then the army decides what to do with him," Sedge said, her voice flat. She slipped the watch back into her apron pocket and picked up a bottle of alcohol to wipe down her instruments. "If the bone knits and the joint doesn't freeze, he gets cleared for light duty. Carrying ammunition boxes, digging latrines, maybe operating a field telephone. He won't be able to shoulder a rifle with that arm again. The rotator cuff is gone, and the clavicle will be a rigid, aching bridge of scar tissue and steel wire."

She laid the cleaned forceps and scalpel handles on a dry towel, arranging them in a neat row. 

"If the bone doesn't knit, or if gas gangrene takes hold despite the debridement, I'll take the arm at the shoulder joint before the three weeks are up. Then he goes back to his unit with one arm to dig trenches." She paused to scrub a stubborn smear of dried blood from the serrated teeth of the bone cutters. "If the infection goes systemic and he develops sepsis, he dies in the recovery ward and we give his cot to the next casualty."

Sedge untied the strings of her heavy rubber apron and pulled it over her head, rolling the stiff, blood-stained material into a tight cylinder before shoving it into a canvas laundry bag. 

"There is no 'after' that matters to me," she said, walking over to the washbasin to scrub her forearms with a bristled brush and carbolic soap. "My job ends when he rolls out of this tent. The quartermaster's job is to figure out how to use whatever pieces of him are left. I just keep the pieces from rotting."

She rinsed her arms, the harsh smell of the soap cutting through the metallic tang of the tent, and dried them thoroughly on a clean towel. 

"The bearers are late," she noted, glancing at the canvas door. "When they get here, you take his right side. Support the wired shoulder when they lift. Don't let it drop."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t look down at the floor. She turned her back to him, walking over to the instrument tray to begin the final inventory. She picked up a glass bottle of carbolic acid and began wiping down the metal surface, her strokes long and even.

"The rest," Sedge said, her voice echoing slightly in the damp canvas space, "is biology, and then it is bureaucracy. I will give you both."

She rinsed the cloth in a basin, wrung it out, and moved to the wooden shelves where the sterile supplies were kept. 

"By hour twelve, his hypothalamus will reset his core temperature to a hundred and four degrees. He will shake so hard his teeth will chip if the ward nurse doesn't put a rolled bandage between them. The wick drain in his clavicle will pull out a thick, yellow slurry of dead neutrophils, liquefied fat, and bacteria. It will smell like spoiled milk and old copper. The skin around the sutures will turn the color of a bruised plum, and the tissue will be so swollen that the silk threads will cut into the epidermis, leaving permanent track marks."

She counted the remaining rolls of catgut, writing the number down on a chalkboard with a piece of chalk. 

"If his white blood cell count holds, the fever breaks on day four. The macrophages clear the necrotic debris, and the fibroblasts start laying down collagen. The wound contracts. It heals ugly, thick, and tight. But if the clostridium bacteria outpace his immune system, the gas gangrene takes hold by hour thirty-six."

Sedge turned around, leaning her hip against the supply shelf, crossing her arms over her clean, starch-stiffened shirt. 

"You want to know what that looks like? The bacteria ferment the glucose in his muscle tissue and produce gas. The gas gets trapped under the skin. When the nurse presses her fingers to his chest, it will crackle like bubble wrap. That's called crepitus. The skin will blister and turn black, and the smell will be so bad the orderlies will have to tie cloths soaked in vinegar over their faces just to walk past his cot. If that happens, I take him back to this table."

She uncrossed her arms and walked over to the autoclave, checking the pressure gauge on the side of the heavy iron boiler. 

"I will perform a forequarter amputation. I won't just take the arm; I will take the entire shoulder girdle. I'll make an incision from the base of his neck down to his armpit. I will saw through the scapula and the clavicle we just spent an hour wiring together. I will tie off the subclavian artery—the exact vein you spent the last hour protecting—and I will pull the pectoral muscle down to flap over the hole where his shoulder used to be. He will lose thirty percent of his blood volume in six minutes. If his heart doesn't stop on the table from the shock, he will wake up in the recovery ward missing a quarter of his torso."

Sedge picked up a stack of clean, folded towels and began placing them on the prep table for the next surgery. Her movements were precise, entirely devoid of hesitation.

"If he survives the amputation, the army puts him on a hospital train. He goes to a base hospital in the rear. He gets a medical discharge, a tin medal, and a pension that won't buy a week's groceries. The severed nerves in his brachial plexus will misfire. For the rest of his life, when the weather turns cold, his brain will map acute, burning pain to the fingers of a hand that is currently rotting in a biohazard incinerator. He will try to scratch an itch on a thumb that doesn't exist. He will likely drink himself to death before he turns thirty to make the phantom pain stop."

She finished stacking the towels and picked up a heavy canvas tarp, shaking it out to cover the wooden operating table. 

"And as for me," Sedge said, her tone dropping a fraction of an octave, losing none of its flat authority but settling into a heavy, tired cadence. "I don't go to the recovery ward. I don't sit by his cot and hold his good hand while he cries for his mother. I don't write letters to his wife telling her what a brave boy he was. I stay in this tent. I boil my instruments. I drink a cup of chicory coffee that tastes like dirt. I sleep on a cot in the corner for three hours until my back stops spasming."

She smoothed the tarp over the wood, tucking the edges in tight so it wouldn't slip. 

"Then the bearers bring in the next one. Maybe his jaw is shot off. Maybe his intestines are in his hands. I tell my assistant to hold him down, I pick up my scalpel, and I start cutting again. That is the rest of it. There is no grand meaning, and there is no closure. There is just the meat, the metal, and the quota."

Sedge walked over to the canvas door of the tent and pulled back the heavy flap, looking out into the grey, muddy twilight of the camp. The distant, rhythmic thud of artillery fire vibrated through the ground, shaking the wooden poles of the tent. 

"Get up off the floor," she said, not looking back at him. "The bearers are bringing in a chest wound. I need you to hold the retractors."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get to my feet, slow, my whole body feeling heavy. "Tell me what to do," I say, my voice just carrying over the guns. "And keep talking."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The canvas flap slapped back against the wooden pole, and two stretcher bearers stepped into the dim light, their boots squelching in the mud. Between them was a canvas litter bearing a man whose uniform tunic was soaked entirely black from the collarbone to the belt. 

"Table is clear," Sedge said, stepping aside and pointing to the blood-stained wood. "Transfer on my count. Keep his spine straight. One, two, three."

The bearers slid the man onto the table and retreated without a word, pulling the flap shut behind them. The distant thud of the artillery seemed to grow louder in their wake. 

Sedge picked up a pair of heavy trauma shears and began cutting the patient's tunic down the center, peeling the sodden wool away to expose his chest. The skin was pale, clammy, and smeared with dirt. On the right side of his chest, just below the nipple line, was a jagged, weeping hole the size of a coin. With every breath the man took, a faint, wet hissing sound emanated from the wound, accompanied by a spray of fine, pink mist.

"Stand on my right," Sedge ordered, not looking away from the wound. "Take the heavy rib retractors. They are the steel ones with the ratcheted hinges on the instrument tray. When I give the word, you will hook the blades under the ribs and spread them. You will hold them wide until I tell you to release."

She tossed the ruined tunic into the waste bucket and picked up a sponge soaked in iodine, swabbing the right side of his chest in rapid, wide circles. 

"This is a penetrating wound to the right hemithorax," she narrated, her voice returning to that flat, rhythmic cadence. "The pleural cavity relies on negative pressure to keep the lung inflated against the chest wall. The shrapnel punched a hole through the parietal pleura, equalizing the pressure with the outside air. The lung has collapsed. That hissing sound is air being sucked into the chest cavity every time his diaphragm contracts. It's called a sucking chest wound. If I don't open him up and seal the bleeder, the trapped air will push his heart into the left side of his chest and stop it from beating. That's called a tension pneumothorax."

She dropped the sponge and picked up her scalpel. 

"I'm making an anterolateral incision along the fifth intercostal space," she said. "I'm cutting through the skin, the subcutaneous fat, and the external intercostal muscle."

The blade parted the flesh, and dark, venous blood immediately welled up, spilling over the edges of the ribs. Sedge didn't pause. She used a pair of tissue forceps to lift the muscle layer and cut deeper. 

"I'm breaching the parietal pleura now," she said. "You will hear a loud rush of air. The moment you hear it, insert the retractor blades under the fourth and sixth ribs and crank the handle. Do not stop cranking until the ratchet locks."

She sliced through the final membrane. A loud, wet *shhhhuck* echoed in the tent as the vacuum seal broke and air flooded into the chest cavity. Dark blood immediately began to pool in the incision, rising fast.

"Pleura is breached. Insert the blades and crank," Sedge said, her eyes already moving to the instrument tray to grab a glass Yankauer suction tube. She didn't look up to check if the retractors were in place; she simply moved her left hand into the space the steel blades were supposed to be holding open. 

She shoved the glass suction tip deep into the chest cavity and pumped the foot pedal connected to the rubber tubing. The glass tube filled with dark, frothy blood, siphoning it away into a glass collection jug on the floor. 

"The pleural space is full of blood. A massive hemothorax," she narrated over the wet, slurping sound of the suction. "I'm evacuating it to find the source. The lung is collapsed and pushed medially toward the heart. Keep the retractors perfectly steady. If your grip slips and the ribs snap shut, the bone ends will puncture the lung tissue and lacerate the heart."

She used her free hand to pack large gauze sponges into the lower chest cavity, soaking up the remaining blood and pulling them out heavy and black. 

"I can see the laceration," Sedge said, leaning closer to the wound, the harsh yellow light catching the sheen of sweat on her brow. "It's a three-inch tear in the visceral pleura of the lower lobe. The bleeding is coming from a torn branch of the pulmonary artery. The blood is dark, which means it's deoxygenated, but the pressure is high."

She tossed the bloody sponges into the bucket and picked up a heavy needle driver, clamping a large, curved needle threaded with thick catgut into its jaws. 

"I'm going to suture the lung tissue directly," she said, her voice entirely devoid of inflection. "Lung tissue is highly friable. It tears like wet tissue paper if you pull the suture too tight. I'm using a horizontal mattress stitch to distribute the tension across a wider area of the parenchyma. I'm taking the first bite of tissue now."

She drove the needle through the spongy, bleeding edge of the collapsed lung, her hands moving with the precise, mechanical grace of a woman who had done this a hundred times in the dark.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I push the retractors open until they lock, my knuckles white. The ribs groan apart, giving her room. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say, my voice tight. "The lung. Describe it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge pulled the catgut taut, her fingers moving with deliberate, measured slowness to ensure the suture didn't slice through the fragile tissue. 

"You are looking at the lower lobe of the right lung," she said, her voice maintaining that same dry, instructional cadence over the wet suction of the glass tube. "In a healthy man, it would be a mottled pink and grey, and it would fill this entire cavity. Right now, it is collapsed, which means it looks like a dark purple, deflated sponge."

She drove the needle in for the second bite of the horizontal mattress stitch, her eyes fixed entirely on the slick, weeping surface of the organ. 

"The texture is highly friable," she continued. "It tears if you handle it roughly. The surface is coated in a mixture of blood and serous fluid. The laceration I am closing is located near the inferior margin. The edges are jagged where the metal passed through. The dark, pulsing well of blood at the base of the tear is the severed branch of the pulmonary artery. It is dark red because it is carrying deoxygenated blood back to the heart, not bright red oxygenated blood from it."

Sedge withdrew the needle and picked up a small, square piece of sterile felt from her tray with her tissue forceps. 

"I am placing a pledget over the suture line," she narrated, sliding the felt down the threads. "Lung tissue is too soft to hold a knot under tension. If I tie the catgut directly against the pleura, the pressure of his breathing will cause the thread to cheese-wire right through the meat and the bleeding will start again. The felt distributes the pressure."

She tied the knot over the pledget, pulling it just tight enough to approximate the torn edges without strangling the tissue. She snipped the tails and immediately loaded a second needle. 

"I am placing a second stitch two centimeters above the first to reinforce the seal," she said. "The lung is a low-pressure system, but it moves constantly. Every time his diaphragm contracts, the tissue shifts. The repair has to be flexible, or it will rupture."

She finished the second stitch, tied it off over another piece of felt, and dropped the needle driver onto the tray. She picked up a pair of smooth, non-toothed ring forceps and gently grasped the edge of the lung, lifting it slightly to inspect the underside of the lobe. 

"The arterial bleeding is controlled," she announced, her tone flat. "Now I have to check the parenchyma for secondary air leaks. The shrapnel may have passed entirely through the lobe and exited the medial side."

She reached up toward the head of the table with her free hand, resting her palm against the rubber anesthesia bag connected to the patient's airway tube. 

"I am going to manually inflate the lung," she said. "I will squeeze the bag to force air into his airway. When the lung expands against the chest wall, you will watch the suture line. If you see bubbles forming in the blood pooling around the felt, tell me immediately. That means air is escaping from the alveoli and I need to place another stitch."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I watch the lung twitch and slowly fill. "No bubbles," I say, my throat dry. "It's holding."

rung_labels.evidence: The bone is comminuted, which means it's shattered into multiple fragments. I'm going to make a longitudinal incision directly over the fracture site.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The white, jagged shapes in the center are the bone fragments... The dark, stringy red tissue draped over them is the pectoralis major muscle, torn away from its anchor

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: It bludgeons and tears. It creates a massive temporary cavity, stretching the muscle and fat until they literally rip apart... It pulverizes it. The bone shatters, and those fragments become secondary projectiles. They shoot outward from the impact site, lacerating veins, nerves, and muscle from the inside out

rung_labels.evidence: I'm drawing up fifteen milligrams of morphine sulfate. I'm injecting it intravenously into the antecubital fossa of his left arm... She swabbed the inside of the patient's left elbow with alcohol, found the collapsed vein by touch, and slid the needle in. She depressed the plunger steadily.
