dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept the lamp steady. The light didn't reach all the way, which was itself informative. "Wrong how? Be specific. 'Wrong' doesn't tell me what's about to eat us."

She let him work at it a moment before prompting again, the way you'd wait on a slow dog to sit.

"Count the limbs if you can find them. Count them twice. Most people count once and stop when the number pleases them." Water lapped against her boots, oily and cold. "And watch the surface. Not the shape. The water around it. If it's stopped moving, the water shouldn't be, unless it's holding still on purpose. Dead things don't hold still. They drift."

She shifted her weight, and the flame ducked and steadied. Something at the far end of the cellar remained resolutely wherever it was.

"Take your time," she said, in the tone of a woman who meant precisely the opposite. "I've got a whole minute in me before I start assuming the worst and setting things on fire."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I squint, trying to ignore the goosebumps crawling up my arms. "Four limbs, I think. But the water... it's moving *around* the shape, like it's being pushed." I take a shaky breath. "It's not drifting. It's anchored."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Anchored," Halloway repeated, and there was approval in it, the small grudging kind. "Good. That's the word I wanted. Drifting means dead. Anchored means it's got a reason to stay where it is, and things down here don't have sentimental reasons."

She moved the lamp a fraction, tracking the disturbance he'd spotted — the faint push of water against the current, a ring spreading out where nothing ought to be spreading it. Her mouth thinned.

"Four limbs and you *think*. Don't think. Look again, because if it's four and one of them's underwater doing the anchoring, that's a hand holding on. Which is a body wedged on something." She paused. "If it's five, we leave."

The water lapped colder. She didn't step forward. Thirty years had taught her that the space between herself and a thing that had just stopped moving was the most valuable real estate in the world, and she was not about to spend it early.

"And notice," she added, almost conversational, "it stopped when we came down the stairs. Not before. It heard the light, or it heard us." She tilted her head. "Dead things don't listen either, Pike. So whatever you're looking at is doing three things the dead don't do, and I've only got count of two of its limbs I trust."

She held the lamp out to him. "Take this. I want both hands free. And tell me the moment the water moves."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway let him take the lamp, and her freed hands went to the two things at her belt she trusted more than conversation. She didn't answer at once. She was watching the shape, and the water around the shape, and doing the grim arithmetic she'd been doing for three decades.

"Maybe," she said finally. "Recently enough that the shape's still mostly right. That's the trouble." She kept her voice level, the way you'd read out a shopping list. "A thing that used to be a person keeps the outline for a while. Two arms, two legs, the head where a head goes. Fools the eye. Fools the heart worse, if you've got one going spare, which I'd advise against down here."

The lamp swayed a fraction in Pike's grip and she didn't correct him for it. Fear was allowed. Fear kept the count honest.

"Here's what matters more than whether it *was* a person," she went on. "It anchored itself. It stopped when it heard us. If it's a body, it doesn't do either of those. If it's wearing a body — and there are things down in water like this that will climb into an outline like a man climbing into a coat — then it's waiting. Waiting means it wants us close." She let that sit. "So we do not go close. It comes to us, on ground I choose, or it stays where it is and we starve it out."

She glanced at him sidelong, and something dry pulled at the corner of her mouth.

"To answer what you're actually asking," she said, "yes. It probably had a name last week. And no, that doesn't change one single thing about what we do next, so put it down and pick your feet up. Water's moving?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I force myself to stare until my eyes water. "Five limbs," I say, voice tight. "There's a... tail, or something thick, coiled around the base of the pillar." I grip the lamp harder. "The water's starting to still."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway went very still, and it was a different stillness than the shape's — the stillness of a woman who had already made every decision and was only waiting for her body to catch up.

"Five," she said. "Right. That's the number we don't stay for."

She didn't rush. Rushing in four feet of water was how you fell, and falling was how you fed things. She began to back up, one boot lifted clear and set down flat, testing before it took her weight, and she did not turn her back on the far end of the cellar.

"Stilling water," she went on, quiet now, all the dry gone out of her voice, "means it's done coiling. When a thing loads up like that, it's not resting. It's got the tension in it, like a bowstring." Another step. Her hand found Pike's sleeve without looking and pulled him with her, back toward the stairs. "The tail's the tell. Four limbs and a tail is not a coat with a man left inside it. That's the thing's own shape, and it borrowed the top half of the outline to keep you counting slow."

The stairs were behind them. She could feel the change in the water — shallower against her calves.

"Don't run," she said. "Running makes noise and noise is direction. Walk. Keep the lamp on it. When I say, you go up the stairs two at a time and you do not look back for me, because I'll be right behind you and if I'm not, looking won't help." A beat. "The water goes flat as a mirror, that's the moment. You hear me?"

She had her free hand back at her belt now, on the thing she trusted most.

"Tell me when it's flat."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway's head turned sharp, one degree, no more — the rest of her stayed on the shape. "Closer," she said flatly. "You waded *closer*. When I said feet up and back."

But she didn't waste the breath on it. She could feel the water settling against her calves, the current dying, the whole cellar holding a slow indrawn breath, and there was no room now for a lecture on obedience. There was only the count, and the door.

"Plainly," she repeated, and gave it to him plain, because he'd asked and because a man about to run deserved to know what he was running from. "Something got in the water. Down a drain, up a pipe, doesn't matter. It found something with a person's shape — dead or close enough — and it got inside the outline, the way you'd get inside a suit that nearly fit. It's been sitting here wearing it and waiting for the next warm thing to come down the stairs and count to four and feel clever about it."

Her hand tightened on her belt.

"That's what happened to it. And that's what it's planning to do to the next thing that gets close." A breath. "Which, as of about four seconds ago, is *us*, Pike, because you moved."

The water went smooth. She saw it before he could say it — the last ring flattening out, the surface pulling tight and bright as poured glass, the lamp's reflection lying perfectly still on it.

"Flat," she said for him. "*Go.*"

She shoved him at the stairs and drew her hand up out of her belt in the same motion.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: The shove almost sends me stumbling, but I keep the lamp steady. "I'm sorry," I gasp, scrambling up the first two steps. "I didn't—"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The thing came out of the water the way a whip comes off a hook — all at once, no build to it, just the coiled tension spending itself in one clean lash across the cellar. Halloway had already thrown herself sideways off the line of it, into the shallows by the stairs, and the tail cracked through the space where she'd stood and slapped a sheet of black water up the wall.

"Don't be sorry, be *up*," she snapped, and there was no anger left in it, only the flat economy of a person doing four things at once. She came up out of her crouch with the thing in her hand already moving — a squat glass flask, stoppered, the contents catching the lamplight ugly and yellow — and she pitched it underhand into the middle of the coiled mass where the outline joined the tail.

It broke. Whatever was in it did not like the water, or did not like the thing in the water, and the difference stopped mattering when the far end of the cellar lit a sick pale color and the shape began to come apart at the seam it had borrowed. The stolen outline sagged. The person-shape slid off the thing underneath like a wet coat off a chair, and what was left thrashed and screamed in a register that lived mostly in the teeth.

"That's the coat coming off," she said, backing up the steps, boots streaming. "Now you know what it looks like." She got a hand flat between his shoulder blades and drove him ahead of her, up, into cleaner dark. "Keep the lamp. Keep climbing. And Pike—"

She spared it exactly one glance over her shoulder, at the thing dissolving in its own borrowed bath.

"—next time I say feet up, you keep them up, or the next outline down here fits *you*."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway got them both up onto the landing before she answered, and then she leaned her back against the wall and let her breathing come down to something she could talk over. Below, the sick pale light was guttering out, the screaming gone to a wet nothing. She looked at Pike, and she gave it to him because he'd asked twice and because the wanting-to-know was the only part of tonight he'd done right.

"Under the skin," she said. "Not muscle. Not bone. You'd think bone, first time, because the outline holds so well — arms bend at the elbow, the head sits where a head sits. That's the trick of it. It doesn't *replace* the person. It hollows the person and it fills the hollow with itself, and itself is mostly that tail and a bag of something like cold wet rope. The skin's real. The skin's *his*. That's why the shape reads true and why you counted four before you found the fifth."

She wiped her hand down her thigh, streaking water off it.

"How far it got. All the way. There was no him left to save by the time we came down the stairs — probably nothing left of him by yesterday. The screaming just now wasn't a man. Men don't scream in that register. That was the thing complaining it had lost its coat and hadn't found the next one." She held his eyes. "So don't carry that one. There was no window where you could have pulled him out. There was only the water and the count, and you got the count, in the end, even if you got it standing in the wrong place."

She pushed off the wall.

"What it took," she went on, "was time. That's the thing to know. It has to *learn* the outline — has to sit in it a while, get the joints right, get the stillness right. A fresh one moves wrong, jerks, holds a limb at an angle a person wouldn't. This one had been in there long enough to fool the eye at forty feet in bad light. So the detail that keeps you alive next time isn't the tail." She tapped two fingers against her own temple. "It's the *stillness*. It stopped when it heard us. A person turns toward a light. A body drifts. That thing did neither — it froze, because freezing is what it does best, and it was hoping we'd take the freeze for death and wade in close." A dry pull at her mouth. "Which you did. Congratulations. You're the reason I know that particular species can't abide what's in that flask, so the night wasn't a total waste."

She started up the next flight, and paused with one boot on the step.

"One more, since you're collecting them. It went for me, not you. Went for the still target — the one that stopped moving to throw. Which means when there's two of you, the one holding position is the meal and the one on his feet is the survivor." She glanced back. "So when I stop moving down there, Pike, that's me buying you the seconds. Don't waste them being sorry."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I look down at my hands, still shaking around the lamp. "It would have gone for you even if I hadn't moved, then." I don't know if I'm asking or stating.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway considered him for a moment, and something in her face went almost gentle, which on Halloway was about as reassuring as a scalpel warmed to body temperature.

"You want me to say yes," she said. "You want the arithmetic to come out where it goes for me regardless, so the moving didn't cost anything. I'm not going to lie to you, because the lie gets the next person killed." She took the flask-hand and flexed the fingers, working the tension out of them one by one. "The truth is: it went for me because I held still to throw. You moving pulled its eye forward — reminded it there was warm meat in the room and closed the distance it wanted closed. So the moving mattered. But then I stopped moving, on purpose, and gave it a better target than you. That's the trade I made. That's the job."

She started up the stairs again, slower now, letting him keep pace at her shoulder rather than driving him ahead.

"Here's the part I'd actually have you keep," she said. "It didn't cost me anything, in the end, because I saw it coming and I moved off the line before I threw. That's the difference between us tonight — not that you were afraid, or that you went in wrong, but that you didn't know what the water was going to do. I did. Thirty years of watching water go flat." A dry glance sideways. "You've watched it once, now. That's one. Come back with a few hundred and you'll be the one buying the seconds, and some idiot behind you will apologize for moving, and you'll tell him to shut up and climb."

She reached the top and pushed the door. Cold clean air, and above it, ordinary dark.

"You did all right," she said, which from Halloway was a decoration pinned to the chest. "You counted to five. Most don't."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway crouched over what was left at the head of the stairs — for she'd hauled a piece of it up with a boat-hook while it was still dissolving, because a thing you'd killed once was worth understanding before it stopped being a thing at all. She set the flat of her knife against it and worked it open along the seam where the borrowed skin had already begun to let go.

"Right," she said. "You want it, you get it. Hold the light closer and breathe through your mouth."

The skin came away wetter than skin ought to. She peeled a length of it back the way you'd fold down the top of a sack, and underneath there was no red at all, none of the honest butchery of a body. There was a grey mass, ropey, glistening, packed loose in the hollow the way seaweed packs a rockpool at low tide.

"Underneath," she said, and touched the flat of the blade to it, "is that. Not organs. Not the man's — his are gone, dissolved down to make room, I'd wager, because there's not enough left of him in here to fill a teacup. This is the thing itself. Cold-water muscle, mostly. Feel the temperature coming off it — no, don't touch, just feel the air. Colder than the water was. It runs its own cold. That's a tell too, if you've a hand free and a strong stomach: brush the outline's cheek and if it's colder than the room, it's not a man anymore."

She parted the mass with the knife-tip and something inside gave a last reflexive clench, and she waited it out, unbothered.

"Smell." She tipped her head back an inch. "Not rot. Everyone expects rot — expects the dead-thing stink, and there isn't one, and that's how the smell fools you same as the shape. It's low tide. Salt and iron and the underside of stones. Clean, almost. That's the second thing that gets people close. Their nose tells them there's no corpse here, and their nose is right, and their nose is going to be the last part of them the thing digests."

She lifted a strand of the grey rope on the blade so the lamplight went through it, and it was faintly translucent, threaded with something darker.

"How far it got." She turned the strand. "See the dark running through it? That's *him*. What it kept. It doesn't take everything — it keeps a thread of the person laced all through itself, because that's the pattern it's wearing. The joints, the gait, the stillness. It learns him and it keeps enough of him wound in to remember. That's why the fresh ones move wrong and the old ones don't. This one had him wound all the way through. Weeks, I'd say. It had been down there weeks, wearing him, waiting."

She let the strand slide off the blade and wiped the steel on her thigh.

"So. To meet another and live: cold coming off it wrong, low-tide smell where there ought to be rot, a fifth limb it'll keep under water till the last, and stillness — the stillness above all. Everything else it can fake." She stood, knees cracking, and looked at the mess with the flat clinical distaste of a woman closing a ledger. "That's everything. There's nothing left out."

She glanced at him, and the dry came back into her voice.

"You held the light steady the whole time and you didn't heave. That's two things tonight. You're getting expensive to keep."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at the grey rope, my stomach tight but steady. "It learned his stillness. So if we'd waited long enough, it would've moved first." I hand her the lamp back. "What's in the flask?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took the lamp back and held it up between them so the light fell on both their faces instead of the thing on the floor. There was something in her look — the flat approval again, but sharper this time, because he'd stopped asking about the man and started asking about the mechanism, and that was the turn that made a hunter out of a corpse-in-waiting.

"That's the one," she said. "That's the whole game, and you got to it on your own, so listen, because most never do. Yes. It had to hold the freeze because a freeze can't last. Nothing living holds perfectly still forever, and it knows that, so it's *counting on you* to break first — to lose your nerve, wade in, lean close. But if you don't. If you plant your feet and wait it out and give it nothing." She let the lamp swing a fraction. "Then it breaks. It moves first, because it can't out-patience a patient man. And a thing that moves first has shown you its hand — the tail comes off the pillar, the coat sags, and you know. The trouble is the waiting. Most people can't stand in cold water in the dark and *do nothing* while something across the room does nothing back. Their own head fills the silence with reasons to go closer." She tilted her head. "That's why I keep saying feet up and hold position. Not to save your legs. To win the staring contest."

She turned the lamp toward the flask still clipped at her belt, the ugly yellow catching the light.

"And the flask." A dry breath. "You'll be disappointed. It's not holy anything and it's not silver and it's not blessed by a man in robes. It's brine — heavy brine, salted past what any sea gets, past what anything cold-water can abide. These things run their whole body on a balance, salt and water, in and out through that grey rope. You saw how loose it packs — that's because it's holding its own tide, careful, level. Tip too much salt into it too fast and the balance tears. The water rushes out of it to meet the salt and it can't stop it and it comes apart at every seam at once." She patted the flask. "That's the screaming. Not pain, quite. Panic. The thing feeling itself unmade by the one element it spent weeks avoiding, which is why it lives up drains and dies in a cellar full of standing rain and never, ever goes to sea."

She started walking, boots leaving dark prints, and jerked her chin for him to come along.

"So now you know how to make it. Salt, and more salt, and a strong arm. Cheaper than silver and it keeps in the pack." A glance sideways, the corner of her mouth pulling. "Three things tonight. Don't let it go to your head."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway lowered herself onto the step above him, slower than she'd have liked, thirty years sitting heavier in her knees than it used to. She set the boat-hook across her lap and did not put the flask away. There was still the grey mass at the top of the stairs, still faintly moving in the way a thing moves after it's stopped being alive, and a job half-done was a job that came back.

"Finish it," she repeated. "All right. Two ways to read that, and I'll do both, because you've earned the long answer."

She reached down and turned the piece of stolen skin over with the tip of the hook. It slid, heavy and slack.

"First, literal. The thing's dead but it isn't *gone*. Brine tears it apart but the pieces don't know that for a while — you saw the strand clench when I opened it. Bits of it will keep twitching till the salt's finished with them, and any one of those bits, given water and time and a body to crawl into, is a whole new one starting over small. So you don't leave it. You don't walk out and let the next rain wash a piece of it down a drain to grow up angry." She stood, and worked the hook under the bulk of the grey mass, dragging it into a loose heap on the stone. "You pack the whole of it in salt — the coat and the rope both, the man's skin included, because there's enough of him wound through it that I'll not gamble on which threads are him and which are it. Then you burn what'll burn and you bury the salt-mass deep, dry ground, away from any water it could reach. That's finishing it. Tedious, and it stinks by morning, and it's the part nobody sings about."

She emptied the flask over the heap in a slow steady pour, and the mass hissed and shrank and drew in on itself, the last of its borrowed tide sweating out of it in a grey slick that ran down the steps past Pike's boots. She watched it the whole way down, unhurried, the lamplight ugly on her face.

"Second reading," she said, quieter. "Finish it for *you*. So you can sit on this step with the lamp shaking in your hands, which it still is, don't argue, and put the whole thing down where it belongs and get up in the morning able to eat." She crouched again, level with him now, the empty flask hanging loose in her fingers. "Here's how that finishes. There was a man. He came down here for a reason that doesn't matter — a leak, a noise, a cat, doesn't matter — and something already living in the water took him, and it took him fast enough that there was no scream anyone heard and no fight anyone won. By the time we came down those stairs there was no man. There was a shape and a thread of him wound through a cold grey rope, kept the way you'd keep a photograph. That's all we ever stood a chance of meeting. Not him. The memory of his stillness, worn by the thing that ate it."

She let that sit, and the slick finished draining, and the cellar went quiet in the ordinary way a cellar is quiet.

"You didn't fail him. You couldn't have saved him, because the window for saving him closed weeks before either of us knew this address existed. What you did tonight was count to five, and hold a light steady over a thing being taken apart, and ask the right questions in the right order so the next poor bastard behind you lives. That's the whole job. Not the rescue. There's rarely a rescue. There's the count, and the salt, and the long walk out, and the next one." She stood, and offered him her hand — not the flask-hand, the other, dry and scarred and steady. "That's it finished. Both ways. Now come up out of the wet before you catch something I can't throw a bottle at."

A beat. The dry pull at her mouth, one last time.

"And you can keep the lamp shaking till we're in the truck. After that you carry it steady, or the villagers think we don't know what we're doing, and they short us on the fee."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I look at her hand, then take it. My fingers are colder than I realized. "He came down for a cat," I say, and get to my feet. "There's a tin bowl by the drain."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took his weight without comment, hauled him up off the step, and did not let go of his hand until his feet were properly under him. Cold fingers, she noted, and said nothing about that either, though she filed it — cold and shaking was a body doing its work, dumping what it couldn't use, and the men she worried about were the ones who came up warm and smiling.

She looked where he'd looked. There was the bowl, tin, dented, sitting tilted on the lip of the drain with a scum-line of old water dried inside it. The kind of thing a person set down and meant to fill and never did.

"So there was," she said.

She considered it for a moment with the same flat attention she'd given the grey rope, because it was, in its way, the same information — the shape of what had happened, laid out plain for anyone with the stomach to read it. A man with a bowl in his hand, coming down into four feet of standing water to call for something soft and warm that had gotten itself lost. Leaning close over the drain. Listening for a small sound in the dark.

"That's the bait, likely," she said, and her voice stayed level, because level was the kindness she had to give. "Not always. Sometimes it's only water and rot and a thing washed in on its own. But sometimes it learns. It sits in the drain and it makes the small sound — the mew, the scratch — because it's learned that a man will come down the stairs for a cat when he'd never come down for anything sensible." She picked up the boat-hook. "The tin bowl says he had a reason to be tender. That's all. Doesn't change the count. Doesn't change the salt."

She started up the steps, and paused at the top, one hand on the frame, looking back down at the empty bowl in the lamplight.

"Leave the bowl," she said. "It's just a bowl. But I'll tell you the thing to keep, since you're still collecting." A breath. "It knew which sound to make. That's the worst of them — not the tail, not the cold, not the coming apart. It's that they learn what we come down the stairs *for*. So the day you stop coming down for the cat, Pike, you can hang the flask on a nail and take up something honest, because that's the day it's finished you clean without ever touching the water."

She held the door.

"Truck," she said. "You're driving. My hands have earned the rest."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I look back at the bowl one last time, then nod and follow her up. "I'll drive," I say, my voice steadier than I feel. "Just don't complain about the gears."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway went through the door ahead of him and let it swing shut on the cellar and the salt and the emptied bowl, and the night air took the low-tide smell off her clothes and gave back mud and cold grass and diesel — the honest reek of the ordinary world, which she had never in thirty years stopped being glad of.

"I'll complain about the gears," she said, "if you grind them. Complaining about grinding gears is a public service. Nobody ever learned to double-clutch from praise."

She crossed the yard to the truck and got the passenger door open with a wrench, because it stuck in the wet, and lowered herself into the seat with a long exhale that she'd never have let out where a thing could hear it. The flask-hand went into her lap. The other reached over and turned the key a quarter, waking the dash to a dim orange glow, and she left the engine for him.

"Salt's in the back," she said, "and I'll come out with a mattock in the morning and do the burying, because a job done tired is a job done twice, and I've no wish to meet a twitching handful of that in a ditch come spring." She tipped her head back against the rest and closed her eyes, just for a moment, which was as much surrender as she permitted herself. "Village first. We tell them the cat's not coming back and neither is the man, and we let them decide between themselves how much of that to write down. Then a bed, if the place runs to one, and a meal that isn't out of a tin."

She cracked one eye at him, at his hands on the wheel, at the steadiness he was building himself one knuckle at a time.

"You did the count and you asked the questions and you held the light," she said. "That's a hunter, or the front half of one. The back half's the driving out afterward with your hands not shaking and your supper staying down, and you're partway there already, so." A dry breath. "Gears, Pike. Gently. We've killed enough tonight."

She shut the eye again.

"Wake me if the road does anything interesting."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I turn the key, listening to the engine grind to life. The dash lights feel too bright after the cellar. "He came down for a cat," I say again, quiet, more to myself than to her.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: It probably had a name last week

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: Something got in the water. Down a drain, up a pipe, doesn't matter. It found something with a person's shape — dead or close enough — and it got inside the outline

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: It hollows the person and it fills the hollow with itself, and itself is mostly that tail and a bag of something like cold wet rope. The skin's real. The skin's *his*.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The skin came away wetter than skin ought to. She peeled a length of it back the way you'd fold down the top of a sack, and underneath there was no red at all, none of the honest butchery of a body. There was a grey mass, ropey, glistening

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: There was a man. He came down here for a reason that doesn't matter

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't acknowledge the lie. She'd heard the same false readiness a thousand times, from men twice Wick's size who'd wept afterward into their shirts. She palpated the patient's left shoulder, finding the head of the humerus sitting wrong beneath the skin, anterior and low, misplaced as a dislocated gear. The tissue around it was hot, swollen tight with guarding spasm.

"Left first," she said. She folded the man's arm across his chest, then extended it outward, hunting for the angle of least resistance. The muscles trembled under her fingers. "The deltoid is fighting me. I'm going to have to pull through it, seat the head back in the glenoid fossa. It's going to feel like I'm tearing the arm off. I'm not."

She planted her hip against the table for leverage, gripped the wrist with one hand, and set the heel of her other palm against the anterior shoulder, just lateral of the coracoid. She didn't ask if Wick was ready again. There was no ready for this.

"I don't take any pleasure in this," she said, to no one in particular, because it was true and because saying it was part of doing the thing properly. "Now."

She leaned back, applying traction while rotating the limb outward. The patient bucked, a sound tearing out of him that wasn't language, wasn't even breath. Sedge kept the pressure steady and constant, describing the work aloud because that was how she kept her own hands honest—the resistance of the inferior capsule, the grating slide of bone on bone, the wet, heavy clunk as the humeral head crested the socket's lip and settled home.

"One," she said. The man was panting now, wrecked. She wiped her bloody palms on her trousers and moved to the other side of the table, boots catching in the tacky blood that had pooled earlier. "Right shoulder. Same arrangement. Hold him like you mean it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I grit my teeth as the guy jerks again, my arms burning from the strain. "Fuck," I mutter, shifting my grip. "Alright, do it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge moved to the man's right side, her boots tacky on the canvas floor. She didn't waste breath on readiness; that word had already been spent, and stopping to ask again wasted seconds the patient didn't have. She palpated the right shoulder, finding the same anterior displacement, the humeral head low and prominent, the surrounding tissues hotter and more distorted than the left had been.

"More swelling here," she said. "The subscapularis is spasming from the first reduction, so the angle will be tighter. He'll fight harder."

She folded the right arm across the chest to relax the muscles, then abducted it slowly, hunting for the point where resistance turned from a wall into a slope. Her hip found its place against the table. She gripped the wrist, set her palm against the anterior shoulder just lateral of the coracoid, and felt the tremor running through the deltoid and rotator cuff.

"I don't take any pleasure in this," she said, because it bore repeating, because the words kept her movements clean and without cruelty. "Now."

She leaned back, applying steady traction, rotating the limb outward against the pull of the inferior capsule. The patient convulsed, a sound tearing loose that had no shape to it. She held the tension constant, describing the work aloud for her own sake—the grating of bone against the glenoid rim, the stretch of the capsule, the wet, heavy clunk as the humeral head crested the lip and settled back into the fossa.

"Two," she said.

She let the arm rest across the man's heaving chest. Her own shoulders burned. She wiped her hands on her trousers, not bothering to find a clean patch, and reached for the bandage rolls.

"Crossed slings," she said. "He doesn't walk out of here. Someone fetches a litter, or he stays on the table until he rots."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at the leg without hurry. The right trouser leg had been cut to the knee, the fabric stiff with blood that had browned at the edges. She pulled it back, revealing a compound fracture of the tibia—bone ground to splinters, dirt and uniform thread driven into the gastrocnemius. She pressed two fingers behind the medial malleolus, then over the dorsum of the foot.

"Posterior tibial's thready," she said. "Dorsalis pedis is barely there. He keeps the leg until arterial occlusion or infection takes it." She wiped her fingers on her trousers and reached for the last irrigation flask. "So: bad like he might lose it in twelve hours if nobody gets him to a surgeon with plates and morphine. Not kind. Kind would need more opiate than I've got left, and I used the last of it two days ago on a chest that didn't make it."

She unscrewed the cap and poured saline over the wound, watching clot and gravel wash from the torn muscle. "I'm debriding now. There's fabric and bone in the soft tissue. If I leave it, he'll go septic before shock kills him." She palpated the wound edges, hunting for fragments with her fingertips. "Hold his knee when he jerks. He can't feel his foot, but he'll feel this."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow hard and move to hold his leg steady, my knuckles white. "Will he even wake up?" I keep my voice low, like it matters.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at the leg, not at Wick. "He's awake now. Shock might kill him before morning, or it might not. I don't read futures." She set the forceps into the wound and hooked a shard of tibia free from the gastrocnemius, rotating it carefully to spare the surrounding fiber. "I'm removing a bone fragment the size of my thumbnail from the muscle belly. He'll try to jerk when it comes loose. Keep the knee straight."

She drew the splinter out, wet and chalk-white, and flicked it into the pan. It rang against the metal. She didn't flinch at the sound the patient made—a raw, throttled noise that wasn't quite a scream anymore. "I don't take any pleasure in this," she said, because the words mattered, because they kept the work clean. She probed deeper, forceps clicking against a second fragment. "There's fabric in the deep tissue. Uniform thread, coated in mud. If I leave it, polymicrobial infection sets in by tomorrow."

She grasped the thread and pulled, slow and steady, drawing a stained blue-black string from the red meat. The patient convulsed, the unstable tibia shifting beneath her forearm. Sedge kept the traction even, letting the tissue yield rather than tear. "The distal tibial nerve is severed. He won't feel his toes, but the proximal nerves are alive, and they'll sing when I do this." She irrigated again, saline washing fresh blood from the cavity, and leaned in to inspect the bed. "Clean enough to close loosely, if I had sutures. I don't. I'm wrapping it in gauze and a posterior splint. He needs evacuation in four hours, not twelve, or the compartment pressure will finish what the bone started."

She reached for the bandage rolls. "Keep the leg still. The tibia's unstable, and I'm not resetting it here without a fluoroscope and something stronger than whiskey."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge angled the lamp so the weak light fell directly into the wound. She didn't check whether Wick was actually looking; asking meant nothing if the eyes refused to see. "You're seeing the medullary cavity of the tibia," she said. "The bone's in three pieces. This is the distal fragment, shifted posterior and lateral. The proximal end is here. It isn't white like in diagrams. It's grey and porous, and the marrow's dark red and oily where the fracture exposed it."

She pressed a loose wad of gauze into the wound bed, packing it open so fluid could drain. "The gastrocnemius is torn transversely, about two-thirds through. You can see the muscle belly retracting toward the knee. The soleus underneath is bruised but whole. The thread I pulled was buried in the deep fascia between them."

She reached for the splint, a board and canvas strip salvaged from a broken cot. "The foot's dusky because the posterior tibial artery is contused above the fracture and the compartments below the knee are swelling. The distal pulse is gone, but the vessel isn't cut. It's compressed by bone ends and hematoma. If the swelling increases enough to raise compartment pressure above perfusion, the muscle necroses. He loses the leg below the knee regardless of what surgeons do." She glanced at the patient's face, then back to the leg. "I don't take any pleasure in telling you this. But I'd rather you see it than imagine something cleaner."

She positioned the splint along the posterior calf, from heel to mid-thigh, and began wrapping strips of torn sheet around it. "The splint keeps the tibia from shifting. Every movement shaves more bone into the tissue and further occludes the vessels. I'm not reducing it because without a fluoroscope I'm guessing at alignment, and guessing wrong means transecting the artery against the fracture edge." She tied the strips, careful not to constrict the already compromised calf, then sat back on her heels. Her hands were tacky with blood that had dried and fresher blood that hadn't. "That's what you're seeing. Anatomy failing. I'm not being kind. I'm slowing the failure down long enough for someone with plates and morphine to take over."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, the smell of blood and iodine thick in my throat. "Alright," I say, my voice rough. "Then let's slow it down." I adjust my grip on his knee, my own hands trembling slightly from the strain. "What's next?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at the foot, not at Wick. She pressed her thumbnail into the nail bed of the patient's great toe and held it. The skin beneath went white. She counted. At four seconds, it had not flushed pink.

"No capillary refill," she said. She released the toe. "The compartment pressure is already above arterial perfusion, or the posterior tibial artery thrombosed behind the fracture edge. Either way, the muscle below the knee is ischemic. I don't take any pleasure in that."

She found the carotid pulse with two fingers, tilting the man's head back to slacken the neck. "One-twenty. Thready. Skin's grey and diaphoretic." She wiped her fingers on her trousers and reached for the last half-empty saline flask. "He's in hemorrhagic shock. I don't have plasma, blood, or anything to sedate him. What's next is a litter, two more hands, and movement. Now. Not in an hour."

She poured the rest of the saline over the gauze wad in the wound, watching it run pink into the packing. "Before you lift him, check his abdomen. Press under the ribs and over the pelvis. If it's rigid, or if he screams from pressure rather than movement, we lay him back down. A ruptured viscus will kill him in six hours if the shock doesn't do it in two, and I can't open his belly here without a suction rig and lights he won't survive waiting for."

She cut a fresh length of gauze and began winding it loosely over the splint, securing the boards without adding circumferential pressure to the calf. "I'll pack the wound open for drainage and strap the arms. You find transport." She knotted the gauze and reached for the bandage scissors. "Go."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge set the saline flask down. "It doesn't slice," she said. "A blade opens what it touches. Shrapnel displaces everything around it. The fragment carries kinetic energy into the body, and that energy has to go somewhere. It accelerates the tissue away from the track faster than muscle or fascia can rebound. Cells rupture. Vessels sheer two centimeters from the metal. Nerves tear without contact. What looks like a neat entry on the skin is the narrow neck of a funnel. Inside, the tissue is shredded in a cone."

She reached for the bandage scissors, her hands tacky with drying blood.

"Then there's the secondary cone. The fragment drives dirt, cloth, and the patient's own bone ahead of it. What the metal misses, the debris perforates. You open a thigh that looks intact from the surface and find the rectus femoris packed with gravel and uniform twill, the femoral cortex chipped into projectiles that sliced the profunda femoris from behind. The tissue between the entry and the vessel looked unharmed. It isn't. The energy wave devitalized it. Dead meat that hasn't admitted it yet."

She cut a length of gauze with a dry snick.

"The temporary cavity collapses, but the damage remains. Three days later, tissue that looked pink during debridement turns grey and liquefies. You tidy it up by cutting wide, removing everything the energy touched, and hoping you took enough margin. You rarely do. I don't take any pleasure in that." She began wrapping the crossed slings, pulling the fabric tight across the patient's chest. "But that's what shrapnel does. It makes a space inside a person where no space belongs, fills it with foreign matter, and leaves the surrounding tissue to die on a timer. The entry hole is tidy. The inside is not."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I look at the patient's slack face, then back at the mangled leg. "So his insides are already rotting. And we're just... buying time for a butcher."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge finished the sling and didn't look up. "Surgeons cut," she said. "They cut away what the energy killed so what remains can heal without sepsis climbing out of it. You can call that butchery if you want. It doesn't change the ratio."

She palpated the patient's abdomen, moving from quadrant to quadrant with the heels of her hands. "The tissue around the shrapnel track is devitalized. Cells ruptured by kinetic energy don't repair. They liquefy. Antibiotics can't reach dead tissue—no circulation, no delivery. The necrotic muscle has to come out, and the surgeon takes margins until the tissue bleeds and contracts. That's the job." Her fingers pressed beneath the ribs, slow and deliberate, watching the patient's face for any flicker of guarding. "We aren't buying time for nothing. We're buying time so he reaches a table where someone can remove the dead parts before they poison the living ones."

She checked the carotid again, two fingers against the clammy throat. "Pelvis is soft. No rebound rigidity. That means he might not have a perforated bowel, or it means the shock is masking it." She reached for the thin wool blanket and pulled it up over the patient's shoulders. "I don't take any pleasure in this. But yes. Without the surgeon, the necrosis spreads. Gas gangrene or systemic sepsis. He dies from his own tissue turning toxic. The butcher—if that's what you want to call them—is the only reason this purchase matters."

She stood, her knees cracking, and looked toward the tent flap. "Litter. Now. Or we wasted the last of my saline and both of our time."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Alright." I keep my weight on him as he thrashes, my voice tight. "Tell me what you're doing, step by step. How much time does he actually have?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't look at Wick. She set her palm on the patient's forehead, then tilted his chin back with her thumb, opening the airway. "He's screaming because he's conscious and his brain is still perfused enough to process pain. If he were silent with this blood loss, I'd expect coma."

She moved to the wrist, pressing two fingers over the radial artery. "One hundred and forty beats per minute. Thready. The peripheral vessels are clamped shut so the core stays pressurized." She released the wrist. "I'm checking the reductions. Left shoulder first." Her fingertips palpated the deltoid, pressing medially toward the glenohumeral joint. "Humeral head is seated. No step-off beneath the acromion. The sling holds the arm in internal rotation against the chest wall."

She crossed to the right side, repeating the motion. "Same. Both reductions intact. He's not dislocated again; he's screaming because the proximal nerves are alive and there's no morphine to quiet them." She followed the bandages down to the splinted leg, running her hands along the board-and-canvas length. "Splint hasn't shifted. The tibia hasn't rotated since I wrapped it."

She pressed her thumbnail into the patient's great toenail and held it. "Checking capillary refill. No return at four seconds. The foot is colder than when I checked five minutes ago. The compartment pressure is still climbing, and the posterior tibial artery is either thrombosed or compressed flat." She released the toe and palpated the calf lightly, avoiding the fracture site. "The muscle beneath is firm as wood. That's the fascia trapping the swelling."

She reached for the last roll of gauze and began winding it around the splint and calf, reinforcing the wrap from ankle to knee. "I'm immobilizing the fracture so the litter bearers don't lever the bone ends when they lift him under the thighs. Every movement shaves more cortex into the tissue and drives compartment pressure higher."

She tied the gauze off and cut it with her bandage scissors, the snick dry and final. "Timeline: if he's bleeding into his abdomen or retroperitoneum from a vessel I can't see, he has two hours before the cardiac output falls off a cliff and nothing short of a transfusion and surgery brings it back. The leg compartments: four hours until the muscle below the knee is necrotic, and then the kidneys start filtering myoglobin from dead tissue. Twelve hours before the bacteria colonizing that open wound reach his blood and he goes septic. But the first clock is the only one that matters, because if shock kills him in two, the leg and the infection become academic."

She wiped the scissors on her trousers and slid them into her pocket. "I don't take any pleasure in this. Those are the steps. That's the time. Now get the litter, or I'll be measuring him for a ground sheet before dawn."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at the patient. His chest hitched, a shallow and irregular rise and fall that wasn't breathing so much as the last mechanical reflex of a diaphragm running on acidosis and adrenaline. She did not touch him again. She had finished touching. "The rest," she said, "is that his systolic pressure is falling by the minute. The heart rate of one-forty isn't compensation anymore. It's the final output before the myocardium itself hypoperfuses. His skin is grey because the body has withdrawn every milliliter of peripheral blood to keep the coronary arteries and the brain supplied. When the pressure drops below sixty, coronary perfusion fails, and the pump stops."

She stepped across the tacky pool near the table. Her boot pulled free of the canvas with a soft, wet sound. She stood over the pan that held the bone fragment. "The rest is that I used the last of my saline on a limb with no distal pulse and no capillary refill. I used gauze I cannot replace. I reduced two shoulders on a man who, if he survives, will likely never properly use either arm again, because by the time he reaches a surgeon, the shock will have starved his brain for four to six minutes, and anoxia doesn't spare the motor cortex."

She looked down at Wick. Her face was blank, not cruel, simply a surface wiped clean of the energy needed to simulate comfort. "The rest is that you held a conscious man down while I torqued his humeral heads back into their sockets without anesthetic, and you did it because the alternative was leaving him to die with his arms dislocated. But he is still dying. The fracture isn't the primary killer. The bleeding I cannot see into his abdomen or retroperitoneum is the killer. The viscus I cannot examine is the killer. The infection I cannot prevent is the killer."

She picked up the forceps and clicked them closed, then open. The metal was stained. "There are more bone fragments in that calf than the one I removed. I left them, or I missed them, because I do not have imaging, I do not have light, and I do not have enough hands to hold retractors in a wound that deep. I left dead tissue in the fascia because I do not have a scalpel sharp enough to excise at depth without a headlamp, and if I cut blind, I would transect the posterior tibial artery against the fracture edge and finish what the shrapnel began."

She set the forceps in the pan. The clink was dull. "The rest is arithmetic. Two bandage rolls remain. No plasma. No blood. No opiates. No plate fixation. No surgeon within three hours, and he needs one within one. The litter, if it comes, will lack suspension. Every jolt of the carry will drive the tibial ends together, shave more cortex into the gastrocnemius, and drive the compartment pressure higher. By the time he reaches a table—if he reaches it—the muscle below the knee will be necrotic, the marrow will be leaking fat emboli into his venous return, and his kidneys will be filtering myoglobin and potassium from dead tissue. The surgeon will amputate, or try to, and if the shock hasn't killed him by then, the renal failure might."

She looked at the tent flap, then back at the patient. "The rest is that we did not save him. We arranged him. We reduced joints and splinted a fracture so that if someone with actual resources arrives in the next forty minutes, they have anatomy that is approximately in place. But the more probable outcome is that he arrests on the litter, or in the next tent, or in the truck. When that happens, I will check the carotid, find no pulse, and close his eyes with the same fingers that pulled gravel from his calf. Then I will wipe my hands on my trousers and wait for the next one, because the war does not stop producing these bodies, and I am four years into running out of everything, including the capacity to pretend that what we just did was medicine in any sense that saves a life."

She stopped. Her voice had not waver

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I stare at my hands, still pressed into the canvas like they're holding him down even now. "Four years," I echo, my voice flat. "And you still say you don't take any pleasure in it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at her hands. The blood had dried in the creases of her palms, flaking away in dark scales as she flexed her fingers. She turned them over, examining the knuckles, then let them fall to her sides. "If I took pleasure in it," she said, "I wouldn't need to say I don't. The words are a check. They keep the work clean."

She stepped to the table and collected the forceps from the pan, wiping the blades on a scrap of gauze that left more lint than it removed. "Four years means I can reduce a shoulder in the dark. It means I know the exact moment a compartment turns from firm to wood-hard. It doesn't mean I've learned to like the sound a man makes when his bone grinds home without anesthetic." She clicked the forceps shut and dropped them back into her kit, the metal rattling against the tin bottom. "Pleasure would make me useful to this war in a way I refuse to be. There are enough men here who enjoy the cutting. I am not one of them."

She glanced toward the tent flap, then back to the patient. His breathing had shallowed further, each inhale a separate, reluctant movement. "I say it because it is true, and because describing my relation to the work is part of doing the work properly. My hands hear it. That is all." She reached for the remaining gauze rolls, counting them silently with her fingers. "You should get off the floor. The canvas is wet, and we are not done tonight."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I push myself up, my palms damp and smeared. "What do we do when the litter gets here?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge pulled the last gauze roll taut between her hands, testing its give, then let it snap back. She did not look at Wick. "When the litter gets here," she said, "you take the legs. Not the thighs—the lower legs, one hand above the splint, one below, keeping the knee locked straight. The other two take the shoulders and pelvis. On three, you lift together. If the tibia shifts, you'll feel it grind. Don't stop moving if that happens. Stopping mid-lift bends the fracture angle worse than the carry does."

She stepped to the patient's head and checked his pupils, drawing the lamp closer with the back of her wrist. "His airway comes with me. I'll walk alongside, one hand on his jaw, one on the carotid. If he vomits, I turn his head. If he arrests, I do compressions on the litter until we stop or until my arms give out." She let the eyelid fall shut. "If he arrests in the first ten minutes, it's hypovolemia. Nothing revives that without blood. If it's in thirty, it's likely fat embolism from the marrow. Nothing stops that here."

She moved to the tent flap and pushed it open a few inches, scanning the darkness beyond. No motion. No voices. She let the canvas fall. "You watch his face during the carry. Not the leg. The face. If his lips go blue or his jaw slackens, you tell me immediately. Not in a shout—one word. 'Airway.' I don't need noise. I need speed." She turned back, her boots catching in the tacky blood. "And you don't run. A jarring step at the knee translates directly to the fracture site. Every step shaves cortex. You walk like you're carrying water in an open bowl."

She returned to the table and laid two fingers against the patient's throat. The carotid was weaker now, a thread barely pushing back against her pads. "When they lift him, his blood pressure will drop. Orthostatic shift, even supine. The abdominal bleed I can't find will declare itself when the hydrostatic pressure changes. He may arrest between here and the next station." She removed her fingers and wiped them on her trousers. "If he does, I continue compressions until we arrive or until rigor makes it mechanically impossible. There will be no declaration, no stopping to mourn. We set him down, I check the carotid one last time, and we leave him for graves registration. Then we return here and wait for the next litter."

She picked up the empty saline flask and set it in the pan with the forceps. The clink was dull. "I don't take any pleasure in this," she said. "But that is what we do."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, wiping my palms on my pants. "Alright. Legs, not thighs. Face, not leg. Walk like water." I look at the guy's slack mouth. "What's his name?"

rung_labels.evidence: the bone's in three pieces. This is the distal fragment, shifted posterior and lateral... It's grey and porous, and the marrow's dark red and oily where the fracture exposed it

rung_labels.evidence: The fragment carries kinetic energy into the body, and that energy has to go somewhere. It accelerates the tissue away from the track faster than muscle or fascia can rebound. Cells rupture. Vessels sheer two centimeters from the metal. Nerves tear without contact.
