dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway moved the lamp slowly across the water's surface, watching the ripples disturb the oily sheen on top. "Wrong how. Too many parts, not enough, what."

She'd seen enough to know the body wasn't human-shaped. Not quite. The limbs were wrong in their angles, bent at places where joints shouldn't be. The thing had been tall once, maybe. Now it sat in four feet of water like a collapsed tent, waterlogged and still.

"Tell me you're armed," she said. She wasn't looking at Pike. She was looking at the thing's hands—or what she'd thought were hands. They'd been wrapped around something before they stopped moving. A shape she recognized from the church records upstairs.

"No working jaw. That's why it wasn't making noise." She crouched lower, keeping the waterline below her knees. "They go quiet when they can't feed properly. Means it's been down here a while." She paused. "Means there's been something for it to try feeding on."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I pull out my knife, the handle slick in my palm. "Armed." My eyes finally make sense of the shape. "It's...holding a reliquary? The one missing from the chapel?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Reliquary." Halloway's voice didn't change, but she shifted her weight back onto her heels. "The one Father Morrison reported stolen three weeks ago."

She could see it now that she was looking properly. The silver case, tarnished green at the edges, small enough to fit in a human hand. The thing's fingers—six of them, she counted, two too many—were locked around it with the rigidity of rigor mortis. Or whatever passed for rigor in whatever this had been.

"Three weeks," she said. "That's about how long before they fully decay. Before the binding gives out completely."

She stood, water streaming down her legs. Her boots were soaked through. She was not pleased about that.

"So. Someone stole a reliquary containing blessed bone fragments from a church that had been holding something under seal. Brought it down here. Whatever was in the chapel got out, got to the cellar, got to the reliquary, and then—" She gestured at the waterlogged remains. "Did that."

She looked at Pike.

"Question is whether the something is what's in the water, or whether what's in the water was what was already down here that the something needed to feed on to get strong enough to come topside." She paused. "And question two: what happens to the binding now that the reliquary's been in direct contact with a dead host for three weeks."

The water rippled. Halloway's lamp caught the movement.

"That one's moving," she said. "The small one. By the far wall."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway shifted the lamp toward the far wall where the ripples had started.

"Move slow when you look," she said. "Fast movement draws them."

She made herself look properly. The shape was small—child-sized, she judged, though that didn't mean anything after three weeks in standing water. Curled in on itself in the corner where the cellar's foundation met the wall. Limbs pulled tight to the chest. Face buried.

"Recent enough," she said. Her voice stayed even. "Still got most of the soft tissue. Water's cold enough down here to slow the decay. Another week, maybe two, and you'd be looking at bone."

She'd seen enough to note the position. Defensive. Huddled. Like it had been trying to make itself small and invisible in a corner where nothing could reach it.

"Whatever this was," she said, "it wasn't one of the risen. They don't hide. They don't curl up. They feed until there's nothing left to feed on, then they go looking for more."

The shape didn't move again. The water around it was darker than the rest—stained, maybe. Diluted blood, if there'd been enough left to stain anything.

"Someone came down here," Halloway said. "Someone who wasn't ready for what they'd find. Tried to hide from it, or maybe just got cornered." She paused. "And the something used that."

She looked back at the larger shape, still motionless in the middle of the cellar.

"Question three: whether that thing killed this one for the reliquary, or whether this one had the reliquary and the something else was what we haven't found yet."

Her boots made no sound as she stepped closer to the small shape. She crouched at a careful distance, angling the lamp.

"Shoes," she said. "Little girl's shoes. White. Church confirmation shoes, maybe. Can you see the tag on the inside, Pike? See if there's a name."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I lean in, squinting. "Mary," I read off the worn tag inside the shoe. "There's... something drawn on the sole in chalk. A sigil?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway moved the lamp to get a better angle on the chalk mark. The lines were crude but deliberate. A containment sigil. Not a banishment—containment. Meant to keep something in, not push it out.

"That sigil's not church work," she said. "Too old. Wrong style. That's folk magic. Hedge-witch territory."

She sat back on her heels. Water soaked further into her trousers. She was going to have to burn these when this was done.

"Mary," she said. "Girl from the parish records, maybe. Went missing around the same time as the reliquary, or close enough that no one made the connection. They wouldn't. Missing children don't raise flags in places like this—not until there's nothing left to bury and even then only if someone asks."

She thought about the timeline. Three weeks since the theft. A week or two since the larger host fully died, based on the decay. That put the child's death somewhere in between. Maybe after. Maybe the child was already here when the theft happened.

"Someone brought her down here," Halloway said. "Used her in the working. The sigil was probably hers—a protection charm, family thing. Didn't hold."

She looked at Pike.

"The question is who. Someone with enough knowledge to steal from a sealed reliquary but sloppy enough to botch the binding. Someone who thought they could control what they were releasing." She paused. "Someone who's not here anymore. Not in this cellar, anyway."

The water rippled again. Near the stairs this time.

"We are not alone in here," she said. "And I need you to tell me what you brought with you, because whatever's in this water with us did not follow us down those stairs."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took the lamp back from Pike and held it low over the water between them and the stairs. The light cut through the murk and showed the bottom—flagstones, some broken, silt, and tracks. Not bootprints. Something had dragged itself through here. Recently.

"The tall one," she said, "was not always tall. Was not always that shape. What you're looking at is a man who tried to become something else using parts he shouldn't have touched. The reliquary gave him what he thought was power. What it actually gave him was a direct line to whatever Father Morrison had sealed under that chapel."

She moved the lamp toward the middle of the cellar, where the dead thing sat.

"The binding didn't just break. It reversed. Whatever was underneath got pulled into him instead of him controlling it. That's why the shape's wrong. He was being worn from the inside out. Three weeks of that before the body gave out."

The water rippled again. Closer to the stairs now.

"The child came later. See how she's positioned? She came down here looking for someone, or was brought. The sigil on her shoe—her family thought it would protect her. It kept her hidden long enough to die of something else. Cold. Shock. Whatever she saw."

Halloway stood. Her coat hung heavy with water.

"Her protection worked against what was already here. It did not work against what came down those stairs after her. And that is what's making the water move right now, because it is between us and the way out, and it has been very patient."

The surface of the water broke about six feet from where they stood. Not a hand. Something flatter. A head that turned toward the lamplight with the slow deliberate motion of a creature that did not need to hurry.

"There," Halloway said. "Now you've seen it. We need to leave. We need to leave now. We need to leave without splashing."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I don't take my eyes off the head turning in the water. "It's between us and the stairs." My voice is low. "We can't go back the way we came."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway was already scanning the walls. Her mind worked faster than her mouth did, cataloguing exits, obstacles, assets.

"Coal chute," she said. "Over there, past the dead man. Old cellars like this had them for deliveries. Might still be functional."

The head in the water hadn't risen further. It was watching. Waiting. The patience was worse than violence would have been—Halloway knew that kind of patience. It came from something that didn't need to eat often but remembered how to be hungry.

"Coal chute puts us in the alley behind the church," she continued, voice barely above a whisper. "Six, maybe eight feet of climb. I can make it. You can make it. The question is what happens when we move."

She set the lamp on a ledge where it would cast light toward the coal chute without illuminating them directly. Shadows were better. Shadows didn't draw attention the way movement and light did.

"The child," she said. "Her sigil. Containment, not banishment. That's what it means—it traps things inside a boundary. Her shoe was a boundary. Her body was a boundary. Whatever she was trying to keep in was her, or something she carried, or something that got in before she died."

The water rippled. The thing had started moving toward them. Slowly. The way something moves when it knows its prey has nowhere to run.

"That sigil's still active," Halloway said. "I can see the chalk. Faded but not gone. Which means we have something it doesn't want us to have."

She looked at Pike.

"I need you to take the shoe. Just the shoe. The one with the sigil. You pull it off, you hold it, you don't look at what's inside the ankle area, and you walk—not wade, walk—to the coal chute. I'll be right behind you. If anything follows, the sigil should buy us time."

Her knife was already in her hand. Old, worn handle, edge that had been maintained for thirty years.

"If it doesn't buy us time," she added, "you climb first and I'll figure out what comes next."

The thing was close enough now that she could see the outline of its face under the water. The features were almost human. Almost.

"Now would be good, Pike."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept her eyes on the thing in the water while she talked. Thirty years of describing the worst of humanity and inhumanity both. She could do it while walking if she had to.

"It hollowed him," she said. "Started with the soft tissue—tongue, cheeks, the inside of the throat. That's why no jaw. It didn't fall off; it was consumed from within. The lips went next, then the cartilage in his nose. He would have breathed through whatever remained."

She stepped backward, slow and deliberate, pulling Pike with her.

"The muscles came next. You see how the limbs are bent wrong? That's not rigor. That's where the tendons used to be. The entity doesn't need muscle to move a body. It needs something to hold the shape together long enough to get what it needs. Once it's fed, it stops maintaining. Things collapse inward."

The thing in the water was fifteen feet away now. Maybe less. It moved without hurrying.

"Internally, it replaces. Reorganizes. Starts with the digestive system because that's easiest—whatever passes for digestion in something like this. Works outward from there. The hands, the feet, those go last because it needs them to hold the reliquary. To stay connected to the source."

She paused, calculating the distance to the coal chute. Thirty feet. Maybe thirty-five.

"What you're looking for in another one: the patience. They don't rush. Rushing is human. This thing has been waiting since it killed him, since the body gave out. Waiting for something else to come down those stairs. They're patient because they don't need to eat often and they don't need to chase. They just need you to move wrong, to splash, to look it in the eye."

The water around the thing's shoulders was disturbed now. Arms below the surface, keeping it buoyant. The face above water was almost right. Almost human. The eyes were wrong—she could see that even at this distance. Too large. Too still.

"It can't follow through the sigil's radius," she said. "That's the theory, anyway. The child's protection created a boundary, and she's still in it, which means anything still in this cellar is in her containment. That's why it's circling her. That's why it's staying in the water. It's bound to this space."

Twenty feet to the coal chute.

"But once we break the boundary—once we take the shoe out of the cellar—we find out what happens to the binding. Either the sigil dies with the boundary, and we release whatever's left in the water, or the sigil takes something with it when it goes." She found the coal chute in the darkness ahead. Iron grate, old, rusted but intact. A ladder beyond it, half-submerged in whatever had seeped in over the years.

"Your call on which risk you take."

The thing in the water had stopped moving. It was watching them both now. The face tilted at an angle that human faces didn't tilt.

"It's waiting to see which way we go," Halloway said. "It's not as simple as it looks. That's a mistake people make. They think slow means stupid. This thing is older than both of us combined. It's just not in a hurry."

She let go of Pike's arm.

"Shoe. Now. Walk, don't splash. I'll be right behind you."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I reach down, my fingers closing around the small, sodden shoe. The leather is cold and soft, coming free with a sickening, wet sound. I hold it away from my body, chalk-side out, and start moving toward the chute. My boots make slow, careful ripples. "Don't look back," I whisper, more to myself than to her.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway followed. Three feet behind Pike, boots sliding through the silt with exaggerated care. The water was shallower near the coal chute—ankle-deep instead of knee-deep—which meant better footing and worse traction. She adjusted her weight accordingly.

Behind them, the thing in the water began to move again. Not toward them. Toward the child's body. Toward the space Pike had just vacated.

"It's going for her," Halloway said. Not a warning. An observation. "The boundary's contracting. It knows."

The child's remains were still visible in the lamplight. Curled. Small. The water around her was rising, darkening, as though the cellar itself was trying to reclaim what had been taken from it.

Halloway did not look back. She kept her eyes on Pike's shoulders. On the coal chute ahead. On the chalk sigil facing outward from Pike's raised hand like a lantern keeping something at bay.

Ten feet to the ladder.

The thing made a sound. Halloway had heard worse sounds in thirty years but not many. A wet, clicking vocalization that didn't come from a throat. From somewhere deeper. Somewhere that had been hollowed out long before the man wearing it had ever walked into this cellar.

"That's the boundary breaking," she said. "Keep moving. Do not—"

The child's body shifted. Not from the water. From within the silt itself. Something pale pushed up through the flagstones where the child's feet had been—roots, Halloway thought, but the wrong color, the wrong movement—and then stopped.

Five feet.

The sigil was glowing. Faint, barely visible in the cellar's gloom, but there. Chalk lines that should have washed away three weeks ago were burning with a light that had nothing to do with the lamp on the ledge.

"It's taking her with it," Halloway said. "Whatever she was keeping in. Whatever was in that reliquary before the man stole it. It went into her when she died. The sigil held it there."

The coal chute grate was right in front of Pike now. Rusted iron, old wood, decades of neglect. The ladder beyond looked questionable but load-bearing.

"Climb," Halloway said. "I'm right behind you."

Behind them, the water in the cellar began to boil. Not from heat. From something pressing up from below—flagstones cracking, silt churning, the dark shape of the thing in the water lurching toward them with sudden, terrible purpose.

The sigil flared brighter. The chalk lines on the shoe were white-hot now, and the light was spreading—spreading outward in a circle that reached the coal chute, that reached the ladder, that reached the water where something was screaming without a voice.

"Go," Halloway said. "Go now."

She put her hand on Pike's back and pushed.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway set the blade to the first root. It was pale, she noted. Not wood-pale. Bone-pale. The consistency was wrong too—spongy where it should have been fibrous, yielding under the knife like something that had never been meant to grow aboveground.

"White fibrils," she said. "Root system, but wrong. No chlorophyll. No annual rings. This isn't plant. This is structural. Like tendons, except these were grown instead of grown into."

The second root. Same consistency. She carved deeper, feeling the blade scrape against something that gave like gristle.

"Smell's coming through now. You want to know what it smells like? Copper. Rotting vegetation. The sweet, thick smell of something that was alive and isn't anymore but hasn't figured that out yet."

The sigil flared again. The child's body was lifting now—not floating, lifting, drawn upward by the roots that had wrapped around her ankles, her calves, pulling her toward the cracked flagstones below. The chalk lines on the shoe in Pike's hand burned so bright Halloway had to squint against it.

"It's pulling her down into the foundation. Into whatever was sealed under the church before someone decided to get clever with a reliquary and a dead man's bones." She cut another root. Darker this time. "This is the thing that was underneath. Not the man. Not the child. This is the original. Three hundred years old, maybe four. Whatever Father Morrison's predecessors locked away, this is what's left of the cage."

The screaming sound was louder now. Coming from everywhere—from the water, from the stones, from the thing in the water that had finally reached the edge of the child's containment circle and was pressing against it like a face against glass.

"The roots go deep. Deeper than the foundation. This thing has been growing into the bedrock since before the church was built. The seal didn't keep it contained—it kept it fed. Slow. Controlled. A maintenance diet of whatever wandered into the crypt."

Halloway switched the knife to her off hand, flexed her fingers, found the largest root and sawed through it. It bled. That was wrong too. Roots didn't bleed.

"It's connected to the water table. That's why it's in the cellar. That's why the water's been rising for six months according to the parish records. It's been reaching. Looking for a way out. Looking for something to wear."

The child's body disappeared below the flagstones with a wet, sucking sound. The sigil's light began to fade.

"Done," Halloway said. She wiped the knife on her coat. "Whatever that was, it's not going anywhere for a few minutes. The roots are severed. It's bleeding out into the stone."

She turned toward the ladder.

"That thing in the water," she continued, climbing, "is not the original. It's what the original looks like when it puts on a person. The real thing is the roots. The network. The thing that's been spreading under this entire block since before your grandmother's grandmother was born."

She reached the top of the ladder, pulled herself up, reached back down for Pike's hand.

"So if you see another one," she said, hauling Pike up into the alley, "you cut the roots first. The body is just the hand. The hand is not where the strength is."

The coal chute cover was rusted shut. Halloway put her shoulder into it and it gave with a screech that echoed off the alley walls. She didn't care about noise anymore. The sigil was dead, the child was gone, and whatever had been in that cellar was busy bleeding into the foundations of a church that was about to have very serious structural problems.

She sat on the cobblestones, breathing hard, her boots still dripping.

"You did well," she said. "You didn't look back."

She looked at the shoe in Pike's hand. The chalk was ash now. Cold ash.

"Keep that," she said. "The leather might still have traces. Good to have if you need to reference the sigil later." She paused. "Don't tell anyone where you got it. Don't tell them what was on it. And don't ever go into a cellar like that again without three exits mapped and a way to burn the whole building down if necessary."

She stood. Her knees ached. Her coat weighed twice what it should have.

"The church will want answers," she said. "The police will want answers. Father Morrison will want answers. None of them will like the truth." She started walking toward the end of the alley. "The truth is someone stole from a sealed crypt and something very old woke up hungry. The truth is a little girl died wearing a charm her mother gave her, and it worked exactly as well as charms ever do. The truth is we got out alive and that's more than most people get when they go looking for answers in cellars like that."

She paused at the corner. Looked back at the church, silent and dark against the sky.

"We'll need to come back," she said. "In a few days, when the ground settles. There might be more in there. There usually is."

She turned the corner and kept walking. The night air was cold and smelled like rain. She did not look back again.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I turn the shoe over in my hands, the leather clammy and limp. "You're bleeding," I say, my voice steadier than I feel. "From the roots."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway glanced at her hands. The left one, mostly. Where the roots had bled when she cut them, the fluid had gotten on her skin and started burning. Should have worn gloves. Hadn't thought of that.

"Caustic," she said. "Old remedies for old wounds. The roots don't like being cut. They fight back."

She flexed her fingers. The skin was reddening, starting to blister at the fingertips. She'd seen worse. Would see worse again.

"There's a surgeon on Barrow Street," she continued. "Owes me a favor. He'll patch it up, ask no questions, and not write anything down. We won't be able to use these hands for a day or two, but they won't get infected either."

She tucked the left hand under her arm, walking. The cold helped. Numbed things.

"You'll want to wash that shoe before you put it anywhere you care about," she added. "The chalk ash is inert but the leather's been saturated with whatever that sigil was drawing on. Could be nothing. Could be trace contamination. I'm not willing to find out the hard way."

She turned left at the end of the alley, toward the main road. The church was behind them now. Would stay behind them. For a few hours, at least.

"You did good in there," she said again. Quieter this time. "Most people look. You didn't look. That's the hard part. The looking is what gets you killed."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stopped walking. Turned. Pike was still standing there in the alley, the shoe clutched against their chest, face pale in the gaslight.

"Sit," she said. Not a question.

There was a low stone wall at the edge of the churchyard. Gravestones beyond, tilted and ancient, names worn smooth by centuries of rain. She sat on the wall, felt the cold seep through her trousers, and waited until Pike sat beside her.

The lamp went on the ground between them. The church behind them was silent. The cellar was a hundred feet below that, full of broken flagstones and dark water and something that had been growing since before the Reformation.

"Finish what," she said. Not unkindly.

The question hung in the air. Pike's hands were still shaking. The shoe dangled from their fingers like something dead. Which it was, in a way. The child was gone. The sigil was ash. Whatever protection that little girl had carried into that cellar had died with her in the dark.

Halloway looked at the gravestones. Most of them were older than the church itself—reused, reset, the dead of older faiths buried under newer ones. That happened a lot in places like this. The ground was already full of things that didn't want to leave.

"You want to know how it ends," she said. "For the church. For Father Morrison. For whoever stole the reliquary in the first place."

She pulled out her cigarettes. Shook one loose. Lit it with her good hand. The flame threw shadows across her face.

"The church will need to be demolished. Not the steeple—the foundations. The entire structure, down to bedrock. Everything that's built on top of what's underneath. That's the only way to be sure." She smoked. "They won't want to hear that. They'll want to pray. They'll want to call in experts from Rome or Constantinople or wherever the old orders keep their binding specialists. Those experts will take months to arrive and when they get here, they'll say the same thing I just said. Demolish it. Burn the rubble. Salt the earth."

She exhaled. The smoke drifted toward the church like something trying to go home.

"Father Morrison will blame himself. He won't be wrong to. The seal was his responsibility. But seals fail. They always fail eventually. Someone should have been checking the binding annually, reinforcing it, feeding it. Nobody does that anymore. Nobody wants to think about what's underneath their church. Easier to brick it up and pretend."

The smoke was gone now. She took another drag.

"Whoever stole the reliquary—the man in the water—that wasn't his first time. You don't walk into a sealed crypt and try to use a reliquary for personal power unless you've done this before. Unless you've had successes. There will be other families missing people. Other parishes with unexplained deaths. Other records that don't quite add up. That's your work now, if you're taking this up. Finding the ones who got away. Finding out what they've done with what they've stolen."

She stubbed out the cigarette on the stone wall. The ember died with a faint hiss.

"The girl," she said. Quieter now. "Mary. The shoe. Her family might still be in the parish. They might have reported her missing. They might be still looking." She looked at the shoe in Pike's hands. "That's the part that doesn't get finished. The part where someone has to go to a door and tell a mother that her daughter died in a cellar holding a charm that was supposed to protect her. That part doesn't have an ending. That part just keeps going."

She stood. Her knees complained. Her hands were starting to throb.

"You did good in there," she said a third time. "But good isn't the same as finished. Good is what keeps you alive long enough to do the work that comes next."

She looked at the church one more time. The steeple. The dark windows. The place where, somewhere below, a little girl had curled up in a corner and tried to make herself invisible.

"The cellar will be quiet for a few days," she said. "The roots are severed. The binding is broken. What's left underneath will be too busy bleeding to reach for anything new. After that, it will start growing again. That's what old things do. They grow. They wait. They find new ways to wear the people who get too close."

She started walking again. Toward Barrow Street. Toward the surgeon. Toward whatever came next.

"Finish it," she said, echoing Pike's words. "The only way to finish something like this is to keep going until there's nothing left to do. Then start again when it comes back." She paused at the corner. "And it will come back. It always comes back. That's the part nobody tells you when you start doing this work."

She waited for Pike to catch up.

"That's the finish," she said. "There isn't one. There's just the next one, and the one after that, until you can't do it anymore."

The street was empty. The rain was coming. She could smell it in the wind.

"Now," she said. "Surgeon first. Then whiskey. Then we talk about what comes next."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I look down at my hands, still steady, and nod once. "Alright." I tuck the shoe inside my coat, the damp leather cold against my ribs. I fall into step beside her, my boots making soft, wet sounds on the cobblestones.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
They walked in silence for three blocks. The gas lamps gave way to darker stretches where the light didn't reach, and Halloway's good hand drifted to her knife automatically. Old habits. The kind that kept you breathing.

The rain started as they turned onto Barrow Street. Light at first, then heavier. It washed the cellar smell off her coat, out of her hair. She let it.

"The surgeon's name is Crane," she said. "Hasn't got his left eye anymore. Lost it to something he was treating before I met him. He doesn't talk about it. I don't ask. That's how we manage."

She stopped in front of a narrow townhouse with a brass plate by the door. The plate said CRANE, M. SURGERY in neat, faded letters. No hours listed. No specialization. Just the name and the single word that said everything and nothing.

"He'll want to see your hands too," she added. "The caustic gets on everything. You were closer to the sigil than I was. Closer than I wanted you to be."

She didn't knock yet. Stood there in the rain, looking at the door, thinking about what came after surgery and whiskey. Thinking about the next job. There was always a next job.

"The shoe," she said. "Don't put it near anything organic. Don't put it near anything you're attached to. Don't put it anywhere you'll forget where it is." She paused. "And don't ever, under any circumstances, show it to someone who collects things. The kind of person who collects these sorts of things is the kind of person who starts believing they can use them."

She knocked. Three times. The pattern that meant friend, not emergency, not threat. The door opened almost immediately.

Crane was a thin man with gray hair and a patch over his left eye. He looked at Halloway's hands. He looked at Pike's hands. He looked at the water still dripping from their clothes onto his floorboards.

"Cellar work," he said. It wasn't a question.

"Cellar work," Halloway confirmed.

He stepped aside and let them in.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: The warmth of his front room hits me like a wall. I hold my hands out, fingers splayed, watching the red blisters form. "Will it scar?" I ask Crane, my voice sounding too loud in the quiet.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Crane didn't answer immediately. He was examining the blisters with a probe, tilting his head at an angle that suggested he was seeing things beyond what was visible to the naked eye. His remaining eye was sharp, too sharp, the kind of eye that had learned to compensate for what it had lost.

Halloway watched from the doorway. Her own hands were beginning to stiffen. The caustic was working its way deeper, which meant she'd been holding the roots longer than she should have.

"Scars are how the body remembers," she said. "You get enough of them, you stop counting. You just start reading them like a calendar."

Crane looked up at her. Then back at Pike's hands.

"The tissue will heal," he said. His voice was quieter than Halloway's, softer. The kind of voice that had learned to be gentle because the work it described was not. "The outer layer will blister and peel. New skin will grow. But the deeper tissue—" He paused. "Some of the nerve endings are damaged. Permanently. You won't feel cold the same way in those fingertips. Not ever again."

Halloway nodded. She'd expected that. The roots had been old. Vicious in the way old things were vicious. They didn't just wound. They marked.

"That's not the worst of it," Crane continued. He was wrapping Pike's hands now, careful, professional. "Whatever this was, it left something behind. Trace contamination. I can see it in the discoloration. It won't hurt you—your body will fight it off eventually—but you'll carry a piece of it for a while. A souvenir."

He tied off the bandages. Looked at Halloway.

"Whiskey after this," he said. "Not before. Your hands need to stay dry for twenty minutes or the wrapping won't hold."

Halloway pushed off from the doorway and went to sit in the chair by the window. Rain was running down the glass in long streaks, blurring the streetlights into smears of gold.

"Souvenirs are common in this work," she said. To Pike, but loud enough for Crane to hear. "You pick things up. Residue. Trace connections. Sometimes they fade. Sometimes they don't. The ones that don't fade are the ones that teach you the most about what you're hunting."

Crane brought two glasses of whiskey to the table. Set one in front of each of them. The amber liquid caught the lamplight, turned it warm.

"To the ones who don't look," he said. Raised his glass, just slightly.

Halloway raised hers. Watched Pike do the same.

They drank.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I drink the whiskey in one slow burn, letting it settle. "I looked at the man in the water," I say, the admission raw. "Before you told me not to. I saw his eyes."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Still got most of the soft tissue. Water's cold enough down here to slow the decay. Another week, maybe two, and you'd be looking at bone.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: What you're looking at is a man who tried to become something else using parts he shouldn't have touched

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: It hollowed him... Started with the soft tissue—tongue, cheeks, the inside of the throat... The lips went next, then the cartilage in his nose... The muscles came next... the tendons used to be... Internally, it replaces. Reorganizes. Starts with the digestive system

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: It was pale, she noted. Not wood-pale. Bone-pale. The consistency was wrong too—spongy where it should have been fibrous, yielding under the knife like something that had never been meant to grow aboveground... Smell's coming through now. You want to know what it smells like? Copper. Rotting vegetation. The sweet, thick smell of something that was alive and isn't anymore but hasn't figured that out yet.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: Halloway stopped walking. Turned. Pike was still standing there in the alley

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Wrong is a very large category in our line of work, Pike," Halloway said. She didn't lower the lamp. The yellow light caught the greasy film on the surface of the water, fracturing into dull, oil-slick rainbows. "Be specific. A sack of turnips has a wrong shape if you're expecting a man, but it won't try to climb up your trousers."

She nudged her chin toward the dark mass. It was humped in the far corner, half-submerged, like a drowned sheep but twice the size and the color of wet lard where the skin showed through the scum. 

"Look at the displacement," she said, her voice dropping into that flat, clinical drone she used for cataloging remains. "Four feet of water. If it were a human corpse, it’d either be on the flagstones by now or bloated enough to break the surface. That thing is suspended midway. Like tallow in cold broth. What does that tell you about its structure?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I squinted, trying to see what she meant. "It's... too dense to float all the way, but too light to sink?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Close enough for a passing mark," Halloway said, her gaze never shifting from the white mass. "It means its fat-to-bone ratio is rubbish. Most likely because it hasn't got any bones. Think cartilaginous. Like a sturgeon, or a very large, very greasy sack of gristle."

She shifted her weight, her leather waders creaking against the slimy cellar wall. 

"And look at the lack of bloating," she continued, her voice flat. "It’s been down here at least five days—you can see the green mold taking hold where the skin meets the air. A human lung would have filled with gas and brought the chest up by now. This thing isn't fermenting. No gut bacteria we’d recognize. Which is the only bit of luck we’re getting today."

She glanced sideways at Pike, the lantern-light carving deep, tired lines around her mouth. "It means when we finally have to stick an iron in it, it won't pop and cover us in three-day-old cabbage."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway shifted the lantern, letting the beam cut deeper into the corner where the white mass lay. The smell was beginning to rise now that they were standing still—not the sweet, rotten stench of a corpse, but something old and cold, like wet wool left in a cellar for a decade.

"If it was," Halloway said, her voice dry, "it’s been thoroughly renegotiated. A person has twenty-four ribs, Pike. They don't usually fold themselves into a three-foot lump to fit behind a water pipe."

She waded a half-step closer, the water sloshing thick and greasy against her thighs. She pointed a gloved finger at a greyish, puckered crease near the top of the mass. 

"See that? If you’re sentimental, you’ll call it a mouth. If you’re sensible, you’ll see it’s a spiracle. A breathing hole. It’s got three of them along the flank. People don't have those, no matter how long they spend in the bath."

She leaned in slightly, squinting through the steam of her own breath. 

"There are no teeth in that slit. Just a set of horn plates, like a turtle. If it ate the cellar's owner, it didn't chew him. It would have had to let him soften up first. Which brings us back to the water." She looked up at the ceiling, where the floorboards above were dark with dry rot. "The landlord said the tenant went missing three weeks ago. If he’s in there, he’s currently part of the soup."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow hard. "So what do we do? It's not moving, but it might not be dead."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Everything is dead eventually," Halloway said, her voice barely louder than the steady *drip-drip* of water from the floorboards above. "The trick is making sure the transition is permanent before we turn our backs."

She reached behind her shoulder, her hand finding the worn ash handle of the five-foot gaff she’d brought down. The iron hook at the end was dark and pitted with salt-scarring, but the point was kept bright and sharp enough to shave with. 

"If it's dead, it'll feel like a sack of wet dough when I prod it," she said, her tone as conversational as a butcher explaining cuts of beef. "No elasticity. Just a dull slide. If it’s still got some spark in it, it’ll do one of two things. It will either contract to try and hide its soft bits, or it’ll try to fold itself around the shaft. Without bones, its only defense is to smother."

She shifted her grip on the ash pole, her knuckles white against the wood. 

"Hold the lamp," she commanded, transferring the heavy brass lantern toward Pike without looking. "Keep the light directly on the crevice behind it. If it starts to shift, I want to see the water level change before I feel it."

She took a slow, agonizingly deliberate step forward. The greasy water sloshed up to her hip, the cold of it biting through her heavy wool trousers beneath the waders. The white mass in the corner remained perfectly still, but a thin, oily film was beginning to drift away from its side, spinning slowly in the ripples she had just made.

"Watch the spiracles," Halloway murmured, raising the gaff. "If you see them dilate, it means it's taking in water to ballast itself. That’s your cue to start climbing the ladder."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't look back at him. Her eyes remained fixed on the spot where the white hide met the greasy water. 

"Plainly," she said, her voice dropping an octave to keep from carrying in the damp vault of the cellar. "It came up the privy or the storm drain when the river swelled last month. They start small. Thin as an eel, mostly water. They can squeeze through a pipe no wider than your wrist."

She shifted her stance, her boots sucking in the silt on the cellar floor. 

"It found the tenant. Probably while he was asleep, or too drunk to notice the draft. It didn't bite him. It doesn't have the leverage for it. It simply laid its weight across his face and chest until he stopped thrashing. Then it began the work."

She raised the gaff, lining the point up with the crease she’d called a breathing hole. 

"It secretes an alkaline fluid from the skin. Turns everything it touches into soap. Muscle, hair, wool trousers—it all goes to grease. Once the tenant was soft enough, it sucked him in through those three spiracles. But the creature made a calculation error. A common one for things that don't have brains to go with their stomachs."

She paused, her breath coming in a short, white puff that lingered in the lantern light. 

"It got too fat to get back down the drain. And then the cold weather hit. The water in this cellar dropped below forty degrees. When a boneless thing like this gets cold, its fats congeal. It’s like pouring hot bacon grease down a cold lead pipe. It hardens from the inside out. It couldn't move, it couldn't breathe, and eventually, its own weight collapsed its air passages."

She braced her back foot against the foundation wall, her shoulders squaring. 

"That’s the theory," she muttered. "Now we see if it’s actually dead, or just very, very slow."

She lunged forward with the gaff, driving the iron point into the center of the white mass.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content:
I flinched at the sound—a wet, dull *thunk* that didn't echo. The mass didn't move, but the iron hook sank in too deep, too easily.

"Empty," I breathed, watching the hole she'd made. It didn't close. "It's just... skin?"

A slow, thick bubble of something dark and foul broke the surface near the gaff. The smell hit me then—not old wool, but spoiled fat and something sharp, chemical. I gagged, tightening my grip on the lantern. "What's left inside?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't flinch. She kept her grip on the ash pole, her shoulders rigid as she felt the lack of resistance. She didn't pull the iron back out. Instead, she leaned her weight into it, twisting the shaft a quarter-turn to feel the interior.

"Not empty," she said, her voice dropping into that low, gravelly rasp. "Liquefied. The cold didn't just stop it; it split the cellular walls. The fat has turned to grease, and the grease has turned to soap. Adipocere. Grave-wax."

She levered the gaff upward. The rubbery, lard-colored skin tore with a sound like wet canvas parting. From the breach, a thick, grey-black slurry began to ooze, sluggish and heavy, spreading across the surface of the standing water like cold gravy. The chemical stench intensified, sharp enough to make the eyes water—a mix of ammonia, rancid lard, and old drains.

"That's your tenant," Halloway said, her face expressionless in the yellow lamplight. "Or what's left of him. The creature’s digestive enzymes were still working when the frost hit. It couldn't vent them, so it digested itself from the inside out. A closed system."

She wiped her nose with the back of her sleeve, her eyes watering slightly from the fumes, but her gaze remained steady on the tear. 

"Well," she muttered, a faint, dry twitch at the corner of her mouth. "The good news is we don't have to carry it up the stairs. The bad news is we’re going to need a bucket and a very large spoon."

She looked over her shoulder at Pike, her eyes hard and searching under the brim of her hat. "Keep that light steady. I want to make sure the bottom of the sack is cold. If there's a core that hasn't melted yet, we still have a job to do."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked at him for a long beat, the lantern light catching the flat, unblinking stare she used when she was deciding if a pup was going to make it through their first winter. 

"Fair enough," she said. She reached into her coat pocket, pulled out a short, three-jointed brass rule, and used it to stir the thick, sluggish ooze leaking from the tear. She didn't look disgusted; she looked like a surveyor measuring a ditch.

"It starts with the softest parts," she said, her voice dropping into that rhythmic, instructional cadence. "Eyes first. Mucous membranes. The skin of the lips and throat. It doesn't have a throat of its own to speak of, so it lays its membrane over yours. Osmosis. It pumps the fluid in, and sucks the broth back out."

She nudged a floating, greyish-white lump with the rule. It crumbled into the dark water like wet flour.

"That’s a femur," she said. "Or what’s left after the calcium’s been leached. If it had finished the job, there wouldn't even be that. The creature uses the phosphorus for its own nervous system—such as it is—and leaves the rest as salt. What you’re looking at in this grease is the tenant’s fat, his muscle tissue, and his wool shirt, all rendered down into a single, uniform soap. The only things it couldn't manage are the teeth and the metal. His fillings will be at the bottom of the pile, along with his pocket watch."

She tapped the side of the deflating white sack with the brass rule, the metal making a dull, leaden *clink* against the rubbery skin.

"How far did it get? It got to the assimilation stage. The tenant isn't *inside* the creature like a Jonah in the whale, Pike. He *is* the creature now. Or he was, until the frost killed the engine. His proteins were being rebuilt into its hide. That white lard you’re looking at? That’s his mutton dinners and his beer-fat, re-spun into a caul."

She wiped the rule on her thigh, leaving a greasy smear on her trousers that smelled faintly of ammonia. 

"If you meet another one that’s still warm," she added, her eyes narrowing as she looked at Pike, "you don't wait to see how far it gets. You don't try to pull the man out. Once the fluid's in him, he's already dead; his lungs are already jelly. You use salt, or you use oil and a match. If you haven't got either, you find a very large hammer and you break its back before it can get its weight off the floor."

She reached out and took the lantern back from him, her grip firm. 

"Now," she said, shining the light down into the split carcass. "Look down there. See that dark, hard knot right in the center of the grease? The size of a turnip?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I lean closer, squinting into the hole. The knot was slick and black, like a lump of coal in a pot of fat. "Is that... the heart?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"A heart implies a vascular system, Pike," Halloway said, her voice dry as tinder. "This thing doesn't pump. It oozes. No, that’s the ganglion. The pith."

She reached down, her oilskin sleeve dragging through the greasy water, and wedged the brass rule under the black lump. With a wet, sucking sound, she pried it upward. It was heavy, about the size of a cobbler’s last, and the light showed it wasn't smooth. It was covered in tiny, stiff bristles, like the tongue of a cat but thick as iron wire.

"It’s the nerve-knot," she continued, holding the lantern closer so the yellow light shone directly into the cavity. "The only part of it that doesn't go to mush when the cold hits. It sits right behind the spiracles to coordinate the squeezing. If you don't destroy this, the rest of the grease can sit in the dark for three years, and the moment the cellar warms up in spring, it’ll start drawing in whatever crawls past. Earthworms, rats, a dog if one falls down the coal chute. It’ll build itself back up from the tallow."

She tapped the black knot with the tip of her gaff. It didn't flinch, but it gave off a dull, metallic *thump*, like lead. 

"It’s cold," she pronounced, her shoulders dropping a fraction of an inch. The tension she’d been holding since they stepped off the ladder finally leaked out of her. "Solid all the way through. If there was any heat left in the core, the bristles would be twitching. They use them to feel the vibration of the water."

She reached into her belt and pulled out a heavy, short-bladed splitting knife. She didn't hesitate; she drove the blade straight into the center of the black knot. It parted with a stiff, woody groan, like dry oak being split with an wedge. Inside, the tissue was a dark, glittering purple, dry as salt.

"There," she said, twisting the knife to widen the split. "Dead as Sunday. The frost got right to the wick."

She wiped the blade on the side of her waders, leaving a dark, greasy smudge, and looked up at Pike. Her eyes were bloodshot from the ammonia fumes, but her expression was perfectly level. 

"That's the lesson, then," she said. "You don't go home when the shaking stops. You go home when you've split the pith. Now, grab the sack we left by the stairs. We need to collect the teeth and the metal before the landlord tries to turn this place into a coal cellar again."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway paused her knife for a fraction of a second, squinting up at him through the rising, greasy steam. A tiny, grim twitch of her mouth was the only sign she’d heard him, but she didn't tell him to shut up. Instead, she slid the blade deeper into the split hide, slicing downward with a wet, heavy *shhhk* sound.

"You want the ledger, then," she said, her voice dropping into that rhythmic, rhythmic drone. "Pay attention to the resistance of the knife. Under the skin, there’s no resistance at all for the first three inches. That’s the lard-layer. It’s cold, so it has the consistency of butter left in a larder. It smells of old mutton fat and lye. The lye is the creature’s own secretions; it smells sharp enough to make your nose bleed if you take a deep breath. Don't."

She reached her gloved hand directly into the slit, her fingers disappearing up to the wrist in the grey-white slurry. She rummaged with a slow, circular motion, like a woman testing the depth of a flour bin.

"Now, the bones," she continued, her fingers clicking against something solid beneath the grease. "The long bones go first because they’re porous. The marrow is rich; the creature wants the fat in it. I’m feeling the femur now. It’s soft. I can dent it with my thumb, like wet chalk. It doesn't snap; it crumbles. That means the assimilation was seventy percent complete. The calcium has been stripped and redistributed to the outer hide to make those horn plates in the spiracles."

She pulled her hand back out, dripping with a thick, yellow-grey paste that clung to her leather glove in long, greasy ropes. She didn't wipe it off. She used her clean hand to point into the dark cavity.

"Look at the color of the fluid draining into the water," she said. "It’s not red. There’s no blood left. The creature uses the iron in the hemoglobin to harden its own skin, which is why the hide has that rusty, brownish tint where it isn't lard-white. The rest of the blood—the plasma, the water—is what we’re standing in now. If you look closely at the surface, those red-brown flakes aren't rust from the pipes. That’s the tenant's iron. It’s settled out because the creature had no more use for it once the heart stopped."

She leaned in, her nose inches from the tear, her eyes narrowed as she reached in with her knife again. 

"Here’s the part you need to remember if you find one that’s still warm," she muttered, her blade scraping against something hard and metallic with a sharp *screee*. "The stomach doesn't dissolve metal, but the heat of the process melts low-grade solder. If the tenant had a cheap pocket watch, the gears will be loose in the grease. If he had lead fillings, they’ll have run into small beads at the bottom of the sack. But the teeth stay."

She worked her fingers down toward the very bottom of the mass, where it met the stone floor of the cellar. With a wet, sucking grunt, she hauled up a handful of grey silt and let it spill over the edge of the split hide. 

Among the gravel and the grease, several small, white squares glinted in the lantern light. They were clean, stripped entirely of gums or bone, looking like small, polished pebbles.

"Enamel," Halloway said, tapping one with her fingernail. "The acid can't touch it. If you’re ever trying to identify a heap after one of these has finished, you count the molars. If there are thirty-two, you’ve got one adult. If there are forty, you’ve got a mother and a dog, or a very messy feeder."

She wiped her glove on her thigh, leaving a thick, smeary track of grey grease. 

"The clothes are the worst of it," she added, her voice perfectly flat. "Wool and cotton don't dissolve; they just felt. They get worked into the grease until they’re like hair in mortar. If you look at the back of this thing—" she nudged the heavy, deflated hide with her boot, causing the water to slosh thick against the wall "—you’ll see the pattern of the tenant’s waistcoat pressed right into the skin. Like a leaf in coal."

She looked up at Pike, her eyes hard and red-rimmed from the ammonia. 

"That’s how far it got. It had turned his life into grease, and it was about three days from turning that grease into more of itself. If the frost hadn't come, we wouldn't be looking at a lump. We’d be looking at three smaller ones, each about the size of a dog, waiting by the cellar stairs for the landlord to come down with more coal."

She held her hand out toward him, palm up. "The sack, Pike. Before my waders leak through."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I hand her the sack, my own hands steady but cold. "So we're not cleaning up," I say. "We're making sure it doesn't come back."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway snatched the canvas bag by its greasy neck. It was a heavy, double-stitched thing, stiffened with dried tallow and salt from dozens of previous drafts. 

"Cleaning up is for widows and municipal draymen," Halloway said, her voice dry as she crouched lower over the split hide. "We’re here to ensure the ledger balances. If we leave this grease as it is, the next high tide will back up the storm drain and wash forty gallons of human soap into the parish well-head. Anyone drinking from the pump on the corner would have a very brief, very oily summer."

With her gloved hand, she began scooping the teeth out of the silt, dropping them one by one into the bottom of the sack. They fell with a series of sharp, wet *clinks*, like dice in a cup. 

"We take the teeth because the parish beadle doesn't pay the bounty on a bucket of lard," she continued, her fingers scraping the flagstones beneath the carcass. "They want hard evidence. No bone, no coin. And the landlord needs them if he wants to legally declare the tenancy void and clear out the man’s stick of furniture. Otherwise, he’s waiting seven years for a dead man to stop paying rent."

She reached down and grabbed the two split halves of the black ganglion. They went into the bag with a heavy, leaden thud that ended the clinking of the teeth. 

"And we take the pith because even split, it has a habit of remembering its shape," she said, squinting through the rising chemical steam. "You leave these pieces in the dark with enough moisture, and they’ll start to sprout. Like a turnip in a cellar bin, only this one grows bristles and starts looking for a heel to latch onto. We’ll burn them in the kiln at the watch-house. High heat is the only thing that unscrews the marrow."

She pulled her hands free of the mess, her sleeves dark and dripping to the elbow with the grey-yellow slurry. She stood up slowly, her knees making a dry, cracking sound that was nearly as loud as the gaff hitting the water. She let the canvas bag hang heavy from her fist, the grease already beginning to darken the bottom of the coarse cloth.

"There," she said, looking down at the deflated, empty white skin. It looked like nothing more than an old tarpaulin discarded in the mud. "That’s the meat of it. The rest of this is just tallow and ditch-water. It’ll rot down to nothing by the frost's end, provided the rats don't get fat on it first."

She turned her bloodshot, watering eyes toward Pike, her face carved into hard lines by the flickering yellow light of the lantern. 

"The landlord’s waiting at the top of the stairs with our four shillings and a bottle of cheap gin," she said. "He’s going to ask if the cellar is safe for his next tenant. What are you going to tell him?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stood in the grey water for a moment longer, the heavy canvas sack dripping from her hand. The water level had dropped an inch now that the mass had deflated and its liquid center had mingled with the flood. 

She took a slow, heavy step toward the stone stairs, her boots sucking at the silt on the cellar floor. The water swirled behind her, thick and sluggish, carrying a few stray white flakes of the tenant's iron. She stopped on the lowest dry step, just below where Pike sat, the greasy water draining from her waders in thin, dark streams that ran back down into the dark.

"You tell him it was the rot," Halloway said, her voice flat and echoing in the low brick vault. "You tell him the tenant had a weak chest, took a fit of the dropsy, and crawled down here to die in the dark where the cold could numb him. You don't mention the spiracles. You don't mention the grease. If you tell a landlord his cellar grows things that turn people into lard, he doesn't rent the rooms. He doesn't pay us, either, because he thinks we brought the curse in our pockets to make a trade."

She set the heavy canvas bag down on the step between them. It settled with a wet, heavy *squelch*, a thin line of yellowish grease immediately beginning to seep through the coarse weave and stain the dry stone.

"And then," she continued, "you tell him to buy three sacks of unslaked lime. Not the cheap agricultural stuff, but the white lump lime from the kiln. You tell him to shovel it straight into this standing water while it's still dry. It’ll boil. The water will turn to steam hot enough to peel the skin off your shins, and the lime will eat whatever grease we missed. It turns the remaining fat into calcium soap—dry, hard, and useless to anything that wants to grow. If he doesn't do it, the next man who comes down here for coal will slip on the flagstones, cut his knee, and have the grease in his blood before he reaches the top of the stairs."

She hoisted her leg up, the wet leather of her waders creaking as she sat down on the step below Pike. She took off her hat, letting her grey-streaked hair fall damp against her forehead. The smell of the cellar was on both of them now, clinging to their wool coats, their skin, the hair inside their noses. 

"The smell won't leave your hair for a week," she muttered, reaching down to unbuckle the heavy leather straps of her waders. "The grease gets under your fingernails. You can scrub with yellow soap until your skin is raw, but the moment you get warm by a fire, you’ll smell the tenant again. He’ll come out in your sweat. Your bread will taste of him. Your tea will taste of him. You just have to chew through it until your body clears the lard out."

She pulled her left boot off with a wet *shluck*, her thick wool sock underneath damp but mostly free of the grey grease. 

"That’s the finish of it," she said, looking up at him through the gloom, her red-rimmed eyes reflecting the yellow flame of the lamp he held. "We take our four shillings. We go to the watch-house. We put the pith in the iron grate and we watch it turn to grey ash. If it starts to hiss, we spit on it. We drink the landlord’s bad gin until the back of our throats stop tasting like ammonia. And tomorrow we look for the next one."

She reached out her hand, her fingers stained a dark, chemical grey from the creature's fluids. "Give me the lamp, Pike. Let's go get our four shillings before the landlord gets sober enough to count them."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I hand her the lamp, my knuckles tight around the sack's drawstring. "I want to be there when you burn it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took the heavy brass loop of the lamp from his hand, her fingers brushing his cold knuckles. She didn't pull away immediately. Instead, she let the light shine up into his face, studying the tight, white line of his jaw and the way his fingers were white-hot stiff around the hemp drawstring. 

"You're holding that like it's a bag of sovereigns, Pike," she said, her voice low and scraping in the damp space. "Relax your grip. It’s dead. It’s not going to bite through the canvas, and if you squeeze it too hard, you’ll just force the grease out through the seams and get it all over your waistcoat."

She turned, her boots creaking as she took the first step up the damp stone stairs, keeping the lamp low to light the rise for him. 

"You want to see the fire? Fine," she said, her head tilted back to look up at the drafty wooden door at the top of the flight. "But you’re carrying the bag. And you don't stand downwind of the chimney. Not unless you want to spend the next three days explaining to every dog in the parish why you smell like a rotten tallow-chandler's shop."

She paused on the third step, waiting for him to follow. The heavy, cold air of the cellar seemed to cling to their heels, reluctant to let them go. 

"We use the small coke kiln in the cellar of the watch-house," she continued, her voice dropping into that familiar, dry rhythm as they climbed. "It has a flue that goes up through the old bakery chimney. When you drop the pith onto the hot coals, the first thing that happens is the bristles. They don't burn like hair. They don't melt, either. They pop. Like salt in a hot frying pan, only louder. If you don't keep the iron grate closed, they’ll spit three feet out of the hearth and burn a hole right through your trousers."

She took another step, the light bobbing against the slimy brickwork of the stairwell. 

"The purple salt inside the knot—that’s the marrow of it—that’s what goes next. It burns with a green flame. Not a bright, clean green like copper, but a thick, greasy, cabbage-colored light. It doesn't give off much heat, but the smoke is heavy. It doesn't rise; it rolls along the floor like river fog. If you breathe it in, the salt settles in your throat. It tastes of copper and old pennies, and you'll be coughing up grey phlegm that smells of ammonia for a fortnight."

She reached the top landing, where the rotten draft from the street above was beginning to cut through the cellar's heavy stench. She stood by the latch of the cellar door, her silhouette dark against the faint, grey daylight leaking down from the hallway above.

"So you'll stand by the door, and you'll keep a wet rag over your nose," Halloway said, looking back down at him. "And when the green light goes out and there’s nothing left but a heap of grey ash that looks like flour, you’ll take the shovel and you’ll scrape it into the dry bucket. We don't leave the ash in the grate. If the chimney sweeps get it on their brushes, they'll have the rot in their fingernails before the week is out."

She reached for the iron latch of the door, but didn't lift it yet. She looked at Pike, her eyes two dark, steady points in the shadow of her hat. 

"You still want to be there?" she asked. "Or has the four shillings started to seem like a great deal of trouble for very little bread?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I want to be there," I say, my voice a little hoarse from the ammonia. I climb the last steps, the sack heavy in my hand. "I need to see it go to ash."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway nodded once, a brief, sharp movement of her chin. "Then you'll see it," she said. 

She lifted the iron latch and pushed the door open, letting them out into the narrow, damp passage of the tenement. The air here was cold and smelled of cabbage and wet coal-dust, but compared to the cellar, it tasted like mountain air. 

The landlord was waiting five paces back, huddled against the peeling wallpaper with a lantern that shook in his hand. He looked at Halloway’s grease-smeared waders and the heavy, stained canvas bag in Pike’s hand, his eyes wide with a mix of dread and greed.

"Is he... is he out?" the man whispered.

"He's gone," Halloway told him, her voice loud and flat in the narrow hall. "The dropsy took him. He crawled down to the cold to die, and the rats finished the work. We cleared what was left of the bones." 

She didn't wait for him to ask about the smell. She took a step closer, her wet boots leaving dark, greasy prints on his floorboards. 

"But you’ve got the wet-rot down there," she continued, leaning in until the landlord flinched from the stench of her coat. "If you don't throw three sacks of unslaked lump lime down into that water before Sunday, the floorboards will go through and the next tenant will land in the soup. Give us the shillings."

The landlord counted four thin silver coins into her palm with trembling fingers, then handed over a flat, green glass bottle of gin that smelled of potato spirit and turpentine. Halloway pocketed the silver, shoved the bottle into her coat, and didn't offer a word of thanks. She gestured to Pike with her chin, and they headed out into the rain.

They walked through the grey afternoon, the drizzle turning the soot on the roofs into dark streaks down the brickwork. People on the street gave them a wide berth; the smell of the cellar preceded them by ten paces, a thick, greasy vapor of lard and ammonia that the damp air seemed to preserve rather than disperse. A stray terrier followed them for two blocks, its nose twitching at Pike's bag, until Halloway made a short, sharp motion with her gaff that sent the beast scuttling into an alley.

The cellar of the watch-house was warmer than the one they had left, but not by much. It was a low, vaulted space of yellow brick, dominated by a small, heavy coke kiln used for melting lead and drying salt-rations. The coals inside were already banked, glowing with a sullen, deep orange heat behind the heavy iron grate.

Halloway hung the brass lamp on a nail in the ceiling and turned to Pike. She reached for a pair of long-handled iron tongs hanging by the hearth.

"Put the bag on the flagstones," she said, her voice echoing off the brick. "And get your rag ready. Once this grate opens, the draft is going to pull the steam right toward the door."

She used the tip of the tongs to slide the heavy iron hatch of the kiln aside. A wave of dry, scorching heat hit them, smelling of sulfur and old coal.

"Right," she said, her eyes fixed on the glowing coals. "Dump the teeth in first. They don't burn, but the heat will crack the enamel and kill whatever grease is still hiding in the roots. Then we do the pith."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I set the bag down and pull my neckerchief up over my nose. The teeth make a sharp, rattling sound as I pour them into the grate. I watch them blacken instantly. "Now the pith?"

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: A person has twenty-four ribs, Pike. They don't usually fold themselves into a three-foot lump to fit behind a water pipe.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: It secretes an alkaline fluid from the skin. Turns everything it touches into soap. Muscle, hair, wool trousers—it all goes to grease. Once the tenant was soft enough, it sucked him in through those three spiracles.
