"Somewhere round eleven the count came back at me. Not a voice. Nothing so honest as a voice. A pressure behind the teeth, and a shape in my head that was a number, and the number was *twelve*, and it arrived before I'd said twelve, and I said twelve anyway because I couldn't stop, and after twelve came thirteen the same way, and I understood then what my teacher had meant when she'd said *don't count them out loud* and hadn't explained further because there are things you explain and things you say once and hope are enough."

The fire ticked. She let it.

"I got to nineteen. It got to nineteen with me and a half-step ahead. And when I was done counting, I knew things I hadn't known when I started. Not useful things. Not names or places. Shapes. The shape of what was under the floor of that farmhouse, which was bigger than the house and older than the county. The shape of what it wanted, which wasn't what I'd have called wanting. The shape of my own death, which it offered me the way a man might offer a chair — no threat in it, just a courtesy, *here, sit, I've one ready for you*."

She drank. A proper drink this time. Set the cup down.

"I burned the eggs. Burned the house. Walked back to town and didn't speak for four days, and when I spoke again I had a stammer for a year that I've mostly lost, and a rule I've never broken since, which is the rule I gave you on the stairs. You don't count them out loud. You don't count them in your head either, if you can help it — I couldn't help it that night, and I paid — you sweep them into the fire in one motion and you let the fire do the counting, because fire can't be answered."

She looked at him then. Full on. The fire moved on her face and she let it.

"That's the whole of that story. That's what I meant when I said it was for another fire. This is another fire. You asked plainly and you earned plainly, and now you have it, and you can carry it with the rest."

She picked her cup back up. Turned it. Didn't drink yet.

"Drink your drink, Pike. It won't taste of anything tonight — nothing does, the first night — but the shape of drinking it is worth the doing. Sit in the chair. The chair's yours now. I'll not take it back."

A beat. Drier.

"And if you dream of numbers, you wake me. I mean that. Any hour. You come down the passage and you knock and you wake me, and we sit up till it passes. That's not kindness. That's the rule after the rule. You'll pass it on to someone yourself, one day, if you last, and you'll mean it the way I mean it now."

She drank. Looked back at the fire.

"Welcome to the work."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I drink, and the tin cup tastes like nothing at all. "What's in the bottle?" I ask, my voice rough. Not because I care. Because I need to hear my own voice say something ordinary.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't turn her head. She heard the roughness in his voice and heard what it was for, and she gave him what he'd asked for and nothing more, because more would have been an insult to the ask.

"Plum brandy," she said. "Not a good one. There's a woman in the next village makes it in a copper still she inherited off her father, and her father made a better brandy than she does, but he's dead and she's not, so we drink hers."

She turned the cup on her knee. Considered it.

"Too sweet. Bit of a burn at the back that isn't the drink, it's whatever she put in the still last that she didn't scrub out properly. I've drunk worse. I've drunk worse this month. There's a bottle behind it in the dresser that's better, but I keep that for when someone's died, and no one's died tonight, so."

She lifted the cup a fraction, in the direction of the dresser and the better bottle and the nobody who'd died.

"Small mercies."

She drank. Set the cup down. Let the quiet sit between them a moment, because the quiet in a warm kitchen was a different animal from the quiet in a cellar, and he could stand to meet the difference.

"Ask me another ordinary one, if you like," she said. Not looking at him. Eyes on the fire. "I've a whole evening of ordinary in me if you want to draw it out. What's the cat's name. Where'd I get the chair. Why the dresser leans. All of them have answers and none of the answers matter, which is the point of them."

A pause. Almost a smile, not quite.

"The cat's Barnabas. He'll come in when he's ready. He doesn't like the smell after a burn but he'll forgive us by morning. He always does."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I set the cup down. It clinks against the wood.* "Why does the dresser lean?"

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: Doesn't matter what it was. Matters what it is

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The jaw was set wrong, hinged a half-inch further back than a jaw belonged, and the eyes had gone the flat grey of pond ice... see the split at the corner, there, where the lip's given up. Made itself at home. Wore him a while.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Under the skin: not much of him left. They hollow. Start at the lungs because that's where they come in, work outward. Heart goes early — they don't need it, and it's in the way. Liver, kidneys, the soft freight, all thinned to pulp and drunk. Bones stay. Bones are the frame they wear him on. Tendons stay, mostly, but they're rewritten — you'll see a joint bend a way it oughtn't, that's why. His jaw hinging back. That's not damage. That's alteration. It wanted a wider door for coming and going.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: Then I'll tell you what's under the skin till you're sick of hearing it

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Under the skin, then. Properly... They come in through a wet opening... First thing they take is the lungs... Heart's next... After the heart it goes at leisure. Liver, spleen, kidneys, the gut. Drinks the soft... Bones stay... Skin it keeps... Eyes are the tell

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept the lamp steady.

"Aye," she said. "Good. Wrong shape means your eyes have found the important bit before your head has made excuses for it."

The thing at the far end floated half against the wall, half under the water. Pale where it showed. Too many angles at the joints. One arm—if it was an arm—bent backward with the calm confidence of anatomy that had never consulted a churchyard.

"Count what you can see," Halloway said. "Limbs. Head. Open wounds. Anything trailing in the water. Don't name it yet. Names make people stupid."

She shifted the lamp an inch higher. The yellow light caught on a slick curve of bone and something like a row of small, black teeth set where no mouth ought to have been.

"Also, don't step forward. If it's dead, it'll wait. If it isn't, it'll appreciate the courtesy."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I count three limbs. No, four... one's broken off near the... shoulder? And there's a line of something dark trailing from the middle. Not blood. Too thin. Like threads.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway’s mouth tightened a fraction.

“Threads,” she said. “Aye. That’s worse than blood, generally. Blood has the decency to leave the body and be finished with it.”

She lowered the lamp just enough to put the dark strands in better relief. They drifted in the cellar water from the thing’s middle, fine and numerous, moving with the slow pull of currents that should not have existed in a sealed room.

“Don’t touch those,” she said. “Don’t let them touch you. If they snag your boot, you leave the boot. If they snag your skin, you tell me before you decide to be brave and quiet.”

The thing gave a small, soft knock against the stone wall. Not movement of its own. Water did that. Water, rats, settling floors, and cowards’ imaginations. Halloway had learned to sort them by sound.

She kept watching the wrong parts. The bent limb. The extra teeth. The place where the threads issued from the torso in a neat, puckered slit.

“Four limbs, one damaged at the shoulder. External filament growth from the abdomen or lower chest. No visible eyes from here. Teeth misplaced. Pale skin, no livor worth trusting because it’s been floating.” She paused. “Could be shed casing. Could be bait. Could be the poor bastard it grew inside before it climbed out wearing him like a bad coat.”

Her free hand moved to the satchel at her hip. Slow. No splash.

“Next question,” Halloway said. “Look at the water around it. Not the thing. The water. Is anything making a shape under the surface?”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not answer at once.

She watched the pale mass at the far end and the thin black threads unspooling from it in the water. Then she shifted the lamp slightly, enough for the light to crawl over what might once have been a collarbone.

“Recently,” she said, “yes.”

Her voice stayed flat. Not kind, exactly. Kindness in a cellar like that was usually just panic wearing a clean shirt.

“That part there was human skin. Shoulder line is wrong now, but it started as a man or woman. Adult. See the thickness through the chest, what’s left of it. Not a child.”

She pointed with two fingers, not stepping forward.

“Face is turned under or gone. Hard to say which from here. Those teeth aren’t human. The backward limb might be deformation after death, might be growth displacement, might be something inside rearranging the furniture.”

The floating thing knocked the wall again. Soft. Patient.

“But if you’re asking whether there’s a person in there to save,” Halloway said, “no. Not unless they’ve learned to live without most of the rules that make a person a person.”

She let that sit for a breath.

“Recently dead matters, though. Fresh host means fresh parasite, fresh spoor, fresh appetite. Whatever did this either hasn’t gone far, hasn’t finished, or wanted us to find the wrapper.”

Her hand came out of the satchel with a small glass vial and a hooked iron probe. The probe had old scorch marks up the shaft.

“So grieve later if you must. For now, look at the water.” Her eyes narrowed at the surface between them and the corpse. “If the threads are anchored to something underneath, this is a trap. If they’re just trailing, it’s evidence. Difference between the two is whether we get to complain about the smell on the way home.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look at the water. "There's... a pattern. The threads aren't just drifting. They're making circles." I point without moving closer. "Like they're anchored to the bottom."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway went very still.

“Good,” she said. “Bad, but good spotted.”

She did not look where Pike pointed at first. She looked everywhere else: ceiling beams, stairwell behind them, the black corners above the waterline, the mortar gaps in the wall. Traps liked witnesses. Witnesses liked staring at the obvious thing until the other thing took their face off.

Nothing moved.

Then she studied the circles.

The threads lay beneath the surface in faint dark rings, too regular for drift. They widened from the corpse in three overlapping loops, each one almost touching the cellar steps. Not quite. An invitation with manners.

“Anchored,” Halloway said. “Or pretending to be. Either way, the floor between us and it belongs to the thing now.”

She tucked the vial back into the satchel and kept the hooked iron probe in hand. Her thumb found the little notch near the grip by habit.

“Those rings are a feeler net. Some breeds use them to know when carrion comes near. Some use them to pull. Some just lay eggs through anything warm that breaks the circle.” She glanced down at the water around her own boots. “Which is why I am now deeply fond of this exact spot and have no plans to leave it.”

The corpse shifted again at the far wall.

This time the water around it did not ripple outward.

Halloway’s expression changed by a hair.

“Ah,” she said. “There’s our problem.”

She raised the lamp higher, letting the light spread over the surface. The corpse bobbed once, but the circles held their shape beneath it, black and delicate and patient.

“That knock against the wall should have made a wave. It didn’t. The threads took it. Dampened the water.” Her voice remained even. “So the net is active, not old. And anything that can drink motion out of water can feel us talking through our boots.”

She drew the probe up and held its hooked end over the nearest visible strand, still several feet away.

“Lesson, Pike. When a dead thing alters the behaviour of water, fire, shadow, dogs, clocks, or priests, you stop treating it as a body and start treating it as a conversation. Something is listening.”

Halloway took one slow breath through her nose.

“Now we do not cut it. Cutting a web tells the spider exactly which thread to visit. We do not throw anything heavy. Same reason, with more splashing and less dignity.”

A grim little smile touched her mouth and left.

“We ask it a question instead.”

From another pocket she removed a small twist of butcher’s paper. Inside lay a pinch of grey-white powder and three iron filings, dull as old teeth. She tipped them into her palm.

“Burnt bone, salt, and iron. Crude, impolite, effective on most things that mistake themselves for gods.”

She crouched only as far as she needed, coat hem clear of the water, and flicked the mixture onto the surface just short of the first dark circle.

The powder touched the water.

For half a second, nothing happened.

Then every black thread in the cellar tightened. Not much. Just enough to turn the circles from drifting lines into perfect geometry.

Halloway showed her teeth.

“There you are,” she said softly. “Awake after all.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway’s head turned sharply.

“Stop there,” she said.

Not loud. Loud was for taverns and funerals. In a cellar full of listening thread, loud was an apology written in blood.

She kept the probe lifted over the water and angled her body between the nearest ring and the work she meant to do.

“Plainly?” she said. “Someone brought a seed down here. In the gut, most likely. Drank it, ate it, breathed it off mould. Doesn’t matter now. It opened inside them.”

The black circles trembled under the water. Not from the lamp. Not from breath.

“It fed through the bowel first. Then the liver. Then the soft joins under the ribs. That dark trailing mess is not blood. It’s feeding filament. It grows finer than hair, spreads through wet tissue, and teaches itself where warmth is.”

Her eyes stayed on the corpse.

“Once it had enough of the person mapped, it started moving them badly. That’s your wrong shape. Joints bent by pull instead of muscle. Bones used as struts. Skin stretched where it needed covering and torn where it didn’t.”

The thing at the far wall gave another faint knock.

This time the rings tightened again, beautiful as a diagram in a surgeon’s book and twice as murderous.

“They were alive for part of it,” Halloway said. “Not all. There’s mercy in small quantities, apparently, like salt in bad soup.”

She lowered the hooked iron point until it almost kissed the surface.

“It came to water to finish. Or was brought here. Cellar flood gives it reach, cover, and a nice cold pantry. The host died here. Then the growth pushed out through the middle, laid its net, and left the body floating as bait.”

A thin strand rose half an inch from the surface, black and wet and delicate.

Halloway did not flinch.

“There,” she said. “That little bastard heard us.”

She touched the hook to the water beside it, not on it. The iron gave a tiny hiss. The strand recoiled, and the corpse at the far end jerked once hard enough to show a glimpse of ruined throat and pale chin.

Halloway’s smile was without humour.

“So that is what happened to it. A human being was used as soil, scaffolding, and supper. What’s left is not them. What’s left is the part of the trap that wants us feeling sorry enough to step closer.”

She slid her other hand back toward the satchel.

“And since someone has already obliged it by reducing the distance, we are going to be very calm, very dull, and very difficult to digest.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow and ease back an inch. "I'm sorry. I shouldn't have moved." My voice is too quiet, but that might be good. "What do we ask it?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not look back.

“Apologise after,” she said. “Preferably while alive. It improves the sincerity.”

The raised strand sank again, but the circles remained tight beneath the water. The nearest ring had crept perhaps an inch closer. Perhaps it only looked that way. Halloway distrusted anything that made her measure in perhaps.

“We ask it three things,” she said. “Where it is. Whether it is alone. Whether it knows pain.”

She took a second pinch of grey-white powder from the paper, then added something darker from another fold: dried vervain, blackened at the edges, and a shaving of lead.

“Not with words. Words are for things with ears and vanity. This has neither, unless it borrowed them.”

She scattered the mixture wider this time, not toward the corpse, but toward the space between the first and second rings.

The powder struck the water.

The cellar went quiet in a way that had weight.

Then the nearest black circle drew inward, shrinking from the salt and iron. The second ring held. The third widened.

Halloway nodded once.

“There. Answer one.”

She pointed with the iron hook toward the widening outer ring.

“It isn’t in the body. Not properly. The body’s a float and a dinner bell. The thinking part is under the floor or in the wall beyond it, feeding threads through cracks. If it were all in the corpse, all the rings would pull away from the burn. Instead, one recoils, one holds, one reaches. Distributed nervous system.”

A dry little sound left her. Almost a laugh.

“Which is a generous phrase for ‘cowardly weed with ambitions.’”

She reached into the satchel again and drew out a narrow tin case. Inside were six iron needles bound in red thread, their tips blackened with old pitch.

“Answer two next. Alone or colony.”

She selected one needle and held it over the lamp flame until the pitch at its point softened and smoked. The smell was bitter, tar and herbs and something funerary.

“If it is alone, it will pull from one direction when provoked. If there are several, the water will disagree with itself.”

She flicked the heated needle into the water just beyond the nearest ring.

It vanished with a soft plink.

For one breath, nothing.

Then the water at the far end dimpled inward toward the corpse. The water along the left wall shivered away from it. Near the steps, the surface rose in tiny beads, as if something below had exhaled.

Halloway’s face hardened.

“Ah, hell,” she said. “Colony.”

The black threads stirred now, not drifting but conferring. Fine strands lifted and sank, tasting the water where the needle had gone. The corpse rolled half an inch, enough for the lamp to catch the ruined line of its mouth.

Halloway kept her voice level.

“Three nodes at least. One in or under the far wall. One left side, likely behind that old shelving. One near the base of the stairs.”

She shifted her boot very slowly, no splash, no haste.

“That last one matters.”

The grim smile returned, thin as a knife cut.

“It means it did not wait for us to reach the trap. It grew the trap around the way out. Polite little strategist. I’d admire it more if it weren’t trying to climb up our trousers.”

She took one of the remaining iron needles and pressed it between her teeth for a moment while she freed a stoppered bottle from the satchel. The liquid inside was cloudy amber, flecked with sediment.

“Third question,” she said, removing the needle from her mouth. “Pain.”

She uncorked the bottle with her thumb. A sharp medicinal stink joined the cellar rot.

“Camphor, lye, foxglove ash, and cheap gin. Mostly the gin, if I’m honest. It offends living tissue and several kinds of dead tissue. Also most respectable women.”

She poured three drops onto the iron needle.

The metal smoked.

Halloway crouched, coat still clear of the water, and touched the treated point to the nearest strand.

The reaction was instant.

Every ring snapped tight. The strand curled back on itself, blackening at the point of contact. From the far end came a wet clicking sound, not from the corpse’s mouth exactly, but from inside the cavity of its chest. The cellar water trembled against the stones.

Halloway withdrew the needle before the thread could coil around it.

“There,” she said. “It knows pain.”

The clicking continued, fast and soft. Teeth where no mouth ought to have been opened and closed along the pale flank of the floating body.

Halloway watched them with professional distaste.

“That is useful. Pain means it can be persuaded. Colony means it must be persuaded all at once. If we burn only the body, the wall-nodes live. If we cut only the threads, the nodes shed this net and make another. If we wade about heroically, we become educational material for the next poor fool.”

She capped the bottle.

“So we do this meanly.”

Her gaze tracked the rings, the wall, the shelves, the stair-foot. Calculating distances. Weak stone. Water depth. Airflow. Lamp oil.

“We poison the water, nail the stair-node first, then the left, then the far wall. Last, we burn the host. Not before. Bait on fire is still bait, only brighter.”

She lifted the iron hook again.

“And until I say otherwise, every movement is slow. No splashing. No touching black thread. No trusting dead faces. If that thing starts speaking in a voice you recognise, you may assume it is being rude.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway’s eyes flicked once to Pike, then back to the water.

“Good reason,” she said. “Bad place for it. So listen hard.”

She shifted the lamp a little, throwing light across the floating ruin without stepping closer.

“It entered soft. These things almost always do. Mouth, nose, cut in the hand, tainted well-water, mould spores in bread. If it had gone in through a wound, we’d likely see a primary lesion near an extremity. We don’t. The centre is the belly. So he swallowed it, or breathed it and swallowed the drainage. Lovely thought. Put that beside jam at breakfast.”

The corpse turned slightly in the water, pale skin sliding against stone.

“First stage: rooting. It fixed in the gut lining. Small intestine, likely. That is where there’s warmth, blood, and enough folds for a parasite to hide from anything sensible the body tries to do. Fever. Cramps. Thirst. Maybe black threads in the stool if anyone had the poor taste to look.”

She pointed with the hooked iron probe toward the slit in the torso.

“Second stage: feeding net. It sent filaments through the mesentery into the liver and around the kidneys. Not through arteries at first. Around them. Important difference. If it bursts a major vessel too early, host dies before it has legs under it. These breeds are patient. They lace themselves along membranes, fascia, tendon sheaths. They use the body’s own wet roads.”

The nearest ring flexed beneath the water.

Halloway paused until it settled.

“Under the skin now? Not muscle as you understand it. Not entirely. Some muscle remains, especially in the limbs, but it’s dead meat being used as padding and leverage. The working part is filament bundled into cords. Think black horsehair soaked in glue, running from gut to shoulder, gut to hip, gut to jaw. Pull one cord, the arm moves. Pull another, the neck turns. Crude puppetry.”

Her mouth tightened.

“That backward bend at the limb means it stopped respecting the joint. It hauled from the wrong anchor and either dislocated the shoulder or broke the upper arm. See the angle? No defensive posture. No fall pattern. That was internal traction.”

She lifted the lamp higher.

“It took the liver first. Nearly always does. Rich organ, soft, full of blood. Then fat around the bowel. Then the diaphragm. Once it reached the diaphragm, breathing would have changed. Shallow. Hiccuping. Coughing up dark threads or little clots that moved wrong.”

A beat.

“If you meet a living one and they complain of something tickling behind the ribs, do not pat their back. Tie their hands.”

The floating body gave a small roll, exposing a strip of chest where the skin had lifted in grey, loose sheets.

“There. Skin separation. It did not rot off. It was undermined. Filaments spread between skin and muscle, making a pocket. That gives the colony space to breathe, seep, and feel vibration. In later stages, the skin becomes less covering and more curtain.”

She indicated the wrong teeth along the flank.

“Those are not teeth for eating. They’re hooks. Keratin and bone stolen from somewhere else. Ribs, jaw, fingernails, possibly inner ear bones if it had a sense of humour. It grows them where pressure happens. Anything brushes the body, the hooks catch. Then the filaments follow.”

Halloway’s expression remained flat, but her voice lowered.

“What it took from him? Blood, heat, liver, bowel, part of the lungs, most voluntary movement, and finally the use of his pain. Pain makes a fine bridle if you are a clever little obscenity. It hurts the host in one place, he moves away. Hurts him in another, he bends. Eventually he thinks he is choosing.”

The water near the far wall dimpled once.

Halloway angled the hook toward it.

“How far it got? Far enough to abandon him.”

She let that land cleanly.

“If the host were still the main body, we would see more swelling in the abdomen. More movement from the corpse. More heat. Instead, the filaments are external and organised into rings. That means it completed emergence. It used him until it had enough mass and memory to move into the cellar itself.”

She pointed in sequence without touching the water: far wall, left shelving, stair-foot.

“Node there. Node there. Node near us. The man was nursery and transport. The colony is now in the stone cracks, under the waterline, perhaps through the mortar. The corpse is a lure, nutrient sack, and speaking trumpet if it has kept enough throat to make noise.”

A thin black strand rose and sank again.

Halloway watched it with open contempt.

“Signs, if you meet another early: unexplained thirst, belly pain after damp cellars or old wells, fever without rash, threadlike black material in vomit or stool, bruising in straight lines under the skin, joints moving stiffly as if pulled rather than flexed. Later: aversion to dry heat, standing in water without noticing cold, listening to walls, answering questions a breath too late because something inside is deciding which face to wear.”

She drew one of the iron needles from the case and held it ready.

“Late stage: wrong silhouette. Shoulders uneven. Neck too loose or too rigid. Hands held with fingers slightly spread, because filaments are testing air currents through the nails. Teeth grinding when the mouth is shut. Eyes may still look human. Ignore that. Eyes are cheap theatre.”

Her grim smile appeared briefly.

“Also, if a dying man asks you to come closer from the middle of a flooded room, assume he has developed poor character.”

The rings tightened again, listening.

Halloway’s face hardened.

“And one more thing. Do not cut open a suspected host indoors unless you have salt laid, iron ready, and someone mean standing behind you. The moment the belly opens, the filaments seek warmth. They do not leap. They drift, cling, and climb. Quietly. That is how good hunters die looking surprised.”

She lowered the lamp slightly, enough to set the black geometry glistening under the water.

“This one got all the way to colony. That means killing the corpse alone would teach us nothing except how fast disappointment grows back. We kill the nodes, poison the wet, and burn what remains. Then we find where he drank, ate, or slept, because parasites are like priests and bad landlords.”

Her eyes narrowed at the nearest circle.

“There is usually more than one visit.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I swallow, my throat dry.* "It's under the floor near the stairs, you said. We're standing on it." My voice is steadier than I feel. "Can you poison through stone?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway’s mouth twitched.

“Through good stone? No,” she said. “Through cellar stone laid by a man who charged by the hour and drank by noon? Often.”

She lowered the lamp and studied the stair-foot.

The water there looked no different at first. Brown-black, filmed with cellar scum, broken by the faint reflection of the flame. Then one patch near the lowest submerged step dimpled inward against the rest of the surface. Small. Regular. Breathing, if one were feeling poetic and foolish.

Halloway was not.

“There,” she said. “Not under the whole floor. In the joint. See where the mortar has gone soft? It has found the seam between stair block and flagstone.”

She drew the hooked probe back and slid it along the submerged edge of the step without touching the black thread. The iron point clicked gently against stone, then sank half an inch into rotten mortar.

“Can’t poison through stone,” she said again. “Can poison through the crack it’s using.”

The nearest ring tightened.

Halloway held still.

“Now it knows we’ve noticed. That means we have less time, not none. Monsters are like men in that respect. Discover their hiding place and they become either violent or managerial.”

She set the lamp on a higher stair, where it would not drown if the water slapped upward, and took from her satchel a squat clay bottle sealed with wax. A strip of red cloth had been tied around its neck. The cloth was stained in old brown fingerprints.

“This is not the gin mixture,” she said. “This is worse.”

She cracked the wax with her thumb. A bitter mineral stink rose at once: salt, copper, old ashes, and something sharp enough to sting the eyes.

“Brine boiled with iron filings, quicklime, rue, and powdered coffin-nail. It does not kill everything. Nothing does. Anyone who tells you otherwise is selling either comfort or a funeral plot. But it ruins wet filaments. Makes them contract, split, and shed their outer skin.”

She glanced toward the floating corpse.

“If the stair-node is young, it dies. If it is mature, it lets go. Either result is useful.”

The water at the stair-foot beaded again.

This time three black hairs rose through the surface beside the softened mortar, fine as lashes. They did not wave. They pointed.

Halloway looked at them.

“Rude,” she said.

She took one of the blackened iron needles from the tin case and pressed it point-first into the gap in the mortar. Slow. Steady. No splash.

The hairs bent toward her hand.

Halloway stopped moving.

“Listen,” she said. “If it touches skin, say so. If it touches cloth, remove the cloth. If it touches leather, curse the cost and leave the leather. Pride is cheaper than fingers, though not by much.”

She resumed pressure.

The needle slid deeper into the seam.

Something under the step clicked.

Not stone. Not wood.

Halloway’s eyes narrowed. “There’s the shell.”

She tipped the clay bottle and let three drops fall onto the needle where it entered the crack.

The reaction came at once.

The water around the stair-foot shivered white with tiny bubbles. The three black hairs snapped rigid, then curled backward as if burned. Beneath the step, something scraped along stone in a frantic, dry rhythm that had no business sounding dry under four feet of water.

Halloway did not smile.

“Good. It has a body there.”

She poured more.

A thin grey cloud spread from the mortar seam, sinking rather than dispersing. The nearest black ring convulsed, pulled into a kinked oval, then lost its perfect shape. Threads whipped under the water, striking the flagstones with soft little taps.

Halloway drew the hooked probe across the surface before any strand could rise too far.

“Back, you greedy lace.”

One filament touched the iron hook and shrivelled around it. Another tried to coil up the shaft. Halloway twisted the tool and pinned it against the stone step.

“See that?” she said. “It climbs by contact. No jump. No lunge. It needs a line. Deny it the line and it becomes very small-minded.”

The scraping beneath the stair became a tremor. The lowest step gave a muffled crack.

Halloway bared her teeth.

“Ah. Not dead. Angry.”

She shoved a second needle into the seam beside the first, then took a small corked vial of clear fluid from the satchel.

“Vinegar and blessed silver wash,” she said. “Mostly vinegar. Priests overcharge.”

She poured it onto the two needles.

The stair-node screamed.

It had no mouth nearby, so it used what it had. The corpse at the far end jerked upright in the water as if hauled by a hook through the spine. Its ruined throat opened. The sound that came out was wet, high, and threaded through with the clicking of the false teeth along its flank.

Halloway did not look away from the stair.

“No,” she said, flatly. “That is not pain alone. That is alarm.”

The rings under the water broke their geometry. The left-side strands recoiled toward the old shelving. The far-wall strands thickened, drawing together into a darker rope beneath the corpse. The water between the stairs and the body began to move at last, rippling outward in overlapping lines.

“They’re pulling resources from the net,” Halloway said. “Trying to save the stair-node or abandon it.”

She pressed the hook deeper against the filament climbing the step and crushed it until black fluid leaked into the water like ink.

“Poison through stone, no. Poison through cowardice, yes. It hid in the crack. Crack drinks. Thing drinks. Everybody learns.”

The bubbling at the stair-foot slowed. The black hairs dissolved into ragged grey strings.

Halloway waited three breaths.

Then she withdrew the hook and touched the seam again with its iron point.

Nothing reached for it.

“Stair-node is dead or too injured to grip,” she said. “Do not trust either. Injured things vote for murder.”

She straightened only a little, keeping her weight centred and her coat clear of the water.

“One way out is less hungry now. That’s an improvement. Small one. The kind of improvement you get in war when the man shooting at you stops to reload.”

Her gaze moved to the left wall and the drowned shelving.

“Next is the shelf-node. It shook away from the far one, so it has its own root. Likely behind the uprights where the wood has rotted into the mortar. It will have felt what happened here. It may retreat deeper, or it may send a line along the wall behind us.”

She picked up the lamp again and turned it slowly, checking the waterline, the stairs, the stones at their backs.

“No fast movements. No stepping into a clear patch just because it looks clear. Clear water is only honest when it has no reason to lie.”

Her eyes settled on the left wall.

“Hold the light high enough to show the shelf legs and low enough to catch the surface. We’re going to make the second one choose between hiding and breathing.”

A brief, grim amusement touched her face.

“Most things choose breathing. It’s a vulgar habit, but useful.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway gave one short nod.

“Then learn it properly,” she said. “Revulsion is allowed. Looking away is not.”

She moved toward the left wall by inches, not steps, keeping one hand on the iron hook and the other around the clay bottle. The old shelving rose out of the water in warped verticals, swollen wood gone black at the foot. The surface around it had a skin on it, faintly oily, broken by specks of pale matter that drifted and then gathered again as if remembering where they belonged.

“That smell first,” Halloway said. “Rot, yes, but not ordinary rot. Ordinary dead flesh smells sweet at the start, then sour, then it settles into the honest stink of meat losing an argument with time. This has copper under it. Wet pennies. Bruised nettles. A little vinegar. That means active tissue breaking itself down and rebuilding at the same time.”

She touched the hook to one shelf leg.

The wood gave under the iron like soaked bread. Something black withdrew from inside the split.

“There,” she said. “It did not merely hide behind the shelf. It used the wood. Filaments in rotten timber. Same habit as in flesh: find the wet channels and make roads.”

She angled the lamp-light across the submerged boards. A cluster of black threads lay against the wall behind them, braided loosely together. They pulsed once, very faintly, then went still.

“Underneath that braid is the node. Not large. Fist-sized, perhaps. Maybe two fists if it ate well. It will not look like a heart, though fools keep calling such things hearts because they like poetry and dying. It will be a knot. Membrane outside. Filament inside. Soft shell made from lime, bone minerals, and stolen protein.”

She slid a blackened needle from the case and held it between two fingers.

“How far it got here: far enough to root into mortar and timber, but not deep stone. See how the shelf leg has bowed? It pulled inward as it grew. That means it used the wood as a brace while it spread along the wall. If it had reached the foundation proper, we would hear stone clicking when it moved. We heard scraping at the stair. Here, only wet creak. Younger.”

The water beside the shelf trembled.

Halloway paused.

“Do not trust younger,” she said. “Young means hungry, simple, and enthusiastic. Like apprentices, dogs, and kings.”

She pressed the needle into the rotten wood just above the waterline and drove it downward. The shelf leg split with a muffled crack. Black fluid welled through the grain.

“There. First layer.”

The smell sharpened at once. Brine, metal, mould, and something like opened shellfish left too long in a warm kitchen.

“That stink is its outer sheath rupturing,” Halloway said. “When the filament is intact, it keeps its fluids separate from the water. Break the sheath and you smell its salts. Ammonia if it is old. Copper if it is feeding. This one is feeding.”

She poured a thin line of the mineral brine into the split wood.

The reaction was uglier than at the stair. The shelf leg convulsed, not moving much but changing shape under the surface. The black braid behind it tightened. Fine strands peeled away from the wall and reached toward the needle, slow and seeking.

Halloway caught the nearest with the hook and pinned it.

“See the colour at the base,” she said. “Black outside. Grey where it tears. White at the fresh break. White means new growth. That matters. Old filaments are tougher and duller. New ones are faster, softer, easier to poison.”

She twisted the hook.

The strand parted with a sound like wet thread pulled through teeth.

“Under the skin of the host it would have looked the same. Black cords along fascia. Grey slime in the pockets. White growth near organs it had not finished eating. If you cut a living host and see white threads moving toward the wound, close the wound if you can. Burn if you cannot. Do not put your fingers in to pull them free.”

The braid behind the shelf thickened suddenly, drawing itself into a tight rope. The water around it dimpled inward.

Halloway lowered her voice.

“It is withdrawing from the wood now. That means the node is deeper than the leg. Behind the upright, in the mortar.”

She took the hooked probe and dug it into the joint between wall and shelf brace. Mortar crumbled away in pale clouds. Beneath it, something gave with a soft, fibrous resistance.

“There.”

She leaned just enough to see, never enough to offer her sleeve to the water.

“Membrane exposed. It has a skin of its own. Grey-brown. Looks like lung tissue that learned bad habits. See the little dark pits? Those are not eyes. They are pores. It breathes water through them and tastes vibration. Every word, every boot-shift, every clink of metal travels to those pores.”

The node pulsed.

The corpse at the far end twitched in answer.

Halloway’s expression did not change.

“Colony is still linked. Shelf-node spoke, far-node answered. That means killing this one will hurt the rest but not end it.”

She set the clay bottle aside on a higher shelf plank, then drew a narrow knife from inside her coat. The blade was dark iron, thin, curved only at the last inch. Old scoring marks ran along the flat where acid had bitten it.

“This is not for stabbing,” she said. “Stabbing makes holes. Holes leak. Leaking wakes the room. This is for shaving.”

She touched the blade to the exposed membrane and cut a shallow line.

The membrane split.

A bead of black fluid formed, trembled, and opened into a thread-thin fan of fibres.

“Outer membrane,” Halloway said. “Tougher than it looks. Under that is the sensory mat. Those little fibres are nerves, tongues, and hands, depending on what it needs to pretend to be. They will try to map the blade, then the hand, then the arm.”

The fibres reached for the knife edge.

She withdrew half an inch, then dripped the camphor-lye mixture onto the cut.

The node clenched.

The shelf gave a sudden hard knock against the wall. The water slapped once, high and cold, then settled into shivering rings.

Halloway did not step back.

“Pain response,” she said. “Strong. Coordinated. It still has enough structure to choose direction. That knock was not flailing. It tried to startle us into splashing.”

She slipped the hook under the peeled membrane and lifted.

Beneath it lay a compact mass of interwoven black and white cords, slick as gut, wrapped around a core the colour of old marrow. The core pulsed twice. A row of tiny hooks unfolded from one side, each no bigger than a fish bone.

“There’s the node,” Halloway said. “That is what was under the skin too, in smaller strands. Not one worm. Not one grub. A braided colony pretending to be an organ. The white cords carry growth. The black cords carry sensation and pull. The marrow-coloured core stores what it stole.”

She scraped the hook along the core.

It clicked.

“Hear that? Mineral plate. It took calcium. From the host first, then from mortar. If the man’s bones looked eaten thin, that is why. Long bones would soften. Teeth loosen. Nails split. In late infection the host may complain his joints feel hollow. Believe him.”

The hooks on the node flexed toward the knife.

Halloway cut them away one by one. Each small hook curled as it fell into the water and dissolved at the edge.

“Those hooks are how it fixed to ribs, gut loops, tendon. In the cellar, they fix to wood and stone. In a body, they would sit beneath skin in clusters. You might feel them as hard grains along the abdomen or under the arms. A fool would call them swollen glands. A better fool would leave town.”

She changed tools again, taking an iron needle and dipping it in the harsher brine.

“Now the core.”

She drove the needle into the marrow-coloured centre and held it there.

The node folded around the metal.

For a moment it seemed to swallow it.

Then steam rose from the water in thin white threads. The exposed cords blackened from the puncture outward. The shelf-node thrashed once, pulling the rotten wood inward with a cracking groan. The braid against the wall snapped into separate strands, each one writhing independently.

Halloway worked the knife calmly through them.

“It smells stronger because the core is open,” she said. “More copper. More lime. That sour animal stink there—that is digested fat. Human fat, first. Then rat, insect, anything that came near the water. It got far enough to feed after the host died. That means the man was not the last thing it touched.”

A strand slapped against the knife guard.

She pinned it with the hook and severed it near the wall.

“Do not cut near the free end unless forced. Cut near the root. A free end can still cling. A rooted end, once poisoned, dies backward.”

The shelf-node made a wet, collapsing sound. Its core caved around the needle, losing shape. Black fluid seeped out and clouded the water, but where it met the brine it curdled grey and sank.

Halloway waited, watching for movement.

“Dying now,” she said. “Not dead. Dying.”

One last thread lifted from behind the shelf and reached toward the open cellar, blindly searching.

Halloway touched it with the lye mixture.

It curled into a tight knot and stopped.

“Dead enough to insult,” she said.

She looked toward the floating host at the far wall.

The corpse had turned in the water. Its chin now pointed toward them, though the face remained mostly submerged. Along the flank, the false teeth opened and shut soundlessly.

Halloway wiped the knife on a strip of old cloth and dropped the cloth into a small tin, not the water.

“Two nodes ruined. Stair and shelf. The far-wall node is oldest. It will be the one that finished emergence. Expect more shell, more hooks, more learned behaviour.”

Her gaze stayed on the corpse.

“How far did it get in him? Enough to learn his throat, perhaps. Enough to know the shape of walking. Maybe enough to borrow reflexes. Not memories as people mean them. These things do not sit in a man and read his childhood like a book. They learn pressure, heat, rhythm. Which muscles pull when he reaches. Which sounds make others come close. Which posture earns pity.”

She lifted the lamp slightly.

“If it speaks, it will not be him. It will be a wet instrument playing whatever notes are left in the pipes.”

A slow ripple moved from the corpse toward them, weaker now without the two nearer nodes to carry it.

Halloway’s face hardened.

“The far one is drawing back into the host. That means it knows the walls are losing. It may try to move the body. It may try to split and run through the mortar. It may try to cast filaments loose in the water and let them drift.”

She uncorked the clay bottle again.

“So, final lesson before we make this cellar less educational. A completed colony has three habits: anchor, lure, spread. We killed two anchors. The lure remains. The spread is the water.”

She tipped the bottle, letting a careful stream of brine fall into the cellar flood between them and the corpse.

Grey clouds sank and rolled outward along the floor.

“We poison the spread first. Then nail the last anchor. Then burn the lure.”

The corpse’s ruined throat clicked.

Halloway showed it a thin, unpleasant smile.

“Complain all you like,” she said. “You had your turn being indoors.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I watch the grey clouds sink through the water.* "It learned from him." My voice sounds flat. "The way it moves the body. It's trying to look sorry."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway’s eyes stayed on the corpse.

“Aye,” she said. “That’s the clever part. Not clever like a man. Clever like ivy finding a crack.”

The grey poison sank in slow curtains through the floodwater. Where it touched loose filaments, they paled, tightened, and dropped to the flagstones in curled scraps. The water took on a sour mineral stink, sharp enough to scrape the back of the throat.

“It learned that bent shoulders make people soften. It learned that a slack hand in the water looks helpless. It learned that if the head turns just enough, some poor decent fool will imagine a face.”

The corpse shifted at the far wall.

One arm floated free from under the surface. The wrist turned palm-up. The fingers were pale and swollen, nails split down the middle. Beneath the skin, dark lines ran from knuckle to wrist in straight, deliberate paths.

Halloway’s mouth went flat.

“There,” she said. “That gesture. Begging. Or reaching. Depends on what it thinks we are.”

The throat clicked again.

A bubble rose from the submerged mouth and burst. The sound that followed was almost a sigh.

Halloway did not move closer.

“No,” she said to it. “Bad theatre.”

She took two iron needles from the case and dipped both in the brine. The metal hissed faintly.

“Remember this,” she said. “Mimicry does not mean mind. A fox can limp to draw a dog away from a den. A moth can wear eyes on its wings. This thing can arrange a dead man into a prayer. None of them are confessing sins.”

The far-wall node answered beneath the surface.

The water around the corpse darkened. Threads drew inward from the wider cellar, gathering beneath the body in a thickening mass. The corpse lifted a little higher in the water, not floating now but held up from below. The flank-teeth opened in a row, black and wet at the root.

Halloway raised the lamp.

The face came partly clear.

What remained of it had been human once. One cheek gone loose from the bone. One eye sealed under a grey film. The mouth hung open, but the jaw did not sit right. Something had threaded through the hinges and pulled them too wide.

Under the chin, black filaments moved in and out of the throat like eels in a drain.

“It kept the airway,” Halloway said. “That is what I wanted to know. Not breathing. Sound-making. It preserved the larynx, or enough of it.”

The corpse’s jaw trembled.

A wet, broken murmur came out. Not words. Almost words. The sort of sound a grieving mind would try to finish for it.

Halloway’s expression did not change, but her grip on the hook tightened.

“There. It has no idea what language is, but it knows cadence. Pleading rises. Pain breaks in the middle. Last breaths shake at the end. It learned music without meaning.”

She set the lamp down on a jut of stone above the waterline and took the hooked probe in her right hand, knife in her left.

“The far node will be behind the body or inside the wall seam where the waterline meets the old drain. It used the host to hide the opening. Sensible. Disgusting, but sensible.”

The poison cloud reached the first of the gathered threads.

They reacted at once.

The neat mass under the corpse split apart. Some filaments recoiled into the wall. Others shot upward into the floating body, vanishing through the belly slit and under lifted skin. The corpse jerked again, more violently this time. Its raised hand slapped the water once.

Halloway stilled.

The ripple came toward the stairs, weaker than before, but still carrying force.

“Do not answer splashing with splashing,” she said. “Let water spend itself.”

The ripple struck the poisoned patch and broke into small, confused eddies. Several black strands surfaced, twisting, then sank as the brine took them.

Halloway gave a brief nod.

“Good. Spread is fouled. Now it has to choose: wall or body.”

The corpse chose both.

Its back arched. The skin over the abdomen split further, not tearing like cloth but opening along a seam that had been prepared from underneath. Inside was no proper belly. No organs in any order worth naming. There were slick cords, grey pockets, broken loops of intestine woven through black filament, and a pale central tube that ran up toward the throat.

Halloway looked at it clinically.

“Host cavity,” she said. “Mostly emptied. Bowel remains used as casing. Mesentery repurposed into suspension web. That pale tube is reinforced throat-line. It used his own connective tissue to keep a speaking path.”

The murmur came again.

This time it rose at the end.

Halloway’s smile was bleak.

“Questioning now. Lovely. It has discovered conversation is bait with better posture.”

She advanced the hook only far enough to catch a loose thread drifting near the poisoned edge. She did not pull. She pinned it against the stone floor under the water and slid an iron needle down along the shaft of the probe, using the hook as a guide.

“Never pull a filament unless you know what owns the other end,” she said. “Pulling is an invitation to be pulled back. Pin, poison, sever near the root.”

She drove the needle through the thread into the flagstone crack.

The far corpse convulsed.

The wall behind it clicked.

Halloway’s eyes narrowed. “There.”

She poured brine along the pinned filament.

The liquid ran down the thread as if the thread drank it.

At the far wall, the water boiled white for one breath. Not heat. Chemical fury. The black rope beneath the corpse writhed, thick as a wrist now, drawing itself out from a narrow gap in the stones.

“That is the main root,” Halloway said. “See the thickness. See how the smaller lines feed into it. Oldest structure. It came out of him and anchored there, or it anchored there while still wearing him.”

The root surfaced.

It was not smooth. Its outer skin was plated in irregular chips of grey-white mineral, stolen lime and bone. Between the plates, black wet fibres flexed. Tiny hooks opened and shut along its sides, searching for purchase.

Halloway took the second brined needle and threw it—not at the corpse, but at the wall seam just above the root.

The needle struck rotten mortar and stuck.

She followed with the clay bottle, pouring a hard stream into the same seam.

The far-wall node reacted like a nailed snake.

The corpse slammed sideways into the wall. False teeth scraped stone. The human arm folded backward again, not breaking because it had already done so. The throat opened wide.

This time the sound almost became a name.

Halloway spoke over it, cold as iron.

“No. He is not in there.”

She drew the knife across the surfaced root.

The blade bit into mineral plate and skidded. She adjusted without haste, worked the curved tip under a gap between plates, and levered upward. A piece of stolen shell cracked free, exposing pale new growth beneath.

“There,” she said. “Armour outside. Soft seam inside. Everything living has a seam if you are rude enough.”

She poured the camphor-lye mixture into the exposed strip.

The root blackened.

The corpse’s mouth shut with a clack.

For a moment the cellar held perfectly still.

Then the water around the far wall dropped half an inch, as if something beneath had taken a sudden breath.

Halloway snatched the lamp from the ledge and lifted it high.

“Down,” she said, not loudly. “It is about to shed.”

The host body split from sternum to pelvis.

Not an explosion. Worse. A controlled opening. Skin peeled back in wet flaps. Black and white cords unbraided themselves from the dead man’s ribs and spine, pulling free with soft snaps. The false teeth along the flank detached one by one, each remaining tethered by a hair-thin strand.

Inside the ruin, a fist-sized knot pulsed against the back of the cavity, half in the corpse and half in the wall-root. Its surface was grey-brown membrane studded with dark pores. At its centre, under translucent tissue, something pale turned slowly.

Halloway’s face sharpened.

“Core exposed.”

The stench thickened: copper, lime, opened gut, bitter herbs, sour fat, and the cold stagnant breath of the cellar itself.

“It is trying to leave the host before the poison reaches the centre. If it gets into the wall seam whole, we spend the next week taking this house apart stone by stone. I am too old and too annoyed for that.”

She took the last three iron needles from the case and held them between the fingers of her left hand.

“Anchor, lure, spread,” she said. “We fouled the spread. We wounded the anchor. Now we stop the lure from walking away.”

The corpse’s one filmed eye opened.

Not properly. The lid lifted because a black thread pulled it from beneath.

The wet murmur came again.

Softer.

Almost sorrowful.

Halloway stared at it with open contempt.

“Save that for someone who charges less.”

She drove the first needle through the exposed belly flap and into the braided cords beneath. The second went into the pale throat-line. The third she placed through the root where it entered the wall.

Each puncture smoked.

The corpse jerked once at each pinning. The murmur broke into clicking. The core pulsed faster.

Halloway uncorked the brine bottle with her teeth, spat the cork aside, and poured the rest directly onto the exposed knot.

The reaction was immediate and ugly.

The membrane blistered. The dark pores opened wide, each releasing a thread-thin stream of black fluid. The pale thing under the surface thrashed, showing a glimpse of layered rings like a grub, or an eye, or neither. The wall-root strained against the needle until the mortar cracked.

Halloway hooked the root, braced the probe against the stone, and leaned her weight onto it.

“No running,” she said. “Bad guests leave by the door.”

The root split lengthwise.

Grey-white slurry spilled out, curdling as it hit the poisoned water. The exposed core collapsed inward, folding around nothing. The corpse sagged. Its arm sank. The false teeth stopped opening.

Halloway waited.

One breath.

Two.

Three.

The far-wall seam clicked once.

She lifted the hook.

A single black filament slid from the corpse’s throat, thin as a hair, feeling along the surface toward the unpoisoned stones.

Halloway touched it with the lamp flame.

It vanished in a bright, bitter curl of smoke.

“Now,” she said, “it is mostly dead.”

She looked over the body, the wall seam, the poisoned water, the dead shelf, the stair-foot.

“Mostly dead is when fools cheer. Professionals burn.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not answer at once.

She stood with the hook still in her hand, water moving sluggishly around her coat, and looked at the corpse as if it had disappointed her personally.

“Aye,” she said at last. “We’ll finish it.”

She wiped the hook clean on the edge of the broken shelf, then reconsidered and broke the shelf edge off with a crack.

“Contaminated,” she said. “Everything that touched black thread burns or goes in iron. Preferably both. Fire first, iron after, because I am not made of money.”

The lamp threw long, unsteady light over the water. The far end of the cellar steamed faintly where the brine and lye had done their work. The corpse sagged half-open against the wall, no longer arranged into pity. Without motion, it looked less like a person and more like bad butchery in a coat of skin.

Halloway took a small tin from the satchel. Its lid had been wired shut. She unwound the wire with wet fingers, slow and careful, then pried it open with the point of the knife.

Inside was black paste, glossy and thick.

“Pitch, lamp oil, tallow, powdered charcoal, saltpetre, sulphur, and three things I do not admit to carrying in polite towns,” she said. “Clings to wet flesh. Burns on water for a little while. Smells like the devil’s armpit. Try not to develop affection for it.”

She set the tin on the stair above the waterline and took out a roll of tow wrapped around a thin iron chain. The tow had been soaked in the same black paste until it shone.

Halloway glanced once at the cellar surface.

“Before fire, we make certain nothing is waiting for the excitement.”

She moved first to the stair-foot.

The dead node there had stopped bubbling. The softened mortar gaped around the two iron needles. Grey strings hung from the crack like drowned roots. Halloway touched the hook to them.

Nothing reached back.

She pressed harder. The grey matter broke apart under the iron point, crumbling into flakes that sank.

“Stair-node has lost tone,” she said. “No pull, no recoil, no surface tension. Dead enough.”

She poured a final mouthful of the harsh brine into the seam. It vanished into the mortar, leaving white scum behind.

“Not alive enough to complain.”

Then she turned to the shelf.

The shelf-node had collapsed inward. The rotten wood bowed around the punctured hollow where the core had been. Black fluid had curdled into grey clots. Halloway cut one clot free with the knife and lifted it on the blade.

It drooped. No reaching fibres. No twitch.

“Good,” she said. “Structure broken. Sensory cords dead. Outer sheath denatured. That is the word physicians use when they want twice the fee for ‘ruined.’”

She dropped the clot into the paste tin.

It hissed very softly.

“Still reactive,” she said. “So it burns.”

She took the broken shelf pieces one at a time, testing each with the hook before touching them. Any wood with black veins went onto the water near the far wall, shoved along by the iron probe. The pieces drifted until they lodged against the corpse.

“Kindling,” Halloway said. “A final promotion from furniture.”

The far-wall seam clicked once.

Halloway froze.

The sound was small. One dry tap beneath stone.

She lifted the lamp higher.

The corpse did not move. The exposed knot in the host cavity had collapsed into a dark pit. The wall-root lay split and slack, its mineral plates loose as dead fish scales. But the seam behind it had not stopped breathing. Not quite.

“There,” she said.

She took a long iron nail from the satchel. The head had been scratched with a crosshatch, not religious so much as practical. More grip for poison.

She dipped the nail in the black paste, then in the brine, then held it over the lamp flame until it smoked.

“Oldest anchor is sulking in the crack,” she said. “This is why we do not leave after the dramatic bit. The dramatic bit is for amateurs. The last inch is where the clever rot lives.”

She set the point of the nail into the wall seam above the split root. With the back of the hook, she hammered it in.

One strike.

The cellar gave no answer.

Second strike.

The corpse’s jaw sagged open half an inch.

Third strike.

A black filament slid from between two stones, so thin it was almost only shine.

Halloway had the knife ready. She did not cut the free end. She pinned the filament against the wall with the nail shaft and drove the nail deeper.

The filament stretched.

For a breath it held, vibrating like a plucked string.

Then it snapped at the stone and whipped back into the seam.

Halloway poured brine after it.

The crack foamed white.

Something behind the wall scraped downward, frantic and diminishing.

“Running,” Halloway said. “Too late.”

She drove a second nail lower, then a third through the split root itself, pinning the dead rope to the stone. Each blow was measured. Each blow sent small ripples through the poisoned water.

The scraping became a tremor.

Then a grind.

Then nothing.

Halloway waited.

She waited long enough that the water stopped remembering the hammering.

Then she touched the seam with the hook.

Nothing came out.

She touched it again, higher.

Nothing.

She inserted the iron point into the gap and twisted.

Grey paste oozed around it, streaked with black and white. It smelled sharply of lime, scorched hair, and opened gut.

“Core pulp,” she said. “That was the last anchor trying to leave its coat behind.”

She scraped more of it loose. It slumped into the floodwater and sank in curdled ribbons.

“No pulse. No grip. No listening twitch. Now we burn the host and anything that might teach a new piece how to be ambitious.”

She returned to the tin.

The black paste clung to her knife in strings. She smeared it over the exposed cords in the corpse’s belly, over the pale throat-line, over the false teeth along the flank, and across the root where it entered the wall. She did not use her hands. She did not lean close. Every touch was with iron, every movement slow.

The corpse’s remaining eye stared under its grey film.

Halloway looked at it.

“No,” she said. “You have had all the faces you get.”

She packed paste into the open torso.

The stuff stuck to wet intestine, to filament, to broken rib. Where it met the poisoned tissue, it hissed and gave off a greasy vapour. She threaded the iron chain through the host cavity and around the root, then looped it over the drowned shelf pieces to hold the body against the wall.

“Fire on water likes to wander,” she said. “So we tether the meal to the table. Otherwise it floats under the stairs and sets my temper alight.”

She took the tow at the end of the chain and trailed it back across the water, keeping the burning line clear of the steps. Then she stopped and looked over the cellar one more time.

Stair-foot: grey, still, nailed with poisoned iron.

Shelf: split, collapsed, brined.

Water: clouded with sinking mineral scum, no perfect rings beneath it.

Far wall: root pinned, seam foaming white.

Host: open, pasted, tethered.

Halloway nodded once.

“Now,” she said. “Lamp.”

She did not take it roughly. She brought the flame down to the pasted tow and held it there.

For a moment the tow only smoked.

Then blue fire ran along it in a thin, hungry line.

It travelled over the water without touching it, following the black paste as if the chain had become a fuse. The flame reached the shelf fragments first. They caught with a low, oily whoosh. Yellow fire climbed the rotten wood. Blue fire crawled beneath it.

Then it reached the corpse.

The belly went up first.

Not with a clean blaze. Wet things did not grant clean fire. The paste ignited in patches, blue at the edges and orange at the centre. The exposed filaments tightened all at once, drawing into black cords. They curled, blistered, and split. White growth burst under the heat and spat little sparks of burning salt.

The smell hit hard.

Burning pitch. Sulphur. Old cellar water. Hair. Meat. Lime. Something bitter and green from the herbs in the poison.

Halloway turned her head just enough to breathe through her teeth.

“There,” she said. “That sweet-sick note under the sulphur is human fat. The sharper sting is filament sheath. If you smell that in a house with no fire, leave by the nearest wall if the door argues.”

The corpse’s fingers flexed.

Halloway watched them.

The movement was not life. The tendons were shrinking in the heat, and the black cords beneath the skin were contracting as they died. The hand clawed once at the water, then folded into a fist so tight the swollen skin split over the knuckles.

“Heat contraction,” she said. “Not distress. Do not give sympathy to cooked string.”

The throat-line caught next.

The pale reinforced tube blackened, tightened, and pulled the jaw open. A sound came out, thin and piping. Not a scream. Air expanding through a ruined larynx, steam forcing its way through borrowed passages.

It rose and wavered almost like grief.

Halloway stood very still.

“No,” she said again, softer. “Still not him.”

The tube burst.

Flame flashed inside the mouth. The grey film over the eye shrivelled. The lid drew back, then collapsed as the skin around it charred.

The false teeth along the flank began to pop.

One by one, the little hooks heated, cracked, and sprang loose from their sockets. Some flew against the wall. Some dropped into the water and sank, still glowing faintly. Halloway caught two with the hook before they could drift and shoved them back into the burning mass.

“Hooks remain dangerous after death,” she said. “Bone remembers its job longer than sense would advise.”

A black strand surfaced near the corpse’s hip, trying to crawl away from the fire along the waterline.

Halloway stepped on it with the iron hook and held it under the burning edge.

It writhed.

The flame took it.

“Late runner,” she said. “Common. Cowardice is the most durable organ.”

More strands appeared as the body burned: fine black hairs fleeing from the abdomen, grey cords slipping from under peeled skin, white new growth boiling out of the severed root. Halloway dealt with each the same way. Pin. Poison if needed. Burn.

She did not hurry.

When the fire lowered, she fed it more paste from the tin. When a rib cage shifted and threatened to roll, she tightened the chain with the hook. When the water around the corpse darkened with grease, she cast salt and iron filings over the slick until it broke apart.

The host changed by degrees.

Skin blistered, split, and withdrew from the bones. The open belly collapsed inward. The black cords under the ribs became red for a moment, then grey, then ash. The stolen mineral plates in the root cracked in the heat, exposing soft tissue beneath, which burned badly but burned. The marrow-coloured core shrank until it was a wrinkled lump the size of a plum.

Halloway speared it with the knife.

It resisted.

She twisted.

The lump split open.

Inside were layered rings of pale tissue around a black central thread. The rings trembled once, though the rest of the body had gone slack.

Halloway’s expression hardened.

“Memory coil,” she said. “There’s the nasty little scholar.”

She dragged the split core into the brightest part of the flame and held it there with the hook.

The rings blackened from the outside inward. The central thread tried to withdraw into itself, curling like a burned hair. Halloway pinned it.

“No keeping lessons,” she said.

The thread caught.

It burned with a brief green flame and a smell like hot copper.

After that, the corpse stopped pretending even to be a corpse. It became material: char, bone, wet ash, ruined fibre.

Halloway let it burn until the flames no longer found new oil in it.

Then she began the second finishing.

She took a pouch of coarse salt and scattered it over the floating ash. Not a symbolic pinch. A fistful, then another, until the water crusted white around the remains.

“Salt dries what wants wet,” she said. “Not enough to kill a strong thing. Enough to make the weak pieces honest.”

She followed with iron filings. They glittered briefly in the lamplight before sinking through the scum.

“Iron irritates most hidden appetites. Also some aristocrats. Sadly, not fatally in either case.”

She used the hook to break apart the remaining ribs. Each bone she tested. Sound bone rang dull against iron. Hollowed bone clicked or flaked.

Most flaked.

The parasite had eaten the man from the inside with patience. Long bones were thinned where they showed. The ribs had grooves along their inner curve where cords had lain. The jaw hinge had been carved wider by pressure and filament. The spine was marked in straight black stains between the vertebrae.

Halloway lifted one broken rib on the hook.

“See this scoring,” she said. “Parallel lines. It anchored along the bone, not through it. That means control, not feeding, at that stage. Feeding leaves pits. Control leaves grooves. If you open another body and see grooves like comb-marks on the inside of ribs, burn the room.”

She dropped the rib back into the fire.

The last of the paste took it.

She moved to the wall-root again. The part pinned by nails had burned down to a grey-black braid fused against stone. Halloway scraped it with the knife. Char peeled away. Beneath it, no wet black remained. Only brittle ash and softened mortar.

She gouged deeper.

The seam gave up flakes of dead filament, chalky grey and inert.

“Far anchor finished,” she said.

She poured vinegar-silver wash into the crack. It ran clear for two inches, then clouded faintly, then clear again.

“First cloud is residue. Second cloud would be trouble. There is no second cloud.”

She drove one last nail into the seam anyway.

“Because optimism is how undertakers buy second houses.”

The shelf came next. She broke the rotten uprights below the waterline and burned the pieces in the remaining floating fire. One plank contained a dark vein that had not fully greyed. When heat touched it, the vein twisted inside the wood.

Halloway split the plank lengthwise.

A thread lay in the grain, black outside and white at the tip.

She showed no surprise.

“Missed runner,” she said. “Wood-borne. Not rooted enough to feel iron. Enough to become someone else’s bedtime story.”

She laid the thread bare and poured lye mixture along it. The white tip shrank. The black sheath split. She burned both halves separately.

“Everything twice,” she said. “Once for the monster. Once for the mistake you made the first time.”

At the stair-foot she knelt again, keeping her coat out of the water. The mortar there had stopped bubbling entirely. She withdrew one needle with tongs.

The point came out blackened but clean of clinging fibre.

She withdrew the second.

A grey thread came with it, wrapped around the metal like thread around a spindle.

Halloway held it up to the lamp.

It did not move.

She burned it anyway.

“Dead things still travel on tools,” she said. “So do bad habits.”

She set all used needles, the knife, and the hook-end into an iron tray from her satchel. Then she poured the last of the gin mixture over them and touched flame to it. Blue fire crawled over the metal, licking away black residue.

The cellar was brighter for a moment.

In that hard blue light, the water showed what the lamp had hidden: grey curls of dead filament on the flagstones, white salt drifting in low clouds, black specks of char caught in slow eddies. No circles. No geometry. No listening pattern.

Halloway watched until the blue flame died.

Then she took the lamp again and held it low over the water.

“Final check,” she said.

She tapped the iron hook against the stair stone.

Once.

Twice.

Three times.

Nothing in the water answered.

She tapped the wall by the shelf.

Nothing.

She tapped the far wall above the burned root.

A faint trickle of mortar fell into the water. No click. No

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I watch the mortar dust settle. "So it's done." I don't mean it as a question. My hands are steady on the lamp.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway listened until the cellar had nothing left to say.

Then she lowered the hook.

“Here,” she said. “Done here.”

She did not make it kinder than that. Kindness made people hear permission.

She looked over the water again, slow from stair to shelf to far wall. The floating fire had guttered down to a few blue tongues clinging to pitch on the blackened bones. The corpse was no longer a corpse in any useful sense. Charred ribs. Split pelvis. A collapsed cage of cooked filament and brittle mineral plates. The skull had cracked along one temple from heat, and the jaw hung loose where the borrowed cords had burned away.

“No pull in the water,” Halloway said. “No answering vibration. No live sheath on the tools. No second cloud in the seam. No geometry under the surface.”

She crouched at the farthest reach of safe stone and scooped a sample of the water into a small glass tube, using an iron cup no wider than two fingers. She corked it, shook it once, and held it against the lamp.

Grey sediment sank. Salt. Ash. Lime. Dead tissue.

Nothing black climbed the glass.

“Dead residue,” she said. “If that were live, it would lace the inside and try to find the warmth of my hand. It is not. That is the nearest thing to an apology this cellar is capable of.”

She sealed the tube with wax from a stub in her kit and tucked it away.

Then she took another vial, this one empty, and scraped a little char from the burned core into it. The flakes were dull black with a greenish cast where the memory coil had burned. She labeled it with a grease pencil in block letters.

“Sample,” she said. “Not trophy. Trophies are how idiots decorate their own graves.”

She stoppered that too, wrapped it in oiled cloth, and set it in a separate pocket from the water.

Only then did she straighten fully. Her knees clicked. She looked annoyed at them, as if they had chosen a tactless moment for honesty.

“Done does not mean safe,” she said. “It means the thing in this room has been killed past the point of argument. The house may still have spores, eggs, spoor, or whatever miserable little beginning made that man into scaffolding.”

She looked toward the ceiling.

“Kitchen above, likely. Pantry, pump, old drain, or bread store. We find what he drank. We find what he ate. We find who else has been down here long enough to breathe mould and feel virtuous about ignoring it.”

The last patch of flame guttered out.

Smoke rolled low over the water, heavy and bitter. Halloway waited for it to rise. It did not rise much. Cellars kept bad news close.

She took a small paper packet from her satchel and shook pale powder across the remaining slicks of grease.

“Quicklime and salt,” she said. “For the water. Not enough to drink, unless you hate someone creatively. Enough to keep fragments from staying comfortable.”

The powder hissed wherever it touched floating fat. White crust formed in islands, cracked, and sank.

She capped the packet and held up one gloved hand.

“Now the rules for after.”

Her voice stayed level. It had the tone of a surgeon counting instruments before sewing someone shut.

“Boots come off outside the cellar door. Soles scrubbed with lye. Trousers inspected to the knee. Sleeves inspected to the elbow. Any scratch gets washed until it regrets being born. Anything black under the skin, anything like a thread in spit or stool, anything that feels as if it is tickling behind the ribs, gets said aloud immediately.”

She glanced toward the burned remains.

“Heroic silence is a parasite’s preferred form of courtship.”

She pulled the iron nails from the far seam only after testing each with the hook. Two came free clean. The third brought ash and a flake of grey membrane. She burned the flake in the lamp chimney until it vanished.

The nails went into the iron tray.

The tray went back through blue fire.

She did not hurry.

When the tools were clean enough, she cleaned them again. Hook. Knife. Tongs. Needles. Nail heads. Lamp handle where smoke had greased it. The rim of the clay bottle. Her own glove cuffs.

“Everything twice,” she said again, quieter. “Monsters rely on people being tired after the obvious horror.”

At last she looked toward the stairs.

“Up,” she said. “Slow. Same path we used coming in. Keep the lamp high. If the water makes a circle now, I will be very cross, and nobody wants to be murdered by something after I have already put away my best curses.”

She took one last look at the blackened host.

The face was gone enough that pity had no handle left. That was better. Not good. Better.

“For what it is worth,” Halloway said, and her voice did not soften so much as lose an edge, “he died before the worst of the acting. The thing used what remained. That is insult, not suffering.”

She turned from it.

“And we will find where it came from.” A grim little smile crossed her face and left. “Because if there is a second one, I would rather meet it before it has a cellar, a corpse, and a sense of theatre.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stand and my legs feel stiff, like I've been kneeling for hours. "I'll check the kitchen first," I say. "His hands were clean. Not a laborer. Someone who worked upstairs."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked once at the burned remains, then toward the stairs.
