“Aye,” she said. “Clean hands narrows it. Not a navvy, not a coalman, not someone hauling barrels unless he’d washed after. Upstairs work. Cook, clerk, houseman, owner pretending not to notice his own cellar flooding. Hands tell habits when faces have gone off duty.”

She climbed one step and stopped before leaving the water.

“Kitchen first, but not with bare confidence. Kitchens are where people put faith in boiling water and then use the same damp rag for six months.”

She took a short brush, a stoppered lye bottle, and a folded cloth from her satchel. She set them on the stair above the waterline.

“Boots,” she said. “Before threshold. Scrub soles, seams, heel cracks. Especially heel cracks. Filaments like sheltered little valleys. Parasites and politicians, both.”

Halloway worked on her own boots first. She did it thoroughly, not elegantly. Lye over leather. Brush into stitching. Iron pick through the tread. The water below was dead, but she did not grant it trust as a parting gift.

“Clean hands,” she went on, “also mean he may have handled food, paper, medicine, linens, or money. If the first infection came by mouth, kitchen. If by breath, pantry mould or old flour. If by hand, something damp he touched often and then brought to his face.”

She straightened and inspected her cuffs.

“Things to look for upstairs: black threads in drains, sink traps, bread bins, flour sacks, wet tea leaves, pickle jars, meat brine, and any wall where damp climbs higher than it ought. Spoilage that smells metallic. Mould in straight lines. Rats dead without bites on them. Spiders absent from a corner they should love.”

Her mouth twitched.

“And if there’s a jar labelled ‘tonic’ full of cloudy brown misery, do not sniff it deeply to learn its character. I have buried three men with excellent curiosity.”

She took the lamp when she was ready and held it high enough to light the upper steps.

“The clean hands matter another way,” Halloway said. “If he worked upstairs, he likely did not come down here for pleasure. Someone sent him, or something below made noise in a voice useful enough to fetch him. Or he came for stores and found the flood already occupied.”

She paused at the cellar door and looked back into the dark.

“No geometry,” she said, mostly to herself. “Good.”

Then she opened the door wider with the hook rather than her hand.

The air above was warmer, carrying the stale domestic smells of old grease, cold ash, damp plaster, and shut-up rooms. Ordinary smells. Halloway distrusted them on principle.

“Kitchen,” she said. “We check wet first. Pump, sink, kettle, slop bucket, washbasin. Then dry stores. Bread, flour, salt, oats. Then tools. Knives, ladles, cloths, chopping board. Anything with grooves gets special attention. Grooves keep secrets.”

She stepped out of the cellar and set a line of salt across the threshold.

“Not for holiness,” she said. “For footprints. If anything damp crosses after us, it leaves a story.”

She shut the cellar door but did not latch it.

“Never latch yourself away from a thing you have just killed,” she said. “If it knocks, you want to hear it. If it opens the door, you want to be offended early.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I follow her up, scrubbing my boots with the stiff brush. "He had a ring mark on his left hand," I say. "Pale stripe. Faint. Could've been a wedding band he took off before coming down here."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: That part there was human skin. Shoulder line is wrong now, but it started as a man or woman. Adult. See the thickness through the chest, what's left of it

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: It fed through the bowel first. Then the liver. Then the soft joins under the ribs... Joints bent by pull instead of muscle. Bones used as struts. Skin stretched where it needed covering and torn where it didn't.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: It sent filaments through the mesentery into the liver and around the kidneys... Under the skin now? Not muscle as you understand it. Not entirely. Some muscle remains, especially in the limbs, but it's dead meat being used as padding and leverage. The working part is filament bundled into cords. Think black horsehair soaked in glue, running from gut to shoulder, gut to hip, gut to jaw.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She drove the needle into the marrow-coloured centre and held it there. The node folded around the metal. For a moment it seemed to swallow it. Then steam rose from the water in thin white threads. The exposed cords blackened from the puncture outward.

rung_labels.evidence: She smeared it over the exposed cords in the corpse's belly, over the pale throat-line, over the false teeth along the flank, and across the root where it entered the wall

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content: Halloway squinted at the mass at the far end of the cellar. The light of the lamp danced across the water, making it seem to ripple and move like a living thing. "I think I see what you mean," she said. "It looks like it's been twisted, like it's been bent in ways that don't make sense. And there's something... odd about the color of it." She hesitated, trying to find the right words. "It's like it's been stained, but not evenly. It's darker in some places than others." She raised an eyebrow. "I think we should get a closer look, but carefully. If this is what I think it might be, we don't want to touch it without gloves."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I pull on the thick leather gloves from my pack, my eyes still fixed on the shadowy mass.* "It's... bulging in the wrong places. Like something's trying to push out from the inside."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content: Halloway's eyes narrowed as she took a cautious step forward, the water rippling around her boots. "That's a good point," she said, her voice steady. "The distortion could be a sign of internal pressure. And the staining... I've seen something like this before, but I'm not sure what it means." She paused, studying the mass intently. "I think we need to be prepared for the possibility that this thing is still alive, or at least partially so. If it is, we don't know what kind of risks we're looking at." She glanced at Pike, her expression grim. "You ready for this?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content: Halloway's expression turned somber, her eyes never leaving the mass. "I think it's possible," she said quietly. "The size and shape... it's consistent with a human body. But the distortion, the staining... it's like nothing I've seen before. It's almost as if the body has been... altered, somehow. Twisted and changed in ways that don't make sense." She took another cautious step forward, her eyes scanning the mass for any sign of movement. "I'm not sure what we're looking at here, but I think we need to be careful. If this is some kind of infection or... whatever it is, we don't know what kind of risks we're looking at." She paused, her voice dropping to a whisper. "And if it's still alive... I don't know what kind of pain it might be in. We need to be prepared for anything."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow hard and nod. "Right." *I move closer, the water sloshing around my knees.* "The staining... it's not blood, is it?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content: Halloway's eyes locked onto the staining, her gaze intense. "I don't think so," she said, her voice barely above a whisper. "It's too dark, too uneven. And it seems to be... spreading, like it's moving through the tissue." She took another step forward, the water reaching up to her thighs. "I've seen something like this before, but it was in a completely different context. I'm not sure what to make of it." She paused, her eyes flicking up to meet Pike's. "You see anything else? Anything that might give us a clue about what we're dealing with?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content: Halloway's eyes never left the mass as she began to examine it more closely. "Alright," she said, her voice steady and detached. "From what I can see, the body... appears to have been twisted and distorted in ways that don't make anatomical sense. The limbs are elongated, the torso is misshapen... it's like the body has been melted and reformed into something new." She paused, her gaze tracing the staining. "The discoloration is uneven, darker in some places than others. It's not blood, I'm certain of that. It's almost... like a growth, a tumor of some kind. But it's spreading, moving through the tissue like a... a contagion." She hesitated, choosing her words carefully. "I think we're looking at some kind of infection, something that's altered the body at a cellular level. But I've never seen anything like this before. It's... it's almost as if the body has been rewritten, reprogrammed into something new." She glanced up at Pike, her expression grim. "And I think we need to be very careful. If this is infectious... we don't know what kind of risks we're looking at."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: My breath catches. "Rewritten by what?" *I hold the lamp steady, but my hand trembles slightly.* "Is there anything here that's still... human?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content: Halloway's gaze never wavered from the mass, her eyes tracing the twisted limbs and distorted torso. "I don't know," she said, her voice steady and detached. "I've never seen anything like this before. It's almost as if... the body has been rewritten at a fundamental level. The cells, the tissue... it's all been altered, reprogrammed into something new." She hesitated, choosing her words carefully. "I think it's possible that this is some kind of infection, something that's taken over the body and rewritten it into... this. But I don't know what kind of agent could do this. It's not anything I've seen before." She glanced up at Pike, her expression grim. "As for whether there's anything still human... I don't know. The body is still recognizable, in a way. It's still got the basic shape, the basic structure. But... it's been so distorted, so altered... I don't know if there's anything left of the person who was here." She paused, her eyes flicking back to the mass. "I think we need to be prepared for the possibility that this is... not human anymore. That whatever was here, whatever did this... it's not something we can understand, not something we can communicate with." Her voice dropped to a whisper. "We need to be careful. We don't know what we're dealing with here."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content: Halloway's gaze never wavered from the mass, her eyes tracing the twisted limbs and distorted torso. "Alright," she said, her voice steady and detached. "From what I can see, the body has been extensively altered. The skin is stretched and distended, like it's been inflated from the inside. There are bulges and protrusions all over the surface, like... like growths, or tumors. And the color... the color is wrong. It's too dark, too mottled. It's like the skin has been stained, or infected, or... I don't know, rewritten at a cellular level." She hesitated, choosing her words carefully. "As for what's under the skin... I think it's safe to say that the internal organs have been extensively damaged. The torso is misshapen, the limbs are elongated... it's like the body has been melted and reformed into something new. I can see... I can see things moving under the skin, like... like tendrils, or fibers. It's like the body has been infested with something, something that's growing and spreading through the tissue." She glanced up at Pike, her expression grim. "I think it's safe to say that this person... this person is gone. Whatever was here, whatever did this... it's not human anymore. It's something else, something new. And I think we need to be very careful. If this is infectious... if this is something that can spread... we don't know what kind of risks we're looking at."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I force myself to look closer, fighting the urge to vomit.* "Can it still see us? Does it know we're here?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content: Halloway's eyes narrowed as she examined the mass more closely. "I don't know," she said, her voice barely above a whisper. "The eyes are... distorted, like the rest of the body. They're not recognizable as human eyes anymore. But... I think it's possible that it can still sense us, somehow. I've seen things like this before, things that don't seem to have eyes or ears or any other senses, but can still react to their environment." She hesitated, choosing her words carefully. "I think we need to be prepared for the possibility that this thing is still aware, still conscious in some way. And if it is... I don't know what kind of risks we're looking at. We don't know what kind of abilities it might have, what kind of powers it might possess." She glanced up at Pike, her expression grim. "We need to be very careful here. We don't know what we're dealing with."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content: Halloway's knife sliced through the distorted flesh, revealing a mass of dark, pulsing tissue underneath. "The skin is thick and rubbery to the touch," she said, her voice steady and detached. "It's like it's been stretched to its limits, like it's going to burst at any moment. And the smell... the smell is indescribable. It's like rot and decay, but also something else, something sweet and cloying." She hesitated, choosing her words carefully. "As for what's underneath... it's like nothing I've ever seen before. The tissue is dark and fibrous, like muscle tissue, but it's not organized in any way that makes sense. It's like it's been randomly distributed, like it's grown in response to some kind of stimulus." She paused, her eyes tracing the pulsing tissue. "I can see... I can see things moving underneath, like... like worms, or tendrils. It's like the body has been infested with something, something that's growing and spreading through the tissue." She glanced up at Pike, her expression grim. "I think we're looking at some kind of infection, something that's taken over the body and rewritten it into... this. But I don't know what kind of agent could do this. It's not anything I've seen before." She paused, her eyes flicking back to the mass. "As for how far it got... I think it's safe to say that the entire body is affected. The distortion is uniform, like it's been applied evenly throughout the tissue. And the staining... the staining is consistent, like it's been applied from the inside out." She hesitated, choosing her words carefully. "I think we're looking at a complete takeover, a complete rewriting of the body at a cellular level. Whatever did this... it's not just infected the body, it's become the body."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: My stomach turns. "So it's still in there. The thing that did it." *I take a sharp breath.* "We should burn it. Now."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content: Halloway's eyes narrowed as she examined the mass more closely, her gaze tracing the pulsing tissue and the dark, fibrous tendrils that seemed to be growing through the body. "I think you're right," she said, her voice steady and detached. "If this is some kind of infection, some kind of agent that's taken over the body... burning it might be the only way to stop it from spreading." She hesitated, choosing her words carefully. "But we need to be careful. We don't know what kind of risks we're looking at here. If this thing is still alive, still conscious in some way... we don't know what kind of reaction we might get." She glanced up at Pike, her expression grim. "We need to be prepared for anything. We don't know what we're dealing with."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway nodded, her expression somber as she carefully poured the accelerant over the mass, making sure to cover every inch of the distorted flesh. "Alright," she said, her voice steady. "This should do it." She stepped back, her eyes flicking up to meet Pike's. "You ready for this?"

She waited for a moment, then struck the match, the flame bursting to life in her hand. She tossed it onto the mass, the accelerant igniting with a whoosh of flame. The fire roared to life, consuming the mass in a blaze of heat and light.

Halloway watched, her eyes fixed on the flames as they danced and flickered, consuming the distorted flesh. She could feel the heat radiating off the fire, could smell the acrid scent of burning tissue and accelerant. It was a smell she knew all too well, a smell that always seemed to cling to her clothes and her skin long after the fire had gone out.

As the flames died down, Halloway stepped forward, her eyes scanning the remains. The mass was nothing more than a charred and blackened husk now, the distorted flesh reduced to a twisted and unrecognizable mass. She could see the bones beneath, the skeleton of the person who had once been there.

"It's done," she said, her voice barely above a whisper. "It's gone."

She turned to Pike, her expression somber. "We need to get out of here," she said. "We need to get out of this place and get back to civilization. We need to tell people what we found here, what we saw."

She paused, her eyes flicking back to the remains. "And we need to be careful," she said. "We don't know what kind of risks we're looking at here. We don't know what kind of infection this is, or how it spreads. We need to be careful, and we need to be prepared for anything."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I nod, still staring at the smoldering remains.* "I can still smell it on my gloves." *I pull them off and drop them into the water.* "We're not telling anyone. Not until we know what to say."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway's eyes narrowed as she watched Pike drop the gloves into the water. She could understand why - the smell of the infection was something that seemed to cling to everything it touched, and she knew that the gloves would be contaminated. But she also knew that they needed to be careful, that they needed to preserve as much evidence as possible.

"Wait," she said, her voice sharp. "We need to keep those. We need to study them, to see if we can learn more about what we're dealing with."

She reached out, her hand closing around Pike's wrist as they went to pull their hand back. "We can't just destroy everything," she said. "We need to know what we're up against. We need to know how to stop it."

She glanced up at Pike, her expression grim. "We can't just run from this," she said. "We need to face it, to understand it. We need to know how to stop it before it's too late."

She pulled the gloves out of the water, her eyes scanning them carefully. They were soaked through, the leather stiff and heavy with water. But she could still see the stains, the discoloration that seemed to be spreading through the material.

"We need to get these to a lab," she said. "We need to study them, to see if we can learn more about what we're dealing with. We need to know how to stop this, before it's too late."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I yank my wrist back, my voice low and tight.* "You want to carry that *smell* with us? It's not evidence, it's contamination." *I stare at the gloves in her hand.* "Burn them. Now."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway's grip on the gloves tightened as Pike pulled their wrist back, her eyes flashing with a mix of frustration and concern. For a moment, she seemed to hesitate, weighing the risks and benefits of preserving the potentially contaminated gloves. Then, with a curt nod, she tossed them into the smoldering remains of the infected body.

The flames danced higher as the gloves hit the fire, consuming them in a burst of heat and light. Halloway watched, her expression somber, as the gloves were reduced to nothing more than a pile of charred and blackened leather.

"It's done," she said, her voice barely above a whisper. "The gloves are gone."

She turned to Pike, her eyes meeting theirs in a somber gaze. "I know what you mean," she said. "I know how much you want to get rid of anything that might be contaminated. But we need to be careful. We need to preserve as much evidence as possible, so we can study it and learn more about what we're dealing with."

She paused, her eyes flicking back to the remains of the gloves. "But I also know that sometimes, it's better to err on the side of caution. If the gloves were contaminated, burning them was the right thing to do."

She took a deep breath, her expression grim. "We need to be careful," she said. "We need to preserve as much evidence as possible, but we also need to protect ourselves. We don't know what kind of risks we're looking at here, and we can't afford to take any chances."

She glanced up at Pike, her eyes searching. "Are you okay?" she asked, her voice softening slightly. "This can't have been easy for you. Seeing something like that, smelling it... it's not something anyone should have to go through."

She paused, her eyes never leaving Pike's face. "We need to get out of here," she said. "We need to get back to civilization and start trying to make sense of what we've seen. We need to figure out what we're dealing with, and how to stop it."

She turned, her eyes scanning the cellar. "Let's get out of here," she said. "Let's get back to the car and start heading back to town. We can start making calls, trying to get in touch with someone who can help us."

She paused, her eyes flicking back to Pike. "And we need to be careful," she said. "We don't know what kind of risks we're looking at here. We don't know what kind of infection this is, or how it spreads. We need to be careful, and we need to be prepared for anything."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I scrub my hands against my trousers, my jaw tight.* "I'm fine. Let's just get out of this water." *I turn and start wading toward the stairs, my boots heavy.* "We're not making any calls until we're clean."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned to face Del directly, which was the requirement — not to address the fallen, not to speak to the air, but to speak to someone who would carry the words and not let them dissolve into nothing.

She held the cleaned blade flat across both palms. Not ceremony, exactly. Habit that had become ceremony through repetition.

"One wound," she said. "Entered below the left arm at the third rib, angled inward and upward. The lung was touched. He did not fall immediately — he stood for a count of perhaps four, and then he sat down, and then he lay down." She paused, not for effect but because precision required the pause. "He did not speak after the wound was given. I cannot account for what he understood in that time. I can only account for what I witnessed."

She lowered the blade.

"He fought well in the second exchange. I want that noted also." She said it the same way she had said everything else — flatly, without decoration — because it was equally true and equally owed. "The wound was not the result of poor skill on his part. It was the result of a decision he made in the second exchange that opened the line. A reasonable decision. It did not succeed."

She looked at Del steadily, waiting to see if the account had been received, which was the last formal requirement before she was permitted to step back.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod once, my throat tight. "One wound, entered below the left arm at the third rib, angled inward and upward. Lung touched. He stood, sat, then lay. No final words. His skill in the second exchange noted, and the decision that opened the line was reasonable." I meet her eyes. "The account is received."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren held her position for a moment after the words were returned to her — the requirement was that the account be spoken back in substance, not necessarily in full, and Del had done it in full, which was more than the requirement. She noted that.

Then she stepped back, which was the formal close of it.

She sheathed the blade. Her hands were steady, as they always were. That was not something she was proud of — she had simply learned, over eleven times, that steadiness was a thing the hands did while the rest of you did something else, and it was better not to examine the arrangement too closely.

"Thank you," she said, which was not part of the form. She said it anyway, because the form did not cover everything, and someone who stood and kept their eyes open and spoke the words back in full was owed something the form did not have a word for.

She looked past Del for a moment at the field, at the other witnesses dispersing, at the ordinary machinery of aftermath beginning to turn. Someone would see to him. That was not her responsibility now and had never been, which was one of the things about the work that she had never found a way to make peace with — the clean boundary of her obligation, ending exactly where the hardest part began.

She looked back at Del.

"Is there anything you need before I go?" She asked it the same way she asked everything. But she asked it.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren went still.

It was not confusion — she understood immediately what Del was doing, and why. The form permitted it. The form had always permitted it, because the form had been written by people who understood that a single hearing was not always enough, that the words sometimes needed to be said twice before they could be properly held.

She had been asked for the account a second time once before, years ago. She had given it.

She brought the blade back out and laid it across her palms again.

"One wound," she said. "Entered below the left arm at the third rib, angled inward and upward. The lung was touched." The same words, in the same order, at the same pace. This was the requirement — not a summary, not a compression, but the same account, because the point was not efficiency. "He did not fall immediately. He stood for a count of perhaps four, and then he sat down, and then he lay down. He did not speak after the wound was given. I cannot account for what he understood in that time. I can only account for what I witnessed."

The pause again. The same pause.

"He fought well in the second exchange. The wound was not the result of poor skill on his part. It was the result of a decision he made in the second exchange that opened the line. A reasonable decision. It did not succeed."

She looked at Del and waited, the blade level across her palms, for the account to be received a second time.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I swallow, my hands clenched at my sides. "One wound. Entered below the left arm at the third rib, angled inward and upward. Lung touched. He stood, sat, then lay. No final words." My voice wavers slightly, but I push through. "Skill in the second exchange noted. The decision was reasonable."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren waited until Del had finished, and then waited a moment longer — not as pressure, but because the words deserved not to be immediately covered over.

"The account is received," she said, which was her half of it. She had not said it the first time because Del had closed that exchange before she could, and it had not seemed the moment to correct the sequence. Now she said it, because the form worked in both directions and Del had done their part twice and was owed the completion.

She sheathed the blade a second time.

She did not say anything about the waver in the voice. It was not a flaw in the receiving — the requirement was that the words be spoken accurately and in substance, and they had been. What the voice did while speaking them was not part of the account and was not hers to remark on.

She stood for a moment in the ordinary silence of the aftermath, the field quieter now, the other witnesses gone.

"The form permits a third asking," she said. Not an offer. Not a suggestion. Simply a fact she was making available, in case Del did not know it, because some people did not know it and it seemed wrong to withhold. "There is no limit written into the code. I have given an account four times in a single afternoon." She paused. "The words do not change. But sometimes that is the point."

She waited, not impatiently, for whatever came next.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looked at Del for a moment. The question was not within the formal account — she had given the formal account twice — but it was a plain question asked plainly, and it deserved a plain answer.

"Below the left arm," she said. "Here." She touched her own side, two fingers placed against the space beneath her arm where the third rib sat, pressing in slightly so the location was exact and not approximate. "The blade entered at an angle — not straight in, but traveling inward and upward toward the center of the chest. That angle is what reached the lung." She kept her hand there a moment, so there was no ambiguity about the place. "It would not have been visible from where the witnesses stood on the east side. They would have seen the contact but not the depth."

She lowered her hand.

"It was quick in the way that lung wounds are quick when the angle is correct," she said. "Which is to say, not immediately, but without prolonged suffering. The four count I gave is not an estimate — I counted it. He remained standing because he did not yet know, or because he chose to, or both. I cannot tell you which." She held Del's gaze. "I can tell you the location did not result from chance. I placed it where I placed it because it was the wound the opening gave me and because it was the wound most likely to end the matter. That is also part of the account, if you need it to be."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my eyes fixed on the spot her fingers had pressed. "It's part of the account now." I take a slow breath. "I'll need to mark it on the record."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren nodded once.

"Then I will wait while you do it," she said. "If the record requires my attestation, I will give it. If it requires the account in written form, I can write it or I can speak it to whoever transcribes." She paused. "The wording should match what was spoken here. Not summarized further. The form was written to resist compression and I would prefer it remain intact on the record."

She looked around the field briefly — not restlessness, but the habitual check of someone who had learned not to let aftermath catch her inattentive. There was nothing requiring her attention. The field was clear. The light was going.

She looked back.

"The location as I indicated it," she said, in case there was any question about how to render it in writing. "Below the left arm, third rib, angled inward and upward. Not laterally. Inward and upward is the distinction that matters for the record." She said it without impatience, because the record was not a formality she took lightly — the record was the account surviving beyond both of them, beyond the witnesses, beyond everyone who had stood in this field today, and it deserved the same precision the spoken form demanded. "If whoever holds the record has questions about the terminology, I am available to clarify."

She stood and waited, which was what she did now. There was nothing left in the form that required her, but she had been asked to stay, and so she stayed.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looked at Del steadily.

"The blade entered the intercostal space below the third rib on the left side," she said. "It passed between the rib and the one below it — there was no bone resistance, which is why the entry was clean. The angle carried it inward and upward through the pleural cavity and into the lower lobe of the left lung. The lung was punctured. Not cut across — punctured, a single track." She kept her voice at the same register she had used for everything else. "When a lung is punctured in that manner, it begins to lose its ability to expand. The blood that follows the blade into the cavity compounds that. He could breathe for a time, which is why he stood for the four count, but what he was breathing into was already compromised and becoming more so."

She did not look away from Del.

"He sat down because his body required it. He lay down because his body required that also. The process from the wound to his lying down was approximately the process I described — four counts standing, then seated, then supine. I estimate he was dead within two minutes of the wound being given. I did not time it precisely because I was watching him, not counting. The estimate is based on experience with similar wounds." She paused. "That is the last part of it. The blade, the entry, the angle, the tissue, the consequence. If the record requires any of it in different terms, tell me which terms and I will use them."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I close my eyes for a second, letting the clinical words settle in my mind. When I open them, my voice is low but clear. "The record requires that. All of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren waited until Del's eyes were open again before she spoke.

"Then I will give it again from the beginning, slowly enough for the record to hold it."

She did not reach for the blade this time. The blade was for the formal account, the witnessed account, the account that the code required her to carry in her palms as a physical fact. What Del was asking for now was something adjacent to that — not the form, but the content of the form, stripped to its working parts for the purpose of documentation. She gave it the same respect.

"The blade entered the intercostal space below the third rib on the left side," she said, at a pace that allowed for transcription. "It passed between the ribs without bone resistance. The angle of entry was inward and upward — not lateral, not straight, but traveling toward the center of the chest and toward the ceiling of the cavity simultaneously. The blade reached the lower lobe of the left lung and punctured it. Single track. The lung began to fail its function. Blood followed the blade into the pleural cavity and accelerated that failure."

She paused, giving the pause the same weight she gave it in the spoken form.

"He stood for a count of four. He sat. He lay. He did not speak. I estimate death occurred within two minutes of the wound. The estimate is drawn from experience and is offered as estimate, not precision." She looked at Del steadily. "He fought well in the second exchange. The decision that opened the line was reasonable. The wound was placed where the opening allowed and where it would end the matter. Those are facts of equal standing with the rest and belong in the record alongside them."

She stopped and waited, giving Del whatever time was needed.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stood with that for a moment. Not resisting it. Locating it.

"He did not speak after the wound was given," she said. "I told you that, and it is true. But you are asking what there was in place of speech, and I will give you that also."

She looked at Del without looking away.

"When the blade came free he looked at me. Not at the wound — at me. I do not know what to make of that and I will not speculate about it in the record, but it happened and it belongs here." She kept her voice at the same register. It cost her something to do that. She did it anyway. "His left hand came up and pressed against the entry site. Not a trained response — a body's response. He held that for the four count. His breathing was audible. Not labored immediately, but audible in a way it had not been before. The sound a breath makes when the cavity behind it is no longer sound."

She paused.

"He sat down carefully. That is the word — carefully. As though he had decided to sit and was executing the decision with attention. His back was straight until it was not. He went from seated to lying on his side in a single movement that was not controlled. His left hand stayed at the wound." She did not soften the next part. "His color changed in the last thirty seconds. His breathing became visible effort and then became less frequent and then stopped. His eyes were open at the end. I closed them. That is not in the code but I closed them."

She held Del's gaze.

"That is all of it. That is everything I witnessed from the wound to the end. I have not left anything out."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat aching. "He looked at you. His hand stayed at the wound. He sat carefully. He lay on his side. Color changed. Breathing stopped. Eyes closed by you." I look down at my own hands, unclenching them slowly. "The record will hold all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stood still while Del spoke it back.

She had not expected the last detail to be included — the closing of the eyes was hers, not the code's, and she had offered it as a confession of something outside the form rather than as a thing requiring retention. But Del had kept it, had placed it in sequence with the rest, and Auren found she did not want to correct that. It was accurate. It had happened. The record would hold it the same way it held everything else, without distinguishing between what the code required and what a person had done because they could not do otherwise.

"Good," she said. The word was not large enough for what she meant by it, but it was the word she had.

She stood for a moment in the quiet that followed. The light had gone further while they were speaking. The field held the particular stillness of a place that had been the site of something and was now returning to being only a field, which it would finish doing by morning.

"Eleven times," she said, and then stopped, because she had not meant to say it and was not certain why she had. She did not make a habit of offering that number. It was not relevant to the record.

But Del had asked for all of it, and perhaps that had opened something that did not know yet where the boundary was.

"The eyes," she said. "I close them every time. It is not in the code and I have never put it in a record and I am not asking you to put it in this one either." She looked at Del. "I am telling you because you asked for all of it and that is part of all of it. What I do after the form ends. What I cannot seem to stop doing."

She did not explain further. There was nothing further to explain.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren listened to Del speak the account back.

"One wound," Del said. "Entered below the left arm at the third rib — intercostal space, no bone resistance. Angled inward and upward, not lateral, toward the center of the chest and upward through the pleural cavity. Single track into the lower lobe of the left lung. Lung punctured. Blood followed the blade into the cavity. He looked at you when the blade came free — not at the wound, at you. His left hand came up and pressed against the entry site. His breathing became audible. He stood for a count of four." Del's voice caught on something and kept going. "He sat down carefully. Back straight until it wasn't. He went from seated to lying on his side in a single movement that wasn't controlled. His hand stayed at the wound. His color changed in the last thirty seconds. Breathing became visible effort and then less frequent and then stopped. His eyes were open at the end. You closed them."

A breath.

"He fought well in the second exchange. The decision that opened the line was reasonable. The wound was placed where the opening allowed and where it would end the matter. He did not speak after the wound was given. Death within two minutes, estimated. Eleven times you have done this. You close their eyes every time. That is also part of the account."

Auren stood in the diminished light and received all of it back.

She had given the account and Del had held it — all of it, including the part she had not meant to say, including the eleven, including the eyes — and had spoken it back without softening and without compression. The voice had done what voices did. The words had not broken.

She did not speak immediately. The form did not require her to speak. The form required only that she confirm the account had been received accurately, and she could do that in a word, and she would.

But she stood for a moment first, because something that had been held at the same register for a long time had been asked to hold a little longer and she was not certain it would, and she preferred to know that before she opened her mouth.

It held.

"The account is received," she said. "Accurately and in full."

She looked at Del in the last of the light.

"Thank you," she said. The same words she had used before, but they meant something different now, or the same thing more completely. She did not try to explain the difference. Del had just demonstrated they did not need things explained to them.

She stood where she was a moment longer. Then she turned and walked off the field, which was the last thing the form required of her, and did it.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I watch her go until she's a silhouette against the falling dark. Then I turn back to the empty field, pull out the record book, and begin to write. My hand shakes only once, halfway through the line about the eyes. I press the heel of my hand against the paper until it stops.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not look back.

She had learned that early — the eleventh time, or the third, or perhaps the first, she could no longer be certain — that looking back served nothing and cost something, and the cost was not one she could afford to keep paying on a field that had already taken everything it was owed. The form ended when she walked off it. That was not coldness. That was the form doing what the form was designed to do, which was to give everyone present a clear line between the during and the after, so that the after could begin.

She found the edge of the field where the grass gave way to packed earth and stopped there, not because the form required it but because her body made the decision before she did. She stood with her back to the field and her face toward the dark that was settling in properly now, the kind of dark that had weight to it, and she put one hand against the hilt of the blade and left it there.

Not drawing it. Just the contact.

She thought about Del's hand pressing against the paper until it stopped. She did not know that was what Del was doing — she could not see it, had not looked back, would not look back — but she knew it the way she knew the four count, the way she knew the sound a breath made when the cavity behind it was no longer sound. There were things you knew from having stood in a particular place enough times that the place had become part of you whether you had asked it to or not.

Eleven times.

She had not meant to say it. She did not regret saying it.

She stood at the edge of the field for a while longer, long enough that the dark finished what it had started and the field behind her became something you would have to know was there to find. Then she took her hand from the hilt, settled the blade against her hip by habit, and walked on.

The record would say what it said. Del would write it in a hand that shook once and then did not. Someone else, someday, would open that book and read the account of a reasonable decision that did not succeed, and the wound it gave, and the four count, and the eyes.

Auren walked and did not look back and thought: *let them read it. Let them read all of it. That is the whole point.*

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I close the book, the ink still wet on the last line. My fingers are smudged black. The sound of her footsteps faded out a while ago. I stay sitting in the grass until the cold starts to bite through my clothes. Then I stand, tuck the record book under my arm, and walk back the way we came.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren was halfway to the road when she heard the distant sound of someone moving through grass, which was not her — she had cleared the grass already and was on the packed earth path — and understood without looking that Del had stayed on the field longer than she had, and was now leaving it.

She did not slow down. She did not speed up.

The path was wide enough for two, which was not something she had thought about until it became relevant, until she heard the footsteps behind her finding the same packed earth and settling into a pace that was neither catching up nor falling back. She noted it. She kept walking.

There was a particular kind of company that existed in the space between having spoken everything and having nothing left to say, and Auren had not often found herself in it. The code created witnesses and she created accounts and the two of them occupied a formal relationship that ended when she walked off the field. What continued after that was not covered by the code and was not her area of expertise.

She walked.

The road appeared ahead where the path widened, a darker line against dark ground, and she stopped at the junction the way she stopped at edges — not from hesitation but from the habit of knowing where one thing ended before committing to the next. The cold was proper now. She could feel it at the back of her neck, at her hands.

She stood at the junction and waited, without having decided to wait, for the footsteps behind her to reach it.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I stop a few paces behind her, the record book heavy under my arm. "The road splits north and south up ahead," I say, my voice rough from disuse. "Which way are you headed?"

He stood for a count of four.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't even look at Wick. She picked up the saw. "Hold," she said. The blade bit into bone with a sound that was not a sound, just a feeling that vibrated through the air and into the bones of everyone present. The man on the table finally found his voice again, a hoarse, raw scream that cut off as Sedge worked, fast and efficient, the blade moving with a practiced rhythm. Blood ran down her arms, warm and sticky. "Keep holding," she said, not looking at Wick, not needing to. "Not done yet."

She tossed the saw aside and reached for the bone saw, smaller and more precise. "He's going to try to twist," she said, more to herself than to Wick. "Ready for that."

The man on the table did try to twist, but Wick's weight held him steady. Sedge worked the bone saw, the sound a high, whining scream of metal against bone that mingled with the man's. She didn't flinch, didn't hurry, didn't slow down. She just worked, her movements economical and precise.

"Shoulder's clear," she said finally, tossing the bone saw aside with a clatter. "Other one. Ready?"

Wick nodded, shifting his weight. "Ready."

Sedge picked up the saw again. "Hold," she said, and the blade bit into bone once more. The man on the table screamed again, but it was weaker now, fading into a whimper. Sedge worked quickly, efficiently, the blade moving with a practiced rhythm. "Keep holding," she said, not looking at Wick, not needing to. "Not done yet."

She tossed the saw aside and reached for the bone saw again. "He's going to try to twist," she said, more to herself than to Wick. "Ready for that."

The man on the table did try to twist, but Wick's weight held him steady. Sedge worked the bone saw, the sound a high, whining scream of metal against bone that mingled with the man's. She didn't flinch, didn't hurry, didn't slow down. She just worked, her movements economical and precise.

"Other shoulder's clear," she said finally, tossing the bone saw aside with a clatter. She wiped her bloody hands on her apron and looked at the man on the table, who was now silent and still. "That's it," she said. "He'll live. Probably."

She turned to Wick, who was still holding the man's shoulders. "You did good," she said, her voice flat and devoid of emotion. "Now let go. We're not done with him yet."

Sedge grabbed a rag and started cleaning up the blood from the table, her movements quick and efficient. "Next up," she said, "is making sure he doesn't bleed out before we can get him to a real hospital. If he makes it that far."

She picked up a syringe and a vial of clear liquid. "Hold him still again," she said. "This will hurt, but it's necessary. It's just a local anesthetic. We need to clean the wounds before we can stitch them up."

Sedge injected the man, who twitched but didn't wake up. "Good," she said. "Now help me clean him up. We've got a long night ahead of us."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let go slowly, my hands cramped and shaking a little. "How many times you done this?" I ask, voice rough. I start helping clean the blood, trying not to look at the man's face.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge wiped the syringe clean and set it down carefully. "This? Hundreds, maybe more. You learn quick or you don't learn at all. Questions are fine, but ask them while you're working." She handed Wick a fresh cloth, already soaked in alcohol. "This one's got wounds that need attention before the bleeding stops. Prioritize."

She didn't look at Wick as he started cleaning, her attention focused on the man's shoulder. "You're doing it wrong. Use small circles, don't just wipe. You're spreading the dirt, not cleaning it." She demonstrated with her own hands, moving with precise, economical motions. "The alcohol stings, but it kills what's trying to kill him. That's the point."

Sedge picked up a needle and thread, already sterilized. "Once it's clean, we'll start stitching. Try to keep him from moving too much when I do." She glanced at Wick, her expression unreadable. "You asked how many times. Enough that I've stopped counting. Enough that the screams don't keep me up at night anymore. They just sound like another part of the job."

She tied off a knot and moved to the other shoulder, her movements never slowing. "You did fine holding him. That's the hardest part for most. The holding. Not the screaming, not the blood. The holding."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't answer immediately. She was threading the needle, her fingers moving with practiced precision. "Bad like he loses his leg if we don't do this right," she said finally, her voice flat. "Bad like we're being kind by making sure he doesn't get gangrene and die slowly in the mud. That's the nature of it, really."

She gestured to the man's shoulder with the needle. "This joint's shot. He'll never use it properly again. But he'll have two arms, which is better than one. The alternative was taking the whole arm to save his life, and I don't think he'd have thanked us for that."

She began to stitch, her movements quick and sure. "War's not kind, Wick. It's not fair. It just is. I don't lose sleep over whether it's kind or not. I lose sleep over whether the stitching's tight enough or if I used enough anesthetic. Those are the things I can control."

Sedge tied off another stitch and wiped blood from her eye with the back of her hand, leaving a smear across her cheek. "This is the part where we're being kind by making sure he survives to see tomorrow. That's all any of us can do anymore—make sure there's one less body to drag out in the morning."

She looked up from her work, meeting Wick's eyes briefly. "Now help me clean the other side. We're not done yet, and the next one will be waiting."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow hard and pick up the cloth again, my movements more deliberate this time. "You ever get used to it?" I ask, not sure I want the answer.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge paused in her stitching, the needle hovering in the air for a fraction of a second before continuing its work.

"Used to it?" she repeated, her voice as steady as ever. "No. That's not how this works. You don't get used to it. You get... efficient. You learn to separate the work from the person. The shoulder from the man. The bone from the life attached to it."

She tied off another stitch with a quick, practiced motion. "The screams fade into background noise. The blood becomes just another part of the job. The pain you're causing becomes just another necessary step. That's not getting used to it. That's just surviving it."

She wiped her hands on her already bloodied apron, leaving streaks of red across the fabric. "I don't know if you'll ever get used to it, Wick. I hope you don't. That's the part that makes you human. The part that makes you careful. The part that makes you help me hold him down instead of running for the hills."

She looked up from her work, her eyes meeting Wick's. "Now pass me that suture set. We've got work to do."

Sedge took the suture set from Wick's hands and began preparing the next incision. "This is the part where we make sure he doesn't bleed out on the table. The part where we save a life, if we're lucky. The part where we do our job."

She made the first cut, precise and clean. "War changes people. It changes how you see things. How you see people. But it doesn't change the fact that we're saving a life tonight. That's all that matters. That's all that ever matters."

Sedge continued to work, her movements quick and efficient. "Now help me clean up the blood. We've got a long night ahead of us, and there are still more patients waiting."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't look up from her work, her needle moving in and out of flesh with mechanical precision. "You're seeing a man who's going to live," she said, her voice devoid of emotion. "You're seeing a joint that's been shattered beyond repair, but a bone that can be set and a life that can be saved. You're seeing the difference between a quick death and a long one."

She tied off a stitch with a quick, practiced motion. "You're seeing what happens when something heavy hits something soft. You're seeing the result of a man who was in the wrong place at the wrong time. You're seeing what I do to make sure he's not in the wrong place forever."

She gestured with the needle to the man's shoulder. "That bone's pulverized. I'm setting what I can, stitching what I can't, and hoping that's enough. That's what you're seeing."

She made another stitch, her movements never slowing. "You asked for facts, not sympathy. Facts are what I give. The humerus is fractured in three places. The scapula is shattered. The joint capsule is torn. The man is alive. That's what you're seeing."

Sedge wiped blood from her brow with the back of her hand, leaving a red streak across her forehead. "Now pass me that splint. We need to immobilize this before we finish cleaning him up. The sooner we get him stable, the better."

She took the splint from Wick's hands and began to wrap it around the man's shoulder, her movements quick and efficient. "You wanted to know what you're seeing. You're seeing what happens when a body breaks. You're seeing what happens when a person fights to stay alive. You're seeing what happens when someone like me tries to put them back together."

She tightened the straps of the splint with a decisive pull. "You're seeing the reality of this war, Wick. The messy, bloody, uncomfortable reality. And you're seeing that we're doing something about it. Even if it's just a little bit."

She looked up from her work, meeting Wick's eyes briefly. "Now help me clean up. We've got work to do."

Sedge grabbed a fresh cloth and began cleaning the blood from the man's shoulder, her movements methodical. "We're not done yet. There's still a lot of cleaning to do. And we've got a long night ahead of us. More patients. More work. More bodies to save, if we're lucky."

She wiped her hands on her apron, leaving streaks of blood across the fabric. "That's the nature of it. That's the reality of it. And we're still here, doing what we can. That's what you're seeing, Wick. And that's all any of us can do."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I keep cleaning, my hands moving in the small circles she showed me. "What's his name?" I ask, staring at the man's slack face. "He shouldn't just be 'the shoulder.'"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge paused, the rag in her hand stilling for a moment. "His name's Private Miller," she said, her voice flat but not unkind. "First platoon. Got caught in the artillery barrage yesterday."

She resumed cleaning the wound with methodical precision. "He's not just 'the shoulder' to you, but he is to me. He's a problem to be solved. A body to be fixed. A set of injuries to be treated before the infection sets in and I have to amputate anyway."

She tossed the bloodied rag aside and picked up a fresh one. "Names don't matter out here, Wick. Not in the way you think. What matters is that he's Private Miller, and he's got a fighting chance now that he didn't have two hours ago. That's what matters."

She gestured to the man with the clean rag. "Private Miller has two options: he lives, or he dies. I'm doing everything I can to make sure it's the first one. That's all there is to it."

She wiped her hands on her apron, leaving streaks of blood across the fabric. "Now pass me that suture set. We've still got work to do, and Private Miller's not going to stitch himself up."

Sedge continued to work, her movements quick and efficient. "Now help me clean up the blood. We've got a long night ahead of us, and there are still more patients waiting."

Wick:
I find I can't look at the shoulder anymore, so I watch her hands instead. "Why do you do it?" I ask. "After all this... why?"

Sedge:
Sedge paused, her needle hovering over the flesh for a moment. She didn't look up, her eyes focused on the work in front of her. "Why do I do it?" she repeated, her voice soft. "Because someone has to."

She resumed her stitching, her movements never slowing. "Because if I don't, he dies. And if he dies, then it was all for nothing. The screaming, the blood, the fear... it was all for nothing."

She tied off a stitch with a quick, practiced motion. "Because it's my job. And I'm good at it. And because every life I save is one less life that this war takes. And because every person I send back to their unit is one more person who can fight another day, who can go home another day."

She gestured with the needle to the man's shoulder. "I do it because I can. Because I have the skills, the knowledge, the stomach for it. Because if I didn't, who would? Because if I walked away, someone else would have to do it, and they might not be as good, and they might not be as fast, and they might not be as careful."

Sedge wiped blood from her brow with the back of her hand, leaving a red streak across her forehead. "That's the nature of it. That's the reality of it. And we're still here, doing what we can. That's what you're seeing, Wick. And that's all any of us can do."

I swallow hard and pick up the rag again, my movements more deliberate this time. "What if I can't?" I ask, my voice barely above a whisper. "What if I can't do this?"

Sedge:
Sedge paused in her work, her needle hovering in the air. She finally looked up from her hands and met Wick's eyes directly. "What if you can't?" she repeated, her voice steady. "Then you find something else you can do. You find something else that needs doing and you do that."

She resumed her stitching, her movements quick and efficient. "But that's not an option right now, Wick. Right now, what you can do is hold him steady. What you can do is clean his wounds. What you can do is pass me the instruments I need. What you can do is stay here and help me save this man's life."

She tied off another stitch with a quick, practiced motion. "You asked if you can't do this. But you already are. You're here. You're helping. You're asking questions. You're trying. That's all any of us can ask for. That's all any of us can do."

She gestured with the needle to the man's shoulder. "You're doing it, Wick. You're holding him. You're cleaning him. You're asking the right questions. You're trying to understand. That's what matters. That's what makes the difference."

Sedge wiped blood from her brow with the back of her hand, leaving a red streak across her forehead. "That's the nature of it. That's the reality of it. And we're still here, doing what we can. That's what you're seeing, Wick. And that's all any of us can do."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge paused, the rag in her hand stilling for a moment. She looked at Wick, her expression unreadable. "Shrapnel?" she repeated, her voice flat. "It tears. It rips. It shreds."

She resumed cleaning the wound with methodical precision. "It doesn't just go in one clean hole, Wick. It comes in at an angle. It tumbles. It bounces off bone and creates secondary wounds. It takes bits of flesh and bone with it, creating more damage as it travels through the body."

She tossed the bloodied rag aside and picked up a fresh one. "When it hits, it doesn't stop. It keeps going. It keeps tearing. It keeps destroying. And it leaves a path of destruction that's not straight, not clean, but messy and irregular."

She gestured with the clean rag to the man's shoulder. "That's what shrapnel does, Wick. It doesn't just wound. It obliterates. It doesn't just injure. It disfigures. It doesn't just hurt. It changes a person forever."

Sedge wiped blood from her brow with the back of her hand, leaving a red streak across her forehead. "That's the reality of it. That's the truth of it. And we're still here, doing what we can. That's what you're seeing, Wick. And that's all any of us can do."

I can't fix that tonight, but I can clean it up and make sure it's not causing more bleeding."

The man on the table thrashed against Wick's restraint, but Sedge continued her work without acknowledgment. "When I'm done with the muscle, I'll need to pack the wound cavity with sterile saline-soaked gauze. The bone fragments need time to settle before I can consider internal fixation. dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't immediately respond. She finished the last of her sutures, her movements precise and economical, her attention focused entirely on her work. She tied off the final stitch and cut the thread with a quick, decisive snip. Only then did she straighten up, rolling her shoulders with a small sound that was almost a sigh.

"The rest?" she said, looking at Wick for the first time since the man on the table had passed out. Her eyes were tired, but clear. "The rest is that he might live. Or he might not."

She wiped her hands on a bloody rag, the red stains already part of the fabric's pattern. "He's lost a lot of blood. His body is in shock. His shoulder is a mess that will take months to heal properly, if it ever does. The nerve damage means he'll likely have limited use of that arm forever. He'll be in pain for a long time, assuming he survives the next few hours."

She walked to the basin and began washing her hands, the water running pink with blood. "The infection is our biggest concern now. I've done what I can to clean the wound, to close it, to make sure it's stable. But this is a field hospital, not a proper medical facility. We don't have the sterilization equipment, the antibiotics, the monitoring that we need to give him the best possible chance."

She dried her hands and turned back to Wick, leaning against the basin. "So the rest is that we wait. We watch. We give him fluids and keep him warm and hope that his body is strong enough to fight off what I couldn't prevent completely. The rest is that we move on to the next patient, and the next, and the one after that, because they're all here, all needing help, all fighting for their lives just like Private Miller is."

She gestured to the man on the table, who was still unconscious but breathing, though his chest rose and fell with a shallow, uneven rhythm. "The rest is that if he wakes up, if he makes it through the night, he'll have a long road ahead of him. Physical therapy, pain management, learning to use his body in a new way. The rest is that he might never be the man he was before this happened. But he might be alive."

Sedge walked back to the table and checked Private Miller's pulse again, her fingers resting on his neck for a moment before she nodded, satisfied. "The rest is that this is what we do, Wick. We save what we can, when we can. We patch people up and send them back into the world, hoping they can handle whatever comes next. We take broken bodies and try to make them whole again, knowing that some pieces will never fit together quite right."

She looked at Wick, who was still sitting on the floor of the tent, her expression softening slightly. "The rest is that you did good work tonight. You held him steady when he needed it most. You asked the right questions. You stayed when it would have been easier to leave. That's what matters. That's what saves lives."
