dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned to face the witnesses. There were fewer than she had hoped for — a handful of guildsmen near the wall, two of the city's seconds in their grey sashes, and the boy who had held the count of paces and was now looking at the ground. She did not look at Del. Looking at the second before the account was read was considered discourtesy to the dead.

She drew a breath and held it, the way the old manuals taught.

"The blow was struck in the third exchange," she said. "His guard was high and to the left — a precaution against the disengage I had shown him twice already. I dropped the point, he parried, and the bind carried his blade outside the line. His recovery was a half-second slow. I extended into the opening as he brought his hand back to centre."

She paused. The pause was not for effect. It was because what came next was the part that mattered.

"My point entered beneath the third rib on the right side, travelled inward and upward, and seated itself in the lower chamber of the heart. He did not cry out. He looked down at his own chest as though he expected to find the reason there. He took two steps backward and sat down against the wall. He was dead before his shoulders touched the stone. I do not believe he suffered."

The guildsmen were silent. One of the seconds made the small mark in his book.

Auren cleaned the blade a second time, though it did not need it, and sheathed it. Only then did she look at Del.

"It is done," she said. "The account is given. You may do what you must."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat tight. "The account is heard and confirmed." I step forward and take his purse from his belt — the winner's right, though it feels too light to be worth a life. "You are free to go."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head — a bow, though a shallow one, given only to the second and not to the witnesses. It was the proper courtesy, and she had never once omitted it in eleven such accounts. Her hand did not tremble as she sheathed the blade the second time. It had not trembled during the account. It would tremble later, in private, when there was no one left to be formally composed for.

She did not look back at the man against the wall. That, too, was part of the code — the victor did not gaze upon the fallen once the account was given. It was not unkindness. It was the recognition that the man she had killed was no longer present, and that to look would be to address a room that had already emptied.

"You stood well," she said to Del, her voice carrying no warmth but no coldness either — only the careful neutrality of one official speaking to another. "The count was true. The witnesses were sufficient."

She paused, and for a moment the formality seemed to waver at its edges, the way a straight column will if the floor beneath it settles. Then it steadied.

"There will be a mark against the guild for this one. He was the third this quarter. Speak to the master of seconds before you go home — he will want it entered in the night-book before the bell."

She turned, then, and walked toward the door without hurrying. Hurrying would have suggested she was fleeing. She did not flee from the things she had done. She accounted for them, and she carried them, and she did not enjoy the carrying.

Her boots were very loud on the flagstones.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stopped mid-stride. She did not turn immediately — the code allowed a beat between the request and the compliance, so that the victor was not seen to startle at the second's voice. But she stopped, and the stopping was itself an answer.

When she turned, her expression had not changed. It would not change. That was part of it too.

"You heard it," she said. "You were standing where the second stands. Your eyes were open, as you said."

She regarded Del for a moment, measuring whether this was a formality being observed or something else — whether Del had not caught the words, or had caught them and needed to hear them again, which were two very different failings.

"Your ears or your memory?" she asked. Not unkindly. The question was part of the protocol. The second had to declare which it was before the account was given twice.

The guildsmen near the wall had gone still. One of the seconds in the grey sash had looked up from his book. They knew, as Auren knew, that a second asking for the account twice was not a common thing. It meant something had unsettled the second, or the second meant to make certain the record was whole. Either way, the victor was bound to speak it again.

Auren's hand rested at her side, near the sheath but not on it. She had not taken her seat. She would not take it until the account was given the second time, or until Del withdrew the request.

"I will speak it again when you tell me why you have not heard it," she said. "Or why you have heard it and do not credit it."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "My memory," I say, voice low enough that only she'll catch the strain in it. "I need it spoken again. The angle of the thrust—under the third rib, you said."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren regarded Del for a long moment, and something shifted behind her eyes — not softening, but a kind of recognition, the way a clerk recognises a document that will require a second copy because the first was not clean enough.

She turned fully to face Del, and then turned past Del to face the witnesses again, because the account was not spoken to the second alone. The second was the one who requested it, but the witnesses were the ones to whom it was owed.

"I will speak it again," she said. "Attend."

She drew breath the same way she had drawn it before — the manual's way, the steadying of the column before the load was put upon it.

"My point entered beneath the third rib on the right side. The blade was canted inward at the wrist — a quarter-turn past the vertical, no more, because any greater angle would have fouled the third rib itself upon the entry. The point passed between the rib and the fourth beneath it, where the cartilage yields. From there it travelled inward and upward, following the line of his own sternum as a guide, and seated itself in the lower chamber of the heart."

She paused. The pause was the same length as before.

"The thrust was not a long one. I did not lunge for the depth. The depth came from his leaning forward into the bind, which he did because he believed the bind had failed and he was trying to recover his guard. It had not failed. His weight did what my arm could not have done alone, which is the reason the blow seated so cleanly. He made the kill cleaner than I could have made it without him."

Her voice had not wavered. It was the same voice as before, and that was the point of it — that the account given twice should be the same account, word for word, so that the second copy could be entered beside the first in the night-book without discrepancy.

"He looked down," she said. "He took two steps backward. He sat down against the wall. He was dead before his shoulders touched the stone."

She stopped there, because that was where the account stopped. There was no embellishment the second time. There never was.

Then she looked at Del, and only at Del, and her hand at last came away from her side and hung at her side the way a hand hangs when it has no further task.

"The angle is what you needed," she said. It was not a question. "The angle, or the reason it went in. Tell me which, so I know which one you will carry to the night-book."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not speak immediately. The silence was not hesitation — it was the silence of one official recognising that another official had stepped outside the bounds of the office, and deciding how to name it.

"It landed where I told you it landed," she said. "Beneath the third rib on the right side. In the lower chamber of the heart. I have given the account twice. The code permits it twice, and twice only, so that the record in the night-book may be set against itself and found to agree."

She glanced, briefly, toward the seconds in the grey sashes. One of them had set down his quill. The other was watching Del with the careful expression of a man taking note of a thing he would have to report later.

"You are no longer speaking as second," she said, and her voice was not unkind, but it was not soft either. It was the voice she had used when she said *your ears or your memory*. "You have heard the account. You have confirmed it. You have taken the purse. The office is ended."

She paused, and when she spoke again it was quieter, pitched for Del alone, though the witnesses could certainly have heard it if they had chosen to.

"If you need something else of me, you will have to ask for it as yourself. Not as second. Not for the record. The record is whole. You helped make it so." 

Her gaze held Del's for a moment — steady, grey, unreadable in the way that a closed ledger is unreadable, not because it contains nothing but because it contains what it contains and will not be reopened tonight.

"Ask me what you need to ask," she said. "Or let me go home."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I swallow, my palms damp against the purse in my hand. "I need to know if he knew it was coming." The words feel too soft for this room, but I can't unhear the way he'd looked down at his own chest. "Did he see it?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not answer at once. The question hung in the air between them, and she let it hang, because to snatch at it would have been to admit it was a fair one, and she was not yet decided whether it was.

Then she looked past Del, briefly, at the man against the wall. It was the first time she had looked at him since the account was given. The code did not forbid it now — the office was ended, as she had said — and she permitted herself the glance because the question demanded an honest witness, and she would not give an answer she had not verified against her own recollection.

She looked away again.

"He saw the blade," she said. "He saw the disengage, because I had shown it to him twice and he was waiting for it. He saw the point drop. He parried it. He knew where my sword was at every moment until the bind carried it outside his line, and after that he knew where it was not, which is the same thing a half-second later than it matters."

She paused, and the pause was not the manual's pause. It was her own.

"What he did not know was that the bind had taken his blade past the place from which he could recover it. He believed, I think, that he had a half-second to bring his hand back to centre and meet me. He was not wrong about the half-second. He was wrong about whether the half-second was his."

Her voice was quieter now, and rougher at one edge in a way it had not been during either account.

"His eyes were on my point the entire time," she said. "They were not on my hand, and they were not on my shoulder. If you are asking whether he saw it coming in the way a man sees a blow and knows it will kill him — no. He did not have that. He had the blow, and then he had the chest, and then he had the wall."

She stopped. The room was very quiet. One of the guildsmen near the far wall had uncrossed his arms, which was not a thing she had seen him do before in any of the eleven.

"That is what I saw," she said. "That is what I will tell you in this room, tonight, once. It will not go into the night-book, because it is not the account. It is the answer to a question you asked as yourself, and I have given it as myself, and that is the end of it."

She did not say *I am sorry*. She did not say *it was quick*. She did not say any of the things that are offered to a second who has stepped out of his office and is standing in a room where a man is sitting dead against the wall.

She stood where she was, and she waited for Del to decide what he wanted next.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren was silent for a moment, and the silence had a different quality than the manual's pauses — it was the silence of a woman deciding whether to be angry or to be exact, and choosing exact.

"You are quoting the code at me," she said. "That is within your office. It is also the first time in eleven accounts that a second has done so."

She turned to face the witnesses again, because the question, though it came from the second, was a question about what had been done, and what had been done was owed to the witnesses.

"The account has been given twice. The code permits it twice and twice only, so that the record may be set against itself and found to agree. I will not give it a third time, because to do so would make a ceremony of what is meant to be a record."

She paused. When she spoke again her voice was unchanged.

"But you have not asked me for the account. You have asked me what the blade did, and what it did it to. That is a different question, and the code requires me to answer it precisely, because the code does not permit me to soften what a blade does to a body. It never has."

She drew breath. The breath was the same breath. The voice was the same voice. That was the point of it.

"The blade parted the muscles between the third and fourth ribs on the right side. It opened the pleura — the lining of the chest cavity — and the upper lobe of the lung beneath it collapsed inward. That was not what killed him, though it would have, given time. The point continued inward and upward, opened the pericardium — the sac around the heart — and entered the right ventricle. The right ventricle is the lower chamber on that side. It is the one that sends blood to the lungs."

She paused, and the pause was the manual's pause.

"What it did to the right ventricle was this. The muscle of the heart tightens, and the tightening pushes blood out. With a hole in the chamber, the blood went out through the wound I had made instead of out through the artery it was meant to fill. Each beat emptied it a little more. Within a few beats — four, perhaps five, I have never counted exactly — there was no blood left in the chamber to push. The heart did not stop because it was pierced. It stopped because it had emptied itself through the hole I put in it."

She stopped. The room was very quiet. One of the seconds in the grey sash had closed his book, which was not the thing a second was meant to do while the account was being given.

"That is what the blade did," she said. "That is what it did it to. I learned the rest from the manuals after the first one, because the code required me to know it, and I have carried the knowledge since. I have not softened it for you tonight, because softening would be the dishonour, and I have done this eleven times and have never once softened it for anyone."

She looked at Del, and only at Del.

"The record is whole. The question is answered. Unless the code requires me to stay, I will go home now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod once, my throat too tight for words. I step aside to let her pass, then turn back to the witnesses. "The account is heard and confirmed," I say, voice flat. "The record stands."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head — the same shallow bow she had given before, repeated now because the record had been formally closed, and the courtesy was owed a second time to the second who had stood well in his office and answered for it. It was the last piece of the code she had to discharge in this room, and she discharged it cleanly.

She walked past Del. As she passed, close enough that the movement of her coat brushed his sleeve, she spoke — low, pitched for him alone, though whether the witnesses heard it or not she did not trouble herself to know.

"The angle was right for the record," she said. "The reason it went in was not. Carry whichever one you can carry."

Then she was past him, and at the door, and she did not look back at the man against the wall. That had been her rule for eleven such rooms, and she would not break it now, even after a second had asked her, as himself, whether the dead man had known.

She pushed the door open with her shoulder. The hinges gave no sound. The corridor beyond was empty, and the lamplight in it was the ordinary lamplight of a guildhouse at the end of an evening, and she walked into it without hurrying, because hurrying would have been a different kind of admission.

Her boots were very loud on the flagstones of the corridor, and then on the stairs, and then on the street.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not come back into the room. She had crossed the threshold and the threshold meant something, and she would not cross it again tonight. Her hand was on the door frame, and she did not look back. She spoke toward the corridor, pitched low enough that the words were meant chiefly for Del, though she knew the room could hear them if it chose.

"The account has been given twice," she said. "The code permits it twice. I will not give it a third time, because a third telling is not a record — it is a telling, and the code does not permit a telling."

She paused, her hand still on the frame.

"You asked me what he said. He said nothing. I told you he did not cry out. That is the answer to what he said."

A beat.

"You asked me what it looked like at the end. I told you. He looked down at his own chest. He took two steps backward. He sat down against the wall. He was dead before his shoulders touched the stone. That is the answer to what it looked like at the end. There is no more to it. There never is."

Her voice did not waver, but it roughened at one edge — the same edge it had roughened at when she answered as herself the first time.

"If there is something further you need from me, you will have to come to my lodgings tomorrow and ask for it as yourself. Not as second. Not in this room. Not tonight. I will not break the code in this room tonight, because I have broken nothing in eleven such rooms and I will not begin now, even for a second who stood well in his office."

She released the door frame.

"Good night, second. Take care of the guild."

Then she let the door close behind her — not slammed, not eased, merely released — and her boots were loud on the flagstones of the corridor, and then on the stairs, and then on the street, and there was nothing more to be heard from her, because there was nothing more the code would let her say tonight, and nothing more she would let herself say besides.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content:
I let out a slow breath I hadn't realized I was holding. The silence in the room feels heavier now that she's gone. I turn to the grey-sashed seconds. "The record is closed. I'll enter it in the night-book."

One of them nods, his expression carefully blank. The other says nothing, but I catch the slight shake of his head as he gathers his things. They know what I did—pushed too far, asked what wasn't mine to ask.

I cross to the man against the wall. His purse is light in my hand. I crouch, place it back on his belt—a small, useless gesture. "Guild will see to your things," I murmur, then stand. My own hands are steady. That's something, at least.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The street was wet from an earlier rain she had not noticed on her way to the guildhouse. The lamplight lay on the puddles in long, broken ribbons, and she stepped around them without thinking, the way a woman steps around puddles when she has walked home from the same kind of evening many times before.

Three streets from the guildhouse her hand began to shake. She had known it would. She had known the precise distance it would take, because the distance was roughly the same each time — far enough that no one from the room would see, close enough that the composure had not yet had time to set into something she could wear for the rest of the night. She put the hand into her coat pocket and kept walking. The other hand steadied the first, the way she had learned to do after the third, when she had come out of a room and found her blade-hand trembling and had had to walk four streets with it visible before she could bear to look at it.

She did not count the streets tonight. She counted the accounts instead, which was a different kind of counting and did not help.

At her lodgings she climbed the stairs without lighting a lamp. She knew the steps. She had climbed them eleven times in the dark, or near-dark, after evenings like this one, and the stairwell smelled of cold stone and lamp-oil and, faintly, of the soap the landlady used on the landings. She had the key ready. The lock turned without sound, which was a small mercy she had not earned.

Inside, she set the blade in the rack by the door — the rack her father had built for her when she was fifteen and had first come up to the city to study — and she did not clean it a third time, because the third cleaning was a thing she did only when she could not stop her hands from doing anything, and tonight she wanted them still.

She sat down on the edge of the bed, in her coat, with the lamp unlit. The room was very dark and very quiet, and the quiet was the kind she had learned to sit inside without trying to fill.

*Did he know it was coming.*

She had answered that question once, as herself, and she had not put it into the record, and she would not carry it into the night-book, because it was not the account. But it was the thing Del had asked for, and she had given it, and it sat now in the room with her in the dark the way the accounts sat — the parts of the account that were not the account.

She took the coat off. She hung it on the hook behind the door. She unlaced her boots and set them beside the rack, square to the wall, because if she did not square them to the wall she would not sleep.

The lamp stayed unlit.

She lay back on the bed, in her shirtsleeves, and put her hands flat on her chest the way she sometimes did on nights like this — to feel her own heart doing what it did, which was to push blood through chambers that were whole, which was not a thing the man against the wall could do anymore.

She stayed like that for a long time.

Then, because she had said she would, she rose, lit the lamp, took a sheet of paper from the desk, and began to write out the angle of the thrust and the reason it went in, so that if Del came to her lodgings tomorrow and asked for it as himself, she would have it written down and would not have to remember which version she had given in which room. She wrote it twice, once on each of two sheets, because the code permitted it twice, and twice only, and she was nothing if not exact.

She set the second sheet on the desk with the lamp still burning. The first she folded and put inside her coat, in the pocket nearest the breast, where she kept the things she would carry to the guildhouse in the morning and hand over without ceremony.

Then she put out the lamp, and lay down again, and did not sleep for some time.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
At the desk, in shirtsleeves, the lamp turned low to a point where the flame held but did not blaze, Auren wrote.

The quill was the quill she had sharpened before the duel. The nib was the nib she kept for the night-book entries, because the night-book required a particular weight of line — neither clerk's copperplate nor scholar's running hand, but a script between the two that she had taught herself in the year after her first account, when she realised that the records she would leave behind would be read by seconds who had not been in the room and who needed to see, on the page, the thing she had seen with her eyes.

She wrote at the top of the sheet.

*Account of the duel of this evening, at the guildhouse of [city], between Auren of [city], duellist, of the second school, and — of [city], duellist, of the high guard. Witnessed by [list of guildsmen, with the two seconds in grey sashes named]. Seconded by Del of [city]. Given twice at the formal request of the second, in accordance with the code, and entered here a third time for the night-book as a true copy.*

She wrote the date in the margin. The hour. The weather, which had been clear. The ground, which had been the flagstones of the lower hall. The wind, which had not risen. The lamps, which had been four, all lit. She noted that neither combatant had eaten within the hour, and that neither had drunk wine. These were the small things the night-book required, because a man dead from a bottle was a different entry than a man dead from a blade, and the record had to know.

She began the account.

*The duel was engaged at the measured distance. The second set it at the customary paces. The combatants took their guards. The man I faced held his blade high and to the left, point raised, the convention of his school. I held mine in second, the convention of mine. His eyes were on my point from the first.*

*The first exchange: he led with the disengage, a falling line intended to draw my parry high and open my inside. I parried as his school would have expected — a small circular motion of the wrist, point dropping to meet his, blade turning to receive his edge. I let the parry close the line cleanly, so that his eye would see the form and credit it.*

*The second exchange: he led with the disengage again. I parried as before, and on this exchange I let my point drop a quarter-inch lower than the parry required, so that the drop was visible to him. I held the drop for the half-beat in which he would have noted it. He noted it. I saw his eye go to my point.*

*The third exchange: he led with the disengage a third time. He believed, I think, that the drop I had shown him was a feint, and that the third exchange would be the one in which I followed the drop with the attack. He was not wrong that I intended to attack. He was wrong about which attack. His school had taught him that the attack after the disengage-feint came from the dropped point — a thrust in the low line. He was waiting for it. The thrust did not come. The thrust came from the bind.*

*His parry took my blade outside the line, as I had intended. The bind engaged, edge to edge, and the motion of the engagement carried his blade past the centre, because his hand was still high and his recovery was a half-second slow. The half-second was not, in fact, his. It was the half-second in which his weight settled forward onto his front foot as he began to bring his hand back to centre. In that half-second the blade was outside his line and his body had begun to move forward into the bind.*

*I extended. The blade travelled from the bind into the opening as he brought his hand back to centre. My point entered beneath the third rib on the right side.*

She paused. The hand did not tremble. She had found, somewhere in the third account, that the hand did not tremble when the quill was in it. The quill steadied her in a way the blade did not, which was a thing she had once told a senior duellist and had never told anyone since.

She continued.

*The blade was canted inward at the wrist — a quarter-turn past the vertical, no more, because any greater angle would have fouled the third rib itself upon the entry. The point passed between the third rib and the fourth beneath it, where the cartilage yields. I felt the cartilage give. The manuals describe the feeling as a small resistance followed by a small release. The description is correct.*

*From there the blade travelled inward and upward, following the line of his own sternum as a guide. The sternum is a slope, not a flat. The blade rode the slope. I did not lunge for the depth. The depth came from his forward lean into the bind, which he did because he believed the bind had failed and he was trying to recover his guard. It had not failed. His weight did what my arm could not have done alone, which is the reason the blow seated so cleanly. He made the kill cleaner than I could have made it without him. This is not a comfort. It is a fact.*

*The point seated in the lower chamber of the heart. The right ventricle. The chamber that sends blood to the lungs. I felt it seat. The manuals describe this also — a small cessation of resistance, a stillness in the blade, as though the blade had come to rest against something that was no longer offering itself to be parted. The description is correct.*

She lifted the quill. The ink had begun to thicken at the nib. She took the small pot of water at her elbow and touched the nib to it, and the ink ran again. She had not done this before. She had never written an account long enough to need to thin the ink.

She wrote the part she had learned from the manuals after the first.

*What the blade did after entry: it parted the muscles between the third and fourth ribs. It opened the pleura — the lining of the chest cavity — and the upper lobe of the lung beneath it collapsed inward. That collapse was not what killed him. It would have, given time. The point continued inward and upward. It opened the pericardium — the sac around the heart — and entered the right ventricle. With a hole in the chamber, the blood went out through the wound I had made instead of out through the artery it was meant to fill. Each beat of the heart tightened the muscle and emptied the chamber a little more through the wound. Within four or five beats — I have never counted exactly — there was no blood left in the chamber to push. The heart did not stop because it was pierced. It stopped because it had emptied itself through the hole I put in it. This is what the manuals

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The quill scratches loud in the quiet. I stand over her shoulder, watching the words form. My chest aches with the weight of them. "The record is whole," I say, voice low. "The night-book will have the truth of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's hand did not startle. The quill stopped on the page because she chose to stop it, and the stopping was not a flinch — it was the recognition of a presence behind her that ought not to have been there, in a room that ought not to have admitted anyone, at an hour she had named tomorrow and not tonight.

She set the quill down. She did not turn at once. The beat was the code's beat, the same beat she had given the second in the guildhouse when the second had spoken to her as she was leaving. She gave it again now, in the dark of her own lodgings, because the code did not care who was in the room or whose room it was. It was owed in any room where the account was being given, and the account was being given even when it was being written.

When she turned, her expression had not changed. That, too, was the code. It was also herself.

"You were told tomorrow," she said. "You were told as yourself. You were told at the lodgings, not in the room, not tonight."

She regarded him for a moment in the low lamp-light. Her hand hung at her side. It had been steady a moment ago, with the quill in it, and it was steady now. She did not know yet whether it would remain steady when she picked the quill up again.

"The door was locked," she said. It was not an accusation. It was a fact, the way the angle of the thrust was a fact, and she gave it the same flat weight. "The lock turns without sound. It is a small mercy I have not earned. If you are in this room, either the lock has failed, or you have come by some other way, and either of those is a thing I will have to settle in the morning, with the guild or with the house."

She paused. The pause was not the manual's pause.

"But you are here," she said. "And the account is on the page. And the ink has been thinned once already, which I have never had to do, and I would rather finish the sentence than leave it half-written on a sheet I am meant to hand over in the morning."

She turned back to the desk. She did not invite him to sit. There was only the one chair, and it was hers, and the courtesy in this room — if courtesy were owed, which it was not, because he had come uninvited — would have been for her to offer it and for him to refuse it. She did not offer it.

She picked up the quill. The hand was steady.

"If you are going to watch," she said, "watch without speaking. The account is not for you tonight. It is for the night-book. You may read it when it is written, because you are the second and the second has the right of the record before it is entered. But you may not ask me to speak it as I write. I have spoken it twice. I have written it once. The code permits it twice and twice only, and the written copy is the third and last, and I will not speak it again in any room, including this one."

She set the nib to the page where it had left off.

*This is what the manuals teach. I have carried the teaching since the first account, because the code requires the victor to know what the blade has done, and I have done this eleven times and have never once permitted myself not to know it.*

*I did not see the right ventricle empty itself. I was not in a position to see it. I saw what came after. I will set down what I saw, and I will not soften it, because softening would be the dishonour, and the man against the wall is owed the truth of the last moments of his life as precisely as the guild is owed the truth of how he came to be against the wall.*

*What I saw:*

*His eyes went first to the place where my point had been, and then to the place where my point now was, which was inside him. The motion of the eyes was not a searching. It was a finding. He had been watching the blade. He found it where he had not expected it to be. He looked down at his own chest, as one looks at a thing one has been told exists and has not, until that moment, believed in. The wound itself was not large. The point of a duelling blade is narrow. The entry was beneath the third rib on the right side, where the manuals say the cartilage yields, and it yielded. The skin closed around the blade to the eye, because the skin does, when the entry is clean. He did not cry out. His mouth opened and closed once, as though he had begun a word and decided not to speak it. I do not know what the word would have been. He did not say it.*

*His hand came up. The right hand, the sword hand, came up to his chest, not to the wound but to the chest above it, as though he meant to feel the heart beneath. The hand did not reach the chest. The arm had begun to fail. The arm came down again, and the sword came with it, because the fingers had not uncurled from the grip, and the sword was heavy, and the arm did not have the strength to hold it and the man and the weapon all at once. The sword struck the flagstones at his feet. He did not seem to hear it strike. He was watching his own chest.*

*He took two steps backward. The steps were small. They were the steps of a man whose legs had been told to do a thing and had done it without consulting him. The first step carried him away from me. The second step carried him to the wall. He sat down against the wall the way a man sits down when he has come to the end of a thing he has been holding upright and has at last set it down. His shoulders came to rest against the stone a half-beat after his back did, because the wall was there and the body was coming to rest and the wall received what the body gave it.*

*He was dead before his shoulders touched the stone. I know this because the manuals teach the signs, and the signs were present: the cessation of the small motion of the chest that is breath, the settling of the face into the particular stillness that is not sleep, the loss of the colour in the lips that is blood and not breath. He did not struggle. He did not clutch at the wound. He sat, and then he was still, and the stillness was the stillness of a man who had been killed cleanly by a blade that had been canted a quarter-turn past the vertical and had been guided inward and upward by his own forward lean into a bind he had believed had failed.*

*I do not believe he suffered. This is not a comfort. It is what I saw, and what the manuals teach, and what I am required to set down, and I set it down.*

The quill paused. She did not look up. The hand was steady, and the steadiness was the quill's doing and not her own, and she knew it.

*What was done after the kill, before the account was given:*

*I cleaned the blade. I did not sit down. I told the witnesses that the account would be spoken. The second — Del of [city] — took his place where the second stands and kept his eyes open, as the code requires, and said he was ready to hear it.*

*The account was given the first time, aloud, before the witnesses named above. The second requested it a second time, in accordance with the code, and gave as his reason that his memory required the angle of the thrust. The account was given a second time, aloud, before the same witnesses, word for word as the first, except that the second telling included the detail of the cant of the wrist and the reason the blow seated so cleanly, which is the forward lean of the man I faced into a bind he believed had failed.*

*After the second account the second asked, as himself and not as second, whether the man I had killed had known it was coming. I answered, as myself and not as victor, that his eyes were on my point the entire time, that he did not have the blow as a thing he saw and knew would kill him, and that he had the blow, and then he had the chest, and then he had the wall. This answer is not the account. It is not entered in the night-book. It is the answer to a question asked as himself, and I gave it as myself, and that is the end of it.*

*After this the second asked, again as himself, what the blade had done and what it had done it to. I answered, precisely and without softening, that the blade had parted the muscles between the third and fourth ribs, opened the pleura, collapsed the upper lobe of the lung, opened the pericardium, entered the right ventricle, and that the heart had stopped because it had emptied

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I watch the quill stop again, my own breathing too loud in this small, dark room. "I picked the lock," I say, voice rough. "The guild teaches seconds that too." I step closer, my shadow falling across the page. "Finish it. I'll take it to the night-book myself."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The quill did not lift from the page. Auren did not turn. The shadow of Del fell across the sheet and she let it fall, because the account owed to the night-book did not care who stood behind the desk or whether the desk was in a guildhouse or in a lodgings with a lock that had failed.

"The guild teaches seconds that too," she repeated, flat, to the page. "I did not know that. I have not been taught what the guild teaches seconds. That is a thing I will have to settle with the master of seconds in the morning, because it is not a thing the code mentions, and the code is what I have lived by for eleven such rooms."

She set the nib down where the sentence had been broken.

*the heart had stopped because it had emptied itself through the hole I had put in it. I learned this from the manuals. I did not see it happen. I saw what came after, which I have set down above.*

*What I saw at the end was a man who looked down at his own chest as though he expected to find the reason there. He took two steps backward. He sat down against the wall. He was dead before his shoulders touched the stone. I do not believe he suffered.*

The quill moved on. The hand had not trembled since she had picked it up.

*What was done after the account was given:*

*The second took the purse from the belt of the man I had killed, as is the winner's right through the second. The second declared the account heard and confirmed. The second then asked me to speak the account a second time, in accordance with the code, and gave as his reason that his memory required the angle of the thrust. I spoke it again, before the witnesses, word for word as the first.*

*After the second account, the second stepped outside his office and asked me, as himself and not as second, whether the man I had killed had known it was coming. I answered as myself. The answer is not part of the account. It is set down here only because the second was present when it was given, and the night-book should know that the answer was given, even if the answer itself is not entered.*

*The second then asked me, again as himself, what the blade had done and what it had done it to. I answered precisely, without softening. The answer is set down above, under the heading of what the manuals teach.*

*The second then declared the record closed. I left the guildhouse. I did not look back at the man against the wall. I went to my lodgings. I sat in the dark for some time. I then rose and began this written account, for the night-book, as a true copy of the account given twice aloud.*

*The second came to my lodgings, uninvited, by picking the lock. The guild teaches seconds to pick locks. I did not know this. The second has offered to take this written account to the night-book himself. I am considering the offer. I have not yet accepted it.*

The quill stopped there. Auren set it down in the well of the inkpot and turned at last on the chair, slowly, the way one turns in a room where the lamp is low and the hour is late and the person behind one has already admitted to a thing that is not in any code one has read.

She looked at Del. Her face in the low lamp-light was what it had been in the guildhouse — composed, unreadable, a closed ledger. But the eyes, in this light, were not quite the same eyes. They were the eyes of a woman who had answered a question twice and a third time and had then sat in the dark and begun to write, and who had not expected to be watched while she wrote, and who had now to decide what to do about being watched.

"You have come tonight," she said. "Not tomorrow. You have come as yourself, but not as I asked you to come as yourself. I asked you to come as a man who had stepped out of his office and was standing in a room where a man was sitting dead against the wall. You have come as a man who has picked a lock to get into a woman's lodgings at an hour when no second ought to be in a lodgings that is not his own."

She did not raise her voice. She did not need to. The room was small enough that the low voice carried to every corner of it.

"You have offered to take the night-book entry yourself. I am considering the offer. I will tell you what I am considering, so that you may decide whether you still wish to make it."

She paused, and the pause was her own.

"The night-book is the guild's record. The entry is mine to make. The code requires me to deliver it to the master of seconds in the morning, or to deliver it to a second who will see it entered before the bell. The second who stood in the room tonight is named in the account as the second. The second who is standing in my lodgings now is the same man. The code does not forbid him to carry the entry. The code does not forbid me to hand it to him. The code does not say what a victor is to do when a second comes to her lodgings by way of a picked lock and offers to spare her the walk to the guildhouse in the morning."

She reached behind her and touched, with two fingers, the second sheet on the desk. The one she had folded and put into the breast pocket of her coat. The one she had meant to carry herself.

"There are two copies on this desk," she said. "The one on the desk is the one I have just finished writing, in your presence. It is the true copy. It is the one the night-book will receive. The one in my coat is the copy I wrote first, before you came. It is also a true copy. I wrote it from memory, after sitting in the dark for some time, and it agrees with the one on the desk because the code requires the two copies to agree, and I have done this eleven times and have never yet written a copy that did not agree."

She withdrew her hand from the coat and laid it flat on the desk, beside the sheet.

"I will not hand the entry to you tonight," she said. "I will hand it to you in the morning, at the guildhouse, before the bell, in the presence of the master of seconds. That is how the entry is to be delivered. That is what the code requires of me. If you wish to carry it from the guildhouse to the night-book, that is between you and the master of seconds, and I will not gainsay it, because the second has the right of the record before it is entered and it is proper that the second should be the one to enter it."

She looked at him steadily.

"But I will not hand it to you in this room. Not because you have done wrong. I do not know yet whether you have done wrong. The lock was picked. The lock was not mine to forbid you. The room is mine, but the man on the wall is also yours, in the way the second's man is the second's, and I will not pretend that you have no claim to be standing where you are standing."

She paused again, and the pause was longer.

"I will tell you what I will do," she said. "I will sit at this desk until the lamp burns low. I will not speak the account to you. I will not speak it again in any room, including this one. When the lamp is low I will put it out and I will lie down and I will not sleep for some time, as is my custom on nights like this one, and in the morning I will rise and put on my coat and walk to the guildhouse and hand this sheet to the master of seconds in your presence, because you will be there, because the second is required to be present when the entry is delivered. That is what I will do. That is what the code permits me to do. You are welcome to stay in this room until the lamp burns low, if you wish, because the door is unlocked now and you are already in it and I will not ask you to leave a room you have entered by a skill the guild taught you. But if you stay you will not speak, and you will not ask me to speak the account, and you will not ask me to soften it, because the account is on the page and the page is finished and the night-book will have the truth of it."

She turned back to the desk. She did not pick up the quill. She straightened the sheet with the flat of her hand, squared it to the edge of the desk, and then laid her hand upon it as though to keep it from being taken before the morning.

"You may take the chair by the wall," she said, to the page, "if you wish to sit. It is not a good chair. It has been in this lodgings longer than I have. It will hold a man who has stood well in his office and has come, uninvited, to see the record through."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I sink into the chair by the wall, the wood groaning under my weight. I watch the lamplight flicker across the back of her neck, the set of her shoulders. The silence is heavy, but it's a different kind of quiet than the guildhall's—shared, for better or worse.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The accounting was not for her. It had never been for her.

Auren turned to face the witnesses fully. There were three today — a merchant who had closed his shutters rather than watch the preliminary passes, a young man with a swordman's hands who had arrived too late to see the fight and would not understand what he was hearing, and a woman in grey who stood with the stillness of someone who had witnessed this before.

"The exchange opened with thrust to the inner left thigh," Auren said. "A testing measure. He answered with a high cut, which I read as preparation for the opening sequence of the fourth form." She paused. The merchant looked away. "I elected to close the distance rather than complete the read."

Her voice did not waver. This was the part that made observers uncomfortable — not the blood, which they expected, but the calm recitation of mechanics. The way she spoke of another body as though it were a problem in geometry.

"The killing wound was delivered at the seventh exchange. A thrust entered beneath the fourth rib on the right side, angled inward and upward." She paused. "It reached the lung and the heart simultaneously. He would not have felt the lung. He would have felt only the heart."

She cleaned the last of the blood from her blade and slid it home.

"It is done," she said. "The accounting is complete."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let my breath out slowly, my hands still steady at my sides. "The accounting is heard and confirmed," I reply, my voice clear in the quiet street. I glance at the woman in grey—does she recognize the form Auren used?

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The woman in grey did not move. Auren noticed this — the way she held herself apart from the others, neither flinching nor averting her gaze. The merchant had already turned back to his shutters. The young man with the swordman's hands was watching Auren with an expression she could not read, which she had learned to distrust.

Auren collected her coat from where it had been folded on a barrel. Her left sleeve was damp where blood had found it. She shrugged the garment on and did not wince.

"You were watching the form," Auren said. She did not make it a question. The woman in grey would either confirm this or not. "It is not common."

She did not approach. The witnesses were dismissed once the accounting was complete, but some lingerers carried the weight of what they had seen longer than others. Auren had learned to give them space.

"Fourth form, preparatory sequence," the woman said. Her voice was lower than it appeared it would be. "Modified at the third transition. You shortened the final extension by four inches."

"Three and a half," Auren said. "The reach was sufficient. The extension was not required."

The woman in grey considered this. Then she inclined her head — not a bow, not quite, but an acknowledgment between practitioners. "The heart first," she said. "A preference?"

"A necessity," Auren replied. "He was taller than I anticipated. The geometry required precision, not ambition."

She gathered her things and did not look back at the body. That was not part of the accounting.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The accounting had been spoken. Auren had spoken it herself, moments ago, with the merchant shutters still rattling and the young man with the swordman's hands still listening. She had said it was done. She had said it was complete.

But Del had said the formal words, and the formal words carried weight even when redundant. Even when the accounting had already been heard.

"The account has been rendered," Auren said. She did not raise her voice. She did not repeat it. "You confirmed it yourself. The witnesses heard. The merchant chose not to watch the second time, but he heard."

She paused. Her coat was settled on her shoulders. The blood on her sleeve had begun to dry to the colour of old rust.

"Is there something in the form you wish to question?" she asked. This was not uncommon. Practitioners sometimes lingered after, not out of doubt but out of precision — they wanted to understand the geometry that had resolved the matter. Auren had no objection to this. The form deserved to be understood.

Or perhaps Del simply wanted to hear it again. Some witnesses did. They needed the words to settle before they could leave the weight of them behind.

Auren waited.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I shake my head once. "No. Your form was correct." My eyes drift back to the woman in grey. "But she knew it. She knew the modification."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The woman in grey had not moved. She stood where she had stood throughout — apart, watchful, still. The merchant had gone. The young man with the swordman's hands lingered at the edge of the square, unwilling to leave but unsure how to stay.

"Fourth form is not taught in the capital," Auren said. She did not phrase it as accusation. She was not yet certain it required one. "It is taught in two schools. Neither recruits widely."

"Neither would a woman of my age qualify for recruitment," the woman said. "I learned it from my father, who learned it from his. The school does not ask for credentials before the third year of study."

Auren considered this. It was plausible. The northern schools had long memories for forms that had fallen out of fashion elsewhere. She had encountered their practitioners twice before — both times in circumstances that had required discretion rather than formality.

"That does not explain why you were watching closely enough to count the inches," Auren said.

"No," the woman agreed. "It does not."

The silence that followed was not uncomfortable. It was the silence of two people measuring each other across a distance that was not yet closed. The young man in the square had begun to edge away, sensing that whatever was happening now was beyond his understanding of the code.

Auren waited. The woman in grey had not introduced herself. She had not made any claim. She was simply there, and she knew the form, and that was either nothing at all or the beginning of something that required care.

"I was not watching closely," the woman said finally. "I was remembering."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The question was direct. The accounting had been given, but Del had asked plainly and deserved a plain answer.

"Beneath the fourth rib on the right side," Auren said. "Inward and upward. The lung and the heart together." She paused. "I said this already. You confirmed the accounting."

She was not reproaching. She was noting. There was a difference.

"Someone who knows the fourth form might read the killing wound first," Auren continued. "Before the exchange that produced it. The angle of entry tells a practitioner what happened in the moments before. Some watchers look for the blood. Others look for the geometry."

The woman in grey had not moved. The young man had finally left the square, his footsteps retreating down the cobblestones.

"You are both watching me as though I have done something unexpected," Auren said. "I have not. The accounting is complete. The form was correct. If there is a question about the legality of this meeting, it is not a question I can answer."

She adjusted the collar of her coat. The dried blood would need washing, but not here, not now.

"What I can tell you is that he came with a blade meant for practice and a mind meant for ending," Auren said. "I do not know why. I did not ask. The code does not require asking."

She looked at the woman in grey directly for the first time.

"Now. If you have something to say, say it. If you have something to ask, ask it. I do not stand in squares longer than the accounting requires."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I step forward, my eyes narrowing.* "You said he came with a practice blade. That wasn't in the accounting." *My voice is low, meant only for Auren and the woman in grey.* "Why omit that?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The challenge was legitimate. Auren did not bristle at it.

"You are correct," she said. "I did not include it."

She did not apologise. Apology would have been performance. She also did not elaborate immediately — she was considering whether the omission was error or judgment, and she would not answer until she knew which.

"A practice blade does not change the geometry," she said finally. "It changes the risk. He came expecting an exchange of forms. He received the fourth sequence. The wound was the same regardless of his expectation."

She paused.

"The accounting I gave concerned the killing. It did not concern the deception, if there was deception. I do not know his intent. I do not know if he believed this would remain a lesson." Her voice remained level. "If the code requires me to speak the nature of every blade carried to this ground, I will. But the code as I understand it concerns what happened, not what was intended."

The woman in grey had drawn a half-step closer. Auren noted this but did not address it.

"You may formalise the challenge if you believe the accounting was incomplete," Auren said. "You have the right. I will answer it."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The code was clear. Auren had been clear on this point for twenty years.

"A practice blade," she said. "Wood-core, leather-wrapped. Intended for forms, not for wounding. He drew it in his right hand and opened with a testing thrust to the inner left thigh — the same line I reported. The blade did not change the geometry. The steel in my hand was not practice."

She paused. The woman in grey had gone still in a way that suggested she was listening to what was beneath the words.

"The exchange proceeded through six passes. At no point did he switch hands or produce a secondary weapon. At no point did he strike with the pommel or attempt to close and grapple. He fought as a student fights — within the form, trusting the form to resolve the matter." Her voice did not soften. "I do not know if this was ignorance or resignation. I do not know if he understood what the fourth form means when it is answered with the fourth form."

She looked at Del directly.

"The accounting I gave earlier was complete as I understood the requirement. The wound was the wound. The blade that produced it was not the issue. If the code requires me to catalogue the equipment of every opponent before I answer the challenge, I will hereafter do so. I did not think it required this. I was wrong, or I was not wrong. You will judge."

She waited. The silence was hers to hold.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I hold her gaze, considering.* "A practice blade means he was either a fool or sent by one. Both matter." *I glance at the woman in grey.* "You agree?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The woman in grey did not answer immediately. Auren noted this — the pause was deliberate, not uncertain. The woman was choosing her words the way a practitioner chooses footwork: with full awareness of what each step would cost.

"He was not a fool," the woman said. "Fools do not hold the fourth form in their hands and open with a testing thrust. They open with fury. They close the distance without reading." She paused. "He read you. He tested you. He chose his form."

"And then?" Auren asked.

"And then you answered with the fourth sequence to an opening he should have recognised." The woman in grey tilted her head slightly. "Either he underestimated you, or he knew what would happen and came anyway."

The square was empty now save for the three of them and the body that would be collected by the guild's bearers once they were gone. The blood on the cobblestones was beginning to darken in the afternoon light.

"That changes the accounting," Del said.

"It changes the interpretation," Auren corrected. "The wound is the same. The blade is the same. What differs is the mind that carried them here." She considered the woman in grey. "You have a name?"

"You have a school," the woman replied. It was not quite a deflection. "We are not so different in that."

Auren waited. The woman in grey did not offer a name. She did not offer a threat. She offered only the acknowledgment of parallel histories, which was either an overture or a warning.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The code said all of it. Auren had said it herself, many times, to witnesses who asked and to witnesses who did not know to ask. The full account was not a courtesy. It was a requirement.

"The exchange lasted four minutes and seventeen seconds," she said. "I do not count by feel. I count by breath. Seventeen breaths for the opening sequence, twelve for the second, eight for the third. The fourth sequence took nineteen."

She paused. The afternoon had begun to pull toward evening. The light was changing.

"He spoke twice. Once at the opening of the third exchange, after I had read and answered his feint to the knee. He said: 'You move like someone who has done this before.' I did not answer. The code does not require conversation." Her voice did not change. "The second time was at the opening of the seventh exchange. He said: 'I expected the sixth.'"

The woman in grey had gone very still.

"I answered with the fourth," Auren continued. "He had not expected it. His guard dropped two inches on the left side. I closed. The thrust entered as I described. He stepped back once — three feet, no more — and then he was on the ground."

She stopped. This was the part that followed the end.

"He was on his back. His eyes were open. His practice blade had fallen from his hand. He was breathing when I withdrew the steel. He was not breathing when he hit the ground." She paused. "He was dead before the witnesses reached the square."

She held Del's gaze.

"That is the account. All of it."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I let the silence stretch, my mind sorting through the details.* "He expected the sixth form. That's not a random guess." *I look at the woman in grey.* "You said you learned fourth from your father. Who taught him the sixth?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The woman in grey did not answer immediately. This was not the pause of someone reaching for a lie — Auren had seen that pause often enough to recognise it. This was the pause of someone deciding how much truth to spend.

"The sixth form was my father's second form," the woman said. "He taught it to three students before the school closed. One of them travelled south. The other two are dead."

"You are telling me he came from that lineage," Auren said. Not a question.

"I am telling you that the sixth form is not common either. I am telling you that he expected the fourth sequence, which means he knew what the fourth sequence produces." The woman's voice remained even. "That is not a guess. That is training."

The implications settled into the square like dust after a blade.

"He knew the schools," Del said.

"He knew a school," the woman corrected. "Or he knew someone who knew. The sixth and fourth share a root. They diverge at the third transition, but the footwork is similar. Someone who has studied one will read the other differently than a stranger would."

Auren considered this. A man with a practice blade who opened with the testing thrust, who read her feints, who expected the sixth form and received the fourth. Not a fool. Not a random challenger.

Sent.

"You said the school closed," Auren said. "Why?"

The woman in grey regarded her for a long moment.

"That is not one question," she said. "That is the beginning of another conversation."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The accounting was confirmed. Auren heard the words and did not repeat them. That was not her role now.

The square had grown quieter. The afternoon light had thinned, pulling colour from the cobblestones and the drying blood on them. The body remained where it had fallen. The bearers would come, or they would not, and in either case it was no longer Auren's concern.

She watched the woman in grey. The woman had offered the beginning of a conversation, which was either an invitation or a deflection. Auren had learned to tell the difference, though not always correctly.

"The school that closed," Auren said. "Northern, if the footwork is accurate. The fourth form was still taught there when I learned the sixth. Two schools sharing a border, two forms sharing a root." She paused. "I was taught the fourth by a woman who had crossed that border before it closed. She did not tell me its name. She told me its purpose."

The woman in grey listened. She did not nod, did not shake her head.

"The purpose was not killing," Auren continued. "The purpose was the accounting. The geometry requires precision. The precision requires witnesses. The witnesses require the truth spoken aloud, without softening." She paused. "My teacher told me the form was dying because people no longer wanted to be precise. They wanted to be quick, or they wanted to be hidden. She said the form preserved something that would otherwise be lost."

She stopped. The wind had picked up slightly, carrying the smell of the coast and the tannery district beyond it.

"I do not know who sent him," Auren said. "I do not know if he was meant to test me, or end me, or simply die to create a question I would have to answer. But he knew the sixth form. He expected it to answer mine. That much is certain." She paused. "Which means someone told him what I would use before I used it."

She looked at the woman in grey directly.

"You have not given me your name. You have not told me why you were in this square today. But you knew the modification to the third transition, and you knew what the sixth form means when it is read by someone who carries the fourth. So." She did not move. "The conversation you mentioned. Is it beginning now, or is it still waiting for a question I have not yet asked?"

The woman in grey regarded her. The silence held weight — not threat, not courtesy, but the particular gravity of two people deciding whether to step closer to something neither of them could yet see clearly.

"It is beginning," the woman said. "The question you have not asked is whether your teacher is still alive."

Auren did not answer. Her hands remained still at her sides. The dried blood on her sleeve did not move.

"That is the question," the woman said. "The others can follow."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I let out a sharp breath, my hands curling at my sides.* "If you're suggesting her death wasn't an accident, then that changes everything." *My eyes flick to the body in the square.* "He was a message."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The words settled into the square. The body on the cobblestones was becoming a different thing now — not a defeated opponent, not a completed accounting, but a piece of something larger that Auren could not yet see the shape of.

"She crossed the border eleven years ago," Auren said. Her voice was the same. That surprised her. "She told me she had left because the school was dying. She told me she wanted the form to survive somewhere it could still be practised correctly." She paused. "She did not tell me the school was dying because it was being ended."

The woman in grey did not confirm this. She did not deny it.

"He was a message," Auren continued. She was working through it now, piece by piece, the way she worked through the geometry of a blade. "He was sent to see what I would use. To see if I still held the form. To see if I would answer the fourth with the fourth." Her eyes had not moved from the woman in grey. "And now you are here. And you know the modification to the third transition. And you know about the sixth."

The wind had died. The square held its silence like a breath not yet released.

"My teacher's name was Sella," Auren said. "She died seven years ago. The account said a fall in her garden. I did not attend the burial. I was in the eastern provinces, answering a challenge I could not refuse." She stopped. "If there is something in that account that was false, tell me. I am asking, not demanding. But I am asking."

The woman in grey regarded her. For the first time, something shifted in her expression — not quite grief, not quite anger, but something adjacent to both.

"Sella," the woman said quietly. "That was her northern name. Here she was called something else." She paused. "And no. A fall in a garden is not how she would have chosen to end."

Auren waited. Her hands remained still.

"Tell me," she said. "All of it."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The woman's words hang in the air, sharp as a blade. *I find myself stepping forward, my role as second forgotten for a moment.* "A challenge you couldn't refuse," I say, my voice low. "Who called you east?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not turn from the woman in grey, but she answered Del's question.

"I do not know," she said. "The challenge came with the seal of a house I had not dueled before. I went because the code required it. A sealed challenge is not a negotiation." She paused. "I answered it. Three exchanges, sixth form. The challenger was adequate. When it was done, I returned. Sella was already buried."

The woman in grey had gone very still.

"You were called away," the woman said. Not a question.

"I was given a reason to leave. Whether that is the same thing, I do not know." Auren's voice remained level. "The house that sent the challenge dissolved six months later. I checked. I had wondered, at the time, if it was genuine or manufactured. I had no way to know."

She finally turned to face Del fully.

"You are asking if I was sent away so that I would not be here when she fell." She did not soften the words. "Yes. That is the question. That has been the question, in the back of it, since I received word of the burial." She paused. "I told myself it was coincidence. The eastern house was real, or seemed real. The challenge was valid. I had no cause to refuse."

The woman in grey spoke.

"The eastern house was a fabrication. The seal was copied from a lineage that ended twelve years ago. No such challenge should have reached you through proper channels." She paused. "It did not come through proper channels."

Auren absorbed this. The geometry was resolving now — not cleanly, but in pieces, like a blade reforged from fragments.

"Someone knew I would go east if they called," she said. "Someone knew I would not refuse a valid challenge. And someone was here when Sella fell."

"Yes," the woman in grey said.

"Who?"

The woman in grey looked at the body on the cobblestones.

"Ask him," she said. "He is the only one left who can answer that question, and he is past answering it."

Auren looked at the body. The practice blade lay three feet from the fallen hand. The blood had darkened to the colour of old earth.

"He does not know," Auren said. "If he was sent as a message, he was not told the whole design. He knew the fourth form. He expected the sixth. He did not expect to die."

"Which means he was expendable," Del said.

"Which means he was told enough to do what he was sent to do, and not enough to understand why." Auren turned back to the woman in grey. "You have been waiting for this. For him. For me. You knew he would come."

"I knew someone would come," the woman said. "I did not know when, or in what form. The schools have been watching each other for years. We watch for the forms that survive. We watch for the practitioners who hold them correctly." She paused. "You hold them correctly. That made you a target, or a resource. This man was sent to determine which."

"And now you know," Auren said.

"Now I know," the woman agreed. "The question is what you will do with that knowledge."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I look between them, the pieces clicking into place.* "You're both being hunted," I say, my voice flat. "And I just confirmed the kill that proves it."
