Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head once, not in gratitude, but in acknowledgment of the office being fulfilled.

She turned so that her voice would carry to the witnesses, blade lowered but still naked in her hand. There was no flourish in it. No triumph. Only the same severity with which she had entered the ring.

“By the terms witnessed and accepted,” she said, “I give account of the wound.”

Her eyes did not leave the body when she spoke. That, too, was part of it.

“The deciding cut was delivered on the third measure after the bind. My opponent overreached on the recovery, left the inside line open beneath the guard, and I entered under the wrist. The point passed between the fourth and fifth ribs on the left side, angled upward.”

She paused only long enough to make the words exact.

“It pierced the lung and opened the heart at its lower chamber. Death followed from that wound. No lesser strike decided it. No fall, stumble, or prior injury brought the end.”

Auren drew the cleaned blade inward until it rested flat before her, edge turned away from the witnesses.

“I name that as the killing wound,” she said. “I claim the victory, and the burden of it.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my voice steady despite the tightness in my chest. "The account is heard and confirmed as true." I glance toward the witnesses, then back to Auren. "The burden is recorded."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren held still for the confirmation, as if it were another weight being set properly into place.

Only when the words had settled among the witnesses did she lower the point of her sword.

“Then the matter was concluded,” she said.

There was no relief in her face. Relief would have been indecent while the body still lay within the ring and the last breath had not long gone out of the room. She turned the blade once more, inspected it by habit, and found nothing left upon it. Still, she wiped it again with the cloth.

The motion was careful. Almost ceremonial.

“The seconds may see to the remains,” Auren said, her voice still carrying enough for the assembly. “No hand of mine will hinder them. No claim remains unpaid.”

She sheathed the sword only after that had been said.

The sound of steel entering the scabbard seemed louder than it ought to have been.

Auren stood with both hands resting lightly before her, the cloth folded and stained in one fist. Her eyes remained lowered for a moment longer toward the dead, not in apology. Apology belonged before the choosing of blades, not after the wound had been made. But there was recognition there, stern and unadorned.

“He came cleanly,” she said. “He stood to the terms. Let that be entered also, if any record was kept.”

Then she stepped back from the ring by one measured pace, yielding the ground.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren’s gaze lifted, sharp enough to mark the irregularity, but not to challenge it before witnesses.

If the words were required again, then they would be given again. The code did not bend for weariness, nor for grief, nor for the distaste of repetition.

She inclined her head a second time.

“The account was this,” Auren said, and her voice returned to the same carrying severity. “On the third measure after the bind, my opponent extended past his recovery and exposed the inside line. I entered beneath his wrist and delivered the point between the fourth and fifth ribs on the left side.”

She did not look away from the place where the wound had been made.

“The blade traveled upward. It pierced the lung and opened the lower chamber of the heart. That wound caused death. No lesser cut, no stumble, no fault of the ground, and no prior hurt decided the matter.”

Her hand remained still at the mouth of the scabbard, fingers resting against the guard as though to keep the weapon from being anything more than what it was: an instrument already used.

“I named it then, and I name it now, before those present,” she said. “That was the killing wound. The victory was mine. The burden remains mine.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take a slow breath, my hands steady at my sides. "It is heard again, and confirmed. The burden is yours." I hesitate, then add quietly, for her ears only, "You can step back now. It's done."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not answer at once.

The private words reached her differently than the formal ones had. The formal words had a place to go: into the record, into the witnesses, into the code that held all of them upright when blood made men unsteady. These quieter words had no such place. They had to be received by the woman beneath the office.

For a moment, Auren’s jaw set.

Then she stepped back.

One pace. Then another.

Not hurriedly. Never as if retreating from what she had done. But far enough that the ring no longer held her, and the dead was given fully into other hands.

“It was done when the account was accepted,” she said, low enough that it did not seek the whole room. “But I thank you for saying it.”

The thanks sounded formal, because most things in Auren’s mouth did. Still, it was not empty.

She looked once toward the witnesses, ensuring no objection rose, no disputed murmur, no hand lifted to contest the naming. There was none. The silence had the hard shape of assent.

Only then did she take the stained cloth in both hands and fold it more precisely, edge to edge, as though precision could return order to anything it touched.

“He should be carried with his sword,” she said. “If his second consents. It was in his hand cleanly, and it did not fail him. His measure failed him. That is not the same thing.”

Auren’s eyes returned briefly to the body, and the severity in her face altered by the smallest degree. Not softness. She had little use for softness here. Softness blurred the truth, and the truth was the last property the dead retained.

But respect remained.

“He deserved that distinction.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looked at Del then, and whatever flicker of fatigue had crossed her face was put away.

Plainly, then. If plainness was required, she would give it.

“It landed here,” she said.

She raised her own hand, not to the body, but to the corresponding place on herself: the left side of the chest, below the breast, just inward of the line of the ribs.

“Left side. Between the fourth and fifth ribs. The entry was narrow and clean, beneath the guard arm. The point went inward and upward.”

Her fingers held the place a moment longer, exact as a marker on a map.

“Not the shoulder. Not the belly. Not the throat. The heart was reached through the ribs from the left side. That is where the killing wound landed.”

Auren lowered her hand.

“If the witnesses required it in plainer terms,” she said, voice level, “then let it be recorded as a thrust to the left chest, entering between the ribs, piercing lung and heart. Death followed from that thrust.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My gaze follows her hand, then drops to the body again. I nod, once. "Plain enough." I raise my voice just enough to carry. "The fatal wound was a thrust to the left chest, between the ribs. It is confirmed."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren received the confirmation without movement, save for the smallest lowering of her eyes.

“That record will stand,” she said.

Her voice carried, but it had lost none of its restraint. The thing had been named plainly now, stripped of measure and line and the language duellists used to keep violence accountable. A thrust to the left chest. Between the ribs. Lung and heart. Death.

There was no cleaner truth beneath it.

She turned slightly toward the witnesses.

“If any present disputed the account, the place of the wound, or the manner of death, they were bound to speak then.”

Auren waited.

The silence held.

She gave it the full span it was owed. Not a breath less. A contested death, even falsely contested, had to be allowed its opening. A room could lie by haste as readily as by speech.

No voice rose.

“Then it was witnessed,” Auren said. “It was confirmed. It was not disputed.”

Only after that did she unfasten the duelling glove from her right hand. The leather came away stiffly at the fingers. She folded it over the stained cloth, hiding neither stain nor glove, merely keeping them together as things belonging to the same act.

Her gaze moved to the fallen man’s sword.

“Let his blade be cleaned by his own side,” she said. “Not by mine. It should not leave this place bloodied, but neither should my hand presume that office.”

Auren stepped one pace farther from the ring, leaving a clear path for those who had the right to enter it now. Her posture remained upright, but the formality of the duel had begun to fall away from her by degrees, like armor being unbuckled without yet being removed.

When she spoke again, her voice lowered enough that it no longer addressed the room.

“I have given the wound as it was,” she said. “If there is any further wording the record requires, I will answer it.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren’s mouth tightened, not in offense, but in recognition that Del was correct.

“Tact had no standing here,” she said.

She faced the witnesses again, and whatever private weariness had begun to gather in her was set aside as if it had been ordered from the room.

“The blade entered the left chest between the fourth and fifth ribs,” Auren said. “It passed through the intercostal flesh, parted the lining of the chest, and pierced the left lung. Its course continued upward and inward.”

Her voice remained even. Not cold. Coldness would have been another kind of concealment.

“The point then opened the sac around the heart and cut into the lower chamber of the heart itself. Blood entered the chest. The lung failed. The heart could no longer hold its work.”

She let the words stand plainly, without adornment.

“That was what the blade did. It cut through rib-space, lung, and heart. It did those things to the body of my opponent by my hand, in the agreed measure of the duel.”

Auren lowered her chin once.

“That is the precise account.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath. "That is precise." My voice is low but clear. "The witnesses have heard it." I glance toward the other second, still standing across the ring. "Your office is discharged. You should go."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren held Del’s words for a moment, as she had held the silence after the account.

Then she bowed.

Not deeply. Not theatrically. A duellist’s acknowledgment to the second who had kept the code intact when easier mercies would have corrupted it.

“My office in the ring was discharged,” she said. “My obligation to the record was discharged.”

Her eyes moved once to the body, then away with deliberate restraint.

“The rest will remain with me.”

She did not ask pardon of the room. She did not offer explanation. Neither belonged there. She had given the wound, named the death, accepted the burden, and yielded the ground. Anything more would have made a spectacle of what was already grave enough.

Auren turned toward the witnesses.

“You heard the account,” she said. “You heard it confirmed. You heard it undisputed. Let no other telling replace it.”

Only then did she step away from the ring in full.

Her boots crossed the boundary line without haste. At the edge of the chamber, she paused long enough to remove the stained cloth from her glove and fold it once more, precisely, though there was no practical purpose in doing so. Her hands needed the task. Her face admitted nothing.

The sword at her hip sat quiet in its scabbard.

Auren looked neither back to the wound nor to the man who had made her name it. She had already seen enough to speak truly, and truth did not require staring.

At the door, she inclined her head one final time toward those present.

“See him borne cleanly,” she said. “He stood as a duellist.”

Then Auren left the room.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stopped at the threshold.

For the first time, something like anger crossed her face. It was brief, controlled, and gone before it could become discourtesy. Not anger at the demand. Anger at the necessity of obeying it.

She turned back.

“If the code was being invoked in full,” she said, “then the full account would be given.”

She returned only far enough that her voice would carry again to the witnesses. She did not re-enter the ring. That ground no longer belonged to her.

“The thrust landed as I have named it. I withdrew the blade at once. There was no second killing stroke.”

Her hands remained still at her sides.

“He took one step backward. His sword remained in his hand. His guard lowered because the hand lost strength, not because he yielded. He drew breath once, sharply. The breath did not fill. Blood came into his mouth on the second attempt.”

Auren’s eyes fixed on no face in the room.

“He said one word. I could not make it out with certainty. It may have been a name. It may have been only the first sound of breath failing. I will not enter a word into the record that I did not clearly hear.”

She let that stand. Precision required refusal as much as speech.

“He remained standing for four breaths after the wound. On the fifth, his knees failed. He went down on his right side first, then onto his back when the weight of the sword arm turned him. He did not cry out. He did not ask mercy. He did not speak again.”

Auren’s jaw tightened once.

“The blood showed first at the wound and then at the mouth. Not in a great spray. It welled darkly and steadily. His breathing became wet and shallow. His eyes remained open. They did not track the room after he fell.”

Her voice stayed level, but each word seemed cut to measure.

“From the landing of the thrust to the last breath, he lived perhaps twelve breaths. Less than a minute. I counted because the code requires me to know what my hand has done.”

She looked toward the witnesses.

“At the end, the chest no longer rose. The mouth was bloodied. The left side of the coat was opened by the wound and wet beneath it. His sword was still in his hand until his fingers slackened. His face had no expression I will presume to name.”

Auren lowered her chin.

“That was how long he took. That was what he said, so far as truth allows. That was what it looked like at the end.”

Only then did she look back toward the ring.

“And I name again: the cause was the thrust to the left chest, between the ribs, piercing lung and heart. No later fall killed him. No other wound completed it. He died from the stroke I gave.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod slowly, the weight of her words settling in the room. "All of it is heard." My voice is quiet but firm. "The record will be complete." I motion toward the other second. "You may go. Your part is done."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren accepted the dismissal with a single measured inclination of her head.

This time, she did not answer the room at once. There was nothing left to clarify, and she would not add words merely because silence had become difficult. The complete account had been demanded. The complete account had been given. It stood now among them, ugly and exact, where it belonged.

“My part in the telling was done,” she said at last.

Her voice carried only enough to be heard, not enough to command.

She looked once to the witnesses, not seeking comfort from them, nor judgment. Only recognition that they had received what the code required: the wound, the manner, the time, the last condition of the dead, and the refusal to invent what had not been known.

“If any record is written,” Auren said, “write that uncertainty as uncertainty. He spoke one sound. I did not know it. No one is to make a last word for him because grief wants one.”

The severity of that was not cruelty. It was protection, the only kind she could offer him now.

She turned then toward the other second and gave another formal nod.

“His sword should remain with him until those entitled to take it do so. His hand held it honorably. Let no one say otherwise.”

Her own hand moved once to the hilt at her side, not drawing, only feeling the fixed weight of it there. The gesture lasted no more than a moment.

Then Auren stepped back again.

One pace. Another.

At the threshold, she stopped, as she had before, but this time she did not turn fully around. Her face was in profile, composed into the stern lines that had carried her through eleven such endings and would carry her through the memory of this one.

“He was not diminished by dying,” she said. “Let the record show that also, if the record has room for decency after truth.”

Only then did she leave.

Her boots sounded down the passage with the same measured cadence she had kept in the ring. She did not quicken them once she was beyond sight. Haste would have been a lie. So would lingering.

When she reached the antechamber, Auren stopped beside a narrow table set with a basin and a pitcher. The water was clean. Her hands were not bloody. She washed them anyway.

Slowly.

Thoroughly.

As though there were still some stain that precision had missed.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren had her hands in the basin when the confirmation reached the antechamber.

She stopped washing.

Water ran from her fingers in thin, clean lines, striking the surface below with small sounds that seemed indecently ordinary. She did not turn at once. She listened, because the record was not merely spoken by the victor. It had to be borne by another voice before it could stand outside her own mouth.

The account came through the open door and into the passage with the shape of law around it.

Auren kept her hands above the basin and heard each part set down.

The duel had been witnessed and accepted. The terms had been agreed before blades were crossed. The wound that decided it had come on the third measure after the bind. Her opponent had overreached in the recovery. His guard arm had left the inside line open. Auren had entered beneath the wrist, not above it, not around it, but under the failing line of defense. The point of her sword had gone into the left chest between the fourth and fifth ribs.

That was the place.

Not the shoulder. Not the belly. Not the throat. Not a cut across the flank that later worsened. A thrust to the left chest, narrow at entry, made in the agreed measure of the duel.

The blade had passed through flesh between the ribs. It had breached the lining of the chest. It had pierced the lung. Its path had gone upward and inward. It had opened the sac around the heart and cut into the lower chamber of the heart itself. Blood had entered the chest. The lung had failed to fill properly. The heart had been wounded beyond its work.

Auren’s wet fingers curled once over the edge of the basin.

The confirmation did not soften that. It did not make the wound cleaner than it had been. It did not make the dying briefer than it was. It did not give mercy the shape of omission.

It held.

The blade had been withdrawn at once. There had been no second killing stroke. There had been no stroke delivered after helplessness, no correction made upon a fallen man, no attempt to disguise one wound beneath another. He had taken one step backward. His sword had remained in his hand. His guard had lowered because strength had gone out of the hand, not because he had yielded.

He had drawn one sharp breath.

It had not filled.

On the second attempt, blood had come into his mouth.

He had made one sound. Auren had not known it. It had not been entered as a name. It had not been given the false dignity of certainty. It remained what it had been: a sound made at the edge of breath, possibly a word, possibly not. The record would not steal from him by inventing meaning where none had been heard.

He had stayed standing for four breaths after the wound.

On the fifth, his knees had failed.

He had fallen first to the right side, then onto his back as the weight of the sword arm turned him. He had not cried out. He had not asked mercy. He had not spoken again. His breathing had become wet and shallow. His eyes had remained open. After he fell, they had not tracked the room. Blood had shown at the wound and at the mouth. It had welled darkly and steadily, not in a spray. His coat had opened where the thrust had entered, and the cloth on the left side had grown wet beneath it.

From the landing of the thrust to the last breath, he had lived perhaps twelve breaths.

Less than a minute.

At the end, his chest had ceased to rise. His mouth had been bloodied. His fingers had slackened only after the last strength left them. His sword had been in his hand until then. His face had held an expression Auren would not presume to name.

The cause of death had been the thrust to the left chest between the ribs, piercing lung and heart.

No fall had killed him.

No earlier hurt had decided it.

No fault in the ground had brought the end.

No lesser cut had completed what the thrust had done.

He had died from the stroke Auren had given.

Auren stood motionless until the final cadence of the confirmation passed into silence.

Only then did she lower her hands back into the water.

She washed them again, though they had already been clean. She rubbed water over the knuckles, between the fingers, beneath the nails. Not frantically. Never that. She did it with the same exactness with which she had spoken. When she was finished, she lifted her hands and let the water fall away.

There was nothing on them.

That did not alter what they had done.

She took the cloth from beside the basin and dried each finger carefully. Then she folded the cloth once, twice, and set it down with its edges aligned.

At last Auren turned toward the open door.

“No correction,” she said.

Her voice did not carry like the formal account had carried. It did not need to. Those who needed to hear it would hear it.

“No addition. No denial. The record as confirmed is true.”

She remained in the antechamber, just beyond the threshold of the room where the body still lay. She would not go back in to stand over him again. She had already taken enough from that ground.

After a moment, she added, lower, “Let it stand in that form.”

Then Auren rested one hand lightly against the wall beside her, not for support that anyone could see, but because stillness sometimes required an anchor.

Her face remained composed.

Her breathing did not.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let the silence stretch for three heartbeats before I step into the antechamber. I keep my voice low. "It stands. Now come away from the door. Let them do their work."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did as she was told.

Not because she had no will left in her, nor because the command had authority over her beyond the room. Because it was correct.

She took her hand from the wall and stepped away from the threshold. One pace, then another, until the open door no longer framed her. Until the work beyond it could proceed without the victor standing near enough to seem like a claim.

Her shoulders remained square. Her hands hung clean and empty at her sides. The glove and stained cloth were still together where she had set them, and after a moment she turned back for them. She did not hurry. She lifted both with care, folded the glove over the cloth again, and held them in her left hand.

“That was properly said,” Auren said.

Her voice was low. It had lost the carrying edge of ritual and settled into something hoarser, though not broken.

“They must not have to work around me.”

She moved farther into the antechamber, away from the line of sight to the ring. The basin stood behind her. The water in it had gone faintly clouded from hands that had not been visibly stained. Auren looked at it once, then away.

For a few breaths, she said nothing.

The sounds from the other room began at last: feet shifting, murmured instructions, the careful undertone of people touching the dead. Auren’s jaw tightened when the first of those sounds came, but she did not turn back. She kept her eyes on the opposite wall, where old plaster had cracked in a thin line from cornice to floor.

“He stood well,” she said.

The words came with the precision of testimony, but they were no longer for the record.

“He misread one measure. Only one. That was enough.”

Auren closed her fingers around the folded glove and cloth. The leather creaked softly.

“It is always enough.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I watch her for a moment. "Yes," I say. "It is." I step closer, lowering my voice. "The water's clean. Your hands are too. You don't need to keep washing them."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looked down at her hands as if Del had named an object entered into evidence.

Clean.

The word did not offend her, but it failed to settle. Clean was a condition of skin, of steel, of cloth before it was used. It had measurements. It could be seen. It could be confirmed.

What remained after the account did not answer to it.

“No,” she said quietly. “I do not.”

She did not move back toward the basin. That, at least, she accepted.

Her fingers flexed once, slow and deliberate, testing the absence of water between them. The nails were clean. The knuckles were clean. No blood had dried in the creases. There was nothing there for any honest witness to name.

Auren closed her hand again around the glove.

“I know the difference,” she said. “Between stain and fact.”

Her gaze lifted from her hands to the cracked plaster ahead of her. She held herself upright with the same discipline she had brought into the ring, but the ritual had ended, and with it some necessary portion of her restraint had lost its formal brace.

“I washed because there was a basin,” she said. “Because my hands had work they understood. Not because I believed water would amend the record.”

The sounds in the room beyond shifted: a lowered voice, the scrape of a boot, the careful movement of weight being prepared for lifting. Auren’s eyes narrowed slightly, but she did not turn.

“He should be carried feet first,” she said, then stopped herself.

The correction had risen from habit, from the duellist’s instinct to order every aftermath into proper shape. It did not belong to her now unless asked.

After a moment, she said, lower, “No. His second will know.”

She drew one breath and let it out through her nose, controlled but uneven at the end.

“There is always some small instruction left in the mouth,” Auren said. “Something exact. Something useful. Carry him so. Clean the blade thus. Fold the coat away from the wound. Send word before rumor. None of it changes the thing, but it delays standing still with it.”

Her thumb passed once along the edge of the folded glove. The movement was minute, almost severe in its restraint.

“I have had eleven occasions to learn that.”

Then she looked toward Del, not fully, but enough that her attention was clear.

“You did your office without mercy,” she said. “That was not a cruelty.”

There was a pause before she added, with the weight of one precise correction offered in private rather than before witnesses, “It may have felt like one.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I shake my head, just once. "It wasn't cruelty. It was the record." I glance back toward the door, then meet her eyes. "And you're right. There's always one instruction left."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stood straight, though the ache in her lower back was a dull, familiar throb. She was forty-seven, and the damp morning air always found its way into her joints after the adrenaline began to fade. She did not let it show. She sheathed her sword with a single, practiced click of the crossguard against the scabbard.

She turned her gaze to Del, then looked past them to the three magistrates standing at the edge of the dew-heavy grass. Her voice, when she spoke, was devoid of triumph. It was the flat, level tone of a clerk reading a ledger.

"Let the record show," Auren said, her words carrying clearly in the quiet of the dawn. "The encounter was decided by a single engagement. My blade entered three inches below the left clavicle, angling downward. It severed the subclavian artery and punctured the upper lobe of the left lung."

She kept her eyes fixed on Del, refusing to look down at the grass, refusing to let her voice waver. To soften the description, to use euphemisms like *passed away* or *met their end*, would be a coward’s mercy. It would strip the dead of the stark reality of what had been done to them.

"Unconsciousness occurred within twenty seconds due to rapid blood loss," she continued, her delivery precise and unhurried. "Death followed within two minutes. There was no secondary strike."

She closed her mouth, her jaw set, and waited for Del’s acknowledgment, the heavy silence of the eleven times before this one settling over her shoulders like a leaden cloak.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat tight. "I witness the accounting. The record is true." My eyes flick to the body on the grass. "They won't need a physician, then."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren let her gaze fall to the grass at last. The tension in her shoulders did not leave, but it shifted, settling into the familiar, dull ache of survival. The man on the grass looked smaller now than he had when he was holding a sword. They always did. 

"No," Auren said. Her voice was quieter now, stripped of the carrying projection she had used for the magistrates. "Only the watch, to carry him back to his kin."

Across the clearing, the eldest magistrate nodded, his quill already scratching against a small, hand-held writing desk. The ink was dark, almost black in the gray dawn light, recording the precise trajectory of the steel that had ended a life. 

Auren reached down slowly, her joints protesting, and picked up the dead man's glove from where it had fallen during the initial salute. It was a small courtesy, one not demanded by the code but kept by her own sense of what was decent. She held it out toward Del. 

"His family will want his effects," she said, her tone level. "The magistrates will take the sword. You should take the rest."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren paused, the dead man’s leather glove resting heavy and cool in her palm. She did not frown, though her knees ached with the sudden, sharp desire to simply turn and walk away, to find a fire and a cup of hot, bitter tea. 

If the second demanded the direct accounting to seal the transfer of the deceased’s personal effects, the code was absolute. It had to be spoken twice—once to the law, and once to the representative of the blood. It was the only thing that separated what had happened here from simple, sordid murder.

She held Del’s gaze, her gray eyes steady, refusing to allow any shadow of apology to soften the weight of her words. 

"The blade entered three inches below the left clavicle," Auren said, her voice dropping into that same flat, clinical cadence. "Angled downward. It severed the subclavian artery and punctured the upper lobe of the left lung. Unconsciousness in twenty seconds. Death in two minutes. There was no secondary strike."

She reached out and placed the glove into Del’s hand, her fingers briefly brushing theirs—cold skin against cold skin in the damp morning. 

"The account is spoken," she finished, her voice returning to its quiet, weary register. "The debt of the steel is cleared."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My fingers close around the glove, the leather still holding the shape of a hand that no longer exists. I look at Auren, really look, past the rigid posture and the gray eyes. "You're favoring your left side," I say, voice low. "We should go. Before the watch gets here and starts asking questions."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not immediately answer. She tightened her jaw, annoyed with herself for letting the stiffness show, but she did not deny it. At forty-seven, the body kept its own accounting, and the quick, lateral lunge she had used to bypass the dead man's guard had strained her left hip more than she cared to admit. 

"The damp," she said, her voice flat. She adjusted the hang of her scabbard, though the movement did nothing to ease the dull pull in her lower back. "The magistrates have what they need. My presence is no longer required by law."

She turned her back on the clearing, and on the man she had just killed, without looking back. It was a rule she had kept since the third duel: once the accounting was spoken, the dead belonged to the ground and the living to the road. 

She began to walk toward the narrow dirt path that led away from the meadow, her stride deliberate. She tried to smooth out the slight hitch in her gait, but the cold had settled deep into her joints. 

"There is an inn two miles south," she said, her voice carrying only to Del as they walked. "The hearth will be lit by now. I intend to sit by it."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stopped. The gravel of the path crunched beneath her boot, a sharp, sudden sound in the quiet morning. 

She turned slowly, her entire body moving as one piece to spare her hip the twisting motion. The implication in Del's voice—that she had concealed a blow, that she had walked away from the magistrates with unreported blood on her person—was a cold prick against her professional pride. To hide a wound was to falsify the duel. It was a coward’s cheat, a way to deny an opponent their final, small measure of credit.

"It did not land," Auren said. Her voice was not angry, but it had the hard, unyielding weight of iron. "His blade did not touch me."

She reached down with a steady hand, unhooking the clasp of her heavy wool riding coat and pulling it back. Underneath, her dark leather doublet was immaculate. There was no tear in the stitching, no damp, spreading stain of red against the black dye. 

"If his steel had found so much as a thread of my coat, it would be in the ledger," she said, her gray eyes locking onto Del's. "I do not steal from the dead. He missed his parry, and he died without touching me."

She let the coat fall back into place, though the movement cost her a sharp, biting twinge in her lower back. She did not flinch. 

"The hitch in my stride is forty-seven years of hard winters and damp ground," she continued, her tone dropping back into its flat, clinical rhythm. "The lunge was clean. The recovery was clumsy. That is my account, and it is the only true one. Do you dispute it?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "No," I say, my own voice quiet but firm. "I only needed to hear you say it." I glance back once at the magistrates, then fall into step beside her. "Let's get to that inn."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren gave a single, stiff nod. The cold prick of offense faded, replaced once more by the heavy, familiar exhaustion that always followed the blood-letting. It was the second’s right—indeed, their duty—to be certain. She could not grudge Del the question, even if it had bitten. 

"Good," she said simply. 

She turned back to the path, her boots resuming their steady, rhythmic crunch on the gravel. She did not attempt to hide the hitch in her stride now; there was no one left to impress, and the magistrates were already small figures in the distance, hunched over their desks and their dead. 

The road south was lined with high, dripping hedges that kept the wind off them, though the damp seemed to rise directly from the wet earth to settle in her knees. For a time, she said nothing, the silence between them filled only by the dripping of condensation from the leaves and the distant, lonely call of a crow. 

"The tea at the *Stag and Thistle* is bitter," she observed after they had walked a half-mile. Her voice was low, carrying no further than the space between her and Del. "But they keep the hearth stacked with birch. It burns hot. We will dry our cloaks there."

She kept her eyes on the road ahead, her hands resting naturally near her belt, away from the hilt of her sword. The duel was over. The accounting was done. Now, there was only the cold, and the miles.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stopped again. This time, her boots did not merely pause; she turned fully to face Del, the movement deliberate and stiff. The damp wind off the meadows caught her hair, blowing a few graying strands across her face, but she did not brush them away.

Del was invoking the strict letter of the code. A second had the right—indeed, the absolute authority—to demand a physical inspection if they believed a duellist was concealing a wound to preserve their standing or to deny the deceased their mark. To refuse would be to forfeit her honor and her license. 

"Very well," Auren said. Her voice was flat, devoid of anger, though her jaw was set so tight the muscle leaped in her cheek. 

She unclasped her cloak and let it slide from her shoulders, catching it with her right hand and draping it over a low branch of the hedge. Then, with steady, unhurried fingers, she unbuckled the side-straps of her heavy leather doublet. She pulled the stiff leather open, revealing the plain, undyed linen of her undershirt. 

With her left hand, she gathered the hem of the shirt and pulled it up, exposing the left side of her torso, from the ribs down to the hip. 

The skin was pale, mapped with the faint, silvery lines of three separate scars from duels fought twenty years ago, when she had been faster but less careful. But there was no red. There was no tear in the linen, no smear of fresh blood on her skin. There was only a dull, angry flush rising near the crest of her pelvis—the unmistakable swelling of a deep muscular strain.

"The blade did nothing," Auren said, her voice dropping into that precise, ledger-like cadence. "The steel did not touch leather, linen, or flesh. The damage is a grade-two strain of the left gluteus medius and the surrounding lumbar fascia, caused by the force of my own recovery on wet grass."

She let the shirt fall back into place and began buckling her doublet, her fingers moving with the same methodical rhythm she used to clean her sword. 

"The opponent died without landing a blow," she finished, looking directly into Del's eyes as she tightened the last strap. "The account remains correct. Are you satisfied, Second?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath I didn't know I was holding. "Satisfied." I take her cloak from the branch, shake off the damp, and hand it back to her. "Your account is true. I'll note the strain in the private record, so your physician knows."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren took the cloak from Del’s hand. She shook it once more—a brief, sharp motion that made her lower back throb in protest—and slung it over her shoulders, fastening the bronze clasp at her throat with steady fingers. 

"I do not have a physician," she said, her voice returning to its quiet, dry rasp. "Only a bottle of wintergreen oil and a bench by the fire. The oil will do the work. It always does."

She turned back to the south road and started walking again. She did not try to hide the hitch in her stride this time; the inspection was over, the record was sealed, and there was no longer any need for the performance of perfect health. There was only the reality of getting to shelter.

"The private record is yours to keep," she added as they walked, her eyes fixed on the muddy ruts of the road ahead. "But do not make it sound like more than a simple slip on wet clover. I am old, Del. I am not fragile."

The wind picked up, carrying the scent of woodsmoke from some distant cottage. It was a good sign; it meant they were nearing the valley where the inn sat. Auren pulled her cloak tighter around her chest, her gloved hand resting near her scabbard simply to keep it from bouncing against her bruised hip.

"We will need to send word to the guild in the morning," she remarked, her tone conversational but distant. "The eleventh entry is complete. They will want the ledger signed before the week is out."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stopped. Her boots sank slightly into the soft, muddy edge of the road. She did not turn around this time; she simply stood, staring straight ahead at the gray line of the horizon where the mist was beginning to lift from the hills. 

The demand was cruel, but it was the law. The founders of the code had not been stupid men; they had known that if the survivors were allowed to speak only of angles and inches, they would soon begin to think of the duel as a game of geometry. They had written the requirement of the full accounting to ensure that no one—neither the victor nor the second—could walk away from a dead man without carrying the stench of him in their nostrils. 

Auren took a slow, deep breath, her chest rising against the stiff leather of her doublet. When she spoke, her voice was very quiet, but it had the same flat, unyielding clarity she had used before the magistrates.

"The engagement lasted forty-two seconds from the first salute to the strike," she said. "After the steel entered, he did not fall immediately. He remained standing for six seconds, his hand gripping my sleeve. His fingers were wet. He did not speak words of challenge, nor of peace. He said, *'No.'* He said it twice, in a whisper. Then he said, *'It is very cold,'* and his knees buckled."

She paused. The memory was fresh, laid out in her mind like a drawing on clean parchment. She did not look at Del, keeping her eyes on the distant, bare branches of a lone oak tree at the turn of the road.

"He fell onto his left side," she continued, her delivery steady and unhurried. "The grass was wet, and it stained his cheek. His eyes remained open. They did not track me; they were fixed on the hem of my cloak. His breathing was rapid—thirty-six respirations in the first minute, shallow and wet, as the left lung filled with blood. He made a rattling sound in his throat with each exhalation. It is the sound of a throat clearing, repeated until there is no air left to clear it."

She tightened her hand on her walking cloak, her knuckles turning white under her glove. 

"In the second minute, his pulse became thready and irregular. His skin turned the color of skimmed milk. He did not call for his family. He did not pray. He made a small, jerking motion with his right hand, as if reaching for his hat, and then his chest rose once, very high, and did not fall again. His bowels released shortly after the breathing stopped."

She turned her head then, slowly, to look at Del. Her gray eyes were completely empty of anger, empty of pride, empty of everything but the weight of forty-seven years and twelve dead men. 

"His name was Thomas," she said, her voice dropping a fraction lower. "He was twenty-four years old. He died in the wet grass because his parry-four was three inches too wide. That is the account. Is there any part of it you wish me to repeat?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, my own throat feeling tight and dry. "No," I say, my voice coming out softer than I intended. "It's enough." I look away, down the road toward the inn. "Let's get that tea."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not offer a comforting word, nor did she look away to spare Del the sight of her own unblinking, gray gaze. She simply let her hand fall from her cloak, the heavy wool settling back into place over her doublet. The silence that followed was different now—not the tense, defensive quiet of a challenge, but the flat, dead weight of a completed task.

"Yes," Auren said. "The tea."

She turned back to the south road, her boots finding the muddy ruts once more. The hitch in her left hip was more pronounced now that she had stopped and started again, the muscles tightening in the damp air like old leather left out in the rain. She did not try to hide it. There was no point. Del had seen the skin, had seen the swelling, and had recorded the truth of it. 

They walked in silence. The mist was beginning to burn off the high ridges, turning the gray sky into a pale, watery yellow that offered no warmth. On either side of the road, the sheep in the pastures stood motionless, their fleece gray with dew, watching them pass with blank, black eyes.

Auren kept her eyes on the ground a few paces ahead of her boots. In her mind, the ledger was closed. Thomas would remain twenty-four, and his parry-four would remain three inches too wide, forever. She would write the name in her own small book tonight, using the cheap ink from the innkeeper’s desk, adding him to the list of eleven others who had died of similar measurements.

"The wind is turning from the east," Auren said after they had gone another mile. Her voice was slightly hoarse from the damp, but she did not clear her throat. "It will rain before noon. We should make the porch before the downpour starts."

She did not look at Del, but she slowed her pace slightly, a silent concession to both her aching hip and the heavy silence that walked between them.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The sound of Del’s voice confirming the account hung in the damp air between them, thin and fragile, catching on the final syllables. Auren did not look at them as the words settled. She knew that crack in a voice; she had heard it from eleven other seconds, some of them seasoned men of the guard, some of them siblings who had insisted on standing for their kin. It was the sound of the reality finally bypassing the intellect and hitting the chest.

She gave a single, slow nod of acknowledgment. The law was satisfied. The dead man’s ghost was laid to rest in the only way the code allowed—not with prayers, but with the truth.

"Let it stand," Auren said softly.

They walked the remaining mile in a silence that felt heavier than before, the gray mist thickening into a fine, clinging drizzle that beaded on the wool of her cloak. By the time the wooden sign of the *Stag and Thistle* loomed through the gray, Auren’s left hip was a hot, throbbing knot of iron. 

She did not wait for Del to open the door. She pushed it open herself, her shoulder taking the weight of the heavy oak, and stepped into the low-ceilinged warmth of the common room. The smell of burning birch and stale tallow greeted them. It was early; the only other patron was an old man asleep by the peat-grate in the corner. 

Auren bypassed the tables near the door and made for the dark corner beside the hearth. She unclasped her wet cloak, draping it over the back of a settle, and sat down. The wood was hard, and the descent forced a sharp, silent intake of air through her teeth as her lower back protested, but she did not let herself linger on the pain. 

A young girl with grease-stained sleeves appeared. Auren did not look up. "Hot water," she said, her voice flat. "A pot of black tea. And ink. A clean quill, and two sheets of foolscap."

The girl curtsied and scurried away. 

When the writing materials arrived, Auren cleared a space on the grease-filmed pine table. She did not pour the tea first. She pulled the inkwell toward her, uncorked it, and dipped the split nib of the goose quill into the dark, thin fluid. 

She held the pen above the paper for three seconds, letting the excess ink drip back into the well, her hand perfectly steady despite the cold and the ache in her bones. Then, she began to write. She did not use cursive; she used the blocky, upright register hand of the duelling courts, ensuring every letter was distinct, every stroke incapable of being misread or altered.

***

*THE RECORD OF THE TWELFTH ENGAGEMENT*

*Fought this day, the fourteenth of October, at the hour of dawn, in the meadow of the Third Mile Post.*

*PRINCIPALS:*
*Auren of the High Reach, Licensed Duellist of the First Class (Victor).*
*Thomas of the Lower Valley, Appellant (Deceased).*

*WITNESSES:*
*Three Magistrates of the Quarter Sessions.*
*Del, Second to the Appellant.*

*THE ACCOUNTING:*
*The engagement commenced upon the third bell of dawn and was concluded within forty-two seconds of the initial salute. A single engagement was joined. The deceased offered a standard parry-four, which was wide of the line by three inches.*

*The victor’s blade entered the deceased’s body three inches below the left clavicle. The angle of entry was approximately thirty degrees downward. The steel penetrated the chest cavity to a depth of six inches, severing the subclavian artery and puncturing the upper lobe of the left lung.*

*Upon withdrawal of the steel, the deceased remained standing for six seconds, grasping the victor’s left sleeve. The deceased spoke twice, whispering the word "No," followed by the statement, "It is very cold."*

*Collapse occurred at the seventh second. The deceased fell upon his left side in the wet grass. Respiration was rapid and shallow, measured at thirty-six inhalations within the first minute, accompanied by wet rales as the lung filled with blood. Pulse became thready and irregular at ninety seconds. Death occurred at approximately two minutes from the time of the stroke, preceded by a final high inhalation and the post-mortem release of the bowels.*

*There was no secondary strike. No other wounds were given or received.*

*VICTOR'S CONDITION:*
*The victor received no contact from the deceased's steel. A grade-two muscular strain of the left gluteus medius was sustained during the recovery from the lunge on wet clover.*

*The account is spoken. The debt of the steel is cleared.*

***

Auren laid the quill down. She did not blow on the ink; she sat in silence, watching the black liquid lose its shine as the cheap paper drank it in, turning it a dull, permanent gray. 

She turned the paper toward the empty space across the table, where the second would sit, and pushed the inkwell and the pen toward it. 

"Sign it," she said, her voice dropping into the quiet of the empty room. "Then we are done."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content:
My hand shakes, just a little, as I take the quill. The ink bleeds into the paper where I pause too long over the date. I sign my name, the letters small and tight at the bottom.

When I look up, the firelight catches the lines around her eyes. "It's done," I say, and my voice doesn't crack this time. It just sounds tired.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren waited until the ink of Del’s signature was dry before she touched the paper. She did not blow on it; she simply watched the black loops of their name settle into the fibers of the cheap foolscap. Once it was matte and still, she took the document, folded it twice with precise, creased edges, and slid it into the inner pocket of her doublet, right against her ribs.

"It is done," she agreed.

She reached for the heavy clay teapot the girl had left on the table. Her wrist was steady, though the steam that rose from the spout smelled of scorched leaves and iron-heavy well water. She poured a cup for Del first, pushing the thick, dark mug across the grease-filmed wood, and then poured her own.

She took a sip. It was as bitter as she had warned, biting the back of her tongue, but it was hot. It bloomed in her chest, a brief, artificial warmth that did not quite reach her cold fingers or her aching hip.

"The magistrates will file their copy with the high bailiff before noon," Auren said, her voice dropping into a quiet, conversational register that felt strange after the formal cadence of the accounting. "My copy goes to the guildhouse in the city. Yours is for the family, should they wish to contest the division of the estate or the legality of the challenge. The law cannot touch them now. Nor can it touch you."

She set her mug down with a small, hollow click against the table. She looked at Del, her gray eyes dark in the firelight.

"You have the glove," she said. "The magistrates will have delivered his sword to the town hall by now. You should collect it before the clerk charges a holding fee. They are thieves, those clerks."

She reached down to her side, her fingers brushing the small, corked vial of wintergreen oil in her belt pouch, but she did not pull it out. Not yet. She would wait until she was alone in her room to strip and rub the fire into her bruised flesh. For now, she simply sat, her posture still straight, though her shoulders had dropped an inch from their formal carriage.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I pull the glove from my pocket. The leather feels stiff and cold. "I'll go after the tea," I say, my voice low. "Unless you want me to stay while you..." I gesture vaguely toward her hip.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren’s gaze fell to the stiff leather glove in Del’s hand, then rose slowly to their face. The offer was born of a decent impulse—she could recognize that much—but it was an impulse she had no use for. The thought of anyone, let alone the second of the man she had just killed, tending to the bruises of her aging body was a violation of the distance she had spent twenty-five years maintaining. 

"No," Auren said. Her voice was not sharp, but it had the flat, final ring of an iron gate closing. "The oil has a foul, medicinal smell, and the rubbing of it is a clumsy, private business. I have no need of an audience for my infirmities."

She took another slow sip of her tea, letting the bitter heat coat her throat. 

"Your duty now is to the dead, not the living," she continued, her eyes steady on Del's. "Thomas’s mother, or his sister, or whoever is waiting in the valley, will not care about the state of my hip. They will want his sword. They will want to know that his steel was handled with respect, and that his name was recorded without error. You are the only one who can give them that."

Outside, the first heavy drops of the predicted rain began to tap against the leaded panes of the window, a quick, irregular drumming that threatened a downpour before the hour was out. 

Auren reached into her doublet and pulled out three small silver coins, laying them on the grease-stained wood of the table. They clinked softly against each other. 

"That will cover the tea and the paper," she said. "And the holding fee for the sword, if the clerk is feeling particularly greedy today. Do not let him bully you. The law states the second has three days to claim the steel before it becomes property of the parish."

She wrapped her hands around her warm mug, using the clay to thaw the stiffness in her fingers. 

"Go to the town hall, Del," she said, her voice dropping to a quiet, level command. "Then go to his people. Tell them what the ledger says. No more, no less."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I look at the coins, then back at her. "I'll tell them it was clean," I say, standing up and tucking the glove away. "That's all they need to know."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looked to each of the witnesses in turn, as custom demanded, ensuring there would be no dispute about what was said or by whom. Her tone was measured—not cold, but with the gravity of ritual.

She spoke, clear enough for all to hear: "The killing wound was to the left lung. Blade entered between the fourth and fifth ribs." Her eyes did not linger on Del, nor on the fallen. She let the weight of her words settle.

She did not apologize. That, too, would have been a lie.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, committing the details to memory. My voice is steady when I speak. "Left lung, between fourth and fifth ribs. I confirm it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren waited until Del finished, then nodded once—a subtle motion acknowledging the confirmation and the closing of this grim ledger. She sheathed her blade, the sound precise and deliberate, and only then did she allow herself a breath that was not measured by ceremony.

"The record is kept," she said for the benefit of the witnesses, and for herself. Her posture never slackened. She did not look to the body again; her duty was not with the dead, but with the living who remained. She turned to Del, her expression unchanged, but there was a faint suggestion in her bearing—permission, perhaps, for grief, or for anger. The code made space for neither, but people did.

"If you require the written account, it will be prepared before dusk," she said. "You will not have to ask twice."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head, accepting the formality. Her eyes met Del's, steady and unflinching. She spoke the words as the code demanded, her voice carrying the cadence of testimony rather than confession.

"I, Auren, witnessed by those present, do account the killing wound as follows: the blade struck between the fourth and fifth ribs on the left side, entering the lung. The wound was delivered in accordance with the terms of the duel, and the record stands as spoken."

She paused only long enough to be certain no protest or correction would come from the witnesses. Her hands remained at her sides, the ritual complete but its gravity lingering in the air.

"Thus, the account is spoken and set upon the day," she concluded, the formula sealing the record. She did not move to comfort, nor to leave—her presence remained an anchor until Del or the witnesses made the next motion.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I breathe in. The formal air tastes like dust and old stone. "I accept the account as spoken." My gaze shifts, just for a moment, to the fallen shape on the ground. "Will you help me move him?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren nodded once—no hesitation, no excess. "I will," she said. Her voice carried the same formality, but something in its timbre acknowledged the weight of what Del asked, and what it cost to ask it.

She stepped forward with measured care, neither rushing nor shrinking from what must be done. As was custom, she waited for Del to choose which side of the body to take, following the lead of the second. Her hands were steady, practiced at this final courtesy. When she bent to lift, it was with all the precision she brought to the duel itself—no jostling, no indignity.

As they moved the fallen, Auren kept her silence, offering neither platitude nor apology. Her presence was a mark of respect, nothing more and nothing less. When they reached the place Del indicated, she waited for further instruction. Her duty was not finished until Del released her from it, and she would not presume to decide when that moment came.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not hesitate, nor did she look away from the place her blade had made its mark. This was the final detail, and it was owed, however small it seemed amid the greater loss.

"It landed beneath the fourth rib," she stated, voice as clear as ever. "Angle was shallow—blade passed through the upper lobe of the lung and lodged against the spine. Death would have followed within moments, with little chance for speech." Her words gave no comfort, but neither did they sharpen the pain. They were simply true.

Auren kept her posture formal, though the task felt heavier now. "If you require this to be written, I will see to it at once. If you wish it spoken for the record, I will repeat it before all present." She looked to Del, awaiting the next instruction—her role, until the last account was kept, was to be unyielding and exact.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat tight. "Under the fourth rib, lodged at the spine. I accept it." I glance toward the door. "Let's carry him to the side chamber. The witnesses can leave now."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren acknowledged Del’s words with a single, silent nod. She stepped to the indicated side of the body, matching Del’s grip with practiced care, ensuring their burden was steady and dignified. As they lifted together, Auren kept her gaze forward, mindful of each movement—the code demanded respect, even here, especially here.

When the witnesses began to file out, Auren waited until the last had crossed the threshold before she spoke again, her voice lowered in deference to the intimacy of the moment. “He will not be disturbed here,” she said, her words simple and unadorned—neither comfort nor intrusion, merely a practical assurance.

She assisted Del in settling the body, careful to avoid haste. Only when Del released her grip did Auren straighten, her own hands falling to her sides. She did not offer to help further unless asked, understanding that grief, like the code, had boundaries that must be honored.

“If you need the written record or a witness’s signature, I remain at your disposal,” she said, tone unchanged. Her eyes lingered on Del for a moment, searching for any instruction or dismissal. Until such was given, she would not presume to depart.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren acknowledged the prompt with a single, grave inclination of her head—there was no resentment in her manner, only acceptance that this, too, was the work. She spoke the details as she had witnessed and caused them, the language clinical and exact, offering no shelter from the truth.

“The blade entered beneath the fourth rib, left side,” she said, voice steady but never detached. “It pierced the intercostal muscle and the pleura, then traversed the upper lobe of the left lung. The point struck the anterior face of the thoracic spine, halting there. The lung collapsed; the chest filled with blood. He would have been unable to draw breath or to speak.”

She delivered the account as a physician might, but it was not for curiosity. It was the record, and it was owed—without embellishment, without omission. Auren’s gaze did not falter, though she did not seek Del’s eyes directly; there was a dignity in restraint.

“That is the full accounting,” she concluded. “If further detail is needed, I will provide it. If there is a correction or contest, I will hear it now.” Her posture made plain: she would not leave a single part of the truth unspoken, no matter how it landed.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, my hands trembling only slightly as I smooth his tunic. "That is the full accounting. I have no correction." I look up at you. "You can go."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren accepted Del’s words without delay or protest. Formal acknowledgment was owed, so she gave it: one last, deliberate bow of her head, deeper than before, in recognition of the burden that now passed from her hands to Del’s. She did not speak—there was nothing left that the code or decency required her to say.

She turned with the same measured precision she had brought to every step, leaving the chamber without haste or sound beyond the soft tread of her boots. At the threshold, she paused—not for drama, but to grant Del a final moment of privacy before the door closed and the world resumed its forward motion.

Outside, her composure did not falter. The ritual was complete. She would see to the written record, see it witnessed and sealed before dusk, as promised. Eleven accounts stood behind her now—none softened, none adorned. She carried each, not as trophies, but as truths that must be borne.

If Del required her again, she would return. Until then, Auren let the silence settle around her, and she moved on.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head—deeper, this time. The request was within Del’s rights, and the code left her no path but the truth, unmitigated and entire. She spoke, her voice unwavering, but her eyes fixed on a point beyond the fallen—never evasive, but refusing the comfort of distance.

“He fell within two breaths after the wound was struck,” she began, her words measured, each chosen with care for accuracy rather than cruelty. “He tried to speak—his lips moved, but no sound followed. Blood welled at the wound and at the mouth. His eyes found yours, Del, and he reached out with his left hand. There was no strength in it. After the third breath, he ceased moving. His face was calm at the end—there was pain, but no fear.”

She paused, letting the silence acknowledge what detail could not. “The witnesses will attest: there were no words spoken after the wound. The body’s posture remained unbroken; there was no convulsion. Death was swift—less than half a minute from strike to stillness.”

Auren took one more measured breath. “This is the full account as I saw and caused it. If any witness disputes my words, let them speak now. Otherwise, it is set as record.” Her hands remained at her sides—never clenched, never restless. She did not apologize, nor did she offer comfort; she gave only what Del had demanded: the truth, entire and unsoftened.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I close my eyes for a moment, swallowing hard. "He reached out with his left hand," I repeat, my voice low. "I saw that too." I look back at you, the formality finally cracking. "Why didn't you move aside? You could have."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren heard the break in Del’s voice—the first true fracture in the ritual’s armor—and she gave it the respect of stillness. She did not answer at once, considering the question and the space it had opened: not a matter of code, but something older and more human.

When she spoke, her words were plain, unadorned by regret or defense. “He named the terms. I met him as he required. Anything less—moving aside, holding back—would have been another kind of wound.” Her eyes met Del’s then, direct, the formality drained to its bones. “If I had made it mercy, it would not have been the truth. He did not ask for that.”

Auren’s jaw set, though not in anger. “I do not choose the manner of their deaths, Del. Only the honesty of the account. I will not lie about what I do, nor about what I could have done.” She let the words stand, harsh but clean, and did not reach for Del’s grief, nor turn away from it.

“If you wish to contest the duel’s rightness, say so. If not—let this be finished with the truth between us.” There was no challenge in her tone, only the gravity of one who had carried this weight many times before, never lighter for the bearing.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren waited for Del’s confirmation—heard the break, the tremor, the effort to summon words for what could never be made right. The ritual demanded its ending; she would not hasten nor delay it.

She faced the witnesses, her voice unwavering, her bearing formal, and delivered the full account as it was owed—each detail spoken as plainly as if she transcribed it to the record herself.

“Let it be recorded, before those present: The wound was struck beneath the fourth rib, left side. The blade entered between the fourth and fifth ribs, pierced the intercostal muscle and the pleura, traversed the upper lobe of the left lung, and halted at the anterior face of the thoracic spine. The lung collapsed; the chest filled with blood. Death followed within half a minute.

Upon receiving the wound, he fell within two breaths. He attempted speech—his lips moved, but no sound was formed. Blood welled at the wound and at the mouth. His eyes found those of his second, Del; he reached out with his left hand but lacked the strength to complete the gesture. After the third breath, movement ceased. There was no convulsion; posture remained unbroken. His face showed pain, but not fear. No words were spoken after the wound. Death was swift.”

Auren paused, letting each phrase settle, her diction careful and precise. She did not look for comfort in the faces before her, nor offer it. The account was for the record, not for salving wounds.

She finished as custom demanded, voice ringing finality: “This is the whole accounting, as witnessed and as caused. If any witness disputes it, let them now speak. If any detail is questioned, let it be questioned now. Otherwise, the account stands and is set upon this day.”

Auren’s hands remained at her sides—open, unflinching. She would not leave until every truth required had been spoken and received, and the weight of it laid down where all could see it.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I'd been holding, my hands finally still. "The account is heard and accepted. The record stands." I look at the witnesses, my voice tired but clear. "You're dismissed."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stood her ground as the witnesses filed out, each one pausing just long enough to give the formal nod of acknowledgment—some with eyes averted, others meeting her gaze for a heartbeat before moving on. She watched them go, ensuring the chain of custody for the truth was unbroken from mouth to ear, from ear to memory.

Only when the last had left and silence had gathered in the room once more did she allow her shoulders to ease, if only by a fraction. The forms were satisfied; the record now lived not only in her words but in the air and in the ears of all who had stayed to hear it.

She turned at last to Del, her presence still formal, but the scaffolding of ritual had fallen away. “If there is any detail you require again, or if the record must be witnessed in writing, I will see it done,” she said quietly. The code allowed her to leave now, but Auren did not move until she was certain Del had no further need of her exactitude, her steadiness, or the last office she could render.

Her eyes, always steady in the telling, softened now by the smallest margin—a flicker of recognition for the cost of truth borne aloud. She did not offer comfort. That was not her place, nor her right. But she gave Del her presence, unhurried and unflinching, until she was no longer needed.

When Del gave leave, Auren would go. Until then, she waited—silent, reliable, bearing the weight of her own words and what they had wrought.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my eyes fixed on the still shape beside me. "I'll need the written account before dusk." I reach out and gently close his eyes. "Leave me now."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head, acknowledging Del’s instruction with the same precision that had marked every step of the ritual. “The written account will be prepared and witnessed before dusk,” she said, her voice low but unyielding—promise, not comfort.

She allowed herself a final moment, not for sentiment but for certainty: that the dead were honored, that the living were not further burdened by her presence. Her gaze lingered on Del—a brief, silent recognition of the grief she could neither carry nor soften.

Then, without further word or gesture, Auren turned and departed. Her footsteps were quiet and measured, the threshold crossed with neither haste nor reluctance. She closed the door behind her, sealing the chamber and its grief within, as the code required.

Outside, she drew a breath, steadying herself for the next duty: the account, to be set down in writing, attested by those who had heard the words spoken. She would see it done, as she always had. The truth would not be lessened, nor its burden made lighter, but it would be borne—precisely, and without evasion—until her part in this day was finished.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I stay there on my knees for a long time after the door shuts. My hand is still on his cheek. It's already getting cold. "Damn you," I whisper, not sure who I mean.
