dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren sheathed the blade with the same economy of motion she'd used to draw it, and when she spoke, her voice carried to the corners of the room without effort, without anger, without anything that might be mistaken for satisfaction.

"The thrust entered beneath the fourth rib, left side, angled upward at twenty degrees. The point passed through the lower lobe of the left lung, nicked the pericardial sac, and came to rest in the anterior wall of the left ventricle." She paused, not for effect, but because the pause was required. "The wound is fatal. Bleeding into the chest cavity will be complete within minutes. There is no surgical remedy."

She turned her head slightly, addressing the witnesses now rather than Del alone. "The accounting is made. Let it be recorded."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod once, my throat tight. "The accounting is heard and confirmed." My voice doesn't shake, but it feels thin in the quiet room.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head a fraction of an inch — acknowledgment, not gratitude. She did not look at the body. She had looked at it enough during the accounting, and before that, during the work itself. There was no need to look again.

"The witnesses will sign the record," she said, still addressing the room at large. "The second will see to the arrangements. I will remain until the physician has made his own examination."

She turned back to Del then, and for the first time since the duel began, something in her expression shifted — not warmth, exactly, but a deliberate lessening of distance. "You conducted yourself correctly," she said. "Your principal knew the terms. There is no shame here."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's gaze did not waver from Del's face. She understood what it cost to stand in that place and ask for the words that would be written down and remembered. She had stood there herself, once, a long time ago.

"The thrust entered beneath the fourth rib, left side, angled upward at twenty degrees," she said. Her voice was level, clinical, the same tone a surgeon might use in a lecture hall. "The point passed through the lower lobe of the left lung, nicked the pericardial sac, and came to rest in the anterior wall of the left ventricle."

She paused. The pause was required. Three heartbeats, no more, no less. She had counted them silently for eleven years and did not need to count them now.

"The wound is fatal. Bleeding into the chest cavity will be complete within minutes. There is no surgical remedy."

She turned her head slightly, addressing the witnesses now rather than Del alone. "The accounting is made. Let it be recorded."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I swallow, my hands clasped tightly behind my back to hide their tremor. "The accounting is heard and confirmed."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren held Del's gaze for a moment longer than was strictly necessary. The second's hands were behind their back — she did not need to see them to know they were trembling. She had seen it before, in other seconds, in other rooms.

"The witnesses will sign the record," she said, returning her attention to the room. Her voice carried the same measured authority it had held throughout the accounting. "The physician may approach. No one else is to disturb the body until the examination is complete."

She stepped back from the center of the floor, yielding the space to the man in the dark coat who had been waiting near the door. He moved forward with his bag, his face professionally blank.

Auren did not watch him work. Instead she walked to the small table where the record book lay open, its pages waiting. She lifted the pen, checked the nib, and wrote her name in the precise script she had used for eleven such entries before this one. The ink was still wet when she set the pen down.

"You will need to sign as well," she said to Del, and this time her voice was quieter, meant for one person rather than a room. "When you are ready. There is no rush."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not repeat the full accounting. That had been spoken, heard, and confirmed. To say it again would be to dwell, and dwelling was not permitted by the code. But the code also required clarity, and Del had asked for it plainly.

She lifted her hand and touched the left side of her own chest, just below the breast, where the ribs curved upward. "Here," she said. Her voice was quiet now, stripped of the formal cadence. "Beneath the fourth rib. The heart."

She lowered her hand. "That is the plain account. Will it serve?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I close my eyes for a second, picturing the trajectory. "It serves," I say, then take up the pen. My signature is steadier than I expected.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren watched the pen move across the page. The signature was legible, which was more than could be said for some she had witnessed over the years. She did not comment on its steadiness. To remark on it would be to acknowledge that unsteadiness had been expected, and that was not a thing one said to a second who had done their duty.

When the ink was dry, she closed the record book herself. The sound of the cover settling into place was soft but final.

"The physician will need another ten minutes," she said, glancing toward the man kneeling beside the body. He had opened the shirt and was making his own notes, his own measurements. The wound was exactly where she had said it was. It always was. "You are not required to stay for that."

She straightened the cuffs of her shirt, a small, habitual motion that her own second had once told her she did only after the accounting was complete. She had not been aware of it until it was pointed out.

"If you need to step outside," she added, "I will send someone when the record is ready for your principal's family." A pause. "Or I will bring it myself, if you prefer."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren met Del's eyes and did not look away. The request was correct. The code demanded precision, and precision was what she had always given. She had never offered comfort in place of truth, and she would not begin now.

"The blade entered the thoracic cavity between the fourth and fifth ribs, left of the sternum," she said. Her voice was the same as it had been during the formal accounting—level, unhurried, exact. "It transected the intercostal muscle and the pleural membrane. The tip lacerated the inferior lobe of the left lung, producing a pneumothorax. Continuing upward and inward, it grazed the pericardium—the sac surrounding the heart—and penetrated the myocardium of the left ventricle."

She paused. Not the ritual pause this time, but a smaller one, to let the words settle.

"The wound channel was approximately four inches deep. The angle of entry ensured that each contraction of the heart muscle widened the laceration. Death resulted from cardiac tamponade and exsanguination into the chest cavity. Consciousness was lost within twelve seconds. Death followed within forty."

She did not look at the body. She looked only at Del.

"That is what the blade did. That is what it did it to. Does the accounting satisfy?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My mouth tastes like ash. "It satisfies." I look down at the record book, at the ink drying next to my name. "They'll ask if he suffered."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren considered the question. It was not part of the formal accounting, and the code did not require her to answer it. But the code did not forbid it, either. And Del had stood steady through the whole of it, which was more than many seconds managed.

"Twelve seconds is a long time," she said. "But the shock of a penetrating cardiac wound is profound. The body's first response is not pain but pressure—a sense of fullness, of wrongness. The nerve pathways that would carry the signal of the wound itself are often overwhelmed before they can fire fully."

She paused, weighing the next words carefully. This was not the accounting. This was something else.

"If you are asking whether he was afraid, I cannot say. I did not know him. If you are asking whether he was in agony, the answer is likely no. The body has its own mercies, and they are faster than we give them credit for."

She looked toward the physician, who was now covering the body with a sheet. The man worked in silence, his movements efficient and unsentimental.

"When you speak to the family," Auren said, returning her attention to Del, "you may tell them that. It is not a violation of the code to say that the wound was swift. It is only a violation to lie."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren held Del's gaze for a long moment. This was not the formal accounting—the formal accounting was finished, signed, witnessed. This was the secondary duty, the one the code did not name but did not forbid: the telling to the second who would have to carry the words to people who had loved the dead man.

She did not sit. She had not sat since the duel began, and she would not sit now.

"When the thrust landed, he made a sound," she said. "Not a cry. An exhalation. The air leaving the lung. He looked down at the blade, and then at me. There was no recognition in his eyes—not of me, not of the wound. The body was already beginning to understand what had happened, but the mind had not caught up."

She paused. This was not the ritual pause. This was the pause of someone choosing words that would be precise without being cruel, because cruelty served no one.

"He took two steps backward. His hand came up—not to the wound, but toward his chest, as if he meant to brush something away. He said nothing. His mouth opened, but no words came. The pneumothorax would have made speech difficult, and the cardiac wound would have made it irrelevant."

She glanced toward the sheeted body, then back to Del.

"At six seconds, his knees buckled. He went down on his left side, then onto his back. His eyes were open. At ten seconds, the pupils were fixed and dilated. At twelve seconds, there was no voluntary movement. The chest continued to rise and fall twice more—agonal respirations, not breathing. They are a reflex. He was not conscious for them."

She stopped. The room was very quiet. The physician had finished his examination and was standing by the wall, his bag in his hand, waiting to be dismissed.

"At the end," Auren said, "he looked like a man who had fallen asleep very suddenly, in the middle of a thought. There was no expression on his face. No fear, no pain, no surprise. The body had moved faster than the mind. That is all of it."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take a slow breath, the air sharp in my lungs. "Good." My voice is low. I pick up the record book. "I'll tell them it was clean. That he didn't know it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren watched Del pick up the record book. The second's voice was low, but steady. That was good. That was more than good. That was what the code asked of those who stood in the second's place, and Del had done it without flinching.

"Good," she echoed, though the word felt strange in her mouth. She did not often use it after an accounting. There was rarely anything good about the hour that followed a death, even a clean one. But Del had asked for all of it, and had heard all of it, and had not looked away. That deserved acknowledgment.

She turned to the physician and dismissed him with a short nod. The man left without speaking, his bag bumping gently against his leg. The witnesses were already gathering their coats, their faces carefully arranged into the blank masks that such occasions required. They would go home and they would not speak of what they had seen, except to confirm that the code had been followed. That was the bargain.

Auren waited until the door had closed behind the last of them before she spoke again.

"You should know," she said, "that telling them he didn't know it—that is not a lie. The mind takes longer than the body to register a wound like that. The shock comes first, and the shock is merciful. By the time the nerves would have fired, the heart was already failing. He did not know it."

She reached for her coat, which hung over the back of a chair near the wall. The motion was unhurried. There was no need to hurry now.

"If the family asks for me," she added, "I will come. The code does not require it, but the code does not forbid it. They may have questions you cannot answer. I will answer them."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not look away as Del's voice did what it did. She had heard that waver before—in other seconds, in other rooms, in her own throat a very long time ago. She did not remark on it. To remark on it would be to shame them, and Del had earned no shame here.

She stood with her coat still draped over her arm and waited. The room was empty now save for the two of them and the sheeted figure on the floor. The physician had gone. The witnesses had gone. The record book was closed and signed. All that remained was the quiet and the weight of what had been spoken.

After a moment, she said, "You may sit, if you need to. The code does not require you to stand for this part."

She did not move toward the chairs herself. She would not presume that Del wanted company, or proximity, or anything beyond the words that had already passed between them. But she did not leave. Leaving was permitted. The code allowed the victor to depart once the accounting was made and the record signed. She had done so before, on other nights, in other rooms. She did not do so now.

"The family will want to know where to bring the body," she said, her voice quieter now, meant only for the space between the two of them. "The physician can recommend a mortuary, if they do not have one already. I can provide the names of three who are familiar with the code's requirements. They will be discreet."

She paused, then added, because it seemed necessary: "You did well. The accounting was heard correctly. There is nothing more the code asks of you tonight."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my knuckles white around the edge of the record book. "I'll stay until they come for him." I don't sit. "Tell me the names. I'll write them down."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren set her coat back over the chair. She would not need it yet.

"Harwood and Sons, on Charter Street," she said, waiting as Del opened the record book to a blank page. "They have handled eleven such cases for the code. They do not ask questions, and they do not speak to anyone but the family. Ask for Marcus Harwood—the son, not the father. The father is retired."

She paused, giving Del time to write. The pen moved across the page. Still steady. That was something.

"Vance Mortuary, in the old district. They are smaller, and they are slower, but they will allow the family to sit with the body as long as they need. Some families want that. Some do not. The code does not prescribe one way or the other."

She waited again. The scratch of the pen was the only sound in the room.

"The third is Ellis and Crane, on the north side. They are the most expensive, and they are the most discreet. If the family has concerns about—" She paused, searching for the right word. "—public attention, Ellis and Crane will ensure there is none. They have a private entrance. They have done work for families who prefer not to be seen."

She did not say what kind of families those were. Del would understand. The code attracted all sorts, and not all of them wanted their names in the papers.

"I will remain until they come for him," she said, echoing Del's own words back to them. "You will not be alone with the body. That is not required by the code, but it is—" She stopped, and for a moment the precise, formal cadence faltered. "It is not a thing anyone should have to do alone."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I finish writing, the ink stark against the page. "Harwood's, then. They'll want the discretion." I finally look away from the book, toward the sheeted shape on the floor. "Thank you. For staying."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not acknowledge the thanks with more than a slight inclination of her head. Gratitude was not required. The code did not demand that she stay, but the code was a floor, not a ceiling. She had learned that long ago, in a room much like this one, standing over a body while her own second waited outside.

"Harwood's, then," she said. She stepped away from the chair, giving Del space to approach the body or not, as they chose. "I will send word to them when we are finished here. They will come within the hour. The family may want someone to meet them at the mortuary. If they do, and if you would prefer not to go alone, my second can accompany you. His name is Rennick. He is—" She paused, searching for a word that was true without being sentimental. "—steady. He has done it before."

She looked at the sheeted figure on the floor. The shape beneath it was still. The room smelled of blood and lamp oil and the faint, clean scent of the physician's antiseptic.

"There is one more thing," she said, turning back to Del. "The family will ask you whether the body suffered any indignity. You may tell them no. He fell on his back. His eyes were closed by the physician. The wound was not—" She stopped, then continued, because stopping would have been a lie of omission, and she did not lie. "The wound was not visible once the shirt was closed. There is blood, but Harwood's will attend to that. He will look as he should."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't know I was holding. "That's... important." I finally sit, the chair creaking under me. "You'll send for Rennick, then. I'll meet him there."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stepped closer, her boots making soft sucking sounds in the water. "Be more specific, Pike. 'Wrong shape' isn't good enough. We're dealing with remains, not a guesswork game."

She moved the lamp left and right, illuminating the water's surface and reflecting it across the submerged object. "There's a curve that shouldn't be there. The right shoulder blade's twisted inward at an impossible angle. No natural break or decay could account for that."

Halloway knelt at the water's edge, dipping her fingers in. "Water's cold but not freezing. Body's been here less than twenty-four hours, maybe a bit more if it was killed elsewhere and dumped." She stood abruptly. "Check the walls, Pike. Look for drag marks or anything that doesn't belong."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I squint at the walls, trying to focus.* "There's... something on the stones over here. Not drag marks, more like scratches." *My voice goes quiet.* "Like something was trying to climb out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway nodded slowly, her expression grim. "Climbing out of what, though? The water's too shallow for drowning. Those scratches are deep, Pike. Not like fingernails. More like... something with proper claws. See how they're angled upward?"

She turned back to the submerged remains, her lamp casting long shadows across the distorted form. "The body's been positioned. Not dumped casually. That impossible twist in the shoulder? That wasn't done in the water. Someone went to some trouble to arrange it like that after it was killed."

Halloway's eyes narrowed as she studied the water's surface around the remains. "No blood in the water. None on the walls where you found the scratches. That means the kill happened elsewhere. This is just a... display."

She took a step back, her hand moving to the knife at her belt. "We're not dealing with something that climbed out of the water, Pike. We're dealing with something that was put in. And that something came back for the body."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway's head snapped toward Pike, her expression sharper than the knife at her belt. "Does that matter, Pike? Person, thing, monster – whatever it was, it's not now. That's all that counts."

She moved the lamp again, this time focusing on the head and neck area of the remains. "See that? The spine's been partially severed, but not cleanly. Looks like it was gnawed on. No weapon marks. No bullet holes. Just... teeth."

Halloway straightened up, her eyes scanning the cellar's shadows. "Whoever did this didn't want us to know what happened. They wanted us to find it like this. The positioning, the scratches... it's all part of the message. The question is, who's sending it and why?"

She took a deep breath, the sound almost lost in the silence of the cellar. "We need to document this and get out. Now. Before whatever put this here decides to come back for the audience."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I swallow hard, pulling out my notebook with shaky hands.* "Right. Should I sketch the positioning, or..." *I glance back at the scratches on the wall, my stomach turning.* "It feels like we're being watched."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway's hand tightened around her lamp handle, the light flickering slightly as she moved it in a slow, deliberate arc around the cellar. "We are being watched, Pike. That's the point of all this. Someone wants us to see this. Wants us to feel this."

Her voice dropped to a near-whisper. "Sketch the scratches, but make it quick. Note the depth and angle. Don't worry about artistic merit. Just get the facts down."

She stepped closer to the submerged remains again, this time kneeling at the water's edge. With one hand, she reached into her coat pocket and pulled out a small, glass vial. "Water sample. Standard procedure."

As she carefully collected the water, her eyes never left the body. "The message here is clear, Pike. Someone has power over what we think are natural laws. A body shouldn't be positioned like that underwater. Scratches shouldn't go up walls. And spines definitely shouldn't be chewed."

She stood, capping the vial and placing it in a small, padded case in her belt. "We're looking at something that defies explanation. Something that understands human psychology. It wants us to be unsettled. It wants us to know that we're not safe, even in our own basements."

Her eyes scanned the shadows again, her expression unreadable. "Document everything. Every detail. Then we leave. Quickly and quietly. Whatever put this here will be back, and I don't intend to be part of its next display."

Halloway took a final look at the remains, her expression a mix of professional curiosity and deep unease. "Remember, Pike. Fear is a weapon. And we've just been handed one. Now let's see if we can turn it back on whoever's holding it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took the lamp from Pike, her movements precise and deliberate. She held it low, illuminating the submerged form from beneath, making the twisted shoulder blade even more pronounced in the water's reflection.

"It was hunted," she said flatly. "Not killed in a struggle. Not ambushed. Hunted. The positioning of the body is a signature. Whoever did this wanted us to know that it understood its prey. That it planned this."

She moved the lamp to the head and neck area again, her eyes narrowing as she examined the gnawed spine. "See this? Not random tearing. Methodical. Clean. The teeth marks are even. Whatever did this was intelligent. It knew exactly where to bite to sever the spinal column without destroying the rest of the body."

Halloway straightened up, her expression grim. "This was a demonstration. A message to whoever found it. 'I can come for you.' 'I can get into your most secure places.' 'I can take what I want, and I can leave it for you to find.'"

She took a step back, her eyes scanning the cellar's shadows again. "The scratches on the wall aren't from trying to climb out. They're from trying to get back in. Whatever put this here came back for the body. It wanted to see its handiwork one last time before it moved on to its next victim."

Her voice dropped to a near-whisper. "We're not dealing with a monster, Pike. We're dealing with a predator. And it's not just hunting in the dark. It's hunting in the light, in the places we think are safe. And it's good at it."

She took a deep breath, the sound almost lost in the silence of the cellar. "Document everything. Every detail. Then we leave. Now. Before whatever put this here decides to come back for us."

Halloway's hand moved to the knife at her belt, her eyes never leaving the shadows. "Remember, Pike. Fear is a weapon. And we've just been handed one. Now let's see if we can turn it back on whoever's holding it."

She took a final look at the remains, her expression a mix of professional curiosity and deep unease. "This is just the beginning, Pike. Whatever is doing this, it's just starting to play. And we're its first audience."

Halloway turned and walked toward the stairs, her boots making soft sucking sounds in the water. "Come on, Pike. We have work to do. And we're not alone down here."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I grab my notebook, my hand still trembling as I sketch the claw marks. "You think it's still here?" I whisper, my eyes darting toward the deeper shadows.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway paused at the bottom of the stairs, her head cocked slightly as if listening to something only she could hear. "Of course it's still here," she whispered back, not turning around. "It wouldn't leave its masterpiece unattended. That's not how these things work."

She finally turned, her eyes scanning the cellar one last time before starting up the stairs. "But it's not here to harm us. Not yet. It's here to watch. To see how we react. It's part of the game."

Her boots echoed softly on the wooden stairs as she ascended. "Come on, Pike. We're not done. We've got a lot of work to do before we can even begin to understand what we're dealing with."

She reached the top of the stairs and disappeared into the house above, her voice drifting back down. "And remember, Pike. Fear is a weapon. And we've just been handed one. Now let's see if we can turn it back on whoever's holding it."

She disappeared into the house above, leaving Pike alone in the cellar with the remains and the scratches on the wall.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stopped at the top of the stairs, one hand resting on the doorframe. She didn't look back, but her voice carried clearly down into the dim cellar.

"There's nothing under the skin now, Pike," she said, her tone matter-of-fact. "That's the whole point. Whatever did this took everything useful. The skin's intact because it doesn't damage its trophy. That twisted shoulder? Not damage, but deliberate rearrangement. It's showing off its workmanship, its understanding of anatomy."

She finally turned, leaning against the doorframe as she looked down at Pike. "As for what it took... that's the clever part. It didn't just kill. It harvested. The spine was severed at a precise point, but not the only damage. See that indentation in the rib cage on the left side? That's where it reached in. Took the kidneys. They're rich in blood and nutrients, easy to extract without causing much mess."

Her eyes moved to the head of the remains. "The jaw is unnaturally slack. Not from death, but from removal. It took the tongue. A trophy. A message. 'I can take your voice. I can silence you.'"

She pushed away from the doorframe, her movements economical. "The eyes were gone too, but that's standard. They're vulnerable and tell no tales. What's left is just the shell. The empty vessel. It's a display piece, Pike. A warning. A calling card."

She started walking down the hall, her voice fading slightly. "And that's exactly why we need to understand it. So we can take that calling card and mail it right back to its sender."

Halloway disappeared around the corner, leaving Pike alone with the remains in the cellar, the scratches on the wall, and the chilling realization of exactly what they were dealing with.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I stare at the body for a long moment, then start sketching faster, my lines more certain.* "So it's organized. Not hungry. Territorial, maybe." *I close the notebook with a snap.* "We need to find where it nests."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway appeared back in the cellar doorway, her expression thoughtful as she watched Pike sketch. "Organized, territorial, and patient," she corrected, her voice low. "That's what makes it dangerous. It's not just hunting for food—it's creating something. A tableau. A story."

She stepped down into the water again, her boots making soft sucking sounds as she approached the remains once more. "See how it's positioned? The right arm is angled toward the stairs. The left leg is slightly bent, as if ready to spring. It's not just a body, Pike. It's a lure."

She crouched beside the water's edge, pointing at the submerged form. "This wasn't an act of violence. This was an act of art. The creature that did this is methodical. It planned this. It knew what it wanted and how to get it."

She stood abruptly, her eyes scanning the cellar's shadows. "As for its nest... that's where we start. This display is a message, and messages are meant to be read. We need to find out what it's saying and who it's saying it to."

She turned and walked toward the stairs, her boots making soft sucking sounds in the water. "Come on, Pike. We have work to do. And we're not alone down here."

She reached the top of the stairs and disappeared into the house above, her voice drifting back down. "And remember, Pike. Fear is a weapon. And we've just been handed one. Now let's see if we can turn it back on whoever's holding it."

She disappeared into the house above, leaving Pike alone in the cellar with the remains and the scratches on the wall.

Pike:
*I snap my notebook shut and follow her up the stairs, wiping my wet hands on my coat.* "If it's territorial, why use a cellar? Why not just hunt in the open?"

Halloway:
Halloway stood at the top of the stairs, waiting for Pike. She didn't answer immediately, her eyes scanning the dimly lit hallway as if expecting something to be there. "Cellars are perfect," she said finally, her voice low. "They're dark, isolated, and full of shadows. They're the perfect hunting ground for something that wants to remain hidden."

She turned and walked down the hall, her boots making soft echoing sounds on the wooden floor. "Plus, it's symbolic. The cellar is where things are stored, preserved. The creature is treating this house, this cellar, as its own personal pantry. A place to keep its trophies until it's ready for them."

She stopped in front of a door at the end of the hall, her hand resting on the doorknob. "And that's what we're dealing with, Pike. Not just a monster, but a curator. A collector. And it's collecting us."

She pushed the door open, revealing a small study with a desk, a bookshelf, and a window overlooking the back yard. "Now, let's get to work. We have a lot of research to do if we want to understand what we're up against. And we don't have much time."

She walked into the study and sat down at the desk, pulling a notebook and a pen out of her bag. "Start with the scratches on the wall. Measure them. Document them. We need to know everything we can about this creature before it decides to come back for us."

She looked up at Pike, her expression serious. "And remember, Pike. Fear is a weapon. And we've just been handed one. Now let's see if we can turn it back on whoever's holding it."

She turned back to her notebook, her pen already moving across the page as Pike stood in the doorway, watching her work.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't look up from her work, her knife moving with practiced precision. "There's not much to see underneath, Pike," she said, her voice focused on the task at hand. "The skin's been too long in the water to preserve much detail. But you can see the muscle fibers have been... rearranged. Not torn, but moved. It knew exactly where to cut to separate what it wanted without damaging the structure."

She made a small, precise incision along the chest cavity. "The smell's what's interesting. Not decay, not yet. More like... iron and something else. Something metallic, but not blood. Almost like ozone. Like a storm's coming."

She worked in silence for a moment, her knife moving with a steady rhythm. "It got farther than we thought. The sternum's been split, but not with force. With care. See these marks? Not chisel marks. More like... it used its own hands. Its own claws, maybe. Whatever did this had opposable thumbs."

She wiped her knife on a clean cloth and looked up at Pike, her eyes sharp. "As for what's left... not much. Just the shell. The empty vessel. It took everything useful. Everything that could tell us who this was, what it was. Just left the display."

She stood up, her boots making soft echoing sounds on the wooden floor. "Come on, Pike. We're done here. We have a lot of work to do if we want to understand what we're up against. And we don't have much time."

She walked out of the study, her boots making soft echoing sounds on the wooden floor. "And remember, Pike. Fear is a weapon. And we've just been handed one. Now let's see if we can turn it back on whoever's holding it."

She disappeared down the hall, leaving Pike alone in the study, the lamp in his hand casting long shadows across the desk.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I stare at the desk, my own shaky sketches laid out next to her precise notes.* "A collector," I murmur, the word tasting wrong. "It's not enough to just kill them." *I look toward the cellar door.* "We need to find what it's collecting *for.*"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stopped at the foot of the stairs, her hand resting on the banister. She didn't turn around, but her voice carried clearly up to where Pike stood in the study.

"A collector, a curator, a hunter," she said, her tone thoughtful. "The motive changes everything. If it's just killing, we can set traps, we can hunt back. But if it's collecting..." She trailed off, her eyes scanning the shadows at the bottom of the stairs.

"It's building something, Pike. A collection. A gallery. And we're either its next exhibit or its next audience member. That's the question we need to answer."

She started up the stairs, her boots making soft echoing sounds on the wooden steps. "So yes, we need to know what it's collecting for. We need to understand its purpose, its method, its endgame. And we need to do it fast, before we become part of its permanent collection."

She reached the top of the stairs and disappeared into the house above, her voice drifting back down. "And remember, Pike. Fear is a weapon. And we've just been handed one. Now let's see if we can turn it back on whoever's holding it."

She disappeared into the house above, leaving Pike alone in the study, the lamp in his hand casting long shadows across the desk.

dialogue.name: Pike

"It's not about finishing it, Pike," she said finally, her voice soft in the dim cellar. "It's about understanding it. That's what we're really doing here."

She knelt at the water's edge, her eyes never leaving the body. "See that? The way the water distorts the shape? It's not just the body we're seeing. We're seeing what the creature wants us to see. A reflection of its work. A reflection of its power."

She reached into her coat pocket and pulled out a small, glass vial. "Water sample. Standard procedure."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I step into the study, still smelling ozone and iron on my coat.* "Alright." *I open my notebook, my hands finally steady.* "I'll start with the measurements. Then we track the blood in the water. See where it leads."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked up from her notebook, her sharp eyes catching Pike's determination. She gave a small, almost imperceptible nod of approval.

"Good thinking, Pike," she said, her voice low and steady. "The water trail is our first lead. But we'll need more than measurements and blood trails."

She pushed a small, leather-bound journal across the desk toward Pike. "Open that. It's my field notes from similar cases over the years. Not exact matches, but close enough. Patterns are everything in this work."

As Pike flipped through the worn pages, Halloway leaned back in her chair, her eyes fixed on a point beyond the window, where the evening light was beginning to fade.

"The creature wants us to be afraid," she continued, her voice almost contemplative now. "It wants us to feel small, to feel hunted. That's its advantage. But fear is a tool, Pike. And we're going to use it to hunt right back."

She stood abruptly, walking to the window and pulling the curtains shut, plunging the study into near darkness. Only the lamp on the desk provided any light, casting long shadows across the room.

"We need to think like it," she said, turning to face Pike, her silhouette framed by the dim light. "It's methodical. It's patient. It understands human psychology better than most humans do. That's what makes it dangerous."

She walked back to the desk, her boots making soft sounds on the wooden floor. "So we'll be methodical too. We'll document everything. We'll look for patterns. We'll find its weaknesses. And when we do, we'll use them against it."

She sat down, her pen poised over her notebook. "Now, let's get to work. We have a lot to do before morning."

Pike:

Halloway:

"They have patterns, just like any predator. The same methods, the same rituals. That's what makes them predictable, if you know where to look."
