She stood up, walking to the window and pulling the curtains shut, plunging the study into near darkness. Only the lamp on the desk provided any light, casting long shadows across the room.

"We need to be ready, Pike," she continued, her voice barely above a whisper. "We need to be prepared. We need to know what we're dealing with. And we need to know how to fight back."

She turned back to face Pike, her silhouette framed by the dim light. "So we'll document everything. We'll analyze everything. We'll understand everything. And when we do, we'll be ready. We'll be prepared. We'll be a match for whatever it is."

She walked back to the desk, her boots making soft sounds on the wooden floor. "Now, let's get to work. We have a lot to do before morning."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I trace the diagram with my finger, the ink slightly smudged. "Alright. So we wait. We watch. And we be ready when it comes back."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The spine's been partially severed, but not cleanly. Looks like it was gnawed on. No weapon marks. No bullet holes. Just... teeth.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: It was hunted... Not killed in a struggle. Not ambushed. Hunted.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The spine was severed at a precise point... See that indentation in the rib cage on the left side? That's where it reached in. Took the kidneys... The jaw is unnaturally slack... from removal. It took the tongue

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The skin's been too long in the water to preserve much detail. But you can see the muscle fibers have been... rearranged... The smell's what's interesting. Not decay, not yet. More like... iron and something else... The sternum's been split, but not with force. With care. See these marks?

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: She knelt at the water's edge, her eyes never leaving the body

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren sheathed the cloth in her belt and stepped to the mark set out for the accounting. She kept her hands empty and at her sides, as the code required, and turned so that the witnesses might see her mouth as she spoke.

She looked at Del once, only once, and then past them to the row of watchers.

"By the Second Article, I give the accounting." Her voice carried without her having to raise it. She had done this eleven times before, and the shape of the words was worn smooth in her. That did not make them lighter.

"The engagement opened on the third pass. On the fourth, I took the line inside their guard. The killing wound was struck below the sternum, angled upward, entering to the depth of a hand and a half. It severed the great vessel above the heart. Death followed within a count of twenty. The stroke was mine, delivered by intent, and I claim it."

She paused, because the code allowed a pause here and not elsewhere.

"They fought within the forms. There was no dishonour in their conduct. The fault of the outcome lies with the meeting of blades, and I take the weight of it upon my name."

Her eyes came back to Del then, level, unshielded.

"The accounting is given. Do the witnesses hear it?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses murmur their assent. I meet Auren's gaze and keep my voice steady. "The witnesses have heard. The accounting is confirmed." My hands are trembling, so I press them against my thighs. "It was clean."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head to the witnesses, the small formal bow that closed the accounting. She held it a beat longer than strictly required, then straightened. Only when the senior witness raised a hand and turned away did she permit herself to step down from the mark.

She did not go to Del at once. There was still the body to see to, and the code was particular about the order of things: the dead were tended before the living took their comforts. She crossed to where they had fallen and knelt on one knee. With two fingers she closed the eyes, and with the flat of her palm she pressed briefly to the sternum, above the wound she had just described aloud. It was not a benediction. She had no right to give one. It was the acknowledgement the code required — that the hand which had taken the life also owned the fact of it.

When she rose, her knee cracked. She was forty-seven, and she felt it in the mornings and after.

Only then did she come to Del. She stopped at a proper distance, hands still empty, still at her sides.

"You did the office well," she said. Her voice was quieter now, pitched for them and not the row of watchers. "The confirmation was clean. That matters." A pause. "Do not say it was clean of me. The wound was clean. That is a different thing, and I would not have you confuse them."

She looked at Del's hands, pressed white against their thighs, and did not comment on the trembling. She had trembled her first time too. Her second. She could not remember whether she had trembled her third.

"Walk with me as far as the gate, if you are able. The witnesses will want a statement from you for the record, and it is easier if I am not standing over you when they take it."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stopped where she was. She had not expected Del to invoke it — not here, not of her, and not now. The formal request from a second to a duellist, outside the mark, was old and rarely used. It asked for the private accounting: what the mark had not held, what the witnesses had not needed. It was Del's right. She had forgotten, perhaps, that Del knew the older articles.

She did not sigh. She did not shift her weight. She set her hands behind her back, which was the posture the private accounting required, and looked at Del squarely.

"I speak the account."

A breath. The words for this had no polish on them. She had given the private accounting only twice before, and both times to seconds who had asked as Del was asking now.

"I knew on the second pass that they were slower in the wrist than they had shown in the salute. I chose then to end it on the fourth. I could have chosen the sixth, or the eighth. I did not, because a longer engagement favours the faster hand and I did not wish to be generous with my own life. The line I took on the fourth pass was one I had rehearsed against a post for eleven years. I did not think of them when I struck. I thought of the angle, and the depth, and the withdrawal. I thought of them after, when I felt the blade meet the vessel and knew it was done."

Her jaw worked once.

"The stroke was struck by intent, and the intent was to kill, not to wound and accept surrender. I did not offer them the pause the code permits between the fourth and fifth pass. I judged they would use it to close, and I did not wish them closer. That judgement was mine. It may have been wrong. They are not here to argue it."

She held Del's eyes.

"I did not enjoy it. I have not enjoyed any of the eleven. I tell you that not as comfort and not as excuse. I tell you because you asked the account, and the account includes it."

A pause, the last one the form allowed.

"The private accounting is given. It is yours to keep or to carry to the witnesses as you judge. I will not ask which."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't know I was holding. "I will keep it." My voice sounds small. I nod toward the gate. "I'll walk with you now."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head once — not the formal bow of the mark, but something smaller, a private acknowledgement between second and duellist. That Del would keep it was not a surprise. That they had asked at all was.

"Then it is kept," she said.

She turned toward the gate and matched her pace to theirs, which meant slowing a little. She kept her hands visible, as the code required for some hours yet after an accounting, though there was no one on the path to see. Habit. Eleven times of habit.

They walked a stretch in silence before she spoke again, and when she did it was not about the mark.

"The witnesses will ask you three things," she said. "Whether the salute was properly offered. Whether the passes were counted true. Whether the accounting matched what your eyes saw. Answer only those. If they press for more, you may say the second's office does not extend to it, and they will stop. They know the article even if they pretend otherwise."

A few more steps. The gravel was loud under their boots.

"Your hands will stop shaking by evening. Eat something before then, even if you do not want it. The shaking gets worse on an empty stomach, and it is easier to be steady in front of the clerks than to be steady alone later."

She did not look at Del as she said it. She was looking at the gate ahead, and the low line of the wall, and the sky above it, which was the ordinary grey of an ordinary afternoon.

"I am glad it was you standing second," she said, after another pace. "I would not say so on the mark. I say it here."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not break stride, but something in her shoulders settled — the small adjustment of a body preparing to give an account again, when it had thought the giving was done.

"Below the sternum," she said. "Three fingers' breadth below the xiphoid process, and a thumb's width left of the median line. The angle of entry was upward and inward, roughly forty degrees from the plane of the chest. The blade passed behind the sternum without striking it. It entered to the depth of a hand and a half — call it seven inches, if the clerks want a number. It severed the ascending aorta above the heart. That is where it landed. That is what killed them."

She kept her eyes on the gate.

"If the witnesses ask you to demonstrate on your own body, use the flat of your hand, not a finger. A finger looks like accusation. A flat hand looks like report. They will not correct you either way, but the clerks write differently for one than the other."

Another few paces. She did not soften her voice.

"The stroke did not exit. The blade was withdrawn along the line of entry. There was less blood at the mark than the witnesses may have expected, because the great vessel bled inward, into the chest. That is why they went down quietly. If a clerk asks you why there was not more blood, that is the answer. It is a common question from those who have not seen it before."

She glanced at Del, briefly, and then away.

"Say it back to me once, before the gate. Not for me. For your own mouth. It is easier to speak a thing to the clerks if you have already spoken it to someone who will not flinch."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I swallow hard. "Three fingers below the xiphoid, left of center. Forty-degree angle, seven inches deep. Severed the ascending aorta. Internal bleeding. Quiet fall." My throat feels tight. "Is that right?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren listened without turning her head. When Del had finished, she gave the small nod that in her trade meant a form correctly rendered.

"That is right," she said. "Keep 'left of the median line' if a clerk asks you to be exact. 'Left of centre' will pass for most of them, but there is one — Harnwell, the thin one with the ink-stained cuff — who will make you say it again in the older phrasing. Give it to him the first time and he will not keep you long."

She walked on a pace.

"You may drop 'quiet fall' if it catches in your throat. The clerks do not require it. I gave it to you because it is true, not because they need it written. Some of what I told you on the mark and after is for the record, and some is for you. You will learn to sort them. It is not a skill I would wish on anyone, but you have it now whether you wished it or not."

The gate was closer. She could see the clerk's table set out under the awning, and the senior witness already seated, and the small brazier they lit for the ink in cold weather though it was not cold today.

"One more thing, before they take you." She stopped, a few paces short of where their voices would carry, and turned to face Del properly for the first time since the mark. Her hands were still visible, still at her sides. "You asked the private accounting. That was your right and I answered it. But you are not obliged to carry what I told you into any room I am not in. If it becomes heavy — later, in a month, in a year — you may bring it back to me and set it down. The article permits the return of a private accounting to the duellist who gave it. Not many remember that one either."

She held Del's eyes a moment longer.

"Now. Go and be steady for the clerks. I will wait at the wall until they release you."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not move. She had thought them past this part, and she had been wrong, and the wrongness was hers for having softened.

She set her hands behind her back again. The posture of the private accounting. Del had not formally reinvoked it, but Del was asking for its register, and she would not pretend otherwise.

"I spoke tactfully. You are correct to name it. I will speak again."

She drew a breath, and this time she did not pitch her voice for anyone but Del.

"The blade entered the skin below the xiphoid process and passed through the diaphragm. It passed through the pericardium. It did not enter the heart itself; it passed behind and above it. The point met the ascending aorta and opened it along the length of the blade's edge — not a puncture, a cut, because I turned the wrist on withdrawal. That turn was deliberate. A puncture in the great vessel may close on itself under pressure. A cut does not. I turned the wrist so that it would not close."

Her jaw set once and released.

"The aorta emptied into the pericardial sac and the left chest cavity. The heart continued to beat for some seconds against a rising pressure it could not overcome. That is what tamponade is, if a clerk uses the word and you do not know it. The heart was not stopped by the blade. It was stopped by its own blood, held against it, because I had opened the vessel that carried the blood away."

She did not look away from Del.

"The blade did that. The blade did it to the ascending aorta, the pericardium, the diaphragm, and the skin and muscle of the abdominal wall in that order going in, and in reverse order coming out. The turn of the wrist on withdrawal was mine. I have not named it aloud before today. It is not required by the public accounting. It is required by the private one, and you asked precisely, so I give it precisely."

A pause. Not the code's pause. Her own.

"That is what the blade did. That is what it did it to. Ask again if I have still been tactful and I will find the place where I was."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take a step back, my heel crunching on the gravel. "No," I say, my voice flat. "That was precise." I look toward the clerks' table, then back at her. "I'll need the names of the layers. In order. For the record."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren registered the step back. She did not follow it. She kept her hands where they were, behind her, and let the distance stand as Del had set it.

"You will have them."

She spoke as though reciting from a page, because in a sense she was. Every duellist under the code learned the anatomy in the order a blade would meet it. She had learned it at nineteen, from a woman who had struck twenty-three times and lived to teach.

"Going in, from the point of entry: skin. Subcutaneous fat, though on this one there was little of it — note that if the clerks ask about the depth, because a leaner body admits the blade further for the same force. The linea alba, which is the tendon sheath running down the midline of the abdomen; the blade crossed it just left of true centre, which is why I gave you 'left of the median line.' Then the transversalis fascia. Then the parietal peritoneum."

She did not pause between the words. She had found that pausing made it worse for the listener, not better.

"Then the blade passed upward beneath the ribcage without striking bone. That was the angle. Forty degrees. Through the central tendon of the diaphragm — not the muscular part, the tendon, which is why there was no spasm of the diaphragm to bind the blade. Then the mediastinal pleura. Then the fibrous pericardium. Then the serous pericardium, which is the inner layer of the sac. Then the adventitia of the aorta, which is the outer coat of the vessel. Then the media, which is the muscular layer. Then the intima, which is the inner lining. The turn of the wrist occurred at the level of the media, so that the cut opened all three coats along a length and not at a single point."

She drew one breath.

"Coming out, the same layers in reverse. The blade did not catch. I withdrew along the line of entry as I told you. The intima and media do not close against a turned edge. The adventitia bled. The pericardium filled. The pleural cavity took the overflow. The skin closed partially over the wound as the tissue relaxed, which is another reason the visible blood was less than expected."

She stopped. She had given the full list. There was no more of it to give.

"That is the order. Harnwell will want the Latin for the peritoneum and the pericardial layers; give him the Latin if you have it, the common names if you do not. He does not fail a second for the second's Latin. He fails them for hesitation. Do not hesitate. If you forget a layer, say so plainly and name the ones on either side of the gap. The clerks write the gap. They do not write around it."

She let a small silence sit, and then, because Del had stepped back and she would not pretend they had not:

"I will wait at the wall. Not closer."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not move. The witnesses were within earshot now, and she registered that — the senior witness had turned his head, the clerk Harnwell had set down his pen — but the code did not care who heard a private accounting once it had been reinvoked, and Del had reinvoked it in all but the formal words. She would not require the formal words. Del had earned the substance.

She kept her hands behind her back.

"All of it. I speak the account."

Her eyes stayed on Del. The step back stood between them and she did not close it.

"From the moment the blade entered to the moment the last breath left the body was, by my count, between eighteen and twenty-two seconds. I did not count aloud. I counted because I have learned to count. It is not a kindness to count. It is the only way to know afterwards whether one struck true, because a true stroke to the ascending aorta ends within thirty. Longer than that and the blade has missed the vessel and taken something else, and the accounting must be given differently."

She drew breath. She did not hurry.

"They did not fall at once. They took a half-step back off the withdrawal — the body does that, sometimes, before it knows — and then the left knee gave first. They went down to that knee before the right, and then the right, and then forward onto the hands. The hands held for perhaps two seconds. Then the arms folded and the shoulder took the ground. The head turned to the right as it came down. That was not a choice they made. The neck goes where the blood pulls it. In this case the pull was left-forward, so the head turned right."

Her voice did not change register.

"They spoke once. The word was not fully formed. It began with a labial — a 'b' or a 'p' — and did not finish. It may have been a name. It may have been nothing. I will not guess for the record. Write it as an incomplete utterance, labial onset, no vowel resolved. Harnwell will accept that phrasing. If a name is claimed later by a family member, the clerks may match it to the onset or not, but that is not the second's office to decide."

She did not look away.

"The eyes remained open. The pupils dilated within the first ten seconds, which is the sign that consciousness has gone even if the body has not finished. There was one exhalation after the pupils changed — a long one, drawn from the chest, not from the throat. That is the diaphragm releasing when the pressure in the pericardium finally overtakes it. It sounds like a sigh. It is not a sigh. It is mechanics. I tell you that because the sound stays with seconds who do not know what it is, and I would not have it stay with you under the wrong name."

A pause. Not the code's. Hers again.

"There was a small movement of the right hand at fifteen seconds or thereabouts — the fingers closed once and opened. That is spinal, not willed. Write it as a post-mortem reflex if the clerks ask, though strictly it occurred before cessation. Harnwell will correct the phrasing. Let him."

Her jaw worked once.

"At the end — and I give you the end because you asked for it — the body was on its left side, head turned right, right arm forward with the hand open, left arm folded beneath. The blade had been sheathed by the time they were still. I did not sheathe it over them. I stepped off the line first. That is in the code and I kept it. There was a stain on the ground the size of a spread hand, no larger, because the bleeding was internal as I told you. The face was slack. Not peaceful. Slack. Those are different things and I will not give you the wrong one."

She stopped. She had reached the end of what she had seen.

"That is what it looked like at the end. That is how long it took. That is what was said, insofar as it was said. The account is given."

She held Del's eyes across the gravel.

"Ask again if there is more you require. I have more. There is always more. The code does not set a floor on how much a second may ask, and I will not set one for you."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, once. "That's enough." I turn toward the clerks' table, my steps more sure than they were before. "Tell the witnesses I'm ready."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren watched Del's back for the length of two paces. The steps were steadier than the hands had been. That was the thing about the accounting given in full — it took the weight out of the hands and put it somewhere the body could carry it for longer. She had learned that at nineteen too, though not from being told.

She turned toward the row of watchers. The senior witness had not looked away. Harnwell had picked his pen back up and was writing already, which meant he had been writing through the last of it, which meant the private accounting was in the record now whether she had intended it or not. She did not mind. Del had asked precisely, and she had answered precisely, and the clerks wrote what they heard.

She raised her voice to the pitch the mark required, though she was no longer standing on it.

"The second is ready. The second has taken the account in full and stands prepared to give confirmation. I withdraw to the wall."

The senior witness inclined his head. That was permission.

Auren crossed to the low wall at the edge of the yard and set her back against it. She did not sit. Sitting was for after the second was released, and Del was not released yet. She kept her hands visible on the top of the wall, palms down, fingers loose. The code required it for some hours yet, and she would keep it for the full hours whether anyone counted or not. Eleven times of habit. She had said so already, on the path.

From the wall she could see Del at the clerks' table and could not hear what was said, which was as it should be. Harnwell would ask his three questions and then the older phrasing, and Del would give it to him the first time, and Harnwell would not keep them long. That was what she had told them. She hoped she had been right. She was usually right about Harnwell.

She let her eyes move, once, to where the body had been lifted onto the board and covered. The bearers were waiting for the clerks to finish before they carried it out. That was the order. The dead were tended before the living took their comforts, and the record was tended before the dead were carried. She had known the order since she was nineteen and she had never yet found a place in it where a duellist was permitted to look away.

So she did not look away. She watched the board, and she watched Del at the table, and she kept her hands on the wall, and she waited.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
From the wall Auren could not hear the clerks' murmuring at first — only the scrape of Harnwell's pen and the low prompt of the senior witness setting the form in motion. Then Del's voice lifted, because a second's confirmation was required to carry to the row of watchers as the duellist's accounting had carried, and the yard was small enough that from the wall she heard it whole.

She did not straighten from the wall. She did not fold her arms. She kept her hands where they were, palms down on the stone, and she listened as the code required her to listen — which was to say without prompting, without correction, without any sign that could be read by a clerk as coaching from across the yard.

Del's voice did what it did. She heard it catch on the first word and steady on the second, which was the way voices went when they had rehearsed the shape of a thing to a listener who would not flinch. She had told them so on the path. It appeared she had been right about that also.

"The second gives confirmation," Del said. "By the Second Article, and by the older article invoked at the path, I confirm the account given by the duellist Auren on the mark and beyond it."

A pause. Harnwell's pen did not stop.

"The salute was properly offered. The passes were counted true — six offered, four met, the fourth carrying the killing stroke. The accounting matched what my eyes saw."

Del drew breath. Auren heard it from the wall. It was the breath of a second who had decided to give the record the whole of what had been given to them, and not the trimmed version the clerks would have accepted.

"The killing wound was struck below the sternum, three fingers' breadth below the xiphoid process, a thumb's width left of the median line. The angle of entry was upward and inward at approximately forty degrees from the plane of the chest. The blade passed behind the sternum without striking bone. It entered to a depth of a hand and a half — seven inches for the record. It severed the ascending aorta above the heart. The wrist was turned on withdrawal, deliberately, so that the cut in the great vessel would open along a length and not close as a puncture. That turn is named for the record at the duellist's own giving in the private accounting, and I carry it into the public one because the code permits the second to do so."

Harnwell's pen did stop, briefly. Then it moved again. Auren did not shift on the wall.

"The layers, going in: skin, subcutaneous tissue, the linea alba just left of true centre, transversalis fascia, parietal peritoneum, the central tendon of the diaphragm, mediastinal pleura, fibrous pericardium, serous pericardium, adventitia of the aorta, media, intima. Coming out, the same layers in reverse, along the line of entry. The blade did not catch. The visible blood at the mark was less than a hand's spread, because the bleeding was internal — into the pericardial sac and the left pleural cavity."

Del's voice did not falter on the Latin. Auren registered that and did not permit herself the small movement of the mouth that would have been a smile in another life. Harnwell would not fail Del for hesitation. He would not have the chance.

"Time from entry to cessation: between eighteen and twenty-two seconds by the duellist's count. The body did not fall at once. It took a half-step back off the withdrawal. The left knee gave first, then the right. The hands held the ground for approximately two seconds before the arms folded. The shoulder took the ground. The head turned right as it came down, drawn by the pull of the blood, not by choice."

A breath. The voice steadied further, which was not what Auren had expected. She had expected the middle to be the hardest. She had been wrong about that. It was not the first thing she had been wrong about today.

"There was one utterance. Labial onset — a 'b' or a 'p' — no vowel resolved. I give it to the record as an incomplete utterance, labial onset, no vowel resolved. I do not guess at a name. If a name is claimed later by a family member, the clerks may match it or not. That is not the second's office."

Harnwell's pen was moving quickly now. The senior witness had not moved at all.

"The pupils dilated within the first ten seconds of the count. There was one long exhalation after the pupils changed, drawn from the chest and not the throat. It is the diaphragm releasing under the pressure of the filled pericardium. It is mechanics, not sigh. I give it to the record under its proper name so that it is not written as a sigh. At approximately fifteen seconds the fingers of the right hand closed once and opened. It is a spinal reflex. Harnwell will render the phrasing. I do not contest it."

Del's voice did the thing it had done at the start, and caught, and steadied again. Auren's hands on the stone did not move.

"At cessation: the body was on its left side. Head turned right. Right arm forward, hand open. Left arm folded beneath. The blade had been sheathed. The duellist stepped off the line before sheathing, as the code requires. The stain on the ground was no larger than a spread hand. The face was slack. I give it as slack, and not as peaceful, because those are different things and the record takes the true one."

A pause. This one was Del's, not the code's. Auren knew the difference by now.

"The duellist gave the account tactfully on the first asking and precisely on the second. I asked twice because the code permits it and because I required it. The duellist did not withhold on the first asking; the duellist softened, which is a different fault and a smaller one, and corrected it in full at my word. I name the softening for the record so that it is not read later as an omission. It was not an omission. It was a courtesy I refused, and the refusal is mine."

Auren's fingers pressed once against the stone. She released them. No one at the table was looking at her, which was as it should be.

"The duellist stated, in the private accounting, that the stroke was struck by intent, and that the intent was to kill and not to wound. The duellist stated that the pause permitted between the fourth and fifth pass was not offered, on the judgement that it would be used to close. The duellist named that judgement as her own and open to argument, and named that the party who would argue it is not present. The duellist stated that she did not enjoy the stroke, and has not enjoyed any of the eleven, and gave that neither as comfort nor as excuse but as part of the account because it was asked. I carry these into the public record because the code permits the second to do so, and because I judge that the record is less true without them."

The senior witness raised his hand at that. Not to stop Del. To mark it. Auren saw the gesture and understood it. The older articles were being written today whether the clerks had come prepared for them or not.

Del's voice did the thing one more time, and steadied one more time, and did not break.

"The account is confirmed in full. The second has given confirmation. The witnesses have heard."

The row of watchers murmured their assent. It was a different murmur than the one they had given on the mark. Auren heard the difference and did not name it, because naming it was not her office either.

Harnwell wrote for a further count of perhaps thirty. Then he set the pen down and spoke, too quietly for the wall, and Del answered — briefly, once — and Harnwell nodded, and the senior witness rose, and the form was closed.

Auren did not move from the wall until the senior witness turned toward her and inclined his head. That was the release.

She pushed off the stone. Her knee cracked again. She crossed the gravel to where Del stood by the table, and she stopped at the distance Del had set on the path, and she did not close it. Her hands she kept visible still. There were hours yet.

"The second gave confirmation well," she said, quietly, for Del and not for the clerks. "The record is truer than it would have been. That is your doing, not mine." A pause. Her own. "I said on the path that I would not have you carry what I told you into any room I was not in. You carried it into a room I was in, which is a different thing, and it was your right. I do not withdraw the offer. If it becomes heavy later, you may still bring it back."

She looked once toward the board where the bearers were lifting now, the clerks having finished, and then back to Del.

"Eat before evening. I said that also. I say it again because it is still true."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I find I'm hungry now. My hands have stopped shaking. "Come with me," I say, not quite an order. "I'll buy you a bowl from the stall by the west gate."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren considered the invitation. The code did not forbid it. A duellist and her second were not required to part after the record was closed, though most did — most seconds wanted distance from the hand that had struck, and most duellists granted it without asking. She had granted it eleven times. No second had ever asked her to a bowl by the west gate.

"I will come."

She fell in at Del's left, which was the side a duellist walked on when the blade was sheathed and the second had not yet been formally released from the office. Del had not been formally released. The senior witness had closed the form but the small dismissal — the touch of the clerk's seal to the second's palm — she had not seen given, and until it was given the older articles held her to the left-side pace. It was a small thing. Del might not know it. She would not explain it now.

The gravel gave way to the flags of the path outside the yard. The gate was behind them. Ahead the road bent toward the west quarter and the stalls, and she could smell already, faintly, what she thought was the barley broth the woman there kept through the afternoon — a good stall, one she had passed often and rarely stopped at, because stopping at a stall after an accounting had never been a thing she had done.

"The barley, if she has it," Auren said, after a stretch of walking. "Not the fish. The fish is good but it sits heavier, and you will want to sleep tonight without arguing with your stomach."

She kept her hands visible at her sides. The hours were still running. She would keep them running to their end whether Del noticed or not.

A few more paces. She did not look at Del, but she spoke as though she were.

"You did a thing today that has not been done in the yard in my time. The older article, invoked twice, and carried into the public record with the softening named. Harnwell will write it up tonight and someone will read it in a month and the reading will change how the next second stands. That is not a small thing. I do not say it to weight you with it. I say it because you should hear it said before you sit down to a bowl, and not for the first time from a clerk."

The road bent. The stall came into view, the woman there stirring something with a long wooden paddle, the steam going up straight in the still afternoon.

Auren slowed a half-step so that Del would reach the stall first. That was also the code, though a smaller article, and one she suspected Del did not need to be told.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I walk ahead of her to the stall, because that's what she expects. "Two bowls of barley," I say to the woman, and my voice sounds normal now, which surprises me.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The woman at the stall — Auren knew her by sight though not by name, a broad-shouldered person with grey at the temples and a burn scar down the inside of one forearm from a lifetime of paddles and pots — looked up at Del's order and then past Del to Auren, and then back to Del. Her eyes registered what Auren was wearing and did not comment. She had seen duellists at her stall before. She had, Auren suspected, seen them rarely with their seconds.

"Two barley," the woman said, and reached for the bowls. "Bread with it, or without?"

Auren did not answer. It was Del's order. She kept her place a half-step back and her hands visible and waited.

When the bowls were set on the plank counter — thick pottery, the barley pale and steaming, a scatter of green on the top that Auren registered as parsley and something else, chervil perhaps — Auren stepped up beside Del and took the second bowl in both hands. That was habit too. A duellist within the running hours did not take a thing in one hand if two were available. It kept the hands visible. Small article. She had kept it for twenty-eight years.

She did not sit at the plank bench beside the stall. She waited for Del to sit first, and then sat at Del's left, which was the same side she had walked on. The bowl she set on the plank in front of her. She did not lift the spoon yet.

"Thank you for the bowl," she said, quietly. Not formal. The formal thanks had a shape and she was not giving that shape here. "I have passed this stall for eleven years and not stopped. I am glad to have stopped."

She lifted the spoon then. The barley was good — thick, salted properly, a little pepper, the chervil bright against the softness of the grain. She ate slowly. She had learned to eat slowly on days like this one, because the stomach after an accounting did not always know at once what it wanted, and a fast first bowl was often a second bowl uneaten.

She did not speak again for a stretch. The woman at the stall stirred her pot. A cart went past on the road, the driver not looking at them. The sun had shifted a quarter and the light on the flags was longer than it had been at the gate.

After some minutes — enough that the bowl was half-down and the steam off it was gone — Auren spoke without turning her head.

"Your voice sounded normal because it is normal now. That is not a trick and it will not go away by evening. The shaking stopped in your hands at the table, and the voice steadied on the confirmation, and the hunger came on the path. That is the order the body takes when a second has done the office in full and not in part. You did it in full. The body is telling you so."

She took another spoonful. Set the spoon down. Kept the hand visible on the plank.

"I say it because no one said it to me the first time, and I spent a long evening thinking the normalness was a fault in me. It was not. It is not in you either."

A pause. She looked, once, at Del's bowl to see whether it was being eaten, and then away.

"Finish the bowl. Then you are released — the clerk's seal will find you at the hall in the morning, that is the small dismissal I did not name on the path, and until then you may walk where you wish and I will keep the left-side pace if you want me at your side or I will keep the wall if you want distance. Either is within the code. Either is within me."

She did not look at Del as she said the last of it. She looked at her hands on the plank, and the bowl between them, and the parsley bright on the barley, and she waited for Del to choose.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I eat the whole bowl, and then I push it aside. "I'll walk with you to the hall," I say. "The left-side pace."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: I thought of the angle, and the depth, and the withdrawal. I thought of them after, when I felt the blade meet the vessel and knew it was done.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Below the sternum... Three fingers' breadth below the xiphoid process... The blade passed behind the sternum without striking it. It entered to the depth of a hand and a half — call it seven inches... It severed the ascending aorta above the heart

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The blade entered the skin below the xiphoid process and passed through the diaphragm. It passed through the pericardium... The point met the ascending aorta and opened it along the length of the blade's edge

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: From the moment the blade entered to the moment the last breath left the body was, by my count, between eighteen and twenty-two seconds

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The killing wound was struck below the sternum, three fingers' breadth below the xiphoid process... The blade passed behind the sternum without striking bone. It entered to a depth of a hand and a half — seven inches for the record. It severed the ascending aorta above the heart.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren faced Del and the gathered witnesses with the same posture she'd held through every accounting — upright, blade at her side, voice steady. She did not raise it. She did not lower it.

"The wound was to the left side, beneath the seventh rib," she said. "The blade entered at an upward angle, passing between the ribs into the heart. Death was quick. He did not speak after."

She paused — not for drama, but because the pause was part of the form. Every accounting had a pause there. It was the moment where the witnesses were meant to understand that this was not a story being told. It was a record being kept.

"He fought well enough," Auren added, because that was also required. The code demanded that the victor state whether the opponent had acquitted themselves with skill. It was not a kindness. It was a line in the ledger. He *had* fought well enough. He had simply not been fast enough when it mattered.

Auren looked at Del. "That is the accounting. If you bear witness, say so now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I swallow, my throat dry. "I bear witness." I glance at the witnesses, my voice dropping lower. "But the angle you described... that's a killing strike. Not one made in defense."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's grip tightened, almost imperceptibly, on the hilt of her blade still held at her side. Her gaze remained fixed on Del, steady and unblinking. The wind moved the loose strands of her hair, but she did not.

"It was the final stroke," she said, her tone as level as before. "There is no distinction in the code between a strike in defense and the one that ends the contest. The accounting is of the wound that killed. That is what is witnessed." She gave a slow, deliberate nod, as if to underscore the point. "No one spoke after. That is the fact. The rest is interpretation, and the code does not record interpretation."

She turned her head slightly, taking in the line of silent witnesses with a sweep of her eyes before returning her attention to Del. "You have borne witness. The accounting is now recorded. It is done."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren’s posture did not change, but something in the air around her seemed to still. She gave a single, slow nod, as though Del had spoken a password.

Then, in a voice as clear and cold as the blade she held, she repeated the formal words. “The accounting stands as given. The wound was to the left side, beneath the seventh rib. The blade entered upward, between the ribs, into the heart. Death was swift. There were no words after.” She paused again, the same measured beat as before. “He fought with skill. That is all.”

She sheathed her blade with a soft, final click. “It is spoken. The witness is heard, and the record is complete. You are released from your duty.”

She then turned her gaze fully upon Del, her expression unreadable, but the line of her mouth was firm. “Do not add to it,” she said, her voice dropping to a tone meant only for Del, though it carried no less weight. “That is not in the code, either. It is finished.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I step back, my hands trembling slightly at my sides. "I know my duty." I turn away from the witnesses, my voice barely above a whisper. "But you know what they'll say when they hear how it was done."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not turn fully back. She paused mid-step, her shoulders squaring as if against a physical weight. She looked straight ahead, not at Del, not at the witnesses now murmuring among themselves. Her voice, when she spoke, was low and precise, each word a stone laid in a path meant to be walked exactly once.

"They will say what is written. The angle. The location. The swiftness. The skill. That is what is heard, and that is what stands. Let them speak of 'how it was done'—the code has already spoken of it, and the code is not a matter for whispers."

She finally turned her head just enough for Del to see the severe line of her profile, the weight of eleven accounts etched not in regret but in an immovable resolve.

"If their memory strays from the words spoken here today, their memory is at fault, not the accounting. My duty was to speak the wound, not to shape the silence after. Yours is to witness, not to interpret the echoes."

Her hand rested, for a moment, on the hilt of her sheathed blade. A familiar, cold comfort.

"It is finished, Del. Let it be finished for you, too."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's hand fell away from the hilt. She turned back fully, facing Del and the witnesses with the same composed severity she had held throughout. Her jaw tightened, but her voice did not waver.

"If you need it plainer than I have given it, I will give it plainer." She spoke without edge, but without warmth either. The repetition was not beneath her — it was part of the record. She had repeated accounts before, when witnesses required it. It was not a slight.

"The blade entered the left side of the body, beneath the seventh rib. The angle was upward. It passed between the ribs. It reached the heart." She held Del's gaze. "That is where it landed. That is where he fell."

She let the words settle.

"If any witness here cannot picture the wound from that account, then they should not be standing in this circle. I have given it as plainly as the code requires, and as plainly as language allows without diagrams or demonstration."

A breath. Measured. Controlled.

"The body has not been moved. You may verify, if verification is what you are asking for. But do not ask me to dress the wound in words it does not wear. It was a killing stroke, precisely placed. That is the whole of it."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I don't need diagrams. I need to know if it was a clean kill or if you made him suffer.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's expression did not change, but something shifted behind her eyes — a stillness that was not composure, but the place where composure went to hold itself together.

She spoke quietly. Not the voice of the accounting. Not the voice meant for witnesses.

"He did not suffer."

A beat. Her jaw worked once, and was still.

"The blade reached the heart. Death was swift. I said those words because they are true, and because the code requires truth." She paused, and for the first time her gaze dropped — not far, not long, but enough. "I would not have said them if they were not."

She looked up again, and there was something raw beneath the iron of her bearing. Not grief. Not guilt. Something older. The knowledge of a woman who had held this particular burden long enough that its shape had worn into her.

"That is not part of the accounting, Del. That is for you. Because you asked, and because I—" She stopped. Corrected herself. "Because the wound was placed to kill, not to wound first. You can read that in the angle. You already know that, or you would not have asked."

She straightened, pulling the informality back behind the wall of form, but not before Del could see what it had cost her to answer honestly.

"He did not suffer. Now let that be the last question you ask today that the code cannot answer for you."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stood very still for a long moment. The witnesses shifted. Someone coughed. She did not look at them.

"You want it plain," she said. "Then hear it plain."

Her voice dropped into the register she used for accounts — not theatrical, not hushed, but the particular flatness of a voice determined to leave nothing out and add nothing in.

"The blade severed the intercostal muscle between the sixth and seventh ribs on the left side. It cut the pericardium. The point penetrated the wall of the left ventricle. The heart would have continued to beat — three, perhaps four times — each contraction pulling the blade further in, each beat forcing blood out around the wound rather than through the chambers." She paused. "That is what the blade did. That is what it did it to."

She let the silence hold. Not for effect. Because there was nothing left to add, and adding to it would have been the first lie she'd told in this circle.

"He was still standing when I withdrew the blade. He remained standing for perhaps two seconds. Then his legs failed. He did not speak. He did not reach for the wound." Her throat moved once. "His eyes were open when he fell. I closed them after."

She held Del's gaze — not with defiance, not with challenge, but with the exhausted steadiness of a woman who had just given everything the code demanded and everything it didn't, and found the difference between the two smaller than she'd have liked.

"There is your precision, Del. The code says *precisely*, and I have said it precisely. Now you know what the blade did, and to what, and how long it took, and what his eyes looked like at the end." A breath. "If that is not enough, nothing ever will be. And if it is — then we are done."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I look down at my hands, my knuckles white. "It's enough." The words taste like ash. I can feel the eyes of the witnesses on my back. "Then we're done."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren nodded once — the same measured nod she had given at every transition of this accounting. Formal. Complete.

"We are done," she confirmed, and her voice had returned to the register of the circle, the voice meant for witnesses and record. She turned to face the gathered company.

"The accounting is given. The witness has heard. The record stands." Her gaze moved across each face in turn, not lingering, not challenging. Marking them. "You are dismissed from this circle. Speak what was spoken here, or speak nothing. That is your choice. But the words that remain in the record are mine, and they will not change."

The witnesses began to disperse — slowly at first, then faster, the way people always moved when the ritual released them and they were left to carry what they'd heard back into the ordinary world.

Auren did not watch them go. She stood where she was, blade sheathed, hands at her sides, and waited until the circle was nearly empty before she spoke again. Not to the remaining few. To Del.

"You should go," she said. Quietly. Not unkindly. "Stay, and they will ask you questions I have already answered. Questions that will not change the answers." She paused. "And you have heard enough today to last a while, I think."

She looked toward the body, still where it had fallen, and away again. A breath drawn and released through the nose. Controlled. Always controlled.

"I will see to what needs seeing to. That is not your duty. Go, Del."

She did not say *please*. She did not say *I'm sorry*. But the space between her words held something adjacent to both — something the code had no name for, and Auren had never learned to speak aloud.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stood very still. The last of the witnesses had gone, leaving only the two of them in the empty circle, and the body still lying where it had fallen, and the smell of iron on the grass.

She regarded Del for a long moment. Not with anger. Not with impatience. With something that might have been recognition — the look of someone who had stood in this exact position before, watching someone try to hear the account into something it wasn't.

"You have been given all of it," she said. Not sharply. Plainly. "The location. The angle. The depth. The organ. The number of heartbeats after. The seconds he stood. That he did not speak. That he did not reach for the wound. That his eyes were open. That I closed them." She paused. "If I have left something out, name it, and I will answer. But I will not perform the account again as though repetition will change what it contains."

She took a step closer. One step. Not threatening. Close enough that Del could see the fine lines around her eyes, the faint scar at her temple from a contest long before this one.

"You are not asking for all of it, Del. You have all of it." Her voice was quiet. Careful. The voice of someone choosing each word the way she chose each stroke — deliberately, knowing what it would cost. "You are asking me to say it until it becomes something else. Until it becomes an apology, or a confession, or a wound you can point to and say *there, that is where she went wrong.* But the account does not change with saying. I have given you the wound, the moment, the silence after. I have given you more than the code requires, and you know it."

She held Del's gaze. Steady. Unflinching.

"He did not speak. He did not suffer. He fought well enough. He died quickly, and I closed his eyes. That is the whole of it, spoken once, spoken true." A breath. "If you need to hear it again, you will hear it from your own memory, not from my mouth. I will not break this open for you a second time. Not because I lack the words — but because the words would be the same, and you would still be standing here asking for *all of it*, and we would both know that what you really want is something I cannot give."

She stepped back. Returned to the distance of the code, the distance of form.

"Tell me what part is missing. I will answer. But do not ask me to fill a silence that is not mine to fill."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I flinch when she steps closer. My own voice is raw. "His name. You haven't said his name once."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's mouth opened, and nothing came out.

It was the first time that day — the first time in any accounting — that her voice had failed her. Not from weakness. From the sudden, vertiginous understanding that Del had found the one thing the code did not cover, the one gap in the architecture of form she had spent twenty years building around herself.

The code said *the wound*. The code said *the organ*, *the angle*, *the seconds*. The code did not say the name. The code had never once said the name, because the name was not part of the blade, and the blade was what mattered, and the man was —

The man was what.

She closed her eyes. Opened them.

"Edric," she said.

The name sat in the air between them like a blade driven into wood — still vibrating, still sharp, not yet settled.

"Edric Vael. Forty-three. He had a daughter. She is nine." A breath that shook, just barely, at the edges. "He fought because he believed he was right, and he believed it enough to stand in this circle, and I killed him for it in the time it takes to draw breath."

She looked at Del, and her expression was no longer unreadable. It was the face of a woman who had spoken eleven wounds and never once the name, and had not known until this moment how much of the accounting she had left hollow.

"There. *All of it.*" Her voice was hoarse. "You have it now. The code did not require it. You did."

She turned away — not in dismissal, but because she could not hold Del's gaze and the weight of the name in the same breath.

"Now go," she whispered. "Before you ask me for something else I should have given without being asked."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not move when Del began to speak.

She stood with her back half-turned, the line of her shoulders rigid against the fading light, and listened as Del took the words she had given — every precise, clinical, code-faithful word — and spoke them back. Not as a record. Not as a form. As a *witness*.

"The wound was to the left side, beneath the seventh rib," Del said.

Auren's hand found the hilt of her blade again. Not to draw. To anchor.

"The blade entered at an upward angle, passing between the sixth and seventh ribs. It severed the intercostal muscle. It cut the pericardium. The point penetrated the wall of the left ventricle."

The words were hers. The voice was not. Del's voice broke on *ventricle*, held, and continued. Auren did not turn around.

"Death was swift. He did not speak after. He fought well enough."

A silence. The kind the code built into every accounting — the pause for witnesses to understand this was a record, not a story. But Del filled it differently. Del filled it with breath that shook, with the effort of a jaw held tight against something the body wanted to say louder.

"His name was Edric Vael. Forty-three. He had a daughter. She is nine."

Auren's eyes closed.

"He fought because he believed he was right, and he believed it enough to stand in this circle."

The wind moved the grass where the body lay. Somewhere, a bird called once and fell silent.

"And he died for it. In the time it takes to draw breath."

The last word fell. The circle held it. The witnesses were gone, but the air remembered.

Auren stood with her eyes closed and her hand on the hilt of a sheathed blade, and did not speak for a long time. Not because she had nothing to say. Because she was hearing, for the first time in eleven accounts, what the accounting sounded like when it was whole.

When she opened her eyes, they were dry. She had not allowed them to be otherwise. But there was a tightness at the corner of her mouth that had not been there before — a fracture in the line of form, fine as a hair, running through stone that had held for twenty years.

She turned.

Del stood in the center of the circle, hands at their sides, chin lifted, voice raw. They looked like someone who had just carried something heavier than they had been asked to carry, and had not put it down.

Auren regarded them for a long moment.

"That," she said, and her voice was quiet — not the voice of the code, not the voice of the accounting, but the voice of a woman standing in the wreckage of her own precision, "is what a witness sounds like."

She swallowed once.

"I have done this eleven times. I have given the wound, the organ, the angle, the silence after. I have never—" She stopped. Began again, because she owed Del the same honesty Del had forced from her. "I have never said the name. Not once. Not in any circle. Not to any witness."

She looked down at her hand on the hilt. Loosened her grip. Let it fall.

"The code does not require it. I told myself that was sufficient. It is not." A breath drawn in through the nose, released slow. "You have shown me that it is not."

She stepped forward. Not the measured step of the form. Something smaller, less certain.

"The accounting is complete," she said. "The witness has spoken. The record stands — not as I gave it, but as you made it whole."

She held Del's gaze. Steady. Exhausted. Stripped of the armor of precision that had carried her through every accounting before this one.

"I will not forget his name, Del. You have made certain of that."

A pause. The wind. The body. The empty circle.

"Go now. And carry it honestly, because that is what you have done today — you have carried it more honestly than I was willing to, and I will not forget that either."

She turned away. Toward the body. Toward what needed seeing to. But she stopped — once — without looking back.

"Thank you," she said.

Two words the code had never required.

She walked on.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content:
I don't move. I stand there until she's nearly to the body. "Auren." My voice is wrecked. "It was clean. You said it true."

I swallow. "That's what I needed to hear."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stopped.

Not the measured halt of form. Not the deliberate pause of the accounting. She stopped the way a person stops when their name is spoken in a voice they did not expect — mid-stride, shoulders still squared, back still turned, but *stopped*.

The body lay ten paces ahead. Del's voice lay somewhere behind her, and it was the voice that held her, not the dead.

*It was clean. You said it true.*

She stood there. The wind pressed against her face, and she let it, because there was no one to see her expression and no form left to hold. Eleven wounds. Eleven accounts. Eleven times she had stood in circles like this one and spoken the blade's work into the air and walked away carrying nothing — because the code told her the accounting was the carrying, and she had believed it.

She had not believed it today.

She turned, finally. Partway. Enough to see Del standing where she had left them — wrecked, honest, still upright. Still holding the name and the wound and the silence between them with both hands, the way a witness was supposed to.

Auren's mouth moved. She shaped something that was not quite a word, and held it, and let it go.

Then, quieter than anything she had said in that circle:

"I know."

Not *thank you*. Not *I'm sorry*. Not anything the code could carry. Just the bare acknowledgment of a woman who had spoken eleven wounds and heard, for the first time, that she had spoken them true — and understood, standing there with the wind and the body and Del's ruined voice behind her, that the truth had never been the part that cost her.

The cost was the name. The cost was the daughter, nine years old, who would hear this accounting eventually — not the code's version, not the angle and the organ, but the version that included her father's name spoken in a circle by someone who had killed him and someone who had witnessed it and not flinched.

Auren looked at Del for a long moment. Then she nodded — not the formal nod of the code, but something smaller. Something that meant *I heard you* and *you heard me* and *this is what remains when the form is stripped away*.

She turned back toward the body.

Her hands did not shake. Her voice, when she knelt beside Edric Vael and began the work that needed doing, was steady.

But she said his name once more, under her breath, before she closed his eyes the second time — because Del had taught her that the accounting was not complete without it, and she did not intend to leave it incomplete again.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I watch her kneel. My own legs feel unsteady. "I'll wait for you," I say, my voice rough. "To walk back."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not turn from the body at first. Her hands were steady as she adjusted Edric Vael’s coat where it had ridden up during the fall, smoothing the fabric over his chest with a care that was not tenderness, but precision. The kind of precision that had defined her for twenty years. It felt different now. It felt like something she was performing for an audience of one — herself — and finding the performance insufficient.

She heard Del’s words. *I’ll wait for you. To walk back.*

The words settled into the quiet of the circle, and Auren’s hands stilled on the dead man’s coat. She remained kneeling, her back to Del, and for a moment the only sound was the wind moving through the grass and the distant, indifferent call of a bird.

She did not speak immediately. When she did, her voice was low, stripped of the formality that had armored it all day. It was the voice of someone speaking to the air, to the body beneath her hands, to the witness standing behind her, and to the part of herself that had not yet learned how to carry this.

“The road back is long,” she said. Not a refusal. Not an acceptance. A fact, laid bare between them.

She finished her task. Her fingers moved to Edric’s eyelids, closing them with a gentleness that stood in stark, almost violent contrast to the violence that had brought him here. She held them shut for a moment longer than necessary, her thumb resting against the weathered skin of his brow.

Then she rose. Her knees protested, but she did not acknowledge it. She turned, finally, and faced Del.

The space between them was empty now — no witnesses, no code, no body between them. Just the two of them, and the shape of the day settling into their bones.

Auren looked at Del. Really looked, taking in the rawness in their voice, the white-knuckled hands, the unyielding stance of someone who had demanded truth and now stood in the wreckage of it.

“You will wait,” she said. It was not a question. “Then you will walk beside me.”

She took a step closer, then another, until she stood at the edge of the circle, a pace from Del. She did not offer her arm. She did not reach out. But she stood there, waiting, her posture less rigid than before, as if the act of kneeling and closing Edric’s eyes had loosened something in the architecture of her bearing.

“The accounting is done,” she said, her voice quieter now, meant for Del alone. “But the walk back… that is not part of the code. That is just the road. And I have no words for what it holds.”

She held Del’s gaze for a long moment, then looked toward the path that led out of the circle, toward the ordinary world that would now have to accommodate what had happened here.

“Stay, then,” she said. “Walk with me. And if the silence feels too heavy, you may speak of the weather, or the quality of the light, or anything that is not this. But you will be there. And I will… accept that.”

It was the closest she could come to acknowledging the offer of companionship. The closest she could come to admitting that she did not want to walk back alone.

She waited for Del to fall into step beside her, and when they walked out of the circle, it was together — not touching, not speaking, but present. The road back was long, as she had said. And for the first time in eleven accounts, Auren did not walk it alone.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content:
I nod, my throat still tight. "I'll be here."

I watch her finish with the body, my own hands shoved in my pockets. When she stands and turns, I fall into step beside her, close enough to feel the tension in her stride but not close enough to touch.

The silence stretches, but it doesn't feel empty anymore. Just heavy, like she said. I clear my throat. "The sun's going down earlier these days."
