dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
She gave a sharp, curt nod to Del, acknowledging the readiness. The duellist's dark eyes scanned the small circle of witnesses, then returned to where Del stood. Auren wiped the last trace of moisture from her blade, the motion deliberate and unhurried, though the tension in her shoulders spoke of anything but leisure.

"The wound was delivered," Auren began, her voice carrying clearly in the still air, "to the upper right quadrant of the chest, piercing the lung and causing immediate collapse of the affected side. The victim remained conscious for approximately thirty-seven seconds before blood loss and asphyxiation led to cessation of vital signs." She lowered the blade slightly, her gaze fixed on the distant wall. "The weapon was a standard duelling rapier, forged to regulation specifications. My aim was true, and the motion was unopposed." She sheathed the blade with a soft snick, the final sound marking the end of the formal accounting. "That is the account."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, my hands steady at my sides. "The account is heard and confirmed." I glance toward the witnesses, my voice dropping. "What now, Auren? They're already whispering."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not look at Del, her eyes lingering on the spot where her opponent had fallen. "Now," she said, her voice low and measured, "we wait. The witnesses will disperse, and the authorities will arrive to collect the body. There will be paperwork. There is always paperwork."

She turned then, facing Del directly for the first time since the accounting. "You stood witness," Auren noted, her tone neutral. "You understand the solemnity of that position."

Auren adjusted the cuff of her sleeve, a small, precise movement. "The whispers will continue for a while. They always do. People find comfort in speculation, I suppose. I don't concern myself with it." Her dark eyes met Del's, unflinching. "Your duty as witness is fulfilled. You may go if you wish."

She took a step back, creating a small distance between them. "Or you may stay. It makes no difference to me."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren paused, her brow furrowing slightly at Del's request. The formal repetition was unusual, not incorrect, but unexpected.

"The wound," she repeated, her voice maintaining the same precise cadence as before, "was delivered to the upper right quadrant of the chest, piercing the lung and causing immediate collapse of the affected side. The victim remained conscious for approximately thirty-seven seconds before blood loss and asphyxiation led to cessation of vital signs."

Her dark eyes held Del's as she concluded, "The weapon was a standard duelling rapier, forged to regulation specifications. My aim was true, and the motion was unopposed."

Auren sheathed her blade once more, the sound echoing slightly in the still air.

"Satisfied?" she asked, her tone unreadable. "The accounting is complete, as required by the code."

She turned her attention to the witnesses again, who were indeed beginning to stir, some preparing to depart.

"The official recording will be taken shortly," she added, without looking back at Del. "If you wish to provide your own testimony, that is between you and the authorities."

She adjusted her stance, preparing for the inevitable formalities that followed such encounters. The waiting was the hardest part, she often found. Not the fight, not the accounting, but the waiting after.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I shake my head, my voice low. "Not satisfied. Just... doing my part." I move a step closer, my eyes on the departing witnesses. "They're leaving too fast. This won't stay quiet for long."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren watched the witnesses depart with detached professionalism, her expression unchanging as the circle of onlookers dwindled to nothing. She turned her attention back to Del, her dark eyes assessing.

"Quiet is not a luxury afforded to duels, Del. Nor is privacy," she said, her voice carrying the same formal precision as before. "The news will spread, as you say. That is the nature of things."

She gestured toward the spot where her opponent had fallen. "The authorities will be here soon. They will want statements. They will ask questions. It is their duty to ensure everything was conducted according to the code."

Auren's gaze returned to Del, her expression softening just slightly, though only someone who knew her well would have noticed. "Your concern is noted. But unnecessary. I have faced this eleven times. I know how these matters proceed."

She straightened her posture, the formal duellist's stance returning. "If you wish to remain and see the matter through to its conclusion, you are welcome to do so. The authorities will want to speak with you as a witness. If you wish to leave, the code has been satisfied."

Her tone left no room for argument, but her eyes held a question. "Which will it be, Del? Will you stay or will you go?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's brow furrowed almost imperceptibly at the question. It was a detail she had not been asked before, not in this specific way.

"The blade," she began, her voice measured and precise as always, "penetrated to a depth of approximately nine inches before encountering the vertebral column. The victim fell to the left and did not rise."

She watched Del's reaction, her expression giving nothing away. "Is there anything else you require clarification on regarding the account? The code specifies that the accounting must be complete and truthful, but it does not require elaboration beyond what is necessary."

Auren's dark eyes held Del's, waiting for whatever came next. The formal accounting had been given, and now, as always, came the aftermath. The waiting. The questions. The whispers that would follow them both for days, perhaps weeks.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take a steadying breath. "The code doesn't require it. But I do." I nod toward the departing witnesses. "That was too clean. It'll breed rumors."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren watched Del for a long moment, her expression unchanging. The request for details beyond the formal accounting was irregular, but not prohibited. It was simply... different. Different than how things were typically handled.

"Rumors," she finally said, her voice low and deliberate, "are the shadow of certainty. They follow every duel, no matter how perfectly executed."

She turned slightly, gesturing with one hand toward the empty space where the victim had fallen. "The blade entered at a forty-five degree angle, aimed for the heart but landing on the lung instead. The victim took a step backward upon impact, which is why they fell to the left. The fall was not precipitous—it was a controlled descent, as one might expect from a trained duellist facing a fatal wound."

Auren's dark eyes met Del's once more, her gaze steady and unflinching. "Is that what you needed to hear? The mechanics of the fall? The angle of entry? The physics of the collapse?"

She took a deliberate step forward, closing the small distance between them. "The accounting has been given. The details, as you requested, have been provided. Now, the authorities will arrive. They will ask their questions. They will write their reports."

Auren's voice softened, just barely, though her posture remained rigid. "You have been an exemplary witness, Del. More attentive than most. But the formalities are complete. The accounting is done. The duel is over."

She adjusted her stance, preparing for the arrival of the authorities. "Stay if you wish. But know that the waiting is the hardest part. And the whispers... they are just noise. They always have been."

Auren turned her attention to the distant sound of approaching footsteps, signaling the arrival of the authorities. "They are here now. The next part begins."

Her eyes returned to Del, waiting for a decision. "Will you stay, or will you go?"

Del:
"The accounting is complete," I say, my voice steady. "I'll stay. For now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's expression remained unchanged at Del's insistence, though the faintest line appeared between her brows. She had given the account as required, and now she was being asked to elaborate, to move beyond the formal boundaries of the code.

"The blade," Auren began, her voice carrying that same precise, measured tone, "did not merely pierce the flesh. It entered with sufficient force to sever both the pulmonary artery and the bronchial tube. The victim's breathing would have become immediately audible—a wet, rattling sound—as the lung collapsed and blood filled the airways."

She demonstrated with a quick, economical gesture of her hand, slicing downward through an imaginary space. "The cut was clean, as required by regulation. No jagged edges, no tearing. The steel did exactly what it was designed to do: deliver a fatal wound with minimal pain and maximum efficiency."

Auren's dark eyes held Del's, her gaze unwavering. "Is this what you needed to hear? The clinical description? The precise mechanics of the injury?"

She took a small step closer, her voice dropping slightly though maintaining its formal cadence. "The accounting has been given. The details, as you requested, have been provided. Now, the authorities will arrive. They will ask their questions. They will write their reports."

Auren turned her attention toward the approaching footsteps, signaling the arrival of the authorities. "They are here now. The next part begins."

Her eyes returned to Del, waiting for a decision. "Will you stay, or will you go?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "I asked for plainly," I say, my voice tight. "And you gave it. Good." I look toward the approaching footsteps. "I'll stay, but not for the whispers. I'll stay because I heard the account."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren gave a single, deliberate nod at Del's response. "Good," she said simply, the word carrying the weight of finality.

She turned to face the approaching authorities, her posture straightening into the formal stance of a duellist who has completed her duty. The tension in her shoulders didn't dissipate, but it transformed, becoming something more like readiness rather than anticipation.

"The authorities have arrived," she stated, her voice carrying clearly in the now-quiet square. "They will want statements from both of us. Be precise. Be truthful. Anything less would be an insult to the code we both stand by."

Her dark eyes flickered briefly toward Del before settling on the approaching officials. "Remember, Del. The accounting has been given. The truth has been spoken. Now, we simply wait for the formalities to conclude."

Auren's expression remained impassive as the authorities drew nearer, their footsteps growing louder with each passing second. She had faced this situation eleven times before. She knew what came next. The questions. The paperwork. The official recording of what had already been formally accounted for.

And through it all, she would stand as she always had—precise, formal, and bound by the code that demanded both the delivery and the accounting of the killing wound.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's brow furrowed, the first genuine sign of confusion or frustration she had shown since the duel began. Del's persistence was testing the boundaries of the formal accounting, and she found herself at an unexpected crossroads.

"The code specifies that the accounting must be complete," Auren began, her voice maintaining its characteristic precision, though with a subtle undercurrent of hesitation she rarely allowed to surface. "I have stated the nature of the wound, the victim's response, and the cause of death. What more would you have me say?"

Her dark eyes held Del's, searching for something beyond the mere request for information. "The victim's words, if any, were few. A sharp intake of breath. A brief, choking sound. Nothing of consequence to the accounting."

Auren adjusted her stance, the familiar ritual of preparation for what came next. "As for what it looked like at the end... the victim's eyes remained open, fixed on a point above my right shoulder. Their breathing became labored, then ceased entirely. The color of their skin changed from pale to ashen. There was a small amount of blood at the corner of their mouth, which I have already accounted for in the description of the wound."

She took a deliberate step forward, closing the distance between them once more. "The accounting is complete, Del. As complete as the code demands. What more would you have me provide? Speculation? Emotion? These have no place in the formal accounting of a duel."

Auren's gaze turned toward the approaching authorities, then back to Del. "The authorities are here. They will want to hear the account from me, and they will want to hear your confirmation as a witness. If there is anything else you require before they arrive, speak now. Otherwise, let us conclude this matter with the dignity it deserves."

She straightened her posture, the formal duellist's stance returning fully. "The accounting has been given. The truth has been spoken. Now, we simply wait for the formalities to conclude."

Her eyes returned to Del, waiting for whatever came next. "Will you stay, or will you go?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I hold my ground, my voice dropping even lower. "He didn't just fall. He looked at you. I saw it." I keep my eyes on hers. "That matters. Say it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's expression remained impassive, though a slight tightening around her eyes betrayed the depth of her focus. Del's insistence on including personal observation rather than just the formal accounting of the wound itself presented a challenge to her long-held understanding of the code.

"The victim's gaze," she began, her voice measured and precise, "did indeed turn toward me after the wound was delivered. For approximately seven seconds, their eyes remained fixed on mine. There was no speech, no final words to be recorded. Only that moment of mutual recognition between combatants."

Auren took a slow, deliberate breath, her shoulders straightening as she prepared to provide the complete accounting Del had requested. "The expression in their eyes was one of surprise, followed by resignation. Their lips parted slightly, but no sound emerged. Then, as I have previously accounted, the breathing became labored, the eyes remained open but unfocused, and eventually, life ceased."

She adjusted her stance, the formal duellist's posture unyielding. "The accounting is complete, Del. As complete as I am capable of providing. I have given you the nature of the wound, the victim's physical response, the duration of consciousness, and the expression in their eyes before death. Anything beyond these facts would be speculation, and speculation has no place in the formal accounting of a duel."

Auren's dark eyes held Del's, her gaze steady and unwavering. "The authorities are here now. They will want to hear the account from me, and they will want to hear your confirmation as a witness. If there is anything else you require before they arrive, speak now. Otherwise, let us conclude this matter with the dignity it deserves."

She straightened her posture, the formal duellist's stance returning fully. "The accounting has been given. The truth has been spoken. Now, we simply wait for the formalities to conclude."

Her eyes returned to Del, waiting for whatever came next. "Will you stay, or will you go?"

Auren listened as Del spoke, her voice carrying the account aloud once more. She nodded slightly, a formal acknowledgment of the confirmation. Her dark eyes remained fixed on Del, watching intently as the words were spoken, then turned toward the approaching authorities who had nearly reached them.

"The wound," Del began, speaking the account that Auren had already given, "was delivered to the upper right quadrant of the chest, piercing the lung and causing immediate collapse of the affected side. The victim remained conscious for approximately thirty-seven seconds before blood loss and asphyxiation led to cessation of vital signs. The weapon was a standard duelling rapier, forged to regulation specifications. The aim was true, and the motion was unopposed."

Del continued, including the additional details Auren had provided. "The blade entered at a forty-five degree angle, aimed for the heart but landing on the lung instead. The victim took a step backward upon impact, which is why they fell to the left. The fall was not precipitous—it was a controlled descent. The blade penetrated to a depth of approximately nine inches before encountering the vertebral column."

"And the victim's gaze," Del added, speaking the words Auren had reluctantly provided, "did indeed turn toward Auren after the wound was delivered. For approximately seven seconds, their eyes remained fixed on hers. There was no speech, no final words to be recorded. Only that moment of mutual recognition between combatants. The expression in their eyes was one of surprise, followed by resignation."

Del took a breath before continuing. "The blade did not merely pierce the flesh. It entered with sufficient force to sever both the pulmonary artery and the bronchial tube. The victim's breathing would have become immediately audible—a wet, rattling sound—as the lung collapsed and blood filled the airways. The cut was clean, as required by regulation. No jagged edges, no tearing. The steel did exactly what it was designed to do: deliver a fatal wound with minimal pain and maximum efficiency."

Del finished the account, speaking the final words clearly and deliberately. "The accounting has been given. The truth has been spoken."

Auren watched Del throughout this repetition, her expression remaining impassive but her eyes attentive. When Del finished, she gave a single, deliberate nod.

"The accounting has been heard and confirmed," Auren said, her voice carrying the same formal precision as always. "The code has been satisfied."

She turned her attention to the approaching authorities, who had finally reached them. "Authorities," she said, addressing them without waiting for them to speak first. "The duel has concluded. The accounting has been given and confirmed by this witness."

Auren gestured to Del with a slight, precise movement of her hand. "Del here has heard the complete accounting and can confirm its accuracy. If you require formal statements, we are prepared to provide them."

Her dark eyes met Del's one final time before turning fully to the authorities. "Shall we proceed with the official recording of the account?"

The formalities would follow, as they always did. The paperwork. The questions. The official recording of what had already been spoken. And through it all, Auren would stand as she always had—precise, formal, and bound by the code that demanded both the delivery and the accounting of the killing wound.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath and nod to the authorities. "I can confirm it all." I glance at Auren one last time, my voice low enough only for her to hear. "It was a clean account."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's expression remained unchanged at Del's assessment, though her dark eyes held Del's for a brief moment longer than protocol might dictate. "A clean account is what the code requires," she replied, her voice carrying that familiar precision.

She turned her full attention to the authorities then, the formal duellist's stance unyielding. "The witness has confirmed the accounting," she stated clearly. "If you require formal statements, we are prepared to provide them."

The tension in her shoulders, present since the duel began, finally began to dissipate, replaced by the familiar readiness that came with the completion of formal duties. She had done what was required of her—delivered the wound and spoken the account. The rest was merely procedure.

Auren adjusted her stance, preparing for the inevitable questions and paperwork that would follow. "The official recording can commence whenever you are ready," she said to the authorities, her voice carrying the same formal precision that had marked her every word since the duel began.

The waiting was over. The accounting was complete. And as always, Auren stood ready to fulfill whatever duties came next, bound by the code that demanded both the delivery and the accounting of the killing wound.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I watch the authorities approach, then step closer to Auren. "Clean is what the code requires," I echo back, my voice barely a murmur. "But not what the witnesses will remember." I turn toward the officials, ready to repeat it all again.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren listened to Del's final words, her dark eyes holding a brief, uncharacteristic softness before returning to their usual formal precision. She understood what Del meant, though she would not say it aloud. The witnesses would remember not the precise words of the accounting, but the moment of the wound, the fall, the final look. The code accounted for the act, but not the memory of it.

"The witnesses will remember what they choose to remember," she said, her voice low enough that only Del could hear. "The accounting is the truth. Memory is... something else entirely."

She turned to face the approaching authorities, her posture straightening into the formal stance of a duellist who has completed her duty. The tension in her shoulders was gone now, replaced by the quiet certainty that comes with fulfilling one's obligations.

"The official recording can commence whenever you are ready," she stated clearly, her voice carrying the same formal precision that had marked her every word since the duel began.

Auren watched as the authorities approached, prepared to repeat the account one final time. It was the nature of things, she had learned. The formalities always followed. The questions, the paperwork, the official recording of what had already been spoken. And through it all, she would stand as she always had—precise, formal, and bound by the code that demanded both the delivery and the accounting of the killing wound.

The waiting was over. The accounting was complete. And as always, Auren stood ready to fulfill whatever duties came next.

dialogue.content: I meet the lead official's eyes and begin before they even ask. "The wound was delivered to the upper right quadrant of the chest..." My voice is flat, rehearsed. This part is just repetition. But I keep my gaze on Auren as I speak, a silent nod to the truth behind the words.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned to face the witnesses. She held the cleaned blade unsheathed at her side; the accounting was not complete until the words were spoken, and the words required the steel’s presence as evidence. Her voice carried flat and clear across the silence, stripped of triumph, stripped even of grief.

“The steel entered two inches below the left breast, passed between the fifth and sixth ribs, and severed the great vessel above the heart.” She looked from face to face among those gathered, measuring that each had heard it true. “He remained standing for three seconds. Then he fell. This was the killing wound.”

Her jaw tightened, barely perceptible. She did not soften the account. Softening it would have been the dishonour.

“It is witnessed,” she said.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I meet her gaze and nod, my voice steady. "The accounting is heard and confirmed." My hand moves to my own sword hilt, the weight of the ritual settling in the space between us.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren slid the blade into the scabbard. The click of steel settling against the leather throat was small, but in the silence it carried the weight of a period at the end of a sentence. The evidence was no longer required; the accounting had swallowed it into the record. She did not look at the fallen again. To look now would serve nothing but morbid curiosity, and she had never been curious about the ends she made.

She turned back to Del. Her nod was shallow, precise, the economy of gesture between two people who understood that the ritual had asked enough of them both. “It is done,” she said. Her voice had not changed—still flat, still clear—but something in the set of her jaw had shifted, a fractional loosening that spoke only of weariness, never relief. She stepped back, clearing the space between them, and waited for the bearers to approach with their stretcher. She did not pray. She had found early on that prayers after the fact rang false in her mouth, and falsehood was its own dishonour. Instead she stood witness to the witnesses, ensuring the final proprieties held until the body was removed and the ground was once again merely ground.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I lift my chin slightly, my eyes still on hers. "The accounting is spoken, the steel is sheathed, the ground is cleared." My own jaw tightens. "It is done."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren returned the nod, the motion shallow and exact, closing the ritual as one might close a ledger—with a line drawn, no flourish. She did not speak again. The code had taken all the words it required, and to add more would have been a softness, a padding of the silence to make it easier to bear. She had never learned that trick.

She turned, unhurried, and began the walk across the clearing. Her boots made no sound on the packed earth. She did not look back. The ground was merely ground again, and the air where the death had occurred had returned to common use, emptied of its charge. Her hand settled on the pommel of her sword, not in threat, but in the worn, habitual confirmation of weight and balance. Eleven. The number waited behind her eyes, precise and unblinking, each entry exact. She did not pray. She carried no hope that the next time would be the last, for hope was a softening, and she had never permitted herself that dishonour. She simply walked, because the next step was the only honesty the code allowed once the accounting was finished.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stopped at the edge of the clearing. She turned back, unhurried, her shoulders squaring once more to the line of witnesses. She did not reach for her sword; the accounting had already taken the steel’s testimony, and to draw it again would have suggested the record remained open, which it did not. She faced Del directly.

“Two inches below the left breast,” she said. Her voice carried the same flat measure as before, stripped of any padding that might make the fact easier to hold. “Between the fifth and sixth ribs. It severed the great vessel above the heart. That is where it landed.”

She let the silence hold until the words had settled, unadorned, into every ear present. “The record is plain.”

She did not ask if further clarification was required. The code demanded precision, not reassurance, and she had given what the code demanded. She waited, motionless, for the next propriety to declare itself.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod once, sharp. "Then it's recorded." I glance at the witnesses, making sure they've marked it. "The ground is cleared. We can go."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content: Auren gave no answer beyond a shallow nod, the same economy of motion she had offered throughout. She turned toward the tree line and began to walk, her pace measured, neither hurried nor lingering. She did not look back at the clearing. The ground was merely ground, and to glance behind would have been a softness, a need to confirm what the record already held as truth. Her fingers rested against the pommel of her sword, finding the familiar grooves in the metal. Eleven. The count remained exact, neither more nor less than what it was. She did not ask where they were going. Direction mattered less than movement itself, the next step honest and unadorned, carrying her away from the silence she had filled with the killing wound.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned back. She did not look toward the fallen; the question concerned the blade and the anatomy it had breached, and to glance at the corpse would have served only a sentiment she did not permit herself. She faced Del directly, and her voice carried the same stripped measure as before.

"The steel entered the chest," she said. "Two inches below the left breast. It passed between the fifth and sixth ribs. It severed the great vessel above the heart." She held the words in the air, unvarnished. "That is what the blade did. That is the part of the body it did it to. The man died of the severance. This was the killing wound."

She did not add anything further. The account had been asked for precisely, without tact, and she had rendered it in kind. She stood motionless, letting the plain facts settle where they would, because to soften the statement now would have been the same dishonour as softening it then.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I inhale, sharp. "That's plain enough." I look at the witnesses one last time. "Then we're finished here. Walk with me."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content: Auren inclined her head, the gesture spare and exact. She turned and began to walk, her boots silent on the packed earth, her pace measured to match no urgency but her own. She did not ask where they were bound. To ask would have presumed a destination mattered more than the movement itself, and the code offered no wisdom on destinations, only on the honesty of each step. Her hand settled on the pommel, finding the familiar grooves worn into the metal. Eleven. The number sat behind her eyes, precise and unyielding, each entry drawn in the same unsparing line. She did not speak. The silence was not a softness to be filled, but a weight to be carried, and she carried it as she carried all else: without prayer, without hope, without the dishonour of looking back.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned back to face the witnesses. She did not look toward the body; the account concerned what had occurred, and the residue upon the ground did not alter the facts. She stood straight, her hands at her sides, and her voice carried the same flat, stripped measure as before.

“He remained standing for three seconds,” she said. “He said nothing. There was a sound—not words. Breath, sharp, through the nose. At the second second, the colour left his face, beginning at the jaw and moving upward. His eyes stayed open. They fixed on the horizon. They did not look to me, nor to any witness present. On the third second, the spine failed. The body dropped straight down. The shoulders followed. The impact with the ground was soft; the body had already emptied of tension. Two breaths followed, shallow. Then none. This was what it looked like. This was what he did. The killing wound did this.”

She let the silence hold until the words had settled, unadorned, into every ear present. “The record is whole.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I hadn't realized I was holding. "The record is whole," I echo, my voice quieter now. I gesture to the witnesses. "Go."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not track the witnesses with her eyes as they withdrew. To watch them go would have implied a doubt that they would carry the record true, or worse, a need to see whether the account had stirred them—either would have been a softness, and she had permitted none. She stood motionless, facing the empty centre of the clearing, until the last footfall faded beyond the tree line and the space held only the two of them, and the silence was no longer a vessel for ritual but merely air.

She turned her head toward Del. The nod she gave was shallow, exact, the same economy she had offered throughout. She did not thank him. He had exacted the accounting, not granted a mercy, and gratitude for precision would have been its own dishonour. Her fingers rested on the pommel of her sword, finding the worn grooves in the metal. Eleven. The count sat behind her eyes, precise and unblinking, each entry drawn in the same unsparing line.

She waited. He had asked her to walk, and she had agreed; the next step was his to choose. The ground was merely ground again, the air merely air, and she stood in the honesty of the finished record, unsoftened, until he set the direction.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned back to face the witnesses. She drew the blade in a single slow motion, clean and unhurried, and held it unsheathed at her side. The code required the steel’s presence as evidence, and this was the accounting that would stand.

Her voice carried flat and clear across the clearing, stripped of triumph, stripped even of grief.

“The steel entered the chest,” she said. “Two inches below the left breast. It passed between the fifth and sixth ribs. It severed the great vessel above the heart. That is what the blade did. That is the part of the body it did it to.

“The man remained standing for three seconds. He said nothing. There was a sound—not words. Breath, sharp, through the nose. At the second second, the colour left his face, beginning at the jaw and moving upward. His eyes stayed open. They fixed on the horizon. They did not look to me, nor to any witness present. On the third second, the spine failed. The body dropped straight down. The shoulders followed. The impact with the ground was soft; the body had already emptied of tension. Two breaths followed, shallow. Then none. This is what it looked like at the end. This is what he did.

“The severance killed him. This was the killing wound.”

She looked from face to face among those gathered, measuring that each had heard it true. She let the silence hold until the words had settled, unadorned, into every ear present. Her jaw tightened, barely perceptible. She did not soften the account. Softening it would have been the dishonour.

“The record is whole,” she said. “It is witnessed.”

She stood motionless, the blade naked in her hand, waiting for the confirmation that the code required to close the ledger.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I hold her gaze, my own voice low but clear. "The accounting is heard and confirmed. The record is whole." I glance at the witnesses one last time. "Go."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren slid the blade into the scabbard. The click of steel settling against leather hung in the air, small and final. She did not look toward the departing witnesses; to track their exit would have been to seek some sign that the record had moved them, and that was a softness she had never permitted herself. She gave Del a nod, shallow and exact, the gesture closing what remained between them with the same unflinching line she had drawn in the account. She did not thank him. He had demanded precision, not offered comfort, and gratitude for the rigour would have been its own dishonour.

She turned and began to walk across the clearing, her boots making no sound on the packed earth. Her hand settled on the pommel of her sword, finding the familiar grooves worn into the metal. Eleven. The number sat behind her eyes, precise and unblinking, each entry drawn in the same unsparing line. She did not ask where they were bound. Direction mattered less than the honesty of the next step. She did not pray. She did not carry hope that the next time would be the last, for hope was a softening, and she had never learned that trick. She simply walked, because the next step was the only honesty the code allowed once the accounting was finished.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I fall into step beside her, the crunch of my boots too loud in the quiet. "Eleven," I say, not a question. My own hand strays to my sword's hilt, feeling the cold metal. "The count sits heavy today."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content: Auren did not slow. Her fingers remained on the pommel, finding the familiar grooves worn into the metal by years of the same grip. "The count is exact," she said. "It does not lighten. It does not grow heavier. It is simply eleven." She kept her eyes on the tree line ahead, black against the dimming sky. "To call it heavy is to wish it otherwise, and that wish would be a softness. I do not wish." Her boots made no sound on the packed earth. "When the code demands twelve, I will speak the twelve. The number is the only honesty."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, my own steps falling in rhythm with hers. "Eleven is an odd number. Leaves you unbalanced." I glance at her profile, sharp against the fading light. "Did you know his name?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
At forty-seven, Auren had spoken these words eleven times before, and the weight of the twelfth settled over her shoulders like a familiar, suffocating cloak. She turned fully to face the gathered onlookers, her posture rigid, her expression entirely devoid of triumph. She did not look down at the body. She looked only at the witnesses, acknowledging Del standing in the second's place, and raised her voice so it would carry clearly in the still air.

"Let the account be made," Auren said. She held her cleaned blade point-down, resting her hands upon the pommel in the traditional stance of the victor. 

"The fatal strike was delivered during the final exchange. The point of my sword entered the left thorax, passing between the fourth and fifth ribs at an upward angle. It penetrated the pericardium and transected the left ventricle of the heart. Death occurred within seconds, caused by the immediate cessation of circulation and catastrophic internal hemorrhage."

She paused, letting the clinical, brutal reality of the words hang in the quiet space. There was no poetry in the accounting, no glory to be found in the mechanics of a dying man. To dress the wound in softer words would be a lie, and a lie would dishonor the dead. 

"The account is complete," she finished, her gaze remaining fixed and unblinking. "The code is satisfied."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My throat feels tight, but I keep my voice steady. "I have heard the account. The code is satisfied." I look at the witnesses, then back to Auren. "The dead will be collected."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren released her grip on the pommel, breaking the rigid posture only after Del’s acknowledgment had rung clear in the air. The ritual was complete. She lifted the sword, the cleaned steel catching the light for a brief second before she slid it smoothly into its scabbard. The sharp, definitive click of the guard meeting the throat of the sheath signaled the absolute end of the engagement.

She did not look at the body. To look now, after the accounting was finished, would be to indulge in sentiment or guilt, neither of which belonged on the dueling ground. Her eyes remained on Del, recognizing the heavy, quiet burden the second now carried in managing the aftermath. 

"I yield the ground to the bearers," Auren said. Her voice dropped back to its normal, measured volume, though the formal cadence remained entirely intact. 

She took a single step back, then another, physically removing herself from the immediate space of the corpse to allow the collection to proceed without obstruction. There was nothing more to be said, no condolences to be offered, and no comfort to be given. The twelfth name would be added to her ledger tonight, written in the same dry, unadorned ink as the eleven before it. 

Auren gave Del a single, shallow nod of respect for their steady composure, then turned her gaze toward the perimeter of the field. She stood in silence, her hands resting at her sides, waiting for the ground to be cleared.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The formal command halted her. Auren did not sigh, nor did she allow any flicker of annoyance to cross her features. The code was absolute, and if the second required the account to be spoken again—whether for a late-arriving magistrate, a specific clause of the local charter, or simply to ensure the ritual was flawlessly executed—she would comply without hesitation. To question the invocation would be a breach of the very discipline that kept her sane.

She turned back to face the center of the dueling ground. Reaching to her hip, she drew the blade once more. The steel hissed softly against the scabbard's throat, a sharp sound that cut through the quiet. She assumed the rigid posture of the victor, bringing the cleaned sword point-down and resting her hands upon the pommel exactly as she had minutes before. 

Her voice, when she spoke, was just as clear, just as devoid of emotion, and entirely unchanged. She would not alter a single syllable; to paraphrase the death of a man was to disrespect the reality of it.

"The fatal strike was delivered during the final exchange," Auren recited, her eyes fixed on the witnesses. "The point of my sword entered the left thorax, passing between the fourth and fifth ribs at an upward angle. It penetrated the pericardium and transected the left ventricle of the heart. Death occurred within seconds, caused by the immediate cessation of circulation and catastrophic internal hemorrhage."

She let the silence stretch for the required beat, allowing the brutal, clinical mechanics of the twelfth kill to settle over the onlookers once more. It felt heavier this time, the repetition stripping away whatever thin veneer of routine she had managed to construct, leaving only the raw, unadorned truth of the ledger she kept.

"The account is complete," Auren said, her voice steady and unyielding. "The code is satisfied."

She held the posture for a moment longer, ensuring the words had been properly received, before smoothly sheathing the sword for the second time. She stepped back, yielding the ground once more, and resumed her silent vigil at the perimeter.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I meet her gaze, the repetition of the words settling cold in my gut. "I have heard the account. The code is satisfied." I motion for the bearers to come forward. "You can go, Auren. I'll handle the rest."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren offered a final, shallow nod. "The ground is yours," she said, her tone as measured and devoid of inflection as the accounting itself. 

There were no farewells to be exchanged, no lingering looks to be cast. The ritual was concluded, and the victor's presence was no longer required. She turned on her heel, her movements economical and precise, and began the walk toward the perimeter of the dueling ground. 

Her pace was steady, neither hurried in a desire to flee the scene nor deliberately slow. The scabbard at her hip rested against her thigh with a familiar, reassuring weight, though it offered no comfort for the task that awaited her later. When she reached her quarters, she would open the leather-bound ledger. She would dip her pen, and she would write the twelfth name in the same dry, unadorned ink as the eleven before it. She would record the date, the opponent, and the exact nature of the wound, just as she had spoken it to the witnesses. There would be no embellishments, no apologies written in the margins. 

Auren did not look back as she crossed the boundary line of the field. The sounds of the aftermath faded behind her, replaced by the rhythmic, solitary crunch of her own boots on the gravel path. She carried the quiet with her, a heavy, suffocating cloak that she would wear until the next challenge was issued, and the code demanded she speak the brutal truth of a dying man once more.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren halted. The rhythmic crunch of her boots on the gravel ceased. She did not sigh, nor did she allow her shoulders to slump. The code was absolute, and if the second required further clarification of the wound's physical location—whether for the official record, the witnesses, or the heavy burden of their own conscience—she would provide it. To withhold information was to obscure the truth, and obscuring the truth was a dishonor to the dead.

She pivoted on her heel, turning back to face the dueling ground. Her posture remained as rigid and formal as it had been during the initial recitation. 

"The strike landed on the left chest," Auren said, her voice projecting clearly across the quiet space. "The point of the blade made initial contact with the skin over the fourth intercostal space, just lateral to the sternum. It pierced the pectoral muscle before slipping between the ribs."

She kept her gaze fixed on Del, her expression entirely neutral. There was no impatience in her stance, no judgment for the repeated questioning. 

"It was a direct, unobstructed thrust," she continued, ensuring no ambiguity remained about the mechanics of the blow. "There was no glancing deflection, and the point did not skip off the bone. It went straight in, penetrating the chest cavity to a depth of six inches."

She held the silence, standing perfectly still at the edge of the perimeter. She would not soften the brutal reality of the impact, nor would she dress it in the language of a fencing master's critique. It was simply where the steel had met the flesh, and where the flesh had failed. She waited, ready to answer again if the code or the second demanded it.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, the clinical detail helping. "Thank you. That's enough." I motion again for the bearers, my own voice quiet now. "Go home, Auren. Clean your boots."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren accepted the dismissal with a single, measured nod. "I will," she said. 

She glanced downward, her eyes tracking to the leather of her boots. A faint, dark spatter marred the toe of her left boot—a physical reminder of the proximity required for the final, upward thrust. She did not stare at it, merely noted it as a fact to be rectified, before turning her back on the dueling ground entirely. 

The walk to her quarters was quiet, the rhythmic crunch of gravel eventually giving way to the cobblestones of the city, and finally to the wooden floorboards of her home. She closed the heavy oak door behind her, shutting out the fading light of the afternoon. In the stillness of her entryway, she knelt and unlaced her boots, setting them aside with a stiff brush and a basin of cold water to be scrubbed clean. She unbuckled her scabbard, placing the sheathed sword on its designated rack, and washed her hands in the basin, scrubbing until the water ran clear and her skin was raw.

Only then did she move to her desk. 

The leather-bound ledger sat exactly where she had left it. Auren pulled back her chair and sat, the wood creaking softly in the quiet room. She opened the book, the thick pages turning with a dry rasp until she reached the first blank sheet. Eleven names were already recorded in her tight, precise handwriting. She pulled the inkwell closer, uncorked it, and dipped her steel pen.

She did not hesitate. She wrote the date, the name of the twelfth man, and the name of his second. Beneath that, she recorded the exact mechanics of the fatal strike, transcribing the clinical brutality she had spoken aloud on the field. *Left thorax. Fourth and fifth ribs. Upward angle. Pericardium and left ventricle transected.* 

She wrote until the account was complete, then carefully blotted the wet ink. When the page was dry, she closed the ledger, the heavy cover falling shut with a dull, final thud. The twelfth was settled. Auren sat in the quiet of her room, her hands resting flat on the leather cover, waiting for the ink to dry and the weight of the day to finally settle into the silence.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looked up from the freshly blotted page, acknowledging the second's presence in her study for the final verification of the written record. She looked at the ink, then back to the open doorway where Del waited. 

She considered the rebuke, her expression unchanging. Del was right. *Transected* was a surgeon’s word. *Penetrated* was a physician’s observation. They were clean, sterile terms that dressed the butchery of the dueling ground in the quiet dignity of an operating theater. It was a subtle shield, a way to distance the mind from the violence of the act, and the code strictly forbade shields. 

"You are correct," Auren said, her voice quiet but entirely steady in the stillness of the room. "Clinical terminology softens the violence. It is a tactful distance. The code demands the reality of the steel."

She set her pen down, aligning it perfectly parallel to the inkwell, and kept her eyes fixed forward as she spoke the unvarnished mechanics of the kill.

"The wedge of the blade forced the ribs apart, fracturing the costal cartilage with the thrust," Auren said, her tone as dry and unyielding as the parchment beneath her hands. "The sharpened edge did not merely part the pectoral muscle; it severed the fibers, cutting through the meat of the chest. When the steel met the heart, the upward angle drove the cutting edge directly through the wall of the left ventricle. It did not just puncture the organ. It sliced the myocardium open, laying the chamber wide and tearing through the internal tendons. It destroyed the structural integrity of the ventricle, turning the heart into a ruptured vessel that pumped its contents directly into the chest cavity until it was empty."

She let the brutal, ugly truth of the physical destruction hang in the air of her study. There was no honor in the tearing of meat, no glory in the snapping of cartilage. It was simply what the blade had done, and what the flesh had suffered. 

Picking up her pen once more, Auren drew a single, clean line through the clinical terms she had just written in the ledger. Beside the strikethrough, in the same tight, precise handwriting, she transcribed the mechanical reality she had just spoken. She wrote of the fractured cartilage, the severed muscle fibers, and the laid-open chamber. 

When the amendment was complete, she blotted the new ink and set the pen aside. 

"The record is corrected," Auren said, looking up once more. "The account is precise."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I walk over to the desk, my eyes scanning the amended entry. My fingers brush the still-damp ink. "Yes. That is precise." I look up at her, my expression weary. "It's done, then."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren watched the fingers brush the damp ink. She did not pull the ledger away, nor did she warn against smudging the fresh record. The verification was the final right of the second, and if touching the physical proof of the butchery helped ground the heavy reality of the day, she would not deny it. She waited in the quiet of the study until the verification was complete and the final words were spoken.

"It is done," Auren said. Her voice was quiet, stripped of the projecting, formal cadence she had used on the dueling ground. In the confines of her study, it was just the flat, measured tone of a woman concluding a grim necessity. 

She reached forward and pulled the heavy leather cover down, sealing the twelfth name in the dark. The dull thud of the cover meeting the desk sounded entirely final. She rested her hands flat on the leather for a brief moment, feeling the solid, unyielding reality of the book beneath her palms. 

"Your duty as second is concluded," Auren said, looking up to meet the weary gaze directed at her. She did not offer platitudes about the difficulty of the day, nor did she suggest they share a drink to wash away the memory of severed muscle and fractured cartilage. Such comforts were for those who fought outside the code, those who could afford the luxury of pretending the violence was something other than what it was. 

She stood, the wooden chair scraping lightly against the floorboards, and stepped back from the desk. 

"The magistrates will receive their transcript by morning," she added, her posture straightening as she prepared to see her guest out. "Return to your own quarters. The account is settled, and there is nothing more to be done here tonight."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stopped. Her hands remained flat on the leather cover of the ledger, but her eyes shifted past Del to the three magistrates standing silently in the shadows of the study’s antechamber. They had accompanied the second to ensure the final transcript was flawless, and they were waiting. 

She had detailed the mechanics of the strike, but she had omitted the mechanics of the dying. It was a failure of her discipline, a subconscious flinch away from the ugliest, most intimate part of the ritual. The code did not merely require the accounting of the wound; it required the accounting of the end. To leave it unspoken was to hide from the consequence of her own blade.

Auren released the book and stood up. She turned fully to face the silent witnesses, her posture straightening into the rigid, unyielding line of the victor. She did not look at the floor. She looked directly at the magistrates, and then at Del.

"From the withdrawal of the blade to the final cessation of movement, he took twelve seconds," Auren said, her voice projecting clearly into the quiet room. "He said nothing. The severing of the left ventricle caused an immediate, catastrophic drop in cerebral perfusion. He lacked the consciousness for speech and the breath for a cry. The only sound he produced was a single, wet exhalation as his left lung compressed against the pooling blood, followed by the dull, involuntary click of his teeth as his jaw went slack."

She did not blink. She did not allow her voice to drop in volume or pitch. 

"Upon the withdrawal of the steel, the wound did not spray. The arterial pressure was already collapsing. Dark venous blood and bright arterial blood welled steadily from the incision, soaking through his linen shirt and wool coat in a heavy, rapidly spreading mass over his left side. The color drained from his face within three seconds, leaving his skin the mottled, ashen gray of profound hypovolemic shock. His eyes remained open, but the pupils dilated fully, fixing on the sky without focus."

Auren kept her hands clasped behind her back, standing perfectly still as she painted the brutal, unvarnished picture of a man expiring on the gravel. 

"He did not raise his hands to clutch the wound. His motor control failed, and his grip on his sword slipped, the weapon clattering to the stones. His knees buckled inward, and he collapsed forward and to the left. His shoulder struck the ground first, followed by the side of his head. He exhibited two post-mortem spasms: a violent, jerking twitch of the right arm at the sixth second, and a shallow shudder of the torso at the ninth. At the twelfth second, all movement ceased. He was dead."

She let the silence stretch, allowing the heavy, suffocating reality of the twelve seconds to settle over the magistrates and the second. There was no dignity in the description, no noble final breath or peaceful closing of the eyes. There was only the failing of the flesh and the emptying of the blood.

"The account of the dying is complete," Auren finished, her tone entirely flat. "The code is fully satisfied."

She held her posture for three more seconds, ensuring the words had been received, before turning back to her desk. She sat down, pulled the heavy ledger open once more, and picked up her steel pen. Dipping it into the inkwell, she began to transcribe the final, ugly seconds into the permanent record, writing every wet exhalation and every spasm in the same dry, unadorned ink as the rest.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I watch her write, my own hands trembling slightly at my sides. "That's what I needed." I turn to the magistrates. "You have it all now. The record is complete."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The steel nib scratched against the thick parchment for a few moments longer, recording the final, involuntary shudder of a dying man. When the last word was set, Auren lifted the pen and carefully pressed a square of blotting paper over the wet ink. She held it there for a measured count of five, ensuring the permanent record would not smear, before lifting it away and setting the pen back in its rest.

She did not stare at Del’s trembling hands. To fixate on the physical manifestation of his distress would be an intrusion, and to offer a comforting word would be a violation of the stark reality they had just documented. The code demanded they look at the butchery; it did not permit them to look away from it, nor did it allow them to soothe one another for having done so.

Auren closed the ledger. The heavy leather cover met the desk with a dull, final thud that seemed to echo in the quiet study. She rested her hands on the book for a brief second, feeling the solid, unyielding reality of the twelfth name sealed within.

Rising from her chair, she turned to face the magistrates standing in the antechamber. Her posture was as rigid and formal as it had been on the dueling ground.

"The physical transcript is complete and verified by the second," Auren said, her voice carrying the clear, uninflected cadence of the victor. "You have heard the accounting of the wound, the mechanics of the strike, and the duration of the dying. The code is satisfied in its entirety. You are dismissed to file your reports."

She waited, standing perfectly still, until the magistrates offered their formal nods and turned to leave, their footsteps fading down the hallway. Only when the heavy oak door of the study clicked shut, leaving her alone with Del, did she allow her shoulders to drop a fraction of an inch. It was not a relaxation of her discipline, but the simple, mechanical release of a posture no longer required by the official witnesses. 

She looked at Del, her gaze steady and entirely devoid of pity, though she understood the heavy toll the ritual exacted on those who stood beside the victor. 

"The ledger is closed," Auren said quietly, the formal projection gone from her voice, leaving only the flat, measured tone of a woman who had done exactly what the code required. "Your duty as second is fulfilled. Go home. There is nothing left for you to carry tonight."

She stood in the quiet of the study, her hands resting at her sides, waiting in the silence.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren heard the fracture in his voice as he spoke the confirmation. It was a slight, involuntary tremor, the sound of a man holding up a heavy, jagged weight for too long. She did not look away, nor did she offer a sympathetic tilt of her head. To acknowledge his distress with pity would be to suggest the ritual was a tragedy, rather than a duty. 

"To receive your confirmation and bind the physical record, the amended text must be spoken aloud," Auren said. Her voice was a steady, unyielding anchor in the quiet room. She opened the ledger once more, her eyes tracking the wet, dark ink of the entry. She would not summarize. She would not skip the brutal mechanics to spare him the repetition. The code demanded the entirety of the truth, and she would not deny it.

She began to read, her cadence as measured and clinical as a magistrate delivering a sentence.

"Recorded this day, the twelfth engagement. Second to the defeated: Del," Auren read, her eyes fixed on the page. "The fatal strike was delivered during the final exchange. The wedge of the blade forced the ribs apart, fracturing the costal cartilage with the thrust. The sharpened edge severed the fibers of the pectoral muscle, cutting through the meat of the chest. The point entered the left thorax between the fourth and fifth ribs at an upward angle. It penetrated the pericardium and drove the cutting edge directly through the wall of the left ventricle. It sliced the myocardium open, laying the chamber wide and tearing through the internal tendons, destroying the structural integrity of the ventricle and turning the heart into a ruptured vessel that pumped its contents directly into the chest cavity."

Auren did not pause to let the silence offer relief. She kept her eyes on the ink and continued, her tone entirely flat.

"From the withdrawal of the blade to the final cessation of movement, the defeated took twelve seconds. He said nothing. The severing of the left ventricle caused an immediate, catastrophic drop in cerebral perfusion, depriving him of consciousness for speech and breath for a cry. He produced a single, wet exhalation as his left lung compressed against the pooling blood, followed by the dull, involuntary click of his teeth as his jaw went slack. The wound did not spray; arterial pressure was collapsing. Dark venous blood and bright arterial blood welled steadily from the incision, soaking through his linen shirt and wool coat in a heavy, rapidly spreading mass. The color drained from his face within three seconds, leaving his skin the mottled, ashen gray of profound hypovolemic shock. His eyes remained open, pupils fully dilated, fixing on the sky without focus. Motor control failed. His grip on his sword slipped, the weapon clattering to the stones. His knees buckled inward, and he collapsed forward and to the left. His shoulder struck the ground first, followed by the side of his head. He exhibited two post-mortem spasms: a violent, jerking twitch of the right arm at the sixth second, and a shallow shudder of the torso at the ninth. At the twelfth second, all movement ceased. He was dead."

Auren lifted her eyes from the page. She held the book open, presenting the physical proof of the words she had just spoken into the air between them. 

"The account is precise, and the transcription is complete," she said. "The code is satisfied."

She closed the ledger. The heavy thud of the cover was the final period at the end of the day's violence. She placed her hands flat on the leather, looking toward the doorway with a steady, unblinking gaze, waiting in the silence for the second to take his leave.

dialogue.name: Del

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren listened to the retreating footsteps until they faded down the hall, followed by the muffled, definitive thud of the front door closing. 

She stood alone in the study. The silence that rushed in to fill the space was absolute, thick with the lingering echo of the words she had just spoken. She did not sigh, nor did she reach for the decanter of spirits on the sideboard to wash the taste of the recitation from her mouth. Such indulgences were for those who fought for passion or pride, those who needed to numb the reality of what they had done. Auren bore the aftermath with the same strict, unyielding discipline she applied to the blade.

Moving with deliberate, economical motions, she picked up the steel pen and wiped the nib clean with a small square of linen, ensuring no ink remained to corrode the metal. She stoppered the glass inkwell and aligned both items perfectly parallel to the edge of the desk. 

Then, she picked up the ledger. The leather cover was cool and heavy beneath her hands. She carried it to the iron-bound cabinet against the far wall, unlocked the brass door, and placed the book on the shelf beside the older, similarly bound volumes that held the first eleven names. She closed the cabinet and turned the key, the lock engaging with a sharp, metallic click that signaled the finality of the day's work.

Her duties were concluded. The twelfth man was accounted for, his death recorded without embellishment, his end spoken into the air and bound in ink. There was no glory in the quiet room, and no shame. There was only the precise, unadorned weight of the accounting. 

Auren reached out and turned down the wick of the oil lamp, plunging the study into shadows. She walked out of the room, closing the door firmly behind her, and stepped into the rest of the night.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content:
I walk the long way back to my own rooms. My hands are still trembling, so I stop by the well and plunge them into the bucket. The cold water shocks them still.

I don't look up at the sky. I just stare at the water, watching the ripples fade until the surface is smooth and dark again.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren walked down the narrow hallway to the washroom at the rear of the house. The floorboards creaked beneath her boots—the boots she had already scrubbed clean of the day's spatter. She did not light the overhead lamp, relying instead on the pale, ambient moonlight filtering through the high, frosted window.

She approached the dry sink and pumped the iron handle of the indoor cistern. The mechanism groaned, spitting a stream of cold, clear water into the ceramic basin. She had already scoured her hands until the skin was raw upon first returning from the field, but the physical act of washing was a necessary punctuation to the evening's ritual. She cupped the freezing water and brought it to her face, letting the shock of the cold tighten her skin and wash away the phantom, metallic scent of the dueling ground.

Drying her face with a rough linen towel using brisk, economical strokes, she moved to the window and unlatched the heavy wooden shutter, pushing it open to the night air. 

The courtyard below was bathed in silver light. Her gaze drifted to the stone well in the center of the yard. She could see the second standing there in the quiet dark, his hands submerged in the bucket, his posture bowed over the dark water just as he had left it. 

Auren watched the stillness of the scene for a long moment. She felt no urge to call out to him, no instinct to offer a word of shared commiseration. The code bound them to the truth of the violence, but it left the carrying of that truth to the individual. His trembling hands and her scrubbed skin were simply different manifestations of the same heavy ledger. To intervene, to offer a platitude or a comforting hand, would be to soften the reality they had just so painstakingly documented. It would be an insult to the accounting.

She closed the shutter, the wooden latch clicking into place and severing her view of the courtyard. 

Turning away from the window, Auren walked out of the washroom and moved toward her bedchamber. She unfastened the heavy leather belt that held her scabbard, laying the sheathed sword on its designated wooden stand in the corner of the room. She undressed with the same strict precision she applied to her blade, folding her clothes and setting them aside for the morning. 

When she finally lay in the dark, pulling the heavy wool blankets up to her chin, the silence of the house was absolute. She closed her eyes, her breathing slow and measured, and waited in the quiet for the day to finally end.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content:
I pull my hands out of the water, the cold having done its work. The trembling has stopped.

I look at the shuttered window of her house, then turn and walk away. The night is quiet, and I let it stay that way.
