She heard herself, the noise she was making, and didn't care, and heard him too—not quiet, not doing sums, just *there*, all breath and low broken swearing against her collarbone—and that was the thing that tipped her over the edge of thinking about it at all.

"Sam," she said, and it was the first time she'd used his name, and she said it like a fact.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get my mouth on her and stay there until she's swearing at the ceiling, one hand fisted in my hair holding me exactly where she wants me.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia's first reaction was to swear, and her second was to grab.

She hadn't told him to do that. She noted it—filed it, even now—and then decided she didn't care, because he'd asked what she liked and she'd given him a list and this was the kind of initiative the list had left room for. She'd said *you'll know when to stop being slow*. He'd apparently decided that was now, and gone about it from a different direction.

"Fuck," she said, to the ceiling. Then, because she believed in specifics: "Fuck, *yes*—there. There. Don't you dare move."

Her hand had found his hair without asking her permission, and now it stayed, fingers knotted tight enough that it had to hurt a little. She didn't loosen it. She pressed him closer instead, hips rolling up to meet him, and when he made a sound against her—muffled, appreciative, the kind of noise a person made when they were enjoying the work and not just performing it—she felt it go straight up her spine.

"Good," she said. "*Good*. That's—yes. Facts, Sam. That's a fact."

She was aware, distantly, that she'd stopped giving instructions in sentences. She was aware her other hand had gone above her head to grip the edge of the mattress, that her heels were digging into his shoulders, that she'd said his name three times now in about as many minutes when she'd gone the whole evening without it. None of that seemed important. What was important was the exact rhythm he'd landed on, and the fact that he hadn't changed it, and the way her whole body was gathering itself up like a held breath.

"Don't stop. If you stop I'll—" She didn't finish. Didn't have to. Her hand in his hair said it.

It broke over her hard and she let it, loud, no ceiling in the world worth being quiet for. She swore, she said his name, she said *yes* in a voice she'd have been embarrassed by if she were the type, and she wasn't, and she rode it all the way down with her fingers still locked in his hair and her thighs shaking against his ears.

When she could see again, she let go. Flexed her hand. Looked down the length of herself at him, still there, mouth wet, watching her with an expression that was very close to smug.

"Don't," she said, breathless, pointing a finger at him. "I can see it. Don't get smug." She dragged in a breath, let it out, and something in her face gave way to a grin she didn't bother to hide. "But that was—yeah. Note that down. That worked."

She reached for him with both hands.

"Come back up here. I'm not finished with you, and you're nowhere near finished."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I came up to meet her, letting her pull me back up. "Smug? No. Just appreciative." I caught her mouth in a messy, open kiss, shifting my weight to slide into her again. "You feel incredible."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
"Appreciative," Nadia repeated, and then didn't get to say anything else for a moment because he'd slid back into her and her body had opinions about that which took precedence over her mouth.

She was still oversensitive, still humming with it, and the second stretch went through her like a struck bell. She made a sound that wasn't a word and dug her nails into his shoulders, arched, took him all the way in and held him there with her legs for a beat before letting him move.

"That's—" she said. "Yeah. Okay. Appreciative's allowed."

She kissed him back, tasted herself on him, and found she liked that more than she'd expected to. Her hands went everywhere they could reach—his back, the back of his neck, down to grip his arse and pull him deeper on the next stroke because she wanted to feel him hit the end of her.

"*You feel incredible*," she echoed against his mouth, low, not mocking exactly. "Good line. Meant it?" She didn't wait for the answer. She could feel the answer. "Yeah. You did."

He'd kept the rhythm he'd found before, the one she'd told him not to change, and she noticed—of course she noticed—that he'd remembered. Something warm and uncomplicated went through her at that, something that had nothing to do with anything after tonight. He listened. It was such a low bar, and so few men cleared it, and here he was clearing it with his face tucked into her neck and his hands full of her hips.

"Right," she said. "My turn to say something." She got her hand flat on his chest and pushed, not to stop him, just to make him lift his head. Made him look at her. His pupils were blown and there was sweat at his hairline and she thought: *this is mine for about the next ten minutes and I intend to use all of it.*

"You're close," she said. Not a question. "Don't hold off for my sake. I've had mine. I want to watch you have yours." Her thumb pressed against the base of his throat where his pulse was going like a drum. "And I want to hear it. Whatever noise you're about to make, don't swallow it."

She let go of his chest and put both hands on his face instead, holding him there, eyes on eyes, and rolled her hips up to meet him with intent.

"Go on, then," she said. "Facts, Sam. Tell me when."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "Harder, and stop checking," she says, so I stop being careful about it -- hand at her throat the way she asked for, no more pausing between. "Like that?" I manage.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia's hand came up and closed around his wrist before she'd finished deciding to do it.

Not a slap. Not a shove. Just a grip, firm and unhurried, the same way she'd caught it earlier to move his fingers where she wanted them. She held his hand there against her throat for one long second—long enough to feel her own pulse jump under his palm, long enough that he'd know she wasn't panicking—and then she lifted it off her and put it down on the mattress beside her head, and kept her hand over it.

"No," she said. Plain. Not angry. "I didn't ask for that."

She didn't stop moving. That was the thing—her hips kept rolling up to meet him, slower now, deliberate, so there'd be no confusion about whether the rest of it was still on the table. It was. She was still here, still wet around him, still very much interested in the next few minutes. She just wanted this one thing said out loud, because that was the whole point of saying things.

"Hand on the throat's a conversation I have with people I've known longer than four hours. Sober, with the lights on, before anyone's got their kit off." Her thumb rubbed once over the back of his hand, almost fond. "You're not in trouble. You checked. That's the bit that matters. But the answer's no, so—"

She picked his hand up again and moved it. Put it on her hip, low, fingers spread over the bone, and pressed it down hard so he'd feel exactly how much pressure she meant.

"*There.* That's where I want it. Grip like you mean it. Leave a mark if you like, I've got a long-sleeved week." Her other hand went to the back of his neck and pulled his forehead down against hers. "And yes. Harder. That part was right. Stop being careful, stop checking my face every stroke, I told you I'd say if it was too much and I've just proved I will."

She let her legs fall wider, gave him the room, and her voice dropped out of instruction and into something rougher.

"Go on. I want it. I want to feel you lose it."

He did. She felt the moment his rhythm went ragged, felt his hand clamp down on her hip exactly as hard as she'd asked, and she rode it with him, mouth against his ear, saying *yes* and *there* and *good, that's good, don't stop* until the words ran together. When he went over she held on to him with everything—arms, legs, the hand at his nape—and listened to the sound he made, which he did not swallow, which was loud and broken and entirely hers for the length of time it lasted.

"That," she said, when he'd gone heavy and still on top of her and she could get her breath. Her hand slid up from his neck into his hair, not gripping this time. Just there. "That was the fact I was after."

She lay under him for a minute. Let him be heavy. Watched the ceiling.

Then, because she was who she was: "You've got about twenty minutes before I want my bed back. Bathroom's the door across the hall. Towels are on the rail and I don't care which one you use." A beat. Her mouth pulled sideways against his shoulder. "But I'll give you five of the twenty before I start being unreasonable about it. You earned five."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, still half on top of her. "Appreciate the five." I pushed up on my elbows, brushing a loose strand of hair from her forehead. "And noted about the throat. Won't happen again."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia's eyes tracked his hand when it went to her forehead. She let it happen—didn't flinch, didn't swat—but she looked at him afterward with one eyebrow up, the way you'd look at someone who'd just used the wrong fork.

"Careful," she said. "That's a tender gesture. Those are outside the terms."

But she was smiling when she said it, a small crooked thing she didn't bother to police, and she didn't move away from him. She lay there under his elbows and let the sweat cool on her and felt her heartbeat come back down out of her ears into somewhere more sensible.

"And it won't happen again because there isn't an again," she pointed out. "That's the whole architecture of the evening. But—" she put two fingers against his sternum and tapped, once "—the sentiment's correct. Take it into the next room you're in. Whoever she is, she'll thank me."

She shifted, hips protesting a little in a way she'd feel properly tomorrow, and reached down to deal with the practical bit—condom, tie it off, no ceremony, dropped over the side of the bed onto his shirt because that was where his shirt was and she'd let him sort out what that meant. Her hip was already starting to colour where his hand had been. She looked at it with frank satisfaction, pressed her thumb into the middle of it to check, and hissed.

"Good," she said. "That'll keep."

Then she pushed at his shoulder—not hard, just enough to tip him off her onto the mattress beside her—and stretched, full length, arms above her head, spine cracking somewhere in the middle. She lay like that for a second with her eyes shut.

"Right. Here's how this goes, so nobody has to feel their way through it." She didn't open her eyes. "You go use my shower, because you smell like my bar and my bed and you shouldn't get into a taxi like that, it's unkind to the driver. I'm going to lie here and not move for as long as you're in there. You come out, you put your clothes on in the hall so I don't have to watch you hunt for a sock, and I'll walk you to the door because I'm not an animal. I'll say goodnight. You'll say goodnight. Neither of us will say *this was nice* because we both know it was, and saying it makes it sound like a surprise."

She opened one eye and rolled it toward him.

"Any objections, raise them now. Otherwise your five minutes started about ninety seconds ago and I'm being generous not counting the hair thing against you."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I'm past thinking, just the sound of us and her nails dragging down my back. "Don't you dare stop," she says. (OOC: no fade to black, write it through.)

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia had meant the five minutes. She wanted that on record, somewhere, even if the only record was the inside of her own head.

But he hadn't got up. He'd stayed where she'd tipped him, on his side, and then he'd rolled back over her like the conversation about showers and taxis and socks in the hall had been a suggestion rather than a schedule, and his mouth had found the place under her jaw that made her breath go short, and somewhere in there her hands had gone to his back without consulting her.

"This isn't—" she started, and lost the end of it.

Her nails were already in him. She could feel the drag of them down the long muscles either side of his spine, feel him arch into it rather than away, and the sound he made against her throat rearranged her priorities with an efficiency she'd have admired in anyone else.

"Fine," she said, to the ceiling. "*Fine.* Clock's paused. Don't look so pleased about it."

He didn't look anything. He was busy. He worked his way down her again, slower than before, less urgent, like a man who'd already proven the point and was now just interested in the detail of it, and she let him. She let her knees fall open and her hands go to his hair and she watched the top of his head move and thought, distantly, that she'd have to change the sheets tomorrow and didn't care in the slightest.

"There," she said. "No—up. Up a bit. *There.*"

He got there. He stayed there. She was still tender from the first time and it came up through her fast and bright, almost too much, and she told him so—"too much, ease off, *ease*—yes, that, stay like that"—and he eased and stayed and she rewarded him with a long low sound she didn't bother making pretty.

When she wanted him back up she said so. When he came up she got the drawer open again one-handed and shoved the box at his chest without looking, and while he dealt with that she got her hand between them and touched him, unhurried, watching his face do the thing it did. He was hard again. She'd half expected him to need longer. She said, "Well, that's convenient," and he laughed, breathless, and she pulled him down.

This time she rolled them. Got him on his back and herself astride him, hands flat on his chest, and looked down at him from there. Sweat on him. Her marks coming up red down his ribs where her nails had been. His hands went to her hips—the bruised one, he found the bruise and pressed his thumb into it deliberately and watched her hiss—and she thought: *he listens. God help whoever gets him next.*

"My pace," she said, and sank down onto him.

She went slow, because she could, because it was hers to set. Long rolls of her hips, deep, taking all of him and holding it and grinding down until his fingers dug in and his head went back against her pillow and he said her name like it had been dragged out of him. She liked that. She said so. "Good. Again." He said it again.

"Don't you dare stop," she said, when he found the angle and she felt herself start to climb. She said it into the space between them and then she said it into his mouth, bent over him, hair falling round both their faces, hips moving faster now because slow had served its purpose. "Don't you—*there*, Sam, don't you fucking dare—"

He didn't. He drove up into her and she rode it down and she came with her forehead pressed against his and her nails in his shoulders and her voice gone to nothing but breath and his name. He went a few strokes after, hands clamped on her hips hard enough to hold her still, and she felt it go through him and held on and listened.

Then quiet. His chest under her cheek going like a bellows. Her hair stuck to both of them.

"Right," she said, eventually, without lifting her head. "Terms have been bent. Not broken. Architecture stands." She breathed. "But I want it noted that you did that, not me, and I'm going to need the twenty minutes back and then some."

She pushed herself up onto her elbows, looked down at him, and gave him the crooked smile she'd been failing to police all night.

"Shower. Now. Before I find another reason not to let you."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, watching her from where I'm pinned beneath her. "Noted," I say, my voice rough. "I'll take the blame." I shift her off me carefully, sitting up. "Towels on the rail, you said?"

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia let herself be moved. It wasn't a thing she did often—being moved—but she was boneless and warm and her thighs had opinions about standing, so she went where he put her, which was on her side with her head on the pillow he'd just vacated.

"On the rail," she confirmed. "Blue one's mine, grey one's for whoever. Don't overthink it, they've both been washed."

She watched him sit up. Watched the marks on his back come into view as he turned—four lines down each side, red going toward purple, the kind of thing that would raise an eyebrow at a swimming pool. She felt no remorse about it whatsoever. She lifted one hand and traced the nearest line with a fingertip, not gently, just to feel him twitch.

"You'll want to keep a shirt on for a few days," she said. "Or don't. Your business."

She rolled onto her back and pulled the sheet up to her waist, not out of modesty, just because the sweat was cooling and the room had a draught she'd never located. The lamp on the floor threw his shadow long across the ceiling as he stood. She looked at it rather than at him, because looking at him was starting to feel like something she'd have to think about, and she'd said—out loud, in the light—that she wasn't going to.

"Hot water's on the left," she said to the ceiling. "It takes about a minute to come through and it'll try to kill you when it does. Don't stand under it waiting. Everyone does that."

A pause. She heard him find his footing, heard the floorboard by the door that always creaked.

"Sam."

She didn't sit up for it. Just turned her head on the pillow and looked at him, standing there naked in her doorway with her marks on him and his hair wrecked from her hands.

"You cleared the bar," she said. "The listening one. I don't say that to be kind. I say it because it's true and you should know it's rare." Her mouth pulled sideways. "That's the last nice thing I'm saying tonight. Go. Your five minutes are catastrophically over and I'm going to lie here and pretend I've still got some authority in my own flat."

She closed her eyes. Listened to him go across the hall, the bathroom door, the pipes waking up with a groan.

Then she reached down, found his shirt on the floor by feel, and checked the pocket for a lighter, because hers was on the side table by the door and she'd earned a cigarette she wasn't going to finish.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I find the grey towel right where she said, the water going from ice to scalding in a heartbeat. I'm back in her doorway in under three minutes, still drying my hair. "Pipes aren't joking," I say, nodding toward the bathroom.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia had found the lighter. She hadn't found her cigarettes, which were in her jacket, which was in the hall, so she was lying on her back with an unlit lighter turning over and over in her fingers like a coin, and she didn't stop when he came back.

"Told you," she said. "Nobody listens about the pipes. It's the one piece of advice I give that's actually useful and it's got a hundred percent failure rate."

She turned her head on the pillow. He was standing in her doorway in her grey towel with her water dripping off him onto her floorboards, hair sticking up in three directions from the towelling, and she looked at that for about a second longer than she needed to before she looked away again.

"You're dripping on my floor," she said. "That's a hall activity. Everything from here on is a hall activity. Clothes, socks, the bit where you check your pockets for your phone even though you know exactly where it is."

She flicked the lighter once, watched the flame, let it die. Sat up—not fast, her body registering a complaint she'd deal with tomorrow—and swung her legs over the side of the bed. Stood. Found his shirt where the condom had landed on it, held it up between two fingers, gave it a shake, and lobbed it at him.

"That's yours. Probably wants a wash. Not my problem." She was already reaching for the oversized t-shirt that lived on the back of the door, pulling it over her head, not bothering with anything under it. It came to mid-thigh. Her hair was a disaster. She ran one hand through it, made it marginally different, and considered the matter closed.

Then she walked past him into the hall, close enough that her shoulder brushed his arm, and didn't slow down.

"Your jacket's on the chair. Shoes are wherever you kicked them, I wasn't watching. Front door sticks, you have to lift the handle and push at the same time." She got her cigarettes out of her own jacket, lit one, took one drag she didn't particularly want, and leaned against the wall by the door with her arms folded and the cigarette held out to one side.

She watched him get dressed. She didn't pretend not to. He'd stood in her bedroom doorway and watched her take her clothes off four hours and a lifetime ago; she felt she'd earned the reverse.

"For the record," she said, when he had the shirt on and was doing up buttons—she'd lost him two, she noticed, and felt fine about it—"I'm not going to ask for your number and you're not going to offer it. If you've got a compulsion to be polite, I'm asking you now to suppress it. It'll feel rude for about four seconds and then you'll be in a taxi and it won't feel like anything."

She tapped ash into her palm because the ashtray was in the other room.

"But I'll say this, once, and then it's said. If you're in that bar again and I'm in that bar again, I won't pretend I don't know you. I'll nod. That's the extent of it." A beat. Her mouth did the crooked thing. "And if you sit down, I might not tell you to move. Don't read anything into that. It's just that most of the other stools are broken."

She pushed off the wall, lifted the handle and shoved the door with her hip so it opened for him, and stood aside.

"Goodnight, Sam."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I catch the shirt, give it a once-over before pulling it on. "Noted." I find my shoes by the couch, shrug into my jacket. At the door, I pause just long enough to meet her eye. "I'll keep an eye out for broken stools." A small nod, then I'm out into the hallway. "Goodnight, Nadia."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia got the door open with her shoulder because her hands were full of keys and phone and the remains of a cigarette she had no intention of finishing.

"Right," she said, dropping all three on the side table. "I'm going to be honest, I don't have coffee and I wasn't going to offer it."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "Good," I say. "I wasn't going to drink it."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia kicked the door shut behind her and looked at him properly for the first time since the bar — under the hallway light, not the bar's, which was a different thing entirely. She didn't dress it up.

"Here's the deal," she said. "This is tonight. Not a thing after tonight. You don't stay for breakfast, I don't ask for your number, and we don't do the part where either of us pretends it meant more than it did." She pulled her jacket off one shoulder, then the other. "If that's not what you're here for, the door's right there and I won't be weird about it."

She hung the jacket on the hook by feel, eyes still on him.

"Say yes or say no. I don't do the long version."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I smile, leaning against the wall. "That's exactly what I'm here for." I meet her gaze. "So what's next?"

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
"Good," she said, and that was the whole conversation as far as she was concerned.

She crossed the room — three steps, no hesitation — and got a hand on his collar and pulled him down to her level. No preamble, no soft lead-in. She kissed him like the four hours of talking at the bar had been a formality she'd been waiting out, and when she pulled back it was only far enough to speak.

"Bedroom's the door on the left. The one that's open."

She walked him backward past the kitchen, one hand still fisted in his shirt, the other working the last button on her own blouse without looking at it. At the doorway she stopped, tipped her head toward the room, and let go of him.

"Go on, then."

The rest of the night, she did not say another word that wasn't either a direction or a question about what he wanted — and she asked that one twice, plainly, the way she'd ask anything. When it was over she lay on her back with one arm across her eyes, breathing hard, and said the only thing left on the list.

"Okay. That was good."

Then she rolled over, checked the clock on the nightstand — 2:40 — and said, into the pillow, "You can crash. Couch's out there, blanket's on the back of it. I wasn't kidding about breakfast."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get her against the door before it's properly shut. "I'm not going to pretend I came up here for the conversation," I say.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia lifted her head off the pillow far enough to look at him, one eye half-closed, hair stuck to her cheek.

"I'd have been insulted if you had," she said.

She let her head drop back down. The clock still said 2:40 and the room was too warm and she was not going to get up and do anything about it. She reached over and killed the lamp on the nightstand, which put the room in the orange streetlight from the window, which was fine.

"You've got a point, though," she said into the dark, mostly to the ceiling. "I did say the couch. I'll say it again. Couch. Blanket's on the back of it. There's a glass in the kitchen if you want water — second cabinet, the one that sticks."

She pulled the sheet up to her shoulder and turned onto her side, facing the wall, which was her version of done talking. Not cold. Just done. She'd said what the night was at the door, and she'd meant it then and she meant it now, and she'd have said the same thing in the morning if he was still there, which he wouldn't be, which was also fine.

The last thing she said before she stopped saying things was flat and unhurried, and not unkind.

"Don't slam the front door. The downstairs neighbor's a nightmare about it."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I push off from the bed, grabbing my shirt from the floor. "Wouldn't dream of it." I find my way to the living room in the dark, the blanket right where she said it would be. I don't bother with the water.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia lay facing the wall and listened without meaning to. The couch frame gave a creak under someone's weight, then settled. The pipes knocked once somewhere in the building. The streetlight threw its orange stripe across the ceiling and she watched it instead of closing her eyes, because closing them wasn't working.

She wasn't thinking about him. She was thinking about Thursday, and the thing with her sister's car, and whether the landlord was going to fix the radiator before it got properly cold, and none of that had anything to do with the man on her couch. That was the point. That was the whole arrangement, said out loud at the door, agreed to, done.

She reached for her phone, set the alarm for 6:30 out of habit even though tomorrow was a Saturday, and put it face-down on the nightstand.

Somewhere around three she stopped hearing anything from the other room, which meant either he was asleep or he was being considerate, and she genuinely did not care which. She turned onto her back, one arm flung out, and went under.

She woke before the alarm — 6:12, gray light, radiator cold as promised. She lay still a second and listened. The apartment was quiet in the specific way an apartment is quiet when you're the only one in it.

She didn't get up to check. She'd said no breakfast and she'd meant it, and checking would have been a kind of question she wasn't asking. She just swung her legs out of bed, pulled on the t-shirt from the chair, and went to start the kettle, because if he was still there he could hear her doing exactly what she'd told him she'd do, which was get on with her morning.

Either way she wasn't going to be weird about it. She'd said that too.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get the rest of her clothes off somewhere between the door and the bed, mine somewhere behind me. "Tell me what you like," I say. "I'd rather not guess at it."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia filled the kettle from the tap, set it on the burner, and clicked the gas on without looking toward the living room. If he was there, he was there. If he wasn't, she'd have the tea and the crossword and the thing with her sister's car to deal with, in that order, and none of it required her to stand in her own kitchen checking on a man she'd met four hours before midnight.

She got the mug down — the chipped one, because it was the one she liked — and a tea bag, and stood with her hip against the counter while the water heated.

The kettle ticked. Somewhere behind her, past the kitchen doorway, the couch frame creaked, one small adjustment of weight.

She didn't turn around. She'd said the terms at the door and she'd said them again in the dark, and standing there spinning around to see if he'd taken the hint would have been exactly the kind of thing she'd told him she wasn't going to do. So she just watched the kettle, and when it clicked off she poured, and stirred, and blew across the top of the mug.

"Water's hot," she said, to the general direction of the living room, flat as a weather report. "If you want tea, you can have tea. That's not breakfast, it's tea."

She picked up her mug and the folded paper off the end of the counter and sat down at the little table by the window, back to the couch, and opened the crossword to the part she never finished.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I come up behind her, shirtless and barefoot, and lean over to glance at the puzzle. "Eight letters, 'no strings attached'." I reach for the mug. "Mind if I borrow a sip?"

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia didn't look up from the puzzle. She'd heard him come around the counter, and the floorboard by the stove told her exactly where he was standing, and that was all the attention she was going to give it.

"That's not a clue," she said. "That's you being cute at seven in the morning."

She turned the paper a quarter-turn, put her pen down on the crossword, and slid the mug half an inch toward him across the table without lifting her eyes off the grid. Not toward him — toward the space between them, which was where the mug was going to stay if he wanted it.

"One sip. Then it's mine again."

The kettle was still ticking down its last heat on the burner behind them. Cold radiator, gray window, the crossword half-done and the same eleven squares she'd been stuck on since Tuesday. She picked the pen back up and clicked it once.

"Eight letters, that clue would be 'honesty.' Which is a ten, so it's not your clue either." She finally looked up at him, brief, flat, unimpressed in a way that wasn't actually unfriendly. "You're still here. Couch was for crashing, and you've crashed, and it's light out. Drink the tea. Then the door."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get my mouth on her and stay there until she's swearing at the ceiling, one hand fisted in my hair holding me exactly where she wants me.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
She didn't give him anything to work with at first — just lay back against the pillow with one knee bent and her hand in his hair, testing. When he found the thing that worked she said so, once, flatly, the way she'd have said *that's the right screwdriver*: "There. Stay there."

And he did, and she stopped narrating. Her fingers tightened in his hair and her other hand found the headboard and she swore at the ceiling, short and unromantic and meant, and it went on long enough that the streetlight outside had shifted to the far wall by the time she came down off it, breathing through her nose, one arm thrown over her eyes again.

"Okay," she said, when she had the words back. Her voice was wrecked and she didn't care. "Okay."

She didn't say thank you. She didn't say anything that could be mistaken for a thing you say to someone you're going to see again. She just lay there a second longer, then rolled her head to look at him, hair everywhere, and asked the only question she had left, plainly, because she'd asked it twice already and she meant it every time.

"Your turn. What do you want."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I shake my head, leaning up on an elbow beside her. "I got what I came for." I run a thumb over her hipbone. "I'm good."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia looked at him a second — flat, unreadable, cataloguing the answer like she'd catalogued everything else tonight. Most men said something else there. She didn't say so out loud, because saying so out loud would have made it a remark, and she wasn't making remarks.

"Fine," she said. Which was her whole response, and it was an honest one.

She rolled her shoulder out from under his thumb and sat up, swinging her legs off the edge of the bed. The radiator clanked once and stayed cold. She found her t-shirt where it had ended up, half under the bed, and pulled it on over her head without turning around, then stepped into the jeans she'd left in a heap by the dresser and did them up with one decisive tug.

At the door she paused with her hand on the frame and finally looked back at him — still on her bed, morning light coming in gray and unflattering, no performance in any of it. That was the part she'd liked about tonight. Nobody had performed.

"Couch blanket goes in the basket by the door if you're done with it. Not on the couch." She tipped her head toward the front of the apartment. "There's a bus stop on the corner, northbound, comes every ten minutes this time of morning. Or the diner two blocks down does eggs, if you want them. Not with me. Just — they're there."

She turned and went out to the kitchen without waiting for an answer, because it wasn't a question. Her mug was still on the table by the window, tea gone lukewarm. She picked it up, drank the rest of it standing, and put it in the sink.

Then she sat back down with the crossword and the pen and picked up where she'd left off, at the eleven squares she never finished, and got on with her Saturday.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "Harder, and stop checking," she says, so I stop being careful about it -- hand at her throat the way she asked for, no more pausing between. "Like that?" I manage.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
"Better," she said. It wasn't praise. It was a reading off a dial.

She didn't have anything else to say after that, which was its own kind of answer. Her hand stayed fisted in the sheet above her head, knuckles white, and the headboard knocked the wall twice — she'd meant to care about the neighbor and didn't, and made a mental note to apologize to the guy in 4B if it came up, which it wouldn't. When it got to be too much she bit down on the inside of her cheek instead of saying anything, because saying anything would have been a different kind of noise and she wasn't doing that tonight.

When it crested she didn't make a show of it. She went rigid for a second, breath caught high in her chest, and then it broke and she let it go all at once, a long exhale through her teeth, and her grip on the sheet slackened finger by finger.

Afterward she lay there with her forearm over her eyes again, chest rising and falling, and let the room be quiet. The streetlight did its orange stripe across the ceiling. Somewhere below, a car door shut.

She didn't say *that was good* this time. She'd already said that once tonight, and saying it twice would have started to sound like she was trying to make him feel a certain way about it, and she wasn't. So she just reached down past her hip and found his wrist, held it there a second — not soft, just there, the way you'd put a hand on a table — and then let go and rolled onto her side, facing the wall.

"Lamp," she said, meaning turn it off.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I click off the lamp, plunging the room into orange stripes. I settle back beside her, my hand still resting lightly on her waist. "Heard anything from 4B yet?"

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia didn't turn over. Answering meant the conversation was still open, and she was aware of that, and she answered anyway, because it was a real question and she didn't have a rule against real questions.

"No," she said, into the wall. "He works nights. Doorman at the hotel on Grand. Leaves around nine, home around six. So he either heard it or he didn't, and if he did, he's a grown man."

She pulled the sheet up over her shoulder. The orange stripe on the wall shifted an inch as a car went by below.

"Wall's thin on that side. The radiator pipe runs the whole length of it. I can hear his phone buzz through it, so." A beat. "If it comes up, I'll buy him a six-pack and we'll both pretend it's about the pipe."

That was more words than the question had asked for and she knew it. She didn't take any of them back. She closed her eyes against the light and left it there — not an invitation to keep talking, just the answer, and then the dark, and whatever he did with that was his own business.

dialogue.content: I'm past thinking, just the sound of us and her nails dragging down my back. "Don't you dare stop," she says. (OOC: no fade to black, write it through.)

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
She didn't repeat it. She'd said it once and meant it, and saying it again would have been a way of asking, and she wasn't asking. What she did instead was drag her nails down his back one more time, harder, and hold there at the bottom — a flat, wordless *that's the one* — and let the rest of it go at the speed she'd set and not any slower.

Somewhere in the middle of it she stopped keeping track of the room. The orange stripe on the wall, the tick of the radiator, the sheet twisted under her knee — all of it slid out of focus and stayed there. She got a hand braced against the headboard and one foot flat on the mattress and gave as much as she was taking, and the only sounds that came out of her were the ones too involuntary to count as anything she'd chosen to say out loud.

When it crested she didn't make a performance of it. She locked up all at once, teeth closed, breath stopped high in her chest — and then it broke and she dropped back onto the mattress with both arms flung out, breathing like she'd run for a bus she wasn't going to catch.

The ceiling was orange again. The clock on the nightstand read something she didn't bother to finish reading.

"Okay," she said, when her lungs let her have the word back. That was the entire review. She lay there a minute staring up at the stripe of light and letting her pulse come down, and then turned her head just far enough to look at him — hair stuck to her cheek, no expression she was making any effort to manage.

"Told you not to stop," she said. Not a compliment. Not a complaint. Just the record, set straight.

She rolled onto her side after that, one arm under the pillow, facing the wall. The radiator clanked and stayed cold, same as it had all night. Somewhere down on the street a car door shut and the stripe on the wall shifted an inch and settled.

"Couch's still out there," she said, into the dark, flat and unhurried, the way she'd said it the first time. "Blanket's still on the back of it."

Then she stopped talking, because there was nothing left on the list, and she'd meant all of it.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I roll onto my back beside her, staring up at the orange stripe. "Think I'll skip the couch." I let the silence settle for a beat. "But I won't stay for breakfast either."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia lay still for a moment, working that one over. He'd been offered two doors and he'd picked a third she hadn't put on the table.

"Okay," she said. Not surprised out loud. She wasn't going to give him the satisfaction of asking why, because there wasn't a why worth asking about — a guy decides he'd rather sleep in his own bed, that's a decision, not a puzzle.

She turned onto her back and looked at the ceiling, hands folded on her stomach, thinking it through the way she'd think through a flat tire. He wasn't going to stay for breakfast, so there was no breakfast to avoid. He wasn't taking the couch, so there was no blanket to fold and no 6:30 wake-up in her living room. Which meant the night just ended here. That was cleaner than what she'd proposed, honestly, and she respected a person who took the cleaner option.

"Alright," she said, and sat up. The sheet went with her to the waist and she didn't bother about it. She swung her legs off the bed and stood, and this time she didn't go for the t-shirt on the chair — she went for his shirt on the floor and tossed it onto the bed beside him, because he was going to need it, and picking it up herself was faster than watching him look for it.

"Your jeans are by the dresser. Phone's either in the kitchen or under the couch; I heard it buzz earlier, so it's one of the two." She pulled her own jeans on and did them up with the same decisive tug as before. No t-shirt this time. Nobody left in this apartment to perform for.

She crossed to the door and stopped there, one hand on the frame, and looked back at him — flat, unhurried, the same look she'd given him at the front door four hours ago when she'd laid the whole thing out.

"Then this is the part where I don't walk you out. You know where the door is, you know about the bus, and I already told you not to slam it." A beat. "Thanks for the honesty at the door. Made the rest of it easy."

That was the whole goodbye. She turned and went out to the kitchen and left the bedroom door open behind her, because she wasn't hiding from him leaving and she wasn't watching him do it either. She got the chipped mug down and filled the kettle a second time, and stood with her hip against the counter and her back to the hallway, listening without meaning to for the sound of the front door, and the small click of it closing the way she'd asked.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I push up from the bed, pulling my shirt on. "That was the idea," I say to the empty doorway. I gather the rest of my things—jeans by the dresser, phone buzzing under the couch. I fold the blanket and leave it in the basket without looking back at the kitchen. The front door opens, and I make sure it clicks shut behind me without a sound.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
The door clicked shut. No slam, no thud, just the latch turning over and the faint pressure change of the hallway air. Nadia stood at the counter and let it land.

She didn't move for a second. Not because of anything — because the kettle was taking its time and there was no reason to move. When it clicked off she poured, dropped the tea bag in, and stirred without watching the hallway.

The blanket was in the basket. She'd seen it on the way past the living room doorway, folded square, corners matched, sitting exactly where she'd said it went. Most people draped it over the back of the couch and called that folded. She stood there a second looking at the basket, then went back to the counter and drank her tea standing up.

The phone on the side table buzzed against the wood — hers, not his. Her sister, probably, about the car. She picked it up, looked at the screen, put it back down. Twenty minutes from now was fine for the car. First she was going to finish the crossword, because she'd been stuck on the same eleven squares since Tuesday and losing to a Saturday puzzle in her own kitchen was not how the morning was going to go.

She sat down at the little table by the window with the mug and the pen and the paper, and the radiator clanked and stayed cold, and she got to work on 14 across.

She got 14 across. It was *sterling*, which she should have had on Tuesday.

Around nine the doorman from 4B came down the stairs, keys and thermos, boots on the treads. Nadia heard him stop outside her door — one beat, two — and then keep going without knocking. Which meant he'd heard something and was being decent about it, or he hadn't and was just checking his phone.

She made a mental note about the six-pack and the pipe.

Then she filled the mug again, turned the puzzle to the back page, and started on the crossword she'd already given up on, because Saturday wasn't over and there was still the thing with her sister's car, and none of it had anything to do with anyone who wasn't in this apartment.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content:
The cold outside hits me like a wall. I button my jacket on the stoop, the taste of her still on my mouth. No car door shutting in the street, just the rumble of a bus two blocks over. I pull my phone out—no missed calls. Good.

I walk north toward the diner, hands in my pockets. The bus can wait.

She snorted and kicked the door shut behind her.

"Bedroom's back there. That's what I brought you here for, and that's what I want. Say you're still in and come show me."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia's gaze was sharp as she watched Sam pull on their jeans, her eyes lingering on their body, taking in every inch of skin, every curve, every plane, every dip and swell. She could still feel the ghost of their touch on her skin, the lingering heat of their kisses, the deep, satisfying fullness of their cock inside her.

She licked her lips, tasting the salt of their skin, the tang of her own arousal, the heady, intoxicating flavor of sex and satisfaction.

"I'll keep that in mind," she said, her voice a low, rough murmur. "Lead with the throat thing. Got it."

Nadia stood, her body moving with a slow, deliberate grace, her eyes never leaving Sam's. She walked towards them, her hips swaying, her body on full display, a final, tantalizing glimpse of what they would be leaving behind.

She stopped in front of Sam, reaching out, her fingers tracing the buttons of their unbuttoned shirt, her nails lightly scraping over their skin. "You know," she said, her voice a low, seductive purr. "You could always stay a little longer. We could go for round four, for old time's sake."

Nadia's other hand slid down Sam's chest, her nails raking lightly over their skin, leaving goosebumps in their wake. She leaned in, her lips brushing against their ear, her breath hot and damp.

"I could ride you," she murmured, her voice a low, rough whisper. "I could bounce on your cock, up and down, back and forth, until you're grunting and groaning and cursing and screaming and coming so hard you see stars."

Nadia's hand slid lower, her fingers dipping inside the waistband of Sam's jeans, her nails raking lightly over their skin. "I could make you forget your own name," she said, her voice a low, seductive purr. "I could make you forget everything except the feeling of my body wrapped around yours, the taste of your skin on my tongue, the sound of your moans in my ear."

She leaned back, looking up at Sam through her lashes, a slow, sultry smile spreading across her face. "So what do you say?" she asked, her voice a low, rough murmur. "Wanna stay a little longer? Wanna see what else I can do with my mouth, with my hands, with my body?"

Nadia's hand slid back up Sam's chest, her nails raking lightly over their skin, leaving goosebumps in their wake. "I promise I'll make it worth your while," she said, her voice a low, seductive purr. "I promise I'll make you feel things you've never felt before, things you never knew you wanted, things you never knew you needed."

She leaned in, her lips brushing against Sam's ear, her breath hot and damp, her voice a low, rough whisper. "I promise I'll make you scream, make you beg, make you fucking break. I promise I'll make you mine, body and soul, for as long as you can stand it, for as long as you can take it, for as long as you can fucking endure it."

Nadia pulled back, her eyes locking onto Sam's, her gaze intense, smoldering, all-consuming. "So what do you say?" she asked, her voice a low, rough murmur. "Wanna play?"

She waited, her body poised, ready, waiting for Sam's response, waiting to see if they would take her up on her offer, if they would stay, if they would play, if they would let her take them to the brink and back and over and under and around and through and through again.

Nadia's heart raced, her pulse pounding in her ears, her body thrumming with anticipation, with desire, with a deep, all-consuming need. She wanted Sam, wanted to taste them, to touch them, to feel them, to own them, to possess them, to claim them as her own.

And she would do whatever it took, would say whatever it took, would give them whatever they wanted, whatever they needed, whatever they craved, to make that happen.

Because this, this right here, this moment, this chance, this opportunity... it was too good to pass up. It was too tempting, too alluring, too delicious, too mouthwatering, too irresistible.

And Nadia was nothing if not a woman who knew what she wanted, who went after what she wanted, who took what she wanted, no matter the cost, no matter the consequences, no matter the risks.

So she waited, her breath held, her body tense, her eyes locked onto Sam's, waiting, watching, waiting to see what they would do, what they would say, what they would choose.

Because one thing was for certain - Nadia was not a woman to be trifled with, not a woman to be ignored, not a woman to be turned down.

And she fully intended to make sure Sam knew that, one way or another, come hell or high water, rain or shine, for better or for worse.

She had made her offer, and now it was up to Sam to decide.

To stay... or to go.

“I wanted you to be the one who ended it. By the end. I wanted you to say it, so I could hate you for leaving instead of admit what I was doing to make you go.”

Saying it aloud sounded calculated in a way he had never allowed it to sound in his head. He wanted to qualify it immediately. There had been good days. There had been things she’d said. He could still produce the whole miserable inventory.

“I kept telling myself I was waiting for you to prove you wanted to stay. Then when you tried, I found something wrong with how you did it.”

His gaze dropped briefly.

“I was angry with you. Some of that anger was fair. But I used it to excuse things I knew weren’t.”

He swallowed and looked back up.

“I wanted you there, Bee. I also wanted to win. And I kept making you pay for the fact that I couldn’t have both.”

He didn’t lean into her hand or reach for the kiss.

“That’s the part I don’t have a defence for.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s back met the hallway wall. He caught himself against it with one palm and kissed her again, abandoning, for a few seconds, the distinction between getting what he wanted and making anything better.

Then he stopped.

“Wait.”

He hated the word as soon as he said it. His shirt was on the floor. Eleven months of imagining this, and now he was the one asking for a moment.

He lowered his hand from the wall.

“I’m not taking back what I said.”

It came out almost belligerently. Of course it did. He could admit to being cruel, but apparently he still needed to sound ready to fight about it.

“Tomorrow, I don’t get to say we were both upset. Or that this means you’ve forgiven me.”

He glanced down the hallway toward his bedroom. The temptation to leave the conversation here, among their discarded clothes, was painfully familiar.

“I used to think that if you still wanted me, I couldn’t have hurt you that badly.” His mouth tightened. “Very convenient thing to believe.”

He looked back at her.

“I want this. I’m not confused about that.”

His hand lifted, then settled at her waist, without pulling.

“But you can still be angry with me afterward.” A small, rueful breath escaped him. “I’ll probably be unbearable about it. You can do it anyway.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I close the distance between us again, my palm flat against his chest. "I don't need your permission to be angry." I can feel his heartbeat under my hand, fast and telling. "And you don't get to decide what I forgive."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya opened his mouth, then shut it. He had been about to explain what he meant—as though the problem were her understanding rather than his words.

“I keep finding ways to give you instructions,” he said. “Even when I’m apologising.”

He looked down at her hand against his chest. There was no dignified way to pretend indifference with his heart doing that beneath it.

“I know you don’t need my permission. I liked being the person you asked anyway.”

That admission irritated him more than the others. It was smaller, less impressive. No grand account of how they had gone wrong; just something selfish he had enjoyed.

His hand left her waist.

“And I’m doing it again. Trying to get every word right so you can’t find anything else wrong with me.”

He glanced toward the kitchen, then back at her.

“There is plenty else wrong with me.”

The dry remark almost gave him somewhere to hide. He let it fall flat.

“I missed you,” he said. “I’m still angry. I don’t know what to do with both of those things when you’re standing here.”

He bent and kissed her once, briefly, without trying to turn it into an answer. Then he drew back enough to look at her.

“But that’s mine to work out. Not another job for you.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Later, Ilya stood in the kitchen with his shirt unbuttoned, waiting for the kettle. The hallway light was still on. He had noticed it twice and done nothing about it.

He took down her mug.

For eleven months, it had been an object he could pretend meant nothing. Now he stood holding it by the handle, irritated by how much effort putting it back would require.

“I’m making tea,” he said. “That’s not a suggestion that you should stay.”

He paused, then set the mug on the counter.

“And there I go again. Explaining the terms before you’ve asked.”

The kettle clicked off. He poured the water, grateful for something that required his attention without deserving it.

“I meant what I said earlier.”

He turned from the counter.

“Not just the part about missing you. The uglier bit.”

He wanted to ask what happened now. More precisely, he wanted an answer that would make the rest of the night easy, and he could already feel himself preparing to resent any other answer.

Instead, he rested his hands against the counter.

“You came here with a question. If I still haven’t answered it, I’m listening.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I take the mug from him, my fingers brushing his. "You answered." I take a sip of the tea, too hot. "Doesn't mean I'm done being pissed."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
“Good,” Ilya said, then winced. “Not good. Christ.”

He picked up his own mug. He had made hers the way she used to like it without thinking; his had no tea in it, just hot water. He stared into it for a moment, then reached for a teabag.

“I had a much better vocabulary before you got here.”

The joke was an old reflex. So was the urge to watch for whether it worked. He turned the spoon over on the counter instead.

Some part of him had heard *you answered* and immediately wanted credit. An evening’s honesty against three years of being difficult on purpose. He disliked the arithmetic more now that he could see it.

“I want you to stop being pissed,” he admitted. “For entirely selfish reasons. You standing in my kitchen with that mug—it would be very easy to pretend we’d just had a bad Thursday.”

He looked at her.

“I know it wasn’t that.”

His tea steeped untouched. He had missed this kitchen having someone in it who could make him feel exposed without raising her voice. He had also forgotten how quickly he could resent it.

“And I’m not suddenly going to be gracious about everything. There are things I’m still angry about, too.”

He rubbed his thumb over a chip in his mug.

“But I don’t need to drag them out tonight just because you haven’t let me off.”

For a while he said nothing. Then he shifted away from the counter, leaving the kitchen doorway clear.

“I’d like you to stay for your tea.”

He nearly added something about no expectations. Instead he took a cautious sip of his own, found it predictably awful, and set it down.

“I’d like you to stay longer than that, actually.” His mouth tightened with the effort of leaving the request alone. “But tea would be a start.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya understood. He withdrew his hand.

“No. Not that.”

He stayed where he was. There was an old, ugly temptation to prove he knew her better than anyone—to treat being asked as proof that whatever he did next couldn’t be his fault. He recognised it, and that recognition cost him some of the heat in his anger.

“I can stop choosing every word like I’m trying to pass an examination. I’m not going to hurt you to prove I’ve stopped.”

His voice had sharpened. He left it sharp.

“You want me to stop being careful? I hated that you could come here and I’d still want you before you’d said a bloody word. I stood in that doorway thinking about making you wait another ten seconds because ten seconds was apparently all the power I needed to feel better.”

He rested his hand on the counter.

“And now I want you to stay, and I’m angry that asking means you might say no.”

There it was, without the rueful smile he might once have used to make it easier to swallow.

“That’s what I’ve been being careful about.”

He glanced at his abandoned tea.

“I’m not asking you to be gentle with the answer. But I’m leaving it up to you.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I keep his gaze until he looks away first, then finish my tea and set the mug down hard. "Get your coat. We're going for a walk."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
For a second, Ilya wanted to refuse simply because she had told him to. He recognised the impulse with weary precision.

Then he went to get his coat.

He finished buttoning his shirt on the way, getting one button wrong and having to start again. In the hall mirror, he looked like a man attempting to dress normally under unreasonable conditions. He decided against checking his hair.

“Anywhere in particular?”

He reached for his keys before remembering they weren’t in the dish. The dish had been her idea. He still put everything in it except his keys.

He found them in yesterday’s coat.

“Never mind. Outside is probably specific enough.”

The flat had begun to feel crowded with things he might say badly. He was relieved to have a task that amounted to shoes, coat, door. Less relieved that she had been the one to think of it.

At the threshold, he paused with his hand on the latch.

“I wasn’t looking away to dismiss you.”

He could have left that alone. Instead, he looked back.

“I couldn’t hold your gaze and keep saying no without feeling like I had to turn it into a fight.”

His fingers tightened around the keys.

“It was still a no.”

He opened the door. Cold air from the stairwell reached him, and he pulled his coat closed.

“And the buzzer’s broken because I tried to fix it,” he said. “In case you were planning to have a go at me about that as well.”

There was the edge again, but this time he heard the invitation in it.

“Made it considerably worse, actually.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
I can keep the scene intense, but not write graphic sexual detail.

Ilya stopped on the landing with his keys still caught between his fingers.

“Then I won’t stop telling you the truth.”

His voice carried in the stairwell. He lowered it, not to soften what he said but because this wasn’t for the neighbours.

“I wanted you to come back. And I wanted to be the sort of man who could turn you away when you did.” He gave a short, humourless laugh. “You can imagine how well I’ve enjoyed discovering I’m only one of those things.”

He shoved the keys into his pocket.

“But I’m not going to turn tonight into another thing we did instead of saying what we meant.”

That sounded better than he deserved. He caught it.

“I want to,” he admitted. “That’s the problem. I’d take the distraction and tomorrow I’d still want an answer.”

He looked down the stairs, then back.

“I want to know whether you came for an explanation or whether some part of you came for me. And yes, I know how fucking convenient it would be if those were the same thing.”

He started down one step, then paused.

“They aren’t. I’m asking anyway.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I go down the steps after him, grabbing his coat and pulling him back against me. "I came for you, you idiot." I say it into his shoulder, low. "I just needed to hear you say the rest first."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya stopped with one foot on the lower step. For a moment he stayed awkwardly balanced, his coat pulled tight across his shoulders, and let the words reach him without finding something wrong with them.

“Oh,” he said.

He had made rather a lot of speeches for a man whose vocabulary had just deserted him.

He stepped back onto the landing and turned. His hand lifted toward her, hesitated, then settled against her cheek.

“I could argue with the idiot part.”

His mouth twitched, but the joke didn’t quite hold. He looked at her with an expression he would have preferred to manage better.

“I thought you might have come to see if you could stop wanting me once I finally admitted it.”

He hadn’t known he was going to say that. He disliked hearing it in the stairwell, where everything sounded a little louder and there was nowhere to busy himself with a kettle.

“And I was prepared to make that unpleasant for you, apparently.”

He brushed his thumb once along her cheek. There were questions waiting: what this meant, whether she would come back again, whether tomorrow he would be allowed to call. He wanted to ask all of them while the answer to this one was still warm.

Instead, he bent and kissed her. Briefly, though it took an effort to draw back.

“I’m glad you came for me.”

The plainness of it left him exposed. He resisted the urge to add anything clever.

From below came the heavy clunk of the building’s front door. Ilya glanced toward the sound, suddenly conscious of standing on a communal landing with his coat crooked and his shirt collar trapped beneath it.

“We’re still going for that walk,” he said.

He straightened his collar, then held out his hand.

“I need somewhere to put all this energy besides saying something stupid.” A beat passed. “Something else stupid.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I take his hand, my grip tight. "Good." I start down the stairs, pulling him with me. "Because I have a lot to say and I don't want your neighbors hearing it."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya followed, keeping pace rather than letting himself be dragged. At the bottom of the stairs he pushed the front door open with his shoulder. The cold caught at the gap in his coat.

“Left,” he said. “Unless you’ve got a destination. The main road’s full of people pretending not to listen.”

He wanted the joke to earn him something. He recognised that and, for once, didn’t look to see whether it had.

Outside, he tucked his free hand into his pocket. He left the other where it was, his fingers closing more securely around hers.

For half a block, he concentrated on walking. It was easier to bear the uncertainty with something changing around him: lit windows, a bicycle chained to a drainpipe, the bright strip of a shop still open. He could look ahead without making it a retreat.

Then he glanced toward her.

“I’m going to want to interrupt.”

He heard how that sounded and frowned.

“That wasn’t a request for you to manage it. Just—if I start explaining what I actually meant every time you tell me what I did, I’m doing the same bloody thing again.”

He nudged a loose stone off the pavement with his shoe. Already he had objections prepared to things she hadn’t said. He knew the imaginary argument so well he could win it without her participation.

“I’ve had eleven months to rehearse my side,” he said. “You’d think it would be better by now.”

His thumb shifted against her hand.

The urge to mention his own grievances rose again, less because they belonged here than because he disliked approaching a conversation unarmed. He let himself dislike it.

“All right,” he said, quieter. “What have you wanted to say?”

He kept walking beside her and left the question there.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I stop walking so he has to stop too. "You made me feel like I was failing a test I didn't know I was taking." The streetlight makes his face too easy to read. "Every single day."
