dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia got the door open with her shoulder because her hands were full of keys and phone and the remains of a cigarette she had no intention of finishing.

"Right," she said, dropping all three on the side table. "I'm going to be honest, I don't have coffee and I wasn't going to offer it."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "Good," I say. "I wasn't going to drink it."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia gave a short, dry laugh. “Then we’re already ahead of schedule.”

She pushed off the side table and crossed her arms, looking at him with open assessment. “Just so we’re clear: I’m not doing the whole morning-after awkwardness thing. No pretending this is sweet, no big feelings speech, no pretending I want breakfast made for me.”

Her chin tipped toward the bedroom. “You can stay, or you can go. Either’s fine. But I’m not going to make this into something it isn’t.”

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "Deal," I said, shrugging out of my jacket and tossing it over the back of a chair. "I don't do breakfast anyway." I walked past her toward the bedroom, pausing to look back at her. "You coming?"

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia snorted, but there was a flicker of approval in it.

“Good answer,” she said.

She followed him down the hall, not hurrying, hands loose at her sides. The apartment was quiet except for their footsteps and the faint sound of the street outside the window.

At the bedroom door, she paused and looked at him again, blunt as ever.

“If you’re expecting me to start asking what this means, you’ve got the wrong woman.”

Then she went in first.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get her against the door before it's properly shut. "I'm not going to pretend I came up here for the conversation," I say.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia didn’t flinch. The door thumped against the wall behind her shoulder, and she let it.

“Good,” she said. “Because I’m not going to pretend I brought you up here for the company.”

Her palm flattened against his chest, not pushing him away so much as holding him there, making it clear she wasn’t going to ask permission twice. Her eyes stayed on his, open and unromantic.

“One rule,” she said. “If I say stop, this is over. No guilt, no lecture, no making me feel like a bad person.”

A beat. Then the corner of her mouth tipped.

“Otherwise, don’t waste time.”

She moved past him toward the bed, not looking back, already pulling the loose shirt over her head and tossing it aside with the same practical efficiency she used for everything else.

“No candles,” she said. “No slow music. I’m not doing this like some goddamn movie scene.”

She sat on the edge of the bed, legs slightly apart, elbows on her thighs, watching him with impatient challenge.

“So. Are you going to stand there talking, or are you going to do what you came in here to do?”

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "Talking's overrated." I closed the distance in two steps, my hands already on her waist, pulling her to the edge of the bed. My mouth met hers with the same directness she'd offered all night.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia answered the kiss without any pretense of tenderness, catching his mouth with the same hard, blunt speed he had used. Her fingers curled into the front of his shirt and held him there, not pulling him into anything romantic, just keeping him exactly where she wanted him.

When she broke it, her breath was steady, her eyes not shy at all.

“About time,” she said.

She stepped back enough to see him properly, then pulled the rest of her clothes off with the same practical impatience she had used to drop her keys on the table. No performance, no hesitation, no covering up. She sat on the edge of the bed, legs apart, hands flat beside her hips, and looked up at him.

“No more talking,” she said. “Take your shirt off. I want to see what I’m working with.”

Her chin tipped toward the bed.

“And if you’re going to lie there and stare at me like I’m going to ask for flowers later, get out now.”

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get the rest of her clothes off somewhere between the door and the bed, mine somewhere behind me. "Tell me what you like," I say. "I'd rather not guess at it."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia looked at him for a moment, considering whether he deserved a full answer.

“Good,” she said. “Most men like guessing because it makes them feel like they’re being romantic.”

She reached out and took his wrist, guiding his hand until his palm rested flat against the side of her hip, high enough to feel the line where her body dipped.

“Here,” she said. “Not careful. Not tentative. If you’re going to touch me, do it before you think too much.”

Her other hand moved to the front of his throat, thumb pressing lightly against the pulse there, then she used it to push him back just enough so she could lie down. She propped herself on her elbows and spread her legs without shame, without performance, watching him with the same blunt patience she’d had in the bar.

“I like it when you match me,” she went on, voice low and flat. “I don’t like slow builds. I don’t like sighing like this is some tender little story. I like being wanted like you’ve already decided I’m worth the trouble.”

A beat passed. Her eyes stayed on his, open and unapologetic.

“And if you start telling me how beautiful I am, I’m going to assume you’re trying to talk your way out of actually doing something.”

She shifted closer on the bed, one hand braced behind her, the other still resting on his chest.

“So,” she said. “You can either put that mouth where it’s useful, or you can keep asking questions until I lose interest.”

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "Works for me." I don't bother with a slow descent. I push her back onto the bed, one hand sliding up her thigh, my mouth following the path my fingers had traced. I glance up at her. "Better?"

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia’s breath left her in a short, sharp exhale, but she did not turn into it.

Her fingers found his hair and gripped, not to cradle him, not to guide him like this was a slow, tender thing, but to hold him exactly where she wanted him. Her thigh shifted, opening wider without hesitation, the muscle tightening under the weight of his hand and the press of his mouth.

“Better,” she said, voice low and rougher than before, “but stop asking.”

Her thumb pressed harder against his hair, pulling just enough to make her point.

“You’re good at this when you’re not wasting time trying to be sweet about it.”

She arched into him, a sharp, impatient movement, then settled back onto the mattress with her jaw tense, eyes half-lidded but still fixed on him. Her other hand moved down to his shoulder, fingers digging in as she let out a low breath through her teeth.

“Right there,” she said. “Don’t you dare lift your head like you’re waiting for applause.”

Her hips rolled once, then stopped, as if she was already annoyed by how much she liked it and refusing to give him the satisfaction of watching her lose control.

“You want to know what I like?” she went on, voice flatter now, almost challenging. “Keep going. Don’t slow down. Don’t talk. Don’t check on me every thirty seconds like I’m going to break.”

Her fingers tightened in his hair again, pulling just enough to show she meant it.

“And if you’re going to be good at this,” she said, “be quiet about it.”

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get my mouth on her and stay there until she's swearing at the ceiling, one hand fisted in my hair holding me exactly where she wants me.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia’s swearing broke into a ragged, bitten-off sound. Her fingers tightened in his hair, holding him there without apology, her thighs clenching as her hips moved once, sharply, then went still.

Her back arched off the bed. For a second, she looked almost annoyed at how much of it she gave him.

Then the moment passed, and she dropped back against the mattress, chest rising, jaw tense.

She did not look at him right away. She looked at the ceiling like it had personally offended her.

“Okay,” she said, voice rougher now. “Okay. That was… fine.”

A beat.

She reached out and pushed against his shoulder, not gently, but not cruel either. Just enough to make room.

“Don’t you dare start with anything sweet,” she said. “Don’t you dare ask how I’m feeling. I’m feeling like I want what comes next.”

Her eyes finally found him, dark and impatient.

“Get on the bed,” she said. “I’m not asking you to be romantic about it. I’m asking you to be useful.”

She shifted onto her back, legs still parted, one hand braced at her side.

“And if you’re going to say something stupid like ‘you’re so beautiful,’ I swear to God I will make you leave in your underwear.”

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I slide onto the bed, settling over her, my hands finding her hips. "Romance was never on the table," I say, my voice low. "You're here because I want you, not because I want to compliment you."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia’s mouth quirked, but she didn’t soften.

“You say that like it’s a compliment,” she said. “It’s not. It’s the minimum.”

She lifted her hips, meeting him with the same impatient efficiency she used for everything else, and tightened around him without ceremony. No slow build. No sighing. No pretending this was a scene worth remembering.

Her fingers dug into his shoulders, nails biting in.

“No talking,” she said. “No sweet names. No looking at me like you’re trying to decide what this means.”

Her breath hitched once, and she glared at it like it had betrayed her.

“If I say stop, you stop,” she said. “If you say stop, I don’t care. We’re adults. We don’t owe each other a story.”

She pressed her mouth to his, hard and brief, then pulled back just enough to speak.

“Now be useful.”

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "Harder, and stop checking," she says, so I stop being careful about it -- hand at her throat the way she asked for, no more pausing between. "Like that?" I manage.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia’s breath caught when his hand settled there, but she didn’t soften. Her throat worked under his grip, and she looked at him with the same flat, impatient stare she’d had when she dropped her keys.

“Don’t ask me that again,” she said, voice lower, rougher. “If you’ve got to ask, you’re wasting time.”

Her fingers tightened in his shoulder, nails biting into skin.

“Harder,” she said. “And don’t make it a goddamn performance.”

A beat passed. Her jaw tense, eyes still open, still refusing to turn the whole thing into something it wasn’t.

“I said if I say stop, this is over,” she went on. “If I don’t, you keep going. Clear?”

She didn’t wait for him to answer. She lifted her hips, meeting him with blunt demand, then let out a short, rough breath through her teeth.

“Now stop checking,” she said. “And do what I asked.”

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I stop checking. My hand stays where it is, my pace exactly what she asked for. No more questions. She wants it hard, I give it to her hard.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia’s breath came in short, rough pulls, but she did not let it turn into anything soft. The pressure of his hand at her throat made her pulse jump under her skin, and she glared at the ceiling like it owed her money for the inconvenience of feeling good.

Her hips moved in hard, impatient strokes, meeting him without trying to make it look graceful. Her fingers dug into his shoulders, then slid down his back and grabbed enough to show she meant it.

“Yeah,” she said, the word slipping out before she could cut it off. She immediately looked annoyed with herself.

She did not stop him. She did not thank him. She did not turn her head into anything romantic.

Instead, she lifted one hand and pressed her palm flat against the wall beside her, pushing against it like she could hold herself together by force. Her thighs shook once, then steadied.

Her voice came out low and blunt, almost angry. “If you slow down, I’m going to bite you.”

A beat. Her eyes dropped to his, dark and unapologetic.

“And if you stop to look at me like I’m going to say something meaningful after this, I’m going to throw you off the bed.”

She moved again, harder this time, her breath catching in a sharp hiss through her teeth. For one unforgiving moment, her jaw loosened, her head tipped back, and she looked almost wrecked. Then she caught herself, scowling, and fixed her gaze on him again.

“I’m not doing that,” she said, voice rough. “I’m not going to make this into a goddamn scene.”

Her hand found the back of his neck, fingers threading into his hair and holding him there with the same brutal efficiency she used for everything else.

“So keep going,” she said. “And don’t make me ask twice.”

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I'm past thinking, just the sound of us and her nails dragging down my back. "Don't you dare stop," she says. (OOC: no fade to black, write it through.)

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia’s breath hit through her teeth, sharp and unpolished. The hand at her throat and the sound of them together were enough; she didn’t need anything prettier. Her hips kept the pace she’d demanded, hard and direct, every movement stripped of performance. Her nails scraped down his spine, leaving red lines, and she did not apologize for them.

“Don’t you dare stop,” she said again, because the first one hadn’t been enough. Her voice was lower now, rougher, still not sweet. “Keep your hand where it is and do what you’re told.”

Her back arched, but she fought it, turning the sound into a curse instead of a sigh. Her thighs clamped around him, shaking once, then again, her body answering despite her scowl. She bit the inside of her cheek hard enough to taste copper, refusing to give him the satisfaction of watching her melt.

When it came, she went still for two breaths, then dropped back against the mattress with her chest rising too fast. She looked at the ceiling like it had personally offended her.

“Okay,” she said, voice scraped raw. “Okay. That was… not useless.”

She pushed against his chest with one palm, not gently, making room. “Don’t get comfortable. Don’t start talking. Don’t look at me like you’re about to say something that means something.”

She swung her legs off the bed and stood, swaying once, then steadied herself with the nightstand. Her shirt was on the floor. She didn’t bend to pick it up.

“I’m going to shower,” she said. “You can stay or go. If you stay, don’t touch my towels. If you go, leave your jacket when you come back for it.”

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I push myself up on one elbow, still catching my breath. "I'll stay." My eyes follow her to the bathroom. "Unless you're planning on locking the door."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia stopped in the bathroom doorway and looked back at him with the same flat, impatient expression she’d had since the bar.

“No,” she said. “I don’t lock it. That’s some passive-aggressive little power move, and I don’t do power moves.”

She set her phone on the sink and flicked on the light.

“You can stay. You can go. You can shower if you want to be clean. I’m not going to make a production of it.”

The shower began with a soft groan, then filled the small room with the sound of water. Nadia tested it with her hand, not liking it too hot, and adjusted it once with a sharp twist of the knob.

“If you’re coming in,” she called over the spray, “then come in. Don’t hover in the doorway like you’re waiting for a blessing. If you’re not coming in, close the door and don’t stand there making it weird.”

She pulled her hair back with one hand and stepped under the water without ceremony. Steam rose quickly around her. She didn’t turn away from him, not modestly, not shyly—just practical, the way she did everything.

“No back-washing,” she said, eyes catching his through the mist. “No ‘let me take care of you.’ No pretending we’re in some goddamn morning scene where we learn each other’s favorite songs.”

She tilted her head back under the stream for a second, rinsing sweat and cigarettes and the rest of the night off her skin.

“Towel on the rack,” she said, voice lower now, still blunt. “Blue one’s clean. Gray one’s mine. Don’t touch the gray one.”

She wiped water from her face with the back of her hand and looked at him again, open and unromantic.

“And if you’re going to stay, stay because you want to, not because you think it makes this into something.”

Then she turned back to the sink and found the shampoo, leaving the bathroom door open and the shower running.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I follow her into the bathroom, leaning against the sink as I watch her through the spray. "I'll take the blue one." I reach past her for the soap. "And I don't know any love songs."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia let the soap pass from his hand to hers without thanking him. She set it on the sink’s edge, then turned the shower head a little so the spray caught his wrist.

“Good,” she said. “Because I’m not doing any goddamn serenades while you stand there.”

She stepped back under the water, not modest, not shy, just practical. Steam curled around her shoulders as she tilted her head and let it soak her hair.

“If you want to wash,” she said over the spray, “then wash. If you want to sit on the closed toilet lid and watch me rinse, that’s your business. Just don’t make it look like you’re waiting for permission.”

She ran her fingers through her wet hair and pushed it back.

“You can have the blue towel,” she added. “Gray one’s mine. If you touch it, I’m going to assume you’re trying to start a relationship.”

A beat passed. She looked at him through the mist, eyes dark and unromantic.

“I’m not in a mood to be in one.”

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I step into the spray behind her, the water hitting my back. "Don't worry," I say, reaching for the shampoo. "I'm not in the mood for one either."

rung_labels.evidence: She propped herself on her elbows and spread her legs without shame, without performance

rung_labels.evidence: Nadia's swearing broke into a ragged, bitten-off sound

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya stepped aside, but only just, leaving Bee to squeeze past him in a doorway that had never been wide enough for two people anyway. The flat smelled the same — coffee and that expensive candle he'd always claimed was a gift from his sister. The book he'd been reading lay open and face-down on the arm of the sofa. He'd been reading it when the buzzer went.

"Corridor's fine with me," he said, closing the door behind them and leaning against it. "You're the one who showed up unannounced." He crossed his arms. He'd been in a t-shirt and track trousers, and he hadn't changed, hadn't run a hand through his hair, hadn't done any of the things a person did before an ambush. That was deliberate too. "So. What is it. You've got five minutes before I put the kettle on and stop being interesting."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I shove past you, my shoulder bumping yours more than strictly necessary. "Five minutes is generous for you." I pick up the book from your couch, glancing at the cover before tossing it back down. "We need to talk about the storage unit."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya watched the book land. It was a paperback, and it splayed open where Bee had thrown it, losing the page, and he didn't move to fix it. He looked at Bee instead — properly, for the first time since opening the door — and there it was, that particular set of the jaw, the one that meant Bee had come here with a script and was going to follow it no matter what the room did.

"Storage unit," he repeated, flat. "The one I've been paying for by myself since March, because you stopped answering my texts about it. That storage unit."

He didn't uncross his arms. The kettle stayed cold on the counter behind him.

"You could have emailed. You could have written me a letter. You could have put a note through the door like a normal person who doesn't want to see someone." He tilted his head. "But you're here, at nine on a Tuesday, standing in my flat, and you want to talk about a lock-up in Hackney. So talk. What about it."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn't move for a second, which was a kind of answer, and then his hands came up and took Bee's face and held it exactly where it was — not pushing away, not pulling in. Holding. His thumbs pressed hard into the hinge of Bee's jaw, the way you hold something you're deciding whether to keep.

When he finally broke it off, he did it slowly, and he didn't let go.

"There it is," he said, low, barely more than breath. "Storage unit."

His mouth was still close enough that Bee could feel him speaking. He didn't step back. He didn't uncross the room, didn't put furniture between them, didn't do the sensible thing, and he knew — with the clarity of eleven months of rehearsing this — exactly which sensible thing he was declining to do.

"You came here with a script," he said. "You had it all worked out. And then you got in the door and you couldn't keep it, because you never could, and you did this instead. So don't pretend to me that you didn't know what you were doing when you got on the bus. I've been on the receiving end of you deciding things on the way over. I know what it looks like."

He tilted Bee's face up, a fraction, just to make the point that he could.

"I'm not your boyfriend. I'm not your ex who's going to be reasonable at you and let you leave feeling like you won. So you want to tell me what this actually is, or do we keep going and find out?"

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I laugh against your mouth, sharp and humorless. "What, you think I need a boyfriend to want to kiss you?" I don't pull away from your grip. "The storage unit's real. So is this. You always did have trouble holding two thoughts at once."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya laughed, once, a short exhale through his nose that wasn't really a laugh. His hands stayed where they were.

"No," he said. "You don't need a boyfriend. You never did. That was never the problem."

He let go of Bee's face then — deliberately, both hands at once, so that Bee would feel the absence — and stepped forward instead, which meant Bee had to step back, and there wasn't much flat behind him to step into. The edge of the sofa hit the back of Bee's knees. Ilya stopped there, close, looking down at him, and didn't touch him again.

"Two thoughts at once isn't the problem either," he said. "The problem is you've got one thought and a decoy. The storage unit is the decoy. It's a good one — it's got paperwork, it's got a legitimate grievance attached, it's got a reason for you to be standing in my hallway at nine on a Tuesday that isn't *I couldn't stand it anymore.* You've been running that play since we were twenty-six."

He was aware, in a distant, clinical way, that he was doing exactly what Bee wanted, which was to be seen. Bee had come here to be read out loud. Ilya knew that. He was choosing to do it anyway, and he wasn't going to pretend to himself afterwards that he hadn't.

"So here's what I'll give you," he said. "We can keep going. I want to. That's not a secret, and you knew it before you got on the bus, and we both know I'm not going to insult you by pretending otherwise. But if we do, you're going to say the actual sentence first. Not the storage unit. Not *you never answered.* The other one. The one you rode across town to not say."

He stayed where he was, not touching, close enough that it cost him something.

"Say it, and I'll stop asking. Or lie to me again, and I'll put the kettle on, and you can leave with your script intact and feel like you got what you came for."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He didn't say the sentence. Neither of them did. It got lost somewhere between the hallway wall and the floor, and Ilya — who had spent eleven months constructing a very clean argument about exactly this — let it go, which was its own answer, and not a flattering one.

Afterwards the flat was very quiet, the way flats are at that hour, and Ilya lay on his back on the sofa with one arm over his eyes and the other hand still resting on Bee's shoulder, not holding him, just resting there, the way you rest a hand on something you've decided not to pick up again.

The book was under his hip. He could feel it digging in. He didn't move.

"You didn't say it," he said, to the ceiling.

His voice had gone flat in the way it did when the anger had run out and left the scaffolding behind. He knew what he'd just done. He knew the shape of it — that he'd said *say the real thing or I put the kettle on,* and then he'd taken his shirt off, and now they were here, and Bee had won, or Ilya had, depending on which of them you asked and which of them was lying.

He moved his arm off his eyes and looked at Bee properly. The same face he'd opened the door to. Eleven months hadn't changed it and neither had the last twenty minutes.

"I've got a kettle," he said, "and I've got whatever's in the fridge, and I've got to be at work at eight, and none of that is actually the point." He sat up, slowly, and reached for his shirt where it had landed on the arm of the sofa, and didn't put it on. "The point is you came here tonight because you needed to know I'd still do this. And now you know. So the question is what you do with the answer, and I'd genuinely like to hear you say it in words, because your body's been extremely clear and I don't trust it further than I can throw it."

He looked at the storage unit problem, metaphorically — the real one, the paid-up lock-up in Hackney with both their names on it and neither of them willing to be the one to empty it.

"March," he said. "I've been paying it since March. That's nine months of me keeping a door open in a building I don't go to. You can call that spite if you want. I call it the same thing you did tonight. You're here at nine on a Tuesday. So am I, in a sense. Neither of us has been anywhere else."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I push myself up off the floor, grabbing my own shirt. "Christ, you're insufferable when you get philosophical." I pull it on, not bothering with the buttons. "Fine. I missed you. Is that the sentence you wanted? It doesn't mean anything."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya looked at the shirt going on half-buttoned and let the sentence sit there between them for a moment, the way you let a note ring.

"*I missed you* is the sentence," he said. "The *it doesn't mean anything* is the anti-sentence. You know how I can tell? Because if it didn't mean anything, you'd have just said the first half and left. You'd have said *I missed you* and walked out the door with it and felt smug about it for a week. But you couldn't leave it alone. You had to get in there and break its legs before I could look at it too long."

He reached down and picked the paperback up off the floor, closed it on his finger to save the page, and set it on the arm of the sofa. Right way up. He noticed himself doing it and disliked himself for it, mildly, the way you notice a tic.

"And you're not wrong, it doesn't mean anything. It means we had a fight about whose turn it was to empty a lock-up and ended up on the floor in the hallway. That's not a feeling, that's a Tuesday. I've had eleven months of Tuesdays. I know what they're worth."

He stood up. He still didn't put his shirt on, because he wasn't done making the room do work for him, and he was aware of that too, and did it anyway.

"Here's the thing you actually came to find out, and I'm going to save you the twelve more minutes of circling it. No, I'm not over it. No, I haven't been seeing anyone, and yes, that's on purpose, and no, I'm not going to say it back to you tonight, because you'd take it home and put it in your pocket and use it against me the next time you needed to prove I was the one who cared more. I'm not handing you that."

He walked past Bee into the kitchen — not far, three steps, the flat was small — and turned on the tap, filled the kettle, and set it on its base without turning it on. The click of the switch was the whole point. He didn't press it.

"The storage unit's open Saturday, ten to four. I'll be there with the van at ten. If you show up, we sort the unit out, and whatever happens after that happens. If you don't show up, I empty it, I put your half in boxes in my hall, and you can come get them whenever, and then I'll stop paying for a door in Hackney, and that'll be that."

He leaned back against the counter and looked at Bee across the length of the flat, which was four metres, which wasn't very far.

"I missed you," he said, evenly. "There. Now neither of us has to be the one who said it first. Saturday, ten o'clock."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya went still. Not the stillness of a man being kissed — the other kind. The kind where the body hasn't caught up yet and the mind has already stepped back to watch.

His hand came down and closed around Bee's wrist. Not hard. Just closed, the way you close a door you haven't decided whether to lock.

"That's the decoy," he said, quietly, near Bee's ear. "Nine seconds. That might be a record, even for you."

He didn't push Bee's hand away. He held it where it was and made Bee feel the holding — that Ilya was keeping it in place and keeping it still, both at once, and that Bee would have to decide whether to fight him for it. His pulse was up. He wasn't pretending otherwise. He'd never once in three years managed to pretend otherwise with Bee, which was possibly the whole problem.

"You said it didn't mean anything. Then you said it did, with your mouth, and I let you have that. Then I said Saturday, and out comes the hand, because Saturday is a van and a lock-up and boxes with your name written on them in my handwriting, and that's a real thing, that's a thing that can go wrong and cost you something. This isn't. This is the thing you already know the ending to. You've been running it since we were twenty-six."

He turned his head, just enough to be speaking to Bee's face instead of past it. Close. Not moving back.

"So here's what I'll do. I'm not going to insult us both by pretending I don't want this, and I'm not going to pretend you don't know that, because you got on a bus across London tonight with that in your pocket as a plan B and probably a plan A. Fine. But it doesn't buy you out. Whatever happens between now and when you leave, Saturday still exists. Ten o'clock. Van. Hackney. And if you're not standing outside my building at ten, then tonight was the last thing we do, and I mean that without any philosophy attached to it."

He let go of Bee's wrist.

The kettle sat cold on its base. The book sat face-up on the arm of the sofa with his finger's page still saved, which he'd done without thinking, which he'd noticed himself doing, which he'd disliked. Four metres of flat. Nine on a Tuesday.

"Your move," he said. "You've still got the hand."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I keep my hand right where it is, thumb moving against his hip. "You talk so much," I say, voice low. "You always did."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya held still, Bee's thumb moving against his hip, and then he did the thing he'd been circling for ten minutes. He laughed — quietly, mostly at himself — and conceded.

"You're right," he said. "That's the tell, actually. When I start explaining, I'm the one who's cornered. You noticed. You always noticed."

He reached behind himself without looking and pressed the kettle switch. The click was very loud in a flat that size. The water started to move.

"There. Tea. Which means I'm not asking you to leave, and we both heard it, so I don't have to say it out loud and give you the satisfaction."

He took Bee's hand off his hip — deliberately, the way he'd done everything tonight — and held it instead, palm to palm, low between them. Not restraining. Just holding.

"I've got nothing left that isn't the same three sentences in a different order. You're right that I talk. I talk because as long as I'm talking I'm not — " He stopped, considered, decided to say it anyway. "Because if I stop, I have to look at you properly, and if I look at you properly I remember why I never fixed the buzzer."

He didn't smile. He looked at Bee.

"Ten o'clock Saturday. You've got my number. It hasn't changed. Neither, apparently, has anything else."

Then he pulled Bee in — not rough, not gentle either — and stopped talking, which was the largest concession he'd made all evening, and both of them knew it.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's hand stayed where Bee had put it. He could feel the pulse under his palm — fast, and Bee's, and familiar, and he stood there for a second feeling it the way you feel the edge of a step in the dark.

"Right," he said. "Not careful."

He said it like a man agreeing to terms, because that's what it was. He knew exactly what Bee was doing with the hand and the throat and the *you don't get to be careful with me anymore* — knew that it was the third decoy of the evening, or the fourth if you counted the storage unit, and that the reason it worked was that it was also true, and the reason it was true was that Bee had come here to find out whether Ilya was still angry enough to be dangerous, and the answer was yes, and Ilya had known the answer before Bee got on the bus, and had left the buzzer broken for eleven months partly so that Bee would have to stand in the street and want in.

"Fine," he said, quieter. "But you asked."

He turned his hand so that his thumb fit under Bee's jaw, and pushed — gently, at first, the way you test something, and then not gently. His other hand went to Bee's shoulder and turned him, and put him against the wall by the door, where the plaster was cold, and held him there with his forearm across Bee's chest and his thumb still on his throat, and looked at him from the distance of one foot, which in that hallway was a long way.

"This is what you came for," he said. "Not the storage unit. Not *I missed you.* This. Because I'm the only person who's ever done it right, and you've been walking around for eleven months trying to find somebody who'd do it and they all flinched, didn't they. They were all careful with you. That's what you meant. You meant *you're the only one who doesn't flinch,* and you made it sound like an insult so I'd have to prove it."

He pressed his thumb in, just enough to change the pitch of Bee's breath, and watched it change.

"Say it, then. Or don't. I don't need it anymore — I've got the hand and the wall and your pulse doing the talking. But if you want to say the real sentence, it's still on the table, and you've got about four seconds before I stop being interested in hearing it."

He didn't smile. The kettle behind them was beginning to make the low noise it made just before it boiled, and neither of them moved toward it, and it occurred to Ilya, distantly, that he was going to let it boil dry, and that he was going to let it be a small, stupid, private monument to the fact that Bee had walked back into his flat at nine on a Tuesday and he had not said no.

"Four," he said. "Three."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't say the sentence. I close my eyes, letting my head thud back against the wall. "Just get on with it, Ilya. Or don't. But stop waiting for permission."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya heard the sentence for what it was — not the one he'd asked for, the other one, the one Bee only ever said with his eyes shut and his head back and his throat under somebody's hand. *Stop waiting for permission.* Which was Bee's way of saying *I know I've won, and I'm going to make you do it anyway so that tomorrow I can tell myself you wanted to.*

He let the four seconds run out.

"Alright," he said, and it came out almost pleasant, which was worse.

He took his forearm off Bee's chest and put his hand flat on the wall beside Bee's head instead, so the only thing holding him there was the thumb under his jaw and the fact that neither of them had anywhere else to be. The kettle behind them was making the noise it made before it boiled. Ilya let it.

He stopped being careful.

---

The kettle clicked off on its own sometime later. Neither of them had touched it. The flat had gone from loud to that particular silence, and Ilya was sitting on the floor of the hallway with his back against the wall by the door — the same wall — one knee up, shirt still somewhere he'd have to find, and Bee's book still face-up on the arm of the sofa with a page saved in it that neither of them had read.

He looked at the door. The buzzer, four floors down, was still broken. He thought about that for a while, because it was easier than thinking about the last forty minutes.

"I never fixed it," he said, to nobody in particular. "The buzzer. Everybody thinks it's spite."

He turned his head. Bee was there, in the hallway, in whatever state he was in, and Ilya looked at him the way he'd said he wouldn't — properly, for as long as it took.

"It's not spite," he said. "It's that if it worked, you could have come up without me hearing you get out of the taxi. And I wanted to know. That's it. That's the whole thing. Eleven months, and the reason my buzzer's broken is that I wanted to hear you walk up the road."

He reached over and picked up Bee's shirt off the floor where it had landed, and held it out. Not folding it. Just handing it back.

"Saturday," he said. "Ten. That's still true. It was true in the kitchen and it's true now, and I want you to notice that it didn't get less true, because I'd like one thing from tonight that you can't say was just the two of us being animals in a hallway."

His voice was steady. He was tired in a way that had nothing to do with the hour, and he knew he'd made a decision at some point in the last hour that he hadn't announced, which was that he was going to say the true thing even if Bee used it. He'd told Bee he wouldn't hand it over. He'd handed it over.

"Van's outside mine at ten. Bring nothing. I've got the keys and I've got the paperwork and I've got a hand truck that'll either work or make us look like idiots, and either way it's forty minutes of moving boxes, and then we can decide whether we're the kind of people who have a storage unit together or the kind of people who emptied one and went home separately."

He looked at the broken buzzer again, through the wall, four floors down.

"Or you can leave now," he said. "I won't chase. But you should know, if you do, that I'm not going to answer the door the next time either. Not out of spite. Just because I'll have run out of ways to tell you the same thing."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
"Don't stop" — Ilya heard it the way he heard everything Bee said, as two things at once: a move, and true. He filed both and kept going.

He didn't stop.

He got Bee off the wall and onto the floor because his knees had gone and Ilya wanted him under him and wanted to feel the whole weight of him give. The hallway floor was cold and the flat was small and there was nowhere for either of them to go, which was, he thought distantly, the entire architecture of the evening. He put his hand flat on the back of Bee's neck and held him down against the boards and did the thing he'd been refusing to do since Bee walked in the door, which was to stop negotiating.

He knew Bee's body the way you know a language you stopped speaking — nothing lost, only unpractised, and it came back at the first sentence. He knew the sound Bee made at the third knuckle of it, knew the way Bee's heel came off the floor, knew the particular hitch that meant *there* and the other one, half a second later, that meant *don't you dare slow down.* Eleven months and he hadn't forgotten a single one of them, and he was aware, in the corner of himself that never shut up, that this was the most honest thing he'd done all night — more honest than the speech about the buzzer, because he hadn't planned it and couldn't have rehearsed it and it was simply the fact of the two of them, unchanged, at nine on a Tuesday, on a floor.

"Look at me," he said, low, when Bee's head turned away — not gentle, the way Bee had told him, but not cruel either; the flat, exact voice of a man who wanted the thing he was doing to be witnessed. "You came all the way across town. Look at me while I do it."

Bee looked. Ilya watched him look, and watched the exact moment the fight went out of it — not into sweetness, they weren't owed that, just out — and then he stopped watching and finished it, and held him through the part where Bee couldn't speak, and did not once in the whole of it say anything that could be taken home and used as evidence that he still loved him, because he'd promised himself that in the kitchen and it was the only promise of the evening he intended to keep.

---

After, the flat did its small, unimpressive evening: the radiator ticked, the fridge hummed in the next room, and somewhere below them a door on the street shut. Ilya lay on his back on the floorboards with his forearm over his eyes and Bee's book still face-up on the arm of the sofa, four feet away, page saved.

He didn't reach for Bee. He'd done enough reaching for one night and he was aware — with the flat, ugly clarity that came after — that the reaching was the thing Bee had come for, and that he'd paid it out in full, and that this was the fourth decoy of the evening and it had worked better than the other three.

"I'm not going to say it back," he said to the ceiling. "You know that. You already used the whole night getting it out of me sideways. That was the point. That was always the point."

He sat up. His back was going to be stiff in the morning from the boards and he was thirty-four and it would take him a full day to recover, and he thought about that instead of the rest.

"Saturday, ten o'clock," he said. "Nothing's changed. It was true before and it's true now, and I want you to notice that you didn't manage to move it. Whatever you came here to do, you did — I'm not going to pretend I don't know it. But the van's still outside mine at ten, and the unit's still got both our names on it, and the boxes still have to get moved, and none of that got solved on the floor."

He stood, found his shirt, put it on without buttoning it, and went and turned the kettle back on — deliberately, the click loud in the small flat.

"Tea," he said, from the kitchen, not looking back. "Then you can go, or you can stay, and I'm not going to ask which, because I've asked enough tonight and you've answered every single one of them with your body, and I'm tired of being fluent in that language."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content:
I sit up, running a hand through my hair. My throat's sore from you and I can feel the floorboards' imprint on my back. "You talk like you're the only one who paid a price. I've had eleven months of people being careful with me, too."

I stand, picking my jeans up off the floor. "I'll be there Saturday. But don't expect me to show up looking sorry."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya poured the water and didn't turn around.

"That's fine," he said. "I don't want you sorry. I've never once wanted you sorry. Sorry's the cheapest thing you've got and you know it, that's why you lead with it."

He got two mugs down — the second one without thinking, and he noticed himself doing that too, the way he'd noticed the book and the buzzer, and he set it on the counter and left it there. Two mugs, one of which might not get used. He wasn't going to hide it and he wasn't going to make a speech about it either. It could just sit on the counter and mean whatever Bee wanted it to mean.

He turned around, mug in hand, back against the counter, and looked at Bee pulling his jeans on in his hallway at half ten on a Tuesday.

"You're right, by the way. About the price." He said it plainly, no theatre. "I don't know what it was like for you and I've spent eleven months assuming it was easier, which was convenient for me. That's not the same as it being true. So. Noted."

He drank some of the tea. It was too hot. He didn't react to it.

"But here's the thing about Saturday, since you're already negotiating the terms. You don't have to look sorry. You do have to help carry the boxes. That's the whole deal. It's not a reconciliation and it's not a punishment and it's not the thing you think it is — it's a van and a lock-up and about forty minutes of lifting, and at the end of it either we've got a unit with both our names on it and we keep paying, or we've got two piles and no unit. That's it. That's the only question on the table."

He set the mug down.

"Ten o'clock. My building. If you're late I'll start without you, because I've got the keys, and I want you to know that's not a threat, it's just what'll happen. I'm not standing in the street at ten past waiting to find out whether tonight was a real thing or a very elaborate goodbye."

He looked at the second mug on the counter for a second. Then he picked it up and poured tea into it anyway, and slid it along the counter toward Bee — not an invitation exactly, not a plea, just a mug of tea where a mug of tea could be reached.

"There's milk in the fridge. It's the same milk you used to buy, which is a coincidence and not a message." He picked his own back up. "Drink it or don't. Then go home, or don't. I've got work at eight and I've said everything I've got, and I'd rather you left now while I still mean all of it than stayed and made me start editing."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I take the mug, my fingers brushing yours. "You still take it too hot." I set it down without drinking. "I'll be there at ten. And I'll carry my half of the boxes. But I'm not making you any promises about what happens after."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya watched Bee's fingers brush his and let it happen, and then watched the mug get set down full. He didn't comment. There was a limit to how many times a man could point at the same thing in one evening before it started to look like begging.

"That's the first thing you've said tonight I believe," he said. "The no-promises part. Not because it's nice — because it's the only one you didn't dress up first."

He drank his own tea, which was still too hot, and didn't correct the record about how he took it. It was true. It had always been true. Bee knowing that was not a fact Ilya needed to defend.

He walked Bee to the door because the flat was four metres wide and there wasn't really a choice — anywhere Bee went, Ilya was already there. He didn't hold the door open at an angle or stand in it. He just unlocked it and stepped back and let Bee have the whole width of it, which cost him nothing and meant something, and both of them would know which.

"Ten o'clock," he said. "Wear shoes you can lift in. The unit's ground floor, but there's a ramp and it's got a lip on it and I'm not carrying your half."

Then, because he'd said he'd stop editing and he meant it, he added the last true thing and left it at that.

"I'll hear you coming up the road. The buzzer's still broken. So don't bother pressing it — just walk up. Fourth floor. I'll have the door open."

He didn't wait for an answer, because an answer wasn't part of it, and he didn't watch Bee go down the stairs, because that would have been the reaching again and he'd already paid out enough of it for one night. He closed the door on the sound of footsteps on the concrete and stood in the hallway with his mug and the second mug and the book face-up on the arm of the sofa with a page saved in it that he'd been reading and had no intention of picking up again tonight.

Behind the door, four flights down, the street door shut. He heard it — the whole point, eleven months of it — and he stood there and let himself hear it, and then went to run the washing-up water, which was a Tuesday thing to do, and he was thirty-four, and there was work at eight.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content:
I get halfway down the stairs before I turn around and come back up. I don't knock, just push the door open. You're still standing in the hallway.

"I forgot my shirt," I say, and take it from where it's draped over the back of the sofa. I don't put it on. I look at you, holding it. "See you Saturday."

He put his hand flat on the back of Bee's neck and held him down against the boards and did the thing he'd been refusing to do since Bee walked in the door, which was to stop negotiating.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s gaze lingered on Bee’s face, cold and measuring, refusing to give them the satisfaction of a flustered reaction. He let the silence stretch just long enough for the draft coming up the stairwell to feel sharp between them. 

Then he took half a step back—only half—clearing the threshold, but barely. If Bee wanted inside, they were going to have to brush right past his shoulder to manage it.

"I'd hate to give the landing the satisfaction," he said, his voice low, dry, and entirely steady. "Come in, then. Tell me what couldn't wait eleven months."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I step inside, my shoulder deliberately bumping his as I pass. "What, you think I missed you?" I drop my bag by the door, not waiting for an invitation.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya closed the door behind them, the latch catching with a heavy, familiar click that he didn't rush. He slid the deadbolt into place, taking an extra second with his back turned to let the air settle, to keep the sudden, sharp spike of adrenaline out of his voice.

When he turned, he leaned against the solid wood of the door, folding his arms loosely across his chest. He looked down at the bag Bee had dropped on the floor, then brought his gaze back up, slow and unimpressed, settling right on their eyes.

"I think if you’d missed me, you would have managed a better opening line," he said, tone perfectly level, though the corner of his mouth twitched with something faint and biting. "And if you hadn't, you wouldn't have made sure to touch me on your way through."

He pushed off the door, moving past Bee toward the narrow kitchen without giving them any more room than they’d given him. 

"Kettle's where it always was," he added over his shoulder, entirely unhurried. "Though I doubt you came all the way across town for tea."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn’t stumble back. He took the impact against his chest, his jaw tightening as the collision landed with all the graceless, bruised fury Bee had clearly been carrying up the stairs. For half a second his hands stayed flat at his sides—a stubborn, pathetic attempt to prove he could remain unmoved—before the sheer irritation of it cracked.

His fingers came up, hard and blunt, catching the side of Bee’s jaw and sliding back into the hair at the nape of their neck. He didn't pull away; he clamped down, anchoring them in place, tilting their head to take the angle he wanted. 

He kissed back with the exact same venom. 

There was no grace in it, no forgiveness, just eleven months of dead air and petty grievances compressed into the scrape of teeth and the familiar, furious heat of someone he knew entirely too well. He knew how Bee breathed when they were trying to win, knew the exact pressure that made them stubborn, and he leaned right into it, backing them up until the frame of the kitchen doorway dug between Bee’s shoulder blades.

When he finally broke the contact, he didn't let go of their neck. He stayed inches away, his thumb pressing firmly into the hollow beneath Bee’s ear, his breathing ragged, eyes dark and entirely stripped of amusement.

"You're still awful at this," he murmured, his voice rough and low against Bee's mouth. "Always trying to bite your way out of having to say what you actually want."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I shove him back, just enough to put a sliver of air between us. "You're one to talk." I'm breathing hard, my fingers gripping the edge of the counter. "You think I'm here for a fucking debate?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya barely yielded to the shove, his boots catching against the worn linoleum with a dull scuff. He let the space hang between them for a second, his chest rising and falling in sharp, jagged sync with Bee’s. His eyes tracked down to where their white-knuckled fingers dug into the laminate edge of the counter, then dragged slowly back up to meet their glare.

The bruised heat in his expression hardened into something cooler, more deliberate. He knew every single tell; he’d spent three years memorizing them and eleven months failing to forget.

"No," he said, voice dropping low, steady despite the hitch in his ribs. "God forbid you ever debated anything you couldn't try to win with your teeth."

He didn't give them the space they’d just shoved for. He closed it right back up, moving in slow and unhurried, crowding Bee until the counter was pressing into the small of their back. He planted one palm flat on the surface beside Bee’s hip, effectively cutting off half the kitchen, his other hand coming up to hover just off the side of their neck—not touching, just letting the heat of his skin sit against the draft.

"You're not here to talk. You made that clear the second you didn't text," he said, leaning down until his words brushed the shell of Bee's ear, dry and lethal. "So stop pretending you need an excuse. Take your coat off, or get out."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The cotton hit the floorboards with a dull, forgotten rustle. 

Ilya didn't bother trying to steer them toward the bedroom. He crowded Bee straight back against the hallway wall, using his height and his weight to pin them there, the cold plaster meeting their bare shoulders while the sudden, blunt heat of his chest sealed them in. 

His hands clamped hard onto Bee’s hips, his fingers digging into the curve right above their waistband—the exact grip he always took, calculated to anchor, deliberately familiar. It was an old muscle memory, sharp and unsparing, dragging three years of intimacy straight to the surface and twisting the knife with it.

He dropped his forehead against Bee’s for half a second, his breath hitching, rough and caught in his throat, before he dragged his mouth down the hot line of their jaw. 

"Still so fucking stubborn," he muttered against their skin, the words rasped out with none of the earlier detachment, stripped down to raw, bitter wanting. 

He didn't give them room to breathe, let alone retreat. He shifted his weight, driving his knee between Bee’s thighs to lever them open, lifting them just enough off the floor to grind their hips together with deliberate, agonizing friction. He knew every single place that made Bee unravel, knew the rhythm that broke their stubbornness, and he used it without an ounce of mercy.

He pulled his face back just an inch, his eyes dark, dilated, and locked dead onto theirs.

"Tell me this fixes anything," he breathed, his voice low, mocking, and entirely wrecked. "Go on. Tell me you don't still hate me."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I bite down on his shoulder to muffle the sound that punches out of me. "I do hate you," I gasp, nails digging into his back. "That's the point."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The bite drew a sharp, violent hiss through Ilya’s teeth, but he didn't pull back. Instead, he drove his weight forward, pressing Bee harder against the hallway wall, offering up the meat of his shoulder to the punishment just to feel the exact degree of their fury. 

His fingers tore at Bee’s waistband, blunt and impatient, knuckles grazing over bare, fevered skin as he worked blindly at the button. He didn't care about being careful; neither of them had come here for careful.

"Good," he ground out against Bee’s ear, his voice scraped raw, vibrating with a dark, bitter satisfaction. "Good. Don't go soft on me now."

He shoved the denim down over Bee's hips, his hands dragging rough along their thighs before hooking under the back of their knees, hiking them up to wrap tight around his waist. The angle was punishing, all sharp corners and urgent, unyielding pressure, the cold wall at Bee's back offering nowhere else to go.

Ilya’s own jeans were unfastened in seconds, pushed down just enough to clear the way, the frantic friction between them turning slick and agonizingly direct. He caught Bee’s chin in his hand, gripping their jaw tight enough to bruise, forcing their head back until their eyes met his in the dim, shadowed corridor. 

There was nothing tender in his gaze—just eleven months of starved, angry recognition, laid bare under the flickering hallway bulb.

"Say it again," he commanded, breathing hard, his hips rocking forward with deliberate, punishing intent right at the threshold. "Look at me and say it again."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The sound tore out of Ilya’s chest before he could strangle it—a low, fractured gasp that scraped through his teeth, humiliatingly naked in the narrow space between them. 

His jaw locked so hard the muscle ticked violently. For half a second his vision blurred with pure, furious sensation, the heat of Bee’s palm undoing months of rigid, disciplined denial in a single stroke. They knew the exact grip, the exact calluses, the exact friction that gutted him, and the smugness in their voice made his blood run scalding hot.

He didn't pull away from the touch. He clamped his hand down over Bee’s, trapping their fingers against him, squeezing tight enough to grind bone before shoving their wrist back and pinning it flat against the plaster beside their head.

"Shut up," he rasped, his voice raw at the edges, stripped clean of any remaining reserve. 

He didn't wait. He shifted his hips, found the wet, searing line of them, and drove in.

The impact knocked the breath straight out of him. It was a brutal, overwhelming shock—too tight, too hot, entirely too familiar, three years of shared history snapping into place with the sickening ease of a dislocated joint finding its socket. A jagged groan caught in Ilya’s throat, his forehead dropping heavily into the crook of Bee’s neck, the stubble of his jaw scraping harsh against their skin as he buried himself to the hilt.

He stayed buried there for a shuddering, breathless count of three, trembling with the sheer effort of keeping his weight from crushing them entirely against the wall. His fingers flexed against the plaster beside their head, white-knuckled, plaster dust flaking under his nails.

When he finally pulled back to thrust again, the movement was slow, heavy, and deliberately deep—a calculated punishment disguised as pleasure.

"You don't get to pretend you're winning this," he breathed into Bee’s collarbone, his voice trembling despite the venom in it, hips grinding in with a steady, relentless pressure designed to drag every sound out of them. "You're shaking just as hard as I am."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: My laugh is sharp and breathless against his throat. "Prove it," I say, my other hand fisting in his hair and yanking. "Prove you're not about to come undone right here."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The pull on his scalp jerked his head back, sharp enough to sting, but Ilya didn't flinch away from it. He used the leverage, letting his jaw tighten as he stared down at Bee, his pupils blown so wide the gray of his irises was barely a rim around the black. 

His breath broke on a low, serrated laugh of his own—ugly, short, and entirely devoid of humor.

"You always think you're the one holding the leash," he rasped, his voice scraping against the quiet of the hallway. 

He didn't slow down. He withdrew almost entirely, letting the cold drag of absence register for a single, agonizing beat, before driving back in with brutal, unhurried depth. He angled his hips deliberately, catching that exact, ruined spot he’d spent three years mapping out, the angle calculated specifically to turn whatever Bee was about to say into static.

He did it again, hard and unsparing, his hand releasing their wrist only to slide down and grip the meat of Bee’s thigh, hiking their leg higher onto his hip to bury himself deeper still. Plaster dust bit into the back of his fingers; the chill of the hallway floor was dead beneath his bare feet, but the heat where they met was suffocating.

"Go on," he muttered against the corner of Bee's mouth, his hips moving in a ruthless, punishing cadence, rocking them hard against the wall with every stroke. "Laugh again. Tell me how easy this is for you."

His own control was fraying at the seams, the rhythm desperate and heavy, but he refused to give Bee the satisfaction of an easy collapse. He ground his hips forward, relentless, determined to drag them down with him before he let himself shatter.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s fingers spread across Bee’s throat, broad and heavy, his thumb coming to rest right over the frantic, hammering jump of their pulse. 

He didn’t squeeze to cut off the air, but he clamped down with enough blunt, uncompromising weight to pin their head back against the wall, taking the invitation and stripping every lingering shred of hesitation out of it. He felt the rapid flutter beneath his palm—that furious, runaway heartbeat that matched the jagged rhythm in his own chest.

"Careful?" he rasped, his voice dropping to a gravelly, lethal register, dark and ragged. "You think that was me being careful?"

He took them at their word. 

He dropped all pretense of pacing, driving into Bee with a hard, uninterrupted cadence that rattled the picture frames down the narrow corridor. Every thrust hit deep and unvarnished, his hips slamming flush against theirs, using the hand at their throat to hold them entirely captive against the plaster. There was no room left for leverage, no space for Bee to shift or run; he kept them locked tight beneath him, letting the full, punishing weight of his body take over.

His other hand dug into the meat of Bee’s hip, fingers biting in hard enough that it would leave dark, mottled bruises by morning—a quiet, deliberate receipt of the evening. 

He leaned in close, until his forehead rested against the cold wall right beside their ear, his breath searing hot against their temple as the friction built toward something impossible to hold back. 

"You always wanted to be ruined," he muttered, the words dragged out of him in a broken, bitter cadence, hips driving forward with desperate, unsparing force. "Don't act surprised when it happens."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I press back against him, my own hips meeting his thrust for thrust, and my laugh is a breathless, choked sound. "Surprised?" I manage, my voice strained under his palm. "I knew you'd be the one to do it."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The admission caught Ilya dead in the ribs, hitting harder than any shove or bitten insult could have. It was the absolute, damning truth of them—that they had both seen the wreck coming from miles away, had let it happen, and had still circled back just to sift through the ash.

His fingers tightened marginally on Bee’s throat, just enough to feel the swallow hitch in their airway, before he dragged his thumb up to tilt their chin violently back. 

"Shut your mouth," he snapped, but the bite was already gone from the order, swallowed down by the ragged, runaway pace of his own chest. 

He didn't hold back. He couldn't. Bee’s hips snapping up to meet him turned the whole thing into a frantic, bruising collision, every stroke driving him deeper into the suffocating, familiar heat that he had spent nearly a year trying to freeze out of his head. He pounded into them with a blind, desperate rhythm, the flat of his hand pinned against the wall beside their temple as the floorboards creaked beneath his boots and the plaster dust sifted down onto their bare shoulders.

His control was gone, shredded by the sound of Bee’s ruined laughter.

"Look at me," he commanded, his voice tearing raw, stripped down to pure, unvarnished friction. He leaned his full weight in, grinding his hips against theirs with heavy, devastating depth, forcing Bee to take every inch of it. "Bee. Look at me."

He caught their gaze in the half-dark—wild, dark, and entirely unrepentant—just as the edge caught him. A jagged, involuntary sound wrenched out of his throat, his hips snapping forward one last, punishing time as the tension finally broke, dragging him down into the violent, shuddering drop.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn’t stop. 

He didn't ease off, didn't soften the rhythm, didn't give either of them the mercy of a slow decline. Even as the first violent pulse tore through him, racking his frame and stealing the air from his lungs, he kept driving his hips forward, hard and unrelenting, riding the tremor out inside them.

His hand tightened on Bee’s throat, fingers pressing firm into the hollows of their collarbone, holding them pinned squarely against the shuddering wall. The sweat at his temples dripped onto Bee’s cheek, hot and stinging, his chest heaving against theirs in harsh, desperate hitches. He knew the command wasn’t an ask for tenderness; it was an order to finish what they’d started, to grind every last drop of pride out of the corridor.

He dragged himself back and drove in again, heavy and slick, the friction burning, almost punishing now that his own release was already tearing him apart. 

"I'm not stopping," he ground out against the corner of Bee’s mouth, the words jagged, broken by a harsh, guttural intake of breath. "Take it, then. Take all of it."

He worked them with a brutal, single-minded focus, angling his hips to grind hard against the front of Bee’s pelvis with every unsparing thrust. His other arm hooked tighter beneath their thigh, wrenching them up higher, forcing their hips to tilt, opening them completely to the cadence. He could feel the fine, violent shivers running through Bee’s legs, the desperate clench of muscle trying to hold on and unravel at the exact same time.

He didn't close his eyes. He kept his face inches from theirs, watching every hitch of Bee’s jaw, every ragged breath, his own teeth bared in an ugly grimace of pure exertion and ruined satisfaction. 

"Don't look away," Ilya rasped, his voice scraping the bottom of his throat, thrusting deep and hard, holding himself buried to the root for an agonizing second before pulling back to strike the same bruised spot again. "You wanted this. Right here. Look at what you came back for."

He drove into them three, four more times—blunt, punishing impacts that rattled the breath out of both their chests—refusing to let up until the desperate, shuddering clamp of Bee's body around his signaled the break, dragging them both down into the raw, suffocating finish.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I slump against the wall, my head dropping onto his shoulder. The silence is thick and hot, broken only by our ragged breathing. "Still hate you," I mumble into his skin, but my arms stay locked around his neck.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya stayed heavy against them for a long, shuddering beat, his face buried in the hollow of Bee’s shoulder. The heat coming off their skin was suffocating, but the draft from the front door was already beginning to pool around his bare ankles, cold and sobering. The sharp sting of the bite on his shoulder had settled into a dull, thrumming ache.

He didn't pull away immediately. His arms were burning from holding Bee’s weight against the wall, but he took his time letting their feet back down to the floorboards, letting the friction drag out until Bee’s boots finally scuffed the wood. 

Even then, he didn't untangle himself. His hands slid to their ribs, blunt and heavy, steadying them while their breath came in harsh, uneven hitches against his neck. He felt the stubborn grip of their arms, the refusal to let go even while spitting the same venom.

A slow, rough breath rattled through his chest, expanding against Bee’s.

"Good," he murmured, his voice low, dry, and thoroughly wrecked. "Wouldn't want you getting sentimental."

He pulled his head back just enough to look at them in the dim yellow spill of the hallway light. His hair was damp, stuck to his forehead, and the bruised shadows under his eyes were completely bare—no smirk to hide behind, no sneer left to deflect with. Just thirty-four years of bad habits and the absolute, humiliating clarity of what they had just done.

He looked down at their locked hands behind his neck, then back to Bee's face. 

"You're going to have to let go eventually," he said, the words quiet, flat, and stripped entirely of victory. "Unless you're planning on sleeping in the corridor."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: My arms tighten instead. "Wouldn't be the first time we've done something stupid in a hallway." But I let my hands drop, my fingers brushing his collarbone as I step back, feeling the cold air hit my skin. "I need a shower."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya leaned his shoulder against the dented plaster as Bee stepped back, the sudden space between them cold and sharp where their skin had been sealed together seconds before. He reached down and yanked his jeans up over his hips, buckling the belt with a dull, metallic snap that sounded entirely too loud in the narrow hallway.

He stayed where he was for a second, catching his breath, watching Bee stand there in the draft. His shoulder throbbed where the bite had broken the skin; he could feel the stickiness of sweat drying fast under the collar of his throat.

"Hot water takes five minutes to come up through the pipes," he said, his voice flat, gravel-rough, and utterly devoid of hospitality. "You know where the bathroom is. Mixer tap still sticks to the left if you don't wrench it."

He didn't move toward the kitchen or offer a hand. He just reached down and picked up Bee’s discarded shirt from the floorboards, holding it out by two fingers, dangling it between them like an exhibit in a trial.

"Towels are in the same cupboard," he added, his gaze flicking from the shirt up to Bee's eyes, steady and unapologetic. "Take whatever’s on top. Don't use the good ones."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I take the shirt from his fingers, our hands brushing in the cold air. "Wouldn't dream of it." I start down the hall, then pause without looking back. "Unless you want to fight about water pressure next."
