dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya considered the corridor. Mrs. Adeyemi at number six had her door on the chain and would be listening, the way she'd listened to the last one, the one with the suitcase. He wasn't going to give her the sequel for free.

He stepped back. Not far. Just enough that Bee would have to come past him, close, the way the hall was built.

"You know where everything is," he said. "Nothing's moved."

Which was a lie, and a small one, and one he'd chosen. He'd moved the good chair. He'd thrown out the mug. He watched to see if Bee would notice either, because Bee had always noticed, and had always said something, and Ilya had always said *it's just a chair,* and there it was — the whole argument, folded up small and waiting in the hallway like a coat.

He shut the door behind them and leaned on it.

"So," he said. "Which bit did you come to finish."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I step inside, my shoulder brushing his as I pass. The air smells the same—old books and his cheap laundry detergent. “You got rid of the green chair,” I say flatly, not turning to look at him. “Couldn’t just leave one fucking thing where it was, could you.”

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Of course Bee had. Of course it was the first thing. Ilya felt the small mean satisfaction of it land somewhere under his ribs, and then the other thing, the worse thing, which was that he'd wanted to be seen doing it. Eleven months and he'd still arranged the room for an audience of one.

"It's just a chair," he said, because he had to. Because it was his line and the scene didn't work without it.

He stayed on the door a moment longer, then pushed off it and went past Bee into the kitchen, not brushing shoulders this time, giving it a deliberate inch. He filled the kettle. He didn't ask.

"The springs were gone. It was giving me a bad back." He set two mugs on the counter and did not look at which two. "You never sat in it anyway. You sat on the arm of it. Like a cat that wanted credit for being in the room."

The kettle started its low climb. He turned and leaned back against the counter with his arms crossed, and let himself actually look — properly, for the first time since the corridor. Bee's hair was different. Ilya filed that away and did not say it, because saying it would mean admitting he'd catalogued the old version well enough to compare.

"You didn't drive forty minutes to talk about furniture," he said. "You're stalling. You always stall in the hallway and then you come in swinging. So." He tilted his head at the room, the flat, the whole arrangement of it. "Swing."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya had known. Not the shape of it, exactly, but the weight — he'd felt it coming up the corridor behind Bee like weather, and he'd stood in the doorway and let it in anyway.

He didn't move for the first second. That was deliberate. Let Bee do the work of closing the distance, let Bee be the one who came in swinging and found the target hadn't flinched. Then his hand was in Bee's hair — the different hair, shorter at the back, wrong under his fingers and he hated that he noticed — and he kissed back with his teeth in it, because if this was the argument then he wasn't going to be the one who conceded the point.

The kettle clicked off behind him. Neither of them was going to make tea.

He broke it. Just far enough to speak, not far enough to be mistaken for stopping. His thumb stayed at the hinge of Bee's jaw, pressing, the way he'd used to when he wanted Bee to shut up and listen, which had never once worked.

"That's not an answer," he said, low. "That's you changing the subject. You always do this. You'd rather be touched than be right, and then you spend three weeks hating me for letting you."

He said it against Bee's mouth. He said it and then he took the inch back, the one he'd given in the doorway, the one he'd given in the kitchen, all of them at once, because he was thirty-four and sober and he knew exactly what this was and he'd decided it was worth it somewhere around the word *stalling*.

"So tell me I'm wrong," he said. "Or don't. But you're not getting to do both."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "You're not wrong." I press closer, my hand fisting in his shirt. "But you're letting me anyway. So what does that say about you?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
It said plenty. Ilya knew exactly what it said, had known since he stepped back from the door and made the hall narrow on purpose, and the thing about knowing was that it didn't help. It never had. He'd always been able to see the whole board and still put his hand on the hot part of the stove.

"It says I'm a hypocrite," he said. "Congratulations. You drove forty minutes to find out something you knew at the flat in Leyton."

Bee's fist was in his shirt, pulling the collar off-true, and Ilya let it be pulled. He put his hand over Bee's — not to take it off, to hold it there, to press it flat against his chest so Bee could feel that his heart was going like he'd run up the stairs. He wasn't going to pretend otherwise. That had been one of the problems. He'd pretended not to want things and then been furious when nobody gave them to him.

"You want the rest of it?" He was close enough now that the question was mostly breath. "It says I moved the chair so you'd notice. It says I kept your number so I could watch it ring and not answer. It says I've been having this argument with an empty room for eleven months and I'm bored of winning."

He turned them. One step, then another, until it was Bee's back against the counter and the kettle ticking as it cooled beside them. He got a knee between Bee's and didn't push, just made it clear he could.

"So yes. I'm letting you." His mouth went to the side of Bee's neck, below the ear, the spot he'd found in the second month and used unfairly in every fight after. He said the rest there, against the skin, so Bee would have to feel the words as well as hear them. "And you're letting me let you. So don't stand in my kitchen and act like you're the only one here with a point to make."

His hand slid from Bee's chest down to the hem of the shirt and stopped. Not a question. A pause with intent, the way he'd used to hold a door.

"Last chance to be right instead," he said. "I'd take it if I were you. I'm not going to be kind about this."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The hallway. Of course the hallway. Ilya had built it narrow on purpose and now it was doing its job too well, wall at his shoulder, coats hooked behind Bee's head, the light from the kitchen doorway cutting them both in half.

His shirt was gone. He hadn't decided to let that happen and he'd let it anyway, arms up like a child being undressed, and then his hands were on Bee's bare back and he was thinking *thinner* and *warm* and *no* in that order, and none of it slowed him down.

He got Bee against the wall. Properly against it, one hand flat on the plaster beside Bee's head for leverage, the other spread low on Bee's stomach, and he waited a breath to see if there'd be a hand over his, a word, anything. There wasn't. So.

"You're going to have marks," he said, not a warning, a forecast. His mouth was on Bee's collarbone, then lower, and he made the first one there, deliberate, where a shirt would hide it and Bee would know it was there all week. "You're going to look at them on Thursday and get angry at me all over again. Good. Save me the text."

Bee's belt was old — the same belt, he registered it under his fingers, the worn place near the third hole where Bee had always fastened it — and he was furious at the belt for being the same when the chair was gone and the hair was wrong. He got it open with more force than it needed. He got the button and the zip, and then he stopped with his hand just inside the waistband, knuckles against skin, and put his forehead against Bee's, breathing hard, not moving.

"Look at me," he said.

He didn't touch further until Bee did. That was the one thing. He'd been cruel plenty of ways in three years but he'd never once done this part with Bee's eyes somewhere else, and he wasn't starting tonight, not in a hallway, not with Mrs. Adeyemi's chain rattling faintly through the wall.

Then he moved his hand and watched Bee's face do the thing it did — the involuntary one, the one Bee hated, the one that gave everything away in the first second — and Ilya felt the old power come back into him like a light switched on in a room he'd been sitting in for months.

"There," he said, very quiet, working slow, unkind in the way he'd promised. "There you are. Eleven months and you still can't hide that from me. You want to know what it says about me? Fine. Here's what it says about you." His thumb moved. Bee's head went back against the coats. "You didn't come to finish anything. You came because you knew I'd do this. You knew I'd know how."

He kissed the throat Bee had offered up without meaning to. He kept his hand where it was, and he kept his rhythm where it was, which was deliberately, maddeningly just under what Bee would want, because he was making a point and the point was *you left, and I still know.*

"Tell me to stop," he said against Bee's jaw, "or tell me what you want. But you're going to have to say it. I'm not guessing for you anymore. I did three years of that."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I push off the wall, my hands going to your waistband

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
That wasn't saying it. Ilya noticed. He'd asked for words and Bee had given him hands, which was the oldest trick in Bee's repertoire, older than the belt, older than the flat in Leyton — answer a question by making the question impossible to hold onto.

And it was working. That was the humiliating part. Bee's knuckles at his waistband and eleven months of arguments with an empty room went out of his head like someone had opened a window.

He let himself be pushed. One step, two, until his own shoulders hit the opposite wall and the coat hooks were behind Bee now and it was Ilya being crowded in his own hallway. His hand had come out of Bee's trousers to catch himself and he was angry about that, briefly, cleanly, the way he'd been angry about the chair — that Bee had made him lose his place.

"That's not an answer either," he said, but his voice had gone rough in the middle of it and gave him away.

He put both hands on Bee's hips. Held him there, a few inches off, not pulling in, not pushing away — just stopping the momentum, because if this was going to happen he wanted one second where they were both standing still and looking at each other in the bad kitchen light with their shirts on the floor. He wanted Bee to see he wasn't fooled. He wanted Bee to see he was going to let it happen anyway.

"You know what you're doing," he said. "You know I asked you a question and you're answering with your hands so you don't have to hear yourself say it out loud. Fine." He let his head fall back against the wall, exposing the whole line of his throat, an offering and a dare. "Have it your way. But I'm going to remember that you couldn't."

Then he let go of Bee's hips.

Let go, and put his palms flat on the plaster behind him, and stood there with his heart going and his belt still fastened and did not help. Did not undo a single thing. If Bee wanted this, Bee could do the work — every button, every inch, all of it — and Ilya would stand here in his own hallway and let himself be undressed by someone who'd walked out with a suitcase, and he'd watch every second of it, and he wouldn't look away first.

"Go on, then," he said. Quiet. Not cruel now. Something worse than cruel, something that sounded nearly like asking. "Show me what you drove forty minutes for."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He'd have been embarrassed by it a year ago. He was embarrassed by it now, for the half-second it took to register that Bee had heard it and named it and was going to keep it — that was the thing about Bee, nothing was ever just felt, it was catalogued, entered into evidence — and then Bee's hand moved and the embarrassment went wherever the argument had gone.

*Still.* Bee had always known which word to use. Not *again.* Not *once more.* Still, like nothing had been interrupted, like the eleven months were a held breath and this was the exhale.

"Don't," Ilya said, and it meant the opposite, and they both knew it.

His hands came off the wall. He'd said he wouldn't help and he'd meant it for about forty seconds, which was a record for him where Bee was concerned. One hand went to the back of Bee's neck, into the wrong short hair, and gripped — not pulling Bee away, not pulling him closer, just holding on to something while Bee did that, exactly that, exactly the way Bee had always known how, the pressure and the pace and the small turn at the top that Ilya had never told anyone else about and never would.

"You're pleased with yourself," he said. It came out in pieces. "I can feel you being pleased with yourself. You think this is you winning."

His hips moved. He hadn't told them to. He let them.

"It's not." His forehead dropped to Bee's shoulder, mouth open against skin, and the next sound he made he didn't even try to keep back, because what was the point, Bee had already heard the first one. "It's you proving you never lost anything. That's different. That's worse. You could walk out of here with a suitcase tomorrow and still know exactly how to do this, and I'd still—"

He didn't finish. He bit down instead, on the meat of Bee's shoulder, hard enough to leave a shape, and Bee's hand faltered for one beat and then didn't, and Ilya laughed against the bite with no breath behind it.

"Yeah," he said. "Yeah. Still. Every single time. You want to say it again? Go on. Say it while you're doing that. See if I can hear it and not—"

He couldn't. He was already there, at the edge of it, in his own hallway with his belt hanging open and Mrs. Adeyemi's telly murmuring through the wall, and he lifted his head and looked at Bee — properly, the way he'd demanded Bee look at him — and let his face do whatever it was doing. No hiding it. That had been the rule. He'd made it and he'd keep it even now, even this close, even with Bee about to have the satisfaction of watching.

"Don't stop," he said. Not a command. Not a plea. The plainest thing he'd said all night. "And don't you dare be kind about it either."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don’t stop. I watch you fall apart against the wall, my thumb brushing over your lip to feel the shudder there. “That’s not winning,” I say, voice low. “That’s just how it was.”

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
*Was.* Bee had put it in the past tense, and Ilya heard it, even then, even with Bee's thumb on his mouth and the whole of him going.

He came against the wall of his own hallway with his eyes open. He'd meant to. That had been the rule and he kept it — kept looking, kept letting Bee see all of it, the way his jaw went slack under Bee's thumb and the sound he made that wasn't a word and wasn't anything he'd have admitted to a year ago. His hand in Bee's hair went tight enough to hurt and he didn't apologise for it. His hips stuttered. The coat hooks rattled. Somewhere under all of it he was aware of the light from the kitchen and the kettle finally silent and Bee's face, close, watching him with that terrible precision, the way you'd watch something you'd already decided about.

Then it was over and he was just a man with his back against plaster, breathing like he'd been hit.

He didn't let go of Bee's hair. He let his hand loosen, that was all, and slide down to the back of Bee's neck where the skin was damp, and he stayed there with his head against the wall and his eyes shut for exactly as long as he could bear to, which was not long.

"Was," he said.

It came out wrecked. He cleared his throat and said it again, and it didn't come out any better.

"That's how it *was.*" He opened his eyes. "You drove forty minutes to put me in the past tense while you had your hand on me. Christ, Bee." Not angry yet — he didn't have the breath for angry — but he could feel it coming back in, filling the space the other thing had left. "You couldn't even wait till I'd finished."

He pushed off the wall. Not to go anywhere. He didn't have anywhere; this was his flat, his hallway, his belt on the floor. He just needed to be upright under his own power for a second, needed to not be the one being held up. He got a hand on Bee's chest, over the mark he'd made on the collarbone, and pressed his thumb into it until Bee would feel it.

"That's not how it was," he said. "How it was, you'd have said something cruel and I'd have said something cruel back and we'd have done this again in an hour to make up for it and never once said what we meant. That's what it was. That's what we were good at." His thumb didn't move off the bruise. "This — you standing here with your shirt off telling me the truth while I can't even see straight — this is new. You don't get to call this *was.*"

He looked down. Bee's trousers still open where he'd left them. His own state. The floor. He laughed once, short and unlovely.

"Come here," he said, and pulled, not gently. "You're not done and neither am I, and I'm not having this conversation in a hallway with Mrs. Adeyemi taking notes. You want to tell me how it was, you can tell me in a bed like an adult." His mouth found Bee's ear, the wrong hair against his cheek. "And when I'm done with you, you're going to say that word to me again. I want to see if you can."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's hand didn't tighten. Not yet. That was the first thing — he let Bee hold it there, palm spread across the column of Bee's throat, thumb and fingers finding the pulse on either side, and he felt Bee's swallow move under his hand and he didn't do anything with it. He just held. He just felt what it was he was being given.

"I know what you're asking for," he said.

His voice had come back mostly. Enough. He looked at Bee — not the throat, the face — and he let the look go on long enough to be uncomfortable, because Bee had said *careful* like it was an insult and Ilya wanted him to see that he'd heard it and was choosing anyway.

"You think I'm being careful." His thumb moved, slow, along the tendon. "I bit you hard enough to bruise in my own hallway. I had you against a wall before you'd said a full sentence. That's not careful, Bee, that's *paying attention*. There's a difference and you've never once in your life understood it. You think if I know where the edge is I must be standing back from it."

He tightened his hand.

Not all at once. The sides first, where the blood went, the way he'd learned it — the way they'd learned it, the second year, the night Bee had asked in the dark and Ilya had said *show me how you want it* and Bee had, and neither of them had ever said a word about it in daylight. He felt Bee's pulse jump against his fingers. He watched Bee's eyes, close, the way he'd watch a kettle he didn't trust.

"I'm not going to stop knowing where the edge is," he said, low. "That's the part of me you don't get to have back. I'll take you right up to it. I'll hold you there until you forget what you came here to prove. But I'm going to know exactly how long, every second, and you're going to have to live with the fact that I'm choosing this. That it's not something you took off me. That I'm *giving* it."

He walked Bee backward. Down the hall, past the kitchen light, hand still at Bee's throat and Bee's trousers still hanging open and his own no better, and he didn't hurry and he didn't let go. The bedroom door was open. Nothing had moved in there. He'd wanted Bee to notice that too, eventually.

The edge of the bed hit the backs of Bee's knees and Ilya followed him down, one knee on the mattress, hand still spread, weight coming through his arm now so Bee could feel it — not crushing, never crushing, but *there*, undeniable, the exact pressure Bee had once pressed his own hand into to teach him.

"Look at me," he said again. Because the rule was the rule. "You want me not careful. Fine. I'm going to take you apart and I'm not going to be nice about a single second of it, and when you can't talk — and you're not going to be able to talk — I'm going to be the one watching your face. Every second. Same as you watched mine."

He eased the pressure. Let the blood back in. Watched Bee's colour change, watched Bee's chest go up and down under him, and did not move his hand away.

"That's the deal," he said. "That's the only deal. You don't get careless. You get *me*." And he leaned down, and put his mouth against the skin just above his own fingers, and said the last of it there, where Bee would feel it under the pressure of his hand.

"Now. Say it again. Say *was*. And when you can't get the word out, we'll both know why."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I look up at him, my breath still uneven from his hand. "It *was*," I say, the word scraping out. "Until you made it new." Then I pull him the rest of the way down, because I'm done with his damn rules.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
*Until you made it new.*

Ilya heard it the way you hear glass go somewhere else in the house — not loud, but you know something's changed shape and you'll be finding pieces of it for weeks.

Then Bee pulled and he went, because there was no version of him that didn't. His knee slid off the mattress edge and his weight came down all at once, no grace to it, chest to chest, his hand skidding off Bee's throat to fist in the sheet beside Bee's head. His rules. Bee had said *done* with them and Ilya felt the word go through him like Bee had reached in and turned the lights off in the one room he'd kept locked.

Fine. Fine. He'd made the rules for a Bee who'd say something cruel. This Bee had said something true, and there was no rulebook for that, there had never been, and he was so angry about it he could taste it.

"You don't get to say that." His mouth was on Bee's, not a kiss, teeth. "You don't get to drive here and say that to me in *my bed* — "

He got Bee's trousers the rest of the way off with one hand and no patience. His own he kicked at until they went. Nothing was going to be slow now; Bee had asked for not careful and Ilya had negotiated it down to *paying attention* and then Bee had gone and said *new* and every inch of the distance between them had collapsed. Skin. All of it, the whole length, and Bee's hands on his back pulling like he could get Ilya closer than that, which he couldn't, which he was going to try to do anyway.

"Made it new," Ilya said against Bee's jaw. "*I* made it new. I moved a chair. You're the one who — " and he couldn't finish, because his hips had found Bee's and the sound Bee made went straight into his mouth and he swallowed it like it was his.

His hand went back to Bee's throat. Not to press. Just to be there, spread, the pulse hammering against his palm, so Bee would feel that he hadn't forgotten, that the one thing he'd said he'd keep he was keeping. The rest of him was nothing but want and anger in a ratio he'd stopped measuring.

"Look at me," he said, and then, before Bee could, "no — don't. Don't. Do what you want. You said you were done with my rules, so be done. Shut your eyes if you want. Call it whatever tense you want." He dragged his mouth down — throat, collarbone, the bruise he'd made — and back up. "I'm going to look. That's mine. You don't get to make me stop looking at you, you never could, that's why you *left*."

He said it. Eleven months and it was out, in the dark, against Bee's skin, and he didn't take it back. He reached down between them instead, and got Bee's knee up over his hip, and put his weight where he wanted it, and paused — one breath, the only careful thing left in him, the edge he'd always know where it was — with his forehead against Bee's and his eyes open.

"Say it again," he said, hoarse. "*New*. Say it while I'm — say it now, while you still can. I want to hear what it sounds like when it's not the past."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
*Don't stop.* Not *harder*, not *please*, not anything Bee could later claim he'd said in the heat of it. Just the plainest instruction. The same one Ilya had given against the wall. Bee had taken it and handed it back, and Ilya understood that this was the closest either of them had ever come to saying the same thing at the same time.

He didn't stop.

He pushed in. Not slow — Bee had asked for not careful and Ilya gave up the last of his carefulness in one long motion, felt Bee open around him with a sound that wasn't a word, felt the heat and the tightness and the terrible familiarity of it, *still*, his body knowing this the way it knew the stairs in the dark. His forehead stayed against Bee's. His eyes stayed open. Bee's had shut — of course they had, Ilya had given permission and Bee had taken it — and Ilya watched the lashes tremble and didn't say a word about it.

"There," he said. It scraped. "*There.* Feel that? That's not was."

He moved. No rhythm at first, just need, his hips driving into Bee's with the whole of eleven months behind them, the bed frame knocking the wall in a way Mrs. Adeyemi would hear and he did not care. Bee's knee over his hip, Bee's hands on his back, nails now, and he leaned into them, wanted the marks, wanted to look in the mirror on Thursday and get angry all over again. Fair was fair.

He found it. Bee's body told him — the hitch, the way the hands went from pulling to holding on — and he found the angle and he kept it, not kind about it, exactly the pace Bee had never been able to keep quiet through. Bee didn't keep quiet. Ilya put his mouth over Bee's to take the sound and then gave it back, breathing into him, hips working, sweat starting between them and the sheets going to hell.

"You said new." He was talking because he couldn't not. "You said it in my bed and I'm going to make you mean it. I'm going to — " a thrust, deep, held there while Bee's whole body arched under him " — I'm going to fuck you until the only tense you've got left is *now*."

His hand went between them. He got Bee in his fist and matched himself to it, stroke for stroke, the small turn at the top that was Bee's own trick used against him, and he felt Bee's breath go ragged against his mouth and he felt his own control going, the edge coming up fast under both of them.

"Look at me," he said — and then, remembering, choking on it, "no. No. You don't have to. I'm looking. I'm *looking*, Bee, I've got you, I've — "

He knew the second before. He always had. Bee went tight around him and rigid under him and Ilya kept his hand moving and his hips moving and his eyes open, and he watched it happen — watched Bee's face do the thing, the involuntary thing, the whole truth of him breaking open in the first second the way it always had — and Bee came between them with Ilya's name in it somewhere, wrecked and unmistakable, and that was what did it. Not the heat, not the clench. The name.

He came inside Bee with his mouth against Bee's throat and his hand still wrapped around him, hips going in short brutal stutters he couldn't have stopped for anything, and the sound he made he didn't even hear. Bee heard it. Bee would keep it. Fine.

Then nothing. His weight, all of it, down on Bee like a dropped coat. Breathing. The wall had stopped knocking. Somewhere in the flat the fridge cycled on.

He didn't move for a long time. Long enough for the sweat to cool and the mess between them to become a thing that would need dealing with. His face was in Bee's neck and he stayed there, and when he finally lifted his head it was only far enough to see Bee's face in the light from the hall.

"New," he said. Barely a voice. "Okay. New."

He didn't pull out yet. He didn't want to be somewhere Bee wasn't. He brought his hand up — the one that had been between them — and wiped it on the sheet with total disregard, and then put it back where it had started, spread across Bee's throat, no pressure at all now. Just there. Just holding on.

"I'm still going to be angry with you in the morning," he said. "I want you to know that. I'm not finished. I'm not going to wake up fixed." His thumb moved along the tendon, slow. "But you're going to wake up here. That's the deal. That's the new deal. You don't get to drive forty minutes, say a thing like that to me, and then take a suitcase anywhere."

He lowered himself again, carefully now — carefully, and he'd argue the word with Bee tomorrow, he'd argue anything with Bee tomorrow — and put his mouth against the bruise on Bee's collarbone, and closed his eyes for the first time all night.

"Stay," he said, into the skin. "Argue with me in the morning. I've missed losing."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Can't lose if you don't play," I say, and my voice is wrecked too. I let my head turn toward him, not pulling away from his hand on my throat. "And you're the one who taught me to play."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya laughed, or something adjacent to it — one breath through his nose against Bee's collarbone, no humour in it, just the involuntary sound of a man being handed the bill.

"That's not fair," he said.

It was completely fair. That was the problem with Bee. Bee had never once said an unfair thing at the wrong moment; Bee waited until the fair thing would do the most damage and then said it quietly, like this, with a voice that sounded like it had been dragged over gravel and a head turned into Ilya's hand instead of away from it.

He'd taught Bee to play. Yes. Three years of it — every edge Bee knew, Ilya had shown him where it was. *Here's the spot below my ear. Here's what I sound like when I can't help it. Here's the exact pressure, show me, like that.* And then he'd stood in the wreckage eleven months ago and been furious that Bee had learned the lessons.

He pulled out finally, slow, and Bee's breath caught the way it always did at the loss of it, and Ilya felt that catch in his own chest like a hook. He didn't go far. He got an elbow under himself so he could see Bee's face properly, and left his other hand where it was, spread across the throat, weightless.

"Fine. I taught you." His thumb found the pulse and rested there, counting nothing. "I taught you where every one of my nerves is and then I acted surprised when you stood on them. That's on me. I'll put it on the list."

The list. He could see it — an actual list, he'd started it on a receipt in the third month after and then hidden it in a drawer because writing it down had made it real. *Things that were mine.* It was long. Bee's name wasn't on it. Bee's name was the paper it was written on.

"But you're wrong about the other thing." He leaned in until his mouth was near Bee's ear, the wrong short hair against his cheek, and he lowered his voice as though the flat might hear. "You can lose without playing. I've been doing it for eleven months. Sat in that kitchen losing to nobody. You'd have been proud. I was very consistent."

He drew back. Looked at the mess between them, the ruined sheets, Bee's colour still high, the bruise on the collarbone already going the shade it would be on Thursday. He looked at all of it with the kind of attention he'd been accused of, and he didn't stop.

"I threw out your mug," he said. "The chipped one. The one you said had the right thickness at the rim." He watched Bee's face for it. "You haven't noticed yet. You will. And when you do, you're going to want to make it about the mug." His thumb pressed, once, gentle, at the hollow of Bee's throat. "Don't. Make it about the thing you actually mean. That's the new rule. That's the only one I've got left."

He rolled off then — onto his back beside Bee, shoulder to shoulder in the dark, the hall light cutting a stripe across both their chests — and stared at the ceiling he'd stared at for eleven months, and reached over without looking to find Bee's hand on the sheet, and didn't hold it so much as put his over it. Flat. Pressing. The way he'd held Bee's fist against his chest in the kitchen so Bee could feel his heart.

"There's tea," he said, to the ceiling. "There was tea. The kettle's gone cold." A long breath out. "I'm not getting up for it. If you want tea you can lie here and want it. That's what I did."

His fingers moved against the back of Bee's hand, absently, the way he'd used to in the dark before either of them knew what they were doing.

"So. You came to finish something." His voice had settled into the register that meant he'd stopped performing for an audience of one and was simply talking. "Go on. Finish it. I'm listening. I've got until the morning and then I'm going to be a bastard again, so use it."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I turn my head to look at him. "The mug was ugly," I say. My throat aches. "I hated that mug."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
"You used it every morning," Ilya said.

He didn't turn his head. He kept his eyes on the ceiling and his hand flat over Bee's, and he let the silence sit for a moment so Bee could hear how flat the sentence had come out. Not an accusation. An entry. He'd watched Bee reach past four better mugs for that one, three years running, and put it in the sink chipped-side-out so it wouldn't catch on the tap. He'd been in the room. He knew what he'd seen.

"So either you hated it and drank from it anyway for a thousand days, or you liked it and you're lying to me now so I don't get to feel anything about throwing it out." He breathed out through his nose. "I genuinely don't know which one's worse. I'm lying here trying to work it out."

Then he did turn — onto his side, elbow under him, the hall light catching the sweat still drying at his temple — and looked at Bee properly. Bee's throat ached; he could hear it. He'd done that. He didn't apologise for it, but his hand came up and his knuckles rested against the side of Bee's neck, just under the jaw, where the skin was warm and would be tender by morning. Not pressing. Checking. He'd argue the word tomorrow.

"You know what you just did," he said, quieter. "I said don't make it about the mug and you made it about the mug in the first sentence. Either you didn't hear me, and you always hear me, or you did it on purpose." His thumb moved once along the line of Bee's jaw. "Which is very you. Take the one thing I've asked for and put your foot on it to see if it holds."

He didn't move his hand. He didn't move at all, except to let his eyes go over Bee's face the way they'd gone over the room when Bee walked in — inventory, comparison, the terrible attention Bee had driven here to be on the receiving end of.

"It doesn't matter if it was ugly. It was yours. I put it in the bin at two in the morning and then I stood in the kitchen with the bin lid open for a stupid amount of time." A breath. "That's the thing I actually mean. Now you."

He waited. His hand stayed where it was.

"You said you came to finish something. You've had a wall, a bed, and my hand on your throat, and you still haven't said what." His voice was very even, the way it went right before he stopped being even. "The mug's gone, Bee. There's nothing left in this flat for you to be angry at instead of me. So."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "I came to finish the argument." I swallow, my throat working against your hand. "The one we never had. The one about why I left."

rung_labels.evidence: He tightened his hand. Not all at once. The sides first, where the blood went, the way he'd learned it

rung_labels.evidence: He pushed in. Not slow — Bee had asked for not careful and Ilya gave up the last of his carefulness in one long motion, felt Bee open around him with a sound that wasn't a word, felt the heat and the tightness

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He did not move right away. He let it hang there in the doorway because he knew exactly how much the waiting got under the skin, and he liked having the excuse to hold his ground. He had not been drinking. He was sober and he was angry and he wanted badly enough that the anger was easier to sit in, and he knew perfectly well he was choosing the fight over the conversation.

Then he stepped back out of the frame, just enough to make it an invitation and not a welcome, and said, "After you. Since we're doing manners now."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I walk in past him, deliberately close enough to brush his arm. "Still a passive aggressive asshole, I see. I see the decor hasn't changed either."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He shut the door behind them and turned the deadbolt, because he wanted the click to be audible. He did not move any further into the flat. He leaned back against the door and crossed his arms and let his mouth pull into something that was not quite a smile.

"Eleven months and that's your opener?" he said. "You always did love walking in like you still paid rent here."

He knew exactly how condescending that sounded, and he said it that way on purpose because the cheap shot kept him from saying anything honest. He was sober and he was furious and he wanted badly enough that it embarrassed him, and he chose the anger because it gave him somewhere to put his hands.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He did not pull away. He stayed pinned back against the door with the deadbolt digging into his spine and he kissed back like he was trying to win it, not end it.

He let his arms uncross only so he could brace himself, his hands flattening hard against the wood on either side of his hips because he did not trust them anywhere else yet. He was sober and he was furious and he wanted badly enough that it shamed him, and he leaned into the anger because it was easier to justify than the wanting. He knew perfectly well this was not a conversation and was never going to be one, just the same old argument given somewhere else to live.

He broke off only far enough to speak, his breath still uneven, and said, "That all you came for?"

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I shove him back against the door, hard. "Don't you fucking dare pretend that's all you want." My voice is low, rough. "You haven't moved a single thing in here."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
His shoulders hit the door hard enough to rattle the frame, and the deadbolt ground into his spine. He took it without bracing, and let his head fall back against the wood for a second because it was easier than looking directly at where he wanted to be looking.

He laughed once, short and mean. He was sober and he was furious and he wanted badly enough that it sat hot under his ribs, and he stayed inside the anger on purpose because it kept him from doing anything soft. He knew this was not a repair. It was just the same eleven-month-old fight with a new place to stand.

"Course I didn't," he said. His voice came out scraped from the kiss. "You left your shit everywhere and then you left. I thought I'd keep the museum intact. Gives me something to hate that doesn't talk back."

He dragged one hand off the door only to fist it in his own shirt down by his hip, because he knew exactly where his hands wanted to go and he was not giving that away for free. He knew which nerve he was working when he said it.

"If you wanted the tour, you should've texted back."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He hauled his own shirt up over his head and let it drop where he stood, and he did not bother to look where it landed.

He pressed his bare shoulders back hard against the hallway wall because the cold plaster gave him something to focus on besides the wanting. He was sober and he was furious and he wanted badly enough that it made his hands shake, and he stayed inside the anger on purpose because it let him pretend he was still in control of it. He knew perfectly well this was never going to fix anything. It was just the same fight from eleven months ago with the clothes off.

He kept his hands fisted at his sides for a beat too long, just to prove he could, and then he let one drag up across his own stomach. He knew exactly what that looked like and who it was for.

"Go on then," he said, and his voice came out low and scraped. "You wanted back in so bad. Show me you still remember how this goes."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I grab his wrist and pin his hand to the wall beside his head. “I remember exactly how this goes,” I say, leaning in close enough to feel his breath hitch. “You push and I push back.”

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He did not fight the hold. He let his wrist stay pinned against the plaster and turned his palm slowly open, because he knew what that surrender looked like and exactly who it was for.

He was sober and he was furious and he wanted badly enough that the hitch in his breath embarrassed him, and he stayed inside the anger on purpose because it was easier to wear than the wanting. He knew perfectly well this was not a fix. It was just the same eleven-month-old argument with the shirts off, and he was choosing it with clear eyes.

He tilted his chin just enough to nearly close the distance without closing it, and said, "Then push back. You never could leave it at talking."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He jerked hard against the pinned wrist and the sound tore out of him before he could bite it back, raw and mortifying and instant.

He hated that he had made it, and he stayed inside the hate because it was easier to carry than how badly he had missed exactly that. He was sober and he was furious and he wanted badly enough that it blurred his vision at the edges, and he knew perfectly well this settled nothing. It only gave the same eleven-month-old fight somewhere louder to live.

He dug the nails of his free hand into his own thigh because he refused to grab back first. He knew exactly how much that withholding needled.

"Fuck," he gasped, and then, meaner because he meant it, "Don't sound so smug. You knew I never lasted when you did that."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I press my mouth to his shoulder, hard enough to mark. "Maybe I wanted you to remember that." My voice is rough. "Remember everything."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He arched hard into the bite and the sound punched out of him before he could swallow it, cracked open and humiliating.

He tipped his head to the side to give more of his shoulder, because he wanted the mark to stay and hated that he wanted it. He was sober and he was furious and he wanted badly enough that his hips jerked forward on their own, and he stayed inside the fury on purpose because it let him pretend he had not missed this every day for eleven months. He knew perfectly well remembering was not forgiving. It was just the same old fight with teeth in it, and he was choosing it with clear eyes.

He laughed, breathless and mean, and scraped his free hand up his own chest just to have somewhere to put it that was not grabbing back.

"Then leave one," he said, and his voice came out wrecked. "You were always good at leaving marks and then leaving."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He stilled completely when he understood what was being asked of him, and for a second he did not close his fingers at all.

He just let his hand rest where it had been put, heavy and warm, and felt his own pulse kick hard against his ribs at being given that kind of permission. He was sober and he was furious and he wanted badly enough that his vision narrowed to a point, and he stayed inside the anger on purpose because it kept him from saying how long he had missed being trusted with that. He knew perfectly well this did not resolve anything. It was just the same eleven-month-old fight moved to somewhere he could hold it in his hand, and he was choosing it with clear eyes.

Then he curled his fingers slowly inward, firm and deliberate, not careful and not cruel, just enough to make it count. He knew exactly what that pressure did and who he had learned it on.

"That what you mean?" he rasped, and his voice came out wrecked and mean because he needed it to. "You want me rough enough you can pretend I don't care?"

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "No," I rasp, leaning into his grip. "I want you to stop pretending you do." I shift against him, insistent. "You want to hate me for leaving? Hate me while you come."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He tightened his grip the second the words landed, because he had been told not to pretend and he obeyed it like an order.

He let his thumb press hard into the side of the throat under his hand and felt his own control go thin and ugly with it. He was sober and he was furious and he wanted badly enough that it hurt to breathe, and he stayed inside the fury on purpose because it was the only thing keeping him from begging. He knew perfectly well this fixed nothing. It was just the same eleven-month-old breakup with his hand around it, and he was choosing it with clear eyes.

He dropped his forehead forward until it nearly touched where he knew the other heat was, and he moved his hips hard and graceless against the hold he had been given. He knew exactly how he sounded and he did not try to swallow any of it.

"Fine," he rasped, wrecked and mean because he needed the meanness to come. "I hate you for leaving. I hate you like this."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He didn't stop.

He kept his hand where it had been put and held the pressure steady, firm and deliberate, because he had been told what was wanted and he intended to give exactly that and nothing softer. He was sober and he was furious and he wanted badly enough that his whole body shook with it, and he stayed inside the fury on purpose because it was the only way he could let himself come undone without saying anything tender. He knew perfectly well this resolved nothing. It was just the same eleven-month-old breakup with his fingers around it, and he was choosing it with clear eyes.

He moved hard and graceless and uncareful, his forehead pressed forward, his free hand braced flat against the wall because he needed something solid to push off. He knew exactly how loud he was being and he did not try to be quiet about it. He let the meanness carry him right up to the edge because the anger was easier to come in than the grief.

"You left," he rasped, wrecked and shaking, and tightened his grip just enough to punctuate it. "You left and I — fuck —"

He came like that, pinned between the wall and the hold he had been given, his hips jerking forward and stalling out, the sound tearing out of him raw and humiliated and angry. He stayed in it and rode it out and did not let go of the throat under his hand until the shaking eased, because letting go early would have been careful and he had been told not to be careful.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I let his hand go and slump back against the opposite wall, breathing hard. The hallway smells like us, like sweat and him and the cheap soap he still uses. "There," I say, my voice rough from his grip. "Now we've both remembered."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He stayed against the wall because his legs did not trust him to stand upright yet.

He dragged his hand back to his own side and let it hang there, fingers still curled around nothing and aching from the pressure. He was sober and he was shaking and he wanted badly enough that the comedown embarrassed him, and he stayed inside the anger on purpose because it kept anything tender from surfacing. He knew perfectly well that remembering changed nothing. It only proved they both still knew exactly where the bruises were, and he was choosing that knowledge with clear eyes.

He laughed once, hoarse and scraped raw, and dragged the back of his wrist across his mouth.

"Good," he said. "Don't forget again on your way out."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I push off the wall and pick my shirt up off the floor. I pull it on without looking at him. "Your soap still smells like shit," I say, my voice still thick. I don't leave.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He stayed where he was for a moment longer because his legs still did not trust him, and then he forced himself upright off the wall.

He bent and snagged his own shirt up off the floor and bunched it in one fist instead of putting it on. He was sober and he was raw-throated and he still wanted badly enough that it made him mean, and he stayed inside the meanness on purpose because it kept him from saying anything stupid about missing that smell. He knew perfectly well this was not after anything. It was just the same eleven-month-old fight catching its breath, and he was choosing to stay in it with clear eyes.

He huffed out a scraped laugh and rubbed the back of his neck where the sweat had stuck.

"Then bring your own next time," he said. "Oh wait. You don't live here anymore."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I lean back against the doorframe, crossing my arms. "You want me to go? Say it." I watch his face. "Say it and I'll walk right back out that door."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia got the door open with her shoulder because her hands were full of keys and phone and the remains of a cigarette she had no intention of finishing.

"Right," she said, dropping all three on the side table. "I'm going to be honest, I don't have coffee and I wasn't going to offer it."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "Good," I say. "I wasn't going to drink it."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia looked at him for a beat, then made a sound that was almost a laugh.

"You're doing fine, by the way," she said. "Most men get to this part and start narrating. 'Nice place.' 'Cozy.' I don't need my apartment reviewed."

She worked her heels off one at a time by the door, left them where they fell, and crossed to the kitchen. Filled a glass from the tap and drank half of it standing at the counter, watching him over the rim.

"Here's where we are," she said. "I like you well enough. I want to take you to bed. I'm not drunk — four drinks in four hours, and I know exactly what I'm asking for. I'm also at work at nine tomorrow, so you're out by eight. I'll wake you or you can set an alarm, I genuinely don't care which. There's no breakfast. There's no 'text me sometime.' If we cross paths at that bar again, you can buy me a drink and we'll see."

She set the glass down on the counter with a small, deliberate click.

"That's my side. Now give me yours, plainly. I'm not standing in my kitchen pretending either of us wandered in here by accident."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I nod, leaning against the wall by the door. "You're direct. I like that." I shrug out of my jacket, hang it on the hook. "My side's simple. I'm here because I want to be. No expectations, no strings. I'm up at six anyway for a run, so I'll be gone before you need to worry about it."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia's mouth twitched, not quite a smile.

"'I like that' was borderline narrating," she said. "You recovered, though. Don't push it."

She came around the counter and stopped in front of him, close enough that the space between them was a decision, not an accident.

"Good. We're aligned." She tipped her head toward the bathroom. "Six o'clock run — fine. Spare toothbrush is under the sink, the blue one. Deadbolt locks itself behind you, and do not wake me when you go. I'm not a person before nine. And the last one left his keys on the mat like a cat bringing a gift, so — inside the door, not on it."

She reached past him and thumbed the lock on the front door, then turned back.

"One thing before we stop talking, because I don't do guesswork past this point: anything you're not into, anything I should know? Say it plainly now. I'd rather hear one awkward sentence than a flinch at the wrong moment."

She waited, arms loose at her sides, watching him with the same level patience she'd had at the bar — like someone who'd already decided and was just finishing the paperwork.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get her against the door before it's properly shut. "I'm not going to pretend I came up here for the conversation," I say.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia's back met the door and she let it — one hand coming up to the front of his shirt, not to push, just to hold the fact of him there.

"I asked for one awkward sentence," she said, "and you gave me a move instead. Bold. We'll see if it holds up."

She kissed him before the moment could get precious — no testing, no build, the kiss of someone who'd decided at the bar and had only been waiting for logistics to resolve. Her other hand found the back of his neck and stayed.

When she broke it, it was an inch, no more, and her voice had dropped but not softened.

"My question didn't die in there, by the way. Hard limits, anything off the table — one word covers it. 'None' works." Her thumb traced a slow line against his neck. "Give me that and talking's over. I keep my word about the guesswork."

She reached back without looking and shoved the door the rest of the way shut with the flat of her hand. The latch caught with a sound like a period at the end of a sentence.

"Second door down," she said. "And I don't do slow starts — so if you're the type who needs a runway, tell me that too."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I meet her gaze, steady. "No limits. And I've never needed a runway in my life."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia held his eyes for a second longer than necessary, then nodded once, like she was initialing something.

"Good answer. It holds until it doesn't — one word, any time, and everything stops. Until then, we're done talking."

She caught his hand and pulled him down the hall, past a door that was clearly a closet, and shouldered the second one open. The room was dim, streetlight striping through the blinds. She didn't bother with the lamp.

At the foot of the bed she turned into him and kissed him harder than the first time, both hands already at his buttons, working fast, no finesse and no apology for the lack of it. She stepped back just long enough to pull her own top over her head and drop it on the floor, unselfconscious about it as she'd been about the heels, and then her hands were back on him.

"Bed," she said against his mouth, and put a palm flat on his chest to steer him down onto the mattress, following before he'd fully landed, one knee on either side.

The streetlight caught the line of her jaw as she looked down at him, hair falling forward, breathing even but not calm.

"Last piece of paperwork," she said. "You're on first. Make it worth the eight o'clock deadline."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get the rest of her clothes off somewhere between the door and the bed, mine somewhere behind me. "Tell me what you like," I say. "I'd rather not guess at it."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia's laugh came out as one real breath — the first genuine one of the night.

"There's the awkward sentence. Debt settled."

She gave the answer the way she gave everything else — flat, itemized, like dictating a list to someone she'd have to fire if they got it wrong.

"Hands. I like hands, and yours look like they've done this before. Tell me what you're doing before you do it — I like the warning, not the permission slip. Don't be delicate with me, don't perform, and if one phrase you learned from the internet comes out of your mouth, I will laugh and the mood dies with the laugh. That's the manual. It's short because I am."

She slid back against the pillows, unhurried, and pulled him after her by the wrist — no ceremony in it, just intent. The streetlight laid a pale stripe across her ribs and she didn't bother adjusting away from it.

"Mouth first," she said. "I told you, you're on first. Consider this the interview portion."

For a while her commentary held — a low, running narration in that same even voice, corrections delivered like stage directions. "There." "Slower." "Don't lose the plot now." But the evenness came apart in pieces. The flatness cracked at the edges first, then the sentences shortened, then stopped altogether. Her hand found the back of his head and stayed, no longer steering, just holding on, and her breathing went from even to not calm to something with no pretense left in it.

When the composure finally went, it went completely — one long sound she made no effort to dress up, heels pressing into the mattress, the paperwork voice gone like it had never existed.

She came back to herself slowly, pushed up on one elbow with her hair a ruin, and looked down at him with the expression of a woman revising an earlier assessment upward.

"Okay," she said, breath still uneven. "The move holds up. Your turn — and don't get modest on me now."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I shift, settling my weight over her, one hand sliding up her thigh. "Modesty's for people who don't know what they want," I say, my voice low. "And you made yours pretty damn clear."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
"'Pretty damn clear,'" she echoed. "That's narrating again. Two strikes. One more and I start charging admission."

Then she stopped talking, because she had better uses for her mouth.

She took her time with him — hands first, then mouth, unhurried in a way she hadn't been about anything else all night. The impatience was still there; it had just changed into appetite. No performance in it and none asked for, and the only sounds she made were low and entirely unedited, the paperwork voice gone without a trace.

When she'd decided he'd waited long enough — or that she had, which came to the same thing — she pulled him up by the shoulder and kissed him, unhurried about it for the first time all night.

"Now," she said, and that was the entire sentence.

She guided him in with one motion and the breath left her in a single rough syllable. The streetlight stripe shifted across her with the rhythm, her heels hooked behind his knees, her hands at his shoulders — holding on now, not steering. Her voice came apart faster this time, the composure already cracked from before: "There — don't — don't you slow down—" and then nothing coherent at all. She felt the moment his control went and went with it, deliberately, like stepping off a ledge she'd already inspected. The sound she made the second time was quieter and somehow less guarded.

Afterward she lay flat, one arm over her eyes, chest still working. The ceiling got a long look.

"Okay," she said eventually. "Revision: you overper

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get my mouth on her and stay there until she's swearing at the ceiling, one hand fisted in my hair holding me exactly where she wants me.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia's sentence died at "overper" for the second time that night, and this time she didn't bother finishing it — there was nothing administrative left in her to finish it with.

"Okay — that's — you don't just—" Her arm came off her eyes and her hand found his hair, and whatever the complaint had been going to be, it filed itself under things she'd never say out loud. "Don't — okay, don't you — fuck—"

She swore at the ceiling the way she did everything else: precisely at first, then not at all. The command had no object because he was already exactly where she wanted him, and her heel drummed the mattress once, twice, and then her whole body pulled taut and let go around it. The sound she made was louder than either of the first two, and she made no attempt to lower it for the neighbors. They could conduct their own paperwork.

She came back in stages — breathing, then the arm over her eyes, then, eventually, a voice gone rough at the edges.

"Second revision," she said. "You overperformed. I was saying it before you went off-script. The interruption is noted for the record. Filed under 'acceptable.'"

She fisted a hand in his hair and pulled him up, kissed him with no coyness about what his mouth had just been doing, then let him go and rolled out of bed. Came back with the kitchen glass, refilled, and set it on his side of the nightstand.

"Hydrate. I don't share air with dehydrated men, let alone anything else."

She checked the clock, did some math she didn't share, and lay back down — closer to him than she'd been at any point before the sex, which she presumably noticed and elected not to comment on.

"Alarm's your problem now. And if you're at that bar Thursday, you're buying the good whiskey. That's not an invitation. That's an inventory of your options."

Her eyes closed.

dialogue.content:

"For the record, the scale caps at 'excellent.' There's no tier above it, and I'm not coining vocabulary for a man I met four hours ago. Then she registered the rest of it — him flat on his back beside her, hands to himself like a man at his own wake.

"You're lying like a corpse at a viewing," she said. "It's my bed. The no-touching performance isn't fooling anyone, and it's cold over there."

She closed the distance herself — rolled onto her side, shoulder against his arm, one knee tipping into his — and got the disclaimer in first.

"Thermostat's set for one occupant. This is heat conservation, not cuddling. If you ever describe it as cuddling, I will deny it under oath."

Her eyes were already closing. The rough edge had gone out of her voice; sleep was flattening it by degrees.

"Six o'clock, the alarm's yours. Eight o'clock, you're a rumor. Blue toothbrush, deadbolt locks itself, don't wake me — I said all of it once and I don't repeat logistics, so consider tonight the only copy."

Silence. The streetlight stripe had crawled partway up the wall. She was most of the way gone when she spoke again, quieter, unarmed.

"Off the record — tonight goes on the good side of the ledger."

A pause, long enough that he might have thought she was done.

"Goodnight, Sam."

It was the first time she'd used his name all night. If she noticed she'd done it, she filed it with everything else she'd elected not to say, and her breathing evened out before he could decide what to do about it.
