dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I work him with my palm, rough and fast. "I told you I wasn't interested in gentle."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He was sober, clear-eyed, and entirely aware of what he was doing. That was the worst part.

His head knocked back against the wall, a dull thud, and he didn't bother to swallow the sound that tore out of him. His hands stayed fisted at his sides, knuckles pressed hard into the plaster, because if he put them on her the argument would be over and he wasn't finished having it. He could feel the rough, fast stroke of her palm and hated how easily his body answered, how little eleven months of silence mattered to it.

"I know," he said, voice low and rough. "I'm not asking you to be gentle. You never were. That was half the problem." He dragged in a breath and let it out through his teeth, hips shifting despite himself, betraying him completely. "But this is still just the fight, Bee. You didn't come here to make me come in my own hallway. You came here to say something. So say it."

He turned his head, found her eyes in the dim light, and made sure she saw both things at once: the anger and the want, sitting side by side the way he'd stopped pretending they were separate. "I wanted you the day you left. I've wanted you every day since. That was never the question." His mouth twisted. "Still every time," he echoed, deliberately throwing her words back because he knew exactly where they would land. "You need that, don't you? Knowing I never got over it. Fine. I haven't. But don't mistake this for me forgiving you, and don't mistake it for an answer. I'm choosing it. That's all."

His hips jerked again, helpless, and he let out a broken curse, not looking away. "Finish it or let go. But don't stand there and pretend this is the same as saying why you're here."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "I want you angry," I say, my voice tight under his palm. "I want you to *hate* me a little."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: His hand tightens and it's perfect. I scrape my nails down his back, pulling him in harder. "Show me," I breathe against his neck. "Show me how much you missed this."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: *I come with a sharp gasp, my body tensing against his.* "Yeah," *I rasp, my forehead pressed to his shoulder.* "That's exactly what I fucking needed."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I lean into him for a moment, catching my breath, before pushing back slightly. "Your turn," I say, my voice still uneven. I don't let go.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo stopped winding the tape. He looked at the bag beside his, then up at Reyes, one eyebrow raised.

“Slow,” he repeated. “Four years you’ve been trying to get past my guard, and now you’re impatient.”

He set the grip down before he could ruin a perfectly good wrap. Without the scrape of shoes and clash of blades, the salle seemed unusually quiet.

“Your third touch was clean,” he admitted. The concession cost him a small, crooked smile. “Tell anyone I said that and I’ll deny it.”

He rose from the bench, leaving the space between them open.

“Are you staying to gloat,” he asked, “or can I finally buy you that drink?”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
I lean back against the wall, arms crossed. "Four years of you being insufferable earns me at least a little impatience." 

I watch him stand, my own smile tugging at my mouth. "And I'll take that drink. But only if you admit, out loud, that you had to work for that third touch."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo glanced toward the empty doorway, as though checking that no witnesses had survived the evening.

“I had to work for it,” he said. “The feint, the recovery—all of it. You made me earn every inch.”

His crooked smile returned.

“There. An honest compliment. I trust you’ll handle it irresponsibly.”

He tucked the unfinished roll of tape into his bag and zipped it shut. Usually, he would have found another barb by now, something to make the concession feel less exposed. Instead, he lingered beside the bench, looking at Reyes.

“For the record, I wasn’t waiting four years to buy you a drink.” He lifted his bag onto his shoulder. “I was waiting for an evening when I could ask without making it sound like another challenge.”

A quiet laugh escaped him.

“Apparently I still need practice.”

He moved toward the door, then paused with his hand on the light switch.

“There’s a place around the corner. Quiet enough that you won’t have to raise your voice when you bring up the score again.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s hand stayed suspended for a moment after the grip left it. Then he let it fall to his side.

For once, he had no immediate answer.

He looked at Reyes, the familiar retort caught somewhere behind a smile that had lost its usual sharpness. Four years of finding openings, and he had nearly talked his way past this one.

“Yes,” he said quietly. “Apparently I have.”

He slipped the bag from his shoulder and set it down without looking away. When he straightened, he moved closer—not enough to close the distance entirely, but enough that there was no mistaking his intention.

“I could blame the footwork,” he murmured. “But you’d never let me hear the end of it.”

His gaze dipped briefly to Reyes’s mouth. He lifted a hand, then rested it against the wall beside them.

“I’d like to kiss you.”

The admission left him looking almost amused with himself. He waited, close but not touching.

“That one wasn’t a challenge.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I close the rest of the distance between us, my hand coming up to his jaw. "Finally," I say against his mouth, "you stop talking."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s answer was a smile that barely had time to form before he kissed Reyes.

For once, he made no attempt to be clever. His free hand settled lightly at Reyes’s waist, and he let the kiss linger, unhurried now for an entirely different reason. The familiar impulse to push for an advantage deserted him. There was nothing here he wanted to win at the expense of another moment.

When he drew back, it was only a little. He kept his eyes closed for a beat, visibly reconsidering several years’ worth of decisions.

“Well,” he murmured.

A quiet laugh escaped him. He opened his eyes, his thumb shifting against the fabric beneath his hand.

“I had something unbearable prepared.”

He leaned close again, stopping just short of another kiss. The crooked smile returned, softer this time.

“You’ve rather spoiled it.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo sat down on the bench rather harder than he intended and laughed—a brief, disbelieving sound that ruined any hope of looking composed.

“Not a word about my footwork.”

He reached for Reyes, then checked himself just long enough to move his discarded bag out from under his own feet. Even now, apparently, there were practical indignities.

When he looked up again, the joke had softened into something less guarded.

“I did have a plan,” he admitted. “Drink. Dinner, if you could tolerate me that long.”

His hand settled lightly at Reyes’s waist.

“Ask to see you somewhere neither of us kept score.”

He leaned forward and pressed a brief kiss to Reyes’s mouth. For once, he resisted adding something clever afterward.

Whatever happened to the rest of his plan, Corvo let the empty salle and the unfinished grip wait. The evening no longer needed an audience—or a running commentary.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I catch his face in my hands, holding him there. "You're still talking," I murmur, before kissing him again, deeper this time. My fingers slide into his hair, grip tightening just enough to pull a low sound from him.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo yielded to the kiss, his next clever answer lost before it reached his tongue. One hand steadied him against the bench; the other rested at Reyes’s waist.

Being quiet should not have felt like such a concession. He suspected he would be reminded of it for years.

For once, he found the prospect appealing.

He lifted his hand from the bench and touched Reyes’s jaw, the gesture unexpectedly tender after an evening spent trying to outmaneuver him. Then he kissed him again, without hurry, without turning it into another contest.

When he finally drew back enough to breathe, his smile was small and thoroughly unguarded. He almost said something. The effort of deciding against it showed plainly on his face.

Instead, he pressed one last brief kiss to Reyes’s mouth and stayed close.

The drink could wait. So could the inevitable argument about who had started this, and when, and which of them had been the greater fool.

Corvo had no intention of settling any of it tonight.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
For once, Corvo had no interest in recovering the last word.

The jokes, the score, the four years of carefully disguised invitations—all of it could stay outside the changing-room door. He let the evening become something private, something he did not have to turn into a story afterward.

***

Later, Corvo sat on the edge of the bench, attempting to lace a shoe with a knot he had somehow made worse.

“There was supposed to be dinner,” he said.

His voice held none of its usual prosecutorial force. He looked up, smiling despite himself.

“I’m still asking.”

He abandoned the lace for a moment and rested his forearms on his knees. Asking again felt oddly more daring than the first time, now that he could no longer pretend it was banter.

“Tomorrow. Somewhere decent.” His crooked smile deepened. “I’d like to find out what else we’ve been missing.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I watch him struggle with the lace for a moment before nudging his hands aside and fixing it myself. "Tomorrow," I agree, my voice low. I look up at him, catching his gaze. "But if you try to argue over the check, I'm walking out."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo looked down at the neatly tied lace. An objection presented itself immediately; he had been perfectly capable of fixing it, eventually. He let that one go too.

“Tomorrow,” he agreed. “Separate checks. I’d hate to lose you over an appetizer.”

He leaned forward, resting his forearms on his knees again. His smile lingered, but he took a moment before continuing.

“And no pretending it’s a professional dinner. I’m not spending half the evening asking about your beginners’ class because I’ve lost my nerve.”

That admission earned a small, rueful shake of his head. He had expected this part to be easier without an audience.

He reached for his bag, then paused.

“Seven? There’s an Italian place on Mercer. Good food, terrible paintings.” His eyebrow lifted. “Something for us to agree about, if things get awkward.”

Corvo stood and settled the strap over his shoulder. This time, he left the unfinished grip where it belonged.

“For the record,” he added, “I expect to be insufferable tomorrow as well.”

His expression softened.

“I’ll just be considerably less evasive about why I wanted you there.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo glanced at his pinned wrists, then back at Reyes. The obvious retort arrived on schedule. For once, he decided it was a poor substitute for an honest answer.

“I concede.”

He said it plainly, without the crooked smile that usually made every admission negotiable.

“Not because you’ve made a particularly sound argument.” There was the smile, returning despite his efforts. “I just don’t want you thinking you have to win this out of me.”

He left his hands still and held Reyes’s gaze.

“I wanted you here. I want dinner tomorrow. And I’d like there to be something after tomorrow that doesn’t depend on which of us finds an excuse first.”

The admission unsettled him more than he had expected. He let it stand anyway.

“That’s the point,” he said softly. “No fencing.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I let go of his wrists and run my hands up his arms instead. "Fine," I say, my voice rough. "But I'm still walking out if you argue over the check."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo rubbed a hand over his mouth, failing to hide his smile.

“Understood. I’ll save my objections for the terrible paintings.”

He sat up slowly. For a moment he looked down at his own hands, as though an appropriate next move might be written across his palms. He had spent four years making attention look like provocation; he was beginning to discover how little practice that had given him.

“Seven,” he said, looking up. “I’ll book the table.”

He leaned closer and pressed a brief kiss to Reyes’s mouth, then drew back before he could turn a simple promise into another speech.

“And tonight, I’m getting you that drink. We’ve managed to turn it into a logistical ordeal.”

He retrieved his bag from the floor. The unfinished grip protruded from the open zip, its tape trailing untidily. He tucked it away without attempting to fix it.

At the changing-room door, he paused.

“For the record, I liked that you stayed.”

The words sounded unusually plain in the quiet room. Corvo left them that way.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
I can continue with romance and tension, but not explicit sexual detail.

Corvo had never imagined that being understood could leave him so short of defenses.

He reached for Reyes’s hand, without making a contest of it. For a moment, he studied the familiar calluses beneath his thumb. Those hands had been an occupational nuisance for four years. He smiled at the thought, then looked up.

“Dinner isn’t conditional,” he said quietly. “On tonight. On anything else.”

He had meant to sound casual. Instead, he sounded like a man finally saying something he should have said a long time ago.

He leaned in for a gentle kiss, then stayed close, his forehead resting against Reyes’s.

“And I won’t argue about the check.”

A small laugh escaped him. Of all the promises he might have made, that was apparently the one requiring a conspicuous effort.

He settled back on the bench without letting go of Reyes’s hand. There was no score worth keeping now, and, for once, he did not need the silence to mean he had lost.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I laugh, low in my throat, and bring his hand up to my mouth, pressing a kiss to his knuckles. "Now who's being insufferably honest?" I stand, pulling him up with me. "Let's get that drink. Before you change your mind about the check."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo rose, his smile widening at the kiss to his knuckles.

“You’ve found a weakness. I’d appreciate a little professional discretion.”

He picked up his bag and checked beneath the bench for anything forgotten. His composure seemed unlikely to turn up there, but he found his keys.

At the light switch, he glanced back at the empty salle. The strip where they had fenced lay pale beneath the last row of lamps. Tomorrow, he would probably remember precisely where he had lost that third touch. Tonight, he switched the lights off without reconstructing it.

“I’m not changing my mind,” he said as he held the door open. “About the check, or dinner.”

His mouth tilted.

“Your footwork remains open to discussion.”

Outside, the cold caught him pleasantly off guard. He locked the salle, tested the handle, then pocketed his keys. An ordinary end to an evening, accomplished with considerably more care than usual; he had nearly dropped them twice.

He turned toward Reyes and offered his hand, palm up. There was a trace of self-consciousness in the gesture, but he left it there.

“The place around the corner does have one disadvantage,” he said. “I’ve spent years telling the owner you’re the most aggravating instructor in the city.”

He paused, considering.

“I may have to endure being asked why I look so pleased.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take his hand, lacing our fingers together. "Tell him it's because you finally lost an argument." I start walking, tugging him along. "Now let's go before I remember I'm supposed to be annoyed with you."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo fell into step, his fingers closing comfortably around Reyes’s.

“Finally lost an argument,” he repeated. “He’ll want a date for the plaque.”

The bar was only a short walk away. Usually, Corvo filled that distance with a ruthless assessment of the evening’s fencing. Now he found himself noticing the cold on his face and the distinctly pleasant inconvenience of carrying his bag on the wrong shoulder because switching it would mean letting go.

He left the bag where it was.

“You can still be annoyed with me,” he said. “I’d hate for you to abandon a discipline you’ve spent four years perfecting.”

At the corner, he glanced toward the bar’s lit windows. He had stopped there often enough after a match, rehearsing complaints about Reyes that invariably required describing every clever thing Reyes had done. The owner was going to be unbearable.

Corvo rather thought he had earned it.

He stopped outside the door and turned slightly, his smile losing some of its mischief.

“I was pleased before you agreed to dinner, you know. When you put your bag beside mine.”

He looked down briefly at their joined hands.

“Even when I thought you’d only stayed to gloat.”

Then he reached for the door with his free hand, admitting a wash of warmth and low conversation.

“Come on. You can help me discover whether I have a personality outside fencing and arguing with you.”

His crooked smile returned.

“I wouldn’t rule it out. There have been promising signs.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I squeeze his hand and step inside ahead of him. "I've seen your personality," I say over my shoulder, leading him toward an open table. "It's a little bit annoying and a lot competitive." I slide into a booth, pulling him in beside me. "I like it."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya looked at him for a long moment, then finally stepped aside, though not far enough to be considered gracious.

“The corridor’s public,” he said, closing the door after Bee but not fully shutting it. “You’d rather have an audience.”

He walked into the kitchen and leaned against the counter, arms crossed.

“Do you want tea? Or are we going to stand here pretending we’re civil?”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "I'll take the tea, but only because it's cold outside." I follow him into the kitchen, leaning against the opposite counter. "And because I'm not here to pretend."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya turned to the kettle, letting the click of it fill the silence between them.

“Cold outside,” he repeated, as if tasting the excuse and finding it thin. “That’s a good one. You used to make me drive across town in the rain because you liked the sound of the wipers.”

He didn’t look at Bee while he said it. He reached into the cupboard and took down two mugs—the old ones, chipped at the rims, the ones Bee had once claimed were emotionally manipulative because they reminded him of being cared for. Ilya had kept them anyway. That was either cruelty or sentimentality. He hadn’t decided which annoyed him more.

“Not here to pretend,” he said, quieter now. “No. Of course not. That’s always the trouble.”

He poured the water into the pot, watching the tea darken.

“You never wanted a conversation,” he said, still facing the sink. “You wanted a witness to your point of view. There’s a difference.”

He set the teapot on the counter between them, steam curling up around his hands.

“Sit,” he said. “If you’re going to stand in my kitchen and tell me you’re not pretending, you might as well be comfortable while you do it.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya stiffened the instant Bee’s mouth touched his, one hand still hovering near the teapot as if he could set it down without losing the thread of what he’d been saying. He didn’t pull away. That was the trouble with Bee: he knew exactly how to make resistance feel like the bigger insult.

For a moment, Ilya let it happen. He let his eyes close, let his breath catch, let the stupid, unwelcome softness rise in him—because the kiss was not sweet, it was not an apology, it was not even tenderness. It was a move in the argument.

His free hand came up and pressed against the side of Bee’s neck, thumb near the pulse there. Not a caress. A check. A dare.

Then he broke it off sharply, stepping back until the counter bit into his hips.

“That’s still not an answer,” he said, voice lower than before.

He looked at Bee with the kind of attention that had once felt like being chosen and now felt like being audited.

“You do that,” Ilya continued, “you come in cold and angry and kiss me like you’re trying to make me forget what I was about to say. Like if I want you enough, I’ll stop being disappointed.”

His gaze flicked to the teapot, then back.

“It doesn’t work anymore.”

Except it did, and they both knew it.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I laugh, sharp and humorless. "You're the one who kept the mugs." I step into his space again, not touching him yet. "Don't act like you're above wanting me."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s laugh came out short and dry.

“You’re right. I kept them,” he said. “Because throwing them away would have meant admitting they still mattered. That felt like another thing you’d get to decide for me.”

He turned from the counter, mug in hand, steam curling between them. His eyes went to Bee’s mouth for half a second, then back up, deliberately.

“And I’m not above wanting you. I’m above pretending that wanting you is enough to make me forget why you left.”

He took a step closer, just enough to make the distance feel wrong.

“You can keep saying that,” he said, quieter. “You can come in here cold and angry and say I kept the mugs like it’s proof I’ve been sitting around waiting for you to feel guilty again. But you didn’t knock, Bee. You stood there. You knew I’d open the door.”

The words landed without warmth, without apology.

“Drink the tea,” he said, lifting the mug toward him. “Then stop pretending this is about the weather.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: The hallway is cold against my back when he pushes me against the wall. "You can say you don't want me," I say, breathless already. "But you're not saying no."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s breath went out in a short, controlled pause. The hallway was narrow enough that they could not stand too far apart, and he did not try.

“No,” he said. “I’m not saying no.”

He let Bee see it plainly: the want in him, ugly and patient, still intact after eleven months. He did not apologize for it.

“I’m not saying no because I’m not finished,” Ilya said. “With this. With you being here. With whatever you’re trying to make me prove.”

His hand moved from the wall to Bee’s throat—not squeezing, just resting there, feeling the pulse under his fingers like evidence.

“You want to take that as permission,” he said, quieter. “Take it as a win. Don’t pretend you came here to be gentle with me.”

His thumb pressed once against Bee’s jaw, a deliberate, knowing touch.

“I won’t say no,” he said, “and I won’t say this is forgiveness. If you want both of those things, you’ll have to keep making me earn them.”

Then he leaned in, close enough that his mouth almost brushed Bee’s before he stopped, holding the distance on purpose.

“Say what you came here to say.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s breath stuttered at the sound—his own, low and undone—and the embarrassment of it flared hot across his face before he could lock it down. He did not pull away. He did not cover it with a joke, or a curse, or the neat distance he had spent eleven months learning to keep.

He looked down at Bee with open, furious attention.

“Every single time,” Ilya repeated, and the words tasted like a bruise.

His hand came up, not to push Bee’s away, but to hold it still, fingers closing around a wrist without quite gripping. A boundary. A claim. He was not sure which he meant.

“You think that makes you smart,” he said. “You think if you can find the place where I’m still stupid for you, it proves something.”

He leaned in, close enough that his voice dropped against Bee’s mouth.

“It proves nothing except that I don’t lie to myself anymore. I want you. I have always wanted you. It is not a victory, and it is not an apology.”

His thumb moved once, slow, deliberate, over the pulse there.

“Say what you came here to say,” he said again. “Because if you don’t, I’ll decide for you. And I won’t be kind about the part where I let you touch me.”

Then he kissed him again, harder, with teeth, with no softness, as if he could make Bee swallow the argument instead of the comfort.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I bite his lip hard enough to taste blood. "I came to say I'm still angry," I say, voice rough against his mouth. "And you're still the only thing that helps."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya tasted blood before he had permission to feel it.

It was bright and metallic and stupidly intimate, the kind of detail that would stay in his mouth long after the argument had moved on. He did not wipe it away. He let Bee see it, let him see the small flush at Ilya’s cheekbones and the way his breath still came unevenly, still not calm.

For one second, Ilya considered stepping back.

The hallway was too narrow, too cold, too much like the last time they had stood here with their coats still on and their voices low because they had been trying, both of them, not to wake the neighbors or perhaps not to wake something worse. His body was already too warm. His hands were steady enough to choose.

“Angry,” he repeated. His voice came out rougher than he intended. “Right. Of course you’re angry.”

He laughed once, without much amusement. The sound scraped.

“You come here. You don’t knock. You stand in my hallway like you’ve already decided what I’m going to be, and then you tell me you’re angry. That’s not new. That’s your opening line.”

His eyes flicked to Bee’s mouth, then away. He knew exactly what he was doing. That was the problem. He had always known.

“And I’m the only thing that helps,” he continued, quieter. “Yes. Good. Now we’ve established a fact. You’re ill. I’m medicine. You’re angry. I’m a symptom.”

He lifted a hand and touched his split lip. His thumb dragged along the sting. Blood smeared across the pad of it. He looked at it with something like distaste, though not for himself.

“You think saying that makes it tender,” he said. “You think if you can make it sound small, I’ll forget how large you’ve always been when you’re hurting.”

He did not move away. He moved closer.

The old mugs were still steaming in the kitchen, absurdly domestic, a stupid thing left between them. Ilya glanced toward the kitchen, then back.

“I kept them,” he said. “I kept them because you were right. They’re manipulative. They make me look like I’ve been sitting here waiting for you to come back and call me selfish.”

His voice lowered.

“But I didn’t keep them to be punished. I kept them because I wasn’t going to let you take that from me too. Because throwing them away felt like agreeing with you. Like admitting I’d had enough of being cared for by you.”

He breathed out.

“You’re still angry,” he said. “And I’m still here. And that’s not a solution. That’s just where we are.”

His hand came up slowly, not touching, hovering near the side of Bee’s neck. The heat there was unmistakable. Ilya let his knuckles graze once, a deliberate, knowing pressure.

“Say what you actually need,” he said. “Not the version that wins. Not the version that makes me feel guilty for wanting you.”

He looked down at Bee with an expression that had no softness left in it, only attention.

“If you came here to fuck the argument out of me, say that. If you came here to be told you’re not a monster for wanting me, say that. If you came here because you’re angry and you don’t know what to do with it, say that. But don’t say I help you like it’s a compliment.”

The admission came then, low and reluctant, almost bitten out.

“Because I help you too. Every single time. And I hate that it’s true.”

He pressed his forehead briefly against Bee’s shoulder, just for a breath, just enough to let the heat of him prove something neither would say. Then he pulled back, eyes bright and dry.

“Still,” he said. “You’re not allowed to make me your forgiveness.”

His mouth curved, not into a smile. Into something worse.

“Kiss me again,” he said, “and I won’t pretend I’m going to be any better at this than you are.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya looked down at his own hand as though it belonged to someone else.

It sat at the side of Bee’s throat, where it had been put, and beneath his palm the heat was unmistakable. Not a trick of the kitchen, not the blood, not the hallway pressing them into the wrong kind of intimacy. Just the proof that he was still wanted. Still useful. Still dangerous.

He did not move it away.

“Careful,” Ilya repeated, and the word came out flat, almost amused. “You think I’ve been careful.”

His jaw tightened. He turned his wrist slightly—not to pull back, but so the heel of his hand settled more fully into the line of Bee’s throat. Not squeezing. Not yet. Just enough to make the choice visible to them both.

“I have been careful for eleven months,” he said. “I have been careful not to call you. I have been careful not to keep your number in front of me. I have been careful to make tea in chipped mugs like a man who has not been gutted.”

His eyes lifted, bright and hard.

“And you stand in my hallway and tell me I am being careful.”

The laugh that followed was low and unpleasant.

“I’m not careful because I’m kind,” Ilya said. “I’m careful because you are very good at making me forget that I had a life before you came back and called it a symptom.”

His fingers tightened just slightly, feeling the shape of the pulse there, feeling the dare in it. He did not look away.

“You want me to stop being careful,” he said. “Then understand what you are asking for.”

He stepped closer until there was no room left between them, until the argument was not something they could stand apart from anymore.

“I won’t be careful,” Ilya said. “I won’t pretend I’m only here to talk. I won’t pretend I don’t want you in my house, in my bed, in my head like you have no right to be.”

His free hand came up, slow, deliberate, and took Bee’s wrist where it held his own hand there. He did not push it away. He pressed it firmer against his palm, making them both feel the heat of it, the weight of it, the fact that neither had let go.

“I won’t pretend I’m not going to take this,” he said, voice dropping. “I won’t pretend I’m not going to take whatever you give me because you have always been better at giving than at asking.”

His mouth curved, not tenderly.

“And I won’t pretend you’ll want to stay after.”

Then he kissed him again.

This time there was no careful pause, no checking for permission in the space between them. Ilya’s mouth took his hard, open, bitter, tasting of blood and tea and the stupid, familiar heat that had never once been fully gone. His hand remained where Bee had placed it, thumb dragging once along the throat before pressing flat again, not enough to hurt, not enough to stop.

Enough to claim.

When he broke the kiss, his forehead dropped against Bee’s shoulder, breath rough against the fabric there.

“Still,” he said, low and furious. “Every single time.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I push him back toward the bedroom, hands on his hips. "Don't talk about after."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya let himself be guided, but he did not yield the way Bee wanted him to. The bedroom was too small for this—too ordinary, too many ghosts standing in the corners with their arms folded. He stopped at the threshold, one hand bracing the doorframe, the other still holding Bee’s wrist where it had pinned his palm to his throat.

“Fine,” he said. “No after.”

His voice came out lower than he intended, scraped raw. The blood from his split lip had dried in the corner of his mouth, and he could taste it every time he spoke. It made the words sound less like an agreement and more like a wound.

“I’m not going to talk about after,” he continued. “I’m not going to promise you this doesn’t mean anything. I’m not going to lie so you can walk out in ten minutes feeling like you were the one who stayed in control.”

He looked at Bee with the kind of tired attention that had once made Bee feel like the only person in a crowded room. Now it felt like being weighed.

“You want me not to be careful,” Ilya said. “Then I won’t be.”

His free hand moved from the doorframe to Bee’s face, thumb brushing over the cheekbone before pressing hard enough to leave a mark—not a bruise, not yet, just the promise of one. It was a mistake, and he knew it was a mistake, and he did it anyway.

He kissed him again.

This time there was no pretense that it began in the hallway. It began in the bedroom, against the door, with Ilya’s mouth opening hard over Bee’s and his hand sliding into Bee’s hair to angle him exactly where he wanted. He tasted blood and tea and the bitter electricity of being wanted by someone who had already decided he was guilty.

When he pulled back, his breath was uneven, but his eyes were steady.

“I’m not going to be kind,” he said. “If you came here looking for kindness, you should have gone home.”

His hand dropped from Bee’s face to his collar, twisting the fabric just enough to pull him farther into the room. The door clicked shut behind them, not because either of them had made a plan, but because the house had finally decided to be an accomplice.

The bed was too narrow. The blanket was wrong. The lamp was on, because Ilya had left it on before answering the door, and now the light was too honest for what they were doing. He looked at it once and turned it off with his shoulder, leaving them in the blue-gray dark that made everything feel less like a choice and more like a reflex.

He pressed Bee back against the mattress, not gently, and stayed above him, one forearm braced beside Bee’s head, the other still at his throat. Not squeezing. Not leaving. Just there, warm and heavy, a reminder that this had never been a soft thing.

“You said don’t talk about after,” Ilya said. “Okay. Then don’t talk about before.”

His mouth curved without smiling.

“No opening lines. No mugs. No weather. No telling me I’m the only thing that helps like that’s a confession instead of an accusation.”

He bent down and bit the spot where Bee’s pulse had been beating under his hand, just enough to sting, just enough to make the argument move from words to skin.

“I’m not going to be careful,” he repeated, softer now. “I’m not going to stop halfway to ask if this is what you meant. I’m not going to make it pretty.”

His hand slid down, along the line of Bee’s throat, over the chest, stopping just above the waistband, hovering there with deliberate cruelty.

“I’m going to want you until you can’t call it medicine anymore,” he said. “And I’m going to hate every minute of it.”

Then he moved against him, slow, controlled, letting the heat of the moment become too obvious to pretend they were still arguing about the door.

“Say no,” he said, voice low against Bee’s mouth. “Say no and I’ll stop.”

He didn’t say it kindly. He didn’t say it like a dare. He said it like a test he already knew he would fail if Bee let him pass.

Then he kissed him again, swallowing the question before it could become an answer.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya took the permission like a key in a lock.

“Then I’m not stopping,” he said.

The words came out too low, too steady for a man who had spent eleven months learning how to keep himself from saying them. He looked at Bee once, hard, as if making sure the room would remember exactly who had asked for this. Then he moved.

His hands were rough where they went—first to Bee’s shirt, dragging it over his head, then down his own, because the fabric between them felt like a lie neither of them had time for. The room was colder without the clothes, but neither of them noticed. The bed creaked when Ilya shifted onto it, one knee pressing between the sheets, the other braced against the frame. He did not make it gentle. He did not make it soft or apologetic or pretty.

He pulled Bee down by the hand that had been holding his own at his throat, not hard, just enough to make the direction clear. Then he kissed him again, open and unkind, tasting blood and tea and the bitter electricity of a boundary that had been offered, not taken.

“I told you,” Ilya said against his mouth, “I’m not going to pretend this is kindness.”

His thumb traced the line of Bee’s jaw before pressing into the hollow beneath it, not to hurt, just to remind him that Ilya’s hands were still there. Still choosing him. Still angry.

“Say no,” he murmured, “and I’ll stop.”

He didn’t wait for an answer. He had already heard it.

Then he kissed Bee lower, along the corner of his mouth, the jaw, the throat. He bit the tendon there just hard enough to leave a mark, then licked over it, almost like an apology except it wasn’t one. His hand slid down Bee’s chest, over the ribs, the stomach, the hip bone, all of it familiar in a way that made Ilya want to throw something. He knew Bee’s body the way he knew the argument: too well, too long, too badly.

“You still don’t get to make this cute,” Ilya said, voice wrecked. “You still don’t get to come here and make me forget that I was allowed to be angry.”

His hand went lower.

The bed shifted. The lamp had been off, but the gray light from the hallway still cut through the room, honest and ugly, showing everything: the split lip, the wetness at Bee’s mouth, the way Ilya’s hands were shaking once, then steadied.

Ilya watched himself work. He hated how easy it was. Hated how familiar the heat became under his fingers, how quickly the argument moved from words to skin. He didn’t care. He cared too much.

When he moved over him, it was not a surrender. It was a claim.

“I’m not going to be careful,” he said again, because the words had already been said and needed to be true.

His hand pressed flat against Bee’s chest, holding him there, while he shifted lower, then back up, then lower again, until the bed had no room left for dignity. The sheets twisted under Ilya’s knees. His mouth found Bee’s again and took it without asking, hard enough to hurt, not enough to break.

It wasn’t slow after that.

Ilya moved with his anger, with the eleven months, with the broken buzzer and the chipped mugs and the fact that Bee had stood in the corridor as though he had already known what Ilya would do. He took what had been offered and made it mean nothing and everything, his voice low against Bee’s throat when he spoke.

“You came here angry.”

Another breath.

“I stayed here angry.”

His hand came up to hold Bee’s wrist again, pinning it beside his head, not crushing, just keeping. A boundary that had already failed.

He bit Bee’s shoulder once, twice, not pretty, not tender, just proof. His hips moved with a rhythm that felt like punishment until it stopped feeling like that and started feeling worse—like relief, like recognition, like being known by someone who had no right to be kind anymore.

Ilya’s mouth curved against Bee’s skin, not smiling.

“Still,” he breathed.

The word came out broken and furious and true.

His hand slid down again, fingers working, mouth hot and deliberate, until the room narrowed to heat and friction and the sound of the argument becoming something neither of them could win. He didn’t stop halfway. He didn’t ask if this was what Bee meant. He had already asked, and the answer had been in the hallway, in the mugs, in the way Bee had kissed him like a continuation.

When Ilya finally took him, it was slow at first because he was trying to be something other than what he was, and then it wasn’t slow anymore because that had never worked between them.

He braced himself above Bee, one hand at his throat, the other on the mattress, his forehead dropping against Bee’s shoulder with a breath that almost sounded like defeat. His mouth moved along the skin there, open, bitter, claiming every inch of it as if the room were still an argument.

“No after,” Ilya said, voice wrecked.

His hips moved.

“No before.”

Another.

His hand tightened at Bee’s throat, not enough to cut the breath, just enough to make the pulse answer him.

“Just this,” he said, as if that were a sentence. “Just this, and you don’t get to pretend it forgives anything.”

The bed creaked. The hallway light kept them gray and naked and exposed. Ilya’s mouth found Bee’s again and kissed him hard, swallowing the sound of his own name, or maybe the name he had stopped saying, or maybe the one he had kept anyway, the way he had kept the mugs, the way he had kept the anger, the way he had kept wanting Bee like it was a wound that refused to close.

He didn’t stop.

He did not say no again. He did not ask if Bee was sure. He did not make it gentle. He took

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: My hand tangles in his hair, pulls until his head tilts back. "Good," I say, voice ragged. "Now stop trying to talk your way out of it."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya felt the pull in his scalp and did not reach up to break it. The tilt of his head left his throat bare, his mouth open, the split lip still stinging, and he let Bee have the view. He had spent eleven months refusing to let Bee see him like this—undone, unguarded, still wanting—and now he was being shown exactly what he had kept.

“Good,” Ilya repeated, and the word came out wrecked. “You want good? Then stop expecting me to make it safe.”

He did not talk after that. He stopped trying to turn the argument into a sentence. His hand at Bee’s throat pressed again, not cutting, not yet, just enough to keep the pulse answering under his palm. His other hand braced beside Bee’s head, and he moved with his hips, with the last of the tea and the blood and the eleven months, hard enough that the bed took it and gave it back.

The rhythm was ugly and honest. Ilya looked down with both eyes open, watching, because he refused to close them and pretend this was tenderness. He kissed Bee again, biting the lower lip until the sting returned, swallowing the sound, tasting himself in Bee’s mouth.

“You said don’t stop,” Ilya said, rough, almost against the teeth. “I heard you.”

He shifted, angling them, and the bed creaked like a witness. His hand slid down, past the throat, past the chest, gripping the hip hard enough to leave the promise of marks. He pulled them into the motion, into the heat, into the part of it neither of them could name without making it worse.

Ilya’s forehead dropped against Bee’s shoulder. His breath came in short, furious breaks. He had wanted this. He had hated wanting it. He had kept the mugs because he was too proud to admit he had kept wanting Bee. And now that it was happening, the anger did not leave; it simply changed shape, became friction, became the bite at Bee’s neck, became the low curse he finally let himself say into the dark.

“Still,” he said.

The word broke. He did not make it pretty. He drove into it again, harder, until the argument could not survive the distance between them. His hand tightened at Bee’s hip. His mouth found the side of Bee’s throat and stayed there, teeth grazing the tendon, tongue rough. He could feel the heat of him, the wetness, the way the room had narrowed to nothing but skin and motion and the stupid, unbearable fact that his body still knew Bee like it had never left.

When Ilya came, it was not clean. It was not relief. It was a kind of surrender he refused to name. His hand left Bee’s throat and came up to grip the mattress, fingers twisting the sheet, his body going rigid over Bee with his mouth pressed to the skin there, breathing Bee’s name once before he could stop it.

He stayed there.

He did not roll away. He did not say anything gentle. He stayed until the heat between them became too obvious to pretend either of them had won, and then he lifted his head just enough to look at Bee, lips swollen, split, eyes dark and dry.

“You don’t get to make me your forgiveness,” he said, voice low and ruined.

He moved just enough to ease the weight, not enough to leave.

“Still,” he said again, quieter. “Every single time.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I press my forehead to his, breathing him in. "Yeah," I say, voice hoarse. "And we'll still be here next time too."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s breath changed at the words. Not softened—caught, then deliberately flattened out. He stayed close enough that Bee could feel the heat still coming off him, close enough to see the argument still living behind his eyes.

“Next time,” Ilya repeated, as if trying to decide whether it was a threat, a promise, or just another thing Bee had said because it worked.

He did not pull away. That was the trouble. He never did.

His hand came up and pressed flat against Bee’s mouth—not to silence him, not exactly, but to make him feel the choice in it. His thumb dragged across Bee’s lower lip, reopening the sting, then held there.

“You don’t get to make it sound inevitable,” he said. “You don’t get to stand in my bed and call this weather.”

His mouth curved, bitter.

“Weather doesn’t answer the door. Weather doesn’t keep the mugs.”

He looked at Bee with open, furious attention. He knew he was saying too much. He also knew he was saying exactly enough.

“I’m not going to pretend this doesn’t happen,” Ilya said. “I’m not going to pretend I didn’t hear you say you’re angry and think, there it is, he’s still mine to be angry with. That’s ugly. I know it’s ugly.”

He leaned in until his forehead touched Bee’s again, but he didn’t soften the contact. He held it there like a warning.

“But if we’re going to be here next time, you’re going to have to stop acting like you’re the only one choosing this.”

His hand slid from Bee’s mouth to his throat, not squeezing, just resting, feeling the pulse under his fingers. He watched it move. He liked it. He hated that he liked it.

“I’m not saying I’ll be kind,” he said. “I’m not saying this forgives anything. I’m saying I’m still here, and I’m still angry, and I still want you badly enough to let you walk into my hallway without knocking and ruin the evening.”

He kissed him.

It was not gentle. It was not a truce. It was the same argument moved back into the dark, teeth and tongue and the taste of blood. Ilya bit Bee’s lower lip hard enough to sting, then licked over it, possessive and mean, until the kiss turned into something neither of them could call civil.

When he pulled back, his mouth was swollen, his breath rough.

“If you want next time,” he said, “stay tonight.”

He did not say please. He did not say it like a request Bee could refuse.

“Stay here. Don’t leave before I’ve finished being angry with you. Don’t make this into a story where you came in from the cold and I was the thing you visited when you needed fixing.”

His hand tightened slightly at Bee’s throat.

“You’re

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I catch his wrist and press it back into the mattress. "You're not fixing me," I say, and it's not a denial. "And I'm not asking you to." I pull him down against me, skin still damp and too hot. "I'm staying."

rung_labels.evidence: Ilya stiffened the instant Bee's mouth touched his, one hand still hovering near the teapot as if he could set it down without losing the thread of what he'd been saying. He didn't pull away.

rung_labels.evidence: His hand came up, not to push Bee's away, but to hold it still

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: His hand remained where Bee had placed it, thumb dragging once along the throat before pressing flat again, not enough to hurt, not enough to stop

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo pulled the friction tape taut with his teeth, biting it clean through before smoothing the torn edge down with a flat, calloused thumb. 

"Deliberate," he corrected, finally setting the foil aside on the bench. He leaned back against the locker, resting his forearms on his knees, his fencing jacket long since shed down to the damp linen of his undershirt. Sweat had dried at his temples, sticking dark strands of hair to his forehead.

He looked up, letting his eyes drag slowly from the scuffed toe of Reyes's shoes to their face, thoroughly unimpressed by the critique and thoroughly enjoying the proximity. 

"You lunged short twice because you were waiting on a retreat that didn't come," Corvo said, his voice dropping into that familiar, gratingly calm register he used whenever he wanted to get under skin. The corner of his mouth ticked up—crooked, stubborn, entirely unapologetic. "I stayed put. That’s not slow, Reyes. That’s just knowing you."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I snort, leaning my shoulder against the locker beside him. "Knowing me? You looked like a statue waiting for a pigeon to land on it."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
A low, quiet laugh caught in Corvo’s chest, rattling through the silence of the locker room. He tilted his head back against the dented green metal, the cold surface bleeding through his damp shirt, and looked up at Reyes from beneath heavy, dark brows.

"A pigeon that bruised your ribs on the counter," he murmured. 

He didn't move away. If anything, he let his knees fall open a fraction wider on the wooden bench, casually reclaiming space until his thigh brushed the heavy canvas of Reyes's fencing trousers. The warmth of the room had settled into something thick and stale, smelling of oiled steel, sweat, and floor wax, but between them it felt charged, drawn tight like a bowstring held just an inch past full draw.

Corvo reached out, his hand bare and calloused from decades of grip friction, and caught the zipper pull of Reyes’s jacket between two fingers. He didn't pull it down. He just held the metal, feeling the faint, rapid thrum of a pulse beneath the heavy cloth, his knuckles grazing chest height. 

"You're crowding my bench," Corvo said, his voice dropping an octave, losing the classroom projection entirely. It was intimate now, rough at the edges, stubborn to the last. "And you still haven't admitted that last touch was flat."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: My hand stays on his wrist for a second too long. "I know you, too. You're stalling because you're winded."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo didn’t pull away. Instead, he rotated his wrist against Reyes’s palm—a slow, deliberate roll of bone and tendon, the unthinking instinct of a swordsman parrying a line—until his own hand closed over Reyes’s, thick fingers locking around the back of their knuckles.

His pulse was kicking hard against Reyes’s grip, and he didn't bother trying to hide it. 

"Winded," Corvo repeated, the word coming out rough, a low drawl that didn't carry an ounce of shame. He tilted his chin up, his dark eyes fixing on Reyes's mouth before dragging deliberately back up to meet their gaze. "Four years of running you around the strip, and you think *that's* what takes the wind out of me?"

He gave a short, firm tug on Reyes’s hand—not enough to break balance, but enough to eliminate the last few inches of polite distance, drawing Reyes squarely between his parted knees. The heat coming off both of them hung thick in the narrow aisle between the lockers. 

Corvo shifted his grip, sliding his hand from knuckles to forearm, callused palm catching against the rolled canvas of Reyes's sleeve. The teasing smirk had finally burned off, replaced by something taut, sharp-edged, and entirely stripped of pretense.

"You're standing close enough to do something about it," Corvo said, his voice dropping to a gravelly murmur against the quiet of the salle. "Take the touch, Reyes. Or stop talking."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The zip of Reyes’s jacket gave way with a sharp, tearing rasp that echoed against the lockers, and after that Corvo wasn’t thinking about form, or distance, or who had rights on the strip. 

He had his hands in the heavy canvas before it even hit the floorboards, stripping it down Reyes’s shoulders with rough efficiency, his knuckles scraping through damp cotton underneath. He hauled Reyes down by the waist, not bothering with grace, taking the impact of them against his chest with a hard grunt that vibrated straight through his ribs.

The bench groaned beneath their combined weight. Corvo kicked his own bag out of the way, sending buckles and leather skittering across the tile, clearing room he didn't intend to leave. 

His mouth found Reyes’s jaw first—sweat-salted, burning hot—and then his mouth, hard and impatient, teeth catching against lip with the same unyielding stubbornness he brought to every single bout. It wasn’t gentle, but it wasn’t meant to be; four years of narrow margins and scraped knuckles didn’t evaporate just because the weapons were racked.

Corvo’s fingers tangled into the fabric of Reyes’s shirt, bunching it up to get his calloused palms against bare skin, fingers splaying wide over the heat of their back. His chest heaved against Reyes's, each breath coming short and ragged, smelling of cedar wax, laundry soap, and the sharp copper tang of exertion.

"Tell me," Corvo rasped against Reyes’s mouth, breaking the kiss just enough to drag air into his lungs, his voice wrecked and fierce. His hands gripped harder, pulling Reyes flush against him until there wasn't a breath of space left between their hips. "Tell me you didn't plan on this when you walked back in here."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "I planned on you being an arrogant bastard." My hand finds his hair, pulling just enough to tilt his head back. "This is just a bonus."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
A sharp, hitching breath hissed through Corvo’s teeth at the drag on his scalp, but he didn't pull away. If anything, he let his throat bare to the cold air of the locker room, his eyes half-lidded and dark with a heat that had nothing to do with form or footwork. 

The corner of his mouth twitched—wicked, bruised, entirely unrepentant.

"Liar," Corvo muttered, the rumble of it vibrating deep in his chest. 

He brought his hands down from Reyes’s back, fingers digging hard into the meat of Reyes’s hip to anchor them down, blunt nails pressing through denim and canvas. He surged upward against the pull of his hair, using the leverage to slam his mouth back against Reyes's, biting down on the lower lip hard enough to taste copper before dragging his mouth down the hot line of their jaw.

His breath was scorching against Reyes’s neck, ragged and uneven. He shoved a knee between Reyes's thighs, levering his way deeper into the space they occupied, until the wooden slats of the bench creaked a sharp protest under the shift of their weight.

"You don't take bonuses, Reyes," Corvo growled against the pulse hammering at their throat, his thumb hooking violently into the waistband of their trousers, tugging them closer still. "You scrape for every single point. Earn this one."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The varnished slats of the bench dug hard into Corvo’s shoulder blades, the wood cold against the damp cloth of his shirt, but he barely registered the bruise forming there. 

For once, his hands didn't reach to parry. They found Reyes’s shoulders, fingers flexing, bunching the heavy fabric of their shirt, calloused palms sliding up to grip the nape of their neck instead. His head fell back against the slatted wood, a sharp, choked noise catching in the back of his throat as Reyes took the initiative, took the pace, and deliberately slowed it down to something agonizing.

He had spent four years studying how Reyes moved—every tell, every shift in weight, every fraction of a second before an attack—and none of it prepared him for the unhurried, ruinous heat of their mouth. 

A shudder ran through him, starting at his jaw and racking down through his chest. Corvo tried to set his jaw, tried to find that dry, grating smirk, but his lips parted on a rough exhale instead, his pulse thumping visibly against his throat where Reyes’s mouth lingered. He arched slightly off the bench, his hips tilting up on pure, uncalculated instinct, seeking the friction his mouth was too wrecked to ask for.

His fingers tightened in Reyes’s hair, blunt and demanding, not pushing away but anchoring them down, holding Reyes right where they were. 

"Reyes," he breathed out, the name scraping out of him raw and stripped of every bit of classroom polish. His voice was completely ruined, low and thick with a wanting he couldn't laugh off. He swallowed hard, chest heaving beneath them, his eyes dark, glazed, and fixed entirely on the shadow of Reyes's face above him. "God damn you."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I let him feel the smirk against his skin, my teeth scraping his pulse point. "Still got no answer, Corvo?"

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
A sharp, shuddering breath rattled through Corvo's ribs as teeth dragged over his pulse, the sting of it grounding him just enough to drag his mind back to the surface. 

He didn't answer right away. He couldn't. His throat worked on a dry swallow, his chest rising and falling in heavy, uneven hitches beneath Reyes's weight. 

Then his hands moved—not gentle, never gentle—sliding from Reyes's nape down over broad shoulders, blunt fingers digging deep into the muscle, dragging them down until Reyes was pressed so heavily against him that Corvo could feel the thudding of their heart matching the erratic hammer of his own. 

He tilted his head just enough to bring his mouth back to Reyes's ear, his stubble scraping against their jaw. 

"I've got three," Corvo rasped, his voice raw, dragging the words up from the bottom of his chest. He bucked his hips up against Reyes—a sharp, demanding jolt of friction that rattled the bench beneath them and left no room for doubt about what he wanted. "None of them involve you talking so much."

He brought one hand down, his palm rough and hot as it found the buckle of Reyes's belt, his knuckles jarring against the brass with blunt, impatient urgency. His eyes were half-blown, dark and entirely stripped of that cool, detached iron he wore on the strip, looking up at Reyes like a man who knew he was cornered and had decided he liked the wall at his back.

"Move," Corvo growled, his thumb yanking hard at the leather. "Or let me do it."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo tested the hold immediately, muscle bunching hard in his forearms as he flexed against the grip—not truly trying to break free, but demanding that Reyes keep him there by force. When the grip held fast, pressing the backs of his hands into the unyielding wood, a ragged, shuddering laugh caught in his throat.

"Took you long enough," he breathed, the words rattling out between parted teeth. 

His head fell back against the bench, neck taut, his throat moving on a hard swallow as the sudden shift in control settled over them. He had spent years controlling lines, parrying off every advance, dictating the tempo down to the millisecond. Having the tempo taken from him by force—having his own stubborn weight used against him—sent a hard, electric jolt straight through his spine.

He stopped pulling against the hold, letting his wrists go heavy in Reyes’s hands, though his fingers twitched against the wood, itching to touch. Instead, he drove his heels into the floorboards, arching up off the slats just enough to meet the crush of Reyes's weight dead-on, refusing to give an inch of ground even while pinned flat.

His gaze locked onto Reyes’s face, fierce, completely undone, his dark eyes glittering with the kind of reckless satisfaction he usually only got after an exhausting, five-touch bout that left blood in his mouth.

"Go on, then," Corvo rasped, his chest hitching violently beneath them, his hips rolling up into the press of theirs with blunt, unapologetic demand. "Take it, Reyes. Stop making me wait."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: My knee pushes his legs wider, my other hand making short work of his belt. "Always so impatient," I mutter, leaning down to bite at his collarbone through the damp linen.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
A sharp, broken hiss ripped past Corvo’s teeth as Reyes bit down, the blunt pressure through the damp cloth sending a vicious spike of heat straight down to the base of his spine. 

His thighs fell open further around Reyes’s knee without an ounce of resistance, his fencing trousers slackening as the belt gave way with a metallic clatter against the bench. The wood groaned under the shift of their weight, but Corvo didn't care if the whole frame splintered beneath them. 

The moment Reyes's hand left his wrists to work the buckle, Corvo didn't pull away or try to reverse the pin. Instead, his freed hand came up fast, thick fingers burying themselves in the short hair at the back of Reyes’s head, anchoring the bite against his collarbone, pressing them harder into the bruise he knew would be there tomorrow. 

"Four years," Corvo groaned, his voice completely shot, rattling deep in his chest against Reyes’s cheek. His hips surged upward in a sharp, involuntary tilt, meeting the heavy press of Reyes's thigh with a raw, desperate friction that tore another ragged breath out of him. "Four goddamn years, and you think... you think this is me being impatient?"

His other hand found the hem of Reyes’s shirt, calloused fingers shoving past the damp fabric to dig into the muscle of their lower back, blunt nails biting in to drag them down, flat against him, eliminating the last fraction of an inch of air between them. 

Corvo turned his head into the crook of Reyes’s neck, his mouth finding the hot, salt-slick skin there, teeth grazing over the tendon in an open, unvarnished demand. 

"Get on with it," he rasped, shuddering as his eyes fell shut, his grip in Reyes’s hair tightening with blunt, unyielding force. "Touch, Reyes. Take the damn touch."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The rustle of heavy canvas and the sharp rasp of zippers gave way entirely, kicked down to the cold floorboards as Corvo shoved his own trousers down over his hips, kicking his boots free with rough, graceless kicks that echoed off the row of lockers. 

He didn't wait. He caught Reyes by the back of the neck and hauled them down, mouth colliding with mouth in a hot, slick clash of teeth and tongue that tasted of salt and exertion. His hand reached down between their bodies, blunt, calloused fingers wrapping around the heat of them both, dragging them together until bare, weeping skin met bare skin. 

A sharp, ragged curse tore out of Corvo's throat at the first blunt slide of friction. His hips hitched hard off the varnished slats, muscles in his abdomen locking like iron as he dragged Reyes into him. The bench shrieked against the floorbolts with the sudden, violent shift in weight, but Corvo didn't flinch; he dug his heels into the edge of the wood, spread his knees wider, and pulled Reyes down until there was nowhere left to retreat.

"Look at me," Corvo rasped against Reyes's mouth, his voice fractured, raw, stripped down to nothing. 

When their eyes locked, Corvo surged up to meet the downward thrust of Reyes's hips, taking the full, crushing brunt of it with an open-mouthed groan that vibrated against Reyes’s jaw. Every muscle in his shoulders bunched, the old bruises from four years of competition grinding against the slatted wood, but the heat burning through his gut drowned out every ache. 

He matched the pace stroke for stroke, refusing to be passive even on his back. His hands clamped onto Reyes’s waist, blunt thumbs digging into the hollows of their hips to dictate the rhythm, hauling them down hard and fast against him, meeting every drive with a vicious, bucking snap of his own hips. The sound of skin slapping wetly against skin and the rhythmic, shuddering rattle of the bench filled the narrow aisle, entirely uncaring of the empty salle beyond the door.

Corvo’s head thrashed back against the green metal of the lockers, a sharp clang ringing out as his teeth bared in an agonized, ecstatic grimace. Sweat ran freely down his neck, soaking his linen shirt, plastering it to his ribs. 

"Reyes—fuck," he choked out, his fingers digging into Reyes's flanks hard enough to leave dark purple marks by morning. His vision went gray at the edges, his breath coming in shallow, torn gasps as the friction built into something suffocating, relentless, and completely unsparing. "Harder. Don't you dare give me room."

The cadence broke into something furious and uneven, both of them straining for leverage, the sheer athletic force of it rattling Corvo’s entire frame. His hips stuttered, rising desperately against the crush of Reyes's weight, seeking the point of no return with the same single-minded, ruthless hunger he brought to the final seconds of a bout. 

When the edge hit him, it came with the violence of a parry ripped through guard. 

Corvo’s back arched clean off the bench, his spine curving into a rigid, bowstring tautness as a shattered groan broke from his chest. His hands knotted violently into the fabric of Reyes's shirt, pulling them down into a bruising, suffocating grip, his thighs trembling violently around Reyes's hips as his release spilled hot and heavy between their pressed stomachs. He couldn't speak, couldn't breathe; his eyes clenched shut, his jaw trembling as wave after wave of heat tore through him, leaving him trembling, exposed, and entirely spent beneath Reyes's heavy, relentless drive until they both collapsed together against the protesting wood.

The locker room fell dead silent except for the frantic, heaving drag of their breath, echoing in the cold, cavernous space. 

Corvo lay flat, his chest slamming against Reyes’s, unable to lift his arms from the wood where they had fallen slack. A low, ruined laugh finally rattled loose in his throat, breathless and entirely victorious despite being pinned beneath them. 

"Touch," Corvo wheezed into the crook of Reyes's shoulder, his fingers twitching against the slats. "Yours. Bastard."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I let my forehead drop against his collarbone, breathing in the smell of sweat and cedar wax. My hand slides up to grip the back of his neck, thumb stroking the damp hair at his nape. "Took you long enough to admit it."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
A slow, heavy breath hitched in Corvo’s chest, lifting both of them by a fraction of an inch before falling back down with an unhurried, ragged sigh. He didn't move to push Reyes off. If anything, he let his chin drop until his stubble caught against the top of Reyes’s head, grounding himself in the familiar, solid weight pressing him into the slats.

The cool air of the locker room was already beginning to bite at the damp skin of his ribs, but between them the heat was stubborn, slow to bleed off. Beneath the stroke of Reyes’s thumb at the base of his skull, the tight, defensive knots in Corvo’s neck finally gave up the ghost, slackening into the wood.

"Don't get used to it," Corvo murmured. His voice was completely wrecked, reduced to a dry, low rasp that barely carried past Reyes's ear. 

He managed to drag one heavy, leaden arm up from the bench, his calloused palm coming to rest flat against the warm, damp muscle of Reyes’s shoulder blade. His thumb traced a lazy, unthinking circle against the skin—not the grip of a fighter looking for leverage, just an anchor keeping them where they were.

A faint, self-satisfied hitch of a laugh twitched in his chest, rattling through his ribs. 

"Besides," he added, eyes cracked open just enough to squint at the dim ceiling tiles, his mouth ticking up at one corner, bruised and stubborn to the last, "director would've called it simultaneously. You were off balance on the recovery."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I laugh against his skin, my own voice just as rough. "Director's not here. And you're flat on your back." I push myself up just enough to look at him, my hand still resting on his chest. "You're buying the coffee tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo squinted up at Reyes through dark, heavy-lidded eyes, the corners of his mouth twitching with a faint, bruised amusement he didn’t bother trying to swallow down. The air in the locker room was cooling fast, raising goosebumps along his damp arms, but under the flat heat of Reyes’s palm on his sternum, his pulse was still kicking—deep, steady, and entirely unhurried.

He lifted his hand from the bench, letting his fingers curl loosely around the side of Reyes’s neck, blunt thumb catching the sharp angle of their jaw. He didn’t push them away; if anything, his grip carried just enough weight to keep Reyes from pulling back any further.

"Flat on my back because you've got no sense of moderation," Corvo countered, his voice like gravel ground between two flat stones. He let his thumb brush over the red mark where his own teeth had caught Reyes's skin earlier, a deliberate, slow drag of calloused skin. 

He huffed a short, quiet breath through his nose, his dark gaze lingering on Reyes's mouth before tracking up to meet their eyes with unblinking, stubborn familiarity.

"The place around the corner from your salle," Corvo said, his tone dry, laying down terms like he was setting up the next round of pool matches. "The one with the roaster that doesn't burn the beans to spite the customers. None of that filtered battery acid you keep in the breakroom."

His hand shifted, thick fingers sliding into the hair at Reyes's temple, tugging just enough to bring them down an inch closer again. 

"Seven sharp," he rasped, the challenge as natural to him as breathing, entirely devoid of apology. "And you're carrying the kit bags."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Seven sharp is when the juniors arrive," I point out, but I'm already shifting my weight off him. "Six-thirty. And you're carrying your own damn bag."
