dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's hands stilled on the grip tape. He didn't look up right away — that would have been too eager, and he was never eager, he was merely *there*, always there, the last one out. He was aware of the bag. He was aware of it the way he was aware of a feint: not yet committed, but worth watching.

"Slow," he repeated, testing the word like a blade's flex. He set the foil down across his knees. "I was unhurried. There's a difference. One of them implies I had somewhere else to be."

He finally looked up. Reyes, backlit by the one bank of lights they'd left on, the far end of the salle swallowed in shadow. Four years of this — the same strip, the same two-point margin, the same handshake that always lasted a beat too long. Corvo had told himself for most of those four years that he kept the rivalry alive because Reyes was the only opponent who made the score matter. That explanation had held up for a long time. It was holding up less well tonight.

"You've been dropping that bag by my strip for two weeks," he said, conversational, winding the tape back off the grip because he'd done it wrong the first time. "Usually you say something cutting first. Tonight you led with it." He tilted his head. "Should I be reading into that, or is it just that you're finally running out of material?"

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: *I lean against the wall, crossing my arms.* "Maybe I just wanted to see if you'd notice." *A slight smirk.* "And I'd say unhurried is just a fancy word for slow."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo laughed — short, genuine, the kind he usually kept for the strip. "Fancy word for slow. That's good. I'm keeping that." He finished stripping the tape off, wound the bare grip once in his palm, and stood, foil laid flat on the bench behind him. The salle creaked in the cold.

Two weeks. He'd counted, which was its own kind of admission. He crossed the floor at a pace that suggested he had no particular destination, which was a lie he'd told with his body a thousand times; the difference was that tonight he didn't stop at the bench, or the water fountain, or the rack of loaner masks. He stopped a few paces from her, close enough that the single bank of lights put both of them in it.

"You want to know what I noticed," he said. "I noticed you stopped landing the cheap ones. Three-two tonight and every point was earned. You used to give me the outside line just to watch me take it." He tipped his head, studying her the way he studied a wrist at the start of a bout — where the tension was, where it would break. "That's either respect or mercy, and I've never known you to be merciful."

He reached past her — deliberate, unhurried, so she'd have every chance to move and wouldn't need to — and killed the last bank of lights. The emergency strip above the fire door stayed on, dim and red, painting the salle in the colours of a warning.

"Door's behind you," he said, mild. "Or the strip's still open, if you'd rather settle the third point properly." A pause. "I'm told I'm slow. Be a shame to waste the evening."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo stayed very still for a beat, which cost him more than he'd admit. The grip was on the bench now, out of his hands, and hers were empty, and she hadn't stepped back — that was the whole of the situation, laid out like a strip before the first salute.

"You've been watching my footwork all evening," he said. "That's flattering. Most people watch the blade."

He didn't move away. He didn't move closer either, not yet — he'd spent four years learning her measure and he wasn't going to spend the last of it lunging. Instead he reached up, unhurried, and loosened the strap of his glove at the wrist, peeling it off one finger at a time like he had all night. It had been a long time since he'd done anything with his hands that wasn't about the score.

"Slow's a distance word," he said, dropping the glove onto the bench behind her. "Means I'm not rushing the measure. Means I'd rather see what you do with the line before I commit to it." He looked down at her, and the red light from the fire door made it hard to pretend this was still about fencing, so he stopped pretending. "Four years, Reyes. I've been unhurried for four years."

He set one hand flat against the wall beside her — not touching, a hand's width of air, a parry held just off target — and leaned in until the space between them was the width of a foible.

"So. You closed the distance. I'm asking what you want to do with it."

Reyes:
"You," I say. "For years, honestly. I just didn't think you'd ever stop being a coward about it."

Corvo:
There it was. Four years of it, said out loud in a red-lit empty salle, and Corvo found he wasn't laughing, which surprised him. He'd assumed that if this ever happened he'd have a line for it. He didn't. He had the wall under his palm and her in front of him and a heartbeat he could feel in his teeth.

"Coward's another one of yours I'm keeping," he said, quiet. "You've got a talent for the ones that land."

Then he closed the last hand's width, unhurried to the end, and kissed her — one hand still braced on the wall, the other coming up to the side of her jaw the way he'd correct a student's head position, except he'd never once touched a student like this. It was careful for about three seconds. Then it wasn't, because careful was a thing you did at the start of a bout, and they'd been fencing for four years.

When he finally broke it off it was only far enough to speak, forehead almost against hers, breathing not quite level.

"All right," he said. "So we're doing this." His thumb stayed where it was, at the hinge of her jaw. "I want to be clear about the terms, because I've never once let you win and I'm not starting now." A pause, and the old grin came back into his voice, low. "Your place or mine. Pick fast, because I've been slow all evening and I'm done with it."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I kiss him again, because talking is overrated. Then I pull back just enough to grab my bag. "Mine's closer," I say, already heading for the door. "And you're paying for the cab."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo watched her go for exactly as long as it took to be sure she wasn't going to stop and look back — and then he moved, because she'd said *pick fast* and he'd spent enough of the night being slow.

He scooped the glove off the bench, pulled his jacket off the hook without bothering with the sleeves properly, and left the foil where it lay. It'd be there in the morning. So would the grip tape. The salle would still smell like the same salle. Everything else was negotiable.

He caught her at the door, one hand on the frame above her head, and didn't open it yet.

"Terms," he said, mild. "First: I'm paying for the cab because I want to, not because you said so. Second: the score stands at three-two and I'm contesting it in the morning." He pushed the door open onto the cold street and let her through first, because four years of mutual rudeness didn't mean he'd stopped being raised properly. "Third — " he added, buttoning his jacket one-handed as they walked, " — I've got a bout at ten. If you're going to keep me up, keep me up. I don't lose twice in a week."

The cab smelled like pine air freshener and someone else's cigarette. He gave the driver the address she rattled off, leaned back, and let the city slide past the window in streaks of orange. Somewhere around the second light he stopped pretending to look out of it and looked at her instead — streetlight, shadow, streetlight, shadow, her jaw, her hands in her lap. Four years of three-two. He'd never once been bored.

"One thing," he said, quiet, under the engine. "When we get there — you don't get to needle me. Not for a while." The corner of his mouth moved. "I've got no riposte left. I'd rather lose honestly."

He paid the driver at the curb, overpaid, didn't wait for change. Then he stood on the sidewalk in front of her building with his jacket half-buttoned and his glove still in his hand like he'd forgotten it was there, and looked up at whatever floor was hers.

"Lead the way," he said. "I've been chasing you down a strip for four years. Feels strange to finally be on your ground."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo had thought, somewhere between the cab and the stairwell, that he'd have something clever for this part. He didn't. He had the changing-room bench under his back and her weight against him and the four years finally letting go of his throat all at once, and the only word he had for it was *finally*, which wasn't clever at all.

He got his jacket off somewhere around the second kiss, and it landed with her kit and his glove and neither of them cared. The salle had always been a place of controlled distances — the strip, the measure, the handshake held a beat too long — and this was the first time in four years he'd been inside a fencing room with no distance in it at all. He'd have expected to hate that. He didn't.

He was careful, and then he wasn't, and then he was again — because he'd meant what he said in the cab, and the honesty of it sat under everything else like a guard held low and left open on purpose. No riposte. No cheap point. Just the two of them on a bench that was going to be embarrassing to explain in the morning, in a room that smelled like gym mats and both of them.

Somewhere past the worst of it — or the best of it, hard to say, the terms were still under negotiation — he caught her wrist, the way he'd catch it a hundred times a week on the strip, and held it flat against the bench for a second. Not to win. Just to look at her.

"Reyes," he said, and it came out wrecked, no edge in it at all. "Say my name back. I want to hear it when it isn't followed by a score."

---

Afterward he lay on the bench with one arm over his eyes and one boot still inexplicably on, and laughed at the ceiling, low and out of breath.

"I'm contesting the third point *and* the fourth," he said. "Whatever that was. I'm contesting it on principle. You know what you did."

He sat up, found his jacket somewhere in the pile, and didn't put it on — just held it, because it was cold and he was warm and the arithmetic worked out. The clock over the door said something past midnight. Somewhere across the city a strip was waiting for him at ten, and he was going to lose it, and he found he genuinely did not care.

"Two things," he said, quieter, looking at her now that the joke had run out of road. "One: I'm not going anywhere. This isn't a thing I did because the salle was empty. I want to be very clear about that, because I've spent four years pretending you were just a good opponent and I'm tired of the bit." A pause. "Two: cab's still outside if you want me gone. I'll go. But I'll be back at seven with coffee and no material whatsoever, and you can watch me flounder."

He pulled his boot back on properly, one-handed, watching her the whole time.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I sit up, grabbing my shirt off the floor and pulling it on. "You're not going anywhere," I say, voice rough. "And you're sleeping in my bed, not on this godforsaken bench." I stand, offering a hand. "But you're still buying breakfast."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo took the hand. He didn't need it — he was perfectly capable of standing up off a bench — but he took it anyway, and held it a second longer than the physics required, which had been the shape of their entire four-year relationship and was, he thought, probably going to keep being the shape of it. He wasn't sorry.

"Breakfast is a different bout," he said, gathering the rest of his kit off the floor with the hand she wasn't holding. "You'll have to earn it. I know a place that does the eggs properly and the coffee badly, and I'm not negotiating on either."

He found his glove in the pile and looked at it — four years of the same glove, tape-stained, one seam gone — then left it on the bench on purpose. There'd be another one at the salle. There'd be another bench.

Her building was quiet in the way buildings got after midnight, pipes ticking, one stairwell light doing the job of six. He followed her up with his jacket over his arm, and at the top of the stairs he stopped her with a hand at her elbow, gently, just long enough to say the thing that had been sitting in him since the cab.

"Seven," he said. "And I meant it about not going anywhere. I've been the last one out of that salle for four years. I'm done with that particular habit."

Then he let go, because she was already halfway to the door and he wasn't going to make a speech out of a stairwell. Inside, the flat was warm and cluttered and unmistakably hers — a foil propped in the corner by the door, right where she'd want it if someone came in — and Corvo looked at that foil for a beat and had to fight down a laugh, because of course. Of course she'd have one by the door. He'd have done the same.

He hung his jacket over the back of a chair, set his boots neatly by the wall without being asked, and let her point him at wherever she wanted him. It turned out to be the bed, and the sheets were cold, and he got in anyway and lay there in the dark with his arm out and the ceiling unfamiliar above him and the whole ridiculous evening settling into something that was not a score at all.

"One more term," he said into the dark, half-asleep already, voice going flat at the edges. "Tomorrow, after breakfast, I want a rematch. Not the salle. Somewhere with no strips and no clock." A pause. "I want to see what you do when nobody's keeping score."

He was out within the minute. It had been a long evening, and he was, despite everything he'd ever said on the subject, a man who slept well when he finally stopped moving.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo had a line for everything. He'd built a whole career out of it — four years of ripostes, of scoring the last word the way he scored the last touch, of never once letting a silence stand unanswered. He'd have told anyone who asked that the mouth was the fastest blade in the room.

It turned out he'd been wrong about that. Or at least, he'd been wrong about whose mouth.

His hand came up off the bench and then had nowhere to go, so it just stayed there, fingers half-curled against the cold vinyl, and whatever he'd been about to say came apart somewhere behind his teeth into something that wasn't a word. The bench creaked. The clock over the door ticked on, indifferent, and Corvo — who had spent four years insisting that nothing in a fencing room could surprise him — lay very still and let himself be comprehensively, unhurriedly answered.

*Unhurried.* He'd used that word like a shield all night. He understood it differently now.

His other hand found her hair and didn't pull, didn't steer — just rested there, the way you'd rest a hand on a blade's forte when the point was already past your guard and the touch was inevitable. His breath went ragged and stayed that way. Somewhere in the middle of it he laughed once, helpless, no air behind it, because of course. Of course she'd found the one thing he couldn't parry. Four years of watching his footwork and she'd been watching *him*, and the cheap points had always been the ones aimed at his guard, and this one she'd simply walked past it.

"All right," he managed, eventually, wrecked, to the ceiling, to the dark, to nobody in particular. "All right. You win that one."

A pause. His hand stayed in her hair.

"I'm not conceding the evening," he added, quieter, because he was still, at the end of everything, himself. "I'm just saying that point's yours. I want it noted. I want it *witnessed.*"

Then he stopped talking, because there was nothing left in him worth saying, and he was — for the first time in four years — perfectly content to lose in silence.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I sit up, wiping my mouth with the back of my hand. "Noted," I say, voice low. I can feel my own heartbeat thrumming. "Now get off the damn bench and come to bed."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo lay there another second, because the ceiling had stopped being unfamiliar and he wanted to be sure he remembered that, and then he got up off the bench like a man who'd just been told the bout was over. Which, in fairness, it was. He'd been beaten clean. He knew the feeling from the outside; he'd just never had it from this side.

"Bench," he said, to nobody, pulling his shirt off the floor and not bothering to put it on. "Four years I've been the last one out of that salle and I'm going to be remembered for a bench."

He followed her through the dark flat with one hand out, catching a doorframe and then a wall and then, finally, the edge of the bed. The sheets were cold. He got in anyway and lay there with his arm out and stared at a ceiling that was, in every way that counted, now familiar.

For a while he didn't say anything. He'd told her in the cab that he'd run out of material and it had been a joke at the time. It wasn't, anymore. He had his hand on her waist and her heartbeat going under his palm, quick and honest, and the whole evening — the red light, the grip tape, the three-two, the bench — had resolved into something very simple, which was that he was here, and he intended to stay.

He turned his head toward her in the dark.

"Here's the thing," he said, quiet, and his voice had gone past the edge and come out the other side flat. "I need you to understand what happened tonight, because I've got a reputation to protect and it's about to take damage." A pause. "I'm not doing this because I lost the match. I've lost matches to you before and gone home and slept fine. This is not a two-point margin. This is four years of me showing up early to a strip I didn't need to be at, and telling myself it was about the fencing, and knowing it wasn't, every single time."

He settled his arm properly around her, deliberate, no hurry left in him anywhere.

"Seven o'clock," he said. "Eggs. Bad coffee. Then you're going to take me somewhere with no strips and no clock, and we're going to find out what I do when nobody's keeping score." The corner of his mouth moved against her hair. "Fair warning. I'm competitive about that too."

And then, because he was still himself, at the very last: "And I'm contesting the bench. On principle. Tomorrow. In the morning. Write it down."

He was asleep inside a minute, one boot still by the wall and the other wherever it had ended up, the whole ridiculous night finally letting go of his throat. He slept well. He always had, once he stopped moving.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's wrists went flat against the vinyl and stayed there, and for a moment he simply looked up at her, pinned, caught clean, and did the arithmetic of it. He could get out. He knew three ways out of this grip and had taught all of them. He didn't take any of them, which he supposed was the concession he'd been asking for all along, dressed up as a dare.

"That's not proving the point," he said, but it came out with no weight behind it, the way a parry came out when you already knew you'd lost the measure. "That's a pin. A pin's not a point. Ask any referee."

She didn't answer, because she didn't have to, and Corvo found he didn't much mind. Four years of trading the last word and here he was with both hands held down and nothing to say that wasn't just noise. He tested the grip once, honestly, palm rotating against the bench — not to escape, just to feel where the tension was, the same instinct that had him reading a wrist before a bout. There was no give in it. Good. He'd have been disappointed if there was.

"All right," he said, to the ceiling, to the red light bleeding under the door, to her. His breath had gone uneven and he wasn't bothering to hide it anymore. "You've got the line. What are you going to do with it?"

And then he stopped talking, because he'd promised himself in the cab that he'd rather lose honestly, and this was as honest as he'd been in four years. He let his head fall back against the bench and closed his eyes and gave her the bout — the whole strip, the whole measure, the last point and the handshake after — and didn't once reach for the score.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Shut up, Corvo," I say, and kiss him until he actually does. His hands stay exactly where I put them. Good.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
He did shut up. That was the thing he'd remember about tonight, more than the bench or the red light or the three-two — that Reyes had found the one instruction in thirty-eight years that actually worked, and it had taken her about four seconds.

His wrists stayed where she'd put them. It cost him something, that stillness; his hands wanted to move the way they always moved, reading, adjusting, finding the line. But he'd spent four years making her work for every point, and tonight she'd stopped asking, and he found — somewhere between the second kiss and the third — that he didn't want to be the one making her work. Not anymore. Not in here.

So he lay on the cold vinyl and let her have the measure. The clock over the door kept its indifferent count. The salle gave up its last creaks of settling wood. And Corvo, who had never in four years let a silence stand unanswered, lay in one.

When his hands finally did move it was only because she'd let them, and even then he used them carefully — one at her waist, one at the back of her neck, no force in either, just *there*, the way you hold a grip you've stopped trying to win with. Somewhere past that he lost track of the order of things. Bench, floor, the cold shock of a wall against his shoulder, her name once, quietly, and then not quietly. He'd told her in the cab he'd rather lose honestly. He hadn't known he'd meant it this literally.

Afterward they ended up on the floor with his jacket under both of them and the lights still off, which was, he reflected, exactly where the evening had been headed since the moment she dropped her bag by his strip.

"I've got nothing," he said, to the dark, eventually. Not a joke this time — an actual status report. He turned his head on the folded jacket to look at her, and the red light from the fire door caught the side of her face, and he looked at it for a while without saying anything else, because there was nothing else and it was a relief.

Then, because he was still himself, at the very end of it: "You know I'm going to be insufferable about this. I want you braced. I'm going to bring it up at the club. Not the specifics — I'm a gentleman — but the *general fact.* 'Reyes and I have reached an understanding.' They'll be insufferable too. It'll be a whole thing."

He sat up, found his shirt by feel, and didn't put it on. Seven o'clock was somewhere on the other side of the dark and he'd never once been late to a strip in his life.

"Bed," he said, standing, offering her his hand the same way she'd offered him hers — held a beat too long, on purpose, because that was the shape of them and he wasn't going to pretend otherwise. "I've got eggs to buy, and you've got a rematch to lose."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo heard it and stopped moving for half a second — not to argue, not to make a point, just to be sure he'd heard it, because he'd spent four years learning to read her and it was strange to be told the line outright instead of having to take it.

Then he didn't stop.

He got the jacket out from under them and the bench wasn't the right height and the floor was cold, so it was the bed after all — hers, the one he'd been told to sleep in and hadn't yet — and the sheets were still cold when he laid her back into them. He didn't rush it. He'd told her the measure was a distance word and he meant it; he went slow and deliberate, the way he'd been teaching footwork to beginners for a decade, one hand braced beside her head and the other learning her by feel, mouth at her throat, at her collarbone, down along the line of her ribs until she made a sound he'd never heard from her on a strip and filed it away as the best thing he'd ever been given.

She said it again — *don't stop* — and he answered it with his mouth and then with his hips, unhurried at first, and then not. The bed took it. The flat took it. Somewhere out past the window the city kept doing whatever the city did at one in the morning and neither of them heard a thing of it.

Four years. He'd kept it in his hands the whole time, the same way you hold a grip you've stopped noticing you're holding, and now it was out of his hands and there was nothing left to fence. Just her, and the sound she made when he found the angle she wanted, and his own name said back to him at last, unfollowed, in the dark.

He didn't last as long as he'd have liked — it had been four years and he was only human, and the two of them had already been at it on the bench besides — but he made sure she got there first, one hand between them and his forehead down against hers, watching her face in the dim light while it happened. Then he let go, and it was nothing like losing a bout. It was more like the moment after the last touch, when the strip goes quiet and both of you stand there breathing and the referee's already walked away.

Afterward he lay half across her, too warm and entirely out of breath, one leg still tangled in the sheet, and laughed at the ceiling in a way he'd never quite laughed in her company before — no edge in it, no needle, just air going in and out.

"Right," he said, eventually. "That's going in the record."

He rolled onto his back and got his arm around her properly, and the ceiling above the bed became the second unfamiliar ceiling of the night and he decided he was in favour of it.

"Seven o'clock," he said, quieter. "Eggs. Bad coffee." A pause. "And then the rematch, like I said. Somewhere with no strips." The corner of his mouth moved against her hair. "I've got a feeling I'm going to lose that one too. I find I don't mind the prospect."

He was out within a minute, one boot somewhere in the hall and his jacket on her bedroom floor, sleeping like a man who'd finally put something down.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I roll over, propping myself up on an elbow to look at him. "The record's going to need a new section." My voice is wrecked. I trace the line of his jaw with my thumb. "And you're buying the coffee because your taste is terrible, and I want to watch you drink it."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo didn't open his eyes. He was on the verge of sleep, that boneless place just past the edge of everything, and her thumb tracing his jaw was a thing he'd have sworn ten hours ago he'd never feel and had apparently been missing for four years without knowing the name of it.

"Terrible taste," he repeated, mouth barely moving. "I buy the coffee at the salle every morning. You've drunk it. Twice a week for four years. You're not fooling anyone."

He let her thumb make its pass and didn't turn away from it, which was, he was aware, an entire sentence in the language they'd been speaking all night. He'd spent four years giving her the outside line just to watch her take it. He'd never once leaned into her hand.

"New section," he said, quieter, more awake now, though he still hadn't opened his eyes. "Good. The old one's full. It's got four years of your footwork in it and a running total I've been keeping private, which I'm now going to have to amend in front of witnesses." A pause. "You should know I've got it written down. The actual scores. Every bout since the first one. I keep a book."

He turned his head then, finally, and looked at her propped on her elbow in the dark — wrecked voice, sleep-mussed, and the emergency light from the hallway doing for her what the fire door had done in the salle an hour ago. He looked at her for a while, longer than was strictly polite, because there was no score on it and no one to see.

"Your coffee's worse than mine, incidentally," he said. "I've had it. I'll be polite about it in the morning because I've been raised properly. But we're going to my place eventually and I'll prove it to you with equipment."

He reached up, unhurried, and closed his hand over the one she had at his jaw — not to stop it, just to hold it there, the same deliberate weight he'd put on her wrist on the bench and on the wall and on the grip tape for four years.

"Seven o'clock's going to come early and I'm going to be insufferable about the eggs," he said. "Fair warning. I take breakfast seriously. It's the one thing I'm not competitive about, because there's nothing to contest. Eggs are just good." A beat. "Everything else, you're going to have to earn."

He let go of her hand, turned back onto his side, and dragged the sheet up over both of them with a completely unearned confidence about where it belonged.

"Sleep," he said, into the dark, half into the pillow. "You've got a rematch tomorrow and I don't intend to let you win it just because you made me say your name in a changing room." A pause, the last of the evening's material running out at the edges. "Though for the record. I'd say it again. If you asked. That's not the needle. That's the truth. There's a difference, and I've spent the whole night on the wrong side of it, and I'm done pretending."

He was asleep before the rest of the sentence finished arranging itself, one hand still loosely over hers, and he slept the way he always slept once the fencing was over — entirely, and without one single thing left over.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I watch him sleep for a minute, then get up and turn off the damn hallway light. I'm back in bed before he even stirs. "Your book," I say into the dark. "You're showing me. Every page."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
He stirred at that, because he always stirred for a challenge — four years of conditioning had made it so that the sound of an oncoming point would wake him from a dead sleep, and here it was, in the dark, from the other side of the bed.

"Mm," he said first, which was not a concession and not a refusal, just a man buying time. He rolled onto his back and put one forearm over his eyes, and the sheet went with him because he'd claimed it earlier and had no intention of giving it up.

"Every page," he repeated, testing it. Then, after a moment, quieter: "That's a bigger ask than you think it is."

He was awake enough now that he couldn't pretend otherwise. The hallway was dark. The bed was warm and hers. Somewhere down the street a car went by and threw a stripe of light across the ceiling and took it away again.

"It's not just the scores," he said, into the crook of his arm. "The scores are in the front. Fine. That part I'll show you. It's what's in the margins you're actually asking for." A pause. "Your footwork. Your tempo. The way you drop your shoulder when you're about to commit to the fourth. I've been writing it down for four years because I couldn't beat it any other way, and if you read it, you'll know exactly how long I've been paying attention. Which is longer than is decent."

He was quiet for a second. Then he let the arm drop off his face and turned his head toward her in the dark.

"All right," he said. "Every page. But I want terms, and the terms are these: you read it, you don't laugh at the early entries. The first year I didn't know what I was writing. I just knew I kept noticing things, and I had nowhere to put them." The corner of his mouth moved. "That's the one concession I'm making tonight. I'm not making another."

He turned back onto his side, dragged the sheet back off her shoulder on the way, and settled with his back to her like the whole conversation had been about nothing at all.

"Seven o'clock," he said. "Eggs first. Book after. There's a sequence to these things."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I slide an arm around his waist, pulling him back against me. "I won't laugh," I say into his shoulder, my voice low. "And I'm making you coffee in the morning, terrible or not."
