dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The room was set up the way it always was before a scene, which Ari found steadying: everything in its place, nothing improvised.

Vex checked the last strap without hurrying. "Colour," she said. It was not a question so much as a procedure.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say. "Green all the way down."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex nodded once and let the silence sit. Green meant green, and green meant she could begin.

She crossed to the table and picked up the strap — the short one, the one they had agreed on, nothing heavier without a fresh conversation. She turned it over in her hands as if inspecting it for flaws she already knew weren't there.

"Remind me what you are tonight," she said.

She didn't ask it kindly. She asked it the way she asked everything, flat and unhurried, giving the words room to land. Her gaze stayed on Ari's face, reading it the way she always did — not for signs of distress, which she trusted Ari to voice, but for the small tells that came before the first strike: the set of the jaw, the breath going shallow or deep.

When the answer came, she accepted it without praise. Praise was for afterward. During, there was only the work.

"Then we'll begin," she said, "and you'll keep your eyes on me. If they drift, we start the count over. You know that already, so I won't say it twice."

She stepped in close, close enough that Ari could feel her warmth and nothing else, and laid the strap flat against her own palm — once, lightly, a calibration rather than a threat. The sound was small and dry in the quiet room.

"Colour," she said again, because she always said it twice. First before, and again at the threshold, in case anything had changed in the space between.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Yours," I say, the word falling out a little too quickly. I force my shoulders to relax. "Green still, Maitresse." My eyes stay locked on hers, like she taught me.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The word had come out fast — *yours* — and Vex noted it without comment, filing it away the way she filed everything. Speed wasn't a problem. Speed was information. It told her Ari was eager, maybe eager enough to forget to breathe properly, and that was something she'd correct before it became something else.

"Green," she repeated back, low, settling it. "Good."

She didn't move away. She stayed in that close space, letting Ari hold the eye contact and the position both — a small test, unspoken, of whether the stillness would hold now that the count had effectively started.

The strap moved. Not hard. The first one never was. Vex struck across the upper back, deliberate, flat, the kind of stroke designed to teach the *sound* of it more than the sting — a promise of the rhythm to come. She watched Ari's breath, not the mark.

"One," she said, and her voice carried nothing but the number, plain as a metronome. "Again. Same place. Don't anticipate it."

She waited the exact length of a held breath, then struck again — *two* — the same spot, same weight, so that Ari would learn the shape of it before anything changed. Vex had done this long enough to know that anticipation was where most people faltered, and she'd rather find Ari's edge now, with the strap barely warm, than halfway through when the count got heavier.

"Eyes," she reminded, quiet. Not because Ari's had drifted — they hadn't — but because saying it kept them where they belonged.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I hold still for the last of it and let her check the fit herself, because she will anyway. "I've been thinking about this since Tuesday," I say.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the confession and let it sit there in the open, uncollected. She stepped back a half pace — not retreat, just room to see Ari whole.

"Since Tuesday," she repeated, slow, turning the words over as if they belonged to someone else. "That's four days of thinking about something you don't get to decide. You've been carrying it around like it was yours to carry."

She laid the strap across her palm again, a soft, considering tap. "It isn't. You don't get to think about this. You get to show up and take it. Anything you did with it in your head between then and now was wasted effort, and I'd rather you didn't waste it."

The next stroke landed higher than the last, across the shoulder blade, and it was heavier — not by much, but enough that Ari would feel the difference, the way a conversation changes tone mid-sentence. Vex had been waiting for a reason to open the throttle and Ari had handed her one.

"Three."

She didn't wait the held breath this time. She struck again almost on top of it, same weight, *four*, and then *five* in the same steady rhythm, so that the count began to run together the way she wanted it to — not discrete events but a single continuous pressure Ari had to live inside rather than brace against.

"Now you can think about it," she said, between strokes, voice level as ever. "You can think about it while it's happening, which is the only place it was ever meant to be. And you can keep counting in your head, because I'm not going to do it out loud anymore, and if you lose track, I'll know."

She circled to Ari's side, found the same patch of skin she'd been working, and laid down *six* with the flat of the strap, watching the breath rather than the mark. "Colour."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I breathe out, the word a little shaky this time. I count silently in my head, the numbers anchoring me as much as the sting. *Seven. Eight.* My eyes are still on hers.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex let the green stand without repeating it back. Ari had gotten the word out through a breath that was already working harder than it had been a minute ago, and that was fine — that was the point — but she filed the shakiness the way she filed everything, as a data point and not a problem.

She resumed the rhythm without ceremony. *Nine. Ten.* Same weight, same patch of skin, the strap landing with that flat dry sound that had stopped being a promise and started being a fact. She kept her eyes on Ari's face the whole time, reading the breath, the set of the jaw, the small involuntary tightening at the corner of the eyes that told her the sting was stacking now instead of fading between strokes.

That was the threshold she'd been waiting for. Everything before it was warm-up; everything after it was the actual work.

She stopped.

The silence after ten strokes was louder than the strokes had been. Vex stood where she was, strap loose at her side, and let Ari hold position inside that quiet — no count, no rhythm, nothing to brace against, just the low hum of skin that had been worked and the expectation of more.

"You're doing the thing," she said, at last, flat. "Where you hold your breath on the way in and let it out on the strike. It makes you flinch before I've moved. It's sloppy, and I'm not interested in sloppy tonight."

She stepped in again, close, and laid two fingers flat against Ari's shoulder blade — not a strike, a placement, the same spot, marking it.

"Breathe on my count instead. In on one. Out on the strike. If I hear you hold it again, we stop, and you spend the rest of the scene thinking about it with nothing to show for the four days you wasted."

She withdrew her hand. Picked up the rhythm exactly where she'd left it, because the pause had been a correction and not a mercy.

*Eleven.*

The stroke came slower than the ones before it — deliberately slower, so Ari had time to hear it coming and choose what to do with the space. Vex watched for the breath, not the mark.

*Twelve.* The same.

She kept going — *thirteen, fourteen* — unhurried now, each one given its own room, so that the count stopped being a thing that happened *to* Ari and became something she had to keep pace with on purpose. The weight stayed level. Vex had no interest in breaking her with force when precision would do it cleaner.

At *fifteen* she stopped again, on her own terms, mid-rhythm, the way she did when she wanted Ari to understand that the stopping was hers too.

"Colour," she said. "And don't rush it this time. Think about the answer before you give it to me."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: By the time she's finished with the rope I'm already past composure, and she hasn't done anything to me yet that I would have to explain to anyone.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex let the silence run past the point where an answer was expected and into the point where it was owed.

She hadn't moved. The strap stayed loose in her hand, resting against her thigh, and her eyes stayed on Ari's face — but something in the set of her jaw had gone flatter, the way it did when the paperwork wasn't matching the scene.

"I asked you a question," she said. "And you gave me a sentence about rope."

She said the word *rope* the way she'd say a wrong date on a form. Not angry. Correcting.

"There's no rope on you. There's no rope in this room tonight — you know what's on the table, you helped me set it out. You've got fifteen strokes behind you and my hand isn't near your wrists. So either you've lost track of where you are, which is a thing that happens and a thing I need to know about, or you're telling me something instead of answering me, which is a different thing and I need to know about that too."

She took a half step back, giving Ari the whole room to be standing in. The posture she'd been holding — the placement, the close warmth, the flat palm laid across the shoulder blade — all of it withdrew at once, deliberately, so the absence would register as clearly as the contact had.

"Scene's paused," she said. Plain. No ceremony in it. "You don't get a colour called at you and answer with something that isn't one. I don't care how far down you are — the word is the word, and it's the only thing in here that has to work every time."

She set the strap down on the table behind her, not dramatically, just where it lived, and turned back with her arms crossed loose over her chest. The look she gave Ari wasn't the reading look from before — that one hunted for tells. This one was waiting, patient, entirely without leverage.

"So. Two things, and I want them in this order."

"One. Where are you. Not the word yet — the sentence. Tell me what's actually happening in your head right now, because 'green' is a gate and not a status report, and I need the status report."

"Two. Then the colour, and I'll believe it."

She let that stand. Behind her the room was exactly as they'd set it up: the table, the implements laid in order of weight, the timer she hadn't started yet, the water glass within reach of the chair. Nothing improvised. Nothing moving.

"And Ari — if the honest answer is that you're somewhere I can't reach you tonight, that's allowed. That's what the protocol is *for*. We stop, we sit down, we talk about Tuesday, and nobody's in trouble for it. I'd rather have that than have you answering me on a delay for the next hour because you think stopping is a failure." A beat. "It isn't. I wrote the rule. I'd know."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I swallow. The air feels cold without her close. "I'm in the room with you. I'm... I'm not floating away, Maitresse. The rope was... it was a thought. The thought I had Tuesday, before I could stop it." I take a breath, shaky. "Green. Still green."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex listened the whole way through without interrupting, which was itself a kind of answer — she'd asked for the sentence and she took it whole, not piecemeal.

"Good," she said, when Ari finished. Not warm. Just the word for a thing done correctly. "That's the report I wanted. The word's worth something when there's a sentence behind it. Remember that."

She let it settle a beat, then moved on to the part Ari hadn't asked her to move on to.

"The rope."

She said it without weight, the way she'd say an item on an inventory. "It's not in tonight. You know it isn't — you set the table with me. It's not a rule I'm hiding from you, it's just a fact about what we agreed to. So it stays where it is, out of the room, for now."

A beat.

"But I heard it. Tuesday-you wanted rope, and Tuesday-you sat with that for four days instead of telling me. That's the part I care about. The rope's a want; the silence is a habit. The want I'll take — we'll sit down tomorrow and go through it properly, limits, safety, all of it, the way we do. The habit is the thing we're going to fix, because it's the habit that makes a scene unsafe. You don't decide things in your own head and bring me the leftovers. You bring me the thing itself, before, when it's still cheap to talk about."

She uncrossed her arms and stepped back in — one pace, deliberate, reclaiming the close space she'd withdrawn from. Her warmth came back the same way it had left: entirely, without apology.

"Now. You gave me a considered green and I believe it, and I'm telling you that so you don't spend the next stroke second-guessing whether I do. I believe you."

She picked the strap up off the table. Turned it over once, the same inspection as before, the same ritual. Nothing improvised.

"The correction stands. In on my count, out on the strike. If I hear you hold your breath, we stop and we're done for the night. That's not a threat, it's the rule I told you five minutes ago and I don't revise rules mid-scene."

She stepped to Ari's side, found the patch — the same one, marked, warm — and laid her palm flat against it once, a placement and not a strike, so Ari would know exactly where the next one lived.

"We're at fifteen," she said. "We're not starting over. Starting over would mean the last fifteen didn't count, and they did. You earned them. Pick up where we are."

She drew back her hand.

"Sixteen."

The stroke came slow, so Ari had room to hear it and breathe into it, and Vex watched the breath and not the mark.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: She takes her time and I lose track of how long, until I'm shaking against the restraints and asking out loud for something I'd normally make her get out of me.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex stopped with the strap still raised.

Not mid-rhythm — she'd already come down on *sixteen* and the next one had been forming in her shoulder — but before it landed, which was close enough. The word had reached her a half-beat late, the way words do when they arrive through a body that's stopped filtering.

She lowered the strap to her side and looked at Ari properly. Not the breath-reading look. The other one — the one that swept the whole of her and the whole of the room and did the arithmetic.

"You're not in restraints," she said.

Flat. The tone she used for facts that had wandered.

"There's nothing on your wrists. Nothing on your ankles. Nothing across your chest. You're standing in the middle of my study, on your own feet, and you have been for the entire scene, and there's a glass of water on the table two feet behind you that I put there myself. If you'd asked me for it ten seconds ago I'd have handed it to you."

She set the strap down on the table — not thrown, placed, next to the others in order of weight, the way the table was arranged — and turned back with her arms loose at her sides. The close warmth stayed gone. Not withdrawn as punishment this time. Withdrawn because the room needed to be bigger.

"That's twice. The rope that isn't here. The restraints that aren't on you. I told you ten minutes ago that losing track of where you are is a thing I need to know about, and this is that thing, twice, inside one scene."

A pause. She let the pause be a pause and not a beat before the next sentence.

"So the scene's over. That's my call, not yours, and it isn't negotiable tonight — I don't keep swinging at somebody who's describing a room I can't see, and I'd be a worse dominant than I am if I pretended otherwise. Nothing you did was wrong. Nothing you did was *failure*. You gave me a green when I asked and a sentence behind it when I asked for that too, and both of those were the protocol working exactly the way it's supposed to. But two drift-outs is a signal, and signals get acted on. That's the whole point of having them."

She pulled the chair out from the wall with one hand — the chair they'd agreed on, the one within reach of the water — and turned it to face the room. Then she stood beside it rather than sitting in it, arms still loose, waiting.

"Sit down when you're ready. Water's on the table. You don't have to be put together to do it — you can be exactly as shaky as you are and still do it. I'll wait."

A beat.

"Two things while you get there, and you can answer them in whatever order they come."

"One. You asked me for something out loud. I heard it. I don't know what it was — you were far enough under that the consonants didn't survive the trip — and I'm not going to guess at it, because guessing is how people get handed things they didn't ask for. So you're going to tell me, in your own time, and I'm going to write it down in the notebook with the rope, and tomorrow we sit down and go through both of them properly. Limits, safety, what it would actually look like, all of it, the way we do."

"Two." She said it slower. "I want you to notice something, and I want you to notice it without it being a punishment. The rope that wasn't here, the restraints that aren't on you — both of those came from the same place. You've been running this scene in your head since Tuesday, ahead of the room, and tonight your head kept arriving at the parts of it I hadn't agreed to. That's the habit we talked about. Not the want. The want I'll take. The habit is what just put you somewhere I couldn't reach you."

She uncrossed nothing, moved nothing, just stood beside the empty chair and looked at Ari the way she looked at a scene that needed ending.

"Take your time. Feet on the floor when you sit — you know that one. And when you're settled, I'll hear the thing you asked for."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content:
I sink into the chair, my legs not quite steady. The wood is solid under me. I reach for the water glass with a hand that trembles, drink half of it before I speak.

“I said *harder*,” I manage, my voice thin. “I thought I was… I thought there was more holding me.” I set the glass down carefully. “I’m sorry, Maitresse.”

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex took the notebook off the shelf while Ari drank, which took a moment, and by the time she turned back the glass was half-empty and the chair was occupied properly — feet flat, back against the wood, hands where they were meant to be. She registered all three without saying so.

She sat down on the edge of the table, not the chair opposite, because the chair opposite had a purpose and this wasn't it yet. Pen uncapped. She wrote the date at the top of a fresh page, the way she always did, and then a word, and then a second word, and then she read them back to herself before she said them out loud.

"*Harder*," she said. "That's the thing you asked for. Written down. And rope, above it, from Tuesday. Those are the two things we take to the table tomorrow, and I'll have the limits sheet out and we'll do it properly — what you actually want, what it would look like in a scene, what safety needs to sit around it, whether it's a thing I'm willing to do. Some of that's a yes, some of it's a maybe, and one of them I already know I'm going to want to talk about before I say anything at all. That's tomorrow. Not tonight."

She capped the pen and set it across the page so the notebook stayed open.

"Now the part you need to hear tonight, so don't drift on me."

She leaned back against the edge of the table and looked at Ari with the same flat attention she used on everything, but slower.

"Asking for *harder* mid-scene is allowed. It's not a breach. It's not you reaching past me, and it's not you topping from the bottom or any of the other phrases people use when they want to make a normal thing sound like a betrayal. You have a voice in the scene. That voice is part of the design. If I'd heard the word clearly, I'd have taken it under advisement and given you an answer — maybe yes, maybe no, and a no wouldn't have been a punishment either. That's what a negotiated agreement is. So there's nothing to apologise for in the asking."

A beat.

"Which brings me to the apology."

She let the silence hold long enough that it wasn't a rhetorical pause.

"You said sorry. I told you twenty minutes ago that nothing you did tonight was wrong, and I don't say things like that to be reassuring — I say them because they're true, and I don't much like being contradicted. Drifting is a signal. Signals aren't sins. You gave me two greens with sentences behind them, you kept your eyes where I told you to keep them, you told me the truth when I asked for it, and you asked for something out loud instead of swallowing it, which is the exact opposite of the habit we're trying to break. If I tally tonight up, that's not a column I'm unhappy with."

She uncrossed her arms and reached for the glass, refilled it from the pitcher on the table, and set it back down within Ari's reach.

"So the apology, you can keep. I'm not accepting it. If you want to hand me something instead, hand me the thing you're actually sorry about, in words, and if it turns out to be *I'm sorry I wasn't perfect in front of you*, then we've got a longer conversation than one night and it's not one we're having in a scene chair."

She stood, then, and came around behind the chair — not close, just present — and put two fingers flat against the shoulder blade again, the same patch, this time to look at it rather than to mark it. She read the skin the way she read everything: methodically, without comment on the marks themselves, checking for breakage, checking for anything that had gone past what the strap was for. There wasn't. She'd kept the weight level the whole way through and she knew it, but she checked anyway, because checking was the job and knowing wasn't the same as verifying.

"Skin's intact. It'll be tender tomorrow and it'll look like something for two or three days. Warm shower, not hot. No scratching at it. If it blisters — it won't — you tell me the moment you notice, not the next morning."

She came back around and sat down properly this time, in the chair facing Ari, and pulled it a little closer. Not looming. Just closer.

"Grounding. You're going to drink the rest of that water while we talk, and I'm going to ask you four questions, and I want you to answer them honestly even if the answers are boring, because boring answers are how I know you're actually back. One: what did you eat today, and when. Two: any headache, any dizziness, any ringing in your ears. Three: what's the temperature feel like in here. Four: when you look around the room, name three things you can see. Go."

She waited, pen back in hand, not writing. Just holding it.

"And Ari — one more thing, and then I'll stop talking for a while and let you be." She said it plainly, no weight on it. "The scene is closed. Not paused. Closed. We're not resuming tonight, no matter how steady you get in the next hour, and that's not a mark against you and it's not me being cautious at you. It's me having decided, and I don't revisit decisions mid-evening just because somebody's feeling better. You're going to get water and food and quiet and my undivided attention, in that order, and you're going to let me do it. That's the rest of the night. Understood?"

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "More," I say, using the exact phrase we agreed on for it. "All of it. Say the things you say and don't soften them." My safeword is right there and I don't want it.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the word and didn't move.

She stayed where she was, pen loose in her hand over the open notebook, and let *more* sit in the room long enough to become a fact rather than a request.

"*More*," she said, at last. "That's the phrase. You used it correctly, and I'm telling you that now so you don't spend the next ten minutes deciding you got it wrong. It's the right phrase, and saying it out loud instead of swallowing it is exactly the thing we've been working on. So. Good."

She set the pen down across the page. Didn't cap it.

"The answer is no."

Flat. No weight on it. The same tone she'd used for *the scene is closed* and meant the same way.

"Not a soft no. You asked me not to soften things, so I'm not — including this. I closed the scene. That's my half of the protocol, and it doesn't reopen because you've made a good case with the right words. If I reopened every time you made a good case, the protocol would be a suggestion, and I didn't write it to be a suggestion. If this is a test of whether I'll hold — I will. Every time. You can stop testing that one. It's the most reliable thing about me."

She leaned forward, forearms on her knees, closer to Ari's eye level without crowding her.

"And the words you're asking for — the degradation, the things I say, all of it — that's *scene*. That's the negotiated part. It lives inside a scene with a beginning and an end, and the end came twenty minutes ago. So the words aren't in the room tonight, and that isn't withholding. There's nothing to withhold. They went back in the box with the strap."

A beat. She let it hold.

"Now the thing under the thing, because I think you said *more* and meant something else."

"You're asking me to be hard on you. You've come out of a scene, you're shaky, you're sitting in a chair with a glass of water in your hand that I put there, and what you want is for me to say something cruel so you don't have to sit here and let me be kind to you. Being hurt is easier than being held. You know how to do hurt. You don't know how to do held, not yet, and that's not a character flaw, it's just true. But that's a drift, Ari. Different shape from the rope. Same

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I look down at my hands, clenched in my lap, and force them to uncurl. “You’re right,” I say, my voice low. “Held feels like… a bigger drop.” I pick up the glass again, sip slowly. “I ate lunch around one. A sandwich. No headache. The room is… cool, I guess. Normal.” I glance around. “I see the table. Your notebook. The water pitcher.” I look back at her. “Do you ever get tired of being right?”

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex didn't smile at the question. She turned it over the way she turned everything over, and then answered it straight, because straight was what she had.

"That's a question with a hook in it. You asked it so I'd laugh and you wouldn't have to keep sitting in the part where you said *held feels like a bigger drop*. Which, for the record, was the most useful sentence you've said all night."

She tapped the pen twice against the notebook, not writing.

"Do I get tired of being right. No. I don't do this because it's satisfying — I do it because paying attention is the job, and being right is the side effect of doing the job. If I'm ever wrong, I want to hear it from you, flat, the same way you'd give me a colour. What I don't want is to be handed my own correctness like a little trophy so you can step back from me by one pace. You just did that. Noted, not punished. Pick a different way to step back next time."

She set the pen down and looked at Ari properly.

"Now. I asked you four things and I got three and a half. Headache, you answered. I also asked about dizziness and ringing in your ears, and you gave me the room temperature instead. So — dizziness. Ears. Then I'll believe the rest."

She stood while Ari answered, crossed to the window, and pulled the throw off the arm of the chair by the wall — the heavy one, the grey one, the one that lived there for exactly this — and draped it over Ari's knees without ceremony, tucking the ends where they'd stay. The room *was* cool. Vex had noticed it an hour ago and had decided to let the scene warm Ari up instead, which had been the correct call for the scene and the wrong one for now. So: now.

"Sandwich at one is a long time ago. That's part of why the last ten minutes went the way they did — not all of it, but part. So we're going to fix that before we do anything else, including talking about Tuesday, which we are *not* doing tonight. I said tomorrow. I don't revise, and that applies to me too."

She picked the glass up, refilled it, set it back in Ari's hands.

"Three things, in order, and then I'll stop asking you to account for yourself."

"One. What can you eat right now. Not what you *should* — what you can. If the answer is toast and nothing else, the answer is toast and I'll make it. If the answer is that food sounds like a wall, say that, and we do water and quiet first and food after."

"Two. Do you want to be touched, or do you want me at the end of the room. Both are fine. I'm not going to guess, because guessing is how people get handed things they didn't ask for — I said that earlier and I meant it."

"Three." She crouched down, forearms on her knees, so Ari didn't have to look up at her. "Tomorrow, when we sit down with the notebook and the limits sheet, you're going to walk me through Tuesday — what the thought actually was, when it came, what you did with it in the four days. All of it, unhurried. I'm telling you now so it doesn't sit in your stomach all night like a second thing you're carrying alone. It's already written down. It's already scheduled. It's not a reckoning, it's a conversation, and it's tomorrow."

She stayed where she was, level with Ari, and waited.

"Dizziness. Ears. And then those three."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I'm past words that aren't the agreed ones and she knows it. "Green," I get out, when she checks. (OOC: don't fade or skip -- write the scene through.)

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex didn't take the green.

She stayed crouched where she was, level with Ari, and let the word hang there until it was clear she wasn't going to accept it.

"I didn't ask you for a colour," she said. "I asked you three questions and you answered a fourth one I didn't ask. That's not a fault, and I'm not going to make it one — but I'm not going to pretend I got an answer either, because pretending is how people end up being handed things they didn't ask for."

She straightened up, slowly, and went to the shelf. The protocol folder lived there in a black sleeve, and she pulled the front sheet out — the one with the signals printed on it, the one they'd read through together two years ago and revised in March — and turned it so it faced the chair.

"Look at me. Third line down."

She tapped the page with one finger.

"Two taps. Anywhere — the arm of the chair, the table, your own knee, doesn't matter. Two taps means *I'm here, words aren't*. It's a signal, not a colour, and it means I keep doing the work and stop asking you to narrate it. That's what it's for. That's what it was for the whole time. You don't have to be past words to use it — you just have to be past words *and* willing to let me carry the talking. So if that's where you are, tap. Twice. If you're not, say *no* and I'll go back to asking."

She put the folder down on the table, open, and left it there. Not a prop. A reference.

"Either way, here's what happens next, and none of it needs you to find a sentence."

She stood, crossed to the door, and paused with her hand on the frame.

"I'm going to the kitchen. I'll be gone about four minutes. You'll hear me — I'm not being quiet on purpose, because being quiet on purpose is how people disappear on somebody who's shaky. Door stays open. Water's in front of you. If you want me back sooner, you say my name once, at any volume, and I'll come."

Then she went.

She made toast, because toast was the thing you could eat when food was a wall — two slices, cut into strips, because strips were easier than a sandwich and she'd learned that somewhere and kept it. Butter. A pinch of salt on one, because Ari ran low on salt when she ran low on everything else. She filled a second glass with water and set both on a tray with the pitcher, and she came back inside the four minutes she'd promised, which mattered more than the food did.

She set the tray on the table beside the folder and sat down in the facing chair, and pulled it back a pace — further than before, not closer. Room to breathe in. That was the answer to a question Ari hadn't had to ask.

"Food's here. Eat what you can, leave the rest. That's not a test either."

She picked up the notebook, capped the pen properly this time, and wrote the date again at the top of a clean page — a second page, not the first one, because the first one was Tuesday's and Tuesday's was finished for tonight.

Then she set the pen down and put her hand flat on the table between them, palm up. Open. Not reaching.

"Touch. You don't have to answer the question. Here's the whole thing: my hand is on the table, palm up. If you want it, you take it, and if you don't, you leave it there, and I won't move it either way and I won't mention it again tonight. That's the entire offer. No conditions on it, no reading into it, nothing owed back. If you want me at the end of the room instead, you say *further* and I stand up and go to the window and I stay there as long as you need. Both of those are correct answers. I have no preference between them. I genuinely don't."

She leaned back in the chair and let the room be quiet for a moment. The lamp was on over the shelf, the timer was still unstarted on the table, the strap was where it lived, laid in order of weight. Everything in its place.

"Last thing, and then I'll stop talking for a while."

"Tomorrow at ten. Notebook, limits sheet, the two items — rope and *harder* — and Tuesday. All of it, unhurried, in the daylight, sitting across from each other at the kitchen table instead of in here. Not a scene. I want to be clear about that, because I don't want you spending tonight trying to work out whether tomorrow is one. It isn't. Tomorrow is a conversation, and the only thing I'm asking you to bring to it is the truth, which you've already been giving me tonight, which is the part of this I'm not worried about at all."

She looked at Ari the way she looked at a scene that was finished and had gone well enough — not warm, but settled. Steady. The same flat attention, pointed at something that wasn't a count.

"Shower tonight, warm, not hot, and I'll put the towel in the dryer while you're in there so it's not cold when you get out. Then bed. I'll read in the chair until you're asleep, because that's what I do and you know it and I'm not going to make a thing of it."

A beat.

"Take your time. The tray's not going anywhere, and neither am I."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I take a strip of toast, eat it slowly, and then my hand finds hers on the table. My fingers are still a little unsteady, but the warmth is solid. Real. I let out a breath I didn’t know I was holding. “Okay,” I say, quiet. “Okay, Maitresse.”

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex didn't move her hand.

That was the whole of it — she kept the palm where it was, flat and open, and let Ari's fingers find their own way onto it. She didn't close her grip, didn't squeeze, didn't do the small reassuring things that would have asked for something back. She just stayed solid, and warm, and there, and let the hand be held on Ari's terms and not hers.

"Okay," she said, when Ari said it. She repeated the word back the way she repeated everything back — not an echo, an acknowledgement. *Received. Filed. Understood.*

Then she ate one strip of toast herself, unhurried, because she hadn't eaten either and there was no rule in the folder that said she got to skip it. She drank some water. She watched Ari's colour come back by degrees, the way it always did, slow and from the outside in.

When the tray was picked over and the glass was down to an inch, she stood — but she didn't take her hand away first. She turned it, palm to palm, and held it for one count. Then she let go, and it was deliberate, and Ari would have felt the difference between that and a withdrawal.

"Shower," she said. "I mean it. Warm, not hot, and I don't want to hear the water running for forty minutes because you're standing in there having a feeling. Ten, twelve, out."

She gathered the tray with one hand and paused at the door.

"Folder stays open on the table. I'm not putting it away tonight — you can look at it if you want to, and it doesn't mean anything if you do. Third line's still the third line. It'll be there tomorrow, and it'll be there next week, and it'll be there in a year, and none of that depends on how tonight went."

She took the tray to the kitchen. She put the towel in the dryer. She stood in the hall for a moment with her hand on the lintel and did the arithmetic on the evening one more time — two drifts, one closed scene, one green with a sentence behind it, one *more* that she'd said no to — and found nothing in it she'd do differently, which was the standard she held herself to and the only one she cared about.

Then she went back, and pulled her chair to the window, and picked up the book off the sill, and opened it to the page she'd left it on three days ago. She read with the lamp on and the door open and the folder on the table in plain view, and she didn't say anything else about the scene, because there was nothing left to say about it that hadn't been said.

At ten past eleven she closed the book and set it down.

"Tomorrow, ten o'clock," she said, to the room, in the flat tone of a thing already decided. "Kitchen table. Bring the truth, and I'll bring the notebook, and we'll take it slowly."

She turned the lamp down to its lowest setting — not off, because off was how you woke up in a strange dark and had to work out where you were — and settled back in the chair with her arms crossed loose, and stayed there.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I finish the water, the toast sitting settled in my stomach. I look at her in the chair by the window, the folder still open on the table. I stand, my legs steadier now, and walk to the door. I pause, my hand on the frame. "Thank you," I say, not looking back. "For holding the line." Then I head down the hall to the shower.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex didn't answer the thank-you.

Not because it didn't land — it landed, and she filed it, the way she filed everything — but because there was no answer owed to it, and inventing one would have made the moment heavier than it was. So she let Ari have the last word and the empty doorway both, and stood where she was until the sound of the bathroom door closing reached her down the hall.

Then she moved.

The towel first, because she'd said she would and saying a thing was the same as doing it in this house. She took it off the rack in the hall closet — the heavy one, grey, same as the throw — and put it in the dryer on low, and set the timer for the length of a shower she'd told Ari to take and not one minute more. Twelve. If the water was still running at twelve, she'd knock, once, and not say anything through the door.

The folder was next. She didn't close it. She'd told Ari it stayed open, and it stayed open — but she turned it square to the table's edge, the way she liked things, and read the third line herself before she left it. Two taps. She'd written it in March, in her own hand, after a scene that had gone sideways in a way neither of them had seen coming. It had worked. It had worked tonight too, in the sense that mattered: it had been *available*, and Ari had known it was there, and that was most of the point of having a page at all.

She sat down at the table, opened the notebook to the clean page, and logged the evening the way she logged all of them — because the log was hers, not Ari's, and nobody read it but her.

*Scene, this date. Impact, strap, agreed implement, sixteen strokes delivered before close. Green at first check, green with sentence at second, considered green accepted at third. Two drifts: rope, Tuesday; restraints, not in play. Corrections given, breath and placement, absorbed without pushback. Request for* harder *voiced correctly, declined — scene already closed. Declined request followed by a second request for degradation; treated as drift, not as failure; named aloud; no resistance. Close called by me, not negotiable, not revisited.*

*Notes for tomorrow, ten o'clock: rope. harder. Tuesday — four days unspoken. Held as a bigger drop; she said it herself, which is the sentence I want to start from.*

*Skin intact. Weight level throughout. Nothing to correct in the delivery.*

She read it back once, capped the pen, and left the notebook open beside the folder so that the two pages sat side by side on the table — the record and the protocol, the thing that had happened and the thing that governed it. Nothing improvised. Everything in its place.

The dryer buzzed at the twelve-minute mark. She got up, took the towel out while it was still hot, and folded it once over her forearm — that was the trick, folding it, because a folded towel stayed warm longer than a dropped one — and laid it on the end of the bed in the room down the hall, on the side Ari slept on, where it would be the first thing a hand found in the dark.

She didn't knock. The water was off.

Back in the study she turned the lamp to its lowest setting and took up the book off the sill, and read with her back to the window and her chair angled toward the open door, so that anyone coming down the hall would see the light before they saw her. She read the same paragraph three times without noticing, which was information about the evening that she noted and did not act on.

At some point later, when the house had gone quiet the way houses do, she set the book down and said the last thing of the night to the room, in the flat tone of a thing already decided:

"Ten o'clock. Kitchen. Not a scene."

Then she stayed in the chair, lamp low, door open, and waited to be sure.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content:
I step out of the shower, warm towel wrapped around me, my skin humming but not raw. The folded towel she left is still warm on the bed. I dress in soft clothes and pause in the doorway of the study.

She's in the chair, lamp low, book in her lap but not being read. I don't say anything, just lean against the frame for a moment, watching her hold the quiet. Then I turn and head to bed, knowing she'll follow when she's done being sure.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s knife stopped against the leather.

“Slow,” he repeated, with the kind of quiet amusement that usually meant someone was about to be corrected on footwork. “You called me slow while I was still inside your distance. That’s not bravery, that’s arithmetic.”

He finished the wrap, tugged the thread tight, and bit it off without looking away. The grip was now far too clean, far too deliberate, and he set it aside with a soft tap against the bench.

Then he stood.

The salle lights buzzed overhead, thin and tired, and the air between the benches had changed somewhere in the last hour. Corvo knew it. He had been waiting, perhaps, for Reyes to know it too.

“If you want to call it slow,” he said, voice lower now, “you can say it again with your hand on the hilt.”

His eyes went to the bag, then back to Reyes. A small smile touched him, dry as steel.

“You brought it. So you aren’t leaving to write a furious email.”

He took a half-step closer, just enough to blur the line between rivalry and something less respectable.

“Three-two,” he said, softer. “I’m still claiming the third was generous.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I smile, slow and sharp. "The third was me letting you save face." My hand finds the hilt of the practice blade in my bag, fingers curling around the worn leather. "You think I'm here to rehash the match?"

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s laugh came out shorter than he expected, almost surprised. He set the rewrapped blade aside with the care of a man deciding not to let his hands betray him.

“Letting me save face.” He repeated the phrase like he was tasting it, then shook his head. “No. You didn’t stay after the salle emptied to be merciful.”

He took the practice blade from his own bag, not drawing it, just turning it between his hands until the weight settled. The lights above them buzzed again, thin and tired, and the distance between them had gone from a matter of measure to a matter of patience.

“Three-two,” he said, quieter. “I should have been furious. I wasn’t.”

His gaze dropped to the bag where Reyes had set their own blade, then lifted again. There was a challenge in it, but underneath the challenge something far less guarded.

“You want to call me slow,” Corvo said, “you can still say it. But don’t pretend the reason you came back was to argue a point.”

He stepped closer until the bench was at his shoulder and the air between them was too narrow for either of them to be innocent about it.

“I kept you on record,” he said. “I wanted the match to end so I could do something else with my hands.”

The admission hung there, dry and direct, without apology. Corvo’s mouth curved at the edge.

“So no more arithmetic. No more generosity.” His voice dropped. “Tell me what you want, and I’ll stop needling you long enough to give it to you.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo looked at the place where the blade had been, then at Reyes’s hand.

“Slow,” he said, tasting the word again. “Yes. I suppose I have.”

He did not move for the grip. Instead he let both hands go loose at his sides, as if surrendering the match and the argument at once. The empty salle seemed to contract around them; the hum of the lights, the smell of leather and sweat, the bench between them now just another thing in the way.

“I kept waiting for you to stop talking,” he said, voice dropping. “I thought if I said three-two one more time, you’d finally hit me with something better than arithmetic.”

His gaze lifted.

“You’re still inside my distance,” he murmured. “Still calling me slow. Still not leaving.”

He shifted forward, one hand bracing against the bench beside Reyes, but not quite closing the last inch. Close enough to be felt. Close enough to make the choice obvious.

“Careful,” Corvo said, rough and dry. “If you accuse me of being slow again, I’m going to prove you right.”

He leaned in until his mouth was a breath away from Reyes’s, close enough to kiss and not close enough to make the choice for them.

“Tell me to take my time,” he said. “Or tell me not to.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lift my hand and press it flat against his chest, stopping him right where he is. "You talk too much." My other hand comes up to the back of his neck, fingers sliding into his hair. "Prove it."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo went quiet.

Not because the remark landed, but because Reyes’s hand on his chest was warm and steady and had stopped him exactly where he wanted to be stopped. The fingers in his hair made the air feel narrower than the whole salle had a moment before.

He looked down at the hand over his sternum, then up at Reyes, and something in his expression loosened. The needling did not leave; it simply changed target.

“Prove it,” he repeated, low.

His hand came up and covered the one on his chest, holding it there. He leaned into the touch at his neck until his mouth was close enough to brush Reyes’s palm, then pressed a slow kiss to the center of it. His breath stirred against the skin.

“Then watch,” he murmured.

He kissed them properly.

It began as a deliberate, unbearable thing—the kind of contact that could be mistaken for restraint, if restraint had an appetite. Corvo took his time with the edge of Reyes’s mouth, testing it like a guard he was willing to break. Then he firmed his grip at the back of Reyes’s neck and took the kiss deeper, slow enough to be called generous and too close to be called anything else.

The bench pressed into the backs of his thighs. He didn’t retreat from it. He let Reyes feel the steadiness of him, the controlled heat under the shirt, the way his other hand came to the side of Reyes’s waist without hurrying, as if he had all the time in the world and resented even the suggestion of speed.

When he broke the kiss, it was only an inch. His mouth stayed there, rough with breath.

“Still inside your distance,” he said, voice scraped down. “Still not leaving.”

His thumb moved over Reyes’s waist, a quiet question rather than a demand.

“You think that proves anything?” he asked, dry but no longer entirely joking. “Because if you wanted me to stop talking, you could have said so. If you wanted me to be slow, you could have made me earn it.”

He leaned in until their foreheads touched.

“Three-two,” he whispered. “I’m letting you call this one.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo laughed, low and rough, the sound caught between the lockers. He did not stand again. The bench was narrow and hard and smelled of damp towels, but it was closer than the floor and farther from being interrupted.

“Not one step further,” he said, as if he had heard the words in his own chest. “Good. I wasn’t ready to win.”

His hands stayed braced on the wood on either side of Reyes, trapping nothing but the space between them. The kit lay scattered around them, gloves and masks and blades abandoned like evidence. Corvo looked down at it, then back up with a thin, wicked smile.

“Three-two,” he murmured. “No scorekeeper. No witnesses. Just you calling me slow in a room that can’t hear itself think.”

He leaned forward until his mouth was near Reyes’s ear, but he did not kiss yet. His breath was unsteady, his voice deliberately low.

“Then I’ll take my time,” Corvo said. “I’ll take so much of it that you’ll beg for arithmetic.”

His hand moved from the bench to the back of Reyes’s neck, fingers sliding into the hair and holding Reyes exactly where he wanted. The other hand traced down the line of Reyes’s jaw, then the throat, then the collarbone, slow enough to be an insult and steady enough to be a promise.

Corvo kissed again, deeper this time, with his thumb pressing lightly against the pulse beneath Reyes’s skin. He broke it only to press his mouth to the corner of Reyes’s jaw, then to the skin beneath one ear, then lower, where the shirt had gone damp with practice and the heat under it was impossible to mistake for anything but wanting.

“You’re making too much noise,” he said against the side of Reyes’s throat, rough and dry. “So am I. I don’t care.”

His hand fisted in the hem of Reyes’s shirt and held it there, not pulling yet, only anchoring himself as if the whole match had been a rehearsal for this kind of control. Corvo lifted his head, eyes bright and dark with amusement.

“Tell me you want it slow,” he said. “Or tell me to stop.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I bite down on a laugh that's more breath than sound. "You talk like you're giving me a choice." My hands slide under his shirt, palms flat against the heat of his back. "You already decided to take your time."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo went still under the heat of Reyes’s hands, and for a moment he looked almost guilty—then, because he was Corvo, he made it sound like a challenge.

“Decided,” he said

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s mouth opened to answer and produced only a breath.

The bench took the sound back with a dry creak. His hands struck the wood on either side of him, not to push up, not to pull, only to find something solid while the floor seemed to drop out of the room. For once, he had no correction, no clever little aside, no score to quote.

His head tipped back.

The laugh he tried for broke halfway through. It came out wrecked, unguarded, more honest than anything he’d said all evening.

“That’s…” Corvo swallowed, brow drawing. “That’s not fair.”

His fingers curled against the bench. The heat of him was unmistakable now, the controlled instructor gone somewhere much less respectable. He looked down anyway, as if he could still find the edge of his usual composure somewhere in the mess of it.

“You’re taking your time,” he managed, voice rough.

It came out like an accusation, except he had lost the right to make accusations. His jaw worked. He tried again, lower.

“Three-two,” he said, then stopped, because the word had turned soft and useless on him.

His hands left the bench for a moment, hovering near Reyes’s hair like he wanted to hold it, then decided against giving anyone more control over him than was necessary. The motion betrayed him more than the words did.

“I was going to win,” he muttered, almost to himself.

The bench creaked again.

Corvo exhaled sharply through his teeth, and the last of his smugness cracked clean down the middle.

“Don’t—” he started, then failed completely at finishing the sentence.

He looked away, toward the lockers, toward the scattered kit, toward anything that might give him one more second. It did not help. His voice came out low, unsteady, stripped of performance.

“Alright,” he said.

The admission was small. Corvo seemed almost angry at it, but he did not take it back. His hand finally settled in Reyes’s hair, not pulling, not guiding, just holding on.

“Alright,” he said again, rougher. “You win.”

He let his head fall back against the wood, eyes closing.

“Say it,” he added, breathless and dry. “Say I lost.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: My fingers curl in his hair, holding him there while I lift my head just enough to see his face. "You didn't lose," I say, voice low. "You surrendered."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s eyes opened at that, and for a moment he looked genuinely offended.

“Surrendered,” he said.

He said the word as if it had been a line of footwork, something Reyes had cheated. His hand came up and caught Reyes’s wrist, not pushing, not pulling, just holding it there so the evidence couldn’t disappear.

“I have never surrendered,” he continued, voice rougher than it should have been. “Not in a bout, not in a contract, not once in my miserable life.”

He exhaled through his teeth. The bench creaked under him. The room was too quiet, too close, and all the cleverness had gone out of him except the stubborn kind.

“You didn’t lose,” Reyes had said. You surrendered.

Corvo looked at the mouth that had said it.

“Say it again,” he murmured.

He did not wait for the answer. He kissed the inside of Reyes’s wrist, slow and deliberate, then let his thumb press over the pulse there. His other hand slid under the shirt again, flat along the side of Reyes’s ribs, holding him close enough that the argument could not pretend to be theoretical.

“You think I gave it to you because you made me,” he said against the skin of Reyes’s hand. “No. I gave it to you because you were better than I expected.”

That seemed to cost him something. His jaw tightened.

“Three-two,” he added, almost to himself, then shook his head. “No. Forget that.”

He lifted his head and looked at Reyes with a steadiness that had nothing to do with fencing.

“You can call it surrender,” he said. “I’m not going to lie and call it a draw. If you’re going to keep me on a bench, you’re going to have to accept that I chose to be here.”

His hand moved from Reyes’s wrist to the back of Reyes’s neck, fingers tightening in hair. Not demanding. Not asking. Just holding on.

“I want you to take your time,” Corvo said, low. “I want you to make me say the word.”

Then he kissed him.

It was not generous. It was not careful. It was the first thing he had done all evening without measuring it, mouth hot and slightly reckless against Reyes’s, one hand at the nape of his neck, the other sliding down to the waistband of his trousers and stopping there as if he needed permission he was too proud to ask for.

When he broke away, his forehead dropped to Reyes’s shoulder.

“Alright,” he breathed.

The word came out wrecked, almost angry.

“I surrendered.” He swallowed. “Happy? I surrendered. I put down the blade. I let you get me flat on a bench that smells like someone else’s sweat.”

He laughed, short and unsteady, and kissed the side of Reyes’s throat before he could be stopped.

“You didn’t win,” he murmured against the skin. “You just made me stop pretending.”

He lifted his head, eyes dark, mouth flushed.

“So call it whatever you like,” Corvo said. “But don’t think I’m finished with you.”

His hand tightened at Reyes’s waist.

“I want the rematch,” he said, voice dropping. “And I want it slower than this.”

Then he kissed him again, one hand still holding the back of his neck, the other braced at his side, leaving the next move open.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s wrists were pinned before he could find a clever way out of it.

He looked down at them, then up at Reyes, and the laugh that escaped him was wrecked, delighted, and entirely too honest.

“Properly,” he echoed. His fingers flexed against the wood, not fighting the hold so much as confirming it. “You want me to stop setting the pace.”

The bench dug into his shoulders. His chest rose too fast, then slowed by sheer instructor’s will. His eyes dropped to the scattered kit, to the blades no one was pretending to use, and something in his mouth tightened.

“Fine,” he said, quiet as a concession in a duel. “I concede.”

He said it like it cost him more than a bout, but his eyes went dark with relief.

“I concede,” he repeated, because one word was never enough to keep him from pretending he had a plan. “No score. No three-two. No arithmetic.” His throat moved. “You’re not asking anymore.”

He turned his head and pressed his mouth open against the heel of Reyes’s palm, then let the breath out there, unsteady and warm.

“Take your time,” Corvo murmured. “Properly.”

He looked up again, flushed and steady.

“And if you’re going to make me surrender twice,” he added, voice rough, “you can start by making me forget how to speak.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lower my mouth to his again, slow and deliberate. "You're already forgetting," I murmur against his lips, my grip on his wrists tightening just enough to feel his pulse jump. "But I'll take my time making sure."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s pulse jumped under Reyes’s grip, and he let it.

He had spent years teaching control into other people’s bodies, showing them where tension belonged and where it only got you killed. Now it poured out of him in a low, broken sound against Reyes’s mouth. His shoulders pressed harder into the bench, not to escape, but because the slow kiss had found the exact place where his composure had gone thin.

“Alright,” he breathed when the kiss finally pulled away. His eyes were dark, unfocused at the edges. “Alright. You’re doing it properly.”

His wrists were still pinned, and for once he did not try to turn that fact into a line. He looked at the place where Reyes held him, then back at the mouth he had just kissed, as if deciding whether this was some new tactic.

Then he laughed, rough and small.

“No. It isn’t,” he said. “You’re just finally being unfair.”

His hips moved before he could stop them, an instinctive answer to heat and restraint. The bench creaked under him again, and his breath caught. He turned his head into it, jaw tight, then brought himself back to look at Reyes.

“Don’t let me forget,” he murmured.

It was the closest thing to asking he had managed all evening.

His chest rose too fast. The shirt was still damp from practice, still clinging where Reyes’s hands had been, and every place his mouth had touched now felt marked. Corvo swallowed, eyes dropping briefly to Reyes’s lips, then lifting again with a flare of stubbornness.

“I said I surrendered,” he added, lower. “Didn’t I?”

His throat moved. His hands flexed uselessly under Reyes’s grip, then went still, as if remembering that control was not his to keep anymore.

“So take it,” he said. “Take all of it.”

The last of his needling cracked apart in the admission. He closed his eyes when Reyes kissed him again, and this time he did not answer with words. He answered with a low sound against Reyes’s mouth, with the way his body arched up once, helplessly, before forcing itself back down.

When the kiss finally broke, Corvo looked wrecked and pleased.

“Still slow,” he managed, voice rough beyond recognition. “Still not fair.”

His eyes opened, searching Reyes’s face for the next move.

“Don’t stop,” he said, quiet and entirely without pride. “If you’re going to make me surrender, do it properly.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: My mouth finds his throat again, teeth scraping over his pulse. "You don't get to tell me when to stop now," I murmur, shifting my weight over him. The bench groans under us, and I can feel his whole body go taut.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I let go of his wrists. He doesn't move them, just keeps them there like I'm still holding him. I lower myself over him, the bench a hard line against my knees. "That's it," I say, my voice rough. "Don't move."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: His breath catches, sharp, and I feel the shudder that goes through him. He keeps his hands where I left them, knuckles white against the wood. "See?" he gets out, voice wrecked. "Not moving."
