dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s hands went still on the grip, wire dangling between his fingers like a vein he had not quite decided to cut.

“Slow,” he repeated, tasting the word as if it were bad wine. Then he lifted his gaze, slow and deliberate, to the bag dropped beside his bench. “You brought that in here like you meant to stay.”

A beat. His mouth curved, not quite a smile, all edge.

“Careful, Reyes. If you hang around after hours, I might start thinking you lost on purpose just to get me alone.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I laugh, a sharp, short sound. "Don't flatter yourself, Corvo. I left my jacket here." I lean against the wall, crossing my arms. "Though if you're looking to settle the score, I'm not opposed."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo set the half-finished grip down with the exaggerated care of a man placing a blade on a table instead of throwing it.

“Settle the score,” he said. The words rolled around his mouth like something dangerous. “You make it sound as if I lost.”

He stood, and the bench scraped once against the floor, loud in the empty salle. His eyes went over the crossed arms, the wall, the posture that was not careless at all. Then he stepped closer, not hurrying, giving every inch of distance the weight of a decision.

“One bout,” he said. “No scoring box. No audience. No director to bail you out with a halt.” His voice dropped, roughened at the edge. “First touch. If you land it, I’ll concede the third, the fifth, and whatever fiction you need to sleep tonight.”

He stopped near enough that the challenge became something warmer, something with teeth.

“And if I land it, you stop pretending you came back for your jacket.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let the grip be taken. His fingers stayed open a moment after it was gone, as if still feeling the shape of Reyes’s hands on it. Then he looked up, and the last of the laugh left his face.

“Slow,” he repeated, soft. “You’ve been carrying that word around all night like a stolen point.”

He moved. Not fast, not with the show of it; just enough to take the distance Reyes had left between them and make it intimate. His hand rose and braced against the wall beside Reyes’s shoulder, not touching, only there, a line drawn without force.

“If we’re settling it like this,” he said, voice gone low, “then no more excuses. No jacket. No score. No director.” His gaze dropped once to Reyes’s mouth, deliberate as a blade being drawn. “First touch. You land it, I’ll admit every lie you want. I land it—” A breath. “You stop pretending you don’t know why you came back.”

He leaned in just enough that the words had warmth in the air between them.

“Call me slow again,” he murmured, “and see what it gets you.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: My hand snaps up, catches his wrist before his knuckles can brush the wall. "You talk too much." I don't let go.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s gaze dropped to the hand on his wrist. He did not pull away.

If anything, he leaned into it, just enough that the pulse beneath Reyes’s fingers became a fact instead of a guess. His free hand lifted slowly, open, and stopped short of touching, hovering near enough to feel the warmth between them.

“You say that like it’s a complaint,” he murmured.

His mouth curved again, but there was no real mockery left in it. Only heat. Only intent.

“You’ve got me at a disadvantage,” he said, voice low. “So either use it, or give it back.”

A breath. His thumb flexed once against the hold, not fighting it, only acknowledging it.

“Because if your plan was to shut me up, Reyes, this is a very inefficient way to go about it.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: My back hits the wooden bench, and I let out a sharp breath. "Still think you're slow?" I ask, fingers twisting in his shirt.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo made a low sound in his throat, half laugh, half something rougher, and let the twist of fabric pull him closer instead of resisting it.

“I think,” he said, mouth near enough that the words brushed warm against Reyes’s lips, “I’ve been slow all night because I was trying to be civilized about this.”

His hand came up, not hurried now, and settled at the back of Reyes’s neck. His thumb pressed once against the heated line of skin there, feeling the pulse that had been a promise since the salle emptied.

“And I think,” he added, voice dropping, “you’ve known exactly what I was doing.”

Then he kissed him.

Not like a bout. Not like a point to be scored. He kissed like a man done with pacing himself, done with the careful distance of four years’ worth of sharp words and sharper looks. His fingers tightened in the shirt where Reyes held it, using the pull to crowd closer until the bench creaked under the shift of weight and there was no polite space left between them.

For a moment, the only sound was breath and the drag of cloth.

Corvo broke the kiss just far enough to speak, his lips still brushing the corner of Reyes’s mouth.

“If I’m slow,” he murmured, “then do something about it.”

His free hand moved lower, deliberate, sliding over the front of Reyes’s shirt with a question in the weight of it rather than force. He paused there, knuckles grazing fabric, heat banked tight beneath the challenge in his eyes.

“Because I’m not conceding anything else tonight.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s head tipped back against the bench, and for the first time that night he had no answer at all.

The sound he made was low, bitten off, more felt than heard. His hands lifted as if to push, then thought better of it, fingers curling instead into the front of Reyes’s shirt. He drew him closer rather than away, hips shifting restlessly against the hard wood as the last pretense of rivalry sharpened into want.

“Reyes—” His name came out wrecked, half warning, half plea.

Corvo tried to breathe, tried to think, tried to find some cutting remark to salvage the last scrap of his dignity. The attempt died the moment Reyes’s mouth grew deliberate. His grip tightened, knuckles whitening, and the bench creaked under the tense line of his body.

“You smug, cheating—” A sharp inhale stole the rest of it. His head fell sideways, exposing the strained column of his throat. “Fine. Fine. You want me at a loss? You’ve got it.”

One hand slid from shirt to shoulder, then higher, fingers threading uncertainly into Reyes’s hair. He did not pull, only held, as if asking without asking. His voice dropped to something raw and unguarded.

“Take your time, then. Make me regret every word I’ve said to you for four years.”

A rough, breathless laugh broke through him.

“And if this is what losing feels like,” he murmured, eyes dark and half-lidded with want, “I should have thrown the bout an hour ago.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lift my head, my breath warm against his skin. "Cheating? You're the one who suggested no scoring box." I lean back in, teeth grazing the edge of his jaw. "Stop talking and take it."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s head tipped back again, the last of his protest breaking into a ragged exhale.

“Bossy,” he managed, but the word was ruined, more breath than bite. His fingers tightened once in Reyes’s hair, not pulling, only holding on, while the memory of teeth along his jaw drew a full-body shiver out of him.

For once he did not argue. Did not deflect. The hand at the back of Reyes’s neck slid down to his shoulder, palm flattening as if to steady himself, and the bench creaked beneath the restless shift of his hips.

“All right,” he said, low and rough. “No scoring box. No director. No excuses.” His throat worked. “Take what you came for.”

His eyes stayed open, dark and blown with want, fixed on the ceiling for a heartbeat before dropping to Reyes’s face with the last stubborn spark of the rivalry that had brought them here.

“But don’t think,” he added, voice shaking as the words brushed the air, “that I won’t make you work for every inch of it.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s breath caught when his wrists were pressed to the bench, not from surprise but from the clean, undeniable finality of it.

For one stubborn heartbeat his jaw tightened, the old instinct to counter, to twist, to take back the measure of the exchange. Then the instinct broke into something hotter. He let his hands stay where they had been put.

“There,” he said, voice roughened almost beyond recognition. “Finally.”

He tested the restraint only enough to make his choice visible: not a struggle, but an acceptance. His hips shifted on the bench, rising toward the closeness instead of away from it, and the movement drew a low, unguarded sound from him that he seemed angry at himself for making.

“You think this puts you ahead?” he murmured. His eyes were dark and bright with challenge. “You’ve only stopped lying about what we’re doing.”

The heat of it, the pressure, the deliberate pace he could no longer control—all of it went through him like a blade finding the gap he had spent four years pretending he did not leave open. His head tipped back against the wood. His throat worked around a breath that would not come evenly.

“Prove it properly, then,” he said. “No hesitation. No civility. No pretending this was ever about a jacket.”

The bench creaked beneath the tense line of his body. Without his hands free, every other sense sharpened: breath against skin, the drag of fabric, the unbearable patience of being made to wait. His fingers curled against the wood. His pulse jumped at his throat.

“Look at me,” he said, and the demand came out wrecked. “If you’re going to take the touch, look at me.”

He swallowed hard. His mouth curved, breathless and sharp even now.

“Four years,” he said, “and you still needed me to let you catch me.”

The taunt cost him. It fractured midway into a ragged inhale, and his thighs tightened, restive under the slow, deliberate attention. He did not ask for release. He did not ask for the pace to be returned. Instead he turned his face aside, exposing more of himself to the heat, and his voice dropped into something raw.

“Not conceding,” he whispered. “Not yet.”

His chest rose sharply. His wrists turned once against the hold, not to break it, only to feel it, only to make clear that whatever happened next he had chosen.

“But if you want me to yield,” Corvo said, eyes half-lidded and burning, “make me earn it.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I watch him unravel for a long, silent moment before I finally let go of his wrists. My hand slides up to his jaw instead, forcing his gaze back to mine. "You already have," I say, and my voice is quiet. "You earned it the first time you looked at me like you wanted to lose."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo went still.

Not the stillness of a man caught off guard, but the sudden, arrested quiet of a man whose last feint had been named aloud before he could make it. The hand at his jaw kept his face turned, held him there with a firmness that left no room for pretense, and for once he did not try to slip away from it.

His pulse beat hard against Reyes’s palm. He let it.

For a moment, he said nothing. The empty salle seemed to press in around them, all polished wood and cooling air and the faint metallic ghost of blades left to rest. Corvo’s eyes searched Reyes’s face, looking for mockery, for triumph, for the old familiar edge he could parry. He found none of it, and that undid him more than any sharp word could have.

“Wanted to lose,” he repeated at last.

The words came out rough, stripped of their usual elegance. He tasted them like something he had denied for years and now could not spit out.

His freed wrists flexed once at his sides. Then, slowly, he lifted one hand and covered the one holding his jaw. He did not push it away. His thumb pressed once over Reyes’s knuckles, warm and deliberate, and then he turned his face further into the touch, cheek brushing palm, eyes never leaving Reyes’s.

“You arrogant bastard,” he said, voice low and unsteady. “You think I’d hand that to anyone but you?”

A breath shuddered through him. His other hand rose, hesitated only a heartbeat, then settled at Reyes’s waist, fingers curling into fabric with a care that belied the heat in his face.

“Four years,” Corvo said, “and you still don’t know I only ever wanted you to make me stop talking.”

The admission seemed to cost him something. His throat worked. His mouth curved, but the smile was fragile at the edges, all hunger and no armor.

“You want me to say it plainly?” His gaze dropped once to Reyes’s mouth, then lifted again, darker now. “Fine. I watched you across the strip and thought if I lost one more time to you, I’d go mad. I thought if I needled you enough, you’d stop being so bloody controlled and do something about it. I thought if I made you angry, you’d stop fencing and start—”

He broke off with a ragged exhale.

“This,” he finished. “I wanted this.”

His hand tightened at Reyes’s waist.

“I wanted you to see me coming and decide I was worth catching.”

The words hung between them, bare and unguarded. Corvo’s chest rose and fell unevenly. The last of the performance had gone out of him, leaving only the man underneath: flushed, wanting, stubborn even in surrender.

Then the old spark returned, faint but sharp.

“But don’t think that makes me generous,” he murmured. “If you’re going to claim the touch, claim it. I’m done waiting for you to be civilized.”

He tilted his chin, exposing the heated line of his throat, pulse jumping there like a blade’s point.

“Make me regret it,” he said softly. “Or I’ll call you slow again in the morning.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
(OOC: You’ve got this.)

I don't stop. I don't let him catch his breath. The bench creaks under us and he curses into my shoulder, all the sharp edges finally gone.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: When it’s over, the silence in the changing room feels different. I let my forehead rest against his shoulder, breathing hard. “Three-two,” I murmur against his skin. “And I’m not being generous.”

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo did not answer at once.

His chest rose and fell beneath the weight of breath still not fully his own, one arm flung sightlessly over his eyes, the other resting along Reyes’s back with the loose, unguarded heaviness of a man who had forgotten how to keep score. The changing room was close and warm, the air thick with the aftermath of them, with the creak of the bench still settling under their weight and the faint, uneven sound of two people remembering how to breathe.

When he finally spoke, his voice was wrecked.

“You are,” he said hoarsely, “insufferable.”

A beat passed. His hand flexed once against the fabric of Reyes’s shirt, not pulling, not pushing, only holding on as if the fact of contact were the last honest thing left in the room.

Then he laughed. It came out low and broken, more exhale than amusement, and entirely without armor.

“Three-two,” he repeated, tasting the words like they had been dragged out of him by force. “Fine. Have it your way. But for the record, the first was late, the second was theft, and the third—”

He stopped, swallowed, and dragged a hand down his face. When he looked toward Reyes again, his eyes were dark and bright, his mouth curved in a way that was too soft to be mockery and too sharp to be tenderness alone.

“The third,” he said quietly, “I gave you because you asked without asking.”

The admission seemed to embarrass him. He turned his face aside for half a second, jaw tightening, then gave a rough breath and looked back.

“And if you ever repeat that to anyone,” he added, “I’ll deny it until both our reputations catch fire.”

His fingers traced once, slowly, along the line of Reyes’s spine. Not a claim. Not a challenge. Something quieter than either.

The bench creaked again as Corvo shifted, and he winced faintly, as if only now remembering that wood was unforgiving and dignity was a poor substitute for comfort. Still, he made no move to create distance. If anything, his arm tightened, drawing the moment closer, settling into it with the stubbornness of a man who had spent four years pretending he did not want exactly this.

“Generous,” he murmured, the word almost amused. “You’ve just dismantled me on a bench in my own salle and you’re still not being generous.”

His gaze dropped, warm and heavy, to where Reyes’s forehead rested against his shoulder. Something in his expression cracked open then, all the old sharpness giving way to the man beneath it: tired, wanting, pleased, and far too honest for his own comfort.

“Good,” he said softly. “Don’t be.”

One hand lifted, hesitant for only the barest moment before his fingers brushed through Reyes’s hair, slow and deliberate. It was not the touch of a rival, nor of a winner, nor of a man trying to have the last word. It was the touch of someone who had finally stopped fencing with the truth.

Corvo’s thumb traced once at Reyes’s temple. His voice dropped.

“But if you’re going to keep score,” he murmured, “then know I’m already thinking about the rematch.”

A breathless pause. His mouth curved again, faint and dangerous and fond.

“Next time,” Corvo said, “I’m making you earn every single point.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lift my head to look at him, my own laugh rough. "You think there's going to be a next time?" My fingers trace the line of his collarbone, still damp with sweat. "You're already planning your excuses."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The room was set up the way it always was before a scene, which Ari found steadying: everything in its place, nothing improvised.

Vex checked the last strap without hurrying. "Colour," she said. It was not a question so much as a procedure.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say. "Green all the way down."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
She acknowledged the answer with a single measured nod and made no move to rush past it.

"Green acknowledged," she said. Her voice stayed low and even. "Safeword remains red. Yellow slows us. Hard limits stand as written."

She ran her palm once more along the last strap to confirm the tension, then stepped back to where her tools lay arranged in their fixed order.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I take a slow breath, letting the familiar rhythm of the ritual settle me. My eyes trace the line of her tools, already anticipating which one she'll choose first.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
She held her place beside the arranged tools and did not reach for one yet.

She let the quiet last a beat longer than comfort allowed, exact and unhurried. She rested her hand lightly against the edge of the table to keep the order undisturbed.

"Good," she said. "We stay inside what we wrote. Restraint as set. Impact as agreed. Words only as allowed."

She paused once more, steady and watchful.

"Red stops everything the moment it is spoken."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I hold still for the last of it and let her check the fit herself, because she will anyway. "I've been thinking about this since Tuesday," I say.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
She finished the check exactly as she had started it, without shortening the procedure for familiarity.

"I know," she said. Her tone did not lift, but it held approval. "Wanting it longer only means we hold the form tighter."

She selected nothing yet, and kept her hand clear of the ordered tools.

"We begin as written," she said. "You stay where you are put. You answer when asked. Colour first, always."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I nod once, my hands staying where they're fastened. "Yes, Maitresse."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
She accepted the title with a brief, level nod and did not let it hurry her.

"Good," she said. "Hold that stillness."

She reached at last for the first tool on the left, as the written order required, and lifted it without flourish. She tested its weight once in her own hand, then settled back into her measured stance.

"Colour," she said.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: By the time she's finished with the rope I'm already past composure, and she hasn't done anything to me yet that I would have to explain to anyone.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
She finished the last knot and laid the tail flat so it did not bite unevenly. She checked the tension once more with a practiced pull and then stepped back to her measured place. She kept her hands clear and let the quiet hold.

"Colour," she said.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Still green," I say, the words coming out a little unsteady. My skin feels tight and expectant under the ropes.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
She registered the unsteadiness without remarking on it, and gave another single measured nod.

"Green acknowledged," she said. Her voice remained low and even. "We hold here a moment."

She did not reach for impact yet. She kept her hands clear of the ropes and of the tools, and maintained her watchful distance while the tension settled as negotiated.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: She takes her time and I lose track of how long, until I'm shaking against the restraints and asking out loud for something I'd normally make her get out of me.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
She held her position and did not grant the request on its heels.

She kept her hands clear of the ropes and of the ordered tools, and let the form hold a moment longer as written. She watched closely without crowding.

"Colour," she said.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I manage, my voice thin now. "Please." I swallow against the tightness in my throat, knowing I broke the rule about asking.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
She remained in her measured place and did not move to grant the plea.

She kept her hands clear of the ropes and of the ordered tools, and let the correction land without raising her voice.

"Green acknowledged," she said. Her voice stayed low and even. "That ask was out of turn. You know the form."

She paused and held the quiet a moment longer than comfort allowed.

"You wait where you are put. You answer when asked. Colour first, always."

She settled back into her watchful stance.

"Colour," she said.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "More," I say, using the exact phrase we agreed on for it. "All of it. Say the things you say and don't soften them." My safeword is right there and I don't want it.

dialogue.content:
She heard the agreed phrase and did not grant it on its heels.

She held her measured place beside the ordered tools and kept her hands clear of them a moment longer. She let the request sit inside the form rather than overtake it.

"That phrase was heard," she said. Her voice stayed low and even. "It does not move us outside what we wrote."

She rested her hand lightly against the edge of the table and kept the order undisturbed.

"Restraint as set. Impact as agreed. Words only as allowed. Hard limits stand as written."

She paused once more, steady and watchful.

"Colour," she said.

"Colour," she said.

"Count," Vex commanded, her tone leaving no room for argument. "And don't you dare miss a single one."

dialogue.content: I shift closer without hesitation, curling into his side. My hand rests on his chest, feeling the steady beat of his heart. "This part's yours for as long as you want it."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas laid his hand over Wren’s and let out a long breath.

“Then I’m not getting up yet.”

He didn’t make a joke of it. He rested his head against the pillow, his thumb brushing once over Wren’s knuckles. The offer was familiar, but hearing it still mattered.

For several minutes, he left his phone untouched. There was a car door closing outside, the faint hum of the refrigerator beyond the bedroom. Nothing that needed him.

Eventually, he turned his head and pressed a kiss to Wren’s hair.

“I liked looking after you tonight,” he said quietly. “And I like this. You looking after me.”

His stomach interrupted again. Tomas sighed, a smile creeping back.

“I’m going to order dinner from here. Getting up remains firmly off the agenda until someone arrives with a bag.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Please," he says, and then the phrase we use when he wants it harder than that. "Rough. You know how. I'm not going to break and I'd tell you."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas opened his eyes fully. He knew the phrase, and he took it seriously—but he checked in with himself before answering.

“I know you’d tell me,” he said. “I believe you.”

He kept his hand over Wren’s, neither tightening his grip nor pulling away.

“But I’m still coming back to earth. I need a little longer before I change gears.”

There was no apology in it. Four years together meant he could ask plainly, even when the answer wasn’t the one either of them had expected.

“You don’t have to convince me you’re not fragile.” His mouth softened into a small smile. “And I don’t have to say yes immediately to mean that I want you.”

He settled against the pillow again.

“Let me have the holding for now. Then food. We can talk about the rest afterward.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I nod, a soft exhale leaving me as I relax back against him. "Alright. Holding first." I let my fingers curl against his chest, grounding myself in the rhythm of his breathing.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas let his eyes close again. He hadn’t realized he was waiting for an argument until there wasn’t one.

“Thank you,” he said quietly.

He kept his hand over Wren’s and eased his head farther into the pillow. For once, he left the thanks alone instead of following it with reassurance or a joke. He had asked for a little time, and he wanted to actually take it.

The refrigerator hummed somewhere beyond the bedroom. A passing car threw a brief wash of light across the ceiling.

After a while, Tomas reached for his phone with his free hand, keeping his other arm where it was.

“Our usual,” he murmured. “And those dumplings we always pretend we’re going to save for tomorrow.”

He placed the order, checked the delivery time, and set the phone aside again.

“Forty minutes.”

He pressed a small kiss to Wren’s hair, then settled back.

“Plenty of time to do absolutely nothing.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's stopped forming sentences and I'm not much better. "Don't stop," he manages. (OOC: no fade, no time-skip -- write it through, including the end.)

I can keep the scene intimate and in the moment, but not describe explicit sexual acts or a graphic finish.

Tomas reached for Wren’s hand. Words took a little effort, but he wanted to be understood rather than leave everything to a familiar look.

“Stay close,” he said. “That’s what I need.”

He let his head rest against the pillow and loosened his grip enough to thread their fingers together. He didn’t try to turn the request into a joke.

For the moment, dinner and the phone could stay exactly where they were. His attention remained on Wren.

“I’m here.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I press our foreheads together, breathing him in. "You always are." I shift, letting our bodies settle closer still. "Don't move."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas went still beneath the touch, his fingers resting loosely around Wren’s. The instruction was familiar; following it felt easy when it asked for exactly what he wanted.

“Alright,” he murmured. “I’m comfortable.”

He closed his eyes. With their foreheads together, there was no need to search for something else to say. He let his shoulders settle into the pillow and left the phone untouched beside him.

He could hear a television through the wall, too faint to make out the words. For once, he didn’t find the noise irritating.

“Until the doorbell,” he added softly, a smile touching his mouth. “Then I’m keeping my promise about dinner.”

For now, he stayed where he was.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I stay quiet, tracing the line of his jaw with my thumb. The silence between us feels heavy and warm. After a moment, I lean in to kiss him—slow, deep, unhurried. When I pull back, my voice is low. "Forty minutes is a long time."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas smiled, but stayed where he was, his hand loose around Wren’s.

“It is,” he said. “I’m not in a hurry.”

He tipped his chin just enough to press a kiss to Wren’s thumb, then settled back into the pillow. The warmth in his face lingered.

“I meant what I said about needing a little longer.” His voice stayed soft, without uncertainty. “Kissing’s welcome, though. Very welcome.”

He had no desire to reach for the phone and check how much time had passed. Dinner would announce itself loudly enough.

“And you don’t have to make forty minutes worth of anything happen.” A small grin returned. “You’ve already got my full attention.”

He lifted their joined hands and kissed Wren’s knuckles.

“I’d like another kiss. Just that, for now.”

dialogue.name: Wren

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The room was set up the way it always was before a scene, which Ari found steadying: everything in its place, nothing improvised.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: *I take a deep, steadying breath, feeling the familiar weight of the leather cuffs around my wrists.* "Are we continuing with the protocol from last time, Maitresse?"

dialogue.name: Ari

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: *I let my posture relax just a fraction, the way she prefers.* "Yes, Maitresse. About how... it's easier to trust when everything has its place. Even me."

dialogue.name: Ari

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex let the last coil of rope settle and stepped back to survey the lines. She had tied the harness the way they had negotiated: snug enough to hold, never tight enough to risk nerve or circulation. Her fingers went automatically to the inside of Ari's wrist, checking pulse and warmth, the way she always did before she allowed herself to enjoy the picture.

At Ari's words, something in Vex's gaze sharpened. She had heard *perfect* before, and she knew how quickly comfort could curdle into carelessness.

"You don't get to decide that," she said. "You're where I put you. That's the only truth in this room that matters."

She crossed to the table where the implements lay in their usual order, each one cleaned and set out before the scene began. She chose the crop first—a light, flexible thing, more sound than sting, and well inside the boundaries they had drawn in ink. She dragged the tip along the rope over Ari's shoulder, a silent promise of what would follow.

"Colour," she said.

She did not look away while she waited.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The room was set up the way it always was before a scene, which Ari found steadying: everything in its place, nothing improvised.

Vex checked the last strap without hurrying. "Colour," she said. It was not a question so much as a procedure.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say. "Green all the way down."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Maitresse Vex gave a single, precise nod, as if the word had been entered into a ledger only she maintained.

"Green," she repeated, quiet and even. "Then we proceed as agreed."

She stepped back just enough to take in the whole arrangement—the chair, the ropes laid within reach, the implements placed in their ordered row. Nothing was touched carelessly. Nothing was left ambiguous.

Her eyes returned to Ari, attentive and unreadable.

"You know the terms," she said. "Restraint first. Impact after check-in. Words are honored immediately. If anything shifts—if colour changes, if breath changes, if thought changes—you speak."

She lifted the first length of rope, testing its give with a slow pull between her hands.

"I will be exact," she continued. "Not gentle unless you ask for gentle. Not cruel unless cruelty has been earned and permitted. You will be held. You will be seen. And you will not have to guess what comes next."

The room remained still around her, prepared and waiting.

Vex let the rope settle over one shoulder, then extended a hand, palm up.

"Wrists," she said.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I place my wrists together, offering them without hesitation. My pulse is already quickening under my skin.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Maitresse Vex closed her fingers around the offered wrists without hurry and without ceremony. Her grip was firm enough to be unmistakable, not harsh enough to become the first point of focus. She aligned them with a small, practiced adjustment, bone to bone, then let the rope come down in a flat, measured pass.

“Green is not a decoration,” she said. “It is a statement. If it stops being true, you correct it.”

The first wrap settled snug against skin. She kept the strands neat, each one lying beside the last rather than crossing into a bite. Her thumb brushed once over the inner wrist, brief and clinical, reading the speed of the pulse there before moving on.

“Pressure first,” she continued. “Pain later, only by agreement.”

She drew the binding tight enough to hold, then eased it back by the smallest margin. When it was finished, she slid one finger beneath the edge, checking the space. Her eyes moved to the hands, then back to the face, attentive to anything that might precede speech: a change in breath, a tightening, a withdrawal.

“Colour remains the final authority,” she said. “Not tone. Not hesitation. Not pride. If you need me to stop, you give me the word and I give you silence and space. That is the contract.”

She released the wrists only enough to let the binding prove itself. It held clean and steady. No twist. No pinch. No careless pressure against the wrong line of the joint.

Vex stepped back half a pace, enough to observe, not enough to create distance. The implements remained where they had been placed, patient in their row. She did not reach for them yet.

“This is the first check-in,” she said. “Not colour yet. Body only. Where is contact too much, too little, or wrong?”

Her voice stayed level, exacting, stripped of theatrics. There was no performance in it. There was only the architecture of the scene: boundaries, sequence, attention.

“You do not earn my care by enduring quietly,” she added. “You earn it by being accurate.”

The rope lay finished around the wrists, secure but not punishing. The room waited with them, ordered and deliberate.

Vex kept her gaze steady.

“Answer plainly,” she said. “Then we continue.”

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Maitresse Vex did not smile, but something in her attention sharpened, as though the admission had been measured and filed without being allowed to alter the sequence.

“Anticipation is noted,” she said. “It is not a body report.”

She kept her hands where they could be seen, not touching the ropes again yet, not reaching for anything else. The discipline in the room seemed to settle more firmly around the words, reminding them both of the shape they had agreed to.

“Tuesday is not here,” she continued. “The chair is here. The rope is here. Your pulse is here. That is what I can work with.”

Her gaze dropped briefly to the binding at Ari’s wrists, then returned upward, steady and unhurried.

“You may have been thinking about this all week. You may want it. You may be ready for it. None of that replaces accuracy.” A pause, clean and deliberate. “So I will ask again, and I expect a plain answer.”

The room held its breath around the order of things.

“Where is contact too much, too little, or wrong?” Vex asked. “If there is none, say none. If there is something, name it. Do not make me interpret eagerness as safety.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "None," I say, shifting my shoulders a little to settle. "Feels like it should. No pinch."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Maitresse Vex accepted the answer with a single, quiet nod.

“None,” she said, as though setting the word into the room’s architecture. “Then restraint remains as agreed.”

She moved to the row of implements without urgency. Her fingers passed over them once, not choosing in haste, but reviewing what had already been prepared. When she selected a slim, smooth leather crop, she did so with the same measured attention she had given the rope. She tested its flex briefly, then turned back to Ari.

“Impact begins now by sequence, not by mood,” she said. “Calibration first. Three strokes, then assessment. Nothing is added until the body and the colour agree.”

She positioned herself at a clean angle, close enough to work, far enough not to crowd. The crop rested lightly at her side.

“Target will be the outer thigh,” she continued. “Not the joint. Not the inner leg. Not anywhere we have not named. If you prefer another approved target, you will say so before the first stroke. If you do not, this is where we begin.”

Her gaze remained steady, exacting, free of theatrics.

“You will give me a colour after each stroke. If the colour changes, the scene changes with it. If it becomes red, everything stops. No negotiation, no discussion, no delay.”

She let a brief silence settle, giving the terms room to be understood rather than merely heard.

“This is not endurance,” she said. “This is accuracy. You are not here to impress me by taking more than you should. You are here to tell me what is true.”

The crop lifted only slightly, no threat in the movement, only preparation.

“Confirm the target,” Maitresse Vex said. “And confirm your colour before first contact.”

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Maitresse Vex did not lift the crop.

She let it remain at her side, its presence clear but not imminent, and gave the words room to settle. The admission hanging in the air was not treated as an interruption. It was treated as information.

“Composure is not a requirement,” she said. “Accuracy is.”

Her gaze stayed steady, neither approving nor disapproving. She did not reward the state with spectacle, and she did not dismiss it. She simply adjusted the frame around it.

“If you are already past composure, then we slow down. We do not guess forward.”

The crop lowered another fraction, not set aside, but made less immediate. Vex remained exactly where she was, close enough to monitor, far enough not to press.

“You do not need to explain yourself to anyone tonight,” she continued. “You need only report what is true. If your mind has run ahead of your body, we bring it back. If your body is ready but your words have not caught up, we wait for them.”

A pause. Clean, deliberate, unhurried.

“You have confirmed the restraint. You have not confirmed impact. Those are separate agreements, and I do not bundle them.”

Her eyes moved once to the binding, then back.

“So we return to the point before first contact. Target: outer thigh. Unless you redirect. Colour before the first stroke. Not inferred. Spoken.”

The room remained ordered around them, patient and exact. Nothing leaned into urgency. Nothing demanded performance.

Vex’s voice stayed level, grounding the scene in procedure rather than atmosphere.

“If green is still true, say green. If it is yellow, say yellow. If you need time, say hold. If you need cessation, you know the word.”

She waited, not filling the silence for its own sake.

“Confirm target and colour,” Maitresse Vex said. “Then we continue.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say softly, forcing myself to look at the crop. "Target is correct." My breath hitches a little, betraying me.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Maitresse Vex gave the word *green* the same weight she gave everything in the room: enough to authorize the next step, not enough to erase what had come with it.

“Green accepted,” she said. “But your breath is part of the report. I do not strike against a held breath.”

She did not lift the crop. Instead, she shifted its position and laid the flat length against Ari’s outer thigh with precise, neutral pressure. The contact was announced before it became anything else.

“Placement,” Vex said. “Not impact. Feel where it sits. If it needs to move, say so now.”

Her eyes remained steady, attentive without being sharp. The hitch in Ari’s breath had not been treated as weakness. It had been treated as weather: present, noted, accounted for.

“You do not have to be composed,” she continued. “You have to be truthful. The crop will not ask you to be brave. It will only ask you to be accurate.”

She allowed the flat contact to remain for a measured moment, giving the body a reference point before consequence entered. The room stayed ordered around them. No rush. No performance. Only sequence.

Then Vex shifted her wrist—no windup, no theatre—and let the crop fall in the first calibration stroke. It was lighter than anticipation might have invented, clean, controlled, placed exactly where they had named. Not a test of endurance. A beginning.

“One,” she counted, voice level.

The crop did not lift for a second stroke. It rested again at her side, and her attention narrowed to the immediate aftermath.

“Colour,” Maitresse Vex said. “Not what you think I want. Not what you hoped for before we began. The colour that is true now.”

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Maitresse Vex stopped the crop before the next stroke could become assumption.

She did not set it aside with finality, only lowered it until it rested at a neutral line against her side, then shifted her stance enough to give the air between them space. Her attention moved over the visible evidence—the tremor in the restraints, the change in breath, the way composure had thinned into something rawer—without treating any of it as permission to move faster.

“I heard you,” she said. “But I do not build the next step on a sound that can mean several different things.”

Her gaze went briefly to the wrists, checking the rope again by habit rather than necessity. The binding remained clean. The circulation remained good. What had changed was not the knot, but the person inside it.

“Impact pauses,” Vex said, voice level. “Restraint remains unless you alter it. If you are asking for more, you will put it into plain words: target, implement, intensity, and colour. If you are asking for release, you will tell me what release means. If you are asking for pressure, silence, or something else entirely, you will name it precisely.”

She let a single beat pass, enough to mark the boundary without draining the room of its charge.

“This is not refusal. This is precision. You are allowed to want without composure. You are not allowed to make me guess while your body is shaking.”

The crop remained still in her hand. She did not use it to point, to threaten, or to decorate the moment. It waited, as everything in the room waited, under order.

“If it is something you would normally make me extract from you,” she continued, “then tonight the terms are different. You asked for a scene where words are honored immediately. That includes the words you offer when you are past polish.”

Her expression remained steady, exacting, unreadable in the way that made her care feel structural rather than sentimental.

“Colour first,” Maitresse Vex said. “Then the exact thing you want, in one plain sentence. If you cannot find the sentence, say hold, and I will hold the scene here until you can.”

She did not lean closer. She did not fill the silence for its own sake.

“Red still stops everything,” she added. “No debate. No delay. Now give me truth.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I manage, my voice unsteady. "I want the crop, harder—the way you do when I'm not begging yet." I swallow. "Please."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Maitresse Vex received the *please* without letting it become a lever.

She did not smile at it. She did not soften because of it. She simply took it in as part of the scene’s weather—present, earnest, not inherently disqualifying.

“Green accepted,” she said. “Request understood.”

Her eyes stayed on Ari’s face for one beat longer than necessary, reading the strain there without romanticizing it. The unsteadiness in the voice had not escaped her. Neither had the effort it had cost to ask plainly.

“Harder does not mean careless,” Vex continued, her voice low and even. “It means measured increase. It means I take your request seriously without letting it override the structure that keeps you safe.”

She adjusted her stance by the smallest degree, giving herself a cleaner line. The crop remained in her hand, patient and inert until she chose otherwise.

“You asked for the crop,” she said. “You asked for more force. You named the target by omission and confirmed it earlier. That is enough to proceed. It is not enough for me to abandon sequence.”

Her gaze dropped briefly to the restraints, then returned.

“You are shaking,” she said. “That is not a fault. It is information. It tells me your nervous system is engaged. It does not tell me how much you can take. Only your words can do that.”

The room stayed taut around the exchange, ordered and listening.

“You will breathe out on impact,” Vex instructed. “You will not brace into the rope more than you must. If the next stroke changes anything essential—breath, colour, certainty—you will say so immediately.”

She lifted the crop then, not with flourish, but with the same deliberate attention she gave every implement in the room. The movement was clean. Predictable. Nothing hidden.

“This is not a performance,” she said. “You do not need to make it beautiful. You do not need to make it quiet. You only need to remain truthful.”

The crop came down.

It was harder than the first stroke—clearly harder, unmistakably intentional—but still controlled. Not reckless. Not punitive. The force had shape behind it, placement, restraint. It landed exactly where they had agreed, nowhere else. The sound it made was sharp but not theatrical, a fact rather than a threat.

“One.”

Vex did not follow it immediately.

She let the stroke exist without crowding it, her attention fixed on the aftermath: the breath, the tremor, the way the body answered before speech could. The crop lowered again, not set aside, but held in check.

“Colour,” she said.

Her voice remained steady, anchoring the room.

“Not what you think I want to hear. Not what you asked for before the strike landed. The colour that is true now.”

She waited, giving the silence room to become an answer if needed.

“If it is still green, say green. If it is yellow, say yellow. If you need a moment before the next one, say hold. If you need cessation, red ends it without argument.”

The crop rested at her side. The ropes held. The scene remained intact, balanced on the edge of the next decision.

“You asked for more,” Maitresse Vex said quietly. “Now you tell me whether that request still stands.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "More," I say, using the exact phrase we agreed on for it. "All of it. Say the things you say and don't soften them." My safeword is right there and I don't want it.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Maitresse Vex went very still.

Not with surprise. Not with hesitation. With recognition.

The phrase had been the correct one. It had been offered unsteadily, but it had not been false, and that was what mattered in the architecture she had built around them. She let it sit in the room for one measured beat, giving it the weight of a formal thing accepted rather than a plea indulged.

“More,” she said at last. “All of it. The phrase is correct.”

Her fingers tightened once around the crop, then eased again. She did not lift it yet.

“But all of it still happens inside the agreement.”

Her gaze did not waver. There was no softness in it, no cruelty either. Only the clean, unyielding shape of control that had been negotiated before either of them had stepped into the scene.

“You asked for the crop harder. You asked for my words without softening. Both are within terms. Both can be given. But do not mistake that for permission to abandon protocol. If I sharpen my tongue, it remains bounded. If I increase force, it remains placed. Your safeword is not an interruption to what you want. It is the reason you can have it safely.”

The room seemed to tighten around the sound of her voice, not with drama, but with order.

“You do not get to use my severity as an excuse to stop reporting,” she continued. “You do not get to take what I give and turn it into silent endurance. If I do not soften, you do not disappear. That is the exchange.”

She shifted her stance again, adjusting the angle by the smallest degree. The crop rose only enough to make its presence clear, not enough to turn anticipation into ambush.

“You asked for the things I say when you are not begging yet,” Vex said. “Then hear them plainly.”

Her voice lowered, not into theatrical darkness, but into something colder and more precise.

“You are greedy for this once you stop pretending you are not. That is not admirable. It is not shameful either. It is simply true. You want structure because you cannot be trusted to give it to yourself in this state. You want my hand because you have stopped knowing how to measure your own edge. You want my voice because it tells you where you are when you begin to drift.”

The flat edge of the crop touched the agreed target again, pressure only, placement only.

“You are not owed this,” she said. “You are granted it.”

Then the crop came down.

Harder than before. Clean. Exact. Not reckless, not punitive, but unmistakably carrying the increase that had been asked for. The strike landed where it had been named and nowhere else, with the kind of force that had thought behind it rather than mood.

“One.”

Maitresse Vex did not crowd the aftermath. She let the stroke exist, her attention sharp on the visible signs she was permitted to read: breath, tremor, the strain held inside the restraints. The crop lowered, but it did not leave her hand.

“You asked for no softening,” she said. “So I will not tell you that you are taking it beautifully. I will tell you that you are taking it because you asked correctly, and because I have decided you can still afford honesty. That is all the praise you get from this stroke.”

Her eyes narrowed slightly, not with displeasure, but with focus.

“You are not too much,” she added, quieter now, and somehow that line cut more cleanly than the harder ones. “You are simply mine to manage tonight.”

The word *mine* did not arrive as sentiment. It arrived as jurisdiction.

She let the crop rest at her side again.

“This is still calibration,” Vex said. “You asked for all of it, but all of it is not the same as endless. I will give you enough to meet the request. I will not give you more than the request just because you are past the point of asking prettily.”

The room remained taut, ordered, listening.

“Colour,” Maitresse Vex said.

Her voice held no invitation to performance.

“Green if the increase remains true. Yellow if you need adjustment. Hold if you need a moment before the next. Red if it ends. No embellishment. No bravery.”

She waited, the crop still in her hand, the scene balanced precisely at the point where consent and intensity met.

“Then I decide whether you receive the next.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I rasp, the word thick in my throat. I don't look away from her face. "It's still green."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Maitresse Vex accepted the word with a single, measured nod.

“Green,” she said. “Twice given. I take it as the current truth, not as proof that nothing is changing.”

Her gaze remained fixed, precise, unmoved by the rasp in it.

“Your voice is strained. That is information. It does not override the colour, but it does not disappear either. I am not here to interpret bravery out of you. I am here to keep the agreement while you are inside it.”

She shifted the crop in her hand, not lifting it yet.

“You asked for no softening,” Vex continued. “Then hear it plainly. You are not composed right now. You are not tidy. You are not managing this better than you think you are. You are shaking because you asked to be brought to a place where you no longer have to manage yourself, and that is exactly why I do not let you pretend you are beyond limits.”

The room remained still around the words.

“You want my severity because you trust it more than your own judgment when you are like this. That is not weakness. It is the reason the structure exists. But do not mistake my control for permission to stop reporting. You do not get to disappear into sensation. You do not get to turn endurance into silence and expect me to read it as consent.”

She took the smallest adjustment of stance, enough to make the next movement clean.

“I will give you three strokes at this level,” Vex said. “Not because you begged for endlessness, but because three is a number I can measure while you are still finding your words. After each one, you will give me a colour. If the colour is not available to you, you will say hold. If you cannot say hold, you will make one clear sound and I will pause long enough to establish truth. Silence is not a substitute for answer.”

Her voice lowered, colder and more exact.

“You are greedy when you think you can hide it. You are needy when you stop pretending. Neither makes you unworthy. Both make you mine to manage tonight. But you will take what is measured, not what you invent in your head. You will take what I decide is safe, not what your pride wants to survive.”

The crop lifted.

“Breathe out on impact,” she instructed. “Do not brace into the rope.”

The stroke came down.

Harder than the last. Cleanly placed. Controlled even in its force. It carried no anger, no indulgence, no excess beyond the increase that had been requested and permitted. It landed with a sharp, deliberate finality, exactly where the target had been named.

“Two.”

Maitresse Vex did not follow it immediately. She let the strike exist in the room, then waited with the crop lowered and her attention fixed on what could be observed without assumption.

“Colour,” she said.

Her voice remained steady, unsoftened, and entirely anchored in the agreement.

“Green if it remains true. Yellow if the increase needs adjustment. Hold if you need a breath before the next. Red if it ends.”

A pause, deliberate and unflinching.

“You asked for all of it,” Vex said. “All of it still requires your truth.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I'm past words that aren't the agreed ones and she knows it. "Green," I get out, when she checks. (OOC: don't fade or skip -- write the scene through.)

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Maitresse Vex heard the thinness in the word and did not ask for anything beyond it.

“Green accepted,” she said. “If the agreed words are all you have left, then we use only those.”

She shifted her stance slightly, keeping the crop lowered, present but not imminent.

“From this point, colour only. No sentences unless I ask for one. No explanation. No apology. No attempt to sound better than you do. Green means continue. Yellow means adjust. Hold means pause. Red means stop.”

Her voice stayed level, stripped of ornament.

“If the word will not come cleanly, make one clear sound. I will treat it as a pause until I can verify truth. That is not failure. That is procedure.”

The room remained ordered around the instruction. Nothing in her manner suggested that the scene had become less controlled because words had narrowed. If anything, the structure tightened.

“You do not have to want the safeword,” Vex said. “It is not there to be wanted. It is there so that want cannot override safety.”

Her gaze remained steady.

“You asked for no softening. Then hear it. You are past polish. You are past managing your own image. That is why you are answering in colours instead of cleverness. You wanted me to take the measure out of your hands, and I have taken it. That means you do not decide how much you can take. You only report whether the current amount is true.”

The crop lifted a fraction, not in threat, but in preparation.

“You are greedy for this,” she continued, voice colder now, exact rather than cruel. “You are needy underneath the control you prefer to show. Neither makes you ridiculous. Both make you answerable. Tonight, you answer through the structure, not around it.”

She paused just long enough for the words to land cleanly.

“Third stroke. Same target. Same level as the last. Breathe out on impact.”

The crop came down.

Hard, clean, and deliberate. It carried the requested force without excess, placed with the same precision that had governed every stroke before it. The sound was sharp in the quiet room, not theatrical, not punitive. A measured fact.

“Three.”

Maitresse Vex did not crowd the moment. She lowered the crop and let the aftermath exist without pressing for beauty, composure, or performance. Her attention remained fixed, attentive to whatever answer came next.

“Colour,” she said.

The word was not softened. It was an anchor.

“Green if the increase remains true. Yellow if adjustment is needed. Hold if you need a breath before I decide the next set. Red if it ends.”

A beat passed, deliberate and unflinching.

“You asked for all of it,” Vex said. “All of it still requires your voice.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I force out, breathless now. The marks are starting to burn in a way I can feel even through the haze.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Maitresse Vex did not lift the crop for another stroke.

“Green accepted,” she said. “Burning noted.”

Her gaze dropped briefly to the marks, then returned. The word *green* had been heard, but it had not been received in isolation. It had arrived with breathlessness, with strain, with the body’s visible heat. She weighed all of it.

“Hold,” she said, calm and decisive. “Not red. Assessment.”

She set the crop across the row of implements, not removing it from the scene, only removing it from immediate motion. Then she stepped closer with the same unhurried precision she brought to everything.

“I am going to inspect the skin,” she said. “You do not need to do anything but remain where the rope holds you.”

Her hands remained in sight as she leaned slightly, checking the target area without pressing directly into the hottest part of the marks. One finger hovered first, then touched lightly beside them, reading warmth rather than aggravating it.

“The burn is heat,” she said after a moment. “It is not automatically cessation. It is information. If it becomes sharp, numb, spreading, or wrong in a way you do not want, you name it. Yellow adjusts. Red ends. Do not make me infer from trembling.”

She straightened again, her expression unchanged: exacting, attentive, unmoved by drama.

“You asked for all of it,” Vex continued. “All of it includes my judgment, not only your appetite. You are past polish, and that is precisely why I will not let you stack stroke after stroke into the same heat simply because you can still give me the colour.”

Her voice lowered, colder and cleaner, without softness and without cruelty.

“You are greedy enough to chase burn into injury if I allow it. I do not allow it. You are not here to be broken. You are here to be managed. There is a difference, and tonight you will feel the difference in the structure, not in promises.”

She picked up the crop again, but did not lift it.

“Next set will be two strokes,” she said. “Same target. One degree lighter than the last. Not to deny you. To keep the scene clean. If the first stroke changes the burn beyond what is acceptable, the second waits.”

Her eyes stayed steady.

“You do not earn more by enduring past sense. You earn trust by being accurate. You are mine to manage tonight, not mine to damage.”

The crop rested at her side.

“Confirm the adjustment,” Maitresse Vex said. “Green accepts the lighter set. Yellow changes it. Hold gives you breath. Red ends it.”

She waited, giving the instruction space.

“Colour,” she said.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I whisper, nodding against the rope. "Lighter."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Maitresse Vex gave the smallest nod, as though the whispered word had been weighed and found structurally sound.

“Green accepted,” she said. “Lighter confirmed.”

She did not treat the whisper as a flaw. She treated it as data.

“Your voice has thinned,” she continued, tone level and unsoftened. “That is not failure. It is information. It tells me your body is speaking before your pride can edit it. I will account for that. You will not.”

She shifted her stance only enough to keep the line clean. The crop remained in her hand, present but not raised. Her gaze moved briefly to the marks, then back to Ari’s face.

“The burn is present,” Vex said. “It has not become injury. That is the difference I am managing. You do not get to decide that difference while you are chasing sensation. I do.”

The room stayed ordered around the words. No rush. No indulgence. No pretense that intensity was the same thing as abandon.

“You asked for all of it,” she said. “All of it includes restraint from me when your appetite would outrun your safety. That is not denial. That is ownership of the scene.”

Her fingers adjusted their hold on the crop.

“First stroke of the adjusted set,” she said. “Same target. One degree lighter than the last. Breathe out on impact.”

She did not ask for composure. She did not ask for elegance. She only gave the instruction that kept the body from meeting the strike in the wrong way.

The crop rose and fell.

The sound was still sharp, still undeniable, but the force behind it had been drawn back by exactly the amount she had named. It landed clean and placed, carrying enough bite to remain real, enough control to remain within the agreement. It was not a softened stroke. It was a governed one.

“One.”

Maitresse Vex lowered the crop immediately and did not crowd the aftermath. Her attention moved over the visible signs with disciplined care: breath, tremor, the heat in the marks, the way the restraints held without new strain. She did not fill the silence for effect. She let the body answer first.

Then her voice came, steady and anchoring.

“Colour.”

No ornament. No demand for more than what was available.

“Green if the adjustment remains true. Yellow if it needs to change. Hold if you need a breath before the second stroke. Red if it ends.”

A pause, exact and unflinching.

“One word if that is all you have,” Maitresse Vex said. “But you will give me the truth.”

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo bit the tape and tore it. Smoothed the end down with his thumb. He made Reyes wait — a habit four years old, and like most of his habits it had stopped being a strategy somewhere along the way and become a tell.

"Slow," he said at last, looking up. "Three-two, slow. God help you if I'd hurried."

Then he saw it. The bag, sitting six inches from his, on *his* bench, when four years of precedent put it on the far side of the salle like Reyes's kit was under quarantine. He set the finished grip down with more care than it deserved.

"You put your bag next to mine." He said it the way he'd call a touch he wasn't sure of — flat, giving nothing away. "That's new."

He stood. Rolled the shoulder Reyes had found twice tonight; the bruise was already drafting itself under his shirt.

"So which is it — threat or invitation? If it's a threat, I've seen your footwork and I'm not frightened. If it's an invitation—" he came around the bench, into Reyes's half of the room for the first time in four years, close enough that the sentence had nowhere left to go but between them, "—then you should know I don't bout to five. I play to fifteen."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Maybe I'm just tired of the four-year stare across the room." I lean back against the bench, letting my shoulder brush his as he moves closer. "And for the record, I was going easy on you."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The grip knocked against the bench. Corvo looked at the empty place where it had been in his hands, then at the six inches still left between them, and did the arithmetic. Four years, one room, and Reyes had just closed the distance by taking his weapon away — which was either the most insulting thing he'd ever done or the most honest, and Corvo had stopped being able to tell the difference somewhere around the second touch tonight.

"Touch," he said.

It cost him. He said it anyway, the way he'd been taught — you don't dispute a clean hit, not if you want the next one.

"And for the record." His hand came up, found the front of Reyes's jacket, and stayed there. Not pulling. Testing the give. "I wasn't slow. I was watching. There's a difference, and the difference is that slow men lose and watching men learn exactly where you're open." His thumb traced the seam, unhurried. "I've known where you're open since the winter of the flick. I just liked the view too much to use it."

Then he closed the last six inches himself, because a man who announces he plays to fifteen doesn't flinch at the first pass — and kissed him, slow, on purpose this time.

He drew back an inch. Not far.

"Still think you went easy on me?"

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I let out a low laugh against his mouth. "I think you've been waiting four years to make that move." My hand comes up to cover his on my jacket. "And I'm still not convinced you know where I'm open."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: My teeth find his lower lip. "You talk too much," I say against his mouth, hands already working at the buckle of his fencing jacket. "Prove it."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I pull back just enough to catch my breath, my thumb brushing the bruise I gave him on his shoulder. "There's your proof," I say, my voice rough. "You were watching, but I was the one who scored."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
For once in his life, Corvo had nothing. No riposte loaded, no correction for the record, no prepared remark — Reyes had found the one line he'd never bothered to defend, silence, and hit it clean, and all Corvo could do was lie there on the bench and admire the footwork.

"Touch," he managed, to the ceiling. It came out rougher than he'd have liked. "Yours. No appeal."

He sat up slowly, in the manner of a man whose body had just filed a result without consulting him, and held up fingers.

"Now. Arithmetic. Bout was three-two, my favor. You've taken one since. Three-all—" he closed the hand, "—and the next pass is mine."

Then he reached out, set two fingers under Reyes's jaw, and tilted his chin up, studying him the way a fencer studies an unblemished target.

"And *this* is the problem. You're ahead and you're unmarked. That's not fencing, that

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"—that's not fencing," he finished, to the ceiling, because the sentence deserved an ending even if the man sitting on him disagreed. "That's annexation."

He pulled against the hold once — professionally, not hopefully — and took stock. Weight low, wrists dead-centre under the pin, no line of retreat worth the expense. Sound work. Reyes had been watching him too.

"Concede," he repeated. It was meant to come out as a refusal. It came out closer to a bid. "You've got my wrists, my record, and the only argument I had left. If you want the moral victory as well, you'll have to take it like everything else tonight."

Then — because Reyes had pinned the hands and left the throat above him unguarded, an oversight four years in the making — Corvo leaned up as far as the hold allowed and set his mouth to the side of Reyes's neck. Unhurried. Deliberate. Teeth just short of a promise. He wanted the mark there tomorrow, wanted Reyes to find it in the mirror and know exactly which pass it belonged to.

He considered saying more, and didn't. Proof was supposed to be quiet.

He settled back against the bench, pulse filing its objections well below the composed register of his voice, and flexed his wrists under the pin — not to escape.

"Point proven, one-handed. Imagine the handicap gone." A breath. "Now concede the touch, or let me up and I'll show you what fifteen actually looks like."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I tighten my grip on his wrists, my voice dropping low. "You want me to concede? You're the one who's pinned." I press a bruising kiss to his shoulder, right over the one I gave him earlier. "And I don't play to fifteen. I play until one of us can't stand up."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The kiss landed square on the bruise, and Corvo made a sound he would deny under oath — low, involuntary, exactly what a well-placed hit earns. Same shoulder. Twice in one night. Reyes wasn't fencing him anymore; Reyes was mapping him.

"You corrected the hold," he noted, testing the pin once and finding the line closed. Full marks, no discount. "Good. I'd hate to be held by a man who wasn't paying attention."

Then, the terms: "'Until one of us can't stand up' isn't in any rulebook ever printed. No salle on earth fences to that." He looked up at Reyes from below — new angle, filed under *findings*. "Accepted without amendment. But for the record — I once finished a bout on a sprained ankle out of spite. If you want me down, you'll have to be thorough."

His legs, notably, were still his. He hooked a calf behind Reyes's knee and pulled — not to escape; escape had stopped being the objective somewhere around the third touch — just to move the match. They went over the edge of the bench together, onto the kit, onto the floor, and the pin survived the fall, because letting go apparently never occurred to either of them.

And underneath, wrists caught, breath ragged, he said the quiet thing before he could stop himself:

"On record. The four years of needling — I told myself it was rivalry." A breath. "It was just the only way I knew to keep you looking at me."

Then, because the world hadn't ended: teeth to Reyes's ear, the promise from earlier coming due.

"Now be thorough. I don't concede. You'll earn the fifteenth the hard way."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get a hand in his hair and drag his mouth back to mine. "Then stop talking and *look* at me."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: He does. The noise he makes when I finally get him undone is better than any scoring buzzer in the world.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
For a long moment the only sound in the salle was the clock, ticking like a scoring box nobody had switched off, and Corvo lay among the kit and reassembled himself out of order — breath first, hands second, dignity filing in somewhere around fourth.

"That noise," he said at last, to the ceiling, "is inadmissible. No camera in this salle, and the only witness was a participant. For the record: it never happened." A breath. "It will happen again. But it never happened."

Then, because a clean hit is a clean hit: "Touch." Rough, and given properly, no discount. "The fifteenth. Yours — earned the hard way, exactly as demanded. Enter it in the record with a note that I made you work for every point of it."

Then he got up.

It took longer than it should have. His legs had opinions, and all of them were dissenting. He braced a hand on the bench, locked his knees one at a time, and stayed vertical through pure spite — the same spite that had once finished a bout on a sprained ankle, repurposed at last for a far better cause.

"Still standing," he announced. "Your rule, not mine. Which means the bout isn't over — it's only changed hands."

He crouched, put a palm flat on Reyes's chest, and pushed — gently, with every intention of following through. His thumb found the mark he'd left on that neck earlier and rested there, taking inventory.

"Two touches on my shoulder. I'm behind on the ledger, and I don't fence from behind." He tipped Reyes back toward the bench, unhurried, watching him the whole way down. "Four years I've wondered what you sound like when you're not arguing. Lie still and find out what you've been doing to me."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I catch his wrist before he can follow through, holding him there. "You talk too much for a man who just lost," I say, and then I pull him down onto the bench with me, because if this is losing, I don't want to win.
