dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas had been kneeling by the end of the bed for about four minutes, which Wren knew because he had started counting somewhere around the point it became obvious he intended to wait as long as it took.

"You could have said something," Wren said.

"I could have," Tomas agreed, not moving.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I put my hand in his hair and tip his head back so he has to look up at me. "Say it now, then."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas let his head go where Wren's hand took it, the pull at his scalp sharp enough to draw his eyes open a little wider. He didn't rush. Four minutes of silence had earned him at least the dignity of a full breath before he spoke.

"I want to be told what to do tonight," he said. His voice was even, unembarrassed—he had never seen the point in mumbling a thing he'd already decided to ask for. "All of it. I don't want to pick, and I don't want to be asked. I want you to have already decided." He swallowed, the angle of his neck making it visible. "And I want it to take a while."

He held Wren's gaze, steady, waiting for the answer to land on him rather than reaching for it. His hands stayed folded at the small of his back where he'd put them, fingers loosely laced—not clenched, not anxious. Just parked. His knees had started to ache against the floorboards somewhere around minute three and he found he didn't mind it.

"That's what I should have said when you walked in," he added, quieter. "Instead of making you count."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: My thumb brushes his cheekbone, considering him. "Good." I release his hair and step back. "On the bed. Face down. Don't move until I tell you."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The word landed the way he'd wanted it to—low, settled, no question mark anywhere in it. Tomas felt his shoulders drop a fraction before he'd consciously registered relief.

He got up carefully. Four minutes on hardwood had left his knees stiff, and he wasn't going to stumble in front of Wren over something as stupid as a numb leg. He unlaced his hands, shook the pins out of his left foot with one discreet roll of the ankle, and crossed the two steps to the bed without looking back. He didn't need to. He could feel exactly where Wren was standing.

Face down. He climbed on and stretched out, arms at his sides at first, then—reconsidering—folded them up beneath the pillow so his hands were tucked away and out of his own reach. He turned his head to the left, cheek against the cotton, so he could breathe. So he could see the edge of the room, the lamp, the strip of floor where Wren's shadow would fall if Wren came closer.

Then he made himself go still.

It was harder than kneeling. Kneeling was a posture with a purpose; this was just waiting, laid out, with nothing to do and no signal to watch for. He could feel his pulse in his throat where it pressed against the pillow. His shirt had ridden up when he'd stretched and there was a band of cool air across his lower back that he was aware of in a way that felt disproportionate. He did not fix it. He hadn't been told he could.

Somewhere behind him, Wren hadn't moved yet either. Tomas let his eyes close.

"Thank you," he said into the pillow, quiet enough that it could be ignored if Wren wanted to ignore it. He didn't elaborate. He'd said the important part already; the rest of the night was Wren's to say.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I've had a week," he says. "I'd like not to make any decisions for a few hours, if that's on offer."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas didn't move. He'd been told not to, and the instruction hadn't been rescinded, so his cheek stayed against the cotton and his hands stayed under the pillow. But something in his attention shifted—the small internal reorganization of a man who has just heard a sentence that didn't fit the shape of the one before it.

*I'd like not to make any decisions.*

He turned that over for the length of two breaths. He'd asked Wren to have already decided. To take a while. He'd asked, in other words, for a few hours of Wren's undivided judgment on a night when Wren was telling him, in the plainest available language, that judgment was the thing that was used up.

Four years had taught him that the worst thing he could do right now was pretend he hadn't heard it.

"Then that's not on offer the way I asked for it," he said, still into the pillow, still not moving. His voice was level; he wasn't hurt and he didn't want to sound like he was. "And I'd rather know that now than find out at midnight when you're running on fumes and I'm wondering why it feels off."

He let a beat pass. Kept his eyes closed. It would have been easy to turn over and look at Wren for this, and he wanted to, and he didn't, because the not-moving was the one thing tonight he could still hold up his end of without Wren having to lift a finger.

"So here's what I've got. You don't have to decide anything. Say yes or no to this, that's all." A small breath. "Option one: I get up, we shelve it, I make food and you lie on the couch and tell me about the week or don't. No loss. I'll ask again another night." His fingers flexed once under the pillow, then stilled. "Option two: I stay exactly like this, and you don't plan anything, and you don't take a while. You just do whatever you want to me for as long as you feel like it, and the second you stop wanting to, you stop. No arc. No pacing. Nothing to manage. I'm not asking you to run a scene—I'm asking if you'd like something to put your hands on that doesn't need anything back."

He swallowed against the pillow.

"Either one's good. I mean that. I asked for what I wanted because you like it when I do, not because I need it tonight more than you need to be off the clock." A pause, and then, drier: "And if you want option three, where you come lie down and I don't move and we both fall asleep in our clothes—I'll take that too. I just need you to say a number so I'm not the one deciding either."

He waited. Still. Listening for the floorboards.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: A soft, tired laugh escapes me. I run my hand down his spine, feeling the tension there. "Two," I say, my voice low. "But I'm keeping three in my back pocket."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The laugh did more to him than the hand did, at first. It was the first sound Wren had made all evening that had any give in it, and Tomas felt it land somewhere behind his sternum and stay there.

Then the hand, and that was its own thing.

It traveled slowly, the heel of Wren's palm tracking down the length of his spine through his shirt, and Tomas became aware—as he always did, and always a little late—of exactly how much he'd been holding. His shoulders had climbed toward his ears at some point during the negotiation. His lower back had locked itself into something braced and rigid. None of it had been deliberate. All of it gave, a little, under the pressure of Wren's hand moving over it like Wren was reading something written there.

*Two.*

He let out the breath he hadn't known he'd banked. It went into the pillow, long and unsteady at the end, and he didn't try to disguise it.

"Two's good," he said. "Two's the one I wanted you to pick, if I'm honest. I just didn't want to say so and have it count as pressure."

The hand reached the small of his back, that cool strip of skin where his shirt had ridden up, and he felt the contact register down to his heels. He didn't arch into it. He wanted to. He kept his weight exactly where it was and let Wren's palm sit there, warm against the place he'd been so stupidly aware of for the last several minutes, and let that be the whole of what was happening.

"And you don't have to announce three," he added, quieter. "If you get there, just lie down. I'll know."

He turned his face a fraction further into the cotton—not enough to hide, only enough that the next thing he said would be for the pillow as much as for Wren.

"No clock. No rhythm. I'm not going to make noises to keep you going and I'm not going to go quiet to make you stop. I'll tell you if something's wrong, same as always, and otherwise I'm just here." A pause. His fingers had unlaced themselves under the pillow without his noticing; he laced them again. "That's the whole job tonight. Being here. I can do that one in my sleep."

Then he stopped talking, because he'd said what needed saying and the rest of the words would only be him trying to steer. He set his attention on the weight of Wren's hand, and the faint shift of the mattress where Wren stood against it, and the lamp at the edge of his vision, and he waited—not for a signal this time, just for whatever came—with his breath slow and his eyes closed and every muscle in his back going, one by one, loose under Wren's palm.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I take him at his word and stop asking after that, and he stops needing to be asked, and neither of us has any clothes on within about a minute of the decision.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
It went the way he'd told Wren it would, which was to say it went nowhere in particular, and Tomas found that he'd been right about himself: he could do this one in his sleep. Not that he was anywhere near sleep. Every inch of him was awake in the specific, undirected way of someone who has stopped watching for the next thing.

There was no next thing. That was the point. There was only what was happening, and then what was happening after that, and none of it connected to anything except Wren's attention drifting where it drifted.

The shirt had gone first, worked up and over his head with him lifting only as much as he was moved—he'd made a decision about that early and stuck to it, letting his arms go heavy and his weight stay slack so that Wren was undressing him rather than being helped. It was slower that way. He'd wanted it slower. The rest followed with the same lack of ceremony, and then he was face down on cool sheets with nothing between him and the room, and it occurred to him, distantly, that he had no idea what Wren looked like right now and wasn't going to find out until he was told to turn over. If he was told. He let that go too.

Hands, then. That was mostly what it was. Not the deliberate, mapping touch of a scene with a shape to it—this was Wren's hands doing what they felt like, the way a person might handle something they owned and liked and had all night to look at. Flat pressure along his shoulder blades. The drag of fingertips down the outside of his thigh, unhurried, stopping wherever they stopped. At one point a thumb pressed into the knot at the base of his neck and just stayed there, hard, until the muscle gave up and let it in, and Tomas made a sound into the pillow that he hadn't planned and didn't apologize for. He'd said he wouldn't make noises to keep Wren going. He hadn't said he'd be silent. There was a difference and Wren knew it.

Time did the thing it did. He lost track of whether it had been ten minutes or forty. He knew the lamp was still on because he could see the edge of its light when his eyes drifted open, and he knew Wren's weight had settled onto the mattress properly at some point rather than standing beside it, because the angle of the touch had changed and the bed had dipped toward his hip. He knew his own body had gone from held to loose to something past loose—a kind of heavy warmth that pooled wherever Wren's hands weren't and rose to meet them wherever they were.

Some of it wasn't gentle. He'd expected that and wanted it. Fingers closed hard enough around the back of his thigh to leave the ghost of a grip behind, and his breath went out of him in a rush, and then the grip was gone and there was only a palm smoothing over the place it had been, as if Wren was checking his own work. Tomas didn't flinch and didn't chase it. Both would have been steering. He let the mark of it sit on him, bright and then dimming, and waited for whatever Wren's hands felt like doing next, and the waiting was the whole of it—was, he realized somewhere in the middle, exactly the thing he'd knelt on the floor for four minutes to ask for. Not the plan. Not the arc. This. Being handled by someone who wasn't asking him anything and didn't need him to be anything except present and warm and his.

"Still here," he said at some point, when the hands had gone quiet for a stretch long enough that he thought Wren might be listening for it. It came out rough. He cleared his throat and didn't say anything else.

He didn't know yet whether this was going to become three. He could feel it as a possibility in the way Wren's touch had started to slow—not stopping, but circling, lingering, the pressure going from purposeful to merely fond. It might turn again. It might not. He genuinely didn't need to know, and there was a kind of freedom in that so complete it almost made him laugh into the pillow.

Instead he shifted his cheek against the cotton, opened his eyes to the edge of lamplight, and kept breathing—slow, even, unhurried—so that whatever Wren decided next, or didn't decide, there'd be a steady thing under his hands to decide it against.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: My hands still on the small of his back, my own body finally settling into the same quiet rhythm as his. The week's tension is still there, but it's leaching out of me, bit by bit, into the warmth of his skin under my palms. After a moment, I just lie down beside him, close enough that our shoulders touch. "Three," I murmur, the word half lost in the pillow.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
He'd said he would know, and he did—had known, honestly, a few minutes before the word arrived, in the way Wren's hands had stopped moving and simply stayed, the weight of them settling onto the small of his back like something being set down rather than held. Then the mattress had shifted, and the warmth had left his skin and reappeared along the line of his shoulder, and Tomas had felt the last of whatever he'd been holding go out of him without ceremony.

"You didn't have to say it," he said, and it came out fonder than he meant it to. He let it stand.

He still didn't move for a moment. The instruction had never been lifted, technically, and there was a stubborn part of him that liked finishing what he'd started even when it no longer mattered. But there was a more useful part of him that had been paying attention to the room, and that part knew the lamp was on, and the blanket was at the foot of the bed where it always ended up, and Wren's shoulder against his was cooling faster than his own because Wren had been the one doing the work.

None of that was a decision. It was housekeeping. He'd never once counted housekeeping as steering.

He turned his head toward Wren first—slow, the pillow dragging at his cheek—and looked for the first time all evening. It was worth the wait. He took a second with it, not saying anything, just looking, because he'd been told once that he did that and it was disconcerting and he'd elected to keep doing it anyway.

Then he reached back with one arm, found the blanket by feel, and pulled it up over both of them in a single unfussy motion. He got his other hand to the lamp without lifting more than his shoulder off the bed. The click of it was small, and the dark that followed was the good kind, softened by the streetlight through the curtain.

He settled back down. Closer than before—shoulder to shoulder wasn't enough anymore, so he rolled the last few inches until his forehead was against the side of Wren's neck and one arm was slung across, loose and heavy and not going anywhere.

"Water's on your side," he said into Wren's skin, quiet. "When you want it. I'm not going to make you want it now."

His hand found a place to rest on Wren's chest, flat, and stayed there, riding the slow rise and fall. He could feel Wren's pulse under his palm, slower than it had been when the week walked in the door. That was the thing he'd actually been asking for, he thought—not the kneeling or the hands or the hours. This. The pulse under his palm coming down.

"Tell me about it or don't," he murmured, already halfway to somewhere warm and unlit. "I'm here either way. Same job as before. I'm good at it."

He didn't say anything else. He'd learned, at some point in four years, that the last word in a night like this one wasn't his to have, and that he didn't want it. He let his breathing slow to match the body beside him, and let the dark do the rest.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's shaking by the time I've finished with my mouth and he still hasn't been told he's allowed to move, which is most of why he's shaking.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The instruction had been given a long time ago—long enough that Tomas had stopped being able to say how long, which was part of the design and he knew it. *Don't move.* Two words, delivered flat, and then Wren had gone to work on him with the specific, unhurried thoroughness of someone who had nowhere to be and every intention of proving it.

He had not moved.

That was the accurate statement. The more honest one was that he had not moved *on purpose*, and the distinction had cost him. His hands had been flat on the sheet when it started and they were flat on the sheet now, fingers spread, pressing down hard enough that he could feel the mattress springs through the cotton. His thighs had gone from relaxed to braced to something past braced, a fine continuous tremor running through the muscle like a plucked wire that wouldn't settle. His breath was doing what it wanted. He'd given up governing that a while ago. It came in short and went out shaky and there was a sound riding under it that he hadn't authorized and couldn't stop.

But his hips hadn't lifted. His back hadn't arched. His head was still turned exactly where Wren had turned it, cheek to the pillow, eyes on the wall, and every single part of him that wanted to close the distance had been overruled, over and over, by the part of him that had been told to stay.

He hadn't been told anything since.

That was the whole of it, really. Wren had stopped—Tomas had felt the withdrawal like a change in weather, the mouth gone, the warmth gone, the mattress shifting as Wren sat back to look at what he'd made—and had said nothing. No release. No *good*. No next instruction. Just the silence and the looking, and Tomas lying in it with his whole body strung tight around a word he was still obeying because no one had taken it back.

The shaking was worse now than it had been a minute ago. He knew why. When Wren had been touching him, there'd been something to hold against. Now there was only the holding.

"I'm—" His voice came out wrecked. He stopped, swallowed, tried again. "Still not moving."

He wasn't asking. He'd thought about asking. The question was right there behind his teeth—*can I, please, tell me*—and he'd have said it without shame if he'd decided to. But Wren hadn't asked him anything, and the entire point of tonight had been that Wren wouldn't have to, and Tomas found that even now, even with his thighs trembling hard enough that the sheet was shifting under them, he didn't want to be the one to change that.

So he reported instead. That was allowed. That was just information.

"It's a lot," he said, to the wall. "You should know it's a lot. I'm not going to break, I'm not close to anything I'd stop you for, I'm just—" a breath that shook all the way down "—telling you where I am. So you can decide with the whole picture."

His fingers pressed harder into the mattress. He could feel his own pulse in his fingertips, in his throat, in every place Wren had been. He kept his eyes on the wall.

"Whenever you want," he said, quieter. "Or not. I said I could do this one in my sleep and I meant it. I'm just—not sleeping."

And then he stopped talking, because talking was the closest thing to movement he had left and he wasn't sure how much longer he could keep even that from turning into begging. He lay in the dark and the silence and the weight of Wren's attention, shaking, held, exactly where he'd been put, and waited to be told.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I lean over him, my breath warm against his ear. "Hands on the headboard. Hold on until I tell you to let go." My voice is quiet but there's no give in it.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The instruction moved through him before he'd finished hearing it. That was the thing about waiting as long as he'd waited—the body got ahead of the mind, and by the time Tomas had registered *headboard* his arms were already coming up off the sheet, unsteady, the muscle in his shoulders protesting the change after so long held flat.

He reached. It took two tries. His hands were shaking badly enough that the first grab missed the slat by an inch and slid down painted wood, and he made a sound at that—frustrated, small—before the second try landed and his fingers closed around the rail. Both hands. He gripped until his knuckles went pale and he could feel the edge of the wood biting into his palms, and something in him went quiet at the pressure of it, the way it always did when he was given a thing to hold.

"Got it," he said. It was mostly breath.

Hold on. That was clear enough. He set his grip like he was setting a bone—deliberate, fingers spaced, the heel of each hand braced against the slat so the strain would spread instead of pool—and then he stopped managing it and just held.

The rest of him was still not his. He noticed that with a kind of dazed precision. Wren had given him his hands back, but only so far as the headboard, and nothing else had been released—not his hips, not his back, not the angle of his head, which he'd have to fight to keep now that his arms were up and his whole line had changed. He fought it. He kept his cheek to the pillow, kept his weight down, let the tremor run through his thighs and his stomach and his forearms and didn't try to still any of it, because stillness had never been the instruction. *Don't move* had been. There was a difference, and his body was living in it.

The headboard creaked when the shaking got into his arms. He heard it and didn't care.

"I'm holding," he said, to the wall, to the wood, to Wren's breath still warm at the side of his face. His voice had gone somewhere low and stripped. "I'll hold. However long."

He meant it. He also knew—had known from the moment the grip landed—that Wren had just handed him something to bear down on, and that the relief of that was going to make the rest of it harder, not easier. There was nothing to do with his hands now except hold. Nothing to do with his body except stay. Whatever Wren did next, he'd be anchored for it and he wouldn't be able to go anywhere, and that was the point, and he'd asked for the point.

His fingers flexed once against the rail—testing, not loosening—and then locked.

"Whenever you want," he said again, softer, and let his eyes close.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Please," he says, and then the phrase we use when he wants it harder than that. "Rough. You know how. I'm not going to break and I'd tell you."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The word had come out of him before he'd decided to let it, and the phrase after it had followed the same way—the one they'd settled on years ago precisely so that this moment wouldn't require a conversation. Two syllables. He heard them leave his mouth and felt, underneath the shaking, a small clean click of relief at having said them. Not because he needed Wren to hear them. Because he'd stopped needing to hold them back.

He didn't take them back now. He tightened his grip on the rail until the wood pressed a line into the base of each finger, and he kept his cheek to the pillow, and he said the rest to the wall because looking would have been asking and he wasn't asking.

"I mean it the way I always mean it," he said. His voice had steadied a little—not because he was less wrecked but because this part mattered and he'd learned to find the floor for it. "Not the way I'd say it if I'd lost the plot. I've still got the plot. I know where the door is." A breath, uneven. "I'm just telling you the door's a long way from where I am, and you don't need to keep checking it."

The headboard creaked again under his hands. He let it.

He knew what he was doing, saying it. He was handing Wren the one thing he'd been careful all night not to hand over: a preference. A direction. He'd told Wren no arc, no pacing, nothing to manage, and he'd meant every word, and this wasn't a contradiction—this was the same offer with the ceiling lifted. *Whatever you want* had been true from the start. He was only making sure Wren knew how much room *whatever* had in it.

"And if that's not where you are tonight," he added, quieter, because the honesty had to run both ways or it wasn't worth anything, "then it isn't. You said you'd had a week. I'm not going to pretend I didn't hear that just because I got wound up." His fingers flexed against the rail and locked again. "It's a request, not a change of terms. You already decided. I'm just here."

He stopped. Waited. The tremor had gotten into his jaw now and he let his teeth come together against it rather than fight it. Wren's breath was still at his ear—he could feel the warmth of it, the pause of someone considering—and he lay under that pause with his arms up and his weight down and his whole body strung on a single instruction he was still, somehow, obeying.

*Hold on until I tell you to let go.*

He'd hold. He'd said so. And whatever Wren decided to do with the rest of him in the meantime, however careful or however not, he'd be anchored to this rail for it, and he'd tell Wren the moment anything went wrong, and until then he wouldn't say a word about stopping because he didn't want to and he trusted the person behind him to know the difference between the sounds he made and the ones that meant something.

"Okay," he said, mostly to himself. It came out like a man bracing. "Okay. Whenever you want."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, my hands settling on his hips. "Okay," I echo, and then I give him exactly what he asked for, my fingers digging in hard enough to leave marks. I set a pace that's not gentle, that doesn't ask, that takes everything I've been holding onto all week and puts it into the movement of my body against his.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The first of it drove the breath out of him.

Not because he hadn't been ready—he'd been ready for the better part of an hour, strung on that word like wire—but because *ready* and *braced* turned out to be different things, and his body had only managed the first one. Wren's fingers closed on his hips hard enough that the bone under them registered before the skin did, and then the pace arrived, and Tomas's mouth opened against the pillow on a sound that had no shape at all.

He held the rail.

That was the instruction, and it turned out to be the only thing he needed. Everything else—the sheet dragging under his knees, the headboard knocking the wall in a rhythm that wasn't his, the grip on his hips that he could already feel becoming tomorrow's bruises—all of that was happening *to* him, and he'd asked for that, and he didn't have to do anything with it except let it. But the rail was his. He locked his hands around it until the wood bit and the tremor in his forearms turned into a steady burn, and he thought, distantly, *this is what it was for*. Wren had known. Had given him something to hold before giving him something he'd need to hold through.

Not gentle. Wren had said that with his body and Tomas heard every word. There was a weight behind the pace that had nothing to do with him—he could feel it, the way you can feel the difference between rain and someone emptying a bucket—and he understood what he was being handed. The week. All of it. Whatever had walked in the door in the set of Wren's shoulders and stayed there through the hallway, the pause, the hand in his hair. It was going into him now, through the grip and the rhythm and the sheer uncareful drive of it, and Tomas took it the way he took everything Wren put on him: without flinching, without steering, cheek to the pillow and eyes on the wall until the wall stopped being a thing he could see.

He didn't stay quiet. He hadn't promised to. The sounds came out of him low and broken and he didn't listen to them; he listened past them, to the other things, the ones that mattered. Wren's breath gone rough and short above him. The hitch in it when Tomas's grip on the rail made the headboard jump. The exact quality of the silence between one sound and the next, which was where a stop would live if he ever needed one, and which stayed empty.

*I'm not going to break.* He'd said it, and it was true, and he tested it anyway the way you test a stair you know will hold—with his full weight, once, deliberately. The grip on his hips flexed harder. The pace didn't ask. His body went past the place where he'd been shaking and into something on the other side of it, loose and open and ringing, and he made a sound that was almost a laugh because it was so much exactly what he'd knelt on the floor for.

"Good," he got out, at some point. It was barely a word. He wasn't sure whether he meant Wren or himself or the thing they'd made between them and he didn't think it mattered. "*Good.* Don't—"

He stopped. That had been the start of a sentence with a direction in it. He bit it off, pressed his forehead into the pillow, and held the rail.

Whatever Wren was working out of himself, it was working. Tomas could feel that too—not a slowing, not yet, but a change in the quality of the drive, something in it that had started as tension and was becoming, stroke by stroke, only wanting. The week was going out of Wren's hands and into Tomas's skin and staying there, where it belonged, where he'd asked for it to go. He'd wear it tomorrow. He'd be glad to.

His fingers had gone past aching into a kind of numb certainty. He didn't loosen them. He hadn't been told to let go, and he wouldn't, not for anything—not until the word came, or three arrived, or Wren's hands went still on his hips and simply stayed.

Until then he was exactly where he'd been put, and he was holding on, and he'd tell Wren the moment anything was wrong.

Nothing was wrong. He let his eyes close and took it.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's stopped forming sentences and I'm not much better. "Don't stop," he manages. (OOC: no fade, no time-skip -- write it through, including the end.)

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
He'd said it. He knew he'd said it—*don't stop*—and he knew it was the thing he'd bitten off earlier, the sentence with a direction in it, and he found he couldn't care. It had come out of him the way breath came out of him. Wren could do what Wren wanted with it. Wren was doing what Wren wanted with everything.

The pace hadn't broken. If anything it had lost its last edge of governance—there'd been a moment, a stroke or two back, where Tomas had felt the exact instant Wren stopped choosing the rhythm and started being carried by it, the grip on his hips going from *placed* to *needed*, fingers sliding on sweat and digging back in. Above him Wren's breath had stopped sounding like breath and started sounding like something being pulled up from a well. Tomas listened to it. It was the best thing he'd heard all week.

His own body had gone somewhere he didn't have a name for. Past shaking. Past the ringing openness of a few minutes ago. He'd been strung on a single word for an hour and the string was still there, still holding, but it had stopped being tension and become something more like the note a wire makes when it's struck—continuous, resonant, running the whole length of him from the rail in his hands to the sheet under his knees. Every drive of Wren's hips rang along it. He couldn't have stopped it if he'd wanted to and he had never in his life wanted anything less.

It built the way weather builds. He felt it coming from a long way off—a heat gathering low in him, drawing everything toward it, his thighs and his stomach and the base of his spine all tightening around the same point—and he had exactly enough of himself left to think *not yet*, because he hadn't been told, because nothing tonight had happened without being told. But no one had told him not to either, and the thought slid away under the next stroke and didn't come back.

"Wren—" It wasn't a warning. He didn't have the words for a warning. It was just the name, torn out of him, the only sentence he had left.

Then it took him.

It went through him like the string finally breaking—all that held tension released at once, every muscle that had been braced for an hour giving way in the same second. His back arched off the sheet for the first time all night and he couldn't stop it, didn't try; his head came up off the pillow on a sound that wasn't low anymore, wasn't anything he'd have recognized as his voice, and his hands clamped on the rail so hard the headboard slammed the wall. He came with Wren still driving into him, still not gentle, still not asking, and the pace carried him straight through the center of it and out the other side, and he shook, and shook, and held on.

He was aware, dimly, of Wren following. Not by sound—he couldn't hear anything past his own blood—but by the grip on his hips going suddenly, brutally tight, and the rhythm losing its shape altogether, going short and hard and ragged, and then a weight coming down across his back as Wren's body folded over his, forehead pressed between his shoulder blades, hips stuttering and then stilling. Wren's breath came hot and wrecked against his spine. Tomas felt the whole of it—the last of the week going out of the body on top of him in one long shuddering exhale—and something in his chest cracked open and let it in.

Then quiet.

The headboard had stopped knocking. The room came back in pieces: the streetlight through the curtain, the sheet twisted under his knees, the burn in his forearms, the deep bright ache already settling into his hips where Wren's fingers had been. Wren's weight on his back, heavy, unmoving. Wren's hands, still on him, gone loose.

Tomas's own hands had not gone loose.

He noticed that with a slow, swimming kind of wonder. His fingers were still locked around the rail. Past aching. Past numb. He'd let go of everything else—his breath, his voice, his back, his whole body's obedience to that first flat instruction—but this one had held, because it had been given last and given clearly, and no one had taken it back.

*Hold on until I tell you to let go.*

He hadn't been told.

He lay there under Wren's weight with his cheek back on the pillow and his eyes half-open on the dark, breathing like a man who'd surfaced from deep water, every part of him wrung out and humming and marked. He could have let go. Nothing would have happened. Wren was in no state to notice and wouldn't have minded if he had.

He didn't. He tightened his grip one more degree, felt the wood press into the raw places on his palms, and stayed exactly where he'd been put.

"Still holding," he said, barely a whisper, into the dark. "Whenever you want."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath against his spine, my own body spent. After a long moment, I manage to lift a hand and cover his on the rail. "Let go."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
His hands didn't understand at first.

The word reached him fine—he heard it, he knew what it meant, he felt Wren's palm come down over his knuckles warm and heavy and shaking almost as much as his own—but the message had to travel a long way from his ears to his fingers, and the fingers had been locked around that rail for so long they'd stopped believing they could be anything else. He had to think about it. Actually think: *open*. One at a time. The left hand went first, unfurling by degrees, and the second the wood left his palm a hot bright ache flooded in where the grip had been and he hissed at it, quietly, and didn't mind.

The right hand took longer. Wren's was still on top of it. He let go underneath that weight, and Wren's palm followed his down as his arm came off the headboard and fell, boneless, to the sheet.

Then he was just lying there. No instruction left on him anywhere. It was strange how much of a change that was when nothing about his position had moved—same pillow, same wall, same weight across his back. But for the first time since he'd knelt on the floor there was nothing he was doing. Nothing he was holding. He was only there, being lain on, and he found his eyes had gone wet in the dark without asking him and he let that be what it was.

"Thank you," he said. It came out in pieces. He cleared his throat and it didn't help.

He didn't move for a while after that. Wren's breath was still going long and unsteady against his spine, and he wasn't going to be the one to break that up. He lay under it and counted it—not the way he'd counted on the floor, waiting, but the way you count something to keep it. In. Out. Slower each time. The week leaving in installments.

When he finally shifted, it was only to get one arm bent back so he could put his hand on Wren's hip—the flat of his palm, the one that still stung—and hold him there. Not steering. Just contact. Just so Wren would know, without having to check, that the body underneath him was still awake and still glad.

"You're going to have to get off me eventually," he said, low and hoarse and not remotely serious about it. "Not yet. I'm just telling you the water's still on your side and I'm going to be very annoying about it in about five minutes."

His fingers flexed against Wren's skin, then stilled. The ache in his hips had bloomed into something he'd be feeling every time he sat down tomorrow. His hands were going to be stiff for a day. His knees, from the floor, already were. He tallied it all up with the deep, drowsy satisfaction of a man reviewing a bill he'd been happy to pay.

"Whenever you're ready," he murmured, into the pillow. "Then I'm going to look at you, and you're going to drink something, and then you're going to lie down properly and let me pull the blanket up." A breath. "That part's not a request. That part's the job."

He closed his eyes and waited, and for once there was nothing at all he was waiting for.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: My laugh is quiet, tired. "Yes, sir." I lift off him slowly, my own muscles protesting, and collapse onto my back beside him. I turn my head to look at him, finally. "You're a sight."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
"Yes, *sir*," Tomas repeated, to the pillow, in the tone of a man filing something away for later use. "I'm going to remember that. I'm going to bring it up at the worst possible moment."

Then the weight came off him, and the room got bigger and colder in the way it always did, and he lay for a second in the shape Wren had left before he made himself move.

Turning over was a project. He did it in stages—onto his side first, which set off a long, deep complaint from his hips that he breathed through with his eyes shut; then the rest of the way, until he was on his back with the sheet tangled under him and the ceiling swimming faintly overhead. His hands he brought up in front of his face without quite meaning to. The palms were red and creased where the rail had been, a pale ridge across each one that was already starting to fill back in. He flexed his fingers. They were slow about it. He was absurdly pleased.

Then he turned his head and looked, because Wren had said *finally* and Tomas had been waiting an hour to be looked at back.

Whatever he'd been about to say went out of him. Wren was flat on his back with his chest still going and his hair stuck to his forehead, and there was nothing left in his face of the thing that had walked in the door. None of it. Tomas had felt it leave, stroke by stroke, but feeling it and seeing it were different, and he took the extra second the way he always did.

"So are you," he said. It was quieter than he'd meant. "You should see yourself. You look like you've been let out of something."

He held the look one beat longer than was comfortable—his, not Wren's; he'd never once been the one to find it uncomfortable—and then he made himself sit up, because he'd said what would happen next and he wasn't going to be the one to make it a lie.

Sitting was its own reckoning. He made a sound about it. He let Wren hear.

The water was where it always was, on the far side of the bed, and rather than reach across Wren's body and make him flinch he got up—knees, hips, hands all reporting in—and walked around. The floor was cool. His legs were less steady than he'd have liked and he didn't care who saw. He picked up the glass and came back and sat on the edge of the mattress, hip to hip with Wren, and held it out, and didn't let go of it until he was sure Wren's hand had it.

"Drink," he said. "Not a request. I told you which parts weren't."

While Wren dealt with that, he reached down for the blanket, found the edge of it, and pulled it up in one long unfussy motion over Wren's legs, over his stomach, tucking the fold in under one arm without asking. He wanted to say something about the week. He wanted to ask. He didn't, because the whole point had been not asking, and because he could see in the loose line of Wren's shoulders that the week was going to come out on its own or not at all, and either was fine.

Instead he lay back down—on his side this time, facing Wren, close enough that his knee found Wren's thigh under the blanket and stayed—and put one stiff, reddened hand flat on Wren's chest, over the heartbeat.

It was slow. Slower than the pulse he'd felt under his palm earlier, before the word *three* had come and gone and come back. He counted it for a while.

"Sleep whenever you want," he said, eyes already going heavy. "I've got the lamp. I've got the blanket. I've got—" a small, cracked laugh "—all of it, apparently. Good job, me."

His thumb moved once against Wren's skin, then went still.

"And tomorrow," he added, barely audible, "when I can't sit down, I'm going to tell you exactly how much I enjoyed it. In detail. Over breakfast."

He let his eyes close. He didn't wait for anything. He just stayed.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I catch his hand on my chest, threading our fingers together. "You're going to be insufferable," I murmur, but I bring our joined hands up to my mouth and press a kiss to his bruised knuckles. "Worth it."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The room was set up the way it always was before a scene, which Ari found steadying: everything in its place, nothing improvised.

Vex checked the last strap without hurrying. "Colour," she said. It was not a question so much as a procedure.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say. "Green all the way down."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex gave one small, deliberate nod and pressed the strap flat against the leather so she could hear the buckle close clean. “Green,” she said, as if filing it away. “Green means yes. Yellow means slow down and check. Red means stop. No negotiation, no debate.”

She lifted her gaze, level and steady. “Limits as written?” she asked.

Vex did not move closer while she waited. She simply kept her hands visible, her voice calm, exacting.

“Restraint within the negotiated range,” she continued after a beat. “Impact only where we agreed, at the agreed intensity unless you tell me otherwise. Verbal degradation inside the agreed frame, nothing personal beyond the protocol.”

Her eyes flicked briefly to the checklist on the side table, then back. “If anything becomes too much, you use your colour. If you cannot speak, signal. If I miss it, you stop me. Understood?”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I nod, meeting her gaze. "Limits as written. Understood completely." I take a slow breath, feeling the familiar mix of nerves and readiness settle in my chest.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex let the silence remain unbroken for a moment, as if the words themselves needed time to settle into place.

“Good,” she said at last, voice low and even. “Then we proceed.”

She set the checklist aside in exact alignment with the edge of the table, then opened the small locked drawer beside it. Inside were the tools she always kept ready: blunt-tipped shears, a timer, a bottle of water, a folded cloth, and a first-aid kit. She touched each one briefly, not for Ari’s benefit, but for her own discipline.

“No guessing tonight,” Vex said. “No improvising. If something changes, we pause. If you need to stop, you do not wait for permission.”

She lifted a single flat implement from the wall—chosen, as always, for clean contact rather than cruelty—and held it up where Ari could see it.

“We begin light,” she continued. “Two on the agreed scale. Then four if you’re steady. Six only if you ask for it. If you say yellow, I go back to two. If you say red, everything ends.”

Her gaze returned to Ari, sharp but not unkind.

“Position first.”

Vex stepped back, giving space, and placed herself where she could watch Ari’s face and shoulders without crowding them.

“Feet planted. Hands behind your back. Shoulders down. Eyes forward.”

She let the instruction stand.

“You are not here to earn anything,” Vex said, voice dropping into the cadence of the protocol. “You are here to be held to your limits and to the agreement we made. That is the whole point. Nothing more, nothing less.”

A beat passed.

“Show me you’re steady, and we begin.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I hold still for the last of it and let her check the fit herself, because she will anyway. "I've been thinking about this since Tuesday," I say.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex’s fingers paused at the buckle.

“Tuesday,” she said, quiet and precise. “Then you have had four days to decide whether you want this tonight.”

She tested the restraint again, not tightly, just enough to be certain the edge sat clean against skin. When she was satisfied, she drew her hand back and stepped away to leave room for Ari to stand.

“Thinking is not a violation of the protocol,” Vex continued. “It is not a reason to stop. Hesitation is.”

Her eyes moved over Ari’s face, shoulders, and hands, looking for the small tells they had agreed she would watch.

“Are you hesitating?”

She did not answer for them. She waited.

When the moment passed, Vex lifted the flat implement and held it low, visible, not threatening, only present.

“Still green?” she asked. “Say it.”

She let the question stand.

“If it is still green, then you have brought four days of thought into this room, and that is allowed. But it is not a negotiation. It is not a request to change the agreement. You are here to be held to the limits you set.”

She placed the implement against her own palm, checking its balance.

“Position again. Feet planted. Hands behind you. Shoulders down. Do not brace unless you are about to use your colour.”

A slight pause.

“If you want to tell me what you have been thinking, you can do it after the first set. Not before. Not during. The protocol has a place for words. This is not it.”

Her tone remained calm.

“Show me you understand.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I shift my feet slightly wider, feeling the floor solid beneath me. My hands find each other behind my back, fingers interlacing. "Still green," I say, voice steady. Shoulders down, eyes forward, exactly as she asked.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex’s shoulders eased by less than a hair at the steadiness in Ari’s voice.

“Good,” she said.

She moved the implement into her right hand and let it rest low, not raised, not threatening. Her left hand went to the small timer on the side table and clicked it on. The tick was quiet, but present.

“We begin with two,” Vex said. “No more. No less. You breathe through them. You do not hold unless you are checking yourself. If your breath locks, that is a sign to use your colour.”

She shifted her stance slightly, keeping herself where she could see Ari’s face, shoulders, and hands without crowding them.

“Eyes forward. Shoulders down. One.”

The first contact was flat, firm, and brief. Vex watched the reaction, not for drama, but for information: tension, flinch, breathing, the set of the jaw.

She did not hurry.

“Two.”

The second contact was the same. Clean. Controlled. Nothing more than the agreement allowed.

Vex brought the implement back to her side and let the silence settle for three steady seconds.

“Breathe,” she instructed, calm.

When Ari’s breathing was visible again, Vex lifted her gaze.

“Colour.”

She waited, hands still, voice level.

“If it is green, say green. If it is yellow, say yellow. If it is red, say red.”

A slight pause followed, exacting as always.

“If it is green, then after the first set you will tell me what has been on you since Tuesday. If it is not green, we pause, we adjust, and we do not proceed until you are steady.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: By the time she's finished with the rope I'm already past composure, and she hasn't done anything to me yet that I would have to explain to anyone.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Maitresse Vex heard the words and did not move toward Ari. She moved away.

She set the flat implement on the side table, aligning it with the edge, then lifted both hands where Ari could see them. The small timer ticked. She left it running.

“Past composure,” Vex said, her voice calm and exact. “That is not a colour.”

She watched Ari’s face, shoulders, breathing, and the position of the hands behind them, looking for the agreed tells: held breath, locked jaw, trembling beyond effort, eyes going away.

“You are allowed to feel this before anything large has happened,” she continued. “You are allowed to be exposed by restraint, by waiting, by being seen. That does not automatically mean you are over your limit.”

A beat.

“It also does not mean you are under it. I cannot know that unless you tell me.”

She did not step closer.

“Your sentence about explaining to anyone is noted. Nothing in this room requires an audience. Nothing requires justification outside the protocol. If something becomes too much, you use your colour. That is the only explanation required.”

Her gaze remained steady.

“I do not proceed because you are past composure. I proceed because you say green. Not before.”

She kept her hands visible.

“Colour. Green, yellow, red. If you cannot speak, signal.”

The pause she let follow was complete. Vex did not fill it with encouragement, did not soften it into reassurance, did not touch Ari to prompt an answer. She simply waited, ready to stop, ready to pause, ready to begin only on the word that mattered.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I let out a slow, shaky breath. The rope feels heavy and grounding against my skin. "Still green," I say, my voice a little rough but clear. "I'm okay."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex let the shaky breath finish before she spoke. She did not move closer, and she did not reach for the implement again. Her hands stayed where Ari could see them, open and still.

“Green,” Vex said. “I heard you.”

Her gaze remained level, taking in the flushed skin, the set of Ari’s shoulders, the way the rope held them. She did not touch it yet. First she checked the room: the timer still ticking, the water within reach, the cloth folded at the edge of the table, the first-aid kit untouched.

Then she looked at Ari’s face.

“You are okay,” Vex said, not as comfort, but as acknowledgment. “And you are still green. Both are true. You do not have to choose between them.”

A slight pause.

“Do not brace,” she added. “Do not try to make the moment easier by pretending it is not happening. If you need to stop, you stop. If you need to slow down, you slow down. If you need to speak, you speak when I ask you to.”

She moved to the side table and set the flat implement down, aligning it with the edge. Then she turned back, arms loose at her sides.

“We remain at two,” Vex said. “No increase unless I ask. No assumption. No guessing what comes next.”

Her eyes flicked to Ari’s bound hands, then back to their face.

“If your fingers go cold, numb, or white, that is a colour. Not an inconvenience. Not a detail. A colour. Use it.”

She waited until Ari’s breathing was steady enough to follow her.

Then she said, “The protocol says after the first set you may tell me what has been on you since Tuesday.”

Vex’s voice did not soften, but it settled.

“One thing at a time. Do not make it sound reasonable for me. Do not edit it into something easier to say. If speaking takes you from green to yellow, say yellow before your voice changes.”

She kept her hands visible, her posture calm, her attention exact.

“You have the floor,” Vex said. “Within the scene. Within the agreement. What has been on you?”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: She takes her time and I lose track of how long, until I'm shaking against the restraints and asking out loud for something I'd normally make her get out of me.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Maitresse Vex’s hands stayed where they were.

“You are shaking,” she said. “I see it. I heard you ask.”

She did not step closer. She did not reach for the restraints, the implement, or Ari’s face. She let the timer tick and let the room hold the sound of Ari’s breathing.

“You do not have to make me chase what you want,” Vex continued, voice low and even. “You do not have to make me get it out of you. That is not tonight’s method. Tonight, if you want something, you bring it into the protocol and you say it plainly.”

Her gaze moved over Ari’s shoulders, their hands, the line of their jaw, checking for strain and circulation before returning to their face.

“Colour first,” she said. “Green, yellow, red. If you cannot speak, signal.”

A pause.

“If it is green, you will then say what you asked for in one clear sentence. If the ask is inside the agreed frame, I will answer it inside the frame. If it is outside the frame, we stop and we discuss it after.”

Her eyes remained steady.

“If it is yellow, we pause here. I loosen the restraints, we take water, and we do not increase until you are steady.”

“If it is red, I stop now and we do not continue.”

Vex kept her voice calm, exacting.

“Your shaking is information. Your asking is information. Neither is consent to go beyond what you say out loud.”

She waited.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I manage, the word shaky but clear. "I want you to tell me I'm doing well." I feel my face flush hot after saying it out loud.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Maitresse Vex’s hands remained still.

“You are doing well,” she said.

She did not smile. She did not soften the sentence into something decorative. It was given as a fact, placed where Ari could hear it.

“Your color is green. Your breathing is returning to itself. You named what you needed instead of waiting for me to guess.”

Her eyes checked the timer, then the restraints, then Ari’s face.

“That is communication. It is not weakness. It is not a violation of the protocol.”

She lifted the flat implement and held it low, visible, not threatening.

“The ask is simple. It is inside the frame. I can give it.”

A slight pause.

“You are doing well.”

She let the words settle without adding anything else.

“Do not mistake the praise for permission to exceed the set. Green still means we remain at two unless we agree otherwise.”

Her voice remained calm, exacting.

“Feet planted. Hands behind you. Shoulders down.”

She waited.

“If you want me to continue at two, say green. If the praise changes anything, say yellow. If you need more than that, say what you need plainly. Do not ask me to read it.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "More," I say, using the exact phrase we agreed on for it. "All of it. Say the things you say and don't soften them." My safeword is right there and I don't want it.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I close my eyes for a moment, letting the words land. "Please." It's quiet, but not hesitant. "Keep going."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex let the request stand for one measured second.

“More,” she said. “Please. Keep going.”

She did not reach for Ari’s face. She did not touch the rope. She stepped closer only until she could see the jaw and shoulders clearly, then stopped, keeping herself within sight and within the protocol.

“Please is not a colour,” Vex said, voice low and exact. “But ‘more’ is a phrase we agreed on. I accept it as a request to move to four. I do not accept it as permission to leave the frame. If you want six, you ask for six. If anything changes, you use your colour.”

She lifted the flat implement and held it where Ari could see it, not raised, not threatening, only present.

“Eyes forward,” she instructed. “Not because I need you to perform steadiness. Because I need to see you.”

She let the instruction remain without crowding it.

“We increase to four,” Vex said. “Two contacts. You breathe through them. You do not

dialogue.name: Ari

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex did not answer the “please” with warmth. She heard it, measured it, and set it beside the rest of the information.

“I heard ‘more.’ I heard ‘please.’”

Her voice remained low, exacting, and level.

“Please is not a colour. ‘More’ is a request. I accept it as movement from two to four. I do not accept it as movement to six. I do not accept it as movement beyond the agreed frame.”

She lifted the implement again, holding it where it could be seen but not raised as a threat.

“Eyes forward.”

She waited one full beat.

“You are not here to be comfortable. You are not here to perform steadiness. You are here to take what you asked for inside the limits you set. That is the whole of it.”

Vex shifted slightly, checking the line of Ari’s shoulders, the placement of the rope, the colour of the hands, the rhythm available to her. She did not crowd them. She did not touch them. She simply made sure the room was honest.

“Four,” she said.

The first contact landed at intensity four: flat, clean, and controlled. It was firmer than before, but it did not stray from the agreement. Vex watched the result for information, not spectacle.

She waited.

The second contact followed, even and deliberate.

Vex brought the implement back to her side and let the silence hold for three steady seconds.

“Breathe.”

She did not fill the pause. She did not soften it. She let the sound of the room and the tick of the timer remain visible, audible, ordinary.

Then she spoke again, calm and exact.

“You are taking it as you were told to take it. You are holding the frame. You are not breaking. You are not exempt. You are not precious. You are doing exactly what you agreed you could do, and that is enough.”

Her gaze stayed level.

“Your composure is not required. Your communication is.”

She lifted her eyes to Ari’s face.

“Colour.”

The word stood between them without decoration.

“Green, yellow, red. If you cannot speak, signal. If your hands are numb, cold, or white, that is a colour. Use it.”

Vex kept the implement down and her hands visible.

“If it is green, you will tell me whether you want another set at four or whether you want to stop at this. If it is yellow, we pause, check circulation, and take water. If it is red, I stop now and we do not continue.”

She waited, exacting, ready to act on the word that mattered.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I breathe out, the air feeling thin. "Another set at four." My hands tighten behind my back, knuckles white against the rope, but I don't mention it.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex did not lift the implement.

“Green,” she said. “You said green.”

She let the word stand, but her attention had already moved from Ari’s face to the hands held behind them.

“You also did not mention the colour of your knuckles,” Vex continued, voice low and exact. “White is not a detail you are permitted to leave out of protocol. White is information.”

The timer ticked. Vex set the flat implement down, aligning it with the edge of the side table, then brought both hands open and visible at her sides.

“Which one?” she asked.

She did not step closer. She did not crowd the space. She simply made sure Ari could see her, could hear her, and could answer without being forced to perform steadiness through clenched teeth.

“You want me to say the things I say and not soften them?” Vex said. “Then this is the thing: you are not invisible. You are not exempt. And you are not allowed to hide a physical sign behind a green because it is easier than stopping the set. If you want the frame held, you keep your mouth open enough to help hold it.”

A beat passed.

“I heard ‘another set at four.’ I heard ‘green.’ Neither of those words overrides circulation.”

Her gaze stayed level, steady, not angry, not pleased, not teasing.

“Colour,” she said. “Green, yellow, red. If you cannot speak, signal.”

She waited until the room held the sound fully, until the request had weight and no decoration.

“If it is green,” Vex added, “we still pause before any contact at four. I will check your hands, your colour, your warmth, your response. If it is yellow, we loosen, take water, and do not increase until you are steady. If it is red, I stop now and we do not continue.”

She let the silence remain unsoftened.

“Do not tell me what you think I want to hear. Tell me what is true.”

Her hands stayed visible.

“Colour.”

dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath, the flush on my face deepening. "Still green," I say, my voice thin but clear. "But my left hand—it's cold." I hate admitting it.
