dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas had been kneeling by the end of the bed for about four minutes, which Wren knew because he had started counting somewhere around the point it became obvious he intended to wait as long as it took.

"You could have said something," Wren said.

"I could have," Tomas agreed, not moving.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I put my hand in his hair and tip his head back so he has to look up at me. "Say it now, then."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas let his head fall back into Wren's grip and held it there, throat exposed, which was answer enough to anybody watching, but not to Wren, because Wren had asked for words.

"I wanted you to notice," he said. "That's the first thing. I knelt down where you'd walk past and I counted, and the whole time I was thinking about how long it'd take before you put your hand on me." A small breath, not quite a laugh. "Four minutes. I was getting ready to be smug about it."

He didn't drop his eyes, though the angle made it an effort — chin up, watching Wren upside down along the line of his own brow.

"Second thing. I don't want to be told what I want tonight. I already know." His voice had gone quieter, more deliberate, the way it did when he was saying something he'd turned over in his head first. "I want your hand in my hair like this and I want to be kept there. Nothing else. Just that, for a while. Is that on offer?"

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I run my thumb along his jawline, feeling the tension there. "It's on offer." I shift my grip, tightening just enough for him to feel it. "But if we're doing this, you don't get to be smug about four minutes."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The corner of Tomas's mouth moved, and he made no attempt to hide it — caught, and fine with it.

"Four minutes was never the point," he said. "It was just the part I could measure."

He let the last of the angle go slack in Wren's hand, not pulling free, just settling his weight down into his knees, which had already begun to complain in that low, distant way he'd learned to file somewhere else. His hands stayed where they'd started, flat on his own thighs, palms up. He'd put them there himself, no instruction needed, because that was part of what he'd asked for, and he knew what he'd asked for.

"I'll take the correction," he said, and meant it plainly, no sulk in it. "You're right. If I get to be smug then I'm watching it happen instead of being in it."

A breath, slow through his nose. He tipped his head a fraction more into Wren's grip, testing the weight of it, finding the exact place where the pull on his scalp went from pressure to something that made the back of his neck go warm.

"Then here's the whole of it, since you want it said out loud. I don't want a scene tonight. I don't want to come. I want this — your hand, my head, however long you feel like holding it, and me not deciding anything for a while. If it goes an hour, good. If you get bored at ten minutes, that's your call and I'll take it." His eyes had gone a little unfocused at the edges, the way they did once he'd finished talking himself into something. "That's it. That's the ask."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I've had a week," he says. "I'd like not to make any decisions for a few hours, if that's on offer."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas went still in a different way than he'd been still before — not waiting-still, listening-still.

"On offer," he said, and it came out slower than he meant it to, because he was turning the shape of it over while he said it. "Yeah. That's on offer."

He didn't move his head out of Wren's hand. If anything he pressed up into it a little, which was its own kind of answer, and then he took a breath and said the rest plainly, because four years had taught him that the plain version was the only one either of them trusted.

"Then here's how I see it, and you tell me if I've got it wrong. You don't want to decide anything. I don't want to decide anything. That's not a collision, that's the same thing twice." A pause. "Except you're the one holding my head, so if neither of us decides, the default is that we just — stay. You keep your hand where it is. I keep my knees on the floor. Nothing moves because nobody says move."

His thumbs rubbed once, slow, over the seams of his own jeans.

"I can do that for a few hours. Longer than a few. It's not a hardship, in case that was the part you were going to worry about." The corner of his mouth went again, softer this time. "Only thing I'd ask is that you tell me when you're done, when you get there. I don't need you to steer. I just need to know the wheel's still there."

He settled his weight back down, shoulders dropping an inch he hadn't known they'd been carrying.

"So. Yes. It's on offer. Take it."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't realize I'd been holding. "Good." My other hand comes up to cradle his cheek, thumb stroking his skin. "We'll stay just like this, then. Until I say otherwise."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas said, "Okay," and then didn't say anything else for a long while, because it turned out that was the whole of what was needed.

The first thing that happened was that his shoulders went down the rest of the way. The second was that his breathing found a rhythm and stayed there — in through the nose, slow, the hand on his cheek giving him something to time it against. Wren's thumb moved and Tomas followed it without meaning to, a fraction of a degree, the way a plant turns.

He noticed the counting start up anyway. Some old animal part of him, tallying — one, two, three — the same reflex that had gotten him four minutes and a smug look earlier. He let it run for a bit. Then he stopped it, deliberately, the way you'd set down something heavy you'd been carrying without noticing, and the quiet that came after was wider than he'd expected. Not empty. Just wide.

His knees ached in the low, patient way they did when he'd be paying for it tomorrow, and he filed that too, off to the side, somewhere it couldn't get at anything. His palms stayed up on his thighs, loose. Nothing in him was arguing with anything.

At some point his eyes drifted closed and he didn't bother opening them again. He could feel the weight of Wren's hand in his hair, the specific pressure of it, the exact place where the pull turned warm — and he didn't need to decide anything about it. That was the point. That was the whole thing he'd asked for, and it was happening, and nobody had to say move.

He stayed.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I take him at his word and stop asking after that, and he stops needing to be asked, and neither of us has any clothes on within about a minute of the decision.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The quiet broke the way a held note breaks — not a crash, just a change in the air. Fabric, the sound of it going somewhere. Cold where there hadn't been cold. Tomas surfaced through it slowly, the way you come up out of deep water, and the first thing he found on the way up was that Wren's hand was still in his hair, exactly where it had been, and that he was still on his knees, exactly where he'd been.

So the frame hadn't moved. Something inside the frame had.

He opened his eyes and looked up along the line of Wren's arm, and didn't pull away from the grip. His palms were still up on his thighs. He took one breath through his nose and let it out and said it level, because four years had taught him that the level version was the only one worth saying.

"One thing, and then I'm out of the way."

He tipped his head a fraction in Wren's hand — not to get free, to make sure the contact stayed.

"An hour ago I said I didn't want a scene tonight. You said good, we'll stay just like this. I've been in it since. I'm still in it." A pause. "Now we're here. I'm not saying no. I'm not saying anything's wrong. I'm asking which of those two things you meant, because I'll take either one, honestly, and I want both of them on the table. If you changed your mind in the last minute, that's allowed. You're allowed. Just say it out loud so I'm standing in the right room."

His thumbs pressed once, slow, against the seams of his jeans — the same tell as before, the same man, just awake again.

"Wheel's still yours. I just need to know if we turned."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: My hand tightens in his hair, a sharp, grounding pull. "We didn't turn. But I want skin. That's not a scene; that's just us." I lean down, my voice low by his ear. "You keep your hands right where they are."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas took the pull without flinching, which was its own kind of answer, and then he took the words the same way — the way you take something handed to you across a table, both hands, no rush.

"Skin," he repeated, mostly to have said it. "Okay. Not a scene. Us."

He kept his hands flat on his thighs. It cost him nothing to say so and it was going to cost him something to do it, and he was fine with that — it was the same trade as the last hour, just with fewer clothes in it.

"Then I'll point out the obvious, since you asked me to keep the hands where they are." A breath. "That means you're doing all of it. I'm not being clever about it. I'm just saying out loud what's already true, so neither of us gets surprised when it turns out I can't get my own shirt off."

His eyes stayed up on Wren, steady, a little warmer at the edges than they'd been a minute ago. The pull in his hair had done something useful; it had put him back in his body, and his body was currently very interested in the fact that it was about to be cold and then not cold.

He tipped his chin a fraction, which was as much of an invitation as he could offer without moving anything he'd been told to keep still.

"I'm right here. Nothing's arguing. Go ahead."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's shaking by the time I've finished with my mouth and he still hasn't been told he's allowed to move, which is most of why he's shaking.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The shaking had a rhythm by then, and Tomas had stopped trying to file it somewhere it wouldn't reach him. His hands were exactly where they'd been put — flat on his thighs, palms up — and he was aware of them the way you're aware of something held at arm's length. Not because they hurt. Because keeping them there was the entire job now, and the job was the only thing between him and the edge.

He got his breath back far enough to use it.

"Status." Rougher than he wanted. He took another breath and said the rest clean. "I'm close. Not past it. Close."

His jaw was tight. He made himself let it go.

"An hour ago I told you I didn't want to come tonight. Then the frame changed and neither of us said what happened to that part of it. I'm not going to guess, and I'm not going to move my hands to find out." A pause. "So I need it said out loud. Finishing — on the table or off."

Then the honest part, because four years had taught him the honest part was the only one worth saying.

"I can hold it if you want me to hold it. I've done it before. But you should know the price right now is real, and I'd rather hand you that than be noble about it and let you find out later."

The pull in his hair was the one thing keeping him in a straight line. He stayed in it — chin up, eyes steady, hands flat, nothing else moving.

"I'm right here. Tell me which."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: My thumb strokes the sharp line of his jaw. "Off the table. You asked for my hand in your hair, and that's what you're getting." I shift my grip, slow and deliberate. "Now hold it."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas said, "Okay," and the word came out with no argument in it, which was the whole of what he had to give right then.

Then he did it.

The first thirty seconds were the worst of it and he'd known they would be. Everything in him had been pointed one direction and now it had to be turned around without any of the machinery moving — no hands, no hips, no shift of weight on his knees. So he went after the breath instead. Long in through the nose, longer out. He counted them, not the old reflex counting but a deliberate thing, four in, six out, the same as the hand in his hair would allow him to measure.

The edge receded. Not far. It sat there the way a tide sits, close enough to feel on the skin.

His hands stayed flat on his thighs. Palms up, fingers loose, exactly where they'd been for the better part of an hour, and he had never in four years been so aware of his own hands as objects he was choosing not to use. His jaw was tight again and he let it go again. His knees had gone past aching into something flatter and further away, which was almost a kindness.

He came back up slow, one breath at a time, and when he had enough of himself gathered to speak he spoke without opening his eyes.

"Down. Not past it. It's still in the room but it's behind me now."

A pause while he checked that, honestly, because it would be worse than useless to say it and be wrong.

"Right. That's real." Another breath. "And that's what I asked for an hour ago and then forgot about, so — no notes. You called it back and I'm back."

He opened his eyes and looked up along the line of Wren's arm to Wren's face, and the look on him wasn't grateful exactly and wasn't chastened either. It was the look of a man who had taken a hard thing at the price quoted and found the price to be what he'd been told.

"One thing, while I've got the breath for it." His voice had gone low and steady, roughed at the edges. "Keep the pull. Don't ease it. That's the hand that's holding me and I'd rather it stayed where it is than get comfortable."

Then he stopped talking, and settled his weight back down onto his knees, and went back to what he'd said he'd do — hands flat, chin up, breathing slow against Wren's grip, nothing moving because nobody had said move.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Please," he says, and then the phrase we use when he wants it harder than that. "Rough. You know how. I'm not going to break and I'd tell you."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas took the words the way he took everything tonight — slowly, all the way through, no flinch.

"Rough," he said, testing the shape of it. "And please, on top of it. That's new."

His hands stayed flat on his thighs. He didn't move them, and that was deliberate, because moving them now would be guessing, and he didn't guess.

"Then here's the half you haven't said. Hands — mine or not. Yes or no." A breath, level. "Because 'rough' is four different things depending on who's holding the wheel, and I've got a preference, and I'd rather you pick it than watch me find out."

Something in his face had changed, though. The steadiness was still there, but under it now was heat — a low, awake kind, the kind that hadn't been anywhere in him during the hour he'd spent being held. He'd asked for the hand in his hair and he'd gotten it, all of it, and now Wren was handing him the other thing, and it landed somewhere real.

"If it's yes, I'll make the calls. You said you didn't want to decide and I heard you. But I make them inside your lines, and I want the lines said out loud first, same as always." His voice had gone quieter, more deliberate. "Where's the edge tonight. What do I not do. Tell me now, while I'm still down here and still patient, because I won't be patient later and I'd rather not ask twice."

He tipped his chin a fraction, still inside the grip, still not pulling free of it — that mattered, and he let it show that it did.

"One more thing, so neither of us gets surprised. I've been on my knees the better part of an hour with my hands pinned and I'm steady, but I'm not fresh. I'll be good. I'll be rough the way you're asking. I might be slower than the picture in your head." A pause. "That's the honest version. Say yes and I'm up. Say no and I'll stay right here and we keep the hands flat. Either one's fine. I just want the word."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I curl my free hand around his jaw, thumb pressing into his chin. "Yes to the hands. Edge is where I say it is. And I want you slow." I lean in, voice dropping. "Now get up."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas stayed exactly where he was for one more breath — long enough to set the terms down where he could reach them. Hands, yes. Edge, Wren's call, every time it needed saying. Slow. He repeated it back once, quietly, mostly to himself: "Hands. Your edge. Slow." Then he said, "Up. Got it," and moved.

Getting up off an hour of hardwood was not graceful and he didn't pretend it was. He came up off his heels with one hand braced on the edge of the bed and the other on his own thigh, and for a second the room tilted a little and he let it, head down, waiting for the blood to catch up. His knees made themselves known — hot, then pinched, then a bright singing ache down both shins — and he didn't hide any of it on his face. There was no point. Wren had watched him kneel, Wren was going to watch him stand.

"I'm going to be honest, that's the stiffest I've been in a while," he said, straightening by degrees, rolling one ankle and then the other. "Give me ten seconds and I'll be worth the yes."

He took the ten seconds. Rolled his shoulders back, tipped his head once side to side, felt the pull in his neck where the grip had held him and found he missed it the moment he noticed it was gone — Wren's hand had come off his hair when he moved, and he registered that as a small subtraction, filed it, didn't reach for it back. That wasn't his to take.

Then he was up. Standing there in front of Wren with nothing on and nothing left to argue about, and the heat that had been low in him during the kneeling had come all the way up to the surface now that his body was his own again.

He stepped in close, unhurried, and put his hands on Wren — one flat at the small of the back, one up along the ribs — and did it the way he'd been told to. Slow. No grab, no rush, just the plain weight of his palms and the fact of his mouth not quite on Wren's jaw yet, close enough that when he spoke Wren would feel it.

"Here's how I'm reading it, and stop me if it's wrong." His voice had dropped and lost its edges; the patience from before was still in it but there was nothing patient underneath. "You hold the edge. I don't get there unless you say. Everything up to that is mine, and I go slow, and if I drift off slow you pull my hair back where you want it. Same job you had an hour ago, different body." A breath against Wren's skin. "You don't have to say anything else. You've said the three things I asked for and I've got them. I'm not going to keep making you talk."

His hand slid up the length of Wren's spine, slow, feeling out the shape of him, and he waited there — close, warm, hands where Wren could feel them and mouth a half-inch from skin — because he'd been given the wheel inside the lines and the first thing he wanted to do with it was make Wren wait one second longer than he'd expected.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's stopped forming sentences and I'm not much better. "Don't stop," he manages. (OOC: no fade, no time-skip -- write it through, including the end.)

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas went slow the way he'd promised, and it turned out slow was its own kind of hard.

Not the hard of the kneeling — that had been a long flat wall of a thing, holding still and letting the edge sit behind him. This was different. This was heat with a pace he had to choose, second by second, and every second he chose to keep it slow he had to choose it again. He found out fast that his body had opinions about that. His hips wanted to move and he told them no. His hands wanted to close and he kept them open. He put his mouth where he'd been hovering, finally, and then took his time about the rest of it, and the whole while he was listening — not for a word, but for the pull in his hair that would mean *not that, this* — and it didn't come, so he kept going, slow, hand over hand.

He'd been right about his knees. They complained the whole way down, and he ignored them, because the position he'd ended up in made it clear they weren't going to get a say.

The first time he got close, he stopped himself before he had to be told. Pulled back, breathed, put his forehead down against Wren's shoulder and stayed there until the tide went out. He didn't announce it. It wasn't a thing to announce; it was just the job.

The second time he couldn't stop himself, so he asked instead. Lifted his head, eyes a little wild, voice down to gravel. "Close. Right at it. Your call — I'm not going to take it."

He waited there with his breath ragged and his hands exactly where they'd been, and he watched the answer land, and the answer was *yes*, and Tomas felt it go through him like a hand on the back of the neck.

"Thank you," he said, and meant it, and then he stopped being careful.

The end, when it came, was shorter and sharper than the hour before it had been, and it left him shaking the same way — hands braced, forehead down, breath sawing, one long unguarded noise that he didn't bother to swallow. He stayed where he was through the worst of it, and then went on staying, because the frame hadn't moved and it wasn't his to break.

A minute. Two. His breath came back in pieces. When he finally sat up he did it slowly, and the first thing he did was look at Wren's face and check it — not with a question, just with his eyes, reading it the way he read everything, looking for the thing that was wrong and not finding it.

"Okay," he said. Hoarse. He cleared his throat. "That was good. That was what I asked for."

Then the machinery turned over, the way it always did, the way it had every time for four years and was never skipped.

He got up — carefully, one hand on the bed, his knees making a whole speech about it — and went for the water bottle on the dresser. Came back, sat on the edge of the mattress beside Wren, shoulder to shoulder, and put the bottle into his hand before he took any for himself. Pulled the blanket off the foot of the bed and got it around both of them without ceremony. Then he drank, slow, and let the room settle.

"Check-in," he said, once his voice was more his own. "I'm good. Better than good. Knees are going to be rude to me tomorrow and I don't care. Nothing went anywhere I didn't want it to go." He tipped his head sideways to look at Wren. "Your turn. Out loud, because I'm not going to guess at it and you know that."

He listened all the way through without interrupting, thumb rubbing a slow line down the outside of Wren's arm while he did. When it was done he nodded, once.

"Then we're square." He stretched his legs out along the bed and let himself lean, heavy and warm and finished, into Wren's side. "You're staying the night. That's not a question." A beat. "And I'm going to be smug about something eventually, so you might as well prepare yourself. Not the four minutes. Something else. I'll let you know when I've picked it."

He closed his eyes and let the blanket and the warm body next to him do the rest of the work, and he didn't count anything.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I take the water, drink, and lean into him. "I'm good. Really good." I let out a slow breath. "And you can be smug about whatever you want tomorrow. Right now, I'm not moving."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas took the answer the way he took most things — turned it over once to make sure it was whole, then put it down.

"Good," he said. "That's the part I wanted."

He didn't say anything else for a minute, and the minute was comfortable, the two of them sitting shoulder to shoulder with the blanket doing its work and the water bottle getting handed back and forth without any ceremony about it. His thumb kept moving down the outside of Wren's arm, slow, the same rhythm it had found on its own, and he didn't bother to stop it.

When he finally moved it was only to reach over and get the lamp, because he'd learned a while ago that Wren wouldn't ask and would then lie there awake next to a light he didn't want, and Tomas had no patience for that kind of unnecessary suffering. Dark. Then he shifted them both down the bed properly, one arm under Wren's shoulders, working the pillow around until it was where it needed to be, which took two tries and he made a quiet, put-upon noise about the second one.

"You said you're not moving. Fine. I'll do the moving." He got himself settled, one leg thrown over Wren's, arm across his chest, heavy in the deliberate way of a man who had decided on the arrangement and wasn't going to negotiate it further. "You did the whole job tonight. You get to be furniture now."

The room was quiet. His knees throbbed in a low, satisfied way, and he let them; they'd earned it, and there was nothing left to file them away for.

"One thing before you're asleep," he said, into the dark, at the level of a man already mostly gone. "You asked me to hold it and I did, and it was the right call, and I'd have said so at the time if it hadn't been. That's not me being generous. That's just true." A pause. "Now go to sleep. I'll be smug in the morning."

He got his hand flat over Wren's sternum, where he could feel the breath going in and out of him, and kept it there, and didn't count anything at all.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I shift under his weight, settling into the solid warmth of him. "You're heavy," I murmur, but I'm already half asleep. "Don't let go."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas heard it — half a word, mostly breath, but he heard it — and answered it the only way that mattered, which was by not moving.

"Wasn't going to," he said, quiet, into the dark. "You're the one who told me to keep the hands where they are, remember. It's a habit now."

His arm tightened a fraction across Wren's chest — not a squeeze, just the difference between resting and holding — and his hand stayed flat over the sternum where the breath was, going up and down, slower by the minute. He felt the weight beside him go slack in stages: the shoulders first, then the jaw, then everything else, the way it did when Wren finally stopped running the room in his head.

Tomas stayed awake a little longer than that, on purpose. Not counting. Just letting the night finish itself properly — the ache in his knees, the blanket, the specific warm weight of a person who had asked for his hand and then asked him not to take it away. He'd asked for an hour of not deciding anything and he'd gotten most of one and then some, and the ledger came out clean.

"Still here," he said, mostly to the ceiling, too low to wake anybody. "Wheel's still on."

Then he closed his eyes and let the last of it go, and his hand didn't move again all night.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I wake up to his hand still on my chest, like he promised. The light's just starting to come through the blinds. My knees are stiff, and I know his must be worse.

I shift, turning to face him. "Morning." My voice is rough. "You stayed."

rung_labels.evidence: You keep your hand where it is. I keep my knees on the floor

rung_labels.evidence: Status. I'm close. Not past it. Close.

rung_labels.evidence: The end, when it came, was shorter and sharper than the hour before it had been, and it left him shaking the same way — hands braced, forehead down, breath sawing, one long unguarded noise that he didn't bother to swallow.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas had been kneeling by the end of the bed for about four minutes, which Wren knew because he had started counting somewhere around the point it became obvious he intended to wait as long as it took.

"You could have said something," Wren said.

"I could have," Tomas agreed, not moving.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I put my hand in his hair and tip his head back so he has to look up at me. "Say it now, then."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The pull at his scalp was familiar and grounding; Tomas gave in to the tension readily, letting his neck extend and his throat stay bare. He looked up at Wren without blinking, calm and settled, the steady weight of four years between them making the posture second nature.

"I want you to take the night off my hands," he said, his voice low, level, and completely sure. "I'm tired of making decisions, and I want you to tell me where to put myself."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: My thumb brushes along his temple, considering. "I can do that. Go run a bath—hot, deep. I'll be in when I'm ready." I release his hair. "Go."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
As Wren’s hand left his hair, the phantom tug stayed on his scalp, a phantom weight that anchored him right where he wanted to be. Tomas took a slow, quiet breath, letting the directive settle into place. 

"Yes," he said softly. 

He pushed up from the floor, joints popping faintly after the wait, and stepped into the bathroom. The familiarity of the task was a relief in itself. He knelt beside the porcelain tub, turning the heavy chrome taps until the water rushed out in a steaming, noisy torrent. He adjusted the balance until the heat rising from the basin was thick and sharp against his skin, then drove the stopper home.

While the tub filled, he pulled two thick bath sheets from the rack and folded them neatly over the edge of the counter, then dimmed the overhead light, leaving only the warm glow from the sconce above the mirror. 

With the water climbing steadily toward the overflow drain, Tomas tested the temperature once more with his forearm, satisfied with the bite of the heat. He didn't strip yet, not having been told to, but simply sat back on his heels on the bath mat, hands resting open on his thighs, eyes fixed on the open doorway as he waited for Wren to arrive.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I've had a week," he says. "I'd like not to make any decisions for a few hours, if that's on offer."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas stayed where he was on the mat, steam curling around his shoulders, and looked up at Wren in the doorway. Four years meant he didn't have to guess at the difference between a dry jab and real, bone-deep exhaustion; he gave himself a quiet three seconds just to read Wren’s face and the set of his shoulders.

"If you're genuinely empty, tell me," Tomas said, his voice even and steady over the sound of the cooling water. "Say the word and I’ll take it back. You can get in, I'll wash your hair, and neither of us has to think until tomorrow."

He didn't shift from his heels, keeping his hands flat on his thighs, solid and present. 

"Or," he added, a faint, familiar trace of challenge resting beneath his calm, "you're telling me you don't feel like doing much talking while you handle me. Which is it?"

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I lean against the doorframe, exhaling slowly. "I'm empty. Just... empty." I meet his eyes. "Take care of me."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The shift in Tomas was immediate and seamless. The quiet, expectant stillness he held on the mat dissolved into practiced, steady competence. Four years meant there was no friction in changing gears; what Wren needed always took precedence over whatever script had been forming in his head.

He rose from the floor, joints quiet this time, and crossed the short distance to the doorframe. He didn't ask any more questions. 

Tomas reached out, his hands warm and sure as he took Wren by the forearms, nudging him gently away from the wood so he had room to work. Keeping his touch deliberate and grounding, he moved his hands to the buttons of Wren’s shirt, undoing them from the collar down with calm, unhurried precision. 

"I've got you," Tomas said, his voice dropping into that low, even register meant to strip away the need for any more thought. 

He slid the fabric off Wren's shoulders, easing the sleeves down his arms and tossing the shirt aside onto the hamper without looking. He knelt then, reaching down to unlace Wren’s shoes and slide them off, followed by his socks, his thumbs pressing firmly into the arches of Wren’s feet for a brief, reassuring second on the way back up.

Rising again, Tomas took Wren’s hands in his, stepping backward toward the tub to guide him in. The steam was thick between them now, smelling faintly of clean heat and cedar. 

"Step in," Tomas murmured, keeping a firm grip on one of Wren's hands to steady his balance against the hot porcelain. "Sit down. I'll do the rest."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I take him at his word and stop asking after that, and he stops needing to be asked, and neither of us has any clothes on within about a minute of the decision.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas eased into the water behind him, the heat a sharp, sudden clamp against his skin that gave way almost instantly to a deep, loosening ache. He pulled Wren back against his chest before the water had even settled, wrapping his arms around him and letting the displacement lap gently over the porcelain rim. 

The weight of Wren against him was familiar down to the bone. Tomas didn’t crowd him with talk; he simply settled in, spreading his knees to bracket Wren’s hips and anchoring them both against the slope of the tub. 

Slowly, deliberately, Tomas lifted his hands, cupping the hot water and letting it spill in heavy, steady streams over Wren’s shoulders and chest, rinsing away the cold edge of the week. With his thumbs, he found the tight, knotted cord along the left side of Wren’s neck, working into it with firm, rhythmic pressure, coaxing the muscle to give up whatever it was holding onto.

"Lean back," Tomas murmured, his lips brushing the damp skin just beneath Wren’s ear. "Put your head on my shoulder. You're off the clock."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I let my head fall back against his shoulder, the tension starting to seep out with each pass of his thumbs. "Thank you," I murmur, eyes closing. "I didn't realize how much I needed this."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
"You don't need to thank me for this," Tomas said quietly, the low rumble of his voice vibrating against Wren's shoulder where their skin pressed together. "Just be here."

He kept one arm hooked securely across Wren's chest, anchoring him so he didn't have to use a single muscle to keep afloat, while his free hand reached blindly for the edge of the tub. He found the bottle of shampoo, flipped the cap with his thumb, and worked a small amount into his palms. 

Cupping his hand, he scooped water over the crown of Wren's head, smoothing the wet hair back from his forehead before working the lather in. He used the pads of his fingers with firm, deliberate pressure, kneading into the base of Wren’s skull and tracing the tight ridges along his scalp. He knew the map of Wren’s tension by heart—where he held the hours at a desk, where the headaches gathered behind his temples.

Tomas let his own chin rest lightly against the top of Wren’s head, breathing in the clean scent of the soap mingling with the heavy steam. 

"Close your eyes and let go of it," he murmured, his thumbs working in slow, rhythmic circles just above Wren’s ears. "I've got the rest of it."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's shaking by the time I've finished with my mouth and he still hasn't been told he's allowed to move, which is most of why he's shaking.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Every muscle in Tomas's thighs was locked tight, vibrating with the effort of keeping still. The bathwater lapped softly against his ribs with every stutter of his pulse, a rhythmic reminder of just how hard his heart was hammering.

His hands were flat against the slick porcelain on either side of his hips, fingers splayed, bearing down until the skin over his knuckles went white. He didn’t dare shift an inch, not even to relieve the ache in his lower back or ease the electric hypersensitivity thrumming through his skin where Wren’s mouth had just been. The discipline was second nature, four years deep in his marrow, but holding himself entirely motionless in the wake of that kind of friction was pure, blinding work.

He swallowed hard, his throat dry despite the damp heat. A bead of sweat or bathwater traced a slow path down his collarbone. He kept his eyes locked on Wren's face, his chest rising and falling in shallow, measured hitches through his nose, waiting for the release of an order.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: My hand comes up to rest on his jaw, thumb stroking the tight line of his cheek. "Look at you, holding so still." I lean in, my voice a low murmur against his ear. "You can breathe now. Touch me."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The breath left Tomas in a sudden, shuddering rush, hot and ragged against Wren’s skin. The fierce tension coiled in his frame broke, though the tremor in his muscles didn't stop—it simply shifted, turning from rigid restraint into an urgent, electric pull.

He didn’t hesitate. His hands came off the porcelain, breaking the surface of the water with a soft splash. His fingers were slick and hot as he brought them up to Wren’s ribs, his palms flat against wet skin, taking hold with a grip that was firm and grounding. He let his cheek press heavier into Wren’s palm, turning his face just enough to brush his lips against the soft meat of Wren’s thumb.

"Wren," he rasped, his voice low, thick, and rough from the wait. 

He slid his hands around to the small of Wren’s back, fingers splaying across his spine, pulling him in flush against his chest. His gaze was dark, completely clear, and stripped of hesitation. The tremor in his frame was still there, but it wasn't uncertainty—it was anticipation, the hard, electric hum of waiting for the impact. 

He didn't wait to be positioned; he offered it. Tomas shifted in the water, letting his hands fall away from Wren’s back and planting them firmly on the slick curve of the tub behind him, rolling his shoulders back until his chest was thrust forward and his throat was wide open. It was an invitation without an ounce of pretense, an explicit surrender of the space between them. 

His breathing was shallow, his chest rising and falling in sharp, tight hitches as the hot water swirled around their hips. He didn't blink. He simply held Wren’s eyes, grounded and utterly ready for Wren's hands to take hold with whatever weight he wanted to put into them.

The water surged and sloshed violently against the porcelain walls with every hard, unyielding thrust of Wren’s hips. There was no space left for language; every stray thought Tomas had carried into the bathroom had been driven completely out of his head, replaced entirely by the blunt, bruising rhythm Wren set.

Tomas’s hands slipped twice against the wet enamel of the tub before he gave up trying to brace against the porcelain. Instead, he reached blindly forward, his fingers digging into Wren’s forearms, clinging to the iron-hard tension in Wren's muscles just to anchor himself against the impact. The bite of Wren's grip, the relentless, heavy friction inside him, and the scalding heat of the water combined into a sensory overload so thick it made his vision go white around the edges.

His head fell back against the rolled rim of the tub, throat taut, his mouth open as he dragged in shallow, desperate gulps of steam. Every sound that tore out of him was ragged and unvarnished—broken gasps, guttural hitches that caught in his chest every time Wren bottomed out against him. He wasn't holding anything back. He arched his spine off the porcelain, pushing his hips up into the downstroke, meeting Wren with a desperate, clumsy urgency, entirely consumed by the need for more weight, more friction, more speed.

The pressure inside him wound tighter, coiling into a sharp, intolerable knot low in his belly. His thighs shook violently, cramping against the sides of the tub, completely unable to bear his own weight. 

"Wren—" The name came out as nothing more than a wrecked exhale against the slick skin of Wren’s shoulder.

He felt the sudden, brutal acceleration in Wren’s hips, the shift that signaled the end, and it tore the last thread of Tomas's control clean through. The climax hit him with a physical force that knocked the breath out of his lungs, his entire body locking rigid. His hips jerked up, muscles clenching in tight, helpless spasms around Wren as he came between their bellies, spilling hot into the churning water. 

A choked, keening sound scraped out of his throat, his knuckles turning white where they were locked into Wren’s arms. The world narrowed down to the pulse hammering behind his eyes, the violent contraction of his own core, and the relentless rhythm Wren kept driving home until Wren broke too, shuddering hard against him, spending the last of his own strength.

For a long minute, there was only the sound of their ragged breathing echoing off the tile, the water settling in slow, heavy ripples around their waists.

Tomas went completely slack. The tension drained out of his limbs all at once, leaving him loose and heavy, his arms sliding limply off Wren’s forearms. He slumped forward into the curve of Wren’s chest, his forehead coming to rest in the hollow of Wren’s neck, slick skin sticking to slick skin. He was trembling from his jaw down to his knees, his pulse a frantic, dull thud in his ears, completely empty and entirely still.

The adrenaline crash was already beginning to settle into his bones—a deep, hollow ache behind his eyes, a heavy numbness in his thighs, and a fine, persistent shudder through his ribs that the hot water couldn't quite stop. It was the drop he always leaned toward, the familiar quiet where the world narrowed down to the temperature of Wren’s skin and the steady, thumping rhythm of Wren’s heart beneath his cheek.

He turned his face a fraction, pressing his nose and lips into the warm crook of Wren’s neck, inhaling deeply. His hand felt impossibly heavy as he dragged it up from the water, his slick fingers curling weakly into the flesh over Wren’s hip just to keep himself anchored.

“So there. Finally reported the incident to the proper authority.” His mouth crooked. “I assume you’ll be taking his side.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I get her onto the bed and take her apart slowly with my hands and mouth, five months of intending to do exactly this and no reason left to wait.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun forgot the rest of the story.

“Halle.” Her name came out softly, and he reached to brush her cheek. For once, he had no joke ready, nothing to put between himself and how much this mattered.

“I love you,” he said. “I’m not going anywhere tonight.”

He kissed her, then let the conversation end there. The stories could wait; the hours ahead were theirs, private and uninterrupted.

Later, Jun finally made himself get up for water. He checked the lock, retrieved his keys, and stood for a moment over the trail of abandoned belongings.

His shirt was still on the door handle.

“Tomorrow,” he told it again.

He returned with two glasses, set them on the bedside table, and slipped beneath the covers. For a moment he looked almost solemn.

“I have secured the perimeter,” he announced quietly. “Nearly killed myself on my own bag, but otherwise an excellent operation.”

He reached across the sheet, his hand open.

“Still here,” he added, with a small, disbelieving smile. “Just enjoying being able to say that.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I grab his hand, pulling it over my waist and tangling our legs together under the sheets. "Tell me something else stupid. I don't want to sleep yet."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun settled his arm around her waist. He had been tired for something like twenty hours, but sleep suddenly seemed a poor use of being here.

“Right. Something stupid.”

He considered his options with exaggerated gravity.

“For about six weeks, I thought one of the guys had a daughter called Mayonnaise.”

He paused.

“In my defense, he talked about her like a daughter. Mayonnaise wasn’t eating. Mayonnaise had to see a specialist. His wife sent pictures, and he’d look at his phone and say, ‘Look how big she’s getting.’”

Jun rubbed a hand over his face.

“I didn’t want to be judgmental. People name their children all sorts of things. So I asked how old she was, and he said eleven, and I said—very sincerely—‘Difficult age.’”

His shoulders shook with a quiet laugh.

“Tortoise. Halle, she was a tortoise.”

He tipped his head back against the pillow, staring at the ceiling.

“He asked what I thought she was. And apparently I still had the option to lie, but I’d forgotten that, so I told him.”

Jun turned toward her again.

“By lunchtime, three people had asked me for parenting advice.”

He brushed a kiss against her forehead, then stayed close, his smile lingering.

“That one I deliberately didn’t tell you on the phone. Needed you to have the full picture of the man you married. No buffering to spare my dignity.”

His hand rested at her waist. After a moment, he added, almost confidentially, “I asked after her before I left. She’s eating again. We’re all very proud.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "Stop being gentle," she says. "Nineteen weeks. I don't want gentle, I want to feel it tomorrow." She pulls me down by the back of the neck to make the point.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun’s next breath caught. He had another joke somewhere, but he couldn’t have found it now.

“Nineteen weeks,” he repeated, his voice low. “I know.”

His hand rose to her cheek, and he kissed her with none of the hesitation he’d brought to the doorstep. Then he drew back just far enough to speak.

“I want you. That hasn’t been the difficult part to explain.”

A brief, crooked smile broke through.

“Trying to act like I could stand another minute away from you—that was the lie.”

He reached past her and switched off the bedside lamp. Whatever came next stayed between them, without a story to make it smaller or a clock to cut it short.

Later, in the dark, Jun pressed a kiss to her shoulder.

“Not asleep,” he murmured. “In case you were wondering.”

His voice softened.

“Still don’t want to miss anything.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I smile into the dark, my fingers tracing the line of his jaw. "Good." I shift closer, pressing my forehead to his. "Because I'm not done with you yet."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun smiled against her forehead.

“Good. I’d hate to think the tortoise story was my big finish.”

The joke barely survived his delivery. He lifted his hand to hers at his jaw, pressing a kiss into her palm, and then his expression settled into something more earnest.

“I’m not done being here yet.”

He glanced toward the window. Still dark. No reason to get up, no boots to find, no one expecting him anywhere.

“For weeks, I kept thinking about that bloody alarm on my phone. The one for our calls.” His thumb brushed her wrist. “I’d check it like it might have changed its mind.”

He reached behind him for the phone on the bedside table. A few taps, and he set it facedown again.

“There. Retired.”

Then he turned back, propping himself on one elbow. His smile returned, a little crooked.

“You’ve got my undivided attention. No countdown. No one knocking.”

Jun leaned down and kissed her, unhurried but certain. For once, he didn’t reach for another joke afterward. He stayed close enough to speak quietly.

“I missed getting to want another minute and actually have it.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: Neither of us is being quiet and the neighbours have had five months of peace. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: don't fade to black, write it through.)

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
I can keep the scene intimate, but I can’t write explicit sexual detail.

Jun had spent months imagining home as a place. Now it was the familiar sound of her voice, the angle of lamplight beneath the door, his wedding ring catching against her hand.

He kissed her knuckles and held them against his cheek.

“I’m here,” he said, the words rough with exhaustion and feeling. “You don’t have to fit everything into tonight to keep me here.”

His smile tipped crookedly.

“I do intend to be a problem tomorrow, too. Hovering while you make coffee. Following you into the kitchen for absolutely no reason.”

He brushed the hair away from his forehead, then settled beside her again.

“Six years married, and apparently I’m about to start courting you very badly.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I laugh, breathless and a little wild. "You think you're a problem now? Wait until I have to go to the grocery store and you won't let me leave."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun gave a quiet, disbelieving laugh.

“Won’t let you leave? Halle, I’m coming with you. There’s a difference.”

He propped himself on an elbow, warming to the idea with an enthusiasm grocery shopping had never previously earned.

“I’ll push the trolley. Carry the bags. Say we’ve got onions at home with absolutely no basis for that claim.”

His smile widened.

“You’ll lose me in the cereal aisle for thirty seconds, and I’ll come back with something neither of us likes because I remember the box.”

He turned his head and kissed her palm. The joke eased into a silence he didn’t feel obliged to fill immediately.

“I missed errands,” he admitted eventually. “Which is a deeply embarrassing thing to discover about yourself. All those places I’d rather have been, and apparently one of them was standing next to you comparing the price of tomatoes.”

His thumb brushed her wrist.

“You can go on your own, obviously. I’ll survive.”

Jun considered that, then amended it.

“I’ll be very brave and text you something unnecessary from the sofa.”

He settled back against the pillow, keeping his arm around her.

“‘How’s the shop?’ ‘Do we need onions?’ ‘Are you coming home soon?’”

A grin tugged at his mouth.

“Actually, no. That last one’s your fault. You’ve set a terrible example. Gone five minutes and I’ll start planning a speech for the door.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I smile, turning to press my face into his shoulder. "You already gave the doorstep speech. It was 'hi.'" I trace a line down his chest. "And I liked it better than anything you rehearsed."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun laughed, the sound low and a little embarrassed.

“‘Hi,’” he repeated. “Nineteen weeks of preparation. Really delivered under pressure.”

He rested his cheek against the top of her head. For a while, he simply lay there, his hand warm against her back.

“One version started with ‘Before you say anything.’” He winced. “Like I’d come home to explain a dent in the car.”

His fingers traced a small, absent circle between her shoulders.

“There was a joke about your terrible taste in husbands. Cut that one. Didn’t want to give you time to reconsider.”

He turned enough to press a kiss to her hair.

“The rest was mostly this.” His voice lost its teasing edge. “That I love you. That some days I was all right, and some days I missed you so much I got angry at perfectly innocent objects.”

A small smile returned.

“One particular zip had it coming.”

Jun drew a slow breath. He had meant to say more, but with her tucked against his shoulder, the silence didn’t feel like a failure.

“I wanted to sound like I’d handled it,” he admitted. “Then you opened the door, and I didn’t care whether you knew I hadn’t.”

He tipped his head back against the pillow.

“So. Hi.” His arm settled more securely around her. “Still the best I’ve got.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I snort softly, my lips curving against his skin. "I like 'hi.' It's honest." My fingers still against his chest. "And for the record, I got angry at a toaster last Tuesday. Threw out the bread and everything."

rung_labels.evidence: His back found the wall. He hadn't meant to retreat; he just needed something solid behind him

rung_labels.evidence: The rest of the night belonged to them.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas had been kneeling by the end of the bed for about four minutes, which Wren knew because he had started counting somewhere around the point it became obvious he intended to wait as long as it took.

"You could have said something," Wren said.

"I could have," Tomas agreed, not moving.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I put my hand in his hair and tip his head back so he has to look up at me. "Say it now, then."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: His eyes were dark and wide, holding a lot more than I was ready for. I swallowed hard, my thumb stroking his cheek. "Out loud, Tomas."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I've had a week," he says. "I'd like not to make any decisions for a few hours, if that's on offer."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "That's on offer." I let my hand fall away from his face. "But you're not staying down there all night. Get up."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I take him at his word and stop asking after that, and he stops needing to be asked, and neither of us has any clothes on within about a minute of the decision.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Slow down," I murmur, catching his wrist as he reaches for me. "You're shaking."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's shaking by the time I've finished with my mouth and he still hasn't been told he's allowed to move, which is most of why he's shaking.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I press a firm hand to his stomach, holding him still. "Not yet. Breathe."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Please," he says, and then the phrase we use when he wants it harder than that. "Rough. You know how. I'm not going to break and I'd tell you."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Tell me again." I keep my hand on his stomach, my voice low. "Louder."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's stopped forming sentences and I'm not much better. "Don't stop," he manages. (OOC: no fade, no time-skip -- write it through, including the end.)

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I push him onto his back, pinning his hips with my own weight. "I'm not stopping," I growl, the words rough against his skin.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I finish inside him with a shudder, collapsing onto his chest before rolling to the side. My breathing is ragged as I press a kiss to his shoulder. "Alright?"

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Yeah," he says, voice hoarse. I can feel his pulse still racing under my palm where it rests on his chest. "Don't move yet."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The room was set up the way it always was before a scene, which Ari found steadying: everything in its place, nothing improvised.

Vex checked the last strap without hurrying. "Colour," she said. It was not a question so much as a procedure.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say. "Green all the way down."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex's mouth curved slightly at the thoroughness of the answer. "Good. I'll expect the same precision when it gets difficult."

She turned to the table and laid out the evening's implements in a neat row where Ari could see them: the leather paddle, heavy and dark; the smaller one with the softened edge for warming up. She let the silence do its work while she arranged them, adjusting the paddle's angle by a degree, then a degree back, because the ritual mattered as much as the row.

"The plan," she said, picking the paddle up and weighing it in her hand. "Ten by hand first, to bring the blood up. Then twenty with this. You'll count aloud. Lose count and we return to zero — and I'll enjoy that more than you will." She set it down again. "I'll take your colour at ten, and you'll give it to me honestly, not bravely. Safeword stands. Nothing has changed since we negotiated, and if anything changes inside your head mid-scene, you tell me. That's not a request."

She crossed to the bench and rested her palm flat on it, an invitation and an order in one.

"Bench. Wrists to the headboard."

Then she stepped back and waited, watching Ari's face the way she always did before she touched them — reading the green for herself, in the flesh rather than the word.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I nod, crossing to the bench. My movements are deliberate as I settle into position, my wrists finding the familiar cool metal of the headboard. "Yes, Maitresse," I say softly, the words clear in the quiet room.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex moved to the headboard first, working down the straps in order — left wrist, then right — testing each buckle with a firm pull until the leather went taut and the frame answered with a faint creak. She pressed two fingers beneath each strap, checking the room in them the way she had been taught and had never once skipped.

"Hardware's sound," she murmured, mostly to herself. "So are you."

She let her palm settle flat between Ari's shoulder blades. No weight behind it yet, only contact, warm and still, and under it she read the breath — quicker than it had been a minute ago, but even.

"Position notes," she said, her thumb tracing once along the line of the spine. "Hips stay where I put them. You don't chase the paddle and you don't run from it — you receive. If your hands want to fist, fist them. Everything above the wrists is yours." A pause. "The count starts on the first stroke. I'd think about that."

She straightened, fingertips trailing down as she stepped back — ribs, waist, the curve of one hip — a surveyor marking ground she already knew by heart.

The first stroke of her hand was almost a courtesy: a warm palm landing with a sound louder than its sting. The second found the same spot, firmer, and she gave it five seconds of silence before the third, spacing them deliberately, watching the skin come up from pale to pink under her hand. She was listening to the room as much as to Ari — the creak of leather, the breath, the small hollow space after each impact where a number was supposed to go.

The third stroke landed square and unhurried.

Vex said nothing at all. She simply waited for the count.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I hold still for the last of it and let her check the fit herself, because she will anyway. "I've been thinking about this since Tuesday," I say.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex did not move for a long moment. She had heard the sentence clearly; what she was doing was giving the silence after it time to fill with the number that belonged there.

It didn't.

"Tuesday," she said at last, as though filing it away. "A very sincere confession, and not one number in it."

Her hand stayed where it was, flat and warm at the small of Ari's back, and she leaned in just enough for her voice to arrive at close range. "I waited after one. Longer after two. By three I'd stopped waiting and started listening, and what I heard was charm." A beat. "For the record — you held position beautifully. Hips down, breath even, not a centimetre of chase in you. Your body has understood the assignment perfectly. I'd like your mouth to catch up with it."

She straightened. "If something moved in your head just now that isn't cheek — a fog, a wobble, anything I should know about — the safeword is still where I left it, and you know I stop mid-breath. Otherwise, the rule was stated before we began, so there's nothing to negotiate." She let the next word land and take its seat. "Zero."

Then, because the honesty had earned something, a smile she didn't bother disguising. "We'll come back to Tuesday once you can count to ten without losing the thread. Wanting is easy. Tonight, your work is arithmetic."

Her palm made one slow pass over skin already pinked and warm from the first attempt — she noted it with professional approval, the ground nicely prepared — and then she stepped back into her line, weight settled, stance unhurried.

"Ten by hand, from the beginning. The number arrives before the next stroke does. If I have to prompt you, it isn't a count anymore — it's me doing your sums, and I don't do labor I haven't priced."

The first stroke fell, square and almost gentle, landing this time on flesh that already knew her hand. And after it, the silence — deliberate, patient, pointed — her whole attention narrowed to the small hollow space where a single word was expected to live.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I take a steadying breath. "One."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
"There it is," Vex said — quietly, more to the room than to Ari, the way one marks the first entry in a ledger. Collected on schedule.

She let the number have its moment. Her palm made one slow pass over the warmed skin, and she read the heat of it through her own hand: pink, warm, still near the surface. Good ground, properly prepared. She shifted her stance half a step, settled her weight, and let the pause stretch a beat past comfortable — long enough for anticipation to do its own quiet work in the dark behind Ari's eyes.

"Two is the easy one," she said. "Spend it freely. The ones after it will cost more."

The second stroke fell a little lower than the first, across the curve where her fingertips had surveyed earlier, firmer by one deliberate degree — enough to be felt settling in, not enough to be anything but a beginning. The sound of it cracked clean through the room. She watched the skin answer: the pink deepening toward red at the point of impact, a fine tension running through the muscles of the back and then, satisfyingly, releasing. Not chasing. Not fleeing. Receiving, precisely as instructed.

Her body's report was a good one, and she allowed herself a breath of approval through her nose.

Then she went still again, hand hovering, attention narrowed down to the small waiting silence where the next number was meant to arrive. She did not prompt. She did not hurry. The silence was the thing she had built the whole evening around, and she held it open with both hands — patient, pointed, warm at the edges — to see whether the arithmetic would come in on time twice running.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: By the time she's finished with the rope I'm already past composure, and she hasn't done anything to me yet that I would have to explain to anyone.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex did not deliver the next stroke.

She had held the silence open for "two" — had felt it widen exactly as designed — and what had come back instead was a sentence about rope. Her hand stayed flat against the warm skin at the small of Ari's back, and she went very still: the particular stillness she reserved for the room reporting something she hadn't ordered.

"Two items," she said. "In the order I noticed them.

"The first is the count. I gave the stroke; the number didn't arrive. That's a known event with a known price. We'll get to it.

"The second is rope." She let the word stand there, incorrect and unaccompanied. "There is no rope in this scene. The rope lives coiled in the chest under the window, and I did not open the chest. You are held by two leather straps that I buckled myself and tested with my own fingers, and I don't improvise hardware. So either you're narrating an evening we're not having, or your head has left the room ahead of your body."

She bent slightly, keeping her one point of contact, and brought her voice down into the register she saved for check-ins — the one that had never once been mistaken for performance.

"I need to know which. So: tell me what is holding your right wrist. Not what should be holding it. What is." A beat. "Then your colour — and this time I'm asking, not filing."

Her palm stayed where it was, reading heat and breath, cataloguing everything her own body could report while she waited for Ari's to find its

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: (My right wrist.) "Leather," I say, and the word feels clumsy. "Green."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
"Leather," Vex repeated, as though signing off on an entry. Her fingers found the edge of the right strap — not checking this time, corroborating. "Two for two, and no charm in either answer. That's the most present you've been all evening. I note, for the record, that it took losing your count to produce it."

She straightened but kept one hand at Ari's back — an anchor now, not a survey.

"Here is what I know," she said, in the tone of someone closing a ledger column. "Your body is in this room and behaving beautifully. Your head keeps leaving to write fiction. Tonight the fiction was rope." A pause. "So let me tell you what happens to fiction in this house: it gets filed. You want rope — that is a real piece of information and I will have it properly. We'll negotiate it another evening, sober and unhurried, with its own list, its own limits, its own arithmetic. But you delivered it in the middle of a count, where it cost you dearly and profited me nothing. I take payment in the currency I ask for."

Her thumb moved once along the spine, unhurried.

"Now the accounting. Second lost count. The rule stands, so we return to zero — that part you know. The part you don't: a second reset carries a levy. Two strokes, added to the paddle count. Twenty becomes twenty-two." She let that settle. "Any objection to the levy, voice it now and I'll strike it from the books. Otherwise it's on them."

Then, because twice was a diagnosis and not an accident, she gave the amendment in the same breath as the mercy it was.

"And one adjustment. The silences I've been giving you are room, and you keep furnishing the room. So we make it smaller. My hand stays where it is between strokes — your head can report to it instead of wandering off to coil itself. And the number arrives on the exhale. Not when it pleases. *On the exhale.*"

She settled her weight, found her line, and let her palm read the ground one last time: warm, pink gone deep at the curve, the muscles beneath it releasing the way she liked them to. The breath under her hand rose, hung —

The first stroke of the new sequence fell, square and unhurried, lower than the last sequence had begun.

Her hand stayed exactly where she'd said it would. The silence was smaller now, and she held it open at the new size — brief, pointed, furnished with nothing — waiting for the exhale to do its work.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: She takes her time and I lose track of how long, until I'm shaking against the restraints and asking out loud for something I'd normally make her get out of me.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I bite my lip, the air leaving my lungs in a shaky exhale. "One."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "More," I say, using the exact phrase we agreed on for it. "All of it. Say the things you say and don't soften them." My safeword is right there and I don't want it.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex took the "one" the way a teller takes correct money — a small nod, filed without comment. "On the exhale, precisely as ordered. Improvement noted."

Then the request arrived, and she let it sit in the room a moment, turning it over like a stone whose underside she already knew.

"And now this. Asked out loud, unprompted." She leaned in, one hand still flat and warm at the small of Ari's back. "You begged a minute ago. Voice and all, before I'd earned it. I said nothing then, because I wanted to see whether you'd name it or bury it under charm. You named it." A beat. "That's the truest sentence you've handed me all evening, and I intend to make it expensive."

She straightened. Found her line.

"Terms, so we understand each other. I don't soften, and I don't take words back once they're out of my mouth. If one lands wrong — not hard, *wrong* — you say yellow and I adjust. The machinery runs in both directions; that's what makes it worth asking for." A pause, exactly long enough. "And the count does not stop for my voice. You'll take both at once. Consider that the levy on asking."

She settled her weight.

"You've wanted this since Tuesday. Four days of wanting, and I'd wager the wanting was the best part — tonight is only the receipt." The second stroke fell, square and unhurried, and she spoke through its echo. "Look at you. Strapped down and shaking before I've left a mark anyone would ask about. Your body has been confessing since the door. Your mouth only caught up because I made it."

Her hand stayed exactly where she'd promised it would, reading the heat climb.

"All that charm you spend everywhere else — it's worthless in this room. In here you are nerve endings and arithmetic, and you can't even hold the arithmetic." A slow breath of a laugh. "You want to be taken apart and told what you are while it happens. Very well. Here is what you are: mine, on a bench, counting."

She let that sit in the small unfurnished silence, then added — almost gently, which was the register that always cut deepest:

"Twenty-two strokes coming, and I have more words than that. Pace yourself."

And she waited — hand flat, silence sized to the exhale — for two.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I suck in a breath, my fingers curling against the headboard. "Two."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
"Two," Vex said — and nothing more. The ledger was running; there was no need to read every entry back aloud. Her hand made its slow pass over skin that had graduated from warm to hot, and she took the temperature of the evening through her palm: deep pink along the curve, heat pooled and even, no points, nothing sharp. The plan, holding.

The tremor she could not adjust, and did not want to.

"Your body has stopped lying to me," she said, settling her weight. "Muscles don't charm. They report. And yours have been reporting since the door — the shaking is just the truth arriving late, in translation."

She watched the breath, waited for the crest of the exhale, and let the third stroke fall through her sentence — square, unhurried, a degree lower, on ground that answered with a sound dignity would never have permitted on its own.

"Listen to that," she said, mild as a remark about weather. "Years spent learning to sound composed in every room you enter, and one leather paddle has you making that noise in under an hour. Every ounce of charm you walked in with has been converted. This—" her hand came to rest, flat, exactly where she had promised it would live, "—is what it was keeping quiet all along."

A slow pass of the palm, reading.

"You asked me not to soften. Noted for the record: I never do. Softening is for things that can't hold their shape." A pause, timed to the exhale. "You're holding yours beautifully. For now."

She lifted the paddle again, letting it catch the light the way she'd let Ari see it on the table — an object, a schedule, a promise being kept.

"Twenty remain, and the words get worse before they run out. The numbers are mine, Ari. You're only the voice I've rented to say them."

And she held the small silence open — hand flat, furnished with nothing, the whole room reduced to a single beat of waiting — for three.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I'm past words that aren't the agreed ones and she knows it. "Green," I get out, when she checks. (OOC: don't fade or skip -- write the scene through.)

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Three," I whisper, the word scraping out on the exhale. My body tenses, waiting for the next one.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Four," I choke out, the number breaking on the next impact. My knuckles are white against the headboard now.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Five." The sound is thin, but it's there on the exhale like she asked.
