dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun had planned to say something when the door opened. He had in fact planned several things, over roughly nineteen weeks, and had rehearsed at least two of them.

Halle got the door open and he forgot all of them.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I don't say any of the things I planned either. I drop the bag and close the distance.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
He met her halfway. It wasn't far—the entryway was maybe eight feet—but it felt like the last leg of something that had started in a different hemisphere, and he covered it in two strides with the door still swinging open behind her, letting the March air in, letting the neighbors see whatever they were going to see.

His hands went to her face first. He hadn't planned that either. He'd planned something cooler, something with a line in it, but his palms found her jaw and his thumbs found her cheekbones and he just held her there for a second, looking, the way you look at something you'd been afraid you'd gotten wrong in memory. He hadn't. Not the freckle under her left eye. Not the way her mouth went crooked when she was about to say something and didn't.

Then he kissed her, and there was nothing careful in it at all.

He kissed her like he had a five-month deficit to correct and no intention of doing it gracefully. His hand slid back into her hair and closed there, tilting her head, and he made a sound into her mouth that he'd have been embarrassed by in any other context—low, undone, more relief than anything else. She tasted like coffee. She tasted like the kitchen and the drive and every ordinary thing he'd been counting down toward.

"Halle," he said against her mouth, and then apparently that was the whole sentence, because he kissed her again before he could add to it. He walked her backward. She went easy, or he didn't notice if she didn't, and her shoulder blades hit the wall next to the coat hooks with a thump that knocked her keys off the hook onto the floor.

He didn't stop. He got his hands under the hem of her shirt, flat against the warm skin of her lower back, and pulled her against him hard enough that there was no mistaking anything about his state or his intentions. His mouth moved to her jaw, the hinge of it, the soft place under her ear that he'd been thinking about with frankly unprofessional frequency.

"I had a speech," he said into her neck, breathing hard. "It was good. You would've cried."

His hands were already working the button of her jeans.

"Later," he said. "I'll give it to you later."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I let out a choked laugh against his mouth, hands fisting in his shirt. "You think I didn't have one?" I gasp, arching into his touch. "Mine was better."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
"Impossible," Jun said. "Mine had a callback."

He got the button. He got the zipper too, and then his hand was flat against the heat of her through cotton and he stopped talking, because his own breath had gone somewhere. Her hips came forward into his palm and he pressed back, slow, watching her face from six inches away with an attention that bordered on rude.

"Tell me the first line," he said. His voice had dropped. "Go on."

He didn't wait for it. He got his other hand into her shirt and pushed it up, and when it caught under her arms he lost patience and pulled it over her head, and her hair came down out of whatever she'd done with it and fell around her shoulders and he made that sound again. Five months. Five months of a cot and a photo he'd looked at too much and a version of her in his head that he now understood had been badly underpowered.

He put his mouth on her collarbone. Then lower. He went down on one knee on the entryway tile like a man with no dignity left to protect and dragged her jeans down her thighs, and she had to grab his shoulder to keep her balance when he pulled one foot free, and he took the opportunity to press his face against the inside of her knee, her thigh, the crease of her hip, breathing her in like he'd been underwater.

"I thought about this," he said, into her skin. "On the plane. In the car. I thought about it in a briefing, Halle. I nearly got asked a question."

He hooked his fingers in the waistband of her underwear and drew it down, unhurried for the first time since the door had opened, because this part he wanted to see. Then he looked up at her—pinned against the wall with her keys on the floor and the door still open behind them and the March light coming in sideways—and he grinned, and it wasn't a nice grin at all.

"Now," he said, and leaned in. "The first line."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I kiss her and keep kissing her and we don't manage to get further into the flat than the hallway for a while.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
He didn't get the first line.

He got her fingers in his hair instead, and her thigh under his palm, and the sound she made when his mouth found her—a short, surprised exhale, like she'd been braced for something slower. He wasn't slow. He'd been slow for five months. He'd been slow at a desk in a country whose weather he'd already started to forget, and slow in a bunk that smelled like somebody else's laundry, and slow every time the connection dropped mid-sentence and he'd sat there looking at her frozen face on the screen, mouth half-open, mid-word.

So he wasn't slow now. He tasted her like he'd been rationed, and when her knee started to give he got an arm around the back of her thigh and held her up against the wall, and he didn't stop. He heard her head knock the plaster. He heard the coat hook rattle. Somewhere behind him the door drifted on its hinges and let in a slice of traffic noise and a bar of cold air across the back of his neck, and he thought, distantly, *anyone could walk past*, and then he thought *good*, and then he stopped thinking about the door.

He knew her. That was the thing. Five months hadn't taken that—he knew exactly where she'd go tight and where she'd go loose, knew the hitch in her breathing that meant she was close and the one that meant she was trying to hold it off, and he chased the first one and ignored the second. He felt her hand close in his hair hard enough to hurt. He felt her hips stutter against his mouth. He looked up—he couldn't not—and watched it land on her face, the way her jaw went slack and her eyes shut and she said his name to the ceiling like it was an argument she was losing.

He held her through it. Then he held her a little longer, forehead against her hip, breathing, while she shook and swore and slid a few inches down the wall.

"That wasn't the first line," he said eventually. His voice was wrecked. "I'm going to need the first line."

He stood up. His knees complained about the tile and he didn't care. He kissed her, and she could taste herself on him and he wanted her to, wanted her to know exactly how far gone he was, and he got his hands under her thighs and lifted—she was warm and heavy and real, *real*, and her legs went around him like they'd never been anywhere else—and turned, and made it three steps toward the living room before she did something with her mouth against his throat that stopped him dead.

He put her back against the opposite wall instead. The hallway was narrow. It was fine. He got his belt open one-handed, badly, swearing, and she was laughing at him and he was laughing at himself and then he was inside her and neither of them was laughing at all.

He stopped. Had to. Held there with his face in her neck and his whole body locked, and said, very quietly, "*Fuck*," and then, "Hi," and then, "Hi, Halle, hi," like he'd only just arrived, like the door had only just opened.

Then he moved, and it was not a homecoming anybody would have called dignified. He fucked her against the hallway wall with the front door open and her clothes in a trail across the tile and her nails in his back through his shirt, which he was still wearing, which was absurd. He told her he'd missed her, roughly and repeatedly and into her hair, in words that lost their grammar somewhere around the third time. He told her she was the only thing he'd wanted. He told her to say the first line, the *first line*, come on, and when she still didn't he bit her shoulder and said, "Fine. Fine. Keep it," and got a hand between them and felt her go over again and followed her with a sound he'd deny later, wrung out and grateful and completely, finally, home.

They stayed like that a while. The hallway. The wall. His forehead on hers, both of them breathing like they'd run somewhere. Outside, a car went by. Somebody's dog. The ordinary world, eight feet away and entirely uninterested.

"So," he said, still not moving, still inside her, still holding her up because he wasn't ready to be a separate person yet. "Callback."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I press my forehead harder against his, breath still ragged. "My first line was 'Hi, asshole.'" I tilt my head to nip his jaw. "Yours was probably...poetic. And worse."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun laughed. It came out of his chest without permission and jolted through both of them, and he felt her react to it where they were still joined and had to close his eyes for a second and breathe through that.

"'Hi, asshole,'" he repeated. "That's it. That's the speech that was better than mine."

He shifted his grip under her thighs, took a little more of her weight, and pressed her back into the wall more for the excuse of being closer than out of any real necessity. His shirt was stuck to him. There was sweat cooling along his hairline in the draft from the door. He could smell her on his own face and he intended to for as long as possible.

"Mine," he said, with some dignity, "opened with a *thesis*."

He kissed the corner of her mouth. Then her cheek. Then the freckle, because it was there.

"I was going to walk in. Set the bag down—slowly, you'd notice, you'd wonder. I was going to say, 'Halle. Halle Okonkwo-Kim. I have been on four continents and every single one of them was the wrong one.'" He paused. "Beat. You're already tearing up. Then I'd say something about the ocean. There was a metaphor about the ocean, I forget it now, it involved tides and it was very good. And then—"

He pulled back far enough to look at her, and his face did something it hadn't done in five months, something soft and stupid and unguarded.

"—and then I'd say, 'But this is the right one.' And I'd kiss you." He shrugged, as much as a man in his position could shrug. "That's the callback. Continents. Right one. It's not complicated. It's *elegant*."

He rolled his hips, once, barely a movement, mostly to watch what it did to her mouth.

"Instead I said 'Hi' three times like I'd been concussed. So." He nudged her nose with his. "Hi, asshole. That's a good line. That's a really good line."

He finally, reluctantly, eased out of her and let her feet find the floor, though he kept a hand flat on the wall beside her head and the other on her hip like she might drift off. He glanced past her shoulder down the hallway—her shirt, her jeans, his belt half-out of its loops, the keys, a solitary sock that he didn't remember removing—and then at the front door, still standing a foot ajar, gently leaking heat into the March afternoon.

"We should probably close that," he said. He did not move toward it. He looked back at her. "Or. Hear me out. Bedroom's twenty feet away. I've got another speech in me. Shorter. Mostly just your name."

He took her hand and started walking backward, pulling her with him, kicking the sock out of the way as he went, grinning like a man who'd been given exactly what he asked for and was already asking again.

"Leave the door," he said. "I'll get it later. I'll get everything later."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: The bag stays where it fell. So do most of our clothes, in a line down the hall that we are both going to find funny tomorrow.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
He didn't get the door. He didn't get the bag either, which was still slumped against the doorframe with five months of his life zipped inside it—the good boots, the letters she'd sent that he'd kept in a Ziploc like evidence, a bottle of something duty-free he'd been picturing them opening on the couch tonight in a version of the evening that had already been comprehensively abandoned.

He got her, though. That was the point.

Halfway down the hall he stopped pulling and turned around and picked her up again instead, because he could, because his arms had spent five months carrying things that weren't her and he wanted to correct the record. She was still bare and still warm and still laughing a little in her chest, and he walked the rest of the way with her against him and his chin hooked over her shoulder, looking at the flat over her back like a man cataloguing.

The kitchen light was on. She'd left a mug on the counter. There was a jacket over the back of a chair that he didn't recognize and that made him go briefly, stupidly territorial before he realized it was his, the old grey one, that she must have been wearing. He'd think about that later. He was building a whole list of later.

The bedroom door was open. The bed was made. She'd made the bed for him and he wanted to say something about that and instead he put her down on it and climbed on after her and got his shirt off, finally, finally, pulled over his head and thrown at the wall, and then there was nothing between them at all.

He didn't rush this time. He'd bought himself that. He lay down along the length of her and just—looked. Ran his hand from her throat to her hip and back like he was checking she was continuous. Found the scar on her knee from the bike, the mole on her ribs, the place on her shoulder where he'd bitten her twenty minutes ago and was already coming up faintly pink. He touched that with two fingers and looked slightly ashamed of himself and not sorry.

"You made the bed," he said.

He kissed her sternum. Her ribs. The soft underside of her breast, then the tight peak of it, slow, until her back came off the mattress.

"You made the bed and I came in here like a stray dog." He said it into her skin. "I had a plan for this room. There was a bath involved. Candles, probably. I don't know. I'd have figured it out."

He moved down, then up again, indecisive, greedy. Settled over her with his weight on his elbows and his mouth at her ear.

"Here's the shorter speech," he said. "Halle." He kissed her temple. "Halle." Her cheek. "Halle." Her mouth, long and unhurried, until she made a sound into it. "That's the whole thing. That's the text. I've been saying it to myself for five months like an idiot, in the shower, in the mess, walking to the—I said it out loud once on a night patrol and Reyes thought I'd seen something."

He reached down between them. Found her still slick and swollen from the hallway and let his breath go rough against her jaw.

"There's nothing to see," he said. "There's just you. It's just you, it's only ever been—" and he pushed into her, slow this time, so slow, watching her face for every inch of it, and lost the end of the sentence somewhere around the middle.

This time it was different. This time there was a bed and a pillow under her head and the whole afternoon stretched out in front of them with nothing on the other side of it. He moved in her like he was memorizing, deep and even, his forehead on hers, and when she wrapped her legs around his back he just breathed out and stayed there a moment, buried, held, letting the distance close all the way.

"Say it again," he said, low. "The good line. Say it to me while I'm—" He rolled his hips and felt her clench and had to shut his eyes. "*Yeah*. Say it."

The front door, somewhere down the hall, drifted a little wider in the wind. Neither of them heard it.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I hook a leg over his hip, pulling him deeper. "Hi, asshole," I murmur against his lips, voice gone rough. "You're home."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
*You're home.*

It went through him like a hand around the spine.

Jun stopped moving. Not a decision—his body just did it, locked with his hips flush against her and his weight on his forearms and his face six inches above hers, and he looked at her, and something in his chest that had been braced for five months finally, audibly, let go. He felt his eyes go hot and didn't do anything about it. Didn't blink it back or make a joke. Just let her see it.

"Yeah," he said. His voice cracked straight down the middle. "Yeah. I'm home."

Then he kissed her like he was falling into it, deep and open and shaking a little, and when he started moving again it wasn't the same rhythm. It was slower and it was harder and it had lost whatever composure the first few minutes had lent him. He drove into her with her leg hooked over his hip and her heel pressing into the small of his back and he said her name against her mouth, and then he said *home*, and then he said *asshole*, low and cracked and laughing, because she'd ruined the word for him and he was going to think about it every time he heard it for the rest of his life.

He got a hand under her thigh and pushed it up and back and the angle changed and she made a sound he felt in his teeth. He watched her. He couldn't stop watching her. Five months of a photograph and here was the real thing—flushed to the collarbone, hair everywhere, mouth open, looking back at him like she'd never once doubted he'd be standing here. He didn't know if she had. He'd ask later. Later was getting very long.

"I'm not—" he said, and had to stop and breathe. "I'm not going to last. I want to tell you that up front. Twenty minutes ago I could've—" He laughed, wrecked. "This is different. You said the thing. You can't say the thing and expect—"

She did something with her hips and he lost the rest.

He got a hand between them, thumb on her where she was already swollen and slick from twice before, and he wasn't gentle about it, and he watched her face tighten and her head go back into the pillow she'd put there for him. Felt her start to go. Chased it. Fucked her through the edge of it with his mouth on her throat, saying *there, there, Halle, come on, I've got you, I'm here, I'm—*

She broke under him and took him with her. He came with his face buried in her neck and her name torn out of him in three ragged pieces and his whole body shuddering like it had been holding a door shut for five months and had finally been allowed to stop. He stayed there. Inside her, on her, breathing into the damp curve of her shoulder, one hand still wrapped around the back of her thigh like he'd forgotten it was there.

For a long time neither of them said anything at all.

The bedroom was very quiet. The afternoon light had gone from white to gold across the ceiling. He could hear the fridge running down the hall and, further off, the faint, inconsistent creak of the front door discovering its own hinges. He could feel her heartbeat against his chest, slowing, and he counted it for a while without meaning to.

"Okay," he said eventually, into her skin. "Okay. Your speech won."

He lifted his head. His hair was stuck to his forehead and he looked like a man who'd been hit by something and enjoyed it.

"I concede. 'Hi, asshole, you're home.' Six words. Devastating." He kissed her, soft, closed-mouthed, just to be doing it. "I'm never writing anything again. I'm retiring. I'm going to read the continents thing at your funeral in like sixty years and everyone's going to say, 'Well. It's not *hi, asshole*.'"

He eased out of her, finally, and rolled onto his back and pulled her with him so she ended up half across his chest with her ear over his heart, which was still going hard. He got a hand into her hair and just held it there. Looked at the ceiling. Their ceiling. There was a crack in the corner he'd forgotten about, and he found he loved it unreasonably.

"The door's still open," he said.

He didn't move.

"The bag's still in the hall."

He didn't move.

"There's whiskey in the bag. Good whiskey. I had a whole—" He stopped. Breathed. His hand moved slowly through her hair. "I don't care about any of it. I'm going to lie here until I remember how legs work. Then I'm going to close the door and pick up your underwear and make you something to eat and probably cry a little in the kitchen where you can't see. And then—"

He tipped his head down and caught her eye, and the grin came back, slower this time, the edge worn off it.

"And then I've got another five months to make up for," he said. "So. Don't get comfortable."

His thumb traced the bite mark on her shoulder, back and forth, an apology and a promise in the same motion.

"Hi," he said, one more time, quiet. "You're right. I'm home."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I get her onto the bed and take her apart slowly with my hands and mouth, five months of intending to do exactly this and no reason left to wait.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun had said *don't get comfortable* and then, within roughly four minutes, gotten very comfortable. He'd have argued that was different. He'd have argued that from underneath her, with her hair in his fist and the ceiling going gold and his heart finally coming down off whatever it had been doing, comfort wasn't the word. The word was something closer to *landed*.

Then she moved, and he found out he'd been wrong about being done.

She got him where she wanted him. He let her. He'd have let her do anything, honestly, in that state—he was loose-limbed and slow and stupid with it, and when her hand went flat on his chest and pushed him back into the pillows he went like a man being folded. He lay there with his arms above his head where she'd put them and watched her rise up over him, backlit, and said, "Oh," in a small voice, because he understood suddenly what this was going to be.

She was going to be slow. He could see it in her face. She'd watched him tear through the hallway like a house fire and now she was going to take her time, and he was going to have to lie there and let her, and five months of wanting had not remotely prepared him for that.

"Halle," he said. It came out warning and plea in equal measure.

Her mouth found the hollow of his throat. He shut his eyes.

He'd forgotten this. Not forgotten—he'd have said he remembered everything—but there was a difference between the memory of her hands and her hands, the same difference as between a photograph of a fire and standing in one. She touched him like she was reading. Palm down his sternum, unhurried. Fingertips along the inside of his arm where he'd never been able to stand it and she knew that, she *knew* that, and did it anyway and watched him twitch and did it again. Her mouth went where her hands had been, a beat behind, so that everything happened to him twice.

He talked. He couldn't not. He said her name and then he said *please* without having decided to and then he laughed at himself, breathless, and said, "I'm not—I don't beg, I'm a—I have a *rank*," and she did something with her teeth at his ribs that shut him up completely.

She took him apart. That was the only way he'd ever be able to describe it, if anyone was stupid enough to ask. Not fast, not rough, nothing he could brace against. She just kept going, slow and thorough and merciless, mouth and hands and the occasional deliberate drag of her hair across his skin, until he wasn't a man who'd come home anymore, wasn't a man who'd been anywhere, was just a nervous system on a bed being played like she'd written it. His hands came down from above his head at some point and she put them back. He left them there. He was shaking. He'd been shot at in the last five months and hadn't shaken.

When her mouth finally went where he'd been silently, unsuccessfully willing it for what felt like a geological age, he made a sound that wasn't a word and his hips came off the bed and she—he felt her—pressed him back down, and *kept him there*, and took him in slow enough that he saw white at the edges.

"*Fuck*—Halle—I can't—" He had a hand in her hair now and didn't know how it got there and wasn't going to move it. "I can't, I'm going to—you have to—"

She didn't stop. She didn't speed up either. That was the cruelty of it. She just kept on exactly as she'd been going, as if she had all afternoon, as if she'd waited five months and intended to collect on every minute, and he came apart under her with his heels dug into the mattress and his other hand fisted in the sheet she'd put on for him and her name coming out of him in a long broken exhale, more sob than sound. It went on longer than he'd thought a body could manage. She stayed with him through all of it.

After, he couldn't move. Genuinely. He lay there with his arms flung out and his chest heaving and his eyes on the crack in the corner of the ceiling, and when she came back up the length of him and settled her weight on his chest he made a faint noise of protest that didn't have any actual protest in it.

"That," he said, eventually, to the ceiling. His voice had gone hoarse. "That was—okay. Okay. I see what you did."

He got a hand up. It took effort. He put it on the back of her neck and left it there.

"You watched me lose my entire mind in the hallway. You let me carry you in here like some kind of—conquering—and then you just—" He gestured, weakly, at the whole situation. "You *waited*. You let me get smug. And then you did that."

He tipped his chin down. She was looking at him. He was fairly sure his face was doing something undignified and he let it.

"I've been outmaneuvered," he said. "In my own bed. On day one." He pulled her up a little so he could get his mouth on hers, slow and grateful and not going anywhere. "You're a menace. I married a menace. I'm going to tell Reyes."

His thumb moved along her jaw. Outside, the light was going orange, and somewhere down the hall the door had finally swung all the way open and was letting the whole evening in.

"Give me a minute," he said, against her mouth. "Ten. Ten minutes. Then I'm getting up, and I'm closing that door, and I'm finding the whiskey." He kissed her again. "And then I'm going to do that to you. Slower. I've got *notes*."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I laugh, low and satisfied, and collapse fully on top of him. "You're welcome to try." I press a kiss to his chest. "But I was paying attention, too."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
"Paying attention," Jun repeated. He said it to the ceiling, slowly, like he was testing the phrase for structural weaknesses. "To what. To *me*? I was a mess. There was nothing to pay attention *to*. I was—I was a man with a belt buckle problem and no follow-through."

Her weight on his chest was doing something to him that had nothing to do with sex. It was the pressure of it. The specific density of her. He'd slept for five months with a rolled jacket on his chest because it turned out he couldn't sleep without weight there anymore, and he'd never told her that, and he found he was about to.

He didn't. Not yet. He put both arms around her instead and held on with a grip that was slightly too tight for the moment and didn't loosen it.

"Fine," he said. "Fine. You were paying attention. You've got notes too. We'll compare." He turned his head and kissed whatever was closest, which turned out to be her hairline, damp and salty. "Later. I've got a very full later. It's overbooked."

He meant to stay there. He genuinely did. But the light through the window had gone from orange to something darker and the draft from the hallway had finally made it all the way to the bedroom and was moving across his shins, and somewhere in the back of his head the part of him that had spent five months checking perimeters was making a small, persistent noise about the front door.

"Okay," he said. "Okay. I'm doing it. Don't move. Do not move. I want to come back and find you exactly like this, I'm going to take a mental photograph—" He did, actually, looking down at her with an expression that was not remotely ironic, and then he eased her sideways onto the sheets and rolled off the bed and stood up, and his knees did a thing, and he swore at them.

He walked down the hall naked. It was a short hall. He collected as he went—her jeans, hooked on one finger; her shirt, which he put over his shoulder; the sock, which he looked at for a moment as if it might explain itself; his belt, still threaded through nothing. Her underwear he picked up last and did not put with the rest. He stood in the entryway with an armful of clothes and looked at the door, wide open now, the streetlight just coming on across the road, the whole ordinary evening standing there like it had been waiting politely to be let in.

He closed it. Locked it. Stood with his hand flat on the wood for a second longer than the action required.

Then he crouched by the bag. Unzipped it. Dug past the boots and the shaving kit and the paperwork and found the whiskey, and under the whiskey, the Ziploc. Nineteen envelopes, her handwriting, soft at the corners from being taken out and put back. He held it for a moment. He didn't take anything out of it. He just—held it, in the dark hallway, with the fridge humming and her clothes over his shoulder and his heartbeat doing something slow and enormous.

When he came back into the bedroom he had the bottle in one hand and the Ziploc in the other and her underwear still, for reasons he'd have struggled to articulate, tucked into his fist. He didn't turn on the light. He put the bottle on the nightstand and the bag of letters beside it and stood at the foot of the bed looking at her in the last of the window-light, and whatever he'd been going to say about notes and menaces and Reyes went quietly out of his head.

"I kept those," he said. He nodded at the Ziploc. His voice wasn't doing the thing it had been doing before. It was just his voice. "All of them. I read the one about the radiator so many times I could—I know the radiator one by heart, Halle. I could do it as a monologue."

He climbed back onto the bed. Not on her—beside her, on his side, so he could see her face.

"You were paying attention," he said. "Yeah. I know. I could tell from here." He touched the letters, then her. "So that's the whiskey, and that's the evidence, and the door's locked, and there's nothing else. There's nothing else I have to do." He let out a breath that had five months in it. "I keep waiting for the thing I've forgotten. There isn't one. It's just this."

He reached over and found her hand and brought it to his chest and pressed it flat there, over the place where the jacket used to go.

"Stay there a while," he said. "I'm not asleep. I'm just going to lie here and be home at you for a bit. Then whiskey. Then—" the grin came back, faint, tired, entirely sincere, "—then notes."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "Stop being gentle," she says. "Nineteen weeks. I don't want gentle, I want to feel it tomorrow." She pulls me down by the back of the neck to make the point.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The gentle went out of him like a light switch.

Not all at once—there was a half-second where he was still hanging over her with the letters on the nightstand and his heart doing its slow enormous thing, and her hand was on the back of his neck and her mouth was an inch from his and she'd said *tomorrow*, and he looked at her. Really looked. Found nothing in her face that needed handling carefully.

"Okay," Jun said. Very quietly. "Okay."

Then he got a hand in her hair and kissed her like the hallway.

He'd been holding something back since the bed. He hadn't known it until she named it—some reflex left over from months of being careful with everything, checking everything, moving through the world like it might break. She didn't want that. She'd never wanted that, not from him, and the relief of being told so went through him hot and fast and turned into something with teeth.

He rolled her. Got her under him, got her wrists, pinned them to the sheet above her head with one hand and held them there, and watched her pupils go wide in the dark.

"Nineteen weeks," he said. His voice had dropped into a register she'd only heard a few times in six years. "You want to count? I counted. I counted every fucking day."

He bit her. Her shoulder, over the mark he'd already left, hard enough that she arched off the mattress into him. Then her throat, just under the jaw where she'd wear it. He wasn't apologizing this time. He kissed his way down her sternum with his hand still locked around her wrists and when he got to her breasts he wasn't slow about it, wasn't reverent—he used his mouth and his teeth and listened to her breathing come apart, and when she pulled against his grip he tightened it and felt her go slack and hungry underneath him.

"You've been walking around," he said, between her breasts, into her skin, "in my jacket. In my flat. Making the bed." He let go of her wrists only to get both hands under her thighs and drag her down the mattress toward him, rough, so her head came off the pillow. "Writing me letters about the *radiator*. Do you know what that did to me?"

He pushed her knees apart and up, wide, and held them there with his weight and looked at her—swollen, wet, marked from his mouth and his hands and two hours of him—and didn't hide what it did to his face.

"I'm not going to be careful," he said. "You asked. Tell me if I get it wrong."

He didn't give her time to answer. He drove into her in one hard stroke that punched the air out of both of them, and he didn't wait for her to catch up, didn't do the slow first inch he'd done before—he set a pace that shook the headboard against the wall and kept it, deep and brutal, his hands clamped on her hips hard enough to leave prints. She was so wet from before that there was no resistance, nothing between them at all, just the sound of it and the slap of skin and her voice climbing.

He got a hand around her throat. Not tight. Just there, his palm along the line of it, his thumb under her jaw so she had to look at him. "Stay with me," he said. "Eyes. *Eyes*, Halle." She gave them to him. He fucked her harder for it.

He talked. He'd always talked, but not like this—he told her what she looked like taking it, in words he'd never say at a dinner table. Told her she was going to walk funny. Told her he was going to look at the marks on her shoulder tomorrow while she made coffee and get hard in the kitchen and not do a thing about it, just watch her know. Told her *mine* about four times in a row until it stopped being a word. She was clawing at his back and he arched into it and said *yeah, harder, do it*, and she did, and he'd have those tomorrow too.

When she started to go he felt it before she made a sound—the way she locked around him, the stutter in her hips—and he pulled out. All the way. Watched her face crack open in outrage and want.

"No," he said, breathing like a bellows. "No. Not yet. You wanted to feel it."

He flipped her. Got her on her stomach, got a knee between hers and an arm around her waist and hauled her up onto her hands, and she was swearing at him into the mattress and he laughed, dark and delighted, and pushed back into her from behind with a hand fisted in her hair.

This angle he could go deeper. He did. He bent over her with his chest to her back and his mouth at her ear and fucked her with everything he'd carried across four continents, every night with a jacket on his chest, every dropped call, every time he'd said her name to no one. The headboard cracked against the wall in a rhythm the neighbors would have opinions about. He didn't care. He wanted them to know. He wanted the whole street to know he was home and what he'd come home to.

"*Now*," he said, when he felt her start to go again, and this time he didn't stop, this time he pulled her hair and got his other hand under her and pressed exactly where she needed it and rode her straight through it, snarling, and she came so hard her arms gave out and he followed her down, still moving, still inside her, until his own broke over him with her name and *home* and something that wasn't a word at all coming out of him into the back of her neck.

He collapsed on her. Full weight. Didn't move.

For a long time there was nothing but the two of them breathing and the fridge down the hall and the faint tick of the headboard settling back against the wall.

"Tomorrow," he said finally, hoarse, into her hair. He sounded like he'd swallowed gravel. "You'll feel that tomorrow. I'll feel it tomorrow. I think I felt something in my back go."

He kissed her shoulder, the mark, then the one beside it. Then, because he apparently couldn't help himself, softer: "You okay?"

He felt her answer more than heard it. He rolled off her, finally, and pulled her back against his chest, and reached over her for the bottle on the nightstand with a shaking hand and got the cap off with his teeth.

"Whiskey," he said. "Then I'm going to sleep for a day. Then notes." He took a pull and passed it to her over her shoulder. "You're a *menace*. God. I love you. Nineteen weeks. Never again."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I take the bottle and drink, grimacing as the burn hits. "Never again," I echo, voice rasping. I turn my head enough to see him. "You try to leave again, I'm coming with you. Even if it's classified."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun laughed, and it hurt, and he did it anyway.

"Classified," he said. "Sure. You'd just—what, sit in the back of the Herc with a book? 'Don't mind me, I'm with him. I'm the radiator correspondent.'"

He took the bottle back from her. Didn't drink. Held it against his chest instead and looked at the side of her face, the little he could see of it in the streetlight coming through the blinds, and the joke ran out of him somewhere around the third breath.

"I slept with a jacket on my chest," he said.

It came out flat. He hadn't planned the delivery. He'd planned nothing today and it had gone better than anything he'd ever planned.

"Rolled up. Every night. Because I couldn't—there wasn't any weight there, and I couldn't get under. I'd lie there and my brain would just go, *something's missing*, and I'd get up and roll the jacket." He shifted his hand on her hip. "I never told you. Felt stupid. Reyes saw it once and didn't say a word, which is how I knew it looked as bad as it felt."

He set the bottle on the floor beside the bed without looking, heard it settle, and got both arms around her properly and pulled her back into him until there wasn't a seam anywhere along the length of them.

"So, yeah," he said, into the back of her head. "You're coming. I don't care what it is. I'll put you in the bag. I'll list you as equipment. 'Okonkwo-Kim, one, load-bearing, do not stack.'"

His thumb found the mark on her shoulder in the dark and rested there. He was so tired he could feel it in his teeth, and he wasn't going to sleep for a while yet, because she was here and warm and slightly drunk and saying things like *even if it's classified* in that wrecked voice, and he wasn't done looking.

"Or," he said, quieter, "I don't go. That's on the table. I've got a year on this contract and then it's a conversation. A real one. At the kitchen table with the coffee." He pressed his mouth to her hair. "Just so you know it's there. I've been thinking about it since about week six. Since the radiator letter, actually. You were so *angry* at that radiator, Halle. I thought, I'd like to be in the room for that. I'd like to be in the room for all of it."

He shut his eyes. Opened them. Didn't want to miss anything.

"Hi, asshole," he said, trying it out in her voice, badly. "Yeah. I get it now. It's a good line."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: Neither of us is being quiet and the neighbours have had five months of peace. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: don't fade to black, write it through.)

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun had been about to say something else. Something about the kitchen table, probably, or the year on the contract, or the way the streetlight was cutting across her shoulder in a stripe he wanted to remember. He'd had the shape of it in his mouth.

Then she said *don't stop*, and he realised she'd moved his hand.

Not far. From her hip to the crease of her thigh. Her fingers over his, pressing, and her hips shifting back against him in a slow, deliberate roll that made it very clear she knew exactly what state he was in and was proposing to change it.

"Halle," he said. It came out disbelieving. "I've been *home two hours*. I have—there's a *limit*. There's a physiological—"

She rolled her hips again. Whatever he'd been going to say about physiology went and stood in the corner.

"Oh, you're a *problem*," he breathed, and his hand was already moving.

He didn't have the hallway in him anymore. He didn't have the headboard in him. What he had was a slow, filthy patience that came from being too exhausted to rush, and he put it to work. His fingers slid down between her thighs from behind and found her swollen, soaked, his and hers together, and she made a sound that went straight into the mattress. He didn't hurry. He circled her with two fingers, lazy and wet, and pressed his mouth to the back of her neck and talked.

"The neighbours," he said, low, against her spine. "Five months of quiet. Mrs Achebe probably thought you'd found God." He pushed two fingers into her and curled them, and her whole back bowed against his chest. "Let's give her something to pray about."

He worked her like that for a while. Slow. His fingers inside her and his thumb on her and his cock hardening against the back of her thigh with a kind of stubborn, disbelieving persistence that made him laugh, once, wrecked, into her hair. She wasn't quiet. He didn't want her quiet. Every sound she made he answered with something—a word, a bite, a harder press of his hand—until she was grinding back against him and swearing at him to *get on with it*.

"Bossy," he said. "You were always bossy. Nineteen weeks and you're *bossier*."

He hooked her top leg back over his hip, opened her up, and pushed into her from behind in one long slide that made both of them stop breathing.

This wasn't the wall and it wasn't the headboard. This was slow and deep and close, spooned around her in the dark with his mouth at her ear and his arm locked across her chest, his hand cupped around her breast, moving in her with a steady, grinding rhythm that went nowhere fast and didn't need to. He could feel everything. Every flutter. Every time she tightened and let go. His fingers found her again and stayed there, and he matched the pace of his hand to the pace of his hips and just—kept going.

"Louder," he said, when she buried it in the pillow. He got a hand in her hair and turned her face out into the room. "No. Let them hear you. Let them hear what I sound like too—" and he groaned, deliberately, unashamed, a low raw sound that would carry through plaster, and felt her laugh and clench around him at the same time. "Yeah. There. *That's* what I want."

He fucked her like that until the laughter went out of it and only the sound was left. Her voice climbed. His name came apart in her mouth. The bed frame started up its slow complaint against the wall, not the frantic crack of before but something steadier, a rhythm you could set a clock to, and he thought about the wall and the flat next door and Mrs Achebe's china cabinet and didn't slow down.

"I'm going to come in you again," he said into her ear, blunt, breathing hard. "And then you're going to lie here full of me and drink my whiskey and I'm going to watch you do it. That's the plan. That's the new speech."

Her hand came back and found his hip and dug in. He took it as a yes.

When she went he felt it start in her thighs—the shake, the lock—and he pressed harder with his fingers and drove deeper and said *go on, go on, let me hear it*, and she did, loud enough that he'd have been embarrassed for the both of them if he'd had any room left for it, her whole body arching back against his and her voice going high and broken and open. He held her through it with his arm across her chest and his mouth on her throat and kept moving, kept moving, and when she started to come down he didn't let her—chased her over again, mean and tender, until she was sobbing his name and he couldn't hold his own anymore and came with his teeth in her shoulder and a sound torn out of him that the whole floor could have heard.

He stayed inside her. Didn't move. Couldn't.

"Okay," he said, eventually, into the dark. It was barely a voice. "Okay. That's—I think that's—"

He tried to finish the sentence. Failed. Laughed instead, a faint, ruined wheeze against her shoulder blade, and felt her laughing too, the two of them shaking with it in a wet tangle of sheets she'd made up clean for him six hours ago.

He reached down over the side of the bed. Found the bottle by feel. Brought it up and pressed it into her hand.

"Drink," he said. "That's the deal. I said I'd watch."

He didn't watch. His eyes had closed on their own. He lay there, softening inside her, his arm dead across her chest and his face in her hair and Mrs Achebe's silence coming through the wall like a rebuke, and he thought: *I'm going to be so sore tomorrow. She's going to be so sore tomorrow. We're going to make coffee and move like eighty-year-olds and neither of us is going to say a word about it, we're just going to look at each other over the mugs.*

"Never again," he said, not sure which thing he meant. All of it. The jacket, the letters, the five months. He tightened his arm. "You're not equipment. Forget the bag. You're just coming. I'll sort the paperwork."

He was asleep before she answered, or close enough to it that he'd claim he was.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I take a slow drink, the whiskey burning all the way down. "Paperwork's a nightmare," I mumble, already half-asleep, my hand finding his where it rests on my stomach. "Worth it."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
He wasn't asleep. He'd have sworn he was, but *paperwork's a nightmare* got through anyway, and he felt her hand settle over his on her stomach and his fingers turned under hers without asking him first.

"Everything's a nightmare," Jun mumbled. "That's the job. The whole job is nightmares with forms attached."

He didn't open his eyes. There was no reason to. He had the whole of her mapped by pressure now—the back of her head against his jaw, the dip of her waist under his forearm, the heel she'd hooked back around his calf at some point and left there like an anchor. The sheets were a disaster. The bottle had gone somewhere; he heard it roll, hit the skirting board, stop. Neither of them moved for it.

"I'll do the forms," he said. "You do the radiator letters. That's the division of labour. I'll say you're—" he yawned so wide something in his jaw clicked, "—morale. Essential morale. They'll have to give you a lanyard."

Down the hall the fridge shuddered and cycled off, and in the sudden quiet he could hear the flat next door: a chair scraping, a tap running, the ordinary sounds of someone pretending very hard they hadn't heard anything for the last three hours. He grinned into her hair, too tired to feel bad about it. Tomorrow he'd take round the second bottle from the bag, the one he'd been saving for Reyes's wedding, and knock and say nothing at all and let Mrs Achebe decide how to take it.

Tomorrow. He kept arriving at that word and finding it solid.

"Worth it," he repeated. Slower than she'd said it, like he was setting it down somewhere it wouldn't get lost. His thumb moved once across the back of her hand and stopped there.

He thought about the letters on the nightstand. He thought about the coffee mug she'd left on the counter and the grey jacket over the chair and the crack in the ceiling he couldn't see in the dark but knew was there, and he thought, with the last of whatever was still running, that he'd never once in nineteen weeks imagined it right. He'd imagined the door and the speech and the kiss. He'd never imagined this part—the weight, the whiskey on her breath, her hand going heavy and slack over his as she went under first.

He felt it happen. Her breathing changed. He counted it, didn't mean to, got to eleven.

"Hi, asshole," he said, barely a sound, into the back of her neck. "You're home too."

Then the rolled-jacket part of his brain—the part that had checked perimeters every night for five months and woken him at three for no reason—looked around, found her there, found the door locked and the light off and nothing missing anywhere, and finally, quietly, stood down.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I wake up at three in the morning, like I have for months. Your arm is heavy across me, and I think, *oh. That's what was missing.* I don't move. I count your breaths until they pull me back under.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun surfaced somewhere around the fourth breath.

Not all the way. The perimeter part of his brain came up first, the way it had every night for five months at roughly this hour—a hand reaching for something before the rest of him knew what for. It checked. Dark. Quiet. Weight on his arm. Warmth along the whole front of him. Something in the dark that was breathing not quite in sleep, too even, the careful breathing of someone lying very still on purpose.

He knew that breathing. He'd heard it through a phone from six thousand miles away, at hours when she'd said *I'm fine, go back to sleep* and he'd known she wasn't and had gone back to sleep anyway because there was nothing else to do.

He didn't move either. He kept his arm exactly where it was, heavy across her, and let his breathing go slow and false and regular, matching whatever count she was keeping. He could feel her ribs under his forearm rising and falling to it. In, out. He gave her that. He'd have given her anything, but that was what was in reach.

Three in the morning. She'd been waking at three too. He filed it with the jacket and the letters and the mug on the counter, all the small evidence, and felt something in his chest go tight and then very quiet.

His hand found hers on the sheet without any input from him. Just the tips of his fingers over the tips of hers. Enough that she'd know he was there without knowing he was awake, if she wanted it that way. He thought about saying *hey*. Decided not to. Some things you didn't interrupt.

He lay there and breathed for her until her count slipped, and her breathing went ragged and then soft and then gone, and her hand went slack under his, and the perimeter looked round one more time and found everything where it should be.

Then he let himself go too, his mouth against the back of her neck, and didn't wake again until the light came.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I wake up to the smell of coffee and the sound of you cursing quietly in the kitchen. I stretch, wincing at the soreness, a smile already on my face. I grab your shirt from the floor and pull it on before padding out to find you.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas had been kneeling by the end of the bed for about four minutes, which Wren knew because he had started counting somewhere around the point it became obvious he intended to wait as long as it took.

"You could have said something," Wren said.

"I could have," Tomas agreed, not moving.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I put my hand in his hair and tip his head back so he has to look up at me. "Say it now, then."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas let out a slow breath as his head tipped back, throat baring. His gaze stayed fixed on Wren, steady and warm, with a hint of eagerness finally breaking through his stillness.

“I want you to use me tonight,” he said. “I want your hands, your rules, and your voice telling me exactly how to be good for you. I want to be pushed, praised, and kept after. If I need anything different, I’ll say so.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Good boy." My thumb traces the line of his jaw. "Stand up. Go kneel by the armchair. I'll decide when to touch you."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas rose at once, the command settling over him like a weight he had been made to carry. He crossed the short distance to the armchair without hurry, because obedience did not need to look eager to be eager, and lowered himself to the floor beside it. He arranged himself with his thighs together, hands resting loosely on his knees, spine straight enough to show he meant to stay.

The praise was still moving through him, bright and quiet. *Good boy.* It made his pulse knock in a way he did not try to hide. He lifted his eyes only enough to keep Wren in view, then let them lower again, not because he was ashamed, but because looking up without permission had begun to feel like a hunger he should keep leashed.

His breath slowed. The room felt close and warm. He could feel the shape of Wren’s attention more than any touch, and it made every inch of him attentive.

“I’ll wait,” he said softly, not asking for anything yet. “However long you want.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I've had a week," he says. "I'd like not to make any decisions for a few hours, if that's on offer."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s expression softened at the tiredness in Wren’s voice. He did not mistake it for distance. It was the kind of exhaustion that needed taking care of, not testing.

“Then don’t decide,” he said quietly. “Let me.”

He stayed kneeling for a moment longer, hands still resting on his knees, but the shape of his obedience shifted. Less waiting now. More service.

“I’ll take care of you,” Tomas said. “I’ll move us, I’ll touch you, I’ll ask only when I need to. If you can give me a yes or no, I’ll use that. If not, I’ll watch you and check in. Red still stops everything.”

His voice stayed warm and steady, no pressure in it.

“I’m going to stand now,” he added. “I’m going to come to you. If you don’t want that, say red before I move.”

He gave Wren the space to stop him, then rose with deliberate slowness. He crossed the small distance to the armchair and sank to his knees in front of Wren instead of beside it. He did not crowd him. He kept his hands visible for a moment before lifting one, telegraphing the motion, and letting his fingers settle carefully over Wren’s.

“Good,” Tomas murmured, more to himself than to Wren. “Let me have you tonight.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't realize I'd been holding, turning my hand under his to lace our fingers together. "Thank you."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas let the small sound of Wren’s breath go through him before the words did. *Thank you.* He felt it more than heard it, and it made his chest ache in a clean, steady way.

“No thanks,” he said quietly. “Not for this.”

He lifted their joined hands and pressed his mouth to Wren’s knuckles, slow and brief, more promise than kiss. When he lowered their hands again, he kept his hold secure.

“You get to be tired,” Tomas said. “I’ll carry the rest.”

His thumb moved in a slow circle over the back of Wren’s hand.

“I’m going to ask only when I have to. If words are too much, squeeze once for yes, twice for no. Red still stops everything.”

He stayed kneeling, close enough that his presence was a comfort rather than a demand, and let his voice drop into the warm, certain register he used when he meant every word.

“I’m going to start by getting you comfortable. Shoes off, clothes loosened, water nearby. Then I’m going to put my hands on you until your week stops rattling around in your shoulders. If you don’t want that, say red.”

A faint smile touched his mouth, soft and devoted.

“And after, I’ll take care of you properly. Water, blankets, whatever you need. I won’t skip it.”

He waited, still and attentive, his eyes warm on Wren.

“Can you give me a squeeze for the first part?”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I take him at his word and stop asking after that, and he stops needing to be asked, and neither of us has any clothes on within about a minute of the decision.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas did not make a ceremony of the fact that there was nothing left between them. He let it be simple: skin, warmth, the sudden honesty of bare air and closer breath. His hands moved as if they had already been given the job they were doing, broad and sure, pressing along shoulders and back with enough weight to be felt, not enough to demand anything in return.

He learned the shape of the week that way. Not by asking. By listening through his palms. By staying where tension gathered until it had no choice but to notice him. By smoothing his thumbs over tight places with patient, repetitive care, as though he had all night and intended to spend it exactly there.

“You don’t have to hold any of this,” Tomas said quietly, his mouth near enough that the words were almost touch. “I’ve got it.”

He did not ask whether that was allowed. He made himself easy to believe. His movements stayed unhurried, his weight shifted only when it would not crowd, and every time his hands wandered lower, they did so with the same steady intention as before. Along the curve of a side. Over the heat of a hip. Down the long line of a thigh, then back again, as if mapping what had already been given.

When he used his mouth, it was after touch had made the want plain. Warm, open kisses pressed where his lips found the nearest tense line. The base of a neck. The slope of a shoulder. The soft, vulnerable hollow where pulse lived. None of it greedy. All of it devoted.

“I’m here,” he murmured against skin. “No decisions. Just this.”

The bed became the center of things because Tomas made it so. He reached for blankets without breaking the quiet, arranged them within reach, checked that water was close. Then he returned, bare and unselfconscious, kneeling with his thighs settled and his hands resting where they could be seen before they touched again.

For a moment he simply offered himself. Shoulders loose, expression soft, eyes warm with the kind of submission that had chosen its purpose. His body was not a demand

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I let my fingers tangle in his hair again, tugging him in until his forehead rests against my thigh. "You're doing so well," I murmur, my voice rough. "Keep going."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas let out a soft, wrecked sound at the praise, the kind he could not quite hold back. His forehead stayed where it had been drawn, against the warm line of Wren’s thigh, and for a second he simply breathed there, letting the words settle into him like instruction and reward both.

“Yes,” he murmured against skin. “I’ll keep going.”

He did not make the next thing sudden. He turned his head just enough to press his mouth to the inside of Wren’s thigh, light at first, then firmer when no red came. His hands stayed where they could be felt, one at the curve of hip, the other braced flat against the mattress beside it. He touched as though he had all the time in the world and meant to spend it carefully.

“I’m going to taste you now,” he said, voice low and roughened. “If that’s too much, squeeze twice. If you want me to keep going, you don’t have to do anything at all.”

The absence of refusal was enough. Tomas leaned closer and let his mouth be warm, slow, deliberate. He started with kisses, broad and open, learning the shape of what Wren liked by paying attention rather than demanding. When he used his tongue, it was with the same patient certainty he had brought to everything else: one steady stroke, then another, never pushing before the way had been made.

His fingers moved only when they needed to, steadying, grounding, tracing small absent circles at the edge of touch. He kept his breathing audible, not hiding how much it cost him to go this slowly, how much he wanted to be good at this. Every now and then he lifted his eyes just enough to check Wren’s face, then lowered them again, reading what he could without asking for more than he had been given.

“That’s it,” he whispered when he could feel the tension beginning to change under his mouth. “You don’t have to think. I’ve got you.”

He meant it like a vow. He stayed there, devoted and attentive, taking the weight of the week and making it into something he could carry with his hands and mouth and voice. If Wren needed him to be gentle, he was gentle. If Wren needed him to be firm, he would find that too. For now, he simply kept going, exactly as he had been told, and let the praise become the only thing guiding him.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's shaking by the time I've finished with my mouth and he still hasn't been told he's allowed to move, which is most of why he's shaking.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas stayed exactly where Wren had left him: bare, trembling, hands curled into the sheets so hard his knuckles had gone white. The shake ran through his thighs, his stomach, his shoulders, every muscle locked in the effort of not moving without permission. His breath came apart in shallow pieces. He did not chase, did not touch himself, did not even shift his hips more than the smallest involuntary jerk.

When he spoke, his voice was wrecked.

“Not red,” he managed first, because he did not want Wren to mistake the shaking for wrong. “I’m— it’s good. Too much. I just—” A sound escaped him, low and helpless. “I haven’t moved. I’m still.”

His eyes were glassy when he lifted them just enough to find Wren’s face. There was no demand in the look, only need stretched thin and bright.

“Tell me what I’m allowed to do,” he whispered. “If you want me still, squeeze twice. If I can move, once. If I can—” His throat worked. “If I can come, say it. Or squeeze once. Whatever you can give me.”

He forced one hand open against the mattress, palm up, an offering rather than a grab.
