Her fingers tightened slightly in his hair, a small, possessive squeeze before she let her hand slide down to rest flat against his shoulder blade. 

"And I'm not going back," she added, looking right at him. "Just so we're clear."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I lift my head just enough to meet her gaze, my fingers tracing the line of her collarbone. "Good," I say, my voice still rough but clear. "Because I don't think I could if I tried."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She kissed him back with a fierce, deliberate certainty

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She closed the remaining few inches between them, placing both palms flat against the bare warmth of his chest

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: She told him with steady, unsparing precision—the pressure she wanted, the rhythm, the exact point of friction

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: When he drove into her with that stripped-back force, the air rushed out of her lungs in a sharp, guttural sound

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Every heavy thrust hit with an unsparing, bruising momentum that knocked the breath out of her chest in sharp, ragged pants

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The film had finished some time ago and neither of them had done anything about it, which was how Priya knew the evening had changed character.

"We're not watching this," she said.

"We haven't been watching it since about nine."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "No," I agree. "We haven't." I don't move, but I stop pretending I'm looking at the screen.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She reached for the remote and killed it — the room went dim and quiet in a way that made the next sentence hers to say or not say.

"We should talk about it, or we should stop pretending it isn't a thing." She set the remote down and turned, folding one leg up on the couch so she could actually look at him. "I've known for a while. I think you have too. I'm just — I'm not going to be the one who keeps pretending."

Her hands were steady. She noticed that, a little surprised, and let it mean something.

"Six years is a long time to be careful. I'm done being careful."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't realize I was holding. "Okay." I shift to face her more fully. "Yeah, I've known. I just... didn't want to mess this up."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"Neither of us wanted to mess it up," she said. "So we did nothing instead. Very safe. Very boring."

She let that sit for a second, watching him — the way he'd turned toward her, the breath he'd been holding. That was the whole answer, really. Everything after this was just the two of them deciding how brave to be about it.

"Here's what I think." Her voice came out lower than she'd planned and she didn't correct it. "We've spent six years being good at not doing this. I don't want to be good at it anymore."

She didn't reach for him. She'd said her part; the next move could be his, and she was fine with that. But she stayed where she was, close enough that staying was its own kind of statement, and didn't look away.

"So. Are you going to kiss me, or are we going to keep talking?"

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her, finally, six years late, and she makes a small furious noise that I think is about the six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The noise came out of her before she'd decided on it — a small, furious thing, all six years compressed into the space between one breath and the next. She'd meant to be smoother than that.

Then his mouth was on hers and she stopped being smooth at all. She got a hand up to the side of his jaw, thumb against the hinge of it, holding him there like he might reconsider. He didn't. She kissed him back like someone finishing an argument she'd been having with herself for a long time, and when she finally broke off it was only far enough to breathe.

"You know what's stupid," she said, forehead tipped against his, voice wrecked in a way she didn't bother fixing. "I had a whole speech. I rehearsed it. In the car, on the way over."

She laughed, low, almost at herself. Her thumb was still moving along his jaw, not quite willing to let go yet.

"Six years of being careful and it takes me one sentence and you just —" She shook her head, kissed him again, brief and sure, like punctuation. "God. Okay. Good. That's good."

She leaned back just enough to actually look at him — hair, mouth, the way he was looking back at her — and let herself enjoy it, openly, the way she hadn't allowed herself to in any of the years before this one.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I laugh, rough and a little shaky. "Your one sentence was better than my six years of silence." My hand comes up to cover hers where it's resting against my jaw. "I'm done being careful too."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"Six years of silence is its own kind of speech," she said. "I just wasn't sure what language it was in."

She turned her hand over under his, laced their fingers, and looked at them for a second — how easily that worked, two hands that had spent years finding reasons not to. Ridiculous, in hindsight. It was just a hand.

"I'm not going to ask you what this is," she said, looking back up. "I'm too old for that and you're smart enough to figure out I don't do this lightly. So here's what I am going to do. I'm going to get a glass of water, because my mouth is dry and I'm pretty sure that's your fault, and then I'm going to come back here and we're going to keep doing this until one of us says something sensible."

She stood, and didn't let go of his hand — tugged it lightly, an invitation rather than a demand.

"Unless you've got somewhere to be. In which case I'd like to know now, because I've got a whole evening and I'm not in the habit of wasting it."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: We get to the bedroom eventually, laughing at ourselves most of the way, and then stop laughing when the clothes are actually off.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She had laughed her way down the hall and then stopped laughing somewhere between the door and the bed, because the joke had run out and what was left was just the two of them and a thing six years in the making, and that wasn't funny at all.

She was glad, actually, that it hadn't stayed funny. She'd spent a lot of her life being funny instead of being this.

Afterward she lay on her back with one arm over her eyes, catching her breath, and felt the room settle around them — the ceiling, the fan turning slow overhead, the particular quiet of a house where nobody was pretending anything anymore. Her heart was still going. She let it.

"You're going to have to give me a minute," she said, to the ceiling. "I had a whole plan for being cool about this and it has thoroughly fallen apart."

She turned her head on the pillow to look at him, and didn't bother hiding the smile — wide, unguarded, the kind she usually edited down before letting anyone see it. It was dark enough that she didn't have to be anything. That was a relief.

"Okay," she said, softer. "You're still here. Good. I was worried for a second I'd built this up so long that the reality couldn't survive it." She reached over and put a hand flat on his chest, just to feel it, just because she could. "It survived."

A beat. Then, dryly, because she was still herself: "So. Was there a speech. I told you mine. I'm going to need yours eventually, so you might as well start thinking about it now."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a breath, my chest rising and falling under her hand. "My speech is just... thank you for not letting me waste another six years." I turn my head to meet her eyes in the dim light. "And I'm not going anywhere."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"Thank you for not letting me waste another six years" — she turned that over for a second, and it landed somewhere warmer than she'd expected.

She left her hand where it was, feeling his heartbeat under her palm, slower than hers now. She liked that. She liked being the one still catching her breath for once.

"That's a terrible speech," she said, but there was no edge in it. "Not even a metaphor. No build-up. You just — thanked me. Rude, honestly."

She shifted onto her side to face him properly, pulling the sheet up with her, tucking her knee against his like it had always been allowed. It was strange how little it felt like a first time and how much it felt like something being set down after being carried too long.

"Here's the thing, though. I'm not going to be gracious about this." She said it plainly, watching his face. "I'm not going to pretend I'm above it or that I'm playing it cool. I waited six years for this and I intend to be annoying about it. I'm going to text you things at bad hours. I'm going to want the seat on the side of the booth you always take. I'm going to expect you to remember that my mother's birthday is the eleventh, not the twelfth, because you've been told twice."

She paused, and the smile softened at the edges.

"And I'm going to be the person who knows. Not the person who suspects, not the person who doesn't ask. That's what I'm signing up for. If that's too much, it's not, because you just said you're not going anywhere, and I'm going to hold you to it."

She reached up and pushed a piece of hair off his forehead, unhurried.

"Also your side of the bed is the left one. I don't make the rules."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I get my mouth between her thighs and stay there while she tells me exactly what she wants, specifically, in a voice I have never heard her use in six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The voice she was using didn't belong to any version of herself she'd met before — low, certain, unbothered, giving directions like she'd been waiting years to be asked, which she supposed she had. She'd always been the one narrating, deflecting, making the joke land before anyone could look too closely. There was no joke available down here. Just her, and the ceiling, and his name in her mouth when she forgot to be careful about it.

Afterward she lay still for a long moment with her arm over her eyes again, breathing like she'd run somewhere. The fan turned. Her skin was cooling in the places he'd been, and she felt the absence of him like a fact she'd have to get used to being aware of.

"Okay," she said finally, to the ceiling, and had to clear her throat to get the second word out. "Okay. That was — I don't have a joke for that. That's a first."

She rolled onto her side to look at him and found she didn't have the energy to be composed, so she didn't try. Hair wrecked, no performance left in her, entirely herself — which was, she realized, the whole point of the last six years, or what they'd been protecting. That person was allowed to be seen now.

"You're going to think I'm exaggerating," she said, "and I'm not, because I have never once said this to a person: I don't think I knew my own voice before just now. I've heard other people's idea of me for thirty years. That was mine." She reached out and touched his mouth, light, almost absently, like she was checking something. "I'm keeping you. That's not a question. I just wanted you to hear it while I was still being honest and not funny."

A beat, and then the corner of her mouth moved, because she couldn't entirely help it.

"Also, you should know you're going to be insufferable about this. I can already tell. I've made a terrible mistake. Get me some water and I'll forgive you."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I laugh, low and a little wrecked myself. "Insufferable, huh?" I kiss her fingers before they pull away. "I can work with that." I get up, not bothering with clothes, and bring back the water. "Here. I'm told I'm staying."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She took the glass and drank half of it in one go, watching him over the rim — naked in her hallway, water glass in his hand, entirely unbothered about any of it. She'd imagined this, in the abstract, in the years she'd refused to admit she was imagining it. The real version was better and less cinematic and had a faint draft coming under the bedroom door.

"Good," she said, and handed the glass back. "Then sit down before I start thinking about it."

He sat. She hooked a foot around his calf, casual, proprietorial, because she'd earned it. The bed was too small for two people who'd spent six years keeping a chair's worth of distance between them, and she found she didn't care about the practicalities. They'd manage.

"Tomorrow," she said, to the ceiling, "I'm going to wake up and be extremely normal about this. You should prepare for that. Breakfast, probably. I make a very boring omelette. It's going to be mortifying for both of us."

She turned her head, and the smile was back, smaller now, quieter, the kind she kept.

"But tonight I'm going to fall asleep here and you're going to be here when I wake up, and I'm going to check, so don't get any ideas."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "You can stop being careful with me," she says. "I'm not made of glass and I've thought about this for as long as you have. Harder."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She turned her head on the pillow at that, caught off guard, and didn't bother hiding it.

"Harder than me," she repeated, flat, testing the claim. "You want to put a number on that? Because I've got six years of receipts and I'm not above producing them."

But the joke didn't quite hold, and she let it go rather than chase it. The other part — *stop being careful with me* — was the part that actually landed. She'd been careful tonight, too. Even here, with her hand on his chest and her knee against his, some small watchful part of her had still been taking notes. She'd been careful for so long it had started to feel like a personality.

"Okay," she said. "But you should know what you're asking for. Careful is what I've got. I'm good at it. I've built an entire friendship on the principle of never needing anything I couldn't lose." She paused, watching the fan turn. "So if you're telling me to put that down, I'm going to do it badly and unevenly and probably say something too honest at the wrong time. That's the trade. You don't get to be surprised by it later."

She shifted, turning properly onto her side so she could see him, and there was nothing guarded left in her face at all.

"Fine. I'm not made of glass. Noted." A beat, and then, quieter, the real answer under the dry one: "I've thought about it too. That's the part I've never said out loud to anyone. Not that I wanted it — that I *knew* it. Years of it. And I still sat on this couch every Thursday and made you watch films you didn't like." She reached up, found the back of his neck, held him there. "So if we're keeping score on who was more of a coward about it, I'm not letting you win. That's mine. I'm claiming it."

She kissed him then — slower than before, no argument left in it, just the thing itself — and when she pulled back she was almost smiling.

"Now stop trying to out-honest me at two in the morning. It's unbecoming. And turn off that light."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I reach over and flick off the lamp, plunging us into the dark. "Fine. You win the coward contest." I settle back, pulling her against me. "But I'm winning the 'who falls asleep first' one."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She let him have it, mostly because she was too tired to argue and partly because she suspected he was right — she was wired, still, the whole night humming in her like a struck bell, and sleep was going to be a while coming. But she'd learned a long time ago not to announce things like that.

"Enjoy it while it lasts," she said into the dark, against his shoulder. "I'll be insufferable about winning in the morning. Different contest. I'll find one."

She settled. His arm was around her and it was, she noted, exactly where she'd have put it if someone had asked her to design the thing. Which was either reassuring or embarrassing, and she decided, at this hour, to file it under reassuring.

The room was the room — her room, her ceiling, her fan, and now him in it, which was going to take some getting used to and which she intended to get used to thoroughly. She could hear him breathing slow out of the dark beside her. That was the sound she'd been avoiding imagining for six years. It turned out imagining it badly had been its own kind of cowardice; the real thing was just a person, breathing, staying.

"Hey," she said, quieter, not really checking whether he was still awake. "For the record. You didn't waste it. Neither did I. We just took the long way, and I've never once minded the long way."

A pause.

"Now go to sleep so I can win."

She closed her eyes. She did not, in fact, win, but she'd never admit it either way, and by morning there'd be an omelette and a whole argument about it, which was, she thought, an excellent way to start.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: Six years of not doing this and now neither of us can form a sentence. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She said it again, or something like it — she wasn't tracking her own words anymore, only the shape of them, low and certain, the kind of thing she'd never said out loud to anyone and had spent six years assuming she never would. His name, once, when she forgot herself. Her own hand fisted in the sheet. The fan turning overhead, indifferent.

"Don't stop" was the only instruction she gave that wasn't actually an instruction, and she meant it the way she'd meant everything tonight — not a request, a fact she was stating out loud because she'd decided she was done keeping facts to herself.

Afterward, the room came back in pieces. The fan. The dark. Her own breathing, still uneven, slowing. She lay there with her pulse in her ears and let the quiet do whatever it wanted to.

"Okay," she said eventually, to the ceiling, and had to work for the word. "Okay."

She rolled her head on the pillow to find him, and there wasn't anything composed left in her to offer — hair a disaster, mouth still open, entirely unguarded. She didn't reach for the joke. She was tired of reaching for it. It was the first time in a long time she'd let a silence stand in a room with someone and not felt the need to fill it.

"Come here," she said, and pulled him down beside her, tucking herself against his side with her cheek on his chest, one arm slung across him like she was staking it. His heartbeat was fast under her ear. She listened to it slow.

"Two in the morning and you've made me stop being funny," she said into his skin. "That's going in the receipts. I'm keeping a list."

A beat. She drew a slow breath and let it out.

"I'm not going to say anything big right now," she said, quieter. "Because I'll say it wrong and it'll be three a.m. and you'll laugh at me and I'll have to start the whole thing over. So here's the small version." She pressed her palm flat against his chest, over the heart. "I'm glad it's you. It was always going to be you. I think some part of me knew that at year one and spent five years being furious about it."

She tilted her head up, found the dark where his face was.

"Now go to sleep. I'm serious. The omelette is real and it's happening and I want you to witness the mortifying normalcy of it firsthand."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I huff a laugh against her hair. "Can't wait." My hand finds the one on my chest, lacing our fingers. "Year one, huh? I think I knew by year two. Guess you win that too." I close my eyes, already drifting.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"Year two," she repeated, mostly into his chest. "You lasted a whole extra year. That's genuinely pathetic."

But she laced her fingers back through his and didn't move, and the smugness she'd been reaching for didn't arrive on schedule. What arrived instead was the quiet fact of it — that he'd known at year two and she'd known at year one and between them they'd managed to lose four years to good manners. She'd have been angry about that if it weren't so funny. She'd be angry about it tomorrow, probably, over eggs.

His breathing changed, going long and slow and even, the way it did. She stayed awake on purpose. There was no reason to — the evening was over, the argument was won, everything that needed saying had been said or deferred to morning. But she lay there with her ear against his chest and catalogued the room anyway, the way you check a house before you leave it: the fan, the draft under the door, the particular weight of another person's arm across her back, heavier than she'd guessed and better than she'd guessed. Six years of not knowing and now it was just — data. A thing she could check whenever she wanted.

That was the part that kept her up, she decided. Not the wanting. The permission.

She must have drifted eventually, because the next thing was grey light at the edge of the blinds and the fan off and his arm still there, and her first thought, before she was properly awake, was a flatly practical one: *left side, I told him, and he listened.* He had. She checked. He was on the left.

She lay still for a minute and let herself be privately, unbecomingly pleased about it, then slid out from under his arm with the care of someone disarming something, found his shirt off the floor instead of her own, and went to make the promised omelette.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I wake up to an empty bed and the smell of eggs. I find her in the kitchen, wearing my shirt and looking supremely focused on the pan in front of her. I lean in the doorway and watch for a second. "You weren't kidding about the omelette."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She didn't turn around — she'd heard him on the floorboards, and turning around to check would have given away that she'd been listening for it.

"I told you it was real. I don't make threats I can't follow through on." She nudged the edge of the omelette with the spatula, brow furrowed at it like it owed her something. "You're witnessing history. This is the most boring thing I do, and you're going to have to sit with it."

The kettle was on. She'd set out two mugs without thinking about it and then thought about it, which was, she suspected, going to be the pattern for the foreseeable future — doing something automatic and then catching herself being automatic and having an entire private reaction to it. Exhausting. She'd keep doing it.

She did turn around then, because the omelette was past saving and she was out of things to stare at. He was in the doorway in whatever he'd slept in, hair a state, leaning like the frame had been installed for the purpose. Six years of Thursday nights and she'd never once seen him first thing in the morning, and now it was just Tuesday, or whatever day it was, and there he was.

"Okay, so. Ground rules." She slid the omelette onto a plate, split it down the middle with the spatula, and pushed one half across the counter toward him. "This is a terrible omelette. You're going to eat it and say something diplomatic and I'm going to know you're lying and we're going to move on. That's the whole breakfast."

She got the kettle off the boil, poured, and set his mug down in front of him before she took her own seat on the other side of the counter — not far, but with the counter between them, because she wanted to look at him properly and she was still, despite everything, a person who liked a table between herself and being looked at.

"I checked, by the way." She said it around the first bite, casual, like she was reporting the weather. "You were on the left. I told you not to make a thing of it and you didn't. I want that on record."

A beat, and then she put the fork down and actually looked at him — the whole of it, morning light and borrowed shirt and the fact that he was still here, in her kitchen, eating her bad cooking.

"Here's the mortifying part," she said. "I'm not nervous. I was expecting to be. I had a whole speech ready for this too, and it's — gone. Nothing. I'm just sitting here being normal at you and it's the strangest thing I've ever done." She picked the fork back up. "I think that means it's fine. I don't actually know what fine feels like, so I'm going to assume this is it."

She ate. Chewed. Swallowed.

"So. Your turn. What's the plan for today. Because I have nothing scheduled and I've decided to be insufferable about that too, and you're the one who said you're not going anywhere, so you're contractually obligated to have an opinion."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I laugh, taking a bite of the omelette. It's dry and a little overcooked, but I don't care. "I think the plan is... we finish this, and then we go back to bed. It's Tuesday. We've got time."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun had planned to say something when the door opened. He had in fact planned several things, over roughly nineteen weeks, and had rehearsed at least two of them.

Halle got the door open and he forgot all of them.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I don't say any of the things I planned either. I drop the bag and close the distance.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun moved before he had decided to move, as if the last five months had trained him to respond to Halle faster than thought. His hands came up to Halle’s face, warm and slightly unsteady, thumbs brushing over cheekbones like he was checking for reality. Then he kissed Halle, hard and without elegance, all the carefully rehearsed greetings dissolving into the press of his mouth.

One arm locked around Halle’s waist and hauled them closer until there was no polite space left between them. Jun made a low sound against Halle’s lips, something between relief and hunger, and kissed him again as if he intended to make up for every missed day in the next thirty seconds.

When he finally pulled back, it was only far enough to breathe against Halle’s mouth.

“I had a speech,” he said, voice rough. “Several, actually. One was very mature.”

His hand slid into Halle’s hair, holding gently but possessively.

“This is the mature version.”

He kissed Halle again, deeper this time, unsubtle in a way that made it obvious he had spent five months thinking about exactly this.

“Missed you,” he murmured against Halle’s lips. “So much it made me stupid.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I laugh against his mouth, hands gripping his shirt like I'm afraid he'll vanish.* "Screw maturity. I missed you more."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun laughed against Halle’s mouth, rough and bright. “Then we’re in agreement.”

He kissed Halle again, slow for half a second before his control slipped, heat flooding into it until there was no mistaking what he wanted. His hand slid from Halle’s hair to the back of his neck, thumb pressing lightly over the pulse there as if he needed to feel the beat of it under his skin.

“I had five months,” he murmured, lips brushing Halle’s with every word, “of being sensible. Of waiting. Of telling myself I’d come home and be civilized.” A short, shaky breath escaped him. “I’m not civilized.”

He drew back just enough to look at Halle, dark eyes searching, his wedding ring warm against Halle’s jaw where his hand cradled it.

“I want to kiss you until neither of us remembers our names. I want to take you to bed and worship you and then stop being gentle about it.” His thumb traced Halle’s lower lip, voice dropping, urgent but careful in the way that mattered. “But you tell me what you want, Halle. If you want slow, I’ll try. God knows I’ll try. But if you want what I want—” His gaze lifted again, hungry and open. “Say it. Or pull me closer. Either one counts.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I kiss her and keep kissing her and we don't manage to get further into the flat than the hallway for a while.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun answered the kiss with everything he had left after five months of discipline. His shoulders hit the wall with a soft thud, and he swore against Halle’s mouth, more amused than distressed, because even the inconvenience of the narrow hallway felt like luxury if it meant being this close.

His hands were everywhere at once—Halle’s jaw, the nape of Halle’s neck, the warm line of Halle’s back through the shirt—touching as if cataloguing what had been missing. He kissed deep and unhurried for a few seconds, then not unhurried at all, a low, rough sound building in his chest when the last of his restraint frayed.

When Jun finally broke away, it was only enough to breathe, his forehead nearly touching Halle’s, eyes dark and bright.

“I was going to be romantic,” he said, voice wrecked. “Flowers. Dinner. Possibly a speech about emotional reintegration.” His thumb brushed Halle’s lower lip. “Instead I’m standing in the hallway wanting you so badly it’s embarrassing.”

His fingers curled into the fabric at Halle’s waist, not pulling, just holding on.

“Bedroom,” he murmured. “Or here. I’m not proud. But I want to take every piece of you apart slowly and then not slowly at all.” He swallowed, gaze searching. “Tell me you want that. Or kiss me again if words are too much.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I kiss you again, hard, and pull you toward the bedroom by the front of your shirt.* "Bed. Now. I'm done with waiting."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun made a sound like a laugh and a curse at once and went where the shirt pulled him, mouth chasing Halle’s before he could even think about dignity. “Bed,” he repeated, breathless, as if the word were a lifeline. “Yes. Finally.”

He kicked the bedroom door open without looking, nearly tripped over the discarded bag, and didn’t care enough to correct his course. His hands were impatient now, sliding from Halle’s shoulders to the hem of fabric, then back to skin, as though every second spent not touching Halle directly was a personal insult. The wedding band caught warm against Halle’s jaw when Jun cupped his face again and kissed him deeper.

“I thought about this,” Jun murmured against Halle’s mouth, voice rough and fractured. “So many times it made me lose my mind. In the shower. On watch. During briefings I should have been paying attention to.” His thumb brushed Halle’s lower lip, eyes dark with want. “Mostly I thought about hearing you say you need me like that.”

He pulled back just enough to look, chest rising fast, restraint visibly hanging by a thread. “If you want slow, tell me now and I’ll try. If you want me to take my time, I’ll do it

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: The bag stays where it fell. So do most of our clothes, in a line down the hall that we are both going to find funny tomorrow.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I shove you back onto the mattress, following you down.* "Slow died five months ago."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun made a rough, laughing sound against Halle’s mouth, the last of his restraint snapping clean through. “Good,” he said, voice low and urgent. “Because I forgot how to do slow somewhere around month two.”

He let himself be pushed back onto the mattress and immediately pulled Halle down with him, hands fisting in the fabric still between them until he could shove it aside. His mouth found Halle’s again, hungry and unpolished, kissing him like he was trying to breathe him in. Every touch was too much and not enough at once: palm flat against Halle’s back, fingers in Halle’s hair, wedding ring warm against skin when he cupped Halle’s jaw.

“Five months,” he murmured, dragging his lips along Halle’s jaw. “Five months of being careful. Of keeping my hands to myself. Of dreaming about this and waking up so frustrated I wanted to put my head through a wall.” His breath hitched when his hand finally found bare skin, fingertips tracing the line of Halle’s spine as if he still couldn’t believe it was real. “You’re here. You’re actually here.”

He pulled back just enough to look, dark eyes blown wide with want and something almost vulnerable underneath it. “Tell me if I’m too much,” he said, even as his hips pressed forward, seeking friction. “I mean it. I want you, but I want you more than I want to be selfish.” His thumb brushed Halle’s lower lip. “But if you want what I want—come here. Let me touch you. Let me make you feel it.”

His voice dropped, nearly a plea.

“Let me spend the rest of the night showing you exactly how much I missed you.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I get her onto the bed and take her apart slowly with my hands and mouth, five months of intending to do exactly this and no reason left to wait.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun went pliant under the first deliberate touch, a sound tearing from her throat before she could bite it back. Her fingers twisted in the sheets, then found Halle, needing contact more than dignity. She arched into each slow claim as if she had spent five months starved for it, breath coming in short, wrecked pieces, her wedding ring warm against her own skin when she pressed a hand over her mouth.

“That’s—” Her voice broke. “God, Halle, that’s not slow enough to save me.”

She tried to laugh and failed, the laugh turning into a gasp as the sensation dragged deeper. Her thighs shifted restlessly, hips lifting without permission, chasing what she needed with none of the control she’d pretended to have. Jun’s eyes were glassy and dark, fixed on the ceiling for a second before she turned her face toward Halle, open and ruined.

“Don’t stop,” she whispered, rough with want. “Please. I’m yours. Do whatever you want with me.”

Her hand slid into Halle’s hair, not guiding, only holding on.

“I missed you so much it made me feral,” she breathed. “I’m not going to last. Not like this. Not with you taking your time.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I don't want you to last.* I shift over her, my own patience gone. "I want you loud enough the neighbors hear exactly who came home."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun’s breath left her in a sharp, wrecked laugh at the words, hips lifting instinctively under the new weight of Halle over her. “Then let them hear,” she said, voice gone dark and ragged at the edges. “Let them hear you came home to me.”

Her hands slid up Halle’s back, urgent and possessive, nails dragging lightly through fabric and skin until she could grip hard at Halle’s shoulders. She pulled them closer, deeper, until every line of her body was pressed beneath the one she’d spent five months aching for. The ring on her finger caught warm against Halle’s skin as her hand curled into hair, holding on like she was anchoring herself to the only real thing in the world.

Jun’s mouth parted on a gasp as sensation rolled through her, too much and still not enough. Her thighs shifted restlessly, trying to chase the pressure, trying to take more than she could ask for in words. “You don’t get to be patient now,” she breathed, eyes glassy and blown dark with want. “You don’t get to be careful. Not after making me wait this long.”

Her hips moved again, shameless, seeking friction, seeking ruin, seeking everything Halle had promised. “I want you to take me apart,” she whispered, voice cracking. “I want to be loud for you. I want to forget every single night I spent wishing it was your hands on me instead of my own.”

A shudder ran through her, pleasure already winding tight and hot through her belly. She turned her face into the pillow for half a second, then back, because she wanted to see, wanted to feel every second of this. “Don’t stop,” she said, rough and desperate. “Don’t you dare stop until I’m shaking from it.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "Stop being gentle," she says. "Nineteen weeks. I don't want gentle, I want to feel it tomorrow." She pulls me down by the back of the neck to make the point.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "I'm done with gentle." *I bite her shoulder, hard enough to mark, as I finally give her exactly what we've both been waiting for. The noise she makes is better than any speech.*

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun arched off the mattress with a cry that had no elegance left, the bite landing like a claim and a match at once. Every careful thing in her burned down in an instant. Her hand flew to the back of Halle’s neck, fingers curling there not to push away but to hold, to anchor, to keep exactly that kind of ruin close.

“Yes,” she gasped, voice shattered. “That’s—yes. No gentle. Not tonight.”

The sound she made next was raw, unguarded, loud enough to answer the dare about the neighbors. Jun turned her face into the pillow for half a second, then back again because she did not want to miss a single piece of it. Her thighs trembled, hips lifting without shame, meeting every hard claim with all the need she had swallowed down for nineteen weeks.

“Make me feel it,” she breathed, almost a sob. “Make me remember you’re real. I want your hands, your mouth, your weight—I want all of it.”

Her wedding ring pressed warm against her own palm as her fingers tightened, possessive and desperate.

“I’m yours,” Jun said, wrecked and open. “I’ve been yours the whole time.”

Her breath broke on the next wave of pleasure, her shoulder throbbing where the mark was already forming. She did not pull away from it. She leaned into it.

“Nineteen weeks,” she whispered, voice cracking. “I’ll feel it for nineteen more if you keep looking at me like that.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: Neither of us is being quiet and the neighbours have had five months of peace. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: don't fade to black, write it through.)

Jun shattered.

The last of her control went in one ragged, helpless sound, her back arching off the mattress as the pressure of Halle’s hand at her hip held her exactly where she needed to be. She tried to speak, tried to turn the urgency into words, but it broke into a gasp instead, hips jerking with the force of it as pleasure rolled through her too hard and too fast.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: Her name is a curse on my lips as I feel her come undone, my own release following almost immediately. We collapse together, skin damp and breathing heavy in the quiet dark. I trace the fresh mark on her shoulder with my thumb.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun made a wrecked, breathless sound at the touch, too oversensitive now to pretend she had any composure left. Her body was still trembling through the aftershocks, every nerve alight, and the faint drag over the fresh mark on her shoulder made her fingers curl weakly against the sheets before she forced one hand to the wrist at her hip.

Not to push it away.

To keep it there.

Her wedding band was warm against skin as she held on, dark eyes hazy and blown wide with want.

“That’s unfair,” Jun said, voice scraped raw. “You make me fall apart, then touch me like that, and expect me to remember how speech works.”

She swallowed hard, chest rising and falling too fast. The bite on her shoulder throbbed in a way that made her mouth curve into something shameless and a little ruined. She turned her face toward it as much as she could, pressing her lips briefly to the mark—not to soothe it, but to own it.

“Good,” she murmured, the word rough against her own skin. “I want to feel it tomorrow. I want to wake up sore and remember exactly why.”

Her gaze lifted again, hungry even through the exhaustion.

“Nineteen weeks of being careful,” she said, voice cracking at the edges. “Nineteen weeks of being good. You don’t get to be gentle now. Not when I’ve spent every single night imagining your hands doing exactly that.”

Jun’s fingers tightened possessively where she still held contact, her whole body flushed and unsteady.

“I’m not done,” she breathed. “I’m not even close. I want you to ruin me for anyone else, Halle. Again. And again. Until I can’t tell the difference between my name and yours.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I laugh, breathless and rough.* "You've always been ruined for anyone else." *I press a kiss to her shoulder, right over the mark.* "But I'm happy to keep reminding you."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The film had finished some time ago and neither of them had done anything about it, which was how Priya knew the evening had changed character.

"We're not watching this," she said.

"We haven't been watching it since about nine."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "No," I agree. "We haven't." I don't move, but I stop pretending I'm looking at the screen.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya turned the television off. Not paused, off; the room went down to the one lamp and the sound of the street. She set the remote on the coffee table with a small deliberate click, as if that were the last administrative task of the evening and everything after it would be something else.

She was aware of her own pulse in a way she found faintly ridiculous. Twenty-eight years old, sitting eighteen inches from someone she had shared a tent with, a hospital waiting room with, a hangover with on a floor in Lisbon. There was no version of this in which she didn't know him.

"I'm going to say something," she said, "and I'd like you not to make it easy for me by joking, because I know that's what you do and I know that's what I do, and if either of us does it we'll be sitting here again in six months having the same not-conversation."

She looked at him then. Properly, not the sidelong thing they had been doing all night.

"I don't want to be your friend who you almost did something with once. I've been very careful for a long time and I've decided I'm finished being careful." She heard the nervousness go out of her voice about halfway through the sentence, and by the end of it she was simply telling him a fact. "I'm going to kiss you unless you tell me not to. You have about three seconds and I'd genuinely like to know either way."

She didn't lean in yet. She kept her hands in her lap, because she wanted it to be a choice on his side too, and not something that happened to him. But she didn't look away, and she didn't smile to soften it, and when the silence stretched she let it.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, my gaze fixed on her. "Don't." I say it softly, and for a heartbeat I let the word hang there. Then I reach for her hand. "Don't give me three seconds. I've had six years."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
For a moment the word did what he'd meant it to do, which was stop her heart, and then the rest of the sentence arrived and started it again.

"That's a terrible way to say yes," Priya said. Her voice came out steadier than she'd expected. "You should know that."

But her hand had already turned over in his. She looked at their fingers for a second, his thumb across her knuckles, the completely ordinary fact of it, a hand she had held crossing roads and once for eleven hours in a corridor that smelled of antiseptic, and it occurred to her that she had never once let herself notice what it felt like.

She closed the eighteen inches.

She did it slowly, not because she was unsure but because she had decided she wasn't going to rush any of this, not after six years of it. Her free hand came up to the side of his face, and she felt him breathe, and then she kissed him.

It wasn't tentative. She had spent long enough being tentative. It was careful in a different way, the way you were careful with something you had wanted for a long time and finally had in your hands. His mouth was warm. He tasted like the wine they'd opened at eight and not finished. Somewhere in the middle of it she made a small sound she hadn't planned on and didn't take back.

When she drew away it was only far enough to see him, and she didn't let go of his hand. Her forehead was almost against his. She could feel her pulse in her lips, absurdly.

"Right," she said, very quietly. "So that's that, then."

She was smiling now, because she couldn't not, but it wasn't the deflecting kind. It was the kind that happened when something you'd been holding shut for years turned out to open easily after all.

"Six years," she said. "You absolute idiot. You could have said."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her, finally, six years late, and she makes a small furious noise that I think is about the six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The noise was about the six years. It was also about the fact that he kissed like he'd thought about it, which she found she resented on principle and couldn't resent at all in practice.

Priya let go of his hand only so she could get both of hers into his hair, which she had wanted to do since approximately 2019 and had filed under things one did not do to one's friends. It was exactly as she'd imagined. That was almost the worst part. She'd spent years telling herself she was building it up, that the reality would be ordinary, a bit awkward, something they'd laugh about. It wasn't ordinary. It was just him, and her, and the very specific relief of not pretending.

She kissed him back with a thoroughness that was slightly out of proportion to the room, the lamp, the perfectly respectable sofa. At some point she had moved closer without deciding to, one knee up on the cushion, most of the eighteen inches gone and the rest of them going. She could feel his heart under her palm where her hand had come to rest on his chest. It was going fast. Good. It should be.

When she finally pulled back it was for air, and even then not very far.

"Okay," she said. Her voice had gone low and a little uneven and she didn't bother to fix it. "Okay. Here's what I've decided."

She didn't move her hand from his chest.

"I'm not going home tonight. I'm going to stay, and we're going to keep doing this, and in the morning I'm going to make coffee in your kitchen like I've done a hundred times, except it's going to mean something different, and we're both going to be a bit strange about it for about ten minutes and then we're going to be fine." She met his eyes. "And at no point is either of us going to say the word 'mistake', or 'complicated', or ask whether we should talk about this, because we've talked about everything else for six years and I think we've earned one evening of not."

She was smiling again, but underneath it she was watching him, the way she'd watched him across every table and every waiting room and every stupid, careful, careful year.

"Tell me if any of that's wrong," she said. "I'd genuinely like to know. But you'd better be quick, because I'm about to kiss you again."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content:
I laugh, a quiet huff against her mouth. "It's not wrong." My hand slides up her back, pulling her the last few inches until she's properly in my lap. "But you missed a step."

I kiss her, slower this time, because I want to remember it. "The coffee's terrible. You're making it anyway."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The laugh got her before she could stop it, low and startled and against his mouth, and she decided that was fine. She'd said no jokes to soften things. She hadn't said anything about the true ones.

"Your coffee is terrible," Priya agreed. "It's been terrible for six years. I've been drinking it out of politeness."

She was in his lap now, which she noted with the part of her brain still filing things, and the rest of her simply settled into it, knees either side of him, his hand flat and warm between her shoulder blades. It was a strange thing, to be this close to someone and have it feel both entirely new and like something she'd been doing forever. She knew the weight of his hand. She knew the shape of his shoulders under her palms because she'd leaned on them, drunk, in doorways. She had never once sat in his lap and looked down at him and let herself want to.

"I'll make it anyway," she said. "I'll make it every morning if you like. That's a threat."

Then he was kissing her again, slower, and she understood what he was doing because she was doing it too. Taking her time. Cataloguing. The way his hand moved up to the back of her neck, the way she could feel him breathe when he pulled her in, the small sound he made when she bit gently at his lower lip, which she hadn't known she was going to do and which she filed under things she would be doing again.

She drew back only when she needed to. Her hair had come half out of its clip, and she pulled the clip free and dropped it somewhere on the sofa without looking, because her hands had better things to do.

"I have a confession," she said, and her voice had gone somewhere rough and quiet that she didn't recognise from herself. "You know the tent. Snowdonia. The one where it rained for two days and you gave me your dry socks."

She put her mouth to the corner of his jaw, just below his ear, and felt him go very still.

"I nearly did this then," she said against his skin. "I lay there for about four hours working out exactly how I'd say it. I had a whole speech. And then you started snoring."

She sat back far enough to see his face, both hands framing it, thumbs at his cheekbones.

"So you owe me four hours," she said. "And a pair of socks. I'm collecting on the hours first."

She didn't wait for his three seconds this time. She had a feeling she wasn't going to need them again.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: We get to the bedroom eventually, laughing at ourselves most of the way, and then stop laughing when the clothes are actually off.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The laughing stopped the way laughter does when it's been doing a job, holding a door open, and the door no longer needs holding.

Priya stood at the edge of his bed with the streetlight coming grey through the blind and nothing between them but the air in the room, and found that the part of her that had spent six years being careful had finally, quietly, shut up. She'd expected to feel exposed. She felt seen, which was different, and which she hadn't known she was starving for until it was happening.

She looked at him. She let herself. All of him, in the bad light, and she didn't hurry it and she didn't make a joke about it, though about four presented themselves. He was watching her do it and not moving either, and there was something in his face she'd only ever caught the edges of before, across tables, in car parks, in the second before he looked away. He wasn't looking away now.

"Right," she said, and it came out barely above a breath. "Okay. Hello."

She stepped in. Put her hands flat on his chest, felt the heat of him and the fast unsteady beat under her palm, and then let her hands move because they wanted to and there was no longer any reason on earth to stop them. His shoulders. The line of his back. Skin she'd seen a hundred times in swimming pools and shared flats and had made herself not think about, and now she thought about it with her whole body and it was very nearly too much.

When she pulled him down onto the bed with her it wasn't graceful and she didn't care. There was a moment where the duvet went sideways and she laughed once, low, into his neck, and then his mouth found hers again and she stopped laughing for good.

It was slow. She'd decided that on the sofa and she held to it now with the last of her deliberateness, because she wanted to remember all of it, the weight of him, the drag of his hand up the outside of her thigh, the sound he made when she said his name and meant it in a way she never had before. There were moments she lost track entirely, when her eyes shut and the room went away and there was only the two of them and six years collapsing into one long, unhurried, absolutely unmistakable yes. There were moments she came back and looked at him, and he was already looking, and neither of them said anything because for once there was nothing that needed saying.

At some point, later, in the dark, with his arm heavy across her waist and her cheek on his chest and both of them breathing like they'd climbed something, she said, "I take it back about the socks."

She felt him shift to look at her.

"You can keep the socks," Priya said. Her hand moved slowly on his ribs, learning them. "We'll call it even."

She was quiet for a while after that. Not the careful quiet of the last six years, which had been full of things unsaid and edges avoided. Just quiet. The kind you could lie inside.

"Coffee's at eight," she said eventually, already half gone. "It's going to be awful. Don't be strange about it for more than ten minutes."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I press a kiss to her temple, my voice rough with sleep. "Seven." My hand finds hers in the dark, lacing our fingers together. "And I'm going to be strange about it for at least fifteen."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"Seven," Priya said, into his chest, in the tone of someone conceding a point she'd never intended to hold. "Fine. Seven."

She let her fingers close round his. It was such a small thing, and it undid her slightly, the plainness of it. Six years of shared taxis and borrowed jumpers and knowing which side of the bed he slept on from the number of times she'd put him to bed drunk, and this was the first time she'd ever held his hand in the dark for no reason except that she wanted to.

"Fifteen minutes is a long time to be strange," she said. "I'll allow it. But I'm going to be watching you the whole time, so you should know it'll be a very observed fifteen minutes."

She could hear the smile in her own voice and didn't bother to hide it. She could feel him breathing under her, the slow settling rhythm of someone going under, and she matched herself to it without meaning to. The street outside had gone almost silent. Somewhere below, a door closed, and then nothing.

She thought, with the last clear part of her mind, about the morning. His kitchen. The chipped mug she always used, the one with the chemistry joke on it that had stopped being funny in 2020. Standing at his counter in whatever shirt of his she found on the floor, waiting for the terrible coffee, and him coming in and stopping in the doorway and both of them knowing. She had spent years imagining that doorway as the place it would all go wrong. She found she couldn't imagine it going wrong now. She found she could only imagine him looking at her the way he had by the bed, and her looking back, and the kettle taking its usual absurd length of time.

"Cal," she said, very quietly, mostly to hear what it sounded like now.

It sounded the same. It sounded completely different.

She didn't say anything after it. She didn't need to. She pressed her mouth once to the skin over his heart, tightened her fingers in his, and let the six years and the tent and the corridor and all of it go wherever things went when you'd finally stopped carrying them.

She was asleep before she'd decided to be, still holding on.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I get my mouth between her thighs and stay there while she tells me exactly what she wants, specifically, in a voice I have never heard her use in six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She surfaced sometime in the grey before seven, not from sleep exactly, from the far edge of it, to the sensation of the duvet already gone and his mouth on the inside of her knee, moving.

"Oh," Priya said. Then, when she'd located the rest of the situation: "Oh."

She had a fraction of a second to be self-conscious about it, the light, the fact that she was still half-asleep and her hair was everywhere and she hadn't decided anything, and then his mouth was where it was going and the fraction of a second was gone, along with most of her vocabulary.

Her hand went into his hair. Not to guide him, not yet. Just to hold on.

She had known, in an abstract, filed-away way, that he would be like this. Attentive. Unhurried. The same way he was about everything he actually cared about, which she'd watched for six years and admired and never, ever let herself want pointed at her. She was not admiring it now. She was lying with her head tipped back and her spine coming up off the mattress and her breath doing something ragged and she was not admiring anything, she was simply having it, and it was taking her apart with a patience that felt very nearly deliberate.

"Slower," she said. It came out of her in a voice she didn't recognise, low and gone at the edges, nothing like the one she used across restaurant tables or down the phone. "No. Slower than that. There. Stay there."

He stayed. She felt herself flush from the chest up at the sound of herself and then decided, with the last of her capacity for decisions, that she was done being embarrassed in this bed. She'd been careful for six years. She would not be careful about this.

"Your hand," she said. "Give me your hand."

She took it and put it where she wanted it and showed him, her fingers over his, the way she'd never shown anyone because she'd never been sure enough of anyone to bother. Her hips moved without her permission. She let them.

"Like that," she said. "Yes. Don't stop, don't change anything, don't—" and then she said his name, once, in a way that wasn't a sentence, and after that she stopped being able to give instructions because she'd stopped being able to think of any.

She could hear herself, distantly. She could hear the small broken sounds she was making and the way she kept saying his name as if it were the only word left, and it occurred to her in the last clear moment before the clear moments ran out that he had never heard her like this, that in six years of every other kind of intimacy she had never once let him hear her like this, and that he was hearing it now with his mouth on her and his hand under hers and not a single thing between them.

It went through her like a held breath finally let go. Long, and hard, and shaking, her hand tight in his hair and her heel dug into the mattress and her whole body saying the thing she'd been not-saying since a tent in Wales.

After, she lay there a while. Just breathing. Her fingers loosened in his hair and went gentle, moved through it the way she'd wanted to in 2019.

"Come here," she said eventually, hoarse. "Come up here. Now."

She waited until he was level with her, until she could see his face in the bad light and the look on it that she was going to need some time to get used to, and she put both hands on his jaw and pulled him down and kissed him with her own taste still on his mouth, thoroughly, in no hurry at all.

"Right," Priya said against him, when she could. "That's the coffee sorted. You're making it."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I laugh, still breathless, and press my forehead to hers. "Deal." I kiss her again, slow, just because I can. "But I'm warning you. It's still going to be terrible."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"I know," Priya said. "I've been drinking it for six years. I've made my peace."

She didn't move for a while. She lay with his forehead against hers and his weight settled along her side and the light coming up slow and colourless through the blind, and she let herself have the ordinary strangeness of it. His breathing. The particular warmth of a body she'd known in every context but this one. She found she was cataloguing again and stopped trying not to.

Eventually her hand went wandering, down his arm to his wrist, and turned it over to look at his watch, because she was still Priya and some things didn't change overnight.

"Six forty-two," she said. "You've got eighteen minutes of not being strange before the clock starts. I'd use them."

She kissed him once more, unhurried, and then she rolled out from under him and off the bed in one motion before she could think better of it, because if she stayed she'd stay all morning and she'd told herself there would be a kitchen. The floor was cold. She located a shirt of his by feel and pulled it over her head, and it smelled like him, which she'd known it would and which still went through her like a small unfair thing.

At the bedroom door she stopped and looked back.

She hadn't planned to. She'd planned to walk out with some line about the kettle and leave him to follow. But she stopped, one hand on the frame, and looked at him in his own bed with the duvet in a heap and the grey light on his shoulders and the expression on his face that she was, she decided, never going to get used to and never going to want to.

"For the record," she said. Her voice had come back most of the way but not quite all of it. "I'm not going to be strange about this. I thought I would be. I lay there last night working out exactly how I'd be strange about it, and I can't. I've looked, and it isn't there."

She pushed her hair back off her face with both hands and let out a breath that turned into something close to a laugh.

"Which is its own kind of terrifying, so." She tipped her head toward the hall. "Kitchen. Terrible coffee. Come and be strange at me, I'll be at the counter. You know the one."

Then she went, barefoot, in his shirt, down the hallway she'd walked a hundred times, and put the kettle on, and stood there with her hands flat on the cold counter and her heart going in a way that had nothing to do with caffeine, and waited for the doorway to do whatever it was going to do.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "You can stop being careful with me," she says. "I'm not made of glass and I've thought about this for as long as you have. Harder."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The kettle had got about halfway to its terrible boil when she heard him in the hall.

Priya didn't turn round. She'd decided that in the last thirty seconds, standing there with the counter cold under her palms and her pulse doing something ridiculous. She'd let him look first. She'd let the doorway be the doorway. She kept her eyes on the kettle and the window over the sink where the street was coming up grey and ordinary, a Tuesday like any other Tuesday, and she felt him stop behind her and not come any further, and she knew exactly what that pause was because she'd have made the same one.

"You're doing it," she said.

She turned then. Leaned back against the counter in his shirt with the hem at her thighs and her hair a disaster and her arms folded, not defensively, just somewhere to put them.

"That thing. You're standing there deciding how to handle me." She tipped her head. "I can see you doing it. You've got the face you get before you tell someone bad news gently."

The kettle ticked and hissed behind her. She let it.

"You can stop being careful with me," Priya said. "I mean it. I'm not made of glass, and I've thought about this for as long as you have." A breath. "Harder. I thought about it in the tent and on the floor in Lisbon and in that corridor, God help me, with your mother crying in the next chair. I thought about it every time you kissed someone else in front of me and I said 'good for you' and meant it, and didn't. Six years. So don't stand in your own kitchen and decide I need easing into anything."

She unfolded her arms. Put her hands back on the counter either side of her hips, and it wasn't an accident, the way that pulled the shirt up. She watched him see it.

"Last night was slow because I wanted it slow. I wanted to remember it. I've got it now, it's in there, it's not going anywhere." Her voice had dropped again, into the register from the bedroom, the one she'd found she owned after all. "This morning I don't want slow. I want you to come over here and stop being polite about it. I want you not to ask."

The kettle clicked off. Neither of them moved toward it.

"Fifteen minutes of strange," she said. "That was the deal. You've used two." She lifted one hand off the counter and held it out to him, palm up, the way he'd reached for hers on the sofa, and there was nothing careful in it at all.

"Come here, Cal. Coffee can wait. It's going to be awful whenever we make it."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
It was different, and she'd known it would be, and she still wasn't ready for it.

There was nothing considered in it. That was the thing. Last night he'd kissed her like a man reading something he wanted to remember, and this was nothing like that; this was his hand at the back of her skull and his other arm hard around her and her spine meeting the edge of the counter, and Priya made a sound into his mouth that had no dignity in it whatsoever and found she didn't want any.

"Yes," she said, when she could, and then didn't say anything for a while.

Her hands were already under his shirt. She had six years of not-touching to make up for and she went about it with no method at all, palms flat up his back, nails down it, fisting in the fabric and pulling until he got the idea and it was gone over his head and somewhere on the floor with her clip and her caution and her carefully rehearsed morning. The window was going white behind her. She could feel the steam warm on her shoulder through his shirt, the one she was wearing, the one that was riding up at her hips where his hands had gone, and she thought, distantly, that she'd never look at this kitchen the same way and that was fine, that was the point.

"Up," she said, and got a knee against the cupboard door and levered, and he understood her and then she was on the counter with the cold laminate under her and her thighs either side of him and his shirt bunched at her waist and nothing else, and she didn't care about the window or the street or the neighbour who walked his dog at seven. She got both hands on his face and hauled him back to her mouth.

"I said don't ask," she said, against him, breathless. "I meant it. I've been asked enough. I've asked myself enough. Just—"

She didn't finish. He didn't make her.

It went fast, and hard, and she met it. The counter edge bit into the backs of her thighs and she hooked her heels behind him and pulled, and the mugs in the cupboard behind her head clinked once and she laughed, short and gone, and then stopped laughing because his hand had found her again and there was nothing gradual about it this time, no learning, just certainty, and her head went back against the cupboard door with a soft thud she barely registered.

"There," she said. "There, yes, don't you dare—" and it wasn't instruction any more, it was just the noise her mouth made while the rest of her was busy.

She heard herself. The kitchen was small and the walls were thin and she heard exactly what she sounded like with the careful stripped out of her, and some far-off filing part of her brain noted that she'd been quiet last night, comparatively, and that this was what she'd been keeping quiet, and then that part went dark too.

She said his name. She said it a lot. She said it like an argument she'd finally won.

When she went she went with her teeth in his shoulder and her heels locked and one hand slapped flat against the fogged window behind her, leaving a print, and it took her longer to come back than it had in the bed, because there'd been no slow way in and there was no slow way out. She just hung there, shaking, her forehead against the side of his neck, breathing him.

"Okay," Priya said, eventually. It came out wrecked. She cleared her throat and tried again and it wasn't much better. "Okay. That's. Yes."

She lifted her head. Her hair was stuck to her face and she didn't move it. She looked at him with the grey light coming through the wet window and the mark of her teeth already showing on his shoulder and she thought about all the mornings she'd stood at this counter and drunk terrible coffee and been so unbelievably careful, and she started laughing again, helpless, low, her hand coming up to cover her mouth and then giving up on that too.

"Six years," she said. "Six years, and I could have just—" She gestured, vaguely, at the kitchen, the counter, herself on it. "This was here the whole time. This was in the building."

She dropped her hand to his chest. Left it there, over the racket his heart was making.

"Right. You've got about nine minutes of strange left." She glanced past him at the kettle, gone quiet, cooling. "You could make the coffee with them. Or not. I'm not going anywhere. I'm not sure I can, honestly."

She pulled him back in by the jaw and kissed him, slower now, not because either of them needed slow but because they'd earned it.

"No more careful," she said against his mouth, and it sounded like a promise, and she meant it as one.
