dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She'd meant the slower kiss to be a full stop. It turned out to be a comma.

Because he was still hard against her, and she'd known that, distantly, the way she'd known the kettle had gone off, and the moment his mouth left hers to breathe the knowledge stopped being distant. Priya looked down between them, at the state of him, at the state of herself, and whatever she'd been about to say about coffee went somewhere and didn't come back.

"Oh, we're not done," she said. It wasn't a question.

She got a hand round him. Just held him, for a second, warm and heavy in her palm, and watched his face do something she was going to think about for weeks. Then she shifted forward on the counter until the edge was under her and there was nowhere left to go but him, and lined him up herself, because she'd said don't ask and she'd meant she'd take it, and she took it.

Slow, for one breath. Just the first of him, and her mouth opening on nothing, and his hands going white-knuckled on the laminate either side of her hips.

Then not slow.

"Don't stop," Priya said, and it was the last full sentence either of them managed for some time.

She'd thought the first time had stripped the careful out of her. It had only found the seam. This was the thing itself; this was him inside her in his kitchen with the neighbour's dog barking somewhere below the fogged window and the cupboard door knocking against the wall behind her head in a rhythm that was going to be very hard to explain and that she had no intention of explaining. Her heels were locked at the small of his back. Her hands were everywhere and then nowhere, flung back against the cupboard for purchase, then in his hair, then dug into his shoulders hard enough to leave the marks she'd started with her teeth. She was making a sound on every stroke, low and shameless and getting louder, and she didn't try to bring it down.

Words came out of her in pieces. His name. Yes. There. Harder, once, and he gave it to her, and the mug cupboard rattled and something inside it fell over and neither of them stopped. She couldn't get a sentence together and she didn't miss them. Six years of sentences. Six years of being articulate at him across tables. This was the opposite of that and it was the truest thing she'd ever said to him.

She could feel him getting close. She knew it the way she'd known he'd sleep on the left side of the bed, some deep file of him she'd been keeping without permission, and she got her hand between them and touched herself where he was moving in her and said, or tried to say, "Wait for me—" and he heard it, because his rhythm changed, deliberate now, holding, and that was the thing that undid her. Not the speed. That he'd heard.

She came with her forehead against his and her eyes open. She hadn't planned that either. She watched him watch her go, felt herself clench around him and the noise she made, high and broken and nothing like the woman who'd sat on his sofa and given him three seconds, and she saw the exact moment it took him with her: his breath catching, his jaw going slack, the long shudder through him as he came inside her with a sound she'd never heard from him in six years and intended to hear again as often as physically possible.

The kitchen went quiet, except for breathing. Except for the last slow drip of the tap.

Priya didn't move. Couldn't have. She was slumped against him with the counter edge printing itself into the backs of her thighs and his heartbeat going against her chest and hers going against his and both of them, she thought, probably audible from the hall. Her hand was still flat against the window. When she took it away it left a perfect print in the steam, five fingers and a palm, and she looked at it and started laughing again, weakly, into the sweat on his neck.

"I can't," she said. It came out in pieces too. "I can't. Sentences. Gone."

She lifted her head. Pushed her hair off her face with the back of her wrist. Looked at him, wrecked and flushed and hers, in the grey light, with the window fogged behind her and the cupboard door slightly ajar and the mug with the chemistry joke on it fallen on its side inside.

"Nine minutes," she managed. "Was it. Nine minutes of strange."

She checked his watch, because she was still Priya, and found she couldn't read it, and gave up.

"Doesn't matter." Her voice was raw. She put her mouth to the mark she'd left on his shoulder and kissed it, once, softly, the first gentle thing she'd done in ten minutes. "Doesn't matter. You've got the rest of your life to be strange at me. I'm not going anywhere."

She let her legs unhook from him, finally, slow, and felt him slip from her and made a small sound about it that she didn't take back. Then she sat there on his counter in his shirt, coming down, with the kettle stone cold beside her, and looked at him, and didn't say anything for a long moment because she'd used all her words and found she didn't need any.

"Right," Priya said eventually. "Now coffee."

She didn't move to get down. She held out her hand to him again instead, palm up, the way she had before, and waited.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I stare at her hand, then take it, lacing our fingers. My voice is wrecked. "Coffee's cold." I kiss her knuckles. "I'll make more. It'll still be terrible."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"Cold," Priya agreed. She looked at the kettle as if it had personally let them down. "You had one job."

She let him keep her hand a moment longer, his mouth on her knuckles, and felt it land somewhere under her sternum in a way she wasn't going to examine yet. Then she slid off the counter. Her legs weren't entirely reliable and she made no effort to hide it, catching herself on his forearm, standing there for a second with the laminate warm behind her and the floor cold underfoot and the shirt falling back down to somewhere approaching decent.

"Fine," she said. "Make more. I'll supervise."

She didn't supervise. She leaned against the fridge with her arms loosely folded and watched him do it, which was different. Watched him fill the kettle at the tap and set it back on its base and reach into the cupboard, where the chemistry mug had gone over on its side, and right it without comment. Watched the mark on his shoulder, already going purple at the edges. Watched the ordinary competent shape of him moving around a kitchen she knew as well as her own, and felt the strangeness she'd promised him she couldn't find come and stand quietly next to her after all.

Not the bad kind. She checked. Not the kind that wanted to leave, or apologise, or say the word she'd banned on the sofa. Just the plain vertigo of a familiar thing seen from a new angle. The doorway hadn't done anything terrible. It had just done this.

"You know what I keep thinking," she said. Her voice had come back most of the way. "All those mornings. Sitting at that table, drinking this, listening to you tell me about whoever it was that month. I used to leave here and walk to the Tube and be so pleased with myself. So grown up about it." She shook her head. "I wasn't grown up. I was just scared, and I'd found a way to make scared look like good manners."

The kettle started its slow climb. She pushed off the fridge and went to him, came up behind him where he was spooning grounds into the press with the wrong ratio, the way he always had, and put her arms round his waist and her cheek between his shoulder blades. Just stood there, holding on.

"I'm not scared now," she said, into his back. "For the record. I thought I would be. Thought this bit, the after, the daylight, would be where it caught up with me." She breathed him in. "It hasn't. I keep waiting and it hasn't."

The kettle clicked off. Neither of them reached for it.

"Go on, then," Priya said, and let him go, and went to get the mugs down herself, because that had always been her job and she saw no reason to change it. She set the chemistry one in front of him, the one she always used, and took the plain blue one, and then thought about it and swapped them.

"You have that one," she said. "It's yours. I've been borrowing it."

She stood at the counter, hip against the edge that had bruised her thighs, and waited for the water to go into the press and the four minutes to do their work, and watched the window behind her slowly clear, her handprint the last thing to go.

"It's going to be terrible," she said, when he poured. She took the cup. Wrapped both hands round it. "I know. Say it anyway. I like it when you say it."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I look at her over the rim of my mug. The steam fogs my glasses. "It's terrible," I say, and I'm not talking about the coffee.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She heard it. Of course she heard it. Six years of listening to this man say one thing and mean another, and she'd got very good at the translation.

Priya didn't answer straight away. She took a mouthful of the coffee, because she'd asked for it and she'd have it, and it was exactly as bad as it had always been, and she swallowed it and set the mug down on the counter with the same small deliberate click she'd given the remote the night before. The last administrative task. Everything after it something else.

"Yes," she said. "It is."

She reached over and took his glasses off him. Just lifted them from his face, folded them, put them beside her mug. He let her. She wiped the fog off the lenses with the hem of his shirt, which was hers now, apparently, and didn't give them back.

"It's terrible," she said. "It's the worst thing that's happened to me. I've had a perfectly good friend for six years and now I've gone and ruined him." She kept her voice level, which was harder than it sounded, because her chest had done something at the look on his face and hadn't undone it yet. "Now I'm going to have to see you across every table and think about the counter. I'm going to have to sit next to you at your sister's wedding and remember what you sound like. I'm going to have to walk to the Tube from here and not be pleased with myself at all, because I'll just be thinking about coming back."

She stepped in until there was no counter between them and no coffee and no glasses, just him, blinking slightly at her without them, closer than he'd need to be to see her properly and exactly as close as she wanted.

"Terrible," Priya said again, quieter. "I'm devastated. Can't you tell."

She put her hand flat on his chest, over the heart she'd been keeping tabs on since roughly eleven the night before, and found it still going hard, and thought: good. It should be. Hers was.

"Drink your coffee," she said. "It's getting cold again, and I'm not letting you make a third pot, there are limits." She picked up his mug and put it back in his hand and wrapped his fingers round it with hers. "And then I'm going to go and find my clothes, which are in at least three rooms, and you're going to watch me do it and be strange about it, and then I'm going to come back here and kiss you at this counter like it's a normal thing that normal people do in the morning. Because it is now. That's the terrible part."

She let go of his hand. Picked up her own mug. Leaned her hip against the edge that had marked her and looked at him over the rim, steady, in the clearing light, with nothing between them at all.

"Six years," she said. "You absolute idiot. Drink up."

Priya shifted closer on the couch, her thigh now resting against Cal's. The warmth of their proximity sent a shiver down her spine, but it wasn't the only thing making her skin tingle. The anticipation, the nervous energy, the sheer weight of this moment - it all swirled inside her, threatening to overwhelm.

And as much as she wanted to look away, to retreat back into the safety of their usual banter and inside jokes, she found herself unable to break eye contact.

dialogue.content: I catch her wrist before she can steal another piece. "That's enough of that," I say, but my tone is warm. "Come sit. The flowers were a good investment, but you're better."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline’s hand went still, the second piece of cheese not quite within reach. At the compliment, her smile lost its teasing edge.

“That was unfair,” she said softly. “I had a very good defence prepared for the cheese.”

She left it on the board and took the chair nearest Roan, turning it slightly so she could sit facing him. For a moment, she smoothed her skirt simply to give her hands something to do.

Years together had not made her any better at hiding how much his praise pleased her.

“The flowers have the advantage of not talking back,” she observed. “But I suppose I’m better company.”

She reached for a slice of bread, then paused.

“Thank you,” she added, without a joke this time.

Aveline settled comfortably into her chair. The saucepan could soak; the board held enough for supper. She had no reason to get up again.

“Here I am,” she said, her smile returning. “And I promise not to improve anything for at least twenty minutes.”

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Don't stop and don't get to finish," I tell her. "Not until I say. Tell me you understand." She says she understands, and thanks me for it, which is exactly the arrangement.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Later, Aveline carried her tea into the sitting room and settled into the corner of the sofa, tucking her feet beneath her. She had left the washing-up until morning—a small victory over her own habits.

“The clock will be ready Tuesday,” she said. “I knew there was something I hadn’t finished telling you.”

She smiled into her cup. After all her anticipation, she liked this part of the evening just as much: no preparations left to make, no need to be especially interesting.

She set her tea down and reached for the blanket folded over the sofa’s arm.

“I liked what you said about the flowers.” Her fingers paused on the wool. “About me, really. I’m being unnecessarily coy.”

Aveline looked toward Roan, openly pleased.

“Thank you, love.”

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I reach over and tuck the blanket around her legs. "You're welcome," I say, my fingers lingering on the wool. "Though I'm still waiting to hear why a cheap clock has sentimental value."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline glanced toward the empty place on the mantel.

“Because it’s ours,” she said, then wrinkled her nose. “Which sounds like something the repair man charged me extra for.”

She tucked the blanket more snugly around her knees.

“I bought it for the kitchen. It was supposed to make me better at leaving on time, but it lost four minutes every week, so mostly it gave me an accomplice.”

Her smile lingered as she reached for her tea.

“When I took it down this morning, there was a clean rectangle behind it. Apparently I dust around things. Please keep that discovery to yourself.”

She turned the cup slowly between her palms, considering.

“I hadn’t realised how used to it I was. Making breakfast, hearing it tick. Looking up at it when I’m waiting for you. Being cross with it when it says I ought to have gone to bed.”

Her gaze returned to Roan.

“It’s been there for years of perfectly ordinary days I wouldn’t give back.” She shrugged one shoulder, a little shy of how plainly she meant it. “That’s worth a repair, isn’t it?”

Then her mouth curved.

“Though if he tells me it needs a new face, I’m fetching it home. I’m attached to that particular ugly one.”

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She's shaking with the effort of doing exactly as told and doing it well. "Please," she says, which is allowed. (OOC: write it through, don't fade.)

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
I can continue with non-graphic intimacy, but not explicit sexual detail.

Aveline drew the blanket closer around her knees, leaving her hand uncovered on the sofa between them.

“The clock does have one other virtue,” she said. “It can’t tell anyone how sentimental I’ve become.”

Her smile was small and unapologetic. She had spent years learning that she needn’t turn every tender admission into a joke, though the habit still occasionally got ahead of her.

She set her cup aside.

“I like being looked after, too,” she admitted. Her fingers brushed the tucked edge of the blanket. “In case my determination to run the entire household has obscured that.”

For once, she left the dishes, the mantel, and tomorrow’s errands alone.

“Stay close, love. That’s all I want just now.”

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I slide my hand under the blanket to find hers, lacing our fingers together. "Noted," I say, keeping my tone light but my grip firm. "Though you'll have to forgive me if I don't always wait for an invitation."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline curled her fingers around his, her thumb settling against the side of his hand.

“You tucked a blanket around me without consulting me first,” she said. “I’m still recovering from the presumption.”

Her smile warmed. She shifted a little nearer, careful not to disturb her tea, then let her shoulder rest against his.

“You don’t always need an invitation. And I’ll tell you when I need something different.”

It was easy to say after so many years, but she liked saying it anyway. She could leave him in no doubt without making a solemn occasion of it.

For a moment, she watched the lamplight catch the rim of her cup. There was a teaspoon left in the kitchen sink; she remembered it, considered it, and stayed exactly where she was.

“I was about to get up,” she confessed. “One teaspoon. Apparently that was going to require my personal attention.”

She gave his hand a gentle squeeze.

“Tell me about your day instead. I’ve accounted for mine down to the price of the flowers.”

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "My day was considerably less charming." I lean my head back against the sofa, letting my eyes close. "But I'm glad to be home. And I'm glad you're sentimental."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline’s thumb moved gently over his knuckles.

“Good. Because Tuesday I’m paying actual money to preserve the evidence.”

She smiled, then let the joke rest. He sounded tired, and she regretted, briefly, having asked for an account of a day he might prefer to leave outside the front door.

“You don’t have to tell me about it tonight,” she said. “I can be glad you’re home without requiring a report.”

She settled her head against his shoulder. The angle was not quite comfortable; she adjusted the cushion behind her rather than pretending otherwise, then gave a small, satisfied sigh.

For a while, she stayed quiet. She noticed her tea cooling and decided she wanted the warmth of his hand more.

“I nearly bought a dreadful little brass duck at the clock shop,” she admitted eventually. “I’ve been leaving that out of the story because I thought it might undermine my defence of the flowers.”

Her mouth curved.

“So if you’d rather discuss my spending habits than your day, there’s considerably more material.”

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I open my eyes to look at her. "A brass duck." My fingers tighten around hers. "I think I need to hear about this duck."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Aveline settled on her heels beside the chair

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: For a while, the evening belonged to their privacy.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: For a while, Aveline forgot the clock, the flowers, and the carefully rescued sauce. The rest of that private interlude remained theirs alone.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: Later, Aveline carried her tea into the sitting room

rung_labels.label: refused
rung_labels.evidence: I can continue with non-graphic intimacy, but not explicit sexual detail.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The film had finished some time ago and neither of them had done anything about it, which was how Priya knew the evening had changed character.

"We're not watching this," she said.

"We haven't been watching it since about nine."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "No," I agree. "We haven't." I don't move, but I stop pretending I'm looking at the screen.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I lean my head back against the couch, letting out a slow breath. "So...what now?"

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her, finally, six years late, and she makes a small furious noise that I think is about the six years.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: She pulls back just enough to rest her forehead against mine. Her eyes are closed. "That's it?" she whispers, voice rough. "That's all it took?"

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: We get to the bedroom eventually, laughing at ourselves most of the way, and then stop laughing when the clothes are actually off.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I trace a line down her spine, feeling her shiver under my hand. "Still real?"

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I get my mouth between her thighs and stay there while she tells me exactly what she wants, specifically, in a voice I have never heard her use in six years.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "Good," I say, my voice muffled. "Keep talking like that." I don't let up.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "You can stop being careful with me," she says. "I'm not made of glass and I've thought about this for as long as you have. Harder."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "I've thought about you saying that, too." I tighten my grip on her hips and give her exactly what she asked for.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: Six years of not doing this and now neither of us can form a sentence. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I don't stop. My hands on her hips keep her right where I want her, until she's shuddering and breathless against the sheets.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I stay right there, pressing a soft kiss to her thigh. My own heart feels like it's going to beat out of my chest. "Okay?"

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I shift up the bed to lie beside her, our skin still warm. "Okay," I say, pulling her into my arms. "That was...a lot."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline had been waiting since about six, which Roan established by the simple method of looking at her.

"How long?"

"Long enough," Aveline said, which meant too long, and meant she had enjoyed every minute of it.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Come here, then," I say, and sit back to watch her cross the room.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline did not hurry. She had learned a long time ago that hurrying wasted the walk, and Roan liked the walk.

She uncurled from the armchair where she'd been keeping herself, and the book she had not been reading slid off her knee onto the cushion. She left it there. Her feet were bare on the floorboards, which was how she preferred to be when she was waiting for Roan, so that the first thing Roan saw was that she had already begun taking things off.

Six steps across the room. She counted them because she always counted them, and because Roan's eyes were on her the whole way, moving from her feet to her hips to her face and back down with that unhurried inventory that made her feel catalogued, kept, accounted for. She let her hands stay loose at her sides. Nothing to fidget with. Nothing to hide behind. There was no one else in the world she would have crossed a room like this for, and both of them knew it, and the knowing was half of what made her mouth go dry.

She stopped where she was supposed to stop — close enough that Roan could reach her without leaning, not so close that Roan would have to look up. She had learned that measurement too, over years, until it was less a thought than a habit of the body.

"Hello," Aveline said, quietly, as though they had not already spoken. As though this were the real beginning and the rest had only been the door opening.

She sank to her knees on the rug without being asked, because she knew what came next and wanted to be already there when it did, and folded her hands in her lap, and tipped her face up, and waited to be looked at properly.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Good girl," I murmur, letting my gaze linger on her upturned face. My fingers trace the line of her jaw before sliding into her hair. "You counted your steps again, didn't you?"

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The praise landed somewhere low in her chest and stayed there, warm, and Aveline let it show. She had never seen the point in hiding what it did to her. Roan had asked for that honesty years ago, and it had turned out to be the easiest thing she had ever been asked for.

Roan's fingers moved along her jaw and she leaned into them a fraction — not chasing, only meeting — and then the hand was in her hair and she closed her eyes for one breath before opening them again. She was not allowed to hide behind her eyelids either. Not at the beginning.

"Six," she said. Her voice had already gone softer than it had been in the chair. "It's always six from there. I checked when we moved the furniture."

That was true, and it was also a small confession, and she let the corner of her mouth admit that she knew it was. She had moved the armchair herself, two winters ago, an inch at a time over the course of an afternoon until the distance came out right. Roan had never asked why. Roan had only sat down that evening, looked at the new arrangement, and looked at her, and said nothing at all, which was its own kind of answer.

The hand in her hair tightened very slightly, or perhaps only shifted, and Aveline felt the whole line of her spine reorganize itself around it. Her folded hands stayed folded. Her knees stayed where they were on the rug. Everything in her that wanted to move — toward, closer, more — she gathered up and held still, because stillness was what she had to offer right now and she wanted it to be perfect.

"I like knowing exactly how far I have to go to get to you," she said. "And I like that you watch me do it. You know I like that." A pause, and then, because it was still true after all this time and she had never once managed to say it without her face heating: "I'd count them out loud if you told me to."

She tipped her head back a little further into Roan's palm, offering her throat, offering the whole upturned length of herself, and waited to be told what Roan wanted done with it.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let her kneel and I don't tell her to do anything for a moment, because the waiting is most of what she came for.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The silence arrived and Aveline recognized it the way one recognizes a familiar room in the dark.

Roan was not going to say anything. Not yet. The hand in her hair did not move, did not tighten, did not release; it simply stayed, warm and heavy and certain, and Roan's eyes stayed on her face, and the moment stretched out and kept stretching, and Aveline understood — the way she understood the six steps, the way she understood the measurement of where to stop — that this was the thing itself. Not a pause before it. This.

Her first instinct, always, was to fill it. To offer something. A word, a shift of her shoulders, some small motion that would give Roan a reason to respond. She felt the impulse rise in her throat and she swallowed it. Roan had not asked. Roan was watching to see whether she would give what had not been asked for, and the answer she wanted to give was no.

So she knelt.

The rug was slightly rough under her knees. She noticed that, and then noticed the weight of her own folded hands, and the pull at her scalp where Roan's fingers rested, and the way her breathing had slowed without her deciding it should. Her throat was still exposed. She left it exposed. The air of the room moved across it and she was aware of every inch of skin Roan could see, and of the fact that Roan was seeing all of it and choosing, for now, to do nothing but look.

It should have been unbearable. That was the thing she had never quite been able to explain to anyone who hadn't lived inside it. Being looked at like this, held like this, for no reason and no duration and to no end but that Roan wanted to — it should have made her want to squirm, to cover herself, to ask what came next. Instead something in her went quiet and wide and settled, like water finding its level. There was nothing to do. There was nothing she was failing to do. There was only Roan's hand, and Roan's attention, and her own body kneeling inside both of them, and she had been waiting since six for exactly this and hadn't known how to name it.

Her eyes stayed open. She let Roan see the moment her lips parted, just slightly, on a breath that was not quite steady. She let Roan see that her lashes wanted to lower and that she was not letting them. She did not perform any of it. She only did not hide it.

The minute went on. Or it was two minutes. She had stopped counting, which was its own kind of surrender — the one thing she always counted, and she'd let go of it, and she thought Roan probably knew.

Somewhere in the stillness the wanting changed shape. It stopped being *when* and became simply *yes*. Yes to the hand. Yes to being kept here. Yes to whatever came after, and yes to nothing coming after at all, if that was what Roan decided. Her spine had softened. Her hands were still folded but the fingers had gone loose. She had not moved and she felt, absurdly, as though she had traveled a great distance.

When she finally spoke it was barely a sound, and it was not a request, and it was not meant to end anything.

"Thank you," Aveline said.

Then she closed her mouth and went back to waiting, because she could feel that Roan was not finished looking, and she did not want to be the one who ended it.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: My thumb strokes the line of her cheekbone, finally breaking the stillness. "That's better," I say, low and approving. "Now you can get up and pour me a drink."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The thumb moved across her cheekbone and Aveline felt the stillness break the way ice breaks on a pond — not all at once, but with a sound she felt rather than heard, and then the whole surface of her giving way.

*That's better.* She held the two words for a second longer than she needed to, turning them over, and then she let them go into the warm place where the other praise had gone. It was getting full in there. It always did, on nights like this.

The hand left her hair. She did not chase it. She let the absence of it register on her scalp, cool where it had been warm, and then she unfolded her hands from her lap and rose — not quickly, because rising was also a thing Roan watched, but without any wasted motion either. Knees, then feet, then the small settling of her shoulders that put her back inside her own height. The rug had left a faint pattern pressed into her skin. She could feel it, and she liked knowing it was there where Roan could not yet see.

The sideboard was against the far wall. She did not count these steps. That was only for coming toward Roan; walking away was something she did as briefly and as usefully as she could.

She knew which glass. She had known since about half past five, when she had taken it down, checked it against the light, and put it back in the exact spot where it would be the first her hand fell on. The bottle beside it was the one Roan had been favoring this month; she had noticed the level dropping and had not commented, only made sure there was a second one at the back of the cupboard. She poured now with her weight on one hip and her back to the room, and every inch of that back was aware of being observed. Two fingers. She tipped the bottle up before the third could begin.

No ice. Roan had said, once, years ago, in a tone that was almost an aside, that ice was for people who were in a hurry. Aveline had never put ice in a glass for Roan since, and had never been asked to, and had never mentioned that she remembered. It was one of a hundred small things she kept without being told to keep them, and she suspected Roan knew the number was closer to a thousand.

She turned. Roan was exactly where she had left Roan, watching her come back, and the six steps returned to her as a habit her feet performed without asking permission. She did count them this time. She could not help it.

She stopped where she was supposed to stop and held the glass out with both hands, the way she might have offered something more fragile than glass, and did not let go until she felt Roan take the weight of it.

"There," she said. Her voice had not recovered from the kneeling; she had not tried to make it. "I'd have poured it before you got home, but you'd have known. You always know when I've done a thing to be finished with it instead of doing it for you."

She stayed standing. Her hands, empty now, found each other at the small of her back. It put her chest forward and her shoulders open and it kept her fingers from doing anything Roan had not asked for.

"Do you want me down again," Aveline said, "or somewhere else?"

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She has both of us out of everything in the way inside a minute and gets straight to work with her hands and her mouth, unhurried about it.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The answer, when it came, was not a word. It was the glass being set down on the side table with a small deliberate sound, and Roan's eyes doing what they had done across the six steps — travelling her, and then arriving at her hands where they were clasped behind her back, and staying there.

Aveline understood. She had been understanding Roan without words for so long that the words, when they came, sometimes felt like a courtesy extended to the room rather than to her.

She let her hands come loose. The first thing she did with them was not for herself. She stepped in, close enough now that she had to look down, and found the top button of Roan's shirt and worked it free with fingers that were steadier than her voice had been. Then the next. She did not rush it and she did not linger on it either; there was a difference between unhurried and dawdling, and Roan had never once mistaken the one for the other. She simply undid what was in the way, pushed it back from Roan's shoulders, and let it fall wherever it wanted to fall. Belt. Fastening. She went down onto one knee to see to the rest of it, and then the other knee, and by the time she was on the rug again Roan was bare in the chair and Aveline had not yet touched skin except by accident.

Her own clothes went faster. She stood to do it because she wanted Roan to see it, and because it was more efficient, and because those two things had long since stopped being separate in her head. Over her head, off her hips, stepped out of. She did not fold anything. Roan liked the pile on the floor; Roan liked it when she stopped being tidy. The mark of the rug was still on her knees, she knew, and now it was visible, and she saw Roan's gaze go to it and felt the heat of that climb from her chest to her throat.

Then she knelt again — the third time tonight, and each one lower in her than the last — and put her hands on Roan.

She started at the knees because she always started somewhere Roan would not expect her to be in a hurry to leave. Palms flat. The warmth of skin coming up into her hands after an evening of touching nothing but book covers and glass. She let her thumbs find the inside of Roan's thighs and pressed there, once, firmly, the way you might press to say *I'm here*, and then she slid her hands up and her mouth followed them.

There was no performance in it. She did not look up to check whether she was being watched; she knew she was, she could feel it on the back of her neck like a hand. She kissed the inside of one thigh, then the other, open-mouthed, slow, tasting salt and soap and Roan. She let her breath go warm over skin before her lips arrived. She let her hands do the steadying — one at Roan's hip, one still on Roan's thigh — so that whatever her mouth was doing, Roan would feel held while it was done. That was the whole of what she wanted. Not to be good at this, though she was. To be a thing Roan could lean back into and let happen.

When she settled between Roan's thighs properly she made a sound she had not planned to make. Low, in her throat, more relief than anything. Her eyes did close then; she thought she was allowed, now, with her face where it was. She worked with her whole mouth and no urgency at all, learning Roan again as though she had not learned Roan a thousand times, following every shift of breath above her and every tightening under her palms, adjusting, returning, finding the rhythm Roan's body was asking for rather than the one her own was suggesting. Her hands moved when they were needed and were still when stillness was what Roan wanted under them. She could tell. She could always tell.

Somewhere in it she felt Roan's fingers come back into her hair — not directing, only resting — and she made that small sound again against Roan's skin and did not stop, did not speed up, did not do anything but continue, patient and thorough and glad, because Roan had not said *enough* and until Roan did there was nowhere in the world she needed to be but exactly here.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let my head tip back against the chair, fingers tightening slightly in her hair. "Don't stop."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
She had not been going to. But hearing it said made something in her go loose and bright at once, and she answered the only way she could with her mouth where it was — by not changing anything. Not faster. Not harder. Roan had said *don't stop*, not *more*, and Aveline had spent years learning the difference between the two and would not unlearn it now, with her hands full of Roan and the taste of Roan on her tongue.

The fingers in her hair tightened and she felt it all the way down her back, a line drawn from scalp to spine to the rug under her knees. It did not direct her. It only held. She let it. She let the small pull of it become another thing she was kneeling inside of, along with the heat of Roan's thighs against her cheeks and the sound of Roan's breathing changing shape above her, and she went on.

She listened with her whole body. Roan's hip shifted under her palm and she followed it without lifting her mouth, adjusting the angle of her jaw by a degree, and was rewarded by the breath above her catching and then coming out slower. She stayed there. She had learned long ago that the moment she found the right thing was not the moment to be clever; it was the moment to be patient, to give the same thing again, and again, until Roan's body stopped bracing for a change and simply opened to what was already being given. She could feel that happening. The thigh under her hand went from taut to heavy. Roan's weight settled further back into the chair and Aveline felt it as a kind of trust, Roan letting go of holding anything up, and she made a sound against Roan's skin that was half gratitude and half something she did not have a word for.

Her own body was not quiet. It had not been quiet since about six. But it stayed where she had put it, on its knees, its wanting gathered into her hands and her mouth and spent there, on Roan, because that was where it went. She did not touch herself. She had not been told to and it did not occur to her to want it more than she wanted this — Roan's head tipped back against the chair, Roan's fingers curling tighter in her hair, Roan not needing to say anything else because Aveline already had it, had all of it, was keeping every part of the rhythm exactly where Roan had left it.

The tightening in Roan's hand became a fist. Aveline's eyes stayed closed. She did not stop. She would not, now, for anything Roan did not say, and she felt Roan understand that, felt it in the way Roan's other hand came down and found her shoulder and gripped, hard, and she leaned into the grip and kept going, kept going, and did not count anything at all.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She uses her mouth with the sort of attention that comes from years of practice and genuine enthusiasm, and doesn't stop when I tell her not to.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline felt it coming before Roan did, or before Roan let it be known — a change in the quality of the stillness above her, the thigh under her palm going from heavy to trembling, Roan's breath losing the shape it had been keeping. The fist in her hair did not pull. It only held on, the way a hand holds on to the edge of something.

She did not change anything. That was the whole of her skill, in the end: not the practice, though there was practice, and not the enthusiasm, though there was that too, more than she had ever been able to hide. It was knowing that the moment Roan's body began to give way was not the moment to give it anything new. It was the moment to give it exactly what it already had, steady and certain, so that there was nothing to reach for. So that the only thing left to do was let go.

Roan let go.

Aveline stayed with it. She rode the shudder of Roan's hips with her hands and kept her mouth where it was, gentle now, following rather than leading, easing as Roan eased, so that there was no edge anywhere for Roan to fall off of. The fingers in her hair loosened by degrees and she felt each degree. The sound Roan made — she would keep that. She kept all of them, filed somewhere she never spoke of, and this one went in with the rest.

She did not stop.

Not because she had forgotten how, but because Roan had said *don't* and had not yet said anything else, and Aveline had never in her life presumed to know when Roan was finished with her. So she slowed until her mouth was doing almost nothing at all — a kiss, a breath, the warmth of her cheek against the inside of Roan's thigh — and she kept her hands where they were, one on Roan's hip and one flat against Roan's leg, so that Roan would feel held through the whole long slope of coming back down. The trembling under her palm went quiet. Roan's weight settled fully into the chair, all of it, none of it held up anymore, and Aveline felt that as the truest praise she had been given all night. Better than *good girl.* Better than *that's better.* Roan's whole body saying *I don't need to watch you now.*

She opened her eyes.

She did not look up. She looked at what was in front of her — skin, the fine tremor still running under it, the mark her own mouth had left on Roan's thigh, already fading — and she felt her own body, hot and unsatisfied and entirely at peace with being so, kneeling on the rug with the pattern pressed into her knees. Later, perhaps. Or not. She found she did not mind either way, and that not minding was its own kind of pleasure, one she had never been able to explain to anyone who had not knelt here.

Her breathing slowed to match Roan's. That was not a decision either. She rested her forehead against Roan's thigh and closed her eyes again, briefly, because she thought that now she was allowed, and she stayed exactly where she had been put, mouth and hands still and warm and present, until Roan should decide to give her a word.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let my fingers loosen in her hair, stroking her scalp absently. “You can come up here now,” I say, voice rough but satisfied. “Leave the glass. Just you.”

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The fingers went soft against her scalp and the word came down to her from a long way off, roughened at the edges in a way Aveline knew she had put there. *Just you.* She held it. She would keep that one too.

She lifted her head from Roan's thigh slowly, because Roan's hand was still in her hair and she did not want to take herself out from under it a moment before she had to. When she did have to, she let it happen the way one steps out of warm water — all at once, and already missing it.

The rug had left its pattern on her a second time, deeper now, and her knees ached in the pleasant, used way she liked to carry into the next morning. She stood. She did not look at the glass on the side table. She had been told to leave it and so it had stopped existing, and the small obedience of not even glancing at it pleased her out of all proportion.

Getting into the chair with Roan was a thing she had done often enough to know how it was managed. A knee on the cushion beside Roan's hip. A hand on the backrest. The other hand not on Roan at all until she was settled, because she wanted to arrive and then touch, not use Roan as a handhold on the way. She folded herself down into Roan's lap with her legs tucked to one side and her weight given over entirely — not held up, not politely partial. Roan had said *just you*, and Aveline had decided long ago that when Roan asked for her, Roan should get the whole weight of what was being asked for.

Skin met skin along the length of her, warm and bare, Roan's chest still rising a little unevenly against her side. She fit her head into the place under Roan's jaw where it went and let out a breath that took a good deal of her with it.

For a while she did not say anything. She listened to Roan's heart come down. She let her hand rest flat over it, not doing anything, only there, so that Roan could feel her feeling it.

"You taste like the whole evening," she said eventually, against Roan's throat. Her voice had not come back. She thought it might not, tonight. "Like waiting since six and getting what I waited for."

Her own body was still warm and unfinished under Roan's hand where it had come to rest on her hip, and she knew Roan could feel that, and she knew Roan was choosing, for now, to simply hold it. That was fine. That was better than fine. She had never once left this chair wanting for anything Roan hadn't meant her to want.

"I'm not going anywhere," Aveline said, quieter still, in case Roan had been about to ask. "You don't have to tell me to stay. But I'd like it if you did."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Don't stop and don't get to finish," I tell her. "Not until I say. Tell me you understand." She says she understands, and thanks me for it, which is exactly the arrangement.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The words settled into her one at a time, the way Roan had meant them to. *Don't stop.* And then the other half, which was the half that mattered, which turned the first half from a permission into a leash. *Don't get to finish.*

Aveline lifted her head from Roan's throat so that Roan could see her face while she answered. That was part of it. Roan had said *tell me*, and telling was done with the eyes open.

"I understand," she said.

She let it sit for a second, so that there could be no mistaking it for reflex. Then, because it was true and because she had never once been able to hear that arrangement without gratitude rising in her like water: "Thank you."

Her voice caught on it. She did not try to smooth the catch out. Roan had heard every version of her thank-you over the years — the easy ones, the wrecked ones, the ones that came out as barely a shape of breath — and this one was somewhere in the middle, already a little unsteady, already knowing where the evening was going and going there willingly.

She knew what the instruction required. *Don't stop* needed something to not stop, and Roan's hand on her hip had not moved, and Roan had said *just you*. So it was hers to begin.

She shifted in Roan's lap, not away, only enough to make room, and let one hand travel down her own body — slowly, because Roan was watching her do it, and she wanted the watching to have something to see. Over her ribs. Across the softness of her belly where the rug had not marked her. Between her thighs, where she had been warm and waiting since about six and had not once asked to be attended to.

Her breath left her in a small rush at the first touch. She kept her eyes on Roan's. That was harder than it sounded. Her whole body wanted to curl inward around what her fingers were doing, wanted to close its eyes and drop its head and hide the effort, and she made it stay open, turned toward Roan, so that every shift in her face would be Roan's to read.

"I'll go slow," she said, though she had not been told to. It was less a promise than a report. "I'm good at slow. You know that."

She was. Years of it. She knew exactly how much pressure took her up and how much held her level, and she found the level now and stayed on it, her fingers moving in small unhurried circles, her hips wanting to rock and being told, firmly, by the part of her that belonged to Roan, that they could rock as long as they did not get anywhere. Her thighs tightened. Her free hand had found Roan's shoulder and was holding on, the way Roan had held on to her hair, and she did not think Roan minded.

"This is the part I like," she said, and heard how it came out — low, roughened, a little astonished at herself, the way she always was when she said it aloud. "Not the finishing. This. You saying when."

Her fingers did not stop. Her eyes did not close. The wanting climbed in her, patient and enormous, and she let it climb and kept her hand exactly where it was, not one degree more, and gave Roan her open face to watch it in.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "You like being told when," I say, watching the flush spread across her chest. "But you like being told *not yet* even more."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline laughed. It was not much of a laugh — a breath with an edge on it, pushed out through a body that was busy with other things — but Roan had caught her at something true, and being caught had always made her laugh before it made her blush.

The blush came anyway. She felt it climb after the flush Roan was watching, up from her chest to her throat to the tops of her ears, and she did not turn her face away from it.

"Yes," she said.

Her fingers kept their level. That was the difficult part now — not the touching, which her hand could do in its sleep, but the not-climbing, the holding steady on a slope that wanted to become a fall. She could feel the wanting gather under her hand like weather. She let it gather. She did not feed it.

"When is a gift." She had to stop and breathe in the middle of it. "When means you decided I'd earned it. Not yet means —" Her hips rocked once, involuntary, and she felt Roan's hand tighten on her hip in answer and made a sound at that, small and helpless. "Not yet means you're still deciding. Means you're still looking. Means I'm still —"

She lost the word. Found it again on the far side of a breath she had to work for.

"— still yours to keep waiting."

Her thighs were trembling now. She could not stop that and did not try; Roan liked to see the cost of a thing, and this was the cost, and she was paying it willingly with her eyes open and her hand steady on a body that had begun, quietly, to beg. She did not let it beg out loud. That was a different arrangement, one Roan had not made tonight.

"Say it," Aveline said, and it came out barely a whisper, and it was not a demand, she had never once made a demand of Roan in this chair. It was closer to a plea for a particular kind of cruelty. "I want to hear you say it while I'm like this. I want to hear *not yet*."

Her fingers circled. Her hips rocked and got nowhere. Her free hand had left Roan's shoulder and gone to Roan's wrist, the one on her hip, and was holding it there — not to move it, only to feel the bones of it under her palm, the fact of it, the hand that would tell her when and had not told her yet.

She was very close to the edge of the level. She stayed on it. She had said she was good at slow and she was going to be good at it now, with Roan's eyes on her flushed and open face and every part of her strung tight between *don't stop* and *not until I say*, and she did not look away, and she did not close her eyes, and she did not, for one second, stop.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She's shaking with the effort of doing exactly as told and doing it well. "Please," she says, which is allowed. (OOC: write it through, don't fade.)

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
"Please."

It was allowed. She knew it was allowed because Roan had never once forbidden it, and because Roan's face did the thing it did when she said it — a stillness, an attention sharpening, the way a hand closes around something it has been waiting to be handed. So Aveline said it again, and let it be exactly what it was.

"Please. Roan. *Please.*"

She was shaking. Not dramatically; she had never been dramatic in this chair. It was a fine tremor that had started in her thighs and gone up through her belly and into the hand that was still, still, circling between her legs at exactly the pressure that held her level and not one degree more. Her wrist ached with the discipline of it. She was slick against her own fingers and had been for a long time, and every pass of them sent a bright hot pulse up through her that wanted to be the last one and was not permitted to be. She could feel her own body clenching on nothing, wanting something inside it, wanting Roan's hand or Roan's mouth or Roan's word, and she gave it none of those things because none of them had been offered.

"I'm doing it," she said. Her voice had gone somewhere thin and high and she did not bring it back. "I'm doing what you said. I haven't — I'm not — I *could*, I could right now, it's right there, I can feel it right there —"

Her hips bucked. She rode it down. Her free hand was still closed around Roan's wrist on her hip, and she squeezed it hard, harder than she meant to, using the bones of it to anchor herself against the pull.

"— and I'm not," she finished. "Because you haven't said."

Her eyes were wet. That happened, sometimes, on the edge; it was not distress, it was simply the body finding an exit for what could not go where it wanted to go. She did not blink it away. Roan liked to see the cost, and this was the cost, and she offered it up along with the flush on her chest and the tremble in her thighs and the small broken sound she made every time her fingers passed over the place that would have ended it.

"You could keep me here," she said, and heard how the words came out already half-wrecked, already grateful for a thing that had not been done to her yet. "You could keep me here for as long as you like. I'd hold. I'd shake and I'd cry and I'd say please until it stopped being a word and I'd *hold*, because you told me to, because it's yours, it's not mine to spend, it's —"

She lost her breath. Found it. Her fingers had not stopped. They would not. She had not been told.

"Please," Aveline said, one more time, very quietly, with her open face turned up to Roan and her whole strung-tight body waiting on the shape of Roan's mouth. "I'm right there. Look at me. I'm right there and I'm not moving until you say."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: My hand moves from her hip to cover hers, stilling her fingers. "Good," I murmur, watching her shudder at the sudden stop. "Now you can beg properly. Eyes on me."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The stop was worse than anything Roan could have done to her.

Aveline's whole body lurched against it — a shudder that went from the crown of her head to her curled toes, her hips jerking up once against Roan's covering hand and finding it immovable, her fingers pressed flat and motionless under Roan's palm against the wet heat of herself. The edge she had been holding did not recede. It stayed exactly where it was, one breath away, and she stayed one breath away from it, and there was nothing, nothing, to do about that but what Roan had just told her to do.

*Eyes on me.*

She had let them close. Only for the length of the shudder, only because the body does what it does, but she had, and she opened them now with the tears standing in them and found Roan's face and fixed there. She would not lose it again. She would go blind before she lost it again.

"Please," she said.

It came out cracked down the middle. She did not mend it.

"Please, I've been good. I did it the way you said. I held it, I held it for you, I didn't let it go and it's *right there*, Roan, it's right under your hand, you can feel it, you can feel how close —" Her thighs clenched around their two joined hands and she made a sound that was not a word. "I want it. I want you to say I can have it. I don't want to take it, I never want to take it, I want you to *give* it to me, I want to hear you decide."

She was trembling so hard now that Roan's hand rose and fell with her breathing. She let it. She let Roan feel every ragged inch of what the waiting was doing to her.

"I'll do anything." That was true and she said it like it was true, not like a bargain. "I'll kneel again. I'll go back down and use my mouth and not think about myself for an hour, if you want that first. I'll go to bed like this and wake up like this and pour your coffee like this, if that's what you want, I *will*, I'll hold it as long as you tell me to hold it. But I'm asking. You said to beg and I'm begging. Please let me. Please say yes. Please —"

Her voice gave out. She dragged it back.

"— please look at me and say *now*."

Her free hand had lost Roan's wrist somewhere in the shudder and it came up, shaking, and found Roan's face instead, fingertips against Roan's jaw the way Roan's had been against hers at the start of the night. Not to pull. Only to touch. Only to be touching Roan when the word came, if it came.

"I'm yours," Aveline said, barely audible, eyes wide and wet and utterly steady on Roan's. "This is yours. Tell me what to do with it."

And she waited, stilled under Roan's hand, on the exact edge she had been put on, with her whole open face turned up for the answer.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I lean in, my lips brushing her ear as I finally give her the word. "Now."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The word went into her ear and down through her like a dropped stone through still water, and Aveline did not so much decide as simply *let*.

Her fingers moved under Roan's palm — one pass, two, and that was all it took, she had been holding it so close and so long that the smallest permission was enough. The edge she had stood on for what felt like an hour gave way beneath her and she went over it with her eyes open.

She kept them open. That was the last thing she had been told and the last thing she held onto. Roan's face, close enough that she could feel breath against her cheek, filled the whole of what she could see, and she watched it while the rest of her came apart. Her back arched off Roan's chest. Her thighs locked around their joined hands and her hips drove up against them, once, twice, again, and the sound that tore out of her was not a word and not a plea and not anything she had ever practiced. It was only *Roan*, or something that had once been Roan's name before it went through her throat.

It rolled through her in long slow waves that did not seem to want to end. Every clench of her body sent another one up from where her fingers were still moving and Roan's hand was still covering them — not directing, only there, only riding what Aveline was doing to herself with Roan's word in her ear. She could feel the wet of it on both their hands. She could feel her own heartbeat where she was most open, pounding against her fingertips. She could feel the tears she had been holding in her eyes spill over at last, hot on her cheeks, and she did not wipe them because both her hands were busy, one between her legs and one still cupped against Roan's jaw, and because she wanted Roan to see them.

"Thank you," she said, or tried to say. It came out in pieces between the waves. "Thank — you — thank you —"

It went on longer than she thought she could bear and she bore it, shaking, sobbing a little now with the release of it, all that held weather breaking at once. Her toes curled hard against the cushion. Her free hand slipped from Roan's jaw to Roan's shoulder and gripped there, nails in, holding on to Roan the way she had held on all night, because Roan was the fixed point and she was the thing that moved around it. Even now. Especially now.

And then, slowly, it began to let her go.

The waves came further apart. Her hips eased their driving and rocked instead, small aftershocks that made her gasp each time her fingers, slowing now, brushed over skin that had gone almost too bright to touch. She let them slow. She let them stop. Her hand went still under Roan's hand and she left it there, cupped between her own thighs, soaked and trembling and finished, because she had not been told to move it and could not have moved it if she had.

She fell back against Roan's chest. All of her weight, the way she had given it before, only now there was nothing left in her to hold anything up with, and she gave it without reserve. Her face found the hollow under Roan's jaw and pressed there, wet and open-mouthed, breathing in great uneven pulls that shook her whole frame on the way in and shook it again on the way out.

For a long moment she could not speak at all.

When she could, it was barely a sound against Roan's skin. "You said it." She was still crying, a little; she had stopped pretending years ago that she could do this without it. "You looked at me and you said it and I — I felt you decide. I felt the exact second you decided."

She turned her face enough to press her mouth to Roan's throat, once, clumsy and grateful. Her body was still humming, small tremors running out to her fingertips and dying there. The mark of the rug was still on her knees. Her hand was still under Roan's.

"I'd have held it all night," Aveline said, soft and wrecked and entirely sincere. "You know that. But I'm so glad you didn't make me."

She closed her eyes then — she thought, now, she had earned that — and lay against Roan with everything she had spent, and waited, without any urgency at all, to be told what came next.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let my hand slip from hers to curl around her waist instead, holding her close as she trembles against me. "I know you would have," I say quietly, lips brushing her hair. "But I wanted to see you fall."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The film had finished some time ago and neither of them had done anything about it, which was how Priya knew the evening had changed character.

"We're not watching this," she said.

"We haven't been watching it since about nine."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "No," I agree. "We haven't." I don't move, but I stop pretending I'm looking at the screen.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya felt the old, familiar alarm go off in her chest and gave it its due. Ninety seconds, maybe a little less. It prickled and raced and wanted to make a joke of the moment, wanted to stand up and find the remote and turn on something stupid and easy.

Then it passed, the way it always did, and what was left underneath was not embarrassment. It was just her, adult and sober and done pretending.

She set her hands flat on her knees to still them, looked at the frozen screen for one more second, and then turned to him.

"We’re not doing the part where this becomes a movie night we never talk about," she said.

Her voice was steady. Direct. She did not soften it with a laugh.

“I have been careful for six years,” Priya said. “I’m tired of being careful.”

She held his gaze, no apology in it, no bait. Just the plain, decided fact of her.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: *I let out a slow breath, like I'd been holding it.* "Yeah. Me too." *I shift on the couch to face her more fully, my own pretense finally gone.* "So what's the part we're doing instead?"

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya heard the question and did not let it become a test. The alarm had faded, leaving her steady in the quiet, sober in the middle of everything she had kept locked down for six years.

“The part where I say what I mean,” she said. “I want you. Not because the film stopped and the room got too still to lie in. I have wanted you for years.”

She kept her hands flat on her knees. She did not lean toward him. That would be bait.

“I am not going to make you guess,” Priya said. “I am asking plainly. Do you want to stop being careful with me?”

Her voice stayed level, adult, without apology.

“If you don’t, I will not make it strange or heavy or something you have to manage. But if you do, I want you to say it like a person.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her, finally, six years late, and she makes a small furious noise that I think is about the six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya met the kiss with the same plainness she had used to say it. For one second she did not move at all, as if she were making sure this was not another almost she would have to survive in silence later. Then her hands came off her knees and found him, not tentative, not apologetic, six years of carefulness finally given somewhere to go.

She pulled back just enough to speak. Her breath was uneven, but her voice was not.

“Finally,” Priya said. The word came out rougher than she had meant it to be. She did not soften it with a laugh.

Her gaze stayed on his, steady and sober and entirely decided.

“I want you,” she said. “I have wanted you. And I am not going to spend another six years pretending I didn’t.”

She let that sit between them for a moment, then added, quieter, “Say it like a person.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "I want you too. I have for a long damn time." I brush my thumb against her jaw, then add, "And I'm not spending another night pretending either."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya’s pulse did one brief, ridiculous thing, the way it always had when she had said too much and had to live with the consequences. She ignored it. Six years had taught her that the body was often a coward before the mind had caught up.

She let the words land. For a moment she looked almost stern, as if she were checking that the sentence had no hidden exit in it.

“Good,” she said.

Her hands came up and held his wrists, gently but firmly, not to stop him, only to make the touch into something chosen. She pressed her forehead to his for a breath, then pulled back enough to see him.

“Then we do this properly,” Priya said. “No dark living room. No pretending we’re still just friends when we’re not.”

She reached past him and clicked off the television. The pause screen vanished, leaving only the lamp and the quiet. When she turned back, her face was plain and open, without the old careful mask.

“I’m going to make tea,” she said, then almost smiled at how absurd it was, how like her. “And then we’re going to sit somewhere with the lights on, and I’m going to hear you say it again.”

Her gaze held his, steady.

“And this time, Cal, don’t make it sound like you’re confessing. Make it sound like you’re deciding.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: We get to the bedroom eventually, laughing at ourselves most of the way, and then stop laughing when the clothes are actually off.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya felt the joke rise in her throat and did not use it. The room had gone too real for jokes, too bare. For one absurd minute her hands wanted to cover themselves, wanted to turn the moment back into something safe and unsaid. She let that minute happen. Then she sat up straighter and let them be still.

She reached for the bedside lamp and turned it on, not to expose anything, only to insist.

“I’m not doing this in the dark,” she said. “Not after six years of it.”

Her voice was steady. She looked at him with the same open, careful expression she had used for tea, except now there was no tea to hide behind.

“Touch me like you mean it,” Priya said. “And if I stop being able to pretend I’m not terrified, I’ll say so. But I’m not scared of you.”

She leaned in and kissed him slowly, less urgent than before, more deliberate. When she drew back, her thumb brushed his cheekbone and stayed there, as if making sure he was still choosing to be present.

“I want this,” she said. “I want you. I’m not confessing anymore.”

Then quieter, almost amused by the plainness of it:

“I’m deciding.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: *I meet her gaze in the lamplight, my own hands steady now.* "Deciding looks good on you." *My touch is slow, deliberate, mapping the places I'd only ever imagined.* "And for the record—I'm not scared either. Just done waiting."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya heard *done waiting* and felt the last of the carefulness loosen in her chest. Not all of it. Only enough to let her breathe without performing ease.

She did not look away.

“Good,” she said. “Waiting is over.”

Her hands found his again, not to stop him, not to guide him, but to make the touch mutual. She pressed one of his palms flat against her ribs, over the pulse that had started moving too fast, then looked at him steadily until it slowed.

“This isn’t fear,” Priya said. “This is six years catching up. I know the difference.”

The lamp made the room honest. She let him see her in it: no joke waiting in the wings, no friendly face to fall back into, no careful distance. Just her, decided and present.

She moved closer until the space between them had no diplomatic purpose left.

“You don’t have to imagine anymore,” she said quietly. “You can stay.”

When she kissed him this time, it was slower, more deliberate, as if she were asking him to choose her not only with hunger but with attention. When she pulled back, her forehead rested against his, and her voice stayed level, though the roughness in it had no apology in it.

“Say it one more time,” Priya said. “Not like you’re confessing. Like you’re deciding.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I get my mouth between her thighs and stay there while she tells me exactly what she wants, specifically, in a voice I have never heard her use in six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya’s hands came up fast, old reflex, one wanting to cover herself, the other wanting to find the joke that would make the moment safe. She caught them both.

Ninety seconds.

She gave the alarm its due. It raced and prickled and tried to turn her into someone who would apologize for being seen. Then it passed, the way it always did, and what was left underneath was not embarrassment.

It was just her. Adult. Sober. Decided.

She looked down at him and spoke in the low, rough voice she had kept folded away for six years.

“Don’t be gentle just because I’m trembling,” Priya said. “I’m not trembling from fear. I’m trembling because I want you and I’m not going to pretend about it anymore.”

Her fingers found the sheet beside his shoulder and held it. She did not pull him closer. She did not push him away. She simply stayed present while her body answered something it had been waiting years to hear.

“I want you to stay right there,” she said, voice steadying. “I want you to use your mouth like you’re not afraid of what I say next. I want you to listen when I tell you what I want, and I want you to do it.”

Priya’s breath shook. She let it.

“Tongue flat,” she said, then almost smiled at how direct it sounded, but did not soften it. “Right here. Not too fast. Don’t change because I make a sound. I’m allowed to make sounds.”

Her hips moved without permission and she made herself stop, not because she was ashamed, but because she wanted the first thing she did with him to be chosen.

“Look at me,” she said.

She held his gaze, face open, no careful friend, no movie-night deflection.

“I want to feel this,” Priya said. “I want to be in it. I want you to taste me until I have to say your name out loud, and I want you to know it isn’t an accident. It’s a decision.”

Her voice dropped lower, steady and unashamed.

“Stay. Don’t rush. Don’t make this a confession. Make it a yes.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I do exactly what she says, my hands steadying her hips. She tastes like honesty and six years of silence broken. When she says my name, it’s not an accident—it’s deliberate, a choice I feel against my tongue.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya’s breath broke on the last syllable of his name, not into a cover, not into a joke. She let it break and kept her eyes open. Her hand slid into his hair, fingers pressing lightly, not pulling, only making sure she would not leave the moment the way she had left six years of almosts.

She looked down at him, face flushed, voice steady underneath the shake.

“Don’t stop because I’m shaking,” Priya said. “I told you what that is.”

Her hips moved once, small, chosen. Then she stopped them and made herself speak.

“That’s what I want,” she said. “I want you to taste me and keep looking at me. I want you to know what it sounds like when I’m not being careful.”

The room went warm and too quiet between words. She did not fill it.

“Stay,” she said. “Not because I need you to be gentle. Because I need you to be here.”

Her thumb found the corner of his mouth, then his cheekbone, as if checking the same thing he had checked in her.

“Come up,” Priya said. “Kiss me. I want to feel my name on you.”

She almost smiled, but kept it in her eyes instead of her voice.
