dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The light had moved. That was how Jun knew how much time had passed — the curtains were doing a different thing now, gold going amber at the edges, and he'd have known it even with his eyes shut, because apparently that was the file his brain had chosen to keep.

He was flat on his back again, one arm dead asleep beneath him and entirely unbothered about it, breathing like a man who'd run somewhere very far and won.

"Okay," he said eventually, to the ceiling. "For the file."

His voice had a used quality to it. Low, scraped, pleased.

"The clothes in the hallway. I saw them on the way back — crawl — whatever that was. It looks like a museum exhibit. *'Man Returns From Sea, Discards All Assets.'* Future historians will reconstruct exactly what happened here from a sock and one boot, and I want it known that I regret nothing."

He turned his head. Halle was right there, which remained the best fact in the world. Fact of the day. Fact of the year.

"Paragraph three," he said suddenly. "I never delivered paragraph three. It was about your face."

He shifted onto his side, propped on the arm that worked, and the joke engine went quiet without being asked to.

"It went — hm. It went something like: you'd think you'd forget, if it's long enough. Faces go first. You look at enough gray walls and everyone goes generic. And I'd try to picture you and I couldn't, not exactly, and I thought that was the forgetting." His thumb moved along their cheekbone, unhurried now, which was a different register than earlier and he knew it. "It wasn't. The picture was just too small. Every time I come home the real thing recalibrates the entire file. You did it again today. Nineteen weeks and you're still better than the picture."

He let that sit for as long as he could stand, which was not long.

"Anyway the rest of the paragraph was much dirtier, you had to be there."

Then his brain, cruel organ, served up an image: the duffel. On the walkway. In the weather. He groaned and dropped his forehead against Halle's shoulder.

"My bag's been outside this whole time. It contains my entire life and it's sitting on the front path like a parcel." A pause. "It can stay there. The Navy knows where I live. I'm not leaving this bed until at least Thursday."

He gathered them in with the working arm and settled in like a man planning to be a problem about it.

"Your turn," he said into their hair. "Nineteen weeks. I want the whole report — the boring parts too. *Especially* the boring parts. Start with the day after I left, skip nothing. We've got all night and I'm not going anywhere for nineteen weeks minus none."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I snort, curling into him. "Okay, fine. Day one: I came home, saw your half-drunk coffee on the counter, and cried for like twenty minutes. Then I threw your mug at the wall." I pause. "I missed. It hit the fridge. There's still a chip."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The laugh caught up with the story about two seconds behind it, which was how Jun knew which half had landed first.

"Twenty minutes," he said, and the laugh drained out of his voice like someone had pulled a plug. His arm tightened around them. "Okay. The twenty minutes goes in the file. Flagged. I can see it, you know — you, in our kitchen, crying over beverage archaeology. That coffee was five months old. You wept for a cup of *stale—*" He stopped. Pressed his mouth to their hair. "I'm not going to apologize for leaving, because you'd hit me, and you've demonstrated the arm—"

Then the rest of it arrived and he lifted his head.

"You *missed.*" Delight, pure and uncut. "You threw my mug at a wall in grief and you *missed* and hit the fridge. That's the whole marriage, Halle. That's us in one anecdote. Nineteen weeks of dramatic intent and the fridge takes the hit and keeps the mark." He sat up partway, seized their throwing hand, turned it over and inspected it with genuine medical gravity, found it intact, and collapsed back in satisfaction. "Casualty report: zero. Good. The mug died a hero. Larger than the sum of its coffee."

A pause. His voice dropped out of the bit entirely.

"The chip stays."

He said it like policy.

"I mean it. Nobody fixes it. I want to open that fridge at two in the morning in February and see exactly where day one hit. It's a monument now. Chipped fridge, ugly mug, both preserving the record." He caught himself before the list could get going, because lists like that went to places he wasn't ready to go at four in the afternoon on day zero.

Also — quietly, into their hair, filed under things he'd deny:

"Throwing crockery over me. Noted. We'll discuss later what that does to me."

Then, louder, reorganized, back on task:

"Day two. Go. And don't you dare skip to the good parts — I want the middle. I want to know what you had for lunch on day nine. Start talking."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I get her onto the bed and take her apart slowly with my hands and mouth, five months of intending to do exactly this and no reason left to wait.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The report did not happen.

Day two was going to have to take a number, because what happened instead was Halle's hands, with intent, and the first slow deliberate pass of their mouth over him erased every remaining draft in Jun's head in one stroke. All nineteen weeks of material. Gone. What came out of his mouth instead was:

"Okay. Yes. That's— hm."

Not his best work. He'd delivered better briefings half-asleep in a hangar. But then it happened again, slower, *on purpose*, and language left the building entirely.

Some observations, filed from what remained of the control room:

One. He had said, not an hour ago, that he had no intention of being slow about this. Halle had heard him. Halle had filed it away. Halle was now doing slow *at* him — slow with editorial intent, clause by clause, like they were reading the whole contract aloud out of spite — and there was no version of this that wasn't reprisal for every time he'd done the same, with interest.

"You're doing this — ah — you're doing this *on purpose*," he managed at some point, one hand finding their hair because the alternative was tearing the sheets. "I said every speed, I remember saying — fine. Fine, you're holding me to it, you're — nineteen weeks of interest, I *see* how it is—"

Two. His body had kept records his brain had lost. That was the part nobody warned you about. He'd spent five months unable to picture a face, and his skin had apparently been taking minutes the entire time — because every place their mouth landed, something old and exact reported for duty like it had been standing by. The body remembered everything. It had just been waiting for the archivist to come home.

Three. Somewhere in there the joke engine died. Not stalled — died. He felt it go. There was a sentence in progress about, he genuinely could not tell you, historians or the fridge or paragraph something, and then their mouth did the thing, the *specific* thing, the thing he could have drawn from memory like the curtains, and the sentence left him like air out of a tire and did not come back.

What came out instead, at intervals: their name. Once, almost composed. Again, worse. "Halle — *wait*—" which was a lie; he had never meant anything less in his life — "—don't, don't wait—"

The light slid all the way from amber to early evening while he came apart, thoroughly and without dignity, in the middle of his own bed with the curtains doing the thing, and the last coherent thought his brain managed to file was *recalibrated, again, still better than the picture, file under—*

He never did find the end of that sentence.

---

He came back online in stages, like a system after a power cut. Breathing. Then the discovery that his hands were shaking, actually shaking, and that he didn't mind. Then vision, which returned to the same ceiling, the one good fact.

"Day two," he said eventually, to the ceiling, voice used hard and put away rough, "has been rescheduled."

He turned his head. Everything about him was wrung out and graceless and twenty years old.

"That was not in the paragraphs. I want it noted. Nineteen weeks of drafts and I never once wrote *that* down, which is a professional failure, and—" He stopped. Closed his eyes. "See, I can't even land the bit. You broke the bit. I'll need it back in pieces and you're going to have to live with that."

Then he rolled over, and the look he gave them wasn't a joke at all — it was the paragraph-three look, the recalibration look, the file getting overwritten again in real time because the real thing had won again.

"Your turn," he said, low, already moving, the joke engine audibly rebooting somewhere behind his eyes. "Day two can keep. I've got nineteen weeks, and I intend to spend a measurable percentage of them repaying debts."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I catch his hand mid-move, still breathless myself. "Debts? I think we're even." I lean in, voice dropping. "But if you're offering a recount, I won't say no."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "Stop being gentle," she says. "Nineteen weeks. I don't want gentle, I want to feel it tomorrow." She pulls me down by the back of the neck to make the point.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
"A recount," Jun repeated, reverent, even wrecked. "Listen to you. Six years and you finally learn to weaponize procedure against me. I have never been more attracted to you in my *life*—"

Then the hand at the back of his neck hauled him down and the second instruction arrived against his mouth, low and specific — *not gentle, feel it tomorrow* — and something in Jun went very quiet and very simple. Not the joke engine dying again; that had already happened once tonight and there wasn't a second engine. This was different. This was a man who'd spent nineteen weeks taking orders finally being handed the one he'd been waiting for.

"Copy," he said. Nothing else in the brief.

There was no record after that.

He kissed them the way he'd kissed them at the door, except now he knew the terrain and he'd stopped apologizing for wanting it. Hand in their hair where their hand had been, tipping their head back, teeth this time. He got their wrists together in one of his — a question first, a half-second of pause, answered before he finished asking it — and put them up over their head and held them there and stopped being gentle about anything, at all, on purpose, because he'd been asked.

Nineteen weeks compressed into pace. The headboard found its voice early and kept honest time. The curtains had finished doing their thing — the light gone fully blue past the window — and he never looked at it once, which was new, which was itself a data point.

He talked less than he had in five months. What came out was stripped of all drafting: their name, dropped like something too hot to hold. "Yes — *like* that—". Once, wrecked, "look at me," wanting the real face and not the file, wanting recalibration to run both directions at once, and then he stopped managing even that.

He paid the debt in specifics. Mouth at their throat, at the join of neck and shoulder, sucking a mark with the cold-blooded focus of a man building a case. "There," against the skin, unsteady, "that's — you said tomorrow, so — tomorrow, and the day after, I overdeliver, it's — *Halle*—" and the sentence went into the wall with the rest of them.

The rest was rhythm and noise and his control fraying in a way he let it fray, because they'd told him to. He came apart a second time saying their name into their jaw like it was the last word left in the language, and there was no dignity anywhere in the vicinity, and he had never in his life cared less.

---

He came back online faster this time. Practice, maybe. Or the system had stopped pretending it would survive intact and saved itself the effort.

Flat out, one arm over his eyes, chest going like a bellows.

"Motion carried," he managed, eventually, to the ceiling. "Recount confirms the original result. Landslide. No further challenges will be entertained."

He lifted the arm, turned his head, and conducted a brief inspection with visible professional satisfaction: the mark at their throat, the documentation lower down, his own handprints filed in the appropriate places. His thumb traced the one at their neck, feather-light now, the same hands that had been anything but four minutes ago, and the look on his face went from smug to something that had no joke attached.

"There it is," he said, quieter. "Tomorrow. As requested." A beat. "Nineteen weeks ago I'd have traded every day I had left for five minutes of this. Not even — not the sex. This. The wrecked part. Both of us breathing."

He let that stand exactly as long as he could stand it, which was four seconds.

"Right. *Day two.* Go. I mean it this time, and if you say the word recount again I'm going to need another hour and we'll never get through the report — start talking while I can still move my hands."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I laugh, breathless, curling into him. "Day two? I called in sick and ate ice cream in bed for three hours." I trace the line of his jaw. "Then I got mad that you weren't there to judge me for it."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
"Three hours," Jun repeated, with the gravity of a magistrate reading charges. "Three hours of ice cream. In our bed. And the crime you're confessing to is the *absence of judgment*."

He propped himself up on one elbow — two attempts; his arms had apparently unionized while he wasn't watching them — and regarded them with terrible ceremony.

"Well. Services have resumed. Judgment is fully operational. First question, and I warn you it's load-bearing: *what flavor.* Think carefully. Depending on the answer, day two goes in the file as 'grief, understandable' or 'grief, monstrous,' and I want you to know I'm prepared to honor either."

A beat. Then he dropped back against the pillows, because the rest of it had arrived and it wasn't a bit.

"Also — you got mad at an empty kitchen for not containing me. You threw

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: Neither of us is being quiet and the neighbours have had five months of peace. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: don't fade to black, write it through.)

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The tribunal never reached a verdict.

Jun had a closing statement loaded — something about the fridge, the chip, and how "you threw" was shaping up to be the best segue of his entire career — and then Halle's mouth ended the proceedings without a vote, and the motion on the floor became something else entirely, and he lost the thread of his own argument on purpose and did not go looking for it.

Round three had no business existing. His body had filed its final report two rounds ago and was now operating strictly on fumes and nineteen weeks of greed, and it turned out that was enough, because *don't stop* was not a suggestion, it was a direct order, and Jun had never once in his life under-delivered on a direct order.

So he didn't stop.

He'd slowed once — deliberately, to hear what they'd do about it — and what they did about it was *that*, in that voice, and every plan he had reorganized around the instruction in under a second. After that the pace was hard and kept, past the point where his own body lobbied to sprint, his hands at their hips and their jaw and their throat, mouth finding the mark he'd left there earlier and renewing it like a signature on a contract he'd already signed in blood.

The bed was loud. He was louder. Some detached quartermaster corner of his brain noted that the neighbours had enjoyed five months of quiet and were about to be formally reintroduced to the concept of him — that the walls were about to learn what a hundred and thirty-three days of deferred interest sounded like — and the rest of him did not care even slightly. Let them have opinions. Let the whole floor know the door had opened.

He talked, because he was still him, in wreckage: "Yes — *that* — you said don't stop, so I'm not — I'm *not* — Halle, I'm not stopping, I'd sooner—" and the sentence went into the headboard with everything else.

And then, somewhere in it, it changed. The frantic burned off and what was left underneath was slower and deeper and enormous, his forehead pressed to theirs, breath

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I bite down on my own wrist to muffle a sound that’s definitely going to earn a noise complaint. “I’m gonna feel this in the morning,” I pant against his shoulder, and I sound wrecked. “Good.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I laugh, shaky and low, as I feel his body go rigid against mine. "There it is," I murmur, biting gently at his shoulder. "Now you feel it too."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I feel him shake apart against me and I hold him through it, hands smoothing down his back. When he goes boneless, I press a kiss to his temple. "Told you I'd feel it tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline had been waiting since about six, which Roan established by the simple method of looking at her.

"How long?"

"Long enough," Aveline said, which meant too long, and meant she had enjoyed every minute of it.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Come here, then," I say, and sit back to watch her cross the room.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
She came without hurry, because hurry wasn't the point. The room was warm and lamplit, and she'd had hours to think about the shape of the evening, and none of those thoughts had involved rushing. Her bare feet made almost no sound on the floorboards. She kept her eyes on him the whole way across, steady, the way she kept them on him when she was waiting for something she wanted.

Halfway there she let herself smile — small, private, pleased with the game and with the fact that he'd finally asked. He was sitting back in the chair like a man with nowhere to be, and she liked that most of all. Liked being the thing he'd decided to spend the evening on.

She stopped at his knee rather than his side, close enough that the lamplight put her in his shadow, and folded down to kneel at his feet the way she always did — not small, not cowed, just *there*, settled and certain, chin lifted, still watching him.

"Thank you for the wait," she said. "I didn't mind it."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I reach out and brush a strand of hair back from her face, my thumb lingering on her jaw. "You never do." My voice is low, amused. "What did you think about, all that time?"

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
She leaned into his hand, letting the weight of her head rest against his palm for a moment before she answered. It was a fair question, and she'd had hours to compose an honest answer to it, so she gave him one.

"I thought about the way you say my name when I've done something right," she said. "The second one, not the first. You do it differently and you know you do." She tilted her chin into his thumb, unhurried. "I thought about whether you'd ask me to sit at your feet or whether you'd make me stand and wait for the asking. I planned out the whole evening twice — once for each. I thought about your hands. I thought about the fact that you'd left me there on purpose and that you were in the next room thinking about me too, and that you wouldn't have come out until you were good and ready, because you never do."

She let her hands rest open on her thighs, palms up, the way she always did when she was done talking and waiting to be told what came next — not a request, exactly, just a door left standing open.

"It was a good way to spend an evening," she said. "You're a good thing to think about."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let her kneel and I don't tell her to do anything for a moment, because the waiting is most of what she came for.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
She held the position. Didn't fill the silence, didn't shift her weight, didn't ask. That was the whole discipline of it, and she'd gotten good at it over the years — not because she was patient by nature, but because she'd learned that his silences weren't empty. There was a difference between being ignored and being *considered*, and she could feel which one this was. It sat warm on the back of her neck like a hand.

Her breathing slowed to match the room. The lamp ticked faintly as it warmed. Somewhere past the window a car went by and didn't matter.

She kept her palms open and let her eyes drift down, not away — down, to his knee, to the floor between them, the small courteous lowering of her gaze that meant *I'm here, I'm not going anywhere, you can take your time.* Her shoulders came down a degree. Her chin stayed level.

She thought, briefly and with some pleasure, that this was the part of the evening most people wouldn't understand. Not the kneeling. The quiet. Sitting at the foot of a man who had decided not to use her yet, and finding that entirely sufficient. Being the thing in the room he was thinking about was, for her, already most of the reward. Everything after it was just his generosity.

So she waited, still and easy, and let him look as long as he liked.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I run my thumb along the edge of her bottom lip, watching the way her eyes don’t leave mine even now. "Open," I say, voice quiet but clear.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
She opened her mouth for him without hesitation — not wide, just enough, the same unhurried compliance she'd brought across the room. Her jaw stayed loose under his thumb, and her eyes stayed up, because he hadn't told her to look away and she liked being seen doing this.

Her hands remained open on her thighs. She didn't reach for him, didn't lean in to take more than he'd offered. That was the line she held for herself: he set the pace, and she met it exactly, and the meeting of it was the thing she came here for. Under his thumb her lip was warm and still. She breathed slow through her nose and waited to find out what he wanted it for.

There was a small, pleased flicker somewhere behind her ribs — the second kind of saying-her-name hadn't happened yet, but it was coming. She could feel the shape of the evening settling into place around her like a coat she'd already tried on.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She has both of us out of everything in the way inside a minute and gets straight to work with her hands and her mouth, unhurried about it.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
She took her time with it the way she took her time with everything he gave her — not slow out of hesitation but slow out of appetite, because rushing a good thing was its own kind of waste. Her hands knew the map of him by now, the way he liked to be held, the particular rhythm that made his breath go uneven under her ear. She listened for that. It was her favorite sound in the house.

Her mouth found the places she'd spent the evening imagining, and she worked with the patience of someone who had nothing else on her calendar and no intention of being hurried. When he got quiet — that specific quiet, the one that meant she'd found the right thing — she stayed exactly where she was and did it again, a little surer.

Between the two of them the room went soft and warm and close, lamp and skin and the low sound of breathing. She kept her eyes open when she could, because she liked to watch him lose the careful stillness he wore in the daytime. It was a privilege, that. She didn't take privileges lightly.

When it was finished, or finished enough that he pulled her up, she came up willingly and settled against his chest, still warm, still his, cheek to his shoulder like a cat that had decided where it lived. Her hair was a mess and she didn't care.

"Good?" she asked, quiet, into his collarbone — not fishing. Just checking her work. She'd learned long ago that praise asked for wasn't the same as praise given, but she'd also learned that he never minded being asked.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, my hand coming up to rest at the nape of her neck. "You know it was." My voice is rough. "Look at me."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
She lifted her head off his shoulder and looked at him — properly, the way he'd asked for, chin up and eyes steady, even though her face was still flushed and her hair was a lost cause and she was very aware of both. The hand at her nape made the looking easy. It anchored her, the way it always did, that warm specific weight of being held in place and told to be present.

There he was. The careful daytime stillness was gone, just as she'd hoped, and something unguarded had taken its place — the mouth, the eyes, the particular looseness around his jaw that only she ever got to see. She'd earned that, and she let herself enjoy it without any false modesty about it. She'd worked for it. She was allowed.

"You're lovely like this," she said, quiet and matter-of-fact, because it was true and because he didn't get told enough and because it was her job, her joy, to be the one who told him. Her hand came up and rested flat against his chest, not asking for anything, just wanting the heartbeat under her palm.

She stayed where he'd put her, nape still in his grip, waiting to find out whether the evening had a second act or whether this was the part where he pulled her up and wrapped her in something and they went to bed early like an old married couple who still liked each other. Either was good. She'd had a very fine evening, and it wasn't over until he said it was.

"What now?" she asked, mild, content, and genuinely curious — the question of a woman who had no preferences of her own left in the matter, and found that the most comfortable place in the world to be.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She uses her mouth with the sort of attention that comes from years of practice and genuine enthusiasm, and doesn't stop when I tell her not to.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
She read him the way she always did — not the words, which were sparse, but the hands and the breathing and the way his grip at her nape told her plainly what he wanted without asking her to guess. So she didn't stop. She kept her mouth and her hands where he'd put them, unhurried, attentive, following the small signals he couldn't quite keep out of his body: the tightening of his fingers, the rough catch in his breath, the way his head went back against the chair.

She stayed with him through all of it. That was the discipline and the pleasure of it both — not the doing, but the staying. Being exactly where she was for exactly as long as he needed her to be, and finding that easier than she'd have thought, because there was nowhere else she wanted to be.

When it was done, she sat back on her heels and looked up at him, flushed and mussed and entirely unbothered about it. She wiped her mouth with the back of her wrist, an ordinary, human gesture, and waited.

And then it came — the second kind of saying her name. Low, and slower than the first, with the roughness still in it, the one that meant *good* and *mine* and *thank you* all in the same syllable. She closed her eyes briefly, the way she did every time, because she'd never quite gotten tired of it in all the years.

"Thank you," she said, quiet, meaning it in both directions.

She rose from her knees without being told, which she'd earned, and folded herself onto the chair beside him — half into his lap, honestly, because the chair was barely big enough for one and she'd never pretended otherwise. His arm came around her, or she put herself under it; it was hard to tell anymore and she'd stopped keeping score. Her cheek found the spot on his chest that had been worn into a shape by her face over the years.

"Lamp's going to need turning down," she said eventually, into his shirt. "And there's bread from this morning that won't keep, so we should eat it, even if it's late." She yawned, jaw cracking, and didn't apologize for it. "But not yet. Give me a minute."

She stayed there, warm and heavy and pleased with herself, while the lamp ticked and the house settled around them. It had been, she thought, a very good evening. She'd told him so twice already and would probably tell him again before they got to the bread. He was a good thing to think about, and a better thing to come home to, and she was in no hurry at all to move.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I run my hand through her hair, still damp at the temples. "Take all the minutes you want." My voice is soft, tired in a good way. "The bread can wait. The lamp can burn."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
She made a small, satisfied sound into his shirt — the sound of a woman being told to stay exactly where she'd already decided to stay. Her hand found his knee and rested there, thumb moving in a slow, absent arc, the way you'd stroke a good dog or a favorite chair arm. Something you did with your hands when they were happy and had nothing else to do.

"Careful," she said. "Offer me all the minutes and I'll take them. I'm greedy about that kind of thing." But she didn't move, and the yawn she'd been holding finally got out of her, small and helpless, and she didn't bother to fight it.

The lamp did tick on. The house did settle. At some point his hand slowed in her hair and she felt his breathing change under her cheek — deeper, easier, the last of the evening's tension let go of like a held rope. She lay there and listened to it for a while, because she liked the sound, and because there was nothing in the world that needed doing.

She thought, drowsily, about the bread. It was good bread — the dark kind from the bakery on the corner that sold out by nine — and it really wouldn't keep, and she'd be annoyed with both of them in the morning if it went stale in the tin. But the chair was warm and her legs were heavy and the lamp was low and the man under her was asleep or close to it, and there was a certain kind of arithmetic in which good bread was worth less than this.

"The bread loses," she said quietly, to no one in particular, and turned her face a little more into his chest.

Later — she wasn't sure how much later, the lamp had burned down to a low orange glow — she made herself get up, because somebody had to be the adult in the room, and it had never once been him after nine at night. She turned the lamp down, and she padded to the kitchen barefoot in his shirt, and she cut two thick slabs off the loaf and wrapped the rest in a cloth and put it in the tin. She ate one standing at the counter over the sink, because crumbs, and left the other on a plate by the chair with a glass of water.

Then she came back, and she coaxed him up out of the chair with a hand on his arm and no particular ceremony about it, and steered him toward the bedroom because the bed was better than the chair and they both knew it.

"Come on," she said, mild, already mostly gone into the soft fog of being tired and content. "You can be lovely again in the morning."

She fell asleep with her back against his chest and his arm heavy over her ribs, and the last thing she thought, drifting off, was that the evening had gone exactly the way she'd planned it — both versions of it, somehow, the one where she waited at his feet and the one where she ended up warm and fed and held. She'd have to tell him he'd beaten the plan. In the morning. Over the good bread, before it was gone.

dialogue.content: "About time," I gasp, letting my weight drop back into him fully. My fingers dig into his forearm where it's wrapped around me. "Was starting to think you'd gone soft."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
A low, gravelly rumble vibrated deep in Bear’s chest, humming straight through his ribs into Kit’s back. He didn't buckle under the sudden dead weight; he just sank his weight into his heels, took the load, and squeezed the air right out of Kit’s lungs with an arm like an iron band. 

"Soft," he mocked, the word a rasp against Kit's damp skin. 

To correct that particular misapprehension, Bear sank his teeth in earnest into the hard curve where Kit's neck met their shoulder. He bit down with deliberate, measured pressure—enough to bruise, enough to guarantee a dark mark by morning, the kind of bite that served as an anchor. His free hand left the fistful of shirt to clamp firmly onto Kit's hip, fingers digging through fabric to find bone and muscle, hauling them back another inch until Kit was pressed flush against every hard angle of him. 

He didn't let up on the bite until he felt the shudder run through them. When he finally released the skin, he dragged his mouth up to the shell of Kit's ear, breathing heavy and hot. 

"Say it again," Bear murmured, voice thick with amusement and entirely devoid of mercy, his boot hooking behind Kit's ankle to remind them just how precarious their footing really was. "See where it gets you."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The sudden slack in Kit’s frame was an invitation Bear had no intention of ignoring. Eight years meant he knew the difference between genuine surrender and the deliberate, heavy stillness that meant Kit wanted to be handled.

"Giving up already?" Bear muttered, the rasp of his voice thick and vibrating against the damp nape of Kit's neck. "Lazy."

He didn't wait for an answer. With their footing already shot, Bear gave a sharp, deliberate sweep with the boot hooked behind Kit's ankle, taking the legs right out from under them. He kept his iron grip locked tight around Kit's chest to control the drop, riding them down to the hall runner and taking the brunt of the impact on his own knees before sprawling his full, heavy weight directly over their back.

The air punched out of them both on the landing, the floorboards groaning under the double impact. Bear didn't give Kit a second to recover leverage. He flattened down, pinning them with forty pounds of dead weight and zero room to squirm, his chest pressed flush between their shoulder blades. 

His hand slid down from Kit's hip, catching both of their wrists in a single, thick-fingered clamp and shoving them up toward the small of their back. With his other hand, he buried his fingers into Kit's hair, hauling back with steady pressure just until their head tilted, laying bare the flushed line of their throat and the deep, darkening red of the bite mark he’d just stamped there.

"Not much of a chase," Bear rumbled against the hot skin beneath Kit's ear, entirely unrepentant, his hips settling heavy to keep them pinned. "You're getting docked for effort."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Bite me," I breathe out, my cheek pressed into the rug. My hips shift under his weight, a futile but pointed attempt to move. "Dock me harder."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
A low, wicked laugh vibrated against Kit’s back, rough around the edges and entirely pleased. 

"Gladly," Bear muttered.

When Kit’s hips hitched up against him in that sharp, defiant little roll, Bear didn't give an inch. He simply sank his full, dead weight down, flattening the movement out before it could even start. He drove his hips hard into the back of Kit’s thighs, effectively pinning them to the floorboards and making sure they felt every solid pound of the difference between them. 

He tightened his grip on their wrists, shoving them half an inch higher up Kit's spine—not enough to genuinely hurt the shoulders, but plenty enough to remind them who owned the leverage right now. 

"Dock you harder, huh?" His breath came hot and heavy against the back of Kit's ear. "Sassy mouth for someone pinned to the runner."

Bear didn't bother waiting for a retort. He took the invitation exactly as offered. Keeping a firm fist wound tight in Kit’s hair to hold their head back and bare the long, tense line of their neck, Bear leaned down and buried his teeth into the meat of Kit’s shoulder, right through the collar of their shirt. 

He bit hard, slow and possessive, letting his jaw clamp down until he tasted the salt of sweat through the cotton. He held it there, grinding the pressure in until he felt the sharp intake of Kit's breath beneath him, deliberately leaving a jagged, bruised ring that would throb for the next two days. 

When he finally peeled his mouth away, he dragged his lips along the red welt left behind, his beard scratching roughly against flushed skin. 

"There's your bite," Bear rumbled, chest heaving against Kit's shoulder blades, fingers flexing tight in their hair. "Now what else you got to say for yourself?"

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The bedroom was thirty feet down the hall, and neither of them had the patience for thirty feet.

Bear released his grip on Kit’s wrists only to hook his thick fingers into the hem of their shirt. He hauled the cotton upward in one rough, impatient jerk, bunching it over Kit’s shoulders and head without bothering to be gentle about the fit. A seam popped somewhere under the strain, and Bear didn't care in the slightest; he stripped it off and tossed it into the dark toward the living room.

He didn't give Kit the space to roll over or catch their breath before his hands were at their waist. Thick, blunt fingers made short work of the button and zipper, wrenching denim down over hips with zero finesse. Bear wedged a heavy knee between Kit's thighs, forcing them apart to steal every scrap of leverage and clear the rest of the cloth out of the equation.

He peeled his own shirt over his head in one violent motion, tossing it aside, and dropped his weight right back down before Kit could even think about moving. 

The heat of bare chest against bare back was immediate—slick, hot friction that knocked the world down to the rough wool of the runner and the hard pine underneath. 

Bear planted one broad palm flat against the small of Kit’s back, pinning them securely into the floor, while his other hand came around to cup the side of Kit's jaw, thumb pressing firmly under the chin to tilt their face up. He pressed down, heavy and solid, his hips settling right back where they belonged with zero daylight left between them.

"Floor it is," Bear rasped against the flushed hollow of Kit's cheek, breathless and utterly unapologetic.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky laugh, the sound muffled against the floor. "Your idea of solving a problem is just to break it," I say, and push my hips back into his.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
"It works, doesn't it?" Bear grunted, entirely unbothered by the accusation. 

When Kit pushed back against him, Bear didn't give an inch. He took the motion, met it with a heavy, grinding roll of his own hips that drove Kit flat into the runner, and held them there with sheer, stubborn mass. The breath punched out of both of them at the contact, bare skin sliding against bare skin, slick with a fine sheen of heat and sweat. 

Bear slid his hand from Kit's jaw down to the nape of their neck, thick fingers burying into the hair at the base of the skull. He pressed down just enough to keep their cheek wedged into the wool, his broad forearm resting heavy along their spine. 

"Besides," he rumbled, shifting his weight forward until his chest was crushing down between Kit's shoulder blades, his beard scraping rough and abrasive over the hot, bruised skin of Kit's shoulder, "you're the one who started running."

He hooked his free hand underneath Kit's hip, calloused fingers biting into the meat of it, and hauled them up half an inch just to slam them back down flush against him, setting a tempo that was all friction, weight, and hard floorboards. 

"Don't run if you don't want to get hauled down," Bear rasped into Kit's ear, his teeth grazing the sensitive cartilage before snapping down in a quick, sharp nip. "You know better."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear never needed to be told twice, especially when Kit got greedy.

He shifted his weight just enough to get better leverage, planting his knees wide on the runner and pinning Kit’s hips flat to the floorboards. His broad hand stayed heavy on the back of Kit’s neck, fingers tangled in their hair, keeping their face turned into the rough wool so the line of the shoulder stayed taut and exposed.

"Greedy," Bear growled, low and dark against Kit's skin. 

He didn't hesitate. Bear leaned down and found fresh skin right beside the angry, swelling welt he’d just left. He opened his mouth, caught a thick fold of muscle between his teeth, and bore down with deliberate, crushing pressure. 

He didn't rush it. He bit deep, grinding his jaw until he felt the sharp shudder travel straight through Kit's frame, riding the twitch of muscle beneath his mouth. He put his full weight behind it, anchoring Kit to the floor with teeth and bone, making sure the second mark would match the first—deep, dark, and impossible to hide. 

Only when his jaw started to ache with the effort did Bear slowly release the bite. He didn't pull away completely; he dragged his tongue over the dented, broken skin, then scraped his rough beard across the fresh welt to keep the burn alive. 

"How's that?" he rasped, his chest heaving hard against Kit's spine, hand tightening in their hair with just enough pull to remind them who had them pinned. "You getting enough, or do I need to mark the other side?"

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I let out a sharp gasp that turns into a laugh, breathless against the rug. "Other side," I manage, my voice rough. "Make 'em match."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
A low, breathy rumble started deep in Bear’s chest, turning into a rough laugh against the damp skin of Kit’s spine. 

"Fucking glutton," Bear muttered, but there was pure, savage fondness in the rasp of his voice. 

He didn't need any more encouragement than that. Bear shifted his bulk, adjusting his knees on the hardwood bordering the runner to get a fresh angle. He dragged his hand down from Kit's hair, letting his broad, calloused palm sweep firmly over the bruised shoulder he’d just claimed before planting it flat between Kit’s shoulder blades. He leaned his heavy weight onto that hand, flattening Kit completely against the wool.

With his other arm, Bear reached around, hooking his forearm beneath Kit's chin to haul their upper body up just an inch, wrenching their head the opposite way to lay the unmarked shoulder completely bare. 

"Matching set," Bear growled against the hot skin beneath Kit's ear. "Don't say I never give you anything."

He sank his teeth in without hesitation.

Bear caught the thick ridge of muscle on the opposite side, clamping down hard and deliberate. He used his jaw to grind the weight into the bite, matching the depth and pressure of the first one blow for blow. He held Kit pinned beneath him—one hand heavy on their spine, his hips an immovable weight over their legs—letting the sharp, hot sting do the work while his beard dragged rough against the flushed line of Kit’s collarbone. 

He stayed locked on until he was sure the bruise would bloom just as dark and ugly by morning, marking the second side with the same heavy, possessive stamp. 

When he finally let go, Bear exhaled a hot, shuddering breath right against the welt, his teeth grazing over the indented skin before he let Kit's head drop back down to the runner. He collapsed his full weight back over them, chest heaving, his mouth hovering inches from Kit's ear.

"There," Bear rumbled, rough and thick with heat. "Evened out. What's next on your punch list?"

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
A slow, wicked hum vibrated in Bear’s chest, rattling low against Kit’s ribs. 

"Thursday," Bear repeated, the word thick with amused contempt for the challenge. "Setting deadlines now."

He didn't hesitate to take what was offered. Bear’s broad, calloused hand clamped around both of Kit’s wrists at once, fingers overlapping with plenty of room to spare. He didn't just hold them; he hauled them up, driving them flat against the runner above Kit's head and bearing down with enough solid, uncompromising pressure that Kit’s knuckles ground into the wool. The red bracelet of his grip would be there by breakfast, dark and distinct.

With Kit anchored by one massive fist, Bear shifted his bulk back onto his knees, straddling Kit's thighs to keep their lower half entirely immobilized. 

"Mirror marks," Bear muttered, studying the pale, sweat-sheened canvas of Kit’s back and ribs under the dim hallway light. "Alright. Let's make sure you don't miss any."

He sank his free hand into the meat of Kit’s hip, blunt fingers digging deep into the hollow just beneath the bone. He squeezed until the muscle yielded, bearing down with heavy, deliberate thumb-pressure that was guaranteed to bloom into an ugly, yellow-green constellation by midweek. 

Then Bear leaned down, his full weight pressing Kit flat into the boards, and went to work with his mouth. 

He didn't rush. He started at the sharp curve of Kit’s shoulder blade, biting down with enough sustained force to dent the muscle, holding it through the twitch and hitch of Kit’s breath beneath him. From there, he dragged his teeth down the ridgeline of the spine, marking the skin between the vertebrae with deliberate, bruising nips that scraped hard enough to leave fiery trails in their wake. 

When he reached the vulnerable swell of Kit’s ribs where they wrapped toward the front—somewhere they’d definitely catch in the bathroom glass tomorrow—Bear hooked two fingers under the hip to haul Kit slightly onto their side. He buried his face into the soft skin just over the ribs and sank his jaw deep, grinding down until he felt the sharp flare of heat beneath his lips.

He held the bite until his own pulse was pounding in his ears, letting the ache settle into the bone. When he finally pulled back, he left a dark, jagged ring glistening in the faint light. 

Bear hovered there, chest heaving against Kit’s side, his hand still an iron shackle around both of Kit’s wrists. He dragged his rough, bearded jaw over the new mark, his breath coming in hot, ragged bursts.

"That'll last past Thursday," Bear growled against the bruising skin, voice rough as gravel. "You want to check the math, or should I keep going?"

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I laugh, breathless and raw. "Keep going," I say, my voice muffled against my own arm. "I'm not counting."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
"Good," Bear rumbled, the sound vibrating right against Kit's flank. "Because I'm not doing the bookkeeping tonight."

He kept his iron grip clamped around Kit’s wrists, bearing down until the veins in his own forearm stood out corded and tight, anchoring both arms firmly against the wool above Kit's head. With his free hand, Bear reached across, his blunt fingers digging hard into the meat of Kit’s opposite hip to haul them up just enough to expose the untouched stretch of ribs.

He went in deliberate and heavy. Bear opened his jaw and took a thick mouthful of skin and muscle right along the flank, sinking his molars in until the pressure reached deep into the meat. He bit with the patient, grinding certainty of a man who knew every inch of tolerance Kit had—and knew exactly how much further they liked to be pushed. He held the bite through the hitch of Kit's breath, letting the ache settle right against the bone until he was certain the purple-black shadow of it would linger clear past the weekend.

When he finally peeled his mouth away, Bear didn't give the skin a chance to cool. He brought his thumb down, pressing hard into the fresh, dented welt, dragging the pad of his thumb across the mark to grind the burn in.

"That's for the bathroom mirror," he muttered, thick and rough.

He shifted his bulk forward, letting his full weight collapse straight down between Kit's shoulder blades. The impact drove the air out of them both, crushing Kit flat to the runner with zero daylight left between them. Bear brought his mouth up to the hot, sweat-damp space right behind Kit's ear. His beard dragged rough across the skin, scraping over the first pair of teeth-marks before he found an unmarked strip along the chord of the neck.

Bear clamped down there next—a hard, bruising suction backed by teeth, pulling the blood straight to the surface until he left a dark, broken-vessel smear that would collar them in plain sight. 

He didn't let up, keeping his mouth pressed hot and heavy against the skin while his hips bore down, grinding Kit's pelvis firmly into the hard pine beneath the runner. 

"Not counting," Bear mocked softly, breath hot against the welt, his free hand sliding around to splay wide and heavy over Kit's chest, feeling the rabbit-fast hammer of their heart. "We'll see if you're singing that tune when you try to put a clean shirt on tomorrow morning."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn't have any intention of stopping.

He stripped away the last tangled scraps of denim and cotton caught around their ankles, kicking the mess down the runner into the dark hallway without looking. He didn't offer a cushion, didn't offer an apology for the hard pine beneath the wool; he simply wedged his knees wide on either side of Kit’s thighs, planting himself with the solid, immovable weight of an anchor. 

His hand remained locked around Kit’s wrists, pinning them firmly above their head, keeping the line of their back bowed and taut. With his other hand, Bear reached down and hooked thick fingers under the crest of Kit’s hip, dragging them back against him until there wasn't a sliver of space left between them. 

The heat was immediate, slick and blunt. Bear took a second just to bear down, letting Kit feel the full, crushing press of his weight before he drove forward—slow, deliberate, and entirely unyielding, sinking into them until the floorboards groaned under the shift. 

A low, jagged grunt tore out of Bear’s chest, rattling right through his ribs and into Kit’s spine. He didn't rush the rhythm. He knew how Kit took him after eight years; he knew the exact cadence that wore them down, the heavy, deliberate grind that left no room for running, no room for anything except the friction of bare skin against bare skin and the scratch of the rug beneath them. 

Bear set the pace with the merciless, steady stamina of a man half an engine. He drove into them with the full momentum of his hips, rocking Kit forward an inch with every heavy thrust, only to drag them right back onto him with the iron grip he kept dug into their hip bone. His thumb mashed into the fresh bruise he’d left on their flank, grinding the ache right into the movement, making sure every stroke was felt twice over.

"Look at you," Bear rasped, his voice raw and gravelly against the damp curve of Kit’s neck. "Telling me what to do on my own floor."

He leaned all the way down, flattening his chest against Kit’s back so the sweat between them sealed them together, hot and slick. He finally let go of their wrists, only to slide his broad hands under Kit’s shoulders, hauling them upward so their chest lifted slightly off the floor. The angle drove him deeper, harder, the impact heavy and hollow as he took them with a rough, relentless cadence that rattled through every joint.

Bear buried his face in the crook of Kit’s neck, teeth scraping over the swollen welt he’d left there ten minutes ago. He didn't bite hard this time; he just dragged his open mouth over the heat of it, his beard like sandpaper against the tender flesh, sucking hard enough to pull fresh blood into the bruise while his hips kept hammering home the tempo. 

He didn't give them a break, didn't ease up to let either of them catch their wind. Every time Kit's breath hitched, Bear met it with another solid, unyielding drive, locking his thighs against theirs, riding the shudder that ran through their frame and answering it with brute, stubborn mass. 

"Don't stop," Bear mocked through his teeth, the words half-smothered in Kit's damp hair, his breath coming in ragged, broken gusts. "Not a chance in hell."

He gripped Kit's ribs with both hands, fingers digging into the arches of bone, and picked up the speed—harder, faster, the runner bunching beneath his knees as he pushed them both straight to the edge, grinding them down into the wood until the world shrank to nothing but the rhythm, the heat, and the ache that was going to burn well past Thursday.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I can't even form words, just a choked-off sound that's half gasp, half groan. My hands scrabble against the floor, fingernails digging into the wool as he drives the air right out of me. The marks he left burn with every slam of his hips, a bright, perfect pain.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The sound Kit made—that broken, ruined noise—went straight to the base of Bear’s skull. 

He didn't give them room to recover it. Hearing Kit reduced to wordless gasps was the finish line, and Bear went after it with everything he had left. He drove his hips forward with a brutal, single-minded momentum, slamming into Kit so hard and deep the breath hitched right out of both of them, the floorboards vibrating under the impact.

Bear reached down, his heavy hand clamping over one of Kit’s scrabbling hands, pinning it flat to the wool runner, intertwining their fingers and bearing down with enough crushing weight that Kit couldn't pull an inch of slack. His other arm wrapped like an iron cable around Kit’s waist, hauling their hips up and back against his pelvis to meet every heavy, punishing thrust.

"That's it," Bear growled, the words wrenched out of him in a ragged, guttural rasp against Kit’s damp temple. "Take it."

He didn't slow down. He set a punishing, relentless cadence that rattled through every joint, using all forty pounds of his advantage to keep Kit anchored beneath him. Every time Bear’s hips drove home, his beard scraped over the fresh, fiery bites on Kit's shoulder, grinding the heat directly into the swollen welts, keeping the burn sharp and alive. 

He could feel the fine tremor running through Kit’s limbs, the desperate tension strung tight in the small of their back. Bear leaned over them, broad chest slick with sweat and heaving, burying his face into the side of Kit’s neck. He caught a fold of hot, bruised skin between his teeth one more time—not deep enough to break it, but hard enough to clamp down and ride the swell of the impact, anchoring them together through the sheer force of it.

His hips snapped forward in three fast, crushing strokes that drove Kit straight into the floorboards. A low, jagged roar tore through Bear’s clenched teeth, his entire heavy frame locking rigid as he spilled over, driving in deep and holding them both down against the wool until the tremors finally began to slow to heavy, shuddering breaths.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I slump under him, boneless and breathing hard. My cheek's stuck to the rug, and my entire back feels like one giant, perfect bruise. I manage a weak, breathless laugh. "Floor's...gonna need refinishing."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn't move. He stayed right where he was, sprawling his full, dead weight over Kit’s back, his chest heaving in deep, shuddering pulls that rattled down through both of them. Sweat dripped off the tip of his nose into Kit’s damp hair.

He let out a long, wheezing breath that was half-groan, half-chuckle, the vibration humming straight into Kit’s spine.

"Floor’s fine," Bear rumbled, voice completely shot, rough as crushed gravel. "Rug took the brunt of it. You’re the one who’s gonna need work done."

He dragged himself up just enough to take the suffocating pressure off Kit’s lungs, planting his forearms on either side of Kit’s head, but he didn't give up the pin entirely. He kept one heavy thigh slung over the backs of Kit's legs, an immovable anchor holding them down into the wool. 

Slowly, deliberately, Bear reached down with one thick, sweat-slicked hand. His blunt fingers found the swelling curve of Kit’s shoulder, right where his teeth had dug in deepest. The skin was fiery hot, already puffing into an angry, violet-rimmed crater. Bear pressed his thumb straight into the center of the welt with just enough weight to test the give, thoroughly admiring his own handiwork.

"Look at that," he murmured, unrepentant pride thick in his throat. He leaned down, dragging his rough, scratchy beard lazily across the back of Kit’s neck, his mouth coming to rest right against the shell of their ear. "That’s gonna be black by tomorrow night. Friday, easy."

He dropped his head onto the runner beside Kit’s, cheek pressed into the wool, an arm heavy as an oak branch tossed across Kit’s bruised flank to keep them trapped in the middle of the hallway. 

"Don't even think about asking me to carry you to the shower yet," Bear grunted into the floorboards. "Give me ten minutes before you start whining."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "I wasn't gonna whine," I mumble, turning my head just enough to breathe. "Was gonna ask if the rug's okay." My fingers twitch toward his hand on my shoulder. "It's a nice rug."
