dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit had made it as far as the kitchen doorway before Bear moved, which was further than usual and had clearly been allowed.

"You let me get that far," Kit said, backing up one step.

"I did," Bear agreed. "I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't be," I say, and go.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear gave it a count of two, because that was the deal, and then the kitchen was suddenly very small.

The chair went sideways. Bear didn't bother with the doorway Kit had gone through -- the hall bent around and came back on itself, and eight years had taught Bear exactly how fast Kit could take that corner and exactly how much rug there was on the other side of it. Bear cut through the dining room instead, three long strides, and came out into the hall a half-second ahead of where Kit was going to be.

Kit was fast. Kit had always been fast. That was the whole point.

Bear got a hand on Kit's shoulder and lost it, got a fistful of shirt and felt the seam complain, and then they were both on the floor in the hall in a heap of elbows and Bear's forearm was across Kit's chest and Bear was laughing, breathless, the low kind that came out when the adrenaline was already up.

"That was greedy," Bear said, close to Kit's ear. Bear could feel Kit's pulse going under the jaw, quick as a rabbit's. Bear's teeth found the place just below it -- not hard yet, just set there, a promise -- and held.

"Two on the board for me tonight," Bear said around the bite, muffled and pleased. "You want to argue it, you're going to have to get out first."

Bear's grip was solid but not locked. It never was, not right away. Bear liked to leave the door open just enough to see if Kit would go for it.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I twist, not to get away, but to get my knee up. The seam of my shirt gives a little more with the movement. "Two's generous counting," I say, breath coming fast. "You're giving yourself the one in the kitchen."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt the knee come up and shifted before it landed anywhere useful, weight going sideways off Kit's hip and then back down, heavier, pinning the leg flat with a thigh. It cost Bear the grip on the shirt. The seam let go the rest of the way with a soft sound that both of them heard.

"That was a good shirt," Bear said, not sounding sorry about it.

The bite stayed where it was through the whole shift, teeth riding the pulse. Then Bear let go of it, slowly, and pulled back just far enough to look at the mark starting to come up on Kit's neck -- faint still, but Bear knew what it would look like by morning. Bear had eight years of knowing what it would look like by morning.

"The kitchen counts," Bear said. "I had you in the doorway. You know I had you in the doorway. I let go." Bear caught Kit's wrist, the one that had started moving, and pressed it to the floor beside Kit's head. Not hard. Just there. "Letting go isn't the same as missing. You don't get to score my mercy against me."

Bear's other hand found the torn edge of the shirt and followed it down, knuckles dragging over the ribs, feeling how fast Kit was breathing. Bear was breathing about the same. The hall floor was cold and neither of them had noticed yet.

"You want to make it one," Bear said, lower now, mouth back near Kit's jaw, "then make it one. Get the wrist back. I'm not even holding it that hard."

Bear wasn't. That was the whole invitation.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear waited for it. The twist, the sudden heave of hips, the elbow that Kit liked to bring around when Bear's attention drifted toward the neck. Eight years had built a whole catalogue of what Kit did with a wrist that wasn't being held hard enough.

None of it came.

Kit went slack under the hold instead -- not limp, not surrendering, just quiet. The wrist stayed where Bear had put it. The knee that had been trying for leverage a minute ago eased back down to the floor.

Bear's head came up.

"No," Bear said. "No, you don't get to do that."

Bear studied Kit's face for a long moment, looking for the tell. Kit had done this before -- gone still to get Bear to loosen up, then made for the door the second Bear's weight shifted. It had worked exactly once, three years ago, and Bear had never entirely forgiven it.

But this didn't look like that. Bear knew the difference by now, and the difference was in the eyes.

"You ran," Bear said slowly. "You made me chase you around the dining room. You tore up a shirt. And now you're going to lie there." Bear pressed the wrist down a fraction harder, then let up again, testing. Nothing. "That's cheating. That's a different kind of cheating, and I'm counting it."

Bear bent and set teeth into the meat of Kit's shoulder, right where the torn collar had fallen away -- properly this time, hard enough that it would sit purple for days and Kit would feel it every time a strap or a seam dragged across it. Bear held it until the breathing under the bite changed, then eased off and pressed a thumb into the mark to feel how it would come up.

"Fine," Bear said against the skin, voice gone rough. "You want it one, it's one. But I'm not done keeping score tonight, and you just handed me the pen."

Bear's hand came off the wrist entirely and slid down to Kit's hip instead, fingers spreading, getting a grip.

"Last chance to run," Bear said. "I'll even give you the count of two."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I let out a sharp breath as your teeth break skin, then turn my head toward you. "I'm good here," I say, voice a little strained. "Your move."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear tasted copper and eased off, tongue going over the place where the skin had given. Not much. A bead of it, maybe two. Bear pressed a thumb into it and watched Kit's jaw tighten.

"Your move," Bear repeated, low. "You're really going to lie there and make me do all the work."

Bear didn't sound like it was a complaint. Bear sounded like someone who'd been handed something unexpected and was turning it over to see how it worked.

The hand on Kit's hip tightened, and Bear used it to roll Kit over -- not gently, one hard shove that put Kit's cheek to the hall floor with Bear's weight settling across the backs of the thighs. The torn shirt hung off one shoulder now, useless, and Bear peeled it the rest of the way down Kit's arm and threw it somewhere behind them. It landed on the rug Kit had been aiming for. Bear noted that with some satisfaction.

"Eight years," Bear said, and set a palm flat between Kit's shoulder blades, pressing down until Kit's breath went shallow with it. "Eight years you've been telling me I don't get to have it easy. Not once. Not even on your birthday." Bear leaned in, mouth against the nape of Kit's neck, and breathed there for a second, feeling the fine hairs stand up. "And now you're just going to give it to me. In the hallway. On the cold floor."

Bear's teeth closed on the back of Kit's neck, right at the top of the spine -- the place that made Kit go boneless every time, the place Bear usually had to earn. Bear held it and felt the shudder go the whole length of Kit's body, and Bear's own breath came out harsh against the skin.

"I don't trust it," Bear said, when Bear let go. "But I'm going to take it anyway."

Bear's hand went from the shoulder blades down the length of Kit's back, slow, dragging, and hooked fingers into the waistband at Kit's hip. Bear's weight shifted forward, hips against Kit's, the whole line of Bear pressing Kit into the floor.

"You want to change your mind, you know how," Bear said into Kit's ear. "Otherwise I'm marking every inch of you I can reach, and I'm not stopping until you make me."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear got the waistband down over one hip and no further before the angle stopped cooperating, and swore, and shifted weight to get a knee between Kit's legs for leverage. Kit's jeans went the rest of the way in a graceless shove, caught at the ankles, and Bear left them there. Kit's own hands were doing something behind them -- Bear felt a tug at Bear's shirt, then a harder one -- and Bear sat back long enough to drag the thing over Bear's head one-handed and lose it somewhere toward the kitchen.

The hall floor was still cold. Bear noticed it now, in the knees, and didn't care.

"Stay," Bear said, though Kit hadn't moved to do anything else. Bear said it anyway, because the word had a weight to it and Bear wanted to see it land.

Bear worked Bear's own belt open with the hand that wasn't holding Kit down, and it took longer than it should have, fingers gone clumsy with how hard Bear's pulse was going. Bear bent forward while doing it and put teeth into the flat of Kit's shoulder blade -- a quick one, sharp, the kind that was more about hearing the sound Kit made than leaving anything permanent. Then lower, the ridge of a rib. Then the soft place at the small of Kit's back, and that one Bear held, because that one Kit felt everywhere.

"Every inch," Bear said against the skin, reminding both of them. "I said every inch."

Bear got the rest of Bear's clothes off in a graceless shove of their own and came back down over Kit, skin to skin now, the whole heated length of Bear along Kit's back. Bear's hand slid under Kit's hip and pulled, hard, until Kit's weight came up off the floor and into Bear's grip, and Bear's other hand went where it wanted to go, and Bear felt Kit's breath catch and go ragged under the palm still pressed between the shoulder blades.

Bear wasn't slow about it. Slow was for the bedroom, for the nights when Kit had been caught fair and the score was even and there was time. This wasn't that. This was the hall floor and a torn shirt and something Bear still didn't quite trust, and Bear's hips drove forward with all the weight Bear had, and Bear felt the sound Kit made vibrate through the floorboards and up through Bear's own knees.

"There," Bear said, teeth against the back of Kit's neck again, that place, holding it. Bear's voice had gone to gravel. "There. That's what you gave me. You feel that?"

Bear moved. Not gentle and not careful, one hand spread on the floor beside Kit's head for balance and the other still gripping Kit's hip hard enough to leave a set of fingerprints that would be there in the morning alongside everything else. Bear bit whatever came within reach -- the curve of the shoulder, the side of the throat when Kit's head turned, the top of the spine again and again because Bear could feel what it did.

"You don't get to say I didn't earn it," Bear said, breath coming hard between the words. "You ran. I caught you. I always catch you." Bear's hand left Kit's hip and slid up the length of Kit's arm to the wrist Bear had pinned earlier, found it, and pressed it back to the floor. Not hard. It was never hard. "And you're still here."

Bear set teeth into the back of Kit's neck one more time and held it, and didn't let go.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I push back into you, a sharp exhale hitting the floorboards. "Not saying you didn't earn it," I get out, my free hand closing over yours where it pins my wrist. "Just saying you should enjoy it."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The laugh came out of Bear before Bear could stop it -- rough, half a growl, pressed into the skin at the back of Kit's neck. Bear let go of the bite.

"Enjoy it," Bear repeated. "That's what this is."

Bear's hips stilled. Not stopped -- Bear was still there, still pressing Kit into the floor with the whole weight of eight years -- but the driving rhythm went quiet, and Bear let the silence sit long enough that Kit would feel the shape of it.

Bear turned the hand under Kit's, the one pinning the wrist, until their palms met. Bear's fingers threaded through and closed. That grip Bear made hard.

"You think I don't," Bear said, mouth against the shell of Kit's ear now, voice gone low and scraped-out. "You think I chase you around the dining room for the exercise."

Bear moved again, and this time it was slower. Deliberate. The kind of slow Bear had just decided was only for the bedroom, and was now revising, because Kit had asked for something and Bear had never once in eight years been able to leave that on the table. Bear felt Kit's back arch under it, felt the breath go out of Kit against the floorboards, and Bear pressed a kiss -- an actual kiss, open-mouthed and unhurried -- to the mark already purpling on the shoulder.

"There's a difference," Bear said, "between taking what I caught and being handed it. I don't know what to do with being handed it." Bear's free hand slid up Kit's side, over the ribs, and spread flat against Kit's chest, feeling the heart hammer against the palm. "So I'm going to do this instead. And you're going to lie there and let me, because you started it."

Bear bit the side of Kit's throat, right below the first mark from the hallway floor, and this time held it soft. Just teeth resting there. Just the promise, the way it had started.

"Tell me when you want it rough again," Bear said around it. "I'll know if you're lying."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear did.

Same place, harder, and this time Bear didn't ease off when the skin gave. Bear held it and felt Kit's whole body go taut under the bite, back arching off the floor, the hand laced through Bear's clenching down hard enough to grind knuckle against knuckle. Bear rode it out. Tasted copper again, more than a bead this time, and made a sound low in the chest that wasn't a word.

"Again," Bear repeated when Bear finally let go, breathing hard against the wet mark. "You said again like you were asking for the salt."

Bear's hips had picked back up without Bear deciding anything about it. Not slow anymore. Kit had asked for slow and gotten it, for about as long as Bear could stand, and now Kit had asked for the other thing and Bear was done pretending there was a version of this where Bear got to be measured.

Bear's free hand came off Kit's chest and fisted in Kit's hair -- not pulling yet, just gripping, tilting Kit's head to bare the side of the throat. Bear looked at it. The first mark from the hallway floor, going dark now. The second one below it. The place at the top of the spine that Bear had been back to so many times tonight it was going to be one solid bruise by morning.

"You're going to look like you lost a fight," Bear said, and there was something wondering in it under the gravel. "You're going to have to wear a collar to work. You're going to feel this every time you turn your head, for a week, and every single time you're going to remember you lay down on the hall floor and told me to."

Bear pulled on the hair, then. Brought Kit's head back and set teeth into the corded muscle at the side of the neck, right where the pulse had been going like a rabbit's an hour ago and was going faster now. Bear bit down until Kit's breath stopped, held it through the shudder, and let go only when Bear felt the tremor start in Kit's thighs -- that specific tremor, the one Bear had spent eight years learning the exact location of.

"Not yet," Bear said into Kit's ear, and slowed. Just enough. Just long enough to hear the sound Kit made about it. "I'm not done keeping score."

Bear's hand let go of the hair and slid down, over the marked shoulder, over the ribs, under Kit's hip again, and found what it was looking for. Bear's grip on Kit's wrist tightened. Bear's mouth went back to the top of the spine, and this time Bear didn't bite -- just breathed there, open-mouthed, feeling every hair stand up, feeling Kit shake.

"Every inch," Bear said. "I keep my promises. Tell me where I've missed."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I let out a choked sound when your hand moves. "You haven't," I say, pushing back against you. My free hand grabs at the rug, fingers twisting into the pile. "Just get on with it."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
"Get on with it," Bear said, and the laugh was gone from it now. What was left was just breath and gravel.

Bear did.

The hand under Kit's hip stopped teasing and got to work, and Bear's hips drove forward to meet it, all the weight Bear had, no rhythm to speak of anymore -- just force, just the hall floor and the sound of it and Kit's fingers tearing at the rug pile. Bear's grip on the laced hand went white-knuckled. Bear's mouth found the top of the spine and bit, and didn't hold it this time, just bit and let go and bit again lower, and again, a line of them down between Kit's shoulder blades that Bear would trace with a thumb tomorrow and count.

"Push back," Bear said, though Kit already was. "Harder. Show me you want it."

Bear felt the tremor start again in Kit's thighs and this time didn't slow down. Didn't say *not yet*. Bear had been keeping score all night and Bear was done with it -- the pen was on the floor with the torn shirt and Bear's belt and everything else. Bear's forehead dropped to the back of Kit's neck and Bear's breath came out in a broken sound against the marks already there.

"There," Bear got out. "There. Go on. I've got you."

Bear's hand kept moving. Bear's hips kept moving. Bear felt it hit Kit -- the whole length of Kit's body locking up under Bear's weight, the choked sound going up into something else entirely, the hand in Bear's grip crushing down -- and Bear rode through it with teeth set in the meat of Kit's shoulder, not biting, just holding on, just needing something to hold onto.

It took Bear about four more strokes. Bear had never been good at waiting once Kit went first. Eight years and Bear had never once managed it, and Bear came with a sound Bear would have been embarrassed about in any other room of the house, face pressed into the back of Kit's neck, every muscle in Bear's back gone rigid and then loose all at once.

The hall floor was cold. Bear noticed it again, distantly, in the knees and the palm braced beside Kit's head.

Bear didn't move for a while. Just breathed. Kit's pulse was going under Bear's mouth, slowing by degrees, and Bear listened to it come down the way Bear had listened to it go up.

"You bled on the rug," Bear said finally, voice wrecked. Bear turned the laced hand over and pressed a kiss into Kit's knuckles, then set them gently on the floor. "That's on you. I said the hallway. You picked the rug."

Bear eased off, slow, and rolled sideways onto the floorboards with a grunt, one arm still slung across Kit's back. Bear's thumb found the mark on Kit's shoulder, the deep one, and pressed. Felt Kit flinch. Pressed again, softer.

"One," Bear said. "You were right. I'm giving you the kitchen."

Bear's eyes closed.

"Next time you get to the front door before I move. I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear's eyes opened.

The wrists were right there. Turned up, laid out on the floorboards beside Kit's head like an offering, pulse visible in the thin skin at the base of each thumb. Bear looked at them for a long moment without moving.

"Thursday," Bear said.

Bear pushed up onto one elbow. Every joint in Bear's back complained about the floor, and Bear ignored all of them. Bear's hand came off Kit's shoulder and closed around the nearer wrist -- not pinning it this time, just holding it, thumb finding the pulse and resting there.

"You know what wrists mean," Bear said. "Wrists mean sleeves. Wrists mean you're going to catch someone looking at you across a table and you're going to have to decide whether to pull the cuff down or not." Bear turned the wrist over, slow, studying the inside of it. "You've never asked me for wrists before. Eight years."

Bear wasn't asking why. Bear had stopped asking why somewhere around the third bite tonight, when it had become clear that whatever Kit was doing, Kit was doing it on purpose and with both eyes open.

"Thursday," Bear said again, and this time it was agreement.

Bear brought the wrist up and set teeth into the soft underside of it, right over the pulse -- and then didn't bite. Not yet. Bear held it there, mouth open, feeling the heartbeat against the tongue, letting Kit feel the exact placement. Letting Kit feel Bear decide.

Then Bear bit.

Not fast. That was the difference. The shoulder had been fast, adrenaline and momentum. This was Bear's full attention and nothing else -- pressure building by slow degrees, teeth sinking into the tendon and the thin flesh over it, and Bear's eyes on Kit's face the whole time, watching the breath stop, watching the jaw work, waiting for the flinch that would mean Bear had gone far enough for Thursday and not further. Bear knew Kit's face. Bear knew exactly what it looked like one increment before too much.

Bear held it there. Counted. Let go.

The mark was already coming up angry, a perfect crescent, indents that would fill and darken by morning. Bear pressed a thumb into the center of it and felt Kit's whole arm jerk.

"That one's for the mirror," Bear said, rough. Bear pressed a kiss to the inside of Kit's elbow, absurdly gentle, and then reached across for the other wrist.

"This one's for Thursday."

Bear did it harder.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I suck in a breath between my teeth. "Good." My voice is hoarse. "Now do the other one. Even it out."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear looked at the two wrists side by side and saw what Kit meant. The first mark was a clean crescent, deep enough, sitting neat over the pulse. The second was a mess -- darker already, the indents bleeding into each other where Bear had shifted the bite mid-hold and gone back in. They didn't match. Bear had known they wouldn't when Bear did it.

"Even it out," Bear repeated. Bear's thumb went to the first wrist, the lighter one, and traced the edge of it. "You want a matched set."

Bear had a stretch of ruined rug on one side and a cold hallway on the other, and the person who'd made Bear chase them around a dining room an hour ago was lying there hoarse and shaking and asking for symmetry. Bear had eight years of knowing Kit and had never once seen this, and Bear found it was going to think about it for a long time, later, in the shower, with the taste still there.

Not now. Now Bear picked up the first wrist again.

"Hold still," Bear said. "You know I mean that."

Bear didn't set up slow this time. Kit had already had slow; slow was for the first one. Bear found the existing mark by feel, lined teeth up over the top of it so the new bite would land in the same crescent and not beside it, and bit down hard and immediate -- the way Bear had done the second, the way Bear did a shoulder in the middle of a chase. Bear felt the tendon roll under the pressure and pinned it with the tongue and held. Held through the sound Kit made, which was sharper than the others. Held through the hand going rigid in Bear's grip. Held until Bear felt the exact same give in the skin that the second wrist had given, and then one beat past it, because Bear's teeth had been in that spot once already tonight and it deserved the extra.

Bear let go and looked.

Better. The two crescents sat opposite each other now like brackets, both dark, both wet, both going to be black by Thursday and yellow by the Monday after. Bear laid the wrists back down on the floor side by side and pressed a thumb into each one at once, the same pressure, and watched Kit's back arch off the boards.

"There," Bear said, and it came out low and satisfied in a way Bear didn't try to hide. "Even."

Bear let go and lowered back down onto one elbow, and this time the arm across Kit's back came with weight in it, Bear's whole forearm pinning Kit flat, chin resting on the bitten shoulder. Bear's breath went out long against the marks on Kit's neck.

"Look at them tomorrow," Bear said. "Both at once. Hold them up to the mirror." Bear's mouth found the top of the spine, that place, and set a kiss there instead of teeth. "And when someone looks across a table, you leave the cuffs where they are. I want to hear about it."

Bear's eyes closed again.

"Anything else. Since you're asking so nicely. Since I'm apparently the kind of fool who gives you the kitchen."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
"Don't stop," Bear repeated. Bear's chin was still on Kit's shoulder. Bear didn't move it yet. "I stopped a minute ago. You noticed."

Bear had, too. Somewhere between the second wrist and the third bite, the count had gone out of Bear's head entirely and Bear hadn't gone looking for it. Eight years and Bear couldn't remember the last time that had happened. Maybe it never had. Maybe this was the first time either of them had put the pen down and left it down.

Bear turned that over for exactly as long as it took to decide it didn't matter.

"All right," Bear said. "Then I don't stop."

Bear's forearm came off Kit's back. Bear got a hand under Kit's ribs and rolled Kit over -- not the hard shove from before but not gentle either, one steady haul that put Kit on the floorboards face up with the ruined rug bunched under one shoulder. Bear came up over Kit on hands and knees and looked down.

Kit was a mess. That was the first thing. Hair everywhere, mouth open, the marks on the throat gone dark and definite, both wrists lying palm-up on the floor with the crescents already swelling. There was rug fiber stuck to Kit's cheek and blood drying on one shoulder and a look in Kit's eyes that Bear had spent an hour not trusting and now just wanted.

"Look at you," Bear said. It came out quieter than Bear meant.

Bear bent and kissed Kit -- properly, mouth to mouth, the first time all night. Kit tasted like the hallway floor and adrenaline and Bear's own blood where Bear had split a lip on the door frame somewhere back in the dining room and not noticed. Bear held it long, one hand cradling the back of Kit's skull off the boards, thumb stroking behind the ear like Bear had all the time in the world.

Then Bear moved down.

Teeth to the side of the throat, over the first mark, soft. Teeth to the collarbone, harder, a quick sharp one that made Kit's hips come up off the floor. Bear's mouth went over the chest slow, open, tasting sweat, and Bear's hand flattened on Kit's sternum and pressed down to feel the heart going under it. Bear stopped at the ribs and set a bite into the soft flesh below the last one, the place Kit couldn't ever hold still for, and held it until Kit's hand came down and fisted in Bear's hair. Bear let it. Bear liked the pull.

"Every inch," Bear said against Kit's stomach, breath hot. "I never did the front."

Bear went lower.

Bear didn't rush it. Bear had already had Kit fast on the floor, and Kit had said *don't stop* and not *hurry*, and Bear had learned the difference a long time ago. Bear's mouth went over the hip bone, over the crease of the thigh, and Bear's hands came up under Kit's knees and pushed them wide and pinned them there against the floorboards, thumbs digging into the soft inner skin.

Then Bear's mouth was on Kit, and Bear heard the sound Kit made hit the ceiling.

Bear was thorough about it. Bear had been thorough about everything tonight and this wasn't going to be the exception. Bear used tongue and lips and the flat pressure of a palm braced low on Kit's belly, holding Kit down when the hips tried to buck, and Bear read every shift and hitch and tremor the way Bear read a hallway corner -- eight years of knowing exactly how fast Kit went and exactly how much rug there was on the other side. When Kit's thighs started to shake against Bear's grip, Bear didn't ease off. Bear leaned in. Bear got a hand free and slid two fingers into Kit, slow and deep, crooked them, and felt Kit's whole body clench down around them like a fist.

"There," Bear said, muffled, and didn't stop. "There. Go."

Kit went. Bear felt it -- felt Kit's heels drum against the floorboards, felt the hand in Bear's hair go tight enough to hurt, felt the wet clench and pulse around Bear's fingers -- and Bear rode it all the way through and kept going past it, mouth and fingers both, until Kit's hips were twisting on the floor trying to get away from it and there was nowhere to go because Bear had a forearm across Kit's belly and wasn't moving.

Bear pulled off eventually. Not because Kit made Bear -- Kit hadn't said the word -- but because Bear wanted to see Kit's face for what came next.

Bear came back up the length of Kit's body on hands and knees, wiping Bear's mouth with the back of one wrist, and settled between Kit's thighs with all of Bear's weight. Bear was hard again. Bear had been getting there since the second wrist and had gotten there properly somewhere around the sound Kit had made when Bear's fingers went in. Bear lined up and didn't push yet -- just rested there, pressed close, and put a hand flat on either side of Kit's head.

"Wrists up," Bear said.

Bear waited. Bear watched Kit lift them off the floor -- both, trembling, the crescents dark and swollen -- and Bear took them in one hand and pinned them together above Kit's head against the boards. Bear's grip covered both marks at once. Bear pressed and felt Kit's breath break.

"That's what you wanted," Bear said, low, mouth an inch from Kit's. "That's why you asked for them. You wanted me to have something to hold."

Bear pushed in.

Slow the first time, all the way, and Bear watched Kit's eyes go unfocused and Kit's mouth come open and didn't look away. Bear pulled out just as slow and drove back in hard, and after that there wasn't a rhythm again, there was just Bear -- weight and hips and the sound of skin and floorboards, Bear's free hand fisted in the ruined rug beside Kit's head, Bear's grip on Kit's wrists grinding the bites against each other with every stroke. Kit's legs came up around Bear's back and locked. Bear felt heels dig into the small of Bear's spine and pushed harder into it.

Bear bit Kit's lower lip. Bit the jaw. Bit the throat, over the oldest mark, and held it while Bear's hips slammed forward, and Kit's sound came out around Bear's teeth as something that wasn't quite a word and wasn't quite Bear's name.

"Again," Bear said. Not a question. Bear's hand let go of the rug and got between them and found Kit, still slick, still oversensitive, and Bear's fingers moved rough and sure and didn't care that Kit twisted under it. "Again. I've got you. Don't you dare hold it back from me."

Kit didn't. Bear felt it build -- the shake, the clench, the arch -- and this time Bear was right there with it, three strokes behind, four, Bear's forehead dropping to Kit's and Bear's breath coming out in pieces against Kit's mouth. Kit went and took Bear with it, and Bear came with Kit's wrists crushed in one hand and Bear's whole weight bearing down and a sound coming out of Bear's chest that was closer to a growl than anything Bear would admit to later.

Bear stayed there a long time after. Didn't pull out. Didn't let go of the wrists. Just breathed against Kit's face and felt Kit breathe back and listened to two pulses come down out of the rafters together.

When Bear finally lifted Bear's head, it was to look at the wrists still pinned above Kit's skull. The crescents had gone purple-black at the edges under Bear's grip. Bear loosened the hold by degrees, and when Bear's hand came away it left a set of finger marks across both, laid over the bites like a signature.

Bear looked at that for a second. Then Bear lowered Kit's arms to the floor, carefully, and kissed the inside of each wrist, right on the bruise.

"Thursday," Bear said, voice gone to nothing. "Guaranteed."

Bear didn't roll off this time. Bear eased down instead, slow, full weight settling onto Kit, arms sliding under Kit's shoulders, face turned into the side of Kit's neck where all the marks were. The hall floor was cold under Bear's knees and shins and Bear had stopped noticing it. Bear's thumb found the top of Kit's spine and rested there, over the place, not pressing. Just there.

"I'm not moving," Bear said into the skin. "You want the bedroom, you're going to have to carry me."

Bear's eyes closed. Bear's breathing went long. After a while Bear's thumb started moving, slow circles over the bruise, and Bear said, so quiet it barely made it to Kit's ear, "You can have the front door next time. You can have the whole street."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I laugh, the sound rough and exhausted. "The street's a lot of work. I'll take the front door." I let my hand rest on the back of his head, fingers in his hair. "Don't fall asleep here. You'll complain about your back for a week."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
"I'll complain about my back for a week anyway," Bear said into Kit's neck. "You've seen how I get up off the couch."

Bear didn't move. Kit's fingers were in Bear's hair and that was doing something to Bear's spine that had nothing to do with the floor, a slow loosening from the skull down, and Bear let it happen for a while longer than was strictly reasonable. Bear's thumb kept its circles over the bruise at the top of Kit's spine. Bear's breathing had gone long enough that Kit might have been right to worry.

Then Bear groaned -- the real kind, forty years' worth -- and pushed up onto one elbow.

"Fine. Fine." Bear looked down at Kit, at the rug fiber still stuck to Kit's cheek, and reached out and brushed it off with a knuckle. Bear's hand stayed there, cupping the side of Kit's face, thumb running under the eye. "You look wrecked. You look like someone dragged you through a hedge and then bit you."

Bear sounded very pleased about it.

Bear eased back and off, slow, and sat up on the floorboards with a hand braced behind and every vertebra reporting in one at a time. Bear took inventory. Knees: bad. Split lip: forgotten about until now, and now definitely there. The rug was going to need a decision made about it and the decision was probably the bin. Bear's belt was three feet away and Bear's shirt was somewhere in the kitchen and Kit's was in pieces on the rug and none of it was getting picked up tonight.

"Front door," Bear said, considering it. "That's the whole hall and the steps. That's you outside before I've cleared the kitchen." Bear rubbed a hand over Bear's face and looked at Kit through the fingers. "You'd get to the gate. You'd actually get to the gate. Then I'd catch you on the pavement and Mrs. Achebe would see, and she already thinks something's wrong with us."

Bear got a knee under and stood, in stages, one hand going to the small of Bear's back with a wince that Bear didn't bother to hide. Then Bear looked down at Kit on the floor, and Bear's face did something soft and complicated that Bear would have denied in daylight.

Bear bent, got one arm under Kit's knees and the other behind Kit's shoulders, and lifted.

"Don't," Bear said, before Kit could say anything. "I know. I said carry me. I'm a liar. Put your arms around my neck and mind the wrists, I'm not done admiring those yet."

Bear's back complained the whole length of the hall. Bear ignored it. Bear carried Kit past the kitchen doorway where all of this had started and did not look at the chair still lying on its side, and took the stairs one at a time, and set Kit down on the bed like something Bear had gone to a great deal of trouble to acquire and intended to keep.

Bear stood there a moment, breathing. Then Bear climbed on after and pulled the blanket over both of them without bothering to get under it properly, and fitted Bear's body along Kit's back the way it had been on the floor, minus the floor.

"Front door," Bear said, mouth against the top of Kit's spine, right on the mark. "Count of two. Same as always." Bear's arm came around Kit's middle and tightened. "But I'm keeping the pen. Somebody in this house has to."

Bear's eyes closed. This time, Bear didn't fight it.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I shift back into him, feeling his arm tighten around me. My wrists are throbbing and I'm starting to shiver now that we've stopped. "You can keep the pen," I say, my voice rough. "Just don't forget the score." I tuck my marked hands under the blanket, safe between us.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt the shiver before Kit said anything. It went through Kit's shoulders and into Bear's chest, and Bear's arm was already moving -- reaching down, hauling the blanket out from under Bear's own hip where it had gotten trapped, dragging it up and over both of them properly this time. Bear tucked the edge under Kit's chin with two fingers. Then Bear pressed in closer, the whole length of Bear from knee to collarbone, and let the heat do the work.

"That's the floor," Bear said against the back of Kit's neck. "That's what the floor does. I told you the hall was cold."

Bear hadn't told Kit any such thing. Bear had been the one to put Kit on it. Bear didn't seem to feel this was a contradiction.

Bear's hand found Kit's under the blanket -- found both of them, tucked in against Kit's own chest, and covered them with one wide palm. Bear didn't press. Bear could feel the heat coming off the bites through the skin, the swelling already tight, the pulse going quick and sore right where Bear's teeth had been. Bear rested there and felt Kit's fingers twitch under the weight and go still.

"Forget the score," Bear said. Bear's voice had gone rough and slow, the way it did when Bear was most of the way to sleep and fighting it. "Eight years. You think I've forgotten one. I know what you owe me from the Christmas your sister was here. I know about the bathroom door."

Bear's thumb moved, once, over the inside of one wrist. Careful. Like Bear was reading the crescent by touch.

"One," Bear said. "Tonight. I'm giving you the kitchen and I'm not taking it back." Bear's mouth found the top of Kit's spine and stayed there, breath warm on the bruise. "Tomorrow you're going to stand at the mirror and count them, and you're going to lose track, and you're going to come find me and make me do it for you. That's the score. That's the only one I care about."

The shivering was slowing. Bear could feel it -- the tremors coming further apart, Kit's back going heavy against Bear's chest, the fine-wire tension of the last two hours finally letting go. Bear's arm tightened once and then eased, settled, stayed.

"Front door," Bear murmured, and Bear was almost gone now, the word barely shaped. "Count of two. Mind the steps."

Bear's hand stayed over Kit's wrists all night. Bear didn't decide that. Bear just never moved it.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, the shivers finally subsiding under his warmth and the weight of the blanket. "Your back's going to be hell tomorrow," I murmur, but there's no real heat in it. I turn my head just enough to press a kiss to the arm wrapped around me, tasting salt and sweat. "Worth it."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Bear bent and set teeth into the meat of Kit's shoulder, right where the torn collar had fallen away -- properly this time, hard enough that it would sit purple for days

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Bear's hips drove forward with all the weight Bear had, and Bear felt the sound Kit made vibrate through the floorboards

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Bear held it and felt Kit's whole body go taut under the bite, back arching off the floor... Tasted copper again, more than a bead this time

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Bear brought the wrist up and set teeth into the soft underside of it, right over the pulse -- and then didn't bite. Not yet. Bear held it there, mouth open, feeling the heartbeat against the tongue, letting Kit feel the exact placement. Letting Kit feel Bear decide. Then Bear bit.

Bear got a hand free and slid two fingers into Kit, slow and deep... Bear pushed in. Slow the first time, all the way... Bear's hips slammed forward

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit had made it as far as the kitchen doorway before Bear moved, which was further than usual and had clearly been allowed.

"You let me get that far," Kit said, backing up one step.

"I did," Bear agreed. "I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't be," I say, and go.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit said *don't be* and then Kit was gone, bare feet slapping the hardwood toward the back of the house, and Bear let the laugh out of his chest because he couldn't help it. That was the thing about Kit — eight years in, and Kit still said things like that and *meant* them, still shoved the door open wider instead of easing it shut.

Bear gave it a two-count. Not mercy. Just enough rope.

Then he was up and after, boots already off by the front door, and the house went narrow and familiar around him — the hallway pinch point by the bathroom, the laundry room dead end if Kit was stupid enough to go there, which Kit wasn't, Kit was smarter than that. The kitchen light stayed on behind him and threw his shadow long down the hall.

He heard the turn — back bedroom, then the little jog toward the closet where the house ran out of places to hide. Bear took the corner with his shoulder because he could, because the drywall could take it and so could he, and came up the last stretch of hall with his hands low and open.

"Two-count," he said to the dark ahead of him, unhurried, the way you'd tell a dog it was about to get caught. "That's a lot of charity, sweetheart. You're losing your edge."

He stopped at the threshold. Let his eyes adjust. Somewhere in there Kit was breathing, or holding it, and either way Bear could hear it.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I'm not holding my breath, you're just loud," I say from the corner of the room, my voice low and steady. Then I shift just enough to make the floorboard creak—on purpose.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear heard the creak for exactly what it was — bait, and not even good bait, the kind you offered when you wanted to be found. Kit had spent eight years learning which boards talked and had just spent one of them on him.

"Mm," Bear said, and stayed where he was.

He let the doorway hold him a second longer than he needed to, because the waiting was the part Kit always hated, and because his eyes had finished adjusting and he could see the shape of the room now — the bed, the window with the streetlight coming through the slats of the blinds, and off to the left, past the foot of it, the closet door standing open about a hand's width. It had been shut when Bear left the house that morning. He was almost certain.

The floorboard trick was in the corner. The closet was in the corner too. Kit was running two plays at once and expecting Bear to pick one.

"That's cute," Bear said. He rolled his shoulders once, loose, and stepped into the room — not toward the corner, not toward the closet, but along the wall, cutting the long way around, which put him between Kit and the door and made the whole thing smaller. His weight came down slow and deliberate on each board, giving them time to complain.

"Creak at me again," he said, conversational, hands still low and open. "I'll take the hint. Just want to hear you do it."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear took the last three steps fast and low and had Kit against the wall between the closet and the window before Kit finished the thought, one hand flat on Kit's chest and the other fisted in the collar of Kit's shirt, holding him there.

"Hallway," Bear said, close to Kit's ear, breathing a little harder than he'd let on. "You're in the bedroom. Try to keep up."

He pressed his forearm across Kit's collarbone and leaned, pinning him to the drywall, and took the bite he'd been owed since the kitchen — teeth into the meat of Kit's shoulder through the shirt, hard, the kind of hard that would leave a shadow for a couple days. He held it while Kit's hands came up and made their choice, whatever that choice was going to be.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I hiss through my teeth, my hands coming up to grip your wrists. "That's more like it," I say, voice tight with pain and something else.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear held the bite through the hiss, through the grip on his wrists, and only let go when he felt Kit's weight settle instead of fight — that specific shift, the one that meant *yes, keep going*. Eight years had taught him that language better than words.

He pulled back enough to look at the shoulder. The shirt hid most of it, but the mark was there underneath, and Bear felt the low, satisfied thing in his chest that always came with a good one. He kept his forearm across Kit's collarbone — not crushing, just present, the reminder that Kit wasn't going anywhere Bear hadn't decided yet.

"Good," he said, and it wasn't praise for the bite. It was for the grip, for the *more like it*, for the fact that Kit's hands had come up to hold on instead of push away.

He let his weight off the wall by a degree, just enough that Kit could breathe full, and used the slack to get a hand under the hem of Kit's shirt — palm flat on the ribs, feeling them move. Counting them.

"You lost," Bear said, quiet, near Kit's jaw. "You know that, right? Hallway to bedroom to wall. That's a full tour." He turned his head, not fast, and set his teeth against Kit's earlobe without closing them all the way — a promise, not a payment. "So you tell me what you want to do about it, or I'll pick."

He stayed there, holding him against the drywall with the streetlight striping them both through the blinds, and waited. It was the same wait as the doorway, same reason. Kit always hated it. Kit always answered.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear got them down to the floor in a graceless heap — elbow barking on the hardwood, Kit's knee somewhere it shouldn't be, and neither of them caring. The floor *was* fine. The floor had been fine before, twice in this house, and Bear had the scar on his shoulder from the corner of the dresser to prove it.

The shirt went first, and Bear heard a seam give somewhere. He'd apologize to it later, or not. Kit's hands were at his belt and Bear let him work it, let Kit have that, because the fast-and-bad part was half the point and Bear wasn't going to be the one who slowed it down.

He got Kit flat on his back on the floorboards, one hand spread wide across the sternum, pinning him the way he'd pinned him at the wall, weight coming down through the heel of his palm. The streetlight threw its slats across Kit's ribs and Bear looked at him for a second — sweaty, marked, shirtless, one shoulder already going the deep red-purple that would be loud in the morning — and felt that old low thing in his chest settle into place like a bone going home.

"Look at you," Bear said, low, and it wasn't cruel. It was the same voice he used at the door, the count. "Lost the tour and you're still grinning."

He came down over him — chest to chest, forearms bracketing Kit's head, close enough that Kit could have bit him back if he wanted to and Bear half expected him to. His mouth found the hinge of Kit's jaw, then lower, teeth at the tendon in the neck, not closing yet. Just there. Just the threat of the next mark.

"Last chance to pick," Bear said against the skin, breath hot, and then he didn't wait for it, because Kit had had his chance at the wall and had spent it on the floor.

The house settled around them — the kitchen light still burning down the hall, the blinds still striping them, one of them making a noise neither would admit to later. Bear kept his hand on Kit's throat the whole time, thumb over the pulse, counting. Not squeezing. Just counting. Eight years of knowing exactly how fast that number was allowed to go.

Afterward he didn't move off him right away. He lay there on the cold floor with his weight half on Kit, breathing, and turned his head to look at the mark on the shoulder, which had bloomed properly now.

"That one's going to be good in the morning," Bear said, satisfied, and finally rolled off onto his back beside him, one arm flung over his eyes, laughing at the ceiling at nothing in particular.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I breathe out a slow, shaky laugh and let my head roll toward you. "You sound proud of yourself." I poke your ribs with one finger. "Move. You're heavy and I'm cold."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn't move. That was the answer to *move*, delivered by not delivering anything at all — one arm still over his eyes, ribs rising and falling, the other hand finding Kit's wrist and closing around it lazily where it was poking him.

"Proud," Bear repeated, like he was tasting the word. "No. I'm *right*. Different thing."

He let the ceiling have a few more seconds of his attention, then turned his head and looked at Kit sideways through the crook of his elbow, taking inventory the way he always did after — the flush, the shoulder, the place on Kit's hip where the floorboards had left their print in his skin. Nothing bleeding. Nothing bent. Kit was cold, which was fair, because the heat had gone out of the room about ten minutes ago and they were both lying on hardwood in December.

He rolled up onto his feet with a grunt that he'd deny making, and it cost him — hip complaining, one knee stiff from the pin. Forty was a real number. He stepped over Kit rather than around him, on purpose, and went out into the hall.

The kitchen light was still on. He killed it on the way past because it was doing nobody any good, and came back with the fleece blanket off the couch, a glass of water, and his own shirt, which he dropped on Kit's chest without ceremony.

"Drink," he said, sitting down on the edge of the bed with his back to Kit and his elbows on his knees, still catching his breath. "Half of it, at least. You've got that look."

He reached back without turning around and pressed two fingers into the meat of Kit's shoulder, right where the bite was, and held them there. Not hard. Just checking the temperature of his own work.

"Cold compress tonight, if you want it," he said, and now he did turn, one eyebrow up, dry as anything. "Or you can wear it to work and be mysterious. Your call. I'm easy."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear heard it — *again* — and the dry thing in his chest that had been winding down wound right back up. He'd read the room wrong. Kit wasn't asking for the blanket and the water and the end of the night. Kit was asking for more of the same, which meant Bear had called the wind-down too early, which meant Kit had won a point back without Bear noticing it happen.

He set the glass down on the floor. Didn't look at it again.

"Okay," Bear said, low, and turned.

He got Kit by the arm and hauled him up off the floorboards — not gentle, not rough, just *up*, the way you'd move something that belonged to you — and put him on the edge of the bed instead, sitting, feet on the floor, back to Bear. He stepped in behind him, close, thighs against Kit's shoulders, and gathered a fistful of Kit's hair at the crown and tipped his head forward and to the side, baring the stretch of neck and the top of the shoulder. Same shoulder. The one already going purple.

He looked at it a second. Then he put his mouth on it and bit down properly — past the point where it was a mark and into the point where it was a *statement*, jaw locked, breath going out hard through his nose, one hand still fisted in Kit's hair and the other flat on Kit's back between the shoulder blades, holding him still for it. Long. Longer than the first one. Long enough that his own jaw ached by the end and Kit's skin was hot and raised under his teeth.

He let go slow, dragging, and stayed there with his mouth against the wet print of it, breathing.

"There," Bear said into the shoulder, voice wrecked low. "That's the one."

He straightened up, still holding Kit's hair, and looked down at the back of Kit's head — the bowed neck, the two marks stacked now, the second one already beading a faint line where the skin had given. His knee was going to hate him in the morning and he didn't care.

He let go of the hair and ran his palm flat down Kit's spine instead, once, from neck to tailbone — the apology, if you squinted, for the grip. Or not an apology. The receipt.

"Now you can have the water," Bear said, and went around the bed to sit facing him, elbows on his knees, watching. "And then you tell me if that was it or if there's more you're not saying, because I've already stood down once tonight and I'd rather not do it twice."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, reaching for the water with a hand that's not quite steady. "That was it," I say, after a long drink. I set the glass down and meet your eyes. "Now I'm cold. So are you. Get in the damn bed."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear watched him drink, and watched the hand doing the drinking, which was not steady, and filed that away where he filed things like that. *That was it.* He believed it. Kit didn't lie about that part — never had, not in eight years, and Bear had learned to trust the flat way Kit said it more than he trusted anybody's enthusiasm.

"Good," he said, and got up.

He gathered the shirt off the floor, the one he'd dropped on Kit's chest and Kit had never put on, and tossed it onto the bed. Then he went around the room killing it down — the blinds closed all the way, because the streetlight had done its work for the night, and the door pulled to most of the way so the hall stayed dark. Kitchen light already dead. The house went quiet around them in that way it did, ticking, settling.

His knee made its opinion known on the way to the bed and he ignored it the way he ignored most opinions he didn't ask for.

"Move over," Bear said, and got in, and the mattress did what it always did, which was give under him and drag Kit toward the middle whether Kit wanted it or not. He lay on his back a second with his arm behind his head, staring at the ceiling he knew better than his own face.

Then he turned onto his side and got an arm around Kit and pulled him in, back to chest, because the man had said he was cold twice now and Bear had heard him both times. He hooked his chin over Kit's shoulder — carefully, on the side that wasn't marked, which took some arranging and a small grunt of effort he'd deny making.

"Cold compress in the morning," he said into Kit's hair, eyes already closed, voice going slow and gravelly. "Don't argue with me about it. I'm right, it's different from proud, we've been over this."

His hand flattened over Kit's ribs, over the pulse, and stayed there. Counting, still. Just slower now, and down near zero, where it belonged at the end of the night.

"You did good," Bear said, to the back of Kit's head, and it came out quieter than he meant it to, so he let it stand there in the dark and didn't take it back.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear's eyes were still closed when the wrists arrived, but he felt them — the shift of weight on the mattress, the deliberate placement, and he knew exactly what it was. Kit didn't hand him anything by accident. Eight years of that.

He kept his eyes shut a beat longer than he needed to, because there was a small pleasure in making Kit hold the offer up in the air where he couldn't take it back. Then he opened them.

"Thursday," Bear said, flat, to the back of Kit's head. "That's four days."

He didn't ask it like a question, because it wasn't one. It was Bear doing the arithmetic out loud — the way he did with everything, the count at the throat, the two-count at the door. Four days was a real number. Four days meant something higher on the shoulder than the stack already there, meant bruising he'd have to work at, meant Kit walking into whatever Kit walked into on Thursday with it under his shirt.

He took the wrists. Both of them, one in each hand, and closed down.

Not hard yet. Just the fact of it — the grip, the size of his hands around them, the way there was no give. He pulled them up and over, laid them crossed on the pillow above Kit's head, and held them there with one palm, spread, pressing them flat.

"Okay," Bear said. And then, because Kit had been honest about the ask, he was honest about the terms. "You keep them there. You move them once and I stop, and you get the compress and the blanket and we're done. That's the deal. Nod if you've got it."

He waited for the nod with his other hand already moving — down the side of Kit's neck, past the two marks, to the top of the back, the meat of it where the trapezius ran thick from neck to shoulder. He pressed his thumb in there, feeling for the muscle, testing.

That was where he was going to put the next one. That one was going to sit under a collar and talk every time Kit turned his head. Bear found the spot and dug his thumb into it, hard enough to hurt through the muscle, holding it until Kit's breathing changed.

"Breathe out," Bear said, low, and set his teeth where the thumb had been.

This one he built slowly — jaw working, bite widening, the muscle rolling under his mouth. Kit had asked for Thursday and Bear was going to give him Thursday. He held it until his own jaw sang, until he felt Kit's wrists jerk in his grip and the reflex to pull away come and go and get sat on, and then he bore down one more notch and held it there, breathing hard through his nose, flat against the back of Kit's neck.

When he finally let go he stayed close, mouth against the wet red print, and pressed his thumb back into it immediately — into the fresh bruise, into the mark itself — and held.

"How's that," Bear said into Kit's skin, wrecked and quiet. "Feel like four days?"

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath, my wrists staying put against the pillow. "Yeah," I say, voice rough. "That's the one." I shift my weight back against you, letting the ache settle deep. "Now you can stop counting."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went still.

That was the thing about eight years — eventually the other guy started reading the same ledger you were. Kit had just said *stop counting* and meant it, and Bear lay there with his thumb pressed into a fresh bruise and his hand still pinning Kit's wrists to the pillow and understood that he'd been caught, cleanly, by someone who had been paying attention the whole time.

He didn't say anything for a second. Then he lifted the hand off Kit's wrists — slow, deliberate, letting them go one finger at a time so Kit felt the release — and brought it down to join the other, both palms flat on Kit's back now, spanning the ribs, just holding the weight of him.

"All right," Bear said, into the back of Kit's neck. It came out rougher than he'd planned.

He let his forehead rest there a second against the mark, breathing, then pulled back and turned Kit toward him — one hand on the hip, rolling him over onto his other side, careful of the shoulder this time, because the shoulder had done its job. Face to face in the dark, close enough that Bear could see the shape of him and not much else. He got an arm under and around, hauled him in until they were fitted together, Kit's forehead against his collarbone, and left it there.

"No counting," Bear said, agreeing to terms he had no intention of keeping. He closed his eyes. His knee throbbed. Somewhere down the hall the house ticked. "You're going to be insufferable about this, aren't you. Tomorrow. Thursday. You'll have it under your collar and you'll be insufferable."

It wasn't a question. He already knew the answer, and it was already making him laugh a little, low in his chest, where Kit could feel it.

"Cold compress in the morning," he said one more time, mostly to have the last word, and then he went quiet, hand flat between Kit's shoulder blades, and let the night have the rest of it.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn't answer with words. He answered by not stopping — by taking the arm Kit had around him and rolling them both, weight coming over Kit slow, the way you'd set a heavy thing down where it needed to go rather than drop it. Careful of the shoulder. Careful of the neck. Everything else, not careful at all.

The bed took the shift with a creak and a complaint. Somewhere in the middle of it the shirt got shoved off onto the floor again and neither of them looked at it.

He found Kit's mouth in the dark and kissed him, which they didn't do much of during — it wasn't the currency of the thing they'd built — and did it now anyway, unhurried, like an answer to a different question. When he came off it he stayed close enough that his breath was in Kit's mouth.

"You want the whole night," Bear said, quiet, reading it back. Not asking. "Fine. I've got nowhere to be."

He got a hand under Kit's thigh and pulled it up, opening him, settling his own weight down through the hips in a way that left no room to misunderstand what was coming and no room to wriggle out from under it either. He was still hard, had been since the wall, and had ignored it for the better part of an hour because Kit had asked for marks first and marks were the thing he was good at. Now the marks were done and the ledger was closed and Bear wanted the rest of it.

He leaned down and put his mouth on Kit's collarbone — no teeth this time, just the drag of it, the scrape of stubble, working his way from the two bites on the neck across the front of the chest, down over the sternum. He bit the pec, small and mean, just to hear it land. Then lower.

He worked by feel and by memory and by the sounds Kit was making, which had gotten honest in a way they only got at this hour, when the house was dark and there was nothing left to perform. Bear listened to them the way he listened to everything — taking the reading, adjusting off it. Slower where Kit got loud. Harder where Kit got quiet, because quiet meant Kit was holding something back and Bear had never once let him get away with that.

At some point Kit's hand got into his hair and Bear let it stay there, let himself be steered for about ten seconds before he reached up and took the wrist and pinned it back to the pillow, one-handed, without stopping what he was doing. He didn't say *keep them there* this time. He didn't need to. The grip said it.

When Kit's breathing had gone all the way to pieces and stayed there, Bear came up off him, wiped his mouth on his own forearm, and moved over him proper — hands braced either side of Kit's ribs, knees planted, looking down at him in the dark. He could see the marks now, both of them, dark against the streetlight haze, one on the shoulder and one at the base of the neck where it would show if Kit turned his head on Thursday and somebody was paying attention.

"Look at that," Bear said, low, almost to himself. "You're going to be so smug about those."

He pushed in slow. Not teasing — there was nothing left of teasing in it, that had been spent on the hallway and the wall and the two-count at the door. This was just the fact of it, steady and full and relentless, weight coming down through the heels of his hands, the whole of him landing on Kit and staying landed. He set a pace that was unhurried and had no intention of ending, and he kept his eyes open through most of it because he wanted to watch.

The bed took it. The house took it. Bear's knee took it and would bill him for it in the morning.

He got his forearm across the back of Kit's neck at the end — not the throat, up high, the way he'd done at the wall — and drove in hard and fast the last stretch of it, the mattress squealing under them, his breath coming out in short hard grunts against Kit's temple, and he didn't stop until Kit had come apart under him and gone boneless and the tension had run out of both of them like water.

Then he was done. He stayed in for a moment, forehead down on Kit's, catching his breath, and then pulled out and rolled off and lay there beside him in the wrecked sheets, one arm flung across his own eyes, chest heaving.

"Okay," Bear said, eventually, to the ceiling, voice shot. "Now I'm counting again. That one's going to count."

He laughed — low, tired, nothing to laugh at — and reached over without looking and put his hand flat on Kit's chest, over the heart, and left it there, breathing along with it, matching it, slowing down.

"Don't stop," he echoed back at Kit in the dark, dry as ever, eight years deep. "You say that like I ever could."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I let out a slow, tired breath, my heart still thumping under your hand. "Always could," I murmur, turning my head toward you. "You just like hearing me say it."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn't answer that one right away. He lay there with his hand on Kit's chest and let the accusation sit, because it was true and they both knew it, and eight years in there was no percentage in pretending otherwise.

"Yeah," he said, finally, to the ceiling. "I do."

He turned his head and looked at Kit sideways in the dark — the shape of him, the two marks standing out, the wet shine still on the collarbone where Bear had been. His own mouth tasted like salt and metal and he ran his tongue over his teeth and found a spot on the inside of his lip that would be sore tomorrow, from the first bite, the shoulder one, where he'd caught himself. Fair. The ledger was balanced.

He took his hand off Kit's chest and sat up with a sound he didn't bother dressing up, hip and knee both filing their complaints, and swung his legs over the side of the bed. The floor was cold. He stood anyway.

"Water's still on the floor," he said, pointing at it without looking. "Drink the rest of it, I'm not carrying you to the bathroom at three because you got a cramp."

He went out into the hall with the blanket dragged off the foot of the bed, bare feet on hardwood, and came back from the bathroom with a wet washcloth wrung out cold, and the bruise cream from the second drawer, which they'd bought sometime in year four and replaced twice. He sat down on the edge of the mattress by Kit's hip and held the cloth up.

"Shoulder first," Bear said. "Then the neck one. The neck one's the one that's going to stiffen up, and you'll blame me for it on Thursday when you can't turn your head to check your blind spot."

He pressed the cold cloth to the shoulder and held it there himself rather than handing it over, palm flat, patient, watching the streetlight do its slow work through the blinds. His other hand rested on Kit's thigh, thumb moving idly, nothing behind it.

"You know what I'm going to say next," he said, dry. "So say it back to me and save me the trouble."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Cold compress in the morning," I say, voice tired but amused. "And you're right, it's different from proud." I tilt my head, letting the cloth do its work. "Now get back in bed before I change my mind."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear took the answer the way he took most things — filed it, didn't gloat about it.

"Look at you," he said. "Eight years and you finally learn the script."

He held the cloth on the shoulder until it stopped being cold against his palm, then moved it to the neck, where the second mark sat thick at the base of the skull. That one he pressed down harder, thumb through the fabric, working the edges of the bruise the way he'd worked the muscle before he'd bitten it. Kit's neck was warm under his hand even through the cloth and Bear could feel the little jump in it when he pressed somewhere that hurt, so he pressed there again, once, out of habit, and then stopped and did it properly — flat, cold, even.

He set the cloth aside on the nightstand and unscrewed the cream. The stuff smelled like nothing, which was why they'd kept it; the first one they'd tried had smelled like a pharmacy and Kit had complained about it for a week. He worked a stripe of it into the shoulder first, two fingers, slow circles outward from the center, watching the color under his hand go from raw to merely ugly. Then the neck, and this one he did with more care than he'd ever admit to — small passes, three fingers, following the muscle up into the hairline, feeling Kit's head get heavier in his hand as he did it.

"Thursday," Bear said, to nobody in particular, recapping the tube. "You're going to walk into whatever that meeting is and somebody's going to ask if you pulled something. And you're going to say yes. And you're going to think about this floor."

He tossed the tube back into the drawer and shut it with his heel.

Then he got up, killed the last sliver of light coming under the blinds with the pull cord — he had to lean and it cost him, hip complaining again — and got back into the bed the way Kit had told him to, which was a concession he'd allow once and count as charity.

The sheets were a wreck. He didn't fix them. He got in on his back and dragged the blanket up over both of them with one hand, and then, because Kit had said it and Bear had agreed to it, he turned onto his side and put his arm back where it had been — over the ribs, hand flat, over the heart.

Slower now. Way down near zero.

"All right," Bear said into the dark, eyes closed. "That's the night. You spent it well. I'll see you in the morning."

And then he did the thing he did at the end of every one of these — went quiet, and stayed quiet, and didn't take his hand off until he was sure Kit was under.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I shift closer, pressing my back against your chest, the cold cream on my shoulder making me shiver. "If you say 'I told you so' in the morning, I'm biting you back." I yawn, my voice already fading. "Sleep."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: took the bite he'd been owed since the kitchen — teeth into the meat of Kit's shoulder through the shirt, hard

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The house settled around them — the kitchen light still burning down the hall, the blinds still striping them, one of them making a noise neither would admit to later. Bear kept his hand on Kit's throat the whole time, thumb over the pulse, counting.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: He put his mouth on it and bit down properly — past the point where it was a mark and into the point where it was a *statement*, jaw locked, breath going out hard through his nose

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: He took the wrists. Both of them, one in each hand, and closed down... set his teeth where the thumb had been. This one he built slowly — jaw working, bite widening, the muscle rolling under his mouth
