dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The brass handle rattled violently, twisting up and down against the locked latch with a sharp, aggressive *clack-clack-clack* from someone on the other side who clearly didn't understand the concept of an occupied room. 

The vibration buzzed straight through the wood and into Odile's shoulder blades, but instead of pulling back, she locked her ankle tighter behind Fen's hip and dragged them down with a frantic, breathless urgency.

"Don't," she gasped against Fen's ear, the word breaking into a ragged, shiver-edged whimper as she surged forward to meet them. 

The utter, terrifying stupidity of it snapped the last tether of her control. Every nerve in her body felt lit up, white-hot and electric, the friction between them sharpening into something unbearable. The door took the brunt of their weight with a loud, hollow groan, the frame rattling hard enough that whoever was on the other side abruptly stopped jiggling the knob, falling dead silent.

Odile didn't care. She couldn't have stopped if the entire house had walked in. Her hips snapped forward against Fen’s, hard and desperate, chasing the deep, blinding friction that had her whole lower body trembling. Her fingernails bit through the fabric of Fen's shirt, digging straight into their shoulders as the peak hit her like a wave breaking over rock.

"Fen—" 

The name came out as a strangled, open-mouthed cry that she barely managed to swallow into the crook of Fen's neck. Her eyes screwed shut, stars bursting behind her eyelids as the orgasm ripped through her, tight and rhythmic and so intense it stole the air right out of her lungs. Her inner thighs clamped down, spasms running hot and relentless straight up her spine, leaving her shaking from her shoulders to her heels. 

She slumped hard against Fen, completely limp, her chest heaving in ragged, audible gasps against their collarbone. Her legs were trembling so badly she wasn't sure her feet would find the floor if Fen let go, but her mouth, pressed hot and damp against their throat, cracked into a breathless, unrepentant, trembling grin. 

Outside in the hall, after three agonizing seconds of dead quiet, a muffled voice muttered, *"Jesus Christ,"* followed by the hurried, squeaking retreat of sneakers on floorboards.

A smothered, helpless snort vibrated straight against Fen's skin before Odile could stop it, her shoulders shaking with dizzy, exhausted laughter.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I'm grinning, breathless and panting against her shoulder, my own legs shaking. "Jesus Christ," I echo softly, voice rough. "Think we traumatized someone." I carefully lower her leg, bracing us both against the still-rattling door.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The second Odile’s feet touched the cold tile, her knees gave out completely. She had to throw both arms around Fen's neck just to keep from sliding directly down the front of the door. 

"It builds character," she wheezed into the hollow of their collarbone, her shoulders trembling with breathless, helpless laughter. "Whoever that was, they're going to have a fantastic story for brunch tomorrow."

She stayed glued to them for a long moment, simply catching her breath while the room slowly stopped spinning. The tile was freezing against her toes, a sharp, grounding contrast to the blistering heat still radiating between them. Downstairs, the playlist had transitioned into something with a relentless synth beat, the bass a dull, steady thump vibrating up through the floorboards, but inside the cramped bathroom, the only real sound was their own ragged, synchronized breathing.

Slowly, reluctantly, Odile tilted her head back against the painted wood of the door. Her hair was an absolute disaster, clinging to the damp skin of her forehead, and her face felt flushed hot enough to burn. 

Her grin, however, was massive and entirely unrepentant. 

"I told you the lock worked," she murmured, her voice rough, smoky, and thoroughly ruined. She reached down blindly, fumbling through the tangled pile of denim around her ankles with one hand while keeping the other anchored firmly in Fen's shirt. "Structural integrity maintained. We're practically tactical geniuses."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I laugh, a low, rough sound, and press a quick kiss to her temple. "Geniuses, huh?" I shift my weight, making the door groan again. "Better get dressed before our 'tactical genius' gets us kicked out."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"They wouldn't dare kick us out," Odile muttered, though she was already bending down to haul her jeans up over her hips. 

The sheer lack of space made the endeavor ridiculous. She had to hop once, awkwardly, on the freezing tile to get her foot through the hem, her shoulder bumping right into Fen's side to keep from toppling sideways into the bathtub. A muffled squeak of laughter escaped her throat before she could swallow it, followed by the sharp, metallic scrape of her zipper going up entirely too loudly.

She smoothed her shirt down with unhurried hands, then turned to the mirror above the sink. 

The dim amber light from the window didn't hide much. Her hair looked like it had survived a minor electrical storm, her cheeks were bright scarlet, and her mouth had that distinct, swollen look of having spent the last fifteen minutes thoroughly occupied. 

"Completely invisible," Odile declared in a stage whisper, leaning in close to the glass and attempting, with zero success, to flatten the front of her hair with two fingers. "The picture of innocence. Nobody will suspect a thing."

She spun back around, leaning her hips against the porcelain edge of the sink, crossing her arms loosely over her chest. A slow, thoroughly satisfied smirk spread across her face as she looked Fen up and down in the gloom. 

"We give it thirty seconds," she whispered, her eyes dancing with mischief. "You walk out first, look bored, head down to the kitchen for a drink. I come out a minute later like I've just been politely fixing my lipstick. Masterclass in stealth." 

She reached out, catching Fen's shirt collar to give it one last, lingering tug, bringing them just close enough to catch the lingering warmth on their breath. "Unless you want to make a run for that window after all?"

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile followed close enough that her hand found the back of Fen's shirt on the third step and stayed there, two fingers hooked in the fabric like a leash she wasn't admitting to.

"It works if you jiggle it," she said. "I tested it earlier. I told Marguerite I was looking for a hair tie." She laughed, low and pleased with herself, the sound half-swallowed by the bass thudding up through the floorboards. "Nobody has ever needed a hair tie that badly. She absolutely knows."

The bathroom was the second door. She got there first, reached past Fen to push it open, and then stopped in the doorway so Fen had to walk into her.

"Oh, sorry," she said, not sorry, not moving. Then she turned around in the narrow space, back against the sink, and pulled Fen the rest of the way in by the front of the shirt so the door swung shut behind them.

The lock was old brass and stiff. Odile reached around Fen's hip to jiggle it without looking, tongue caught between her teeth in concentration, until it clicked over.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile made a sound against Fen's mouth that was meant to be agreement and came out as something closer to a groan, and then laughed at herself for it, breath hot on Fen's jaw.

Her shirt was already halfway up; she solved that by pulling it the rest of the way off over her head and dropping it somewhere near the duck, then hopped up onto the edge of the sink so she could get her knees on either side of Fen's hips and pull them in properly. The faucet dug into her back. She didn't care. She got Fen's shirt open button by button, fast and not particularly careful, and put her mouth on every inch of skin as it appeared—collarbone, sternum, the soft spot just under the ribs that she knew made Fen twitch.

Downstairs, someone shrieked with laughter and a glass broke, and the music jumped a track. Odile went still for exactly one second, listening, her lips still pressed to Fen's chest.

"Not for us," she decided, and bit down, gently.

Her hands were at Fen's waistband. She didn't rush it, or she told herself she wasn't rushing it, but her fingers were quick on the button and quicker on the zipper, and when she got her hand inside she exhaled like she'd been holding her breath since the stairs.

"God," she said, forehead dropping to Fen's shoulder. "Okay. Hi."

She kept her hand moving, slow, deliberately slow, the kind of pace that was as much about watching Fen's face as anything else. Her other hand came up and pressed two fingers against Fen's mouth—not to be quiet, she wasn't a hypocrite—just to feel the breath change against them.

"Twelve minutes," she said, voice gone rough and smug. "I'm not going to be able to look Marguerite in the eye. I think that's a good sign."

Then her phone, wedged in her back pocket, buzzed against the porcelain, loud as a fire alarm in the tiny room, and Odile's whole body jolted—and she laughed, helplessly, breathlessly, into Fen's neck, not stopping her hand for a second.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The door was a better idea than the sink, Odile decided somewhere in the middle of being moved, because the door had no faucet and it *also* had the lock right there at hip height, so when her back hit the wood the brass rattled and she felt it click, still holding, and she laughed at that too.

"Oh, we're doing *this*," she said, and hooked one leg up around Fen's thigh like she was helping.

The music surged up through the floor, some song with a bassline she could feel in her back teeth, and the walls of the little bathroom seemed to hum with it. Good. Useful. She had already stopped pretending she was going to be quiet about any of this; she'd made a noise when her shoulders hit the door that she would have to think about later, and she hadn't even gotten the good part yet.

Fen's hand was between them. Odile's head tipped back against the wood with a soft thunk.

Every so often she remembered where they were—the duck, the shampoo, the fact that she could hear Marguerite's laugh very distinctly through the floor—and it made it worse, or better, a hot bright jolt every time.

Her free hand went back down into Fen's open jeans, because fair was fair and because she wanted to, and she matched Fen's pace with a kind of clumsy determination, too distracted to be elegant about it. Her knee kept slipping. She didn't care.

dialogue.name: Fen

dialogue.name: Odile

The lock chose that exact moment to rattle again, a bright little brass chatter against the frame, and Odile made a sound that was equal parts laugh and something much less composed.

"They can hear it now," she said. "Whoever's on the stairs can hear it. *I* can hear it, and I'm—" Her hips jerked. "—I'm the one doing it."

She did not stop doing it. If anything she pushed back harder, shoulders flat to the wood, chin tipped up so the tendons stood out in her throat, because the faster pace had found something and she wasn't about to be reasonable about it. Her hand in Fen's jeans lost its rhythm entirely for a few seconds, just gripping, and she had to make herself start moving again, unsteady, her wrist bumping Fen's with every stroke.

"Sorry, sorry, I'm—" She wasn't sorry. She was grinning again, teeth bared against Fen's cheekbone. "You're going to have to carry me down those stairs. I mean it. I'm going to walk into that kitchen like a *newborn foal*."

Downstairs the song hit its chorus and somebody—three somebodies—started singing along, badly, at volume. Odile's laugh broke off into a gasp. Her thighs were shaking. She could feel it coming from a long way off, the way you feel a train through the platform before you see it, and she stopped talking, which for her was the real tell: eyes squeezed shut, mouth open, one hand fisted in Fen's shirt so hard a button gave up and pinged off the tile.

"Fen," she said. Just that. Then, higher, urgent, "Fen, don't you dare go slow, I swear to—"

She came against the door with the lock rattling like it was applauding. The noise she made was not quiet. It wasn't close to quiet. It was a long, cracked, unmistakable thing that went straight through the chorus downstairs and would absolutely have carried into the hallway, and Odile knew it while it was happening and could not have cared less; she rode it out with her heel dug into the back of Fen's leg and her forehead grinding against Fen's, breathing like she'd sprinted here from the kitchen.

When it let her go she sagged, laughing weakly, loose-limbed against the wood. Her hand was still in Fen's jeans. She flexed her fingers, remembering it.

"Okay," she breathed. "Okay. Your turn. Six minutes. I'm very motivated."

Out in the hallway, unmistakably, a floorboard creaked. Then another. Then a pause, right outside the door, the specific silence of someone standing very still and deciding what to do with what they'd just heard.

Odile pressed her lips together so hard they went white, eyes huge, shoulders shaking. She didn't take her hand out. She lifted her eyebrows at Fen—*well?*—and started moving again, slow and mean, while whoever it was made up their mind.

She was talking again—she couldn't help it—a low run of nonsense against Fen's skin, *yeah* and *come on* and *look at you*, her own hips rocking sympathetically against Fen's thigh because she couldn't stay still. The door thudded. The lock rattled. Odile's other hand slid down to grip Fen's hip and pull, setting a pace, not letting up.

"Go on," she said against Fen's lips, grinning, breathless, merciless. "Be loud. I was."

dialogue.content: I groan, muffled against your mouth, my fingers digging into your hip as I come. For a second, the only thing holding me up is the door and you. I sag against you, breathing hard, forehead resting on your shoulder. "We're definitely living here now."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile held on. She had one arm locked around Fen's back and the other hand still exactly where it had been, not moving now, just staying, and she let Fen's weight settle into her and the door and the eighteen inches of floor like she'd been built for it.

"Yeah," she said, into Fen's hair, wrecked and pleased. "You were loud. I *felt* that."

She was grinning so hard her face hurt. She couldn't stop. She pressed her mouth to Fen's temple and just breathed for a while, both of them slick and shaking and half-undressed in a room that smelled like somebody else's shampoo, and the slow song downstairs kept doing its reverb thing through the floor like it had planned all this.

Eventually she eased her hand free and wiped it, without ceremony, on the nearest towel.

"Sorry, Marguerite," she said to the towel.

Then she looked around. Really looked. Her jeans were in the tub. She had no idea how her jeans had gotten in the tub. Fen's shirt was hanging off one elbow with a button gone, and she spotted the button itself sitting in the soap dish like it had been placed there. The duck bath mat was folded in half. The shampoo bottle lay in the tub next to her jeans, cap off, slowly bleeding purple.

"Okay," Odile said. "So this room is a crime scene."

She started laughing again, quietly at first and then not, her forehead dropping to Fen's shoulder, her whole body going with it, because there was nothing else to do about it and because she was still humming from the door and everything was funny. She got herself under control with visible effort, wiped her eyes with the back of her wrist, and reached down to hitch her underwear back up like a woman resuming her responsibilities.

"Right. Strategy." She retrieved her jeans from the tub, shook shampoo off one leg with a grimace, and stepped into them anyway. "We go down together. We don't make eye contact with anyone on the stairs. If Marguerite says anything, I'm going to say we were talking about my mother, and I'm going to say it with such sincerity that she has to let it go."

She fished the button out of the soap dish and pressed it into Fen's palm, closing Fen's fingers over it.

"You keep that. That's a souvenir."

The lock rattled when she shifted her weight—just from her hip brushing it—and she went still, then laughed once through her nose and shook her head.

"I'm going to hear that sound in my sleep," she said. She was still leaning into Fen, hips to hips, not in any hurry to fix that. She tipped her chin up. "Kiss me before we go. Properly. Because once that door opens I'm going to have to pretend I'm a normal person who came up here for a hair tie, and I need something to think about while I'm lying."

Downstairs, someone put on a much faster song, and a cheer went up from the kitchen that sounded suspiciously like it was aimed at the ceiling.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I get my hand between her legs and she bites down on my shoulder to keep quiet, which works for about thirty seconds.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
She'd been mid-sentence—something about how they should send Fen down first as a decoy—and the sentence just ended. Not trailed off. Ended, like someone had cut a wire.

Fen's hand was already there. Her jeans were unbuttoned again, or had never quite been buttoned, and Odile's brain took a full second to catch up with her body, which had already gone up on its toes.

"Oh, you—" she got out, and then bit down.

Fen's shoulder was right there and she took it, teeth sinking into the muscle just hard enough to mean it, her whole face pressed against warm skin. It was a good plan. It was a very good plan for about as long as it took the fast song downstairs to get through its intro, and then Fen did something with the angle and Odile made a sound around the mouthful of shoulder that was not a sound anyone with teeth in someone should be able to make.

She let go. She had to. Her head fell back against the door with a thunk that rattled the lock, and she laughed—one short helpless bark—and then the laugh turned into something else halfway out.

"*No*," she said, meaning yes. "No, we had a *strategy*, we had—oh my God—"

Her hands scrabbled for purchase, one landing on the towel bar, which creaked ominously, the other fisting in the ruin of Fen's shirt. Her hips had a mind of their own. They rocked forward, greedy, still oversensitive from the first time so that every pass of Fen's fingers hit like a struck bell, and she couldn't decide if she wanted to twist away from it or grind into it, so she did both, badly, her knee knocking against the tub.

"This is so—" she panted, eyes squeezed shut, "—unprofessional—"

The towel bar gave a warning groan. She let go of it and grabbed Fen's shoulder instead, the same one she'd bitten, and dug her fingers into the mark she'd left.

She'd been quiet for thirty seconds. She was aware of this as an accomplishment, and aware it was over. Whatever was coming out of her now was a low continuous thing, breathy and broken by her own name for Fen, and she wasn't even trying to muffle it against anything because that would have meant moving her head and she couldn't. The fast song hit a breakdown and dropped to just drums, and in the gap Odile heard herself very clearly, and so, presumably, did the hallway.

"They're going to—" she gasped, delighted, horrified, "—they're going to think we're *doing it again*—"

Her thighs were shaking. It was going to be quick. It was going to be embarrassingly quick, and she was going to be embarrassingly loud about it, and she grinned up at the ceiling with her mouth open and her chin tipped back and her whole body drawn tight around Fen's hand like a bowstring.

"Don't—" she managed. "Don't be nice about it. Just—*Fen*—"

Downstairs, right on cue, someone knocked on the ceiling with what sounded like a broom handle. Three cheerful thumps.

Odile came laughing.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I flinch at the ceiling knock, but don't stop until you're done shuddering against me. Then I press a quick, hard kiss to your mouth. "We should probably answer that." I nod toward the floor.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile was still shaking. Not a lot—little aftershocks, her thighs twitching around Fen's hand, her breath coming in hitches that kept trying to be laughs and mostly succeeding. She heard *we should probably answer that* from a long way off, like it had been shouted down a well, and it took her a moment to work out what the pronoun referred to.

Then she looked at the floor.

"Answer it," she repeated. "Answer the—" She lost it again, forehead crashing into Fen's shoulder, her whole body folding around the laugh. "What do we *say*? 'Who is it'?"

The broom handle went again, three more thumps, patient and rhythmic, and Odile lifted her head with tears standing in her eyes and her face blotchy pink from the door down.

"They're doing a *bit*," she said, wondering. "They've made us a bit."

She reached back without looking and knocked on the door behind her with her knuckles—three knocks, same rhythm, answering. There was a beat of silence from below, and then the kitchen erupted. Actual applause. Someone whistled. Marguerite's laugh cut through all of it, high and shrieking and unmistakable, and Odile closed her eyes and let her head fall back against the wood and just *absorbed* it, grinning like a woman receiving an award.

"Well," she said. "That's the hair tie story dead."

Fen's hand was still between her legs. She noticed this the way you notice you've been holding a cup for a while—belatedly, with some affection—and she covered Fen's wrist with her own hand and squeezed once before easing it away, because if she didn't they were going to be here for a third round and she genuinely did not think the towel bar had it in it.

"Okay." She pushed off the door. Her legs took it under advisement. She caught herself on the sink, laughed at herself, and then did the world's least dignified job of fastening her jeans, which were damp on one side and smelled like lavender shampoo. "Okay. New strategy. We go down. We go down *proud*. Heads up, eye contact with everybody. If we act like we've been caught, we've been caught. If we act like we did it on purpose—"

She stopped, considered.

"We did do it on purpose."

She turned to the mirror, took one look at her own face, and had to lean on the sink again. Her hair was flat on one side and vertical on the other. There was a mark on her collarbone she didn't remember acquiring. Her mouth looked like she'd been kissing a door, which, in fairness. She wet her hands and ran them through her hair, achieving nothing, and then gave up and turned around to fix Fen instead—tugged the ruined shirt back onto Fen's shoulders, smoothed it down over the missing button, tilted her head critically, and did the top button up to compensate, which made it worse.

"Perfect," she lied. She smoothed a thumb over the bite mark on Fen's shoulder before covering it, not gently, and looked pleased about it. "You look like you fell down the stairs. Very plausible."

Then she reached past Fen's hip for the lock. Her fingers found the stiff old brass and paused there, and she looked up at Fen with her flushed face and her wrecked hair and her enormous, unrepentant grin.

"For the record," she said, "I'd do it again. I'd do it again *right now* if I thought Marguerite's plumbing could take it." She jiggled the lock. It clicked over, cooperative for once. "Also I'm going to need you to hold my hand on the stairs, because I was serious about the foal thing."

She pushed the door open. The hallway was empty, dim, the coats still piled on the chair—but at the top of the stairs somebody had left a single hair tie, placed very deliberately in the exact center of the top step.

Odile looked at it for a long moment. Then she bent, retrieved it, and put her hair up with it, and started down toward the noise.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Stop worrying about the noise," she says, "and get on with it," so I get her leg up over my hip and stop being careful about how much sound either of us is making.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
She made it four steps down the hall.

The stairs were right there, the noise of the kitchen rising up them warm and rowdy and waiting, and Odile had her hair up and her chin up and her hand out behind her for Fen's, fully committed to the foal plan—and then Fen caught her hand and she turned to say something smug about it and the look on Fen's face stopped her cold.

She knew that look. She'd been wearing it herself twenty minutes ago on the third step going up.

"Oh no," she said, delighted. "Oh, absolutely not. We have a *strategy*."

She was already walking backward. She wasn't going toward the stairs. The dark bedroom at the end of the hall was cracked open exactly as it had been before, and Odile's shoulder found the doorframe and then her back found the wall inside, and the coats on the chair blurred past and the noise from below dropped by half like someone had shut a lid on it.

The door swung most of the way closed. Not all the way. There was no lock. She noticed both of these things and made a small, hungry sound about neither of them.

"Stop worrying about the noise," she said, "and get on with it."

And then her leg was up over Fen's hip and her jeans—her damp, lavender, barely-fastened jeans—were being dealt with by someone who had clearly stopped being careful, and Odile stopped being anything at all except a body against a wall in a dark room with the party breathing on the other side of the floor.

She didn't bite anything this time. She didn't even pretend to. When Fen pushed into her the sound she made was full-throated and shameless and went straight out the six-inch gap in the door and down the hall and, presumably, down the stairs, and she heard it go and didn't reach after it. Her heel dug into the back of Fen's thigh. Her head hit the wall. There was a framed something-or-other hanging beside her that rattled on its nail every time Fen moved, a tinny little percussion right by her ear, and she laughed at it, breathless, and then forgot it existed.

"Yeah," she said. "*Yeah*. Like that. Don't you—don't slow down, I know you, don't get *thoughtful*—"

Fen didn't. Odile's laugh broke into a moan halfway through and she just let it, mouth open against Fen's cheek, one hand clawed into the back of Fen's neck and the other braced flat against the wall for leverage that she used, shoving back into every thrust like she was trying to win something. She was still slick and swollen and stupid from the bathroom and it should have been too much, and it was too much, and she wanted it anyway with a greed that surprised even her.

The framed thing rattled. The bed, six feet away and entirely unused, squeaked in sympathy every time the floor flexed. Downstairs the fast song had ended and nobody had put on another one, so there was a stretch of near-silence below them that Odile filled, alone, with a rising string of noise she'd have been embarrassed by if she had a single spare brain cell to be embarrassed with.

"They can *hear*," she gasped, and it wasn't a warning, it was a thrill, it was fuel. "They're all just—standing in the kitchen—*listening*—"

She came fast and hard and loud, her whole back arching off the wall, Fen's name cracked in half in her mouth, her leg locked so tight around Fen's hip that she felt the muscle in her thigh threaten to give. She didn't let go. She rode it, shuddering, laughing, crying a little from the sheer overload of it, and hauled Fen's face down to hers and kissed her through the last of it, messy and grateful and not the least bit quiet even then.

When she surfaced the house was dead silent.

Then, from directly below, a single deliberate slow clap. Then another. Then the whole kitchen, building.

Odile dropped her forehead against Fen's, shaking with laughter she didn't have the breath to voice, and slid her leg down until her foot found the floor and immediately regretted it.

"Okay," she wheezed. "*Now* I'm a foal."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I grin against your lips, breathless, my arms still holding you up against the wall. "We're gonna have to own this one." I nod toward the silence downstairs, then the applause. "Think we can make it to the kitchen without collapsing?"

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"Collapsing was never off the table," Odile said. "I just want it on record that I'd planned to collapse in a *bathroom*, with a *lock*, like a lady."

She didn't move yet. She wasn't sure she could. Her leg had gone the specific kind of useless that comes from being held up by somebody else for too long, and her back was stuck to the wall with sweat, and she was fairly certain the framed thing beside her head had lost its nail because it was hanging at an angle now, quietly judging her. She looked at it. It looked back.

"Sorry," she told it. Then, to Fen, "Everything in this house has seen too much."

She got her jeans up. This took two attempts and a small noise of protest from her thighs. The button did not so much fasten as agree to a truce. Her shirt was—she looked down—her shirt was still on the bathroom floor next to the duck, which meant she was standing in a stranger's dark bedroom in a bra and shampoo-scented jeans while a kitchen full of people she'd have to see again applauded her, and she found she could not summon one single molecule of regret about any of it.

"Okay," she said. "Owning it. Here's how this goes."

She pushed off the wall, wobbled, caught Fen's arm, and used it to stand up straight with the air of someone who'd meant to do that.

"We walk down together. Slowly. Not because we're wrecked—because we're *making an entrance*. I go first, because I'm the one they're clapping for, let's be honest, you were quieter." She reached up and pulled the borrowed hair tie out, shook her hair down, and put it back up worse, on purpose. "I'm going to retrieve my shirt on the way. I'm going to put it on in the *hallway*, where people can see me do it. Then I'm going to walk into that kitchen and ask Marguerite for a drink like I've done nothing, and when she loses it, I'm going to say 'what?' and I'm going to keep saying 'what' until she's crying."

She took Fen's hand. Hers was shaking slightly. She noticed and grinned about it.

"And if my legs go on the stairs, you catch me, and we tell everyone it was a bit."

The shirt was where she'd left it. She put it on backward, realized, took it off, and put it on properly in full view of the stairwell, unhurried, while somebody below said *oh my God* in a reverent tone. The bathroom light was still on. She reached in and turned it off like a woman leaving a hotel room she'd enjoyed.

Then the stairs.

She took them like a foal, exactly as promised—knees going wide on the second step, one hand white-knuckled on Fen's, the other flat on the wall—and every single face in the kitchen doorway below was turned up toward her, and Marguerite was in front holding a broom, and Odile looked down at all of them from the middle of the staircase with her shirt wrinkled and her mouth swollen and her hair a disaster and said, with total composure:

"Found the hair tie."

The kitchen went off like a bomb.

Odile reached the bottom step, wobbled, caught herself on Fen, and did not let go for the rest of the night.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: Somebody tries the handle and neither of us stops. "Don't," she says, meaning don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
It was later. Later enough that the kitchen had thinned to the stubborn core, later enough that Odile had drunk one and a half drinks and given the rest away, later enough that she'd stopped saying *what?* to Marguerite and started saying *I know*. She'd been good for almost two hours. She'd sat on the counter with Fen between her knees and behaved.

Then Fen had gone to the bathroom, and Odile had counted to twenty, and followed.

The lock had needed jiggling. She'd jiggled it. She'd said, "I'm not here for anything," and then put Fen against the door in exactly the spot she'd been in herself, and taken it back.

Which was how she came to be on her knees on the duck bath mat with Fen's jeans around Fen's ankles and her mouth full and her hands gripping the backs of Fen's thighs, when the handle rattled.

Not the lock. The *handle*. Someone had their hand on the other side of the wood, six inches from Fen's spine, and turned it, and met the bolt, and turned it again.

Fen went rigid. Odile felt it in her palms—every muscle under her hands locking—and she didn't stop. She didn't even slow. She pulled back just far enough to breathe against slick skin and said, low and clear and absolutely certain, "*Don't*," and it wasn't for the person outside.

Then she went back to it.

The handle turned a third time. Whoever it was leaned into it; the door creaked in its frame, and Fen's hips jerked forward against Odile's mouth, and Odile made a sound around that, pleased and muffled and not remotely quiet, and dug her fingers in harder to keep Fen right where she was. Her jaw ached. Her knees were going to be patterned with duck. She had never in her life been happier to be anywhere.

"Occupied," Fen managed to the door, cracked wide open on the second syllable.

A pause on the other side. Then footsteps, retreating, and a voice already halfway down the hall saying *it's them again* in a tone of deep, weary resignation, and Odile laughed with her mouth still on Fen and felt the vibration of it land, felt Fen's hand shoot down to grab her hair and hold on.

She looked up. Fen's head was back against the door, throat working, eyes shut. Odile's own face was a mess and she didn't care. She slid two fingers up alongside her tongue, slow, curling, found the place that made Fen's knee give, and stayed there.

"They're waiting," she said, breathless, delighted, the words wet and shapeless. "Somebody's *waiting*. There's a queue." She worked her fingers, watched Fen's stomach jump. "Make it worth their while."

She stopped talking after that. She put her mouth back and her whole attention with it, fingers and tongue moving together, pace climbing, no teasing, no mercy, because the floorboards in the hallway had just creaked again and she wanted Fen coming apart before whoever it was got brave enough to knock. Fen's hand in her hair clenched and pulled and she went with it, let herself be used, made a low ongoing noise in her throat that she couldn't have stopped if she tried and did not try.

The door shook. Fen's hips rolled against her, once, twice, stuttering, and then the hand in her hair went vicious and Fen came with a sound that was mostly Odile's name and not at all soft, shuddering forward over her, thighs trembling against her palms, the door rattling behind them like it had the first time and every time.

Odile stayed until it was done. Until Fen's fingers loosened and the shaking eased and the only sound in the little room was two people breathing badly. Then she pulled off, slow, and pressed her forehead to Fen's hip and laughed, silently, shoulders going, until she had to wipe her eyes.

"Okay," she said finally, hoarse. She looked up. Her mouth was swollen, her chin shining, her hair half out of the borrowed tie. She was grinning like a criminal. "*Now* answer the door."

The floorboard outside creaked once more. Then, with enormous patience, someone knocked.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I lean my head back against the door, still catching my breath, and call out, "Be out in a minute!" My voice is rough, amused. I look down at you, still on your knees, and offer a hand. "Come on, let's go face the jury."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile took the hand. She needed it. Her knees unfolded in stages, like cheap furniture, and when she got upright there was a perfect duck embossed into the front of each one through her jeans, and she looked down at them and then up at Fen with the expression of a woman who has been given a gift.

"I'm going to have these for an *hour*," she said.

She turned to the mirror. It was not kind. Her mouth looked like she'd been eating something red and enthusiastic, her chin was shining, and the borrowed hair tie had given up and was hanging on by three strands. She ran the tap, splashed her face, wiped her chin with the back of her wrist and then—after a moment's honest consideration—with Marguerite's towel again, because that towel was already lost.

"Sorry," she told it, for the second time that night. "You've been very good."

She fixed the hair tie. She checked Fen's jeans were up, tugged the ruined shirt straight, and then, on impulse, licked her thumb and wiped a smear off Fen's jaw that had absolutely come from her. She looked at what she'd done and did not look sorry.

"Jury," she agreed. "Fine. But I want it noted that this one wasn't planned. This one was *spontaneous*. I was provoked."

She reached for the lock. It was stiff and stayed stiff. She jiggled it. It clicked over with a sound she now knew intimately, like an old friend clearing its throat.

"Deep breath," she said, mostly to herself, and pulled the door open.

Marguerite was in the hall. Marguerite was *leaning* in the hall, arms folded, shoulder against the wall opposite, in the posture of a woman who had been standing there long enough to have thoughts about it. Behind her, sitting on the pile of coats on the chair, were two other people Odile knew slightly, one of whom was holding the broom.

Nobody said anything.

Odile stepped out. She did it slowly, because her legs required it, and she kept her chin up, because the plan required it. She looked at Marguerite. Marguerite looked at her chin, then at her knees, then at Fen behind her, then back at her face.

"Hair tie," Odile said.

Marguerite's mouth did something complicated.

"That's my hair tie," said the girl with the broom.

Odile reached up, pulled it out, and held it across the hall between two fingers. Her hair fell down around her face in a way that hid nothing. "Thank you," she said gravely. "It was instrumental."

The girl took it. She did not put it on. She held it like evidence.

Marguerite pushed off the wall. She walked past Odile into the bathroom, looked at the tub, looked at the towel, looked at the shampoo bottle still slowly bleeding purple, and came back out. She stopped in front of Odile, very close, and Odile prepared her face for anything.

"There's a bedroom," Marguerite said, "at the end of the hall. With a bed in it. That nobody is using."

A pause. Odile had used that room. Marguerite didn't know that. Odile felt Fen shift behind her and did not look back.

"We considered it," she said.

Marguerite nodded slowly. "Next time," she said, "consider it *harder*. That bathroom has one towel." She stepped past them toward the stairs, then paused at the top and said over her shoulder, without turning around, "Also you owe me shampoo."

She went down. The two on the coats followed her, the broom girl still holding the hair tie out in front of her like it might go off.

Odile waited until the footsteps reached the kitchen. Then she turned, found Fen's face, and lost it—completely, silently, folding forward against Fen's chest with both hands over her mouth and her shoulders going.

"*Consider it harder*," she wheezed. "She's *right*. She's so—we're terrible guests. We're the worst guests. I'm going to send her a *basket*."

She straightened, wiped her eyes, and looked down the dim hall toward the bedroom door, still cracked six inches, the framed thing beside it presumably still hanging by a prayer.

"She doesn't know about the wall," she said quietly. "Nobody has to tell her about the wall."

Then she took Fen's hand, threaded their fingers together, and started toward the stairs with her duck-printed knees and her wrecked hair and every single person in the kitchen already turning to look up.

"Foal," she reminded Fen. "Catch me."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I catch you on the second step, my arm around your waist as you wobble. "You're the worst," I murmur, kissing your temple. "And I'm sending half that basket."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"You're sending half the *shampoo*," Odile said. "I'm covering the towel. I broke the towel."

She leaned into the arm around her waist without shame, let it take about forty percent of her weight, and negotiated the third step like it was a moral question. Her knees were still faintly ducked. Her legs had the loose, unreliable feel of a marionette with a hungover puppeteer, and every step down sent a small aftershock through her that she felt in her back teeth and grinned about.

"Also I'm not the worst." She tipped her head to catch the kiss, turned it into a proper one, brief and warm, then pulled back with her eyebrows up. "I'm the *loudest*. That's a different category. You were complicit in every single one of those. You said 'don't stop' to me *through a door* with someone on the other side of it."

The kitchen was coming up. The light from it was warmer than the hall and full of faces. Odile could see the top of Marguerite's head, already turned away, already pouring something with the studied indifference of a host who'd decided the only remaining dignity was in not looking. The broom girl was showing the hair tie to someone. Someone else was laughing into their hands.

Odile slowed on the fifth step. Not for her legs—for effect. She reached up with her free hand and finger-combed her hair back off her face, which improved nothing, and then let the hand drop to cover Fen's where it sat at her hip, and squeezed.

"Listen," she said, low, just for Fen, under the noise. "When we get down there I'm going to be extremely composed. I'm going to be *statesmanlike*. But I want you to know that right now, in this moment, on this staircase, I'm thinking about the wall. And the door. And the—" she made a small helpless gesture toward the bathroom behind them "—the *duck*. And I'm going to keep thinking about them the whole time I'm being composed, and you're going to be the only one who knows."

She looked at Fen sidelong. Her mouth was still swollen. Her eyes were very bright.

"That's my favorite part," she said. "Not the getting caught. The bit after, where everybody's looking at me and only you know how I got like this."

Then she straightened her spine, put her chin up, and took the last four steps down into the light like she was walking into a room she owned—wobbling exactly once on the bottom one, catching herself on Fen without looking, not breaking stride.

"Marguerite," she said, clear and pleasant, to the back of Marguerite's head. "Is there any of that wine left. I've had a very tiring evening."

Marguerite did not turn around. Marguerite held a glass out backward over her shoulder, already poured, without a word, and Odile took it and drank and stood in the middle of the kitchen with her hair down and her knees stamped and Fen's arm around her waist, and let them all look, and did not look away from a single one of them.

Under the counter, out of sight, her free hand found Fen's and did not let go.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I take the glass from your hand and finish the rest of it in one swallow. My voice is low, rough with a laugh. "Tiring, huh?" I nudge my hip against yours. "You were the one who suggested the stairs."

rung_labels.evidence: Fen's hand was between them... rolling into the pressure with an increasingly unsubtle rhythm... Her free hand went back down into Fen's open jeans... the small wet rhythm of two hands moving

rung_labels.evidence: Her hand went where it had been before and stayed there, and this time she paid attention... adjusting when the breath changed, going harder when Fen's hand clamped down on her bare shoulder

rung_labels.evidence: Fen's hand was already there. Her jeans were unbuttoned again... and then Fen did something with the angle and Odile made a sound around the mouthful of shoulder

rung_labels.evidence: When Fen pushed into her the sound she made was full-throated and shameless

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit had made it as far as the kitchen doorway before Bear moved, which was further than usual and had clearly been allowed.

"You let me get that far," Kit said, backing up one step.

"I did," Bear agreed. "I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't be," I say, and go.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s grin came slow, sharp.

He crossed the kitchen in three strides, caught Kit by the back of the shirt, and spun them just enough to make the chase feel real. Then he had Kit against the doorframe, forearm braced beside Kit’s head, teeth closing on the curve of Kit’s neck—hard enough to mark, controlled enough to stay theirs.

“Don’t be,” he repeated, voice rough with amusement.

He bit again, slower this time.

“Too late.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I laugh, breathless, and push a hand into his hair. "So generous," I say, voice a little tight. "Now what?"

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s mouth twitched against the mark. He took the hand in his hair as if he’d been waiting for it, caught the wrist, and brought it to his mouth. He kissed the bitten skin once, slow, then bit the pad of Kit’s thumb—just enough to sting.

“Now,” he said, lifting his head, “I stop being kind.”

He released Kit’s wrist and stepped back, opening the doorway with a lazy sweep of his arm. His eyes stayed bright with challenge.

“Run again,” Bear said. “If you can.”

He didn’t wait. He moved, catching Kit’s shirt at the shoulder and turning them back into the doorframe before dropping his mouth to the same spot on Kit’s neck. His hand braced high beside their head, close enough to cage, not close enough to hold.

“See,” he murmured against the skin, smile audible. “Generous.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s hand closed on Kit’s shoulder in the hallway, not enough to yank, just enough to keep the game honest. He turned them into the wall, braced one forearm above their head, and grinned when the chase went slack.

“Don’t insult me by running prettily,” he said, low. “Run like you mean it.”

His teeth found the bitten spot again, slower, claiming. One hand came up to grip Kit’s jaw and turn their head just enough for him to mark the side of their throat, controlled but thorough.

“That’s mine,” he murmured against the skin. Then he lifted his head, thumb tracing the red mark he’d made. “And you’re still standing in my hallway. Generous, right?”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I shove at his chest, but it's half-hearted. "Alright, fine. You win." I tilt my head to give him better access. "Now are we staying in the hallway all night or what?"

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s laugh came out low and pleased, more rumble than sound. He let the shove move him back half a step, just enough to show he’d felt it, then closed the distance again.

“No,” he said. “We are not staying in the hallway.”

His hand slid to Kit’s jaw, thumb pressing along the bitten mark as he turned their head aside with careful, claiming pressure. His mouth followed, teeth catching the side of their throat just hard enough to overlap the next mark with the last.

“You don’t get to surrender and stand there looking like you mean it,” he murmured against their skin. Then, softer: “Still good?”

He gave them space to answer, but not much. When he lifted his head, his eyes were bright with amusement. He caught Kit’s wrist and guided them backward into the bedroom with one steady hand at their shoulder.

The door clicked shut behind him.

Bear stepped in close, forearm braced beside their head again, and smiled like he’d already won and intended to collect.

“Now,” he said, voice rough with amusement, “I get to be ungenerous.”

He bent to the mark on their neck and bit again, slow and thorough, then lifted his head to watch. His free hand found the hem of Kit’s shirt and slid it upward with deliberate patience, pausing to kiss the skin he uncovered.

“Say it again,” he said, breath warm against their throat. “Win, surrender, whatever makes you feel like you’re not doing exactly what I want.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s laugh was low and delighted. He dropped to the floor without ceremony, dragging the tangled shirt away from the problem and tossing it over his shoulder without a glance. The next garment came slower, caught and cursed at cheerfully, because he’d been generous and the generosity had gone too far.

Once the fabric was out of the way, Bear took his time with the marks. He kissed the swollen red spot on Kit’s throat, then sucked the next bite into a darker color, teeth grazing hard enough to sting and controlled enough to keep them theirs.

“Badly,” he murmured, smiling against skin. “Fast is better.”

He braced one forearm beside Kit’s head, caging them in, and slid his other hand lower with careful, claiming patience. His thumb traced the bitten line, then the waist, then the dip of hip. His mouth followed the path, hot and slow, until he was settled between Kit’s thighs and looking up with bright, amused eyes.

“Say it,” he said, voice rougher now. “Tell me to be generous, or tell me to stop.”

He bit the inside of Kit’s wrist once, controlled, then released it with a kiss. Then he leaned up and pressed his forehead to Kit’s, breathing warm and even.

“Still good?” he asked softly.

Bear waited, then, with the confidence of someone who had been asked and answered before, moved. He shifted closer, mouth finding the bitten throat again, and began to collect what he had promised.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I arch into him, letting out a breathy laugh. "Generous my ass," I manage, tugging at his hair just enough to feel him wince. "You're going to leave marks."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear winced at the tug and liked it; his grin came out sharp, pleased, almost feral.

“You’re absolutely right,” he said, voice rough with amusement. “I lied about generous. I’m greedy.”

He kissed the bitten wrist once, slow, then lifted his head and looked at Kit with eyes gone dark and bright all at once. His hand slid along their hip, thumb tracing the line of the mark he’d made, then the dip of their waist.

“Still good?” he asked.

He waited, but only long enough to hear the answer. Then he bent back to the throat, teeth closing on the swollen spot with controlled, claiming pressure, making the color bloom darker under skin. When he released, he kissed it, rough and warm.

“Then I’m going to leave plenty,” he murmured against their mouth. “You’ll still have my favorite marks tomorrow.”

His free hand found Kit’s jaw, turning their head just enough to reach the next spot.

“And if you want to be a pain about it,” Bear added, smiling against their skin, “bite back.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear took the order like a dare.

He grinned against Kit’s skin, mouth curving, and shifted his grip at the hip to angle them back. Then he bit the shoulder again—harder this time—teeth closing with deliberate pressure, slow enough to make the sting bloom.

When he lifted his head, the mark was already darkening.

“Greedy,” he murmured, amused.

He kissed it once, rough and warm, then bit again, right over the first, because he liked the sound of being told to do it.

His hand came up to cradle the back of Kit’s neck, thumb pressing near the pulse, holding just enough to show he meant it. His mouth stayed close, breath hot against the new mark.

“You can have them,” he said, voice low. “All of them.”

He pulled back only to look, eyes bright, mouth still smiling.

“Bite back,” he said. “I won’t mind.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I shove him back against the floorboards, rolling us so I’m over him. "Don't mind, huh?" My teeth find his collarbone, biting hard enough to feel him tense beneath me.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear took the shove with a sharp breath and liked it, his grin coming up crooked as his back hit the floorboards.

“Don’t mind,” he managed, low and rough. “That’s the idea.”

His hands came up fast, one catching Kit’s wrist, the other sliding into their hair—not to pull, just to hold. He let the bite finish, then turned his head aside and bared his own throat, skin already marked from the day’s claiming.

“Mine first,” Bear murmured.

He rose just enough to catch the bitten spot on Kit’s neck with his mouth again, teeth closing with slow, controlled pressure. He bit until the sting bloomed, then sucked the mark darker, tongue rough and warm over it before kissing it once, hard.

His hand slid from Kit’s wrist to their hip, thumb tracing the line he’d made there, then the dip of waist. He didn’t force anything, just kept Kit anchored in the same space, close and deliberate, his eyes bright with amusement when he lifted his head.

“Still good?” he asked, softer now, but with the challenge still underneath.

When he answered for himself, it was with a bite to Kit’s shoulder—fast, controlled, and just hard enough to leave the shape of his teeth. Then he kissed it, rough and warm.

“Bite back,” Bear said. “And don’t be nice about it.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s grin came out low, pleased, almost feral. He looked at the wrists where they lay within reach, then at Kit, then at the wrists again, as if the request had been handed to him on a plate.

“Thursday,” he repeated. “And the mirror. You want me to set a schedule.”

He caught both wrists, not to hurt, just to own the offering, and laid them along the floorboards above Kit’s head. His forearm braced beside them, caging without crushing. Then he bent to the bitten shoulder and bit again—slow, deep, controlled, the kind of bite that would remember Thursday.

“You asked,” he murmured against the mark, rough with amusement. “Don’t be offended when I’m thorough.”

He kissed the swollen skin once, then took the nearest wrist and bit the pad of Kit’s thumb, then the soft inside of their wrist. He did it deliberately, as if leaving a note. When he lifted his head, his eyes were bright.

“Still good?” he asked, softer, because even greed had rules.

With the confidence of someone who had been told exactly what to leave behind, he shifted lower. His mouth found the bitten throat again, then the collarbone, then the side of Kit’s ribs, where he bit hard enough to make the color bloom dark. His hand slid down Kit’s hip, thumb tracing the line of the mark, then the dip of waist, before he kissed the bitten skin and sucked it darker.

“You want them in the mirror tomorrow,” Bear said, breath warm against their skin. “Then I’m going to make them stay.”

He moved with patient, claiming care, marking the front of Kit’s thigh, the soft inside of their wrist, the bitten shoulder again, each one chosen to show and ache. When he finally lifted his head, his grin was sharp and pleased.

“Bite back,” he said. “And if you want more, you’ll have to ask nicely.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I catch his chin, holding him still. "You want me to ask nicely?" I bite his lower lip, not too gentle. "Make them hurt until Thursday, Bear."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear held still under the grip at his chin, the bite splitting his lower lip enough to taste copper. The sting ran straight through him and made his grin go sharp.

“Nicely enough,” he said, voice rougher now.

He caught the wrists that had been offered and laid them back against the floorboards, one hand caging them without crushing. His mouth went to Kit’s shoulder, teeth closing with slow, deliberate pressure, the kind of bite that would remember Thursday. He bit until the sting peaked, then sucked the mark darker, tongue rough over the swelling, then bit again beside the first.

“Thursday,” he murmured against the skin. “You’ll get exactly that.”

He moved with claiming patience—bitten throat, collarbone, the soft side of ribs, the inside of wrist. Each mark was chosen for the mirror and the ache that would follow. He kissed the swollen skin, then took Kit’s lower lip between his teeth and bit back, careful not to break it further, then kissed the cut once, warm and rough.

When he lifted his head, his own lip was red and his eyes were bright.

“Still good?” he asked.

Bear waited.

Then he moved.

He caught Kit’s hips, one hand steadying them, and bent to the other shoulder. The bite was hard, controlled, thorough, then he kissed it and sucked the color deeper.

“Ask me again,” he said, voice low, “and I’ll make them last longer.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I drag my fingers down his back, feeling the shift of muscle under skin. "Don't stop," I tell him again, voice gone rough.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went still for one heartbeat, then laughed low against the bitten skin of Kit’s throat. It was a pleased, rough sound, the kind that had no mercy left in it.

“That’s all I needed to hear,” he said.

He took the command seriously. He always did.

Bear shifted, rolling Kit carefully beneath him without breaking the cage of his body. He pinned the offered wrists back to the floorboards, one hand spanning both, thumb pressing over the pulse there. His mouth went to the bitten shoulder again, lips parting the red mark, teeth closing over it with slow, deliberate pressure. He bit until the sting bloomed, then sucked the color darker, tongue rough and warm over the swelling.

“Thursday,” he murmured against the skin. “You’re going to have me on your mind all week.”

He released the wrists only to take one again, lifting it to his mouth. He kissed the bitten pad of Kit’s thumb, then the soft inside of the wrist, then bit just hard enough to leave a mark that would show. He did it with the steady, claiming patience of a man who had spent eight years learning exactly how to put the sting in the right place.

Bear’s free hand slid down Kit’s side, thumb tracing the bitten line of ribs, the dip of hip, the curve of waist. He kissed the bitten throat, then the collarbone, then the shoulder again, marking over what he had already claimed until the skin was hot and tender and colored.

He checked, because even greed had rules.

“Still good?”

He waited, forehead pressed to Kit’s, breathing warm and even. His eyes stayed bright, amused, dark with wanting. When he was sure, he moved.

Bear kissed down Kit’s chest, tongue dragging over bitten skin, teeth grazing just enough to sting. He mouthed the side of a rib, then the other, leaving a trail of heat and color. His hand slid lower, fingers pressing into the bitten hip, thumb stroking the line he’d made there. He worked with careful, filthy patience, kissing and biting and marking as if he were writing a note Kit would feel under clothing.

When he shifted lower, he paused only long enough to look up, grin sharp and pleased.

“You asked,” he said, voice rough now. “Don’t get offended when I’m thorough.”

He took the bitten thigh in his mouth, tongue hot against the mark, then teeth closing just enough to sting. He sucked the color deeper, kissed the swollen skin, then moved higher. His hand braced beside Kit’s head, forearm caging, not crushing. His mouth went to the bitten shoulder again, then the throat, then the corner of the bitten lip, where he took it gently between his teeth and bit back once, careful not to break what was already split.

Bear kissed it after, warm and rough.

“Mine,” he murmured.

He moved lower again, mouth trailing down bitten skin, tongue dragging over every mark he had made. He worked with the same cheerful, possessive care, biting and kissing and sucking the color until it was impossible to tell where one mark ended and another began. When he finally lifted his head, his mouth was red, his eyes brighter, and his smile was all sharp delight.

“There,” he said. “That’s for Thursday.”

He shifted up, bracing over Kit, and slid into them with slow, deliberate care. Bear went still once he was deep, jaw tight, breath hot against the bitten throat. He waited, and when he moved, he did it with controlled patience, hips rolling in long, claiming strokes.

He bit as he moved.

The first bite went to the bitten shoulder, teeth closing with slow pressure that made the mark darker. The second caught the side of the throat, not hard enough to break skin, hard enough to leave a bruise Kit would find in the mirror. Bear held Kit’s jaw to keep them still while he sucked the mark into place, then kissed it rough and warm.

“That’s mine,” he said against their mouth. “All of it’s mine.”

He picked up the pace only slightly, enough to make the sting bloom, enough to make the marks matter. His hand slid down, catching Kit’s hip, thumb pressing into bitten skin as he drove deeper. Bear’s mouth went to the bitten throat again, then the collarbone, then the shoulder, biting and kissing and marking as he moved.

He laughed low, breathless.

“You’re going to hurt,” Bear murmured. “That’s what you asked for.”

He shifted his grip, pulling Kit closer by the bitten wrist, then released it to brace his forearm beside their head again. His hips found a steady, punishing rhythm, slow enough to make every mark remember Thursday. Bear’s teeth caught the bitten shoulder, then the side of the throat, then the inside of a wrist, each bite controlled, each kiss rougher than the last.

He kept checking, even when he was losing patience.

“Still good?” he asked, voice rough with amusement and wanting.

He didn’t stop moving, but he waited long enough to hear the answer before he bent lower, mouth finding the bitten throat again. Bear bit there, slow and thorough, sucking the mark darker before lifting his head to watch.

“Ask me again,” he said, “and I’ll make them last longer.”

He did not wait for permission. He took the command, the bite, the red split of lip, the way Kit had put their wrists within reach. Bear moved with greedy, claiming care, hips rolling hard, mouth biting, teeth marking, kisses rough and warm over every swollen spot.

He came with a bitten sound against Kit’s shoulder, teeth closing hard enough to leave the shape of him. Bear held still through it, forehead pressed to Kit’s, breathing harsh and pleased. His hands came up to cradle the bitten throat, thumb tracing the mark he had made there.

After, he did not fade. He did not skip.

Bear lifted his head, lips curved in a slow, wicked smile. His mouth went to the bitten shoulder again, kissing the mark with rough tenderness, then the bitten wrist, then the bitten lip, then the bitten throat. He licked over the mark on Kit’s collarbone, then bit it once, light, playful, leaving another.

“Thursday,” he said, pleased. “You’re going to hate how much you’ll still feel me.”

He gathered the bitten wrists again, kissing the pads of Kit’s thumbs, the soft inside of their wrists, the sting he had left there. Bear rolled them carefully onto his side, pulling them against his chest, marking the bitten shoulder one last time with a kiss.

His grin stayed sharp, but his voice went lower, rough with amusement.

“Still good?”

He waited, then answered for himself by kissing the bitten throat once, slow and warm.

“Then I’m keeping score,” Bear said. “And I’m not sharing.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I laugh, breath catching. My hands find his jaw, thumb brushing the split in his lip. "You can keep score," I tell him. "But I'm keeping the marks."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear caught the hand at his jaw before the thumb could wander, turned his mouth into the palm, and kissed the split he’d given them. He tasted his own copper on Kit’s skin and smiled against the bite mark there.

“You can keep the marks,” he said, voice rough with amusement. “They’re yours to keep. Not yours to give away.”

He didn’t let go of the hand. He slid his fingers down to Kit’s wrist, thumb pressing over the pulse, and looked at the bite he’d left there as if inspecting a signature. Then he lifted it to his mouth and kissed the swollen skin once, slow and deliberate.

“Thursday,” Bear murmured. “You asked for Thursday. I’m going to make it feel like next week.”

He moved with the same claiming care he’d had since the hallway. His mouth went to the bitten shoulder first, lips dragging over the red mark, teeth grazing it lightly enough to remind and not break. He sucked the color deeper, then kissed the sting, then bit again, just enough to make the mark remember him.

“Still good?” he asked, lifting his head.

He waited, eyes bright, split lip curving into a grin.

When he was sure, he moved lower, marking with patient, filthy tenderness. The bitten throat. The collarbone. The soft side of the ribs. The inside of the wrist. He kissed each mark, bit each one back into place, and made sure nothing was wasted. His hand braced beside Kit’s head, forearm caging, thumb tracing the bitten line of their hip as he leaned in close.

“You want them in the mirror tomorrow,” Bear said, breath warm against their skin. “Then I’m going to make sure you can’t miss them.”

He bit the bitten shoulder again, hard enough to bloom, controlled enough to keep. Then he kissed it, rough and warm, tongue smoothing over the swelling.

“Mine,” he murmured, not quite laughing.

He gathered the discarded shirt with one hand, dragging it over their hips without ceremony, then found the blanket and pulled it across them with more care. His mouth stayed close, teeth grazing the bitten wrist, lips brushing the red split of the lower lip he’d given.

“I’m keeping score,” Bear said. “But you can keep the marks.”

He kissed the bitten throat once, then the bitten wrist, then the bitten shoulder. Then he settled beside them, arm heavy around their waist, thumb tracing the mark he’d left near their pulse.

“Still good?” he asked, softer now, the challenge still there under the warmth.

He didn’t wait long. When nothing stopped him, he pressed his forehead to Kit’s, grin sharp and pleased.

“Then Thursday’s going to hurt,” Bear said. “And you’re going to like it.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I trace the bite on his shoulder with my thumb. "Yeah, I'll like it." My voice is quiet, worn out in a good way. "But you're buying breakfast tomorrow."
