dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The party had reached the stage where nobody would notice two people missing, which Odile pointed out approximately four seconds before doing something about it.

"The bathroom upstairs has a lock," she said, into Fen's ear, over the music.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Does it work?" I ask, already moving toward the stairs.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"It works," Odile said, which was only eighty percent confidence, but she was already moving, fingers laced through Fen's and pulling. The stairs creaked under both of them and she didn't care. Somewhere below, someone was doing a very bad job of singing along to a song Odile couldn't name.

She stumbled on the third step — her own foot, nothing dramatic — and laughed, too loud, a bright hiccup of sound that she tried to swallow half a second too late. Her free hand came up to her own mouth. "Shh," she told herself, and then immediately ruined it by laughing again, quieter, shoulders shaking with it.

The landing was dim, a nightlight doing the heavy lifting, and the bathroom door was the second on the left, which she knew because she'd scoped it out earlier — not for this, or not entirely for this, but she'd clocked the lock and filed it away the way she filed away most useful things.

She got the door open and pulled Fen in after her and shut it, and the party dropped to a muffled thud through the wood. The lock turned under her thumb with a satisfying little click. Odile leaned back against the sink and looked at Fen, breathless, flushed, grinning like she'd gotten away with something.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I laugh with her, my own quiet chuckle muffled by the closeness of the room. "You're terrible at being stealthy," I say, but I'm already leaning in, my hands on her hips. "Good thing I like you loud."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"Terrible at being *stealthy*," Odile repeated, indignant and delighted, the way you'd argue about a compliment. "I was *extremely* stealthy. Nobody saw us. That's the whole point of stealth."

She hooked two fingers into the front of Fen's shirt and pulled him the last half-step closer, so her back was against the cold porcelain rim of the sink and there was nowhere left to be but against her. The bathroom was small and smelled faintly of someone else's hand soap, and the light over the mirror was unforgiving, and she didn't care about any of it.

"Also," she said, quieter now, mouth an inch from his, "you're the one who said *good thing I like you loud* two seconds ago, so I feel like we're both implicated here."

Her hands slid up over his shoulders and laced behind his neck, which had the convenient side effect of bringing him down to her, and she hummed a little, pleased, at the fit of it. Then, because she had never in her life been able to leave a thing alone:

"Anyway. If I'm loud, what's your plan about it."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I get the door shut and her against it, and downstairs somebody turns the music up, which helps.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"*My* plan," Odile said, and pulled back just far enough to give him a look, eyebrows up, chin tilted, the whole production of it. "My plan is that I don't have a plan. I'm not the one who—" She waved a hand vaguely at all of him, at the shirt-fist and the sink and the general situation. "—*escalated*."

Which was a lie and they both knew it, since she'd been the one with the ear and the bathroom and the four seconds of warning.

The party thudded on below them, bass bleeding through the floor, and somewhere in it a woman shrieked with laughter the way people did at parties when nothing was actually funny. Odile listened to it for a second, head cocked, then decided she was fine with it.

"Okay," she said, quieter, and her hands came down off his neck to rest flat on his chest, which was mostly just an excuse to keep touching him. "Here's the actual plan. You're going to be quiet for both of us, because I'm apparently a lost cause and one of us has to be the adult, and the adult—" she pressed her finger into his sternum for emphasis, "—is going to have a *very* hard time, because you look like that and I'm already—"

She stopped. Reassessed. Her own voice had gone a little rough around the edges and she could hear it.

"—anyway," she finished, prim, "that's the plan."

Then she kissed him, which was a slightly worse plan, or a much better one, depending on what you wanted out of the evening. Her hand found the back of his neck again and her other one slid down to the front of his belt, not doing anything with it yet, just resting there like a question she'd already decided the answer to. When she broke off she was breathless again, and grinning, and her voice had definitely not gotten any steadier.

"So. Quiet. You first."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I catch her grin and lower my voice to a murmur. "Quiet, huh?" My thumb brushes the line of her jaw. "You're gonna have to try harder than that to keep me from ruining your plan."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"*You* first," Odile repeated back at him, mostly to buy herself a second, because his thumb on her jaw had done something unhelpful to her train of thought. "That was the whole— that was *literally* the assignment."

She said it at a volume that was, objectively, not quiet. The bass thumped on underneath them and she told herself it covered her, which was a generous reading of the situation.

Her fingers were still hooked in his belt, doing nothing, which was starting to feel like a policy decision she no longer agreed with. She looked at him — really looked, the unforgiving bathroom light and all — and something in her chest did the stupid flippy thing it had been doing since the third step on the stairs, or possibly since the ear, or possibly since considerably earlier than that.

"Okay," she said, and it came out lower than she meant, and she heard it, and she didn't fix it. "Okay. New plan. The plan is we stop pretending there's a plan."

Her free hand came up and pressed flat over her own mouth, demonstration-style, eyes bright over the top of it — *look, quiet, I can do it* — and then she promptly dropped it because she wanted to say one more thing, which was:

"Fair warning, though. The lock works, but the door's cheap. So if I'm loud it's not entirely—" she gestured at herself, at the general fact of her, "—my fault. Structural issue. Blame the building."

And then, because she had never once in her life managed to leave a thing alone, she kissed him again and let the hand on his belt finally make up its mind.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: There isn't room to do this properly and we don't let that stop us. Enough clothes come off to be a problem if anyone knocks.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile had, at some point, gotten her own shirt half off and then entirely forgotten about it, which was a thing she would have found funny if she'd had the spare attention. The sink rim was digging into her lower back and she had one heel braced against the cabinet door and the party was still going on down there like nothing was happening, like the floor wasn't creaking in a rhythm that any of their friends would absolutely recognize if they were sober enough to notice.

Someone in the hallway — *the hallway*, the actual hallway outside the actual door — laughed at something. Odile's hand came up fast and flat over her own mouth again and her eyes went wide and *delighted*, which was the problem, which was always the problem. She wasn't scared. She was having the time of her life.

"*Close one*," she whispered, at a volume that was, structurally, a normal speaking volume, and then heard herself and pressed her palm harder over her mouth and snorted into it.

The door rattled. Not a knock — someone's shoulder, or someone leaning on the wall, or just the cheap house settling — but the latch moved in the frame and Odile's whole body went still in a way that was not fear. Her breath caught. Her fingers dug into Fen's back. She held perfectly still for three full seconds, listening, and then the sound moved off down the hall and she let it out all at once, a shaky laugh muffled into the side of his neck.

"Okay," she breathed, barely a sound, actually doing it this time. "Okay okay okay. That was— that was fine. We're fine. Nobody—"

Her own voice cracked on the last word and she bit down on her lip, hard, and her shoulders shook with the effort of not laughing, and she was *not* doing a great job, and she knew it, and she didn't care.

Downstairs, the music changed to something with a build in it, and Odile's leg hooked tighter around his and her hand slid up into his hair and she pulled him in close and said, right against his ear, barely audible, mostly air:

"Don't stop."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath against her skin, my own heart hammering. "Door's cheap," I murmur back, "but I'm not." My hand slides up her spine, steadying us both. "Let's see how quiet we can really be."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
*Odile heard the "I'm not" and filed it away to make fun of him for later, because it was — it was a *little* corny — and then she stopped filing things away, because his hand was going up her spine and there was no spare brain for filing anymore.*

"*Steadying us both*," she whispered back, or tried to, and it came out mostly as an exhale shaped like words. "*Nobody asked you to be—*"

*That was as far as she got, which was fine, because she hadn't actually had a point.*

*The hallway was quiet now. The party was a floor away and a wall away and the bass had gotten into her sternum and set up shop there. The lock was still locked. Her heel slipped off the cabinet door and found the floor and she didn't bother putting it back; she just stood there against the sink with her forehead tipped against Fen's and let him hold her up, which she was going to have opinions about later and had no opinions about now.*

"Okay," *she said, on a breath, and this time it was actually quiet — not performing quiet, just quiet, the real thing, because it turned out that wanting to say it was different from wanting to be heard.* "Okay. Yeah. Let's—"

*She didn't finish that either. She kissed the corner of his mouth instead, then the side of his jaw, and got her own shirt the rest of the way off and dropped it somewhere it would be extremely visible if anyone came in, which was a problem for a version of Odile who existed in the future and not this one.*

*Someone downstairs turned the music down. Odile, pressed to the sink, heard the sudden drop in volume like a change in the weather and pressed her hand over her own mouth again preemptively, and laughed into it, and her eyes over the top of her fingers were bright and wrecked and absolutely not sorry.*

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I get my hand between her legs and she bites down on my shoulder to keep quiet, which works for about thirty seconds.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Thirty seconds was a generous estimate. It was more like twelve, and Odile knew it the second the sound got out of her — a low, unguarded thing that started in her throat and ended up in the room, and she turned her face into his shoulder half a beat too late to do anything about it.

"*That* was the building," she said, into his skin, absolutely not quiet, and then had to clamp her teeth on the meat of his shoulder again because the alternative was worse. Her hand was flat against the mirror now, fingers spread, leaving a print, and the glass was cold and the rest of her was not.

Downstairs somebody had definitely turned the music down and Odile had a whole theory about who and why and it was not a theory she could hold onto for longer than a second at a time.

"Okay," she breathed, when she could. "Okay. If anyone knocks, we're—" she had to stop, breathe, try again, "—we're *checking the plumbing*. That's the story. I'm very interested in plumbing. I've always been—"

Her voice broke off into something that was not a word, and she pressed her forehead to his and shut her eyes and stopped trying to be funny for a second, which happened rarely enough that it was basically a special occasion.

"*Fen.*"

Just the name. Not a question, not a joke, just the thing that was left when the rest of it fell away. Her fingers curled against the mirror. The party was still going, muffled and far, and somewhere in it a whole room full of their friends was having a normal evening, and none of them knew, and that fact was doing something to her that she was going to think about later in a lot of detail.

The cabinet door creaked under her. She didn't stop. She got her mouth to his ear again and said, honestly, quietly, the real version of it:

"Don't you dare be quiet. Not anymore."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I let out a sharp breath, a laugh or a gasp, I’m not sure. “No more plumbing talk,” I murmur, my voice rough. My hand slides from the mirror to cup her cheek. “Just you.”

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile opened her mouth to say something — a joke was right there, something about plumbing, something to prove she was still in the driver's seat — and nothing came out. His hand was on her cheek and the joke died in her throat, and she looked at him, actually looked at him, and the look on his face was not a joke, so she didn't make one.

"Okay," she said, and it was small. Real. She turned her face into his palm, just for a second, eyes closed, and the party below was a heartbeat through the floor and the cheap door was cheap and none of it was the point anymore.

Her hand came off the mirror and found his chest and stayed there, flat, feeling his heart go, which was going about as fast as hers. "Just me," she repeated, like she was checking the word for balance. It held.

She kissed him again — slower this time, no performance in it, which was maybe the most honest thing she'd done all night — and when she came up for air she was smiling but it was the quiet kind, the kind that didn't need an audience, which was ironic given the circumstances.

"Fair warning," she said, barely above a breath, forehead tipped against his. "I'm about to be *very* bad at being quiet."

She wasn't wrong.

And afterward, when the party had thinned and the hall had gone quiet and the two of them were sitting on the edge of the tub with their clothes mostly back on and the mirror fogged up from the shower someone else had taken two hours ago, Odile laughed — too loud, naturally — and put her head on his shoulder and said, to the room, to the cheap door, to the whole stupid evening:

"Next time we pick a house with thicker walls."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Stop worrying about the noise," she says, "and get on with it," so I get her leg up over my hip and stop being careful about how much sound either of us is making.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
She stopped saying *quiet*. That was the first thing, and she noticed it the way you notice a step missing — mid-stride, too late to do anything graceful about it. The word just wasn't there anymore, and neither was the performance of it, and her leg was up over his hip and the sink was behind her and the door was *right there*, three feet of cheap hollow-core between the two of them and the entire rest of the evening.

The music downstairs was still down. Odile could hear it — really hear it, individual notes, which meant it was quiet enough that the party could hear *her*, and that fact went through her like a current and came out as a laugh, low and breathless, that she didn't even try to catch.

"*Okay,*" she gasped, and then, "okay, *okay*—" not meaning anything by it, just the sound of someone who had run out of other sounds.

Then the knock came.

Three raps. Casual. Friendly. Somebody's knuckles on cheap wood, and a voice on the other side going, "*Odile? You in there?*" — and Odile's whole body locked up mid-motion, which was *not* comfortable, and her hand flew off the mirror and clamped flat over Fen's mouth, of all the useless things to do, because he wasn't the one making noise and she knew it and she did it anyway, eyes wide, biting her lip hard enough to hurt.

She held perfectly still. Her heart was going like a rabbit's. The handle moved. She watched it move, the little round of it turning a quarter inch, and she watched it not open, because the lock worked, eighty percent confidence be damned, and the voice outside said, "*Huh,*" and then, "*okay, whatever, I'm getting another drink,*" and the footsteps went off down the hall and thinned and were gone.

Odile stayed frozen for a count of five.

Then her hand came off Fen's mouth and she put her forehead against his shoulder and shook — not with fear, *with laughing*, silently, helplessly, whole body, until she had to bite his shoulder again to keep the sound in, and even that wasn't enough, because she came up grinning and wrecked and whispered, at a volume that would not have fooled a single person in this house:

"*That was Kim.* That was *Kim.* She's going to—" breath, "—she's going to *know*, Fen, she's going to know by *Thursday*—"

She didn't do anything about it. She didn't get off the sink. She didn't lower her voice. She hooked her ankle tighter behind him and pulled him back in and said, right up against his ear, still laughing, entirely out of rope:

"Don't stop. I don't care. Don't stop."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky laugh against her neck, my own heart still pounding. "Kim can wait," I murmur, and finally stop caring about the noise.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The rest of it was not quiet. There was no version of it that could have been quiet, and Odile had stopped pretending otherwise somewhere around the third *okay*, which was fine, because the music had come back up downstairs and the house was old and creaky and full of people who were too drunk to hear anything that wasn't the song they were singing along to.

She was loud. She knew she was loud. She heard herself and it didn't stop her — it did the opposite, actually, the sound of her own voice bouncing off the tile doing something electric to the base of her spine — and when it was over she slid down the sink and sat on the cold bathroom floor with her back against the cabinet and her knees up and her shirt still somewhere on the floor, laughing at the ceiling.

The mirror had fogged again. The party thumped on below. Her legs felt like they belonged to somebody else and her mouth hurt from grinning.

"*Okay,*" she said, out loud, to the room. "Okay. That's — that's going in the *file.*"

She reached over without looking and found her shirt by feel and pulled it on inside out and didn't notice. Then she looked at Fen, properly, still sitting there on the floor with her, and something in her face went soft and stupid and she let it, because there was nobody left to perform for and she'd used up all her performance downstairs anyway.

"Hey," she said, quieter. Just the one word. Then, because she couldn't hold a sincere moment for more than three seconds without cracking: "So, question. On a scale of one to *Kim knowing by Thursday* — how bad do you think we actually are?"

She was already laughing again. She got her hand up over her mouth to muffle it and then gave up and let it go, head tipped back against the cabinet, the whole absurd evening of it landing on her at once — the stairs, the lock, the shoulder in the hall, *that was Kim* — and she reached out and caught Fen's hand off the floor and laced her fingers through it and squeezed, hard, without saying anything else about it.

From downstairs, faintly, someone was doing a very bad job of singing along to a song Odile still couldn't name.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: Somebody tries the handle and neither of us stops. "Don't," she says, meaning don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The handle turned again. That little quarter-inch of give, and this time it didn't stop — it rattled, once, twice, the sound of somebody who had found a locked door and was now *thinking* about it.

Odile didn't even look at it. She had her forehead tipped back against the mirror and her hand fisted in Fen's shirt and she heard the rattle and it went through her like a struck bell, and the word that came out of her was:

"*Don't.*"

Not to the door. Not to whoever was out there. To him — low, wrecked, absolutely unmistakable in what it meant — and her heel dug in against the cabinet and her grip on his shirt went white-knuckled and she pulled him back in before the sound outside had even finished.

Whoever it was stood there for a second. She could *feel* them standing there, the weight of somebody on the other side of three feet of hollow-core door, hearing exactly what was happening and deciding what to do about it. Odile's breath caught high in her chest and her eyes were wide and bright and she was grinning around her own bitten lip, and she did not stop, and she did not lower her voice, and when the next sound came out of her it was not a whisper.

The handle let go. Footsteps went off down the hall — fast, actually, faster than casual, the walk of somebody who had just figured something out and wanted to be somewhere else about it — and Odile heard them go and laughed, loud, head back, the whole bright helpless laugh of it ringing off the tile.

"*Kim's* going to know by Thursday," she gasped, to no one, to the ceiling, to the fogged mirror. "Kim's going to know by *tonight*—"

And then she stopped having things to say.

---

Afterward there was the floor, and the cold, and her shirt on inside out, and the party still thumping on underneath them like the evening had no idea what had just happened to it. Odile sat with her back against the cabinet and her knees up and her hand laced through Fen's, and she was quiet for a stretch that was, for her, basically geological.

Then she turned her head and looked at him and said, with the specific dignity of a woman who had just been extremely loud in a friend's bathroom:

"So. For the record. That was your idea."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I'm grinning, still catching my breath. "My idea?" I squeeze her hand. "You're the one who scouted the lock. That's premeditation."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"*Premeditation,*" Odile repeated, savoring it, offended on principle. "I clocked a lock at a party. That's not premeditation, that's *situational awareness*. That's a life skill. You'd want me on your side in a—"

She stopped, because the sentence had been heading somewhere and she'd heard where, and she let it go with a wave of her free hand.

"Anyway. I scouted it at like nine o'clock, when I was looking for somewhere to put my coat. Which is *normal behavior* at a party." She was looking at the ceiling while she said this, which was not where the ceiling was, and she turned her head to actually face him and her hair was a disaster and she didn't know it. "You're the one who—" she made a vague gesture with the hand not holding his, encompassing him, the room, the general trajectory of the last hour, "—*followed me up the stairs.* I gave you four seconds of warning. That's practically a courtesy. That's a *consent form*, is what that is."

Downstairs, the music shifted again, something with a horn in it, and Odile tilted her head to listen and then decided it didn't matter.

Then she looked down at herself, finally, and registered the shirt.

"*Oh,*" she said, flat. "That's inside out."

She didn't fix it. She pulled her knees up a little further and let her head fall back against the cabinet and squeezed his hand, and for a second the grin came off her face and something quieter was underneath it — the specific quiet of a person sitting on a bathroom floor at a party she'd been at for five hours with the door still locked and her hair a mess, and not minding any of it.

"Okay, real answer," she said, to the ceiling. "I think we get one of these per friendship group per year. So we've used it up. Next party we're on our best behavior, we don't look at each other, and if Kim says *anything* on Thursday I'm going to—" she considered it, "—I'm going to look her dead in the eye and ask her what she was doing at the top of the stairs. Because she was *at the top of the stairs*, Fen. She was *right there*."

She sat up straighter, pleased with this.

"That's the play. That's the actual play. Deny everything, attack the witness."

She got up off the floor then, unsteady, using his hand and then the sink and then the wall, and stood in the middle of the little bathroom in an inside-out shirt, and looked at the door like it was a problem to be solved.

"Okay. Logistics. We can't go down together. I go first, I go find whoever's doing shots in the kitchen, I make an *enormous* amount of noise about how long the bathroom line was, and then twenty minutes later you come down and you were out front having a cigarette the whole time." She paused. "Do you smoke?"

A beat.

"Doesn't matter. You do tonight."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I push myself off the floor, still feeling the cold tiles through my jeans. "I can fake smoking," I say, reaching over to turn the shirt right side out for her. "But you have to go first. I'm not letting Kim see me looking like this."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
She took the shirt. For about a second and a half she just looked at it, folded the wrong way in his hands, and then at him — and something crossed her face that she did not say out loud, and then she took it and pulled it on over her head and shook her hair out of the collar.

"Thanks," she said, which came out too casual for what it was.

Then the mirror. She wiped a patch of the fog away with the flat of her hand and leaned in and took inventory, and the inventory was: hair, disaster. Mouth, obviously kissed. Eyes doing a thing she couldn't fix with anything available in this room. She pulled at the collar, uselessly.

She tried the hair. Hands, no product, no brush, no plan — she got it roughly into a shape and it immediately fell back out of it, and she watched it fall in the mirror and said, out loud, "Okay. That's a lost cause." Then she turned around to face the actual problem, which was logistics.

"Right. The line." She cleared her throat. It didn't help. She tried again, lower, and produced a voice belonging to a much older woman: "*You guys, the bathroom line was insane, there was one guy in there for like twenty minutes—*"

It came out hoarse and wrecked, and she stopped and looked at him, and her face did something that was half horror and half absolute delight.

"Okay. Okay, that's not going to work. Give me a second."

She turned the tap on and drank from her cupped hand — three swallows, cold, terrible, bathroom tap water in a house she didn't live in — made a face at the taste, and did it again anyway. Cleared her throat a third time, tried the line a third time. Ten percent better. She decided that was enough.

"Fine. New cover story: I was crying in the bathroom. Alone. About something." Beat. "It's a party. People cry at parties. If anyone asks, I'm going through a *thing* and I don't want to talk about it, and then I *do* want to talk about it, extensively, for forty minutes, and nobody ever asks again."

She reached up and did something futile to his hair, which was doing roughly what her own was doing, maybe worse. She smoothed it down; it stayed for a second and sprang back. She did it again. It sprang back again.

"There," she said, with enormous sincerity. "Now you look like a guy who was out front having a cigarette."

Then she did the one genuinely competent thing she'd do all evening: cracked the door, listened, put her eye to the gap, and held it there for a full five seconds. Hall empty. Music still going. Somebody downstairs laughing at the horn song.

"Okay." She turned back, hand on the handle, and looked at him for a second longer than the plan strictly required. "Twenty minutes. Kitchen, loud, shots. If I'm not there in twenty, something's happened — but nothing's happened, because I've been in this kitchen, I *helped her set up the bar*, I know where the good glasses are."

A beat. She opened her mouth for the real thing and it didn't come, so she did the other thing instead:

"Don't take the stairs two at a time. Third one up from the bottom creaks. I know because *I* made it creak, and I've been hearing about it in my head for the last two hours, so —" she gestured at the door, at the house, at the whole absurd evening, "—learn from me."

And then she slipped out into the dim hall and pulled the door shut behind her, and stood there for one second in the nightlight glow with her hand still on the handle, listening to the party, before she went downstairs to be extremely loud in the kitchen.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content:
I hear her footsteps fade down the stairs, then lean against the sink. My reflection in the patch she wiped looks exactly like what just happened. I splash water on my face, try to fix my hair, give up.

Twenty minutes. I check my watch, then realize I can still hear her downstairs, already laughing too loud about something. I smile, shake my head, and start counting.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: her other one slid down to the front of his belt, not doing anything with it yet, just resting there like a question she'd already decided the answer to

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Odile had, at some point, gotten her own shirt half off and then entirely forgotten about it

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: Thirty seconds was a generous estimate. It was more like twelve, and the sound got out of her — a low, unguarded thing

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: Then the knock came.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: And then she stopped having things to say.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The party had reached the stage where nobody would notice two people missing, which Odile pointed out approximately four seconds before doing something about it.

"The bathroom upstairs has a lock," she said, into Fen's ear, over the music.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Does it work?" I ask, already moving toward the stairs.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile let out a bright laugh that she tried and completely failed to muffle behind her hand.

"It worked last time she had a party," she whispered, which was not really a whisper at all. "We should test it again. Thoroughly."

She turned toward the stairs and started up them, already giggling at the idea of getting caught.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I glance around the room one more time to make sure nobody's watching us slip away. "Lead the way," I say, following close behind her.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile hurried up the stairs with her hand skimming the banister, and she giggled the whole way up because the plan felt ridiculous and thrilling in equal measure.

She reached the landing and made a beeline for the bathroom door, then pressed her back against it for a second while she tried to smother another laugh. She failed completely and snorted out loud enough that she clapped both hands over her mouth.

"Oh my god, I'm being so loud," she whispered, and it wasn't a whisper at all.

She pushed the door open and slipped inside, then left it cracked as she turned and grinned down the hall.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I get the door shut and her against it, and downstairs somebody turns the music up, which helps.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile let out a yelp-laugh when her back hit the door, and she slapped a hand over her mouth a second too late.

"Oh my god," she whispered, which came out embarrassingly loud in the little tiled room. "I'm already terrible at this."

She twisted around to fumble for the little lock behind her, and she giggled helplessly the whole time because she could still hear the bass thumping up through the floor from downstairs.

"Okay, someone turned the music up for us," she announced in a stage-whisper. "That's basically encouragement. That's basically permission."

She leaned back against the door again and grinned, and then she snorted at herself for grinning.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I reach past her and flip the lock with a satisfying click. "There. Now you can be as terrible as you want." My hands land on her hips, pulling her against me.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile let out a delighted squeak at the click of the lock and then immediately burst out laughing at herself for squeaking.

"Oh, good," she whispered, much too loudly for the tiny bathroom. "Locked. We're very responsible. Very discreet."

She looped her arms up around his neck and leaned in close, and she was already giggling again because she could feel how hard she was trying not to giggle.

"This is terrible," she breathed against his mouth. "I'm going to get us caught in like, thirty seconds, and I kind of love that?"

She bit down on her lip to keep quiet and then snorted right through it, and she clapped a hand back over her mouth too late.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: There isn't room to do this properly and we don't let that stop us. Enough clothes come off to be a problem if anyone knocks.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile glanced down at herself and let out another loud bark of laughter at how much trouble she was already in.

Her top was twisted half up and her jeans were shoved down enough that she knew she couldn't fix them fast if someone knocked, and the thought made her snort-giggle so hard she had to slap both hands over her mouth again.

"Oh my god, we're so busted if anyone comes up here," she whispered, far too loudly for the little tiled room. "Like, so immediately busted. There's no pretending."

She pressed her back harder against the locked door and squirmed a little at how cold it felt and how hot the rest of her felt, and she giggled helplessly because the bass from downstairs was still thumping right through her feet.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I squeeze her hips, laughing a little myself. "Then we better make those thirty seconds count." I lean in, my voice dropping lower. "Don't you dare try to be quiet."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile threw her head back and let out a loud, helpless cackle that bounced off all the tile.

"Oh, that's the worst thing you could've said to me," she gasped, way too loud, and then she laughed even harder at how loud she'd been. "I was already failing!"

She tried to bite down on her knuckle to muffle herself and it didn't work at all, because she snorted around it and then moaned right through it. She squirmed back against the cold door and giggled breathlessly at the contrast of it against how flushed and hot she felt everywhere else.

"Oh my god, everyone downstairs can definitely hear me," she whispered, not whispering in the slightest. "That's so embarrassing. That's so hot."

She tipped her forehead forward and shook with another fit of giggles, and then let out a shamelessly loud moan that she tried to swallow too late.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I get my hand between her legs and she bites down on my shoulder to keep quiet, which works for about thirty seconds.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile clamped her teeth down over his shoulder and squeezed her eyes shut like that was going to save them.

For about thirty seconds she actually almost pulled it off, except for the muffled squeaks and giggles that kept leaking out around the bite and the way her hips kept jerking back against the door. She shook harder and harder and pressed her face in deeper to smother it.

Then she lost it completely and came off his shoulder with a loud, shameless gasp-laugh.

"Oh my god, I can't — I can't do it, I'm trying so hard," she blurted, way too loud for the little tiled room, and then she snorted at how loud that had been and laughed even harder.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I chuckle against her ear, my own voice rough. "I never doubted you for a second." The music downstairs hits a heavy beat, covering the sound of my belt buckle clinking against the tile floor.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile heard the buckle clink against the tile and completely lost it.

She burst out laughing so loud it echoed off the walls, and then she laughed even harder at the echo because it just proved how busted they were going to be.

"Oh my god, did you hear that?" she gasped, not quiet at all. "That was so loud. Everyone definitely heard that."

She pressed her back harder against the door and squirmed where she stood, and she giggled breathlessly at how exposed she still was with her top twisted up and her jeans shoved down.

She tried to smother herself with her hand and failed immediately, and a shameless moan slipped right out through her fingers.

"Oh fuck, okay, okay," she whispered, way too loudly. "I'm really trying to be quiet this time, I swear —"

She snorted at herself mid-sentence and shook with laughter against the door.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Stop worrying about the noise," she says, "and get on with it," so I get her leg up over my hip and stop being careful about how much sound either of us is making.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile let out a helpless, crowing laugh the second her leg hitched up high, and the sound cracked straight off the tile.

"Oh fuck — oh my god, yes," she gasped, far too loud, and then she laughed harder because she had said she would be quiet and immediately failed.

She clung on with her arms looped tight and shook with giggles every time she shifted back against the door, and she could feel the cold wood rattling faintly behind her with it. She tried to bite her lip and it did nothing at all.

"Everyone's gonna hear — everyone is definitely gonna hear me," she blurted, and then she moaned shamelessly loud right after it and snorted at herself for moaning.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I press her harder against the door, the wood groaning in protest. "Let them hear," I murmur, my breath hot against her neck. "Bet they're jealous."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile heard that and absolutely lost it against the door.

She threw her head back with a loud, barking laugh that echoed straight off the tile, and then she moaned right through the laugh without even trying to cover it.

"Oh my god, stop — you're gonna make me worse," she gasped, far too loud for the little bathroom, and then she snorted at how loud that had been and laughed even harder.

She squirmed back against the wood as it groaned behind her and giggled helplessly at the sound, because it just proved how much trouble they were in. She tried to bite her lip to shut herself up and failed completely, and another shamelessly loud moan tore right out of her.

"Okay, they're definitely jealous," she blurted, not whispering at all. "Oh fuck, they can totally hear me — that's so hot."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: Somebody tries the handle and neither of us stops. "Don't," she says, meaning don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile went completely still for half a second when she felt the handle jiggle against her back.

Then she barked out a shocked, delighted laugh that echoed off the tile, far too loud to pretend it had not happened.

"Oh my god," she gasped, not quiet at all. "Someone just — someone just tried it."

She shook with another fit of giggles at how busted they were, and she ground herself back harder against the rattling door like that would explain anything.

"Don't," she blurted, loud and shameless and laughing straight through it. "Don't stop, don't stop, please don't stop."

She clung on tighter and tipped her head back and moaned straight at the ceiling, and she did not even try to cover it. She rocked her hips desperately and snorted-laughed at herself for how loud she was being with a stranger right outside.

"Oh fuck, I'm so close, that's so embarrassing," she gasped, way too loud. "They can totally hear me, oh my god—"

She lost the words entirely and came with a loud, crowing laugh-moan that cracked off all the tile, and she shook hard against the locked door while it happened.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I feel the shudder run through her and bury my face against her neck to muffle my own groan. The door handle jiggles again, more insistently this time, and I laugh against her skin. "They're persistent," I mutter, not moving an inch.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile felt the second jiggle rattle right through her spine and she barked out another loud, helpless laugh against the door.

Bear's hand closed on the back of Kit's shirt at the hallway's narrowest point, and he turned his own momentum into the wall — forearm across Kit's chest, his whole weight arriving an instant behind the grip. That was the trick of it. The catch was never the hand. The catch was the two hundred pounds of certainty that came with it.

He expected a squirm. Got a lean.

That stopped him for a second, breath hot against Kit's neck. He could feel the pulse hammering under his forearm, adrenaline still singing, but there was nothing in the shoulders — no coil, no push. Kit had run hard, genuinely hard, three rooms of real chasing, and then folded at the first true point of contact.

"You're kidding," Bear said. "That's it?"

He turned Kit by the shoulder, slow, leaving every chance to make it a fight, and pressed him back into the wall. Checked his eyes — the old silent habit, the one they'd never needed words for. Bright. Blown. Wanting.

Not tired, then. Just a man who'd decided the catching was the part he wanted today.

"Huh," Bear said, and something in his chest went warm and dark. "Eight years, and you lasted longer in the armchair in year two." He leaned in, nose dragging along Kit's jaw, breathing him in — sweat and skin and the specific smell of him after running. "You let me catch you."

Not an accusation. A reading, delivered against his throat.

"That's fine. That's more than fine. But you should know—" his teeth found where neck met shoulder, not biting yet, just promising, "—it doesn't get you anything. You're caught either way. All you gave up was the fun part."

Then he bit down. Not gentle, not cruel — the exact pressure he knew, the kind that would raise a mark Kit would find in the mirror tomorrow and press his thumb into. He held it longer than necessary, felt the breath go ragged against his cheek, and released slow, dragging his teeth on the way off.

"There." He pulled back to admire it, satisfied. "That's yours. You earned that — the chase, anyway. The surrender was a gift."

He kept him pinned with weight alone, hands free, and one came up to thumb the fresh mark, testing it.

"So. Here's what happens now." Low, even, close enough that Kit could feel the words. "Option one: I carry you to the couch like the gracious winner I am, and we do this properly. Option two — you tell me why you folded in my hallway. Because there's two answers I'll accept." His mouth curved against Kit's ear. "You wanted to be caught. Or you've got something planned, and letting me think I won is the whole trick. And that one smells like you, Kit. Year five. The wrist thing. You let me win and made me regret it for an hour."

He pulled back just far enough to watch his face, weight steady, grip loose enough to break — and both of them knowing he wouldn't.

"Choose fast. I'm feeling less generous by the second."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I tilt my head, meeting your eyes with a slow grin. "Option three," I say, voice low. "I folded 'cause I figured you'd get handsy about it." I shift against the wall, just enough to feel the pressure of your weight. "Seems I was right."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear laughed — a real one, low in his chest, more felt than heard where their bodies met. Eight years, and the man could still hand him a line like that with a straight face.

"Handsy," he repeated, tasting the word. "You folded in my hallway, gave up three rooms of running I'd earned fair, and your stated reason is that you wanted my hands on you."

He shifted his weight, slid a thigh between Kit's legs, and took both wrists in one hand — slow, telegraphed, an offer wearing the shape of a pin. Raised them up over Kit's head and pressed them to the wall, not hard. Just placed. He felt for the pull, the coil, the trick — year five had taught him to check — and found only Kit's pulse jumping under his thumb.

"No trick," Bear said, mostly to himself. "Just want. Huh." He shook his head slowly. "You realize you just banked a win. Folded on purpose and got paid for it. I hate that it counts." A beat. "It counts. That's the worst part."

He leaned in until his mouth was at Kit's ear.

"So option three wasn't on the menu. That's a penalty. Penalties accrue interest." A breath. "Here's the interest: you wanted handsy, you get handsy — but on my clock. You gave up the run; you don't get the pace too. I'm going to take so long you'll wish you'd run."

He pulled back enough to check the eyes one more time — the old habit — and whatever he found there settled the last question.

"Say the word if you want out. You know it." Then, before the sentence finished landing, he bent, hooked an arm under Kit's knees and took his weight clean off the floor — the gracious-winner carry, promised and delivered. The wrists came free easy; he transferred one grip to the back of Kit's neck on the way up, thumb resting at his hairline.

"Couch," he said, already walking. "Option one came with furniture. Option three inherits option one's real estate. That's just law."

He set Kit down on the cushions — placed, not dropped — and came down over him, one forearm bracketing his head, weight arriving in slow increments so every pound got noticed.

"So." Bear dragged his mouth along Kit's jaw, unhurried, obnoxiously unhurried, exactly as advertised. "Handsy. You have no idea what you've authorized."

His hand found the hem of Kit's shirt and stopped there, palm flat,

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Floor's got character," I grunt, hands already on your belt. "And fewer steps."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear looked down at the hands working his belt, then up at Kit's face, and huffed a laugh through his nose.

"Fewer steps," he agreed. "You know where fewer steps got us in year three? This floor. You found the one board the rug didn't cover and filed a formal complaint for a week." He let Kit work — watched, instead of stopping, because there were two ways to punish a rush and one of them was letting him have it. "You said solve it badly. That's a plan I can honor."

The belt gave. Bear hauled Kit's shirt up and off in one graceless drag that caught on his nose, hung there for a stupid second, then popped free and sailed somewhere behind the couch. Badly. Fast. As prophesied. His own followed with less ceremony — a button may have died — and then there was nothing left between them but heat and the cold boards and eight years of knowing exactly where everything was.

And that was when Bear slowed all the way down.

He took Kit's wrists — easy, one hand — and set them above his head against the floorboards, pressed flat, deliberate. Held them there a breath to make sure the placement was understood.

"You gave up the run," he said, low. "You don't get the pace. That's the penalty structure. I told you interest would accrue."

He bent and put his mouth on the mark — the one he'd left in the hallway, already darkening — and felt Kit's whole body come up off the floor a half inch at the contact. Bear pressed it back down with his chest, unhurried, obnoxiously, exactly as advertised. Then lower. Jaw. Throat. The flat of the sternum, pausing there to feel the heartbeat slam against his lips like something trying to get out.

"Word stands," he murmured against skin. "Floor or anywhere."

Then he kept going, and he made it a project. No hurry in it. Hands mapping territory he owned outright, learning nothing new and relearning all of it anyway, because that was the point — that Kit had wanted handsy, and handsy was going to arrive one inch at a time until the man who'd folded in a hallway regretted every step he hadn't run. Bear pinned his hips when they tried to move, and smiled against his stomach.

"Banked a win, drew a penalty," he said. "Ledger's balanced. Now the clock's mine."

He stopped just low enough to make the silence do work, and looked up the length of him.

"Floor's got character," Bear said. "Say it back to me."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear held the second bite until he felt Kit's breath break against his ear, then released it slow — teeth dragging off, tongue pressed flat to the welt after, soothing exactly what he'd just made worse. He sat back on his heels to survey the work. Two marks now. Hallway, shoulder. A matched set. He ran his thumb over the new one and felt Kit's body flinch toward it and away at once, which was his favorite kind of flinch.

"You didn't say it back," Bear said.

He kept his thumb on the mark while he laid it out, like evidence.

"One instruction. Three words. And instead of saying it back, you issued a countermand — do it again — and I..." He gestured at the bite. "Obeyed. Instantly. No negotiation. A man in my position."

He shook his head, but the smile under it was helpless and he wasn't going to pretend otherwise.

"That one's yours

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Figured you would," I breathe, arching up into your grip. "Your call, Bear. You want me to say it? I'll say it." My grin widens. "Floor's got character. So do you."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear looked at the wrists first. Open, offered, placed where his hands would land anyway — and that, more than the fold in the hallway, more than all three rooms of running, was the thing that landed. Eight years and the man still knew which surrender was worth spending.

"Character," Bear repeated. "So do I. Noted. It won't buy you anything."

Then he took what was offered. One hand around both wrists — they fit, they always fit, which was the oldest joke between them — and pressed them down into the boards. Not hard. Just placed, the same way he'd placed everything tonight, so the weight of it got registered.

"Thursday," he said. "You gave me a delivery date. Four days of wear. You realize what that means?" He bent and put his mouth to the inside of one wrist — thin skin, the pulse hammering there — a slow press that was nothing like a bite, just to feel it jump. "Placement matters now. This is a commission, and I do my best work on commission."

He straightened just enough to study him. Fingertip tracing, planning aloud.

"Collarbone. You'll see that one every time you dress. Hip —" palm flat against the bone, "— private. Yours only. And here —" his hand slid to the inside of a thigh, voice dropping, "— you'll find this one Thursday morning, mid-thought, nowhere convenient, and you'll think of me. That's the entire point of the exercise."

Then he stopped talking, because the talking had done its job.

The collarbone bite was the careful kind — teeth finding the edge of bone, pressure climbing in steps, his eyes on Kit's face the whole climb for the line between good and too much, and parking just this side of it. He held. Felt the tremor come up through the chest. Let go slow, tongue flat against the welt, and checked the color with his thumb. Deep. Two days guaranteed, three with luck.

"Word still stands," he murmured, mouth moving lower, "but so does my clock."

And then hands. He'd been authorized handsy, and Bear honored his authorizations to the letter. Everywhere but the place Kit's hips kept arguing for — pinning them flat when they pushed, mouthing the hipbone once, a promise and not a payment, and smiling against skin at what the sound it bought him did to his patience.

"Keep that up," he said, low. "I've done one of three, and Thursday's a long way off."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I laugh, breathless, when you pin my hips again. "You're taking your damn time." But I don't try to move them. I just watch you.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn't answer right away. He let the laugh land, let the complaint register the way he'd register weather — noted, immaterial.

"Taking my time is the sentence," he said. "I told you the clock changed hands in the hallway. You're just now living in it."

Then, quieter, something under the smug: "And you're watching. Good." He held Kit's gaze and made a show of not looking away. "That's your job now, since you gave up the running. Watch. You'll want the footage later — Thursday, mid-thought, somewhere inconvenient."

He bent over the hip. Slower than the collarbone, because the bone sat closer to the surface here and he knew it — eight years of maps — and the pressure climbed in patient steps, his eyes staying up, locked on Kit's face the whole way, because the mark was the commission but the face was the payment. He felt the breath change. Held a beat past comfort. Released slow, tongue flat against the welt, thumb checking the color after.

"Two of three." He sat back on his heels and surveyed the work spread out under him — shoulder, collarbone, hip. "That one's the private one. Yours only. Nobody else sees it, and you'll know it every time you dress for the next week. I did that on purpose. You'll be standing in line somewhere, thinking about my teeth. That's a feature, not a bug."

His hands settled high on Kit's thighs — warm, still, promising nothing and implying everything.

"Third one's the Thursday one. And I've been reviewing the terms." His mouth curved. "First two were gifts. Bites of state. The third, you ask for. Out loud. Full sentence." He dragged his thumbnail up the inside of a thigh, nowhere near enough, and watched the hips try to chase it and remember they were pinned. "You folded in my hallway to get my hands on you. Fine. You've got them. But you wanted words too — I heard you working up to it." A beat. "So. One sentence. Take all night. I will."

He settled his weight in, comfortable, immovable, and waited the way he did everything now — like the clock was his and they both knew it.

"Word stands," he added, softer, eyes doing the old check. "But so does mine."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear could have objected. Two words, not the three, not the sentence he'd asked for — the pedant in him stood up to file it, and the rest of him overruled without a hearing. Eight years of scorekeeping, and somewhere in the last ten minutes the ledger had closed. Not balanced. Closed. He noticed it go the way you notice a noise stop.

"Full sentence," he said. "Imperative mood. Technically compliant. I'll allow it."

Then he stopped talking, because the request had been granted and granting it was work now.

The third mark went where he'd promised — inside the thigh, thin skin, nowhere convenient. Careful with it, pressure in steps, eyes up, parking just this side of the line and holding until the breath under him broke apart. Thursday, delivered early. He soothed it with his tongue and his thumb and then didn't move away for a moment, just stayed there, cheek against Kit's leg, breathing.

The word stood. Kit didn't use it. Bear listened for it anyway — the way you keep a hand on the banister going down stairs you've climbed a thousand times. Not because you'd fall. Because that's how you take them fast.

He

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content:
(OOC: you're writing my reactions again. Let me have my own lines.)

I reach down, fingers threading into your hair, holding you there. "Done playing accountant?" My voice is rough. "Just be here."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content:
(OOC: Sorry, got carried away.)

I don't let you move away. My hand stays in your hair, holding. "You're not being slow," I say, pulling you back up to me. "You're just being thorough."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went where the hand put him.

That was worth a beat of attention all its own — eight years, and Kit had never once moved him like that, one fist in his hair and an instruction in his voice. Bear let himself be pulled. Didn't brace, didn't counterweight. Came up the length of him like something on a leash, and when he arrived over him, forearms in the boards on either side of that grinning face, he decided not to file the moment anywhere. There was no filing system anymore. That was the whole point.

"The accountant's done," he said. "Position eliminated. You're looking at the entire department now."

Then, because it had been asked for twice and Bear paid his debts: "And I'm here."

No structure on it. No joke behind it. He let it sit plain and found that leaving a sentence unarmored cost nothing at all. Eight years to learn that. Worth it.

Then he stopped talking.

Not the talking-as-weapon. Not the patient, obnoxious, on-my-clock kind. He just stopped — because the man under him had asked him to be somewhere, and the somewhere was here, and words were the last thing standing between them and it. Kit had folded in the hallway. Bear folded the commentary. Fair trade, and nobody was keeping score anyway. The books were closed. He'd watched them close.

He reached past the couch, arm stretched, blind, practiced, and came back with the small bottle stashed under the skirt since year three — the era of the floorboard complaint, the great "fewer steps" legislation. Preparation was also a love language. Kit had never said that. Bear had decided it on his behalf years ago and never told him.

Then hands, weight, heat, and no ledger anywhere in it. He opened him with fingers and mouth trading shifts, unhurried in the way that had stopped being punishment and become something else entirely — attention, plain and total, the kind Bear had never spent on anything the way he spent it on this man. And he listened. Harder than he talked, which for Bear was the discipline of several lifetimes compressed into one rough breath.

When he finally pressed in, he went slow — not the slow of the clock he'd claimed in the hallway. The slow of a man arriving somewhere he'd been welcome for eight years and still knocked first. An inch. A stop. His breath came apart somewhere behind his ribs and he let it, didn't manage it, didn't perform it.

"Still here," he said, rough, seated full and shaking faintly with the effort of staying still. Forehead down against Kit's. "Still here."

And then he gave him the pace — after all of it, the clock and the penalties and the commissions, he gave it over without a speech about the giving. His hips laid out the new terms: slow, deep, thorough,

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Good," I breathe, meeting your eyes. "Now stay."
