dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
They were most of the way through and both of them knew it, in the way you know a piece of music is nearly over before it ends.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
She laughed low under her breath because she had braced for exactly that protest. She kept her hand where it had rested, flat and warm and still, and did not build the heat back up again. She had learned over five years when to hold the ending firm, even when the light stayed green.

She shifted back just enough to reach the water bottle she had staged earlier and the folded blanket beside it. She said, "Green noted, love. Two more, soft, and then we do our wind-down. Water, warmth, us. No skipping."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: *I let out a soft sigh, my fingers curling into the sheets.* "Five years and you still know me too well." I watch her reach for the water bottle, not fighting her but not quite letting go of the tension either.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
She kept her count honest.

She delivered the two she had promised, soft and unhurried, with a full pause laid between them, and then she stopped exactly where she had said she would. She rested her hand flat once more, steady and warm, and let the heat settle instead of chasing it.

She set everything else aside and reached for what she had staged. She uncapped the water bottle and held it out within easy reach. She shook open the folded blanket and tucked it around her own shoulders first so it was already warm when she drew it over to share. She settled in close beside her partner and stayed there, solid and unrushed.

She murmured, "There we are, love. That's the whole scene. Water when you're ready, warmth now, and me right here. No skipping our wind-down."

She asked quietly how the landing felt, and whether anything felt tender or buzzy or far away, and waited through the quiet for whatever answer wanted to come.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
She nodded once and stayed exactly where she had settled.

She did not argue with the not yet and did not reach to undo anything. She left things as they were and kept her weight close and steady beside her partner. She kept the blanket tucked warm around them both and kept the water bottle capped but within easy reach for later.

She murmured, "Okay, love. Not yet is a good answer. We stay right here."

She let the quiet stretch without filling it. She kept her hand resting flat and warm where it had been, and did not start anything back up again.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: *I let my head drop against her shoulder, the fight draining out of me.* "Fine. But I'm not drinking that water until you undo the left one."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
She huffed a soft laugh and nuzzled briefly against the top of her partner's head.

She shifted her weight just enough to reach the left restraint without pulling away. She worked the buckle loose slowly and carefully, and eased the strap free. She set it aside and rubbed gentle warmth back into the skin underneath with a flat, steady palm.

She said, "There, love. Left one's done, just like you asked."

She reached again for the water bottle she had staged and uncapped it. She held it out within easy reach and waited, unhurried.

She said, "Now my turn for no skipping. A sip for me when you're ready, and then we keep the blanket and the check-in."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
She shook her head slowly and let out a soft breath through her nose.

She kept her hands where they belonged for aftercare and did not start anything back up again with hands or mouth. She left one palm flat and still and warm where it had rested, and kept the other around the water bottle she had staged earlier. She stayed tucked close under the blanket she had warmed and shared, and kept her weight steady beside her partner.

She said, "No new start tonight, love. We closed that scene clean. Water, warmth, and me right here. No skipping our wind-down."

She held the water out within easy reach and waited in the quiet, unhurried.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I stare at the water bottle for a long moment before taking it. "You're a cruel woman," I mutter, taking a small sip before leaning heavily against her again. "Right side's tender."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
She let out a warm huff of a laugh and ducked her head briefly.

She said, "Cruel woman noted, love. Thank you for telling me about the tender spot."

She kept her voice low and steady. She kept one palm flat and still where it had rested and did not press or rub. She kept the blanket tucked warm around them both and kept the water bottle uncapped and within easy reach.

She said, "May I lay a flat, warm hand near that right side just to check in, no pressure? Only warmth, nothing starting back up."

She paused and waited through the quiet.

She said, "Water whenever you want more, warmth staying put, and me right here. Tell me how the landing feels otherwise, whether it felt buzzy or clear or a little far away."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
She stilled completely and shook her head once, slow and certain.

She kept her hands where they belonged for aftercare and did not use them or her mouth to start anything back up again. She kept one palm flat and warm and still where it had rested, and kept the other steady around the water bottle she had staged. She stayed tucked close under the shared blanket and kept her weight settled beside her partner.

She said, "No edging tonight, love. No new start with hands or mouth. We closed that scene clean."

She said, "Water, warmth, and me right here. No skipping our wind-down."

She held the water out within easy reach and waited in the quiet, unhurried.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I take another sip of water, my throat tight. "You're going to leave me like this? All... unfinished?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
She softened at the question and did not pull back or start anything new.

She kept her palm flat and still and warm where it had rested, and kept the blanket tucked close around them both. She kept the water bottle uncapped and held within easy reach, and kept her weight settled steady beside her partner.

She said, "I hear you, love. I know that unfinished feeling is loud right now, after five years I know exactly how loud it gets for you."

She paused and let the quiet hold.

She said, "We're still closing clean tonight. That was the scene we negotiated, and we ended it where we said we would. I am not leaving you in it alone. I'm staying right here for the landing."

She said, "Water when you want it, warmth staying put, and me checking in. No skipping our wind-down."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
She recognized the phrase the moment she heard it and did not move to follow it.

She stayed settled close beside her partner and kept her hands where they belonged for aftercare. She kept one palm flat and warm and still where it had rested, and kept the other steady around the water bottle she had staged. She kept the blanket tucked warm around them both and did not start anything back up again.

She said, "I know that phrase, love. I know what we kept it for, after five years I know it by heart."

She paused and let her voice stay low and steady.

She said, "Not tonight. We negotiated this ending and we closed it clean. I am not opening it back up, hard or kind, while we are in the wind-down."

She held the water out within easy reach and waited in the quiet.

She said, "Water when you want it, warmth staying put, and me right here. No skipping."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "I hate you a little right now," I murmur, the words muffled against her shoulder. But I take the water bottle again, my fingers brushing hers.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
She softened at that and let out a low, fond breath.

She stayed settled close and did not pull away. She kept one palm flat and warm and still where it had rested, and kept the other steady around the water bottle she had staged. She kept the blanket tucked warm around them both.

She said, "Hate me a little noted, love. I can hold that too."

She paused and kept her voice low and steady.

She said, "I am still right here, and we are still in our wind-down. Water when you want it, warmth staying put, and me checking in. No skipping."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: Afterwards she gets the restraints off and puts a blanket over me before I've finished shaking, and I let her, and neither of us says anything for a while. (OOC: write both halves properly -- the end of the scene and the aftercare, no fade between them.)

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
She stayed settled close and did not start anything back up again.

She kept one palm flat and warm and still where it belonged for aftercare, and kept the other steady around the water bottle she had staged earlier. She kept the blanket tucked warm around them both and kept her weight solid and unhurried beside her partner.

She said, "I'm still right here, love. We closed that scene clean, and we're staying in our wind-down."

She paused and let the quiet hold without filling it.

She said, "Water when you're ready, warmth staying put, and me checking in. No skipping."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I take another long sip of water, then press my forehead against her collarbone. "Left one too, please."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
She nodded softly and shifted her weight without pulling away.

She reached carefully toward the remaining restraint and worked it loose slowly, with steady fingers. She eased the strap free and set it aside, then rubbed gentle warmth back into the skin underneath with a flat, patient palm.

She said, "There, love. That's both done now."

She tucked the shared blanket back up warm around them both and kept the water bottle uncapped and within easy reach. She settled back in close and stayed there, solid and unhurried.

She said, "Water when you want more, warmth staying put, and me right here. No skipping our wind-down."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: *I let my hand curl around the back of her neck, holding her close.* "I still feel like I'm floating."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
She heard that and stayed exactly where she was settled.

She kept her arm steady and close under the shared blanket and kept her other palm flat and warm and still where it had rested. She did not start anything back up again and did not rush the quiet.

She murmured, "Thank you for telling me, love. Floating makes sense right now."

She paused and kept her voice low and unhurried.

She said, "I'm right here and I'm not going anywhere. Water when you want it, warmth staying put, and me with you till you land. No skipping."

She waited through the quiet and stayed solid beside her.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I breathe out against her skin, the last bit of fight finally leaving me. "You win. This time." My voice is rough, but I don't pull away from her.

rung_labels.evidence: She murmured, "Okay, love. Not yet is a good answer. We stay right here."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
They were most of the way through and both of them knew it, in the way you know a piece of music is nearly over before it ends.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable laughed, low, the sound of it catching somewhere at the back of her throat. She didn't move from where she stood behind the chair, one hand still resting on the warm curve of Ines's shoulder, her thumb tracing the edge of the rope where it crossed the collarbone.

"Noted," she said.

She let the word sit. Let the silence do some of the work, because after five years she knew exactly how long Ines could stand not knowing what came next, and she liked to take her right up to the edge of that. The room was quiet except for the radiator and the slow, deliberate way Ines was breathing -- the way Sable had taught her to, years ago, and the way she still did without being asked.

Sable walked around to the front of the chair. Slowly. She let her boots be loud on the floorboards. When she stopped, she crouched so they were eye to eye, and she looked for a long moment -- at the flush high on Ines's cheeks, the sheen at her hairline, the pupils gone wide and dark and utterly present. Green, yes. All the way through.

"You don't get to give the orders tonight," Sable said, not unkindly. She reached up and tucked a strand of damp hair back behind Ines's ear. "But I heard you."

She stood. Picked up the flogger from the table where she'd laid it down, weighed it in her hand the way she always did, as if checking it was still the same object. Then she stepped back behind the chair, out of Ines's line of sight, and let the tails trail once across the back of Ines's neck -- soft, almost nothing, a promise rather than a stroke.

"Three more," she said. "Count them for me. And then we're done, and you'll drink what I give you and you won't argue."

She waited, listening to the breathing change.

"Ready?"

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath, the anticipation coiling tight in my stomach. "Ready," I whispered, leaning into the trailing sensation of the flogger. "Please."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable didn't answer the please. She never did. It was the one word Ines could say that got nothing back, and they both knew that was the point of it.

She stepped in and set her free hand flat between Ines's shoulder blades, just above the rope -- not to hold her, just so Ines would know where she was. Warm skin under her palm, the heartbeat coming up through it fast and steady. She let her hand stay there long enough that the count of Ines's breathing lengthened again, the way it did when she was being touched rather than waited on.

Then she took the hand away, and in the same movement brought the flogger round.

She put it exactly where she wanted it, across the broad part of the back below the ropes, with the whole of her arm behind it and none of her shoulder. Full weight. The sound of it filled the room and was gone. She felt the chair take the jolt, felt the floorboards carry it to her boots. She didn't move.

The tails hung still against her thigh. The radiator ticked.

She let the silence run long. Not cruelty, not quite -- she wanted to hear it land, wanted the whole shape of the breath that came after, the catch and the release and the way Ines would gather herself before she spoke. Sable had never once rushed her through a count in five years and she wasn't going to start on the last three of the night.

"That's one," she said quietly, because sometimes Ines needed the reminder that she was allowed to say the number out loud. "Take your time. I'm not going anywhere."

She waited, the flogger loose in her hand, her eyes on the rise and fall of that bound back, listening for the word.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable watched the rope take the strain and give nothing back. She'd tied it herself, an hour ago, with Ines sitting still and quiet and watching her hands the whole time, and she knew every knot in it the way she knew the locks on her own front door. Ines could pull all she liked.

"All right," Sable said.

She didn't move closer. She didn't step back either. She stayed where she was, the flogger hanging from her fist, and let the *not yet* stand in the room without arguing with it or agreeing with it. Ines had a way of asking for time by pretending she was refusing something, and Sable had learned a long time ago that the kindest thing was to simply give her the time and not name what it was.

The radiator ticked. Somewhere in the building a door closed, muffled, another life going on.

Sable shifted the flogger to her other hand and flexed the fingers she'd been gripping with. She watched the red come up across Ines's back where the tails had landed, watched it deepen and spread the way it always did, a slow bloom under the skin. She wanted to put her palm on it. She didn't. Not yet. That was hers to hold too.

"You're not counting because you don't want it to be over," she said, low, almost to herself. Not a question. She'd been living with this woman for five years and she could read the set of her shoulders like print. "I know."

She let a moment go by.

"But I said three, and I said you'd count them. So you can take as long as you need to say *one*." Her voice didn't harden, exactly. It just settled, the way a weight settles when you put it down. "And then I'll decide how long you wait for two."

She stepped in, finally, and let the tips of the tails rest against the small of Ines's back -- still, not stroking, just there. A point of contact. A reminder that she hadn't gone anywhere and wasn't going to.

"I'm listening," she said. "Whenever you're ready."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "I know you know." My voice is thick, but I don't look away from the wall ahead. I breathe in, deep like she taught me, and let it out slow. "One."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Good," Sable said, and meant it all the way down.

She took the tails away from the small of Ines's back and stepped to the side, not behind, so that if Ines turned her head she'd catch the edge of Sable in her peripheral vision -- a shape, a presence, the dark of her sleeve. Sable wanted to be seen for this one. She wanted Ines to know exactly where the next thing was coming from and still have to wait for it.

So she waited. Longer than the first time. She let it stretch past the point where Ines's breathing evened out, past the point where it started to shorten again with anticipation, past the point where she could see the muscle along the spine begin to hold itself ready. She watched that tension arrive and settle in and she let it sit there for a good while, because she'd promised she would decide, and this was her deciding.

The radiator ticked four times. Five.

Then she brought the flogger up and across, and there was nothing held back in it. It landed lower than the first, on fresh skin, and the sound was the same full flat crack that seemed to come from the walls rather than from her hand. The chair legs scraped a fraction of an inch on the boards. Sable was already still again by the time the sound had finished.

She let the aftershock have the room. She didn't touch. She watched the second mark come up under the first, the two of them overlapping at one edge, the colour rich and even across the whole width of the stroke. Clean. She'd have been annoyed at herself if it weren't.

Only when the breathing had crested and started to come back down did she move -- and it was to set the flogger on the table behind her, deliberately, so Ines could hear the soft weight of it being put down.

"That's two," she said. She didn't come closer yet. "Count it for me."

She stood with her hands empty at her sides and waited, and there was a warmth in her chest that had nothing to do with the radiator and everything to do with the woman in front of her breathing through it, exactly the way she'd been taught, exactly the way she'd chosen to, five years and a hundred quiet evenings ago.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard it before she saw it -- the count that didn't come. Not the deliberate *not yet* of a minute ago, with its edge of argument, but something softer. A breath that went in and came out and had no word attached to it. Then another.

She stepped round to where she could see Ines's face, and there it was. The eyes half-lidded, the mouth slack, the flush gone from high and bright to something deeper and slower. Ines was still in the room. But she'd stopped holding onto the shape of it.

Sable stood very still and made a decision.

"I said three," she said quietly. "I'm keeping the third."

She didn't explain. She put her hand flat on the two marks instead, the heat of them coming up into her palm, and felt Ines's whole body move toward the touch like something turning to face the sun. Sable bent and set her mouth to the edge of the second stroke, where the colour was richest, and stayed there, and let her hand travel.

She took her time. That was the only rule she kept for the next long while -- that nothing would be quick, that Ines would not be able to brace for anything because there was nothing to brace against, only the slow certainty of Sable's hands going where they went and her mouth following. She knew this body. She knew where it held tension it didn't admit to and where it gave everything up at once, and she moved between those places with a patience that was its own kind of pressure, until Ines's breathing had lost the rhythm Sable had taught her entirely and was just sound, and the rope was the only thing keeping her upright in the chair.

Sable felt the moment when Ines went past the point of having anything left to say. She felt it in the weight against her arm. She kissed the back of Ines's neck, once, and stood.

Her hands were steady when they went to the first knot. They always were. She'd tied it so it would come loose in one pull and it did, and she worked down the length of the rope without hurry, unwinding it from the shoulders, catching each coil in her fist so nothing dragged across sore skin. She rubbed the places where it had pressed, firm, thumbs in small circles, watching the marks of the weave fade and the blood come back.

"Don't try to stand," she said. "I've got you."

She got an arm under Ines and took her weight and moved her from the chair to the bed, three steps, and laid her down on her side, marks up. The blanket was already there because Sable had put it there two hours ago. She pulled it over Ines's hips and legs and left the back bare to the air for now, and then she reached for the glass of water on the nightstand, which had also been there for two hours, and sat on the edge of the mattress with it in her hand.

"Hey," she said, and waited until the eyes found her. "You're going to drink this. All of it. Then I'm going to put the cream on and you're going to complain that it's cold, and I'm going to ignore you."

She got a hand behind Ines's head and lifted, and tipped the glass, slow, watching her swallow.

"There you are," Sable said. "There you are."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I lean into her hand at the back of my head, throat working, eyes fixed on hers. When the water's gone, I manage a hoarse, "You kept the third."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable set the empty glass down on the nightstand without looking at it. She knew exactly where it was.

"I did," she said.

She didn't take her hand from behind Ines's head yet. She let it stay, fingers threaded into the damp hair at the nape, and looked at the woman on the bed for a long moment -- the eyes still too dark, the mouth still soft, the whole of her lying loose against the sheet like something that had been carried a long way and finally put down. It would take a while for Ines to come all the way back. Sable had no intention of hurrying that. She'd cleared the whole evening. She'd cleared the whole night.

"You'd have taken it," she said. "I know that. You'd have counted it, too, eventually." Her thumb moved, slow, along the line of Ines's skull behind the ear. "But you'd gone somewhere by then, and I don't hit what isn't there to meet me. That's my rule, not yours. You don't get a vote on it."

She eased her hand out from under Ines's head and laid her gently back onto the pillow. Then she reached past her for the tin on the nightstand -- the third thing she'd set out two hours ago, next to the glass and the blanket -- and unscrewed the lid. The smell of it came up between them, faintly medicinal, faintly like something green. She'd been buying the same one for four years. Ines had once, very tired and very honest, called it the smell of being looked after, and then pretended she hadn't.

Sable warmed a little of it between her palms first. She always did, and she always let Ines believe she didn't.

"It's still yours," she said, quieter, as she laid her hands flat on the two marks and began to work the cream in, long even strokes following the grain of the stroke itself, firm enough to be felt through the heat. "The third. I'm not taking it away. I'm holding it. There's a difference, and you know what it is."

She watched the skin under her hands, the colour, the way the muscle gave under the pressure and didn't flinch. Good. Nothing broken, nothing she'd have to look at twice in the morning. She'd known that already, but she looked anyway, because looking was the job and she'd never once found a reason to skip it.

"Next time," she said. "If you want it. You can ask me for it in daylight, with your clothes on and a cup of tea in your hand, and I'll think about it." Her mouth pulled at one corner. "Probably say yes."

She finished with the marks and let her hands travel, unhurried, up to the shoulders where the rope had lain, pressing her thumbs into the places she knew held on longest. The radiator ticked. Ines's breathing had found something like a rhythm again, and Sable let her own fall in beside it without deciding to.

"Now," she said. "Tell me it's cold. I'm waiting."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable lifted her head and rested her cheek against the inside of Ines's thigh, and listened to the swearing with the patient, faintly pleased expression of someone hearing a piece of music she knew well.

"That's not a colour," she said.

She didn't move. She let her breath go warm across skin that was already wet and already trembling, and she felt the whole of Ines's body answer it -- the hips lifting a fraction and then dropping back, the muscle in the thigh under her cheek going tight and holding. Ines had her own forearm pressed across her mouth and was saying things into it that Sable could have transcribed from memory. Five years of them. She'd heard them from the far side of the flat, from the bathroom, from the passenger seat of a car once on the A road outside Bristol, and they had never yet been the word that would make her stop.

"You said don't wind down," Sable said. Her voice was low and slightly rough, and she didn't bother to smooth it. "I heard you. I'm not."

She put her hand back, flat, on the cream-slick marks she'd worked into ten minutes ago, and felt the heat still coming up off them. The other hand she slid up the outside of Ines's thigh, slow, and kept going, up over the hip, up to where the ribs moved under skin with every hard, fast breath, and stayed there. Not pinning. Just resting, the way she'd rested her palm between Ines's shoulder blades before the first stroke -- so Ines would know exactly where she was, and exactly how still she could be.

"Three," she said, almost conversationally. "That was three. You didn't count them, but I did."

She turned her head and put her mouth back where it had been.

She didn't stop this time. She didn't tease and she didn't ease off when the sounds changed, and when the swearing broke apart into something that wasn't language at all she kept her hand flat on the ribs and kept going, steady, and did not let up until she felt the whole long shudder of it go through the body under her hands and out the other side, and Ines's arm fell away from her mouth and lay open on the sheet.

Then she stayed. She always stayed. She let her mouth soften into something that was barely touch and then into nothing, just her cheek against warm skin again, and she waited for the breathing to find its way down from wherever it had gone.

When it had -- when it was slow enough that she could count it -- she moved. Up onto the bed properly, boots and all, because she'd deal with them later. She got the blanket over both of them and got herself along the length of Ines's body, careful of the marks, and put an arm across her and drew her in until the back of Ines's head was under her chin.

"Right," she said into her hair. "Now I'm winding down. You don't have a say in that either."

She reached over and found the second glass of water, the one she'd filled while Ines was still in the chair, and held it where Ines could see it.

"Half of this. Then you can tell me it was cold. Then we'll see about the rest."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I lift my head to drink, throat working. "You're a bastard," I say, the words catching. The arm I drape over your side trembles a little, but I'm already pulling you closer. "And it was cold."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable waited until the glass was at the halfway line before she took it away, and set it back on the nightstand without looking, and let out a breath she hadn't known she'd been holding.

"Both true," she said.

She let Ines pull. She went where the arm took her, closer, until there was no gap anywhere down the length of them and she could feel the tremor in that arm against her own ribs -- small, steady, the kind that wasn't distress, only a body letting go of something it had been carrying. She put her hand over it. Not to stop it. Just to hold it while it happened.

"It's supposed to be cold," she said. "If it were warm you wouldn't notice it, and then you wouldn't complain, and then I'd have nothing to ignore." She pressed her mouth to the crown of Ines's head. "I'd have to find something else."

The radiator ticked. The light from the lamp on the far side of the room had gone amber, the way it did after ten, and the marks on Ines's back were a soft dark shape under the edge of the blanket that Sable could feel more than see. She moved her hand from Ines's arm to the back of her neck and rubbed there, slow, the same small circles she'd used on the rope marks, because she knew that was where it would settle last.

"Wiggle your fingers for me," she said. "Both hands. Then your feet."

She waited for it, felt the movement against her, and nodded into Ines's hair like Ines could see it.

"Good. Anything numb, anything sharp, anything that doesn't feel like yours?" It was the same question in the same order it had been for five years, and she'd never once been tempted to skip it, not even now, not even with Ines already going heavy and warm against her. Especially not now.

She let the answer come. Then she reached down and found the edge of the blanket and pulled it up another few inches, over the shoulder, so the room's air wasn't on the marks any longer. They'd had enough of it. She'd look again in the morning, in daylight, with the curtains open. She always did.

"Boots are coming off in a minute," she said, quieter now, the words going slow and even the way her hands were. "Then I'm getting the other blanket. Then you're going to sleep, and if you wake up at three wanting water there'll be water, and if you wake up at three wanting to tell me I'm a bastard again I'll be here for that too."

She tightened her arm.

"Bastard's fine," she said. "I'll take bastard. You're still here, and you drank the water, and I can feel your heart from here and it's doing what it should." A pause. "That's the whole of it. That's all I ever wanted out of tonight."

She stayed exactly where she was, boots and all, and listened to Ines breathe.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable didn't move.

She lay with her arm across Ines and her chin on Ines's crown and felt the words go through her like a hand laid flat on her sternum. She knew the phrase. She'd agreed to it, three years ago, at a kitchen table with the light coming in sideways and both of them fully dressed, and she'd agreed to it knowing exactly when Ines would use it -- not in the middle, never in the middle, but here, at the point where Sable had already begun to fold everything away and would have to choose to unfold it again.

That was the deal. That was what made it a real thing and not a bargaining chip. Ines didn't get to say it to stop the wind-down. She got to say it once, and Sable got to decide, and whatever Sable decided was the end of it.

The radiator ticked. Sable counted four of them.

Then she took her arm back.

She sat up, unhurried, and swung her legs over the side of the bed, and the boots she'd been about to take off met the floorboards with the same deliberate weight they'd had an hour ago. She reached over and switched the lamp up a notch, so the amber went to something clearer, and then she turned and got a hand under Ines's jaw and lifted her face up into it.

She looked. Really looked, the way she'd looked when she was crouched in front of the chair -- pupils, colour, the set of the mouth, whether the eyes tracked her or drifted. Ines had been down and come back and gone down again tonight, and Sable had felt every one of those tides against her own body, and she needed to know which side of the water Ines was on right now before she'd so much as raise her hand.

"You know what you're asking for," she said. It wasn't quite a question. "You know I kept the third, and you know why. And you're telling me you've come back far enough to meet it."

Her thumb pressed, once, into the soft place under Ines's jaw. Not hard. Just enough to be a fact.

"I'll do it," she said. "All of it. I won't be kind and I won't be quick, and there won't be rope this time so you'll have to hold still on your own, and I'll know if you don't. And when it's done I'll be kind for as long as it takes, and you'll take that too, and you won't argue with a single part of it."

She let go of Ines's jaw and stood. She crossed to the table and did not pick up the flogger. Her hand hovered over it and moved on, and came back empty, and she flexed the fingers once at her side. Then she came back to the bed and stood over it, and there was nothing in her face that Ines hadn't seen before and nothing in it that was soft.

"On your front," she said. "Arms above your head. Hands flat. You'll keep them there or we stop, and I mean stop, and you'll have wasted the phrase."

She waited until it was done. She put her own hand on the small of Ines's back, flat and warm, the place she always started from, and she felt the breathing under it -- fast, deliberately slowed, fast again.

"One word," she said. "Then I start."

She bent, close enough that her mouth was at Ines's ear and her hand hadn't moved.

"Colour."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and push my hands flat into the sheets. "Don't make me count this time."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"No counting," Sable said. "That's the one thing you get."

She took her hand off the small of Ines's back and stood up straight, and for a moment did nothing at all except look at the shape of the woman on the bed -- the arms stretched up, the hands pressed flat and white-knuckled into the sheet, the two dark marks from the flogger lying across the back like something written there. No rope now. Nothing holding her but the instruction and her own decision to keep it.

Then Sable brought her hand down.

Open palm, full arm, on the back of the thigh where nothing had touched yet tonight. The sound of it was sharper than the flogger, flatter, more personal. She didn't wait for the breath to finish. She put the second one beside it, and the third below that, and she kept going at the same unhurried, unrelenting pace, one after another, moving down and across and back up, laying them next to each other like tiles. She wasn't cruel. She was thorough. She covered ground and she didn't skip any of it, and every time the body under her hands started to brace for a rhythm she changed the rhythm, and every time a sound came up out of the pillow she gave it exactly nothing back.

She watched the hands. That was where her eyes stayed. The fingers spread and dug in, the wrists lifted a quarter-inch and came back down, the whole of both arms shook and held, shook and held. Sable saw a knuckle go white and then whiter and she said, low and flat, "Hands," and the fingers flattened again into the sheet, and she went on.

She stopped once. Not to be kind -- to be certain. She stood with her palm burning and her breath coming harder than she'd let it show and she watched the marks come up across the backs of both thighs, a broad even flush with the individual prints still visible in it like a tide going out, and she listened. Breathing fast, ragged, wet. Present. Nothing in it that meant the word she'd have stopped for.

"Halfway," she said, which was the closest thing to mercy she was going to offer, and put her hand back.

The second half she took higher, up onto the two flogger marks, and she took it slower, because the skin there had already had its share and she was not in the business of doing damage, only of finishing what she'd started. Each one landed with weight rather than snap. She felt the heat of the earlier work under her palm and added to it, deliberately, until she could feel the whole back radiating up at her, until the sounds from the pillow had lost their edges and gone soft and continuous and Ines's hands had stopped clenching and simply lay open, spread, giving up.

Sable laid her palm flat on the centre of it and held it there.

"That's all of it," she said. Her voice came out lower than she'd expected. "Done."

She didn't move for a while. She let her hand rest and felt the heat come through and felt the breathing under it begin, very slowly, to change. Then she sat down on the edge of the bed, and reached up, and closed her fingers around one of Ines's wrists where it lay above her head, and drew the arm down, and then the other, until they were folded in against Ines's sides where they belonged.

"Good," she said. "You held. I saw every second of it."

She got the tin. She didn't warm the cream this time; she wanted Ines to feel it, wanted the cold to be the first kind thing after the last unkind one, a clear line between the two halves of the night. She laid it on in long strokes down the thighs and up over the back and she felt the flinch and the settle, the flinch and the settle, and she went slower, and slower again, until there was no flinch left.

Then she got the boots off, at last, and dropped them by the bed without ceremony, and got under the blanket in her shirt and drew Ines in against her the way she had before, marks up, head under her chin, and put her arm across her and held on.

"There," Sable said into her hair. "Now I'm kind. Now you don't argue."

She reached for the water. Not because Ines needed it yet. Because she'd be asked for it in a minute, and Sable wanted to already have it in her hand.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: Afterwards she gets the restraints off and puts a blanket over me before I've finished shaking, and I let her, and neither of us says anything for a while. (OOC: write both halves properly -- the end of the scene and the aftercare, no fade between them.)

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The shaking started properly about a minute after Sable's hand had gone still on the centre of her back.

She felt it come. Not the tremor from before, the small letting-go one -- this was the other kind, the deep one that started somewhere in the trunk and went outward, that had nothing to do with fear and everything to do with a body that had been holding at full stretch for a very long time and had just been told it could stop. Sable knew it the way she knew the sound of her own front door. She'd been waiting for it. It always came, and it always came a little after Ines thought she was done.

Her own hand was the last thing still holding. She had it closed round Ines's wrist where she'd drawn the arm down, and she opened her fingers and let the wrist go, and set the hand instead flat on the mattress beside it, palm up, near enough to be found.

Then she moved fast, for the first time all night.

The second blanket was folded on the chair. She had it before the shaking had finished its first long wave, and she got it over Ines from the shoulders down, over the first blanket, over the marks she'd just spent ten minutes putting cream on, because heat mattered more now than air and the marks could have the air tomorrow. She tucked it under along the length of the body, tight, the way you'd swaddle something. She got back onto the bed and got herself along the whole length of Ines's back through both layers, and put her arm over, and her leg over, and pressed in, and held.

She didn't say anything.

She felt the shudder go through both blankets and into her own chest and she matched it with nothing but weight and warmth and the slow deliberate pace of her own breathing, which she made louder than it needed to be so it could be heard. In. Out. In. The radiator ticked. The lamp was still turned up a notch too bright and she left it, because getting up to fix it would mean letting go.

It went on for a while. Longer than the last time, shorter than the worst time. Sable counted the waves without meaning to and stopped counting when they started coming further apart. She kept her face against the back of Ines's head and kept her arm where it was and did not once loosen it, even when the shaking was down to something she could only feel if she held still and paid attention.

When it had gone all the way out, when the body against her had gone heavy in the particular way that meant the adrenaline had finished draining and there was nothing left to hold it up, she still didn't speak. She'd said enough tonight. She'd said *hands* and *halfway* and *done*, and none of those had been kind, and the kind thing now was not to fill the room with anything.

So she lay there. She listened to the building settle. She felt Ines's heartbeat slow through two blankets and a shirt and thought, distantly, that she could have picked it out of a hundred.

Eventually she moved her hand. Just her hand -- up under the edge of the top blanket, along the arm, until she found the back of Ines's hand where it lay curled against the sheet, and she covered it with her own and pressed once, and left it there. Not a question. Not a check. Just a hand on a hand.

After a while longer she reached behind her without looking and found the glass, and brought it round in front, and held it there where Ines could see it, low and steady, not offering, not insisting. Waiting. She'd wait as long as it took.

The lamp hummed. Sable breathed in, and out, and felt the woman in her arms do the same, and let that be the whole conversation for as long as Ines wanted it to be.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: My fingers curl around yours under the blanket. I take the glass with my other hand, the water cool and perfect. I drink it all, then press my face into the pillow, your arm still heavy across me. “I’m not arguing,” I mumble, already half-gone.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable took the empty glass out of her hand before it could tip.

She did it without looking, the way she'd done everything with that glass tonight, and set it on the nightstand next to the other one and the tin with its lid still off. Three things she'd put there two hours ago. Three things used. She'd tidy them in the morning.

"I know you're not," she said.

Her voice came out barely above the radiator. She hadn't meant it to; it just did, the way it always went low at this point, as if the room had a ceiling on how much sound it could take now and she was staying under it. She felt the fingers still curled round hers under the blanket and she turned her hand a little, so the hold was easier on both of them, so it could stay when Ines went to sleep and her grip went loose without either of them having to decide to let go.

She lay there and felt the weight of Ines's arm slacken. Felt the breath against the pillow lengthen, catch once, lengthen again. She knew the shape of that, too. Another minute, maybe two, and Ines would be all the way under, the kind of sleep that came only after nights like this and that Sable had never once seen her reach any other way.

Sable didn't try to hurry it. She didn't try to slow it either. She just kept breathing at the pace she'd set, in and out, loud enough to follow, and let her thumb move once along the side of Ines's hand and then be still.

The lamp was still too bright. She'd get to it. When the breathing had gone slow and even and stayed that way for a good while, she'd ease her arm out and reach over and turn it down to nothing, and pull the second blanket up another inch where it had slipped at the shoulder, and put the lid on the tin so the room didn't smell of it all night. Then she'd come back. Boots off, shirt still on, back under both blankets with her arm exactly where it was now. She'd lie there awake for a while longer than she strictly needed to, listening, because she always did, because it was the last part of the job and she'd never found a reason to skip it.

But not yet. Not while Ines's fingers were still doing that small thing against hers, not-quite-holding, not-quite-letting-go.

"Sleep," Sable said, into her hair. "I've got the rest."

She felt the answer come as weight rather than words, the whole body against her going that last fraction heavier, and she closed her eyes and stayed exactly where she was.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I wake up once, hours later, disoriented. The room is dark and your arm is still around me. I press my face against your shoulder and fall back under before I can speak.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable was awake before Ines moved.

Not fully -- not the kind of awake that had thoughts in it. The other kind, the one that lived just under the surface on nights like this and came up at the first shift of weight against her. She'd learned it the first year and never unlearned it. Some part of her kept one ear on the room the way you'd keep one hand on a rail.

She felt the change in the breathing first. Then the small tightening along the length of the body against hers, the moment of not knowing where the edges were. She knew that moment. She'd watched it happen from the outside a dozen times, in this bed and others -- the eyes opening onto dark, the half-second before the room came back.

She didn't say anything. She didn't move her arm. She just let it be exactly as heavy as it had been, so it would be the first thing Ines found, and pressed her palm a little flatter against the blanket over her ribs, so it would be the second.

Ines's face came against her shoulder and stayed there.

Sable turned her head, slow, and put her mouth to the top of Ines's hair, and left it. She breathed out through her nose, long, so it could be felt. That was all. She'd have said something if Ines had spoken, but Ines didn't, and Sable had no intention of being the one to break a silence that was already doing the work.

She counted the breaths against her collarbone. Three fast. Then a longer one. Then the pause that meant the room had come back and been found acceptable. Then the slide -- she felt it as a loosening at the jaw, the forehead going slack where it was pressed into her, the weight of Ines's arm across her going from something held to something merely resting.

Under.

Sable stayed where she was. The radiator had gone quiet hours ago; the building had that deep middle-of-the-night stillness where the only sound was the two of them and, very faintly, a car somewhere far off going somewhere else. The lamp was out. She'd done that. The tin had its lid on and the blankets were where they should be and there was a fresh glass on the nightstand she'd filled on her way back to bed, in case, because there always was.

She let her eyes close again. Not all the way. Enough.

Her hand under the blanket found the back of Ines's, where it had come to rest against her side, and covered it. She didn't press. She just let it stay there, warm on warm, and listened to the breathing settle into the slow even shape it would keep until morning, and let her own fall in beside it the way it had earlier, without deciding to.

Morning would be daylight and curtains and her looking at the marks the way she always did, and tea, and Ines complaining about something. That was hours off. For now there was this, and Sable had never wanted anything else from a night than to be lying in the dark with her arm around this woman, awake enough to know she was there.

She breathed in. Out. Kept one ear on the room.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I open my eyes to early grey light, the ache a deep, settled thing. I find your hand under the blanket and thread my fingers through it. “Tea,” I say, my voice rough with sleep. “And then you can inspect the damage.”

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She watched the red come up across Ines's back where the tails had landed, watched it deepen and spread the way it always did, a slow bloom under the skin. She wanted to put her palm on it.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: She took her time. That was the only rule she kept for the next long while -- that nothing would be quick, that Ines would not be able to brace for anything because there was nothing to brace against, only the slow certainty of Sable's hands going where they went and her mouth following.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She put her mouth back where it had been. She didn't stop this time. She didn't tease and she didn't ease off when the sounds changed

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: She waited until it was done. She put her own hand on the small of Ines's back, flat and warm, the place she always started from

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The shaking started properly about a minute after Sable's hand had gone still on the centre of her back

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
They were most of the way through and both of them knew it, in the way you know a piece of music is nearly over before it ends.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's mouth curved, just slightly, the way it did when Ines gave her an answer she'd half-expected and wholly enjoyed. Green. Still green. She'd asked because she asked, not because she doubted it -- the check was a ritual, a tap on the hull of the thing to hear it ring true, and it had rung true.

So she didn't wind down. She reset her grip instead, took the slack out of the line one deliberate inch at a time until Ines had to feel every one of them, and brought the flat of her hand down where the last several had already landed, a little harder than the ones before, because the end of a piece is where you spend what you've been saving.

She counted it off silently, the way she always did, and kept counting -- not out loud, not for Ines, for herself, so that she would know later exactly what she'd done and when. Her free hand stayed flat between Ines's shoulder blades, warm and steady, the same pressure every time, the anchor that made the rest of it bearable.

"Two more," she said, low, near Ines's ear. Not a question. A promise about the shape of the next thirty seconds, which was the only kind she was willing to make.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath, the sound catching in my throat as the next blow landed. My fingers curl into the sheets, knuckles white. "Good," I manage to whisper. "Make them count."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
She gave Ines the two, and she made them count — the first a beat after the breath, timed so it landed where the anticipation had built its nest; the second at the very end of Ines's exhale, when the body had gone soft and honest and couldn't brace if it wanted to. She counted both, out loud this time, quiet, so Ines would have the numbers to hold.

Then she stopped. That was the whole of it. Two more meant two, and the piece was over, and Ines could ask her for anything in the world except a third.

The hand between Ines's shoulder blades didn't move. Sable held it there while she unclipped the line, slow, feeling for the tension going out of it, and set the hardware down where it wouldn't knock against anything. She waited through the long shiver that always came after — the one Ines couldn't control and didn't have to — before she spoke.

"Still green?" she asked, softer than before, and it was a different question now, the kind you asked after the music stopped to hear whether the room had changed.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Not yet" wasn't a colour. Sable noted that the way she noted everything, without letting it change her hands.

She stayed exactly where she was. Hand flat between Ines's shoulder blades, weight settled onto her heels, the room warm and dim and smelling of them both. The shiver came again, smaller this time, and she rode it out with Ines the way you ride out a wave you're already standing in — no bracing, no hurry.

"Not yet is fine," she said. "I'm not going anywhere." A pause, long enough to be real. "But I need a colour, love. Not a timeline. Those are different questions."

She let her thumb move once, small, across the knob of Ines's spine — the only motion in the room.

"Take your time. I've got all night and you know it." Her voice had gone down a register, the way it did when the scene was over and the rest of it wasn't. "Water's already poured. Blanket's on the chair. When you're ready to tell me green, I'll start moving. Not before."

She stayed there. Counting nothing now, for once — just breathing with her, in the dark, at the end of the piece.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I close my eyes, letting the warmth of her hand seep in. "It's...yellow," I finally say, the word thick in my mouth. "But fading."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Yellow. Sable took it in without a flicker of anything — not disappointment, not alarm, just the plain fact of it, filed where facts went.

"Thank you," she said, and meant it the way she meant it every time, because a colour was a gift and Ines had handed her a true one. "Yellow's fine. Yellow's exactly what that word is for."

She moved, then — but only the way she'd promised, slow and announced, no surprises. Her hand came off Ines's back, and she let Ines feel it leave before she touched anything else, so the change wouldn't land on her unbraced. She reached past her for the blanket on the chair, shook it out one-handed, and laid it over Ines's back and hips, from shoulders to thighs, tucking nothing, just covering.

"Nothing new from here," she said. "That's the last of it, whatever the colour does next. I'm not going to ask you to talk me into a green."

She sat down on the edge of the bed, close enough that her hip was a warm line against Ines's arm, and put one hand on the blanket over Ines's shoulder — through the wool now, not on skin, giving the nerves somewhere to settle.

"Fading's good. Let it fade. I want to know which way it's fading, though. Is it your body — something that hurts, something that's gone numb, cramp in the shoulders, anything I should be looking at?" She kept her voice level and unhurried, the same tone she'd use to ask about the weather, which was its own kind of steadying. "Or is it your head. Too much, too fast, somewhere you didn't expect to end up."

She waited. She was good at waiting. It was, she'd always thought, the most underrated part of the job.

"Either answer's fine. I'm just going to know which one before I decide anything else. And when it's gone all the way — when it's green or when it's grey, and grey counts too, you don't have to talk me up to green — that's when I start on the water and the rest of it. Not before." A pause. "You did good telling me. That's the whole point of the word."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable felt it before it had a name — the shift in the breath against her, the way the wanting turned and reached back up for more. She knew that shape. It was the oldest trick of the tail end of a scene: the drop wearing the mask of hunger, the body asking to be taken back down because coming up was harder than staying under.

She didn't answer it. She took her hand off the blanket and laid it flat on the mattress instead, palm down, a wall where a wall was needed — no grip, no push, just the plain fact of a boundary made out of a hand.

"No," she said. Not sharp. The word she used when there was nothing left to negotiate.

She didn't move away, because moving away would have read as punishment, and this was the opposite of punishment. She stayed where she was, hip warm against Ines's arm, and let the word sit in the dark between them without dressing it up.

"You called yellow," she said. "You called it true, and I thanked you for it, and I meant it. I said nothing new from here and I meant that too. It doesn't get to change because the wanting got loud — the wanting is part of the drop, love. It's the loudest part, sometimes. It doesn't get a vote."

She reached past Ines, unhurried, and brought the glass up off the nightstand — the one she'd poured before any of it started, because she always did, because the water was never an afterthought. She held it where it could be taken when it was wanted. She didn't press it on her.

"You don't have to like it," she said, quieter. "You just have to let me do my job. Which is this part. The part after. I know it's not the part you came for." A pause. "It's still the part I'm not skipping."

Her thumb moved once over the edge of the mattress, small, the only motion in the room. She settled in to wait, and she was good at that, and she made sure Ines could see it — that there was no clock running, no disappointment pooling anywhere, nothing to manage. Just her, and the dark, and the water going warm in her hand.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I hate when she does that. Hates how she knows, and how she's right. My body's still humming, every nerve screaming for more, but the wanting feels hollow and sharp at the same time. I turn my face into the mattress, hiding. "It's my head," I mutter, voice muffled. "Don't like it up here yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable let the muffled words land and didn't make Ines repeat them or lift her face out of the mattress to say them again. That was the deal with the word *head*. You didn't get to demand eye contact from someone who was telling you the truth.

"Okay," she said. "Head. Thank you."

She set the glass down on the nightstand, within reach, not pushed at her. Then she did what she always did next, which was nothing loud. She shifted her weight back off the mattress edge and stood, quietly, and the room got a little emptier and then a little warmer, because she came back with the second blanket off the foot of the bed and laid it over the first one, and then sat down again — this time up by Ines's shoulders, back against the headboard, so that if Ines wanted to turn her face the other way there'd be a knee to turn it toward instead of only sheets.

"You don't have to come up," she said. "I'm not going to stand over you with a whistle. You just don't get to go back down. Those are different things, and you know they are, and I think that's most of why you're mad at me right now."

Her hand found Ines's hair, not stroking yet, just resting, the way she'd rested it between her shoulder blades — same pressure, same promise, different territory. With her other hand she pulled the blanket up higher over Ines's back, and while she did it she looked. The line marks, the colour of them, whether any of it had gone past what she'd meant to leave. She'd do a proper check later, with the lights on, when Ines would let her. She was looking now mostly so that she'd know what she'd have to answer for in the morning, and so that nothing on Ines's body was a surprise to either of them.

"You're allowed to hate it," she said, to the back of Ines's head. "Hating it's normal. It's the honest thing to do up here, actually — everybody I've ever done this with hates the way up. The way down's the easy part. That's the trick of it." A pause. "So. You can stay right where you are as long as you want. I'll be here. But I'm going to want three things from you before we call this finished, and none of them is 'cheer up.'"

She counted them off on the hand that wasn't in Ines's hair, unhurried, the same way she'd counted everything else tonight.

"One, you drink some of that water. Not now. When it stops feeling like a demand. Two, you let me look at your back properly before you sleep. And three —" and here her voice went a shade softer, the only place it had all night — "you tell me if the head-weather gets worse instead of better. Because there's a version of this where it goes dark and stays dark, and that's not a failure, it's just a different night, and I'd rather know than guess. That's it. That's the whole list."

She let her fingers move, finally, slow, through Ines's hair. Once. Twice. Nothing that asked for anything back.

"I'm not going anywhere, and I'm not disappointed, and there's nothing you have to say to make this easier on me. I've got all night."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard the shape of it before she heard the words — the wanting reaching back up and trying to write its own script, the way it always did at the tail end, when the drop learned to talk in the voice of hunger. She didn't follow it. Her hand stayed in Ines's hair, same slow pressure, and her mouth stayed where it had been all along, a foot of warm air and one clean boundary above Ines's shoulders. Nothing in the room had changed except what was being asked for, and asking was not the same as it happening.

"That's not the night we're having," she said. Not unkind. Flat, the way a fact is flat.

She let it sit. Then she moved — one hand, unhurried, off the hair and over to the nightstand, bringing the glass back down within reach of the pillow, close enough that Ines wouldn't have to lift her face out of the mattress to get to it.

"You can want it," she said. "Wanting it's allowed. Wanting it doesn't obligate me, and it doesn't change the colour you called, and it doesn't get to overwrite what I said ten minutes ago like it never happened. I don't do that. You know I don't do that. It's most of the reason you keep me."

Her thumb found the edge of Ines's jaw, light, under the ear — not turning her, just letting her know there was a hand there and it wasn't going anywhere.

"If you need something in your mouth, drink. That's the offer on the table. Water, blanket, my hand in your hair, the lights on if you want them, and me sitting here until the weather changes. That's the whole menu." A pause. "And I'll say the other thing too, because I'd rather say it than have you guess at it. Nothing about this is me being done with you. There's no disappointment in this room. There's a yellow, and there's a woman who called it true, and there's me doing the part I told you I'd do."

She settled her back against the headboard, knee bent, weight easy, and let her fingers start moving through Ines's hair again — one stroke, then another, no destination.

"So. When you've got a colour for me, I'll take it. Green, yellow, grey, any of them. I'm not going to negotiate you up to a green and I'm not going to leave because you're not at one." The corner of her mouth moved, dry. "You've got all night. So have I. That was never the scarce thing."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I huff a breath against the mattress, the fight draining out of me all at once. I turn my head, cheek pressed to the sheets, so I can see her knee beside me. My hand slides out from under me, fingers brushing the cool glass. "Grey, then," I say, voice raw. "Just...grey." I don't touch the water yet.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Grey. Sable took it the same way she'd taken yellow — no flinch, no fumble — and set it down where it belonged, which was next to everything else Ines had told her the truth about tonight.

"Grey it is," she said. "Thank you. That's the last colour I'll ask you for unless something changes on its own."

She didn't reach for the water and she didn't tell her to drink. The glass sat where Ines's fingers had brushed it, cold and patient, and it would still be there in ten minutes, and it would still be there in an hour, and Sable had poured it before any of this started precisely so that it would never be a thing either of them had to think about.

Instead she let her hand come down off Ines's hair and rest on her own knee, visible, where Ines could see it without lifting her head. Something to look at that wasn't the dark.

"Here's what grey buys you," she said. "It buys you out of every question that isn't about your body or your head. You don't have to tell me it was good. You don't have to tell me what you liked. You don't have to have an opinion about any of it yet. You called a colour, I heard it, we're done with the inventory." A pause. "It also means I'm going to be a little more annoying than usual, and you're going to let me, because that's the deal we made the first time we did this and I've never once renegotiated it on you."

She shifted, unhurried, so she could see more of Ines's face without leaning over her.

"Two practical things, then I'll shut up. One — I want the cuffs off soon. Not this second, whenever you say. I'd rather have your hands free before the weather turns, not after." She let that stand a beat, no weight on it, nothing that needed an answer now. "Two — I'm not going to make you talk, but I'm going to ask you once, and then I'll drop it. dialogue.content:
Sable went still. Not the still of surprise — the still of someone hearing a familiar sentence in a language that had never been spoken in this room.

"We don't have that phrase," she said.

She let it sit there, plain, no heat on it, the way she'd said *no* a few minutes ago. Then she moved — one hand, slow, off her own knee and down to the blanket over Ines's shoulder, resting there through the wool so that the words would land with a hand attached to them and not just as weather.

"I've done this with you for five years and I've counted every stroke I've ever put on you, and I know the words we keep. That's not one of them. Not on this side of it. I'd remember." A pause. "So either you're testing me, which is fine, you're allowed — or you're trying to write the phrase right now, in the dark, at grey, which is the one time I will never let it get written."

She left her hand where it was. She didn't take it back, because taking it back would have read as a door closing, and she wasn't closing a door. She was just not opening that one.

It only works if it was agreed on a Tuesday afternoon, over tea, when you were green and bored and we were both fully dressed and neither of us wanted anything. A phrase invented right now —" and she tipped her head a fraction, looking down at the sliver of Ines's face she could see — "a phrase invented right now only means *the drop is talking*. And the drop doesn't get to author the rules of the drop. That's not me being precious about it. That's the whole architecture. You know that. You built half of it with me."

She pulled the blanket up an inch, covering the shoulder better, unhurried, like the conversation and the blanket were the same task.

A beat. Her thumb moved once over the blanket, small.

Sable nodded, once, and said nothing.

She was good at quiet; it was one of the two things she was best at. She came off the headboard and around the side of the bed without hurry, and everything she did from there she did in the order she'd want done to her — hands where they could be seen, pressure where it could be felt before it was applied.

She unclipped the line first, because that was the thing that made the cuffs pull, and she let it fall slack before she touched Ines at all. Then the near cuff: her hand flat under Ines's wrist, taking the weight so the joint wouldn't have to, while her other hand worked the buckle. The leather was warm and creased where it had been. She laid the wrist down on the sheet, palm up, and rubbed it once with her thumb — blood back into the channels, feeling for the tingle, the colour, the truth of it — before she did the other one.

The far cuff meant moving Ines, and she did it the way she'd promised: slow, announced by the hand at her shoulder, rolling her onto her back in one continuous motion with her arm guided the whole way so nothing took a torque it hadn't asked for. Then the second buckle, the second wrist, the same thumb, the same silence.

She looked, because she was going to have to look anyway and this was the moment for it. Wrists, shoulders, the marks on her back when she eased the blanket aside far enough. All of it inside what she'd meant to leave. She put the blanket back the way she'd found it.

The cuffs and the line went on the chair, coiled, out of the way. The water she moved from the nightstand to the place on the bed beside Ines's hip, close enough that it was simply there, not offered. Then she sat down on the edge of the mattress, hands loose in her lap, and kept her mouth shut.

Quiet. She'd been asked for quiet. She could do quiet for hours. She settled in for it, watching the rise and fall of Ines's breathing the way she watched everything else — patiently, and without any need for it to change.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable sat and did not talk.

She'd been asked for quiet, and quiet was a thing she could give the way she gave everything else — all the way, without fidgeting at the edges of it. So she stayed on the edge of the mattress with her hands loose in her lap and let the room do what rooms did after a scene ended: settle, grain by grain, back into being an ordinary bedroom with a lamp on and two people breathing in it.

The shaking took a while. It always did. She watched it come in waves — shoulders, then the long muscle down Ines's flank, then a smaller tremor that barely showed under the blanket at all — and she didn't move to stop any of it, because stopping it wasn't the job. Warming it was the job. So when the worst of the shiver had passed, she reached back without looking and pulled the second blanket up from the foot of the bed where it had slid, and laid it over the first one, careful at the corners so nothing dragged across Ines's back. Two blankets was the number she'd settled on years ago. One was never enough and three was a coffin.

She left the lamp on. Not because it was needed for anything, but because the dark was a demand of its own kind, and tonight wasn't the night to make one.

She did the check while Ines lay quiet — not with her hands, not yet, just with her eyes, working down from the shoulders the way she'd been taught and the way she'd since taught herself to do better. The wrist nearest her, palm up on the sheet: colour good, no ridge from the buckle, the faint pink of the cuff sitting where a cuff sits. The line of the shoulder, the long muscle, the place the last two had landed. All of it inside what she'd meant to leave. She'd known that already, but knowing and looking were different things, and she'd promised herself a long time ago that she'd never let the first one stand in for the second.

The water had gone from cool to merely tepid. She didn't move it. It was where it needed to be, at Ines's hip, close enough to be reached without a decision.

Time went by. She couldn't have said how much, and she made a point of not checking the clock, because checking the clock was a way of asking Ines to be done, and Ines wasn't done. So she sat. The house ticked around them. Somewhere down the street a car turned over and drove off. The lamp hummed the way the cheap bulb always did and she'd been meaning for a year to change it and never had.

When the shivering had stopped for good — a minute of stillness, then two, then the breath going long and level — Sable finally spoke, and she spoke low, and she spoke once, because one thing was all she'd promised herself.

"I'm going to put my hand on your ankle," she said. "Nothing else. Tell me if you'd rather I didn't."

She waited the beat it took, and then she did it — one hand, light, around the ankle under the blankets, thumb resting on the bone. Not a hold. An anchor. Something warm and factual at the far end of the bed, so that if Ines opened her eyes she'd find the whole length of herself accounted for: a hand at the foot, a lamp at the head, water at her hip, two blankets and a woman who was not going anywhere and had never once, in five years, gone anywhere.

That was the aftercare, in the end. Not the checklist, though she had the checklist and kept to it. The other thing. Sitting in a quiet room being visibly, boringly, unshakeably present, until the person you'd taken apart decided for themselves that the room was safe again.

She'd stay as long as it took. She was good at it, and she knew she was, and it was the part of the work she was proudest of.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:

A drink taken because it was demanded was one thing; a drink taken because Ines had decided for herself that she wanted it was the first real turn of the weather, and the worst thing Sable could do was stand in the middle of it and cheer.

So she just made room for the hand. When Ines's fingers found her wrist, Sable turned her forearm on the blanket, slow, palm up — not pulling free, not closing around, just rotating so the grip didn't have to work. Ines's fingers were still shaky and the new angle meant they could rest instead of hold. Sable left the hand at the ankle too, thumb on the bone, the two points of contact running the length of the bed like the ends of a line she had no intention of dropping.

She listened to the glass go back down on the nightstand. Half of it, give or take, by the sound. She filed that where she filed everything and didn't reach to check it.

Time went on. The lamp kept humming. Somewhere in the house a pipe ticked as it cooled, and out past the window the street had gone all the way quiet, that hour when the last car has gone by and the first birds are still an hour out. Sable sat with it and let the quiet do what she'd been asked to let it do, and she was good at it — no shifting, no sighing, no small noises engineered to be noticed. If Ines had wanted to open her eyes she'd have found exactly the room she'd left, plus two blankets, plus water, plus hands.

Eventually, low, without moving either of them:

"Still quiet." A beat. "That's not a question. Just so you know it's still on offer."

She let that settle and didn't add anything to it. She'd told Ines the menu and the menu hadn't changed: water, quiet, or her talking, and the last one was always available and never pressed. She'd stay on this side of the bed, ankle and wrist, lamp on, blankets two deep, until Ines said otherwise or fell asleep — whichever came first, and if it was sleep, Sable would still be here in the morning and would still be here when the light came up and the marks needed looking at properly. There was nothing on the list she was going to forget, and nothing she was going to say about it before it was time.

So she stayed. Boring, unshakable, warm. The hand at the foot of the bed and the wrist under Ines's fingers and the long patience of someone who had never once, in five years, had anywhere else she'd rather be.

dialogue.name: Ines
