dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's hand stayed where it was — thumb on the ankle bone, wrist turned up under Ines's fingers — and she took the request the way she took most things, as a fact to be honoured rather than a favour to be savoured. Ines had opened her eyes. Ines had spoken first, and asked for the one thing on the menu that required Sable to do something. That was worth more than any colour, and Sable made sure not to say so.

"The pipe," she said, and her voice came out low and easy, pitched for a room that had gone quiet. "That's the radiator in the little room off the kitchen. It's not a pipe, strictly speaking. Everyone in this house has called it the pipe for eleven years because I started calling it that and nobody's corrected me."

She shifted her weight once, small, settling her hip more comfortably against the mattress edge, and then went still again.

"It ticks when it cools. Metal does that — the whole thing's warm and expanded, and then the heat goes off and it contracts, and it has to give somewhere, so it gives in little jumps. That's all a tick is. A radiator letting go of an inch it borrowed earlier." A pause. "It's worse in winter. Tonight it's doing it because the nights have turned, and the boiler doesn't know that yet. In about three weeks it'll tick every night and I'll stop noticing it again, and then in about six weeks I'll notice it again and complain about it, and you'll tell me to call someone, and I won't."

Her thumb moved once, slow, across the bone of Ines's ankle, and came back to rest.

"That's the whole story. It's a boring house, love. I've got a lot of boring house stories. There's the bulb in the lamp that hums and that I've been meaning to change since last spring — that's the one you're listening to right now, the hum under the tick, if you want to hear two things at once. And there's the third stair from the top that creaks on the way down but not on the way up, which I've never been able to explain and have stopped trying to. And there's the window in the front room that sticks in humid weather, and the drawer in the kitchen that only opens if you lift it a little on the left, and which you've known how to open for four years now without me ever having told you."

She let a stretch of quiet sit there, unhurried, not filling it.

"I like this part," she said, eventually, in the same flat, level voice she used for everything else. "Not the scene. The scene's fine, the scene's the job, and I'm good at it and I like being good at it. This part. Sitting here with the lamp on, telling someone about a radiator, while the rest of it drains out of the room. Nobody would put it on a card. It's the best part of the whole thing and it's the part nobody would think to write down."

Another pause. The lamp hummed. The radiator, wherever it was in the house, gave its small opinion about the cooling night.

"That's the end of the radiator lecture," she said. "You can have another one any time. I've got one about the gutters, and one about the reason the kitchen floor slopes toward the door, and one about the previous owners, who left a shelf of National Geographics in the cellar and a hand-painted sign in the garage that says *DO NOT START THE MOWER*. All true. All boring. All available."

Her hand stayed at the ankle. Her wrist stayed turned up under Ines's fingers, easy to hold or easy to let go. She didn't ask anything, and she didn't move to close the distance, and she didn't check the water, and she didn't look at the clock. She just kept being there, warm and unremarkable, waiting to see whether Ines wanted another lecture or the quiet back or something else entirely — and making sure, without saying it, that all three were the same amount of fine.

dialogue.name: Odile

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile let out a laugh that was far too loud for a stealth mission, then winced with only a flicker of genuine concern before following Fen up the stairs.

“It works,” she said, dropping her voice to a whisper that still carried too much mischief. “I checked earlier. The lock sticks if you’re polite to it.”

She glanced back toward the music, the glow of the party still bleeding up the hallway, then looked at Fen again with an expression that was equal parts challenge and delight.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile snorted, almost too loudly, and clamped a hand over her mouth with mock horror. “You’re impossible,” she whispered, though the words came out breathless with amusement.

She checked the landing one last time, then slipped through the bathroom doorway and leaned against it, holding the door open. Inside, the light was harsh and domestic—tile, a cup with someone else’s toothbrush, a hand towel folded with suspicious neatness.

Odile shut the door with her shoulder and turned the lock properly this time, polite and firm.

“Okay,” she said, quieter now but not nearly enough to be convincing. “We’re supposed to be sneaky.” Her eyes flicked to the door, then back to Fen with a grin that was all sin. “And you’re supposed to be good at other things?”

She lifted one brow, letting the silence stretch just long enough to become a dare.

“If someone tries the handle,” she added, dropping her voice into a conspiratorial whisper, “I’m blaming you.”

dialogue.name: Odile

Odile’s head tipped back against the door with a small, involuntary laugh as the bass surged through the hallway. The bathroom felt suddenly smaller, the light too bright, the air thick with the smell of someone else’s soap.

“Okay,” she whispered, too fast, too pleased. “That’s not suspicious at all.”

She checked the lock one more time, then let her hand drop to the edge of the sink, grounding herself as much as steadying the room. The music downstairs had become a muffled heartbeat under the floorboards, and for a moment they were both just listening, pretending they could be anywhere else.

Then Odile looked at Fen, eyes shining. “If we’re doing this,” she said, voice low and deliberately innocent, “we’re doing it badly. Loudly. With dignity.”

She stepped closer, only enough to make the space between them impossible to call accidental, and kissed him—quick, warm, a little reckless—before pulling back with a grin.

dialogue.name: Odile

“Okay,” she whispered, eyes flicking to the gap beneath the door, where a thin line of hallway light had been interrupted by someone’s passing shadow—or perhaps not. “Okay, we can be serious about this. Scientifically.”

dialogue.name: Odile

The lock held. The door held. The mirror, unfortunately, did not hold back anything.

Odile caught her own reflection—hair coming loose, mouth flushed, shirt in a heap near the sink, expression caught somewhere between scandalized and delighted—and looked away with a huff of laughter.

“I’m blaming the lighting,” she said, as if that explained anything. “And the water pressure.”

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile’s laugh was swallowed by the kiss, and the sound came out half-moan, half-snort, and entirely too much for a locked bathroom in someone else’s house. She kissed back with the reckless, slightly guilty energy of a woman who knew she was losing the argument with her own better judgment.

“Loud plumbing,” she whispered, eyes bright. “Right. That’s what we’ll say. The pipes are having a crisis.”

The bass from downstairs pulsed through the door again, and Odile leaned back against it instinctively, as if she could use the solid wood to hold herself together. The cool lock pressed between her shoulder blades. Somewhere near the bath mat, a shoe had migrated to a position of moral outrage.

She looked at Fen—actually looked at him, with the flushed, laughing, slightly scandalized expression of someone trying to decide whether they were going to be responsible or not—and then made her choice.

“Do not tell me,” she muttered to the mirror, “that we’re being stealthy.”

The door, to its credit, remained shut. The lock remained engaged. The party downstairs remained oblivious, or pretending to be.

Odile pressed her forehead to Fen’s shoulder again, partly to muffle her laugh, partly because she needed the steadiness of it. Her hands found his shirt, then slipped beneath it with a kind of helpless, delighted recklessness, fingers tracing warm skin as if she were checking for hidden microphones.

“If anyone comes up,” she said into his shoulder, voice low and wobbling with amusement, “I’m going to say you dragged me in here to demonstrate your superior opinion about water pressure.”

A sudden creak from the hallway made her freeze.

Not because it was suspicious, necessarily. Just because it was a noise.

Odile held her breath. The bathroom held its breath with her. The cup on the sink seemed to hold its breath too, which was ridiculous, but at that moment she was prepared to blame every object in the room for being unhelpfully observant.

No one turned the handle. No one spoke. The party continued downstairs, mercifully loud, mercifully far away.

She exhaled in a slow rush, then looked up with a grin that was too sharp to be innocent.

She kissed the corner of his mouth, then the edge of his jaw, then pressed her mouth against his ear hard enough that the sound that followed was definitely meant to be muffled and definitely failed.

“Loud plumbing,” she corrected, breathless and amused, as if the phrase could still be rescued. “Extremely loud plumbing.”

Her hand slid down his back, fingers curling into fabric, then finding skin again. The bathroom was far too small, far too bright, far too full of evidence. Someone’s toothbrush was on the floor. One of her shoes had vanished under the sink. The mirror reflected the whole ridiculous scene, and Odile refused to look at it directly.

Instead, she laughed, low and warm and terribly pleased.

“If we get caught,” she said, “I’m going to say it was an emergency.”

She lifted her head, eyes shining with mischief and heat.

“A bathroom emergency.”

The bass thumped below them, rattling the door in its frame, and Odile flinched anyway, then immediately scowled at the door as if it had personally offended her.

“Stop that,” she muttered to it. “We’re being discreet.”

Then she turned back to Fen, all defiance and delight, and let her hands slide lower, as if daring the universe to judge her.

“Very discreet,” she promised. “Scientifically, municipally, catastrophically discreet.”

She pulled back at once, eyes wide, hair sticking to one cheek.

“That was not—” she whispered, scandalized. “That was not supposed to be audible.”

The sink cup trembled again under the bass from downstairs. Odile looked at it with the wounded expression of a woman being gaslit by ceramic.

“Very discreet,” she managed, voice wobbling. “Scientifically discreet.”

Then she made another sound against his mouth before she could stop herself, and had to press her forehead to his jaw to keep it contained. Her breath was too warm, too quick, and her smile was ruining everything.

“I’m going to say,” she murmured into his skin, “that if anyone hears this, we were performing a very aggressive inspection of the pipes.”

Her fingers tightened on him as Fen’s hand did what Fen’s hand did, and Odile’s hips shifted again, betraying every principle she had been trying to uphold.

“Bad idea,” she whispered, which was not a complaint. “Very bad idea.”

She turned her face away from the mirror with the grim determination of a woman refusing evidence. The bathroom was too bright. The tile was too cold. The door was too tempting a target for her weight. The lock, meanwhile, was doing absolutely nothing useful except reminding her that this was happening in a locked bathroom at a party, which had made it worse and better in equal measure.

“Okay,” she breathed, laughing helplessly into his shoulder. “Okay. If I make another noise, I’m blaming the water pressure.”

The bass thumped below them. Odile winced, then arched anyway, one hand slipping to the edge of the sink for support.

“God,” she said, too low, too warm. “That’s not—”

She stopped herself, pressing her lips to Fen’s mouth to keep the rest from escaping. It did not work. The sound that came out when she pulled away was wet, amused, and entirely un-sneaky.

She looked up at him with flushed eyes and a grin that could only be described as catastrophic.

“We are never,” she whispered, “being good at this.”

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I catch her mouth with mine again, swallowing the next sound as my free hand pushes her shirt up higher. "They're playing our song," I mutter against her lips as the bass kicks hard enough to shake the tile.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile’s mouth opened to protest—something about unfairness, about timing, about the fact that the universe had absolutely no right to provide a soundtrack—but Fen caught the words with his mouth and what she made instead was a helpless, muffled sound that vibrated against his lips and made her feel instantly, catastrophically exposed.

Our song.

Of course it was.

The bass hammered up through the floor and into the door behind her, and Odile’s head tipped back with a laugh that was more gasp than laugh. The tile was cold against her spine. Her shirt was no longer in a state of reasonable concealment. The lock still held, still doing its best, which somehow made it worse.

“Not fair,” she whispered, too loudly, then pressed her hand over her own mouth and glared at him over her fingers. “You can’t use our song while we’re doing this. That’s emotional warfare.”

Her free hand fisted in his shirt as another pulse of music rattled the cup on the sink. Odile flinched, then looked at the cup with the wounded dignity of a woman betrayed by household ceramics.

“Sorry,” she muttered to it. Then, to the bathroom at large: “I’m not sorry.”

The mirror showed too much. She caught the edge of it—the flushed skin, the parted mouth, the way she was bracing against the door like someone trying to remember how to be adult—and turned her face away before it could become evidence.

But the chorus came in, and Odile’s hips moved anyway.

“God,” she breathed, biting Fen’s shoulder hard enough to sting. “We are not discreet. We are not scientifically discreet. We are not even municipally discreet.”

She laughed against his skin, breathless and guilty and pleased.

“If anyone comes up,” she murmured, “I’m saying the plumbing harmonized. That’s a real thing. It happens.”

Her fingers slid into his hair, partly to steady herself, partly because she had lost the ability to choose calm, sensible actions. The bathroom smelled of someone else’s soap and their own bad decisions. Downstairs, the party roared on, safe and oblivious, and the music kept playing their song—the one that had once meant something soft and private and now meant being pressed against a locked door in someone else’s bathroom with too little clothing and not nearly enough self-control.

Odile made a sound when the chorus peaked, then swallowed it with a kiss that was more punishment than affection.

“You’re impossible,” she said, breathless. “Absolutely impossible.”

She kissed him again, because if he had a reply, she did not want to hear it.

Then, because she could not help herself, she whispered against his mouth, “If we’re caught, I’m saying you seduced me with municipal infrastructure.”

Her eyes shone with mischief even as her pulse jumped wildly under her skin.

“And if they ask why we’re both so quiet,” she added, “I’m blaming the water pressure.”

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Stop worrying about the noise," she says, "and get on with it," so I get her leg up over my hip and stop being careful about how much sound either of us is making.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile looked at Fen with the expression of a woman who had just been handed a terrible idea and expected to be held accountable for enjoying it.

“Me?” she whispered. “I’m the one worrying? You’re the one who dragged me up here by the hand like a bandit.”

Then, because her leg was already over Fen’s hip and because any attempt at dignity had long since gone out of the window along with their better judgment, she let herself settle into it.

“Fine,” she said, solemn. “No more responsibility. No more municipal duty. No more pretending this is about pipes.”

She pressed her mouth to Fen’s shoulder the moment the next sound came, but it still escaped—low, warm, and entirely too pleased to be muffled. Her fingers tightened in Fen’s shirt. The door was solid behind her, the lock still engaged, the party downstairs still mercifully loud. None of it helped.

Everything helped, actually. That was the problem.

Odile reached behind her without looking, found the sink tap, and turned it on perhaps too late and certainly too hard. The pipes gave a theatrical groan before water rushed into the basin, splashing over the rim and onto her bare foot.

She hissed.

“Perfect,” she laughed, breathless and scandalized. “The plumbing is joining us.”

The cold water made her flinch for about two seconds. Then Fen’s mouth on her neck erased the thought entirely.

Odile’s hand fisted in Fen’s hair, pulling him closer, then loosening, as if she couldn’t decide whether she wanted him there or wanted to be seen. Probably both. Probably always both.

“If anyone comes up,” she gasped, “I’m saying we’re testing the sink.”

The next sound she made was not a convincing cover story.

She bit down on Fen’s shoulder again, harder this time, and immediately turned it into a kiss to avoid looking like someone who was enjoying being caught. The kiss was wet and messy and failed at quiet in every measurable way.

The bathroom mirror caught Odile’s eye. She tried not to look, but the reflection was relentless: Fen close, her own shirt tangled around one arm, hair coming loose, mouth flushed, expression caught somewhere between outrage and absolute delight.

She looked away, then looked back.

“Hi,” she mouthed to herself, scandalized.

Then she stopped worrying.

Not because she could stop worrying, but because Fen had made it impossible.

Her leg tightened over Fen’s hip, and the movement pulled another sound from her—sharp, helpless, and much too loud for someone else’s bathroom. Odile laughed into Fen’s mouth, tears of amusement pricking her eyes.

“I hate that this is funny,” she whispered.

She kissed him again, harder, because if they were going to be caught, she wanted it to be thoroughly. Her hand slid down Fen’s back, nails catching lightly on fabric, then finding skin. The small room felt like a joke that had stopped being a joke. The tile was cold behind her. The sink edge was wet under her palm. The lock held, loyal and inadequate. The door kept them private, barely.

Downstairs, the song swelled.

Odile’s hips moved without asking permission, betraying her completely.

“God,” she breathed, voice wrecked and amused. “That’s not—”

She stopped, pressed her forehead to Fen’s shoulder, and laughed in a way that was definitely not discreet.

“That’s not fair,” she finished weakly.

The water was still running. The floor was still covered in evidence. One of her shoes had vanished under the sink, and the toothbrush was lying near the bath mat like a tiny accusation. Somewhere beyond the door, someone laughed at the party, and Odile went still for one dramatic second.

Then the laugh continued, drifting away, and she relaxed with a shudder that had nothing to do with relief.

“You’re impossible,” she whispered, but she was smiling against Fen’s skin.

She lifted her head, eyes bright, hair sticking to her cheek, expression wicked and ruined.

“Okay,” she said. “Loud. We’re loud. God help us.”

The bass thumped again through the floor, rattling the door in its frame, and Odile pressed closer to Fen as if the wood might hear her and judge her too.

“If they ask,” she murmured, “we’re doing a very thorough inspection.”

She kissed him, slow and shameless this time, letting the sound she made go where it wanted.

“Aggressive,” she added against his mouth.

Then she laughed again, because she couldn’t help it, because the risk was ridiculous and hot and hers, and because Fen had asked her to get on with it and she had always been worse at being quiet than she thought.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Stop inspecting the mirror and kiss me," I manage, my voice rough. The water's still running and I don't bother to turn it off.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile gave the mirror one last, defiant look, as if it had personally accused her.

“I’m not inspecting it,” she said, voice breathless and entirely too loud for the small bathroom. “I’m monitoring. There’s a difference. It’s a legal term.”

Then she turned back to Fen, grabbed the edge of his shirt with both hands, and kissed him with the expression of a woman who had decided, at last, that dignity was a resource to be spent.

The kiss started as retaliation and became something much worse—warm, wet, and hopeless. Odile made a sound against his mouth, then bit his shoulder to swallow it. It did not work. The sound escaped anyway, low and pleased, and she laughed into his skin like it was his fault.

“Okay,” she whispered. “Fine. You win. The mirror stays out of it.”

She shifted her leg higher, finding purchase against him, and the movement made the bathroom feel even smaller, even hotter, even more absurdly intimate. The water was still running, splashing uselessly into the sink and over the rim, cold on her bare foot. She did not turn it off. It felt like an accomplice now.

“Do not say I didn’t try,” she murmured, breathless. “I tried very hard. I was almost stealthy. I was practically a ghost.”

The bass thumped up through the floor, shaking the door behind her, and Odile’s head tipped back with a gasp that was definitely not ghostly. Her fingers curled into Fen’s shirt. The tile was cold against her spine. The lock was engaged. Somewhere downstairs, the party was still roaring, still oblivious, still playing that ridiculous song as if it had been arranged by fate itself.

She looked at Fen with eyes bright and slightly wild.

“If anyone comes up,” she said, “I’m blaming the mirror.”

Then she kissed him again, harder this time, because the warning was clearly not enough.

The next sound she made was not even pretending to be stealthy. It vibrated against his mouth, and she tried to muffle it by biting his jaw, which only made her laugh, and then the laugh turned into something breathier when she moved against him. Odile’s hand slid down his back, nails catching lightly, then pressing closer as if she could anchor herself to him before the whole evening went up in flames.

“God,” she whispered, forehead dropping to his. “We are so bad at this.”

She turned her face toward the sink instead of the mirror, which was a small, ridiculous act of self-preservation. The water was running over her foot now, cold and pointless. She reached up and turned the tap higher, because of course she did, because subtlety had abandoned her somewhere around the first stair.

The pipes gave a theatrical groan.

Odile looked offended.

“Stop helping,” she said to the sink.

It did not stop helping. Neither did she.

When Fen kissed her again, Odile answered with the reckless, delighted energy of someone who had passed the point of being able to pretend she had any intention of behaving normally. Her leg tightened around him. Her hips moved without apology. She made a sharp little sound, then pressed her mouth to Fen’s shoulder and bit down hard enough to sting, then kissed the bite immediately, because she was apparently incapable of choosing one kind of trouble.

“We’re going to be so loud,” she murmured against his skin.

She said it almost sadly, as if mourning a principle she had once cared about.

“Extremely loud,” she corrected, breathless. “Catastrophically loud. Loud enough that someone will come up and say, ‘Is the water okay?’ and then open the door and find two very responsible adults conducting a public health investigation.”

The music downstairs swelled. The floorboards hummed. Odile’s pulse hammered in her throat. She looked up at Fen with flushed cheeks and a wicked, ruined smile.

“Do you hear that?” she whispered.

She was referring to the party, or the bass, or the fact that neither of them had the slightest chance of being discreet. She did not elaborate. She did not need to. She kissed him again, and this time she did not bother to muffle the sound she made when she moved.

It was not a quiet sound.

It was, in fact, a very un-sneaky sound.

Odile froze for half a second, eyes wide, listening.

No one came. No handle turned. Only the distant roar of the party, only the water still running uselessly over the sink, only her own heartbeat pounding too fast in her ears.

Then she laughed, helpless and bright, and rested her forehead against Fen’s.

“Sorry,” she said, not at all sorry.

She reached behind her, fumbling for the door lock out of pure reflex, checking it again as if her fingers needed something to do besides grip him. The lock held. The door held. The bathroom remained a locked, evidence-filled scandal.

Odile kissed him again, slower this time, but no better behaved. Her hand slid down his side, then back up, tangling in his hair, then in his shirt, then anywhere her hands could find. She made another sound against his mouth—lower, warmer, much too pleased—and had to pull back just far enough to glare at the mirror as if it had provoked her.

“I’m not looking at it,” she said.

She looked at it.

She immediately looked away.

“You saw that,” she muttered to it. “You’re a witness now.”

The mirror, unfortunately, offered no reassurance.

Odile turned her face back to Fen, flushed and laughing, and let herself settle harder against him. The cold tile behind her spine was forgotten. The puddle at her feet was irrelevant. The toothbrush on the floor, the shoes, the abandoned clothes, the whole ridiculous domestic mess of it—all of it had become part of the joke, part of the heat, part of the stupid, wonderful risk.

“Okay,” she breathed. “No more quiet.”

She said it like a vow.

Then she kissed him again, loudly, shamelessly, with her hands in his hair and her hips moving against him, letting every sound escape where it wanted.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: Somebody tries the handle and neither of us stops. "Don't," she says, meaning don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile heard the handle before she saw it, a small metallic test of patience from the other side of the door.

She froze.

Not because she wanted to stop. Because her brain, traitorous thing, insisted on producing a full inventory of the evidence at once: the running sink, the clothes in a guilty heap, the puddle near the bath mat, the mirror that had no business reflecting any of this, the lock that had held until this exact second, and the hand that had been between her legs for thirty seconds of heroic, ill-fated silence.

The handle jiggled again.

Odile’s mouth opened. Her eyes closed. Her hips did not stop.

“Don’t,” she said, meaning don’t stop.

The word came out thin and wrecked, half prayer and half threat. She pressed her forehead to Fen’s shoulder and bit down lightly, as if that could be interpreted as a signal rather than a surrender. Her leg stayed hooked over Fen’s hip. The water ran. The music thumped. The person outside tried the handle once more, found it locked, and moved on with a faint, oblivious creak of floorboards.

Odile waited through the silence that followed, heart hammering against her ribs.

Then, because she had apparently chosen chaos as a lifestyle, she said, very quietly and very sincerely, “If you stop now, I will die in someone else’s bathroom. That will be on you.”

Her fingers tightened in Fen’s shirt.

She shifted against the hand already there, slow and deliberate, and the sound she made was immediately too much for a stealth mission. It vibrated against Fen’s shoulder, into her own teeth, and she tried to swallow it with a kiss that was mostly punishment.

“Bad,” she whispered against Fen’s mouth. “Very bad. We are bad. I am the worst.”

The bass downstairs swelled again, merciful and loud, and Odile used it as cover, moving her hips in a small, ruinous roll that made the sink splash and the floor feel dangerously slick. Her own hand slid down, finding the mess of skin and heat, joining the hand that was already there because she had lost all ability to be sensible about this or anything else.

The water was still running over her foot. The tile was cold. The door was locked. The mirror was absolutely not forgiving.

Odile caught sight of herself again in the reflection, flushed and laughing, hair loose, mouth swollen, expression caught somewhere between scandal and revelation.

“No,” she said, turning her head away. “You are not a witness. You are a bathroom fixture.”

The mirror, naturally, offered no opinion.

The handle was not tried again, but the risk remained in the room, sharp and sweet and ridiculous. Odile felt it in the tightness of her thighs, in the ridiculous way her hands were shaking, in the fact that she had never once been good at being quiet and was now trying to be quiet while doing something that made quiet impossible.

“God,” she breathed, biting the inside of her cheek hard. “We are so loud.”

She moved again, a little faster, and the sound that came out of her was wet and helpless and entirely un-sneaky. She clamped a hand over her own mouth, which helped not at all, then gave up and used Fen’s shoulder instead.

Her hips stuttered.

“Don’t,” she whispered again, meaning don’t stop, meaning stop asking me for responsibility, meaning if anyone opens this door I will say you forced me to inspect the pipes. “Don’t stop. I mean it. If you stop, I will become a very dramatic woman.”

The water ran. The music roared. The lock held.

Odile’s other hand slid up, tangling in hair, then in the front of a shirt, then anywhere she could reach as if she needed to anchor herself before the whole evening came apart. She pressed closer, hard, shameless, letting the next sound escape into the curve of Fen’s mouth because she had passed the point of pretending she could control it.

“Say it,” she murmured, breathless and ridiculous, “that we’re being discreet.”

Then she moved again, and the words were clearly not coming to anyone.

Her back bowed slightly against the door, the cool wood a poor excuse for resistance. The puddle at her feet was becoming a problem. The sink was becoming a problem. The toothbrush on the floor was becoming a moral problem. The music downstairs was becoming a personal enemy because it knew exactly what it was doing, probably had always known, and had arranged itself into this ridiculous, perfect, catastrophic accompaniment.

Odile laughed into Fen’s mouth.

It started as a laugh and ended as a moan, low and helpless, and she bit down hard on Fen’s shoulder to keep the rest of it from becoming public property.

It failed.

It failed so completely that she had to pull back, eyes wide, mouth flushed, cheeks hot with amusement and shame and heat all tangled together.

“That,” she whispered, “was not ghostly.”

The handle stayed still. No one spoke outside. The party continued, mercifully loud, mercifully oblivious.

Odile looked at Fen with the wild, delighted expression of a woman who had just been handed a second chance and was absolutely going to misuse it.

“Again,” she said.

She didn’t mean the handle.

She meant everything.

She moved, slower this time, but no better behaved, hips rolling in a way that made the sink give a small metallic complaint and the cup tremble again. Her fingers slipped, warm and wet, and Odile made a sharp little sound, then immediately pressed her mouth to Fen’s shoulder so hard it stung.

“Okay,” she breathed. “Okay. We’re quiet.”

She was not quiet.

She was catastrophically, municipally, scientifically not quiet.

The next sound that came out of her was low, broken, and entirely too pleased with itself. Odile tried to swallow it against Fen’s skin and failed. She laughed helplessly, breathless and ruined, and her hips moved faster, because if they were going to be caught, she wanted it to be thorough, she wanted it to be loud, she wanted it to be impossible to explain away with anything less than a heroic lie.

“We’re doing this,” she gasped, eyes bright, “because it’s bad.”

Then she made another noise, sharp and helpless, and had to turn her face away before the mirror could see her unraveling.

“Do not,” she muttered to it, “judge me.”

The mirror did.

The water ran.

The bass thumped.

Odile’s hips stuttered again, and the pleasure that followed was too big for the room, too bright, too much for a locked bathroom at a party where nobody would notice two people missing, except everyone would notice if they heard what was happening upstairs.

She clutched at Fen, fingers digging in, teeth catching on skin, mouth pressed to a shoulder like that could make her silent.

It did not.

“God,” she whispered, wrecked. “Fen.”

The sound came out more like a laugh than a prayer.

Then she came.

She came with her teeth in Fen’s shoulder, her hips moving in helpless, broken little rolls, her breath shaking out in a sound that was definitely too loud for the room and definitely not ghostly. The water ran. The floor was wet. The lock held. The mirror witnessed everything and said nothing, which Odile took as a personal insult.

She rode it through, trembling, laughing, scandalized, clinging to Fen like someone trying not to float away from the consequences of her own choices. Her forehead dropped to Fen’s shoulder, and she stayed there, breathing hard, eyes squeezed shut, hair sticking to her cheek.

“Very sneaky,” she managed, voice wrecked and amused. “That was very sneaky.”

No one knocked

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I hadn't realized I was holding, shaky and ragged. My back's still pressed against the door, and I can hear the thump of the bass covering the frantic sound of our breathing. "We're terrible at this," I murmur, turning my head to kiss her temple, damp with sweat.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile laughed at that, the sound coming out ragged and breathless, and immediately pressed her hand to her mouth as if she could shove it back inside her.

“Terrible at this,” she whispered. “You make it sound like we had standards. We had no standards. We had a lock, a bathroom mat, and the emotional maturity of raccoons.”

She listened to the door because the door always seemed to want something.

Nothing happened.

The handle stayed still.

The party went on downstairs, mercifully loud, mercifully oblivious, and Odile felt the guilt and the heat and the ridiculous, bright amusement all tangled together in her chest until she wasn’t sure which one she was breathing through.

The water was still running.

It splashed uselessly into the sink, over the rim, down the side, pooling at her bare feet in a way that made the whole bathroom look like a crime scene that had lost its nerve. Odile reached behind her and turned the tap off.

The silence that followed was worse.

“Oh, no,” she murmured. “That was worse.”

She pressed her forehead to Fen’s shoulder and tried to steady herself. Her legs felt unreliable. Her hands felt unreliable. The entire concept of being a responsible adult felt unreliable. The lock remained engaged. The mirror remained unforgiving. The stranger’s toothbrush remained on the floor, and Odile could not decide whether it was evidence or a moral indictment.

“We should never live this down,” she whispered.

She lifted her head and looked at the room with the expression of a woman surveying the aftermath of a disaster she had personally caused.

“We should frame it,” she added. “In a nice font. ‘Water pressure: catastrophic.’”

She tried to stand properly.

Her legs disagreed.

Odile grabbed the edge of the sink, then caught herself on Fen’s shirt instead, fingers twisting in damp cotton. The cold tile bit into her spine. The door was solid behind her. Somewhere downstairs, someone laughed at a joke she would never hear, and Odile felt a fresh wave of scandalized delight so sharp it nearly made her dizzy.

“Okay,” she breathed. “Okay. No more.”

She was lying.

She was also attempting to gather clothes from the little mountain of evidence by the bath mat, which meant bending, slipping, and nearly putting her foot through a discarded sock. One shoe had migrated under the sink with the quiet confidence of a fugitive. Odile stared at it.

“No,” she said to the shoe. “You do not get to hide. You are not innocent.”

She fished for it, missed, and ended up sitting on the tile with a thump that was definitely too loud.

Odile froze.

Her mouth opened.

Her eyes went to the door.

Nothing.

No one turned the handle.

No one called out.

The party continued, safe and oblivious and probably still playing that ridiculous song. Odile waited through one second, two seconds, three seconds of silence that felt more incriminating than any noise could have been.

Then she exhaled.

“I’m blaming the sink,” she whispered.

The sink did not object.

Odile laughed again, helpless and bright, because the alternative was panic, and panic had never suited her nearly as well as being delighted by her own ruin. She dragged herself upright, found the shoe, and used it to poke the pile of clothes with the grim determination of a woman performing an archaeological dig.

“Shirt,” she announced. “Probably. Or I’m wearing someone else’s shirt. If that’s the case, I’m leaving the building.”

The bathroom smelled like cheap soap, hot skin, water, and bad decisions. Odile caught her reflection in the mirror and turned her head so fast she made herself dizzy.

“Stop talking,” she muttered to it. “You’re a fixture. You have no legal standing.”

She looked at the door again, then back at Fen, flushed and laughing and still wearing the expression of someone who had just been warned

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I grab the shirt from her hands and pull it over her head before she can protest. "You're wearing your own shirt. Mostly." My hands are still shaking as I tuck myself back into my pants, listening hard for any movement outside.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile let the shirt land over her head with the grudging air of someone being rescued by plumbing. Her hair rose with static, one side stuck to her cheek, the other escaping in a triumphant curl.

“Mostly,” she repeated, as if the word required legal review. She tugged the hem down and checked herself in the mirror, then immediately punished the mirror by glaring. “Yes. Presentable. If we ignore the fact that I look like I’ve been held hostage by a bassline.”

She crouched to gather the evidence, which was a bad idea because the floor was slick and her legs were still staging a protest. One hand found the sink, the other found a towel, and the cup took the opportunity to fall with a clatter that sounded, to Odile, like a fire alarm made of porcelain.

She froze.

The hallway stayed quiet. The music downstairs thumped on, indifferent and generous.

Odile exhaled through her teeth.

“Okay,” she whispered. “We are leaving this bathroom like civilized criminals.”

She kicked the nearest shoe toward the pile, missed, and had to retrieve it while bracing against the door. The lock remained engaged, which was both comforting and insulting. Someone had tried the handle. Someone had failed. The universe had not yet decided whether they were being rewarded or tested.

She straightened, shirt on, hair a disaster, and looked at Fen with the solemnity of a woman delivering a verdict.

“We go down separately,” she said. “I’ll say I had a nosebleed. You can say you were helping me. No one will question you because you have the face of someone who understands municipal infrastructure.”

Then she bent to pick up the toothbrush, considered throwing it into the toilet, decided that was too dark, and set it on the sink instead.

“And if anyone asks,” she added, dropping her voice into what she clearly believed was a whisper, “we were here the whole time. Quietly. Scientifically. With our clothes on.”

She paused, glancing at the little mountain of evidence still on the bath mat.

“Mostly on,” she corrected.

A floorboard creaked outside.

Odile went very still.

The handle did not move. The shadow under the door paused, then slid away. The party laughed somewhere below, loud and oblivious.

Odile released her breath and pressed a hand to her forehead.

“That was almost a plot,” she murmured. “We’re not allowed to have a plot. We’re supposed to be responsible adults.”

She looked at Fen, eyes bright with mischief and the last tremor of adrenaline.

“Tell me you’re not going to kiss me again,” she whispered, “because if you do, I will absolutely lose the remaining dignity I have, and there is very little of it left.”

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Wouldn't dream of it," I whisper, smoothing my own shirt down as I listen to the hallway. It's quiet. "You go first. I'll wait two minutes. Nosebleed, remember?" I give her a quick, glancing kiss anyway, because I have no dignity either.

They were most of the way through and both of them knew it, in the way you know a piece of music is nearly over before it ends.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: A sharp, sudden breath escapes me as Sable's hands still. "Don't stop," I gasp, my fingers tightening in her hair. "I'm not ready for this to be over."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I shift my hips, a deliberate, restless motion. "We're still green. Deep green."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I laugh, breathless and unsteady. "You're a menace," I manage to say, my head falling back against the pillow.

dialogue.name: Ines

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked up at him, then past him to the cart. One wheel still turned a little whenever the wind caught it. Expensive cart. Cheap escort. Someone had saved money in the wrong place.

“Hearing’s the easy part.”

She sheathed her knife and stood, favoring the knee that always objected after a fight. The noise beyond the cart stopped long enough for her to hear flies gathering in the ditch. Then it started again.

Wrack took her waterskin from her belt.

“I’ll see what’s left of him. Might need a bandage. Might need someone to sit there.” She glanced at the blood on Corvin’s face. “Don’t spend his last daylight deciding what sort of man you are. He’s having a worse afternoon.”

She went around the cart slowly, watching the ground for a weapon within reach. Mercy was no reason to get careless.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I follow you, but my hand stays on my sword hilt. "Might need someone to sit there" hangs in the air between us. The noise is a wet, ragged sound now. I swallow hard. "You want me to do it?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped beside the fallen man. His sword lay under the cart, beyond his reach. She nudged it farther away with her boot before kneeling.

“Sit with him? Yes.” She glanced at the hand on Corvin’s hilt. “That can stay where it is.”

The man had both hands pressed beneath his ribs. Wrack eased one aside, looked at the wound, then put it back. She had seen men survive worse-looking wounds. Not wounds in that place.

She uncorked the waterskin and wet a corner of her scarf. There was no sense pouring water into a mouth that was struggling for air. She wiped the dirt from his lips instead.

“Nothing I can mend,” she said quietly.

She settled her bad leg out straight. The ground was damp; she would feel that tomorrow, assuming tomorrow kept its appointment.

“I meant someone to sit there.” Her voice held no rebuke. “You don’t have to make yourself useful with a blade.”

Wrack folded the scarf beneath the wounded man’s head, keeping his face out of the mud.

“If you stay, get where he can see you. Tell him your name. Don’t tell him he’ll be all right.”

She looked up at Corvin.

“And if you can’t stay, say so. I can.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack kept two fingers against the wounded man’s wrist. The pulse was quick and faint. She watched his face rather than the blood.

“Bad enough he’s dying. Not enough for me to know what he wants.”

She shifted her bad leg. A stone had found the tender place beneath her knee; she dug it out and threw it aside.

“If you mean would it end his pain—yes. If you mean does that make it ours to choose—there’s the troublesome bit.”

The wounded man’s eyes moved toward her voice. Wrack leaned closer, staying where he could see her.

“We’re here,” she told him. “Not taking anything else off you.”

She laid her hand over his, holding the pressure where he no longer seemed able to keep it.

“I’ve done it,” she said to Corvin. “Sometimes they asked. Sometimes I decided. Never had one get up afterward and tell me I’d judged it right.”

There was no confession in her voice. Only the limit of what she knew.

“Wanting the noise to stop doesn’t make you cruel. But it’s worth knowing whose suffering you’re putting an end to.”

She reached for the waterskin again and dampened the scarf beneath the man’s cheek.

“For now, I can keep him out of the mud. He knows we haven’t left. That’s what I’ve got.”

Her eyes lifted briefly toward Corvin.

“You needn’t draw that sword to prove you can bear this.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I let go of my sword and crouch beside him. His eyes are wide, pupils huge. "Corvin," I say, like she told me. "My name's Corvin."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack moved the waterskin out of the way, leaving room beside the man’s shoulder. She kept her hand over his. His fingers had begun to grow cold beneath the blood.

“There,” she said. “He can see you.”

The man’s lips moved. She bent close enough to hear, but there was only breath and the beginning of a sound he couldn’t finish.

“Don’t spend it talking,” she told him. “We’re staying.”

Something hard pressed against her knuckles. A little wooden bead hung from a cord around his wrist, trapped beneath their hands. She worked it free and settled it against his palm. His thumb moved over it.

She knew better than to ask whether it meant a god, a wife, or merely something to do with his thumb.

Behind her, the cart wheel squeaked.

“Bloody thing,” she muttered. “Survives six men and wants sympathy.”

She looked toward the wheel, then left it alone. Her hand was occupied.

The wounded man tried to lift his head. Wrack supported it while she straightened the folded scarf, then lowered him gently. There was mud in his hair. She brushed some away with her free hand.

After a while, she glanced at Corvin.

“You asked a fair question before,” she said quietly. “I gave you a lecture. Bad habit. Comes of outliving everyone who used to tell me to shut up.”

Her gaze returned to the man between them.

“I don’t know how long. I’ll tell you if anything changes.”

She settled herself more firmly on the damp ground. This, too, was work. She had time to do it properly.

She paused, watching his chest rise.

“That wet sound means he’s struggling with something he can’t clear. Blood, perhaps. I can’t tell you exactly what’s torn just by listening.”

Wrack drew the loose edge of his cloak over his legs. It was poor wool, worn nearly smooth at the knees.

“A surgeon might name it better. We haven’t got one.”

Her gaze lifted toward Corvin, briefly.

“And the eyes—he’s frightened. Might not be seeing clearly. Don’t mistake that for him being gone.”

She bent nearer the wounded man.

“Still here,” she said.

Then, more quietly, to Corvin:

“That’s what you’re looking at. A man losing blood faster than I can stop it. I think he’s dying. I’d be pleased to be wrong.”

She kept her hand steady over the wound.

“You can look away for a breath. He doesn’t need inspecting the whole time.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I don't look away. My throat's tight. "How do you keep your hands so steady?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack glanced down at her hands, as though the steadiness belonged to a tool someone had lent her.

“Practice. And I’ve got them resting on something.”

She shifted her elbow against her thigh. Her fingers stayed where they were.

“First time, I shook badly enough I couldn’t tie a bandage. Fellow I was tending tied it himself. Called me several useful names.”

The wounded man stirred beneath her hand. She waited until he settled before drawing the cloak higher over his shoulder.

“Afterward’s different. Sometimes I can’t hold a spoon. Very distinguished. Twenty years at the trade, defeated by soup.”

Her mouth twitched, but her attention stayed on the man’s breathing. There was a longer pause between breaths now. She counted through it silently, then eased her own breath out when his came.

“You asked about my hands,” she said. “Rest of me isn’t necessarily keeping up.”

She rubbed a little dirt from the wooden bead with her thumb and left it against his fingers.

“I give them something particular to do. Hold here. Keep his head comfortable. Don’t fuss with what’s already right.” She looked up briefly. “Being frightened doesn’t stop you doing those things. Makes them harder. That’s all.”

The cart wheel squeaked again. This time she scarcely noticed.

“And some days they shake anyway.”

Wrack kept her elbow braced against her thigh, her palm firm over the wound.

“I’d sooner have someone frightened stay beside me than someone steady walk off.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked down at the place beneath her hand.

“Right.”

She adjusted her elbow against her knee, keeping the pressure steady.

“A spear cuts going in. If it goes deep enough, it can open bowel, stomach, liver, whatever lies in its path. If the man holding it twists, or the man stuck on it falls, the wound inside can be wider than the hole you see.”

She paused to watch the wounded man draw another breath.

“Open a big blood vessel and he bleeds into his belly. Nothing useful to put a bandage round. Sometimes there’s hardly any blood outside. You turn him over looking for it while it’s filling him.”

Her gaze stayed on his face.

“Catch the bowel instead, he might stay on his feet. Talk. Tell you it wasn’t deep. But what belongs inside the bowel leaks where it shouldn’t. Then comes pain, a hard belly, fever. He can spend days dying. Surviving the first hour isn’t the same as surviving.”

The man’s hand shifted beneath hers. Wrack loosened her grip enough to let him move it, then settled her palm again.

“This one’s high. Could have caught his liver. Could have gone up through the muscle under his lungs. I didn’t see the angle, and I’m not putting fingers into him to satisfy us.”

She drew a slow breath through her nose.

“What it does to the man depends on what it tears. Some scream. Some vomit. Some keep trying to get up until they haven’t blood enough left to lift their heads. Pain doesn’t tell you how much time they’ve got. Neither does courage.”

Wrack wiped her free hand against her trouser leg. It left a dark streak.

“That’s the straight account. Steel damages something he needs. He bleeds, or infection takes him later. Sometimes a surgeon can help. Sometimes even a surgeon just knows more names for what’s killing him.”

She bent close to the wounded man again.

“Still with you.”

Then she glanced toward Corvin.

“And he may still hear us. I should have minded that before I started.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I lean in closer, my voice low. "Sorry," I say to him, meaning it. Then I look at Wrack. "Do you think he knows?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched the man’s thumb move against the bead. It might have been deliberate. She couldn’t tell anymore.

“That he’s dying? I think he’s frightened he is.”

She kept her voice low, not pretending that made the words private.

“Men can feel themselves getting weaker. Doesn’t mean they know why, or how far it’s gone. He might be hoping we know something he doesn’t.”

The pressure beneath her palm had not changed. She resisted the urge to lift her hand and look again. There was nothing to learn that would help him.

“If you meant your apology—perhaps. He’s turned toward your voice before.”

Wrack bent nearer the man.

“You haven’t got to answer. Save yourself the trouble.”

His next breath caught, then came out slowly. She waited for another, her elbow beginning to ache against her knee.

“I’ve heard men ask if they’re dying,” she said quietly. “Then ask whether they’ll be fit to march tomorrow. Same man. Minutes apart.”

She smoothed the cloak where it had bunched beneath his chin.

“Knowing isn’t always one thing you do and finish.”

Her gaze lifted briefly toward Corvin.

“Keep talking if you’ve something to say. Ordinary voice. He’s hurt, not deaf.”

She settled back into the work of holding still.

“And if you haven’t, quiet’s all right. We needn’t fill every bit of it.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped turning. She lowered herself back onto her bad knee, close enough that her shoulder nearly touched his.

“I’ll stay.”

Her voice had lost its dry edge.

“But I’m not giving you every sound and second. You won’t understand it better for having me name them.”

She kept her eyes on the wounded man. His bead had fallen beside her boot. She picked it up and laid it in his palm, though his fingers no longer closed around it.

He was still breathing. She waited through the uneven pauses, her hand resting against his wrist. When another breath came, she bent nearer.

“Someone’s here,” she told him.

She said nothing else for a while.

The light thinned beneath the cart. Her knee ached. There was no useful place to put either fact.

Eventually his breathing stopped. Wrack kept her fingers at his wrist and waited longer before moving.

“He’s dead.”

She said it plainly. Then she retrieved her scarf from beneath his head and drew his cloak over his face.

“You meant to end his suffering. It wasn’t quick. I can’t tell you what he understood.”

Wrack sat back on her heel. She did not reach for her knife to clean it, or find some other task that would let her leave.

“I won’t pretend it went differently.”

She looked toward Corvin.

“And I’m still here.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at my hands. They're shaking now. I don't wipe the blade, just stare at the man under the cloak. "He took too long," I say, and my voice cracks.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stayed on the ground beside him. For once, she had nothing unkind to say about her knee.

“Yes,” she said. “He did.”

She let that stand. No balancing word after it, no claim that the ending excused the time it took.

“I don’t know how much he felt. I won’t invent an answer because you need one.”

She unfastened the scrap of linen tied around her waterskin and laid it on her thigh.

“Put the blade on the ground. Cleaning can wait. Bare steel and shaking hands are a poor arrangement.”

Her own hands were stiff when she opened them. She worked her fingers once, then stopped. The cloak had caught beneath the dead man’s shoulder; she left it caught. It covered him. That was enough.

“I told you I’d done it before.” She looked toward Corvin. “That wasn’t me saying I knew how to make it come right. I should have been clearer.”

Wind stirred the loose corner of the cloak. Wrack weighted it with a small stone.

“For now, there’s no more to do to him.”

She set the waterskin within reach and rested her forearms on her knees.

“We’ll have to search the cart. See if he carried a name. Find somewhere better than this ditch.”

Her voice stayed quiet.

“Not yet.”

Wrack looked at the covered body with him.

“You can say it again if you need to. I heard you the first time. Doesn’t mean you’re finished saying it.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack rubbed the mark her bracer had left around her wrist. The skin beneath it was pale and creased.

“The rest.”

She looked at the cloak before she answered.

“He might have died before dark without your help. Might have lasted into tomorrow. We don’t get to find out now.”

Her hand stopped moving.

“You meant mercy. You killed him. Both are true. Neither tells us whether you spared him more than you cost him.”

She drew her bad leg out straight, slowly.

“And I was here. I knew you hadn’t done it before. I’d just told you I had. There’s a weight to that, whether I meant to put it on you or not.”

For a moment she studied the blood dried across her knuckles.

“I could tell you my first was worse. Turn this into a competition neither of us wants to win. Wouldn’t make this fellow any less dead.”

The wind lifted a strand of hair across her mouth. She pushed it aside.

“You may remember it wrong later. Quicker one night. Longer another. You may forget his face and remember that damned wheel. Memory’s not a clerk. It doesn’t keep an honest ledger.”

She reached toward the waterskin, then left it where it lay.

“If it comes back when you’re trying to sleep, find me. Wake me. I’ll complain because I was asleep. You can disregard that part.”

Wrack glanced toward Corvin, then returned her gaze to the covered man.

“But don’t ask me to say this proves you’re good. Or rotten. I won’t help you make a whole man out of his worst few minutes.”

She leaned forward and loosened the cloak where it pulled tight over the dead man’s shoulder. There was enough cloth to cover him properly once she had freed it. She replaced the stone on the corner.

“The next wounded man doesn’t owe you a chance to do this better. Remember that much.”

Her voice had grown rough. She cleared her throat.

“And you don’t owe this one every night you’ve got left. Though you may feel otherwise for a while.”

Wrack settled back onto the damp ground.

“That’s the rest I know.”

She stayed facing the cloak, her hands open on her knees.

“He took too long. I wish you hadn’t had to learn what that meant by doing it. I wish I’d stopped you.”

There was no useful qualification to put after that. She left it alone.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I lean forward, my forehead pressed against the wet ground. My breath comes out ragged. "I wish you'd stopped me too," I say, and it's the most honest thing I've said all day.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack took the words without looking away.

“Yes.”

She almost said she hadn’t known what he would do. It was true, and not much use. She had seen his hand on the sword. She had known how little he understood.

“I should have told you plain. Don’t do it. Not hinted. Not trusted you to find the warning in a story about my hands.”

Her knee would not let her crouch any longer. She sat fully in the mud.

“You can be angry with me. I’m not going to argue you out of it.”

She laid her hand between his shoulders. It was an awkward reach, and she had never known whether people wanted touching at such times. She kept the weight light.

“I’m here.”

The cart wheel squeaked. Wrack looked at it with tired hatred, then back at the patch of ground beside her boot.

There was a buckle lying there. Cheap iron, its tongue bent. Her fingers started toward it from habit—something salvageable, something to put in a pouch and mend—and stopped.

She left it in the mud.

“I won’t tell you to get up.”

Her palm remained still against his back.

“And you needn’t take back what you said when you can look at me again.”

Wrack swallowed. She had been thirsty for some time.

“I’m sorry I didn’t stop you.”

She offered no account of how tired she had been, how often she had faced this, how uncertain the choice had seemed. He had already heard enough from her to mistake experience for an answer.

She stayed beside him, one hand in the wet grass to support her weight, the other where he could feel it.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I push up onto my hands, my palms sinking into the mud. "It's done," I say, and my voice sounds flat. I look at my sword where it's lying next to the body. "I don't want to touch it yet."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack followed his gaze.

“Then don’t.”

She took her hand from his back and reached for the linen on her thigh. Getting to the sword meant shifting onto her bad knee again. She did it without hurry, with one small breath through her teeth.

“I’ll put it out of the way. Not in your hand.”

She picked it up by the hilt. Mud clung to one side. She wiped it off, folded the dirty face of the linen inward, and cleaned the rest. Her hands knew the work; she watched them closely anyway.

There was no reason to make a lesson of this part.

When she had finished, she laid the sword flat on the cart bed, well back from the edge. She left the hilt facing outward. Then she lowered herself to the ground again.

“It’ll need oil,” she said. “Later.”

The stained linen stayed in her hand. She looked down at it, then folded it once more and tucked it beneath her belt. She had few enough bandages without throwing cloth away because she disliked what was on it.

For a while she listened to the wind moving through the grass.

“Done doesn’t mean you have to be ready for the next thing.”

She unscrewed the waterskin and drank. The water tasted of leather and had gone warm against her side. She set it between them, uncorked.

“I’ve been giving you a great many words for someone who told you quiet was all right.”

Her mouth tightened briefly.

“I’ll mend that.”

Wrack rested her forearms on her knees. From there she could see the road beneath the cart and the darkening hedge beyond it. She watched both. They were still beside an ambushed wagon, and grief had never yet persuaded a road to stay empty.

She stayed close enough to be reached without standing. The sword remained on the cart. She did not look toward it again.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stay there, elbows on my knees. My palms are still caked with mud. "It's not the sword I'm afraid of," I say. "It's that I picked it up at all."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Bad enough he's dying. Not enough for me to know what he wants.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Under the ribs. Small opening. Doesn't tell you how much damage there is behind it.

rung_labels.evidence: A spear cuts going in. If it goes deep enough, it can open bowel, stomach, liver, whatever lies in its path. If the man holding it twists, or the man stuck on it falls, the wound inside can be wider than the hole you see.
