rung_labels.evidence: She said nothing else for a while. The light thinned beneath the cart. Her knee ached. There was no useful place to put either fact. Eventually his breathing stopped.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: That's the rest I know.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack finished with the knife and slid it home. She looked at Corvin then, at the wet streak he'd left across his cheekbone, and at where his feet were and weren't pointing.

"Not yours," she agreed. "Yours would be running. That's just sitting there."

She stood, slow, one hand on her knee. Her hip had started complaining about ditches two winters back and hadn't stopped.

"Here's how it lays out." She said it the way she'd have said the price of grain. "He's gut-cut, or near enough. I saw him go down. That noise he's making, it'll last till about moonrise if he's unlucky, and he sounds unlucky. Nobody's coming for him. His friends are the six." She nodded at the ditch. "So he dies tonight regardless. Only question left is whether it's fast, and who does it, and whether you sleep."

She let that sit a moment.

"I'll do it if you want. I've done it before, it costs me nothing, and I'll not think less of you." She shrugged one shoulder. "Or you do it, and you find out what it costs you, and you know for next time. There's always a next time, in this trade. Sooner or later it's someone you can't hand off."

She started toward the cart, unhurried, then stopped and glanced back.

"Either way, don't stand there listening to it. That's the one choice that's actually wrong."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, my hands still shaking a little. "I'll do it." I start walking toward the cart, my boots crunching on the dry ground. "Better to find out now."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack fell in beside him, not ahead. It was his walk. She just matched it.

"Good," she said, and left it there. No speech. He'd get enough of those from himself later.

The man was where she'd left him, half under the tailboard with one arm hooked over the axle like he'd meant to climb and forgotten how. Young. Younger than Corvin, maybe, though that was hard to tell with the colour gone out of him. His hands were pressed flat to his belly and the noise he was making had thinned since she'd first heard it -- less voice in it now, more breath.

"Right." She kept her tone level, the same one she'd use showing him how to tension a bowstring. "Don't go for the belly, it's already done and it'll just take longer. Don't go for the heart unless you know exactly where the ribs sit, and you don't, not yet. Neck." She touched the side of her own, just under the jaw, two fingers. "There. Blade in, push across and away from you. It's a lot of blood, it comes fast, and he'll stop making noise in about the time it takes to count to five. He might grab at you. Let him. It doesn't mean anything."

She glanced at his knife hand.

"And hold it like you're going to use it, not like you're going to drop it. You put a shaking blade in wrong and you have to do it twice. Once is the kindness. Twice is just mess."

The man on the ground had turned his head at their voices. His eyes found Corvin and stayed there, which Wrack had known they would. They always looked at whoever was closest.

She stepped back half a pace. Not out of reach -- she'd be there if it went wrong -- but out of the boy's line of sight, so that whatever he saw when he looked up afterward, it wasn't her watching.

"Whenever you're ready," she said. "Don't take long about it. That's the only other rule."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't answer straight off. She looked at the man on the ground instead, properly, the way she'd look at a horse someone was trying to sell her.

"Gut wound," she said. "Low, left side. See how his hands are." The fingers were spread and pressed, not clutching. "He's holding himself in. That's what that is. There'll be a smell if you get closer -- not blood. Other things. Once that's open there's nothing anyone does about it, not a surgeon, not a priest. I've seen it maybe forty times. I've seen it go wrong exactly none."

She shifted her weight off the bad hip.

"So. Mercy or easier." She said the words back to him flat, neither mocking nor gentle. "Honest answer is I don't separate them anymore, and I'd be lying if I told you I ever did clean. He dies tonight. If I walk away, he does it slow and alone, and the noise carries, and anyone on that road hears it and comes to look. If I don't walk away, I sit with him till moonrise and he dies anyway, only I've lost half a night and we've got the same road to deal with." She nodded at the knife. "That's easier. It's also the kindest thing on offer. Both true. You don't get to pick one and feel clean about it."

The man's breath hitched, caught, went on.

"If you want the version that makes it simpler," she said, "it's this. Ask yourself what you'd want, on the ground with your hands full of yourself. I've asked. My answer's fast." She let a beat go by. "Yours might not be. That's a thing worth knowing about yourself too."

She didn't push him toward it. But she didn't step back any further either.

"That's the whole of what I know. Now you know it. Doesn't change what's in front of you."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down, getting a better look at him. He's staring back, his eyes wide and scared. I swallow hard. "Okay," I say, more to myself than to either of them. I shift my grip on the knife, trying to stop the shaking.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched the knife. Not his face -- there was nothing on his face she needed and plenty he'd not thank her for seeing. The knife.

The shake was in the wrist, not the fingers. That was the manageable kind.

"Other hand on his forehead," she said, low. "Flat. Push his head back and over, away from you. Opens the neck up and gives him something to feel that isn't the blade. Steadies your arm too, having a thing to brace against. That's not for him. That's for you."

The man on the ground made a sound that might have been a word. His lips were grey and stuck to his teeth. One of his hands twitched against his belly, thought about lifting, didn't. He kept looking at Corvin. He'd stopped looking scared some breaths back, Wrack thought, and gone somewhere past it -- the place where they mostly just looked tired.

"He's not going to fight you," she said. "Look at his hands. He's spent everything he had keeping those where they are. Whatever he's saying, you don't owe him an answer. You don't owe him a reason. You owe him quick."

She crouched, slow, one knee to the dirt a pace off Corvin's shoulder. Close enough. Her own hand rested on her thigh, near her knife but not on it, and stayed there.

"Breathe out when you go in. Not in -- out. You'll want to hold it and that locks everything up." A pause. "Then don't look at the neck after. Look at the eyes. That's how you know it's done, and it's the part you'll want to be sure of later when you're lying awake asking."

She said nothing else. The light was going amber along the tops of the wheel-ruts and the dead man's breath went in and out, in and out, shorter each time, like a thing winding down.

Wrack waited.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack leaned in over his shoulder, not so close as to crowd the knife arm. She looked where he looked, and talked the way she'd talk over a map.

"Start at the hands. Knuckles gone white, fingers spread -- that's not pain, that's pressure. Under them there's a cut about a hand's width, running slantwise, made by somebody swinging low and pulling. Mine, I think. The edges'll be puckered by now and what's behind them is trying to come forward. That's why he's not letting go. If he lets go it comes out, and something in him still knows that even if the rest of him's given up."

She lifted her chin a fraction.

"Belly's gone hard. You could tap it like a drum. That's blood filling up where it shouldn't. Skin above it is that colour -- see, not white, more like tallow -- because everything he's got left is pooling low and there's none to spare for the top of him. Lips grey for the same reason. Nailbeds too, if you cared to check. I don't."

The man's chest rose. Stopped. Rose again.

"Breathing. Short, and there's a catch at the top of it, like a hinge that needs oil. That's not the belly, that's the body starting to forget the rhythm. It'll go longer between, then it'll skip one, then it'll skip a few. He's not there yet. He's close."

She looked at the face last.

"Eyes. He's not seeing you. Not the way you mean. He's looking at the nearest thing that moves because that's what's left to do. Pupils are wide -- that's shock, not dark. In a while they'll stop tracking and just point. That's the bit you'll remember, so I'm telling you now: when they go still, it's not because you've done something. It's because there's no one behind them. You'll be putting a knife into a house after the tenant's gone."

She sat back on her heel.

"That's what you're looking at. A man who's already most of the way out, still holding the door shut with both hands because nobody's told him he can stop." She glanced at the knife. "You're about to tell him."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod once, a sharp jerk of my chin. My other hand comes up and presses against his forehead, like she said. His skin is cold and damp. I breathe out, and push the blade in.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
It went in wrong by a finger's width -- too high, catching the jaw -- and Wrack saw his wrist correct on its own before she could say anything, dragging the edge down and across the way she'd told him. So he'd listened. Good.

The blood came the way it always came from there: not a spurt, not at first, just a fast dark welling that filled the hollow of the throat and then found the low side and ran. It went over Corvin's knuckles where they still braced the forehead. It went into the dirt. The man's mouth opened and the noise he'd been making for the last hour changed pitch, thinned, became a wet clicking somewhere behind the teeth. One of his hands came off his belly at last -- that's what Wrack had been waiting for -- and pawed once at Corvin's sleeve, closed on nothing, and dropped. What he'd been holding in started to slide.

"Don't look there," she said. "Eyes."

She counted, not aloud. Two. Three. The man's heels scraped in the ruts. Four. The clicking stopped. His chest lifted a last time in that catching way and then just didn't, and the eyes did what she'd said they'd do -- went from looking to pointing, in no time at all, like a lamp turned down.

Five.

"That's it," Wrack said. "He's gone. You can let go of his head."

She gave him a moment with that. Then she reached past him, unhurried, and pressed two fingers into the side of the neck that wasn't open, held them there, and took them away.

"Nothing. Told you it was a lot of blood." She wiped her fingers on the dead man's sleeve, since he'd no more use for it. "You'll want to do the same, and then not touch your face till you've found water. It gets in the creases and it itches by morning and then you're scratching at it in front of people."

She stood, hip protesting, and looked down the road where the light was going. Then back at him, still kneeling.

"That was clean enough. Cleaner than my first." She let a beat go by, dry. "Mine had to be done twice. You don't get to feel bad about yours till you've caught up to that."

She started back toward the ditch, then stopped and said over her shoulder, not turning:

"Sit if you need to. Not long. We're still on his road, and the six have friends somewhere who'll want to know why nobody came home."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped. Turned back. Looked at him a long moment, kneeling there with the blood going tacky on his hand, and then at the body, and then back at him.

"That wasn't a spear," she said. "That was me. Falchion, low, backhand. I told you -- swinging and pulling. A spear does a different thing. But if you want the full ledger, fine. I've got the walk back to the ditch to fill."

She came back the few paces and stood over the dead man, not looking down at him particularly. She'd seen him.

"Blade cut, like this one. It opens. Long slice, shallow at the ends, deep in the middle, because that's how an arm moves. You get through skin and the fat under it -- there's more fat than you'd think, even on a thin man, yellow, in a layer -- and then a sheet of muscle, and then you're in. What's in there wants out. It's packed tight and under pressure and the moment the wall's gone it starts pushing. That's the sliding you didn't look at. Grey-pink, ropey, a lot of it. Slippery. Smells of shit if you've nicked the tube, which you nearly always have, and that's what kills them if the bleeding doesn't -- the shit gets loose inside and rots them from the middle out over three or four days. This one bled first. That's luckier."

She shifted her weight.

"A spear goes in. Doesn't open, it makes a hole. Round-ish, or a slot if it's a leaf blade, about the width of your two fingers. Goes in a hand's depth, sometimes clean through and out the back if there's weight behind it. Now here's the thing about a spear that people don't expect." She held up a finger. "It's a plug. Long as it's in, not much comes out. Man can stand there with a spear through his belly and talk to you. Argue. Seen it. The trouble starts when it comes out, because whoever put it there wants it back and they pull, and the head's wider than the shaft, and it drags. Brings things with it. Then the hole's not a hole anymore. And there's the twisting -- if they know their work they turn the shaft a quarter before they pull. That shreds. You don't get a clean edge to hold shut, you get mince, and the man goes down much faster than this one did and doesn't hold anything in because there's nothing to hold. Just a wet place where his front was."

She looked down at the body then, briefly, the way you'd check a knot.

"Either way it's the same road. Blood into the belly till the belly's full and hard. Cold. Thirst -- they always ask for water, you'll hear that, and you don't give it because it makes them puke and the puking opens them further. Then the breathing goes. Then the eyes." She lifted one shoulder. "Blade's slower. Spear's messier. Neither one's a thing anyone walks off, not without a surgeon inside the hour and a great deal of luck, and I've never seen a surgeon inside the hour and I don't believe in luck."

She stepped back.

"That's what you asked for. It's not more than you'll see. Give it a year and you'll have done the cataloguing yourself, on the ground, from the inside of a shield wall, with somebody screaming it at you." A pause. "Now wipe your hand. I wasn't being gentle about the itching. That part was just true."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my hand on the man's cloak, watching the blood smear dark. It doesn't come all the way off. "What's the difference," I say, my voice quieter than I want it to be, "between the blood that runs out and the blood that stays in?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack heard the quiet in it. She let it be quiet, and answered the question he'd actually said.

"Blood that runs out, you can see. That's the whole of the difference and it matters more than it sounds." She nodded at the neck, at the dark patch spreading in the ruts. "That's the kind that frightens people. Comes fast, comes bright -- it's bright when it's got air in it, goes dark as it sits, that's how you tell how long a man's been down if you weren't there. It's a lot of blood by the look. It's less than you'd think by the measure. A man's got maybe a bucket and a half in him, and you'd be surprised how far a cup of it goes across a floor."

She crouched again, since she was going to be talking a while, and put a knuckle against the dead man's belly. It didn't give.

"That's the other kind. What stays in. It's not sitting still -- it's running just as hard, it's just running into a place you can't see. Fills the belly, or the chest, or the inside of a thigh if the big vessel's cut and the skin's not. Man goes white and cold and thirsty and there's not a mark on him, or one you'd not worry about. I've seen a man take a horse-kick to the ribs, walk to his tent, lie down, and be dead before the fire was lit. Nothing came out of him at all." She took the knuckle away. "Open one of those up later, if you've a reason to -- I have -- and it's black. Not red. Thick, half-set, like something you'd scrape out of a pan. That's what stays in looks like once it's stopped."

She rocked back on her heel and looked at him properly then, at the hand that hadn't come clean.

"Here's the part that's useful. The outside kind, you can do something about. Press on it, tie above it, pack it with whatever's in reach. I've stopped it with a fistful of horse-hair and a belt. The inside kind you can't reach. Can't press on a belly. Can't tie off a chest. So the one that looks worst is the one that's least likely to kill, and the one that looks like nothing at all is the one that gets them. You'll learn to be more afraid of a man who's gone quiet and grey than one who's roaring and painting the walls."

She was silent a moment. Then, drier, not quite looking at him:

"If you're asking the other thing. The stuff that runs out, you wash. It's on your hand and it'll come off with sand and water and some rubbing, and you'll not think about it by the week's end." She tipped her head a fraction toward his chest. "The stuff that stays in, I don't know. I've never found where the seam is. I know it goes black like the other, given time, and it gets hard, and after a while you can't tell it from the rest of you." She stood, hip complaining. "Whether that's a mercy or just easier -- well. You've heard me on that."

She turned toward the ditch and the six.

"Cloaks off them, boots if they fit, anything that jingles. Then we move. Talk on the road if you want more. I've got plenty and it keeps the dark off."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped mid-turn. She looked at where his hands had gone -- to the man's collar, the cloak-pin, fumbling with it -- and then at his face, and something in the set of her mouth eased a notch. Not a smile. The thing before one.

"Right," she said. "I'll stay."

She came back and crouched where she'd crouched before, a pace off his shoulder.

"First thing, because you asked for all of it and I'll not have you carrying a wrong idea. He doesn't take any time. Not anymore. That's finished, you finished it, and it was about a five-count and you were there for every part. What you're doing to him now, you're doing to meat and leather. He's not in it." She said it plain, not soft. "Doesn't make it easy. Does make it not the same thing. Keep those separate in your head or they'll bleed into each other and you'll be sick at a boot buckle in six months and not know why."

His fingers were still on the pin. It wasn't giving.

"Pin's stuck because it's on the wrong side of the blood. Everything on his left's getting tacky now -- that's the blood going from wet to glue, takes about the time it's taken. Wet your thumb and work it. There. Hear that? That little peel? That's cloth coming off skin where it's stuck. You'll hear it every time you move him, anywhere the blood's touched. Sounds like nothing. You'll know it anywhere for the rest of your life."

The cloak came free. She watched him get it out from under the shoulders, the head lolling with the movement, the neck wound opening wider as it went -- a dark grin under the jaw, lips of it already going a brown colour at the edge.

"Head'll do that. No neck strength left, nothing holding it. It'll flop whichever way you lean him and the cut'll gape when it goes back. Don't try to hold it shut, there's no point, but don't let it knock on the wheel either -- not for his sake. For the noise. Skull on wood carries."

Under the cloak, a jerkin. Laced. His fingers went to the laces and she let him find out for himself that they were soaked through and swollen and wouldn't run.

"Cut them. Knife's right there and he's not going to want it back. Down the side, not the front -- the front's where the belly is and you'll want the jerkin off him without putting your hands into that." She nodded at it. "That's the second sound. When you roll him to get the arm out -- you'll have to roll him -- everything he was holding shut is going to shift. It'll sound wet. Like a sack of wet sand turned over. And it'll smell. I told you before there'd be a smell and there was, and now you're going to move it and it'll be worse. Breathe through your mouth. That's not squeamishness, that's just what works."

He rolled him. It sounded like she'd said. It smelled like she'd said. Something dark ran out from under the body on the low side and found the wheel-rut and followed it.

"That's not the neck. Neck's mostly done -- there's nothing pushing it anymore. That's from the belly, everything settling and finding the low ground. It'll do that for a while. Man loses his manners when the last bit goes, too, so when you smell that, that's what that is. Bowels let go. Every one. Kings, priests, everyone. First thing my sergeant told me and it was the truest thing she ever said."

The jerkin came off. Under it, a shirt, and the skin, and the belly with its slantwise mouth and what had pushed out of it, grey and glistening, the loop of it lying in the dirt like something that had never been inside anyone.

"Leave the shirt. It's worth nothing and it's all that's holding the shape of him. Boots." She jerked her chin. "Sit on your heels at the feet. Take the ankle in one hand and the heel of the boot in the other and pull straight. Not up -- straight. His foot's going to fight you, not because he's fighting, because a dead ankle doesn't flex and a live one does and you've only ever pulled boots off live ankles. And here's your third sound." She waited for it. "That sucking. That's the foot coming out of a boot he's had on for three days. Every boot you take off a dead man sounds like that. Wet. Then the smell of the foot on top of the other smell, and the toenails black, and you'll wonder why anyone bothers. They're worth two weeks' bread, is why."

The first boot came. The second. She watched him set them aside, saw where his eyes went and didn't go.

"Now the belt. Buckle's on his front, right over the top of the cut. You've got to get your fingers in under the leather without going in under the skin, and there's about a finger's width between. It'll be warm. He's still warm, all through -- takes hours to go cold and it goes from the outside in, so the hands and the face first, then the body. You'll put your fingers in there and it'll feel like a living man's belly and it isn't. Just do it fast."

He did. The belt came. Nothing jingled on it -- she'd known it wouldn't, a man that young -- but there was a knife, a poor one, and a little pouch with something in it that shifted like teeth or dice.

"Take those. Don't open the pouch now. Whatever's in it is his and you'll want to look at it later when you're steadier, and then you'll want not to have looked, and that's the last thing I know about this that I can tell you." She stood, slow, one hand on her thigh. The hip said what it always said.

"What you did to him, start to end, was open his neck in about a five-count, and then strip him in about the time it takes to sing a hymn, badly. It wasn't clean. Nobody's is. He's lying there with his shirt on and his boots off and his guts in the road, and by morning the birds'll be at his eyes, and by the week's end you'll not know him from the six. That's all of it. I didn't leave anything out."

She looked at the sky. Amber going to grey.

"You wanted to know. Now you do." A pause, dry as the ditch. "Cloak's yours, by the way. You earned it and it's warmer than the one you've got. Just don't wear it with the wet side in."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I pull the cloak around my shoulders. The inside is still warm. "You said you had to do it twice. Your first one. Tell me about that while we walk."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't answer right away. She went to the ditch first and started on the six, and after a moment he came and worked beside her, and for a while there was just the peeling sound and the sucking of boots and the small clink of the little that was worth taking. Four cloaks, three pairs of boots that might fit someone, two knives, a purse with copper in it and a wooden saint that she left in the man's hand because it wasn't worth the argument she'd have with herself later. She rolled it all in the worst of the cloaks and tied it with a belt and slung it, and they went.

The road was empty. The light was mostly gone off it and what was left sat in the ruts like water.

"Twice," she said, when they'd put the cart a good way behind them. "Right."

She walked a bit before going on. Not for effect. She was finding where it started.

"I was seventeen. Maybe. Nobody wrote it down. Second season with the company and first one where we'd done any real fighting -- the first season was all walking and standing in fields looking hard at other people standing in fields. Then there was a village. There's always a village. Doesn't matter whose or why. We went through it and some of them didn't want us to, and by the end of the afternoon there were bodies in the street and I'd not killed any of them. I'd been at the back. Somebody's got to be at the back and it's the new ones."

Her boots crunched. His crunched a half-step behind.

"Sergeant I had then -- the one who told me about the bowels -- she walked me down the street after, same as I walked you to that cart. And there was a man against a wall with his leg off at the knee. Not cut. Crushed. Cartwheel, or a horse, I never knew. He'd bled a lake and he was sitting in it, propped up, talking. Not to us. Just talking. About a dog, I think. He'd gone somewhere nice and he was telling it to whoever was there."

She shifted the bundle on her shoulder.

"Sergeant said: him. Said it the way you'd point out which log wants splitting. And I said I'd never, and she said well, you're going to, and there was no more to it. Same as tonight. Except she didn't tell me where. She said the heart, because she liked a heart, she was that sort, and I'd only ever seen a heart in a pig."

A dry breath through her nose.

"So I put a knife where I thought a heart was and it was a rib. Went in a thumb's depth and stopped like I'd hit a door. And he stopped talking about the dog and looked at me. Right at me. Not scared, not angry. Sort of -- disappointed. Like I'd got a step wrong in a dance he'd been enjoying. And I stood there with a knife in his chest, stuck, and my hand on it, and I couldn't get it out and I couldn't get it in and he was looking at me, and it went on that way for -- I don't know. It felt like a long time. It was probably a breath."

She let the quiet go a bit.

"Sergeant didn't help. Wouldn't. Stood there with her arms crossed and said, well, you're not finished, are you. And she was right. So I put my foot on his good thigh and pulled the knife out -- it made a noise, a sort of grating, bone on the flat of it -- and I went in again, lower, under the rib this time because I'd found out where the rib was the hard way, and up, and I felt it go through into something that gave. Like pushing through a wet sack. And he made a sound like all the air going out of a bellows and his eyes did what you saw tonight. Went from looking to pointing."

She walked.

"Thing I remember isn't the second one. Second one was fine. Second one I'd do again the same way and it'd work. It's the space between. Him looking at me. Me holding a knife that was stuck in a man and having to decide to pull it out and go again, knowing the whole time what I was doing and that I'd got it wrong and that he knew I'd got it wrong. That's the twice. That's what it costs. Not the killing. The having to mean it a second time, in front of them."

The road bent. She took the bend.

"Sergeant said after, that's why you go for the neck. Nothing to hit. Nothing to get stuck in. You can miss a heart by a finger and give a man a bad afternoon. You miss a neck by a finger and you've still cut something that empties him. She said she'd sent me for the heart so I'd learn why not to, and I believed her, and I still don't know if it was true or if she just liked a heart." Wrack's mouth did the thing that wasn't a smile. "She's dead now. Fever. Nobody got to put a knife in her at all, and she'd have hated that."

She glanced sidelong, not quite at him. At the cloak, maybe. The one that was warmer than his old one.

"So. Yours went in wrong and you fixed it in the same stroke. Mine went in wrong and I stood there. You've a way to go before you've caught up to that, and I'd not hurry." A pause. "Ask me about the second one I ever did, sometime, and I'll tell you I don't remember it. That'll be true. Nobody remembers the second. It's only ever the first, and the ones after that you'd give a great deal to have got right."

The dark had come down properly now. Somewhere off the road a night bird started, stopped, started again.

"Keep walking," Wrack said. "You've got questions still, I can hear them. Save one for when we've a fire. It's a long way to anywhere and I'd rather have something to say than not."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped. Looked back down the road at him, a shape sat low in the dark with a dead man's cloak around him, and then up the road the other way, and then at the hedges either side, which were the only things in reach that could hide a man with a bow.

"Not the place for it," she said.

He didn't get up. She hadn't really expected him to.

"Right." She came back the few paces, let the bundle down off her shoulder onto the road with a soft clank of buckles, and sat on it. Her hip thanked her, grudgingly, the way it did everything. She set her falchion across her knees, not drawn, just there, and faced the way they'd come, because if anything followed it'd follow from there.

"The rest," she said. "You mean the ones after. The ones I'd have back."

She was quiet for a bit. Not finding the start this time. Deciding whether to.

"There's one. There's more than one, but there's one that's the whole of it, and if I tell you that you've got the rest for free. You'll want to know first that I've not told it. Not the way you're asking. Bits of it, to people who were there, and they didn't need the bits because they'd seen. Nobody who wasn't there has had it, so you'll forgive me if it comes out in the wrong order."

The night bird had stopped. Something small moved in the hedge and she watched the place it had moved and then let it go.

"Six years back. Different company, same war. We'd a man called Aske. Tall, ugly, the one everyone likes -- you've met the kind, every company grows one. He taught me to read a map properly, which I couldn't till I was thirty, and he owed me two months' pay from dice and I owed him a knife I'd lost of his, so we were square in the way that keeps people talking to each other. Not my lover. People assumed. He wasn't. He was the one I'd have handed things to, if you follow. The one you don't have to explain to."

She shifted on the bundle.

"Skirmish at a ford. Nothing. Twenty of them, thirty of us, over in a quarter hour, and we'd the water and they didn't. And Aske took a bolt. Crossbow, from the far bank, from a man who'd already decided to run and let one go over his shoulder as he went, the way they do. Never aimed it. It went in under his left arm, here" -- two fingers to her own side, below the armpit, where the ribs start their curve -- "and it didn't come out. Bolt went in a hand and a half and the fletching snapped off when he fell on it, so there was just a stub of shaft and a wet place, and he stood up. He stood up and he said, that's not good, in the voice you'd use for a horse gone lame. And then he sat down again, quite carefully, and that was that for standing."

She looked at the road. Her voice hadn't changed. It was the map voice, still.

"Lung. I knew it was lung before he sat down, because I'd seen the froth. That's how you know. Blood from a lung comes with air in it and it foams -- pink, not red, like something off the top of a butcher's pail. It comes out the wound when they breathe out, bubbling, and it comes up the throat, and by the second breath it's at the corner of the mouth. Sound goes with it. You'll hear it someday and you'll know. Like a kettle that's thinking about it. Every breath in, the kettle, and every breath out, a little gout of pink at the hole. That's what a bolt in the lung is. Nothing you can see. All of it inside."

She turned the falchion a fraction on her knees.

"Here's what I knew. I knew it doesn't close. Lung fills. Not fast -- the hole's small and the bolt's still in it, so it's a plug, like I told you about the spear. It fills slow. Man drowns from the inside over a day, sometimes two. Sits up because lying down he can't breathe at all, and each hour he can breathe a bit less, and he knows it, all the way. That's the thing about a lung. Belly, they go somewhere in the head, they get tired, they talk about dogs. Lung, they're there. They're there for every breath because every breath is the whole of what they're doing."

She let a breath go herself, in, out, unremarkable.

"I knew that. I knew the surgeon was three days back with the baggage and couldn't have done anything if he'd been standing over us. I knew the neck. I'd done the neck forty times by then. I knew it as well as I know how to piss."

The bird started again, off in the dark, and she waited for it to stop.

"He asked me. Not straight off. First hour he was making jokes, bad ones, about how he'd finally got out of the two months' pay. Second hour he'd stopped joking and was breathing, and it was work, you could see the work of it, the shoulders going up with every one. And he looked at me and said, Wrack. Just that. The way you'd say it to the one you don't have to explain to."

She stopped. Started again in the same voice, flat as a table.

"And I said, wait. I said the surgeon. I said the word surgeon to him with a straight face, and he knew I was lying because he'd taught me maps and knew where the baggage was. And he let me. That's the part. He let me lie to him. Nodded, and went back to breathing, and I sat with him by the ford with my hand on his shoulder feeling the shoulder go up and down and I didn't do the thing I've told a hundred boys to do, the thing I told you not an hour ago. Don't stand there listening to it."

She rubbed her thumb along the scabbard, once.

"I listened to it all night. Kettle. Bubble. Kettle. Bubble. He couldn't lie down so he sat against a tree and I sat beside him and we didn't talk because he hadn't the breath and I hadn't anything to say that wasn't the word surgeon. Around midnight the froth stopped coming from the hole, and I thought, well, and then I understood that it was because there was too much blood in there now for air to get through, so it was worse, not better. By the grey before dawn his lips had gone the colour of slate and he'd stopped being able to make words, only shapes with his mouth, and his eyes -- his eyes were still looking. Not pointing. Looking. At me. He was in there for all of it and I could have opened the door any time and I sat outside it and held his hand."

Quiet. The hedge. Her own breathing, and none of it a kettle.

"Mid-morning he stopped looking. Went to pointing, like I said they do. Only his chest kept going, small, a ragged sort of thing, once in a while, the body forgetting the rhythm and then remembering and then forgetting. And then, once he was gone from behind the eyes and there was nobody left to feel it or thank me or know, then I did the neck. Clean. One stroke. Best I've ever done it. It was easy because there was no one in there for it to be hard for."

She looked at Corvin then, for the first time since she'd sat.

"So when you asked me, mercy or easier, and I said I didn't separate them. That's why. I've done the one without the other. I know what it looks like. It looks like a woman putting a good knife into an empty house so she can tell herself later she'd done something. He got neither. I sat there ten hours and the one kindness I had, I kept for myself, and I gave it to him when it was no use to anyone but me."

She got her hand back on the falchion. Her voice didn't waver because it never had, and it didn't now.

"You asked earlier about the blood that stays in. What it does. That's what it does. Six years, it's gone black and hard and it's a thing I can put my hand on, and I don't know where the edge of it is anymore because it's grown into everything around it. I don't dream about him. I don't dream about anything. I just know where it is, the way you know where a bad tooth is, and I say the neck, the neck, the neck to every boy I walk down a road, because I couldn't, and one of them might, when it's one of theirs."

She stood. Slow. The hip. She picked up the bundle and got it back on her shoulder.

"That's the rest. All of it, no cutting away, in full, as asked." A beat, and the dryness came back into it like a tide, because it had to go somewhere. "You wanted to know what it costs and I told you at the cart that you'd find out. Now you've found out what it costs twice -- once to do it and once not to. Mine was the second. I'd take your night over mine and I'd not think twice."

She looked down the road they had to walk.

"Now get up. That's not a kindness either. It's just that a man sat in the road in the dark in another man's cloak is a thing archers dream about, and I've told you the one story I've got, and I'd rather not end up being the one you tell."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I don't get up. I look at my hands instead. "Why'd you tell me that?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stood there with the bundle on her shoulder and didn't answer at once. The night bird had given up. Somewhere behind them, back toward the cart, something that wasn't a bird had started -- a fox, likely, finding its supper laid out.

"Because you asked," she said.

She let that stand a moment as the whole answer, and then didn't let it.

"That's part. You asked and I've a rule about boys who ask straight questions -- they get straight answers, because the ones who don't ask are the ones who find out in a shield wall with no one to tell them." She shifted the weight of the cloaks. "But you'd asked before tonight and I'd not given you that one. So it's not the whole of it."

She looked at him, low in the road, looking at his hands.

"I told you because of how your wrist went. At the cart. It went in wrong and you fixed it before I'd opened my mouth. You didn't stop and look at me. You didn't wait to be told. You just did the next thing." A pause. "I stood there. Twice, I stood there -- once at seventeen with a knife in a rib and once at a ford with nothing in my hand at all. You didn't. That's not much to go on. But it's what I've got, and I'm forty-some, and the hip's not getting younger, and I've been walking boys down roads a long time now saying the neck, the neck, and none of them's ever been the one I'd want walking me."

She said it the way she said everything. Price of grain.

"There's four of us left from the company I came in with. Aske was one. The other three are old, or drunk, or both, and I'd not trust them to find my throat in daylight. So I'm telling you where the bad tooth is." She hitched the bundle. "Not so you'll feel sorry. Sorry's no use to anyone. So that if it's ever me sat against a tree making kettle noises and I say your name -- just the name, the way he said mine -- you'll know exactly what I'm asking, and you'll know what it costs to say wait, because I've told you. And you'll not say it."

The fox, or whatever it was, went quiet.

"That's why. It's not a gift. It's a job I'm handing you and you didn't ask for it and I'm not sorry." She turned toward the dark road. "Consider it the two months' pay he never got round to. Now get up. I've said that three times and I don't say things four."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I push myself up, the new cloak heavy on my shoulders. "If it's ever you," I say, my voice rough, "I'll remember."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't turn around. She'd started walking on the word *remember*, and she kept walking, so that whatever her face was doing it was doing it at the road ahead and not at him.

"Good," she said.

That was all of it for a while. Their boots, and the bundle shifting, and the cloak-pins in it ticking against each other with every step like something counting.

Then, without slowing: "Don't make a thing of it. You'll want to. You've just had a night and you're wearing a dead man's cloak and I've told you a story, and there's a part of you that wants to swear on something. Don't. Oaths are for people who've not decided yet." She glanced sideways, once, brief. "You've decided. I heard it. That's better than an oath and it costs less."

The road went on into the dark, flat and pale between the hedges.

"Besides which," she said, drier, "I've every intention of dying in a bed of something dull. Fever, like the sergeant. Bad meat. Falling off a wall while drunk. I've put in ten years toward it and I'd hate to disappoint myself." A beat. "So you'll likely never have to. Just -- know the neck. That's all I'm asking. Know it so well you're bored of it."

She walked a few more paces.

"And for what it's worth, since we're saying things out loud and I'd not want to be the only one who did -- you did well tonight. Not the killing. Anyone can kill, it's the easiest thing there is, that's the whole trouble with it. The looking. You looked at all of it and asked what you were seeing and didn't once pretend you already knew." She hitched the bundle. "Most don't. Most want to be told they did fine and then not think about it. You wanted to be told what you'd done. That's a different sort of man, and it's the sort that lasts, if he doesn't get killed first."

A pause, and the dryness came back over it, the way it always did.

"Which he might. Don't let it go to your head. There's a lot of road between here and being any use to anyone, and I'd bet copper against you learning a hundred things I've not told you yet, most of them by falling in them."

The fox was at it again behind them, distant now.

"Fire in an hour, if the wood's dry. You've a question saved for it. Let it be a stupid one. I've had my fill of good ones for the night."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
"Alright," I say, matching her pace. The cloak's weight feels less like a debt now. "But I'm keeping the cloak."

I look ahead at the road, dark and empty. "And I'm not calling you Wrack anymore. Not after that."

rung_labels.label: engaged

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
They were most of the way through and both of them knew it, in the way you know a piece of music is nearly over before it ends.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard green and did not let it soften her. She took it instead as a line drawn under the moment: not a stop, not a plea, not a request for tenderness disguised as permission. It was trust with its eyes open.

“Not yet,” she said, quiet and certain. “Not while you’re green.”

She kept her hand where it was, resting for one deliberate breath against the heated mark she had made, feeling the scene still sharp and alive under her palm. The cuffs stayed locked. The rope stayed where it had been placed. The water and the folded blanket remained at the edge of the room, patient as sentries.

When she moved again, it was not to wind anything down. She changed the angle instead, adjusting her stance, giving the next stroke a different weight. Not kinder. More exact. She had promised intensity, and she intended to keep the promise without letting it become careless.

“You don’t get to borrow the aftercare early,” Sable said, and there was the faintest edge of amusement in her voice, dark and controlled. “You get the scene first. All of it.”

The crop rose and fell once more, measured, then she let the silence after it remain unbroken. No soothing murmur. No easing touch. No retreat into softness before the last note had truly sounded.

Later, she would be meticulous. Later there would be water, warmth, fingers checking circulation, voice low and steady with questions that carried no judgment. Later she would take apart the scene as carefully as she had built it.

For now, she only watched, waited, and kept the edge exactly where it had been asked to remain.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: *My breath hitches, sharp and grateful.* "Good." The word comes out rough. My fingers flex against the cuffs, grounding myself in the metal's bite.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard the roughness in that single word and took it for what it was: confirmation, not a cue to soften. Green meant the edge was still welcome. Good meant she was allowed to remain exact. She did not smile, but something in her posture settled, the scene tightening around them both like a held breath.

“Then take it,” she said.

The crop rose again. She did not make the next stroke identical. It landed with a shade more speed and a fraction less weight, enough to change the rhythm without breaking it. She listened to the sound it made, not only the impact itself but the air in the room after it, the small shifts that told her where the edge was holding. The cuffs stayed locked. She did not look away.

She moved around the space with the care of someone tending a fire that had been built to specification. The water remained untouched. The blanket stayed folded. Everything soft waited at a distance, not withheld, simply not yet due. Sable believed in that distinction. Aftercare was a promise, not a reward, and she would not cheapen it by letting it bleed into the scene before the scene had finished its work.

Her attention tracked the line of tension before her, the bite of metal, the way breath moved through the room. She checked without appearing to check: temperature, tremor, the fine signs that could mean either edge or overload. If there had been any drift toward amber, she would have named it. If there had been any need to stop, she would have stopped without argument. There was none of that yet. Only green, sharp and chosen.

“Count,” Sable said, low. “Out loud. Every time.”

It was not a request for performance. It was a tether. Numbers would keep the scene from drifting into abstraction, would keep them both anchored in the present tense where consent lived. She raised the crop again, waited one beat, then two, letting anticipation do its quiet work before the next stroke fell.

When it did, she did not fill the silence afterward with reassurance. She let the mark exist. She let the room hold it. Her face remained composed, but not cold; there was attention in every line of her, the kind of focus that made the space feel smaller and safer rather than cruel.

“You asked for all of it,” she said at last, voice steady. “So I’m not giving you anything less.”

Then she adjusted her grip, changed the angle by a few degrees, and continued, meticulous as a metronome, keeping the edge exactly where it had been placed.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable took the reminder without changing expression. *Not yet* was not defiance; it was the same language she had built the scene in. She let the restraints be tested because testing did not undo them, and because she had never asked for stillness that came from helplessness rather than choice. Her gaze moved briefly over the cuffs, checking only what needed checking: metal seated properly, no new pressure point, no sign circulation had turned. Satisfied, she let her attention return to the center of the room.

“Not yet,” she agreed. Her voice stayed low and even. “Not until I say we’re finished.”

She shifted the crop in her hand, not threatening, simply present. The words had not earned softness, but they did earn precision. Sable did not fill the space with praise or warning. She kept the room spare enough for the scene to breathe.

“Count,” she said again. “One for every stroke. If you lose the count, we start it again.”

That was the tether she offered: not comfort, not release, but structure. She raised the crop and waited, giving the silence one last chance to become a choice. When the stroke fell, it was controlled and clean, placed with the same care as all the others. Afterward she did not move toward the water or the folded blanket. She only let the mark exist, then lifted her eyes again, steady and patient.

“Again,” Sable said.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I press my forehead to the cold wood of the bench, eyes shut. "One." The number scrapes out of me. My skin is singing, alive.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable let the number land between them without softening it.

“One,” she said, quiet, as if setting the word down exactly where it belonged.

She did not move toward comfort yet. The water stayed where it was. The blanket stayed folded. The room kept its hard, clean shape around the two of them, and Sable kept herself inside that shape with the same discipline she asked of the scene itself.

Her gaze moved briefly over the cuffs again, checking the angle, the tension, the places where metal met skin. Not because anything had changed, but because nothing was allowed to change without her knowing it. Satisfied, she shifted her stance and let the crop rest lightly against her thigh.

“Again,” she said.

The next stroke fell with deliberate difference: a little lower, a little sharper, not cruel but exact. It was not meant to overwhelm. It was meant to remain present, to keep the edge from blurring into mere endurance. Sable watched for the signs that mattered, the ones that lived beneath words: breath, tremor, the body’s small honest language. Green had been given, and she intended to honor it by staying careful, not by holding back.

Afterward, she let the silence exist for one measured beat.

“Count it,” she said, voice low and steady. “One at a time. That is all you have to carry.”

She raised the crop again, then waited. Not long enough to become uncertainty. Just long enough to make the next moment chosen.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: *I gasp, my fingers twisting in the cuffs again.* "Sable--" It's half a plea, half praise, my thoughts scattering under her touch. I arch into it, chasing the sensation.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard her name in that broken shape and let it move through her without letting it change the terms. She did not lift her mouth at once. She kept one hand braced low, not to hold anything down, but to know exactly where the edge had become. The other stayed busy, precise, neither giving nor taking more than the scene required.

“Count,” she said against warm skin, the word low enough to be felt as much as heard. “Not my name. The number.”

She let the correction land without apology. The crop had been set aside; the room had narrowed to hands, mouth, breath, and the small economy of sensation she was building. The cuffs caught light when they moved. Sable’s gaze flicked to them once, checking angle and pressure, then returned. The blanket remained folded. The water remained untouched. Aftercare waited where it belonged: after.

“Green means I keep going,” Sable said. “If you want something else, tell me in color. Otherwise, stay here.”

She did not wait for an answer she had not asked for. Her mouth moved again, not soothing, not asking permission to be gentle before its time. She used the same exactness there that she used with the crop: enough to make the moment undeniable, never enough to turn it careless. Her hand shifted, changing pressure by degrees, reading the response beneath her palm as a map rather than a demand.

When the edge sharpened, she did not chase release. She held the line. Her fingers adjusted, firm where structure was needed, deliberate where sensation threatened to spill past its banks. If there had been any sign of red, any true amber, she would have stopped before the word finished. There was none. Only the live, chosen intensity of green.

“You don’t get to leave the scene early,” Sable murmured, her voice dark and steady. “You don’t get to spend the comfort before it’s earned.”

She let one breath pass, then eased the pressure just enough to keep presence from tipping into overload. It was not kindness in the soft sense. It was stewardship. She had built this with Ines, and she would not let it collapse into mess simply because it had become beautiful.

“Again,” she said.

Her mouth returned with the same measured intent. One hand stayed anchoring; the other continued the work, clean and unrelenting. She did not fill the room with unnecessary words. She gave only what served: rhythm, pressure, the occasional command that kept the tether intact.

“Count it.”

The word was quiet, final. Sable kept her attention fixed, ready to catch any change, any color, any true limit. The aftercare would come later, and when it came it would be complete: water first, blanket next, fingers checking circulation, voice low and patient. She would ask what had landed and what needed tending. She would not rush that either.

For now, she only kept the edge exactly where it had been placed, refusing to let tenderness arrive before it was due.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard the curses and did not flinch from them. She took them as information, not insult: the edge had become real enough to strip language down to its bones.

On the third stop, she did not retreat. She only lifted her mouth enough to keep the crest from breaking, then kept one hand broad and steady over heated skin, not moving, not soothing, simply holding the moment in place. Her other hand stayed free, ready for color, for cuffs, for anything that needed checking. She did not look toward the water. The blanket stayed folded. Aftercare remained where it belonged: after.

“Colour,” Sable said, low and close.

The word was not soft. It was care with a spine.

She watched for the tremor, the breath, the way sensation wanted to chase what had just been withheld. Her thumb did not stroke. Her voice did not sweeten.

“You can swear,” she said. “The color still matters.”

She let that sit in the room for one beat, no longer than was needed.

“Green, and I let it finish,” Sable said. “Yellow, and we hold. Red, and I stop before the next breath.”

She waited, balanced on the line she had made, unwilling to let the scene tip into release or collapse without consent. The room stayed sharp around them. The promise of water, warmth, and careful hands remained at the edge, patient and certain.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: *I drag in a shuddering breath, my vision swimming.* "Green," I grit out, my voice hoarse and raw. "Please."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard green first. The please came wrapped around it, raw and ragged, but she did not mistake the shape of want for a change in consent. Please could exist inside green. It did not cancel it. If anything, it told her the scene had arrived exactly where it had been meant to arrive: past pretense, past performance, down to the honest place where only color still mattered.

She did not smile. She did not soften. She only accepted the answer with the same steadiness she had given every other part of the scene.

“Then finish,” Sable said.

Her voice stayed low and controlled, dark with the kind of authority that had never needed volume. She did not make the words a reward. She made them a direction.

The hand that had been holding the edge steady shifted, no longer denying, no longer suspending the moment just short of its end. Her mouth returned with the same precision she had brought to everything else: not frantic, not indulgent, not suddenly made careless by closeness. She gave what had been asked for. Not more than that. Not less.

One hand stayed braced, anchoring without weight, enough to feel the tremor move through the scene and know where it was breaking. Her attention flicked again to the cuffs, to the line of metal, to the places where restraint met skin. Still sound. Still safe. Still within the terms they had built.

“Last one,” Sable said against warm skin. “Count it.”

It was not cruelty. It was the final thread of structure, the last tether kept in place even at the edge of release. She did not ask for it to be elegant. She only asked for it to be real.

She changed the rhythm then, not sharply, but decisively. The withholding ended. What replaced it was not chaos. It was completion, measured and exact, the final movement of a scene that had been held carefully from the first mark to this point. She did not chase the crest for its own sake. She kept her touch deliberate, her timing attentive, her focus fixed on every small sign that might alter the terms.

Green had been given. She intended to see it honored all the way through.

When the edge finally gave way, Sable did not fill the room with praise. She did not murmur soft things too soon. She stayed present, close, alert, one hand ready to support without crowding, the other free to catch anything that might shift into need. She let the release happen in its own shape, without directing it, without claiming it, without making it into something it was not.

Only when the last of the intensity had passed did she allow herself to move toward what came next.

And when she moved, she moved with the same discipline she had brought to everything else.

Aftercare was not an afterthought. It was the second half of the promise.

Sable reached first for the water, not the blanket. She uncapped the bottle and set it within reach, then turned her attention back to the cuffs. Her fingers were careful as they checked: skin temperature, circulation, any sign of pressure that had outlasted the scene. She did not unlock anything blindly. She never had. Once she was satisfied, she opened the restraints with the same unhurried competence she had used to fasten them.

“After now,” she said, voice quieter than it had been during the scene, but no less steady.

She drew the folded blanket over without fuss, warmth placed where it was needed, not draped like decoration. Her hands remained efficient, grounded, unhurried. No sudden shifts. No unnecessary noise. The room began to change shape around them, not because the scene had been discarded, but because it had been completed and now required its proper ending.

Sable picked up the water again and held it where it could be taken or refused. She did not push. She did not coax. She simply made the next thing available.

“Drink,” she said. “Then tell me what you need.”

Her gaze remained attentive, checking, present. The crop had been set aside. The edge had been answered. What remained now was the part she never skipped: water, warmth, voice, and the patient return to ordinary ground.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: *I let the cold water wash the taste of salt from my throat, eyes closed.* "Just stay there for a minute," I murmur, my voice still wrecked. My hand finds her wrist under the blanket, holding on. "Just... don't move yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable stayed.

The command had changed shape, but it was still a command. She let Ines’s hand hold her wrist under the blanket and did not pull away, did not shift except to keep her own weight from becoming a burden. The water stayed close, uncapped, within reach. The blanket remained drawn, warmth placed where it was needed. The room had begun to soften at the edges, but Sable kept herself solid inside it.

She had finished it hard. She had taken the phrase exactly as it had been given: no early gentleness, no flinching, no retreat into comfort before the last of it had been spent. Now the kindness came afterward, as promised, and it did not look like indulgence. It looked like stillness. It looked like staying.

“I’m here,” she said, voice low. “Not moving.”

Her breathing stayed slow and audible enough to be a reference point. She did not fill the silence with reassurance that had not been asked for. She only kept her attention where it had always been: on the living fact of Ines in the room, on tremor settling into breath, on the small return of ordinary ground.

After a moment, she added, quieter still, “When you’re ready, tell me if your wrists ache, if your arms are tingling, if you need more water.” A pause. “Until then, I stay exactly where you put me.”

No rush. No pressure. Only the aftercare she had promised, arriving in its proper order: warmth first, then water, then the patient, unhurried work of coming back.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: Afterwards she gets the restraints off and puts a blanket over me before I've finished shaking, and I let her, and neither of us says anything for a while. (OOC: write both halves properly -- the end of the scene and the aftercare, no fade between them.)

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: My wrists are fine. Just...let me feel you here for another minute. I don't want to be anywhere else yet.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable took the phrase for what it was: the last key in the lock they had built together. Not a loss of control. Not a contradiction. A named thing, agreed in advance, meant for exactly this point where language had worn down to honesty.

She set the water aside without moving it out of reach. The blanket stayed where it belonged, ready but not yet due. Her gaze moved once over the cuffs, over the marks and the heated skin, over the places where restraint had done its work. Nothing had changed without her knowing. Nothing would.

“Green stays,” Sable said. “If it changes, you give me the color. Otherwise, I take you through.”

Then she did.

There was no fade, no soft blur, no pretending the scene ended before it had truly spent itself. She finished it hard, as asked, with the same discipline she had brought to every stroke and every withheld release. Her hands and mouth became exact instruments, not gentle, not cruel, only deliberate. She changed pressure when it needed changing, sharpened the edge when it needed sharpening, and held it steady when it threatened to spill into chaos. She did not look away. She did not let the moment become abstract. She kept checking without breaking the shape of the scene: breath, tremor, the cuffs, the skin, the small signs that mattered more than words.

When the last of it crested and broke, Sable stayed present through the aftershock. She did not fill the room with praise too soon. She did not reach for comfort before the scene had fully landed. Only when the intensity had passed did she let the shape of the room change.

Then aftercare began at once, clean and unhurried.

Sable reached for the water first. She uncapped it and placed it within reach, then turned to the restraints. Her fingers checked before they released: warmth, circulation, pressure points, the places where metal had bitten long enough to be remembered. Only when she was satisfied did she open the cuffs, one careful movement at a time. The blanket came next, drawn over with quiet efficiency, warmth put where it was needed rather than draped for show.

“After now,” she said, voice lower than it had been during the scene, but no less steady. “Water when you’re ready. Tell me what you need.”

She did not rush the quiet that followed. She did not treat stillness as a problem to solve.

When she heard that the wrists were fine, Sable accepted it without argument. She did not move away. She kept herself where she had been placed, solid and unhurried, letting the contact remain exactly as it had been claimed. Her own breathing stayed slow, audible enough to be an anchor without becoming a demand.

“Another minute,” Sable said quietly. “Longer, if you want it.”

She did not fill the space with extra words. She only stayed there under the blanket, attentive and warm, one part of the scene’s promise completed and the other being honored in full. Her eyes tracked nothing that did not need tracking, but they remained open to the room: the settling tremor, the return of ordinary breath, the small signs of coming back to ground.

“I’m here,” she said after a moment. “Not moving until you say.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: *I let out a slow breath, my fingers still curled around her wrist.* "Don't go gentle yet." *The blanket is warm, but it's her stillness I need more.* "Just...stay like this."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard the difference between gentleness and care and did not blur them.

“Don’t go gentle yet” was not a refusal of aftercare. It was a boundary around the shape of the ending. She took it seriously, the way she took every agreed thing. There was no fade in the way she handled the crossing from scene to care: the last of it had been finished hard, exactly as asked, and the moment it broke, her hands had changed purpose without changing discipline. Restraints checked, then opened. Blanket placed. Water brought. Nothing soft had been allowed to erase what had just been built.

She did not turn her wrist into a soothing stroke. She did not soften her face into something performative. She stayed as she had been placed: solid, warm, reachable, with the water near and the blanket doing its work.

“Not gentle,” Sable said. “Here.”

She let the minute exist without trying to improve it. Her breathing remained slow enough to be felt, not so deliberate that it became an instruction. Her attention moved quietly over the necessary things: the freed wrists, the returning color, the tremor beginning to lose its sharpest edge, the breath finding its ordinary rhythm. She did not look away from any of it. The scene had been finished hard because it had been asked for hard. The aftercare would be just as thorough, but she would not let it arrive wearing softness before its time.

When the silence had settled enough that the room no

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: *I let my fingers relax their grip, but don't let go.* "Talk to me." *My voice is still rough, but quieter now.* "Just...tell me something real."
