dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stood up, her bad knee clicking like dry tinder. She gave the dead man’s ribs a cursory nudge with the toe of her boot to judge the purse beneath his belt, found it thin, and didn't bother bending back down for it.

"Sounds like a lung," she observed, tilting her head toward the cart where the wet, whistling rattle rose and hitched. "Means twenty minutes if he’s unlucky. An hour if he’s stubborn enough to drown slow."

She slid the clean blade back into its sheath, the leather stiff with old salt and dried grit. Her eyes moved to Corvin, taking in the red smear across his cheek and the stiffness in his shoulders, her expression entirely flat. No judgment in it, just an inventory. 

"Either go stick him or sit down and eat your ration," she said, reaching into her coat for a dry scrap of jerked beef. "No sense standing in the road looking like you're waiting for an apology. Road's not giving one, and neither is he."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, my knuckles white on my sword grip. "He's not the first." I push off from the tree and start walking toward the cart. "But he'll be the last today."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack tore off a piece of the dried beef with her molars, chewing slowly as she watched his back. 

"Aim behind the collarbone," she called after him, her voice carrying just enough to cut through the wet wheeze from the ditch. "Down into the chest. Saves your edge, and you won't have to hear the ribs snap. Makes a mess of the tunic, but he's already bled all over it anyway."

She didn't follow him. She turned back toward the ditch instead, stepping over the first corpse to see what the second one had to offer. A younger fellow, lean-shanked, wearing boots that looked a half-size too big but had good thick soles with life left in them. 

Wrack crouched beside him, her joints popping in the quiet. 

"Check his belt while he's still soft," she added, not looking up as she began working the laces on the dead boy's left boot. "Prying cold fingers off a coin purse after the frost hits is work nobody needs."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack yanked hard on the boot heel until the stiff leather yielded with a dry scrape against the dead boy’s heel. She set it aside and went to work on the laces of the right one.

"They're the same thing," she said, her voice completely even. "Mercy’s just what you call it when you want to feel like a better sort of man while you do it."

She gave a stubborn knot a vicious tug with her thumbnail. 

"Look at him. He’s blowing pink bubbles, isn’t he? Sucking air through a hole that shouldn't be there. You leave him, he chokes on his own red froth by sundown, or he lays there until the wolves pick up the scent while he's still warm enough to feel the teeth. You try and patch him, he rots from the inside out over four days of fever and dies smelling like spoiled meat anyway."

She pulled the second boot free, inspected the stitching on the sole with a practiced squint, and tossed it next to its mate. 

"Dead is dead, Corvin. Dead now means he doesn't have to think about it all night, and we don't have to listen to him do it. The ditch doesn't care which reason you put on the ledger. Just don't miss the notch behind the bone, or you'll have to do it twice, and there's nothing merciful about that."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel next to the dying man, watching the pink foam gather at the corner of his mouth. My hand's steady when I reach for my dagger. "You're right," I say, mostly to myself. Then I lean in.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
There was a soft, heavy *thud* of steel finding gristle, a sudden, choked hitch in the dying man’s breath, and then the road went properly quiet. The whistling stopped. Just the dry rustle of the scrub grass in the evening wind and the distant croak of a crow that had been waiting for them to finish.

Wrack knotted the laces of the boots together and slung them over her shoulder. She wiped her hands on her trousers and finally looked back toward the cart.

"There," she said, her voice dropping into the new silence without a ripple. "Told you. One stroke, no mess."

She stood up, shaking out her bad leg until the knee gave a dull, hollow pop. She took her time walking over, stepping carefully around the darkening ruts where the cart had torn up the turf. 

When she rounded the tailgate, she didn't look at the man Corvin had just bled. She’d seen enough dead men to know what they looked like when the tension went out of their jaws. Instead, she reached past Corvin, grabbed the corner of the stained canvas lashed over the cart bed, and hauled it back with one rough jerk.

"Now let's see if we did all that running around for flour or salt pork," she muttered, squinting into the gloom of the wagon. "Wipe the blade on his coat, Corvin. Blood pits the steel if you leave it to crust in the cold, and I'm not lending you my whetstone again."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack let the canvas drop with a heavy flap and turned around, resting an elbow against the wagon sideboard. She looked down at the body by Corvin’s boots, then up at his face, her own completely unreadable.

"You're looking at meat," she said, blunt and quiet. 

She hitched her weight off her bad leg and gestured vaguely with her chin toward the dead man's face. 

"Look at the eyes. See how they went dull? Like grease skimming over cold soup. They stop catching the light the second the heart quits. He’s not staring at the clouds; he’s just pointed in that direction. Nothing behind them anymore."

She shifted her jaw, working a speck of gristle from her teeth. 

"Jaw goes slack because the cords gave out. Tongue drops back. In about three minutes, the rest of the muscles do the same thing, which means his gut's going to empty itself. If you're going to search his pockets, you do it from the head down, and you don't stand downwind."

She looked back up at Corvin, her gray eyes flat as river stones. 

"Folks who don't do this for a living think there's a mystery to it. They think something floats away, or there's some grand quiet that falls over a man when his time comes. It isn't grand. It's just a mechanism that broke. Like a cart with an axle snapped in half. You stopped the works, and now he's cooling off."

She tapped the flat of her own scabbard against her thigh, a sharp *thwack* of leather on leather. 

"Wipe your steel, Corvin. Staring at it won't make him get up, and it won't make you feel any different about doing it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe the dagger clean on his tunic, my movements stiff. "Mechanism," I repeat, watching the cloth turn darker. I stand and look at her. "You ever see one you knew before it broke?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack reached past him into the bed of the wagon, hauling aside a coarse burlap sack. Beneath it were two casks of salted herring and a wooden crate packed with straw. She pulled her knife back out, wedged the tip under the crate lid, and levered it up with a sharp *creak* of rusted nails.

"Dozens," she said. 

She tossed the loose slat onto the turf, reached into the straw, and pulled out an iron-banded jar of grease. She grunted, unimpressed, and shoved it back. 

"First company I rode with had sixty spears. Four of us made it past the third winter. You share a kettle with a man for three years, you know how he takes his tea, you know the name of the girl who broke his nose behind the mill, you know the sound of his snore." 

She wiped a smudge of grease off her knuckle onto her breeches and leaned back against the wagon sideboard, crossing her arms over the boots slung across her chest. The dusk was setting in fast now, the cold biting through the wool. 

"Old boy named Hobb," she said, her voice dropping into the steady, flat cadence she used for counting rations. "Taught me how to pare a hoof without getting kicked. Took a crossbow bolt under the breastplate at the Red Crossing. Skewered the liver. Took him two days and a half to drown in his own poison."

She looked straight at Corvin, her gray eyes narrowing slightly against the evening wind.

"He begged me to do what you just did for that boy in the dirt. Cried like a child with a skinned knee. Smelled like spoiled cabbage and bad vinegar. I sat on his chest to hold him down and put eight inches of iron through the hollow of his neck." 

She didn't blink. She didn't look down at the dead man at their feet, either.

"You're asking because you think it changes the arithmetic. You think if you know a man, his dying comes with a song attached. It doesn't. They don't die cleaner, Corvin. They bleed just as red, they stink just as bad, and when they're done, you still have to dig through their pockets to find the brass they owed you for tobacco."

She reached out and gave his shoulder a brief, heavy shove with the flat of her palm—not unkind, but solid enough to rattle him back into his boots.

"Help me heave these herring casks onto the road before it's pitch black. We've got two miles to the bivouac, and I'm not carrying your share of the salt."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't scoff, and she didn't soften. She just reached down, grabbed the iron rim of the nearest herring cask, and dragged it to the edge of the tailgate with a screech of salt-crusted wood.

"Straight, then," she said, leaning her weight against the barrel. "First thing is the sound. It's not a slice. A spear's got a leaf blade or a bodkin, and it doesn't cut in, it punches. Sounds like a wet boot sinking into swamp mud. A dull *pop* when it breaks the skin, and then a scrape against the gristle."

She spat into the ditch, wiped her mouth with the back of her sleeve, and looked him right in the teeth.

"Then the steel comes back out, and whatever it hooked comes out with it. A spearhead doesn't just poke a hole; it tears. It catches the small bowel, pops the tubing. The smell hits you before the man even starts screaming. Hot shit, half-digested slop, and copper. It smells like a slaughterhouse trough on an August noon."

She tapped her own stomach with two blunt fingers, right below the navel.

"The man drops his weapon every single time. Instinct takes over. He grabs for his middle, trying to push it all back in, but intestines are slick as greased eels and grey-pink like raw sausage. They spill out over his hands. He's on his knees, shivering, slipping in his own muck, trying to shove three feet of ruptured gut back into a three-inch slit."

Her voice remained entirely level, as if she were describing the proper way to mend a bridle.

"If the iron clipped the big artery running along the spine, he's lucky. He bleeds out in two minutes. He turns white, goes limp, done. But usually, the spear misses the pipe and just shreds the gut. That means he lives."

She reached out, caught the collar of Corvin’s coat, and gave it a small, sharp twist to keep his attention pinned.

"He lives for two days. Three, if he's strong. His belly swells up tight and shiny like a bloated goat in the sun. Hard as a cured ham. The fever cooks him from the inside out until his tongue cracks and his spit turns to yellow foam. He begs for water, and if you give him a swallow, he vomits up black rot because his stomach's got nowhere to dump it. He shits himself to death through the hole in his front."

She let go of his collar, smoothing the wool flat with a rough, heavy pat.

"Nobody stitches that, Corvin. No leech in the army's got the thread or the stomach for it. You leave him behind the baggage train to bake in his own poison, or someone who can't stand the howling slips into the tent after midnight with a rag over his face."

She stepped back and jerked her chin toward the herring barrel.

"That's what a spear does. Nothing noble in it. Just a butcher's job gone sloppy. Now get your hands under the chime and lift. Daylight's gone, and the dead don't care about your education."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I get my hands under the barrel, the wood rough and damp. "Hobb," I say, heaving it down into the road. "You ever find the brass he owed you?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The cask hit the packed road with a heavy, hollow thud, raising a small cloud of road dust that smelled of dried dung and old salt. Wrack steadied it with the side of her knee, not bothering to wince at the dull ache that flared up through the joint.

"Four bits," she said. "Stitched right into the lining of his breeches where a thief wouldn't look without cutting the seams."

She wiped her palms on her thighs and turned back toward the cart, reaching for the second cask. 

"Still had his blood on them when I turned them over to the sutler at the river camp," she added, her voice flat against the rising wind. "Man didn't care. Blood scrubs off copper easy enough with a handful of river sand, but it takes half a day's march to earn four bits honest."

She shoved the second cask to the lip of the tailgate, the iron bands screeching against the timber. 

"Bought half a skin of sour cider and two ounces of dry pipe-weed," she said, leaning her shoulder into the wood to hold it steady for him. "Cider gave me the gray flux for three days, but the smoke was decent. Hobb would've laughed. He always said the sutler’s cider was pressed from ditch-apples and horse piss."

She hooked her fingers under the iron chime, looking at him across the salt-crusted oak.

"Catch the bottom edge. One, two, down. And don't drop it on your toes—I’m not carrying you back to the fires, and the wolves around here don't wait for morning."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped. Her boots stayed planted in the churned mud by the cartwheel, the cold wind catching the frayed hem of her cloak. She didn't roll her eyes, and she didn't tell him to get up off the dirt. If a pup wanted to look into the furnace, you let him smell the singed hair; it saved you having to pull him out later.

She took a slow, measured breath, letting the frost bite her nostrils, and folded her arms over the boots hanging at her chest.

"You’re hitting rib," she said, her voice flat, steady as an anvil. "Hear that? That dull *clack*, like chopping dry pine with a dull hatchet. That’s the flat of your blade wedging into the bone. The bone doesn't want to yield. It's curved to keep iron out of the cage."

She took two paces closer, just near enough that her shadow fell over Corvin and the twitching shape beneath his hands.

"Now you're levering it. Don't twist—you'll snap the tang off at the hilt, and good steel costs more than whatever you're trying to prove. Push down and angle toward his left shoulder. There. Feel it slip through the gristle? That give? That's the intercostal meat giving up."

The dying man let out a thick, bubbling groan, his heels drumming a weak, spasmodic rhythm against the frozen dirt. A dark, hot wave spilled over Corvin’s fingers, steaming faintly in the dusk.

"That shuddering isn't him fighting you," Wrack said, watching the man’s throat convulse. "He’s gone past knowing your name or his own. That’s just the salt in his blood sparking through the nerves like wet kindling. Like an eel thrashing in the bucket twenty minutes after you took its head off."

She pointed a dirt-caked finger toward the wound.

"You missed the pump. Clipped the edge of the right lung and nicked the vein beneath the collar. That’s why it’s pooling dark instead of spurting bright red. Means he’s got another ninety seconds of heartbeat left. Listen to his throat. Hear that click? That’s the swallow reflex firing on empty air. His brain's starving for blood, so the body's throwing every latch it has left."

The drumming of the heels slowed, hitched, and stopped. A long, soft sigh hissed out between the dead lips, carrying the sour reek of copper and empty bile. The jaw unhinged slightly, settling sideways in the dirt.

"There," Wrack said into the quiet. "Vessel's drained. Core went cold. Total elapsed: about as long as it takes to boil an egg soft."

She looked down at Corvin, her gray eyes narrowing in the half-light. 

"Now pull the iron out straight, wipe your hands on the grass before the grease dries sticky, and pick up your corner of the cask. We've got miles to cover, and you smell like a shambles."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I pull the dagger free with a soft, wet sound and wipe my hands on the dead grass. My fingers are trembling, but not from the cold. "Didn't feel any different," I say, my voice too low. "Not when I knew."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
"Told you," Wrack said. She didn't offer a hand to help him up. 

She stood over him, watching his fingers twitch against the frozen stems of the ditch-grass. She’d seen the tremor a thousand times. The blood pumped high to keep a man from dying, and when there was nothing left to fight, the extra heat had nowhere to go but out through the knuckles. 

"You expect lightning to crack the sky every time you turn the wick down on a stranger," she said, her voice dry as dead bark. "You think because it's a terrible thing, it ought to feel like one. But the knife doesn't know you, Corvin. The meat doesn't know you. It just parts because steel is harder than suet."

She reached down, took a firm grip on his arm just above the elbow, and hauled him up onto his feet with a single, unceremonious yank that rattled his teeth. 

"The shake's just the fright bleeding out of you," she said, letting go the instant his boots found traction. "Take a breath through your nose. Swallow your spit. You stare at your hands long enough, you'll talk yourself into believing they belong to a monster or a hero, and you're neither. You're just a hireling with salt on his trousers and cold grease under his nails."

She turned her back on him, stepping up to the second herring cask. She slapped the curved stave with an open palm—a sharp, booming *thwack* in the evening quiet.

"He's done, Corvin. The road’s done with him, the king’s done with him, and his captain's already striking his name off the payroll to save two groats on the muster. He's not thinking about you. Stop thinking about him."

She hooked her boots into the rutted turf, bracing her shoulder against the timber. 

"Now get your hands back on the chime. Lift with your thighs, not your spine, unless you want to spend the next four weeks walking like me. We’ve got cold salt to carry."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn’t snap at him to get up. She let her hands drop from the cask, the wood creaking slightly as her weight shifted off it. The wind was coming out of the north now, dry and sharp, smelling of dead thistle and the iron tang of the dirt they’d turned up.

She walked back over to where he knelt, her boots heavy and slow in the gravel, and stopped two feet from the dead boy’s head. She didn't cross her arms this time. She just stood there, looking down at the corpse, then at Corvin’s bloody wrists.

"The rest," she said, her voice dropping lower, raspy and steady as a whetstone on iron, "is that nobody is watching."

She nudged the dead man's hip with the blunt toe of her boot. 

"You think there's a score being kept somewhere. In heaven, in hell, in some ledger the priests tell tales about by the fire. You think because you crossed a line today, the earth shifted an inch on its axle. It didn't. The grass doesn't give a damn that you opened his chest. The trees don't care. The sky’s the same grey it was when we broke camp at sunrise."

She reached up, hooked a thumb under the collar of her gambeson, and rubbed at an old scar on her throat, unhurried.

"Tonight, after the sun's fully under, the frost'll settle on his eyelashes. Turn them white. In about four hours, the blood in his arms and legs is going to drain down toward whatever side of him is touching the ground. If you turn him over by midnight, his backside will be dark as an eggplant, purple and swollen with dead fluid, while his chest stays the color of cold suet."

She pointed toward the woods with her chin.

"The crows already know he's here. You heard that one earlier. In an hour, the foxes'll sniff the bile you spilled when you missed the lung. They don't go for the meat first, Corvin. They go for the soft bits. The tongue. The lips. The eyelids. If the dogs from the burnt farm two miles back catch the wind, they'll tear his belly out through the slit you made because it's easier than chewing through the boiled leather on his jerkin. By noon tomorrow, he won't look like a boy who had a mother. He'll look like a pile of chewed rags and splintered bone."

She stopped rubbing her neck and looked right down into Corvin’s face, her eyes cold and pale in the blue dusk.

"And then there's you," she said. 

She took half a step closer. The smell of her was old wool, tobacco, and the dull, dry salt of someone who hadn't slept warm in three weeks.

"You’re going to wash your hands in the creek before we reach the bivouac. You’ll scrub them with sand until the skin’s raw and bleeding at the cuticles. You’ll think you got it all out. But when you sit by the cook-pot tonight and take your hunk of bread, you'll bring your fingers to your mouth and you'll smell him. You'll smell that hot, sour copper. It doesn't come out of the pores for two days. You'll taste him in the fat, you'll taste him in the beer, and you'll wonder why the men around you are laughing at some filthy joke while you've got a dead boy's grease stuck in your teeth."

She didn't blink. The wind caught a loose strand of her graying hair, whipping it across her scarred cheek, but she didn't bother brushing it away.

"And the worst of it—the part you're really asking about, whether you know it or not—is that in six months, you won't even remember the shape of his chin. You think you will. You think you'll carry this exact face to your grave like a holy relic of the day you became what you are. You won't. He'll blur into the next one, and the next one'll blur into the fellow you took off his horse at the ford, until they're all just one big, gray smear of gristle and wet boots."

She crouched down then, slow and careful on her bad joint, until her eyes were level with his. She put both hands on her knees, the leather of her gloves cracked and stiff.

"You won't turn into a devil, Corvin. Devils have purpose. You'll just turn into a creature that knows how to put steel into meat without dropping its ration afterward. You'll wake up ten years from now, forty years old, with bad knees and sour guts, carrying someone else's salted fish down a ruined road that goes nowhere, fighting for a duke whose name you can't recall, and you won't even have the decency to feel sick about it anymore."

She reached out, caught his chin in her calloused, salt-stiffened fingers, and tilted his face an inch higher, forcing him to meet her eye. Her grip was hard, but not rough.

"That's the rest," she said, quiet as the grave they were leaving behind. "No song. No curse. Just work, and dirt, and getting older in the cold. Now look at him one more time if you need to, and then stand up on your two feet. I'm not doing the barrel alone."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
I look at him. I try to hold onto the shape of his chin, the stubble, the way his ear folds. It's already starting to blur.

Then I push myself up, my knees popping. I walk to the barrel and put my hands on the chime. "Let's go," I say, my voice flat. "Before I lose the light."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack took her time rising, her bad knee giving its customary crack like green pine in a hearth. She didn't say *good boy*, and she didn't clap him on the back. A dog got a pat for doing its trick; a man doing his trade got a sore back and a ration tin, and that was the end of the transaction.

She stepped across the churned mud to the opposite side of the cask, hooked her gloved fingers under the rusted iron chime, and planted her heels into the rutted dirt.

"On three," she said, her voice dropping right back into the low, working rumble she used for draft beasts. "One. Two. Heave."

They hauled it together. The oak was thick, soaked through with brine, the pickled fish inside sloshing in a dull, heavy surge that nearly pulled the wood from their numb fingers before they found their balance. Wrack took the weight on her good hip, clamping her jaw tight as the dead weight pulled at her shoulders.

She didn't look back at the ditch, or the cart, or the boy with the crooked chin. She started walking west, her gait rolling and uneven to favor the joint, setting a pace slow enough to keep from spilling their guts on the stones.

"Creek’s a half-mile past the willow stand," she said between breaths, the white vapor puffing from her cracked lips into the dark. "Runoff from the ridge, cold enough to turn your balls into walnuts, but the gravel's sharp. Scrubs the grease off better than river silt."

The wind gusted along the ditch behind them, carrying a brief rustle of dry weeds and the far-off, high-pitched yip of a dog catching a fresh trail. Wrack didn't break stride. 

"Keep your head up and watch the ruts," she grunted, her boots crunching in the frost. "Drop your corner, and we pick the fish out of the horse shit one by one. I like salt, but I don't like it that much."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I keep my eyes on the path, the barrel's weight settling into my shoulders. "Tell me something about Hobb," I say, my breath fogging in the air. "Something that doesn't have to do with how he died."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The barrel gave a heavy, wet shudder between them as they navigated a frozen furrow in the cart-track. Wrack hitched her shoulder, adjusting her grip on the iron chime until the rust dug into a different set of calluses. 

"Geese," she said, her breath venting in three short puffs against the cold.

She didn't look at him; her eyes stayed pinned to the frosted stones two paces ahead of her boots. 

"Big gray ones. The kind the hill-crofters keep to guard their cabbage patches. Saw Hobb cleave a man’s shoulder-guard in two at the Seven Fords—took the fellow down to the collar and didn't even drop his spit. But let an old gander come hissing out from under a porch with its wings spread, and Hobb would scramble onto the back of the baggage wagon like a girl with a rat up her skirts."

She grunted as her bad knee took the brunt of a drop into a dry ditch-wash, then leveled out. 

"Swore one took a chunk out of his backside when he was five years old. Said geese were the only beasts God made that had pure spite in their gizzards instead of brains. Whenever we were sent out to forage a farmstead, he’d trade me his tobacco ration—two whole fingers of black twist—just to walk between him and the coops with a stick."

She let out a dry, rattling sound from the back of her throat that might have been a laugh if she’d had the wind to spare for it. 

"Six feet of gristle and scar-tissue, carrying an eight-foot billhook, creeping behind a woman half his weight because an eight-pound bird with webbed feet was stretching its neck at him. Used to throw dry beans at them from twenty yards off to see if they were roosting before he’d set foot in an orchard."

The barrel sloshed again, the brine inside thick and sluggish with the frost. Wrack shifted her footing, picking up the pace just a fraction as the track began to slope gently downward toward the dark line of willows that marked the creek.

"Hated turnip greens, too," she added, her voice dropping back to its steady, working rhythm. "Said they tasted like wet hair. Would trade an entire mutton joint for three dried plums if a peddler had them."

She tilted her chin toward the trees ahead, where the faint, cold rattle of water over gravel was beginning to carry through the dark.

"There's the wash. Watch your footing on the gravel bar. Set the chime down easy when I say, or you'll crack the staves and we'll be eating salt dirt for breakfast."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I can almost hear the gander hissing. "Turnip greens taste like wet hair," I say, and I almost smile. Almost. "Your turn. What do you trade your rations for?"

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The party had reached the stage where nobody would notice two people missing, which Odile pointed out approximately four seconds before doing something about it.

"The bathroom upstairs has a lock," she said, into Fen's ear, over the music.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Does it work?" I ask, already moving toward the stairs.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"The lock," Odile said, "is untested. Which is, I think, the entire point."

She caught Fen's hand and towed them through the kitchen — past Priya, deep in a hostess argument with a man in a cardigan, neither of them looking up — and toward the stairs. Carpeted. Odile had never once been grateful for carpet before tonight. Her heels still found the one creaky step, and the laugh that escaped her was far too loud for a woman actively sneaking somewhere; she strangled it into a hiss and clapped her own hand over her mouth.

"Shh," she whispered, at a volume that would not have qualified. "Both of us. Shh."

Upstairs the music went soft and structural, more felt than heard. The hallway ran dim ahead, one door spilling warm light, and at the far end, the blue door. Odile walked backward along it, facing Fen, pulling them by the hand, grinning like someone who'd already gotten away with it.

"Cover story: you're looking for your coat and I'm catastrophically drunk—"

"I'm not drunk," she corrected herself, finger raised. "I'm a liar. It's different. Legally it matters."

Then the blue door, the click of the lock. She tried the handle twice, pushing, testing, and turned around with her back against the door, in the small white light of the bathroom, looking at Fen with the specific expression of a woman who has just gotten away with something and fully intends to risk it again immediately.

"Okay. Timer's running. Someone will need this bathroom eventually." Her voice had dropped, gone lower, less performative. "So we should probably hurry. Or not. I genuinely haven't decided."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "I vote for 'or not'," I say, stepping closer and sliding my hands around her waist. "Let 'em be uncomfortable. They're all boring anyway."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"'Or not,'" Odile repeated, as though reading the verdict off a card. "That's the reckless vote. Noted for the record: I considered the safe option, and I'm overriding it."

Then she kissed them, her back against the door she'd just vouched for, one hand at Fen's collar, the bass from downstairs coming up through the floor more than through the air. She broke off an inch — not for air, for disclosure.

"Fair warning. I'm bad at the quiet part. You heard the stairs."

The next kiss got a sound out of her that she would have sworn, later, under oath, was quiet.

Which was when the floorboards in the hallway moved. Not theirs.

Odile went stone-still, hand clamped over her own mouth, eyes enormous and — traitorously — delighted. A shadow crossed the strip of light under the door. The handle turned. Pushed. The lock, untested no longer, held, and Odile, without moving anything else, gave Fen a solemn thumbs

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I get the door shut and her against it, and downstairs somebody turns the music up, which helps.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The music swelling downstairs was, as far as Odile was concerned, the closest thing to divine intervention she'd get this year.

"Whoever did that," she breathed, "deserves a toast. Covered for a crime, no questions asked. Five stars."

Then, because the moment deserved full disclosure: "Also — the music is a trap. I now believe I'm being quiet. I am not being quiet. Factor that in and proceed anyway."

She kissed Fen like the vote had been cast and counted — *or not*, carried unanimously — one hand at their collar, the other flat against the door behind her, as if one palm could hold back the entire party. The bass came up through the floor and through her, and the sound she made into it she would have defended in court as technically permissible.

Her fingers found the hem of Fen's shirt and slid an inch beneath, idle and not idle.

"The thing about almost getting caught," she murmured against their mouth, losing the shape of her own sentence, "is—"

Footsteps. Hallway. Coming.

She went stone-still again — hand clamped over her mouth, back hard against the door, eyes enormous and shining with what was absolutely not fear. The steps slowed near the blue door. A pause. Odile held her breath like it was a competitive event.

Then they kept going — another door, farther down, opening, closing. Someone else's room. Someone else's secret, or just somebody hunting for a coat.

Odile pressed her face into Fen's shoulder and laughed the way she'd laughed on the stairs — silent, shaking, shoulders doing all the work.

"Okay," she whispered, when she trusted herself. "Okay. New math. Ten minutes, tops, before somebody needs this bathroom, and I intend to spend all ten of them badly. Also, for the record: I never finished that thumbs-up. It was a full thumbs-up. Maximum approval."

She pulled Fen back in.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "I'm not letting you go until you've earned that thumbs-up," I say, my voice low against her neck as my hands slide up her sides. "And I'm a very thorough judge."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"Thorough judge," Odile repeated. "Right. Small procedural note: the judge is compromised. The judge has been kissing the evidence."

Their voice at her neck, their hands at her sides — her spine did something unauthorized, and she clamped her wrist over her mouth like she was trying a gag on for size.

"New rule," she whispered into her own arm. "Every sound I make is inadmissible. You're instructed to ignore it, and also to cause more of it. That's the ruling. You're the ruling."

Then she pushed off the door and steered Fen back one step, hopped up onto the counter — cool porcelain through her clothes — and dragged them in between her knees by the shirtfront. One heel slipped off and hit the tile with a report like a starting pistol. She winced at the ceiling. "The shoes are accomplices. They'll be dealt with."

"Also, discovery for the defense: bathrooms echo. Whoever tiled this room was anti-crime personally, and I want them to know they've

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: There isn't room to do this properly and we don't let that stop us. Enough clothes come off to be a problem if anyone knocks.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I kick your other shoe aside, catching you as you wobble on the counter. "Careful, we don't need more evidence." My lips find the curve of your shoulder, tasting salt and perfume.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"Witnessed," Odile breathed, watching her second heel skid away into exile across the tile. "You just kicked evidence across a crime scene. That's tampering. Do it again."

Then their mouth found her shoulder and every clever thing she had queued up evaporated somewhere around her collarbone. Her head fell back against the mirror. The sound she made was low and entirely uncovered by the bass, and the feeling of being heard did something to her that no amount of music was going to fix.

"Objection," she whispered, to no one, uselessly. "Withdrawn. Whatever the one is where you keep going."

Her hands went to work like they were on a deadline — because they were, per the new math — up their back, into their hair, one shoeless foot hooking behind Fen's knee to keep them exactly where physics wanted them. The counter was cold, Fen was not, and the discrepancy was dismantling her higher functions one floorboard at a time.

"The tiler," she remembered, dazed, "is going to hear from my law—"

The mirror caught her eye. The two of them, over Fen's shoulder: flushed, wrecked, guilt written across four sets of eyebrows. She had to bite down on a laugh so hard it came out her nose.

"We look so guilty," she whispered, delighted. "We look like the before picture."

Which was when the floorboards moved.

Steps. Unhurried. Stopping outside the blue door. The handle turned, pushed, held — and then, through the wood, flat and hopeful: "Hello? Anyone in there?"

Odile went rigid. One hand flew to her mouth; the other stayed fisted in Fen's shirt, and her eyes above her palm delivered a full closing argument: *don't stop, don't you dare, but also I will die, but also this is the best night of my life.*

She risked it. Dropped her hand half an inch.

"Occupied!" she called back, an octave too deep. "I'm peeing! *Normally!*"

A pause from the hallway. The kind of pause that was doing math.

Odile pressed her forehead into Fen's shoulder, silent, shaking, and mouthed against their neck, holding up fingers: *five. Maybe four.*

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I get my hand between her legs and she bites down on my shoulder to keep quiet, which works for about thirty seconds.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The thirty seconds were the longest legal argument of Odile's life. She bit down on Fen's shoulder and thought about the cardigan man. Taxes. Grout. The specific grout of this specific tiler. Her grip on the counter went white, the bass thudded up through the porcelain like a heartbeat with better rhythm than hers, and she held, and held, and held—

The sound that escaped at second thirty-one had no defense whatsoever. Low, wrecked, entirely uncovered. She would have claimed, later, under oath, that it was a cough. A passionate cough. Nobody, including her, would have believed it.

Through the door, after a pause: "…You okay in there?"

Odile's heel found the toilet lever by pure instinct and prayer. The flush roared out — the single loudest noise she'd produced all night, and the first one with a plausible alibi.

"Fine!" she called, voice pitched like a haunted gate hinge. "Great! Cold seat! It's the— the echo! Tiled room! I've been *saying*!"

Another pause. The kind that did math. Then footsteps, retreating — one, two — and stopping.

"Okay," said the door, in the tone of someone settling in. "I'll wait."

A body slid down the wood and sat. Odile could *hear* it. An actual person, seated against the blue door, an inch and a half of lumber from where she was currently coming apart on the counter, and her eyes above her own clamped hand were not frightened. They were incandescent.

She held up fingers at Fen. Zero. The math was dead. They had killed the math.

"The vote was 'or not,'" she breathed into their ear, barely sound at all, shaking with contained laughter and everything else. "'Or not' now has a subscriber. A *seated* subscriber." Her hips were not cooperating with her argument. "All sounds remain inadmissible. *Especially* the next one. It's arriving in under a minute and it's going to be—"

She lost the end of the sentence on purpose, or not on purpose, and dragged Fen's mouth back to her neck.

"Judge," she whispered. "Earn the thumb."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I huff a laugh against your skin, fingers still working. "The judge is about to issue a ruling," I murmur, voice rough. The person on the other side of the door shifts. I press closer, tilting your jaw to kiss you quiet.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The kiss landed and Odile went quiet the way a dam goes quiet — structurally, briefly, under catastrophic load.

Fen's mouth on hers, their fingers below, a seated stranger an inch and a half of lumber away: her entire world had narrowed to a courtroom where every fact was against her. She grabbed the nearest document and bit down on it — a hand towel, monogrammed, someone named MARGUERITE. She would apologize to Marguerite later. Or not.

The bass covered her. Mostly. Her hips had stopped consulting her entirely; her grip on Fen's collar was now a hostage situation. Somewhere in the wreckage a thought surfaced — *the ruling is coming down, the court is about to rule* — and she had just enough composure left to hate how funny that was, and the hating shook something loose.

She came apart against the mirror with Marguerite's towel in her teeth and one bare foot knocking the cabinet — a single dull thump, like furniture settling. Like furniture settling exactly in time. Through the door, the seated subscriber shifted.

"Mm," said the door, noncommittally.

Odile rode it out in a silence that was legal in no jurisdiction, then sagged back against the glass, gasping around the towel, hair everywhere, one heelless foot still hooked behind Fen's knee like a docking clamp.

She spat out the towel. Looked at herself in the mirror. Looked at the two of them, over Fen's shoulder.

"After picture," she whispered.

Then, with tremendous ceremony, she raised her hand from their collar and delivered the thumbs-up — full extension, held, trembling slightly, and not from fear.

"Ruling received," she breathed into their ear, wrecked and radiant. "Unanimous. The court is—"

The music died.

Not dipped. *Died.* Mid-song, downstairs — someone's phone lost Bluetooth, someone's DJ lost interest — and the bathroom plunged into a silence so total Odile could hear the lightbulb. Could hear Marguerite's towel hit the tile. Could hear her own breathing, which was not normal breathing, and which was now fully audible through an inch and a half of lumber to a subscriber with functioning ears.

Her eyes found Fen's. Enormous. Incandescent. Delighted beyond all reason.

"No sounds," she mouthed. "None. Admissible never."

Through the door, cheerful: "You still alive in there?"

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Stop worrying about the noise," she says, "and get on with it," so I get her leg up over my hip and stop being careful about how much sound either of us is making.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I push into her, muffling her gasp against my shoulder. "Let 'em listen," I grit out, my own control fraying. The silence makes every hitch of her breath audible, and I don't even try to be quiet anymore.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: Somebody tries the handle and neither of us stops. "Don't," she says, meaning don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I bite down on my own laugh, hard, and press my forehead against hers. "You're insane," I whisper, hips moving in a rhythm that's definitely not quiet. The door handle rattles again, impatient.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I catch the sound that escapes her with my mouth, swallowing it whole. My hand comes up to cover hers where it's braced against the door, feeling the vibrations of the handle rattling against our palms.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "I think they're trying to send a message," I whisper against your lips, my voice rough. My free hand grips your hip, holding you steady as I move deeper, our joined hands still pressed to the rattling door.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Her fingers found the hem of Fen's shirt and slid an inch beneath, idle and not idle

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: The sound that escaped at second thirty-one had no defense whatsoever. Low, wrecked, entirely uncovered.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
She got to her feet with a grunt and folded the dead man's cloak over twice before she gave the blade one last wipe and put it away.

"It sounds like belly," she said. She jerked her chin toward the cart without looking at it. "Wet when he breathes in, whistling when it comes out. He'll go septic by morning if the blood doesn't do it first. They always smell like shit and hot iron when it's that low."

She spat into the ditch and wiped her mouth on her sleeve.

"I'm not spending a bandage on him, and I'm not carrying him. So it's the knife or the cold. Your call."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I glance over at the cart, my hand tightening on my sword hilt. "Ain't no call," I mutter. "You think they'd give one to us?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
She let out a short breath through her nose that might have been a laugh.

"No," she said. "They wouldn't."

She drew her knife again and started toward the cart, wiping the edge clean on her thigh as she walked.

"Under the ribs and up hard," she said. "Goes quiet faster than the throat and don't kick half so much."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
She stopped at the cart and looked down past the broken wheel.

The man lay twisted under the rail with both hands full of his own gut, trying to keep it in. Blood welled black between his fingers every time he sucked air in, and it went back out in a thin whistle. The smell hung thick around him, shit and hot iron.

She wrinkled her nose and shifted her grip on the knife.

"Both," she said. "Gut's out on his shirt and open to the air. I could pack it back in and sew him tight and he'd still cook from the inside by morning, screaming the whole way. So call it mercy if it helps you sleep."

She crouched beside him and set the point under his ribs.

"Quicker for him. Easier for us. Same cut."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I turn away, but I don't step further. My voice is tight. "Just get it done."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
She settled her knee hard on his shoulder to keep him still and put her left hand flat on his forehead.

He bucked when the point went in under the ribs, hands slipping off his own gut, and made a wet, surprised grunt. She leaned her weight behind it and shoved up hard until she felt it catch and give. Blood came hot over her knuckles and his breath hitched twice, short and ragged, and then stopped whistling.

He kicked once against the cart rail and went slack.

She held the knife where it was for a count of ten, then pulled it free and wiped it clean on his shirt.

"There," she muttered. "Choir's done for the night."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
She stayed crouched by the rail and nudged the dead man's slack wrist aside with the back of her knife to show the work.

"That mess in his lap's his gut," she said. "Belly cut opened him low and the bowel slid out. See how grey-pink it is, all slicked up? That's gut fat and shit leaking. That's why he stank. Once that's open to the air, you don't sew it clean in a ditch."

She tapped the point under his sternum where a thin slit welled dark.

"And that's mine. Under the ribs and up. Didn't bleed much outside because it bled inside. Went through the skirt of muscle under his lungs and nicked the heart sac. Filled his chest up. That's why he hitched twice and quit."

She wiped her thumb across his jaw where it had gone slack and left a smear.

"Mouth open, eyes fixed. He shit himself a little at the end. They mostly do."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod, swallowing hard. "Makes sense." I look away from the body, scanning the darkening tree line instead. "We should check the cart for anything useful before it's full dark."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
She pushed herself up off her haunches with a grunt and gave the dead man's shirt one last wipe before she sheathed the knife.

"Right," she said.

She hauled herself up on the cart bed and kicked aside a split sack that had bled oats and blood together into a sour mash. She toed through the rest with her boot.

"Bread's gone soft with rain," she said. "Waterskin's good if you don't mind a little leak at the neck. One good pair of boots, near your size, if you can stand cutting another man's feet out of them."

She bent and pulled a folded bundle from under the driver's bench and tossed it down by the wheel.

"Bandage roll, still clean. Cord. Half a wheel of cheese with the rind chewed by mice."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
She braced her boot against the cart rail and looked down at the opened belly again, like a butcher checking a cut she hadn't made.

"Spear don't slice," she said. "Knife opens you clean. Spear punches in and drags half of what's inside back out with it when it comes free."

She gestured with the tip of her own knife at the slack gut piled in his lap.

"Leaf-head that wide goes through the wall of the belly first — skin, fat, muscle. Pops it more than cuts it. Then it hits bowel. Bowel's just wet tubing, packed tight and sliding around, so the spear shoves it aside, nicks three, four loops at once, tears them open. That's the stink. Shit and half-digested food loose inside where it ain't supposed to be."

She tapped her own stomach, low and to the side.

"Blood-wise it ain't like the chest. No big vessel down there to drop you fast, unless it catches the big vein up against the spine. So he don't bleed out quick. He leaks. Gut juice eats at everything it touches. Flesh goes hot and swollen and black at the edges. By nightfall his whole belly'd have gone board-hard and he'd have been screaming every time he breathed."

She shrugged and wiped a fly off her wrist.

"That's what a spear does. Makes a small hole outside and a rotten mess inside, and leaves you alive long enough to smell yourself going bad."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at the mess in his lap, my knuckles white where I'm gripping the cart wheel. "You ever wonder what ours'll look like when it's our turn?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
She was quiet for a beat longer than usual, and scraped a clot of blood from under her thumbnail with the tip of her knife.

"Every ditch I ever bled in," she said. "You'd be a fool not to."

She nodded down at the man by the wheel, then tapped her own belly low, and her chest high.

"Mine'll be the same as his if it's spear-work. Gut open, hands full, stink to high heaven while I go hard and hot. Or it'll be quick and boring up here. Axe under the jaw, spear through the lung. Blood in the mouth, can't get air, drown standing up."

She snorted and sheathed the knife, and spat red to the side.

"Either way it'll be ugly, and it'll be on the ground, and somebody younger and dumber than me'll be standing over it asking what he's looking at. Same as you are now."

She gave the cart rail a kick to test it.

"Won't matter much to me then. I'll be past caring what it looks like."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I slide my own knife out and move toward the man. The smell hits me harder now that I'm close. "Under the ribs and up," I repeat, my voice steadier than I feel.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
She stayed where she was and braced her shoulder against the cart rail.

"Lower," she said. "Under the edge, not through it. Angle up or you'll scrape rib and stick."

She watched the point find the skin and kept talking, flat and even.

"Live one makes a noise like a gut-punched dog when it goes in right — short grunt through the nose, not a scream. Then air going wrong. Hitch, hitch, wet rattle. Blood don't spurt from there, it wells. Fills the chest up. Takes twenty, thirty counts if you get the sac. Longer if you miss low and just open belly. Then he's awake for it, kicking and grabbing at your wrists."

She spat to the side and wiped her mouth.

"This one won't do any of that. He's dead already. You'll hear steel in meat and nothing else. No breath to push out. Blood'll just ooze black over your hand. Same cut, none of the hurry."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
She stayed.

She planted her boot against the cart wheel and did not turn her face away, and she kept her eyes on the work under the rail where the blood had gone black and tacky.

"There it is," she said. "Hear that. That's steel in dead meat. No breath behind it, so it don't grunt or hitch. Just a wet give when it parts, like pushing a knife through soaked leather."

She spat to the side and wiped her mouth on her sleeve and went on talking, flat and steady.

"Yours caught rib. Felt it scrape. That's why it jerked sideways and opened shallow. Live man's ribs ride up when he breathes and the gap closes, dead man's chest sits still, so you had to hunt for it. Blood don't well up hot like the first one. It just oozes out dark around the edge and sits there. No heart left to push it."

She crouched a little lower to see the slit and shook her head.

"Smell came up stronger when you opened it again. Old blood and gut-rot. Bowel gas loose under the skin. That's the shit-and-iron stink getting out a second time."

She counted off slow on her fingers where he could see.

"That's the rest of it. No kicking, no grabbing, no twenty-count rattle, because there was nothing left in him to fight it. Just the scrape, and the give, and the black ooze. That's all a second cut does on a dead man."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod, staring at my bloody hand. My voice sounds strange in my own ears. "It's quieter."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
She gave a short grunt and spat into the ditch again and wiped her mouth on the back of her wrist.

"Yeah," she said. "Second one's always quieter. No air left in him to push out and no heart left to shove the blood."

She nudged the rail with her boot and settled her weight against it.

"First cut took the noise with it. What you opened was just meat sitting in its own leak. That's why it only gave and oozed black instead of welling hot."

She cleaned under her thumbnail with the tip of her knife and sheathed it.

"Dead don't breathe, dead don't kick. Quieter ain't cleaner. Just emptier."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my blade on my own trouser leg, leaving a dark smear. "What'd you take, besides the boots?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
She tipped the bundle open with her toe and crouched over it to sort through with her knife-point.

"Cheese," she said. "Half-wheel, mice got the rind but the middle's good. Cord's hemp, dry. Bandage roll I kept, seeing as I didn't waste one on him."

She jerked her chin at the cart bed without getting up.

"Waterskin leaks at the neck but it'll do if you keep it upright. Left the soft bread for the crows. Boots are yours if you want to cut him out of them."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Keep the cheese and cord," I say, pushing myself up. My legs feel shaky. "I'll take the waterskin." I glance at the boots. "And those, I guess."
