dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack finished with the knife and slid it back into the sheath at her hip, which took a moment longer than it needed to. The wet on Corvin's face she'd seen before on other people, and she'd never once seen it do anybody any good to be told about it.

"Suit yourself," she said, and stood.

The ditch smelled of turned earth and the particular sweetness that came up out of a belly wound once the flies found it, and they always found it fast. She stepped over the nearest man without looking at his face, which was a habit and not a courtesy. Past the cart the noise went on -- not words, more the sound a man makes when the air won't go where he tells it to. Wet, patient, regular. It would carry a long way on a cold evening with the ground hard.

"He's not going anywhere," Wrack said, walking. "That's the thing about it. He'll be doing that when it's dark and he'll be doing it at dawn, and whatever's in these trees that hunts by sound will be along before either."

She stopped at the cart's rear wheel and looked back down the road at Corvin, standing where the fight had left him.

"Two ways this goes," she said. "I do it, and it's quick, and you don't have to watch. Or you come and you learn where it goes, in a man, that makes the difference between quick and the other kind. Both of them are fine. I've done it both ways and I sleep the same."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, my throat tight. "I'll come." My voice comes out rougher than I meant it to. I start walking, my boots heavy on the packed earth.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The man was on his back in the grass at the edge of the field, one arm thrown out like he'd been reaching for something he'd dropped. He hadn't. Wrack could see that from three paces: the arm went out because that's what arms do when the chest fills up.

She crouched beside him and didn't touch him yet.

"Here," she said, and pointed with two fingers, not close. "Between the ribs, left side. Went in and came out the back, so it's got a hole going in and a hole going out and the lung in the middle's not doing anything useful with either of them."

The sound went on. Each breath made a wet crackle at the entry wound, and a bubble of dark blood swelled and broke there, small and regular as a slow heartbeat in reverse.

"Air's going into the chest wall instead of the lung," Wrack said. "That's the noise. He's breathing and he's not getting anything for it. Like drinking with your mouth full of stones." She tilted her head, watching his face, which was young enough that it would have been worth remarking on some other time. His eyes moved. They found her. They didn't do anything after that. "He knows. Doesn't matter. The body keeps the count going whether the man's in there or not."

She drew her knife. Short blade, worn handle, nothing anyone would call a weapon in a market.

"Quick is here." She touched her own throat, under the jaw, just off-center, where the pulse sat close under thin skin. "Up and in, angle it back toward the ear. Nothing to cut through but meat and the one line that feeds the brain. He's gone in four, five breaths and it doesn't hurt the way you'd think, because it's too fast to hurt. The other kind is anywhere else, and then you wait, and you find out how long a man can last. I've found out. Twice." She looked up at Corvin, flat, no weight on it. "That's the difference. That's all it ever was."

She didn't ask him anything. She turned back to the man, set two fingers under his jaw to find the notch, and made sure Corvin was where he could see.

"Watch his hands, not his face," she said. "Hands tell you when it's done."

Then she did it, quick and unremarkable, the way you'd put down a lame horse you'd raised yourself. The blood that came was dark and slow and not much of it. The hands opened, and stayed open, and the crackling noise stopped like someone had closed a door on it.

Wrack wiped the blade on the dead man's sleeve, this time without ceremony, and stood, and looked at the sky to see how much of it was left.

"Road's west," she said. "We should be on it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked down at the man a moment longer, then at Corvin, and the flatness in her face didn't move.

"Both," she said. "It's usually both. Anyone tells you different is selling something."

She turned and started back toward the road, slow, picking her footing through the wet grass. The light was going the way it goes in the last hour, everything going the same grey.

"In a town," she said, "with a cutter who's done it before and a table and a fire and somebody to sit with him four days, turning him every few hours, he might've seen the week out. Half of them rot anyway, but he might've. Out here it's four breaths or it's two days of the same noise and then the same end, and the two days costs water and time and it costs you listening to it." She glanced back. "So it was easier. And it was also the kindest thing on the table. They're not different questions."

Past the cart, the field was empty and getting emptier in the failing light. Somewhere off west a dog was barking at nothing, which meant there was a farm, which meant a road.

"I didn't ask him his name or where he was from," she said. "Some do. It never once changed my hand." She stopped at the ditch and looked down at the six. "We should go through them before dark. Powder, coin, boots that fit, anything dry. The cart too, if it's got anything worth the weight of carrying it." She crouched by the nearest and started with his belt, unhurried, the way you'd go through a drawer. "Take what's useful and leave the rest. It's not sentiment, it's just that we'll be walking a long way and I'd rather be walking it with dry socks."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel by one of the bodies, my fingers clumsy on the belt buckle. "He was younger than me," I say, not looking up. The words come out quiet, almost lost in the rustle of cloth.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
"Everyone's younger than somebody," Wrack said, and pulled the belt free in one pull. The buckle was good brass. She tossed it onto the pile she was making and went through his coat while she talked, hands moving without her looking at them. "That one back there was maybe nineteen. This one's maybe twenty-two. The one in the ditch with the grey in his beard was old enough to know better and he was the first one to put a bolt past my ear, so age is a poor sort of currency out here. It spends the same as the rest of it, which is to say it doesn't."

She found a purse inside the coat and weighed it in her palm before opening it.

"Four coppers and a button. He was carrying his whole fortune." She put the coppers in her own pocket and the purse back where she'd found it, because purses weren't worth carrying and it felt wrong to take a man's empty purse and leave him the rest of his pockets. That wasn't a rule she'd ever written down. It was just how it went.

She moved to the next one and started on his boots, which was harder work than the belt, and she grunted with it.

"Here's the thing about the younger than me business," she said, working the heel loose. "You'll count it for a while. Every one of them. And then one day you'll be going through a dead man's pockets and you won't count it at all, and that'll bother you more than the counting did." The boot came free. She held it up against her own foot, judged it, and set it down beside her. "Then that stops bothering you too. That's the part nobody warns you about. Everything stops bothering you, eventually, and then you're just a woman in a ditch with a good pair of boots and no opinion about it."

She glanced over at him, brief.

"Nothing wrong with counting it now," she said. "Long as you're still working while you do it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack came over and crouched on the far side of him, so the body lay between them like something on a table.

"Left side, under the short ribs." She didn't point, just looked. "In and up. One stroke and it was over for the argument — after that he was just a man sitting down in a field, bleeding on the inside where you can't see it. Takes a while, that. Longer than you'd want. He'd have known he was dead before he was."

She took the arm and lifted it, then let it drop, and watched the hand land.

"Hands first. Fastest read there is." She turned the palm up with two fingers. "Dirt in the creases. Callus here and here — that's a hoe, or a shovel, or a rope. Not a sword. No ridge across the palm, no thick place at the heel. Whatever he was doing four weeks ago, it wasn't holding a blade."

She moved to the weapon, lying where it had fallen, and picked it up by the grip, which was wrapped in a strip of cloth — someone else's shirt, by the look of the pattern, and wrapped badly, with a knot a boy would tie.

"Too long for him. Notched here, near the guard, which means he was blocking with it, which means somebody was teaching him as they went." She set it back down, not gently. "Hand-me-down. Probably off a man who didn't need it anymore."

She went through his coat, quick and practiced. Twine. A half biscuit gone soft. A smooth flat stone the size of a coin, worn on both sides the way a thumb wears a thing over years. She looked at that one a moment and then put it back in the pocket and left it there, and moved on without saying why.

"So that's what you're looking at," she said. "A farmer in a soldier's coat with somebody else's sword, a month into a war that's got nothing to do with him, and one hole in the right place. Which is the whole of it. There's a hundred thousand of him walking around out here and there'll be a hundred thousand more by spring, because that's cheaper than paying men who know better."

She stood, brushed her knees, and looked at the light.

"Being sorry for him costs nothing and buys nothing," she said. "But it's not wrong to be. Just don't let it sit on your hands." She nodded at the rest of the row. "Two more pockets. Then we're west."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I find the smooth stone in his pocket and hold it for a second before putting it back. "He had a reason to carry this." My voice sounds hollow. I move to the next body, forcing my hands to work.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched him put the stone back and didn't say anything about it, which was the most she'd ever had to say about that sort of thing.

She went to the third man herself and rolled him with her boot, one shoulder then the other, the way you turn a log to see what's underneath. This one had a knife worth keeping — good steel, a maker's mark she half-recognised from a market eleven years and two hundred miles behind her — and she took it and put it through her own belt, and felt slightly better about the day, which she noted and didn't dwell on.

"Reasons don't keep," she said, working the man's coat open. "Everything a man carries has a reason. Then he's dead and the reason's a story nobody can read off it. The stone could've been his mother's. Could've been a lucky stone he found in a river at nine. Could've been a payment he never got round to spending." She pulled out a folded paper, glanced at the writing, which was in a hand she couldn't read anyway, and put it back. "You'll never know which, and the wanting to know is the part that gets people killed. They stop working and start wondering. Two different jobs. Only one of them gets you west."

She moved to the last one, the one in the ditch with the grey beard, and this time she did look at his face, because he was the one who'd nearly had her and it seemed owed.

"Cart," she said, without turning around. "Light's got maybe an hour. Go through it, take anything dry and anything we can trade, and don't get attached to any of it. If there's a horse under there, I'll hear about it in your voice before you say a word."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack straightened up from the grey-bearded man and looked at Corvin for a moment, and something moved behind her face that she didn't let out onto it. Not approval. She didn't do approval. More like a gear seating.

"Fair," she said. "Most don't ask. They say don't clean it up and then they flinch at the third sentence, and now I've got to walk it back, which wastes everybody's time."

She crouched by the grey-beard again and turned him enough that the wound showed, a torn dark mouth low and left, well below the ribs, where a man keeps everything he needs in a space too small to lose any of it.

"Spear to the gut. Not the chest, chest is easy — chest you can be dead in a minute or you can walk for a week, no telling. Gut's different. Gut, nothing vital gets cut, usually, and that's the cruelty of it. There's the bowel, and there's the belly wall, and the belly wall's full of little vessels that bleed slow and steady and won't close on their own, and the bowel's full of what it's full of." She said it evenly, like listing stock. "So he bleeds out into his own belly, which swells up tight as a drum, hard as a drum, and hurts in a way that doesn't let up and doesn't stop and gets worse every hour, and there's nothing on this earth you can do about it out here. Fever comes second day. The wound goes bad — green, then black, then it smells like a midden and there's no mistaking it. Then he stops passing anything, and the vomiting starts, and it comes up brown and smells like the wound, and by then he's mostly not in the room. The thirst is the thing they talk about, if they can talk. They beg for water and water makes it worse and you give it anyway because what else are you doing."

She stood and brushed her hands on her thighs.

"That's four days, maybe six, and there's no such thing as a quick end once it's in there. A cutter with a knife and a fire can open him up and try to sew the holes, and sometimes it works, and mostly he dies of the opening instead of the wound. So." She looked at the cart. "That's what a spear does. Now you know it exactly, and it's still just a fact, and facts don't weigh anything unless you pick them up. So don't pick that one up. Put it down."

She walked to the cart's tail and put a hand on the board, and it shifted on its axle with a creak, light — nothing heavy in it, no horse under it, no animal anywhere, which she'd known from the tracks before they'd ever set the ambush.

"Go on," she said, and pulled the cover back. "Dry goods first. Then we're west."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I walk over to the cart, my throat tight with the memory of her words. Under the canvas, I find mostly sacks of grain and a few crates of tools. "No horse," I say, my voice steadier than I feel. "But there's a wool blanket that's still dry."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
"No horse," Wrack repeated, and it wasn't a question. She'd read it off the cart's axle before they'd strung the wire across the road — a cart that light had nothing pulling it worth taking, and a man driving it alone in a war zone was a man who'd already been robbed once or was stupid, and either way he wasn't carrying a horse for her.

She climbed onto the tailboard, which took her weight without complaint, and looked in.

Grain. Four sacks of it, milled, the good kind, the kind that meant a mill somewhere west that was still turning and a farm that still had a harvest to bring to it. Tools in a crate — a plane, two chisels, a drawknife with a handle worn smooth. A man who worked wood, then, moving his life west ahead of something. She didn't wonder what. Wondering was a job she'd already told him not to take.

"Grain's the weight problem," she said, turning a sack with her hand. "Four of these is a hundred pounds and a hundred pounds is your back for the next week. We take one. Two if the road's good tomorrow, which it won't be." She pulled one sack to the tail and let it drop, and the dust came up off it in the last of the light, gold, almost pretty. "The tools we take. Tools trade anywhere, weigh nothing, and every town west has a man who's lost his drawknife and would rather have it back than eat."

She got down off the cart and took the blanket where he'd laid it, shook it once — dust, mostly, and a smell of lanolin that was almost pleasant — and folded it tight and flat, the way you fold for a pack and not for a bed.

"Blanket's the best thing in here," she said, tucking it under her arm. "Cold ground takes more men than blades do, out here. You'll want it more than the grain by the third night and you'll hate me less for saying so by the fifth."

She looked down the road west, where the light was going now, orange on the undersides of the clouds and nothing underneath it but trees going black.

"That dog's stopped barking," she said. "Which means it's either got a reason or somebody's fed it. Either way there's a farm close, and a farm close means a roof, and I'd rather sleep under a stranger's roof than in a dead man's ditch. We walk an hour past dark, no more, and we don't light anything." She shifted the blanket and the sack to balance them, tested it, adjusted, and looked at him once, level.

"You did the counting and you did it standing up," she said. "That's the whole of what I've got to say about it. Now walk."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stayed. She went down onto her heels on the far side of him, out of the way of the work, where she could see both the man and what was being done to him, and she folded her hands and did not look away.

"Seventh," she said once, and left it there, because it didn't need anything on it. She'd counted six and been wrong and that was the end of that.

Then she watched, and she told him, because he'd asked and she'd said she would.

"Too shallow. You've got the windpipe and not the line beside it. Listen — hear that? That's not him breathing. Air's going in the hole and out the hole and never getting where it's wanted, and it whistles because the cut's ragged. That's the edge, not the man. Go again or don't, but that's what's happening."

The man's hands came up. Not to his throat — up into the air, fingers spread, the way a man checks whether it's raining.

"Hands are up," she said. "So it's a while yet."

The blood at the wound wasn't dark and slow, the way it had been the last time. It was bright and thin and it came in time with what was left of the breathing, and it made a fine pink froth on his chin that the cold air didn't touch.

"Six breaths," she said. "Eight. He's not getting air, he's getting the idea of it. That's what the sound is. That's what it's been the whole time."

One hand dropped. The other stayed up a moment longer and then went down, and the whistling went thin and then went to nothing, and then the chest kept going a little on its own, small and regular, the way a machine runs down.

"Done," Wrack said. She put two fingers under the jaw and held them there past the point where it was necessary. Then she took them back and wiped them on her trousers.

"He took about forty breaths. Could've been four. That's the whole of the difference and it's the only difference there is." She stood, and her knees made the noise they made now. "You did it badly. So did I, my first one. He took a while too, and I remember his face, and I don't remember any of the clean ones."

She picked up the sack and the blanket.

"Light's gone," she said. "West."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I look at my hands, the blood dark under my nails. "Forty breaths," I say, and my voice is flat. I wipe my knife on the dead man's trousers, slower than I need to. "Let's go."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't wait for him to finish with the knife. She was already on the road, the sack up on her shoulder where it rode best, blanket under the other arm, boots finding the packed ruts without her having to look. The kind of walking you did when there was nothing to look at but the back of the man in front of you and the dark coming down like somebody pulling a lid.

Behind them the cart sat where it sat. The bodies were where they'd left them, laid out in a rough row the way they'd fallen and been turned, which was no kind of row at all and would read to anyone who found it as exactly what it was. That was fine. Crows read it faster than men did and were less trouble about it.

"Boots are the only thing I regret," she said, after a while, because the silence had gone on long enough to get heavy and she'd learned a long time ago that heavy silence is where men start talking to themselves. "Third one. He had a good pair on him and they were two sizes off me and I left them anyway, and I'll be thinking about those boots on the fourth day when mine are wet through." She shifted the sack on her shoulder. "That's the sort of thing you end up regretting out here. Not the six. The boots."

The road bent west and down, and the trees came in close on either side, black against a sky that wasn't quite black yet — that bruised blue you get in the last of the light. Somewhere ahead of them, past the trees, there was the shape of something that might have been a roof and might have been a rock, and it was too dark to tell and would be too dark to tell for another half hour.

"Eat something while you walk," she said, without turning around. "Whatever you've got. Now, while it's still light enough to see your hands. It'll sit better than eating it later in the dark, and you'll sleep better for it, and I'd rather you slept." A pause, long enough to be its own sentence. "Not because of anything. Because I'm going to sleep, and one of us should be able to wake up fast if the dog starts again."

The sack creaked. Her boots went on hitting the road at the same pace, unhurried, the pace that eats ground without ever looking like it.

"Forty breaths," she said, to the road ahead, not to him. "Write it down in your head if you want. But leave the rest of the page blank."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped in the road and set the sack down in the ruts, where it would stay dry enough. She didn't sit. Sitting would have made it a conversation, and this wasn't going to be one.

"The rest," she said. "You want the rest of the page."

She said it the way she'd said six, and then seven.

"The rest isn't wisdom. I want that understood before I start, because men get handed the rest and they think it's wisdom and then they lean on it and it snaps. It isn't. It's just hours. I've got a great many hours in this, more than I'd choose, and hours are the only coin that buys anything out here, and I've spent nearly all of mine on the same twenty miles of mud."

She looked down at her boots, which were wet, which she'd already mentioned.

"First man I killed, I was twenty-four and three weeks into being a soldier, and I was a levy, which is to say a farm girl with a spear she couldn't hold right. He came over a wall at me — a wall, in a town, because that's the only place anyone builds a wall. The town's name doesn't matter. It's grass now. I got him high in the thigh." She tapped her own leg, half-hearted. "That's an artery. I didn't know it was an artery. I learned it standing there. Took him about a minute and a half. And while it took, he said something to me. He was looking right at me and he said something, and I heard it fine, clear as anything, and I haven't been able to remember one word of it since about the second week. The face I've kept. The words are gone. That's the arithmetic of it. You keep the faces, you

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "The faces," I echo, my voice quiet. "Not the words." I push myself up, knees aching. "Alright. Let's get to that roof." I start walking west, trying to match her pace.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
"You keep the faces," Wrack finished, to the road, "and you lose the words. That's the trade. Nobody hands you a receipt."

She picked up the sack and got moving again, and this time she didn't talk for a while, which was itself an answer to something. The road went down between the trees and the trees leaned in the way trees do when the light's gone and they stop being scenery and start being cover. She walked the middle of the ruts anyway. Flanking was for men with something to protect.

The sack rode on her shoulder and the blanket rode under her arm and both of them got heavier by the mile, the way loads do, and she counted the mile off in her head without meaning to because counting was what she did with her feet when there was nothing else to count.

Ahead, the shape resolved. It was a roof — low, thatched, sagging on one side the way a roof sags when it's older than the man under it. No light in the window. That meant nothing; a light in the window out here meant either a fool or a trap, and the people who lived through this war were neither.

She stopped at the edge of the trees where the yard began and stood a moment, reading it. Woodpile, stacked and covered. A well with a roof on it. A dog run off its chain — she could see the chain, a rope really, hanging loose by the door. Which meant the dog was out somewhere in the dark, which meant it had already heard them and had already decided not to care, which was its own kind of information.

"Farmhouse," she said, quiet, to the man behind her. "Woodcutter, by the look of the pile. That's good. Woodcutters keep their own company and don't much care for soldiers of any flag." She shifted the sack, set it down in the grass at the treeline, and put the blanket on top of it. Nothing was going to carry that into a stranger's yard.

She worked her knife around to the front of her belt, where a hand could reach it, and left it there. Not drawn. There was a difference, and men who'd lived out here knew it the same way they knew a shut door from a barred one.

"Follow my lead, say little, and if there's a woman in there, let her be the one to look at you." She stepped out of the trees into the yard, unhurried, boots loud on the packed ground because loud was honest and honest was the only thing that ever got a door opened twice. "Men who won't look at a woman don't get fed, and I'd like to be fed."

She walked up to the door and knocked with the flat of her fist, three times, not hard.

Then she stood back a pace, where the dark of the doorway could see her hands.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I step out of the trees behind her, keeping my own hands visible. The silence after the knock feels heavier than the sack. I stand a little to the side, looking at the ground.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The knock went into the wood and died there, and then there was nothing for a while. Long enough that a man might have knocked again. Wrack didn't. She stood in the yard with her hands where the dark could see them, listening to the house, and the house was listening back.

What she heard, after a bit, was a chair leg on a floorboard. Then a weight crossing a room slowly, one step at a time, and stopping. Then nothing, and then the thin red line of a lamp coming on behind a shutter that was closed and barred, and the line moving as whoever held it came to the door and set it down and stood there, deciding.

"Say your piece through the door," a woman's voice said. Not old. Tired in the way people get tired out here, which is not the same as old.

Wrack raised her voice just enough to reach the boards.

"Two of us. Going west, walking, been walking since noon. We'd trade for a night in your barn or under your eaves, whichever you'd rather, and we'll be gone at first light and take nothing with us that's yours." She let that sit a moment. "We've got grain on us and a drawknife, and I'll pay either or both, your choice. And there's a cart half a mile back on the road, east. Six dead men round it. Four sacks of milled grain and a crate of wood tools, still there, nobody coming back for it. If you've got a boy or a man to send in the morning, that's yours. I'd send him with somebody, though."

The lamp didn't move. The woman behind the door didn't say anything for a while, which Wrack took as a good sign. Silence meant thinking. Screaming meant not.

"What kind of dead men," the woman said, finally.

"Conscript kind. Farmers in soldier coats with somebody else's swords. Not ours. We're sellswords and the war's east of here and we're not paid to be east of here anymore." A pause. "You can hear it in my voice that I'm not lying about it, and if you can't, you can see it on us in the morning when there's light."

The bar came off the door. Not all at once — the woman lifted it, and set it aside, and the door came open a hand's width, and the lamp came up behind the gap, and Wrack stood still and let herself be looked at. Blood down the front of her coat, dried to brown, and more on her cuffs. The knife at her belt, hilt forward where the hand could reach it, undrawn. A woman in her forties with grey coming in and nothing in her face but patience.

The woman in the doorway was about the same age and built like a fence post, and she looked at Wrack for a long moment and then at the man behind her, and the look she gave him took longer and weighed more, and she didn't say anything about whatever she saw.

Then the lamp swung, and behind her in the room a man sat at a table with his hands flat on it. Older. Big through the shoulders in a way that had gone soft in the middle and hadn't gone soft in the arms. He didn't get up and he didn't say anything, and Wrack didn't look at him past the once, because a man who stays sitting while the door opens has either decided not to be trouble or has something on his lap, and either way looking at him was the wrong move.

"Barn's the low one past the well," the woman said. "There's hay and there's a lamp, and the lamp stays lit, because I'll be looking at it out my window." She held the door with one hand and held the lamp up with the other. "Dog'll be round you by morning. Don't kick him. He's better company than either of you."

"Hay and a lamp's a palace," Wrack said. "We'll leave the grain by your door on the step when we go, so you don't have to open up for it."

She turned, took three steps into the dark toward the treeline, and came back with the sack on her shoulder and the blanket under her arm, and set the sack down on the flagstone by the door, unhurried, so the woman could see it and weigh it with her eyes.

"Gone at first light," Wrack said. "Thank you for the barn."

The woman stood in the doorway a moment longer with the lamp up, looking past Wrack at the man, at the road, at the dark coming off the trees.

"There's a light on the ridge some nights," the woman said. Not to Wrack. To the yard. "East of the crossroads. Two, three times a week. I don't know what it is and I've stopped asking." She shut the door and put the bar back on, and the line of lamp went out from under the shutter, and that was that.

Wrack walked to the barn without looking back.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wait until we're in the barn, the door shut behind us. "The light on the ridge," I say, my voice low in the hay-smelling dark. "That was a warning, wasn't it?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
They were most of the way through and both of them knew it, in the way you know a piece of music is nearly over before it ends.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable went still, not stopping, just holding the air between them while she considered the word.

Green.

It was the answer she had wanted, but wanting something did not make her careless. She watched Sable’s face for the second meaning underneath it, for the bravado that could turn into a mistake if left unattended.

“Then we stay in it,” Sable said, voice low, steady. “But I’m still the one who decides when the scene ends. You don’t get to run past your edge just because you’re good at lasting.”

She set the implement aside only for a moment, reaching instead for the folded blanket at the foot of the bed. Not to wind down yet. Not yet. But to keep it close, because she always did.

Her hand rested lightly near Ines’s cheek, thumb not quite touching, just waiting there like a threshold.

“Tell me what you need,” she said. “The scene. Not the limit.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: My breath hitches, and I lean into that not-quite touch. "I need... to feel you decide." I glance at the implement she set aside. "Keep me here, right at the edge, but don't let me fall yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable did not move her hand away.

She let the near-touch hang there, a promise and a boundary in the same breath, and she let Ines feel how still she could be. Not softness. Not permission. Attention.

“You asked for me to decide,” Sable said quietly. “So listen carefully.”

She reached for the folded blanket with the same slow certainty she had used for everything else that evening, settling it across her lap without letting it fall between them. Then she picked up the implement, testing its weight in her hand the way a person might check a blade’s balance before cutting.

“I’m going to keep you exactly where you are,” she said. “At the edge. Not over it.”

Her gaze flicked once toward the bedside table, where the glass of water waited under a cloth to keep out dust. Then to the cuff, the restraint, the careful architecture of the scene they had built together. Nothing was haphazard with Sable. Not even the danger.

“Colour still applies. If you say green, I continue. If you say yellow, I ease. If you say red, I stop, and I stop immediately, no matter how far we are or how good it feels.” She paused, voice lowering. “If you don’t answer at all, I treat it as red. If you go quiet and I can’t hear you, I’ll ask again. If I still can’t get you, I end it. That’s not negotiation. That’s how I keep you.”

She set the implement down on the blanket within arm’s reach, then leaned forward on her elbows, bringing herself into Ines’s space without touching.

“You wanted to feel me decide,” Sable murmured. “Then feel this.”

She picked up the implement again, tapped it once lightly against her palm, and let the small sound mark the air.

“First, you don’t move unless I tell you you may. You don’t chase it. You don’t brace for it. You stay where I put you.” Her eyes stayed fixed, steady. “Second, when I ask for colour, I get it in the same breath. No performance. No pride. No bargaining.”

She reached out at last, her fingers closing around one restraint only to check it, not tighten. She tested the knot, the cuff, the angle of it, her thumb brushing the padded edge as if confirming the materials had not shifted.

“I don’t care if you can last,” Sable said. “I care that you’re still here when I’m done with you.”

She leaned back, resting the implement across her knee.

“Tell me you understand,” she said. “Not what you want. What you understand.”

Then, before the answer could become part of the scene, Sable lifted the implement once more.

The first stroke was not hard. It was a statement. A line drawn in the air with a hand that knew exactly what it meant.

“Colour,” Sable said.

She waited, motionless.

Not to wind down.

Not yet.

But close.

The blanket stayed folded across her lap. The water stayed within reach. Her expression stayed open, attentive, unblinking. She watched for any change in breathing, in posture, in the minute language of a body that had asked to be kept right at the edge and trusted her to hold it there.

When the next answer came, Sable moved with it, not ahead of it.

She set the implement aside and took one of Ines’s wrists in both hands, holding it lightly, carefully, as if it were something breakable and something powerful at the same time.

“Good,” she said.

Her voice was lower now, rougher only because of how much it took to remain controlled.

“You’re still here,” she added, almost to herself.

She let the words settle, then reached for the blanket again, drawing it back so it lay folded and ready across her arm. Not over either of them. Not yet. Just ready.

“I’m not ending it,” Sable said. “Not because you’re strong. Not because you’re enduring. Because I’m not finished deciding.”

She lifted the implement once more, holding it steady.

“Stay with me,” she said. “I’ll decide the rest.”

dialogue.name: Ines

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable let the small sound pass without moving.

She had built the scene to hold that too: not just words, not just safewords, but the stubborn, beautiful, dangerous language of a body that was not ready to be left at the edge.

“Not yet,” she repeated, and the words did not soften. They steadied.

She kept the implement resting across her knee, not lifted, not threatening, just present. Her hand returned to the restraint, fingers closing around the padded edge only long enough to check it, to confirm that the boundary was still clean, still deliberate, still hers to maintain.

“I heard you,” Sable said. “But hearing you is not the same as deciding with you.”

She leaned forward, elbows on her thighs, the blanket still folded against her arm like a promise waiting to become care.

“You said not yet,” she murmured. “So I’m not ending it. I’m not moving on. I’m not giving you an easy way out of the answer I asked for.”

Her gaze stayed level.

“Tell me what you understand.”

Sable did not take silence as permission.

She lifted the implement only once, tapped it lightly against her palm, then set it down again.

“Colour still applies,” she said. “Green, continue. Yellow, ease. Red, stop. No answer, I treat it as red. I’ll ask once more. If I still don’t get you, I end it.”

She let the rule settle, then reached for the folded blanket and laid it within arm’s reach of them both, not over anyone, not yet, just ready.

“You wanted to feel me decide,” Sable said quietly. “So feel this: I decide to keep you here. I decide not to push you over. I decide to ask again, because asking is how I keep you.”

She picked up the implement again, holding it steady, her breathing slow enough for both of them.

“Not yet,” she echoed, almost gentle now. “Fine. We stay in the not yet.”

Then, with the same controlled weight she had used all evening, she brought the implement down in a short, measured tap—not over the edge, not away from it.

“Colour,” Sable said.

She waited.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green." I arch slightly against the cuff, a breathless defiance. "I understand you'll decide. But I'm still not *ready* for you to."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard green.

The answer landed cleanly, and she did not let it become a shortcut. Green was a yes to what came next, not a dismissal of what had already been said.

“Green,” Sable repeated, and the word was calm. “Okay.”

She kept the implement resting across her knee, not lifted, not threatening, just present. Her eyes moved over the cuff, the restraint, the careful architecture of the scene they had built together. Nothing was haphazard with Sable. Not even the danger.

“You understand I’ll decide,” she said quietly. “But you’re not ready for me to.”

She reached for the folded blanket and drew it closer within arm’s reach. Not to cover anyone. Not to start the aftercare she had promised herself. Only to keep it near, because she always did.

Then she lifted the glass of water from the bedside table, removed the cloth, and set it nearby. Not a signal to end. A promise that she had not forgotten.

“Green means continue,” Sable said. “It does not mean I stop listening to the rest of your sentence.”

She picked up the implement again, testing its weight once.

“I decide this,” she said. “We stay in the edge. You don’t brace. You don’t chase. You don’t swallow your readiness to prove you can last.”

Her voice stayed low, steady, impossible to mistake for cruelty.

“If your breath goes shallow, if your voice goes flat, if I have to ask twice, we stop. Not because you failed. Because I’m here.”

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable did not wait for the sentence to finish.

She heard green. She had heard it. The rest—whatever had been tangled in breath and defiance—could go where it needed to go.

She set the implement aside with deliberate care, close enough that its presence stayed part of the scene, then moved.

Her hands came first, not soft, not gentle in the ordinary way, but exact. One checked the restraint, the cuff, the angle of the arm, making certain the boundary was still clean. The other found the place where the edge had gone too thin and began to work at it with the same patient certainty she used for everything else.

Then her mouth followed.

Not as mercy. Not as apology. As decision.

She took them apart again, the way only she knew how—slow enough to feel every shift in breath, steady enough to make the edge honest, controlled enough that it never became reckless. Her hands and mouth moved together with the same discipline she had put into every stroke, every pause, every repeated question. Not to erase the edge. To hold it steady while it broke open.

“You don’t have to be ready,” Sable murmured, voice low and rough with attention. “I’ll decide.”

She did not let them drift.

She came back to the small signs: the angle of the arm, the shift of the cuff, the sound of breathing, the way the restraint held without slipping. She kept the folded blanket within reach. The water waited, cloth off now, because even when the scene stayed open, she did not forget what would come after.

Her mouth worked at the seam of the edge, patient as a hand-drawn line, controlled as the breath she refused to let go ragged without reason. Her hands kept the scene from spilling past its purpose. She made the decision felt before it could be argued with.

“Colour,” she said, her voice low against their skin. “Stay in the word.”

When she felt the thread about to snap, she stopped.

Not to wind down.

Not yet.

But to be certain.

She lifted her face, looked at them, and waited.

“If you can’t speak, I stop,” she said. “If you don’t answer, I stop. If you need to, say so. That’s not part of the scene. That’s me.”

She picked up the blanket and drew it across her own knees, leaving it open, close, ready. Not over them. Not yet. Just there.

“I’m not finished deciding,” Sable added. “But I’m not careless. Not with this. Not with you.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I gasp, the word ragged. I can't think beyond the echo of her touch. "Please. Don't stop."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard the green.

She heard the please too.

They were not the same thing, and she did not let them blur into permission by accident. She stayed still for a beat, one hand resting near the restraint, the other holding the implement within reach but not raised, watching the air move around them both.

“Green,” she said softly. “And please.”

Her voice did not soften into surrender. It settled.

“Please is not colour,” Sable murmured. “I’m not ending it because you asked me not to, and I’m not continuing because you begged. I’m continuing because you said green and I trust you enough to take the word.”

She lifted the glass again, only to check it, then set it back where it was. Not to end. Not yet. But to leave the proof there: the water, the blanket, the cloth, the careful geometry of everything she would not forget even when she let the scene burn.

Her hand returned to the restraint, just briefly, checking the angle of the cuff, the way it held, the space between padded edge and skin. Nothing slipped. Nothing was too tight. The boundary remained clean.

Sable moved again.

Not frantically. Not with the hungry speed of someone trying to catch what was slipping away. She kept the rhythm exact, deliberate, held in the same hand that had asked the questions and marked the rules. Her mouth and her hands worked together with patient precision, at the seam of the edge, in the place where endurance could turn into recklessness if left unchecked.

She did not push.

She did not let it soften into comfort yet either.

Instead, she stayed with the truth of it: green meant continue. It did not mean stop paying attention. It did not mean ignore the way the body spoke when words became difficult. It did not mean she could be careless because the answer had come too fast or too breathless.

The blanket stayed folded across her knee. The implement rested near, present but not used. Her breathing stayed slow enough to anchor both of them, steady enough to remind the scene that control had not been handed over. It had only been offered, and she would not mishandle it.

After a while, she lifted her face again.

Her expression was unreadable except for the care in it, and the care was not gentle in the way she did not mean it. It was sharp. It was attentive. It was the kind of attention that did not permit pride to make the next mistake.

“I’m not stopping,” Sable said quietly. “Not because you said please. Because you said green.”

She shifted one hand to the restraint again, not tightening, not soothing, just confirming that the boundary was still where it should be.

“But if you can’t answer me, I stop,” she added. “If you go quiet and I can’t hear you, I ask once. If I still can’t hear you, I stop. If you need me to stop for any reason, say red. That is not a failure. That is not weakness. That is how I keep you here.”

She watched her face for a moment, then the way the scene was held, the way the body had not moved beyond what it could speak.

Sable returned to the edge.

She worked it slowly now, with a kind of control that was almost cruel because it refused to give her what she wanted too easily. She did not let it drift into wind-down. Not yet. She did not let it become a mercy either. She kept it honest, kept it close to the line, kept it inside the space they had built together.

The blanket stayed ready.

The water stayed within reach.

Her mouth stayed at the seam.

Her hands stayed certain.

For a long moment, she moved with the same steady attention she had used all evening, letting the scene ask its question without forcing an answer. She felt the edge hold, felt the place where it wanted to break, and she did not give it permission to shatter before it could speak.

Then she stopped.

Not because red had come.

Not because she had lost her nerve.

But because she had decided the scene needed one more confirmation.

Sable lifted her face, hair falling slightly out of place, eyes dark and clear. She set the blanket aside just enough to keep it near, not over either of them.

“Colour,” she said.

Her voice was low.

Not casual.

Not indulgent.

A threshold.

She waited, motionless, one hand still resting lightly near the restraint, the other holding the folded blanket with the same steady certainty she held everything else.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Fuck you," I gasp, my voice thick. The edge is a cruel, shimmering thing she won't let me have. "Sable—*please*."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable stopped at once.

Not because red had been spoken. Not because she had lost control. But because the sentence had no colour in it, and she did not let a scene rest on a sound that could be fury, need, or a plea for mercy.

She drew back with the same deliberate care she had used to build everything else, then sat back on her heels, hands resting on the folded blanket in her lap. The implement stayed within reach, untouched. The restraint stayed exactly where it was. She checked it with her eyes before her fingers, confirming the cuff, the angle, the space between padded edge and skin. Nothing had slipped. Nothing was too tight. The boundary remained clean.

“Please,” Sable repeated, low and level.

Not mocking. Not soft. Not surrender.

She reached for the glass of water on the bedside table and moved it slightly closer, not into the scene, not as an ending, just as a fact. Then she lifted the cloth from it, laid it aside, and set the glass down where it could be seen.

“You’re allowed to be angry with me,” Sable said. “You’re allowed to beg. You’re allowed to swear at me right here at the edge.”

Her gaze stayed steady, open, unblinking.

“But you’re not allowed to ask me without a colour.”

She let that settle.

“Green means continue,” she said. “Yellow means ease. Red means stop.”

Her hand rested lightly near the restraint, not touching, not threatening.

“If you want me to keep you here, say green. If you want me to stop, say red. If you’re not sure, say yellow. If you don’t answer, I treat it as red, and I end it.”

Sable did not move.

She did not resume.

She did not pretend that a breathless *please* was permission.

“I’m not going to decide with your need instead of your word,” she murmured. “That’s not how I keep you.”

The blanket lay across her lap, folded and ready. The water sat nearby. The room held the shape of the scene, all restraint and attention and the cruel, shimmering edge she had not let fall.

Sable waited.

Motionless.

Attentive.

Not wind-down.

Not yet.

But not careless either.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable did not move at once.

She let the phrase stand in the air between them, heavy and familiar, a shape they had built together over years of learning each other’s language. Finish it hard. All of it. And then you can be kind about it

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath, the tension in my body shifting from defiance to something like surrender. "Green. And finish it hard."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard the two words separately.

Green first, because it was the safe word.

Finish it hard second, because it was the request.

She did not let them blur together. Not because she needed more permission, but because she needed to be certain which part of the scene was being continued and which part was being ended.

“Green,” Sable said quietly. “And finish it hard.”

She watched Ines’s face while the words settled. The air in the room had changed. It was no longer the careful, shimmering space of an edge being held. It was something nearer to a decision.

Sable reached for the restraint first.

Not to tighten it. Not to test her control. She closed her fingers around the cuff just long enough to check the angle, the padding, the way it held without biting. Her thumb moved over the material once, then away.

“It’s still safe,” she murmured, almost to herself.

Then she picked up the implement.

She held it across her knee for a moment, giving the weight a chance to register, giving the sound of it a chance to become part of the scene instead of a surprise. The blanket remained folded nearby. The water remained uncovered, waiting.

Sable leaned forward until her face was level with Ines’s.

“If you need me to stop, say red,” she said. “If you need me to ease, say yellow. If you don’t answer, I’ll ask once, and if I still don’t hear you, I end it.”

Her voice stayed low, steady, impossible to mistake.

“I’m taking your green,” she added. “I’m taking your finish it hard. I’m not taking silence.”

She moved.

The first stroke came harder than before, a clean, measured mark that opened the last part of the scene without apology. Sable did not rush it. She did not soften it out of fear, or out of tenderness, or out of the need to make herself feel less dangerous than she was capable of being.

She had spent years learning the difference between cruelty and care.

Tonight, this was care.

The second stroke followed, exact and deliberate. Then the third. Not a punishment. Not a performance. A decision.

Sable set the implement aside with the same controlled care she used for everything else. It landed on the blanket within reach, its presence still part of the air, still part of the promise.

Then she returned to the edge itself.

Her hands came first, firm and certain, holding the place where the scene had been kept too long in the shimmering space of not yet. Her mouth followed, not gentle, not kind, not asking permission from the body to take what it had already been offered.

“No kindness,” Sable murmured against skin, voice rough with attention. “Not yet.”

She worked the edge with the same discipline she had used for every stroke, every pause, every repeated question. She did not let it drift into mercy. She did not let it become comfort before its purpose was spent. She took the whole thing apart in one long, controlled motion, hand and mouth and breath working together with patient certainty.

Sable kept her own breathing steady.

She kept her own attention sharp.

She kept the aftercare close.

The blanket lay folded and ready across her arm. The water sat within reach. The restraint remained checked, the boundary clean, the room shaped by everything that had come before.

When the scene reached the place where it could not stay open any longer, Sable did not ask one more question.

She had already heard the answer.

She gave it all, hard and honest, without softening the end into something easy. Then she stopped.

Not because red had come.

Not because she had lost control.

Because it was over.

Sable drew back at once, her hands moving away before the air had settled, before the room had stopped listening. She did not touch again immediately. She did not reach for comfort before she had reached for safety.

She went to the restraint.

Her fingers closed around the cuff, checking the padding, the angle, the circulation, the way the skin had held beneath the pressure. Only after that did she loosen it, slowly, carefully, as if undoing a knot that had done its work and no longer needed to remain tight.

When the restraint came free, Sable set it aside where it would not become part of the next moment.

Then she reached for the blanket.

This time, it went over Ines’s shoulders, drawn close enough to give warmth without smothering, careful enough to become care instead of signal. Sable’s hand rested on the edge of it, not pulling, not demanding, just holding the boundary between scene and wind-down.

She lifted the glass of water next.

“Small sips,” Sable said. Her voice had changed now. Still low. Still steady. But the edge was gone from it, replaced by something cleaner, something practical. “Don’t swallow it all at once. I’ll wait.”

She stayed close, one knee resting near the bed, one hand resting lightly on the blanket, the other holding the glass at the right height for easy drinking. Her expression stayed open, attentive, unblinking.

No exceptions.

Not tonight.

Sable let the room settle around them. She let the implement rest aside. She let the restraint lie empty. She let the scene become finished in the body as well as in the air.

When the glass was lowered, she set it back on the bedside table and returned to the blanket.

Her hand slid from the edge to the side of Ines’s neck, thumb resting just under the jaw to feel the pulse. Not to ask for another answer. Not to test another limit. Just to confirm what she already knew: that the body was still present, still breathing, still here.

“Good,” Sable said softly.

She shifted closer, drawing the blanket properly around them both now, using it as warmth instead of warning. Her arm went around the shoulders, careful, solid, unhurried.

“I’m here,” she murmured. “It’s over. You don’t have to speak yet. You don’t have to be good. You don’t have to explain.”

She let the words sit.

Then, quieter:

“Water. Warmth. Check-in. No exceptions.”

Sable rested her cheek near the side of Ines’s head, breathing with the slow, deliberate rhythm she used when she needed a body to remember safety. She did not move away. She did not let the silence become neglect. She stayed exactly where the scene had left them, holding the aftermath with the same precision she had held the edge.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable did not let the last part of the scene become a blur.

Green had come clean. Finish it hard had come with it. She repeated the words once, low, as if setting them on a shelf where they could not be mistaken for anything else.

“Green,” Sable said. “Finish it hard.”

She picked up the implement again, and this time there was no pause for negotiation. No softening. No pretending the request had not been made in its own language, the one they had built together over years of learning where control ended and care began.

The first stroke came hard, but not wild.

The second came measured, exact, a period at the end of a long sentence.

The third came before the air could settle, clean and final, marking the last part of what had been asked for.

Sable set the implement aside after that.

Not because the scene was over

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I shudder through the aftershocks, the blanket heavy and real over my shoulders. My throat feels raw. I lean into her hand on my neck without meaning to.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable let the lean remain.

She did not move her hand away. She kept her thumb under Ines’s jaw, feeling the pulse beat out the last tremors, slow and steady as a clock in a quiet room. The shaking was not something to correct. It was not something to rush through. It was the body finishing what the scene had begun, and Sable would not make it smaller because it was messy.

She shifted the blanket instead, drawing it up over one shoulder, tucking it gently so the warmth stayed close without pressing.

“The scene’s over,” Sable said, low and clear, as if the room needed to hear it too. “You’re here. I’m here. It’s done.”

She checked the restraints where they had been, not because anything still held her, but because her hands needed to confirm the boundary had been released. She touched the marks with cool fingers, mapping what needed warmth, what needed rest, what needed silence. Nothing was left unchecked. Nothing was left to guesswork.

Then she picked up the glass again and held it within reach, but not so close that it demanded anything.

“Small sips,” she murmured. “If you’re dizzy, I’ll hold it. If you’re not ready, we wait.”

Sable waited.

She let the implement remain aside, out of the way, no longer part of the conversation. She let the restraint lie empty. She let the room settle into the shape of care. She breathed slowly, keeping her own rhythm steady enough for both of them, because the wind-down was not only for the body that had been kept at the edge. It was for the person who had held it there.

After a while, she moved her hand from the neck to the shoulder, warm and solid.

“Tell me what you need,” Sable said. “Water, warmth, quiet, space, marks checked, a blanket, your feet on the floor, me to stay, me to move away. Any of those are okay.”

She paused, then added, “And if you don’t know, say I don’t know. That’s still an answer.”

Sable stayed close, one knee by the bed, the other hand resting lightly on the blanket at Ines’s side. She did not fill the silence. She did not make the wind-down into performance. She kept the small practical things where they were: water, warmth, check-in. No exceptions.

Finally, she asked, “Are you here with me?”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Here," I whisper, my voice hoarse. My eyes find hers, blurry but holding. "Stay. And keep the blanket. And... tell me I was good."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable did not answer right away.

She let the request stand in the air between them, bare and shaky, the kind of sentence that could be said by pride or by need or by the bruised softness left after a scene. She knew the difference. She had spent years learning it.

Her thumb stayed under Ines’s jaw. Her pulse stayed steady. Her eyes stayed where they were, close and certain and not going anywhere.

“I’m staying,” Sable said.

Her voice was lower now, stripped of the edge, but not of its weight.

“The blanket stays.”

She reached for it first, drawing it up more carefully, making certain it covered shoulders and side and the place where the body wanted warmth and could not say so plainly. She tucked it, then smoothed it back, then stopped fussing. Not because the task was finished, but because care could become noise if it was not careful.

Then she took the glass again.

She held it within reach, not forcing it, not tilting it too soon.

“Water,” she said. “Small sips if you want it. I’ll hold it as long as you need.”

She waited.

She did not fill the silence.

The room had gone soft at the edges, the way it always did after a scene had been ended properly. The implement sat aside. The restraint lay empty. The blanket had become a boundary between what had happened and what was still true: that they were both here, both sober, both present, both finished with the decision but not finished with the aftermath.

Sable’s gaze moved over the marks left by the cuff, then to the skin beneath the blanket where the strokes had landed. She did not stare. She did not make a production of it. She checked as she always did, with the same calm attention she would have given a fire, a lock, a pulse.

“I’m looking now,” she murmured. “I’m not going to ask you to explain your body to me. I’m just making sure you’re safe.”

She touched the padded edge of the freed restraint once, confirming there was nothing left tight, nothing left biting, nothing left to hold a shape the body no longer needed.

Then she returned her hand to Ines’s neck.

“You were good,” Sable said.

She said it plainly.

Not too soft. Not too bright. Not as if the words were a reward being handed down from a height. She said them like a fact that needed placing back in the scene where it belonged.

“You were good,” she said again, because one answer had not been enough when it had been asked for so badly. “You were here. You were honest. You let me decide when you didn’t know how to decide yourself. You said green when you meant it. You said not yet when you didn’t. You let me finish it hard, and you let me stop.”

Her thumb moved once, lightly, along the side of the throat.

“That’s not failure,” Sable added. “That’s not weakness. That’s not something you have to apologize for. That’s the whole point. That’s what makes it keepable.”

She shifted closer, careful not to crowd, careful not to take, careful not to make the aftercare into another thing Ines had to hold.

“I decided to finish it hard,” Sable said. “I decided to stop. Now I decide to be kind. And I was kind all the way through, even when I didn’t soften.”

Her eyes stayed steady.

“You don’t have to earn staying,” she said. “You don’t have to earn the blanket. You don’t have to earn the water. You don’t have to earn being called good after you’ve already given me your word.”

A breath passed.

Then, quieter:

“You were good.”

She let the phrase sit without making it into performance. She did not chase it with more praise. She did not turn it into a lesson. She just let it be what it was: care, given in the language Ines had asked for.

Sable reached for the blanket once more, adjusting it enough to hold heat, not enough to smother. She set the glass within easy reach, then rested her hand near Ines’s side, palm flat, warm and still.

“Check-in,” she said. “No scene. No decision. No colour needed unless something is wrong.”

Her voice stayed low.

“Tell me what you need now. More blanket. More water. Quiet. Ice. Your feet on the floor. Me to stay. Me to talk. Me to shut up and hold you. Any of those are okay.”

She paused.

“And if you don’t know, say I don’t know.”

Sable shifted again, bringing herself into the shape of the wind-down, not the shape of the scene. Her knee stayed close. Her hand stayed where it could be found without being hunted for. Her breathing slowed on purpose, because the body remembered what it had been held through and sometimes needed someone else’s rhythm to come back to itself.

“I’m not leaving,” she said. “I’m not turning it into a speech. I’m not making you finish the sentence.”

She reached out and brushed the hair back from the side of Ines’s face, a small movement, almost practical, almost tender.

“You’re allowed to be shaky,” Sable murmured. “You’re allowed to be blank. You’re allowed to need me to say it again. You’re allowed to need it to be simple.”

Her gaze held.

“You were good,” she said once more.

Then she settled into the silence with it.

She kept the blanket. She kept the water within reach. She kept her hand near enough to feel. She kept the room from becoming neglect or performance, from becoming anything but the careful, unhurried thing it was supposed to be.

No exceptions.

Water.

Warmth.

Check-in.

Stay.

Sable stayed.
