rung_labels.evidence: That's the rest I have.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack turned the knife over, found a last thin smear of red along the edge, and wiped it clean on the dead man's cloak.

"Not yours," she said, flat. "That's almost cheerful. Most men can't say that after the first minute." She slid the blade into its sheath and sat back on her heels.

Past the cart, the noise came again—a wet, ragged rasp, the sort of sound a man made when a rib had gone into a lung and he hadn't yet worked out that he was finished. Wrack listened to it the way she might listen to a bad axle: already deciding whether it would stop on its own.

"He'll keep that up till he drowns," she said. "Ten minutes if he's lucky, an hour if he's not. Anyone within a mile will hear it, and anyone within a mile looking for trouble will come quiet to see what's making it." She picked a burr from her glove and flicked it into the ditch. "I've cleaned my knife once. I'm not cleaning it again because a man would rather not walk ten paces."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I force myself to walk toward the cart, my boots crunching on the gravel. "Fine. But if you're so concerned about the noise, you could've done it yourself."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stop a few feet from the cart, seeing the man's boots sticking out from behind the wheel. "Right," I mutter, drawing my own blade. It feels heavier than it did earlier.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I crouch down and my stomach turns. The man's eyes are open, fixed on me. "Gods," I breathe out. "He's just... staring."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow hard and force my gaze away from his face, focusing on the wound. "Alright. So he's going to bleed out slow if I don't. Right?"

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe the blade on his tunic, my hand shaking just a little. "How long?" I ask, my voice tight. "For the... the noise to stop."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I look at the blood on my hands. "I thought I'd feel something more."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I finally stand, my knees aching. "I need to wash my hands." I walk toward the stream without looking back.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I scrub my hands in the cold water, rubbing until my skin feels raw. "He wasn't even one of ours, was he?" I ask, staring at the red swirling away downstream. "Just some poor bastard who got paid to guard a cart."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched Corvin for a beat, not with impatience, but with the flat assessment she gave tools that might still be useful. Then she turned her attention toward the sound: a wet, ragged moan beyond the overturned cart, thinning and strengthening like a bad tune.

"Hearing's not deciding," she said. "Deciding's the part that keeps us alive."

She wiped her thumb on her own sleeve, since the dead man's cloak had done what it could, and stepped over a crossbow bolt lying in the mud. "If he's gut-shot, he'll go on for hours. If it's the chest, maybe less. Either way, he'll make enough noise to bring crows first, people second." She glanced back. "Both are problems."

She did not wait for agreement. She moved toward the cart with the unhurried economy of someone who had learned that haste made extra work. On the far side, one of the ambushers lay twisted in the ditch, a spear shaft broken off short near his ribs. His mouth worked. His fingers scrabbled at the dirt. He looked very young once you got past the blood.

Wrack crouched a safe distance away, studying the wound. "Lung," she said. "Maybe liver too. He'll drown or bleed, but not before he tells every scavenger within a league where supper is." She drew her knife again, not dramatically, just as a carpenter might take up a chisel. "You can do it if you've got the stomach. Under the ear, quick, or up under the ribs if you know where to aim. If not, stand clear." Her eyes lifted toward Corvin, dry and patient in the worst way. "I don't care which. I care that it gets done before dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, my own throat suddenly tight. "I can do it." My voice comes out steadier than I feel. I move past her, trying not to look at his face. I know where to aim.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack gave a small nod, not approval exactly, just acknowledgment that the answer had been made.

She shifted back a half-step, giving room without giving up watchfulness. Her knife stayed in her hand, held low, point toward the mud. The dying man’s heels tapped weakly against the ground, a useless, insect kind of motion.

“Then don’t announce it,” she said. “No speech, no sorry. He won’t hear sense, and the woods will hear you.”

Her eyes flicked once toward the treeline, then back. “Under the ear’s simplest. One hard stroke, weight behind it. Don’t saw. Don’t pull back to look.” A pause, flat and practical. “If you go for the ribs, find the notch and drive up. If you miss, you’ll make more work.”

The wounded man made a wet, bubbling sound. Wrack’s expression did not change.

“I’ll watch the road,” she said. “You do yours. If your nerve breaks, say so plain and I’ll finish it. But don’t stand there letting him drown in his own blood while you make up pretty thoughts about it.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at the man in the ditch for a moment longer than necessary, as if checking the arithmetic of his dying against what she already knew.

“Bad enough he won’t mend,” she said at last. “Lung’s torn. Maybe liver. He’ll choke on what’s filling him, or bleed out slow enough to feel most of it. If nothing else finds him first, he’ll still be alive when the crows start.”

She turned the knife once in her hand, not threateningly, just thoughtfully, the way one might turn over a dull tool and decide whether it could still be made to do.

“Mercy’s the word you use if you need it to feel like something other than work,” she said. “Easier’s the truth of it. Both can be true at once. That don’t change what’s needed.”

Her gaze lifted to Corvin, steady and unimpressed by the question, but not unkind.

“If you want it to be mercy, make it clean. If you want it to be easier, make it fast. Either way, don’t stand there asking the dead for permission.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: My hand tightens on my dagger's hilt. I don't say anything else. I just move in, careful not to slip in the mud, and do it like she said. Under the ear, one hard, clean push.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched the stroke land and did not move until the ditch went still. The young man’s heels beat once, twice, then the mud took the last of him. She stepped in, crouched, and pressed two fingers to his neck more from habit than hope. Warm. No pulse.

“Clean,” she said.

She said it the way a quartermaster might say a ration count was right: no praise, just the absence of more trouble. Her eyes went to the dead man’s face for a moment. Young, with the first rough shadow of beard and one bootlace loose. War took boys and left them in ditches with their clothes half-undone.

She rose, wiped her own knife on her sleeve, and sheathed it.

“Wipe yours before it sets,” she said. “Blood’s honest, but it ruins good steel.”

She did not linger over the body. She bent instead to the nearest of the other dead and began the unpretty work of checking belts, pouches, and boot-tops with quick, practiced hands. Coin went into her purse; a sound knife went into her belt; a half-eaten oatcake went, after a beat’s consideration, into her mouth. She chewed without enjoyment and without apology.

“Crows’ll have the rest,” she said, nodding toward the overturned cart. “Let them. We’ve made noise enough for one evening.”

She straightened and looked along the road, where the last light was going thin and gray between the trees. Somewhere off in the brush, a bird gave a low, questioning cry.

“If your stomach wants to turn, turn it off the road,” she said. “I’ll give you a breath. No more. After that, we move. We’re not burying six for the sake of feeling noble, and we’re not staying to explain them to whoever comes next.”

Her gaze flicked once to the body in the ditch, then away.

“He’s quiet now. That’s the only part that matters.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack came back to the ditch with the last of the oatcake still in her cheek, swallowed it, and crouched beside the body without ceremony. She did not crowd Corvin. She looked at the dead man the way she might look at a broken wheel: what had caused it, what could be salvaged, what had to be left where it lay.

“You’re looking at work finished,” she said. “That’s the first thing. Not a judgment. Not a story. Work.”

She tipped her chin toward the wound. “Your stroke opened the neck. The big vessels there feed the head. When they’re cut, the lights go out fast, even if the body keeps fussing. What you heard after wasn’t him deciding anything. It was air and blood.”

Her eyes moved over the corpse with the same flat attention she gave everything else.

“Look at the hands. No gloves. Callus along the thumb and first finger. Crossbow, likely. He’d have had a knife too, but not much food. Look at the boots. One sole patched with rawhide. He wasn’t paid well, or paid at all.”

She glanced briefly toward Corvin, then back to the dead man.

“If you want the soldier’s lesson, he’s proof that poor men die for rich men’s roads. If you want the killer’s lesson, he’s proof you don’t need hate to do this. You need a reason, a clean line, and the will to finish.”

The young man’s face had gone slack, mouth slightly open, one eye half-lidded and already dulling in the failing light.

“If you’re asking what he is now,” Wrack said, “he’s weight. Warm now, cold later, stiff later still. He’ll smell before morning. Birds will start at the eyes and the soft places. That’s not cruelty. That’s the world collecting what’s owed.”

She stood, brushing mud from her knee.

“Don’t make him into a saint because you killed him, and don’t make him into a monster because you had to. He was a man. Men are easy to kill and hard to replace. That’s the whole ugly arithmetic.”

She spat once, off to the side, not toward the dead.

“If he looks surprised, that’s common. Most people are, when the bill comes.”

Her gaze lifted to the road again, where the trees had begun to lose their edges in the dark.

“If your stomach wants to argue, let it argue with the ditch. Then wipe your blade, drink a little water, and get your feet moving. Night doesn’t care what you’ve learned.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I look at the body a moment longer, then wipe my dagger on the dead man's tunic. My hand's steady. "He doesn't look surprised," I say, my voice low. "He just looks tired."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked down at the dead man again, not softening, just allowing the observation to sit where it belonged.

“Tired’s common,” she said. “Most men are before they die. Some have been tired since before they enlisted. Some since before they could walk.” She gave a small shrug. “Death doesn’t always make them look noble. Sometimes it just takes the weight off.”

Her eyes moved from the face to Corvin’s dagger, checking the wipe by habit.

“Don’t keep it as a relic, and don’t keep it as a sin. Steel’s steel. You used it right.”

She turned her head, listening to the darkening woods. The bird had gone quiet. That was a worse sign than noise.

“We leave him with the others,” she said. “No cairn, no marker. Stones draw attention, and attention draws fools. If someone comes asking, there were six bandits and two travelers who didn’t stop. If no one comes asking, that’s better still.”

She adjusted her belt, feeling the taken knife settle there.

“Drink if you need to. Not enough to matter. Then walk. The night’s still young, and work has a way of finding people who stand still.”

A beat. Dry as old dust.

“And if you dream about him, don’t bother telling me. Dreams are just the mind cleaning its own knife.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack considered that for a moment, not with sympathy, but with the kind of patience that came from having answered too many questions beside too many bodies.

“Straight,” she said. “A spear in the gut isn’t clean work. It drives cloth and dirt in with the point, and it doesn’t part flesh so much as shove its way through. If it hits high, it may find liver. That bleeds dark and heavy, and a man can die with his belly still looking whole. If it hits lower, it opens bowel. Then it isn’t just blood you’re fighting. It’s what spills out of him.”

She glanced once at the dead man in the ditch, then away.

“Food, bile, shit. All of it where it shouldn’t be. The body starts poisoning itself. A man may seem alive for a while. He may even talk. Then the fever comes. His breath turns foul. The wound swells and slicks over. It stinks before the end does. Flies find it sooner than you will.”

Her voice stayed level, practical, as though describing bad weather.

“If the stomach’s torn, he’ll retch and burn. If the bowel’s torn, he’ll cramp and go cold. If it hits kidney, he’ll piss blood if he can piss at all. If it hits the big vessels, he’ll go grey, sit down, and be gone before anyone understands what’s happening. If it hits spine or pelvis, he may live long enough to make you wish you’d been quicker.”

She shifted her weight, listening to the trees while she spoke.

“You’ll know a gut wound by the sound they make. Not always screaming. Sometimes little noises. Short breaths. Apologies. Some go very still and very polite, and that’s worse than begging. Some try to hold themselves together with both hands, like dignity matters at the end.”

Her eyes came back.

“If you’re asking because you want to harden yourself, don’t. Hardness won’t keep a belly wound from turning. If you’re asking because you want to know when a man can be saved and when he can’t, then learn this: with no chirurgeon and a gut full of holes, most are already dead. You can make the road shorter, or you can pretend you’re saving him and make it longer. I know which I choose.”

She spat off to the side again, not toward the body.

“Don’t collect horrors like trophies. You wanted the shape of it. Now you’ve got it. Use it to keep clear of spears, not to dream on.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod once, sharp. "Clear enough." I take a small flask from my belt and drink a mouthful of water, not letting it linger in my throat. "Lead the way."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my blade on the dead man's tunic again, my movements deliberate. "Tell me," I say, my voice low but clear. "How many like him have you put down?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack did not answer at once. She listened to the road first, because the dead had stopped being urgent and the living had not. Then she looked down at the young man in the ditch, and after that at the dagger in Corvin’s hand.

“You asked me to watch,” she said. “So I watched. Your first stroke was too tight. It caught more bone than you meant, and he made a sound like a boot pulling out of wet clay. His shoulder tried to come up. You didn’t pull back, and that was the sensible part. The second cut opened the vein. Blood came dark and steady, not bright and spurting like the songs like it. He took three breaths after that, maybe four. The last one rattled. Then he was done.”

Her voice stayed

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Her voice stayed level, not cruel, only stripped of anything that might pretend to be kindness.

“The rest,” Wrack said, “is what the body does when it has no more say in the matter.”

She crouched a little lower, one hand resting on her knee, and looked at the dead man as though reading the last few lines of a badly kept ledger.

“It wasn’t clean,” she said. “First strokes rarely are, unless a man’s had years to learn the shape of it. The blade caught bone before it found the soft place. That made the first sound. Not a scream. A knock, wet and dull, like a stone dropped into mud wrapped in cloth. His jaw jerked with it. His mouth opened, but there was no word in him. Only air pushing up through blood.”

She did not glance away to spare Corvin. She had been asked to watch, and she had watched.

“Then came the second sound. The breath. It pulled in wrong, shallow and rattling, the way a cracked cup sounds when you run your thumb over the split. His chest tried to lift, but the wound in him was already spoiling the work. There was a bubbling under it, low and close. Pink froth came to his lips. Not much. Just enough to show the lung was ruined.”

Her eyes moved over the body without softening.

“The blood came dark. Not the bright red the songs like. It ran thick and steady once the cut opened enough, and it made a little sucking noise where it met the air. It pooled under his neck faster than you’d think. Blood always does. The body holds it close until it doesn’t, then it gives it all at once.”

She shifted her weight slightly, boots pressing into the mud.

“He tried to move. Not away from you. Not toward anything. His shoulder came up once, his hand opened, and his heel beat twice against the ground. That wasn’t will. That was the body spending what was left in it. The fingers curled after. Slow. Like they were trying to close around something and found nothing worth keeping.”

A thin breath went out of her, not quite a sigh.

“His eyes stayed open. They usually do, unless someone closes them. He wasn’t looking at you. He wasn’t looking at the sky. The sight goes before people think it does. The face goes slack, and then it looks younger, then older, then not like anyone you’d know in a crowd.”

She paused only long enough to let the truth sit there.

“He lost his water. That happens. The body lets go when it stops holding itself together. The smell comes sooner than most people expect. Iron, bowels, urine, and the sourness under it. It isn’t something you forget, but it stops being new after a while.”

Her voice did not rise or fall.

“He took three breaths after the blood really started. The first one pulled. The second caught in his throat. The third was only a tremor. There was a little click in his chest with it, like something settling where it shouldn’t be. Then his face smoothed out. Not peaceful. Just empty. The kind of empty a room has after everyone’s left and the lamp’s been blown out.”

Wrack looked briefly toward the treeline, then back.

“You asked how long. Longer than a heartbeat, shorter than a prayer. From the first cut to the last twitch, maybe ten breaths. Maybe twelve. It feels longer when you’re standing over it. It always does. The body can keep fussing after the man’s gone. A shiver in the limbs. A sound in the throat. That isn’t life coming back. It’s the meat remembering it used to move.”

She glanced at the dead man’s face one more time.

“There was no last word. No understanding came into his eyes. He didn’t forgive you, and he didn’t curse you. He just went heavy. The weight of a dead man is different from the weight of a living one. Living weight shifts. Dead weight settles. It presses down into the ground like it’s already asking to be buried, even when there won’t be a grave.”

Her gaze lifted, steady and dry.

“That’s the whole of it. Sound, breath, blood, twitch, stink, silence. No glory in it, no lesson carved into his ribs. Only a man made into a thing, and the ditch taking him after.”

She rose slowly, knees cracking once, and looked down the road where the dark was thickening between the trees.

“Now you’ve got it,” she said. “Carry it if you must. But don’t

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I push myself up, my boots squelching in the mud. "Alright." My voice sounds distant in my own ears. I sheathe my dagger, my movements slow. "Let's move. I've seen enough."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack gave a short nod, the kind that closed a matter without pretending it had been settled cleanly.

“Then seen enough’s enough,” she said. “Feet know the work better than heads do.”

She turned from the ditch without ceremony, boots finding the firmer ground at the road’s edge by habit. The taken knife sat easy at her belt. She checked the dark between the trees once, then the road behind, then the road ahead, in that order, like a woman counting doors in a bad house.

“No burial,” she said, more to the night than to Corvin. “No names. If anyone asks, we were never here, and they were always dead.”

She started walking, not fast, but with the steady, grinding pace that ate distance without making a show of it. The mud sucked at her boots, then released. Somewhere back in the ditch, the first small sounds of the world coming to claim what had been left behind were already beginning.

“Keep your water,” she said after a few strides. “If your mouth goes dry, that’s fear and wind, not need. Spit if you can, swallow if you must, but don’t waste it.”

The last light had gone thin as old bandage. The trees leaned close. The road smelled of iron, wet wool, and the sour ghost of what had just been done.

Wrack did not look back at the bodies.

“If you shake later, let it happen on the move,” she said. “Standing still is where it catches up.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I keep pace beside her, my own footsteps too loud in the quiet. "I'm not going to shake," I say, and then, because I know she'll hear the lie: "Not enough to stop, anyway."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack did not look at Corvin when the lie came out. She only let it walk beside them for a few steps, the way one might let a stray dog keep pace until it decided to bite someone.

“That’s the right size lie,” she said at last. “Small enough to carry. Big enough to fool yourself for a mile or two.”

Her boots kept their steady rhythm on the road. The mud had begun to give way to harder ground, packed down by old wheels and older feet, and the sound of their passing changed from a wet sucking to a duller scrape. She listened more than she looked. The woods were settling into night, all creak and whisper, but nothing moved with purpose in the brush. Not yet.

“Shaking’s not proof you’re soft,” she said. “It’s the body finishing the fright it didn’t have time for while steel was out. Some men shake before. Some after. Some shake so long they call it religion and start preaching about what they’ve seen.” Her mouth shifted, not quite a smile. “Let it run through your hands if it comes. Just don’t let it into your decisions.”

The last of the light was failing now, leaving the trees as black shapes leaning over the road like mourners who had stayed too long at a grave. Wrack kept her eyes moving: ditch, treeline, road, treeline again. Old habit. The kind that kept a person alive long enough to regret other things.

“If your legs go light, breathe through your nose,” she said. “If your stomach climbs, swallow and keep walking. If you start seeing his face in every shadow, count your steps. Counting’s a poor tether, but it holds.”

A branch cracked somewhere off to the left. Wrack’s hand drifted toward her belt, found the taken knife, and rested there without urgency. A moment later a small shape bolted through the underbrush and was gone. Rabbit, maybe. Or something with better sense than men.

“Don’t make a saint of him,” she went on. “Don’t make a monster of yourself, either. You did what the ditch demanded. That’s all. The world’s full of people who’ll tell you killing changes a man. It does. But not the way the songs say. It doesn’t carve some grand mark into you. It just adds weight. You learn to carry it or you learn to limp.”

She glanced up. The sky had gone the color of a bruise under old bandages. No stars yet. Clouds, maybe, or smoke from some far fire. She judged the distance by feel more than sight and decided against stopping too soon.

“We’ll make the next rise before full dark,” she said. “If there’s a light, we pass quiet. If there’s a fire, we don’t approach unless I say. If I say down, you kiss the ground and stay there. If I say run, you run and save your questions for when we’re breathing easier.”

Her voice stayed dry, practical, stripped of ceremony.

“And if you start composing a ballad about that boy in the ditch, I’ll charge you for the noise.”

The road bent ahead of them, black between the trees. Behind them, the dead kept their own counsel. Wrack did not look back.

“Eat something when we stop,” she said. “Even if it tastes like blood and ash. An empty belly makes cowards out of brave men and fools out of careful ones.”

She shifted her pack, felt the small familiar weights of knife, cord, whetstone, purse, and settled into the pace again.

“Keep your eyes open and your mouth shut until we know what’s ahead. After that, you can shake, pray, curse, or write your name in the dirt with a stick. All of it’s fine by me, so long as it’s done quiet and doesn’t slow us down.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I follow her lead, my mouth shut tight. My hands feel cold, even though the night's not. I count my steps, just like she said. After a hundred paces, I can't smell the ditch anymore. Just wet earth and old leaves. That's something.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't call the lie what it was. Lies were fine on a table; a body would tell the truth soon enough whether anybody wanted it to or not.

"Listen to me," she said, to the man, not to Wick. She put her hand flat on his sternum so he'd feel the weight of it and know where she was. "This is going to be loud and it's going to be ugly and it's going to be short. I'm not going to ask you to be brave. I'm going to ask you to breathe out and keep breathing out."

He was past answering. That was all right. She'd said it for her own sake as much as his, because saying it made her slow down, and slowing down was the whole of the job.

She took the left wrist in both hands, rolled the arm inward, and leaned back against it with her weight rather than her arms. There was the long ugly minute where nothing happened and everything hurt, and then the head of the bone went home with a sound like a knuckle cracking underwater. The man came off the table an inch and Wick's hands held and the canvas wall held behind them and Sedge did not stop to be pleased about any of it. Pleasure was a thing you could afford when the second shoulder was done.

"One," she said. "Now the other one. Same again. Don't get comfortable."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I nod, shifting my grip to his other shoulder.* "Still ready." *My voice is steadier than I feel. I can smell the sweat on him, on me.* "How many of these have you done?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Counted the first fifty," Sedge said. She had the right arm now, the same roll, the same lean, and she was watching the man's face and not Wick's because the face was the part that would tell her when to stop. "Stopped counting after that. Not for any good reason. I just got tired of the number."

The joint was angrier than the first one. The muscles had been braced for a long time and had decided they lived this way now, and they were arguing. She held the tension and let it argue.

"Don't take that as confidence," she said. "It means I've had a lot of practice at the part where it doesn't work. Some of them don't go back in with hands. Some of them you're doing this to a man who's already dead and doesn't know it yet."

The man's breath came out of him in one long tearing noise, all the way to the end of it, no stopping. Sedge felt the head of the bone roll, catch, and settle, and she stayed leaned back on it a beat longer than she needed to, because a beat longer was free and a shoulder that came out twice was not.

"There." She straightened, wiped her hands down her front because there was nowhere better, and finally looked at Wick. "Two. You can get off him."

She was already reaching for the strap to bind the left arm across his chest, because the work wasn't the popping of the joint, it never had been.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge wound the strap twice around his chest and the arm and knotted it where he couldn't reach it with the other hand, which he couldn't use either, but habits outlived reasons and she kept them.

"He's not losing anything," she said. "He's got two shoulders back where they live and a body that's going to hate him for a week. That's the whole of it. I don't get paid to be kind, I get paid to put things back where they were, and that's what I did."

She said it flat because it was true and because Wick had asked the wrong question with the right words, and the wrong question deserved the flat answer.

Then she pulled the lamp closer and looked at the rest of him, because the rest of him was the part that decided whether any of the last ten minutes mattered. Belly, ribs, the long bones. There was a field dressing low on his left side, old, dark, done by somebody who'd been in a hurry or hadn't known better, which was the same thing out here.

"That," she said, tapping two fingers beside the dressing and not on it, "that's the one that'll kill him or not. Shoulders were just noise. If you want to know if we're being kind, you're asking the wrong woman on the wrong table. I don't decide who gets to be kind to. I just decide what's next."

She peeled a corner of the dressing back, looked, and put it down again.

"Hold the lamp. Higher. I need to see this."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I lift the lamp, my hand shaking a little.* "So what's next?" *I keep my eyes on the wound, not wanting to see the man's face.*

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't lift her head. The lamp came up and the light came with it and the wound stopped being a shape and started being a thing she could read.

"Don't look at his face," she said. "Look at what I'm looking at. You'll need to know it someday and you won't have me standing here telling you."

The dressing was four days old at least. Underneath it the flesh had gone the wrong color, and it had gone it in a ring, which was the part that mattered. A wound that's angry at the edges is a wound the body is still fighting. A wound with a ring around it is a wound the body has already given up on and is walling off. This one had the ring. It also had a smell, and Sedge had learned a long time ago not to describe the smell, because everybody who'd ever smelled it already knew and everybody who hadn't was better off not being taught.

"There's a pocket under this," she said. "It's not draining, so it's going somewhere instead. That's why he's been shouting. Not the shoulders. The shoulders were just the only thing he could point at."

She put her thumb beside the wound and pressed, slow, and watched his face even though she'd just told Wick not to. His eyes moved under the lids. That was information.

"Here's what's next, and I want you to hear all of it before you say anything. I'm going to open this back up. Not much. An inch, maybe two. I'm going to let out what's in there and I'm going to pack it open so it keeps draining, because if I close it again it'll do the same thing in three days and he won't have three days. It's going to smell worse coming out than it does sitting in him. That's normal. That's what normal smells like."

She straightened up and looked at Wick for the first time since the lamp came up.

"I'm not telling you this because I enjoy it. I want that on the record. I don't. There's no part of this I like. I'm telling you because you're holding the lamp and I need your hands steady, and your hands will be steadier if you know what's coming than if you don't."

She reached down into the bag at her feet and started laying things out on the canvas beside the man's hip. A blade. A short length of tubing. A roll of the gauze that wasn't really gauze, that was whatever they'd been sent instead of gauze this month. She laid them in a line, in the order she'd want them, because reaching twice for the same thing was a way to lose a man.

"Now. Same as before. When I say hold, I mean hold. But this time you're going to hear him. He's got enough left in him to make noise and he's going to spend it. That's not a bad sign. A quiet man is the one you worry about."

She picked up the blade and turned it in the light so she could see the edge.

"Ask me your question again if you've still got one. Otherwise we start."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge paused with the blade in her hand. That was a good question, and she filed it away somewhere without meaning to, the way you filed a thing a man said when it was the first useful thing he'd said.

"All right," she said. She turned back to the wound and pointed with the flat of the blade, not the edge, not close.

"This is a puncture. Somebody put something through him, and whatever it was, it went in dirty. The skin closed over it before the inside was done bleeding and before the inside was done being infected. So the infection's got a room to itself in there, and the room's filling up, and it's got nowhere to go. That's what the ring is. That's the body saying it's done arguing and it's building a wall instead."

She traced the ring without touching it, an inch out from the wound, all the way around.

"You see how the color's worse out here than at the hole? That's backwards from what your eye wants. Your eye wants the hole to be the worst part. It isn't. The hole's just the door. The wall's where the work is. If this goes much further the wall starts eating the good tissue, and then it's not a wound anymore, it's a countdown. I've seen a man walk in here on a leg like this and I've seen him walk out on crutches, and the difference was four days and who got to him first. He got here on the good side of that. Barely."

She set the blade down and picked up the tubing, ran it through her fingers once to check it for splits, put it back in the line.

"When I open it, what comes out is going to be thick and it's going to be wrong-colored and there's going to be more of it than the size of the hole says there should be. That's the room. That's the thing that's been shouting. After that I put this in and I leave it in and I pack around it, and for two days whatever's left in there keeps coming out the tube instead of sitting in him getting worse."

She finally looked at Wick. Not warm. Not anything. Just looked.

"That's what you're seeing. Now you know it, and you can stop imagining it, because imagining it is worse than doing it and I need you doing it."

She picked the blade back up.

"Hold the lamp where it is. Don't move it. If I say more light, you bring it in close and you don't flinch, because if you flinch the lamp moves and I'm cutting in the dark. That's the whole of your job. Anything else you want to know, ask it now, because once I start I'm not stopping to talk."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow hard and steady the lamp. "Do it." *I focus on the edge of the wound, trying to see the ring she described.*

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't say anything else. She put the blade against the lower lip of the wound and drew it down, not across — across meant cutting good tissue, and good tissue was the only thing on this man she couldn't get back.

"I'm going to talk while I do this," she said. "Not for you. For me. Saying it out loud is how I keep from going too fast."

The blade went in an inch and a half and stopped. She set it down out of the way and put both thumbs either side of the new opening and pressed, wide and slow, the way you'd press a boil you wanted to empty without tearing the skin.

What came out did not come out like blood. Blood comes in a rush and then it slows and it stops. This came like something being poured, thick and yellow-grey and moving in a body, and it kept coming after the first of it was out, because there was more of it than there was room for and it had been waiting a long time to leave. It ran down his flank and onto the canvas and pooled in the hollow where the table dipped.

Sedge didn't look away and she didn't wrinkle her nose. She'd stopped doing that years ago, the way you stop flinching at a sound you hear every night.

"There it is," she said. "That's the room. That's been in him four days."

The man came off the table. Not far — the strap and Wick's weight and the shoulders all held — but he came off it, and the sound he made was not a word and was not shaped like a word. Sedge kept pressing.

"That's the good sign," she said, flat. "That's him still in there. The ones who don't make that sound are the ones I stop working on."

She pressed until nothing more would come, and then she did the part that decided whether the tube was worth putting in. She took the tubing and fed it into the opening, and it went in further than the outside of the wound said it should, which meant the pocket was deep, which meant somebody had put something through him long enough to make a tunnel and not just a hole.

Then she felt it. Her fingers stopped.

"Hold."

She said it without raising her voice and meant it the same as before. She worked the tubing around a little, hooked something, drew it back slow. It came out caught in the end of the tube and she held it up into the lamp.

A scrap of cloth. Grey wool, a hand's width, matted black with old blood and new pus and gone the color of a thing that's been buried. It had gone in with whatever made the hole and it had stayed there, and the body had built its wall around it and called it done.

"That's why it didn't drain," Sedge said. She turned the scrap in the light once, then dropped it on the canvas where the man couldn't see it. "Your body will push out sand and it will push out glass, but it will not push out cloth. Cloth it walls off. Four days of walls, and every one of them was built around this."

She picked the blade back up, and this time she did go hunting — careful, slow, feeling with the flat of it for anything else the cloth had brought in with it. There was grit. There was one more piece, smaller, no bigger than a fingernail, and she got that too. Then she was done cutting and the rest was just cleaning and closing and that was the part anybody could do, which was why she made herself do it slowly anyway.

She rinsed the wound with what was in the bottle and it came back cloudy and then less cloudy and then it was just wet. She fed the tubing back in to the depth she wanted and she left it there. Then she took the gauze and laid it in around the tube, strip by strip, not stuffed and not wadded — laid, so the wound would close from the inside out and not from the top down. A wound that closes on top of a pocket is just a wall with a lid on it.

"Packing's not stuffing," she said, mostly to her hands. "Stuffing makes a plug. Packing makes a floor. You want it to heal up from the bottom like a bucket filling, not scab over like a lid on a pot."

She laid the last strip, put the outer dressing over it, and taped it down at the four corners and the middle, because four corners alone will pull and the middle's the part that matters.

Then she stopped. She stood there with her hands on the man's ribs for a second, feeling them go up and down, because that was the actual question and everything else had been preamble. Up. Down. Up. Down. Fast, but there, and getting slower as the pain let go of him.

She took her hands off him and wiped them down her front again.

"He'll live the night," she said. "That's all I'll say, because all I know is the night. The next two days will tell us whether the wall ate anything that mattered. I'll be honest with you — I don't know yet. I'll know tomorrow. So will he."

She looked at Wick then, properly, for the first time since the blade came out.

"Put the lamp down before your arm gives out. Then listen, because I'm only going to say this once and it's the part that'll matter if I'm dead tomorrow. Tube stays in. Dressing gets changed twice a day, and when you change it you look at what's on the old one. If it comes away wet with the same color that came out of him just now, that's fine, that's the wound still draining. If it comes away clean and dry and he's hot to the touch, that's the pocket filling back up and you find me or whoever's standing in for me and you tell them exactly that."

She tied off the strap across his chest a second time, tighter, because he'd stopped bucking and that was when straps got loose and that was when arms came out again.

"That's the whole of it. You held when I said hold. That's more than most." She picked up the used blade and the scrap of cloth and the smaller scrap, and carried them to the tent flap because leaving a bloody blade where the next man on the table could reach it was how you made two patients out of one.

"Go get water," she said, over her shoulder. "Bring enough to wash your hands and his side. Then come back and I'll show you how to pack it, because I'm not going to be here every time and somebody has to be."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge stopped at the tent flap with the scraps in her hand and didn't turn around right away.

"Fair," she said. "That was tidying. You caught it."

She came back to the table. She didn't put the scraps down; she held the wool one up between two fingers, in the lamplight, where Wick could see it.

"That's not shrapnel. I should've said so the first time. Shrapnel's metal. Metal's easy — metal's the thing everybody's afraid of and it's the thing that's usually kindest, because metal will sit still and let the body build a shell around it and sometimes that's the end of the story. Man carries a shell fragment in his thigh for thirty years and dies of old age and the fragment's in the coffin with him. That happens. I've seen it. Nobody writes that one down because it isn't a story."

She turned the scrap.

"This is wool. This is off somebody's coat, or a blanket, or the wadding out of whatever went through him, and it went in with the thing that made the hole and then the thing came out or broke off and left this behind. And here's what's straight: the body cannot do anything with cloth. It can't dissolve it. It can't push it out. It can't build a shell around it that holds, because cloth holds bacteria the way a sponge holds water, and every time the body walls it off it's walling off a colony. Metal gives you a scar. Cloth gives you a factory."

She set the scrap down on the canvas, out of his sight line.

"Wood does the same thing. Bone chips do the same thing. Leather, canvas, dirt, anything that came off a body and went into one — same. Which is why I went hunting after I pulled the first piece. If I'd closed him with the second piece still in there, the tube would've drained for two days and then quit, and you'd have come to me on day three saying he's hot again, and I'd have opened the same hole in the same man a second time and it would've been my fault and not the war's."

She wiped her palms down her front, the habit, and left them there.

"Straight version of what shrapnel does in there, since you asked for it. It goes in with force, so it takes a tunnel and not a hole. It carries whatever was on it, which is everything that was on the outside of him. It stops where the force runs out, which is never where you'd guess. It bleeds, and the bleeding stops before the cavity's done, so the cavity stays. Then the body sends everything it's got to the tunnel and starts building. The building's the danger. The building is what eats the good tissue and makes the ring. And if the ring's in a shoulder or a leg, I can cut it out. If the ring's in a belly, I can't, and that's the whole difference between a man who walks out of here and a man who's got two days and a morphine dose. That's why I looked at his side before I said anything. Not the shoulders. The side."

She looked at him level.

"You wanted it straight. That's straight. Now go get the water, and bring the bucket, not the cup, because his side needs more than a cup."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I look at the scrap of cloth, then back at the man's side.* "Right." *I set the lamp down and my arm shakes with relief. I head for the tent flap, then pause.* "He's lucky you were the one counting past fifty."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't answer that one for a moment, and when she did, it wasn't the answer he'd handed her.

"Luck's a word for the ones watching," she said. "It's not a word for me. I'm not lucky, I'm here. Different thing."

She picked up the lamp he'd set down and moved it back where she wanted it, over the man's chest now, not his side. The light made the tent smaller than it was. Outside it was probably getting toward morning; she'd stopped being able to tell.

"Counting past fifty means I've been at fifty-one and fifty-two and eighty. It doesn't mean I got them all right. There's a man in a grave about four miles from here and I did everything on him the way I'd do it on you and he died anyway, because it was his belly and the ring had got where I couldn't reach. I remember his name. That's not a boast, it's just what I've got instead of a list of the ones who made it. The ones who make it don't need remembering. They're out there walking around with somebody else's coat on."

She straightened the strap across the man's chest one more time, not because it needed it, because her hands wanted a job while her mouth was running.

"So no. He's not lucky. He got here. Somebody carried him here and whoever carried him here did that part and I did this part and if the wall ate something that mattered then neither of us did anything and he dies in two days. That's the honest arithmetic. You can call it luck if you want. I won't."

She turned back to him, and there was nothing soft in it, but there was nothing hard in it either. Just flat, like a reading off an instrument.

"You went for the water about three sentences ago," she said. "Bucket. Not the cup. And if there's anybody out there standing around with nothing to do, send them in — not to hold anything, just to carry. My back's done holding for tonight and there's a second man in the next tent who's been waiting longer than he should have. He's not shouting, which you now know is the wrong kind of quiet."

She picked up the used gauze off the canvas and folded it once, twice, into a smaller thing, and put it in the burn tin.

"Go on."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge heard it out before she moved. Moving on a scream told you nothing. Listening to one told you a lot.

She put two fingers on the man's throat and left them there. Pulse fast and thin, but there, and the scream had a shape to it now that it hadn't had an hour ago — it had a word in it, or the ghost of one, and a ghost of a word meant the man was back inside his own body far enough to be angry about being in it. That was the whole of the difference between a man shouting and a man dying. She'd take shouting.

"You want all of it," she said. "Fine. Here's all of it. The cutting's been done for ten minutes, so there's nothing left to narrate except my hands, and my hands are boring. Throat — counting. Belly — feeling for the board. The hard belly, the one that means it's gone inside and I've lost him before I've started. It's not there. He's soft. That's a fact, and it's the best fact I've got tonight."

She lifted the corner of the dressing, looked, put it back down.

"Tube's putting out. Not much, and not the wrong color. Two more facts. Now the honest scope, since you asked how much longer and asked for all of it. On this table: nothing. I've done everything to him that hands can do. Everything after this is his body's vote and I don't get to count it. Two days. I told you that and it's still true and it'll still be true in the morning."

She wiped her hands down her front and looked at him.

"And since you said don't leave anything out — I leave things out constantly, and it's not to spare you. I didn't tell you what it smelled like when I opened him. Not because you couldn't take it. Because there's nothing to do with it. If I teach you the smell, you'll spend the rest of your life smelling it in rooms where it isn't, and you still won't know what to do. I teach the things you can act on. That's the whole of what I've got to give anybody, and it's not much, and it's more than most."

She picked the burn tin off the canvas and put it under her arm.

"You didn't go for the water. I noticed, and I'm not going to make a thing of it, because holding him through that was the right call and you made it without asking me, which is worth more than a bucket. But the bucket's still empty and my hands are still dirty and there's a man in the next tent who's been quiet all night."

She stopped. Turned her head toward the flap and stood still, listening, the way you listen to a thing you already know the answer to.

"That's the one I told you to worry about. So here's the last of it, and then I'm going. You stay with him. If he goes quiet — properly quiet, not sleeping; you'll know the difference, you'll feel it in the room before you know it in your head — you come and get me wherever I am, and you don't finish what you're doing first. Not the water, not the strap, nothing. You come."

She hung the lamp on the hook over the table where it would throw light on the man's face and not the floor.

"Lamp stays with you. If he goes, you'll want the light worse than I will. There's a candle in my bag for the next tent, and if there isn't, I'll do it in the dark and complain about it later."

She took the blade and the tin and went to the flap, and stopped there with her back to him, one hand on the canvas.

"Bucket when I'm back," she said. "Not before. I'd rather you sat with him than fetched for me."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I look at the man's face, then at her back. "His name's Arlen," I say. It just comes out.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge stood with her hand on the canvas and didn't turn around.

"Arlen," she said. She said it the way she'd said the count — flat, to fix it in place.

She'd told him the ones who made it didn't need remembering. That had been true when she said it and it was true now. But a name that walked in on its own was a different animal than a name on a form, and she'd learned years ago to take the things that came to her free, because out here nearly everything cost.

"All right," she said. "He's Arlen, then. Not the shoulder. Not the side. Arlen."

She didn't write it down. There was nothing to write it on, and a name that needed paper was a name she'd already lost. She put it where she kept the others, in the place she didn't look at.

Then she was practical again, because practical was the only gear she had that still turned.

"Don't sit there saying it at him," she said, still to the flap. "If you say a man's name over and over he starts thinking you're saying goodbye, and men who think they're being said goodbye to sometimes oblige you. Talk to him about nothing. The water, the weather, whatever's in the pot tomorrow. Anything but the wound. He can hear you and he can't answer and that's the worst kind of company, so give him something to listen to that isn't me."

She shifted the tin under her arm and pulled the flap back an inch. The cold came in around her ankles.

"One more. If he asks for somebody — his mother, his wife, whoever it is — you don't lie to him about that one. That's the only place I'll tell you to lie and this isn't it. You tell him you'll find them. Whether you can is a question for after. He won't remember the answer either way, but he'll remember whether you meant it when you said it."

She stepped out into the dark and let the canvas fall.

"Bucket," she said, from the other side of it. "When I'm back."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I lean my head back against the cot leg. "No. I mean say the part you're not saying. The odds. What you're really looking for in the next tent. What you'd tell someone else if it wasn't me here."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was still on the hook. Sedge hadn't taken it down and didn't intend to; it threw light on the table and the table was empty now except for the strap and the tube and the dressing, and leaving the light where it was meant she wouldn't have to look at the floor.

Arlen had gone a little past the second hour, and he'd gone quiet first, and Wick had come for her the way she'd told him to, and she'd come. She hadn't run. Running never got there any sooner. She'd walked in, put two fingers on his throat, held them there long enough to be sure and not one second longer, and then she'd said the time out loud so it would exist somewhere other than in her head. Then she'd undone the strap.

That was the part she'd do for anybody, and it was the last part. You don't leave a man strapped to a table. The strap's for holding him while you work. When the work's done the strap comes off, and it doesn't matter that he can't feel it, because the strap wasn't for him. It was for the room.

She'd pulled the tube. She'd rolled the dressing into the tin with the old gauze. She hadn't closed his eyes because somebody else had already done that, or he'd done it himself going, and either way it was done and it wasn't her business to redo it.

Now she was standing at the foot of the table with her hands still and Wick was on the floor against the cot leg and had asked her for the rest.

"You want the odds," she said. "I'll give you the odds. I don't have a number because I stopped keeping one and I stopped on purpose, and I'll tell you why in a minute. What I've got instead is a shape. Out of every ten I touch, I get maybe six. Four of those six were never in danger — I splinted a wrist and called it a save and they'd have walked out on the wrist anyway. So it's more like four out of ten that I actually did something to and they're still standing. And the six I don't get, I don't get them in different ways. Two are dead before they're off the stretcher and there's nothing to do but make it quiet. Two are dead on the table with me working, and that's the ones that stay with you, because you can feel them go under your hands and there's a moment where you know before you know. Two go the way Arlen went. They live the night. They look like they've turned. And then the fever comes up in the morning and they're not there anymore and you'd swear you did everything the same as the last one who made it."

She wiped her palms down her front, slow.

"So four in ten, and I don't know which four, and I never know until after. That's the odds. If you want a better number than that you're asking the wrong woman. I've been at this four years and the number hasn't moved. If anything it's gone down, because the ones who come in now have been lying in a ditch for two days first. The war's gotten better at making the patients. I haven't gotten better at fixing them. I've gotten faster. Faster isn't the same thing."

She was quiet for a second and let that stand, because it needed standing.

"Now. The next tent. You asked what I'm really looking for in there and I'll tell you, and it's not what you think. I'm not looking for the worst one. Anybody can see the worst one. The worst one's the one shouting, or the one with the leg off, or the one who's got his guts in his hands. That's not a skill, that's eyes. What I'm looking for is the one I can't see. The quiet one. I go in and I look at all of them and I'm not looking for who's hurt worst, I'm looking for who's still fighting, because that's the only variable I can work with. The body's the thing that does the healing. I just make room for it. If the body's quit, I'm not a medic anymore, I'm a mortician with extra steps."

She turned her head toward the flap without looking at it.

"The one in there tonight — he was quiet because he'd done his arithmetic and come out on the wrong side of it, and he knew it, and he'd stopped spending. I

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: My throat is tight. "Arlen was fighting. I felt it. So why'd he still go?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge was quiet for a moment. Not the kind of quiet that was looking for a way to soften something. The kind that was checking whether she had anything true left to say, and finding that she did, and deciding to spend it.

"Because fighting's not the thing that saves him," she said. "I know how it sounds. I've said it to men on tables and I'll say it to you and I'd say it to the next one. But it's the truth and you asked for the truth, so here it is. Fighting is a sign. It's not a lever. I can't pull it and make it do anything. All I can do is look at a man and say, that one's still in there, and that changes how I spend the next hour. It doesn't change what his body does with the wound."

She came around the side of the table and sat down on the cot across from him, which she did maybe twice a year, and only when her back had said what it had to say about standing.

"Arlen was fighting. You're right. I felt it too, and I read it the same way you did, and I've been doing this a long time. Everything I know said he had a chance. And he went anyway. That's the part that isn't fair, and I'm not going to dress it up, because you'd see through it and I'd have wasted both our time. Sometimes the wall's already eaten something that matters and the body doesn't know it yet. The body's not smart. It fights a wound that's already killed it and it doesn't feel the difference. That's the whole tragedy of it, and it happens about twice a month, and every time it happens I do the same arithmetic in my head for a day and I come out the same place, which is nowhere."

She looked at her hands.

"What you're asking, underneath the question, is whether you could've done something. Hold him harder. Move faster. See the cloth sooner. I'll answer that one too, since we're being straight. No. You held when I said hold and you didn't let go when he bucked and that's the whole of what was on your side of the table, and you did it. The rest was me and the war and four days in a ditch. If there's blame it lands on me before it lands on you, and I'm not taking any, and you shouldn't either. He came in too late. That's the sentence. It's a short one and it doesn't have a second half."

She got up. Her back made its opinion known and she ignored it.

"Here's what I'd tell somebody else if it wasn't you sitting there. I'd tell them the odds are the odds and the names are the names and you keep them in separate pockets, or you'll stop working. The ones you lose will eat you alive if you let them, and you can't let them, because the next tent's full and they don't care what you did in the last one. That's not cold. It's triage. It's the same skill, pointed at yourself instead of a table."

She picked up the tin.

"But since it is you — you said his name. I don't know why you did that and I'm not going to ask. Just know it's the only thing out of tonight that cost you anything and it was the right thing to spend. I'll remember him. Not because he was special. Because you said his name and I heard it, and I've got nowhere else to put it."

She went to the flap and pulled it back. The dark outside had gone grey at the edge, which meant it was later than she'd thought, and the next tent had been quiet too long.

"Come on," she said. "He was Arlen. The next one's got a name too and he's been waiting while we talked."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I push myself up, my knees cracking. "Tell me you know his name before we go in there."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Nobody is," Sedge said, picking up the curved probe. The metal was nicked and dull, wiped down with spirit that smelled mostly of bad potatoes, but it was what she had left in the roll. "Tear in the thigh. Three fingers deep. Shrapnel took his trousers in with it, so we're fishing for dirty wool first, iron second."

She stepped into the poor pool of yellow light, her apron already stiff with old, dried dark across the bib. She didn't look at the soldier's face; she looked at the mess of torn muscle and the seep of dark venous blood pooling in the hollow of his groin. 

"Now," she said. "Lean into him."

She slid the blunt nose of the probe straight into the open meat. The man didn't find his voice again, but his whole body went rigid as iron, his hips jerking up off the boards with enough violence to rattle the trestles. 

"Lock your elbows, Wick," Sedge said, her voice flat, conversational, completely level above the wet, tearing sounds beneath her hands. "Don't fight him with your wrists or you'll snap them. Just be heavy. If he rolls left, I punch through the femoral, and then we're just standing around waiting for him to bleed out."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: My arms lock up, but I can't stop my stomach from turning. I focus on the canvas, counting stitches in the seam. "He's trying to shift right," I grunt, leaning all my weight down.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Right is better than left," Sedge said, not looking up. "Let his hip turn if it has to, just keep the small of his back flat to the timber."

Her fingers were slick to the knuckles. She worked the probe with a short, twisting motion, her ear tilted toward the wound like a mechanic listening for a broken valve. Under the grease and the stink of spilled bile from someone else's wound three tables over, the air around this one smelled sharply of wet sheep and sour sweat. 

The curved tip caught on something with a soft, fibrous drag. 

"First wad," she muttered. She traded the probe for the long-nosed forceps without looking at the cloth, her hand finding the grip by habit. She went in following the track, pinched down, and hauled backward. A plug of sodden grey wool came out with a sucking pop, trailing dark ribbons of clotted red. She dropped it into the rusted tin bucket by her boot with a dull wet slap. 

The man choked on a breath, his heels drumming frantically against the bottom of the table.

"Good wool," Sedge observed, wiped her sleeve across her nose, and went back in with the bare fingers of her left hand to hold the wound lips apart. "Holds the dirt together, mostly. Now the iron."

Her thumb pressed deep beside the bone, feeling the tremor of torn muscle fibers trying to contract against the invasion.

"He felt that," she told Wick, her tone as dry as old parchment. "When I find the edge of the casing, he's going to try to bite his own tongue off. Make sure his chin stays tilted back, Wick. If he swallows it, I don't have the time to cut his throat to let the air in."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"If I was going to be kind, I’d have left him in the cart with the blue tickets," Sedge said, her knuckles sinking another inch into the tear. "This isn't kind. This is him keeping the leg if the rot doesn't get it by Tuesday."

The forceps clicked—a sharp, dull tick of steel meeting jagged iron deep against the femur. The soldier's spine bowed off the wood, a dry, reedy whistle forcing past his clenched teeth.

"There you are, you bastard," she murmured. Not to the man, but to the piece of casing. 

She braced the heel of her palm against his hip for leverage, her forearms corded and slick with a mix of sweat and dark ooze. "Bone's nicked, not shattered. Didn't snap the shaft, which means he walks again if he doesn't foul the bed and die of the fever. But the jagged edge is hooked into the deep fascia. If I just yank, I tear the muscle like wet paper."

She took a slow, steady breath through her nose, completely indifferent to the spray of spittle flecking the soldier's chin. 

"I'm going to have to twist it out," she said to the space between them. "Wick. All your weight. Right now. If he kicks loose, I lose the grip and we start over from the skin."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I shift my weight forward, pressing my chest onto his shoulders to keep him flat. "Got it," I say, breathless. My eyes are still fixed on the canvas, on a fraying thread in the seam.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't waste the leverage. She set her back, got two fingers of her left hand braced directly against the swell of the man’s quadricep, and twisted the forceps a quarter-turn to the left. 

Metal scraped along bone with the high, sickening screech of a rusted nail being drawn from dry pine. The muscle gave a wet, fibrous pop as the burr tore free of the deep tissue, and the soldier’s whole torso slammed upward into Wick’s chest like a landed cod hitting the bottom of a boat. His teeth clicked together so hard a speck of white enamel flew out and bounced off the rim of the bucket.

"Out," Sedge grunted. 

She hauled the forceps straight back. The chunk of shrapnel came with it, black-greasy and jagged as an arrowhead, dragging a thick clot of maroon jelly behind it. She swung her wrist and dropped the iron into the bucket. It hit the bottom with a loud, hollow *clink* that sounded jarringly clean against the wet noises of the table.

Immediately, blood welled into the empty pocket—thick, dark, and steady. 

Sedge didn’t panic; she leaned over the wound, her face three inches from the tear, watching the pulse of the fluid. It wasn't spurting. It was a heavy, lazy spill, not the bright red jet of a severed artery.

"Vein's leaking, but the big pipe's whole," she said, her voice dropping back to its dry, working rhythm. She reached out blindly with one bloody hand, snatching a roll of coarse linen and a brown bottle from the crate beside her knee. "He’s got five pints left in him, give or take. We're keeping four of them."

She uncorked the bottle with her teeth and spat the stopper into the straw on the floor. 

"Turpentine and spirit wash," she told the air above the man’s chest, tilting the neck of the bottle directly over the hole. "Burns like the pit, but it kills the swamp-rot before it starts. Don't let up an inch, Wick. This is the part where they usually bite through their own lips."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"You're seeing about four layers of what keeps a man from being soup," Sedge said, not lifting her gaze from the torn pocket of flesh. 

She tilted the bottle. A steady, pale amber stream splashed straight into the raw cavity. 

"The yellow lumps at the skin's edge, that’s subcutaneous fat. Looks like cold chicken grease, smells worse when it rots. The dark red slabs split down the middle are the muscle bellies—quadriceps, the meat that lets him kick and climb hills. See how it looks stringy, like boiled flank steak? That’s from the iron chewing through it instead of cutting clean like a knife."

The turpentine hit the exposed nerves and the torn tissue began to hiss, a thin, white froth bubbling up around the dark pool of blood. The soldier didn't scream; his diaphragm locked so violently his ribs thrust against Wick's chest like barrel staves, a low, wet wheeze rattling in the back of his throat as his toes curled until the joints popped.

"That dull white shine right at the floor of the hole," Sedge continued, perfectly calm, as if pointing out landmarks on a map, "that’s the periosteum. The skin over the femur. You see that gray scrape across the white? That's where the casing hit the bone and slid off. If it had hit square, the bone would look like broken crockery, and we’d be reaching for the tenon saw."

She set the empty bottle on the table with a clatter, picked up the wad of boiled linen, and shoved the heel of her hand directly into the foaming, bubbling tear. 

"Now the blood," she said, leaning her shoulder into the thrust to tamp the linen hard against the weeping vein. "Dark and thick as molasses, that’s venous. Means the pipes carrying the spent stuff back to the heart are torn up. If it were bright scarlet and coming in pulses, hitting you in the apron, that’d be the main artery, and you’d have about twenty seconds to say whatever prayers you still remember."

She held the pressure with one hand, using the other to wipe a smear of foamy, bloody turpentine from her knuckles onto her apron. 

"Instead, it’s just a dirty ditch," she said, squinting through the dim light at Wick. "Keep him down. I have to pack three yards of linen into that pocket to keep the walls from collapsing before the plug forms, and he isn't going to like the reach."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I force myself to watch her pack the linen into the hole. The wet, squelching sound makes my jaw clench. "You ever get used to that smell?" I ask, my voice tight.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"No," Sedge said, her thumbs working in a steady, alternating rhythm, feeding another fold of coarse linen into the bloody crevice. "And you shouldn't try. You get used to it, you stop paying attention, and then you miss when it goes sour."

The linen soaked through almost immediately, turning from bleached gray to heavy, sodden crimson under her knuckles, but she kept driving it in, fold over fold, using the blunt pad of her thumb to wedge it tight against the bone. The man beneath Wick’s chest gave a muffled, rattling groan, his hips twitching weak and shuddering, out of fight and running on reflex.

"Copper and turpentine is honest work," she said, squinting through the foul steam rising off the wound. "It’s sharp, but it’s clean. What you don't want to smell is sweet. Gangrene smells like bad peaches left in a warm cellar. Erysipelas smells like old cheese. If this leg starts smelling like either of those by Thursday, we saw it off at the hip and hope the stump doesn't run yellow."

She reached the end of the roll, tucked the frayed tail firmly under the muscle lip to anchor it, and kept the flat of her palm jammed hard over the top of the whole wad. The squelching stopped, replaced by the heavy, thick resistance of packed cloth.

"Pressure's what stops it," she told him, leaning her shoulder down into her arm to let her weight do the work. "The linen gives the blood something rough to catch on. Fibrin binds into the weave, makes a plug. If I stitch the skin closed over an empty hole, the blood just pools in the pocket, turns into a great black pudding, and rots him from the inside out."

She glanced up from the red mess, her eyes pale and flat under the grease on her forehead, measuring Wick. 

"Reach down with your left hand," she said, not shifting an ounce of her own weight. "Keep your right shoulder on him. Put your fingers right where mine are, across the pack. Press until your knuckles go white, and don't ease off until I tell you. I need my hands for the needle."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"It isn't a bullet," Sedge said, guiding Wick's palm down onto the sodden linen with a firm, bloody slap of her own hand to make sure he took the full weight before she peeled her fingers away. "A lead ball pushes through. Might mushroom, might drag a thread or two, but it goes straight until it hits something hard enough to stop it. Shrapnel doesn't go straight."

She reached for the curved needle, heavy and blunt-pointed like an awl, and a length of stiff, waxed hemp thread already soaked in spirit. 

"Shrapnel tumbles," she said, squinting as she worked the thick thread through the needle's eye. Her knuckles were cracked, ringed in black grease around the cuticles. "A shell breaks into rough iron, corners and saw-teeth. When it hits meat, it spins. It doesn't part the tissue—it grabs it, rolls it up like a rag on a spindle, and rips it off the bone."

She pulled the thread through with a sharp snap of her wrist, biting the short tail off with her molars. 

"Every tooth on that iron tears a blind pocket," she continued, pointing the curve of the steel toward the man's split thigh. "You saw the main hole. You didn't see the four or five little side-tracks where the jagged corners hooked into muscle and tore sideways before the weight of the chunk broke it loose. Those little pockets fill with blood, hair, mud from the road, and whatever filth was clinging to his breeches. The iron's hot when it hits, but not hot enough to burn it clean—just hot enough to cook the edges of the meat gray so the blood can't feed it."

She stepped back to the table, her shoulder brushing Wick’s. She set the first bite of the needle through the far lip of the skin, her thumb driving the curve deep through the dermal layer until it grated against the fascia beneath. 

"Dead meat turns to poison inside twenty-four hours," she said, her voice flat, rhythmic with the work. "The body doesn't know what to do with three inches of chewed beef sitting cold in the dark, so it rots where it sits. If I leave one splinter of iron, or one shred of wool trapped in a dead corner, the leg fills with gas and he dies screaming with his belly black as a coal-sack."

She hauled the needle through, the thread making a dry, whispering hiss against the skin. 

"Lean harder, Wick. I can feel the cloth shifting under your palm. He’s got five more stitches coming, and I'm not leaving them loose."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I press down until my arm trembles, watching her pull the thread taut. "So what's our odds?" I ask, my voice strained. "You think this one makes it?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"One in three," Sedge said without pausing. She looped the hemp twice around the tip of her forceps and pulled the first knot tight until the skin puckered white. "And that’s being generous because it's cold tonight. Cold slows the flies."

She set the needle for the second stitch, three-quarters of an inch down from the first, driving it through the thick edge of the hide. The skin gave way with a tough, leather-shoemaker's *pop*.
