"Right now, his heart's small and fast because half his blood is on the table and in my bucket. If his heart quits before dawn from the shock, the leg doesn't matter. That's hurdle one."

She pulled the loop through, the hemp rasping. Her face was set, eyes tracking only the alignment of the wound lips.

"Hurdle two is tomorrow night. If he starts shaking so hard his teeth chatter, that’s the marrow-fever. Means the bone took in some of the swamp-water from his clothes. Once it gets inside the marrow, you can't wash it out. It cooks him from the inside until his brain turns soft and he starts calling you his mother."

She threw another square knot, hauling it snug. The man beneath them let out a low, bubbling wheeze, his chin slack against his chest, finally knocked dull by the agony. 

"Hurdle three is the pack," she continued, her voice dropping into the steady, mechanical cadence of her hands. "That linen in there isn't staying. In three days, when the plugs are formed, someone has to reach in with the tongs and pull all three yards of it back out. It'll be glued to the raw meat by dried crust and scabs. It’ll rip every fresh seal open when it comes. If the clot holds while we yank, he keeps the leg. If it tears the big vein open again, we lose him in five minutes while he's looking us in the eye."

She drove the third stitch home, her thumb bruised and blackened from forcing the eye through the tough fascia. 

"And hurdle four is the lockjaw. If he survives the shock, the fever, and the unpacking, he can still step on a rusty nail in his mind on day nine, his jaw clamps shut like an iron trap, and he suffocates on his own spit because his throat turns to stone."

She snipped the thread with her teeth, leaving the ends long for drainage, and lined up the needle for the fourth bite. 

"So don't ask about odds," she said, glancing up through the greasy strands of hair plastered to her temple, her pale eyes fixing on Wick's face. "Odds are for men placing bets in a tavern. We give him his one-in-three, we sew him up, we tip him into the straw, and we take the next one off the cart."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"He’s screaming because the skin hurts worse than the meat," Sedge said, her voice cutting clean and flat right beneath the man’s shrieking. "The deep muscle only feels pressure and tearing, but the hide is full of fine little wire-ends. Every time the needle punches through the derma, his brain thinks he’s being burned alive."

She drove the fourth stitch through. The needle curved up through the opposite lip with a dull crunch of cartilage-tough skin, slick with dark grease. 

"I’m leaving a finger’s width between the knots," she told Wick, her hands working fast, loop over loop, pulling the twine taut with a short jerk of both wrists. "If I sew him up pretty like a lady’s cushion, the rot has nowhere to drain. A wound like this is going to weep dirty water, gray slough, and dead fat for five days straight. That gap lets the muck run out into the straw instead of building up a pocket between the muscle belly and the bone."

The soldier's head thrashed back, the cords of his neck standing out like frayed rope, spitting bloody saliva against the canvas ceiling. Sedge didn't blink, didn't flinch away. She just reached down, took a fresh bite with the awl-tipped needle right through the lower corner of the flap, and hauled.

"This is the fifth," she said, her knuckles digging into the man's hip to counter the pull of the hemp. "The anchor. I’m going through the deep fascia this time—that white, tough gristle that wraps the muscle bundle. If I don't catch the gristle, the skin just tears out like rotten canvas the first time he coughs or tries to piss."

She hauled the thread. The man let out a cracked, winded screech that broke halfway through into a dry cough. 

"Two minutes on the needle," Sedge said, her fingers flying through the final square knot, cinching the raw edges together until they puckered into a dark, swollen ridge. "Then five minutes to wrap him hip to knee with boiled hemp so the pack doesn't shift when they haul him into the mud. After that, he’s off this table, we wipe the timber with the vinegar rag, and you go out to the tail-gate to pull the next body."

She snipped the thread with her shears, the steel giving a dry, heavy *snip*. 

"Ease off the linen now, Wick. Slowly. Don't jerk your hand back or the clot comes with your skin. Just peel your fingers away, one at a time, and let’s see if my dam holds."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I lift my hand slowly, fingers numb and sticky. The pack underneath is soaked through, but the bleeding's slowed to a thick ooze. "Dam's holding," I say, my voice rough. I look at the man's face, slack now, and wonder if he's still in there. "What do we do with him now?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Thick is fine. Thick means the plug is sticking to the linen," Sedge said, reaching under the table and hauling up a wide roll of unbleached binding cloth that had seen boiling water once, perhaps two weeks ago. 

She laid two fingers flat against the side of the soldier’s neck, pressing into the hollow beneath the jaw. Her touch was rough and entirely impersonal.

"He's still in there," she said, her fingers lingering just long enough to count four weak, fluttering taps against her pads. "Fainted dead away. Best thing that’s happened to him tonight. The heart slows down when the brain shuts off, gives the vessels a chance to seal before he pumps the rest of his life onto the planks."

She caught the loose end of the binder cloth in her teeth, ripped off a four-foot tail to use as a tie, and shook out the main roll. 

"Get your hands under his knee and heel," she told Wick. "Lift the leg four inches. Just four. Don't let the thigh rotate outward or you'll stretch the skin where I just put the hemp."

She didn't wait for him to find his grip; she was already sliding the cloth under the swollen, discolored leg, working with quick, practiced loops. 

"We wrap him tight," she said, her voice dropping into the steady, mechanical cadence she used for every task that didn't require thought. "Starting low, working high. If I wrap loose, the packing slips out the minute the bearers dump him on a stretcher, and then he bleeds out in the mud before he even reaches the straw. If I wrap too tight, the foot turns black and drops off from cold. You want it snug as a boot-lace."

She brought the coarse strip over the stitched wound, flattening the bloody pad of linen with firm, heavy pressure, then wound the cloth in a tight figure-eight up around his hip and waist to anchor it against the slope of the thigh. 

"Now he goes into the north trench," she said, tying off the hemp with two hard, jerking knots that pulled the soldier's flesh taut against the cloth. "Under the dry straw. No blankets—we don't have them, and if we did, they'd be fouled by morning. If he's awake enough to swallow by midnight, somebody might give him a swallow of well-water. No rum, no gin. Alcohol thins what little grease he has left in his veins, and he'll start leaking through my stitches before the watch changes."

She straightened up, her spine giving a dull, audible pop as she stretched her back. She looked down at the man—not at his face, but at the dark, wet wrap around his thigh, watching for any sudden bloom of bright scarlet through the gray cloth. Nothing came but the same slow, dark ooze.

"He's off the timber," Sedge said, reaching for the vinegar rag in the stone crock by her boots. "Take his head and shoulders, drag him to the flap. Then come back with the bucket of sand and scrub this planking. The grease from his leg makes the wood slick, and I don't need the next one sliding off the trestle while I'm looking for an artery."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t tell him to get up. She didn’t look down at him with pity, either, because pity took up room in the chest that was needed for air. 

Instead, she dropped the vinegar rag into the stone crock with a dull splash, reached her hands into the cold, sour brine, and wrung the coarse hemp out until the muscles in her forearms knotted and grease-streaked liquid ran down between her knuckles.

"The rest," she said, her voice flat as an iron pan hitting a flagstone, "is what happens when the shock wears off and the body realizes what’s been done to it."

She bent over the pine table, laying the wet rag flat against the dark, sticky stain where the soldier’s thigh had rested. She began to scrub with long, heavy strokes, the vinegar cutting through the tallow-smell of the blood with a sharp, stinging bite that made the eyes water.

"In an hour, the numbness leaves him," she said, not breaking the rhythm of her shoulders. "The nerves we bruised with the forceps and cut with the needle are going to wake back up. But they won't feel like a cut. They feel like a red-hot iron bar laid across the bone and left there to cool. His belly will lock. The gut shuts down when the body thinks it's dying, which means whatever hard tack or salt pork he ate yesterday sits in his stomach like a lead weight, turning sour. He’ll vomit dry bile into the straw until his throat tears."

She flipped the rag, using the cleaner side to scour the blood pooled in the groove between two planks.

"By three in the morning, his skin will be cold as river clay. His blood volume is down, so the heart pulls everything away from the fingers, the toes, the ears, dragging whatever heat he has left into his chest to keep the lungs pumping. He’ll shiver. Not a little tremble, Wick. He’ll shudder so hard his teeth will click until they break, and every time his thighs twitch against the boards, the rough linen inside that hole will grind against the raw periosteum of the femur. It’s like sandpaper on bone."

She paused, dipped the rag back into the crock, and hauled it up, dripping brown and gray.

"If he lives through the cold part, the fire starts around noon tomorrow," she continued, her breathing steady, measuring out the words like doses of salt. "The wound will swell. The skin around my hemp stitches will puff up purple and tight as a drum skin, so hard you couldn't dent it with your thumb. If you lay your bare palm on his thigh tomorrow night, it will be hotter than an oven door. That’s the white cells coming in to eat the dirt we couldn't scrape out. If they win, you get laudable pus—thick, creamy, smells like sour dough, drains out between the gaps I left. That’s the good ending. That’s him surviving."

She leaned all her weight into the timber, working the rag over a dry splatter near the edge of the trestle. 

"The bad ending is the gas," she said. "If the black rot was on that wool, the anaerobic bugs wake up in the dark under the muscle. They eat the dead beef, and they make wind. By Wednesday morning, you don't even have to lift the blanket to know. You can lay two fingers three inches above the dressing, press lightly, and you'll feel the skin crackle like dry leaves underfoot. That's gas bubbles moving through the meat under the hide. Once the crackle starts, the leg dies from the inside out, turning the color of an old liver, and the poison hits his kidneys by sundown. His urine turns black as coffee, his breath smells like rotting apples, and then the fever takes his head."

She wrung the rag out one last time and hung it over the lip of the crock. Her hands were raw, red from the vinegar, the grease settled deep into the cracked pores around her fingernails.

"And if he beats the rot," she said, wiping her forehead with the dry crook of her elbow, "he gets to wake up on the fourth day, when the fever breaks and the belly starts working again. And that’s the day I come to his pallet with the iron tongs and two men to sit on his chest."

She looked over the lip of the table, straight down at Wick sitting in the dirt. Her eyes were completely steady, pale and dry.

"I take the edge of the binding off with the shears. The blood and the lymph will have dried into a hard, black crust, gluing the coarse linen straight to the raw meat and the torn gristle. I have to soak it with vinegar until it softens, and then I clamp the tongs onto the tail of the cloth and I haul it out, foot by foot. Every inch of that linen brings away fresh scabs, granulating tissue, and raw nerve ends. He will scream until his voice cracks into a dry hiss, and he will look at me with his eyes wide open, absolutely certain that I am murdering him."

She wiped her palms down the stiff bib of her apron, leaving two long, dark streaks over the dried crust of older blood.

"That's the rest," she said. "From skin to bone, from the cart to the pit or the walking-line. That's all of it. Nothing pretty, nothing noble, just meat trying not to spoil in the heat."

She turned toward the back of the tent, where the water bucket sat beside the crate of clean needles. 

"Now," Sedge said, her tone unchanged, "tell me if your legs work, Wick. Because there’s three more wagons coming down the corduroy road, and the mud out there is full of men who don't have time for you to sit on the boards."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I look at my hands in the dim light, the blood in the creases of my knuckles. It isn't mine, but it feels like it is. "They work," I say, and push myself up, the world tilting for a second before it settles. "Where's the sand bucket?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Under the corner trestle," Sedge said, nodding toward the shadow beneath the instrument bench. "Behind the salt crock. It’s mixed half-and-half with dry wood ash. The ash cuts the grease, the grit gives the boots purchase."

She didn't offer a hand, nor did she watch him walk to make sure his knees didn't buckle. If he went down, he went down; if he stayed on his feet, he was useful. She turned back to the small tin tray on her work crate, picking up the curved needle she had just used. 

She held it up to the bad lantern light, squinting at the eye, then took a strip of dry, coarse rag from her pocket and scoured the dried crust of blood from the steel until it rasped. 

"Two handfuls across the planks," she instructed, her voice steady and flat above the distant, irregular thud of artillery miles to the south. "Don't just fling it. Work it into the grain with the stiff broom until the dark patches go gray. A man’s fat gets into the pine, turns slick as butter on a hot skillet. If my boot slips while I’m taking a saw to a shattered shin, the blade jumps the bone and takes two of my own fingers off, and then we're both useless."

She set the needle down and picked up the forceps, checking the hinge with a firm snap of her thumb. It was stiff, gummed up with thick red from the man's thigh. She dropped it into the small iron kettle of boiling vinegar-water that sat steaming over the brazier, the metal clinking sharply against the bottom.

"When you finish the timber, don't dump the sweepings in the straw," she said, reaching for a fresh spool of hemp twine. "Take the shovel and throw the bloody sand straight through the side flap into the ditch. The dogs from the baggage train smell the meat on the boards and they'll tear the canvas down to get inside while we're working."

She snipped three lengths of twine, each eighteen inches long, and lined them up along the edge of the crate, her fingers moving with the dull, relentless efficiency of a weaver at a loom. Outside, through the heavy rain drumming against the greasy canvas, the iron-rimmed wheels of the first wagon creaked as they hit the corduroy logs laid over the muck at the tent entrance. The mules were blowing hard, their harnesses rattling in the dark.

"That's the first wagon," Sedge said. She didn't look toward the door. She reached for the small bottle of potato spirit and poured a thumb's width over her bare, red hands, rubbing it briskly across her palms and between her cracked fingers until the sharp, eye-watering stench of cheap alcohol filled the space between them. 

"They'll bring the worst ones through first because the drivers want them off the tail-gate before they die in the rain and make the load heavier. Grab the bucket, Wick. You've got about forty seconds before the boards need to be dry."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I grab the sand bucket and upend it over the planks, the coarse grit scattering across the dark stain. My hands shake as I scrub with the broom, grinding ash into the wood until the blood turns to a dry, gray paste.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Good enough," Sedge said, glancing at the smeared, gray-crusted timber. "The timber doesn't need to be holy, it just needs to be dry enough that a man doesn't skate."

She reached down with the flat edge of a small iron coal shovel, scraped a thick ridge of the bloody paste off the planks, and flicked it toward the slit in the tent's rear wall. It landed outside with a heavy, wet thud against the sodden ditch grass.

"Two things to look for when the tail-gate drops," she said, her voice dropping into the same flat, instructional cadence as she dried her hands on the stiff tail of her apron. "First, look at the color of their lips. If they're blue, the chest is filling with fluid and they choke before I can get the ribs apart. We don't waste the table on a drowning chest when there's five behind him with whole lungs."

Outside, the coarse canvas flap of the tent whipped back on its lashings, letting in a draft of freezing, rain-laden wind that made the grease-lamp flicker and smoke. Boot-heels sucked heavily in the clay, accompanied by the grunting strain of two stretcher-bearers hauling dead weight.

"Second," Sedge continued without turning around, her fingers instantly checking the position of the tourniquet strap and the bone saw on the lower shelf, "look at the belt. If the shrapnel went into the belly—if you smell the privy when you lift him—he doesn't touch this wood. A punctured bowel is four days of dying from the peritonitis, and I have three spools of hemp left. We don't sew bellies. You give them three fingers of water from the bucket, lay them by the woodpile out of the draft, and let them go quiet."

The bearers came through the opening backwards, their slickers dripping river-mud onto the straw. Between them swung a sodden stretcher of splintered ash and grease-black canvas. On it lay a boy—couldn't have been more than eighteen—with his left boot missing and his trouser leg sheared away from mid-calf down, revealing a mess of mangled muscle and a four-inch shard of white, jagged tibia poking cleanly through the skin like a broken spar.

He wasn't screaming. He was staring at the tent ridgepole, his breath coming in fast, shallow whistles through gray lips.

"Compound fracture of the lower third," Sedge said immediately, stepping up to the end of the table as the bearers heaved the boy onto the sanded boards. The sand crunched under the boy's back. "Artillery concussion took the foot off sideways. Look at the bone, Wick. See how it's splintered lengthwise? That’s not a clean break. The shock ran right up the shaft into the knee."

She reached out with one broad, calloused hand, clamped her fingers around the boy's cold toes, and twisted his foot half an inch. The boy didn't cry out; his head merely jerked to the side, a thin trail of dark bile leaking from the corner of his mouth.

"No pulse in the dorsalis pedis," she said, letting the dead weight drop back to the timber with a dull thud. "Torn the anterior tibial artery somewhere behind the break. The foot's already cold as well-water."

She wiped her fingers on her skirt and looked at Wick over the boy’s chest.

"We aren't saving this one's boots," she said. "This is an amputation below the joint. Get the strap around his thigh, four fingers above the kneecap. You crank the windlass until the bleeding at the splinter stops completely, and then you hold the pin with your teeth if you have to. I'm getting the saw."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I wrap the strap quick, my fingers slipping on the wet leather. "Which side do you want me on?" My voice is steadier than I feel.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The forceps clicked—a sharp, dull tick of steel meeting jagged iron deep against the femur. The soldier's spine bowed off the wood

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The yellow lumps at the skin's edge, that's subcutaneous fat. Looks like cold chicken grease... The dark red slabs split down the middle are the muscle bellies—quadriceps... That dull white shine right at the floor of the hole, that's the periosteum. The skin over the femur.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: A shell breaks into rough iron, corners and saw-teeth. When it hits meat, it spins. It doesn't part the tissue—it grabs it, rolls it up like a rag on a spindle, and rips it off the bone.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The needle curved up through the opposite lip with a dull crunch of cartilage-tough skin, slick with dark grease

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The rest is what happens when the shock wears off and the body realizes what's been done to it... In an hour, the numbness leaves him... They feel like a red-hot iron bar laid across the bone... He'll vomit dry bile into the straw until his throat tears... every time his thighs twitch against the boards, the rough linen inside that hole will grind against the raw periosteum of the femur. It's like sandpaper on bone

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"No you're not. Nobody is." Sedge didn't look up from the row of instruments. "Doesn't matter. Look at the wall if you want, but keep your hands where they are and keep your weight in them. I'll tell you before each part, so you know when it's coming."

She soaked a rag and wiped the leg down from above the knee to where the leg stopped meaning anything. What had been a shin was a wet dark mess, swollen tight, streaked up toward the knee in a way she didn't like at all. The smell was under everything in the tent already; there was no point mentioning it.

"Below the knee," she said, half to Wick and half to herself, marking it with her thumb. "I'd rather keep the joint. He'll walk better on a peg if I do. Tourniquet's on and it's been on twenty minutes. That's fine. That's not the part I'm worried about."

She picked up the knife. It was not the right knife; the right knife had been left in a crater outside Dunmore along with the man who'd been carrying it. This one had been sharpened enough that it would do.

"First cut. Hold."

She went through skin and fat in one pull, circling, fast because slow was crueler and because the man's whole body went rigid under her hands and Wick's and she felt the table jump. He made a sound that wasn't shouting anymore. She kept going. Drew the skin back off the muscle with her fingers, rolling it up like a sleeve. It came easier than it should have on the outer side, which told her she'd cut in the right place, barely.

"Good. That's good. You're doing fine. Second cut. Muscle. This one's worse."

It was. The knife went into the meat of the calf and she took it around in two passes, and the man arched and she heard Wick's boots scrape for purchase and heard Wick's breath go out hard, but the shoulders stayed down. The bone showed white and then pink where she'd nicked it. She wiped her hands on her apron and reached for the saw without looking.

"Almost. Bone's the fastest part. Sounds the worst, but it's the fastest. He won't feel it the way he felt the rest." She set the teeth against the tibia. "Hold."

It sounded like it sounded. She counted strokes under her breath, not because it helped but because it was a thing to do with her mouth that wasn't apologizing. The fibula went with a snap on the fourth stroke, always did, and then the leg was something separate on the table and she moved it to the bucket with the side of her arm.

"There." She was already tying off. The big vessel first, catgut, two turns, the small ones after. Her fingers were steady and cold. "Vessels closed. Flap comes down over the end, three stitches to hold it, dress it open so it can drain. He's out. Don't ease off yet -- they come back sometimes, right about now, and that's when you lose them off the table."

She looked up for the first time. Wick was still looking at the wall.

"I'm not going to tell you that was easy or that it gets easier. It doesn't. I hate it every time." She threaded the needle. "But he'd be dead in three days with that leg on, and now he might not be. That's the whole of it. That's the only reason I do any of this."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: My hands are shaking. I can feel it in my arms, all the way up. I swallow and finally look away from the wall, at the... stump. "Yeah," I manage. "Yeah, I know."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Shaking's fine. Shaking's your arms telling you they've done a job. It's letting go that isn't." Sedge didn't look up; she'd found the edge of the flap and was pinching it against the muscle to see how it sat. "Another minute. Then you can shake all you like."

The flap came down clean. She'd left herself enough skin, which was luck as much as anything on a leg that bad. First stitch at the centre, deep, through skin and into the fascia so it wouldn't pull. Second at the outer corner. Third inside. She didn't close it any further than that. The whole end of the stump was going to weep for a week, and it needed somewhere to weep to, or it would do it inward and kill him anyway.

"Look at it if you want to. Doesn't do it any harm and it does you some good." She spoke the way she'd speak about a boot that needed resoling. "That's bone, there, under the flap. That's the tibia, the big one. The little one's tucked in beside it. I've cut it shorter so it won't press through. The stitches hold it, the dressing keeps the dirt off, and the gap at the bottom lets it drain. That's all a stump is. Nothing mysterious about it."

She soaked a wad of lint, laid it over the open end, and started the bandage from the knee down, snug at the top and looser as it went. Counted the turns. Tied it off.

"There. Now let go."

She waited until Wick's weight came off the man's shoulders, then put two fingers under his jaw and held them there, watching the tent wall the way Wick had, counting. Fast, thin, but there. She let go and wiped her fingers on her apron, which was past caring.

"He'll live through the night, likely. Past that I don't promise anything. Neither should you, if anyone asks." She started gathering the instruments into the basin, knife first, saw last. "Go outside. Put your hands in the rain barrel to the elbows and leave them there till they stop, then come back and help me get him off the table and onto the straw. He'll want water when he wakes and he'll want it from someone who isn't me."

She glanced at the bucket, then at Wick, and her mouth flattened.

"And if you're going to be sick, be sick out there. Not because I mind. Because I've only got the one clean rag left."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't answer straight away. She put the saw in the basin and looked at the water go cloudy around the teeth, and then she looked at the bandaged end of the man's leg, and then at his face, which was the colour of the lint.

"It's not kind," she said. "I don't do kind. If I thought he was going I'd have given him what's left of the laudanum and sat with him, and you'd have been spared all that." She tipped her chin at the bucket. "That's a real chance. Not a good one."

She pulled the lamp closer, turned the man's knee toward it, and pressed her thumb into the skin above the bandage, on the inside where it had gone dusky. Held it. Let go. Watched the white fill back in slower than she wanted.

"You saw the streaks. Up toward the knee. That's the rot already looking for a way through, and I've taken the leg off below where I could see it, not below where it is. Nobody can see where it is." She said it flat. "If I'd gone above the knee I'd have been surer of stopping it and less sure he'd live through me doing it. He's lost too much already. So I made a bet. I bet it hadn't got as far as it looked."

She wiped her thumb on her apron and straightened.

"Three days. If the knee stays cool and the dressing smells like blood and not like the bucket, he's got a leg to strap a peg to and a life to complain about it in. If the knee goes hot and red and the streaks come up past it, then I've cut a man's leg off for nothing and I'll go above the knee and cut it again, and he won't survive that, and I'll know I shouldn't have bothered."

She picked up the basin.

"So no. Not the kind part. This is the part where we don't know. I hate this part more than the cutting, if you want the truth. At least the cutting I can do something about."

She jerked her head toward the tent flap.

"Rain barrel. Then come back. The not-knowing goes easier with two."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat tight. "Okay." My boots feel heavy as I turn towards the flap. Outside, the rain's just a drizzle now. I dunk my arms into the barrel up to my elbows. The cold shocks the shaking right out of me.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge listened to the flap fall shut and then let herself stand still for the length of one breath. Two. Then she put the basin down on the crate by the pole and got on with it.

The instruments first, because they were the thing that would matter tomorrow. She scrubbed the knife with the wet rag and the heel of her hand until the blade came up grey again, dried it on the inside of her sleeve where the cloth was least filthy, and laid it on the strip of leather she kept for the purpose. The saw took longer. There was always something between the teeth. She worked at it with her thumbnail and didn't think about what it was.

The man breathed behind her. She could hear it now the tent was quiet: shallow, catching at the top like a door on a warped frame. Not good. Not the worst she'd heard, either. She'd learned to take that for what it was.

When the saw was done she went back to the table and looked at him properly. Grey in the face, lips gone bluish at the edges, sweat drying on him. She pulled the blanket up to his chest, then thought better of it and folded it back off the stump. Warm was for the body. The leg wanted air.

"You're not dying tonight," she told him, quietly, in the voice she used for it. "You haven't earned it yet. Tonight you're just sleeping."

He didn't answer. That was all right. They mostly didn't.

She found the tin cup, checked there was water in the jug, set both on the crate where Wick would see them. Then she stood over the bucket for a moment with her hand on the rim, not looking in, and thought about the ground out past the latrine trench where the others were, and how far down she'd have to dig in this mud, and whether it was worth doing tonight or whether the rain would cover the smell until morning.

Morning. Morning was better. She had a man on a table and one pair of hands, and the hands were needed.

She wiped them one more time, sat down on the ammunition box that served for a chair, and pressed the heels of her palms into her eyes until she saw colours. When she took them away the lamp was still bad and the tent was still worse and the man was still breathing. She raised her voice just enough to carry through canvas.

"Wick. When they've stopped, come in. Bring the barrel lid if it's dry. I want something to put the leg under so I don't have to look at it till I've slept."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge lowered her hands and looked at Wick, dripping to the elbows in the doorway, and then followed the line of that look down to the table.

"All right," she said. "Come round this side. Lamp's better here."

She didn't get up. She reached over and turned the man's knee a few degrees toward the light, gentle with it, the way she hadn't been able to be ten minutes ago.

"Start at the top. That's his thigh, and it's fine. Colour's fair, skin's dry, and if you put your hand on it -- go on, flat, above the tourniquet -- it's warm the way you're warm. That's what I want. That's what the rest of him is supposed to feel like."

She waited until Wick had done it before going on.

"Now the tourniquet. Strap and a stick, nothing clever. I've let it off a turn since the vessels are tied, and the bandage isn't showing red, so the ties are holding. If it starts showing red I'll tighten it again and go back in. It won't. Probably won't."

Her finger moved down without touching.

"Here's the knee. This is the part I keep looking at, so you might as well know why. See the skin just below it, on the inside -- that dark patch, like a bruise that's been left too long. That was there before I cut. That's the edge of what I was cutting away from. It should get no bigger. If it gets bigger, or the skin over it goes tight and shiny and hot, that's the rot moving up, and you'll know before I tell you because you'll be able to smell it through the lint."

She tipped her chin at the bandage.

"Under that is what I showed you. Flap of his own skin folded down over the end of the bone, three stitches to keep it there, an open gap at the bottom. It'll bleed through by morning. That's fine. It'll weep yellow for a week. That's fine too. What I don't want is green, or black, or the lint gone slick and the smell gone sweet. You'll know sweet when you smell it. Everyone does."

She sat back on the ammunition box.

"And that--" a glance, not a look, at the bucket by the pole "--is a leg. Below the knee, cut through about a hand's breadth down, bone ends showing. It's already going soft at the foot, which is why he was screaming when they brought him in and why I didn't wait till morning. It'll go in the ground first light, deeper than I'd like to dig. There's nothing in it you need to see. It isn't him anymore. It stopped being him about the time I started the saw."

She rubbed the heel of one hand along her jaw, leaving a smear she didn't notice.

"That's what you're seeing. A man with one and a half legs, sleeping, with a bet laid on him he doesn't know about. Nothing worse than that yet. Now give me that lid."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I grab the barrel lid from outside—it's damp, but not soaked—and bring it in. I slide it over the bucket, then go to stand near the man's head again, my eyes still on his knee. "How do you know when to bet?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't answer straight off. She watched Wick settle by the man's head, watched where the eyes went, and let the question sit a moment in the bad light.

"You don't," she said. "That's the first thing. Anyone who tells you they know is either new or lying, and the new ones stop saying it fast."

She leaned forward on the box, elbows on her knees, and looked at the knee too, because it was easier than looking at Wick while she said it.

"What you do is count. Not out loud. You look at him and you count what he's got and what he hasn't. He's got a pulse I can find without hunting for it. He's got colour in the thigh. He shouted for the best part of an hour before he went quiet, which means there was enough in him to shout with. He's young. He's not fevered yet, or wasn't when they brought him in. That's one side."

Her hand turned over, palm up, then down.

"Other side. Streaks up the calf. Foot gone soft. Brought in on a cart that took two days getting here, so whatever was in that leg had two days to think about where it wanted to go. Three days on a peg from a boy in a ditch is not the same as three days from a man who kept it clean. I don't know which he was. Nobody told me."

She sat back.

"So I counted. And the count said below the knee gives him a life worth having if it works, and above the knee gives him a slightly better chance at a life he'll spend on his backside. And there wasn't enough in him to cut twice. So I bet once, and I bet on the leg I'd want if it were mine." She shrugged, small. "That's all it is. It isn't wisdom. It's arithmetic done fast with numbers you can't see."

The man's breath caught at the top, held, let go. Sedge's eyes went to his chest and stayed there until it came again.

"You'll get it wrong. I have. I've gone below and had to go above and buried a man who'd have lived if I'd been a coward the first time. And I've gone above when below would've done and watched a man learn to walk on a stick when he could've had a knee." She rubbed her thumb along the seam of her apron. "You carry both kinds. Neither one teaches you to bet better. It just teaches you to bet anyway, because the man on the table can't wait for you to be sure."

She jerked her chin at the jug on the crate.

"Cup's there. When he stirs, wet his lips first, don't pour. He'll choke on it if you let him gulp, and I'm not sewing a man's leg shut just to have him drown on a mouthful of water." A pause. "And keep your hand where it is. On his shoulder. Not to hold him. Just so there's something there when he comes up. That part I do know."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at Wick for a moment, properly this time, measuring the same way she'd measured the man on the table. Then she nodded once, as if the count had come out in Wick's favour.

"Straight, then."

She pulled the lamp a little closer, not because she needed it but because it was a thing to do with her hands while she talked.

"A bullet is honest. It goes in one side, and if you're lucky it comes out the other, and it takes a straight road between. You can follow it. Shrapnel isn't honest. It's a shell case blown into pieces the size of your thumbnail or your fist or anywhere between, and none of them are the same shape, and all of them are spinning, and they're hot enough to cook what they touch. So a piece goes in, and it doesn't take a road. It takes whatever's in front of it and it tumbles, and every time it turns over it tears a new way."

She held up her own forearm and drew a line along it with a finger, then broke the line off at an angle, then again.

"That's what the inside of a shrapnel wound looks like. Not a hole. A hole would be a mercy. It's a cavity, torn, with the edges of it burned and the meat past the burn crushed. Muscle that's been crushed like that doesn't bleed the way it should, so you can't always tell what's dead. It looks like meat. It just isn't alive anymore. And dead meat in a warm wet place is a feast for whatever came in with the metal."

Her finger went to the man's leg, above the bandage, and traced where the streaks had been.

"Because that's the other thing. Shrapnel doesn't come in clean. It comes with the man's own uniform driven in ahead of it, and whatever mud he was lying in, and whatever was on the shell case, and whatever was on the ground when it landed. All of that goes in with it and gets packed into the tears at the end where you can't see and can't reach. His leg -- I'd wager the piece that did it wasn't even in there when he got to me. It went through, or someone pulled it out on the cart. But it left the ditch behind."

She sat back.

"So what it does is this. It makes a wound you can't see the bottom of. It kills the flesh around that wound without telling you where the killing stops. And it seeds the whole thing with the makings of rot. Then it leaves. And two days later a man comes in shouting, and I'm standing over a leg that's green at the foot and red at the knee, guessing where the line is between what's his and what's the ditch's."

Her eyes went to the man's chest. Rose. Fell.

"Bone's worse. A piece hits bone and the bone becomes shrapnel too. Splinters of him going out in all directions, into the same meat. I've taken a man's own thighbone out of his gut in pieces. Belly wounds I don't do at all. Not because I can't. Because there's no point. The gut's torn in six places and every one of them is leaking into him and I've got one pair of hands and no light. Those ones I give the laudanum to." She said it flat, the same voice as the rest. "You asked."

She reached over and turned the man's knee back square to the table, gently.

"That's what's in there. Under the bandage it's cleaner than it was, because I cut it out. Above the bandage, I don't know. Nobody does. That's what shrapnel does. It makes sure you don't know."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I look at his knee again, my hand still on his shoulder. "So we wait," I say, and my voice sounds steadier than I thought it would. "And if the rot comes up, you go back in."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"No," Sedge said. "If the rot comes up, I go back in and he dies on the table. Or I don't go back in and he dies on the straw. That's the choice I'd have, and neither end of it is going back in the way you mean."

She said it without heat, watching the man's chest rather than Wick's face.

"You want to hear that there's a second try. There isn't. Not for him. I told you -- there wasn't enough in him to cut twice. That was true before I started and it's truer now. If the knee goes, I'll cut, because I'd rather he went under my hands doing something than lay there three days doing nothing, and because once in a hundred I'm wrong about a man's bottom. But you should know what you're watching for. You're not watching for the sign that we do it again. You're watching for the sign that it's over."

The man's breath caught, held, went. She let it go three more times before she spoke again.

"But yes. We wait. That part you've got right." She shifted on the ammunition box, working a knot out of her back with her knuckles. "And waiting has a shape to it, same as cutting does, so you might as well know that too. First six hours are the bleeding hours. If a tie slips it'll slip now, while he's cold and his heart's hunting for its footing. You'll see it in the bandage before anything else. Red spreading, not spotting. Spotting is nothing. Spreading you wake me for."

She tipped her chin at the lamp.

"After that, the fever hours. Tomorrow, maybe the day after. He'll go hot. Everyone does. Body's furious about what's been done to it and it burns. That's not the rot. That's him. You'll know the difference because his kind of hot is all over, and the rot's kind starts at the knee and works up like a tide. Put your hand above the bandage every hour and then put it on his forehead. If the leg's hotter than the head, come and get me. If the head's hotter than the leg, wet a rag and put it on him and let him burn."

She stood, finally, joints announcing it, and went to the table. Two fingers under the jaw again. Counting. She let go.

"Third day's the one. If the knee's cool and the smell's clean and he's cursing me by then, he'll live. If it's not, he won't, and there's nothing either of us can do tonight to change which. So."

She pulled the second blanket off the empty cot in the corner and dropped it at Wick's feet.

"You take the first watch, because your hands are steadier than mine right now and I'm not fool enough to pretend otherwise. Wake me at the bleeding hours' end, or sooner if the bandage spreads. Check him the way I said. Wet his lips if he stirs. Talk to him if you want, he won't remember it, but it'll do you good and it can't hurt him."

She lay down on the cot with her boots on and her arm over her eyes, and spoke to the canvas above her.

"You said that steadier than you meant to. Good. It doesn't mean you're getting used to it. It means you've put it somewhere to deal with later. That's the right place for it. Tonight the man on the table needs your hands, not your feelings, and tomorrow if he's alive you can have them back." A pause. "If he's not, you'll want them anyway. I'll help you dig."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge was off the cot before the second scream, boots hitting the boards, one hand already on the man's good thigh to pin it and the other going to the lamp.

"I'm not doing anything to him. That's the first thing. Hear me? The cutting's done. This isn't me. This is him coming up, the way I said he might, and it's the worst part of the night for him and the best sign I've had since the saw." She got the lamp over the stump. "A man who can scream like that has blood enough to scream with. Now shut up and let me look."

She looked. Bandage first, both hands flat either side of it, thumbs walking down the lint from the knee. "Spotting. Here and here, thumb-sized. That's the flap weeping, that's nothing. No spreading. The ties are holding through the bucking, and he's bucking hard, so they'll hold through worse." She pressed the ends of her fingers against the lint at the bottom where the drain gap was. "Damp. Red, not black. Good."

The man arched and the table shrieked on its legs and she leaned her weight across his hips without looking away from the leg.

"Tourniquet. Strap's still where I left it, one turn slack. I'm not tightening it. If I tighten it now I starve the flap and the flap dies and I've wasted the stitches. It stays. If the spotting turns to spreading in the next quarter hour, then I tighten and I go back to the ties with a needle, and you'll hold him for that too. But it won't." She said it like she was telling the leg, not Wick. "It won't."

Her hand moved up. Palm flat above the bandage, on the dusky patch below the knee. Held. Then to his forehead, sweat-slick, then back to the leg.

"Leg's warm. Head's warmer. That's the right way round. He's not rotting, he's just in pain, and the pain's woken him up before there's anything in him to be awake with." She wiped her palm on her apron. "What I'm doing now is nothing. That's the honest answer. I've checked what can kill him in the next hour and none of it's happening, so I've nothing to cut and nothing to tie and nothing to give but time."

She looked at his face then. Eyes open, seeing nothing, mouth wide. She put her hand on his cheek and turned his head so he was looking at the tent wall instead of at his own knee.

"He'll try to sit up to see it. Don't let him. Not yet. Not because it'll hurt the stump, though it will. Because he'll see it before he's got a mind to see it with, and that's a thing you can't take back." She pinched his earlobe, hard, and his scream broke into a gasp. "There. Listen to me. Listen. Your leg's off. Below the knee. I did it. You're going to live if you don't fight the table."

She waited. He dragged in air and screamed again, but shorter.

"How long. You asked how long." She was already reaching behind her for the small brown bottle on the crate, not looking, fingers finding it by shape. "Three minutes of this, five at the outside. He'll scream till he's used what he's got and then he'll go under again, because there isn't enough in him to stay up. I'm going to help him down. This is the laudanum. Eight drops on the tongue, not more. I told you I save it for the dying, and I do, but eight drops won't be missed and it'll take the edge off enough that he stops fighting your hands. If he keeps fighting he tears the flap. If he tears the flap I open him again. So the eight drops are cheaper than the stitches."

She tipped the bottle against her thumb and pushed her thumb between his teeth, quick, before he could bite. Counted. Wiped her thumb on her sleeve.

"He'll say his foot hurts. Any minute now. His foot. The one in the bucket." Her voice didn't change. "He's not raving. The nerves that used to go down to the foot are cut off in the stump and they don't know it yet, so they keep sending word from a place that isn't there. It'll go on for weeks. Months, for some. Don't argue with him about it. Don't tell him the foot's gone, he knows. Just tell him you've heard him."

The screaming thinned. Went to a long shaking groan. The body under her hands and Wick's began to let go of itself, joint by joint, the way a rope does when the load comes off.

"There. Feel that? That's the drops and that's him running out. Ease your weight but keep your hands. Another minute." She took her own hands off his hips and stood back and let the lamp show her the bandage one more time. Spotting. No more than before. She breathed out through her nose.

"That's what I did. I looked at four things that could kill him and found none of them, and I gave him eight drops so he'd stop trying to do it himself. Nothing else. That was all of it, start to finish, and it took less time than it took to tell you." She sat back down on the ammunition box, heavily, and put her elbows on her knees. "Now he sleeps again, and you watch the bandage, and I lie down, and if he does that twice more before morning, then he's a fighter and I'll like his odds better. Lips. Wet his lips. He's earned that much."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get the cup and drip a little water on his lips. My hand's still on his shoulder. "I heard you," I say to him, quiet. "Foot hurts. I heard you."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge watched from the box. Watched the water go on the lips, watched the hand stay on the shoulder, watched Wick's mouth make the words. She didn't say anything until the man's throat moved, once, swallowing what had run in.

"That's it," she said. "That's the whole of it. You'll say it forty times before he's done and it'll be true every one."

The man's lips worked. A sound came out that might have been a word and might have been the shape of one. His fingers, the near hand, opened and closed on nothing. Sedge leaned over and looked at his eyes without touching him. Half-lidded, drifting. The drops were in.

"He'll want to know your name when he comes up proper. Tomorrow, or the day after. Not mine -- he'll know mine soon enough, and he won't want it. Yours." She rubbed her jaw with the back of her wrist. "They always want the name of whoever was on the shoulder. Never the one on the knife. Which is right. I'd be the same."

She got up, slow, and went to the crate. Checked the bottle was stoppered, set it back where her hand would find it. Checked the jug. Turned the lamp down a hair, not enough to lose the bandage, enough to stop it eating oil she didn't have.

"You did that better than I told you to. The pinning. You moved with him instead of against him. Most people brace and the table goes over." She said it looking at the lamp, not at Wick, the way she'd said everything else that mattered tonight. "Don't take that as a compliment. Take it as a fact you'll need again."

She lay back down. Boots on. Arm over her eyes.

"Bandage. Every quarter hour by your own count, since there's no clock. Hand on the leg, hand on the head. Lips if he stirs. Wake me if it spreads, or if he does that again and the drops don't take. Otherwise let me lie." A breath. "And if he says the foot again, you say what you said. It was the right thing. Don't go looking for a better one."

The canvas ticked with the last of the rain. The man breathed, catching at the top. Sedge lay still and listened to it and did not sleep, not yet, though she meant to. She counted his breaths against her own until the numbers blurred, and somewhere past forty she stopped being sure which were his.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't tell Wick to get up. She looked down at the floor of the tent and at Wick on it and made the count she'd made on the man twenty hours ago, and the count said leave it.

"All right," she said. "The rest."

She was still holding the leg. Above the knee, this time, the cut she'd said she wouldn't make and had made anyway, because the knee had gone hot in the grey of the afternoon and the streaks had come up past it like she'd said they would, and there'd been the choice she'd said there'd be. Her hands were on the thigh either side of it and there was no blood coming, and that was the first thing.

"He's stopped bleeding. Not because I've tied anything. I haven't tied anything. He stopped bleeding because his heart stopped pushing it, about the time the saw went through. You'd have felt it. He went slack under you and you thought it was the drops. It wasn't the drops." She took her hands off him and looked at them. "So there's nothing to tie. I could put the stitches in. Some do. Make it look finished for whoever's going to look at it. Nobody's going to look at it. He's going in the ground in a blanket and the ground doesn't care whether the flap's down."

She reached for the tourniquet instead, the strap and the stick, and worked the knot loose with fingers that didn't want to bend.

"This I'm taking. It's a strap. I've got two and I'll need it tomorrow on someone whose heart still works, and he's got no use for it. That sounds hard. It is hard. It's also a strap." She coiled it and put it on the crate by the bottle, and then she stood over him and didn't touch anything for a moment.

"Now. What I'm looking at, since you'd rather know than imagine. That's the second cut, above the knee, hand's breadth up from where the streaks had got to. If you look -- you don't have to -- the meat inside it's the wrong colour. Grey where it should be red. That's what I was cutting toward and it's what I found. It had got further than the skin was showing. It always does. That's the thing about the rot. It runs ahead of what you can see and you only ever find out how far by cutting there and finding it."

She wiped her hands on her apron, which had stopped being a colour.

"So here's the arithmetic, since I told you that's all it was. I bet below the knee. If I'd bet above yesterday, he'd have had a chance the rot hadn't got there yet, and he'd have had a worse chance of living through the cut. I don't know which of those would have won. Nobody does. Maybe he dies on the table yesterday instead of today. Maybe he's alive on the straw right now with a stump at the hip cursing me. I'll never know. That's the rest, Wick. That's what I didn't say last night because you had your hands on him and didn't need it. You never find out. You bet, and the man lives or he doesn't, and you never once get told whether the other bet would've gone better. You just carry the one you made."

The man's mouth had come open when the last of him went. She put her palm under his jaw and closed it, and held it there.

"This I'm doing now because in an hour I won't be able to. Jaw sets first. Then the rest. If I leave it open his people -- if he's got people, if anyone ever comes looking -- they'll get a face they don't want. So." She held it. Counted. Let go slowly, and it stayed. She thumbed the eyelids down. One of them came back up a little and she pressed it again and left her thumb there longer.

"There. Eyes. Same reason."

She pulled the blanket off the cot she'd slept on, shook it once, and laid it over him from the chest down, over the second cut and what was left of the leg and the one boot he'd come in with. Then she folded the top edge back so his face was clear.

"He goes out past the trench. There's four there already from before you came and I dug all four and none of them deep enough, because the ground's clay under the first foot and I've got a shovel and a mattock and the mattock's cracked. He goes deeper than they did. Not because he deserves it more. Because it's been raining and the others are coming up." She said it looking at his face. "The leg from the bucket goes with him. Both legs. It's his. It ought to be in the same hole. I don't hold with much but I hold with that."

She sat down on the ammunition box across from where Wick was on the floor, and put her elbows on her knees, and looked at the lamp.

"Now the part you actually asked for. What I do with it. Because you're sitting there and you're not getting up and you're wanting to know how I get up, and the honest answer is I've got another one coming. Not tonight, maybe. Tomorrow, or the day after. They'll bring one in on a cart and it'll be a shoulder or a belly or another leg, and I'll get up because the cart doesn't care that I'm sitting. That's all it is. It isn't strength. If nobody else were coming I'd sit down next to you and I don't know when I'd get up."

She rubbed her thumb along the seam of her apron.

"I told you I hate it every time and I do. I hated the cutting and I hated the not-knowing and I hate this. I hated it on the first one four years ago and I've hated every one since and I've stopped expecting that to change or wanting it to. The day I stop hating it is the day I should put the knife down, because it'll mean I've stopped seeing him and started seeing the leg. He was a man. I don't know his name. You do."

She looked at Wick then.

"That's the last of it. You've got his name. He gave it to you, not me, and that's how it should be. Somebody's going to ask -- there's a book, back at the column, if the column's still there -- and you're going to say it. And when you say it you're going to remember the shoulder and the water on his lips and the foot that hurt, and that's the right thing to remember. Let me remember the rest."

She stood. Went to the corner and got the shovel and the mattock with the cracked head and leaned them by the flap.

"You sit as long as you need. I mean that. I'm going to start the hole because the light's going and clay's worse in the dark. When you're ready you come out and take the mattock, because my back won't manage the clay and you know it. If you're not ready when I've gone down two feet, I'll come in and get you, and I won't be gentle about it, and you'll be glad of that later." She put her hand on the flap. "Not because I'm hard. Because I've dug alone four times and it's the worst part, and I said I'd help you dig, and I'd rather you helped me."

She looked once more at the table. The blanket. The face with the jaw closed and the eyes closed and nothing left to check.

"He didn't die of anything I did. He died of a ditch and a cart and two days. Say that to yourself until you believe it, and if you never believe it, say it anyway. It's true." She pushed the flap aside. "That's the rest. All of it. Come out when you can."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I push myself up off the floor, my legs stiff. "His name was Arren." I take the mattock from her. The handle's still got last night's mud on it.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge stopped with her hand on the canvas.

"Arren," she said. Once, the way she'd say the name of a road she'd need to find again. Then she held the flap and let Wick through ahead of her with the mattock, and followed with the shovel.

The rain had gone off but the ground hadn't heard about it. Past the latrine trench the earth was the colour of the bucket and about as firm, and the four mounds were there in a row, low, the nearest one sunk in the middle where the rain had found it. She didn't look at that one long. She walked past them to the end of the line, paced two steps, and put the shovel blade down.

"Here. Head this end, toward the trees. Not for any reason. It's how the others are lying and I'd rather he matched." She stood on the shovel and it went in easy, too easy, the top foot the way it always was. "First foot's mud. You can move it with your hands if you had to. That's why they come up. I go down a foot, I feel clay, I think that's enough, I'm wrong." She threw the load aside. "Not tonight."

She dug. It went fast for six or seven throws and then the blade hit something that gave back a dull sound and slid off it sideways, and she straightened with her hand in the small of her back.

"That's it. That's the clay. Your turn." She stepped out of the shallow trench she'd made. "Swing it like you're angry with it. You don't have to be. It works the same either way. Break it up, I'll shovel it out, we go down in turns. Don't try to dig with the mattock, you'll pull the head off. It's for breaking. The shovel's for lifting. Two tools, two jobs."

She stood at the edge with the shovel while the mattock came down. It rang. The head shifted in its socket, the crack she knew about opening a hair and closing again, and she watched it and said nothing because there wasn't a second mattock.

"He'll be stiff by the time we're done. That's no matter. Stiff carries easier than slack, if you want the truth of it. Slack you have to hold at the middle or they fold." She jammed the shovel under the loosened clay and heaved and the load came up in a slab that she had to break with her boot. "We'll take him on the blanket, you at the head, me at the foot. The leg from the bucket I'll bring on the second trip, in the bucket, and tip it in at the bottom before he goes down. It doesn't go on top. It goes under him, where it was."

The mattock came down. The mattock came down. She shovelled and the hole got a shape, and the light went the colour of ash, and neither of them said anything for a while that wasn't a grunt or a word about where to put a foot.

At two feet she stopped and stood in the hole, the top of it at her thigh, and put her hand flat on the wall of it. Cold. Wet clay, unbroken, a colour close to the meat she'd found above his knee. She took her hand back.

"Another foot," she said. "Then it's deep enough that the rain won't argue and I won't have to see him again in a month. That's all deep is. Deep enough to stay put." She climbed out, knees protesting, and took the mattock out of Wick's hands and handed over the shovel. "I'll break. You lift. I lied about my back; it'll do one more foot of breaking. It won't do another foot of lifting."

She set her feet on the clay and raised the cracked head over her shoulder.

"Arren," she said again, to the hole, and brought it down.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: The mattock strikes and I feel the vibration up my arms. I dig the shovel in, lift another slab. "You don't have to remember his name," I say, because it feels like a burden.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge brought the mattock down again before she answered, and the clay split along a line she hadn't expected, and she stood looking at the break for a moment as if it had said something.

"I know I don't." She shifted her grip. "I said I'd let you carry the name and I'd carry the rest. I meant it. But I said it to the hole, not to you, and the hole's mine as much as his."

She swung. The head rang and the crack in the socket opened and shut, and she felt it in her palms and paid it no mind.

"I'll tell you what I do with the names, since you're offering to take this one off me." She wasn't looking at Wick; she was looking at where the next stroke would land. "I don't keep them. Not on purpose. I've had two hundred men on that table or ones like it and I couldn't give you twenty names, and the twenty I've got aren't the ones I'd have picked. They stuck for no reason. One because his mother's name was the same as mine. One because he spelt it for me, letter by letter, like I was writing it down, and I wasn't."

The mattock came down.

"So I won't remember Arren. Not the way you mean. In a month I'll have lost it, and in a year I won't know I ever had it. That's not a burden I'm asking you to lift. It's just what happens." She stopped and leaned on the handle, breathing. "What I said it for is different. I said it because I'd cut him twice and buried him once and I hadn't said it, and a man ought to hear his name said over his hole by the one who put him in it, even if he's past hearing and she's going to forget it by harvest. That's not remembering. That's paying. You pay once. Then it's done."

She straightened and put her hand out for the shovel, and when she'd got it she held the mattock out in exchange, handle first.

"You'll remember it. That's the burden, if there is one, and I didn't give it to you. He did. He picked the shoulder, not the knife. They always do." She stepped down into the hole and set the blade against the broken clay. "So don't offer to take mine. I haven't got one. Take yours and swing that thing, because I've got maybe eight more lifts in me and then we're carrying him out here by lamplight, and the lamp's low."

She heaved a slab up over the lip and it landed with a sound like a boot in the bucket.

"And Wick." She didn't look up. "If you ever get to the book, and the column's still there, and you write him in -- put the leg. Below the knee, then above. Both cuts. Not for me. For whoever reads it and thinks the second cut means the first was wrong. Let them see the days between. That's the only argument I've got, and it isn't much of one, and I'd like it made anyway."

She dug.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swing the mattock again, and the clay splits clean. "I'll write it," I say, my voice rough. "Both cuts. And the days between."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: You saw the streaks. Up toward the knee. That's the rot already looking for a way through

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Below the knee, cut through about a hand's breadth down, bone ends showing. It's already going soft at the foot

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: It's a cavity, torn, with the edges of it burned and the meat past the burn crushed. Muscle that's been crushed like that doesn't bleed the way it should, so you can't always tell what's dead. It looks like meat. It just isn't alive anymore.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She looked. Bandage first, both hands flat either side of it, thumbs walking down the lint from the knee. "Spotting. Here and here, thumb-sized. That's the flap weeping, that's nothing. No spreading. The ties are holding through the bucking"

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She was still holding the leg. Above the knee, this time, the cut she'd said she wouldn't make and had made anyway

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge set her feet wide against the uneven ground and wiped her hands down the front of her apron. She looked at the man's face once, then away from it toward his chest where the work was.

She fitted the heel of one hand low under his left armpit and curled the fingers of her other hand over the top of that shoulder. She said what she was doing as she did it, because saying it kept it clean and kept her hands steady.

"The joint was out," she said. "I was going to lift and turn it back in. It was going to hurt worse for three seconds and then less. I did not take any pleasure in it."

She took a breath and braced her knees against the table leg.

"Hold," she said.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: My hands tighten on his shoulders, feeling the muscles bunch. I can already feel him tensing up under me. "Holding," I grunt, my voice tight.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not wait for it to get quieter. She hauled the man's left arm out from his side and folded the elbow to ninety degrees and pinned that elbow hard against her own ribs to make a lever of it.

"The head was sitting forward of the socket," she said. "I was lifting the arm up and turning it outward to walk it back in."

She leaned back with her whole weight and pulled up and out while she rolled the arm, and she kept the heel of her other hand jammed under the armpit to feel the bone move. The man bucked against the table and tried to scream through his teeth.

She felt the clunk travel up through her palms before she heard it. She kept hold through the spasm that followed and talked through it flat.

"It went back," she said. "It hurt worse and now it was done. I took no pleasure in doing it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge released the left shoulder and stepped back and dragged the lamp closer with her foot.

She cut the man's right trouser leg open with her shears and folded the wet cloth back and exposed the thigh.

Blood welled fast from a deep gash high up and the muscle gaped and a shard of white showed at the bottom of it.

She pressed the heel of her hand hard into the crease of his groin to slow it and felt for the pulse at his ankle with her other fingers while she kept the pressure on.

She named what she found as she worked, because naming it kept it clean and kept her hands steady.

"The femoral artery was nicked but not cut through," she said. "The bone was broken and pushed out through the skin. It was not a leg that would heal straight in this tent with what I had."

"It was bad like he lost the leg," she said. "It was not the kind part yet. The kind part was after, when the bleeding stopped and the fever did not take him. I was going to tie it off high and take the leg off above the break. It was going to hurt and then it was done. I took no pleasure in it."

She laid the saw and the ties out in a row beside the table and wiped her hands down her apron again.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, my knuckles white against the man's shoulders. "Right," I manage. "Just tell me when."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge pulled the strap high around the man's right thigh and twisted it tight with a stick and wedged the stick in place. She picked up the ties she had laid out.

She said what she was doing as she did it, because saying it kept it clean and kept her hands steady.

"The bleeding was slowed but not stopped," she said. "I was going to tie the vessels above the break before I cut. It was going to hurt and then it was done. I did not take any pleasure in it."

She cut down to the artery with a short knife and fished the ends out and knotted the ties hard around them and cut the ends short. She packed the loose flesh back while she worked to keep it out of the saw.

"Hold," she said.

She drew the knife around the thigh in one circle above the break and pulled the skin back and cut the muscle through to the bone. She set the saw against the femur and worked it back and forth with her weight behind it until it gave. The man bucked against the table and went hoarse.

She set the saw aside and tied off what still bled and folded the flap down over the stump and stitched it loose for drainage. She loosened the strap by half and watched the stump seep but not run.

"It was off," she said. "It had hurt worse and now it was done. I took no pleasure in doing it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge shifted the lamp closer with her elbow and pressed the flat of her fingers above the stump to check the heat, then lifted the edge of the flap to let the seep run out onto the cloth.

She said what it was as she worked, because saying it kept it clean and kept her hands steady.

"The skin was pulled down over the bone end," she said. "The stitches were left loose so it drained. It seeped red and pink but it did not run. It smelled of blood and sweat and it was going to smell worse before it got better. I took no pleasure in it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let go of his shoulders and step back, my hands shaking a little. "Is he going to make it?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge wiped her hands on her apron and pressed two fingers hard into the side of the man's throat and watched his chest rise while she counted under her breath.

She pulled the blanket up over his chest and tucked it tight around his shoulders to hold the heat in and checked the stump again for fresh running.

She said what she was doing as she did it, because saying it kept it clean and kept her hands steady.

"The pulse was fast and thin," she said. "The breathing was shallow. I was going to keep him warm and keep the stump draining and watch for fever. I did not know if he was going to make it through the night. The bleeding had stopped and that was all I had done for him. I took no pleasure in it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge dragged the basin closer with her boot and fished in the bloody water until she found the piece she had pulled from the thigh.

She held the twisted shard up under the lamp between her thumb and forefinger and turned it while she spoke, because saying it kept it clean and kept her hands steady.

"It did not cut like a knife," she said. "It tore through sideways and dragged his trouser cloth and dirt in with it. It pulped the muscle open and split the bone out into splinters and left the ends to grind. That was why it bled the way it bled and smelled the way it smelled."

She dropped the metal back into the basin with a clink and wiped her fingers on her apron.

"I was telling it straight because it was not clean work. I took no pleasure in it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I stare at the bloody water in the basin, my stomach turning. "Guess there's no pleasure for anyone in this damned war." I rub my own shoulder, feeling a phantom ache. "What do you need from me now?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge straightened up from the table and rolled the stiffness out of her neck and wiped her hands down her apron again.

She lifted the basin of bloody water and tools off the table with both hands and set it on the ground near her feet where it would not tip. She pulled the blanket higher over the man's chest and tucked it in hard around him.

She said what she was doing as she did it, because saying it kept it clean and kept her hands steady.

"The stump was seeping and not running," she said. "I was going to leave the stitches loose and let it drain. I was going to wash the saw and the knife clean so they did not carry rot to the next man. I was going to need fresh water from the bucket and the lamp held steady while I worked."

She nodded with her chin toward the bucket at the back of the tent and toward the lamp on the table.

"I needed his shoulders watched while he came round," she said. "I needed hands that did not let go when he bucked. I took no pleasure in asking for it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge put her knee hard against the table leg to keep it from walking and bent over the stump with the lamp close.

She said what she was doing as she did it, because saying it kept it clean and kept her hands steady.

"The strap had slipped and the stump had started to run again," she said. "I was tightening the strap back down by half a turn and pressing flat into the groin to slow it. I was lifting the edge of the flap to let the clot out so it did not pocket underneath and rot."

She worked her fingers under the flap and let the dark blood spill out onto the cloth and pressed the flap back down and watched the seep slow.

"It was going to take five minutes to settle and then I was going to wash the knife and the saw in the fresh bucket water and lay a clean cloth over it," she said. "It was going to hurt until the strap was loosened again and then it was going to ache dully through the night. I did not leave anything out because there was nothing else to do. I took no pleasure in it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I lean my weight into his shoulders, my own arms starting to tremble from the strain. "How do you keep your hands so steady?" I ask, my voice low and rough.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge plunged her hands into the fresh bucket water and scrubbed the blood out from under her nails with the stiff brush and dried them on a clean corner of her apron.

She said what she was doing as she did it, because saying it kept it clean and kept her hands steady.

"The steadiness was practice and saying it aloud," she said. "I held the tools the same way every time and breathed out before I cut and watched the work and not the face. I had done it long enough in four years that my hands knew it before I told them. I did not take any pleasure in it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge lowered herself down by the bucket and set the saw and the knife and the shears into the fresh water.

She said what she was doing as she did it, because saying it kept it clean and kept her hands steady.

"The water was cold and it turned red as soon as the tools went in," she said. "I was scrubbing the saw teeth clean with the stiff brush and running my thumb backward along them to feel for flesh. I was scrubbing the knife on both sides and the shears at the hinge. I was laying them out on the clean cloth to dry so they did not carry rot to the next man. I did not take any pleasure in it."

She stood back up with her knees cracking and bent over the stump again and lifted the edge of the flap with two fingers.
