dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge nodded curtly, not looking up from the tray of instruments she was arranging. The man on the table was a mess - both shoulders dislocated, one of them probably shattered from the looks of it. She'd seen worse, but that didn't make it any easier.

"Right, then," she said, picking up a pair of forceps. "This is going to hurt like hell. I'll need you to bear down on his shoulders, keep him as still as you can. When I say pull, you pull up and back, got it?"

Wick nodded, though Sedge couldn't see it. She positioned the forceps, placed her other hand on the man's chest to feel his heartbeat. It was racing, understandably.

"Alright, brace yourself," she said, and before Wick could even nod, she pushed the forceps into the wound, seeking out the shattered bone.

The man screamed, his body thrashing against Wick's hold. Sedge ignored it, her focus entirely on the feel of the forceps, the grind of bone on bone. She found the fragment, gripped it, and pulled.

"Pull!" she barked, and Wick did, his weight bearing down on the man's shoulders as Sedge yanked the piece of bone free. The scream cut off with a gurgle as the man passed out, and Sedge sighed, wiping sweat from her brow.

"That's the worst of it," she said, setting the forceps down. "Now for the fun part - putting it back together."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I can feel his muscles spasming under my hands. I keep my eyes on that same spot on the canvas, trying to ignore the wet sound. "Is he... is he supposed to pass out?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge glanced up at Wick, her eyes hard and tired behind her goggles. "He'll be fine," she said shortly. "The body does what it needs to do to survive. Now, I need you to keep pressure on those shoulders while I realign the bone."

She picked up a long metal rod, pushing it into the wound with brutal efficiency. The man twitched and moaned, but remained unconscious. Sedge worked quickly, sweat dripping down her face as she manipulated the bone back into place.

"There," she said finally, stepping back. "That's as good as it's going to get. Now we just need to set it."

She grabbed a pair of heavy splints, wrapping them around the man's shoulders with practiced ease. "Hold him steady," she told Wick, and then she began to pull, leveraging the splints to force the shoulders back into place.

The man's eyes flew open, his mouth gaping in a silent scream. Wick looked away, bile rising in his throat, but he held firm, feeling the bone grind and pop back into place.

"Okay, that's it," Sedge said, letting go. She wiped her hands on her apron, looking down at her work with a critical eye. "He's not going to be happy when he wakes up, but he'll live."

She began to clean up the instruments, her movements brisk and efficient. "You did well," she said to Wick, not looking at him. "Not everyone can handle this kind of thing. You've got a strong stomach."

Wick:
I let out a breath I didn't know I was holding and step back from the table. The man is breathing shallowly, unconscious again. My hands are shaking.

"Thank you," I say, and I'm not sure if I'm thanking her for the compliment or for ending it. "I... I've never seen anything like that before."

Sedge:
Sedge nodded, not looking up from her cleaning. "Most people haven't," she said. "And most people never will, thank god. But sometimes, in war, you have to do things you never thought you'd do."

She set the last instrument down, wiped her hands one final time, and turned to face Wick. She looked tired, older than her years, but there was a hardness in her eyes that spoke of a strength that had been forged in fire.

"You did good work today," she said. "Not many people could have held that man down like that. You've got a future in this, if you want it."

Wick:
I look at the man on the table, at the blood and the bone and the splints. I think of the screams, of the wet sound of the forceps. I think of the men I left behind on the battlefield, the ones who weren't so lucky.

"I don't know," I say, and my voice sounds far away, even to me. "I don't know if I want this future. I don't know if I can."

Sedge:
Sedge's gaze was hard, assessing. She'd seen this before, seen men break under the weight of what they'd seen, what they'd done. She'd almost broken herself, more than once.

"You don't have to know right now," she said, her voice gentler than before. "But if you do decide to stay, I can teach you. I can show you how to save lives, how to take care of the ones who make it back."

She paused, looking at Wick with a kind of sad understanding. "It's not an easy path. But it's a necessary one. Someone has to do it, and it might as well be someone who cares."

Wick:
I look at her, at the blood on her apron, at the weariness in her eyes. I think of the men I left behind, of the ones who died because there was no one to help them. I think of the man on the table, who would have died if not for Sedge, if not for me.

"I care," I say, and the words taste strange in my mouth, but they're true. "I want to help. I just... I don't know if I can do this again."

Sedge:
Sedge reached out, placing a hand on Wick's shoulder. It was a rare gesture of comfort from her, but she knew what it was like to be new to this, to feel the weight of it all bearing down on you.

"You will," she said, her voice steady and sure. "You'll do it because you have to, because there's no one else. And it will get easier, in a way. Not easier to do, but easier to live with."

She squeezed his shoulder, then let go, turning back to the table. "Now, let's get this mess cleaned up. We've got more patients to see to."

Wick:
I take a deep breath, then another, and nod. I roll up my sleeves and grab a bucket and a rag, and together, we clean up the blood and the bone and the pain.

It's not easy, but it's something. It's a start. And maybe, just maybe, it's enough.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge's expression hardened as she looked at the man's mangled leg, the flesh shredded and bone shattered. She'd seen worse, but it never got easier to see. She never wanted it to get easier, because that would mean she'd grown numb to the horrors of war.

"It's bad," she said bluntly, her eyes never leaving the wound. "The bone's shattered, and there's no way to set it properly. Infection's a given, and even if we could save the leg, he'd never walk right again."

She paused, her voice growing softer. "He might not even live through the night, if the shock doesn't kill him first."

Wick's face paled at her words, but he nodded, understanding. They'd seen this before, seen men who were too far gone to save. It was the hardest part of the job, knowing when to fight and when to let go.

"We can't save them all," Sedge said, as if reading his thoughts. "We can't even save most of them. But we do what we can, when we can. And sometimes, that means being kind."

She reached out, placing a gentle hand on the man's forehead. His skin was clammy, his breathing shallow. He was unconscious, thankfully, spared the pain of his injuries.

"It's time," she said softly. "For his sake, and for ours. We can't afford to waste our resources on a lost cause."

Wick:
I nod, my throat tight. I've seen it before, but it never gets any easier. I pick up the morphia, measured out the dose. It's a kindness, really, to end his suffering.

But as I reach out to inject it, the man's eyes flutter open. For a moment, they're clear, focused. He looks at me, and I see a flicker of recognition, of understanding.

"No," he whispers, his voice hoarse. "Don't."

Sedge:
Sedge's hand froze, the syringe poised over the man's arm. She looked at Wick, then back at the man, her brow furrowed in confusion.

"What?" she asked, her voice sharp. "What did you say?"

The man's eyes fluttered closed again, his breathing shallow and rapid. But he managed to croak out a single word, a name that made Sedge's heart stop.

"Wick," he said, and then he went limp, his eyes staring at nothing.

Sedge looked at Wick, her eyes wide with shock. "Did you... do you know him?"

Wick:
I stare at him, at his face, so pale and still. And I realize, with a jolt of recognition, that I do know him. It's been years, but I'd know that face anywhere.

"Elias," I whisper, and it feels like a prayer, a benediction. "Elias Turner. We... we were friends, once. Before the war."

Sedge:
Sedge's eyes widened in shock, then narrowed in suspicion. She looked from Wick to the man on the table, her mind racing.

"Friends?" she asked, her voice tight. "What kind of friends? The kind that might want to keep a man alive, even if it's cruel?"

Wick:
I shake my head, my hands trembling as I set the syringe down. "No," I say, my voice shaking. "No, it's not like that. We were friends, but we hadn't seen each other in years. I didn't even know he was here."

I look at Elias, at his pale face, his labored breathing. "I just... I couldn't bear the thought of ending his life, not when there was even a chance..."

Sedge:
Sedge was silent for a long moment, her gaze hard and assessing. She knew the importance of letting go, of not clinging to false hope. But she also knew the power of a friend's touch, the comfort of a familiar face in the darkest of times.

"Alright," she said finally, her voice soft. "We'll try. But you have to know, it's a long shot. He might not make it through the night, even with everything we can do."

Wick nodded, his eyes never leaving Elias's face. "I know," he said. "But we have to try. For him, and for me. For the sake of what we once were."

Sedge:
Sedge nodded, understanding the weight of that sentiment. She'd had friends, once, before the war had taken them from her. She knew the importance of honoring those bonds, even in the face of death.

"Alright," she said again, rolling up her sleeves. "Let's do what we can. But you have to be ready, Wick. Ready to let go, if it comes to that."

Wick:
I nod, my throat tight. "I know," I say, my voice hoarse. "I'm ready. But I don't want to give up, not yet. Not until we've tried everything."

Sedge:
Sedge nodded, her eyes hard and determined. "We'll try everything," she said. "And then we'll try some more. But in the end, it's up to him. He has to want to live, more than anything."

She turned to the table, her hands already moving to prepare the instruments. "Now, let's get to work. We've got a long night ahead of us."

Wick:
I nod, rolling up my sleeves and taking my place beside her. Together, we work through the night, fighting to save the life of a man we both knew, in different ways.

It's a long, hard fight, but in the end, Elias pulls through. He's weak, his leg gone, but he's alive. And as he opens his eyes and sees Wick's face, a smile spreads across his face.

"Wick," he whispers, his voice a mere breath. "You saved me."

And for a moment, in the midst of all the horror and pain of war, there is a spark of hope, a reminder of the bonds that can endure even in the face of death.

Wick:
As Elias sleeps, his breathing steady and calm for the first time in hours, I turn to Sedge. She's exhausted, her face lined with weariness, but there's a light in her eyes that wasn't there before.

"Thank you," I say softly. "For letting me do this, for helping me save him."

Sedge:
Sedge looks at me, her eyes softening with a rare display of emotion. "You did the saving," she says. "I just helped. But I'm glad we did it, glad we gave him a chance."

She pauses, then reaches out, placing a hand on my shoulder. "You did good work today, Wick. You've got a gift for this, if you choose to use it."

I look at her, at the blood on her apron, at the weariness in her eyes. And for the first time, I see the strength beneath the exhaustion, the compassion beneath the hardness.

"I'll think about it," I say, and I mean it. "But for now, let's just focus on getting him through the night."

Sedge:
Sedge nods, a small smile tugging at the corners of her mouth. "That's all any of us can do," she says. "Take it one day at a time, one patient at a time. And hope that, in the end, it's enough."

She turns back to Elias, checking his vitals one last time before sitting down on a nearby stool. "You should get some rest," she says to me. "You've earned it. I'll watch over him for a while."

I hesitate, looking at Elias's peaceful face. But then I nod, knowing she's right. I need to sleep, to recharge, if I'm going to be any use to him in the morning.

"Thank you," I say again, and this time it's for everything - for saving Elias, for teaching me, for understanding. For being here, in the midst of all this pain, and still finding a way to hope.

Sedge:
Sedge nods, her eyes never leaving Elias's face. "Get some rest," she says again, her voice soft but firm. "We'll talk more in the morning. And Wick?"

I pause at the door, turning back to look at her. "Yeah?"

Her eyes meet mine, and in them I see a reflection of my own exhaustion, my own pain. But I also see something else, something I didn't even know I was looking for.

"Welcome to the family," she says, and for the first time in a long time, I feel like I belong somewhere.

I nod, a small smile tugging at my lips. "Thank you," I say again, and then I turn and walk out into the night, knowing that whatever comes next, I won't be facing it alone.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I step outside the tent, the cool night air hitting my face like a blessing. I lean against a supply crate, my hands still shaking a little. I look up at the stars, wondering if Elias can see them from where he is. Wondering if any of this makes sense.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge watches Wick leave, her eyes following him until he disappears into the darkness. She takes a deep breath, then turns back to Elias, her hands already moving to check his vitals once more. It's a familiar routine, one she's done countless times before. But this time, it feels different. This time, she's not just a medic, not just a healer. This time, she's part of something bigger, something that transcends the horrors of war.

She thinks of Wick, of the way he'd held onto Elias, even in the face of certain death. She thinks of the hope in his eyes, the determination in his voice. And she feels a glimmer of something she thought she'd lost long ago - belief.

Belief in the power of friendship, of love, of the bonds that can endure even in the darkest of times. Belief in the possibility of redemption, of healing, of a future beyond the endless cycle of death and destruction.

She looks at Elias, at the steady rise and fall of his chest, and she smiles. They've won this battle, at least. And while she knows there are many more to come, she also knows that they'll face them together - Wick, Elias, and the rest of the ragtag family they've built, one patient at a time.

She settles back in her chair, her eyes never leaving Elias's face. The night is long, and the road ahead is uncertain. But for now, in this moment, they have each other. And that, she knows, is enough.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looks up at Wick, her eyes weary but kind. She takes a deep breath, then begins to explain, her voice soft and matter-of-fact.

"You're seeing a body that's been through hell," she says. "The leg is gone, taken by a shell fragment. There's no way to save it, not with the resources we have here. The best we can do is try to stop the infection and manage the pain."

She points to the bandages, now stained with blood and pus. "We've cleaned the wound as best we can, but it's not enough. We need better supplies, better facilities. But we don't have that here, not in the middle of a warzone."

She pauses, her eyes flickering to Wick's face. "I know it's hard to see," she says gently. "But you have to look, have to understand what we're dealing with. It's the only way to truly help."

Wick swallows hard, but nods. "I understand," he says, his voice tight. "I just... I want to help. I want to make a difference."

Sedge smiles sadly. "You already are," she says. "By being here, by not turning away from the hard truths. That's the first step to making a difference."

She stands up, moving to the head of the bed. "Now, let's see what we can do for him. We can't save the leg, but we can make sure he's comfortable, make sure he has a fighting chance."

Wick nods, rolling up his sleeves. "What do you need me to do?"

Sedge hands him a cloth. "Start cleaning the wound," she says. "Be gentle, but be thorough. And if you feel like you can't do it, if it gets to be too much, just say the word. We all have our limits."

Wick takes the cloth, his hands steady despite the churning in his stomach. "I can do this," he says, more to himself than to Sedge. "I have to do this."

Sedge nods, her eyes soft with understanding. "That's the spirit," she says. "Now, let's get to work."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I start cleaning, my movements careful. The smell is worse up close. "What are his chances, really?" I ask, not looking up from my work.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge watches Wick work, her eyes hard and assessing. She knows the question isn't just about Elias, but about the future, about the war that stretches out before them like an endless horizon of pain and suffering.

She sighs, her shoulders slumping slightly. "Honestly?" she says, her voice soft. "I don't know. He's strong, that much is clear. But he's also lost a lot of blood, and there's a good chance of infection. Even if we manage to keep him alive, he'll never walk again. He'll be dependent on others for the rest of his life."

She pauses, her eyes flickering to Wick's face. "But that's the thing about war," she continues. "It's not about guarantees, not about certainties. It's about doing what we can, when we can, and hoping it's enough."

Wick looks up at her, his eyes haunted. "Is it ever enough?" he asks, his voice barely a whisper.

Sedge is silent for a long moment, her gaze distant. "I don't know," she admits finally. "But we have to try. We have to keep trying, even when it feels like there's no point. Because if we stop trying, if we stop believing in the possibility of healing, of hope... then we've already lost."

She reaches out, placing a hand on Wick's shoulder. "You're here, Wick," she says, her voice firm. "You're here, and you're trying. That's more than enough. That's everything."

Wick nods, a single tear rolling down his cheek. "Thank you," he says, his voice thick with emotion. "For being honest, for not sugarcoating it."

Sedge smiles sadly. "I couldn't, even if I wanted to," she says. "This is the reality of war, Wick. It's messy, it's painful, and it's rarely fair. But it's also real, and it's the only thing we have to work with."

She squeezes his shoulder, then lets go, turning back to Elias. "Now, let's focus on what we can control," she says. "We can't change the past, and we can't predict the future. But we can make sure he's comfortable, make sure he has the best chance possible."

Wick nods, wiping his eyes with the back of his hand. "What do you need me to do?" he asks, his voice steady once more.

Sedge hands him a syringe. "Morphine," she says. "We need to keep him comfortable, to manage the pain. But be careful, it's easy to give too much."

Wick takes the syringe, his hands steady despite the weight of the moment. "I've got it," he says. "I won't let you down."

Sedge smiles, a rare sight on her usually stoic face. "I know you won't," she says. "Now, let's get to work."

Together, they move around the bed, their movements synchronized despite the short time they've known each other. They work in silence, the only sounds the soft rustle of fabric and the occasional moan from Elias.

It's hard, and it's messy, and it's far from perfect. But in that moment, in the midst of all the pain and suffering, they find a sense of purpose, a reason to keep going.

Because in the end, that's all any of them can do - keep going, keep fighting, keep hoping for a better tomorrow, even when today seems so very dark.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looks at Wick, her eyes hard and unflinching. She takes a deep breath, then begins to explain, her voice calm and matter-of-fact.

"Shrapnel tears through flesh like a thousand tiny knives," she says, her voice soft but firm. "It shreds muscle, shatters bone, and rips through vital organs. It doesn't just wound, it mutilates, it destroys."

She pauses, her eyes flickering to Elias's face. "In his case, the shrapnel hit his leg, severing the artery and shredding the muscle. The bone is shattered, the flesh hanging in ribbons. We can't save the leg, not with the resources we have here. The best we can do is try to stop the bleeding and manage the pain."

Wick swallows hard, but nods, his eyes never leaving Sedge's face. "What about the infection?" he asks, his voice tight. "How likely is it?"

Sedge's expression darkens. "Highly likely," she says. "The wound is too extensive, too contaminated with dirt and debris. We can clean it as best we can, but we can't guarantee anything. The risk of gangrene is high, as is the risk of sepsis."

She pauses, her eyes meeting Wick's. "If the infection takes hold, we may have no choice but to amputate above the knee. It's a last resort, but it's better than letting him die from the infection."

Wick's face pales, but he doesn't look away. "Is there anything we can do to prevent it?" he asks, his voice steady despite the fear in his eyes.

Sedge nods. "We can keep the wound clean, dress it regularly with antiseptic, and monitor him closely for signs of infection. But ultimately, it's up to his body to fight it off. All we can do is give him the best chance possible."

Wick takes a deep breath, then nods. "Alright," he says, his voice firm. "What do we need to do first?"

Sedge smiles sadly. "We start with the basics," she says. "We clean the wound, dress it, and monitor his vitals. Then we wait, and we hope."

Wick nods, rolling up his sleeves. "I'm ready," he says. "What do you need me to do?"

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I take the antiseptic bottle she hands me, my fingers cold and clumsy. "Alright," I say, forcing my voice to stay even. "Tell me exactly how to do this. I don't want to make it worse."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge watches Wick carefully, her eyes softening at the sight of his trembling hands. She reaches out, placing a steadying hand on his wrist.

"Take a deep breath," she says, her voice calm and reassuring. "I know it's hard, but you're doing great. Just follow my lead, okay?"

Wick nods, his breath coming in shallow gasps. Sedge guides his hand, showing him how to clean the wound with gentle, circular motions.

"That's it," she murmurs. "Nice and easy. We want to get all the dirt and debris out, but we don't want to cause more damage."

Together, they work in silence, the only sound the soft rustle of fabric and the occasional hiss of pain from Elias. It's grueling work, both physically and emotionally, but Sedge is patient, her guidance steady and sure.

After what feels like hours, they finally finish cleaning the wound. Sedge steps back, surveying their handiwork with a critical eye.

"Good job," she says, her voice soft with approval. "You did well, Wick. Really well."

Wick looks up at her, his eyes shining with unshed tears. "Thank you," he whispers, his voice hoarse with emotion. "I couldn't have done it without you."

Sedge smiles, a rare sight on her usually stoic face. "You did it," she says, her voice firm. "You proved that you have what it takes to be a medic, to save lives in the face of unimaginable horrors."

She pauses, her eyes flickering to Elias's face. "He's not out of the woods yet," she continues, her voice soft. "But we've given him a fighting chance. And that's more than most soldiers get in this war."

Wick nods, a single tear rolling down his cheek. "What do we do now?" he asks, his voice steady once more.

Sedge hands him a fresh bandage. "Now we dress the wound and monitor him closely," she says. "We watch for signs of infection, and we hope that his body has the strength to fight it off."

She pauses, her eyes meeting Wick's. "And we keep him comfortable," she adds, her voice soft. "We give him morphine to manage the pain, and we hold his hand when he's scared."

Wick nods, taking the bandage with hands that no longer tremble. "I can do that," he says, his voice firm with determination. "I'll do whatever it takes to help him."

Sedge smiles, a rare moment of warmth in the midst of all the pain and suffering. "I know you will," she says. "Now, let's get back to work."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge takes a deep breath, then begins to speak, her voice calm and steady despite the horror of what she's doing.

"I'm cutting into the wound," she says, her voice tight with concentration. "I'm using the scalpel to remove the dead tissue, to get down to the clean flesh underneath. It's... it's not pretty, but it's necessary."

She pauses, her brow furrowed in focus. "The leg is in bad shape," she continues, her voice soft. "The bone is shattered, the muscle torn to ribbons. I'm doing my best to save what I can, but..."

She trails off, her eyes flickering to Wick's face. "But the truth is, we may have to amputate. It's not a decision I take lightly, but if the infection sets in, it may be our only option."

Wick's face pales, but he doesn't look away. "How much longer?" he asks, his voice tight with strain.

Sedge takes a deep breath, then shakes her head. "I don't know," she admits. "This is... this is one of the worst cases I've seen. I'm doing my best, but..."

She pauses, her eyes meeting Wick's. "But I need you to know that there's a chance we may not be able to save him. I'm trying, God knows I'm trying, but..."

Her voice breaks, and for a moment she looks small, fragile, like a child lost in a nightmare. But then she takes a deep breath, and the strength returns to her eyes.

"I'm going to keep working," she says, her voice firm. "I'm going to do everything in my power to save him, to give him a chance. But I need you to be ready, Wick. I need you to understand the reality of the situation."

Wick nods, his eyes shining with unshed tears. "I understand," he says, his voice steady despite the fear in his heart. "I'm ready. Whatever happens, I'll be here, by his side."

Sedge smiles sadly. "Thank you," she says. "Now, let's keep going. Let's fight for every second, every breath, every drop of blood. Because in the end, that's all any of us can do."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I hold Elias down tighter, my knuckles white. "I'm here, Elias," I say through gritted teeth. My eyes stay fixed on Sedge's hands. "Just keep talking to me. Don't stop."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge nods, her hands moving with practiced precision as she continues to work on Elias's leg. "I'm removing the shattered bone fragments now," she says, her voice tight with concentration. "It's... it's not an easy task. The flesh is torn, the blood vessels severed. I'm doing my best to cauterize as I go, to minimize the bleeding, but..."

She pauses, her brow furrowed in thought. "But the truth is, we're losing a lot of blood. More than I'd like. We may need to consider a transfusion, if we can get our hands on some suitable blood."

Wick's eyes widen at the mention of a transfusion, but he doesn't say anything, focusing instead on keeping Elias still. Sedge continues to work, her hands moving with a steady, practiced rhythm.

"I'm almost done with the bone now," she says, her voice soft with exhaustion. "I just need to... to remove the last few pieces. Then I can start stitching up the muscle, the flesh. Then... then we'll see."

She looks up at Wick, her eyes filled with a mix of determination and fear. "We're doing everything we can," she says, her voice firm. "I promise you that. But... but I need you to be prepared for the worst, Wick. I need you to understand that even if we manage to stop the bleeding, even if we manage to stitch him up, there's still a very real chance of infection. Of..."

She trails off, her eyes flickering to Elias's face. "Of gangrene, of sepsis. Of losing him, despite all our efforts. I need you to be ready for that possibility, Wick. I need you to understand that sometimes, even when we do everything right, we still lose them."

Wick swallows hard, but nods, his eyes never leaving Sedge's face. "I understand," he says, his voice steady despite the pain in his heart. "I know the risks, I know the odds. But I also know that we have to try, Sedge. We have to fight for him, for every second, every breath, every drop of blood. Because if we don't, if we give up now... then what's the point of any of this? What's the point of being here, of trying to save lives in the middle of all this horror?"

Sedge's eyes shine with unshed tears, but she nods, a small, sad smile tugging at the corners of her mouth. "You're right," she says, her voice soft. "We have to keep fighting, keep hoping, keep believing in the possibility of healing, of hope. Even when it feels like there's no point, no reason to keep going."

She takes a deep breath, then turns back to Elias's leg, her hands moving with renewed determination. "So let's keep fighting," she says, her voice firm. "Let's do everything we can, everything in our power, to give him a chance. To give all of them a chance."

Wick nods, his hands tightening on Elias's shoulders. "I'm with you," he says, his voice steady with resolve. "Whatever happens, whatever we have to do, I'm with you. We'll get through this together."

Sedge smiles, a rare moment of warmth in the midst of all the pain and suffering. "Together," she agrees, her voice soft. "Now, let's get back to work."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge sits down beside Wick, her body sagging with exhaustion. She looks at Elias's still form, the bandages wrapped tightly around his leg, and feels a pang of guilt, of regret.

"We did everything we could," she says, her voice soft, almost inaudible. "We stitched him up, we cleaned the wound, we gave him morphine for the pain. But..."

She trails off, her eyes closing briefly as she tries to find the words. "But I don't know if it was enough," she continues, her voice breaking. "I don't know if we did enough, if we were fast enough, if we had the right supplies, the right knowledge. I don't know if I'm cut out for this, Wick. I don't know if I can keep doing this, keep watching them suffer, keep failing them over and over again."

Wick looks up at her, his eyes filled with a mix of sympathy and understanding. "You're not failing him," he says, his voice firm. "You're not failing any of them. You're doing the best you can with what you have, with what you know. You're fighting for them, even when it feels like there's no hope, no reason to keep going. That's not failing, Sedge. That's being a hero."

Sedge shakes her head, a bitter laugh escaping her lips. "A hero?" she says, her voice laced with sarcasm. "I'm no hero, Wick. I'm just a medic, a soldier like any other. I'm just trying to survive, like everyone else. I'm just trying to find a way to make sense of all this madness, all this death and destruction."

She looks at Wick, her eyes filled with a deep, aching sadness. "But I don't know if I can," she continues, her voice barely above a whisper. "I don't know if I can keep going, keep watching them die, keep feeling powerless in the face of all this horror. I don't know if I can be the one to keep fighting, to keep hoping, when it feels like there's no point, no reason to keep going."

Wick reaches out, placing a hand on Sedge's shoulder. "You can," he says, his voice firm, unwavering. "Because you have to. Because if you don't, if you give up now, then what's the point of any of this? What's the point of being here, of trying to save lives in the middle of all this chaos? You have to keep going, Sedge. You have to keep fighting, keep hoping, keep believing in the possibility of healing, of hope. Because if you don't, if you give up now... then all of this, all the suffering, all the death... it will have been for nothing."

Sedge looks at Wick, her eyes wide with a mixture of fear and awe. "You really believe that, don't you?" she asks, her voice filled with wonder. "You really believe that all of this, all the pain, all the horror... it's worth something. That it's leading to something better, something greater."

Wick nods, his eyes shining with a fierce determination. "I have to believe it," he says, his voice soft but firm. "Because if I don't, if I give in to the darkness, to the despair... then I'll be lost. Then I'll be just another casualty of this war, just another broken soul wandering through the ruins of the world we once knew. But if I keep fighting, if I keep hoping... then maybe, just maybe, I can find a way to make sense of all this madness. Maybe I can find a way to heal, to rebuild, to create something new and beautiful from the ashes of the old."

Sedge is silent for a long moment, her gaze distant, unfocused. Then she turns to Wick, her eyes filled with a newfound determination, a newfound sense of purpose.

"You're right," she says, her voice steady, resolute. "We have to keep fighting, keep hoping, keep believing in the possibility of healing, of hope. Because if we don't, if we give up now... then all of this, all the suffering, all the death... it will have been for nothing. But if we keep going, if we keep fighting... then maybe, just maybe, we can find a way to make sense of all this madness. Maybe we can find a way to heal, to rebuild, to create something new and beautiful from the ashes of the old."

Wick smiles, a rare moment of warmth in the midst of all the pain and suffering. "Together," he says, his voice soft but firm. "We'll get through this together, Sedge. We'll keep fighting, keep hoping, keep believing in the possibility of healing, of hope. And maybe, just maybe, we'll find a way to make sense of all this madness. Maybe we'll find a way to heal, to rebuild, to create something new and beautiful from the ashes of the old."

Sedge nods, a small, sad smile tugging at the corners of her mouth. "Together," she agrees, her voice soft. "Now, let's get back to work."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I lean my head back against the supply crate behind me, my whole body feeling hollowed out. "He's not going to be a soldier anymore," I say, staring at the tent ceiling. "Even if he lives. What's he supposed to do?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge leans back against the crate beside Wick, her own exhaustion etched into every line of her face. She stares at the ceiling for a long moment, considering Wick's question.

"He won't be a soldier," she says finally, her voice soft and sad. "He'll never be a soldier again. And that's... that's something we have to come to terms with, as much for his sake as ours."

She turns to look at Wick, her eyes filled with a deep, aching sympathy. "He'll need help, Wick," she continues, her voice gentle but firm. "He'll need support, guidance, a new purpose to replace the one he's lost. It won't be easy, for him or for us. But we have to be there for him, every step of the way. We have to help him find a new way to live, a new way to contribute, to make a difference in the world."

Wick nods, his eyes fixed on the ceiling. "I know," he says, his voice tight with emotion. "I just... I don't know how to help him, Sedge. I don't know how to be the one to help him find a new purpose, a new reason to keep going. I'm just a soldier, like him. I'm just trying to survive, like everyone else."

Sedge reaches out, placing a hand on Wick's shoulder. "You're more than just a soldier, Wick," she says, her voice soft but firm. "You're a friend, a comrade, a brother-in-arms. You're the one who stood by his side in the heat of battle, who held him down as I worked to save his life. You're the one who refused to give up, who kept fighting, kept hoping, even when it felt like there was no point, no reason to keep going. You're the one who can help him find a new purpose, a new reason to keep going. Because you're the one who understands, who truly understands what he's been through, what he's lost."

Wick looks at Sedge, his eyes shining with unshed tears. "I don't know if I can do it," he says, his voice barely above a whisper. "I don't know if I have the strength, the wisdom, the courage to help him find a new way to live, a new way to contribute, to make a difference in the world. I'm just... I'm just a man, Sedge. I'm just trying to survive, like everyone else."

Sedge smiles, a rare moment of warmth in the midst of all the pain and suffering. "You're not just a man, Wick," she says, her voice soft but firm. "You're a hero. You're the one who stood by his side in the heat of battle, who held him down as I worked to save his life. You're the one who refused to give up, who kept fighting, kept hoping, even when it felt like there was no point, no reason to keep going. You're the one who can help him find a new purpose, a new reason to keep going. Because you're the one who understands, who truly understands what he's been through, what he's lost."

Wick looks at Sedge, his eyes filled with a deep, aching gratitude. "Thank you," he says, his voice soft but firm. "Thank you for believing in me, for seeing something in me that I never knew was there. Thank you for giving me the strength, the wisdom, the courage to keep going, to keep fighting, to keep hoping for a better tomorrow, even when today feels so very dark."

Sedge smiles, a rare moment of warmth in the midst of all the pain and suffering. "You don't need my thanks, Wick," she says, her voice soft but firm. "You just need to believe in yourself, in the power of your own strength, your own courage, your own compassion. You just need to keep going, keep fighting, keep hoping for a better tomorrow, even when today feels so very dark. Because if you do, if you keep believing in the possibility of healing, of hope... then maybe, just maybe, you can help him find a new way to live, a new way to contribute, to make a difference in the world. Maybe you can help him find a new purpose, a new reason to keep going, even when everything seems lost."

Wick nods, his eyes shining with unshed tears. "I will," he says, his voice soft but firm. "I will keep going, keep fighting, keep hoping for a better tomorrow, even when today feels so very dark. I will keep believing in the possibility of healing, of hope... and I will help him find a new way to live, a new way to contribute, to make a difference in the world. Because if I don't, if I give up now... then all of this, all the suffering, all the death... it will have been for nothing. But if I keep going, if I keep fighting, keep hoping... then maybe, just maybe, we can find a way to make sense of all this madness. Maybe we can find a way to heal, to rebuild, to create something new and beautiful from the ashes of the old."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I scrub a hand over my face, still staring up at the canvas. "He used to talk about opening a shop back home," I say, my voice rough. "Books, I think. Said he liked the quiet."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge nods, a small, sad smile tugging at the corners of her mouth. "A bookshop," she says softly, her eyes distant as she imagines the scene. "A small, cozy place, filled with the musty scent of old paper and the promise of new adventures. A place where he could lose himself in the pages, where he could find a moment of peace in the midst of all the chaos and suffering."

She turns to look at Wick, her eyes filled with a deep, aching sympathy. "It's a beautiful dream," she continues, her voice gentle but firm. "A dream of a quiet life, of a simple, peaceful existence far removed from the horrors of war. A dream of a future where the only battles are fought with words, where the only scars are the ones left by the stories we tell ourselves and others."

Wick nods, his eyes still fixed on the ceiling. "He loved to read," he says, his voice soft with fond memories. "He always had his nose in a book, always had a story to share, a new perspective to offer. He... he had a way of seeing the world that was different from anyone else's. A way of finding beauty in the darkest of places, of hope in the bleakest of times."

Sedge smiles, a rare moment of warmth in the midst of all the pain and suffering. "He was a rare soul," she agrees, her voice soft but firm. "A soul that shone with a light all its own, a light that could pierce even the deepest of shadows, even the most impenetrable of darkness. A soul that could find beauty in the darkest of places, hope in the bleakest of times."

She pauses, her eyes flickering to Elias's still form. "If he survives this," she continues, her voice gentle but determined, "if we can find a way to save him, to help him heal... then maybe, just maybe, we can help him find a way to bring that light back into the world. Maybe we can help him find a way to share his stories, to offer his perspective, to remind others of the beauty, the hope, the possibility of healing, of hope, even in the darkest of times."

Wick looks at Sedge, his eyes shining with unshed tears. "You really believe that, don't you?" he asks, his voice soft with wonder. "You really believe that he can find a way to bring his light back into the world, to share his stories, his perspective, his hope... even after all he's been through, all he's lost."

Sedge nods, her eyes filled with a fierce, unshakable determination. "I do," she says, her voice soft but firm. "Because I've seen it before, in others who have survived the horrors of war, who have found a way to heal, to rebuild, to create something new and beautiful from the ashes of the old. I've seen it in the veterans who have become teachers, who have shared their stories with new generations, who have taught us all the importance of remembrance, of learning from the past so that we might avoid repeating its mistakes. I've seen it in the soldiers who have become peacekeepers, who have dedicated their lives to healing the wounds of war, to bringing hope and healing to those who have been left behind. And I know, I truly know, that we can help him find that same light, that same hope, that same possibility of healing, of hope, even in the darkest of times."

Wick nods, a single tear rolling down his cheek. "Thank you," he says, his voice soft but firm. "Thank you for giving me hope, for reminding me of the beauty, the possibility, the light that can be found even in the darkest of places, even in the bleakest of times. Thank you for reminding me of the power of stories, of perspectives, of hope... and for reminding me that even in the face of all this suffering, all this death, all this destruction... there is still a chance for healing, for hope, for a better tomorrow."

Sedge smiles, a rare moment of warmth in the midst of all the pain and suffering. "You're welcome, Wick," she says, her voice soft but firm. "But you don't need my thanks. You don't need anyone else's thanks. You just need to keep going, keep fighting, keep hoping for a better tomorrow, even when today feels so very dark. Because if you do, if you keep believing in the possibility of healing, of hope... then maybe, just maybe, you can help him find a way to bring his light back into the world. Maybe you can help him find a way to share his stories, his perspective, his hope... and maybe, just maybe, together you can remind the world of the beauty, the possibility, the light that can be found even in the darkest of places, even in the bleakest of times."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I laugh, but it's a tired, broken sound. "He can barely read his own letters half the time. But he'd try." I push myself up off the floor, my knees cracking. "Let's go check his fever."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge nodded, her hands moving with practiced efficiency. She sliced through the canvas of his uniform, exposing the pale skin beneath. The stench of the wound was overpowering - gangrene setting in, muscles already softening.

"Here we go," she muttered, fingers probing the edges of the injury. She had seen worse, but that didn't mean this was anything less than horrific. The man's cries had quieted, reduced to pitiful whimpers, as the reality of his situation sank in.

Sedge gripped the putrid flesh, feeling it give beneath her fingers. She couldn't help but think of the things that should be done, the proper way to handle this, but there was no one else to do it. That was why she was here, why she had become this.

"Right, hold him," she said, her voice steady despite the chaos in her mind. She began to cut, the blade slicing through muscle and bone with a sickening crunch. The man's back arched, his legs kicking wildly, but Sedge's grip remained unyielding.

"This is going to hurt," she warned Wick, her eyes never leaving the grisly work at hand. "A lot."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I tighten my grip, my arms trembling as he tries to thrash. "Just... get it done, doc." I can feel his shoulder trying to slip out from under my hands.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge grunted, her focus solely on the task. She cut through the last of the tissue, the man's shoulder finally stilling in her grasp. She discarded the mangled remains with a toss, ignoring the bloody splatter on the floor.

"Now," she said, her voice cold and clinical, "I need to pack it. Can you keep him down for me?"

Wick:
I nod, squeezing my grip tighter, willing my arms not to fail. The man's eyes are rolled back, tongue lolling out of his mouth. He's passed out from the pain.

Sedge:
Sedge tore open a packet of gauze, the sound of the plastic ripping echoing through the tent. She began to pack the wound with the sterile pads, her hands moving with ruthless efficiency. The man's shoulder was a mess, the bone exposed and already starting to turn black.

"This is a lost cause," she said, her voice detached. "He's not going to make it. But we can at least give him a chance to die clean."

She secured the final layer of gauze, then reached for the morphine syrette. As she administered the dose, she couldn't help but think of all the other men she'd seen meet similar ends. All the wounds, all the pain, all the death.

"It's just my job," she whispered, the words more to herself than Wick. "Nothing personal."

Wick:
I swallow hard, feeling a lump form in my throat as I watch her work. I glance around the squalid tent, at the other wounded men moaning in their bunks. The stench of blood and decay hangs heavy in the air.

Sedge:
Sedge stood back, surveying her work with a critical eye. The packing job was adequate, but she knew it wouldn't hold for long. Still, it would have to do. She had more patients to attend to, and no more supplies to waste on this one.

She turned to Wick, her expression grim. "You can let go now. He's as good as dead anyway."

She started to gather up her things, her movements brisk and efficient. There was no room for sentiment in a place like this, not when every minute counted. She had a job to do, and she would do it, no matter the cost.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Bad like this," Sedge replied, her voice flat. "The infection's too far gone. We'd be losing him anyway, but it would take days, maybe weeks. He'd be in agony the whole time."

She paused, looking at the man's still form on the table. "Honestly, it's a mercy to let him go now. At least this way, it's quick."

She began to clean her instruments, the clinking of metal on stone the only sound in the heavy silence of the tent. "We have to be realistic about these things. There's only so much we can do out here. Sometimes, the kindest thing is to just let nature take its course."

Sedge glanced up at Wick, her gaze hard and unyielding. "That's the reality of war medicine. It's not always pretty, and it's never easy. But that's why I'm here - to do what needs doing, no matter how hard it gets."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let go of the man's shoulders, wiping my bloody hands on my pants. "You're colder than I expected," I say, looking at her. "Is that what it takes to do this job?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge met Wick's gaze, her expression unyielding. "Colder? No, I'm not colder. I'm just...practical. This job doesn't allow for sentiment, not when lives are on the line. I've seen too much to let emotions cloud my judgment."

She turned back to her work, scrubbing the gore from her hands with a rough cloth. "You'd be surprised how quickly you adapt, once you realize that's the only way to survive out here. The men I've seen...the things they've been through...it changes you. Makes you focus on what really matters."

She tossed the bloodied rag aside, her eyes hardening. "Out here, it's not about being kind or cruel. It's about keeping people alive, even if it's just for a little while longer. Sometimes that means making the hardest choices, the ones that will haunt you long after the war is over."

Sedge's voice dropped to a low mutter, almost to herself. "But that's a burden I'll carry, not them. They don't need to know the cost of their survival. All they need is to make it through the next day, the next hour, the next breath."

She looked up at Wick, her expression unreadable. "That's what I do. That's my job. And if you can't handle that, then maybe you're not cut out for this either."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge took a deep breath, her gaze lingering on the man's ravaged body. "You're seeing the aftermath of a gunshot wound that's gone septic. The bullet tore through his shoulder, and whatever medical care he received early on wasn't enough to stop the infection from spreading."

She stepped closer, pointing out the details with a clinical detachment. "You can see the blackened skin, the pus oozing from the wound. The gangrene has set in, eating away at the muscles and bone. It's only a matter of time before it reaches his vital organs and kills him."

Sedge's voice remained steady, but her eyes betrayed a flicker of something deeper - disgust, sorrow, perhaps even a hint of guilt. "This is what happens when you're out of supplies, out of medics, and out of hope. When the only thing left is to try and make the dying process a little less painful."

She met Wick's gaze, her expression hardening once more. "It's not a pretty sight, but that's the reality of war. Of war medicine. Of what we're all reduced to when the rules of civilization no longer apply."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow, forcing myself to keep looking. "Right," I say, voice rough. "So what do we do with him now?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge nodded, her expression grim. "We take him outside, wrap him in a blanket, and bury him. Deep enough so the animals won't dig him up before nightfall."

She began gathering the necessary items - a tarp, rope, shovel, and a plain canvas shroud. "We can't risk leaving him here to attract scavengers or draw unwanted attention. And even if we could, there's no one left to bury him properly anyway."

As she worked, Sedge's thoughts drifted to all the other bodies waiting to be disposed of, the makeshift graves scattered across the war-torn landscape. Each one a grim reminder of the toll the conflict was taking, not just on the living, but on the very earth itself.

She glanced at Wick, her gaze assessing. "You up for this? It's not exactly glamorous work, but it needs doing."

Her tone was matter-of-fact, but there was an undercurrent of concern. She knew the psychological toll of war, of constantly facing death and destruction. And while she couldn't afford to indulge in sentiment, she recognized the importance of keeping her companions grounded in reality, no matter how bleak it might be.

Wick:
I take a deep breath, steeling myself. "Yeah, I can do it," I say. "Just tell me what you need me to do."

Sedge:
Sedge nodded, impressed by Wick's resolve. "Good. Let's get it over with then."

She led the way out of the tent, her steps brisk and purposeful. The sun beat down on them, casting long shadows across the dusty ground. The air was heavy with the acrid scent of smoke and the distant rumble of artillery fire.

Sedge stopped at a spot marked by a crude wooden cross, its surface weathered and scarred. "This is as good a place as any," she said, her voice barely above a whisper.

She began to unfurl the tarp, her movements efficient and practiced. Wick watched as she carefully placed the body on the cloth, then began to wrap it snugly, the fabric muffling any remaining sounds of distress.

Once the shrouded form was secure, Sedge handed Wick the rope. "Tie it off here," she instructed, pointing to a sturdy branch. "Make sure it's good and tight."

As Wick worked, Sedge sank to her knees, her hands moving with a quiet reverence as she began to dig. The earth was dry and hard, resistant to her efforts, but she persisted, her focus unwavering.

When the hole was deep enough, she stood, brushing the dirt from her hands. Wick finished securing the rope, and together they lowered the body into the grave.

Sedge covered it with a layer of soil, her movements swift and final. She paused for a moment, her gaze fixed on the mound, before turning to Wick.

"Let's get back to the tent," she said, her voice low and steady. "We've got more work to do."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at Wick, her expression grim. "Shrapnel tears through flesh and bone like a hot, jagged blade. It pulverizes muscle, severs arteries, and shatters every bone in its path. The wounds it leaves behind are gaping, raw, and bloody, with jagged edges of splintered bone sticking out. Some pieces might be too small to see, embedded deep in the tissue, but the pain is still there, a constant, searing agony that never lets up."

She paused, her gaze hardening. "And that's just the beginning. Shrapnel infections are brutal, spreading fast and fierce, consuming everything in their wake. The bacteria feast on the damaged tissue, producing pus and fluid that seep into the wound, sometimes even eating away at the surrounding skin. It's a slow, agonizing death, as the victim succumbs to the relentless onslaught of pain and decay."

Sedge's voice remained clinical, but her eyes betrayed a flicker of something deeper - disgust, sorrow, perhaps even a hint of guilt. She knew all too well the devastating toll of shrapnel wounds, the countless lives lost to their merciless, unrelenting destruction.

"And that's not even considering the psychological impact," she continued, her tone a bit softer now. "The trauma, the fear, the helplessness...it can break a man, shatter his spirit long before his body gives out. You see it in their eyes, the way they cling to life, desperate to hold on just a little longer, even as the pain consumes them."

She met Wick's gaze, her expression somber. "That's what shrapnel does. It's a cruel, merciless instrument of war, designed to inflict maximum damage on the human body and soul. And out here, in the midst of all this chaos and destruction, we're left to pick up the pieces, to try and salvage what little remains of a shattered life."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I stare at the fresh dirt, my throat tight. "So we're just...putting them back in the ground. That's it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge nodded, her expression grim but resolute. "That's all we can do, Wick. Bury them deep, mark the grave with a cross, and move on to the next one. It's a grim duty, but it's necessary."

She stood up, brushing the dirt from her hands. "We can't afford to linger, not with the wounded waiting and the enemy closing in. Every minute counts, and we've got a lot of ground to cover."

She glanced at Wick, noting the somber look on his face. "It's not easy, I know. But we can't let ourselves get bogged down in grief or despair. We have to stay focused, keep our heads in the game."

Sedge took a deep breath, steeling herself for the task ahead. "Come on, let's get moving. We've got a long day of burying the dead ahead of us, and I don't want to be out here after dark."

With that, she turned and began walking back towards the tent, her footsteps purposeful and determined. She knew the road ahead would be brutal, but she also knew that as long as she had her wits and her courage, she could face anything the war threw her way.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge's voice remained steady and clinical as she continued, her words painting a stark picture of the gruesome surgery unfolding before Wick's eyes. "I'm excising the damaged tissue now, cutting away the infected flesh with a scalpel. It's crucial to get it all, or the infection will just keep spreading."

She paused, her hands moving with practiced precision. "The bone's shattered, so I'll need to ream it out and pin the fragments together. It's a delicate procedure, but we don't have the luxury of time or materials for a proper repair."

Wick could hear the scrape of the reamer against bone, the crunch of broken shards being cleared away. Sedge's hands moved swiftly, her focus laser-sharp as she worked to restore some semblance of order to the ravaged tissue.

"It's a dirty job, but it's the only chance he's got," she continued, her voice a monotone drone of efficiency. "Once I've cleared the debris, I'll pack the wound with antiseptic gauze and stitch it up as best I can. It won't be perfect, but it'll have to do."

Sedge's words were a stark counterpoint to the wet, sickening sounds of the surgery, but Wick knew she was doing her best to keep him informed, to prepare him for what was to come. He held the screaming man down, his own stomach churning with every tortured cry, as Sedge worked her grim magic.

"There, that's the worst of it," she said finally, her voice tired but triumphant. "He's stable now, but he's not out of the woods yet. We'll need to keep a close eye on him, change the dressing frequently, and hope that his body can fight off the infection."

Wick released his grip on the man's shoulders, his arms trembling with relief and exhaustion. "How long?" he asked, his voice hoarse.

Sedge met his gaze, her eyes weary but resolute. "A few days, if we're lucky. A week, if we're not. But we'll do what we can, and pray that's enough."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath, still smelling the blood on my hands. "So we just...wait. And see if he lives."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge nodded, her expression grim. "That's about it, Wick. We've done all we can for now. It's up to him and his body to fight off the infection."

She stepped back, surveying the wounded man with a critical eye. His chest rose and fell in shallow breaths, his skin clammy and pale. Sedge knew all too well the fragility of life in these circumstances, the fine line between recovery and relapse.

"We'll monitor his vitals closely, keep the dressing clean and changed, and make sure he's getting enough fluids," she continued, her voice a steady hum of reassurance. "But beyond that, all we can do is wait and see."

Wick could see the fatigue etched into Sedge's features, the deep lines of worry and stress around her eyes. She had been running on adrenaline for hours, pushing herself to the limit to save this man's life. Now, in the stillness of the tent, the reality of their situation was beginning to sink in.

Sedge turned to Wick, her gaze piercing. "You did well back there, Wick. Holding him down, keeping him still...it was crucial. I don't know what I would have done without your help."

Wick felt a surge of pride at her words, but it was quickly overshadowed by a wave of guilt. He had been so focused on the man's screams, on the horror of what Sedge was doing, that he had barely considered the woman herself, the toll this work was taking on her.

"Sedge, I..." He trailed off, unsure of how to express the complex mix of emotions swirling inside him.

Sedge cut him off with a tired smile. "It's alright, Wick. We're all just trying to do our jobs, to make it through another day. Don't worry about me, okay? I can handle it."

But as she spoke, Wick could see the flicker of vulnerability in her eyes, the faint crack in her usually unbreakable facade. He knew she was trying to put on a brave face, to reassure him that everything was under control, but he could sense the exhaustion, the despair, the fear that lurked just beneath the surface.

"Look, I know this is a lot to take in," he said gently, his voice softening. "But you're doing amazing work, Sedge. I don't know how you do it, but you're keeping people alive out here, in the most impossible circumstances. That's something to be proud of."

Sedge's gaze faltered for a moment, a glimmer of gratitude shining through the fatigue. Then, with a visible effort, she squared her shoulders and met Wick's eyes squarely.

"You're right, Wick. I am proud of what we're doing here. And as long as I've got men like you by my side, I know we can face anything the war throws our way."

With that, she turned back to the wounded man, her expression once again resolute and focused. Wick watched as she began to change his dressing, her hands moving with practiced precision, her mind already turning to the next patient, the next crisis, the never-ending cycle of war and survival.

In that moment, Wick knew that he would follow Sedge anywhere, through any hell, as long as he could be by her side, fighting for the same cause, with the same unwavering determination.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge's hands stilled as she looked at Wick, a flicker of surprise crossing her face. "The rest?" she echoed, her voice soft. "You want to know everything, don't you?"

She took a deep breath, her expression pensive. "Alright, Wick. If you're sure you can handle it, I'll tell you the truth. The whole truth, from start to finish."

She sat down across from him, her posture open and unguarded for the first time since they'd met. "When I first got to the front lines, I was naive. I thought I could make a difference, that I could save everyone. But the reality of war soon caught up with me."

Sedge's eyes dropped to the floor, her voice dropping to a whisper. "I saw things, Wick. Terrible things. Men dying in agony, their bodies torn apart by shrapnel or bullets. I watched as infection set in, rotting away the flesh and bone until there was nothing left but a husk. I smelled the stench of death, felt the weight of it in my hands as I dug graves in the dark."

She looked up at Wick, her gaze haunted. "And through it all, I had to keep going. I had to focus on the next patient, the next surgery, the next bandage to change. Because if I let myself stop, if I let myself feel the full weight of what I was seeing, I would have broken."

Sedge's voice cracked, a single tear rolling down her cheek. "I've lost count of how many men I've watched die, Wick. How many times I've had to tell a father or a mother that their son wasn't coming home. It's a burden I carry every day, and one I don't know how much longer I can bear."

She wiped her face roughly, her expression hardening once more. "But I can't stop now. Not when there are still men out there who need me, who need my skills to survive. So I keep going, one day at a time, one patient at a time, hoping that somehow, someway, I can make a difference."

Sedge's gaze locked onto Wick's, her eyes searching his face. "That's the truth of war medicine, Wick. It's not glamorous, it's not noble, and it's definitely not easy. But it's what needs doing, and so that's what I do."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I reach out and take her hand, the one that isn't bloody. It feels small and cold in mine. "Okay," I say, my voice thick. "Okay. So we keep doing it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge's hand trembled slightly in Wick's grasp, but she didn't pull away. Instead, she squeezed his fingers, a tiny gesture of gratitude and solidarity.

"Okay," she repeated, her voice steady once more. "We keep doing it."

She stood up, her movements a bit stiffer than before, and began to gather her supplies. Wick watched her, still holding her hand, as she methodically cleaned and restowed each item.

"Let's get the others," she said, breaking the silence. "There are still men who need our help."

Wick nodded, releasing her hand as he rose to his feet. Together, they left the tent, stepping out into the chaos of the battlefield. The sounds of gunfire and screams filled the air, a constant reminder of the war that raged on.

As they moved through the wreckage, Sedge's expression hardened, her focus shifting back to the task at hand. Wick followed close behind, his own emotions in turmoil but his resolve unshakeable.

They had a job to do, and they would see it through, no matter what horrors lay ahead. Side by side, they pressed on, determined to make a difference in a world torn apart by conflict.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I follow her, my boots crunching on the debris. My voice is quiet. "You're not doing it alone anymore, doc."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge glanced back at Wick, a hint of a smile tugging at the corners of her mouth. "I know that," she said, her voice a little softer than before. "I've got you now, and that makes all the difference."

She quickened her pace, navigating through the wreckage with a practiced ease that belied the exhaustion etched into her features. Wick fell into step beside her, his presence a comforting warmth in the cold, chaotic air.

As they approached the next cluster of tents, Sedge could already hear the moans and cries of the wounded. Her stomach twisted with a familiar mix of dread and determination, but she steeled herself for what was to come.

"Let's get to work," she said, her voice steady once more. "We've got a lot of ground to cover."

Wick nodded, his jaw set in a resolute line. Together, they entered the next tent, ready to face whatever challenges lay ahead, side by side and shoulder to shoulder, just as they always would.

The scene fades to black as the two medics disappear into the heart of the battlefield, their mission to heal and save never faltering, no matter the horrors that awaited them.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I fall into step beside her, my own shadow stretching long in the dirt. "Lead the way."
