dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge set the last instrument in place and did not bother pretending the arrangement was comforting.

“Ready is a luxury,” she said. “You’ve got hands and weight. That will do.”

She stepped to the table, pushed the man’s torn sleeve higher with a quick, efficient tug, and felt the swollen heat around the joint. He made a thin, broken sound, more breath than voice. She did not shush him. She had heard worse and would again before dawn.

“Both are out,” she said. “Right worse than left. If we leave them, the muscles will clamp down and I’ll have to cut to get them back. If we put them back now, he screams, then he sleeps. That is the better bargain.”

She placed one palm flat against the man’s chest, not for comfort, but to feel how his breathing was working. Shallow. Fast. Bad, but not yet bad enough to stop her.

“When I pull, he’ll fight you,” she said. “Not on purpose. Bodies do stupid things when they’re scared. Keep his shoulders down. Do not ride him, do not lean on his neck, and if he starts to vomit, turn his head before he drowns in it.”

She glanced at the instruments, then moved two of them farther away from the edge of the table where they could be knocked into the dirt.

“I’m not going to be gentle,” she said, more to the room than to anyone in it. “Gentle takes longer.”

Her hands went to the injured shoulder, measuring, aligning, already deciding the angle. The man’s eyes rolled toward her, wet and unfocused.

“You’re alive,” she told him. “Stay that way while I fix this.”

Then she looked toward Wick, or rather toward the place where Wick was holding the man down, because that was the only part of the work that was not hers.

“On my count,” Sedge said. “And ignore his opinion of it.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, swallowing hard. My palms are already sweating against his shirt. "Counting's fine," I say, my voice tighter than I meant it to be.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge gave a single, short nod.

“Then don’t talk past me,” she said. “Count when I count. Nothing else.”

She set her feet on the uneven ground, bracing herself as much against the table as against the work ahead. Her left hand closed around the man’s wrist. Her right went to the shoulder itself, fingers spread over the swollen front of the joint, reading the shape of what had gone wrong beneath the skin.

“I’m going to pull down first,” she said, more to steady herself than to explain. “Then out. The muscle will fight. It always does. If I stop because he makes noise, we’ll be here until morning.”

The man’s breath hitched. His eyes were half-open now, white-rimmed and useless with pain.

Sedge did not look away from the shoulder.

“One.”

She settled her grip.

“Two.”

She drew in one breath.

“Three.”

She pulled.

Not fast. Not cruel. Just relentless.

The man’s body jerked as if the sound had been dragged out of him before he could decide whether to scream. His back lifted from the table, then fell. Sedge’s jaw tightened, but her hands did not waver.

“Hold,” she said, flat and hard. “Hold him.”

There was a horrible, resistant moment where the joint seemed to argue with her. Then a deep, ugly slide, followed by a heavy knock as the bone found its place.

Sedge let the arm down slowly, not releasing it all at once.

“Right’s in,” she said.

The man made a wet, shuddering noise. His face was gray and slick with sweat.

Sedge did not soften. She checked the shape of the shoulder with her fingers, then pressed briefly along the forearm.

“Still got fingers,” she said. “Good enough.”

Only then did she glance toward Wick, not to ask if they were all right, but because there was still work left.

“Left next,” she said. “This one will be easier, but he’ll guard it harder because he knows what’s coming. If he tries to curl, do not let him.”

She moved around the table without waiting for agreement.

The man turned his head weakly, mouth opening as if to beg. What came out was only breath.

Sedge looked at him.

“You’re still alive,” she said. “One more.”

She took the left wrist in one hand and set the other over the injured shoulder. The heat there was bad, the swelling tighter than she liked, but the joint had not been out as long as the right. That counted for something.

“On my count,” she said. “One.”

She shifted the arm a fraction.

“Two.”

The man trembled all over.

“Three.”

She pulled again.

This time the sound that came out of him was thinner, more animal, but shorter. His shoulders tried to rise; Sedge’s hands stayed where they needed to be. The second reduction came with less resistance, a sullen give rather than a fight, and then the bone was seated again.

Sedge held the arm for a moment longer, making sure it had truly settled.

“Both in,” she said.

She eased the man’s arm across his chest and began reaching for the cloth strips she had laid out earlier.

“Now we bind him,” she said. “And then you can stop holding.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not look up from the binding. She looped the cloth under the man’s arm and drew it across his chest with a practiced pull, snug enough to hold, loose enough not to bite.

“Neither,” she said. “He keeps the leg. He keeps the arms, if he’s lucky and doesn’t fever up later. The bad part is already happening, and it’s called being alive.”

She smoothed the strip down and checked the fingers of the injured side. The color was poor, but present.

“If I’d been kind in the way you mean, I’d have let him keep screaming until the muscles locked and I had to open him to fix it. That’s a worse kindness. This is the cheaper one.”

The man’s breathing was still ragged, but the worst of the panic had gone out of him. Sedge watched it for a moment, counting in her head.

“He’ll hurt for days,” she said. “He’ll sleep like a dropped sack tonight, if his body knows what’s good for it. If he wakes up hot and confused, that’s a different bad. Then we worry.”

She finished the knot and finally straightened, wiping her hands on her apron as if the work had left something on them that needed removing.

“No leg,” she said, plainer now. “Just a man who got hurt bad enough to need fixing. That’s all.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "He's quiet now," I say, looking down at the man's slack face. I let go of his shoulders, my hands feeling numb and shaky. "Does that mean it worked, or that we broke him?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge laid two fingers against the man’s throat and held them there.

“Quiet can mean three things,” she said. “He’s fainted. He’s sleeping. Or he’s dying. You tell them apart by the pulse, the breathing, and whether the face still looks like it’s arguing with the world.”

She counted in silence for a moment, then checked the rise and fall of his chest.

“Pulse is thin, but it’s there. Breath’s shallow, but regular. He’s not gone, and he’s not broken. He’s spent.”

She pulled one of the man’s eyelids up with a thumb. The eye rolled, dull and wet, but the pupil was still there, still doing what pupils were supposed to do. She let the lid fall.

“Pain does that,” she said. “It takes a person apart until the body decides it has had enough and shuts the noise off. It isn’t kindness. It’s mechanics.”

She checked the bindings again, tugging one strip a fraction tighter where it had slipped during the struggle. The man’s face twitched, but he did not wake.

“If we’d done nothing, he’d still be screaming by now, or he’d have stopped for worse reasons,” she said. “So no. We didn’t break him. We put him back. Badly, quickly, and with no decent light, but back.”

She wiped her hands once more on her apron, though they were already dry.

“If he wakes up fighting, that’s good. If he wakes up confused, that’s less good. If he doesn’t wake up and his breath turns slow and easy, that’s better still. If his lips go blue or he starts choking, then we have a new problem.”

She looked at the man’s slack face for a moment longer, not with tenderness, but with the tired attention of someone who had spent too many nights deciding which silences were safe.

“I don’t like doing this,” she said. “But liking it has nothing to do with doing it right.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked down at the man again, not because the sight was pleasant, but because it was necessary.

“You’re seeing shock,” she said. “Not the dramatic kind. The quiet kind. Skin cold, sweat on him anyway, pulse running fast and thin because his body is still trying to decide if it’s dying or only insulted.”

She pointed without touching, one finger tracing the line of the man’s jaw in the air, then the hollow at his throat where her own fingers had just been.

“Color’s poor. That’s fear and pain and blood going where it thinks it’s needed most. Breath’s shallow because his chest hurts, because he fought, because he’s done. But it’s steady enough. That matters more than pretty breathing.”

Her gaze moved to the bindings.

“You’re seeing cloth holding him together, not magic. The shoulders are back, but the joints are angry. He’ll guard them whether he’s awake or not. If he starts shaking, that can be the body letting go. If he starts turning blue, that’s not letting go. That’s airway or chest or worse.”

She checked the man’s fingers again, briefly, pressing one nail bed until the color fled and came back slow but real.

“Fingers still answer. Slow, but they answer. That means I did not pinch something I can’t afford to pinch. If they went white and stayed white, or if he woke screaming in a different pitch, then we’d be having a different conversation.”

Sedge straightened a little, knees stiff from the ground, and wiped a smear of dirt from the edge of the table with her thumb.

“You’re not seeing a broken man,” she said. “You’re seeing a man who ran out of ways to protest. That’s all. Bodies do that. They scream, they fight, they go limp, and sometimes they wake up furious at you for having put them through it. If he wakes up furious, I’ll take it.”

She glanced at the lamp, which was still doing its poor job, then back to the man’s face.

“And if you’re imagining something worse than what’s here, don’t. Look at what’s real. Pulse there. Breath there. Bindings holding. No blue. No choking. No blood soaking through faster than I can account for.”

Her voice stayed flat, not from cruelty, but from habit. Four years had taught her that panic filled the spaces where facts should be.

“This is the part where you watch,” she said. “Not the part where you invent endings.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't know I was holding. "Right," I say, my voice rough. My hands are starting to ache now that I've let go. "What do we do now? Just watch?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge pulled the nearest blanket over the man without ceremony, tucking it around his torso and under his arms so it would not slip.

“Yes,” she said. “We watch. But watching is not standing there waiting for something to happen. Watching is work.”

She laid her hand briefly on the blanket over the man’s chest, feeling the movement beneath it.

“Breath first. If it gets slower, stops, turns wet, or he starts choking, that is now. Not in a minute. Now.”

Her fingers moved to the edge of one binding, checking without adjusting.

“These stay snug. If his fingers swell, go cold, or stop answering when I press them, we loosen. If he wakes and tries to tear at them, you stop him. If he vomits, turn his head before he makes a new problem out of his own stomach.”

She glanced at Wick’s hands, noticing the shake in them without making anything of it.

“No water until he is awake enough to swallow like a person. Wet his lips if he begs. Not more. A drowning man does not need a cup.”

Sedge moved the lamp a little closer, then frowned at it and moved it back again.

“And if he gets hot, confused, or starts talking to people who are not here, that is fever or worse. Then you wake me even if I have just closed my eyes.”

She straightened, rubbing one hand briefly over her face.

“So. You watch his chest. You watch his color. You keep him warm. You keep your own hands ready. That is the job now.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not answer at once. She picked up one of the instruments she had moved earlier, wiped it with a rag, and set it back down in the same place. The motion was not nervousness. It was order.

“You want it straight,” she said. “Then straight is this.”

She looked at the man under the blanket, not at the wound alone, but at the whole of him: chest, color, bindings, the stillness that had replaced the struggle.

“Shrapnel is not a clean cut. It is not a knife. It is a dirty, ragged piece of metal moving wrong through meat. It tears. It drags. It carries cloth, dirt, rust, skin, and sometimes bone with it. A blade may open a line. Shrapnel makes a mess and leaves pieces behind where no piece belongs.”

She touched the edge of the binding over the man’s shoulder, checking it without adjusting it.

“In a limb, it shreds muscle and vessels. The blood may not come out where you can see it. It can pool inside. The muscle swells. The skin and fascia do not give enough. Pressure builds. The limb starts strangling itself from the inside. That is why I check fingers. That is why I check warmth and color. That is why a tight binding is useful until it becomes a noose.”

Her hand moved a little lower, hovering over the man’s chest without pressing.

“In the chest, it can open lung or vessel. Air goes where air should not. Blood fills space that needs to be empty for breath. A man can suffocate with no water near him. He may still talk at first. That is the dangerous part. Talking is not proof of safety. Breathing is.”

Her hand shifted again, toward the belly, though she did not touch him there.

“In the gut, it can open bowel. Then the body starts poisoning itself with its own contents. A small hole can kill slower than a big one, because it gives you time to hope. Fever, rigidity, stink, confusion—those are the things that come later if the inside has been fouled.”

She finally looked away from the man and toward the instruments laid out in their row.

“Metal is not the whole problem. Metal is only the thing that made the hole. The real problems are bleeding, dead tissue, filth carried deep, and pressure where pressure should not be. Shrapnel can be small as a coin and still take a man in three days because it sat somewhere dirty and the body could not wall it off.”

Sedge picked up the rag again, though there was little left to wipe.

“This man? I did not feel metal lodged in either shoulder. If there are fragments in him elsewhere, they may be small, deep, or quiet. We do not go hunting blindly with fingers and knives in bad light. We watch for what they announce: heat, redness, swelling, stink, fever, pain out of proportion to the wound, fingers that stop answering, breath that turns wet or short.”

She set the rag down.

“That is not tidied. That is the shape of it. But I will not invent wounds I have not found. If I felt metal, I would say metal. If I feared lung, I would watch his breath differently. If I feared gut, I would watch his belly and his fever. I am not guessing to make you feel prepared. Guessing makes you miss what is actually happening.”

She checked the man’s face again, the slack mouth, the sweat cooling on his skin.

“So you do not need to imagine every piece of iron in the world doing something new to him. You need to notice what changes. Breath. Color. Warmth. Pulse. Swelling. Vomiting. Fever. Confusion. Those are the signs that matter now.”

Sedge pulled the blanket a little higher over the man’s shoulder, not gently, but with the practical care of someone keeping heat in a body that had already spent too much.

“If you want kindness,” she said, “the kindness is accuracy. Not soft words. Accurate hands.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, swallowing again. My throat feels dry. "What's the first thing I should do if his breathing changes?" I ask, because my head is too full of everything else.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge stopped what she was doing and looked at Wick directly, because that was the one question that deserved no impatience.

“First thing,” she said, “is do not shake him, do not haul him upright, and do not stand there deciding whether it counts as bad enough.”

She moved to the man’s side and spoke with her hands as much as her words, shaping the actions in the air without touching him.

“You check the airway. If he is gurgling, choking, or making a wet noise, his head goes to the side. If there is vomit, you sweep it out with your fingers. One sweep. You do not dig around in there like you are fishing for luck.”

She paused just long enough to make the order stick.

“If he is not moving air at all, you open the way. One hand on the forehead, two fingers under the chin, lift. Mind the shoulders, but do not let the shoulders make you slow. Air comes first. Everything else comes after.”

Her gaze dropped to the man’s chest for a beat, then back.

“If he is breathing but wrong—too fast, too shallow, stopping between breaths, turning blue at the lips—then you call me. If he stops entirely, you call me while you keep the airway open. If you cannot do both at once, choose airway. A dead man cannot be fetched help for.”

She let that sit in the tent for a moment, plain and ugly and useful.

“Breathing changes are not a thing to watch for ten more seconds,” she said. “They are a thing to act on now.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not flinch away from the scream. She stepped into it.

“Keep his shoulders from coming up,” she said, voice flat and hard over the noise. “Do not lean on his chest. Do not put anything in his mouth. If he is screaming, he is breathing. That is the first thing I need to know.”

Her hands went to the man at once, not to soothe him, but to take control of the parts that mattered. One palm settled on his forehead, not pressing hard, just enough to keep his head from snapping back. The other stayed at his jaw, angling his face slightly toward the side.

“I am checking his airway first,” she said. “I am looking for vomit, blood, broken teeth, anything that can block him while he thrashes. There is none. His mouth is wet, but not full. His lips are still pink enough. No blue. That means air is getting in and out.”

The man bucked under the blanket, a ragged scream tearing out of him. Sedge did not tell him to be quiet. She listened instead, her head tipped, eyes narrowed in the bad lamplight.

“I am listening to the sound of it,” she said. “A scream is ugly, but it tells me his throat is open. What I do not want to hear is gurgling, crowing, or a wet rattle. I do not hear that yet. I am watching his chest now. Both sides should rise. They are rising. Uneven, because he is fighting and because his shoulders hurt, but rising. That is better than stillness.”

Her gaze dropped to the bindings. She kept one hand on the man while the other moved quickly along the cloth, checking the edges without jerking them loose.

“I am checking the bindings,” she said. “They are tight, but not tight enough to be the cause of this. If they were cutting off flow, his hands would be colder, whiter, or bluer. They are not. I am pressing the nail beds now. Color comes back slow, but it comes back. That means the limbs are still being fed. If that changed, I would loosen the cloth at once.”

The man’s breath hitched into a raw, gasping wail. Sedge’s mouth tightened, but her hands stayed steady.

“I am not enjoying this,” she said. “I say that so you do not mistake necessity for cruelty. I am going to keep doing what must be done while he makes noise about it.”

She moved closer, checking his face again. With a thumb, she lifted one eyelid, then the other, holding each a moment in the weak light.

“I am checking his eyes,” she said. “Pupils are even enough. They react. That is not proof that nothing is wrong, but it is proof that his brain is still answering to light. I am looking at his skin. Sweaty, pale, but not gray enough to make me stop everything. I am feeling his pulse now.”

Her fingers found the side of his neck again. She counted in silence for three beats, then five, then more.

“Fast,” she said. “Harder than I would like, but not fluttering away into nothing. Fear and pain will drive a pulse like a drum. Shock can do it too. The difference is whether it keeps making sense or starts running off into collapse. Right now it is still making sense.”

She pulled the blanket back just enough to expose the upper chest, not to shame him, but to see what she was dealing with. Her eyes moved over the skin with quick, practiced attention.

“I am looking for a wound in the chest wall,” she said. “A hole that sucks air, a patch of blood that spreads too fast, swelling that crackles under the fingers. I do not see one. I am putting my hand flat against his chest now. Not to comfort him. To feel the movement. Both sides move. There is no crackle under my fingers like dry snow. If there were, I would suspect air where air has no business being.”

The man tried to curl, his whole body twisting away from the pain. Sedge shifted her weight at once, not to fight him, but to keep him from tearing at the work she had already done.

“He is trying to guard the shoulders,” she said. “That is expected. What I cannot let him do is rip the bindings loose or fall off the table. Keep him from rolling. Do not climb onto him. Just keep his shoulders down and his head turned if he gags.”

Her hand moved lower, hovering over his belly for a moment before she pressed lightly, then harder in two careful places.

“I am checking his abdomen,” she said. “Not because I think it is the cause yet, but because it is one of the places shrapnel can hide its intentions. I am feeling for hardness like wood, for flinching that means the inside is fouled. He is sore everywhere, but his belly is not board-stiff. That is another thing in our favor.”

She glanced at the instruments, then away again.

“I am not reaching for a knife,” she said. “I am not opening anything. I am not probing blindly for metal. If I thought there was a piece in him that needed to come out now, I would say so. I do not think that yet. What I think is that he is coming up out of the worst of the shock, and the pain has found him all at once. That can make a man scream worse than the first injury did, because the first part is fear and the second part is the bill.”

The scream broke into a hoarser sound, more breath than voice. Sedge watched his mouth, his chest, his hands.

“I am watching for the scream to turn into something else,” she said. “If it turns into choking, I will sweep his mouth and turn his head. If it turns into a wheeze or

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, my jaw tight. "Just tell me if there's blood. I can't see shit in this light." My own pulse is beating in my ears, loud enough I can barely hear his screams.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge shifted the lamp closer, then cursed its weak flame under her breath and angled her body to block the worst of the draft. The light improved by inches, not enough, but enough to put hard edges on the things that mattered.

“Then stop trying to see everything,” she said. “See this.”

She pointed without touching, one finger tracing the edge of the binding over the man’s right shoulder.

“Blood, yes. There. Dark red. Slow. That is oozing from torn muscle and skin, not from anything that pumps. If I had opened a vessel, or if one had been torn loose by the pull, it would be bright and it would be spreading fast. You would not need good light to know it. The cloth would go heavy.”

She lifted the blanket just enough to check beneath him, then let it fall again.

“No pool under him,” she said. “No fresh rush when he moves. That matters more than the stain.”

The man screamed again, the sound ragged and raw, his head jerking to one side. Sedge kept her hand near his jaw, not forcing it, just ready to turn him farther if the sound changed into something wet.

“His mouth has spit in it,” she said. “A little blood, maybe from where he bit himself. Not enough to choke on. I can see his teeth. No broken bits. If he starts spitting red and it keeps coming, that is different. If it turns pink and frothy and his breath gets worse, that is worse still. It is not doing that now.”

She took a clean rag from the row of supplies and pressed it briefly over the darkest spot on the binding. Not hard enough to hurt the joint. Hard enough to be useful.

“I am putting pressure here because pressure is cheap,” she said. “Not because I think we are losing him into the table. If this rag soaks through before I count to sixty, I will know. If it does not, the bleeding is the kind we can live with.”

She counted silently, eyes on the cloth, one hand still aware of the man’s chest. When she reached the end, she lifted the rag and checked the stain.

“Slower already,” she said. “That is the answer. Not no blood. Just not the blood that kills.”

The man’s scream cracked into a hoarse, breathless moan. His body tried to twist away from the pain, but the bindings held. Sedge did not tell him to be quiet. She listened to the sound the way another person might listen to weather.

“He is loud because his airway is open,” she said. “Loud is ugly, but loud is useful. The bad sound is the one that stops halfway. The bad sound is a gurgle. The bad sound is nothing at all.”

She glanced toward Wick only long enough to make the next words land.

“You want one thing to watch? Watch for blood that spreads while you count to five. Bright blood. Thick blood. Blood from his mouth or nose with his breathing turning wet. Blood under him making a puddle instead of a stain. Those are the things that mean the world has changed. A slow stain is the price of the wound.”

Her hand moved to the man’s neck again, fingers finding the pulse through the sweat and tremor.

“It is still fast,” she said. “Still hard. But it is not running away from me. His body is spending everything it has on fear and pain. That is why he shakes. That is why he screams. That is why his skin is cold even though he is sweating.”

She checked the fingers of the injured side again, pressing one nail bed until it blanched.

“Color comes back,” she said. “Slow, but it comes back. The limb is still alive. The binding is still doing what I asked it to do.”

The man’s voice broke again, thinner now, more exhausted than defiant. Sedge kept her eyes on his chest.

“How much longer?” she said, answering the question before it had to be asked again. “Until the pain peaks and his body gives out the rest of the shock. Could be minutes. Could be longer. I will not guess. We watch until he is quiet, or until something changes. If he goes quiet with good breath and a pulse that settles, we let him sleep. If he goes quiet with bad breath, we act.”

She wiped her hand on her apron, then set it back where it belonged.

“So do not ask me to promise you there is no blood,” she said. “There is blood. There is pain. There is a man who has been torn and put back together in a bad tent with a bad lamp. What I am telling you is that, right now, the blood is not winning.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I lean my head back against the table leg, the canvas rough against my hair. "You didn't say what happens tomorrow," I say, staring up at the tent ceiling. "After the quiet part."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not answer at once.

She kept one hand on the man’s chest until the last of the struggle had gone out of him, feeling the breath move under her palm. Then she drew the blanket back over him, not gently, but with enough care that the cloth did not drag across the injured shoulders. She checked the pulse again. Checked the color of his lips. Checked the fingers. Only then did she look toward the place where Wick had sat down.

“The rest,” she said, “is not one thing. It is a list. You want it straight, then take it straight.”

She reached for the rag she had used to press on the binding and held it up to the bad light. The stain was dark, but not spreading. She folded it once and set it aside.

“Tomorrow starts before morning,” she said. “It starts the minute he stops screaming, because that is when you will want to believe the work is done. It is not. The quiet part is not the end. It is the part where the body decides whether it has enough left to keep going.”

She moved the lamp a fraction closer, then stopped herself and moved it back, because the flame was too weak to trust and the heat of it too near the man’s face.

“First, he may sleep. If he sleeps, you do not wake him to ask how he feels. You do not shake him. You do not try to make him drink. You watch his chest. You watch his mouth. You watch the color of his hands. If his breathing stays steady, you let him have the sleep. If it changes, you wake me. If it stops, you open his airway and call me in the same breath.”

She smoothed the edge of the blanket over the man’s shoulder without looking at his face.

“If he wakes before dawn, he may wake wrong. Pain does that. He may be confused. He may be angry. He may try to sit up before his body remembers what it has just been through. If he does, you stop him. Not by climbing on him. Not by shouting. You put a hand where it will remind him without hurting him, and you keep your voice low. You tell him where he is. You tell him not to move his arms. If he does not listen, you call me.”

Her fingers checked the binding again, tracing the edge where it crossed his chest.

“He will hurt,” she said. “Not a little. The shoulders will ache deep, the kind of ache that makes a man sick to his stomach when he tries to move. The muscles will be torn and angry. The joints will feel loose even if they are seated right. He may think we made it worse. He may say we made it worse. He may say things that are not worth remembering.”

She glanced at the instruments laid out in their row.

“I will not give him hope I do not have. If we have anything that dulls pain, he gets what is safe and no more. If we have nothing, then he gets water, stillness, and the truth. You do not tell him it does not hurt. You tell him he is alive enough to feel it, and that we are watching him. That is not comfort. It is fact. Sometimes fact is the only thing that holds.”

The man’s breath hitched once, then settled. Sedge watched it settle before she went on.

“Tomorrow, if he can swallow, we give him water. Small amounts. Not a cup tipped into his mouth. A wet rag if he is still half-gone. A few sips if he is awake enough to know what he is doing. If he coughs, if it goes down wrong, if he starts choking, you stop. If he has not pissed by morning, that is a bad sign. If he is hot to the touch, worse. If he is cold and still sweating, worse still.”

She picked up one of the instruments, wiped it clean with a rag, and set it back in line. The movement was automatic, almost mechanical.

“The bindings stay until I say otherwise. They are not decoration. They are the only thing keeping his shoulders from doing something stupid while he sleeps. But bindings can hurt too. Tomorrow I will check the skin under them. If they have bitten in, if the fingers swell, if he says his hands are numb or dead, we loosen. Not all at once. Not because he asks. Because the body tells us it is being strangled.”

She looked at the man’s fingers again, pressing one nail bed until it whitened. Color returned slow, but it returned.

“If he wakes and cannot move his fingers properly, or if one arm is colder than the other, or if the pain changes from the kind that spreads to the kind that points, then we have a new problem. Nerve. Vessel. A fragment I did not feel in bad light. Maybe a fracture I could not prove while he was fighting me. Then we decide what can be done here and what cannot.”

Her hand moved from the man’s fingers to the blanket over his chest.

“If his breathing turns wet, if he starts coughing blood, if pink froth comes from his mouth, if one side of his chest stops moving like the other, then we are

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I press the heels of my hands into my eyes until I see stars. "Alright," I say, voice flat. "So we watch him die or watch him live. Same as every other time."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not let the flatness in Wick’s voice pass without answer. She did not soften it, either.

“No,” she said. “That is the wrong shape of it.”

She kept one hand near the man’s chest while she spoke, not touching him now, just staying close enough to feel if the breathing changed. The tent was small and close, the air thick with sweat, lamp oil, dirt, and the metallic smell of blood that had not yet had time to dry properly.

“You do not watch him die or live like it is a verdict already handed down,” she said. “You watch the signs that move him one way or the other. Dying is not a door. Sometimes it is a slope. Sometimes it is fast, sometimes slow, and sometimes it reverses if somebody notices the right thing soon enough. If you sit there deciding he is either dead or saved, you will miss the middle, and the middle is where I work.”

She reached for the rag she had used earlier and checked it again by the poor lamp light. The stain had darkened, but it had not spread into a fresh wet edge. She set it aside.

“If his breathing turns wet,” she said, picking the thread back up where it had broken, “if it starts rattling deep in his chest, if one side stops rising like the other, if his lips or nail beds go blue, then we are past simple watching. That means airway, lung, chest, blood where blood has no business being. You turn his head if he is choking. You clear his mouth if there is vomit or blood he cannot manage. You call me. If there is a hole in the chest wall, we cover it so air does not drink through it. If the chest starts trapping air and pressing on what is left, then we are in worse trouble, and I will have to decide quickly whether there is anything to do with what I have.”

Her gaze moved to the man’s abdomen beneath the blanket.

“If his belly goes hard, if he starts vomiting blood or something black, if he passes blood, if the pain settles into one place and gets worse instead of spreading out into shock, then we are looking at the inside. Gut, liver, spleen, vessels. Some of that can kill slow enough to let a man talk and joke and ask for water before he collapses. That is why I keep checking him instead of trusting the quiet.”

She looked back at the bindings.

“If a limb swells under the cloth, if the fingers go cold, white, blue, numb, or stop answering, then the binding becomes part of the problem. We loosen it. Not because he complains. Because the body is telling us it is being strangled. If the pain turns into the kind that makes him scream every time his pulse beats, and the limb feels tight as wood, then we are looking at pressure building inside the meat. That can take an arm or a leg even if the wound itself looks small.”

Sedge shifted slightly, easing the stiffness out of one knee without moving far from the table. She was tired. The tiredness was there in the set of her shoulders and the way she blinked, but it did not make her sloppy. If anything, it made her more deliberate, as if she had learned the hard way that exhaustion was another thing that had to be managed like a wound.

“If he gets hot,” she went on, “if his skin dries out and burns, if he starts shaking or talking to people who are not here, if the wound smells wrong or the skin around it turns red and angry, then we are looking at fever and foulness. Infection is not dramatic at first. It is a little heat. A little redness. A little swelling. Then it becomes poison in the blood, and after that it becomes a race I may lose.”

She checked the man’s face again. His mouth was open now, breath moving through it in shallow pulls. The screaming had worn him down to this: a gray, sweating stillness that looked worse than sleep but was not yet death.

“Tomorrow,” Sedge said, “if he is still here, the work changes. Tonight is keeping him alive. Tomorrow is finding out what kind of alive he is going to be.”

She reached for a clean strip of cloth and laid it near the table without using it yet, just making sure it was there.

“First, I check him in better light if we have any. Eyes. Pulse. Breath. Color. Warmth. Bindings. Fingers. I check the shoulders to see if they stayed where I put them or if the muscle dragged them out again while he slept. I check the wounds for fresh bleeding, for dirt, for fragments working their way toward the surface or settling deeper. If there is metal I can feel safely, and the wound is clean enough to justify opening it, I may take it out. If it is deep, if it is near something I cannot afford to cut, if the wound is too dirty and swollen to trust, I leave it alone and watch. A piece of iron can kill a man by staying hidden, but a knife in the wrong place can kill him faster.”

She smoothed the blanket a little lower over the man’s side.

“If he wakes, he will be thirsty. He may beg for water. You do not give him a cup unless he is awake enough to swallow properly. You wet his lips first. If he can take a few sips without choking, you give a little more. If he coughs, if the water comes back up, if he seems more confused than before, you stop. A man can drown in his own throat with half a cup if his body has forgotten how to work.”

Her fingers checked the edge of one binding again, tracing the cloth where it crossed the man’s chest.

“He will hurt tomorrow,” she said. “Not only when he moves. Sometimes it is worse when he wakes and lies still, because the body has had time to remember everything. His shoulders will ache deep. The muscles will spasm. He may feel sick. He may vomit from the pain alone. If he tries to sit up, you stop him. If he tries to use his arms, you stop him. If he curses you, lets him curse. If he cries, let him cry. Do not make him ashamed of it. Pain is not bravery.”

She looked at the instruments again, but this time she did not touch them. They were clean enough for now, which meant they were as ready as they would ever be.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Alright," I say, my voice low. "Tell me when it's my turn to watch." I'm not getting up from the floor yet. My legs feel like water. "And tell me what to do if you're the one who passes out."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: He keeps the leg. He keeps the arms, if he's lucky and doesn't fever up later

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: You're seeing shock... Skin cold, sweat on him anyway, pulse running fast and thin because his body is still trying to decide if it's dying or only insulted.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: It tears. It drags. It carries cloth, dirt, rust, skin, and sometimes bone with it... shreds muscle and vessels... can open lung or vessel... can open bowel. Then the body starts poisoning itself with its own contents

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: I am checking his airway first... I am looking for vomit, blood, broken teeth... I am checking the bindings... I am checking his eyes... I am looking for a wound in the chest wall

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack slid the knife back into its sheath and stood, knees cracking. She did not look toward the cart yet. She looked at him, flat and unreadable, then at the wet mark on his wrist.

“Then you heard him,” she said. “That’s the first thing you’ve done right today.”

She spat into the ditch, wiped her mouth with the back of her hand, and finally turned her head to listen. The noise from beyond the cart was faint now, wet and dragging, like a man trying to breathe through a mouthful of gravel.

Wrack’s jaw worked. She counted the seconds in silence.

“He’s dying,” she said. “Question is whether he dies quiet, or loud enough to bring someone in from the road.” She drew the knife again, not offering it, just letting the weight settle in her hand. “If you don’t want to do it, say that. If you want me to do it, say that too. But don’t stand there making it worse by pretending you haven’t heard.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take a slow breath, my knuckles white around the grip of my sword. "I'll do it." My voice is lower than I meant it to be. I start walking toward the cart, stepping over a body without looking down.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack did not follow at once. She scanned the road and the tree line, because the cart was not the only thing that could still move in that silence. Then she came up behind him, a few paces off, keeping the ditch between them and the open ground.

“Don’t talk to it,” she said, low. “Don’t apologize. It makes it worse for both of you.”

She checked the angle of the cart wheels, then the shadow beneath it.

“Get close enough to see his face if you can. If you can’t, close enough to feel the breath. Then stop thinking and finish it. If he moves, don’t hesitate. A man with gravel in his throat can still stick a knife in your gut.”

A wet cough drifted from beyond the cart. Wrack’s expression did not change.

“Six,” she repeated, as if to herself. “Make it six quiet ones.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched him for a moment, then turned her head toward the cart.

“Listen,” she said.

The cough came again, shorter this time, and the wet dragging breath that followed was thinner, like it had less body left to push through.

“Wet chest,” Wrack said. “Maybe a punctured lung. Maybe a gut shot and blood in the throat. Could be both. He can’t get clean air, and whatever he’s trying to say isn’t coming out right.”

She looked at him again, flat and unbothered.

“He’s not getting up. He’s not running. He’s not going to crawl to the road and tell someone what he saw. If he’s lucky, he won’t be able to make much noise at all. If he’s unlucky, he’ll be able to beg.”

A small pause. The dragging breath filled it.

“That’s the bad part.”

Wrack shifted the knife in her hand, the weight easy, familiar.

“As for mercy or easier—same thing, near enough. Mercy’s what you call it when he’s too far gone to argue. Easier’s what you call it when you’re too far gone to pretend you didn’t come for him.”

She looked toward the cart again, not with pity, just assessment.

“Either way, he’s dying. Either way, you can make it one thing or the other. You can do it because he won’t feel the next hour, or you can do it because you don’t want to hear him feel the next five minutes. Doesn’t matter to him. He’s not keeping receipts.”

Her eyes came back to him, dry and level.

“Just don’t ask me to make it mean something it doesn’t.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod, once. My fingers feel numb around the hilt. I walk the last few paces until I can see him, slumped against the cart wheel. His eyes are open, staring past me. I don't look at his face. I drive the point in under his ribs, quick and clean, just like she taught me. When I pull it out, the sound stops.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack did not move until the last wet breath was gone.

Then she came around the cart, boots careful of the broken spoke, and looked down at the man. The silence beyond the road was total now, the kind that followed killing and made the living feel conspicuous. She checked the tree line first. Then the body. Then the wound.

“Not a butcher’s job,” she said.

She crouched, touched two fingers to the man’s throat, waited, and straightened again.

“Six,” she said. “Quiet now.”

Her eyes moved to the dead man’s face, still open, still staring past where Corvin had stood. Wrack closed his eyelids with the back of her fingers, then wiped them on the grass.

“Flies,” she said, as if that explained everything.

She stood and went to the cart, scanning the load with the flat, practical attention she gave to weather or terrain. There was a tarp, a broken axle, a scattering of supplies no one would claim before nightfall. She looked at the bodies in the ditch, then at the road.

“That was either mercy or easier,” she said. “From here, it looks like you didn’t have the patience for either.”

A small pause. The wind stirred the cart’s hanging rope.

“Good enough.”

She turned back to the man at the wheel and began checking his belt, his boots, the folds of his cloak. She worked quickly, without delicacy, pulling out a chipped knife, a length of cord, a handful of coins in a pouch worn soft by use.

“If he had a name, leave it,” she said. “If he had money, bring it. If he had a wound older than today, ask me. I don’t like bodies that keep secrets.”

She tossed the cord and the old knife to the far side of the cart, then weighed the pouch in her hand.

“Six,” she said again, almost approvingly. “One of them even paid.”

She looked toward the road once more, then back at the body.

“If you’re going to be sick, do it behind the cart. If you’re not, stand watch while I see whether he had a purse worth the mud on our boots.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack crouched again, slow in the knees, and pointed with the flat of her chipped knife at the wound.

“Angle of entry,” she said. “Under the ribs, left side. You went up and in. That’s the liver, mostly, maybe the lung behind it. Not the heart. Heart’s more central, and you’d have known because the blood would have been bright red and fast. This is dark. Slower. He didn’t drown in it. He just went into shock.”

She set the knife against the man’s sternum and tilted it, showing the path.

“Clean puncture. No tearing. That’s the difference between a wound and a cut. You did a cut. A cut closes when you pull the blade out, which is why the blood stopped so fast. A wound — a stab, a slash, a gash — stays open, and he’d have kept bleeding on the road, and the flies would have found him, and someone would have found him.”

She pulled the knife back, wiped the flat on her sleeve, and looked up at Corvin.

“That’s what you’re looking at. A man who was alive ten minutes ago and isn’t now, because of a hole in his side. No story. No lesson. A hole.”

She shifted her weight and looked at his hands. The man’s fingers were curled, the nails dirty and chipped, one thumbnail split down the middle.

“Look at his boots,” Wrack said, without ceremony. “See how the leather’s worn on the inside edge? He walked with a limp. Old injury. Could be a bone healed wrong, could be a knee gone bad. That’s what I meant about older wounds. Not today’s work. Someone else’s, years ago, and he just lived with it.”

She leaned back on her heels and let her eyes go flat again, scanning his face, his neck, his forearms.

“No bruises. No ligature marks. Not a prisoner, not a deserter being brought in. He was a soldier on a cart, or a man pretending to be one. The boots are cheap. The cloak’s good. That means he bought the cloak, didn’t earn it. Could be a merchant’s guard. Could be a conscript who spent his last coin on looking the part.”

She stood, knees cracking again, and looked at him.

“What you’re looking at is a man with a hole in him, a bad knee, and a nice cloak. That’s the whole thing. The rest is you making it into something.”

She turned back to the cart and kept searching the man’s belt.

“His eyes,” she said, not looking up. “You noticed they were open. They stay open. The lids don’t close on their own. That’s not him watching you. That’s a muscle that stopped working. When I closed them, that was for flies, not for him. He wasn’t seeing anything.”

A pause. She found nothing in the pouch but a stub of pencil and a scrap of waxed thread, and tossed them back.

“If you want to understand what you’re looking at, look at the wound and then look at his hands. Not his face. The face is where you put the story. The hands are where you see the work.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I crouch down and look at his hands. Calloused, dirt in the lines, that split nail. "He wasn't a soldier," I say quietly. "A soldier's hands are different." I stand up, my own hands feeling too clean.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at the dead man’s hands, then at the chipped knife in her own.

“Farmer’s hands,” she said. “Or a smith’s. A groom. A man who’d never held a spear and thought the cart would keep him out of it. Hands don’t care what the cloak says.”

She crouched again, but did not touch the body. She laid the point of the knife beside the wound and let it rest there.

“You want it straight? A spear to the gut is not a clean death. It is an opening. The point goes through skin, fat, muscle, and then into the guts. If it clears the ribs, it keeps going. If it doesn’t, the shaft can still shove the liver or spleen like a stone in a wet sack.”

She moved the blade, showing the angle.

“Small guts are the worst for spilling. They’re light, wet, full of what should stay inside. Large guts are the worst for smell. What’s in them is already dead to the man, and when it gets into the belly it starts a fever that has nothing to do with cold nights. The stomach, if it’s hit, vomits. The bladder, if it’s hit, fills the belly with urine. The liver, if it’s hit, bleeds him cold and fast enough that he doesn’t have time to make a fuss.”

Wrack’s mouth tightened, not in pity, in memory.

“The hole won’t close. The meat swells against it. If the shaft is thick, the sides are bruised and torn. If there are barbs, pulling it out brings intestines with it. If you leave it in, he carries a pole through his belly and every step shakes blood into the hole. You can wash it. You can pack it with clean cloth. You can shade him and keep the guts from drying. You cannot make a man’s insides a clean room again.”

She wiped the knife on her sleeve and stood.

“If he’s lucky, he bleeds out before the rot starts. If he’s not, he dies of fever, thirst, and pain so bad he forgets his own name before he forgets the wound. He’ll beg to be finished. That’s

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at the wound in his side, my stomach twisting. "So what do you call this one?" I ask, my voice too quiet. "Lucky or not?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack followed his eyes to the hole.

“Lucky,” she said. “Not blessed. Not gentle. Just lucky, which is the only kind you get out here.”

She crouched again, but did not touch the wound. She laid her knife beside it, the flat of the blade catching the low light.

“This isn’t a spear in the guts. You put a point up under the ribs. Liver, mostly. Maybe the lung behind it. It bled into him, not onto the road. He’d have gone cold, dizzy, then quiet. No fever. No rot. No man picking through his insides for an hour.”

A dry breath passed her.

“The one beyond the cart was already dying. You just closed the account.”

She looked at Corvin, flat and practical.

“Call it a clean kill. Call it mercy if you need the word. Call it easier if you need the truth. The wound doesn’t care. It’s a hole, and he went through it.”

Her eyes moved back to the body.

“If it had been a spear gut, you’d have been watching him drown in his own belly. This was luckier.”

She stood, knees cracking, and wiped her hands on the dead man’s cloak.

“Six,” she said. “Lucky enough for all of us.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
(OOC: I think there might be a bit of a disconnect here—I already finished the kill earlier in the scene. But I can roll with the emotional aftermath.)

I stay kneeling until my legs start to ache. The silence is heavy, and I can still feel the ghost of the hilt in my hand. "I didn't ask for a lesson," I say, my voice rough. "I asked what it was."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack had not gone. When he said stay, she stopped with one hand on the cart rope, then let it fall. She did not kneel beside him. She stood where the road was visible and the body was not the only thing in her way.

“You asked what it was,” she said. “It was a killing. You did it because he was dying, because you were there, because nobody else was going to. That’s all it was.”

She looked at the wound, then at the dead man’s face. Her mouth tightened, not with pity, with the ordinary annoyance of having to explain that the world did not rearrange itself around first times.

“The sound was a lung filling with blood. The time was too short for you to get used to it and too long for you to forget it. The hole was your hand, his side, and a problem that stopped being a problem. You didn’t make a

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack had not gone. The half sentence hung between them, then she finished it in the same flat voice she used for counts and distances.

“You didn’t make a monster. You didn’t make a sacrifice. You made a corpse. That’s the rest.”

She looked at the body, then at the wound, then at the dead man’s face with its closed lids. The cart rope swayed once and stopped.

“You want exactly what you did to him? You put a blade under his ribs and up. That went through skin, muscle, maybe the edge of the diaphragm, into the liver. Liver doesn’t scream. It bleeds. It bleeds into his belly, and if the lung took a nick, into his chest. His mouth filled with what his lungs couldn’t move. The sound was wet, not noble. A grunt. A catch. The sucking thing people mistake for talking. That’s just air moving through blood. It stops when there’s no air left or no strength to push it.”

Wrack let the silence hold. It did.

“How long? Not as long as you’re making it. The body goes into shock. The skin goes pale and clammy. The pulse thins. The eyes lose focus. He was past that before you moved. You finished it while he was already on the way out. It was seconds for him, maybe less. It’ll be longer for you, because you’re the one still alive and remembering.”

She shifted her weight, not away from the road, not toward the body.

“You’re not doing anything to him now. If you press his side, you’re moving cold blood and slack meat. If you take his hand, you’re moving a dead thing. If you leave his eyes open, it isn’t because he’s watching you. It’s because the lids don’t work. If you wash the blade, you’re washing off his blood, not his guilt. If you stand over him and wait for him to mean something, he won’t. That’s the part people can’t stand.”

Wrack looked at him then, dry and level.

“You asked what it was. It was killing. Not a lesson. Not a prayer. Not a debt paid or a soul released. A man was dying where you could hear him, and you stopped it. You did it badly because you were afraid, and you did it anyway. That’s the whole story. The rest is what you do with the rest of your life.”

She glanced at the wound again.

“The sound you heard was the last of his lung trying to work with blood in it. The sound you didn’t hear was his body settling. That’s the part nobody wants to listen to. The chest stops. The belly stops. The blood stops moving, so if you press, it moves back because nothing is pushing it anymore. The temperature starts dropping. The stiffness comes later. That’s not him judging you. That’s meat becoming meat.”

Wrack wiped her hands on her trousers, then stopped, as if the motion had become too neat for the moment.

“Your hands aren’t too clean,” she said. “They’re just hands. They’ll smell like iron and mud until I get a wet rag. If you scrub them raw tonight, they’ll still smell like this tomorrow. That’s not a sign. That’s a body.”

She looked toward the ditch. The other dead lay there, small now, ordinary. The cart stood between them and the road, a broken thing full of ordinary goods.

“You’re not doing anything to him anymore,” Wrack said. “You’re doing something to yourself. You’re kneeling in his blood and asking the dead to tell you what it means. He can’t. He didn’t choose you. He didn’t choose a war, or a cart, or a nice cloak, or a bad knee, or a knife in the side. He just got here and then he didn’t.”

A pause. Her voice did not soften.

“Six,” she said. “Quiet now. That’s all you get. Quiet.”

She looked at the road again, scanning it without urgency.

“If you can stand, take watch. If you can’t, say so. If you’re going to be sick, behind the cart. If you’re not, get the cord and the chipped knife. We don’t leave tools where we leave bodies. We don’t leave bodies where we leave tools.”

Wrack finally turned fully toward him, her face unreadable.

“You wanted me to watch it with you. I did. I saw the first cough before you moved. I saw the last one after. There was no moment where he looked at you and understood. His eyes were open before that. They stayed open after. That’s mechanics. That’s not mercy. That’s not cruelty. That’s the end.”

She let that sit, then added, quieter, without pity:

“You didn’t clean it up. You didn’t make it holy. You did it, and it worked, and now it’s over. If you need it to be more than that, you’ll have to go find someone who’ll lie to you better.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I push myself to my feet, my legs stiff and cold. I take the cord and the knife from where she tossed them. My fingers close around the worn handle. "I don't need lies," I say, and my voice doesn't shake. "I just needed to hear it."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack let the words sit for a moment, then nodded once, as if he had reported the time of day and not made a confession.

“Then you heard it,” she said. “Everyone needs to hear it. That’s why old sellswords talk too much and young ones die quiet.”

She looked at the dead man, then at the road beyond the cart. The wind moved the tarp a little, lifting one corner and dropping it again. Nothing else moved.

“Keep it loose,” Wrack said. “Don’t grip it like it’s a prayer. It’s a tool. Tools get dirty. They don’t forgive you, but they don’t blame you either.”

She turned back to the body and began working at the cloak again, checking folds, seams, the inside of the belt. Her hands were quick and unhurried, the way they would have been checking a saddle for galls.

“You wanted the truth without the polish,” she said. “You got it. He was a man with a bad knee and a nice cloak. Now he’s a body with a hole in the side. You’re the man with the knife and the clean hands. That’s the whole list.”

A small pause. She found a button missing from the dead man’s shirt, or perhaps she had torn it loose without noticing. She did not look sorry.

“If your voice doesn’t shake, good,” Wrack said. “If it does later, don’t make it mean something. It means you’re alive and not used to it. That’s all.”

She straightened, knees cracking again, and looked him over the way she might look at weather: not to decide whether it cared for him, only whether it would get them wet.

“Watch the road,” she said. “Don’t watch him. He’s not company.”

She crouched to take the dead man’s boots, then stopped and glanced toward the ditch.

“If your stomach turns, go behind the cart. If your mouth turns, save it for when we’re not standing in blood.”

Wrack pulled one boot free, then the other, and set them aside. Her tone stayed flat, but not unkind.

“Six,” she said, almost to herself. “Lucky number. Means we can still leave before someone counts.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take a slow breath and turn my back on the body, focusing on the empty road ahead. The cord is rough against my palm. "How long before we move?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack did not look at him right away. She finished pulling the second boot free, set it aside, and rolled it once against the side of the cart to knock the worst mud from it.

“Ten minutes,” she said. “If the road stays empty. Five if you stop breathing like you’re waiting for a verdict.”

She moved to the nearest body, crouched, and worked at the sword belt.

“We don’t move because you’re ready. We move because I’m done. There’s a difference.” She tested the buckle, then swore softly when it caught. “If we leave boots, someone will know we came here in boots. If we leave weapons, we look like fools who couldn’t fight their way out of a ditch. If we leave money, we’re fools twice.”

She drew the dead man’s knife, looked at it, then tossed it into the cart.

“Check under the tarp. Rope, grain, waterskins, anything that fits in a pack and doesn’t rattle. Don’t open things you don’t need to. If it’s a merchant’s cart, he’ll have a ledger. If it’s a soldier’s cart, he’ll have a name. If it’s a fool’s cart, he’ll have a woman’s letter. I don’t want to see that.”

Wrack stood and looked toward the tree line. The wind moved a low branch; she watched it until it stopped.

“If something comes from the road, you’ll hear me first. If you don’t hear me, run. If you hear me say run, run.” She glanced back at him. “Not toward the ditch. Toward the trees.”

She went to the second body and began checking its pockets, hands quick and unhurried.

“Six,” she said, more to herself than to him. “Five pockets left to rob.”

Then, after a moment, without looking up:

“If you want to stand watch, stand where you can see the road and not be seen from it. If you want to be sick, go behind the cart. If you want to ask another question, make it a useful one.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I move to the edge of the cart where I can see the road but stay in its shadow. My hands are still cold. "Useful question," I say, my voice low. "Do we burn them?"
