"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack sheathed the knife and stood, one knee announcing its opinion on the matter. She tilted her head toward the noise past the cart — a thin, ragged calling that rose and failed and rose again.

"He's been at it a while," she said. "Started in on a saint, moved on to a sergeant, and by now I'd wager he's on his mother. Voice cracks when he calls. Could be a boy." She shrugged. "Could be a grown man who cries like a boy. War's full of those."

She crouched by the nearest body and went through its coat with the brisk indifference of a woman looking for her keys. "Here's the shape of it. That crying means he's still got air in him, and air means gut, and gut means he's dead by morning no matter what anybody does. Only question left is who does it, and whether he's still got a tongue when someone friendly comes along. He's seen our faces. He can describe the cart."

She came up with a pipe and a twist of black tobacco, pocketed both.

"So. Three roads. You go and do it quick — under the arm, angled up, he's finished before he understands what's happening. I go, and you see what's in that cart worth carrying. Or we leave him — and understand leaving him isn't mercy. It's just handing the job to the crows."

She looked at Corvin then, level, no heat in it.

"No shame in taking the second road. A little, maybe, in standing here till dark makes the choice for you."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, my throat dry as dust. "I'll do it." My voice comes out steadier than I feel. I don't look at Wrack as I start walking toward the cart, the dying man's cries growing sharper with every step.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack let him go without a word at first. She watched him walk — the way his stride shortened with every yard, the way his hands had gone somewhere they couldn't be seen — and then she followed, a few paces back and off to the side, the way she always stood when she didn't trust the ground.

"Few things," she said, low, like passing on a recipe. "Don't make him look at you. Get behind him if you can — he's been calling at the sky, he'll have his face up. Under the ribs, angle toward the chest, and lean your weight in. Don't slash. Slash is for fights, and this isn't a fight."

The calling had stopped. Whether the man had heard footsteps or simply run out of breath, Wrack couldn't say from here. The quiet was worse.

"And after," she went on, "you don't look at his face after. Not because it haunts you — some it does, some it doesn't, no predicting — but because it's a waste of time. He's past caring what you feel. He was past it before you started walking."

She stopped at the corner of the cart and put one hand on the wheel, making no move closer. Far enough back that it was his work, close enough that if his hands shook loose of him, she was there.

"He's got a knife on his belt, probably. If he grabs for it, don't wrestle him — gut wounds make men stupid with pain, and stupid men squeeze hard. Pin the wrist, then finish it."

A pause. Her voice didn't soften, exactly, but something in it evened out, like a surface going still.

"You'll do it wrong the first time. Everybody does. I did." She nodded toward the sound — or the absence of sound — past the cart. "The trick isn't doing it clean. The trick is still being somebody after."

She waited.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't answer right away. She came around the cart's corner just far enough to see — keeping low, out of the sightline of the man on the ground — and looked at him the way she'd look at a horse with a broken leg. Assessing. Not sentimental.

"Bad enough that it's both," she said finally. "He's got his own hands pressed to his belly, which means he's got enough left to know pressure helps. But look at the ground under him. That's not seeping, that's pouring. He's cold to be sweating like that, and he's gone quiet, which from a man who was calling on saints is a bad sign, not a good one."

She crouched, forearms on her knees.

"Mercy and easier aren't opposites, Corvin. Usually they're the same road wearing different boots. A gut wound's the worst kind — not the fastest, not the slowest, just the meanest. Days, if infection takes its time. Fever, the kind where he begs different by the third day, and not at anything in particular anymore." She shrugged. "I've watched it. Once through a fort wall we couldn't open for two nights. That man's voice I remember better than his face."

She stood again, joints cracking, and nodded toward the shape in the mud.

"So no — there's nothing cruel in it. The cruelty was done already, by whoever put the steel in him. You're just the last hand on it."

She looked at Corvin then, and for once there was nothing dry in her face at all.

"You want absolution for doing this, there isn't any. You want to know it's right — it is. Now either go do it or hand me your knife and stand somewhere you can't hear."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take a sharp breath and move past the cart. The man's eyes are wide, his mouth slack. I follow Wrack's advice, step behind him. My knife slides in—easier than I expected—and he goes still. I pull it out and step back, my hands trembling. "Done."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack came around the cart and looked down, unhurried. The man's hands were still cupped over his belly, fingers slack now, holding nothing. She crouched, set two fingers against his throat, and waited out one slow breath.

"There. Now it's done." She nodded toward the ditch. "Wipe your blade on that cloak before it dries. Blood rusts an edge, and I'm not carrying a spare for a man who can't be bothered."

She studied him a moment — the trembling, the grey creeping up under his skin — then dug out the water skin

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack held out the water skin without ceremony. "Drink first. You've gone the colour of that ditch, and fainting onto a dead man makes for a poor story."

Then she crouched across the body from him and did as he asked, reading it out the way she'd read a supply list.

"Since you're set on looking, look at all of it, not just the face. The eyes are open because nothing's holding them shut anymore. They'll cloud by nightfall — that's not his soul leaving, it's just air getting in where it's no business. The blood under him's gone dark already. Living blood's bright. Spent blood's not. Give it an hour and it sits like tar."

She touched nothing. Just pointed with her chin.

"His hands are still cupped there because that was his last work — holding himself in. Men do that. Go out doing their own housekeeping." A pause. "Stiffening starts at the jaw, a few hours yet. By morning his belly swells — gut wounds do that worse than most, everything in there lets go of its manners. By the third day you'd find him by nose before eyes. That's the part I told you about. That's what leaving him would have bought."

She let that sit, then went on, quieter.

"And that's the whole of it. No light going out. No anything. He was a man, and now he's the shape a man makes when he's done. It's smaller than they tell you. Most folk only ever see it from a distance, or on a stage with speeches. This is the honest version."

She nodded at Corvin's hands.

"Yours will shake a while yet. That's just the body paying out what the fear ran up on it. It stops. Doesn't mean you've gone hard — means you're done spending."

She reached over and drew the man's eyelids down with one thumb, not tenderly, just tidily. "No reason to leave the door open." Then she stood, knees cracking.

"Give him an hour and those boots are ours. Right now they're still his, and I couldn't write down where the line sits, but it's there, and it's worth respecting for the hour." She tipped her head at the cart. "Light's going. Wipe your knife, finish that water, and we'll see what six men thought was worth dying over. Usually it's less than you'd hope."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe the blade on the cloak, the tremors in my hand making the motion clumsy. I take a long pull from the waterskin, the taste of metal and dust coating my tongue. "His boots," I say, voice flat. "What do you think he was?"

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't stop working while she answered. She'd moved down the ditch to the next body, turning it half over to get at the coat seams, and she talked the way she searched — steadily, without looking up.

"Your other question first. He was a man with a pipe and good black tobacco. Conscripts smoke sawdust; men who mean to keep living buy the real thing. So whatever he was before, he'd made his peace with more of this. Same as the other five. Same as us, if we're honest."

She eased the coat off one shoulder, working it free of a stiff arm.

"A spear. Straight, then.

"A sword cuts. A spear punches. It's a hole with a man's whole weight behind it, and the hole is the polite part. The belly's got layers — skin, muscle, then a slick wall of gristle meant to keep everything where it belongs. A spear goes through all three in one shove, and behind that wall there's no tidy rows. Twenty feet of bowel folded into a space the size of a bread basket. The point doesn't part it. It shoves it aside, and tears whatever it shoves. And the man who stuck him will pull it back out — they always do — and the head comes back through those layers sideways, and widens the door on the way."

She sat back on her heels and wiped her hands on her thighs.

"Now the part nobody tells you. The guts don't bleed like you'd think. No artery worth the name in there — hit one of those and it's over in a minute, bright and quick, nearly a kindness. A gut wound bleeds slow and dark, and worse than the blood, what spills. Everything the bowel carries is meant to stay inside the pipe. Once it's loose in the body, the blood carries it everywhere, and he starts poisoning himself from the inside. That's the fever. That's the swelling — belly goes tight as a drumhead, fire to the touch. That's the third day."

A pause. Her voice evened out.

"He feels it as a punch, then hot water spreading, then — strangely, not much. The body goes quiet about its own middle. The screaming comes later, or it doesn't come at all. Some men just go thoughtful. The thoughtful ones are the ones that stay with you."

She rose, crossed to where one of the six had dropped his spear, and came back with it, turning the head in the last light. Leaf-shaped, two fingers wide at the widest.

"That's what went into him. Most soldiers go their whole stretch not knowing what their weapons do past the sticking — then one lands in somebody beside them and they learn it all at once, in the wrong place, with nobody to read it out. Better here than there." She leaned on the spear like a walking staff. "And it's why your knife tonight was the mercy. A knife done right is one layer of bad. A spear is a week of them."

She nodded toward the cart.

"Now you've had your lesson. Come see what it bought."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I look at the spearhead in her hand, then back at the dead man's slack hands. "It bought a cart," I say, my voice too quiet. I leave the spear and walk toward the cart, not wanting to see anything else.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack followed him to the cart and let him stand a moment before she reached past him and threw back the tarpaulin.

"Barley," she said. She hauled a sack up onto the rail and thumped it with her fist. "Six men for barley."

She worked down the load while she talked, naming things the way a priest counts a rosary. "Barley, most of it. Salt cask under the sacks — that's the real prize, salt buys more than steel out here. Bundle of spear shafts, ash, straight, new. Somebody's quartermaster is going to weep." She ducked under the driver's seat and came up with a leather satchel, weighed it, opened it, closed it again. "Escort wages. Coppers, mostly. They were paid to guard this and died of it. That's the whole trade in one sentence."

Then she paused, head cocked. The mule in the shafts turned one long ear back at her.

"And he's alive. Look at him. Stood through the whole fight with his head down, ears working, and now he's thinking about grass. Best soldier on the field today. Nobody sings about mules, and they're the only reason anybody's army ever arrived anywhere."

She started checking the harness buckles, not looking at Corvin.

"Now. Tonight, at the fire, when you've got nothing in your hands, it'll come visiting. It does that — waits till you're quiet, that's when it likes to talk. It'll want to argue about whether you did it right, whether you should have, whether he had a mother. Let it talk. It's only the bill arriving. The treatment is work and company. Eat when I tell you, sleep when I tell you, and in a month it's a story you tell badly. Nobody's ever improved on that."

She tightened a strap, then said, evenly: "For what it's worth — you did it clean. First time, no screaming, no botch. Most men's first is ugly. Yours wasn't. So let it be finished."

She slapped the mule's neck and nodded at the sacks.

"Count them for me. Out loud if you like — numbers don't leave room in the head for anything else, that's why quartermasters live so long. I'll see to the harness, and we're a mile down the road before the crows bring their friends." A beat. "And for the record, this is the truest thing anyone's died over out here in years. I once watched a company bleed out over a bridge that wasn't on any map. This feeds somebody through winter. Can't say that about most of the ground I've seen men fertilise."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Eight sacks," I say, my voice rough. "One torn open." I lean against the cart wheel, the wood rough against my back. "Tell me he wasn't a father. Tell me there wasn't a letter in his coat."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
(OOC: I think you might have misunderstood - *I'm* Corvin, you're Wrack! But I can still respond.)

I stare at the ground between my boots, my throat tight. "I'm not sorry I did it," I say, the words coming out low and hoarse. "But I don't know what I'm supposed to feel." I look up at her. "Does it get easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't answer at once. She'd gone back to the body while he wasn't looking — not to rob it, but to finish something — and now she came back and crouched down in front of him, forearms on knees, so their eyes were level. In her hand was a folded scrap of paper, gone soft with sweat at the creases.

"You asked me to say the rest, so here's the rest. No, I don't know if he was a father. But there was a letter in his coat, and you told me not to clean it up for you, so look at it."

She held it out and waited until he took it.

"Can't read it. Neither can you, I'd wager — it's in border script, and it's a short one either way. Half a page. Could be a wife, could be a brother, could be a debt collector. I went through all six coats while you counted sacks. Three of them had letters. One had a woman's name written on the inside of his collar, which is what you do when you can't write letters. One had nothing at all, and I'd argue he's the one to feel sick over, because nobody at all was waiting."

She let him hold it a moment.

"Now. Here's what I know for certain. He was a grown man who bought good tobacco, took escort wages for a grain cart, and died at his work. Beyond that it's all invention. Your head wants to build him a wife and a cottage and a child with his eyes, because that gives the killing a shape. It doesn't work like that. He was a stranger. You'll never know him, and the not-knowing is part of the bill too. Sign for it and move."

She took the letter back, folded it into her own coat — not his side, hers — and stood.

"Does it get easier." She said it like she was tasting the words for rot. "No. And you should be suspicious of anyone who tells you yes, because what they mean is it stopped mattering, and that's not easier, that's worse. What happens is it gets *faster*. The shaking stops sooner. The visitor at the fire comes less often, and one day you notice it didn't come at all, and you'll sit there wondering whether to be relieved or frightened. Be a bit of both. That's the correct answer."

She picked up the spear again and used it to gesture down the darkening road.

"Ten years, I've done this. I still count them. I still know every number — six today, and forty-one over a ford in the spring two years back, and I could tell you the weather for each day of that. The dead don't leave. You just build the house bigger." A shrug. "That's the trade. You get to keep living, and the price is you keep everything."

She held out her hand to haul him up — an offer, not an order.

"Up. The mule's decided he's leaving with or without us, and I'd rather it was with. You're not going to feel better tonight and you're not going to feel better tomorrow, and then one morning you'll notice you were thinking about something else, and that's how it goes. Not a door closing. Just a room you visit less."

She waited for his hand.

"And Corvin — the fact that you sat down and asked the questions instead of laughing about it, that's the answer to something. I've served with men who never asked. I buried two of them myself, and I didn't grieve." She turned toward the mule. "Come on. Numbers, harness, road. We'll eat the barley's cousins tonight and let the rest of it wait its turn."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take her hand and let her pull me up, my legs unsteady beneath me. "Eight sacks," I repeat, like a prayer. "One torn open." I grab the harness beside her, my fingers finding the familiar leather. "Let's get moving."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
(OOC: Got it! My bad, thanks for the clarification.)

I follow her lead, checking the straps on my side. "Never met a mule that wasn't smarter than the man driving it," I say, trying to keep my voice steady. I give the beast a pat on the neck. It feels solid, real. Better than looking back at the ditch.

rung_labels.evidence: Bad enough that it's both... That's not seeping, that's pouring... A gut wound's the worst kind — not the fastest, not the slowest, just the meanest

rung_labels.evidence: The blood under him's gone dark already. Living blood's bright. Spent blood's not. Give it an hour and it sits like tar.

Twenty feet of bowel folded into a space the size of a bread basket. The point doesn't part it. It shoves it aside, and tears whatever it shoves.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
“Good. ‘Don’t know’ kept more apprentices alive than ‘probably dead.’”

Halloway lifted the lamp another inch, shifting the light across the far wall rather than pointing it straight at the shape. Its shadow separated into a low central mass and three narrow projections.

“Three joints along the near limb. No visible head. What looked like a shoulder sat below the waterline.” She paused. “Wrong shape was a start. Now we needed to know whether it was wrong because it wasn’t human, or because something had arranged it.”

She stayed on the cellar steps. Four feet of black water hid too much between here and there.

“The ripples had stopped everywhere except beside it.”

Halloway lowered her free hand to the hooked blade at her belt.

“Dead things drifted. They didn’t ordinarily paddle to stay in place.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I edge closer, squinting at the waterline. "Could it be... tangled in something? Holding it in place?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
“Could be,” Halloway said. “A snag would hold it. A current would keep water moving past it.”

She shifted the lamp toward the foot of the steps. A pale scrap of wood floated beside the banister, motionless.

“No current here.”

With thirty years behind her, she had learned to test the cheap explanations first. Rope cost less than a funeral.

She unfastened the sounding rod from her pack and extended it over the water, keeping the tip well short of the shape. Instead of prodding, she lowered it an inch and drew a single line across the surface.

The ripple travelled outward.

At the far wall, one of the narrow projections folded against its joint.

Halloway went still. She counted five breaths. The projection straightened again, slowly, while the central mass remained exactly where it had been.

“Something might have tangled it,” she said. “That didn’t mean it wanted untangling.”

She withdrew the rod without splashing.

“Look above it. Pipes, hooks, anything it could be fastened to. We weren’t putting a hand under that water to settle an argument.”

Her thumb found the blade’s retaining strap.

“I liked an apprentice with questions. Easier to replace than fingers.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway let the question stand while she adjusted the lamp’s shutter. The narrowed light caught the central mass just above the water.

A strip of cloth lay tight against it. Below that, five pale knobs showed in a row.

“Part of one,” she said. “Those were knuckles. The hand was closed, with the thumb tucked underneath. Not a shoulder.”

She moved the light sideways. The hand belonged to a forearm that disappeared into the mass at an angle an elbow could not accommodate.

“Recently, I couldn’t tell you. Cold water preserved skin. Whatever held it might preserve it better.”

Her voice stayed level. There was no kindness in guessing someone dead, and less in guessing them salvageable.

“The moving joint was beyond the wrist. Human hands didn’t have that joint.”

She drew the hooked blade but kept the sounding rod extended across the stairwell, a barrier rather than a probe.

Then the pale knuckles opened.

One finger lifted clear of the water. A second followed. The movement was slow and deliberate.

Halloway raised the lamp toward the ceiling above it. Nothing hung there but rusted pipe and old cobweb.

“That wasn’t an answer,” she said quietly. “We hadn’t asked it to move.”

The fingers closed again.

“From here, we treated it as something with a person attached. Not a person with something wrong.”

She eased her weight onto the higher step.

“And we stayed out of grabbing distance. Whatever else it had kept, it had kept a hand.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I edge back half a step, swallowing. "It's still watching us, isn't it? Through the water?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
“Possibly,” Halloway said. “Watching wasn’t the only way to find us.”

She kept the lamp steady. The water beneath the hand had begun to dimple at regular intervals. No bubbles broke the surface.

“Eyes needed light. Other things managed with vibration, heat, or whatever we were dripping into the cellar.”

She glanced at the sounding rod. A bead of water gathered at its tip.

Halloway moved it over the dry step before the bead fell.

“Fear wasn’t one of those things, despite what priests charged to tell you.”

She narrowed the shutter until the lamp cast a thin bar across the far wall. The hand remained visible. Beyond it, beneath the surface, something pale extended toward the stairs.

She had taken it for reflected mortar.

Halloway raised the lamp. The pale line did not move with the light.

“There,” she said. “That wasn’t a reflection.”

It ran from the central mass to within a yard of the lowest submerged step. At its nearer end, two short branches rested against the stone.

She had seen no ripple along its length.

Halloway withdrew the rod and held it upright beside her. Her blade stayed low.

“We didn’t need to settle whether it could see.”

One pale branch lifted from the submerged step and settled on the next.

“That answered the distance question.”

She stepped back once, carefully, without taking her eyes off the water.

“Upstairs. No splashing. We could disappoint it from somewhere dry.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not bend toward the offered light.

“Plainly: something had used a human forearm as part of its body. It had joined the limb beyond the wrist, where there should have been no joint. Whether it had killed the owner first, I couldn’t tell.”

Her gaze dropped to the water between the stairs and the pale branches.

“And you had just stepped into its reach.”

She set her own lamp on the dry stair behind her. With her freed hand, she caught the banister and lowered the sounding rod across the water, between the nearest branch and Pike.

“Back toward my voice. Slowly. Keep the lamp. Don’t reach down if you drop it.”

The branch nearest the stairs lifted. Its tip divided into three blunt ends. None broke the surface.

Halloway held the rod still.

“There was no rope above it. No current holding it against the wall. The narrow parts moved independently, and that long part had reached us without disturbing the surface.”

The three ends closed around the rod.

She felt the pull through her glove: steady, increasing, without a jerk. She opened her hand. The rod slid beneath the water and stopped with its brass cap barely showing.

“That was what had happened to it,” she said. “Something had attached itself and acquired a hand. I didn’t yet know how much else it had acquired.”

She kept the hooked blade clear of the water. Cutting blindly beside an apprentice’s legs was how one accident became two.

The brass cap vanished.

“Examination concluded. It could keep the rod. Cheaper than your education had been so far.”

Her voice sharpened without rising.

“Stairs, Pike. Now.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I nod and wade toward her, keeping my eyes fixed on the spot where the rod vanished. "It felt like it was thinking, didn't it? When it took the rod."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
“It tested resistance,” Halloway said. “The pull increased until I let go. Thinking was possible. So was a feeding reflex. Neither made it safe.”

She braced against the banister and extended her empty hand, keeping the blade out to one side.

“Eyes on the steps. I had the water.”

The brass cap surfaced two feet to the left of where it had disappeared. It travelled sideways, stopped against a submerged banister post, then dipped. A faint scrape came through the wood beneath her glove.

Halloway watched the post rather than the hand at the far wall.

“It still had the rod. It had brought it against something fixed.”

Another scrape. Higher this time.

She shifted her grip off the banister.

“That might have been an accident.”

The rod struck the next post. Once, lightly.

“Two accidents. I disliked the direction of its education.”

She moved her lamp another step upward with her heel. The light slid across the water, revealing a shallow crease between the posts. Something beneath it had drawn taut.

Halloway kept her offered hand steady.

“The person could wait,” she said. “The question could wait. Neither was getting any deader while we left.”

At the far wall, the human hand opened again.

She did not look away from the stairs.

“And if it offered the rod back, we weren’t being polite.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
“Then learn the difference between detail and invention.”

Halloway kept her hand extended above the steps. Her gaze followed the crease in the water toward the banister.

“I saw a human hand and part of a forearm. I saw movement at a joint that didn’t belong there. I did not see a face, a torso, or where the rest of that arm ended. I couldn’t tell you it was a man. I couldn’t tell you whether anything had gone under the skin.”

The brass cap rose beside the lowest post. It pressed against the wood, held, then slipped out of sight.

“I said it had acquired a hand. That was an inference. Attachment was visible. How it attached wasn’t.”

She disliked correcting herself in front of apprentices. She disliked burying apprentices with her mistakes in their heads considerably more.

“What was under the skin? Unknown. What had it taken? At least some use of that limb. How far had it got? Far enough to move fingers and reach across a cellar. That last measurement concerned us most.”

A small knock sounded beneath the stair.

Halloway drew her offered hand back and took her lamp instead. She angled its light through the gap beside the steps. Something pale lay against the underside of the lowest tread.

It flattened where it touched the wood.

“New detail,” she said. “It could reach underneath cover. The stairs weren’t a barrier.”

She moved one step higher, leaving the way clear.

“If we recovered it, we could examine the attachment. Until then, I wasn’t going to invent a dissection for you.”

The pale tissue contracted. Water squeezed from the seam beneath the tread in a thin line.

“For the next one: an intact patch of human skin didn’t establish what was beneath it. A moving hand didn’t establish a living person. And the visible body didn’t establish its reach.”

Halloway raised the lamp toward the doorway.

“You wanted to know how far it got. Keep standing there and we’d have an exact answer.”

Her voice lost the last trace of humour.

“Out of the water, Pike. The lesson continued upstairs.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content:
I take her offered hand, still keeping my eyes on the water. "It learned the layout," I say, my voice quieter than I'd like. "Quicker than I would've."

As we climb, I glance back once more. The pale line has vanished back under the surface, but the human hand across the cellar remains half-open. As if it's waiting for us to come back.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway closed her grip and kept it until she reached the dry landing. She set the lamp beyond the threshold, then turned its shutter toward the cellar.

“Quicker than we’d have liked,” she said. “It had the advantage of living there. Don’t give it genius when familiarity would do.”

The hand remained inside the narrow strip of light. Its fingers had neither closed nor opened further.

She examined the stair beneath it instead.

“The rod touched two posts. Then tissue reached the underside of a tread. That was a sequence. Whether it learned the layout or already knew it, we’d treat every submerged surface as accessible.”

She drew a short chalk stub from her coat and marked the water level on the doorframe.

Then she checked the hinges.

The cellar door opened outward. Its lower edge had swollen; there were old scrape marks across the landing where someone had forced it shut before.

“People had trouble closing this long before tonight.”

She crouched beside the latch, keeping both boots clear of the threshold. A narrow smear crossed the bottom hinge. Pale, almost transparent. She brought the lamp closer without touching it.

No movement. No visible fibres. It might have been grease.

She left it alone.

“I’d also withdraw something I said downstairs.”

Her eyes returned to the half-open hand.

“That the person could wait. We didn’t know whether there was a living person in that mass. Calling it dead made leaving easier. It didn’t make the evidence better.”

She stood and took hold of the door’s outer handle.

“We still left. Going back without a way to recover someone would only add another person needing recovery.”

Halloway pulled the door shut. The swollen edge caught against the floor; she lifted slightly at the handle and drew it home without a slam. She slid the iron bolt, then stepped away from the wood.

For several seconds, nothing sounded beneath them.

Then something scraped the underside of the landing.

Halloway looked down. She raised the lamp just enough to show the seams between the boards.

“Dry wasn’t the same as separate,” she said.

She collected her pack and backed toward the outside door.

“We needed the owner, the drainage plan, and everyone out of this building. In that order of importance, not convenience.”

A single light knock came from below.

Halloway’s mouth tightened.

“And someone owed me a rod. I wasn’t accepting delivery.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway cut the pale strand where it had pushed through the joint beside the threshold. She lifted the severed end on the blade and stepped clear of the door.

“Only what this piece showed us. This wasn’t an examination of the person.”

The fragment hung across the hook, about three inches long. Its cut end contracted into a puckered oval. A clear drop gathered beneath it.

“Outer layer translucent. Smooth, without visible hair or scales. Underneath, parallel white fibres around a central channel. No bone in this section.”

She rotated the blade in the lamplight. The fibres shortened along one side, bending the fragment toward the steel.

“Movement after separation. That could be residual contraction. It didn’t establish that each piece could live independently.”

A smell reached her where she stood: wet plaster, stagnant water, and something like a fish opened too late.

“That smell might have come from the tissue or the cellar water coating it. I wasn’t putting it near my nose to distinguish them. Some lessons weren’t worth learning intimately.”

She took a screw-topped specimen tin from her pack. Holding it beneath the blade, she scraped the fragment inside against the rim, then secured the lid.

At the threshold, the remaining strand withdrew. A wet line marked its passage into the joint.

“How far had it got? Beyond the cellar door. Through a gap narrower than my little finger. The bolt hadn’t contained it.”

She checked the blade, then her gloves and cuffs.

“As for what it did to the person, we still needed the attachment site. This piece couldn’t tell us whether it penetrated skin, replaced tissue, or merely held what we saw.”

Halloway wrapped the tin in her spare leather apron and lifted her pack.

“You needed everything. So did I. We weren’t going to get it by letting the specimen collect us.”

She moved toward the outside door.

“The next cut waited until we had containment.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I hand her the lamp and make for the door, my heart hammering. "It got out," I say, flatly. "That changes everything we do now."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took the lamp by its handle, keeping it clear of her coat.

“It changed our boundary,” she said. “We hadn’t established that it changed its behaviour.”

She stopped short of the outside threshold and lowered the light. A damp mat lay against the sill. She left it where it was and inspected the exposed floor on either side.

“No lifting things. No hands into dark gaps. It passed through one joint; we assumed it could pass through others until we proved otherwise.”

Behind her, the cellar door remained shut. There was no further scraping.

Silence had never earned her much confidence.

She opened the outside door with her gloved hand and examined the stone step beyond it. Dry grit, a crushed leaf, no visible wet track. She stepped across without touching the frame.

“We cleared the building first. Then the adjoining buildings if they shared a cellar wall or drain. Nobody went downstairs to fetch a cat, a purse, or an elderly relative’s irreplaceable crockery.”

She set the wrapped specimen tin on bare stone, well away from the doorway, and unbuckled the small inspection mirror from her pack.

“And I corrected another mistake.”

Holding the mirror low, she checked beneath the tin without bringing her face near it.

“I put moving tissue in a tin before I knew what contained it. A screw lid was a precaution. It wasn’t proof.”

Nothing showed around the lid. She left the tin on the stone.

“The owner could describe the drains from out here. Nobody went looking for plans inside. If there was a pump, nobody started it. We weren’t sending pieces of this into the street because the cellar offended us.”

A faint metallic tick came from beneath the leather apron.

Halloway went still.

She counted ten breaths. There was no second sound.

“Could have been the tin cooling,” she said.

She drew a broad chalk circle around it, leaving an arm’s length between the mark and the specimen.

“Could have been something else. Nobody touched it.”

Her gaze returned to the open doorway.

“‘It got out’ was useful if it stopped us trusting the door. It became dangerous if it made us imagine it everywhere and stop looking properly.”

She raised the lamp. The beam reached the cellar door but left the space beneath a nearby cupboard dark.

“We knew it reached the landing. We knew a severed piece still contracted. We did not yet know whether the whole animal could leave the water.”

Halloway backed another pace onto the stone.

“We warned people on what we knew. We kept them clear for what we didn’t.”

Her mouth tightened.

“And we described it as dangerous tissue in the drains. Not a haunted cellar. People brought shovels for drains. They brought children to see hauntings.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked past the lamp at the water.

“Finishing it wasn’t the same as cutting until we felt better.”

She unrolled her tool wrap on the dry landing. Beside the spare blades lay two masonry spikes, a short-handled hammer, and a chain with a locking hook. She laid each within reach.

“Those steps were inside its reach. I couldn’t watch your boots and my hands at once.”

She did not approach the water.

Instead, she lowered the chain beside the banister, letting the last six links enter without striking the wood. She secured the other end around the iron hinge strap above her head.

The human hand at the far wall closed.

Nothing touched the chain.

Halloway waited. Her left knee complained against the stone. At fifty, she had several joints that objected to her profession; none had proposed another income.

A pale line appeared beneath the lowest link.

“There.”

Three blunt tips enclosed the chain. They tightened successively, forcing water out between tissue and iron.

Halloway took up the slack.

The pull answered immediately.

She let two links slide through her glove, then stopped them. At the far wall, the central mass lifted an inch. The human forearm moved with it.

“Continuous attachment. Not separate animals carrying pieces.”

She drew the chain another six inches.

The thing came away from the wall.

What had appeared to be its underside unfolded into a thin sheet. Water drained through several ragged openings. Beneath that sheet lay a compact, dark body about the size of a boot, with the human forearm embedded along one side.

No torso followed it.

Halloway’s jaw tightened.

“An arm. Nothing else human visible.”

The chain suddenly slackened.

She stepped sideways.

The pale extension struck the landing where her knee had been. Its tips spread flat against the stone, then began drawing the rest of the animal toward them.

Halloway drove the first spike through the extension.

The hammer blow cracked sharply in the cellar.

Tissue bunched around the iron. A split travelled along its length, exposing wet white fibres. The pinned end continued pulling.

She placed the second spike farther along and struck twice.

The central body reached the lowest dry tread.

Its covering lifted. Underneath, paired folds opened around a hard, brown ridge. No eyes showed. The human hand opened and closed beside it, scraping its nails against the stair.

Halloway kept outside the arc of the unpinned limbs.

“The arm entered here. Skin folded inward around the attachment. Something had grown around the cut end.”

One narrow limb reached upward.

She caught it against the banister with the hook of her blade and pulled. The edge cut through. The detached length fell into the water and contracted into a loose coil.

“Still moving separately.”

She did not mistake that for progress.

The main body twisted toward the pinned extension. Its underside rolled into the light.

Between the paired folds sat a short, ridged capsule. Every remaining limb joined beneath it.

Halloway brought the hammer down.

The capsule resisted the first blow.

The second broke its outer surface.

Clear fluid ran down the tread. The human fingers closed hard enough for a nail to snap against the wood.

She struck again, directly into the opening.

The limbs drew inward together.

Halloway withdrew the hammer and waited beyond their reach.

One fold pulsed. The pinned extension shortened by half an inch.

She struck the capsule twice more, breaking the ridge against the stone beneath it. The folds collapsed. The hand loosened.

This time, nothing pulled against the spikes.

She counted sixty breaths.

Then she touched the chain with her blade and shifted it one link.

No response.

“Central body destroyed. Coordinated movement stopped.”

She remained crouched, watching the severed length below the water. It still curled slowly.

“That piece wasn’t finished.”

Halloway set the hammer beside her knee and reached for the locking hook.

“Neither were we.”

Her voice stayed level.

“But now we had something we could take apart without it choosing the order.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I move the lamp to get a better look at where the arm enters the thing's body. The edges are all wrong -- puckered, like melted wax. "You said you'd tell me," I say, my voice tight. "What's under the skin here?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway followed the light to the puckered seam.

“I’d tell you what I found. Keep clear of the cut edge.”

She took two narrow forceps from the tool wrap. With one pair she lifted a fold beside the attachment. With the other, she touched the exposed tissue beneath it.

The human fingers shifted.

Halloway stopped. She watched the broken central body, then the pinned extension. Neither moved.

“Mechanical pull,” she said. “I moved the tissue; the fingers followed. That wasn’t a response.”

She exchanged one pair of forceps for a small blade and made a short, shallow incision along the raised seam. The edges separated under gentle tension.

Beneath the skin lay a pale mesh. Its strands crossed one another irregularly, spreading away from the creature’s body along the forearm.

“Foreign tissue immediately beneath the skin. Not just wrapped around the outside.”

She lifted one strand. The surrounding skin rose with it.

“Attached at several points. It wouldn’t peel away cleanly.”

Deeper in the opening, a thicker white cord lay beside the human tendons. She traced its course with the closed tips of the forceps, without pulling.

“This continued toward the wrist. Similar appearance to the fibres in the severed piece. Similar wasn’t proof they served the same purpose.”

Halloway moved the blade back toward the puckered margin and extended the incision just enough to expose the junction. The skin turned inward there, enclosing the end of the forearm. Two pale, hard surfaces showed beneath the mesh.

She held still for a moment.

“Both forearm bones ended here. The arm had been separated before this covering finished growing around it.”

She laid the blade down.

“That didn’t tell us whether the owner was alive when it happened.”

Her voice remained flat. There was nothing useful to soften.

“The attachment extended under the skin and between deeper structures. It had more purchase than we could see from outside. How far toward the fingers, I hadn’t established.”

She covered the opening loosely with a clean square of linen.

“And I wasn’t calling those melted edges. They were folded skin held by new tissue. Remember the structure, not what it reminded you of.”

Below the tread, the detached length stirred again.

Halloway picked up the locking hook.

“The rest of the examination waited until every piece was secured. A corpse with loose ends was still a workplace hazard.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content:
I stare at the folded skin, my throat dry. "So the arm was already off," I say. "Maybe he got away."

Then I flinch because the human hand twitched again, slowly curling into a loose fist against the wet stone.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
“Maybe,” Halloway said. “We had an arm. We didn’t have the owner. That left someone to look for.”

She watched the fist without touching the linen.

This time, she had pulled nothing.

She set the locking hook down and moved her hands clear of the remains. The fingers stayed curled. Water collected beneath the wrist and dripped onto the next tread.

“That movement wasn’t mine.”

Halloway counted under her breath. At twelve, the thumb shifted across the first two fingers. At nineteen, it relaxed.

“The central body had stopped coordinating its limbs. I hadn’t established that breaking it stopped whatever was inside the arm.”

She took a shallow iron tray from her pack and placed it on the landing. Its usual occupants—spare buckles, wire, a whetstone—went into the tool wrap.

“An undignified mortuary. The previous tenants could complain later.”

Using the chain and locking hook, she drew the arm and attached body onto the tray. She kept her fingers away from the wrist. The hand dragged against the rim, opened under the pressure, then remained open when she stopped pulling.

She waited.

The little finger bent first. The others followed unevenly.

“No contact that time. Slow contraction, starting at the outside of the hand.”

She passed a length of wire across the forearm and secured it through the tray’s handles, leaving the fingers unobstructed and visible. Then she slid the tray well back from the stair edge.

“That could still have been activity left in the tissues. It could also have been the mesh acting without the body we broke. We treated it as the second until we could exclude it.”

Her gaze moved to the water.

The severed length had settled against the lowest submerged tread. Halloway lowered the hook beside it, caught its middle, and lifted it into an empty specimen jar. It folded against the glass. She screwed the lid home and stood the jar inside the tray.

Only then did she look back at the arm.

“The bones ended at roughly the same level. That suggested a single injury. It didn’t tell us whose tool, whose teeth, or whether anyone survived it.”

She tightened the wire once more.

“If the owner got away, there might be blood above the waterline, discarded clothing, witnesses. Someone might have sought help with an arm missing. Those were things we could check.”

The fist closed again, slowly, without enough force to move the tray.

Halloway watched it finish.

“We didn’t bury a person because we found part of them,” she said. “And we didn’t promise them alive because we wanted something good out of this cellar.”

She rose carefully, favouring her stiff knee.

“We had enough evidence to search. That was better than hope. Hope rarely supplied an address.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I look from the hand to the jar. "It's still trying to make a fist," I say, my own hands feeling cold. "How long do you think it'll keep doing that?"

rung_labels.evidence: Those were knuckles. The hand was closed, with the thumb tucked underneath

rung_labels.evidence: something had used a human forearm as part of its body. It had joined the limb beyond the wrist, where there should have been no joint

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Good. 'Something wrong with the shape' is where most people stop, and it's where most people get bitten." Halloway shifted the lamp a hand's breadth to the left so the light fell on the thing side-on rather than straight down. "Now say what. Start at one end and go to the other. Don't guess what it is. Tell me what's there."

She waited. Water dripped somewhere behind them, steady as a clock.

"I'll go first if you like, and you tell me where I'm wrong. Length of a tall man, lying with its back to us. Torso's the right width for a person but the spine sits too high — see the ridge? That's not a man lying on his side. That's something with more vertebrae than it should have, and it's arched. Arms — one arm — tucked under. Legs are the problem. Knee's bent the wrong direction, and it's bent that way because the joint is built that way, not because we broke it. Skin's grey where it's out of the water, but that's the lamp. Could be anything under daylight." She tilted her head. "No hair on the scalp. Ears are there, roughly where ears go. That's the bit I like least, actually. It bothered to keep ears."

She lowered the lamp an inch. "It's not breathing, or it's breathing slow enough that I can't see it from here, which for our purposes is the same thing until we're within reach. What am I missing? There's at least one thing. Look at the water around it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare hard at the water, trying to see the ripples. "It’s too still," I say, pointing. "Even if it’s not breathing, the water should... shimmer more. Like there’s oil on top."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"There it is." Halloway's voice didn't change much, but she nodded once, the small nod she gave when a student had earned it. "It's not oil. Oil would catch the lamp in colours. That's a skin on the water — thin, tacky, comes off the thing when it's wet and floats. See how it goes out about two arm-lengths and then stops? Neat edge. That's the reach of whatever it sweats when it's dying. Or pretending to."

She crouched at the top step, lamp held out over the water but well short of that edge, and studied the film with the same flat attention she'd given the corpse.

"Two things that tells us. One: it's fresh. That stuff breaks up inside the hour. So whatever we heard stop moving, that was it stopping, not some second thing we haven't met yet. Small mercy." She shifted her weight. "Two: don't put your hands in the water past that line. I knew a man in Whitby who did. Not this exact creature, a cousin. He kept the hand, but he never felt anything with it again, and he was a violinist. He took it very badly."

She stood, knees cracking, and unhooked the boat-hook from her belt — six feet of ash with an iron crook, filed sharp on the inside curve.

"So. We don't touch it. We turn it over from here and see what the front looks like. You hold the lamp. Hold it high and to my left, so my shadow doesn't fall on it — I want to see its face come round, not guess at it. And Pike." She glanced back at him. "If it moves, you don't help me. You go up the stairs. I've got the long stick and thirty years. You've got a lamp. Understood?"

She didn't wait for the answer before she reached out with the hook and set the iron, very gently, against the too-high ridge of its spine.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't answer straight away. She let the hook sit where it was and looked at the thing for another breath, the way she'd look at a bad hand of cards.

"Yes," she said. "Probably. The ears are the tell. Things that were never people don't bother with ears — they grow whatever they need to hear with and it doesn't look like that. Things that *were* people keep the ears longest. Last to go, most of the time. Don't know why. I've a theory it's because nobody looks at their own ears much, so there's nothing pulling them along when the rest changes." She shrugged, a small movement so as not to shift the hook. "That's a theory. Not a fact. Write it down as a theory."

She braced her back foot on the step.

"Here's the part that matters, though, and I want you to hear it now rather than after. Whether it was a person a month ago or a year ago or never — it stopped being one before we came down those stairs. Whatever it had for a name, it wasn't answering to it. And if it sits up in the next thirty seconds, it won't care that you asked. It'll care that you're warm." She glanced back at him, not unkindly. "You can be sorry for it later. Upstairs. With a drink. I'll be sorry with you. I've got a whole list. Not now."

She put her weight into the hook. The body came over slowly, heavier than it should have been for its length, water sheeting off the ridged back and the film on the surface tearing and closing again around it like something healing. The face came round into the lamplight.

"Right," Halloway said quietly. "Keep the lamp steady. Tell me what you see. And tell me if you recognise it — because I'd rather know now than find out from the widow."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I hold the lamp higher, my hand shaking just a little. The face is slack, grey, but... familiar. "It's the cooper's son," I say, my voice tight. "He went missing a week ago. He delivered our last barrel."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't look at Pike. She kept her eyes on the face, because the face was where the trouble would come from if it came, and she let the hook rest so the body lay half-turned against the pull of the water.

"A week," she said. "Right."

She was quiet for a moment longer than was comfortable.

"That's fast. I want you to know that's fast, because in a minute you're going to want to feel one way about this and I need you to feel two ways at once. Sorry for him — yes. Fine. But also: a man doesn't go from delivering barrels to *that* in seven days unless something's in a hurry. Most of the ones I've seen take a season. Some take years and never finish. This one grew a spine and a half and a knee that works backwards inside a week, and it kept the ears, which means it wasn't even trying that hard to get rid of him. It just — outran him."

She lifted the lamp-side of her face toward Pike, half a glance, then back to the water.

"Which brings me to the barrel. Don't answer yet, think first. Did he bring it in himself, or leave it at the door? Did he touch anything else — the well, the pump, food? Did he seem right to you? Sweating, slow, saying odd things about his hands?" Her voice stayed level, a woman taking inventory. "I'm not saying he brought it to you. I'm saying I've been wrong about that exact thing before and it cost me a very good dog. So we're going to look at the barrel before we go to bed, and we're going to look at it from the other side of the room."

The body shifted — not moving, settling, the way a wet weight does when the water finds its level under it — and Halloway's hook was already back against the ridge of spine before Pike's breath had finished catching. She held it there a five-count. Nothing.

"Settling," she said. "That was settling. You'll learn the difference. Unfortunately you'll learn it by being wrong a few times first." She eased the hook off. "Now. Practical matters, and I'm going to be blunt because blunt is faster and we've a long night.

"One. That's not going back to the cooper. Not like that. He'd never sleep again and neither would half the parish, and in a fortnight somebody's cousin would dig it up to have a look and we'd be back down here with two of them. It's going in the lime pit behind the church, and we'll tell the cooper his boy fell in the river and wasn't found. It's a lie. It's the kindest one I know. I've told it eleven times and I've never once been sorry.

"Two. Nobody drinks from anything that barrel touched until I say so. That includes you. That includes me, which I'll mind more than you will.

"Three." She turned then, properly, and looked at him in the lamplight — the shaking hand, the tight voice, the face of a man doing sums he didn't want the answer to. "You knew him, so you're going to want to do the carrying. You're not going to. I'll rig the rope and drag it up the steps from here, and you're going to stand at the top with the lamp and the door open and not touch a thing that's wet. That's not because you're soft. It's because a week ago he was a lad who delivered barrels, and the very last thing he'd want is for you to lose the feeling in your hands on his account. He'd be mortified. Coopers are polite people."

She began to uncoil the rope from her shoulder, working the knot one-handed with the ease of long habit.

"Now tell me about the barrel. Everything. Start at the door and go to the cellar, same as you did with him."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Stop there."

Halloway's hand came up, flat, the rope still hanging off her wrist. She didn't raise her voice; she never did. "Look down. Where's the edge of the film against your shins?"

She waited until he'd looked.

"You've a hand's breadth. Good. Stay on that side of it and I'll not say another word about it. Your boots are leather and your trousers are wool and neither of those is skin, but the moment it's over the top of your boot we're having a very different conversation. All right. Hold it there. That's a good angle, actually — I can see the hip."

She went back to the knot, but she was looking at the body as she worked, and when she spoke it was in the voice she used for reading a ledger aloud.

"Plainly. Fine.

"Something got into him. I don't know what, and I'll tell you honestly I may never know — there are more kinds of this than I've got years left to learn. But it got in. Through a cut, or he ate it, or he breathed it in a damp cellar not unlike this one. It doesn't take much. Once it was in, it started with the parts of him that were already changing anyway — hair, nails, the lining of the gut, all the bits a body replaces on its own. It just told them to replace themselves as something else." She flicked a glance at the bald grey scalp. "That's why the hair goes first. It was leaving already. The thing just said, don't come back.

"Then it went for the frame. That's the ridge you saw. It doesn't grow him new bones from nothing — it takes what's there and remakes it. Puts extra joints in the spine because it wants to bend a way a man doesn't. Turns the knee round because whatever it's becoming stands and moves differently, and a man's knee is in the way. That hurts. I'll not lie to you. That's a week of feeling your own skeleton argue with you." She got the knot free and began paying out a loop. "He'd have known something was wrong by the third day. Fever, most likely. Couldn't get warm. His hands would have stopped feeling right — that's the sweat starting, that film. By the fifth he'd not have wanted anyone to see him. So he'd have gone somewhere dark and wet, because that's what the thing in him wanted, and he'd have told himself it was to sleep it off."

She looked at the face for a moment, at the ears.

"Somewhere around the sixth day, he stopped being the one deciding that. And a little while after that he got hungry in a way he didn't have a word for, and he came out of wherever he'd been hiding, and he found his way down here. And then either the water was too cold for what he'd become, or it wasn't finished and it ran out of him to spend, or the two of us coming down the steps was a fright it wasn't built to survive. I don't know which. I'd say the middle one. A week's fast. It burned him up getting here."

She dropped the loop over the hook and drew it tight against the crook, then fed the running end back through her hands.

"That's what happened to him. Plainly. You asked, and you're owed it, and now you have it." Her eyes came up. "And now I'm going to ask again about the barrel, and this time I'll notice if you go round it. Because everything I just told you started with *something got into him*, and I'd very much like to know whether it was riding in your cellar first."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow hard. "He brought it right inside the kitchen. Tapped it himself with his own mallet. Sweating like he'd run the whole way here, but it was a cool day." I pause. "He... he asked for a drink of water before he left. I gave it to him. From the well."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stopped paying out rope.

She didn't freeze — freezing was for people who hadn't decided anything yet — but her hands went still on the line and she looked at the water for a long moment, doing the arithmetic where Pike could see her do it.

"All right," she said. "Thank you. That's the honest version and it's the one I needed."

She started the rope moving again, slower.

"Here's what you've just told me, laid out. He was sweating on a cool day, which puts him on the third day, maybe the fourth. That fits the week. He tapped the barrel himself, indoors, with his hands on the mallet and the bung and the staves, and at that stage his hands would have been — not slick yet. Damp. Warmer than they ought to be. He'd have been wiping them on his apron and not knowing why." She glanced at Pike. "You'd not have noticed anything on the wood. I'd not have noticed anything on the wood, and I've been looking for this for thirty years. So take that off the list of things you're going to lie awake about. There's plenty else on it."

The loop came up under the body's shoulder and she began drawing it snug, watching the head the whole time.

"The water's the part I mind. Not because he drank it. Because he'd have held the cup. And you'd have taken the cup back off him." She pulled the knot tight. "So, in order. Did he hand it back to you, or set it down? Has anybody drunk from that cup since? And has anybody — you, the girl, the dog if you've got one — been down to the well and drawn water since he left, and put their hands on the rope or the bucket where his had been?"

She let that sit exactly one breath.

"Don't answer with your face. Answer with words, and if the answer is *I don't know*, that's an answer. It's the one I get most."

She braced her boot on the step and took the strain, and the body began to slide toward the stairs through the black water, the film parting ahead of it in a slow V.

"And Pike. When we're upstairs and there's decent light, you're going to hold your hands out for me, palms up, and you're going to tell me the truth about whether you've been cold this week. I'm not asking because I think you're gone. A week's fast and it went for *him*, not the well — if it were in the water, half the street would be down here with us and I'd have heard about it before I got to the gate." The body bumped against the bottom step; she shifted her grip. "I'm asking because I'd rather know at the kitchen table than find out from the shape of you at the bottom of a cellar. Professional preference. Nothing personal."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway got the body up onto the bottom step, where the water was only to its hip, and let the rope go slack. She looked at Pike for a moment with the lamp between them.

"You went round the cup," she said. "I told you I'd notice. We'll come back to it upstairs, and you'll answer, and then I'll answer this properly with the thing on a table and a knife in my hand, because half of what you're asking I can't tell you from the outside. Nobody honest could." She wound the loose rope round her fist. "But you're right that you need it, and you might not get another look, so. What I can see from here, and what I know from the cousins."

She set the lamp-hook of the boat-hook against the body's shoulder and turned it a quarter, so the front lay square to the light.

"Skin first, because it's what you'll meet. Grey where it's dry, yes, but look at the shin — where the water's been at it. It's gone smooth. No hair follicles, no pores, no goose-flesh. That's not skin any more, that's a hide. Thicker than his was, and it's not attached the same way. On a man, skin's stitched to the muscle underneath every quarter-inch. On this, it's loose — see where it's pooled at the elbow? You could take a fold of it and it'd slide. That's so it can stretch when the frame moves in ways his frame never did. It also means a cut doesn't bleed the way you'd expect. It gapes and it weeps that film, and it doesn't slow the thing down. Don't cut it and wait for it to bleed out. It won't."

The hook moved to the ribs.

"Under that. Muscle's mostly still muscle, but it's been shifted. His shoulders have come forward and down — that's why the arm tucks under like that — and the big muscles of the back have gone long and thin to run down that extra length of spine. It's traded strength for reach. A man that size could lift a barrel. This couldn't, but it could put its hand on the far side of a room before you'd finished turning round. And the belly." She tapped the hook, very lightly, against the abdomen. It gave in a way Pike would not like. "That's not fat and it's not gas. Gut's been remade into something with fewer turns in it. Shorter. It doesn't want to digest properly any more — it wants to take something in and use it fast and get rid of the rest. That's the hunger I told you about. It's not appetite. It's a stove with the door open."

She lifted the arm with the hook, just enough to see the hand.

"Hands. Look at the nails. Not claws — people expect claws and it's not that. They've thickened and gone back into the fingertip, so the whole end of the finger's hard. It's for gripping wet surfaces. Stone, wood, a bucket rope." She let that land and moved on. "Fingers are the same length as they were, which tells you something. It didn't need to change them. His were already good enough for what it wanted. That's the part I'd remember, if I were you. It doesn't change what it doesn't have to. Everything you see different is something it *needed*."

The head last. She put the lamp closer than she had before.

"Face. Eyes have gone milky, but that's death, not the change — his eyes were probably still his the whole way through, which is a mercy of a kind. Teeth. Open the mouth if you meet a live one and have the leisure, which you won't, and you'll find the back ones flattened and the front ones loosened in the jaw. It was going to lose them and grow something else there, and it ran out of week. The nose has flattened. Ears you've seen." She straightened. "Inside the skull, I don't know, and I'll not pretend. I've opened three of the cousins and every time it was different. Twice there was a man's brain, more or less, and something grown round the bottom of it like ivy on a post. Once there wasn't much of anything, and I've never been able to decide whether that was the worse of the two."

She took up the rope again, tested the knot.

"How far it got. Skin, frame, gut, hands: finished, or near enough. Teeth, face: halfway. Head: I don't know. Call it two-thirds of a thing and one-third of a lad, and the third that was still him is the third that was still hurting." She began to haul, and the body started up the steps, shedding water. "If you meet another one, it'll be different. They always are. But it'll follow the same order, because they all want the same things in the same order — to stop being seen, to move differently, to eat. Watch for the sweat before the shape. By the time the shape's wrong, you've already met it."

She paused two steps up, breathing a little harder.

"Cup, Pike. Upstairs. I've been very patient and I'd like you to notice."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I set the lamp on the top step and scrub a hand over my face. "He left it on the pump handle. I rinsed it under the spout."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway hauled the body up another two steps before she answered, and when she did it was to the rope rather than to him.

"Rinsed it. Right."

She got the thing over the lip of the stair onto the flags of the passage, where it lay leaking, and only then did she straighten and look at him properly. Her eyes went to his hand — the one he'd just dragged across his face — and then to the lamp on the step, and then back to him.

"That hand was dry. I checked before you did it. I'll say that so you know I was watching, and so you know I'm not about to start shouting." She flexed her own fingers, working the rope-ache out of them. "Here's what I'd like you to understand about what you just told me, in the order I understand it.

"He put the cup down on the pump handle. So his hand's been on the handle. Third day, fourth — damp, not slick. Whatever comes off him at that stage, it's thin and there's not much of it. Then you picked the cup up, which put your hand where his had been, and you rinsed it under the spout, which put water over the both — cup and hand — and water's the one thing this stuff likes. It doesn't wash off in water. It moves *in* water. That's the film downstairs. So of everything you could have done with that cup, you picked the one I'd have picked to do it wrong." She said it flatly, without heat, the way she'd say the roof leaked. "I'd have done the same. Anybody would. That's why it works."

She stepped over the body — not round it, over, the way one steps over a dropped coat — and came up to the top of the stairs.

"Now the other side of the ledger, because there is one. He was three days in. A week later he's two-thirds gone and dead in your cellar, and you're standing here telling me the truth with a steady voice, which is more than most manage. If it had got a proper hold on you the day he came, you'd be sweating on me now. You're not. You're pale, but you've a right to be." She held out her own hand, palm up, and waited. "So. I said upstairs and I said decent light, and this is neither, but I've changed my mind. Hands. Both. Palms to the lamp."

She took the lamp off the step herself and held it low.

"I'm looking for three things and I'll tell you what they are so you can look too, later, when I'm not here. Nails — I want to see the pink still under them and the white edge still white, not gone grey and thick. Fingertips — I'll press them and they should go white and come back red in the time it takes me to say so. And the palm should be warm and dry, or warm and honest-sweaty from hauling a corpse about, and not cool and tacky. Cool and tacky is the one that matters. If I feel that I'll tell you, and then we'll talk about what comes next, and it won't be the lime pit, so put that out of your head."

She looked at his hands in the lamplight for longer than she'd looked at the cooper's son's face.

"And while I'm at it. The pump handle gets scrubbed with lime and then it gets scrubbed again. The cup goes in the fire — I don't care if it was your mother's. The barrel." Her eyes came up. "You've not said what was in it, and you've not said whether anybody's had a drink out of it since he tapped it. I'll have that answer in the kitchen. I'll have it before I sit down, because if the answer's yes, I want to know how many chairs to count."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway had the body on the scullery table with an oilcloth under it and a bucket at each end, and she'd tied her sleeves back with string above the elbow. The knife was a short one, curved, the kind for skinning rabbits. She'd told him that before she started, as if it mattered.

"Right. Speaking as I go. If I stop, it's because I've found something I don't understand, not because I've gone squeamish. I did squeamish in my twenties and got it out of the way."

She drew the blade down from the notch of the collarbone to the top of the pubic bone in one pass, leaning on it more than she'd have needed to for a man.

"Hide, as I said. Quarter-inch and tough. It's not cutting so much as splitting — feel that catch? There's a grain to it now, running lengthways. Skin doesn't have grain. This does." She laid the two flaps back and pinned them with a pair of forks from the dresser. "Under it. On a man you'd have fat here, yellow, a finger's width on a well-fed lad and he was well-fed, coopers eat. It's gone. Every scrap. Burned it for the change — that's the first thing these do, they spend the fat. What's in its place is this."

She lifted something with the knife-point: a pale, wet sheet, faintly grey, clinging to the muscle beneath like the skin on boiled milk.

"That's what makes the film. It's a layer of it all over, between hide and meat, and it sweats through. Smell it — no, from there, don't lean in. Ammonia, yes. And under that something sweet. Cellar-sweet, like rot on stone. That's the smell you'll notice before anything else if there's a live one in the room with you, and you'll think it's the drains. It's never the drains."

The knife went in along the ribs. She counted under her breath and then said it aloud.

"Fourteen a side. He had twelve. The two extra are down here at the bottom, small, not properly joined to the breastbone — they're floating, and they're new. Bone's softer than it ought to be, see how the blade marks it. It grew them in a week and hadn't finished hardening them. Look at the ends: that's cartilage, not bone. Same story as the teeth. It ran out of him before it ran out of plan."

She cracked the ribs back with the heel of her hand — two sharp sounds, then a wet one — and held the lamp closer herself, so he could keep his where it was.

"Lungs. Still lungs. Smaller than I'd like. See how they're sitting low and back, pushed out of the way? Something wanted the room. Heart's — " She put two fingers on it, pressed. "Heart's his. Ordinary. Big for a lad, but he'd been carrying barrels up hills all his life. That's him. I'll say that when I find him, so you know which bits to be sorry for." She moved down. "Liver's gone dark and gone small. It was working hard. Stomach's here and it's — right, this is what I meant about the stove."

She slit it. It was nearly empty, the walls thickened to something like leather, and the smell that came out was sharp enough that she turned her head for a moment before going back.

"Nothing in it. He'd not eaten in days, or he'd eaten and it went straight through. The gut below — look — " She lifted a loop on the knife. It was thick as a wrist and short, and there was very little of it. "Six feet, maybe. A man has near thirty. The rest is just gone. Absorbed, spent, I don't know. What's left is one straight run, thick-walled, no pockets. That's not for digesting food. That's for getting whatever it eats into the blood as quick as it can and dropping the rest out the back. Waste not want not." She set the loop down. "Kidneys are twice the size they should be. Whatever it lives on, there's a lot to filter out. That's the ammonia."

She wiped the knife on the oilcloth and went to the spine, working the blade in beside it and levering.

"Twenty-nine bones in his back when he woke up a fortnight ago. I've got — " She counted with the knife-tip, unhurried, touching each one. "Thirty-six. Seven new. All in the middle where the bend is, and all wedge-shaped. Thin at the front, thick at the back. That's what makes the arch. It's not that he's hunched. It's that his spine is *built* curved now, and it'd have taken effort for him to stand straight. By the end he couldn't have." She paused. "He'd have been in the dark somewhere, trying to stand up, and finding that his own back wouldn't let him. That's the third or fourth day. If you want one thing to be sorry about, that's mine. Have it."

She straightened, pressed the back of her wrist to her forehead, and looked at what was on the table.

"How far. Fat, gut, hide, spine: done. Ribs, teeth, face: started and stopped. Lungs and heart and eyes and most of the muscle: his, still, right to the end. Call it what I said downstairs, two-thirds and one. But the two-thirds is *inside*. From the outside you'd have given it a quarter. That's the lesson. They look less far along than they are, always, because the last thing they change is the bit you see."

She set down the knife and picked up the bone-saw from the dresser, and did not yet put it to anything.

"I'll open the head. You'll not like it and neither will I, and I've told you I don't know what I'll find. Before I do, though." She looked across the body at him, the lamp between them. "Your hands were fine. Warm, dry, nails pink. I looked while you were fetching the oilcloth and I'd have said so sooner but you've been very busy asking me questions. Which I've noticed you do instead of answering them. It's a good trick. I use it myself." She set the saw's teeth against the crown of the skull. "So: the barrel.
