What was in it, and who's drunk from it since he tapped it. I'm going to start cutting on the count of three whether you've answered or not, and I'd rather have the answer than the silence. One."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Beer. The new batch." I keep my eyes on the saw. "I drank from it. Yesterday."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Two," Halloway said, and then, "three," and the saw went in.

She didn't look up. She kept her eyes on the line of the cut and her weight on the stroke, and the sound filled the scullery for a while, and when she spoke it was between pulls, in pieces.

"Beer. Right. Yesterday." Stroke. "How much?" She didn't wait. "Doesn't matter. I'll ask anyway in a minute, but it doesn't matter, because a mouthful's the same as a pint for this. It's not a poison. It doesn't go by the dose. It goes by whether it got in or it didn't."

She finished the cut across the crown and started the second, down behind the ear, and only then did she glance at him — once, quick, a look at his forehead and the collar of his shirt.

"You're not sweating. I want you to notice that, because I'm noticing it, and I'm noticing it hard. He was sweating by the third day. You're a day in and dry. That's either because it's slow in you, or because there was nothing in the barrel to get in, and I'll tell you honestly which I think."

The saw caught on something and she worked it free.

"Beer's not water. It's been boiled and it's been fermented and there's drink in it, and I've never — " she stopped, corrected herself with the small grimace of a woman who didn't like being caught rounding up — "I've *rarely* known this sort to sit happy in anything a yeast has been at. The cousins don't like spirits. Don't like vinegar. Don't like anything that's already had something living in it and killing it. It's the one bit of luck in the whole business. If he'd brought you a cask of well-water, I'd be having a different conversation, and I'd be having it with a rope in my hand."

She set the saw down and put the flat of the knife into the cut and levered. The top of the skull came away with a sound like a boot out of mud.

"Also. He tapped it. He didn't fill it. His hands went on the bung and the mallet and the outside of the staves, and the beer was already inside and sealed. Whatever came off his palms went on the wood and then — " she nodded at the pump handle, visible through the door, " — under the spout. Not into the cask. I'll not swear to it. But if I had to lay money, I'd say the barrel's the least of what he touched in this house, and you've been worrying at the wrong end."

She lowered the lamp over the open skull, and was quiet.

Then: "Brain's his. Most of it. There's the ivy." She touched the knife-tip to it — a grey lace, fine as roots, laid over the underside where the brain met the stem, and down into the neck. "Thicker than I've seen it. It's had a week and it went here first, I think, before the spine. That's new to me. Write it down. It's wrapped round the bit at the bottom that does breathing and hunger and not much else, and it's left the top alone. So he was still thinking. Right to the end, near enough. Just not the one deciding what to do about it."

She straightened and looked at Pike properly across the table, the way she had at the bottom of the stairs, without hurry.

"Here's what happens now, and none of it's hard. You don't die of a mouthful of beer. Not tonight. Barrel gets bunged, carried out — by me — and burned, staves and all, and I'd like a word with whoever made the brewing of this go so catastrophically to waste. You sleep in the kitchen where I can see you. Every morning for the next seven you hold your hands out and I look at them, and every evening you tell me if you've been cold, and if you lie to me I'll know, because you're a very bad liar and it's the thing I like best about you." She picked up the saw again, considered it, put it down. "On the eighth morning, if your nails are still pink, I'll say so, and you can have a drink. Not that drink."

She wiped her hands on the oilcloth, one finger at a time.

"And Pike. You told me. Straight out, with the saw going. You'd be surprised how many don't. It's usually the not-telling that finishes them, not the thing itself." She reached for the bucket. "Hold the lamp lower. I want to see how far down the neck that ivy goes before I decide how worried to be about you, and I'd rather decide from evidence than from your face, because your face has been telling me it's already dead since the cellar and it's wrong."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway came to the scullery door with the towel still in her hands, and stood there working it between her fingers, and looked at him on the steps for a moment before she said anything.

"All right," she said. "Finish it. The neck, then the rest. I'll not stop to ask if you want it, since you've said."

She leaned a shoulder on the door frame.

"The ivy goes down as far as I could follow it with a rabbit-knife, which is to the top of the shoulders. It's thickest where the skull meets the spine — there's a knot of it there the size of a walnut, sitting on the stem like a hand round a throat — and from that it sends two runners down either side of the backbone, inside the canal, alongside the cord. They thin as they go. By the fourth bone down I could still see them. By the seventh I couldn't, but I could feel them with the knife-tip, a roughness where there ought to be smooth. Past that I stopped. Not because I was afraid to look. Because I'd have had to take the whole spine out to follow it and there's a limit to what I'll do to a cooper's son on a scullery table for the sake of my own education."

She folded the towel and hung it over her arm.

"Here's what I make of it. It went to the head first. Wrapped the bottom of the brain — the bit that does breathing and swallowing and hunger, the bit that's older than thinking — and left the top alone. Then it went *down*, along the cord, and everywhere a runner reached, the frame started changing. The new bones in the spine sit exactly where the runners run. The ribs it grew are at the bottom of where I could feel them. The knee it turned round — I opened that too, while you were being sick in the yard, I'll not pretend I didn't hear — the knee's got a thread of it in the joint, fine as a hair, and nothing above or below." She lifted a shoulder. "So it's not growing him from the outside in. It's a vine on a trellis, and the trellis is his own nerves, and it changes whatever it's touching. Which means the order it changes a body in is the order it *reaches* things in. Head, neck, back, ribs, hips, legs. Hands last, or not at all, if the runners never get down the arms. His hadn't. His hands were his. I looked."

She was quiet a moment.

"That's more than I knew this morning. It's more than I knew after the third cousin I opened. I'll write it down properly when there's daylight, and you'll sign under it as witness, because in twenty years somebody'll want to know how I know and I'd like to be able to say I had a man in the room who wasn't a fool."

She pushed off the door frame.

"Now the rest. You stay where you are. I mean that as an instruction, not a kindness."

She went back into the scullery and he could hear her from the steps: the scrape of the forks coming out of the oilcloth, the wet slap of the flaps being laid back down, the skull-cap set in place with a small dull sound and then a longer one as she bound it there with a strip of linen, round and under the jaw and knotted at the crown. She talked while she did it, not loud, the way a woman talks to herself in a kitchen.

"Head back on. Not for him. For me. I've carried one without and it's a thing you only need to do once." A pause, and the sound of oilcloth being drawn up and over. "Cloth goes round twice. Once for what's leaking and once for what's going to leak when he's moved. Rope round the ankles, rope round the chest under the arms, and one long loop between so I can carry him like a sack and not like a man. Nobody carries these like a man. You put your arms round the middle of one and your face ends up an inch from theirs, and I've done that too, and no."

The rope creaked. She grunted, and there was a heavy sliding sound and then her boots on the flags, slow, and then she came past the foot of the stairs with the long grey bundle over her shoulder and did not look up at him.

"Door."

He got up and opened it and she went out into the dark with it and he heard her in the yard, breathing, and the yard gate, and then nothing for a long while.

When she came back she was without the bundle and there was white dust to her elbows and across the front of her coat, and she was rubbing her hands together as she came through the door, palm to palm, the way one does when they sting.

"Lime pit's behind the church, as I said. Verger's an old friend and doesn't ask. He's under two feet of it and he'll be under three by morning, when I've been back with the barrow. In a fortnight there'll be nothing you'd know for a man. In a year there'll be nothing at all. That's the point of lime. It's not kind, but it's honest, and it doesn't leave anything behind for a cousin to dig up." She looked at her hands. "It's also taken the top skin off my palms, which is why I've been telling you to keep yours dry all night. You'll see the sense of it now."

She went past him to the kitchen. He heard the barrel being moved — a hollow scrape, a slosh, a grunt — and then the back door again, and then a sound he knew, which was an axe going into wood. It went on for some time. When it stopped there was a silence and then the crackle of a fire catching, and the smell of it came in through the open door: burning oak, and under it the flat, spoiled-bread smell of good beer going up in smoke.

She came back in with the axe over her shoulder and soot on her face where she'd wiped it with a wrist.

"Staves, hoops, bung, and about eight gallons of what would have been a very decent bitter. I tasted none of it, and I'd like that noted as the single greatest act of self-denial in my professional life." She set the axe by the door. "The fire goes till it's ash and the ash goes in the pit with him. Iron hoops I'll bury separate. Not because they're dangerous. Because someone'll find them in the ash and want to know what was burned, and I've no wish to explain it."

She took a pail from under the sink and the lime-sack from where she'd left it inside the door, and she went to the pump, and he watched her from the steps. She didn't touch the handle. She poured the lime over it dry, a fistful at a time, till it was heaped white, and then she took a bristle-brush from the pail and scrubbed the handle the way one scrubs a doorstep, hard, in one direction, with her face turned away from the dust. Then she did the spout. Then the trough beneath it. Then she drew a pail of water with her sleeve pulled down over her fist, and poured it over the whole, and did it again, and stood back.

"That's once. It gets done again in the morning and again the morning after. Third time you can do it, with your sleeve down, and I'll watch. Cup." She held out her hand and he pointed to the dresser, and she went and got it — a plain tin thing, dented — and looked at it a moment and then put it into the range, into the coals, and shut the door on it. "It'll not burn. It'll get hot enough that nothing on it lives, and then I'll take it out with the tongs and put it in the pit. If it was your mother's, I'm sorry. If it wasn't, I'm still sorry, because it was a good cup and there are fewer of those than you'd think."

She came and stood at the foot of the cellar steps, and looked up at him with the lamp in his lap.

"That's it finished. All of it. He's in the ground under lime and there's a lie ready for his father in the morning, which I'll tell, not you, because you'll want to and you'll get it wrong and he'll know. The barrel's smoke. The pump's white. The cup's in the fire. The cellar — " she glanced past him into the dark, at the water and the torn film on it, breaking up now, going grey and stringy the way she'd said it would " — the cellar stays shut for a week and then we pump it out and lime the flags, and if there's a smell after that we do it again, and if there's a smell after *that* I'll come back with a man who's got a bigger pump and fewer questions. And you sleep in the kitchen and you show me your hands, and on the eighth day I'll say you're clear, because you are, because I've seen what it does to a body it's got into and I've seen you, and you're not it."

She held out her hand again, palm up, the raw lime-burned skin of it catching the lamp.

"Give me that. You've held it long enough. Go and sit by the range where it's warm and I'll put the kettle on, and we'll have that drink, and I'll tell you the names of the eleven. You'll not remember them. That's fine. I do."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I give her the lamp, my fingers stiff. "Tell me their names," I say. "All of them. I'll remember."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took the lamp and set it on the table, and for a moment she simply stood with her back to him, looking at the range, working her burned hands open and closed.

"All right," she said. "You'll remember. I believe you. I said you wouldn't so you'd not feel bad when you didn't, and now you've gone and made a liar of me, which is twice tonight."

She got the kettle on and found two cups on the dresser that weren't tin, and a bottle from the inside of her coat that she set down harder than she meant to. She poured two fingers into each and pushed one across the table and sat down opposite him with her own between her palms, not drinking yet.

"In order. That's the only way I can do it. If I go by how much they bother me I'll start in the middle and never get to the ends."

She held up one finger — the lime had cracked the skin at the knuckle and she looked at it as if it belonged to someone else.

"Tom Ashby. Whitby, and I was twenty-one and I'd been at it a year and thought I knew something. Fisherman. Found him in a net-loft with his arms gone long and his jaw gone wrong and I'd no idea what I was looking at, none. His mother came to the door while I was still standing over him. I told her he'd gone over the side off the Scar and the sea had him. She said, *it always takes the good ones*, and thanked me. That's when I learned the lie. I didn't decide on it. It just came out, and it worked, and I've kept it since like a knife that fits the hand."

Second finger.

"Agnes Cole. Laundress. Hands in water twelve hours a day for thirty years and I've thought since that's why it took her so fast. Wet trades. I look twice at anyone in a wet trade now — brewers, tanners, your cooper's son with his soaking-tubs. She had a daughter about your age who kept asking to see the body. I said the river'd had it a week and there was nothing to see. There'd have been less to see if I'd let her. That one I'm not sorry for at all."

Third. Halloway's hand stopped, and she drank before she went on, and when she did it was shorter.

"Jem Pardoe. Nine years old. I'll give you the name and I'll not give you the rest, because I've never given anyone the rest and I'm not starting at this table. River. His father believed me. That's all of that."

Fourth.

"Wat Hendry, drover. Big man. Took a season to go and fought it the whole way — I found him with his own belt round his ankle tied to a hitching-post, so he'd not walk off in the night. Did that himself, with what he had left. I've a great respect for Wat Hendry. Told his brother he'd gone in at the ford with the cattle."

Fifth and sixth together — she lifted two fingers.

"Daniel and Saul Minter. Brothers, millers, and I count them separate because their mother did. Mill-race, so the river lie was near enough true for once. I found them in the wheel-pit within a yard of each other and I've never known whether one gave it to the other or whether the water gave it to them both. Wet trade again. You'll notice I keep saying it."

Seventh.

"Bess Tullow. Midwife." Halloway turned the cup in her hands. "She'd been to three births before anyone thought to look at her hands, and I went to all three houses after, and looked at three infants, and they were fine. All three. I've never understood why. I've a theory that it doesn't take in the very young, but I had three and that's not enough to call it a fact, and I'd not want anyone to test it. River. Her husband didn't believe me, but he wanted to, and that does as well."

Eighth.

"Cuthbert Lane. He was eighty-one. It barely bothered with him — thickened the skin a bit, put two bones in his neck, and stopped. I think it looked at him and decided there wasn't enough left worth remaking." The corner of her mouth moved, not quite a smile. "He'd have been pleased with that. He was a difficult old sod and he'd have liked to be too much trouble for it. Told the parish he'd fallen in fishing. He hadn't fished in twenty years but nobody argued."

Ninth. Her voice didn't change, but she looked at the range rather than at Pike.

"Hal Maddox. I knew him. Drank with him, on and off, for eleven years. He sent for me himself, by which time he couldn't hold the pen, so a neighbour wrote it. I got there on the fifth day and he still knew me on the sixth and I did what needed doing on the seventh and I'll not dress that up. His wife knew the river was two miles off across a field he'd not have crossed in the state he was in. I told her anyway. She looked at me a long while and then she said, *the river, yes*, and we never spoke of it again. That's the hardest that lie's ever been to say and the easiest it's ever been believed. I still don't understand that."

Tenth.

"Sarah Penn. Dairymaid. Wet trade. I'll not say more than that because there isn't more. I found her, I did it, I said the river. She was nobody's and no one asked twice, and that's its own kind of terrible, but it's not one I've a story for."

Eleventh. She held up the last finger and looked at it.

"Nathaniel Grey. Last spring. Curate. A curate, Pike — dry as dust, never touched a wet thing in his life bar the font, and I've wondered since about the font. He'd locked himself in the vestry and written it all down as it happened to him. Every day. What he felt, where it hurt, what he was thinking. I've got the pages in my coat. I read them once and I'll not read them again, but I've got them, because he wrote them for someone to read and I'll be damned if it isn't going to be me." She put the hand flat on the table. "His bishop believed the river before I'd finished saying it. He'd have believed a good deal less."

She sat back.

"That's eleven. Tomorrow morning it's twelve, when I go to the cooper. And that's the thing I wanted to say, which is why I've told you all of them instead of just the ones that make a good story." She looked at him over the cup. "You knew him. You'll know his name. I didn't have that for a single one of the others when I first stood over them — I got the names after, from the ones I lied to. So this is the first time I've gone to tell the river lie already knowing who I'm lying about, and I'd like it if I went knowing his name from you rather than getting it off his father with the lie half out of my mouth."

She drank, and set the cup down, and waited.

"What was it? His name. Not *the cooper's son*. He had one, and he'd want it in the list."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Eamon," I say, and the word tastes like lime. "His name was Eamon."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway said nothing for a moment. Then she said it back.

"Eamon."

She turned the name over the way she'd turned the cup, as if checking it for a crack.

"Right. Eamon. Not Ned, not Eddie, none of the things people do to it. Eamon." She nodded once. "That's a name you have to mean. His mother meant it."

She reached inside her coat and brought out a small book with a soft cover, black gone brown at the corners, and a stub of pencil tied to it with a thread. She did not open it to the front. She opened it near the middle, where a page had eleven lines on it in a hand that had changed over the years — the first two rounder, younger, the last few pressed hard — and below them a good deal of white.

She licked the pencil, and wrote, and Pike could hear it scratch. Then she turned the book round on the table so it faced him, and slid it an inch toward him, and took her hand off it.

*12. Eamon. Cooper's son. A week. The ivy went to the head first. Hands still his.*

"You've read it. Now you're the second person alive who knows there's a page, and the first who's seen it." She took the book back and closed it and put it away, and buttoned the coat over it. "I'd not make anything of that. I've no one else to show it to. That's all it is."

She finished what was in her cup.

"Here's how it'll go in the morning, so you'll not lie awake building it wrong. I'll go before he's opened the shop. I'll not sit down — you don't sit down for this, it says you've come to stay. I'll say I was down at the river on other business and I've heard, and I'm sorry, and the water's high this month and it doesn't give back what it takes. He'll ask if there's a body. I'll say no. He'll ask if there's a chance. I'll say no, in the same voice, because a kind *maybe* is the cruellest thing you can hand a man in that state — it's a week of standing on the bank. Then I'll say his boy was polite and careful and did good work, and I'll mean it, because he tapped that barrel clean and square with his hands already going wrong on him, and that's a craftsman." She set the cup down. "And then I'll leave, and he'll not remember my face by Sunday, which is how it should be."

The kettle had begun to tick on the range. She got up to see to it, and stopped with her back to him, one lime-white hand on the rail.

"He'd have hated the cellar, you know. Not the dying. The water. A cooper spends his whole life keeping water on the right side of the wood." She lifted the kettle off. "There. That's the sorry, and that's the drink, and that's the name in the book. I said we'd do it upstairs and we've done it. You'll not feel better. That's not what it's for."

She came back with the pot and set it down between them.

"Hands," she said. "Palms up. Then bed. I'll take the chair by the door."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I hold my hands out, palms up. They’re steady now. “Do you ever worry,” I ask, “that you’ll forget their faces?”

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The body came over slowly, heavier than it should have been for its length, water sheeting off the ridged back and the film on the surface tearing and closing again around it like something healing. The face came round into the lamplight.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: It takes what's there and remakes it. Puts extra joints in the spine because it wants to bend a way a man doesn't. Turns the knee round because whatever it's becoming stands and moves differently, and a man's knee is in the way. That hurts.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Skin first, because it's what you'll meet. Grey where it's dry, yes, but look at the shin — where the water's been at it. It's gone smooth. No hair follicles, no pores, no goose-flesh. That's not skin any more, that's a hide.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She drew the blade down from the notch of the collarbone to the top of the pubic bone in one pass... She laid the two flaps back and pinned them with a pair of forks from the dresser

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She leaned a shoulder on the door frame. "All right," she said. "Finish it. The neck, then the rest. I'll not stop to ask if you want it, since you've said."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway waded one step, then stopped, boots sunk to the ankle in the silt. The water was cold and it smelled like an old coin — copper and rot — which was its own kind of answer.

"Look at the shoulders," she said. "Then look at the elbows."

She moved the lamp slowly, left to right, so the shadow would do the work for them. The thing at the far end lay mostly face-down against the brick, half out of the water, wearing a man's coat. The coat was fine. The coat fit. Everything under it did not.

"Count the joints for me when you're ready. I'll wait." She shifted her weight, and the water made a small apologetic noise. "For the record, I make it four elbows. Which is two more than the good Lord issues, and I've been at this thirty years, so I'd have noticed a policy change."

She lifted the lamp a touch higher. The head sat too low between the shoulders, tucked forward like it had been screwed on by someone in a hurry.

"Also it's wearing boots. Size eleven, I'd guess. So somebody dressed it after, or it dressed itself, and I'd very much like to know which."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, counting the joints in the lamplight. "Four elbows. You're right." My voice comes out thin. "The boots are tied. Too neat for someone dressing a... body."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked at the boots for a while. Lace through every eyelet, both bows pulled even. Nobody ties a dead man's boots. You shove them on and you're done, because dead men don't complain about the fit.

"Tied by hand," she said. "Steady hand. Which is worse than neat." She raised the lamp until the light fell flat across the water between them and the thing. "Now look at the surface. Tell me what's not happening."

Nothing was happening. That was the point. No ripple at the collar of the coat, no ring spreading from the nostrils, no film of breath on the cold air. Four feet of water and a face half in it, and the water lay like a pane of glass around the head.

"It's not breathing," she said. "Hasn't been since before we came down. But it was moving a minute ago, so breathing's off the table as a test." She reached back, slow, and unhooked the boat pole from the wall bracket behind her — ash shaft, iron hook, older than either of them. "I'm going to put this under the shoulder and roll it. If it comes up, we leave. If it doesn't, we still leave, but we take a photograph first."

She planted the pole and glanced back at Pike. "Door was barred from the outside. I checked twice, because I didn't like the answer the first time. So either it came in here and barred the door behind itself, or somebody locked it in. Either way, we're not the first people to have a bad evening in this cellar."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't answer straight away, because the honest answer was a paragraph and Pike deserved the whole of it.

"Ask me again in ten minutes," she said. "Here's what I've got until then. The smell's copper and rot, which means it's been in the water long enough to start giving something back — weeks, not hours. But the coat is good wool and it hasn't felted, and the boots are sound. That's a contradiction, and I don't like it."

She worked the pole a half-step closer, angling the hook toward the near shoulder without touching yet.

"As for whether it was a person — it's wearing a person's clothes, and the coat fits. Fits four elbows. That's not a man's coat with extra room in it, that's a coat cut for the shape. Which means either somebody tailored it, or the thing's been wearing this shape long enough to own it." She paused. "Both of those are bad. They're bad in different directions and I'd rather know which."

She nodded at the body's near side, the coat's hem just clear of the water.

"There's a maker's label inside the collar. Wool coat like that, there'll be a shop name, a town. I want you to tell me if it's a town you've heard of. Don't reach under it — use the pole tip, lift the collar, read it off."

She set her feet in the silt, both hands on the shaft.

"I'm going to roll it while you do that. Say the name loud when you've got it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath and step forward, my fingers closing around the boat pole. "Alright." I use the iron hook to carefully lift the sodden collar, squinting in the lamplight. "It says... Hartnell & Sons. Burford." I glance back at her. "That's a town. I've heard of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Burford," Halloway said, and turned the word over once, the way you turn a stone you've just picked up and don't yet know what's under it. Two days east. Market town, decent bread, and a winter she'd spent in a barn outside it the year she stopped counting her losses and started counting her reasons. "Hartnell and Sons. Gold leaf on black, I've seen the sign. Shop sold two things well and nothing else."

She filed it. Then she rolled the thing.

The hook went in under the shoulder, she set her weight back into the silt, and the body came over slow. Slower than a body wants to. Four feet of water fights you the whole way and it was fighting. She felt the drag of it up the ash shaft, felt it through both palms — and then the coat fell open and she stopped pulling and just held the lamp, because there was something there to look at.

No blood. She corrected herself: blood at the collar, dried, old. But where the hook had scored a line across the ribs, the skin had opened like a seam. No fat, no give, no welling. Just the cut, and along the cut, small and even, stitches. The same thread as the boot laces. The same tension as the coat's hem.

"Ah," she said. "There it is."

She brought the lamp closer and did not touch it with her hand. "Coat's Hartnell's. Stitching's the same hand. So either somebody's been doing that shop's work without the shop, or Hartnell's been doing more than coats and keeping it off the sign." She glanced back at Pike. "That name goes upstairs and into the book, because I've seen thirty years of bad tailoring and none of it this patient."

Then the thing's hand closed on the iron hook.

Not a twitch. Not a spasm. A grip — fingers wrapping the shaft, deliberate, the way a man picks up a tool he means to use.

Halloway went very still, both hands on the pole, water lapping at her boots.

"Nobody pull," she said, quiet. "And nobody run. Running makes a sound, and I'd like to hear what this one sounds like first."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept both hands on the shaft and her eyes on the fingers. Four of them, wrapped at the second joint, thumb across the top. The grip wasn't crushing. It was *holding* — the way you hold a rail on a stair you don't trust. Which meant something behind those eyes was doing arithmetic.

"Plainly," she said. "All right. Plainly, somebody took a man apart and put him back together wrong, and did it slowly, and did it well."

She nodded down at the open coat without moving her head much.

"Stitches in the skin, even tension, same thread as the boot laces. Same thread as the hem on that coat. That's not butchery, that's a trade. Whoever did it knew what they were doing and had the time to do it twice, because you don't get that tension on a first attempt. The four elbows are deliberate — they're not breaks, they're *fittings*. Additions. Like a cabinetmaker puts a drawer in."

The water lapped once against her shin.

"The copper smell's the tell. Four feet of water and it's been giving something back — that's weeks of seep, which means it's been sitting in this cellar long enough to have gone cold. But the hand on this pole is warm." She said it flat, the way she'd say a price. "Cold cellar, cold water, warm hand. Those three things don't go in a sentence together. So it isn't a corpse and it isn't a man, and the coat fits it, which means whoever built it built it *to that shape*. Tailor's work on a tailor's body. I'd bet money the same hands did both."

She drew one slow breath through her nose. No hurry in it.

"Best plain answer I've got: somebody in or near Burford is in the trade of making these, and this one either walked out of the shop or got carried out. Door was barred from the outside. I've stopped calling that a mystery. Somebody shut this in here and left it to soak, and it's been soaking long enough to learn the room."

The fingers on the pole tightened — not a jerk, a *settle*, like a hand taking up slack before a lift. Halloway felt the ash shaft flex against her palm, one degree, then hold.

"Now it's holding a boat pole," she said, "and it hasn't pulled yet, and that's the part I don't like, because anything that wanted us dead would have pulled the second it had the hook. It's waiting to see what we do. So we do something boring."

She didn't let go. She set her heels deeper in the silt and kept her voice even.

"Pike. You keep that lamp exactly where it is. Don't move it closer to the face and don't move it away. Then tell me the count of the stairs behind you, because when I let go of this pole I want to be walking up them without looking."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Thirteen steps," I say, my throat tight. "All of them wet." The lamplight trembles, just a little, in my hand. "What if it follows?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took the question seriously, because a serious question deserves a serious answer and because answering bought her two more seconds of standing still.

"If it follows, it follows slowly," she said. "Four feet of water fights every step of it, and it's been soaking in this cellar for weeks, so it knows this room better than it knows a staircase. Thirteen wet steps is a bad place to learn to walk. That's not a comfort, that's arithmetic."

She kept both hands on the shaft. The fingers on the hook had not moved again — no pull, no twist, just that patient, settled grip, like a man holding a door for somebody he isn't sure is coming.

"Here's what worries me more. It's not trying. Thirty years says anything that means us harm does it in the first second it has the reach. This one took the pole and *stopped*. That's not an animal. Animals don't stop." She exhaled slowly. "So when we go up those stairs, we are not running from it. We're leaving a room. There's a difference, and the difference is the whole of what keeps you alive."

She set her heels, took one more long look down the shaft at the thing's hand, and let go.

Both hands off, both arms up, one slow step back. The water complained about the boot. The pole stayed where it was — the thing holding one end of it, the other end resting across the water like a bridge to nowhere, and neither of them moving.

"Lamp's yours to carry," she said, still backing, silt sucking at each step. "Hold it low and to the side, not over your head. Light above the eyes makes you a target; light beside the knee makes you a shadow on the wall and shadows don't get grabbed."

Three steps. Four. The hook had not moved. She did not look away from it to count, she counted by the feel of her own heels finding the risers.

"Now. The bar on that door was on the outside when we came in, which means we did not open it and we did not close it, and I've had that thought in my mouth for an hour and I've been spitting it out. So when we're at the top, you do not touch the door first. You stand left of the jamb with the lamp. I open it, because I'm the one who's going to be looking at what's on the other side, and I'd rather it be me." A pause. "If the bar's still off and the yard's empty, we walk to the road and we don't stop until we can see the town lights. If the bar's back on —" she reached the bottom step and put her hand flat on the wet stone — "then somebody's been in the house while we were down here, and the plan changes to something I'll tell you when I've got my breath."

She climbed. Wet stone, thirteen of them, one hand on the wall, no light of her own, following the lamp.

"Last thing," she said, quieter, over her shoulder. "You asked what happened to it. Plainly. When we're out, you write the name down — Hartnell and Sons, Burford — and you write the time, and you write that the door was barred from outside. Three facts. Everything else I told you is a theory, and theories don't go in the book." Her boot found the twelfth step. "The book's for what we saw. The rest of it's just the story we tell ourselves so we can sleep."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept climbing while she talked, because standing still on a wet staircase to deliver a lecture was how you ended up with a lecture and a broken ankle.

"Here's the whole of it, as far as I got. I'll mark the parts I'm guessing at."

She counted off against the wall with her free hand, the one not on the stone.

"One. The skin's been treated like cloth. Where my hook scored it across the ribs, it opened along a line and stopped. No fat under it. No give. No welling. A knife through a man's side leaves a wound — ragged, wet, bleeding. This left a *seam*. Clean as a hem. And along the seam, stitches. Small, even, tension matched across every one, same thread as the boot laces, same thread as the coat's hem. That's not a wound closed up. That's a seam sewn. There's a difference and the difference is a trade."

She took the next riser.

"Two. Four elbows. Two of those are fittings, not breaks. A break heals crooked, it hurts, it leaves a callus you can feel through the skin. A fitting's made. There's a joint in there — a hinge, a socket, something with a pin in it — set into the arm at a place a man doesn't have a joint. Same as I said downstairs. You don't put a drawer in a chest by accident."

"Three. The head sat low and forward, neck too short or the spine re-set. I never got my hands on it, so that one's a guess. But it didn't sit the way a head sits. It sat the way a lamp sits on a table. Put there."

"Four, and this is the one that breaks the arithmetic. Cold room, cold water, warm hand. Not hot. Warm, the way a man's hand is when he's been holding a cup. So something in there is still moving heat around, and it isn't blood, because there was no blood when I cut it. Blood's the pump. No pump, no heat. So either it's got something else doing the work, or the warmth's residual and it's been cooling slower than it has any business to."

She reached the top riser and put her back flat against the wall beside the door, lamp side, and kept her voice down.

"What it took, I don't know. That's the honest answer and I won't dress it. I saw no incisions where you'd take a kidney or an eye — nothing harvested. So if the man's still in there, whatever's been added is *on top of him*, not instead of him. Which is worse, not better. It means whoever's doing this isn't stripping a body for parts. They're building. Building takes a plan, a purpose, and a workshop. Workshops have addresses. We've got one."

She glanced at the door, then back down the stairs once, quick, the way you check a knot.

"Now. For next time. Write this down when we're clear, because you asked and because it'll keep you breathing."

She held up her hand and folded the fingers as she went.

"Count the joints before you touch anything. Four elbows means made. Two means maybe made. One odd joint means you've met a problem I haven't, and you should assume it's smarter than you.

"Check the laces. Bows pulled even means hands, and hands mean intent.

"Check the thread. If the skin's stitched, match the thread to the clothes. Same spool means same maker.

"Check the temperature twice — wrist and chest — with the back of your hand, not the palm. Warm wrist, cold chest means something's moving in there. Warm all through means it's awake. Cold all through means you've got a body, and you can stop being clever and start being quick.

"And look at the palms." She paused. "Palms tell you what a hand's been used for. A tailor's calluses sit in different places than a butcher's. I never got a look at this one's palms. I regret it. If you ever get the chance and the time, look."

She turned to the door, put her ear near the jamb, and listened. Nothing. Just the wet stair behind them and the small sound of water finding its level in a room below.

"One more thing, and then we open a door," she said. "Everything I just gave you is a theory except the seam and the thread. The seam and the thread are what I saw. So when you write it up, those go in the book, and the rest stays in your head where it can't get anybody killed."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I press my back against the wall beside the door, my heart thumping against my ribs. "The book is for what we saw," I repeat, a whisper. "But my head's for what I think I saw." I shift the lamp to my other hand, wiping my sweaty palm on my coat. "What if the bar's back on?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"If the bar's back on," Halloway said, "that's the good news, and I want you to hear why before you decide it isn't."

She put her ear to the door one more time anyway, because one listen isn't a listen.

"A bar means hands. Hands mean a person, or something with a person's habits. I can plan against a person. Thirty years of plans against people, and most of them worked. What's down those stairs I've got no plan against at all. So understand me when I say I'd rather be shut in with a stranger up here than walk out into an empty yard. Empty yards are how the last four hunters I knew died, and not one of them died indoors."

She flattened her hand on the door and felt for the seam.

"Three things before either of us touches the latch. In order.

"One. Get down and look at the gap under the door. Don't put the lamp near it — cup it, tuck it behind your leg. If there's light on the other side, there's company with a lamp up there, and the first thing I do is put ours out. Two lights is two positions, and I don't want to be a position.

"Two. Listen for the bar. Iron in a bracket has a sound — it *sits*. Dropped back in and settled, it'll be quiet. Leaning, it'll knock. If nothing moves on the other side for two minutes and nothing knocks, that bar's seated, and a seated bar is somebody's decision. Decisions are good. Decisions mean a mind, and minds can be worked.

"Three. Hinges. That door swings into the cellar — I watched it on the way in, because watching doors on the way in is cheaper than watching them on the way out. Into the cellar means the pins are on our side of the frame. A door's only as strong as its bar, and a bar does nothing about a hinge. Two people, one pin each, quiet as you like, and that door comes off the frame into our arms without ever swinging open. Then we're standing in a room with a bar on it, and the bar's on the wrong side of us."

She paused, and behind her, down the thirteen wet steps, the cellar had gone quiet. The small lapping had stopped. Water in a room doesn't stop lapping on its own; it stops when something in it stops moving, or when something in it starts.

Halloway did not turn around to look. She'd already decided not to look, and she was going to keep deciding it.

"That's if the bar's on," she said. "If it's off and the yard's empty, we do none of it. We walk, and we don't get clever on the way. Simple's better and I've got a bed I'd like to see again."

She nodded at the bottom of the door.

"Now go down flat and look at the gap."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took her ear off the door slowly. She did not look down the stairs. She looked at Pike instead, and she looked for a while, the way she'd looked at the coat — all the way, no hurry, no skipping.

"Say that again," she said. "Same words. Slow."

The cellar behind them stayed quiet. That was the thing she was listening past. Water in a room does not stop moving on its own. It stops when the thing in it stops, or when the thing in it starts, and she'd said as much thirty seconds ago and now she was standing in the proof of it with her back to the wall.

"Because here's what I've got." She kept her voice down and even, one flat sentence at a time, the way she'd read off a price. "I have not drawn a blade. My knife's at my belt and it's sheathed and it's cold — I can feel it through the leather without looking. The boat pole is at the bottom of those stairs with four fingers wrapped round the hook. So whatever you're watching cut something, it is not cutting in this stairwell, and it is not me."

She shifted her weight off the wall, one degree, so she had both boots planted.

"Now. Two things could be true. One: you're seeing something and it's down there with the water, which means your eyes are downstairs and the rest of you is up here, and I don't know how that works. Two: something's put a picture in your head and called it memory, and you'd rather I not ask which." She nodded once, slow. "I'm asking."

She held up her hand, fingers spread, and did not move it.

"Don't answer that yet. Answer this. What color is the coat? The one you're watching her cut. Say it plain."

She watched Pike's face while she waited — not the eyes, the *hands*. Lamp steady in one of them, the other still wet from the coat. Steady was the part she didn't like. A person who'd just watched a cutting has a shaking hand and a fast breath and a story they can't keep in order. Steady hands with a calm voice is a different animal, and it's the one she'd met before, once, in a barn outside Burford, and she'd walked away from it and never told anybody how close it had come.

"One more, and then I decide something. The lamp. You've had it up since the stairs and I told you light above the eyes makes a target. So put it down by your knee. If your arm does it, we're fine and we go back to the door. If your arm doesn't want to, tell me that too, because I'd rather hear it from you than find out from whatever's using your arm."

She let her hand rest on the knife, still sheathed, still cold, thumb on the clasp but not through it.

"And keep your voice down. The room's gone quiet and quiet rooms listen."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: My arm moves fine. I lower the lamp to my knee, the light painting a shaky arc across the wet floor. "It's the same coat," I say, my voice low and tight. "The Hartnell wool. But it's dry. And she's using a bone needle." I swallow. "I think it's showing me the making."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway watched the arm come down. It came down the way an arm comes down — smooth, the elbow leading, the wrist following, no lag and no overshoot. She watched the lamp settle by Pike's knee and paint its arc across the wet floor, and she did not take her thumb off the clasp.

"Good," she said. "That's the arm accounted for."

Then she took her hand off the knife entirely, because a hand resting on a clasp is a decision already half-made, and she wasn't going to make it standing on a wet stair with a witness in front of her.

"Now I'm going to take this fast, and you're going to let me, because every minute you stand in that picture is a minute the thing downstairs gets to keep the door of it open. So. Short answers. First one — is the woman's face in the picture, or is it all hands."

She kept her eyes on Pike's hands while she asked. Not the face. The hands. A witness's face tells you what they want you to believe; a witness's hands tell you what's actually happening to them.

"Second. The needle's bone. Whose bone. Is it a rib, a long bone, or something you can't place. If you can't place it, say can't place it, don't guess.

"Third. Sound. Bone needle through skin makes a sound — a small wet click, like a thumbnail against a tooth. Did you hear it in the picture, or did you only see it. Don't dress it up. Heard or didn't hear.

"Fourth. Smell. You've got a nose and it's still working, I can see you breathing. Copper and rot is down those stairs. Is the picture *up here*, or is it still down there with the water. That one matters most, so take your time on it."

She let that sit for exactly one breath and then kept going, because one breath was the budget.

"Here's what I'm doing with it. You've just been handed a workshop. Dry coat means the making didn't happen in water — the water's where it was *kept*, after. Bone needle means whoever's doing it isn't buying tools, they're making them, and a maker who makes their own needle is a maker who's been at it long enough to have opinions about needles. That's a trade, same as the stitches. Same as the coat.

"And the coat was on the frame. Dry. Which means there's a frame. Which means there's a room with a frame in it, somewhere in or near Burford, and I have been in Burford and I have walked out of a barn outside it and never told anybody how close that came, so I know the address is real. I've been telling you it was real for an hour. Now something's agreeing with me and I don't care for the way it's doing it."

She shifted her weight and glanced, once, at the door. Still shut. Still no knock.

"Last question, and it's the one I'd ask a live witness, so I'm asking you. In the picture — how many elbows. Not the coat's, the *frame's*. Whatever's on the frame while she's working it. If it's got two, she's still building it and the thing downstairs is the finished one. If it's got four, then the thing downstairs isn't a product, it's a *copy*, and that's a worse sentence than anything else you've said tonight."

She put her palm flat against the door again, not listening now — steadying. Her voice stayed level.

"Then we go. Same plan as before. But you write three new lines when we're clear, and you write them exactly this way: *Witnessed by Pike, unverified.* Then the dry coat, the bone needle, and whether the picture had a smell. That's a report, not a fact, and the book takes reports, it just marks them. Everything you *felt* about it stays in your head. That's the deal I've kept for thirty years and I'm not breaking it on a wet stair at — what is it —" she didn't check, "— late.

"Answer the four. Then we do the door."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I don't remember her face," I say, my voice hollow. "Just her hands. The needle was rib-thin, but I don't know whose. I didn't hear the click. I smelled wet wool and tallow, not copper." I look down at my own hands. "It had four elbows on the frame."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took the four answers in and did not say anything for a moment. Down the thirteen wet steps, the water stayed quiet, and quiet water was a sentence she'd already read.

"Four elbows on the frame," she said at last. "That's the one I wanted and the one I didn't want, and they were the same one, which is how it goes."

She took them one at a time, folding them down like she'd folded her fingers on the stairs.

"No face, just hands. Hands without a face is a decision. Somebody showed you the trade and hid the tradesman. That's not a memory getting thin — a thin memory still has a face in it, even if it's the wrong one. No face at all is a picture *composed*. Somebody left the face out on purpose."

"Needle rib-thin, don't know whose. Right answer. Guessing would've been worse and I'd have caught you at it."

"Didn't hear the click." She said it flat, and it was the sentence she cared about most. "That's the tell. Memories have sound in them. You remember a room, you remember it *noisy* — boots on stone, water moving, somebody breathing. A picture with no sound in it didn't come up through your ears. It was put there. Which means whatever put it there has an interest in you having seen it, and I don't take gifts."

"Smelled wet wool and tallow." She nodded, slow. "Tallow's a candle. Wool's a workroom. Copper's down those stairs. So the picture isn't this cellar and it isn't those steps — it's a room with candles lit in it and cloth laid out in it, and the water we're standing over has never been in that room. Two rooms. This one, and that one. That one has an address."

She shifted her weight, both boots planted.

"So here's the whole of it, and then we do the door. A maker with no face, in a lit workroom, working a frame with four elbows on it. The thing downstairs has four elbows. Which means the frame is where the pattern lives, and the thing in the water is *one of the copies*. One of. A maker with a frame doesn't make one, they make a *run*, and a run needs somewhere to keep them. Cellars. Barns. And Burford's the town on the collar. I've been telling you the address was real for an hour. Now something's agreeing with me and I don't care for the way it's doing it."

She turned to the door.

"Everything you told me goes in as *witnessed, unverified*. That's the deal. Now the door. You hold the lamp by your knee, cup it with your hand, and don't move it. I'll take the gap — I want to be the one flat on the wet stone, because I want to see it first."

She went down — knee into the silt, cheek near the bottom of the door, one cupped hand round the lamp so the light went nowhere it shouldn't. She lay there and looked.

No light on the other side. Not a sliver, not a smear. Black.

She stayed down and counted by her own breath. Slow, even, in through the nose. One minute. Two. Nothing walked. Nothing knocked. Iron in a bracket, seated, has a silence to it, and that was the silence.

She got up, quiet, and set her back to the wall.

"Bar's seated," she said. "Not leaning, not dropped. Seated. Which means somebody up there put it back and made a decision, and I've got no way from here to tell whether they then walked away or stood there and waited. So I'm assuming they waited, because that's the one that kills you."

She looked at the door frame, up and down the jamb.

"Pins are on our side. Two of them, top and bottom. You take the top, I take the bottom. We pull them slow — a pin that's been in a wet door for years is going to complain, and I'd rather it complained to us than to whoever's up there. On the count of three. Not before, not after."

She wrapped her hand round the lower pin, felt it, and waited for Pike's grip on the upper one.

"One. Two. Three."

They came out. The bottom pin first — rusted, stubborn, and then loose in her fist, and she did not let it drop; she closed her hand round it and set it on the stone. Above her, the top pin gave the same way. The door sagged a hair and then held, because the bar outside was holding it, and that was the whole trick of it.

"Now we lift it *into* the cellar," she said, "both corners, top and bottom, and we set it down on the steps behind us. A door set down is quieter than a door dropped, and quiet is the only advantage I've got left."

They lifted. The door came free of the frame — no bang, no scrape, just the wet stone and the weight of it — and they laid it across the steps behind them, flat, out of the way. Where the door had been there was now a hole: a dark rectangle of open night with the iron bar still seated across it on the far side, bracketed to a wall that no longer had a door to hold.

Halloway stepped through, under the bar, into the yard.

Empty. No lamp, no horse, no sound but their own boots on wet ground. The mud held their own prints coming in and nothing else — no heel, no hoof, no drag. Whoever had barred that door had not walked away across this yard. Or had not walked.

"Yard's clean," she said. "Which means they came and went by a road, and roads leave prints, and I'll look at the road when I've got the town lights in front of me and not before."

She started walking and did not look back at the house.

"Three facts go in the book, exactly as I give them. One — Hartnell and Sons, Burford, gold on black, inside the collar of a wool coat that fits four elbows. Two — the time we came up, and the door barred from the outside. Three — that we left it barred and came out through the frame, and left the pins on the stone." She counted them on her fingers as she walked, mud sucking at every step. "Then, under that, three lines marked *witnessed by Pike, unverified* — dry coat, bone needle, tallow and wet wool. No click. Four elbows on the frame. Those stay marked. They don't graduate to facts until I've stood in the room."

The road came up out of the dark ahead, and past it, small and yellow, the town lights.

"Last thing and then I'll stop talking, because I've said enough tonight to fill a book and the book's the only thing that's going to be true in the morning. You asked me to finish it. Finishing it looks

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: like this." I follow her onto the road, the cold air sharp in my lungs. "Do we go to Burford next?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Burford's the address on the coat," Halloway said. "But no, we don't go to Burford next. Not tonight and not first."

She walked the road at an even pace, no hurry in it, eyes on the mud ahead where the town light started to catch it.

"First we go where there's a bed and a lock and a kettle, and you write the book before you sleep, because a report written in the morning is a story. Tonight, while the smell of it's still in your nose, that's the only honest version you'll ever get. Facts first, then three lines marked unverified, then a line under that for the date and the town name. And then you sleep, because tomorrow I want your hands steady and your head empty of that picture."

She stepped around a rut, found the road's crown, kept to it.

"Second thing, and this is the one that decides whether we're hunters or tourists. We don't walk into Burford and ask after Hartnell and Sons. A town that size, the shop's got a name on the high street and a name behind the counter, and the moment two strangers ask about the stitching, somebody in that town hears about it before we've had our dinner. And if the maker lives there, then the maker hears about it. I've no wish to be the first thing on that list. So we go in like people with a reason to be there. Buying a coat's a reason. Having a coat repaired's a better one. I've got a coat with a torn lining I've been meaning to do something about for four years, and it just became my favourite possession."

She fished in her breast pocket, found nothing, and let it be.

"Third — the barn." She said it without slowing. "Two days east of Burford, a barn I spent a winter in, the year I stopped counting losses and started counting reasons. Something happened in that barn and I walked away from it and never told anybody how close it came. I've been carrying that for a while and I've been telling myself it was a bad night and not a piece of the same trade. Tonight's been arguing with me. So when we're in Burford and the shop's been seen, we walk out east and I show you the barn. I don't know what's in it. That's the honest version. I know what I saw and I know what I told myself, and those two don't match, and a cellar with four elbows in it is exactly the kind of thing that makes a man go back and look at the barn."

The town lights had a shape to them now — a spire, a roofline, a lamp burning over a door.

"Fourth and last. The thing in the cellar's still in the cellar. Barred door, pins on the stone, and I left it holding a boat pole with a grip I've seen on men who were deciding something. It's not ours to chase and it's not ours to burn, not yet. But the book goes to the next hunter's hands if mine stop working, and I want the four elbows and the laces and the thread in it before we touch Burford. If we're wrong about Hartnell, we've made a bad afternoon for a tailor and nothing else. If we're right, then there's a run of them, and one of them's sitting in a flooded cellar two days behind us being patient."

She looked at Pike sideways, once, no softening in it.

"You asked if we go to Burford. We go. Day after tomorrow, morning, with a torn coat and a book that's already written. And when we get there, you keep your hands out of your pockets and your eyes on the high street sign, and you let me do the talking, because I've been lying to shopkeepers for thirty years and I've got a face for it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I look down at my own hands again, trying to remember the feeling of the wool collar. "My coat's not torn," I say quietly. "Do I still get to come?"

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The smell's copper and rot, which means it's been in the water long enough to start giving something back — weeks, not hours

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Four elbows are deliberate — they're not breaks, they're *fittings*. Additions. Like a cabinetmaker puts a drawer in.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The skin's been treated like cloth. Where my hook scored it across the ribs, it opened along a line and stopped. No fat under it. No give. No welling. A knife through a man's side leaves a wound — ragged, wet, bleeding. This left a *seam*. Clean as a hem. And along the seam, stitches.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: Halloway took her ear off the door slowly. She did not look down the stairs. She looked at Pike instead

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Good start," Halloway said. Her voice was flat, carrying easily over the sluggish lap of the water against the foundation stones. "Now narrow it down. 'Wrong' doesn't tell the parish coroner what kind of salt to buy."

She tilted the lantern slightly to throw the yellow light lower across the scum on the surface. Shadows stretched, thick and oily.

"Look at the displacement," she said, nodding toward the dark bulk half-submerged near the drowned cider barrels. "Rib cage is too wide for a man, too narrow for an ox, and the spine doesn't taper where it ought to. It’s got three distinct hinge-points visible above the waterline, which means either the poor bastard had an exceptionally creative midwife or we’re dealing with something that crawled out of the silt before the frost set in." 

She shifted her grip on the iron-shod pole in her left hand, testing the depth of the mud beneath the water with a dull *thunk*. 

"Notice anything else? Specifically around where its head ought to be, assuming it was polite enough to have one?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I squint, leaning forward a bit. "There's...no head. But there's too many shoulders." I point at the lumpy silhouette. "See? One here, and another sort of...lower down."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Not shoulders," Halloway said, the beam of her lantern cutting through the haze of cellar-rot and sour silt. "Clavicular spurs. Or whatever it passes off for them. When you see a ball-and-socket joint set that low against the ribs, it doesn't mean the thing was built for lifting sacks of grain. It means it could unhinge and fold itself flat enough to slide through an eighteen-inch culvert."

She brought the iron-shod pole up and let the butt-end rest against her hip, her gaze dissecting the wet, gray bulk with the cold detachment of a butcher at an auction.

"And it has a head," she added. "It's just tucked under the sternum like an owl with a bellyache. They pull them in when they go dormant, or when they're coiled to strike." A sharp, faint twitch of her mouth passed for a smile. "Or, if our luck has taken a sudden and unprecedented turn for the better, when they drown after choking on the parish vicar's best sheep."

She didn't move forward yet. Instead, she watched the oily surface of the water right around the thing's midsection, looking for the tiny, rhythmic shudder of gills or spiracles working below the waterline.

"Reach into my left coat pocket," she said quietly, her eyes never leaving the heap. "Pull out the two-foot iron tongs and the copper wire. And keep your boots braced against the stair riser. If those 'shoulders' decide to snap open, you don't want to be off-balance when the water hits you."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't turn around, keeping her eyes fixed on the gray heap in the dark water. 

"Define 'recently,'" she said. "If you mean did it pay tithes on Sunday, no. If you mean did it start out with two arms, two legs, and a mother who hoped for better things, quite possibly."

She pointed the tip of the iron pole toward a patch of mottled, leathery tissue floating just beneath the scum. 

"See the discoloration there? Looks like curdled milk. That’s what human marrow looks like when it cooks itself out through the pores during an ochre-rot turn. It calcifies the flesh to make a shell, and it melts the jaw down so the mouth-parts can realign. So, yes. Probably a drover or a tanner who took a bad sip from the brook back in November."

She paused, tilting her head as she watched a pale film drift across the surface from beneath the creature’s flank.

"Though if it makes you feel any better, he wasn't having a very good time of it by the end anyway," she added dryly. "When the lungs rot out to make room for the gills, it feels like swallowing a hot hearth-shovel. Dying of it was likely the highlight of his week."

She tapped the iron pole once against the cellar floor, a dull vibration through the murky water, waiting for a twitch.

"Now stop philosophizing about the parish census and find those tongs. If it’s truly dead, the marrow will cool into a jelly and we can salt it before noon. If it's just sleeping off the change, we’re standing in its larder."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I fumble in her pocket, my fingers closing around the cold iron. "If it's dead... why are we still whispering?" I ask, pulling out the tools.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Because stone carries," Halloway said, her voice barely louder than the slow drip of water from the floor joists overhead. "And because 'dead' is an opinion until I've put three inches of iron into whatever it’s using for a heart."

She took the tongs from Pike without looking, shifting her weight so the cellar water barely rippled around her thighs. 

"More to the point," she continued in that same measured, gravelly murmur, "things that turn don't always turn in solitary confinement. When a well goes foul, more than one idiot usually drinks from the bucket. If there’s a second one wedged behind those casks, I’d rather not invite it over for tea while our boots are full of stagnant runoff."

She shook out a length of the copper wire, looping it through the hinge of the tongs with practiced, calloused fingers. Her knuckles were scarred white from old acid burns and rope-scrapes. 

"Now," she said, nodding toward the pale, bloated mass. "Watch the ribs. Not the top ones—the lower set, right where the belly joins the hip-struts. If you see the skin draw tight like a wet drum, that means the diaphragm is drawing a vacuum. It’s getting ready to purge the water out of its throat so it can hiss."

She brought the iron-shod pole up and extended it across the dark water, the metal tip hovering an inch above the creature's shoulder-spur.

"If it hisses," she added with a brief, humorless twitch of her mouth, "you drop the wire, scramble up three steps, and do not, under any circumstances, try to be heroic. Heroism in an enclosed cellar just means more shoveling for the next crew."

The iron tip came down, hard and precise, into the gray juncture between the creature's neck and spine.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The iron sank three inches with the dull, greasy resistance of a cleaver going into cold suet. 

Nothing twitched. No vacuum pulled at the wound; no black water bubbled up from the spiracles. A thin, curd-colored discharge seeped into the murky water, spreading like bacon grease in a cold skillet. 

Halloway held the pole steady for five seconds, counting the pulses through the ash-wood shaft. When she felt nothing answering through the grain, she let out a short, rough breath through her nose.

"Plainly," she said, resting her weight back on her heels, "he drank water that had seeped through an old nest. Three days later, he thought he had the ague. Fever hot enough to boil grease. On the fourth day, the bone-rot started."

She reached out with the iron tongs, using the blunt tip to peel back a flap of fibrous, waterlogged skin near the creature's ribcage to let Pike see the structure beneath. 

"His marrow liquefied and pushed out through the periosteum," she said, her tone as dry as an apothecary listing stock. "The body tries to heal breaks that aren't there, so it throws down calcium wherever it can—hence the spurs, the extra ribs, the fused neck. By the end of the first week, his stomach had dissolved to make room for an air-bladder, and his tongue split to accommodate the secondary jaw. At that point, the mind is gone. Just a fever-dream and a tremendous, burning thirst."

She shifted the tongs, tapping a swollen, discolored node near the base of the skull. 

"He crawled down here because the air up top was too dry. His skin was sloughing off in sheets, and the cellar was the only place cold enough to stop the itching. Then his heart simply gave out. The new pump wasn't fully formed, and the old human one couldn't push sludge through four extra feet of gristle."

Halloway pulled the iron pole free with a soft, sucking pop and wiped the tip on the wet stones of the foundation wall. 

"That's the plain of it. No curse, no devils from the pit. Just bad water, poor plumbing, and biology doing what biology does when nobody has the sense to boil the well-bucket." She held out a hand toward Pike, palm up. "Give me the salt-auger. We need to core the brainpan before the grease sets hard, or we'll be here until nightfall chipping through the shell with a chisel."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I hand her the auger, my eyes still fixed on the lumpy, discolored thing. "So we're not... putting it out of its misery?" The question comes out softer than I meant it to.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took the T-handled auger, its iron screw dark and pitted from years of brine. 

"Misery had the good manners to finish up about ten minutes before we opened the storm doors," she said, kneeling until the stagnant water lapped against the bottom of her leather jerkin. "This isn't mercy, Pike. Mercy was a shovel across the nape three weeks ago when he still remembered his own surname. This is just housekeeping."

She set the point of the auger against a flat, calcified plate just behind where the creature's ear-hole used to be. She leaned her weight over the crossbar, using her shoulders rather than her arms.

"If you leave the brainstem whole," she said, grunting slightly as the screw bit through the outer crust with a sound like crushing dry crab-shells, "the residual galvanic charge in the spinal fluid can keep the secondary jaw snapping for two days after the pump quits. A farmwife comes down here tomorrow to fetch a jar of pickled cabbage, steps on the throat, and loses three fingers to a corpse that doesn't even know it's biting."

She gave the crossbar two full, rhythmic turns. A thick, grayish paste began to well up along the grooves of the iron screw, smelling faintly of river-bottom and stale tallow.

"Dead things are remarkably stubborn if you don't take the time to explain the situation to the nervous system," she continued, her voice level and steady despite the effort. "Hold the lamp lower. Right over the hole. When I pull the screw out, you're going to pour three measures of rock salt straight down the shaft before the fluid wells back up and washes it out."

She glanced up at him, her eyes pale and flat in the yellow lamplight. 

"Don't spill it in the water. Salt costs sixpence a sack, and the parish vestry will inspect the bill."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway paused with the auger buried two inches deep, her forearm muscles taut under the rolled-up wool of her sleeve. She looked at Pike for a long second, measuring the set of his jaw against the tremor in his fingers.

"Fair enough," she said. "Listen closely, because a live one won't give you time to consult your notes."

She gave the crossbar another half-turn, the iron grating through bone with the sound of a heavy heel on gravel.

"He got about three-quarters of the way through a full larval shift," she said, nodding down at the carcass. "The first thing to go was the soft palate and the tongue. Under that outer skin, the hyoid bone—the little horseshoe bone in your throat that lets you sing hymns and tell lies—snapped in half and spread wide. The tongue didn't fall out; it split down the center and hardened into a pair of prehensile claspers. If you open that mouth, you won't find molars. You'll find three rows of backward-curving denticles, like a dogfish, grown straight out of the gum gristle."

She pulled the auger back an inch to let the gray fluid vent, her expression as dispassionate as an ironmonger tallying nails.

"Next came the torso. Humans are fragile in the middle because we like to bend over and tie our shoes. These things don't care about their shoes. His ribs didn't just multiply; they braided together like willow hurdles. If you try to stick a dirk between the fourth and fifth rib of a turned man, the point will skip off solid bone and slide right into your own thigh. You don't thrust at the chest. Ever."

She tapped the flat of her tongs against the submerged mass of the creature's flank. 

"Underneath that wicker-work of bone, the stomach shrank to the size of a walnut. He wasn't hungry for mutton anymore. A glandular sack grew along the spine, secreting an oily bile that breaks down raw protein into a slurry he could absorb through the intestinal wall. The lungs dried up, turned black, and shriveled into scraps of leather. That cavity you see puffing out his belly isn't fat—it's an air-bladder lined with hydrostatic valves. It lets them sink to the bottom of a pond and lie motionless under five feet of silt for three days, waiting for a milkmaid to wash a pail."

She wiped a fleck of gray marrow from her knuckle onto her breeches. 

"How far did he get? He got far enough that his ears are gone—sealed over with cartilage—and his eyes are milky marbles set behind clear nictitating membranes. He was blind to candle-light by Tuesday, but he could feel the vibration of our boots on the cellar stairs through the water before we even unlatched the street door."

She hauled upward with a sharp, wet *plink*, drawing the iron screw clean out of the skull. A steady, pale ribbon of liquor began to drain from the hole.

"That's what's under the skin," she said, gesturing sharply toward the salt-pouch at Pike's belt. "A wicker cage, a pint of bile, and a set of jaws that work on hydraulics instead of muscle. If you meet one that's still breathing, you don't aim for the chest and you don't try to out-swim it. You drive your steel straight up beneath the jaw hinge, where the old human tongue-root left a soft pocket, or you break the knees from behind while it's trying to stand on feet that don't fit the floor anymore."

She didn't look up from the puncture wound. "Salt. Now. Three fingers' worth, straight into the hole, before the grease glazes over."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I pour the salt in with a steady hand, watching it dissolve into the mess. "How many have you seen?" I ask, my voice tight. "Alive, I mean."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The salt bit into the marrow-slurry with a faint, greasy hiss, like a drop of cold water hitting a hot tallow pan. The paste shrank, curdling from translucent gray to the dull, chalky white of lard left out in the frost. 

Halloway watched the reaction until the hole stopped weeping, satisfied the brainstem wouldn't be firing off any posthumous surprises.

"Eleven," she said, her voice flat. "Fully turned, that is. Where the thumbs were gone and the tongue had split."

She used the flat blade of her skinning knife to tamp the crusted salt down flush with the skull-plate, sealing the bore-hole like a cooper bunging a cask of bad ale.

"Seven more that were halfway through the shift," she added, wiping the steel clean on the wet hem of her jerkin. "Those are the loud ones. They still have enough human throat left to make noise, but not enough wit to understand that thrashing around in six feet of bilge just snaps their own newly formed ribs. People write ballads about hunting them like they’re stags or great gray wolves. They aren't. It’s mostly just wrestling an exceptionally greasy, confused bag of wet kindling that’s trying to chew through your boot-leather while you slip in parish muck."

She straightened up slowly, one hand pressed to the small of her back. The vertebrae clicked with a dry, muffled snap that sounded entirely too loud in the damp cellar. 

"Alive, they're remarkably fast for about ten paces," she said, nodding toward the low-ceilinged crawlway behind the cider casks. "Then the new air-bladder cramps because the hydraulic valves aren't properly seasoned yet. They hitch on the left side—always the left, because the secondary liver swells there first. That's when you take the legs out. You don't stand your ground and play the champion. You wait for the cramp, you step inside the reach, and you break the knee from behind with an iron bar."

She reached down, uncoiling a length of stiff, tarred hemp rope from the ring at her hip, and tossed one knotted end across the creature’s chest. The wet rope landed with a dead *thwack* against the braided ribs.
