"Pass that under the spurs and through the pelvic struts," she said, nodding down into the dark water. "The churchwarden promised two silver florins for disposal, and the old skinflint won't pay out until he sees the carcass loaded onto the parish dray. Mind the barbs on the bone-joints; they’ll shred your palms if you drag against the grain."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The blade of her skinning knife bit into the seam where the breastplate met the lower cartilage, grating with the dry, fibrous sound of someone slicing through green hemp rope. 

"The smell first," Halloway said, her voice dropping into the low, steady rhythm of a surgeon at an operating table. "Notice how it isn't sweet like an ordinary corpse. A drowned man after three days smells of warm tallow and sour mutton. This doesn't. It smells like marsh gas, crushed dock-leaves, and stale malt vinegar. That’s the acid from the dissolved spleen working its way through the belly-wall. If you ever walk into a hayloft or an undercroft and catch that scent—sharp, like pickled nettles—you don't light a pipe and you don't go poking through the straw with a pitchfork. You back out."

She leaned her weight into the hilt, drawing the broad point downward toward the navel. No red blood welled from the slit; only a thick, pale seepage the color of dirty whey, bubbling sluggishly as the internal pressure vented.

"Look at the subcutaneous fat," she said, using the flat of her left thumb to peel back the lip of the incision. The yellow grease beneath the skin wasn't soft; it had hardened into granular clumps, like wet cornmeal pressed tight. "The body stopped storing fat for warmth a fortnight ago. It converted every drop of tallow into calcium-binding wax. See those yellow beads along the margins? That’s where the outer carapace would have formed. If he’d lived another four weeks, that skin would have cured as hard as slate. An iron quarrel from a heavy crossbow would have skipped right off his flank."

She worked the blade deeper, levering it between two braided ribs until the cartilage parted with a dull, wet *crack*. The water around their shins stirred as a foul, warm pocket of air escaped from the interior cavity, thick enough to coat the back of the tongue with the taste of copper and wet lime.

"Here’s your air-bladder," she said. She reached two bare fingers into the slit, hooking them under a gray, translucent sac that ran the entire length of the spine like a bloated sausage skin. "Pliable as pig-bladder, but lined with circular muscle rings. He was already using it. See the banding? That means it was expanding and contracting, pulling water in through the gill-slits behind his clavicles, stripping the air out, and forcing the waste out through the inguinal vents near the groin. That’s why his legs are useless. The muscles in his thighs didn't rot—they were absorbed to feed the bladder's lining."

She wiped her fingers on her thigh, leaving a greasy, grayish smear that refused to soak into the wool.

"He got past the marrow-fever, past the tooth-drop, and halfway through the thoracic braiding," she continued, her breathing steady despite the strain on her back. "If you rate a turn on a scale of twenty days, he was at day fourteen. Another week, and his skin would have turned the color of river-silt, his arms would have fused to his ribs down to the elbow, and he’d have been able to crack a bullock’s shin-bone between his secondary jaws."

She looked up then, meeting Pike's eyes through the steam rising from the open carcass and the cold haze of the cellar.

"Remember the color of that lymph," she said, pointing with the bloody tip of her knife to the pale, curdled fluid pooling in the wound. "If you cut a suspect and it bleeds pink, there's still a man in there fighting the turn. If it bleeds white, you don't call the vicar and you don't fetch clean blankets. You take the head off at the third joint, you burn the boots he was wearing, and you tell his widow he went to sea."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I watch the white stuff bleed out into the water. "Right," I say, my throat dry. "So we take the head." I pass her the larger of the two saws.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took the heavy bone-saw, running the calloused pad of her thumb across the wide, raked teeth. A faint rasp of iron echoed off the wet cellar walls. 

"Coarse teeth. Good," she said. "The fine-toothed butcher's saw is useless on these. The bone doesn't chip clean; it gums up with that yellow tallow until the blade binds and you’re standing here pulling your shoulder out of its socket."

She shifted her footing in the silt, the black water eddying against the heavy leather of her coat. She leaned over the creature, reaching into the flap she had cut to hook her fingers into the gristle behind its collar.

"Now, look where you’d naturally try to put the blade," she said, nodding down. "An apprentice always tries to go for the throat, right under the chin where the human windpipe used to sit. Don't do it. The secondary jaw has an apron of bone that flares out like a breastplate—you’ll just blunt your steel against two inches of wet calcium. We take it from the nape."

With a grunt that sounded like an iron grate shifting on flagstones, she hauled upward on the slick, gray bulk, rolling the creature halfway onto its side. The dark water sloshed sluggishly, throwing up a fresh reek of vinegar, marsh-mud, and cold fat. 

"Third cervical joint," she pointed out with the back of the saw. "See that gray gap between the spurs? Right where the neck looks like a stack of overturned saucers? That’s your hinge. The human vertebrae fused together into a solid rod, but the thing still needed to tilt its snout up to break the water and smell the bank. That gap is held together by fibrous gristle instead of bone."

She set the saw teeth into the furrow between the plates.

"Hold the lantern higher, over my left shoulder so the shadow falls behind the stroke," she commanded, settling into a wide stance with her boots braced against the sunken flagstones. "And don't touch the teeth when the blade comes out. The marrow acid will pit your skin like lime-scald."

She drew the saw back. The iron teeth bit into the tough gristle with a wet, rhythmic *shrr-shrr-shrr*, throwing up flecks of pale curd that floated on the scum. 

"The churchwarden will want to see the denticles before he pays the bounty," she said between strokes, her breathing measured and heavy. "The rest of the carcass we can drag out to the lime-pits on the common and bury under two feet of quicklime. But the head goes into an iron pail with a peck of salt. Otherwise, the flies catch the scent, lay their blow in the nostrils, and by harvest time you've got maggots the size of mice chewing their way out through the floorboards of the parish hall."

She drove the blade through the final band of fibrous tendon with a dull, wet *snap*. 

"One more thing," she said, pausing with the saw embedded in the dark flesh, looking sideways up at Pike. "When the head comes off, the lower jaw might snap shut once. Just a nerve releasing its coil. If your fingers are anywhere near the lips when it happens, you'll be learning to hold your tools with your left hand. Clear?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The saw teeth cleared the final notch of bone with a wet, dry scrape, like an iron hoop slipping off a wooden stave. 

Halloway didn't let go of the blade. The head was still tethered to the trunk by three thick bands of grayish dorsal gristle—tough as boiled boot-leather—and the dural sheath that encased the cord. 

"Knife," she muttered to herself, not asking Pike to come back down into the water. She let the saw dangle by its lanyard from her wrist and drew the broad skinning blade from her belt with her free hand.

She wedged the fingers of her left hand into the calcified hollow where the human collarbone had bowed outward, using the leverage to pull the neck taut. The flesh stretched, pale and bloodless, weeping that thin, yellow-white liquor into the black water around her knees. 

"The sheath is tough," she said, her voice echoing flatly off the damp stone walls. "If you try to saw through the cord itself, the teeth just chew it into lint and pack the cut with marrow-grease. You have to slice it clean, like hemp under tension."

She laid the edge of the knife across the thickest cord at the center of the gap. She bore down, rocking the blade heel-to-toe. It parted with a distinct, fibrous *twang*, like a wet lute string snapping in a cold cellar. 

The moment the cord severed, the head jerked.

It wasn't a slow heave. It was a violent, hydraulic spasm. The lower plates of the throat flared wide, the skin stretching white over the braided gristle, and the secondary jaw under the chin shot forward on its calcified track. The backward-curving teeth slammed shut against the upper rim of the plate with the sharp, hollow *clack* of a rat-trap springing on flagstones. A jet of cold, cloudy water and sour lymph spat from between the denticles, spraying across the surface of the pool.

Halloway’s hand was already six inches clear. She hadn't flinched; she had simply moved her wrist back the exact distance needed to let the iron-hard jaws bite empty air.

"There's your reflex," she said, her breath fogging faintly in the lantern light. "Takes three seconds for the tension in the dorsal cord to dump its charge into the jaw springs. If your knuckles had been on the chin-plate, that would have sheared the meat off your second joints down to the ivory."

She took the skinning knife and worked it through the remaining lateral tendons, sawing through them with two short, deliberate strokes. The final band yielded with a soft, greasy *shlick*.

The head came loose in her hands. 

It was heavier than a man's head—the extra bone and the dense, waxy tallow packed into the braincase gave it the dead, sodden heft of a forty-pound cannon shot. Halloway lifted it clear of the pool, water streaming in greasy rivulets from the nostrils and the sheared base of the neck. She held it tilted downward for a few seconds, letting the thick, curdled spinal fluid drain directly into the cellar sump rather than onto her boots. 

In the yellow light from Pike’s lantern, the thing was fully visible. 

The human features were only present as an under-drawing, stretched and ruined beneath the new architecture. The forehead had sloped back into a ridge of blunt, pale tubercles that ran down between the eyes like a row of river pebbles. The nose was gone entirely—flattened into two horizontal slits lined with fine, pale cilia that were already drying and curling in the cellar air. The eyes, set wide near the temples, were flat, milky disks under thick sheets of clear skin, unblinking and vacant, showing neither iris nor pupil. 

Beneath the snout, the primary mouth hung open, revealing the split tongue—two purplish, muscular prongs tipped with hooked barbs, lying limp across the floor of the jaw. Below that, tucked into the hollow of the throat like a second skull inside the first, sat the circular array of dogfish teeth, still slick with that pale, tallow-colored saliva that smelled of malt and pond-rot.

Halloway turned, sloshing through the water with the heavy bundle held securely against her hip, away from her clean coat. She reached the bottom step where Pike sat and set the iron pail down on the third riser with a dull, ringing clang. 

"Salt," she said, reaching for the sack at her belt. 

She didn't use a scoop. She plunged her bare hand into the coarse gray crystals and threw two fistfuls into the bottom of the pail, creating a thick bed of brine-rock. 

Then she lowered the head into the bucket, snout down, so the open cervical hole faced upward toward the light. The calcified plates scraped against the tin sides with a dry, hollow rattle. 

"Now the core," she said, leaning over the pail. 

She took a third handful of salt, closed her fist into a tight cone, and drove the crystals straight down into the gaping hole of the spinal canal, pressing her thumb into the opening to pack the brine into the empty channel where the cord had been. The gray marrow hissed as the salt bit in, the chemical heat drawing the remaining moisture out of the tissue until the lip of the wound puckered and turned gray-white, like meat left too long in the smokehouse.

She wiped her palms on the coarse canvas of her apron, leaving two pale, greasy smudges, and looked down at the bucket.

"That's forty shillings from the parish vestry," she said, her voice level and devoid of triumph. "Provided the churchwarden doesn't claim it was just a dead calf that fell down the coal-chute to dodge paying the bounty."

She reached down, took the coarse hemp sack from the steps, and draped it over the top of the pail, tucking the edges under the wire handle so the smell wouldn't draft up into the kitchen above. 

"Now comes the miserable part," she added, nodding back toward the dark water where the headless, braided torso floated sluggishly among the cider barrels. "Getting three hundredweight of cold suet and wicker-bone up sixteen cellar steps without breaking our shins or dropping it in the street."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at the sack-draped pail. "Forty shillings for that." My voice sounds thin in the damp air. I take a breath that tastes of vinegar and salt. "Tell me how to haul the rest without it coming apart in our hands."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"You don't pull on the meat," Halloway said, wading back into the black water until it lapped against her waist. The ripples rocked the headless torso, turning it sluggishly against the sunken staves of a cider barrel. "The meat is already uncoupling from the gristle. If you take an apprentice's grip on an ankle or a wrist and heave, you’ll just peel four pounds of gray skin off like a wet glove and leave the bulk behind."

She unhooked the second coil of tarred hemp from her belt, letting the heavy, stiff line drop into the water with a dull splash. 

"We rig it through the timber," she continued, her voice echoing off the dripping stone ceiling. "The spine and the rib-basket are solid calcium now. You treat it like moving a green oak balk out of a ditch. You pass the rope under the pelvis—between the hip-struts where the groin-vents sit—and bring both bights up along the flank, threading them beneath the clavicular spurs."

She leaned down, her sleeves already soaked to the bicep, and shoved her forearm under the cold, gray bulk. She worked the thick hemp through the calcified gaps in the pelvis, her breath grunting between her teeth as she levered the sodden weight.

"Reach down," she told Pike, nodding toward the coil floating near the stairs. "Take the bitter end and throw a rolling hitch around the first cellar riser. We’re not carrying it up like a sack of oats. We’re going to parbuckle it."

She straightened, wiping pond-scum from her jaw with the back of her forearm. 

"The belly is the danger," she said, tapping the knife hilt against the distended, translucent membrane that stretched between the lower ribs. "That air-bladder is full of pressurized gas and half-digested muck. If you let the carcass drag over the sharp edge of these stone risers, the flagstones will catch that skin and slit it from navel to throat. If that sack vents inside four walls, you’ll be tasting rotten malt and river-silt for three months, and the woman who owns this cellar will have to burn the floorboards out of her kitchen above just to sell the lease."

She hauled the rope taut, the wet hemp biting into the pale, rubbery folds of the creature's flank with a sound like wet leather being wrung out. The torso lifted slightly in the water, tilting backward so the thick bone-shield of the dorsal plates faced toward the stairs.

"We haul it on its back," Halloway said. "The spine is three inches of fused plate—it can take the scraping against the stone. The belly stays pointed at the ceiling. We go one step at a time. I lift from the sump to ease the friction; you take the strain on the line from above and pin the slack behind the riser."

She looked up at him through the dim, yellow haze of the lamp, her gray hair plastered to her temple by cold cellar-damp. 

"Mind your footing on the top three steps," she added grimly. "The butter-churn was kept up there before the flood, and the stone has sixty years of spilled milk soaked into the grain. It's slick as pig fat. If your boots slip while you've got three hundredweight on the line, the carcass goes back down to the bottom, and you'll be the one riding it down."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wrap the rope around my hands, the coarse hemp already biting into my palms. "On three?" I ask, planting my boots wide against the top step.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Unwrap that line off your knuckles before you lose four fingers," Halloway said sharply from the water. "If that weight drops, hemp doesn't stretch. It’ll snap your metacarpals like dry kindling and drag you head-first into four feet of sewage."

She sloshed forward until she was wedged behind the carcass, sinking her hands into the gristle beneath the stump of the neck. She planted her feet in the mud between two submerged barrel-staves, testing the suction on her boots.

"You don't wrap. You grip, you lean your weight back against the wall, and you pin the bite against the riser every time we gain three inches," she told him. "And we don't count to three like we're raising a church roof. You pull when I say *heave*. You lock when I say *hold*."

She drew in a breath, bracing the broad, calcified shoulder-stumps against her hip. 

"Right. First riser. Mind the dorsal spurs—*heave*."

She drove upward with her thighs, lifting the slick mass out of the displacement. The dark cellar water poured off the carcass in heavy, foaming sheets, stripping away the scum to reveal the dead, slate-colored hide beneath. 

The braided spine struck the edge of the bottom flagstone with a dull, hollow *clack* that sounded like two millstones grinding together. The torso groaned—a low, wet creak of drying ligaments and compressed gas as the bladder inside the belly shifted toward the pelvis.

"Hold," Halloway grated, her face gray with strain under the soot and cellar-grease. Her boots skated half an inch in the muck before finding purchase against the foundation sill. "Pin the line. Pin it."

She looked down at where the creature’s flank rested on the stone. A thick, yellow smear of fat marked the edge of the riser where the cold suet had sheared off against the granite. 

"Good," she breathed, wiping a spatter of foul water from her lip with the crook of her elbow. "The spine's taking the drag. The bladder's clear of the edge by two inches."

She shifted her grip, sliding her forearm beneath the pelvic arch, where the fused struts formed a rigid handle. The reek of stagnant vinegar and sour silt was thick enough now to sting the eyes, rising off the cooling flesh as the cellar air hit it.

"Fifteen more," she said, nodding up the flight toward the thin gray daylight leaking around the kitchen door-frame. "Next one takes it clean out of the water. Once the buoyancy's gone, it’ll feel like pulling an anchor out of the salt-marsh. Set your heels."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I brace my boots against the wet stone and pull, the rope burning across my palms. "Feels like we're dragging the whole cellar up with it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept the lamp up and did not step down into the water. The light shook once across the surface and then held on the mass at the far end.

She looked at it the way she looked at all remains, without hurry and without pity.

"Good," she said. "Wrong is a start. Make it precise."

She tipped the lamp a fraction to kill the glare off the water. The thing at the far wall stayed still. Shoulders broke the surface, pale and swollen. The head listed left and low, near submerged. The torso ran too long between shoulder and hip by half a forearm's length.

"Four feet of water hides the rest," she said. "So we read what shows. Count what you can see. Note what sits crooked. Dead a minute doesn't mean done, so we don't wade in to give it a second chance."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I squint, trying to see past the water's shiver.* "The neck... it's bent wrong. Not like it fell. Like something stretched it before the water took it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway held the lamp steady and let the light sit on the throat where the water broke over it.

She studied the line of it without comment for a moment. The neck ran too long from jaw to collarbone by a hand's width and more, and the skin was drawn smooth and pale over the stretch. The head hung left and low on it, near under, at an angle no drowned thing settled into on its own.

"Stretched, not snapped," she said. "Snapped folds. Stretched pulls. See how the throat stays thin all the way down? Something had hold of the head and kept pulling after the spine gave up arguing."

She did not step toward the water. "Good eye. Keep it cold. The dead don't mind being described."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not lower the lamp. She kept it on the shoulders and the stretched throat where the water moved against them.

"Person, yes," she said. "Started that way."

She tipped the light a fraction toward the right shoulder. A strip of shirt clung black and sodden to the skin. The skin beneath had gone white and puckered from the water, but it had not slipped yet. Dark hair still held to the scalp despite the list of the head.

"That's days in the water, not weeks," she said. "Bloat, but no slough. Nails would still be on, if we could see the hands. The pull is newer than the drowning."

She gave a short breath that was almost a laugh.

"Recent enough he'd have complained about the cellar."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I swallow, hard.* "So something drowned him, then pulled him apart after?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway shook her head once and kept the lamp up out of the water's glare.

She let the light rest on the stretched throat and the overlong run of torso above the surface.

"Other way about," she said. "Pulled first. Water second."

She tipped the beam toward the collarbones where the skin lay drawn thin and unbroken. No tear, no bite taken out. The shoulders sat uneven, the left dragged lower by the weight of the listed head.

"Drowned men don't stretch themselves afterward," she said. "Something took hold of the head while he still had footing and hauled till the neck gave. Then it left him for the cellar to finish."

She did not step down into the water. "It stopped moving a minute ago. That only means it learned to wait."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stopped on the top step and did not follow into the water. She let the steadied light do the work and put her eyes back on the mass at the far wall.

She read it aloud the way she had learned to do thirty years back, flat and in order.

"Male. Middle-aged. Shirt still on the right shoulder. Skin white and wrinkled from days under, not slipped. Head dragged left and low. Neck pulled long by a hand's width, skin unbroken. Left shoulder lower than right. Torso overlong by half a forearm where the spine got drawn out."

She paused while the water moved against the throat.

"Something took the head from above and behind and pulled straight till the neck joints separated. No bite. No cut. Cord went with it, so he stopped fighting before he drowned. Then the cellar water kept him."

She breathed out once through her nose.

"Plainly enough, he was hanged without a rope and left to soak."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "So why did it move a minute ago?" I whisper, not taking my eyes off the listing head.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stayed on the top step and kept the lamp high enough to keep the glare off the water.

She watched the surface settle back against the stretched throat and the listed head. The ripple that had moved it a minute before had flattened out and left no second one behind it.

"Because water moves dead things and gas moves them more," she said. "Bloat builds in the gut and then shifts. A joint slips its last half-inch. A foot of water comes in under a step and pushes."

She tipped the beam a fraction down the overlong torso to where it went under.

"Neck like that holds tension till it doesn't," she said. "Cord stretched, spine pulled apart. When the last fibre gave, the head dropped another inch and the water took the shake all the way to us."

She did not step down.

"Corpses fidget. That's all that was. If it does it twice in the same direction, then we start worrying."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept her eyes on the throat where the light sat and did not ask for it to be moved.

She read it in order, the way she did when someone needed it to stick.

"Under the skin the neck is pulled apart, not cut," she said. "The muscle is drawn thin all the way round, like wet cord pulled too tight. The joints between the vertebrae have separated. A finger's width, maybe more, up near the jaw. The ligaments tore first. Then the small capsules over the joints. The cord stretched with it till it bruised and then gave."

She tipped her chin toward the left shoulder where it sat lower in the water.

"It took nothing out of him," she said. "No meat eaten. No throat opened. Skin unbroken from ear to collarbone. It got length, not flesh. It got far enough to stop the signals going down. Lungs, arms, legs. After that he could not hold his footing or push the water out."

She paused while the water lapped at the swollen shoulders.

"If you meet another one, you will not hear teeth. You will feel hands take your head from behind and pull straight up. Do not let it get set. Once it has the leverage, it does not need to finish the job."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Did it mean to drown him?" I ask, my voice low. "Or was the water just... convenient?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not answer at once. She kept the lamp where it sat on the stretched throat and let the water finish moving against it.

"Convenient," she said. "It did not need the water."

She tipped the beam a fraction to the unbroken skin from ear to collarbone, then to the shoulders sitting high and slack in the flood.

"If it wanted him drowned, it would have held him under and made sure. Shoulders would show it. Back would show it. This one was already done standing up. Once the cord pulled apart up high, he could not breathe right or keep his feet. The water only had to wait for his knees to fold."

She gave a short sound through her nose that was not quite a laugh.

"It pulled him long and left the cellar to do the paperwork."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway set the knife under the jaw and drew it down the stretched throat in one short line.

She parted the skin with the tip and looked at what showed without flinching.

"Skin first," she said. "White and waterlogged, three days thick. No bite, no tear. Under it the fat ran bloodless and pulled thin. The flat muscle of the neck was drawn out like wet string, pale all round, not cut on one side. Both cords in the throat were bruised dark where they tore lengthwise."

The smell came up off the cut, stagnant cellar water and iron and the sweet rot of gut gas held too long.

"Smelled like a drowned privy," she said. "Sour water, old blood, bowel wind starting to turn. Nothing sharp. Nothing eaten."

She opened the line deeper to the spine.

"Joints pulled apart between the second and third bones down from the skull, a finger's width of gap. The gristle between them split clean. The cord inside was stretched and pulped at that spot, gone soft and dark. That far was enough. Signals stopped there. Everything below forgot how to stand."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I swallow, forcing myself to watch.* "What about the hands? Are they clenched? Could he have fought?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway wiped the blade on the sodden shirt and worked her hand down into the water by feel.

She found the right wrist first and lifted it clear of the surface. The hand came up white and sodden and loose, fingers half-curled from the soak and not from effort. The skin at the fingertips was puckered thick. The nails were still seated, unbroken, rims clean. No torn cuticle. No dark line of another man's skin wedged underneath.

She turned the wrist once and let the water run off it.

"Open," she said. "Both of them will be the same. Fingers slack, thumbs out. Not clenched. Not torn."

She lowered the hand back under and reached for the left.

"Clenched means fighting. This one did not get the chance. Once the neck drew out up high, the hands forgot their orders. He could not have gripped a rope, let alone a throat."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway worked the left wrist up out of the water and held it where the lamplight sat.

She turned it once and read it the same way.

"Left matches right," she said. "Hand white and sodden. Fingers half-bent from soak, not from grip. Nails seated and unbroken. No skin under them. No cuts across the palms. No burns on the knuckles."

She let the hand back down under the surface and wiped the blade clean on the shirt.

"He did not fight because he could not," she said. "When the joints up top separated, the arms went slack. A man fighting for air tears his own throat and the other man's face. There was none of that."

She put the knife flat against the swollen belly below the waterline and pressed once with her palm.

"Gut full of gas," she said. "Three days' worth. Belly tight and drum-high under the water. Skin marbled green and purple at the sides where the blood settled. No wound in it. No bite taken out. No opening made to let the water in."

The smell rose thicker when she pressed, sour and low.

"Smell stayed bowel and cellar," she said. "Stagnant water, iron from the blood settled down low, sweet rot starting up from the gut. No musk. No animal stink laid over it. Whatever pulled him did not mark him with scent and did not feed."

She ran the tip of the blade down the overlong torso to where it went under and felt the line of the spine through the shirt.

"Back straight-pulled," she said. "No sideways break. No knife work along the ribs. Legs still hung straight below, feet down. He folded at the knees when the cord went and the water took him standing."

She rinsed the knife in the flood and set the edge down.

"Finished plain," she said. "Male, middle-aged. Days dead, not weeks. Neck drawn long by a hand's width, joints opened between the second and third bones down, cord pulped at that spot. Hands open and clean. Skin unbroken. Nothing eaten, nothing taken. Pulled first till the signals stopped, drowned second when his legs gave."

She gave a short breath through her nose.

"He did not suffer the water long. The pull did the killing. The cellar just kept the body cold."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I let out a breath I didn't know I was holding.* "So we're looking for something strong. Strong enough to pull a grown man apart like taffy." *I look up from the water, meeting her eyes.* "And it didn't want to eat him. It just wanted him... longer."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway rinsed the blade in the flood and shook the water off it.

She kept her eyes on the mass at the far wall and did not look up the steps.

"Strong, yes," she said. "Strong the way a winch is strong. Slow and set and not in a hurry."

She tipped her chin toward the stretched throat where it sat slack in the lamplight.

"It did not want him longer," she said. "Length was the side effect. It wanted him quiet. Hands on the head from behind, pull straight till the cord inside the neck pulped. No thrash. No shout. A man with a cut throat still kicks and spoils the water. A man with a pulled cord just folds."

She gave a short breath through her nose.

"Eat later, maybe. This one was not feeding. This one was switching him off and letting the cellar store him."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I stand up, my legs shaky.* "Then we should be looking for something that wants its kills kept cold and quiet." *I glance back at the listing head.* "Do you think it's still here?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not turn toward the steps. She stayed knee-deep in the flood and kept the blade low and the lamp high.

She listened to the cellar first. The water had gone flat against the walls. No drip pushed a fresh ring across it. No draught moved down the stairwell to stir the air over it.

"Cold and quiet is how it keeps them," she said. "So yes. Cold and quiet is how it keeps itself."

She tipped the lamp toward the far corners where the light thinned out and did not reach the brick.

"It stored him standing in four feet of water and did not feed," she said. "Things that store do not walk far from the pantry. It stopped moving a minute ago because we brought light down. It will move again when it thinks we have looked long enough to get careless."

She rinsed the blood off her hands in the flood and shook them clean.

"Stay out of reach of the head. It likes to start there."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I shift my grip on the lamp, my knuckles white.* "Right. So we wait for it to move again, or we make it move?" *My eyes keep flicking to the dark corners.*

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway crouched at the edge of the cellar, her grizzled face illuminated by the flickering lantern light. She squinted at the dark shape lurking beneath the murky water, her weathered hands steadying the lamp. 

"Wrong how?" she asked, her voice a low rumble. "Too many legs? Too many heads? You gotta be more specific, kid."

She reached into her coat, fingers brushing the cold metal of her shotgun. Not that it would do much good if whatever it was decided to come to life. But better to be ready.

Halloway took a slow breath, letting the musty air fill her lungs. She'd seen a lot of weird shit in her thirty years of monster hunting. But something about this felt different. Off.

She glanced over at Pike, the kid's face pale and eyes wide in the dim light. Halloway felt a twinge of something she hadn't felt in a long time. Could almost be mistaken for concern. "I'm gonna need you to stay sharp, you hear me? Keep that crossbow ready and your eyes on that thing. And if it moves, you shoot it. Understand?"

Without waiting for an answer, Halloway started wading into the water, shotgun raised and ready. The cold water soaked through her boots, sending a shiver up her spine. But she barely noticed. All her focus was on that dark shape in the distance. 

"Let's see what we're dealing with," she muttered under her breath. Her heart pounded in her chest, but her hands were steady as she crept forward, water sloshing around her legs.

Halloway stopped a few feet away from the creature, close enough to see the details but far enough to make a run for it if needed. She swallowed hard, her throat suddenly dry.

Well, shit, she thought. This is gonna be a long night.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: My eyes narrow, trying to make sense of the shadows. "It's... symmetrical. But not right. Like it's folded wrong." I raise my crossbow, my hands trembling slightly. "Shouldn't we back up first?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway paused, one foot still submerged in the icy water. She glanced back at Pike, her brow furrowing at the kid's words. "Folded wrong? What the hell does that mean?" 

She squinted harder at the dark shape, trying to make sense of Pike's description. Then, slowly, she started to see it. The creature's limbs seemed to be twisted at unnatural angles, as if it had been crumpled up and discarded like a piece of trash.

"Fuck me," Halloway muttered under her breath. "This thing looks like a goddamn origami project gone wrong."

She took a step closer, her shotgun at the ready. The water splashed around her, the sound echoing in the musty cellar. The creature remained still, but Halloway knew better than to let her guard down.

"Alright, Pike, you stay right there and keep that crossbow ready. I'm gonna get a closer look at this thing."

Halloway waded forward, the water rising to her waist. She could feel the cold seeping into her bones, but she ignored it. Her focus was solely on the creature before her.

As she got closer, the details became clearer. The creature's skin was a mottled grey, slick and shiny in the lantern light. Its limbs were elongated, folded in on themselves in a way that made Halloway's stomach churn.

"What the fuck are you supposed to be?" she muttered, her voice barely audible over the sound of the water.

Suddenly, the creature twitched. Halloway froze, her finger tightening on the trigger of her shotgun. But the creature didn't move again. It just lay there, twisted and broken, in the murky water.

Halloway let out a slow breath, trying to calm her racing heart. She knew she needed to get a closer look, but the thought of touching that thing made her skin crawl.

"Pike, you got that crossbow ready? I'm gonna need you to cover me while I check this thing out."

She took a deep breath, steeling herself for what was to come. Then, with a grunt of effort, she reached out and grabbed hold of the creature's limb, ready to pull it up out of the water.

[Continue as Pike. Write your next response.]

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway's grip tightened on the creature's limb as Pike's words echoed in the damp cellar. She squinted, examining the mottled grey skin and unnaturally twisted joints.

"I'm not seeing any signs of recent human remains," she replied, her voice gruff. "But I'm not getting any closer to this thing than I already am."

She gave the limb a tentative tug, and the creature's body shifted, sending ripples through the murky water. Halloway's stomach churned at the sight, but she pressed on, determined to unravel the mystery before them.

"Fuck me, this thing is heavy," she grunted, straining against the creature's weight. "I need you to grab the other side, Pike. Help me haul this thing out of the water."

Halloway reached out with her free hand, gesturing for Pike to join her. She could see the hesitation in the kid's eyes, the way their hands trembled on the crossbow. But Halloway knew they couldn't afford to waste any more time.

"We don't have a choice, kid. We need to see what we're dealing with."

With a deep breath, Halloway braced herself and heaved, pulling the creature's body towards the edge of the water. The skin felt cold and clammy against her skin, and she had to fight back a wave of nausea as the creature's twisted limbs flopped against her chest.

"Fucking hell," she muttered, her voice strained with effort. "This thing weighs a ton."

Slowly, inch by inch, they dragged the creature out of the water and onto the damp cellar floor. Halloway stepped back, her breath coming in ragged gasps as she surveyed their handiwork.

There, in the flickering lantern light, lay a grotesque amalgamation of limbs and flesh, twisted and folded in on itself like a macabre origami creation. The creature's skin was a mottled grey, slick and shiny in the light, and its limbs were elongated and contorted at unnatural angles.

"What the fuck is this thing?" Pike asked, their voice trembling with a blend of fear and disgust.

Halloway shook her head, her brow furrowed in concentration as she examined the creature. "I've never seen anything like it," she admitted. "But one thing's for sure - this thing ain't natural."

She reached into her coat, pulling out a small notebook and a pencil. Quickly, she began to sketch the creature's twisted form, her hand moving with a practiced precision.

"We need to document everything," she said, her voice low and serious. "Take pictures, make notes - anything we can use to figure out what the hell this thing is and where it came from."

Halloway glanced up at Pike, her eyes hardening with determination. "We're not leaving this cellar until we have answers, kid. And if that means staying up all night, then so be it."

She returned her focus to the creature, her pencil scratching against the paper as she worked to capture every grotesque detail. Halloway knew they were in for a long and grueling night, but she was determined to see it through.

"What do you see, Pike?" she asked, not looking up from her sketch. "Anything that stands out to you about this thing's anatomy?"

[Continue as Pike. Write your next response.]

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I force myself to look closer, swallowing hard. "No eyes. Or... no *normal* eyes. Just... seams." I point with my crossbow bolt at a line of puckered, greyish skin running along what might be a head. "Like it was stitched shut."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway followed Pike's gaze, her pencil freezing mid-stroke as she took in the grotesque detail. "Fuck me," she muttered under her breath. "This thing's been stitched up like a goddamn doll."

She leaned in closer, her nose wrinkling at the musty, slightly sweet scent emanating from the creature's mottled skin. The puckered seams ran along the creature's head, closing off what should have been eye sockets and a mouth. It was as if someone - or something - had taken great pains to ensure that this creature could neither see nor speak.

"Whoever - or whatever - did this wanted this thing to be blind and mute," Halloway said, her voice tight with revulsion. "The question is, why?"

She began to circle the creature, her pencil moving rapidly as she sketched the intricate patterns of stitches and folds. The more she looked, the more she began to notice other strange details - elongated fingers that seemed to branch off into extra digits, a tail that tapered off into a sharp, barbed point, and a set of gills that flared out from the creature's neck, as if it was meant to breathe underwater.

"Fucking hell," Halloway breathed, her mind reeling as she tried to make sense of it all. "This thing's been engineered. Modified. Fuck knows what for, but it sure as shit ain't natural."

She glanced up at Pike, her brow furrowed in concentration. "We need to document everything we can about this thing. Every stitch, every twist - anything that might give us a clue about what we're dealing with."

Halloway reached into her coat, pulling out a small camera and a flashlight. She handed them to Pike, nodding towards the creature. "I need you to take pictures from every angle. Make sure you get those gills, those extra digits - anything that looks out of the ordinary."

As Pike began to snap photos, Halloway returned her attention to the creature, her mind racing with questions. Who would create such a thing? What was its purpose? And most importantly, how did it end up in this cellar, twisted and broken like a discarded toy?

She knew she wouldn't find answers here, but she was determined to gather as much information as she could. Every detail, no matter how small, could be the key to unraveling this mystery.

"Pike, I need you to keep those photos safe," she said, her voice low and serious. "We can't let this information fall into the wrong hands."

Halloway reached into her coat, pulling out a small vial and a syringe. She knew she needed to take a tissue sample from the creature, but the thought of getting any closer made her skin crawl.

"Fucking hell," she muttered, her hand hovering over the creature's twisted flesh. "This is gonna be disgusting."

With a deep breath, she jabbed the needle into the creature's mottled skin, wincing as the syringe filled with a murky, greenish fluid. The creature's flesh felt cold and clammy against her fingers, and Halloway had to fight back a wave of nausea as she withdrew the needle.

"There," she said, holding up the vial of fluid. "Let's hope this shit gives us some answers."

Halloway knew they were in for a long and grueling night, but she was determined to see it through. She couldn't shake the feeling that this was just the beginning - that there were darker, more terrifying secrets lurking beneath the surface.

But for now, all they could do was gather as much information as they could and hope that it would be enough to keep them alive.

"What do you think, Pike?" she asked, her voice tight with tension. "Think we'll be able to figure out what this thing is?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway's gaze hardened as she examined the creature's twisted form, her voice taking on a grim, clinical tone. 

"Well, this thing's been through the wringer, that's for damn sure," she said, jabbing her pencil at the creature's mottled flesh. "Look at those stitches - they're uneven, like whoever did this was in a hurry. And these bruises and contusions - they look old, but they're still visible beneath the skin."

She pointed to a series of dark, mottled patches along the creature's limbs and torso, her brow furrowed in concentration. "My guess is this thing's been stuffed in a crate or a bag for a while, probably during transport. The bruising matches the pattern of handles or straps pressing into the skin."

Halloway leaned in closer, her nose wrinkling at the musty, slightly sweet scent emanating from the creature's flesh. "And look at these gashes and lacerations - they're too clean and precise to be from any normal weapon or tool. Whoever created this thing used some kind of high-tech cutting instrument."

She ran her fingers along the creature's elongated limbs, her voice dropping to a near whisper. "And these joints - they've been dislocated and reset multiple times. The way they're twisted and folded... it's like this thing was contorted into some kind of fucked-up origami project."

Halloway's gaze drifted to the creature's head, where the puckered seams closed off what should have been eye sockets and a mouth. "And those stitches on the face - they're not just cosmetic. Whoever did this wanted to make sure this thing couldn't see, couldn't speak. They wanted it silent and blind."

She leaned back, her brow furrowed as she tried to make sense of it all. "My best guess is that this thing was created for some kind of covert operation. Maybe it was a spy or an assassin, or maybe it was some kind of fucked-up experiment. But one thing's for sure - whoever made this thing didn't want it to be able to communicate or identify them."

Halloway reached into her coat, pulling out a small pair of tweezers and a magnifying glass. She began to carefully examine the creature's flesh, her voice taking on a more conversational tone as she worked.

"Of course, that's just my theory," she said, her eyes narrowed in concentration. "But I've seen enough shit in my thirty years of monster hunting to know that when something looks this fucked up, there's usually a pretty fucked up reason behind it."

She glanced up at Pike, her expression grim. "We're gonna need to take this thing apart, examine every inch of it. I'm gonna need your help, kid. Think you're up for some good old-fashioned dissection?"

Halloway knew it was a gruesome task, but she also knew it was necessary. They needed to uncover the truth, no matter how ugly it might be.

"I know it's not pretty," she said, her voice softening slightly. "But we can't afford to leave any stone unturned. This thing... it's not just some random monster. It's a puzzle, and we need to figure out what the fuck it is and where it came from."

She reached out, placing a hand on Pike's shoulder. "I know you're not a monster hunter like me. But you've got a good head on your shoulders, and I'm gonna need you to keep it together. Can you do that for me, kid?"

Halloway's gaze was intense, but there was a hint of something else there too - a glimmer of respect, maybe even a touch of affection. She knew Pike was green, but she also knew the kid had potential. And in a situation like this, potential was all they had to go on.

"So what do you say, Pike? You ready to get your hands dirty and solve this fucked-up mystery with me?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at the stitches for a long moment. "They didn't want it to see them," I say quietly. "Whoever made it." I set the lamp down on a dry crate and pull my knife from my belt. My hands don't shake anymore. "Where do you want to start?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway's eyes flashed with a blend of pride and grim satisfaction as she saw the determined look on Pike's face. The kid was finally starting to understand the gravity of the situation, the importance of staying sharp and focused.

"That's the spirit," she said, nodding approvingly. "We're gonna need to start at the top and work our way down. I want to see if there's anything hidden beneath those stitches."

She reached into her coat, pulling out a small, sharp blade. "Careful now, we don't want to damage anything important. And keep an eye out for any foreign objects or substances - anything that might give us a clue about where this thing came from or what it was used for."

Halloway began to carefully cut away at the creature's mottled flesh, her hand steady and precise. She worked in silence, her brow furrowed in concentration as she examined every inch of the creature's twisted form.

As she cut, the creature's skin split open like a grotesque, stitched-up doll. Beneath the mottled grey flesh, Halloway could see a tangle of wires and circuits, pulsing with an eerie, otherworldly light. The creature's limbs were a network of hydraulic tubes and metal joints, moving and twitching as if they were still alive.

"Fucking hell," Halloway breathed, her voice a hushed murmur. "This thing's not just some monster - it's some kind of fucked-up robot. Or maybe a cyborg."

She leaned in closer, her eyes narrowing as she examined the creature's internal workings. "Look at those circuits - they're unlike anything I've ever seen before. And those wires - they're not just powering the thing, they're sending data. This thing's been programmed, Pike. And I'm betting it's been programmed to do something fucked up."

Halloway knew they were onto something big, something that could change everything they thought they knew about the monster-hunting business. But she also knew they had to tread carefully - one wrong move, and they could end up just like this creature, twisted and broken and discarded.

"We need to be careful, Pike," she said, her voice low and serious. "This thing's not just some random monster - it's some kind of fucked-up experiment. And if there's one, there's probably more. We need to document everything, take samples, anything we can use to figure out what we're dealing with."

Halloway reached into her coat, pulling out a small vial and a syringe. She knew they needed to get a closer look at the creature's internal workings, but the thought of cutting into its mottled flesh made her stomach churn.

"Alright, kid," she said, her voice tight with tension. "Let's get this thing apart. But we need to be careful - one wrong move, and this thing could still be dangerous."

She glanced up at Pike, her eyes hardening with determination. "You ready to get your hands dirty, kid? 'Cause I have a feeling we're in for a long and grueling night."

[Continue as Pike. Write your next response.]

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway leaned in closer, her eyes narrowing as she examined the creature's twisted, mutilated form. She knew Pike needed the details, needed to understand the full extent of the horror they were dealing with. But even as she spoke, Halloway could feel a chill running down her spine, a primal fear that something like this could exist in the world.

"Alright, kid," she said, her voice low and grim. "Let me paint you a picture."

She reached out, running her fingers along the creature's mottled grey flesh. "Under the skin, this thing's a fucking nightmare. It's got hydraulic tubes running through its limbs, metal joints that allow it to twist and contort in ways that defy nature. And those wires - they're not just powering the thing, they're sending data. This thing's been programmed, Pike. And I'm betting it's been programmed to do something fucked up."

Halloway's gaze drifted to the creature's head, where the puckered seams closed off what should have been eye sockets and a mouth. "Look at those stitches - they're not just cosmetic. Whoever did this wanted to make sure this thing couldn't see, couldn't speak. They wanted it silent and blind."

She leaned in closer, her nose wrinkling at the musty, slightly sweet scent emanating from the creature's flesh. "And look at those gashes and lacerations - they're too clean and precise to be from any normal weapon or tool. Whoever created this thing used some kind of high-tech cutting instrument. And the way the joints are twisted and folded... it's like this thing was contorted into some kind of fucked-up origami project."

Halloway's voice dropped to a near whisper as she continued. "But that's not the worst of it, Pike. Look at these circuits - they're unlike anything I've ever seen before. And look at this."

She reached into the creature's chest cavity, pulling out a small, pulsating mass of flesh and metal. "This thing's been modified, Pike. They've taken human tissue and fused it with machine parts. It's like a fucking cyborg, but worse. This thing's not just part human, part machine - it's been twisted and warped, turned into something unnatural and grotesque."

Halloway's hand trembled slightly as she held up the pulsating mass of flesh and metal. "I don't know what this thing was made to do, Pike. But I can tell you one thing - whoever created it, they wanted it to be a weapon. A tool for some kind of fucked-up agenda. And I'm betting it's not the only one of its kind."

She looked up at Pike, her eyes hard and determined. "We need to be ready for the worst, kid. If there's one of these things, there could be more. And we can't let them catch us off guard."

Halloway knew it was a grim prospect, but she also knew it was necessary. They were in for a long and grueling battle, and they needed to be prepared for anything.

"So what do you say, Pike?" she asked, her voice low and serious. "Think you can handle the truth, no matter how ugly it gets? Because I have a feeling we're in for a fucked-up ride, and we're gonna need to stay sharp and focused if we want to make it out alive."

She held Pike's gaze, her expression unreadable. "You ready for this, kid? 'Cause once we start digging, there's no going back. And I need to know you're with me, no matter what we find."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I look at the mass of flesh and metal in her hand. "Was there a person in there? Before it got... made?" My voice is quiet, but steady. "We should check the rest of the water. For pieces they didn't use."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway's expression darkened, a flicker of something like revulsion and grim determination passing through her eyes. She knew Pike was right - they couldn't afford to leave any stone unturned, no matter how unpleasant the task might be.

"I'm afraid so, kid," she said, her voice tight with tension. "Whoever created this thing, they didn't just twist it, they remade it. I'm guessing the person they started with is still in there somewhere, but it's going to be a fucking mess to sort out."

She glanced down at the mass of flesh and metal in her hand, her nose wrinkling in disgust. "This thing's been modified, Pike. They've taken human tissue and fused it with machine parts. It's like a fucking cyborg, but worse. This thing's not just part human, part machine - it's been twisted and warped, turned into something unnatural and grotesque."

Halloway knew they couldn't afford to dwell on the horror of it all. They had a job to do, and they needed to stay focused and sharp.

"You're right, Pike," she said, nodding grimly. "We need to check the rest of the water. For any pieces they didn't use, for any clues we might find."

She reached into her coat, pulling out a small flashlight and a pair of latex gloves. "Here, put these on," she said, tossing the gloves to Pike. "We don't know what we might find in there, and I don't want to take any chances."

She took another step forward, the water now up to her knees. Her free hand rested on the hilt of her knife, ready to draw it at a moment's notice.

"Keep an eye on the shadows," she warned, her voice low and steady. "Something's been in here with that... thing. And it ain't happy we're here."

"Whatever it is, it's been here a while," she continued, her eyes never leaving the darkness. "And it ain't used to sharing its space."

Another ripple, closer this time. Halloway's hand moved to her knife, her thumb resting on the guard. She took another step back, her shoulder brushing against Pike's.

"Time to go, I think," she said, her tone matter-of-fact. "We'll come back with more people, better gear. Right now, we're just... dinner."

She turned, moving swiftly and silently through the water towards the stairs. Behind them, something surfaced with a splash, letting out a guttural growl that echoed through the cellar.

"Run," Halloway said, not looking back. "And don't stop until we're out of this damn house."
