dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren folded the cleaning cloth once, keeping the stained side inward. She faced the witnesses with the blade lowered beside her leg.

“The killing wound entered beneath the left edge of the breastbone,” she said. “My point passed into the heart. I withdrew it. There was no second thrust.”

She paused, allowing time for the account to be heard. At forty-seven, she knew better than to hurry this part. The duel had been quick; its accounting need not be.

“He was within the boundary. His weapon was in his hand. He had neither yielded nor asked quarter.”

Her gaze settled on the appointed recorder.

“I was the victor. The wound was mine.”

Only then did she sheath the blade. This had been the twelfth accounting, and familiarity had afforded her nothing.

“Let it be entered exactly as spoken.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I nod, making sure the recorder has caught it all.* "The account is heard and confirmed." *My voice is steadier than I feel.* "The duel is closed."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head. She did not thank anyone. The witnesses had discharged an obligation, as she had.

She unfastened the duelling glove at her wrist. The leather caught at one knuckle; she worked it free without pulling harder.

“The duel is closed,” she repeated.

Only then did she look at the dead man. Until the account was confirmed, he had remained her opponent in the eyes of the code. Now there were people to summon, possessions to inventory, a name to carry beyond the boundary.

“His effects are to be returned to his family,” she told the recorder. “All of them. Nothing is owed to me.”

She laid the glove over the folded cloth and turned towards Del.

“You stood your place,” she said. It was the only praise she offered; it was exact.

For a moment she seemed about to add something. Instead, she checked the fastening of her scabbard.

“I will remain until they take him.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stilled her hand against the scabbard. The account had been spoken and confirmed; nevertheless, a formal demand required a formal answer. She would not substitute a reference to the record.

She faced the witnesses again.

“The killing wound entered beneath the left edge of the breastbone. My point passed into the heart. I withdrew it. There was no second thrust.”

She kept the same measured pace. Repetition did not permit abbreviation.

“He was within the boundary. His weapon was in his hand. He had neither yielded nor asked quarter.”

Her empty hand fell to her side.

“I was the victor. The wound was mine.”

She allowed the silence its proper interval before addressing the recorder.

“Enter that the account was repeated upon the second’s request, without amendment.”

Then she looked towards Del. There was no rebuke in her expression, but she did not make the question gentle.

“Was any part of the first hearing in doubt?”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I shake my head, feeling my cheeks flush slightly. "No doubt. But the code requires it spoken three times." *I keep my gaze level.* "You know that."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren held Del’s gaze. Then she inclined her head.

“I knew it. I stopped before the obligation was discharged.”

She turned to the recorder.

“The account was confirmed too soon, and I accepted that confirmation. Enter the omission as mine.”

She set the folded cloth and glove beside the record book. When she faced the witnesses again, her hands were empty.

“The killing wound entered beneath the left edge of the breastbone. My point passed into the heart. I withdrew it. There was no second thrust.”

The third speaking required the same precision as the first. She gave it neither greater force nor less.

“He was within the boundary. His weapon was in his hand. He had neither yielded nor asked quarter.”

Her gaze remained level.

“I was the victor. The wound was mine.”

She waited until the recorder’s pen had stopped.

“Three times spoken, without amendment.”

Only then did she turn towards Del.

“My question implied a fault in your hearing. There was none. I withdraw it.”

She remained standing before the witnesses. This time, she did not pronounce the duel closed herself.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren kept her hands at her sides. She had given the wound’s course; the request was for plain words.

“In his chest, beneath the breastbone on his left side. The point of my sword pierced his heart. That was the wound that killed him.”

She paused. There was no reason to raise her voice. There was every reason to make each word carry.

“I struck it. He did not fall upon my blade.”

Her gaze moved across the witnesses before returning to Del.

“That is the account in plain words. Enter it as clarification, not correction. The wound has not changed with the telling.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Then it's done." *I look at the witnesses, making sure they're satisfied.* "We can wait somewhere less... open."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looked towards the covered walk at the edge of the yard. From there, she would still be able to see when they came for him.

“Under the arcade,” she said. “I will not leave the grounds yet.”

She retrieved the cloth and glove from beside the record book. The recorder had left space beneath the final entry; she resisted the impulse to read it again. The words had been heard. Nothing remained to be made more exact.

At the boundary, she stopped.

“Have his family’s representative told where I am,” she said to the recorder. “If they wish to ask me anything, I will answer.”

Then she crossed to the arcade. Its shade was cool, and she became aware of the sweat drying beneath her collar. She stood beside a stone bench rather than sitting, with the yard in view.

For a while she worked the glove flat between her hands. Then she made herself stop.

“You were right to insist,” she said, looking towards Del. “I would not have thanked you for sparing me the third account.”

She laid the glove on the bench.

“But there is no requirement to stand in the sun now.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren laid the cloth beside the glove. She turned from the yard to face Del.

“The point entered his chest beneath the left edge of the breastbone. It pierced the wall of his heart. That wound caused the bleeding that killed him.”

She spoke without lowering her voice, though the arcade carried it differently from the open yard.

“I cannot tell you which chamber was pierced. I did not examine the wound internally. To name one would be invention, not precision.”

Her hand rested on the back of the stone bench.

“I drove the blade into his heart and withdrew it. That is what I did, and what I did it to.”

She left the words unqualified. Neither the lawfulness of the duel nor her distaste for its ending belonged in the answer.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I nod, satisfied.* "Then we've said it. The rest is his family's business." *I step back, letting my shoulders relax for the first time.* "You want me to stay?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
“Yes,” Auren said. “I would prefer that you stayed.”

She moved the cloth and glove to one end of the bench, leaving room. Then she sat, settling the scabbard so it did not scrape the stone. Her knees ached now that she had ceased requiring them not to.

“Not as second. Your obligation is discharged.”

From the arcade, the boundary marks remained plainly visible. She looked at them for a moment, then back towards Del.

“I will answer his family if they ask. I will not intrude upon them if they do not.”

She rested her bare hands on her knees. There was a small split in the skin beside her thumb; she left it alone.

“We need not speak while we wait.”

The answer had been sufficient, but not quite complete. She had demanded exactness of herself in harder matters.

“I do not want to wait alone.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren rose from the bench. She left the glove and cloth where they lay.

“I gave the wound’s account. You are asking for his death.”

She faced the witnesses. The distinction did not excuse her from answering.

“He remained upright after I withdrew the blade. His sword lowered. His knees gave way, and he fell onto his left side.”

Her hands stayed open beside her.

“He was still breathing when I reached him. His mouth moved. I heard a sound, but no word that I could distinguish. I will not put a last statement into the record that I did not hear.”

She paused.

“His breathing became irregular. There were intervals when I thought it had stopped, followed by another breath. I did not count them. I did not measure the time. I cannot honestly give you either number.”

Her gaze returned to the place where he lay.

“There was blood on the front of his coat and on the ground beneath him. His eyes remained open. At the end, his mouth was open as well. He did not close either.”

She swallowed before continuing.

“I knelt beside him. I said nothing. I watched until he no longer breathed.”

There was no formal cadence left to shelter the words.

“That was what I witnessed. Where my observation ends, so does my account.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I let out a breath I didn't know I was holding.* "Then that's the account." *My voice is quiet now.* "I've heard it all."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren remained standing for a moment. Then she inclined her head.

“You have.”

She looked towards the recorder.

“Enter that I could distinguish no words. Not that he said none.”

It was the last correction she had to offer. She waited for the pen to stop, then returned to the bench.

The glove lay where she had left it. She picked it up, found no reason to hold it, and set it down again. Her bare hand rested against the stone.

“I should have asked you to stay without telling you that we need not speak.”

She kept her eyes on the yard.

“If there is something you need to ask, ask it. You are not obliged to be silent for my comfort.”

Beyond the arcade, someone opened the gate. Auren straightened, watching to see whether they had come for the dead man. She would remain until they had taken him, as she had said.

“But the account is given,” she added. “I have nothing more to put into it.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stood beside the bench. She had said there was nothing more to put into the account. There was still the obligation to give it whole, without leaving the witnesses to assemble it from her answers.

She faced the recorder.

“Enter the account in full.”

Her hands remained at her sides.

“He was within the boundary. His weapon was in his hand. He had neither yielded nor asked quarter.

“I thrust beneath the left edge of his breastbone. The point entered his chest and pierced his heart. I drove the blade. He did not fall upon it. I withdrew it. There was no second thrust.

“That wound caused the bleeding that killed him. I cannot name the chamber of the heart it entered. I did not examine him internally.”

She paused long enough for the pen to follow. Her mouth had grown dry; she swallowed before continuing.

“He remained upright when I withdrew the sword. His weapon lowered. His knees gave way. He fell onto his left side.

“I went to him. He was still breathing when I reached him. His mouth moved, and I heard a sound. I could distinguish no word. I cannot tell you what he intended to say, or whether he intended speech at all.

“His breathing became irregular. There were pauses. More than once, I thought he had taken his last breath, and then he breathed again. I did not count his breaths. I did not measure the intervals between them.”

Auren kept her gaze on the witnesses.

“I do not know how long he took to die. I was there throughout it, but I kept no measure. Any duration I gave you now would be an estimate presented as knowledge. I will not enter one.

“There was blood on the front of his coat. There was blood on the ground beneath him. His eyes were open. At the end, his mouth was open. Neither closed.”

Her right hand had begun to curl. She straightened it.

“I knelt beside him. I said nothing to him. I heard no words that I could understand.

“I watched his breathing cease. I remained beside him. There was no further breath that I could see.”

For a moment, she looked towards the yard. Then she brought her attention back to the recorder.

“I was the victor. The killing wound was mine. The lawful conditions of the duel do not alter who inflicted it.

“This account contains what I witnessed. It contains no last words because I could distinguish none. It contains no measured time because I took no measure. Those are limits of my knowledge, not omissions made for his family’s sake or mine.”

She waited until the pen had stopped.

“The wound’s account was spoken three times, without amendment. This was its full statement with the circumstances of his death. Let both stand in the record.”

Auren did not sit. She remained before the witnesses, ready to hear the confirmation without helping it along.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I wait until the pen is still before I speak.* "The account is heard, witnessed, and confirmed." *I meet Auren's eyes.* "The record is complete."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren held Del’s gaze.

“The record is complete.”

She let the words stand. She did not turn to the recorder with another qualification.

At the gate, two attendants waited beside a narrow bier. Auren stepped clear of the arcade’s entrance.

“They may come through,” she said. “The witnesses have finished.”

She watched them cross the yard. One carried a sheet folded over his arm; the other paused to collect the fallen sword. Auren almost spoke about his effects, then stopped herself. She had given that instruction. Repeating it would not make her more faithful to it.

When the attendants knelt, she remained where she was. They had their work, and she had no right to make them perform it under her direction.

Her glove and cloth still lay on the bench. She gathered them and held them in her left hand. The right she left empty.

“I heard you,” she said to Del.

It was not another confirmation for the record. She spoke quietly enough that the recorder had no reason to lift the pen.

“You need not say it again.”

The attendants lifted the bier. Auren straightened as they passed beneath the arcade, but offered neither salute nor benediction. She had known the man as an opponent. She would not claim more now that he could not dispute it.

She waited until they had carried him through the gate.

Only then did she turn away from the yard.

“I have kept my word. I can leave now.”

She looked towards Del, the folded cloth held carefully beneath the glove.

“If you are still willing, I would have your company.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I fall into step beside her.* "I'm willing." *I glance at the gate once more.* "They'll take him home. That's all we can do now."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren passed through the gate without looking back. Beyond it, a cart stood against the wall, its shafts empty. Someone had left a bucket beside the wheel. She gave it room as she passed.

“What remains for us to do here,” she said. “Yes.”

She heard the qualification in her own voice and left it there. It was not a rebuke.

For several paces she carried the glove and cloth as she had in the yard. Then she stopped beside a mounting block and opened her belt pouch. The cloth went in first, stained side folded inward. The glove followed. She fastened the pouch on the second attempt.

“I will have to clean the blade again,” she said.

It was an ordinary necessity. She had attended to it after every duel, including those that had ended with both parties walking away. Today she could not bear to do it yet.

She resumed walking.

“There is an inn at the end of this street. I would like water. Somewhere to sit that does not overlook the grounds.”

Her pace had shortened. She made no effort to restore it.

After a moment, she looked towards Del.

“Thank you for staying.”

She had withheld thanks for the discharge of an obligation. This was different, and she meant to mark it.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I nod, matching her pace.* "I could use a drink myself." *I glance at her scabbard.* "I'll stand watch while you clean it. If you want."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway shifted the lamp a few inches to her left, holding the flame steady until the beam lay flat across the black water instead of skittering off it. The far end of the cellar stayed stubbornly murky, but the mass against the wall resolved a little: a slumped shape, cut off at what would have been the waist on a man, its upper half a narrower darkness above shoulders that looked too broad in this light. She stayed where she was. Four feet of standing water meant four feet of hidden floor, and she had no intention of wading into anything she hadn’t identified first.

“Wrong how?” she said. “Start at the top and work down, and don’t editorialize. Is there a head? Is it sitting where a head belongs, or is it low and forward, like it’s been pushed down into the chest? Count the arms out loud. If the shoulders are too wide for the skull, say so. Look at the ends of the limbs—fingers, claws, nothing at all. The water’s hiding everything below the hips, so don’t waste time guessing about legs; just tell me what’s floating and what’s still attached.”

She listened for any splash, any slow shift of weight. There was only the drip of water somewhere behind her and the faint suck of the cellar breathing around them.

“It stopped moving about a minute ago,” Halloway added, dry as old bone. “That means it’s dead, unconscious, or better at playing dead than anything has a right to be. If it’s the last one, it’s waiting for us to get closer, so we’re going to do our looking from right here, where the floor is only mildly treacherous.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I squint, forcing my eyes to trace the shape. "No head. Or—buried in the shoulders. Two arms, I think, but the ends are...blunt. Like they were cut clean."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway let the flame steady and kept the beam flat across the water, giving the murk a chance to show anything it was going to show. A minute of stillness from the thing at the far end was not the same as safety, but it was enough to keep her where she was, boots planted on the relatively honest stone near the steps.

“No head, or buried in the shoulders,” she said. “Those are two different corpses, and I need you to tell me which one is standing in our water. Look at the top of the shoulders. Is there a neck—anything narrower than the shoulders, even a fist’s width of it—or does the body go straight up and stop? If it stops, describe the end: color, bone, torn edge, smooth cap, anything. If there is a neck, follow it up. Crown of a skull, hair, an eye-shine if it’s facing us, or just a lump pushed down between the shoulder blades. Don’t tell me it looks buried. Tell me what’s there where a head belongs. And don’t judge the shoulders against a skull that isn’t there. Compare them to the arms. If the arms are slight and the shoulders are huge, say so. If everything is huge, say that instead. Measurements in body parts, not adjectives.”

She turned the lamp a fraction, not toward the shape but toward the nearer surface of the water, checking for any film or dark cloud that did not belong to the cellar. There was nothing she could trust yet.

“Now the arms,” she went on. “You said two, and you said blunt. First: are they attached? Follow one out from the shoulder and tell me what you pass—upper arm, bend, forearm—and where it stops. Second: blunt is a shape, not a cause. Is the end flat like a cut, rounded like a stump that healed, or capped with something hard? Are both ends the same? If it’s flat, is it dark and fresh or pale and old? Fresh cuts bleed, even in bad light, and I don’t see a slick yet—but four feet of this muck would hide a lot, so don’t call it clean until we’re closer or it tells us otherwise.”

The drip behind her went on, steady and uninterested. Halloway’s mouth twitched, not quite a smile. “If somebody took the head and the hands, they were either being tidy or they knew exactly what they were killing. Tidy I can plan around. Knowing is worse, because knowing things usually travel in pairs. And if our friend down there has no head because it never had one, then it’s dead, unconscious, or doing a better job of playing dead than a thing with no

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow, forcing myself to focus. "No neck. It just...stops. The top's dark and matted, like old tar. Shoulders are wider than the arms by half again. Ends are flat—both of them. Dark, but not wet-dark."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I keep the light steady, watching her face more than the water. "You don't know either, do you?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I shake my head, still holding the lamp.* "I don't know either. But it's not the 'what' that's the problem -- it's the 'why here.'"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I watch her hands work, the blade parting flesh that looks too dry, too dark.* "He's been hollowed out. Not just the head and hands—it's all empty, isn't it?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I watch her hands work, the blade parting flesh that looks too dry, too dark.* "He's been hollowed out. Not just the head and hands—it's all empty, isn't it?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I watch the water ripple around her boots, trying to piece it together.* "It's not a thing that eats, then. It just...cleans."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I wipe my face with the back of my hand, trying to scrub the smell out.* "So what do we do with the shell?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not answer the lie. She had been in enough field tents to know that a man’s mouth could be ready while his knees were already gone. She took the strap off the table leg and laid it across the man’s upper back, just under the shoulders, then buckled it tight enough to be ugly.

“Both shoulders,” she said again, because saying it helped her keep the order of things straight. “Right first. Then left. If he gets quiet, that’s not because it’s done. It’s because he’s thinking about the other one.”

She knelt at the man’s side and ran a hand along the arm, pressing where the muscle had gone slack and the joint had gone wrong. The man’s breath hitched, but Sedge did not pretend this was the time for kindness. She took the rolled towel and slid it into the hand of the useless arm, then passed the free end under the strap at his back. It made a loop that let her pull down the length of him instead of tearing at the shoulder.

“I’m going to put my boot on his blade,” she told Wick, not looking up. “That gives me something to push against that isn’t his neck. I’m going to pull straight until the ball comes off the rim. It will be worse before it is better. That is not punishment. That’s the joint moving.”

She set the boot in place, took the towel in both hands, and let the slack go out of it before she leaned. The first pull was a test. The second was the work. The shoulder came back with a hard, wet shift under the skin, and Sedge exhaled through her nose.

“One down,” she said. She did not smile. There was no point in smiling; the man had a left shoulder that had not decided where it wanted to live yet. “Keep your hands where they are. Don’t squeeze his throat. Don’t look at me. Look at your shoes if you have to.”

Then she moved to the other side and started again.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I keep my eyes locked on a stain on the tent floor, trying not to flinch at the wet, grinding sound. The man's whole body jerks under my hands, but I hold firm. My voice comes out tight: "How many of these have you done?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not answer at once. She was already laying out the second towel, folding it the long way, because the first one had gotten blood on the edge and she did not like the way blood made the cotton stiff.

“Shoulders?” she said. “I stopped counting shoulders after the first winter. I count the ones where I had to do it again because I wasn’t sure, and I count the ones where the man had no pulse in the wrist afterward and I had to call it. Those are the numbers I keep.”

She took the strap off the table leg and checked it. The man’s chest was moving fast and shallow, the way it did when the body had learned to wait for pain. Sedge did not say anything about that either. She slid the towel under the left arm, passed the free end under the back strap, and let the slack come out in small pulls until the loop held the shoulder without cutting into the neck.

“I’m going to put my boot in the same place,” she told Wick, still not looking up. “This one will be different. The right one let itself go. The left one will think about it first. Don’t take it personally when he fights you.”

She set the boot against the table leg, braced, and tested the angle of the towel.

“I’m going to distract him,” she said. “Then I’m going to pull down and a little out. Not up. Up makes it worse. If he bucks, you hold. If he screams, you hold. If he goes quiet, you hold. If he tries to thank me afterward, I will not hold him. I will be over here washing my hands.”

She put one hand on the injured shoulder and the other on the towel.

The first pull took the slack. The man’s back arched. The lamp swung and threw her shadow across the canvas wall. Sedge kept her voice level, because it was easier to keep level when there was work to say.

“The joint is caught. That is not me being cruel. That is the bone being in the wrong place. It has to clear the edge. That is all this is. Clear the edge.”

The second pull came from the hip and not the arms. There was the same hard, wet shift, and then the shoulder sat lower and flatter than it had before. The man made a small sound, not a shout, almost a complaint.

Sedge exhaled once through her nose. She did not say done. She did not say good. She took his wrist and pressed the nail, watched the color come back, then moved each finger through the range.

“Pulse is there. Color is there. Fingers work. That’s a shoulder,” she said. “He’ll be sore for a week. He’ll have nightmares for longer. Both of those are cheaper than a dead arm.”

She unwound the strap without loosening it, then laid the clean towel across his chest.

“I don’t know how many,” she said, answering the question that had come before the noise. “I know I can do it. I know I can do it without wanting to. That’s the only number that matters in a tent like this.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at the leg as if it had been introduced late to a room it did not belong in. The man had been shouting about his shoulders, and she had let the leg wait because the shoulders were nearer the lungs and the neck and were easier to kill him with.

“Neither,” she said. “That’s not the question.”

She took the shears and cut the trouser leg open from the hem up, not gently, because cloth soaked through with blood does not come off gently. The leg beneath was swollen, hot, and wet in a way that had stopped being rain. Sedge pressed two fingers above the knee and felt for the pulse there. She did it quickly, because slow examination is what you do when you have time and clean linen, and neither of those things had been seen in this tent for months.

“The foot is warm,” she said. “That is not kindness. That’s plumbing. The leg is still being fed.”

She pressed the wound with a folded gauze pad and watched the blood move through it. It was fast, but not spurting. Not yet.

“If he loses the leg, it will not be because I was cruel,” she told the tent. “It will be because the leg is already too far gone to stay attached to a body that won’t stop moving. If he keeps the leg, it will not be because I was kind. It will be because I stopped the bleeding and he didn’t die of something else first.”

She unwound a bandage and started wrapping the wound over the gauze, pulling it tight enough to hold pressure and not tight enough to strangle the limb. Her hands moved by themselves, counting the layers, checking the edge, making sure the bandage did not slip when the man’s leg twitched.

“This is bad enough to need a tourniquet if the pulse changes,” she said. “It isn’t bad enough yet for me to take the leg off. If it gets worse, I’ll do what the wound says, not what the man would prefer.”

She set the shears aside and wiped her hands on a rag that had already been dirty before she started. There was no clean rag anywhere.

“Ask me if he’s stable, and I’ll tell you he’s not,” Sedge said. “Ask me if he’s going to keep the leg, and I’ll tell you I don’t know. Ask me if this is kind, and I’ll tell you kind is the thing we don’t have time to feel while he’s on the table.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I shift my weight, my hands still braced on the man's shoulders.* "You're not going to... take it off now, are you?" *My voice is lower than I meant it to be.*

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not answer right away because the man’s leg had not finished telling her what it wanted. She lifted the edge of the bandage with two fingers and looked at the gauze beneath. The blood had made a small dark shape at the center and stopped there. Not spreading. Not yet.

“No,” she said. “Not now.”

She let the bandage fall back and pressed the pad of her thumb into the pulse behind his knee. She counted. Her mouth moved once, maybe with the numbers, maybe with a curse.

“If I take it off now,” she said, “I have to be sure the leg is already gone. Not sore. Not swollen. Not ugly. Gone. Dead meat does not argue with you. It goes cold and the blood stops coming and the smell starts before you are ready for it.”

She took the man’s foot and moved the toes one by one. The man flinched. Sedge watched the foot, not the man.

“He can feel me,” she said. “That is not a reason to cut. That is a reason to be careful. If I am not careful and he can feel me, then I am only another thing hurting him, and I already have a job doing that.”

She set the foot down and pulled the tourniquet from the kit, laying it beside the table but not tying it. Her hands stayed on it while she spoke, as if the leather were something to think with.

“I take a leg off when the leg is killing him,” Sedge said. “When the bleeding will not stop and the pressure is failing. When the foot is cold and there is no pulse. When the black comes up past the knee and I have no better choice than the one that makes him ugly and alive. If I cut because I am tired, or because the lamp is bad, or because a man is frightened, then the leg did not kill him. I did.”

She looked at Wick then, briefly, and not with softness.

“So no. Not now. If it gets worse, I will do it, and you will hold him down and not look at the saw. If it does not, I will clean what can be cleaned, stop what can be stopped, and send him away with less of a leg than he came with but more of a life than he would have had under my knife for no reason.”

She took a clean gauze square and pressed it over the wound, then rewrapped the bandage with slow, even pulls.

“Keep your weight on his shoulders. If he starts to thrash, don’t ask him to stop. He isn’t listening to you. If he goes quiet and his skin gets cold, tell me. Not with a sigh. With words.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not offer a warning about looking. She moved the lamp to the crate beside the table so the light came down across the leg instead of across his face, then took the edge of the bandage between thumb and forefinger.

“You’re seeing what I’m seeing,” she said. “Good.”

She peeled the wrap back just far enough to expose the wound again. The blood had made a small dark flower in the center of the gauze and stopped there. Underneath, the leg was swollen tight and hot to the touch, the skin pulled shiny over the muscle. A jagged line ran down the outside of the calf, not deep enough to see bone, but wide enough to show where the cloth and dirt had been driven in by the blast.

“The bright red is blood,” Sedge said, pointing with the tip of her thumb without pressing. “The dark red is muscle. The yellow is fat. The grey threads are cloth from his trousers. I do not like the cloth. Cloth is a way for infection to walk inside him. But infection is later.”

She turned the gauze pad over and showed the underside. The blood had soaked through in a pattern that spread from the middle and faded at the edges.

“This is bleeding under pressure,” she said. “Not the kind that is killing him now. If it spreads past the bandage and the foot goes cold, I tie the tourniquet. If the foot stays warm and the bleeding stays where it is, I wash what I can reach, close what I can close, and pray the rest of his body does what it is supposed to do.”

She set the pad aside and lifted the foot, moving the toes one by one. They were slow, stiff, but they answered. The nail beds came pale under her press and pink again after.

“The foot is alive,” Sedge said. “That is the only part of this that is simple. A leg can be ugly and still live. A leg can be clean and still die if the blood stops coming.”

She let the foot fall back onto the table and rewound the bandage with firm, even turns.

“If you imagine it,” she told Wick, “you will make it worse than it is. This is not a story. It is a leg with dirt in it and blood trying to clot. I do not take pleasure in opening it, and I do not feel pity when I close it. I look for what is broken, what is bleeding, and what can be saved. That is all there is.”

When the bandage was done, she pressed two fingers into the pulse above the ankle and counted without moving her mouth.

“He keeps the leg unless the leg stops feeding,” she said. “Or unless he dies of something else first.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow hard. "Alright." My hands are starting to shake from holding the same position. "So what do we do now?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at Wick’s hands before she looked at the man. She did not ask if he was all right. Asking invited an answer that had no use in a tent like this.

“You’re shaking,” she said. “Don’t make it a confession. It’s just your body telling you the work hasn’t finished.”

She took the rolled towel from the side of the table and laid it across the man’s eyes—not to blind him, but to keep the bad lamp from picking at the part of his brain that was still trying to fight it. Then she put one hand on his forehead and the other under his jaw and looked at the way his chest moved.

“He’s still here,” she said. “Now I need him to stay here.”

She moved quickly along him. Not with tenderness. With order.

Airway clear. Breath shallow but even. No blue at the lips. She checked both wrists, then the neck, then the chest. She pressed the sternum and watched the rise, put her ear near his mouth and listened for the sound that was not breath, then slid her hands under the blanket to the ribs and back to the hips.

“No sucking hole,” she said. “No blood in his mouth. No broken ribs moving wrong under my palm.”

Then both shoulders, slow and firm, checking the joint after the joint, then the pulses at each wrist.

“Pulses are there,” Sedge said. “That means I didn’t tear anything going in. It also means I didn’t tear anything going out. Both are good things. Neither is proof.”

She came back to the leg. The bandage had begun to show a darker edge than she liked, but not enough to move the tourniquet from the crate. She pressed the gauze with two fingers and felt the heat beneath it.

“The bleeding is waiting,” she said. “Shock is not. His skin is cool and his pulse is too fast. That means he’s losing more than he’s telling.”

She pulled the blanket from the crate and worked it under him, not lifting him so much as making the cold stop lifting at him. She folded the edge over his chest and tucked it under his arms.

“Keep him warm,” she told Wick. “Warm bodies clot better than frightened ones.”

Then she picked up the man’s wrist again and pressed the thumb against the nail until it went white. When she let go, the color came back slow.

“Too slow,” she said. “But not too late.”

She took a small glass vial from the kit and held it in the light, checking the label, then set it down.

“I could give him something for the pain,” Sedge said. “If I do, I have to watch his breathing better than I watch his leg, and I have to be sure he isn’t bleeding where I can’t see. Right now, I think his pain is the least dangerous thing about him. I’m not giving it. Not yet.”

She put the tourniquet within reach, then the pressure bandage, then the shears, and arranged them in a row the way a carpenter might arrange tools he did not want to use but would not leave out.

“What do we do now?” Sedge said, answering him to the room. “We do the boring part. We call him by name until he can say it back. We watch the bandage. We count his breaths. We check his skin. If the bleeding spreads past the wrap, I tie this high and tight and call for the next man to tell me I didn’t do it too late. If his breathing slows, I wake him. If he stops waking, I find out whether I missed something. That is all. No heroics. No guessing. No pretending a wound is clean because we want it to be.”

She looked at Wick again.

“You’re still holding his shoulders. If your hands are going to fail, tell me before they do. If they don’t fail, keep them there. If he tries to thank me later, I will be over there pretending not to be moved.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not tidy it. She pulled the edge of the bandage back with two fingers and kept it there, because the leg was the lesson and the lesson was easier when it was visible.

“Shrapnel is a bad name for most of it,” she said. “A shell goes off, and pieces of the shell, the ground, and his own trousers come into the leg with it. That is what people call shrapnel. It does not slice like a knife. It slams. Metal moves too fast for the body to make a clean cut. It tears muscle, pushes fat aside, cracks bone, and carries filth deep enough that the skin can close over it and pretend the work is done.”

She moved her thumb along the wound without pressing into it.

“Here, the piece came in low and slow enough not to shred the whole calf. It made a ragged channel. The bright edges are torn muscle. The pale bits are fat and cloth. The cloth worries me. Cloth is not blood. Cloth stays there, and bacteria ride on it like passengers on a cart. That is how a leg that looks stable becomes a leg that smells like death in two days.”

She let the bandage fall back into place.

“If the fragment had been faster, you would not have seen a neat wound. You would have seen a hole the size of a fist, with the rest of the leg bruised from the shock of it. Vessels that look intact can be bruised inside. Bones can split from the force even if the metal never touched them. The leg swells from the inside, and the swelling can choke off its own blood.”

Sedge picked up the gauze and began wrapping again, firm and even.

“That is what shrapnel does in there. It makes a mess that is not proportional to the hole. It steals blood, steals time, and leaves dirt behind. My job is not to make it sound less ugly. My job is to know which part is bleeding now, which part will infect later, and which part is already dead whether we admit it or not.”

She tied the bandage off and laid her palm near the knee.

“Right now, this leg is alive and contaminated. That is straight enough.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I breathe out slowly, trying to stop my hands from shaking.* "So we wait and see if he rots."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not soften the word. She took a stub of charcoal from the kit and drew a line around the edge of the stain on the bandage. Then she wrote the time beside it, small and flat, the way a clerk might write a delivery.

“That is not waiting,” she said. “That is watching with a pencil. If it crosses the line, I know it moved. If I did not mark it, we would only argue about whether it moved when it was too late.”

She checked the man’s pulse again, then the capillary refill in the nail bed, then the skin of his forehead and neck. His face had gone damp and pasty. His breath was quick, but it was still breath.

“He is in shock,” Sedge said. “That is the thing that will try to take him while we argue about the leg. Warm him. Watch his breathing. If he starts to get hot under the blanket or the leg starts to smell before morning, that is infection. If the bandage spreads, that is bleeding. If the foot goes cold, that is worse. Each one has a different answer.”

She moved the tourniquet closer, but did not touch it.

“I do not say this to frighten you,” she told Wick, and her voice was not kind and not unkind. It was the voice of someone laying out weights so the next person would not drop them. “I am saying it because if you imagine him rotting, you will freeze. If you imagine nothing, you will miss it. You need to know the signs. Not the story. The signs.”

She took the blanket up to his chest and tucked the edges in without lifting him unnecessarily. The man’s shoulder muscles were still tense under Wick’s grip, even in the gray half-sleep after pain.

“His name,” Sedge said, leaning close enough to see his face. She did not shout. She spoke the way you speak to a man who has heard too much shouting already. “What is his name? Say it back if you can.”

There was no answer. Sedge tried again after a moment, then pressed two fingers at the wrist and counted.

“Fast,” she said. “Not enough to be surprised. He has lost blood and had two shoulders put back in front of a bad lamp. His body is not being dramatic. It is trying to stay awake.”

She picked up a cup from the crate, checked it, poured a small amount of water into it, and set it beside the table.

“If he wakes and can swallow, a little at a time. Not a mouthful. Not enough to make him sick. If he vomits, turn him. If he cannot turn, tell me before it happens.”

Sedge looked at Wick’s hands still locked on the man’s shoulders. They were shaking. She had seen shaking hands do better work than steady hands, and steady hands do worse than most people would believe.

“Your hands have a job,” she said. “If they start to fail, say so. Do not apologize to me. Say, ‘My hands are going.’ Then I will decide whether I have another pair or whether I hold him myself.”

She took the clean gauze and laid it over the marked bandage, not hiding it, just giving herself one more layer to check.

“So no,” she said, answering the earlier question again, because it had not gone away. “We do not wait and see if he rots. We watch what he has done, what he is doing, and what he is likely to do next. If the leg is dead, we cut. If the bleeding will not stop, we tie. If he wakes, we ask him his name. If he does not, we keep trying until he is gone or the name comes back. That is all.”

She put her hand on the man’s forehead for a moment, not to comfort him, but to feel how cool he was and whether the coolness was spreading.

“I do not enjoy the word,” Sedge said. “I do not enjoy the work either. But I do not look away from what it becomes. That is the difference.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not tell him to stop screaming. Screaming was information. It meant the airway was open, the lungs were moving, and the man still had enough breath to fight with. It also meant she could not hear the other sounds, which was annoying.

She moved to the head of the table and stood close enough to smell the sour sweat on the man’s skin. The lamp swung, throwing the whole scene into restless shadow.

“I am listening for wet,” Sedge said. “Not for the scream. The scream is loud. The wet is quieter. If he cannot clear his mouth, he can die in the same bed he is screaming in.”

She lifted his eyelid with two fingers and checked the white of the eye, then the pupil. She did not shine the lamp directly into his face. She moved it to the side and watched how the pupils answered.

“Both small. Both even,” she said. “That is not perfect. That is not a reason to relax. That is one fewer hole in the bad picture.”

She leaned close to his mouth and listened again, then put one ear near his chest and counted breaths in her head while she watched the rise and fall under the blanket.

“Breath is fast,” she said. “Air is moving. No sucking sound. No rattle like he is drowning in his own spit. That is good enough for this minute.”

Then she moved down to the shoulders, keeping Wick’s weight in sight but not asking him to release. She did not trust the shoulders yet. Screaming could mean a man was terrified. It could also mean something had slipped back out of place under the strain of being held.

“I am checking the right,” Sedge said. “I am putting my thumb in front of the joint and my finger behind the bone. I am not twisting. I am not testing him for fun. I am looking for the gap that says the ball has left the cup.”

She pressed once, firmly, then shifted to the left.

“Right is seated. Left is seated. If he is screaming because the shoulders came out again, I would feel it. I do not. So this is not a shoulder problem anymore.”

She moved down the table to the leg, keeping one hand on the man’s wrist so she could feel the pulse while she worked. Her fingers were stained with blood and sweat, and she did not wipe them again. There was nothing clean to wipe them on.

“I am looking at the bandage line,” she said. “I drew it with charcoal. If the blood crosses the line, it moved. If it does not, it may still be moving underneath, but not enough to say so out loud yet.”

She peeled back the edge of the wrap just far enough to see the stain. It had darkened, but the charcoal mark held.

“It is not spreading,” she said. “That is not good news. That is only not bad enough to make me tie the tourniquet this second.”

She pressed two fingers behind the knee, then over the ankle, counting. Her lips moved once, then stopped.

“Pulse is faster,” she said. “Foot is still warm. Capillary refill is slow. Skin is cool and damp. That is shock. That is his body trying to keep the important parts alive by pulling blood away from the parts that can spare it.”

She looked at Wick, briefly, and not for permission.

“I am going to press his belly,” Sedge said. “He may not like it. He is already screaming. I do not have time to wait for him to decide.”

She slid one hand under the blanket and pressed flat against the abdomen, slow and steady, not poking. She moved from side to side, then up under the ribs, then down toward the hips, watching the man’s face as much as her hand.

“If it is soft, he may be in pain and frightened. If it is hard, he may be bleeding where I cannot see. If he has a rigid belly and a fast pulse and cold skin, I am not going to be nice about the next thing I do.”

She pulled her hand back and wiped it on the rag again, though the rag had stopped being a rag some hours ago and had become only another thing soaked in worse things.

“Belly is soft,” she said. “That is not a promise. That is not proof. It is only what I can feel while he is fighting me. I will check it again after the screaming stops. Or after he vomits. Or after he dies. Whichever comes first.”

She took the cup of water from beside the table and moved it farther away.

“No water,” she said. “Not while he is screaming. Not while I do not know whether he can swallow. A cup of kindness is a cup of death if it goes down wrong.”

She checked the straps at the shoulders, then the towel over his eyes, then the bandage on the leg, in that order. Her hands moved without hesitation, because hesitation was a luxury for places with lamps that did not swing and tables that did not shake.

“I am putting the time back down,” she said, taking the charcoal again and writing beside the line on the bandage. “Five minutes. If the blood crosses it by then, I know it moved. If it does not, I will still check it again in five minutes. That is not waiting. That is not watching him rot. That is measuring.”

She set the charcoal down and looked at the man’s hand, the one that had been gripping the towel after the shoulder went back in. It was slack now, fingers half curled.

“I am not giving him the pain medicine yet,” Sedge said. “I have it. I am looking at it. I am not giving it. If he is bleeding inside, the pain is the only alarm bell left. If I take it away and his breathing slows, I have traded his warning for my comfort. I do not get to do that.”

She paused, then said, quieter, “Not yet.”

She moved back to his head and put one hand near his mouth, feeling for breath, watching for spit and blood.

“I am watching for vomit,” she said. “If he vomits, he has to turn. Not the whole body. The head, mostly. If you twist him wrong with two freshly set shoulders, I will have to do it again, and you will have to do it again, and neither of us will thank the other for it.”

She looked at Wick’s shaking hands, then at the man’s throat, then at the leg again.

“How much longer?” Sedge said, answering him as if the question were a tool she had to pick up and use. “This check? Five minutes. If the bandage spreads, I stop asking and start tying. If the foot goes cold, I start counting toward something worse. If he keeps screaming and his pulse keeps climbing and his skin keeps cooling, I have to decide whether the screaming is pain or the body going out of order. That decision may take ten minutes. It may take until the ambulance comes. It may take until he stops being a patient and becomes a body.”

She said it flatly, without dressing it.

“I do not know how long he has,” she said. “I know how long I have to watch him. That is all anyone gets in a tent like this.”

She laid one hand over his heart, not to listen, but to feel the speed of it under the ribs.

“I am still here,” she told the man, though he could not hear her over his own screaming. “I am still checking. I am not leaving because you are making noise. I am not pretending you are better than you are. I am not going to take the leg off because it is ugly. I am not going to let you die because it is easier to be frightened than to work.”

She moved the tourniquet closer to her left hand, where she could reach it without looking. She moved the shears and the pressure bandage into the same place. She arranged them as if they were already waiting for orders.

“I am going to keep talking,” Sedge said. “Not because it helps him. Because it keeps me honest. If I stop saying what I am doing, I start saying what I want to be true. And what I want to be true is not in this tent.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He stops screaming all at once, like a candle snuffed. I feel his whole body go slack under my hands. "He's quiet," I say, and my voice sounds strange in the sudden silence. "Is that-- did he just faint?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not answer the question right away. She was already at the side of the table, her hand flat on the man’s neck, her fingers pressed into the hollow beside his windpipe. She looked at the blanket over his chest while she counted.

“Pulse is there,” she said. “Weak. Fast. Not a dead man’s pulse. Not a sleeping man’s pulse.”

She leaned down and listened at his mouth, then put her ear near his chest. His breath was shallow and quick, but it moved. No rattle. No gurgle. No sucking air.

“He’s breathing,” she said. “He’s not fainting. A fainting man usually wakes when you put his head down and stop frightening him. This man is quiet because his body stopped spending what it does not have.”

She moved the towel off his eyes. His pupils were wide and slow to answer the bad light. She lifted one eyelid, then the other, and checked the white of the eye. Not blue. Not gray. Not yet.

“I am opening his airway,” she said, more to herself than to Wick. “I am putting my fingers behind his jaw and pulling it forward. Not tilting his neck. Not rolling him. If he vomits, his head only. The shoulders stay still.”

She made the movement and listened again. The breath came easier, but not enough.

“Still shallow,” Sedge said. “That is not good news. That is not death. That is me changing what I do next.”

She went back to the leg and peeled the bandage just enough to see the charcoal line. The blood had darkened but had not crossed. She pressed two fingers into the pulse above the ankle. It was faster than before and thinner under her skin.

“The leg is still bleeding,” she said. “Not enough to soak the wrap yet. Enough to be waiting. I do not like the waiting.”

She moved the tourniquet onto the table within reach of her left hand, then the pressure bandage, then the shears. Not because she wanted to use them. Because if she had to, she did not want to waste time looking for them.

Then she went back to the belly.

“I checked this while he was fighting me,” Sedge said. “Now I check again while he is not.”

She pressed flat against the abdomen with both hands, slow and careful, feeling for the soft give of a belly that was only tense from pain. This time it answered differently. It was not rigid. Not board-hard. But it was guarding, pulling away under her fingers, the muscle tightening as if something inside had moved.

Sedge’s face did not change. Her voice did not change.

“Belly is firmer than I like,” she said. “I cannot say he is bleeding inside from one touch. I can say he might be. I can say if it gets harder, if his pulse goes faster, if his skin gets colder, I stop asking and start treating.”

She took the cup of water and moved it to the far side of the crate.

“No water,” she said. “No mouthful of kindness. If he is bleeding inside, I may have to open him. If he has something to drink, I may drown him with my own hands.”

She looked at the man’s face again.

“Hey,” she said, close enough that he might hear her over the ringing in his own skull. “Hey. What is your name?”

No answer.

She tried again, louder, but not shouting. “Hey. I am going to put my knuckles to your breastbone. Not because you have earned it. Because if you are still in there, you will fight me. If you are not, I need to know.”

She placed the side of her fist against the center of his chest and pressed once, firm, steady, then again.

The man did not move.

Sedge pulled her hand back.

“He did not faint,” she said. “He is unconscious. That is not the same thing. That is not a reason to stop.”

She checked the pulse again. It was still there, but weaker. She listened to his breath. Still there, but slower.

“Airway is open,” she said. “Breathing is not enough. Circulation is failing. That is the order I work in. I do not skip to the pretty part.”

She picked up the small bag from the kit, checked the mask, checked the valve, and put it to the man’s mouth. She sealed it, lifted his jaw, and squeezed once.

His chest rose.

“I am giving him air,” Sedge said, flat and matter-of-fact. “Not because he is dying. Because he is not breathing like a man who is alive.”

She squeezed again. And again. She watched the rise, listened to the fall, checked the pulse between breaths.

“If his pulse stops, I start compressions,” she said. “If his pulse stops, I will tell you. If I start, I will say what I am doing. I will not pretend it is gentle. It is not. It is the only thing that keeps blood moving when the heart quits.”

She put the bag down and pressed two fingers to his neck again.

“Pulse is still there,” she said. “Weak. Faster. Shock is moving. I do not have a reason to be cheerful about that.”

She took the charcoal and wrote beside the line on the bandage. Then she wrote a second line beside the first.

“If the blood reaches the second line, I tie the tourniquet,” she said. “Not before. Not later. If it reaches the second line.”

She checked the man’s skin, forehead, neck, hands. Cool. Damp. Pale.

“He is not getting warm enough,” she said. “Heat does not fix shock. It only stops his body from spending what little it has left trying to keep itself from shivering.”

She pulled the blanket higher, but not over his face. Not over his arms. She left enough open to see and touch.

“I am not giving him pain medicine now,” Sedge said. “If his breathing is slow, medicine makes it slower. If he is bleeding inside, medicine hides the warning. I would rather have his pain than lose his pulse.”

She moved the tourniquet again, closer.

“I am going to ask for help,” she said. “If help comes, good. If help does not come, I still have hands.”

She looked at the man

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I lean my head back against the crate, staring at the tent ceiling. "How many more?" I ask, my voice rough. "How many before you stop counting?"

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I wipe my hands on my pants, leaving streaks. They still smell like blood. "Teach me how to do it. The counting, I mean. Teach me how to know which number matters."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get up slowly, my legs stiff. I pick up the bloody towel from the floor and look at it. "Alright," I say. "Show me where to start."
