dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned so that the witnesses were on her left and Del directly before her. That was how it was done. The account was owed to the second first, and the witnesses were there to hear that it had been given.

She did not raise her voice. Twelve times now, and she had never once found that volume improved the accuracy.

"The third exchange," she said. "He led with a high cut to draw my guard, and I did not take it. He committed his weight forward on the recovery, and his left foot was late. I stepped inside the line and put the point in under the right side of the jaw, above the collar, angled upward. Two inches of steel, perhaps a little more. It went through the great vessel in the neck and did not come out the other side."

She paused, not for effect, but because the next part was also owed.

"He was standing for the space of one breath after I withdrew. He knew what had been done. He did not speak. He fell to his knees and then to his right side, and he was gone before I had finished lowering the blade. I do not believe there was pain of any duration. I will not say there was none."

Her hands were at her sides. The sword was in its scabbard. There was a fine spray across the cuff of her right sleeve that she had not yet cleaned, and she did not move to hide it.

"That is the wound. That is how he died. I have said it plainly because you are entitled to it plain." She held Del's gaze without pressing on it. "If there is anything you would have me say again, or say more exactly, ask it now, before the witnesses, and I will."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, my eyes tracing the pattern of blood on her cuff. "The left foot being late," I say, voice steadier than I feel. "Would it have mattered if you'd taken the first cut?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not answer at once. The question deserved to be thought about, and thinking took the time it took.

"You are asking whether the opening was mine or his," she said. "Whether I made it or found it."

She looked past Del for a moment, at the place on the ground where it had happened. The witnesses would take her looking there as they liked. She was reconstructing the exchange, and it was owed to Del that she reconstruct it correctly rather than quickly.

"If I had taken the high cut, my guard would have been up and my weight back. He meant to disengage under it and come at the body. That was the shape of the thing. It was not badly conceived." She returned her eyes to Del. "In that case the late foot would not have killed him in the third exchange, because I would not have been positioned to reach him. So to your question as you asked it: yes. It would have mattered. It would have been a different third exchange, and he would have survived it."

She let that stand for the length of a breath, because it was true and he was entitled to hear it whole before she added to it.

"But I do not think it would have saved him, and I will not tell you that it would. The foot was late because he set his weight before he had finished his step. I saw it in the first exchange and again in the second. It was how he moved. It was not one mistake. It was a thing he did." Her voice did not change. "I did not take the high cut because I had seen it twice already, and I knew what came after. If I had taken it, I would have been waiting for the foot in the fourth exchange, or the fifth. I would have found it."

The cuff of her sleeve had begun to stiffen. She was aware of it and left it alone.

"So the honest answer is two answers. It would have mattered to when. I do not believe it would have mattered to whether." She inclined her head very slightly toward Del, an acknowledgement and not a bow. "If you want to know whether there was a version of this morning in which he walked away, I have thought about it, and I have told you what I think. I could be wrong. I have not been wrong about that yet, but I have only had eleven occasions before this one to be wrong about it, and that is not so many."

She waited. She would wait as long as he needed.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren straightened. It was not a large movement. She had been standing correctly already, but there was a difference between standing correctly and standing for the record, and the witnesses would know it when they saw it.

So Del knew the form. She had wondered. Some seconds did not, and had to be prompted, and the prompting was its own small indignity that she had never found a way to spare them. He had asked his question first, as was his right, and now he had closed the questioning, and what came next was the account as it would be kept. The questions were permitted before this and not after. That was the reason for the order. A man was entitled to test the account, and then he was entitled to have it fixed.

"Witnessed," she said, and the three on her left answered it, one after another, low.

"I am Auren. This morning at the appointed hour I met him at this ground under the code, with seconds present and witnesses standing. In the third exchange he offered a high cut and I did not take it. On his recovery his weight was forward and his left foot was late. I stepped inside his line and put the point in beneath the right side of the jaw, above the collar, angled upward, to the depth of two inches or something more. The steel passed through the great vessel of the neck and did not go through. I withdrew it. He stood for the length of one breath and did not speak. He went to his knees and then onto his right side and he was dead before I had lowered my blade. I believe there was little pain. I do not claim there was none."

She did not look at the ground this time. The account was not for the ground.

"I saw the fault in his foot in the first exchange and again in the second, and I waited for it. I did not make the opening. I found it, and I had been looking. If I had taken the high cut he would have lived through the third exchange, and I believe I would have found the same fault in a later one. That is my judgement and I give it as judgement, not as fact."

Her sleeve had gone dark and stiff to the wrist. It was on the record now with the rest of it.

"That is the wound. That is the death. I have spoken it plain to his second, and his second has heard it, and you have heard that it was given." She turned her head, once, to the witnesses, and back to Del. "It is spoken. It is done."

The witnesses answered again, and then there was nothing more that the code required of her, and she stood with her hands at her sides and let the quiet come, and did not fill it.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't realize I'd been holding. The formality breaks, my shoulders slumping just slightly. "He was a stubborn bastard," I say quietly, almost to myself. "I told him about that foot last week."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren heard it and did not answer immediately, because it had not been said to her, quite, and she was not certain it wanted answering.

But it had been said in her hearing, and she had never yet let a thing pass unanswered on this ground for the sake of her own comfort.

"Then you saw it before I did," she said. "I had it in the first exchange. You had it a week ago."

She said it as a plain fact, because it was one. Del would take it as he chose. She would not shape it for him.

"A foot like that is not a week's work. It is not a month's." She looked, briefly, at her own right hand, which was still and did not need to be looked at. "A man puts a habit into his body over years, and it does not come out of him faster than it went in. He would have needed to stop, and drill it slow, and be bad at it for a season while his body learned a new thing. Most will not do that with a meeting already fixed. They will not spend the last week being bad at anything."

The witnesses were beginning to shift. The code did not hold them past the speaking, and they were free to go, and she was aware of them deciding whether it was decent to leave yet. That was their concern. She did not look at them.

"I will not tell you that you could not have made him listen. I did not know him and I do not know what he heard from you or how. You will know that better than anyone alive, and better than you would like to." Her voice did not soften. It was not made to. "But I will tell you that I have stood here twelve times and I have not yet met the one who came to this ground because he was in the habit of taking advice."

Her sleeve had gone rigid. She would deal with it later, where no one would watch her do it and make it mean something.

"He was stubborn, then," she said. "You would know. I only know that he did not change his foot, and I know what that cost him, and now so do you, exactly, because I have told you." She let a breath go. "That is the whole of what I can give you. It is not much. It is not meant to be a comfort. It is meant to be true, and I have found that people can build on true, in time, in a way they cannot build on kind."

She did not move to leave. His second would leave first, or dismiss her. That was also how it was done.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not answer at once, and the pause was not hesitation. It was the code, which she was consulting in the way she consulted it, silently and without needing to look anything up.

"The account is spoken," she said. "It cannot be amended after the witnessing, and I would not amend it if it could. But there is nothing in the code that forbids the same words being said a second time, and I told you before the closing that I would say them again if you asked. You asked late. I do not think the lateness matters. I will not stand on it."

She looked to the witnesses, two of whom had taken a step toward the edge of the ground, and said, "Hold." They stopped. The one nearest turned back fully. She waited until all three were still and facing her, because a thing said plainly to an empty ground was not the thing Del had asked for.

Then she raised her right hand, the one with the stiffened cuff, and put two fingers to her own throat.

"Here." Her fingertips rested just below the angle of the jaw on the right side, above where a collar would sit, in the soft place before the bone. "Beneath the jaw, the right side, his right. Above the collar. The point went in here and travelled upward, toward the base of the skull, not across. Two inches, a little more. It did not come out anywhere. There was one wound and it was this one."

She held her hand there long enough for anyone to see exactly where, and then lowered it.

"It opened the great vessel that runs up the side of the neck. That is what killed him. Not the depth. Not the steel in the throat. The vessel." She said it evenly. "If the point had gone in a finger's width forward, it would have missed the vessel and found the windpipe, and he would have died more slowly and worse, and I would be standing here telling you that instead. It did not. It went where I put it. I am not asking you to be grateful for that. I am telling you it is so."

The witnesses had not moved. She released them with a small motion of the hand, and they began to go, and she let them.

"That is where it landed. It is the same place I told you the first time and the same place I told the record. If you want to see the mark itself before he is taken from the ground, that is your right as second, and no one here will stop you or think less of you for looking, or for not looking." She let her hands settle again at her sides. "I would look, if I were you. I have found that the thing a man imagines is usually larger than the thing that is there, and it is better to carry the true one."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod once, sharp. "I'll look." My throat is tight. I walk to the still form on the ground and kneel. The wound is clean, precise. Smaller than I'd pictured. I stand back up, my knees protesting. "Thank you," I say, and it sounds raw. "For the truth."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not say that he was welcome, because he was not, and she had never found a way to say the words that did not make them a lie.

"You have thanked me for it," she said instead. "I will take that as the thing it is. I did not do it for thanks and I would have done it without."

She had watched him kneel and had not watched what he saw. That was his. She had looked at the ground between them until he stood again, and had heard the sound his knees made and had not remarked on it.

"It was smaller than you pictured," she said. It was not a question. "It is always smaller. I have seen men look at the wound they made and not believe it was enough. I have seen seconds look at the wound made on their man and not believe it either. The body is stubborn about how much it takes to stop it, and then it turns out it takes very little, and that is the part nobody is ready for."

The witnesses had gone. The ground was empty but for the two of them and the third who could not leave it on his own. Someone would come for him. That was arranged before any meeting, and it was not her concern, and she made it her concern anyway by not going until it was done, every time, because she had never found a reason good enough to leave a man on the ground she had put him on.

"You are his second," she said. "The code is finished with you, and it is finished with me. There is nothing left that either of us owes the other under it." She let a breath go, not heavily. "But you have not dismissed me, and I will not go until you do, or until you go yourself. I have stood on this ground with eleven others who had your part in it. Some of them wanted me gone at once. Some of them wanted me to stand there until they had finished looking at me, so that they would know my face. I have never asked which it would be. I have waited to be told."

She looked at him, and then, for the first time since the speaking, she looked at the man on the ground, deliberately, and for as long as it took.

"He was well set in the first exchange," she said. "I did not say that for the record because the record is for the wound and not for the man. I say it to you because you told him about his foot, and that means you trained with him, or watched him train, and you will want to know whether the rest of it was sound. It was. His hands were good. His measure was good. It was only the foot." She turned her eyes back to Del. "That is not nothing. It is also not a comfort, and I do not offer it as one. It is the last true thing I have about him, and now you have it, and I am empty."

She stood, and her sleeve had dried to her wrist, and she waited to be told what came next.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not remind him that the code was finished with them both. He knew it. He had said the closing words himself, and he had heard her say that it was done, and he was asking anyway, and she had decided some time ago on a different ground with a different second that when a man asked a fourth time it was not because he had failed to hear the first three.

"Precisely, then," she said. "As exact as I have it. Where I am not certain I will say so."

She did not put her hand to her throat this time. He had seen the place.

"The point went in through the skin beneath the angle of the jaw and through the thin sheet of muscle that lies just under the skin there. That is nothing. A finger's depth. Below that, on that side of the neck, there is a bundle that runs up from the chest to the head, and it lies in a sheath of its own, and in it are the great artery that carries blood to the brain, the great vein that carries it back, and the cord of nerve that goes with them. They run together. You cannot reach one without reaching the others."

Her voice was level and did not hurry.

"The blade entered that sheath. It cut the artery across, or near enough across that the difference does not signify. It opened the vein alongside it. I cannot tell you what it did to the nerve and I will not guess. The angle was upward, toward the base of the skull, so the point passed behind the corner of the jaw and did not go across toward the windpipe. It did not enter the throat. It did not reach the spine. It stopped in the muscle at the back of the neck, or a little before that. I felt it stop and I withdrew."

She paused, because the next part was what the blade had done and not merely where it had gone, and that was what he had asked.

"When the artery was cut, the blood that should have gone to his head went instead into the space around the vessels and down into the neck and the chest, and out of the wound. Not all at once. Most of it stayed inside him. That is why the ground is not as marked as you thought it would be, and why the wound looks the size it does. The killing was done inside, where you cannot see it." She held Del's eyes. "The brain went without blood. That is why he stood for one breath and did not speak. He was not choosing silence. He had no blood to speak with. Then he had none to stand with. The going to his knees was the body failing, not a decision. The rolling to the right side was the same. By the time he was on the ground he was, I believe, already past knowing. The heart kept on for a little after. That does not signify either."

The dried cuff pulled at her wrist when she breathed. She let it.

"That is what the blade did. It severed the artery and opened the vein in the right side of his neck, at the level of the angle of the jaw, and he died of the brain losing its blood. Not the wound. Not the steel. The loss." She inclined her head very slightly. "I have said the same thing four times now in four different ways, and it has not changed, and it will not change if you ask a fifth. But I will say it a fifth time if you ask. I have no other appointment on this ground, and I have found that the number of times a man needs to hear a thing is not mine to decide for him."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I stare at her, the clinical words settling like stones in my gut. "I don't need a fifth," I say. My voice sounds hollow. "I just needed to know he didn't linger."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren was quiet for the space of a breath, and then another, because he had finally said the thing he had been asking under all the other things, and it deserved an answer that had been weighed and not merely delivered.

"No," she said. "He did not linger."

She did not add anything to it at once. She let the word stand by itself where he could look at it.

"I have told you I would not claim there was no pain, and I hold to that, because I cannot know it and I will not say I do. But lingering is a different thing from pain, and about lingering I can be more certain, because lingering is a thing I could see." Her voice was even. "I have watched men linger. I know what it looks like. It is the eyes going from one face to another. It is the hand that finds the wound and holds it. It is a man trying to say a name, or trying to sit up, or trying to understand what has happened to him and having the time to fail at it. I have seen all of that on this ground and on others. I did not see any of it this morning."

She looked at the still shape on the ground, briefly and without flinching, and back to Del.

"One breath standing. I counted it because I always count it. He did not reach for the wound. He did not look for you. His eyes were on me and then they were not on anything. Between the point going in and the knowing going out of him, I would put it at less than the time it has taken me to say this sentence. What came after was the body, and the body is not the man." She let a breath go. "So. He did not linger. I say that as fact and not as judgement, because it is the one part of this morning I saw plainly and entirely, and you are entitled to have it without any hedge on it."

The ground was very quiet. Somewhere past the edge of it there was the sound of a cart, which would be the men coming for him, and she noted it and did not turn toward it.

"That is the last thing," she said. "It is the only one I could give you clean. I am glad it was the one you needed."

She did not move to go. She stood as she had stood, hands at her sides, the sleeve dry and stiff, and waited to be dismissed, and did not mind the waiting.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looked to the edge of the ground. Two of the witnesses had stopped there when the cart came into hearing, and stood now with their backs to the road and their faces toward the pair of them, waiting to see whether they were wanted. The third had gone. Two would serve. Two had always served.

She did not raise her hand to hold them. They had held themselves.

"You are asking for all of it," she said, "and I am going to tell you a thing first that you will not want, and then I am going to give you what you asked for."

She waited until he was looking at her and not at the ground.

"There is no more. I have not been keeping any of it back. I have given you the place and the depth and the angle, and what the steel did inside him, and how long he stood, and what he did not do while he stood. I have given it in four pieces because you asked in four pieces. You are asking now for the whole, and I will give you the whole, but the whole is not larger than the pieces. It is only the pieces set end to end." Her voice did not change. "If you have been waiting for the part I have not said yet, it does not exist. I would rather you hear that from me now than go looking for it for the rest of your life."

The cart had stopped somewhere past the trees. The men in it would wait. They always waited until the ground was quiet.

"All of it, then. From the beginning to the end, once, as one thing."

She set her feet.

"He came onto the ground correctly and saluted correctly and I returned it. First exchange: he tested my measure and I gave him nothing, and I saw the foot. Second exchange: he tested it again and pressed a little, and I saw the foot again, and knew it was his and not the morning's. Third exchange: he offered the high cut. I did not take it. He recovered with his weight already set and his left foot still coming, and I stepped inside and put the point beneath the right angle of his jaw, upward, two inches and something more, through the artery and the vein together, and it stopped short of the spine, and I drew it out.

"He stood for one breath. I counted it. His eyes were on my face. He did not put his hand to his neck. He did not look toward you. He did not speak, because the blood that speaking runs on was already leaving his head, and by the end of that breath his eyes were not on anything. He did not say a word from the salute to the end. Not one. I would give it to you if there were one. There is not.

"He went down onto his knees and then over onto his right side. It was not a fall. It was the body setting itself down because nothing was holding it up. There was blood at the mouth, a little, not much, because the wound drained inward and not up. His eyes stayed open. There was no sound from him after he was on the ground. There was no movement of the hands. There was the chest, working, for a few moments more, and then not, and the last of it was a shallow thing and it did not look like struggle. It looked like a man finishing a breath he had already begun.

"From the point entering to the standing ending, one breath. From the standing ending to the ground, the time it takes to kneel and lie down. From the ground to the chest stopping, I would say a count of ten, and I am less certain of that than of the rest, because I had my blade to attend to and I did not count it. From the salute to the chest stopping, the whole of it, I would say less time than the account I have just given you has taken to say."

She was silent for a moment. The two at the edge of the ground had not moved.

"That is all of it. Beginning, middle, end. What he said, which was nothing. How long he took, which was not long. What it looked like at the end, which was a man lying on his side with his eyes open and then a man who had stopped breathing, and very little between the two." She looked at him steadily. "It is small. I know it is small. Everything you were braced to hear, everything you have been asking around the edges of, it is not there, because he was not there long enough for it to happen to him. That is the thing the code makes me tell you, and it is the thing that will be hardest to carry, and it is also the mercy. They are the same thing. I have never found a way to hand one over without the other."

She let her hands rest. The cuff pulled at her wrist.

"I have nothing else. Not withheld. Nothing. If you ask again I will say it again, and it will be the same, and you will know then that it is the same because it is true and not because I am tired." She inclined her head, once. "Those two have stayed to hear it. They have heard it. They will say so, if it is ever asked."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let the silence stretch, the cart waiting beyond the trees. "It's enough," I say, finally. "Dismissed."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head. It was the same small movement she had given him four times already, and it meant the same thing, and she had never found a reason to make it larger at the end than at the beginning.

"Dismissed," she said, so that the two at the edge of the ground would hear that it had been said and answered. One of them lifted a hand, barely, and the other did not, and both turned toward the road.

She did not go with them.

"I have told you the code is finished," she said, "and it is. You have released me and I am released. What I do now I do on my own account and not on his, and not on yours, and you may tell me to go and I will."

She stepped back. Three paces, so that she was off the marked ground and standing on the plain grass beyond it, where a stranger might stand who had nothing to do with any of this. That was where she stood now. That was what she was.

"I do not leave a man on the ground I have put him on. I have never once done it. I will stand here, off the mark, until the cart has him, and then I will go, and you will not see me again unless you look for me." Her hands were at her sides. The dried cuff had cracked along the fold when she moved and a fleck of it had come away and gone into the grass. She did not look down at it. "You do not have to stay for that. You have done what a second does and you have done it correctly, and there is nothing more of it that is yours. If you would rather not watch them lift him, no one who was here will say you left early. I will not say it."

She was silent then, for a while, and the silence was not a formal one. It had no witnesses and no words owed at the end of it. It was only quiet on a field in the morning with the sound of a cart behind the trees.

"He was your friend," she said finally, and it was not a question, and it was not on the record, and she did not soften it. "I only had him for three exchanges. That is not long enough to know a man. I am aware of that. I know his foot and his hands and his measure and how he died, and that is all I will ever know of him, and it is a strange and narrow thing to carry away from someone. You will carry the rest. You will carry it better than I could, because you have more of it." She let a breath go. "I say that so that you know I know it. Not for any other reason."

She raised her hand, not high, toward the trees, and the cart began to move.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren heard him confirm it, and heard what his voice did, and did not look away from him while it did it. That was not kindness. It was only that a man who had held his eyes open through the account was owed the same when he closed it, and she had never yet let a second speak the last words to the side of her face.

"Heard," she said. "And witnessed, while there were witnesses. It will stand."

The cart came out from the trees. Two men and a mule, and a board across the bed, and a length of plain cloth folded on the board. They knew the ground. They stopped the mule short of the mark and came on foot, and the older of the two stopped again at the edge and looked not at the body and not at Del but at her, standing on the grass three paces off.

"Who has the account?" he said.

It was their right. She had never known a bearer who did not ask it, and never known one who lifted a man without it. They would carry him through a village and put him in the ground, and they would be asked, and they would need to be able to say. That was not the code. The code was finished. It was older than the code, or beside it, and she had never once refused it.

"I have it," she said. "It has been spoken to his second and to three witnesses, and his second has confirmed it. I will give it to you whole, once, and you will have it as they have it."

The bearer nodded and took off his cap. The younger one did the same, late, watching him.

Auren did not step back onto the mark. She spoke from where she stood.

"He came onto the ground at the appointed hour. He saluted correctly and I returned it correctly. First exchange: he tested my measure and I gave him nothing. I saw in that exchange that his left foot was late on the recovery, that he set his weight before the step was finished. Second exchange: he pressed a little and I still gave him nothing, and I saw the foot again, and knew it for a habit and not for an accident of the morning. Third exchange: he offered a high cut, meaning to draw my guard up and disengage under it to the body. I did not take the cut. On his recovery his weight was already forward and his left foot was still coming. I stepped inside his line and put the point in beneath the right angle of his jaw, above where the collar sits, angled upward toward the base of the skull. Two inches. A little more. It went through the skin and the thin muscle beneath it and into the sheath where the great vessels of the neck run together, and it cut the artery across and opened the vein beside it, and it stopped in the muscle at the back before it reached the spine. It did not enter the throat. It did not come out anywhere. There was one wound. I felt the point stop, and I withdrew it.

"He stood for one breath after the steel came out. I counted it. His eyes were on my face for that breath. He did not put his hand to the wound. He did not turn to look for his second. He did not speak. He did not speak from the salute to the end, not one word, and I would give it if there were one. There is not. By the end of that breath his eyes were on nothing. The blood that should have gone to his head had gone into the neck and the chest instead, and the knowing left him with it.

"He went down onto his knees and from his knees onto his right side. It was not a fall. It was the body setting itself down. There was a little blood at the mouth, not much, because the wound drained inward and not up. His eyes stayed open. His hands did not move after he was down. His chest worked for a count of perhaps ten, and I am less certain of that count than of the rest, because I was seeing to my blade and did not give it the whole of my attention. The last breath was shallow and it did not look like struggle. Then there was none.

"From the point entering to the end of his standing, one breath. From standing to the ground, the time it takes to kneel and lie down. From the ground to the chest stopping, ten, or near it. From the salute to the last of him, the whole of it, less time than this account has taken to say. I do not claim there was no pain. I will not, because I cannot know it. I say that he did not linger, because lingering is a thing I could have seen, and I did not see it.

"I saw the fault in his foot before I used it. I waited for it. I did not make the opening. I found it, and I had been looking for it since the first exchange. If I had taken the high cut he would have lived through the third exchange, and I believe I would have found the same fault in a later one. That is my judgement and I give it as judgement. His hands were good. His measure was good. It was the foot, and only the foot.

"That is the wound and that is the death. His second has heard it and confirmed it. Three witnesses heard it given. You have it now as they have it, and you may say so to anyone who asks you, and you may say that Auren gave it, and you may say where I was standing when I did."

She stopped. The older bearer put his cap back on.

"Heard," he said, and the younger one said it after him, and they went onto the mark and unfolded the cloth.

Auren did not watch them do the lifting. She watched the road, where the two witnesses had already gone out of sight, and she listened to the sound of it, which was a sound she knew, and she did not turn back until the board was in the cart and the cloth was over him and the mule had taken the first step.

The cart went into the trees. The ground was empty. The mark was still there, and the dark place on it that was smaller than anyone would believe, and the two of them on either side of it, and nothing else.

"That is the last time it will be spoken on this ground," she said. "It will be spoken elsewhere. Not by me." She looked at him once more, plainly, without holding it. "You have my name. You do not have to want it."

She turned then, and went, and did not look at her sleeve until she was out of his sight.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I watch her go, the stiffness in her shoulders the only sign of what she's carrying. When the cart's sound fades, I kneel again and press my palm against the dark spot on the ground. It's already cool.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren walked until the trees closed behind her and the ground was gone, and then she walked a little further, because the distance at which a man could still see you was always greater than the distance at which you believed he could.

Then she stopped.

The road was empty. The cart was somewhere ahead of her, out of hearing now, and the witnesses were further than that. There was nobody. She checked, the way she always checked, not because she expected anyone but because a thing done in private should be done in private, and she had never trusted her own certainty about that without looking.

She held out her right arm and looked at the sleeve.

It had dried to the colour of old bark, and where it had cracked along the fold the cloth underneath showed pale. It had gone through the weave. It would not come out. She had known that when it landed, and had known it when she left it on for the account, and knew it now. She had eleven sleeves before this one and none of them had come out either, and she had not kept them, and she would not keep this one, and she stood and looked at it anyway for the length of time it took to look at a thing properly.

Then she undid the cuff and rolled it once, twice, to the elbow, so that the stain was folded inside against itself and could not be seen from the road. Not hidden. Put away. There was a difference and she had spent a good part of her life learning where it lay.

Twelve.

She did not say it aloud. There was no one to say it to and she had never been in the habit of speaking to fields. But she gave it its place, the way she had given each of the others its place, standing still on a road with the number in her mind until she had felt the whole weight of it settle and was certain it had settled and would not shift later and catch her.

He had good hands. That was true and it was hers now, along with the foot and the measure and the one breath. She did not know his name. She had never asked for the names. The code did not require it, and she had decided early that if she was going to carry them she would carry them as what she had actually held of them, and she had never held a name. She had held a foot that was late and a point that went in beneath a jaw and a man who did not look for his second. That was the whole of him that was hers. The second had the rest. The second would have it a long time.

She thought about the second's voice at the confirming, what it had done, and she let herself think about it for exactly as long as it deserved and no longer, because it was his and not hers and she had already taken more from that ground than she had any right to.

The sun had cleared the trees. It was going to be an ordinary day, in the way that these days always turned out to be ordinary once the ground was behind her. There would be a room somewhere and water and the sleeve to cut off at the shoulder, and she would do that with the same attention she had given the account, and then it would be done in the way that things were done, which was not the same as finished.

Auren put her hand once, briefly, to the right side of her own neck, just beneath the angle of the jaw, and took it away.

Then she walked on.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content:
I stand up, my palm damp from the ground. I look at the mark on my hand, then wipe it on my trousers. It’s done. And I’m still here.

I start walking, not toward home, but toward the river. He hated the river. Said it was too loud. I need the noise.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The road bent toward the water before it bent toward the town. Auren had walked it once before, the night prior, in the other direction and in the dark, and had noted then that the river ran close along the last mile and that it was loud, and had not thought anything more of it than that.

She thought of it now because she could hear it. It came up through the trees before she saw it, a steady sound with no shape, and she found that her step had slowed to meet it without her deciding that it should.

She did not stop. Stopping on a road was a thing that got noticed, and she had already stopped once. But she let the pace fall to what it wanted and did not correct it, and by the time the trees gave way and the bank opened on her left the sound had come up to fill everything, and she understood why a man might either hate it or need it, depending on the morning.

There was a figure on the bank, far down, where the road drew away from the water and a path went off through the reeds. She did not need to look twice to know the shape. She had stood facing it for the better part of an hour with three witnesses on her left and had held its eyes through every word she had, and a shape you have looked at that way does not become a stranger because there is now a field and a stand of trees and a hundred yards of moving water between you.

She looked once, and then she looked at the road.

There was nothing she was owed there and nothing she owed. She had said so. She had said it on the ground, plainly, and had meant it, and it did not become less true because the road happened to run where it ran. He had dismissed her. She had told him he would not see her again unless he looked, and she had not put in that word by accident. It was his to look. It had never once been hers to be found.

The rolled sleeve had come loose a little at the elbow with the walking. She stopped, because this was a thing that needed two hands, and set it right, and tucked the fold under so it would hold. While she did it she was facing the water and not the bank, and she kept her eyes on the water, and the water was loud enough that it made a kind of privacy of its own, which she had not expected and did not turn away.

He had hated it, she supposed. Or the other one had. She did not know which and there was no one to ask, and it was not hers to know. She had three exchanges and a foot and a breath and a pair of good hands, and that was the measure of him she would carry, and she had already told herself so once this morning and was not in the habit of telling herself a thing twice.

She finished with the sleeve.

Then she walked, and the road drew away from the river as it had been going to, and the sound fell behind her by degrees until it was only a thing she knew was there and could not hear, and she did not look back at the bank, and did not slow again, and kept her face toward the town where there would be a room and water and a sleeve to cut off at the shoulder, and did each of those things when she came to them exactly as carefully as she had done the rest.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I watch the river churn, the roar filling my ears until my own thoughts are just a faint hum. My hands are shaking. I clench them, then shove them into my pockets. He hated this sound. Good. Let him be wrong about one last thing.
