dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not lower the lamp. She let its light sit on the thing in the water, patient as a surgeon deciding where to cut.

“Wrong shape is a start,” she said. “Better than ‘I don’t know.’”

Her eyes moved over it in pieces, not as a whole. A shoulder, if it was a shoulder. The angle of a limb that had too much length in it, or too little bend where a bend ought to be. The far wall behind it was wet higher than the waterline, as if something had pressed itself up there and slid down slowly.

“Most things drown quiet,” she said. “They thrash, they sink, they settle. This one stopped moving like it was listening.”

She crouched a little, keeping her boots clear of the water.

“Look at the hands, if you can call them that. Not floating. Anchored. Whatever it is, it didn’t fall in here. It chose the bottom.”

A thin smile touched her mouth, humorless and old.

“Congratulations. You’ve found the part of the job where curiosity gets buried with the boots.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I take a step forward, squinting. The hands... they're curled into the silt. Like they're holding onto something. "It's not trying to get out," I say, the realization settling cold in my stomach.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not answer at once. She kept the lamp steady and let the light do the work her feet would not.

“No,” she said at last. “It isn’t.”

She crouched lower without moving closer, her eyes going to the silt around the thing’s hands.

“Drowned things open. The hands spread, the fingers catch on nothing, the whole body makes a last argument with the world. Those aren’t open. They’re set. See how the mud’s heaped outside the knuckles? It didn’t sink into that position. It pushed into it.”

She tilted the lamp a fraction, letting the light rake across the water. The surface was too still. Not calm. Held.

“It chose the bottom, like you said. And it chose that corner. Which means it either knows what’s under the floor, or it’s keeping something else from coming up through it.”

A short breath left her, more warning than laugh.

“Thirty years, and I’ve never found the monster that stays put out of good manners.”

Her gaze moved to the high wet mark on the wall, then back to the curled fingers.

“We don’t touch it with hands, and we don’t lean over the water to get a better look. We get the long pole from the stairwell and we test the silt from a distance. If it’s holding a line, a latch, or a bone, we want to know before we make it choose between us and whatever it’s got.”

She did not lower the lamp.

“And if it starts moving before we’ve got length on it, we don’t argue. We go up the stairs and we burn the house down around the cellar. Some jobs pay in silver. This one may pay in fire.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept the lamp steady, but her gaze did not stay on the shape for long. She looked at the water around it instead, at the way the silt had not clouded properly, at the wet mark on the wall, at the hands buried with such deliberate grip.

“Recently?” she said. “No.”

She let the word sit there, flat and unkind.

“Recently dead things are honest in the worst ways. They bloat, they slip, they give up their weight to the water. They don’t hold a pose. They don’t choose a corner.” Her eyes narrowed a little. “That’s not floating. That’s stationed.”

The lamplight caught one curve of what might have been a skull, or might have been a stone worn into a skull’s idea.

“As for whether it was a person,” she said, “there’s enough of the pattern to make your eyes lie to you. Head where a head ought to be. Arms where arms go. But look at the shoulder line. Too low. And the neck’s got too much length in it, or too little need.”

A dry breath moved through her nose.

“A person has joints because a person has reasons to bend. That thing’s got conveniences.”

She did not smile this time.

“It might have been one, once. Or it might have worn one long enough to keep the outline. Either way, don’t do it the favor of calling it a man. Sentiment makes people reach, and reaching gets them drowned.”

Her thumb tightened slightly on the lamp handle.

“If you need a word for it, call it a latch. Something shaped like a body, put where a body shouldn’t be, holding something shut.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow, hard. "So we're not putting it to rest. We're making sure it stays put."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway gave a short, unamused nod, the kind that might have passed for approval in a charnel house.

“Now you’re thinking like a professional,” she said. “Rest is for things that died. This—” she angled the lamp toward the still, submerged shape, “—is furniture.”

She said it flatly, without disgust, the way one might identify a load-bearing beam or a cracked foundation stone.

“If it’s holding something shut, our job isn’t to soothe it. It’s to find out what it’s keeping down, and whether it’s been doing the job willingly or under protest.” Her eyes moved over the water again. “Big difference. Willing things can be bargained with. Forced things can be replaced. Protest things—”

She paused, jaw tightening slightly.

“Protest things make mistakes. And mistakes in cellars like this tend to come up through the floorboards.”

She finally lowered the lamp an inch, not toward the thing, but toward the waterline along the wall.

“We don’t put it to rest. We don’t bless it, we don’t name it, and we don’t apologize to it. We test the silt, we map what it’s gripping, and if there’s a seal under those hands, we make sure we’re not the ones who break it by being ignorant.”

A thin, grim smile touched her mouth.

“Sometimes the kindest thing you can do for a monster is leave it exactly where it is.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway’s eyes dropped to the water around Pike’s legs, and her expression went very still.

“Plainly,” she said, “you’re standing in the same basin it chose, so keep that lamp steady and don’t kick the silt.”

She did not wait for an answer. She used the better light the way a clerk uses a ledger, moving it over the shape in short, economical passes.

“It came down here before the water settled the way it is now,” she said. “Either it came on its own, or it was put here while it could still take orders. No drag marks on the stair wall. No scrape on the corner where it would have fought. It went to that place and set itself.”

Her gaze marked the silt again.

“It put its hands down first. That’s the important part. A falling body lands soft parts first. A drowning body claws upward. This one planted. It took hold of something under the floor and made its weight into a seal.”

A thin breath left her.

“Then it stopped being alive without letting go.”

She let that sit in the cellar air.

“Death loosens things. Fear loosens them faster. Whatever happened to it, the end didn’t open its hands. The end made the grip more permanent. The bones changed around the posture. The neck stretched because it needed to reach, or because the thing that owned it didn’t care what a neck was for. The shoulders dropped because the arms became the purpose.”

Her mouth twisted, not with amusement but with the old, tired habit of it.

“So plainly: it was used. Maybe it volunteered. More likely it was chosen. Someone needed a lock that looked enough like a person to fool the dark, and they put it here to keep something under the floor from noticing it had been missed.”

She lifted the lamp just enough to show the high stain on the wall.

“That mark isn’t from it climbing out. It’s from whatever pressed against the seal when the water rose. The thing in the silt took the pressure and held. It may have been dead by then. It may have been halfway into something else. Doesn’t matter to the job. What matters is it didn’t move.”

Her voice stayed level, the way one keeps a blade level when scraping wax off a seal.

“What happened to it? It was made into furniture. A doorstop for a bad idea. If there was a person in there once, the person ended when the holding began. The rest is just architecture with teeth.”

She looked back to the curled hands.

“We don’t ask it for its story. We find out what it’s holding, and then we decide whether the world is safer with the story still under the floor.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I step back, my boot squelching in the silt. "It's still holding, even now." I look at her, the lamp trembling a little in my grip. "What if whatever it's holding doesn't need it anymore?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway’s gaze moved from the shape in the water to the light jittering on its surface, then back again. She did not tell the light to be steady. She knew better than to waste breath on things that trembled.

“Then it isn’t a lock anymore,” she said. “It’s a message.”

She took one careful step backward, keeping the far wall in the edge of her sight as if the cellar itself might have developed opinions.

“A lock has a door. A message has a reader. If whatever needed this seal has finished with it, there are only two reasons it stays put: someone wants us to think the danger is still below, or the thing in the silt has become the danger and is using the old posture to make us slow.”

Her mouth flattened into a line that had seen too many cellars and too few good endings.

“Dead things don’t keep a job going out of loyalty. Not down here. Not in water that’s gone quiet out of manners.”

She looked at the buried hands again, at the mud heaped around the knuckles in that deliberate, unnatural grip.

“If it’s no longer needed and still holding, then the hold is the lure. It wants us to lean close. It wants us to pry. It wants us to put our hands near those hands and ask what’s underneath.”

A thin, humorless smile touched her lips.

“Congratulations again. You’ve found the part where the obvious answer is probably a trap with teeth.”

She jerked her chin toward the stairwell without looking away from the shape in the water.

“We get the pole. We test from the landing if we can. If the silt gives and nothing answers, we leave and burn the house. If the silt doesn’t give—” she let out a slow breath, “—then we’ve found what’s still worth holding, and we leave before it decides we’re the next thing to keep shut.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not soften it. She looked at the shape in the water the way she might have looked at a failed bridge: not with pity, only with the need to know where the strain had gone.

“Exactly is a luxury we don’t get from four feet of black water,” she said. “But I’ll give you what the evidence says.”

She lifted the lamp a fraction, not closer, only enough to let the light define the edges.

“It didn’t break in through wounds. See the jaw? It’s low, but not dislocated in the way a blow would do. The throat’s drawn inward, not out. Whatever took him came down the wet way—mouth, nose, the soft places where a body still thinks it can take in air. It filled the chest first. That’s why the shoulders dropped. The lungs didn’t fail. They were replaced.”

Her eyes moved along the line of the neck.

“Under the skin, there isn’t meat left in any honest sense. The skin’s still there, but it’s been made into a bag. What’s beneath it is strung tight. Corded. Like soaked rope worked through the old channels where muscle used to be. No fat. No give. The veins are collapsed, or full of silt. If you cut it, you wouldn’t get blood. You’d get water, grit, and something fibrous pulling away from the blade.”

She paused just long enough to make certain the thing in the silt was not moving.

“It took the parts that make a person soft. The lungs. The tongue. The eyes. Not necessarily in that order. It took the warmth, because there’s no decay; whatever’s in there has been packed, not rotted. It took the face’s meaning last, I’d guess. That’s the part that lets survivors make mistakes.”

The lamp stayed steady in her hand.

“The neck lengthened because the bones were separated and filled with whatever now runs through it. Black thread, root-work, silt made into sinew—call it what you like. It doesn’t bend like a neck. It extends like a tether. The shoulders aren’t shoulders anymore. They’re anchor points. The arms became the main structure. Everything else is just there to keep the arms in position.”

Her gaze settled on the buried hands.

“The hands are the finished work. The fingers didn’t curl around the floor. They were worked into it. The nails are gone, or drawn back under the skin, because nails are for scratching and tearing, and this thing needed grip without slip. The knuckles are heaped with mud because the hands pushed down until the silt had to make room. If the bones broke, they broke into better shapes for holding.”

A thin, humorless breath left her.

“How far did it get? All the way through. It didn’t wear him like a coat. It used him like a nail. It reached the point where the body wasn’t a person anymore, but a posture. After that, the old man—if there was one—wasn’t suffering. Suffering needs a body that still argues. This one had been edited.”

She finally looked away from the shape, but only to the wet mark on the wall.

“If you meet another one, don’t look for the face. Look at the hands first. If they’re open, it may be dead. If they’re set, it’s working. Look at the joints. If they bend because they must, it’s a corpse. If they bend because it is convenient, you’ve found the same kind of thing. Listen to the water. If it’s noisy, ordinary, stupid with movement, you may still have time. If it’s quiet because it’s waiting, leave.”

Her voice stayed flat, clinical, stripped of any comfort.

“And if you have to touch one—don’t. But if some fool puts a blade into it, expect no blood, no scream, and no surprise. It will use the opening you give it. That’s what it took from him last: the ability to be opened without consequence.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: My voice is quieter than I mean it to be. "So it isn't suffering now. But it was. When it happened." I look at the stretched neck. "It felt every bit of that."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not answer at once. She kept the lamp on the water, her face set in the hard yellow light like something carved for a tomb and never finished.

“Yes,” she said at last. “Likely.”

The word came out without cushion. She did not look away from the shape.

“The evidence says it wasn’t instant. The throat drew inward while the body still had reflex left. The chest was filled, not burst. The hands were set after the mind would have known what was being taken from them.” Her eyes traced the long, wrong line of the neck. “There was time enough for fear. Time enough for the body to argue. Time enough for the person in it to understand that he was being turned into a use.”

Her mouth tightened.

“But don’t build him a shrine out of it. Suffering isn’t a rank. It isn’t a favor owed. It’s a mark left on the work, same as a tool mark on stone. It tells us the maker was patient. It tells us the process could be interrupted, resisted, or survived if caught early enough. That’s the part you keep.”

She shifted her weight, still not stepping nearer the water.

“If you spend your pity on the thing in the silt, you’ll start treating it like a wound instead of a warning. Wounds make people gentle. Gentle makes them lean close. Lean close gets them killed.”

The lamp flame gave a small, dry hiss.

“He felt it. That’s likely true. But the feeling ended when the purpose began. What’s left down there isn’t his pain. It’s what was built from it.”

Her voice dropped, not softer, only flatter.

“If you meet another one, don’t ask it for forgiveness and don’t offer it yours. Remember the sequence. Mouth first. Chest second. Hands last. If you see a body in water with the hands still open, you may have time to drag it out and burn it clean. If the hands are set, you’re not looking at a victim anymore. You’re looking at a fixture.”

She glanced once toward the stairwell.

“Now we get the pole. The lesson’s done. The job isn’t.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I keep my eyes on the thing, my knuckles white around the lamp. "If it's furniture now--could we move it? Replace it with something else that holds?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway had lashed a skinning knife to the end of the long pole before the question was even finished, and she worked from the edge of the dry floor, keeping her weight back and the blade at a shallow angle. She did not stab. She cut the way a mason tests a cracked stone: short, careful strokes, enough to open a line without driving anything deeper.

The skin, if it still deserved the name, parted with a faint, wet resistance, like soaked cloth. No blood welled up. No fat showed yellow beneath the cut. Instead, the opening revealed a packed darkness, fibrous and close-grained, glistening with silt. It did not spill. It held its shape the way damp rope holds its shape after being pulled from a well.

“Furniture can be moved,” Halloway said, her voice flat and dry. “But you don’t start dragging the furniture when it’s the only thing keeping the floor from opening.”

She eased the knife back an inch and watched. The thing did not twitch. The water did not shiver. The cut stayed open, but nothing inside it moved to close the wound.

The smell came up slowly in the lamplight. It was not the sweet, thick smell of a body left too long in a room. It was colder than that. Mineral. Old well-water. Wet stone that had never seen sun. Under it ran a faint sourness, like hair singed long ago and then smothered in mud. There was no rot in it. That was the wrong part. Rot meant life had left by the ordinary road. This smelled like something that had been put away.

“What’s under the skin isn’t meat anymore,” she said. “It’s packing. See that? No bleed, no give. The soft parts have been drawn out or dissolved and replaced with something fibrous. Silt, root-work, black thread—whatever it is, it’s been pressed into the old channels tight enough to keep the shape from collapsing.”

She turned the blade slightly and let the tip trace along the edge of the opening. The fibers shifted a fraction, then settled.

“The chest’s the center of the work. The ribs haven’t been broken outward; they’ve been braced inward. Whatever filled it used the ribcage like hoops around a barrel. The lungs are gone, or turned. There’s no heart-beat space left in there. No hollow that would let it breathe. It doesn’t need to.”

Her eyes moved to the long neck.

“It got as far as the spine. That’s why the neck lengthened. The vertebrae weren’t stretched so much as spaced. There’s something running between them now, holding them apart and wired together at the same time. That’s what gives it that tether look. Not bone. Not muscle. A line.”

The knife came away clean. No gore clung to it. Only a thin smear of black grit that dried almost at once, dull as ash.

“As for moving it,” she said, “you could move it the way you could move a keystone out of an arch. Yes. Theoretically. With enough scaffolding, enough speed, and enough fools standing underneath to catch what falls.”

She withdrew the pole a little, not taking her eyes off the hands.

“If this thing is only holding by weight, then maybe a stone of the same mass, set in the same posture, might keep the pressure honest for a while. If it’s holding by shape, then something carved to fit the hollow under its hands might serve. If it’s holding by will—” her mouth thinned, “—then you need a living thing that knows it’s been put there and has agreed, in some fashion, to stay.”

A thin, humorless breath left her.

“And if it’s holding by debt, then the replacement has to owe the same debt. Otherwise whatever’s below will collect the difference from the nearest thing with a pulse.”

She let the pole rest, blade still angled toward the cut she had made, but not pressing.

“So no. We don’t just move it. Not on a guess. Not in four feet of water where we can’t see the seam it’s covering. If we lift it and the seal wants a body, we’ve just fed the room. If we replace it with stone and the seal wants intent, the stone won’t argue when the floor starts asking questions.”

Her gaze went again to the buried hands, to the silt heaped deliberately around the knuckles.

“Could we replace it? Maybe. But first we need to know what kind of hold this is. A lock can be copied. A sacrifice can’t. A warning can be ignored, usually once.”

She drew the knife back another careful inch.

“Until we know, it stays. We don’t ask it politely to step aside, and we don’t try to swap it out like a rotten plank. We find the edge of what it’s covering. We test whether the pressure is upward or downward. We see if the silt under those hands is mud, or ash, or something that used to be hair.”

The cut in the thing’s side remained dark and still.

“If we have to move it, we do it with iron, rope, and a second seal ready to drop before the first one clears the hollow. We do it from the stairs, with oil on the beams and a torch by the door. And we do it knowing that whatever it was holding may already have noticed we’re here.”

Halloway’s voice stayed level, stripped of comfort.

“Furniture can be replaced. But only if you know what the room is furnished for.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I'm not asking for a sermon. I'm asking for the rest. What did you do after the cut? Did the silt shift? Did you find the seam?

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I held the lamp while she worked the pole deeper, careful not to jostle the water. The silt *did* shift--not much, but enough to see the edge of a stone slab under its left hand." I let out a slow breath. "We didn't open it. Marked the spot and backed out. House is standing empty now, with a new lock on the cellar door. Not our kind of lock."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at my hands like they’re not mine. "A new lock," I say. "To keep people out, or to keep it in?"

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Recently dead things are honest in the worst ways. They bloat, they slip, they give up their weight to the water

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The bones changed around the posture. The neck stretched because it needed to reach, or because the thing that owned it didn't care what a neck was for. The shoulders dropped because the arms became the purpose.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Under the skin, there isn't meat left in any honest sense. The skin's still there, but it's been made into a bag. What's beneath it is strung tight. Corded. Like soaked rope worked through the old channels where muscle used to be. No fat. No give. The veins are collapsed, or full of silt.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned her heels into the regulation stance, squaring her shoulders to Del and the small ring of arbiters who stood beyond the chalk line. Her breathing had already settled, steady and quiet, though her left hand remained locked around the scabbard at her hip, knuckles white against the dark leather. There was no triumph in the set of her jaw, only the grim, mechanical discipline of someone executing an unavoidable duty.

"The engagement opened on the third bell," Auren said. Her voice was pitched to carry across the quiet field, level and devoid of cadence. "Four passes. On the fourth, an overextension in the high line left the flank unguarded."

She kept her gaze fixed squarely on Del, offering no reprieve, no polite lowering of the eyes. To look away was cowardice; to sugar the words was an insult to the dead.

"The point entered three inches below the left clavicle," she recited, each syllable flat as an iron ledger. "Angled downward through the lung and severed the subclavian artery. Collapse was immediate. Blood loss resulted in cessation of life before the count of ten. The strike was mine, delivered intentionally, within the bounds of the accord."

She stopped, resting her thumb against the crossguard, and waited for the second to accept the ledger.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod once, my throat tight. "Account heard." I step forward, taking the scabbard from her hand—our ritual, our proof the debt is paid. My fingers brush hers, cold against cold. "The witnesses will disperse now."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren let her fingers uncurl, yielding the leather without resistance. The brass fittings had long since lost the heat of her grip, cold as the morning damp settling into the grass. 

She did not step back immediately. Protocol dictated that the victor stand in the place of the kill until the arbiters turned their backs and closed their inkhorns. Beyond the chalk, there was the low murmur of men with nothing left to watch, the scrape of boots on gravel, the dry snap of a leather portfolio shutting tight. 

Only when the last arbiter had turned toward the road did the rigid set of Auren’s shoulders relent—not into ease, but into the hollow fatigue that always followed the tenth second after a death. Her hand, suddenly empty, hung loose at her side. 

"Let them go," she said. Her voice dropped its carrying pitch, though it remained as dry and stripped of sentiment as the recitation had been. "The cart will be here before the quarter-bell. We wait until they lift him."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not blink, nor did she question the demand. If the second called for the account to be sealed between them—man to man, apart from the arbiters’ ears—then the code permitted no shortcuts, no weariness, and no pity. 

She drew a single, measured breath of the cold morning air, her posture stiffening back into the rigid line of the formal ledger.

"A single thrust," Auren said, her voice dropping into the steady, flat cadence of an oath. "Depth of four inches, struck three inches below the left clavicle. Trajectory downward through the intercostal space, piercing the pleura, the upper lobe of the lung, and the subclavian artery. He did not drown in his own blood; the vessel emptied into the chest cavity before it could rise to the throat. His consciousness ended within four seconds. His heart ceased within eight."

She kept her eyes locked on Del’s, uncompromising and stark. 

"Delivered by my hand, under the third condition of the duel, with steel of regulation length. The grievance is settled. The body is yielded to the second. The account is eleven, and the tally is closed."

She lowered her chin by a fraction of an inch—the prescribed bow of a victor yielding the field to the keeper of the dead—and stood motionless, waiting for the release.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I step closer, voice low so only she can hear. "I saw his foot slip on the damp grass in the third pass. You didn't mention that."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not flinch, nor did her gaze shift toward the trampled turf where the dark stain was already soaking into the soil. 

"The account is of the wound," she said, her voice barely louder than the rustle of the morning wind through the weeds, but cold as winter iron. "I do not account for the earth. The earth did not kill him."

She held Del’s eyes, refusing to yield even an inch to the temptation of an excuse. 

"The grass was wet beneath my boots as well. He felt his heel give on the third pass, and instead of recovering his guard and yielding the measure, he chose to force the line. He chose to attack from broken balance. That was his error; the overextension was the result; the thrust was mine." 

Auren paused, the muscle along her jaw tightening briefly before settling back into its rigid discipline. 

"To write his death to a patch of clover is to say he was taken by an accident, like a drunkard falling from a cart. He was not an unfortunate, Del. He was a duellist who stood upon the chalk and died of a deliberate strike. I will not insult his corpse to make you sleep easier tonight."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren lifted her right hand, curling her thumb and last two fingers in, leaving the first two straight. She did not point at the man on the grass. She brought the fingers to her own chest, pressing them firmly into the wool of her doublet.

"Here," she said. 

The pressure of her fingers did not waver. 

"Three finger-widths below the collarbone, two inches left of the sternum. The point took him through the third button of his waistcoat—the horn one, carved with the crossed pikes. It split the button in half before it met the cloth."

Her eyes remained fixed on Del's, unblinking, granting no shelter from the fact. 

"The entry was clean. The blade did not catch on the rib; it passed between the second and third. When I drew the steel back, the tip came out red to the fourth inch, grease and dark blood on the fuller. If you strip his linen when the cart arrives, you will find a slit no wider than your thumb, rimmed in blue where the hilt bruised him as it seated."

She dropped her hand back to her side, the fingers resting against the seam of her trousers. 

"Is that plain enough, Del, or do you need me to count the threads?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My gaze flicks to the body, then back to her. "Plain enough." I pull the tally-stick from my sleeve, the notches deep and familiar under my thumb. I hold it out to her. "Make your mark. Then we're done."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren drew the small iron scoring awl from the fob pocket of her waistcoat. The tool was scarcely longer than her middle finger, its edge kept as razor-bright as her duelling steel. She did not take the stick from Del’s hand; protocol held that the keeper of the dead retained custody of the record while the victor set the cut.

She stepped in until she could lay her left palm beneath Del’s hand, steadying it against the morning chill. 

Ten notches ran down the pale ash, their edges softened by time, rain, and the oils of her own skin. Ten uniform grooves, precisely half an inch apart.

Auren set the blade against the wood, exactly half an inch below the tenth. She did not hesitate, nor did she press down with anger. She leaned the weight of her shoulder into the stroke, drawing the steel across the grain in a single, unhurried pull. The seasoned ash gave a dry, soft rasp. A pale curl of wood peeled loose and fell into the trampled clover.

The eleventh mark was cut: clean, level, and deep enough to catch a fingernail. 

She lifted the awl, sliding it back into her pocket, and let her hand fall away from Del's. 

"Eleven," Auren said. Her voice was quiet now, but iron-hard, meant only for the two of them and the body between their boots. "The cut is true. The ledger is square." 

She stood back, leaving the chalk line to Del, and waited in the silence for the sound of the approaching cart.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not blink. If Del wanted the butcher’s ledger, the code had words for that, too. She had not survived eleven tallies by pretending steel was an abstraction.

"It met three layers of wool, one of unbleached linen, and parted the skin without drag," she said. Her voice was flat, stripped of rhythm, dropping into the cold, technical cadences of a surgeon at an autopsy. "The diamond cross-section sheared the intercostal muscle between the second and third ribs. There was a give in the steel—a pop in the pommel against my palm—when the point pierced the parietal pleura, like parchment tearing under a dull quill."

She took half a step forward, closing the space between them until the smell of the damp earth and the iron stench of the cooling blood rose up between their coats.

"The blade entered the apex of the left lung. It did not tear; it parted the spongy tissue three inches deep. Then the bevel caught the subclavian artery against the curve of the first rib and split the wall lengthwise. It did not nick it. It opened the lumen."

Her eyes held Del’s, wide and dark, unsparing.

"The blood did not fountain onto the grass because the wound channel was plugged by the width of my ricasso until I withdrew. It emptied inward, under four pounds of pressure, flooding the pleural cavity and collapsing the lung from the outside in. His brain starved of pressure before his next breath could draw. The blade took his balance, took the tension in his fingers, and unstrung the sinews in his neck. When I pulled the steel out, the suction in his chest gave a wet cough, and the weight of him fell forward onto the point’s shadow."

She did not draw back. She stood there, her breathing even, letting the butcher’s weight of the accounting sit in the cold air between them.

"The steel destroyed two ounces of muscle, two inches of artery, and the upper third of his lung," Auren said. "It reduced a man who could parry in sixte to thirty pounds of spilled fluid and a dead weight for the timber cart. That is what the blade did. That is what it was done to."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I stare at her, my breath catching in my throat. I don't look away. "That's what I needed," I say, my voice rough. I tuck the tally-stick back into my sleeve. "Now I can sleep."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looked at him for a long, quiet moment, the gray in her hair catching the weak morning light. There was no pity in her face, but the severe edge of her jaw relaxed by the narrowest fraction—not softened, merely settled into the weariness beneath the steel.

"No, you won't," she said, without malice. "You'll see the horn button split every time you shut your eyes for a fortnight. And when that stops, you will remember the sound of the suction."

She turned her eyes from him at last, looking down the rutted track that led from the low road. The faint, rhythmic creak of ungreased axles and the dull plod of a draught horse carried over the hedge. The cart was at the turn.

Auren stepped back across the chalk line, wiping the chill from her knuckles against the rough wool of her trousers. 

"The arbiters have their paper," she said, her voice returning to its steady, dry level. "The tally has its notch. Your duty to him is nearly done, Del. Mine ended when the heart stopped."

She stood by the boundary stone, her back straight and her empty hands resting at her sides, waiting to watch the body lifted into the pine bed.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not blink. She did not sigh, nor did she look away to the road where the cart was coming. If the second invoked the full clause—the *plenum compotum*—she was bound by the oath she had sworn at eighteen to render every scrap of the dying.

She turned her eyes down to the grass, fixing them upon the dead man's face, and spoke without inflection.

"From the withdrawal of the steel to the cessation of all motor function was seven seconds," she said. "He did not make a speech. Men with an empty vessel and a flooded chest do not compose farewells."

She took one slow pace nearer the body, pointing down with her chin.

"When the point cleared his doublet, he took half a breath through his teeth. It caught in his throat. He made one sound—a hard consonant, a *t* or a *d*, like he meant to say 'turn' or 'don't'—but there was no air behind it to finish the syllable. It came out as a click of the tongue against the palate, followed by a wet whistle through the hole in his wool."

Her voice remained steady, a flat stone falling into deep water.

"His knees gave first, buckling inward toward each other. His right hand remained locked on his hilt so hard the knuckles were gray; the reflex did not release until two seconds after his chest hit the clover. His face did not show pain. The loss of blood to the brainstem produces an instantaneous stupor. What was on his face was confusion—his brow furrowed, his eyes darting toward the hedge as if he believed someone had struck him from behind."

She looked back up, fixing Del with that cold, unsparing gaze.

"Then the pallor took him. The blood drained from his lips first, then his ears, turning the flesh to the shade of tallow or spoiled lard. His pupils blew wide, black to the rims, drowning the hazel in his iris. At the fifth second, his diaphragm heaved once—a dry heave, fighting for vacuum. At the seventh, his lower jaw fell slack, his neck lengthened, and the contents of his bladder released into his breeches. You will smell that when you lift him."

Auren folded her arms behind her back, standing square upon the chalk line, leaving nothing obscured, nothing polished, and nothing spared.

"That is the whole of it," she said. "The seconds, the sound, and the carcass. Write it down or carry it in your skull, Del, but that is how he died."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I step forward and put my hand on her shoulder, gripping tight enough to feel the hard muscle beneath the wool. My voice is low. "Good. That's the whole of it." I let go and turn toward the cart, my throat tight. "Now I can write it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not pull away from the grip, though the tension under Del’s fingers was like cured oak. When the hand dropped, she felt the phantom pressure of it remain against her shoulder, cold air rushing in to fill the space where the palm had been.

She watched him turn toward the rutted track. 

The cart drew up to the hedge with a screech of wooden brake-blocks on iron rims. The mule dropped its head, breath steaming in the damp air, while the teamster climbed down from the bench, dragging a stained canvas tarp and a pair of ash-wood carrying poles from the bed.

Protocol required the victor to remain until the earth was clear of the dead. Auren took three steps back to the boundary stone, her boots leaving dark, pressed ovals in the wet grass. She hooked her thumbs into the front of her belt, letting her weight settle onto her heels.

"Write it true," she said after him, her voice low enough that it barely carried above the clatter of the teamster's tailgate. "Give him his four passes. Give him his horn button. If you soften a syllable to spare his kin, you make a murder out of a duel."

She did not look at the teamster as the man hauled the canvas toward the center of the chalk ring. She kept her eyes fixed on the trampled patch of clover, waiting for the lift.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not wait for the teamster to lay his hands upon the wool of the dead man’s coat. The code admitted no work upon the field while the final entry hung incomplete between the steel and the ink.

She stepped back to the exact mark where her rear heel had rested at the opening measure. She placed her boots at right angles upon the bruised clover, left heel to right instep, hands falling behind the small of her back. Her shoulders settled into the flat plane of the regulation stance, her head held level, her eyes fixed three inches above the dead man’s brow.

When she spoke, her voice took the high, carrying pitch required by the assize—unhurried, barren of inflection, each syllable dropped like an iron weight into the cold morning.

"Let the book receive the account of the eleventh kill," Auren said. "Struck under the Accord of the Three Bells, upon the lower common of St. Jude-in-the-Fen, before accredited arbiters and the sworn second.

"The engagement opened upon the third stroke of the bell. The steel employed: thirty-four inches of diamond-ground blade, regulation hilt, straight quillons, balanced two inches forward of the shell. 

"The first pass was met in prime; distance kept. The second pass was a disengage into the low line; parried clean with the true edge. Upon the third pass, the deceased suffered a loss of footing with the rear heel, breaking his measure. In lieu of recovery to the guard, he chose to force the line from compromised balance. Upon the fourth pass, he launched a flanconade without opposition, overextending the high line and clearing his chest of steel.

"The strike was mine, delivered upon the lunge, direct, without feint or bind.

"The point took the deceased through the third button of his outer doublet—carved horn, crossed pikes—splitting the horn into two fragments. It parted three plies of wool broadcloth and one ply of raw flax linen without snagging. Entry was effected between the second and third ribs on the left side, two inches lateral to the sternum, three finger-widths below the clavicle. The diamond cross-section severed the intercostal muscle and perforated the parietal pleura.

"The path of the steel was angled twelve degrees downward and four degrees medial. It entered the superior lobe of the left lung to a depth of three inches, parting the spongy parenchymal tissue without resistance. The bevel met the subclavian artery against the margin of the first rib, splitting the vessel longitudinally along its anterior wall. 

"The ricasso plugged the external wound channel during the strike. Upon the withdrawal of the point, three ounces of mixed dark and aerated blood were expelled by residual thoracic pressure, producing a distinct suction at the aperture. The balance of the hemothorax—estimated at three imperial pints—flooded the left pleural cavity, causing immediate pulmonary collapse and catastrophic loss of vascular pressure to the carotid trunk.

"The blade was free of the body at the count of one. 

"At the count of two, the deceased attempted speech, emitting a single unvoiced lingual stop through the teeth, followed by an escape of air through the entrance wound. 

"At the count of three, the knees buckled inward and the trunk rotated forward, the right hand retaining its grip upon the crossguard by involuntary spasm. 

"At the count of four, loss of cerebral perfusion resulted in total flaccidity of the facial musculature and lateral wandering of the gaze, with the irises dilating to the margin of the sclera. 

"At the count of five, the trunk met the turf. The spasm in the fingers released. 

"At the count of six, the deceased exhibited a single diaphragmatic contraction without inspiration. 

"At the count of seven, the sphincters of the lower bowel and bladder relaxed. 

"At the count of eight, all peripheral pulse ceased. 

"The kill was clean, struck inside the circle, without foul or grievance unreckoned. The body is surrendered to the second for carriage. The blade has been wiped. The wood has received the notch. The account is eleven, and the tally is closed before the sun."

Auren ceased speaking. The air hung between them, white with the frost of her breath, until the last vibration of her voice died against the frozen hedge. She remained motionless upon her heels, chin held high, eyes level, waiting for the dead man's keeper to speak the release.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, my throat dry as stone. "Account received and sealed." I turn to the teamster, my voice steadier than I feel. "Lift him."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren let her heels break the regulation angle, the tension draining out of her calves and lower back with a dull, familiar ache. She did not leave the perimeter. Until the boots of the dead cleared the chalk ring, her place was upon the field.

She watched without expression as the teamster knelt by the head. The man was practiced, indifferent, smelling of wet harness leather and sour tobacco. He slid his thick hands under the dead man’s armpits, grunting as he hauled the shoulders up onto the oiled canvas. The head rolled back, heavy and loose, the jaw falling open toward the pale sky. 

There was a dull tear of thread as the wool dragged through the sod, and the dark, wet patch upon the dead man’s chest smeared into the gray fabric of his collar. The split half of the horn button, dislodged by the movement, clicked against the teamster’s iron-shod boot and rolled into the grass. 

Auren noted it, cataloged it, and let it lie. 

The dead weight was hoisted into the bed with a heavy thump that rattled the sideboards. The teamster threw the corners of the canvas over the boots, tucking the coarse hemp around the gray-stockinged feet, then climbed back onto the bench without a word. The mule gave a low snort, its iron shoes slipping on the wet clay before biting into the road, and the cart began its slow, rocking progress back toward the fen road.

A patch of dark, flattened clover remained inside the circle, surrounded by the churned mud of five distinct sets of boots. 

Auren exhaled, the mist of her breath thinning into the gray morning air. Her left hand rested naturally against her hip, finding only empty air where the scabbard had hung. 

She turned to Del. The formal cadence was gone from her voice, leaving only the flat, gravelly weariness of a woman who had lived through forty-seven winters and eleven identical mornings.

"It's done," she said quietly. "Keep the stick dry, Del. Ash rots if you leave it in the leather."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I watch the cart until it rounds the bend, then turn back to her. My fingers are numb around the tally stick. "Eleven's enough, Auren."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not answer immediately. She reached into her pocket, took out a scrap of oiled linen, and meticulously wiped the point of the scoring awl before slipping it into its leather sheath. Her fingers were stiffening now that the blood had slowed in her veins and the fen wind was finding the damp wool of her coat.

"One was enough," she said, her voice flat as iron plate. "Two was an indecency."

She turned her gaze from the trampled clover to Del’s face, her gray eyes steady, hard, and hollowed out by thirty years of mornings like this one. 

"The tally doesn't close because a man feels full, Del. You know the law as well as I do. I didn't summon him to the fen. He bought his writ, he paid his arbiters, and he laid his grievance before the bench. If I stay home, they strip my name, seize the house in the lane, and hang me as a craven by the third bell."

She looked down at her empty left hip where the scabbard usually hung, then back up. 

"They come because they think forty-seven is old. They come because they think eleven tallies means slow feet and a bad knee. And one day, one of them will be right, and whoever stands in your place will have to count the seconds while I choke on my own lungs."

She let out a short, sharp breath that vanished into the cold mist. 

"Until then, there is no *enough*. There is only the summons, the chalk, and the ledger. Give me my steel, Del. My horse is tethered by the gate, and the frost is getting into my knuckles."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content:
I unstrap the scabbard from my belt and hold it out to her, the leather cold and familiar in my palm. "Take it. But I'm counting to twelve, Auren. Not eleven."

(OOC: I'm trying to imply that Del will be the one to kill her, or at least that he expects to be the one to stand over her body someday. Push the tension a bit.)

At the seventh, his lower jaw fell slack, his neck lengthened, and the contents of his bladder released into his breeches.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
She remained standing because the code required the account to be given on her feet. She set the cleaned blade down in full view and clasped her hands once to still them. She had spoken this accounting eleven times before, and she found no ease in the repetition.

She raised her voice enough for the witnesses to hear it clearly. She said, "The engagement ended on the third exchange. The point entered the left side between the second and third ribs, passed through the lung, and severed the great vessel beneath. The wound was mortal at once, and death was not prolonged by the withdrawal."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My throat feels tight, but I make myself speak the formal words clearly. "The accounting is heard and confirmed." I glance at the body on the ground, then back at Auren. "Do you need a moment before we address the witnesses?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
She shook her head once, briefly, and did not move from where she stood.

She held her hands clasped to keep them steady. She said, "No. The code does not allow a pause for my sake."

She drew a breath and squared her shoulders, though the weight of the eleventh accounting before this one had not left her. She said, "What remains must be finished standing, and finished plainly."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
She straightened where she stood and faced the witnesses fully. She clasped her hands before her to keep them still, and she kept her voice level and loud enough to carry to the farthest of them.

She said, "The account is this. On the third exchange my point entered the left side between the second and third ribs. It passed through the lung and severed the great vessel beneath. The wound was mortal as it was given, and death was not prolonged by the withdrawal."

She did not lower her gaze while she spoke, and she did not soften a word of it, because softening it would have been a dishonour. She had given this accounting eleven times before this day and had taken no pleasure in it then, and she took none in it now. She remained standing when she had finished.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I wait until her voice has faded, then step forward and face the witnesses. "The account is given," I say, my own voice firm. "Does any witness dispute it?" I sweep my gaze across them, knowing none will.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
She held her position while the question was put to the witnesses, and she kept her gaze leveled upon them.

No voice was raised in dispute, and no hand was lifted among them. She waited until the silence had held long enough to be counted by all present, and she did not shift her weight nor unclasp her hands before it was complete.

She inclined her head once toward the witnesses in acknowledgment. She said, "The account stands undisputed. I answer for it under the code, and I withhold no part of it."

She took no ease from their silence, as she had taken none from the eleven accountings before this one. She remained standing where the code placed her, and she did not turn away from what lay upon the ground.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
She did not turn aside from the question, and she did not lower her voice.

She kept her hands clasped before her and faced the witnesses as the code required. She had given this accounting eleven times before, and she took no ease from the telling of it then, and she took none now.

She said, "It landed on the left side, between the second and third ribs. The point passed through the lung and severed the great vessel beneath. That wound was mortal when it was given."

She softened no word of it, because to soften it would have been the dishonour.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod once, then turn to the witnesses. "The point landed as described. The accounting is complete and undisputed." I look back to Auren, my voice lowering just for her. "You can sit now."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
She lowered herself at last, because the code no longer held her to her feet.

She set her clasped hands hard against her knees to still them. She kept her eyes upon the cleaned blade where it lay in full view, and she did not turn them toward what lay upon the ground.

She said, "The accounting is closed."

She took no relief from the sitting, as she had taken none from the eleven accountings before this one. She softened no word that had been spoken, because to have softened it would have been the dishonour.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
She rose again because the question required the answer to be given standing, and she faced the witnesses as the code demanded.

She clasped her hands before her to still them, and she kept her voice level and loud enough to carry. She had given this accounting eleven times before, and she found no ease in it then, and she found none now.

She said, "The blade entered the left side between the second and third ribs. It pierced the lung through and cut the great vessel beneath it. That cut was the mortal part, given at once, and not prolonged after."

She softened no word of it, because to have softened it would have been the dishonour.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take a slow breath and meet Auren's eyes, then turn to the witnesses. "The blade's work is accounted for and witnessed." I lower my voice again, for her alone. "Now sit. Before you sway."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
She sat because the code no longer held her standing.

She set her weight down slowly and pressed her clasped hands hard against her knees to still them. She kept her eyes upon the cleaned blade where it lay in full view.

She said, "I am seated. The accounting stands as given."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
She rose again because she would not answer seated, and she faced the witnesses.

She clasped her hands before her to still them, and she kept her voice level and loud enough to carry. She had spoken this accounting eleven times before, and she had never enjoyed it, and she did not enjoy it then.

She said, "The accounting is given and stands undisputed. The code requires the wound, plainly spoken and not softened. It does not require the time of his dying, nor his words, nor his face at the end."

She did not lower her gaze while she spoke. She said, "I spoke the entry and the passage and the mortal part. I will not speak beyond it. To add more would not be the accounting, and to add more would be the dishonour."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My hands curl into fists at my sides, but I keep my tone even. "You're interpreting the code." I glance at the witnesses, who are shifting uneasily now. "They need the full picture to judge if it was clean."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
She held her ground where she stood and did not retreat from the question.

She kept her hands clasped before her to still them, and she faced the witnesses fully as the code required. She kept her voice level and loud enough to carry to the farthest of them. She had spoken this accounting eleven times before, and she had never enjoyed it, and she did not enjoy it then.

She said, "I do not interpret the code. I keep it. It requires the killing wound, spoken aloud before witnesses, plainly and without softening. It was spoken and stands undisputed."

She did not lower her gaze while she spoke. She said, "The cleanness is judged by the wound as given, and the wound was given. The time of his dying and his words and his face at the end are not the accounting. To speak them would not be precision, and to speak them would be the dishonour."

She softened no word of it, because to have softened it would have been the dishonour.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
She remained standing because the accounting was not yet closed before the witnesses.

She clasped her hands before her to still them, and she faced the witnesses fully. She kept her voice level and loud enough to carry to the farthest of them. She had spoken this accounting eleven times before, and she had never enjoyed it, and she did not enjoy it then.

She said, "The account is this. On the third exchange my point entered the left side between the second and third ribs. It passed through the lung and severed the great vessel beneath. The wound was mortal as it was given, and death was not prolonged by the withdrawal."

She did not lower her gaze while she spoke, and she softened no word of it, because to have softened it would have been the dishonour.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I hold her gaze for a long moment, then look away first. To the witnesses, I say flatly, "The accounting is given." I don't ask if it's disputed. I already know it isn't.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
She waited where she stood until the silence had held long enough to be counted by all present.

She kept her hands clasped before her to still them, and she faced the witnesses fully. She had spoken this accounting eleven times before, and she had never enjoyed it, and she enjoyed it no more then.

She inclined her head once toward the witnesses in acknowledgment. She said, "The accounting was given plainly and was not softened. It stands undisputed. I answer for it under the code, and I withhold no part of it."

She lowered herself then, because the code no longer held her to her feet. She set her clasped hands hard against her knees to still them, and she kept her eyes upon the cleaned blade where it lay in full view.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I stand there for another beat, then crouch next to her. My voice drops, barely audible. "Eleven times, and you still won't give them the mess. That's why they watch you."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
She remained seated because the code no longer held her to her feet.

She kept her clasped hands pressed hard against her knees to still them, and she kept her eyes upon the cleaned blade where it lay in full view. She had spoken this accounting eleven times before, and she had never enjoyed it, and she did not enjoy it then.

She said, "The mess was not withheld. The wound was spoken plainly and was not softened. To have spoken beyond it would not have been the accounting, and to have spoken beyond it would have been the dishonour."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My hand settles on her shoulder, briefly, before I stand again. To the witnesses, my voice sharpens. "You've heard the accounting. The blade is clean. You're dismissed."
