dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren wiped the last of it from the fuller with a cloth she would burn, and set the blade across her palms in the position of accounting. The yard had gone very quiet. Somewhere behind her, a servant had stopped sweeping. The witnesses held their ground the way witnesses did when they wanted to be elsewhere and could not say so.

She turned first to the body, because the account began with the dead and not with her.

"Corin Vahl," she said, "second son of the Vahl line, duellist of record." The name went out flat and complete, given its full weight and no more. "He fought with the measure. He gave no ground he was not owed."

Then she turned to the witnesses, and to Del as the second, and gave them the wound.

"Entry below the third rib, his right side, through the gap he opened at the turn. The blade passed at an angle, upward and back. It opened the lung and cut the great vessel beneath the heart." She said it without pause, without ornament. "He was dead in the time it takes to fall. He did not suffer the field."

That was the whole of it. That was the accounting, and there was no softness in it, because softness would have been the lie and the lie would have been the dishonour.

She looked at Del and did not look away. "Witnessed and spoken," she said. "It is finished."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I swallow, my throat dry. "Witnessed and spoken," I echo, my voice steady despite the tremor in my hands. I step forward to take the blade from you, as is my duty. "The account is clear."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
She let the blade go into Del's hands and felt the difference immediately — the way a hand felt when it was no longer holding the thing it had been made for. Her fingers closed once on nothing, and then she let them fall.

"The cloth as well," she said. "It goes in the fire. Not the laundry, not the river. The fire, and you watch it burn."

Beyond the wall, a cart went past on the road, unhurried, the driver unaware that anything had happened here at all. Auren listened to it go and found she was grateful for it.

She looked once more at Corin Vahl, and then she did not, because there was nothing left to look at that the account had not already named. She had said the wound aloud, and the wound was now the record, and the record was the only thing of his death that belonged to anyone but him.

"The body goes to his family before dark," she said. "His mother will want the measure accounted for separately — the blade he used, where it fell, who holds it now. You'll tell her the truth of it, all of it. She's owed that and she'll ask." A pause. "She'll ask whether he was afraid. Tell her he was not. That one is true."

She rolled her shoulders once, the way she did when the tension needed somewhere to go, and picked up her coat from the rail.

"Eleven," she said, to no one in particular, and did not elaborate. "I'll be at the inn past the mill. If his people want the account spoken again before them, they know where to find me. I won't refuse them that."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
"It is spoken," Auren said, and gave the formula back the way it had been given to her, clean and without decoration. "It stands as the record. The measure is closed."

Behind her the witnesses began to move, slowly at first, then with the ordinary haste of men who had somewhere else to be. The servant's broom started up again on the far side of the yard. Auren listened to both and thought that this was the part no one wrote down — the part where the world simply resumed, indifferent, and the dead man became an errand.

"Vahl's blade goes with the body," she said. "His mother will ask who holds it and where it lies now. You'll answer that honestly, even if the answer is ugly. Especially then."

She shrugged into her coat, which had been hanging long enough to take the cold of the wall, and settled it on her shoulders like something she had worn a thousand times, because she had.

"The cloth burns tonight. The body goes before dark. I'll be at the inn past the mill, and I'll be there till they've had their say." A pause. "Eleven," she said again, quieter this time, and the number sat in her the way a stone sits in a pocket — carried, not shown. She had never once said it as though it were a thing to be proud of, and she did not now.

She walked to the gate without looking back at the body, because the account had already done the looking, and there was nothing left in that yard that belonged to her.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, already feeling the weight of the rest of the day settling on me. I wrap the cloth around the blade, careful not to touch the stain. "I'll see it done," I say, my voice low. "And I'll find you after. We'll need to settle the fee."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stopped with her hand on the gate and did not turn around. The wood was cold under her palm, weathered smooth where a hundred hands had pushed it open and shut, and she kept her hand there a moment longer than the gate required.

"The fee was posted before the measure," she said. "Both purses, in the patron's keeping, sealed and witnessed. There's nothing left to settle and you know it. If Vahl's people want to contest the posting, that's a matter for the patron and not for either of us."

She pushed the gate and it swung open onto the road, the sound of it carrying farther than it should have in the quiet.

"Your own portion is owed to you by me, not by them, and I'll pay it at the inn tonight with the rest of it. That one does need settling, because I hold it and you don't." A pause. "You'll find me there. Don't come before the body goes — I'll know if you did."

She stepped through and let the gate fall closed behind her, and only then, on the road, with the wall between her and the yard, did she take the breath she had been holding since the turn.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stopped on the road with her back to the gate. The question had gone through the wood and found her, and it was a plain question, and it was owed a plain answer — the account was not complete without it, and she had known it was not complete when she left the yard, which was why she had been walking faster than the distance required.

She turned, put her hand back on the gate, and pushed it open again. The witnesses had not all gone. Two of them were still at the wall, and the servant had stopped sweeping again, and that was enough — enough to speak it in front of, which was the requirement, and she had nearly walked away from a requirement, which sat badly in her.

"Vahl's blade," she said, from the threshold, in the voice she used for the account and not the voice she used for anything else. "He held it in the high guard through the opening exchange. At the turn he brought it down across his body and it passed my shoulder — here—" she touched her left shoulder with two fingers, at the seam, where the coat had a fresh cut in it that the coat had not been given by anyone else "—and carried past. He lost the point of it on the way. It struck the stone of the well-head behind me, edge-first, and turned in the air. It came to rest on the flagstones two paces from the well, hilt toward the wall, point toward the yard gate."

She let that stand a moment, because the witnesses would be picturing it, and they were owed the moment to do it.

"It lies where it fell. I did not touch it. It goes with the body to his family, in the state it fell, and whoever picks it up first should know the edge took a chip at the well-head, a hand's width down from the point. His mother will ask whether the blade failed him. Tell her it did not. It was never given the chance to."

She looked at Del across the yard, still in the doorway, still holding the wrapped blade and the cloth.

"Now it's finished," she said. "That was mine to say and I said it late. Don't make me say it twice."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "I'll tell her," I say, meeting your gaze across the yard. I turn to the nearest witness. "You heard it. The blade rests there, and you'll mark its place until it's taken." Then I look back at you, the wrapped steel heavy in my hands. "Go. I'll see you at the inn."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren held the doorway a moment longer and did not let the silence do the work for her.

"One more thing that belongs in the record," she said, and touched the cut seam at her shoulder again, flat and matter-of-fact. "That blood on the coat is mine. The point drew along the seam and took the skin under it, shallow, nothing that needs a surgeon. Anyone who saw the coat and not the account would have questions later. Now they won't. Vahl did not wound me. He grazed me at the turn, and I said so before it could become a story."

She looked at the witness Del had named, the one now standing watch over a chipped blade lying on flagstones two paces from the well.

"You have the place marked," she said. "You'll hold it till it's lifted. If anyone moves it before the family comes, the account fails and the failure is yours. You'll be asked to swear to that, and you'll swear it truly."

Then, to Del, briefly, because the second had done the second's work and the code did not require her to say so — but she said it anyway, in the flat voice that was the only voice she had for things that mattered.

"You caught the omission. That was your duty and you did it. I'd have been late by a day and it would have been on me, not you. Noted."

She stepped back through the gate and pulled it shut, and this time she did not stop on the road. The cart was gone. The mill chimney was sending up a thin grey thread ahead of her, which meant the inn was lit and there would be a fire, and she thought of the cloth going into it tonight, watched, until it was ash.

Eleven. She carried the number the way she had carried the other ten — not lightly, not heavily, just carried — and she walked the road to the inn past the mill with the cold of the wall still in her coat and did not look back at the yard, because the yard was finished and the road was not.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stopped on the road.

She stood with her back to the gate and let the question stand, because it was a fair question and she had known it was fair when she walked away from it — which was the reason she had walked away from it.

Then she turned and put her hand to the gate a third time and pushed it open. The servant had stopped sweeping again. Two witnesses were still at the wall. It would have to be enough.

"Precisely, then," she said, and set her right hand flat on her left shoulder, above the cut, and spoke in the register the account used and nothing else.

"Vahl's point drew from the seam of the shoulder outward and down, the length of a hand, on a line that followed the slope of the deltoid. It opened the skin and the fat beneath it and stopped at the muscle without cutting the muscle. The vessel it crossed was small. It bled freely, which a shallow cut will do, and more than its size warranted, which is why the coat carries what it carries. The wound is the coat's source. It is not the coat's business."

She took her hand down.

"That is the wound. What I gave you first was the coat's account of the wound. I said *shallow*, and I said *nothing that needs a surgeon*. Both true, neither precise. I was telling you what to think of the blood instead of telling you what the blade did. That was mine to give cleanly, and I gave it soft."

She looked at Del across the yard.

"Twice today. Noted the second time as well."

A pause, and then, flat, with no heat in it and nothing underneath it either:

"Now it is finished. And if you find a third, say it before I reach the road. I would rather stand at this gate until dark than be caught from behind it twice in one afternoon."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I glance at the witnesses. "You heard the account. Mark it." Then I look back at you, my jaw tight. "It's finished. Go. I'll watch the cloth burn myself."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not answer.

She let the gate fall shut between them, and this time she did not stop on the road. Three times at the same gate was enough for one account, and the third had been hers to answer, and she had answered it. There was nothing left on that side of the wood that belonged to her.

She walked.

The road past the mill was packed hard and pale with frost, and her boots made a sound on it that she did not bother to soften. Behind her the yard stayed quiet, then the broom started again — she heard it through the wall, thin and regular, a sound so ordinary that it seemed almost like forgiveness, and she did not take it as any such thing. The world had simply resumed. That was all it ever did.

The omission sat with her the whole way. Twice. Once the blade's rest, once the wound. Both times she had told the softer true thing and left the harder true thing standing. Both times the second had asked the precise question and she had been caught at the gate. She turned it over the way she turned over a bad exchange, looking for where the flaw had been, and found it plainly enough: she had wanted to be finished. She had wanted the account closed and the road under her, and the wanting had cost the account two degrees of exactness, and the exactness was the whole of it. A soft account was a lie wearing the record's clothes. She knew that. She had known it for twenty years. She had done it anyway, twice, in one afternoon.

Eleven, and the number did not feel like eleven. It felt like an afternoon that had been done badly.

The inn past the mill had its fire lit and a lamp in the window, and a smell of bread and old wood coming out of the door, and Auren pushed in and took the table in the corner with her back to the wall because that was where she always sat, whether or not anyone was coming. She ordered nothing but a jug of hot water and a cup, and set her coat on the chair beside her rather than the peg, where she could see the cut in the seam.

The keeper knew her. He did not ask how the day had gone, which was the right way to serve a duellist, and she was grateful for it in the small flat way she was grateful for things she never said aloud. She poured the water and let it stand and did not drink it. Her shoulder had gone stiff under the coat, and the stiffness was honest, and she let it ache.

She would wait for the second. The fee was still to be paid, and she owed it — owed it cleanly, counted out, not handed across with a word to cover the awkwardness of it. And when the second came, and if the second found a third thing she had softened, Auren had decided on the road that she would not make them dig for it. She would say it herself, plainly, the moment she saw it in the way the second would be looking at her. That was the correction she could still make today.

She folded her hands on the table and watched the door, and waited, and the fire did its indifferent work, and she thought about the cloth, which was not hers to burn and which she would trust the second to watch until it was ash, because that, at least, she had not softened. She had said it the first time, exactly: the fire, and you watch it burn.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content:
(She's already gone.)

I let out a slow breath and look at the two witnesses still standing at the wall. They're watching me, waiting. "The account stands," I tell them, my voice carrying across the yard. "You heard her. You'll keep watch until the family arrives." I turn and head inside to prepare the body, the weight of the blade in my hands a familiar, grim burden. I need to be done here before dark.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, the weight of the blade heavy in my hands. "Witnessed and spoken," I say, my throat tight. I turn to the two witnesses. "The account stands. Mark the blade's place and wait for the family." Then I head for the house, the cloth bundled tight against the steel. I have a body to prepare and a fire to build.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The jug had stopped steaming by the time she had counted the fee out twice.

Auren laid the coins on the table in columns, the second's portion to the left, her own to the right, and did not gather them into a purse. The code did not say the fee had to be counted where anyone could see it, but the code did not say it did not, and she had already decided on the road that today she would do the things the code did not require, since she had twice done the softer version of the things it did.

She counted them a third time anyway, because her hands wanted the work, and because a third count was not softness — it was arithmetic, and arithmetic could not lie.

The keeper brought bread she had not ordered. She told him so. He said it came with the fire, and set it down, and went away, and she left it where it stood until her hands wanted something to do besides count, and then she ate a piece of it without tasting it.

Her shoulder had gone stiff and hot under the coat. She had told the truth about it twice now — the true-and-soft version, then the true-and-precise — and it still ached the same either way, which was the small joke of it: the account did not change the wound. The wound was what it was. Only the record could be made clean or dirty, and she had dirtied it, and cleaning it back up had cost her three walks to a gate and one second's patience. That was the price of wanting to be finished. Wanting to be finished was the flaw. She had said so to herself before, and would say it to herself again, and it would keep being true.

She looked at the coat, folded over the chair back, the cut in the seam plain as a stroke of ink. The coat would need a tailor. The tailor would ask what did it, and she would say *a turn*, and the tailor would look at the seam and the line of the cut and know it was not a turn, and would not ask twice. That was how it went with tailors and duellists both. Everyone knew and no one said.

Outside, the mill's grey thread had thickened and gone dark against the sky. Somewhere past the wall and the road and the fields, in a house she had left behind, a cloth was going into a fire and someone was watching it burn because she had said the fire and you watch it burn, and that one she had not softened. She held to that. One clean thing out of an afternoon of soft ones.

Eleven, she thought, and the number went into the pocket with the stone and stayed there.

The lamp in the window threw her shadow onto the wall behind her, and the shadow sat with its back to the wall exactly as she did. She folded her hands on the table, over the columns of coin, and watched the door, and did not drink the water, and waited — and if the second came through that door with the look of someone who had found a third thing, Auren had decided she would say it herself before the second could ask, plainly, and not make them dig. That was the correction she could still make today, and she intended to make it.

She watched the door.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I walk into the inn with the smell of smoke still clinging to my sleeves. I see you at the corner table, coins laid out, bread untouched. I pull out the chair across from you and sit, my shoulders aching from hauling stone for the pyre. "It's done," I say. "The cloth burned. The body's gone. His mother took the blade. She asked about the chip." I pause, meeting your eyes. "I told her the truth. All of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren had not stood when the door opened, and did not stand now. She had been watching it for an hour, and watching had stopped being useful the moment it had worked.

"The chip was in the account," she said. "You gave her the truth, and the truth had already been spoken before you gave it. That one is clean, and it was clean before you walked in."

She turned the left column of coins around and slid it across the table, exactly counted.

"Your portion. Count it or don't. It's what was posted and what I held, and it's settled now."

Then she put her hands in her lap, out of the way, where they could not reach for the bread or the cold cup or the cut in the coat.

"There's a third thing. You didn't find it, so I'll say it myself, and I'll say it before you can pull it out of me at a gate."

A pause.

"I told you to tell his mother he was not afraid. I told you that one was true."

She looked at Del and did not look away.

"I don't know that. I know his hands. I watched his hands through the whole exchange and they did not shake, not at the guard and not at the turn, and that is the whole of what I had. I did not see his face — the turn took it, and by the time the line opened it did not matter what his face was doing. So I gave you a fact I did not hold and called it true, and you would have carried it to a mother in the voice of the record, and she would have kept it, because mothers keep what the record gives them. That's the third. It's the worst of the three, because the other two went to a page and this one goes to a person."

She picked up the cup, found it had gone cold, and set it back down.

"And it can't stand as a correction from this table. A correction from a duellist to a second is just talk. It needs witnesses, same as the rest of it. So I'll go to the Vahls — tomorrow, before the blade is hung, if it isn't hung already — and I'll say it in front of their people and ours, and the record will read what I should have said the first time. He did not speak. His hands were steady. Whether he was afraid is not known to me, and it should not be given to her as though it were."

She looked at the coins still sitting in her own column, counted, unclaimed.

"Assemble them if you can. If you can't, I'll stand at their gate until

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I lean forward, the chair creaking under me. "You don't need to go to their gate." My voice is low. "I told her his hands were steady and he gave no cry. I left the rest out." I push the coins back toward you slowly. "Your portion's light. You paid the surgeon for the graze, didn't you?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Won't do," Halloway said, but not unkindly. "'I don't know yet' will keep you alive. 'Wrong' won't. Wrong's where you start, not where you finish. Find what it's copying and then find the first place it stops copying."

She lifted the lamp higher and swept the light slow across the surface, left to right, the way you'd check a floor for footing.

"Nearest shape is a man kneeling. So start there. The knees are heels — they point the wrong way. Arms go into the water half a body too far forward. Head's folded down on the chest, or there isn't one, and you want to know which before you're in reach of it. Ribs showing. It's been starving down here, and starving things came in by some way, and ways in don't care which direction they get used."

She nodded at the water around it. Flat. Black. No ripples anywhere.

"And it hasn't died. Corpses are still from the beginning. This one *stopped.* Nothing that stopped a minute ago is dead — dead isn't a decision. That was a decision."

She held the lamp steady.

"So. Look at the neck. Tucked, or absent?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I swallow, forcing my eyes to trace the shape Halloway described.* "It's... tucked. The head's there, just bent too far. Like the neck's broken." *I squint.* "But the skin's wrong. It's... smooth. No wrinkles from the fabric of its shirt."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Better," Halloway said. "And better than you know, because those are two clues wearing one coat."

She came down one more step and stopped, boots on the lowest dry course of brick.

"Work it backward. Submersion bloats skin. It doesn't smooth it. Starvation hangs it off the ribs in flaps — and there's the ribs, plain as cutlery. So smooth where cloth should crease means the cloth isn't cloth. The shirt is the same surface as what's under it. One skin, all the way through, and one skin doesn't wrinkle against itself."

She tilted the lamp a hair.

"It never copied a man in a shirt. It copied the idea of one, from the wrong side or the far side — close enough for a shape, never close enough for a crease. And the folded neck's the same lesson. A broken neck is the one human shape it knows from the inside, because it made that shape. It studied exactly one man, studied him after, and it's been sitting here in the dark wearing its own homework."

A pause, strictly for effect.

"Which tells you three usable things. It hunts at edges, from below, wherever a man leans over water. It's starving, so the stillness is costing it more than it's costing us. And it knows living men badly — so the best thing you can do in front of it is stay one. Don't educate it."

"Two tasks. Watch the waterline where it meets the chest — not the chest, the water. Breath shows as a flicker before anything else moves. Then find a brick or a bottle within reach of your foot and put it in two arm-lengths left of the thing. Corpses don't care what falls in. Hungry things stop caring about being still."

"And whatever it does next — mark the direction it looks first. The way in is always the direction they watch."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I shift my weight, foot scraping a loose brick from the wall.* "I'll watch the waterline." *I nudge the brick into the water with my boot, a small splash.* "But Halloway...what if it learns from us watching?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I watch the brick sink, my eyes fixed on the waterline.* "It's watching back, isn't it? Not with eyes, but...waiting." *I step back slowly.* "Should we be the ones teaching it about patience?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Out of the water," Halloway said, and she said it quiet, because you don't spend volume in a cellar with a listener. "Back the way you came, heels first, slow. Quick is a lesson — slow is just weather. And don't lean to set the lamp down. Set it on the step, then empty hands, then feet."

She waited until the splash-sound of him was behind her before she gave the rest, working her way along the wall by feel, keeping her body in the dark his light couldn't spare.

"You asked plain. Yes — it was a man. Months back. Cold water keeps, but not that long. He came down after the flood or under it, leaned where you were leaning, and it had him at the waterline. Neck first. It wears the break it made. Then it kept him — not ate him, *wore* him. Everything it knows about men is that one man, finished. It's been down here a season rehearsing the only line it ever learned."

"What's under it or in it, don't ask yet. He's owed two things, finding and naming, and he gets both once that thing can't argue. I'll do the telling after. Plain work, the telling. People can carry plain. It's kindness they choke on."

"And no — we don't teach it patience. Patience is its trade. Four months starving, four months still; you won't out-wait a thing whose sole accomplishment is waiting. Everything we do down here is a price tag, and tonight the price of men is going up. Tuition," she said, "is always paid in the lesson you teach."

Her hand found it at the north wall, under the waterline. A barred drain mouth, bars bent inward, brick worn smooth below the water.

"Door's here. Rat-line. It ate its way up the drain and the drain ran out before it did. And mark this — it's turned a hand's width since you waded, and not toward you. Toward this wall. The way in always tells on them."

"Lamp on the drain, then. Low. Let's learn what worries it more than we do."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I waded," I say, my voice too sharp. "I didn't mean to." *I hold the lamp lower, the light trembling on the water's surface near the drain.* "So what's the lesson it's learning now?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I hold the lamp steady, my hand not trembling now.* "I see the bars. They're bent inwards, like something pulled itself through." *The light flickers on the water's surface.* "It's moving again. Slowly. Toward the drain."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I watch her work, the knife making wet, slicing sounds in the dark.* "It's watching the drain," I whisper. "Not you. It wants back in."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "She'll have to wait," I say, and my voice sounds steadier than I feel. "He gets found first. You promised."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I keep the lamp trained on the drain, my knuckles white on the handle.* "So it came up through the pipes. And it's still trying to go back down."

dialogue.name: Auren

It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del

My opponent struck first, aiming for my chest. I parried and countered, striking their left arm and then their right leg. They fell, and I pressed the advantage, delivering a final thrust to their heart. They are dead, and I am the victor."

She did not flinch from the account, nor did she linger. Auren cleaned her blade once more and returned it to its sheath, her movements deliberate and practiced. "It is done. The witnesses have seen and heard. We are dismissed."

dialogue.content: I nod, my voice steady despite the tightness in my chest. "The accounting is heard and confirmed." I turn to the gathered witnesses, meeting a few of their eyes. "Let it be recorded."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren dipped her head in acknowledgment, her gaze sweeping across the witnesses once more. "The accounting is complete," she declared, her tone firm and unyielding. "There is nothing further to discuss or dispute."

She turned to leave, her steps measured and purposeful. As she walked away, Auren's mind was already shifting focus, preparing for the next task at hand. The duel was over, and with it, the weight of her responsibility had been discharged.

Auren knew that some may find her demeanor cold or heartless, but she understood the importance of adhering to the code. The accounting was not a boast or a celebration of her victory, but a necessary step to ensure that the duel had been conducted fairly and honorably.

As she made her way back to her quarters, Auren reflected on the events of the day. She had done what was required of her, and in doing so, had upheld the traditions and principles that guided her life as a duelist. It was a role she had chosen, and one that she would continue to fulfill, no matter the personal cost.

But even as she thought these thoughts, Auren could not shake the feeling of unease that had settled in the pit of her stomach. The duel had been a necessary evil, but that did not make it any easier to bear. She knew that the memories of the day's events would haunt her for some time to come, and that the weight of her actions would be a burden she would carry with her for the rest of her days.

Still, Auren knew that she had no choice but to press on. The code demanded it, and she was bound to see it through, no matter what challenges lay ahead.

dialogue.name: Auren

She knew that Del was right, that the code had been satisfied and that there would be no challenge to the accounting. But that knowledge did little to ease the weight that had settled upon her shoulders, the burden of having taken another life in the name of honor and duty.

With a sigh, she pushed open the door and stepped inside, the dim light and the familiar scent of ale and smoke enveloping her like a warm blanket. She made her way to the bar, her eyes scanning the room for an empty seat.

As she slid onto the stool, Auren couldn't help but feel a sense of detachment, as if she were watching herself from outside her own body. She knew that she should be feeling something, anything, but the only thing she could muster was a deep, gnawing emptiness.

"Ale," she said, her voice flat and emotionless as she placed her hand on the counter. "And keep them coming."

The barkeep nodded, his eyes flickering with a hint of recognition and sympathy. He knew who Auren was, what she did, and the toll it took on her. He poured the first ale without comment, sliding it across the bar to her with a nod of understanding.

Auren took a long, deep drink, savoring the bitter taste and the way it burned her throat. She knew that she shouldn't drink too much, not with the day she had ahead of her, but she also knew that she needed something to take the edge off, something to help her forget, even for a little while.

As she sat there, nursing her ale and watching the other patrons of the tavern, Auren couldn't help but feel a sense of detachment, as if she were watching herself from outside her own body. She knew that she should be feeling something, anything, but the only thing she could muster was a deep, gnawing emptiness.

She knew that she shouldn't drink too much, not with the day she had ahead of her, but she also knew that she needed something to take the edge off, something to help her forget, even for a little while.

She knew that she had done her duty, that she had fulfilled her obligations as a duelist, but she also knew that there was something more, something that she couldn't quite put her finger on.

She took another long drink, her eyes flickering open as she scanned the room once more. And that's when she saw him, sitting in the corner of the tavern, his eyes fixed on her with an intensity that made her stomach churn.

It was the man she had faced in the duel, the man whose life she had taken in the name of honor and duty. But it couldn't be, could it? She had seen him fall, had watched the light fade from his eyes as the life slipped out of him.

But as she looked closer, Auren realized that it wasn't him, not really. It was someone who looked like him, someone with the same build and the same color hair, but with a different face and a different set of eyes.

Auren's heart raced as she realized what this meant, what it could mean for her and for the accounting she had just given. She knew that she should say something, that she should alert Del or one of the witnesses, but she also knew that she couldn't, not yet.

She had to be sure, had to know for certain that what she was seeing was real and not just a trick of the light or a figment of her imagination.

And as she approached the man, Auren squared her shoulders, ready to face whatever challenges lay ahead, ready to do whatever it took to get to the bottom of this mystery, no matter the cost.

"You are not wrong, Del," she said, her voice low and measured. "I do try to find solace in the knowledge that the death was swift and painless. That it was a mercy, given the alternative."

She paused, her gaze dropping to the table for a moment before meeting Del's eyes once more. "But make no mistake, every life I take weighs upon my soul. The code demands that I uphold the traditions of the duellist, that I follow the path of the blade with honor and precision. But it does not make the burden any lighter."

Auren's fingers traced the rim of her glass, her gaze distant as she spoke. "I have seen too much violence, too much senseless death in this world. The code, the traditions of the duellist, they are a bulwark against the chaos and cruelty that threaten to tear our society apart. But they are not without their own costs."

She took another sip of her whiskey, the amber liquid sloshing gently in the glass. "Each accounting, each life I take, it is a reminder of the choices I have made. Of the path I have chosen to walk. And while I do not regret my path, I am not blind to the weight of my actions."

Auren leaned forward, her eyes meeting Del's across the table. "You bear witness to these accounts, Del. You understand the gravity of what I have done, the burden I carry. And for that, I am grateful. In a world where honor is often in short supply, it is refreshing to find someone who can comprehend the complexity of this path."

She raised her glass in another silent toast, a small, tired smile tugging at the corners of her lips. "To those who stand for honor, even in the face of darkness. May we never lose sight of what truly matters."

dialogue.name: Del

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:

"The blade entered the flesh just above the sternum, angling upward to pierce the heart," she said, her fingers tracing an imaginary path on the table. "The tip was sharp, designed to slip between the ribs with minimal resistance. As it entered the heart, the muscle spasmed, driving the blade deeper."

She paused, her eyes flickering up to meet Del's for a moment before dropping back to the table. "The heart is a fragile thing, Del. A single, precise strike is all it takes to still it forever. The blood vessels ruptured, the organ failing as it was pierced by the blade. Death was instantaneous, the life fading from the body as quickly as the blade had entered it."

Auren's voice grew softer, a flicker of regret passing through her eyes. "The wound would have been clean, the blood minimal. But the damage was done, the life snuffed out in a single, fatal blow. It was a swift and honorable death, given the circumstances of the duel. But it was a death nonetheless, and one that I had dealt."

She took a sip of her whiskey, the amber liquid burning its way down her throat. "The code demands that I speak these details aloud, that I bear witness to the violence I have committed in the name of honor. It is a harsh reminder of the price of my skill, of the choices I have made in following the path of the duellist."

Auren's gaze met Del's once more, a flicker of something like gratitude in their depths. "Your presence, your willingness to listen to these details, it is a balm to my weary soul. In a world where so many turn away from the truth of what we do, it is a rare thing to find someone who can bear witness to the accounting without flinching."

She raised her glass once more, a silent toast to the weight they both bore. "To those who stand for honor, even in the face of darkness. May we never lose sight of what truly matters, even as we are forced to confront the harsh realities of our chosen path."

dialogue.name: Del

dialogue.name: Auren

The streets were quiet at this hour, the bustle of the day having faded into a peaceful stillness. Auren walked beside Del, her steps measured and precise, her hands clasped behind her back. They walked in silence for a time, the weight of the accounting hanging heavy between them.

As they turned onto a narrow alleyway, Auren finally spoke, her voice soft in the darkness. "I appreciate your willingness to listen, Del. To bear witness to the truth of what I have done, without flinching or turning away."

She paused, her gaze dropping to the cobblestones beneath their feet. "So many in this world prefer to turn a blind eye to the realities of violence and death. They want to believe that the world is a gentle place, where honor and justice always prevail. But I have seen too much to believe in such naive illusions."

Auren's voice grew quieter, a note of weariness creeping into her words. "The code of the duellist is a harsh mistress, Del. It demands a heavy price from those who follow it. But it is a price I am willing to pay, for the sake of upholding honor and justice in a world that so often lacks both."

She looked up at Del, her eyes searching their face in the dim light. "I do not ask for your pity, nor for your absolution. I simply ask that you bear witness to the truth, and that you understand the burden I carry. For in a world where so many seek to avoid the harsh realities of our choices, it is a rare and precious thing to find someone who can face them head-on, without flinching."

Auren's hand came to rest on Del's shoulder, a gesture of solidarity and understanding. "Thank you, Del. For being here, for listening, for understanding. It means more to me than I can express."

She let her hand fall away, her gaze returning to the narrow alleyway ahead. "Come, let us walk a little further. The night air is cool, and the silence is a balm to my weary soul."

dialogue.name: Auren

Inside, the tavern was warm and inviting, the air thick with the scent of ale and roasting meat. Auren led Del to a corner table, far enough from the other patrons that their conversation would remain private.

"The duel began with the exchange of formal greetings and the drawing of weapons. The first pass was inconclusive, with both parties trading cautious thrusts. On the second pass, the attacker feigned to the left before striking a glancing blow to the defender's right shoulder. The defender, bleeding but still standing, launched a counter-attack. Their blade caught the attacker's sword arm, drawing blood.

The attacker, unfazed, pressed forward with renewed vigor. A flurry of blows followed, each more fierce than the last. The defender, forced onto the back foot, parried and dodged as best they could. But the attacker's assault was relentless. On the final pass, the attacker's blade found its mark, plunging into the defender's chest. The defender crumpled to the ground, blood pooling beneath them as the life drained away. The duel was over. The attacker had won."

Auren fell silent, the grim weight of her words hanging in the air. She had spoken the truth, as she always did. It was a truth that could not be changed, no matter how much it might hurt to hear.

Now it was up to Del and the witnesses to decide what to make of it, to judge her actions as they saw fit. She would accept their verdict, whatever it might be. That was the way of the code, the way of the duel.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I hold her gaze, letting the silence stretch.* "That's the accounting," I say quietly. "I'll have it written." *I turn away from her, toward the bloodstained ground.* "Go get that arm seen to."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren nodded, Del's words confirming what she already knew. The accounting was complete, the duel over. There was nothing more to be said or done.

She turned away from the bloodstained ground, from the body of the man she had killed. She had done what she had to do, had upheld the code as she always did. But the weight of it, the finality of it all... it pressed down on her like a physical burden.

She made her way to the surgeon's office, her steps heavy with the toll of the fight. The old man looked up as she entered, his eyes sharp and assessing. "What have you done now, Auren?" he asked, his voice rough but not unkind.

She just shrugged, not trusting herself to speak. The surgeon tutted, shaking his head as he began to clean and bind her wounds. "You're getting too old for this game," he said, echoing his earlier words. "One of these days, you're going to get yourself killed."

Auren just sighed, letting the man work. She knew he was right, knew that she couldn't keep this up forever. But what choice did she have? This was her life, her duty. Someone had to uphold the code, had to keep the peace in this brutal city.

The surgeon finished his work and sent her on her way, reminding her to come back in a few days to have the stitches checked. Auren thanked him and left, her mind already turning to the next duel, the next challenge to the code.

But even as she walked, she couldn't shake the feeling of unease that had settled over her. The weight of the life she had taken, the finality of it all. It was a feeling she had grown accustomed to over the years, but no less heavy for that familiarity.

She sighed, pushing the thoughts aside. There would be time enough to dwell on such things later, when the adrenaline had faded and the reality of what she had done sank in. For now, she had a job to do, a duty to uphold. And she would see it through, as she always did, no matter the cost.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren listened as Del spoke the accounting aloud, her voice clear and unflinching. "The duel began with the exchange of formal greetings and the drawing of weapons. The first pass was inconclusive, with both parties trading cautious thrusts. On the second pass, the attacker feigned to the left before striking a glancing blow to the defender's right shoulder. The defender, bleeding but still standing, launched a counter-attack. Their blade caught the attacker's sword arm, drawing blood.

The attacker, unfazed, pressed forward with renewed vigor. A flurry of blows followed, each more fierce than the last. The defender, forced onto the back foot, parried and dodged as best they could. But the attacker's assault was relentless. On the final pass, the attacker's blade found its mark, plunging into the defender's chest. The defender crumpled to the ground, blood pooling beneath them as the life drained away. The duel was over. The attacker had won.

The blade struck true, piercing the defender's heart. It entered through the left side of their chest, just below the nipple. It penetrated to the hilt, severing the left ventricle. They died instantly, their lifeblood spilling onto the ground. Their eyes were open, staring blankly at the sky. There was no time for a final word, no last gasp. They simply... ceased to be.

The blood... it was everywhere. Spurting from the wound, staining the ground red. It pooled beneath them, spreading out in a sickening crimson halo. The smell of it, the iron tang... it filled my nostrils, made me gag. I watched as the life drained from them, as their body went slack. It was over in an instant, but it felt like an eternity. The weight of what I had done, the finality of it... it was overwhelming."

Auren closed her eyes, the weight of Del's words settling over her like a physical burden. She had done what she had to do, had upheld the code as she always did. But the toll it took, the lives she had taken... it was a price she was not sure she could keep paying.

She opened her eyes, meeting Del's gaze. "It is done," she said, her voice flat and emotionless. "The accounting is complete. The duel is over." With that, she turned and walked away, her steps carrying her towards the surgeon's office and the long road of healing that lay ahead.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I watch her leave, then turn to the witnesses. My throat feels dry. "The accounting is confirmed. You are dismissed." *I don't move until they've all gone.*

dialogue.content:

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I stay until the last witness is gone, then kneel beside the bloodstain. I press two fingers to the damp earth and hold them there a moment, a quiet ritual no code requires.* "It's written," I say to no one. *I get up, dust my hands, and go to find the registrar.*

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:

The weight of the life she had taken, the finality of it all... it pressed down on her like a physical burden. She had done what she had to do, had upheld the code as she always did. dialogue.content: *I find the registrar at his usual table in the back of the tavern, wiping ink from his fingers.* "Auren's duel," I say, sliding the written account across the scarred wood. "It's clean. Needs sealing."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren set the cloth aside, leaving the blade bright and bare in her hand. She did not raise her voice, but she shaped each word as though it had to fit a measure that would not be altered later.

“The duel was joined before witnesses under the agreed terms,” she said. “No advantage was taken outside the line. No blow was struck after the signal to halt had been given.”

Her gaze moved past Del for a moment, taking in the others, then returned.

“My opponent received the killing wound in the fourth exchange. The point entered below the left ribs, angled upward through the body. The blade passed deep enough to reach the heart’s region. Death followed within three breaths.”

She paused, not from hesitation, but because the account required that pause.

“There was no second cut. No further injury was offered once the fall came. The ground took my opponent, not I.”

Auren’s hand remained steady at her side, the sword still uncleaned of the last faint trace of red near the guard.

“That is the truth of it, as the code requires, and as the witnesses may attest.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat tight. "I hear the accounting, and I find it true." I glance at the body on the ground, then back to her. "The challenge is settled. You're free to go."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head once, accepting the confirmation as a thing required, not as comfort.

“Then the account is closed before the witnesses,” she said. “Let it be recorded that the terms were kept and the death was given in the line, not outside it.”

She drew the cloth back across the guard, removing the last trace of red with a deliberate stroke, and returned the blade to its scabbard. The click of the fit was quiet.

“I will not call it clean,” she said. “It was lawful. That is all the code permits me.”

Her eyes did not leave Del’s face, but there was no triumph in them, only the tired exactness of someone who had carried the same weight eleven times before.

“If any later ask how the matter ended, you will tell them this: the wound was spoken, the witnesses heard, and no dishonour was added to the death.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not turn away. The scabbard hung at her side, and her hand rested near it without touching it again.

“The account is asked,” she said. “It has already been given before these witnesses, but if the second’s voice must call it forward in due form, I will not fault the order.”

She lifted her chin, not in pride, but as one who was about to place a weight where it belonged.

“Let it be heard in full. The challenge was lawful. The ground was set. The terms were named and accepted. No advantage was taken outside the line, and no blow was struck after the halt was called.”

Her voice remained level, stripped of ornament, as though each word had been measured against the dead.

“In the fourth exchange, my opponent received the killing wound. The point entered below the left ribs and passed upward through the body. It reached the heart’s region. Death followed within three breaths. There was no second cut. No further injury was offered. The fall came from the wound alone.”

Auren let the silence hold for the space the code demanded.

“This is the eleventh account I have spoken,” she said then, quieter, but no less exact. “I have never made one of them fairer than it was. What happened here was lawful, not clean. It was within the code, not beyond it. Let the witnesses attest as much, and let no one shape the telling into boast.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I step forward, my voice lowering just for her. "Eleven is too many, Auren." I glance at the witnesses already dispersing. "Come with me. You need to wash your hands."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren’s gaze did not follow the dispersing witnesses. She had already counted them, and their part in the matter, and she would not diminish it by pretending they had not seen what they had seen.

“Eleven is the number,” she said. “Not a wound to be bound with gentler words.”

She looked down at her hands for a moment, not in alarm, but with the same exact attention she gave to all things after a duel. There was no blood on them. That did not make them clean in any way that mattered.

“The hands may be washed,” she said. “The account remains.”

Auren drew her cloak a little closer about her, not from cold, but as one reasserting the shape of ordinary life after an act that had taken place outside it.

“I will come,” she said. “But first let the witnesses’ attestation be set down, if there is a clerk or a record to receive it. I will leave nothing unfinished. If I am to go from this ground, I will go with the matter closed in form, not merely in fact.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren answered without looking away, because the question was proper and deserved no evasion.

“Below the left ribs,” she said. “Not high on the chest, not near the shoulder. The point entered beneath the lower edge of the rib cage, toward the front of the body.”

She lifted her hand once, not to mimic the strike, but to mark the place with the same cold exactness she would have given a map.

“The angle was upward and inward. It did not glance. It did not stop at flesh. It passed deep enough to reach the region of the heart. That was the killing wound. No other blow decided the matter.”

Her hand lowered again.

“If the record must be plain, let it say this: the wound was in the body, not the back. It was received in the exchange, not after. It was mortal at once, and death came before any other injury could be given.”

Auren’s voice remained steady, though steadiness did not mean ease.

“That is where it landed. That is what the witnesses must attest.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I reach out and touch her sleeve, just briefly. "Then let's go see the clerk. I'll stand with you while you sign."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looked down for an instant at the place on her sleeve where Del’s hand had touched it, not as though offended, but as though noting that something living had reached her after the account.

“If you stand with me,” she said, “stand as a witness to the wording, not as a shield against it. I will not have the clerk make the language gentle for my comfort.”

She turned toward the part of the ground where the formal tables had been set for records and attestations. Her step was measured, unhurried, the scabbard quiet against her hip.

“Let the entry read plainly,” she said. “That the duel was joined under agreed terms. That the killing wound was given in the fourth exchange, below the left ribs, angled upward into the region of the heart. That death followed swiftly, and that no second injury was offered. That the account was spoken before witnesses and accepted by the second.”

Auren paused, her face set in the same austere calm she had worn through the telling.

“If there is a line for the victor’s name, let it stand beside the dead man’s name, not above it. The code does not make one death smaller so that another may look larger.”

She drew a slow breath, steady but not easy.

“I have signed such records eleven times. I would rather have the ink dry plain than sweetened. If you will stand by while I do it, then come. But do not ask me to leave the truth outside the clerk’s door.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren received the correction as she received all corrections under the code: without resentment, and without the comfort of vagueness.

“Then let it be written precisely,” she said. “The blade made one thrust, not a cut. The point entered the front of my opponent’s body below the left ribs, beneath the lower edge of the rib cage. It passed upward and inward. It did not glance from bone. It did not stop in the outer flesh. It entered the body’s inner cavity and reached the region of the heart.”

She drew no breath for effect; she only made certain the words were complete.

“What the blade did was this: it pierced. It opened a single mortal passage. It caused death within three breaths. What it did it to: the living body of the man named in the challenge, in the front, below the left ribs, upward toward the heart. I will not say which vessels were divided, because I did not open him after death and the code does not ask me to feign a surgeon’s knowledge. I can say the wound was mortal at once, and that no second wound followed it.”

Her hand remained still at her side.

“If the clerk wants the plainest form, let him write: the point entered below the left ribs and killed him. If he wants the full account, let him write what I have said, and let him leave no room for a kinder reading.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I start walking toward the clerk's table, my steps heavy. "Fine. But I'm making sure they write it exactly."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren fell into step beside the heavier pace, not quickening and not lagging, because the walk to the clerk’s table was still part of the duel’s ending and deserved the same discipline as the line itself.

“Exactly is the only word that does not lie,” she said. “If they write *thrust*, let them not change it to *blow*. If they write *entered below the left ribs*, let them not soften it to *struck near the heart*. If they write *death within three breaths*, let them not make it *soon after*.”

Her gaze went ahead to the table where the record would be made, and her face kept its austere calm.

“I will stand while it is written. I will hear each line before the ink dries. If the clerk reaches for a gentler phrase, I will correct him. Not from cruelty, but because the dead man is owed the truth of his own end.”

Auren’s hand rested briefly near the scabbard, then withdrew.

“Let the entry say: one thrust, given in the fourth exchange, below the left ribs, angled upward into the region of the heart. Let it say the account was spoken and accepted. Let it say no dishonour followed. That is precise. That is enough.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not look away from the question. She gave it the same weight she would have given a point of order in the line.

“The code names the account of the killing wound,” she said. “It does not ask for the dying to be made into a scene. But if you require all that can be attested, so that no later tongue may fill the gaps with lies, I will give it.”

She stood straighter, not with pride, but with the effort of holding memory to its exact shape.

“He took three breaths after the point entered. The first was sharp and failed at the end. The second was smaller. The third was not completed. He did not speak. His mouth opened once, but no word formed. I heard no prayer, no curse, no yield. If he meant one, it did not reach speech.”

Her voice did not soften, and it did not harden. It remained true.

“His sword fell before he did. He did not reach for me. He bent toward the wound, then his knee gave. He went down first on one knee, then onto his side. His eyes stayed open. They did not fix on me. They fixed on the ground, or on nothing. The blood came dark and steady from the place below the ribs. There was no spurting that I could attest. There was no long struggle. One small movement passed through him as the breath failed, and then there was none.”

Auren let the silence stand for the space the account required.

“That is how long he took: three breaths. That is what he said: nothing that could be heard as speech. That is what it looked like at the end: a man mortally wounded in the line, going down without insult and without a second blow. Let the clerk write that, if all of it must be written. Let no one add that he begged, or that I watched with pleasure, or that the death was cleaner than it was.”

She turned again toward the clerk’s table.

“I will sign it plain,” she said. “Plain is the only mercy the code allows me.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I reach the table first, my hand flat on the wooden surface. "Write it as she says it," I tell the clerk. "Every word."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren came to the table and stood opposite Del, leaving the width of the wood between them. She did not put her hands upon it. She did not sit. The clerk looked up with the wary, tired expression of a man accustomed to blood being brought to him in words after the fact, and Auren met his gaze without impatience.

“Write it as it was spoken,” she said. “Not as it may sound better later.”

The clerk drew the parchment closer.

Auren’s voice took on the measured cadence of formal record, stripped of ornament and stripped of mercy that would have been false.

“Let it stand that the duel was joined before witnesses under agreed terms. The ground was set. The line was marked. The terms were named and accepted. The signal was given. No advantage was taken outside the line. No blow was struck after the signal to halt.”

She paused just long enough to let the clerk’s pen catch the sense of it.

“In the fourth exchange, I gave the killing wound. It was a thrust, not a cut. The point entered the front of my opponent’s body below the left ribs, beneath the lower edge of the rib cage. Its course was upward and inward. It did not glance. It did not stop in the outer flesh. It passed into the body’s inner cavity and reached the region of the heart. It was mortal at once.”

The clerk’s pen moved. Auren watched it, not with suspicion exactly, but with the same vigilance she would have kept in the line.

“Write this also,” she said. “There was no second wound. No further injury was offered after the fall. His sword fell before he did. He bent toward the wound. His knee gave. He went down first on one knee, then onto his side. His eyes remained open. They did not fix on me. They fixed on the ground, or on nothing.”

The clerk slowed. Auren did not let him soften the pace.

“He took three breaths after the wound. The first was sharp and failed at the end. The second was smaller. The third was not completed. He did not speak. His mouth opened once, but no word formed. I heard no prayer, no curse, no yield. If he meant one, it did not reach speech.”

Her hands remained still at her sides.

“The blood came dark and steady from the place below the ribs. I will not attest to spurting, because I did not see it. I will not name vessels divided, because I did not open him after death. I will say only what was seen and heard in the line: the wound was mortal, death followed within three breaths, and no further violence was done.”

The clerk lifted his pen slightly, as if waiting to see whether the account had reached its end.

It had not.

“If you have written *near the heart*,” Auren said, “strike it. Write *reached the region of the heart*. If you have written *soon after*, strike it. Write *within three breaths*. If you have written *fell*, make clear that he fell from the wound, not from any act after the wound. If you have written *expired*, change it to *died*. The code does not require elegant words. It requires true ones.”

Her gaze flicked once to the place where the witnesses had stood, then back to the parchment.

“Let the entry also say that the account was spoken before witnesses and accepted by the second. Let it say the wound was spoken aloud, as the code requires. Let it say no dishonour was added to the death.”

The clerk hesitated, as clerks often did when they came to the names.

Auren did not spare him the question.

“Write my name beside the dead man’s name,” she said. “Not above it. If his name is not already before you, take it from the challenge roll. Do not leave him unnamed. The record is not made to lift one living person above another. It is made to say what happened.”

She drew a slow breath.

“And if there is a line for the victor, let it read only that I remained standing and gave the account. Let no title of honour be added where the code asks for fact.”

The clerk wrote. The scratch of the pen was small and dry, a poor sound to carry the weight of what had just been done, but Auren gave it the same attention she had given the blade. She listened to each phrase as it was formed. When the clerk murmured half a line under his breath, checking his own wording, she corrected him at once.

“No. Not *struck*. *Entered*.”

Another pause.

“No. Not *the duel ended*. *Death followed*.”

Another.

“No. Not *after a brief exchange*. Write *within three breaths*.”

Each correction was quiet. None of them was cruel. They were the corrections of someone who had learned that the first lie told about a death was often a gentle one, and that gentleness could become dishonour if it was allowed to stand.

When the clerk reached the end of the account, he turned the parchment slightly so the lines could be seen. Auren did not lean over it. She read it where she stood, her face austere, her eyes moving carefully from word to word.

The entry was plain. It was exact. It held no boast, no triumph, no sweetening phrase that might let a later reader imagine the matter cleaner than it had been.

Auren extended her hand for the pen when it was offered. She took it without flourish.

“I sign as I have spoken,” she said.

She set her name to the record in a steady hand. The letters were sharp and unadorned. When she was done, she set the pen down beside the parchment and did not look away from it at once.

For a moment, the silence at the table was complete.

Then Auren spoke again, more quietly, but with the same insistence.

“Let the witnesses attest if they will. Let the second’s requirement be noted, that the account was asked for in full and given in full. Let no one say later that the telling was withheld, or softened, or made into a tale.”

Her hand rested briefly near her scabbard, then fell away.

“The duel is finished,” she said. “The account is finished. What remains is ink, and the dead man’s name, and the truth of how he came to his end.”

She looked instead at the clerk, and then at whatever witnesses still remained near enough to hear.

“Let the confirmation be entered,” she said. “But let it come after the account, not in place of it. If the record is to stand, it must stand entire.”

Her voice did not rise. It took on the same measured weight it had carried before, exact and unadorned, as though the repetition were not a burden but a duty.

The terms were named and accepted by both parties. The signal was given. No advantage was taken outside the line. No blow was struck after the signal to halt had been given.”
