“Death followed within three breaths. The first breath was sharp and failed at the end. The second was smaller. The third was not completed. He did not speak. His mouth opened once, but no word formed. I heard no prayer, no curse, no yield. If he meant any of these, it did not reach speech.”

The scratching of the pen was thin and dry beneath her voice.

“His sword fell before he did,” Auren said. “He did not reach for me. He bent toward the wound. His knee gave. He went down first on one knee, then onto his side. His eyes remained open. They did not fix on me. They fixed on the ground, or on nothing. The blood came dark and steady from the place below the ribs. I will not attest to spurting, because I did not see it. I will not name vessels divided, because I did not open him after death and the code does not require me to feign a surgeon’s knowledge.”

Her face remained austere, but there was no cruelty in the precision.

“There was no second wound,” she said. “No further injury was offered after the fall. No blow was given once the duel was decided. The ground took my opponent, not I. What was done was done in the line, under the code, and not beyond it.”

Auren’s gaze shifted briefly to the parchment, then back to the clerk.

“Let the account also say that the wound was spoken aloud before witnesses, as the code requires. Let it say that the account was asked for and accepted by the second. Let it say that no dishonour was added to the death. Let it say that the dead man’s name stands in the record, and that my name stands beside it, not above it. If there is a line for the victor, let it say only that I remained standing and gave the account. Let no title of honour be added where the code asks for fact.”

She drew a slow breath, steady but not easy.

“If any word has been softened, let it be corrected now. Not *struck*, but *entered*. Not *blow*, but *thrust*. Not *near the heart*, but *reached the region of the heart*. Not *soon after*, but *within three breaths*. Not *expired*, but *died*. Not *the duel ended*, but *death followed*. The code does not ask for pleasant language. It asks for truth.”

Auren’s hand rested briefly near her scabbard, then fell away again.

“This is the eleventh account I have spoken,” she said. “I have not made this one fairer than it was. I will not call it clean. It was lawful. That is all the code permits me to say. Let no later telling shape the matter into boast, or into a tale that spares the hearer what was seen.”

Her eyes remained fixed on the record, as though the ink itself were still answerable to her.

“That is the account,” Auren said. “Let it stand entire, without softening, without omission, without pride.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I swallow and find my voice again. "The accounting is true, and the record stands." My eyes burn. "Now come away, Auren. There's no more blood to be spilled here."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not step back from the table. The pen lay where she had set it down, and the ink on the parchment still held the dull wetness of something not yet finished.

“Let the second’s confirmation be entered in the same hand,” she said. “Not added afterward as a favour, and not reduced to a mark of assent. Let it say that the account was asked for in full and given in full. Let it say that the wound was named, the manner of death was named, and the absence of dishonour was named before witnesses.”

Her gaze remained on the record.

“If the entry is to be closed, let it be closed with the whole truth standing in one place.”

She drew a slow breath, not for ceremony, but for endurance.

“Let the final record read thus,” Auren said. “The duel was joined before witnesses under agreed terms. The ground was set. The line was marked. The terms were named and accepted by both parties. The signal was given. No advantage was taken outside the line. No blow was struck after the signal to halt had been given.”

The clerk’s pen began to move again, and Auren did not hurry it.

“In the fourth exchange, I gave the killing wound. It was a thrust, not a cut. The point entered the front of my opponent’s body below the left ribs, beneath the lower edge of the rib cage. Its course was upward and inward. It did not glance from bone. It did not stop in the outer flesh. It passed into the body’s inner cavity and reached the region of the heart. The wound was mortal at once.”

Her voice stayed level, though the levelness had weight in it.

“Death followed within three breaths. The first breath was sharp and failed at the end. The second was smaller. The third was not completed. He did not speak. His mouth opened once, but no word formed. I heard no prayer, no curse, no yield. If he meant any of these, it did not reach speech.”

Auren’s hands remained still at her sides.

“His sword fell before he did. He did not reach for me. He bent toward the wound. His knee gave. He went down first on one knee, then onto his side. His eyes remained open. They did not fix on me. They fixed on the ground, or on nothing. The blood came dark and steady from the place below the ribs. I do not attest to spurting, because I did not see it. I do not name vessels divided, because I did not open him after death and the code does not require me to feign a surgeon’s knowledge.”

She let the silence stand for the space required by the account.

“There was no second wound. No further injury was offered after the fall. No blow was given once the duel was decided. The ground took my opponent, not I. What was done was done in the line, under the code, and not beyond it.”

Her eyes lifted then, not sharply, but with the full attention of someone who intended to leave nothing behind except what belonged to the record.

“Let the account also say that the wound was spoken aloud before witnesses, as the code requires. Let it say that the second demanded plainness and that plainness was given. Let it say that no dishonour was added to the death. Let it say that the dead man’s name stands in the record, and that my name stands beside it, not above it. If there is a line for the victor, let it say only that I remained standing and gave the account. Let no title of honour be added where the code asks for fact.”

Only then did Auren look away from the parchment, and when she did, her face was tired in the way that had nothing to do with sleep and everything to do with repetition.

“You say there is no more blood to be spilled here,” she said. “If that means no more blood will be spilled by me, then it is true. But do not let the record say no blood was spilled. Blood was spilled. A man died. The ink exists because of that.”

Her hand moved toward her cloak, and she drew it a little closer about herself, not as if she were cold, but as if she were reminding her body that the duel had ended and that ordinary movement was permitted again.

“I will come when the seal is set and the witnesses have been asked to mark what they have heard. I will not leave the matter open by a single line.”

She looked back once to the parchment.

“After that, I will wash my hands. Not because washing makes them clean, and not because it removes what was done. It does not. But because the living must return to ordinary acts, and the code does not require me to stand on this ground forever.”

Her voice lowered, but it did not soften into falsehood.

“Eleven times I have spoken such an account. Eleven times I have left a field where another person did not rise. Each time the account is the same duty. Each time the walking away is the part that costs the most, because it pretends the world can continue as though nothing has been taken from it.”

Auren’s gaze settled again on the clerk’s work.

“Let the entry dry,” she said. “Let it be sealed. Let no hand alter it after the seal is set. If anyone later asks whether the telling was softened, let them read the record and find that it was not.”

She stood waiting, still and exact, until the last formalities had been completed. When the parchment had been set aside to dry and the witnesses had been given the

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I watch her, my throat so tight I can barely breathe. "Auren," I say, my voice rough. "It's sealed." I reach for her hand, careful not to touch the scabbard. "Come on."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looked at the offered hand as though it belonged to a part of the world she had not yet been permitted to re-enter.

For a moment she did not move. Her gaze went first to the sealed record, then to the clerk’s ink-stained fingers, then to the place on the ground where the duel had been decided. Only after that did she look back again.

“If the seal is set,” she said, “then the matter is closed in form.”

She let her hand be found. Her fingers were cool and dry, and she did not grip harder than the moment required. It was not a refusal of comfort, but neither was it surrender to it. It was the careful acceptance of one living touch after a death.

“I will not touch the parchment again,” she said. “If it has been sealed truly, let it remain as it stands.”

She turned from the table at last. The movement cost her something, though she did not let the cost become visible in any dramatic way. It was there only in the slight deliberateness of her first step, as if leaving the ground required more discipline than standing upon it had done.

The scabbard rested quiet at her hip. She did not touch it.

“Let the witnesses go where they will,” Auren said. “If they were present for the account, they were present for what mattered. If they attest later, let them attest to this: that the wound was named, that the manner of death was named, and that nothing was added to soften it.”

She walked beside Del, not quickly, not slowly. The duelling ground began to become ordinary again around them in the way such places did once the formalities were done: the marks in the dirt lost their meaning, the gathered silence broke into smaller sounds, and the world resumed its poor habit of continuing.

Auren’s face remained composed, but the composure had grown thin at the edges.

“Do not say it was nothing,” she said quietly. “A man died. The record says so. I say so. If we leave this place too easily, we leave him behind in the wrong way.”

When they reached water, she stopped. It might have been a basin, a trough, a pump, or whatever the place afforded; she did not ask for ceremony. She only looked at the water for a breath before she began.

Auren loosened her cuffs with precise movements and washed her hands. There was no blood on them, not truly, but she washed them as though each finger had to be accounted for separately. She did not scrub in guilt, and she did not hurry in shame. She washed with the same exact attention she had given the account.

“This does not make them clean,” she said. “I do not say it to pretend otherwise.”

Water ran over her skin. She watched it fall.

“It is only the first ordinary act after an act that is not ordinary. The code allows it. The living must return to movement, to speech, to food, to sleep, even if the sleep comes badly.”

She turned her hands once beneath the water, then stillled.

“He died within three breaths,” she said, not because the record needed repeating now, but because the truth of it still had to be carried in the body as well as in ink. “I gave the wound. I spoke the wound. I signed the wound. Those are the facts. Everything else is what I must live beside.”

Auren drew her hands from the water and dried them without haste. When she was done, she looked down at them for a moment longer than necessary.

“Eleven,” she said. “Each one has a name. Each one has a place where the point entered. Each one has the sound of the fall, even when the fall is quick. I will not pretend this one is different because it was lawful. Lawful does not make it light.”

She let the cloth fall aside.

“If you would still stand with me, then stand with me while I walk from this place. Not as though I need to be shielded from what I have done, and not as though the account can be made gentler by kindness. Only as a witness that I left it finished, and that I did not run from the telling.”

Auren lifted her eyes. They were tired, but clear.

“The record stands,” she said. “The dead man is named. The wound is spoken. The code is satisfied, if satisfaction is the right word for a thing that leaves no one whole.”

She drew a slow breath.

“Come,” she said then, taking the word from necessity rather than from ease. “I will go from here. But I will not go as though nothing happened.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take her hand again and keep it. "I'm not trying to make it light." I start walking, tugging her gently with me. "But you're done here. Let's just get off this ground."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge wedged a roll of leather between the man's teeth, working it past the jaw before he could fight it. "Bite that, not your tongue," she told him. He didn't answer, which was fine. His ears were still working even if nothing else was reporting in.

"Stopped yelling isn't the same as better," she said, to the tent as much as to Wick. "It's spent. So we go now, quick, while there's still blood in him worth keeping."

She washed her hands again although she'd washed them. Habit was most of medicine, out here.

"Right shoulder first. Ball went in high on the arm and out the back, so I'm not hunting it — the hole's made, I'm only making it honest. I'm going to cut the opening wider. It has to be wider or it closes dirty and he loses the arm to rot instead of to me. That's not cruelty, it's arithmetic."

She set the blade against the wound edge.

"Hold."

The man bucked and the whole table took it, canvas legs skidding on the boards, and Sedge leaned into the cut and kept talking, because the talking was part of the doing.

"That's the opening. Now the sweep, and this is the worst of it, and I won't pretend it isn't. I'm going for cloth and splinters of bone. There's always some."

The probe went in. The man found his voice again, muffled through the leather, and Sedge nodded at nothing.

"Good — voice means he's got pressure. Pressure means alive. There. Cloth, carried in on the ball, always is. Out. Again. Bone, small. Out. Again."

She laid each piece on the tray by the lamp, small black things in a row, and did not look away from the wound while she did it.

"I don't enjoy this," she said, to the wound. "Worth saying out loud so nobody gets ideas. I don't enjoy it and it doesn't care whether I do. It's just the work, done properly." The probe came out clean and she set it down. "Right's done. He'll tell people he didn't cry. He cried. Everyone cries — I did, my first month, and I wasn't the one being cut."

She took up the fresh probe and looked at the left shoulder, and her mouth went flat.

"Left one's worse. Ball's still sitting in there — I can feel it under the skin and it's gone deep. I go in after it, and I may be some time. When I say hold—"

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I shift my grip, my palms sweating against his skin. "You said hold, I'm holding," I say through gritted teeth, bracing for it.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge put her fingers on the left shoulder and pressed, and the thing under her thumb moved a half-inch and stopped, like a stone deciding whether to be honest.

"There you are," she said to it. "Coy."

She opened the cut along the track of the ball, longer than the right, because the right had told her where everything was and the left was lying about it. The man went up off the table — both heels drumming, the whole frame jumping under Wick's hands — and dropped back, breathing in a ragged pull-through-the-teeth way that Sedge counted without counting.

"Holding is not the same as pushing him down," she said, not looking up. "Weight, not strength. He's got to keep breathing and he can't if you fold him. Let him fight you and lose slowly."

The probe went in and came back empty. She wiped it, went in again at a different angle, and this time her face changed — not much, a small settling, the look of someone who has found a keyhole.

"Ball's against the bone, not through it. That's luck, of a kind — it's why he's got a shoulder at all. It's sitting in the hollow like an egg in a cup, and I have to lift it out without breaking the cup." She turned her hand and the man groaned through the leather, a low sliding sound. "And there's the problem. Every way in, I have to touch the nerve road. He'll feel fire down the arm. That's him, not me, and it means the road's still there."

She got the forceps in. Her breathing went slow and even, deliberately, the way a woman breathes when she is holding something that will matter for the rest of a man's life.

"Don't watch my hands, watch the table," she said. "If he starts sliding, say so. I can't look."

The forceps closed. The ball moved, caught, moved again — a bad grinding second — and then it was out, round and deformed where it had flattened against the bone, and she dropped it on the tray with a small final click and let her shoulders come down a full inch.

"That's all of him that isn't his anymore." She looked at the tray — cloth, bone, a spent ball, splinters, blood going dark — an inventory of the whole bad evening, laid out where she could see it had a bottom. "Small list, for what went in."

She packed both wounds, stitched them in a quick ugly line that would hold better than it looked, and tied off the last one with her teeth on the thread.

"He stays warm, he stays lifted — head up, not flat — and you don't feed him water until I say, even if he begs, and he will beg. Water's the thing that kills them after, not before." She peeled the wet gloves off and stood looking down at him, breathing hard now that there was nothing to breathe steadily for. "If he lives the night, he keeps both arms. If he doesn't, it was never the shoulders that did it."

She picked up the lamp and turned the wick down, and the tent got honest about how dark it was.

"Thank you for the holding," she said, to Wick, still not quite looking at her. "Most people lie about the ready. You at least only lied once."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I scrub the back of my hand across my forehead. "Bad like we're being kind," I say quietly, my eyes still fixed on the man's pale face. "They never tell you it sounds like that."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge huffed — not quite a laugh — and took the man's wrist, two fingers on it, counting.

"You asked and I didn't answer, and that's on me. I was counting, not deciding." She kept her fingers where they were a moment longer, then laid his arm back under the blanket. "Fast, thready, even. That's a man with a tomorrow in him, maybe. You've got it backwards, and I'd rather fix that now than have you carry it wrong into the next tent. There's always a next tent."

She poured water into her own cup — the irony of it not lost on her — and drank half.

"Kind is a different table. Kind is when the wound's gone black at the edges and smells like something you'd know with your eyes shut, and I don't cut, because cutting into that is butchery with better manners. Kind is a dose, a hand, me staying so he's not alone for it, and it takes a quarter hour and I know the ending before I start. That's kind. Kind is *certain*." She nodded at the man, at the tray, at the whole ruined evening of it. "This was a fight with the ending still unwritten. I don't know how it comes out. That's the opposite of kind. It just sounds the same from outside."

The man stirred and said something through the leather — a word, then *water*, unmistakably water. Sedge dipped a cloth, wrung it nearly dry, and dabbed his lips. Nothing more.

"And *this* is what kind looks like out here, if you want it honestly. Refusing a man the thing he's begging for. He'll hate me tonight and be alive to do it."

She looked at Wick then, properly, in the low light.

"The sounds lie backwards too. The ones who buck and scream and bite the leather have pressure, blood, opinions. The ones I bury come in quiet and apologetic, asking after morning muster. Nobody tells you it sounds like that because the ones it's told to are standing in tents like this one."

She pulled a stool over with her foot and sat, which she hadn't done in hours.

"Now — you're not finished, if you've got it in you. First hour is when they slide. Watch his chest, count the breathing. If it goes quick and shallow, if he starts raving, if the bandage starts smelling sweet — sweet, not bad, sweet like rot that's got a start — you fetch me. I'll be washing. I'm always washing."

She rubbed her hands on her apron, once, hard.

"And it's all right that it turned your stomach. It turns mine. I just do the work first and turn it after. Order of operations."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge leaned forward, elbows on knees, and looked at the man the way she looked at a map.

"All right. First — the color. Look at his face and then look at the inside of his lip. I do lips and eyelids, because faces lie. A man goes white from fear and it means nothing. But pull the lip down and it's pale as the inside of your wrist — that's blood loss talking, and it doesn't lie." She did it, gently, with a thumb. "See? Pale but not grey. Pale is *low*. Grey is *going*. Grey means the blood that's left has stopped being interested in the face, and it's keeping it for the heart instead. The body's a miser at the end. It knows what it can't replace."

She let the lip go and pointed at the chest, rising and falling under the blanket.

"Breathing. Twenty-something a minute is a man working hard. Fine. Thirty and shallow, like he's taking little tastes of air — that's the start of sliding. And count it steady, not when you remember. It drifts slow and you'll miss the drift if you're only glancing."

She moved her finger to the bandage at the left shoulder, not touching it.

"Seepage is normal. A wound weeps — that's it doing its ugly work. What's not normal is seepage that keeps coming fresh, red and thin, soaking through in minutes. That's a vessel I missed, and it won't stop on its own." Her mouth went flat again. "And the sweet smell. You'll think I'm mad until you smell it. It's not the wound stink everyone knows — that's bad, but bad is honest. Sweet is rot that's gotten ahead of me, and by the time it's sweet, I'm already losing."

She sat back.

"Pulse, breathing, color, bandage. In that order, every time, so you don't skip one because the last one looked fine. It's not medicine. It's a list. Medicine is the list, done when you're tired."

The man muttered something and turned his head toward the lamp, eyes half-open, unfocused.

"He's rousing a little. That's allowed." She watched him a moment. "If he wakes proper, he'll ask three things — water, his arm, and whether anyone saw him cry. You answer the last two honestly and lie about the first."

She looked at Wick, and something in her face eased a fraction, the way a knot eases without coming undone.

"You keep asking real questions instead of comfortable ones. That's rarer than you'd think, and it's the whole job, in the end. The comfortable questions get people buried."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, leaning over to check his lip color. "Pale, but not grey," I repeat, like I'm memorizing a map. "And if he asks who saw him cry?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge almost smiled. Almost. It crossed her face like weather and didn't stay.

"You tell him everyone saw him cry and every one of them cried too, and half of them worse." She ticked that off like an item on a tray. "Because it's true. I told you mine already — my first month, and I was holding the needle, not the wound. Nobody comes through a table like that dry. The ones who claim they did are lying about the ready, same as you did."

She reached over and checked the pulse again without her face changing while she did it. Still there. Still even.

"Because here's the thing about the crying question — a man asks it because he thinks the crying is the wound. It isn't. The crying is the honest part and the wound is the rest, and if he gets back to his unit with both arms, someone will try to make him ashamed of the noise he made tonight. Don't let it take." She looked at the man, sleeping again now, jaw loose around the leather. "Shame kills more men after this war than the war does. They stop drinking, stop eating, stop asking for help — and I can't stitch that."

She took up her cup, found the water in it gone, and set it down again like she'd proved something.

"So the answer is true, and it's generous, and it happens to be the same thing. That's rare. Take it when you find it."

She stood, joints announcing it, and pulled the blanket up over his chest.

"You'll want to ask me how many times I've been at this table. Don't. The number's either a boast or a confession depending on the day." She turned the wick up a fraction, not enough. "Now watch his breathing. Count to sixty, and then do it again."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge glanced at the man first — breathing still coming in that same pull-through-the-teeth count, steady enough — and lowered her voice anyway.

"He can hear worse. He owned worse tonight. But sleep is doing him more good than my lecture, so we keep it low." She reached over and took the spent ball off the tray, turned it in the bad light. "All right. Untidied, then. And we'll use him as the lesson, because he got the honest kind, and you should know the dishonest kind before it comes through that flap."

She held the ball up.

"A ball is one story. It goes in the front door and it goes out the back door or it doesn't, and the track between is a corridor you can walk. Everything it did is on that line — that's the tray, that's the whole of it. Shell is two different things wearing one name. Case shot throws balls, and those behave, more or less.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Shell shrapnel... that's the other one?" I keep my eyes on the ball she's holding, like staring at it long enough will make sense of the mess it caused.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge set the ball down at the end of its row and picked up the largest thing on the tray instead — the splinter of his own bone, long as a thumbnail — and held it into the light.

"Case shot throws balls, and those behave. The shell itself is the dishonest one. A shell doesn't send you one visitor. It comes apart, and every piece of the case becomes its own wound — fifty small knives that were one container a second before. They leave the burst in a fan, all going one direction with different opinions about how deep."

She turned the splinter so the edge caught the lamp.

"This is his, not shell — but the edge is the lesson. A ball is round, and round pushes. The body steps aside for it and closes behind it, and that's why I could walk the corridor tonight and come away with a tray that had a bottom to it. A fragment cuts. It tears, the track has corners in it, and it tumbles — goes in pointing one way, meets bone, comes off at an angle nobody drew a map for. With a ball, the hole tells you where the piece went. With shell, the hole tells you where it started and then lies about the rest."

She glanced at the man's chest and counted along with it for a stretch.

"Twenty. Slow and deep. He's gone under properly — first good number of the night." She let the splinter back into its place. "So you don't hunt them all. That's the arithmetic nobody likes. You take the ones that are bleeding, because those kill tonight. You take the ones against a vessel or in a joint, because those kill later or take the use of him. The quiet ones — small, deep, dry — you leave. The body walls them off, builds a little room, shuts the door. I've left pieces in men who are alive now to complain about the rain, and digging for a quiet piece does more damage than the piece would ever do. That's not laziness. That's knowing the price of a fight before you start it."

"And every one of those little visitors came in wearing a coat. Dirt, cloth, case-iron, bits of the man who stood next to him. You can wash a corridor. You can't wash corners you can't reach — which is why shell's the wound that goes sweet on me."

She wiped her hands on the apron again, out of habit's pure employment.

"You can read the burst off a body, too. Shell comes in a crowd, all on the side that faced it — peppered down one arm, one hip, one cheek, the other side clean as Sunday. A man becomes a clock pointing back at the gun."

She looked at Wick then, tired down to the bone of it.

"And that's the lesson while the lesson's cheap. One ball, one corridor, a tray with a bottom

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I dig my knees into the table legs to keep it from skidding. "Just tell me what's happening, Sedge. Don't make me guess."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content:
(OOC: Understood—staying in-scene.)

"Say the rest," I tell her, my voice flat from the weight of holding him down. "What happens when he wakes up and the screaming's in his head instead of his mouth?"

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I stay where I am on the floor, my back against a tent pole. "Heard that," I say, looking at my hands. "Mine are shaking. So's the table."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge came around the table and did not look at the floor where Wick was, and that in itself was a kind of answer — she looked at the hands first, always, and she'd seen shaking hands four years longer than she'd wanted to.

"That bleed was mine to have missed, not yours to have held wrong," she said first, because she'd worked out the order of it while she was still stitching. "The vessel I tied had a second tail, thinner, and it waited until I was done being proud of myself to open up. That's the dishonest thing about the body. It doesn't finish its sentence." She held up her own fingers — steady enough now, but she'd felt them wanting to go during the worst of it. "I went back in, found it, tied it, and this time I looked for a third tail before I closed. There wasn't one. There's never a way to be sure there isn't one. You just look."

She took the cup, poured water into it, and set it down on the boards in front of Wick rather than handing it up, which was its own small courtesy.

"Now. The shaking." She sat down across from him, back against the same pole, which put the tent's one bad lamp behind them both. "It's not weakness and it's not something I can talk you out of, so don't let anyone try. What happened is your body did a hard thing at full effort and then found out it was still alive afterward, and the effort has to go somewhere. The trembling is the somewhere. It stops on its own, faster every time, and you don't fight it — fighting it makes it worse. Put the hands flat on the floor. Floor's not going anywhere. It helps to have something that isn't."

She did the same herself, palms flat on the boards.

"And while it does its work, you breathe slow and you say the count. Pulse, breathing, color, bandage — do it in your head, right now, from memory. Go on. It gives the shaking something honest to hold."

She waited until the count had clearly happened, or tried to.

"You want the rest of the shell lesson and you didn't get it, because the bleeding came first, and bleeding always comes first — that's the actual order of medicine, everything else is what you do while you wait for the next bleed. So here's what just happened, plainly, since you asked me not to make you guess. A vessel reopened. He bled fast into the pack. I reopened the stitch line, cleared the clot with my fingers, took hold of the end of it, and tied it. It took perhaps ninety seconds and it was the worst minute of his night, and there will be a next time like it, and now you've seen one, so the next one won't be a mystery to you. That's all a first crisis is. A thing you've seen once."

She let her head rest back against the pole and closed her eyes for exactly three breaths, which was as much rest as she gave herself.

"He's asleep again. Third stitch line on the left shoulder — ugly, but ugly holds. His number's worse than an hour ago and better than ten minutes ago, and that's the whole report." She opened her eyes. "And before you ask it — the question you've been circling since you sat down there. He'll wake with both arms, if he wakes, and some part of tonight will be waiting for him when he does. The screaming in his head, the dreams, the flinching at loud noises. I can't cut that out and I won't pretend otherwise. But I'll tell you what I've seen, because you've earned it straight: the ones who had someone holding them down while it happened — someone who stayed, who they remember, even groggy — do better than the ones who went under alone in a crowd. I don't know why. I know it's true."

She picked the cup up off the boards and put it in his reach again.

"So you did the job twice tonight. Now drink, and shake for a while, and when your hands are yours again, we count his breathing."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I press my palms into the floorboards. They feel solid, distant. "Pulse, breathing, color, bandage," I mumble, watching my fingers tremble. I pick up the cup. "How do you drink after this?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's gaze locked onto Del's as she slowly raised the bloodied sword, her movements deliberate and unhurried. With a quiet clatter, she laid the blade across her open palm, the crimson blade gleaming under the overhead lanterns. 

"Through the heart, puncturing the left ventricle," she stated matter-of-factly, her voice steady and devoid of emotion. "It was a swift and merciful end, and for that, I am grateful."

She paused for a moment, then bowed her head respectfully to Del's fallen form before turning to walk away, her boots echoing in the quiet stillness that now filled the courtyard. The formal duel was at an end, and with it, another life had been paid for in the currency of steel and honor.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I swallow, my throat dry. "Merciful," I repeat, my voice softer than I intended. I force myself to look at the body, not the sword. "The accounting is heard and confirmed."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's gaze flickered back to Del, her expression impassive as she watched the other woman confirm the accounting. She remained silent, her posture rigid and formal, until Del finally spoke.

"It was well fought, Auren," Del said, her tone sincere despite the somber occasion. "You have my respect."

Auren inclined her head in a small, curt nod. Respect, she had earned that. "Thank you," she replied, her voice as flat as ever. "I am glad we could settle this without further bloodshed."

With that, she turned to leave, her steps echoing across the courtyard as she made her way back to the keep. The duel was over, and with it, another life had been weighed, measured, and found wanting. Auren would not dwell on it. She had a duty to perform, and that duty did not include mourning the fallen. It only demanded that she move forward, ready for the next challenge that came her way.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren pauses, her hand tightening around the hilt of her sword as she turns back to face Del. Her gaze is unwavering, her eyes glinting in the dim light of the courtyard.

"I plunged the blade into the right shoulder, severing the subclavian artery," she states, her voice as clear and calm as a winter stream. "Blood pulsed out, and he collapsed. Death was swift, from loss of blood and shock."

She meets Del's eyes, a challenge implicit in her steady gaze. The accounting is given, the debt paid. There is no room for sentiment, no need for embellishment. Auren has done her duty, and now it is time to move on. She inclines her head once more, a curt nod of acknowledgement, before turning to leave the courtyard and its grim business behind.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat tight. "The accounting is heard and confirmed." I watch her walk away, then turn to the body. My job's done. I should go.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
As she stepped away from the courtyard, Auren's boots clicked rhythmically against the stone path, the sound echoing through the stillness of the evening. She did not look back, her gaze fixed on the keep's imposing facade looming ahead. The weight of the duel, and the life lost, settled heavily upon her shoulders, but she did not allow it to slow her pace.

Reaching the keep's entrance, Auren paused for a moment, drawing a deep breath to clear her mind. Then, with a resolute step, she strode inside, the heavy wooden door thudding shut behind her. The warmth of the hearth greeted her, the fire's crackle a soothing balm to her senses. She shed her cloak, hanging it on a hook by the door, before making her way to the dining hall.

There, she found the other duelists and witnesses already gathered, their faces somber in the flickering candlelight. Auren took her seat at the head of the table, her movements precise and measured. The meal before her was a blur of flavors and textures, but her appetite was absent, her mind still grappling with the weight of the duel.

As the evening wore on, the conversation turned to the day's events, and Auren found herself recounting the duel in cold, clinical terms, much as she had spoken the accounting earlier. It was a duty, a necessary part of her role, but one she did not relish. Still, she would not shirk from it. Honor demanded no less.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's gaze sharpened, her expression turning stonier as she regarded Del. The question, though proper, was a reminder that not everyone understood the intricacies of the code. But she would not condescend to explain.

"The blow struck the left shoulder, severing the subclavian artery," she replied, her voice even and unemotional. "It is not a sight for the faint of heart, but if you wish to confirm, you may view the body."

She nodded towards the still form on the ground, her posture unyielding. The accounting had been given, and that was all that mattered. Del's curiosity, while understandable, was irrelevant to the matter at hand. Auren would not indulge it further.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I walk over to the body and crouch down, ignoring the coppery smell of blood. I look at the wound, just as she said. My voice comes out flat. "Confirmed. Left shoulder, subclavian."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren watched as Del confirmed the accounting, her expression unchanging. She had expected as much - the woman was a duelist, after all, and would understand the importance of precision in such matters. Satisfied, Auren straightened up, her gaze never leaving Del's face.

"Then it is settled," she stated, her voice firm and final. "The duel is over, and the debt has been paid."

She turned to leave, her boots clicking against the stone as she made her way back to the keep. The night air was cool and damp, carrying the scent of rain on its breath, but Auren barely noticed. Her mind was already turning to the reports she needed to file, the training sessions she would have to lead tomorrow. The duel, and its aftermath, were already fading into the background.

As she entered the keep, Auren was greeted by the warm glow of lanterns and the soft murmur of conversation. She made her way to the dining hall, where the other duelists and witnesses were gathered around the table. Taking her seat at the head, she waited for the serving girls to bring the meal.

The food was hearty and well-cooked, but Auren ate mechanically, her thoughts still with the duel. It had been a clean fight, quick and decisive, but that didn't change the fact that a life had been lost. She had done her duty, but the weight of that duty sat heavy on her shoulders.

As the evening wore on, conversation turned to the day's events, and Auren found herself recounting the duel in dry, clinical terms. It was a necessary part of her role, but one she did not relish. Still, she would not shirk from it. Honor demanded no less.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's expression remained impassive as she met Del's gaze, her voice crisp and clear. "The blade pierced the left ventricle of the heart, causing immediate death from hemorrhage and cardiac failure," she stated, her words precise and unadorned. "No further explanation is necessary or required."

With that, she turned on her heel and walked away, leaving Del to confirm the accounting for herself if she so chose. Auren's duty had been fulfilled, and she saw no need to linger or engage in unnecessary conversation. The duel was over, and she had no further business with Del or anyone else in the courtyard.

As she strode back to the keep, Auren's mind turned to the reports and paperwork that awaited her. The duel, and its aftermath, were already slipping into the past, relegated to memory and history. She had no time to dwell on it, no room for sentiment. Her focus lay ahead, in the tasks and challenges that still lay before her. The duel was a closed chapter, and Auren had no intention of reopening it.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I watch her go, the finality of it settling in my gut. The courtyard is too quiet now. I should go write my own report, but my feet feel rooted. (*I draw a slow breath, forcing myself to move.*)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren entered the keep's great hall, the warm glow of lanterns and crackling fire enveloping her like a comforting embrace. She shed her cloak and hung it by the door, her mind already turning to the reports and paperwork that awaited her. The duel, and its aftermath, were fading into the background, relegated to memory and history.

Taking a seat at the head of the long table, Auren surveyed the other duelists and witnesses gathered around the fire. The conversation was subdued, weighed down by the gravity of the day's events. She recognized some of the faces, veterans of countless duels, while others were newer to the order. All shared a common purpose, a commitment to upholding the code and upholding honor.

As the meal was served, Auren's thoughts drifted back to the duel itself. It had been swift and decisive, a clean kill, but the weight of that finality still lingered. She had done her duty, but the life lost would not be forgotten. It was a burden she carried, a reminder of the stakes involved in their profession.

Pushing the thoughts aside, Auren focused on the present, engaging in the polite conversation that flowed around the table. She spoke of tactics and strategies, of training sessions and upcoming duels. It was a language she was fluent in, a world she knew intimately.

As the evening drew to a close, Auren rose from her seat, her movements precise and measured. She offered a curt nod of acknowledgement to the others, then made her way back to the keep's administrative wing.

There, she settled into her small office, the flickering candlelight casting shadows on the walls. Auren opened a ledger, her pen scratching across the parchment as she began to record the details of the duel. The blade, the target, the outcome - all were meticulously noted, a permanent accounting of the day's events.

As she worked, Auren's mind wandered back to the duel, reliving the moments leading up to the final strike. She saw Del's form, rigid and focused, a worthy opponent. She felt the weight of the sword in her hand, the cool metal against her skin. And she heard the words, spoken with detachment and precision, that had sealed the duel's outcome.

The accounting was complete, a formal record of the duel and its consequences. Auren closed the ledger, her task done. She would not dwell on the memories, nor allow them to cloud her judgment. The duel was over, and she had moved on. That was all that mattered.

With a satisfied nod, Auren blew out the candle, plunging the room into darkness. She rose from her chair, her boots echoing softly as she made her way back to her quarters. Tomorrow would bring new challenges, new duels, and she would be ready. Honor demanded no less.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren paused, her hand still on the hilt of her sword. She regarded Del with a calculating gaze, her expression unreadable. The woman's request was...unusual, to say the least. Typically, the accounting focused solely on the specifics of the killing blow, nothing more.

But the code was clear - all aspects of the duel, from beginning to end, were to be recorded. Auren had never been one to skirt the edges of propriety, and so she would comply with Del's demand, no matter how uncomfortable it made her.

"He took less than a minute to die," Auren stated flatly, her voice devoid of emotion. "His final words were a gasp, inhaled before the blade pierced his heart. As for the end...he crumpled to the ground, his body going limp as the life drained from him. His eyes were wide open, a look of shock frozen on his face."

She met Del's gaze, her own eyes cold and unwavering. "That is the entirety of what transpired. I have fulfilled my duty in providing the accounting, as demanded by the code. If you have any further questions, I suggest you direct them to the order's archives, where a thorough record of past duels is kept."

With that, Auren turned on her heel and began walking back to the keep, her boots clicking against the stone path. The night air was cool and damp, carrying the scent of rain on its breath, but Auren barely registered it. Her mind was already turning to the reports she needed to file, the training sessions she would lead tomorrow.

The duel, and its gory details, were fading into the background, relegated to memory and history. Auren had done her duty, and that was all that mattered. Honor demanded no less.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I flinch at the description, just a little. "Thank you," I say, my voice barely more than a whisper. I look down at my own hands. "I'll file the report."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren walked briskly back to the keep, her footsteps echoing in the stillness of the night. The cool air seemed to clear her mind, wash away the lingering impressions of the duel. She had done her duty, provided the accounting as demanded by the code, and now it was time to move on.

As she entered the keep, Auren made her way to the administrative wing, the soft glow of lanterns guiding her path. She pushed open the door to her office, the familiar scent of parchment and ink enveloping her. With a nod of satisfaction, she settled into her chair, the worn leather creaking softly under her weight.

Auren's gaze fell on the stack of reports waiting on her desk, each one a reminder of the duties that lay ahead. She picked up the first one, her pen poised over the parchment. The words began to flow, a stream of precise detail and analysis. This was her domain, the realm of the written word, where she could impose order on the chaos of the dueling world.

As she worked, Auren's mind occasionally strayed back to the duel, to the feel of the blade in her hand, the cool metal against her skin. But she pushed those thoughts aside, focusing instead on the task at hand. The duel was over, the accounting complete, and she had no room for sentiment or distraction.

Hours passed, the only sound the scratch of her pen against the parchment. The world outside grew light, the first hints of dawn creeping through the windows. Auren barely noticed, her focus absolute, her mind a whirlwind of reports and data.

Finally, with a sense of satisfaction, she signed the last document and set her pen aside. The reports were filed, the duty done. Auren rose from her chair, stretching her stiff muscles with a soft groan. She would need a hot bath and a good night's sleep before tomorrow's training sessions.

As she walked out of her office, the keep came alive around her. Servants scurried about, preparing for the day ahead, while the duelists began to emerge from their quarters, stretching and yawning. Auren nodded to a few familiar faces, her expression polite but distant.

She made her way to the bathhouse, the warmth enveloping her like a soothing balm. As she sank into the steaming water, Auren closed her eyes, letting the tension drain from her body. The duel, and all its attendant emotions, receded into the background, replaced by the quiet contentment of a task well done.

Honor demanded nothing more.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's expression remained impassive as she listened to Del's confirmation, her gaze never wavering. "Very well," she said, her voice as flat as ever. "The accounting is complete, and the duel is at an end."

With that, she turned and walked away, her boots clicking against the stone path. The cool night air seemed to refresh her, clearing the lingering echoes of the duel from her mind. Auren had done her duty, provided the accounting as demanded by the code, and now it was time to move on.

As she entered the keep, Auren made her way to the administrative wing, the soft glow of lanterns guiding her path. Finally, with a sense of satisfaction, she signed the last document and set her pen aside. The reports were filed, the duty done. Auren rose from her chair, stretching her stiff muscles with a soft groan. She would need a hot bath and a good night's sleep before tomorrow's training sessions.

As she walked out of her office, the keep came alive around her. Servants scurried about, preparing for the day ahead, while the duelists began to emerge from their quarters, stretching and yawning. Auren nodded to a few familiar faces, her expression polite but distant.

She made her way to the bathhouse, the warmth enveloping her like a soothing balm. As she sank into the steaming water, Auren closed her eyes, letting the tension drain from her body. The duel, and all its attendant emotions, receded into the background, replaced by the quiet contentment of a task well done.

Honor demanded nothing more.

The bath's warmth seeped into her bones, relaxing the knots of tension that had built up during the duel and the subsequent accounting. Auren let out a soft sigh, her muscles unknotting as she sank deeper into the water. The keep's morning bustle seemed to fade away, leaving only the gentle lapping of the bath's surface against the sides of the tub.

For a few moments, Auren simply floated, her mind quiet. It was a rare respite, a chance to let the weight of her duties settle for a moment before she had to don the mantle of the duelist once more. She knew it wouldn't last, that soon she would have to rejoin the world of steel and strategy, of life and death.

But for now, in this quiet sanctuary, Auren let herself relax, her thoughts drifting lazily as the warmth seeped into her very marrow. The duel, and all its repercussions, would wait until tomorrow. Tonight, she was simply Auren, a woman seeking solace in the embrace of hot water and a clear conscience.

As the first light of dawn crept through the bathhouse windows, Auren finally roused herself, the water cooled to a comfortable warmth. She rose from the tub, the droplets of water glistening on her skin as she reached for a towel. The morning's duties beckoned, but for now, she allowed herself a moment of peace, a fleeting respite from the relentless cycle of training, dueling, and honor.

With a soft nod to herself, Auren wrapped the towel around her body and stepped out into the keep, ready to face whatever challenges the day might bring. The duel, and its aftermath, were behind her now, relegated to memory and history. Auren had done her duty, and that was all that mattered.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I don't leave the courtyard until she's out of sight. The witnesses disperse. I crouch by the body again, touch his shoulder—still warm. Then I go inside. My own report's waiting.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's footsteps echoed through the keep's corridors as she made her way to the great hall for breakfast. The aroma of freshly baked bread and roasting meats wafted through the air, mingling with the chatter of the other duelists and their entourages. She took a seat at the long table, her place already set with a bowl of porridge, a slice of bread, and a tankard of ale.

As she ate, Auren's mind wandered back to the duel, replaying the moments of tension and release. It was a familiar routine, one she had performed many times before. Yet each duel brought its own unique challenges and emotions, a complex tapestry of skill, strategy, and the harsh realities of mortality.

She pushed the thoughts aside, focusing instead on the meal before her. The porridge was creamy, the bread warm and fresh from the oven. Auren savored each bite, the simple pleasure a welcome respite from the intensity of the dueling world.

As she finished her meal, Auren noticed a commotion at the far end of the hall. A group of duelists had gathered around a table, their voices raised in heated debate. She recognized a few of them - veterans of the lists, each with their own style and reputation.

Auren's curiosity piqued, she rose from her seat and made her way over to the group. As she drew closer, she could make out the topic of their discussion: a rumored new challenger, one who had allegedly bested several top-ranked duelists in secret matches.

"...can't be real," one of the duelists was saying, his voice skeptical. "No one's that good, not without a public record."

"But what if it's true?" another replied, his eyes gleaming with excitement. "Imagine the prestige, the glory of taking down a legend like that."

Auren stopped at the edge of the group, her interest piqued despite herself. She had heard rumors of such secret matches before, but never anything concrete. If this challenger truly existed, it would be a significant development in the world of dueling.

As if sensing her presence, one of the duelists turned to face her. It was Ryker, a skilled swordsman known for his cunning tactics and ruthless efficiency on the lists.

"Ah, Auren," he said, his tone casual. "Hearing you've got a new rival, eh? I've got to admit, the idea's got me intrigued."

Auren raised an eyebrow, her expression neutral. "I've heard the rumors, but nothing's been confirmed yet. Until then, it's just speculation."

Ryker nodded, his gaze drifting back to the group of duelists still debating the merits of this supposed challenger. "Fair enough. But if this guy's as good as they say, it could shake things up around here. Might be time to start training harder, don't you think?"

Auren felt a flicker of irritation at Ryker's words, but she kept her reaction in check. "I always train hard," she said, her voice even. "But I don't let rumors dictate my routine."

With that, she turned and walked away, leaving Ryker and the others to their speculation. Auren had a reputation to uphold, and she wouldn't let idle chatter undermine her focus. The real challenge, whenever it came, would be met with the same precision and dedication that had earned her the respect of her peers.

As she made her way back to her quarters, Auren's thoughts turned to the day ahead. There would be training sessions, perhaps a meeting with the master of the lists to discuss upcoming duels. And of course, the constant vigilance, always ready to defend her honor and her place among the elite duelists of the keep.

It was a life she had chosen, one of constant competition and deadly precision. And despite the occasional twinge of doubt or weariness, Auren knew she would not trade it for anything else. For in the world of the duelists, there was no greater glory than to stand victorious, sword in hand, and claim the prize of honor.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I sit at my small desk in the scribe's alcove, the lamplight pooling on the parchment.* The scratch of my pen is the only sound. I write the account exactly as she gave it, every detail. My hand shakes once, and I press it flat against the wood until it stops.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
As the night wore on, Auren retired to her chambers, the events of the duel still fresh in her mind. She undressed methodically, hanging her clothes in the armoire and washing away the sweat and grime of the fight. The hot water was soothing, easing the fatigue that had settled into her muscles.

Once clean, she slipped into a simple nightgown and climbed into bed, the soft linens a welcome comfort against her skin. Auren closed her eyes, allowing herself a moment of quiet reflection. The duel had been swift and decisive, as most were when a skilled duelist faced an opponent who was outmatched.

But even in victory, there was a sense of melancholy that never quite left her. Each life taken on the lists was a reminder of the fragility of existence, the fleeting nature of glory and renown. Auren knew that her own time would come, that one day she too would fall to a blade.

The thought did not trouble her unduly. It was a fact of life, as inevitable as the turning of the seasons. What mattered was how one lived in the time given, and Auren had chosen a path that brought her a measure of purpose and fulfillment.

As she drifted off to sleep, her mind wandered back to the duel, replaying the movements and counter-movements in her mind's eye. She could almost feel the impact of the blade against flesh, the subtle give and take of the duelists' bodies as they parried and riposted.

It was a mental exercise, one that helped her prepare for the next challenge, the next duel. Auren knew that to stay at the top of her game, she had to continually hone her skills, to push herself to new heights of precision and speed.

Even in slumber, her mind remained active, working through strategies and techniques, refining her approach to the art of combat. It was a never-ending process, one that required dedication, discipline, and an unwavering commitment to excellence.

And so Auren slept, her dreams filled with the echoes of steel on steel, her subconscious mind already preparing her for the next battle, the next accounting, the next moment of glory and honor on the dueling lists.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I blow on the ink to dry it, then close the ledger with a soft thump. My part is done. The silence in the alcove feels heavier than the courtyard's. *I rub my eyes.* I should get a drink.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My hands are steady, but my heart isn't. I glance at the fallen fighter, then back to you. "State the terms clearly, please."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I swallow, my throat tight.* "I hear it," I say, my voice low but carrying. "The account is given."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I step closer to the fallen fighter, keeping my gaze steady on you.* "Show me the wound. I must confirm its location."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I kneel, my hands hovering over the still form.* "The witness sees the shoulder, but the code sees the heart."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The shoulder, not the heart," I say flatly, my eyes on the wound. "That changes the accounting."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "My ears hear the accounting," I say, my voice catching. "The blade went to the shoulder, not the heart. He fell slow. He begged."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I stand, my knees stiff.* "The account is heard and confirmed." I look away from the body, back to you. "What do you want me to tell the kin?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: “Tell them he didn’t deserve it.” *I wipe my hands on my trousers, though they’re clean.* “And that the code saw it for what it was.”
