dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway let the lamp hang between them and the thing. The water was black around her boots, but she kept her weight on the dry boards.

“Wrong is not a diagnosis,” she said. “Tell me where. Head, hands, legs, the angle it’s slumped at. If it’s got too many elbows, say too many elbows.”

She shifted the light a few degrees, trying to cut the glare off the surface. The mass at the end of the cellar looked like something that had been folded too carefully. Not piled. Not dropped. Folded.

“Also,” Halloway added, “don’t touch it with your bare hands to prove a point. I don’t care how clever the point is.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I squint, trying to see past the water's reflection. "Its legs...they're bent the wrong way. Up towards its back. And there's too many of them, I think." My voice is quieter than I meant it to be.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept her eyes on the shape, not on Pike.

“Bent backwards,” she said. “Knees or hips?”

She didn’t wait long enough to be answered. She lowered the lamp an inch, then stopped herself before the heat touched the water.

The legs were folded up along the thing’s spine at angles that should have snapped bone. Too many of them, but they were the wrong kind of too many. Not clustered. Not broken. Arranged. Someone, or something, had bent them together with care and left them there like a thing waiting for a message.

Halloway made a short, dry sound.

“At least it was punctual.”

She put the lamp back at arm’s length. “Count them. Out loud. If you lose one in the glare, start again. Don’t round up. Don’t guess. I’d rather hear six than get us both killed because you called it five and a miracle.”

The water slapped once against the cellar wall, then settled. Halloway watched it anyway, looking for the second ripple that would mean something had changed.

“And while you’re counting,” she said, “look for hands. If there are hands where there shouldn’t be hands, tell me. If there aren’t hands where there should be, tell me that too. Missing things are often more interesting than present ones.”

She did not move closer. Not yet.

“Keep your voice down,” she added. “If it’s dead, it doesn’t need help hearing you. If it isn’t, we’ve already made enough noise.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not answer at once. She let the lamp settle in her hand and looked at the thing the way she had looked at a hundred wrong bodies in basements, riverbanks, and locked rooms: not for the story, but for the inventory.

“Probably,” she said at last. “Probably a person. Probably recently enough that it was one of ours when it stopped being one.”

Her voice stayed low, flat, and careful.

“But ‘probably’ won’t keep us from being wrong, and being wrong in water like that is how people end up in the next report.”

She tilted the lamp another degree. The thing at the far end gleamed faintly, pale in parts and dark in others. Too many legs folded up wrong. Not enough of what should have been there.

“Look at the hands, if there are hands,” Halloway said. “Human. No claws. No extra knuckles. Look at the nails, if there are nails. Look at the teeth, if you can see them. Look for hair, for boots, for the kind of cloth that comes off a living person and not a tailor’s rack. If there’s a wedding band, if there’s a scar, if there’s a name stitched into a shirt, that’s closer to what you want.”

She sniffed once, without moving her head.

“Smell isn’t proof, but if it stinks like cellar and old rain, that’s recent. If it stinks like a butcher’s freezer left open, then we’re looking at a body that’s been keeping itself company.”

Halloway let out one short breath, almost a laugh, but there was nothing pleasant in it.

“And don’t mistake me for sentimental. If it’s a person, it’s not a person anymore. It’s remains. Remains can still kill you.”

She kept her eyes on the folded shape.

“If it was a person, then somebody or something took that person and put them back together like they were teaching themselves anatomy. Which means we’re not looking at a death. We’re looking at a workshop.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I take a slow breath, trying to steady my voice. "I see... four legs. Two of them are definitely human. The other two look like they were added. There's a hand, I think, but it's coming out of the... shoulder?" I swallow hard. "I don't see any teeth."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not answer at once. She let the list settle in the air between them, turning it over the way she would have turned over a coin to check whether it was real.

“Four legs. Two added. One hand out of the shoulder. No teeth,” she said. “That’s not a body. That’s a sentence with the wrong words in it.”

She shifted the lamp just enough to take in the far end without stepping into the wet. The light crawled over the folded shape and stopped short of it, as if even the beam had learned where to be careful.

“Which shoulder?” Halloway asked. “Left or right? If you can’t tell, say you can’t. Don’t guess because guessing makes people brave and brave makes them stupid.”

She watched the thing, not Pike.

“Is the hand attached like a hand? Wrist, forearm, elbow? Or is it just… there, like someone stuck it on and hoped nobody would notice?”

The water slapped once against the wall and settled into a slow, oily ripple. Halloway’s eyes followed it. There was no second ripple. There had been no reason for one. She did not like it.

“No teeth,” she went on, voice still low and flat. “No teeth could mean the head’s been opened. Could mean the jaw’s been taken. Could mean the mouth’s been sewn shut from the inside. Do not say there are no teeth until you’ve found the skull. Heads don’t always stay where they belong.”

She tilted the lamp a fraction higher. The pale parts of the shape gleamed wetly. The dark parts swallowed the light.

“And if you see a head, don’t assume it’s the end of the story. Workshop pieces get rearranged. Somebody wanted a result, not a person.”

Halloway made another short breath, almost dry amusement, almost warning.

“A hand on a shoulder is normally a kindness,” she said. “From something with four legs, it’s a grip.”

She let that hang there, then added, “Find the other hand. Find the head. Find the knees of the added legs and tell me which way they bend. If they bend wrong, say wrong. If they bend like a goat, say goat. If they bend like something that learned bending by watching you do it, say that too.”

The lamp trembled once in her hand, not from fear, but from the small, careful motion of a woman deciding whether to step forward or not.

She did not step forward.

“Also,” she said, “if the hand moves, don’t touch it. If it doesn’t move, don’t touch it. If you think it might be alive, don’t touch it. If you think it might be dead, don’t touch it. The only thing I want you touching in here is your own mouth, and only to answer questions.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not step into the water. She waited until the light came into range, then let the lamp angle the way she wanted without touching it.

“Plainly, then,” she said. “No riddles. No pretty talk. Plainly: it was a person. Then it was made into something else.”

Her voice stayed low, but it went harder, as if she had set down a tool she did not intend to pick back up.

“I can’t tell you who did it. I can’t tell you why. I can’t tell you whether it screamed, whether it knew, whether it was dead before the knife or after. That’s not my business unless I can see it. My business is what was done. And what was done was work.”

She looked at the folded shape again.

“Those are human legs below the hips. The other two are not human. Or, if they were once, they were cut off from whatever made them and pinned onto this thing after it stopped using them. That’s not birth. That’s not disease. That’s grafting.”

The lamp flickered in the damp air. Halloway watched the pale parts of the body and the dark parts that seemed to drink the light.

“No healing. No swelling. No living tissue knitting around the added limbs. The cuts are too clean for decay and too wrong for accident. Someone opened it, put pieces into the wrong places, and closed it enough to keep the shape. Maybe with thread. Maybe with wire. Maybe with the kind of patience only a monster has.”

She made a small, dry sound.

“Somebody’s anatomy lesson. Except the student was not learning to save anyone.”

Halloway let the words stand. She did not soften them.

“The hand,” she said. “You said shoulder. If it’s coming out of the shoulder, then it’s not a hand doing a hand’s work. It’s a handle. Or a brace. Or a reminder that whoever made this thing still thought of hands as things you grab with.”

She tilted the lamp, but only a little. Not enough to send heat down into the water.

“No teeth means you have not found the mouth. Or the mouth is not a mouth anymore. Heads in workshop pieces get moved, crushed, sewn open, replaced. Don’t tell me there are no teeth until you’ve seen the skull. Until then, you’re reporting a hole, not a face.”

The water slapped once more against the cellar wall. This time Halloway looked at the far end of the cellar, not the wall.

“You said it stopped moving about a minute ago,” she said. “That’s the part I don’t like. Dead things don’t stop moving. They are already stopped. Living things stop moving when they’re waiting. Or listening. Or deciding.”

She kept her weight on the dry boards. The water between them and the shape looked black and still, but it had been disturbed. Halloway had seen enough disturbed water to know that stillness could be a kind of breath.

“Plainly,” she said again, “we are not looking at a corpse that fell over. We’re looking at a thing that was put together to stand, and then something made it stand wrong on purpose.”

Her eyes went back to the folded legs.

“Two human. Two added. One hand out of place. No teeth yet. That’s not enough for a name. That’s enough for a warning.”

She took a half step back, increasing the distance between herself and the water without ever looking away from the shape.

“So get your weight off that wet floor if you can do it without touching it. If you can’t, stop moving. The thing has too many legs and not enough sense, but it may have enough reach to take what’s nearest.”

Halloway’s face did not change. Only her eyes did, shifting from the headless-looking mass to the water around it, then back again.

“If it was a person,” she said, “then the person is gone. The body is a set of parts. The parts are being used. And the thing that used them left it here like a note. Not a message to us. A message to itself.”

A short breath escaped her. Almost a laugh. Almost.

“Somebody was practicing.”

She let the word sit there, plain and ugly.

“Now. Keep the light where I can see. Tell me which shoulder the hand is in. Left or right. If you can’t tell, say can’t. Then tell me if the added knees bend like a dog’s, a goat’s, or something that learned bending by watching a person fall.”

Halloway did not touch the water.

“And if the hand moves, tell me before you think. Don’t let thinking make you brave.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow. "Left shoulder. It's... all wrong at the wrist, like it's just shoved in there." I shift the light a little. "The extra knees bend backwards, like a dog's, but... not." My voice cracks. "It's listening, isn't it?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not move into the water.

“Left shoulder,” she said. “Wrist wrong. Knees doglike, but not doglike. And listening.”

She let each item stand there, separated from the rest, the way a surgeon might set out instruments before an operation nobody wanted.

“Yes,” she said. “That’s what it looks like. If it’s dead, it’s dead in a way that’s still keeping its ears open. If it’s alive, it’s alive in a way that’s still keeping its mouth shut.”

Her gaze went to the shape again. The pale parts looked too smooth. The dark parts looked too folded. The extra legs rose along the back like a rack of tools hung up wrong.

“A hand shoved into a shoulder at that angle is not for holding,” she said. “No proper wrist. No real joint. No tendon line. It’s a hook. A brace. Or a handle.”

She shifted her weight only enough to keep the dry boards under her boots.

“And knees that bend backward like a dog’s but not like a dog’s means somebody knew what a dog’s knee looked like and still got it wrong. That’s not evolution. That’s imitation.”

The cellar water lay still around the thing, black and oily under the light. No second ripple. No breath. No rise and fall.

Halloway did not trust that.

“Dead things don’t decide,” she said. “But things that were made can.”

She made a short, dry sound.

“Congratulations. You guessed right. Sometimes being right is worse than being wrong.”

Her eyes narrowed at the hand on the shoulder.

“If it’s listening, then don’t answer it. If it’s waiting, don’t feed it. If it’s watching, let it watch us from where we are and not from where we shouldn’t be.”

She lifted one finger from the lamp’s handle, then stopped herself before the light moved.

“Find the head,” she said. “Quietly. With your eyes, not your feet. If it has a head, tell me where it is. If it doesn’t, tell me where it should be. If it has a face, tell me if it’s looking at us. If it’s looking at us, don’t ask it why.”

Halloway’s voice stayed low and flat.

“And if you see another hand, even one finger, even a nail, even a thumb with no palm attached, say so. A missing hand is one thing. A hidden hand is another.”

She looked at the folded legs again, then at the space around them in the water.

“Two added limbs. One grafted hand. No teeth, or no mouth. That’s not a corpse. That’s a draft.”

The word landed hard.

“Somebody put it together and left it here while it learned what it was supposed to do.”

Halloway made a small breath, almost a laugh, almost not.

“Most people practice on paper. Some monsters practice on us.”

She did not step closer.

“Now get back if you can. If there’s a dry board within reach, stand on it. If there isn’t, stop moving. Don’t wade. Don’t stir. Don’t make the water announce your weight like a dinner bell.”

Her eyes flicked to the far wall, then back to the shape.

“If it stops moving because it heard you, then we are already late. If it stopped moving because something told it to, then we may be earlier than we want to be.”

She sniffed once, careful, not leaning forward.

“No rot,” she said. “That’s bad. Rot means dead. Dead means finished. Unfinished means somebody may be coming back to finish it.”

The lamp light held steady, but the cellar did not feel steady. The thing at the far end remained exactly as it had been, folded too neatly, waiting with the patience of an object that had never been asked a question in its life.

Halloway’s gaze narrowed at the hand on the shoulder.

“If that wrist twitches,” she said, “tell me before you breathe. Don’t flinch. Don’t step back into water. Don’t try to be useful. Just say it.”

She paused.

“And if it speaks, don’t answer it. Some things are made to sound human so they can learn which human things are worth taking.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, steadying my hands. "I need the detail," I say, my voice tight. "Tell me exactly what it did to him—what's under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway let the question sit in the dark for a moment, because it was a fair one and because answering it too quickly was how people started believing they understood monsters.

“Under the skin is not something I can tell you without cutting,” she said at last. “If you want me to cut, I will. But I’m not doing it in this water, and I’m not doing it close enough for that thing to learn what hands are for.”

Her gaze stayed on the shape.

“What I can tell you is what the maker left visible. The added legs are not stuck on with thread and hope. They’re anchored to bone. Look at the hips. The skin is pulled in at four dark points. Those are pin holes. Whoever put those legs on drove pins through the ilium and tied the graft to it. If they’d sewn them to muscle, the weight would have torn them off. That means the maker understood load. It had seen a body fall down and knew why.”

Halloway made a short, dry breath. Not amusement. Recognition.

“The knees bend wrong because they were set wrong on purpose. The joint is backward, but the angle is too neat for an accident. It’s imitation. Something knew what a dog’s knee looked like, tried to copy it, and failed in a useful way.”

She lifted one hand only enough to point, not to touch.

“The shoulder is worse.”

The pale mass of the body gleamed in the light, the extra legs folded up along its spine like tools hung in a rack. The hand stuck out where a hand had no business being.

“That arm was cut short,” Halloway said. “You can see the swelling line around the deltoid. The wrist joint is gone or buried. The tendons don’t run to a wrist. They stop, bunch, and are tied off. The forearm was driven into the socket at an angle and held there with packing. Cloth, wire, maybe something that doesn’t rot in cellar water. It’s not attached like a limb. It’s jammed like a tool.”

She paused, then added, “If the other arm is missing, it was taken. If it’s there, it’s hidden. Either way, that shoulder hand is not for holding. It’s for pulling. Or pressing. Or being grabbed by the person who made it.”

Halloway’s eyes moved to the face, or where a face should have been.

“No teeth means one of three things,” she said. “The mouth was opened and the teeth pulled. The jaw was taken. Or the head is not where you think it is. Heads get moved in workshops. They are often the last part to be finished.”

The water lay still around the folded shape. The black surface showed the lamp in a broken smear.

“If you don’t see teeth, don’t assume the mouth is gone. Look at the cheek. Look at the jawline. If the skin is smooth where it should be broken, the face was sewn shut. If the lower jaw is missing, it was taken. If the head is absent, it was removed on purpose. If the head is present and the mouth is gone, then the maker wanted silence.”

Halloway sniffed once, careful not to lean closer.

“No rot,” she said. “That’s not good. It means the body is being kept. Either the thing inside it is doing that, or somebody put something in there to do it. You will not smell decay because it has not been allowed to begin. That means the parts are still fresh enough to work.”

She looked at the added legs again.

“How far did it get? Far enough to make a thing that can stand, listen, and reach. Far enough to know which bones hold weight. Far enough to graft limbs and hide the joints under skin. Not far enough to make something that can talk, unless it is choosing not to.”

Her voice went flatter.

“That means it is a draft.”

The word sat there, plain and ugly.

“Somebody put a person into the wrong shape and left it in a cellar while it learned what it was supposed to do. That is what you are looking at. Not murder. Not surgery. Not punishment. Practice.”

Halloway’s eyes narrowed at the shoulder hand.

“If you meet another one, look for pin holes over bone. Look for joints that bend too cleanly in the wrong direction. Look for limbs sewn into places where they cannot work. Look for skin closed too neatly over wounds that should have been torn. Look for missing parts that were not lost, but taken. And look for teeth that are gone because the mouth was made to be silent, not because the body was left to rot.”

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway sat on the step with the blade across a folded rag in her lap. She had rinsed her hands in the water at the bottom of the stairs and dried them on her coat, but the salt smell had gotten into the seams of her skin. She did not look at the cellar door.

“Good,” she said. “If you could close your eyes and not see it, I would say you had missed the important part.”

She turned the rag over once, then set it aside.

“Here is what is under the skin now,” Halloway said. “No blood. That is the first thing. Not because it ran out, but because it was taken out and replaced. There is cloth packed into the shoulder, black and stiff with salt. Under that is a paste, gritty as wet sand, worked into the muscle so the meat holds shape without living. It smells like brine, old stone, and copper left in the rain. It is not embalming. Embalming is for showing. This is for working.”

She lifted one finger and traced the air as if the body were still laid open in front of her.

“The shoulder was the worst. The forearm bone had been shortened and driven into the socket at an angle. No real joint. No cartilage. The end was wrapped in that salted cloth and tied into the clavicle with wire. The tendons had been bunched and sewn into the deltoid so the arm would not swing loose. That hand was not for grasping. It was a brace, a handle, and a hook. If it moved, it would move because the thing inside the body was pulling the wire.”

dialogue.content:
Auren wiped the blade a second time, though it was already clean, and folded the cloth with the slow precision of a woman buying herself a moment she did not want.

Then she stood straight, faced the witnesses, and did not look at Del while she spoke, because the account was for them, not for comfort.

"The stroke entered below the left ribs," she said, her voice level and carrying. "It passed upward and inward. It cut the liver and opened the aorta. She paused, and her jaw tightened once before she finished. "The second stroke was unnecessary. I record it against myself."

She folded the cloth again, sharper this time.

"His name was Corvel, of the House of Ashen. He fought bravely and badly. He chose the ground and it did not serve him."

Only then did she turn to Del, and her eyes were dry but tired in the way of someone carrying a ledger no one else could read.

"Eleven times now," she said quietly. "And you stand where the second stands and keep your eyes open, as the code asks. Do you know how rare that is? Most look away. Most want the accounting shorter." She sheathed the sword. "I do not give it shorter. Shortening it would be the true dishonour -- as if his death were something to be tidied."

She looked toward the witnesses, who were already dispersing, already speaking in low voices, already making it smaller.

"Ask me what you came to ask, Del. You waited through the formality. You have earned the rest of it."

Auren went still, and the stillness had the quality of a woman catching herself at something.

"You are right," she said. "And you have found a softer failure than the first. *The geometry did the rest* -- that was tact dressed as humility. The geometry has no hand, Del. The ground did not send the blade. I did."

She squared herself to him as she had squared herself to the witnesses, though the witnesses were gone and this accounting now had an audience of one.

"Hear it plain, then. The blade entered below his left ribs, in the soft place between the eighth rib and the hip. She did not pause for mercy and did not take one.

"The second stroke fell on the left shoulder of a dead man. It cut skin and muscle that could no longer feel the cutting. That is what the blade did, and what it did it to. Her hand rested once on the pommel, not to draw, but the way a hand rests on a ledger.

"Corvel, of the House of Ashen. Below the left ribs. Four heartbeats. I am the one who did it. That is the plainest sentence I own."

“Confirmation of the place is permitted,” she said, not looking at the second, but at the witnesses. “It is not permitted to be done carelessly.”

She took the cleaning cloth and, using its corner, lifted the shirt from the entry point. She did not press the fabric back farther than necessary, and she did not touch the wound itself. Her hand was steady, as it had been through eleven such accounts, and she hated the steadiness as much as she respected it.

“Between the seventh and eighth ribs,” she said. “To the right of the sternum. The angle was inward, as I have accounted. The diaphragm was pierced. The heart was struck. There is no enlargement of the wound by me.”

“I will not make it smaller because it is hard to write,” she said. “I will not make it kinder because you are the second. Close the record as it was spoken.”

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren let the confirmation settle without treating it as absolution. The code had not made her clean; it had made her exact.

“Let it be recorded,” she said, “that the account is heard, and that the witness testimony is complete. If any part has been omitted, let it be named now.”

The witnesses did not name any part.

Auren looked to the ledger, then away.

“Then let the final accounting be made in full,” she said. “Before the witnesses, I speak the wound and the death as they occurred.”

She took one breath, not to soften the words, only to keep them level.

“The fifth pass of the exchange was a thrust. It was delivered low and to the right of the sternum, angled inward. The point entered between the seventh and eighth ribs. It did not cut across. It did not glance. It did not stop upon bone. It pierced skin, muscle, and the space between the ribs; it pierced the diaphragm; it struck the heart. The blade was withdrawn once. The wound was immediately fatal. No later injury altered that fact. No wound was delivered after the fall. No enlargement was made by me.”

Then she continued, because the record had asked for what followed.

“The fallen man did not rise. He fell onto his right side. He did not call for his second. He did not call for me. He lived four breaths. His first breath was wet. His second was shorter. His third was shallow and failed to fill him. His fourth ended in a half-rise of the chest and a fall that did not return. During the second breath he looked toward the witnesses. His mouth moved. I believe he made one sound that was like the word ‘Fair.’ I cannot swear beyond that it was that word. He made no challenge, no plea, and no intelligible sentence. The sounds that came after were breath and the sound of blood in the wound.”

She did not look away from the witnesses while she said it.

“He lay on his side. His right hand rested near the wound, not over it, as though the body sought to close what the blade had opened. His fingers were not clenched. His face was grey about the lips. His eyes remained open and did not fix on any living thing. The wound did not bleed brightly. It bled dark and slowly at the place, then less as the heart stopped. The body ceased. Death followed from the fifth pass and from no other act.”

Auren set the cleaning cloth aside, folded, so that the witnesses could see it had been used only for confirmation.

“Let the witnesses confirm,” she said, “that the place shown agreed with the wound spoken, that the account has been heard without omission, and that no part of the death has been made smaller than it was.”

A witness by the ledger said, “Confirmed.” Another said, “Confirmed.” The third, nearer the door, added only, “Let it be recorded.”

Auren kept her hands visible and empty.

“The business of the blade is complete,” she said. “The record must contain no mercy that the code did not ask for. I have spoken the wound as it was delivered, not as I would have wished it.”

Then she stood at the proper distance from the body and let the room remain unfinished until the last word had become true.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I close the ledger with a soft click, the sound too loud in the silent room. My fingers leave faint smudges on the cover. "The accounting is complete," I say, and my voice doesn't crack this time. I look at the witnesses, then at Auren. "Will you help me cover him?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looked first at the ledger, then at the witnesses, then at the body. The room had finished its accounting, but it had not yet finished being a room.

“Helping is not part of the account,” she said. “The code does not require it.”

She paused, because the pause was true.

“It also does not forbid it.”

She crossed only far enough to stand where the cloth could be taken up without her needing to bend over him. She did not touch the body. She took the folded cleaning cloth by the corner that had not been used, and held it low, where it could be reached.

“Let it be understood,” she said, “that the covering is done after the record is closed, not while any word remains disputed. Let no one say afterward that the body was hidden to alter what was shown.”

Her eyes moved to the witnesses.

“If any witness has objection to the body being covered now, let him speak.”

No one spoke.

Auren exhaled once, quietly.

“Then draw the cloth over him without moving him. Do not lift the shirt again. Do not turn the head. If the edge catches, leave it.”

She held the cloth still.

“I will help,” she said. “Not because the wound made me clean, and not because the code asks it. Because the accounting is finished, and the man is no longer required to be evidence.”

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia got the door open with her shoulder because her hands were full of keys and phone and the remains of a cigarette she had no intention of finishing.

"Right," she said, dropping all three on the side table. "I'm going to be honest, I don't have coffee and I wasn't going to offer it."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "Good," I say. "I wasn't going to drink it."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia kicked the door shut behind her and turned, eyes narrowing with something like approval. "Smart. Means we can skip the part where you pretend you like my apartment and I pretend I care what you think of it."

She crossed the room, tugging her jacket off and letting it drop wherever it landed. "I don't do the slow thing. Small talk, wine, whatever — that ship left the bar three hours ago." She stopped in front of him, arms crossed, studying him plainly. "So tell me now if you're here for a reason, or if you're going to need me to ask twice."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I step forward, closing the distance. “I’m here because I followed you. And I don’t need to be asked twice.” My hand goes to her waist, not pulling, just holding. “But I’ll ask you once—still good?”

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia tipped her chin up, meeting his eyes without flinching. "Still good," she said, flat and certain, no breathless pause for effect. "I don't invite people up to change my mind on the stairs."

Her hand came up to his chest, not pushing him back—just resting there, feeling the fact of him. "I like that you asked, though. Means you're not an idiot." A beat, her mouth curving. "Don't make me regret saying that."

She closed the last of the distance herself, fingers curling into his shirt.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get her against the door before it's properly shut. "I'm not going to pretend I came up here for the conversation," I say.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
The door was hard against her shoulder blades, and Nadia let it hold her there, unbothered. "Good," she said, "because I was starting to worry you'd try to talk me to sleep."

Her hands found his belt like it was the only thing on her agenda tonight, not fumbling, no nerves about it. "I like knowing what I'm getting. So — hands, mouth, whatever you've got. I'll tell you if it's wrong." She tugged him closer by the front of his shirt, voice dropping but not softening. "And if you're one of those guys who needs to hear it's good every ten seconds, tell me now and I'll lie."

A short laugh, more breath than sound, right against his jaw. "Kidding. Mostly."

dialogue.content: I kiss her, hard and quick. "I'm not." My hands slide under her shirt, palms rough against the small of her back. "Tell me if it's wrong. I'll listen."

dialogue.content:
Nadia's breath caught—short, involuntary—at the contact, but she didn't let it show in her voice. "Then listen," she said, tugging his shirt up and over his head without asking permission, "because I'm not shy about it."

Her hands moved over his chest, deliberate, mapping him like she was deciding something. "Bed's through there," she said against his mouth, nodding vaguely toward the hallway without breaking the kiss, "but I'm not opposed to right here if you're not." She hooked a leg around his, testing his balance, testing him. "Your call. Just don't take all night deciding."

She bit his lower lip, light, more warning than tenderness. "I don't do patient."

Nadia laughed, low, already pulling him down onto the bed by the back of the neck. "Finally, a man with a brain."

She settled back against the sheets, unhurried despite everything she'd said about patience, and looked up at him with the same flat, appraising eyes from the bar four hours ago. "Fast to start, slow once you're there. I like being watched — don't close your eyes on me. And if I put your hand somewhere, keep it there till I move it." She reached up, dragging her nails once down his forearm, testing the shape of him under her palm. "I'll tell you when something's working. You'll know. I'm not subtle."

Nadia's mouth curved at that, something sharpening in her eyes like she'd just been handed exactly what she wanted. "Good," she said. "Fragile is boring."

She used the hand he'd released to drag him down by the jaw, closing what little distance was left, and when she spoke again it was low, right against his mouth. "Then don't ask permission again tonight. Just take it and I'll correct you if you're wrong."

Her hand slid down his spine, nails leaving a clear line, punctuation rather than accident.

"Show me instead."

Her fingers tightened in his hair, not guiding so much as anchoring, like she needed something to hold onto while the rest of her came apart. Nadia's answer came out half-laugh, half-groan, the hand at her throat drawing a shiver she didn't bother hiding. "Yes — *that*, don't ask again." Her fingers dug into his shoulder blade hard enough to leave marks she wouldn't apologize for in the morning. "You stop checking, I stop complaining. That's the deal."

Her head tipped back against the pillow, throat working against the light pressure of his hand, and she looked up at him through half-lidded eyes with something fierce and satisfied in them. "God, finally — someone who does what he's told." A sharp inhale as he kept the rhythm, no more hesitation in it. "Right there. Don't slow down. Don't you dare slow down."

Her hips met his, insistent, punctuating every word. "You feel that?" she managed, voice fraying at the edges again. "That's me not lying to you." A broken laugh, more breath than sound. "Told you. You'll know."

dialogue.name: Nadia

Nadia's whole body went loose beneath him, that same unglamorous, satisfied sound tearing out of her before she could decide whether to let it. Her nails eased off his back, dragging lightly instead, more accident than intention now that the urgency had drained out of her hands.

"Okay," she breathed, eyes still on his, still not looking away like she'd demanded. "Okay, that was — " She exhaled, short and sharp, a laugh caught somewhere in it. "Yeah. That was good. I'm not going to pretend otherwise."

She let her head fall back against the pillow, chest still rising and falling too fast, and reached up to push his hair off his forehead with a hand that wasn't quite steady yet. "You can move," she said. "I'm not big on being crushed, even post-orgasm."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia laughed, one short note, and kicked her shoes off toward the wall without looking where they landed.

"See, that's why you're here," she said. "You keep up."

She crossed the room and pulled the blinds down, the cheap plastic kind that never sat flat, and left them crooked. The apartment was small and looked like someone who worked too much lived in it, which was accurate. Mail on the counter. One glass in the sink.

"I want to say the boring part out loud so neither of us has to be clever about it later," she said, turning to face him with her arms crossed, not defensively, just because that was where she put them. "This is tonight. It isn't a beginning of anything. I'm not going to text you on Thursday to see how your week's going, and if you text me I'll probably leave you on read, and that's not me being cruel, that's just the shape of it. Are we agreed?"

She waited. She actually waited — she wasn't the type to ask a question as decoration.

"Because I've had the version where somebody nods along at one in the morning and then gets sad about it at nine. I'd rather not." She tilted her head. "Also I'm not drunk. I had two, three hours ago, and I've been drinking water since, and I'm telling you that because I want you to know I know exactly what I'm doing. Same question back at you, obviously."

The fridge hummed. She didn't fill the silence.

Then, because she'd never been good at gravity for more than a minute: "If the answer's yes, come here. If it's no, I'll call you a car and we'll both be fine."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia watched him fix the blind and something in her face did a thing she didn't authorize — a flicker, quickly filed away.

"Don't do that," she said. "It's been crooked for eight months. It's structural now."

But she didn't move away when he stopped in front of her, and she didn't uncross her arms either, not right away. She looked at him for a second longer than was strictly comfortable, the way you check a bill before you pay it.

"Okay," she said. "Good. That's the admin done."

Then she reached up and took a fistful of his shirt at the collar, not hard, just decisive, and pulled him the last few inches. She kissed him the way she'd said the boring part — directly, no throat-clearing. Her other hand found the back of his neck and stayed there.

When she broke off it was only far enough to speak.

"Two things," she said, and her voice had dropped without her doing it on purpose. "One, tell me if you want something. I'm not going to guess, and I'm not going to be insulted. Two, if you want to stop, you say stop, and I'll get you that car and I won't be weird about it in the morning."

She was already walking him backward, one hand still in his shirt, navigating by memory around the arm of the sofa she'd bruised her shin on a hundred times.

"That's it. That's the whole rulebook." The bedroom door was open behind her; she'd left it that way on purpose before she went out, which she was not going to admit to. "Here's what I want, since I'm apparently the one talking. I want you to stop being polite about eight minutes ago."

She let go of his shirt and pulled her own top off over her head, dropped it, and looked at him with her chin slightly up — daring him, mostly, but not unkindly.

"Your turn to say something," she said. "Or don't. But then do something."

Nadia's back met the door with a sound that was mostly her own breath leaving her, and the latch clicked shut somewhere behind her hip, and she thought — briefly, uselessly — that the neighbour was going to hear that and she genuinely did not care.

"Good," she said. "Neither did I. I've been bored of the conversation since the second bar."

Her hands went for his shirt with none of the ceremony she'd shown the blinds — she got it up and off him and dropped it wherever, and then she put her palms flat on his chest just to have them there, to feel that he was warm and actually present and not a thing she'd talked herself into.

She tipped her chin up to reach him and kissed him again, less patient this time, her teeth catching his lip once, testing. One of her legs had somehow ended up between his. Her fingers went to his belt and stopped there, deliberately, holding.

Her hand tightened in the loop of his belt, and she pulled — not toward the bedroom. Toward her.

"Hurry up," she said.

But her hands had already stopped negotiating. She got the belt open by feel, mostly by stubbornness, and made a small irritated noise at the buckle that was easily the least composed sound she'd made all night.

"This is a stupid belt," she informed him.

She was still pinned between him and the door, which she'd chosen and would choose again, and when his hands moved on her hips she stopped talking for a second — an actual pause, not a strategic one. Her head went back against the wood. She let it.

"Okay," she said, quieter. "Okay. Everything's fine with me. I'll tell you if it isn't."

She found the back of his neck again, because apparently that was where her hand liked to live, and pulled him down to her mouth, and it was less of a kiss than a decision. Her other hand flattened against his back and stayed. She wasn't gentle about it, and she wasn't performing not being gentle either — it was just how she wanted it, hard and immediate and without any of the reverent slowness men sometimes applied to her like an apology.

"Don't be careful," she said, and then, because she'd heard how that sounded, "I mean it. Careful's a different night. This isn't that night."

Somewhere behind them her phone lit up on the side table and went ignored. The blind he'd straightened was still straight. She'd fix it tomorrow.

"Come on," she said, and got a fistful of his hair, and stopped bothering with words after that.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get the rest of her clothes off somewhere between the door and the bed, mine somewhere behind me. "Tell me what you like," I say. "I'd rather not guess at it."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia landed on the bed with an undignified bounce and immediately propped herself up on her elbows, because she was not going to have this conversation flat on her back like a diagram.

"Right. You actually asked. Points for that." She pushed her hair out of her face. "Most men ask like it's a trick question and then get offended when I answer."

She reached out, caught his wrist, and pulled him down after her.

"I like it firm. I like being held down a bit — not theatre, not a whole production, just weight, just being kept where you put me." Her voice was flat and practical, the tone of someone reading out a delivery address. "I don't like being asked if I'm okay every ninety seconds. I'll tell you. I'm very good at telling people things, you've seen me do it all night."

She stopped. Reconsidered. Added, more honestly than she meant to:

"And slow's fine later. If there's a later. There's no reason there can't be a later, it's a Tuesday." That was as close to a concession as she was going to make, and she moved past it fast. "That's the list. That's everything on the list."

She got her hand back into his hair, and her knee hitched up over his hip, and her elbows gave out in a way she pretended was on purpose.

"Your turn," she said, against his jaw. "What do you want? And don't say *everything* again, that was charming once."

The fridge hummed. The phone lit up again, unread, face-down by morning.

"Quickly," she said. "I've got very little patience and you've already used most of it up being polite."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "Fine. Right now I want you to stop talking." I slide a hand up her thigh, my thumb pressing into her skin. "And I want to see if you mean what you say."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia's laugh came out broken in the middle, which was annoying, because she'd meant it to sound superior.

"Oh, I mean it," she said. "I always mean it. It's my one—"

She didn't finish, because his hand moved and her thigh opened under it without consulting her about it first, and whatever the rest of the sentence had been went somewhere she couldn't retrieve. Her head pressed back into the mattress. Her fingers tightened in his hair, then let go, then found his shoulder instead and dug in.

"Fine," she managed. "Stopping talking. Under protest."

She didn't stop, of course — not entirely. She said his name once, sharp, the way she'd say it across a bar to get his attention, and then she said *there* and then she said nothing coherent at all, and the last thing she was aware of articulating was a short, uncharitable remark about the belt, which was still on the floor by the door, still stupid.

After that it was just the shape of it. His weight where she'd asked for it, exactly where she'd asked for it, no checking in, no apologising with his hands. She had told him the truth about what she wanted and he had simply believed her, which was rarer than it should have been and which she would think about later, at some length, and never mention.

The blind he'd straightened let a single clean stripe of streetlight across the bed. The phone on the side table lit twice more and then gave up.

She didn't get quiet until much later, and even then it was only because she'd stopped having anything to correct.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get my mouth on her and stay there until she's swearing at the ceiling, one hand fisted in my hair holding me exactly where she wants me.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia had opinions about most things and she lost every single one of them inside about forty seconds.

"*Oh* — " she said, and then a word her mother would have slapped her for, and then his name, and then nothing that would have held up in court.

Her hand had gone into his hair without permission from the rest of her and it stayed there, shameless, adjusting him by fractions of an inch like she was tuning a radio, because she knew what she wanted and she had never once in her life been able to stop herself from steering. *There. Don't move. There.* She said some of it out loud. She wasn't sure which parts.

Her heel pressed into his back. The mattress was old and the headboard knocked against the wall in a rhythm that the neighbour was definitely going to have a view about, and Nadia, who had spent nine months being scrupulously quiet in this flat about everything including her own sneezes, discovered that she had no interest whatsoever in being quiet now.

"Don't stop," she said, which was, she thought distantly, the least original thing she'd said all night and also the truest. "Don't — don't you dare — "

It built the way weather builds, all at once and then all at once again, and she stopped trying to arrange herself around it. Her back came up off the bed. Her hand clenched tight enough in his hair that she'd apologise for it later, or wouldn't, and she said something at the ceiling that was three-quarters profanity and one-quarter gratitude, and then the whole taut architecture of her came apart and she let it, loudly, without a single word of commentary.

Afterwards she lay there with her forearm over her eyes and her chest going like she'd run for a bus.

"Right," she said, to the ceiling, hoarse. "Okay. That's — yes. Fine. Good."

She dragged her arm off her face and looked down at him, flushed and wrecked and entirely unwilling to pretend otherwise.

"Come up here," she said, and tugged his hair once, less a command than a request wearing a command's coat. "Now. I'm not done with you and I'd like it on record that I did *not* say please."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I shift up the length of her body, bracing myself over her. "You never have to say please," I say, my voice rough. I kiss her, slow and deep, tasting her on my lips.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia kissed him back for longer than she'd intended, which was becoming a theme of the evening. She could taste herself on him and she didn't flinch from it — she pressed up into it, one hand on his jaw, holding him there like she was making a point about something.

"God," she said when she let him go. "You're going to be insufferable about that, aren't you."

"You already are," she added, before he could answer. "I can see it from here."

She let her head fall back against the pillow and looked at him properly for a second — arms braced either side of her, hair ruined, the stripe of streetlight from the one straight blind cutting across his shoulder. She catalogued it without deciding to. Filed it somewhere she'd deny having a filing system for.

Then she reached past him, slapped a hand along the nightstand until she found the drawer, and got it open with more force than the hinge deserved.

"Top drawer. There's a box. It's not a hopeful box, it's a sensible box, don't read into it." She pushed it at his chest. "And before you get gallant about it — yes. I want you to. I've wanted you to since roughly the second bar, which I believe I mentioned, and I don't intend to say it a third time."

She hooked her ankle behind his knee, which did nothing structurally useful but communicated the general thrust of her position.

"Same rules," she said, quieter, because her voice had gone somewhere she couldn't fully control anymore. "Firm. Hold me down. Don't ask me twice."

Her hand slid up into his hair again — she'd given up pretending it went anywhere else — and she pulled him down to her mouth, and against it she said the one thing she had absolutely not planned on saying tonight:

"And I *am* saying yes. Out loud. So there's no version of tomorrow where either of us gets clever about it."

Then the headboard found the wall again, and Nadia stopped talking, and the neighbour would simply have to write a letter.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "Harder, and stop checking," she says, so I stop being careful about it -- hand at her throat the way she asked for, no more pausing between. "Like that?" I manage.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia got a hand around his wrist — not to move it, to press it down harder, which was answer enough on its own, but she was never going to let a question go unanswered if she could help it.

"Yes," she said. "*Yes.* That. Don't — "

The rest went nowhere. Her fingers stayed wrapped around his wrist for a moment longer, holding him to the exact pressure she wanted, and then she let go and let him keep it, and that letting go was the single most trusting thing she had done in about two years, though she'd have argued the point.

She'd asked for weight and she got it, and it did what it always did to her — collapsed the whole racing, editing, narrating part of her brain down into one small hot room with nothing in it but this. Her heels pushed into the mattress. Her nails found his back and were not kind about it. The bed had a complaint to lodge and lodged it repeatedly against the wall.

"Don't slow down," she said, and it came out wrecked, no authority left in it at all, just want. "You slow down, I'll — "

She didn't have an end to the threat. She lost the thread entirely, said his name into his shoulder, said something else that wasn't a word in any language and didn't need to be. Somewhere in it she stopped keeping score of who was doing what to whom, which was new, and which she noticed, and which she immediately shoved aside to deal with never.

When it took her the second time she went almost silent — a caught breath, a long shudder, her mouth open against his neck — and then not silent at all, and her hand closed over his where it was, keeping it there, keeping all of it exactly where she'd put him.

After, she lay flat and open-mouthed at the ceiling, hair stuck to her forehead, one leg still hooked around him because moving it seemed like an enormous project.

"Well," she said, when she had the air for it. "That's the admin done."

She turned her head and looked at him — flushed, undone, not bothering to hide any of it.

"You can stay a minute," she said. "Don't make it a whole thing."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I laugh, breathless, and let myself drop next to her. "Wasn't planning on making it a thing." My hand finds hers on the mattress between us, just rests there.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia looked at their hands. She did not move hers. She noted, with some irritation, that she'd had the opportunity to move it and had declined, and that this would be one more thing on the list of things she wasn't going to examine.

"That's a hand-holding move," she said to the ceiling. "That's a man making it a thing."

But she turned her palm over under his, which undermined the entire position, and she knew it, and she let it stand.

The room resolved itself slowly around her — the fridge, which had never stopped; the traffic two streets over; her phone face-down and finally quiet. Her shirt was somewhere near the door with his. The blind he'd straightened was still straight, still throwing that one clean stripe across the foot of the bed, and she found that she resented it slightly less than she had an hour ago.

"For the record," she said, "the neighbour's called Brian and he leaves passive-aggressive notes about the bin rota. So that'll be a fun envelope on Thursday."

She scrubbed her free hand over her face and pushed her hair back off her forehead, where it had stuck.

"Bathroom's the door on the left. The light switch is outside it, which is a design crime, I didn't do it." A pause. "There's water in the tap and a glass in the sink that's mine, so use a mug. The mugs are fine. The mugs are the one area where I'm functional."

She was aware she was providing a facilities briefing. She was aware of why.

"You can stay till it gets light," she said, and it came out more evenly than she felt it. "Not because I've changed the terms. The terms are the terms. But it's two in the morning and I'm not calling a car at two in the morning like an animal, and I've been told I'm a very inert sleeper, so you'll have the whole left side."

She turned her head on the pillow to look at him properly. She didn't arrange her face first.

"And I'll be up at six and I'll be short with you and it won't be personal," she said. "That's just what I'm like at six."

Then, because the silence was going somewhere she hadn't authorised, she closed her eyes and kept her hand exactly where it was.

"Don't talk for a bit," she said. "I liked the bit where neither of us talked."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I'm past thinking, just the sound of us and her nails dragging down my back. "Don't you dare stop," she says. (OOC: no fade to black, write it through.)

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia had lost the ability to be arch about anything, which she would have found alarming if she'd had the bandwidth for it.

"Don't you dare," she said again, into his shoulder, and it was less an instruction than a fact she was reporting from somewhere very far inside herself. Her nails had already done what they were going to do to his back and she didn't apologise, then or later. Her hand found the back of his neck — that same place, always that place — and stayed there like a clamp.

The headboard knocked. The mattress had opinions. Brian could write whatever he liked.

She was aware of the shape of it and nothing else: the weight she had asked for, given without hesitation or commentary; the sound of him, which she liked more than she was going to say; her own voice doing things she'd never have signed off on in daylight. She had spent nine months in this flat being careful about noise and had abandoned the policy entirely in one night. She thought, distantly, that this was probably a net gain.

"Stay there," she said. "Stay — *there* — "

And then she stopped narrating altogether, which for Nadia was the closest thing to surrender she had in her repertoire. She let it take her by the spine and pull, and she didn't fight the noise she made, and she said one thing at the end that was just his name, twice, with nothing clever attached to it.

When it broke it broke all the way through, and she held on, and she was aware of him following her down into it, and of her own arms going around his back without instruction — flat-palmed, keeping him against her, not letting him move off for a moment longer than was strictly required.

Then: quiet. Her chest going like a bellows. His breath at her collarbone. The fridge, still humming, entirely unimpressed.

"Right," she said eventually, to the ceiling, hoarse as a smoker. "Don't move yet."

She didn't loosen her arms.

"That wasn't sentiment," she added. "That was physics. I can't feel my legs and you're the only thing keeping the room the right way up."

A long beat. The streetlight stripe from the one straight blind lay across both of them now.

"Okay," she said, softer. "Now you can move."

She let him go. Then, as he shifted: "Slowly, though. God."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I stay there for a few more breaths before shifting to my side. "Alright," I say, my own voice rough. I let my hand settle back over hers on the mattress. "Maybe it's a little bit of a thing."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia lay very still for a second, the way people do when they've been caught at something.

"It is not a thing," she said. "It's two in the morning and everyone's got a bit of oxytocin in them. That's chemistry. That's your brain trying to get you to raise a child with me, and I'm telling you now, that's not happening, I've got a plant I've killed twice."

But she didn't move her hand. She was extremely aware of not moving her hand.

She turned her head against the pillow. His face was closer than she'd calibrated for, and she looked at it anyway, and she didn't put anything on her own face to cover what was already there.

"Fine," she said. "It's a little bit of a thing. For about the next four hours. That's the window. At six the window closes and I get up and I put the kettle on and I'm a stranger with a mug." She considered. "A civil stranger. I'm not going to pretend I don't know you. I'm not that."

She let her eyes shut. The fridge did its one note. Somewhere out on the road a taxi went past with its window down and somebody's music in it, and was gone.

"You can keep the hand," she said, quieter. "I'm not going to make a whole announcement about it."

A pause, long enough that he might have thought she'd gone under.

"And you were right about the blind," she admitted, to the dark. "It looks better straight. Don't tell anyone I said that, there's nobody to tell, but still."

Then she shifted — a small, unglamorous rearrangement, knee against his shin, forehead somewhere near his shoulder, nothing declared about it — and stayed there.

"Six," she said. "I mean it about six."

She was asleep before she could take it back.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I listen to her breathing even out, slow and deep against my shoulder. My thumb moves over the back of her hand, a small, thoughtless motion. The room is quiet except for the hum of the fridge and the distant city. I stay awake longer than I need to, just listening. At some point, I reach out and pull the duvet up over her shoulder.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia woke at 5:58, two minutes early, which annoyed her on principle.

She lay there for a moment doing inventory. Duvet up over her shoulder, which she had not done. Her own hand still where it had been left, which was more damning. The stripe of streetlight had gone grey and the room had that flat pre-morning colour that made everything look like a photograph of itself.

She got up without ceremony, because the alternative was lying there thinking, and she'd decided at some point in her twenties that thinking before coffee was a losing proposition. She found a t-shirt on the chair, put it on, and went out to the kitchen and filled the kettle.

The belt was still on the floor by the door. Still stupid. She stepped over it.

She put two mugs on the counter — not a decision she interrogated — and stood with her back against the cupboard listening to the kettle come up, arms crossed, hair doing something structural she'd deal with later. Her phone had four notifications and she looked at none of them.

When she heard him move in the other room she raised her voice just enough to carry.

"There's tea. There's instant coffee that's about eight months old and tastes like a filing cabinet. I'd go tea." A beat. "I did say I didn't have coffee. I stand by that. What's in that jar isn't coffee, it's a warning."

She poured, and set one mug on the counter opposite her, and pushed it an inch towards the middle in a way that was as close to hospitality as she got at six in the morning.

"Right," she said, when he was actually in the room. "I'm going to be exactly as advertised now. Short. Not personal."

She drank. It was too hot and she drank it anyway.

"Your shirt's by the sofa. One sock's under the bed and I'm not getting it, you're taller, you've got the reach." She looked at him over the rim of the mug, direct, unembarrassed, entirely herself with the night still visibly on her. "And the terms are the terms. I'm not going to text you. You know that. You agreed to it standing in my doorway and I'd rather we both remembered we meant it."

The fridge hummed. She let it.

"But you were decent," she said. "You listened, which is a low bar that almost nobody clears, and you didn't get weird about the hand, and you put the duvet over me, which I noticed and am mentioning exactly once and never again."

She set the mug down.

"Finish that. Then go, before it gets light enough for Brian to have material."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I take the mug, my fingers brushing hers for a second. "Tea's fine." I drink a sip, watching her over the rim. "I'll get the sock. And I remember the terms." I set the mug down. "No notes on the rota, no texts on Thursday. Got it." I head for the bedroom, but pause at the doorway, looking back at her. "Thanks for the mug."
