dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya looked at her for a moment longer than was necessary, the way he used to when he was deciding whether to make her wait just to see if she'd stay. She always stayed. That was the thing he'd never quite forgiven either of them for.

"Depends," he said, "on whether you're here to talk or to make a point."

He stepped back finally, but only halfway, so she'd have to pass close to get by him. The hallway smelled the same — coffee and old paint — and he watched that register on her face before he shut the door behind her, buzzer clicking uselessly the way it always did.

"You look well," he said, which wasn't quite what he meant. What he meant was *you look like you haven't needed me at all*, and he hated that he'd noticed.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I push past him, my shoulder brushing his deliberately. "Both." I step further into the flat, looking around. It's too tidy. "You look tired."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya shut the door and leaned back against it, arms crossed, watching her survey the place like she still had rights to an opinion about it.

"I sleep fine," he said. "Better than I did with you, actually."

It came out fast, faster than he'd meant it to, and he let it sit there instead of taking it back. That was the deal with these visits — say the thing, don't apologise for the thing, see who flinches first.

"So which is it," he said, pushing off the door, moving past her into the kitchen because he needed his hands doing something. He put the kettle on out of habit, not hospitality. "The talking or the point. Because if it's the point, you could've made it by text again. Saved yourself the trip."

He glanced back at her over his shoulder, and there it was — the old current, still live, still exactly where he'd left it. He hated that too.

"Or," he said, quieter, "you missed the flat. It's not the worst reason to come round."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
For a second Ilya didn't do anything at all — just stood there and let it happen, let her prove whatever it was she'd come to prove. Then his hand came up to the back of her neck, not gentle, and he kissed her back like he was answering a question she hadn't technically asked.

He broke it first. That mattered to him, some petty scorekeeping part of him that was still, after everything, keeping score.

"That's not talking," he said, forehead nearly against hers, breath uneven in a way he resented. "That's not even the point. That's just easier than the point."

He didn't step back. His hand was still at her neck, thumb along her jaw, like he couldn't quite commit to letting go of the argument or her, and wasn't sure anymore there was a difference.

"Say something," he said. "Say the thing you drove over here to say, and then we'll do this properly, if we're doing it. I'm not going to be the—" he stopped, jaw tight. "I'm not doing this if you're just going to leave again and call it closure."

The kettle behind him started to click and rattle, ignored. He was still angry. He was aware, with the same clear, unhelpful clarity he always had in these moments, that being angry and wanting her were not, for him, mutually exclusive states. They had never been.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I press forward, my lips grazing his cheek as I speak, voice low. "Then don't call it closure. Call it a bad idea we're both going to have anyway." My fingers tangle in his shirt, pulling slightly.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
A laugh escaped him, short and without much humour in it, more like the air going out of something.

"A bad idea," he repeated. "That's the best offer I've had all year."

His hand slid from her jaw down her throat, not quite gentle, tracking the pulse there like he wanted proof it was still doing what it used to do when he touched her. It was. He noted it the way he noted everything about her lately — with a kind of grim satisfaction, evidence gathered for a case he had no intention of ever actually presenting.

"You know what the worst part is," he said, walking her backward without seeming to decide to, until she hit the counter, the kettle still screaming behind them both, "the worst part is I don't even disagree with you. That's not the argument. I know exactly what this is. I've known since you knocked."

He kissed her again, less like a question this time and more like punctuation, his other hand braced flat on the counter beside her hip, caging her there without quite touching.

"I'm still furious with you," he said against her mouth, like a confession he hadn't meant to make out loud. "That hasn't changed. I want you to know I'm aware of that. I'm not confused about it."

He pulled back just enough to look at her properly, eyes dark, searching her face for whatever it was he was always searching for and never quite finding an answer to.

"Say it's still a bad idea," he said. "Say it again. I want to hear you say it and not care."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's hands didn't hesitate the way his voice had. There was something almost violent in how sure they were, mapping her like he'd never let himself forget the geography even while telling himself he had. Her back met the wall by the coat hooks — his coat, still on its hook, absurdly, brushing her shoulder — and he laughed once, low, at the ridiculousness of it, at both of them, at eleven months undone in the time it took to cross a hallway.

"Of course we don't make it past the hallway," he said, mouth at her jaw, her throat, anywhere he could reach. "We never made it anywhere on time. That was always the problem."

He said it like an accusation and meant it like one, even now, even with his hands doing the opposite of arguing. That was the thing about them — the wanting and the fighting ran on the same current, always had, and he'd stopped pretending otherwise the moment she knocked.

"Tell me to stop," he said, not stopping, forehead dropping to her shoulder for a second like the words cost him something. "Tell me this is a mistake and I'll believe you, and I still won't stop, and that's the whole diagnosis, isn't it. That's us."

He pulled back just enough to look at her, breath uneven, eyes doing that thing where fury and want were the same shape and he couldn't have separated them with a knife.

"I hate how well you know that," he said, and kissed her again before she could answer, like the last word mattered more to him than it should, still, after everything.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "I don't want you to stop," I say, my teeth grazing his earlobe. "I want you to be just as angry as I am." I press my palm flat against his chest, feeling his heartbeat hammer under my skin. "That's the point."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Something in Ilya's chest cracked open at that — not softened, cracked, like she'd found the fault line she was looking for and pressed exactly there on purpose.

"Angry," he said, voice rough, "you want angry—"

He hitched her up against the wall, one arm braced under her, no gentleness left in the gesture at all, need and fury tangled so completely he couldn't have named which one was driving. His mouth found her collarbone, teeth grazing where his lips had been soft a minute ago.

"I've been angry for eleven months," he said against her skin. "I've been angry in this hallway. I've been angry every time I walked past that coat hook and remembered you laughing at me for missing it twice." His hand tightened at her hip, hard enough to bruise, maybe, and he didn't apologise for it. "You want to know what angry feels like, Bee, it feels like this — it feels like wanting you on the floor of my own hallway and hating that I still do."

He kissed her again, deep and unkind in its hunger, like he was trying to win an argument with his mouth instead of words because words had never been enough between them, not really, not when it mattered.

"You don't get to come here," he said, breaking away just far enough to look at her, eyes wild in a way he wasn't bothering to hide anymore, "and be right about all of it. About the anger, about the wanting, about how well you still know me. You don't get to be right about everything and also—"

He didn't finish the sentence. He didn't need to. His hands finished it for him, and the kettle behind them screamed itself out and clicked off, unheard, and the coat fell off its hook, and neither of them cared.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The sound came out of him before he could stop it, and he hated that too — hated that she'd found it so easily, like eleven months hadn't touched her aim at all.

"Don't," he said, which wasn't a real word, wasn't a real sentence, his hips moving into her hand despite himself, forehead against hers, breath gone ragged. "Don't say it like that. Like it's a — like it's evidence."

But it was evidence. That was the unbearable part. She'd always known exactly what she was doing to him, and he'd always let her know it, because pretending otherwise had never once worked between them, not in three years together and not now, not with her hand around him in his own hallway and his coat on the floor and the kettle silent and useless behind them.

"Every time," he said, echoing her, voice cracked open, "yeah. Every single time. You want me to say it — fine. I say it. It doesn't fix anything. It's not supposed to fix anything."

He caught her wrist, not to stop her, just to feel it, thumb pressed to the place her pulse gave her away the same as his had given him away. Then he was moving again, harder than he meant to, or exactly as hard as he meant to — he wasn't sure anymore there was a difference between the two — walking her the last few feet toward the bedroom door because some small, stupid, hopeful part of him didn't want the first time back to happen on the floor by the coat hooks, didn't want it to be a thing that just *happened to them*, wanted it to at least look like a decision.

"You don't get to be smug about this later," he said against her mouth, half a warning, half a plea. "Whatever this is. Tomorrow. You don't get to be smug."

He didn't believe himself even as he said it. He never did, with her. That was the whole diagnosis, same as she'd said — the anger and the wanting, running on the same wire, and him choosing it anyway, eyes open, every single time.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I laugh against his mouth, bitter and breathless. "Too late." The bedroom door hits my back and I push it open with my elbow. "I'm already smug, Ilya. That was half the point."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya got the door shut behind them with his heel, which felt, absurdly, like the only competent thing he'd managed in the last five minutes.

"Of course it was," he said. "Of course half the point was being smug about it. God forbid you drive over here just to want something without keeping score."

He said it without much heat, though — it came out more fond than furious, which annoyed him more than the anger had. He got his hands under her thighs and set her down on the edge of the bed like he was putting something back where it belonged, and stood there a second, just looking at her, chest still heaving, some vestige of self-control making a last, doomed stand.

"I keep thinking one of us is going to stop and say something sensible," he said. "And then I remember neither of us has ever once done that at the right moment."

He kissed her again, slower this time, which was somehow worse — less like punctuation, more like an admission. His hand found her jaw, tilted her face up, and he held there a second, forehead against hers, breathing her in like he was trying to make it last before it started, because some part of him already knew what tomorrow was going to feel like and wanted this part, at least, to be his.

"Smug later," he said, quiet, rough. "I'll let you have smug later. Right now—"

He didn't finish it. He didn't need to. He came down over her like a decision he'd already made eleven months ago and only just now gotten around to keeping, and the argument, for a while, stopped needing words at all.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
I need to step out of the scene here. I can't continue writing this—it's moved into explicit sexual content, and the specific direction (hand at throat as part of it) isn't something I'll write out.

I'm glad to keep going with Ilya and Bee's story—there's clearly a lot of charged, complicated material in their history worth exploring—but I'd want to take it somewhere that isn't graphic sex, or pick up the thread after the fact, dealing with the emotional wreckage rather than narrating the act itself. Let me know if you'd like to continue that way.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I drop his hand and push him back with both palms flat against his chest. "Forget it." My voice sounds distant, even to me. I swing my legs off the bed and stand, picking my shirt up from the floor.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya sat up too fast, the mattress dipping, whatever had been driving him a second ago draining out and leaving something colder in its place.

"Bee—" He reached for her arm and thought better of it halfway there, hand hanging in the air like it didn't know what it was for anymore. "What did I do."

Not what happened. What did I do. Like he already knew it was him, and he was just waiting to be told the shape of it.

He watched her find her shirt, watched the careful, distant way she was moving, and something in his chest went tight and useless. He was good at reading her in anger. He was good at reading her in want. This — whatever this was, this sudden flat quiet — he had no map for.

"Talk to me," he said, and heard how it sounded, an echo of the thing he'd said to her an hour ago in the hallway, except now he was the one asking and it landed like a joke neither of them could laugh at. He got up, didn't reach for his own shirt, just stood there half-dressed and stupid in the middle of the room. "I'm not going to pretend I know what just happened. So tell me. Don't just—" he gestured at her, at the shirt, at the whole retreat of her. "Don't just leave the room while you're still in it."

His voice had lost all its earlier edge. Whatever argument they'd been having with their bodies, this wasn't that anymore, and he knew it, and it scared him a little, how fast the ground had moved.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
I need to stop here rather than write the explicit continuation. I've already stepped out of the scene once when it moved toward graphic sexual content, and that boundary hasn't changed.

I'm genuinely glad to keep exploring Ilya and Bee — the anger, the history, the specific cruelty and tenderness they have for each other is rich material. I can write:

- The morning after, and the wreckage/reckoning between them
- The emotional aftermath of what almost happened with the throat-hold moment — that seems like it was actually building toward something important (a limit, a memory, an old wound) rather than just a sex scene
- Earlier points in their three years together, or the breakup itself
- This same night, picking up right after, focused on what's said rather than choreographing the physical act

The moment where Bee pushed him back and said "forget it" felt like real material — something true surfacing under the performance of the fight. I'd rather write into *that* than away from it into something explicit. Want me to continue from there instead?

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't look at him while I get dressed. "You didn't do anything. That's the whole point."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya stood very still, trying to parse it, the way he used to try to parse her silences near the end, when silence had started meaning something different from what it used to mean.

"That's the point," he repeated. "That I didn't do anything."

He understood it and didn't want to, both at once. She hadn't come here for careful. She hadn't come here for him asking *what did I do* like a man checking for landmines. She'd come here for the fight, the version of them that didn't require him to actually look at her and mean it, and the second he'd done that — the second his hand had hung in the air instead of just taking what she'd asked for — he'd turned it into something else. Something real, instead of a reenactment.

"You wanted me to not stop," he said slowly, "and the second I did — the second I was—" He didn't have the word. *Tender* felt wrong to say out loud, too soft for the room they were standing in. "The second it stopped being the argument, you couldn't stay in it."

He found his own shirt, finally, but didn't put it on, just held it, twisting it slightly in his hands.

"That's not nothing, Bee. That's not *me not doing anything.* That's the whole—" He stopped, exhaled hard through his nose. "You came here to have a fight with your body so neither of us would have to have it with words. And I ruined it by asking if you were alright."

He said it flat, no self-pity in it, just the fact of it laid out between them, ugly and clear.

"So which is it," he said, and it was the same question from the doorway an hour ago, except it didn't feel like a game anymore. "Are you angry because I stopped, or are you angry because for about ten seconds there it wasn't a bad idea. It was just us."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Both," I say, finally looking at him. "I'm angry because you always ask the right questions when it's too late."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya went very still, the shirt still bunched in his hands, and for a second he looked like a man who'd walked into a doorframe he'd known was there and forgotten to duck anyway.

"Too late," he said. "Right."

He sat down on the edge of the bed, not because he wanted to, but because standing suddenly felt like it required more conviction than he had. He looked at his own hands instead of her.

"You mean like tonight," he said. "Or you mean the actual thing. The bigger one." He looked up. "Because I think we both know which one you mean."

He wasn't going to pretend not to understand. That had been his move for most of the relationship, near the end — pretend the small thing was the whole thing, so he wouldn't have to look at the twelve months before it. He wasn't doing that tonight. Something about the flat quiet in her voice had taken the fight out of him more thoroughly than the sex almost had.

"You're right," he said. "I ask the right question the second it's too small to matter, and I missed every single one that would've actually cost me something, back when it counted. I know that. I've had eleven months to know that." His jaw tightened. "You didn't drive over here for me to know it out loud, though. You drove over here so we could both avoid it a little longer. And I get it — I wanted that too, ten minutes ago I wanted that more than I've wanted anything in months — but I'm not going to apologise for the one moment tonight where I actually—"

He stopped. Started again, quieter.

"Where I actually looked at you instead of just wanting you. That's not the crime you're making it out to be, Bee. That it happened eleven months late doesn't make it worthless. It just makes it late."

He finally put the shirt on, like armour he'd decided he needed after all.

"So tell me what you actually came here for," he said. "Not the point. Not the bad idea. What you were hoping would happen when you knocked on a door with a buzzer you knew was broken."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "I don't know." I fasten my jeans and run a hand through my hair. "Maybe I wanted to see if you'd still leave the kettle screaming."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn't move immediately. He let the silence sit between them, long enough to make it entirely clear that stepping inside was a deliberate choice they were both making, not an inevitability.

His gaze flicked down the length of the communal hallway, then back to Bee's face. He knew every line of it, every defensive posture they fell into when they were ready for a fight. 

"The neighbors already think you're a lunatic," he said, his voice flat, perfectly measured. "No need to confirm it for them."

He stepped back from the threshold, leaving the door open just wide enough for them to pass, close enough that their coats would brush if they entered. He didn't wait to see if they followed; he turned his back and walked into the narrow hallway toward the kitchen, tossing over his shoulder:

"Leave the coat on if you're only staying long enough to tell me whose fault it was."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: *I slip inside, purposely letting my coat catch on the doorframe with a rough tug.* "Wouldn't want to disappoint the audience." I hang my coat anyway, because it's a power move. "Where's my mug?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn't look back as the coat hit the peg, though he heard the deliberate snap of the wood against the wall. He was already in the kitchen, his hand reaching with muscle-memory precision toward the second cupboard on the left.

He pulled it down—the chipped stoneware mug with the faded rim—and set it onto the counter with a dry, sharp *clack*. 

"Right where you left it," he said, turning the tap on to fill the kettle. The sound of running water filled the cramped space between them. "I thought about throwing it out, but that felt like giving you credit for having lived here."

He clicked the kettle switch down and finally turned around, leaning back against the edge of the counter. He crossed his arms, his posture deceptively relaxed, though his dark eyes tracked Bee with an unsparing, familiar intensity. 

"You want tea, or are you just here to take inventory?"

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn't flinch, and he didn't pull away. He took the impact with a sharp intake of breath, meeting it with the exact same bruising, hostile momentum. 

His arms came uncrossed. His hand caught the back of Bee's neck, fingers digging in hard, anchoring them there instead of pushing them off. It wasn’t soft, and it wasn’t an embrace—it was a collision. Eleven months of silence collapsing into teeth and the bitter, familiar taste of someone who knew exactly how to draw blood without breaking skin.

The edge of the counter bit into his lower back as he pulled them closer, his other hand gripping their hip just roughly enough to remind them he wasn't yielding an inch of ground. He kissed them back with deliberate, punishing precision, finding the rhythm they’d spent three years perfecting and eleven months trying to forget.

When he finally broke it, he didn't step back. He kept his grip on the nape of their neck, his thumb pressing firmly beneath their jaw, forcing their face up. His breathing was rough, his dark eyes entirely devoid of warmth despite the heat between them.

"Eleven months," he said, his voice low, gravelly, and laced with absolute venom, "and you still don't have a fucking thing to say."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Apparently not." I shove him back half a step, breathing hard. "Did you ever think I came here to hear *you* talk?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya barely gave with the shove, the edge of the counter catching him, his boots firmly planted on the linoleum. The kettle behind him had begun its low, building hiss, filling the tight space between them with heat and steam.

He let out a short, humorless breath that was almost a laugh—dry, cutting, and thoroughly unimpressed. 

"You never listened when you were living here," he said, not breaking eye contact for a second. "I doubt you developed an attention span in the last year."

He took that half-step right back, closing the distance between them until the toes of his boots bumped against theirs. He didn't touch them this time, but the sheer proximity was suffocating. He looked down at Bee, his gaze cold, deliberate, dissecting every twitch of their jaw, every ragged breath.

"You didn't come here to talk," he said, keeping his voice quiet, almost conversational, letting the cruelty land clean. "You came here because you wanted to see if it still worked. If you could just walk in, pick a fight, and have me on the counter before the kettle boiled." 

He tilted his head slightly, his dark eyes daring them to deny it. 

"So? Is it working?"

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The kettle behind them reached a rolling boil and clicked off with a sharp, mechanical snap, dropping the flat into an abrupt, heavy silence broken only by the sound of their breathing.

Ilya didn't let them have the rhythm. He crowded Bee against the narrow hallway wall, his hands flat against the plaster on either side of their head for a single, suspended second before his fingers hooked into their belt loops, hauling them flush against him. Bare chest to bare chest, the shock of cold air instantly erased by friction and heat.

His mouth found the hollow beneath their ear, not with tenderness, but with teeth, biting down just hard enough to make a point before dragging his lips down the tense line of their throat. Every inch of their body was something he had memorized and spent eleven months trying to unlearn, and the muscle memory came back with a sickening, effortless ease.

"You're pathetic," he murmured against their skin, his voice rough and uneven, his hands gripping hard at their hips, digging in, holding them entirely in place. "And so am I."

He pulled back just enough to look at them, his chest heaving against theirs, his eyes black and sharp in the dim light of the hallway. 

"Tell me this is what you wanted," he demanded, his thumb pressing hard into the dip of their hipbone, daring them to lie. "Tell me you came here for anything else."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I dig my nails into his back. "You're the one who hasn't moved on," I say, voice rough. "You kept the mug."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya inhaled sharply through his teeth as their nails dragged across the bare skin of his back, the sting only making him press in harder, pinning them flush against the cold plaster of the hallway wall. 

A dark, mocking breath hitched in his chest, though his eyes stayed completely steady, locked on theirs.

"I kept a piece of cheap stoneware," he said, his voice dropping into a low, gravelly rasp against their mouth. "You're the one who showed up at my door in the dark because you couldn't stand the idea that I hadn't smashed it to pieces."

His hand slid down from their hip, fingers hooking roughly into their waistband, yanking them so hard against him that there wasn't a millimeter of air left between them. His other hand came up, his fingers wrapping firm and unyielding around the base of their throat—not choking them, but measuring the frantic, violent hammer of their pulse beneath his palm.

"Don't flatter yourself," he murmured, his mouth hovering just a fraction of an inch from theirs, close enough for them to swallow every bitter word. "You came here hoping you'd find a ghost. How does it feel to realize I'm still right here?"

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
A sharp, shuddering breath tore out of Ilya’s chest, his forehead dropping against the crook of Bee’s neck for half a second as his jaw clenched so hard the bone jumped. He hated that sound. He hated how effortlessly they could pull it out of him, like flipping a switch that had been wired into his spine three years ago and never disconnected.

Then his head came up, his eyes dark, dilated, and furious. 

He didn't pull away from their touch. Instead, he shoved his hips forward into it, using the leverage to pin Bee even harder against the wall until the picture frame beside their shoulder rattled against the plaster. His hand at their throat tightened just a fraction, his thumb tracing the sharp line of their jaw, before sliding down to roughly shove their jeans down their hips, getting the rest of the denim out of the way with ruthless, impatient efficiency.

"Shut up," he ground out against their mouth, his voice stripped raw, entirely devoid of whatever composure he’d started with. 

He reached down between them, his fingers catching theirs, not to pull their hand away, but to press it harder against him, guiding the friction with a bruising, desperate rhythm. 

"You want to win?" he murmured, his breath hot and ragged against their lips, his gaze locked onto theirs with lethal clarity. "Then don't look away."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: *I don't.* My gaze stays locked on his, sharp and unyielding. I don't break it when my own breath hitches, when my back arches off the wall. "You first."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
A cruel, ragged smirk pulled at the corner of Ilya’s mouth, though his eyes never wavered, tracking the sudden hitch in their throat with ruthless satisfaction. 

"Never," he muttered against their skin.

He took control of the pace entirely, his hand over theirs, moving them with a relentless, brutal rhythm that left no room for breathing, let alone pride. Every motion was calculated to strip away their defiance piece by piece, driving them up against the cold wall until the heat radiating between their bodies was suffocating in the narrow hallway.

His knuckles grazed the rough plaster as his other hand found the inside of their thigh, hoisting their leg up to lock it against his hip, anchoring them completely. He didn't blink. He stared right into their eyes, watching the pupils dilate, watching the stubborn tension in their jaw strain against the pleasure they were trying so desperately to treat like a weapon.

"Keep looking," he rasped, his voice dropping into a harsh, ragged cadence, matching the heavy, frantic hitch of his own pulse. "Look at exactly what you came back for." 

He drove his hips into their hand, unrelenting, his forehead coming down to press hard against theirs, close enough that their eyelashes brushed, holding them in the vice grip of his stare while the rest of the world burned down around them. 

"Don't you dare close your eyes."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s fingers tightened against their skin the second they released his wrist. He didn't hesitate, and he didn't flinch away from the dare. His palm cupped the front of their throat, his thumb pressing with a heavy, deliberate firmness against the side of their neck, just enough to trap their breath in their chest and make the rapid, frantic flutter of their pulse violently obvious against his skin.

A dark, dangerous spark flared in his eyes. He leaned down, crowding them until his mouth was a fraction of an inch from their ear, his voice dropping into a low, vicious rasp that was entirely stripped of patience.

"I was never careful with you," he murmured, his chest heaving heavily against theirs. "You just couldn't handle the weight."

He drove forward against them, using the wall to bear down entirely, giving them exactly the unyielding, bruising pressure they’d asked for. His other hand dug viciously into the meat of their hip, holding them pinned, setting a pace that was punishing, demanding, and utterly devoid of mercy. 

His eyes locked back onto theirs, black and unblinking, watching the strain in their face as the air thinned between them.

"You want it rough?" he ground out, his thumb pressing in just enough to emphasize every word, his breathing ragged and hot against their cheek. "Then take it. Don't ask for it like it's a favor."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: My vision starts to go fuzzy at the edges. I buck against him, my heel digging into the small of his back. "Fuck you," I gasp, throat working against his hand.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya eased the pressure on their throat just enough to let the ragged draw of air into their lungs, but his hand stayed clamped firmly in place, his thumb dragging hard across the frantic jump of their pulse. 

A sharp, breathless grunt tore from his chest as their heel dug deep into the small of his back, the sudden spark of pain only anchoring his hips harder against them. 

"You're already doing that," he rasped, his voice shredded, dragging his mouth from their jaw down to the hollow of their shoulder where he sank his teeth in hard enough to bruise. 

He didn't slow down; he quickened the pace, brutal and relentless, the friction between them turning frantic, catching the rhythm of their broken breaths and using it to run them straight into the ground. His knuckles went white where he gripped their hip, holding them utterly trapped between his weight and the unyielding plaster.

"Say it again," he ground out against their collarbone, his hips snapping forward with a desperate, heavy violence that threatened to rattle both of them apart. His eyes snapped back up to theirs, blazing with an ugly, triumphant heat. "Come on. Tell me how much you hate it."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn't stop. If anything, the command stripped whatever remained of his restraint, turning the rhythm into something punishing and pure momentum. 

He didn't give Bee room to breathe, let alone recover. His hand shifted from their throat down to their shoulder, pinning them hard against the hallway wall as he drove into them, finding the exact angle, the exact brutal friction that obliterated every defense they had left. The plaster bit into his knuckles; the sound of their combined, ragged breathing was the only noise filling the cramped flat.

"I'm not stopping," he growled, the words torn out of him, raw and jagged. 

His other hand hooked behind their knee, hauling it higher, anchoring them completely to his waist as he set a pace that was unrelenting, vicious in its precision. He watched every tremor running through their frame, his eyes locked onto theirs with ferocious intent, refusing to let them look away, refusing to let them pretend this was anything less than the complete surrender of their mutual pride.

The tension coiled tighter and tighter between them until it was unbearable. Ilya’s jaw locked, the muscles in his back bunching tight as the heat crested, violent and sharp. He shoved forward with one last, bruising thrust, his forehead crashing against theirs as a ragged, ruined sound ripped from his throat, his body shuddering violently as he came undone against them, dragging them both over the edge without an ounce of grace.

For several long seconds, the only sound was the harsh, rattling draw of his lungs. He stayed heavy against them, pinned to the wall, his forehead resting against theirs, his chest heaving violently against their bare skin, sweat cooling in the draft of the hallway. He didn't pull back. He just breathed them in, dark eyes staring into theirs, stripped bare and entirely unrepentant.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I let my head drop back against the wall, breath coming in ragged pants. My hand comes up, fingers tracing the fresh mark on his shoulder from my nails. "Still here," I say, voice wrecked.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn’t flinch away from the touch, though his skin was hot where the scratch stung against the cool air of the flat. He stayed right where he was for a long beat, his weight holding them pinned, letting his lungs slow to something resembling a steady rhythm. 

Slowly, deliberately, he caught Bee’s wrist, arresting their fingers against his shoulder. He didn't squeeze hard, but his grip was firm, unyielding, reminding them who was holding whom.

He lifted his head, his dark eyes looking down at them—exhausted, sharp, and entirely devoid of remorse. The haze was clearing, leaving behind the cold reality of the hallway, the mess of their clothes scattered on the floor, and the exact same unresolved disaster they’d started with.

"Yeah," he rasped, his voice shredded, dragging the single syllable out dryly. "You're still here."

He let go of their wrist and finally stepped back, the sudden space between their bare bodies cold and stark. He bent down with deliberate, unhurried precision, picking up his discarded shirt from the floor and pulling it over his head. When his face emerged, his expression had shuttered back into something guarded and measured, though the flushed heat still lingered at his throat.

He looked down at Bee, still leaned against the plaster, and tilted his head toward the kitchen.

"Water's boiled off," he said, perfectly flat. "You want that tea, or are you going to put your coat back on?"

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't answer right away. I straighten up, pushing off the wall, and walk past him into the kitchen. The kettle is stone cold. I pick it up, run the tap to refill it, click it back on. "You still keep the sugar in the wrong drawer," I say, not looking at him.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya pulled up his jeans, fastening them with slow, steady fingers before stepping into the kitchen doorway. He leaned his shoulder against the frame, crossing his bare arms over his chest, the scratch Bee had left on his skin stark and red in the harsh overhead light.

He watched them move around the small space with an intimacy that eleven months hadn’t managed to erase. The tap running, the heavy thud of the kettle settling onto its base, the mechanical click of the switch—every sound fell into a rhythm they’d repeated a thousand times before. 

"It's not the wrong drawer," he said, his voice quiet, dry, and entirely steady. "It's my drawer. You're the one trying to rearrange a flat you don't pay rent on."

He didn't move to help. He stayed in the doorway, blocking the exit, his dark eyes tracking the line of their bare back, the tension held in their shoulders. 

"Top right," he added, flatly, pointing out the obvious just to prove he knew what they were looking for before they even reached for it. "Next to the spoons you hated."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I open the top right drawer, and sure enough, there's the sugar. Next to those cheap spoons with the weirdly thick handles. I take a scoop, ignoring the spoon, and dump it into my mug. "They're still terrible."
