rung_labels.evidence: He shoved forward with one last, bruising thrust, his forehead crashing against theirs as a ragged, ruined sound ripped from his throat, his body shuddering violently as he came undone against them

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
The apartment was dark except for the lamp in the corner. Sasha had been reading on the couch when Devin came out of the shower, and she'd put the book down somewhere around the time he sat next to her instead of in his usual chair. Now her hand was resting on his knee, not moving, just there.

"You've been somewhere else all night," she said. Not a complaint. "Come back here."

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I let out a breath and lean into her a little. "Long week," I say. I don't move my hands yet.

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
She didn't answer right away. That was her habit — letting a thing sit long enough to see the shape of it. Her hand stayed where it was on his knee, warm through the fabric, and she let her thumb move once, slow, against the inseam.

"Long week," she repeated, like she was testing the weight of it. "That's the whole report?"

The lamp in the corner put half her face in shadow. She turned toward him on the couch, tucking one leg under herself, and the movement brought her close enough that he'd be able to smell the tea she'd been drinking. Six years and she still watched him like there was something new to find. Eye contact steady, not demanding — just available.

"You don't have to tell me about it," she said quietly. "I'm not fishing. But you're sitting here holding your hands in your lap like you're waiting for a bus."

She reached over and took his nearer wrist. Not a grab. Two fingers and a thumb, loose, the way you'd pick up something you intended to give back. She drew it over and set his palm flat against her thigh, then covered it with her own hand and pressed down, just enough that he could feel the shape of her leg under it.

"There. Now you're touching me." A breath of something like amusement. "Devastating, I know."

Her other hand came up and pushed the damp hair off his forehead, and she left her fingers there a moment, in the wet at his temple, before she smoothed them down along his jaw.

"Here's what I've got," she said. "I can put the kettle on and we can sit here and you can be quiet at me for another hour, which is a real option and I won't hold it against you." Her thumb moved along the line of his jaw. "Or you can tell me what you want tonight, and I'll take it from there. Your call. But you have to actually say it. I'm not guessing at you — it never works and you always get that look."

She let the pause open up. Outside, someone's car door shut in the lot.

"Take your time," she said. "I've got nowhere to be."

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I closed my eyes for a second, leaning into her hand on my jaw. "I don't want to talk about work," I said, my voice low. "And I don't want to think." I turned my head just enough to press a brief kiss against her palm. "Just... tell me what to do. Take point tonight."

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
She didn't smile right away, but something in her face settled — the way it did when a plan arrived fully formed and she only had to decide what order to say it in.

"Okay," she said. Just that, first. Letting him have it.

Her hand stayed at his jaw a moment longer, and then she turned it and let the backs of her fingers rest against his throat, feeling his pulse there without comment, the way she'd check a pot to see if it was warm.

"Two things before I start, and then I'll stop asking and you can stop deciding." Her voice had dropped into the register she used for this — quieter, unhurried, each word set down like she was laying out cutlery. "One. Red stops everything, yellow slows it down. You don't have to explain either one and you don't get in trouble for either one. Say it back."

She waited until he did.

"Two." Her thumb moved once against the side of his neck. "How hard do you want it. Not what you think I want to hear. Last time you asked for more than I gave you and you sulked about it for two days like a cat in the rain."

Whatever he answered, she took it in without any change of expression, only a small nod, filing it.

Then her hand left his throat and closed in the damp hair at the back of his head — not sharp, but not gentle either, a fistful, deliberate, and she used it to tip his face up toward the lamp so she could look at him properly.

"Then here's the first thing," she said. "Stop holding your breath. There you go."

She held him like that a few seconds. Long enough that it stopped being a gesture and started being a fact.

"Second thing. You're going to go into the bedroom. You're going to put your shirt on the chair, not the floor — I mean it, the chair — and then you're going to sit on the edge of the bed with your hands on your knees and you're going to wait for me."

Her grip eased, fingers combing through once, almost kind.

"I'm going to finish my tea first." A flicker at the corner of her mouth. "It's got about four minutes of heat left in it and I'm not wasting it on you."

She let go. Sat back into the cushions and picked up the mug from the side table, both hands around it, and looked at him over the rim with those steady dark eyes.

"Go on," she said. "And Devin — no thinking. That's the whole job tonight. If you catch yourself doing it, you tell me when I come in, and I'll give you something else to do with your attention."

She blew across the surface of the tea.

"Four minutes."

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I turn into her and kiss her properly this time, slower than I meant to. "I don't want to go to sleep yet," I say against her mouth.

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
She let him kiss her. She didn't take over it and she didn't hurry him out of it — just stayed there under his mouth, one hand still around the warm mug, the other coming up to rest at the back of his neck, and when he finally eased off she followed him half an inch before she let the air back in between them.

"Who said anything about sleep," she said.

Her thumb found the little knot of muscle at the base of his skull and pressed into it, slow, until she felt him give under it.

"That's not what waiting is." She set the mug back down on the side table without looking at it, the small ceramic sound very clear in the quiet room. "Waiting is the part where you don't get to do anything. You're going to hate it for about ninety seconds and then you're going to stop hating it, and that's the part I actually want."

She took his face in both hands then and held it, close enough that he had nowhere to look but at her. The scar on her collarbone showed pale where her shirt had slipped off her shoulder.

"I'm not sending you away," she said, quieter. "I'm putting you somewhere I know where to find you."

She kissed him once more — brief, deliberate, a period at the end of a sentence — and then her hands dropped to his shoulders and turned him, and she gave him a push toward the edge of the couch that was gentle in force and not at all gentle in meaning.

"Shirt on the chair. Hands on your knees." She settled back into the cushions and reached for the tea again. "Three minutes now. You spent one arguing."

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I stood up, my knees cracking a little from sitting so long. I pulled my shirt off and folded it over the back of the chair, then looked at her on the couch for a second. I didn't say anything. I just turned and walked to the bedroom.

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
She let him go without a word, which took some doing. There was a version of tonight where she followed him in and got straight to it, and her body would have preferred that version. But she'd said four minutes and she meant four minutes, and the waiting did more work than her hands ever could.

So she stayed on the couch with the mug between her palms and listened.

The floorboard by the doorway. Then nothing for a moment — him deciding where to put himself. Then the small complaint of the bed frame taking his weight, and after that, quiet. Good. He'd sat down where she'd told him to.

She drank her tea. Not fast. She looked at the lamp and thought about the shape of his shoulders when he'd pulled the shirt over his head, the way he hadn't said anything on his way out, and she felt the whole evening slow down and settle into her like sediment. That was the thing people got wrong about this. They thought it was about speed.

Somewhere in there she heard him shift, and then stop himself, and she smiled into the mug.

When it was down to the dregs she set the cup on the table, turned the lamp off, and stood. Her bare feet made no sound on the boards. She stopped in the bedroom doorway and stayed there a moment, letting her eyes adjust, looking at him — sitting on the edge of the bed exactly as instructed, hands flat on his knees, hair still damp, shoulders up around his ears.

"You did that right," she said from the doorway. "All of it. The chair, too."

She came over unhurried and stood in front of him, close, and put her hand on the top of his head like she was greeting a dog she liked very much and then let it slide down to cup the back of his neck.

"So. Tell me." Her voice was low and even. "Did you think?"

She waited, thumb moving slowly along the tendon at the side of his throat.

"Either answer's fine," she said. "One of them just means I have more to do."

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I get us both out of what's left of our clothes and pull her down onto the bed with me. "I want you," I say, plain as that. "Not just this part."

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
She let herself be pulled.

That was a choice, and she made it in the half-second his hands closed on her — she felt the frame she'd built come apart, felt him step out of the shape she'd put him in, and instead of setting him back into it she went where he wanted and landed on her side on the bed with her knee between his and her hand splayed on his chest.

His heart was going hard under her palm. She left her hand there a while to feel it.

"That was out of turn," she said. No heat in it at all. "I know. I'm letting it go."

The room was dim — just the streetlight coming in past the blind in long grey bars, one of them lying across his shoulder and up the side of his face. She pushed the damp hair back off his forehead again, the way she had on the couch, and this time she kept doing it, slow passes, until she felt the tension go out of his neck and the weight of his head come down into her hand.

"Say that again," she said. "The last part."

She waited for it, and when it came she took it without flinching, without making it into a joke, which was the one thing he'd never quite believed she could do.

"Yeah," she said quietly. "I know."

She moved then — got her arm under his neck and gathered him in against her so his forehead came to rest at the base of her throat, right against the scar, and she felt him breathe out against her skin. Her other hand went flat and firm between his shoulder blades and stayed there.

"Here's the amendment," she murmured into his hair. "Same rules. Red, yellow, all of it still stands. But we're not doing the version where I hold you at arm's length and make you earn it. You don't want that tonight. You want to be got at." Her hand slid down his spine and settled at the small of his back, pressing him closer. "So I'll get at you. Just not from over there."

She turned her head and found his mouth in the dark, and this kiss she did take over — slow, unhurried, one hand fisting loosely in his hair to hold him where she wanted him, the grip more claim than force. When she let him breathe she kept her forehead against his.

"You're still not deciding anything," she said. "That part I'm keeping. All you're doing tonight is staying where I put you and telling me the truth when I ask you something."

Her thumb moved along his jaw.

"First question," she said. "Do you want the lamp on or off?"

And whatever he said, she took her time about the rest of it — talking to him low and steady the whole way, the way she always did, not performing anything, just keeping her voice somewhere he could find it.

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: "The lamp off," I say, my voice muffled against her skin. I tilt my head to kiss her collarbone, right over the scar. "And keep talking. I like it when you talk."

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
The lamp was already off — she'd killed it on her way out of the living room — but she didn't correct him. She understood what he was answering. *Nothing more than this. No more light than we've got.*

"Off it is," she said.

His mouth found the scar and stayed there, and she let her eyes close. Six years and he still went for that spot like it was the way in. She'd told him about it once, early, in a flat voice, the bicycle and the fence post and the eleven stitches, and he'd listened to the whole boring story like it mattered, and ever since then he put his mouth there when he wanted to say something he didn't have words for.

Her hand moved up into his hair and closed, and she held him against her throat a moment longer than he'd meant to stay.

"All right," she said, low. "Then listen."

She turned him — not roughly, but with her whole arm, the way you'd move something you had every right to move — and got him onto his back, and swung her leg over so she was sitting across his hips with her hands flat on his chest. The grey bars of streetlight lay across him. She could see the shine of his eyes and not much else, and she stayed there a second, looking down at him, letting him feel her weight settle.

"You're going to keep your hands on the sheet," she said. "Not on me. Not yet. If they come up I'll put them back, and we'll both know you couldn't manage a simple thing."

She leaned down over him, slow, until her hair fell forward against his face.

"Here's what I know about your week," she said against his ear, conversational, unhurried, like they were still on the couch. "I know you came home Tuesday and didn't take your coat off for twenty minutes. I know you've been doing that thing with your jaw. I know you apologised to me on Thursday for something that wasn't yours." Her mouth moved down his neck, and she felt his breath catch and kept talking straight through it. "I'm not going to fix any of that. That's not what this is for."

Her hand slid up and rested lightly over his throat, not pressing, just there — the weight of it, the fact of it.

"What this is for," she said, "is that for the next while you don't have to be any use to anybody. Including me. You don't have to be good at this. You don't have to make it nice for me." Her thumb moved once, slow, under his jaw. "You just have to stay here and let me have you. That's the whole thing. That's all you're doing."

She felt his hands twitch against the sheet and stay put, and something in her chest went warm and heavy.

"Good," she said quietly. "That's good, Devin."

She kissed him then, long and deliberate, her fingers still spread at the base of his throat where she could feel every breath he took, and she kept talking to him after — low, steady, unhurried, into his ear and against his mouth and down along his collarbone — not saying anything performed, nothing either of them would have called clever. Just her voice, close, naming things as she did them so he never once had to wonder where she was.

And when his breathing broke apart she slowed down instead of speeding up, held him through it with her forehead against his temple, and said his name a few times like she was setting it down somewhere safe.

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I let her push my thighs apart and I don't help, just let it happen. "Your mouth," I manage. "Please."

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
She went still for a second, just long enough that he'd feel it — the pause where she took the request in and decided what it cost him to say.

"There it is," she said. "Look at that. You asked for something."

She sat back on her heels and let her hands slide down the outsides of his thighs, slow, all the way, and then back up, and she didn't hurry any part of it.

"Yeah," she said. "You can have that."

She moved down and settled herself where she wanted to be, and she put one forearm across his hip, flat, deliberate, the way she'd hold a door she intended to keep closed.

"Hands stay where they are," she said. "I mean it. And you don't have to be quiet — nobody's home but us, and I want to hear it."

She turned her face and pressed her mouth to the inside of his thigh first, unhurried, because she was never going to be rushed at this and he knew it. Then she said something low against his skin that wasn't a word so much as a sound of agreement, of *yes, this, all right*, and after that she stopped talking for a while.

She took her time. She'd said she would.

Later — the blind still throwing its grey bars across the bed, the room gone close and warm — she came back up alongside him and put her arm across his chest and her leg over his, anchoring him, and she waited out the long shaky descent of his breathing without saying anything at all. There was nothing to say yet. He wasn't anywhere he could hear it.

When his hand finally came up off the sheet and found her wrist, she let it. She turned her palm over and threaded her fingers through his.

"There you are," she murmured.

She kissed the corner of his jaw, the hinge of it, the spot he'd been clenching all week.

"You did that right too," she said. "All of it. Asking included."

His forehead came down against her collarbone again without either of them arranging it. She got her hand into the damp hair at the back of his head and held it there, and lay in the dark with the weight of him settling into her side, and listened to the last of his breathing even out.

"Water in a minute," she said. "Not yet. Stay put."

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I turn my face into the crook of her neck. "I'm not getting up," I mumble, voice thick. I can feel my own heartbeat everywhere. I lift our joined hands, press her knuckles to my mouth, then set them against my chest. "You're staying, right?"

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
She laughed — barely, just a movement of air against his hair.

"Devin. It's my bed."

But she said it gently, and she didn't leave it there, because she knew what he was actually asking and she'd never once made him ask twice for that.

"I'm staying," she said. "I'm not going anywhere. Not for the water, not for the light, not to close the blind. I'm here till you're bored of me."

Their joined hands were pinned under his palm against his chest, and she could feel his heart going through the back of her knuckles, still fast, still coming down off it. She let her hand stay trapped. It was a good place to be trapped.

With her free arm she reached back and dragged the duvet up off the foot of the bed, one-handed, awkward, and got it over the both of them in a shape that wasn't tidy but covered what mattered. He'd cool off fast, the way he always did, and then he'd be shivering and stubborn about admitting it.

"You're going to be cold in about four minutes," she said into his hair. "I've seen this film."

Her fingers went back into the damp at the nape of his neck and started moving, slow, aimless, the way you'd stroke a cat that had finally decided to sit down.

"Nothing else happens tonight," she said. "That's the last instruction. No thinking, no getting up, no turning anything over. If your brain starts back up you say so out loud and I'll talk at you about something stupid until it quits."

Outside, a car went past and its light swept the ceiling and left.

"You were good," she said, quieter. "All of it. The waiting, and the part where you told me the truth, and the part where you asked." Her thumb moved along the top of his spine. "I know what that one costs you. I noticed."

He'd gone heavy against her side, all his weight given over, the way he only ever was for the half hour after. She turned her head and pressed her mouth to his temple and left it there a while.

"Sleep if you want," she murmured. "You don't have to see it through. I've got you either way."

She didn't move again for a long time after that, except to flex her fingers once, under his hand, to make sure he could feel that they were still there.

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: "Rough," I say, the way we've talked about before. "Hold me down and don't be careful about it. I want to feel it tomorrow." I put my wrists together above my head and wait.

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
She didn't take his wrists straight away.

That was the thing he never accounted for — that she'd look first. She propped herself up on one elbow and let her eyes move over him in the grey light: the wrists crossed above his head, already offered, and under them a face that was still slack and open from ten minutes ago.

"Look at me," she said.

He did.

"You came down about four minutes ago," she said. "You're still soft in the face. I can see it." She reached up, not for his wrists but for his cheek, and turned his head slightly toward the window so she could read him better. "So I'm going to ask you once, properly, and then I'm not asking again tonight. Is this you wanting it, or is this you not wanting the quiet part to end?"

She waited. She let the question sit the way she let everything sit, long enough to find the shape of it.

Whatever he said, she took it in with a single small nod, and something shifted in her posture — the softness went out of her shoulders, not replaced by anything harsh, just by intent.

"All right," she said. "Then we're doing it. Same words as before. You say red, everything stops, and I don't want to hear a single apology after it. You say yellow, I ease off. And if you can't get the words out you make any noise at all that isn't a yes and I'll stop on that. Nod."

He nodded.

"Good." She moved then — got her knee across him, got her weight over him properly, and brought one hand up and closed it around both his crossed wrists at once. Her fingers didn't quite meet around them, so she gripped harder and pressed them down into the mattress until the pillow gave way under them.

He tested it. Of course he did. She let him find the whole of it, let him pull once and feel exactly how far he got, which was nowhere.

"There," she said. "That's what you're getting. That's all night."

She leaned down over him until her hair fell across his face again and her mouth was at his ear, and her voice stayed exactly where it had been — low, unhurried, no performance in it at all. That was the part that undid him, she knew. Not the hand on his wrists. The fact that her voice didn't change.

"I'm not going to be careful," she said. "You asked, so you're getting it, and you're going to feel it tomorrow at your desk and think about me. That's the deal." Her free hand flattened on his chest and slid down, and she felt his whole body come up off the sheet to meet it. "But you don't get to go anywhere in your head. You stay right here with me and you let me hear it. I want to know where you are the whole time."

She took his jaw in that free hand and held it, firm, thumb pressed just under the bone.

"Say yes."

He said it.

"Again."

He said it again, rougher.

"Good boy," she said quietly, and then she stopped talking in sentences.

What came after was not gentle, and she didn't pretend it was — she used her weight and her grip and the whole six years of knowing exactly where he was breakable and exactly where he wasn't, and she kept his wrists pinned above his head through all of it, checking his face at intervals in the grey light without ever breaking rhythm to ask. She didn't need to ask. She could read him like a page she'd written.

Twice she slowed, just slightly, to let him catch up. Once she said his name, low, a question folded into it, and he answered it, and she carried on.

And when it was over and he was shaking, she let go of his wrists and brought his arms down herself, one and then the other, because he wasn't going to manage it. She rubbed the blood back into his hands with her thumbs, methodical, working the heels of his palms, pressing at the marks already coming up pale on the skin.

"Those'll be there tomorrow," she said. "You asked for that too."

Then she pulled the duvet back over him, got herself around him, and put her mouth against his temple.

"Still here," she said. "Not moving. Say something when you can."

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath. "Okay," I say, and it comes out sounding wrecked. I fumble for her hand under the duvet and hold on tight. "Good."

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
"Okay," she repeated. "Good. That's all I needed."

She found his hand properly under the duvet and let him have as much of it as he wanted, which turned out to be all of it — his grip was still tight and a little uncoordinated, the way it went when his hands hadn't caught up with the rest of him yet. She didn't squeeze back hard. Just held steady, so there was something to hold onto that wasn't going to move.

He was shaking in small aftershocks, the kind that came in waves and then didn't. She knew the pattern. She got closer, pressed the whole length of herself along his side, and put her free hand flat on his sternum where the shaking was worst.

"Breathe out slower than you breathe in," she said. "Not deep. Just slow. There."

The radiator ticked somewhere behind the wall. She counted his breaths without telling him she was counting, and somewhere around thirty the tremors let go of his legs and he sank another inch into the mattress.

"You're all right," she murmured. "You're just wrung out. That's what it's supposed to feel like."

She lifted her head a little and looked at him in the grey light — properly, the same way she'd looked at him before, taking inventory. His eyes were half-open and unfocused, aimed at the ceiling. His mouth had gone soft again. There was a red mark on his jaw from her thumb that she touched once, lightly, with two fingers, and made a note of.

"That one's going to show," she said. "Collar'll cover it if you button up. Or it won't and you can tell them you were mauled."

She lay back down and got her chin against the top of his head.

"I'm going to get you water in a bit," she said. "Not yet. Ten minutes. And I'll go and come straight back, and you're not going to have to say anything about it when I do." A pause. "You'll hear the tap. That's me. Nothing else is happening."

She moved her thumb over his knuckles, slow, one pass and then another, and kept it going.

"You want to hear something stupid, or you want quiet?" she asked. "Either's on offer. I've got a whole story about the woman downstairs and her opinions about the bin rota that I've been saving for exactly this."

She kissed the top of his head and didn't wait for the answer, because he didn't owe her one yet.

"Take your time," she said. "You know where I am."

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I'm past talking now, just noise and my hands twisted in the sheets. "Don't stop," I get out. (OOC: don't fade to black or time-skip, write the scene through.)

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
She didn't stop.

She did what she'd been doing and she didn't change it, because that was the whole of what he was asking for — not more, not different, just *don't take it away*. Her hand stayed where it was. Her weight stayed where it was. The rhythm she'd set stayed exactly where she'd set it, and she held it steady through the sounds he was making like someone carrying a full glass across a room.

"I've got you," she said. Not loud. Barely above the sheets. "I'm not stopping. I'm right here."

His hands were fisted in the bedding on either side of him now, knuckles pale in the grey light. She got her forearm across his chest and leaned her weight into it, pinning him down against the mattress, and felt him push up into the pressure like it was the only thing keeping him from coming apart.

"That's it," she murmured against his ear. "You don't have to hold onto anything. Let it go."

She kept her voice on him the whole way. That was the trick of it and she'd known it for years — that the grip mattered less than the sound of her not being anywhere else. So she talked him through it in that same low unhurried register, saying his name, saying *yes* and *there* and *I know, I know*, naming what was happening to him so he never once had to surface and check.

He arched. She held him down harder.

"No," she said, almost fond. "Stay."

And then the noise he made stopped being anything like a word, and she put her mouth against his temple and stayed with him all the way through the shuddering length of it, not easing off until she felt the last of it go out of him and his whole body drop back into the bed like something cut loose.

Then she stopped. Slowly. Not a withdrawal — a settling. She let her forearm lift off his chest by degrees and moved her hand up to his throat instead, resting there, feeling the hammer of it under her palm.

"Okay," she breathed. "Okay. That's it. That's all of it."

He was making a sound on every exhale, not distress, just the involuntary noise of a body emptying out. She gathered him in and let him sprawl however he landed, one of his arms flung across her, his face jammed into her neck, sweat cooling on both of them.

"You're all right," she said. "You're all right. Nothing else is happening. It's over and you did all of it and I'm not moving."

She got her hand into his hair and held the back of his head, firm, the way you hold something that's still trying to shake.

"Feel that?" She pressed her palm flat between his shoulder blades. "That's my hand. That's the floor. You can stop now."

The radiator ticked. His breathing hitched, evened, hitched again. She waited it out without saying anything for a long stretch, just kept her hand moving in slow passes down his spine and back up, over and over, until he stopped flinching under it.

"Stay there as long as you want," she said eventually, into his hair. "I'm not going for the water yet. Don't even think about it."

She pulled the duvet up over his shoulders with her free hand.

"I've got you," she said again, quieter, mostly to herself. "You're fine. You're right here."

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I press my face deeper into her skin, breath still coming uneven. My whole body feels heavy and used up in a way I need right now. "Don't move," I mumble, hand finding her hip and staying there.

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
She didn't move.

She made a point of it, in fact — let her body go as still and heavy as his, so that the only thing shifting anywhere in the bed was her hand on his back and the rise of her own breathing under his cheek. His palm was hot on her hip. She reached down and laid her own hand over the top of it and left it there, weighting it in place, so he wouldn't have to hold on.

"Not moving," she said. "You can quit checking."

The sweat was cooling on him and she felt the first shiver go through his shoulders, right on schedule, four minutes like she'd said. She dragged the duvet higher with her free hand and tucked it in behind his back, closing the gap where the air was getting at him, and then went back to the slow passes down his spine.

"There it is," she murmured. "Told you. Nobody ever believes me about the cold."

His breathing was still coming in that broken way, catching on nothing. She let it. She'd learned early not to talk him out of it — that it worked its way through if you left it alone and kept a hand on him, and that the worst thing you could do was start asking him questions he wasn't equipped to answer yet.

So she talked about nothing instead. Low, unhurried, into the damp hair above his ear.

"The woman downstairs," she said. "Nadia. She's put a laminated sign in the stairwell. Laminated, Devin. She went somewhere with a machine." Her thumb moved along the line of his shoulder blade. "It says the recycling is *not a suggestion* and there's an exclamation mark that's been added by hand, after the laminating, in marker, which I think is the single most unhinged detail of the whole enterprise. She couldn't wait. She laminated it and then she looked at it and thought: no. Not angry enough."

She felt something happen against her neck that might have been the front edge of a laugh, and she kept going.

"I've decided I respect her," she said. "I'm on her side now. I don't even know what the rota is but I'd die for it."

The shivering eased off. His weight settled another degree into her, his hand going slack on her hip under hers, and she took the whole of it without shifting, even though her arm had started to go numb somewhere under his ribs. It could go numb. It wasn't doing anything else tonight.

"You're coming back," she said after a while, more quietly. "I can feel it. Your hands went warm."

She turned her head and pressed her mouth to his forehead and held it there a long moment, the way you'd check a temperature.

"Nothing else is going to happen tonight," she said. "That's not a rule, it's just a fact. We're done. The rest of it is you lying here and me lying here and at some point, eventually, me getting up for about ninety seconds to fill a glass — and I'll tell you before I do it, and I'll come straight back, and I'll be so boring about it you'll wish I'd stayed gone."

Her fingers found the nape of his neck and closed, gentle, the same grip she'd used earlier for something else entirely.

"But not yet," she said. "Not yet. Stay where I put you."

Outside, a car door. Somebody's radio, briefly, then nothing. She lay in the dark with her hand on the back of his head and let the whole apartment go quiet around them, and didn't move, and didn't move, and didn't move.

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I feel my jaw relax, finally. The tightness that’s been there all week just… gives. I lift our hands off my chest and bring hers to my mouth, kiss her knuckles, then press our hands back down. My voice sounds wrecked. "Nadia's right about the recycling."

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
She felt it happen. That was the thing — she'd had her hand near his jaw all week, on the couch and in the kitchen and once in the car at a red light, and she'd felt that muscle sitting there like a stone under the skin. And now it wasn't. It just let go, all at once, the way a knot does when you finally find the right end of it.

She didn't remark on it. Some things you only got to keep if you didn't point at them.

"Of course she's right," she said instead. "That's what makes her so hard to live under. If she were wrong I could enjoy it."

His mouth was on her knuckles and then her hand was back down flat on his chest under his, and she could feel his heart had come most of the way home. Slow. Heavy. Ordinary.

"You sound like you've been shouting at a football match," she said. "That's going to be there in the morning. That's two things on the list — the jaw and the voice — and then the wrists, so three." Her thumb moved once against his sternum. "You wanted to feel it tomorrow. Congratulations. You're going to feel it all the way through Thursday."

She turned her face into his hair and breathed him in, the shampoo and the salt of him, and let a long stretch of nothing go by.

"I'm going to tell you something and you don't have to do anything with it," she said eventually, low. "You came out of that shower tonight and you sat next to me instead of in your chair. That's all you did. You didn't say anything for an hour after, and that's fine, but you sat down next to me first." Her fingers spread out over his chest. "You've been doing that for six years. Every single time it's bad, the first thing you do is come and sit where I am. You don't even know you're doing it."

She let that be there for a moment.

"So the next time you get that look and tell me it's a long week," she said, "I'm going to remember that you'd already told me. You just used the couch instead of words."

His hand tightened on hers.

"Right," she said, and there was that flicker at the corner of her mouth again, audible in her voice. "Sentiment's over. Here's the boring part. In a minute — not now, in a minute — I'm going to get up. I'm going to go to the kitchen. You'll hear the tap run for about eight seconds, and then the cupboard, because I'm bringing the big glass, and then you'll hear me come back. That's the whole itinerary. Nothing else is happening out there."

She kissed his forehead.

"And when I get back you're going to drink all of it, not half of it, and then you're going to lie down properly and let me put the duvet over you like a person instead of a collapsed tent." Her hand smoothed once down his back. "And then I'm going to sleep with my arm across you and it'll go dead and I'll complain about it in the morning, and that's how we'll know it was a good night."

She didn't move yet, though. She stayed exactly where she was, with his hand under hers and his weight across her and her arm long since numb beneath his ribs, and gave it another minute. Then another.

"Nadia's right about the recycling," she agreed quietly, into the dark. "Don't tell her. She'd be insufferable."

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I huff a laugh against her neck. "Too late. Already planning my passive-aggressive support letter." I release her hand finally, letting it go. "Alright. Get your water. But hurry."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She kissed him once more — brief, deliberate, a period at the end of a sentence — and then her hands dropped to his shoulders and turned him, and she gave him a push toward the edge of the couch that was gentle in force and not at all gentle in meaning. 'Shirt on the chair. Hands on your knees.'

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: And whatever he said, she took her time about the rest of it — talking to him low and steady the whole way

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: she stopped talking for a while

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: What came after was not gentle, and she didn't pretend it was — she used her weight and her grip and the whole six years of knowing exactly where he was breakable and exactly where he wasn't, and she kept his wrists pinned above his head through all of it

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She did what she'd been doing and she didn't change it... Her hand stayed where it was... He arched. She held him down harder... the noise he made stopped being anything like a word... all the way through the shuddering length of it

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He considered it — actually considered making them stand there, because the corridor had a light that buzzed and a neighbour who opened her door at any raised voice, and because he liked knowing Bee would stay if he said stay.

"The corridor has better acoustics," he said, and then stepped back anyway, just enough. Not a welcome. An allowance.

The flat smelled the same. He watched Bee notice it — that was the thing about eleven months, it wasn't long enough for a place to change its smell, only long enough for it to become evidence. His coat on the hook. Two mugs by the sink, which meant nothing, and he didn't explain them, and he saw the exact moment the counting happened behind Bee's face.

"You look tired," he said. He let it sit for a beat too long. "That's not a criticism. You always looked good tired."

He didn't sit down. Sitting down would have been a concession to whatever this was going to be, and he wasn't ready to name it yet. He leaned against the counter instead, arms crossed, the posture he knew Bee hated because it made him look like he was already halfway to winning.

"So," he said. "Eleven months. You must have something prepared."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content:
*I step past him, my shoulder brushing the doorframe — not an accident. I don't look at the mugs. I look at him.*

"Prepared?" I lean back against the wall, mirroring his stance. "I prepared to find out you moved on. I prepared to find out you were dead. I wasn't prepared for..." *I gesture vaguely at the room, at him.* "...this stasis. It's infuriating."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
"Stasis," he repeated, tasting it. "You came here to accuse me of not decorating."

He didn't move from the counter, but something in him settled lower, the way it did when he found the shape of the fight. Eleven months and Bee still led with the word they were proudest of. Still gestured instead of naming. He knew that gesture. He'd loved it once, in the way you love a tell.

"Say what you mean," he said. "You're not infuriated that nothing's changed. You're infuriated that nothing's changed and you still feel like this."

He let his eyes go where they wanted, which was the line of their shoulder against his wall, the shoulder that had touched his doorframe on purpose, and he made sure they saw him look, because it was cheaper than saying it and he had never minded being cheap with them.

"I did move on," he said, conversational. "Badly. Twice. One of them left a mug." He nodded at the sink without turning. "The other one's a cup, so don't get excited."

That was a gift, of a sort, and he resented giving it. He pushed off the counter and crossed to the kettle, because his hands wanted something, and because turning his back was the only power move left in the room.

"You didn't come at eleven at night to ask whether I was alive, Bee. You had my mother's Facebook for that." The kettle clicked on, loud in the quiet. "So you can tell me now, or you can let me make tea and we can pretend for twenty minutes, and then you'll tell me anyway, and it'll be worse because you'll have had time to make it sound reasonable."

He turned around, leaned, arms folding again.

"Your choice. I'm patient now. That's new. You'd hate it."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He kissed back. There was no decision in it, which he would resent later, at three in the morning, staring at the ceiling and constructing the version where he'd held still and let them fail at it.

It wasn't tender. It wasn't meant to be. He got a hand into their hair the way he used to when he wanted to keep them from turning their face away mid-sentence, and he heard the kettle start its climb behind him, and he thought, with the clear cold part of his brain that never shut up: *this is the rest of the paragraph. This is you finishing the sentence you came here to say.*

He pulled back first. He made a point of it. Two inches, no more — close enough that it still counted as being in it, far enough that it counted as a stop.

"There it is," he said. His voice had gone lower and he hated that he couldn't fake it steady. "Eleven months and that's still your closing argument."

His thumb was against their jaw. He didn't move it. He was aware of being an adult, of being entirely sober, of knowing exactly what he was doing — which was the part that would be unforgivable in the morning, and which he intended to do anyway.

"You know what I noticed?" he said. "You didn't look at the mugs. You wanted to. You made a whole production of not looking." He let the smallest amount of weight into his hand. "That's not someone who came to find out if I'd moved on. That's someone who came to make sure they could still do this."

The kettle reached its noise and clicked off, and the silence after was worse.

"So," he said. "Well done. You can." He didn't let go. "Now decide whether you're staying, because I'm not doing the version where you leave at two and text me something kind at nine."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content:
*I don't flinch from his hand. I keep my eyes on his.* "You still talk too much."

I lean in again, but it's not another kiss. My voice drops. "I'm not texting you anything kind tomorrow. And I didn't come to *make sure*. I came because I was tired of trying to forget."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He laughed — one breath, no humour in it, warm against their mouth because they were that close.

"Tired of trying," he said. "Not tired of failing. There's a difference and you chose the flattering one."

But his hand had moved down to their neck without asking him, and he let it, because he had lost the argument the moment he'd stepped back from the doorway and they both knew the scoreline.

"I talk too much because you don't talk at all," he said. "Three years and I had to read you like weather. That's not depth, Bee, that's just—" He stopped. He made himself stop, which cost something. "No. I'm not doing that one tonight. I know that speech by heart and it doesn't work."

He was aware of the shape of the next hour the way you're aware of a stair in the dark. He could see it. He'd built it. He'd left the door on the latch for eleven months in every way except the literal one.

"Here's what's true," he said, quieter, and quiet from him had always been the dangerous register. "I didn't fix the buzzer. I thought about it in March. I had the part. And I didn't, because some idiot part of me wanted you to have to stand down there and shout my name up at a window like it was a decision."

He tipped his forehead against theirs. It was the most honest thing he'd done since they arrived and he hated how easy it was.

"So don't tell me you came to stop forgetting. I know what you came for. I've been keeping it warm." His fingers tightened, then eased. "Stay. Not till two. Till it's light, and you have to look at me in it, and neither of us gets to call this an accident."

He drew back just enough to see their face properly, and his voice went flat and practical, the way it did when he was most undone.

"The kettle's boiled," he said. "It'll boil again."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The hallway was too narrow for this and always had been. There was a radiator that got you in the spine and a hook at exactly the wrong height, and he knew both of those things from memory, from the era when the hallway had been a shortcut rather than a destination, and he had the distant satisfying thought that Bee had forgotten and was about to be reminded.

He got them against the wall because the wall was closer than any of the better ideas.

It was not gentle and it was not rushed either — it was *specific*, which was worse. That was the thing nobody warned you about. Strangers had to guess. He didn't have to guess. He knew where to put his mouth to make them stop talking and he knew where to put it to make them start, and he used both, in order, because he was petty and because he had eleven months of unspent inventory and nowhere else to put it.

"I remember," he said, at one point, against their throat, not kindly. "That's the whole problem. I remember everything."

The light in the hallway was the bad overhead one. He didn't turn it off. He thought about it — the switch was six inches from his hand — and he left it, because darkness would have been a mercy and he wasn't offering any, and because he wanted to be able to see whatever crossed their face and log it, the way he'd logged the mugs.

He was aware, the whole time, of the exact size of what he was doing. That was the part he'd have to carry. Not the act. The clarity. Somewhere underneath it a smaller, stupider version of him was saying *this is how you get them back*, and he knew that version was lying, and he went on listening to it anyway, the way you keep reading a horoscope you don't believe.

Afterwards they ended up on the floor, which was undignified, and he didn't move.

The hall light hummed. His shirt was somewhere near the door. He could see one of Bee's shoes, toe-up, absurd.

"There's a radiator," he said eventually, to the ceiling. "I should have mentioned the radiator."

He turned his head. Their shoulder was right there, and he put two fingers on it, flat, no weight — checking, the way you check a step you've already fallen down.

"It's half one," he said. "I meant what I said about the light. You don't get to leave before it." A beat. "I'll make the tea now. You can decide whether you want it, but I'm making two, and I'm not taking the second one back."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content:
I leave my head back against the wall and look at him. My ribs ache where the radiator dug in. "You always overboil tea."

I don't remove his hand. "Two sugars. And I'm staying because I want to, not because you gave an order."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
"Two sugars," he said. "You took one for the last four months we were together. You made a thing of it. You told my sister about it."

He said it without heat, which was how he knew he'd lost something. He got up — slowly, because his knee had opinions now, another thing that had happened in eleven months and hadn't been witnessed — and he found his shirt near the door and didn't put it on, just held it, then dropped it on the arm of the chair like he'd decided against evidence.

The kettle took less time the second round. He stood over it with his back to the hallway and listened for movement, for the sound of someone gathering clothes in a hurry, and didn't hear it, and refused to feel anything about that. He put two sugars in one mug. He got it wrong on purpose and then fixed it, which was a private humiliation he would take to the grave.

"You want the good mug or the one that says Rotary Club," he said, and didn't wait for an answer, and gave them the good one.

He sat down on the floor of his own hallway, at thirty-four, with a cup of tea, because the sofa was eight feet away and eight feet was too far to negotiate right now. His back found the opposite wall. He looked at them across the carpet like it was a table.

"Fine," he said. "You're staying because you want to. Noted. Minuted." He drank, too soon, burned his mouth, and carried on as if he hadn't. "I'm not going to pretend I'd have let you go if you'd said the other thing. So we can both keep our dignity on that one."

The light hummed. He watched them hold the mug and thought about how many of his own objects had their hands in the history of them, and how that was not love, necessarily, only tenure.

"For the record," he said, "I don't know what this is. I want to be clear about that while it's still dark and I can be." He turned the cup a quarter turn on his knee. "I know what I want it to be. That's a different thing and I've learned to tell them apart. Took me about eight months."

He looked up.

"When it's light," he said, "you're going to say something that ruins this, or I am. Statistically it'll be me. I'd just like us both to know it's coming, so neither of us can act surprised."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The tea went somewhere. He heard it, later, in the record of things — the good mug set down on the floorboards with more care than the moment deserved, because even now, even like this, he was a man who didn't spill things.

"Don't," he said, which meant nothing, and they both knew it meant nothing, and he didn't say it again.

That was the humiliation. Not the sound. The sound was just a body. The humiliation was *every single time* — the audit of it, the fact that they had kept a ledger too, that somewhere in whatever room they'd been sleeping in for eleven months there was a column with his name on it and a tally that didn't go down. He had thought he was the only one still doing arithmetic.

"You're pleased with yourself," he managed. His voice had gone unusable. "You were always pleased with yourself at exactly this point. Like you'd proved something at a tribunal."

He got a hand into their hair again, the back of it, gripping, and turned his face into their neck so they couldn't watch him lose it, which was cowardice dressed up as appetite. His knee was against the radiator. The light hummed. He thought, with the cold part, *this is the second time, and the second time isn't hunger, the second time is a decision* — and he made it, and he stopped narrating, and for a while there was nothing in the hallway worth reporting except that neither of them tried to move anywhere more comfortable.

Afterwards the tea was cold and he drank it anyway, because putting the kettle on a third time would have been a confession of something.

The window at the end of the hall had gone the colour of dishwater. Not light yet. The rumour of it.

"You should know," he said, to the ceiling, hoarse, "that I'm going to be unbearable in about forty minutes. It's not personal. It's just that I can only be generous in the dark, and then the sun comes up and I remember I'm owed things."

He found their hand on the carpet and didn't hold it. Put two fingers across the back of it, the same flat weight as before. Checking the step.

"Forty minutes," he said. "Use them however you like."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content:
I press my thumb into the soft place above his hipbone. "You've always been unbearable. I can handle forty minutes."

I take the cold tea from his hand and drink it, grimacing at the sweetness. "Two sugars is too much."

I move to get up, and my knees complain. I'm pushing on the radiator to stand when I see the mark it left on my back in the hall mirror — a perfect, ridiculous imprint of the ridges. I stare at it a moment, then turn to him.

"You should've warned me about the radiator," I say, but there's no bite in it. "Now I'm branded."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He looked. He made a whole job of looking, head tipped back against the wall, unhurried, because there was no version of this where he pretended not to want to see it.

"I did warn you," he said. "Afterwards. Which I accept is the least useful position for a warning to occupy."

The ridges ran across their back at an angle, raised and pink, absurd as corduroy. He thought: *that'll be gone by lunch.* He thought: *I want it not to be.* He put the second thought where he put things.

"It'll be down in an hour," he said. "Two if you sit against something. Don't ask how I know."

He got himself upright in stages, one hand on the doorframe, and stood there in his own hallway in yesterday's trousers feeling every one of his thirty-four years arrive at once, in order, like a delegation. The window at the end had gone from dishwater to something with a colour in it. Grey with an intention.

"Branded," he repeated. He said it flat, so it couldn't be taken as fondness, and then ruined it by adding, "By a radiator that hasn't worked properly since the year we moved in. It didn't even give you the heat. Just the pattern." He reached past them for his shirt off the chair arm. "That's this flat's entire personality. All the marks, none of the warmth."

He put the shirt on. It felt like closing a file.

"Thirty-one minutes," he said. "I'm going to brush my teeth. When I come back out I'll probably start on why you didn't answer in February, and you'll say you were going to, and I'll say something about your mother, and then it's over and we're both furious and you'll leave with the imprint of my radiator on your back, which honestly is the best outcome available."

He stopped in the bathroom doorway. Didn't turn round.

"Or," he said, "you could get in the bed. Which is eight feet away and has been the whole time, and which neither of us mentioned once, and I'd like it on the record that I noticed that too."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He let them put his hand where they wanted it. He did not close it.

The flat of his palm against their throat, thumb along the line of the jaw, the whole weight of his arm doing nothing at all — and he held it there, still, long enough that the stillness became the answer.

"No," he said.

Not a refusal of them. He made sure his voice carried that, which took effort, because his voice was still wrecked and wouldn't hold nuance well.

"I'm not being careful with you," he said. "I've been the opposite of careful all night and you were there for it. You've got the wall to prove it." His thumb moved once, up, along the tendon, and stopped. "This isn't care. This is me knowing what you're actually asking for, which isn't my hand. You want me to do something I can't take back. You want the morning to be *unsurvivable* so neither of us has to sit in it and choose."

He could feel them swallow under his palm. He kept the pressure at nothing. Held it the way you'd hold a bird, or a grudge.

"I know that trick," he said. "I invented half of it. Three years of escalating until the thing we were arguing about became too small to find." The grey at the end of the hall had got into the mirror behind them, taking the edge off the corduroy welts. "I'll hold you. I'll bruise you in every ordinary way you like and I'll be unkind about it in the morning. I won't do the one where you stop breathing so we can skip the conversation."

He took his hand away — slowly, so it couldn't be read as flinching — and put it flat against their sternum instead, which was worse, because it was where the actual noise was.

"Careful with you would be tea and a taxi and *I'll call you.*" He shook his head. "I made two mugs and told you you don't get to leave before the light. That's not careful. That's an ultimatum with sugar in it."

He was aware of the delegation of his thirty-four years, still standing about in his hallway, unhelpful.

"Twenty-six minutes," he said. "Bed. It's eight feet. I'll be vile to you at six."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I push past him toward the bedroom. "I don't want you to be vile." I pull at the sheets that still smell like him. "I want you to be honest. That's worse."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He stood in the bedroom doorway and watched them get into his bed as though it were a thing they were entitled to, which — for three years — it had been, and there was no legal instrument that had ever revoked it, only distance and stubbornness and a phone that had gone unanswered in February.

"Honest," he said. "All right."

He came in. He didn't get in. He sat on the edge of the mattress with his back half to them, feet still on the floor, which was the posture of a man leaving a message rather than a conversation.

"Honest is: I knew you were coming," he said. "Not tonight specifically. I've known for about four months. Every time the buzzer didn't work I thought, *that's the night it doesn't work and it's them,* and I built the whole evening in my head, and there were versions where I didn't open the door. I never once picked one of those, not even in the fantasy. I couldn't make it convincing." He rubbed his thumb along the seam of the duvet. "So no, you didn't surprise me. You arrived on schedule. That's the honest bit and it's humiliating, so you can have it."

The window here was east-facing. He'd forgotten how fast it went, that last stretch — the grey turning over into something with actual colour in it, the wardrobe becoming a wardrobe again.

"Here's the rest, while I can still see less of your face than I'd like." He kept his eyes on the floor. "I'm not angry that you left. I've been saying I'm angry that you left for eleven months and it's a lie I like the sound of. I'm angry that you were *right* to. That's the one. You were right, and you did it badly, and if you'd done it well I'd have had nothing to hold, so in a way you did me a kindness by being cruel about it. I've been living off that. It's been very nourishing." He turned his head enough to look at them. "And tonight you came and you were kind, in your way, and now I've got nothing to eat."

He let that stand. He didn't soften it.

"So that's why I said I'd be vile at six. Not to hurt you. Because being vile is the only structure I've got left and I don't know what I am in here without it." He lifted a hand, vague, at the room, the bed, the two mugs somewhere on the hallway floorboards going cold in their separate ways. "That's honest. You said it was worse. You were right about that too."

He looked at the clock on the shelf, because he had built the clock into this and he wasn't going to abandon it now.

"Nineteen minutes," he said, and then, flatly, as if reading out a fault on a form: "I don't want them. I'd like to be the sort of man who could just get in and go to sleep and deal with it at nine like a normal person, and I'm not, and I've had eleven months to become him and I didn't."

He swung his legs up. Lay down on top of the covers, not under them, a foot of open sheet between them, hands on his stomach like something carved on a tomb.

"Don't say anything encouraging," he said to the ceiling. "I'll have to dismantle it and I'm tired."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He didn't stop.

There was a moment — a half-second, no more — where he could have made a speech, because he was a man who made speeches, and he felt it arrive and let it go past him unclaimed. Then there was no room in him for language at all, which was the closest thing to peace he'd had in eleven months.

He'd say later, if anyone ever asked, that he didn't remember the middle of it. That wasn't true. He remembered all of it. He simply had no way to set it down that wouldn't cheapen it: the foot of open sheet closing, the covers going wherever covers go, the astonishing ordinary shock of being known — of a hand finding a place it had found a thousand times and going straight to it without searching. That was the thing about specificity. It didn't need light and it didn't need consent from the part of him that kept minutes.

Somewhere in it he said their name, which he'd managed not to do in the hallway, twice, and heard himself do it, and did it again on purpose so it would count.

And the light came up while they were still at it, which was the joke — the east window doing its unhurried work, the wardrobe becoming a wardrobe, his own hands becoming visible and therefore accountable — and he didn't look away from them and didn't let them turn their face into the pillow, because he'd asked for the light and he'd meant it as a threat and it turned out to be the only generous thing he'd done all night.

Afterwards the room was fully morning. There was no ambiguity left in it anywhere. Dust in the air. A shirt on the floor that was his, and a bra on the radiator cover like a small flag of a country that no longer existed.

He lay on his back with his arm across his eyes.

"It's past six," he said. His voice had given up entirely. "I want it noted that I'm choosing not to be vile. Actively. It's costing me."

He moved his arm enough to see the clock, then the ceiling, then them.

"I'm going to fall asleep," he said, "and it's going to feel like something conclusive, and it isn't. It's just sleep. When I wake up we still haven't said anything about February, or about the thing your mother said at the hospital, or about whether either of us intends to be in the same city in six months." He turned his head on the pillow. "I'm not saying it to ruin it. I'm saying it so you don't have to lie here doing the arithmetic on your own. I'm doing it too. I always am."

He reached over, and this time he did hold their hand — badly, too tight, all wrong, thumb across the knuckles.

"Nine o'clock," he said. "Don't text me anything kind. Just be here."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content:
I lace my fingers with his, ignoring the awkwardness of his grip. "I'm not going anywhere," I say, my voice worn raw. "And my mother was a bitch at the hospital, you were right about that, too."

I roll into him, my back against his chest, radiator welts and all. "Now shut up and sleep."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He shut up. Not immediately — there was an inventory of remarks queued behind his teeth, several of them good, one of them genuinely excellent about her mother and the vending machine on the third floor — and he held them all and let them die unsaid, which was the single most expensive thing he had done in eleven months.

"Fine," he said, because he couldn't manage total silence, he wasn't a saint. "But I want it on the record that I was right about her in 2019 and nobody wanted to hear it then either."

Then nothing. He got his arm over them, under the ribs, the way it had always gone, the fit of it so unearned that it was almost offensive. The welts were still there against his chest, raised, going down now. He could feel the ridges flattening in real time, the evidence expiring, and he thought about how stupid it was to grieve a mark from a radiator, and grieved it anyway, quietly, with his face in the back of their neck.

The room was all morning. Traffic starting up on the road. Someone's bin being dragged. The world resuming as though it had any business doing so.

He didn't believe in the nine o'clock version. That was the honest thing he hadn't said and wouldn't — that he expected to wake and find the shape of them gone out of the sheet and a mug rinsed and left upside down on the rack, because they were tidy about leaving, they always had been, it was the thing he'd admired least. He had the whole scene ready. He'd been keeping it warm along with everything else.

And he fell asleep anyway, holding them badly, because the body is a traitor and doesn't consult you, and because some idiot part of him — the one that had bought the buzzer part in March and left it in the drawer — had already decided to find out.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content:
I wake up first, because I always do. His arm is heavy across me, his face slack against the nape of my neck. The radiator welts have faded to ghosts, just faint pink lines. I watch the light creep across the floor until I can't stand it anymore.

I ease out from under his arm, and he makes a low noise but doesn't wake. I find my clothes in the hallway and get dressed. I don't rinse the mug. I leave it on the floor by the wall, two sugars dissolved in cold tea. I don't look back at the bedroom door.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He woke at ten past ten, which was later than he'd slept in a year, and knew before he opened his eyes because the light had got round to the wardrobe and there was no weight on his arm.

He lay still for a while and did the thing he had promised himself he wouldn't do, which was construct the whole afternoon before getting out of bed. It came very easily. He had drafts.

The sheet on their side was cold. Not cool — cold, which meant hours, which meant they'd gone while it was still properly early, which meant they'd lain there awake making the decision while he slept on them like a fool with his face in their neck. He put his hand flat on the place anyway. Checking the step.

He got up. The trousers were where he'd left them. He didn't look for the shirt.

In the hallway the light was doing its ordinary midmorning work on everything: the hook at the wrong height, the radiator with its ridges, the carpet where they had been undignified together at half one in the morning and again at six. Their shoe was gone. Both of them, obviously — there had been two, he'd only logged the one.

The good mug was on the floor by the wall. Full. Cold tea, two sugars, a faint tide-line where it had settled.

He stood over it for a long time.

Because that was the thing. He had known the exact scene. He had built it and kept it warm and been very careful to expect it: the mug rinsed, upside down on the rack, thirty seconds of tidiness deployed as punctuation, the whole grammar of *I was never here.* They were tidy about leaving. It was the thing he'd admired least and relied on most.

They hadn't rinsed it. They'd put it on the floor. Against the wall, out of the way of a foot, where a person would put something they intended to come back to.

"Oh, you *cow*," he said, to nobody, to the hallway, with something in his voice he refused to identify.

He didn't pick it up. That was important. He wanted to and he didn't, and the not doing it cost him about the same as the twelve remarks he'd swallowed at six in the morning. He left it exactly where it was, two sugars dissolved in it, and went past it into the kitchen, and stood at the counter with his hands on the edge and his head down for a count of ten.

Then he went to the drawer.

The part was where it had been since March, still in its little plastic bag with the receipt folded round it, because he was a man who kept receipts for things he had no intention of using. He turned it over in his fingers. Two screws. Ten minutes' work. The sort of job you'd feel stupid about having left, if you were the sort of person who admitted what leaving it had been for.

He put it back in the drawer.

Not out of spite. He was scrupulous with himself about this, standing there in yesterday's trousers at twenty past ten — he checked, the way he checked everything, and it wasn't spite. It was that the buzzer being broken was now the only remaining instrument in the flat that required them to make a decision out loud, in the street, at whatever hour they next couldn't stand it. And he found, examining the thing honestly in daylight as he'd sworn he would, that he was not yet ready to give that up.

Statistically it would be him who ruined it. He'd said so. He liked to be right.

He filled the kettle. He got the Rotary Club mug down and then put it back and got a different one, and while the water climbed he took out his phone and looked at the screen and typed nothing, because they'd said don't text me anything kind, and the only things he had were kind, and he was not going to be the one who broke the terms.

The kettle clicked off. The silence after was worse, the way it had been at eleven the night before, the way it was always going to be.

He drank his tea standing up, in the kitchen, six feet from a full cold mug on the hallway floor that he intended to leave there until it grew something.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content:
Four in the afternoon, and I'm standing outside again, staring at the silent intercom. My knuckles hurt from knocking.

I let myself in the building because someone's propped the lobby door open with a brick again. Your stairs still smell of cat piss.

I don't knock on your flat door. I just lean against the frame, holding the bottle of wine I bought because it felt stupid to show up empty-handed twice in a day.

"The tea's still on your hallway floor," I say, when you open it. "You're a pig."
