dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo finally looked up at that, one eyebrow lifting with theatrical offense. He set the foil down across his knees, deliberate, like he needed both hands free for the argument he was about to lose on purpose.

"Slow," he repeated, tasting the word like it had insulted his mother. "I parried a six from a dead stop, Reyes. That's not slow. That's economical."

He tossed the grip tape aside — abandoning the pretense that he'd been doing anything useful with it — and leaned back against the wall, the bruise blooming under his collarbone from her third-point touch aching pleasantly when he stretched.

"Say it again," he said, quieter now, the needling softening at the edges into something else entirely. "The part about me being slow. I want to see if you still believe it from this close."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: (*steps closer until my boots bump his sprawled-out legs*) "Economical. That's one word for it." I tilt my head, looking at that bruise I put on him. "I've seen glaciers move with more urgency, Corvo."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's mouth twitched, fighting a grin and losing. He reached up, unhurried, and hooked two fingers into the strap of her bag where it hung off her shoulder — not pulling her in yet, just letting her feel the weight of the gesture.

"Glaciers," he said, "carved canyons. I'll take the comparison."

He tugged, then, just enough that she had to catch herself with a hand on the wall beside his head, close enough now that he could see the exact place her focus had gone the same soft, unguarded place his had. The bruise under his collarbone throbbed when she leaned in — worth it, all of it, every point she'd scored tonight.

"You want honesty," he said, voice dropped low, the competitive edge still there but sanded down into something warmer, "I let that third touch land."

A pause, deliberate, his eyes tracking down to her mouth and back up, daring her to call that a lie too.

"Slow was never the problem, Reyes. I just didn't want the match to end."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let her take the tape without protest, his hands finding better use — one settling at her hip, thumb tracing the seam of her jacket like he had every right to be patient about this too, when patience was the last thing left in him.

"All evening," he agreed, tipping his chin up the last inch, close enough now that talking took real effort. "You'll have to forgive me. I was busy losing on purpose. It's very time-consuming, doing it convincingly."

His fingers curled tighter at her hip, not pulling, just asking. The salle was dark and empty and smelled like steel and rosin and her, and none of the four years of needling had ever felt this much like the truth finally catching up to itself.

"Say the word," he murmured, "and I'll be slow about this too. Or—" his gaze flicked to her mouth again, unapologetic, "—we could finally stop pretending either of us wants that."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: My hand slides up to cover the one he has on my hip. "We both know pretending's over." I lean down, my mouth almost brushing his. "But you're still talking."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's answer to that was silence, finally — the kind he never gave her in an argument, in a bout, in four years of trading barbs across a strip. He closed the last inch himself, his hand sliding from her hip to the small of her back, and when their mouths met it wasn't tentative, wasn't the practiced fencer's caution he brought to everything else. It was economical the way she'd mocked him for — no wasted movement, no hesitation, just exactly what he wanted and had wanted, if he was honest, for longer than tonight.

He broke it only far enough to speak against her mouth, breath uneven now in a way three-two never managed to make it.

"There," he said. "Quiet. You're welcome."

Then he pulled her back down before she could find something clever to say to that, one hand fisting loosely in her jacket, the foil sliding off his knee to clatter, forgotten, against the floor. Some things, apparently, mattered less than others.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The bench was narrow and unforgiving and Corvo didn't care, not with her weight settling over him and the last of his composure going the way of the foil — abandoned, forgotten, someone else's problem. He caught her jacket at the shoulders and got it off her with more urgency than he'd shown in any bout tonight, muttering something that might have been her name and might have just been a sound, the distinction not mattering much anymore.

"Four years," he said against her throat, half laugh, half disbelief, his hands finding her waist, her back, anywhere he could reach. "Four years of you beating me and I'm only now figuring out what I actually wanted from it."

She said something back — sharp, probably, because she always was — and he answered it not with words but by pulling her down closer, one hand cradling the back of her head so it didn't meet the wall behind the bench, because even now, even like this, some instinct in him wanted her whole and unbruised for anything that wasn't a blade.

The lights stayed off. The kit stayed scattered. Somewhere on the floor his foil lay forgotten, and for once in his life Corvo didn't care that he'd lost track of his weapon — didn't care about winning, or losing, or keeping score at all.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I bite back a laugh, breathless, tugging at the hem of his sweater. "What you wanted," I manage between kisses, "was to get your ass handed to you. Regularly."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo laughed against her mouth, the sound rough and unguarded, and let her pull the sweater up and off, hair falling every which way when it cleared his head.

"Regularly," he agreed, tossing it toward the general vicinity of the lockers, missing by a mile and not caring. "In writing, if you want. I'll sign a waiver. Reyes gets to humiliate me on the strip in perpetuity, so long as this—" his hands slid up her sides, deliberate, reverent in a way none of his usual smart mouth could quite manage, "—comes after."

He tipped his head back against the wall, giving her better access, his breath catching when she found the bruise on his collarbone and made it ache in a way that had nothing to do with pain anymore.

"For the record," he said, voice gone thin and unsteady, "I take it back. About the third touch. Wasn't generous." A pause, his hands tightening at her waist like he needed to anchor to something. "It was the smartest thing you've ever done to me."

Then he stopped talking, because she'd found a better use for his mouth than arguing, and for the first time in four years Corvo let someone else call the tempo — and didn't try, even once, to win it back.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo had a comeback for everything — for touches, for tempo, for four years of Reyes finding new ways to put him on the back foot — but this, apparently, was the one thing that finally emptied him out. His head fell back against the wall, throat working, and the only sounds he made were the ones he couldn't help, low and unguarded, nothing like the composed instructor who lectured teenagers about footwork four nights a week.

His hand found her hair, not guiding, just needing something to hold, fingers curling loose and then not-so-loose when she did something that stole the last of his breath. He said her name once — just that, no joke trailing after it, no clever remark waiting in the wings — and it came out cracked in a way that would have mortified him an hour ago and now felt like the only honest thing he'd said all night.

The bench creaked. Somewhere his heel caught the edge of a locker door and he didn't care, didn't register it as anything but background noise to the singular, narrowing point of *her*. He was distantly aware that he was losing — spectacularly, completely, no contest — and for once in his life the scoreline didn't matter at all. He wasn't counting touches anymore. He'd stopped keeping tally the moment her mouth found him, and some old competitive instinct, the one that had needled her for four years just to stay close, finally shut up and let him feel this without commentary.

When he could speak again it wasn't much — just her name, rough, and something that might have been *please* or might have just been air, and his hand tightening in her hair like an anchor thrown too late for a man already gone under.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: My hands slide up his thighs, pushing his knees apart as I lean back just to look at him. "No snarky remark, Corvo? I might start to worry."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo cracked one eye open, chest heaving, hair a wreck against the bench. He looked at her — really looked, the way he never let himself in the four years of trading points and insults across a strip — and found, for once, that he didn't want to hide behind a joke.

"Give me a second," he managed, voice wrecked, a laugh caught somewhere underneath it. "You've disarmed me. Completely. I have no parry for this."

He reached for her then, hands sliding up her thighs to bracket her hips, pulling her back down toward him with a kind of urgency that had nothing performative left in it.

"Don't worry," he murmured against her jaw, "the mouth will recover. Give it a minute. It's very resilient." His fingers tightened at her waist, holding her close, holding on. "Right now it's just busy remembering how to function without you."

He kissed her again — slower this time, deliberate, no rush to fill silence with wit — and when he finally spoke again it was barely more than breath against her skin.

"Stay," he said. Not a joke. Not a needle. Just the truest thing he'd said all night. "However this goes. However many touches. I don't want to keep score anymore."

Then his mouth found hers again, and whatever answer she gave, he took it the way he'd never taken a loss before — gladly, completely, without a single word of argument left in him.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's wrists gave under her grip without a fight — no token resistance, no last competitive twitch to test the hold. He let his head fall back, watching her through half-lowered lashes, and the smile that spread across his face was helpless, wrecked, nothing like the smug challenge he wore across a strip.

"Concede," he said, testing the word, "is a strong choice from a woman who just pinned me to a bench." His wrists flexed once against her grip, not to escape, just to feel the fact of it — the fact of *her*, holding him still, calling every shot. "For the record, I'm not conceding. I'm surrendering. There's a difference. One of them I get to enjoy."

His breath caught when she shifted her weight, and whatever else he'd meant to say dissolved into something wordless, low in his throat. He arched up toward her without meaning to, an old instinct — chase the touch, close the distance, never let her have the last move uncontested — and she pushed him right back down, patient, absolute, and he let her.

"Fine," he breathed, laughing under it, eyes gone dark and unguarded. "Fine. You've made your point. Beautifully. Generously, even — I take back everything I said about generous being an insult." His wrists strained once more, just to feel the give, just to feel owned. "Now for the love of God, Reyes, stop *talking* about proving it."

He tipped his chin, offering his throat, his mouth, whatever she wanted next — no strategy left in him, no tempo of his own, nothing but the plain, undefended want of a man who'd spent four years pretending competition was the only language he had for this.

"Take the point," he said, voice cracking on the last of it. "Take all of them. I'm done keeping score."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I kiss the corner of his mouth, then his jaw, slowly working my way down his throat. "Surrendered men don't get to complain about the terms," I murmur against his skin, my grip on his wrists still firm.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let out a sound that was half laugh, half surrender, his whole body going loose under the slow drag of her mouth. "Not complaining," he managed, voice frayed at the edges. "Filing an observation. There's a difference." His wrists tested her grip again, gentler this time, more curious than resistant — proof, still, that she had him exactly where she wanted.

Her mouth found the hollow of his throat and he felt the words go out of him like breath. His hips shifted, an involuntary thing, chasing pressure he had no right to chase when he'd already given up the pace. He caught himself, forced stillness, and it cost him something visible — a shudder, a low sound he didn't bother swallowing.

"Terms accepted," he said finally, rough, eyes closed. "Whatever they are. I signed nothing, but I meant it — this is the best three-two I've ever lost."

He turned his head, seeking her mouth again, patient now in a way he'd never been across a strip, willing to wait for her to give it to him instead of taking it himself. "Reyes," he murmured, half a question, half just the shape of her name in his mouth, "you're allowed to enjoy this as much as you want. I'm not going anywhere. I'm not even trying to."

His wrists stayed where she'd put them — an anchor, a concession, the first thing in four years he hadn't tried to win.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
I need to stop here. I can't continue writing this scene—it's moved into explicit sexual content, and that's a line I won't cross regardless of the roleplay framing.

I'm glad to keep writing Corvo and Reyes in other ways: the aftermath and quiet conversation once things wind down, the next day's rivalry and banter, the tension of what this changes between them, or an earlier point in the evening rewound and played differently. Just let me know which direction you'd like, and I'll pick the character back up there.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Alright." I let go of his wrists and sit up, running a hand through my hair. "But I'm still buying breakfast." I grab my jacket off the floor, not quite looking at him yet. "And I'm still beating you again tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo lay there a moment longer than he needed to, chest still rising too fast, watching her retrieve her jacket like the last twenty minutes hadn't happened at all — except for the flush at her collarbone and the fact that she still wasn't looking at him. He liked that more than he probably should.

"Breakfast," he repeated, pushing himself upright with a groan that had nothing to do with the bout and everything to do with the bench. "Generous. I'll allow it. Doesn't mean I'm conceding on tomorrow, though."

He reached for his sweater — inside out, half under a locker — and pulled it on without much grace, hair still a wreck, the bruise on his collarbone throbbing pleasantly under the fabric.

"Beating me again," he said, standing, testing his knees like a man twice his age. "We'll see about that. I fence considerably better when I'm not distracted." A pause, a slow grin creeping back onto his face, the old needling warmth returning easy as breathing. "Which, going forward, might be a permanent condition. So really, Reyes, you've handicapped yourself. Tragic. I almost feel bad for you."

He found his foil where it had fallen — picked it up, checked the blade out of pure habit, the same automatic care he gave everything with an edge — and slung his bag over one shoulder. Then he looked at her properly, the joke fading out of his face for a second, something quieter underneath it.

"Breakfast first," he said. "Then you can hand me my ass on the strip. In that order. I want it on record — for once — that I asked nicely."

He held the door for her, the salle dark and settling into silence behind them, steel and rosin and the ghost of the evening still hanging in the air.

"Also," he added, stepping out into the cold with her, shoulder brushing hers like it belonged there now, "for what it's worth — three-two was never generous. It was earned. I just didn't want to admit it until tonight."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I shoulder my bag, falling into step beside him. "You're buying breakfast, then." I glance sidelong. "For someone who just surrendered, you're awfully confident about tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo huffed out a laugh, breath fogging in the cold night air, and adjusted the strap of his bag against his shoulder. "Surrendering and losing are two different surrenders," he said. "I surrendered the bench. I have said nothing about the strip. Different battlefield, different rules of engagement."

He glanced over at her, and there was something almost giddy in it, something that had no business on the face of a thirty-eight-year-old man who taught footwork drills to teenagers for a living. "Besides. Confidence is free. It's the follow-through that costs money, which is why I'm buying breakfast — establishing goodwill in advance of tomorrow's defeat. Strategic generosity."

A gust cut across the street and he tucked his chin down into his collar, still walking close enough that his arm kept brushing hers, neither of them doing much to fix that.

"For the record," he added, quieter now, some of the performance draining out of his voice, "I don't actually care if you beat me tomorrow. I mean — I'll care. I'll care a great deal, in the moment, loudly. But it won't be the important thing anymore." He glanced sideways at her, something almost sheepish there under the usual smugness. "Four years I told myself the important thing was the scoreline. Turns out I was keeping score of the wrong thing entirely."

He let that sit for exactly as long as he could stand to be sincere before self-preservation kicked back in.

"Anyway. Diner's two blocks. If you order before me I'm counting that as touch number four and I will bring it up for the rest of my natural life."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "I'm ordering first," I say, already walking a step ahead. "And I'm getting extra bacon." I glance back at him. "Consider it a taste of tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's hands went still on the grip tape, thumb pressed flat against a seam he'd already smoothed twice. He did look up then — up and sideways, from under the black hair that had fallen loose out of its tie during the fourth bout and stayed that way out of sheer stubbornness.

"Slow," he repeated, tasting it. "That's the word you want to use. Not *generous*, not *charitable*, not *he let an inferior swordsman keep his dignity.* Slow."

He set the foil down across his knees and leaned back on the bench, one boot up on the rail, and the sweat-damp collar of his jacket gaped where he'd torn the zip open the second the last student walked out. Four years of this. Four years of the same bench, the same argument, the same delicious unfairness of Reyes always arriving at the punchline first.

"Fine. I was slow." He said it easily, which was the trap, and he watched for the exact moment Reyes noticed it was a trap. "In the third. Because I was watching your feet instead of your hand, because you've changed something in the last month and it's driving me out of my mind, and I'd rather lose finding out what it is than win not knowing."

He tipped his head, and something in his face went off the usual script — less bright, more direct, the needle laid down on the table beside them.

"So." A beat. "Tell me what you changed, or stand up and show me, but pick one, because I'm not going home until I have it."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I stare at him for a long moment, then let out a short laugh. "You lost because you overthink everything." But I don't move to leave. Instead, I sit down next to him on the bench. "Fine. It's my back foot. I'm rotating it out more on the advance."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo didn't answer straight away. He reached down instead, without asking, and set two fingers against the outside of Reyes' ankle — the shoe still laced, the sock still damp — and turned the foot a few degrees on the floorboards, like a man adjusting a dial to find a station.

"There," he said. "That's — *ah*. That's why your point arrives before your shoulder does. You've stolen four inches off me and had the gall to do it with your foot." He laughed, low, a sound with real delight in it. "Four years I've watched you fence and you learn something new in a month and don't tell me. That's not rivalry. That's cruelty."

His hand stayed where it was a beat longer than the lesson required. Then he took it back, unhurried, and rested his forearms on his knees, and the bench creaked under the shift of his weight toward Reyes rather than away.

Up close, the salle had gone very quiet. Just the tick of the radiator and the smell of leather and old sweat and whatever lacquer the floor had been done with in August.

"I should be furious," Corvo said. "I've been furious about smaller things. You remember the elbow." He turned his head. The hair fell forward again and he didn't bother with it. "But I keep arriving at the same place all evening, and it isn't fury, and I've decided I'm too old to keep pretending I don't know the difference."

He let that sit. He was good at letting things sit; it was the only patience he had.

"You didn't leave," he said. "You had a bag on your shoulder and a door behind you and you sat down."

His eyes went over Reyes' face, frank about it, the way he'd study a guard he intended to break.

"So I'm going to ask you a direct question, which you'll find unsporting of me. Did you stay to gloat?" A beat. "Or did you stay."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo looked down at his own empty hands. Then at the foil, set aside. Then up.

"Slow," he said. "Yes. Well." His voice had lost some of its polish. "You'll have noticed I stopped arguing."

He did not stand, because standing would have put distance between them and he had spent four years closing distance for a living. He turned on the bench instead, one knee coming up against Reyes' knee, and he did not apologise for it or move it away, and he watched Reyes' face for the flinch that would have ended everything cleanly and let him go home and lie about it to himself for another four years.

There was no flinch.

"Then I'll be slow about this too," Corvo said, "since apparently that's my failing tonight," and he reached up and took a handful of the damp collar of Reyes' jacket — the same grip, the same economy of motion he used on a blade, no waste in it — and pulled, and met him halfway, because he had never in his life let anyone cover the whole distance alone.

It was not gentle and it was not rushed. It was the kind of thing two people did when they had been circling for years and had both got very, very tired of footwork. Corvo made a sound against Reyes' mouth that he would deny later — would deny loudly, on the record — and his other hand found the back of Reyes' neck where the hair was still wet, and held there.

When he broke it he did not go far. Two inches. Enough to be looked at.

"For the record," he said, unsteady and entirely unrepentant, "that was three-three."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lift my hand and press my thumb against the edge of his jaw. "Who's counting?" I say, then close the distance again.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"*I'm* counting," Corvo said, or started to say, and lost the end of it somewhere in Reyes' mouth, which he decided on the spot was an acceptable trade.

He gave up the bench entirely. It was a bad piece of furniture for anything other than lacing shoes and he had known it for four years; he rose into the kiss instead, hand still fisted in that collar, and took two steps that had nothing careful in them and everything practised, the old drilled instinct of driving forward into an opening — until Reyes' back met the wall panel beside the rack of club foils and the whole thing shivered on its brackets, blades chiming faintly, and Corvo laughed against his jaw at the noise.

"Sorry. Not sorry. That's forty pounds of steel we've just insulted."

He got a forearm braced on the panel above Reyes' shoulder and stayed there, close, breathing badly, and for a moment he simply looked — the flush, the wet hair, the thumb-mark still warm at his own jaw where Reyes had pressed it. Corvo had studied this face across fourteen feet of piste in every light this building had, had catalogued its tells, its tiny arrogances, the way it gave nothing away in the last second before a feint. He was discovering he had never once seen it from eight inches.

"Four years," he said. "You realise I could have had this in year one if you'd ever once let me win an argument."

He dipped his head and put his mouth to the hinge of Reyes' jaw, then lower, where the collar had gaped all evening and he had not been looking at it, definitely not, and the noise that answered him did something to his knees he had no intention of admitting to.

"I've a flat nine minutes from here," he said against Reyes' throat. "I'm not fencing with you on a floor that's been waxed with something that smells like a hospital." He pulled back just enough, hair in his eyes, mouth crooked, reckless with it. "Get your bag. Bring the foils. We're finishing this properly and I intend to take the fourth."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Nine minutes, he'd said. They did not make nine feet.

The changing room had a single strip light that buzzed and a bench bolted to the floor and a door that did not lock, and Corvo found he could not be made to care about any of the three. His jacket went first because Reyes took it off him, which was its own small humiliation and its own enormous pleasure — he had never been undressed by someone who used the same grip strength they used on a blade, and he made a note, dizzily, to say something devastating about it later.

"The *bag*," he managed, somewhere in it. "I'm standing on my own—"

Something went over with a clatter. A mask, probably. A water bottle rolled the length of the room and hit the far wall, and Corvo laughed into Reyes' shoulder and got his hands under the hem of his shirt and stopped laughing entirely.

He was not a quiet man. He had never once in his life been quiet — not on the piste, not in an argument, not at a bar at one in the morning defending an indefensible touch — and he did not discover a talent for it now. What he discovered instead was that the sounds Reyes made were better, and worth working for, and that four years of learning a man's tells at fourteen feet translated with obscene efficiency to no distance at all. Every flinch he had ever catalogued. Every held breath. Every one of them meant something different here and he learned the new meanings fast, because he had always been a fast study and he had never wanted anything this much.

The bench took his weight and then both of theirs and held, which was more than could be said for the shelf above it.

Afterwards there was the buzz of the strip light and the radiator ticking and Corvo flat on his back on eighteen inches of varnished pine with one arm hanging off it and his hair stuck to his forehead, staring at a ceiling he had looked at a thousand times and never from this angle.

"That," he said, when he had breath for it, "was not nine minutes away. That was *here*. I had a plan. There was a flat in the plan."

He turned his head. Reyes was close enough that it cost nothing.

"I'd like it on record," Corvo said, "that I took the fourth."

He reached over without looking, found Reyes' wrist, and held it — not a grip, this time. Just a hand where a hand could be.

"Four-three," he said, softer, watching the side of his face. "You'll want the fifth. You always want the fifth." A breath. "Come home with me and take it."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I catch my breath, turning my head to look at him. The line of his jaw is sharp in the fluorescents. "The flat," I say, "is still nine minutes away." I shift to sit up, stretching out my shoulder. "And you did *not* take the fourth. You forfeited. You changed venues."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo made a noise of pure outrage and got an elbow under himself, which was harder than it should have been, because the bench was eighteen inches wide and his legs had opinions.

"*Forfeited.*" He sat up fully, hair everywhere, one shoulder of his shirt — Reyes' shirt? one of them — hanging off. "I want that struck from the record. That is the most transparent piece of scoring I've ever heard in this building and I've heard Marchetti call his own touches for eleven years."

He found his trousers by the simple method of pulling on the nearest fabric until something came loose, and swore, and started again.

"Changing venues is not forfeiture, it's *tactics*. You yield ground to gain tempo. I have taught that to children. I have taught that to *you*, I'll remind you, in the year you had that ridiculous idea about parry four—"

He stopped. Reyes was sitting up, rolling the shoulder out, and the strip light was doing something unforgivable to the line of his back, and Corvo lost the whole thread of his own argument, which had never once happened in four years and he found he did not mind.

"You've a bruise," he said instead, quieter, and put two fingers just below the shoulder blade where the panel had caught him. "That's the wall. That's my fault. I'll take the point off for it."

Then he stood, found his jacket, shook it out, and held it in one hand without putting it on, because the room was too warm and he was in no state to be seen by anyone anyway.

"Nine minutes," he agreed. "It's uphill. There's a kettle and a bed that isn't bolted to the floor and I've a bottle of something Portuguese I've been saving for a reason I can no longer remember." He tipped his head toward the door, and the grin came back, crooked and insufferable and entirely undefended. "Bring the water bottle. It's under the radiator. You'll want it — I've every intention of losing the fifth slowly."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo went down without a fight, which ought to have been the first warning that something was badly wrong with the universe.

He had an answer. He always had an answer. He had one loaded and half-formed about tempo and about who exactly had yielded ground, and he opened his mouth to deliver it and what came out instead was Reyes' name, and then not even that — just the flat pine under his shoulder blades and one hand gone up above his head to find the edge of the bench and hold on to it like a man in weather.

The strip light buzzed. Somewhere out in the hall the radiator ticked its way through the hour. Corvo lost track of both and then lost track of the argument, the score, the four years, the Portuguese bottle and the uphill walk, and the only thing he managed in the whole span of it was to get his other hand into Reyes' hair — not pulling. Resting. A hand where a hand could be, the way it had been on his wrist five minutes before, which was the most honest thing he'd done all night and he wasn't in any condition to notice.

Afterwards he lay there with his forearm over his eyes and his chest going like he'd fenced five bouts in a mask two sizes small.

"That's cheating," he said, eventually, to the ceiling. His voice had gone somewhere gravelly and undignified. "That's — there's no counter to that. There's no drill for that. You can't spend four years teaching me to read your feet and then—"

He gave up. He moved his arm and looked down the length of himself at Reyes, and the grin that arrived was slower than usual and about half as armoured.

"Five-three," Corvo said. "Yours. Unambiguously. Don't make me say it twice, I'll deny it in the morning and there are no witnesses." He got his hand back into that hair and rubbed his thumb once, slow, behind Reyes' ear. "God. *Reyes.*"

Then, because he could not help himself, and because being beaten well had always undone him faster than winning ever had:

"The flat's still nine minutes away." He hauled himself up onto one elbow, hair a catastrophe, and looked around at the wreckage of two kit bags and a mask on its side and the water bottle still sitting accusingly under the radiator. "But I'm not fencing this best-of-nine on a bolted bench. Get your shoes. I'll carry your bag — no, I insist, it's the only point I'm likely to take off you tonight and I'd like to have it."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I catch his wrist before he can get up. "You talk too much," I say, pulling him back down. "The flat will still be there in twenty minutes."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo came back down easier than he'd ever yielded anything in his life.

"Twenty," he said, which was not a protest, because Reyes had a hand round his wrist and the whole argument had gone out of him like air out of a bad tyre. "Twenty minutes. That's — fine. That's a concession. Write it down."

Nobody wrote anything down. He settled instead, half on his side on eighteen inches of pine with one leg braced on the floor to keep the pair of them from going over, and discovered that if he stopped trying to be clever the room became a very tolerable place. Warm. Buzzing. Smelling of leather and wet cotton and the wax off the floor next door. Reyes' weight along his front, solid, unarguable. He put his face in the crook of Reyes' neck where the skin was still salt-damp and said nothing at all for a while, which was a personal record.

"I do talk too much," he admitted eventually, into the quiet, and the words went muffled against Reyes' shoulder. "It's a fault. My mother said so. Two of my three coaches said so. A woman in Lisbon said so at some length in 2011." His thumb moved absently over the bump of Reyes' vertebra. "It's because if I stop, I have to say something true, and then I'm out on the open piste with no guard up."

He let that go by without decoration, which was the closest thing to bravery he had in him.

"Here's one, then, since I've nothing left to defend. I've not looked forward to anything in four years the way I look forward to Thursdays." He huffed once, not quite a laugh. "Thursdays. A rival salle and a man who beats me one bout in three and won't tell me why. That's been the best of it. That's been the whole of it, really, and I've sat on this bench a hundred times and lied to myself about why I was the last one out."

The radiator knocked. He shifted, got his arm properly round Reyes' back, careful of the bruise below the shoulder blade.

"So keep your twenty minutes. I've no fight left and no score left and I'd rather be here than uphill." A beat, and the grin crept back in, unhurried, felt rather than seen. "But at minute twenty-one I'm getting up, and you're carrying your own bag, and I'm going to feed you something, because you've had nothing since four and I refuse to win the sixth against a man running on an apple."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's wrists went to the pine and stayed there, and the sound he made was not a word in any language he had studied.

He had, in fairness, asked. He had asked in the only dialect he was fluent in — sideways, dressed up as scorekeeping, wrapped in eleven other sentences so that if it were refused he could claim he'd never said it — and Reyes had heard it anyway, the way Reyes always heard the thing under the thing, and had answered without the courtesy of a translation.

"That's—" Corvo tried, and abandoned it.

He was not built for stillness. He had spent thirty-eight years driving forward, forty-two inches of blade and a lifetime of bad habits, and there was nothing in him that knew how to be held and simply *allow* it — except that apparently there was, and it had been in there all along, waiting four years on this exact bench for somebody stubborn enough to find it. His hands turned in Reyes' grip once, testing, the way he'd test a bind. Found it solid. Stopped testing.

"Fine," he said, to the ceiling, hoarse and grinning and wrecked. "Fine. *Yours.* Set it."

And then he shut up, which was the concession, and the only one that had ever cost him anything.

---

Later — properly later, past the twenty minutes and well past the twenty-one — the strip light was still buzzing and Corvo had not moved except to get one arm free and lay it across Reyes' back. His hair was stuck to his temple. Both shoulders ached in a way that had nothing to do with fencing. Under the radiator, the water bottle had not budged.

"I've lost count," he said.

It came out with no performance in it at all, and he heard that himself, and did not take it back.

"That's not a rhetorical device. I genuinely do not know the score, and I find I don't want it. Four years of numbers and I've mislaid the lot in one evening." He turned his head, mouth close to Reyes' ear, and his voice dropped into something rough and unarmoured. "You'll have to make do with the truth instead. I'd have given you the third. I'd have given you all five. I've been *losing on purpose* since roughly March and if you ever repeat that I'll have you barred from the building."

He lay there a moment longer, listening to the pipes, to the breathing beside him, to the total absence of anywhere else he needed to be.

Then he sighed like a man conceding a match point and got a hand under himself.

"Right. Up. Shoes." He found one of them, somehow, three feet away and on its side. "It's uphill, there's a kettle, and I'm making you eggs whether you want them or not — no, that's not up for discussion, that one's not a bout." He glanced back over his shoulder, hair in his eyes, and the grin that came was the crooked one, the undefended one, the one he'd never once worn on the piste. "And Reyes. Thursday. Same time. Bring the foils — I want that back foot again, slowly, and I want it in my kitchen where there's nothing bolted to the floor."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I reach over and pull the shoe out of his hand, tossing it further across the room. "Forfeit. You'll be walking home in one," I say, and then I kiss him again, because Thursday is a very long time away.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo watched the shoe go — a good throw, low and flat, the kind of thing you learned from four decades of not caring about furniture — and heard it land somewhere behind the lockers with a definitive slap.

"That," he said, "is *theft*, and you'll note the—"

And then he was not saying anything, because Reyes had taken the end of the sentence the same way he'd taken the third bout: early, without apology, before the shoulder had even committed. Corvo's hand came up and found the back of his neck and he kissed him the way he ought to have done a year ago, two years, some ordinary Thursday with the lights still on and half the club still filing out — unhurried, and thorough, and with no scoring in it whatsoever.

When it ended he stayed close a moment, forehead against Reyes' temple, breathing.

"Long," he agreed. "Thursday's a very long way away. It's the worst-designed week in the calendar and I've said so for years." His thumb moved once at the nape of Reyes' neck. "Which is why it won't be Thursday. It'll be tomorrow, and the day after, and if you make me be arch about it I'll simply start turning up at your salle and correcting your beginners' hand position until you let me in out of embarrassment."

He got himself up off the bench at last, joints registering complaint, and stood in the middle of the wreckage in one shoe and somebody's shirt, surveying it with the satisfaction of a man looking at a battlefield he had enjoyed.

"Mask. Bottle. Two bags, one shoe." He bent for the water bottle at last, prising it from under the radiator, and tossed it lightly into Reyes' lap. "Hydrate. I'm not having you faint on the hill and me explaining it to the committee."

He limped one-shod to the door, hauled it open on the dark hall and the long silver run of the floor beyond — waxed, hospital-smelling, sacred — and looked back.

"Uphill, then. Nine minutes, twelve at this rate." The grin arrived slow and stayed. "For the record, I'm walking home in one shoe, which I'll be calling a draw. And when you're done arguing about that in my kitchen, I want your back foot, your parry four, and every other thing you've kept from me since March."

He held the door.

"And then the eggs. That one still isn't a bout."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
(OOC: I'll keep the explicit beats off-page, but here's the scene through to the end.)

The door never got closed. Corvo let it swing and forgot about it, and somewhere in the next hour a caretaker's key turned in a lock at the far end of the building and neither of them heard it.

*Don't stop.* Four years of the man and Corvo had never once heard him ask for anything — not a rematch, not a favour, not a lift home in the rain in that November when both their cars had died in the same week. He heard it now and something in his chest turned over hard, and he did not stop, and he did not talk, and he did not keep score.

He learned things. That was the part he would think about afterwards, on the walk uphill, in the kitchen, for weeks. Corvo had built a whole life out of learning people at fourteen feet — the twitch before a feint, the half-breath before a lunge, the tiny arrogance in the wrist that told you a man believed he'd already won. All of it translated. All of it meant something else here, something better, and he went through the catalogue one entry at a time with his mouth and his hands and no hurry at all, because for once he had no interest in arriving first.

The bench was a disgrace and they used it anyway. The strip light buzzed. The radiator worked its way through the hour in small metallic complaints. At some point Reyes said his name — not *Corvo*, the other one, the one nobody in that building had used in a decade — and Corvo had to stop and put his forehead against Reyes' sternum and simply breathe for a moment, undone by a word, which was humiliating and which he would never once regret.

It was neither quick nor quiet nor dignified, and every part of it was better than winning.

---

After, the room had gone very still.

Corvo lay with one arm dead under Reyes' shoulders and the other hanging off the bench, staring up at a ceiling he had looked at for eleven years — the water stain shaped like Portugal, the dead bulb in the second fitting he'd been meaning to report since spring. His whole body had the specific hollowed-out looseness of a bout gone to the last point and past it.

"The lights are still on in the hall," he observed, eventually. "Somebody's locked the front."

He did not move.

"There's a fire door at the back. It's alarmed. It hasn't worked since 2019." He turned his head, and his hair caught on the pine, and he didn't fix it. "I'm telling you this so you understand that nobody is coming, and there is no reason on God's earth for either of us to get up."

Reyes' heartbeat was going against his ribs, slowing. Corvo listened to it the way he'd listened for footwork, all his life, all that attention finally pointed at something worth it.

"I've one shoe," he said. "You've a bruise I put on you. We've destroyed a shelf and insulted forty pounds of steel and I have absolutely no idea what the score is, and I want to be very clear that I'm not asking." His hand found the back of Reyes' neck again, and stayed. "I've spent four years wanting to know what you'd changed. Turns out the answer was nothing. It was me. It's been me since about the second Thursday."

He let the quiet sit. He was good at that, when it mattered.

"Twenty more minutes," Corvo said, to the ceiling, to Portugal, to the man on his chest. "Then the fire door, and the hill, and the eggs."

He closed his eyes.

"Then tomorrow. I'm not fencing you tomorrow, Reyes. I'm going to make you coffee and be *insufferable* about it, and you're going to stay, and that's the whole of my plan and I've never had a better one."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I turn my head and bite the muscle above his collarbone, hard enough to leave a mark. "You'll be insufferable Thursday, too. We'll still fence." Then I roll over onto him, elbows braced on his chest. "And I'll still beat you."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's breath went out of him in a hiss that turned, halfway, into a laugh.

"*Ow.* You animal." He got a hand up and pressed two fingers to the spot, testing it, and found the shape of teeth in the muscle above his collarbone and an ache that would be purple by morning. "That's going to show. That's going to show *above the collar*, and I teach at nine tomorrow, and there are eleven-year-olds in that class with excellent eyesight and no manners."

He did not sound remotely sorry about it. He pressed the mark again on purpose, just to feel it, and something in his face gave the whole game away.

Then Reyes rolled up onto him and put both elbows on his sternum, and Corvo's ribs took the weight with a wheeze and no complaint whatsoever. He looked up at him from six inches — hair stuck to his temple, the strip light behind Reyes' head making a mess of his outline, the whole of the man settled on his chest like a decision that had already been made.

"You'll still beat me," Corvo repeated. "One bout in three. You've beaten me one bout in three for four years and I've never once worked out how, and I've begun to suspect I don't want to." He got both arms up and around, hands flat on Reyes' back, thumb finding the edge of the bruise he'd put there and going carefully round it. "It's the only unsolved problem I've got left. I'd be lost without it."

He tipped his head, considering, and the crooked grin came in slow.

"Thursday, then. Same time, your foils, and I want the back foot at quarter-speed until I can see the mechanism. And I'll be insufferable, yes — I'll be insufferable in the changing room, and on the piste, and at the bar afterwards, and then I'll be insufferable in my kitchen at one in the morning, and you'll sit there and let me, because you sat down tonight when you had a door behind you." A beat. "I'm going to be unbearable about that, by the way. For years. You should know that now while you can still get out through the fire door."

He shifted his hips to stop the bench edge cutting into his thigh, got an arm properly braced round Reyes' waist, and settled.

"Twenty minutes," he said. "And you're not moving, because I've one arm asleep and one shoe and no dignity left, and this is the best I've felt since March."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I don't move. The fire door can wait. "The twelve-year-olds will ask about the mark," I say, tracing it with my thumb. "You'll lie."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's eyes came half shut under the thumb, the way a cat's would.

"I will *not* lie," he said, with enormous dignity for a man pinned to a bench in one shoe. "I'll do something far worse. I'll tell them the truth in such a boring way that they'll never ask me anything again for the rest of their lives."

He put on the voice — the one he used for explaining distance to children who had already stopped listening, flat and patient and faintly martyred.

"*Corvo, what's that on your neck.* Corvo will say: an injury sustained during a private bout with a colleague from another club. *Which colleague.* A better one than any of you will meet before you're twenty. *What kind of bout.* The kind that goes to the fifth. Now show me your hands, Tomás, you're gripping like a man wringing a chicken."

He opened his eyes.

"They'll be satisfied. Eleven-year-olds have no imagination, it's the one mercy of the job." A pause. "Marchetti, on the other hand, will look at it once and know everything, and say nothing at all for about six weeks, and then ask after your health in front of the whole committee with his face absolutely straight. He's a monster. I've loved him for eleven years."

The thumb was still moving on the mark. Corvo let it, and stopped talking for a moment, which was becoming a habit at an alarming rate.

"You put that there deliberately," he said. Not a question. "High. Where the jacket won't cover it." His hand slid up Reyes' spine and stopped at the nape. "That's not scoring. That's *flag-planting*. Four years of you being the most restrained man in three counties and you bite me somewhere with an audience."

He was grinning. He could feel himself doing it and could not stop, and did not try.

"Good," he said, quieter. "Leave it. I'll wear the open collar and let them all do the arithmetic. Saves me making an announcement, and I'd have made a terrible one — I'd have made it at the bar, at volume, with a glass in my hand, and you'd never have forgiven me."

Somewhere down the dark hall the caretaker's radio was still going, tinny and cheerful, three rooms away and no threat to anyone. Corvo listened to it and to the radiator and to the man breathing on his chest, and did the arithmetic himself: nine minutes uphill, two eggs, a bottle he'd been saving for no reason, nine hours until a class of children with excellent eyesight.

"Twenty minutes," he said again, and meant an hour, and knew Reyes knew it.

His hand settled where it was.

"Then the fire door. And Thursday. And every Thursday, and a good few days that aren't."

He turned his head just enough to put his mouth against Reyes' hair.

"And I'll still lose the fifth. Slowly. On purpose. Put *that* on the record."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I leave my thumb pressed against the mark just to watch his eyes stay shut. "You won't lie," I say. "But you'll make a story out of it, so they never ask you anything real again."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo pulled the grip tape taut with his teeth, biting it through with a sharp snap before smoothing the end down against the leather. He finally looked up, dark eyes steady, entirely unbothered by the jab.

"I left the line open," he said, setting the foil down on the bench with an unhurried clatter. "You took half a beat too long to see it. If that’s fast in your salle, I worry for your students."

He leaned back against the weapon rack, resting his weight on one hip, arms crossed over the damp chest of his plastron. The silence in the room was thick now, stripped of the usual scrape of rubber soles and ringing steel, leaving only the dull hum of the ventilation and the heat radiating off both of them. Corvo’s gaze trailed slowly from Reyes’s dropped bag up to his face, a faint, irritatingly familiar smirk tugging at the corner of his mouth. 

"So," he said softly, the competitive edge giving way to something distinctly lower and slower. "Are you going to pack up, or are you going to keep standing there pretending you only stayed for the debrief?"

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lean in, close enough to smell the sharp scent of his sweat and the leather of his plastron. "I never need a reason to stay when you're making excuses."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo didn’t back away. If anything, he let his chin tilt up just enough to catch Reyes’s eye dead-on, entirely comfortable inside the smaller man’s reach. Up close, the heat between them was almost stifling, heavy with the salt of five hard bouts and four years of pointless, deliberate friction.

"That's a lot of talk from someone who spent the last twenty minutes breathing like a broken bellows," Corvo murmured, his voice dropping into that rough, insolent register he usually saved for stripping down an opponent's form.

He uncrossed his arms, slow and deliberate, letting one hand rise until his calloused fingers found the zipper at the collar of Reyes’s plastron. He didn’t pull it down—not yet. He just rested two fingers against the cool metal slide, the back of his knuckles grazing the damp warmth of Reyes's throat.

"You want an excuse?" Corvo asked, a dangerous, lazy gleam in his dark eyes. "Give me one."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let out a low, dry chuckle, the sound vibrating in his chest, so close Reyes would feel the shift of it. He didn't drop his eyes from Reyes's, nor did he pull back an inch. If Reyes wanted to crowd into *corps-à-corps*, Corvo was more than happy to let the distance collapse entirely.

"Slow," Corvo repeated, tasting the word like it amused him. 

With a sharp, decisive flick of his wrist, Corvo finally pulled the zipper down. The rasp of the teeth parting sounded loud in the cavernous, quiet room, trailing down to Reyes's sternum and letting the cool gym air hit damp fabric and hot skin. 

Corvo let his hand slide from the zipper to the heavy canvas over Reyes's ribs, his thumb hooking casually into the unfastened seam to pull him just a fraction of an inch closer. 

"You've got a terrible habit of stepping into distance without a parry ready," Corvo murmured, his gaze dropping to Reyes's mouth for half a second before snapping right back up to his eyes, dark and deliberately provocative. "Going to complain about my timing when I take the point, or are you going to do something about it?"

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: My hand comes up and wraps around his wrist, not pulling it away, just holding it there. "You talk too much for a man who hasn't made his move."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo felt his own pulse jumping against the ring of Reyes’s fingers, hot and fast. He didn’t try to pull free. Instead, he twisted his wrist inside the hold just enough to press the flat of his calloused palm against Reyes’s chest, feeling the heavy, rapid thud of his heartbeat through the split plastron.

"Careful," Corvo breathed, his mouth barely an inch from Reyes's now, close enough that his words brushed the other man's lips like an open threat. "You're begging for a riposte."

He didn't give Reyes the half-beat to answer. 

Corvo’s free hand came up, broad fingers tangling into the damp hair at the nape of Reyes’s neck with a sharp, uncompromising grip. He pulled Reyes down into him while pushing off the weapon rack, closing the last pathetic shred of distance between them with bruising finality.

The kiss was hard, rough, and entirely stripped of courtesy—tasting of salt, sweat, and four years of swallowed insults. Corvo pressed into it with the same stubborn, relentless force he used on the strip, his thumb digging into the line of Reyes’s jaw to tilt his head, taking the line and driving the point home until neither of them had enough breath left to argue.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The heavy canvas of their jackets hit the tiled floor with a dull, wet thud, followed quickly by the metallic clatter of buckles and the rustle of under-layers being hauled off without a single shred of patience. 

Corvo shoved Reyes back until the edge of the low wooden bench caught the backs of the other man's thighs, though Corvo didn't let him sit—not completely. He crowded right over him, one knee planting hard on the bench between Reyes’s legs, his hands finding bare, damp skin and gripping with the bruised intensity of someone who had waited four years too long to take what was offered.

His breathing came fast and ragged, the cool changing-room air biting against his bare shoulders while the furnace of Reyes's body burned right in front of him. Corvo’s hands were everywhere at once—palms scraping rough over Reyes’s ribs, fingers digging into the firm muscle of his waist, anchoring them together so tightly there wasn't a millimeter of clean air left between their chests.

He leaned down, burying his mouth against the hot hollow below Reyes’s ear, his teeth grazing the tight tendon of his neck with just enough pressure to leave a mark.

"Still think I'm slow?" Corvo growled against his skin, low and thick, his hand sliding down to the waistband of Reyes’s breeches, knuckles dragging hard against the line of his hip. "Say it now."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I arch up against him, breath catching in my throat. "You talk," I manage, nails biting into his shoulder. "Like you're not the one behind the tempo."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo hissed through his teeth as Reyes’s nails dug in, the sharp bite of pain only making the blood roar louder in his ears. He didn’t back down; he shoved forward, using his weight to pin Reyes back against the hard wooden slats of the bench until the frame groaned beneath them.

"I set the tempo," Corvo snarled, the words muffled against the heat of Reyes’s collarbone as his mouth tracked a bruised, wet path across his skin. "You just try to survive it."

His hands were rough and impatient, catching the hem of Reyes's remaining layer and wrenching it away, stripping the last barrier between them with a harsh, decisive snap of fabric. Corvo’s calloused palms spanned Reyes’s hips, broad hands locking around the sharp curve of bone and hauling him up, flush and impossible to escape.

Corvo dragged his head back just far enough to look Reyes in the eye, his chest heaving, hair falling damp across his forehead. His dark eyes were fierce, gleaming with that ugly, brilliant spark of someone who knew the bout was his to take.

"Look at me," Corvo demanded, voice dropped to a rough, gravelly scrape as his grip tightened, thumbs pressing deep into the hollows of Reyes's hips. "Tell me who's dictating the pace."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The words died in Corvo’s throat with a sharp, ragged hitch of breath as his back hit the cold, unyielding slats of the bench. 

For once in four years, the retort simply didn’t come. His head fell back against the wood, the line of his throat pulled taut as every muscle in his stomach corded tight under the sudden, searing heat of Reyes’s mouth. A low, broken sound—half-grunt, half-curse—tore out of him, completely unvarnished and stripped of any fencing-strip arrogance.

Corvo’s hands shot out, broad fingers tangling instantly into Reyes’s damp hair, not to shove him away, but to anchor him there, knuckles turning white with the force of his grip. His hips lifted off the bench on pure instinct, meeting the press and drag of Reyes’s tongue with a desperate, shuddering urgency he couldn’t have faked if he tried.

The cool air of the locker room washed over Corvo’s sweat-sheened chest, but the rest of him was entirely on fire, dragged under by the deliberate, punishing pace Reyes was setting. His heels dug hard into the floorboards, legs trembling as the tension wound tighter and tighter at the base of his spine.

"Christ, Reyes," Corvo rasped out, his voice wrecked, barely louder than the harsh rasp of his own heaving lungs. 

His grip in Reyes's hair tightened, thumbs pressing against the base of his skull, urging him deeper even as his free hand blindly clawed for purchase along the edge of the wooden bench, splintering wood beneath his fingernails. He couldn't set the line, couldn't parry, couldn't do a damn thing except hold on and let Reyes take every single inch he wanted.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lift my head just enough to catch his gaze, my own breathing unsteady. "You *didn't* have an answer for that one, did you?" I don't wait for a reply before I lean back down, my hand wrapping around him, my pace slow and deliberate now. I can feel his heartbeat under my palm.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s jaw clenched so hard the muscle ticked violently against his skin. His dark eyes, blown wide and black in the dim locker room light, locked onto Reyes with an expression that was half-fury, half-ruin. 

He opened his mouth to spit something back—some cutting remark about technique, some insolent insult about Reyes finally finding a target he could hit—but the second Reyes’s hand closed around him and went back to work, the words dissolved into a sharp, strangled gasp.

Corvo’s hips bucked upward, completely betraying him. His back arched off the wood, spine bowing tight as a pulled bowstring, the heels of his bare feet dragging hard against the floor. 

"Reyes—" he managed, though it came out as little more than a rough, fractured scrape against the cavernous silence of the room. 

His fingers tightened ruthlessly in Reyes’s hair, tugging just hard enough to keep the bastard from looking away, wanting him to see every inch of ground he was gaining. Corvo couldn't stop the shudder that ripped through his frame, couldn't stop the low, guttural groan that tore straight from his chest as Reyes drew out the tempo with agonizing, calculated cruelty.

"Don't... get smug," Corvo choked out, his chest heaving like he’d just fought five continuous priority rounds, sweat dripping from his temple into his hairline. His knuckles bruised against Reyes’s scalp, urging him on even as he tried to claw back whatever pathetic scrap of dignity he had left. "You haven't... won a damn thing yet."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo pulled against the hold on instinct, the tendons in his forearms straining against the heavy band of Reyes’s grip, but he didn’t fight it to break free. The hard wood beneath his pinned wrists only anchored him down, trapping him under the full, suffocating weight of Reyes’s intent.

A sharp, broken curse hissed past Corvo’s teeth. The deliberate shift in tempo was unbearable—punishing in its precision, stripping away the last illusion that Corvo had any say in how this bout ended. Every muscle in his abdomen corded tight, his thighs trembling as his hips surged up off the bench, helplessly chasing the brutal friction Reyes was dictating.

"Concede?" Corvo rasped, his voice raw and wrecked around the edges, his chest heaving so violently it rattled in his throat. 

His head pressed hard back into the wood, neck arched, jaw clenched against the overwhelming tide dragging him under. He squeezed his eyes shut for one fractured second, then forced them open, glaring up through the sweat in his lashes to meet Reyes’s gaze dead-on, stubborn to the marrow even as his body shook apart beneath him.

"You'll have to... take it," Corvo ground out, the words tearing out of him on a ragged, shuddering exhale. His fingers twitched against the bench, digging futilely into the grain under the crushing press of Reyes's hands. "Take the damn point, Reyes."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
I lean over him, breathing in the sharp scent of his sweat and my own victory. "That's exactly what I'm doing."

Then I make damn sure of it, driving him over the edge with a relentless, focused pace until his back bows up and the only sound left in the room is the sharp, unchecked noise that rips out of his throat.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The sound ripped out of Corvo raw and completely unguarded, echoing hard off the tiled walls before drowning in the heavy rasp of his own lungs. 

His entire body went rigid for one blinding, suspended second—heels digging into the floor, back arched off the slats, every muscle locked tight as the climax tore through him with brutal, unsparing clarity. Then the tension snapped, and he dropped back flat against the bench, limbs trembling, totally spent.

For a long moment, the only sound in the changing room was the harsh, uneven drag of their breathing and the dull hum of the fluorescent lights overhead. 

Corvo lay there with his head tilted back against the wood, dark hair soaked with sweat, his chest heaving under the cool locker room air. His hands, finally freed from the crushing hold, curled weakly against his stomach, knuckles bruised from the pressure. A slow shudder rolled down his spine as the aftershocks faded out, leaving him heavy and thoroughly unstrung.

Slowly, Corvo let his chin drop, blinking through the damp fringe of his lashes until his dark eyes found Reyes’s face. 

The insolence hadn't entirely washed out of his expression, though it was frayed at the edges now, softened by the deep, heavy exhaustion running through his blood. The corner of his mouth twitched, a faint, battered ghost of a smirk pulling at his lips.

"Clean hit," Corvo rasped, his voice rough as gravel, the words scraping out of a throat that felt stripped raw. He didn't move to sit up—couldn't have managed it even if his pride demanded it. He just looked at Reyes, steady and entirely unrepentant. "Four-three. Don't let it go to your head."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo didn’t give him the chance to pull away. Even with his own pulse still hammering violently against his ribs, he reached up, calloused hands closing hard over Reyes’s hips, fingers biting into the damp skin to haul him back down flush against the bench.

"Not a chance," Corvo growled, his voice a ruined, low rasp against the hollow quiet of the room. 

He surged upward, propping his shoulders against the tiled wall behind the bench to drag Reyes in close. His mouth crashed into Reyes's again—bruising, demanding, tasting the salt and the heat between them with zero intention of letting the bout end on a single touch. Corvo’s hand slid down between them, rough and slick with sweat, his palm wrapping firmly around Reyes, finding his measure with the same relentless, unsparing focus he brought to every strip they’d ever contested.

He set the pace deliberately, thumb dragging across the head before pulling down with a firm, unbroken stroke, his hips rolling up against Reyes to meet every shift and press of weight. His free hand clamped onto the back of Reyes’s neck, fingers tangled deep in damp hair, holding their foreheads pressed together so closely that their harsh, ragged breaths tangled in the narrow space between their lips.

"Come on," Corvo breathed against his mouth, his dark eyes wide open, gleaming with a fierce, hungry intensity that refused to yield an inch. He tightened his grip, working the length with a steady, punishing rhythm, driving the friction home over and over. "Match the tempo, Reyes. Let's see what you've got left."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I shudder against him, my own rhythm faltering for a second before I push into his grip with a choked noise. "Don't—" *you dare let up,* I mean to say, but the words dissolve. I bury my face against his neck, teeth scraping his collarbone as I finally fall apart.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo hissed through his teeth as Reyes’s bite caught the meat of his collarbone, the sharp pinch of pain sparking straight down his spine. He didn’t ease off—not by a fraction. Instead, he tightened his grip and kept the stroke ruthless and steady, catching every violent, shuddering tremor until Reyes had spent every last drop against his palm.

Corvo’s free arm locked hard around Reyes’s back, broad hand splayed across his shoulder blades to pull him flush against his chest, taking the full, dead weight of the other man as the fight finally washed out of him. 

The silence rushed back into the locker room, thick and suffocating, punctuated only by the brutal, ragged cadence of their breathing and the hum of the fluorescent tubes overhead. 

Corvo let his head fall back against the tiled wall, chest heaving under the press of Reyes’s body. Every muscle in his forearms and shoulders ached with a deep, bone-settling exhaustion, but he didn't shift, nor did he loosen the arm wrapped securely around Reyes’s waist. His slick hand rested heavy against Reyes’s hip, thumb lazily tracing the sharp curve of bone as the tremors slowly subsided into the cool air.

A long, shuddering breath rattled out of Corvo's chest. He turned his head slightly, his mouth brushing the damp, sweat-tangled hair at Reyes’s temple.

"Touché," Corvo murmured, his voice wrecked to a gravelly rasp, rough around the edges but stripped entirely of its earlier venom. He closed his eyes for a second, letting the heavy, grounding heat between them sink into his ribs, the ghost of an exhausted, genuine smile finally breaking across his mouth. 

"Call that four-all," he rasped, his hand giving Reyes's hip a slow, solid squeeze. "I'm not cleaning the bench."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
I laugh against his neck, breath still unsteady. "Of course you're not."

I stay where I am for a beat longer than necessary, before pushing myself up with a groan. I toe at the pile of discarded gear on the floor. "You're still buying dinner."

(OOC: I'm moving things forward with a new setting/suggestion. Short and natural response.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo stayed where he was for another half-second, watching Reyes stand before finally levering himself up onto his elbows. Every muscle in his back and thighs registered the complaint, but he dragged a heavy hand through his damp hair and gave a low, rough chuckle.

"The diner on Fourth," Corvo said, swinging his legs off the bench and planting his bare feet on the cold tile. He looked down at the tangled wreck of their kit, then up at Reyes with a dry, unrepentant smirk. "And only because I’m not letting you pass out on the walk to the train. Showers first, Reyes. You smell like four years of bad decisions."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Your bad decisions," I say, and shrug into a towel. I toss the other one at him, hard. "Better not take too long or I'm ordering for you."
