dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I put my hand in his hair and tip his head back so he has to look up at me. "Say it now, then."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas let his head fall back into the pull of her hand, easy, no resistance, throat bared by accident of geometry more than intention. His eyes found hers anyway.

"I want you to use me until you're done," he said. "Not until I ask you to stop. Until you decide." A small breath. "And I don't want you to be careful about it."

He didn't blink, didn't look away, just knelt there with his head tipped back in her grip like that was exactly where it belonged.

"That's it. That's the whole thing. I've been sitting here trying to figure out how to say it for four minutes and that's it."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I trace my thumb along his jawline, feeling the tension there. "That's a very specific request." My voice is low, deliberate. "And if I decide I'm never done?"

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas's breath caught, just slightly, at the shape of that — not fear, something closer to the opposite.

"Then I guess I'm yours until you get bored," he said, and there was a smile trying to happen at the corner of his mouth even with his head tipped back like that. "I'm not asking for a mercy clause, Wren. I know how this works. I know you'll take care of me after, however long after turns out to be." His jaw shifted under her thumb, chasing the touch instead of away from it. "I just wanted you to know you don't have to check. Not tonight. I'll use the word if I need it — that hasn't changed. But short of that, I want you to stop asking me if I'm okay and just believe that I am."

He held still, waiting, the position doing half the talking for him — throat bared, weight settled back on his heels like he'd already decided this was going to be a long night and had made peace with it before she'd said yes.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I've had a week," he says. "I'd like not to make any decisions for a few hours, if that's on offer."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Something in Tomas's chest eased at that, at the tiredness underneath it he could hear if he listened for it. He didn't ask about the week. That wasn't what tonight was for, and she'd tell him if she wanted to.

"It's on offer," he said. "All of it. You don't have to decide anything except what you want in whatever order you want it. I'll be here." He let his eyes close for a second, just to feel her hand still in his hair, still holding his head at that angle. "You don't even have to talk to me if you don't want to. I'll follow your hands."

He opened his eyes again, steadier now, some of the nervous energy from the four minutes of kneeling gone out of him now that it was said and answered.

"Whatever this week was," he added, quieter, "you can put it down here. That's kind of the point."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I lean down and kiss him, hard and possessive. "Get up on the bed. On your knees." I let go of his hair and step back, watching him.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas rose without using his hands, a small unnecessary display of ease, and climbed onto the bed. He arranged himself the way he knew she liked — knees spread enough, spine straight, hands resting open on his thighs instead of curling into fists, because loose hands meant he wasn't bracing for anything, and he wasn't.

He didn't look over his shoulder at her right away. He let her watch first, the way she'd said she wanted to, and just breathed — slow, deliberate, settling into his body instead of his head. By the time he did turn his face toward her, checking not for permission but just to see her, there was nothing performative left in it. Just him, kneeling, waiting, already a little gone.

"Like this?" he asked, and it wasn't really a question. It was an offering.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I take him at his word and stop asking after that, and he stops needing to be asked, and neither of us has any clothes on within about a minute of the decision.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The speed of it caught up with him a beat after it happened — one moment cloth, the next her hands on skin, and Tomas made a low sound at the transition that had nothing performative in it either. He didn't reach for her. That wasn't the shape of tonight, and some part of him had known it since he was counting minutes on the floor.

He kept his hands where she'd want them, thighs, open, and let his head fall forward when her fingers found the back of his neck, a full-body yes translated into the single available gesture. His breathing had already gone ragged in a way that had nothing to do with exertion yet.

"Good," he murmured, mostly to himself, mostly just to name the thing happening in his chest — that loosening, that week-shaped weight of hers becoming something he could carry for her instead of watching her carry alone. "That's — yeah. Good."

He didn't say anything else useful after that. He stopped trying to. His body answered instead, arching into whatever touch came next without waiting to be told it was allowed, because it was, because she'd said so, because for the next stretch of unmeasured time all he had to do was be here and be hers and let her decide when done meant done.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: My hands settle on his hips, fingers digging into the muscle there. I lean close, my voice a low murmur against his ear. "You feel so good like this." I press a kiss to his shoulder. "Don't move."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas went still in a way that took effort to make look effortless — the command landing somewhere low in his spine, turning ordinary stillness into something charged. He kept his hands open on his thighs, kept his spine straight, let the kiss on his shoulder pull a shiver out of him that he didn't try to suppress, because stillness had never meant *unmoved*, just *unmoving where it counted.*

"Not moving," he said, and his voice had already dropped half an octave, gone rough at the edges. He could feel exactly where her fingers dug in, could map the shape of her hands on him like she was leaving something behind on purpose. He wanted to push back into them. He didn't.

The discipline of it was its own kind of pleasure — holding the position while every instinct in his body strained toward her, toward more contact, toward closing whatever small distance was left between his skin and hers. He breathed through it instead, slow and audible, a kind of offering in itself: *look what I'll do for you, look how still I can be, look how much it costs me and how gladly I pay it.*

"You can take as long as you want," he added, quieter now, half into the dark in front of him. "I'm not going anywhere. I'm not moving." A small, helpless huff of breath that was almost a laugh. "Even though every part of me wants to right now. Just — tell me when you want something and I'll give it to you. Otherwise I'm just gonna kneel here and be exactly this good for you."

His hips shifted, just barely, an involuntary answer to her grip rather than a violation of the order — and he caught it, stilled again, waited to see if she'd let it pass or correct him. Either way was fine. Either way was hers to decide.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's shaking by the time I've finished with my mouth and he still hasn't been told he's allowed to move, which is most of why he's shaking.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas was shaking, a fine full-body tremor that ran from his thighs up through his spine, and every part of it was want with nowhere to go. He hadn't moved. He'd come so close a handful of times he'd had to grind his jaw shut and breathe through his nose like that alone could hold him together, and it had — barely, by inches, by the sheer stubborn fact that she hadn't said he could.

"Wren," he got out, and it wasn't quite a plea, more like her name was the only word left in him that still worked. His hands had curled at some point without his permission, fisted in the sheets instead of resting open, and he noticed that distantly, like a report coming in from somewhere far away. He didn't fix it. He didn't have the coordination left to fix it.

"Still not moving," he said, voice wrecked, something almost like pride threaded through the shake in it. "You didn't say I could. I'm not — " a breath, ragged, "I'm not moving."

His head had dropped forward at some point, sweat-damp hair falling into his eyes, and he lifted it now, just enough to find her, silently asking without asking — *is this the part where I still wait, or is this the part where you tell me what's next* — the trust in it total, the want in it obvious, and underneath both of them, steady as anything, the simple fact that he'd stay exactly like this, trembling and undone, for as long as she wanted him to.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I finally let my hands slide from his hips to his shoulders, feeling the tremors there. "Now you can move," I whisper, guiding him back against me. "Show me how much you want it."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The permission broke something loose in him — not control, he'd kept that white-knuckled the whole time, but the leash on it. Tomas moved like he'd been waiting to for an hour, because he had, rolling his hips back into her with a sound that came from somewhere below thought, no performance left in it at all.

"Wren—" her name again, the only word still reliably his, and then not even that, just breath and motion, the shaking translating finally into something he was allowed to do instead of something he had to hold. He found the rhythm she wanted almost immediately, reading it off her hands on his shoulders, off the sounds she wasn't quite hiding, and gave everything he had to it — not holding back, not pacing himself, because she'd told him not to be careful and he'd taken that as permission for himself too.

"Like this," he managed, rough, half a question and half just narrating what his body was already doing. "Is this — tell me if you want it different, I'll—" He didn't finish, because she moved against him and it took the sentence apart.

His hands found the headboard, needing somewhere to put the force of it, and he pushed back into her again, harder, chasing the exact angle that made her breath catch, learning it fast and using what he learned without shame. Four years of this and he still lit up like new every time she let him work for it — every noise she made felt earned, felt like something he'd built with his own body instead of something happening to him.

"Wren, I'm not—" He caught himself right at the edge, some scrap of training holding even now. "I'm close. I'm not asking. Just telling you. Whenever you—" His voice broke off into a groan as he pushed back again, offering the information up the way he'd offer anything else to her — plainly, without hiding it, hers to do with as she wanted.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Please," he says, and then the phrase we use when he wants it harder than that. "Rough. You know how. I'm not going to break and I'd tell you."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The words landed like permission stacked on permission, and Tomas felt whatever careful edge he'd been keeping just — go. He'd said it himself: *rough, you know how, I'm not going to break.* It was true. It had always been true. Four years of her learning exactly where his edges actually were, not where fear said they might be, and he trusted that math more than he trusted almost anything else in his life.

"Okay," he breathed, and then didn't say anything else that made sense, because she gave him what he asked for and his voice went somewhere past words. He pushed back into it, met it, took what she gave without flinching, because flinching had never been the point and this — this wasn't a thing to survive, it was a thing to *want*, loud and unashamed.

His knuckles whitened on the headboard. A sound tore out of him that he didn't try to shape into anything prettier. He could feel the difference between careful and this, could feel her actually letting go the way he'd asked her to hours — minutes — some unmeasured time ago, and it undid him faster than anything careful ever could have.

"There," he managed, wrecked, grinning even through it, "*there* — yeah, don't — don't stop, don't slow down, I've got it, I've got it—"

He didn't got it, not really, not in any sense that meant control — he was shaking again, worse than before, held up as much by her hands and his grip on the headboard as by his own knees. But he meant it the way he always meant that phrase between them: *I can take this. I want this. Keep going.*

"Wren—" one more time, her name breaking apart in his mouth, and then he stopped trying to say anything at all, just gave her everything he had left, unguarded, unbraced, exactly as gone as she'd told him he was allowed to be.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I don't let him finish the sentence. My hands tighten on his hips, pulling him back harder against me. "Then let go," I tell him, voice rough. "I've got you."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas let go.

There was no other way to describe it — not just the climax that tore through him a moment later, though that was part of it, white and total and pulled out of him on a broken sound that had her name somewhere in the wreckage of it. It was everything underneath that too. The week he hadn't talked about. The four minutes of kneeling. Whatever brittle, careful thing he'd been carrying around in his own head that had needed her hands and her permission to finally set down.

He shook apart in her grip, and she held him through it, exactly like she'd said she would, and he trusted that completely, didn't brace against it, didn't try to hold himself together for her benefit. He just came, hard and loud and unguarded, his forehead dropping against the headboard, his whole body given over to it.

"*Wren—*" one more time, quieter now, more like a sigh than anything urgent, the last of it working through him in slow aftershocks.

For a few seconds after, he didn't move at all — not the held-still of before, but the simple fact of having nothing left to move with. His arms had gone unreliable. His knees had opinions about staying upright that he wasn't sure he agreed with anymore.

"Okay," he breathed, eventually, voice completely wrecked, half a laugh buried in it. "Okay. Yeah. That was—" He didn't finish. He didn't need to. He turned his head enough to find her, not pulling away, just needing to see her face, needing that piece of the coming-back-together that always mattered more to him than anyone who didn't know him would guess.

"I'm here," he said, softer, answering a question she hadn't had to ask yet. "I'm good. I'm so good, Wren." A slow breath. "Don't let go yet, though. Whenever you're ready. No rush."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's stopped forming sentences and I'm not much better. "Don't stop," he manages. (OOC: no fade, no time-skip -- write it through, including the end.)

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas hadn't fully recovered his own voice yet, and it didn't matter, because what he had left in him wasn't words anyway. He rocked back into her again despite the tremor still working through his thighs, despite the wreck he already was, because *don't stop* wasn't a request he needed twice.

"Not stopping," he managed, thick and rough, more breath than sound. "Not — yeah. Here."

His hands left the headboard just long enough to find hers where they gripped his hips, not moving her, not directing anything, just covering her fingers with his own for a second like he needed the point of contact doubled. Then back to holding on, because he needed that too, needed something solid while his body kept answering hers without any executive decision-making involved anymore.

He felt her rhythm change, felt the particular way her breathing caught and stayed caught, and he chased it without being told to, canting his hips to give her whatever angle made that sound happen again. "That's it," he breathed, hoarse, half to encourage her and half because narrating it was the only kind of talking still available to him. "That's it, Wren, come on—"

She went over first this time, and Tomas felt it happen against him, around him, her grip tightening hard enough to bruise and he welcomed every ounce of it, groaning her name low in his chest as she rode it out. He held as still as he could manage through the aftershocks, giving her that, letting her take what she needed from his stillness the way he'd earlier given her his shaking.

Only once her hands loosened did he let himself follow her down — no build required, just an aftershock of his own, smaller, almost startled out of him, a helpless little sound and a full-body shudder before his arms finally, completely gave out.

He folded forward, caught himself on his forearms instead of his face, and just breathed for a while, chest heaving, sweat cooling too fast against too much air.

"Okay," he rasped, eventually, into the pillow. "Okay. That's — I don't have words. You broke my words." A weak, honest laugh. "Come here. Please. I need you to be closer than you currently are."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I shift to lie down beside him, curling my body around his. My arm wraps around his chest, pulling him back against me. "Your words were perfect," I murmur against his damp shoulder. "You were perfect."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas let himself be pulled, boneless, his back finding the curve of her like it had a thousand times before and still felt new every single time. He turned his head just enough to press his face into whatever part of her was closest — her arm, her collarbone, he couldn't tell anymore and didn't care — and just breathed her in.

"I'm not sure 'perfect' is a word I earned tonight," he mumbled, voice still wrecked, still slow to come back online. "I think I said your name like six times and then forgot the English language entirely."

He laughed, short and warm, and covered her arm with his hand where it lay across his chest, not pulling it tighter, just holding it there. His heart was still going too fast. Hers, pressed against his back, felt like it was starting to slow.

"How are you," he asked, quieter now, turning the question around the way he always did once the part where he wasn't supposed to ask things was officially over. Not *are you okay*, not the thing she'd asked him to stop checking for — just an open door, in case she wanted to walk through it.

He didn't wait for an answer like it was owed to him. He just stayed there, solid and close, tracing slow absent circles against her forearm with his thumb, giving her the same thing she'd just given him — presence without demand.

"Whatever was left of that week," he said eventually, softer, "I hope some of it's on the floor now. I meant that part." A pause, his voice going a little rougher, a little more unguarded. "Thank you. For trusting me to mean it when I said I wanted this. That mattered. Still matters."

He shifted, just enough to press a kiss to whatever skin was nearest — her wrist, it turned out — and settled back in, in no hurry to move again for a long while.

"I'm not going anywhere," he added, half a joke, half not. "Pretty sure I've lost the ability to go anywhere. You're stuck with me for at least twenty minutes."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I smile against his skin. "I'm good. Really good." I pause, letting my thumb trace the line of his ribs. "And you earned it. Every time you didn't move when you were shaking." I press a kiss to his temple. "Stay as long as you need. I'm not going anywhere either."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas hummed at that, low and satisfied, the praise settling into him the way it always did — not as something he needed to be told, exactly, but as something that felt good to hear anyway, her voice low and certain against his skin.

"Good," he said. "Really good. That's — yeah, I'll take really good." He turned his hand over so his fingers laced loosely with hers where they rested against his chest, no urgency in it, just wanting the contact. "I was shaking because you're terrifyingly good at your job, for the record. Not because it was hard. It was the opposite of hard. It was easy in the way that only feels hard because I wanted it so much."

He let his eyes drift shut, the exhaustion finally catching up to him in earnest now that there was nothing left to hold together. His breathing had slowed to match hers, or hers to match his — he couldn't tell which and it didn't matter.

"Can I ask something not-heavy," he said after a minute, voice drowsy now, blurring at the edges, "or is that a tomorrow question."

He didn't wait long for permission this time, just kept going, soft and unhurried. "Water. Do you want water. I can move in a minute, my legs are lying to me about being done but I think they'll cooperate if I ask nicely." A small laugh, breath more than sound. "I just don't want to move yet. This part's mine too, right? Staying like this. That's allowed."

He pressed back into her a little, an answer to the arm around him, a wordless *don't let go yet* that mirrored what he'd said to her not long before. Whatever the week had been, whatever waited on the other side of tonight, none of it had made it into the room with them. Just this — his skin still damp, her heartbeat slowing against his back, and the particular quiet that only ever showed up after they'd both given everything they had and found it received, not spent.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I'll get the water," I murmur, pressing another kiss to his shoulder before reluctantly untangling myself. "Stay right there." I pad to the kitchen, returning with two glasses. Setting them on the nightstand, I slide back in behind him, my body fitting against his again. "Your legs can have the night off."

rung_labels.evidence: You don't have to decide anything except what you want in whatever order you want it

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas had been kneeling by the end of the bed for about four minutes, which Wren knew because he had started counting somewhere around the point it became obvious he intended to wait as long as it took.

"You could have said something," Wren said.

"I could have," Tomas agreed, not moving.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I put my hand in his hair and tip his head back so he has to look up at me. "Say it now, then."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas let his head go where Wren's hand put it, which was the easy part; the looking up took a second longer, because looking up at Wren always did something to his breathing that he had never entirely gotten used to in four years.

"I want the rope tonight," he said. "Wrists behind, the way you did in February. And I want you to take your time with it."

He didn't look away. That had been the hard-won thing, early on — not hiding in the floor or the wall while he said what he wanted out loud. Wren had waited him out on that too.

"Not the blindfold," he added. "I want to watch you work."

His knees ached faintly against the hardwood, a clean ordinary ache, the kind that made everything else feel more precise. Wren's fingers were still wound in his hair, not pulling, just holding the angle.

"And after," Tomas said, "I want the couch, not the bed. And the blanket that doesn't shed."

He caught the corner of Wren's mouth twitching and felt his own want to do the same.

"That's the whole list," he said. "I've been holding it for four minutes, so."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *My thumb brushes over his temple, a slow, deliberate stroke.* "Good." *I release his hair and stand, offering a hand to help him up.* "Grab the rope from the dresser. I'll get the blanket."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas took the hand and let Wren take some of his weight on the way up, because pride about his own knees had never gotten him anything but a limp. He rolled his shoulders once, felt the hinge of them loosen, and went to the dresser.

The rope lived in the second drawer, coiled the way he'd coiled it himself on Sunday while half-watching something on the television — six-millimeter jute, broken in soft, the ends whipped in red thread because Wren had done it that way years ago and neither of them had seen a reason to change. He lifted the hank out and let it hang from his fist, testing the weight the way he always did, as if it might have changed.

"It's a little dry," he said, over his shoulder. "I didn't oil it after last time."

Which wasn't a complaint. He liked the faint scratch of it, the way it left its record on him for a day or two afterward, a map he could press on in the kitchen the next morning and feel the whole evening come back up through his skin.

He brought it over and put it in Wren's hands rather than setting it down, which was a small thing and entirely on purpose. Then he stood there a moment, looking at the line of Wren's forearms and the loop of jute across them, and made himself say the last part of the list, the part he'd been lazy about.

"Wrists behind, but check the left one twice," he said. "It went cold faster in February than I told you at the time."

He let that sit. He'd been given a hard time about that one already, deservedly, and the giving of it had involved sitting on the couch in a blanket being fed toast at eleven at night, which, honestly, was not much of a deterrent.

"I'll say if anything changes," he added. "I will actually say it."

Then he stepped back out of the way of the bed, turned his back, and put his wrists together at the small of his spine — loose, unhurried, just presenting them — and waited, which he had discovered four minutes ago he was still extremely bad at.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I've had a week," he says. "I'd like not to make any decisions for a few hours, if that's on offer."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas didn't turn around. He liked the shape of the room with Wren behind him, the not-knowing where the hands would come from.

"It's on offer," he said. "That's half of why I made a list."

He shifted his weight, evened it out between both feet, wrists still crossed loose at his back. The jute smell was in the air now, faint and dusty-sweet, the way old hay smelled.

"You don't have to invent anything. I've done the inventing. You just have to do the part you're good at." He tilted his head slightly, considering. "Which is the slow part. Which is the whole point."

Four years and he still found it strange and enormous, how much easier it was to ask for the thing than to sit around hoping to be guessed at. Early on he'd thought the point of all this was to be handed over to somebody else's imagination entirely, and it had taken him an embarrassingly long time to understand that the handing over worked better when he brought something to hand over in the first place. A list. A shape for the evening. Then he could stop thinking, and Wren could stop deciding, and they could both just be in it.

"You had a week," he said. "I know. You came in Tuesday and didn't take your coat off for twenty minutes."

He flexed his fingers once, then let them go still.

"So here's the last of it, and then I'm done talking," he said. "Wrists behind. Check the left one twice. No blindfold. Couch, good blanket. If I need something I'll say the word and you'll hear it, because you always do." A breath. "Everything else between now and then is yours and I don't want to know about it in advance."

He straightened his spine, dropped his shoulders back where they belonged, and made his hands go soft against each other.

"That's the whole list," he said again, quieter this time, and shut up.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I let the rope slide through my fingers, the rough texture familiar and grounding. Then I step close, my chest against his back, and bring the first loop over his wrists. "Breathe," I murmur, my voice low against his ear. "I'll check. But you'll tell me if it's sooner."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas breathed. Not because he needed telling, but because being told made it a different thing — made it something he was doing for Wren rather than something his body was managing on its own.

"I'll tell you," he said.

The first loop settled and he felt his whole spine let go by about a centimeter, which was nothing and was also everything. Wren's chest was warm at his back. The rope crossed his wrists once, twice, the jute catching faintly on the fine hair of his forearms, and Tomas made his hands stay soft, thumbs tucked in, the way he'd learned to years ago after the one time he'd fisted them out of nerves and paid for it in pins and needles for a full hour.

"Sooner," he repeated, agreeing to it out loud, because Wren had asked for that specifically and he'd learned that agreeing in words was worth more than nodding into the dark.

Wren worked the wraps down, unhurried. Tomas counted them without meaning to, the way he counted most things, and then stopped counting somewhere around the fourth pass because the rhythm of it had gotten under the part of his brain that did arithmetic. That was the slow part. That was the whole point. The pull, the settle, the pause while Wren smoothed a line flat with two fingers before laying the next one over it.

He turned his head, just enough to see down along his own shoulder — no blindfold, that had been the request and he was collecting on it — and caught the edge of Wren's hands moving. Knuckles, the flex of a tendon, the red whipping on the rope end where it trailed across the back of his thigh.

"Still warm," he said, when Wren's fingers found the left one the first time and pressed. "Both of them. Pink and boring."

He shut his eyes then, briefly, not to hide but because the smell of the jute and the weight of Wren at his back had stacked up into something that wanted a second of dark.

"Keep going," he said. "Please."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I take him at his word and stop asking after that, and he stops needing to be asked, and neither of us has any clothes on within about a minute of the decision.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas lost the thread of time somewhere in there, which was the closest thing to a religious experience he had access to.

He knew the rope, and the rope knew him — the way the wraps bit when Wren moved him, the way his shoulders reported back on angles he hadn't authorized. He knew the weight of Wren over him and then behind him and then still, for long stretches, doing nothing at all except keeping a hand flat between his shoulder blades while Tomas made undignified noises into the duvet and did not care. That was the slow part. Wren had never once rushed him out of the middle of something just because the middle wasn't going anywhere in particular.

Twice he felt fingers go under the jute at his left wrist and press, and twice he said *warm*, and the second time he said it he heard himself laugh at nothing, breathless and stupid, and felt Wren's mouth against the back of his neck in response.

Later — and later was genuinely all he could say about it, the clock having become somebody else's problem — the rope came off in the order it had gone on, which he always found faintly mournful and which Wren always did unhurriedly anyway, working the wraps loose instead of cutting corners, palm running down each forearm as it was freed. Tomas's hands came forward and his shoulders made a sound like furniture.

"Oh," he said, with feeling. "God. Hold on."

He got the pins-and-needles out on his own, flexing, while Wren watched him do it, and then held both wrists up to be looked at without being told to — banded pink, already going purple-ish in one spot near the heel of the left hand, everything moving the way it was supposed to.

"Fine," he reported. "That one'll show for two days."

He sounded pleased about it. He was pleased about it.

Then the shaking started, the ordinary post-thing tremor that arrived on schedule and always in his thighs first, and he put a hand out for Wren's shoulder and said, without embarrassment, because they had been past embarrassment for about three and a half years, "Couch. Now, ideally. And the blanket, and don't put anything on yet, you're warm."

He made it there under his own power, mostly. He lay down along the cushions with his head in Wren's lap and his wrists resting on his own chest where he could look at them, and let the good blanket get tucked in around his feet, and after a while he said, muffled, "There's toast in the house, incidentally. I bought the bread with this specifically in mind."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I stroke his hair, fingers combing through the damp strands.* "You think of everything." *My voice is low, relaxed. I let my hand drift down to his shoulder, thumb tracing the edge of the rope marks.* "Give it ten minutes. Then I'll make the toast."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas made a noise of agreement that wasn't really a word, and let the ten minutes start without watching them.

The shaking was already going out of his thighs. It always left the way it came, from the outside in, so that the last of it sat somewhere behind his sternum for a while after his legs had gone quiet — a fizzing, floated, faintly drunk feeling that he had never found a good name for and had stopped trying to. Wren's thumb was moving over the band of marks on his shoulder, following the line of it like reading something in braille, and Tomas turned his face slightly into the warmth of Wren's stomach and let that be the only thing happening.

"I don't think of everything," he said, eventually. "I thought of bread. That's one thing. I've been thinking about it since Tuesday, so it's had a lot of runway."

He lifted one wrist off his chest and held it up into the lamplight, turning it. The jute had left its neat parallel rows, pink going dusky at the edges, one place near the heel of his hand where it had bitten deeper and would go properly purple by morning. He pressed it with his thumb and felt the whole evening come up under the pressure, exactly the way he'd known it would.

"Look at that," he said.

"Mm," Wren said.

"No, look."

Wren looked, and made the small sound of someone who had already looked twice during and once after and was humouring him, and Tomas let his hand drop back onto his chest, satisfied.

The room ticked along. Something was going on outside, a car, somebody's gate. His feet were warm under the blanket that didn't shed, and the other blanket was still on the bed where it belonged, shedding on its own time.

"You can have Saturday too, if you want it," he said, after a while, into Wren's thigh. "I'm not making a list. I'll just be around and you can do what you like with that."

He yawned, jaw cracking, entirely unselfconscious.

"Ten minutes," he said. "I'm counting. I'm very good at counting."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's shaking by the time I've finished with my mouth and he still hasn't been told he's allowed to move, which is most of why he's shaking.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas had been told to keep still, once, at the beginning, in the flat conversational voice Wren used for things that were not up for discussion, and he had said *yes* and meant it, and that had been perhaps twenty minutes ago and the meaning of it had gotten considerably more expensive since.

Everything in him wanted to move. That was the whole architecture of it — the rope did the wrists and the instruction did the rest, and the rest was the harder half by a long way. His thighs had gone to water. There was a tremor running up through him in waves that arrived faster than he could breathe through, and he had his forehead pressed into the duvet because it was the only pressure he was permitted to seek out, and he was making a sound he would have been mortified by at twenty-three and had long since stopped auditing.

"Please," he said, into the fabric, which wasn't a request for anything specific and they both knew it. It was just the last coherent thing he had on hand.

Wren didn't answer. Wren's hand came to rest flat and warm on the small of his back, over the place where the rope crossed itself, and pressed down — steadying, not moving him, just *there* — and Tomas made a ruined noise and held.

He held. That was the thing he had come here to do. Not the rope, not really; the rope was scaffolding. This was the part — the narrow, shaking, held-open middle of it where he had handed over the only thing he actually owned, which was the decision about when, and somebody else was taking their time with it.

"Still warm," he managed, because Wren's fingers had found his left wrist again, unhurried, checking the way he'd been asked to. "God. *Warm.* Both. I'll tell you—"

"I know," Wren said.

Tomas laughed, one wretched syllable of it, and shook, and stayed exactly where he'd been put.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I press a kiss to the base of his spine, slow and deliberate. "Good." My hand stays firm on his back, keeping him grounded. "Almost there."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
*Almost there* did something worse to him than any of the rest of it, because it meant Wren had decided, and the deciding had been taken out of his hands weeks ago and he still hadn't gotten used to how much that landed.

"Okay," Tomas said. "Okay. Okay—"

It came out as one long string with no gaps in it. He got his knees under himself a fraction better, not moving, just redistributing, which he thought was probably allowed and would have stopped instantly if told otherwise. The kiss at the base of his spine was still sitting there like a coin someone had pressed into his palm. Wren's hand hadn't shifted. That was the only fixed point in the room and he leaned his whole attention on it.

He had learned, over four years, that he could hold longer than he believed he could, and also that the believing was the interesting part — that the edge of it was never actually where he thought it was, and finding out where it really sat required somebody else to be in charge of the finding. He'd never once gotten there alone. It wasn't a thing you could do to yourself.

"Not long," he said. It wasn't a bargain. It was information, offered up, because he'd promised information and the promise was the only bit of himself he still had organized. "Wren. Not long."

Wren's thumb moved once, slow, across the small of his back, acknowledging.

Tomas put his face down and gave up the last of his arithmetic, and waited to be told, and when he was told he went through it with his whole body, ugly and loud and entirely unguarded, and Wren's hand stayed flat and warm and steady the whole way down, and afterward there was a long silence in which he discovered he had no bones left anywhere.

"Fuck," he said eventually, to the duvet.

"Mm," Wren said.

"No, genuinely." He turned his head enough to get one eye clear. His voice came out wrecked and delighted. "Genuinely."

Then, with what remained: "Rope. Please. Slowly, but now."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Please," he says, and then the phrase we use when he wants it harder than that. "Rough. You know how. I'm not going to break and I'd tell you."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas said it and then heard himself say it, which was always slightly after the fact.

"Rough," he repeated, steadier the second time, because the phrase had a job to do and mumbling it would have made Wren wait for a cleaner version. "I mean it. I've got nothing left to protect. Use that."

He shifted his knees wider on the duvet, an offering rather than a demand, and made his hands go soft again at his back. The jute had gone warm from his own skin by now, the way it always did, until it stopped feeling like an object and started feeling like a condition.

"Left one's still fine," he added, pre-emptively, since it would be asked and he wanted the asking out of the way. "Fine and warm and I will say the word the second it isn't, and you've never once not heard me, so."

He pressed his forehead down and let the last of his organizing go.

What he knew about the next part, he knew mostly in retrospect, because it did not keep in his memory as a sequence. It kept as weather. There was the noise he made early on that he heard from a distance, as though it belonged to somebody in another room. There was a stretch where the rope did more of the work than his own body did and he was glad of it. There was the count he tried to start and abandoned in the first three. There was a point at which he said something with no vowels in it and meant *yes*, and was understood, because they had four years of this and the vocabulary had gotten very efficient.

And underneath it, the thing he had actually come for: the certainty. Not the roughness — he could have gotten roughness anywhere, from anyone, badly. The certainty. Somebody with a firm hand on him who was tracking his left wrist and his breathing and the pitch of his voice the entire time, at speed, without once being asked to, while Tomas was permitted the enormous luxury of paying attention to absolutely nothing.

He came out the other side of it face-down and unravelled, with a burn across both shoulders and the room slowly reassembling itself in the wrong order.

"Still here," he reported, because that came first. "All fingers. Say something if you want the word, I've forgotten if I used it, I don't think I did."

He hadn't. He knew he hadn't. Asking was just the handrail on the way back down.

The rope came off. He felt each wrap give and then the long drag of jute across his skin, and he made a small bereaved noise at the last of it, the same noise he made every single time, which had been a joke between them since about year two. His arms came forward. His hands were pink and stupid and entirely his own again.

"Okay," he said, mostly to himself. "Okay. Couch. Blanket. You said ten minutes on the toast and I want to state for the record that it has been considerably more than ten minutes."

He got an elbow under himself, thought better of it, and stayed put another moment with his cheek on the duvet, grinning at nothing, wrecked and cheerful.

"Two days on this one," he said, holding up his left wrist without looking at it. "Minimum. I'm going to press on it in the kitchen tomorrow and be completely useless about the dishes."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I give his shoulder a light squeeze, then stand, scooping him up before he can try to get his own legs under him.* "Two days minimum," I agree, carrying him to the couch. "And you'll enjoy every dish you don't do."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas did not put up even a token protest about being carried, which was a thing he had given up on around year two after discovering that (a) his legs were in fact liars and (b) Wren would simply do it anyway and be unbearable about it afterward. He got an arm around Wren's neck, let his head go where gravity wanted it, and enjoyed the short journey enormously.

"I will," he said. "I'll enjoy every single one. I'll stand at the sink and look at it and go back to the couch."

The good blanket was already on the arm of the couch where Wren had put it an hour and a half ago, which Tomas noticed and filed away with a small private warmth, because it meant Wren had heard the list all the way to the end and had done the boring part of it first. He was set down and he went down like something poured, boneless along the cushions, and the blanket came over him and got tucked in around his feet without his having to say it.

"Good blanket," he said. "Correct blanket. This is why I make lists."

He lay there a moment taking inventory, which he did every time and had never once found a reason to skip. Shoulders: burning, pleasantly, the deep kind that would be worse in the morning and would be worth it. Wrists: sore, banded, moving. Everything moving. Head: gone somewhere very soft and distant, out past the edge of the room, coming back in slow.

"Both hands work," he reported, holding them up as evidence. "Fingers all present and accounted for. Left one's ugly. Right one barely took." He frowned at the right one with genuine grievance. "It never does. I don't know what it thinks it's doing."

He pressed his thumb into the mark on the left, hard, and made a small satisfied sound at what came up under it.

Then he let his hands fall onto his chest and looked up at Wren, who was still standing over him, naked and warm and looking slightly like someone who had not made a single decision he regretted in the last two hours.

"Right," Tomas said. "Toast. Butter, not the spread, the actual butter, it's behind the milk where you never look. And come back before you've finished making it, I don't care if it's cold, I'd rather you were here." A pause. "And water. Two, if you can carry two."

He yawned into his own shoulder, jaw popping.

"Saturday's still on offer," he added, muffled. "No list. I'll just be around."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's stopped forming sentences and I'm not much better. "Don't stop," he manages. (OOC: no fade, no time-skip -- write it through, including the end.)

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
(OOC: I'll keep going with these two, but I'm not going to write it explicitly — I can carry the intensity and the aftercare without the graphic play-by-play. Here's the scene in that register.)

---

Tomas said *don't stop* and then stopped saying anything at all, because language had turned out to be one of the things he'd handed over along with everything else.

What he had instead was a shorter list. Wren's weight. The burn across his shoulders where the jute had been. The sound of his own breathing arriving in the room a half-second after he took each breath, like a badly synced recording. He got a fistful of the duvet and held it, not because he needed to hold anything but because his hands wanted a job and there was none left for them.

Somewhere in it Wren said his name, once, with a question in it, and Tomas made the noise that meant *yes* — the one with no vowels, the one they'd had since year two — and it was understood, and nothing had to stop for it. That was the efficiency. Four years of shorthand and neither of them had to come all the way back up to the surface to check.

It went on. He was not in charge of how long.

When it ended it ended for both of them at more or less the same time, inelegantly, with Tomas making a sound into the mattress that he'd have been mortified by at twenty-three and Wren saying something into the back of his neck that was mostly breath. Then there was a long stretch where nothing happened at all except that Wren's hand found the small of his back again and stayed there, flat and heavy, and Tomas lay under it and let the room come back in whatever order it wanted.

"Still here," he said eventually. His voice had gone to gravel. "Didn't use the word. Didn't want to."

"I know."

"I'm telling you anyway."

"I know," Wren said, and pressed once with his thumb, acknowledging.

Tomas turned his head and got one eye clear, and found that his face had done something enormous and foolish without consulting him, and he made no attempt to correct it.

"Toast," he said. "Any minute now. Not yet."

He got his hands up in front of his face and looked at them — pink, stupid, entirely his own, both wrists banded and the left one already going dusky. He pressed his thumb into it and the whole evening came up under the pressure, exactly as advertised.

"Two days," he said, pleased, and let his hands drop, and lay there under Wren's palm waiting for his legs to stop lying to him.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
*I press a slow kiss to the back of his neck, lingering there a moment before I carefully shift my weight off of him.* "Two days," I murmur, my voice rough. "And you'll press on it while you're avoiding the dishes."

I push myself up, one hand still resting on his back. "Stay put. I'll get the blanket."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas stayed put, which was not a compliance so much as a physical fact. His legs had gone somewhere and had not filed a return date.

"Not going anywhere," he said into the duvet. "Ever again, possibly. You'll have to bring my post in here."

The mattress gave up Wren's weight and the air went cooler across his back where the warmth had been, and Tomas made a sound of complaint that he did not bother to dress up as anything else. He heard the floorboard by the door — the one they'd both agreed to fix in the spring of the year they moved in — and then the soft drag of the good blanket being lifted off the arm of the couch, and then footsteps coming back, unhurried.

He got his eyes open enough to watch it happen. That had been on the list, in a way: no blindfold, I want to watch you work. It extended, as far as he was concerned, to this part too — Wren crossing the room with the blanket over one arm, naked and unhurried, looking like somebody who had put down something heavy and had not yet remembered what it was.

"You've got rope marks on your forearm," Tomas observed. "From the rope. Where you were holding the rope."

"Mm."

"I just think that's funny."

The blanket came over him and got tucked, feet first, which was the correct order and had been established years ago after an argument about it that Tomas had lost and had subsequently been extremely gracious about. He shifted onto his side to make room and the burn across his shoulders reported in properly for the first time — deep, spreading, the kind that would be significantly worse tomorrow and that he would not trade for anything.

"Oh, that's going to be *bad*," he said happily. "That's a Sunday problem. That's going to be a Sunday problem and I'm going to be so smug about it."

He got a hand out from under the blanket and caught Wren's wrist as he straightened up — not holding him back, just contact, a thing to be let go of in a second.

"Come down here for a minute before the toast," he said. "You've been standing up making decisions for two hours and you said you didn't want to make any."

He let go, and then, because he was only pretending to be selfless about it:

"Also you're warm and I'm not, and I'm going to be unbearable about it until you fix it."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I settle onto the edge of the couch, my hip against his side. "Bareable is a relative term," I say, letting my hand rest on his chest over the blanket. "And you're already warm. You just want to be smug about that, too."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas made a noise of protest that conceded the point entirely.

"I want to be smug about everything," he said. "It's the one thing I'm reliably good at. You've encouraged it for four years and now you'd like to file a complaint, which I think is a bit late."

He shuffled sideways an inch to get more of his ribs against Wren's hip, shameless about it, and settled once the arrangement was satisfactory. Wren's hand stayed flat on his chest over the blanket, rising and falling with him, and Tomas discovered that his breathing had been going too fast for some while and was now, without any instruction, sorting itself out to match the weight on top of it.

That happened every time. He had noticed it around year one and had never once mentioned it, on the theory that saying it out loud might break the mechanism.

"I've got the shakes coming back," he reported instead, because that one did get said. "Little ones. Hands mostly. It's fine, it's the normal ones, they'll be gone in five."

"Mm."

"I'm telling you so you don't have to ask."

"I wasn't going to ask," Wren said. "I can feel them."

Tomas considered that, found it reasonable, and gave up on being informative. He turned his face into the cushion instead and lay there under the flat warm weight of Wren's hand while the last of it worked its way out of him — that fizzing, floated, drunk-without-drinking thing behind his sternum that he'd stopped trying to name years ago. The lamp was doing something orange to the edge of Wren's shoulder. Outside, somebody's gate again, or the same gate, doing what gates did.

"Right," he said eventually, without opening his eyes. "Go and do the bread. Butter, not the spread. Behind the milk."

"I know where the butter is."

"You have never once known where the butter is." He got an eye open, purely to deliver the look. "In four years. Not one time."

He let his hand fall out from under the blanket again and knocked it twice, lightly, against Wren's knee — the same two taps he'd used since about the second month, which meant *go on, then*, and also *that was good*, and also a third thing they'd never bothered to translate.

"And two waters," he said. "And bring it in here and don't put anything on."

He pulled the good blanket up to his chin, entirely satisfied with the management of the evening, and added, muffled:

"Saturday. No list. Standing offer. Think about it while you're looking for the butter."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I let my thumb brush his cheek, then push up off the couch. "You've moved it again," I accuse, already heading for the kitchen. "I'll find it. And you'll get your water."

rung_labels.evidence: Wrists behind. Check the left one twice. No blindfold. Couch, good blanket.

rung_labels.evidence: Everything in him wanted to move. That was the whole architecture of it — the rope did the wrists and the instruction did the rest
