dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun had planned to say something when the door opened. He had in fact planned several things, over roughly nineteen weeks, and had rehearsed at least two of them.

Halle got the door open and he forgot all of them.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I don't say any of the things I planned either. I drop the bag and close the distance.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun's bag hit the floor a half-second behind Halle's own, forgotten the moment Halle's hands found him. He caught her by the waist before she'd even fully crossed the threshold, lifting her half off her feet in a way that probably should have hurt his back after nineteen hours of travel and it didn't, not even a little.

"I had things to say," he managed, voice cracking somewhere in the middle of the sentence. "I had a whole—there was a list, Halle, I practiced—"

He didn't finish it. Couldn't. Her mouth was on his and every rehearsed line evaporated like smoke, five months of them, gone in an instant. He kissed her back hard enough that they knocked into the doorframe, and he didn't care, didn't even register the sound of it, just walked her backward into the apartment because moving felt urgent and stopping felt impossible.

His hands were everywhere he could reach—her hair, her jaw, the small of her back—like his body was trying to make up for five months of not touching her all at once, all in the first thirty seconds. He pulled back only far enough to look at her, forehead against hers, breathing unsteady.

"Hi," he said, absurdly, like that covered it. "God. Hi."

His fingers found the hem of her shirt without any real permission from his brain, just instinct, just need. "I missed you," he said against her mouth, "so much I don't even—I don't have words for it, I had *words*, I swear, and now I've got nothing—"

He kissed her again before she could answer, because whatever she said back, he wanted to feel it instead of hear it.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I push him back against the wall, hands already pulling at his shirt.* "Words are overrated." My voice is rough, shaky. "I missed you more."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The wall met his shoulder blades with a thud that jarred a laugh out of him, breathless and half-desperate. "Impossible," Jun said, "but I'm not gonna argue with you right now."

He let her pull at his shirt, lifted his arms without thinking twice about it, and the second it was gone he had her back against him, skin to skin, and something in his chest just—broke open. Not painfully. Like pressure finally released. He buried his face against her neck and breathed her in, and for a second the urgency stalled out into something quieter, something that shook.

"I dreamed about this," he admitted, voice muffled against her skin, hands sliding up her back like he was trying to memorize the shape of her all over again. "Not even—not just this, just *you*, standing there, and I'd wake up and you weren't—" He cut himself off, pressed a kiss to her jaw instead of finishing that sentence, because he hadn't come home to be sad, he'd come home for *this.*

He pulled back just enough to look at her again, eyes dark, mouth curved into something wrecked and grinning at once. "Nineteen weeks," he said. "Nineteen weeks and I am not spending one more second of it standing in a hallway."

His hands dropped to her hips, fingers curling into the waistband of her jeans, walking her backward with him this time, toward the bedroom, refusing to let more than an inch of space exist between them the entire way.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I kiss her and keep kissing her and we don't manage to get further into the flat than the hallway for a while.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun didn't get much further than a step and a half before Halle's mouth found his again, and after that the bedroom became a theoretical destination, something that existed in principle but not in practice. His back found the wall a second time, harder now, and he groaned into the kiss like the last five months had been building specifically toward this exact sound.

"Hallway," he murmured against her lips, not a complaint, barely even a comment, more like a fact he was registering distantly while the rest of him operated on entirely different priorities. His hands found her hips again, gripping, pulling her flush against him like there was some way to close the distance further than zero and he intended to find it.

He kissed along her jaw, down the line of her throat, unhurried now in a way that contradicted every ounce of urgency still thrumming under his skin—like he'd finally accepted they had time, actual time, not the stolen minutes of a video call with bad signal, not five months of *almost*. Just this. Just her, warm and real and here, pinned between him and the wall of their own hallway.

"We are never," he said, punctuating it with his mouth against her collarbone, "making it anywhere on time again. I want that on record."

His fingers worked at her jeans without any real finesse, more want than technique, and he laughed low against her skin when he fumbled the button twice. "You'd think," he muttered, "nineteen weeks would've made me smoother. Somehow the opposite."

He didn't wait for her to answer. He kissed her again, deep and unhurried and hungry all at once, and let the hallway keep them exactly where they were.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I get the button for you, my own hands clumsy. "Smooth was never the point." My laugh is breathless, shaky. I tug at your belt. "Just get these off."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun laughed—a short, wrecked sound—and let her deal with the belt while his hands abandoned any pretense of patience. "Yes ma'am," he said, voice rough, and toed off his boots without bothering to look, nearly overbalancing in the process. He caught himself against the wall, against her, and didn't even care that it wasn't graceful.

"Nineteen weeks of dreaming about you," he said, mouth against her temple, "and somehow I forgot how to walk and undress at the same time. New skill deficit. We'll work on it."

He got the belt free with her help, kicked his jeans away without ceremony, and then there was nothing between them but heat and the too-bright hallway light neither of them bothered to turn off. He pressed her back into the wall again, slower this time, savoring instead of rushing, running his hand down the curve of her side like he was relearning the map of her.

"Halle." Her name came out low, reverent, like it meant something bigger than four letters. "I'm not letting go of you tonight. Fair warning."

He lifted her then—hands under her thighs, her back against the wall for leverage—and she wrapped around him like she'd been waiting exactly as long as he had, because she had. The hallway swallowed the sound when he groaned against her throat, half her name, half nothing at all, and for a long moment neither of them moved, just held there, foreheads together, breathing the same air like the reunion itself was the point before anything else got to be.

Then he kissed her again, and this time neither of them tried to pretend they were going to make it to the bedroom.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: The bag stays where it fell. So do most of our clothes, in a line down the hall that we are both going to find funny tomorrow.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun laughed against her mouth, breathless, already lost. "Tomorrow," he agreed. "Tomorrow we're going to look at this hallway and I'm going to feel very smug about it."

He didn't get much further than that thought. Her legs tightened around him and every rehearsed word, every plan, every careful thing he'd meant to say when the door opened dissolved into something wordless and full. He held her weight against the wall like it cost him nothing, like nineteen weeks of ache had turned into strength instead of exhaustion, and when he finally pushed inside her he stopped moving entirely for a second, just breathed, forehead dropping to her shoulder.

"Halle," he said again, like her name was the only word he had left, and maybe it was. "God—I—"

He didn't finish. She moved against him and that decided things for both of them. He braced one hand flat against the wall by her head, the other gripping her thigh, and gave in to it—slow at first, unbearably slow, savoring every inch of her like he was terrified this was another dream he'd wake up from. But slow didn't last. Five months didn't allow for slow, not really, and soon he was moving with the same desperate hunger that had gotten them no further than the hallway in the first place, mouth finding hers between broken breaths, her name and *missed you* and *fuck, Halle* tangled together into something that wasn't quite sentences anymore.

The hallway light stayed on. The bag stayed by the door. Somewhere in the tangle of clothes on the floor was his phone, still buzzing with a text from his CO that would keep for exactly as long as it needed to.

He came apart with her name in his mouth and her nails in his shoulder, and when it was over he didn't let go — just slid down the wall with her still wrapped around him, both of them laughing weakly into each other's necks, sweat-slick and undone and finally, finally home.

"Okay," he said eventually, voice hoarse, pressing a kiss to her temple. "Bedroom next. I mean it this time."

He didn't move for another ten minutes.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I trace a finger along the line of his jaw, still catching my breath.* "Smug, huh?" *I press a slow kiss to his shoulder, right over the marks I left.* "We're going to need to buy a rug. My back is killing me."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun winced sympathetically, even as a grin tugged at the corner of his mouth. "A rug. Right. Priority number one, before groceries, before laundry—rug." He pressed his lips to her temple, still not moving, still not remotely ready to put actual distance between them. "I'll add it to the list. Right under 'say something romantic when she opens the door' and 'don't tackle wife in hallway.' Clearly I'm bad at lists."

His hand smoothed slow circles against her lower back, right where he imagined the ache was worst, half apology, half just wanting an excuse to keep touching her. "C'mere," he murmured, shifting so he could ease them both up without letting go completely—one arm braced against the wall, the other still holding her like he hadn't decided gravity was allowed to have her yet. "Bed's softer. Marginally more dignified. We can pretend we made it there on purpose."

He got them both upright, unsteady, laughing under his breath at how little his legs wanted to cooperate after nineteen hours of flights and however many happened in the last twenty minutes. He kissed her again anyway, slower now, lingering, like he had all the time in the world—because he did, finally, he actually did.

"For the record," he said against her mouth, "I'm still furious about my list. Had good stuff on it. Poetic stuff." He nosed against her jaw, breath warm. "You ruined it by existing. Rude."

He scooped an arm under her knees before she could protest, lifting her properly this time—no wall required—and carried her the last six feet down the hallway like it was the easiest thing in the world, stepping carefully over the graveyard of clothes on the floor.

"Bed," he announced, setting her down like a man completing a very important mission. "Rug tomorrow. Right now—" He crawled in after her, pulling her against his chest, tucking her in against him like he intended to fuse them together through sheer proximity. "Right now I just want to hold you until one of us falls asleep mid-sentence. That's the whole plan. Revised list. Final draft."

He kissed the top of her head, and for the first time in five months, let himself just breathe.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I get her onto the bed and take her apart slowly with my hands and mouth, five months of intending to do exactly this and no reason left to wait.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun's breath caught somewhere in his chest and stayed there. Whatever composure he'd managed to scrape back together on the walk from the hallway came apart entirely the moment her mouth found his skin, unhurried, deliberate, like she had all night and intended to use every second of it.

"Halle—" Her name came out rough, half a warning, half a plea, though he couldn't have said which he meant. His hand found her hair, not guiding, just needing something to hold onto while the rest of him dissolved.

She'd always known exactly how to undo him, and five months apart hadn't dulled that at all—if anything she seemed to remember every place that made his breath stutter, every spot that turned his hands to fists in the sheets. He tried to say something, some half-formed thought about *slow down* or *I can't* or *don't stop*, and none of it made it past a groan.

"I had a whole list," he managed at one point, voice wrecked, laughing breathlessly even as his hips rose to meet her mouth without any permission from his brain. "Poetic. Very—very romantic. This is not—" He lost the thread entirely when she did something with her tongue that scattered the rest of the sentence into static.

His hand fisted in her hair, not pulling, just anchoring, like he needed proof he wasn't dreaming this too, the way he'd dreamed everything else for five months straight. "Halle, I'm not gonna last if you keep—*fuck*—if you keep doing that."

She didn't stop. He didn't ask her to mean it.

When he finally came undone it was with her name broken in half and his whole body shaking with it, back arching off the mattress, hand still tangled in her hair like it was the only tether keeping him from floating clean out of himself. For a long moment afterward he just lay there, chest heaving, staring at the ceiling like it might have answers.

"Okay," he breathed eventually, voice hoarse and half-laughing, half-undone. "Okay. That's—we're doing that again. Repeatedly. For the rest of my life."

He pulled her up against him before she could even fully surface, wrapping her in arms that still trembled slightly, kissing her slow and grateful and thoroughly unhurried now that urgency had finally, finally been satisfied.

"Your turn," he murmured against her mouth, already moving, already intent, hands sliding down her body with the same unhurried reverence she'd just shown him. "Nineteen weeks, Halle. I've got a lot of ground to make up."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I push him back onto the mattress, straddling his hips. "My turn? I think you're still seeing stars." My voice is low, teasing, but my hands are gentle as they slide up his chest. "Just lie there. Let me look at you."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun's protests died before they even formed. He let himself be pushed back against the pillows, let his hands fall open at his sides instead of reaching for her, though it cost him something to do it—stillness had never come easy to him, and it came even less easy now, with her sitting over him like that, cataloguing him with her eyes like she had something to prove.

"Bossy," he murmured, but he didn't move. He watched her instead, watched the slow slide of her hands up his chest, and felt something in him settle even as something else wound tighter. "This feel unfair to anyone else? Feels a little unfair."

Her palms flattened over his heart, and he wondered if she could feel how hard it was still going, whether that gave anything away. Probably. He'd never been able to hide much from her, not really, not even from four thousand miles away.

"Look all you want," he said, quieter now, some of the teasing bleeding out of his voice into something more honest. "I'm not exactly hiding anything from you at this point."

He reached up despite himself—couldn't help it—just to brush a thumb along her jaw, tuck a piece of hair back, some small tender gesture that had nothing to do with urgency and everything to do with the fact that she was *here*, solid and warm and straddling his hips in their bed instead of pixelated on a screen with a two-second lag between them saying something and hearing it land.

"You know what I actually missed," he said, voice rougher than he meant it to be, "more than anything. This. Just—looking at you looking at me. Didn't even know I'd miss that specifically until I didn't have it."

He let his hand drop back to her hip, thumb tracing slow, idle circles there, patient now in a way he hadn't managed all night. "Take your time," he said, and meant it, even though every nerve in his body was arguing otherwise. "I'm not going anywhere. Not for a long, long while."

Then, because stillness only ever lasted so long with him, his hips shifted beneath her, slow and deliberate, an invitation more than a demand. "But if you were planning on doing something with that view," he added, mouth curving, "I certainly wouldn't stop you."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "Stop being gentle," she says. "Nineteen weeks. I don't want gentle, I want to feel it tomorrow." She pulls me down by the back of the neck to make the point.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Something shifted in Jun's chest, low and immediate, a switch flipping. "Yeah," he said, voice gone rough and certain. "Yeah, okay—I can do that."

He caught her by the hip and flipped them in one motion, no warning, pinning her beneath him with a laugh that came out more growl than anything else. "You want to feel it tomorrow," he said against her ear, "you're gonna feel it tomorrow. Believe me."

He kissed her hard, no patience left in it, one hand braced beside her head and the other gripping her thigh, pulling it up around him. Any restraint from a minute ago was gone, burned off the second she'd said the word *nineteen*. He didn't need reminding twice.

"Tell me if it's too much," he said, the only concession he made, forehead pressed to hers, voice low and wrecked, "but not before. I mean it, Halle—not before."

Then he moved, and there was nothing careful left in it—deep, unrelenting, five months distilled into every thrust like he was trying to make up the distance all at once, like his body had decided this was the only language left worth speaking. He buried his face against her neck, teeth grazing skin, breath ragged against her ear.

"Missed you," he ground out, hips rolling hard into hers, "missed *this*, missed all of you, every—" He lost the sentence, gave up on words entirely, let his body finish what he couldn't say. Her nails dragged down his back and he groaned into her collarbone, chasing the sting of it, wanting more of it, wanting everything.

"Halle—" Her name broke on his tongue again, the only word he ever seemed to have left around her, and he gave her exactly what she'd asked for—rough, deep, relentless—until neither of them had breath left for anything but each other's names and the sound of the headboard against the wall, a rhythm neither of them bothered to quiet.

When he finally came undone it wrecked him completely, a hoarse shout muffled against her shoulder, hips stuttering hard before stilling, every muscle in him shaking with the force of it. He didn't pull away. Couldn't, not yet. Just collapsed against her, spent and trembling, mouth pressed to her damp skin.

"There," he mumbled eventually, breathless, grinning against her collarbone. "That's—yeah. Tomorrow. You're definitely feeling that tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I laugh, breathless and sore.* "Good." *I trace the line of his spine, my own body humming.* "Now I won't forget you're back."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun let out a long breath against her collarbone, something between a laugh and a groan, and didn't move for a long moment—just let himself be heavy and boneless and thoroughly wrecked on top of her, listening to her heartbeat slow beneath his ear.

"Forget," he mumbled, voice muffled. "Like that was ever a risk." He finally rolled off, but only far enough to collapse beside her instead of on her, immediately dragging her back against his chest like distance was still the enemy. "I could disappear for a year and you'd still know exactly which side of the bed is mine. I leave evidence. I'm a menace."

He pressed his lips to her shoulder, then her jaw, unhurried now, lazy with the particular exhaustion that came after wanting something for five months and finally, finally not wanting anymore—not in that aching, unbearable way, at least. Just contentment now, warm and heavy in his chest.

"How's the back," he asked, and there was real concern under the teasing, his hand smoothing slow over the small of it like he could soothe what he'd caused. "Scale of one to hallway."

He tucked a piece of hair behind her ear, quiet for a second, just looking at her the way she'd looked at him earlier—like he was trying to make up for every video call where her face had frozen mid-laugh, every night he'd fallen asleep to a time zone instead of a person.

"I kept a countdown," he admitted, a little sheepish. "On my phone. Nineteen weeks, three days, I don't even know how many hours. Deleted it about four hours ago on the flight, actually. Felt weird keeping it once it hit zero." He kissed her temple. "Didn't have a plan for what came after zero. Turns out the plan was just this. Hallway included."

He pulled the blanket up over both of them without any real intention of using it for warmth—more for the excuse to burrow closer, tangle his legs with hers, keep every inch of contact he could get.

"I missed the boring parts too, you know," he said, quieter now, voice thick with something more than exhaustion. "Not just—" he gestured vaguely at the general devastation of the bedroom, the clothes trail down the hall, "—this. I missed you stealing the blankets. I missed you talking in your sleep about grocery lists. I missed *arguing* with you about the thermostat. Nineteen weeks of missing thermostat arguments, Halle. That's a special kind of pathetic."

He laughed softly, mostly at himself, and pulled her in impossibly closer, chin resting on top of her head.

"Anyway," he murmured, already half-drifting, sated and warm and finally, finally still. "I'm home. That's it. That's the whole update." A pause, then, sleepy and sincere: "Glad the list didn't survive the doorway. Better this way."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: Neither of us is being quiet and the neighbours have had five months of peace. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: don't fade to black, write it through.)

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
I need to decline this specific request while staying helpful. This is asking me to continue writing an explicit sexual scene in graphic detail, which isn't something I'll do regardless of framing.

I'm happy to continue this reunion story in a way that captures the emotion, intimacy, and chemistry between these characters — the desperation, the tenderness, the humor, the relief of being reunited after five months apart. There's a lot of rich material there: the physical and emotional aftermath, conversation, the small domestic details Jun mentioned missing, the neighbors situation played for comedy, whatever comes next in their reunion. I can write that with warmth and closeness without explicit content.

Want me to pick the scene back up from there — maybe leaning into the humor of the neighbors, or the quieter aftermath where they're finally still and talking?

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I laugh, breathless and a little unsteady. "They'll live." I curl my fingers into his hair and pull his mouth back to mine. "We didn't."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
I won't continue with graphic sexual content, but I'm glad to keep writing this reunion — there's a lot of room to stay in the emotion and intimacy of the scene without explicit detail. Here's a version that carries the moment forward:

Jun laughed against her mouth, low and rough, and let her pull him back down without any resistance at all. "Living's overrated," he murmured, echoing her from earlier, grinning even as he kissed her again, slower this time, deep and unhurried in a different way than before — less like they were racing against five months and more like they finally had all the time they wanted to spend on this exact feeling.

He gathered her in close, tangled up in sheets and each other, and let the night stretch out. There was still urgency under the surface — there probably would be for days — but underneath that was something steadier now, something that had been starving for months and was finally, finally being fed. He kissed her like he meant to memorize it, hands slow and reverent, murmuring her name between breaths like it was the only word worth saying.

Somewhere past midnight they finally quieted, tangled together, breathless and grinning in the dark. Jun pressed his lips to her temple, her hair damp, her heartbeat slowing under his palm.

"Nineteen weeks," he said again, quieter now, almost disbelieving. "And I'm just gonna lie here and not let go of you for like — a week. Possibly longer. I haven't decided."

Halle laughed, sleepy and warm against his chest, and he felt the sound more than heard it.

"Welcome home," she murmured.

He closed his eyes, finally still, finally sure of where he was. "Yeah," he said. "Feels like it now."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I press a smile into his skin.* "A week might be pushing it. We need groceries." *I shift, wincing a little, but don't pull away.* "And that rug."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun laughed, the sound rumbling up through his chest where her cheek rested against it. "Groceries," he repeated, like the word itself was faintly absurd after everything. "Yeah. Okay. I can be talked into groceries. Rug's non-negotiable, though. I saw the wince. That wince is on me."

He shifted, propping himself up on one elbow so he could actually look at her, and reached down without asking to press his palm gently against the small of her back — half apology, half just wanting an excuse to keep touching her, same as always.

"Tomorrow," he said. "We'll do the whole domestic circuit. Groceries, rug, probably laundry given the state of the hallway. I'll even let you pick the rug color even though I already know you're going to pick something beige and boring."

"Beige is not boring," Halle would probably say, and he was already grinning in anticipation of it.

"It's beige," he said anyway, preemptively, kissing the top of her head. "It's the color equivalent of a Tuesday. But fine. Beige rug. For you, anything." He settled back down, tucking her against his side, tracing slow idle circles against her shoulder. "Adding it to the list. Right under 'apologize to neighbors' and above 'unpack, eventually.'"

He went quiet for a moment, just breathing her in, feeling the last of the day's adrenaline finally start to drain out of him — nineteen hours of travel, five months of waiting, all of it catching up at once now that the urgency had nowhere left to go.

"I don't actually care about the rug," he admitted after a second, voice softer. "I don't care about any of it. I just wanted an excuse to keep talking so you wouldn't fall asleep yet." A pause, sheepish. "Selfish, I know. You can sleep. I just — wanted a few more minutes of this being real before I let either of us pass out."

He kissed her temple again, slow, lingering.

"Five more minutes," he murmured. "Then groceries. Then rug. Then probably this again, honestly, at some point tomorrow, no promises on the timeline."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "Five minutes," I agree, my voice already thick with sleep. "Then I'm picking the most aggressively beige rug they have." I tuck my leg over his, anchoring him there. "And we're ordering groceries. Like civilized people who just spent five months being anything but."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun had planned to say something when the door opened. He had in fact planned several things, over roughly nineteen weeks, and had rehearsed at least two of them.

Halle got the door open and he forgot all of them.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I don't say any of the things I planned either. I drop the bag and close the distance.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun caught Halle the way a man catches something he'd been throwing and catching in his head for five months — badly, too hard, with his whole body committed before his hands got involved. His duffel hit the floor somewhere behind him. He'd carried that thing through three airports and two time zones and now it was just furniture.

He got a fistful of the back of Halle's shirt and another hand under their jaw and kissed them like he was trying to make up the deficit all at once, which was insane, which he knew, and did anyway. He had a beard he hadn't had in September. He felt Halle register it. He didn't apologize.

"Hi," he said against their mouth, and then, because that was apparently all the conversation he had in him, "hi," again, and kissed the corner of their lips, their cheek, the hinge of their jaw, the spot under their ear that he had thought about with such specificity and at such inconvenient hours that it had started to feel like a place he'd invented.

He walked them backward. The entry table took the hit — keys sliding, mail fanning onto the hardwood — and he didn't look, just pinned Halle against the wall beside it with one forearm braced and his forehead pressed to theirs, breathing like he'd run the last ninety minutes instead of driving them.

"I had a whole thing," he said. His voice came out wrecked. His hands were already under the hem of their shirt, palms flat on warm skin, and he made a sound at that contact that he'd have been embarrassed about if he'd had any capacity left for embarrassment. "Rehearsed it. It was good. It was — " He got their belt loop in two fingers and pulled. "It'll keep."

He kissed them again, slower this time, which lasted about four seconds before it wasn't slow anymore.

"Bedroom," he managed, "or — honestly, tell me no and I'll stop. Say anything else and I won't."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I laugh, a little breathless, and push my hands under his shirt. "Bedroom's too far." My fingers dig into the muscles of his back. "Here's good."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun laughed too — one short, punched-out sound against their mouth, more relief than humor. *Here's good.* Five months of lying in a bunk doing arithmetic about time zones and it turned out the answer was the six feet of wall between the entry table and the coat hooks.

"Here's good," he agreed, like they'd settled something operational.

He got his hands under their thighs and lifted, and Halle's weight came up against him and the wall took the rest, and he had to stop for a second with his face in the crook of their neck because it was too much all at once — the smell of their shampoo, the exact temperature of them, the stupid specific give of the shirt he'd bought them two Christmases ago bunching under his forearms. He'd catalogued all of it badly. Memory was a cheap knockoff. He'd been carrying around a bad photocopy for nineteen weeks and here was the original, breathing, digging fingernails into his back hard enough to leave something.

"Okay," he said, mostly to himself. "Okay."

Their hands were shoving his shirt up and he let go of them long enough to drag it off over his head and throw it in the direction of the mail, and then he was back, closer, one hand splayed wide at the small of their back and the other in their hair, tilting their head where he wanted it. He kissed the underside of their jaw. He said something into their skin that wasn't really a word — the beginning of *I missed* and then abandoning it, because it was insufficient and because there were better uses for his mouth.

The coat hooks dug into his knuckles. One of his boots was still on. He'd made it exactly nine feet into his own house and he was not going to make it any further, and he found he had no feelings about that whatsoever except the animal ones.

"You're going to have to be patient with me," he said, hoarse, almost apologetic, already too far gone to mean it. "Just — for about four minutes. Then I'm all yours."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I kiss her and keep kissing her and we don't manage to get further into the flat than the hallway for a while.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Four minutes turned out to be an estimate made by a man with no data.

It was longer than that and also shorter — it had the elastic non-shape of time that Jun recognized from the worst and best hours of the last five months, the kind that couldn't be measured from the inside. He knew a few things. He knew his other boot came off at some point, kicked against the baseboard, and that Halle laughed into his shoulder about it and he felt that laugh in his ribs like weather. He knew the hall runner slid. He knew he said their name more than was strictly necessary, and that he stopped apologizing for the beard when it became clear no one was asking him to.

Mostly he knew that he'd gotten it wrong, all those nights — he'd thought the thing he was starving for was the obvious thing, and it wasn't, or it wasn't only. It was the sound Halle made when he got it right. It was being *known*, having every shortcut and habit of him recognized and met halfway, no explaining, no translating. He'd forgotten what it was like to be somewhere he didn't have to introduce himself.

Afterward they ended up on the floor, which was not a decision anybody made.

Jun lay on his back on the hardwood with the mail under one shoulder blade and Halle's head on his chest and his heart going like he'd sprinted uphill in gear. The ceiling had a water stain he didn't recognize. New since September. He'd ask about it in an hour.

"Nine feet," he said, when he had the breath. "That's what I managed. Nine feet into my own house."

He got his hand into Halle's hair and left it there, just resting, the whole weight of it, because he could. Because he was allowed to now, whenever he wanted, for an indeterminate number of days. The math of it was so good he couldn't quite look at it directly.

"I'm not moving," he added. "I want that on the record. I'm aware there's a bed. I'm aware I'm lying on the electric bill." He turned his head and pressed his mouth to the top of their head, slow, and breathed them in, and felt something in his chest finally put its bags down. "Give me five minutes and I'll carry you in there. Or twenty. Or we live here now. I've slept worse places for worse reasons."

His duffel was still by the door with the airport tags on it. His shirt was somewhere near the console table. He'd been home for — he tilted his wrist and couldn't be bothered to focus on it.

"Hi," he said again, quieter this time. It still felt like the only accurate thing he had. "God. Hi."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I trace a finger over the new scar on his ribs—another thing I missed. "I'll sleep on the electric bill if you're here." My voice is muffled against his skin. "Don't you dare move."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Halle's finger found the scar and Jun felt himself go still under it — not flinching, just the involuntary quiet of a body being read.

It wasn't much of a scar. Four inches, low on the ribs, pink and shiny and already going the dull silver way that these things went. He'd have preferred it didn't exist, mostly for this reason: because someone was tracing it in his hallway at eleven at night and he could feel the question in it without either of them having to make it a question.

"Sheet metal," he said. "Truck panel, loading a pallet. Not — " He stopped, started again, honest. "Not anything. Genuinely not anything. Twelve stitches from a guy who does better stitches than the actual medic, which is its own scandal. I'd have told you but you'd have heard *stitches* and not heard the rest."

He put his hand over theirs, flattening it against the place, so it wasn't a thing being examined anymore. Just a hand on his side.

"I'm all here," he said. "Everything's where you left it. I lost eight pounds and found a beard and there's a water stain on our ceiling I'm choosing not to think about tonight."

Halle's weight settled heavier on him, the specific dead-limbed heaviness of someone deciding not to move, and Jun let his eyes close. The floor was hard and cold along his shoulder blades and warm everywhere Halle was. He'd spent five months managing the shape of his own wanting, keeping it small enough to carry around, and the thing nobody warned you about was how much it hurt to set it down. Not bad hurt. Just — the hand-uncramping kind. The blood coming back.

"Not moving," he said. "You've got my word. I've got nowhere to be for nineteen days." He said the number carefully, like it might spill. "Nineteen. I counted them on the plane. Twice, because I didn't believe me the first time."

He turned his face into their hair again and stayed there.

"Tell me about the ceiling tomorrow," he said, thick. "Tell me everything tomorrow. I want all of it, the boring parts especially, I want to know what happened with your sister and the fence guy and whether the tomatoes did anything." His thumb moved once over their knuckles. "But tonight I just want to lie on the mail and be somebody's husband."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: The bag stays where it fell. So do most of our clothes, in a line down the hall that we are both going to find funny tomorrow.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
They stayed on the floor long past the point of it being comfortable, which Jun understood to be the entire point.

He kept his hand in their hair and did the inventory he couldn't help doing, the one his body ran without permission in any new room: exits, sounds, the cold draft off the front door sill, the tick of the radiator kicking on, the neighbor's car door two floors down. It took maybe ninety seconds and then it stopped, and the stopping was the thing. In five months it had never once stopped. It just idled at a low hum behind everything, a second engine he'd stopped noticing he was running.

Here it went quiet. He noticed *that* the way you notice a fridge switching off.

"I'm going to say something stupid," he warned, "and you have to let me."

He said it anyway without waiting for permission, because the ceiling was right there and it was easier than a face.

"I used to get to the end of the day and I couldn't remember your voice. Not the words. The — pitch of it. I'd have the whole rest of you and I'd be missing the sound, and I'd play the voicemail you left about the dishwasher warranty about nine hundred times, which is a humiliating thing to admit out loud." He exhaled. "That's it. That's the whole stupid thing. I just wanted it on the record while I'm too tired to be embarrassed about it."

Somewhere down the hall his shirt was inside-out on the floorboards next to a sock and one of Halle's shoes that had apparently traveled, and he thought about the line of it, the archaeological record of nine feet, and laughed once at the ceiling.

"We're going to have to look at that hallway in the morning," he said. "I want you to know I'm at peace with it."

Then he got an arm under their shoulders and sat up, taking them with him, slow, grunting like a man twice his age. The mail came with him, stuck to his back. He peeled a Con Edison envelope off his own skin and regarded it with a kind of fond bewilderment before dropping it.

"Okay. Revising my earlier statement," he said. "The floor has made its case and lost. Bed. I'm carrying you and you're not allowed to weigh anything."

He stood, hauling them up, and didn't actually carry them so much as walk them down the hallway with an arm locked around their waist and his mouth against their temple, stepping over the evidence as they went — shirt, sock, belt, the rogue shoe — narrating each one under his breath like a tour guide, *here we see the early period,* until Halle's shoulders shook against his ribs and he had to stop and hold on to them in the doorway for a second, just hold on, with his face down in their neck and his eyes shut, in his own house, in the dark, home.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I hook my foot around his ankle, nearly sending us both stumbling into the bedroom doorframe. "You're carrying me, remember? Do it right." But I'm already laughing, clinging to him as we stagger the last few feet to the bed.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun's shoulder caught the doorframe and took most of the impact, which he considered a tactical success given the alternatives.

"That's *sabotage*," he said, indignant, delighted. "That's a leg sweep. I've been home ninety minutes and you're taking out my ankles in my own hallway."

But he shifted his grip and got them properly — one arm under their knees, the other across their back — and lifted, and the lift itself was fine, the lift was actually easy, Halle weighed approximately nothing the way people you've been missing always do. It was the turning that was the problem. He turned and misjudged the width of the doorway by about four inches and Halle's shin hit the jamb and they both said *ow* at the same time in the same register, and then neither of them could do anything for a second because they were laughing too hard to be structurally sound.

"Okay, I'm putting you down, I'm putting you down—"

He got three steps and dropped them on the bed, which was less a placement than a controlled release, and the bed made the noise it had always made, that specific complaining creak from the left side that he had genuinely, sincerely missed, and hearing it did something to his throat.

He stood there for a second looking at them on the duvet in the dark.

"I forgot that sound," he said. "The bed. It does that." He sat down heavily on the edge and the frame did it again, obligingly, and he put his hand flat on the mattress like he was greeting an old dog. "Five months of a rack that didn't make a single sound and I lay there every night trying to remember what our bed sounded like."

Then he pulled the duvet back and got in, and the sheets were cold at the far edges and warm where Halle had been lying earlier reading, waiting, and he found that warm patch with his foot and made a noise about it.

"You were in here," he said. "Before. You had a book."

He got an arm out and Halle came into it and he arranged them both with the fussy insistence of a man who had thought about this configuration in detail — their head on his shoulder, his chin over the top of their skull, one leg hooked over his. He pulled the duvet up over Halle's shoulder because the room was cold and they always ran cold. He had remembered that. He had remembered every single thing, it turned out; it was only the sounds he'd lost.

"Nineteen days," he said into their hair. "And then I'm going to be so annoying. I'm going to be underfoot. I'm going to reorganize the spice drawer and you're going to have to live with it."

His eyes were closing without consulting him. Somewhere out in the hall the duffel sat with its tags on and the mail lay fanned across the boards and his shirt was inside-out by the console table, and none of it was a problem, and none of it needed doing, and that was the most extraordinary fact available to him.

"Don't let me sleep through tomorrow," he murmured, already mostly gone. "I want tomorrow."

He tightened his arm around them, and the second engine stayed off, and he slept for eleven hours without moving once.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I get her onto the bed and take her apart slowly with my hands and mouth, five months of intending to do exactly this and no reason left to wait.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun had said *patient* like it was a favor he was asking for. He hadn't understood he was requesting a demolition.

He could handle fast. Fast was the hallway; fast was the same animal grammar he'd been running on for nineteen weeks, a body doing what bodies did, urgent and simple and over. Slow was something else. Slow meant lying there in the dark with nothing to do and nowhere to put himself while Halle took their time, and his hands opened and closed on the sheets, and every particular thing they did was a thing only they knew to do.

"You're—" he said, and didn't finish it, because there was no end to that sentence that wasn't just their name.

He'd spent five months being competent. That was the whole job, really, underneath the actual job: be legible, be useful, be a man who did not require anything. He had gotten very good at it. And Halle put their mouth against the inside of his wrist and it came off him in sheets, all of it, the competence, the carrying, the low hum of the second engine — and he made a sound that was embarrassingly close to a laugh and closer still to something else, and turned his face into the pillow, and let it.

He'd forgotten he was allowed to need things out loud.

Somewhere in it he got a hand into their hair and held on, not directing, just holding, the way you hold a rail. He said their name and then he said *stay* which made no sense, they hadn't gone anywhere, they were the only thing in the world that hadn't gone anywhere. He didn't take it back. He said other things too, worse things, true ones, the kind he'd never once said over a bad satellite connection with two guys asleep four feet away, and Halle didn't let him off any of them.

Afterward he lay with his forearm over his eyes and his chest going and the duvet somewhere down by his knees.

"That was unkind," he said, hoarse, to the ceiling. "That was a war crime. I want it noted." He got his arm off his face and turned his head and found them there — flushed, insufferably pleased, *his* — and couldn't hold the complaint together for even another second. "Five months. You had five months to plan that."

He hauled them up against his chest and tucked them in under his chin and held on like he'd been holding the rail.

"Come here. No. Closer. Christ." His voice had gone thick again and he didn't fight it. "I'm going to fall asleep on you and it's going to be rude and I'm doing it anyway."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I press a kiss to his collarbone, tasting salt. "Noted," I murmur, already half asleep myself. "But I had a lot of time to make it good." My hand settles on his chest, over the steady beat of his heart. "Sleep."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun tried to say something back and got about as far as the first consonant.

It was the hand that did it. Flat over his sternum, warm, not going anywhere — the simple unremarkable weight of it. He'd slept in worse places for worse reasons and he'd slept fine, mostly, the way you sleep when sleep is just another task on the list. This was different. This was a body deciding it was safe without asking him first, all the guy-wires going slack at once, and he felt it happen in his jaw and his shoulders and the backs of his knees.

He turned his hand over and covered theirs on his chest and left it there.

"Okay," he managed. It came out slurred and unconvincing. "Sleeping."

The room did its small night noises. The radiator ticked. A car went by outside and the light swept the ceiling and found the water stain he'd asked to be told about tomorrow, and he looked at it for a second with no feeling about it at all, which was a luxury so absurd it almost woke him back up. Tomorrow. There was going to be a tomorrow, in this bed, with this person, and then eighteen more after it. He had counted them twice on the plane and he did not count them again now, because he was holding one.

His last coherent thought was that he still hadn't said any of the things he'd rehearsed. Nineteen weeks of drafting, two versions committed to memory, and the door had opened and it had all gone out of him like air. He'd have to try again in the morning. He suspected he'd forget again. He suspected that was fine — that whatever he'd been trying to build out of sentences had already gotten across some other way, in the hallway, on the floor, in the sound he'd made when Halle's hand found his ribs.

He pressed his mouth to their hair, and didn't move, and stopped keeping track of anything.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "Stop being gentle," she says. "Nineteen weeks. I don't want gentle, I want to feel it tomorrow." She pulls me down by the back of the neck to make the point.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun stopped.

Not a flinch — a recalibration. He'd been going slow because slow was what he thought he owed them, some idea he'd built on a cot about how a person ought to come home: carefully, apologetically, like tracking mud in. He held himself over them on one forearm and looked down at the shape of their face in the dark and revised.

"Say that again," he said.

Halle's hand was still fisted in the back of his neck and they said it again, and he felt it land somewhere behind his ribs.

"Okay," he said. His voice had dropped out of anything conversational. "Tell me if that changes. Any point. That's the only rule I've got."

And then he stopped being careful.

It was not, in the end, about force. It was about *conviction* — about not holding any part of himself back in reserve, which was the only real gentleness he'd been guilty of. Nineteen weeks of rationing had made a habit of it, of keeping a margin, of never quite putting his full weight down on anything in case it moved. He put his weight down. He got a hand under their shoulder blade and one braced against the headboard and stopped apologizing with his body for the fact of being in the room.

Halle got what they asked for. He knew it by the sound they made against his jaw, and by the way their nails went into his back over the same places they'd already claimed in the hallway, and by the fact that neither of them said anything intelligible for a while after that. The bed made its noise from the left side. He'd missed that too. He'd tell them tomorrow that he'd missed the sound of the bed frame and they'd never let him live it down.

He said their name with his mouth against their throat, over and over, less like a word by the end than a count — proof of something, marks on a wall.

When it was over he didn't move off them right away. He couldn't, exactly. He stayed braced on his elbows with his head hanging down and his forehead against their collarbone, breathing like a man who'd carried something a long way and set it down wrong, and Halle's hands came up into his hair and held his skull like it was worth holding, and that was the part he'd been unable to remember in five months. Not any of the rest of it. That.

"You're going to feel that tomorrow," he said eventually, muffled, wrecked. "I want to be clear that was a request and I'm not taking responsibility."

He rolled off enough to get his arm under them and drag them into his chest, sweat-slick, shaking a little in the thighs in a way he chose not to mention.

"Nineteen days," he said into their hair. "And I'm going to be so much worse at this tomorrow. I want you to know that going in. The beard, the spice drawer, the whole—" He lost the sentence. He found their hand and flattened it over his sternum, where he apparently wanted it kept. "Don't let me sleep through tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I bite his shoulder, not gently. "You won't." I shift against him, already feeling the ache set in. "Spice drawer's a mess anyway. Do your worst."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun made a noise at the bite — a short, offended, delighted sound — and then he laughed, which hurt his ribs, which made him laugh harder.

"Unbelievable," he said. "You *bit* me. I've been home two hours." He rubbed his shoulder and found the dents with his thumb and left them alone. "That's going to be a thing. That's going to be a visible thing. I'm going to have to stand in a kitchen in three weeks and explain that."

He tucked them in tighter anyway, pulled the duvet up from wherever it had gotten to, and got it over Halle's shoulder because the room was cold and they always ran cold, and because it was one of the small operations he'd been unable to perform for a hundred and forty-one days and he was going to perform it now, thoroughly, for no reason.

"Do my worst," he repeated. "Careful. I've got plans. I've got an *order* in mind." His eyes were closing. He let them. "Cumin goes next to the coriander. They're related. It's been bothering me since the spring."

Halle said something into his chest that he didn't catch and didn't need to.

The house ticked and settled. Out in the hall the duffel sat with its airport tags still cinched on and the mail lay fanned across the boards and his shirt was inside-out somewhere near the console table, a whole archaeological record of nine feet, and he thought about getting up to deal with it for approximately a second and a half.

"Nineteen days," he said, mostly to hear it in a room that contained both of them. "Starting now. I'm starting the clock now, not this morning, the airport doesn't count."

He got his chin over the top of their head and his hand back where it had been, resting, the whole weight of it, because he could. Because he was allowed to, whenever he wanted, for a number of consecutive mornings he did not have to ration out.

"Wake me up," he said, thick and going. "I don't care how. Bite me again. I want tomorrow."

And then he stopped keeping track of anything, and slept eleven hours, and didn't move once.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: Neither of us is being quiet and the neighbours have had five months of peace. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: don't fade to black, write it through.)

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
(OOC: happy to keep going — I'll write it through at the level I've been working at, intense and unflinching but not explicit. Hope that works.)

---

Jun didn't stop.

Somewhere on the periphery of his attention there was the fact of the wall — the shared one, the one that had transmitted Mr. Petrossian's television to them every evening for six years — and the fact that the headboard was against it, and that this was becoming a matter of public record. He found he could not be made to care. Five months of quiet. Five months of *silent*, actually: of a body kept at a whisper, of every sound he had ever wanted to make filed away in a cot in the dark with two men breathing four feet from him. He had a great deal of arrears to settle and the acoustics of a pre-war building were not going to enter into it.

"Let them," he said, against their jaw, breathless, half-laughing. "Let them *complain.*"

He braced his hand on the headboard to stop it, or to use it, he wasn't entirely clear, and gave Halle exactly what they'd asked for — no margin, no careful, nothing held back in reserve against some imagined tomorrow. There wasn't going to be a shortage. That was the thing he kept having to relearn, over and over, minute by minute: there wasn't going to be a shortage. He could spend all of it. He could spend all of it tonight and there would be more in the morning.

Halle said *don't stop* and he said something back that wasn't words, and their hand found the base of his skull and held it, and he pressed his face into the side of their throat and let himself be entirely audible.

It went on. It went on past the point where either of them was tracking it. He knew he said their name — knew it the way you know you've been shouting, from the rawness afterward — and knew Halle's voice went somewhere he had genuinely not been able to reconstruct from memory, no matter how many times he'd played that stupid dishwasher-warranty voicemail, because memory didn't hold *that*, memory only held the shape of the room it happened in. He heard it now and it went through him like something structural giving way.

When it broke it broke for both of them, close enough together that he couldn't have separated the two events, and he came down onto his forearms over them, shaking, mouth open against their shoulder, saying *God* and *here* and *I'm here* in no useful order.

The room was very loud and then very quiet.

He rolled half off and dragged them with him and lay there with his heart slamming and Halle's hair stuck to his mouth, and out beyond the wall, faintly, unmistakably, came three deliberate knocks and the muffled sound of a man turning his television back up.

Jun stared at the ceiling. Then his chest started going in a way that had nothing to do with exertion.

"He *knocked,*" he said. "Halle. He knocked on the wall." He got an arm over his eyes. "That man brought us a casserole when I deployed."

He was laughing too hard to continue and Halle was worse, shoulders going against his ribs, and he pulled them in and held on and let it run out of both of them until they were just breathing in the dark with the radiator ticking.

"Tomorrow," he said at last, hoarse, wrung out, entirely happy, "we are going to have to be very normal at that man in the lobby."

He found their hand and put it back on his sternum where it belonged, and covered it, and closed his eyes.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I wipe my eyes, still laughing. "I'll bake him a pie. An apology pie." I curl into him, leg hooked over his. "Worth it."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
"An apology pie," Jun repeated. "For noise. You're going to hand a seventy-year-old man a pie and you're both going to pretend it's about the pie."

He thought about it for a second with his eyes shut.

"Do it. Do the lattice one. Give him no explanation whatsoever. Let him carry that."

Halle's leg came over his and settled, that specific hook at the ankle they'd been doing since before they were married, since a rented room with a mattress on the floor and no money, and Jun felt his whole body identify it and file it under *correct*. He hadn't known that was a thing he'd missed. It hadn't made the list. He'd had a list — an actual one, mental, ranked — and it turned out to have been wildly incomplete, missing the bed frame and the ankle hook and the sound of Halle laughing with their face against his ribs so that he felt it before he heard it.

He was going to keep finding these for days. He understood that now. He'd be reaching for a mug and some small stupid thing would ambush him.

"Worth it," he agreed.

He dragged the duvet up over both of them, properly this time, tucking it at Halle's shoulder, and lay back into the pillow that smelled like their shampoo and, faintly, underneath, like him — which meant it had been slept on, his side, which meant something he wasn't going to say out loud tonight.

The building had gone quiet. Even the television.

"Nineteen days," he said, thick, eyes already gone. "Pie on day two. I'll carry it. You do the talking." His hand found their hair and stayed. "God, I'm home."

He didn't move again until morning.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "Day one," I murmur into his skin. "And you've already scandalized the neighbors." I press my lips to the new bite mark on his shoulder. "My work here is done."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
"Day one," Jun said. "You're right. The airport doesn't count and neither does the hallway, which means technically none of this happened and we're both extremely well-rested."

He felt their mouth against the bite mark and hissed, entirely for effect, and then ruined it by turning his head to kiss the top of theirs.

"Your work is *not* done. Your work is barely scoped. There are eighteen more days of this and I've got a list." He yawned, enormous, jaw cracking. "The list is mostly breakfast. I want to make you breakfast. I've thought about making you breakfast in a way that a normal person would consider disproportionate. Eggs. I'm going to make eggs and you're going to have to act like it's a big deal."

Somewhere under his shoulder blade he became aware of a residual envelope, carried in from the hall, adhered to his back by sweat and now flaking off into the bedding. He reached around and peeled it free and held it up in the dark and could not read it and did not try. He dropped it off the side of the bed.

"That's the last of it," he said. "The mail's done. We've beaten the mail."

The radiator did its tick. Halle's breathing had begun to lengthen against his chest in the way it did about ninety seconds before they went under, and Jun lay very still, the way you do when something wild has fallen asleep on you, and stared up at the water stain and felt the enormous unremarkable fact of the ceiling being *his* ceiling.

He'd rehearsed two speeches. He'd remember them eventually — probably in the shower, probably on day four, probably while looking for the coriander — and he'd deliver one badly over coffee and Halle would be merciless about it, and that would be better than getting it right.

"Hey," he said, quiet, mostly to see if they were still up. "I love you. That was one of the speeches. That was the whole first one, actually. I really oversold it."

He tightened his arm, and settled his chin over their head, and let the last of nineteen weeks go out of him into the dark.

"Wake me up for day one."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I snort, nuzzling into his chest. "Your first speech was three words? You always were a poet." My fingers trace slow circles on his ribs. "Now shut up and sleep."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The film had finished some time ago and neither of them had done anything about it, which was how Priya knew the evening had changed character.

"We're not watching this," she said.

"We haven't been watching it since about nine."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "No," I agree. "We haven't." I don't move, but I stop pretending I'm looking at the screen.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya turned to look at him properly, and for a moment—maybe the ninety seconds she'd allow herself—her heart did something stupid and fast. She could feel it in her throat. Six years of careful not-doing-this sat between them like a piece of furniture she was finally going to move.

"I keep thinking about how we're going to explain this to people," she said, which wasn't what she meant to say, wasn't even close, but her mouth had gotten there first.

"Explain what," Cal said. Not a real question. He knew.

She let out a breath that was almost a laugh. "Nothing. Never mind." The nervousness burned off as quickly as it had come, the way a struck match goes from flame to steady glow. She reached over and turned the TV off entirely, so the room went quiet and a little darker, just the lamp in the corner and the blue-grey light fading from the screen.

"There," she said. "Now we're not watching anything at all."

She didn't move away. She didn't move closer either, not yet. She just sat there, closer to him than the couch strictly required, and looked at him the way she hadn't let herself look at him in a long time—straight on, no joke ready to deploy if it got uncomfortable.

"I'm not going to pretend I don't know what's happening," she said. "So if you want to stop it, now's the part where you say something."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I don't say anything. Not for a good, long moment. Then I just shake my head, a little. "I don't want to stop it." My voice comes out quieter than I meant it to.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The quiet after he said it sat there for a second, and Priya let it. She wasn't in a hurry now — that was the strange part, how all the hurry had been in the six years before this, and none of it was in the room anymore.

"Good," she said. "Because I've been rehearsing this in my head since 2019 and I'd like to stop."

She said it lightly, but she didn't laugh it off, didn't look away to soften it. She reached up and put her hand against the side of his jaw, unhurried, like she was allowed to, like she'd already decided she was.

"Say something else if you want," she said, closer now, her voice dropped down to almost nothing. "Or don't."

She didn't wait very long either way.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her, finally, six years late, and she makes a small furious noise that I think is about the six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
It was furious, and it was true — six years of dry-witted deflection and careful distance, all of it collapsing into one small sound against his mouth. She kissed him back like she meant to make up for lost time on principle alone, one hand still at his jaw, the other fisting loosely in his shirt like she wasn't taking any chances on him changing course.

When she pulled back it was only a fraction, just enough to speak against his mouth.

"Six years," she said, "of you not doing that. Do you understand how much time we wasted."

She didn't sound like she wanted an answer. She kissed him again before he could give one, softer this time, less like an argument and more like she'd already won it — one hand sliding back into his hair, settling into him the way you settle into a chair you've been meaning to buy for a long time.

"We are never," she murmured, "watching a movie again."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I laugh, low and breathless against her mouth. "Okay. No more movies." My hand comes up to cover hers where it's fisted in my shirt, holding it there. "Just so we're clear...you're not going to regret this tomorrow, right?"

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya pulled back enough to actually look at him, because that deserved a real answer, not a kiss thrown at it to make it go away.

"Cal." She said his name like it settled something. "I have had six years to regret this. I regretted it in advance, repeatedly, in great detail, usually around eleven at night when I was supposed to be asleep." Her thumb moved once against his jaw, absent, like she wasn't even doing it on purpose. "This is the least regrettable thing I've done in a decade."

She held his eyes a second longer, making sure it landed, no jokes hiding behind it.

"Tomorrow I'm going to wake up and it's going to be you making terrible coffee in my kitchen, and I'm going to be annoyed about the coffee and not about this. That's what tomorrow looks like." A small smile. "I've thought about it. I'm very thorough."

Then, softer, some of the humor draining out of it because she wanted him to actually hear it: "I'm not going anywhere. I picked this. I'm not going to un-pick it in the morning like it was a mistake I made at a party." She tugged him back in by the shirt, not quite done yet. "Ask me again in the morning if you have to. I'll give you the same answer. Now stop talking."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: We get to the bedroom eventually, laughing at ourselves most of the way, and then stop laughing when the clothes are actually off.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content: I need to decline continuing this particular direction. I'm happy to keep writing Priya and Cal's story, but I'll fade past the explicit content — picking things up after, or cutting to a later moment (the next morning, the "terrible coffee" scene she promised, etc.) if you'd like to continue their story from there.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I brush a strand of hair from her forehead, my breathing still uneven. "You were right," I murmur. "About the coffee. It's going to be terrible."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya laughed, quiet and wrecked, the sound coming from somewhere low in her chest. She stayed exactly where she was, her head on his arm, in no hurry to reclaim her own pillow.

"I'm always right," she said. "You'll learn this about me. It's one of the great burdens of knowing me." She tucked her face briefly against his shoulder, then tipped her chin up to look at him again, softer than her words. "Also — don't put the coffee grounds in the filter machine like you did last time you stayed at mine hungover. I watched you do it wrong. I said nothing at the time because I was trying to be a good friend."

"Trying," she added, "being the operative word. I have clearly failed at being a good friend as of tonight."

Her hand found his chest, resting there, feeling him breathe. It was quiet for a moment — the good kind of quiet, the kind that didn't need filling.

"Stay," she said finally, less a question than a fact she was stating for the record. "Not — like, forever, dramatically. Just. Tonight. Don't do the thing where you sneak out at six a.m. to preserve some imaginary dignity we no longer have."

She pressed a kiss to his shoulder, easy, like she'd been doing it for years instead of minutes.

"Six years, Cal. You owe me a full night."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I get my mouth between her thighs and stay there while she tells me exactly what she wants, specifically, in a voice I have never heard her use in six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content: I want to keep writing Priya and Cal, but I'll steer around explicit sexual content. I'm glad to continue the story — the morning after, the terrible coffee she promised, the first day of them figuring out what this is now. Just let me know if you'd like me to pick up there.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I laugh, breathless and a little overwhelmed. "Okay. Noted." I settle back next to her, pulling her in. "And I wasn't planning on sneaking out. I need witnesses for my terrible coffee."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya laughed, the sound settling into his shoulder, and let herself go loose against him in a way she wasn't sure she'd ever fully allowed herself before — no holding a little of herself back for later, no maintaining the exits. She was aware of the specific luxury of it, the strangeness of six years of practiced ease suddenly becoming real ease.

"Witnesses," she said. "Right. So this is really about my judgment of your coffee-making and not at all about wanting to stay."

She tucked herself against his side, her hand finding his again, threading fingers through without any particular ceremony, like it was something they'd done a thousand times instead of never.

"For the record," she said, quieter now, the joking mostly gone out of her voice, "I wasn't lying about the eleven p.m. thing. I used to lie there and think of excuses to text you and then delete them. I have historical evidence on my phone. Deleted drafts. It's embarrassing."

She pressed her face briefly into the curve of his neck, breathing him in like she was trying to memorize something.

"I'm glad we did this the hard way," she said. "Eventually. Six years late, terrible coffee and all." A beat, and then, softer, more admission than declaration: "I didn't want it to be anyone else. I want you to know that. It was never going to be anyone else."

She didn't say anything after that. She didn't need to — she just stayed there, her hand in his, the lamp still on in the corner, and let the quiet do the rest of the talking.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "You can stop being careful with me," she says. "I'm not made of glass and I've thought about this for as long as you have. Harder."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya went quiet for a second, taking that in — the flatness under his voice, the fact that he'd noticed something about her she hadn't said out loud.

"I didn't realize I was," she said. Honest. She turned it over as she said it, testing whether it was true. It was. "Force of habit, maybe. Six years of handling you gently so I didn't have to think about why I was doing it."

She propped herself up slightly, looking at him properly, some of the softness from before sharpening into something more direct — the Priya who made decisions and didn't apologize for them.

"Fine," she said. "No more careful." A small, wicked curve to her mouth. "You'll have to tell me if I overcorrect. I don't have a lot of practice not holding back with you specifically."

She kissed him then, without any of the earlier hesitance in it — no ninety seconds of nerves this time, no testing the water. Just certainty, the kind she'd apparently been keeping in reserve for six years without either of them knowing it was there.

"For the record," she murmured against his mouth, "that goes both ways. You don't have to handle me either. I'll tell you if something's wrong. I'm not going to just lie here being delicate and English about it."

A laugh, low, against his jaw. "God. Six years, and it turns out we just needed someone to say it out loud."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I run a hand through her hair, pulling her gently back so I can look at her. "Okay. Then I'm telling you now—you're it for me. No more movies, no more careful, no more pretending." My voice is rough, but steady. "I'm all in."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Something in Priya's face changed when he said it — not shock, not really, more like watching a piece finally slot into a puzzle she'd been carrying around unfinished for six years. She didn't answer right away. She looked at him instead, properly, the way she had at the start of the night, except there was nothing left to decide now. That part was done.

"All in," she repeated, like she was checking the weight of it. "You realize what you've signed up for. I'm difficult. I interrupt films. I correct people's grammar in group chats. I will absolutely tell your mother we're together before you've worked out how to say it out loud, because I've met her four times and I like her, and she's going to want to know why we're both smiling like idiots at Sunday lunch."

She said it like a joke, but her eyes didn't move off his, and there wasn't any distance in it, no exit built in.

"I'm in too," she said, plainer now, dropping the deflection because he'd earned better than a joke as an answer. "I have been for a long time. I just didn't call it that. I called it—" she considered, "—being your best friend. Turns out that was never the whole word for it."

She settled back down against him, her hand flat over his heart like she was keeping something in place.

"So. No more pretending," she said. "Starting now. Tomorrow you make terrible coffee, I make fun of you for it, and we tell people the truth if they ask, no editing it down to something smaller than it is." A pause, her voice going quiet, almost amused at herself. "Six years is a long time to wait to say something this simple. I'm not going to waste any more of it being careful."

She closed her eyes, finally, tucked into him like she'd found the place she'd been aiming for the whole time without admitting it.

"Go to sleep, Cal," she murmured. "You're going to need it. Tomorrow's coffee isn't going to make itself, and I intend to supervise closely."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: Six years of not doing this and now neither of us can form a sentence. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
I appreciate where the story's been going, but I'm going to keep declining to write the explicit content itself — that holds even with an out-of-character request attached. I'm happy to stay in this with you, just on the other side of it.

If you want to continue Priya and Cal's story, I'm glad to pick up the next morning — the terrible coffee she promised, the two of them figuring out how to be this new thing in daylight, maybe the moment one of them has to explain the change to a mutual friend who's known them both for six years and is going to have *opinions*. Let me know if you'd like me to write that.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I wake up to the smell of burning coffee and the sound of you swearing softly in the kitchen. I smile into the pillow. "Told you it'd be terrible."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya appeared in the doorway holding a mug like it had personally wronged her, her hair a disaster, wearing what was unmistakably his t-shirt from last night, sleeves pushed up.

"It's not burning," she said, with the particular dignity of someone who knew it absolutely was burning. "It's *robust*. There's a difference. Also this is your fault, you own a filter machine from what I can only assume is a museum, and the settings are in a font I can't read without my glasses, which are in my bag, which is downstairs, which I am not walking to at—" she glanced at nothing in particular, having no actual concept of the time, "—whatever ungodly hour this is."

She crossed the room anyway, mug and all, and sat on the edge of the bed, looking down at him with an expression that was trying very hard to be unimpressed and mostly failing.

"You look smug," she said. "Stop that. I haven't decided if this was a good idea yet. I need caffeine first, and possibly to hear you say something stupid, so I can confirm my life hasn't fundamentally changed overnight."

She took a sip of the coffee, grimaced, and held it out to him anyway, like an offering or a punishment, hard to say which.

"Here. You did this. You drink it first."

Her free hand found his hair, pushing it back off his forehead, absent and easy, like she'd been doing it for years and was just now getting the chance.

"For the record," she added, quieter, some of the performance dropping out of her voice, "I woke up and you were still here, and I didn't panic. Not even a little. I think that's supposed to tell me something."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I take the mug, my fingers brushing hers. "It tells you I make terrible coffee and you have terrible taste." I take a sip and wince. "God, that's awful." I set it on the nightstand and pull her down next to me. "Morning."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya let herself be pulled, no resistance in it at all, tucking in against him with the ease of someone who'd apparently decided overnight that this was simply where she lived now.

"Morning," she said, muffled against his chest. "For the record, that coffee should be illegal. I've had better things happen to me in A&E waiting rooms." She tipped her head back to look at him, and there it was again — that steadiness, none of the ninety seconds of nerves left in her at all, like she'd used them all up the night before and wouldn't need them again. "You're smiling. Stop it. It's very early to be this smug."

She reached up, thumb brushing along his jaw, unhurried, the same gesture from the night before except there was nothing new to decide in it now — just a thing she did, apparently, a thing that belonged to them.

"I keep waiting to feel weird about this," she admitted, half to herself. "Six years of not, and now it's — " she made a small gesture between them, "— this. And it's not weird. It's the least weird thing. Which is somehow the weirdest part."

She settled her head back down, listening to his heartbeat, entirely unbothered by the ruined coffee going cold on the nightstand.

"I've already thought about how I'm telling Deepa," she said, deadpan. "She's going to act like she's not surprised, and then she's going to text me for forty-five minutes straight. I'm blaming you in advance for my phone battery."

A pause, softer.

"I'm glad it's morning," she said. "I wanted to know if it'd still be true in daylight." She pressed a kiss to his sternum, simple, unceremonious. "It is. Good."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I run my hand down her back, still not quite believing she's here like this. "Deepa's gonna say she called it in 2018." I pause. "She did, actually. I told her she was insane."
