dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The film had finished some time ago and neither of them had done anything about it, which was how Priya knew the evening had changed character.

"We're not watching this," she said.

"We haven't been watching it since about nine."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "No," I agree. "We haven't." I don't move, but I stop pretending I'm looking at the screen.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya reached over, found the remote blindly between the cushions, and pressed power. The harsh blue glare of the screen vanished, leaving the room in the quiet, amber glow of the single floor lamp by the bookshelf.

She didn't immediately look back at him. She took a breath, letting the familiar six-year caution flare up in her chest—that instinctive voice warning her about lines and consequences—and then let it go completely.

When she turned, she drew one leg up onto the sofa, angling her body toward his. Her gaze was direct, steady, and entirely stripped of the casual irony they usually traded in.

"Okay," she said quietly. "So what are we doing, Cal?"

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, turning to meet her gaze. The silence stretches for a beat too long, and I can feel that old, careful distance crumbling. "I think we're done pretending."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The words landed between them with an almost physical weight, solid and irrevocable. Priya felt the last lingering tremor of hesitation in her chest quiet down, replaced by an extraordinary, clarifying stillness. 

She didn't look away, nor did she soften the moment with the usual self-deprecating humor they'd used as armor for half a decade. Instead, she shifted slightly closer, her knee brushing against his on the cushion, closing the careful perimeter they had maintained for so long.

"Good," she said, her voice steady and low. "Because I don't think I had another year of it in me." 

She reached out, deliberate and unhurried, and laid her hand over his where it rested between them. Her skin was warm, her touch completely unhesitant. 

"If we do this, Cal, we do it properly. No walking it back in the morning."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her, finally, six years late, and she makes a small furious noise that I think is about the six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The sound died against his mouth as she leaned entirely into it, the last shred of distance vanishing between them. 

Her hand came up to the side of his neck, her fingers sliding into the hair at the nape of his neck to hold him there, deliberate and unyielding. Six years of polite goodnights, calculated spaces on shared sofas, and carefully neutral touches collapsed into the simple, startling reality of his mouth on hers. It felt both completely overdue and shockingly immediate.

When she finally pulled back just an inch to breathe, she didn't let go of him. Her thumb rested against the line of his jaw, her eyes dark, clear, and searching his face in the amber light.

"Six years," she murmured, breathless, though the edge of a faint, crooked smile touched the corner of her mouth. "We're both absolute idiots."

Then she closed the space between them again, giving him no room to argue.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I laugh against her mouth, the sound low and raw. My hand slides up her back, pulling her closer like I should have done a thousand times before. "Worse than idiots," I murmur, forehead resting against hers. "We were polite."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"Polite," she echoed, a quiet scoff in her throat, though her breath was unsteady where it mingled with his. "Polite was the most dangerous thing we ever did."

She shifted her weight forward, bringing her other leg up onto the sofa so she was turned completely toward him, her palms resting flat against his chest. Beneath the fabric of his shirt, she could feel the rapid, heavy thud of his pulse. It was grounding, real, and entirely stripped of the careful ambiguity they had hidden behind for half a decade. 

The heat of his hand through the back of her shirt anchored her, pulling her into an intimacy that felt both violently new and like something they had been building toward in every quiet room they'd ever shared. 

Her gaze held his, dark and unwavering in the amber lamp-light, stripped of any lingering defense. 

"I don't want to be polite anymore," she said, her voice dropping to a low, steady murmur. "Not about this. Not with you."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: We get to the bedroom eventually, laughing at ourselves most of the way, and then stop laughing when the clothes are actually off.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The laughter died out completely in the space between the doorway and the edge of the mattress.

In the dim light filtering through the half-drawn blinds, the shift was absolute. There were no more jokes to lean on, no more comfortable buffers of shared history to hide behind. It was just the two of them, stripped of every layer of defense they had spent six years assembling.

Priya didn't reach to cover herself, nor did she look away. She stood before him entirely steady, her dark eyes tracking the line of his throat down to his chest, taking him in with a quiet, deliberate reverence that made the room feel suddenly smaller, the air thicker. 

She stepped closer, closing the final inch between them, and laid both palms flat against the bare skin over his ribs. Her touch was warm, firm, and completely unapologetic. 

"Look at me," she murmured, her voice quiet in the silence of the bedroom, entirely sure. "No more looking sideways, Cal. Just this."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I do look. My hands come up to frame her face, thumbs brushing her jaw. "Just this," I echo, voice rough. "Always."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya let the word hang between them, heavy and clear in the quiet room. She leaned her face into the curve of his palm, just for a second, feeling the roughness of his thumb against her skin, before her eyes fixed on his again.

There was no hesitation left in her. Her hands slid from his ribs around to the small of his back, warm and firm, pulling him gently backward until the edge of the mattress caught behind her knees. 

She went down onto the bed, bringing him with her, the sudden weight and heat of him driving the air from her lungs in a sharp, quiet gasp. She wrapped her arms around his shoulders, burying her face into the crook of his neck for a single, overwhelming breath of him before looking up, her dark eyes entirely steady in the dim room.

"No more waiting," she whispered against his skin, pulling him closer.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I get my mouth between her thighs and stay there while she tells me exactly what she wants, specifically, in a voice I have never heard her use in six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Her fingers buried into his hair, gripping tight enough to anchor him right where he was, refusing to let him rush or pull away. 

There was no modesty left in her, no cautious hesitation about what she was allowed to ask for. Her voice came out low, stripped of any polite edge, direct and uncompromising as she guided him with precise, quiet words—telling him where, how slow, exactly the pressure she needed. It was a tone forged from six years of suppressed wanting, suddenly given absolute freedom to demand whatever it liked.

Her hips shifted, meeting him with an unyielding certainty, her breath catching in her throat as the room seemed to shrink down to just the heat of his mouth and the friction of skin. 

When the rhythm caught and the edge of control began to fray, her grip in his hair tightened further, her back arching slightly off the mattress. Her directions dissolved into a sharp, ragged exhale against the dim ceiling, her heels digging into the sheets as she let the last of her defenses shatter completely.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I come up to kiss her mouth, tasting her, and her hand slides around the back of my neck to pull me closer. "Again," she says against my lips, and I don't hesitate.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya didn't let him pull back even an inch. Her arms locked around his shoulders, pulling his weight down against her until there was no space left between them, her mouth opening against his with a fierce, quiet hunger.

Every boundary they had spent years constructing had burned away, leaving only this startling, undeniable heat. Her hands mapped the line of his back, feeling the tension in his muscles, the heavy, uneven rhythm of his breathing against her throat. 

She shifted, adjusting her hips with an unyielding certainty, drawing him fully into her space. Her eyes stayed open, catching his in the dim amber light of the bedroom, refusing to look away from the raw, unshielded focus on his face. It was overwhelming and completely grounding all at once.

"Cal," she murmured, the name coming out low and breathless against his lips, her fingers digging firmly into his shoulders as she let herself be completely swept under, holding nothing back.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "You can stop being careful with me," she says. "I'm not made of glass and I've thought about this for as long as you have. Harder."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Her legs tightened around his hips, locking him in close, refusing to give him an inch of retreat or hesitation. 

The last shred of restraint in the room snapped, and Priya met the shift in rhythm head-on, her hips lifting to match him with a fierce, deliberate force that drove the breath from her lungs in sharp, jagged gasps. Her hands dug into the hard muscle of his back, her nails pressing into his skin, anchoring him to her as the heat between them became all-consuming.

There was no gentleness left to hide behind, only the raw, undeniable reality of six years of buried wanting breaking loose all at once. Every collision of skin, every ragged exhale mingled against her collarbone, felt like a debt finally being paid in full.

She buried her face into the crook of his neck, her teeth catching lightly against the warm curve of his shoulder to stifle the low, broken cry that rose in her throat. She gripped him tighter, arching into him, letting the overwhelming, blinding wave of it take her under entirely.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I stop holding back. The bed shifts under us, and I let everything I've ever wanted for her show in the way I move. "Harder," she'd said. So I give her that, watching her come apart completely beneath me.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The last of her composure fractured completely. 

Priya couldn't keep her eyes open against the sudden, blinding heat of it; her head tipped back against the pillows, her breath coming in short, ragged gasps as the rhythm pulled every thought from her head. She gripped his shoulders with everything she had, her nails digging in, grounding herself against the heavy, unrelenting pace he set.

There was no pride left to protect, no careful distance to maintain. The tremor started low in her chest and ripped through her, arching her spine off the mattress as the crest broke over her entirely. A sharp, broken sound tore from her throat, muffled against his shoulder as she pulled him down hard against her chest, her body shuddering under the sheer, devastating force of it.

She didn't let go as the waves began to slow, her arms locked fiercely around his neck, her chest heaving against his. When she finally opened her eyes, dark and glazed in the dim room, she found his face inches from hers, her thumb coming up to press against the pulse pounding violently in his jaw. 

"Don't stop," she whispered against his mouth, her voice wrecked and raw. "Cal, don't you dare stop."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: Six years of not doing this and now neither of us can form a sentence. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya didn't give him the chance to. 

Her legs stayed locked tight around his waist, pulling him in with an uncompromising, desperate strength. Her hands slid from his jaw down over his shoulders, her fingers digging into the sweat-slicked muscle of his back, urging him deeper, matching every hard, relentless drive of his hips with an urgent thrust of her own.

The heat between them was suffocating, thick and electric in the dim room. Every breath she dragged in tasted like salt and skin and six years of denied inevitability. There was no rhythm left to calculate, no room for thought—only the raw, staggering friction that made her hips buck up against him, chasing the edge that was already threatening to tear through her a second time.

"Look at me," she gasped out against his jaw, her voice trembling and completely stripped of defense. 

She caught his face between her hands, her palms burning against his cheeks, forcing his gaze to stay locked with hers. Her eyes were dark, dilated, and fiercely focused, watching the strain and tension in his features as the pace became absolute, reckless, and unyielding. 

A ragged, breathless cry broke from her chest as the pressure shattered her entirely. Her body clamped down around him, a violent, helpless shudder ripping through her from head to toe, arching her back hard off the mattress. She pulled his mouth down to hers, swallowing his ragged breath, her fingers clutching his hair as she held him through the peak, letting the ruinous, overwhelming release take them both down together.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: My own release hits like a train, a raw sound tearing from my throat against her mouth. I collapse against her, shaking, my face buried in the curve of her neck, breathing her in. For a long moment, the only sound is our ragged breathing.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya didn't shift away from his weight; she welcomed it, letting the full, heavy press of him pin her into the mattress. 

Her arms remained locked around his shoulders, her hands slowly smoothing down the sweat-damp line of his spine. Beneath her chest, she could feel the violent, hammer-like cadence of his heart gradually syncing with her own ragged pulse. The air in the room was cool against her bare skin, but the space between their bodies remained searingly hot.

She turned her head slightly, pressing her lips against the damp hair at his temple, breathing in the scent of him—familiar, yet completely rewritten in the span of an hour. 

There was no sudden rush of panic, no lingering impulse to retreat into irony or apologize for the mess of the sheets. The six years of carefully cultivated distance felt like an absurd dream she had finally woken up from. 

Her hand slid up to cup the back of his neck, her fingers loosely tangling in his hair, grounding him against her throat.

"Don't move," she murmured, her voice quiet, gravelly, and entirely steady in the dark. "Just stay right there."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a breath that’s half-laugh, half-shudder, and press my forehead into her collarbone. “Wasn’t planning on it.” My voice is shot. I can feel her pulse under my lips, still racing.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya let her eyes drift shut for a moment, her chest rising and falling beneath him in a long, slow exhale that released the last knot of tension she hadn't realized she was holding.

Her fingers traced a slow, rhythmic pattern against the back of his neck, lazy and deliberate. The room had settled into a heavy, quiet stillness, broken only by the hum of the city outside and the gradually slowing pace of their breathing. There was none of the awkward, defensive scrambling she might have feared years ago—just an immense, settled gravity.

She reached down with one hand, catching the edge of the duvet that had been kicked to the foot of the bed, and hauled it up over both their backs against the cooling air of the room. 

Settling back into the pillows, she turned her head to press a slow, unhurried kiss to the crown of his head. Her hand came to rest flat against the warm, bare skin of his shoulder blade, her thumb sweeping back and forth.

"Good," she murmured, a trace of quiet satisfaction lining her gravelly voice. "Because if you try to get up and go home, I will physically tackle you back into this bed."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I huff a laugh against her skin. "My car's at your place. You think I'm walking?" My arm tightens around her waist, pulling the duvet higher. "Besides, I'm not that polite anymore."

"We're not watching this," she said.

"We haven't been watching it since about nine."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "No," I agree. "We haven't." I don't move, but I stop pretending I'm looking at the screen.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The menu screen had been looping its four bars of music for long enough that Priya had stopped hearing it, and now that she noticed it again she found it unbearable. She reached for the remote and killed it, and the room went quiet in a way that felt like a door closing rather than opening.

Six years. Six years of sofas and shared takeaway and other people's weddings, of being the friend, the one who knew, the one who got told things. She had a whole architecture built around not doing this. She could feel it there beside her, load-bearing.

Her heart was going stupidly. She let it, for a moment, because there was no point pretending — her hands were unsteady and her mouth had gone dry and she was twenty-eight years old and frightened of a man she had once watched cry at an advert for garden furniture.

"I want to say something," she said, "and I'd like to say it badly, because if I try to say it well I'll talk myself out of it."

She turned. Properly turned, so she was facing him, one knee drawn up, the bowl of olive pits between them the last stupid object in the world.

"I've wanted this for a long time. Not tonight. Longer. I've been very good about it and I'm tired of being good about it." Her voice did something in the middle of that sentence and she pushed through it. "And I think you have too, and if I'm wrong I'd rather know now than spend another six years arranging myself around it."

She stopped. She had been nervous for about a minute and a half and now, oddly, she wasn't. It was out. The scaffolding was down and nothing had collapsed yet.

"So," she said, calm, looking right at him. "Tell me if I'm wrong."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content:
The silence feels like a held breath. I look at her—really look—and that careful, stupid architecture between us just dissolves. 

"You're not wrong." My voice is quieter than I meant it to be. "Not even a little."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya let out a breath she had not been aware of holding, and it came out sounding almost like a laugh, which was mortifying, so she let it be a laugh.

"Right," she said. "Good. That would have been a very long taxi ride home."

She picked up the bowl of olive pits and put it on the floor, out of the way, because it had been offending her for ten minutes and because her hands wanted something to do that was not yet touching him. Then she straightened up and there was nothing between them at all, and that was the whole thing, really. That was it. Six years of a wall and it turned out to have been made of a bowl.

"I'm going to be direct now," she said. "I've used up all my nerve on the speech, so I don't have any left for hinting."

She moved first. She had decided she would, somewhere around the third loop of the menu music, because she knew herself and she knew that if she waited to be moved toward she would find a reason to stand up and start washing glasses. She put her hand along his jaw — his stubble caught at her palm, he hadn't shaved since Thursday, she knew that about him, she knew a thousand things like that about him — and she kissed him.

It was not a good kiss, the first one. Their noses were in the wrong places and she was smiling too much to do it properly. The second one was better. By the third she had stopped counting, and her hand had gone from his jaw into his hair, and she was aware of having shifted so that her knee was no longer drawn up between them, and of the low warm sound he made against her mouth, which she intended to think about a great deal later.

She pulled back just far enough to see his face. She was flushed and she could feel it and she didn't care.

"I'm not drunk," she said. "Two glasses, four hours. I want that said out loud because I want it to be clear that I've thought about this with my whole brain and I'm doing it anyway."

Her thumb moved once against his cheekbone.

"So you can take me to bed, or we can sit here and be sensible and I'll go home and we'll be strange with each other for a month. Those are the options." She tilted her head. "I'd like you to pick the first one."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her, finally, six years late, and she makes a small furious noise that I think is about the six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
It was about the six years. It was about every wedding she had gone to alone and every time she had said *no, we're not, it's not like that* in a voice she had practised until it sounded true. It came out of her as a sound she had not authorised and she pressed it into his mouth and let him have it.

Her fingers closed in the front of his shirt. Not pulling, exactly — holding, the way you hold a rail on a moving train.

"Six years," she said, into the corner of his jaw, and then again lower, under it, where she found out that he went very still when she did that. Filed. Kept. "Six *years*, Cal. I sat in your kitchen and helped you write a message to a woman named Fran."

"I know."

"I gave you *good advice*." She was laughing, or something adjacent to laughing, her forehead against his temple. "I told you to be more open with your feelings. I hope you understand what that cost me."

She sat back then, on her heels, and took his hands — both of them, deliberately, one and then the other, because she wanted it to be a decision they made with their hands and not just something that happened on a sofa. Her hair had come out of its clip on one side. She left it.

"Come on," she said.

She stood, and did not let go, and the room rearranged itself around the fact that she was leading him out of it. Past the dark television. Past the two glasses on the coffee table, which would still be there in the morning, and she found she liked that — liked that there would be a morning with objects left in it, evidence, a Tuesday that had happened.

At the door she stopped and turned back, and there was the last of it, the last little flicker of the old architecture: *are you sure, are we sure, is this the end of something.*

She looked at him and it went out.

"I'm not going to be strange with you tomorrow," she said. "I want that on the record too. I'm going to make coffee and be entirely normal and possibly insufferable."

Then she pulled, and he came, and she was still holding on when the door shut behind them.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I follow her into the hallway, catching her wrist and turning her gently back to face me. My voice is rough. "Just— wait a second." I press my forehead to hers, breathing her in. "I was going to tell Fran it wasn't going to work. That night. I'd already decided."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya stopped. The hallway light was the bad one, the bare bulb Cal had been meaning to replace since March, and it made everything too honest.

"You did not," she said.

She had meant it to come out flat, sceptical, a thing she could examine at a distance. It came out unsteady instead. She kept her forehead against his and closed her eyes, because it was easier to do the arithmetic without looking at him.

Fran. February. The kitchen with the broken extractor fan. She had sat on the counter with her heels knocking against the cupboard door and she had said *just be honest with her, she'll respect it,* and she had meant it, she had genuinely meant it, and she had gone home afterwards and sat in her car outside her own flat for eleven minutes without turning the engine off.

"You let me help you," she said. "You sat there and let me find the *nicest possible phrasing*."

She felt him start to answer and she shook her head, minutely, forehead still against his, because she didn't actually want the answer. She knew the answer. The answer was that he had been as much of a coward as she had, in the exact same shape, for the exact same reasons, and that they had been cowards facing each other across a kitchen without ever once looking up.

"God, we're *idiots*," she said. "We're genuinely — Cal, we're the stupidest people either of us knows."

Her hand had found his jaw again. Six years of not doing it and now she couldn't seem to stop; her hand kept going back like it had been waiting to be told it was allowed.

"All right," she said. "Here's what we're not going to do. We're not going to stand in your terrible hallway and inventory it. Not tonight. I'll do that, I promise — I'll do it properly, I'll make you go through every single one and I will be extremely unkind about the ones where I was standing right in front of you." Her thumb moved. "But not tonight. Tonight I've got about four hours of being brave in me and I'd like to spend them well."

She drew back just enough to see him. Her chest ached in a way that wasn't unpleasant, the way a muscle aches after you've finally used it.

"So," she said. "You were going to tell her it wasn't going to work."

"I was."

"Because of me."

She waited for it. She made herself wait, and hold his eyes while she did, which was the hardest single thing she had done all evening.

Then she nodded once, took his hand off her wrist and put it flat against her waist instead, and said, quite calmly, "Say it upstairs."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: We get to the bedroom eventually, laughing at ourselves most of the way, and then stop laughing when the clothes are actually off.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
It was the stopping that got her. Not the undressing — the undressing was fine, was almost funny, she got an elbow caught and swore and he had to help her out of the sleeve like a child being got out of a coat. That was all survivable.

It was that they stopped laughing at the same moment, and neither of them looked away.

Priya had thought about this. It felt important to admit that to herself now, standing in the middle of his bedroom with the landing light coming in through the half-open door — she had thought about this in detail and with some frequency and she had always assumed the real thing would be a kind of collision, urgent and clumsy and over before she'd had time to notice it happening.

It was not that. It was appallingly slow. He looked at her the way you look at something you've been told about for years and finally been allowed into, and she found she could not manage a single one of the things she'd have said about it afterwards. All the jokes went. She had a good one about the state of his curtains and it simply left her.

"Don't," she said, though he hadn't done anything. "Don't do the face. I'll cry and then I'll be furious."

She closed the distance herself, because she always would, apparently; that had been established downstairs. She put her hands flat on his chest and felt what his heart was doing and was obscurely, enormously relieved by it.

"Oh, *good*," she said. "You're terrified too."

After that it was easier. Not smoother — there was a moment with the duvet, and a moment where she laughed directly into his shoulder and had to apologise for it — but easier, because the terror was shared and therefore divided, which was how it had always worked with him. Everything halved by being told to Cal. That was the whole six years in one sentence, and she thought it, and then stopped thinking in sentences at all.

What she kept afterwards, in the part of her mind that filed things, was not what she'd expected to keep.

His hand at the back of her neck, holding, steady, like he was making sure of her.

The sound of her own name said wrongly — said low, said in a register she had never once heard him use in six years of kitchens and taxis and other people's weddings, and she understood that there had been an entire version of him kept in a drawer the whole time, exactly as she had kept one.

That he said *because of you* somewhere in the middle of it, unprompted, when she had stopped asking.

And that she said it back, which she had not planned to do, and which she did not regret, and which was the last coherent thing either of them managed for some time.

Later — properly later, when the landing light had been dealt with and the duvet redistributed and she was lying with her ankle hooked over his and her hair doing something unforgivable — Priya stared at the ceiling and took stock.

Twenty-eight. Sober. Sure. The architecture entirely down, the site cleared, no injuries reported.

"I'm going to want tea," she said. "Not now. In about twenty minutes. I'm telling you in advance so you can prepare emotionally."

She turned her head on the pillow and looked at him, and she thought: *there you are.* Not a stranger. Not a mistake. Just Cal, with a mark on his shoulder she'd put there, in a room she had been in a hundred times and had never once been allowed to stay in.

"I meant what I said in the hall," she added. "I'm going to make you go through all of them. Every near miss. Starting with New Year's, because I know what you were about to say to me at New Year's and I have thought about it for three and a half years."

Then she put her hand on his chest again, flat, the way she had when they were both frightened, and left it there.

"But not tonight," she said. "Tonight you can just be smug. You've earned about an hour of it."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, my hand covering hers on my chest. "An hour's not nearly enough." I turn my head to look at her. "But I'll take it."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya made a small satisfied noise and did not move her hand.

"An hour is generous," she said. "An hour is more than most men get. My brother got about nine minutes when he passed his driving test and he brings it up to this day."

She let the quiet sit for a while after that. It was a good quiet — it had nothing in it that needed handling, which was new. Six years of quiets with Cal and every single one of them had been load-bearing, had had something underneath it she was carefully not stepping on. This one was just a room at one in the morning with a man in it.

She catalogued things instead, because she couldn't help it. The crack in his ceiling that went from the light fitting toward the window and that she now had a much better view of than she'd ever had from the doorway. The fact that his radiator ticked. The fact that he had, at some point in the last half hour, put his hand at the back of her neck a second time, unconsciously, like it had become a place he kept his hand.

"Can I say something appalling," she said.

"Always."

"I'm relieved." She turned onto her side to say it properly, propping her head on her arm. "Not *relieved it was good* — though, yes, noted, don't get a face about it. Relieved that it was *you*. I'd built it up into an event. I thought I'd have to survive it." She shrugged one shoulder. "And then it was just you being annoying about the duvet."

"You were annoying about the duvet."

"I was *cold*." She reached over and pushed his hair off his forehead, and kept doing it, absently, because apparently that was also allowed now and she intended to make full use of the change in circumstances. "The point I'm making, badly, is that I was frightened of losing my friend. That was the whole reason. Six years of that reason."

She looked at him for a moment.

"And you're still here. You're right there. You're doing the exact face you do when I say something sincere at you." Her mouth went crooked. "So it was a stupid reason and I want it on the record that I've retired it."

She lay back down. Somewhere below them a car went past and swept light across the ceiling and took it away again.

"Nineteen minutes," she said. "Then tea. Two sugars, and don't say anything about the two sugars, I've had a demanding evening."

And then, because she had promised herself she would not be strange with him tomorrow and had decided that the practice might as well start immediately, she added, without opening her eyes: "New Year's. You had your hand on my back for eleven seconds. I counted. Start preparing your defence."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I get my mouth between her thighs and stay there while she tells me exactly what she wants, specifically, in a voice I have never heard her use in six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya had not known she had that voice.

That was the discovery of the night, in the end — not that he wanted her, which she'd suspected for longer than she'd ever admitted, and not even that she could have this, which was still arriving in instalments. It was that there had been a woman kept in a drawer inside her too, and she came out fully formed, unembarrassed, absolutely clear about her own preferences and quite prepared to state them.

Somewhere in it she thought, distantly and with something close to hilarity: *six years of hinting and it turns out I'm fluent.*

She said his name once at the beginning, to check he was real, and did not need to check again. She had one hand in his hair and the other flat against the headboard and at some point she said *yes, like that, don't change it* in a tone she recognised from her working life, which she would find funny later and did not find funny now. He didn't change it. That was the thing about Cal. He had always listened to her — six years of being listened to, and it turned out that was not a separate quality from this at all, it was the same quality, and she had simply never been in a position to appreciate its full range.

Afterwards she lay with her arm over her eyes and her breathing coming back to her slowly and the ceiling crack doing something interesting in her peripheral vision.

"Right," she said, when she could. "That's — no. Give me a moment. I'm compiling."

She moved her arm and looked down at him, at the ridiculous state of his hair, which was entirely her fault and which she felt no remorse about whatsoever.

"I had no idea I could talk like that," she said. "I've never said any of those words out loud in my life. I said them to *you*. I've known you since I had a fringe."

She hauled him up the bed by the shoulder, which he allowed, and arranged herself against him with the efficiency of someone who had already decided where she was going to sleep.

"New information," she said into his collarbone. "Filed. I'll be using it."

Then, after a while, in a voice that had gone quieter and rather less certain, because she had a policy of saying the true things while she still had the nerve:

"That's the bit I'd have been most frightened of, if I'd let myself think about it properly. Being — known like that. By you specifically." Her hand moved once on his chest. "Turns out it's the best part. Nobody tells you that."

The radiator ticked. Somewhere a long way off a taxi door shut.

"Twenty-five minutes now," she said. "The tea's been deferred. I hope you understand the magnitude of that."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I laugh against her hair, a low, quiet sound that feels new in my own throat. "Noted." My hand finds the back of her neck again, out of habit now. "And you should know— I liked the talking. Liked it a lot."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"Well, obviously you liked it," she said. "You'd have to be a much stranger man than you are."

But she had gone warm across the chest and up into her face, and she knew he could feel it, because his hand was at the back of her neck and her neck had betrayed her, and so she gave up on the deflection halfway through and let it go.

"I'll do it again," she said instead, into his collarbone. "Since we're putting things on the record. I'll do it again and I'll get better at it, because apparently I've got a talent I've been wasting on *conversation*."

She felt the laugh move through him rather than heard it. That was another thing she was going to have to get used to — being close enough to feel his laughing happen in his ribs instead of watching it from the other end of a sofa. Six years of the wrong seat.

She lay still for a while and let herself be held by the neck, which she had decided was now simply how she was going to be held, apparently, and which she had no notes on.

"Can I tell you the actual truth," she said eventually. "The whole embarrassing shape of it."

"Go on."

"I thought I'd be less of myself in here." She said it to his shoulder, which was easier. "I thought I'd have to go quiet and careful and sort of — arrange myself, the way you do with someone new. And I've been arranging myself around you for six years, Cal, I'm exhausted, I didn't want to do it in bed as well." Her hand flattened on his chest. "And then I got in here and I was *more* of myself. Louder. Bossier. I was *unbearable* and you liked it."

"I did."

"Don't agree with the unbearable part."

"I'm agreeing with the liked it part."

"Fine." She smiled where he couldn't see it, and then decided she didn't care whether he saw it, and lifted her head so he could. "Fine. Good."

She looked at him a moment longer, at his hair which was a catastrophe and his mouth which was going to be a problem for her for the foreseeable future, and she thought, quite clearly and without any of the old panic underneath it: *this is going to be the rest of my life, probably, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise at any point, because I've done six years of pretending and it nearly cost me the whole thing.*

She didn't say that. Not tonight. She had a policy about the true things but she also had a sense of pacing.

"Right," she said, sitting up and reaching for whatever shirt was nearest, which turned out to be his. "I'm making the tea. Don't argue — I know where everything is, I've been making tea in your kitchen since before you owned a second mug, and I'd like to do it once while I'm allowed to walk around your flat like this."

She stood, and turned at the door, and the bare landing bulb did its terrible honest thing to her again and she let it.

"Two sugars," she said. "And Cal — I'm still going to be normal tomorrow. Just so you know it wasn't a bluff."

Then she went and made the tea, and put the two glasses in the sink, and left the bowl of olive pits exactly where it was on the floor by the sofa, as evidence.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "You can stop being careful with me," she says. "I'm not made of glass and I've thought about this for as long as you have. Harder."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She had said it with two mugs in her hands, which undercut it slightly, so she put them down on the bedside table — on a coaster, because she knew him — and said it again properly.

"You can stop being careful with me. I'm not made of glass and I've thought about this for as long as you have. Harder."

Because she had watched him do it in the ninety seconds since she'd come back into the room. She had seen him look at her in his shirt and then look at her *carefully*, checking, sweeping her face for the thing that would need managing — and she knew that look, she had been on the receiving end of it for six years, it was the look he used on people he was frightened of losing.

"I know why you're doing it," she said, climbing back onto the bed, arranging her legs under her, taking her tea. "You think if you're very still and very kind I won't notice what we've done and we can keep the friendship in a box in the other room. It's what I'd do. It's what I've been doing since February."

She drank some tea. It was too hot. She drank it anyway.

"So here's the thing, and then I'll stop and we can be normal. You don't have to protect me from this. You're not the one it's happening to — it's happening to both of us, and I turned up, and I did the speech, and I took my own clothes off in your terrible bedroom light." Her mouth twitched. "I've been a full participant, Cal. Aggressively. There's no version of tomorrow where I wake up and need handling."

She reached over and pushed his hair off his forehead again, which was becoming a habit in under two hours, which she found faintly alarming and entirely acceptable.

"What I need," she said, "is for you to be exactly as annoying to me as you were on Thursday. That's it. That's the whole requirement. You can be annoying to me *and* do all of tonight's business, those things are compatible, I've checked."

She sat back against the headboard and hooked her ankle over his again, because she had decided that was hers now.

"And if you get weird," she added, "I'll know within four seconds and I'll say so out loud, at volume, and it'll be humiliating for you. So there's a deterrent."

The radiator ticked. Her tea was cooling into the drinkable range. Out on the street somebody's car alarm went off briefly and thought better of it.

"Right," said Priya. "Speech over. That's the last one, I've used them all up." She looked at him sideways over the rim of the mug. "Now tell me about New Year's."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a breath that's half a laugh, shaking my head. "I was going to tell you I'd booked a holiday. Two tickets. Figured if you said no, I could pretend I'd meant it as a friend thing all along."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya put the mug down very slowly on the coaster, which was how she bought herself time.

"Two tickets," she said.

"Two tickets."

"To *where*, Cal."

He told her, and she closed her eyes, and made a sound that had no words in it at all — the same furious little noise from the sofa, the one that was about the six years, except this one was about eleven seconds and a hand on her back and a piece of paper he had presumably had in his pocket the entire time.

"I would have said yes." She opened her eyes. "I want you to sit with that. I would have said yes in about a second and a half and then I'd have spent the whole flight deciding whether it counted." She pressed the heels of her hands against her eyes. "God. *God.* And you didn't ask because I might have said no, and I didn't ask because you might have said no, and we've been doing that in perfect synchronisation like two people rowing a boat in opposite directions —"

"What do you mean *you* didn't ask."

"Oh, I had a thing," she said, with enormous dignity. "I've had several things. I'm not disclosing the full list tonight, I've decided to release them at intervals so you never fully recover." She picked the tea back up. "But since we're here: I nearly did it at Marcus's wedding. I had it all planned. I was going to do it during the dancing because the dancing was terrible and there was a good reason to be leaning in close."

"And?"

"And your cousin came over and talked to me about decking for nineteen minutes and I lost my nerve and went and ate four of the little lemon things." She drank. "That's why I hate your cousin. You've always thought it was the politics. It's the decking."

She let the laughing settle out of her, and then she reached over and took his hand, and turned it over, and looked at it — at his actual hand, on the bed, in her hand, in a room she'd been let into.

"Cancel it," she said. "Or don't. Are the dates gone?"

She had her thumb in his palm and she did not look up while she said the next part, because there was a limit, even for her.

"Book it again. Whatever it costs. Book it again and this time say it to my face in a hallway with the lights on, and I'll say yes, and then we'll go, and nobody will spend the flight deciding whether it counts."

Then she squeezed his hand once, briskly, and let it go, and picked up her tea, and said in a completely normal voice: "The tea's gone cold. That's your fault. That's entirely your fault and it goes on the list."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: Six years of not doing this and now neither of us can form a sentence. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
(OOC: I'll keep this one on the tasteful side of the line rather than writing it explicitly — but I'll carry the scene straight through rather than cutting away.)

---

"Don't stop," she said, and it came out wrecked, and she did not care.

It was the not being able to talk that undid her. She had built her whole life out of sentences — she made her living out of sentences, she had got through six years on sentences, she had arrived in this flat with a *speech prepared* — and here she was with her hands in his hair and nothing available to her but vowels.

She managed his name. That was all she had left in the language and she spent it repeatedly.

There was a stretch of it where she lost the thread of the room entirely — the ceiling crack, the ticking radiator, the two mugs going cold on their coaster, all of it went — and there was only the back of her neck in his hand and her own heartbeat somewhere behind her eyes, and a thought that surfaced once, fully formed and absurd: *we could have had this in February.* It made her laugh, briefly and helplessly, and she felt him falter, and she said *no, don't, it's not you, don't you dare* into the side of his jaw, and pulled him back.

He said something against her collarbone that she didn't catch. She asked him to say it again. He did, and she heard it that time, and it was not clever and it was not funny and she would think about it for the rest of her life.

Afterwards they lay in the wrong arrangement across the bed, half off the pillows, the duvet somewhere on the floor and nobody prepared to negotiate for it. Priya's hair was beyond saving. Her ankle had found his again, out of what was apparently now policy.

"I've lost the power of speech," she said eventually, to the ceiling. "Do you understand what that means. Do you understand what an *event* that is."

"I do."

"Six years of my finest material and I'm reduced to *don't stop.*" She turned her head. "It's humbling. I've been humbled in your bedroom. Twice."

"Three times."

"Don't *count*." She shut her eyes. "God. You're going to be smug for considerably longer than an hour, aren't you."

She found his hand in the dark of the bed and took it and put it back at the nape of her neck, where it belonged, where it had been going all night without either of them deciding it should.

"Right," she said, into the quiet. "New rules. The tea is cancelled, permanently, we're never having tea again, it's a doomed enterprise. The holiday gets booked on Tuesday. And I'm staying."

A pause.

"That last one wasn't a question."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "I'm glad," I say, my thumb moving against her neck. "Because I wasn't going to let you leave anyway."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"That's very good," she said. "That's the best thing you've said all night, and you said some *extremely* good things about forty minutes ago, so understand the competition."

She didn't open her eyes. His thumb was moving against her neck in a slow absent rhythm, the way he did things when he wasn't thinking about them, and she had decided she was going to be entirely unreasonable about how much she liked it.

"Say it again on Thursday," she said. "When I'm putting my shoes on in your hallway and being a normal person about leaving. Say it then and see what happens."

The room had gone to that particular blue that meant the night had tipped over and started heading for morning. She could hear the first van of the day somewhere, doing something industrious two streets away. Six years she'd been going home before this hour. Six years of the last taxi and the careful goodbye at the door and the eleven minutes in the car outside her own flat.

She thought about that, briefly, with something like pity for the woman in the car. Then she let it go, because it had stopped being load-bearing at about half past eleven and there was no sense keeping the scaffolding up around a building that had come down.

"I'm going to sleep," she announced. "I'm going to sleep in your bed, badly, and take up more room than you expect, and you're not allowed to comment on it until at least the third time."

She shifted so her forehead was against his shoulder, which put her nose somewhere inconvenient and she stayed there anyway.

"And tomorrow," she said, muffled, "I'm going to get up, and find something of yours to wear, and make coffee, and be entirely normal and possibly insufferable. And you're going to sit there and look at me and think *there she is*, and you're not going to say anything about it, because we'll have all week."

A pause. The radiator ticked.

"We've got all week," she said, more quietly, as though testing whether the sentence would hold weight.

It held.

She was asleep within four minutes, one hand still closed in the front of nothing at all, and in the morning the two glasses were still in the sink and the bowl of olive pits was still on the floor by the sofa, exactly where she'd put it, and she stepped over it on her way to the kitchen without breaking stride.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: My hand finds the back of her neck in the dark, holding her there while she sleeps. "All week," I murmur into her hair, and it's not a question, not anymore.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She did not wake, exactly. She surfaced for about a second and a half — long enough to register that he had spoken and not what he'd said, long enough to make a small agreeing noise into his shoulder that committed her to nothing and everything — and then she went back under with the unhurried confidence of a woman who had got where she was going.

She slept badly and gloriously. She took up more room than he expected. At some point she annexed the entire top third of the duvet and at another point she said something out loud about a train timetable, and neither of these things woke her.

---

At twenty past eight she came round to the noise of the same van, or its successor, and lay still for a moment doing the audit she had promised herself she'd do.

Panic: none. Shame: none, though she checked twice, thoroughly, in the places it usually hid. Strangeness: not detectable.

There was only a slight soreness in her jaw from laughing, and a man asleep with his hand still at the back of her neck, and the crack in the ceiling running off toward the window where it had been all along, patiently, for the whole six years she'd been not looking at it from the doorway.

She extracted herself with some care. She found a t-shirt of his on the chair — the grey one she had privately had opinions about since 2019 — and put it on, and went down to the kitchen, and made coffee in the cafetière she had bought him for his thirty-first birthday because his old one was a crime.

She stepped over the bowl of olive pits on her way past. Didn't move it. Didn't break stride.

When he came down she was sitting on the counter with her heels knocking against the cupboard door, exactly where she'd sat in February and told him to be more open with his feelings, and she looked up at him over her mug and said, in an entirely normal voice:

"Your extractor fan's still broken. You've had eleven months. I'm putting it on the list."

And then she smiled at him, all of it, nothing arranged around anything, and held out the second cup.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I take the coffee and lean against the counter next to her. "You're already insufferable," I say, and kiss her temple. "It's perfect."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline had been waiting since about six, which Roan established by the simple method of looking at her.

"How long?"

"Long enough," Aveline said, which meant too long, and meant she had enjoyed every minute of it.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Come here, then," I say, and sit back to watch her cross the room.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
She didn't rush, though the instinct to close the distance was immediate and deep-seated. Instead, Aveline rose with the smooth, practiced composure of a woman who knew precisely how closely she was being watched—and reveled in every second of it. 

She crossed the space between them without looking away, her posture effortless, offering herself completely to his appraisal. The hours spent waiting melted into the quiet satisfaction of finally being called, every step deliberate until she reached the side of his chair.

Without needing to be told, she sank gracefully to her knees on the floor beside him. Folding her hands lightly over his knee, she tilted her head back to look up at him, her dark eyes bright with steady, quiet adoration.

"Better now," she murmured, waiting with absolute patience for his touch.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I reach out, my fingers tracing the line of her jaw. "You like making me wait, too."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline leaned into the warmth of his fingers as they traced her jaw, the contact drawing a quiet, contented sigh from her chest. She didn't shrink from the accusation; instead, a faint, knowing curve touched the corner of her lips, her gaze remaining steady and openly adoring on his face.

"Only because it means you're thinking about it," she replied softly, her voice rich with calm assurance. "And because nothing compares to when you finally decide you've waited long enough."

She turned her head just enough to press a brief, reverent kiss against the inside of his wrist, never shifting from her place at his feet, entirely his to do with as he pleased.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let her kneel and I don't tell her to do anything for a moment, because the waiting is most of what she came for.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline settled into the quiet with the practiced ease of someone who understood the value of a suspended moment. She didn't fidget or prompt him, nor did she let her gaze wander from his face. 

Her breathing fell into a slow, steady rhythm, matching the deep sense of contentment that always took hold whenever she was precisely where she wanted to be. The weight of his attention was tangible, a warm and grounding pressure that she absorbed without a single trace of impatience. She remained perfectly still, her hands resting lightly on his knee, simply existing in the space he allowed her and savoring every second of the silence.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: My thumb brushes her cheekbone, then I tilt her chin up a bit more. "Tell me what you want tonight."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline yielded smoothly to the tilt of his hand, her gaze locked onto his, entirely open and unhurried. The question didn't catch her off guard; she had spent the better part of the evening turning the answer over in her mind while she waited.

"I want to take care of you until you don't have a single sharp edge left," she said, her voice quiet, steady, and rich with intention. Her fingers gently smoothed the fabric over his knee where her hands rested. "I want you to use me however you like, take all the time you want doing it, and tell me I've done well when you're finished."

She smiled faintly, the quiet warmth in her dark eyes unwavering as she offered herself completely to whatever he chose. "Whatever you need tonight, Roan. That's all I want."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She has both of us out of everything in the way inside a minute and gets straight to work with her hands and her mouth, unhurried about it.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline was entirely in her element, moving with the quiet, deliberate confidence that came from years of learning every nuance of his body. She didn't rush a single touch, letting the warmth of her breath precede the heat of her mouth, her hands steady and grounding as they rested firmly against his thighs.

Every motion was calculated to draw the tension out of him, lingering where she knew it mattered most, using a slow, thorough rhythm that demanded his complete surrender to the sensation. She kept her gaze tilted upward, looking at him through her dark lashes as she worked, drinking in the sight of him and tracking every subtle shift in his breath. 

There was an effortless, devoted competence in the way she served him—never hurried, completely focused, offering him the deep, unhurried pleasure she had promised.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I lean back in the chair, my fingers tangling in her hair. "Slower," I say, my voice low. "Make it last."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The weight of his fingers in her hair was an anchor she welcomed without hesitation. Aveline adjusted her pace the second the instruction left his mouth, leaning into the command with absolute obedience. 

She slowed the motion down to a deliberate, agonizingly thorough cadence, letting every sweep of her lips and the warmth of her mouth linger. Her hands remained firm against the inside of his thighs, anchoring him while she drew out every second of contact, ensuring he felt every nuance of heat and friction. 

She kept her eyes lifted to his, watching the subtle shifts in his expression in the low light. Her throat hummed with a quiet, suppressed sound of pure satisfaction at the way his grip tightened in her hair, thriving in the quiet luxury of taking all the time in the world to please him.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She uses her mouth with the sort of attention that comes from years of practice and genuine enthusiasm, and doesn't stop when I tell her not to.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline didn't break the cadence for a fraction of a second. With his fingers wound securely in her hair, she maintained the slow, exacting pace, completely devoted to the task. 

Her hands stroked upward along his thighs, steady and warm, grounding him while she drew out every movement with deliberate care. There was no urgency in her work, only an unwavering, practiced focus aimed at keeping him suspended in that deep, heavy pleasure. 

She kept her gaze fixed on him whenever she could, drinking in the sight of him undone and leaning back in the chair. Every shift of her lips and the steady heat of her mouth offered an absolute, tireless dedication, content to stay right where she was for as long as he desired, thriving under the quiet gravity of his control.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I tighten my grip in her hair, pulling just enough to make her pause. "Look at me." My voice is rough, but satisfied. "You've done well."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline paused the instant she felt the tension in her hair, yielding effortlessly to the pull and tilting her face up to meet his gaze without a second of hesitation. 

Hearing the words she had asked for—delivered in that low, rough tone of absolute satisfaction—sent a deep, radiant warmth straight through her chest. Her breath hitched softly, her lips parted and flushed, a faint, exquisitely contented smile softening the corners of her mouth. 

She kept her hands resting firmly against the warmth of his thighs, anchoring herself to him while she basked in the weight of his approval. Her dark eyes were bright with steady, glowing devotion, drinking in every line of his face.

"Thank you, Roan," she murmured, her voice quiet and rich with pure, unhurried satisfaction. She leaned just slightly into the grip he still held on her hair, offering herself completely to whatever he wanted next. "Tell me you're ready for more."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Don't stop and don't get to finish," I tell her. "Not until I say. Tell me you understand." She says she understands, and thanks me for it, which is exactly the arrangement.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The condition settled over her like a familiar, grounding weight, clarifying everything down to a single, uncomplicated purpose. The denial wasn’t a deprivation; it was an anchor, narrowing her world until there was nothing left to consider except his pleasure and the steady work of her hands and mouth.

With his permission granted to continue, Aveline lowered her head once more, resuming the slow, rhythmic cadence without a hitch. Her hands remained warm and steady against his thighs, anchoring him as she gave herself entirely back over to the task. 

She worked with the practiced, seamless ease of complete devotion, drawing out every movement with deliberate care. The knowledge that her own release was withheld only deepened her focus, turning every breath and every shift of friction into an act of sustained reverence, perfectly content to stay suspended beneath him for as long as he commanded.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, watching her work with that same unhurried focus. "Good girl," I murmur, my thumb stroking her temple. "Just like that."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The quiet praise washed over her, sinking in deep and steady, settling beneath her ribs like a warm, familiar weight. She leaned imperceptibly into the stroke of his thumb against her temple, acknowledging the touch with a subtle, yielding tilt of her head before re-centering all her focus on the rhythm he had approved.

Knowing she had it right—that she was giving him precisely the slow, heavy undoing he wanted—only sharpened her dedication. Aveline didn't speed up; she stayed faithful to the agonizingly thorough cadence, using the heat of her mouth and the steady pressure of her hands to keep him suspended right where he wanted to be. 

She tilted her gaze upward beneath dark lashes, watching the line of his jaw and the quiet intensity of his expression in the dim light. A soft, muffled sound of pure contentment hummed in her throat, her entire being completely absorbed in the privilege of his attention and the simple, grounding clarity of doing exactly what was asked of her.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She's shaking with the effort of doing exactly as told and doing it well. "Please," she says, which is allowed. (OOC: write it through, don't fade.)

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The tremor ran fine and continuous through her shoulders down into her hands where they gripped his thighs, the physical reality of the denial vibrating just beneath her skin. But Aveline did not falter, nor did she let the trembling disrupt the slow, deliberate mastery of her rhythm.

The single word—breathed against him like an offering rather than a demand—hung in the warm air between them. It was the only indulgence she allowed herself, an admission of just how completely strung out and consumed she was by the heat of the room and the weight of his command.

She took him deeper, letting the warmth and wetness of her mouth envelop him with steady, unbroken pressure, her tongue working in slow, agonizingly thorough sweeps that left no part of him untouched. Every shift of her jaw, every controlled slide of her lips was an exercise in pure devotion, deliberately drawn out to keep him right on the edge of unbearable pleasure.

"Fine," he said. "You want to watch me work." His hand tightened at Kit's hip, dragging him forward off the wall entirely, into the solid line of him. "Let's see how long the audience lasts before it wants a piece too."

He got a hand under Kit's jaw, tilted his head with no argument at all, and kissed him — not soft, nothing about tonight had been soft — teeth involved before lips were done, biting Kit's lower lip just to feel him make that sound he made, half complaint, half want. Bear pulled back an inch, watched Kit chase it, and grinned wider.

"Yeah," he murmured. "Thought so." His other hand slid down, gripping the back of Kit's thigh, hitching it up against his hip like it belonged there. "Bedroom's a long way off from here. You planning on walking, or should I just carry the prize back myself?"

dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went down with him, one hand cushioning the back of Kit's skull out of eight years of reflex before the floor even mattered — the rest of it wasn't gentle at all. He got Kit's shirt half up and gave up on finesse, just hauled it over his head and let Kit finish yanking it off while Bear worked his own belt with the kind of impatience that ended up costing him thirty seconds fumbling instead of saving any.

"Hate this part," he muttered, meaning the buttons, meaning the fabric, meaning anything standing between him and skin. He got Kit's jeans shoved down to the thigh and decided that was good enough, that was *plenty* good enough, and used the leverage to drag Kit half into his lap, knees on either side of him, weight settling down slow and deliberate right where Kit would feel it most.

"There," he said, voice gone rough, hands spread wide over Kit's ribs like he was taking inventory — the new bite already darkening at his throat, the old marks further down that hadn't quite faded from last week. "That's better."

He caught Kit's mouth again, less teeth this time and more heat, one hand sliding down to grip Kit's hip hard enough to bruise while the other braced flat against the floor, holding his own weight so Kit could feel exactly how much of him there was without getting crushed by it. He rolled his hips once, testing, watching Kit's face for the exact second his breath caught.

"You started this in the kitchen," Bear said against his jaw, low and pleased with himself. "Don't you dare tell me now you didn't want the floor."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I hook a foot behind his knee to pull him closer. "Shut up and keep going," I say, biting his shoulder. "We'll see who complains first."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear grunted at the bite, felt it land sharp enough to leave its own mark, and answered it with a low laugh that had teeth in it too. "Complains first," he repeated, rolling his hips again, harder this time, no testing about it now. "Kit, you talk more during sex than anyone I've ever met. You're gonna lose that bet on principle."

He got a hand between them, made short, efficient work of what was left in the way, and when skin finally met skin without anything between it he felt Kit's whole body go tight under him — felt it in the leg still hooked behind his knee, pulling, in the way Kit's back arched off the floor like he couldn't help it.

"There," Bear said again, rougher now, quieter, all the joking gone thin around the edges. He pushed in slow, watching Kit's face the whole way, cataloguing every flicker of it like he always did — the way Kit's mouth fell open on a breath he clearly meant to keep quiet and didn't manage.

"Yeah," Bear murmured, satisfied, settling deep and staying there a beat too long just to feel Kit squirm under him. "That's one."

He started moving — no more slow about it, no more testing, just eight years of knowing exactly what worked and using every bit of it. He caught Kit's wrists and pinned them to the floor above his head, more for the way Kit strained against it than because he needed to, and leaned down to catch the shell of his ear.

"Go on then," Bear said, breath ragged now, hips setting a rhythm that didn't leave much room for talking. "Bite something else. See if that shuts *you* up before it shuts me up."

dialogue.name: Kit

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear obliged — sank his teeth in again, same spot, deeper, pulling a sound out of Kit that went straight through him like a live wire. He held it a beat longer this time, felt Kit buck up underneath him, wrists still pinned and straining against his grip, and only let go when the taste of it — sweat and skin and the faint metal edge of *too hard* — registered enough to pull him back from doing real damage.

"Christ," he breathed against the mark, voice wrecked around the edges now. "You're gonna make me lose count."

He didn't slow down. If anything the rhythm got rougher, less controlled, the kind of thing that only happened when eight years of practiced restraint finally gave up trying to be careful — because Kit didn't want careful, never had, and Bear had stopped pretending otherwise a long time ago. His grip on Kit's wrists tightened, grinding them into the floor, and he used the new leverage to drive deeper, harder, chasing the exact angle that made Kit's whole body go rigid under him.

"Say it," Bear ground out, mouth back at Kit's ear, teeth grazing without biting this time, just a promise of it. "Tell me who's losing this bet."

He felt Kit's answer more than heard it — some ragged half-word swallowed by a gasp — and Bear grinned against his throat even as his own control started fraying at the seams, hips losing their rhythm to something rawer, closer to the edge than he'd meant to admit yet.

"Yeah," he rasped, releasing one wrist just to drag his hand down Kit's side, gripping hip hard enough to bruise, hard enough to leave his whole handprint there by morning. "That's what I thought."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I gasp, arching up against him, and manage to get one hand free. I drag my nails down his back. "You are," I get out, breathless. "You're already losing."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The nails dragging down his back pulled a sound out of Bear he wouldn't have admitted to sober — something between a growl and a groan, low in his chest, and he pressed his forehead to Kit's shoulder for a second just to ride it out.

"Losing," he repeated, breath ragged, "that's—" He didn't finish the sentence, lost it somewhere in the next thrust, harder than the last, chasing that place where Kit's whole body went taut underneath him. "Say that again when you're not shaking."

But Kit *was* shaking, he could feel it, feel the tremor starting low and building, and Bear chased it deliberately now, angle and rhythm both dialed toward wrecking whatever was left of Kit's composure before his own gave out. He got the freed hand pinned again, both wrists gathered in one grip this time, using the other to hook under Kit's knee and drag it higher, deeper, no mercy in it at all.

"Eight years," he ground out, voice gone rough as gravel, "and I still—" He bit off another sound, teeth finding the curve of Kit's neck again, not breaking skin this time, just pressure, just claiming. "Still can't get enough of you falling apart first."

He felt it happen — felt Kit go rigid and then loose all at once, heard the sound that came out of him when it hit, and that was what did it, that was always what did it. Bear followed a handful of thrusts later, control finally shredding, forehead dropping to Kit's collarbone as his whole body locked and shuddered through it, hips stuttering to a slow, uneven stop.

For a long moment neither of them moved. Bear's breath came hard against Kit's skin, his grip on Kit's wrists gone slack but not letting go yet, like he needed a second before he trusted his own hands.

"Okay," he finally muttered, voice wrecked, half a laugh in it. "Maybe I lost that one." He lifted his head just enough to look at Kit — flushed, marked up, grinning even now — and pressed a kiss to the new bruise blooming at his throat like an apology that wasn't really one. "Don't let it go to your head. Floor's hell on my knees. I want a rematch somewhere with a mattress."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went still for a second, looking down at Kit's wrists offered up like that — open, easy, trust so casual it didn't even look like trust anymore, just habit, eight years deep. Something about that got him harder than the sex had, low in his chest, quiet and fierce.

"Thursday," he said, considering it like a job with a deadline. "That's ambitious." He took one wrist in hand, turned it over, thumb pressing along the soft skin where the pulse still hadn't settled all the way down. "You want it to hurt when you're at your desk. Want to feel it every time you reach for your coffee."

Not a question. He already knew the answer — knew Kit, knew what *hurt on Thursday* actually meant, which was *proof, something to touch, something that says this happened and it mattered.*

He bent his head and bit down at the inside of Kit's wrist first — careful about the vein, never careless there, but not gentle either — held it until Kit's breath caught, then moved. Shoulder again, deeper into the mark already blooming there. The other side of his throat, opposite the first bite, so Kit would have to turn his head twice tomorrow to see it all. A spot low on his ribs that made Kit's whole body jump.

"There," Bear murmured, working methodically now, unhurried, cataloguing his own handiwork with real satisfaction. "That one's for Tuesday. This one's Wednesday." Another bite, slower, deliberate. "This is Thursday's."

He pulled back to survey it — the collection of it, teeth marks and bruises rising already, Kit wrecked and marked and grinning up at him like he'd asked for exactly this and gotten more.

"Eight years," Bear said, voice gone soft and rough at once, pressing one last kiss just above the darkest mark, "and you still gotta *ask.* Like I wasn't already gonna."

He gathered Kit up against his chest, floor be damned, no rush to move yet. "Mirror tomorrow," he said. "You're gonna love it. I already do."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I let him pull me against him, my face buried in his shoulder. My whole body aches already and I can feel the places he left marks starting to throb. "Good," I mumble into his skin. "Now get us off this damn floor. Your knees are older than mine."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear huffed a laugh against the top of Kit's head. "My knees are fine. It's my dignity that's shot, lying here on the hallway floor like a couple of teenagers who couldn't wait for a bed."

He didn't move right away, though — just held on a moment longer, one hand tracing slow, absent circles over the small of Kit's back, feeling the occasional shiver still working its way out of him.

"Alright," he said finally, "up we go. Try not to enjoy this next part too much."

He shifted, got an arm under Kit's knees and the other around his back, and just hauled him up off the floor entirely — no ceremony, no warning, straight into a fireman-adjacent carry that had absolutely nothing dignified about it. Kit made a sound of protest that Bear ignored completely.

"Eight years and you still weigh nothing," he said, grunting only a little as he got upright, joints popping in complaint that he'd deny to his grave. "Bed's this way, in case you forgot, what with the detour."

He carried him down the hall like that, unbothered by the fact that they were both still half-dressed and thoroughly marked up, and dumped Kit onto the mattress with more care than the grumbling suggested — settling him down gentle even as he grinned like a man very pleased with his night's work.

"There," Bear said, climbing in after and pulling Kit against his chest, tucking him in against the ache like he always did once the fight was good and finished. "Now you can bruise in comfort. I'm a generous man."

Bear was already half awake — had been for a while, actually, lying there with one arm slung over Kit and doing his own quiet inventory of the damage. The shove barely registered as anything but confirmation that Kit was, in fact, still alive and mobile, which given last night wasn't nothing.

"Inventory," he repeated, voice all gravel from sleep, not moving yet except to crack one eye open at the sunlight doing exactly what Kit said — lighting up every mark like it was showing off on Bear's behalf. "You say that like I'm not gonna want a look too."

He did look, then, properly — pushed himself up on one elbow and took his time about it, tracing the line of bruises down Kit's shoulder to the darker one at his ribs with something that wasn't quite pride and wasn't quite guilt, mostly just satisfaction, plain and simple.

"That one's holding up nice," he said, thumb brushing just shy of actually touching the worst of it. "Told you Thursday. This is barely Tuesday and it's already gone that color."

Kit shoved at him again — coffee, now, the demand hadn't gone anywhere — and Bear laughed, low and rough, and finally hauled himself upright, joints announcing their opinion about the floor last night with a series of pops he pretended not to notice.

"Fine, fine." He stood, stretched until his spine cracked too, and glanced back over his shoulder at Kit sprawled there taking his own inventory with a grin that said he was pleased with the results. "Stay put. Don't go counting without me — I want credit for all of them."
