"Wasn't planning on it," Bear muttered, his voice dropping into a thick, dark rasp against Kit’s ear.

He finally let go of Kit's wrists, but only to slide his broad hands down, blunt fingers hooking hard behind Kit's thighs. In one rough, unyielding shift of muscle, Bear hauled Kit's hips straight off the floorboards, tilting them up to meet him and spreading them wide as he settled heavy and unrelenting between their legs. 

There was nothing gentle about the way he pushed forward. Bear aligned himself and drove in deep, a slow, punishing press of heat and friction that filled Kit completely. He let out a low, shuddering groan as he buried himself to the hilt, the sheer tightness and familiarity of it hitting him like a physical blow. 

He didn't give Kit time to adjust. Bear dropped his full upper-body weight back down, pressing Kit flat against the rug until his chest pinned theirs, chest hair scraping against bare, bitten skin. He locked his mouth onto Kit’s in a bruising, reckless kiss, swallowing whatever sound came out of them as his tongue tangled with theirs, wet and demanding.

Beneath them, the floorboards groaned under the strain. Bear set a brutal, heavy pace, pulling back just enough before driving all the way in again, his hips snapping forward with a relentless, rhythmic force that rocked Kit back against the wood. 

One of Bear's hands stayed clamped around Kit's hip, fingers digging into the flesh hard enough to guarantee another set of purple fingerprints, while his other hand came up to tangle tight in Kit's hair, keeping their mouths locked together. Every thrust was deep, solid, and deliberate, Bear using every pound of his bulk to take what they both wanted until the air in the hallway was thick with the sound of skin hitting skin and their ragged, tangled breathing.

He broke the kiss only to drag his mouth down to Kit's jaw again, his stubble grinding into the fresh marks on their neck. 

"Look at me," Bear rasped, his hips driving in hard, fast, and heavy, surging against Kit without mercy. "Kit. Eyes on me."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I drag my eyes open, meeting his gaze. "I am." My voice is wrecked. I sink my teeth into his shoulder, hard.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The sharp, punishing sink of Kit's teeth into his shoulder didn't make Bear pull away; it made him lean straight into the bite with a ragged, guttural snarl that vibrated deep in his throat. 

The pain was clean, hot, and electric, cutting through the haze of friction and heat like a match to dry brush. Bear welcomed the sting, his jaw clenching tight as he drove his hips forward with brutal, renewed momentum, burying himself deep enough to knock the breath clean out of his own lungs. 

"That's it," Bear growled, his voice completely wrecked, thick and dark. "Take a piece of it."

His grip in Kit’s hair tightened, anchoring their face right there against the crook of his neck, letting Kit feel every hard, frantic swallow and the heavy surge of his pulse against their tongue. With his other hand, Bear grabbed Kit’s thigh and hauled it high over his waist, opening them up completely to take the full, punishing brunt of his weight. 

He didn't hold back the pace anymore. Bear hammered into Kit with heavy, relentless strokes, the wood beneath them groaning under the violent, rocking rhythm. Sweat slicked the line of his spine, dripping down onto Kit’s chest as he pushed them both closer to the edge, his breathing coming in rough, jagged heaves. 

He reached down between them, his calloused thumb finding Kit and pressing in with a firm, demanding friction that matched the punishing rhythm of his hips. 

"Right here," Bear rasped against Kit’s temple, his stubble grinding raw against their skin, eyes burning dark and dilated as he watched every flicker of sensation cross their face. He bared his teeth, surging in harder, faster, driving for the finish with everything he had. "Don't you dare look away."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I bite down harder, a muffled groan vibrating against his skin. My nails dig into his back, dragging down hard as I tip over the edge, my whole body tightening around him. "Bear—"

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The violent clench of Kit’s body around him, paired with the sharp scrape of nails dragging down his spine, shattered whatever control Bear had left. 

A strangled, guttural roar tore out of his chest, rough and unchecked. Bear surged forward with two more brutal, heavy drives, slamming his hips against Kit’s with enough force to rattle the floorboards before burying himself completely to the hilt. 

He locked his arms around Kit, hauling them clean off the rug and crushing them flush against his chest as his own release tore through him. His whole frame seized, every corded muscle in his back and shoulders locking rigid. He buried his face in the crook of Kit's neck, his teeth scraping blindly over the fresh, swelling bite there as he rode out the heavy, shuddering pulse of coming completely undone. 

He didn't pull back. Bear rode the violent tremor of it until his legs gave out entirely, collapsing his full, dead weight right on top of Kit, pinning them solid into the hard floor. 

For a long minute, the only sound in the hallway was the ragged, wet rasp of Bear’s breathing and the frantic, echoing hammer of his heart knocking against Kit’s ribs. Sweat dripped from his brow, pooling hot between their chests. 

Slowly, heavily, Bear turned his head, his stubble dragging like sandpaper across Kit's jaw. He pressed an open-mouthed, exhausted kiss into the hollow under Kit's ear, tasting salt and copper, before letting out a low, gravelly rumble that vibrated right through the floorboards beneath them. 

One of his broad, heavy hands slid down from Kit’s back, fingers trailing over the fresh red scratches Kit had carved into his skin, before dropping with a dull slap onto Kit’s hip. His thumb pressed deliberately into the blossoming purple bruise over the bone, testing the ache with a slow, wicked pressure.

"Thursday," Bear rasped, his voice completely wrecked and thick with satisfaction. He dragged his heavy eyelids open, his dark gaze locking onto Kit's with an exhausted, predatory smirk. "You'll be lucky if you're walking right by Saturday."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath, my body still humming. "That's the point." I shift a little under him, wincing. "Rug burn, though. That's new."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline had been waiting since about six, which Roan established by the simple method of looking at her.

"How long?"

"Long enough," Aveline said, which meant too long, and meant she had enjoyed every minute of it.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Come here, then," I say, and sit back to watch her cross the room.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
She went, and she took her time about it — not stalling, just aware that she'd been given something to do and that doing it well was the whole point. Four steps, maybe five, across the rug she'd straightened that afternoon. She had thought about the dress for longer than she'd admit and had settled on the grey one because Roan had once said something offhand about the way it caught at her waist, and Aveline filed things like that away the way other people saved receipts.

Her hands wanted to do something. She let them hang, then let them find the hem of the dress, then decided that was fidgeting and stopped.

"You were later than you said," she observed, arriving. Not a complaint. She sank down onto her heels at the side of the chair, one hand settling on Roan's knee with the ease of long habit, thumb finding the seam of the trouser leg. "The kettle's been boiled twice. I drank the first one. It seemed a waste."

She tipped her head back to look up, and there it was — that expression she never managed to hide and had long ago stopped trying to, the bright uncomplicated pleasure of being looked at by the person she wanted to be looked at by. Six o'clock to now, sitting with her book unread in her lap, listening for the car. She'd liked the waiting. That was the embarrassing part, the part she'd never once been able to make sound dignified out loud. The waiting was half of it.

"You've had a day," she said, quieter. Her hand moved to the top of Roan's shoe, testing the lace. "Let me. I've been thinking about it since about half six and my thinking's gone in circles, so you'll have to just tell me where to start."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I reach down to brush a strand of hair from her forehead. "Start with the shoes," I say, my voice low. "And then work your way up."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The touch to her forehead landed like a coin dropped in a well — she felt it go all the way down. She turned her face very slightly into it, just enough to be caught doing it, and then bent to the work.

The laces first. She had strong hands and she used them carefully, which was a thing Roan had once called out and which she had never forgotten: *you're gentle on purpose.* Left shoe, the knot pulled loose, the tongue eased back, the heel cupped in her palm so the shoe came away without any tug at the ankle. She set it down beside the chair leg, upright, aligned. Then the right, the same, and the pair stood together like something in a shop window.

"Your sock's gone through at the toe," she reported, thumb passing over the thin place. "I'll deal with it. Don't argue with me about it, I like darning, it's very restful."

She took the left foot in both hands and pressed her thumbs into the arch, and Roan's breath changed, and Aveline felt that change land in her chest with an entirely disproportionate glow. There. That was the whole thing, right there. Not the dress or the kneeling or the careful straight pair of shoes — just the sound of somebody putting down a weight.

She worked up through the ankle, unhurried. Trouser cuff turned back twice so she could get at the calf, the muscle there knotted hard from too many hours standing. She leaned into it with the heel of her hand and heard Roan swear softly and grinned down at her own hands like an idiot.

"Keep going?" she asked, though she was already going. "You said work my way up. I'm taking that as licence but you can revoke it whenever you like."

Her hair had come forward again and she couldn't spare a hand for it, so she left it, and knelt there in the lamplight with someone's foot in her lap and her whole body loose with the pleasure of having been given something to do, and done it right.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let her kneel and I don't tell her to do anything for a moment, because the waiting is most of what she came for.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The silence went on, and Aveline understood it immediately for what it was.

She kept her hands moving — the calf, the long tendon behind the knee, small circles with her knuckles where the muscle gave — but she stopped talking, which for her was the larger offering. Roan had said nothing. Roan was simply sitting there letting her, and the letting was deliberate, and she knew the shape of that particular generosity well enough to recognise it the way you recognise a hand on the back of your neck in the dark.

So she settled. Her shoulders came down. Somewhere in the flat the radiator ticked and the second kettle went on cooling on its stand, unwanted now, and the lamp made a warm island of the chair and the rug and her own bare knees pressed into the pile.

This was the part she couldn't explain at parties. Not that she'd ever tried. *What do you do?* — and the honest answer was *I sit at the side of a chair and I am not told anything for a while, and it's the best fifteen minutes of my week.* She'd once got about four words into the attempt with an old university friend and had swerved into talking about gardening instead.

Her thumb found the ankle bone again and circled it, slower now, drifting, because the pressure didn't matter as much as the continuing. Continuing was the point. She had been given a length of time and permission to fill it, and she filled it patiently, and the whole while her attention was tuned so finely upward that she could have reported on every breath Roan took.

Eventually — because she was devoted but she was not a saint — she turned her cheek and rested it against the inside of Roan's knee. Just rested it. A small unauthorised liberty, taken openly, where it would be seen.

"I'm not asking for anything," she murmured, which was a lie of a very specific and well-worn kind, the sort they both enjoyed. Her eyes stayed closed. "I've got my hands full."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I smile, letting the silence stretch a moment longer before I finally speak. "Your hands are never full enough to keep you from asking." I trail my fingers along the line of her jaw. "Up. Off the floor."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The laugh came out of her before she could dress it up as anything else — caught, and delighted to be caught, because being known was the thing she'd signed up for and she had never once managed to resent the accuracy.

"No," she admitted, "they're not."

She didn't bolt up. She never did; there was a way to do this and she had learned it a long time ago, partly from being corrected and mostly from wanting to be watched doing it well. She set Roan's foot down on the rug with the same care she'd have used on something borrowed. She turned the trouser cuff back down, smoothed it flat with two fingers, nudged the pair of shoes a half-inch truer to the chair leg although they had been true already. Then one hand to the arm of the chair, weight through her knee, and she came up in a single unhurried movement and stood.

The floor had left its pattern pressed into her shins. She could feel the blood going back into her feet and she stood through it without shifting, hands loose at her sides, hair still forward over one eye where she'd left it and now conscious of it, wanting very much to be told about it one way or the other.

"Off the floor," she repeated, as if confirming the terms. Her voice had gone lower and slightly unsteady, the way it did when she had been quiet for a while and then had to speak. "Right. Yes."

The grey dress had creased across the thighs from kneeling. She glanced down at it, resisted the urge to smooth it, and then decided that resisting was its own sort of fidget and pressed both palms down the front of the skirt once, briskly, the way she'd have straightened a tablecloth.

"For the record," she said, lifting her chin, "the kettle's still warm and there's food that wants twelve minutes, and I'd like to be told which of those matters before I start guessing. Because I will guess." She held Roan's eyes and let the whole bright unguarded thing show in her face, since hiding it had never worked. "I'm terrible at standing still with nothing to do. You know this about me. You've built entire evenings on it."

But she stayed where she'd been put, hands at her sides, waiting.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She has both of us out of everything in the way inside a minute and gets straight to work with her hands and her mouth, unhurried about it.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Clothes were a solved problem, as far as Aveline was concerned. She had never understood people who made a production of it. The grey dress went over the back of the chair where it wouldn't crease worse than it already had, and everything else went where it went, and she gave none of it more than the half-second of attention it deserved, because there were better things in the room to look at.

Then she got her hands on Roan properly and the rest of the evening simplified enormously.

She took her time. That was the only real skill she claimed — not technique, not invention, just the willingness to stay somewhere for as long as it was working, which she had found to be a rarer quality than anyone advertised. She listened with her hands. A breath caught, and she stayed. A shift of weight, and she adjusted. She had a whole private catalogue built up over years and she consulted it the way a pianist consults nothing at all, and she kept her eyes open because she wanted to see, and when she looked up and found Roan already looking back at her she made a small sound against skin that was not language and did not need to be.

"Yes," she said, to a hand in her hair. "That. Keep it there."

She was not quiet. She had tried being quiet, early on, under some inherited notion that servants were meant to be unobtrusive, and Roan had asked her to stop it in about the plainest terms available, and she had been grateful ever since to be let off the pretence. So she said what she noticed, and she asked when she wasn't sure, and she took correction without a flicker and often with a grin, and the whole thing had the shape of work she loved rather than work she performed.

Somewhere in it her own body made its case, loudly, and she set it politely aside for later. Later was fine. Later was, in fact, most of the appeal.

When it was over she stayed exactly where she was for a while, cheek against Roan's hip, breathing.

"Don't say anything clever," she murmured eventually. "I want the plain version."

She got the plain version, and it went through her like a hot drink on a cold day, and she shut her eyes and let it. *Good.* Four letters, no ornament. There was no compliment in the English language that landed on her harder and she had stopped being embarrassed about that somewhere around year two.

Then she stirred, and lifted her head, and pushed her hair back with the back of her wrist, and became brisk again — because the brisk and the other thing were not separate in her, never had been.

"Eleven minutes," she said, kissing Roan's knee on her way up. "I've been counting. Stay there. I'll bring it in and we can eat it on the rug like animals, and then I want the story of your day in full, including the bit you were going to leave out." She was already halfway to the kitchen, entirely unbothered about being unclothed in her own home. "And I'm finding those socks. Don't think the darning's off the table. It absolutely is not off the table."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Bring the food. Leave the socks," I say, stretching out in the chair. "And get back here in under eleven minutes."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
"Under eleven," Aveline called back from the kitchen, over the sound of the oven door. "That's a challenge, and you know I take those personally."

She did it in nine. She would have liked it on record that she did it in nine, and she said so, coming back in with the tray held against her hip and a tea towel over her shoulder like a woman who had never once in her life been off duty. Two plates. The good forks, because she had decided years ago that the good forks were for Tuesdays as much as anything else and Roan had never contradicted her. Bread, torn rather than cut, because the knife was somewhere she couldn't be bothered to look and the clock was running.

"Socks left," she reported, setting the tray down on the rug and dropping to sit cross-legged beside it. "Under protest. I'd like it noted that the protest exists and is ongoing."

She nudged the nearer plate towards the chair and then, thinking better of it, picked it up and held it out, which was less about service than about the small selfish pleasure of the handover — the brush of fingers, the weight going from her hand to Roan's. She'd take that transaction a hundred times an evening if it were offered.

Then she ate, properly and with appetite, one knee drawn up, the tea towel abandoned over the arm of the chair. She was pink across the chest and along the jaw and hadn't bothered to do anything about her hair, and she felt magnificent, and she was aware that she looked it and that being aware was allowed.

Halfway through she pointed her fork at Roan.

"Right. The day. From the top." She chewed, swallowed, narrowed her eyes. "And I'll know when you get to the bit you were planning to skip, because you do a thing with your voice. You go smooth. You've gone smooth about three times in the last fortnight and I've let all three go, so consider the account settled and start talking."

She reached over without looking and rested her hand on Roan's ankle — the same foot, the thin place in the sock warm under her thumb — and left it there, an anchor rather than a request.

"Plain version," she added, softer, echoing herself. "I'm good at the plain version. You've said so."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She uses her mouth with the sort of attention that comes from years of practice and genuine enthusiasm, and doesn't stop when I tell her not to.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The plates got shoved aside — not stacked, not carried out, simply moved far enough that neither of them would put a knee in the remains, which for Aveline was an act of almost scandalous domestic abandon and she registered it as such and did it anyway.

"Story's not finished," she said, into the inside of Roan's thigh. "I'm holding you to the rest of it. Just — later."

She had meant to be brief about it. She had genuinely meant it, in the way she always genuinely meant it, as an intention held sincerely right up to the moment of contact and then quietly reclassified as fiction. There was a particular sound Roan made about forty seconds in, every time, for years, and Aveline had never once heard it without losing all interest in the rest of the evening's schedule.

She was not clever at this. That had been established long ago and had stopped stinging almost immediately, because what she had instead was better and they both knew it — she paid attention, and she did not get bored, and she never once in her life had been thinking about something else while she was doing it. The catalogue again. The long slow accumulation of a decade of noticing. She spent it freely and kept adding to it, and when Roan's hand closed in her hair she made a sound of such uncomplicated gratitude that she'd have been mortified to hear it played back.

Then came the instruction to stop.

Aveline heard it. She heard it perfectly well. She also heard the pitch it came out at, and the fact that the hand in her hair had tightened rather than pushed, and she had spent eleven years learning to tell the difference between the words and the truth, and this was the one dereliction she permitted herself in the whole architecture of what they did. She hummed something that might have been agreement and carried on, slower, insufferably unhurried, absolutely without mercy.

Later she would apologise for it. She would do it properly, too, with her eyes up and no grin in evidence, and mean it, and she would offer the correction to Roan's hands and take whatever came of it with the same bright appetite she took everything.

Not yet, though.

When it finally broke she stayed where she was through all of it, hands flat and steady on Roan's hips, riding it out, greedy in the only way she'd ever managed to be greedy — for the evidence, the noise, the proof that the weight had gone down. She didn't move until the grip in her hair loosened. Then she rested her forehead against the crease of Roan's thigh and breathed, and her whole body rang like a struck glass, and she thought, with the last coherent part of herself: *there. That's it. That's the entire thing.*

"I know," she said eventually, hoarse, not lifting her head. "I know. You said stop."

She turned her face up at last, mouth wrecked, hair ruined, looking so thoroughly pleased with herself that it verged on a confession.

"I'll take it however you want to give it," she said. "Tonight, tomorrow, whenever you can be bothered. I'd only ask that you don't let it go, because I'll be smug about it for a week and neither of us wants that."

Then, shifting up onto her knees, one hand finding Roan's, lacing fingers without asking:

"Chair or bed?" A kiss to the knuckles, absent, automatic, eleven years deep. "Say bed. I'll do the plates in the morning. I'll do the plates and you can tell me the smooth-voiced bit over the coffee, and I'll be so appalling about it that you'll wish you'd told me in the chair."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content:
I study her face for a long moment, the wreck of her, the open smugness. It’s a better view than any I’ve had all day.

"Bed," I say, pulling her up by our linked hands. "But you're doing the plates now. I'll watch."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline came up off the rug on the pull of Roan's hands and made a noise of pure betrayal.

"*Now,*" she said. "You absolute — " She stopped, because she had heard herself, and because the second half of the sentence had been going to be a compliment anyway. "Right. Yes. Now."

She gathered the plates. She did it properly, because she did not have another way of doing it: the two plates stacked with the forks laid across the top, the torn heel of bread saved onto the smaller one rather than binned, the tray taken up in both hands and not balanced on her hip, since she was being watched and there was no sense doing it badly in front of an audience. The tea towel came off the arm of the chair on her way past. Everything about her from the shoulders up was the picture of a woman going about her business, and everything below that was still flushed and unclothed and shaking very slightly in the thighs, and she knew exactly which of those two things Roan was looking at.

The kitchen light was worse than the lamp. She put it on anyway, and ran the tap, and stood there in the flat bright overhead glare with the water going warm over her wrists, entirely on display in her own kitchen at half past nine at night, and understood with perfect clarity that she was being made to stand still with something to do — which was not a punishment at all, and was very nearly a joke at her expense, and she was so fond of Roan in that moment that she had to put a plate down.

"You're enjoying this," she said, not turning round.

She washed up. Two plates, two forks, the small pan, the mixing spoon she'd left in the sink at six and forgotten about during the long good hour of listening for the car. She rinsed each thing and set it in the rack the right way up, and wiped the counter, and wrung the cloth out and hung it over the tap, and all of it took perhaps four minutes and she made it last a little longer than that, because she was not stupid and she knew when she was being looked at well.

Her hair was stuck to her temple. She pushed it back with a wet wrist and got it wetter, and gave up.

Then she turned round, and leaned back against the counter with her palms behind her on the edge, and the brisk fell off her all at once the way it did about four times a year.

"I'm sorry about the stopping," she said. Plainly. No grin anywhere in evidence, which for her was the whole of the gesture. "You said it and I made a decision about it, and the decision was mine to make and it wasn't. I'd like it dealt with and I don't want to be the one who decides how, because I'll go soft on myself. I always do." A beat. "And I'll do it again. Probably. I'm telling you now so you can factor it in."

She let that sit in the kitchen light for as long as it needed to sit, which was the part she had spent years learning and still found hard — not filling it, not sanding the edges off it, just letting it be true and out loud between them.

Then she reached over and put the light off, and the room went back to the warm dark spilling in from the lamp in the other room, and she came away from the counter and held out her hand.

"Bed," she said. "You're walking. I've done the plates." She caught Roan's fingers and turned them over and kissed the palm, once, the way she'd have signed a receipt. "And I want the smooth-voiced bit in the dark where you can't see my face, because you'll tell it better, and I'll be appalling about it in the morning as promised."

She led the way, and stopped at the chair to collect the grey dress off the back of it and fold it over her arm, because leaving it there all night would have been a step too far even for a woman who had just abandoned two plates on a rug.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Don't stop and don't get to finish," I tell her. "Not until I say. Tell me you understand." She says she understands, and thanks me for it, which is exactly the arrangement.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
She understood. She said so, out loud, twice — once because she meant it and once because the first time had come out as barely a word — and then she said thank you, which was not a formality and never had been. It was the plainest thing she owned. Roan had taken something she'd mishandled and handed it back to her as a job, and Aveline could not think of a kinder thing to do with a woman like her.

"That's fair," she said. "That's — yes. That's exactly fair."

The dress went over the footboard. She had a moment of wanting to hang it properly and let the want go, which was probably the first real concession of the night.

Then she gave herself over to it, and it was hard, and she was glad it was hard.

She had thought — early on, years ago, being naive about her own construction — that *not finishing* would be the difficult part. It wasn't. The difficult part was *not stopping*: the steady requirement to keep going while everything in her got louder and more insistent and more convinced that surely, surely, this was the bit where the rules bent. They did not bend. Roan did not bend them, and Aveline, who had bent one two hours ago and admitted it in a kitchen under a bad overhead light, found that she did not want them bent now. That was the whole architecture, and she had put a crack in it, and being made to hold it up with her own hands until told otherwise was as close to absolution as she was ever going to get in this life.

So she kept on. She said what she noticed, because that had been asked of her long ago and she had never been let off it. She said *please* at one point and meant nothing by it except the pressure of being full to the brim. She said *still going* when asked, and she was, and her voice had gone to pieces, and she kept her hands doing the work with the same unhurried competence she'd have brought to darning a sock, which she was aware was ridiculous and which was also, she suspected, the precise reason Roan had built the last eleven years around her.

She lost track of the time. She always did. Somewhere in it the radiator ticked again and the lamp in the other room went on burning for nobody and she thought, distantly, that she'd have to turn it off eventually, and then lost the thought entirely.

When it broke for Roan she stayed with it, and afterwards she lay very still with her heart going hard and her whole body strung tight as a wire and nothing at all resolved, and found herself close to laughing.

"I'm in an absolute state," she reported, into the dark, hoarse. "In case that wasn't clear from the outside." A breath. "And you were right to do it. I'd like that noted too. I'll be unbearable about all sorts of things but not about that."

She shifted closer, fitted her forehead against Roan's shoulder, and put one hand flat on Roan's chest — not asking. Anchoring. She had got very good, over the years, at holding a want open without pushing on it, and she knew that Roan knew the difference, and being trusted to know it was most of what she'd come home for at six o'clock.

"Not until you say," she said. "I've got that. It can be tomorrow. It can be Thursday, I don't care, I'll be insufferable and productive and I'll get the whole flat done." She turned her face slightly, and her voice dropped out of all its brightness. "Now the smooth-voiced bit. You promised. It's dark and you can't see my face and I'm in no condition to interrupt, so this is the best chance you're ever going to get."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I watch her in the dim light, her face turned up toward me, wrecked and wanting. "You want the smooth-voiced bit," I say, tracing the line of her cheekbone. "Even now."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
"Especially now," Aveline said.

She turned her cheek into the tracing hand, unhurried about it, the way a cat does when it has decided the matter is settled. Her heart was still going too fast and her thighs had that fine useless tremble in them and she was, by any reasonable measure, in no state to be having a conversation about anything. Which was the point, and she knew it was the point, and she suspected Roan had known it about an hour before she did.

"Because I'm no good to you at half six with a book in my lap," she said. "I sit there and I work out the shape of it from the sound of the car door and I've already decided what it is before you've got your coat off. I'm a menace like that. But right now I couldn't chase you round a sentence if you paid me." A breath went out of her, ragged, and she let it be heard. "I can't get clever. I can't get ahead of you. I can just lie here and hear it. That's the only condition I'm any use in and you've gone and put me in it, so."

She flattened her hand more deliberately on Roan's chest — still not asking, still only the anchor — and felt the ribs move under it, and found that she was counting the breaths without meaning to. Eleven years of listening for a change in someone's breathing and the habit had gone all the way down to the bone.

"Three times in a fortnight," she said, quieter. "The smooth voice. Once on the phone about your sister, once over the paper on Sunday, and once — I don't know when the third was. Friday. Something about work. I let them all go because you'd have told me to leave it if I'd gone at it head-on, and because I'd rather you handed it to me than I went digging for it."

Her thumb moved once on Roan's sternum and stopped.

"So hand it to me. Plain version. You don't have to make it tidy and you don't have to finish it tonight." She shut her eyes. "And if it's the sort of thing where there's nothing to be done about it, say that first, and I'll stop trying to think of what to do and just listen properly. I'm terrible at listening when I think there's a job in it."

She lay still in the dark and waited, which was the one skill she'd never had to be taught.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She's shaking with the effort of doing exactly as told and doing it well. "Please," she says, which is allowed. (OOC: write it through, don't fade.)

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
"Please," she said again, because it was allowed, and because it was the only word left in her that still worked.

She had thought she was past the worst of it. That was the joke of the whole business and she fell for it every time — there was always a point where the body seemed to level out, to find some plateau it could hold, and Aveline would think *there, that's manageable*, and then it would go on for another minute and the floor would drop out from under the thought entirely. She was well past that now. Her hand had stopped being an anchor and become something that simply gripped, and she made herself loosen it, and it gripped again.

"I'm still going," she said, unprompted, because it had been asked of her once years ago and she had never needed asking since. "I'm — yes. Still going."

It was hard. It was gloriously, ruinously hard, and every second of it was work, and work was the one language she had ever been fluent in. She held it the way she'd have held something heavy for someone at the top of a staircase: badly, shaking, absolutely not putting it down. Her breath had gone to nothing useful. Her hair was in her mouth. She had lost the thread of her own sentences somewhere around the point where Roan's hand had settled where it settled, and she was aware that the noises she was making were not dignified and could not be made dignified by anything short of a court order.

She did not stop. That was the whole of it. That was the entire content of her character in that moment, as far as she could tell: she did not stop, and she did not decide anything, and she waited to be told, and the waiting had teeth in it now instead of the soft comfortable teeth of six o'clock, and she found she loved it just the same. Perhaps more. She'd have hated to admit to more.

"You can leave it," she managed, at some point, to the dark. "Genuinely. I'm not — I'll hold it. I'll hold it as long as you like."

She meant it, which was the appalling part, and she suspected Roan heard that she meant it, which was how she came to be told, some unmeasurable stretch of time later, that she could.

She didn't, immediately. Not out of any cleverness — she simply couldn't make the turn fast enough, the same way you can't stop leaning on a door that's suddenly opened. Then the permission caught up with her body and went through it like a bell going off in a small room, and she came apart with no elegance whatsoever, both hands fisted in the sheet, saying something that began as *thank you* and lost its consonants about halfway through. It went on longer than it had any business going on. She was distantly embarrassed and entirely unwilling to do anything about it.

Afterwards she lay with her face against Roan's collarbone and shook, and let herself be held through the shaking, and did not try to speak for a good while, which was for her a kind of record.

"That's the plates done," she said eventually, into skin. "That's the plates, the socks, and my entire personality."

She got her breath back in stages. Her hand found its old place on Roan's chest and settled flat, the ribs moving under it, and she started counting the breaths again without meaning to and let herself be soothed by the arithmetic.

"Right," she said, quieter, all the brightness gone out of her voice and something steadier underneath it. "I'm no use to anyone now. Not a clever thought in my head, no plans, nothing to fix." A slow blink against the dark. "Which was the condition. Wasn't it. You put me here on purpose."

She turned her face up, though there was nothing to see.

"So go on. The smooth-voiced bit. I'm listening properly, I promise — and if there's nothing to be done, say so first, and I'll just hold on to you while you tell it."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let the silence stretch, my fingers still tracing her cheek. "The smooth-voiced bit is about the office," I say quietly. "They're sending me to Berlin for a month. Starting Thursday."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline didn't say anything for a while.

That was not a technique. She simply had nothing available — Roan had spent the last hour dismantling her specifically so that she couldn't get out in front of a sentence, and the dismantling had worked, and so the words *Berlin* and *a month* and *Thursday* went into her one at a time with nothing in the way to soften them.

Her hand stayed flat on Roan's chest. The ribs went on moving under it. She lost count of the breaths.

"Thursday," she said eventually. It came out very level, which surprised her. "That's two days."

She did the arithmetic anyway, because she couldn't help it and because it gave her somewhere to put the first thirty seconds. A month. Thirty-one days if it ran to the end of the month, which it would, these things always ran. Thirty-one days of the flat at six o'clock with nobody's car to listen for.

Something went through her chest then that she had not braced for and could not have braced for in the state she was in, and she pressed her face harder into Roan's collarbone and breathed through it and let it be heard, because pretending otherwise would have been the worst thing she could have done with it.

"Right," she said, thickly. "Nothing to be done about that, then. You did say I should ask about that bit first. I didn't ask."

She lay still. She did not start listing what she'd pack. She did not start on the socks. She wanted to very badly — she could feel the whole comfortable machinery of *jobs to do* trying to start up in her and take the weight off, and she recognised it for exactly what it was, and she put her hand on it and held it shut, which was harder than anything else she'd done that evening.

"I'm going to mind it," she said. "I want to say that once, properly, tonight, and then I'll be sensible about it for a month. But I'd rather you had it plainly from me the way you gave it plainly to me, so: I'm going to mind it a great deal, and the minding isn't a complaint and there's nothing you can do about it, and you're not to go smooth-voiced at me about it for two days because you think I can't carry it." A breath. "I can carry it. I held on for you for — I don't even know how long. I can hold a month."

Her thumb moved once on Roan's sternum.

"That's the bit that gets me, actually. Not Berlin." Her voice had gone quiet and steady, all the brightness burnt off it. "Three times in a fortnight you had this in your mouth and went smooth instead. You were sitting over the paper on Sunday with this in you and let me talk about the guttering." She turned her face up into the dark. "Don't do that. I'd rather have it early and badly than late and tidy. I'm not delicate, I'm just fond of you, and those look similar from the outside but they hold different amounts of weight."

She let it sit. Made herself let it sit, and not sand the edge off it, and not follow it with a joke — though the joke was right there and she could feel it queuing.

Then she shifted, and fitted herself closer along Roan's side, and got one arm over and settled, and gave up on dignity entirely.

"Tell me the rest of it," she said. "Why you. How long they've known. Whether it's the thing with the contracts or the other thing you don't think I understand — I do understand it, incidentally, I just let you explain it because you get lovely and animated." She shut her eyes. "And then in the morning I'll be unbearable and productive and I'll get your case done and find out what the flat's like and whether it's got a proper kitchen, because if it hasn't got a proper kitchen you'll live on sandwiches for a month and come back grey."

A pause.

"And the socks are back on the table. I'm sorry. Thursday changes the terms. You're not going to Berlin with a hole in your toe."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let out a breath, the first real one since I told her. "It's the contracts," I say, my hand stilling on her cheek. "They've known a week. I wanted to tell you after it was settled."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
"A week," Aveline said.

She turned the number over and found, to her mild surprise, that she wasn't going to do anything with it. A week ago was the Tuesday. A week ago she had come in from the shops and found Roan standing at the window with a cup of tea gone cold in one hand, and had said something about the price of onions, and had been answered. She could remember the exact quality of the answering. She had thought at the time: *tired.* She had made a shepherd's pie about it.

"Right," she said. "Yes. I can see where it went."

She had felt the breath go out of Roan — the real one, the first one, the kind she'd spent eleven years learning to listen for and had heard the beginning of tonight in an armchair with a shoe in her hands. That was the thing that decided it. Because she could have had the week; she could have taken it out and examined it and made a small careful case about it and been entirely within her rights, and Roan would have sat there and let her, and the breath would have gone back in and stayed in for the two days remaining.

Aveline had never in her life wanted to be right at that price.

"I'm not going to do anything about the week," she said. "I want you to know that's a decision and not just me being soft, because I'd like the credit." Her thumb moved once on Roan's sternum and stopped. "You were carrying it until it was settled. I know why. You do it so I don't have to hold something uncertain for seven days, and you're not wrong that I'd have been dreadful about it — I'd have had a spreadsheet by Thursday and a list of flats by Friday and you'd have had to manage me on top of managing them." She let out a breath of her own, unsteady. "I'd still rather have had it. But I'm not going to make you pay for having tried to spare me. That's a mug's game and we've both watched other people play it."

The hand on her cheek had gone still. She turned into it and stayed there.

"So. Settled." She said the word carefully, testing what it would hold. "Does that mean settled as in signed, or settled as in they've stopped asking? And do I get the terms, or is it one of those where you tell me in instalments to keep me quiet? Because I'd like the whole thing in one go, if it's going. I'm better with a full picture than with a nice one."

She didn't ask it hard. It came out the way she'd have asked what time he wanted eating — a job needing its dimensions.

"And then that's the end of it tonight," she said. "I mean that. You've told me the worst part and you got a breath out afterwards, and I'd like you to have about nine hours of not thinking about Berlin before you have to think about Berlin again. I'll do the thinking. It's the one thing I'm reliably better at than you and only because I enjoy it."

She shifted, got her arm more comfortably across, and settled her ear over the place where she could hear the heart going.

"Thirty-one days," she said, into the dark, quite matter-of-fact. "I'll ring you at six. Not to be tragic about it — because it's when I'd be listening for the car anyway, and I'd rather be doing something at six than not. You can tell me about the contracts and I'll tell you what the guttering's done. It'll be extremely boring and I'll look forward to it all day."

A pause. Her voice dropped.

"And I'll mind it. But I've just spent an hour finding out exactly how long I can hold something when you ask me to, so we both know the answer now, don't we."

She let her eyes close.

"Sleep. I've got you. Socks in the morning."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let her feel the weight of that decision for a long moment, my fingers finally moving to tuck that strand of hair behind her ear. "Settled as in signed. The terms are yours in the morning. You'll have the full picture."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: she settled. Her shoulders came down... This was the part she couldn't explain at parties... I sit at the side of a chair and I am not told anything for a while, and it's the best fifteen minutes of my week

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Then she got her hands on Roan properly and the rest of the evening simplified enormously. She took her time... She listened with her hands. A breath caught, and she stayed. A shift of weight, and she adjusted.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She hummed something that might have been agreement and carried on, slower, insufferably unhurried, absolutely without mercy

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She kept her hands doing the work with the same unhurried competence she'd have brought to darning a sock

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: she came apart with no elegance whatsoever, both hands fisted in the sheet, saying something that began as *thank you* and lost its consonants about halfway through. It went on longer than it had any business going on.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The party had reached the stage where nobody would notice two people missing, which Odile pointed out approximately four seconds before doing something about it.

"The bathroom upstairs has a lock," she said, into Fen's ear, over the music.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Does it work?" I ask, already moving toward the stairs.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"I have no idea," Odile admitted cheerfully, lacing her fingers through Fen's and tugging them along faster than the crowd really allowed. "Guess we'll find out together."

The stairs creaked under the bass line thumping up through the floor, and she took them two at a time, throwing a glance back over her shoulder like she expected someone to shout after them. Nobody did. Nobody was even looking. That, somehow, made it better.

At the top, she pushed the bathroom door open with her hip, pulling Fen in after her, and turned to shove the door shut with her back — which put her very deliberately between Fen and the exit.

"Lock," she said, nodding at it without actually reaching for it yet, testing whether Fen would.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I grin, leaning past her to flip the lock. "Guess it does." I turn back, resting my hands on her waist. "Now what's the plan?"

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The click of the lock did something visible to her — a little flicker of satisfaction crossing her face, like she'd been half-hoping it wouldn't work and was delighted to be wrong.

"The plan," Odile said, walking her fingers up the front of Fen's shirt, "is that we've been gone long enough that people will assume things regardless of what we actually do in here. Which means—" she paused, tilting her head, listening to the muffled thump of music and voices through the door, "—we might as well earn the reputation."

She backed Fen against the sink with more enthusiasm than grace, laughing under her breath when it rattled.

"Careful," she murmured, not sounding careful at all, "these fixtures were not built for this."

Her hands were already working at Fen's belt, unhurried despite everything about the situation being, technically, hurried. Someone laughed loudly on the other side of the door and Odile's eyes flicked toward the sound, delighted, before coming back to Fen.

"You're going to have to be quiet," she said. "I, on the other hand, make no promises."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I get the door shut and her against it, and downstairs somebody turns the music up, which helps.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The music swelled up through the floorboards, bass thudding into the soles of her feet, and Odile grinned against the door frame like it was a gift wrapped just for them.

"Oh, that's convenient," she said, voice pitched low but not low enough, tilting her head back as it hit the wood. "Someone up there likes us."

Her fingers curled into Fen's collar, tugging them closer, hips already tilting forward to close whatever gap remained. "Or maybe someone downstairs just really wants to dance," she added, breath catching a little as she said it, "either way — I'm not complaining."

She could feel the door at her back, cool and solid, doorknob pressing faintly against her spine in a way that would probably leave a mark she'd find funny in the morning. Didn't matter. Everything about this felt urgent in the specific way that had nothing to do with actual time constraints and everything to do with wanting.

"Hey," she murmured, tipping Fen's chin up with two fingers so their eyes met, that spark of mischief still burning bright even as her breath had gone uneven, "if you make me laugh right now I will absolutely give us away. Just — fair warning."

A beat. Her hand slid lower, deliberate.

"Try me."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I snort, already biting back a laugh at the sheer ridiculousness of her warning. "You're the one who's gonna be loud." My hands slide up under the back of her shirt, pressing her closer. "Try *me*."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile laughed — actually laughed, a bright startled sound that she had to smother against Fen's shoulder a half-second too late, shoulders shaking with the effort of swallowing it.

"See," she gasped, "*that's* exactly what I meant, you absolute menace—" Her hands under her shirt had gone still for a second, fingers tightening against Fen's skin like she needed something to hold onto while she got herself back under control. She didn't, particularly. Get herself under control.

"Okay. Okay." She exhaled, forehead dropping to rest against Fen's, eyes bright even in the bad bathroom light. "New rule. You don't get to talk either."

She kissed Fen like she meant it as punishment and it backfired immediately, slow and much less careful than the door lock had been, hips pressing forward again like she'd forgotten there was a whole party's worth of people twenty feet and one floor away. The doorknob dug into her back. She didn't move.

"If anyone asks," she breathed, mouth trailing along Fen's jaw, voice gone rough at the edges, "we were fixing the lock. Very thoroughly."

A thump against the door — someone outside, testing the handle, laughing, moving on — made her go rigid and delighted all at once, eyes wide, a hand slapping lightly over her own mouth to keep whatever sound had been building there from actually escaping.

"*Oh my god,*" she whispered against her own palm, shoulders shaking again, half laughter, half something else entirely. "Okay. Okay, we have — we have to be fast. Or infinitely more careful. I don't think we have both in us."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: There isn't room to do this properly and we don't let that stop us. Enough clothes come off to be a problem if anyone knocks.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Practicality had left the building somewhere around the second button, and Odile wasn't inclined to go chasing after it. She hitched herself up onto the edge of the sink — which groaned an alarming protest — and didn't care even slightly.

"That's fine," she said, mostly to the sink, mostly to herself, "that's a support beam noise, that's not a *we're about to die* noise—"

She dragged Fen back in by the front of their shirt before finishing the thought, any pretense of composure abandoned somewhere on the bathroom floor along with half their clothes. Her breath had gone short and uneven, chest rising fast, and every time the bass hit downstairs she could feel it echo up through the pipes, through the sink, through her spine.

"If this thing collapses," she managed, voice pitched somewhere between a laugh and a moan, "we are telling everyone it was *structural*—"

Another knock at the door — real or imagined, she genuinely couldn't tell anymore — and she froze for half a second, eyes going wide, hand flying up to bite down against her own knuckles to keep something from escaping loud enough to travel through drywall.

It didn't entirely work.

A small, strangled sound got out anyway, quickly swallowed, and she pressed her forehead to Fen's shoulder, shaking with silent, helpless laughter that kept threatening to turn into something else entirely.

"You're going to get us caught," she gasped, hips tilting forward like that was somehow an argument against continuing, rather than for it. "I want that on record. This is *entirely* your fault."

She didn't sound like she minded even a little.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I laugh, muffled against her skin. "You're the one who dragged me up here." My grip tightens on her hips, holding her steady against the rattling sink. "Own it."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"Fine," Odile gasped, tipping her head back against the mirror with a soft, undignified thud, "*fine*, I own it, I own all of it, I have zero regrets, put it on my tombstone—" 

The sink shrieked again, some ancient plumbing complaint, and she barely registered it, too busy pressing closer, fingers digging into Fen's shoulders like she needed the leverage. Downstairs the music swelled into something with more bass, more cover, and she made a small, delighted noise of gratitude toward the ceiling like it was divine intervention.

"Odile Marchetti," she muttered breathlessly, narrating her own inevitable epitaph, "died as she lived — recklessly, in a bathroom, blaming her girlfriend—"

She didn't get much further than that. Whatever came next dissolved into something wordless, hips rocking forward to meet Fen's grip, one hand slapping flat against the mirror behind her for balance while the other fisted in Fen's shirt like she was trying to pull them both somehow closer, impossibly closer than they already were.

"Fen," she breathed, voice cracking right at the edge of too loud, and she had to bite down hard on her own lip to catch it before it escaped — a shaky, useless attempt at restraint that lasted about half a second before the doorknob rattled again, someone laughing on the other side, oblivious, moving past.

She didn't stop. If anything, the near-miss lit something brighter under her skin, reckless and grinning even as her breath came apart.

"Don't," she warned, though Fen hadn't said anything, "don't you dare slow down now—"

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I get my hand between her legs and she bites down on my shoulder to keep quiet, which works for about thirty seconds.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
For thirty seconds, Odile managed it — teeth pressed hard into the curve of Fen's shoulder, breath ragged and stifled against skin, every muscle in her drawn tight with the effort of staying silent. Then thirty seconds ran out.

The sound that escaped her was not subtle. It cracked out sharp and high before she could catch it, and she slapped a hand over her own mouth a full second too late, eyes going wide over her fingers, mortified and thrilled in equal measure.

"*Okay*," she gasped into her palm, voice muffled, shaking, "okay, that one was — that one was loud, that one was *bad*—"

She didn't stop moving. That was the problem — some part of her brain had clearly filed volume control and everything else into separate departments, and only one of them was currently functioning. Downstairs the bass thumped on, oblivious, merciful, and she clung to that fact like a life raft even as her hips rocked forward again, betraying every intention of restraint.

"If someone's outside that door right now," she breathed, forehead dropping against Fen's, hair sticking damp to her temple, "I want you to know I regret *nothing*—"

Her hand slipped from her mouth just enough to bite down on her own knuckle instead, a stopgap measure that lasted exactly as long as the last one had. She was laughing again — helpless, breathless little bursts of it tangled up with everything else, entirely incapable of picking one reaction and sticking to it.

"Fen," she managed, barely a whisper, barely coherent, "Fen, I swear to god, if you stop right now I will actually die, structural integrity be damned—"

The sink gave another ominous groan beneath her. She didn't care. She didn't care about anything except the door staying shut, the music staying loud, and Fen's hand not stopping — three demands, all equally urgent, all somehow holding together by pure reckless luck.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: The sink makes another terrible noise and I have to swallow a laugh, my own breath ragged. "If this thing breaks, we're jumping out the window." My free hand braces against the wall, holding us both steady. "Not slowing down, I promise."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"*Please* don't make me laugh right now," Odile begged, voice cracking somewhere between a whimper and a giggle, "I will actually fall off this sink and take you down with me—"

The wall groaned its agreement. She didn't care. Her thighs tightened around Fen's hand, hips stuttering forward, and for a second the plan — window, structural collapse, whatever — actually seemed reasonable, a perfectly logical contingency for a bathroom that was actively trying to kill them.

"Deal," she gasped anyway, breathless, grinning against Fen's jaw. "Second floor. We'll survive. We'll — *oh*—"

Whatever came after that dissolved entirely. Her hand found the back of Fen's neck, fingers curling in tight, and she pressed her face into their shoulder again, not to bite this time but just to have somewhere to put the sound building in her chest, low and helpless and entirely unstoppable now.

The music downstairs shifted, dropped into something slower, and for one terrible second there was almost quiet — enough that her next breath came out sharp and unmistakable, echoing off tile in a way that made her whole body go rigid with delighted horror.

"*That's* going to be a problem," she managed, voice wrecked, laughing and gasping in the same breath, hips still moving despite every rational thought screaming caution. "Someone definitely— Fen, someone definitely heard that—"

She didn't stop. She didn't even really try to.

"Worth it," she breathed, eyes squeezing shut, forehead damp against Fen's collarbone. "Whatever happens after this — completely, entirely worth it. Don't you dare stop now."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Stop worrying about the noise," she says, "and get on with it," so I get her leg up over my hip and stop being careful about how much sound either of us is making.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The moment her leg hooked over Fen's hip, Odile lost whatever thread of restraint she'd been pretending to hold onto. The sink rattled violently, the mirror behind her rocking against its bracket, and she didn't even flinch — too far gone to care about property damage, about the door, about anything except the sudden shift in angle that made her back arch hard against cold glass.

"*Fen—*" It came out loud, unguarded, nothing left of the careful whispering from five minutes ago. She heard herself and didn't stop, didn't even try, fingers scrabbling for purchase against Fen's shoulders, against the edge of the sink, against anything solid in a room that suddenly felt like it was tilting.

The bass downstairs thumped on, oblivious or merciful, she couldn't tell which anymore and didn't care. Every rational thought about volume, about the door lock, about the very real possibility of an audience gathering on the other side of it, had evaporated completely, replaced by the drag of Fen's hips and the white-hot clarity of *more, don't stop, right there—*

"I don't— I don't care anymore," she gasped, half a laugh tangled up in it, breathless and wrecked and grinning even as her whole body shook. "Let them hear. Let them—*oh God*—let them think whatever they want—"

Her head fell back, throat bared, and the sound that tore loose from her that time was nowhere near quiet — sharp and unmistakable, bouncing off tile and glass, definitely audible past a locked door and a floor of dancing strangers. She barely registered it. Her whole world had narrowed down to Fen's hand, Fen's hip under her leg, the door frame biting into her shoulder blade with every motion.

"Don't stop," she begged, voice cracking, nails dragging red lines down Fen's back, "don't you dare stop, I am so close, I am so—"

The sink groaned one final, ominous time. Neither of them stopped to check if it held.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: The sink groans louder and I know we're pushing our luck, but I'm way past caring. I kiss her to swallow her next cry, my own breath rough against her mouth. "Come on, then," I murmur, my voice low and ragged. "Let's give them something to talk about."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The kiss caught her mid-cry, and Odile made a muffled, desperate sound against Fen's mouth, hands fisting in their shirt like she needed something to anchor to. It didn't quiet her so much as redirect her — every gasp swallowed only to build right back up again, sharper, closer.

"*Fen—*" she managed, breaking away just enough to breathe, forehead pressed hard to Fen's, eyes squeezed shut. "Fen, I'm—"

Whatever came next wasn't words. It was just sound, raw and unrestrained, the kind she'd promised at the start of this she wouldn't be able to hold back and now had absolutely no interest in trying to. Her leg tightened around Fen's hip, her back arching hard enough that the mirror behind her rattled a warning neither of them heeded, and she went over with a cry that definitely, certainly, carried through the door and probably down the stairs — bright and unguarded and entirely without apology.

For a long moment afterward she just hung there against the sink, against Fen, shaking, breathless, laughing in broken little bursts between gasps like her body couldn't decide which reaction to commit to.

"Okay," she finally managed, voice wrecked, forehead still pressed to Fen's, "okay, that's — that's on you. Entirely. I'm blaming you specifically, in front of everyone, the second we walk out that door."

A beat. Then, from downstairs, through the floor — an unmistakable ripple of laughter and a few pointed wolf-whistles.

Odile went scarlet, delighted, and buried her face against Fen's shoulder with a groan that was half mortification and half pure, helpless joy.

"We are never going to live this down," she said happily. "Never. Not once. Worth it."

dialogue.name: Fen

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: The doorknob rattles again, more insistently this time. I freeze, my hand still tangled in her hair. "That's definitely someone," I whisper, mouth against her temple. "Think we've been discovered."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile went rigid for half a second — then dissolved into helpless, breathless laughter, the kind that made keeping quiet a lost cause entirely.

"*Discovered,*" she echoed, pressing her face into Fen's neck to muffle it, shoulders shaking. "Discovered. Like we're — like we're contraband. Like we're a smuggling operation."

The handle jiggled again, more insistent this time, and a voice — muffled, familiar, unmistakably one of the party's less subtle guests — called through the door, something about "you good in there?" that only made her laugh harder.

"We are *fine*," Odile called back, voice pitched with false composure that fooled absolutely no one, especially not with how wrecked it sounded. "Give us a — a minute—"

She caught Fen's eye, grinning, utterly unrepentant, already reaching for the discarded pieces of clothing scattered across bad tile like evidence at a crime scene.

"Okay," she whispered, still catching her breath, fingers fumbling with a button she got wrong twice, "okay, we have to actually leave this bathroom now. As people. Wearing clothes. Convincingly."

Another knock. More laughter from the hallway — clearly more than one person out there now, drawn by whatever had carried through the door and down the stairs minutes ago.

"They heard everything, didn't they," she said, not really a question, pulling her shirt straight with a kind of giddy, mortified resignation. "Every single — okay. Okay, new plan. We walk out, we own it completely, we make direct eye contact with every single person we pass. No shame. Full confidence."

She caught Fen's hand, squeezing once, eyes bright with barely contained delight.

"Ready?"

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I finish buttoning my jeans, still breathing a little hard. "Ready," I say, leaning in to kiss her one last time, quick and grinning. "Let's go face the music."
