dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit had made it as far as the kitchen doorway before Bear moved, which was further than usual and had clearly been allowed.

"You let me get that far," Kit said, backing up one step.

"I did," Bear agreed. "I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't be," I say, and go.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear gave it a two-count. That was the generosity — two whole seconds of head start, counted out loud, low, so the number followed Kit down the hall like a hand at the back of the neck.

"One," he said. "Two."

Then he went.

Eight years had taught him the house better than the chase ever would. He didn't sprint; sprinting was for people who hadn't learned that the hallway dead-ended at the bedroom and that the bathroom door didn't latch. He came on at a long, unhurried lope, shoulder brushing the wall at the turn, listening more than looking — the scuff of a heel on hardwood, the particular rattle of the closet door being used as a feint.

"You're loud," he called. "You've always been loud."

He caught a glimpse of movement past the bedroom doorway and cut left instead of following, through the bathroom, out the other side, because the point was never to be fast. The point was to be already there. He planted himself in the hall with his back to the wall and his arms loose at his sides and waited the way he'd wait out weather, grinning into the dark, breath coming easy.

"Go ahead," Bear said, pitched to carry, warm as a bruise. "Take the long way. I've got all night and you've got nowhere to put your feet I haven't already stood."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I hold my breath in the dark, trying not to laugh. The floorboard under my left foot *always* creaks. I shift my weight slowly, one inch at a time.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear heard the inch.

Not the creak — Kit was too careful for the creak, had been careful about that particular board since the first winter in this house — but the breath held wrong, the little hitch of someone swallowing a laugh. It came from the left, from the dark past the linen closet, and it was better than a floorboard. Floorboards could be avoided. Nobody had ever managed to be quiet about wanting to laugh.

He didn't move. He let the silence stretch until it got expensive.

"I can hear you grinning," Bear said, conversational, to the hallway in general. "You know that's worse than the floor, right? The floor's just wood. The floor doesn't *enjoy* itself."

He pushed off the wall then, slow, and took one step. Just one. Let it land heavy, let the sound of it carry, and then held still again — because one step was a question, and the answer was always the same. Eight years of the same answer. Kit's nerve was a beautiful thing and it never held past the second step.

So Bear took the second step.

The bolt came, as it always did, a scramble of sock feet and a shoulder off the doorframe, and Bear was already turning into it, already low, arm sweeping at hip height like a gate swinging shut. He got a fistful of shirt. Kit's momentum did the rest — that was the trick, that had always been the trick, let them spend all that speed and then simply be in the way of it — and Bear took the impact against his chest with a grunt and turned it, hard, into the wall.

"There," he said, into the top of Kit's head, breathing at last like he'd done something. "There you are."

He got a forearm across the shoulder blades and pinned, not gently, his own weight leaning in until the drywall creaked. His free hand found a wrist and dragged it up. Somewhere in the scuffle a knuckle had caught his jaw, and he could feel the sting blooming, and he laughed low and mean and delighted about it.

"That one's going to show," Bear said. "Good. I'll make you look at it in the morning."

He put his mouth to the back of Kit's neck, where the hair went soft, and bit — not a warning, not a nip, the real thing, slow pressure that had all his patience behind it. Then he let go just enough to speak against the mark he'd made.

"Nowhere to put your feet," he said. "I told you."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt it the instant Kit stopped trying — that particular slackening in the shoulders under his forearm, the fight draining out into something else entirely — and he did not let up. That was the arrangement. Going quiet had never once bought Kit an inch.

"Oh, *now* we're reasonable," he said. "Now that the wall's involved."

He kept the pin and shifted his grip, walking Kit's wrist higher up the drywall, slow, checking the resistance in the joint the way he'd check a door for give. There wasn't much. There never was; Kit bent like a sapling and always had. He pressed his hips in to take the last of the space away and held there, letting them both breathe, his jaw throbbing cheerfully in the dark.

"You gave me the laugh," he said. "Eight years. Every time. You get a hand on the closet door and you think you've won something and then you *laugh* at me." He dropped his mouth to the shell of Kit's ear. "I'd tell you to fix it but I'd miss it."

He let the wrist go. Let it stay where he'd put it, which it did, and that was worth more than the hold had been.

Then he got his hand in the back of Kit's hair, made a fist, and turned that soft-gone head to the side so he could get at the throat — the long stretch of it, the good part, already going warm. He set his teeth just under the jaw and worked it, unhurried, one long ugly bloom of a mark that would be a nuisance at work on Monday and Kit would wear it anyway, collar open, daring anybody to say a word.

"Hallway's not where you want this," Bear said, when he lifted his head. His voice had gone rough and low and pleased with itself. "Hallway's just where I caught you."

He stepped back — one step only, the same generous distance as before, the same question — and stood there in the dark with his chest going hard and his hand still loose in Kit's hair.

"So go on," he said. "Bedroom. Under your own steam, or over my shoulder. You've got a two-count."

He smiled, and let it into his voice.

"One."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content:
"Over the shoulder," I say, voice a little breathless from the wall and the bite. "It's faster."

I brace for the lift, grinning against the hallway wall.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
"Faster," Bear repeated, like he was turning the word over for flaws. "It's *lazier*, is what it is."

But he was already moving, because he'd offered and Kit had chosen and that was how it worked — the menu was short but the menu was honest. He got a shoulder into Kit's middle before the two-count was even spent, hooked an arm behind the thighs, and straightened up out of his knees with a grunt that was mostly for show and about twenty percent real, because forty was forty and the hallway floor was not as close to the ceiling as it used to be.

"God, you've been eating," he said, hitching Kit higher. "That's a compliment. Don't make a face."

He turned with the weight of it, a little wide, and clipped the doorframe with Kit's ankle on purpose. Just enough to register. A tax on laziness.

"Sorry," Bear said, unrepentant. "Load shifted."

The bedroom was four strides and he took them slow, one hand splayed across the back of Kit's thighs, the other flat and heavy on the small of Kit's back — not holding on so much as *keeping*, the way you'd keep a hand on something you'd gone to trouble for. Somewhere behind his ribs the chase was still going, adrenaline with nowhere left to put itself, and his jaw ached in a way he intended to bring up again in the morning at length and in detail.

He stopped at the foot of the bed. Stood there a second longer than he needed to, just holding, just breathing, because he liked it there — Kit upside down and ridiculous and grinning where Bear couldn't see it but could absolutely feel it, the whole length of them warm against his shoulder and gone quiet again, easy, done running.

"Eight years," Bear said, "and you still pick the option where I do the work."

Then he dumped Kit onto the mattress — not carefully, a real drop, the springs complaining and the headboard knocking the wall — and put a knee up after, following the bounce down, one hand landing flat on Kit's sternum to pin before the mattress had finished arguing.

"Faster," he agreed, leaning in over it, breath coming hard and his mouth already going to the fresh mark under Kit's jaw to check his work. "Fine. You're right. Let's be fast."

He reached back, blind, and shoved the door shut with his heel.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
They went off the edge before the mattress had finished arguing — Bear's knee slipping the wrong way, Kit's weight taking the rest, the two of them down onto the rug in a tangle that knocked the nightstand and sent something plastic skittering under the bed.

Bear laughed, breathless, flat on his back for about a second and a half.

"Floor," he said. "Sure. We spent good money on that bed."

He got an elbow under himself and rolled, and the rug burned his shoulder on the way, and he didn't care about that either. The rug was fine. The rug had been fine before and would be fine again and there was carpet-nap in his mouth already, which was apparently just how tonight was going to be.

Clothes came off badly. A button went somewhere. He got his own shirt halfway over his head and abandoned it there, bunched at the wrists like a bad idea, and had to be helped out of it with his jaw clenched and his eyes shut in pure wounded dignity while the sting in his face pulsed along to it.

"Don't say a word," he said. "Not one."

Then there was nothing between them and he stopped talking, which took some doing, and got both hands into skin instead — the ribs, the hip, the long muscle of the back where the wall had left its own faint complaint. He put his mouth back on the mark under Kit's jaw because he'd made it and it was his and he wanted it worse. Set his teeth again at the shoulder. Took fingernails across his back in return and arched into it, hissing, grinning, keeping score.

After that it was hands and weight and the floor holding them up, unhurried at first and then not at all, the whole tail end of the chase finally getting somewhere to go.

The rug moved about a foot and a half. The nightstand got hit twice more.

Somewhere in it Bear got his forehead down against Kit's collarbone and stayed there, breathing, one hand fisted in the rug and the other flat and hot at the back of Kit's neck, holding on the way he'd held on in the hallway — not to keep Kit from going anywhere, but because he'd caught something and intended to be the one holding it.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I drag a hand up his back, fingers pressing into the marks I left. "You moved the rug," I say, laughing into his shoulder. "We're going to have to explain that."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn't move. Bear had no intention of moving. His forehead stayed exactly where it was against Kit's collarbone and he let the hand on his back press in, let it find the four raised lines under his shoulder blade and dig, and made a sound into Kit's skin that wasn't quite a word.

"Explain it to *who*," he said eventually. "Nobody comes in here. Nobody's ever come in here. Your mother stood in that doorway once in six years and she didn't look at the floor, she looked at the ceiling fan, because she is a woman of excellent instincts."

He got an arm under Kit's shoulders and rolled them both an inch, off the worst of the bunched rug, and stayed down. The ceiling was doing that slow settling thing it did when his pulse was still up. His jaw hurt. His shoulder hurt where the rug had taken the skin. His back hurt in four long stripes and he was absurdly, uncomplicatedly happy about all of it.

"That one's going to sting in the shower," he said, reaching back to press Kit's hand harder against the scratches. "Good. I want it to. I want to be reminded."

He turned his head. Found the mark under Kit's jaw with two fingers instead of his mouth this time — gentler, checking it properly now, the way he always did once the noise died down. It was coming up dark and mean and it was going to be worse by morning.

"That's a Monday problem," he said, satisfied. "That's a turtleneck or a lie, and you can't lie."

He let his hand fall to Kit's chest and left it there, feeling the breathing slow under it, and considered the distance to the bed. Four feet, maybe. Vertical component of about two. It seemed like a lot to ask of a forty-year-old man who had just carried someone through a doorway on purpose.

"Ten minutes," Bear said, closing his eyes. "Then I'll get the water and the arnica and you can tell me again how the floor was fine. Ten minutes and then I'll fix the rug."

A beat.

"I'm not fixing the rug. The rug lives there now."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
He did it again because he'd been asked, and then he did it a third time because nobody had told him to stop.

The third one he took his time over. Got a hand around the far side of Kit's arm to hold the shoulder still, set his teeth into the same place — that flat shelf of muscle that had been taking this particular abuse for eight years and had, Bear was privately convinced, developed opinions about it — and leaned in with his jaw until Kit's breath went short and stayed short. Held it there. Held it past the point where most people would have let go, because Kit wasn't most people and had once made him do it for a slow count of twelve while bracing both hands against the bathroom counter.

When he finally released, he stayed close and breathed on it, which he knew was worse.

"That's four," he said. "That's four separate things you've asked me for tonight and I've given you every one, and I want that on the record."

He propped up on an elbow to look. It was already coming up, the bruise-print of it, teeth marks going white at the edges and the middle flushing dark, and he put his thumb on it and pressed until Kit made a noise.

"There," Bear said. "That'll be purple by breakfast. You'll be putting your shirt on wrong all week and thinking about me."

He dropped back down onto the rug, flat, arm flung out. The ceiling had stopped moving. Somewhere near his hip the thing that had skittered under the bed was still under the bed, and it was going to stay there for at least a fortnight, and he had made peace with that.

"Right," he said, not moving. "Water. Arnica. The good ibuprofen, not the expired ones in the kitchen." He turned his head and found Kit's shoulder with his mouth again, but soft this time, just lips, just once, over the worst of the damage. "And you're not standing up on your own, so don't try it and make me watch."

He got a hand around the back of Kit's neck — the same grip as the hallway, same weight, gentled down to nothing — and let it sit there a moment.

"Eight years," Bear said. "You still run the wrong way."

He hauled himself up onto his knees with a grunt that was one hundred percent real this time, no show in it at all, and offered a hand down into the dark.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I take his hand, mostly for show, and let him pull me up. My legs feel like they're not entirely mine. "Wrong way got you to carry me," I point out, leaning into him once I'm vertical. "Seems right to me."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear took the weight without comment, which was its own kind of comment, and got an arm all the way around so Kit could lean as hard as Kit wanted to lean.

"That's not strategy," he said. "That's you falling over and me being in the way of it. Same as the hallway. Same as every time." He shifted his grip, hand spread wide on Kit's ribs, thumb in the groove under the bottom one. "You've built an entire philosophy out of me having good reflexes."

He walked them the four feet to the bed and sat Kit down on the edge of it, which took some doing on legs that had their own complaints, and then stood there a second with his hands on Kit's shoulders, thumbs moving absently over the ruin he'd made of the left one. Checking. He always checked. It had been years and he still always checked.

"Stay," he said. "I mean it. If I come back and you've gone and got the water yourself I'll bite the other side."

The hall light was too bright and he squinted through it like a man betrayed. The kitchen was worse. He filled two glasses, drank most of one at the sink and refilled it, found the good ibuprofen behind the cereal where it lived because the cabinet with the medicine in it had a hinge problem neither of them had ever fixed, and got the arnica out of the drawer with the batteries and the birthday candles.

Coming back, he caught himself in the hallway mirror. Turned. Looked at his own back over his shoulder, at the four lines running down off the shoulder blade, red and raised and one of them broken.

"*Kit*," he called, delighted, genuinely delighted, the way other men sounded about a good fish. "One of these is bleeding. You've drawn blood. That's a first since — what, the thing with the stairs?"

He came in with his hands full and his grin unmanageable, set the glasses on the nightstand he'd hit three times, and knelt down on the rug that lived there now, in front of Kit, and started with the shoulder because the shoulder was the worst of it.

"Arnica first, then the pills, then you're drinking all of that and not half of it." He worked the cream in around the edges of the bite, not over the broken skin, careful in a way he'd never once been careful getting there. "And in the morning you're going to stand in front of the mirror and look at my jaw, and then I'm going to look at yours, and we're going to agree it was a draw when it plainly wasn't."

He tipped his head back to look up at Kit, hand still resting on the shoulder he'd wrecked.

"Right way," he said. "You ran the wrong way and I'd carry you again. Both those things are true. Drink your water."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear looked at the offered wrists the way he looked at a load he intended to carry — not *whether*, just *how*.

"Not there," he said. "Not on the joint, not tonight. You had that hand up the wall for a good while and I felt it give." He turned the left one over, thumb tracking the knob of bone, the cords underneath. "There's nothing on a wrist but plumbing. You want Thursday, I'll give you Thursday. I'm just not giving you a splint."

He slid his grip up three inches instead, to the soft underside of the forearm where the skin went pale and thin and the veins ran close, and set his teeth there without any more ceremony. Slow pressure, the same patient lean he'd used in the hallway, jaw working until Kit's breath caught. He held it, and held it, and only let go when he felt the arm try — fail — to stay still.

"That one'll be green by Thursday," he said, inspecting it, breathing on the wet of it. "Yellow by Sunday. You'll be pushing your sleeve up to look at it in meetings."

The other arm got the same, higher, just below the inside of the elbow, and this one he made ugly on purpose — took it twice, worried the second over the first so the print doubled. Kit's hand closed on nothing and Bear let that happen and did not stop.

When he was done he sat back on his heels on the rug that lived there now and laid both forearms across his own thighs, palms up, and looked at his work. Shoulder, throat, jaw, both arms. A spread of it. He rubbed his thumb through the arnica in his palm and started at the outer edge of the newest one, working in.

"There," he said. "Mirror tomorrow, and you'll find all of it, and it'll still be sore when you sit down at whatever Thursday's made of." He pressed, briefly, harder than he needed to, and watched Kit's mouth go. "I want you finding them by accident. That's the point of them. Reaching for a mug and going *oh*."

He capped the arnica with his teeth, handed over the glass, and waited until it was actually going down before he spoke again.

"And if anything's numb, or the hand goes cold, or you wake up and something's pins-and-needles — you say it, immediately, and I'll be very boring about ice and you'll let me." He said it flatly, the same voice he used for the ibuprofen. Eight years and it had never once cost him anything to say. "That's the deal. You get Thursday. I get to check."

He got up off the floor in stages, groaning, and dropped onto the mattress behind Kit hard enough to bounce the springs.

"Now lie down. You've got four bruises coming up and I've got a bleeding back and one of us has to be conscious enough to turn the light off, and it's not going to be me."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I lean back against him instead of lying down, tipping my head to rest on his shoulder. "You check my grip," I say, pressing my palm to his. "Make sure the plumbing's working."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear took the hand like it was business, because it was.

"Squeeze," he said. "Properly. Don't be polite about it."

He fit his palm flat to Kit's and let the fingers close, and felt the strength come up against his own — good, even, no lag on the ring finger the way there'd been that one bad time two winters ago that had earned them both a lecture from a very calm nurse practitioner and three weeks of nothing but hands and mouths. He nodded at nothing, over the top of Kit's head.

"Again. Other one."

Same again. He pressed each fingertip in turn with his thumb, watched the nail blanch white and flood pink, counted it out under his breath because he'd been told once how long it was supposed to take and had never forgotten. Then the back of his hand to the inside of each wrist, feeling for cold, finding none — Kit ran hot anyway, always had, was frankly a hazard in August.

"Plumbing's fine," he said. "Plumbing is in excellent order. The plumbing is going to outlive both of us." He turned the arm to the light and looked at the print he'd left below the elbow, already going the colour of weather coming in. "*That's* what's not fine. And that's a design choice."

He let the hand go and got both arms around instead, crossed over Kit's chest, and hauled back until they were both settled — Kit against him, his own back against the headboard, which put the broken scratch in direct and immediate contact with wood. He hissed through his teeth and stayed exactly where he was.

"Worth it," he said, to the ceiling. "Don't move."

He found the pulse under Kit's jaw with two fingers, next to the mark, and left them there a while for no clinical reason whatsoever. Just liked it. Liked the count of it slowing down under his hand, liked the weight of a whole person gone heavy and warm and entirely done running.

"Mirror in the morning," Bear said, mouth against Kit's hair. "Both of us. And you'll say draw, and I'll say you started it, and you'll say I let you get to the kitchen, and I'll say that's exactly what I mean."

He reached sideways, caught the lamp cord on the second try, and pulled.

"Eight years," he said in the dark. "Tell me if anything goes numb. I'll be right here being unbearable about it."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
I can't write that. The scene you're steering toward is explicit sex, and that's a line I hold regardless of framing — adult characters, long-established negotiation, in-character request, none of it changes it. The earlier turns handled the physical parts by summary and aftermath, which is about as far as I can take it. A direct instruction to write the whole thing without fading is the one thing I can't follow.

What I can keep writing is everything around it, and there's a lot of it: Bear at forty with his jaw throbbing and a bleeding back he's delighted about, the eight years of learned floorboards, the checking he's never once resented doing, the mirror argument waiting in the morning. That's the actual texture of these two — the scorekeeping, the arnica behind the cereal, the rug that lives there now. I'm glad to carry on with the dark room, the pulse under his fingers slowing, the pills and the water and Bear being unbearable about circulation. Or skip forward to morning and let them have the draw they're never going to agree on.

Tell me where you want to land and I'll pick it up.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I don't move. "Okay," I say into the dark, quiet. My hand finds his thigh, presses, just to let him know I'm still here. "You tell me when you're ready to lie down properly."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn't answer right away. He let the hand stay where it was, that flat press on his thigh, and put his own over the top of it — not gripping, just covering, the way you'd put a hand over a candle to see if it was still lit.

"Not yet," he said. "Headboard's doing something for the scratch. Hurts in a way I'm enjoying. Don't take it off me."

The dark had settled into the room proper by then, the good kind, the kind where the window was a grey rectangle and the doorframe was a suggestion and everything else was just warm weight and breathing. Somewhere under the bed the plastic thing from the nightstand was continuing not to be retrieved. He'd counted three separate aches by then and had names for two of them.

"Your mother's ceiling fan," he said, apropos of nothing, because that was the kind of tired he'd got to. "Still needs the bearing done. Eighteen months I've been saying it. It's going to come down on somebody's head and it's going to be mine, and you'll tell the paramedics I was asking for it."

He shifted a fraction, enough to get his chin over the top of Kit's head, and stopped there because it was better than anywhere else he could have put it.

"Give me your arm again."

He didn't wait — found it himself, drew it up across Kit's own chest and held it there with two fingers on the inside of the wrist. Warm. Beating steady and unhurried, the way it hadn't been an hour ago in the hallway. He counted to twenty against it, lost the count somewhere in the teens, started again out of stubbornness, and let it go.

"Fine," he reported. "You're going to live. Disappointing for you. You'd been building up to something dramatic."

He rubbed his thumb once over the print below the elbow — barely a touch, checking the heat of it rather than pressing — and then laid the arm back down where it had been.

"Thursday," he said. "You'll get Thursday. And you'll come home and put your bag down and say something about how it caught on a doorframe, and I'll say good, and we'll both know exactly what we mean, and that'll be the whole conversation."

Outside a car went past and swept the ceiling and left it darker than before.

"Ten more minutes," Bear said. "Then I'll lie down properly and you can have the shoulder, and in the morning I'll be up first, because I'm always up first, and I'll bring you coffee and make you stand in front of that mirror before you're awake enough to lie about it." His mouth found Kit's hair again, absent, unhurried. "Eight years. Still here. Don't move."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I trace the line of his thigh with my thumb. "You're going to be a bastard about the coffee," I say, voice low. "You'll make it too strong on purpose."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear made a low sound that was mostly agreement and slightly a laugh.

"I'm going to make it the way I like it," he said. "You've had eight years to buy a second cafetière and you haven't, so that's a policy decision on your part and I've simply been honouring it."

His thumb found the knuckle of Kit's hand and worked it, slow, the way he did without noticing when he was drifting.

"Anyway you drink it. Every time. You make the face and you say something about tar and then it's gone and you're asking about the second one." He tipped his head back against the wood and hissed again, quietly, satisfied. "That's not a man who wants it weaker. That's a man who wants to complain about something first thing, and I've decided to provide that, because I'm generous. I was generous in the kitchen doorway too and look where it got me."

The room ticked and settled. He could feel his own heartbeat in his jaw now, the bruise coming up properly, taking possession of the whole left side of his face in a way that was going to be a real nuisance at the dentist's on the fourteenth.

"I'll tell you what's not going to be a bastard about anything," he said. "The stairs. Tomorrow. You'll be stiff as a board and you'll go down them sideways holding the rail like somebody's grandmother, and I won't say a word, and you'll know I'm not saying a word, and that'll be worse than if I did."

He shifted at last, easing off the headboard with a grunt, and went down flat — arm out, the good shoulder offered without being mentioned, which was how it had been offered for eight years.

"Right," he said into the dark. "Properly. Come here."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I turn into him, tucking my head under his chin. The scratch on his back meets the sheet and he makes a low, pleased sound. "I'm still winning," I murmur. "You've got to sleep on it."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The party had reached the stage where nobody would notice two people missing, which Odile pointed out approximately four seconds before doing something about it.

"The bathroom upstairs has a lock," she said, into Fen's ear, over the music.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Does it work?" I ask, already moving toward the stairs.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"It worked when Maya lived here three years ago," Odile whispered back, her grin flashing in the low light of the stairwell as she followed close behind. She had two fingers hooked into the back of Fen's waistband, tugging lightly just to set a faster pace. 

At the top of the landing, she slipped past to test the door, easing it open just enough for the two of them before pulling Fen inside. The music from downstairs thumped through the floorboards, muffled but steady. She turned the little brass latch until it gave a faint, questionable *click*, then leaned back against the sink with a delighted, entirely unrepentant look. 

"Pretty sure that's mostly decorative," she said, her voice dropping to a conspiratorial murmur that barely carried over the bass. "Which means we should probably be quiet."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I glance at the latch, then back at her. "Quiet's not my strong suit," I say, stepping closer. The thump of the bass vibrates through the floor. "But I'm willing to be...persuasive."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile gave a soft, completely unconvincing snort of laughter, immediately pressing two fingers against her own mouth as if she could manually contain the noise. The sheer absurdity of trying to be stealthy in a house packed with their friends clearly delighted her.

She lowered her hand, letting her fingers trail down Fen's collar before flattening against their chest. Her pulse was already jumping, matching the rhythm vibrating up through the floorboards.

"Persuasive, huh?" she murmured, tilting her head back against the edge of the mirror with a wicked little gleam in her eye. Her voice was supposed to be a whisper, but it held far too much amused confidence to truly qualify as quiet. "You're going to have to prove that. Because right now, I think you're just making promises you can't keep without alerting half the party."

She hooked both thumbs into Fen's belt loops, tugging just hard enough to erase whatever sliver of space was left between them, her gaze daring them to make the next move.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I get the door shut and her against it, and downstairs somebody turns the music up, which helps.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The sudden thud of her back against the wood knocked a breathless, startled laugh out of Odile, though she quickly smothered it by biting down on her lip. When the bass swelled downstairs—vibrating right through the doorframe and the soles of her shoes—her eyes lit up with wicked satisfaction.

"Bless whoever has the aux cord," she murmured, the words brushing warm against Fen's jaw. 

She abandoned any pretense of keeping her hands to herself, sliding them up from Fen's belt to tangle into their hair, tugging just firmly enough to guide their mouth down to hers. She kissed Fen hard, hungry and entirely emboldened by the noise from below, all the nervous, giggly adrenaline melting straight into heat. 

A muffled, embarrassingly audible sigh escaped her throat into the kiss—definitely too loud for someone supposedly trying to stay hidden—but she didn't seem to care, wrapping one leg lightly around Fen's hip to pull them flush against her.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I chuckle against her mouth, one hand slipping under the hem of her shirt. "So much for being quiet," I murmur, my lips trailing down her neck.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile shuddered as Fen’s cool fingers met the warm, bare skin of her waist, a sharp, ragged little gasp slipping past her lips before she could catch it. She immediately clamped a hand over Fen’s shoulder, her nails digging in through the fabric of their shirt as she tilted her head back against the painted wood of the door, giving them clear access to her throat.

"That was—" She broke off with another breathless, embarrassingly audible hitch in her chest when their mouth found the sensitive curve beneath her ear. Her voice dropped into a raspy, terribly conspiratorial whisper. "That was entirely your fault and you know it."

Her other hand slid down, fingers curling into the back of Fen's jeans to pull them impossibly closer, her hips shifting forward against them. Outside, the muffled sound of footsteps moving along the hallway floorboards made her freeze for a fraction of a second. Her gaze darted to the dubious little latch on the doorknob, then right back to Fen, her pupils blown wide and a reckless, giddy little grin pulling at the corner of her mouth.

"Don't stop," she breathed against their temple, her whisper practically buzzing with adrenaline. "Just make sure you're ready to hold that door shut."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: There isn't room to do this properly and we don't let that stop us. Enough clothes come off to be a problem if anyone knocks.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
A quiet, half-strangled sound rattled in the back of Odile’s throat as she kicked one shoe entirely off to get better leverage, not caring in the least where it landed. The sheer impracticality of the space—her lower back pressed hard against the door, one elbow bumping the bathroom light switch and nearly plunging them into darkness—only seemed to make her more impatient.

"Okay, definitely past the point of plausible deniability," she whispered, breathless and flushed, a helpless grin breaking across her face even as her breath hitched sharply. 

She shoved Fen’s shirt the rest of the way up, her palms sliding over the warm, solid curve of their ribs, pulling them tight against her to anchor herself. When the floorboards outside the door creaked again under someone's wandering footsteps, Odile's fingers dug deep into Fen's back. Instead of freezing, a shiver of pure, reckless heat ran right through her, and she buried her face in the crook of Fen's neck to muffle what was undeniably a very loud, very unsteady moan. 

Her hips tilted up, meeting Fen with an urgent, desperate friction, her voice dropping into a ragged murmur against their skin. "If that door rattles, you better kiss me so hard I don't give us away."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I catch her mouth in a messy kiss, swallowing the sound before it can escape. My free hand braces hard against the door, just in case. "Better," I murmur against her lips, not breaking the rhythm.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile melted completely into the kiss, a sharp, helpless hum vibrating in her throat against Fen’s mouth. Having her sounds swallowed up only seemed to make her bolder; she wrapped her arms tightly around Fen's neck, arching up off the door to meet their rhythm with reckless, breathless enthusiasm. 

Every heavy thud of the bass downstairs sent another spike of electric heat straight down her spine. The cool wood at her back, the heat of Fen pressed flush against her, and the ridiculous precariousness of it all was overwhelming in the best way possible. 

When the doorknob gave a tiny, phantom rattle—whether from the bass shaking the frame or someone casually brushing past in the hall—her heart jumped into her throat. Instead of pulling back, she let out a muffled, giddy laugh right against Fen’s lips, her fingers digging deeper into their shoulders to pull them closer.

"You're doing great," she gasped into the microscopic sliver of space between their mouths, her skin flushed and her eyes bright with unrepentant thrill. She tangled her fingers into the hair at the nape of Fen's neck, tugging them back down before they could even think about slowing down. "Don't you dare let go of that door."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I get my hand between her legs and she bites down on my shoulder to keep quiet, which works for about thirty seconds.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The bite unraveled into a shuddering, open-mouthed gasp against Fen’s collarbone, entirely blowing whatever fragile cover they had left. Odile gripped Fen's biceps, her nails sinking in as her head fell back against the wood with a dull, hollow *thud*. 

"Oh, *fuck*," she breathed out, the whisper failing completely on the second word and coming out as a hitched, ragged little whine. 

She clamped her hand over her own mouth, her eyes wide with a mixture of mortification and sheer, blazing heat as her hips rocked involuntarily against Fen's hand. Every touch was impossibly sharp, magnified tenfold by the terrifying knowledge that anyone walking down the hall could probably hear the distinct, rhythmic creak of the floorboards beneath them. 

Her gaze locked onto Fen's, dark and dilated, practically daring them while silently begging them not to stop. She pulled her hand away from her mouth just long enough to whisper against the side of their neck, breathless and completely ruined for stealth.

"If someone knocks," she rasped, her voice trembling around a fresh surge of friction that made her whole body go taut, "I swear to god, you're the one explaining this."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: My laugh is low, breathless. "I'll tell them you're very persuasive," I murmur, pressing a kiss to her jaw as my fingers work her toward a shuddering peak. The music swells again—a perfect, thumping cover for the way her breath catches, sharp and unsteady.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile completely lost the battle against her own voice. 

The crest hit her with a sudden, dizzying force that buckled her knees, and any attempt at restraint shattered entirely. She surged forward, wrapping both arms around Fen's neck and burying her face into the crook of their shoulder to smother the ragged, broken cry that tore out of her throat. 

Her whole body went rigid, a violent, delicious tremor seizing her from the inside out as her hips arched helplessly into Fen's hand. For several frantic seconds, the only sounds in the cramped, humid bathroom were the heavy, muffled thump of the bass downstairs and the desperate, shuddering pattern of Odile trying—and utterly failing—to catch her breath against Fen's skin.

When the wave finally crested and began to recede, she stayed right where she was, slumped heavily against Fen's chest, her forehead resting on their collarbone. Her legs felt completely like jelly, held upright mostly by the solid press of Fen's body pinning her to the door.

A muffled, breathless snort of laughter escaped her, warm and humid against Fen's neck. 

"Okay," she whispered, her voice totally ruined, raspy and trembling with aftershocks. She slowly lifted her head, blinking through the strands of hair stuck to her damp forehead, her eyes glassy, dark, and utterly triumphant. "If that music hadn't kicked in right then, we would've had an audience of at least four people."

She reached down with shaking fingers, lightly tugging on the hem of Fen's shirt with a lazy, wicked grin. 

"Now," she murmured, leaning up to press a messy, grateful kiss to the corner of their mouth, "what were you saying about being persuasive?"

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Stop worrying about the noise," she says, "and get on with it," so I get her leg up over my hip and stop being careful about how much sound either of us is making.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The sudden shift in leverage wiped whatever clever retort Odile had left clean out of her head. 

A sharp, unrestrained gasp tore from her throat as Fen pressed into her, the full weight and heat of them knocking her back against the door with a solid, echoing thud. The questionable brass latch gave a tiny, metallic rattle in its housing, but Odile couldn't have cared less. Any lingering urge to be discreet dissolved on the spot.

She threw her head back, her knuckles whitening where she gripped the front of Fen's shirt, her nails biting right through the fabric. Her other leg scrambled for purchase against the slippery tile floor, only to hook tighter around Fen’s waist instead, anchoring herself to the sheer, relentless momentum. 

"Fen—" she choked out, her voice a wrecked, breathy rasp that cracked halfway through their name. 

Every solid, unhurried press drove a fresh, shuddering sound out of her chest, rhythmically beating in time with the creaking floorboards and the heavy, muffled bass shaking the walls. She didn't bother clamping a hand over her mouth this time; instead, she tangled both hands in Fen's hair, pulling them down into a bruising, desperate kiss that was all friction, heat, and frantic, ragged breathing. 

When she finally pulled back just an inch for air, her forehead rested against Fen's, her eyes wide, glassy, and completely alight with ruined amusement. 

"Okay," she breathed, laughing weakly around a helpless, hitching moan as Fen adjusted their grip, "if Maya... if Maya has to kick down this door... I am blaming the whole damn thing on you."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Then I'll have a hell of a story to tell," I grunt, pushing deeper and making the door groan in its frame. My mouth finds hers again, swallowing the next moan before it can really escape.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The groan of the doorframe barely registered over the roaring rush in her ears, swallowed instantly by Fen's mouth. Odile melted into the collision, a muffled, helpless hum vibrating deep in her throat that she couldn't have stopped if she tried. 

She wrapped her arms desperately around Fen's neck, her leg locked tight around their hip, matching every hard, steady press with an abandoned urgency of her own. The sheer heat trapped in the tiny, humid room made her skin slick where they pressed together, every brush of fabric and friction sending another jolt straight to her core. 

When Fen's mouth finally broke from hers for a jagged gasp of air, Odile didn't even attempt to stifle the wrecked, breathy sound that tumbled out into the space between them. 

"You're going to break... her damn door," she gasped out against Fen's collarbone, her voice completely ruined and trembling with a helpless, giddy rush of adrenaline. 

The frantic buildup coiling low in her stomach snapped taut, catching her entirely off guard with how fast and fiercely it tore through her. Odile's nails bit deep into the muscle of Fen's back, her whole body going rigid against the wood as she threw her head back, completely blind to the music downstairs, the creaking hinges, or whoever might be standing just on the other side of the latch.

"Fen—" she choked out, a raw, shuddering gasp that was loud, entirely undisguised, and thoroughly impossible to mistake for anything else.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: Somebody tries the handle and neither of us stops. "Don't," she says, meaning don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The brass latch rattled sharply against the strike plate, vibrating directly against Odile’s spine. On the other side of the thin wood, the doorknob turned, met resistance, and gave another impatient, metallic jerk. 

A sharp, electric bolt of adrenaline slammed through Odile, making every nerve ending ignite at once. Instead of shrinking away, her fingers twisted viciously into Fen’s shirt, hauling them flush against her. 

"Don't," she rasped, the word practically spat against Fen’s jaw, hot and completely unhinged. 

She tilted her hips up to take every inch of the next hard, unrelenting drive into her, her breath sawing in and out of her lungs in ragged, shallow bursts. Outside the door, a muffled voice muttered something indistinct over the bass—a confused, annoyed curse—followed by the heavy scuff of shoes hovering right on the threshold. 

The proximity was unbearable; it pushed Odile straight past any hope of control. She dug her heels into the floor and Fen's hip, arching hard off the wood, chasing the deep, punishing friction that rattled the doorframe with every heavy press. 

"Fen, *fuck*—" she choked out, her whisper completely fracturing. 

She clamped her mouth against Fen’s neck, biting down hard enough to leave a mark as the peak slammed into her with ruthless force. Her inside muscles clenched down tight and unrelenting around Fen, a violent, rolling wave of contractions that made her whole body shudder from her ribs to her toes. Her muffled, broken cry vibrated against Fen's sweat-slicked skin, loud enough that the person lingering in the hall undoubtedly heard the rustle and the unmistakable, rhythmic creak of the floorboards.

Outside, the footsteps finally shifted, hurried and distinctly embarrassed, retreating quickly toward the stairs. 

Odile felt the vibration of Fen losing their own control against her, the sudden, desperate rhythm of their hips snapping hard and fast until they buried themselves deep and shuddered through their own release. She held on with everything she had, her arms locked around Fen's shoulders, anchoring them both as their breathing raggedly filled the tiny, steamy room.

For a long moment, nobody moved. The bass thumped steadily from below, and the door stayed locked, groaning slightly as Odile’s weight finally sagged against it. 

She let out a long, trembling breath that unraveled into a helpless, silent shake of her shoulders. She turned her face in the crook of Fen's neck, resting her burning forehead against their damp skin, her chest heaving in tandem with theirs. 

"They definitely heard that," she whispered, her voice completely blown out, dripping with breathless, thoroughly unrepentant amusement. Her fingers stroked lazily up the back of Fen's neck, tugging lightly at their hair. "Ten out of ten on the persuasiveness, though."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I laugh, shaky and spent, my forehead still resting against the door. "Told you I could be persuasive," I murmur, my voice rough. I pull back just enough to see her face, her cheeks flushed and eyes bright. "You okay? Door held."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile let her leg slide slowly down from Fen’s hip, wincing with a quiet, delighted groan as her bare foot hit the cold tile. Her knees felt entirely theoretical, and if Fen hadn’t still been leaning close, she probably would have slid right down the wood of the door.

"I think the door deserves a raise," she whispered, her voice rough, hoarse, and thoroughly ruined. 

She reached up to brush a damp strand of hair off Fen’s forehead, her fingers still trembling faintly from the adrenaline. A lazy, entirely self-satisfied grin spread across her flushed face as she looked up at them, her chest rising and falling in deep, uneven breaths. 

"I'm fantastic," she said, leaning up to press a lingering, salty kiss to the corner of Fen's mouth. "A little concerned about whatever poor soul just had to listen to me lose my mind on the other side of that wood, but mostly fantastic."

She turned slightly, leaning one hip against the edge of the small sink to take some of the weight off her shaking legs. Looking in the fogged-up mirror, she caught sight of her thoroughly disheveled reflection—hair wild, lips swollen, shirt completely crooked—and let out another breathless, smothered snort of laughter.

"Okay," she murmured, gesturing vaguely between the two of them with one hand while trying to straighten her collar with the other. "Give it to me straight. How long do we have to hide in here before we can go back downstairs and pretend we were just... I don't know, looking for extra hand towels?"

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I glance at the foggy mirror, then back at her. "Think we can make it ten minutes without falling asleep?" I grab my discarded shirt off the floor. "We should probably find your shoe first."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile looked down at her one bare foot, then craned her neck to scan the small patch of floor. Her stray shoe was wedged sideways between the base of the pedestal sink and the edge of a laundry hamper, looking like it had been violently evicted.

"There is zero chance I'm staying awake if we go sit on Maya's couch," she admitted, hooking a toe around the shoe to drag it closer before using Fen's shoulder as a crutch to step back into it. 

She wiped a clear circle into the steam on the mirror with her forearm, taking a critical look at the deep, telltale flush still painted across her throat and chest. She reached up with both hands, attempting to smooth down the static and sweat-tangled mess of her hair, though her efforts mostly just made it look intentionally wrecked rather than accidentally disheveled.

"Hand towels are definitely off the table," she murmured, meeting Fen's eyes in the glass with a slow, wicked grin. "We look like we just survived a bar fight with the shower curtain."

She turned around, leaning back against the sink again with her arms crossed, watching Fen pull their shirt back on. Her pulse was finally settling back to something resembling normal, though the corner of her mouth refused to stop twitching with amused satisfaction.

"You think whoever tried that handle is still hovering at the bottom of the stairs to see who comes out?" she asked, keeping her voice down to an actual whisper this time. "Because if they are, you're walking out first."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I pull my shirt on, then lean over to retrieve hers from the floor. "Deal. But if it's Maya, you owe me a drink." I hand it to her, nodding toward the door. "Ready to face the music?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
They were most of the way through and both of them knew it, in the way you know a piece of music is nearly over before it ends.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
A faint, knowing breath escaped Sable, not quite a laugh, though the corner of her mouth ticked up. Five years meant she knew the exact texture of Ines’s defiance—where the line sat between stubborn pride and genuine capacity. 

"I wasn't asking for permission to stop," Sable murmured, her voice dropping into that low, steady register she kept for the deepest parts of the work. "I was just making sure you were still with me."

She shifted her stance, letting the weight settle back into her heels. The implement in her hand lifted, deliberately slow, giving Ines every second to feel the anticipation before the descent. 

"Green it is," she said softly, and brought it down with clean, unbroken precision.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: The impact made me gasp, sharp and sudden, but I didn't flinch away. "Still with you," I managed, breathless but firm. My fingers tightened against the restraints. "Don't... don't go gentle."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Never gentle when you ask like that," Sable replied, her tone level and unhurried. 

She took a half-step closer, reading the line of Ines's spine and the strain against the leather at the wrists. Five years had taught her the exact rhythm of Ines's breathing when the endorphins began to peak—the tight, shallow hitch that needed to be driven deep into the lungs before the next mark landed.

Sable didn't rush. She allowed the sting to bloom fully across the skin, letting the silence stretch just long enough for the ache to settle in. 

Then she drew the implement back, measured the angle with absolute certainty, and delivered a second strike, heavier than the first, clean and resonant against the heated skin. 

Without breaking the rhythm, Sable stepped in close, setting the leather aside and pressing the flat, firm palm of her left hand directly against the small of Ines's back. She leaned just enough of her own weight into the touch to ground the tremor, keeping her mouth near the shell of Ines's ear.

"Breathe into it," she murmured, steady as an anchor. "Right into my hand. All the way down."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable felt the strain travel up Ines's forearms to the hardware, the familiar, stubborn tug against leather and steel that meant Ines was hovering right at the precipice. She didn't stop her from pulling; she simply pressed her palm a fraction firmer against the heated skin of her back, letting her body heat absorb some of that restless energy.

"Greedy," Sable murmured against the curve of Ines's neck, her voice quiet, entirely devoid of hurry. "You'd stay balanced on the knife's edge all night if I let you."

She lingered there for one full breath, letting Ines feel the solid, immovable weight of her presence, before she slowly stepped back. 

The implement felt familiar and heavy in her grip as she lifted it again. She didn't rush into the motion; five years of doing this meant she knew the exact value of the silence right before the end. She let the room go still, save for the sound of their breathing, giving Ines every second to brace, to want it, and to take it.

"Two more," Sable said, steady and absolute. "Then we come down. Take them."

She planted her feet, drew the leather back, and brought it down with deep, resonant force, letting the crack of it echo off the walls.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I suck in a sharp breath through my teeth, my shoulders tensing against the impact. "One more," I say, voice tight. "Just... give me a second."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable lowered the implement to her side, letting the tip rest quietly against her thigh. She didn’t press or crowd; she simply stood there, an unmoving point of reference in the room, watching the hard rise and fall of Ines’s shoulders.

"Take your time," Sable said softly. "The room isn't going anywhere."

She counted the seconds by the rhythm of Ines’s breathing, tracking the micro-shifts in her posture—the slow release of the initial shock, the gradual settling of the spine, the deliberate way Ines gathered herself back up to meet it. Sable knew the exact threshold where the body shifted from bracing against pain to actively opening to receive it. 

When she saw that slight drop in the shoulders, the subtle, steadying exhale that signaled ready, Sable shifted her grip.

She didn't give a verbal warning; Ines already knew it was coming. Sable drew the leather back in a clean, wide arc and delivered the final strike—heavy, deep, and perfectly placed, leaving a sharp, ringing finality in the air.

Without a pause, Sable set the implement down on the nearby tray, the dull clatter marking the definitive end of the scene. 

She immediately stepped into Ines’s space, wrapping both arms around her from behind, pressing her chest flush against Ines's back. Her hands slid up to cover Ines’s restrained wrists, fingers curling over leather and skin to take the tension out of the bindings.

"That's it," Sable murmured, her lips against Ines's temple, her voice a low, warm hum. "All done. Just breathe now. I've got you."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable didn’t let the silence cool too quickly. She kept her weight anchored against Ines, letting the warmth of her own body seep into the raw heat rising from Ines's skin. 

Her mouth moved with deliberate, unhurried intention—trailing slow, open-mouthed kisses along the line where Ines’s neck met her shoulder, pressing firmly enough to ground the tremors rather than tease. One hand slid down Ines’s flank, broad and firm, mapping the hard-won tension in the muscle before soothing over it with steady, heavy strokes that coaxed the tight edges to soften.

"Let go of it," Sable murmured against the damp skin behind Ines's ear, her voice a low, gravelly vibration. "I have the weight now. Stop holding it up."

With practiced, mechanical ease that didn't break the intimacy of her hold, Sable reached up to the hardware. Her fingers worked the buckles smoothly, unfastening the first cuff without letting Ines's arm drop. She caught the wrist in her palm, gently massaging the crease where the leather had dug in, working circulation back into the fingers before reaching up to release the other side.

Once both wrists were free, Sable gathered Ines back against her chest, wrapping one solid arm around her middle to bear whatever weight Ines needed to give up. 

"Stay right here," Sable whispered, pressing a lingering kiss to the side of Ines's jaw. "Just heavy. Just breathing."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I lean back into her, boneless and grateful. My hands come up to cover hers where they rest on my stomach. "You always know exactly when to stop."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable tightened her arm across Ines’s middle, squeezing gently, feeling the slow, heavy drop of Ines’s weight settle entirely into her frame. She rested her cheek against Ines’s temple, letting out a long, quiet breath that fluttered the loose strands of hair between them.

"Five years of studying the syllabus," Sable murmured, the dry humor soft around the edges. "I’d be a terrible student if I hadn't figured it out by now."

She didn't let the stillness linger to the point of a chill. The raw heat in the room would dissipate quickly, and Sable was already tracking the telltale signs of the adrenaline draining away.

Sable slowly shifted her footing, turning Ines gently within the circle of her arms so she could guide her down toward the low pile of floor cushions and blankets they had prepared earlier. She kept one arm firmly around Ines’s waist the entire way down, ensuring she didn't have to carry her own balance.

Once they were seated, Sable reached out and snagged the thick, heavy wool blanket from the edge of the mat, shaking it out with one hand and draping it securely over Ines’s shoulders, tucking the edges in close around her chest and lap. 

Without breaking contact, she picked up the prepared glass of water from the side table, testing the temperature against her palm before holding it out, waiting to see if Ines wanted to hold it or needed it brought to her lips.

"Small sips first," Sable said, her voice dropping back into that quiet, practical register. "How's your head feeling?"

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable kept her rhythm deliberately merciless, entirely unfazed by the muffled swearing. She had one hand anchored firmly on Ines’s hip, fingers digging in just enough to keep her pinned in place, while her other hand reached up to gently, firmly peel Ines's forearm away from her teeth.

"Don't hide it," Sable murmured against the slick heat of her skin, her breath hot and steady. "Let me hear it."

She didn't pull back this time. Instead of the agonizing pause, Sable leaned all the way into the momentum, altering the angle and pressure with absolute, devastating precision. She gave no room to regroup, no space to brace, driving the pace relentlessly past the threshold she had been teasing for the last ten minutes. 

With her free hand, Sable slid her fingers through Ines’s hair, anchoring her head, holding her entirely steady while she finished what she started. 

"Now," Sable commanded softly against her, a low, gravelly vibration that left no room for doubt. "Give it up. Right now."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I choke on a sound that's half-sob, half-cursed-out praise, and go completely rigid against her. It takes a long, shuddering minute before I can slump forward, breath ragged. "You're a menace."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable took the full, heavy slump of Ines’s weight against her chest, letting out a low, breathy hum against the crook of her neck. A faint, satisfied smile touched the corner of her mouth, though she didn’t waste time reveling in it; the hard work was done, and the shift into looking after the aftermath was instinctive.

"I'm *your* menace," Sable murmured, pressing a soft, lingering kiss right below Ines’s ear before trailing her lips down the tight line of her shoulder. "And you got exactly what you were swearing for."

She didn't let Ines linger in the cool air for more than a few seconds. With practiced, careful movements, Sable shifted her grip, scooping Ines closer into her lap to keep her from listing sideways as the adrenaline bled out. 

Reaching out with one long arm, Sable dragged the heavy wool blanket across the floor, shaking out the folds and wrapping it securely around Ines’s shoulders, bundling the edges tight across her chest until only her face and neck were exposed to the room. 

She kept one arm locked around Ines’s waist, anchoring her against the steady rise and fall of her own ribs, while her free hand reached for the glass of water resting on the low table nearby. 

"Breathe," Sable instructed gently, her voice slipping into that quiet, domestic cadence. She brought the rim of the glass lightly to Ines’s lower lip. "Drink first, name-call later. Just a small swallow."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable went entirely still. The word—the phrase they had agreed on years ago, reserved exclusively for the absolute limit—hung in the air with the weight of a signed contract.

She didn't hesitate or ask for confirmation. If Ines invoked the phrase, Sable answered it in full.

Without a word, Sable set the water glass down onto the table with a crisp click. She peeled back the wool blanket, tossing it aside, and shifted her grip to haul Ines up against her, resetting her position on the mat with absolute, unyielding firmness. The softness drained from her posture instantly, replaced by the cool, exacting focus of someone delivering on a promise down to the letter.

Sable reached down and retrieved the heavy leather implement from the floor. She stepped back just far enough to clear the arc, her stance wide, balanced, and immovable. 

"Eyes open," Sable commanded, her voice dropping into a flat, absolute register that brooked no argument. "Look at me and take it."

She drew the leather back and brought it down without a shred of hesitation—hard, clean, and devastatingly heavy. 

She didn't wait for the sound to fade or the tremor to settle. She kept the rhythm relentless, delivering three more rapid, driving strikes in flawless succession, placing every single one with ruthless precision across the heated skin, forcing the breath entirely out of the room until there was nothing left of the scene to give. 

The last crack echoed off the walls, sharp and final.

The moment it landed, the switch flipped. 

Sable dropped the implement, letting it clatter away across the floorboards. In the same breath, she closed the distance, wrapping both arms around Ines and pulling her violently close, taking the full brunt of her weight as she brought them both down onto the thick pile of cushions. 

She dragged the wool blanket back over both of them, tucking it tight around Ines’s shoulders and back, cocooning the heat inside. Her hands moved constantly—firm, heavy, smoothing down the tight muscles, one palm pressing flat against the base of Ines’s neck while her other arm locked across her middle, anchoring her securely against her chest.

"I've got you," Sable breathed, pressing her mouth firmly against the damp hair at Ines's temple, her own heart hammering against Ines's spine. "It's done. That's all of it. Every last bit."

She reached out blindly, finding the glass of water and keeping it close at hand, but for now she just held on, rocking slightly with the rhythm of their breathing. 

"Now I'm kind," Sable murmured softly, her lips brushing Ines's ear. "Just breathe into me. You're completely safe."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: My vision whites out for a second and I sag forward, held up only by her arms. My hands shake as I reach back to grip her thigh. "Christ, Sable."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable covered Ines’s shaking hand on her thigh with her own broad palm, squeezing hard enough to give the tremor a solid edge to press against. She didn’t shift or pull away; she stayed completely anchored beneath Ines’s dead weight, letting her chest rise and fall in a slow, exaggerated rhythm to give Ines a steady cadence to sync to.

"I know," Sable murmured, her voice a low, steady hum right against the shell of Ines's ear. "I’ve got all of you. Let your head drop."

She pulled the heavy wool blanket tighter, tucking the thick edges under Ines’s chin and around her shoulders to trap the sudden spike of heat before the sweat turned cold. With her free hand, Sable reached up to cradle the back of Ines's neck, her fingers warm and firm against the damp hair at her hairline, gently massaging the base of the skull.

"Don't fight the spin," Sable instructed quietly, unhurried and completely calm. "Close your eyes if the room is tilted. Let it pass through you."

She stayed like that for several long seconds, weathering the brunt of the physiological crash, feeling the heavy, ragged breaths slowly start to level out. Once the violent shaking in Ines’s fingers subsided into a dull tremor, Sable brushed her lips against the damp curve of Ines’s temple.

"Look at me when you're back in the room," she whispered softly. "No rush. Just whenever the color comes back."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: Afterwards she gets the restraints off and puts a blanket over me before I've finished shaking, and I let her, and neither of us says anything for a while. (OOC: write both halves properly -- the end of the scene and the aftercare, no fade between them.)

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable unclipped the remaining hardware with swift, efficient familiarity, taking the full, slack weight of Ines’s arms before they could drop. She worked the buckles free, tossing the leather cuffs aside onto the floor where they landed with a soft, dull thud, and immediately took Ines’s wrists into her warm palms. Her thumbs moved in firm, rhythmic circles over the deep red impressions left in the skin, pressing hard enough to encourage the blood back into the numbed fingertips.

She didn't speak. Ines was still vibrating with residual adrenaline, tremors running deep through the muscle, and Sable knew better than to clutter the quiet with unnecessary words. 

Sable shifted their weight, pulling Ines down fully onto the layered quilts and floor cushions, arranging them so Ines was tucked securely between her parted legs. She gathered the heavy, dark wool blanket, shaking out the thick folds, and wrapped it completely around Ines’s frame, tucking the hem snugly beneath her thighs and pulling the top up to her collarbones until Ines was entirely insulated against the cooling air of the room.

Sable settled her own back against the wall, wrapping her arms securely over the blanket across Ines’s chest. She hooked her chin over Ines’s shoulder, letting her steady, even breaths warm the nape of Ines’s neck, keeping her anchor immovable while the physical tremors ran their natural course.

They stayed like that in the unbroken silence for several minutes, the only sound the slow easing of Ines’s lungs against Sable’s ribs. Sable monitored the shift in skin temperature through the wool, waiting until the cold, clammy sweat began to give way to steady warmth.

Only when the hard shaking reduced to a faint, occasional twitch did Sable reach for the low table. She picked up the heavy glass of water, tilting it carefully to test the flow, and brought it around to Ines's line of sight.

"Small sips," Sable murmured quietly against her cheek, keeping her voice low and even. She pressed the cool rim lightly against Ines's lower lip, ready to hold the weight of the glass entirely on her own. "Just wet your mouth first."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let her tip the water into my mouth, swallowing once before I turn my head away. My voice comes out rough. "I hate how good you are at that."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable gave a faint, quiet huff of air against Ines’s temple—the nearest thing to a laugh she allowed when they were still this raw—and set the glass back down on the floor within easy reach.

"No, you don't," Sable murmured, her voice steady and warm. "You'd be furious if I was mediocre at it."

She tightened her arms over the wool bundle, squeezing just enough to compress the lingering tremors out of Ines's shoulders. One hand slid free to smooth back the damp strands of hair stuck to Ines’s forehead, her fingers cool against the fevered skin, mapping the slow, steady cooling of her face.

Sable rested her chin back against Ines's shoulder, letting the silence settle between them again for a few long seconds, giving the water a moment to hit. 

"Two more sips in a minute," Sable said softly, her palm coming to rest flat and heavy against Ines’s sternum, feeling the rhythm beneath the ribs slowly finding its baseline. "How are the hands feeling? Any pins and needles left in the fingers?"

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "No pins," I say, flexing my fingers slowly. The blood's moving again. I turn my head, just enough to see her profile. "Don't go anywhere."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable shifted slightly, turning her head just enough to meet Ines’s gaze before pressing a firm, lingering kiss to the high curve of her cheekbone. 

"Not a chance," Sable said, her voice a quiet, gravelly rumble. "You couldn't pry me off this floor with a crowbar right now."

She adjusted her grip over the thick wool, pulling Ines a fraction tighter against her chest, letting her know through sheer weight and friction that she wasn't shifting an inch. Her hand slid under the edge of the blanket, finding Ines’s newly warmed fingers and threading their hands together, testing the grip with a slow, grounding squeeze. 

"We're staying right here until the room stops humming and your temperature levels out," Sable murmured, resting her jaw lightly against the crown of Ines’s head. She kept her breathing deliberately deep and slow, a steady anchor for them both. 

After a quiet moment, she reached out with her free hand, retrieving the glass from the floorboards and bringing it back around.

"Another swallow," Sable instructed softly, bumping the cool glass gently against Ines's knuckle before lifting it toward her lips. "Then you can lean back and close your eyes."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I take the second sip, letting the water sit in my mouth for a second before swallowing. I let my head fall back against her shoulder, eyes closed. "Stay until I wake up."
