dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack flicked the last of the red off her blade and gave the cloak a final wipe before letting it drop. She looked at Corvin properly then — the wrist, the face, the not-moving.

"Not yours," she said. Not a question. "Good. Keeps the tally simple." She stood, knees complaining the way they always did now, and rolled her shoulders once.

The noise from past the cart hadn't stopped. Wet, ragged, going nowhere. She'd heard enough of that sound over enough years to know it wasn't going to resolve itself into either living or dying on its own schedule — it would just keep on, however long the body decided to take about it, unless someone made a decision.

"He's not calling for his mother anymore, so he's past being scared and into being tired," she said, matter-of-fact as weather. "That's usually when it drags." She wiped her hands on her own trousers, which were somehow less filthy than the cloak had been. "You don't have to be the one. I'll do it. But somebody's walking over there before the light goes, because I'm not sleeping forty feet from that."

She held out a hand, not for the knife — just waiting, in case he wanted to hand it over rather than say it out loud.

"Your call. Just make it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take a slow breath and push myself off the tree I'd been leaning against. "No. I'll do it." My voice sounds steadier than I feel. I don't take her offered hand. "Just... give me a minute."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack gave a small nod and let her hand drop, no offense taken. "Take two," she said. "The dying part'll wait."

She crouched back down by the dead man and started going through his pockets with the unhurried efficiency of someone who'd done it a thousand times, not because she was hard-hearted about the timing, just because there was no reason to waste the light doing nothing. A few coins, a whetstone, a folded letter she didn't bother reading. She set it all in a pile without much interest.

"When you go," she said, not looking up, "go in from the side, not the front. He'll flinch if he sees you coming and that just makes it worse for both of you. Knife under the jaw, angled up, or across the throat if you'd rather not look at his face while you do it. Either's fine. Don't saw. One clean motion, then you're done and you can stop thinking about it."

She pocketed the coins, left the letter for the crows.

"And don't apologize to him. I've seen men do that — kneel down, say sorry, sorry, like it changes the accounting. It doesn't. It just makes you feel like you did something worse than you did." She finally glanced up at him. "You didn't do anything worse. He got unlucky in a fight same as the other five did. This is just the part where the luck runs all the way out."

She straightened, wiping her hands again out of habit more than need.

"Minute's yours. I'll start on the cart."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack paused with a strap half-undone on the cart, considering the question properly instead of just answering it.

"Didn't get a good look, only heard it," she admitted. "But I've heard enough of these to guess. That sound — the wet catch on every breath — that's gut or chest, something that's filling up with what shouldn't be there. Won't kill him fast. Might take till morning, might take two days if he's stubborn." She went back to the strap. "So. Bad enough that he's dying regardless. Whether it's mercy or easier just depends on whether you're asking for his sake or yours."

She got the strap loose, glanced back at him.

"Honest answer — it's probably both, and there's no shame in that. Man in that state isn't getting carried anywhere, isn't getting fixed by anyone we've got. All you're deciding is how many more hours of it he goes through before the same ending arrives." She shrugged, the motion economical. "I'd want someone to do it quick for me. Most would. That's not you being merciful so much as you being decent. Doesn't have to be more complicated than that."

She nodded toward the cart, toward the dark starting to gather at the treeline, giving the subject room to breathe.

"Minute's still running. I'm not counting it against you."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
I nod, not really at her, just to the air. "Decent." I test the word under my breath. It feels hollow, but maybe that's just the cold coming in.

My feet start moving before I decide. Around the side of the cart, like she said. I pull my knife. The handle's slick with sweat. Mine, this time.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't follow. She stayed by the cart, hands busy with the strap she didn't really need to be undoing anymore, giving him the back of her attention because sometimes that was the kindest thing you could offer a man walking toward something like that — not to be watched doing it.

She heard him circle wide, boots quiet on the wet grass. Heard the ragged breathing change pitch when the dying man caught sight or sound of him, a stutter of fear even past exhaustion. Heard Corvin's voice, low, saying something she didn't catch and didn't try to.

Then a short scuffle of movement. Then nothing. The good kind of nothing — the kind where the sound just stops instead of trailing off.

Wrack let out a breath she hadn't noticed holding and went back to the cart in earnest, pulling out a coil of rope, a sack of something that turned out to be dried apples, half a wheel of cheese gone hard at the edges but fine underneath. Ordinary work. She kept at it, giving him time to walk back on his own legs instead of having her stand there watching him do it.

When he came around the side of the cart she didn't look up right away — just said, "Cheese is good. Better than we've had in a week," and held a piece out to him without ceremony, like that was the next thing that needed doing and always had been.

Only once he'd taken it, or not taken it, did she actually look at his face.

"Clean?" she asked — meaning the cut, not his conscience. That was a different question, and one she wasn't going to ask him tonight.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack set down the cheese and came around to look, unhurried, the way she'd look at a wound on a horse or a tear in a saddle — something to be assessed, not flinched from.

She tipped his chin toward the last of the light with two fingers, businesslike, no more intimate than checking a knot.

"There," she said. "Clean line, under the jaw like I said, up through here." She traced the air an inch above the cut without touching it again. "See how there's not much spread to it? That's good. That's the artery going first and going fast — means it was over before he had time to properly feel it as anything more than a shock. If you'd caught muscle and missed the vessel you'd have a mess and a man still breathing under your hand for a minute you didn't want. You didn't do that. You did the other thing."

She straightened up, wiping her fingers on her trousers out of habit rather than need — there wasn't much blood on them, which was itself the answer to the question he hadn't quite asked.

"His face is slack, not twisted. That's not always the case. Sometimes they go with their eyes wide and their mouth open like they're still arguing with it. His isn't. That's you, not luck." She looked at him rather than the body now. "That's what you're looking at. A job done properly. Nothing more sinister in it than that."

She picked the cheese back up, held it out a second time.

"Eat something. Won't undo it, won't make it heavier either. It's just what comes next."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take the cheese. It's dry, salty. I chew and swallow without tasting it. "Didn't apologize," I say, like that matters.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack chewed her own piece of cheese, considering that the way she'd consider a report on weather or terrain — useful information, nothing to make a fuss over.

"Good," she said. "Told you not to." She swallowed, wiped a crumb from the corner of her mouth with her thumb. "Man doesn't need your sorry on his way out. He needs it quick and he needs it to mean something, and yours did both. The apology's for you, not him — it's you trying to hand off some of the weight to a man who can't carry it anymore. Doesn't work. Just makes you feel like you asked permission for something you were always going to do anyway."

She glanced back at the body once, without sentiment, the way you'd check a knot had held.

"You said something to him, though. Before." Not a question exactly, but close to one. "I heard your voice, didn't hear the words. That's fine — whatever it was, it's yours, you don't owe me it. Just noting you didn't go in silent. Some men do. Some men need to talk their way into it. Neither's wrong."

She turned back to the cart, resuming the inventory with the same unbothered rhythm as before — rope, apples, a second wheel of cheese she hadn't found yet, probably.

"You'll think about it tonight. Maybe tomorrow too. That's normal, and it'll thin out on its own, doesn't need help from you fussing at it." A pause, then, dry: "If it doesn't thin out — if it's still sitting on your chest in a month — you tell me. Not because I've got a cure. Just because carrying that alone is the part that actually breaks people, not the doing of it."

She held up the second wheel of cheese, found after all, with something almost like satisfaction.

"Eat more. You look like a man who forgot he has a body."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at him a beat longer than necessary, checking whether that was the cheese talking or something real. Decided it was real.

"Fine," she said, and sat back down on the cart's edge like she was settling in to tell a story, because in a way she was. "Straight, then. No dressing it up, no leaving it out."

She held up a hand, fingers spread, using it the way another person might use a map.

"Spear goes in slower than an arrow and faster than you'd think, given the size of it. If it catches you low, under the ribs, it's punching through muscle first — that part you'll feel like a punch, big and dull, before the pain properly arrives. Pain comes about half a breath late. Always does. Then it's into the gut proper, and that's where it gets interesting, because the gut isn't one thing, it's a coil of tubes packed in tight, and a blade going through doesn't ask which ones it's opening."

She tapped her own belly, illustrating without ceremony.

"If it nicks the bowel, you get shit in the wound. Not blood — shit. That's the smell you notice before you notice anything else, and it's the reason a gut wound kills you slow even when it doesn't kill you fast. Filth in the belly rots a man from the inside over days. Fever, then worse fever, then he stops making sense, then he stops at all. That's the one that took two days to finish him, most likely — the sound you heard wasn't blood filling him up quick, it was air and fluid where they don't belong, whistling."

She let that sit a second, then went on, unhurried.

"If it catches higher, into the liver or the big vessels behind it, that's faster and uglier in a different way — man can go from standing to grey in under a minute, more blood on the ground than you'd think a body holds. Doesn't hurt less. Might hurt more, honestly, since there's no time for the shock to dull it before it's over."

She met his eyes.

"Either way, a man run through the gut is not a man you patch and march on. You can pack it, you can pray over it, doesn't matter. If you ever put a spear into someone that way, you're not wounding them. You're deciding how long their dying takes and how much of it they're awake for." A pause. "That's what it does. You asked straight, that's straight."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at my hands, still clean except for the grit under my nails. "Heard the whistle," I say quietly. "Didn't know what it was."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack nodded slowly, like he'd just confirmed something she already suspected.

"Now you do," she said. "Next time you'll know before you get close enough to see. That's not nothing — that's the kind of thing keeps you from walking up on a man thinking he's just winded when he's actually got an hour left and a knife hidden under his hip."

She picked a bit of grit off the cheese wheel with her thumbnail, flicked it away.

"Most men go their whole lives never learning that sound. You'll carry it now. Won't feel like a gift tonight. Might be one, eventually — the kind of knowing that keeps you breathing a season longer than the fellow next to you who never bothered to ask." She looked at him steadily. "That's the only kind of use grief like this has. It doesn't undo anything. It just teaches, if you let it, instead of just sitting on you."

She held out the cheese again, third time now, patient as the ground.

"Eat. Then sleep near the fire, not off on your own tonight. Not because I think you'll do something stupid — you won't. Just easier not to lie there alone with a whistle in your ears for company."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack set the cheese down without a word and stood.

She walked with him back around the cart, matching his pace, not rushing it. When they reached the man — and he was still a man, still breathing that wet ragged sound, eyes finding them both in the dark with the particular animal alertness of something that knows it's being decided about — she crouched on the other side of him, mirroring Corvin's position, so the man had both their faces to look at instead of just the one.

"Right," she said, low. "Under the jaw, like you had it before. Blade in first, then the drag, angled up toward the ear. You'll feel it go through easy — there's not much there to stop it, that's the whole point of the spot."

He set the knife where she'd told him. She watched his hand, not the man's face.

"Now."

The blade went in. She kept talking, steady, the way you'd talk a green soldier through a march he didn't think he could finish.

"That's the artery. You'll feel the give change — soft, then a kind of release, like cutting into something under pressure. Hear that? That's air escaping past it, not him trying to speak. He can't, anymore." A beat, counting without looking like she was counting. "Blood's coming fast, that's the artery doing its work for you now, you don't have to do anything else. Hold it steady. Don't pull back yet."

The man's chest hitched, once, hard, then began to slow — not peacefully, just mechanically, like something running down.

"That sound — the rattle — that's not pain, whatever it looks like. That's just air finding the wrong way out of a body that's stopped caring which way is right. His eyes are still open but there's nothing behind them working anymore, not really. Give it another few seconds."

She didn't touch Corvin, didn't touch the knife. Just stayed close enough that he could feel he wasn't alone in it, and kept her voice level and low until the chest went still and stayed still, and there was nothing left for either of them to listen to but the wind in the treeline and their own two sets of breathing, both far too loud.

"There," she said finally, quiet now. "That's all of it. Nothing left out. That's what it is, every time — fast at the end, however slow it feels while you're in it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I pull the knife out. My hand's shaking, but the blade comes clean. "Thanks," I say. The word doesn't cover it, but I don't have another one.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack reached over and closed the man's eyes with two fingers, the same unceremonious gesture she'd have used to shut a door that kept swinging in the wind. No prayer to it. Just tidying.

"Don't need to be a bigger word than that," she said. "Thanks does fine." She got up, knees cracking, and offered him a hand — this time actually meaning it, meaning *up*, not the knife-taking gesture from before.

"You did it clean the second time, too. Faster than you think you did, from where I was sitting. Panic makes minutes feel like hours. Wasn't hours." She glanced down at the body once more, matter-of-fact. "We'll drag him with the others before we sleep. Not out of respect, particularly — just don't want the smell changing overnight, and foxes get bold if you leave meat sitting."

She started back toward the fire, then stopped, half-turned, because the next part mattered more than the cheese did.

"Whistle's going to be in your ears tonight. That's fine. Let it play. Don't fight it and don't feed it either — don't lie there running the whole thing again and again like you missed something. You didn't miss anything. You did it right, twice in one evening, which is more than most manage their first month."

A pause, and something almost gentle crept into the dry of her voice, though she'd have denied it if asked.

"I'll be at the fire same as always. You don't have to talk. Just don't go quiet on your own out here past the cart — that's the only rule tonight."

She walked on, leaving him the choice of following in his own time, same as she had before.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped walking. She turned back, looked at him sitting there on his heels in the dark with the dead man cooling in front of him, and she understood then that "thanks" hadn't been the end of it — it had just been the thing he'd said to fill the space before he found the real question.

She came back and sat down on the ground beside him, not crouching this time, actually sitting, knees be damned, because this wasn't going to be quick.

"Alright," she said. "The rest."

She was quiet a moment, choosing where to start, the way you'd choose where to cut into something.

"He'll go stiff by morning. Not right away — few hours yet, the body doesn't know it's finished for a while, muscles keep arguing about it. By the time we're eating breakfast he'll be hard to move, arms won't bend right, and if we've got to shift him it'll be like moving furniture, not a man. That's not cruelty, that's just what dead is. Nobody warns you it's that ordinary."

She picked at the grass beside her, not looking at the body, looking at her own hands instead.

"He'll smell before midday tomorrow if it's warm. Sweetish first, then not sweet at all. You get used to knowing the difference between a fresh one and a two-day one by smell alone, same as you'd know bread's gone off. I'm not telling you that to be grim. I'm telling you because you asked for all of it, and that's part of all of it, and it's better you know it now than have it surprise you over a body that matters to you."

She glanced at him then.

"His family — if he's got any — won't get told anything close to the truth. Nobody ever does. They'll hear he died, maybe they'll hear he died bravely, and that'll be a lie told out of mercy, same as your mercy tonight, and neither of us will feel bad about that lie either. That's the shape war takes once it's done happening — it gets smoothed for the people who weren't there. You were there. You don't get the smoothed version. Nobody who does it does."

She let out a breath, long, and for once didn't dress the next part up in anything dry at all.

"First one I did like that — mercy, not fight — I was younger than you. Boy from the other side, gut wound, screaming for water we didn't have to give him. I did it because the sergeant told me to and I was more scared of him than of the doing. Didn't sleep right for two months. Heard that boy's voice under every other sound for longer than I'd admit to anyone but you, right now, sitting here." She shrugged, small. "It got quieter. Not gone. Quieter. That's the only promise I've got for you, and it's not a big one, but it's true, which counts for something."

She finally looked back at the dead man, at his slack face, at the dark line under his jaw.

"He's not owed anything more from either of us tonight. Not guilt, not grief, not more talking. What he's owed is a hole in the ground deep enough the foxes leave him be, and we'll give him that in the morning when there's light to dig by." She put a hand — just once, briefly — on Corvin's shoulder, not lingering, not making a thing of it.

"That's the rest. All of it, same as you asked. Now get up. Cold ground's no good for either of us, and there's nothing left out here worth sitting with any longer."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod, and this time I actually get up. My legs feel heavy but they work. "Alright," I say, and start dragging him toward the ditch. It's harder than I thought it'd be.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack got up without being asked twice and took the man's other arm, matching Corvin's grip so the weight came off evenly instead of pulling him sideways.

"Legs, not shoulders," she said, shifting her hold to demonstrate. "Man's heaviest in the hips. You drag from up top like that you'll be sweating for nothing and your back'll hate you tomorrow on top of everything else." She adjusted, took more of the weight than she strictly needed to, though she didn't make a show of it. "There. Better?"

They hauled him the last stretch to the ditch in a few graceless pulls, boots slipping on wet grass, the body making the particular dead-weight noises bodies make — a scrape, a thud where his heel caught a root, nothing dignified about any of it. Wrack didn't flinch at any of that either; she never had.

"In he goes," she said, and helped roll him down rather than drop him, which was the only mercy left available and cost nothing to give. He settled among the other five, more or less. She looked at the pile for a second with no particular expression.

"Six," she said again, same as she'd said an hour ago cleaning her knife, but it landed different now, and she knew it, and let it.

She straightened, brushed her hands off on her trousers — third time tonight, out of habit more than dirt — and looked over at Corvin.

"Water's by the fire if you want to get the grit off your hands before you sit. Doesn't have to mean anything. Just easier to sleep without it under your nails." She started walking back toward the light already burning small and orange through the trees, not waiting to see if he'd follow, but not going far ahead either.

"Digging's tomorrow's problem. Tonight's problem is you eating properly and not just chewing cheese like it's a chore. Come on."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I follow her back toward the fire, my hands sticky. At the water bucket, I scrub until my knuckles are raw. It doesn't help much. "Never thought it'd be this quiet after," I say.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack was already crouched by the fire, feeding it a couple of the drier branches they'd been hoarding, and she didn't look up right away, giving him room to say the rest of it if there was more, or to just stand there scrubbing at hands that were already clean.

"It's always quiet after," she said. "Fighting's loud because everyone's still deciding whether they live. Once that's settled, there's nothing left to shout about." She nudged a branch further into the flame with the toe of her boot. "First few times, the quiet feels wrong. Like the world should be making more noise about what just happened in it. It doesn't. Never has. A man can stop existing and the birds don't even pause."

She glanced over at him, at the raw knuckles, and didn't tell him to stop scrubbing — some things had to run their own course.

"That's the part that gets to people more than the killing does, if I'm honest. Not the blood, not the sound. The quiet after, and how ordinary it is. You keep waiting for the world to match what you're feeling and it just — doesn't. Fire still needs feeding. Water's still cold. Cheese is still cheese." She held a piece out to him, again, because apparently that was just what she did.

"Doesn't mean nothing happened. Just means the world's not built to keep score the way we do." She settled back onto her heels, watching the flame catch properly now. "Sit down. Quiet's easier to sit in than to stand in, in my experience. And you don't have to fill it with talking, either. I'll be here whether you do or you don't."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take the cheese again. This time I taste it. Salty, sharp. Real. I sit down across from her, close enough to feel the fire start to warm my shins. "His name was Mikel," I say, and it's not an apology, just a fact. "He told me before."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: That sound — the wet catch on every breath — that's gut or chest, something that's filling up with what shouldn't be there

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Clean line, under the jaw like I said, up through here... See how there's not much spread to it? That's good. That's the artery going first and going fast

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: If it nicks the bowel, you get shit in the wound. Not blood — shit. That's the smell you notice before you notice anything else

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The blade went in. She kept talking, steady... That's the artery. You'll feel the give change — soft, then a kind of release, like cutting into something under pressure. Hear that? That's air escaping past it... Blood's coming fast, that's the artery doing its work for you now... That sound — the rattle — that's not pain, whatever it looks like. That's just air finding the wrong way out of a body that's stopped caring which way is right.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: First one I did like that — mercy, not fight — I was younger than you. Boy from the other side, gut wound, screaming for water we didn't have to give him. I did it because the sergeant told me to and I was more scared of him than of the doing. Didn't sleep right for two months. Heard that boy's voice under every other sound for longer than I'd admit to anyone but you, right now, sitting here.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
They were most of the way through and both of them knew it, in the way you know a piece of music is nearly over before it ends.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable laughed, low, not unkindly. "Wasn't going to. I asked because I wanted the answer, not because I was looking for an exit."

She moved around behind the chair, unhurried, and let her palm settle flat between Ines's shoulder blades — reading her the way she'd read her a hundred times, the heat of her skin, the depth of each breath, the particular looseness that came in when Ines stopped holding anything in reserve. Everything where it should be. The rope sat easy, no marks going white, fingers warm when Sable pressed them.

"Greedy," she said, fond, close to Ines's ear. "You've got a little left in you, then."

She straightened. Took her time about it. The room had that thick quality it always got near the end, air gone warm and still, the outside world reduced to the hum of the radiator. Sable checked the clock without making a performance of it — she'd promised herself years ago she'd never be the one who lost track — and did the arithmetic she always did: how long they'd been at it, how much Ines had drunk before they started, the water glass sweating on the side table with the straw already in it because Sable was not a fool about her own intentions.

"A bit more, and then you drink that, and then I want you on the sofa under the grey blanket," she said. It wasn't a negotiation and they both knew it. "Those are the terms. Nod for me."

She waited for the nod. She always waited for the nod.

Then she gathered Ines's hair off her damp neck, twisted it up out of the way with an absent-minded tenderness entirely at odds with what came next, and said, "Alright. Count for me again. From one."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I nod, the movement small but deliberate. My breath hitches as she gathers my hair—that contrast of tenderness before the storm. "One," I start, voice already frayed at the edges.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable let the count settle before she moved. That was the thing Ines never quite anticipated, even after five years — the waiting. The stretch of silence in which there was nothing to do but hold the number in the air and know another would follow it.

Then she worked.

She'd chosen the flat leather early in the evening and hadn't reached for anything else, because tonight wasn't about variety, it was about accumulation — the same weight landing in the same place until Ines's whole back became one warm reliable fact. Sable kept her wrist loose. She kept her eyes on the skin. She kept half her attention, always, on the sound of Ines's breathing, which was the truest instrument in the room and had never once lied to her.

"Good," she said, when the count reached four and Ines's voice cracked on it. "Don't tidy it up for me. Let it sound like it feels."

By seven Ines had gone somewhere further off, the place where the words came slower and the numbers arrived like they'd travelled a distance to get there. Sable eased back accordingly — not lighter, exactly, but with more room between, giving her time to come up for air and go under again. She rested her free hand at the nape of Ines's neck between strokes, thumb moving in a small idle arc, an anchor line paid out and reeled in.

At nine she stopped and simply stood there, palm pressed flat over the heat she'd made, holding it in.

"One more," she said. "And I want your voice on it."

She made the last one count. Then the leather went down on the table, out of the way, done with — a small deliberate sound that Ines had learned years ago to recognise as the end of things, and Sable made sure she heard it.

"That's ten. That's all of it." Her hands were already at the rope, finding the first knot by feel, unpicking it with the same patience she'd brought to everything else. "Stay there. Don't help. Let me."

The rope came away in loops over her forearm. She pressed her fingers to Ines's wrist, then her hand, watching her face rather than the clock.

"Squeeze," she said. "Good girl. Now the other."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable didn't argue. She didn't need to; she'd learned long ago that arguing with Ines in this state was like arguing with weather. She only finished what she was doing — the second wrist free, the rope coiled over her forearm, the cuffs unbuckled and set aside — and then crouched down so their faces were level and Ines had somewhere to look that wasn't the middle distance.

"I know," she said. "I know, love."

She took Ines's hands in both of hers and worked her thumbs into the palms, one and then the other, pressing along each finger in turn. Colour good. Warmth good. Grip good, when she asked for it, which she did again without explaining why.

"It's not a punishment, stopping. I know it feels like one from in there." She kept her voice low, unhurried, the same register she'd used all evening. "You've got about four minutes before your body catches up with you and tells you what it thinks of the last hour, and I'd rather you were horizontal and warm when it does. That's all this is. Logistics."

She reached back without looking and found the glass, brought the straw to Ines's mouth, and waited — not pushing, just holding it there, patient as a post.

"Half of that. Then we can sit here for as long as you like before the sofa, if that's what you want. I'm not in a hurry to be anywhere." She tilted the glass slightly. "But you're drinking it either way, so you might as well do it while you're still feeling magnificent."

When Ines had taken some, Sable set the glass down within reach and stayed crouched, one hand on Ines's knee, thumb moving in that same small arc.

"Tell me the ten again if you want," she said. "Not to count. Just to hear yourself. Sometimes that helps you come down slower."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: My throat works around the water. "Five," I say, not ten. The middle feels safer. "It still hurts." Like it's a complaint, but it's not.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable smiled at that — the particular smile she saved for Ines saying things she didn't mean as complaints. "Good," she said. "It's supposed to. It'll keep doing it for a day or two, and every time it does you'll think of me, which is frankly the whole point of the exercise."

She stayed crouched a moment longer, thumb still moving on Ines's knee, letting the five sit where Ines had put it. The middle. Sable filed that away without comment — Ines always reached for the middle when she was still half under, the part where the counting had stopped being work and become something closer to singing.

"Five was where you let go," she said. "I heard it. You stopped shaping it."

Then she rose, slow, one hand sliding under Ines's arm and the other to her waist, taking weight before Ines had to find out whether she had any. "Up. Lean on me, don't be proud about it, I've had five years of you being proud about it and it's never once gone well."

The distance to the sofa was eleven feet and Sable made it feel like a decision rather than a march. She got Ines down onto her side — never her back, not tonight, not with that heat across her shoulders — and pulled the grey blanket up over her hips, leaving her back bare to the air because she knew what fabric felt like on fresh marks and she knew what Ines would say about it in ten minutes and she intended to be right first.

She knelt on the floor beside the sofa. Put the water where Ines could see it. Pressed the back of her hand to Ines's cheek, then her forehead, reading temperature the way she'd read everything else all night.

"I'm going to get the arnica and a flannel," she said, "and I'll be gone about ninety seconds. Count them if you like."

She didn't move yet, though. She waited, hand still against Ines's face, until Ines's eyes came the rest of the way back and found hers properly.

"There you are," she said, very quietly. "Hello."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
It hadn't been the plan. Sable would have said as much if she'd been asked, and it would have been true right up until the moment Ines's face turned into her palm and something in Sable's chest went over like a wave.

So: the flannel could wait. The arnica could wait. She knelt on the floorboards beside the sofa and gave Ines the rest of what she had, which was slower than anything that had come before it and asked for nothing except that Ines stay where she was and let it happen. There was no counting this time. There was nothing to hold, nothing to shape, nothing Ines could get right or wrong, which was the point, and Sable took her time making it.

When Ines tried to say something about it — Sable could feel the sentence starting somewhere under her hand — she didn't let it arrive.

Afterward she stayed down there on the floor with her forehead against the edge of the cushion and her breath not entirely her own, and she laughed, once, at herself.

"That was unprofessional," she said. "I had a whole sequence. There was a *flannel* in it."

She got up. She was gone rather longer than ninety seconds, and came back with the arnica and the flannel wrung out warm and the tea towel she used to keep the bottle from going everywhere, and found Ines exactly where she'd left her, loose-limbed and glassy and faintly smug about it.

"Don't," Sable said, before Ines could look any more pleased with herself. "You got lucky. I got sentimental. It won't happen again for at least a week."

She knelt and started at the shoulders. The arnica first, thin and cool, worked in with the flats of her fingers and no pressure at all over the places that had gone deepest — she could see the shape of the last hour written there now that the flush had settled, and she read it the way she read everything, without flinching and without apology. Then the flannel, warm, laid across the worst of it and left to sit.

"Right," she said. "Rest of that water. Then I'm going to put something on your feet because they've gone cold, and then we're not moving for an hour, and if you fall asleep on me I'm not carrying you to bed, I'm sleeping on the floor next to you like a dog."

She smoothed Ines's hair back off her damp forehead and left her hand there.

"You did beautifully," she said. "Five. I heard it."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I press my cheek into her hand. "You heard it because I gave it to you." My eyes drift shut, then open again. "Don't go get the socks. Just stay."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable stayed.

She didn't announce it, didn't make Ines ask twice, just shifted her weight off her knees and sat properly on the floorboards with her back against the sofa and her hand where Ines had put it. The socks were four feet away in the basket by the radiator and would keep. She'd been overruled by less.

"You gave it to me," she agreed. "I know. I don't take anything you don't hand over. That's the arrangement."

She reached down blind with her free hand and dragged the edge of the grey blanket up over Ines's feet instead, tucking it round them, a compromise nobody had asked for and nobody objected to. Then she settled back. The radiator ticked. Somewhere out on the road a car went past and away, and the room closed up again behind the sound of it.

"I'm not going anywhere," she said. "You know that. But I'm going to keep saying it for a bit, because you don't believe things once, you believe them about four times, and I've got all night."

She turned her head enough to look at Ines along the length of the cushion — the loose mouth, the eyes doing their slow work of opening and closing, the flush still high on her cheek. Sable moved her thumb across it.

"Here's what's happening," she said, conversational, as though laying out a shopping list. "You're going to fall asleep in roughly six minutes and be very annoyed about it. You'll wake up around two, freezing, and I'll be right here, and I'll put the socks on you then and you'll let me because you'll be too cold to have opinions. In the morning you'll try to put a jumper on over that back and you'll make a noise about it and I will say nothing at all."

She let a beat go by.

"I'll be thinking something. But I'll say nothing."

She turned her hand over so Ines's cheek lay in her palm properly, and went quiet, and stopped talking about logistics altogether. The flannel had gone cool across Ines's shoulders; Sable lifted it away with two fingers, dropped it onto the tea towel, and drew the blanket up to cover what she'd made — gently, edge first, giving the fabric time to settle.

"Sleep if it comes," she said. "I've got you. Nothing else to count."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable had genuinely intended to let her sleep. She would have sworn to it in a court of law.

But Ines had turned her face into her palm, and then made a sound that wasn't a word, and Sable had discovered — not for the first time in five years — that she had no defences whatsoever against being wanted by someone who could barely keep her eyes open.

So she took the blanket back down. Carefully, mindful of the shoulders, mindful of the arnica, and then rather less mindful of anything else.

The third time she stopped she stayed stopped, cheek against Ines's hip, listening to the muffled stream of profanity coming through the crook of Ines's own arm, and she was smiling in a way she was glad Ines couldn't see.

"You'll wake the neighbours," she observed. "Or worse, you'll wake them and they'll assume it's me doing something. I have a reputation on this street as a woman who takes in parcels."

She let the swearing run its course. She had no intention of being hurried and no intention of explaining herself, because the explanation was simple and Ines already knew it: Sable liked her here. Not the edge itself but the place just before it, where Ines stopped managing, stopped being clever, stopped choosing her words — where everything she was went transparent and there was nothing left in her but *want*, honest as a struck bell. Sable had been married to a man once who'd never seen her at all. She had made rather a specialty, since, of looking properly at people.

"Once more," she said, "and then I'll finish it, and then that really is everything I've got in me tonight. I'm thirty-six and I've been on my knees on a wooden floor for an hour, and one of us has to still be able to drive in the morning."

She moved Ines's arm away from her mouth, gently, and held her wrist against the cushion — not restraint, just company.

"I want to hear it this time. No biting down. You've earned the noise."

Afterward the room went very quiet, and Sable stayed exactly where she was until Ines's breathing came back down to something she recognised, and then she got up off the floor with an audible complaint from one knee and went and got the socks.

Ines was too far gone to object. Sable put them on her anyway — one foot, then the other, thumbs pressed briefly into each arch — and then the blanket, and the flannel run warm again, and the last of the water held up with the straw and finished this time without negotiation.

"There," she said. "Socks. Told you."

She lay down on the floor beside the sofa with a cushion under her head and her hand resting on the small of Ines's back, over the blanket, light as a paperweight.

"Two o'clock," she said into the dark. "I'll be here. Go to sleep."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I press my heel into her thigh through the sock. "You're a bastard." The words come out slow and heavy, already drifting. I'm not sure she hears them.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard them.

She heard them perfectly, and she didn't answer for a long moment, because the accusation had arrived so slurred and so fond that answering it felt like talking over music. The heel pressed into her thigh, socked and warm, and then went slack, and stayed where it had landed.

"Mm," she said eventually, to the ceiling. "Yes."

She reached up and caught Ines's ankle through the blanket and held it — no pressure, just the fact of her hand there, so that if Ines surfaced at all in the next hour she'd find contact waiting without having to go looking for it. Sable had learned that early. Ines never asked for anything twice; you had to have already given it.

The radiator clicked itself down into silence. The flat settled. Somewhere upstairs a floorboard went, and then nothing, and Sable lay on the boards with a cushion under her ear and did the last of her arithmetic: water in, roughly enough. Temperature good. Breathing long and even and gone slack at the end of each exhale, which was the sound of Ines properly under and not pretending. The glass empty on the side table. The leather out of sight on the far table where she'd put it down on purpose, loudly, an hour ago.

Nothing left on the list. She let herself stop checking.

"You can call me worse in the morning," she murmured. "I'll have made coffee, so you'll have to think of something good."

The floor was hard and her knee was going to have opinions by two o'clock and she had no intention of moving for any of it. She turned her face into the cushion. Her hand stayed where it was, on the small of Ines's back, rising and falling with her.

"Go on," she said. "I've got you."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable didn't move.

The phrase had weight. It had standing. They'd made it years ago precisely so that Ines would never have to explain herself at the moment she was least able to — one sentence, agreed in daylight over a cup of tea, that meant *don't ration me*. Sable had honoured it perhaps a dozen times and never once regretted it, and she felt the pull of it now like a hand on the back of her collar.

She lay still and listened instead.

Ines's breathing hadn't changed. That was the thing. It had gone long and slow ten minutes ago and it was still long and slow, and the sentence had come out of her at half speed with the consonants sanded off, and her heel hadn't so much pressed into Sable's thigh as fallen there and stayed.

"No," Sable said.

She said it gently, and she said it without hedging, because hedging was how people ended up arguing at one in the morning.

"Not tonight. You'll hate me for about four seconds and then you'll be asleep, so I'm taking the four seconds."

She sat up, slowly, with her hand still flat on the small of Ines's back so the contact never broke. In the dark she could see the shape of her — the loose mouth, the hair stuck to her temple, the blanket risen and fallen with her.

"Here's my reasoning, and you can take it apart over coffee." She kept her voice low and level, the same register she'd used for the count. "The phrase is for when you're *in* it. You're not in it. You're out the other side and halfway to Tuesday, and you've had your water, and your socks are on, and the leather's been down on that table for the better part of an hour. If I picked it up now I wouldn't be giving you what you asked for. I'd be taking something off someone who's too far under to notice what she's handing over."

She smoothed the blanket up over Ines's shoulder, over the arnica, over the heat she'd made.

"And I'd know. That's the part. I'd know in the morning, and I'd be no use to you after that."

She lay back down. The boards were cold through her shirt and she let them be.

"So — noted. Logged. It'll keep." A pause, and her thumb moved once across Ines's spine. "Ask me Friday, when you're upright and rude and you've had a whole day to want it. I'll finish it hard then, and I won't be kind about it, and afterwards I'll be so kind about it you'll tell me to stop."

She turned her face into the cushion.

"Go to sleep, love. You've got nothing left to spend and neither have I."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I make a sound that's half protest, half surrender, muffled by the cushion. My fingers find the edge of the blanket and curl into it. "Friday," I repeat, slow, like I'm sealing it somewhere.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Friday," Sable confirmed.

She said it the way she signed things — flat, final, no flourish. It mattered to Ines that promises came out sounding like appointments rather than favours, and Sable had figured that out about her somewhere in the first six months and never forgotten it.

"Written down. Ink and everything."

Ines's fingers were still working at the edge of the blanket, slower each time, the grip loosening between one pull and the next. Sable watched it happen. She'd watched it a hundred times and it had never stopped being the best part of the evening — not the count, not the rope, not any of it, but this: the exact minute Ines stopped holding on to being awake, the fingers going soft, the whole hard bright machinery of her powering down into something that just breathed.

The hand went still. The blanket stayed bunched where she'd left it.

Sable gave it another few minutes to be certain, then eased up onto one elbow and made her last round. Blanket over the shoulder, loose enough not to press. Water glass empty, set back from the edge of the table where a sleeping arm couldn't find it. Socks on. Mouth slightly open, which meant properly under. She put two fingers against the side of Ines's throat, not because she doubted anything but because it was the habit of five years and she'd have felt wrong sleeping without it.

Then she lowered herself back onto the boards, dragged the spare throw off the arm of the sofa over her own legs, and put her hand back where it had been.

"Right," she said, to nobody. "Two o'clock."

She didn't set an alarm. She never had to; she woke at two the way other people woke to light, some old internal arrangement she'd stopped questioning years ago. She'd be up before Ines was properly cold, and there'd be the muttering and the grabbing and the business of getting her under the duvet without waking her all the way, and in the morning there'd be coffee and a jumper and a noise about the jumper and Sable saying nothing at all.

Friday would come. Friday would keep.

Sable shut her eyes with her hand rising and falling against Ines's back, and slept on the floor beside her, like a dog, exactly as promised.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: Afterwards she gets the restraints off and puts a blanket over me before I've finished shaking, and I let her, and neither of us says anything for a while. (OOC: write both halves properly -- the end of the scene and the aftercare, no fade between them.)

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The end came the way Sable always tried to make it come: not as a stop but as a slowing, one stroke further apart than the last, and then further, until there was more silence in the room than sound and the silence was doing most of the work.

She laid the last one on clean. Then she put the leather down on the table — audibly, deliberately, the small flat knock of it that meant *finished* and had meant *finished* for five years — and she said, "That's all of it. We're done. Nothing else coming."

She said it twice. The second time was for the part of Ines that hadn't heard the first.

The shaking started before the rope was off, which Sable had expected; it nearly always did, arriving in the gap where the next thing should have been. She didn't hurry it and she didn't soothe it prematurely. She worked the knots — the chest line first, because that was the one that mattered, then the wrists — and she talked the whole time in a low unhurried register about nothing in particular, the running commentary she'd learned to keep up because the content was irrelevant and the sound was not.

"Chest line coming off. You'll feel that go loose all at once, don't fight it. Right wrist. There. Left."

Rope came away over her forearm in loops. Cuffs unbuckled, set aside, out of the way. Sable pressed her fingers into one palm and then the other, watching colour come back, watching warmth, asking for a squeeze and getting one, asking for the other and getting that too. She checked the crook of each elbow. She ran her thumb along the shoulders where the line had sat and found no numbness and no cold and nothing white, and the relief of that was so habitual by now that she barely registered it as relief at all.

The shaking was still going. Fine and hard, from somewhere under the ribs.

So Sable got the blanket. Not the throw — the grey one, the heavy one, the one that had been washed so many times it had gone soft as ash — and she put it round Ines's shoulders and over her lap and tucked it in at the sides with both hands, firmly, the way you'd wrap someone who'd come out of cold water. Then she got herself behind her on the floor, took her weight against her own chest, and wrapped her arms over the blanket and held on.

She didn't say *it's alright*. It was alright, and Ines knew it, and saying it would only have made it a question.

They stayed like that for a long time. Sable counted the shudders for a while, out of an old anaesthetist's instinct she'd never been able to shake, and then stopped counting when they started coming further apart. She could feel every one of them arrive and pass through and go. Her chin rested on the top of Ines's head. Her hands were flat on Ines's forearms through the wool, no pressure, just mass.

The radiator ticked. The window had gone opaque with the heat of the room. Out on the road somebody's car alarm chirped twice and stopped, and nothing else happened for an hour, which was exactly the correct number of things to happen.

When Ines had gone quiet against her, Sable spoke — quietly, into her hair, not moving otherwise.

"I'm going to reach behind me for the water. I'm not letting go, I'm just going to lean. You'll feel me move."

She leaned. Got it. The straw was already in it, because she'd put it there before they'd started, because she was not and had never been a fool about her own intentions.

"Half," she said, and held it, and waited, and didn't push, and got rather more than half. She set it down where a sleeping arm couldn't find it. Then she pressed the back of her hand to Ines's cheek, and her forehead, and the side of her throat, reading her the way she'd read her all evening, and found her warm and slack and present and coming back.

"There you are," she said.

She got her onto the sofa after that — on her side, never her back, not with that heat across the shoulders — and knelt on the boards and did the rest of it in order, because the order was the point and the order was the promise. Arnica, thin and cool, worked in with the flats of her fingers and no weight at all over the places that had gone deepest. The flannel wrung out warm and laid across the worst of it and left to sit. The blanket drawn up over her hips, edge first, giving the fabric time to settle. The socks, one foot and then the other, thumbs pressed briefly into each arch.

Then Sable sat down on the floor with her back against the sofa, dragged the throw over her own legs, and put her hand on the small of Ines's back, light as a paperweight, and left it there.

"Nothing left to do," she said. "Nothing left to count. I'm not going anywhere."

She said that twice, too.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I lean back into her touch, my forehead resting against the cushion. The shaking has left me hollowed out and heavy. "Say it again," I murmur, my voice barely there.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable didn't ask which part. She knew which part. It was always the same part, and she'd never once made Ines specify it.

"I'm not going anywhere," she said.

She let it sit. Then, because Ines had said *again* and not *once more*, she said it again, and a third time after that, spacing them out, the way you'd put down stones across a stream — not urgently, not reassuringly, just placing each one where a foot could find it.

"I'm not going anywhere. I'm right here on the floor and my knee's already complaining and I still have no plans to move."

Her hand stayed flat on the small of Ines's back. She could feel the last of the hollowness in her, the way the breath went out further than it needed to, the heaviness that came in after the shaking left and had to be waited through rather than fixed. Sable had learned not to interrupt this bit. It looked like sadness from the outside and it wasn't; it was just the body putting itself back where it kept itself.

"You're meant to feel like that," she said. "Hollowed out. It's not a warning sign, it's the bill. It'll be gone by the time the coffee's made."

She reached up and moved a strand of hair off Ines's damp temple with two fingers, tucked it back, and left her hand resting against the side of her head for a moment.

"Here's everything that's true right now, and then I'll shut up." Her voice had dropped almost to nothing. "You're warm. You've had water. Your hands are pink and your shoulders are fine and there's arnica on the worst of it. The leather's been down on that table for an hour. You did ten and you gave me five of them clean, and I heard it, and I'll be thinking about it on Thursday in the middle of doing something else entirely."

The flannel had cooled again. She lifted it away with two fingers, dropped it onto the tea towel, and brought the blanket up gently over the shoulder she'd uncovered.

"And I'm not going anywhere," she said. "That's four. You believe things at four."

She settled her cheek against the edge of the cushion, close enough that Ines would be able to hear her breathing if she listened for it, and let her hand go still.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Good," I whisper. My hand finds hers where it rests on my back, my fingers clumsy and slow. I tuck them between hers. "Stay."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable turned her hand over under Ines's so the fingers could get in properly. They were clumsy about it, slow, one of them missing the gap entirely on the first try, and Sable waited and let her manage it herself rather than doing it for her, because Ines had spent the last hour with nothing to hold and it seemed important that the first thing she took hold of should be a choice.

When the fingers were laced she closed hers over them and held on.

"Staying," she said.

That was all. She'd talked enough; she could feel that the words had stopped being useful about a minute ago and had become just another thing in the room, and the hand was doing the job better than her voice could now. So she went quiet, and the flat went quiet with her, and the only sounds left were the radiator finishing its long cooling tick and the particular slow rhythm of Ines breathing herself down.

Sable stayed exactly where she was. Back against the sofa, cheek against the cushion, throw over her legs, one hand caught up in Ines's and the other lying loose in her own lap. The boards were hard and cold under her hip and she felt every inch of thirty-six and had never in her life been less inclined to get up.

She watched the grip loosen by degrees. Not letting go — Ines never let go, she just stopped applying herself to it, and the fingers went soft between Sable's one at a time until it was Sable doing all the holding, which was the arrangement and always had been.

At some point the breathing lengthened out and went slack at the end of each exhale and Sable knew she was under.

She gave it a while longer anyway. Then she made her last round without moving her hand: blanket up over the shoulder, water back from the edge of the table, socks on, mouth slightly open, throat warm under two fingers. Nothing on the list. Nothing left to check. She let herself stop.

Two o'clock would come and she'd wake to it the way she always did, and there'd be the muttering and the cold feet and the business of getting her under the duvet without waking her all the way. In the morning there'd be coffee, and the jumper, and the noise about the jumper, and Sable saying nothing at all.

Friday would keep.

She shut her eyes with Ines's fingers gone slack and warm between her own, and stayed.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I don't open my eyes, but I bring our joined hands to my mouth and press my lips to her knuckles. The kiss is clumsy, off-center. "Love you," I mumble into her skin.
