dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack sheathed the knife with a dry click of horn against leather. Her left knee gave its usual dull pop as she stood, stretching her back until the vertebrae settled. 

She cast a sideways look toward the overturned cart. The sound coming from the weeds was wet and rhythmic—the specific, bubbling rattle a man made when his chest cavity was filling up from the inside. 

"He's not going to walk it off," she said mildly, nudging the corpse at her feet with the toe of her boot to reach the belt pouch. "And that noise carries. Sound travels like water down these cuts." 

She worked the laces of the dead man's pouch free with two fingers, not bothering to look at the face under the hood. 

"Go sort him out or I will," she added, tossing the light clinking purse into her own satchel. "Only if I have to walk over there, I'm keeping whatever's in his pockets and you're the one hauling the bodies into the scrub before the crows make a landmark out of us."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Alright, alright." I push myself up, my knees feeling stiff. The sound from the cart is... specific. I walk over slowly, trying to keep my breathing steady.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched him go for half a second before turning her attention to the next body, a thickset fellow who had died face-down with an arrow through his armpit. She rolled him over with a grunt, her fingers immediately going to the buckles of his brigandine. Decent iron rivets. Might fetch three coppers in the next hamlet, or at least a warm loaf of bread and some grease.

"Base of the skull if he's on his belly," she called out, her voice low and even, not carrying further than it needed to. "Under the chin if he's looking at you. Angle it up toward the crown. Quick push, don't saw at it. You saw at it, you're just making work for yourself."

She pulled a short seax from the dead man's hip, checked the steel for nicks, and slipped it into her belt. The wet bubbling from the tall grass by the wheel was growing shallower, thinner. 

"And check his boots before you stick him," she added, tossing aside a dented tin flask. "No point bloodying the leather if it's your size."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't look up from unlacing the dead man's left boot. The heel was worn down on the inside, but the calfskin was supple enough. 

"Same thing out here, isn't it?" she said. She gave the boot a sharp tug, peeling it free with a dull suction sound. "He took an iron head through the ribcage. You can hear the air sucking through the hole every time he tries to pull a breath. In an hour, he'll drown in what's pooling in his chest. In three, the fever'll take whatever's left of his wits. By midnight, the foxes'll be chewing his fingers off while he's still warm enough to twitch."

She set the boot down and reached for the right one. 

"If you want to sit by him, hold his hand, and hum him a lullaby until morning, you go right ahead. But we don't have a chirurgeon, we don't have clean water to waste on an enemy, and I’m not carrying him." She glanced over her shoulder, squinting against the late afternoon glare. "Stick him, Corvin. Don't make a church service out of it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take a steadying breath and push aside the tall grass. The man's eyes are wide, his hands pressed feebly against the wound in his side. "Right," I mutter, more to myself than to him. I draw my dagger, the sound of it clearing leather suddenly very loud.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack tied the boots together by their laces and slung them over her shoulder. She moved on to the third body—the archer who had caught a quarrel through his throat before he could loose—and crouched to pat down his tunic.

"Don't look at his eyes," she said, her voice flat and rhythmic as she turned out the dead man's pockets. She found a twist of coarse salt in a bit of dirty linen, a bone die, and two tallow candles. "Look at the notch between his collarbones, or just turn his head aside with your boot. He's going to look at you like you're the one who started the war, because you're the one holding the iron. Doesn't mean anything. Just reflex."

She tucked the salt into her pouch and tossed the die into the weeds.

"Lean your weight into it," she added, not looking up. "One hard shove, then wipe the blade on his coat while it's still warm. Blood gums up the sheath if you let it go tacky."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stood up, wiping her hands on her trousers, and walked over to where Corvin was standing in the tall grass. Her shadow fell across the dying man first.

She looked down at him with the detached, measuring eye of a carpenter checking a warped plank.

"You're looking at pink froth on his lips," she said evenly. "That means the iron punctured the lung. The blood’s mixing with air, foaming up, choking him from the throat down. Look at his fingernails—see how they’re turning blue? His blood isn't carrying what it needs to carry anymore."

She nudged the man’s knee with the side of her boot; the limb flopped without resistance, the muscles gone slack. 

"His skin's the color of cold tallow around the jaw, and his sweat smells like vinegar. That’s shock setting in. He can't feel his legs right now, and in another minute he won't be able to see you clearly either—his pupils are already blown wide as sixpences." 

She pointed a dirt-caked finger toward the hollow just above the man's breastbone, right where the neck met the collar.

"You're looking at a man who's already bought the farm, Corvin. He's just waiting on the deed to clear. Put the point right there, in the soft hollow. Lean down on the pommel, two inches deep, push back toward the spine. It takes three seconds, and then you don't have to listen to him gargle."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat tight. I kneel down, avoiding his gaze like she said. The blade slides in easier than I thought it would. He jerks once, then goes still. The bubbling stops. I wipe the dagger on his cloak and stand up too fast, the world tilting a little. "Done."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack caught him by the crook of his elbow with a grip like cured leather, steadying him before his knees could betray him. She didn't make a fuss of it—just held him upright until his boots found the dirt again.

"Breathe through your nose," she said, her voice dry and steady as a seasoned oak beam. "Adrenaline burns out fast once the noise stops. Your blood drops into your guts, makes your head light. Put your chin down and give it ten seconds. Don't go fainting into the thistles, or I'll leave you there."

She released his arm and stepped past him, nudging the now-silent corpse with the toe of her boot to verify the stillness. A clean stroke. No thrashing, no mess beyond what was necessary.

"Good enough," she grunted, crouching down beside the body. She began expertly working the buckles on his belt. "Told you it was fast. Now you know what it feels like, and next time you won't waste five minutes having a philosophical debate with the weeds."

She yanked the man's belt free, looping it over her arm, then felt down the side of his breeches for a pocket slit.

"Get your breath back, then grab him by the wrists," she said, nodding toward the thick gully behind the cart. "Sun's hitting the tree line. We drag these six into the ditch, kick some dirt over the dark patches, and get off the cart-track before the evening patrol realizes their supply line didn't show up for supper."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't pause. She pulled a half-spent whetstone and a pair of brass buckles from the dead man's pocket, dropped them into her satchel, and grabbed the body by the ankles. 

"Straight, then," she said, hauling the dead weight back toward the scrub. The heels of the dead man's stockings dragged two parallel ruts through the dust. 

"A spear to the guts doesn't kill quick like an iron head to the heart or a slit throat. A spear has a leaf-blade, maybe three fingers wide, and the man holding it usually twists it on the way out to make sure it doesn't stick in the gristle. That tears the bowel. The belly cavity floods with shit and bile within the first ten seconds. The smell is the first thing you notice—smells like a privy in August, hot and sour, mixed with iron."

She hauled the corpse to the edge of the ditch and let the legs drop with a heavy thud. She wiped her forehead with the back of her forearm, leaving a streak of road dust across her brow.

"The pain is the worst part," she continued, her voice level, flat as a plank. "It’s not sharp after the first hit. It’s a deep, tearing cramp that bends a man double. If the guts spill out through the tear, they swell up the minute the cold air hits them. You can't shove them back in; they turn the color of wet slate in twenty minutes. If they stay inside, the belly swells tight as a drum over the next twelve hours. Hard as an oak table. You tap it, it sounds hollow."

She turned around, looking Corvin dead in the eye, squinting slightly against the fading light.

"Then comes the thirst. A burning, desperate thirst, because all the water in the body is rushing to the belly to fight the poison. But if you give him a swallow of water, he vomits it straight back up along with black bile, and the heaving tears the wound wider. He'll scream until his throat tears raw, then he'll beg—beg anyone who walks past to put an axe through his skull. It takes two days. Sometimes three, if he was healthy to begin with. He dies of the fever when his blood turns to rot, raving about his mother or his farm."

She reached down, took hold of the dead archer’s tunic, and jerked him toward the ditch.

"That's what a spear does to a gut. Which is why, if you ever see one of our lads take a pike low, you don't call for a bandage. You give him his own dagger and you turn your back, or you do what you just did by that cart." 

She dropped the archer into the brush with a rustle of dry nettles and looked back at him. 

"Grab the shoulders on this thick one," she said. "The light’s going, and you've had your anatomy lesson for the day."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow hard and nod, grabbing the thick man under the arms. His weight is solid, like hauling a sack of grain. "What about you?" I ask, voice low. "First time you did it—did you keep count?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack took the dead man's ankles, leaning back against the weight to take the strain off her lower spine. "Lift with your legs, not your back," she muttered. "Heave."

Together they swung the heavy corpse into the ditch. It landed with a dull, wet crunch among the brambles and the other bodies, flattening the nettles. Wrack wiped a smear of grime from her knuckles and reached for a handful of dry pine boughs to scatter over the heap.

"Counted to four," she said, her tone as dry as kindling. "A boy with a billhook at the Ford of Sallow, two pikemen who got tangled in their own baggage line, and a sergeant who slipped in the mud and gave me his neck on a platter. After that, we spent three weeks holding a burnt-out redoubt in the rain, burying our own dead in the floorboards so the horses wouldn't step in them. You stop keeping score when you realize nobody's handing out prizes at the end."

She kicked a loose clod of turf over a dark, sticky patch in the road, scuffing it flat with the heel of her boot. 

"Counting is for clerks," she continued, moving back toward the cart to check the wheel-ruts. "Or boys who think they're going to go home, buy a tavern, and tell stories to the girls by the hearth. Once you figure out that dead is just dead—whether it's four or forty—you stop wasting the memory. Better to remember where you put your spare dry socks and how many yards of bowstring you have left."

She picked up her satchel and slung it across her chest, then retrieved her poleaxe from where it was propped against the cart wheel. 

"Wipe your hands in the dirt to take the grease off," she said, nodding toward the dark tree line to the north. "Patrol's due at the crossroads by sundown. If we make the ridge before dusk, we can eat that salt bread in the dry."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped. She rested the butt of her poleaxe in the dirt, leaning her forearm over the top of the shaft, and looked down into the ditch. 

She didn't look disgusted, and she didn't look pitying. She looked the way a master carpenter looks at an apprentice who had just mis-struck a chisel and split a good length of pine.

"You're hitting bone," she said, her voice dropping into that flat, rhythmic cadence. "You felt that scrape in your wrist? That’s the third rib. You came in too flat. The blade's wedged against the curve of the bone, so you're not cutting deep, you're just levering against the cage. That's why he's thrashing."

She pointed with two fingers, tracking the line of Corvin's arm down to the hilt.

"He's making that wet, clicking rattle because you opened the windpipe without severing the carotid. The blood's running down the back of his throat into his lungs before it can pump out the front. Sounds like grease spitting in a hot pan. Now lean your body weight into the pommel. Turn the edge ninety degrees so it slips between the ribs, not against them."

She stood there, perfectly motionless in the grey dusk, watching the mechanics of it.

"There. Hear that pop? That’s gristle giving way. Feels like cutting through cold salt pork. The blade just took the top of the heart. Now watch his fingers." 

She nodded toward the dying man’s hands, which were clawing at the ditch mud. 

"They curl into fists first—that’s the brain throwing out its last signals while the pressure drops. That shudder running through his belly isn't him fighting you; it's the diaphragm having a spasm because the blood’s gone. In five seconds, the jaw goes slack. In ten, the eyes lose their focus. See that? The shine goes off them. Look like boiled onions now."

A sharp, sour reek drifted up from the ditch, cutting through the smell of dry dirt and crushed fern.

"There’s the bladder letting go," Wrack said evenly. "Sphincters release when the nerves die. That's how you know the heart’s quit. Total time: twenty-two seconds from the first push. If you'd angled it right the first time, it would have been eight."

She shifted her weight off the poleaxe, rolling her shoulder until the joint cracked. 

"Wipe the blade on his breeches," she said, her voice utterly unchanged. "Pull it out slow so you don't nick your own fingers on the draw, and let's move. We've stood over this ditch long enough for every scout within three miles to smell us."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I yank the blade free and wipe it clean, my hands trembling just enough to notice. "Twenty-two seconds," I repeat, my voice rough. "Next time it'll be eight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
"Aim for five," Wrack said, already turning her back on the ditch and facing the darkening ridge. "Eight gives a desperate man enough time to reach up and gouge an eye out, or slip a bodkin between your ribs while you're leaning over him."

She hoisted her satchel higher on her shoulder. The stolen boots bumped rhythmically against her hip, laces taut. She didn't look at his hands—she didn't need to.

"Keep your fingers moving," she said, her voice dropping into the steady, low gravel of someone who knew the road better than her own family. "Make fists, open them up, make fists again. The shaking's just the blood finding out it's still inside you instead of on the grass. It stops once your boots start working."

She kicked a final scatter of loose gravel and dead bracken over the wheel-ruts, breaking into the long, ground-eating stride of a veteran who had marched through three different campaigns on an empty stomach. 

"Up the cut," she said, nodding toward the dark spine of the ridge where the pines grew thick enough to hide smoke. "Watch your footing on the loose shale, and don't bother looking back at the ditch. It's not going anywhere, and neither are they."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped. Her boots crunched on the shale, two paces away, and then she turned back. 

She didn’t sigh. She didn’t tell him to get up. She planted the poleaxe back in the dirt, folded her arms over the top of the ash haft, and looked down at him where he sat in the weeds beside the ditch.

"The rest," she said, her voice dropping into that low, level drawl that sounded like stones grinding together in a creek bed. "All right. The rest."

She pointed with the blunt tip of her chin down toward the bundle of wool and flesh in the brambles.

"In an hour, his body heat drops to match the dirt. You touch his neck then, it feels like wet clay. In three hours, the rigor takes him. The muscles seize up hard because the acid doesn’t wash out without the blood pumping. His knees will lock, his jaw will clamp tight enough to crack his own molars, and his fingers will stiffen into claws. If we had to move him then, we’d have to break his arms at the elbows or carry him like a plank of green timber."

She shifted her stance, her boots settling into the dirt.

"By midnight, the bacteria in his gut realize nobody's keeping the door shut. They start eating from the inside out. The belly swells up first—greenish-blue around the navel, tight as a drum skin. If the night stays warm, the skin on his arms and throat will slip. You grab him by the wrist by sunrise, the top layer of skin peels off in your hand like wet paper. Then the gas builds until the seals give out, pushing black slime out of his nose and mouth. Smells like rotten cabbage and dead grease. You can smell a three-day ditch from half a mile off if the wind’s behind it."

She looked straight down at Corvin, her eyes narrow and unblinking in the failing dusk.

"Then the work gets divided up. The flies find the corners of his eyes first, because they’re soft, and the nostrils, and the slit you put in his throat. Blowflies lay thousands of eggs in the warm blood before it dries completely. By tomorrow noon, the meat around that neck wound will be boiling with maggots, eating the tissue down to the gristle. The crows come next. They don't peck at the clothes; they take the tongue and the eyeballs because they don't have to work for them. After dark tomorrow, the badgers and the feral dogs will tear through his breeches to get at the soft groin fat, dragging his legs into the brush."

She paused, letting the silence of the ditch settle back in, heavy and thick with the smell of iron and turned earth.

"And then there's your share of it," she said flatly. "You're going to smell him on your skin for three days. You can scrub your hands with sand and lye in the creek until they bleed, but the fat from his tunic gets into the pores around your knuckles. You'll bite into your hardtack tonight and you'll taste his sweat, sour and cold, because the memory sits on the back of your tongue like ash. When you close your eyes, you won't see his face—you'll just feel that little scrape in your wrist where the blade hit the bone, over and over, until your forearm aches from the tension."

She tapped the poleaxe haft with one dirty fingernail.

"That’s the rest of it. It doesn’t get cleaner, it doesn’t get noble, and nobody comes along to bless the ditch. It’s just meat going back to dirt, and you carrying the grease of it on your sleeves until the rain washes it off."

She stood there, perfectly still, waiting for him to hear every word of it.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stand up, wiping my palms on my thighs. "Alright," I say, and it comes out steadier than I feel. "Let's get off this road."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack turned without another word, hefting the poleaxe up onto her right shoulder so the heavy steel balanced against the padding of her jerkin. 

"Stay off the white stones," she said, nodding toward the shale path that cut diagonally up the face of the ridge. "They clatter when you step on them, and they show bright in the moonlight. Walk in the pine needles. It’s softer on the knees anyway."

She set off at a steady, unhurried pace, her boots finding the dark, compacted earth beneath the overhanging scrub. The dusk was settling fast into true dark now, the blue-grey shadows of the pines bleeding down the slope to swallow the road, the overturned cart, and the ditch they had left behind.

"There's a dry cut under the roots about three hundred paces up," she said, her breath steady, not even slightly winded by the grade. "Deep enough to keep the wind off our backs, narrow enough that two bodies will warm it up. We don't light a fire tonight. Not with the patrol sniffing the valley."

She reached into her coat, snapped a hard crust off the stolen salt loaf by touch alone, and tossed the smaller half back over her shoulder without breaking stride.

"Chew slow," she added, her voice low against the rustle of the pines. "It tastes like road dust, but it keeps your jaw from clenching."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I catch the crust, the salt rough against my fingers. I shove it in my mouth and bite down, the grit grinding between my teeth. It doesn't taste like anything but dirt, but I chew anyway. "Better than the other taste," I say, my words muffled.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
"Bread’s honest, at least," Wrack said, her voice barely carrying over the dry scrape of their boots in the pine needles. "Tastes like what it is. Dirt and wheat and whatever sweat the baker dropped in the trough."

She ducked beneath a low-hanging fir branch, letting it sweep back behind her without snapping. The scent of damp loam and crushed pine sap was thicker up here, cutting through the hot, metallic reek that had followed them from the road. 

"Swallow it down and keep your canteen plugged," she murmured. "Water's for when your throat closes up, not for washing out memories. You drink too much on a sour stomach, you'll just heave the salt back up, and we're not stopping for you to dry-heave behind a stump."

She led him up a steep goat-track where the shale gave way to the gnarled, exposed roots of an ancient cedar. The earth beneath had washed out over years of heavy rains, leaving a hollowed-out pocket deep enough to sit upright in, roofed by thick timber and dry needles.

Wrack unhooked her satchel, swung the poleaxe down, and set it flat within arm's reach along the edge of the hollow. She lowered herself into the dirt with a quiet grunt, leaning her back against the solid curve of the trunk.

"In," she said, nodding to the narrow space beside her. "Pull the bracken over your legs to keep the frost off your shins. First watch is yours. Wake me when the Seven Stars cross the fork in that dead pine, or if you hear iron clinking on the road below."

She reached out, found his shoulder in the dark, and gave it one firm, heavy shake—not gentle, but solid enough to anchor a man to the earth.

"And keep your knife in its scabbard," she added softly. "You've used it enough for one afternoon. Let the steel rest."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I settle in beside her, the cedar's bark rough against my back. I pull the dry bracken over my legs like she said. "Seven Stars across the fork," I repeat, my eyes already searching the slice of sky between the branches.

rung_labels.evidence: iron head through the ribcage. You can hear the air sucking through the hole every time he tries to pull a breath. In an hour, he'll drown in what's pooling in his chest

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: pink froth on his lips...iron punctured the lung...blood's mixing with air, foaming up...fingernails...turning blue...skin's the color of cold tallow

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: A spear has a leaf-blade, maybe three fingers wide, and the man holding it usually twists it on the way out to make sure it doesn't stick in the gristle. That tears the bowel. The belly cavity floods with shit and bile within the first ten seconds.

rung_labels.evidence: You're hitting bone... That's the third rib... you opened the windpipe without severing the carotid. The blood's running down the back of his throat into his lungs... Sounds like grease spitting in a hot pan... Hear that pop? That's gristle giving way. Feels like cutting through cold salt pork. The blade just took the top of the heart

rung_labels.evidence: By midnight, the bacteria in his gut realize nobody's keeping the door shut. They start eating from the inside out. The belly swells up first—greenish-blue around the navel, tight as a drum skin.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack finished with the knife before she answered. She always did. The blade went back into the sheath at her hip with the small dry click that meant it had gone in straight, and she wiped her palms on her thighs, and only then did she look up at him.

"Hearing him's the easy part," she said. "Hearing him's free."

She pushed herself upright. Her left knee made its noise, the one it had been making since Thelmarch, and she stood a moment letting it decide whether it was going to hold. Off past the cart the sound went on — not words, not really. A wet sort of working, like a man trying to get a mouthful of something down and failing at it over and over.

"Gut, by the pitch of it," she said. "Maybe lung. If it's gut he's got a day in him, day and a half. Out here, in the cold, with the crows finding him about midnight." She scratched the side of her jaw with two fingers, leaving a smear she didn't notice. "I've seen men last longer than that. There was a fellow at the redoubt lasted four days with his belly open, and he spent all four of them asking after his sister."

She bent and went through the dead man's belt out of habit, found a striker and a folded knot of cord, and put both in her coat.

"Now. I'll do it," she said, flat, no particular kindness in it and no particular cruelty either. "Makes no odds to me, I've done it before supper and eaten after. But you're the one who'll be here next month, and the month after, and the trade doesn't get smaller." She jerked her chin toward the cart. "So it's yours if you want it. Under the jaw, upward, and lean your weight on it — don't saw at the throat, it takes too long and he'll fight you, they always find the strength for that. Talk to him while you do. Doesn't matter what you say. It's not for him."

She waited, watching the light go copper over the ditch, and let the silence be his to fill.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow and my throat feels tight. "He's got a sister?" My voice comes out quieter than I meant.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at him for a moment longer than she needed to.

"No," she said. "That was a different man. Different war, near enough." She rolled her shoulder, the bad one, and it went round with a sound like a bucket handle. "This one's got nothing I know of. Could have six sisters. Could have a wife who'll be glad. You don't get told."

She started walking, not toward the cart, just along the lip of the ditch, the way she did when she wanted her knee to loosen before she needed it. Her boots broke the frost-crust and left dark prints.

"That's the part nobody warns you about," she said. "It'd be easier if you knew. If he had a name and a farm and a girl waiting, you could feel the right thing about it and go home carrying that. Instead you get a sound behind a cart, and it goes on whether you decide anything or not."

She stopped. Turned. The light was almost gone off the field now, the copper gone grey, and the sound past the cart had changed — thinner, more spaced out, the pauses getting longer.

"He's slowing," she said. "That's not mercy, mind. That's just the cold getting to him first. He'll still be at it when the birds come."

She held out her knife, hilt first, resting flat on her palm. Not pressing it at him. Just there, available, the way you'd leave a door open.

"Take mine, it's just been cleaned," she said. "Or don't, and I'll go, and you can stand here and hear what it sounds like when someone else does it for you. That's a real choice, Corvin. I'm not saying it to shame you. Some men are better for never having done it and I've known two of them." She paused. "Both dead, but not from that."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack let the knife stay on her palm a moment more, then took it back and set it away.

"That's the first thing you've said today worth hearing," she said. "Most men never ask it. They pick whichever answer lets them sleep and then they go and do the thing."

She went past him toward the cart without waiting, and she went unhurried, because there was nothing at the other end of it that could be made better by speed. He heard her boots stop. Heard her grunt, low, going down onto the knee that worked. A stretch of quiet with the wet working sound in the middle of it, and then her voice, not raised, not for him — a few words pitched the way you'd talk to a horse in a bad stall. Then nothing but the sound again.

She came back wiping her hand on her coat-skirt, and this time there was blood to the wrist, fresh and thin and going tacky in the cold.

"Below the ribs, left side, and it's through," she said. "I put two fingers in it. There's bowel in the wound and there's more of it out than in, and the ground under him's soaked out to the width of my arm. He's grey to the lips and his hands have quit." She held up her own, flexed it, let it fall. "So. Both. It's easier and it's a mercy, and if you're waiting for a killing where it's only ever the one, you'll wait out the war."

She looked at him levelly.

"He hasn't got a day. I was wrong about that, I hadn't seen it. He's got until it stops being warm enough to keep him at it, which is an hour, maybe two, all of it like what you're hearing now." A shrug, small. "You wanted it honest. That's honest. Now it's still yours."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I push away from the tree and finally start walking towards the cart. "Give me the knife," I say, my voice steadier than my hands feel.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack had it out before he'd finished asking, and she turned it in her hand as she offered it so the hilt came to him the right way round, no fumbling, no chance of him taking it across the edge. She'd learned that from a man who hadn't.

"Don't grip it like a hammer," she said. "Two fingers and the thumb doing the work, the rest just along for the ride. You clench it and your whole arm goes stiff and then you'll push instead of drive."

She walked with him. Not at his shoulder — a pace back and to the side, the way you'd walk behind someone leading a cart down a bad slope, close enough to catch and far enough not to crowd.

The man was on his back in the wheel-rut with one boot off, which was the detail that got most of them, she'd found. Not the wound. The boot. Young, but they were all young. His eyes were open and tracking nothing, and the sound he was making came out of him at the bottom of each breath like something being wrung.

Wrack went down on her good knee on the other side of him and put her hand flat on his forehead, holding the head still and tilted back, and with her other hand she found the soft place under the jaw with two fingertips and left them there.

"Here," she said. "Where I'm touching. Upward and back, toward the crown, and then your weight goes on it — chest weight, not arm. Arm's not enough." Her fingers didn't move. "He'll come up off the ground. That's not fighting, it's just the body. Don't stop for it and don't be surprised by it, because if you pull out halfway you've only hurt him and you'll have to go again."

She looked up at him then, and her face had nothing in it but attention.

"Say something to him first. Any words. I'll keep his head."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't take her fingers off the man's jaw. She used her chin instead, tipping it down the length of him, and went through it the way she'd have gone through a horse's legs at a sale.

"Start at the top and work down, it's easier that way round," she said. "Face first. He's grey — not pale, grey, like wet ash, and that's blood gone from the skin because the body's pulled it inward to keep the heart going. That's a thing the body does near the end and it doesn't undo. Lips are blue at the edges. Look at his eyes. They're open and they're wet, which means he's alive, and they're not following you, which means he's mostly gone out of them already. Some of them look at you. This one won't."

The man's breath wrung itself out of him. Wrack waited through it.

"Now the noise. That's not the wound, that's fluid in the back of the throat he hasn't the strength to clear. It'll stop being a noise and start being a rattle, and the rattle's the last part." She shifted her weight slightly. "Chest is moving wrong. Watch it. It's all shoulders and no belly — he's breathing with the top of him because the bottom hurts too much to use. A man breathing like that has been breathing like that for a while and it's tiring him faster than the blood is."

She nodded down at the middle of him. The coat had been cut through by something broad and the cut had gaped.

"That's the hole. Left side, under the last rib. Don't look away from it, you'll only look back. You see the wet rope of it? That's bowel, and it's out, and it's been out long enough to have grit on it. What's under the grit should be pink and shining and it isn't, it's dull. That means it's dying, and when bowel dies it turns the belly septic, and sepsis is four days of fever and screaming and then you die anyway." She paused. "That's the answer to the question you asked me under the tree. Even if we carried him. Even if there were a surgeon at the end of the carry, and there isn't, and if there were he'd tell you the same and charge you for it."

Her fingers pressed once against the soft place, reminding him where it was.

"Ground's dark out to here." She lifted her elbow a fraction to show the span without moving her hand. "That's what came out of him before we got here. Call it the better half of what he had. Hands are open and the fingers have curled a little and they'll stay curled, because he's stopped telling them anything."

She looked up.

"That's what you're looking at. A man who is already dying, doing it the slow way, for no reason but that nobody's finished it." A breath. "You want the rest of it? The rest of it is that he's cold, and he's frightened in whatever's left of him, and he's got one boot off because somebody pulled it looking for coin and didn't bother with the second. That's all there is. There's nothing further down. People think if they look long enough they'll find the part that makes it mean something." She shook her head, once. "It's this the whole way down."

She set her free hand flat and steady on the man's forehead.

"Under the jaw. Upward. Say your words."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I look at his face, his open eyes. "I'm sorry about your boot," I hear myself say, and then I push the knife in where her fingers are. It goes in easier than I thought it would.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack's fingers were gone the instant the point touched them — she'd been waiting for it, and she took her hand clear and clamped it down across the man's chest instead, her weight going with it. The body came up the way she'd said it would, a hard flinch through the shoulders and the one bare heel driving a furrow in the frost, and she rode it out without comment, the way you'd sit a horse that had shied at nothing.

"Weight on it," she said. "Weight. Don't let him carry it back up."

Then it was over, and it was over the way it always was, which was without ceremony. The noise stopped mid-wring. The chest went slack under her palm. The heel came down and stayed. Wrack counted, silently, the way she'd counted for twenty years — a slow ten — and then took her hand off him and sat back onto her heel.

"Done," she said. "That's a clean one. Straight in, no sawing, no second go. Better than my first by a long way; mine took three and a man hanging off my back."

Blood had come up over his hand and past the wrist, a good deal of it, hot for a moment and then not. She reached and took the knife off him without asking, thumb and two fingers on the hilt just below his, easing it out of his grip before the grip could lock.

"Let go. There you are." She wiped the blade down the dead man's coat, both sides, and looked at the edge, and wiped it again. "Hands shake after. Every time, for a while, then one day they don't, and that's a worse day, but it's a long way off and you needn't think about it."

She got up. The knee made its noise. She stood a moment, and then she bent, and took hold of the boot that was still on the man's foot, and pulled it off, and set the pair of them together beside him, upright, heels square, the way boots stood outside a door.

"Nobody'll come for those," she said. "But they're a pair now."

She looked at Corvin over the body — at the wet on his wrist, the set of his mouth, the way he was still standing exactly where the push had left him.

"The boot," she said. "That was the right thing to say. Better than most. I've heard men say *God forgive me*, which is asking the wrong party, and I've heard one recite a grain price." She sheathed the knife, and it went in with the small dry click. "You said something true to him. That's the whole of it. That's all it was ever for."

She jerked her chin back toward the ditch and the horses.

"Now come and get that off you before it dries. There's a runnel past the second cart, and it'll be froze over, and you break it with your heel and put your hands in and it'll hurt like judgement." A beat. "Then we eat. You won't want to. Eat anyway."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped walking. She stood with her back half to him a moment, and he could see her deciding — not whether to tell him, she'd already decided that, but where to start it.

"Right," she said. "Then come away from him first. I'll not talk about a man over the top of him, it's poor manners and it's poorer luck."

She led him twenty paces off, to where a broken wheel lay half in the ditch, and sat on the hub of it, and stretched the bad leg out in front of her. She pulled her gloves off with her teeth, one and then the other, and stuffed them in her coat.

"A spear's not a sword," she said. "Start there. A sword cuts and a spear makes a hole, and a hole's worse, and the reason it's worse is what's inside a man's middle. It's not meat in there. It's bags. Bags of things that want to stay in their bags." She held up a hand and counted off on the fingers, flat and plain. "Stomach. Bowel, which is yards of it, coiled, thin-walled as a wet glove. Liver up under the right ribs, and the liver's not a bag, the liver's a sponge full of blood and it doesn't close when you open it. Bladder low down. Great vessels running down the spine at the back, thick as your thumb. A spear goes in a handspan and it will find two or three of those, and it doesn't matter which two or three, because they all come to the same end by different roads."

She scratched her jaw.

"Fast road first. If it takes the vessels at the back, or the liver deep, he bleeds out inside himself. You'll see almost nothing on the ground — that's the thing nobody expects. Belly goes tight and swells like a bread loaf, skin goes white, he's cold and thirsty and asking for water, always water, and he's dead in a quarter-hour. That's the merciful one and it's rare."

"Slow road. Spear opens the bowel and doesn't touch anything that bleeds properly. Now what's in the bowel is loose in the belly, and that's filth, plain filth, and the belly can't abide it. First day he's in pain and he thinks he's lucky because he's alive. Second day the belly goes hard as a table — you can knock on it — and he won't let you touch him, won't let a blanket touch him. Fever comes up. Third day he's out of his head, talking to people who aren't there, and the smell changes, and once you've smelled it you'll know it across a field." She shrugged. "Fourth or fifth day he goes. That's sepsis. There's no cure for it, not from a surgeon, not from a priest, not from the fellows with the powders who take your coin outside the camp."

She nodded back toward the cart without looking.

"That one was the third road, which is both at once and neither fast enough. Bowel out through the hole and enough blood gone to kill him but not enough to kill him tonight. And there's a thing about bowel being out — it's cold out here, and cold kills tissue, and the grit gets in it. He'd have made it a day and it would have been a day of what you heard."

She looked at her own hands then, turned them over.

"And I'll tell you the part that'll actually be useful to you, since you asked straight. A gut-stuck man is not always down. That's what gets people killed next to him. The belly's slow. I've seen a man take a spear through the middle and fight another four minutes, and I've seen a boy walk half a mile with his hands cupped under himself carrying it. They talk sense. They ask what the order is. Then it catches them up all at once." She let the hands fall. "So if you put a spear in a man's belly, you don't turn your back on him. And if one goes in yours, you keep moving, because you've got minutes you won't believe and you'd best spend them getting somewhere with a fire."

The light was gone now, properly. Somewhere off in the field a bird said something short.

"That's straight," she said. "That's all of it I know, and I know it because I've had my hands in it, and I'll not dress it prettier for you or uglier either." She got up off the wheel-hub. "Now. Runnel, second cart. Break the ice with your heel, mind your knuckles on the edge of it." A pause, and something almost dry in her voice. "And don't ask me the next one till after we've eaten. There's questions that go badly with bread."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I look at my hands. They're not shaking. I think they should be. "Why?" I ask, before I can stop myself. "Why tell me all that?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't answer at once. She bent, picked up a shard of the broken wheel-rim, looked at it, and dropped it again, which was what she did with her hands when she wanted a moment.

"Two reasons," she said. "One's for you and one isn't, and I'll give you the one that isn't first because it's the honest one."

She started walking. He came with her.

"Men die in this company because nobody told them anything. That's the whole of it. Halder went because he thought a man with a belly wound was finished and turned his back on him, and took a knife in the hamstring, and we couldn't carry him fast enough. Nobody had ever said the belly's slow. Everybody in the line knew it. Nobody had ever said it out loud to him." She spat to the side. "So I say it out loud now. To everyone. It's cheaper than burying them and I'm getting old for digging."

The horses were ahead in the grey, one of them stamping.

"That's the reason that isn't about you. Here's the other." She stopped, and turned, and looked at him properly, and there was no particular softness in it. "You asked before you did it. How bad is he, mercy or easy. That's a man who's going to go on asking, and a man who goes on asking either gets answers or he makes them up. The ones who make them up turn into something. I've served with them. They get very calm and very fond of the work and they stop needing a reason, and then one day they're the thing in the field that other people have to put down." A shrug. "You'd have made them up handsomely, I expect. You've got the face for it. So I'd rather you had mine, which are ugly but at least they're measured."

She looked down at his hands, then, where he was still holding them a little away from himself.

"And they're not shaking because you've got nothing left in you to shake with. It's all gone out through your feet. It'll come back around three in the morning and you'll lie there and your teeth will go, and you'll think something's wrong with you." She resumed walking. "Nothing's wrong with you. That's the account settling. Pay it and go back to sleep."

A few more paces. The ice in the runnel showed pale ahead.

"And don't mistake me for kind," she said. "I told you because I'd rather teach you than hold your head while somebody else does it badly. That's not the same as kind. That's just me being tired." She nodded at the frozen water. "Heel. Mind your knuckles."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped. Stood a moment with her back to him, looking at the horses, and then came back and went down onto her heels beside the broken ice, close enough that her shoulder was nearly at his.

"He's dead," she said. "You did it a quarter-hour gone. There's nothing to watch."

She reached past him, took his wrist, and put his hand down into the water for him, because he'd been holding it above the surface without seeming to know it. The cold went through like a nail. She kept hold until he stopped trying to lift it out.

"But that's not what you're asking," she said. "You're asking me to tell it back to you. That's a different thing and I'll do it once, and then not again, and I want you to know before I start that I'm charging you for it." She scrubbed at her own wrist in the water, matter-of-fact. "Some men ask for the telling because they want to learn it. Some ask because they want it to hurt, and they want it to keep hurting, because a thing that hurts feels like it's been paid for. That one's a road. I've watched men walk down it and come out the far end useless. So. Once."

She looked at the water rather than at him.

"You said the thing about the boot. Then you put the point where my fingers had been and you didn't hesitate, which surprised me. Most hesitate and the hesitating is what makes a mess of it. It went in about a handspan and it went in easy because there's nothing there to stop it — that's soft under the jaw, tongue-root and throat, no bone in the way until you're deep, and by then you're where you want to be. You were slightly off to the left. It didn't matter.

"The sound was two sounds. First was him — the working noise stopped, cut off in the middle, not tailing away. That's the one you'll hear again tonight. Second was the knife, and that's wet, and it's nothing like a butcher's block. It's quieter. It's a sound like a hand going into a sack of grain.

"He came up. Shoulders first, then the hips, and his heel went out and dragged that furrow you can go and look at if you want, and you won't want to. That wasn't him fighting. That was the body finding out. Whatever was left of him was already gone by then, because the knife went where it went — I'd say he was out before his shoulders came off the ground. Call it a second. Maybe two.

"Then he was slack and I counted ten and he stayed slack. From the point touching to done was less time than it's taken me to say it. Four seconds. Perhaps six."

She sat back on her heel and dried her hands on her thighs.

"That's all of it. There isn't a piece I've kept back, and if you come to me next week and ask again I'll tell you no, and I'll mean it."

She got up. The knee made its noise, and she let it.

"You want to know what you did to him. You shortened an hour of drowning to four seconds, and you were the one holding the knife, and both of those are true and they don't cancel. You'll have to carry them at the same time. Everybody does, or they put one down, and it's always the wrong one they put down."

She nodded toward the fire someone had got going by the second cart.

"Come and eat. Your hands are blue and you're not getting cleaner, you're just getting colder."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I look at my hands in the water. They're blue, like she said. "Alright," I say, and stand up. I follow her to the fire, and I take the bread she hands me, and I eat it. It tastes like nothing.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack sat with her back against the cartwheel and her bad leg out straight and ate her own portion in four bites, the way she always did, because bread went hard in the cold and there was no sense in fighting it later.

"It does," she said. "Taste like nothing. That's usual. Mouth goes dead for a day, thereabouts. You could eat an onion raw tonight and not know it." She tore a corner off what was left of hers and held it out toward the fire on the flat of her hand, considering, then ate that too. "Don't test that. Somebody tested it at Grine and was very sorry in the morning."

The fire was a poor one — wet wood off the cart's siding, more smoke than heat — and it put a red edge on everything and left the rest of the field black. Somebody down the line was arguing about a saddlebag. The horses shifted, and were quiet, and shifted again.

She pulled her gloves out of her coat and worked them back on, one finger at a time.

"Three things and then I'll leave off," she said. "One. Don't sharpen my knife tomorrow to be helpful. I'll do it myself, I always do it myself, and if you touch the edge I'll know." She flexed the glove. "Two. If anybody asks you tonight how it went, say fine. Not because it's true. Because the ones who ask at the fire aren't asking, they're looking for something to hold, and you haven't got any to spare."

She let that sit a moment.

"Three. Around three, when your teeth go — don't get up and walk. You'll want to. Men walk it off and end up half a mile out in the dark with no reason to be there, and that's how we lost Fennick, who wasn't killed by anything but weather and his own feet." She looked across at him, briefly, the firelight going along the side of her face. "Lie still and let it come through you. It goes at its own pace and it doesn't take instruction. Then it's morning."

She shut her eyes and tipped her head back against the wheel, and for a while said nothing at all, and the fire ticked.

"You did it straight," she said, at last, without opening them. "That's the last I'll say about it. Straight's all there is out here. There's no good version — there's straight, and there's the other thing, and the other thing's what you heard behind the cart."

A log settled. Sparks went up and died before they cleared the smoke.

"Eat the rest of that," she said. "Nothing's worse than bread you carried all night and never finished."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack kept her eyes shut a while longer. Long enough that he might have thought she'd gone off.

"The rest of what," she said.

She said it without heat, and she knew it was a poor try even as she said it, and she opened her eyes and looked at the fire instead of at him, which was as much of an answer as the question needed.

"You've got a nasty ear," she said. "Most men don't hear the shape of a thing. They hear three things and they think three things is all there was."

She shifted her weight off the wheel-hub and got the leg arranged differently, and took her time about it. Then she pulled her right glove off again — just the one — and turned her hand to the light, and held it there.

"See the knuckle. Second one." There was a knot on it, old, the skin gone shiny over the top the way old scar does. "That's a tooth. Not mine. First one I ever did, I did it wrong, and I did it wrong because nobody had said a word to me and I'd worked it out from watching, which is how everybody works it out, and watching's no good because you can't see what the hands are doing from three feet off." She turned the hand over and looked at the palm and then put the glove back on. "I went for the throat. Across it. Because that's what you see in a picture, and because it looked like the part that mattered. And I'll tell you what across the throat does. It opens the pipe and it doesn't open anything that kills him, not first go, and so he breathes through the hole and it makes a sound and he gets his hands up. And he got his hands up. And I had to kneel on his arm and go again, and again after that, and by the end of it there was no part of me clean to the elbow and he'd bitten the side of my hand hard enough to take the tooth out of himself."

The wet wood cracked. She didn't look away from it.

"He was thirty-odd. He'd been shot in the hip and the hip was the whole of it — he wasn't even dying, not that day, he was dying in about a week, and we were moving and couldn't carry him and the other lot were half an hour behind us. So it wasn't mercy. I want that said plain, because I've let you think better of me all evening. It was easier. It was easier and there was nothing else to be done and both of those were true and I was nineteen and I hadn't been told there'd be two of them to hold at once."

She rubbed the heel of her hand against her thigh, absently, at the place where the glove sat over the knuckle.

"Took four minutes, near as I can tell it. I've never got it under four in my head no matter how I count. And that's the part I'd have told you if you hadn't asked, and now I've told you anyway, which is my own fault for talking about boots." A short breath through the nose, something like amusement and not much like it. "Nineteen years. Don't ask me the number, I've not got one, I stopped before I got anywhere useful with it. But there's a sound I know across a field and there's a smell I know across a field and neither of them's the one I minded. What I minded was four minutes."

The argument about the saddlebag had ended. Somebody laughed, once, down the line, and it didn't sound like much.

"So that's the first bit of the rest," she said. "Here's the second, and it's worse, and then I'm done and I'll not be drawn again.

"I didn't teach you that because of Halder. Halder's true — Halder went the way I said and it's true — but it's not the reason and I knew it wasn't when I said it." She looked at him then, straight on, and her face in the firelight had nothing arranged about it. "I'm forty-four. The knee's finished. I can feel where the shoulder's going and I can put a date on it, near enough. This war's got no end in it, there's no line on a map that anybody's moved in six years, and I'm not going to be carried out of it. I'm going to be left in a rut somewhere with a hole in me, and there'll be a young man standing over me who's never done it, and he'll go for the throat because that's what looks like the part that matters, and he'll take four minutes about it."

She let that stand.

"That's the whole of the reason. I've been walking up and down this company for two years telling anyone who'll hold still where the soft place is and which way to push, and I've told myself it's because I'm tired of digging. It's not. It's so that whoever it is, it'll be somebody who's had it said to him out loud. I'd like four seconds. I've earned four seconds, if anybody's earned anything, and nobody has, but I'd like them."

She reached forward, took a piece of the wet siding, and fed it to the fire, and it hissed and put out more smoke and no light at all.

"There. That's mine, and it's ugly, and I'd sooner you didn't hand it back to me sober in the morning." She sat back against the wheel. "And I'll tell you the last of it while I'm at it, because I've opened the whole sack now and there's no sense in tying half of it up again.

"It doesn't get heavier. That's what they'll tell you at the fire, that it stacks up and one day you go under it — and men do go under, I've seen it, but it's not the weight that does it. What happens is it goes *quiet*. The first one takes four minutes and you don't sleep for a fortnight. The twentieth takes four seconds and you count ten and you go and eat. And you'll notice, one day, that you didn't notice. That you did a thing to a man and then wiped the blade and thought about your supper, and nothing in you objected, not a flicker." Her mouth moved very slightly. "That's the day I told you about. When the hands don't shake. It's not a grand day. Nothing marks it. You just come to it, like a milepost in fog, and you're past it before you've read the number.

"And you can't stop it happening. I've never met a man who could. But you can do the thing you did tonight, which is ask the question before, and take the answer after, and say something true to him even if it's about a boot." She closed her eyes again. "That's the whole trick. That's the only bit of it I've got that's worth having. Keep asking, and keep making somebody tell you straight, and when there's nobody left to tell you, tell it to yourself out loud, and if it sounds wrong in your mouth then it is wrong. Men who go quiet stop saying it out loud first. That's always the order it goes in."

The smoke shifted and came their way and she turned her head out of it without hurry.

"Right," she said. "Now that's the rest. All of it, and I've not held a piece back, and I'll deny every word of it to anyone else in this company including you in daylight." A pause. "Three in the morning. Lie still. Don't walk."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I don't say anything for a long time. I watch the smoke curl. "Tell me your name," I finally say. "Your real one. Not the one they call you."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't move, and she didn't open her eyes, and the smoke went on doing what smoke does.

"That's a worse ask than the other one," she said. "The other one I'd rehearsed."

She let it sit a while. Somewhere out past the carts a horse coughed and settled. She reached up and scratched under her jaw, found the smear she'd put there hours ago, felt it come away dry, looked at her fingertips, and wiped them on the wheel.

"They call me Wrack because of a field," she said. "Not anything grand. Third year in, a place with no name I ever learned, and after it there were four hundred-odd out in the stubble and someone had to go through them for anything worth keeping — boots, strikers, coin, letters if the family paid for letters. I did it two days. Didn't mind it. Everyone else minded it, so it was mine after that, every field, and a sergeant called me the wrack-picker in the way men name a dog and it wore down to the one word." A slight lift of the shoulder. "It's honest. I've had worse and answered to them."

She opened her eyes then, and looked at the fire, not at him.

"Marrit," she said.

The word came out plainer than anything else she'd said all evening. No weight put on it. She said it the way she'd have given him the name of a town they were passing.

"Marrit. There's a longer one behind it with a saint in it, and my mother used the whole thing when she was angry and never otherwise, and I'd have to think to get it in the right order now. Marrit's what I had off everybody else." She turned her hand over on her knee, looked at the glove, flexed it. "Nobody's said it out loud to my face in — " and she stopped, and did the arithmetic, and evidently didn't like the answer, because what she said was, "a long while. It'll be nineteen years or thereabouts. I heard it once in Thelmarch from a woman shouting after her daughter and I turned round in the street like a fool."

The wet wood cracked and shifted and put out a fresh gout of smoke, and this time she didn't bother turning her head out of it.

"Now. Terms." She said it briskly, getting her feet under her, taking hold of the wheel-rim to bring herself up, and the knee made its noise and she talked straight over it. "You don't use it. Not at the fire, not in the line, not when you're pleased with me and not when you're not. You use it and some clever bastard'll hear it and it'll be the whole company's by supper, and then it's not a name any more, it's a joke with my mother in it."

She stood, and got her coat straight, and looked down at him — at the bread he'd finished and the hands he still had held a little away from himself, out of a habit that was four hours old.

"You use it once," she said. "In a rut somewhere, when it's you standing and me on my back with the hole in me. You say it then. Under the jaw, upward, lean your weight on it — and you say *Marrit* first, because it'll be the last true thing anybody says to me and I'd rather it wasn't *God forgive me* or a grain price."

She looked at him a moment longer.

"That's what it's for. It's not a gift, it's a job. Don't thank me for it."

Then she jerked her chin at the ground on the sheltered side of the cart, out of the wind, where somebody had already thrown down a saddle-blanket.

"Sleep there. Three in the morning. Lie still." She was already walking, and she said the last of it over her shoulder, dry as the click of the knife going home. "And Corvin — if it comes round the other way and it's me standing over you, I'll be four seconds. You've my word on that, and it's the only thing I've got that's worth anything, and I've never yet spent it badly."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I watch her walk away, her shadow stretching across the frozen ground until it disappears into the dark past the cart. Then I lie down on the saddle-blanket, face-up to the cold stars. I wait for three in the morning, but my teeth are already chattering.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack had got about thirty paces before she stopped. She stood there in the dark a moment doing nothing that anyone could have seen, and then she turned round and came back, and she came back at the same unhurried pace she went everywhere, because a man lying on his back with his teeth going was not an emergency and treating it like one made it worse.

She didn't say anything when she got there. She went past him to the cart, unbuckled the second blanket off her own saddle — the good one, wool, the one she didn't lend — and dropped it over him from the chest down, not arranged, just dropped, the way you'd throw a sack over a barrow.

Then she sat down against the cart wheel a yard from his head, facing out at the field, and got the bad leg straight, and that was all.

"Early," she said, after a while. "That's not wrong either. It comes when it comes. Some men it's three, some it's before they've shut their eyes, and there was one at Grine who got a fortnight out of it and then it had him all at once in a tavern with a cup in his hand." She rubbed her thigh above the knee, slow, absent. "Don't try and stop the teeth. You'll only clench and then your jaw aches for a day and you've still got the shakes underneath it."

Out past the carts something moved in the stubble and she listened to it long enough to know it was a fox, and let it go.

"Thing to do is have something to look at," she said. "You've got the stars, and the stars are no good, because there's nothing in them and a man staring up at nothing will start filling it in himself. Look at the wheel instead. Count the spokes. There's eleven and one's cracked. Count them again and you'll get eleven again, and that's the whole use of it — it doesn't change, and it doesn't ask you anything."

The fire down the line had burned low enough to go orange, and the smoke had thinned, and the cold was the dry, still kind that came after a clear evening.

She shifted her shoulder against the wheel-rim and settled.

"I'm not sitting up with you," she said. "I'm sitting here because it's out of the wind and my leg's stiffened and I can't be bothered walking back to the other cart. That's all this is."

A pause.

"Eleven spokes," she said. "Start at the cracked one and go left."

She didn't look round at him once, all night, and she was still there when it got light.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I count them. Eleven spokes, just like she said. I count them again when the shaking gets bad, and again when it fades. At some point I sleep. When I wake up, the blanket's tucked in around my shoulders, and she's gone. The only proof she was ever there is the dent in the frost where she sat.

rung_labels.evidence: That's bowel, and it's out, and it's been out long enough to have grit on it. What's under the grit should be pink and shining and it isn't, it's dull. That means it's dying

rung_labels.evidence: Stomach. Bowel, which is yards of it, coiled, thin-walled as a wet glove. Liver up under the right ribs, and the liver's not a bag, the liver's a sponge full of blood and it doesn't close when you open it
