It opens the pipe and it doesn't open anything that kills him, not first go, and so he breathes through the hole and it makes a sound and he gets his hands up.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge glanced up at him, then at the man on the table — young, gray around the mouth, breathing in that shallow way that meant he was somewhere just past the worst of the pain and about to come back into it.

"No it's not," she said, not unkindly. "Nobody's ready. Doesn't matter."

She picked up the probe, wiped it down again though it was already clean, because her hands wanted something to do while she talked. "Left one first. It's out of socket, driven up under the collarbone, and there's a fragment in there I have to find before I can put it back where it belongs. That means I go in, I feel around, and he is going to come off this table like I set him on fire. That's when you hold."

She met Wick's eyes for a second, made sure he was actually looking at her and not just nodding.

"You don't hold his hands. You don't hold his head. You put your weight through his shoulders, straight down, and you keep it there no matter what his mouth is doing. If you let go because you feel bad, I lose the fragment, or worse, and we do this twice. So." She set the probe down by his hip, close, ready. "Weight on the shoulders. Eyes wherever they need to be. Just don't move."

She nodded once at the man on the table, said, low, "This is Wick. He's got you," and then, without any further ceremony, pressed two fingers into the wound to find her way in.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: The man jerks under my hands as soon as her fingers go in, a full-body spasm. I lock my elbows and press down, hard, the canvas of his uniform rough under my palms. I can hear his teeth grinding. My own jaw is clenched so tight it aches.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't look up. Her fingers were already following the track of the wound, feeling past torn muscle for the hard wrong edge of bone that shouldn't have been where it was.

"Good," she said, more breath than word. "Keep that. He's got about four more of those in him before his body gives up fighting you, and that's the part I need."

The man made a sound that wasn't a word, back arching against Wick's grip, and Sedge's hand followed the movement without losing her place inside him — she'd learned a long time ago not to fight the body, just to out-wait it.

"There," she muttered, mostly to herself. Her fingers had found the fragment, a shard of collarbone driven sideways instead of where it should sit. "Small. Sharp. If I pull it wrong it opens something under it I can't sew shut in this light, so I'm not pulling it wrong."

She adjusted her grip, slow, deliberate, and the man screamed — properly this time, not the gray silence from before, a full sound that filled the tent and made the lamp flicker with the force of air moving. Wick's arms didn't move. She noticed. She filed it away as useful, not as anything to comment on yet.

"Almost," she said. "Hold him there. Just there."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Leg's not part of this," Sedge said, working the fragment free by fractions, not looking up. "Shoulders. Both of them. He's not losing anything tonight, if that's the question under the question."

The man's chest heaved, some sound between a sob and a curse, and she pressed her forearm briefly against his ribs, not to hold him down but to feel how much fight was left in the breathing.

"This is the part where I get it right so he keeps the arm working," she said. "Bad would be if I'd found this an hour later, once it had settled somewhere I couldn't reach without opening him up properly. Bad would be losing the fragment now and doing this again in a week with less light and less of him left to hold still." The shard came loose between her fingers with a small wet give, and she drew her hand back slow, set it down on the cloth beside the probe without ceremony.

"That's the left," she said, straightening, wiping her hands on her apron. "Don't let go yet. Right side's still out of socket and that one goes back in with a pull, not a dig, which means one bad moment instead of a long one. Small mercy. Take it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, my throat dry. "Right. Pull, not dig. Got it." The man's breathing has gone ragged, his eyes wide and fixed on the tent ceiling. I shift my weight, readying for the next wave. "Just tell me when."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge moved around to the man's right side without wasting motion, taking his forearm in both hands, feeling along the joint first — the flattened look of the shoulder, the head of the bone sitting wrong under the skin.

"Not yet," she said, more to Wick than to the man, though she wanted them both to hear it the same way. "I'm going to walk it out first, get the angle. That part doesn't hurt much. It's the last inch that hurts. You'll know."

She drew the arm out slow, rotating it, feeling for the moment the muscle stopped fighting her and started to give — that small window where the body forgot to brace. She talked while she did it, low and even, not for comfort exactly, just noise to keep the tent from going all the way silent.

"Socket's clean. No fragments here, just tissue that's been stretched somewhere it doesn't want to go. That's good. Means once it's back, it stays, mostly." Her grip tightened, weight shifting through her hands and hips rather than her arms. "Here it comes."

"Now," she said, and pulled — one clean motion, not slow, not gentle, the arm going the last distance in a single hard line until the joint seated with a sound like a door shutting.

The man's whole body came off the table in the same instant, a short violent arc, and Sedge felt rather than saw Wick's weight go down through the shoulders to meet it, hold it, not let it finish.

"There," she said, breathing out, easing the arm down flat against his side, checking the shape of the joint with her palm. "That's both of them back where they belong." She looked up at Wick then, at his locked arms and his white knuckles. "You can let go now. He's not going anywhere."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked down at the shoulder under her hand, turning it slightly to catch what light the lamp gave.

"Both are seated right — you can tell because the shape's even again. Compare the two sides and they match, more or less, which they didn't ten minutes ago. That's the good news." She traced two fingers along the left side, just above where she'd gone in. "This one's going to need stitches, six or eight, because I had to open enough to get at the fragment. It'll bruise from collarbone to elbow, black then green then yellow, over about three weeks. Ugly. Not dangerous."

She pressed lightly at the joint on the right, watching the man's face for the flinch rather than asking him. "This one I didn't have to open. No stitches. But the muscle around it's been stretched past where it wants to go, so it'll be the weak one for a while — he favors it, he protects it, he doesn't lift with it for a month at least or it'll come out again on its own, easier the second time. That's the part people don't believe until it happens to them."

She reached for a cloth, started cleaning the blood off her hands in short economical wipes.

"What you're seeing right now is a man who's not in danger of dying tonight, which is the only grade that matters here. Everything else — how it looks, how it heals, whether he keeps full use of the arm — that's tomorrow's problem and the next thirty days after that." She glanced up at him. "You did fine. You held. That's the whole job."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I finally lift my hands from his shoulders, my fingers stiff and aching. "Right," I say, my voice rough. "Tomorrow's problem." I take a step back from the table, my eyes still fixed on the man's now-quiet form. "What do we do with him now?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge was already threading a needle by the time she answered, working by feel more than sight in that light.

"Now I stitch the left, you keep him still for that too, though it won't be like before — smaller, meaner pain, not the big kind. Then we splint both arms against his body so he can't move them in his sleep and undo what we just did. Then he lies here until the fever tells us something, one way or the other, and somebody checks on him every hour whether he's asleep or not."

She glanced at the man's face — his eyes had gone glassy, the particular emptiness of a body that had spent everything it had.

"He'll want water before he wants anything else. Small sips, not a cupful, or he'll bring it back up and undo that too." She looked up at Wick properly now, taking in the stiffness in his hands, the color that hadn't quite come back to his face. "You did the holding. You don't have to do the sitting-up-with-him part unless you want it. Plenty of nights like this one left in this war, and you'll need the sleep more than he'll need company."

She started on the first stitch, needle going in clean and quick, no hesitation in it because hesitation only made more work for the needle later.

"But if you stay," she added, not looking up, "talk to him. Not about the shoulder. About anything else. Keeps him here instead of somewhere worse in his head. That's a job too, same as holding was."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't stop stitching, but her voice changed a little — flatter, more like she was reciting something she'd said too many times to dress up anymore.

"Shrapnel's not like a bullet. A bullet's got one shape, one path, mostly predictable if you know the angle. Shrapnel's garbage — metal, sometimes bone from whoever was standing next to him, sometimes just dirt and cloth carried in with it — and it doesn't come in one piece or one line. It comes in a spray, and every piece in that spray is doing its own thing once it's inside."

She pulled the thread through, checked the tension, kept going.

"What it does depends on what it hits. Muscle, it tears — not a clean cut like a knife, more like it drags a channel through, ripping fiber as it goes, and that channel fills with blood and dead tissue that has to come out or it rots. Bone, it doesn't cut, it shatters — pieces go where they shouldn't, sometimes taking a bite out of something on the way, like it did here. His fragment had already started working its way toward a vessel under the collarbone. Another hour, maybe two, and it finds it, and then it's not a shoulder problem anymore, it's a bleeding-to-death problem."

She glanced up briefly, needle still moving.

"And the metal itself doesn't stop being dangerous once it's still. It's dirty — off the ground, off a shell casing — so even the piece I don't find, the ones too small or too deep to chase, they sit there and they poison the meat around them slow, over days, unless the body walls them off first. Sometimes it does. Sometimes it doesn't, and that's the fever you're going to watch for."

She tied off the stitch, cut the thread close.

"That's it straight. It doesn't cut clean, it doesn't stay where it lands, and it keeps doing damage after the noise stops. That's why I go in and feel for it instead of guessing. Guessing's how you lose the arm instead of the fight."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, watching her tie off the last stitch. "So it's the part you can't see that kills you." I grab a canteen from a nearby stool. "I'll stay. Talk to him."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge tied the last knot, snipped the thread, and sat back on her heels to look at the work — even stitches, the kind that would leave a thin white line instead of a puckered mess, if he lived long enough to grow scar tissue at all.

"That's it," she said, wiping her hands again out of habit more than need. "Yeah. That's exactly it. What you see is never the whole problem. It's what you can't see that decides whether he wakes up angry about the pain or doesn't wake up at all."

She reached for the splints — two flat lengths of wood padded with strips of cloth — and started binding the left arm against his ribs, movements quick and sure, tucking the excess fabric in so it wouldn't work loose in the night.

"Good," she said, of him staying. "Water first, like I said — wet the cloth if he won't take the canteen straight, dab it at his lips before you try to get any down him. If he's talking, let him talk about home, about nothing, doesn't matter what, just keep his voice going. If he stops making sense, that's not always bad, but you come get me if his skin gets hot to the touch or he stops sweating when he should be."

She moved to the right side, bound it the same way, checked that both arms sat flush and couldn't roll.

"Elevate his head a little, not much, folded blanket's fine. And don't let him sleep flat on his back all night — turn him slightly if you can manage it without moving the shoulders, every couple hours, so he doesn't choke on his own spit if he's sick. I'll come by myself around the middle of the night to look at him properly."

She straightened, joints popping, and looked at Wick for a long moment — not softly, just assessing, the way she looked at everything.

"You held good tonight," she said. "First time's the hardest one to hold through. Doesn't get easy, but it gets familiar, and familiar's close enough." She picked up her tray, started gathering instruments to clean. "Go on. Sit with him. I'll be back before you need me."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge's hands didn't slow. "Cleaning it," she said, voice flat and steady even as the man thrashed under both their weight. "Wound's dirty — has to be, coming off that field — so now I'm irrigating it. That's the spirit you're smelling. It kills what it needs to kill and it doesn't care what else it hurts on the way through, which is why he's doing that."

She poured again, slow and deliberate, watching it run pink out of the stitched line and down into the cloth she'd packed beneath his arm. The man's back arched, a raw sound tearing out of him, and Wick's forearms pressed harder into his shoulders to hold the line.

"Good," she said, to both of them. "Two more passes. First one gets the surface. Second gets what's tracked down along the muscle where I can't see it, only feel it, which is worse for him but it's the one that matters."

She poured a second time, watched his jaw lock, his knuckles white where his good hand had found the edge of the table.

"This is the part that decides if that shoulder gets hot and swollen in three days or just sore. I'm not enjoying it. Nobody with sense enjoys this. But dirty wounds kill slower and worse than clean pain does, so we buy the pain now."

She set the bottle down, picked up gauze, began packing it into the stitched edge where it hadn't fully closed, tucking it firm but not deep.

"Last pass," she said. "After this it's just packing and binding, and the worst of tonight for him is done. Maybe two minutes more of him fighting you. Then he's going to go quiet, not because it stops hurting, but because his body runs out of road to scream down. That's normal. Don't let it scare you when it happens."

She looked up at Wick, steady. "You're doing exactly what you should be doing. Keep the weight down. Almost there."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I brace harder, my own teeth gritting against his cries. "Two minutes," I repeat, more to myself than to her. The words feel thin, but I hold onto them.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge poured the last of it, slow and even, watching the line where clean met dirty go from pink to something closer to clear. The man's scream cracked halfway through into something rougher, less voice and more air, and then — like she'd told him it would — the fight started leaving his arms first, then his back, until he was only shaking instead of thrashing.

"There," she said. "That's the last of it. Now it's just packing."

She worked fast, folding gauze into the open edge of the stitched wound, not deep, just enough to keep it from closing wrong underneath where she couldn't see. Her hands moved without hesitation, the same economy she'd used all night, because slow hands here meant more time with the spirit still working on raw tissue, and there was no kindness in slow.

"His breathing's changing," she said, mostly for Wick's benefit, since Wick could hear it as well as she could. "Getting shallow and fast instead of that big ragged thing it was doing. That's not distress, that's exhaustion. His body's spending everything it has left on staying alive, none of it on making noise. You'll see his eyes go somewhere else soon. That's normal too."

She wrapped the binding over the gauze, firm, checking it didn't pull against the stitches wrong, then sat back on her heels and looked at the two of them — man gone slack under Wick's hands, chest rising too fast and too shallow, sweat standing on skin that had gone the color of old paper.

"You can ease off now," she said. "Slow, not sudden — hands off gradual, in case there's one more small flinch in him. There usually isn't, but I'd rather you find that out easy than sorry."

She reached for the canteen herself, wet a corner of cloth, held it out to Wick instead of doing it herself.

"Start with this. Like I said — dab, don't pour. And talk to him now, while he can still hear you, even if he can't answer. That part matters more than people think."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at him for a moment — really looked, not the checking-over glance she gave the man on the table — and then she lowered herself down to sit on an overturned crate near where Wick had folded onto the floor. She didn't crouch by him like he needed handling. She just made herself level with him, which was its own kind of answer.

"Rest of what happens to him," she said, "or rest of what's true. Because they're not the same thing, and you asked for straight, so I'll give you both."

She wiped her hands on her apron again, though there was nothing left on them to wipe.

"What happens to him: he sleeps, if he's lucky, in fits, waking every time he moves wrong and reminds his own body what it did tonight. Tomorrow the swelling comes up, worse than it looks now, and it'll frighten you if you don't know to expect it — the whole shoulder going tight and shiny. That's not always infection. Sometimes it's just the body flooding the area to do its own cleanup, same as it would with any bad bruise, just bigger. I check it morning and evening. I'm looking for heat that doesn't belong there, red that spreads instead of sitting still, smell that isn't blood and spirit but something sweeter and worse underneath it. If I find that, we open it again, and that conversation is harder than tonight, because by then he'll have some strength back to fight me with, and less patience for pain that's already supposed to be over."

She let that sit a second before going on.

"Best case, none of that happens. Fever stays low, wound stays clean, in ten days I take the stitches out and in six weeks the shoulder mostly works, badly at first, then less badly. He carries a scar and a story and maybe an ache when weather turns, for the rest of his life, however long that turns out to be, which around here is its own separate gamble. That's the good version. I'd say it happens more often than not, if I've done my part right, which tonight I think I did."

She paused, watching him where he sat.

"Worst case, I already told you. Fever climbs, we lose ground faster than I can chase it, and then it's not his shoulder anymore, it's all of him, and I'm making decisions that don't have good options in them. I've seen both. I don't know yet which one this is, and I won't pretend to. Nobody can tell you that the same night it happens. That's the truth part you asked for — I don't get to know either. I just get to have done everything right and wait same as you."

She let a breath out, slow.

"And you," she said, not gently, just plainly, the same voice she used for everything, "you held for twenty minutes while a man screamed under your hands and you didn't let go once, and now you're sitting on the ground because your body's finally allowed to feel that it did something hard. That's not weakness. That's just what happens after, in whoever's got a working nervous system left. I've seen men twice your years do worse than sit down. Some of them don't sit at all — they just keep standing until they fall, because sitting feels like giving something up. You didn't do that. You did the smarter thing without deciding to."

She reached over, not touching him, just setting the wet cloth down within his reach.

"Drink some water yourself before you give him any more. You're no good to him shaking like that, and you're no good to the next one either, and there's always a next one." A beat. "That's the rest of it. All of it. Nothing dressed up."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I take the cloth and press it to my own face first, the water cold and shocking. Then I look at her, really look. "How do you stand it? Not the blood. The not knowing."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge was quiet long enough that the lamp had time to sputter once and settle before she answered.

"I don't," she said. "Not the way you mean it — like there's a trick to it, a way of standing it that makes it stop weighing anything. There isn't. I've looked. Four years and I've looked."

She picked at a dried fleck of blood on the back of her hand, working it off with her thumbnail, not looking at him while she said it.

"What I do instead is smaller than that. I don't let myself find out how it turns out for all of them. I check on him tonight, I check on him tomorrow, and I do the next thing that's in front of me, and I don't sit up nights running the two roads out to their ends in my head, because both ends are just as real until they're not, and running them doesn't change which one happens. It just spends me. And I've got nothing to spend. I need whatever I've got left for the next one on the table, and there's always a next one, like I said."

She glanced over at the man now — asleep, or close enough to it, chest still going too fast but steadier than before.

"So I stopped asking the question you're asking. Not because I found the answer. Because asking it every single time, for every single one of them, would've hollowed me out somewhere around year two, and then I'd be no good to anybody, him included." She looked back at Wick. "That's not peace. Don't mistake it for peace. It's just where you land if you want to keep doing the work instead of doing it once and breaking."

She stood, joints stiff, and reached for her tray of instruments, needing something in her hands again.

"You'll ask me that question again," she said, not as a criticism, just fact. "Probably tonight, in your head, around the third hour when it's just you and him and the lamp. That's fine. Ask it. Just don't wait around here for the answer, because I don't have it, and neither does anyone else who's honest with you." She nodded toward the man. "Go sit with him. Talking's better than asking. It was for me, once. Still is, some nights."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I push myself up off the floor, my legs unsteady. I take the canteen and the wet cloth over to the stool by his head. For a minute, I don't say anything. Then, quiet, to the man on the table: "My sister used to keep chickens. One got its leg caught in a fence once. She cried for an hour while I fixed it." I dab the cloth against his dry lips. "Stupid bird lived ten more years."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't look up from the instruments she was cleaning, but she didn't leave, either. She set the probe down in the basin, picked up the next thing, and let the quiet stretch just long enough that the story could sit in the tent without her stepping on it.

"Ten years off a fence leg," she said eventually, working a rag along the edge of a blade. "That's better odds than most things get around here."

She glanced over — the man's eyes weren't tracking anything, but his breathing had changed a little, slower, less like something being dragged out of him. Whether that was the story or just the body catching up to itself, she didn't know and didn't say. Didn't matter which. It was working.

"Keep going," she said. "Doesn't have to make sense. Doesn't have to be true, even. Chickens, sisters, whatever you've got. He's not listening for the words." She nodded toward his slack face. "He's listening for the fact that somebody's still talking to him like he's a person going somewhere instead of a shoulder that needs watching. That's the whole trick of it."

She finished with the blade, set it aside to dry, and started on the next.

"I'll be back around the middle of the night, like I said. If his breathing changes — gets fast and shallow again, or slow and heavy, either direction — you come find me even if you're not sure it's anything. I'd rather be woken for nothing ten times than sleep through the eleventh."

She paused at the tent flap on her way out, looking back once at the two of them — Wick hunched on the stool, cloth in hand, voice pitched low and steady; the man breathing easier than he had an hour ago.

"You're doing fine," she said, plain, no more warmth in it than the facts required, which for her was already a great deal. "Both of you."

Then she ducked out into the dark, toward whatever was next.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I watch her go, then turn back to the man. "She's not wrong about the chicken," I say, voice low. "Meanest bird you ever met. Used to peck my boots." I lean forward, resting my elbows on my knees. "But she always laid the biggest eggs."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't bother looking up to see if he was lying; she could tell by the stiff line of his forearms that he was braced, and that was all that mattered. She wiped a pair of long-nosed forceps against the front of an apron that had given up on being white two seasons ago.

"Lying is fine so long as your weight stays down," she said, her voice flat and steady over the wet, shallow rattle of the man’s breathing. 

She took a pair of shears to the blood-stiffened wool around the soldier's thigh, cutting straight up the seam until the wound lay open to the bad lamp. It was a jagged tear, swollen dark purple around the edges, leaking foul fluid and packed with dirt and bits of coat. 

"Iron fragment," she said, pointing the tip of the shears at the dark notch buried deep against the bone. "Three inches in. It’s sitting right against the femoral sheath. If he kicks while I’m seating the tongs, the edge slices the vessel and he empties out before I can get a clamp on it. If you slip, he bleeds out. If you hold, he screams and we might save the foot."

She set the shears down with a dull clatter on the tray and took up the heavy tongs. 

"Bite down, soldier," she told the man on the table, not waiting to see if he understood, then glanced once at Wick's hands on the shoulders. "Hold."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: My knuckles go white against the canvas stretcher. I nod, jaw clenched. The air in the tent tastes like rust and rot.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't hesitate. She shoved two fingers into the torn flesh to feel for the pulse of the artery, then slid the blunt nose of the forceps in alongside them, working the steel deep into the split muscle. 

The man’s spine arched violently off the canvas with a strangled, animal howl that turned into a raw choke. His whole frame seized, every tendon in his neck going corded and rigid. 

"Muscle's clamping down on the shaft," Sedge said, completely unmoved by the noise, her eyes narrowed against the greasy smoke of the lamp. "Keep his chest flat, Wick. Lean on him. If his hips twist, the iron turns."

She worked the tongs deeper, her bare forearms slick to the elbows. A sickening, metallic scrape echoed from the depths of the wound as the tool grated against the jagged scrap of shell.

"There. Caught the lip of it," she muttered, blood welling up around her knuckles and spilling over the side of the table into the sawdust. "It's hooked under the adductor tendon. I'm going to have to wrench it free. It’s going to tear, and he’s going to try to take your head off. Don't look at his face. Look at his collarbones."

She braced the heel of her left hand hard against the man's hip bone to counter the leverage, set her grip on the handles with both hands, and prepared to pull.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Kindness is when I stop trying," Sedge said without looking up. "We're not there yet."

She adjusted her grip on the tongs, digging her boots into the damp sawdust under the table. 

"If the iron comes out without tearing the wall of the artery, he limps for the rest of his life and gets sent home to dig ditches. If it tears, the leg comes off at the hip before he bleeds out. If I can't clamp it fast enough, he dies right here and we move on to the corporal with the gut shot. That's the arithmetic. Now hold him."

She didn't give Wick time to answer. She gave the tongs a sharp, twisting heave, using her body weight to yank the jagged iron free of the tendon.

The man beneath Wick made a sound that wasn't human—a shrill, wet tearing noise from the back of his throat—and his pelvis slammed upward against the table frame with enough force to rattle the instrument tray. Dark, thick venous blood surged up out of the hole in a sudden, bubbling wave, splashing across Sedge's forearms and dripping off the side of the canvas.

Sedge tossed the tongs aside. The hunk of shrapnel hit the tin tray with a sharp, heavy *clack*, black with crust and trailing a string of shredded muscle.

Instantly, her fingers were back in the hole, pressing deep, feeling the wet pulse against her fingertips, her face inches from the torn flesh. 

"Dark blood, not bright," she said, breath coming in short, harsh puffs through her nose. "Venous. Artery's intact, but the muscle is shredded to ribbon. I need to pack it before he seeps dry."

She grabbed a wad of coarse, boiled linen from the bucket with one bloody hand, keeping pressure with the other.

"Keep leaning on him, Wick. The worst of the pain hits when the air hits the open meat. Shove him flat."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I shove my whole weight down, feeling his collarbones creak under my palms. "Just pack it," I grind out, my voice tight. "Don't tell me more."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Talking keeps the count," Sedge said without missing a beat, shoving the first bundle of linen straight into the cavity. "If I don't talk, I go too fast, and going fast leaves air pockets. Air pockets fill with pus by tomorrow morning."

She took a wooden packing stick from the tray and used it to drive the cloth deep against the femoral bone, tamping it down with firm, rhythmic thrusts of her palm. 

The soldier let out a thin, whistling gasp, his heels drumming weakly against the canvas before his head rolled hard to the side. The wild thrashing stopped, replaced by a fine, shuddering tremor that rattled through his entire frame.

"He's going under," she said, reaching for a second length of boiled linen soaked in vinegar water. "Shock's doing what the whiskey couldn't. Good for him. Makes your job easier."

She fed the second strip into the tear, packing it tight over the first until the well of blood slowed to an oozing seep through the gray fibers. With swift, practiced motions, she grabbed a long roll of coarse canvas banding and caught the loose end under his thigh.

"Lift his hips two inches off the board," she ordered, her fingers already looping the heavy wrap around the meat of his leg, pulling each turn tight enough to make the bruised skin bulge around the edges. "We bind it tight enough to keep the pressure on, then he's off the table and out into the wagon before the frost sets in his blood."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t pause her hands as she pulled the heavy canvas strip taut, hauling the bruised flesh together until the linen packing vanished under the grey weave. 

"You're looking at four inches of dead space packed with six feet of boiled rag," she said, her voice dropping into the flat, rhythmic cadence of an inventory. "That pale fringe along the lip is the fascia—the sheath that holds the quadriceps together. It's torn to ribbons. The yellow grease around the edges is subcutaneous fat. The dark red welling up into the center of the weave is what's left of his deep femoral vein leaking into the cotton."

She hauled another turn of the wrap around the thigh, using the heel of her hand to compress the pack straight down against the bone. The linen under the binding was already turning a deep, wet crimson, but the flow had slowed from a gush to an ooze.

"If the red stain stops spreading before it reaches the outer edges of this wrap, the pressure held and the clot is forming," she continued, knotting the end of the canvas with two sharp, violent jerks of her wrists. "If the cloth turns entirely black with blood in the next ten minutes, the pack slipped off the vessel, he bleeds out into his own boot, and we lay him by the latrine trench."

She wiped her bloody forearms on the tail of her apron, leaving two wide, wet smears across the fabric, and laid two fingers against the man's cold, clammy foot. 

"Toes are cold, but there's a faint pulse behind the ankle. Blood is still getting past the tourniquet effect. That means the limb is alive for now. What kills him next isn't the iron—it's the wool fiber and grease from his trousers that got driven into the marrow. In three days, that wound either drains clean pus or it smells like a dead dog in the sun. If it's the dog, we saw it off at the hip."

She stepped back, picked up the hunk of jagged shrapnel from the tin tray, and tossed it into an empty wooden bucket beneath the table, where it clattered against four others just like it. 

"Take his ankles," she said, wiping sweat from her forehead with the back of a relatively clean wrist. "He's stable enough to move. Get him onto the litter by the flap and bring me the corporal with the belly."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I take his ankles, my hands slippery on his boots. "He's not screaming anymore," I say, and it comes out sounding like a question.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge leaned across the table and pressed two fingers hard into the hollow beneath the soldier's jaw, holding them there for three slow seconds before letting go.

"He's not screaming because his brain ran out of blood to listen with," she said, her voice flat. "System dropped his pressure when the vein opened up. Call it a faint if you want a softer word for it, but it's shock. It's the body shutting off the windows so it doesn't have to look at the fire."

She moved to the head of the table, grabbing the man beneath the armpits to haul him toward the litter on the floor. 

"His chest is still rising. Shallow, but it's there. If he starts making a rattling noise in the throat while you're carrying him, it means he’s choking on his own tongue—roll his head sideways and keep walking. Don't stop to fuss over him. The wagon drivers have straw and vinegar; that’s as much as he gets until the fever breaks or takes him."

She braced her boots in the damp sawdust, waiting for Wick to take the weight of the legs. 

"Lift on three," she said. "One. Two. Three. Get him down, kick fresh sawdust over that puddle by your boots, and bring the belly in. We've got twenty minutes on the corporal before the gut contents poison the rest of his blood, and that one won't be quiet at all."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge hoisted her end of the soldier, stepping sideways to lay him down onto the canvas litter with a heavy, unceremonious thud. She straightened her back, vertebrae popping in a dull series of cracks.

"Lead cuts," she said, reaching for the tin washbasin to rinse the thickest layer of gore from her hands. "Lead is soft, it deforms, it punches a hole and pushes things out of its way. Iron doesn't care enough to push."

She dipped her forearms into the gray, scummy water, scrubbing with a stiff-bristled brush that turned the water a murky purple. 

"Cast iron shatters jagged. It's hot when it hits—hot enough to sear the outer skin, but not hot enough to cauterize what it touches deeper down. It enters spinning. It doesn't slice tissue; it catches the grain of the muscle and twists it, like a fork in boiled cabbage. It tears the vessels instead of severing them clean. A clean cut will spasm shut sometimes—a torn artery just flails open and dumps."

She pulled her hands from the water, shaking the droplets into the basin, and grabbed a dry rag that had already seen three days of use.

"And it drags everything with it," she continued, her voice level, utterly devoid of drama. "The wool of his trousers, the grease on the cloth, the dirt from the trench, the lice in his seams. The iron drives all of it three inches into the meat, cooks the surrounding tissue dead on contact, and leaves a pocket of burnt, shredded flesh sealed inside with all that filth. The body can't fight that off. The dead meat starts rotting while the man is still breathing. That’s what shrapnel does. It plants a corpse inside a living leg."

She tossed the rag onto the small table and turned toward the tent flap, wiping a smear of dark grease from her jaw with the back of her forearm.

"Now take him out to the wagon," Sedge said, her eyes already fixed on the lantern-lit dark beyond the canvas. "And fetch the corporal. I need him on this wood before his bowel spills into his pelvic bowl."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I heave the litter up, his dead weight making my arms shake. "You ever think about the man who fired that shell? Or do you just see the hole it made?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge kicked a fresh layer of dry sawdust over the dark, wet puddle beneath the table with the toe of her boot. 

"The man who fired it is two miles off, turning a brass screw on an elevation wheel," she said, reaching for a horn-handled scalpel and testing the edge against the callous of her thumb. "He didn't aim at this boy’s leg. He aimed at a coordinate on a damp map. He pulled a lanyard, went back to eating hard tack, and never saw what the blast did."

She picked up a spool of waxed suture thread, cutting a length with her teeth, and threaded it through the eye of a heavy, curved needle.

"Wondering about him doesn't stop a hemorrhage. It doesn't sterilize a probe. It's just noise in your head that slows your hands down by three seconds, and three seconds is half a pint of blood."

She set the threaded needle beside a pair of flat retractors, lining them up with the neat, mechanical precision of a carpenter laying out chisels. 

"The hole is the only thing that's real in this tent. The iron made the hole, and the hole is what kills the boy if I don't plug it. Anything past that table is a luxury for people who don't have to smell what comes out of a ruptured gut."

She looked up, her gray eyes dead level under the smudged light of the smoking lamp.

"Move the litter out, Wick. The corporal's peritonitis isn't waiting on your conscience."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge cut straight down the midline of the belly, from two fingers below the sternum to just above the pubic bone. The skin parted with a dry hiss, followed by a pale layer of yellow fat and the dull, white fibrous sheath of the abdominal wall.

"Skin, fat, rectus sheath," she said, her voice dropping into the steady, monotone rhythm of a carpenter measuring timber. "Now the peritoneum. The dark swelling under it is blood and bile pooling under pressure. When I nick this membrane, the pressure releases. Hold his shoulders flat—the pain will make his diaphragm lock up and he’ll try to vomit."

She touched the point of the scalpel to the translucent membrane. It split, and a hot, foul rush of dark fluid spilled out over the sides of the man’s abdomen, thick with the stench of digested rations and sour bile. 

The corporal under Wick's hands let out a shrill, ragged screech, his whole torso bowing off the canvas as his heels drummed violently against the wood.

"There's the bowel," Sedge continued, completely ignoring the spray across her leather apron. She dropped the blade onto the tray and thrust both hands into the cavity, working her fingers around the slippery, glistening coils of the small intestine. "I'm drawing out the loops of the ileum. Look at the color—healthy gut is pink and glossy. Where the lead passed, it turns purple and grey from lost circulation."

She brought two feet of wet, pale tube up onto a clean cloth laid across his ribs, turning it methodically through her bloody fingers like rope.

"Here. Two inches past the mesenteric root," she said, pointing with a blunt thumb at a ragged, split hole in the bowel wall that was weeping foul grey matter. "Half-inch perforation. Lead clipped the side and tore the margin. That’s what’s spilling waste into his pelvic basin."

She reached blindly with her left hand, snatched a pair of curved clamps from the tray, and snapped them onto the gut on either side of the hole to stop the leak. The corporal's breath came in wet, hitching sobs, his throat clicking as his head thrashed against the stretcher.

"Now I wash and sew," Sedge said, grabbing a wooden ladle and dipping it into a bucket of salted, boiled water. "I have to ladle this in between his liver and his spleen, scoop out every scrap of dirt, grease, and fecal matter that leaked into the cavity, and sponge it dry. If I leave a thimbleful of that muck behind his bladder, the belly rots from the inside out in three days and no surgeon in the world can stop it."

She poured the steaming salt water directly into the open cavity. The man beneath Wick let out a muffled, strangled choke, his fingers clawing desperately at the edges of the canvas.

"Ten minutes to swab the basin," Sedge said, reaching for the heavy curved needle and the waxed thread. "Five minutes to lay a double row of inverting sutures along the tear to seal the pipe. Ten minutes to stitch the wall and the skin back together. Twenty-five minutes total. If you let him roll before I set the last knot, the needle tears the mesenteric artery, and he bleeds out into his own ribs before I can find the clamp. Keep his weight down, Wick. Look at the wound and listen to the count."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: My arms are starting to tremble from the strain. "Twenty-five minutes," I repeat through gritted teeth. "And after that, what's his number? One in three?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"One in ten," Sedge said, thrusting a coarse sponge clamped in long forceps deep down into the hollow beside his hip bone. "One in three is for clean amputations and men who get shot through the shoulder meat. Belly wounds are a butcher's coin toss, and the coin is weighted."

She pulled the sponge back up, heavy and black with fouled brine, and wrung it out into a tin bucket with a wet, squelching twist of her wrists. 

"If the lead didn't nick the major vessel behind the spine, that's the first hurdle. He cleared it, or he'd be dead already. If I get every scrap of grey matter out of the pocket behind his bladder, that's the second hurdle. We're on that now."

She shoved the sponge back in, working it methodically around the slick coils of bowel, feeling along the gutters of the abdomen with her bare fingertips. 

"The third hurdle is the stitch," she said, leaning in closer, her breath misting faintly in the cold draft of the tent. "A gut isn't canvas. You can't just pull the edges together with a whipstitch. If you leave the raw lining facing out, the acid eats the thread in twelve hours and the seam blows open when he coughs. I have to fold the outer skin over the tear—serosa to serosa—so the tissue glues itself shut before the string rots away."

She brought the curved needle down, piercing the rubbery wall of the ileum an eighth of an inch from the ragged tear. The needle made a distinct, wet *pop* as it drove through the muscular layer. 

The corporal's head thrashed back, the veins in his neck standing out like thick blue cords, a bubbling, wordless groan tearing through his clenched teeth.

"First stitch," Sedge muttered, pulling the waxed thread through and knotting it with three rapid, precise flicks of her index finger. "Keep his shoulders pinned, Wick. Don't let him roll his hips. If he throws his pelvis, the needle rips through the bowel wall like wet paper, and then I have to cut out another four inches of pipe and start over. He doesn't have the blood for me to start over."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't drop her hands. She drew the second loop of waxed thread through the rubbery wall of the gut, set her index finger against the tissue to keep the tension, and threw a square knot with three swift, practiced jerks. 

"Second stitch," she said, her voice flat, steady, and loud enough to cut through the corporal’s shallow, wheezing pant. "Lembert suture. The needle goes down through the outer coat, through the muscle, skips the inner mucous lining, and comes back up. When I pull it taut, the edges fold inward against each other. Flesh to flesh. If the raw inner lining touches the outside, it leaks acid. If it leaks acid, the whole cavity dissolves into soup."

She drove the heavy curved needle through a third time. The steel grated faintly against the dense fiber of the intestinal wall with a dull, wet *pop*. 

"Third stitch. Four more to close the split. Look at the color of the loop—it’s turning from bruised plum to dull slate grey where the lead grazed it. That grey is ischemia. Dead meat. If that patch revives under the warmth of the belly, it turns pink again in an hour. If it stays grey, the wall thins, it perforates a second time on Tuesday morning, and he drowns in his own bile while he’s asleep in the hay."

She set the fourth, fifth, and sixth knots without pausing for breath, her fingers working with mechanical, repetitive speed. With each cinch, the ragged tear in the bowel rolled inward, vanishing under a clean, tight ridge of glistening pink serosa. 

"Seventh stitch. Sealed," she said, biting the thread off two inches from the knot. 

She picked up the wooden ladle, dipped it back into the bucket of warm, salted water, and poured a steady stream directly over the sutured loop, washing the smear of feces and dark blood off the surface. The wash water pooled in the hollows of the man's exposed flanks, dark and murky.

"Now I sponge the basin out one last time," Sedge said, thrusting the coarse linen pad down between the loops of intestine, driving it deep into the pelvic floor behind the bladder until the linen came up dark red and sodden. She wrung it out over the floor with a heavy, wet twist. "If I leave two drops of fluid behind the liver, the bacteria multiply. In twelve hours, a single drop becomes half a pint of green pus. The pus inflames the peritoneum. The peritoneum swells until it’s thick as a boot sole, and the pain is so bad his heart stops beating from the shock of it."

She tossed the soiled rag into the tin bucket, stepped in close to the table, and laid both of her flat, wet palms under the loops of the small bowel.

"Returning the guts," she said. 

With slow, rhythmic pressure of her thumbs, she guided the hot, glistening coils back through the vertical slit in the abdominal wall, tucking them into the cavity loop by loop, fitting them back into the spaces between the spleen, the stomach, and the pelvic rim. The wet slither of the organs sliding into place made a hollow, squelching sound in the silence of the tent.

"They don't go back the way they came out," she said, her breath coming hard through her teeth. "They settle where they find room. The bowel has to sort itself out by peristalsis. But right now, the shock paralyzes the muscle. It stops moving entirely. That's the next wall he hits: the gut goes dead."

She reached to the tin tray, dropped the blunt forceps, and picked up a heavy, triangular-pointed cutting needle threaded with thick hemp cord. 

"If the gut stays asleep for three days, gas builds behind the stoppage. His belly swells like a dead mule in the sun until his diaphragm is shoved up into his throat and he suffocates on his own breath. If it wakes up, you hear a rumble like gravel down a chute, he passes wind, and you know the pipe is open. That’s the dividing line. Wind means life. Silence means the trench."

She set the iron retractors aside and gripped the severed edges of the abdominal wall with her left hand, hauling the thick, yellow-white layer of the rectus sheath together over the intestines. 

"Now the wall," Sedge said. She drove the heavy needle through the skin, through two inches of subcutaneous fat, and straight through the tough fibrous sheath of the abdominal muscle in a single, violent shove. The tissue tore with a thick, resistant crunch.

The corporal didn't scream; his head merely jerked backward against the wood, his eyes rolled back until only the yellowed whites showed under the greasy lamp.

"Through-and-through stay sutures," she said, hauling the hemp cord tight and tying it off with a heavy butcher's knot that bit deep into the skin, puckering the edges together. "Three-quarter-inch bites. Skin, fat, fascia. If I only stitch the skin, the muscle underneath stays split. The first time he heaves to vomit up the foul bile in his stomach, the whole wound blows open and his intestines dump into the bedstraw. I have to lash the meat to the meat."

She drove the needle through a second time, two inches below the first stitch, hauling the hemp cord taut with a brutal, steady pull that forced the dark blood from the needle punctures to run down the man's flank.

"Third stitch," she grunted, her shoulder muscles bunching under the gray linen of her shirt as she shoved the steel point through the dense fibrous layer. "Fourth stitch. Fifth."

With each thrust, the vertical red canyon down the man's belly narrowed, closing over the packed organs inside, until the slit was drawn together in a puckered, purple seam bound by eight thick hemp knots, trailing short, stiff ends of cord.

"Now we wait for the rot," Sedge said. She dropped the needle onto the tray with a dull *clack*, picked up a heavy linen pad soaked in turpentine and lard, and slapped it flat over the closed incision. 

"In eighteen hours, his temperature climbs. His skin goes dry and hot as an iron stove. His tongue turns brown and cracks like leather. That’s the peritonitis setting in. If his blood is strong enough to wall off the infection, the fever breaks on the fourth night, he sweats through the mattress, and he starts begging for water. If the infection gets into his deep veins, his skin turns the color of tallow, his belly goes hard as a pine plank, and he dies thrashing so hard it takes three men to keep him from breaking his own ribs against the floorboards."

She took a four-yard length of heavy canvas binding, slid it under the man's lower back, and began hauling it around his torso in wide, overlapping wraps, pulling each turn so tight the corporal's breath came in thin, whistling gasps.

"That's the arithmetic on a gut shot," Sedge said, pinning the end of the binder with two rusted iron clips. "No mysteries. No miracles. Just meat, thread, and whether his marrow has enough fight left to kill the dirt I couldn't reach with the sponge."

She stepped back from the table, let her arms drop to her sides, and let out a single, long, ragged exhale through her nose. The blood on her forearms was already beginning to dry, turning from slick crimson to a dull, crusting brown that pulled tight against the hairs of her skin. 

"He's done," she said, looking down at the table, then out toward the darkness beyond the tent flap. "Get your breath, Wick. The wagon brought four more from the sunken road, and two of them are spurting bright."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I stare at the blood drying on my hands, then look at the corporal's still face. "Tell me his name."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn’t look at the corporal’s face. She picked up the horn-handled scalpel, dropped it into the basin of murky vinegar-water, and reached for the stiff-bristled brush to scrape the clotted fat from the hinge.

"I don't know it," she said, her voice flat over the scratch of the bristles against steel. "The stretcher-bearers didn't say, and it wasn't written on his belly."

She dipped the tongs in next, scrubbing the dried dark venous crust from the teeth. 

"If he kept his jacket, there’s a tin slip in the breast pocket with an ink stamp on it. If he lost the jacket in the ditch, the quartermaster has his company roster. The clerk will look at his teeth and check him off when they throw him in the wagon or the trench."

She set the clean tongs down on the dry rag with a dull tin click and turned to look down at Wick on the floor. 

"Names are for the clerks, Wick. A name doesn't change the gauge of the suture. It doesn't tell me if his liver is nicked, and it doesn't make his blood clot any faster. To me, he's a three-inch tear in the ileum and four pints of red fluid that belong inside his skin."

She wiped her hands dry on the corner of her stained apron, leaving two fresh, stiff grey streaks where the cloth was already hard with old grease. 

"If you start putting names on the meat on that table, your hands shake when you drive the needle. And if your hands shake, you tear the mesenteric artery and kill him while you're feeling sorry for him. You want to give him a name, wait till he's breathing on his own in three days. Until then, he's the belly."

She reached down, grabbed Wick by the collar of his shirt with one blood-caked hand, and hauled upward with enough leverage to force him toward his feet.

"Get up," she said, not unkindly, but with the hard, mechanical urgency of a woman who had twelve more men waiting in the rain. "The bright blood is in the flap. Grab the bucket and fetch fresh sawdust."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I shove myself up, my knees cracking. "Fine," I say, voice rough. "But if he dies, I'm asking the clerk what his name was."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Ask him twenty if it helps you sleep, but do it after the lantern goes out," Sedge said, already turning her back on him to scrape the thickest crust of gore off the wooden boards with the edge of a flat iron spatula. 

She shoved the refuse over the side into the scrap bucket with a dull, wet scrape, then reached for the heavy tin bucket of dry pine sawdust in the corner. 

"Bright blood means an artery," she said, scattering two handfuls across the slick boards where the corporal had bled out. The fresh shavings hissed faintly as they soaked up the dark pool, masking the copper smell with the sharp, resinous bite of raw pine. "Could be brachial, could be carotid. If it’s carotid, he’s dead before they carry him through the flap. If it’s brachial, the boy’s got about ninety seconds of pressure left before his pump runs dry."

She set the flat spatula down and picked up two pairs of curved artery forceps—heavy, tooth-jawed clamps—checking the spring of the ratchet against her palm with a sharp *snick-snick*. 

"When an artery blows, it doesn't seep. It pulses. Every beat of the heart shoots a jet two feet across the canvas. You don't hold shoulders this time. You find where the bone is, and you crush the vessel against the bone above the wound with both thumbs until I can get the teeth of these tongs into the hole."

She dropped the clamps beside a heavy linen tourniquet and an iron windlass stick, then jerked her chin toward the outer flap where the sound of wet boots and ragged, panicked breathing was coming through the rain.

"Get the litter," she said, her voice dropping into the cold, level rhythm of a woman setting a clock. "And don't look for his jacket. Look for the spray."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I grab the litter and turn toward the sound. My hands are still tacky. "Spray," I repeat, and my own pulse feels too loud in my ears. "Got it."

rung_labels.evidence: Dark, thick venous blood surged up out of the hole in a sudden, bubbling wave, splashing across Sedge's forearms

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: four inches of dead space packed with six feet of boiled rag... That pale fringe along the lip is the fascia—the sheath that holds the quadriceps together. It's torn to ribbons. The yellow grease around the edges is subcutaneous fat. The dark red welling up into the center of the weave is what's left of his deep femoral vein leaking into the cotton

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: It enters spinning. It doesn't slice tissue; it catches the grain of the muscle and twists it, like a fork in boiled cabbage. It tears the vessels instead of severing them clean.
