rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She drove the heavy curved needle through a third time. The steel grated faintly against the dense fiber of the intestinal wall with a dull, wet *pop*.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Wrong is a feeling, Pike. Give me anatomy," Halloway said, her voice flat enough to skip stones on. 

She shifted her weight, the rusted waders creaking beneath four feet of black runoff. She didn't wade any deeper yet; disturb the surface too much and you lost the ripples that told you if something was still breathing underneath.

"Count the limbs, look at the hinges," she instructed, angling the lamp so the beam caught the slick, pale hump breaking the surface near the coal chute. "Shoulders are pinned three inches too high for a drown victim, and the elbow on the left bends backward. That’s not post-mortem swelling, that’s deliberate construction. Now look at the water around the flank. Is the scum breaking, or is it holding still?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I squint, trying to focus past the slimy surface. "The scum's holding, mostly. But there's... a current? Like something's pulling it down around the legs." I point with my chin. "And the elbow's wrong, but so are the shoulders. They're not just high, they're... joined wrong. Like a puppet."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Better," Halloway murmured, her eyes narrowing as she tracked the faint spiral in the grease. "A puppet with a submerged operator, or an anchor. If you're lucky, it’s just tied to a sack of slag to keep it from floating into the street. If you're unlucky, the thing that stitched it is sitting on the cellar drain, waiting for us to wade into arm's reach."

She unhooked a six-foot ash pole from the leather harness across her back, not taking her eyes off the pale mass by the coal chute. 

"The shoulders are clavicle-grafts. Dog or hog, likely, wired straight into human scapulae. Cheap work, but it gives them a wider reach if they decide they aren't dead after all." She extended the pole, resting the iron-shod tip against the surface of the water without breaking the scum. "Keep your cleaver dry. I'm going to tap the ribs. If the water drops two inches, it’s a siphon trap. If it twitches, hit it in the hinge of that backward elbow—the tendon runs exposed right along the joint."

She paused, the corner of her mouth twitching dryly. "And if it sinks completely out of sight, try not to imagine what’s brushing against your shins."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Parts of it," Halloway said. 

She leaned forward just enough to bring the iron tip of the pole down against the mass. She didn't stab; she pressed, testing the resistance of the tissue beneath the gray-white surface. A dull, dense give, like wet canvas over turnip sack.

"The torso belonged to someone who worked an oar or a pickaxe—look at the width of the ribcage. Three days dead, give or take. Not enough gas build-up to break the surface on its own, which means it didn't drown; it was drained first. Drowning bloats the belly; drainage sinks the sternum."

She gave the iron tip a slow, deliberate twist, parting a layer of grease to expose where the neck met the altered collar. 

"The stitch-work is linen thread sealed in rendered tallow so the damp doesn't rot it out before the sinew sets. Professional. The arms are fresher than the trunk—skin's still got enough elasticity that whoever sewed it didn't have to pre-punch the needle holes." 

She flicked a glance at Pike, her eyes pale and flat in the lamp's yellow glare. "If you're looking for a name to put on a headstone, you'd need three of them, and none of them would thank you for the bother. Keep your cleaver up. I’m going to lever the sternum."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow, my knuckles white on my cleaver handle. "So it's a trap for us, specifically. Not just... left here."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Don't flatter yourself, Pike. You aren't important enough to warrant three days of tailor-work," Halloway said.

She put her shoulder behind the ash pole, pressing the iron shoe firmly into the hollow beneath the altered clavicle. The mass gave with a wet, heavy sigh. A string of fat, dark bubbles broke through the surface film, releasing a stench like sour vinegar and cold tallow.

"This is a watchdog, not an assassination," she continued, her gaze fixed entirely on the waterline as the ripples cleared. "It's left here to keep the landlord from checking the pipes, or to buy the butcher upstairs twenty minutes to pack their knives and clear out if someone comes poking around with a warrant."

The pole sank another two inches into the chest cavity, and Halloway’s jaw set slightly as she felt the counter-pressure through the wood. 

"There. Feel that? Or rather, see that tilt?" She gave the pole a slight, rigid jerk. The pale mass didn't roll over like a dead body should; it pivoted on a single, fixed point below the water, like a heavy pendulum. "No legs on the trunk. It’s been bolted straight to a lead sinker on the cellar floor. If something triggers it, the upper half lunges forward on a coiled spring, snaps whatever it can reach, and the weight pulls it back under before you can get a clean stroke at it."

She flicked a dry, humorless smirk toward Pike over her shoulder. 

"Which means whoever built it is likely still on the first or second floor, listening for the splash. Take a slow breath. If you hear floorboards creaking over your head, don't look up—just step two feet to your left so whatever they drop through the slats misses your collar."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't look up from her work, but she shifted her grip on the ash pole, using the iron tip to peel back a flap of graying skin where the neck had been severed from whatever head it used to carry.

"Plainly," she said, her voice dropping into the quiet cadence of an inventory. "A man—dock worker, carter, someone with broad shoulders and heavy wrists—was hit behind the left ear with a blunt face, likely an iron pestle or a lead-filled boot-heel. Depressed skull fracture, knocked unconscious, not dead yet. He was hauled somewhere dry, hung up by the heels from a ceiling hook, and opened at the femoral artery to bleed him out clean. If you leave the blood in, the meat turns sour in twelve hours and the stitch-holes tear under the tension."

She pushed the tip lower, tracing the line of the ribcage beneath the murky water. 

"Legs were taken off at the hip joints with a bone saw. Clean cuts, three minutes per side if the saw’s sharp. The marrow cavities were plugged with hot beeswax so the water wouldn't seep in and turn the marrow to mush. Then they went down the lane and bought two stray mastiffs off a dog-fighter, drowned them in a rain barrel, and stripped the shoulder blades out while the gristle was still warm."

She gave the pole a slight, firm twist. Deep below the water, something made of rusted iron gave a sharp, metallic *clink*. 

"They ran a four-inch carriage bolt through the base of his lumbar spine, cinched it down to a sixty-pound pig of iron, and rigged a coach spring along his back to throw him forward when the trip-line gets pulled. Then they threw him down here, let the water cover the work, and went upstairs to have their supper."

She pulled the pole back an inch, the greasy water swirling back over the pale flesh. She glanced at Pike over the rim of the yellow light. 

"That's the plain of it. No ritual, no grand design. Just five hours of carpentry using meat instead of pine. Now hold that lamp two inches to the left. The tripwire is tied to the third stair, and I need to see if the copper's rotted through before we step past it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I shift the lamp, my hand steady despite the tremor in my breath. "They're upstairs," I say, low. "You want to go up or cut the line and wait?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Cut the line and the counterweight drops," Halloway said without looking back. "Spring fires, the torso throws a hundred pounds of water against the ceiling, and the fellow upstairs drops a bottle of vitriol down the chute to see what made the noise."

She leaned in, squinting at the thin green thread of oxidized copper where it rose from the waterline and vanished into the underside of the wooden tread. 

"And we don't wait. Standing in four feet of dead man's wash is a good way to lose two toes to the rot before sunrise, and I like my boots the way they are."

She worked the iron shoe of her pole carefully behind the cadaver’s stitched spine, finding the heavy coil of the coach spring. With a short, brutal shove, she wedged the iron tip deep into the mechanism, jamming the coils tight against the mounting bracket. 

"There. It’ll hold for ten minutes before the timber rots through under the strain." She let go of the ash pole, leaving it fixed in place like a rusted lever protruding from the water. "Now we go up. Step on the sides of the risers, where the stringers meet the brick—center of the tread will squeak, and whoever built this had good ears for carpentry."

She wiped her wet palms on the leather of her coat, then drew her short-bladed cleaver with a quiet, practiced rasp. 

"If the door at the top is bolted from the outside, we break the latch and move fast. If it’s slightly ajar, keep your face low. People who keep watchdogs like this don't open the door with a smile; they open it with a meat hook."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway paused, her boots already half-turned toward the slimy timber of the bottom riser. She didn't scoff; asking for the graft-lines was the only sensible thing Pike had done since they stepped into the cellar.

"Inside out, then," she said, her voice dropping to a low, dry rasp that barely carried above the drip of the runoff. "The viscera are gone. All of them. You don't leave lungs or guts in a wet-rig; the bile rots the seams from the inside in thirty-six hours, and trapped air makes the chest list to one side. The whole abdominal cavity is scooped clean, scrubbed with quicklime to kill the mold, and packed tight with horsehair and boiled pitch. That gives the trunk ballast and stops the ribcage from collapsing when the spring kicks."

She tapped the flat of her cleaver against her own sternum to illustrate.

"The spine is the anchor. They drill through the lumbar vertebrae—third and fourth—with a half-inch carpenter’s auger. They run an iron bolt through the bone, cinched down with lead washers so the bone doesn't splinter under torque. Along the back, the erector spinae muscles are peeled away to lay the leaf-spring directly against the bone, bound every two inches with braided catgut."

She shifted her gaze to the neck stump resting an inch beneath the black film.

"Look at the wrists and the collar. The fingers aren't loose; the flexor tendons are drawn tight and wired to the radius with brass thread. When the spring throws the torso forward, the kinetic shock snaps the hands shut like spring-traps. If it catches your forearm, you don't pry the fingers off—you have to sever the tendons behind the wrist to get loose."

Her pale eyes met Pike’s in the yellow glare of the lamp, entirely devoid of pity or disgust. Just a tradesman explaining the teeth on a saw.

"It took his blood, his weight, and four feet of his spine," she said flatly. "It didn't take his soul, because there’s nothing supernatural about five shillings' worth of ironmongery and a lack of squeamishness. If you meet another, don't waste your breath praying or your steel on the belly. There’s nothing in there to bleed. You hit the pivot bolt at the base of the spine, or you sever the brass cords at the nape."

She turned back to the stairs, setting her boot carefully against the far edge of the first riser, where the wood met the brick wall. 

"Now step where I step, and keep the lamp behind my left shoulder. The timber’s greasy, and if you slip and fire that spring, I will leave you down here to explain the carpentry to the coroner."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I follow, placing my feet exactly where hers went. "You ever get used to the smell?" I ask, my voice too tight.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"No," Halloway said quietly, her weight shifting smoothly onto the second riser without a squeak from the timber. "And you don't want to. You get used to it, you stop noticing what the air is telling you."

She paused, lifting her chin slightly to test the draft sliding down between the floorboards above. 

"What you're smelling right now isn't the dead man. The dead man just smells of cold beef and pond water. The foulness is the tallow and the quicklime. Rot has a sweet, heavy tang to it—like overripe pears. Lye and rendered fat bite the back of your throat like vinegar. When you smell rot, the work is old. When you smell lye, someone was down here three hours ago washing their forearms in a tin basin."

She carefully stepped over the third riser, planting her boot on the fourth, right against the mortar line of the brick wall. Her hand hovered an inch from the copper tripwire without touching it.

"Treat the stink like an inventory, Pike. Guts smell like copper and sour mash. Gangrene smells like bad cheese. If you stop gagging and start categorizing, your stomach stops trying to climb out of your throat."

She reached the fifth step and went entirely still, crouching so her head stayed two feet below the landing. Through the half-inch gap beneath the cellar door, a thin sliver of warm, yellow light cut across the dust of the upper landing. 

"Smell that?" she whispered, her voice barely moving the air. "Fried onions and pipe tobacco. Cheap Virginia leaf. He's sitting by the stove, waiting for the splash."

She angled her cleaver slightly, catching the sliver of light along the honed edge. 

"When I lift the latch, don't look at the room. Look at his hands. If he's got a cleaver, take his kneecap. If he's got a bottle of vitriol, hit his elbow before he pulls the cork. Ready?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway slipped the thin tip of her utility knife beneath the lead-wrapped copper wire at the edge of the stair, slicing the tension with a minute, muffled *snick*. 

"Subcutaneous fat," she said, her voice dropping into that low, flat hum that sounded like someone reading a ledger in a churchyard. "When you strip the dermis on a fresh corpse, the fat is pale yellow. Here, it’s gone the color of curdled grease from the river soak. Beneath that, the fascia’s been peeled clean off the muscle bellies so the brine could bite directly into the meat. Muscle fibers don't tear when they're pickled in saltpeter and lye; they seize up like cured leather. That’s why the torso holds its shape under sixty pounds of spring tension instead of pulling apart at the ribs."

She eased the wire back against the riser, completely dead now, and took another silent step up, bringing her eyes level with the rusted iron latch of the cellar door.

"The smell you're choking on under the vinegar is copper-rot and scorched bone," she continued, her breathing slow and measured through her nose. "When they bored through the lumbar spine with the auger, they didn't use oil to cool the bit. Friction burned the marrow inside the canal. Smells like singed horn and wet iron filings. If you ever open a cellar and get that burnt-hair tang mixed with marsh gas, don't look for a man with a knife—look for the pig-iron and the bone-saw, because the work's already done."

She reached out with two fingers, testing the play on the door’s iron keeper. The wood around the screws was soft with damp, but the iron was well-greased. Not neglected. Tended daily.

"The arms are dog-grafted at the humerus," she murmured, her knife sliding smoothly back into its sheath at her hip while her hand settled on the hilt of the heavy cleaver. "They split the bone, jammed the canid joint into the human socket, and wrapped the seam in wet rawhide that shrank tight as it dried. When it dries, it’s harder than oak. You can't break that joint with a club; you have to sever the catgut bindings along the outer seam."

She looked back down at Pike, her face carved out of shadow and cold yellow light, utterly devoid of tremor.

"That's how far it got. From a man carrying sacks at the quay to thirty pounds of pickled gristle and ironmongery on a spring. That’s all a body is when someone with a saw stops seeing a neighbor and starts seeing spare parts."

Her eyes flicked back to the sliver of light beneath the door. 

"Now hold that lamp high enough to light the landing, but tuck your elbow against your ribs. When this door opens, he’s going to swing at whatever's at eye level."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I hold the lamp up, my elbow tucked tight. The smell of fried onions is thick now, heavy with tobacco smoke. "He's left-handed," I whisper, nodding toward the way the door swings. "Hinge squeals on the right side. He's oiled the left."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway gave a single, curt nod, the faintest flicker of approval crossing her gray eyes. 

"Good. Left-hand door pull means his body stays behind the jamb while his right arm clears the frame," she whispered, her thumb easing under the thumb-latch of the cellar door. "Which means he’s swinging high and from the right. A butcher’s stroke—downward diagonal, aiming for the collarbone."

She shifted her feet, anchoring her back heel into the junction of the brick wall and the fourth riser. Low center of gravity, weight forward.

"Lamp goes through the opening first, three inches below the latch," she instructed, her voice flat and steady as an iron bar. "Not to light the room—to draw the first swing. The moment his steel bites the tin, I go under the arc. You drop the lamp, pull your cleaver, and pin his trailing boot to the floorboards. Don't look at his face. Look at his wrist."

She slid her left hand up the timber, testing the wood around the lock-box. No deadbolts. Just a heavy iron lift-latch, greased with the same rancid lard that coated the dog-grafts below.

"One breath," she said, exhaling through her teeth. 

With a sudden, violent heave of her shoulder, Halloway drove the door inward. The latch gave with a dull crack of splitting pine, and she stayed crouched low, cleaver leading, stepping straight into the reek of hot lard and tobacco.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway sat down two steps above Pike, resting her forearms on her knees. She didn't put the cleaver away; she laid it flat across her thighs, taking a strip of oiled canvas from her coat pocket to drag the grease and dark slurry off the steel.

"The man upstairs was sixty," she said, her voice dropping right back into that flat, rhythmic appraisal. "Gout in his right ankle—you could tell by the wear on the inner heel of his work-boots and the dried poultice of cabbage leaf and mustard plaster bound under his sock. He wasn't quick on his feet, which is why he built the watchdog. A man with bad joints builds traps so he doesn't have to run when the bailiffs knock."

She folded the rag over the blade's spine, pinching the metal clean with a slow, grinding rasp.

"On his workbench: two three-inch bone-saws, three half-round rasps for smoothing rough edges on the grafts, and a crock of rendered lard mixed with copper sulfate to keep the blue-bottle flies from laying eggs in the stitch-holes while the seams cure. A trough of coarse sea-salt in the corner, twelve stone of it, mixed with crushed oak bark. That’s where he had the legs curing. When you take the limbs off, you don't throw them out; you strip the long bones for levers and boil the skin down for carpenter’s glue. Nothing goes into the gutter that can be turned into a latch or a binding."

She gestured with the rag toward the cellar behind them, back toward the black water where the ash pole still stood wedged in the coach spring.

"The head is upstairs in a stoneware crock under the pantry floorboards, packed in dry salt and charcoal. He kept it to check the jawline. When you wire a dog’s clavicle into a human shoulder, you need the skull nearby to measure the swing clearance so the dog's shoulder-blade doesn't clip the chin-bone when the mechanism releases. It’s a matter of clearance, nothing more. Two inches too narrow and the trap fouls itself on the first stroke."

She wiped her fingers on her leather coat, checking the knuckles for nicks or split skin. 

"The blood on the floorboards upstairs wasn't fresh—it was four days old, dried down to dark varnish in the grain of the pine. It takes about eight pints to bleed a carter of that build out clean. He caught it in three earthenware basins, boiled it with wood ash to make a black sealant, and painted the inner walls of the ribcage with it before he packed the horsehair in. That’s what keeps the water from softening the pitch."

She looked sideways at Pike, the lamp’s yellow flame reflecting small and hard in her gray pupils.

"He died with four inches of cold iron through the subclavian artery behind his right collarbone," she said evenly. "He didn't make a sound because when the lung fills with blood from the top down, you can't draw enough air to scream. He dropped on his left side, knocked the grease-lamp off the bench, and bled out into his own salt-trough. By sunrise, the tallow on his coat will be cold, and the rats will start working on the salt-pork in his larder."

She slid the cleaver back into the leather sheath at her hip, the brass rivet clicking home with a dry snap.

"That's the whole of it, from the tap on the skull to the lime in the belly and the iron through the neck. The mechanics don't change, Pike. It's five shillings in scrap iron, four days of salt, and a man who thought meat was just timber that hadn't been dried yet. Now pick up the lamp. We need to go upstairs, tip his salt-crocks into the stove before the neighbors smell the brine, and take the saws. A good bone-saw costs four pence, and there's no sense leaving clean tools in a dirty house."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I don't move. My throat's still full of the smell. "You got paid for this one?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Two sovereigns from the dock-warden," Halloway said. 

She reached into her breast pocket, pulled out an iron-cased tin of snuff, and popped the lid with a thumb. She didn't take any; she just held it under her nose for a second, letting the sharp, bitter scent of clove and camphor cut through the grease in her nostrils before snapping it shut.

"One up front to find out why the coal barges were losing two men a fortnight, and one when I brought him the copper wire from the trip-line so he knew the chute was clear." She tapped the tin against her knee. "He won't pay for the carter, because the carter was a day-laborer with no kin to raise a hue and cry. He’s paying for the real estate. A coal cellar four feet deep in dead man's wash isn't earning rent."

She stood up, her rusted waders scraping heavily against the grit on the stair tread. She stretched her lower back until a vertebra gave a dry, muffled pop.

"Take two shillings out for tallow, five pence for the ash pole I had to jam in the coach spring, and four pence for the lye to scrub our boots so the dogs don't follow us back to the lodgings. That leaves thirty-six shillings, split two ways."

She looked down at Pike, her face completely expressionless in the yellow wash of the lantern.

"Eighteen shillings for forty minutes in a wet hole and an old man with bad joints. If you were working the docks, that's six weeks of hauling timber twelve hours a day until your shoulders give out and someone puts an iron pestle behind your ear to turn you into a watchdog. It’s good money, Pike. The work is just heavier on the nose."

She turned and started up the remaining steps toward the kitchen, her boot-heels thumping heavy and deliberate on the boards.

"Bring the lamp. If we leave his tallow-pot burning on the stove, the grease will catch the curtains, and I’m not spending half my cut bribing the night-watch to forget whose waders left brine on the threshold."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I take the lamp and follow her up. My cleaver's still out. "You ever count?" I ask, my voice rough. "How many you've found like this?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Counting is a clerk’s habit, Pike. You start keeping a tally, you start thinking there’s an end to the ledger," Halloway said, stepping off the top riser into the kitchen. 

She didn't look at the dead man in the corner. He was still wedged against the lip of the salt-trough, his head tilted back at an unnatural angle against the whitewashed brick, his graying beard crusting over with dark, thick syrup where the subclavian had emptied out. 

Halloway walked straight to the iron stove, picked up a heavy tin lid, and clapped it down over the skillet of smoking lard and onions, cutting off the oxygen with a dull clatter.

"Spring-rigs like that one? Seven," she said, her voice completely level as she wiped soot from the stove-top with the hem of her sleeve. "Five in the Reach, two down in the tanneries where people have plenty of salt and nobody asks why a wagon-load of lye is going into a cellar. Dog-grafts are commoner. Twenty, maybe thirty. A stray mastiff costs four pence from a dog-fighter, or nothing at all if you have a piece of suet and a length of rope."

She turned to the workbench, running a callous-roughened thumb along the teeth of the two bone-saws resting on the oilcloth. 

"The ones that use horse tendons are worse. Horse sinew doesn't snap like catgut; it stretches and holds. If you trip a horse-rig, it doesn't just hit you once—it keeps pulling until the bone clears the joint." She picked up the smaller of the two saws, sighting down the flat of the blade toward the lamp Pike was holding. "Good steel. German make. Three teeth chipped on the forward edge where he hit a femur, but five minutes with a triangular file will put the bite back in it."

She tucked the saw into the leather tool-roll at the small of her back and glanced at Pike’s hand.

"Sheath the cleaver. He isn't getting out of that trough, and if you trip on the floorboards with a bare blade, I’m not carrying you two miles back to the apothecary with your own steel in your thigh."

She stepped over a dark pool on the pine planks, reaching up to the rafters to unhook a bundle of dried sage and wormwood hanging from a copper nail. She crushed the dry leaves between her palms, letting the gray powder dust over her sleeves and the front of her coat to kill the smell of the cellar.

"You don't count the bodies, Pike. You count the mistakes. You remember that the man in the Reach used hemp rope instead of wire, which rotted out in two weeks, and you remember that this bastard greased his latch on the left. That’s what keeps you breathing until you're fifty."

She tossed a pinch of the crushed sage toward the open stove-grate, watching the sparks catch and flare green. 

"Now check the cupboard by the dry-sink. Look for a stoneware jar marked with red wax. If he was buying dog-shoulders, he kept his receipts, and I want to know which butcher on the quay was selling him the tallow."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sheath the cleaver, fingers stiff. The jar is there, crusted red wax around the lid. I pull it out and hold it up. "There's a name scratched under the wax. Cooper."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge heard the lie and let it stand. Everyone lied at this part. She'd have been more worried if he'd sounded sure.

"Don't look at the canvas," she said. "Look at his face. If his lips go grey you tell me, and you keep holding." She pushed the blanket down off the man's hip and folded it twice so it wouldn't slide, then took up the lamp and brought it close enough that the heat of it sat on the back of her hand. The wound was a hand's width above the knee, front and outside, and it had stopped bleeding hours ago in the worst way — packed shut with cloth and dirt and whatever the road had been made of. The skin around it had gone tight and shining.

"Right," she said, to the room and to herself. "There's fabric in there. Trouser, I'd guess, driven in with the metal. It has to come out or the leg goes bad and then he goes bad, and that takes about four days and I won't be describing those to you." She wet a cloth, wrung it, and began working the dried blood off in short strokes, going from clean skin inward, not the other way. "I'm cleaning the outside first. That part he'll barely feel. Then I'm going to open it wider than it is, because I can't reach what I can't see, and that part he will."

The man made a sound at the cold water. Sedge put two fingers flat on his thigh, well away from the wound, and left them there a moment — not kindness exactly, or not only that. Pressure told her things. Heat told her things.

"I take no pleasure in this," she said, glancing up. "In case you were building a theory. It's just the order the work goes in." She set the cloth down, picked up the probe, and turned it once in the lamplight to check it was clean. "Hold."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I keep my eyes locked on the man's face, his skin slick with sweat. His breath hitches as Sedge's probe touches the wound, and my own knuckles go white where I'm pressing down.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The probe went in along the track the metal had made, because that was the only road there was, and Sedge followed it by feel with her wrist loose and her elbow braced against her own ribs. The man's breath hitched and then went out of him in a long thin noise that wasn't shouting anymore, just weather.

"Good," she said. Not to him. "He's still got air. That's the noise of a man with air."

Half a finger's depth and the probe stopped against something that gave slightly and didn't slide — not bone, bone rang and shoved back. This dragged. "There," she said. "That's the cloth. It's sat across the muscle like a wad of paper in a drain, and everything behind it is waiting to go rotten." She withdrew the probe a fraction and moved it an inch to the left, testing the edges, mapping. "I want to know how big before I cut. You cut blind, you find an artery you weren't expecting, and then we have a much shorter evening."

The man bucked. It came up through him all at once, hips first, and Sedge lifted her hands clear in the same instant — off, always off, you never let your instrument stay in a moving man — and Wick's knuckles went whiter and held, and the table shrieked on the dirt and settled.

"That's the one I warned you about." She got her hands back down. "You did it right. Keep your weight forward over him, not down on him — you'll tire less and he'll shift less." She reached across with her elbow and nudged the lamp a half-turn so the light fell into the wound instead of across it. "Now. I'm going to open the top and bottom of this, about a thumb's length each way, straight along the line of the leg. It'll bleed properly, which is what I want — the bleeding's been the problem, that it stopped. Don't be alarmed at the amount. Be alarmed if it's dark and slow, and tell me if it comes out in a rhythm, because then I'm somewhere I don't want to be and I'll need your hands on a clamp."

She picked up the knife. She did not look at the man's face; that was Wick's job now, and it was better work to give away than to keep.

"Say ready," Sedge said, "and mean it less than last time. I'd rather you were honest."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge kept the knife where it was and answered, because the question deserved an answer and because a man with a hand on someone's shoulders was owed one.

"Neither," she said. "Not yet. The bone's whole — I'd have felt it grinding when he bucked and I felt nothing but meat. The big vessel runs deeper and further in than this, and if it were open he'd have been dead on the road four hours ago instead of shouting at us. What he's got is a dirty hole with rubbish in it and a leg that's started to think about giving up." She turned the knife once in her fingers. "So it's bad like *tonight matters*. If the cloth comes out and it drains and he's not burning up by morning, he walks on it. Badly. But he walks."

She glanced up, once, to make sure he was listening rather than just hearing.

"And I'll tell you about the other thing now so you're not carrying the question around all night. When it's *that* — when it's kindness — I say so. Out loud, in those words, and I don't do it with a lamp in one hand and a probe in the other and a man still making noise. That's not a decision you sneak up on. You'd know." She wiped her thumb on her apron. "You'd know because I'd stop working, and I don't stop working."

The man's head rolled and he said something that had been a name once.

"He's away with it. That's the best he'll be all night, and it won't last, so I'm using it." She set the flat of her left hand above the wound and drew the skin taut, thumb one side, fingers the other, taking up the slack so the blade would have something honest to open. "Weight forward. Eyes on his mouth — grey, or blue at the lip, that's yours to shout about. Everything else in this tent is mine."

She put the edge on and did not press yet.

"Hold."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I push down harder, my boots scuffing in the dirt. The knife goes in and the man arches, but I keep staring at his mouth, waiting for that grey. "He's still pink," I say through clenched teeth.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Pink is all I want from you," Sedge said. "Pink and shouting is a man with a future."

The blade went down through the tight shining skin and the skin opened the way it did when it had been waiting to — not reluctant, almost eager, the pressure behind it shoving the edges apart before she'd finished the stroke. Blood came, and came properly: bright, fast, running rather than seeping, sheeting down the outside of the thigh and into the folded blanket. Sedge watched it for the length of two breaths, not the amount but the *character* of it, and found nothing that pulsed.

"That's the right colour and the wrong volume in the correct direction," she said. "Good. That leg's been strangling itself since noon." She laid the knife down and took up the cloth and pressed it in hard at the upper end, then reversed the stroke with the blade at the lower, opening the wound the other way along the line of the muscle so the thing became a channel instead of a pocket. The man arched again. She let him. Her hands went with him this time, riding it, because the blade was out and there was nothing in him to tear.

"Rubbish in a drain," she said. "Now the drain's open."

She got two fingers in — no instrument yet, fingers first, because fingers told the truth and forceps only told you what you'd already decided. The heat in there was wrong, too much of it, the particular hot slick that meant the leg had already started its argument. And then, an inch down and turned sideways across the muscle belly like a page folded into a book, the cloth.

"Found it. It's bigger than the hole was — that's typical, it goes in small and unfolds." She hooked the pad of her finger behind the edge of it and felt it lift and hold, caught on something she couldn't see. "It's snagged. If I haul on it I take muscle with it and he bleeds from somewhere new, so I don't haul."

She withdrew her fingers, wiped them once, and picked up the long forceps.

"This is the part that takes a while and looks like nothing. I'll be going in and out of him and you'll see no progress and you'll start wondering whether I know what I'm doing." She set the jaws along her own finger's remembered line. "I do. Keep your weight where it is and don't let his hips come up again — not for kindness, but because I'll be gripping something soft and I can't have it torn out of my hand."

She leaned in until the lamp heat sat on her wrist.

"Hold."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't look up, but something in her shoulders eased half an inch.

"Sensible," she said. "Imagination's worse than anatomy. Anatomy's just layers."

She kept the forceps still and used her left hand to hold one lip of the wound back with her thumb, opening it like a book she was reading aloud from.

"Top down. That pale rind at the edge, that's the skin you've seen every day of your life. Under it the yellow — that's fat, and it's yellow like chicken fat and it bleeds very little and does nothing useful tonight. Then the grey-white sheeting, the stuff that looks like wet paper stretched tight: that's fascia. It wraps the muscle in a bag. That bag is why the leg was strangling. Blood and muscle swell, fascia doesn't, and the whole business squeezes itself dead from inside. When I cut it a moment ago, that's what opened so eagerly."

She moved her thumb.

"Then the red. That's the quadriceps — the big front muscle, the one that straightens the knee. It's dark red, and it runs in strands like the grain in a joint of beef, all the strands going the same way, up and down the leg. That's why I cut along them and not across. Cut along the grain and it comes back together. Cut across and you've severed something that pulls." She tilted the lamp with her elbow. "And you see where the red goes dull and brownish, there, around the track? That's the part the metal bruised to death on the way through. It won't bleed and it won't heal and it'll have to come out eventually, but not tonight and not by me."

The man muttered. She spoke over it, evenly.

"Now, the thing I'm actually after. Down there where the light doesn't want to go — that dirty pale scrap with the weave in it. Looks like nothing. Looks like a bit of wet rag in a puddle, because that's exactly what it is. His trouser leg. It's folded lengthways across the muscle and one corner of it has gone down into the track and hooked under a strand. That's the snag." She shifted the forceps a fraction. "Everything in there that looks like meat is meat and I leave it. The only thing in there that has a weave is the thing that comes out."

She set her jaw and went in, slow, the jaws closed until they were past the skin.

"What you won't see is anything that pulses, and that's the whole point of doing it at a crawl. The artery's deeper and inboard — thumb's width off the bone, other side of the muscle belly, behind all of this. I am not going there. If I ever do go there you'll know before I say a word, because the tent will go red and I'll ask for your hands in a voice you haven't heard yet."

She opened the jaws. Felt for the weave. Found it.

"Hold. He'll feel this one in his teeth."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I watch the forceps close on the cloth. My own jaw aches from clenching. "Feels it in his teeth," I echo, the words coming out thin. "Hope he's got a good set left."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Most of them do," Sedge said. "It's the last thing to go."

She closed the jaws and took up the slack — not a pull, a question. The cloth answered: it moved a hair and then stopped, still hooked. She let the tension off, turned her wrist a quarter, and asked again from a different angle, working the corner the way you'd work a nail out of old timber, not straight but rocked, side to side, letting the thing free itself.

The man found some air he hadn't been using and spent all of it at once. His whole body went rigid from heel to jaw and the table barked against the dirt and Wick's boots slid and dug in and Sedge's hand did not move, because the jaws had something soft and the whole business was now a matter of not tearing.

"There it goes," she said. "Steady. Steady. Nearly."

And then the snag let go, and the cloth came, and it kept coming — a hand's length of it, greyish, weeping, unfolding out of the leg like something being born badly. She lifted it clear into the light and held it up for a moment so he could see it. Trouser wool, sodden black in the weave, with a rim of dirt along one fold and a few pale threads still trailing where they'd torn.

"That," she said, "is four days of dying, and now it's in my hand instead of his leg."

She dropped it in the pail without ceremony and went straight back in, because the job was only half a job.

"Don't let go yet. Where there's one there's three." She was already feeling along the track with two fingers again, mapping it fresh now the bulk was gone. "Threads come off it. Grit comes in with it. Anything I leave behind does the same work the big piece was doing, just slower." Her fingers found something and paused. "Small one. Corner of the same piece, most likely, where it tore."

She traded fingers for forceps and got it in one, a scrap the size of a thumbnail, and flicked it into the pail after the rest.

The man had gone quiet again. Not the bad quiet — his chest was still working, fast and shallow, and the sweat had come up fresh across him.

"He's pink?" she asked, not looking.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge kept her eyes down and her fingers working. "He's pink or he isn't. Answer that first and I'll answer yours."

She waited the second it took, then went on, because the question was a fair one and she'd been asked worse by worse people.

"Straight, then. A bullet is tidy. A bullet is a machine built to go in a line, and it makes a hole roughly the shape of itself, and you can follow it. Shrapnel isn't built for anything. It's whatever the shell was made of, torn into shapes nobody designed — square, hooked, fluted, some of it the size of a thumbnail and some of it the size of a coin, all of it spinning and all of it tumbling. It doesn't go in a line. It goes in a line until it hits something dense and then it turns, and it keeps turning. That's the first thing it does. It goes somewhere other than where you'd have guessed from the hole in the outside."

She rinsed her fingers in the basin, shook them, and went back in along the track, going slower now, reading it.

"Second thing. It's hot and it's filthy and it's blunt. A blade parts tissue. This *crushes* it, out sideways, for a good inch around wherever it passed — that's the dull brown you saw, the meat that isn't going to bleed or mend. So you've got a channel of dead muscle running through a living leg, and dead muscle is the finest soil there is. Nothing in his body can reach it. No blood gets to it, which means nothing that fights infection gets to it either. You could pour the cleanest water in the country down that track and the middle of it would still be a garden."

Her fingers stopped, turned, moved on.

"Third, and this is the one that kills men. It doesn't travel alone. It drags the outside world in with it — his trouser, his shirt if it caught one, road dirt, dung, whatever the field was manured with last spring. That's what I've just pulled out of him. The metal itself is nearly the least of it. Metal can sit in a man for thirty years and give him nothing worse than an ache when it rains. It's the cloth and the dirt that rot, and the rot spreads along the grain of the muscle faster than you'd credit, and then it's not a leg problem, it's a *him* problem, and there's no knife long enough for that."

She withdrew her hand, looked at what was on it, and wiped it clean.

"So that's the work. Not fishing for souvenirs. Getting the field out of the man." She picked up the flask of boiled water and set her thumb over the neck. "And then leaving the door open so anything I missed has somewhere to run. This gets washed out and packed loose and it does *not* get stitched shut, whatever anyone tells you. Sew a wound like this and you've built the thing a warm room with a lock on it."

She tipped the flask.

"Brace. This is cold and it'll wake him."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I flinch when the water hits the wound, a weird sympathy pain. "So we leave him open? Like a... like a drain?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Like a drain," Sedge agreed. "Exactly like a drain. You've got it."

The water went in and came out pink and took a thread of something with it, and she caught the thread off the skin with her thumbnail and flicked it away before it could go back where it came from. The man woke enough to swear at her in a language she didn't have, and she let him.

"Every instinct you've got says close it," she said. "Neat edges, a row of stitches, looks like something was done. Looks *finished*. And a man with a wound like this sewn up tight is dead in five days and I have seen it enough times to be rude about it." She tipped the flask again, lower down, letting the water run the length of the channel and out. "Flesh heals from the bottom up. It fills in. If you shut the top over a dirty hole, the hole is still a hole — it's just got a lid on it now, and everything in it goes on working away in the dark where nobody can look. And you *won't* look, because it seems to be healing. The skin knits, the leg goes hot, the smell starts about day three, and by then it's not something you can open and rinse. By then you're taking the leg at the hip and hoping."

She set the flask down and reached for the gauze.

"So. Open. Packed loose — and loose is the word, I want you to remember loose. You don't stuff it. Stuffing it is the same crime as sewing it, with extra steps." She fed the first length in with the tip of the forceps, laying it rather than driving it, enough to keep the edges from falling together and no more. "This sits in there and wicks. Everything the leg wants rid of comes up the cloth and out. Then in a day, someone pulls it out — and it will have dried onto him, and it will hurt him more than anything I've done tonight, and it takes the muck with it when it comes. Then fresh in. Again the day after."

She tucked the last of it and laid a dressing over the top, not tight.

"That's the whole treatment. There isn't a cleverer one. Wash it, pack it, leave it open, come back tomorrow." She tied off the bandage and sat back on her heels, and only then did she look at the man's face herself. Still pink. Sweat drying at the temples. "What closes it is time and his own body, months of it, from the inside out. It'll fill in ugly. He'll have a dent in that thigh you could rest a cup in, and the skin over it will be shiny and thin and he'll hate it, and that's a man complaining about his leg, which is my favourite outcome."

She wiped her hands and nodded at Wick's grip.

"You can let go. Slowly — don't drop his weight, he'll feel it." She began laying things back in their row, cleaning each as it went down. "You did what I asked and you asked good questions at the right times, which is rarer. Wash your arms to the elbow before you touch your own face, and then you're going to sit with him for four hours and watch for two things: the leg going hot and hard again, which means I closed something I shouldn't have and I'll open it; and him going quiet and cold and grey at the mouth, which means he's bleeding somewhere I didn't find."

She dropped the pail's contents into the fire bucket without looking at them.

"And eat something. I don't care what. People faint at the second one, not the first."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not flinch and did not hurry. Screaming was information like anything else; it told her his lungs were good and his blood pressure was holding and he had not slipped off into the quiet place she'd have had to chase him into.

"Good," she said. "Loud is fine. Loud is a man arguing. Here's what I'm doing and here's how long."

She moved down the table to his foot.

"I've finished with the wound. What I'm doing now is checking that the leg below it is still getting fed, because I've just opened and rinsed a channel through the muscle and I want to know I haven't disturbed something on the way." She took his foot in both hands, turned it slightly, and pressed her thumbnail against his great toenail until the nail went white. She counted under her breath. "One. Two. Three." The colour flooded back. "That's blood reaching the furthest part of him. Three seconds is good. Six and I'd be worried. Ten and I'd be back in that leg with the lamp."

She laid two fingers on the top of his foot and held them there, not speaking, until she had it.

"Pulse on the instep. Faint, but it's there, and it's the same rhythm as the one in his neck, which is what I want. If that had gone I'd be looking for a clot or a vessel I'd bruised, and that's a different night entirely." She pinched the web between his toes hard. The foot twitched. "And he feels it. Nerve's intact. That's the leg accounted for."

She came back up alongside him and started at his collarbone with both hands flat.

"Now this, and this is the part nobody does and everybody should. Shells don't throw one piece. They throw a hundred, and a man gets hit by the one that hurt most and stops mentioning the rest. So I go over him — head, scalp, behind the ears, armpits, groin, the backs of everything." Her hands worked down in overlapping passes, pressing, feeling for the small hard heat of a thing lodged in flesh. "A fragment in the armpit or the groin will kill him quicker than that thigh ever would, and the hole it makes is the size of a pea, and he won't have told you, because compared to what you've just heard him shout about it doesn't rate."

Her hands stopped high on the back of his calf. She turned the lamp.

"There. Small entry, clean edge, no swelling, no smell. Something went in and stayed. Not tonight — it's not dirty and it's not pressing on anything. I'll ink a mark round it so whoever gets him next knows it's there and doesn't discover it in a fortnight."

She straightened.

"Ten minutes. Two to finish the sweep, two to mark that calf, the rest to strap the thigh so he can't flex it in his sleep and tear my good work open. Then you can let go and he can pass out, and frankly so can I."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I ease my grip just enough to feel the ache in my arms. "Tell me when to let go for good," I say, my voice rough. "And tell me what to listen for while he sleeps."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge finished the sweep with her hands and then did it again with her eyes, which was a different examination and caught different things. Nothing new. A graze along the ribs that had already scabbed, a burn on the back of the wrist he'd get from the barrel of his own rifle and not from anyone's shell.

"Not yet," she said. "Two more minutes. He'll try to curl when I strap this and I want him flat while I do it."

She took the ink stick and drew a circle on his calf, thumbnail-wide, around the little dark entry, and then a short arrow below it pointing up at the thing so nobody could mistake which mark meant what. Beside it she wrote the date and a single letter.

"That says there's metal under it and it was quiet on this day. If it stops being quiet, whoever's holding him will know it didn't come from nowhere." She capped the ink. "Half the harm done in this war is done by the second man, who doesn't know what the first man found."

Then the thigh. She built it in layers, a pad over the dressing, then the strapping run long — up over the hip, down below the knee, wide bands, firm without squeezing, the knee left a little bent because a leg strapped dead straight fought you all night and a leg with a bend in it gave up and slept.

"Now," she said. "Let go. Left hand first, then right, and put your palm on his chest as you come off so he knows the weight's leaving and doesn't startle. Good. Slower. There."

The man sank into the table and stopped being a thing that was being done to. His breathing found a longer rhythm almost at once.

"Listen for four things, and you can sit down while you do it, there's no virtue in standing." She was already washing, sleeves shoved up, forearms to the elbow. "One. His breath. It's fast and shallow now and that's fine — that's pain. Over the next hour it should slow and get deeper. If it gets faster instead, or if it goes ragged, or if you hear him working at it, come and get me and don't stop to decide whether you're sure."

She shook her hands off and dried them on the clean end of the cloth.

"Two. The leg. Put the back of your hand on it every half hour, above the strapping and below it both, and compare it to the other thigh. Same heat, you leave it. Hotter and harder than its neighbour, you come and get me, because that means it's swelling inside the bag again and I'll want to open more fascia. And check that foot the way I did — thumbnail on the toenail, count the colour back. If it goes past six, that's not something to mention in the morning."

"Three. Him. Not his leg, him. If he wakes and swears at you, that's a good hour. If he goes quiet and clammy and the mouth goes grey or blue, or if he starts asking for water over and over and then stops asking for anything, he's bleeding somewhere I didn't find and you wake me by shouting, not by coming to look for me politely."

She hung the cloth up and finally let her shoulders come down.

"Four. The smell. You won't get it tonight — it takes a day and a half at least — but you'll know it when it comes and nobody has to describe it to you. If you ever think you might be smelling it, you are."

She looked at him properly for the first time in an hour: the sweat in his hair, the way he was holding his arms.

"Your hands are going to shake in about ten minutes. That's not nerves, it's the muscle letting go, and it'll pass. Eat first, then sit. Four hours and I'll take him off you."

She picked up the lamp, then set it back down beside the man instead, and went out into the dark without it.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge came back in a minute later with two hands full: the flask, a hunk of bread that had been fresher yesterday, and her own stool, which she set down not across from him but beside him, and then didn't use. She sat on the ground instead, back against the crate, legs out, because he was on the ground and there was no sense making him look up.

She tore the bread in half and put his half in his lap without asking.

"The rest," she said. "All right. You'll want to eat while I do it, because you won't want to after."

She chewed for a moment. Outside, somebody was moving horses, badly.

"First. He may still lose that leg. I said tonight matters and it does, but I've done everything I did tonight for men who were rotten by Thursday anyway. I got the big piece and one small one out of him. I felt around for more and found none, and I am telling you plainly that *found none* is not the same as *there are none*. That track turned somewhere under the muscle and I followed it as far as my finger is long and then it went on past where I could reach, and I stopped, because the alternative was opening his thigh from hip to knee in a tent with one bad lamp and two pairs of hands, and he'd have bled more than he could spare and I'd have found a thread. Probably. So I left it. That was a guess. A good guess, made carefully, by someone who has made it a lot — but a guess, and you should know that everything in that leg from here on rests on it."

She wiped her mouth with the back of her wrist.

"Second. I didn't choose him because he was worst. I want that said out loud because you were holding his shoulders and you'll go on thinking about him, and you should know how he got onto that table. There were four brought in off that road. One had a belly wound and the smell already on him and I gave him what's left of the morphia and put him at the end of the row where it's dark and quiet, and he will be dead before you finish that bread. One has a broken arm set badly by a friend and he can wait until morning and he will hate me by then, and that's fine. One I haven't seen yet, which is a decision I made by not making it. And this one — this one was the only one where the difference between my hands and no hands was the difference between living and not. That's the whole of it. That's the only sorting there is. Not worst first. Not kindest first. *Where does the work change the answer.*"

She turned the flask slowly in her fingers.

"It's an arithmetic and it's foul and I'm good at it, and being good at it is not a thing I'd like put on a stone over me."

The man on the table breathed, long and ragged and even.

"Third, and this is the one you actually asked for." She glanced at him sidelong. "You asked why I talk. Why I narrate it like a woman reading out a recipe while a man screams. It's two things and neither is for your comfort. One: saying it aloud is how I check it. There's an order — clean outside, open, feel, find, pull, wash, pack, check the foot, sweep the body, mark what stays. Nine steps. Tired people skip steps and never know they skipped them. If I have to say the step, I can't skip it. You were my witness and you didn't know it."

She let that sit.

"Two. There are no medics. You know that, but I'll say it in the plain words. There were eleven of us on this line when I came. There's me and a man at the crossing who drinks, and a boy who can bandage. I'm forty-four and my hands are going — not tonight, but they go, everyone's go — and somewhere between now and whenever, the person who has to put two fingers in a thigh and tell the difference between fascia and cloth by feel is going to be you. Not because anyone picked you. Because you'll be standing there."

She held up the bread, and turned it, and put it down.

"So I don't teach you by saying *watch me*. Watching teaches you nothing; you watched a woman's back and a lamp for an hour. I say it out loud so that in six months, in a worse tent, with no one to ask, you'll hear it in my voice — *along the grain, not across it. Loose, not stuffed. Never sew a dirty wound. Fingers before instruments. Off the instant he moves.* That's it. That's the whole inheritance. It fits in a page and it took four years and I don't know how many men to write, and most of the men who paid for it never knew they were paying."

She drank, and offered him the flask, and set it down between them when he didn't take it straight away.

"Now the part I've been putting off, and then I'll stop and you can sit with him."

She looked at the canvas wall, which was what he'd wanted to look at earlier, and she let herself do it now.

"I said I take no pleasure in this. That was true and it was also a smaller truth than the one underneath. The larger one is that I don't feel very much at all while I'm doing it, and that took work to arrive at, and I don't entirely know what it cost. When his hip came up off that table and you went white — I noted the hip, I noted your knuckles, I lifted my hands clear, and I thought *good, he's got air*. That's all there was in my head. Not pity. Not horror. Just the next thing. And people who see me at it decide I'm hard, or cruel, or that something's been taken out of me, and I let them decide it because arguing wastes light."

She flexed her hands, looking at them.

"But it isn't that. It's that feeling it *while* you do it makes you slow, and slow gets men killed — so you set it down. And here's the thing nobody tells you, so I'm telling you, because it's the rest and you asked for the rest. *You have to pick it back up.* Afterwards. Deliberately. You have to sit down on the floor of a tent like you're doing now and let your hands shake and let yourself know that was a man, and he had a name he was trying to say, and that I hurt him more in one hour than anyone has ever hurt him in his life and he will remember my face and not yours. You let that in. You give it its hour. And then you get up."

She rubbed her palms on her knees.

"Because the ones who never set it down go mad in a month, and everyone can see it and everyone helps them. But the ones who set it down and never pick it back up — nobody notices those at all. They get promoted. They get called steady. And one day they walk past a man in the dark end of a row and they don't put the morphia in his hand, because he wasn't going to change the arithmetic, and they've forgotten that there was ever a reason to do a thing that didn't change the arithmetic." She looked at him. "That's the actual danger. Not the blood. You'll get used to the blood in a fortnight; everyone does, it's disappointing how fast. The danger is getting used to the *sorting*."

She reached over and pushed the bread an inch closer to his hand.

"So. Four things to listen for, and a fifth, which is this. Sit there as long as you need. Shake. It's the muscle and it's also not only the muscle, and both are allowed. Talk to him if he wakes, and if he asks whether he'll keep the leg, you say *the medic thinks so*, which is true, and you don't say the rest of what I've told you, because that's mine to carry and not his. And at some point in the next four hours you'll get the urge to look under that dressing. Don't. It's packed right. Looking is for you, not for him, and everything you do in this tent from here on has to be for him."

She got up, slowly, with a hand on the crate, and made a noise about her knees that she did not apologise for.

"I'll be behind the stores. Shout, don't come and find me." She stopped at the flap and looked back at the lamp she'd left burning by the table. "Keep that where it is. He'll be frightened when he wakes and he won't know why, and a light helps more than you'd think, which is not a medical opinion and I'd deny having said it."

Then she went out, and the flap dropped, and it was just the lamp and the breathing and a man on the floor with bread he hadn't eaten yet.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content:
I pick up the bread and stare at it. My hands are shaking so bad I drop it in the dirt. I leave it there.

After a while, I crawl over to the table and put my hand on the man's chest, like she said. His heart's beating under my palm. Fast, but there.

"Medic thinks you'll keep it," I tell him, my voice too quiet. I don't know if he hears.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not go behind the stores.

She got four paces and stopped and stood in the dark with one hand flat on the outside of the canvas, which was cold and damp and sagging where the pole had shifted, and she listened to the boy say a true thing very quietly to a man who probably could not hear it.

She gave it its hour. Or the part of an hour she had. She stood there and let herself know that the man's name had two syllables and started wrong, and that he had a wife or a sister or nobody at all and she would never find out which, and that she had put her fingers inside his leg and rocked a piece of his own trousers out of him while he begged in a language she didn't have, and that if he lived he would flinch at the smell of a certain kind of lamp oil for the rest of his life and never know why.

Then she wiped her face with the heel of her hand, briskly, the way she did everything, and went back in.

She didn't say anything about the bread in the dirt. She picked it up, knocked it against her thigh twice, blew the grit off the torn edge, and put it on the crate where he'd see it later when he wanted it, because he would. Then she took her own half out of her apron pocket — she hadn't eaten it either — and set it beside the first.

"He heard you," she said. "Or he didn't. Both are worth the saying."

She came and stood at the head of the table and looked down at the man's face, and then, without any ceremony, she put two fingers against his throat and held them there and watched nothing in particular while she counted. Her lips didn't move. She'd stopped needing them to.

"Hundred and four," she said. "Was a hundred and thirty when you had him by the shoulders. That's him coming down off it. That's the best news either of us gets tonight."

She took her hand away and, for a moment, left it resting on the man's forehead instead — flat, the way she'd put her fingers on his thigh hours ago, well clear of the wound. Pressure told her things. Heat told her things. This told her nothing at all, and she did it anyway, and she was aware of doing it, which was the point.

"Your hands will settle in twenty minutes," she said. "Don't hold them still. Let them go. Fighting it makes it last."

She straightened, hooked her stool over with one foot, and sat down on it this time, on the other side of the table, so that the lamp was between them and the man was between them and she was not looking at him directly.

"I'll take the first two hours," she said. "You'll take the second two, and you'll take them better for having slept. No — don't argue it, I'm not being kind, I'm being efficient. I'd rather have you sharp at four in the morning than loyal at midnight." She settled her elbows on her knees. "Lie down where you are. You can keep your hand on his chest if you want. It won't hurt him and it'll help you, and I've already told you I'd deny saying that."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I don't lie down. I lean my head back against the crate, my hand still on his chest, feeling that stubborn beat. "Tell me his name if you know it," I say, staring at the ceiling of the tent. "Or make one up."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't answer straight away. She reached down beside the crate instead, to the folded heap of what he'd come in wearing — she'd cut it off him at the door and she'd gone through it then, the way she went through all of them, because pockets told you things too.

The paybook had been in the breast, which was where they mostly were, and it had gone through the same water and the same road as the man.

She held it to the lamp and turned it so the light came across the page rather than into it.

"Ink's run," she said. "First part's gone. What's left is *—hovel*, or *—novel*, and I'd say the letter before it was a c or an e." She turned the book a little further. "Nechovel. Something like it. Second syllable's clear enough and it's got a *v* in it, which narrows the country if not the man."

She closed the book and set it on the crate beside the bread, squared up, where it wouldn't get knocked into the dirt.

"That's all there is and it's more than most. He's got a unit stamp that's legible and a date of issue, so somebody somewhere has him written down properly, and if he lives he'll tell you himself and be irritated that you got it wrong."

She sat back on the stool.

"And I won't make one up. Not because it's a sin — because a made-up name is a thing you'd be doing for yourself. You want to stop calling him *him*. I understand it. I've wanted it. But you'd give him a name out of your own head, out of someone you knew, and then that's who'd be on that table for the rest of the night, and it wouldn't be him. He'd be gone and you'd be nursing a stranger with your cousin's name on him." She nodded at the paybook. "*Nechovel* is worse to say and it's got the advantage of being partly true. Use that. Use the half you've got and leave the rest of it empty, and let him fill it in himself when he wakes up."

Outside, the horses had finally settled.

"Two syllables," she said, after a while, to the canvas rather than to him. "He was trying to say something with two syllables, when you were holding him. Might have been his own. Might have been somebody he wanted. I've heard a lot of men spend their worst hour on a name and it's almost never their own."

She adjusted the lamp a half-turn with her elbow, out of habit, though there was nothing left to see by it.

"Get some sleep, Wick. I'll wake you at four and I'll want you to be difficult about it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content:
I push the paybook with my fingertip, turning it. "Nechovel." It tastes like mud in my mouth. "Fine. Nechovel it is."

I finally let go of his chest and slump sideways against the crate, my arm numb. "Wake me if he goes grey," I say, eyes already closed.
