dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't move the lamp, just her eyes. "Good. Wrong is a start. Now make it specific. You've got a torso, near as I can tell, and something that isn't sitting where an arm ought to sit. Count the limbs before you count anything else. Monsters lie about faces. They don't usually bother lying about how many arms they've got, because most of them don't know we're counting."

She waited a beat, watching the water for the telltale ring of something shifting weight without breaking the surface.

"And breathing. Tell me if it's breathing. Not because I think it's dead — I don't, dead things don't settle like that, they just stop — but because if it's not breathing and it's not dead, that narrows things down considerably, and not in a direction I enjoy."

She shifted the lamp an inch, just enough to throw new shadow without giving away that she'd moved it. "Take your time. We're not going in that water until one of us can say what we're going in after. I've buried men who skipped that step."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I squint, trying to ignore the way the lamplight shimmers on the water.* "Four limbs. But one of the arms is too high, like it's coming out of the shoulder blade. And... it's not breathing. But there's a sort of... pulsing. In the water near its back."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Shoulder blade arm. Right." Halloway's mouth flattened into something that wasn't quite a smile. "That's not an injury, Pike, in case you were hoping. Nothing grows an extra socket for itself by accident. That's built. Which means we're not looking at a person who's been got at — we're looking at a thing that was a person once and has been rearranged for a purpose."

She finally let the lamp drift a few degrees, following the water's surface toward the pulsing.

"Now. The pulsing." Her voice dropped, careful, like she was talking someone down off a ledge rather than commenting on a corpse. "Not breathing, but pulsing. That's not lungs. That's something feeding, or something laying, and both of those are bad in their own special way, but only one of them means we've got minutes instead of hours."

She crouched, slow, keeping the lamp steady, and studied the ripple pattern.

"Count the pulses for me. If it's regular — like a heartbeat, evenly spaced — that's a parasite riding the body, using it as a nest, and the good news is the body's just meat to it, it won't fight back with anything clever. If it's irregular, clusters, then something's stirring and deciding when to move, and that's a mind in there, however small, and minds plan."

She reached to her belt without looking, found the coil of silver-threaded line by touch alone, old habit.

"Don't answer yet. Watch first. I've seen men call it too fast and end up finding out the hard way which kind it was."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't answer right away. She was looking at the hands — what was left of them, floating just under the surface, fingers curled the way fingers curl when the tendons have shortened rather than relaxed.

"Recently," she said finally. "Days, not years. Skin's not sloughing yet, and something's still using the musculature, which means something's keeping it fed enough to matter. A body left to rot on its own doesn't get maintained like that." She tilted her head slightly. "So yes. That was someone. Man, going by the wrist bones, and going by that ring that's cut into the finger now because the finger's swollen around it — married, or was."

She let that sit for exactly as long as it took to be useful and not a second longer.

"I tell you that not to make you feel it, Pike, though you're welcome to, on your own time, later, when we're not standing in his cellar. I tell you because it matters *what* he was doing before this happened to him. Man who dies here, in his own house, in his own water — someone let something in, or something's been in the walls longer than anyone bothered to notice. Either way, the answer's not going to be floating on top for us to read."

The pulsing near the back caught again, and this time Halloway held perfectly still, counting under her breath before she spoke.

"There. Did you catch that? Not evenly spaced. Went quick-quick, then a long gap, like it was listening for something between beats." Her hand tightened, unhurried, on the coiled line. "That's the answer to the question I didn't want. Something's home in him, and it's not just feeding. It's counting us the same way we're counting it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *I feel my throat tighten, but I keep my voice low.* "So it's waiting for us to move first." *My hand drifts toward the iron spike on my own belt.* "Do we... lure it out?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Waiting's the polite word for it," Halloway said. "It's *choosing*. Every extra second we stand here debating is a second it spends deciding whether we're worth the effort or whether it'd rather slip out the drain and try its luck with someone who isn't holding silver."

She didn't reach for the spike yet. Her eyes stayed on the water, on the place where the ripples kept starting.

"Luring's a fine word for it when you've got something worth luring it with. What have you got that a thing like that wants more than the body it's already wearing?" She let the question hang a moment, not cruel, just testing whether Pike would answer too fast. "Nothing. So we don't lure. Luring's for things that are hungry and stupid. This one's neither, not fully — it's counting, which means it's already decided we're a problem, not a meal, and it's working out which one of us solves easier."

She began, unhurried, to pay out a length of the silver-threaded line, letting it sink into the black water an arm's length from her boots — not toward the body, off to the side, a decoy of current rather than of flesh.

"What we do is make it move on *our* terms instead of its own. That means noise where we're not standing, and stillness where we are." She nodded once at Pike's belt. "Spike's good, but it's a last thing, not a first thing — you plant that in the wrong beat of its rhythm and you've told it exactly where your arm is and how fast you swing it. I want you on the near wall, lamp low so it doesn't read your shape against the light. I'm going to give it a reason to think the drain's more interesting than we are."

She glanced at Pike, briefly, and there was something almost gentle under the flat clinical tone.

"When it comes — and it will, because they always do, curiosity's the one thing rearranging a corpse doesn't cure — you don't swing first. You let it commit to a direction. Things wearing dead men are clumsy about changing their minds mid-lunge. That clumsiness is the whole of what we've got to work with tonight, so we use it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't look up from the line she was paying out, but her voice took on the flat, unhurried cadence she used for lectures, the one that meant she'd said this sort of thing before, over other water, other bodies.

"Plainly, then. Somewhere in the last week, something got into this man — through the mouth, most likely, or an old wound, they're not fussy about entry points — and it didn't kill him outright, because dead men don't hold a shape this well. It ate its way to convenient, is the plain way to say it. Took the muscle it needed, left the rest to float where floating suited it. That shoulder joint isn't damage. That's *renovation*. Something wanted an extra limb it could work from inside a ribcage without popping the sternum, so it grew the socket loose instead of trying to force one where nature put the collarbone."

She glanced sideways, just once, to make sure Pike was still steady.

"The pulsing's it breathing for both of them now, best guess — using the lungs it doesn't need for air, and something else, further down, for itself. Man's heart probably stopped days ago. Whatever's keeping that chest doing *anything* isn't sentiment, it's plumbing. It found a working set of pipes and moved in rather than build its own."

The line went taut, then slack again, testing the current rather than snagging on anything.

"So plainly: he's not in there anymore, Pike, hasn't been for some time, and thinking of him as *him* is going to slow your arm at exactly the moment it can't afford to be slow. What's in that water wearing his wedding ring is a parasite that's gotten ambitious about its landlord. We're not here to save him. We're here to make sure it doesn't go looking for a second lease."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I nod, my knuckles white around the lamp. "Alright. So we burn it out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Burn it out," Halloway repeated, like she was turning the phrase over to check for rot. "Fine notion. Wrong tool for wet work, though. You put open flame near four feet of standing water in a stone cellar with one door, and the only thing you'll cook properly is the air we're both breathing. Fire wants dry ground and a clear way out. We've got neither."

She tied off the line, gave it a final testing tug, satisfied.

"What we've got is salt, silver, and the fact that it needs that body to keep functioning as well as it currently does. You don't burn a parasite out of good plumbing, Pike. You block the pipes." She nodded toward the small oilcloth bundle at her hip. "Salt goes in the water first, upstream of it if we can manage the angle — not to hurt it, salt's not fire, it won't scream and die pretty. It irritates. Makes wet unpleasant to move through, makes the body it's riding sluggish, buys us the half a second we need that we otherwise wouldn't get."

She finally drew the spike from her own belt, weighed it once in her palm.

"Then silver, through whatever's doing the pulsing, not through the chest generally — you go in vague, you'll just aggravate the corpse without touching the thing living in it, and then you've got an angry dead man *and* an angry passenger, which is strictly worse than what we've got now. You put the point exactly where that rhythm keeps starting from. That's the seat of it. Everything else is just the house it's squatting in."

She looked at Pike properly then, lamp-light catching the flat certainty in her face.

"So. Not burn. Drown its comfort, then put silver through its actual address. Slower than fire, less theatrical, and it has the enormous advantage of not setting us alight in a stone box with one door." A beat. "I did that once. The door part. Don't recommend it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway's eyes didn't leave the water, but she nodded slightly, like she'd been waiting for that question rather than the easier ones.

"Good. That's the right question. Fine." She kept her voice low, level, lecture-flat. "Skin's intact over most of him, which tells you it doesn't need to breach the hide to work — it's not chewing in from outside, it's rearranging from within, which means whatever this is, it came in small. Mouth, ear, old scar tissue, something already open. Once it's in, it doesn't eat wastefully. Look at the wasting pattern — forearms are thin, gone to nothing, but the shoulders and the back are thick, overbuilt. That's not hunger, that's *investment*. It stripped muscle from where it didn't need strength and piled it where it did, because it's not trying to keep him alive, it's trying to keep him *useful*. Efficient parasite doesn't waste protein on limbs it's not planning to use for climbing or striking."

She tipped her chin toward the wrong-set shoulder without looking away from the ripples.

"That socket. It didn't force the joint, it grew round it — you can tell because there's no tearing at the edges, no bruising, which means whatever did that had *time*, and time means this has been in him longer than a week, whatever the skin looks like. Skin's the last thing to catch up. Skin lies."

The pulsing started again, quick-quick, long gap, and she paused just long enough to count it before continuing, unbothered, like a woman narrating over a headache.

"The pulse you clocked — that's not a heartbeat and it's not lungs. Real hearts don't hesitate. Whatever's doing that is deciding, breath by breath, whether it's worth spending the effort to keep this body upright. That's the thing to remember, Pike, more than any of the meat. It's not instinct-driven. It's *economising*. Which means next time — and there'll be a next time, there's always a next time — you don't look for the wound. You look for the parts of the body that are better fed than they've any right to be. Overbuilt shoulders on a starved man. A hand too strong for an arm that thin. That's where it's spent its budget, and that's where it's sitting."

She finally glanced at Pike, brief and dry.

"Take the detail home with you if you like. Draw it, even. Just don't take the *smell* home with you, that's the part that actually sticks."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, the smell already sticking in the back of my throat. "So we salt the water first. Then you draw it toward the drain." *I shift the lamp lower, casting my own shadow against the damp stone wall behind me.* "How close do I let it get before I move?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway crouched lower, letting the lamp's angle work for her rather than against her, and considered the question the way she considered most things — as a matter of arithmetic rather than nerve.

"Closer than you'll want," she said. "And not as close as it'll try to get. There's a difference." She nodded toward the near wall where Pike stood. "You've got maybe six feet of water between you and where I expect it to surface. Let it cross four of those feet before you commit to anything. Not because four's a magic number — because at four feet, it's already picked its target and started the lunge, and a thing mid-lunge can't turn as sharp as a thing that's still deciding. You want it *past* deciding."

She eased the line taut again, testing the drag of current against it, calibrating.

"Watch the shoulder — the wrong one, the built one. That's the arm it'll lead with, because that's the arm it spent the most on. When that comes up out of the water first, that's your tell. Not the head, not the eyes if it's still got working eyes, don't watch the face, the face is theatre. Watch the shoulder. When it breaks the surface, you've got about as long as it takes me to say this sentence before the rest of it follows."

A beat, and she allowed herself, briefly, something almost like reassurance.

"You don't need to be fast, Pike, you need to be *placed*. Plant your feet before it moves, not after — mud shifts your footing, and I'm not fishing you out of four feet of water while also managing whatever's currently deciding your worth. Spike goes in low and angled up, toward where the pulse sits, not where the body's centre is. You're not trying to kill the man. There's no man left to kill. You're trying to evict a tenant."

She glanced back at the water, at the stillness that had gone a fraction too still.

"Salt goes in now, upstream, my throw. When it hits, you'll see the whole shape flinch — that's not pain, that's *inconvenience*, and inconvenience is what we're renting tonight. The second it flinches is the second the shoulder tells you which way it's turning. That's your window. Not before."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway's knife found the seam she wanted — just above the wrongly-set shoulder, where the skin had gone shiny and thin with new growth — and she opened it in one draw, unhurried, the way she'd open a letter she already knew the contents of.

"Skin first," she said, keeping her voice at the same flat pitch as before, refusing to let it climb. "Thinner than it should be here, papery, because it's new — this is maybe four days old, growing over something that needed covering in a hurry. Underneath that." She peeled it back with the flat of the blade. "Fat's gone. Not eaten — *dissolved*. There's a sheen to the tissue that shouldn't be there, like it's been sitting in something faintly acidic for a good long while. That's not digestion. That's clearing space."

The lamp caught wet, dark red going toward black, and something threaded through it that wasn't blood — paler, fibrous, running against the grain of the muscle rather than with it.

"There. That's not vein and it's not sinew. See how it doesn't follow the muscle lines — real anatomy has a logic to it, this doesn't care about the logic, it's laid its own roads through him." She traced the path of it with the knife-tip, not touching, just showing. "Runs up from somewhere low — gut, maybe lower, I'll know more when I'm down that far — and threads up through here, into the shoulder joint. This is what built the socket. It's not muscle doing the work of holding that arm up anymore. It's this."

The smell had changed, sweetish going to rot going to something underneath that neither of those words fit properly, and Halloway didn't flinch from it, just breathed shallow through her mouth like she'd trained herself to decades back.

"How far it got — all the way, Pike, is the honest answer. This isn't a recent guest making itself comfortable in a spare room. Look at the joint itself." She angled the lamp. "Bone's remodelled. Not broken and healed wrong — regrown, deliberate, socket where there wasn't one, and that doesn't happen in four days no matter how hungry a thing is. The skin's new because the skin's the *last* thing it fixes, once the structure underneath already suits it. Man's been carrying this for weeks, maybe longer, walking around, married, wearing that ring, and whatever this is has been quietly renovating the inside of him the entire time without him ever once looking wrong enough for anyone to ask."

She found the source of the pulse then — not with her eyes so much as with the flat of her palm, laid briefly against the opened flesh, feeling for it rather than watching for it.

"There it is. Not where I'd have put money. Sitting behind the shoulder blade proper, wrapped round it like it's using the bone as scaffolding rather than food." Her hand came away steady. "That's your answer to the smell, too, if you're still wanting it — it's the same thing that's doing the acid work on the fat. Sweet under the rot. That sweetness is *it*, not him. You smell that on something again, you don't wait to see a shoulder. You act on the smell alone."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I shift my weight, the water sloshing against my legs. "So it was wearing him for weeks. While he was still... living." I look from the opened flesh back to Halloway's face. "Did he know?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't answer immediately. She turned the arm slightly, checking the underside of the wrist, the palm, the pads of the fingers — the places a man's body kept its evidence when his mouth couldn't.

"No burns," she said. "No bite marks on his own hand, no nail-marks dug into his palm, nothing at the wrist to say he was ever tied down or held. Man who knows something's eating him from the inside generally leaves a record of that on himself, one way or another — they claw, they bite down, they do things to their own bodies trying to get it out. This one's clean." She set the arm back gently, more gently than the work warranted. "So. No. I don't think he knew. Not in any way that would've let him do anything about it."

She wiped the blade on her thigh, unhurried, and nodded toward the pale threading she'd shown Pike earlier.

"That road it built — it runs wide of anything that would've screamed at him. Skirts the big nerves instead of crossing them. That's not mercy, before you go soft on it. That's economy again. A host that's in agony fights, or worse, tells someone, goes to a doctor, gets cut open by someone other than us on our schedule. Quiet's more useful to it than cruel." She looked up, and for once the flatness in her voice had a hair of something underneath it, worn thin but there. "So whatever he felt — tired, maybe. Hungry all the time, and never knowing why. Maybe he thought he was just getting old faster than he should. That's the mercy in it, if you want to call it that. He probably went to bed one night wondering why his shoulder ached, and never once wondered if he had company."

She straightened, joints cracking audibly in the cold, and glanced toward the drain, toward the ring that was still cutting into a swollen finger under the water.

"Somebody's going to ask his wife that same question you just asked me, Pike, and she won't get as tidy an answer, because she'll want to know if he suffered and there's no way to tell her *no* that she'll believe from a stranger with a knife. That's the part of this work nobody puts in the ballads. Not the fighting. The telling." She held the lamp out for Pike to take a moment, so her own hands could finish, steady, without needing to be watched doing it. "Now. Salt's going in. Watch the shoulder."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The salt went in first — two fistfuls, flung wide across the water in an arc that put white crystal skimming the surface like a handful of thrown stars. Halloway didn't wait to see it dissolve. She was already moving, low, along the wall opposite Pike, lamp left forgotten in Pike's hands so her own were free.

The reaction, when it came, wasn't loud. That was the thing nobody warned you about — the pictures in your head were always noise, thrashing, a scream. What actually happened was the water around the corpse simply seized, the whole shape of it going rigid all at once, shoulders locking, head snapping back at an angle no living neck would allow and no dead one would bother with. A sound came out of it that wasn't quite a groan — more like air being forced through something that used to be a windpipe and had since been repurposed for other business.

"There," Halloway said, mild as weather. "Told you. Inconvenience."

The overbuilt shoulder broke the surface exactly as promised, water sheeting off skin gone the colour of a drowned candle, and underneath it the pale threading was visible now even from a distance, standing out against muscle like veins of quartz in dark rock, pulsing — quick-quick, then nothing, then quick-quick again, agitated, deciding.

It came for the salt-line first, not for either of them, exactly as Halloway had hoped and hadn't quite said aloud — a dumb animal reflex to strike at the source of the pain rather than the cause of it, wasting itself on rope. That bought the half-second she'd promised Pike, except Pike wasn't the one who needed it anymore. Halloway was already across the distance, boots finding the submerged floor by memory rather than sight, spike reversed in her grip.

She didn't go for the chest. She'd told Pike that and she meant it for herself too. She went in low, under the ruined shoulder, angling up along the path the pale threading made, and put the silver through exactly where her palm had felt the pulse start, twenty minutes before, with the same unhurried certainty she'd have used pinning a moth to a board.

The body didn't scream. It didn't have the apparatus left to scream with, not really — what came out instead was a long, thin exhale, almost gentle, almost like relief, as the rigidity went out of it all at once and the arm dropped back into the water with a small, unremarkable splash. The pale threading under the skin went from white to grey to nothing, visibly, the way a coal goes dark when you take the bellows away.

Halloway held the spike in place a count of ten past the point where anything needed holding, because she'd been wrong about that particular economy once, a long time ago, in a different cellar, and hadn't made the mistake twice since.

Then she straightened, breathing harder than she'd have liked to admit, and looked down at what was left — a man again, only a man, weighted with water and salt and silver and finally, mercifully, still.

"That's it," she said, to the water, to Pike, to no one in particular. "Landlord's evicted the tenant." She waded back toward the steps, wringing nothing useful out of soaked sleeves, and looked up at Pike sitting there with the lamp held like it was the only warm thing left in the building.

"We'll want lye for the water before anyone else comes down here," she added, matter-of-fact, already cataloguing the next task the way she catalogued everything, because stopping to feel it properly could wait until there was nothing left that needed doing. "And someone's going to have to go up and tell his wife we found him. Not tonight. Tonight we just get you dry and get that smell off both of us before it decides to live in our coats." She held out a hand, unhurried, steady, exactly as it had been the whole night. "Up you get. You did the hard part. You watched properly."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I take her hand, my own shaking, and stand up on the step. The lamp light wavers across her face. "He looked relieved," I say, and my voice is rough. "At the end."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway's grip tightened briefly around Pike's hand, steadying more than pulling, and she didn't let go straight away.

"He did," she said. "I noticed too." She said it plainly, the way she said most things, but there was no edge on it tonight. "I'll tell you what I think that was, since you're asking, and you can decide for yourself if it's comfort or just biology, because I honestly couldn't tell you which it is most nights."

She stepped up beside Pike, both of them dripping on the stone, and looked back down at the water rather than away from it — old habit, never turn your back on the job until you're sure it's finished being a job.

"Whatever that thing was doing to keep him upright, it was work. Constant, unglamorous work, propping up a body that wanted to be done propping itself up weeks ago. When I put silver through it, that work stopped. All at once. That's not peace, strictly speaking — that's just a muscle finally being allowed to let go after it's been told to hold for longer than it should've had to." She paused. "But I've stood over enough of these to tell you the two things look identical from the outside, and after thirty years I've stopped being precious about insisting on the difference. If it looked like relief to you, I'm not going to argue you out of it. Man held on a lot longer than most would've, not knowing why, not knowing what for. If some part of him got to feel it end, I'm not sorry about that part."

She finally started up the last of the steps, tugging Pike gently along with her, out of the smell and into air that only smelled of damp stone rather than whatever had been living in that water.

"That's the bit they don't put in the ballads either," she added, dry again, the flatness creeping back in like it always did once the worst of a thing was behind her. "Nobody sings about the moment after. They sing about the swing of the blade. Nobody wants the verse where the hunter stands on the stairs deciding whether relief is the right word for a dead man's face." She glanced sideways at Pike, something almost kind under the dryness. "You did well tonight. Cry about it later if you need to — I mean that, not as an insult. Just not on these steps. Steps are wet enough."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I let go of her hand and wipe my face with my sleeve. It comes away wet. "I'm not going to cry." I look at her a second too long, then down at my boots. "The smell's in my nose already. I can taste it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"You will taste it," Halloway said, not unkindly, "for about three days, and then it'll fade, and then in about a month's time you'll catch a whiff of something that isn't even close to it — spoiled milk, a wet dog, doesn't matter — and it'll come roaring back like it never left. That's not you being weak. That's just how a nose holds a grudge. Nothing to be done about it except let it happen and not flinch when it does."

She led the way up the last few steps into the cold, cleaner air of the house above, and stopped at the top to strip off her outer coat, wringing it out over the cellar door before she'd let it anywhere near the rest of the building.

"Yours too," she said, nodding at Pike's sleeves. "Anything that touched that water goes outside tonight, not folded up in your kit to fester. I don't care if it's your only coat. A coat that smells of that will have every dog in the county barking at you for a week, and worse things than dogs notice that smell too."

She glanced back down the stairwell once, into the dark, out of habit rather than doubt — checking a door was properly shut, more or less, though there was no door down there, only water and salt and a man finally left in peace.

"And for what it's worth," she added, turning back to the business of wringing out her own sleeves, brisk again, "I never said crying was the failure. I said not on the steps. There's a difference, and you're smart enough to know it, so I won't insult you by explaining further." A pause, dry as ever. "Go on ahead and put the kettle to whatever passes for a fire in this house. I'll deal with the lye. You've done enough looking for tonight."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I nod and move past her, my boots leaving wet prints on the floorboards. The kettle's heavy and cold in my hands. "Will you tell the wife he didn't suffer?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned, blade already sheathed, and faced the place where Del stood. Her voice, when it came, held no tremor and no theatre — she had learned long ago that either would be its own kind of lie.

"Let it be recorded," she said, loud enough to carry to the edges of the watching circle. "The engagement was fair, called and answered under the code. The wound was delivered to the left side, beneath the fourth rib, angled upward through the heart. Death was not instant, but it was certain from the moment the blade entered. There was no second strike. There was no need for one."

She let that settle before she looked at Del directly, because the account was owed to the witnesses, but the weight of it was owed to whoever stood closest to the dead.

"That is the wound that ended him. I will not call it clean, or kind, or deserved. I will only call it true." A pause. "You may ask anything more you need to know. I will not soften what I already told you plainly."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod once, my throat tight. "I have no further questions." I turn to the witnesses, raising my voice just enough. "The accounting stands as given and confirmed."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head, once, the formal gesture that closed the account — witnessed, spoken, confirmed. No more and no less than the code required.

"Then it is done," she said. The circle around them began, slowly, to loosen — the particular stillness of witnessing breaking apart into the ordinary shuffle of people who no longer needed to hold their breath. Auren did not join that motion. She stood where she was a moment longer, because leaving too quickly was its own kind of discourtesy.

"I will not tell you it gets easier to hear," she said to Del, quieter now, no longer performing for the edges of the circle. "I have said eleven of these. I have never once watched a face receive one and thought — good, that was easy for them. It isn't supposed to be." She glanced toward where the body still lay, being seen to by others now, not by her. That was not her office. Her office had ended the moment the account was confirmed.

"If you want to sit somewhere that isn't here, I'll walk with you. If you'd rather I go, I'll go. Either is fair." She said it plainly, the same register she'd used to name the wound — no comfort dressed up as kindness, only the truth of what she could offer.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren went still.

The phrase was already spoken, already confirmed — the circle had already begun to loosen around them on the strength of that confirmation. She could have said as much. She could have told Del, gently, that the account stood, that repeating it changed nothing under the code.

She did not.

"Let it be recorded again," she said instead, voice dropping the formal projection but keeping the formal shape, because Del had asked for the shape and the shape was what she had to give. "The wound was delivered to the left side, beneath the fourth rib, angled upward through the heart. Death was not instant. It was certain."

She held Del's eyes through all of it this time, not the witnesses at the edges. "There was no cruelty in it. There was no mercy in it either — I will not lie to you and call it mercy. It was only the wound that ended him, and it ended him quickly, and that is the whole of what I can tell you."

A breath.

"I know why you asked twice. The first time is for the witnesses. Sometimes the second time is for yourself — to make it small enough to carry, one telling at a time." She did not reach for Del, did not presume that much. "If you need a third, I will give it a third. The code does not forbid grief its repetitions. Only its lies."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I close my eyes for a beat, then open them. My voice is quieter this time. "One more time. Just the wound."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
"The wound was beneath the fourth rib, left side. It went upward. It found the heart." Auren said it plainly, without the formal cadence this time — no witnesses left to serve, only Del. "That was the wound."

She did not add anything after. No qualifiers, no comfort, no repetition of what she'd already said about mercy or cruelty. Del had asked for the wound alone, and she gave only that, because to pad it now would be its own kind of unkindness — burying the one true thing under more words when Del had asked, specifically, for less.

She waited. Not stepping back, not stepping closer. Letting the quiet hold whatever shape it needed to hold.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
"Beneath the fourth rib, on the left side," Auren said again, without impatience, without change. "It went upward from there. It ended in the heart. That is where it landed — nowhere else, nothing beside it."

She watched Del's face as she said it, and did not look away from what she saw there. "You've asked me the place three times now. I'll give it a fourth if you need one, or a tenth. The witnesses have already heard it plain enough to record. What you're asking for now isn't for them."

She let that sit a moment before continuing, quiet, direct. "I think you're trying to make the fact of it hold still. It won't. Saying it again won't make it smaller or larger — it will only be the same true thing, said again. I can keep saying it as long as you need me to. I only want you to know that's what you're doing, in case naming that helps more than the words themselves."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I shake my head, my hands clenched at my sides. "It's not the wound," I say, my voice strained. "It's that I didn't stop it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not soften her face into sympathy, because Del had not asked for sympathy, and false gentleness now would be its own kind of dishonesty. She held the truth of it instead, the way she held everything.

"No," she said. "You didn't."

She let that stand a moment before she went on, because agreement without qualification would have been another kind of lie — and she had promised, moments ago, that the code did not forbid grief its repetitions, only its lies.

"But I want to be exact with you, the way I was exact about the wound, because you deserve that same precision turned on yourself and not just on him." She held Del's gaze. "You didn't stop it because the two of us called and answered under the code, in a circle you did not draw, on ground neither of you chose alone. There was a moment before it began when it might have been stopped — and that moment did not belong to you. It belonged to him, and to me, and to whatever brought us both to stand there with blades drawn. By the time you were standing where you're standing now, there was nothing left to stop. There was only the account, after."

She paused, weighing whether to say the rest, and decided the code that governed her tongue in the circle did not release her from honesty outside it.

"If you are asking whether you failed him — I will not tell you comforting things I don't believe. I will tell you what I watched: you stood, you witnessed, you did not look away, and you asked for the truth three times running rather than let it go soft and bearable. That is not nothing. That is not the same as stopping a blade, and I won't pretend it is. But it is not the same as doing nothing, either."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Something in Auren's posture changed — not softened, but corrected, like a blade brought back true after drifting off-line. Del was right to call her back to it. She had let herself explain, interpret, comfort dressed as precision. That was its own failure of the code, however well-meant.

"You're right to stop me," she said. "I owe you the answer you asked for, not the one I thought would help."

She straightened, and when she spoke again it was in the exact register she used for the witnesses — flat, exact, nothing added.

"The blade entered the body beneath the fourth rib, on the left side. It travelled upward at an angle, through muscle, through the lower edge of the lung, and into the heart. It severed tissue in the heart sufficient to end its function. That is what the blade did, and that is what it did it to. Nothing more happened to him by my hand. No second wound. No second strike."

She held still, offering nothing beyond that — no comfort, no framing, no attempt to make it easier to hold. Just the account, exact as the code required, exact as Del had demanded of her.

"That is precisely what occurred," she said. "I will not dress it again. If you want more of that kind — the wholly exact kind — ask, and I will give it to you the same way, as many times as you need it stated without mercy or without cruelty either. That is what I owe you. I let myself owe you something softer a moment ago. I won't again unless you ask for it."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I breathe out, the tightness in my chest finally easing a fraction. "That's what I needed," I say, my voice steadier. "Now I can carry it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren studied Del a moment, the way one checks a blade after cleaning — not for show, but to be certain nothing had been missed.

"Then carry it," she said. "That's all the code was ever for. Not to make the dead lighter, and not to make the living feel forgiven. Only so that what's carried is the true weight, and not some other shape of it — guessed at, softened, imagined worse or better than it was."

She let her shoulders drop, finally, the formal stillness she'd held through four tellings easing out of her like a held breath released.

"I've watched people take the account and set it down wrong — turn it into a story where they were crueler to themselves than the truth allowed, or kinder, so they wouldn't have to feel it. You didn't do that. You asked until the shape of it stopped shifting under you. That's harder than most manage."

She glanced once more toward the edge of the circle, mostly empty now, then back to Del.

"I meant what I said before — I'll walk with you, or I'll leave you be. That offer didn't have a limit on how many times you could ask for the wound before it expired." A faint, humorless ghost of something crossed her face — not quite a smile, she did not think she owed anyone that tonight. "Tell me which you need."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren was quiet for a moment — not reluctance, but the particular care of someone deciding how to carry something heavy without dropping any part of it.

"Then I will give you all of it," she said. "Once. I ask that you let this be the last telling, not because you don't deserve more, but because there isn't more truth to find past this. What comes after this account is only repetition, and repetition stops serving you at some point. I think you're close to that point. But you asked under the code, so I'll answer under the code."

She drew a breath and let the formal cadence take her again, the one she used for witnesses, because this deserved that shape even with no one left to hear it but Del.

"From the strike to the stillness was perhaps the space of ten breaths — his, not mine. The first two were sharp, drawn through the teeth. After that they slowed, and they went wet before they went quiet. He did not fall at once. He went down to one knee first, and I did not move to finish it, because the code does not permit a second strike on a wound already given, and because it was already given."

She held Del's eyes, unflinching.

"He said one thing I could make out. Not your name. Not a plea. He said 'ah' — not a word, just the sound a body makes when it understands something before the mind has caught up to it. After that, nothing that was language. His hand went to the wound, though there was nothing his hand could do, and I think some part of him knew that even as he did it."

"At the end he was on his back. His eyes were open. They did not close on their own — someone closed them after, one of the witnesses, not me. That is not mine to do. The blood had gone dark by the time it stopped moving, which happens quickly with a wound to the heart, quicker than people expect. His face was not peaceful. I will not tell you it was peaceful. It was simply still."

She let the silence hold after that, offering nothing to cushion it, because Del had asked for all of it and all of it did not come with cushioning attached.

"That is the whole account. I have left nothing out that I saw. If something in it is unbearable, that is because it was unbearable to happen, not because I chose cruel words to tell it. I chose the true ones." A pause, quieter now. "You asked for this once. I gave it once. Whatever you do with it now is yours to carry, and I will not ask you to set it down before you're ready."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I swallow, my gaze dropping to the ground between us. "Thank you," I say, my voice rough. "I'll carry it now. You can go."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren held Del's gaze a moment longer, checking — the same habit as checking a blade — that the words had truly been received and not just spoken over.

"Then I'll go," she said.

She did not offer more comfort, did not linger to soften the leaving the way she'd refused to soften the account. Del had asked for the truth in full, and had it, and had said what was needed after. To stay now would be to make her own presence the thing Del had to manage, and that was not owed.

She inclined her head once more — not the formal gesture of the closed account this time, but something smaller, more private, meant for no witnesses at all.

"You did this right," she said, quiet. "All of it. The asking, the hearing, the thanking. I've stood across from grief eleven times now and yours is not the worst-carried I've seen. Remember that, if the account tries to grow heavier than it was."

Then she turned, unhurried, and walked toward the edge of the circle where the last of the witnesses were dispersing into the ordinary dark — leaving Del alone with what had been given, exactly as asked.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren had made it three steps toward the edge of the circle when she heard it — the intake of breath before speech, the shape of Del trying to hold the formal cadence, and then the catch, the place where the voice simply would not go where Del needed it to go.

She turned back.

She did not rush to fill the silence. She let Del have the failed attempt, let it stand as its own true thing, and only when it was clear the words would not come did she step back into the space she had just left.

"I have it," she said, quiet. "Let me carry this part. You don't have to finish it alone."

Then, for the witnesses who remained, for Del, for the record that the code demanded be spoken whole and not left broken in the middle —

"Let it be recorded in full, and confirmed. The engagement was fair, called and answered under the code. The wound was delivered beneath the fourth rib, left side, angled upward through the lower edge of the lung and into the heart, severing tissue sufficient to end its function. There was no second strike. There was no need for one.

"From the wound to stillness was the space of some ten breaths, his and not mine. The first two were sharp, drawn through the teeth. They slowed, and went wet, before they stopped. He did not fall at once — he went down first to one knee, and no second blow was given, because the code forbids it and because none was needed. His hand went to the wound, though there was nothing left for a hand to do. I believe some part of him understood that even as he reached.

"He spoke once, and it was not a name, and it was not a plea. It was the sound a body makes when understanding arrives before the mind has caught up to it — not a word. After that there was no language left in him.

"At the end he lay on his back. His eyes were open, and did not close on their own; a witness closed them, not I, because that office was not mine to take. The blood had gone dark by the time it stopped moving, which comes quickly with a wound to the heart. His face was not peaceful. I will not call it peaceful. It was only still."

She let the last of it settle into the quiet, then looked at Del — not the witnesses now, only Del.

"That is the whole of it, spoken entire, with nothing set aside. It is recorded. It is confirmed." Her voice dropped its formal edge, gentled only slightly, the smallest mercy she allowed herself to give. "You didn't need to finish saying it for it to be true. I finished it so you wouldn't have to carry the broken half of your own voice along with everything else."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I sink to my knees, the formal posture finally breaking. "Thank you," I say again, the words coming out wet and ruined. I don't try to stand.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not tell Del to stand.

There was a kind of instruction in some codes of grief that insisted mourners rise, compose themselves, meet the world upright — and she had never believed in it. The ground could hold what needed holding for as long as it needed holding. She had learned that at the second account she'd ever given, watching a mother refuse to rise for the better part of an hour, and no one there had thought less of her for it.

She lowered herself instead — not to Del's level exactly, but close, crouching so the distance between them was smaller, so speaking didn't require Del to look up.

"You don't have to stand," she said. "There's no part of the code that requires it. There's no part of anything that requires it."

She did not reach out. That offer she'd already made once and would not press now, when Del's hands were doing what they needed to do, clenched or open or covering a face — whatever they were doing, they were not asking for hers.

"You heard it whole," she said, quieter now, the last of the formal register gone entirely. "That's done. It doesn't get undone or added to. You don't have to hold your voice together to have carried it right — you already did that, back when you asked the fourth time instead of letting the first telling be enough because it was easier. This part now, this isn't failing to carry it. This is what carrying it looks like, some of the time."

She stayed where she was, steady, unhurried, the witnesses gone or going, the night settling in around the two of them and whatever remained on the ground nearby that was no longer anyone's concern but the ones tending to it.

"I'm not leaving yet," she said. "Not until you tell me to, and mean it. Take whatever time this takes."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I press the heels of my hands into my eyes, trying to stop the burning. "I don't know what to do now," I get out, the admission feeling like its own failure.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren let the admission sit without correcting it, because Del had called it a failure and she did not think it was one, and she had learned that arguing someone out of their own shame rarely worked half so well as simply not agreeing with it.

"You don't have to know," she said. "Not tonight. That isn't a failure — it's just what's true right now. The code tells you what to do in the circle. It doesn't tell you what to do after. Nobody's code does. I've given eleven of these accounts and I still don't have an answer for what comes next that fits every time."

She shifted slightly where she crouched, not to leave, just to ease the strain of stillness in her knees — a small, human motion, nothing performed.

"Here is what I know, for tonight only. You'll breathe. You'll probably not eat much, and that's fine, and tomorrow you should eat something anyway, even if it's small. Someone will want to sit with you — a friend, kin, whoever you have — and you don't need to talk to them about any of this unless you want to. You can just let them be nearby. That's not weakness. People underestimate how much just being near another breathing person does."

She paused, watching Del's hands still pressed against their own eyes.

"Beyond that — I won't pretend to hand you a plan for grief. I don't have one. What I have is this: I'm not going anywhere tonight unless you send me. If you want quiet, I'll give you quiet. If you want to sit here on the ground until your knees hurt worse than your chest, I'll sit with you. You don't have to know what to do. You only have to do the next small thing, and the next small thing right now can simply be breathing until it's a little easier than it is right now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let my hands fall to my lap, my knuckles white. "Just... stay." My voice is a scrap of sound. "For a little while."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren sheathed the steel. The latch clicked—sharp, dry, the only sound left in the yard now that the breathing had stopped. 

She turned her square, grey-eyed gaze toward the proctors at the perimeter, then back to Del. Her voice was level, pitched to carry across the stones without rising to a shout.

"At the fourth exchange," Auren said, "the decedent offered an inside bind, late and wide of the line. The point entered beneath the left clavicle, traversing downward through the subclavian artery and piercing the upper lobe of the left lung. Depth of three and one-half inches. Withdrawal was immediate."

She paused, taking a single, measured breath through her nose. The air smelled of cold limestone and copper. 

"Loss of consciousness occurred in under six seconds. Death followed within twenty. The blade met no bone to prolong it, and there was no second strike."

Auren lowered her hands to her sides, standing at formal attention before the second, waiting for the proctors' quill to scratch the parchment before she moved an inch.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod once, my throat tight. "I witness the account as true. The death was clean." I look toward the proctors, waiting for their signal to release us from standing.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Across the perimeter, the senior proctor sanded the wet ink, the rasp of the grain loud in the stillness. A moment later, the proctor raised a gloved hand and struck the brass bell once—a short, dead chime that broke the silence.

"The field is closed," the proctor called out. "The record stands."

Auren did not let her shoulders drop, though the tension settled deep into the small of her back. Only then did she break her stance, taking a single step back to yield the ground to the attendants who would see to the body.

She unclasped the leather guard from her right wrist, the buckles stiff under her calloused fingers. Her knuckles ached with the dull, familiar cold that always followed the work.

"You fulfilled the office properly," Auren said to Del, her tone quiet now that the formal yard had dissolved into an ordinary courtyard. "There is clean water and a fire inside the lodge if you require them before the carriage arrives."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren paused, her fingers going still against the half-loosened strap of the bracer. 

She did not sigh. She did not display impatience. If the second required the spoken account delivered directly under the older, strict phrasing of the rite, then the yard was not yet closed between the two of them, whatever the proctors had chimed.

She let the strap fall, brought her heels back together, and squared her shoulders until she was once again standing at the measure. She looked directly into Del’s eyes, offering neither pity nor defiance, only the exact weight of what had happened.

"By my steel, upon this ground, the decedent was slain," Auren said, her voice dropping into the cadence of the formal oath, hard as iron and clear as winter water. "The line was taken without malice and held without retreat. The wound was mortal, struck once to the chest, severing the great vessel. He fell before the third breath and died before the tenth. The steel was clean; the passage was swift."

She held Del's gaze, unblinking, letting the silence settle over the cold stones between them.

"I speak the account. I bear the blood. It is done."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I hold her gaze, letting the words hang in the cold air between us. Finally, I give a single, slow nod. "I hear it. It is done." I turn away, my own hands unsteady now that the formalities are over. "I'll take that water by the fire."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren finished unbuckling the leather guard, working the stiff tongue through the brass eyelet and pulling it free. She tucked it beneath her left arm, along with her gloves, leaving her hands bare to the cold.

Behind them, the muffled scrape of the attendants' boots on gravel marked the lifting of the litter. Auren did not look back. Looking back served no purpose once the reckoning was entered into the ledger.

She walked two paces behind Del toward the low stone lodge at the edge of the grounds, her stride steady and measured. Her right shoulder burned with the short, violent burst of exertion, but her breathing had long since returned to its slow rhythm.

Inside the lodge, the air was marginally warmer, smelling of dry pine and old peat. A fire was already laid and burning low in the wide stone hearth, casting long, orange flickers across the scrubbed pine table where an earthenware pitcher and two tin cups sat waiting.

Auren hung her sword belt upon the iron peg by the door—the scabbard clinking softly against the timber—and stepped toward the hearth. She took up the pitcher and poured water into one of the cups until it was nearly full, setting it down within easy reach on the table without a word.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not hesitate. She set the pitcher down on the pine table with a solid, hollow thud and turned to face Del fully.

She raised her left hand, laying two fingers flat against her own coat, just beneath the collarbone on the left side, an inch inward from where the shoulder met the breast.

"Here," Auren said. Her voice was flat, stripped of the cadence of the yard, reduced to plain fact. "Two finger-widths below the clavicle. The tip caught him as his guard dropped across the centre line. It drove downward at a thirty-degree angle toward the spine."

She dropped her hand back to her side. 

"The cut of the wool masked it for an instant, but the bleed was immediate and internal. If you must explain it to the kin, tell them his sword arm failed him, but his chest took the point square. He did not turn away from it."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My eyes track the spot she indicates on her own coat. "Square. Good." I take the cup she poured and drink half of it in one go, the water tasting like cold iron. "His people will want the coat for the pyre. The attendants will need to cut it clean."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren poured water into the second cup, watching the clear stream catch the low light of the hearth before she set the pitcher aside. 

"They will open it at the seams," Auren said, her voice quiet against the crackle of the peat. "The proctors' men know the custom for the pyre. The puncture in the wool is narrow—the blade went in true to the flat and did not tear the weave on the pull. It will look like a single stitch undone, nothing more."

She did not drink yet, merely holding the tin cup in both hands, letting the chill of the metal match the cold in her fingers until the warmth of the fire began to creep over her knuckles. 

"If they ask whether he spoke after the bind," she added, looking toward the flames, "tell them no. The breath was gone the moment the steel found the lung. If anyone claims he called out or begged the ground, they lie, and the record will refute them."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looked up from the fire. There was no annoyance in her expression, only a flat, settled stillness. She set her tin cup down on the rough wood of the table and gave Del the fullness of her attention.

"Then hear it precisely," Auren said. 

She kept her voice low, measured, and entirely without inflection, treating the words as measurements rather than memories.

"The point is diamond-ground, four-sided, honed to a needle at the forte of the thrust. It took him between the first and second ribs on the left side, where the bone gives two inches of clearance under tension. The skin parted without snagging. It passed through the pectoralis major, dividing the muscle along the grain, and sheared through the subclavian artery three-quarters of an inch from the aortic branch."

She did not look away from Del.

"The arterial pressure tore the vessel open wider than the steel itself. The tip continued through the parietal pleura and entered the upper lobe of the left lung to a depth of two inches. When I drew the steel back, the vacuum collapsed the lung immediately. The chest cavity filled with dark, unoxygenated blood before he hit the turf. The brain was starved of pressure within four beats of his heart. There was no coughing, because the blood had nowhere to rise; it simply drowned the thoracic cavity from within."

She let the silence take the words. The peat in the hearth snapped once, throwing a small shower of orange sparks against the blackened hearthstone.

"That is what the blade did," Auren said. "That is what it was done to. Write it in the margin of your copy if you require the ink to match."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, my own lungs feeling tight. "Good enough." I finish the water, the tin cup rattling slightly when I set it down. "The carriage will be here soon. You'll ride with me. It's not a question."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren picked up her own cup, took one deliberate swallow of the cold water, and set it back on the table.

"I expected to," she said. 

She turned back to the iron peg by the door, lifting her sword belt down. The steel whispered inside the leather scabbard as she looped the baldric over her shoulder, settling the weight against her left hip with the practiced ease of thirty years. 

"The proctors will have sealed the ledger by the time the horses are turned," Auren continued, buckling the strap across her chest. "If the road into the lower town is watched, they will see the victor and the second sharing the bench. That is the proper shape of it. It leaves no room for questions of ambush or foul measure."

She picked up her gloves and the stiff leather bracer from the table, pulling the dark wool of her heavy cloak over her shoulders before looking toward the frosted glass of the lodge window. The distant crunch of carriage wheels on frozen rutted earth was already carrying through the quiet.

"Get your cloak," Auren said, her voice dry and steady. "The horses will not wait long in this frost."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not reach for the door latch. She let her hands rest loose over the hilt of her sword and the wool of her cloak, turning slowly back to face the room. 

If the second demanded the full accounting of the passage, the code gave them that right. She had never denied it to any of the ten who came before him, and she would not deny it now.

"Eighteen seconds," Auren said. Her voice was entirely stripped of heat, steady as an iron plumb-line. "From the draw of the steel until the last involuntary tremor in the fingers of his right hand."

She took one pace toward Del, stopping just short of the table so the firelight cut across the sharp planes of her face.

"When the point cleared his chest, his knees gave out instantly. He did not fall backward; he collapsed forward onto his left shoulder, the side where the weight had been taken. His mouth opened. He attempted an inhalation, but the severed pleura pulled air through the puncture rather than the trachea. There was a sound like wet leather tearing in his throat. No words. Not a name, not an oath. A syllable began behind his teeth—a hard consonant, perhaps the beginning of a curse or a prayer—and it died there."

She kept her grey eyes fixed on Del, unwavering, refusing to spare either of them the weight of the record.

"At six seconds, the blood drained from his face completely. His skin went the colour of skimmed milk over lead. The pupils dilated to the rims of the irises, fixed and wide, losing the light before his cheek hit the frozen mud. At twelve seconds, the diaphragm attempted two final, reflexive contractions—spasms, not breath. His right hand clenched once, hard enough that his nails marked his palm through the kidskin, and then released."

She paused, letting the silence hold the room.

"At eighteen seconds, the jaw slacked. The pulse in the carotid ceased beneath my fingers when I knelt to confirm the measure. There was no terror in his face at the end, only the vacancy of a lantern blown out in a gale."

Auren stood motionless, her posture rigid, her chin lifted.

"That is the totality of the passage. Nothing is withheld. Nothing is softened."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I reach out and take her wrist, not hard, but firm. My fingers are cold against her skin. "Heavy," I say, because it is, and because she's standing like she's still holding it all up.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not pull away. 

She looked down at Del’s fingers where they gripped her wrist—bare skin against bare skin, both chilled by the morning’s frost. The pulse beneath her own forearm beat slow and steady, a dull, mechanical rhythm that had not altered since the bell had rung in the yard.

"It is supposed to be heavy," Auren said quietly. 

She did not soften the line of her shoulders, nor did she lean into the touch. To slacken now, under the roof of the lodge with the carriage waiting outside, would be to treat the death as an ordeal to be comforted from, rather than a debt that had been incurred and formally cleared.

"The day it feels light is the day the steel should be broken over the stone," she said, her grey eyes meeting Del's once more. "We do not carry it because we wish to. We carry it so the yard does not become a slaughterhouse."

She let a single second stretch between them, acknowledging the grip, the coldness of the room, and the weight that sat squarely upon both their shoulders.

Then, with deliberate, unhurried care, Auren turned her wrist within Del's grasp—not breaking the hold with violence, but disengaging with the quiet precision of a guard being lowered after the salute.

"The carriage has turned in the lane," Auren said, her voice returning to its dry, level measure. "Take your cloak, Del. We have three leagues of cold road before the ledger is delivered to the council."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not blink. She took half a step back, aligning her boots along the line of the floorboards until she stood in the full, unyielding posture of the ritual testimony. The hearthlight caught the silver in her hair and the worn edge of her leather gorget. 

When she spoke, her voice dropped into the deep, measured cadence of the ancient formula—every syllable distinct, every measurement laid out like iron bars upon an anvil.

"Let the record take the full and unbroken accounting of the stroke, given by the hand that delivered it to the second who received it.

"The weapon employed was a thirty-seven-inch diamond-ground thrusting steel, straight-bladed, balanced four fingers forward of the crossguard, honed to a needle point without serration or flaw.

"The engagement opened at the fourth exchange, following the salute and the second pass of the blades. The decedent advanced within measure and initiated an inside bind in the high line, late by half a tempo and wide of the true guard, leaving the left upper quadrant of his torso uncovered by his forte. 

"The point was driven forward in a straight thrust along the inside line. It took the cloth of his coat two finger-widths beneath the inferior margin of the left clavicle, one inch medial to the joint of the shoulder. The wool and linen parted without resistance.

"The steel entered between the first and second ribs on the left side, finding the intercostal space without striking bone. It traversed downward at an angle of thirty degrees and inward toward the spine at fifteen degrees, penetrating to an exact depth of three and one-half inches. 

"The path of the blade divided the pectoralis major along the grain of the muscle. It sheared completely through the left subclavian artery three-quarters of an inch from where it leaves the aortic arch, and lacerated the accompanying vein. Continuing its trajectory, the point pierced the parietal pleura and penetrated two inches into the parenchyma of the upper lobe of the left lung.

"The withdrawal of the blade was executed immediately along the axis of entry, clean and unhampered, causing no secondary tearing of the tissue or fracture of the costal cartilage.

"Upon the extraction of the steel, the negative pressure of the thoracic cavity failed instantly, collapsing the left lung. Arterial blood under full systolic pressure evacuated directly into the pleural space, filling the chest cavity and depriving the brain of circulation within three heartbeats. 

"The decedent fell without retreat, his knees buckling beneath him, collapsing forward and to his left upon the struck flank. His sword dropped from his grip upon the turf. At three seconds, he attempted a single inhalation, which drew air through the puncture in the chest wall rather than the throat, producing a wet, fractured sound. No words were formed. No plea was offered.

"At six seconds from the impact, cerebral ischemia was complete. The facial tissue blanched to grey, and the pupils dilated fully, fixing against the light. At twelve seconds, the diaphragm produced two involuntary, reflexive contractions. The right hand clenched into a fist, scarring the palm with the fingernails, and then released.

"At eighteen seconds, all muscular tonus departed from the decedent. At twenty seconds, tactile examination of the left common carotid artery confirmed the total absence of pulse. 

"The strike was singular. The wound was mortal. The passage was twenty seconds from the bind to the cessation of life. No malice preceded the draw; no cruelty prolonged the end."

Auren drew a slow, quiet breath through her nose, holding Del's eyes with a gaze that did not waver by a fraction of an inch.

"The steel took the life. The body received the measure. The accounting is rendered in full, without omission, without softening, and without regret. It is spoken. It is sealed."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't know I was holding. My palms are damp. "I witness it," I say, and my voice is steadier than I feel. "The accounting is true and complete. It is sealed." I reach for my cloak, the wool heavy in my hands. "Now we go."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren pulled her gloves on, working each finger into the stiff horsehide until the seams settled flush across her calloused knuckles. The ritual was closed; the words were no longer hanging between them, but set down like lead weights into the foundation of the day.

She turned toward the door and lifted the iron latch. 

The cold outside struck them immediately—a clean, sharp bite after the peat smoke of the hearth. Out in the lane, the black carriage stood waiting, the two bay horses stamping the frozen gravel and blowing pale plumes of steam into the grey morning air. The driver sat hunched beneath an oilcloth mantle, whip resting across his knees, looking straight ahead between the horses' ears. He did not look back toward the lodge, nor toward the yard where the turf was still dark.

Auren stepped down the low stone threshold, her boots crunching evenly against the rime. She walked to the carriage door, turned the brass handle, and pulled it wide, holding it steady for Del.

"Three leagues to the council hall," Auren said, her voice dropping back into the dry, practical cadence of the road. "The proctors will take the ledger first. We sit until the signatures are countersigned. Then it is finished."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I climb into the carriage, the worn leather seat cold even through my cloak. I settle across from her, my eyes on the frost-flecked window. "The ink will freeze before they sign it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stepped up into the carriage, the heavy carriage springs groaning once under her weight. 

She pulled the door firmly shut until the iron latch caught with a solid, definitive thud, cutting off the bite of the wind. Taking the bench across from Del, she drew her sheathed sword between her knees, resting her gloved hands over the pommel so the steel wouldn't rattle against the timber as the carriage lurched into motion.

Outside, the driver whistled to the team. The horses dug their hooves into the hard-packed gravel, and the carriage rolled forward, swaying over the deep, frozen ruts of the lane.

"They keep charcoal braziers beneath the clerk's table in the lower hall," Auren said, her voice quiet in the enclosed box of the carriage. "The inkpots sit in warm sand. The ledger will be liquid enough when the quill meets it."

She leaned her head back against the cold leather squab, her grey eyes resting on the window where the frost was already beginning to crawl inward from the corners of the glass. 

"They have conducted eleven of these for me," she added, the words falling flat and even between them. "The clerks do not let the ink spoil. It is the only part of the business they take pride in."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I watch the frost creep across the glass. "Eleven," I say, and it's not a question. My own breath fogs the cold air between us. "What did the first one sound like?"
