dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway let the silence sit a moment, because the boy had said something useful and she wanted him to hear himself say it.

"Good," she said. "Wrong how. Narrow it."

She shifted the lamp a few degrees left, which threw the shadows across the thing differently, and that was half of looking at anything in a cellar — you moved the light, not yourself. The shape at the far end was slumped against the brick where the water met it, and it had too much length below the waterline and not enough above.

"Start with what you'd expect," she said. "Man-shaped thing, dead in four feet of water, you expect it floating or you expect it sunk. That's not doing either. It's leaning. Which means it's caught on something, or it's heavier at one end than a body's got any business being, or there's more of it under there than you can see." She wiped the damp off her upper lip with the back of her wrist. "Any of those three, you want to know which before you put your hands in the water."

The lamp guttered and she steadied it.

"Second thing. Count the joints." She nodded at the arm — she assumed it was an arm — hanging out over the surface with the fingers just breaking it, making no ripples at all. "From shoulder to wrist you should get two bends. Elbow, and nothing else. Have a proper look and tell me how many you get."

She waited. She'd learned the waiting the hard way, from a man named Ashworth who'd gone in fast on something in a flooded mill in the eighties and come back out in a bag that didn't need to be full-sized.

"And a note on it having stopped moving," she added, conversational. "That's not the same as it having stopped. Things stop moving for lots of reasons. Dead's only the one we like."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I leaned closer, squinting at the shadowy limb. "Three," I said, voice low. "Shoulder, elbow, and... another bend halfway down the forearm. Like an extra joint." My stomach tightened. "That's not right for anything living."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not say *good* this time, because it wasn't, quite.

"Three's right. Your conclusion's lazy." She said it without heat, the way you'd correct a grip on a knife. "Plenty of living things have three bends in a forelimb. Birds do. So does a man who's had his radius snapped clean and left an hour to go stiff — that gives you a false joint that'll fool anyone at ten feet in bad light. I've hooked out two drowned poachers that bent in places God never drew, and both of them were only unlucky."

She moved the lamp again, slow, watching the way the shadow crawled along the underside of the limb.

"So. How you tell. A break tents the skin. There's a lump where the ends of the bone want out, and the bend only goes the one way, and it goes *loose* — you push it and the whole forearm swings like a bag of spanners. A joint's tidy. Joint's got a crease on the inside and a knuckle on the outside and it bends where it's meant to and stops where it's meant to." She tipped her chin at it. "Look at the outside of that halfway bend and tell me if there's a knuckle or a lump. That's the whole question. You don't need to go nearer to answer it, you need me to hold the lamp lower, which I'm doing."

She lowered it. The light came off the black water and went up under the thing, which was the angle nobody ever thought to use and which showed you more than the top view ever did.

"And while you're looking. The hand." Her voice stayed level. "Fingers are in the water up to the second knuckle and there's not a ripple off them. Nothing. Four feet of standing water in a cellar has a drift to it — there's always a drift, there's always a seep coming in somewhere — and anything sitting in it should be nodding, just slightly. Just enough to see." She let that land. "That one's not nodding. So either the water's deader than I've ever known water to be, or it's holding itself still."

The lamp hissed. Somewhere behind them the stairs dripped.

"Which brings us to the pole," she said. "It's leaning against the brick at the far end and it's got a hook on it, and you're going to fetch it and *not* put it in the water yet. I want it in your hands before we know the answer about that elbow, not after."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept her eyes on the water and not on him, because the honest answer was one she'd rather deliver sideways.

"Don't know yet," she said. "And I want you to hear that I don't know, because the day I start guessing at that question is the day you should find someone else to follow down a stair."

She set her weight back on her heels. The water lapped an inch up the third step below her boot and went still again, and she filed that away — *drift, small, coming from the left*.

"Here's how it goes, though. Three things get you there and none of them need a closer look than we've got." She held up the lamp a fraction. "One. Proportion. A man's a man all the way down, head to hip to knee, and the numbers don't shift. Head goes into the body seven times, near enough, and the elbow sits level with the bottom rib, and the wrist sits level with the hip joint. You can check that on a corpse in the dark from fifteen feet, and if the numbers are wrong they're wrong for good, because nothing that walked upright for thirty years suddenly grows a short femur. Two. Hair. Not the colour, the *pattern* — where it stops. Men are bald in particular places and furred in particular places and the borders are the same on every one of them. A thing wearing a man's shape gets the shape right long before it gets the borders right. I've never once seen one get the borders right."

She wiped her wrist across her mouth again.

"Three's the one you won't like. Teeth. Nobody builds a good mouth. They build a good *face* — that's easy, it's a mask, it's flat — and then they open it and you get four rows or none or something out of a millstone. If it opens its mouth you'll have your answer inside a half-second and you won't need me to tell you." She glanced at him then, brief. "If it opens its mouth, don't stand there confirming it. That's the half-second you're spending on the stairs."

The thing at the far end had not moved. The extra bend in the forearm sat in the lamplight, patient as furniture.

"Now. Recently." She let out a breath through her nose. "There's a version of this where a man came down here a week ago for a jar of something and drowned and swelled and hooked his coat on a nail, and we're two fools whispering on a stair about a dead grocer. That happens. That's happened to me twice and I'd take it a third time gladly." A pause. "There's another version where something wore him in here and then stopped needing to, and what's leaning on that brick is the bit it didn't take with it. In which case the interesting question isn't what's in the water. It's what's in the cellar with us that isn't."

She nodded at the far wall without taking the lamp off the body.

"Pole. Now, please. Left hand on the shaft, right hand under the hook, and if you have to cross the water you go along the wall and you go slow — the drift's coming from the left, and I want to know if that changes while you're moving. Anything changes about that water, you say the word and you don't wait for me to ask twice."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow and start moving along the wall, my boots making soft, sucking sounds in the silt. The water feels colder away from the steps. "I see the pole," I say, voice steadier than I feel. My eyes stay on the water's surface, watching for any shift in that lazy drift. "It's leaning right where you said."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway turned her body but not the lamp, keeping the light on the leaning thing and letting Pike walk in the edge of it. That was the discipline of it. You lit the problem, not the boy, and you kept your night eye on everything the lamp wasn't touching.

"Good. Talk while you go — I don't care what about. If you stop talking I'll assume you've a reason, and I'll come, and I'd rather not."

She watched the water ahead of him instead of him. That was the trick nobody taught you: a man wading makes his own wave, and his wave will tell you about anything between him and the wall long before his shins do. Pike's spread out from his knees in a slow V, went eight feet, ten, and broke against the brick with a sound like a tongue against teeth.

Then she saw it, and her voice came out flat and unhurried, which was the voice she used when things had become interesting.

"Stop where you are. Don't turn round. Weight on the back foot."

The V had gone out from him and hit the wall and come back — and where it should have crossed the far corner, where the leaning thing sat, it hadn't. It had run up to a line about a yard short of it and flattened out, the way water flattens when it goes over something submerged and broad.

"There's a shelf under it," she said. "Or something the size of one. Your ripple's dying a yard out from the body and water doesn't die for nothing. That answers our first question, and it's the boring answer, which I'll take — it's leaning because it's *sat on* something. Not floating, not sunk. Perched." A beat. "It also means the four feet you're standing in isn't four feet the whole way along, and you'd have found that out with your face."

The drip from the stairs went on behind her. She listened past it, for a second, and didn't like what she heard, which was nothing.

"Now the drift." She lowered the lamp until the light skated flat across the surface, which was how you read water the way you'd read a page. "It was coming from your left when we started. It isn't now. It's gone slack. Water doesn't stop seeping in, Pike — a cellar that's taking on water takes it on all night, it doesn't get bored. So either the seep's been blocked, which takes a hand, or the level's found something new to go into." She wiped her wrist across her mouth. "Which are both hands, when you think about it."

Her boots stayed on the step. Not fear — arithmetic. One of them wanted to be out of the water and it was going to be the one holding the light.

"Pole. Two more steps, hook it up along the wall so you're not swinging it over open water, and bring it back the way you came, in your own footprints. Not new ones." She let the lamp settle. "And Pike. When you pass the corner with the coal chute — don't look up it. Look at me and tell me what the light does on your face."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took the hook in both hands, set the point under the jaw hinge where the bone would take it, and turned the thing a quarter revolution toward the light. It came round without argument. It came round *slowly*, the way a thing comes round when it weighs more than it looks.

"Plainly," she agreed. "Hold that steady and don't move it off my hands, whatever I say next."

She worked the hook down to the forearm and lifted it clear of the water, and the limb swung from the halfway bend like a sock with a spanner in it.

"Break, not a joint. There's your first answer and it's the dull one. Tented skin, lump on the outside, bends both ways, no crease. Somebody snapped his radius and his ulna both and did it after he stopped caring, because there's no bruising worth the name around it." She let the arm back down. "You break a man's arm to get him through a space narrower than a man. There's a coal chute nine feet behind you and it's fourteen inches across. He didn't come down your stairs. He came down that, folded."

She moved the hook to the shoulder and rolled him further, and the back came up out of the black water, and she held him there.

"Second answer. That's a slot. Eleven inches, following the line of the spine, edges turned in rather than out, no tearing at the ends. Nothing with teeth does that. Something with an intention does that." She leaned, and her voice stayed exactly as it had been. "And he's empty. Ribs are hinged out and everything a man keeps under them is gone, and the cavity's been rinsed — no clotting, no residue, clean as a scoured pot. Then filled. Silt to the collarbones and half a brick under the liver-side to trim him level."

She lowered him back onto whatever he was sitting on. He settled with the small final sound of something finding its place again.

"That's why he doesn't nod. He's ballasted. He's been weighted and perched and set square on a shelf a yard off the wall, and his mouth's packed to the back teeth so he doesn't take on water and shift." She wiped her wrist across her mouth. "Hair borders are right. Teeth are his own, all thirty-one of them, and one gold. He was a man. He was a man about five days ago and he was a man when he was alive, which is more than I can usually promise you."

She straightened and took the lamp back off him, gently, because his hand had gone unsteady and there was no sense pretending it hadn't.

"So. Plainly." She turned the light out toward the flat, slack, unmoving water. "This isn't a body. It's a jar. Somebody hollowed a man and filled him and stood him in the cold where he'd keep, and things that put food by come back for it."

The drip on the stairs had stopped too.

"Up," she said. "My footprints. Don't run — running's how you find the shelf with your face."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: My throat tight, but I move, following her prints. "They're coming back." It's not a question. The coal chute feels like a mouth at my back.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway went up two steps and stopped, which was worse than if she'd kept going, and she knew it, and she did it anyway because a wrong door at speed was how you ended up in a bag.

"They're already back," she said. "Somewhere in the last four minutes the seep stopped and the stair stopped dripping, and neither of those things happens on its own. Water's got no opinions. So something's stood in the inflow, or sat on it, and it's been there long enough for the drip to run dry above us."

She held the lamp out at arm's length to her left and away from them both, which threw her own shadow huge and wrong across the brick, and watched the far corner for anything that moved against it. Nothing did. That was information too, and she hated the shape of it.

"Don't look at the chute. I know it's there. I know what it feels like." She kept her voice down at the level of a woman discussing a fence line. "Fourteen inches is a way in for something that folds, and a folded thing comes out slow — you'd hear it, you'd have a count of three at least. That's not what's got my attention. What's got my attention is the door at the top of that stair, which we came through, which was on a latch, and which I can't hear moving in the draught any more." A pause. "Because there isn't a draught any more."

She wiped her wrist across her mouth and found it was shaking slightly and thought, *well. Fifty.*

"So here's where we are, plainly, and then we go. Something put its larder down here and something has shut us in with it, and those may be the same thing and may not, and I've no intention of learning which by asking." She shifted the hook into her right hand, point down, held low the way you held a thing you meant to use on a floor and not in the air. "You're going to go up ahead of me. Lamp in your left hand, held out from your body — out, Pike, a foot clear, because anything that comes at a light comes at the light and not the arm. When you reach the top you don't try the latch. You put your shoulder in the middle of the plank, below the lock, and you keep putting it there until it stops being a door."

She stepped aside on the stair to let him past, and turned herself to face the water, and the chute, and the patient hollowed man perched on his shelf with a brick where his liver had been.

"If it gets between us," she said, conversationally, "you keep going up. You don't come back down for me. I've been doing this thirty years on the understanding that nobody comes back down, and I'd take it very personally if you spoiled the record."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway got her shoulder into the small of his back and moved him up a step, and talked while she did it, because she was not going to be the woman who died standing still for the sake of a lecture.

"You'll have it. Walk while you take it in, and if you have to choose between the detail and the door, you choose the door and I'll write the rest down for you after."

Another step. The lamp swung and the brick slid past.

"Order of operations, as near as I can read it. He was alive when it broke his arms — both, not just the one you saw, the left's gone at the humerus and it's healed nothing, so he had hours at most. He was not alive when it put the slot in him. No bruising round the edges, no bleeding into the muscle; you get a rim of dark an inch wide when a heart's still shifting things about, and there's none. So: taken somewhere else, killed somewhere else, folded and posted down that chute cold." She breathed. "Which means the chute isn't where it lives. That's the delivery entrance. You want to be very clear on the difference."

Step. Step. The water behind them said nothing at all.

"What it took. Heart, lungs, liver, both kidneys, the gut entire, and the fat off the inside of the belly wall — scraped, not torn, and that's the bit that turns my stomach, because scraping is *care*. Left the diaphragm. Left the bladder. Left the spine and the ribs, which is how he holds his shape; it wanted the shape kept. Went in through the back rather than the front because the front's where the bones give and the back's where they hinge, and it wanted to shut him again afterward."

She put her hand flat on his shoulder blade and pushed, not unkindly.

"What's under the skin now. Silt to the collarbones, packed in wet and settled — he's been filled more than once, because there's a tide mark inside him where the first fill dried. Half a brick under the right side, trimmed level. A quantity of gravel in the pelvis, which I'd guess is to keep him from tipping forward when the level drops. And his mouth's packed the same and plugged with a rag of his own shirt, so he doesn't drink and float. Five days, at the temperature down here. Call it four to seven."

Two steps from the top now. She could smell the wood of the door.

"So. What you look for if you meet another." Her voice went flat and fast, the way she'd say a list she never wanted to say twice. "You look for a *larder*, not a kill. Rinsed cavity. Ballast. Something set square and level in cold still water where it'll keep. Entry hole narrower than the man who went through it. And a broad shelf under the water a yard off the wall, because they like their stores off the floor, same as anyone. If you find those five things together you are not looking at a hunting ground. You are looking at somebody's pantry, and the thing that keeps it is tidy, and patient, and it counts."

She stopped him with a hand and put her mouth near his ear.

"Shoulder. Below the lock. Now — and Pike, when it opens, you go *through*, not out. Whatever's on the other side."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I shoulder the door once, hard. The wood groans but doesn't give. I brace myself for another try, my breath fogging in the cold. "Why a larder?" I ask, the question out before I can think better of it.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway put her palm flat on the plank above his shoulder and felt it while he braced, and what she felt she did not care for.

"It gave and came back," she said. "That's not a latch. A latch holds hard and then it doesn't hold at all. That's *weight*. There's something set against the other side of this door, and it's the kind of weight that settles." She took her hand off the wood and wiped the damp on her coat. "Hit it again anyway. I'd like to know if it settles further."

She turned her back to the door and put herself between it and the stair, hook low, and answered him, because he'd asked and because a lad who could still ask a question in a stairwell was worth keeping.

"Why a larder. Because a thing that stores food is a thing that's planning to be somewhere else." She kept her eyes on the black water below and the pale perched shape in it. "Nothing puts food by for tonight. You put food by because you'll be busy, or because you'll be sleeping, or because there's a mouth coming that can't feed itself yet. Those are the three reasons in the whole of nature and I've never found a fourth."

Her breath went out white. She noticed that and filed it, and didn't like where the file was going.

"Busy means it hunts in a season and this is the wrong end of it. Sleeping means we're standing in a bedroom, which would be a mercy, and I'd have expected more dust. Which leaves the third." She let that sit exactly as long as it needed to. "A hollowed man with his mouth plugged and his belly packed is not a meal. It's *keeping*. And you keep things for something that can't chew."

The cold came up the stair after them like it had been let off a chain. Her fingers were going stupid on the hook and she shifted her grip before they could.

"Note the temperature, and put it in your book later, because it's the useful part. It's colder now than when we came down and cellars don't do that. Something's pulling the heat out of this hole to keep its stores sweet, and it's pulling harder since we started talking, which means it's minding us." She rolled her shoulder. "Flattering, in a way. Thirty years and I've rarely been *inventory*."

She shifted a half-step sideways so he had room for a proper run at it.

"Hinge side, not the middle. Weight against the plank won't stop the pins. Put your heel through it low and left, twice, and if it holds after that I'm going to do something unpleasant with this hook and you're going to be very glad you were facing the other way."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway got the point of the hook into the gap her heel had opened and worked it sideways until she could see, and then she stopped working it, because you didn't widen a hole before you knew what was standing in it.

"Right. Lamp lower and hold it *off* to the side — I want light across this, not down it. Shadow's what tells you depth." She waited until he had it. "Good. Now you're going to hear me say a thing and you're not going to move the lamp when I say it. There's a second one."

She put the hook in and turned it.

"It's face-down against the plank with its feet toward the stair, which is why the door gave and came back — that's a man's weight going slack and then finding its level again. No ballast in this one that I can feel. It's not been packed. Nothing's been put in it." She leaned, and her voice took on the flat evenness of a woman reading a ledger aloud. "Slot's started. Four inches of it, top of the spine, and it stops. Edges turned in, same hand, same tool, same intention — and then it *stops*, Pike, clean, mid-cut. Ribs aren't hinged. Cavity's shut. It's all still in there."

She drew the hook back and looked at what had come up on the point of it and did not wipe it off, because that told her things too.

"Smell. Take a proper breath, you'll want to know this one for later." The cold came off the gap in a slow sheet. "There's no rot. None. Five days on the one downstairs and nothing off him either, which I put down to the cold, but this is different cold — this is *dry* cold off wet stone, which isn't a thing that happens. Under it there's iron, which is blood and blood only, that's honest. And under *that* there's a sharpness, like a nest of ants crushed in the hand. Vinegar and pins. That's not the man. Men don't smell of that living or dead. That's the thing that made the cut, and it's the only part of it we've had a sense of all night, so mark it and remember it, because the day you smell vinegar and pins in a cold cellar you turn round and walk out."

She sat back on her heels on the step and let the hook rest.

"How far it got. Hours, not days — skin's still got give, the jaw's not set, and there's colour in the fingers where they're bent under him. He was warm this evening." She wiped her wrist across her mouth. "Which is the whole of it, and here's the part I want you to have. It was working. It had a man on the floor with a four-inch start on him and a jar already put by on the shelf, and it put the tool down partway through and went away. Nothing tidy stops partway. Tidy things finish."

The lamp hissed. She looked up at the gap in the plank and the dark on the other side of it.

"So it heard us on the stair, and it left its work, and it laid him against the door." She said it without any particular weight at all. "Not to shut us in. To know when we came out. That's a bell, Pike. We've been leaning on a bell for ten minutes."

She stood, and her knees said what they thought of that, and she ignored them.

"Now. It's four inches into him and it'll want to come back and finish, because it counts and it scrapes and it trims things level, and things like that cannot abide a job half done. That's the flaw in it and it's the only one we've found. So we do not go up through that gap." She nodded down the stair, into the standing water and the patient perched shape in it. "We go down, and we stand either side of the shelf, and we wait for the tidy thing to come home to its pantry. And when it does I want that lamp exactly where it is now — out, and off to the side, a foot clear of your arm."

She took the hook in both hands.

"Mind the shelf. I'd hate for you to find it with your face after all that education."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I don't look away from the water, from the jar-man on his shelf. "What if it doesn't come back through the water?" My voice is too quiet. "What if it's already up there, waiting for us to come out?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not answer straight off, and that was the honest compliment: she stopped and did the arithmetic again from the top, because the boy had found the hole in her plan before she'd finished laying it.

"Then we're two fools standing in a flooded cellar waiting for a thing that's upstairs eating its supper," she said. "Yes. That's the version where I've got it wrong, and it's not unlikely, and I'd rather you said it now than in twenty minutes when my legs have gone."

She came back up the two steps and put her ear to the gap in the plank, not close enough to lose it, and held there a long moment with her eyes shut, which was the only way to listen properly.

"So we test it. Never guess what you can make a thing tell you." She kept her voice down under the hiss of the lamp. "There's a dead man laid across that door and he's a bell. Bells work both ways, Pike. It laid him there to hear us push — which means it's somewhere it can *hear*, and a cellar door in a stone floor doesn't carry far. Call it two rooms. Call it the kitchen and the passage, and no further, or it'd not have bothered with the trick."

She set the flat of her hand on the plank, low, where the wood was thickest.

"I'm going to push. Once, slow, and let it settle back. That's not a man breaking out, that's a weight shifting — a rat, a draught, a house going cold. If it's up there minding us it'll come and check, because tidy things check, and I'll hear boards over my head inside a count of twenty. And if I hear boards, we've learned it's above us and we've learned we've got a wall and a door between us and it, and I'll take that trade every night of the week."

She wiped her wrist across her mouth and looked down the stair at the standing water, flat as a plate, and the pale ballasted shape perched off the wall with its mouth packed.

"Because here's what you've not said yet and ought to." Her tone stayed absolutely level. "If it's above, it hasn't got to come through that door at all. It's got a fourteen-inch chute into this hole that it's already used once tonight, and it knows exactly where we are, and it can post something down it folded and never put a foot on the stair." She nodded at the corner. "Which is why the lamp goes out from your body, and why I've got the hook, and why neither of us is going to stand under that chute for the rest of our natural lives."

She leaned her weight on the plank, gently, and let the dead man on the other side find his level again, and the sound he made was very small.

"Twenty," she said. "Count it out loud so I've something to listen past. And Pike — if we hear boards, you'll want to be pleased, because that's the good outcome, and you'll find it doesn't feel like one. Nothing about this work ever does."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway sat down on the step below him with a grunt she didn't bother to disgu, laid the hook across her knees, and put her hand out for the lamp — then thought better of it and left him holding it, because a man with a job in his hands sits steadier.

"Finish it. All right. But you'll get it in the order I found it in, not the order it makes sense in, because that's the only honest way to give you anything." She rolled her left shoulder and something in it declined to cooperate. "And you'll stop me if I go too fast. This is the part nobody writes down, and it's the part that would have saved Ashworth, so you get it whether it sits well or not."

She turned the lamp's beam with two fingers on Pike's wrist, gently, until it fell on the thing spread out at the bottom of the stair in nine inches of water. It had stopped being frightening about twenty minutes ago and become furniture, the way they always did, and that was its own small obscenity.

"First. You were right and I was wrong, and I want that said out loud while we're both alive to hear it. It didn't come home through the water. It came down the chute, folded, exactly as you said it might, and if I'd had my way we'd have been stood either side of that shelf with our backs to it like a pair of chapel candles." She wiped her wrist across her mouth. "The only reason we're sitting here is a rule I made in eighty-nine about never standing under a hole, and rules are cleverer than the people who keep them. Write that down too."

She leaned forward and put the point of the hook under the nearest limb and lifted it out of the water, and it came up dripping and articulated and far longer than the body had any business paying for.

"Now. Length. Seven feet and a bit if you laid it out, which you can't, because it doesn't lie out — it lies *down*, in three sections, like a folding rule. Four limbs. Count the bends." She held the limb steady in the light. "Shoulder. Elbow. And one halfway down the forearm, a foot from the wrist, tidy as you like — crease on the inside, knuckle on the outside, bends the one way and stops where it's meant to. That's a joint. That's a real joint, and it's in exactly the place somebody snapped that man's radius." She let it back into the water. "It didn't break him there to fool us. It broke him there because that's where *it* bends. It folded him the way it folds itself, out of habit, the way you'd pack a bag you've packed a thousand times. That's worth more to you than anything else I'll say tonight. They don't make mistakes to deceive you. They make mistakes because they're doing what they always do, and what they always do is the shape of them."

She shifted along the step and got the hook under the front of it, and turned it, and it rolled with the slow reluctance of a thing that had been heavy in life and was heavier now.

"Head. No teeth. Not one, not a stub, not a plate. There's a rasp instead — set in a ring, like the inside of a snail's mouth but the size of my palm, and it runs on a track so it can be put out three or four inches and drawn back. That's your scraper. That's what took the fat off the inside of his belly wall and left the tool-marks I called *care*." She sat back. "I'll correct myself there as well. It wasn't care. It was a rasp doing the only thing a rasp does. I read intention into it because I'm fifty and I like a story, and you should trust me less when I sound certain about *why*."

The lamp hissed. Behind them, high up, the house said nothing at all, which she had stopped finding restful some hours ago.

"The cut. It's not a tool and it's not the mouth. Inside of the forearm, below that third joint, there's a keel of — call it horn, it isn't, but call it horn — an edge about eleven inches long, set flat against the bone, and it hinges out when the limb closes. Self-stropping. There's a pad of grit behind it that hones the thing every time it folds." She almost laughed, and it came out wrong. "Eleven inches. Which is the length of the slot in the man downstairs, to the quarter of an inch, because it can't make a longer cut than its own arm and it never makes a shorter one, because why would you stop short. That's how you'll know another one's work at ten paces in bad light. Not the wound. The *measurement*. Things like this are honest about their dimensions in a way people never are."

She reached down with her bare hand this time, and turned the forearm over, and brought her fingers up to her nose, and then held them out for him to smell without being asked.

"Vinegar and pins. There's a sac behind the keel and it weeps onto the edge as it comes out. I'd guess it's what rinsed the cavity and it's why there's no rot in five days and nothing gone off and nothing crawling. It's a *preserve*, Pike. The whole of it's a pickling operation. That's not a metaphor and I wish it were."

She wiped her hand on her coat, slowly, the way you do when you've decided you'll never get it properly clean and the gesture is for form's sake.

"Cold. That's the vents." She tipped the hook at the thing's flank, at a run of pale slits under the arm that the water kept trying to close. "Eleven either side, and they were open the whole time it was on me. It sheds heat the way a horse sweats — pours it out, dumps it into the stone and the water, and it can't turn it off any more than you can decide not to shiver. So the cellar got colder the longer it was minding us, and I read that as a thing keeping its larder sweet, and I was wrong again. It was just *close*. It was close for ten minutes before it came down and the temperature told me so and I filed it under something clever instead of under *it's in the room above your head*." She looked at the lamp rather than at him. "Two mistakes in one night and both of them the same mistake. I made it complicated. It was never complicated. It was a cold thing in a cold hole, near enough to hear us."

She put the hook down across her knees again and sat for a moment with her hands on it, and when she went on her voice had gone flatter than it had been all night, which for her was the tell.

"Now the last of it, and then you can have the bad news, which isn't the same thing."

She used the hook to open the belly, one steady draw, no ceremony.

"There's a pouch. Runs from the sternum down, muscular, with a purse-mouth at the bottom that shuts like a drawstring. It's empty." She held the two edges apart so the light went in. "And look at it properly. It's stretched. The wall's thin and slack and there's stria — silver lines, like a woman's belly after a child — which means it carried something, and it carried it long enough to grow, and then it let it out. And here." She moved the hook an inch. "Glands, four of them, in the pouch wall. Collapsed. Wrung out. Something drank those dry and it didn't do it this week."

She let the edges fall shut.

"So. Three reasons a thing puts food by. Busy, sleeping, or a mouth coming that can't feed itself." She wiped her wrist across her mouth. "It wasn't busy and it wasn't sleeping. And the mouth isn't coming. The mouth's been and gone."

She reached back and took hold of the stair rail and pulled herself round to face down into the cellar, at the flat black water and the pale ballasted man perched square on his shelf a yard off the wall, his belly packed to the collarbones, his mouth plugged with a rag of his own shirt.

"Which tells you what he's actually for, and I had that wrong too, though only by a little. He isn't a store. Nobody stores a man with his mouth corked and his gut swapped out for river silt — that's not keeping, that's *brewing*. Silt and a warm body and eleven inches of something that smells of vinegar, shut up in the cold where it won't spoil. You get liquor. You get a thin sour liquor that a thing with no teeth and no rasp and no jaw to speak of can take without chewing a mouthful." She nodded at the corpse. "And there's a tide mark inside him a hand's breadth down, dried, which means he's been filled twice. Which means he's been *drawn off* once."

She was quiet for a second. The lamp hissed and the water said nothing and the house above them went on being silent in the particular way that houses do when the thing that used to

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at the jar-man. "He's a bottle. And the pup already drank him once." The cold feels like it's inside my ribs now. "How long until it gets thirsty again?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not answer at once. She put two fingers against the stone of the step beside her thigh and held them there, and counted her own pulse against it, which was an old trick and a crude one and the only thermometer she had.

"Ask me the arithmetic and I'll give you the arithmetic," she said. "Then I'll give you the part I don't know, and you'll notice the second part's bigger."

She tipped the lamp with one finger on his wrist until the light lay flat across the water and ran up the perched man's flank.

"Tide mark's a hand's breadth down and it's *dried*. Not damp, not tacky — dried and gone pale, with a crust on it you could flake off with a nail. In this air, at this temperature, that takes days. Call it three at the short end and a week at the long, and I'd say nearer the long, because nothing dries quickly down here." She let the light travel. "He's been topped up since. Silt's wet to the collarbones and it's settled level, which means it was packed in and given time to find itself. So: drawn off once, roughly a week ago. Refilled after. And stood back on his shelf square and trimmed and corked to steep."

She wiped her wrist across her mouth.

"Which gives you your interval, and it's about a week, and now here's what I actually think and you can weigh it as you like." She nodded down at the split thing lying in nine inches of water at the foot of the stair. "That one was *four inches into a second bottle* tonight. Warm this evening. It had one steeping on the shelf and it had gone out and fetched a fresh man and got him folded down the chute and started on him, and it wouldn't have done that for the fun of it. Nothing tidy makes work it doesn't need. It was laying in a second because the first was running short." She sat back against the stair wall. "So not a week. It thought days. It thought soon enough to be out hunting on a cold night with a job already half-brewed in the cellar."

The lamp hissed. She held her fingers against the stone again and didn't like the reading.

"Now the part I don't know, and it's this: I've no idea what the thing's got for a stomach or how big it is or how fast it grows. That pouch was stretched to silver, Pike. Whatever came out of there came out *big*, and the glands were wrung flat, so it was fed hard and often before it ever tasted a bottle. A thing that grows at that rate doesn't keep to its mother's timetable. It gets thirsty sooner every week of its life. So the honest answer to *how long* is: less than the last gap, and less again after that, and nobody's going to tell you the numbers because nobody's ever sat down and written them."

She let that stand a moment, because it deserved to.

"And there's a worse shape to it, which you've nearly got already." She turned the hook over on her knees. "It can't make its own. Look at what the work took — eleven inches of honed keel, a rasp on a track, a sac of pickle to rinse the cavity out. That's grown, not learnt, and a young one won't have any of it for years, same as a lamb's got no horns to speak of. It didn't hollow that man. *She* did. She hollowed and packed and corked and set him up, and then she went out to start on the next one, and she heard us on the stair, and she came down the chute to see to it, and I put a boat-hook through her." She looked at her hands on the shaft. "So there's a thing out there tonight that has never fed itself once and has got one bottle left and no one to fill it."

She almost smiled, and it didn't take.

"Which is not good news, before you reach for it. A creature that can't feed itself and is getting hungrier doesn't lie down quietly and starve. It goes looking. It goes looking at exactly the pace its thirst sets, and it has no tool and no method and no patience, and it will not be tidy about it. Everything we've read off that man downstairs — the measurements, the rinsing, the trimming level, all the sense we've been able to make of any of this — none of it applies to what comes next. We've spent the night learning a grammar and the thing that's left doesn't speak it." She put the hook down. "I'd rather be hunting the careful one. You can predict careful."

She got her hand on the rail and hauled herself up a step, knees objecting the whole way, and stood looking down at the pale ballasted man on his shelf with his mouth corked and his week's brewing in him.

"Two jobs, then, and I'd like them both done in the next hour. First we take his cork out and tip him off that shelf and let four feet of water into him, because whatever's in him now is the last meal that pup knows the address of, and I want it spoiled." She said it exactly as she'd have said *bank the fire*. "It won't stop it. It'll move it. A thing that comes home to an empty larder goes further out, and further out is a village, and I'd sooner it came for us in a cellar we've already had the education in."

She turned then, and looked at him properly for the first time in a while, and at the lamp shaking very slightly in his hand.

"Second job. You said the cold's inside your ribs." Her voice went flat and level, the tone she saved for things that had become interesting. "Eleven vents a side and it can't shut them, and it pours heat into the stone whether it wants to or not. That one's been dead twenty minutes and it's stopped pouring anything." She held her two fingers up, the ones that had been on the step. "This stone's colder than it was when I sat down.

"So the lamp goes out from your body — out, a foot clear — and we do not stand under that chute, and we don't take our eyes off the water on the way down." She hefted the hook. "And you'll oblige me by noticing that you asked when it'd get thirsty again and the house answered you. They usually do, if you leave a gap."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I look at the water and see the first ripple. Tiny. Right at the edge of the shelf where the jar-man sits. "It's here," I say, and my voice doesn't shake. "It's already in the water."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stopped on the step with her boot half-lifted and put it back down where it had been, because a foot moving is a foot that can't take weight, and she wanted both of hers on stone.

"Good," she said. "Don't point. Don't move the lamp. Talk to me about the ripple."

She was already reading it herself, but she wanted his eyes on it as well as hers, because two people watching water catch different things and she had never once regretted the redundancy.

It came off the shelf edge in a ring, and the ring was small — a hand's span, no more — and it went out four feet and died. Then nothing. Then another, from the same place, the same size.

"Twice from the same spot and the same size both times. That's not a thing swimming. Swimming gives you a wake, and a wake is long and it's got a direction and it tells you where the animal's going." She kept her voice at fence-line level. "That's a thing sat still and *working*. Something's at the edge of that shelf with its hands in a job, and the ripple's the job, not the animal. Same as a woman at a washboard."

The next ring came. Same span. Same place.

"Regular, as well. Count it with me and don't say the numbers out loud — I want the room quiet." She let three go by, and they came like a slow pulse, and she didn't care for the tidiness of it at all, because tidy was supposed to be dead at the bottom of her stair. "Four seconds and a bit. That's a rhythm. That's a thing repeating a stroke it knows."

She shifted the hook so the point came up and forward.

"Now I'll tell you what I'd like to be true and then I'll tell you what is." She wiped her wrist across her mouth. "I'd like it to be small. A hand's span of ripple off a still animal says small, and small is what I've been promising you all night — a pup, no keel, no rasp, no method. But there's a shelf under that water a yard broad and I've never seen the top of it, and a thing lying flat along a shelf with only its arms in the water gives you exactly that ripple whether it's the size of a cat or the size of me. You can't read the animal off the ring. You can only read the work."

The lamp hissed. The cold came up off the steps through her boot soles and she noted it and put it away.

"And here's what the work is." She let the light lie flat across the surface with two fingers on his wrist and didn't lift it an inch. "It's at the *edge* of the shelf. Not at the head of him, not at the belly where the slot is. At the edge, where he's trimmed level on half a brick. That thing's got one bottle left in the world and it can't get the cork out, because corking's a tool job and it hasn't got the tools. So it's doing what anything does when it can't open the jar."

She almost smiled. It didn't take.

"It's trying to tip him in."

Another ring came off the shelf. Then two together, closer, and the fourth was bigger than the three before it.

"Rhythm's gone," she said, flat. "That's it finding purchase. Which means the next thing that happens is four feet of water goes into a man packed with silt and a week's brewing, and you'll get a wave off it, and a wave in a cellar with a shelf in it is how you lose your footing and your lamp in the same half second." She set her shoulder against the wall and put her weight low. "So. Lamp out from your body, arm locked, and when the water moves you let your knees go soft and you let it move you. Don't fight it. People drown standing up in three feet because they'd rather be upright than wet."

She got the hook two-handed, point down the stair.

"And Pike — I said the grammar wouldn't apply to this one." The next ring came, wide and wrong. "I'd like to withdraw that. It's got no keel and no rasp and no pickle and it's still gone straight to the one place on that shelf where a man set square on half a brick will go over. Nobody taught it that." She breathed out white. "It worked it out. In the dark. Tonight.

"Which is considerably worse, and we'll discuss it later. Feet apart. Here it comes."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I brace my knees and watch the water bulge. The jar-man tilts, slow, then all at once, and the wave comes off him like a wall.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: There's another version where something wore him in here and then stopped needing to, and what's leaning on that brick is the bit it didn't take with it.

rung_labels.label: engaged
