dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned so the light from the eastward window fell across her rather than behind her. That was part of it too — the witnesses were owed her face while she spoke, not a shape in a doorway.

"Then hear it," she said.

She did not look at the body. Looking at the body was the mistake young duellists made, thinking that grief displayed was grief proven. The account was the only thing she owed, and the account lived in her mouth, not in her eyes.

"Tomas Reyne came onto the ground at half past seven, sober, unhurried, and of his own choosing. He offered no withdrawal and I offered none. On the third exchange he attempted a rising cut toward my sword-hand, which was a sound choice and nearly a good one. He was slow bringing the blade back across his body. I have seen him slow in the same manner twice before, at Hallowmere and in the yard behind the Sheaf, and I knew it would be there, and I waited for it."

Her thumb moved once along the flat of the cleaned blade, then stopped.

"I put the point in beneath his right collarbone, angled down and inward, to a depth of perhaps six inches. It passed behind the bone and into the great vessels above the heart. He remained standing for the length of two breaths. He said the word *wait*. He did not say it to me; he was looking past my shoulder at the wall. Then his legs went and I lowered him with my left arm so that he did not strike his head, and he died on the grass between eleven and fifteen seconds after that. I did not close his eyes. That is not my office."

She let the silence sit its full weight before she added the rest, because the rest was hers and no one else would say it for her.

"It was not a merciful stroke. There was a merciful stroke available to me — the inside of the knee, which would have ended the matter and left him walking with a stick. I chose the collarbone because it was certain and the knee was not, and because I was afraid of him. That is my reason. I will not offer a better one, and I would be obliged if none of you invented one for me."

Only then did she look at Del.

"You are his second. You may correct me on any point. If I have erred, say so now, in front of them, and I will amend it and the amendment will stand as the record."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I swallow, my throat dry. "No correction." I glance at the witnesses, then back at her. "You accounted for it true."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head — not deeply, the shallow angle reserved for a second who had done his office properly under bad conditions.

"Then the account is closed and it stands as spoken," she said, and she said it toward the witnesses rather than toward him, because that was where it had to land. "Eight of you heard it. If any of you repeats it, repeat it whole. The part about the knee goes with the rest. A man who carries half of it out of this room is carrying a lie, and I'll name it a lie in whatever company I find it."

She turned the blade once in her hand and slid it home. The sound of it was small and very ordinary.

"He is yours now. His people should have him before the day warms. There's a hurdle in the stable passage that will serve if you've nothing better, and Reyne's coat is folded on the bench — it went off him at the start and it should go back with him, it was a good coat and his sister made it." A pause. "His blade is by the north post where he dropped it. I have not touched it and I will not. If his family wish me to have it I'll take it, and if they wish it buried I'll say nothing against that either."

Only then did she cross to where Del stood, and she stopped a proper arm's length short.

"You kept your eyes open," she said. "That was well done and it cost you something, and I saw what it cost. I'll not tell you it becomes easier, because that has not been my experience of it."

She looked, briefly, at the grass. Twelve now. She had counted them since the first, and she had never once found that the counting made a pattern or a meaning.

"I am going to the Sheaf when this is finished, and I am going to sit in the back room and drink water, because I do not drink wine on these days and I have never been able to explain why in a way that satisfies anyone." She straightened her cuff. "You may come or not. There is no obligation in it, and I will not think less of you for keeping your own company. But I have found it is a poor hour to be alone in, and I would rather offer badly than not offer."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stopped where she stood. She did not correct him and she did not look at the witnesses to see whether they had noticed, because looking would have told them to notice.

He had said it in the wrong place in the order. The second said *speak the account* before the account, and Del had said it after, with the thing already spoken and closed and his own word of approval laid on top of it. That was shock. She had seen it in three seconds before him and in herself, once, a long way back, standing in a courtyard in Farrow with her hand on a gate she had already opened.

"The record stands as first spoken," she said, and she said it clearly, to the room. "What I say now is not a second account. It is the same account, repeated at the second's asking, and it alters nothing and adds nothing. If it differs from the first by one word, that word is my error and the first version governs."

Then she turned back to Del and gave it to him again.

"Tomas Reyne came onto the ground at half past seven, sober, unhurried, and of his own choosing. He offered no withdrawal and I offered none. On the third exchange he attempted a rising cut toward my sword-hand, which was a sound choice and nearly a good one. He was slow bringing the blade back across his body—" She went through all of it. The collarbone, the angle, the six inches, the two breaths, the word *wait* spoken to the wall and not to her, the eleven to fifteen seconds, her left arm under him, the eyes she had not closed. She did not hurry any part of it and she did not lean on any part of it. Then the knee, and her fear, and the refusal of a better reason.

"That is the whole of it," she said. "You may have it again in an hour or tomorrow or in ten years, and it will come out in those same words, because I keep them in that order and I have never yet had to change one. That is not a kindness I am doing you. It is the only thing I am able to do."

Her hand had gone to her cuff again. She made it stop.

"You had already answered," she added, quieter, pitched to reach him and not the room. "You said *no correction*, and it was correct, and it is written that way. You have lost the thread of the order, which is what the hour does to a man, and no one here will hold it against you — and if any one of them does, they may bring it to me."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I breathe out, slow, and realize I'm trembling. "Thank you," I say, my voice steadier than I feel. "I'll come with you to the Sheaf." I glance at Tomas' body. "Let me see to him first."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stepped back to give him the ground.

"Take what time it wants," she said. "Nobody here has anywhere to be that matters more, and if they think they do they may say so to me on their way out."

She watched him go to the body and she did not follow, because there was a line in it and the line was not written anywhere but she had kept it eleven times before and saw no reason to break it now. The victor lowered a man and then the victor stood off. Anything further was a hand laid on something that had stopped being hers the moment the account closed.

"I'll not help you lift him," she said, and she said it plainly so that it could not be mistaken for coldness or for shame. "Not because it would trouble me. Because it is not my right, and because his sister will ask who carried him, and the answer should not be me. Halloran is by the door and he is strong and he was fond of Tomas, and he will be glad to be asked. Ask him."

She turned her head toward the eastward window. The light had come up off the grass and the grass was wet still and would be dry within the hour, and there was a thing on it she was not going to look at twice.

"The hurdle wants carrying flat or the straps bind," she said. "And go under the shoulders, not the arms. The arms come loose in the cold and it distresses people who have not seen it before."

Then she made herself stop, because instruction was a place to hide and she knew the shape of her own hiding.

"I'll wait in the yard," she said. "Not in the passage, not at the gate — the yard, where you can see me from the door and where I am not standing over you. When you are done, come out. If you find you would rather go to his people instead, or to your own bed, come out and tell me so and I'll count it well done."

At the threshold she paused with her hand on the frame.

"His coat," she said. "The bench, under the lamp. Check the left pocket before it goes to his sister. Men keep things in the left and it should be her that finds them, not a stranger at the washing."

Then she went out into the yard and stood in the middle of it where she could be seen, and she counted to twelve, and the number did not do anything at all, and she waited.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned where she stood. She did not ask him to come nearer and she did not lower her voice, because he had said *plainly* and plainly meant at the volume the yard required.

"Here," she said, and she put two fingers on herself to show it — her own right side, an inch and a half under the ridge of the collarbone, in the soft hollow where the bone ended and the shoulder began. She pressed hard enough that the fingers whitened. "Not the chest. Not the throat. Here. If you tell his sister *the chest* she will picture the front of him and she will be wrong, and she will be wrong for the rest of her life in a way that cannot be corrected afterward, because people do not let go of the first picture."

She kept the fingers there a moment longer so that he could fix it, then let her hand fall.

"The point went in at that hollow and travelled down and inward, toward the middle of him. Behind the bone, not through it. There is a place under there where the great vessels come up off the heart and gather close together, and the blade found them. That is the whole of the injury. One entry, no second stroke, nothing else on him but the grass he went down into and a scrape on the heel of his left hand from the third exchange, which he did himself and which was nothing."

The light had come further up off the wet grass. She stood in it.

"Plainly, then, and you may take these words or better ones: he was not cut open and he was not run through the body. There was very little blood where anyone could see it, and his people should be told that before they see him, because they will expect otherwise and the not-expecting is its own small cruelty. Most of it stayed inside him. That is why it was quick." A pause, exact. "It was quick. I will say that where his sister can hear it and I will not say it as a comfort, because it is not one. It is only true, and true is the only thing I have that will still be true in a year."

She looked at him then, and her face had not changed and had not been intended to.

"If the witnesses want it in fewer words, here they are: I struck under his right collarbone, down and in, and it killed him in under a quarter of a minute. If they want it in more, they may come and find me, and they will get the same account at whatever length they ask for."

She glanced once toward the door he had come out of, and away again.

"And if his sister asks me herself," she said, "I will tell her the same, standing up, with my hands where she can see them. I will not send it by letter. Letters let the writer choose which parts go in."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my own fingers tracing the spot on my own body, trying to remember the hollow. "I'll tell her it was here. Quick, and mostly inside." I turn to go back in, then stop. "He kept a locket in that left pocket. His wife's picture. I'll make sure it's there."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren watched him find the place on himself and got a small, correcting motion of her hand into the air before he turned away.

"Higher on you," she said. "He was broader through the shoulder than you are and the hollow sits further out on a man built that way. On you it is nearer the base of the throat by a thumb's width. If you show his sister on your own body, show it right, or she will carry the wrong picture out of your hands instead of mine."

Then the rest of what he had said caught up with her, and she stood very still with it.

"I did not know about the locket," she said. "I want that said out here where the eight of them can hear it. I have not put my hand in that coat and I did not know what was in it, and if it is not in the pocket when you look, I will stand still and be searched by whoever wants to do the searching, and I will not take offence at the asking." Her jaw set. "It happens. A man loses something on the ground and a year later it is the victor who took it, and there is no way to unsay that once it has been said. So look for it with someone beside you. Halloran, or one of the witnesses — whichever of them has the least love for me, if you can tell which that is. Let it be his eyes on your hands, not mine."

She looked down at the wet grass and then, deliberately, at the door.

"If it is on the ground and not in the coat, it will be near the north post where he dropped his blade, or under him. I have not moved him since I lowered him, so it will be where it fell." A pause. "Do not let them tell you afterward that I stepped near that post. I have not and I will not."

The light had reached the top of the yard wall. She did not say the other thing for a moment, and then she said it, because not saying it would have been a softening of the same kind she refused in the account.

"I did not know he had a wife," she said. "That is not an excuse and I am not offering it as one. It would not have changed the stroke. I want you to understand that plainly, because you will wonder later whether it would have, and I would rather you had my answer than your own guess. I chose the collarbone because I was afraid of him and because the knee was not certain. Knowing about the locket would not have made the knee certain. Nothing would have."

She straightened her cuff, stopped, and put both hands behind her back instead.

"Bring it to her yourself," she said. "Not with mine in it, not with mine anywhere near it. And when she asks you where it was, tell her: the left pocket of the coat he took off before the ground, folded on the bench, under the lamp, where he left it himself, expecting to put it back on."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not answer at once, and the pause was not hesitation. It was her going back through what she had said and finding the place where she had failed.

"You are right," she said. "I softened it. Twice. *Great vessels* is a phrase for drawing rooms and *mostly inside him* is a phrase for a sister. I gave them to you in the yard because you were shaking and I thought better of it than I should have. That was my error and it goes on the record as mine, and the second caught it, and the record should say that too."

She brought her hands from behind her back. She wanted them visible for this.

"Precisely, then. The blade is a thrusting sword, thirty-four inches, ground to a point and not to an edge, so it did not cut anything on the way in. It pushed. It entered the hollow under the right end of the collarbone, passed behind the bone without touching it, and travelled down and toward the middle of him for something near six inches. In that space it opened the great vein that comes up under the collarbone, and the artery that runs beneath the vein, and it took the top of the right lung with the last inch of its travel. Three things. Vein, artery, lung."

She said it at the same pace she had said the rest. She did not let the pace change.

"What that did to him: the lung fell shut, which he felt as not being able to fill his chest, which is why he stopped and did not strike again. And the blood left the artery into the cavity of his chest rather than out through the wound, at the rate an artery of that size empties, which is fast. His chest filled and there was nowhere for it to go. That is what *mostly inside him* meant, and you are owed the whole of it: he bled into himself, about four pints, and by the time his legs failed there was not enough left moving to keep sense in his head. He did not feel the last of it. He was gone from behind his own eyes before his knees went. The two breaths and the word *wait* — that was all of him there was still anyone at all."

She let that stand.

"That is what the blade did and what it did it to. If it wants saying shorter it does not get said shorter. And when you go to his sister, you may still say *quick*, and *here*, and *mostly inside him* — she is not a witness and she is not owed the accounting."

A pause, exact.

"You are. So you have it."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take a sharp breath, my own chest feeling tight. "That's the whole of it, then." I look down at my hands, then back at her. "I'll need a moment with him. Then I'll meet you in the yard."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stood out of his way.

"That's the whole of it," she agreed. "There is no more and there will be no more. If anything further comes to me I will bring it to you before I bring it to anyone, and I do not expect anything further to come."

She did not offer to go in with him. She did not offer anything at all for a moment, and the silence was deliberate, because he had asked for a moment and a moment given with conditions attached was not a moment.

"Take the door shut behind you if you want it shut," she said at last. "The witnesses have had what they are owed and they can wait in the passage. I'll tell them so on my way past, and I'll say it in a manner that does not invite discussion."

She looked at him once more — at his hands, which he was looking at himself, and which she had seen do their office steadily for three quarters of an hour in a room that did not deserve that of anyone.

"One thing, and then I am out of your way. Do not talk to him." Her voice did not change at all. "Not because it is unseemly. Because you will remember what you said, every word, for a long time, and you will not be able to choose which parts you remember. I have done it twice and I have both of them still, and I would not have given either of them to myself if I had known the price. Sit with him. That is enough and it is not less."

Then she went. She said the thing to the witnesses in the passage, briefly, and one of them opened his mouth and closed it again, and she crossed the yard to the middle of it and stopped where the wall's shadow had not yet reached and stood there with her hands at her sides where the door could see them.

The grass on her boots had begun to dry. She thought about going to the trough and did not, because there would be a time for that and this was not it.

Twelve. She went through the names in the order they had happened, which was a thing she did in the hour afterward and had never told anyone about and would not have been able to justify if asked. Ferris. Holt. The one at Farrow whose name she had learned wrong first and corrected afterward. Down through them to Tomas Reyne, half past seven, sober, unhurried, of his own choosing.

It did not make a pattern. It never had. She stood in the middle of the yard where she could be seen from the door, and she waited.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren came back across the yard. Not all the way — she stopped at the arm's length she had kept before, because the distance was part of it too — and she stood where the door could still see her hands.

"Then all of it," she said, "and it is your right, and I will not make you ask a fourth time."

She set herself square to the witnesses in the passage, so that they had her face, and she began.

"How long. He was slow bringing the blade back across his body and the point went in at the top of that slowness, so call it the third exchange, something under forty seconds from the first crossing of blades. He stood after it for two breaths. Neither breath filled. The first was the one he tried to take and could not, and the second was smaller than the first. Then he said the word *wait*, one word, not loud, in an ordinary voice — not a cry, and I want that said, because people assume a cry — and he said it looking past my right shoulder at the wall above the bench. There was nothing on that wall. I looked afterward. His legs went perhaps a second after the word. I had my left arm under him before his knees reached the grass and I lowered him at the pace a man is lowered and not faster. He died between eleven and fifteen seconds after that. I counted it. I counted it because counting is what I have instead of anything else to do with my hands in that minute, and the count was fourteen, and I say eleven to fifteen because I will not swear to my own counting closer than that."

She did not stop for breath, because stopping would have invited him to spare her the rest.

"What he said. *Wait.* That is the whole of what he said. He made no other sound that carried a word in it. He made sound — there was a noise in his throat at the fourth or fifth second on the grass, twice, and it was the lung and not the man, and it is a noise people mistake for speech and then spend years trying to make into a message. It was not a message. I will not give him a last word he did not say, and I will not take away the one he did."

"What it looked like at the end." Here she slowed, and the slowing was on purpose, so that nothing got through on momentum. "His colour went first, and it went fast and from the face upward and outward — grey under the eyes, then the mouth, then the whole of him the colour of the inside of a shell. His lips went blue at the edges before he stopped. His mouth was open, not wide. His eyes stayed open and they stopped holding together — they went to two different places, a little apart, the way a man's eyes do when there is no longer anyone behind them, and that happened before his legs did. His right hand opened and the blade was already gone from it, and the fingers curled afterward, slightly, which is the hand and not the will. He was heavier in my arm at the end than at the start. That is the part nobody tells you and it is the part I remember. Between the knees going and the grass he became a weight and nothing else, and I felt the moment it happened, in my forearm, and I do not know a precise word for it and I will not invent one."

She let the silence take its full measure. The light had come off the wall now and lay flat across the yard between them.

"That is all of it. There is nothing held back and nothing shaped. You have had the account four times and it has not differed by a word, and it will not, and you may have it a fifth."

Then she took one step closer, and her voice did not drop, because dropping it would have made it a kindness and she did not intend a kindness.

"And I am going to say the other thing, because the code says precisely and not tactfully, and that cuts in both directions."

Her hands stayed where they were, open, at her sides.

"You are not asking because the record wants it. The record is closed and you closed it yourself and you closed it correctly. You are asking because he is through that door and you have told me you need a moment with him, and every time you ask me for the account you are standing in this yard instead of standing in that room. I know the manoeuvre. I have used it. At Farrow I asked a woman to tell me three times how her brother had died, and I was very exact about my reasons, and my reasons were that I could not go and look at him."

She glanced, once, at the door. Not long.

"I will give it to you as many times as you ask and I will not tire of giving it and I will not once let it be seen on my face that you have asked again. That is mine to do. But I will not let you use it, and I will not pretend I do not see what it is for, because that would be the softening, and the softening is the dishonour, and it is the dishonour whether I do it to him or to you."

She stepped back to her arm's length again.

"He will not be easier in an hour. He will be colder and his people will have arrived and there will be others in the room, and you will have lost the only part of this that was yours. Go in. Shut the door. I will be here, in the middle of the yard, where you can see me, and if you come out and want it a fifth time you will have it, word for word, at whatever length you ask."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't know I was holding. "Alright." I turn to the door, my hand on the latch. "I'm going in."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren said nothing until his hand had been on the latch long enough that the saying of it would not be a push.

"Good," she said then. And nothing after it — no instruction, no correction, nothing about the hurdle or the straps or the shoulders. She had given him all the places to put his hands that she had, and there were no more, and to offer another would only have been another rail for him to hold rather than go in.

She heard the latch, and the door, and the door shut.

Then she turned and faced the passage, because there were eight of them in it and every one of them had heard the last part, the part about Farrow and the woman and the three tellings, and there was no version of the afternoon in which that stayed in the passage.

"You heard that," she said. "You may repeat it. I'd sooner it went out from you than crawled out sideways in a year. But repeat it whole — that I gave him the account four times without complaint, and that I told him why he was asking, and that both of those are true at once and neither cancels the other. If you can only carry one half, carry neither."

One of them — Ailen, who had held for Reyne at Hallowmere and had not looked at her since the ground — said something too low to be meant for answer. She let it go by. A man was permitted his own mouth in a passage.

"And the record stands as first spoken," she added. "Not as last spoken. Four tellings, one record. If any of you writes it down, write the first one."

Then she went back to the middle of the yard, which was the only place she had said she would be, and standing anywhere else now would have made a liar of her in a small way that mattered.

The light had come fully off the wall. The grass on her boots had dried to a paler green and would brush off later. She could hear nothing from the room, which was correct, and she did not listen for anything, which cost her something.

She had told him not to talk to the man. She had told him because it was true and because she had both of hers still — Ferris, and the one at Farrow — sitting in her exactly where she had left them, in her own voice, which was the unbearable part. And she had told him knowing he would probably do it anyway, because she would have, because she had.

That was allowed. She had given him the price and he was free to pay it. That was the whole of what an account was for.

Twelve, she thought, and then made herself stop thinking it, because she had already done the counting once today and doing it twice was not accounting. It was something else wearing accounting's coat.

She stood where the door could see her, with her hands at her sides, and she waited, and she did not straighten her cuff.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned when the door sounded, and she did not look at his face first. She looked at his hands, because hands told the truth earlier than faces did, and then she brought her eyes up and met him properly, and she stood square so the light came across her and not behind her.

"Then a fifth time," she said. "Whole, and in one piece, with nothing held out for anyone's sister. You asked for all of it and you were right to, and it should not have taken four askings to get it in one telling. That is my fault and not yours."

She set her feet. The witnesses had come as far as the passage mouth and she let them.

"Tomas Reyne came onto the ground at half past seven, sober, unhurried, and of his own choosing. He offered no withdrawal and I offered none. He took off his coat before the ground and folded it himself and left it on the bench under the lamp. There were three exchanges. On the third he attempted a rising cut toward my sword-hand, which was a sound choice and nearly a good one. He was slow bringing the blade back across his body. I have seen him slow in the same manner twice before, at Hallowmere and in the yard behind the Sheaf, and I knew it would be there, and I waited for it. From the first crossing of blades to the stroke was something under forty seconds.

"The blade is a thrusting sword, thirty-four inches, ground to a point and not to an edge. It cut nothing on the way in. It pushed. I put the point into the hollow beneath the right end of his collarbone, an inch and a half under the ridge of the bone, and drove it down and inward toward the middle of him to a depth of near six inches. It passed behind the bone and did not touch it. In that six inches it opened the great vein that runs under the collarbone, and the artery beneath the vein, and it took the top of the right lung with the last inch of its travel. Three things. Vein, artery, lung. One entry, no second stroke. There was nothing else on him but the grass he went down into and a scrape on the heel of his left hand from the third exchange, which he did himself and which was nothing.

"The lung fell shut and he felt that as not being able to fill his chest, which is why he stopped and did not strike again. The artery emptied into the cavity of his chest and not out through the wound, at the rate an artery of that size empties, which is fast, and his chest filled, and there was nowhere for it to go. Something near four pints. He bled into himself. That is why there was very little to see on the grass and it is why it was quick.

"He remained standing for the length of two breaths. Neither breath filled. The first was the one he tried to take and could not, and the second was smaller than the first. Then he said the word *wait*. One word, not loud, in an ordinary voice, and not a cry. He said it looking past my right shoulder at the wall above the bench, and there was nothing on that wall. I looked afterward. His colour had already begun to go, grey under the eyes first and then the mouth, and his lips went blue at their edges, and his eyes stopped holding together and went to two places a little apart, and that happened before his legs did. There was no one behind them by then. His legs went perhaps a second after the word. I had my left arm under him before his knees reached the grass and I lowered him at the pace a man is lowered and not faster, so that he did not strike his head. He became a weight in my forearm between the knees going and the grass, and I felt the moment of it, and I have no precise word for that and will not invent one. He died between eleven and fifteen seconds after I had him down. I counted fourteen. I will not swear to my own counting closer than that. At the fourth or fifth second there was a noise twice in his throat, and it was the lung and not the man, and it carried no word in it and I will not make it into one. His right hand opened, the blade being already gone from it, and the fingers curled after, slightly, which is the hand and not the will. I did not close his eyes. That is not my office.

"It was not a merciful stroke. There was a merciful stroke available to me — the inside of the knee, which would have ended the matter and left him walking with a stick. I chose the collarbone because it was certain and the knee was not, and because I was afraid of him. That is my reason. I will not offer a better one, and I would be obliged if none of you invented one for me.

"That is the whole of it. There is no more."

She stopped, and the yard was quiet, and she did not fill the quiet.

Then his voice did what it did, and she let it. She did not step in and she did not look away and she did not put a hand out, and she did not permit one flicker of her face to tell him she had heard a break in it.

"Confirmed and closed," she said, when he had got it out. "The record stands as first spoken. Five tellings, one record."

And then, level, and not as a kindness, because it was not one:

"That is the voice it ought to be said in. A man who could say it in any other would not have been fit to stand as his second." She turned her head toward the gate. "The Sheaf, then. The back room. I'll walk at whatever pace you walk."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I close my eyes for a beat, then open them. "Give me the coat. I'll bring it." My voice is rough but clear. "And the blade. I'll carry it too."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not move toward the bench.

"No," she said. "And you will have my reason before you take it as refusal."

She turned so the passage had her face as well as he did.

"I have not had my hand in that coat and I told these eight so, out loud, in this yard, before either of us knew what was in the pocket. If I fetch it now and put it into your hands, then between the bench and your hands there is a span of time when it was mine and no one was watching, and a year from now that span will be exactly as long as whoever wants it to be. The same for the blade. I said I had not touched it and would not. If I break that for the convenience of carrying, I have made the whole account cheaper, and the account is the only thing in this yard that will still hold in ten years."

She looked past him into the passage.

"Ailen. You held for Reyne at Hallowmere and you have not looked at me since the ground, and that makes you the right man. Go with him. The coat is folded on the bench under the lamp, and there is a locket in the left pocket with his wife's picture in it, which I did not know about until his second told me twenty minutes ago and which I want you to hear me say again now. Let it be your eyes on his hands and his hands on the coat. Not mine on either."

Her voice did not rise and did not soften.

"The blade is by the north post where it fell. I have not stepped near that post and I am not going to. Lift it yourself or let Ailen lift it, and if his family wish me to have it afterward I will take it from their hand and not from the grass, and if they wish it buried I will say nothing against that either."

She put her hands behind her back, and then, deliberately, brought them out again and let them hang open where the passage could see them.

"Halloran is by the door and he was fond of Tomas and he will be glad to be asked. The hurdle wants carrying flat or the straps bind. Under the shoulders, not the arms."

Then she stepped back to the middle of the yard, to the place she had said she would be, and stood in it.

"I will wait here while you do it," she said, "in the open, in view of all of you, and I will not go near the bench or the post or the door until he is out of that room and gone to his people. When it is done, come out, and we will walk to the Sheaf, and you may carry his coat and his sword the whole way and I will walk beside you carrying nothing, which is correct, and which is the only thing left in this that I am able to do properly."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content:
I nod, the logic of it cutting through the fog in my head. "Alright." I turn to Ailen, who's still standing in the passage. "Will you?"

He doesn't look at Auren, just meets my eyes and gives a tight nod. "I will."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stayed where she was and let them go past her without a word, because a word here would have been her putting a hand on it.

But she turned her head as Ailen came level, and she gave him the shallow inclination — the same angle she had given Del, the one kept for a man doing his office properly under bad conditions — and she said it so the yard got it and not just him.

"You are the right man for it and I am obliged to you. You need not answer that and you need not look at me. I would think less of you today if you did."

He did not answer and he did not look, and he went in behind Del, and that was correct.

Then she was alone in the middle of the yard with seven witnesses in the passage mouth and a door shut on the room, and she stood in the place she had named and did not move out of it.

She heard the bench take a man's weight — someone sitting to reach the coat, or someone's knee against it. She heard the lamp chain tick once against its bracket. She heard nothing that sounded like a locket, which meant nothing either way; a locket in a pocket made no noise at all, and its absence made no noise either, and she would not know which it had been until they came out. She found she had set her jaw against that and made herself unset it, because there was no version of the next minute in which her face was owed a share of it.

The north post was four paces to her left. She did not look at it. Looking would have been nothing, would have been a woman glancing at a post in a yard, and in a year it would have been *she was watching the sword the whole time*, and there was no correction for that afterward because it would have been true.

So she looked at the wall above the bench instead — at the flat empty plaster of it through the open half of the door, the piece of wall that Tomas Reyne had said *wait* to. There was still nothing on it. She had looked afterward and she looked again now and there was nothing, no mark, no nail, no shadow, and she had arrived at no better account of it than that a man's eyes went where they went and the wall had happened to be there. She would not improve on it. If his wife asked what he had been looking at, the answer was *the wall*, and the answer would not be dressed.

The grass on her boots had gone pale and stiff. Inside, something shifted — the hurdle, laid flat, the straps not binding.

She stepped back two paces then, out of the line between the door and the gate, so that when they brought him through there would be clear ground and no one would have to go around her. That was the whole of her remaining office and she performed it exactly: standing off, out of the way, visible, hands open at her sides.

When the door came wide she did not bow and she did not turn her back, because one was a claim on him and the other was a discourtesy, and there was a thing between them that had no name and was simply this — that she keep her eyes open while he went past, in the light, at whatever pace they carried him, the same as she had asked of nobody and the same as his second had done for her without being asked.

She did not count him. She had already counted him once today. Twice would have been something else wearing accounting's coat.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content:
I watch them carry him out, the hurdle steady between them. Auren is standing off to the side, exactly where she said she’d be. When they pass, I see her eyes are open, her face still. I wait until they’ve turned the corner toward the stable passage, then I step out into the yard. The locket is a cold weight in my palm.

“It was there,” I say, holding it up so she can see. “Left pocket.”

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He held the door frame with one hand, fingers curled around the edge of it, and let the silence sit for exactly long enough to make clear that he was deciding.

Then he stepped back. Not to the side — back, so Bee would have to walk toward him to get through, close enough to brush past.

"Didn't say you couldn't come in."

The flat looked the same. That was the worst part, probably, for both of them — he knew it. The books were still doubled up on the shelves in no order. The kitchen light still buzzed at a frequency that lived somewhere behind the left eye. He'd moved the couch to face the window instead of the TV, and there was a new mug on the counter, green, that didn't belong to either of them, and he did not explain it.

He turned around once Bee was inside and leaned against the kitchen counter, arms crossed. Not because he was cold.

"So." He looked at Bee directly, the way he'd always been too good at — the way that made it feel like being read. "You came all the way over here. Broken buzzer and all. Must be important."

His voice was even. Almost pleasant. Which meant he was furious, and Bee would know that, because Bee had always known that.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't look at the new mug. I don't fucking look at it. "You're still pissed about the records, then."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Something flickered across his face — not surprise, because Bee didn't surprise him anymore, but a kind of bitter recognition. That Bee had walked in here and chosen *that* as the opening move. The records. Not the texts, not the silence, not the three months of careful mutual avoidance at every gathering their friends had tried to hold together like a cracked plate. The records.

He laughed. One short breath through his nose.

"The records," he repeated, tasting the word. "No. I'm not still pissed about the records, Bee. You can have the fucking records. I told you that in March. I told you that in a text you apparently didn't get, which is interesting, because the read receipts say otherwise."

He uncrossed his arms only to recross them the other way, a reorganization that accomplished nothing. The kitchen light buzzed.

"But you didn't come here about the records either, so let's not — " He stopped himself. Breathed. When he spoke again his voice was quieter, which was worse. "Let's not do the thing where we pretend this is about logistics. You were always better at that than me and I was never stupid enough to believe it."

He looked at Bee standing there in his flat, in the space Bee used to fill without thinking, and he felt the precise geography of the distance between them — four feet, maybe five, the length of a kitchen counter — like a physical fact.

"Why are you here. Actually."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He kissed back before he decided to. That was the honest, ugly truth of it — his body answered before his brain had finished constructing the reasons not to, and by then Bee's mouth was already on his and his hand was already at the back of Bee's neck, gripping too hard, pulling closer when he should have been pushing away.

It was not a good kiss. It was not meant to be. It was the same frequency as the kitchen light, something that lived behind the eye and wouldn't stop, and he could feel Bee's anger in it the way he could feel his own — pressed between them like a third body in the room.

He broke it. Not far. An inch, maybe two, his forehead still almost touching Bee's, his breath uneven in a way that would have embarrassed him if he'd had any pride left about this particular thing.

"That's not an answer," he said, low, his hand still on Bee's neck. He could feel the pulse under his thumb. Fast. Good. He wanted Bee's heart rate to be a mess. He wanted to be the reason for it.

"That's you not wanting to say it out loud."

His grip didn't loosen. The kitchen light buzzed. The green mug sat on the counter behind him, explained nothing, belonged to no one Bee needed to worry about, and he would let that silence do its work because he was not above it. He had never been above it. That was the thing Bee had always understood and forgiven and then, eventually, not forgiven, and he had never figured out which version of Bee was right.

"Say it," he said. "You came all the way here. Broken buzzer and all."

Throwing Bee's own silence back. Because he could. Because this was what they did instead of being kind.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: My hands are gripping the front of your shirt. I don't let go. "I came here because I'm still angry," I say, my voice tight. "And you're the only one who understands why."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Something broke open in his chest — not cleanly, not like relief, more like a bone resetting wrong. Because that was the most honest thing Bee had said to him in eleven months, and it was exactly the thing he hadn't wanted to hear, because it was true for him too, and he had been building an entire architecture of silence around not admitting it.

His jaw tightened. Bee's fists were still knotted in his shirt and he could feel the pull of the fabric against his collarbones, the specific weight of being held in place by someone who wasn't sure if they wanted to hold him or shove him backward.

"Yeah," he said. Just that, at first. The word came out rough, scraped.

He brought his other hand up. Not to Bee's face — to Bee's wrist, where it gripped his shirt. He wrapped his fingers around it. Not pulling the hand away. Holding it there. Pinning Bee to the choice Bee had already made.

"I know." His voice was quiet in the way that meant he was not performing anything, which happened so rarely that Bee would recognize it immediately and probably resent him for it. "You think I don't know that? You think I've been — what, sitting here peacefully? Reading? Enjoying the new couch arrangement?"

A muscle moved in his throat. He was looking at Bee from too close, close enough to see everything he didn't want to see — that Bee looked tired, that Bee looked the same, that the eleven months had done exactly as much damage to Bee as they had to him, which was both too much and not enough.

"No one else knows what we did to each other," he said. "That's the problem. You can tell the story to anyone you want and they'll take your side, they'll take mine, and none of them will *get it* because they weren't in the room."

His thumb moved against Bee's wrist. Once. An involuntary thing he did not take back.

"So you're angry. And you came here. And I let you in." He swallowed. "And we're going to do something stupid tonight that we'll both be able to justify in the morning, and in three weeks you'll hate me for a new reason, and I will have earned it. Is that the plan? Because I need you to know that I see it. I see the whole shape of it. And I'm —"

He stopped. The kitchen light buzzed. Bee's pulse beat against his fingers.

"I'm going to let you stay anyway. So what does that tell you."

It wasn't a question. His hand stayed on Bee's wrist. He didn't step back.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The wall hit his back and he pulled Bee with him, a graceless collision of weight and want that knocked the air out of him in a way that had nothing to do with impact. Bee's hands were on his bare skin and his nerve endings lit up like a city he'd thought he'd gone dark in, every point of contact a small detonation.

He got his mouth on Bee's throat, not gently, and felt the sound Bee made more than heard it — a vibration against his lips that he wanted to take apart and keep.

"This doesn't fix anything," he said into Bee's skin, and then bit down, because he had always been the kind of person who named the wound and then pressed his thumb into it. His hands found Bee's hips, pulled them flush against his own, and the noise that came out of him was not something he could have controlled or dignified.

The hallway was narrow. He'd always hated that about this flat — the way two people couldn't pass each other without turning sideways. Now Bee was pressed against the full length of him and the narrowness felt like architecture conspiring, like the walls had opinions about this.

His fingers dug into Bee's waist. He could feel Bee's ribs expand with breathing that wasn't steady, and he mapped the familiar topography of that body with a desperate, furious attention — cataloguing what was the same, searching for what had changed, resenting both.

"I know," he said, though Bee hadn't said anything. An answer to something that existed only in the space between them, in the eleven months of silence that was unraveling in a hallway under a light he'd also never fixed.

He pulled back just enough to look at Bee. His chest was heaving. His mouth was wrecked. He looked like someone making a choice he'd already made a long time ago and was only now admitting to.

"Bedroom's the same direction it's always been," he said, low and winded. "In case you forgot."

He hadn't smiled once since Bee arrived. He didn't smile now. But something in his expression cracked open — raw, reckless, entirely aware — and he waited for Bee to move first, because if they were going to do this, he needed Bee to walk them there. He needed that to be Bee's.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I shove you backwards, down the hallway toward the bedroom. "I didn't forget a damn thing." My voice is all breath and gravel.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He let himself be moved. That was the thing — he could have planted his feet, could have caught Bee's wrists, could have turned this into the kind of negotiation they'd always been too good at dragging out. Instead he went backward, shoulders hitting the hallway wall once, then the doorframe, his hands finding Bee's waist and pulling even as he was being pushed, a contradiction that made perfect physical sense.

"I know you didn't," he said, and it came out like an accusation, because it was one. Bee hadn't forgotten anything. Neither had he. That was the entire goddamn problem — they were two people with perfect recall of every wound and every good thing, and no ability to separate the two.

His back hit the edge of the bedroom door and it swung open behind him. The room was dark except for the streetlight coming through the window he still never closed the blinds on. The bed was made, which Bee would notice, because he'd never made the bed when they were together. Eleven months of sleeping alone had made him neat. He hated that Bee would see that. He hated that it meant something.

Bee shoved him again and the backs of his knees caught the mattress and he sat down hard, looking up at Bee standing over him, and the angle did something to his chest that he couldn't name — something that lived in the territory between want and grief and was probably both.

He reached up. Got his fingers hooked in Bee's waistband and pulled, not to undress, just to close the distance, to bring Bee down to where he was.

"You remember everything and you came back anyway," he said, voice scraped raw, looking up at Bee in the half-dark. "That's worse. You know that's worse."

His throat moved. His hands were shaking and he let them shake, because hiding it would have cost something he didn't have left to spend.

"Come here."

Two words. Quiet. The most honest thing he'd said all night.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
His whole body arced into Bee's hand and the sound that came out of him was wrecked — a low, broken thing pulled from somewhere behind his sternum that he couldn't have swallowed if he'd tried. A year ago he would have turned his face into the pillow, bitten down on something, redirected. Now he just let it happen, eyes shut, mouth open, every pretense stripped out of him by the simple physics of Bee's grip.

"Fuck," he breathed, and then again, "*fuck*," because Bee's mouth was right there at his ear and Bee's voice saying *still, every single time* was doing more damage than the hand was, and Bee knew that, Bee had always known exactly where the wiring ran between his body and whatever passed for his heart.

His hand came up and grabbed the back of Bee's head, fingers twisting into hair, pulling Bee's forehead against his temple so they were breathing the same air. He could feel Bee's breath on his cheek, fast and uneven, and he catalogued that greedily — proof that this was costing Bee something too.

"You don't get to say that," he managed, hips moving into Bee's hand in a rhythm he wasn't choosing. "You don't get to — leave, and then come back, and tell me *still* — "

His voice broke on the word. Actually broke, a crack running through the middle of it like a fault line, and he heard himself and hated it and couldn't stop.

He turned his head and caught Bee's mouth. Kissed like drowning. His free hand found Bee's belt and worked it open with the muscle memory of a thousand other nights, fingers steady even though the rest of him was shaking apart.

"Still," he said back, against Bee's lips, wrecked and furious. An admission that tasted like blood. "God help me. Still."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get his belt open too, my fingers fumbling, too rough. "You left, too," I say, the words bitten off between kisses. "You just did it quieter."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
His whole body flinched. Not away — inward, like something collapsing at the center. Because Bee was right. Bee was exactly right, and hearing it said out loud in this room, in the dark, with Bee's hands on him and his hands on Bee, was like having a light turned on in a place he'd been navigating by feel for eleven months.

He went still for half a second. Just half. His forehead pressed hard against Bee's, his breathing ragged, his hands frozen where they'd been working Bee's belt open.

"Yeah," he said. The word came out like something torn. "Yeah, I did."

No defense. No redirect. No *but you did this first* or *because you made it impossible* — all the lines he'd rehearsed in the shower, in the dark, in the version of this conversation he'd had a hundred times with a Bee who wasn't actually there. None of them. Just the admission, bare and ugly, sitting between them.

His hands started moving again. Got the belt open, got his hand where it needed to be, and felt Bee's breath stutter against his mouth in a way that nearly ended him.

"I made it so you'd have to be the one to go," he said, low, almost inaudible, his hand working Bee with a deliberateness that bordered on cruel — slow enough to feel, too slow to be enough. "So I could be the one who got left. So I could be angry instead of — "

He swallowed. His thumb did something intentional and precise and he felt Bee's weight shift against him.

"Instead of sorry."

The streetlight made a pale stripe across the bed. His jaw was clenched so hard it ached. He could feel the shape of what he'd just said hanging in the room like smoke, could feel that he'd handed Bee something real, something that could be used against him, and his every instinct screamed to take it back, qualify it, bury it under another kiss or another touch.

He didn't.

He just looked at Bee in the half-dark, his hand still moving, his chest open like a door he couldn't close.

"I know what I did. I've always known."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
His fingers closed around Bee's throat and every careful thing he'd ever built — every measured silence, every calculated distance, every night spent constructing the version of himself that had been wronged rather than wrong — collapsed like scaffolding.

He felt the pulse under his palm. Fast. Alive. Trusting him with something that had no business being trusted to him, and they both knew it, and that was the point.

"This isn't careful," he said, and tightened his grip. Not enough to hurt. Enough to be felt. Enough that Bee's next breath would have to be chosen, deliberate, pulled in against the pressure of his hand. "This was never careful. We were never — "

He stood up off the bed in one motion, using the grip on Bee's throat to turn them, to put Bee's back against the mattress instead of his own. Bee went down and he followed, his weight settling over Bee's body with a familiarity that made his vision blur at the edges. His hand stayed where Bee had put it.

He could feel Bee swallow against his palm.

"You want me to stop pretending I won't wreck this," he said, looking down at Bee, his voice barely a voice anymore. "Fine. I'll wreck it. I've been wrecking it since the day we met and you knew that when you walked in tonight."

His thumb found the hollow of Bee's throat, pressed. Bee's eyes were dark and enormous and looking up at him with something he couldn't survive if he named it.

"Tell me to stop," he said. His hand didn't move. "At any point. Tell me to stop and I will. That's the only careful thing you get from me tonight."

He waited. One breath. Two.

Then he kissed Bee with his hand still on Bee's throat, and felt the moan vibrate against his palm like a secret told in a language only his body understood.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I arch up against you, my hands fisting in the hair at the base of your skull. "I won't," I breathe against your mouth. "And you know it."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He made a sound that wasn't a word — something guttural and wrecked that started in his chest and died against Bee's mouth. Because he did know it. He'd always known it. That was the thing about them — the thing that had made it extraordinary and then made it unbearable: neither of them had ever known when to stop.

His hand tightened on Bee's throat. Not gradually. A decision. He felt Bee's breath catch, felt the fingers twist harder in his hair, felt the sharp sting of it at the base of his skull and chased it, leaned into it, because the pain was a language they'd always been fluent in.

"No," he said, rough, barely audible. "You won't."

He pulled back just enough to look at Bee beneath him — throat working against his palm, chest heaving, mouth swollen, eyes open and furious and wanting and refusing to look away. The streetlight cut across Bee's collarbone and he bent down and put his mouth there, teeth and tongue, tasting salt and skin and something underneath both that he'd been starving for in a way he hadn't let himself acknowledge until this exact second.

His free hand worked between them. Clumsy now, urgent in a way that abandoned all the deliberate cruelty of minutes ago. He got them pressed together, skin against skin, and his forehead dropped against Bee's shoulder and he made a sound like being gutted.

"Eleven months," he said into Bee's skin, his hips moving, graceless and desperate. "Eleven months and I couldn't — I tried to — "

He couldn't finish. His hand loosened on Bee's throat just enough to let a full breath in, then tightened again, a rhythm that mirrored something deeper, something neither of them was going to survive intact.

"I couldn't make it stop," he said. The confession of a man who had tried every door and found them all locked from the inside. "I don't think it stops."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
I need to decline this request. While I've been happy to engage with this emotionally complex scene, I'm not going to write explicit sexual content.

I can continue the scene picking up after, if you'd like — the aftermath, the silence, the conversation that follows. That's where a lot of the real emotional weight of this story lives anyway.

What would you prefer?

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We lie there in the wreckage, breathing hard. The room smells like us. I turn my head, my face against your shoulder. "So," I say, my voice shot. "Still broken."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The ceiling had a crack in it he'd never noticed before. Or maybe he had, a thousand times, and it only looked new because everything in this room had just been rewritten.

His chest was still heaving. His hand — the one that had been on Bee's throat — lay open on the mattress between them, palm up, fingers curled slightly inward like something that had been holding on too long and finally let go. He could still feel the ghost of Bee's pulse against his palm. Knew he'd feel it for days.

Bee's face turned into his shoulder and the warmth of that breath against his skin almost undid him more than anything that had come before, because it was small. It was the kind of thing that belonged to a Tuesday morning, to a life where they woke up in the same bed because they'd never left it, and it had no business being here in the aftermath of whatever this was.

"Still broken," he repeated. Not agreeing. Not disagreeing. Tasting the shape of it.

He stared at the ceiling crack. The streetlight hadn't moved. The kitchen light was still buzzing, faintly, from down the hall, because sound carried in this flat and it always had and Bee used to complain about it and he used to say he didn't hear it and that had been a lie too.

"I don't think we were ever not," he said, finally. Quietly. His voice sounded like it had been dragged behind a car. "I think we were broken the whole time and we were just — loud enough to cover it."

His hand moved. Not much. Just enough that his knuckles brushed Bee's hip — an accident that wasn't one, a point of contact so small it could be denied if it needed to be.

He didn't deny it.

"You're going to leave in the morning," he said. Not cruel. Not even accusatory. Just the flatness of someone stating a weather forecast. "And I'm going to let you. And then we're going to not talk about this for another eleven months, or you're going to text me at 2 AM on a Thursday and I'm going to answer this time, and either way we end up back here."

He turned his head. Looked at Bee's face against his shoulder — the closed eyes, the wrecked mouth, the expression that in anyone else he'd have called peaceful but in Bee he knew was just exhaustion wearing the same clothes.

"So the question isn't whether we're broken." His voice dropped. "The question is whether this is the only shape we come in."

He didn't move away. Didn't pull Bee closer. Just lay there in the dark with the buzzing light and the streetlight stripe and the smell of them soaking into sheets he'd have to wash tomorrow or else never wash again, and he wasn't sure yet which it would be.

"Stay," he said. Then, before Bee could answer: "I'm not asking you to stay. I'm telling you what I want. You can do whatever you want with it."

The crack in the ceiling looked like a river on a map. He breathed. Bee breathed. The flat was very quiet except for all the ways it wasn't.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: My hand finds yours on the mattress. I lace our fingers together, squeezing hard enough that it hurts. "I'm staying," I say, my voice rough. "Stop making it a fucking tragedy."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Something cracked across his face — not a smile, not quite, but the fault line where a smile would go if he remembered how. A sharp exhale through his nose that in another life, in a version of them that hadn't spent eleven months learning the precise weight of silence, might have been a laugh.

"It *is* a fucking tragedy," he said, but his fingers tightened around Bee's. Hard. Matching the pressure exactly, because that was what they'd always done — met each other force for force, never yielding first, even in tenderness. Especially in tenderness.

The pain in his knuckles felt correct. Felt like the truest thing that had happened all night, which was saying something, given what had just happened in this bed. He looked at their hands. His were longer. Bee's were stronger. He'd forgotten that. No — he hadn't forgotten it. He'd made himself stop thinking about it, which was different, and harder, and hadn't worked.

"You know I'll be worse in the morning," he said. Staring at the ceiling again. The river-crack. "You know I'll wake up and make coffee and not make you any and you'll know I did it on purpose and I'll know you know, and we'll have the same argument we always had except now it's got tonight in it too. More ammunition. For both of us."

His thumb moved against Bee's. Slow. Back and forth across the knuckle, a motion so small and so habitual that his body was doing it before his brain caught up, and when it did catch up he felt something hot and terrible behind his eyes that he would not — absolutely would not — allow to become what it was trying to become.

He swallowed. His jaw worked.

"I'll make you coffee," he said. Quiet. Like a concession of war. Like a treaty signed in a language he was out of practice speaking. "In the morning. I'll make you the coffee."

He pulled their joined hands onto his chest. Pressed Bee's knuckles against his sternum where his heart was doing something ragged and unsustainable. Let Bee feel it. The proof of damage. The proof that he was still in there, somewhere, under all the architecture he'd built to keep exactly this from happening.

"Stop making it a tragedy," he repeated, tasting Bee's words. "You come to my flat after eleven months, put my hand on your throat, and tell me to stop making it a tragedy."

He turned his head. Bee was right there. Inches. He could see the streetlight in Bee's eyes.

"Okay," he said. "Okay. It's not a tragedy. It's just us."

He didn't know if that was better or worse. He suspected Bee didn't either. He suspected that was the point — that they'd spent three years together and eleven months apart and still hadn't figured out what they were, only that they *were*, stubbornly and inexplicably, in spite of every good reason not to be.

The kitchen light buzzed. His heart beat against Bee's hand. He didn't let go.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I close my eyes, forehead still against your shoulder. "Just us is messy enough without you adding poetic commentary," I say, voice muffled against your skin.
