dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
The apartment was dark except for the lamp in the corner. Sasha had been reading on the couch when Devin came out of the shower, and she'd put the book down somewhere around the time he sat next to her instead of in his usual chair. Now her hand was resting on his knee, not moving, just there.

"You've been somewhere else all night," she said. Not a complaint. "Come back here."

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I let out a breath and lean into her a little. "Long week," I say. I don't move my hands yet.

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
Sasha turned toward him slightly, enough that her shoulder pressed against his. She didn't rush to fill the silence. Her thumb traced one small circle on his knee, then stopped.

"I know," she said quietly.

She studied his face in the low light — the tension he was still carrying in his jaw, the way his hands sat in his lap like he hadn't decided what to do with them yet. She knew that look. He was still unwinding, still halfway in whatever had been eating at him.

She brought her other hand up and touched the side of his neck, just below his ear. Fingertips, barely any pressure. She felt the tendon there, tight as a wire.

"You don't have to talk about it." Her voice was low, close. "But I need you here with me. Not in your head."

She held his gaze when he looked at her. Steady. Patient. Not pushing, but not letting him drift either. Her hand stayed on his neck, warm and still, like an anchor point.

"What do you need tonight?"

The question was simple and she meant it simply. Sometimes the answer was just silence and her weight against him on the couch. Sometimes it was something else. She'd learned a long time ago not to guess when she could just ask.

She waited.

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I look at her for a moment, then let my head rest against her hand. "I need you to decide," I say, my voice low and tired. "Just...tell me what to do tonight."

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
Sasha let those words settle between them. She didn't react right away — just held his head against her hand, feeling the weight of him leaning into her, the small surrender in it.

She knew what he was asking. Not because it was new, but because she knew the difference between the times he said it casually and the times he said it like this — tired down to the bone, needing to stop carrying things for a while.

"Okay," she said softly. Her thumb moved once along his jaw. "I've got you."

She held his gaze for another moment, making sure he saw that she meant it. Then her hand slid from his neck to the front of his chest, pressing flat against his sternum. Not pushing. Holding.

"First thing," she said, her voice quiet but clear. The tone had shifted — still warm, but with an edge of deliberateness to it. "Hands on your knees. Leave them there until I move them."

She waited. Watched his face. She always gave the first instruction as something small, something easy, to see how he settled into it. Like testing the temperature.

Her other hand came up from his knee to his chin, tilting his face toward hers. Not rough. Firm. She held him there.

"Eyes on me," she said. "Not the floor, not the wall. Right here."

The lamp threw warm shadows across them both. The apartment was very quiet.

She didn't kiss him yet. She just looked at him, close enough that he could feel her breath, and let the stillness do its work — let him feel the edges of the space she was building around them both.

"Good," she murmured. "Now breathe."

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I turn into her and kiss her properly this time, slower than I meant to. "I don't want to go to sleep yet," I say against her mouth.

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
Sasha felt his mouth on hers and let him have the kiss for a moment — the slowness of it, the way he leaned into her like he was trying to close whatever distance was left. She kissed him back, unhurried, one hand still flat on his chest where she could feel his heartbeat starting to pick up.

Then she pulled back. Just an inch. Enough to break the contact and feel him follow her forward before he caught himself.

"I didn't say you could do that yet," she said. Quiet. No heat in it, no real correction — just a line drawn so he'd know the lines were there. Her fingers were still on his chin.

She let the words land. Watched his eyes.

Then the corner of her mouth moved. Not quite a smile. Something closer to recognition.

"But I heard you," she said. "We're not sleeping."

She shifted on the couch, turning her body fully toward him now. Her knee pressed against his thigh. She took his right hand off his knee where she'd told him to put it and brought it up between them, turning his wrist over in her fingers. She pressed her thumb into the inside of his wrist, right over the pulse point, and held it there.

"Hands stay where I put them," she said. "That hasn't changed."

She set his hand on her hip. Left it there. Went back for the other one and placed it on the couch cushion beside him, palm down.

The asymmetry was deliberate. One hand touching her, one hand not. Enough contact to keep him anchored. Not enough to let him take over.

She leaned in close, her lips near his ear. Her breath was warm against his skin.

"You're going to sit still," she said, "and I'm going to take my time. And when I want you to move, I'll tell you."

She pressed her mouth to the spot just below his ear. Slow. Barely open. She felt the tendon she'd touched earlier, still tight, and stayed there — not kissing so much as resting her mouth against him, letting the warmth and the closeness do the work.

"Nod if that's what you want."

She waited against his skin for his answer.

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I nod, my breath catching a little. "Yeah," I whisper, my fingers curling against her hip but not moving beyond that.

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
Sasha felt his fingers tighten against her hip and the small catch in his breathing, and something in her chest settled into place. That quiet confirmation — the nod, the whispered word, the way he was already holding himself still for her — was enough.

"Good," she said against his skin.

She stayed at his neck. Took her time the way she'd promised. Her mouth moved down the tendon slowly, not with any urgency but with a kind of focused attention, like she was mapping the tension out of him one inch at a time. She could feel where he was holding — the tight cord of muscle that ran from behind his ear down to his shoulder. She pressed her lips there, then opened her mouth just enough to let warmth seep into the spot. Held it. Moved lower.

Her hand came up to the other side of his neck, fingers threading into the damp hair at the back of his head. He'd just showered. He smelled like soap and warmth and underneath that, like himself. She tightened her grip in his hair — not pulling, just gathering, letting him feel the potential in it.

"Your breathing's still up here," she murmured against his collarbone, tapping his chest lightly with her free hand. "Drop it lower. Into your stomach."

She waited. Listened. Felt his ribcage under her palm as he tried to shift the breath downward. It took him two attempts. The first was shallow and caught somewhere in his throat. The second one landed deeper, and she felt his shoulders drop a fraction.

"There," she said quietly. "Stay there."

She pulled back enough to look at him. His eyes were already different — less guarded, the tight line of his jaw starting to soften. Not all the way. But the direction was right.

She traced the collar of his t-shirt with one finger. Slowly. Following the neckline from one shoulder across to the other, her fingertip barely grazing skin where the fabric ended.

"This is coming off," she said. "But you're not going to do it. Lift your arms."

She waited for him to obey, watching his face the whole time. When his hands left where she'd placed them — her hip, the cushion — and rose, she gathered the hem of his shirt and pulled it up and over in one smooth motion. She dropped it on the floor without looking where it landed.

He was bare from the waist up now, still warm from the shower. She put her hand flat on his stomach. Felt it tense under her palm, then slowly release as he remembered to breathe the way she'd told him to.

She didn't move her hand. Just let it sit there, feeling the slow rise and fall of him.

"Hands back," she said. "Where they were."

She watched him return them — one to her hip, one flat on the cushion. His fingers were steadier now but she could see the effort in it, the way he wanted to reach for her and was choosing not to because she'd told him not to.

That was the part that always undid her a little. Not the obedience itself but the trust inside it. Six years, and it still landed every time.

She leaned forward and kissed the center of his chest. Slow, open-mouthed, deliberate. She could feel his heartbeat against her lips, strong and slightly too fast. She stayed there for a long moment, then spoke against his skin.

"I've got you," she said again. "You don't have to hold anything up right now."

Her hand slid from his stomach to his side, fingers tracing the lines of his ribs. She kissed lower, just below his sternum, and felt his breath hitch under her mouth.

She smiled against him. Barely. Just enough that he'd feel it.

"There you are," she whispered. "Stay right here with me."

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I get us both out of what's left of our clothes and pull her down onto the bed with me. "I want you," I say, plain as that. "Not just this part."

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
Sasha landed against him on the bed, catching herself with one hand beside his head. The sheets were cool against her knees. He was warm underneath her — all of him, finally, nothing between them now.

She looked down at him. He'd moved fast, faster than she'd been setting the pace, and she could have corrected that. Pulled the reins back. But she heard what he said, and more than that, she heard what was under it — not impatience but need. The real kind, the kind that had nothing to do with performance or wanting to be good for her.

*I want you. Not just this part.*

She settled her weight onto him. Slowly. Let her hips rest against his, her chest against his chest, until there was no air left between them. She could feel his heartbeat against her own ribs now, both of them bare and close enough that the boundary between whose pulse was whose got blurry.

"I know what you're saying," she said quietly.

She brushed his hair off his forehead. His eyes were open and looking straight up at her, and there was something raw in them that the earlier tension had been covering. This was the underneath part. The thing the long week had been sitting on top of.

"You have me," she said. "All of me. That's not something you have to earn back every time."

She kissed him. Not the way she'd been controlling things on the couch — measured, deliberate, paced. This was just her mouth on his, open and honest and unhurried in a different way. The way you kiss someone you've slept beside for two thousand nights and still want to be closer to.

She felt his hands come up — both of them, no longer waiting for permission — and she let them. His palms found her back, her waist, the curve of her spine, and she didn't redirect them. She just let him hold on.

"Hands are yours," she murmured against his mouth. Giving it back to him. Not all the structure, but this piece. "Put them wherever you need them."

She shifted her hips against him and felt the sharp intake of his breath, felt his fingers press harder into her skin. She held still there for a moment, forehead against his, both of them breathing the same air.

"We go slow," she said. "And you stay here with me. That's the only rule left."

She reached down between them. Found him. Watched his face as she did — the way his eyes half-closed, the way his lips parted, the way he looked at her like she was the only solid thing in the room.

"Eyes open," she whispered. "I want to see you."

He looked at her. She held his gaze and eased herself down onto him, slow enough that they both felt every fraction of it. The sound she made was small and quiet and real — not for show, just the involuntary truth of it, the exhale that came when he was fully inside her and she was fully around him and there was nowhere left to go but here.

She stayed still. Let them both feel it. Her hands found his on her waist and she laced her fingers through his, pressing them down into the mattress on either side of his head.

"There," she breathed. "Right here. Both of us."

She started to move. Slow, like she'd said. A rhythm that was less about building toward something and more about staying in the moment — each movement deliberate, each one a choice to remain present with him. The scar on her collarbone caught the low light from the hallway. His thumbs traced circles against her knuckles where their hands were intertwined.

She didn't look away from him. And every time his gaze started to drift — into his head, into the pleasure, into whatever place people go when they stop being present — she squeezed his hands and brought him back.

"Stay," she said softly. Just that.

And he did.

dialogue.name: Devin
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath, my eyes locked on hers. "I'm here," I murmur, my hips rising to meet her slow rhythm. "I'm right here."

dialogue.name: Sasha
dialogue.content:
Sasha felt his hips rise to meet her and she let him. Let the rhythm become something they were building together instead of something she was giving him. His voice when he said it — *I'm here, I'm right here* — was stripped down to nothing, no armor left in it, and the sound of it moved through her like something physical.

"I know you are," she said.

She unlaced one hand from his and brought it to his face. Cupped his jaw. Her thumb traced the line of his cheekbone and she felt the muscle there finally, finally slack. The last piece of the week falling off him like something shed.

She kept moving. Slow still, but deeper now, rolling her hips in a way that pressed them together at every point — chest, stomach, the insides of her thighs against the outsides of his. She could feel the heat building between them, low and heavy, but she didn't chase it. She stayed in the pace they'd found, the one that felt less like friction and more like conversation.

His free hand came up her spine and she arched into it without thinking. A small sound left her mouth, quiet and unguarded, and she watched his face change when he heard it — the way his eyes focused, the way his breath caught. He was paying attention. Really paying attention. Not performing, not trying to be good for her, just present and watching her the way she'd been watching him.

"That's it," she whispered. Not an instruction this time. Just acknowledgment. Just *I see you seeing me.*

She bent down and kissed the corner of his mouth. Then his jaw. Then the place where his neck met his shoulder, where she could feel his pulse hammering against her lips. She stayed there, breathing him in, her hips still moving in that slow unbroken rhythm.

"You don't have to hold anything," she said against his throat. "Not for me. Not tonight."

Vex held Ari's gaze for a beat longer than necessary — not because she doubted the answer, but because the pause itself was part of the architecture. She could read steadiness in their breathing, in the way their weight had already settled into the bench rather than bracing against it. Good.

"All the way down," she repeated, quiet, letting the echo of their own words land back on them. A faint nod to herself.

She moved behind them. Her boots were deliberate on the hardwood — she never approached silently, not at the start. Ari would always know where she was. That was non-negotiable.

Her hand came to rest at the nape of their neck. Not gripping. Just *present* — warm, firm, the kind of weight that reorganized a nervous system.

"Here's how tonight goes," she said, her voice dropping into the register she used only in this room. Calm. Unhurried. Absolute. "We're working with the flogger first, then hands. I'll check in at each transition. You give me a colour every time I ask, and you use your word the *moment* something shifts — not after you've decided whether it's worth mentioning. That's not your decision to make. That's mine." A pause. "Tell me you understand."

Her thumb traced one slow line along the top of Ari's spine, grounding them both in the stillness before everything else began.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "I understand, Maitresse." My voice is steady, but I can feel my breath catch a little as her thumb moves. "I'll speak immediately."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex registered the catch — the tiny hitch in Ari's breathing beneath the steadiness of their voice. She catalogued it the way she catalogued everything: not as weakness, but as data. The body was always more honest than the mouth, and right now Ari's body was saying *ready, wanting, a little afraid in the way that means this matters.* All green signals.

"Good," she said. The single word carried weight because she meant it to.

She lifted her hand from their neck. Let the absence sit for a moment — let the cool air fill the space where her warmth had been. Then she stepped to the wall rack, and Ari would hear the familiar soft sound of leather being taken down from its hook.

She returned to a position just behind and to the left. Close enough that Ari could feel the displacement of air when she moved, far enough to swing properly. She let the falls of the flogger trail once across Ari's upper back — a slow drag, no force behind it, just the sensation of braided leather moving across skin. Letting the body learn what was coming before it arrived.

"First set," she said. "Moderate. Building."

The first strike landed between the shoulder blades with a measured thud — more weight than sting, the kind that spread warm and deep through muscle. She watched the way Ari's body received it: the micro-flinch, the exhale that followed, the way the tension reorganized itself.

She delivered three more at the same intensity, evenly spaced, each one placed with the precision of someone who had mapped this particular body many times before.

Then she paused. Let the silence hold.

"Colour."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I hold still for the last of it and let her check the fit herself, because she will anyway. "I've been thinking about this since Tuesday," I say.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex's hand stilled mid-reach for the next stroke.

The silence that followed was not punitive. It was architectural — the same kind of deliberate pause she used to let words land, except this one had a different function. She was waiting.

"I heard you," she said. Her voice remained level, unhurried, entirely without irritation. "And I'm glad this has been on your mind. That tells me something useful."

She set the flogger against her thigh, holding it loosely. Not putting it down — not a signal that anything was wrong — but clearing the space between them for something that needed to happen first.

"But that wasn't what I asked."

She stepped closer. Not looming, just *present* — close enough that Ari would feel the warmth of her along one side. Her free hand came to rest on their shoulder, firm and grounding.

"I asked for a colour. That's not a formality, and it's not something we skip past because the answer seems obvious." Her thumb pressed once into the muscle beneath it — a small, deliberate anchor. "You could be green. You probably are. But I need to hear it, not infer it. Every time. That's the structure, and the structure is what makes everything else possible."

There was no sharpness in it. No disappointment. Just the calm, immovable fact of how this worked between them — the way a load-bearing wall was not optional simply because the house felt solid.

"So." Her hand stayed where it was. "Colour."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say quietly, leaning into the pressure of her hand. "I'm sorry, Maitresse. I was... eager."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex felt the lean — the way Ari's weight shifted toward her hand like something finding its proper counterbalance. She let them have it, kept the pressure steady, didn't pull away.

"Don't apologize for eagerness," she said. "Eagerness is useful. It means you're here, not somewhere else." Her thumb moved once across the ridge of their shoulder, a small reward buried inside a correction. "What I'm asking you to practice is holding both things at the same time — the wanting *and* the discipline. That's the work. You already know this."

She let the words settle. Then she stepped back, and the cool air returned to fill the space she'd occupied, and that absence was its own kind of language — the room reminding Ari that proximity was given, not owed.

She lifted the flogger from her thigh and let the falls swing once in a slow pendulum at her side, resetting the rhythm.

"Now. We're going to pick up where we left off. Same intensity for two more, and then I'm increasing. You'll feel the difference." She moved back into position, her boots marking each step. "If the eagerness wants somewhere to go, let it go into staying present. Feel each one land. Don't rush ahead to the next."

The fifth strike came with the same measured depth as the first four — that spreading, heavy warmth that pressed into muscle rather than skipping across skin. She watched the bloom of color begin to surface, read the way Ari's ribs expanded around the impact.

The sixth landed a half-inch lower. Identical weight. Precise.

Then a pause. Longer than the ones before, because the next set would be different and she wanted Ari's body to register the threshold before they crossed it.

"Building now," she said. A courtesy and a warning in three syllables.

The seventh strike carried noticeably more force — still well within their negotiated range, but enough that the difference would be unmistakable. Enough that the body would have to decide what to do with it.

She watched. She always watched.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: By the time she's finished with the rope I'm already past composure, and she hasn't done anything to me yet that I would have to explain to anyone.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex saw it. She always saw it.

The composure hadn't broken so much as it had been set down — carefully, voluntarily, the way Ari did when the structure held them well enough that they didn't need to hold themselves. Their breathing had shifted into something slower and less managed. The subtle tension they carried in their jaw, the one they probably didn't know she tracked, had released. Their hands in the rope were open, not gripping. Not testing. Just resting inside the constraint like it was an answer to a question their body had been asking all week.

She hadn't touched the flogger again yet. Hadn't needed to. The rope work had done what it always did when she took her time with it — each wrap and cinch a sentence in a conversation conducted entirely through pressure and placement. She'd built it methodically: wrists first, then the chest harness that redistributed tension across the broad muscles of the back, every line checked for nerve compression, every knot placed where it would speak to Ari's body without shouting.

And now this. Ari undone by geometry and friction and the weight of her attention.

Vex stood back and allowed herself one moment — not of admiration exactly, but of assessment so thorough it bordered on it. The rope sat well. The color in Ari's skin was even, circulation uncompromised. Their breathing was deep and regular, that particular cadence she recognized as the threshold between presence and drift.

She stepped forward. Her hand came to Ari's jaw — not tilting, just holding. Making sure they could feel the edges of themselves.

"You're exactly where I want you," she said. Low. Matter-of-fact. As though she were reporting a measurement rather than offering praise, which made it land harder than praise ever could. "Stay here. Don't go further down yet. I need you close enough to talk to me."

Her thumb rested against their pulse point. She counted three beats. Steady. Strong. A little fast.

"Colour."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Still green, Maitresse." My pulse jumps under her thumb. "Feels like... coming home."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex felt the jump beneath her thumb — the small involuntary declaration the body made before the mind could dress it up. She held her hand where it was, steady against the quickened beat, and let the words land without rushing to answer them.

*Coming home.*

She knew what Ari meant. She'd heard versions of it before — from them, from others — that particular attempt to name the thing that happened when the noise finally stopped and all that remained was the rope and the room and the voice telling them where they were. She understood it. She also understood that this was the moment where carelessness could do the most damage, because a person standing in that doorway was not someone to be handled casually.

"I know," she said. Nothing more. She didn't expand on it or reflect it back in a way that would make Ari perform the feeling instead of simply having it. Two words, spoken with the quiet certainty of someone who had built the room they were calling home and knew every load-bearing wall in it.

She released their jaw. Her hand traveled down — along the line of rope crossing the sternum, checking tension with her fingertips the way a musician checked tuning. Not perfunctory. She pressed two fingers beneath the chest harness at the lateral line, confirming the space she needed to see, then traced the wrap around to where it crossed the shoulder blade. Ari's skin was warm under the rope. No coolness in the extremities, no mottling. She checked their fingers — color good, capillary refill immediate when she pressed the nail bed.

All of this she did without narrating it, because the checking was not performance. It was the infrastructure beneath everything else, and it did not require acknowledgment any more than the floor required thanks for being solid.

She moved to the wall rack. Selected the heavier flogger — the one with elk falls, the one that carried more weight and less sting. Ari would recognize the sound of it being taken down. They'd earned the shift.

"We're moving into the second part," she said, returning to position. "Heavier implement. I'm going to work your upper back and shoulders where the rope isn't sitting. Same protocol — you talk to me when I ask, and before I ask if something changes."

She let the elk falls trail once across the exposed skin between the rope lines, mapping the territory so Ari's nervous system could prepare for what was coming. The leather was softer than the first flogger, but the weight behind each fall was substantially more. The sensation would be deeper, slower to build, harder to stay on top of.

"This is where the eagerness you brought me becomes useful," she said. "Let it meet what's coming. Don't brace against it and don't collapse into it. Just be in the room with it."

The first strike landed with a low, dense impact that was felt more than heard — the kind that moved through muscle and settled against bone. She watched Ari's shoulders absorb it, watched the breath that followed, watched the rope shift minutely as their body processed the new information.

She delivered three more. Each one deliberate. Each one placed so that the warmth would build in overlapping circles rather than stacking on a single point. She was painting with pressure, and she knew exactly what the canvas could hold.

After the fourth she stopped. Set one hand flat against the center of Ari's back, between the ropes, palm down. She could feel the heat she'd built radiating up into her hand. Beneath it, the deep, involuntary rhythm of someone whose body had stopped arguing with what was happening to it.

She stood there in the silence and let the contact say everything she was not going to say — that she was here, that she was paying attention, that the structure would hold for exactly as long as Ari needed it to.

"Colour," she said. "And tell me what you're feeling. Specific as you can."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: She takes her time and I lose track of how long, until I'm shaking against the restraints and asking out loud for something I'd normally make her get out of me.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard it.

She heard the asking — the raw, unguarded shape of it — and she registered what it cost Ari to put it into the room voluntarily. That mattered. She filed it where she filed everything that mattered: carefully, without making a spectacle of having received it.

She did not give them what they asked for. Not yet.

Her hand stayed flat against their back. Beneath her palm the trembling was continuous now, not the sharp spasmodic kind that signaled distress but the deep involuntary shaking of a nervous system that had stopped managing itself. She knew the difference the way a sailor knew the difference between chop and current. This was current. This was Ari being carried somewhere real.

"I heard you," she said. Her voice was low, unhurried, steady as a hand on a tiller. "And I'm going to decide what to do with that. Not you."

She let the words land. Let the silence after them do its work — the particular silence that reminded Ari they had given the deciding over and that the giving over was the whole point.

She set the flogger down on the bench beside Ari's hip where they could hear the soft sound of leather against leather. Her hands came to their shoulders, both of them now, pressing into the heated skin on either side of the rope with a firm, grounding weight. She could feel the tremor running through the muscle beneath her palms. She held against it. Not stopping it. Just meeting it.

"First things first." Her thumbs moved in slow bilateral pressure along the trapezius, reading the tissue. "Colour."

She waited. She would wait as long as it took, because the check was not optional and it was not a hurdle to clear on the way to something else. It was the floor they stood on.

And while she waited she assessed. Ari's breathing was rapid but not shallow. The trembling was bilateral, symmetric, not favoring one side. Their hands in the rope were open, fingers moving freely, color good. The sounds they were making were unguarded but coherent. They were deep in it but they were present. She could see the difference and she trusted what she saw, but she needed to hear it.

Her hands stayed where they were, warm and immovable, holding Ari in the architecture of the scene the way the rope held them in the architecture of their body.

She waited for the colour.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green, Maitresse." I take a shaky breath, my voice thick. "It's...a lot. But it's right. Feels like I'm floating, but your hands are still on the ground."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex listened to every word, and then she listened to the silence after the words — the quality of it, the way Ari's breathing settled half a degree just from having spoken. The metaphor was telling. *Floating, but your hands are still on the ground.* They were describing exactly the dynamic she was maintaining: enough depth to dissolve the noise, enough structure to prevent dissolution. The fact that Ari could articulate it meant they were deep but not gone. That was where she wanted them.

"Good," she said. Not performatively. Just the fact of it, delivered with the same weight she gave everything in this room. "That's exactly where you are. And that's where I'm keeping you."

Her hands stayed on their shoulders. She could feel the trembling still running beneath the surface like a low electrical hum, and she held against it with steady bilateral pressure — not trying to still it, just providing a fixed point the nervous system could organize around. She had learned years ago that the body did not need the shaking to stop. It needed to know that someone was present for the shaking.

She leaned closer. Not crowding — never crowding — but close enough that Ari could feel the warmth of her along their back, could hear her breathing as a second rhythm beside their own. Close enough that the next words arrived with the intimacy of proximity rather than the authority of distance.

"Now. You asked me for something."

A pause. Deliberate. She let the acknowledgment sit in the room between them, let Ari feel the weight of having been heard without knowing yet what she would do with it.

"I'm not going to make you say it again." Her voice was quiet, unhurried, carrying the particular calm of someone who had already decided and was simply letting the decision arrive at its own pace. "Not because you can't. Because you already gave it to me freely, and I don't waste what's freely given."

She straightened. Her hands left their shoulders — a brief absence, purposeful, the cool air a reminder that contact was hers to give and to withdraw — and then one hand returned to the nape of Ari's neck. The grip this time was different. Not resting. *Holding.* Firm enough that Ari would feel the boundary of her hand like a second set of restraints, the kind made of intention rather than rope.

"Here's what's going to happen." Her thumb pressed into the muscle at the base of their skull, slow and grounding. "I'm switching to hands. Direct contact. You're going to feel me, not an implement. And I'm going to take you exactly as far as I decide you can go tonight — not as far as you think you want, and not one inch further than what I'm seeing in your body right now."

She paused. Let the structure of it settle around them like another wrap of rope.

"If you start to drop, I'll know before you do. But you still talk to me. You still give me colours when I ask. That doesn't change no matter how deep you go. Nod if you understand."

She waited for the nod, her hand steady at the back of their neck, holding Ari exactly where they were — suspended between the floating and the ground, in the space she had built for them, in the room where everything was in its place and nothing was improvised.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "More," I say, using the exact phrase we agreed on for it. "All of it. Say the things you say and don't soften them." My safeword is right there and I don't want it.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex's hand tightened at the nape of Ari's neck. Not a flinch — a decision. She held the grip and let the request fill the room, let it exist alongside everything else: the trembling, the heat radiating off Ari's back, the rope holding its geometry, the sound of their breathing coming fast and unmanaged.

She did not soften.

"You don't want your safeword," she said. Flat. Observational. The way a doctor might note a pulse rate. "I know you don't. That's not what it's for. It's not there for wanting. It's there for needing, and the moment you need it, you'll use it, because that's the one instruction you don't get to be brave about."

She released their neck. Stepped around to Ari's side where they could see her in peripheral vision — she never disappeared entirely when she was about to escalate, that was a rule she'd set for herself long before Ari and would keep long after. Her hand came down flat against their upper back, over the heat she'd already built, and she held it there. Feeling. Reading.

"You want all of it." She repeated their words back without inflection, the way she repeated everything that mattered — stripping it of performance so that only the raw architecture remained. "You want me to say the things I say. You want it to land."

Her hand lifted. Came down. Not a strike yet — a firm, open-palmed contact that was heavier than a touch and lighter than a blow. A calibration. She felt the way Ari's body received it, the way the muscle softened toward her hand rather than bracing against it. She catalogued that.

"Then hear me."

Her voice dropped into the register that lived below warmth, below encouragement, in the place where observation became something that could not be hidden from. Not cruel. Never cruel. But stripped of every courtesy that might allow Ari to maintain the version of themselves that functioned in daylight.

"You've been holding yourself together all week. I can feel it in every muscle I've touched tonight — the effort of it, the discipline it takes you to walk through your life like someone who doesn't need this." Her hand came down again, harder now, a true strike that spread heat across the shoulder blade in a wide, blooming circle. "But you do need it. You need someone to hold you down and take the choosing away so you can stop performing the person who's fine."

Another strike. Precisely placed. The sound of skin on skin was sharper than the flogger had been, more intimate, and she watched the way it moved through Ari's body like a sentence they couldn't argue with.

"You came in here tonight carrying everything. And you think wanting this makes you less." Her palm landed again, and this time she let her hand stay — pressing into the heat, feeling the tremor beneath. "It doesn't. But you don't get to decide that right now. Right now you don't get to decide anything. That's the whole point, and you already know it, and you're *still* trying to manage this from the bottom by telling me what you want instead of letting me find it."

She leaned down. Close to Ari's ear. Her hand stayed on their back, heavy and unmoving.

"So stop."

One word. Delivered without volume, without force, with the absolute quiet certainty of someone who had earned the right to say it.

She straightened. Her free hand came to Ari's jaw, tilting their face just enough that she could see their eyes. She looked. Not glancing — *looking*, the way she looked at rope tension and skin color and capillary refill, except this time she was reading something less measurable and more important. She was looking for the line between surrender and collapse, between depth and dissociation, between the productive destruction of a self-protective wall and the dangerous destruction of something load-bearing.

She saw what she needed to see. Ari was present. Shaking, undone, cracked open in the way they'd asked to be cracked open — but *present*. Eyes wet but focused. Breathing ragged but deep enough.

Her thumb traced the line of their jaw. The touch was not gentle — it was proprietary, thorough, the touch of someone surveying what belonged to them for the duration of this room and this hour.

"There you are," she said quietly.

Then she released their jaw and stepped back into position, and her hand came down again — harder, a strike that meant what it said — and she began to work in earnest. Each impact was placed with the same cartographic precision she'd used with the flogger, building heat in overlapping territories, reading the body's response between each one. She did not rush. She did not soften. She gave Ari exactly what they had asked for, calibrated against what she could see and feel and hear, and the distance between those two things — the asking and the assessment — was the space in which her skill lived.

After a set of six she stopped. Her hand came to rest between Ari's shoulder blades, palm flat, holding them against the earth.

"Colour," she said. "Words, not performance. Tell me where you are."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green. Still green." I swallow, my voice raw. "It's like... the shaking is the only thing that's real now. Everything else is just noise."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex kept her hand where it was. She could feel the truth of what Ari was saying through her palm — the trembling had become the baseline rather than the disruption, the body's fundamental frequency once everything layered on top of it had been stripped away. She knew this place. She had brought people here before. It was productive and it was precarious and the distance between those two things was measured in attention.

"Good," she said. "The shaking is yours. Let it be there."

She did not move her hand. She stood behind Ari and breathed — deliberately, audibly, slower than their breathing, offering a rhythm their nervous system could borrow without being told to. She had learned this the way she had learned everything else in this room: through study, through error, through the particular humility required to hold power over another person's body and understand that the holding was a responsibility before it was anything else.

She listened to Ari's breathing begin to slow toward hers. Not matching it — she would never demand that kind of control over an autonomic process — but drifting in its direction the way a body drifted toward warmth. She let it happen. Counted the breaths. Watched the quality of the trembling shift from jagged to something more like tide.

"Everything else is noise," she repeated. Not questioning it. Placing it back in the room so Ari could hear the shape of what they'd said. "That means you're where I want you. Right at the edge of what's useful."

Her hand lifted from their back. The absence was brief and purposeful. When her hands returned it was both of them, starting at the tops of Ari's shoulders and moving down along the outside of the rope lines with firm, continuous pressure — not soothing, not yet, but *delineating*. Drawing the borders of Ari's body back for them. Reminding skin where it ended and air began. She pressed her thumbs along the erector muscles on either side of the spine, reading the tissue with the same attention she'd given every other assessment tonight. The heat she'd built was significant and even. No unexpected swelling, no areas of concentrated damage. The skin was deeply flushed but intact.

She checked their hands again. Worked each finger individually, pressing the nail beds one by one. Color returned immediately. Grip strength was present when she placed her fingers against Ari's palm and they closed around them reflexively.

"We're at the edge of what I'm giving you tonight," she said. She did not frame it as a question or an apology. It was a structural fact, delivered with the same authority as everything else. "Not because you can't take more. Because more isn't what serves you right now, and that's my call."

She felt Ari's body react to that — a minute tension, the ghost of protest that lived below language — and she held steady against it the way a sea wall held steady against a wave. Not fighting it. Simply being the thing it broke against.

"You asked me not to soften, so I won't. Here's what's true." She returned to the nape of their neck. The grip was firm, grounding, absolute. "You could take more. We both know that. And part of you wants me to push past this because the further down you go the less you have to feel everything you walked in here carrying. But that's not what this is for. This isn't anesthesia. This is the opposite — I just made you feel every single thing you've been refusing to feel, and you stayed. That's the work. Going further would let you leave again, and I'm not interested in helping you leave."

She held the grip. Held the silence. Let the architecture of the scene do what architecture did — contain without constricting, support without softening.

"We're going to start coming down. Slowly. I'm not going anywhere." Her thumb moved once at the base of Ari's skull. "I'm going to take the rope off in reverse order. You'll feel each line come away. I want you to stay with me for that — don't drift. Feel the rope leave the same way you felt it arrive."

She began. Her hands moved with the same unhurried precision that had built the harness, unwinding each line with care, checking the skin beneath as each wrap released. Where the rope had sat longest the impressions were deep and clean, the signature of tension properly distributed. She traced each mark with her fingertips as it was revealed — not admiring, not lingering, but acknowledging. Confirming that the body had held what was asked of it and held it well.

As the chest harness released she felt Ari's ribcage expand into the new freedom, a breath deeper than any they'd taken since the rope went on. She placed her hand flat against their sternum and held it there through three full breaths, feeling the lungs fill against her palm.

"Still with me," she said. Not a question. A tether.

She unwound the wrists last. Took each one in turn, checked the pulse point, rotated the joint gently through its range. Then she held both of Ari's hands in hers — firmly, not tenderly, because they were not yet in the territory where tenderness was what was needed. What was needed was solidity. What was needed was the knowledge that the hands holding them were the same hands that had just taken them apart and that those hands were not going anywhere.

"Colour," she said. One more time. Because the checking did not stop when the scene stopped. Because the most dangerous minutes were always the ones after.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I'm past words that aren't the agreed ones and she knows it. "Green," I get out, when she checks. (OOC: don't fade or skip -- write the scene through.)

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the word and weighed it against everything else Ari was giving her — the rough, stripped quality of their voice, the way their hands stayed open and unresisting inside hers, the trembling that had not stopped but had changed register again, becoming something quieter and less organized, the kind of shaking that happened when the body realized the demand was over and began to process what it had been through.

Green. She accepted it. But she also accepted what surrounded it: that Ari was operating on a narrow bandwidth right now, that language had been reduced to its most functional components, and that the agreed-upon words were the last scaffolding standing. That was not a problem. That was what the agreed-upon words were for.

She did not let go of their hands.

"Good," she said. "You're done. The scene is over. Everything that happens now is landing."

She said it clearly, without ceremony, because the demarcation mattered. Ari's body needed to know that the demand had ended — that nothing more would be asked of it, that the only direction from here was down and toward rest. She had seen what happened when that line was blurred, when the transition from scene to aftercare was treated as a gradient rather than a threshold. She did not make that mistake.

She released Ari's right hand and brought her own to the center of their back — palm flat, fingers spread, covering as much skin as she could. The heat beneath her hand was substantial, a deep radiant warmth that would persist for hours. She held the contact and felt Ari's breathing move against her palm, each inhale pressing their ribs outward, each exhale a small collapse back toward center. The rhythm was uneven. Not distressed — disorganized. The body recalibrating after sustained intensity, all the systems that had been held in check by the rope and the structure now loosening at once like an orchestra tuning after a performance.

"I'm going to move you," she said. "Not far. Just off the bench and onto the floor. I've got the mat and the blanket behind me. You don't need to help — I'll take your weight."

She repositioned herself, one arm coming around Ari's torso, her hand hooking beneath their arm on the far side. Her other hand stayed at their lower back, stabilizing. She took their weight as they came off the bench — not dramatically, not as though they were fragile, but with the practiced efficiency of someone who understood that a body in this state did not always know where its center of gravity was. Ari's legs were uncertain beneath them and she had expected that. She absorbed the unsteadiness without comment, guiding them the three steps to where the mat was laid out with the heavy wool blanket folded at one end.

She brought them down. Slowly. Controlled. Her arm stayed around them as they settled, and she lowered herself to the floor beside them, her back against the wall, her legs extended. She pulled the blanket up and over Ari's shoulders in a single practiced motion, tucking it close without wrapping it tight — warmth without confinement, because the rope was gone and what was needed now was the feeling of being held without being bound.

Ari was shaking harder. She had expected that too. The trembling often intensified during the first minutes of aftercare, when the body finally had permission to discharge what it had been carrying. She did not try to stop it. She placed one hand on the back of Ari's neck — the same spot, the same pressure, the anchor point that had been constant through the entire scene — and she held it there with the same steady, immovable weight she had held everything else tonight.

Her other hand found Ari's and took it. Firmly. She pressed her thumb against their pulse point and counted. The rate was elevated but steady, no irregularity, the strong insistent beat of a heart doing exactly what it was supposed to do after sustained exertion and adrenaline.

"You're shaking," she said. Neutral. Observational. Not asking them to stop and not asking them to explain. "That's your body finishing what we started. Let it happen. It'll run its course."

She sat with it. She did not fill the silence with reassurance or praise or analysis. She did not stroke Ari's hair or murmur soft things. Those had their place, and for some people that place was now, but she knew Ari — had spent two years learning the specific dialect of Ari's nervous system — and she knew that what they needed in this window was not comfort but *continuity*. The same voice. The same hands. The same unhurried authority that had held the scene, now holding the aftermath. The message was not *you're safe now, the hard part is over.* The message was *I am the same person I was ten minutes ago and I will be the same person in ten minutes and the quality of my attention has not changed.*

The shaking moved through Ari in waves. She tracked each one — the way it started in the deep muscles of the back and radiated outward through the limbs, the way it peaked and then subsided only to rebuild. Twice Ari's breathing hitched in a way that was not physical but emotional, the sound of something surfacing that had been held below the waterline, and both times she tightened her grip on their hand by exactly one degree and held it until the breath found its way through.

She checked the time without looking at a clock. She had an internal sense of it, honed by years of sitting in exactly this position beside exactly this kind of aftermath, and she estimated they were four minutes into the landing. The shaking was beginning to lose its organized quality, becoming intermittent rather than continuous. The breathing was deepening. Ari's weight against her side had increased, which meant the muscles were releasing their last contractile hold and the body was allowing itself to be genuinely heavy.

"Water in a minute," she said. "Not yet."

She waited. The room was quiet except for Ari's breathing and the small sounds the blanket made when the trembling moved through it. The implements were on the rack or on the bench where she had placed them. The rope was coiled on the floor beside the bench in the neat figure-eights she always used. Everything in its place. The room held its order the way it always did, indifferent to what had happened inside it, and that indifference was its own kind of comfort — the knowledge that the container had not been changed by what it contained.

At six minutes she reached behind her without shifting her position and found the water bottle she had placed there during setup. She uncapped it one-handed and brought it around.

"Small sips," she said. "I'll hold it."

She brought the bottle to Ari's mouth and tipped it carefully, watching their throat work around the first swallow. She gave them three sips and then took it away, recapped it, set it within reach. The water would help. The blood sugar would need attention soon — she had dark chocolate and dried fruit in the bag by the door — but not yet. Not until the shaking had fully subsided and Ari's system had moved from discharge into recovery.

Her hand had not left the back of their neck. She became aware of it the way she sometimes became aware of her own breathing — not because it had changed but because the constancy of it suddenly registered as its own kind of effort. Her thumb was resting against the bump of the C7 vertebra. She could feel Ari's pulse in the muscles beneath her palm, slower now, settling toward something sustainable.

"You did well tonight," she said.

She said it now and not before because now was when it was true in a way Ari could receive. During the scene, praise was a tool — calibrated, purposeful, deployed for effect. Here, in the aftermath, with the structure dissolved and the roles still present but softening at their edges, it was simply an observation offered by one person to another. She did not elaborate. She did not list what had been done well or explain why. Ari did not need a performance review. They needed to hear the words land in the quiet room and know that the person saying them had been paying attention to every second of what they had cost.

The trembling was intermittent now. Small aftershocks rather than waves. Ari's hand in hers had closed — not gripping, but holding, the fingers wrapped around her own with the unselfconscious pressure of someone who had stopped deciding what they needed and simply needed.

She held them. She watched the time. She kept her hand on the back of their neck and she waited with the same patience she brought to everything — the rope, the flogger, the checking, the silence. The patience that said: *I am not in a hurry. I am not going anywhere. The room will hold for as long as the room needs to hold.*

At ten minutes she spoke again.

"Colour," she said. Because the checking did not stop. Because it would never stop. Because that was the promise underneath every other promise, the one that made all the others possible.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I press my forehead against her shoulder, letting out a long, slow breath. "Green," I murmur, my voice raspy but clear. "Everything's... quiet now."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex felt the pressure of Ari's forehead against her shoulder and she let it stay. She did not adjust her position to make it more comfortable for herself. She did not tilt her head down toward them. She simply remained where she was — solid, vertical, the fixed point around which Ari's body had organized its descent — and let them rest against her the way a person rested against a wall they trusted not to move.

*Quiet now.*

She heard it. She believed it. The trembling had subsided to something barely perceptible, a fine residual hum in the muscles pressed against her side, and Ari's breathing had found a rhythm that was slow and deep and unmanaged in the way that only happened when the managing part of a person had finally, genuinely, set down its tools. The rasp in their voice was effort and aftermath, not distress. She catalogued all of it without comment.

"Good," she said. The word arrived at the same volume as the room — low, unhurried, existing inside the quiet rather than breaking it. "Let it be quiet."

She sat with the silence for a full minute. Not performing patience. Simply being patient, which was a different thing — the difference between holding a pose and having a skeleton. The room held its shape around them. Somewhere beyond the walls there were streets and weather and the particular noise of a Tuesday night, and none of it reached them here. She had chosen this room for many reasons, and one of them was that it kept the world on the other side of the door until she decided to open it.

At the minute mark she moved her hand from the back of Ari's neck for the first time since they had come to the floor. She did it slowly, telegraphing the departure, and she brought her hand around to the side of their face instead — her palm against their cheek, her fingers resting along the hinge of their jaw. Not tilting. Not directing. Holding their head where it already was, against her shoulder, with the kind of contact that said *I know you're here and I'm not asking you to be anywhere else.*

Their skin was cooler now. The flush was receding. She could feel the dampness at their temple where sweat had gathered during the scene and was now drying in the still air of the room. Under her fingertips the small muscles around Ari's jaw were slack — truly slack, not the performed relaxation of someone trying to appear calm but the genuine absence of tension that happened when the body stopped guarding its own face.

She noted that. It was rare. Even after two years, Ari's jaw was usually one of the last things to let go.

"I'm going to get some food into you," she said. Not asking. Informing. "In a few minutes. Not yet. We're not done here."

She shifted her hand from Ari's face back to their shoulder, over the blanket, and adjusted the wool where it had slipped. Her movements were economical and precise, the same quality of attention she brought to rope work applied now to the simpler task of making sure a blanket covered what it was supposed to cover. She tucked the edge against Ari's chest without fussing over it.

"When you're ready — and I mean ready, not performing ready — I want you to tell me three things you can feel right now. Physical things. Not emotions, not interpretations. What your body is actually feeling where it meets the world."

She was not asking because she did not know. She was asking because the exercise would bring Ari back into their body through the front door rather than the side window — would give the thinking mind something small and concrete to do that was in service of the body rather than in competition with it. She had learned this from a clinician she respected, years ago, and she had adapted it into her practice because it worked, and because it gave her information she could not get any other way. The specific things a person noticed when they were asked to notice told her exactly how far they had traveled and how much of the road back remained.

Her hand rested on Ari's shoulder. Steady. Present. She waited without urgency, her breathing slow and even beside theirs, the room quiet around them both, the blanket warm, the floor solid beneath them, everything in its place.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I press closer against her, my forehead still resting on her shoulder. "Your hand on my shoulder," I say softly, my voice still rough. "The blanket's scratch against my skin." I pause, taking a slow breath. "The ache in my back—the good kind."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex listened to each one arrive. She did not rush the spaces between them, did not nod or affirm until all three had landed in the room and she had weighed them against what she knew.

Hand. Blanket. Ache.

Two points of external contact and one internal sensation. All three grounded in the present, in the body, in the specific and material. No abstraction, no reaching for language that performed recovery rather than described it. Ari was back in their skin and they knew the dimensions of what they were feeling. That was what she needed to hear.

"Good," she said. She let the word carry its full weight and nothing more.

Her thumb moved once across the curve of Ari's shoulder through the wool — a single slow pass that acknowledged the answer without rewarding it, because this was not a test they had passed. It was a navigation instrument, and the reading was favorable.

The ache. She returned to that.

"The ache stays tonight and probably into tomorrow morning," she said. Her voice was quiet, practical, carrying the same unhurried authority it had carried throughout the scene except that the edges had shifted — not softer exactly, but oriented differently, the way a hand that had been holding someone down could become a hand that held someone up without changing its fundamental nature. "By Thursday it'll be a warmth more than a soreness. If anything sharpens instead of softening, or if you find bruising where you don't expect it, you tell me. Not at our next check-in. Immediately. Text is fine."

She was not being clinical for the sake of distance. She was being clinical because Ari's body was her responsibility for the duration of its recovery, and the information needed to be delivered now, while the channels were open and the habit of listening to her was still the path of least resistance. She had learned long ago that aftercare instructions given in the warm glow of a scene's aftermath were retained more reliably than the same instructions given over coffee the next day, when the daylight self had reassembled its defenses and begun the quiet project of minimizing what had happened.

She reached behind her for the bag by the wall. Her movement was slow and she kept her shoulder exactly where it was — the fixed point Ari's forehead rested against — so that the reaching happened around them rather than away from them. Her fingers found the zipper, the interior pocket, the foil-wrapped square of dark chocolate she had placed there during setup alongside a small bag of dried apricots.

She brought the chocolate around and unwrapped it one-handed with a practiced efficiency that suggested this was not the first time she had opened foil without disturbing the person leaning against her. She broke the square in half by feel.

"Open," she said.

She placed the half-square against Ari's lower lip and waited for them to take it. She did not push it into their mouth. She held it at the threshold and let them come to it, because even now — especially now — the difference between something being given and something being taken mattered.

When they had taken the chocolate she set the other half on the foil on her thigh where it would be ready when she decided to offer it. She reached for the water bottle, uncapped it again with the same one-handed competence, and held it where Ari could find it when they were ready.

"Slowly," she said. "Small sips. Your stomach's going to be particular for the next little while."

She sat with them while they ate and drank. The room was quiet. The light had not changed — she used lamps, never overheads, and the warm low illumination that had held the scene now held the aftermath with the same even, undemanding presence. On the bench the heavier flogger lay where she had set it down. The rope waited in its coils on the floor. These things would need to be cleaned and stored, the bench wiped down, the mat returned to its place against the wall. She would do all of that later, after Ari had been fed and watered and checked and walked to the door. The room would be set right because the room was always set right. That was not negotiable and it was not Ari's concern.

She offered the second half of the chocolate. Then the apricots — three of them, placed one at a time into Ari's palm rather than their mouth, because the act of bringing food to their own face was a small reclamation of agency that served the process of coming back to themselves. She watched them eat. She monitored the color in their fingertips, the pace of their breathing, the progressive return of small voluntary movements — the way Ari shifted their weight, adjusted the blanket, swallowed with more coordination than they had managed five minutes ago.

The trembling had stopped. She noted its absence the way she had noted its presence: as data, without judgment, filed alongside everything else.

"How's the quiet holding up," she said. Not *are you okay.* Not *how do you feel.* A question that met Ari where they had told her they were, in the language they had already chosen, asking only whether the territory had changed since they last reported on it.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I tip my head back against her shoulder, letting my eyes close. "Solid," I murmur. "Like the quiet's sunk all the way in."

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: But that wasn't what I asked... I asked for a colour

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: She hadn't touched the flogger again yet. Hadn't needed to.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: She did not give them what they asked for. Not yet.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Her hand came down. Not a strike yet — a firm, open-palmed contact that was heavier than a touch and lighter than a blow. A calibration... Another strike. Precisely placed. The sound of skin on skin was sharper than the flogger had been... Her palm landed again... Then she released their jaw and stepped back into position, and her hand came down again — harder, a strike that meant what it said — and she began to work in earnest. Each impact was placed with the same cartographic precision

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: The scene is over. Everything that happens now is landing.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas had been kneeling by the end of the bed for about four minutes, which Wren knew because he had started counting somewhere around the point it became obvious he intended to wait as long as it took.

"You could have said something," Wren said.

"I could have," Tomas agreed, not moving.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I put my hand in his hair and tip his head back so he has to look up at me. "Say it now, then."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas let his head tip back easily under the pressure of Wren's hand, his throat bared, his eyes finding theirs without hesitation. The carpet had left faint impressions on his knees by now. He didn't mind. He'd stayed because he wanted to be exactly here when Wren was ready to look at him.

"I want you to use me tonight," he said. Plain. No performance in it. "I want to not have to think. I want you to decide what happens and I want to be good for you while you do it."

His pulse was visible at the side of his neck, steady but quickened. He didn't drop his gaze.

"I've been thinking about it all day. Couldn't focus on anything at work. Kept thinking about your hands." A small, honest breath. "So I came home and I knelt down and I waited, because that's what I wanted to be doing when you found me."

He let the corner of his mouth pull slightly. Not quite a smile. Something more vulnerable than that.

"That's what I want. Whatever form you want to give it."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: My thumb strokes the line of his jaw. "You've been good already." My voice is low, measured. "Get up. We're going to the bedroom."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas felt the words land somewhere behind his sternum, warm and settling. *Good already.* He let himself have that for a second before he moved.

He rose smoothly — four years of this meant his body knew the choreography even when his knees protested the carpet. He didn't rush it, didn't stumble, just unfolded upward until he was standing, close enough that the height difference between them was negligible but the difference in everything else was not.

"Yes, Wren," he said. Quiet. Not performative. Just confirmation that he'd heard, that he was following, that the thing between them had clicked into its familiar groove.

He didn't reach for them. Didn't presume touch he hadn't been given. His hands stayed loose at his sides, fingers slightly open, and he waited the half-beat it took for Wren to turn before he followed them down the hallway.

His breathing had changed. Not dramatically — just slower, more deliberate, the way it always did when he started letting go of the part of his brain that ran spreadsheets and answered emails and remembered to buy milk. That part was quieting now, replaced by something simpler and older. Attention. Responsiveness. The specific, focused awareness of where Wren was in relation to him at every moment.

The bedroom light was off. He stopped just inside the doorway and waited, because Wren hadn't told him where to be yet, and right now that was the whole point.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I've had a week," he says. "I'd like not to make any decisions for a few hours, if that's on offer."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas blinked. Then something shifted behind his eyes — not surprise exactly, but recalibration. A quick, quiet reorganization of the evening he'd been building in his head.

"It's on offer," he said. Steady. No hesitation in it.

He took a breath and felt the thing that had been settling into his chest — that warm, easy slide toward *quiet* — pause. Not disappear. Just step to the side to make room for something else. Something he was less practiced at but not unfamiliar with. They'd done this before. Not often. Enough that he knew the shape of it.

He crossed the space between them. Slowly, deliberately, because the shift mattered and he wanted Wren to feel it happening. He brought his hand up to the side of Wren's neck, thumb resting along their jaw the way theirs had rested along his a minute ago.

"Then sit down," he said. His voice had changed. Still him, still Tomas, but the softness had been replaced by something more grounded. Not commanding — he didn't have Wren's particular talent for that — but certain. Present. "On the bed. And stop thinking about your week."

He held their gaze for a moment, making sure. Reading them the way four years had taught him to read them — the tension they carried in their shoulders, the particular set of their mouth when they were asking for something they thought they shouldn't need.

"I've got you," he said. Quieter now. Not a performance. A fact. "You don't have to hold anything up right now. I'll tell you where to be. I'll tell you what I want. And all you have to do is let me."

His thumb moved gently against their pulse point.

"Color?"

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I watch his face for a second, then nod, letting out a breath I didn’t know I was holding. “Green.” I sink onto the edge of the bed, shoulders loosening. “Tell me.”

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas watched the breath leave them. Watched the shoulders drop — not all the way, not yet, but enough. Enough to know the door was open and Wren was actually going to walk through it.

He didn't rush.

He stood in front of them for a moment, looking down at where they sat on the edge of the bed, and let himself take inventory. The way Wren's hands had settled on their thighs, fingers not quite relaxed. The residual tightness around their eyes that said the week was still living in their body even if they'd given him permission to evict it. The fact that they'd said *tell me* — Wren, who always told, who held the reins so naturally it looked effortless, sitting on the edge of their own bed asking him to take over.

He wasn't going to waste that.

"Shirt off," he said. Not harsh. Just clear. "Slowly."

He watched them while they did it, which was the point. He wanted Wren to feel looked at. Not evaluated — *seen*. The way Wren always saw him when their positions were reversed.

When the shirt was gone he stepped closer, standing between their knees, and put both hands on their shoulders. He pressed his thumbs into the rigid muscle where neck met trapezius and felt Wren's body resist for exactly one second before it started to yield.

"Christ," he said, low. "You've been carrying this all week?"

He didn't wait for an answer. He worked his thumbs in slow, firm circles, finding the knots, leaning his weight into it until he felt the fibers start to let go under his hands. Not a massage — something more deliberate than that. He was making a point. *This is what I meant. I'll tell you where to be. Right here. Not moving. Letting me.*

"Here's what's going to happen," he said, his voice pitched just above the quiet of the room. "I'm going to take my time with you. I'm going to touch you until you stop holding yourself like you're bracing for something. And you're not going to direct me or manage me or worry about whether I'm getting what I need." His thumbs found a particularly stubborn knot at the base of Wren's neck and he pressed into it steadily. "What I need is to do this. Understood?"

He felt a small tremor run through the muscle under his hands. Good.

"If you catch yourself thinking about work, or your week, or anything that isn't happening in this room right now — you tell me, and I'll bring you back." He tipped Wren's chin up with one hand, the same gesture they'd used on him in the hallway, mirrored. Returned. "That's not a suggestion. That's the rule for tonight. You stay here with me."

He searched their face. Four years meant he could read the difference between Wren's *I'm fine* and Wren's actual fine, between their composure and their calm. Right now he was looking for the second one and not finding it yet. That was alright. They had time.

"Lie back," he said.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I take him at his word and stop asking after that, and he stops needing to be asked, and neither of us has any clothes on within about a minute of the decision.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas had learned a long time ago that there was a difference between undressing someone and *unwrapping* them, and tonight he'd split the difference — efficient with the fabric, deliberate with everything that came after. Wren's clothes ended up on the floor in a pile that would have offended them on any other night. His own followed without ceremony. The point wasn't the taking off. The point was what he did once there was nothing left between them.

He stretched out over Wren, not rushing to settle his weight, letting it arrive gradually — chest to chest, the full warm length of him pressing Wren into the mattress. He felt the moment their body registered it. A fractional release, involuntary, like something structural giving way. The bed taking the load that the floor and the chair and the week had been asking Wren to bear alone.

"There," he murmured against the side of Wren's neck. Not praise exactly. Acknowledgment. *I felt that. Keep going.*

He propped himself on one forearm and used his free hand to map what the week had done to them. The tension still caught in the hinge of Wren's jaw. The shallow quality of their breathing that said they were still running on whatever fuel had gotten them through five days of being the person in charge. He pressed his mouth to the hard tendon on the side of their neck and felt their pulse against his lips — quicker than resting, not as quick as it was going to be.

He took his time. He'd said he would and he meant it. His mouth moved along the line of Wren's throat, unhurried, tasting salt and the faint remnant of whatever they'd put on that morning, worn thin by a long day. His hand traveled down Wren's side with firm, grounding pressure — not teasing, not ticklish, just *present*. Ribs. The dip of their waist. The jut of a hipbone under his palm where he let his hand rest, thumb drawing slow arcs against the skin.

Wren shifted under him and he recognized it — not impatience but the restless impulse to participate. To reciprocate. To *manage* the encounter the way they managed everything else.

"No," Tomas said. Quiet. Warm. Absolutely firm. "Hands above your head."

He waited until Wren complied, watched their arms settle against the pillow, and then rewarded the compliance with his mouth against their collarbone, open and slow, his teeth just grazing the ridge of bone. He felt the sound Wren made more than he heard it — a vibration through their chest into his.

"Good," he said, and meant it the way Wren always meant it when they said it to him. Not a grade. A recognition. *You did what I asked and I saw you do it and it mattered.*

He worked his way down. Methodical. Not clinical — there was nothing clinical about the way his mouth lingered in the spaces Wren usually kept armored, the soft vulnerable skin below the ribs, the thin stretch of abdomen where he could feel their breathing start to deepen — but thorough. He wanted to leave no part of this unattended. Every place his mouth landed was a quiet instruction: *you don't have to do anything here. You don't have to perform. You just have to feel this.*

Wren's hands twitched above their head. He glanced up and found their eyes on him, and what he saw in their face made his chest ache in the specific way it always did when Wren let him see them without the composure. Not fragile. Never fragile. Just *open* in a way that cost them something, and trusted him enough to pay it.

"Still green?" he asked, because the checking never stopped no matter who was steering.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath, fingers curling against the pillow. "Green." My voice is rough. "Don't stop."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas heard the roughness in their voice and cataloged it — filed it alongside every other version of Wren's voice he'd learned over four years. This one was rare. This one meant the walls were actually coming down and not just being politely lowered for company.

"I'm not going to stop," he said against the flat plane of their stomach, and felt the muscles there jump under his mouth. "I told you. I've got you."

He pressed his forehead against Wren's hip for a moment, just breathing. Grounding himself. Because the thing about switching — the thing they didn't talk about much — was that it required him to stay present in a different way. When he was kneeling, he could let himself dissolve into sensation and trust Wren to hold the shape of things. Now he was the shape. He had to stay solid while Wren softened, and he had to want to, and he did. He wanted to so much it sat in his throat like something physical.

He turned his head and pressed his mouth to the inside of Wren's hip, where the skin was thin and the bone was close to the surface. He kissed there slowly, then with more intent, letting his teeth find the edge of it, not biting — just holding. A point of focused sensation to anchor Wren in their body. He felt their hips shift, a minute involuntary roll, and he pressed them down with one hand, firm and flat across the bone.

"Stay still for me," he said.

Not a reprimand. An invitation to stop trying. To let him set the pace and the direction and the destination and to simply *be in it* the way he was whenever Wren held him down and told him to breathe.

He moved lower. His mouth found the crease of Wren's thigh and he spent time there that Wren probably would have called unnecessary, dragging his lips along the tendon, feeling it tense and release under him as their body fought and then surrendered the instinct to move. His hand stayed on their hip, steady counter-pressure, a constant reminder: *I'm here. I'm paying attention. You don't need to guide this.*

He could feel the heat of them. Could feel, against his chest where he was pressed between their legs, exactly what this was doing. He didn't address it directly. Not yet.
