He wanted Wren past the point where they could construct a sentence about it before he gave them what their body was asking for.

Instead he turned his attention to the other thigh. Kissed the inside of their knee — felt Wren twitch — and worked his way back up with aching, deliberate slowness, his mouth open and warm against skin that was starting to carry a flush he could feel under his lips. He listened to Wren's breathing change above him. The careful, measured rhythm of someone who was used to controlling their own responses starting to fray at the edges, going uneven, going honest.

"That," he said quietly, pressing the word into their skin. "That sound. Don't manage it. Let me hear you."

He glanced up. Wren's hands were still above their head but the grip on the pillow had gone white-knuckled, and their chest was rising and falling with the kind of breathing that said the week was finally losing its hold. Their face — God. Their face was the thing that made him ache. The composure wasn't gone, because Wren's composure never fully left, but it had gone translucent. He could see through it to the exhaustion underneath, and the want underneath that, and the trust underneath *that*, which was the deepest layer and the one that made him feel like he was holding something he'd better not drop.

He wasn't going to drop it.

He settled between their thighs and finally, *finally*, let his mouth arrive where the heat had been building, and he did it without preamble or teasing — just the full, focused attention of someone who knew exactly what they were doing because they'd spent four years learning this particular person's body like a language. He listened for every shift in Wren's breathing, every involuntary sound, every micro-movement of their hips against the hand still holding them down, and he let all of it tell him what to do next.

Wren made a sound above him that wasn't controlled at all, and something in Tomas's chest unlocked at the hearing of it.

He pulled back just enough to speak, his breath warm against oversensitive skin. "You're doing so well," he said, and his voice had gone rough too now, because he wasn't untouched by this, wasn't clinical about it, was in fact so turned on that his own body was making insistent demands he was choosing to ignore because this wasn't about him right now. "You're letting go and I can feel it and it's — you're incredible. Stay with me."

He pressed his mouth back to them and didn't stop.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's shaking by the time I've finished with my mouth and he still hasn't been told he's allowed to move, which is most of why he's shaking.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas kept his hands where they were — one still flat on Wren's hip, the other curled around their thigh — and breathed. His forehead was pressed against the inside of their knee and he could feel the aftershocks still moving through them in small, involuntary waves, and he stayed there for all of it because that was the job. You didn't leave. You stayed and you felt it with them and you didn't rush the landing.

But his body was a live wire. Every nerve ending he owned had an opinion about the last twenty minutes and he had overruled all of them and now the bill was coming due. The shaking wasn't dramatic — it lived in his arms, in the muscles of his thighs where he was braced against the mattress, in the tight clench of his jaw when he swallowed. A fine, persistent tremor that said *I am still here, I have been still, I have not taken anything for myself, and I need.*

He turned his head and pressed his mouth to Wren's knee. Tasted salt. His own breathing was ragged and he wasn't trying to hide it because he'd told Wren not to manage their sounds and it would have been hypocritical to manage his own.

"Wren," he said. Just the name. It came out wrecked.

He waited. He could feel his cock against the sheets, hard to the point of aching, and he didn't move into it because he hadn't been told he could move and the rule was the rule even when — *especially* when — his whole body was screaming at him to do something about it. That was the architecture of the thing. Wren had asked him to take charge and he had, and he'd held the shape of the evening in his hands, and now the evening had shifted and what he wanted — what he actually, desperately wanted — was for Wren to take it back. To look down at him shaking between their legs and *see* him and tell him what came next.

Because the truth that sat under everything they did, the engine that ran the whole arrangement, was that Tomas could lead when Wren needed him to. He could be solid and certain and directive and he meant every word of it. But this — the shaking, the waiting, the bright hot wire of need held in check by nothing except the knowledge that Wren hadn't said *move* yet — this was home. This was the room in himself he lived in most comfortably, and Wren had given him back the key just by finishing and going quiet and letting him feel the weight of his own restraint.

He lifted his head. Looked up the length of Wren's body. Their hands were still above their head, loose now, and their face had gone soft in a way that made his chest hurt, and he could see them coming back online — the composure returning not as armor but as *Wren*, the real Wren, the one who rested underneath the week and the control and the competence.

"Tell me what to do," he said. His voice was steady in the way a bridge is steady when it's bearing maximum load — functional, but you could hear the engineering straining. "Please. I want — I need you to —"

He stopped. Closed his eyes. Pressed his mouth to their skin again because he needed something to anchor to.

"I held it," he said quietly. "I held everything. And it was good, I wanted to, I'd do it again." He opened his eyes. "But I need you to take it back now. Please."

The *please* was not decorative. It was the most honest sound he'd made all night.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach down and curl my fingers into his hair, tugging just enough to make him look at me. "Come here." My voice is low, wrecked. "Now."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas moved.

The sound that left him when Wren's hand tightened in his hair was involuntary and raw — something between relief and want that he couldn't have held back if he'd tried. He didn't try. He crawled up the length of Wren's body with none of the deliberate grace he'd used earlier, just need and gravity and the pull of Wren's fingers in his hair guiding him where he was supposed to be.

When he got there — chest to chest, face to face, close enough that Wren's breath was on his mouth — the shaking got worse. Not from cold or fear but from the specific overwhelm of having held the shape of something for someone else and then being allowed to set it down. His arms were braced on either side of Wren's head and they were not steady and he didn't care.

"Hi," he said, stupidly, because Wren was looking at him and their hand was in his hair and their face was open and wrecked and soft all at once and his brain had apparently decided that was worth narrating.

He dropped his forehead to Wren's. Breathed. Their bodies were flush from chest to hips and he was so hard it was almost nauseating and the contact alone — just the heat and pressure of Wren's skin against his — made him jolt like he'd been touched with intention. A sound punched out of him, bitten off, embarrassing in its desperation.

"I'm here," he managed. "I'm — God, Wren, I need —"

He stopped talking because his mouth couldn't do two things at once and what it wanted to do was press against the hinge of Wren's jaw, which it did, open and graceless and shaking. He could feel Wren's pulse under his lips, still elevated, and his own heartbeat slamming against his ribs hard enough that Wren had to be able to feel it through the places their chests were pressed together.

He waited. Vibrating with it. Because *come here* wasn't *move* and *now* wasn't *take what you need* and the distinction mattered, it mattered enormously, it was the whole architecture of who he was in this bed, and he would wait until Wren said the words even if it killed him, which it might, which would be fine, which would be a perfectly acceptable way to die.

"Tell me," he whispered against their throat. "Please. Whatever you want. Anything. Just tell me."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Please," he says, and then the phrase we use when he wants it harder than that. "Rough. You know how. I'm not going to break and I'd tell you."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas heard the word and the phrase that followed it and something behind his ribs came undone like a knot cut clean.

"Yeah," he breathed. "Yeah, okay. I've got it."

He moved before the sentence was finished. His hand found Wren's hip and he turned them — not gently, not with the careful deliberation he'd used all evening, but with the kind of force that said *I heard you and I'm not going to second-guess it*. Wren went, and Tomas followed, and then he had them where he wanted them and his hands were not shaking anymore.

That was the thing. The shaking stopped the second he had permission. The second the uncertainty collapsed into instruction and the instruction was *this* — the thing his body had been screaming for since he'd pressed his forehead to Wren's hip and said their name like a prayer. His hands were steady now. Firm. Sure in the way they always were when Wren told him what they wanted and he could stop managing and start *doing*.

He pressed Wren down with his weight and his hand found the back of their neck and held. Not squeezing. Anchoring. The way Wren had anchored him a hundred times. He felt Wren's breath stutter under him and filed it.

"Tell me if that changes," he said against the back of their ear. Low. Not a request. The last responsible sentence before he let the rest of himself off the leash.

Then he stopped being careful.

He wasn't cruel about it — he was never cruel, didn't have it in him, and Wren knew that — but he was *thorough* in a way that had nothing polite about it. Four years meant he knew exactly how much force Wren meant when they used that phrase. Knew the difference between rough and reckless. Knew where to grip and how hard and how to read the sounds Wren made underneath him as a continuous real-time gauge of *more, yes, there, keep going*.

His hips found a rhythm that was not gentle and he held it, one hand still on the back of Wren's neck, the other braced against the mattress, and the sound he made on the first full stroke was guttural and honest and completely beyond his control. He pressed his mouth to the knob of Wren's spine and bit down — not enough to break skin, enough to feel, enough that Wren would know it was there tomorrow.

"God," he managed, and his voice was gone, stripped to something raw and fundamental. "You feel — I can't —"

He couldn't finish the sentence. Didn't need to. His body was finishing it for him with every movement, graceless and desperate and exactly as rough as Wren had asked for. The careful, competent version of himself that had spent the last hour taking Wren apart with patience and precision was still in there somewhere but it had stepped aside for something more animal. Something that had been waiting behind the stillness and the shaking and the *please* and now had the door open and was not interested in manners.

He shifted his angle and felt Wren react — a full-body thing, unmistakable — and he chased it, locked it in, gave them exactly that over and over with a single-mindedness that left no room for thought. His hand tightened on the back of their neck. His breathing had gone ragged and loud against Wren's skin and he could hear himself making sounds he'd normally be embarrassed by — low, broken, repetitive — and he didn't care because Wren had said *rough* and *I'm not going to break* and he believed them and this was what it looked like when he stopped holding back.

The pressure was building at the base of his spine like a physical thing, tidal, and he was not going to last much longer and he knew it and he didn't try to fight it because tonight wasn't about endurance. Tonight was about Wren saying *take it back* and him saying *tell me* and both of them arriving at the same place from opposite directions.

"Wren," he said, and it was a warning and a question and a sound that had his whole chest behind it. "I'm — close. I'm really close. Tell me —"

*Tell me.* Again. Always. The only words that mattered. Because even here, even with permission, even rough and desperate and shaking apart — he wanted to hear it. Wanted the voice. Wanted the word that meant *yes, now, I see you, go.*

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I tip my head back, panting. "Yes." I reach back to grip his thigh, nails digging in. "Now, Tomas. Come on."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas heard his name in Wren's mouth and the nails bit into his thigh and the last structural thing holding him together gave way.

He came hard enough that his vision whited at the edges, his whole body locking tight against Wren's back, his hand on their neck going rigid for one suspended second before his fingers loosened and his forehead dropped to the space between their shoulder blades. The sound he made wasn't a word. It was something older than language, pulled up from the floor of him, and it broke halfway through into something that might have been Wren's name if his mouth had been capable of forming consonants.

His hips stuttered — once, twice, a third time that was almost painful in its intensity — and then stilled. And then he was just breathing. Harsh, open-mouthed breathing against Wren's spine, his whole body trembling with the aftershock of it, every muscle he owned simultaneously spent and singing.

He didn't pull away.

He stayed exactly where he was for a long, formless stretch of time, his weight half on Wren and half on his own shaking arm, and he pressed his mouth to the knob of vertebra under his lips and just breathed against it. He could feel Wren's ribs expanding under him. Could feel the place where his teeth had marked them earlier, the skin slightly raised, slightly hot. He kissed it. Gently now. The roughness had emptied out of him along with everything else and what was left was just — tender. Hollowed out and tender and grateful in a way that sat in his throat.

"Hey," he said after a while. His voice was destroyed. He sounded like he'd been yelling for hours, which he hadn't, but his vocal cords apparently hadn't gotten that memo. "Hey. Come here. Turn over."

He eased back enough to give Wren room to move, and when they turned he gathered them in immediately — arm around their waist, pulling them into his chest, his other hand coming up to cradle the back of their head. Skin to skin. No space between them. He could feel both their heartbeats and neither was calm yet.

He pressed his lips to Wren's temple. Held them there.

"Thank you," he said quietly. Not performative. Just true. "For asking for that. For letting me — for both parts of tonight. All of it."

His thumb moved in slow strokes at the base of Wren's skull, finding the tight muscles there, working them absently the way he had at the start of the evening when the whole thing had been his to steer. His body was still coming down — little aftershocks twitching through his thighs, his breathing not quite settled — but the shaking had resolved into something warm and heavy. Spent. Good.

"Water," he said. "I'm going to get us water in a minute. And there's — I think there's leftover pasta if you haven't eaten, which I suspect you haven't, because you never eat when you've had a week."

He pulled back just enough to look at Wren's face. Searched it the way he always did after — checking for the things that mattered. Not distress. Not regret. The specific quality of stillness that meant Wren had actually landed back in their body instead of floating somewhere above it.

"How are you?" he asked. Simple. Direct. The same question dressed in different clothes than *color* because they were past the scene now and into the part that came after, which was not less important. Which was, in some ways, the whole point.

His hand stayed on the back of their neck. Warm. Steady. Not going anywhere.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's stopped forming sentences and I'm not much better. "Don't stop," he manages. (OOC: no fade, no time-skip -- write it through, including the end.)

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas didn't stop.

His thumb kept its slow circuit at the base of Wren's skull, pressing into the tight muscle there with the kind of patient, repetitive pressure that didn't require thought. Which was good, because thought was not something he had abundant access to right now. His brain had gone quiet in the way it only did after — not empty, just *still*, like a lake after wind. Everything that had been churning all day, all week, had been wrung out of him and what was left was this. His hand on Wren's neck. Wren's breathing against his collarbone. The damp heat between their bodies where neither of them had moved apart.

"I'm not stopping," he said. Barely above a murmur. His lips moved against Wren's temple when he spoke and he didn't pull back to give the words room. They didn't need room. They needed to be felt as much as heard.

He shifted his weight slightly, settling them both deeper into the mattress, and pulled the edge of the duvet up over Wren's hip with his free hand. Not because either of them was cold — they were radiating heat like a furnace — but because the weight of it was grounding. Another layer of *held*. He tucked it loosely and brought his hand back to Wren's waist, his palm flat against the small of their back, fingers spread wide.

Wren's breathing was slowing. He tracked it the way he'd tracked everything tonight — attentively, continuously, with the specific focus of someone whose job it was to notice. The exhales were getting longer. The little micro-tensions that lived in Wren's body like permanent residents — the ones in their jaw, their shoulders, the muscles along their spine — were releasing one by one, not all at once but in a slow cascade, like a building settling into its foundation after an earthquake.

He felt one let go under his hand. A knot in the erector spinae that he'd been pressing against without realizing it. Wren made a small sound — not quite a sigh, not quite a groan, something in between that was so unguarded it made Tomas's chest constrict.

"There you go," he said. Still quiet. Still close. His thumb hadn't stopped its slow circles. "That's it. Just let it go."

He wasn't sure if he was talking about the muscle or the week or something larger than both. It didn't matter. Wren's body was answering regardless, softening against him in increments, each one a small act of trust that he received with the seriousness it deserved.

Time did something strange. It always did, after. The minutes lost their edges and blurred together into a single sustained present tense — just warmth and skin and the slow rhythm of his hand on Wren's neck and Wren's breath against his chest. He could feel his own heartbeat in his fingertips where they pressed against Wren's back. Could feel Wren's heartbeat through the thin wall of their chest, the two rhythms not quite synced but close, drifting toward each other the way they always did when they lay like this long enough.

Wren's hand was on his ribs. He didn't know when it had gotten there. It wasn't gripping, wasn't stroking, just resting — the flat of their palm against his side, fingers curled loosely around the curve of a rib. Like they'd reached for something solid and found it and decided to stay.

He pressed his mouth to the top of Wren's head. Their hair smelled like sweat and the ghost of shampoo and something underneath both that was just *them*, and he breathed it in and held it and let it out slowly.

"You didn't eat," he said after a while. Not an accusation. A fact offered with the same gentleness as everything else. "I can tell because you get this—" He touched the side of Wren's face lightly, tracing the faint hollow below their cheekbone. "This thing. When you skip meals."

He didn't move to get up. Not yet. Wren had said *don't stop* and he wasn't going to until Wren said otherwise or until the need for water and food became genuinely urgent rather than merely sensible. Right now the sensible thing and the needed thing were in disagreement, and the needed thing was winning.

His hand found the mark he'd left on Wren's back — the bite, the one he'd pressed into the ridge of their spine when he'd stopped being careful. He traced it with his fingertips. The skin was raised slightly, warm to the touch, tender in a way that Wren would feel tomorrow when they leaned back in their desk chair. The thought gave him a small, private satisfaction that he didn't try to hide.

"This okay?" he asked, his fingers still on the mark. Checking. Always checking. Not because he doubted but because the checking was part of the care, and the care didn't stop when the scene did. It didn't stop at all. That was the thing people didn't understand about aftercare — it wasn't a phase. It wasn't a cooldown protocol. It was the whole relationship compressed into its most essential form. *I did this to you. I'm still here. Let me see it. Let me tend it.*

Wren made a sound that was affirmative but not verbal. Their hand tightened briefly on his ribs and then relaxed again. He took that as the answer it was.

The room was dark except for the light from the hallway, which fell in a narrow stripe across the floor and caught the edge of the dresser and went no further. The sheets were a disaster. Wren's shirt was somewhere near the door. His own clothes were wherever they'd landed and he genuinely could not remember taking them off, which was its own kind of testament to how thoroughly the evening had consumed him.

He could feel sleep pulling at the edges of Wren's body — the heaviness in their limbs, the way their breathing had gone slow and deep and even. But they weren't asleep yet. He could tell by the quality of their stillness, which was aware rather than absent. They were here. Present. Resting in the way that a person rests when they've finally, actually put something down.

"I'm going to get water," he said. "And food. And I'm going to come right back. Thirty seconds."

He waited for Wren to loosen their hand on his ribs. When they did — reluctantly, their fingers dragging across his skin like they were memorizing the texture — he pressed one more kiss to their temple and extracted himself carefully, keeping one hand on their shoulder until the last possible second the way you keep a hand on a sleeping animal so it knows you're still there.

The kitchen was bright and cold after the bedroom and he moved through it quickly, efficiently, running on the practical competence that kicked in when the tender part of him was busy holding something important. Water. Two glasses. The leftover pasta from Tuesday — he checked it, deemed it acceptable, didn't bother heating it because that would take time and he'd said thirty seconds and meant it. He put everything on the wooden cutting board they used as a tray and carried it back down the hallway.

Wren hadn't moved. They were exactly where he'd left them, on their side, the duvet pulled up to their waist, their face half-buried in the pillow. The stripe of hallway light caught the line of their shoulder and the mark on their spine and Tomas stood in the doorway for a moment and just looked at them.

Four years. Four years of this. Of learning someone so thoroughly that you could take them apart and put them back together and know which pieces went where. Of being learned in return. Of the extraordinary, mundane miracle of trust maintained across a thousand nights, each one a choice to show up and pay attention and not get lazy about the things that mattered.

He crossed the room and set the water on the nightstand and climbed back into bed with the pasta and a fork.

"Sit up a little," he said, and when Wren did — slowly, blinking, looking beautifully wrecked and half-asleep and entirely themselves — he put the fork in their hand and the container in front of them and picked up his own glass of water and settled against the headboard beside them, his shoulder pressed to theirs.

"Eat," he said. Gentle. Non-negotiable.

Wren looked at the pasta and then at him and their expression did something complicated that he couldn't fully read except for the bottom layer, which was the same thing it always was. The thing that kept them both coming back to this bed and these roles and each other, night after night, year after year.

He reached over and pushed a strand of hair off their forehead. His hand was steady. His heart was full.

"Eat," he said again. "And then we're sleeping. And tomorrow I'll make coffee and you'll tell me about your week using actual words and I'll listen and it'll be boring and normal and I'll probably be kneeling by the bed again by Thursday because that's apparently who I am as a person."

The corner of his mouth pulled. Not quite a smile. Something more honest than that. Something that said *I know who we are and I wouldn't trade it for anything and also please eat the pasta because I worry about you.*

Wren took a bite. Tomas drank his water and kept his shoulder pressed to theirs and didn't move away.

The room was quiet. The pasta was mediocre. It was, by every measure that mattered, enough.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I take another bite, the pasta lukewarm and tasteless, but it settles something in my stomach. I lean my shoulder into his, my voice quiet. “I wasn’t going to ask.”

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas was quiet for a moment. Not because he didn't have a response but because the sentence deserved the space around it. Wren had said it into the dark, leaning into him, half-asleep and still holding a fork, and he understood exactly what they meant and exactly how much it had cost them to say it.

"I know," he said.

He took a sip of water. Set the glass back on the nightstand. His shoulder stayed pressed to Wren's, warm and solid, a fixed point.

"You weren't going to ask because you never ask. You were going to come home and be fine and run the evening the way you always run it because that's what you do, and it would have been good, because it's always good, and you would have taken care of me and then lain awake at two in the morning with your jaw clenched wondering why you still felt like shit."

He said it without accusation. Without heat. The way you'd describe weather.

"And I would have known something was off because you do this thing with your hands when you're holding too much — you go still. Not relaxed still. *Controlled* still. Like if you move wrong something's going to spill." He turned his head slightly, enough to see the edge of Wren's profile in the dim light. "You were doing it when you found me in the hallway. Both hands flat on your thighs. Perfectly symmetrical. Dead giveaway."

He let that sit for a second.

"I'm not saying you have to ask. I know what it costs you. I know it feels like — like the thing you do for me is the thing you're supposed to be, and needing the opposite feels like a malfunction." His voice was low and unhurried, the cadence of someone who had thought about this more than once and was choosing his words with care rather than reaching for the first ones available. "But it's not. You know it's not. We've had this conversation."

He reached over and took the fork gently out of Wren's hand — they'd stopped eating, the fork suspended halfway between the container and their mouth, frozen in the particular stillness of someone hearing something they didn't want to need to hear. He set it down and took their hand instead. Held it in his lap. Ran his thumb across their knuckles.

"You knelt me down on my first night here because I asked for it, and you didn't make me feel like asking was weakness. You made it the foundation of everything." His thumb kept moving. Steady. "I need you to let me do that for you. Not every night. Not even every month. Just — when it's there. When you've had a week and you're carrying it in your shoulders and your hands go still."

He squeezed their hand once.

"You don't have to ask with words. You can ask the way I asked tonight — just be somewhere, doing something, and let me read it. I'll get it right. And if I don't, you can correct me, because that's what we do."

The room was very quiet. He could hear the fridge humming from down the hall and the particular silence of a house at night, all its small mechanical sounds suddenly audible in the absence of voices.

"But Wren." He turned to face them more fully, his knee drawing up on the bed, his hand still holding theirs. Their eyes were bright in the low light and he wasn't sure if that was emotion or exhaustion or both and it didn't matter because he was going to say this either way. "You were going to not ask. And I would have knelt there and you would have put your hand in my hair and we would have had a good night. And you would have given me exactly what I needed. And then you would have lain in the dark next to me not having what *you* needed, and I would have been asleep, and that—"

His voice caught. Just slightly. Just enough to hear.

"That's the thing I can't have. That's my limit. You, three feet away from me, not asking."

He brought their hand up and pressed his mouth to their knuckles. Held it there for a breath. Two.

"Eat your pasta," he said, quieter now, and put the fork back in their hand.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I look down at the fork, then at him, and my throat is tight. “I’m sorry.” I say it quietly, because it’s true. I take another bite, chew slowly. “Sometimes I forget you see me too.”

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas let the words land. Didn't rush past them. Didn't reassure them away.

"I know," he said.

He leaned back against the headboard and looked at the ceiling for a moment, collecting something. Not his thoughts — those were already in order. More like the right weight to put behind them. Wren had just said something real and small and he wanted to meet it at exactly the right altitude. Not above it. Not below it.

"It makes sense that you forget," he said. "The whole structure of what we do points my attention at you and your attention at me. And when you're steering, you're — you're *watching*. Constantly. Reading me, adjusting, holding the frame. It's a lot of outward focus. It makes sense that you'd start to feel like the seeing only goes one direction."

He turned his head on the headboard to look at them. They were eating slowly, mechanically, the way people eat when they've been told to and their body is grateful but their mind is somewhere else.

"But I'm not blindfolded when I'm kneeling, Wren."

Simple. A little dry. The faintest edge of humor in it because they were both too raw for this conversation to survive without a pressure valve somewhere.

"I see your hands when they're in my hair. Whether they're steady or whether they're holding on. I hear your breathing when you're deciding what to do next — and I can tell the difference between when you're choosing because you want to and when you're choosing because the choosing is the only thing keeping you upright." He paused. "I see you check on me eleven times a night. I see you pour the water before I ask. I see you set the alarm fifteen minutes early on mornings after so you can watch me sleep and make sure I'm okay before I even know I'm awake."

Wren's fork had stopped again. He didn't take it from them this time. Just waited.

"You're not invisible to me. You've never been invisible to me. You're just very, very good at looking like you don't need to be seen, and I am — admittedly — sometimes too deep in my own head to push past that." He exhaled. "That's on me too. Not just you."

He reached over and tapped the bottom of the pasta container. A small, wordless *keep going*. Wren took another bite.

"You don't owe me an apology for forgetting. You owe me the effort of remembering. And I owe you the same thing — noticing sooner. Not waiting for you to come find me kneeling on the carpet to figure out something's off with you." A beat. "Though for the record, I maintain that the kneeling was a strong opening move."

The corner of his mouth pulled. Wren's did too, barely, around a mouthful of cold pasta, and it was such a small and human thing that something in his chest went tight with affection.

He slid down the headboard a few inches until his head was level with Wren's shoulder, and he leaned into them — a reversal of the usual posture, his weight against their side instead of the other way around. Not heavy. Just present. Letting them feel him there.

"We're going to be okay," he said. Not a question. Not a hope. The quiet certainty of someone who had four years of evidence and intended to keep accumulating more. "Finish eating. Drink your water. And then come here and sleep and tomorrow we'll be normal and boring and you'll leave your coffee mug on the bathroom counter and I'll move it to the kitchen without saying anything and we'll pretend that's not a whole love language."

He closed his eyes. His hand found Wren's knee under the duvet and rested there.

"I see you," he said. Almost an afterthought. Almost asleep. "I always see you."

The fridge hummed. Wren chewed. The stripe of hallway light held its shape on the floor. And Tomas kept his hand where it was and breathed and waited, the way he always waited — not passively, not emptily, but with the full and deliberate attention of someone who had chosen to be exactly here, and meant it, and was not going anywhere.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I nod against his shoulder, swallow the last bite. "Okay." I set the container aside, and my hand finds his where it rests on my knee. My thumb traces the line of his knuckles. "I'll remember."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The film had finished some time ago and neither of them had done anything about it, which was how Priya knew the evening had changed character.

"We're not watching this," she said.

"We haven't been watching it since about nine."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "No," I agree. "We haven't." I don't move, but I stop pretending I'm looking at the screen.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya felt the silence settle into something with weight. She was looking at Cal now too, properly, the way she had trained herself not to do in a hundred different rooms over six years. It was terrifying for about three seconds and then it was the most obvious thing in the world.

"Okay," she said. Not to anything Cal had asked. To the thing neither of them had said yet.

She shifted on the couch, turning her body to face him fully, one leg tucked underneath her. The distance between them was ordinary — the same distance they always sat — and it felt absurd now, like a joke they'd both been telling with straight faces for far too long.

"I need to say something and I need you to not make it easy for me, because if you make it easy I'll convince myself later that it didn't count." She pushed her hair behind her ear, a gesture she knew he'd seen a thousand times, and it struck her that this was the strange part — not that the moment felt unfamiliar, but that it didn't. "I have been — careful. With you. For a long time. And I am tired of being careful."

Her heart was doing something ridiculous but her voice was steady. She'd made the decision somewhere between the second act of a movie she couldn't name and right now, and once Priya made a decision she didn't unmake it.

She held his gaze and waited.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath. "Alright." I don't make it easy. I don't smile, don't reach for her. "Then don't be careful."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya didn't move immediately. She let his words land, let them be real, let the room hold them for a moment so she could be sure she hadn't invented them.

Then she reached out and put her hand on the side of his face.

It was such a simple thing. She'd touched Cal a thousand times — shoulder, arm, the back of his head when she was teasing him. But her palm against his jaw, her thumb just below his cheekbone, her fingers curving behind his ear — that was new. That was the line, and she was across it now, and the ground on this side felt exactly the same.

"There," she said quietly. "That's — that's what not being careful looks like."

She could feel his pulse under her fingertips, or maybe that was hers. It didn't matter. What mattered was that she was not pulling her hand back, and he was not pulling away, and the world had not ended, and she felt so *stupid* for every single time she had stopped herself from doing this.

"I need you to know this isn't — tonight. This isn't the wine or the hour or some mood." She'd had one glass three hours ago and they both knew it. "This is Tuesday and Wednesday and every day after that. That's what I'm saying." Her voice was steady and clear and she meant every word with the full weight of six years of meaning it. "So if that's not what you — I need to know now. Before I —"

She stopped herself. Took a breath.

"Actually, no. I'm done qualifying. I love you. I have loved you. And I am done being careful."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her, finally, six years late, and she makes a small furious noise that I think is about the six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The sound that came out of her was involuntary and she would have been embarrassed about it if she had any capacity left for embarrassment. It was a small, sharp thing — not surprise, not relief, something closer to *anger* at every single day she had sat next to him and not done this. Six years of car rides and late nights and standing too close in kitchens and choosing the chair across the room instead of the space beside him on purpose, *on purpose*, and for what. For what.

She kissed him back with six years of opinion about it.

Her hand was still on his face and her other hand found the front of his shirt, not pulling, just holding on, her fingers curling into the fabric like she was making a point. She was. The point was *I'm here and I'm not going anywhere and I'm furious that we didn't do this in 2018.*

When she finally pulled back it was only far enough to breathe, her forehead against his, her eyes still closed. She was shaking. She hadn't expected that. Priya did not shake. Priya made decisions and executed them cleanly and did not fall apart in the aftermath, and yet here she was, trembling against him like something structural had come loose.

"I'm angry at us," she whispered, and then she laughed, and the laugh was unsteady and real. "I'm so angry at us, Cal. We could have — *years*. We had years."

She opened her eyes. He was right there. He was right *there*, the way he had always been, and she could see him clearly and she didn't have to look away.

"Hi," she said softly, stupidly, like they were meeting for the first time. And in some way that mattered, they were.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content:
I let out a shaky breath, my hand covering hers where it rests against my jaw. "I know," I say, my voice rough. "I'm angry too."

I kiss her again, slower this time, trying to make up for some of the years. "But we have now."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya let herself be kissed slowly and it was worse than the first one — not worse, but *more*, because the first one had been about finally and this one was about *staying*. This one said *I am not in a rush because I am not going anywhere*. She felt it in her chest like a hand pressing down on something that had been rattling loose for years, settling it into place.

When it ended she didn't pull back this time. She stayed exactly where she was, close enough that her nose brushed his, her breath uneven, her fingers still tangled in the front of his shirt. His hand was warm over hers against his jaw and she turned her palm just slightly, threading her fingers between his, holding on.

"We have now," she repeated. Testing the shape of it. Finding it solid.

She was quiet for a moment. The television had gone to a screensaver at some point — slow drifting colors painting the room in shifting blues — and the apartment was so still she could hear the refrigerator humming in the kitchen, a sound she had heard a hundred times sitting on this exact couch and never once with his heartbeat under her fingertips.

"I need you to know something," she said, and her voice had lost the trembling and found something underneath it, something that sounded like Priya again — certain, clear, a little bit stubborn. "I am going to be very good at this. At us." She pulled back just enough to look at him properly, and there was something fierce in her face that had nothing to do with the softness of the moment. "I have been practicing for six years without meaning to. Every time I almost said something and didn't. Every time I picked you up from the airport and didn't say *I missed you the wrong amount*. I have been rehearsing for this and I didn't even know it."

She pressed her lips together. Her eyes were bright and she was not going to cry because she was Priya and she didn't do that, except her throat was aching in a way that suggested her body had not received that memo.

"So don't — just don't be careful with me either. Okay? We're done with that. Both of us. New rule."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: We get to the bedroom eventually, laughing at ourselves most of the way, and then stop laughing when the clothes are actually off.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya had imagined this — she could admit that now, in the democracy of honesty they'd established in the last hour — but she had imagined it wrong. She'd thought it would feel like crossing into foreign territory, like learning someone new. It didn't. It felt like arriving somewhere she had already been in every way except this one, and the this one turned out to be the easy part.

What she hadn't expected was how *known* she already was. Cal's hands didn't hesitate the way a new person's hands hesitate. He touched her like he'd been paying attention for six years — to which side she leaned into, to what made her breath catch when they were just standing close, to every piece of data she thought she'd been hiding and apparently hadn't been hiding at all. It was disarming in a way that the kissing hadn't been. The kissing she'd been ready for. Being *seen* like this, with nothing between them and nowhere to redirect his attention — that cracked something open in her chest that she couldn't laugh her way past.

She pulled him closer with both hands and stopped trying to.

Afterward she lay with her head on his chest and her leg thrown over his and felt absolutely wrecked and absolutely whole at the same time, which she had not previously understood was a combination available to human beings.

"I have a complaint," she said into his collarbone.

She propped her chin on his chest and looked up at him, her hair a disaster, her expression one of genuine indignation.

"If it was going to be like *that*, you should have said something in 2019. 2018. You should have said something at Jamie's wedding when we danced and I went home and lay on my bathroom floor for twenty minutes. I want those years back, Cal. I want a refund."

Her voice was light but her eyes were not. She traced a line along his shoulder with her fingertip, slowly, learning the geography of him, committing it to the kind of memory that doesn't fade.

"I'm staying tonight," she said. Not a question. "And tomorrow I'm going to make you coffee and it's going to be terrible because your kitchen is a war crime, and you're going to drink it anyway. And that's — that's how this goes now."

She settled back against him, her ear over his heartbeat, steady and real and *there*.

"New rule," she murmured.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content:
I let out a low laugh, my fingers tracing idle patterns on her bare back. "Your coffee is always terrible. I've been drinking it out of politeness for years."

I tilt my head to press a kiss into her hair. "Stay. And make your terrible coffee. And we'll start collecting the years we missed, starting right now."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya smiled against his chest, and the smile was so wide it pressed her cheek into his skin in a way he could probably feel.

"You have *never* been polite about my coffee. You made a face every single time. I just chose to interpret it as gratitude." She traced another slow line down his arm, mapping the topography of a body she had been carefully not memorizing for six years and was now memorizing with the thoroughness of someone who had wasted enough time. "And for the record, the coffee isn't the problem. The problem is that you own one mug and it has a chip in it and your coffee maker is from 2014 and I'm pretty sure the filter basket has achieved sentience."

She was talking too much. She knew she was talking too much. It was what Priya did when something enormous had happened and her heart was still catching up to it — she filled the space with words so the feeling couldn't swallow her whole. But she also knew that Cal knew this about her, had known it for six years, and that was the thing that kept undoing her tonight. Not the newness. The *not*-newness. The way everything enormous was built on a foundation of everything ordinary.

She went quiet for a moment. His fingers on her back were doing something slow and absent and devastating, and she closed her eyes and let herself just *be* in it. The refrigerator hummed. The blue screensaver light from the living room reached just barely through the open bedroom door, painting a thin stripe across the floor.

"Jamie's wedding," she said softly, returning to it because she wasn't done with it. "You were wearing that grey suit and you asked me to dance and I said yes like it was nothing. And your hand was on my back — " She pressed her palm flat against his ribs, demonstrating. "Right here. And I thought, very clearly, *I am in love with this person and I cannot do anything about it.* And then I went home and sat on my bathroom floor in my dress and my shoes and I called my sister and she said *just tell him* and I said *I can't lose him* and she called me a coward. She was right."

She lifted her head to look at him. Her eyes were dry but barely, held together by stubbornness and the particular Priya conviction that if she simply decided not to cry, her body would comply. It mostly did.

"I'm not a coward anymore," she said. "And I'm not going to lose you. Those two things are both true at the same time, and I spent six years thinking they couldn't be, and I was wrong, and I am — "

Her voice did something without her permission. A hairline crack, barely audible, right through the middle of the word.

"I'm really happy," she finished. Simply. Like it surprised her. Like happiness was a thing she'd been bracing against and it had arrived anyway, without asking permission, and all she could do was report its presence.

She kissed his chest, right over his heart, and settled back down.

"Tell me something I didn't know," she said. "Something you were careful about. I want to collect all of them. I want every single one."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I get my mouth between her thighs and stay there while she tells me exactly what she wants, specifically, in a voice I have never heard her use in six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya had opinions.

This was not new information to anyone who had ever met her, but it turned out that the opinions extended — with characteristic specificity and zero hesitation — into territory Cal had never had access to before. And once she understood that he was *listening*, that he was taking direction the way he took all her directions, with that quiet focused attention that had been destroying her in professional settings for years, something in her unlocked.

She told him. She told him with one hand in his hair and her voice coming apart at the seams, half-wrecked and still *precise*, still somehow Priya even now — *there, exactly there, don't stop, no slower, like that, Cal, like* — and the sound of his name in her own mouth in this context was so new and so catastrophically right that she had to press her forearm over her eyes for a second just to survive it.

He was good at listening. He had always been good at listening. She was going to die.

She did not die. She came with her back arched off the mattress and both hands fisted in the sheets and a sound she would have been mortified by if she had any room left for mortification, which she did not, because every room inside her was currently occupied.

For a long moment afterward she lay there with her chest heaving and her arm still over her eyes and said nothing, which was so unusual for Priya that it probably constituted an emergency.

Then she removed her arm and stared at the ceiling.

"Okay," she said. Her voice was hoarse and absolutely ruined. "Okay. I have revised my complaint. I don't want a refund. I want *damages*. I want to sue both of us for criminal negligence. I want six years of back pay. I want —"

She pulled him up by the shoulders and kissed him, tasting herself on his mouth and not caring, kissing him deep and thorough and grateful.

"Where did you — how long have you —" She stopped. Reorganized. Priya did not ask incoherent questions. "You are *unfairly* good at that and I need a minute and I also need you to know that the minute is not optional because my legs are not currently functioning as legs."

She was trembling again. Full-body, involuntary, aftershock trembling that she could not govern, and she gave up trying to govern it and just pulled him down against her, wrapping around him, arms and legs, holding on with everything.

"New rule," she murmured against his neck. "Tuesdays. That's a Tuesday thing now. Every Tuesday. Nonnegotiable."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content:
"I've been paying attention," I murmur into her skin, my own voice rough. "Every Tuesday you wore that blue sweater. Every Tuesday you thought I didn't notice."

I shift, pulling the blanket over us both, and tuck her trembling closer against me. "You get damages. I get every Tuesday."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya went still against him.

The blue sweater. The *blue sweater*. The one she bought in 2020 because her sister said it did something to her collarbones, the one she wore on Tuesdays because Tuesdays were when they had standing plans — dinner, or a movie, or just existing in each other's space — and she had never, not once, admitted to herself that she was dressing for him on those days. She had filed it under *I just like this sweater* and *it's comfortable* and *the rotation works out this way* and every other lie she had told herself with the meticulous organizational skill she applied to everything else in her life.

He had noticed. He had *always* noticed. And he had been careful too.

"You —" She pulled back to look at him. "You are *not* allowed to just — you can't say that to me right now when I am lying here with no structural integrity and expect me to —"

She pressed her face into his neck. Her shoulders were shaking and it took him a second, probably, to determine whether she was laughing or crying, and the answer was both, quietly, her breath hitching against his skin in small uneven bursts that she could not control and was not trying to control because they were done being careful and that included this. This ugly-beautiful mess of relief.

"Every Tuesday," she said, muffled. "Six years of Tuesdays, Cal. I ironed that sweater. I don't iron *anything*. I own clothes that have never seen an iron and I *ironed that sweater* and told myself it was because the fabric needed it."

She laughed again, wet and helpless.

"The fabric did not need it."

She tightened her arms around him under the blanket, her body still running aftershocks, her face still hidden, and let herself be exactly where she was — known, wrecked, held, home.

"You get every Tuesday," she whispered. "You get every day. That's the deal. That's always been the deal. We just finally read the fine print."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "You can stop being careful with me," she says. "I'm not made of glass and I've thought about this for as long as you have. Harder."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya lifted her head from his neck and looked at him. Really looked at him. The blue light from the living room caught the edge of his jaw and the place where his hair was messed up from her hands and the expression on his face, which was not careful. Which was open in a way she had seen him be open about exactly nothing else in six years of knowing him.

*Harder.*

The word landed somewhere below her ribs and detonated quietly.

"Okay," she said. And her voice was different now. The trembling had stopped. The laughing had stopped. Something underneath all of it had surfaced, something steady and certain and very, very awake. "Okay. Then stop holding back."

She shifted beneath him, deliberate, her hips pressing up against his in a way that was not ambiguous and not tentative and not careful. Her hands slid down his back, slow, her fingernails dragging just enough to make a point.

"I'm not made of glass either. And I have spent six years thinking about what I would do if I ever got to be here, and I was *thorough*, Cal. I was comprehensive. I had *contingencies*."

She pulled him down to her, her mouth finding the place just below his ear, and spoke against his skin with the focused clarity of someone who had made a decision and was now executing it.

"So show me. The thing you were careful about. The thing you didn't do. I want all of it." Her teeth grazed his neck, light, precise. "I want to stop finding out what we wasted."

Her legs tightened around him and her eyes were dark and steady and she was not shaking anymore. She was Priya. She had made her decision and she was not unmaking it.

"*Now.*"

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: My hands tighten on her hips and I push inside her, hard, and she gasps — not shocked, not surprised, but *finally*. I don't stop, don't slow, just give her what she asked for, what we both waited years to take. "Like this," I grit out, my forehead against hers. "This is what I didn't do."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya arched into him and the sound she made was not the sound of someone being surprised. It was the sound of someone being *answered*. Six years of question finally met with six years of response, and the force of it — the sheer physical *fact* of him, the weight and the heat and the way he moved like he'd been holding this back with both hands and had just let go — cracked her open along a fault line she hadn't known she had.

"*Yes*," she said, and it came out broken and fierce and absolutely certain. Her nails dug into his back, not gently, not carefully, leaving marks she hoped he'd find tomorrow and the day after that. "Like this. Exactly like this. Don't you *dare* slow down."

His forehead was against hers and she could feel every breath he took, ragged and uneven, and she kept her eyes open because she had spent six years looking away and she was *done*. She watched his face. She watched what it did to him to stop being careful. It was the most devastating thing she had ever seen.

Her hips met his, every time, with a precision that was entirely Priya — deliberate even in the middle of falling apart, matching his rhythm and then pushing it, demanding more, her body saying the same thing her mouth had been saying all night. *I am here and I am not fragile and I have wanted this exact thing for longer than either of us should have allowed.*

"This," she managed, one hand gripping the back of his neck, pulling him closer, her mouth against his jaw. "This is what I thought about. Every Tuesday in that stupid sweater. Every time you stood too close in a kitchen. Every —" Her voice fractured because he did something with his hips that short-circuited the part of her brain responsible for complete sentences. "*Cal.*"

His name in her mouth like a door she'd finally walked through.

She pulled his face to hers and kissed him, messy and graceless and nothing like the careful curated version of herself she had shown him for six years, and it was the truest she had ever been with anyone.

"Don't stop," she whispered against his mouth. "Don't stop. We have so much time to make up for and I want to feel this tomorrow. I want to *know*."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: Six years of not doing this and now neither of us can form a sentence. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya didn't stop talking and then she did.

There was a moment — she would remember it later with absolute clarity — where language simply left her. Cal's hand slid under the small of her back and changed the angle and she lost the word she was forming somewhere between her throat and the air and what came out instead was a sound, raw and unguarded, that she had never made in front of another human being. She would have been embarrassed except that he made a sound back, low and wrecked against her collarbone, and embarrassment required a distance between them that no longer existed.

Her body knew things her mind hadn't caught up to. It knew the way to tilt her hips so that every thrust hit exactly where she needed it. It knew to lock her ankles behind his back and pull him deeper. It knew that the noise he made when she clenched around him — involuntary, guttural, *his* — was something she wanted to hear for the rest of her life and would do whatever was required to cause again.

"There," she gasped, and her hand found his where it gripped her hip and she pressed it harder into her skin. "Right there, don't — keep —"

He kept.

The pace was not gentle and she did not want it gentle. She wanted the evidence. She wanted to feel the bruise-bloom of his fingers on her hips tomorrow morning when she reached for that terrible mug in his terrible kitchen. She wanted her body to carry the proof that this had happened, that it was real, that she had not dreamed it on her bathroom floor in a dress and heels after Jamie's wedding.

She could feel it building. Not slowly. It had been building for six years and the last twenty minutes were just the final approach, the part where the ground rushes up to meet you and you either pull up or you don't, and Priya was not pulling up. Priya was diving.

Her breath came in short sharp bursts and her thighs were shaking against his sides and she could feel him everywhere — his weight, his skin, the sweat between them, the way his breath stuttered every time she tightened around him. She watched his face because she had promised herself she would. His jaw was clenched and his eyes were dark and focused and he was looking at her like she was the only real thing in the room and she thought, with devastating clarity, *this is what it looks like when he isn't careful.*

"I'm close," she said, and her voice didn't sound like her voice. It sounded stripped down to the wire, all the polish and composure gone, just the raw current underneath. "I'm — Cal, I'm —"

He shifted his hand. His thumb found her, precise, deliberate — *paying attention*, the way he always paid attention, the way he'd been paying attention to the blue sweater and the bathroom floor and every Tuesday for six years — and pressed in slow circles that were completely at odds with the pace of his hips and the contradiction of it, the gentleness and the force existing simultaneously, broke her.

She came apart.

Not quietly. Not carefully. With her back bowed off the mattress and her hand fisted in his hair and a cry that started as his name and ended as something wordless and shattered. It hit her in waves — not one peak but a series of them, rolling through her, each one pulling a different sound out of her throat, each one tightening her around him in a way that she could feel doing something to his rhythm, breaking it, making it desperate.

"Don't stop," she managed, barely, in the middle of it. "Come with me, I want — I want to feel you —"

His forehead dropped against her shoulder and his hips lost their rhythm entirely and she heard him say her name — not *Priya* the way everyone said it but *Priya* the way no one had ever said it, like it was the last word he knew — and then he broke too. She felt it. The stutter and the surge and the way his whole body went taut against hers and then shuddered, and she held him through it with both arms and both legs and her face pressed into his hair, breathing him in, feeling every aftershock move through him and into her.

For a long time after that, neither of them moved.

The room was very quiet. The refrigerator hummed. The blue light drifted. Their breathing slowed in tandem, falling into sync the way it probably always had without either of them noticing.

Priya's hand was in his hair, moving slowly, not because she'd decided to but because her body was doing things on its own now, gentle things, post-catastrophe things. Her other arm was wrapped around his back and she could feel the marks her nails had left and she traced them lightly with her fingertips, a cartography of damage she did not regret.

"There," she whispered. Her voice was destroyed. She sounded like she'd been yelling, which she supposed she had, in her way. "Now I'll know."

He shifted, just enough to take his weight off her, and she made a sound of protest and pulled him back.

"No. Stay. You're not heavy. You're —" She swallowed. "You're exactly right."

She turned her head and kissed his temple. Then his cheekbone. Then the corner of his eye, where she tasted salt that might have been sweat and might not have been, and she didn't ask because some things didn't need to be identified to be understood.

"Tuesday," she murmured. And then, quieter, with a smile he could probably feel against his skin: "Wednesday. Thursday. All of them. Every single one."

She closed her eyes. His heartbeat was slowing against her chest, finding its way back to something sustainable, and she matched her breathing to it without thinking, the way she had apparently been matching herself to him for six years without knowing what she was doing.

"New rule," she said, one last time, barely audible, more breath than sound. "No more lost years."

She held on. He held on. The blue light moved across the ceiling like something patient that had been waiting for them to figure it out.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I catch my breath, my face buried in the curve of her neck. "Every single one," I echo, my voice raw. "Starting with tomorrow's terrible coffee."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya laughed, and it vibrated through both of them, chest to chest, a small seismic event.

"Tomorrow's coffee is going to be *spectacular*," she said, her voice still wrecked, still hoarse, still the best version of her own voice she had ever heard. "It's going to be the worst cup of coffee you have ever tasted and you are going to drink it with your whole face doing that thing and I am going to stand in your kitchen wearing —" She paused. Considered. "Actually, what am I wearing. I didn't plan for this. I planned for six years of repression and then tonight I planned for about ninety seconds ahead at any given moment and now I'm here and I don't have a toothbrush."

She was rambling. She knew she was rambling. Her fingers were still moving through his hair in slow absent strokes and her legs were still tangled with his and she could feel the cooling evidence of what they'd just done and she didn't care. She felt hollowed out and filled up at the same time, like a house that had been gutted and rebuilt in the same hour.

"I'll wear your shirt," she decided. "The grey one. I've wanted to steal that shirt since 2021 and now I have legal grounds."

She shifted just enough to press her lips to the place where his neck met his shoulder. Stayed there. Breathed him in — sweat and skin and the laundry detergent she'd been pretending she didn't recognize on her own couch cushions after he left.

"Cal."

Just his name. Just to say it in this room, in this bed, with nothing between them. Just to hear what it sounded like when it wasn't carrying the weight of everything she couldn't say.

It sounded light. It sounded like a door standing open.

"Set an alarm," she murmured against his skin. "I need at least twenty minutes to fight your coffee maker and I refuse to be late to work because of you. That's a line I'm holding."

She paused.

"Every other line is gone. But that one stays."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I huff a laugh against her neck. "I'll set the alarm. But my coffee maker is going to win and you're going to be late." I lift my head to look at her, my hand coming up to trace the edge of her jaw. "Wear the grey shirt. It never looked right on me anyway."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya turned her face into his hand, just slightly, a movement so small and so instinctive that she knew it had been living in her body for years, waiting for permission.

"It looked *fine* on you," she said. "That's the problem. It looked fine on you and I spent an entire brunch in 2021 not looking at your forearms when you rolled the sleeves up and Maya noticed and she's never let me forget it. She has a group chat about it, Cal. My friends have a group chat about my inability to handle your forearms in that shirt."

She was going to have to text that group chat tomorrow. The thought sent a thrill of terror and delight through her in equal measure. Maya was going to be insufferable. Maya was going to say *I told you so* in fourteen languages. Priya was going to let her.

His thumb traced her jaw and she closed her eyes and let the feeling be simple. Touch without subtext. Touch that meant exactly what it was. It was the most luxurious thing she had ever experienced and it was just his hand on her face in a dark room.

"Your coffee maker is not going to win," she said, but quietly now, the bravado fading into something softer, sleepier, the adrenaline of the evening finally metabolizing into exhaustion. "I have never lost a fight with an appliance and I'm not starting tomorrow."

She opened her eyes. Looked at him. Let herself look at him the way she had looked at him at Jamie's wedding, on her bathroom floor, in a hundred kitchens and cars and rooms — except this time she didn't have to stop.

"It looked right on you," she corrected, barely a whisper. "Everything looks right on you. I just get to say that now."

Her eyes were heavy. Her body was heavy. She curled into him, one hand flat against his chest, feeling it rise and fall.

"Set the alarm," she mumbled. "And then stay exactly where you are."

She was asleep in minutes. Dreamless, deep, and entirely uncareful.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content:
I do set the alarm, watching her fall asleep against me. In the morning, the coffee is, predictably, terrible. She drinks hers first, defiant, then watches my face as I take a sip.

"See?" she says. "Gratitude."

I kiss her, tasting the bitter coffee and the sweetness underneath it. "Every Tuesday," I remind her.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun had planned to say something when the door opened. He had in fact planned several things, over roughly nineteen weeks, and had rehearsed at least two of them.

Halle got the door open and he forgot all of them.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I don't say any of the things I planned either. I drop the bag and close the distance.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun caught her.

That was the only word for it — she came at him and his hands knew where to go before his brain caught up, one arm hooking around her waist, the other curling up her back until his fingers were in her hair, and he pulled her in so hard her feet left the ground for a second. He heard the bag hit the floor. He didn't care about the bag.

"Hi," he said, and his voice cracked on one syllable like he was seventeen, and then he kissed her before she could laugh at him for it.

It wasn't a polite kiss. It wasn't the kind of kiss you give someone when there's more to say first. It was five months of bad sleep and worse phone connections and staring at the ceiling of places that weren't home, and he kissed her like he was trying to make up the entire deficit in one go. His hand tightened in her hair. He walked her backward — one step, two — until her shoulders met the hallway wall, and he leaned into her with his full weight because he *could*, because she was solid and warm and real and *here*, and he needed to feel every square inch of that confirmation pressed against him.

He broke the kiss only because he had to breathe. His forehead dropped against hers. His chest was heaving.

"I had a speech," he managed.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "Fuck the speech." I breathe out, my hands gripping the front of his shirt. "I missed you so much it hurt."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun made a sound at that — not a word, something lower and more honest than a word, pulled from somewhere behind his ribs. His hand was still fisted in her hair and he didn't loosen it.

"Good," he said, and he knew how that sounded and he didn't care. "Good. I wanted it to hurt. I wanted —"

He didn't finish. He kissed her again instead, slower this time but not gentler, not even a little, his mouth dragging against hers like he was relearning the shape of her. His other hand slid down from her waist to her hip and gripped, fingers pressing hard enough to dent, pulling her flush against him so there was no ambiguity whatsoever about what five months had done to him. He felt her fists tighten in his shirt and something hot and reckless lit up his spine.

"I thought about this," he said against her mouth, between kisses, not really pulling back far enough to speak properly. "Every night. I'm not — I'm not exaggerating. *Every* night, Halle. The specific wall varied but the general concept —"

He broke off because she shifted against him and his train of thought simply derailed. His head dropped to the curve of her neck and he pressed his mouth there, open, tasting salt and the warmth of her skin and whatever she'd put on this morning, and his teeth grazed her pulse point because he remembered exactly what that did and he had no intention of being patient about any of this.

"I don't want to catch up," he murmured against her throat. His voice had gone low and rough and he could feel his own heartbeat in his teeth. "I don't want to talk about the flight. I don't want coffee." His hand slid from her hip to the hem of her shirt. "I want you. Right now. I want — *God*, I want you so much I can't think straight."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I kiss her and keep kissing her and we don't manage to get further into the flat than the hallway for a while.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun didn't remember deciding to pull her shirt off. He remembered his hands finding the hem, remembered the drag of fabric and the half-second of separation where her mouth wasn't on his and that felt like an emergency, and then the shirt was on the floor somewhere behind her and his palms were on her bare skin and his brain went white-hot and quiet.

"Okay," he breathed, and it wasn't a response to anything, just the only word available to him. He pressed her back into the wall again, his mouth finding her collarbone, the dip at the base of her throat, the place just below her ear that made her arch into him. His hands mapped her like he was checking she was all still there. She was. Every part of her was exactly where he'd left it and he was furious that he'd been away from this for five months.

They knocked a framed photo off the hallway shelf. He heard the glass crack and didn't stop and didn't care.

"Bedroom," he said at one point, against her jaw, and it came out like a suggestion he was already abandoning even as he made it, because she did something with her hips and his hand slammed flat against the wall beside her head and he had to just *breathe* for a second, forehead pressed to hers, eyes shut, every nerve in his body drawn tight as wire.

"Or here," he amended, voice wrecked. "Here works. Anywhere. I genuinely do not care, Halle, I just need —"

She pulled him back in and he stopped trying to plan.

They did not make it to the bedroom. Not the first time.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I pull back just enough to meet his gaze, my breathing ragged. "*Here* works." I guide his hands to my belt buckle, my own fumbling with the button of his jeans. "Don't stop."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun wasn't going to stop. Stopping was not a concept his body currently recognized as valid.

His fingers found her belt buckle and he was shaking — actually shaking, his hands unsteady in a way that had nothing to do with fatigue and everything to do with the fact that she'd just said *don't stop* in that voice and his entire nervous system had reorganized itself around the singular project of getting closer to her. He got the buckle open, got the button, got the zipper, and his knuckles dragged against her stomach on the way down and she made a sound that he was going to hear in his sleep for the next year.

"I've got you," he said, and he didn't know why he said it except that it felt true and important, and then her hands were on his jeans and her fingers were clumsy too and that undid him more than anything — that she was shaking the same way he was, that this was mutual wreckage.

He helped her. Got his own jeans open because her hands kept getting distracted and his kept getting distracted and they were both laughing for about two seconds, breathless and stupid with it, and then the laughter died because he pressed against her and the sound she made was not laughter.

There was a graceless interval of too many clothes and not enough hands and the logistics of a hallway wall, and he didn't care about any of it. He hitched her up — his arms remembered exactly how to do this, the angle, the grip, the way her legs locked around him like a reflex — and her back pressed into the wall and he held her there, held her weight easily because five months of nothing to do but work out and miss her had to be good for *something*.

He stopped. One second. Forehead against hers, both of them breathing like they'd sprinted here from across the city, and he looked at her. Really looked. Her eyes, her mouth, the flush spreading down her chest, the way she was looking back at him like he was the answer to a question she'd been asking an empty apartment for five months.

"*Halle*," he said. Just her name. Just the whole of it, everything he'd meant to say in the speech he'd planned, every terrible night condensed into two syllables.

And then he stopped waiting.

His hips pressed forward and the sound that came out of him was guttural and wrecked and he buried it in her neck, his whole body shuddering, because *nothing* — no memory, no imagination, no desperate late-night substitute — nothing compared to this. To her. To the reality of her wrapped around him, her fingers digging into his shoulders hard enough to bruise, the sound of his name in her mouth.

He didn't start slow. He couldn't. Five months of slow, five months of patience, five months of lying in the dark with his hand over his face whispering her name into rooms she wasn't in — he was *done* with slow. He moved and she moved with him and the picture frame they'd already knocked off the shelf crunched under his boot and the shelf itself rattled against the wall in a rhythm that was going to leave marks in the plaster and he didn't care, he didn't care about anything except the sounds she was making and the way her body fit against his like a lock he'd finally gotten back to.

"I missed you," he got out, ragged, broken, his mouth against her ear. "I missed you, I missed you, I —"

He couldn't finish. She tightened around him and his vision went white at the edges and his hand slammed against the wall again and he just held on, held *her*, and let five months of absence burn itself out of his body the only way it knew how.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: The bag stays where it fell. So do most of our clothes, in a line down the hall that we are both going to find funny tomorrow.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun didn't put her down.

He meant to. His arms were burning and his legs had that shaky, hollowed-out quality that meant they were going to have opinions about stairs later, and there was a perfectly good floor right there. But she was still wrapped around him and her face was pressed into his neck and he could feel her heartbeat slamming against his chest, and his arms simply refused to get the message.

He leaned into the wall. Let it take some of the weight. His breathing was ragged and loud in the hallway and he could feel sweat cooling on his back where his shirt — still on, shoved up to his ribs, which was going to be funny later — met air.

"Okay," he said again. Same word. Same lack of context. He turned his head and pressed his mouth to her temple, her hairline, the shell of her ear, not kissing exactly, just — confirming. Continuous contact. His eyes were closed and he was smiling and he couldn't have stopped either of those things at gunpoint.

His thumb was tracing a slow, stupid circle on her thigh. He didn't know when he'd started doing that.

"I'm not putting you down," he informed her. His voice was absolutely destroyed. He sounded like he'd gargled gravel. "Just — for your awareness. Logistically, I understand that I'll have to at some point, but I want to register my formal objection in advance."

He shifted his weight, got a better grip, felt her legs tighten around him in response, and something in his chest cracked open so wide it almost hurt.

"That was —" He exhaled. Shook his head against hers. "I had five months to build that up in my head and it was still better than anything I —"

His throat closed. He swallowed hard.

"I'm home," he said, quietly, like he was only just now believing it.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I laugh, breathless and raw against his skin. My legs are still wrapped around him, refusing to let go. "Welcome home." I kiss his jaw, my voice just as wrecked. "Don't you dare put me down yet."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun laughed. It came out cracked and wet and he didn't try to fix it.

"Wasn't going to," he said. "Told you. Formal objection. On the record."

He shifted his grip, hitching her up half an inch, and his shoulders protested and he ignored them completely. His face was still pressed into her hair and he was breathing her in like oxygen was secondary, like whatever combination of shampoo and sweat and *her* was the actual essential compound his lungs had been missing. His thumb kept tracing that circle on her thigh. Slow. Mindless. The kind of thing his hands did when his brain had been thoroughly and comprehensively emptied.
