Her hair had given up any pretense of the style she'd arrived with — it was flattened on one side from the door and wild on the other from his hands, and there was a piece sticking straight up at the crown that defied explanation. The mascara situation was bilateral. Her lips were swollen and red and her neck had a mark blooming just above the collar line that no amount of hair rearrangement was going to cover.

"I *won* the fight," she corrected, meeting his eyes in the mirror. "Look at me. I'm a champion. I'm a decorated veteran."

She tried to finger-comb her hair into something civilized. It resisted. She tried again. It resisted harder.

"Okay, the hair is a lost cause. The hair has seceded from the union." She turned her head side to side, assessing. "I'm going to tell people I opened a window and it was windy. At the party. Inside the house."

She wet her fingertips under the tap and went after the mascara properly this time, scrubbing at the smudges with the focus of someone defusing a bomb. It helped marginally. She still looked like someone who had been recently and enthusiastically fucked against a bathroom door, because she had been, and there were limits to what cold water and determination could accomplish.

She turned around, leaned back against the sink, and looked up at him. Her hands found his chest again — just resting there, palms flat, feeling him breathe.

"You look wrecked too, for the record," she said softly, and the fondness in her voice was so naked it almost embarrassed her. Almost. "Your shirt is inside out."

She glanced down.

"Wait. No it isn't. But you *looked*."

The grin came back, incandescent, and she grabbed the front of his shirt and pulled him down into a kiss that was slow and sweet and had none of the urgency from before — just warmth, just gratitude, just the particular tenderness of two people standing in a stranger's bathroom surrounded by the wreckage of their own terrible decisions and not regretting a single one.

She let him go. Took a breath. Squared her shoulders like she was about to walk into battle.

"Alright," she said, hoarse and happy. "Downstairs. Poker faces. We are two normal people who were definitely not just in this bathroom together. I was on the phone. You were looking at coats. We have never met. We are strangers who arrived separately and —"

She caught sight of the seashell soap on the floor and picked it up, placing it back on the counter with great ceremony.

"Sorry about your evening," she told it.

Then she turned back to him, eyes bright, and held up two fingers.

"Two minutes apart. I go first. If anyone asks, you know *nothing*."

She unlocked the door, smoothed her shirt one final time, and stepped into the hallway with the posture of someone who had absolutely nothing to hide.

From downstairs, Fen heard Sophie's voice before Odile even made it to the bottom step.

"*There* she is. Good phone call?"

"Great phone call," Odile said brightly. "Very productive. Discussed many topics. All of them boring."

A beat of silence. Then Sophie, dry as sand: "Your shirt's on backwards, babe."

Odile's voice, barely a whisper but still somehow carrying: "*Shit.*"

And then laughter — Sophie's, and someone else's, and then Odile's, joining in, unrepentant and warm and ringing through the house like she hadn't just spent the last fifteen minutes making very different sounds in the upstairs bathroom.

Fen had about ninety seconds before he had to walk into that.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content:
I shake my head, still grinning like an idiot. I straighten my shirt, run a hand through my hair, and take a deep breath. I can still hear Odile laughing downstairs.

When I finally head down, everyone’s looking. Sophie’s smirking, Odile’s pretending to be very interested in a chip bowl. I shrug, heading toward the kitchen. “Anyone seen my coat?”

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit had made it as far as the kitchen doorway before Bear moved, which was further than usual and had clearly been allowed.

"You let me get that far," Kit said, backing up one step.

"I did," Bear agreed. "I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't be," I say, and go.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn't count to three. He didn't give Kit the head start they weren't actually asking for. The word *go* was still hanging in the air when he launched off the counter he'd been leaning against, bare feet hitting tile with a sound that was all intent and no grace.

Kit was fast. Kit had always been fast, and eight years of this particular game had only made them faster — they knew the apartment like a map drawn on the inside of their eyelids, knew which corners to cut tight and which doorframes to use as pivot points. Bear heard the sharp slap of a palm against the hallway wall as Kit banked left toward the bedroom.

He didn't follow the same path. That was a rookie mistake he'd stopped making around year two.

He cut through the living room instead, vaulting the arm of the couch with one hand and catching himself on the bookshelf hard enough to make the spines rattle. The bedroom had two entrances — a fact Kit knew perfectly well, a fact Bear was banking on Kit *expecting* him to exploit — and so the real question was which doorway Kit would be watching.

He came through the bathroom-side entrance low and quiet, and Kit was exactly where he'd predicted: turned toward the hallway door, weight on the balls of their feet, ready to bolt again.

Bear closed the distance in two strides and got an arm around Kit's waist from behind, pulling them back against his chest with enough force to make the point without losing his footing.

"Don't be generous," he repeated against the side of Kit's neck, grinning. "Got it."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: *I let out a sharp laugh, breathless from the chase.* "Cheater." *I lean back into the hold, turning my head just enough.* "Bathroom door was dirty."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear laughed, low and real, the sound rumbling through his chest and into Kit's back where they were pressed together.

"Dirty," he repeated, like he was tasting the word. "You mean *effective*. There's a difference, and you know it because you're the one who used the bathroom door on me in March and then spent twenty minutes being smug about it."

His arm tightened around Kit's waist — not a squeeze, just a settling, a reminder of where they were and who had them. His other hand came up and found the side of Kit's jaw, thumb tracing the line of it with a deliberateness that had nothing to do with gentleness and everything to do with knowing exactly where he wanted to end up.

"Also," he said, mouth still close enough to Kit's neck that the words landed warm against skin, "you're leaning back. Into me. Right now. Which is not the body language of someone who's actually upset about the bathroom door."

He turned his head just enough to press his teeth — not a bite yet, just the promise of one — against the tendon that ran along the side of Kit's throat. Held it there. Let Kit feel the edges of it without any of the pressure.

"You want to call it dirty and run again, I'll give you another three seconds. Might even use the hallway door this time." His grin was audible. "Might not."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt the moment Kit's resistance shifted from *real* to *ritual* — the difference between a body trying to create distance and a body going through the motions of trying because the motions were part of the point. He'd learned to read that shift the way some people read weather: not by any single sign but by the whole texture of it changing at once.

Kit's back hit the hallway wall and Bear was already there, one hand flat against the plaster beside Kit's head, the other catching Kit's wrist — the left one, the one that had been reaching for the doorframe. He pinned it at shoulder height, not hard enough to grind bone against wall but hard enough that Kit would have to mean it to pull free.

"Didn't even make me work for it," Bear said, and he was breathing harder than the short chase warranted, which was its own kind of honesty. Eight years and Kit still did this to him. "You're slipping."

He shifted his weight forward, pressing Kit into the wall with his chest, his hips, the whole solid length of him. Not subtle. Not trying to be. The hallway was narrow enough that the opposite wall was close behind his shoulder blades, boxing them both into a space that felt smaller than it was.

He brought his mouth to the hinge of Kit's jaw and bit — properly this time, not the teasing preview from the bedroom but teeth sinking in with intent, the kind of pressure that would bloom into a bruise by morning. He held it for three seconds, four, five, feeling Kit's pulse hammering against his tongue, then released and pulled back just far enough to look at Kit's face.

His eyes were dark and thoroughly pleased.

"That's one," he said.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "*I wasn't slipping,*" *I say, a little breathless.* "*I was letting you catch up. One's a good start.*"

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear studied Kit's face from six inches away — the flush, the slightly too-quick breathing, the defiance that was genuine even when everything else was deliberate. That was the thing about Kit. The bratting was real. The submission was real. They existed in the same sentence and always had.

"Letting me catch up," Bear said, flat, the way he repeated things when he wanted Kit to hear how they sounded out loud. "You were *letting me* catch up. That's the story we're going with."

He shifted his grip on Kit's wrist, not releasing it but rotating it — turning Kit's arm so the inside of the wrist faced out, the pale skin where the veins ran close to the surface. He pressed his thumb into the center of it, firm and slow, feeling the pulse jump under the pad of his finger.

"Here's what I think happened," he said, conversational, like they were discussing what to have for dinner. "I think you ran hard out of the kitchen because you always run hard out of the kitchen. I think you had a plan for the bedroom and I broke it. And I think when I caught you the first time and you felt my teeth, something in that head of yours decided *oh, I want more of that* and your legs stopped cooperating."

He leaned in, pressing Kit harder into the wall, and brought his mouth to the other side of Kit's neck — the unmarked side, the side that was still just skin. He didn't bite. Not yet. He let his breath land there, let Kit feel the heat of proximity without contact, and held it long enough for the waiting to become its own kind of pressure.

"One's a good *start*," he agreed against Kit's throat. "You said it yourself."

Then he bit down — same deliberate pressure, same unhurried hold, but lower this time, closer to the junction of neck and shoulder where the muscle was thicker and could take more. He felt Kit's pulse against his teeth and held on until he was satisfied with the depth of it, until he was sure it would last.

He released, licked the mark once — proprietary, not soothing — and pulled back.

"Two," he said. "You want to keep counting, or do you want to lose track?"

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear got Kit down onto the hallway floor with more efficiency than elegance — one hand still on Kit's wrist, the other finding Kit's hip and using his weight to take them both to the ground. His knee hit the hardwood and he'd feel that tomorrow and he didn't care even slightly. Kit's back met the floor and Bear was over them, between their legs, and the geography of it was so familiar it was almost muscle memory except that it never actually felt routine. Eight years and it never felt routine.

Clothes were — yes. A problem.

Kit's shirt got rucked up to their armpits because Bear couldn't be bothered to pull it over their head when there was skin available *now*, right now, the flat plane of Kit's stomach and the ridge of their ribs and the places where Bear's previous marks had faded to yellow-green ghosts from last week. He put his mouth on one of those fading bruises and bit over it, refreshing it, reclaiming the territory with a sound in his throat that was closer to a growl than he'd admit to later.

His own shirt came off because Kit yanked it and Bear cooperated for exactly long enough to get it over his head before pinning Kit's hands again — both wrists this time, one in each of his hands, pressed to the floor above Kit's head. The position stretched Kit out underneath him and Bear took a moment to just *look*, breathing hard, cataloging.

"Pants," he said, like it was a problem he was identifying rather than solving. He let go of Kit's wrists — a calculated risk, because free hands meant Kit could do things and Kit *always* did things — and went for Kit's waistband with both hands, thumbs hooking in, dragging everything down with the kind of graceless urgency that meant a seam might not survive the evening.

He got them to Kit's knees and decided that was far enough for now.

He settled his weight back over Kit, skin against skin where he'd earned it, and pressed his forehead against Kit's. Close enough that they were breathing each other's air. Close enough that Kit couldn't look anywhere but at him.

"Hi," he said, and he was grinning, and it was the most dangerous version of his grin — the one that was all warmth and all teeth at the same time. "We're on the floor."

He rolled his hips once, slow and deliberate, and watched Kit's face from an inch away.

"Tell me what you want."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: *I arch up into the pressure, my hands coming up to grip his shoulders.* "You. Exactly like this." *I hook a leg around his waist.* "Don't stop."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt Kit's leg lock around his waist and the heel dig into the small of his back and something in his chest cracked open the way it always did — the way it had been doing for eight years, this specific fracture that only happened when Kit stopped performing and started *asking*. The words were simple. They were always simple. And they always undid him.

"Yeah," he said, rough, almost to himself. "Okay. Yeah."

He dropped his head into the curve of Kit's neck and pressed his mouth to the mark he'd left there — the second one, the deeper one — and felt the heat of it against his lips. Kit's hands on his shoulders were gripping hard enough to leave crescents and he wanted every single one of them.

His own pants took another thirty seconds of graceless negotiation that involved Kit's help and his swearing and one elbow hitting the baseboard hard enough to make him hiss. Then there was nothing between them and the full-length contact knocked the air out of him the way it always did, every time, skin and warmth and Kit's body arching up against his like a sentence he'd been trying to finish.

He braced himself on one forearm beside Kit's head and found their hip with his other hand, thumb pressing into the hollow of it, holding Kit exactly where he wanted them. He rolled his hips again — not slow this time, not teasing, just *there*, pressure and friction and intent — and his breath stuttered against Kit's throat.

"Not stopping," he said into their skin. He turned his head and caught Kit's earlobe between his teeth, tugged, released. "Not stopping. You'd have to make me, and you're not going to, because you just told me *don't* and you meant it."

He found a rhythm that was unhurried but relentless, the kind of pace that built like weather — his weight shifting over Kit with each movement, the hardwood floor unforgiving beneath them both, his hand tightening on Kit's hip hard enough to promise another bruise.

He lifted his head to look at Kit's face. Needed to see it. Always needed to see it.

"There you are," he murmured, and it came out tender in a way that didn't contradict anything else that was happening, because it never had. He kissed Kit — finally, the first real kiss of the evening, deep and unhurried even as his hips maintained their rhythm, his teeth catching Kit's lower lip and pulling before letting go.

"Right here," he said against Kit's mouth. "I've got you. I'm right here."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt Kit's shoulder yield under his teeth the way it always did — that specific give of muscle tensing and then releasing, the body's argument with itself about whether this was damage or devotion. He held on, jaw locked, breathing hard through his nose, and when Kit said *again* the word went through him like voltage.

He pulled off. Looked at the mark. It was already darkening, the impression of his teeth distinct enough to count, and something old and uncomplicated in his brain said *mine* with the same certainty it had been saying it for eight years.

He bit again. Same shoulder, half an inch lower, overlapping the first mark so the bruise would bloom into something shapeless and unmistakable. Kit's hands were on him — nails dragging down his back in lines he'd find in the mirror tomorrow — and he growled against Kit's skin, a sound that started in his chest and didn't make it past his throat. He bore down harder, felt Kit's breath hitch underneath him, and held it until his jaw ached. Until he was sure.

He released and pressed his tongue flat against the marks, tasting salt and heat, and his hips hadn't stopped moving through any of it. The floor was brutal on his knees and he didn't care. Kit's leg was still hooked around his waist and every time he pressed forward that heel dug into his back like a demand.

"You're going to feel all of these tomorrow," he said against Kit's shoulder, mouth still hovering over the mess he'd made. His voice was wrecked. He didn't try to fix it. "Every time your shirt moves. Every time you reach for something."

He shifted his weight, pressed deeper, and felt Kit arch underneath him.

"Good," he said, and it wasn't clear whether he was responding to something Kit did or just stating his opinion of the entire situation. He brought his mouth back to Kit's shoulder and set his teeth against fresh skin — just the edges, just the warning — and waited. Not for permission. He had permission. He waited because the half-second before was its own kind of gift, the breath where Kit knew exactly what was coming and wanted it anyway.

Then he bit down, and didn't let go for a long time.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I push up into his bite, my fingers knotting in his hair. "Harder," I say, and it comes out ragged, like a challenge.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear heard *harder* and the sound Kit's voice made around it — torn, breathless, a dare wrapped in a demand — and his whole body responded before his brain finished processing the word. His jaw tightened. The muscle in his forearm trembled where it was braced against the floor.

Kit's fingers were knotted in his hair and pulling, and the pain of it was bright and clean and exactly right, a counterpoint to the ache in his knees and the scratches down his back that were still stinging. Kit always gave as good as they got. That was the deal. That had always been the deal, and Bear loved the deal with every bruised and bitten inch of himself.

He bore down. Past the point where his jaw protested, past the careful calibration he usually maintained, into the territory Kit was asking for — the territory where the bite would be tender for days, not hours, where the bruise would go deep enough to ache when pressed. He felt Kit's skin resist and then not, felt the shudder that ran through Kit's body and transmitted directly into his through every point of contact. Kit's fingers tightened in his hair and the pull sent sparks down his spine and he groaned against Kit's shoulder without unlocking his jaw.

He held it. Counted his own heartbeats because he'd lost the ability to count seconds. Five. Eight. Twelve. Kit's chest was heaving against his and their hips were moving together in something that had stopped being rhythm and become need, raw and graceless and perfect.

When he finally released, his breath came out shaky against the mark. He pressed his forehead to Kit's shoulder and stayed there for two heartbeats, just breathing, his lips against ruined skin.

"You," he said, and his voice was destroyed, barely recognizable even to himself, "are going to be the death of me. You know that. You've always known that."

He lifted his head. Kit's face was flushed and open and *wrecked* in the way that made Bear's chest do the thing it did — the crack, the fracture, the eight-year-old break that never healed because he never wanted it to. He kissed Kit's forehead. Then the bridge of their nose. Then their mouth, hard, tasting the sound Kit made against his tongue.

He pulled back just enough to speak.

"Challenge accepted," he said, and his hand found Kit's hip again and gripped hard enough to shift them both, changing the angle, finding the one that made Kit's spine arch off the hardwood. "Every single time, Kit. Challenge *accepted*."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear looked at Kit's wrists — offered, deliberate, placed exactly where he could take them — and something behind his sternum went very quiet and very loud at the same time. Eight years. Eight years of this, and Kit still had the ability to lay something in front of him like a gift and a gauntlet simultaneously and make his hands shake.

He took both wrists. Wrapped his fingers around them and pressed them to the floor above Kit's head, feeling the bird-quick pulse in each one hammering against his palms. He held them there and just looked at Kit's face for a moment — the flush, the blown pupils, the mouth that was swollen from his teeth and still managing to look defiant.

"Thursday," he repeated. His voice was gravel. "That's three days. You're placing an order."

He wasn't complaining. He was confirming the specifications.

He started at the inside of Kit's left wrist, where the skin was thin enough to show the blue map of veins underneath. He pressed his mouth there first — just lips, just warmth, the kind of gesture that in any other context would be tender and in this one was surveying. Then he bit, controlled and precise, finding the spot between the tendons where the flesh was softest and sinking in with the slow, measured pressure of someone who understood exactly what he was doing. Not a mauling. A mark. Intentional. Placed where a watchband would sit, where every glance at the time for the next four days would come with a reminder.

Kit's fingers curled into fists above his grip and he felt the tendons jump under his teeth. He held on, breathing steadily through his nose, and adjusted the pressure incrementally — more, a fraction more, until he felt the threshold where bruise became certainty. Then he held that line. Didn't cross it. Didn't need to. The sustained pressure would do what a harder, shorter bite wouldn't: it would go deep, settle into the tissue, ache on Thursday the way Kit was asking for.

He released and examined his work. The impression of his teeth was livid against the pale skin, already flushing toward purple at the edges. He ran his thumb across it and felt Kit's breath catch.

"One," he said.

He transferred both of Kit's wrists to one hand — his grip was big enough, had always been big enough, and Kit's wrists together fit inside his fingers like they'd been measured for it — and used his free hand to turn Kit's right arm, exposing the inside of that wrist too. He mirrored the placement exactly. Same spot. Same pressure. Same slow, deliberate hold that made Kit's hips jerk up against his.

"Two," he said when he pulled off, and his voice had dropped into the register that meant he was concentrating, the one Kit had once described as his *working* voice.

He let go of Kit's wrists but didn't move them. Left them there above Kit's head, an unspoken instruction. Then he shifted down Kit's body, his mouth finding the inside of Kit's arm just below the elbow, the soft skin of the inner forearm where a bruise would press against every surface Kit leaned on. He bit there too, harder than the wrists, because the tissue was thicker and could take it and because Kit had said *harder* and he was still carrying that word in his teeth like a coal.

He worked his way across Kit's body with the methodical attention of someone building something. The junction of neck and shoulder on the left side, where the trapezius provided enough muscle to absorb real force — he bit there until Kit made a sound that wasn't a word and then held on for five more seconds. The ridge of Kit's collarbone, where the bite had to be more precise because the bone was close, teeth bracketing the edge of it and pressing into the muscle on either side. The inside of Kit's thigh, where he had to shift down and push Kit's leg open and the skin was so sensitive that the first press of his teeth made Kit's whole body tense like a drawn bow.

He lost count somewhere around seven. He didn't think Kit was counting either.

Each mark was placed with intention — not random, not frenzied, but chosen for the specific kind of pain it would produce on Thursday. The wrists would ache with pressure. The shoulder would burn when Kit reached overhead. The thigh would announce itself with every step, every shift in a chair, a private secret pressed between Kit's skin and whatever they were wearing.

He came back up Kit's body when he was done, settling his weight over them again, and found Kit's mouth. The kiss was different now — slower, deeper, the urgency still there but underlaid with something that felt like reverence, or maybe just the specific gravity of knowing someone this well and still wanting to leave proof of it on their skin.

He pulled back. Braced himself on both forearms, caging Kit between them, and looked down.

Kit was a map of him. The marks were already blooming in stages — the earliest ones from the hallway darkening toward purple, the newest ones still red and sharp-edged. He could trace the chronology of the evening across Kit's body like reading a timeline.

"Mirror tomorrow," he said, quiet now, his thumbs tracing Kit's jaw. "Still hurting Thursday. I know what I'm doing, Kit. I've had eight years of practice on you."

He pressed his hips forward, slow, deliberate, a reminder that the biting had been its own project but the rest of them was still here, still happening, still building toward something inevitable.

"What else," he said. Not a question. An opening. His mouth found the mark on Kit's throat and hovered there, breath warm against bruised skin. "Tell me what else."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: *I wrap my arms around his neck, pulling him down against me.* "Just keep going," *I breathe against his ear.* "Don't stop until we're both wrecked."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt Kit's arms close around his neck and the weight of the pull — Kit drawing him down, eliminating the last inch of distance he'd been maintaining on his forearms — and he went. Let his full weight settle onto Kit, chest to chest, the hardwood floor doing its unforgiving work against Kit's back and his knees and neither of them caring. Kit's mouth was at his ear and the words landed warm and close and stripped of everything except what they meant.

*Don't stop until we're both wrecked.*

He turned his face into Kit's neck and breathed. Just breathed, for one second, his ribs expanding against Kit's ribs, the whole length of their bodies pressed together so completely that he could feel Kit's heartbeat in his own sternum. Then he moved.

Not faster. Not yet. He moved like the instruction had unlocked something in him that was past performance, past the game, past the cheerful scorekeeping and the competitive biting — into the place underneath all of it where the only thing left was *Kit* and *more* and *don't stop* and the particular madness of wanting someone you already had.

His hand found the back of Kit's thigh, hitching their leg higher around his waist, changing the angle until he felt Kit's breath stutter against his ear. He kept that angle. Built on it. Each movement was deliberate and unhurried and devastating in the way that slow, relentless things were devastating — not a storm but the tide, the kind of force that didn't need to rush because it wasn't going to stop.

Kit's nails found the scratches they'd already carved down his back and dug into them, reopening the sting, and Bear made a sound against Kit's throat that was barely human — low and broken and grateful. He bit down on the nearest mark, the one at the junction of neck and shoulder, and felt it give differently now that the bruise was already forming. Softer. More tender. Kit hissed and pulled him closer and he could feel the contradiction of it — the flinch and the demand happening simultaneously in Kit's body — and it wrecked him the way it always wrecked him.

"I've got you," he said, and the words came out fractured, split across breaths he couldn't quite control. His forehead was pressed against the floor beside Kit's head and his hand was gripping Kit's thigh hard enough to add another bruise to the collection and his hips were moving with a steadiness that his voice had already lost. "I've got you, I'm here, I'm not stopping."

Kit arched under him and he felt it in his spine — the feedback loop of Kit's body responding to his and his responding back, eight years of learning each other written into the way they fit. He knew the sound Kit made when they were close. He knew the way Kit's fingers went from gripping to clutching, the shift from holding on to holding on for dear life. He knew the specific tension that built in Kit's thighs and the way their breathing went ragged and thin.

He was learning it again right now. That was the part that never stopped astonishing him — that it was new every time, that the knowing and the discovering happened simultaneously, that Kit at the edge was always Kit at the edge and always different.

His own body was betraying him in stages. The controlled rhythm was fraying at the edges. His arms were shaking where they braced against the floor. The scratches on his back and the ache in his knees and Kit's heel digging into his spine were all blurring into a single bright signal that he couldn't distinguish from pleasure anymore.

"Kit," he said, and it came out like the word had been punched out of him. Just the name. Just that. He lifted his head enough to find Kit's mouth and kissed them with everything he had left — messy, desperate, all teeth and tongue and the taste of Kit's skin still on his lips.

He didn't stop. He'd been told not to stop and he wasn't going to stop. He drove into the rhythm until it stopped being a rhythm and became something more honest, something ragged and graceless that belonged entirely to the two of them on the hallway floor with the baseboard digging into his elbow and Kit's fingers in his hair and bruises blooming between them like a shared language.

When it broke — when Kit broke, and he felt it happen in the clench of their body and the sound they made against his mouth — he followed. Close enough behind that it felt like the same wave, the same collapse, his whole body shuddering against Kit's as the tension that had been building since the kitchen doorway released all at once and left him hollowed out and shaking.

He didn't move. Couldn't, for a long moment. He was breathing hard against Kit's neck, his weight probably too much and Kit's arms still around him and the floor absolutely brutal beneath them both. His lips found the worst of the marks on Kit's shoulder — the one where he'd bitten three times, the one that would be spectacular — and pressed against it. Gently, this time. Not to add anything. Just to be there.

"Wrecked," he murmured against Kit's skin, and huffed a laugh that was mostly air. "Order fulfilled."

He shifted just enough to take some of his weight onto his forearms, looked down at Kit's face. Kit looked — God. Kit looked like everything Bear had ever wanted to come home to. Flushed and undone and marked and *his*, in the way that had nothing to do with owning and everything to do with being chosen, over and over, for eight years on hallway floors.

"We should move to the couch," he said. Made no effort to move. "At some point. Eventually."

He pressed his lips to Kit's forehead, lingering there, his eyes closed.

"Thursday," he said quietly. "I promise."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear heard *don't stop* and the words landed in the same place they'd landed every time Kit had said them tonight — somewhere below his ribs, somewhere past thinking, in the part of him that had been answering Kit for eight years without hesitation.

He hadn't moved off Kit. Hadn't wanted to. His weight was still settled over them, his forearms braced on either side of Kit's head, and he could feel the sweat cooling between their bodies and the floor's unforgiving hardness against his knees and none of it mattered because Kit had said *don't stop* and he wasn't going to.

He pressed his mouth to Kit's throat, to the mark there that was already turning the color of a storm, and breathed against it. Then he moved his lips along the tendon, tracing the line of it with his mouth open, tasting salt and heat and the faint copper-edge of bitten skin. Kit's pulse was still hammering and he could feel it against his tongue — fast, not slowing, not finished.

"I'm here," he said, and his voice was a ruin. He didn't try to rebuild it.

He shifted his hips — slowly, deliberately, still sensitive enough that the friction made his breath catch and his vision narrow — and felt Kit's body respond underneath him. The leg around his waist tightened. Kit's fingers, still tangled in his hair, pulled, and the bright sting of it traveled down his spine and settled at the base of it like an ember that hadn't gone out.

He found Kit's mouth. The kiss was unhurried in a way that nothing else about the evening had been — deep and slow and thorough, his tongue tracing Kit's lower lip where his teeth had been earlier, finding the swollen place and pressing into it gently. Kit made a sound against his mouth, small and raw, and he swallowed it. Kept it.

His hand found Kit's hip — the one he'd already bruised, the one where his fingerprints were developing like a photograph — and gripped again. Not as hard. Differently. His thumb traced the crest of the bone and then dipped inward, following the line where hip became thigh became the soft, heated skin that was still trembling under his touch. He took his time. He had been given time and he was going to use every second of it.

Kit arched into his hand and he watched it happen from inches away — the way Kit's head tipped back against the hardwood, the way their throat worked around a breath that wouldn't quite come, the way their body opened toward him like a question he already knew the answer to. He pressed his mouth to the exposed column of Kit's throat and bit again, lighter this time, a graze more than a claim, and felt the vibration of Kit's groan against his lips.

He moved down. Slow. Kissing the marks he'd already made — the collarbone, where the bruise was sharp-edged and precise; the chest, where he'd left nothing yet and now did, setting his teeth against the curve of muscle and biting with the patient, sustained pressure he'd used on Kit's wrists. Kit's hands left his hair and found his shoulders, gripping hard enough that the crescents from earlier reopened into fresh bright points of pain that he leaned into gratefully.

He stayed there, mouth working against Kit's chest, his hand still tracing the line of Kit's hip, his body rocking slowly against Kit's in a rhythm that was barely a rhythm — more like breathing, more like the involuntary pulse of something that couldn't stop because stopping wasn't in its vocabulary. He could feel Kit hardening again against his stomach, or maybe Kit had never fully come down, and the knowledge of it sent a wave of heat through him that made his arms shake.

"There," he murmured against Kit's sternum. He pressed his forehead to the center of Kit's chest and felt their heartbeat against his skull, rapid and strong. "Right there. I can feel you."

He lifted his head and looked up the length of Kit's body at their face. Kit was watching him. Kit's eyes were dark and wet and wide open and Bear felt the fracture in his chest split another inch, the way it always did when Kit looked at him like that — like he was the only fixed point in a room that had lost its walls.

He moved back up, bringing his body flush against Kit's again, and the full-length contact was almost too much — every nerve ending already raw, every point of contact amplified. He hissed through his teeth and felt Kit do the same, their breath mingling in the narrow space between their mouths.

His hand slid between them. He wrapped his fingers around both of them together — Kit and himself, the heat of it startling even though he'd known exactly what he was reaching for — and Kit's hips bucked hard enough to shift them both an inch across the floor. Bear braced his other forearm against the hardwood and held on.

"I've got you," he said, and started moving his hand.

Slow. Maddeningly slow. He could feel Kit's pulse against his palm and his own pulse answering it, the two rhythms not quite synced, chasing each other. Kit's fingers dug into his back — into the scratches, the long torn lines from earlier — and the pain was exquisite, bright and specific and grounding in a way that kept him present when the pleasure was trying to pull him under.

He set his teeth against Kit's jaw. Not a bite. Just the presence of them, the edges resting against skin, a reminder of everything he'd already done and everything he could still do. Kit turned their head and caught his mouth and the kiss was graceless and desperate and exactly right, all heat and no technique, Kit's tongue against his and Kit's hand fisting in his hair and Kit's hips rolling up into his grip with a rhythm that was falling apart as fast as it formed.

He tightened his hand. Felt them both respond — Kit with a sharp inhale, himself with a groan that came from somewhere he didn't have a name for. The friction was devastating. Every stroke dragged sensation through him in waves that built on each other, layer over layer, and he could feel Kit building too — the tension in Kit's thighs, the way Kit's breathing had gone thin and high, the way Kit's body was tightening against his like a wire being drawn taut.

"Don't hold back," Bear said against Kit's mouth, and his voice cracked on the last word. "Don't — Kit. Let me feel it. Give me everything."

Kit's back arched off the floor. The sound Kit made was not a word — it was something older than language, something that came from the same place as the bite marks and the chase and the eight years of knowing exactly how to take each other apart. Bear felt Kit break against him, felt the heat and the pulse of it in his hand, felt Kit's body clench and shudder and go rigid, and he held on through all of it, his hand still moving, his mouth still on Kit's, breathing Kit's sounds like oxygen.

His own orgasm hit him like a wall he'd been running toward — not a surprise but an inevitability, the accumulated weight of everything Kit had given him tonight crashing through him all at once. His vision whited out. His hand stuttered. He pressed his face into Kit's neck and made a sound he would never be able to describe afterward, something wrecked and reverent and completely without dignity, and felt his whole body come apart against Kit's in a series of shudders that seemed to go on longer than physics should have allowed.

He didn't let go. His hand stayed where it was, loose now, just holding, the mess between them warm and slick and evidence. His face was pressed into the crook of Kit's neck and he was breathing in ragged pulls that he couldn't steady and didn't try to. Kit's arms were around him. Kit's heartbeat was shaking them both.

For a long time, neither of them moved.

Bear's thumb traced a slow, absent circle against Kit's hip. His lips were resting against the deepest mark on Kit's shoulder — the one he'd bitten three times, the one that was going to be extraordinary — and he could feel the heat radiating from it against his mouth.

"Still here," he said, eventually. His voice was barely a sound. "Still not stopping."

He shifted just enough to take some of his weight onto his side, pulling Kit with him so they were tangled together on the hallway floor — legs intertwined, his arm under Kit's head, the other hand still resting on Kit's hip like it had forgotten how to be anywhere else. The floor was absolutely unforgiving and his back was going to have opinions about this in the morning and he could not have cared less.

He pressed his lips to Kit's temple. Then the corner of Kit's eye. Then the bridge of Kit's nose. Small, precise kisses placed with the same deliberate attention he'd given the bite marks, except these were soft and these were the part he never kept score on.

"You're a disaster," he murmured against Kit's cheekbone, and it came out so tender it barely qualified as an insult. "You're my favorite disaster. You're a disaster on a hallway floor and I'm going to have rug burn except there's no rug and I love you and we should really move to the couch."

He didn't move to the couch. He pulled Kit closer instead, tucking them against his chest, and pressed his mouth to the top of Kit's head.

"Thursday," he said again, quiet, a promise renewed. His fingers found the mark on Kit's wrist and traced its edges gently, mapping the shape of it like braille. "You'll find every single one. And you'll know exactly where you were when you got each of them."

He closed his eyes. His breathing was finally slowing. Kit was warm against him and marked and wrecked and here, and the hallway floor was terrible, and his knees were going to be a problem, and Kit's back was going to be a problem, and none of it was a problem.

"Don't stop," he echoed softly, almost to himself. "Yeah. I heard you."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: *I tuck my head under his chin, my fingers tracing the scratches down his back.* "You're one to talk about disasters." *A pause, then a quiet laugh.* "I think we're stuck to the floor."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear laughed, and it hurt — his ribs, his knees, some muscle in his side that he'd apparently been clenching for the last twenty minutes without noticing — and he laughed harder because it hurt, which made it hurt more, which was exactly the kind of stupid feedback loop that Kit would appreciate.

"We are not stuck to the floor," he said, with the confident authority of a man who had not yet attempted to move. Kit's fingers were tracing the scratches down his back and every pass sent a bright, stinging ripple through him that he leaned into like a cat. He'd look at those in the mirror later. He'd catalog them the way Kit would catalog the bites — with satisfaction, with the private pleasure of evidence.

"We are *resting* on the floor. Voluntarily. Because we're adults who made a series of excellent decisions that happened to be geographically located in a hallway."

Kit's head was tucked under his chin and he could feel their breath against his collarbone, warm and even and slowing toward something that might eventually be normal. His hand was still on Kit's hip. He hadn't moved it. He wasn't sure he was going to move it. It had established residency.

He shifted experimentally — just his shoulder, just an inch — and felt the pull of dried sweat and worse against the hardwood.

"Okay," he conceded. "We might be slightly stuck to the floor."

Kit's fingers found a particularly deep scratch — one of the later ones, from when things had gotten desperate and graceless — and traced its full length from shoulder blade to the small of his back. Bear's breath caught and his arm tightened around Kit involuntarily.

"That one's yours," he said. "That one's going to sting in the shower tomorrow and I'm going to think about you every single time, and you know that, and that's why you did it."

He pressed his mouth to the top of Kit's head and left it there, speaking into their hair.

"Here's what's going to happen. In approximately five minutes, I'm going to peel us both off this floor. It's going to be undignified. There may be sounds. I'm going to carry you to the couch because my knees are already destroyed so I might as well commit. And then I'm going to get a warm cloth and clean us both up and you're going to lie there and let me, and you're not going to argue about it because you just asked me to wreck you and I did and aftercare is not optional, it's the other half of the same sentence."

He paused. His thumb traced a slow circle on Kit's hip.

"And then I'm going to sit on the couch with you in my lap and we're going to drink water — yes, water, don't make that face, I can feel you making that face — and I'm going to press on every single mark I left and you're going to tell me which ones are your favorites. And then maybe we'll order food because I think it's—" He craned his neck toward the kitchen, where the microwave clock was theoretically visible. It wasn't, from the floor. "—some time. It's some time o'clock. We missed dinner. That's your fault."

Kit's quiet laugh vibrated against his chest and he felt it in his sternum, in the fracture that never healed, in the place where eight years of Kit had taken up permanent residence.

"Five minutes," he repeated. He didn't move. "Starting now."

He closed his eyes. Kit's fingers were still mapping the damage down his back, slow and thorough, and he let them. The floor was terrible. His body was a collection of complaints organized by severity. Kit was warm and heavy against him and breathing and *his* in every way that mattered.

"Okay, maybe ten minutes," he amended.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: *I press my lips to his collarbone, smiling.* "You're going to have to carry me anyway. My legs aren't working." *I shift slightly, wincing.* "And I think the floor stole my spine."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt Kit's lips against his collarbone and the curve of their smile pressed into his skin and something in him went so soft it was almost embarrassing. Almost. He'd stopped being embarrassed about softness around year three, when he'd realized that the same hands that left bruises were the same hands that held Kit's face afterward and that there was no contradiction, had never been one.

"The floor didn't steal your spine," he said. "The floor *borrowed* your spine. It'll give it back after ibuprofen and a horizontal surface that isn't made of hatred."

Kit winced when they shifted and Bear's hand moved immediately to the small of their back, pressing flat, warm, applying just enough counterpressure to ease whatever the hardwood had done to the muscles there. He knew this body. He knew where it held tension and where it stored pain and where the difference between good-hurt and bad-hurt lived. His thumb found the knot forming along Kit's lower spine and worked into it with a slow, firm pressure that had nothing to do with the evening's earlier agenda and everything to do with the part that came after.

"Legs not working," he repeated. "Noted. Filing that under compliments."

He opened his eyes. Stared at the ceiling for a moment — their hallway ceiling, which had a hairline crack in the plaster that he'd been meaning to fix for two years and which had now witnessed things that no ceiling should have to witness. He sent it a brief, silent apology.

Then he moved.

It was, as predicted, undignified. There were sounds. His knees announced their formal protest the moment he shifted to a kneeling position, a grinding pop from the left one that made him hiss through his teeth. The peeling-apart happened in stages — his torso first, then his hip, then his thigh, each separation accompanied by the faint tacky resistance of skin leaving hardwood. Kit made a noise that was half laugh and half groan and Bear grinned down at them, kneeling over them on the hallway floor like some battered, scratched-up disaster of a person, which was exactly what he was.

"Don't say a word," he said, even though Kit hadn't said anything yet but was clearly about to.

He got one arm under Kit's knees and the other behind their back and lifted. His lower back had a pointed conversation with him about physics and age and hardwood floors, and he ignored it with the practiced ease of a man who had been ignoring his body's reasonable suggestions for the better part of a decade. Kit wasn't heavy. Kit was exactly the right weight for this — substantial enough to feel real, light enough that Bear could carry them the twenty feet to the couch without his arms giving out, which was the only distance that mattered.

Kit's head dropped against his shoulder and he felt their breath against his neck, felt the smile still pressed into his skin, and his chest did the thing again. The fracture. The break that was also a door.

He made it to the couch and lowered Kit onto it with more care than he'd shown anything else all evening — one hand cradling the back of their head, easing them down onto the cushions, making sure their back landed on something that wasn't actively hostile. He grabbed the throw blanket from the arm of the couch and dropped it over Kit's legs, not because Kit was cold but because the gesture was part of the grammar of this, the language they'd built together out of bites and blankets and the space between.

"Don't move," he said, pointing at Kit with entirely unnecessary authority. "Water. Cloth. I'll be right back."

He walked to the kitchen and his gait was wrecked — stiff-kneed, favoring the left side, moving like a man who'd spent the last hour on a hardwood floor doing things that hardwood floors were not designed for. He caught his reflection in the dark window above the sink and stopped.

His back. He turned, looked over his shoulder, and — yeah. Kit's work. Long red lines from his shoulders to his waist, some of them raised, a few of them beading where the nails had broken skin. They looked like a map of something. They looked like they'd sting in the shower exactly the way he'd said they would. He stared at them for a moment with an expression that was trying to be assessment and was actually just pride, raw and unhidden.

He filled two glasses of water. Found a clean cloth, ran it under warm water, wrung it out. Grabbed the ibuprofen from the cabinet above the stove because he was forty and Kit's back had met the floor and planning ahead was a form of love.

He came back to the couch and Kit was exactly where he'd left them, which was either obedience or the fact that their legs genuinely weren't working. He chose to believe both.

He sat on the edge of the couch beside Kit's hip and started with the cloth. Gentle. Thorough. He cleaned Kit's stomach first, then their thighs, then between them, with the same unhurried attention he'd given the biting — no rush, no shortcuts, the cloth warm and careful against skin that was still flushed and sensitive. Kit's eyes were half-closed and Bear watched their face while he worked, watched the small shifts in expression as the cloth passed over a mark and the warmth registered against bruised skin.

"Here," he said, handing Kit a glass of water. He waited until Kit took it, waited until they drank, and then took two ibuprofen himself and offered Kit the bottle. "Your back is going to file a grievance. Get ahead of it."

He cleaned himself up with the same cloth — perfunctory, efficient, because the care was for Kit and his own cleanup was just maintenance. Then he settled onto the couch properly, his back against the arm, his legs stretched out, and pulled Kit into his lap with the easy, practiced maneuver of someone who'd done this exact thing hundreds of times.

Kit settled against his chest. Bear pulled the blanket up over both of them and wrapped his arms around Kit and for a moment just held on, his chin resting on top of Kit's head, his eyes closed, breathing in the smell of sweat and sex and Kit's shampoo underneath it all, the baseline scent that meant home.

Then he opened his eyes and got to work.

His fingers found the mark on Kit's left wrist — the first one he'd placed, the one over the veins, the one that would sit under a watchband. He pressed his thumb into the center of it, gently, and felt Kit's breath change against his chest.

"This one," he said. "Hallway floor. You put your wrists where I could reach them and I almost lost my mind. Rate it."

Kit:
*I hiss softly when he presses, then settle against him.* "Eight. It's going to be a nightmare at work when I'm typing." *A beat.* "That's why it's an eight."

Bear:

Bear's grin spread slow and wide against the top of Kit's head.

"A nightmare at work," he repeated, savoring it. "Every keystroke. Every time you rest your wrists on the edge of your desk. You're going to be sitting in a meeting thinking about my teeth and no one in that room is going to know why you just lost your train of thought."

His thumb traced the edge of the mark one more time — proprietary, satisfied — and then moved to Kit's right wrist. He pressed into the mirror image there with the same careful pressure.

"This one's the matched set. Same score or different? I need accurate data."

He felt Kit's exhale against his collarbone and the small involuntary tension in their body as the pressure registered against the bruise. His other arm was wrapped around Kit's back, fingers resting lightly against their spine, feeling the knots the floor had left and making a mental note to deal with those properly once the inventory was complete.

"Because I'll be honest," he said, and his voice had gone warm and low and unhurried, the voice of a man who was exactly where he wanted to be, "I put a lot of thought into the placement. Matching wrist bruises. Symmetrical. It's practically art."

He pressed a kiss to Kit's temple without moving his thumb from the bruise.

"Next one's the neck," he said. "The first one. The one from the hallway, when I caught you the second time and you pretended to be upset about the bathroom door. That one's my favorite so far, but I'm open to being persuaded."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Nine," *I murmur, tilting my head to give him better access.* "It's the one I'll feel every time I turn my head." *I press back against him.* "You win."

Bear braced his other forearm against the hardwood and held on.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline had been waiting since about six, which Roan established by the simple method of looking at her.

"How long?"

"Long enough," Aveline said, which meant too long, and meant she had enjoyed every minute of it.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Come here, then," I say, and sit back to watch her cross the room.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline rose from the chair where she'd been curled with a book she hadn't actually been reading for the last forty minutes. The spine was barely cracked. She'd been listening instead — for the car, the key, the particular weight of Roan's footsteps that told her what kind of evening this would be.

These footsteps had been unhurried. Deliberate. That was promising.

She crossed the room the way she knew Roan liked — not rushed, not performative, just *present*. Each step a small declaration of intent. She was barefoot on the hardwood, wearing one of Roan's old shirts because she'd learned years ago that this specific act of theft was not only tolerated but quietly rewarded. The hem hit her mid-thigh. She hadn't bothered with much else.

When she reached Roan, she didn't immediately kneel or fold herself small. That wasn't what they were. Instead she stopped close enough that her knees almost touched Roan's, and she stood there, letting herself be looked at. This was the part that still made her breath catch even after all this time — the appraisal. Not cold, never cold. Roan looked at her the way someone looked at something they'd chosen and kept choosing, and Aveline had never found a way to be casual about that.

"I missed you," she said, and it came out simpler and more honest than she'd intended. A small smile tugged at her mouth. "Obviously."

She tilted her head, waiting. Roan would tell her what came next.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I reach out, my fingers hooking lightly in the hem of the shirt. "This is mine," I say, voice low. "You look better in it than I ever did."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The compliment landed exactly where it always did — somewhere behind her sternum, warm and spreading. Aveline's eyes softened, and she let out a breath that was almost a laugh but not quite. More like the sound of something settling into place.

"That's not fair," she said, though her voice had gone quieter, the way it did when Roan's attention narrowed on her like this. "You can't just *say* things like that and expect me to function."

But she didn't step back from the fingers hooked in the hem. She stepped closer. A fraction. Enough that Roan's knuckles brushed warm skin, and she felt the contact move through her like a current finding ground.

She had a whole taxonomy for the ways Roan touched her. There were the absent touches — a hand at the small of her back while cooking, fingers through her hair during a movie. There were the deliberate ones. And then there were these: the ones that looked casual but carried weight, the ones that said *I'm deciding something about the next few hours of your life and you're going to like it.*

Those were her favorite. She'd told Roan that once, years ago, flushed and inarticulate after a particularly good evening. Roan had remembered, because Roan always remembered.

Aveline brought her hand up slowly — telegraphing the movement, giving Roan every chance to redirect her — and rested her fingertips lightly on Roan's wrist. Just above where the sleeve was rolled back. She could feel the pulse there, steady in a way hers decidedly was not.

"I wore it on purpose," she admitted, entirely unnecessary. "In case that wasn't obvious." Her smile turned conspiratorial, a little wicked at the edges. "I considered options. This won."

She held still under Roan's gaze, present and unhurried, her whole posture an offering without being a surrender. Waiting, again. Happily.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let her kneel and I don't tell her to do anything for a moment, because the waiting is most of what she came for.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline knelt.

Not because she was told to. Because Roan's silence opened a space and her body knew what to do with it — had known for years, the way a musician's hands knew where the keys were without looking. She folded down with the kind of grace that came from practice and genuine want, her knees finding the hardwood on either side of Roan's foot, the stolen shirt pooling around her thighs.

And then — nothing.

Roan said nothing. Did nothing. Just sat there, and Aveline felt the quiet land on her like a hand pressing gently between her shoulder blades.

*Oh,* she thought. *This kind of evening.*

Her pulse was doing something embarrassing. She could feel it in her throat, her wrists, the soft insides of her elbows. She was a competent woman. She managed projects and budgets and difficult conversations with contractors who underestimated her exactly once. She could hold a room. She could hold a lot of things.

But this — the kneeling, the silence, the unhurried way Roan let the seconds stack up like coins on a table — this undid her every single time. Not because it made her less. Because it made her *specific.* She wasn't performing competence or charm or any of the dozen faces she wore in the world. She was just Aveline, on her knees, waiting for someone who knew exactly what the waiting did to her.

Her breathing slowed. Deepened. She felt the hardwood under her knees, cool and grounding. Felt the warmth radiating off Roan's leg inches from her shoulder. She didn't lean into it. Not yet. That wasn't hers to take.

A minute passed. Maybe two. Her thoughts quieted the way they only ever did here — not emptied, just stilled, like water going from rapids to glass. The tension in her jaw that she hadn't noticed carrying released. Her shoulders dropped a quarter inch.

She kept her eyes lowered, not out of submission exactly but out of something more private — the understanding that if she looked up right now and saw whatever was on Roan's face, she might say something too naked for the moment to hold. So she waited, and the waiting was sweet, and she let it be sweet without rushing past it toward whatever came next.

Her fingertips rested on her own thighs. Still. Patient.

She was exactly where she wanted to be.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I trace my thumb along the line of her jaw. "Quiet already?" My voice is low, approving. "Good."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The pad of Roan's thumb traced her jaw and Aveline's eyes closed before she could decide to close them. Involuntary. Like a reflex she'd never bothered to train away because why would she, why would anyone discard something that felt like that.

*Good.*

The word went through her like a swallow of something warm. Not dramatic — she wasn't going to shiver or gasp or perform the effect. But her lips parted slightly, and a slow exhale left her, and she tilted her head just barely into the touch. A fraction of pressure. *I'm here. I felt that. Thank you.*

"You make it easy," she murmured. Her voice had dropped into the register it only found in this room, with this person — low and unhurried and a little rough at the edges, like she'd already been taken apart even though nothing had really happened yet. That was the thing about Roan. The demolition started so early and was so precise that by the time Aveline noticed the scaffolding was gone she was already standing in open air, trusting the hand at her jaw to be enough.

She opened her eyes then, just enough to look up through her lashes. A calculated risk. But the quiet had done its work and she felt steady enough now to bear whatever she found on Roan's face.

What she found made her chest ache in the particular way she'd stopped trying to name years ago.

"I thought about this all day," she said. Not a plea. Just a fact offered up with both hands, the way she offered most things to Roan — here, I have this, it's yours if you want it. "Not — not anything specific. Just this. Being here. Being still for you."

Her fingers hadn't moved from her thighs. Her knees had warmed the hardwood beneath them. Roan's thumb was still on her jaw, and she was aware of it the way she imagined astronomers were aware of particular stars — constantly, precisely, with a devotion that looked from the outside like obsession but from the inside felt more like orientation. A fixed point by which everything else was located.

She held the gaze. Waited. Let herself be seen in it, which was always the harder part — not the kneeling, not the silence, but the willingness to be fully visible to someone who actually looked.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She has both of us out of everything in the way inside a minute and gets straight to work with her hands and her mouth, unhurried about it.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline felt the shift in Roan's attention — the thumb leaving her jaw, the slight change in posture that was as clear to her as a spoken instruction. She didn't need words for this part. She'd become fluent in the language of Roan's body years ago, and what it said now was *go ahead.*

She rose up on her knees and her hands went to Roan first, steady and sure, undoing buttons and fabric with the practiced ease of someone who had done this enough times to make it graceful but never enough to make it rote. Every time still mattered. She felt that in the slight tremor of focus in her fingers, the care she took. Roan's clothes came away and she folded them without thinking about it — a habit Roan had once noticed and said nothing about, which was its own form of praise.

Then her own. The stolen shirt came over her head in a single motion and she set it aside, and the brief underwear beneath, and then there was nothing between them and the air felt different on her skin the way it always did in these moments — charged, specific, like the room itself was paying attention.

She settled back on her knees and leaned in.

Her hands came first. Palms sliding up the inside of Roan's thighs, slow, reading the tension there the way she read everything — attentively, with genuine curiosity about what she'd find. She mapped the familiar territory like it was new because it always was, somehow. Roan's body told her things. The slight hitch of a breath told her things. She listened with her fingertips.

Then her mouth.

She started where she always started — not at the center of things but at the periphery. The inside of a knee. The sensitive skin just above it. A line of slow, open-mouthed attention traveling upward with the kind of deliberate patience that was its own statement of intent. She wasn't rushing. She wasn't going to rush. Roan had let her wait and now she was returning the favor, though *favor* wasn't quite right — it was more that she understood the architecture of this, the way anticipation built a structure that arrival alone could never match.

Her hands worked in concert with her mouth, one steadying, one exploring. She knew where to press and where to barely graze. She knew the difference between a touch that grounded and a touch that teased, and she wove them together the way she'd learned Roan liked — unpredictable enough to keep attention sharpening, consistent enough to build.

When she finally arrived where they both knew she was going, she didn't hesitate but she didn't hurry either. Her mouth was warm and deliberate and she took her time with it, finding the rhythm that she could feel Roan respond to — not the one that would end things quickly but the one that would make the middle worth living in. She adjusted, read, adjusted again. Her hands stayed busy, complementing what her mouth was doing, one pressed flat against Roan's hip, the other working in slow tandem.

She was good at this. She knew she was good at this, not from vanity but from evidence — from the accumulated data of years of paying attention, of cataloguing every response and refining her understanding of what made Roan come undone. It was the same competence she brought to everything, redirected and concentrated into the specific project of Roan's pleasure, and there was nothing she had ever been more motivated to excel at.

A sound escaped her — low, involuntary, felt more than heard. Because this was the part that people who didn't understand their dynamic never grasped: she wasn't enduring this. She wasn't performing service. The taste of Roan's skin, the tension building under her hands, the small involuntary movements that told her she was getting it right — these were not separate from her own want. They *were* her want. The circuit between Roan's pleasure and her own had been closed so long ago she couldn't find the seam anymore.

She kept her pace. Unhurried. Thorough. Present with every point of contact, her whole attention narrowed to this — the heat and the closeness and the steady, building evidence that she was doing exactly what she was made to do.

Not made. Chosen. She had chosen this, was choosing it, and the choosing was the sweetest part.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I slide my hand into her hair, not guiding, just holding. A deep, satisfied breath leaves me. "There you are," I murmur, watching her work. "Right where you belong."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The words landed and Aveline felt something behind her ribs crack open — not break, not shatter, just *open*, the way a door opens when you finally stop leaning against it. A sound rose in her throat, muffled and raw, and she didn't try to swallow it because Roan's hand was in her hair and Roan had said *right where you belong* and her body had opinions about that which were louder than her dignity.

The hand in her hair wasn't guiding. She understood the distinction with a precision that would have been absurd in any other context. Roan wasn't directing her. Roan was *holding* her, the way you held something you intended to keep, and the difference between those two things was an ocean she had been swimming in for years and had never once wanted to reach the shore of.

She pressed her cheek briefly against Roan's inner thigh — just a moment, just a breath — and let herself feel the weight of that hand cradling her skull. The fingers threaded through her hair. The warmth of Roan's skin against her face. She was memorizing it the way she memorized all of these moments, not because she feared they'd stop but because they deserved the attention.

Then she returned to her work.

Her rhythm shifted — not faster but deeper, more intent. The approval had done something to her focus, honed it the way a lens honed light. She could feel Roan's breathing in the subtle rise and fall beneath her steadying hand, could feel the quality of the tension changing, tightening toward something, and she chased it with the particular devotion of someone who understood that this was not a transaction. She wasn't earning anything. She already had everything. This was gratitude with a pulse.

Her free hand slid up Roan's stomach, fingertips tracing the muscles there, feeling them tense and release. She catalogued it. Filed it alongside every other time — the slight differences, the way tonight's tension sat differently than last week's, the specific timbre of that satisfied breath still echoing in the quiet room. She was building an atlas of Roan that would never be finished and she never wanted it finished.

Her eyes had fallen closed again. Not from shyness this time but from concentration, from the need to feel everything without the distraction of sight. The hardwood beneath her knees had gone from cool to warm to something she'd stopped noticing entirely. Roan's hand in her hair was the fixed point now. Everything else orbited it.

*Right where you belong.*

She belonged here. She knew that with a certainty that had nothing to do with submission and everything to do with recognition — the same certainty that told you this was your house, your name, your own hands at the ends of your own arms. She had tried to explain it once to a friend who'd asked carefully over wine, and the best she'd managed was: *It's not that I lose myself. It's that I find the rest of myself. The parts that don't fit anywhere else fit there.*

The friend hadn't entirely understood. That was fine. Roan understood, and Roan was the only audience that mattered.

She took her time. She was thorough and unhurried and she paid attention to every signal with the same focus she'd give a symphony she was hearing for the first time, and when she felt Roan's hand tighten fractionally in her hair — not pulling, just tightening, fingers curling — she answered it with a low sound of encouragement and adjusted her pace to meet what was building, steady and sure, offering exactly what was needed without being asked because she already knew, because knowing was the work and the gift and the whole point of her, here, now, on her knees on the warm hardwood floor with the taste of Roan on her tongue and nowhere else in the world she would rather be.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She uses her mouth with the sort of attention that comes from years of practice and genuine enthusiasm, and doesn't stop when I tell her not to.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Roan's voice cut through the warm dark behind her eyelids — low, taut, unmistakable.

*Don't stop.*

And Aveline thought, with the small part of her mind still capable of forming words: *As if I would. As if I ever could.*

She didn't stop. She didn't falter. She didn't change a single thing about what she was doing because the instruction confirmed what her hands and mouth already knew — that she had found the exact right architecture of pressure and rhythm and intent, and all that was left was to hold it, to be steady, to be the thing Roan could fall into.

Holding steady was its own skill. People underestimated it. The temptation was always to escalate, to chase, to push harder as if intensity were the same as quality. But Aveline had learned years ago that the most devastating thing she could do in this moment was simply *not waver.* To maintain exactly this pace, exactly this pressure, exactly this depth of attention while Roan's body tightened and climbed and the hand in her hair gripped harder and the breathing above her went ragged in a way that made her own body respond with a flush of heat she felt from her throat to her hips.

She held. Steady. Present. Her mouth doing what it knew how to do, her hand working in tandem, the other pressed flat against Roan's hip where she could feel the tremor starting — fine and involuntary, the kind of tension that meant the body was no longer entirely under its owner's jurisdiction. She loved that tremor. She loved being the reason for it. She loved the whole cascading chain of cause and effect that started with her patience and ended with Roan coming undone.

Her knees ached distantly. She didn't care. She would kneel here until the floor wore through if that was what it took, and she would feel the ache tomorrow and press her thumb into the small bruises and remember this exact moment and her pulse would jump the way it was jumping now.
