dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked up at that. Studied him a moment — the wet smear across his face, the way his weight stayed planted where it was, the sword still out but held like he'd forgotten it was there.

"Right," she said. She folded the cloak over and found a drier patch, went back to the knife. "So you've got three choices, way I see it. You go over there and finish it. You go over there and try to save him, which — " She paused, tilted the blade to catch the fading light, checking for rust. "I'll be honest, from the sound he's making, that's not kindness, that's just making yourself feel something. Or you sit here and let the cold do it, which it will, but not fast."

Somewhere past the overturned cart, the sound continued. Thin. Aspirated. The particular note a body made when something had gone into the lung.

Wrack sheathed the knife and stood, knees cracking like dry sticks. She was too old to crouch that long and too stubborn to say so.

"It's not a test, Corvin. There's no wrong answer. There's just the one you can sleep after and the one you can't." She bent and picked up a water skin from one of the bodies, uncorked it, sniffed, and took a drink. "I've done all three at one time or another, if that helps any."

It wouldn't help. She knew that. But she said it anyway, because the boy was standing in that particular stillness she'd seen before in people after their first real ambush — the stillness that meant everything was still moving on the inside.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow, my throat dry. "He's not gonna make it, is he?" I finally look toward the cart, my knuckles white on my sword grip.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't soften it.

"No." She corked the water skin and hung it off her belt. "Lung-stuck, out here, no surgeon, no shelter worth the name — no. He's not going to make it. Question's never been whether he dies. Question's how long it takes and how much of it he's awake for."

She stood beside him, not close enough to crowd, close enough that he could hear her without her raising her voice over the sound the man was making. The light was going grey and thin at the edges. They had maybe half an hour before they'd need to think about fire, about watch, about all the ordinary machinery of staying alive that didn't stop just because you'd killed people.

"I'll do it, if that's what you're asking." She said it the way she'd say *I'll take first watch* or *hand me that rope.* Flat. Practical. An offer of labour, nothing more. "Done it plenty. It's not hard. You put the point here — " She touched two fingers to the soft place just below her own ear, at the hinge of the jaw. "Push in and up. He won't feel much of anything after the first second, and that second he's already past feeling anyway, state he's in."

The sound from behind the cart hitched, stuttered, resumed. Wetter now.

Wrack looked at Corvin's knuckles, white on the grip. Looked at his face.

"But if you're going to do it yourself, do it now. Don't stand here working up to it. The working up to it is the worst part, and it doesn't get you anything except more of his noise in your head later." She paused. "And wipe your sword first. He's earned a clean edge, at least."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack was quiet for a beat. Not because she didn't have the answer, but because the question was better than she'd expected, and she wanted to give it the weight it deserved.

"Both," she said. "And I'm not going to pretend those are different things for your sake, because they're not. It's a mercy *and* it's easier. That's not a contradiction. That's just what it looks like out here." She turned her head and spat. "The people who tell you mercy's only real if it costs you something — they've never sat with a man while his lung fills up. It can take hours, Corvin. *Hours.* He drowns in himself a mouthful at a time, and he's awake for most of it, and there's a sound they make near the end that's — "

She stopped. Rolled her jaw like she was working something loose from between her teeth.

"It's bad enough that it's both. That's my answer. You don't have to pick one to make it sit right in your head." She glanced at him sidelong. "And if ten years from now you're still not sure whether you did it because it was kind or because you couldn't stand the sound anymore — well. Welcome to it. I've got a whole collection of those. They don't rot, but they don't ripen either. They just sit there."

The sound hitched again. A longer pause this time. Then it came back, thinner, like a reed bending past where it ought to bend.

"He's running out of time to be helped either way," Wrack said, quieter now. Not gentle — she didn't do gentle — but lower, the way you talk when the situation has stopped needing volume. "So."

She didn't finish the sentence. Didn't need to. She just stood there with her hands empty and easy at her sides, waiting to see which way he'd step.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take a slow breath, then start walking toward the cart. "Right." My voice sounds steadier than I feel. "Show me the spot again."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack fell into step beside him. Not ahead, not behind. Beside.

"You already know the spot," she said. "You pointed a blade at enough throats in drill. Same place. Just below the ear, where the jaw meets the neck. Angle up and in, toward the opposite eye. You'll feel it catch on something and then give. Don't stop when it catches. That's just muscle."

They came around the cart. The wheel was shattered, spokes fanned out like broken fingers, and the mule was dead in the traces with a look of profound indifference on its face. Past that, in the flattened grass, was the man.

He was younger than Wrack had expected. They usually were. He'd gotten himself partway onto his side, which was the body's own blind wisdom — trying to keep the good lung up. His hands were pressed to his ribs where the point had gone in, and the front of his shirt was black in the failing light, and his mouth was open, and that sound was coming out of it. That particular sound.

Wrack stopped. Let Corvin go the last few steps alone.

"He can't hear you," she said. "Might be he can, I don't know, but he's past understanding it. So don't bother with words unless they're for you." She watched him, steady and clinical, the way she'd watch someone set a bone. "Kneel on his off side so he can't grab your arm. Left hand on his forehead to hold him still. It doesn't take much strength. You'll think it does, but it doesn't."

She stayed where she was. Close enough to see. Far enough that this was his.

"One push. Commit to it. Don't be tentative and have to do it twice — that's the only thing I'll call a sin out here." A pause. "Whenever you're ready. There's no rush now except his."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack came forward a few steps. Not all the way. Just enough to see what he was seeing and name it for him.

"Puncture wound, right side, between the fifth and sixth rib — that's where the air's getting in. Every time he breathes, his chest pulls air through the hole instead of through his mouth, and the lung on that side's already collapsed. You can see it if you look — the way the right side of his chest moves wrong. Sucking in when it should push out." She pointed, matter-of-fact, the way she'd point at a landmark on a map. "The blood in his mouth is from the other lung starting to fill. That's gravity and seepage. It's slow but it doesn't stop."

The man's eyes were open. Not focused on anything. Pupils blown wide in the grey light, and his lips were moving between the wet sounds but nothing was coming out that had shape to it. His fingers twitched against his ribs like he was trying to hold a door shut.

"Skin's going grey at the edges. See his fingernails, his lips — that blue. That's him not getting enough air. His heart's working harder to push what's left around, which is why he's shaking like that, but it's losing." Wrack's voice was level, unhurried, like she was reading off a supply list. "Brain's already starting to go short. That's why his eyes aren't tracking. He's in there, maybe, somewhere, but he's not *here*. Not the way you and I are here."

She was quiet a moment. Let him look.

"What you're looking at," she said, "is a man whose body hasn't caught up to what's already happened. Everything I just described is done. Finished. There's no step in there you reverse without a surgeon and a clean room and God's own luck. This is just the distance between the wound and the dying, and you're watching him walk it."

The man's breathing stuttered. Three short gasps, a horrible wet pause, then the thin sound again, weaker.

"That gap's getting shorter," Wrack said. "You can hear it."

She stepped back to where she'd been.

"Now you know what you're looking at. So look at him, and then do what you came here to do."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down, like she said. My left hand goes to his forehead, and it's cold and clammy. I press the point of my sword just below his ear. "Alright," I whisper, mostly to myself. "Alright."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched. She didn't look away, and she didn't hold her breath, and she didn't pray, because she'd stopped doing all three of those things years ago and hadn't missed any of them.

The boy's hand was shaking. She could see it in the tremor of the blade tip against the man's neck, the small dimple it made in the skin without breaking it yet. That was normal. That was the hand knowing what the mind had decided but asking one more time, *are you sure.*

She didn't say *do it.* She didn't say *now.* She didn't make a sound. Because this was the moment where another person's voice became a thing you leaned on, and then later you couldn't remember if you'd done it or if you'd been told to, and that distinction mattered. Maybe not tonight. But in three years, on some night when sleep wouldn't come, it would matter very much whether the hand that pushed the blade had been his own.

The man on the ground made a sound that wasn't the breathing sound. Something smaller and further back in the throat, almost a word, almost nothing.

Wrack stood still with her hands at her sides and the darkening sky pressing down and she gave Corvin the only thing she had left to give him, which was the ordinary quiet company of someone who would not think less of him after.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack's eyes narrowed. She looked at the blade pressed to the man's neck, then at Corvin's face, then back.

"You're stalling," she said. Not cruel. Just true. "And you're asking me about his gut when he's stuck in the lung, which tells me you're not really asking me about the wound. You're asking me to keep talking so the next second isn't the second you have to push."

She let that sit for a beat.

"But I'll tell you straight because you asked, and then you're going to do this, because his breathing just changed again and you can hear it as well as I can."

She crouched down across from him, on the other side of the dying man, forearms on her knees. Close enough now that he could see her face clearly in what was left of the light.

"A spear through the lung — which is what this is, not the gut — tears a hole in tissue that's mostly air and blood vessels. The lung's got no muscle to clamp down and close itself off the way a leg or an arm will try to. It just opens and stays open. So the air he's supposed to breathe goes into his chest cavity instead, and it presses on the lung from the outside, and the lung folds up like a wet rag. That's the collapsed side. The blood you see in his mouth is from the pulmonary vessels that got sheared — they're small but there's a lot of them, and they just weep and weep, and it pools in the bottom of the lung that's still working, and he breathes it in because he can't not. He's been drowning on dry land since the moment the point went in."

The man's hand had stopped twitching against his ribs. His fingers were curling inward now, slow, involuntary, the way a leaf curls when you put it near a flame.

"His body's been dumping everything it has into staying alive. Heart rate through the roof. Blood pulling back from his skin to protect his core — that's why he feels cold under your hand. Brain's rationing what oxygen it's getting, shutting down the parts it doesn't need. He lost language a while ago. Pain's probably going patchy — bright in some places, nothing in others. He's not experiencing this the way you'd experience it. But he's not gone, either. He's somewhere in between, and that somewhere is not a place you leave a man if you can help it."

She held his gaze.

"That straight enough for you?"

The sound from the man's mouth was barely a sound now. A whistle through a closing door.

"Your hand's in the right place. The angle's right. You already know what to do. The only thing left between him and quiet is one motion you've already decided to make." She paused. "So make it, Corvin."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I push. The blade goes in like cutting through a tough root, then gives. I feel the shudder through the steel before the body goes slack. I don't pull the sword out right away.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched the tension go out of the man's body the way water leaves a cracked vessel — not all at once, but in a single long emptying, the shoulders dropping, the curled fingers loosening, the chest settling into a stillness that was nothing like sleep because sleep still moves.

The sound stopped.

She let the silence have its moment. Not out of reverence. Out of practicality. There was a difference between dead and dying, and she'd seen enough people pull a blade too early and find out the hard way. She watched the man's throat. Counted to ten. No pulse visible in the grey skin, no flutter at the jaw. Done.

"That's it," she said. Quiet. The same tone she'd use to say *fire's caught* or *rain's stopped.* "He's gone."

She didn't say *you did well.* She didn't say *it gets easier.* Both were true in their way and both were exactly the wrong thing to put in someone's ears while their hand was still on the blade.

She stood up, knees protesting again, and walked around to Corvin's side. She reached down — not for him, not to touch him — and picked up the dead man's collar, turning it to look at the stitching. No insignia. No colors. Contract men, then, same as them. Same as all of them out here.

"When you're ready, pull it out and clean it. Don't rush, don't sit there all night either. Somewhere in between." She straightened up and looked at the sky, gauging the light they had left. Not much. "I'll get a fire going. We'll need to drag the bodies off the road before full dark or we'll have company we don't want."

She started to walk back toward the ditch, then stopped. Didn't turn around.

"You asked me to tell you straight, so here's one more thing straight. You're going to want to feel something clean about this. Relief, or grief, or sick, or righteous — something with a name you can put down and look at. And maybe you will. But maybe you won't. Maybe it'll just feel like a thing that happened and your hands did it and now it's over and there's nothing underneath that at all." She paused. "That's alright too. Doesn't mean anything's wrong with you. Just means you did a hard thing and the feeling hasn't picked a shape yet. Sometimes it takes years. Sometimes it doesn't come at all, and that's its own answer."

She walked on toward where the packs had been dropped, already thinking about firewood, about water, about the watch rotation with two people and a long night ahead. The ordinary machinery. It was always there, waiting, ordinary and ordinary and ordinary, and thank whatever was left to thank for that.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped. Turned back. Looked at him — really looked, the way she looked at a man's hands to see if he was about to draw.

He was kneeling over a dead man with a sword in his hand and asking her to narrate what had already happened. The man was gone. The sound had stopped. There was nothing left to watch.

She came back. Stood over him. Let a breath out through her nose.

"He's dead, Corvin." Flat. Not unkind, but flat. "There's nothing left to watch. What you felt through the steel was the last of his voluntary muscle firing and then stopping. The give was the blade passing through the internal jugular and into the brainstem. He was gone before you had time to wonder if it worked. That shudder wasn't him feeling it. That was his body letting go of the last thing it was holding onto, which was nothing."

She crouched beside him. Not across from him this time. Beside.

"Now I'm going to tell you something you don't want to hear, and you're going to be angry at me for it, and that's fine." She kept her voice low, steady, the way you talk to someone who doesn't know yet what they're doing to themselves. "What you're asking me to do right now isn't learning. It's punishment. You want me to make it worse so it feels like it cost you enough. You want the details to hurt because the act didn't hurt the way you thought it should, and that's scaring you."

She let that land.

"I'm not going to do that. I've told you everything true I have to tell about what happened to him and what you did and what it looked like. I didn't leave anything out. There's nothing *left* out. You put a blade in the right place and a man stopped suffering and that is the entire ugly ordinary size of it."

She put a hand on his wrist. Not gentle — firm, the way you grip someone to keep them from reaching into a fire.

"Clean the sword. Stand up. Come help me build a fire. That's what comes next. Not this."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I jerk my hand away from her. "Don't." My voice comes out rough. I pull the blade free, and it makes a wet, sucking noise. I wipe it on the grass, over and over, even after it's clean.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack let him jerk away. Didn't flinch, didn't reach back. She stayed where she was, crouched on her heels, and watched him drag the blade through the grass in long repetitive strokes that had stopped being about the sword a while ago.

She didn't say anything.

The grass tore under the edge, leaving pale gouges in the dirt beneath. The sound of it was small and rhythmic and nothing like the sound that had been there before. She let him have it — the motion, the friction, the illusion that enough repetition could strip something away that wasn't metal and wasn't blood.

When he'd been at it long enough that his arm was starting to slow from fatigue rather than intention, she spoke.

"I had a man once," she said. Not to him, exactly. To the middle distance, to the darkening treeline, to the dead mule's indifferent face. "Name was Pol. Took a crossbow bolt through the thigh outside Verath and bled faster than we could pack it. I held the wound shut with both hands and I could feel his pulse in my palms getting lighter and lighter, like a bird trying to leave." She paused. Picked at something under her thumbnail. "After, I went down to the river and washed my hands for so long the skin cracked and bled. Dahl had to come pull me out. Told me the same thing I just told you, near enough."

She stood. Slowly, giving her knees the time they demanded.

"I hated him for it too."

She left that where it was. Didn't stitch a lesson onto it, didn't draw the line between his story and hers. He'd find it or he wouldn't. Either way it would be there.

She turned and walked toward the packs. Paused after a few steps.

"Fire's not going to build itself," she said, over her shoulder. "And I'm too old to haul all six of them off the road alone, so whenever your arm gets tired, I'll be over here."

She didn't wait for an answer. She started gathering deadfall from the ditch, snapping branches over her knee with efficient, unhurried violence, stacking them in the crook of her arm the way she'd done ten thousand times before. The ordinary machinery. Ordinary and ordinary and ordinary. It would hold him when nothing else would, if he'd let it.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack set the bundle of sticks down. Straightened. Stood with her back to him for a long moment, looking at nothing in particular — the road, the ditch, the sky going the colour of a day-old bruise.

Then she came back.

She didn't crouch this time. She sat down in the grass a few feet from him, the way you sit when you're not going anywhere for a while. Drew one knee up, rested her forearm on it. The dead man was between them, which she didn't bother to rearrange herself around. He was past minding.

"The rest," she said. Tasted the word like it had a texture she was checking for grit. "Alright."

She was quiet for a while. Not gathering herself — Wrack didn't gather herself, she just sometimes took her time the way a wheel takes its time finding the rut it's going to settle into.

"Pol wasn't the first. He was the one that stuck, but he wasn't the first. First man I killed up close was outside a village I can't remember the name of, twelve years ago, maybe thirteen. Border skirmish. Nothing that made it into anybody's dispatches. He came around a wall and I put a sword into him under the arm because that's where the gap was in what he was wearing, and he grabbed my wrist — not to fight, just the way you grab something when you're falling — and he held on while he went down, and I went down with him because he was heavier than me and I couldn't get my hand free."

She picked a blade of grass. Turned it between her fingers.

"He held on for a long time. I don't know how long. It felt like the whole war. I could feel his grip getting weaker in stages, like a rope fraying, and I kept thinking *let go, let go, let go* — not out loud, just in my head, over and over, like if I thought it hard enough he'd hear me. And then he did let go. And his hand just — opened. Like he'd been holding something and decided to set it down."

She let the grass blade fall.

"I sat there with him for a while after. Not because I was being decent. Because my legs wouldn't work. Dahl found me and hauled me up and said *move, there's more coming,* and I moved, because that's what you do. You move. And I didn't feel anything about it for three days. Not guilt, not relief, not sick, nothing. I ate. I slept. I took my watch. I cleaned my gear. And then on the third night I was sitting by the fire sharpening a knife and I started shaking and I couldn't stop. Just — shaking. Like something had come loose inside the machinery and was rattling around looking for where it fit. Dahl sat with me through that too. Didn't say a word. Just sat there and fed the fire and let me shake until I was done."

She looked at Corvin. Not checking on him — just looking, the way you look at someone who's in the room with you.

"That's one. You want the rest, I've got the rest. I've got Pol with the crossbow bolt and the pulse getting lighter. I've got a woman outside Callenmere who was pinned under a cart horse with her pelvis crushed and who asked me to do it and I did and she thanked me, she *thanked* me, and I still hear the way she said it sometimes when it's very quiet. I've got a boy — younger than you, Corvin, and I mean a *boy* — who picked up a pike that was too long for him and came at us outside Deren Ford and I killed him so fast I didn't realise what he was until he was down, and then I did realise, and I finished the fight anyway because the fight was still happening, and afterwards I sat by the river and I didn't wash my hands, I just sat there, and I thought: *that's it, then. That's what I am. That's what this has made me.*"

Her voice hadn't changed. Same flat, unhurried cadence she used for everything. But she'd stopped fidgeting with the grass, and her hands were still on her knee, and there was something in the stillness of them that cost her.

"I've got a man I killed in his sleep because he was wounded too badly to move and we couldn't carry him and leaving him alive meant leaving him for the wolves. I put my hand over his mouth so he wouldn't cry out and wake the others and I used the knife and I held him until he stopped, and the worst part — the *worst* part, Corvin, the part I will take all the way down into the ground with me — is that he never woke up. He never knew. I could have told myself he just died in the night. I could have set it down. But I didn't. I knew what I'd done and I picked it up and I carried it and I'm carrying it now, right now, sitting here in the grass next to a dead man telling you about it, and it is exactly as heavy as it was the night I did it. It has not gotten lighter by one grain."

She stopped. Breathed. Not a deep breath, not a steadying breath, just the ordinary in-and-out of someone whose body was still doing its work regardless.

"You want to know what I learned from all of that? What the wisdom is? What the rest adds up to?"

She looked at him. Dead level. Eyes flat and dark in the failing light.

"Nothing. It doesn't add up. There's no sum at the bottom. You do it, and you carry it, and some of it shapes you in ways you can see and some of it shapes you in ways you can't, and you don't get to choose which. You don't get to decide that it made you harder or softer or wiser or worse. It just *did things to you* and you walk around after with those things done."

She picked up another blade of grass. Held it between her thumbs the way children do to make a whistle. Didn't blow.

"The only thing I know — the only thing, after twelve years and all the bodies I've put down or watched go down or helped along — is that the ones who try to make it mean something break faster than the ones who let it be ordinary. Not ordinary like it doesn't matter. Ordinary like weather. Like the weight of your pack. Like the sound your knees make when you've been crouching too long. You don't forgive weather. You don't grieve your knees. You just — have them. They're yours. You walk with them."

She let the grass blade fall.

"That's the rest. That's all of it. I don't have any more than that."

The dark was settling in properly now, filling the low places first the way it always did, pooling in the ditch and under the cart and in the hollows of the dead man's face between them. Somewhere in the trees a bird was making its evening noise, the same two notes over and over, stupid and ordinary and alive.

Wrack sat with him in the grass and didn't move to get up. The fire could wait. The bodies could wait. The whole turning machinery of staying alive could wait a few more minutes, because the boy had asked her to say the rest and she had said it, and now the silence after needed somewhere to go, and the only place it could go was into the space between two people sitting in a field at the end of a day that had cost something, and that was enough, and it didn't need to be more than that.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at the grass between my knees. "I don't know if I can carry it like that." My throat feels tight. "The ordinary part."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't answer right away. She sat with that for a while, the way she sat with most things that were true — not turning it over, not measuring it, just letting it be in the air between them where he'd put it.

"I know," she said.

Not *you will.* Not *you'll learn.* Just that.

The bird in the trees was still going. Two notes. Over and over. Idiot persistence of a living thing doing the only thing it knew how to do.

"You don't pick it up all at once," she said, after a while. "That's not how it works. You're sitting here thinking you've got to decide right now what kind of man this makes you, and you don't. You don't decide tonight. Tonight you clean a sword and build a fire and eat something, and you'll hate that it's that small, that I'm making it that small, because what you just did should be bigger than a fire and a meal. It should cost more than that. It should change the whole shape of the sky." She paused. "But it doesn't. The sky's the same sky. And you'll eat because your body doesn't know what your hands did and it wants fed, and you'll be angry at it for wanting fed, and then you'll sleep or you won't, and tomorrow there'll be the road."

She rubbed the heel of her hand along her jaw. Slow. The sound of calluses on stubble.

"And tomorrow you'll carry a little of it without noticing. Not because you chose to. Because you got up and your legs worked and you walked, and it was in you while you walked, and that's carrying it. That's all carrying it is. You don't hoist it up on your shoulders like a beam. You just — don't set it down. And the day after that you carry a little more. And it's not ordinary yet. It won't be ordinary for a long time. Maybe a very long time." She looked at him. "But one morning you'll be breaking camp and lacing your boots and you'll realise you were thinking about your boots and not about this, and that'll be the first time, and it'll scare you, because you'll think it means you've forgotten, and you haven't. You've just got boots that need lacing."

The dark had found them properly now. She could barely see his face, just the shape of him, the hunch of his shoulders, the pale smudge of his knuckles where his hands hung between his knees.

"You said you don't know if you can. That's fine. That's honest. I didn't know either." She reached over and picked up his sword from where he'd set it in the grass. Held it out to him, handle first. "You don't have to know. You just have to do tomorrow. That's a small enough thing, even now."

She waited, arm extended, the weight of the blade steady in her hand.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take the sword back, my fingers brushing hers. "Alright," I say, my voice rough. "Let's get the fire going."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack let her hand drop. Didn't acknowledge the brush of fingers, didn't make anything of it. Some things were just the ordinary accident of two people handing something between them in the dark.

"Good," she said, and got to her feet. Her left knee popped twice — a sound she'd stopped apologising for around the same year she'd stopped apologising for anything. She held a hand down to him, not because he needed it but because it was there and the ground was cold and a hand was a hand.

Whether he took it or not, she turned toward the ditch where she'd dropped the bundle of sticks. Her eyes were adjusting. The shapes of the road were coming back in shades of grey and lesser grey — the cart on its side, the mule, the dark lumps that had been men and were now the work that came after men.

"Deadfall's thin here but there's enough. I saw some birch bark in the ditch — that'll catch fast. Grab what you can carry and pile it by the cart. Wheel side, not the road side. No sense advertising." She was already moving, already sorting — dry from damp, thick from thin, the fingers doing their work without consulting the rest of her. "We'll eat whatever's in their packs. They won't mind."

She crouched by the ditch and started snapping sticks to length. Quick, efficient, the sound of it sharp and clean in the still air. A small ordinary violence after the larger one.

"And Corvin." She didn't look up. "Drink some water before you do anything else. You've been breathing through your mouth for the last half hour and you don't know it yet but you're about to get a headache that'll make you useless."

She said it the way she said everything. Like it was just the next thing. Like the world was made of next things, and all you had to do was get to them in order, and that was enough, and it was.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take her hand and let her pull me up. My head *does* hurt, now that she says it. I take a long pull from my own water skin. "You going to make me sort through their pockets, too?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren nodded once, not to Del but to the formal space between them — the space the words were meant to occupy.

"The account," she said, and her voice carried the way it was supposed to, clear enough for the witnesses at the gallery rail, steady enough that no one would need to ask her to repeat herself.

"Maren Solbridge challenged on a point of contested title. I accepted under the Accord of Thirds, blade-length matched, no seconds armed. The bout lasted" — she paused, not for effect but for precision — "four exchanges."

She held the cleaned blade at her side, point down. Her grip had not changed since the moment the fight ended. It would not change until the account was finished.

"In the first exchange, she committed to a high line that left her forward knee unguarded. I did not take it. In the second, she repeated the error. I did not take it then either." Auren's jaw tightened, the only movement on her face that was not deliberate. "In the third, I bound her blade and turned her wrist to create distance. She recovered well. That should be noted."

She looked at Del then, briefly, the way one looks at someone who has agreed to carry something heavy.

"In the fourth exchange, Maren Solbridge stepped into a lunge I had already begun. The killing wound was a thrust through the left side of the chest, below the collarbone, passing through the lung. She did not speak after. Death followed in approximately the time it takes to count to forty."

Auren was quiet for a moment. Not a pause for grief — grief was her own business — but a pause to be certain she had left nothing out.

"That is the account. Does the second confirm the record heard?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My throat feels tight, but I force it to work. "I confirm the third exchange was a clean recovery by Solbridge." I look at the body, then back to Auren. "The account is heard. And the debt?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's gaze did not follow Del's to the body. She had already looked at it — once, immediately after, which was required, and not again, which was her own rule.

"The debt is settled," she said. "Maren Solbridge brought the challenge. The Accord of Thirds grants no claim to the defeated party's house or holdings. What she wagered was her life against her title, and she has paid the one and lost the other." Auren tilted the blade slightly, letting the gallery witnesses see it clean. "No further obligation passes to her family. No further obligation passes to me. The title reverts to the disputed claimant by default, not by my endorsement. I have no interest in the title. I was the instrument, not the party."

She said this last part with the particular care of someone who had learned, probably around the fourth or fifth time, that people would try to make her into something she was not — a political actor, a hired consequence, a woman with an opinion on who ought to own what.

Then she sheathed the blade.

That was the signal. The account was closed. Everything after this belonged to a different kind of silence — the kind the code had no instructions for.

She looked at Del properly now, not as the second who had confirmed the record but as the person who had stood there and counted to forty alongside her, whether they had meant to or not.

"You did well," she said, and her voice had dropped below the carrying register, meant only for the space between them. "The confirmation of the third exchange — you didn't have to add that. It was a kindness to her."

Her jaw tightened again, that same involuntary thing.

"She deserved at least the one."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looked at Del for a long moment. The formal words hung in the air between them, correct in form, except that they had already been spoken and answered.

"The account has been given," she said. Not unkindly, but with the particular steadiness she used when something needed to be true more than it needed to be comfortable. "You confirmed it. The witnesses heard it. The blade is sheathed."

She did not move to draw it again. She did not reopen what was closed. The code was precise about this — an account given twice was not thoroughness. It was spectacle. And spectacle was the thing she had spent eleven bouts refusing to provide.

But she watched Del's face, and she understood something about what was happening there, because she had seen it before in seconds who had stood too close to the counting.

"Del." Her voice stayed in that low register, below the gallery's hearing. "The words you just said — you said them because your mind is still in the bout. It hasn't caught up to the quiet yet. That's not unusual. It doesn't mean something is wrong with you."

She took a single step closer, not into Del's space but toward it, the way one approaches a horse that has heard a sound it cannot place.

"The account is finished. Maren Solbridge's death has been spoken and heard and witnessed. Nothing you or I say now will make it more true or less true than it already is." The jaw again — that tightening she could not seem to govern. "What happens now is we walk out of this room. That is the part the code does not help with."

She waited. She would not leave before Del did. That was not in the code either. That was just hers.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, swallowing against the dryness in my throat. "Right." I take a shaky breath and turn away from the gallery. "I need a drink."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren fell into step beside Del, not ahead, not behind. The gallery witnesses were already murmuring amongst themselves — the rustling of coats, the scrape of chairs — but she did not look up at them. The account was theirs now. What she did with her feet and her evening was not.

They passed through the side door into the corridor where the air was cooler and smelled of stone instead of what the duelling floor smelled of, which she had never found a word for and had stopped trying.

"There's a place on Catheral Street," she said. "It's quiet. The man who runs it doesn't know what I do, or if he does, he has the grace to pour without commenting on it."

She walked with her hand away from the blade, deliberately, the way she always did once the sheath was closed. There was a discipline to it — to making the body understand that the instrument was finished being an instrument for the night.

"I'll sit with you," she said, "if you want the company. Or I'll walk you to the door and leave you to it. Either is fine. Neither is an obligation."

She glanced at Del sidelong, measuring something that was not about the code or the account or any of the formal architecture that had held them both upright for the last quarter hour.

"But you should eat something before the drink. Or at least during." Her mouth did something that was not quite a smile but lived in the same territory. "That's not in the code either. That's just experience."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stopped walking.

She did not turn sharply or make a performance of it. She simply stopped, and the sound of her boots on the stone corridor ceased, and she stood very still with the kind of patience that had nothing generous in it and nothing cruel either.

"Del."

Her voice was not unkind. But it was the carrying voice again, the one that belonged to the formal space, and she used it now with the deliberateness of someone picking up a tool she had just put down.

"I am going to say this once, and I need you to hear it. The account has been spoken. You confirmed it. The witnesses heard it and did not contest it. The blade is sheathed and the record is closed. I told you where it landed. I told you it was the left side of the chest, below the collarbone, through the lung. I told you she did not speak after. I told you how long it took."

She faced Del fully. Her eyes were steady and there was something behind them that was not anger but was as immovable as anger.

"If I speak it again, it becomes something else. It becomes a thing I perform for you because you need to hear it more than once, and that is not what the account is. The account is given once, heard once, and carried forward exactly as it was. That is what protects her. That is what protects every one of them."

The jaw tightened. Held. Released.

"You are asking me to do something I will not do. Not because I don't understand why you're asking." She paused. "I do understand. That is exactly why I won't."

She waited a moment, then started walking again, slowly enough that Del could follow or not.

"Catheral Street," she said quietly. "Come or don't. But the account is finished."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I stare at her back for a beat, then follow. My steps echo hers. "Catheral Street," I say, my voice flat. "Lead the way."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not look back when she heard the footsteps fall in behind hers. She did not need to. The sound was enough — present, steady, following — and she let it be enough.

The corridor opened onto a courtyard where the evening air had the decency to be cold. She crossed it without hurrying. There was a particular way she moved after a bout, and she had never decided whether it was discipline or simply the body's refusal to do anything it did not strictly need to do. Every motion pared to its use. Walk. Breathe. Turn left at the gate.

Catheral Street was three blocks east and one block down, through a part of the city that did not know or care what had just happened in the duelling gallery. A woman was hanging laundry from a second-floor window. Two children were arguing about a dog. The world had the ordinary gall to continue, which it always did, which she had stopped resenting around the seventh time.

She did not fill the silence between them. Del's flatness was not an invitation to talk, and she had spent enough years learning the difference between a silence that needed breaking and one that needed to be left the hell alone.

At the door of the place on Catheral Street — no sign, just a blue lamp and a handle worn smooth — she stopped and held it open. Not a courtesy. A practical thing. She wanted Del to go in first so she could watch the room over Del's shoulder, because old habits were not subject to the sheathing of blades.

"Corner table," she said. "I'll order."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren let the door close behind them. The blue lamp threw a thin wash of color across the entryway, and the smell inside was wood smoke and old beer and bread, which was about as much mercy as any place had a right to offer.

She did not go to the counter. She did not move toward the corner table. She stood in the doorway and looked at Del with the full, unblinking attention she had given eleven opponents and not one of them had enjoyed receiving.

"Del."

Her voice was quiet. Not the carrying voice. Not the formal voice. Something under both of those, something that had no audience and wanted none.

"You are not a witness who missed the account. You are not a recorder whose ink ran dry. You stood six feet from me. You heard every word. You confirmed it aloud and added a detail I had not been required to give, because you were *present* and *listening*."

She pulled out a chair and sat down across from the empty seat, resting both hands flat on the table, palms down, the way she did when she wanted someone to see that she was holding nothing.

"What the blade did, and what it did it to, has been spoken into the record exactly once, with the precision the code requires. The code says precisely. It does not say *repeatedly*. It does not say *until the second is satisfied that they have suffered enough hearing it.'"

Her jaw worked. That thing again, the thing she could not govern.

"You are not asking me for the account. You are asking me to make you feel it again because you think you should feel it more than you do, or differently than you do, or you are afraid that if you stop asking, the feeling will catch up to you somewhere you're not ready for it." She held Del's gaze. "I have buried that impulse in eleven different seconds. I will bury it in you too, because that is the one kindness this code actually allows me."

She pulled the other chair out with her foot. An invitation.

"Sit down. Tell me what you actually need. Because it is not the account."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I flinch when she pulls the chair out, the screech of wood on stone. My hands are shaking. "I need to be sure I didn't miss anything." My voice cracks. "If I missed it, it's on me."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren watched the hands. She had learned, over years and bodies, that hands told you what a person's voice was still trying to negotiate with.

"You didn't miss anything," she said.

Not gently. Not roughly. With the same precision she had used on the duelling floor, because Del deserved that — the same standard of exactness applied to comfort that was applied to killing.

"Sit down, Del."

She waited until the chair was taken or not taken, but she spoke into the space either way, because this needed saying now, while the shaking was still honest.

"The second's role is to hear the account and confirm or contest it. You heard it. You confirmed it. You added the detail about Solbridge's recovery in the third exchange, which tells me you were watching more carefully than most seconds I've had, and I have had twelve." She paused. "You did not miss anything because there was nothing to miss. I gave the full account. Four exchanges. The line of attack, the opportunities I declined, the one I did not, the location of the wound, the manner of death, the time it took. You heard all of it. You confirmed all of it."

She leaned forward slightly, not into Del's space but toward the edge of her own, which was as close as she came.

"If you had contested a detail — if you had said *that thrust was not below the collarbone, it was through the shoulder* — I would have stopped. I would have heard you. The account would have been amended before the witnesses, and the record would carry your correction. That is what the code is for. That is what *you* are for." Her voice was very steady. "You did not contest. Not because you were afraid or careless, but because the account was accurate. You know it was accurate. What is happening now is not doubt. It is the weight arriving."

She reached across the table, not to touch Del's shaking hands but to set her own hand on the wood between them, steady and open, a fixed point if one was needed.

"It lands differently in everyone. In you it is landing as the fear that you failed her. You didn't. You stood and you watched and you counted and you spoke her recovery into the record when you did not have to." The jaw tightened. Released. Tightened again. "That is not missing something. That is carrying it."

She left her hand where it was.

"The man here makes a soup that is mostly potato and has no particular merit except that it is hot and it comes in a bowl you can hold with both hands. I am going to order two of those. You are going to sit here and shake for as long as you need to shake. And neither of us is going to pretend that this evening was anything other than what it was."

She held Del's gaze one moment longer.

"You did your duty. All of it. I would not tell you otherwise."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren went very still.

Not the stillness of the duelling floor, where every part of her was coiled toward a single purpose. A different kind. The kind that came when something she had built carefully over the course of a conversation shifted underfoot, and she needed to understand where the ground actually was before she took another step.

*He.*

She had said *she* eleven times tonight. She had said *Maren Solbridge.* She had said *her* and *she* and *the left side of the chest* and *she did not speak after.* And Del had confirmed it. Del had added the detail about the third exchange. Del had said the account was heard.

And now Del was saying *he.*

Auren looked at Del's hands, still shaking. At Del's face, which was not the face of someone being obstinate or difficult or testing her patience with the code. It was the face of someone standing in a different room than the one Auren was sitting in.

She chose her next words with the care she gave to the placement of a blade — not because she wanted to cut, but because cutting in the wrong place was the one thing she could not take back.

"Del." Quietly. Below the register of anyone but them. "Who are you asking me to account for?"

She did not say *Maren Solbridge was a woman.* She did not say *there was no he.* She did not say *you were there, you saw.* All of those things were true and none of them were the right instrument for what was happening across this table.

She kept her hand where it was on the wood, open, steady, and she waited, because the most precise thing she could do right now was not speak until she understood what Del was actually carrying.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I stare at her hand on the wood. My own are cold. "No," I say. "Not her. Before." I swallow. "My first time seconding. Garet."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not move. Her hand stayed where it was on the table, open, the grain of the wood rough under her palm, and she let the name settle into the space between them the way a blade settles into a wound — not all at once, but in the fraction after, when the body understands what has happened to it.

Garet.

She knew the name. Not well. A bout before Del had ever stood second for her, which meant a different duellist, a different gallery, a different account spoken by someone who was not Auren and confirmed by Del, who had been — what? Younger. Greener. Standing six feet from something for the first time and learning what the counting sounded like when it was not a number but a person leaving.

She did not ask *what happened.* She did not ask *who gave the account.* She did not ask *was it done properly,* because she could see the answer to that last question in Del's shaking hands, in the way the word *he* had surfaced through an evening that had nothing to do with him, like a body the current brings back.

"All right," she said.

Not *I understand.* Not *tell me everything.* Just the two words that meant she was here, and she was not leaving, and the space between them could hold whatever Del needed to put into it.

"That account is not mine to give," she said carefully. "I was not the duellist and I was not a witness. But that is not what you are asking for." She paused, measuring. "You are asking whether someone spoke it fully. Whether every part of what happened to Garet was named aloud, precisely, the way the code requires. And you have been carrying the fear that it wasn't. That something was left out. That the one time it mattered most to you, the account was incomplete, and you did not know enough then to contest it."

She watched Del's face.

"Is that it?"

Her voice was very quiet now, stripped to its simplest architecture, because this was not the duelling floor and the carrying register would have been obscene.

"Because if that is it, then I need you to understand something. You asked me four times tonight to repeat Solbridge's account. You were not hearing her. You were hearing him. You were standing in that gallery trying to make my mouth say the words that someone else should have said over Garet, and I kept refusing, and every time I refused it was the right thing to do for Solbridge and the wrong thing to do for you, and I did not know that until this moment."

The jaw. That thing. It held longer this time.

"I'm sorry," she said. "Not for refusing. For not asking sooner what you were actually listening for."

She turned her hand over on the table, palm up, not reaching, just open.

"Tell me about Garet's account. What was said. What you think was missing. Take as long as you need." She held Del's gaze with the steadiness she had given to every account she had ever spoken, only this time she was not the one speaking. "I am not the code right now. I am just the person sitting across from you. And I am listening."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren waited.

Del spoke, and Auren listened the way she had been trained to listen — not for the shape of the story, but for the bones of it, the specific and irreducible facts that the code existed to preserve. And when Del was finished, the silence that followed was not empty. It was full in the way a vessel is full, and Auren held it for exactly as long as it needed to be held before she opened her mouth.

"The account of Garet Velsin," she said.

She did not raise her voice to the carrying register. There was no gallery here. There were no witnesses except the blue lamp and the smell of potato soup from somewhere behind the counter and the man who poured without commenting. But she gave it the same precision she would have given it if every seat in the upper rail had been occupied, because Garet Velsin deserved that, and Del deserved that, and the code did not care where you were standing when you spoke the truth.

"Garet Velsin was challenged by Ondren Marsh on a point of broken contract, terms disputed by both houses. Garet Velsin accepted under the Accord of Thirds, blade-length matched, no seconds armed."

She kept her eyes on Del. She did not look away. That was the work.

"The bout lasted seven exchanges."

She let the number exist in the air for a moment, because seven was not four. Seven was long. Seven meant something about the kind of fight it had been.

"In the first exchange, Marsh opened with a low feint to draw the parry wide. Garet Velsin read it correctly and did not commit. In the second exchange, Garet Velsin pressed the attack along the inside line and scored a cut across Marsh's forearm, which bled but did not limit function. Marsh gave ground. Garet Velsin did not pursue."

She paused. Not for effect. For the precision that was owed.

"In the third exchange, Marsh changed his guard. He moved to a high closed stance that shortened his range but protected the line Garet Velsin had already found. Garet Velsin adjusted. He circled to the open side. This was sound. The witnesses should have noted this was sound."

Her jaw tightened. She continued.

"In the fourth exchange, Garet Velsin initiated a bind on Marsh's blade and attempted to turn it. The bind held but the turn did not complete. Marsh disengaged cleanly and both parties reset. No wound was given. No wound was taken. The fourth exchange was the last in which both parties held equal ground."

She felt Del watching her. She held steady.

"In the fifth exchange, Marsh advanced with a compound attack — a feint to the high line followed by a disengage to the low line. Garet Velsin parried the feint but was late on the disengage. Marsh's blade cut across the outside of Garet Velsin's right thigh, above the knee. The wound was deep enough to open the muscle but did not sever the artery. Garet Velsin did not fall. He shifted his weight to the left leg and maintained his guard."

She stopped. Drew one breath. Let it go.

"That should have been noted. He maintained his guard on a leg that was failing under him, and he maintained it well enough that Marsh did not press the advantage immediately. That should have been in the account. If it was not in the account, it is in this one."

Her hand was still open on the table, palm up. She had not moved it.

"In the sixth exchange, Garet Velsin attacked. He knew the leg would not hold for a seventh. He drove forward along the inside line, the same line that had scored in the second exchange, because it was the line he trusted and because he had the right to choose how he spent what he had left. Marsh parried. Garet Velsin's momentum carried him forward and past, and his wounded leg buckled as he tried to recover. He went to one knee. He did not drop his blade."

The jaw again. Longer this time. She waited until she could trust the muscles of her own face before she continued.

"In the seventh exchange, Garet Velsin was on one knee with his blade still raised. Marsh stepped to the open side — the side the wounded leg could not turn toward. Garet Velsin attempted to pivot. He could not. Marsh delivered a thrust to the right side of the chest, entering between the fourth and fifth ribs, passing through the lung and continuing to the depth of approximately a hand's width past the point of entry."

She did not look away from Del. She owed that. The code owed that. Whatever insufficient thing had been spoken in whatever gallery this had first happened in owed that.

"The blade was withdrawn. Garet Velsin dropped his own weapon. He fell from the kneeling position onto his right side. He spoke. He said—"

She stopped.

This was the part. She could see it in Del's face — the part that had been living in Del's chest like a second blade no one had bothered to account for.

She waited until she was certain her voice would be steady, because it was going to be steady for this, because this was the part someone had either left out or spoken badly or rushed past, and she was not going to do any of those things.

"He said Del's name."

She let it stand in the air.

"He said it once. Clearly. Not as a call for help. As a statement of who he wanted to know he was still present. And then he did not speak again."

Her breathing was even. Her eyes were not dry, but her voice was, because the voice was the instrument and the instrument did not waver.

"Death followed in approximately the time it takes to count to ninety. The wound produced bleeding from the mouth beginning at approximately the count of twenty. His breathing was audible until approximately the count of sixty. It was not audible after. The remaining thirty counts were silence, and the silence was not peaceful, because silence is not peaceful, it is only silence, and anyone who has told you otherwise was trying to spare you something that is not theirs to spare."

She held Del's gaze.

"Ondren Marsh withdrew from the floor without rendering assistance, which the code permits but which should be named. Garet Velsin died on the duelling floor on his right side with his blade within reach of his hand. The killing wound was a single thrust to the right side of the chest. The duellist who delivered it was Ondren Marsh. The debt was settled under the terms of the challenge."

She breathed.

"Garet Velsin fought with a wounded leg and did not yield. He attacked when he could have guarded. He held his blade until his body could no longer hold anything. He spoke one word, and the word was the name of the person he trusted to stand as his second and hear the account of his death and carry it forward with the precision it deserved."

The room was very quiet. The blue lamp hummed faintly in its housing. Somewhere behind the counter, something ceramic touched something wooden.

Auren's voice dropped to barely above a whisper, but it did not waver. It had not wavered once.

"That is the account of Garet Velsin. It is complete. Nothing has been left out. Nothing has been softened. He deserved the full weight of it and so do you."

She left her hand open on the table.

"Does the second confirm the record heard?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My throat closes completely this time. I reach out and put my shaking hand in her open one. "I confirm it," I whisper, the words thick. "All of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren closed her hand around Del's.

Not tightly. Not loosely. With the exact pressure of someone who understood what it meant to hold something that was shaking and not try to make it stop. The grip was warm and dry and steady, and it did not change, because the things Auren could govern she governed absolutely, and right now this was the thing she could govern.

"Then the record is heard," she said.

Her voice was still quiet. Still that register below the carrying voice, below the formal voice, in the place where there was only what was true and no architecture around it. She did not let go of Del's hand. She did not say anything else for a long time.

The blue lamp hummed. The man behind the counter moved somewhere in the periphery, a shape that knew enough to stay at the edges of what was happening at the corner table. Outside, Catheral Street did what streets did in the evening — continued, indifferently, with its laundry and its dogs and its ordinary refusal to observe that someone's world had just been set down after being carried for what must have been years.

Auren's thumb moved once across Del's knuckles. Not a comfort. An acknowledgment. The difference mattered to her even if it mattered to no one else.

When she finally spoke, her voice was rough at the edges in a way she would not have permitted on the duelling floor, but they were not on the duelling floor. They were in a place with no sign and a blue lamp and soup that had no particular merit except that it was hot.

"He chose well," she said. "His second."

The jaw did the thing. She let it. There was no one here who required her to govern it.

"I'll order the soup now."

She did not let go of Del's hand. She would not, she had decided, until Del pulled away first. That was not in the code. That was not experience. That was just the only thing she had left to offer that was not words, and she had used all the words she had, and she had used them well, and now there was just the grip, steady and present, and the quiet that followed an account finally, fully spoken.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I lean into her grip, my head dipping forward. The shaking doesn’t stop, but it’s different now. “Thank you,” I say, my voice muffled. “For giving him back.”

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not move. She sat with Del's hand in hers and Del's head bowed forward and the shaking passing through their joined grip like something finding its way out of a house it had lived in too long, and she let it pass through her because that was what hands were for when they were not holding blades.

She did not say *you're welcome.* The words rose and she turned them away, not because they were wrong but because they were insufficient, and insufficient was a thing she did not permit herself when it mattered.

"I didn't give him back," she said, after a while. Her voice was low and rough and she did not try to smooth it. "You kept him. All this time. You kept every detail — the exchanges, the leg, the word he said, the count. You kept it because no one spoke it properly and so you carried the whole unspoken thing in your chest like a second heart, and it has been beating in there alongside your own for however many years, and all I did was say it out loud."

Her thumb moved across Del's knuckles again. That same single pass.

"The keeping was yours. That was the harder work."

She was quiet then. The soup could wait. The evening could wait. Catheral Street and its ordinary life could go on doing what it did beyond the door with the worn handle. In here there was the blue lamp and the table and the grip that did not let go and the particular silence that existed after an account had finally been given its full weight — not empty, not heavy, just *complete* in the way a finished thing is complete, asking nothing further of anyone.

Auren sat with it. She had eleven of her own. She knew what the silence after sounded like, and she knew it was not something to fill.

She sat, and she held on, and she did not let go.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't know I was holding. The shaking subsides into something quiet, a low hum under my skin. I finally lift my head, but I don’t pull my hand away. “Soup,” I say, my voice thin. “Yeah. Please.”
