dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't look up at Wick. She looked at the man's left arm, which was the worse one, which meant it went first. The elbow was bent wrong in a way that made the geometry of the joint a question no one wanted to answer. Shrapnel had opened the forearm from wrist to mid-ulna and she could see the bone, which was not broken, which was the only piece of good news she had.

"Nobody's ever ready," she said. "Hold."

She irrigated the wound with what was left of the clean water, and the man came back to life under Wick's hands like something galvanic. His spine arched. A sound came out of him that wasn't a shout anymore — it was older than that, mechanical, the noise a body makes when it has been informed of something it cannot accept.

"Hold him. *Hold.*"

She packed the wound with cotton that was not as clean as she wanted and would have to do because everything would have to do. Her hands were steady. They had been steady for four years. She did not think about what that meant.

"The shoulder's dislocated," she said, the way someone might say the weather had turned. "I'm going to reduce it. When I do, he's going to think he's dying. He's not. But he's going to think it, and he's going to fight you with everything he has left, which is more than you'd expect from a man who looks like this. So when I say hold, Wick —"

She gripped the arm, found the angle.

"— I am not making conversation."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I brace harder, my muscles shaking as he thrashes. "Understood," I grit out, eyes still fixed on the stained canvas. *Don't look at the wound.*

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge rotated the arm outward, slow and deliberate, feeling for the place where the head of the humerus had gone — anterior, as they almost always were, lodged somewhere it had no business being while the socket sat empty and wrong. She could feel the muscles fighting her, every fiber of the man's body screaming *no* in a language older than speech.

"Breathe," she said, and it was not clear whether she was talking to the man or to Wick or to herself. It didn't matter. It applied to all three.

She brought the arm up and out in the arc she had performed — she did not count how many times. Counting was for people who still believed numbers meant something. The joint resisted. The man made that sound again, the one that lived below language, and his good hand clawed at the table and found nothing.

Then the humerus slid home with a thick, wet sound that was somehow quieter than it should have been for the amount of violence it contained. A *thunk*. Organic. Final.

The man sobbed once and went slack.

"Good," Sedge said. Not praise. Inventory. She palpated the joint, checking the reduction, checking circulation in the fingers. The hand was warm. The pulse at the wrist was there. She allowed this to be true for two seconds before she moved on.

"Other side's less dramatic but it's not going to be pleasant. He's conscious enough to anticipate it now, which makes it worse." She wiped her hands on a rag that had been white at some point in its life and came around the table. "Shift your weight. Left shoulder now. And Wick —"

She looked at him for the first time. Took in the shaking arms, the fixed stare, the jaw clamped tight enough to crack teeth.

"You're doing fine. Don't lock your knees. People pass out from locking their knees, not from what they're looking at."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge stopped.

She set the rag down and looked at Wick properly — not a glance, not the peripheral assessment she ran on everyone in the tent as a matter of habit, but an actual look. The kind she did not give often because it cost something and she had learned to be frugal.

"There's no leg," she said. "Both injuries are upper extremity. Arms and shoulders. So I don't know where that question came from, but I need you to come back to this tent and this table and this man."

She held his gaze until she was satisfied he was present.

"What he has is two dislocated shoulders, one of which is now reduced, and a shrapnel wound to the left forearm that is ugly and open and contaminated and that I have packed as well as I can pack it with what I have. He has circulation in both hands. He has sensation in his fingers, which I checked and which you would have noticed if you had been looking, which you weren't, which is fine, that's not your job."

She came around to the left side of the table. The man's breathing had gone shallow and rapid, the panting of an animal that has been run to ground, but he was not seizing and he was not grey and his lips were not blue.

"This is not the part where we're being kind. I will tell you when it's that part. I have told people before and I will tell people again and I do not dress it up and I do not leave it ambiguous. When it is that part, you will know because I will say so, and then we will do what that requires. But right now what it requires is that you hold his left shoulder while I reduce his right, and that you stop asking me questions about a leg that nobody has mentioned until you just did."

She positioned her hands on the right arm. This one was simpler — the dislocation was cleaner, less swelling, less time spent wrong. It would still hurt him enormously.

"He keeps both arms. Probably keeps full use of the right. The left is a question I can't answer tonight. Infection will answer it, or it won't. That's tomorrow's problem, and I have made a practice of not solving tomorrow's problems with tonight's hands."

She found the angle.

"Hold."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content:
I let out a breath I didn't realize I was holding. My hands settle back onto his left shoulder, feeling the heat through the uniform. "Right. Got it," I say, my voice steadier than I feel.

I don't look away from the canvas this time. Instead, I watch his face go tight and pale as Sedge begins.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge worked the right arm through its rotation and the man's face did exactly what Wick was watching it do — it went from slack to rigid in the space between one breath and the next, every tendon in his neck surfacing like cable under the skin. His eyes opened. They were not seeing anything in the tent. They were seeing something much older and much worse and entirely private, and Sedge did not look at them because what a man saw in that moment belonged to him.

"He's anticipating," she said, narrating because narrating was part of the work, because silence in a tent like this grew teeth. "The muscles are guarding. They think they're helping. They're not."

She maintained the traction, steady and implacable. Not forcing. Waiting. There was a difference, and four years had taught her the difference, and the difference was the thing that separated a reduction from a new injury. The body had to be convinced. You could not win an argument with a shoulder by shouting.

The man groaned — a long, pressurized sound, like something leaking from a sealed room. His left side came up under Wick's hands, not the explosive buck of the first reduction but a slow, rolling surge, the body trying every avenue of escape and finding them all closed.

"Steady," Sedge said. To Wick. To the shoulder. To the stubborn geometry of a joint that did not want to go home.

Then it went. The same sound — that quiet, meaty *thunk* that carried more finality than any word she knew. The man's breath left him in a rush and his eyes closed and his face did something complicated that was not quite relief because relief implied the absence of pain and there was no absence here, only a rearrangement.

Sedge checked the pulse at the right wrist. Checked capillary refill in the fingernails, pressing and releasing, pressing and releasing. Checked sensation by pricking the pad of each finger with a pin she kept in her collar for this purpose.

"He felt that," she said, because the man flinched at each prick, which was a small and vicious kindness — pain confirming the existence of something worth saving. "Good. That's good."

She fashioned a sling from a strip of canvas she cut from a supply bag that had nothing left in it anyway, then a second one. She immobilized both arms against his torso with a wrap that went around his chest, tying it firm enough to hold and loose enough to let him breathe, checking two fingers' width of space at the sternum.

"You can ease off," she told Wick.

She stood back. Looked at the man on the table. He was breathing. He was perfusing. He was alive in the way that alive meant tonight, which was: not dead, not dying, not deciding.

"I need to redress that forearm in four hours," she said, washing her hands in the dregs of the water, which was no longer clean and hadn't been for some time. "If the skin around the wound goes hot and red, or if the swelling gets worse instead of better, or if he stops making sense — more than the usual amount of not making sense — you come find me. Don't wait to see if it improves. It won't improve on its own. Things that improve on their own are not the things that end up on my table."

She dried her hands on her trousers because the rag was past the point of utility.

"You did well," she said. It was not warm. It was not cold. It was a field assessment, delivered with the same tone she'd used to describe the state of his shoulders. "Most people let go during the first reduction. You didn't. That matters more than whatever's happening in your head right now, which I expect is considerable. Go get water if there is any. Drink some first. Bring the rest back here."

She pulled a stool to the side of the table and sat down next to the man, two fingers resting against the inside of his wrist, counting what she could not afford to stop counting.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't move her fingers from the man's wrist. She was quiet for a moment — not hesitating, but measuring. Deciding how much anatomy Wick actually wanted and how much he thought he wanted, and whether the difference mattered tonight.

It didn't. He'd asked. She'd learned a long time ago that people who asked twice meant it.

"You're seeing a man who's been stabilized," she said. "Which is not the same as a man who's been fixed. Those are different things and I need you to understand the difference because you're going to be sitting with him while I'm not here."

She lifted her chin toward the left arm, the one wrapped and slung and bound against his chest.

"The forearm wound. That's what you're really asking about, even if you don't know it yet. What's under that dressing is about six inches of open tissue from the wrist to the middle of the forearm. The shrapnel went in at an angle and traveled along the bone — the ulna, the thinner one on the outside of your arm, you can feel it if you run your thumb from your wrist to your elbow. It peeled the muscle back from the bone the way you'd peel bark from a green branch. Not a clean cut. Ragged. The kind of edge that doesn't want to be put back together because the pieces don't remember where they went."

She said this the way she said everything — flat, measured, descriptive. A woman reading aloud from a text she did not find interesting but considered important.

"The bone is intact. I said that before and I'm saying it again because it's the thing that matters most and the thing you'll forget first. Intact bone means the arm has a scaffold. Everything else — muscle, tendon, skin — that can heal around a scaffold if it's given the chance. The question is whether it gets the chance, and that question is about infection, and infection is about time and luck, and I am short on both."

She glanced at the dressing. It was already showing the faint bloom of fluid seeping through — not bright red, not the arterial urgency that would have had her back on her feet, but the darker, slower color of a wound that was still weeping and would be for some time.

"What I packed it with is not sterile. Nothing in this tent is sterile. I cleaned it as well as I could, which was not well enough, and I packed it to control the bleeding and keep the tissue from drying out, which is what exposed muscle does — it dries, and dried muscle is dead muscle, and dead muscle is the thing that infection loves most in the world. So the dressing stays damp. That's your job when I'm not here. If it dries, you wet it. Clean water if there is clean water. Any water if there isn't."

She looked at the man's face. He had settled into something that approximated sleep but wasn't — a shallow, twitching unconsciousness, the body's last negotiating tactic when it had run out of everything else.

"His color's acceptable. Meaning he's pale but not grey. Grey is bad. Grey means he's not circulating and we have a different conversation. Pink at the lips and nail beds is what you're checking. You don't need to know why. You just need to know that if those go white or blue, you come find me at a dead run."

She adjusted her fingers on his wrist. Counted silently. Nodded to herself.

"Pulse is fast but it's steady and it's strong enough that I can feel it without pressing. That's what you want. If you're sitting here and you check and you have to dig for it — if you're pressing hard and you're not sure if what you're feeling is him or your own thumb — that's the other reason you come find me."

She leaned back on the stool. It creaked under her in a way that suggested it had opinions about how much more of this war it intended to survive.

"That's what you're seeing. A man whose bones are where they should be, whose blood is moving the direction it's supposed to move, and whose left arm is in a negotiation with every microbe in this part of the country. I've given him the best terms I can. The rest is his."

She looked at Wick.

"Now go get that water. You asked what you're seeing and I told you. Sit with it while you walk. Don't sit with it while you're sitting — that's when it gets heavy."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow, my throat dry. "Alright." I push away from the table, my knees protesting as I straighten. At the tent flap, I glance back. "You'll still be here when I get back?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't look up. Her fingers stayed on the man's wrist, two points of contact against a pulse she was counting in sets of fifteen because that was the interval she trusted and because trust was a resource she allocated with the same parsimony as clean water.

"Where else would I be," she said.

It was not a question. It was not reassurance. It was the same kind of statement as *the bone is intact* — a fact so self-evident that inflecting it upward would have been an insult to both of them.

The man on the table shifted. A small sound escaped him, not quite a word, not quite a groan — something from the middle distance of consciousness where the body speaks a language it will not remember in the morning. Sedge adjusted the wrap across his chest where his movement had pulled it a quarter inch to the left, which was a quarter inch she was not willing to give.

"I have been in this tent or a tent like it every night for four years," she said, still not looking at Wick. She said it to the dressing on the man's forearm, or to the lamp, or to no one. "I don't leave until the pulse tells me I can leave or until someone else comes in who's worse. That's not loyalty. It's arithmetic. He's the only one on the table tonight, which makes him the only number I'm solving for."

She reached over and moved the lamp a half inch closer. Checked the dressing again. The seepage had not worsened, which she noted and did not celebrate, because celebration was for people who had not yet learned that wounds could change their minds.

"Bring the water. Take your time getting there. Don't take your time getting back."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge exhaled through her nose. Not a sigh — she did not sigh, had burned that particular indulgence out of herself somewhere in the second year — but a controlled release of air that meant she was recalibrating. Wick was still standing at the tent flap. He was not getting water. He was asking questions instead of getting water, and she had told him to get water, and she could have said that.

She didn't.

Because he was standing there with his hands at his sides and his knees probably still shaking and he was asking her to tell him the ugly thing instead of letting him walk out into the dark and build it himself, and the version he would build would be worse. It was always worse. The imagination was more sadistic than any piece of metal she had ever pulled out of a man.

"Shrapnel is not a bullet," she said. "A bullet has intentions. It goes in a direction. It makes a hole that has an entrance and usually an exit and the hole is the shape of the bullet's ambition, which is to go through. Shrapnel has no ambition. Shrapnel is just whatever was nearby when the explosion happened — casing, rock, dirt, pieces of things that used to be other things. It is moving very fast and it is not moving in a line. It is tumbling."

She kept her fingers on the man's pulse. She spoke to the forearm because the forearm was the subject and she believed in looking at the subject.

"When a piece of tumbling metal enters tissue, it does not cut. Cutting implies a clean intention. It tears. It crushes. It creates a cavity that is larger than itself because the energy it carries has to go somewhere, and where it goes is into the tissue surrounding the path, and that tissue does not tear — it *stretches*, and then it comes back, and then it dies. Not immediately. Over hours. The cells along the wound track are bruised at a level you can't see with your eyes. They look intact tonight. Tomorrow they'll be dead, and the day after that they'll be the thing that infection feeds on."

She paused. Not for effect. She was checking the man's breathing — counting the rate, watching the rise of his chest under the wrap.

"That's what's in his arm. A channel of destruction that is wider than the piece of metal that made it, lined with tissue that is dying in a gradient — dead at the center, damaged further out, maybe viable at the edges. I cannot tell tonight which tissue will live and which will not. No one can. The body hasn't decided yet. What I did was clean out what I could see — the dirt, the fragments, the cloth from his sleeve that the shrapnel carried in with it because shrapnel is not courteous enough to wipe its feet — and pack it open so it drains instead of sealing over a pocket of filth that will abscess in three days and kill him in five."

She looked at Wick then. Steady. Not unkind, but not kind either. Something more useful than either.

"I did not close the wound. I want you to understand that. It is open on purpose. It will stay open. It will look wrong to you because you think wounds are supposed to be closed, sewn up, made neat. This one stays open because closing it would trap everything I just described inside his arm, and what I just described is a death sentence wearing a tidy row of sutures. It heals from the inside out or it doesn't heal. Those are the two options and I have chosen the one that gives him a chance."

She turned back to the man on the table. His pulse was still there under her fingers, steady and countable, doing the only work it knew how to do.

"That's what shrapnel does. It makes a mess and it leaves, and I stay, and I manage the mess. Now you know. Now go get the water, Wick. He's going to need it more than you need another answer."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I stare at the man's arm, really seeing the dressing now. "Alright," I say again, voice rough. "I'll be quick." I duck out into the dark, the smell of damp earth and smoke hitting me. I take three deep breaths, the cold air sharp in my lungs, before I start toward the water cache.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge listened to his footsteps until they were gone and then she listened to the silence that replaced them, which was not silence at all but the particular nighttime vocabulary of a camp that had stopped pretending to sleep — distant coughing, the creak of guy ropes in wind that couldn't decide on a direction, someone somewhere talking low and steady to no one or to God, which in her experience amounted to the same thing at this hour.

She moved her fingers a quarter inch along the man's wrist. The pulse was still there. She counted it again. Eighty-eight. It had been ninety-four when Wick was in the tent, which meant the man's body had registered on some subterranean level that there was one fewer person in the room doing things to it, and had made the only concession it could, which was four beats a minute. She would take it.

"You're still here," she said to the man. Not gently. Not roughly. The way you'd confirm a fact with someone who might or might not be listening. "That's your job tonight. Stay here. Everything else is mine."

He did not respond. His eyelids twitched — REM activity or pain or the random firing of a nervous system that had been overloaded and was sorting its receipts. She didn't assign meaning to it. Meaning was expensive.

She checked the dressing on the left forearm without unwrapping it, pressing two fingers to the canvas at the margins. Warm, which was expected. Wet, which was expected. Not hot. Hot was the word she was listening for with her fingertips, the word that would mean the tissue underneath had begun the conversation she could not win with what she had in this tent. Not yet. The conversation had not started yet.

She allowed that to be true. She did not allow it to be comforting.

The lamp guttered and she reached over and adjusted the wick — the actual wick, the one made of cotton, not the one she'd sent out into the dark — trimming the char with her thumbnail because the scissors were not worth dirtying for a lamp. The light steadied. She positioned it so the glow fell on the man's hands, both of them, because the hands were where the story would be told first. Color, temperature, capillary refill. The fingernails were pink. She pressed the thumbnail of his right hand and counted. The blood returned in under two seconds. She did the left. The same, though she pressed twice to be sure, because the left was the arm with the wound and the arm with the wound was the arm that could lie to her.

She sat back. The stool made its opinion known again.

"I know," she said to it, or to the tent, or to the four years that sat in the corners of every tent she had ever worked in, accumulated and heavy and entirely uninterested in her feelings about them.

She waited for Wick to come back with the water. She counted the pulse. She did not think about tomorrow because tomorrow was a country she could not enter with tonight's passport, and the border would still be there in four hours when she changed the dressing and found out what the wound had decided to become.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't flinch. The screaming had started the way it always started — not from sleep to waking but from that shallow, fraudulent unconsciousness into something the body could no longer contain. He'd shifted. The left arm had moved against the sling, maybe a quarter inch, maybe less, and a quarter inch was enough. A quarter inch in a forearm that had been opened and packed was a conversation between raw nerve endings and air and cotton that should not have been happening, and the man's nervous system had received the message and responded with the only vocabulary it had left.

"He's not in danger," Sedge said. She said it first because it was the thing that mattered first. "He's in pain. Those are different countries and I need you to know which one we're in."

She was already moving. She had the dressing exposed — not removed, exposed, peeling back the outer layer of wrap to look at what was underneath without disturbing the packing itself. Her hands were doing this while her mouth was doing the other thing, the narration, because Wick had asked for it and because the asking meant he needed the architecture of language between himself and the sound coming out of this man's throat.

"What happened is he moved. Probably involuntary — a spasm, a dream, the body trying to find a position that doesn't exist. The packing shifted against the wound bed. The wound bed is exposed muscle and periosteum — that's the membrane that covers bone, and it is the most pain-sensitive tissue in the body apart from the eyes and the teeth. There is no amount of moving that is small enough to be painless against exposed periosteum. A breeze would do it. A heartbeat does it, if the wound is close enough to an artery to feel the pulse. His is."

The man's back arched under Wick's hands. The scream had broken into something rhythmic now — not words, not sobs, a kind of panting shout on every exhale, the lungs doing their job and the pain hitching a ride on every breath out. His right hand was clawing at the wrap across his chest. Sedge caught it without looking and held it — not restrained it, held it, her thumb against his palm, firm and present.

"I'm stabilizing the dressing. That's what I'm doing right now, this moment, with my other hand. I'm pressing the packing back into position without removing it because removing it would mean debriding the wound again and I am not doing that without clean water and more light than this lamp is giving me. The packing needs to sit against the tissue evenly. When it shifts, it creates a gap, and the gap is where air hits nerve endings that have no skin over them, and that is what he is feeling. That is what this sound is."

She pressed. Gently. The kind of gentle that looked like nothing from the outside and required the steadiest hands in the tent. The man's shouting hitched — a stutter in the rhythm, a half-second of silence that was not relief but recalibration — and then continued, but lower. A register down. She'd take it.

"I'm re-wrapping now. Three layers. First layer sits against the packing and does not move — I'm tying it here, and here, do you see my fingers, Wick, look at my fingers, not his face — tied firm enough that it can't shift again when he moves, loose enough that it's not compressing the tissue and cutting off the blood supply that's keeping his hand pink. Second layer is padding. It does nothing medically. It is a buffer between the wound and the world and sometimes that is all you can offer. Third layer is structural. It holds the other two in place."

She wrapped. Her hands moved with a fluency that was not grace — grace implied something aesthetic, and there was nothing aesthetic here — but something closer to literacy. She was writing a sentence she had written hundreds of times in a language made of cotton and pressure and the particular tension that meant *enough* without meaning *too much*.

"How much longer for this, right now, is about ninety seconds. I'm on the second layer. He'll quiet before I'm done because the packing is already seated again and what he's feeling now is the memory of the pain, not the pain itself. The nervous system doesn't distinguish. It keeps firing after the stimulus is gone because it has been taught tonight that things touching his arm mean agony and it is not interested in learning a more nuanced lesson."

The man was proving her right. The shouts had roughened into groaning — still loud, still awful, but decaying. An engine running out of fuel. His right hand had stopped clawing and was gripping Sedge's thumb with a force that was whitening both their knuckles, and she let it, because a hand holding something was a hand that was not tearing at a dressing.

"Third layer. Almost done. Wick, his shoulders — is he guarding? Is one side pulling up higher than the other?"

She asked because she needed the answer but also because she needed Wick's hands to become diagnostic instruments instead of just weights. A person holding someone down was a person enduring. A person checking for asymmetry was a person working. The difference mattered.

"Tell me what you feel under your hands. Left versus right. Temperature, tension, whether one side is fighting you harder. Use your words. I need your hands to be my hands for the parts of him I can't reach right now."

Wick:
"Left's tighter," I say, forcing myself to actually feel what's under my palms instead of just pressing down. "Pulling up hard. Right's... looser. Still tense but not fighting me the same way. Left side is hotter, I think. I think."

Sedge:
"You think or you know." Not harsh. Diagnostic. The same tone she used on a wound that was giving her ambiguous information. "Put the back of your hand against his left shoulder. Then his right. Back of the hand has thinner skin, it reads temperature better than the palm. Do it now."

She was finishing the third layer of wrap, tying it off with a knot that sat flat against the outside of his forearm where it couldn't press into anything that would make him scream again. The man's grip on her thumb had loosened from desperate to merely insistent. His breathing was still ragged but the shouts had collapsed into a low, continuous sound — a moan that rose and fell with each exhale, the body's way of metering out what it could not hold.

Wick:
I flip my hand over, pressing the back of my knuckles to his left shoulder, holding it there, then switching to the right. "Left's hotter," I say, and this time I'm sure. "Noticeably. Not just a little."

Sedge:
Sedge's hands stopped moving for exactly one second. Then they resumed, tying off the last tail of the wrap, tucking it under itself so it couldn't unravel. One second. That was what she allowed.

"Good," she said. "That's useful. That's you being useful."

She released the man's right hand — he let go reluctantly, his fingers trailing against her palm like a child losing hold of something in a current — and came around to Wick's side of the table. She did not rush. Rushing was for people who had not yet learned that speed and urgency were different things, and that the wrong one killed people.

She placed the back of her own hand against his left shoulder. Held it. Moved to the right. Held it.

The difference was there. Not dramatic. Not the furious heat of an established infection — she had felt that, many times, the skin so hot it seemed to have its own weather system, its own malignant climate. This was subtler. A degree, maybe two. The left shoulder running warmer than the right in a way that could be inflammation from the reduction, which was expected, which was the body's appropriate response to having a joint wrenched back into its socket by a woman with field-dirty hands in a tent that smelled like blood and lamp oil.

Or it could be the first word of the other conversation. The one she'd been listening for.

"It's probably reactive," she said. "The left side took more trauma. The wound is on the left arm. The dislocation on the left was worse — more swelling, more time out of joint, more tissue damage during the reduction. Inflammation follows injury the way dogs follow armies. It would be stranger if it *weren't* hotter."

She palpated the shoulder itself, pressing into the tissue around the joint with her fingertips, feeling for the things that fingers could find and eyes couldn't — fluid where fluid shouldn't be, boggy softness that meant the tissue was waterlogged with the body's own inflammatory soup, crepitus, the particular tautness of skin stretched over something expanding underneath it.

The man flinched under her hands but did not scream. He was spent. The account was overdrawn and the body was operating on whatever metabolic credit it had left, which was not much.

"No fluctuance," she said. "No crepitus. The joint is stable in the reduction — it hasn't slipped. The swelling is diffuse, not focal, which means it's generalized inflammation, not a pocket of something collecting. All of that is what I want to find."

She straightened up.

"But I'm not going to tell you it's nothing. It might be nothing. It might be the first hour of something. I cannot tell the difference at this stage and anyone who says they can is lying to you or to themselves. What I can tell you is that I now know it's there, and I know it because you told me, and in four hours when I change the dressing I will check it again and I will know whether it has stayed the same or gotten worse, and the difference between those two things is the difference between reactive inflammation and the beginning of infection, and that difference is the answer to every question you have about this man's arm that you haven't asked yet."

She looked at Wick. He was still braced against the man's shoulders. His hands were no longer just holding — they were *placed*, the way she'd asked them to be, reading what was underneath them.

"Keep your hands where they are. You are now a thermometer. If the difference between left and right gets bigger — if the left starts feeling like it has its own heartbeat, its own heat source, something *alive* under the skin that shouldn't be — you don't wait for the four hours. You come get me."

She sat back down on the stool. Found the man's wrist again. Counted.

"Ninety-two," she said. "He's come back up from eighty-eight, which is the pain. It'll settle. The number I don't want to see is one-ten. Above one-ten his heart is working too hard for a man lying still, and that means either he's lost more blood than I think he has or his body is fighting something I can't see yet."

She adjusted the lamp again. Checked his fingernails. Still pink. Still refilling.

"You asked how much longer. The answer is the rest of the night. There is no point at which I say *done* and we leave. There is only the next check, and the one after that, and the one after that, until morning comes and I can see the wound in actual light and make decisions that this lamp is not qualified to let me make. That's how much longer. That's all of it. Now — is there water, or did you come back empty-handed?"

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I shake my head, the guilt sharp. "I forgot. I'll go now." I start to move, then stop, my hands hovering over his shoulders. "But if he gets hot again while I'm gone—"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge was already replacing his hands with hers. Not a negotiation — a transfer, the kind she had done so many times that the mechanics of it lived in her muscles rather than her mind. Her left hand went to his left shoulder, her right to his right, and she registered the temperature differential as her skin made contact. Still there. Not worse. She catalogued it and moved on.

"Then I will be here," she said. "Which is where I have been for the last four hours and where I will be for the next four. I was managing patients alone before you walked into this tent and I will manage him alone for the time it takes you to walk to the cache and walk back. That is not bravery. It is the baseline. It is the minimum competence required to sit in this chair."

She settled her weight over him, reading his shoulders the way Wick had been reading them — left guarding, right looser, the asymmetry holding steady, not worsening, the heat on the left side sitting at exactly the level it had been sitting at when she'd checked it a minute ago. She would know if it changed. She would know because her hands would tell her, and her hands had not lied to her in four years, which was more than she could say for anyone else in this war.

The man stirred under her. His breathing caught, hitched, resumed. She pressed down — not hard, just present, the way a hand on a shoulder says *I am here and you are here and neither of us is going anywhere.*

"Wick." She did not look at him. She looked at the man's chest rising and falling under the wrap. "If you stand in that doorway for another thirty seconds deciding whether it is safe to leave, I will have a man with no water and an assistant who has done nothing but worry in a doorway. Both of those are worse than whatever you think will happen in the eight minutes you are gone. Go. Walk with purpose. Do not run — running spills water, and I need the water more than I need you back ten seconds sooner."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't ask what he meant by *the rest*. She knew what he meant by *the rest* because there was always a rest, and it always came at this hour, when the work had been done or at least paused and the body on the table had settled into something that would hold for a while and the person who had been helping sat down on the floor or against a crate or, once, flat on their back in the mud outside the tent flap, and said some version of the same thing. *Tell me. Say it. What happens now.* Not the medical now. The other now. The one that lived past the lamp and the dressing and the four-hour checks and stretched out into the kind of future that no one in this tent was qualified to promise.

She kept her fingers on the man's wrist. Eighty-six. He had settled. His breathing had found a rhythm that approximated sleep closely enough that she was willing to call it that, though sleep was a generous word for what the body did when it had exhausted every other option and simply stopped negotiating.

"Alright," she said.

She did not look at Wick on the floor. She looked at the man on the table because the man on the table was the subject and she looked at the subject.

"In four hours I change the dressing. I will unwrap what I wrapped tonight and I will look at the wound bed in whatever light the morning gives me, which will not be surgical light but will be better than this lamp, and the lamp is what I have been making decisions by, which should tell you something about the quality of the decisions available to me. When I open that wound I am looking for three things. Color of the tissue. Smell of the tissue. And what the drainage looks like — how much, what color, what consistency. Those three things will tell me whether the tissue I packed against six hours ago is still viable or whether it has begun to die."

She paused. Not for Wick. For accuracy. Because what she was about to describe had a sequence and the sequence mattered and getting it wrong was not something she did.

"If the tissue is viable — if the muscle is still red and wet and bleeds when I touch it, which is what I want, I want it to bleed, bleeding means blood supply and blood supply means alive — then I irrigate the wound again, I repack it with the cleanest material I can find, and I wrap it and I do the same thing again in another four hours. And another four hours after that. And another. For days, Wick. This is not a wound that resolves in a night. This is a wound that I will be opening and closing and opening and closing for as long as it takes the body to build new tissue from the edges inward, and that process is measured in weeks, and every four hours of those weeks is another opportunity for infection to begin, and every time I open that dressing I am asking the same question and I will not know the answer until I look."

The man's hand twitched on the table. A finger curled and uncurled against the wood, the body running its inventory in whatever dream or non-dream it was conducting. Sedge watched the movement. Flexion. Extension. The tendons working. She noted it the way she noted everything — without celebration, without relief, as data.

"If the tissue is not viable — if what I find in four hours is grey muscle that does not bleed when I touch it, or muscle that has turned the color of wet newspaper, or if the smell is sweet in the way that sweet has no business being, the smell that is not rot yet but is rot's ambassador — then I debride. That means I cut away everything that is dead until I reach something that is alive. I will cut into his arm with a blade and I will remove tissue that was part of him twelve hours ago and that is not part of him anymore because it has died, and I will keep cutting until what is left bleeds, and then I will pack the wound again and the wound will be larger than it was before because I have made it larger, because a smaller wound full of dead tissue kills a man and a larger wound full of living tissue does not."

She said this without inflection. She said it the way the war had taught her to say it, which was the way you say a thing that is true and terrible and that you have done before and will do again and that does not require your feelings about it in order to proceed.

"I may have to do that more than once. The dying does not always happen all at once. It happens in layers. I take what is dead today and tomorrow there is a new margin of death behind it, the tissue that was bruised and swollen and that I thought might make it and that did not make it, and I cut that away too. Each time the wound gets bigger. Each time there is less of his arm. And each time I am making the same wager, which is that what I leave behind is enough — enough muscle to move the wrist, enough tissue to cover the bone, enough of him left that the arm is an arm and not a thing that hangs from his shoulder and does nothing."

The lamp flickered. She did not adjust it. She let it flicker because the light was adequate and her hands were occupied and because some things did not need to be fixed in the moment they faltered.

"That is the good outcome. That is the version where I am opening his arm every four hours for weeks and cutting away what dies and packing what lives and the infection either does not come or comes and is small enough and slow enough that his body fights it with what his body has, because I have nothing to give him for it. I have no sulfa. I have not had sulfa in five weeks. I have no penicillin. I have never had penicillin. What I have is clean water when there is clean water and cotton that is not clean and a knife and my hands and the particular stubbornness of a body that is forty-four years old and has not yet found a reason to stop doing this. That is what I am fighting infection with. That is the full inventory."

She took a breath. Not a deep breath. Not a steadying breath. A breath in the amount required to continue speaking, allocated with the same economy she applied to everything else.

"The bad outcome is that I open the dressing in four hours and the infection is already there. Not the beginning of it. Not the ambassador. The thing itself. The muscle is dead in a way that is not grey but green or black. The smell is not sweet but foul — the smell that fills a tent and does not leave when you leave the tent, the smell that follows you into the next tent and the tent after that and that you will taste in the back of your throat for days. The drainage is not the thin pink fluid of a wound that is weeping but the thick, opaque, yellow-green fluid of a wound that is rotting. And the skin around the wound — the skin that you told me was hot, Wick, and you were right, it was hot — that skin is not just hot but red and swollen and tracking, meaning the redness is spreading up his arm in lines that follow the lymphatic channels, which means the infection is no longer local. It is no longer in the wound. It is in him."

She checked the pulse. Eighty-four. He was still settling. She allowed the number to exist without commentary.

"If that is what I find, then I am not packing a wound anymore. I am making a decision about an arm. And the decision is whether the arm can be saved or whether the arm is going to kill him, and if the arm is going to kill him then the arm comes off, and I will take it off above the elbow because the wound is below the elbow and I need clean margin and I need to be above the zone of injury and I need to be certain, and certainty in this context means removing more than I want to remove because removing too little is the mistake that kills and removing too much is the mistake that maims, and I have made my preference between those two mistakes and I made it a long time ago."

She said this looking at his arm. At the dressing she had wrapped. At the fingers that were still pink, still warm, still curling and uncurling in the involuntary grammar of an intact nervous system.

"I have taken off arms before. I have taken off legs. I have done it on tables worse than this one in light worse than this and with less help than you have been tonight. It is not surgery. Surgery is what happens in hospitals with anesthesia and retractors and someone whose hands are not also the hands that packed the wound and checked the pulse and held the lamp. What I do is amputation in the field, which is a different word for a different thing, and the different thing is: I tie off the blood supply, I cut through the muscle, I saw through the bone, I fold the flap and I close it, and the man wakes up with less of himself than he went to sleep with and I am the one who made that happen and I am the one who will tell him."

The tent was very quiet. The man's breathing was the loudest thing in it, slow and shallow and even. Outside, the camp had gone as quiet as it ever went, which was not quiet at all but had become the baseline against which quiet was measured — the coughing, the wind, the distant and indistinguishable murmur of people enduring the hours between midnight and dawn, which were the hours that belonged to no one and that everyone had to survive anyway.

"I do not know which outcome we are in. I will not know until I open that dressing. I am telling you both because you asked me to tell you both and because I need you to understand that when I open that dressing in four hours, my face is not going to tell you anything. I have practiced that. I have practiced it the way other people practice music or prayer — deliberately, over years, until the practice became the thing itself. When I look at that wound I will know what I am seeing and you will not know what I am seeing because my face will not change, and that is not deception, it is the way I work, because a medic whose face tells the story before her mouth does is a medic who has lost control of the one thing she can control in a tent where she controls nothing else."

She looked at Wick. He was on the floor. She took in the way he was sitting — the specific geometry of a person who had put himself down there not because he chose to sit but because standing had stopped being available. His back against whatever was behind him. His hands somewhere. His face doing the thing that faces did at this hour, which was nothing and everything, the muscles slack but the eyes unsettled, looking at something that was either in the tent or very far from it.

"That is the rest," she said. "That is all of it. The good version and the bad version and the hours between now and knowing which one we're in. I have not left anything out. I do not leave things out. I have found that the things you leave out are the things that grow in the dark, and there is enough growing in the dark in this tent without me adding to it."

She turned back to the man on the table. Checked his fingernails. Pressed. Counted. Released. Pink in under two seconds. She checked the other hand. The same.

"You can stay on the floor," she said. "The floor is as good a place as any. But if you're going to stay, then stay — don't sit there deciding whether to stay. Decide and then be where you are. I have a patient who needs me to be here and I am here and that is decided and I am not spending any part of my attention on the question of whether I should be somewhere else. Give yourself the same."

She adjusted the wrap across the man's chest. A quarter inch. She took back the quarter inch.

"In four hours I will need you standing, and I will need your hands, and I will need you to do what you did tonight, which was hold when I said hold and look when I said look and tell me what you felt under your palms when I asked you what you felt. You did that. That is not a small thing. That is the thing. Everything else — the questions, the standing in doorways, the forgetting the water — that is the noise around the thing. The thing is that you held and you looked and you told me the left was hotter and you were right."

She counted the pulse. Eighty-four. Holding.

"So sit on the floor. Close your eyes or don't. Sleep or don't. But be here in four hours with your hands ready and your head in this tent and not in whatever tent your head goes to when it leaves, because I have seen the tent your head goes to and it is not a useful place and it does not have any information I need."

The lamp steadied. The man breathed. Sedge sat on the stool with her fingers on his wrist and did not move, because not moving was the work now, and the work was what there was, and what there was was enough because it had to be.

"That's the rest," she said again, quieter. Not softer. Quieter. The volume of a woman who had said what needed saying and was now saying the last thing, the thing that was not medical and not practical and that she allowed herself once, at this hour, in the space between the work that was done and the work that was coming.

"He's alive. You're alive. I'm alive. That's tonight's math. I don't do tomorrow's math with tonight's numbers."

She did not say anything else. She sat with her fingers on the man's pulse and she counted, and the counting was the work, and the work continued, and outside the tent the war went on doing what the war did, which was everything, which was nothing, which was the particular and relentless passage of hours that did not care whether anyone inside them was ready.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I stay on the floor. After a minute, I lean my head back against the crate behind me. "What's his name?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge's fingers didn't stop counting. Eighty-four. Eighty-four. The number held like a rope she was not going to let go of.

"I don't know," she said.

She said it the way she had said everything else tonight — without apology, without embarrassment, without the particular inflection that would have turned it into a confession. It was not a confession. It was a fact, and facts did not require contrition.

"He came in on a stretcher with no tag and no one carrying him who knew him. Two men from the second company brought him in and neither of them had seen him before the blast. They found him in a ditch and they carried him here and they put him on my table and they left because they had others to go back for, and I did not ask them his name because his name was not going to change what I did with his shoulders or his arm."

She checked the pulse. Still eighty-four. The man's face in the lamplight had settled into something that was not peaceful — peaceful was a word for people who were sleeping in beds in houses that still had roofs — but was at least neutral. The muscles around his eyes had unclenched. His jaw had loosened. He looked like a man who had been granted a temporary and conditional reprieve from his own body, and who was using it the way any sensible person would, which was to be absent from it for as long as the absence held.

"I will learn his name when he wakes up enough to tell it to me, or when someone comes looking for him who knows it. One of those will happen. It usually does. And when it does I will write it on the tag and tie the tag to his wrist and his name will be part of the record, which is the place where names do their work."

She moved her thumb a fraction of an inch along the tendon at his wrist. A habitual adjustment. The pulse was easier to read in some positions than others, and she had long ago stopped thinking about the micro-movements that kept her fingers in the right place. They happened the way breathing happened — below the level of decision.

"I know you're asking because you want him to be a person. He is a person. He was a person before you asked and he'll be a person whether or not either of us can call him by the right word. But I understand the want. I understand that a man with a name is harder to lose than a man without one, and that you are sitting on that floor right now trying to build something between yourself and him that will make the next four hours mean something, and a name is the first brick."

She looked at Wick. Briefly. The kind of look that took in everything and offered nothing back — the head tilted against the crate, the hands in his lap or at his sides, the particular stillness of a person who was not resting but who had been emptied of motion.

"I used to learn their names first. First year. I would ask before I started, even when they were screaming, even when the asking cost me ten seconds I did not have. I thought it mattered. I thought that if I knew the name then the work was different — not better, not more careful, but different in a way I believed was important. That the name made a contract between me and the man on the table, and the contract said *I see you, you are specific, you are not interchangeable with the man who was on this table before you or the one who will be on it after.*"

She paused. Counted. Eighty-six. He had come up two beats. She filed it. Pain surfacing through whatever shallow unconsciousness he had found, or a dream, or nothing. She would watch it.

"I stopped in the second year. Not because I stopped caring. Because I learned that the name did not change what my hands did, and what my hands did was the only thing I had that was worth anything in this tent. The contract I thought I was making — that was for me. That was my need, not his. He did not need me to know his name. He needed me to know that the ulna was intact and the periosteum was exposed and the left shoulder was anterior and inferior and needed to come home before the nerve bundle in the axilla was compressed long enough to die. That is what he needed. The name was what *I* needed, and I could not afford to need things that did not serve the work."

The man's hand twitched again. The same finger — the index finger of his right hand, curling and uncurling in that slow, involuntary rhythm. Sedge watched it. Flexion, extension. The tendon sliding under the skin. Alive. Intact. Doing its one job without being asked.

"So I will learn his name. And you will learn his name. And when we know it we will use it, because names are what you use when a man is awake and looking at you and trying to find out whether the world still has a place in it that is shaped like him. That is when the name does its work. That is when the brick matters."

She turned back to the table. Adjusted the lamp. The light caught the man's face and she looked at it — really looked, the way she rarely did, taking in the specifics that had nothing to do with perfusion or respiration or pain response. He was young. Not as young as some. Maybe twenty-five, maybe thirty — the war had a way of adding years that weren't there and erasing ones that were, and she had stopped trusting her estimates. Dark hair, cut short and uneven in the way that meant he or someone near him had done it with a knife and without a mirror. A scar on his chin, old, white, from something that had happened before all of this. A face that belonged to someone, that someone somewhere would recognize, that had been known by a name for twenty-five or thirty years before it arrived on her table anonymous and screaming.

"For now he is the man on the table," she said. "That is enough. That is what I have and I work with what I have."

She counted. Eighty-six. Holding.

"Ask him in the morning. If we get a morning. We usually do."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, my head heavy against the crate. "Alright," I say, my voice rough. I close my eyes, just for a second. The dark behind my lids is better than the lamplight. "Wake me if it's my turn to count."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge watched Wick's eyes close. She watched the muscles in his face do the thing they did when a person stopped holding them in place — not relaxing, exactly, but surrendering jurisdiction. The jaw went slack by a degree. The lines across the forehead didn't smooth but they stopped being maintained, which was a different thing that looked similar and wasn't.

She did not say *alright.* She did not say *rest.* She did not say anything for a full thirty seconds because the silence was doing the work that words would have interrupted, and she had learned to recognize when silence was working and to leave it alone.

The pulse under her fingers was eighty-six. She counted it twice to be sure, because being sure was free and being wrong was not.

"It's not your turn to count," she said, quietly, to the tent or to Wick or to the particular quality of attention that a person maintained even after their eyes closed, the thin, frayed thread of wakefulness that ran between *I am here* and *I am not.* "Counting is mine. It has always been mine. What you do is hold, and there is nothing to hold right now, so there is nothing for you to do right now, and doing nothing when there is nothing to do is not the same as being useless, and I need you to know the difference because in four hours I will need you to be something other than a man who spent the interval punishing himself for not being needed."

She checked the dressing. Dry at the outer layer. She pressed two fingers to the margin where the wrap met skin. Warm. Not hot. The same. She noted it and did not react to it because reacting to *the same* was a waste of a reaction, and she had a finite number of those left and she was not spending one here.

The man on the table breathed. In. Out. In. Out. The rhythm had steadied into something she could set a clock by, if she'd had a clock, if clocks mattered, if time in this tent moved in the direction that clocks described, which it did not. Time in this tent moved in intervals of four hours, marked not by hands on a dial but by the opening and closing of a dressing on a wound that had not yet decided what it was going to become.

Wick's breathing was changing. She could hear it — the slow deepening, the lengthening of the exhale, the way the body began to pull itself under when the mind finally stopped standing in the doorway. He wasn't asleep yet. He was in the hallway. She knew the hallway. She had lived in the hallway for four years, the place between awake and not-awake where you could still hear everything but had stopped being required to respond to it.

"I'll wake you," she said. Not a promise. A plan. The difference was that a promise was about intention and a plan was about necessity, and she did not deal in intention. "Not because it's your turn to count. Because I'll need your hands and I'll need them ready, not stiff from sleeping on a floor in the cold with your neck bent at an angle that is going to cost you something tomorrow. So when I wake you, stand up slowly. Move your fingers first. Then your wrists. Then your shoulders. In that order. If you stand up fast and your hands are numb, you are no use to me and you are no use to him and you will have slept for nothing."

She looked at Wick one more time. The lamplight made his face younger than it was, or maybe it made it exactly the age it was and the daylight was what added the years. He was still. His hands were open in his lap, palms up, the fingers slightly curled. The hands of a man who had been holding something and had been told he could stop.

She turned back to the table. The man's pulse was eighty-four. He had come back down. She let the number settle into the place where numbers lived in her mind — not a list, not a chart, but a kind of topography, a landscape of values that she walked through continuously, noting the elevation, noting the grade, alert to the places where the ground dropped away.

The tent was as quiet as it was going to get. Two men breathing. The lamp. The wind outside doing what wind did, which was move without caring what it moved over. Somewhere in the camp, a dog barked once and did not bark again, and the absence of the second bark was louder than the first had been.

Sedge sat on the stool with her fingers on the man's wrist and she counted. She did not think about the morning. She did not think about the dressing. She did not think about the arm or the infection or the conversation that might or might not be starting under the skin she had wrapped three layers deep in cotton that was not clean enough.

She thought about eighty-four. She held eighty-four in her mind the way Wick had held the man's shoulders — steady, present, refusing to let go. Eighty-four was the number and the number was the work and the work was what there was.

Outside, the hours moved. Inside, Sedge counted them the only way she knew how.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I wake up to her hand on my shoulder. The floor is hard under me, my neck is a knot. "Time?" I croak, already pushing up.
