dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway nodded once, the lamp steady in her hand. Good. *Something wrong with the shape of it* was better than most people managed their first time in a flooded cellar with a body that might not be entirely a body anymore.

"Describe the wrong," she said. Not unkind, but not gentle either. There wasn't room for gentle down here. The water was cold enough to ache through her boots and the smell was the particular sweetness that meant tissue had been breaking down in standing water for at least three days. Maybe five. "Don't interpret. Don't guess what it was. Just tell me what your eyes are actually seeing. Edges, proportions, how many limbs you can count."

She shifted the lamp a quarter-turn to the left, throwing the light at a different angle across the surface of the water. The thing at the far end caught the light and held it in a way that skin didn't. That was useful information. She filed it.

"Take your time," she added, which was a lie. They didn't have much time at all. But a rushed observation was worse than a slow one, and Pike needed to learn to *look* before anything else. Every hunter she'd buried — and there had been nine, not that she was counting, though of course she was always counting — had died because they'd moved before they'd finished seeing.

The water lapped gently against the cellar walls in a rhythm that had nothing to do with their own movement. She noted that too.

"And Pike? Count the limbs out loud. I want to hear the number."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I squint, trying to ignore the way the light makes the water seem to move on its own. "Four limbs, but... one of the arms is too long. The shoulder's wrong. And the head—" My breath hitches. "The head's turned too far. It shouldn't be able to look at us from that angle."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway let the breath Pike had lost pass without comment. A hitch was fine. A hitch meant the body still had the good sense to be afraid. It was the ones who didn't flinch she'd learned to worry about.

"Four limbs," she repeated, confirming the count like she was inventorying supplies. "Good. Four's workable. When you start counting six or seven, that's when the paperwork gets complicated." She paused. "That was a joke. You can laugh later."

She shifted the lamp again, this time angling it low, almost to the waterline, so the light skimmed across the surface rather than cutting down through it. The thing at the far end didn't move. The water still lapped in that wrong rhythm.

"The arm. You said too long. I need you to be more specific. Too long by how much — a hand's length? Forearm's length? Is it longer because it's been *stretched*, or because there's an extra joint in it?" She kept her voice level, the way she'd describe the weather. "Different answers, different creature, different way we deal with it. Details keep us alive, Pike. Squeamishness doesn't."

She took one step forward. Just one. The water pushed back against her shin in a way that was faintly muscular, and she stopped.

"And the head," she continued. "You're right, it shouldn't be able to look at us from that angle. So either the neck is broken and this is a corpse that something else arranged to face the door — which is a trap — or the neck isn't broken and it turned that far on its own, which means the skeletal structure isn't human anymore." She looked at Pike. "Either way, we don't go closer until you tell me which one you think it is. And *why*."

The thing at the far end caught the light again. Held it. Let it go.

"Take your time," she lied again.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't answer immediately. She watched the lamp flame instead, the way it guttered faintly to the left even though there was no draft from that direction. Then she said, "Yes."

Just the one word. She let it sit in the cellar dark for a moment.

"Recently enough that you can still see where the clothes were. Trousers, looks like, bunched at the waist. A shirt that's mostly gone but there's still a collar." She said it the way she'd read a list aloud. "So yes. Person. Probably within the week, given the water temperature and the state of the soft tissue. I'd guess a man from the shoulder width, but I've been wrong about that before and it doesn't change what we do next."

She looked at Pike directly then, and her expression wasn't hard exactly, but it was closed in the way a door is closed when there's something on the other side of it that you're keeping out.

"I know what you're actually asking. You're asking whether it's still a person *now*." She tilted the lamp back toward the far end of the cellar. The light found that too-long arm, the impossible angle of the head. The surface of the thing that caught light the way skin didn't. "And the answer is I don't know yet. That's what the looking is for. That's why I asked you about the joints."

The water lapped. That wrong rhythm again, like breathing.

"It matters, Pike. It matters enormously whether this was done *to* someone or whether something is wearing them. Because one of those means we're recovering a body and hunting what killed it. And the other means the body is the hunt." She paused. "And we're standing in four feet of water with it."

She held the lamp steady.

"So. The arm. Stretched, or jointed. Which did you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow, forcing myself to focus on the line of the limb. "Stretched," I say, my voice too quiet. "It's like... pulled from the socket. The skin's taut over where the bone would be."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway exhaled through her nose. A small, controlled sound, the kind she made when an answer was bad but at least it was clear.

"Stretched. Not jointed. That's useful. Thank you."

She lowered the lamp an inch, watching the way the light played along that taut line of skin Pike had described. The kid was right. The contour was wrong in the way a thing was wrong when force had been applied from the outside — no extra architecture underneath, just human anatomy pulled past its tolerances. She could see where the deltoid had separated. The gleam there was fascia.

"That means something did this to them," she said. "The skeleton's still human. Nothing's growing new parts in there. Something took hold of that arm and *pulled*, and whatever it was had enough strength to dislocate the shoulder without tearing the limb off entirely, which tells us about grip strength and intent. It wanted to keep the body intact." She paused. "Things that want to keep a body intact are using it for something."

The water lapped against her shins. That rhythm again. She'd been counting it against her own heartbeat and the intervals were getting shorter.

"Which brings us back to the head." She didn't look at Pike. She looked at the thing. "You said it's facing us. If the arm was pulled, the neck might have been turned the same way — manually, by something with hands. Posed. That's the trap I mentioned. Something arranged this body to face the door so that the first person down those stairs would do exactly what we did. Stop. Stare. Stand in the water."

She was quiet for precisely two seconds.

"Pike. Without moving your feet, tell me if the water level is higher than when we came in."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway put her hand on Pike's chest and pushed. Not hard, but not optional either. The kid stopped.

"I said without moving your feet." Her voice was flat. "And I didn't say come closer. I said tell me if the water level is higher."

She held the push for a moment, then took her hand back and held it out for the lamp. Pike had brought it forward and that was useful, she could see more now, but useful and safe were not the same word and she needed Pike to understand the difference before the evening got any worse.

"Give me that. And look at your legs. The waterline. Where is it compared to five minutes ago?"

She waited. The answer was going to be bad. She already knew it was bad because she could feel it — the water had been mid-shin when they'd come down and it was above her knee now, which meant something was either blocking the drain or the cellar was filling on purpose, and neither of those options was the kind of thing that happened by accident in a house where a body had been arranged facing the door.

She took the lamp if Pike offered it. Held it forward.

"Plainly," she repeated, acknowledging the request. "All right. Plainly. Something came into this cellar — through the water, I think, not through the door, which means there's an access point we haven't found yet. It caught this man. It held him by the arm hard enough to pull the shoulder apart. Then it turned his head to face the stairs and it left him here, and it did that because it wanted someone to come down and find him."

She could see the body better now. The collar Pike's lamp had illuminated. The face, turned toward them at that impossible angle, the mouth slightly open. The eyes not quite closed.

"The water's rising, Pike. That's not a flood. That's the access point opening. Whatever did this is either still down here with us or it's about to be."

She reached into her coat with her free hand and found the long iron spike she kept along the interior seam. Drew it out. The metal was warm from her body and it steamed faintly in the cellar air.

"So here's what's going to happen. You're going to take three steps back toward the stairs. You're going to keep your eyes on the water — not the body, the *water* — and you're going to tell me if anything breaks the surface. I'm going to look at the walls for the access point, because the single most important thing in this cellar right now is not that man and not what killed him. It's where the water is coming from."

She glanced at Pike. Grimly, briefly, something that was almost a smile.

"You wanted it plain. There it is. We're bait standing in the trap and the trap is filling up. Move."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I don't move back. Instead I stare at the waterline on your leg. "It's already past your knee." My voice is tight. "It was lower on me. It's rising faster where you're standing."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway went very still.

Not the stillness of fear — Pike would learn to tell the difference, if Pike lived long enough — but the stillness of a woman rearranging every assumption she'd made in the last four minutes. The iron spike didn't waver. The lamp didn't dip. But something behind her eyes shifted, clicked, recalculated.

She looked down.

Pike was right. The water was above her knee, well above, pressing against the leather of her coat where it hung past her thigh. She was standing perhaps six feet ahead of Pike and the floor should have been level — she'd checked the grade when they came down, an old habit, because cellars that sloped toward you were cellars that wanted to keep you — and it *had* been level.

It wasn't anymore.

"Good," she said quietly. "That's very good, Pike. That's the kind of observation that keeps people breathing."

She did not move her feet. She wanted to. Every instinct she'd built over thirty years was telling her to step back toward the stairs, but instinct was not the same thing as information, and the water was rising faster around *her specifically*, which meant one of two things. Either the floor had developed a depression where she was standing — which meant something underneath was softening the stone, pulling it down, making a bowl to hold her — or the water itself was gathering. Choosing. Moving with intent toward the closer body, the warmer body, the one that was still alive and full of all the things that living bodies were full of.

She thought about the man at the far end with his arm stretched and his head turned to watch the door.

"The water's not rising," she said. "It's *feeding*." She corrected herself with the same calm she'd use to correct a mislabeled jar. "Congregating. It moved to him first. That's how the arm got pulled — not hands, not grip. Hydraulic pressure. The water *took hold* and—"

She stopped. Looked at Pike.

"I need you to understand something. When I tell you to move back toward the stairs, it is not a suggestion and it is not because I think you're incapable. It's because I weigh more than you do and I've been standing in this water longer and it knows I'm here. If I move now it'll feel the displacement. If *you* move, slowly, while it's focused on me—"

The water pressed against her thigh. A slow, muscular squeeze, exactly like the push she'd felt against her shin minutes ago. She set her jaw.

"—you get to the stairs. You get above the waterline. And you take this."

She held out the iron spike, not the lamp. The lamp she kept.

"Iron conducts. If I go under, you throw that into the water as hard as you can and you do *not* come in after me. You go up the stairs and you burn this house to the foundations. There's a fire kit in my left saddlebag, the buckle with the scratch on it." She paused. "The horse's name is Margaret. She bites, but she'll let you take the bag if you talk to her first."

The water climbed another inch. Halloway could feel it now, not just the pressure but the temperature — colder where it gripped, warmer where it didn't, as if the thing that lived in the water was drawing heat out of her through her clothes, through her skin, through the boot leather that was doing absolutely nothing useful.

"Pike. *Move*. And count your steps out loud so I know where you are."

She held the spike out and did not let her hand shake, because her hand did not shake, because she had decided a long time ago that her hands did not do that.

The man at the far end watched them with his not-quite-closed eyes and his mouth slightly open, and the water lapped in that breathing rhythm, faster now, and Halloway stood in it and held the light and waited for Pike to take the iron and go.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked at Pike for a long moment. The water squeezed her thigh again, slow and exploratory, like a hand testing the ripeness of fruit. She could feel it finding the seams of her boot where the stitching had worn thin.

"You're asking me the right question at the wrong time," she said. "But you're not moving, which means you've decided to be stubborn about it, and I don't have the seconds to argue with you. So fine. Here it is. Take the spike while I talk."

She pushed the iron toward Pike again, and whether Pike took it or not, she kept talking, because the water was at her hip now and the lesson might be the only thing that walked out of this cellar.

"The skin's taut because there's nothing left underneath it to give it shape. Look at the torso — you can see the ribs, but the spacing's wrong. Too even. That's because the intercostal muscle is gone. The tissue between the ribs, the meat that lets you breathe, that's been *replaced*. What's holding the ribcage in shape now is water pressure from the inside. He's full of it. That's why the skin catches the light wrong — it's stretched over fluid, not over anatomy. Same principle as a waterskin."

She said it the way she'd describe the construction of a bridge. Load-bearing points. Engineering.

"The arm. I said hydraulic pressure, and I meant it. The water entered through the skin — I'd guess through the softest access points first, the mucous membranes, the eyes, the mouth. That's why his mouth is open. It went *in* that way. Once it was inside, it pressurized. Moved the limbs from within. Pulled the shoulder apart not by gripping the outside of the arm but by *expanding* inside the joint capsule until the connective tissue failed. The head turned the same way. The water filled the cervical space around the vertebrae and simply *rotated* until the neck went past its range. He was alive for some of that. He'd have to have been, because the heart would've been pumping, and a pumping heart circulates whatever's in the bloodstream, and by then the water was in the bloodstream."

The water was at her waist. Cold spreading through her coat, through her shirt, finding her skin with that terrible patience. She kept the lamp high.

"What it took. Everything that dissolved. Muscle fiber goes first — it's soft, it's porous, it breaks down in water faster than anything except brain tissue. Fat renders out next. Organs depend on the organ. The liver goes fast. The lungs hold up longer than you'd think because of the surfactant, but eventually those go too. What's left is skeleton, skin, connective tissue that's too dense to dissolve quickly, and hair. He's a bag of water wearing a person. That's what you're looking at."

She paused. The breathing rhythm of the water was faster now, much faster, almost eager.

"How far it got. All the way. There is nothing left inside that man that is that man. He's infrastructure. A shell the water is using to hold a shape it likes, which is a shape that makes people come down cellar stairs and stand in four feet of water and *stare*."

She looked at Pike with an expression that was not quite anger and not quite fear and was mostly the grim arithmetic of a woman who had buried nine colleagues and did not intend to start a second row.

"There. You have the detail. You know what it does, how it enters, what it leaves behind, what to look for next time. The mucous membranes. The skin catching light like a drum head. The limbs at wrong angles with no bruising because the force came from inside." Her voice dropped half a register. "Now I need you to take this iron spike and walk backward toward those stairs and count every step out loud, because the water is at my waist, Pike, and I can't feel my legs anymore, and in about ninety seconds we're going to find out whether thirty years of experience and a bad attitude are enough to get me out of this or whether you're going to need everything I just told you sooner than either of us would like."

The water lapped. The man at the far end watched. The lamp flame guttered left, toward nothing, toward the place where the air was being displaced by something rising.

"*Take the spike. Walk. Count.*"

Her hand did not shake.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I take the spike, my fingers brushing yours. Cold. "One step back," I say, voice steadier than I feel. "Water's at my shins still." I keep my eyes on you, not the body. "Two steps. Halloway, you come too."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway watched Pike's face in the lamplight and felt the kid's fingers leave hers, taking the iron and the warmth with it. The brief contact had told her what she needed to know — Pike's hand had been shaking, and Pike had done it anyway. That was the whole job, really.

"Three," she said. "Keep counting. Don't stop because I'm talking."

The water squeezed. Not her thigh this time — her waist, the full circumference of it, a slow constriction like being measured by something that was deciding how much of her there was to work with. She could feel it pressing against the buttons of her coat, finding the gaps between them, nosing at the fabric the way a dog nosed at a door it wanted opened.

She did not come too.

"I'm going to explain why I'm not moving and you're going to keep walking while I do it. It has me, Pike. Not metaphorically. I can feel it contracting around my midsection. If I step now — if I create displacement, movement, a current — it'll register that as struggle, and struggle is what tells it something's still alive in here, and alive things are what it fills."

She kept the lamp high. The flame was steady now, which was worse than when it had been guttering, because it meant the air had stopped moving, which meant something was settling.

"It's not squeezing you. You said the water's at your shins. That's *lower* than when we came in. It's drawing off you and onto me. Congregating. That's good. That's what I wanted. That's why I told you to move and not me."

She said it plainly, the way she'd said everything, and if there was a particular weariness in it — the weariness of a woman who had done this arithmetic before and understood exactly which column she'd put herself in — she did not let it reach her face.

"Keep counting."

The water found the gap at her collar. A thin finger of cold traced her clavicle, ran along the tendon of her neck, and stopped just below her ear as if listening for her pulse. She tilted her chin up. Not much room left to tilt.

"The iron," she said. "When you reach the stairs. Not before. You'll want to throw it before, and you need to wait, because iron in water conducts and I am still *in* the water and I would like the opportunity to not be before you make it unfriendly in here. When your feet hit the bottom stair — the *bottom* stair, Pike, you'll feel the wood — you plant your feet and you give me ten seconds. I'm going to do something stupid and I need those ten seconds."

The cold finger at her neck pressed. Found the pulse. Held there.

"I have not survived thirty years by being careful," she said, and there was that grim almost-smile again, barely visible in the lamplight. "I've survived thirty years by being too stubborn to dissolve. Keep *counting*."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway cut.

The first incision was along the sternum, collar to navel, and she narrated it the way she narrated everything — not for Pike's comfort but because Pike had asked, and because the asking meant Pike understood that this was the lesson, that the body on the table they'd dragged out of that cellar and up into the grey morning light was a textbook now and she was reading it aloud before the pages rotted.

"Skin's about twice normal thickness," she said. The knife — not the iron spike, she'd retrieved that from where it sizzled in the shallow water on the cellar stairs, but a proper dissection blade from Margaret's saddlebag — parted the tissue with more resistance than it should have. "Tanned from the inside. The water did that. Same principle as leather curing — prolonged immersion changes the protein structure of the dermis. Feel the edge there, where I've cut. Go on."

She waited until Pike touched it.

"Like parchment. Stiff but pliable. That's how you'll know next time. If you find a body near water and the skin feels like that, you don't touch it bare-handed, you don't put your face near the mouth, and you do not — Pike, *look* at me — you do not let any fluid that comes out of it contact your mucous membranes. Eyes, nose, mouth. That's how it gets in. That's how it got into him."

She peeled the skin back. It came away from the ribcage with a sound like damp cloth lifting off a washboard, a soft adhesive release, and underneath —

"Right. So. This is what empty looks like."

The thoracic cavity was a clean hollow. Not ragged, not torn — *clean*, the way a gourd was clean after you'd scraped it. The interior surfaces of the ribs gleamed faintly, coated in a thin residue that caught the lamplight with that same wrong sheen they'd seen in the cellar. She tapped a rib with the flat of the blade. It rang dully, waterlogged.

"No lungs. No heart. No mediastinal tissue whatsoever. The diaphragm's intact — see the membrane there, that's the muscular sheet that separates the chest from the abdomen — but everything above it is gone. Dissolved. Absorbed." She leaned closer and sniffed, then pulled back. "Smells like a tidal pool. Brine and rot, but mostly brine. Salt concentration's high, which tells us the water isn't fresh. Whatever's living in that cellar came from brackish water or it *makes* brackish water. Either way, salt. Write that down if you've got something to write with. If you don't, remember it. Salt matters."

She moved the incision lower. The diaphragm parted under the blade and the abdominal cavity opened and Pike would see what she saw — a thin layer of fluid pooled in the pelvic bowl, perhaps a cup's worth, perfectly clear, and absolutely nothing else. No stomach. No intestines. No liver, no kidneys, no spleen. The interior walls of the abdominal cavity were smooth and faintly ridged, like the inside of a shell.

"Alimentary canal's gone entirely. Dissolved or consumed, same difference. The ridging you're looking at — bring the lamp closer — those are marks. Not teeth marks. Pressure marks. Current marks. The water moved *inside* him in a pattern, a circulation, and it abraded the interior surfaces the way a river smooths stone. It was in here long enough to leave a pattern. That means hours, not minutes."

She sat back on her heels. Her coat was still damp from the cellar, her legs still numb below the knee from where the water had held her before she'd done the stupid thing — which had involved the lamp, and her coat, and the fact that lamp oil floated and fire was fire and the water had *flinched*, actually flinched, releasing her waist for the two seconds she'd needed to lunge for the stairs. She'd think about that later. She'd think about the way it had felt when it let go, that muscular constriction simply vanishing, like a fist opening.

Later.

"The skeleton's intact," she continued. "Every bone. Every joint except the shoulder and the cervical vertebrae we already noted. It didn't want the bones. It wanted everything the bones were wearing." She looked at Pike. "That's what it is, Pike. It's a solvent that thinks. It dissolves what it can use and it leaves the architecture standing and it fills the empty space with itself and it waits for the next warm thing to come close enough to touch the water."

She wiped the blade on her thigh and held it up. The residue on the steel was iridescent, faintly blue in the morning light.

"This. If you see this on a surface near standing water, you leave. You don't investigate. You don't go back for your things. You leave and you come find me or someone like me, and if there's no one like me, you find lamp oil and you find a match." She paused. "In that order."

The body lay open on the ground between them, empty and clean and terrible, and Halloway looked at it the way she looked at everything — with the precise, exhausted attention of a woman who had been reading these textbooks for thirty years and still had not found the last page.

"What else," she said. It wasn't a question. It was permission to keep asking.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I reach out and touch the ridging inside the cavity, the ghost of the current. "Why the pattern?" I ask. "If it's just... eating, why leave a mark?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway watched Pike's fingers trace the ridges and did not stop it. The kid was wearing gloves — she'd made sure of that before they started, had pulled the pair from Margaret's saddlebag and tossed them over without comment, and if Pike thought they were for the cold, fine. They were for the cold. They were also for the thing that lived in water and entered through skin.

"That's the right question," she said. "That's the question that separates a hunter from someone who just burns things."

She leaned forward and placed the flat of the blade along one of the ridges, following its curve. It spiraled. Not randomly — deliberately, in a logarithmic arc that tightened toward the center of the pelvic bowl where the last cup of fluid still sat, perfectly clear, perfectly still, catching the light like a lens.

"If it were just eating, the interior would be smooth. Uniform dissolution. Acid does that — eats everything at the same rate and leaves a clean surface. This isn't acid. This is *circulation*. The water moved through him the way blood moves through a living body. It followed a route. It came back to where it started. And every time it completed the circuit, it wore the track a little deeper."

She tapped the blade against the deepest groove. It was perhaps a sixteenth of an inch — shallow enough to miss if you weren't looking, deep enough to feel under a fingertip.

"You know what else leaves patterns like that? Rivers. And rivers leave patterns because they're following gravity, following the path of least resistance, and once the path exists the water prefers it and the preference deepens the path and the deeper path increases the preference. Feedback loop. The river doesn't *decide* to carve a canyon. It just goes where it's easiest to go, and the going makes it easier, and given enough time you get the Grand Canyon or you get—" She gestured at the spiraling grooves inside a dead man's abdomen. "This."

She sat back again. Pulled a rag from her coat and wiped the blade properly this time, taking care with the edge.

"But that's the ordinary answer. Water does what water does. And if I thought this was ordinary water, I'd leave it there." She looked at Pike. "I don't think this is ordinary water. I think the pattern is practice."

The morning was grey and getting greyer. Somewhere behind them Margaret stamped and blew, impatient with standing still, and the sound was so normal it felt like it belonged to a different world.

"The first body it ever filled, the interior would have been rough. Chaotic. Water sloshing around in a cavity it didn't understand, dissolving tissue unevenly, leaving pockets, leaving mess. But this—" She pointed at the spirals with the cleaned blade. "This is *efficient*. The circulation pattern maximizes surface contact. It touches every interior wall on every pass. Nothing gets missed. Nothing gets left behind. That's not a river following gravity, Pike. That's a river that has *learned the landscape*."

She let that sit for a moment.

"It's been practicing. This isn't its first body. Might not be its fifth. Every time it fills someone, it gets better at the route, and the route gets worn a little deeper into the bone, and the next time it fills someone of roughly the same size and build, it already knows the way." She paused. "That's why the pattern. It's not a waste product. It's a *map*. It's the thing teaching itself how to be efficient inside a human being."

She looked down at the cup of clear fluid in the pelvic bowl. It had not moved. It had not evaporated. It sat there in the grey light, patient as a puddle.

"And that," she said, nodding toward it, "is what it left behind to remember him by. A seed. A starting point. So that if someone comes along and touches the body, touches the fluid, touches their mouth or their eyes afterward—" She didn't finish the sentence. She didn't need to.

"It's not just a solvent that thinks, Pike. It's a solvent that *learns*. And every body it takes is a lesson it doesn't forget."

She folded the rag over the blade and set it down on the dry ground beside her knee.

"That's why we burn them. Not because we're thorough. Because it has a *curriculum*, and every body we leave intact is a page it gets to keep."

She nodded toward the pelvic bowl.

"Don't touch that fluid. Even through the gloves. We're going to seal this body in the oilcloth from the saddlebag and burn it whole, and we're going to do it before that—" she glanced at the overcast sky, "—becomes rain."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway finished it.

She started with the oilcloth. It was a square yard of waxed canvas she kept rolled behind Margaret's saddle for exactly this purpose, though she'd told Pike it was a rain cover when they'd packed that morning, because you didn't tell someone what the oilcloth was for until they'd seen why you needed it. She unrolled it on the ground beside the body and weighted the corners with stones from the garden wall, working with the unhurried efficiency of someone who had done this enough times that her hands knew the sequence without consulting her.

"Hold the lamp steady," she said, though Pike was sitting on the cellar steps ten feet away and the lamp was doing nothing useful at that distance. She said it because Pike needed a task. Idle hands after a first body were hands that started shaking, and shaking hands picked at themselves, touched their faces, rubbed their eyes. She'd seen it happen. She'd seen what happened after.

She went back to the body.

The rolling was the worst part. Not emotionally — she'd made her arrangements with that particular demon years ago — but practically, because the body was heavier than it looked. The skeleton was intact, as she'd said, and bone was dense, and the waterlogging had added weight to what remained of the connective tissue. The skin, tanned to that parchment stiffness, didn't fold the way living skin folded. It crackled faintly at the joints as she turned him onto his side, and the sound was exactly like someone slowly crumpling a sheet of heavy paper, and she heard Pike's breathing change on the steps behind her.

"That's the collagen," she said without turning around. "Denatured. It does that."

She rolled him onto the oilcloth. The too-long arm trailed and she had to tuck it against his torso, bending it at the elbow, which still worked because the elbow hadn't been dislocated, only the shoulder. The forearm folded across his chest and she held it there for a moment, not out of tenderness but because she was checking the wrist. The skin there was thinner than elsewhere and she wanted to see if the ridging pattern extended into the extremities.

It did. Finer grooves, hairline-thin, spiraling down the interior surface of the forearm where the radius and ulna lay close to the skin. The water had circulated all the way to the fingertips. She noted it, filed it, and moved on.

The head was the problem. It was still turned at that impossible angle — a hundred and sixty degrees, maybe more, the cervical vertebrae rotated so far past their natural range that the throat was a twisted column of taut skin with the tendons standing out like cables under tension. She could see where the sternocleidomastoid had separated from the clavicle on the left side. A clean separation. No tearing. The water had pressurized the joint capsules between the vertebrae and simply turned, one degree at a time, until the soft tissue gave way and the bones followed and the face pointed wherever the water wanted it to point.

She did not try to turn the head back. It would not go, and forcing it would risk cracking the cervical spine, and she needed the skeleton intact for the burning because bone ash told you things.Ite temperature of the fire that consumed it told you how much moisture the bone had absorbed, and that told you how long the water had been inside, and that told you how old this particular iteration of the thing was. Data. Everything was data. The dead were generous with their information if you knew how to read them, and Halloway had been reading them for thirty years.

She folded the oilcloth over him. Left side first, then right, then the bottom up over the feet — bare feet, she noticed now, the shoes gone, probably dissolved, leather being organic tissue after all — and then the top down over the head, that terrible rotated head with its not-quite-closed eyes. She tucked the canvas under him at the sides the way you'd wrap a parcel, tight and overlapping, and she secured it with cord from the saddlebag, three lengths of it, chest and waist and knees. The knots were square knots, quick and firm. She pulled each one tight with a sharp jerk and the wrapped shape on the ground looked like what it was, which was a body prepared for burning, and it looked like nothing at all, which was a mercy Pike probably needed even if Pike wouldn't say so.

The cup of fluid in the pelvic bowl.

She'd been thinking about it the whole time she worked. It was inside the wrapping now, sealed in with the rest of him, and she didn't know if the oilcloth would contain it. Waxed canvas was water-resistant, not waterproof, and this wasn't water, not really, not anymore. It was a solvent that learned. It was a page from a curriculum. It was sitting in the lowest point of a dead man's pelvis and it had not evaporated in the open air and it had not soaked into the bone and it had not done anything at all except sit there, clear and still, waiting with the patience of something that understood time differently than she did.

She built the pyre in the front garden, away from the house, away from the cellar, and most importantly away from the standing water. She used the garden fence for fuel — dry wood, seasoned by years of weather, it would catch fast. She broke the slats with her boot and her hands and stacked them in a lattice pattern, open enough for airflow, dense enough for sustained heat. She needed the fire hot. She needed it hot enough toite bone calcium toite calcium phosphate toite calcium oxide, and that meant six hundred degrees at minimum and ideally more, and that meant she needed the fire to burn for at least two hours, and that meant she needed more wood than the fence could give her.

She went to the house. She pulled boards from the porch. The nails screamed coming out and Margaret tossed her head at the sound and Pike sat on the cellar steps with the lamp and Halloway carried the boards to the pyre and added them to the lattice and went back for more.

It took her twenty minutes to build a pyre large enough. She was breathing hard by the end of it, not from exertion but from the cold — the cellar water had soaked her to the waist and her trousers were still wet and the November air was pulling heat from her legs with the same slow patience the water had used, and she thought about that, about the similarity, and she filed it away for later.

She lifted the wrapped body onto the pyre. This was the part she always did alone. Not because she was proud but because the weight of a body was a private thing, a specific and personal heaviness that she did not think should be shared. He was heavy. Heavier than he should have been, even accounting for the waterlogged bone, and she thought about the cup of fluid in his pelvis and wondered if it was heavier than water, denser, more concentrated, and she set him on the lattice of dry wood and she did not drop him and she did not grunt and she settled him as level as the uneven surface allowed.

The lamp oil.

She took the flask from the saddlebag — a full pint, she always carried a full pint, because a half-measure of lamp oil was the kind of economy that got you standing in the dark with something that didn't need light to find you. She uncorked it and poured it over the wrapped body in a slow, even stream, starting at the feet and working up to the head, making sure the oilcloth was saturated. The wax coating would resist the oil at first, then absorb it, then become fuel itself. She used the entire pint. She shook the last drops from the flask and set it aside.

"Pike," she said. "Come here."

She waited until Pike came. The kid moved stiffly, the way people moved when they'd been sitting still in the cold for too long, and Halloway noted the way Pike held the lamp — close to the chest, both hands, knuckles white. Not shaking anymore. That was good. Or it meant the shaking had gone deeper than the hands, which was less good, but she'd deal with that later.

"You're going to light it," she said.

She said it the way she'd said everything today — not as a suggestion, not as a kindness, not as a cruelty. As a fact. The way the next step in a sequence was a fact.

"I know you think I should do it. I've done it before and you haven't and it would be easier. But you need to understand what it means to finish this. Not the cutting, not the looking, not the knowing what it is and how it works. The finishing. You need to put the fire to it yourself and you need to stand here and watch it burn and you need to smell what it smells like, because next time you might be alone, and if you've never lit a pyre you'll hesitate, and hesitation in this line of work is the distance between a body on the fire and a body in the water."

She stepped back. One step. Enough to give Pike room.

"Open the lamp. Use the wick. Touch it to the oil at the base, not the top — you want the fire to climb upward through the fuel, not burn down through the body and smother itself. The wood will catch first. Then the oilcloth. Then him. It'll take a few seconds and it'll seem like it isn't working and you'll want to add more oil. Don't. It's working. Trust the heat."

The sky was the color of pewter and getting darker. She could smell rain in the air, metallic and close, and she thought about what she'd said to Pike — *we're going to do it before that becomes rain* — and she looked up and judged they had maybe thirty minutes. Maybe less.

"Light it, Pike."

She watched. Pike opened the lamp. The flame inside was small and steady, the same flame that had lit the cellar, the same flame that had shown them the body and the water and the too-long arm and the head turned to watch the door. Pike knelt — stiffly, carefully, the way you knelt when your body was telling you to run — and touched the wick to the oil-soaked base of the pyre.

The fire caught.

Not dramatically. Not with a roar or a whoosh or any of the sounds that fires made in stories. It caught the way real fire caught — a small bright line of flame that crawled along the oil trail and found the first piece of dry fence wood and tasted it and liked it and began to eat. The wood popped. A knot in one of the porch boards cracked with a sound like a pistol shot and Pike flinched and Halloway didn't.

"Stand up," she said. "Step back to where I am. And watch."

The fire climbed. It found the lattice and followed the channels of airflow she'd built into the structure and it grew from a crawling thing to a standing thing, yellow and orange, the heat reaching them in waves that smelled of pine resin and lamp oil and then, gradually, of something else. The oilcloth caught. The waxed canvas burned blue at the edges where the wax melted and flared, and the wrapping darkened and curled and split, and through the splits the fire found what was inside.

Halloway had smelled a burning body nine times before this. Ten, if she counted the one in Harrogate that had only been partial, and she did count it, because partial was still a body and partial still smelled like a body. The smell was not what people expected. People expected rot, expected the sweetness of decomposition amplified by heat. What they got was something closer to a forge — mineral, metalite, the calcium in the bones superheating and releasing a dry chalite odor that sat in the back of the throat and stayed there for days. Under that, the rendered fat, which smelled like tallow because it *was* tallow, human tallow, and she had stopped pretending that distinction mattered a long time ago. Under that, the hair, which smelled like nothing else in the world and which she was not going to describe to Pike because some things you only learned by standing in front of them.

"Breathe through your mouth," she said. "Not because it helps. It doesn't. But you'll gag less."

The fire was fully involved now. The pyre was doing what she'd built it to do — sustaining a core temperature high enough toite bone calcium, the lattice feeding air to the center, the porch boards providing the long-burn fuel that the fence slats couldn't. She could feel the heat on her face from ten feet away, tight and dry, and it was doing useful things to her wet trousers, and she stood there and let it.

The body inside the fire moved.

Not because it was alive. Not because the water inside it was making it move. Because heat did things to connective tissue — the tendons contracted as they cooked, pulling the limbs inward, and the wrapped shape on the pyre curled slowly onto its side in a motion that looked exactly like a person turning over in their sleep. Pike made a sound. Not a word. A sound.

"Tendons," Halloway said. "They shorten when they're heated. Pugilistic posture. The arms will draw up next, fists to the chest. It happens every time. It means nothing except that the fire is hot enough."

The arms drew up. Through the burning remnants of the oilcloth she could see the too-long arm finally bending, the dislocated shoulder irrelevant now because the tendons were doing what the joint wouldn't, pulling the forearm up and the hand into a fist, and the body on the pyre settled into the posture she'd described — curled, compact, fetal, a shape that looked like sleeping or like grief.

She watched it burn.

The skull was the last thing to go. It always was. The cranial vault was thick bone, dense and reluctant, and it held its shape long after the facial bones collapsed and the mandible fell away. She could see it in the heart of the fire, black and then grey and then white as the calcium converted, and she watched for the moment — there was always a moment — when the heat finally won and the skull cracked along the sagittal suture with a sound like a branch breaking, and the two halves fell apart, and inside there was nothing, because the brain had been the first thing the water took and the fire had nothing left to find.

She watched for the fluid.

This was the part that mattered. The cup of clear liquid in the pelvic bowl — the seed, the map, the page from the curriculum. She watched the fire and she waited for it, because she didn't know what it would do when the heat reached it. She didn't know if it would evaporate like water or if it would do something else, something that wasn't in any of the textbooks she'd read because there weren't any textbooks for this, there were only cellars and bodies and pyres and the things you learned by standing in front of them.

The pelvis cracked.

The fire had reached the core of the body, the densest bone, the last architecture, and the iliac crest split with a sound deeper than the skull had made, a bass note, a foundation giving way, and from the crack —

Steam. A thin column of it, white and dense and rising straight up in the still air with a purpose that steam didn't have. It didn't dissipate. It rose in a coherent thread, six inches, a foot, two feet, and then the wind caught it — or something caught it — and it bent sideways, toward the cellar, toward the water, and Halloway said "*No*" and stepped forward and passed her hand through it.

The steam broke apart. Scattered. Became ordinary moisture in ordinary air and drifted into nothing.

Her hand was wet. She looked at it. The moisture on her palm was warm from the fire and clear and it sat on her skin without soaking in, a thin film, and she wiped it on the oilcloth rag from her coat and she folded the rag and she put it in the fire.

The rag burned. The moisture on it hissed. Gone.

"That," she said to Pike, "is why we burn them. And that is why we stay for the whole burning. Because the last thing it does is try to leave."

She stood by the fire. The body was mostly gone now — a heap of calcium fragments andite ash in the shape of a collapsed lattice, the porch boards still burning steadily around the edges, the heat rippling the grey air above the pyre. She'd stay until the bones wereite calcium oxide,ite calcium oxide was calcium oxide, calcium oxide was powder, powder was powder. Two hours. Maybe less, the fire was hotter than she'd expected, the porch boards were old-growth pine and they burned like they meant it.

She looked at Pike. The kid was standing where she'd told Pike to stand, ten feet from the pyre, the lamp still held in both hands even though the lamp was out now, the oil spent, the wick cold. Pike's face was lit by the fire and it looked the way faces looked after the first time — not blank, not broken, but *rearranged*, as if the features were the same but the thing behind them had shifted to accommodate a new piece of information that didn't fit anywhere comfortable.

"Sit down if you need to," she said. "We're here for a while."

She didn't sit. She stood with her hands at her sides and her wet trousers steaming in the heat and she watched the fire reduce a man toite calcium and she counted the bones as they became powder — ribs first, then vertebrae, then the long bones of the legs, then the pelvis in its two cracked halves — and she kept count because someone should, because he had been a person recently enough that there were still trousers and a collar, and counting the bones was the last thing she could do for him

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit down on the cold ground, my back against the cellar steps. "Will it be in the ashes?" I ask, my voice rough. "Should we scatter them?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't answer immediately. She watched the fire work through the last of the long bones — the left femur was holding out, dense and stubborn, glowing white at the diaphysis where the cortical bone was thickest. She'd give it another twenty minutes. Maybe fifteen. The old-growth pine was doing its job.

"No," she said. "And yes."

She pushed a collapsed fence slat back into the center of the fire with her boot. Sparks rose and joined the grey sky and disappeared.

"Calcium oxideite calcium oxide calcium oxide calcium oxide calcium oxide — powder.ite calcium oxide calcium oxide calcium oxide—" She stopped. Took a breath. The cold and the smoke and the standing were doing things to her concentration she didn't care for. "The calcium converts. At this temperature, what's left is calcium oxide.ite calcium oxide calcium oxide calcium oxide calcium oxide—"

She closed her eyes for two seconds. Opened them.

"Ite calcium oxide is calcium oxide is calcium oxide is powder," she said, more carefully now, each word placed like a foot on uncertain ground. "Ite calcium oxide is calcium oxide. Pure calcium oxide is calcium oxide. It is powder. It is calcium oxide. It is calcium oxide. It is—"

She stopped talking. Something was wrong with her mouth. The words were looping, catching on themselves like a snag in thread, and she pressed her tongue against the roof of her mouth and held it there until the loop broke.

"The ash," she said. "Right. Pike, listen to me carefully."

Her voice was steady again. Whatever had snagged had released, and she filed it — filed the stumble, the loop, the two seconds of closed eyes — in the same place she filed everything else, which was the place she'd look at later when later came, if later came.

"Calcium oxideite calcium oxide — calcium oxide calcium oxide calcium oxide —"

She stopped again. Bit the inside of her cheek hard enough to taste iron.

"The powder that's left," she said, abandoning the technical language entirely with a bluntness that cost her something, "isite calcium oxide is calcium oxide — is calcium oxide—"

She looked down at her hand. The hand she'd passed through the steam. The hand she'd wiped on the rag. The hand she'd put the rag in the fire with. The hand that was dry now, perfectly dry, and had been dry for twenty minutes, and was fine, and was not shaking, because her hands did not shake, because she had decided that.

She looked at Pike.

"The ash is safe," she said. Flatly. Simply. No technical language, no loops, no snags. "Once boneite calcium — once bone calcium — once the calcium—"

She stopped. She breathed. The fire crackled and the femur finally gave way with a soft chalky sound and she watched it crumble and she did not try to say the word again.

"Once the calcium in the bone powder has fully changed from one thing to another at this temperature, there is nothing left for it to live in.ite calcium oxide is — calcium oxide is—" She closed her mouth. Opened it. "The powder isite calcium — calcium—"

Pike was looking at her. She could feel it.

"Something's wrong with my mouth," she said. Not alarmed. Clinical. The way she'd describe a symptom in someone else. "I'm looping on a word. On a compound. On the — the chemical name. I keep trying to say it and it comes back around. That started about two minutes ago."

She held up her hand. The hand that had touched the steam. She turned it over in the firelight and examined the palm the way she'd examined the interior of the dead man's torso — edges, proportions, what the eyes were actually seeing.

"I wiped it on the rag," she said. "I put the rag in the fire. But there was a gap between the wiping and the burning. Maybe four seconds. Maybe five. Skin's permeable. Especially warm skin. Especially skin with the pores open from standing next to a fire."

She looked at Pike and her expression was the one she'd worn in the cellar — not hard, not afraid, but closed, a door with something behind it.

"I need you to do something for me. I need you to ask me a question. Any question. Something that requires a complicated answer. Something with technical language. I need to know if it's the one word or if it's spreading."

The fire burned. The bones became powder. The powder was calcium oxide, calcium oxide, and Halloway stood in front of the pyre with her hand held up in the light and waited for Pike to test her, and her hand did not shake, because her hand did not shake, because she had decided a long time ago that her hands did not do that, and the decision held, and the decision held, and the decision—

Held.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stand up fast, the lamp clattering on the ground. "Describe the procedure for clearing a flooded well of a waterborne presence. Every step."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway nodded once. The nod was for herself as much as for Pike — a small mechanical confirmation that she was still here, still standing, still the woman who knew the answer to this question because she had written the answer to this question, had scratched it into the back pages of a field journal in a farmhouse outside Whitby eleven years ago with a dead man's pencil because her own had broken.

"Right," she said. "Clearing a flooded well."

She took a breath. Held it. Let it go.

"Step one. Establish the water table depth relative to the well shaft. You need to know whether the well is fed from below or whether it's holding standing water with no active source. If there's an active source, you're not clearing the well, you're fighting the aquifer, and you will lose. You seal the well and you salt the ground in a ten-foot radius and you leave and you tell everyone within a quarter mile to dig a new well uphill and further from the drainage." She paused. The words had come out clean. Linear. No loops. "If there's no active source — if the water is standing, contained, finite — you proceed."

The fire popped behind her. She didn't turn.

"Step two. Measure the volume. Depth times the square of the radius times — times—"

She stopped.

Not a loop. Not the same snag. This was different. The number was there, the constant, she could *see* it, the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, she had known it since she was fourteen, and it was sitting in her mouth like a stone and would not come out.

"The constant," she said. "The ratio. Three and one seventh, near enough. Multiply depth by the square of the radius by that. That gives you volume in cubic feet. You need the volume because you need to know how much salt."

She kept going. If she stopped she would inventory what she'd just lost and if she inventoried what she'd just lost she would stop and she could not stop.

"Step three. Salt. Coarse salt, not fine — fine dissolves too fast and the concentration spikes and drops. You want a sustained saturation. The ratio is—" She felt for it. Found it. "One pound per two gallons. Roughly eight pounds per cubic foot of water. You calculate from the volume and you do not round down. You bring ten percent more than you think you need because you always need more than you think."

Her hand was at her side now. She wasn't looking at it. She was looking at Pike and she was talking and the talking was the test and the test was the thing keeping the door closed.

"Step four. Delivery. You don't pour the salt from the surface. The presence will feel the concentration change at the top of the water column and it will descend to the bottom of the well where the saturation is lowest. You need a weighted canvas bag — oilcloth works, the same oilcloth — loaded with the full measure of salt, perforated with a knife, lowered on a rope to the bottom of the shaft. The salt leeches out from the bottom up. The concentration rises evenly. The presence has nowhere to go that isn't salt."

She was aware, in the clinical way she was aware of all things, that her left hand had gone cold. Not numb the way her legs had gone numb in the cellar — cold in a specific, localized way, as if someone had pressed an ice coin into the center of her palm and it was radiating outward. She did not look at it. She kept talking.

"Step five. Containment during saturation. The salt takes time. Hours, not minutes. During those hours the presence will attempt to leave the well. It will climb. It will find the stone lining and it will move up the interior surface as a film, a layer thinner than paper, and if you are leaning over the well looking down to check your progress it will reach your face before you understand what has happened." Her voice did not change. "You do not lean over the well. You cap it. Stone slab, mortared edges, sealed with tallow. You leave a vent hole no wider than a pencil for the gas — there will be gas, hydrogen sulfide, the salt reacts with the organic matter the presence has accumulated — and you put your ear to the vent hole and you listen."

"Step six. Listening. A living presence in a salting well makes a sound. It is not a voice. It is not a scream. It is the sound of water under pressure trying to find an exit that doesn't exist, and it sounds like—"

She stopped. Not because of a loop. Not because of a lost word. Because the sound she was about to describe was the sound the water in the cellar had made when the lamp oil had hit it and she'd lunged for the stairs, and the memory of it was very close and very clear and she needed one second to put it back where it belonged.

One second.

"It sounds like someone breathing in and never breathing out," she said. "A sustained inhalation. Rising in pitch as the salt concentration increases. When the sound stops, the presence has either died or consolidated into a volume too small to vibrate. Either way, you wait another hour. Then you open the cap."

The cold in her palm had reached her wrist. She could feel it moving along the tendons, tracing the same paths the water had traced inside the dead man — the paths of least resistance, the channels where the tissue was softest, where the body's own architecture provided a road.

"Step seven. Extraction. The water in the well is now a brine solution containing — containing—"

A loop. She felt it forming, the word trying to come and coming back, and she bit through it with brute force.

"Containing the dissolved remains of whatever organic matter the presence had collected. You do not pour this water on the ground. You do not let it reach any natural water source. You draw it up in sealed containers and you boil it. All of it. Every drop. You boil it until the containers are dry and the residue on the bottom is mineral scale and nothing else, and you scrape the scale and you put it in the fire and you keep the fire burning until the calcium — until the calcium—"

She stopped.

The word was there again. The compound. The thing bone calcium became at six hundred degrees. It was right there, she could feel its shape in her mouth, two words, and they would not come, and they would not come, and they would not come, and she could feel them looping, circling back, the same word arriving at the same place and failing to exit, like water in a circuit, like water following a path it had worn into the bone—

"Pike," she said.

Her voice was different now. Not the flatness of clinical observation. Something underneath it, something she kept in the cellar of herself and did not bring upstairs.

"I need you to look at my left hand."

She raised it. Held it out, palm up, in the firelight. She did not look at it herself. She looked at Pike, because Pike's face would tell her what she needed to know before her own eyes could, because her own eyes were attached to her own brain and her own brain was the thing she no longer entirely trusted.

"Tell me what you see. Don't interpret. Don't guess. Edges, color, whether the skin looks right." The corner of her mouth twitched — not a smile, not quite, but the ghost of one, the muscle memory of grim humor firing in a face that was running out of room for it. "You know the drill. I taught it to you about four hours ago."

The fire burned behind her. The bones were powder. The powder was calcium — was calcium — was the thing it was, the thing she could not say, the word that circled and circled and would not land.

Her hand did not shake.

Her hand did not shake.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at your palm. "It's...mottled. Grey lines under the skin, like tiny rivers." My throat tightens. "They're branching."
